en: The Great Collection of Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtras, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha. As for that mountain...
It was lofty, steep, majestic, and beautiful to behold; it supported all manner of things like the great earth, and its various flowers, plants, and trees were all in full bloom.
Within it, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, piśācas, kiṃnaras, and others constantly dwelt and wandered.
Furthermore, there were various kinds of diverse beasts dwelling therein, namely lions, tigers, wolves, qilin, elephants, horses, bears, and brown bears.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various birds—namely peacocks, parrots, mynas, wild ducks, geese, ruddy sheldrakes, and jīvañjīvaka birds—who dwelt therein.
By the Buddha’s majestic power, these sentient beings are not afflicted by greed, hatred, or delusion, nor do they devour one another;
they regard each other with mutual affection, just like a mother and her child.

Within this king of mountains, there are many various trees; the groves are lush and verdant, their branches and leaves flourishing. There are celestial *tagara* trees, *āmra* trees, *kiṃśuka* trees, *nyagrodha* trees, sandalwood, and aloeswood; indeed, all such trees as these are present without exception.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable varieties of flowers on both land and water, namely: *atimuktaka* flowers, *campaka* fragrant flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, *vārṣika* flowers, *sumana* flowers, *yūthikā* flowers, *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *kārasa* flowers, and *mahākārasa* flowers. Such various kinds of famous flowers adorned the King of Mountains, filling it everywhere.

Within this king of mountains, at midnight, great dense clouds arise, accompanied by gentle peals of thunder and fine rain; from beginning to end, they gradually pervade the entire mountain. The waters of the eight virtues flow and nourish all things until they are universally saturated; then, in the time it takes to milk a cow, they vanish away into vast emptiness. A cool breeze stirs gently, bringing delight and serenity to both body and mind.

The sentient beings dwelling within this king of mountains, as well as all the herbs and trees, are moistened and lustrous like exquisite flower garlands; when even a slight sprinkling of water is applied, their radiance and color become vivid and grow even more excellent.
The sentient beings, grasses, and trees within this king of mountains likewise absorb nourishment and radiate brilliance in this same way.

The various soft grasses growing upon this mountain sway gently to the right, endowed with both color and fragrance; they are a greenish-blue hue that reflects light like the throat of a peacock. Their fragrance is comparable to the *vārṣika* flower, and their touch is like that of light *tūla* cotton. Their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are so lush and flourishing that there is never one that is not complete.
The mountain terrain is soft and supple, causing no injury to the feet; when the foot is set down, it sinks four finger-widths deep, and when lifted, it returns to its former state.

Within it are many ponds, springs, and pools, filled with clear, cool water and blooming various lotuses—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, crystal, gold, and fire-colored—each as large as a chariot wheel, their fragrance pervading one *yojana*.

Upon the summit of this king of mountains arose a great and wondrous precious lotus throne: it had a stem made of the invincible, imperial-blue vajra; great vaidūrya formed its various jeweled bells; Jambūnada gold formed its broad and pure petals; seasonal, pure sandalwood formed its pedestal; and agate, the king of jewels, formed its filaments.
The flower was as vast in length and breadth as the great ocean;

it was constantly upheld by ten billion asura kings, covered above by ten billion nets of multicolored maṇi jewels, with ten billion nāga kings raining down a rain of exquisite incense, and ten billion garuḍa kings holding silk streamers in their beaks; ten billion kiṃnara kings arrived...
Truly gazing upward, ten billion mahoraga kings looked down with reverent devotion; ten billion gandharva kings sang praises in song;

ten billion times a hundred thousand great celestial emperors raised auspicious clouds, raining down powdered incense, burning incense, garments, flower garlands, banners, pennants, and precious parasols; and ten billion Brahmās...
The king bowed his body in reverence; ten billion devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens joined their palms in prostration;
ten billion wheel-turning monarchs, accompanied by their retinues of the seven treasures, arrived at his presence;
ten billion sea-kings emerged from the great ocean to pay him homage; ten billion luminous maṇi-jewels shone forth as illumination; ten billion pure...
The *puṣparāga* mani-jewel serves as the supreme ornament; ten billion *vairocana* mani-jewels constitute the stainless treasury;
ten billion *sūryaprabha* mani-jewels serve as the great illumination; ten billion *citravarṇa* mani-treasury jewels provide universal radiance;
the *jambudhvaja* jewel provides excellent stability; and ten billion *vajra* [jewels]...
It was adorned with invincible lion-maṇi jewels; it was extensively embellished by being interspersed and inlaid with ten billion sun-treasury maṇi jewels;
it was wonderfully adorned by ten billion inconceivable maṇi jewels emitting various colors;
and it displayed inexhaustible adornments produced by ten billion wish-fulfilling jewels.
This great lotus flower is born from the roots of goodness that transcend the world, produced by the Tathāgata, and cherished by the aspirations of Bodhisattvas.

It manifests throughout all directions, arising from the illusory nature of phenomena and born of the karma of wholesome dharmas. Adorned with the principle of the non-contentious nature of reality, it is like the dream-like nature of phenomena; following the seal of non-action and the principle of non-attachment, it pervades all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions—this being brought about by the merit of conforming to the realm of the Buddhas.
If one were to praise his physical marks and the adornment of his merits for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they could never be exhausted.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged upon that flower, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus, whose names were as follows:

The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Māṣpāyaṇa, Mahānāman, Udāyin, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Subāhu, Gavāmpati, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Subhūti, Revata, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Upāli, Rāhula, Nanda, and others were the leaders; they had all awakened to the truth of their own intrinsic nature, realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), entered the fundamental nature of phenomena, and crossed over the ocean of existence.
They practice the space-like conduct of the Tathāgatas, being able to forever sever all latent tendencies and fetters, while dwelling in the non-abiding state of the treasury, empty and tranquil.

Having forever severed doubt and confusion regarding the Tathāgata, they enter the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom and the path of supreme faith; they benefit the world as uninvited friends, constantly able to protect all sentient beings, acting as unfailing companions for all living beings.

They have attained mastery over the Buddha-dharma; they guard the sublime Dharma within their spheres of activity; they vow to uphold the true teachings of all Buddhas; they manifest birth within the lineage of the Tathāgatas; and they are well able to advance toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Furthermore, there was an assembly of eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas together,
with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva as their leaders; namely, Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom-Knowledge,
Bodhisattva Supreme Jewel-Wisdom, Bodhisattva Wisdom of All Languages, and Bodhisattva Unattached Wisdom.
Bodhisattva Flower-Supreme-Wisdom, Bodhisattva Sun-Supreme-Wisdom, Bodhisattva Moon-Supreme-Wisdom,
Bodhisattva Stainless-Supreme-Wisdom, Bodhisattva Vajra-Wisdom, Bodhisattva Dust-Distant-Wisdom,
Bodhisattva Light-Banner, Bodhisattva Wondrous High Banner, Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, Bodhisattva Unobstructed Banner, and Bodhisattva Flower...
Dhvaja Bodhisattva, Viśuddhadhvaja Bodhisattva, Sūryadhvaja Bodhisattva, Prāsādikadhvaja Bodhisattva,
Vimaladhvaja Bodhisattva, Samantaprabhādhvaja Bodhisattva, Dhāraṇītejas Bodhisattva, Ratnatejas Bodhisattva, Mahātejas Bodhisattva, and Vajrajñānatejas Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Vimalatejas, the Bodhisattva Sūryatejas, the Bodhisattva Candratejas, the Bodhisattva Puṇyaparvatejas, the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabhātejas, the Bodhisattva Samantavijayatejas,
the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, and the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha.
Sāgaramati, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Viśuddhaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Dharmasāgaragarbha Bodhisattva, Samantālokagarbha Bodhisattva, Samantabhadragarbha Bodhisattva, Jyotirpadmagarbha Bodhisattva,
Sūryanetra Bodhisattva, Viśuddhanetra Bodhisattva, Vimalanetra Bodhisattva, and Asaṅganetra Bodhisattva.
...the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Eye, the Bodhisattva Wholesome Benefit Wisdom Eye,
the Bodhisattva Vajra Eye, the Bodhisattva Jewel Eye, the Bodhisattva Space Eye, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, the Bodhisattva Celestial Crown,
the Bodhisattva Mani-Crown Illuminating the Dharma Realm, the Bodhisattva Mani-Crown of Wondrous Bodhi, and the Bodhisattva Illumination...
The Bodhisattva Ten Directions Crown, the Bodhisattva Appearance of the Treasury of All Buddhas Crown,
the Bodhisattva Surpassing All Worlds Crown, the Bodhisattva Universal Illumination Crown, the Bodhisattva Unobscured Crown,
the Bodhisattva Grasping the Lion Throne of All Tathāgatas Crown, and the Bodhisattva Universal Illumination of the Dharmadhātu and Space Crown.
...Brahmā-Crown-Bodhisattva, Dragon-King-Crown-Bodhisattva, Crown-of-All-Buddha-Emanated-Images-Bodhisattva,
Wondrous-Enlightenment-Crown-Bodhisattva, Crown-of-Maṇi-Kings-with-Sounds-of-the-Ocean-of-All-Vows-Bodhisattva,
and Crown-of-Thunderous-Sound-Maṇi-Jewels-Emitting-the-Halo-Rays-of-All-Tathāgatas-Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sarvagaganāsaṃbhedanirdeśamaṇiratnajālapraticchannacūḍa, the Bodhisattva Sarvatathāgatadharmacakranirghoṣacūḍa, the Bodhisattva Sarvatryadhvanāmanicakranirghoṣacūḍa,
the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha, and the Bodhisattva Virajaprabha.
...the Bodhisattva Sāra, the Bodhisattva Dharmaprabha, the Bodhisattva Śāntiprabha, the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Ṛddhiprabha, the Bodhisattva Devaprabha, the Bodhisattva Puṇyaprabha, the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Dharmāvabhāsaprabha, the Bodhisattva Abhijñāprabha, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, and the Bodhisattva Puṣpaprabha.
...Bodhisattva Jewel Light, Bodhisattva Awakened Radiance, Bodhisattva Brahma Light, Bodhisattva Universal Illumination Light,
Bodhisattva Brahma Sound, Bodhisattva Ocean Sound, Bodhisattva Earth-Roar Sound, Bodhisattva World-King Sound,
Bodhisattva Mountain-King Sound, and Bodhisattva Mountain-King Colliding Sound.
The Bodhisattva Pervasive Sound of the Dharma Realm, the Bodhisattva Thunderous Sound of the Ocean of All Dharmas, the Bodhisattva Sound that Subdues All Māras,
the Bodhisattva Cloud-Thunder Sound of the Principle of Great Compassion, the Bodhisattva Sound that Universally Pacifies All Suffering and Affliction in the World,
the Bodhisattva Surging Excellence of Dharma, the Bodhisattva Surging Sublimity, and the Bodhisattva Surging Wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Undefiled Surge, the Bodhisattva Merit-Sumeru Supreme Surge, the Bodhisattva Supreme Virtue Surge, the Bodhisattva Renowned Supreme Surge,
the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Supreme Surge, the Bodhisattva Great Compassion Supreme Surge,
the Bodhisattva Wisdom Illumination Supreme Surge, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata Lineage Supreme Surge, and the Bodhisattva Radiant Virtue...
Sattva, Śrīguṇa Bodhisattva, Dharmodgataśrīguṇa Bodhisattva, Samantālokaśrīguṇa Bodhisattva,
Dharmaśrīguṇa Bodhisattva, Candraśrīguṇa Bodhisattva, Gaganaguṇa Bodhisattva, Ratnaguṇa Bodhisattva,
Prabhāśrīguṇa Bodhisattva, Jñānaśrīguṇa Bodhisattva, Brahmarājendra Bodhisattva, and Dharmarājendra Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattvas: Elephant King Sovereign Bodhisattva, Brahma King Sovereign Bodhisattva, Mountain King Sovereign Bodhisattva,
Multitude King Sovereign Bodhisattva, Deva King Sovereign Bodhisattva, Tranquility King Sovereign Bodhisattva,
Immovable King Sovereign Bodhisattva, Supreme King Sovereign Bodhisattva, and Bodhi Tranquil Sound Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sa, the Bodhisattva Unattached Sound, the Bodhisattva Earth Sound, the Bodhisattva Great Ocean Sound,
the Bodhisattva Melodious Sound, the Bodhisattva Illuminating Dharma Sound, the Bodhisattva Space Sound, the Bodhisattva All Sounds,
the Bodhisattva Thunderous Sound of Roots of Goodness, the Bodhisattva Sound of Awakening to Original Vows, and the [Bodhisattva] Who Subdues All...
The Bodhisattva Sound of the Māra Army, the Bodhisattva Wisdom-Sumeru Awakening, the Bodhisattva Space Awakening, the Bodhisattva Pure Awakening,
the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Awakening, the Bodhisattva Awakened Enlightenment, the Bodhisattva Illuminating the Three Times Awakening,
the Bodhisattva Jewel Awakening, the Bodhisattva Vast Awakening, and the Bodhisattva Universal Light Awakening.
The Bodhisattva Illuminating-Awakening to the Principle of the Dharma-Domain, and eight thousand such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were present together.
They all dwelt securely in the vows and practices of Samantabhadra; their conduct was unattached because it pervaded all buddha-fields.
The transformation into boundless bodies is for the sake of drawing near to all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
The purity of the objective sphere that is without limits is for the sake of thoroughly understanding the spiritual transformations of all Buddhas.
"Proceeding to the immeasurable" means that one proceeds without rest to the places where all Buddhas manifest equal enlightenment.
"Boundless radiance" means that within the ocean of the true reality of all phenomena, one attains the boundless light of wisdom.
That which is inexhaustible when its merits are proclaimed throughout boundless eons is due to the purity of eloquence;
that which is equal to the realm of empty space is due to the purity of the sphere of activity of wisdom.
Being without dependence means manifesting a form-body (rūpakāya) in accordance with the inclinations of worldly beings.
Being able to remove the cataracts [of ignorance] means thoroughly knowing that there is no realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu).
Having the wisdom of space means emitting a net of light-rays that pervades the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
The one who is ultimately tranquil, because of having a most tranquil mind; the one whose sphere of knowledge consists of the seed-natures of all dhāraṇīs;

the one who is courageous and fearless in samādhi; the one whose eye abides in the dharma-realm to its furthest limit; the one who abides in non-apprehension regarding all phenomena; the one who wanders in the boundless ocean of wisdom; the one who has already crossed to the further shore of knowledge; the one who is Prajñāpāramitā; the one who, through Prajñāpāramitā, has reached the perfection of all worlds; and the one who has attained mastery over the further shore of samādhi.

Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs together with him, headed by the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, the bhikṣuṇī Gautamī, the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, and the bhikṣuṇī Prālambā Gautamī.

Furthermore, there were five hundred upāsakas together, headed by such as the upāsaka Kalyāṇatejas, the upāsaka Devatejas, the upāsaka Prajñāprabha, the upāsaka Yaśastejas, the upāsaka Atiyaśastejas, the upāsaka Kalyāṇamati, the upāsaka Candratejas, the upāsaka Candranandana, the upāsaka Mahānandana, the upāsaka Rāhudeva, and the upāsaka Mahādeva.

Furthermore, there were five hundred upāsikās together, headed by the upāsikā Mahāprabhā, the upāsikā Suprabhā, the upāsikā Sukāya, the upāsikā Rucitakāya, the upāsikā Bhadrāśrī, the upāsikā Candraprabhā, the upāsikā Prabhāvatī, the upāsikā Jyotiṣprabhā, and the upāsikā Sunetra.

He was surrounded and honored by an immeasurable multitude of others, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth, as he preached the Dharma for them.

This refers to the extensive exposition of the chapter on the threefold restraint, the *vinaya* dharma of all Tathāgatas; it reveals and manifests all bodhisattva practices, illuminates the *dharmadhātu*, and enters into all dharma-gates; it is able to purify and adorn all buddha-fields, to refute false doctrines, to subdue Māras and enemies, and to cause the minds of the realm of sentient beings to attain joy.

He opens and enlightens the minds within the dense forest of sentient beings, preaching according to their inclinations; he reveals and illuminates the faculties of sentient beings, causing them to turn toward and progress upon the path.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If sentient beings seek the powers and fearlessnesses of the Buddha-dharma, what dharmas should they embrace and practice?
What dharmas should they embrace to increase and bring to maturity the path of all Tathāgatas?
“By embracing what dharmas does one take up all merits, increase and enter into the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and attain non-retrogression?
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!”

Kāśyapa! What you have now asked brings great peace and security, out of compassion for the world; it provides benefit, profit, and happiness to humans and devas, that you are able to ask the Buddha about such a matter.
"Listen attentively now, and reflect upon it well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there are sentient beings who seek the power and fearlessness of the Buddha's wisdom, for these beings there is not even the slightest dharma that can be obtained; they have nothing upon which to rely as they cultivate various roots of goodness."
Kāśyapa! When a bodhisattva, even while seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, perceives anything as obtainable, this constitutes attachment to conceptualization.

If one is attached to conceptualization, one gives rise to the notion of the conditioned outside of the Buddha-dharma, and outside of the conditioned, one gives rise to the notion of the unconditioned; thus, one generates attachment and conceptual grasping toward the Buddha-dharma. When such conceptual grasping arises, one remains firmly established within the Buddha-dharma and does not relinquish it.
It should be known that such a person is not said to be "proceeding toward the unsurpassed Buddha-way. Why is this?

Because they give rise to conceptualizations regarding the Buddha-dharma and grasp at a self while practicing with diligence; thus, being associated with the habitual tendencies of self-clinging, they do not abandon it, and consequently engage in the discrimination between the subject and the object of discrimination.

From this, the locus of conceptualization and that which is conceptualized become objects of harm; if they are harmed, there is wandering; if there is wandering, there is transmigration; if there is transmigration, there is piercing; if there is piercing, there is false imagination; if there is false imagination, there is discrimination; if there is discrimination, false imagination increases; if false imagination increases, there is pervasive calculation; if there is pervasive calculation, one departs from tranquility; if one departs from tranquility, there is pursuit; if there is pursuit, there is roaming; and if there is roaming, one comes to ruin.
What is ruin? It is the loss of security. What is security?

This refers to non-discrimination. If it is lost or destroyed, one then enters [into it] constantly; if one enters constantly, one then becomes intimate with it; if one is intimate with it, there are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); if there are latent tendencies, there is continuity; if there is continuity, continuity increases; if continuity increases, there is pervasive continuity; if speech involves pervasive continuity, it becomes deranged; if speech is deranged, one then becomes deluded; if there is delusion, there is distress; for one who has distress, there is regret; and if there is regret, one relies upon ignorance, which results in the harm of sorrow and joy.

Within this, there is not even the slightest dharma upon which one can rely; yet, because they arise from the flowing stream of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they are bound by conceptualization. Because they proceed from the bondage of conceptualization, conceptualization continues in succession; therefore, it is called the "bondage of conceptualization" (*saṃjñā-bandhana*).

There is no real locus; all loci of greed, anger, and delusion are entirely false conceptualizations, proliferations of discrimination, and exaggerations of calculation. Therefore, such persons cannot quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa! This is called a locus of craving.
What is meant by a locus of craving?
There is no fixed dharma that can be called craving;
what is called craving refers to the locus of craving.

However, the existence of craving arises solely from firm attachment. If, at the time of firm attachment, one regards space as craving, and if one gives rise to clinging toward this "craving for space," that person will then incur the attachment of craving.
I am one who clings through attachment to self, who clings through attachment to sentient beings, and who clings through attachment to the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Kāśyapa, such a person gives rise to the discrimination of "not empty" regarding all dharmas that are empty; they give rise to the perception of substantiality regarding that which is not a substance.
What is meant by "a thing"?

If one takes bodhi as a thing, or if bodhi is taken as a thing for them, then those various sentient beings, because of the notion of a self, possess the notion of a self; such individuals are not bodhisattvas.

In this regard, if perception is unattainable, then that which perceives within it is likewise unattainable; this is called the "phrase of the non-reality of the self-perception," and this is a designation.
What is meant by the notion of a self?
Furthermore, if one can fulfill the being (sattva), then one fulfills awakening (bodhi).
What is meant by awakening?
What is called "perfection" is like an illusion.
In what way is it like an illusion?

It refers to those who speak of the notion of a "great self" or the notion of a "great life-force," or those who rely upon a notion by means of a notion; these, in turn, rely upon the absence of notions by means of the absence of notions.
If one relies on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of that which is not perception, then one is intoxicated by madness.
If one is intoxicated by madness, then one pursues suffering with suffering.
If one pursues suffering with suffering, then all those Tathāgatas declare such a person to be one who dwells in mad speech and runs about in distraction.
Why is it called "dwelling in the galloping of mad speech"? It refers to the intensification of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

If there is an intensification of mental attention, there is arrogance (*māna*); if there is arrogance, there is verbal expression; if there is verbal expression, there is an increase in talkativeness. Regarding this increase in talkativeness, the Tathāgata has declared that such a person is a mere speaker, a teacher, and one who merely upholds [the words].
Therefore, all phenomena arise and grow from mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Kāśyapa, it is like a mass of clouds arising in the sky above; they do not come from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below.

Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the Speaker of Truth; knowing that this mass of clouds does not come from the ten directions, he speaks of it as it truly is—speaking according to its meaning, speaking in accordance with principle, and speaking by way of ultimate truth.
What is called a "mass of clouds" is, in fact, not a mass; therefore it is named a "mass of clouds.
Why is it called a "mass of clouds"?
Because its various individual characteristics arise separately.
What is the distinct characteristic of their various types?
It is because all these various characteristics are a vast continuity of delusion, within which not even the slightest mark of smallness or greatness can be found.
Observe that when clouds gather and manifest as vast appearances, they are in fact non-appearances.
If they are non-conceptual, it is simply because the appearance of ultimate vastness is not a real cloud-gathering.
Kāśyapa! It is as if someone were to say to another:
"Shall we go together to sit in a place of shade?"
The wise one said, "I will not go and sit.
He spoke these words:
"I do not say this now; I merely speak of these aggregates.
At that time, the wise one spoke again to him, saying:
"That which you call an aggregate is, in fact, no aggregate."
"Kāśyapa! Observe that person; even while conforming to worldly conventions, they are still able to awaken to understanding.
Just so, just so, Kāśyapa!"
The Tathāgata, having realized the true nature of all phenomena as they truly are, utters the authentic lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata intentionally maintains the perception of non-conformity regarding phenomena that are actually conformable; and as for the notion of a "self" held by sentient beings, this is, for the Tathāgata, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Why is this? The Tathāgata now knows those perceptions; he fully knows that the perceptions of all sentient beings are themselves non-perceptions. This is the most supreme secret teaching.
There may be foolish people who give rise to opposition and contend with the Tathāgata; for this reason, I say: "The world contends with me, but I do not contend with the world."
What is meant by "the world"?
It refers to sentient beings.
For what reason are sentient beings called "the world"?
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands such a world; therefore, sentient beings are called "the world.
If one were to follow the understanding of those foolish ordinary beings, one would then be destroyed and utterly harmed.
This is what they constantly perceive as their abiding faith; it is what is conventionally termed "ignorance" (avidyā). Why is this?

Those who dwell in great darkness are called "world-dwellers. If one is a world-dweller, there is craving (rāga); if there is craving, there is aversion (dveṣa); if there is aversion, there is delusion (moha); if there is delusion, there is impurity (aśubha); and if there is impurity, there is contradiction.
With whom is he in conflict?
It is with the Tathāgata and the assembly of śrāvakas.
If one is in conflict, then one is at variance; if one is at variance, then one is in grave conflict. Grave conflict...
One who transgresses thus delights in existence; one who delights in existence seeks it with the mind;
one who seeks existence then seeks it everywhere; one who seeks everywhere does not know contentment; one who does not know contentment performs many actions;
one who performs many actions possesses much desire; and one who possesses much desire has underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Within the three realms, if one’s latent tendencies (anuśaya) follow those of the three realms, they cause others’ latent tendencies to arise;
for those whose latent tendencies are caused to arise by others, there is a flowing along with them, and for those who flow along, they proceed toward death.
Those who proceed toward death do not proceed toward nirvāṇa, and those who do not proceed toward nirvāṇa [do not attain it].
They go to a place of no resort; those who go to a place of no resort proceed to hell.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

Because they are associated with inauspicious dharmas, their minds are filled with the poison of anger and resentment, and they lack concealment. To lack concealment means not to contemplate the notion of "self. Not contemplating leads to the formation of a unified conception [of identity], whereby one is unable to extinguish the notions of "I" and "mine."
What is called the grasping at a self?
Because it is unreal, one dwells in various perceptions and performs all worldly karmas.
If this is so, that grasping at the mark of a self is taken as "self."
What is meant by "what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*)? It refers to craving; therefore, it is called "what belongs to me.

Because one gives rise to a mind of craving when various desires unite with the body, and having given rise to such attachment, one is able to destroy the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*); furthermore, one generates unwholesome thoughts toward others, being obscured by anger and thus mutually disparaging one another, as well as grasping at material wealth as one's own and becoming attached to its protection—this is called "what belongs to me."

Where there is the notion of "mine," there is cyclic existence; where there is cyclic existence, there is delusion; where there is delusion, there is slander; where there is slander, there is anger; where there is anger, there is devouring harm; where there is devouring harm, one is consumed by fire; and where one is consumed, one is utterly consumed. Such faults as these all arise from craving.
To conceive the notions of "male" and "female," as well as the notion of "life," as being "mine" is called "what belongs to me" (*mama*).
For this reason, it is said that one who speaks of "what belongs to me" is reviling their own self.
All foolish persons take the latent tendencies of "I" (asmimāna-anuśaya) as the dharma of a fool; therefore, they speak of it as "mine" (mamakāra).
Kāśyapa, if there are sentient beings who have not heard this Dharma, yet speak of bodhi and the practices of a bodhisattva, that is not true practice.
Regarding what is called "the practice of a bodhisattva," in reality there is no practice; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if bodhisattvas attain the perfection of practice without deficiency—being pure, utterly pure, and completely pure—such persons are able to expound this Great Dharma. They are called those of great power and courageous diligence; the Dharma they teach is equal to space and without accumulation. It is for those who act according to principle, those with merit, and those capable of practice, and never for those who do not act according to principle, those without merit, or those who do not practice.
"You all should receive and uphold this Dharma, yet do not give rise to attachment toward it. Why is this?

What the Tathāgata has spoken is the most supreme; because you have asked these questions for the sake of the most exalted beings worthy of offerings, I have explained them to you with the most excellent Dharma."
What is the supreme dharma?
It is the absence of the notion of dharmas. Kāśyapa!
In this way, the bodhisattva fully maintains the initial pure precepts: his mind is free from arrogance;
he does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*); he does not violate a bhikṣuṇī; nor does he associate with the households of laypeople.
He remains far removed from killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct; he abstains from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
Regarding frivolous speech, one should distance oneself from sensual desire, ill will, and wrong views;
neither afflicting oneself nor afflicting others, one does not associate with desire nor accept it,
does not engage in gambling nor teach it, never associates with those of the third gender, and does not go to the homes of prostitutes, widows, or virgins.
He does not approach the wives of others, nor does he associate with fishermen, fowlers, hunters, executioners, or caṇḍālas;
he does not take the hands of those who drink alcohol, nor does he engage them in quarrels.
One should avoid these various things as one would shun a vicious dog or a *caṇḍāla*.
By abiding in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one does not give rise to even a single thought of malice toward all those who are to be avoided.
There are twenty places that should be avoided.
What are these twenty? They are:
avoiding women, and not engaging with others in frivolous talk, coarse speech, or contentious disputes.
One should avoid showing disrespect toward one's parents, as well as toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
One should not preach the Dharma to women if they are fewer than twenty in number.
Unless a man is present, one should never go to a gathering where bhikṣuṇīs are preaching the Dharma.
One should not inquire after the health of bhikṣuṇīs,
nor should one compose letters for women,
or act as a messenger to deliver letters to them on behalf of others.
One should entrust matters to a man, not to a woman.
At all times, one must never accept private invitations from kinsmen.
One should not, with a mind of desire, remain before a woman for even a single moment.
Furthermore, one should not abandon one's original dwelling to go to a secluded place to engage in conversation with a woman.
One must not follow after a bhikṣuṇī.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives clothing that should not be used as an offering, she must not accept it, except when clothing is offered by someone for the purpose of preaching the Dharma while she is expounding the teaching before the fourfold assembly.
One should generate a mind like the great earth and then accept [the gift], without looking at the face of the donor.
If one hears that a bhikṣuṇī has exhorted others to give clothing, one should not use it.
If a bhikṣuṇī invites one to receive food, even if she is suffering from illness, one must ultimately not accept it, let alone when she is not ill.
If a widow comes to invite one to eat, and the number of the monastic assembly is incomplete, one must likewise not accept it.
Furthermore, one should not enter the midst of the community of bhikṣuṇīs,
nor should one summon those bhikṣuṇīs to come.
If a bhikṣuṇī should come and summon the bodhisattva, he should leave his dwelling place, fold his hands, look upward, turn his back, and depart.
If, while preaching the Dharma, a bhikṣuṇī comes to prostrate at one’s feet, do not let the feet move; rather, you should simply gaze into the palms of both hands.
Son of good family!

One should not merely cultivate diligence with the body; one must also diligently apply the mind to right mindfulness on a single object, refrain from giving rise to greed or hatred toward any sensory realm, and make firm vows for the sake of seeking all-knowledge.
Having heard this Dharma, one should cultivate and study it with perfected faith. Kāśyapa!

If any sons or daughters of good family who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, upon hearing this Dharma, are unable to give rise to true and profound faith, they will ultimately never attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? It is because one realizes that bodhi through cultivation and study; it cannot be realized without cultivation and study.
If one could attain bodhi without practicing, then even cats, rabbits, and the like should also be able to realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Why is this? Because those who practice incorrectly cannot realize unsurpassed enlightenment. Why is this?
If one could attain enlightenment through improper conduct, then sounds and speech should also realize unsurpassed enlightenment by saying:
"I shall become a Buddha!"
"I shall become a Buddha!
Because of this realization, boundless sentient beings should attain perfect enlightenment. Kāśyapa!

If there are sentient beings who cultivate and study this practice, it is extremely rare; they are still unable to maintain single-minded concentration upon it for even a single day and night, let alone for one kalpa or even a thousand kalpas.
Therefore, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is an exceedingly rare event. Kāśyapa!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were, for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or even for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, to join together and cry out these words for the sake of a single sentient being:
"You shall become a Buddha! You shall become a Buddha!
Thus all these sentient beings surrounded him together, chanting in succession:
"You shall attain Buddhahood!
You shall attain Buddhahood!
Thus, in this sequence, even though his exhalations and inhalations might cease, the words he spoke never faltered.
Such words as these cannot even bring the initial bodhicitta to maturity, let alone enable one to realize the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood;
for it is impossible that one could so realize it.
“Kāśyapa! After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the final dharma, and when you and the others have already entered parinirvāṇa, [the teaching] will no longer be protected by the devas.”
At that time, many sentient beings, having heard of my merits, will resolve their minds upon *bodhicitta*.
Among them, there may be certain bhikṣus and others who, although they have already resolved their minds upon unsurpassed *bodhicitta*, will nevertheless abide in twenty dharmas.
What are these twenty? They are:
associating with bhikṣuṇīs; accepting impure food; being greedily attached to delicious flavors; and accepting invitations for food and drink from bhikṣuṇīs.
Kāśyapa! Just as in the present age there are learned bhikṣus who dwell in araṇyas or within villages and diligently practice the Dharma, so too will it be with the bhikṣus of future ages;
whether in villages or in araṇyas, they will gather with bhikṣuṇīs to converse and engage in questions and answers regarding the meaning of the Dharma.
Those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs give rise mostly to defiled minds and little to the mind of the Dharma.
Kāśyapa! Observe these types of people who, while bearing the name of "bodhisattva," fall into great peril and take rebirth in evil destinies.

At that time, having first become close through their affinity for the Dharma, once they saw one another, the fire of desire burned within their hearts, and they moved their lips to manifest their lustful intentions.

When they first drew near, he acted as her disciple and paid his respects according to the rites of an *ācārya*. From that time forward, he gradually sent messengers to convey messages, arrange meetings on the road, or gaze at one another from afar—either in the streets or within the monastery. When she entered or left, he would inquire about her affairs, and they mutually claimed kinship, becoming sisters.

Because they saw one another frequently in this way, they became habituated to each other; once habituated, they gave rise to defiled minds; having given rise to defiled minds, they engaged in impure acts together; and having engaged in impure acts, they began to address one another by the name of "unholy conduct" (*abrahmacarya*).

By practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, they fall away from bodhi and the happy realms; they distance themselves from nirvāṇa, abandon the Tathāgata, oppose the true Dharma, and harbor aversion toward the Saṃgha.

If one dwells in seclusion and gives rise to evil thoughts of desire, malice, and harm, that person lacks the superior karma of a bodhisattva and the fourfold pure brahma-conduct; this is just as those bodhisattvas who now diligently cultivate brahma-conduct will likewise be so in future ages if they give rise to the evil thoughts of desire, malice, and harm.
Kāśyapa! At that time, people will abide in such categories as those of evil conduct, thievery, and hypocrisy.
Observe, Kāśyapa, that those who violate the precepts, upon hearing sūtras such as these, will immediately give rise to slander.

If there are those who, having already been able to abide in the precepts and practice giving, give rise to joy and resolve upon bodhicitta, yet later hear this sutra and again give rise to slander and disparagement—observe such signs at that time; they may serve as a mark of verification.

If one hears this sutra and gives rise to slander, those among them who are wise, who cultivate pure precepts, and who uphold the true Dharma, knowing that within this sutra it is said that such bhikṣus do not understand the Dharma, should immediately distance themselves from such persons, for these individuals lack the heart of love and reverence for the Dharma.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The First Assembly on the Threefold Discipline, Part Two:
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, at that time,
there will be those who falsely pretend to practice the bodhisattva path, proclaiming themselves while falling into negligence."
Having become negligent, they claim to be superior to Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats; dwelling in what is unreasonable, they are called incurable and shall fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

In the future, there will be those who dwell in non-action and non-activity; because they grasp at the signs of sentient beings in order to preach the Dharma, they will wander everywhere performing only semblance practices—practices that most closely resemble the blazing and widespread propagation of the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
If there are those who speak of this sutra according to reality, they will be hated, disliked, and abandoned by others, and will give rise to views of false attachment toward this sutra;
for these deluded people do not know that this sutra censures the breaking of the precepts, Kāśyapa!

At that time, they will all be defiled by the conduct of thieves; therefore, those people will not reflect upon their own faults and will be able to utterly destroy right and equal enlightenment. Because they conceal [their transgressions], they will harbor shame and slander the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
At that time, they will not accord with the Saṃgha, and they will act for the sake of development without knowing how to repay kindness. How do they develop?
[They develop] as follows:..."
This refers to those who seek to probe the minds of others.
The Tathāgata has said that such people deceive others with their speech for the sake of obtaining food and drink. Kāśyapa!

At that time, they will fail to guard their speech, revile and disparage the Tathāgata’s Pratimokṣa precepts, and engage in the same activities as those who do not guard their speech. They will not maintain dignified deportment but will dwell in impure places, teaching various Dharma gates to those who dwell in impure places; thus, this Dharma will gradually be held in contempt by others.
In this way, gradually many women abandoned their husbands and entered the monastery, sitting down for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu preached to them a counterfeit version of nirvāṇa.

Kāśyapa! When I contemplate that time, there will be five hundred gates of unrighteousness; practitioners who do not cultivate themselves will constantly follow them, such that their five hundred afflictions will not diminish at all, and everything they do will be no different from that of worldly people.
Since there are such greatly fearsome matters as these, yet one still hopes for benefit therein, those who seek Bodhi should not associate with bhikṣuṇīs, nor should they engage in such conduct.

One should always abandon all social associations and, at all times, renounce all gain and offerings, practicing the alms-round. One should discard beloved garments and accept rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), abandoning all towers, pavilions, houses, beds, and bedding. One should dwell by mountain streams, in rock caves, or beneath trees, and renounce all medicinal requisites and necessities for treating illness, relying instead on discarded medicines. Knowing that all sentient beings were once one's own kin, one should practice great loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*). One should always endure being struck or reviled, and never strike or insult others.

Having renounced all companions, patrons, and households of kinsmen, one should act in accordance with the wisdom of one's own karma and should not be the same as those householders who remain in the secular world.
One should always respectfully follow the teachings of the Prātimokṣa. “Kāśyapa!
If there is anyone in the world who conceives a sense of opposition toward the Prātimokṣa, they are thereby creating opposition toward the Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses.”

If one should give rise to opposition toward the Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses, one thereby gives rise to opposition toward all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; consequently, one will experience immeasurable great suffering as the ripening result in the future.

Even if all sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to undergo the sufferings of the hells, compared to the bitter poison endured by the aforementioned sentient beings, it would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part; it would not even equal one part in a hundred thousand koṭis, nor even by calculation, analogy, or upaniṣad-part.
If one wishes to remain far removed from such suffering and affliction, one should distance oneself from such types of misconduct.
A bhikṣu should avoid them even from as far away as a thousand yojanas, let alone when they are near.
If one should abandon even the mere hearing of its name, how much more so should one distance oneself from seeing or hearing it?
Therefore, one should draw near to a single dharma.
What is this one dharma?
This means that all phenomena are entirely non-existent.
If one attains the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of the non-existence of all phenomena, one will not associate with, make offerings to, or serve such evil persons.
This person should further cultivate two dharmas. What are these two?
They are seeking that all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and seeking the nature of all dharmas; yet, one should not give rise to a mind of seeking.
How should one seek?

One should seek such that nothing whatsoever can be obtained; within this non-attainment, one should not give rise to a mind of "non-attainment" like that of wrong views. Thus, by being free from all minds associated with the three realms, one accords with the practice of Bodhi;
by being free from all marks, one accords with the practice of a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the "bodhisattva practitioner," this refers to what was previously described as the bodhisattva practice.

Therefore, having heard this Dharma, one should abandon it; thus, in a future life, one will personally attend upon the World-Honored One Maitreya with a mind that is neither arrogant nor inferior, and shall proclaim:
"How wonderful! What peace and joy!"
"I have attained liberation from the snares of Māra and from all evil destinies. "Kāśyapa!

If, at a later time, one hears this sutra and is neither startled nor terrified, and seeing themselves as being in accord with it, further resolves to take up and uphold these teachings, the Buddha knows that such a person will certainly protect my True Dharma."

Kāśyapa! It is like a householder whose wealth and treasures are immeasurable; even when his son sees within the house a single vessel filled with water, he conceives the thought that it is his father’s property.
At another time, after his father had passed away and his wealth had been dissipated, he suddenly saw that vessel and thought to himself:
"This is my father's property.
He then placed it by his side or sometimes hid it away.

Kāśyapa! At that time, the bhikṣus will likewise be thus: having heard this sutra, they will think to themselves, "This is what has been expounded by the Tathāgata’s soft, subtle, and sublime Brahma-voice."
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who, upon hearing this, slandered it. Those bhikṣus who upheld the Dharma spoke thus:
"This is the most authentic teaching spoken by the Tathāgata.
Yet those upholders of the Dharma had few followers and their dwelling places were weak; they concealed and protected such sutras day and night, encountering extreme slander.

I also know and see such persons as these; I entrust them all to the World-Honored One Maitreya, who in the final age shall protect the city of the Tathāgata’s Dharma and subsequently provide unimpeded great giving.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if a son of good family,
having heard this Dharma, practices it according to his wisdom, he will become a being who has achieved profound faith and right view, and in a future age will encounter Maitreya Buddha."
In the first assembly, they fully cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and at the final time, they shall likewise protect the Dharma-city of the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa!

Now I observe universally and do not see even a single person who does not draw near to me; that there should be anyone who, during the fifty years of the future age, upon hearing this sutra, would not give rise to slander, but would instead be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it—such a thing is impossible.
If, at this time, one should behold my body and serve and make offerings to it, that person shall, in the coming fifty years, be able to read, recite, and uphold this sutra.

Without waiting for me to praise their merits, when they themselves have realized the single essence of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they will, upon recollecting me, give rise to joy in their hearts and speak thus:
"How rare and extraordinary is Śākyamuni Buddha!"
"You have been able to skillfully embrace and protect us with your mindfulness. Therefore, Kāśyapa,
you should train in this Dharma.
"One who studies this Dharma will, according to whatever they seek and aspire to, realize all merits without difficulty.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I have reached the ultimate end and no longer have any aspiration or seeking.
Within this Dharma, I have regressed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
I am extremely content with this state and shall ultimately never be able to achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
“World-Honored One!
Unsurpassed Bodhi is a rare and marvelous matter; it is difficult for us śrāvakas to realize.
The Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I did not speak this for your sake; however, I shall now expound it for others because of you.
You must not harbor doubts regarding such a great matter; you, too, shall swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
if sentient beings develop a mind that thirsts for the Dharma and a mind that seeks the Dharma, they will gradually all realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Having realized it, in order to sever all minds of seeking, they shall proclaim the True Dharma to all sentient beings.
Kāśyapa! A bodhisattva should accomplish four dharmas to arouse great diligence. What are these four?
What is diligence? It is said to be not seeking form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, but seeking untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma).
That is to say, there is no earth element, and no water, fire, or wind elements.
One does not speak of the earth element, nor does one speak of the water, fire, or wind elements.

All verbal expressions are termed "representations"; these representational phenomena are all devoid of substantial reality, and a bodhisattva should not grasp at representational phenomena as being solid or real.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We truly have no doubts or hesitations regarding the Tathāgata.”
If someone were to ask:
"If these designating dharmas are not ultimate reality, then are the sounds and verbal expressions of the Buddha's voice also false?
Should one answer this question in such a way?
The Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:

"In future ages there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body or the precepts, whose minds do not understand the principles of meaning, whose anger is fierce, and whose speech is coarse and vulgar; they will be unable to receive, uphold, read, or recite this sūtra in accordance with the Dharma."
Why is this? Because they give rise to a mind that dwells upon form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Future bhikṣus will dwell within the teachings expressed in this sūtra just as they dwell in the arising of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Furthermore, there is another class of bhikṣus who abide in the ways of householders and have no further aspiration for the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), like a person born blind who wears a golden flower garland upon their head but cannot see it themselves.

At that time, the bhikṣus will be just like this: they will not even accept or uphold the words and letters of such sūtras as these, much less be able to enter the ultimate truth (paramārtha) that is cultivated.
For example, suppose there is a young boy or girl who has been scolded by an adult man;
later, at another time, when that boy or girl hears the name of that person, they become startled, terrified, and afraid.

At that time, the bhikṣus will likewise be just like this: having heard these sūtras which speak of faults as they truly are, they will not feel regret upon understanding them; instead, they will delight in fine robes and, conversely, give rise to fear toward these very sūtras.
Kāśyapa! It is like a monkey with a frog tied to its hand, yet the monkey does not turn its face back to look at it.
At that time, the bhikṣus will be just like this: hearing such sūtras as these, they will oppose them and disregard them, and will not remain in their presence.
Kāśyapa! It is just as when a jackal, pursued by dogs, flees toward a cemetery, a cave, or a deep pit.
At that time, the bhikṣus will be just like this, fleeing like the jackal when they hear this sutra being preached.

The "running jackal" refers to those who violate the prohibitive precepts and slander this sutra; having heard this sutra, they retreat from the Path and return home, rushing to seek the realm of desire and approaching women; they engage in strife, clamor, medical arts, and legal adjudication, wherein they frequently violate the prohibitive precepts—I say that such people are like those heading toward a cemetery;
when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms, as if heading toward a burrow;
they gallop through the various great hells of sword-leaves, razor-edged blades, and forested spears, as if heading toward a deep pit.

Kāśyapa! At that time, those bhikṣus will have perfected such qualities of a jackal; they will be unable to awaken to and enter into sūtras such as these, but will instead only slander them and proclaim their faults, falling into the great hells upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
if there is a bhikṣu who speaks thus:
'If the dharmas that are expressed are not real, then are the words of the Tathāgata also not real?'"
If he should say: "The Buddha’s designations are called true; therefore, all designated phenomena should also be called real," a wise bhikṣu should ask him:
"Venerable One! What do you now maintain?
Do you maintain emptiness?"

"Is it for the purpose of representation? If he should say, "I grasp it for the purpose of representation," [the response is: "If you grasp it for the purpose of representation, then that which is grasped for the purpose of representation must itself be something that can be represented. If he should say, "That which is grasped for the purpose of representation is itself something that can be represented," then one should ask him: "Does that which is grasped for the purpose of representation represent itself? If he should say, "It does not represent itself," then one should ask him: "If it does not represent itself, how can it represent others? If he should say, "It represents others," then one should ask him: "By what means does it represent others? If he should say, "It represents others by means of its own nature," then one should ask him: "If it represents others by means of its own nature, then that which represents others by means of its own nature must itself be something that possesses a nature capable of representing. If he should say, "It represents others," then one should ask him: "By what means does it represent others? If he should say, "It represents others by means of its own nature," then one should ask him: "If it represents others by means of its own nature, then that which represents others by means of its own nature must itself be something that possesses a nature capable of representing. If he should say, "That which represents others by means of its own nature is itself something that possesses a nature capable of representing," then one should ask him: "Does that which represents others by means of its own nature represent itself? If he should say, "It does not represent itself," then one should ask him: "If it does not represent itself, how can it represent others? If he should say, "It represents others," then one should ask him: "By what means does it represent others? One should reply to them, saying:
"You are indeed the Buddha. Why is this so?"
"Because you possess speech that expresses phenomena. If he were to say,
"I grasp at emptiness," [then...]
One should ask him:
"Please tell me, what kind of emptiness do you grasp?
For what reason?"
That which is ineffable is called emptiness.

If one clings to the expression itself as being emptiness, one may instead cling to the notions of self, what belongs to a self, sentient beings, and a life-span as being non-empty while regarding them as empty.
He asks him again: "What do you think?
Do you delight in the emptiness of all phenomena? If he should answer:
"I do not delight in the emptiness of all phenomena. The wise one said:
"You have long since forgotten your status as a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas."
Why is this? Because the Buddha has taught that all things are empty and without self; he has not taught that there is a self, a sentient being, a life-span, or a person. If they should say:
If they say, "All phenomena are empty; I delight in emptiness," one should say to them:
"If your mind still delights in the emptiness of all phenomena, how much more so should it delight in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Furthermore, Venerable Sir!
Is the eye the Tathāgata?
Are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the Tathāgata?
If he should say, "The eye is the Tathāgata; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the Tathāgata," you should say to him:
"You are also a Tathāgata at this very moment. If he should say:
"The eye is not the Tathāgata; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also not the Tathāgata."
One should say to him: "Virtuous one!
You have made this statement that the eye does not represent the Tathāgata, and so on, up to the mind does not represent the Tathāgata;..."
"It is not that the Tathāgata is represented by these [faculties]; how could I not have realized this? If he were to say:
'The eye is not the Tathāgata, yet the Tathāgata does not exist apart from the eye; and so on, up to: the mind is not the Tathāgata, yet the Tathāgata does not exist apart from the mind.'"
One should say to him:

"The twelve bases (āyatana) spoken of by the Tathāgata exist—namely, the eye-base and the form-base, up to the mind-base and the phenomena-base—and these are precisely sentient beings and the names of sentient beings."
"O Benevolent One!
Is the eye the Tathāgata or not the Tathāgata?
And so on, up to: is the dharma the Tathāgata or not the Tathāgata?"
If he should answer,
"The eye is the Tathāgata," or even "The dharmas are the Tathāgata," you should tell him:
"If, as you say, all sentient beings, the mountains, forests, and the great earth should be the Tathāgata," and if they should answer,
"The eye is not the Tathāgata, and so on, up to the mind is not the Tathāgata."
One should further say to him:
"As you have stated, the Tathāgata is both the Dharma and the non-Dharma. If he should say:
If they say, "Form is not the Tathāgata, and so on, up to: phenomena are not the Tathāgata," you should tell them:
"If that is so, would you then take what is not a phenomenon to be the Tathāgata?"
If they should say, "One takes what is not the Dharma to be the Tathāgata," one should tell them:

"If it were so, then all sentient beings who are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders, who take life, commit theft, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, sow discord, utter harsh or frivolous speech, and harbor greed, hatred, and wrong views—these would have to be Tathāgatas."
If he should say, "It is neither non-Dharma, but rather the Tathāgata," you should tell him:
“The Tathāgata must be neither dharma nor non-dharma.
If the Tathāgata were neither dharma nor non-dharma, he would be without representation.
O Noble One!...”
"That which cannot be indicated is the Tathāgata! Kāśyapa,
one should thus subdue foolish people.

I do not see any among the people of the world, whether gods or humans, who are able to debate with one who speaks thus in accordance with the Dharma, except for those who are angry, deluded, and intolerant; though they are shown this teaching, they fail to give rise to faith, disparage the Dharma of emptiness, and depart.
“Kāśyapa! You all should receive and uphold this sutra.
In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who uphold this sutra; they shall obtain three names by which they are designated.”
What are these three? They are:
teaching annihilationism, the non-existence of things and aggregates, and a lack of reverence.
At that time, such a sūtra as this will be slandered by others.

Observe that at that time, they did not revere the Buddha nor revere the Dharma; they merely relied upon designations, names, and language to falsely bear the name of "Saṃgha" while lacking any actual virtue.
Although they recite the Buddha's name, they cannot understand it when explained to others; how, then, can they behold and serve the Tathāgata?
Although they speak of the Buddha-dharma, they cannot comprehend the Tathāgata’s intent; how, then, can they be called skilled in preaching the Dharma?

The four pairs and eight ranks are the disciples of the Buddha, the Sangha of Śrāvakas; yet they know only their names and do not understand the meaning of those virtues. Unable to receive the true merit that corresponds to the names, for the sake of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, they slander the Dharma.

Within this, a bodhisattva should apply diligent effort; regarding such sūtras as these, they should give rise to a sense of profound wonder and aspiration, and uphold, receive, read, and recite them. Why is this?
Such a person shall, in future lives, become a protector of the city of the Dharma. "Kāśyapa!
I recall that ninety-one kalpas ago, during a period when the Dharma was empty and non-existent, sūtras such as these were no longer circulated."

Furthermore, he recalled that in the past, beyond a thousand kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Resting from the Heat of Affliction; he remained in the world for eighty-four thousand kalpas, bringing bodhisattvas to maturity and benefiting the world.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past there was another Tathāgata named Anantabala, who remained in the world for twenty billion kalpas.
During those twenty billion kalpas he practiced the bodhisattva path, and only thereafter did he realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa! Behold the Buddha: how many difficult practices has he cultivated to gather in all sentient beings?
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
In this world at the end of the kalpa-turbidity, we should not disparage ourselves. Why is this?
Within the kalpa-turbidity, it is extremely rare for even a single person to be able to have faith and understanding in this Dharma from me.
That all sentient beings do not pursue us with swords or staves is also rare. Why is this?
This Dharma is the Dharma of the true man (satpuruṣa), namely, the perception of non-action regarding all actions; it is difficult to comprehend.

If there is the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a person, or the view of existence; if one gives rise to views regarding the precepts based on the aggregates; or if there are views of extensive learning, views of a Buddha, views of the Dharma, or views of Nirvana—if anyone gives rise to such views of Nirvana, the Tathāgata knows and perceives them all as wrong views.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has no conceptual discrimination regarding nirvāṇa, nor does he have any attainment therein.
If one were to give rise to conceptual discrimination or seek attainment regarding nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata declares that such is entirely false view.

One who holds wrong views is called ignorant; one who is ignorant is called harmful; one who is harmful is called a fool. One who is a fool lacks any aspiration for great enlightenment, and even becomes estranged from the superior path leading to rebirth in the heavens.

Kāśyapa! In future ages there will be bhikṣus who are twenty-three, twenty-four, forty, or even a hundred years old. Overcome by old age, they will adorn themselves with robes; though they have shaved their hair and beards, they have ruined their dignified deportment. Worn out by old age and illness, devoid of majestic radiance, they will incline toward false teachings.

At the time of death, being obscured by the mental disposition of one's transgressions, and having reflected upon the laziness and lack of cultivation committed, one manifests the realization of the three places.
What are these three?
Either they falsely manifest dignified deportment, or they deceitfully pretend to practice pure conduct, or they raise their hands and proclaim, "There is no one equal to me."

By manifesting realization through these three points, such people all fall into the trap of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); at the time of their death, remorse arises in their hearts, and once they have passed away, they are reborn in the hells.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, I now declare this clearly to you all:

I am your true and virtuous spiritual friend. Out of my desire to benefit and out of compassion for you, I do not wish for you to suffer great torment in the future, such as was experienced by Mūlīkā (translated into Chinese as Wěi-xù), Paṇḍikā (translated into Chinese as Lù-shēng), and Pālibhāralīkā (translated into Chinese as Nǚ-fànzhì), who underwent various bitter afflictions.
Kāśyapa! I never permit those who are attached to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, or the view of a person to go forth within my Dharma.
If I do not grant permission and they nonetheless force themselves into the homeless life, they are all thieves.
Even if they consume the heavy offerings of the faithful, they will not achieve the true precepts of a bhikṣu. Kāśyapa!

It would be better to fast for as many as six days than, having gone forth in my Dharma, to consume the heavy offerings of the faithful while giving rise to views of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, a person, or even a view of nirvana.

Therefore, a bodhisattva should arouse diligent effort and should not cling to views of a self, a sentient being, a life span, a person, existence, or nirvana; rather, for the sake of severing all such views, they should preach the Dharma.
Kāśyapa! Such sūtras as these I now entrust to the bodhisattvas and others. Why is this?
Because their intentions are identical to mine;
if their intentions are identical to mine, they are my companions, and as my companions, they are capable of receiving my entrustment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Oppressed by manifold sufferings, There is none at all who can provide protection,
Except for the Teacher of the World, The one who is free from conceptual proliferation."
Sentient beings afflicted by various sufferings, practicing inferior and deviant paths, gradually increase their craving for desires; because of this, they fall into evil realms.
Without a guide and without protection, they dwell in a place that is perilous, desolate, and remote.
Amidst the pursuit of wrong paths, there is ultimately no place of peace and security.
It is like a person who, carrying wealth and seeking profit, travels a long road;
therein a band of thieves arises and plunders all his possessions.
Having lost their wealth, they return home empty-handed; for the sake of profit, their feverish distress increases.
When borrowing the property of others, the burden of debt brings double the suffering.
These people are just like this: though they have left the household life for the sake of the Dharma, [they act otherwise].
The Dharma-wealth they originally possessed has all been extinguished by their white karma.

They have merely shaved their hair and beards in vain; these fools fall into various views, clinging to the notions of "self" and "sentient beings," and harboring the conception of a "person" (pudgala).
Those bhikṣus who preach the Dharma of emptiness do not cling to the notion of a person (pudgala);
yet those who give rise to a mind of slander toward them will swiftly fall into hell.
Due to the causes and conditions of hatred, they will mutually revile one another.
Fearing that others might know of one's own transgressions, One falsely proclaims the faults of others.
With evil deeds of body and speech, And a mind full of flattery and deceit,
Following the stream of inverted views— Such a person is born in the miserable realms.
Having committed various evil karmas, they swiftly go to the three miserable realms,
where they are scorched by manifold sufferings, and no one is able to rescue or protect them.
In the future there will be bhikṣus who are impetuous and full of anger.
They will harass those who have gone forth and are advancing toward enlightenment.
These terrifying multitudes will slander such sutras as these;
they will no longer be able to believe or accept the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas.
Mutually giving rise to hearts of anger, they alternately inflict suffering upon one another;
by proclaiming each other's faults, their evil reputations spread throughout the ten directions.
To falsely attribute wicked rumors to others brings shame upon oneself.
The gentle are weak, while the power of evil friends increases;
know that thus the True Dharma declines and those of evil character gain great influence.
Those whom I love as my own children are the virtuous bhikṣus.
One should turn toward another direction, Go to seek a place of peace and security,
Attain liberation from evil, And give rise to a heart of compassion for this [world].
Within this sutra, one should Reflect upon it with careful self-examination.
The Buddha has given such instruction: one should joyfully dwell in other regions.
When the True Dharma is being destroyed, those who are gentle and mild are difficult to find;
therefore, let us go together to that place praised by the Tathāgata.
Some said, "This place may be left but not inhabited;
one should go to the Great Seer to attain the ground of great enlightenment.
Others addressed the Benevolent One, saying, "What you have truly spoken is well said."
Circumambulating the stupa to seek the Truth— this is called the teaching of the World-Honored One.
It would be better to reach that delightful ground of Bodhi than to dwell forever here, submerged in the oppression of anger.
The bhikṣu should go there; for my sake, he should travel to see the regions where the Buddha once roamed and where he formerly dwelt—
places for walking meditation and sitting in tranquility, whether they be rocky outcrops or secluded spots.
Having gathered together, they lamented and wept many times for him, saying:
"This was the place where that Great Sage practiced walking meditation and took his sustenance;
here he once dwelt in the past and turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma."
All conditioned things are impermanent; we now see neither humans nor non-humans, nor do gods and nāgas gather here.
Having skillfully transformed them to bring them joy, why is it that we now see only emptiness?
Then, having gone to the site of the path, the most supreme ground of enlightenment,
and having gathered together there, one should contemplate according to the truth:
"In this very place, the World-Honored One attained the fruit of unsurpassed Buddhahood."
The demonic hosts are struck with terror, like a pack of jackals;
this is the site of enlightenment where the Great Awakened One dwells,
the seat of all Buddhas of the past and the future.
The Great Hero, the Honored One, dwelt in peace, revered by billions of devas.
For seven days he sat cross-legged, gazing intently at the Bodhi tree;
having completed his contemplation and offerings, he next proceeded to the Deer Park.
When it is said that he turns this wheel of Dharma, its sound shall reach the Brahma world.
Those bhikṣus will surely weep with great sorrow,
for the Guide has come here to discipline the five companions.
When the five men first saw the Buddha, each gave rise to a mind of anxiety and distress;
they established a rule among themselves, vowing, "We shall not rise for him.
At that time, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, out of pity for all classes of living beings, [approached them].
He preached for the five bhikṣus, and the fruit of the nectar was then realized.
Bowing toward the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, his heart was filled with such grief that he wept again and again;
next, he went to the site of the parinirvāṇa, moved by the Buddha’s final body.
Beneath these twin śāla trees, for the benefit of all classes of living beings, you have shattered your body into its constituent parts and entered parinirvāṇa here.
Alas, Great Holy One! Śākyamuni, the Great Nirvāṇa!
Now I hear only his name; alas, I do not see him.
Here once more, the Great Teacher has delivered the virtuous Subhadda as his very last convert;
he was able to know this beforehand through his wisdom that this would be his final conversion.
Whether their lifespan ends while practicing, or they pass away while setting out on the path,
or they die after having completed their practice— they all will be reborn in the happy realms.
From that time onward, however, they shall sink into the deep and vast Dharma.
Whether one upholds the precepts or violates them, all should receive offerings;
yet by accepting the heavy, trusted gifts of others, one quickly falls into the evil realms.
Behold, O bhikṣus, such are the distinctions among you.
Though the wise may practice later, they swiftly receive the bodies of gods and humans.
These lamps that illuminate the world, who have compassion for the world—
these Bodhisattvas of great wisdom, with hearts of loving-kindness, benefit all sentient beings.
Constantly performing the deeds of diligent cultivation with a heart of leaping joy,
one shall become a Great Awakened Honored One; furthermore, encountering and serving Maitreya,
one will make offerings to that Tathāgata and receive the prediction of enlightenment amidst the assembly.
According to what their minds recollect, they receive that great majestic power.
I speak these words of truth to comfort such as these;
though they do not see the Buddha, it is the same as seeing him.
In the past, when I sought awakening, I paid homage to all the Buddhas;
if women likewise aspire to unsurpassed awakening,
I and immeasurable Buddhas shall all comfort them.
Quickly attaining a male body, one shall behold Maitreya;
by making offerings to that Tathāgata, all that is sought shall be fulfilled as desired.
One should follow the example of the wise and go forth into homelessness with pure faith.
With a mind of firm resolve and aspiration, Having heard much and learned,
and upholding the precepts, One shall receive a prophecy from Maitreya Buddha.
Therefore, hear the excellence of this benefit, And give rise to faith to cultivate the virtues of the noble.
Abiding in a firm mind, one gathers all classes of sentient beings.
Who, in such a state, would seek and fail to find it?
For those with wisdom and diligence, enlightenment is not difficult to realize.
Cultivate the mindfulness of loving-kindness and compassion, abandon a deceitful and crooked mind, and always delight in dwelling in solitude; this is the path to bodhi.
If a person speaks of this Dharma in vain without being able to practice it, [they will not attain the goal].
The multitude all pay him reverence; he is a formidable thief.
If, for the sake of food and drink, or for matters of profit and gain, one upholds this gateway of the True Dharma and transmits it to one another, [one shall attain liberation].
Such a person who lives this life in evil is said to have passed through the world in vain;
having cast off this human body here, they will undergo manifold sufferings in the woeful realms.
Or, within the Buddha’s Dharma, they may merely bear the provisional name of a bhikṣu.
Slandering the sūtras, while claiming to well-expound the precepts for liberation,
saying, "I have widely propagated all the teachings of the Prātimokṣa"—
though bearing the appearance of a bhikṣu, one will ultimately lose the body of a human or a deva.
If one slanders gods and humans, or disparages the All-Knowing One,
such a person who slanders the Dharma incurs an even greater offense than those [previously mentioned].
By well-guarding body, speech, and mind, one prevents all evils from arising.
"One who can eliminate these three modes of conduct will certainly attain nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, those bhikṣus who previously planted deep roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddha will all enter parinirvāṇa; likewise, those classes of sentient beings endowed with superior aspirations will, at the end of their lives, come to an end as well.

In the future, when the True Dharma is extinguished after fifty years, there will be monks whose nature is full of attachment; their minds will be overwhelmed by fierce and intense greed, they will delight in divisive speech and seek to harm others, and their words will be coarse, harsh, and scowling as they abide in three things.
What are these three?
They are the practice of medicine, commerce, and intimacy with women.
Abiding in these three things, one falls away from four matters.
What are these four? They are:
