the decline of the aggregate of ethical discipline, of the happy destinies, of the realization of the fruits, and of seeing the Buddha as he truly is.
Due to the decline of these four, four further states arise, whereby one fails to develop weary detachment and instead experiences their intense increase.
What are the four? They are:

the increase and intensification of envy; the increase and intensification of malice and hatred; the increase and intensification of attachment to one's clan; and the greedy attachment to food and drink and the accumulation of various flavors.

Because their attachment to clothing obscures the mind, they place it in chests and trunks, making this their sole constant practice; thus, within the dharma of a śramaṇa, they obtain nothing at all, nor do they give rise to the realization of the path of a śramaṇa.
Upon hearing such sutras as these, one shall fall into four states.
What are these four? They are:

falling into the slander of the Dharma by preaching what the Buddha did not authorize; preaching the essentials of the Dharma exclusively for women; and slandering the Tathāgata’s Pratimokṣa precepts.
Upon hearing such sutras as these, they further increase their destruction of the Dharma and fall into the growth of evil karma. Kāśyapa!
It is like a wicked dog having bitter gall poured into its nose.
"What do you think?
Would that dog not become even more fierce and malicious?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so. The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“Those evil persons are like wicked dogs or piśācas; when they see a bhikṣu who dwells in pure intention and upholds this Dharma, who speaks this Dharma, who abides in truth and possesses few desires, and who praises having few desires—they do not give rise to joy toward such a person but instead develop aversion and opposition. With hearts full of timidity and inferiority, they further give rise to feverish distress.
Because their minds are shrouded by anger, they think to themselves: ‘We dwell at an improper time and in an improper place; at an improper time, others disparage us.’”

Therefore, upon hearing such sutras as these being preached, they give rise to slander and personally insult them, speaking with anger and harsh words, saying: "This is not the Buddha's teaching; these people indulge in the causes and conditions of great desire; they are not those of few desires."

Kāśyapa! I have praised in various ways the state of having few desires and being content; it is called being easy to support and easy to satisfy, and is termed the one who purifies, the one who practices the dhūtas, and the one who is most supremely dignified.
I also praise those who dwell in forest hermitages (araṇya), those who exert diligence, and those whose livelihood is completely pure.
You should not practice the methods of accumulating and storing goods such as boxes and baskets.
Why is this? It is because you should cultivate such dharmas as these.
You should not be like a bronze gong that possesses sound in vain; rather, you should follow the Tathāgata in practicing this dharma.
Furthermore, one should not give rise to intense anger, nor should one grasp at things; one should abide in the state of neither thing nor object.
Do not give rise to a mind of attachment toward any location; one should abide nowhere.

One should not praise oneself, nor should one keep cattle, donkeys, or similar animals; one should not remain established in indolence, but should instead arouse sublime diligence, abandoning what is unwholesome and embracing wholesome dharmas.

Kāśyapa! I have praised dwelling in various ways as being peaceful and secluded in the forest hermitage rather than in the midst of bustle; now, within this context, I shall speak in various ways of the practice of ultimate purification.

If there are those who do not abide in ultimate purification, who possess great desire, and who have committed evil deeds, they will immediately slander all those who do abide in ultimate purification.
Kāśyapa! It is like a fool who, having consumed ghee during the fourth month and suffering from thirst, goes at once to a pond to seek and drink water.
Another person says to him:
"You have already consumed the ghee; do not drink water again, lest it cause your death.
At that time, because his mind was obscured by anger, the foolish man reviled and cursed him, refusing to follow the other's words, and died from drinking water.

Kāśyapa! It is even so, it is even so. In the future, there will be bhikṣus who are attached to views and dwell in unwholesome conduct; among them, those who uphold the Dharma will give this instruction: "This is what should be done;..."
"This should not be done. Because their minds were obscured by anger, those wicked bhikṣus reviled, abused, and slandered this sūtra. Kāśyapa!
Even now there are many who give rise to disputes and contention regarding the Tathāgata, let alone in the future.
You should observe this bhikṣu Bhadrapāla: the Tathāgata established the precepts and commanded all bhikṣus to eat in a single sitting.
Because their minds were obscured by anger, they did not come to me during the three months of the summer retreat. Kāśyapa!

Even now, before my very eyes, there are those who thus slight fellow practitioners of the holy life; how much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa? Attached to food, drink, robes, bowls, and medicinal requisites for the sick, and shrouded by sleep while their anger is fierce and intense—when such bhikṣus hear this Dharma, they will not even show respect to the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher; how then could they ever respect those bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma?
Kāśyapa! This shall be called unwholesome and even utterly evil; thus, this Dharma-treasure will surely disappear.

Among those who seek great benefit, if there are sons or daughters of good family who have faith in my teaching, they will find it difficult to encounter virtuous people during the subsequent age of dregs and extreme concealment. Having heard such profound teachings as these at that time, one should explain them to those who act according to reason and not to those who do not, and explain them to those who have faith and not to those who lack it.
I now speak for those who act in accordance with reason, not for those who do not; I speak for those who have faith, not for those who lack it.

Kāśyapa, it is like a wicked horse that cannot endure being armored; if such a horse were to be armored like a fine steed, it would instead become terrified. How much less could it endure hearing the sound of conchs, horns, and drums? There is no possibility that it could bear such things.
In this way and that way, a precept-breaking bhikṣu is never capable of enduring the Dharma of a virtuous man; he is like a vicious horse that instead gives rise to alarm and fear.

Kāśyapa! When a precept-breaking bhikṣu hears even a single word spoken regarding the selflessness of all phenomena, he gives rise to fear and contention therein because he clings to the notion of a self; how much more so when he hears it said that one should don the armor of goodness?
Once the armor has been donned, one is able to subdue ten billion demonic armies and ensure that conflict never arises again.

When virtuous bhikṣus don the armor of diligence, they do not break the fundamental dhūta virtues; they purify the root, being free from the roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, free from the root of envy, possessing the root of solitude, and the root of wakefulness. At all times and in every manner, they should not give rise to thoughts of anger or greed, nor should they seek after various objects. Donning the armor in this way is called "rootless."

Once one has donned such various armor, one should resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta; one should not cling to anything anywhere, much less give rise to the notion of a self. Therefore, one should not give rise to the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, the notion of a person, the notion of a woman or a man, the notion of earth, water, fire, or wind, the notion of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, the notion of observing precepts, the notion of breaking precepts, or the notion of emptiness.
To state the essential point: one should not give rise to any conceptualizations whatsoever, because all conceptualizations are unattainable.

"Kāśyapa, if greed were truly existent, it would have to be known; one would approach it to extinguish the mind of craving. Yet, there is no abiding in a single place from which 'non-abiding' could be attained, except for false speech. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the Speaker of Truth."
The Tathāgata has taught that all forms of craving are non-self; such dharmas as these are the dharmas of a śramaṇa, and all the dharmas of a śramaṇa are unattainable.

If there should be another person who clings to this notion, that person would be clinging to notions such as "self" to the extent of Mount Sumeru; they would fall away from the holy teaching, and not even a small portion of the qualities of a śramaṇa could arise within them, nor could they abide in the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Such vast and supreme Dharma is [lost] to those foolish persons who are impaired by ignorance; one should not speak of it even slightly.
Why is this? If one clings to even a small portion of the Dharma, one will be seized and dwell for an eon within the great hells, which are places of extreme terror.

Kāśyapa! Observe these bhikṣus: Kokālika (translated as "Evil Time"), Devadatta (translated as "Bestowed by Heaven"), Khaṇḍadravya (translated as "Broken Wealth"), Kāloṣṭha (translated as "Vessel Ghost-Lord"), Mūdrarata (translated as "Ocean Bestower"), Aśvajit (translated as "Horse Ascendant"), Punarvasu (translated as "Willow Star"), and Sugati (translated as "Good Star"). These were my personal attendants who stood before me; they heard me preach the Dharma, saw me walking in meditation, saw me sitting upright, and saw me traveling through the air with supernormal powers. They witnessed me subduing thousands of non-Buddhists amidst the great assembly, crushing their false teachings.
Such persons as these do not even give rise to faith or joy toward me; at every step they constantly seek to disparage me, and by doing so, their malice increases with every step.
Furthermore, if one says that faith in the name of the Buddha is the reality, one should take a superior vessel as large as Mount Sumeru, fill it with powdered sandalwood, and scatter it upon him.
One should fashion a parasol as vast as the trichiliocosm, holding it in mid-air to cover him from above. Why?
Because of faith in the Buddha.
How much more so for those who, having already developed faith, renounce desire to leave the household life and practice the various meditative concentrations (dhyāna) without any dependence?

Kāśyapa, such sentient beings who find conviction therein are extremely rare; being able to skillfully guard and uphold the precepts established by the Buddha, they will be able to understand that nectar-like Dharma.

It is like when, in a great assembly, one uses animal hides and other foul, putrid materials to fashion a human figure, or constructs various composite facial features, painting and decorating them until they appear extremely magnificent.
Some carry it on their faces, or wrap it in clothing and travel about.
Would one consider it beautiful by its outward appearance?
Only upon realizing its filthiness does revulsion arise.

In this way, when those evil bhikṣus observe with careful scrutiny the majestic power, dignified demeanor, and solemn composure of the Tathāgata, they finally realize that their extreme wickedness arises from the self-other dichotomy and the resulting birth of craving and attachment.
If a person understands that the notion of a self is not real, they will not give rise to anger upon hearing such sūtras.
Why is this? Because when others revile or oppose them, hearing these sūtras causes their sense of weary detachment to increase all the more.
If there are sentient beings whose minds harbor attachments, you should know that they are people of wrong views.
If they give rise to wrong views, they will produce anger toward such sutras and their authentic instructions.
Why is this? Because those who harbor the notion of a self possess anger.
"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, upon hearing such sūtras as these, respond with anger, disparagement, or slander, they are not śramaṇas."
Although one may still be said to bear the name of a śramaṇa, such a person is not my disciple, nor am I their teacher. Why is this?
One who is my disciple does not speak falsely; I am not a teacher of falsehood.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, able to explain that all phenomena are empty according to reality. Kāśyapa!

The Tathāgata is able to shatter the grasping at a self and contend with it; whoever contends with the Tathāgata is called an evil Māra, and the Tathāgata does not permit such followers of Māra to leave the household life or receive full ordination.
Suppose someone were to say:
"The small blue jay bird gives birth to great dragons and elephants.
What do you think of this?
"Is such a statement to be believed? Kāśyapa replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
“What do you think?”
"Are they of equal status?
Kāśyapa replied, "They are not of equal status."
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is as when it is said:
'The King of Birds, the Garuḍa, is born from among the winged creatures.'"
"What do you think? Is this credible?
Is it consistent with reason?"
Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One."
This, too, is a category of the dissimilar.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is as when it is said: "
"A tiny firefly insect carries Mount Sumeru and flies through the air.
What do you think? Is this believable?
"Are they of the same kind? Kāśyapa replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
It is likewise not of the same category.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Such evil persons, if they dwell in the notion of a self up to the notion of nirvāṇa, yet claim me as their teacher, they become, in turn, of a different kind. Kāśyapa!

It is like a universal monarch who dwells securely within his realm, nurturing all living beings with boundless happiness; various foods and drinks are spontaneously provided, while attendants stand by to carry out the king’s righteous governance.

At that time, there was a man whom the multitude had never known before; for the sake of wealth and profit, he followed and imitated the conduct of ministers. Without receiving the king's command, he falsely proclaimed the royal decree among the assembly of great ministers and the king, speaking thus:
"You all should remain and dwell here."
Or they may say: "You all have done such a thing. Kāśyapa!

The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, is likewise: he rules over the great trichiliocosm, gathering and transforming all sentient beings of the three vehicles; his ten powers and merits are perfectly accomplished, he performs the deeds of a Buddha for boundless peace and happiness, and food and drink for his offerings are naturally abundant.

Among them, there is a certain class of people who have never understood [the truth]; for the sake of their livelihood, they speak of "self," "sentient beings," and even "nirvana. They do not accept the Tathāgata’s noble teaching of selflessness, but instead say:
"That which the Tathāgata has spoken—this should be done, and this should not be done."

Among them, there were those who believed in the Buddha and followed his teachings without disparaging them; upon hearing what he said, they regarded him as a supreme, wondrous, and pure field of merit. They set aside their own resources and even the portions belonging to their wives and children, bestowing them with profound and sincere faith according to the Dharma, continuing without interruption until they had realized his faults.

Such evil persons, like those unknown to the general public, once their meals are finished, daily discuss at crowded places matters concerning the king, bandits, food, sexual pleasure, women, medical prescriptions, drinking wine, solar and lunar eclipses, the comings and goings of rulers, and clan affairs; or they say, "This is an auspicious day; one should travel elsewhere and shall obtain food."

Engaging in various such discourses and deliberations day and night, they return to the saṃghārāma; after staying for two nights or even up to six nights, wherever they dwell, they constantly speak of such matters. Lacking right mindfulness and wisdom, their deportment is ruined; overcome by dullness and sleep, with saliva flowing from their mouths, they see in their dreams whatever they have imagined, such as seeing themselves traveling to other places, walking quickly or slowly, and performing all manner of such activities.
Having awakened, they spoke to one another, saying: "In our dreams, we saw your body walking and sitting in such a manner, and that from such a place there would be both gain and loss.
Others further said:
"This dream is auspicious; you should depart at once for the villages, towns, and royal cities."

When they enter and exit, come and go, or move about among the households of others, their faces and eyes flicker; because they are oppressed by suffering and affliction, their minds are neither peaceful nor harmonious. Lacking meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are arrogant and self-exalting; their faculties are defiled and mixed, no different from those of the laity. Their speech is untimely and their minds are largely distracted; they delight in wandering through the villages and the homes of various clans. Unable to uphold the *prātimokṣa* vows, they preach the essentials of the Dharma to women alone. While preaching, their minds dwell in lustful attachment, and therein they increase their gain and offerings. Their hearts of stained attachment are like gnawing teeth; through delusion and craving, they increase their dwelling in and clinging to it. Because they do not give rise to remorse, they weep as they depart at the time of parting.
Furthermore, he instructs others in two ways. What are these two?
When one obtains pure and excellent offerings, he praises them; when one obtains that which is impure or inferior, he censures it.
When they met, they looked at what each had received and asked one another:
"What is it that the donor is giving now?
To whom is he giving it?"
"How much food, drink, and wealth do they possess?
Kāśyapa! You should know that such a person is called one who does not practice.
Furthermore, there are other faults for those who do not practice even until the end of their lives: they give rise to malicious intentions, which is to say, they slander the True Dharma. Kāśyapa!
One should give rise to a heart of compassion for such bhikṣus.
Why is this? Because they are destined to experience the fruit of suffering and affliction.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Fools, for the sake of their livelihood, Follow and imitate the king’s ministers;
Therefore they go to other places And falsely proclaim royal decrees.”
When transmitting secret words to them, do not provoke the King’s anger or punishment.
Even a fool would act in this way for the sake of his own livelihood;
how much more so the Most Victorious Buddha, who [strived] throughout many hundreds of eons?
Having sacrificed my limbs and members, and performed many difficult deeds,
I am not of a royal house of Dharma; even when servants are punished,
there is no one capable of questioning whether they acted as they should or not.
Giving a dwelling to a bhikṣu, Exquisite, choice, and delicious delicacies,
And bestowing superior, fine robes— All these are given with reverence.
Having sought wealth and goods through diligent toil, One offers them as gifts to those who uphold the precepts.
Not for one's own sustenance, nor to provide for one's children;
those who do not abide in accordance with the Dharma, upon eating it, simply depart.
When meeting one another, they say, "I ate this to my heart's content."
In whatever gathering places they congregate, they speak of matters concerning kings and bandits,
matters of frontier guards and military outposts, various discussions on food and drink,
predictions of solar and lunar eclipses, and accounts of kings coming and going.
Some say they shall be victorious, while others say they shall perish;
these are not things one should speak of, yet they constantly engage in such idle discourse.
Upon the most exquisite bedding, they indulge in sleep day and night.
By day one goes to the homes of the virtuous, seeking those places of great wealth.
One says, "This gift is not small, nor is it the most supreme.
Having reflected on these matters, one settles down and sits idly in empty talk.
The foolish and indolent do not apply themselves to cultivation, like a donkey constantly burdened with heavy loads.
Within their sleep and dreams, they perceive various conceptualized appearances;
having awakened, they proclaim them to others, and together they discuss these images at length.
"Do not grieve, do not laugh; you shall obtain peace and happiness.
This matter shall be swiftly accomplished; do not give rise to further distress.
Go frequently to villages and towns, yet remain without dignified deportment."
Like a monkey walking about, turning its face and eyes in every direction;
having entered into a village, it preaches the Dharma to women,
abandoning the Buddha’s sūtras and the well-expounded Prātimokṣa.
Having departed from the donor's house, he observes the quantity of the goods;
seeing that they are few, he reviles the host and likewise disparages his kinsmen.
When they meet again, he speaks words of inquiry to one another.
"What did you obtain? What food did you eat?
What matters did you discuss in your conversations?"—briefly recounting such things for the span of a hundred years.
Thus they engage in such mental investigations, making them their means of livelihood.
They contend over the taste of grape wine, as well as fragrant flowers and the like;
they use these as medicine to treat their bodies, seeking thereby to have few ailments and afflictions.
Even if there were a hundred Buddhas, none could do anything for one who abandons their practice and becomes no different from a householder,
cherishing the body and remaining bound by the notions of "I" and "mine."
By practicing in such a manner, one falls into the evil realms;
if a person slanders the True Dharma, they will be consumed by heavy suffering.
Such a fool, lacking wisdom and discernment, is no different from a householder.
If those lions of the Śākyas, practicing the conduct of true śrāvakas,
do not, for the sake of their livelihood, violate even the slightest precept;
if the wise do not crave food, but always conceive of it as a heavy burden—
Cultivating the mind through the contemplation of impurity, one repays the debt to the donor.
Because of abandoning the outflows of desire and thoroughly understanding all perceptions,
I have declared that such as these have gone forth within this Teaching.
The wise person does not disparage the Dharma; regarding the emptiness that has been taught, they repeatedly apply diligent inquiry, finding no solid core to be grasped.
The courageous person of great wisdom thoroughly understands the principle of emptiness.
Able to terrify the armies of Māra, they are worthy of receiving offerings.
If one can remain free from the defilement of craving and does not disparage emptiness,
such a courageous son of the Buddha is the one to be honored among two-legged beings.
The True Dharma will not endure for long; In this world, delusion shall abound.
With few monks who are gentle and mild, And those seeking heedfulness being rare, The wise should give rise to sorrow, For it will soon perish of its own accord.
Later, during the day and night, they will speak of how there once was a self;
that this world has no protector except for the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings;
and that all those who practice and train in the precepts shall utterly perish.
Failing to understand such intentional terminology,
they will show no reverence for the Buddha nor for the unsurpassed True Dharma.
As the True Dharma is about to perish, you should swiftly exert diligent effort.
"Even for as little as a short moment, hearing [this] shall not be for long.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle 2.3, *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle 3.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The First Assembly on the Threefold Discipline, Part Three.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
That such people as these do not feel revulsion upon hearing sūtras such as this.
The Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who accomplish four dharmas, they will not feel revulsion or detachment upon hearing this sutra preached. What are these four?

Because of excessive negligence, they cannot have deep faith; because of the ripening of karma, they likewise do not have deep faith; because of the great hells, they cannot have reflective faith; and because they think 'I shall die.'"
If a person accomplishes these four dharmas, they will not give rise to weary detachment.
Kāśyapa! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who accomplish four dharmas and do not give rise to weary detachment.
What are these four?

In the prime of youth, relying on one's own physical strength, one becomes addicted to sensual pleasures and greedily indulges in various liquors, being unable to understand, discern, or contemplate with clear wisdom.
If a person accomplishes these four dharmas, they will not give rise to weary detachment.
Kāśyapa! If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes four dharmas, he slanders the Buddha’s bodhi.

What are the four? Because they have already brought to fruition the evil karma they originally committed, they destroy the True Dharma; such bhikṣus do not themselves confess the various evil karmas that are the unwholesome maturation [of their deeds].

Because he committed impure acts with a bhikṣuṇī, his preceptor or ācārya—who was revered by many—slandered the Buddha’s bodhi; thus, the disciple who followed and learned from that teacher also gave rise to slander.
These persons of little learning, out of envy, slander and revile the Buddhas.
A bhikṣu who accomplishes these four dharmas slanders the Bodhi of the Buddha. “Kāśyapa!
If there were a single dharma by which one could become a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, what would that one dharma be? It is this:
the mind abiding nowhere among all dharmas.
In this way, through a single dharma, one becomes a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa.
It is like a person who has fallen from the summit of a high mountain; perceiving no earth, trees, or forests, he gives rise only to the thought of emptiness, and his inhalation and exhalation cease.

Kāśyapa! Those who are attached to various phenomena are also like this. If they grasp at the perception of the eye and the characteristics of the eye; if they grasp at the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, up to the characteristics of the mind; if they grasp at the perceptions of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; or if they grasp at the perception of pure morality, extensive learning, shame and remorse, walking meditation, coming and going, and the attainment of Bodhi—all such dharmas do not constitute being a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa.
If one gives rise to conceptualization, one will be harmed.
By whom is one harmed?
It is by greed, hatred, and delusion.
If one grasps at the characteristics of the eye, because of attachment to the characteristics of pleasant and unpleasant forms, one is harmed by the eye.

Likewise, by grasping at the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and so forth, up to attachment to the characteristics of pleasant and unpleasant phenomena, one is harmed by the mind.
If one is harmed, then one is extremely harmed within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.
For what reason is one harmed?
Due to attachment through perception (*saṃjñā*), what is meant by "perceptual attachment"?

It refers to the attachment to the perception of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātma-ātmīya-saṃjñā*); the perception of female and male; the perception of earth, water, fire, and wind; the perception of bones, the perception of decay, the perception of bluish discoloration, the perception of being smeared with blood, the perception of change of color, the perception of disintegration, and the perception of supreme liberation (*adhimukti-vimokṣa-saṃjñā*).
Therein, some have the perception of having attained partial liberation, while others have the perception of not having attained partial liberation.

There are immeasurable kinds of perceptions regarding the direct realization of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), such as: "My perception of recollection is different from the past and different from the present; I was the past, and I am the present."
Regarding all phenomena, they give rise to conceptualizations and attachments, even to the concept of nirvāṇa and the thought, "I have attained nirvāṇa.

Kāśyapa, to speak briefly, those who are attached give rise to conceptualizations everywhere, even giving rise to all manner of conceptualizations regarding emptiness itself; none of these constitute the dharma of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, nor do they constitute the conduct of a śramaṇa or the conduct of a brāhmaṇa.
Kāśyapa! When the Tathāgata speaks of the dharmas of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, they are like space and the great earth. Why is this?
The nature of space never thinks or says, "I am space.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas never claim for themselves, "I am a śramaṇa" or "I am a brāhmaṇa"; therefore, all dharmas likewise do not claim for themselves, "I am performing the dharma of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa."
The Dharma of a śramaṇa is neither to create nor to eliminate; this constitutes being a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa. Kāśyapa!
It is, for example, as if someone in the darkness of night were to wave their arms and move their face and features, saying these words:
"I am deceiving the world;
I am deceiving the world. What do you think?
“Whom does he intend to deceive?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
This person is merely deceiving himself. Why?
Because within that [state], there is no person who can be deceived.
The Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"It is so, it is so. If there is a bhikṣu who goes to an araṇya, or to the foot of a tree, an empty dwelling, or an open space, he should form this thought:
"The eye is impermanent; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all impermanent.
He further reflects: "Forms are impermanent;
sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are also all impermanent."
Thinking thus, "I am proceeding toward nirvāṇa," such practices as these involve self-exhaustion and are not the conduct of a śramaṇa.
Why is this? Because there are various false attachments.
Having understood the characteristics of the eye, one diligently practices for the sake of its cessation.
Having thus understood the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one diligently practices until the mind is extinguished.
If one understands and accepts [the truth] regarding these three bases, then conceptual discrimination arises with respect to those three bases.
If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding various views, how can one attain one-pointedness of mind?
Kāśyapa, profound bodhi is difficult to enter, difficult to approach, and difficult to fulfill through the necessary provisions.
Regarding one-pointedness of mind: by how many names is "one-pointedness of mind" designated?
When one searches exhaustively, not even a single dharma can be found.
That is to say, reality cannot be found in the eye; reality cannot be found in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and reality cannot be found in any dharma whatsoever.
Why is this? Because such is its fundamental nature: the nature of the mind does not arise, and all phenomena have no reality that can be apprehended; therefore, that mind cannot be apprehended.
Because the past, future, and present are non-apprehendable and because there is nothing to be done, this is called "non-action" (*akṛta*).
What is meant by "non-action"?
Whether new or old, that which cannot be produced is called "non-action."

In this regard, the past mind is not liberated, the present mind is not liberated, and the future mind is not liberated; that which, following whatever mind exists, is non-apprehensible—this is one-pointedness of mind.
This is precisely what is called the reckoning of entering the mind. "Kāśyapa!

In the future, there will be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who, being attached to the eye and so forth, will speak of their destruction and give rise to the notion of substantial entities within the aggregates."

The Tathāgata has taught that the aggregates are like a dream; yet they claim that the dream is substantially existent because it is said to exist within the world. If there were no dream, we would not have the experience of dreaming thoughts.
Because there is representation, we conceive of dreams within our sleep and dreaming.
In this very way, because the aggregates have a cause, they are said to be like a dream; if the aggregates did not exist, one should not say that the aggregates are like a dream.
Those foolish people will take dreams to be real; upon hearing such sutras as these, they will give rise to slander.
Among them there will be bhikṣuṇīs and others who, in the homes of donors, falsely claim, "I am an Arhat," or based on shallow wisdom, say that they have attained realization in this very life.
"If upāsakas, upāsikās, and others hear the sūtras, vinaya, and verses proclaiming that I have realized this through direct perception, Kāśyapa, at that time— "

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, for twenty or thirty years, has constantly delighted in dwelling in an araṇya and has diligently practiced for the sake of the Buddha-dharma; yet he comes before a newly converted upāsaka of only one day’s standing and, with mere empty words, proclaims to one another: "Because it is emptiness and emptiness, I have fully known; I have fully known."
There may be bhikṣus who, having heard this sutra and other such teachings, discuss them among themselves; someone hearing this may then give rise to fear and say:
"Those who are householders or renunciants should not be associated with; they should be shunned, for these are not teachers."
"Why is this? Because that which they know does not accord with one another.
Furthermore, there are those who proclaim the profound Dharma, yet they are abandoned and treated with contempt by both householders and renunciants.

Why is this? Even now, those who understand the sublime and wondrous holy life that I proclaim are few; how much more so in future ages, when even the very few who know it shall have utterly perished.
In that age, among a thousand bhikṣus who preach the Dharma, it will be difficult to find even one who can understand and enter the Dharma according to reality;
even among two thousand, it shall be likewise.
Among them, there may even be other bhikṣus who are unable to utter a single word for even a moment, let alone comprehend it.
"Kāśyapa! At that time, both householders and renunciants will together disparage this teaching."

If there is a bhikṣu who exerts diligent effort for the sake of eliminating unwholesome states and giving rise to wholesome dharmas, and who practices with diligence by reducing sleep during the first and last watches of the night, he may be reviled, disparaged, and abandoned by others, or even have his life taken.
Sūtras such as these shall then be destroyed, and the bhikṣus who dwell in the Dharma shall likewise all perish.
Among them, those wise ones who possess profound, supreme, and untainted understanding should, with deep-seated respect and reverence, gather together and dwell in araṇya hermitages.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The wholesome dharmas I have taught are in accord with the ultimate truth;
They declare that the aggregates lack any solid core, And should be contemplated as being like a dream."
At that time, the bhikṣus were agitated by quarrelsome minds;
they lacked propriety and failed to distinguish between the honorable and the lowly, possessing nothing but empty names and appearances.
Whatever the bhikṣus spoke, the laity spoke in the same way.
Such is the teaching of the Dharma; the words of the monastic and the laity are identical.
When a bhikṣu addresses a layperson, saying, "Your understanding of the Dharma is rare and extraordinary;
this is called the Bodhi of the Buddha," it signifies that the fruit of the first stage has already been attained.
That mind is said to see the Dharma; being close to laypeople, they frequently offer gifts to bhikṣus and provide them with the highest offerings.
As such a bhikṣu speaks, his words are without deviation and are entirely true.
Intimate with them, they claim, "I have seen the Dharma.
Born at that time, they have gone forth for the sake of gain;
not abiding in the True Dharma, they destroy the path to Bodhi.
I show you the path: stay close to me and do not associate with others.
Before long you shall attain it, just as I have attained it—this most peaceful state, which I speak of as I face you.
Within the assembly of the harmonious multitude, they destroy my teaching,
like bandits plundering a village; harboring a nature of ferocity and danger,
they ravage various kingdoms, cities, and great settlements.
So it is with the bhikṣu: lacking wisdom and largely deluded, with little insight he gives rise to various errors;
clinging to the notion of a life-principle, he wanders through the realms of rebirth.
Having departed from the teachings I have proclaimed, his mind relies upon various views.
Those who claim to be arhats are all possessed of overweening pride.
In this great assembly, before the multitude of bhikṣus, they proclaim their own wisdom and renown;
yet such a person is rare indeed to find among them.
At times there may be a bhikṣu, established in accordance with reality,
who is slandered with an evil reputation, being called "not a disciple of the Buddha.
At that time, the Great Bodhi of the Dharma King will be reviled.
The hosts of devas harbor grief and sorrow, weeping repeatedly as they face one another.
Before those devas of faithful mind, they cast their own bodies to the ground;
beholding this Lion of the Śākyas, the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma has been shattered.
Alas, we lament for the Buddha, the Tathāgata! How wonderful is the Dharma he has taught!
How extraordinary are the Saṅgha, the field of merit, and the beloved sons of the Buddha!
We shall no longer hear the words spoken by the King of Dharma.
The Muni has now entered parinirvāṇa; Those without awakening harbor deluded minds.
Immediately thereafter, the gods dwelling on earth Produced a great sound, proclaiming to all the devas:
"The torch of Dharma is now about to be extinguished."
Having heard of the Buddha, you must not fail to draw near to the Tathāgata;
lest on a future day, as devas or nāgas, you should harbor regret.
Throughout incalculable kalpas, for both yourselves and others, [strive to practice].
Having fully experienced all manner of sufferings, one shall then finally attain Buddhahood.
This is the gateway to the sublime Dharma taught by all the World-Honored Ones for the sake of all classes of sentient beings; now it shall all vanish into obscurity.
When a person of evasive speech appears in the world, they commit various wrongs that are truly fearsome;
as an emissary of Māra and a wicked Māra himself, he indulges in malicious speech at will.
Deceitful, fraudulent, and largely dull-witted, he deludes and misleads inferior and foolish men.
Whether out of anger or without anger, those who revile their teacher and the sublime teaching—
upon hearing the voices of the Earth-dwelling devas, the higher heavens all grew somber;
humans and the Four Great Kings likewise harbored grief and distress.
The hosts of yakṣas gathered at the city of Aṭavī;
they all raised terrifying cries, their faces streaming with tears of grief.
Their celestial dwellings were adorned with various jewels, and the city walls were exquisitely decorated.
All have utterly lost their radiance, like heaps of earth.
The cities and palaces are no longer as they were, such that one could feel love and joy for them;
now that I behold this city adorned with jewels, it cannot bring even a moment’s pleasure.
The devas all went together to that land, the birthplace of the Sugata;
they leaped about and wailed, their great sorrow and suffering increasing all the more.
I descended from the heavens to the earth and traveled to various kingdoms and cities.
The True Dharma has utterly sunk away; looking everywhere, it is nowhere to be seen.
Reaching down to the realm of Jambudvīpa, one sees the Dharma utterly collapsing and crumbling, afflicting all those who have gone forth, as they raise their voices in great lamentation and weeping.
Within seven days of the Conqueror’s city, every place lost its radiance;
for seven days as well, the gods repeatedly lamented and wept.
Alas, Great Hero! You whom I once personally attended face-to-face.
Who would have expected that now he is not seen, and even his speech has become empty?
Having once dwelt in the city of Śrāvastī, all who came there paid him respect;
within the boundaries of that land, they wept and wailed again and again out of grief.
Beholding the grove where the Buddha sat, they said:
"The Buddha once turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths here; we ourselves heard it directly.
Now the world has returned to darkness, and people no longer honor one another."
Having created the causes for various sins, they are reborn in the three evil realms.
The many palaces of the devas are now entirely empty;
the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have no lord and no protection.
Where the Buddha once walked, all is now ruined and overgrown with weeds;
the Dharma King has entered parinirvāṇa, and the world is no longer a place of joy.
Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, stands there in his midst.
Afflicted by suffering, they gave rise to grief and sorrow, wailing aloud with great lamentation.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and others raised their hands and cried out together in mourning;
as soon as they heard [the news] within the garden, they immediately rushed forth.
These hosts of devas constantly extol the Buddha, the Tathāgata;
lamenting that they have been separated from the World-Honored One, who was once their teacher of the Dharma,
they can no longer partake of the nectar of immortality, nor do the sounds of song and music ever again reach them.
Thus these various devas remained in a state of anxiety for six months.
When the asuras heard it said that the teachings were empty and without a master,
they immediately called out to one another and raised their armies to attack the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
When the kings of Jambudvīpa and others destroy the stūpas of the Buddha,
at that very time, the devas and asuras shall wage war.
There will be many bhikṣus, as well as many bhikṣuṇīs.
Born within the various evil realms, they undergo all manner of bitter suffering.
Those who, while at home, commit various transgressions and as lay followers violate the precepts,
mutually proclaiming each other’s ill repute, thereby give rise to rebirth in the miserable destinies.
When women practice unwholesome deeds, they too shall all enter the three miserable realms;
when such things arise, the world is not at peace.
At times they wander through villages, and at times they flee into the mountain forests.
The masses flee in all directions, and their lifespans are suddenly shortened.
Robbers and thieves arise in great numbers, and there is likewise famine;
crops do not ripen in their proper seasons, and locusts swarm as a violent calamity.
If, during an age of famine, a person’s life comes to an end,
they will be reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta) and undergo manifold suffering and hardship.
Whatever has been offered to stupas and temples, as well as to the Sangha of the four quarters—
At that time, the bhikṣus will all divide and take [the relics] among themselves.
After my parinirvāṇa, such manifold sufferings will arise;
you should swiftly exert yourselves with diligence and no longer look back.
All those who are of the class of fools, Lacking the person of wisdom, Having completed their foolish karma, Will swiftly be born in the various evil realms.
One should delight in reading, reciting, and explaining; From this, wisdom is born.
One who cultivates the mind of wisdom can swiftly ascend to the happy realms.
By constantly observing with wisdom and training as I have done,
one will forever be free from all fetters and swiftly reach nirvana.
The True Dharma will not remain for long; you should arouse firm and diligent effort.
I have already spoken thus: you should quickly engage in correct contemplation.
Once this kalpa has passed, sixty full kalpas [shall elapse].
If one does not hear the name of the Buddha, how could one give rise to faith and joy?
If people encounter one another while being afflicted by the suffering of famine,
even mother and son will at that time devour each other’s flesh.
The children born at that time, their steps unsteady with panic,
felt great terror even while staying within their own homes.
Having seen and heard these things, they knew them to be the burning of birth and death.
What wise person would find delight therein?
Ignorance is the root of birth; women are the root of desire;
the aggregates are the root of suffering. Therefore, one should abandon suffering.
In this world there are foolish sentient beings who are addicted to the desires of women;
those who can distance themselves from such delusion shall swiftly attain nirvāṇa.
When this Dharma is proclaimed, one will not encounter evil retribution.
It is not said that the fruit is with outflows, for one would thus fall into the evil realms.
All dharmas without outflows are empty and void, possessing nothing;
they are quiescent and fundamentally lack solidity—one should quickly realize this.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if there is a bhikṣu or any other sentient being who, by accomplishing this foremost dharma, seeks the untainted (anāsrava), they should speak thus: 'The mind abides nowhere in any phenomena.'"
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva should practice with firm resolve.
What is meant by 'firm resolve'? "
How is it practiced?
That which is called "firm" refers to a firm mind and firm diligence. What is meant by a "firm mind"?
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Even after making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one then gives rise to a single thought seeking the Buddha-way.

Subsequently, after further passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and a single Buddha appearing in the world, because of having given rise to minds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one attains a human body for the first time; through a single phrase of Dharma heard by a body as many times as the sands of the Ganges, the light of wisdom brings great benefit toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
One should give rise to such a firm and resolute mind.
Furthermore, one should gather the Buddha’s wisdom through various skillful means, seeking it through various ascetic practices, and embracing the Buddha’s wisdom through various ascetic practices.
Furthermore, there is such a firm resolve.
"Moreover, Kāśyapa, I shall now proclaim a parable for you;
by means of this parable, those who possess wisdom will be able to understand the meaning of what has been said."
By means of these various difficult practices and ascetic austerities, one can attain bodhi; this should not be abandoned or discontinued for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
If one studies without ceasing or abandoning them for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, then one will be able to realize unexcelled bodhi through direct manifestation.
One should generate such a firm and resolute mind, making it one's strength and applying diligent effort, never abandoning *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* until the end.
Furthermore, there is such a firm mind as this.
Kāśyapa! If there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to this mind, by what means should it be sustained?
This means not grasping at what is possible and not grasping at what is impossible.
Why is there no grasping at the possible and the impossible?
Because if one were to grasp at what is possible and what is impossible, it would constitute an obstacle to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Because they do not grasp at what is possible or impossible, they swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Kāśyapa, suppose there were a person who took precious jewels filling the trichiliocosm and offered them as a gift; yet if another were to receive, uphold, and abide with faith in the teachings of various sūtras such as these spoken by the Tathāgata, which accord with enlightenment, the mass of merit generated by the latter would be many times greater than that of the former.
Kāśyapa! Furthermore, a bodhisattva possesses a firm mind, yet even this firm mind cannot be apprehended; therefore, one must not cease or abandon the practice.
Regarding "cultivation," it refers to practicing extensively.
To what extent? It refers to as many dharmas of extensive cultivation as there may be; if one gives rise to a single mind, one cannot understand them all.
Why is this? Because that dharma cannot be expressed by signs.
Nevertheless, it is the most supreme method of cultivation, namely, the nature of a firm mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Without a mind, one gives rise to mental conceptions; there shall be great fear:
'Shall I succeed or not?'"
What is this matter? Constantly giving rise to discursive thought and investigation, dwelling in one-sided views,
and slandering the true path, one shall not attain bodhi.
This is a mind of indolence; it is not the mark of bodhi.
Such a person doubts all—the Buddhas and the śrāvakas—and though failing to practice, they long for the dharmas of the noble ones and the various Buddhas.
Not merely through verbal expression can the fruit of peace and happiness be accomplished;
it requires a mind of faith and joy that can accomplish the vast Dharma.
Nor is it by mental construction alone that one can attain supreme capability.
"Since a single dharma can accomplish all that is to be done,
once one has recognized its excellence, one should cultivate it for the sake of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:"
When a bodhisattva is able to accomplish this dharma, even though they do not personally attend upon or make offerings to the Buddhas, they themselves declare:
"I shall attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
“Kāśyapa! There are three kinds of cultivation for a lay bodhisattva that can bring benefit to awakening.
What are these three?
For the sake of all-knowledge, one generates deep love and joy, does not fall back into former karma, and firmly upholds the five precepts.
Possessing these three factors, one can accomplish six dharmas. What are these six?

That is to say, one attains the state of a noble one; one is neither mute nor speech-impaired, neither deaf nor lacking in keen hearing; one’s physical form becomes transformed and dignified; one swiftly attains deep faith and does not give rise to fear toward the profound Dharma; one is able to comprehend whatever Dharma is heard without laborious effort and swiftly attains non-retrogression—one should well understand these six dharmas.
There are five obstacles to transformation. What are these five?
They are: divisive speech, all false speech, lack of resolute intention, harboring envy in the mind, and being addicted to various sensual desires.
These five factors act as obstacles to progress.
Furthermore, there are three factors that should be practiced. What are these three?

This means that because one constantly gives rise to the aspiration to leave the household life, one should show respect and reverence toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts; however, those who do not teach the Dharma in accordance with the same class [of practitioners] should be avoided.
Why is this? A bodhisattva should not train in those dharmas; if one were to train in them, it would be like carrying a load of straw. Why is this?
Because it is not the Buddha-way.
To carry such burdens is to be attached, which is identical to the state of the ignorant; therefore, one should not practice or study those teachings.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should train in three dharmas.
What are these three? They are:

always following and conforming to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; expounding the Dharma for others while diligently practicing it oneself; and cultivating a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Having received [instruction] in these three places, one should train accordingly.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three dharmas. What are these three?
That is to say: one should abstain from beating others, refrain from disparaging others by calling them lowly or base, and grant fearlessness to those who are afraid;
these are the three dharmas that one should cultivate and draw near to.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Do not associate with inferior people; When you see those who are not upright, Having seen them, you should distance yourself from them, Just as one avoids a venomous snake."
One should not follow the example of others, nor should one pay them homage;
one should keep far away from them, just as one avoids a vicious dog.
For those who harbor attachments, by following their example, one enters the same evil realms.
Upon hearing the teaching of the sublime Dharma of emptiness, one should give rise to a heart of love and joy;
likewise, one should also show reverence toward bhikṣus who delight in emptiness.
One should increase the path of extensive learning and give rise to a mind of beneficial wisdom.
One who approaches supreme enlightenment should be revered by sentient beings;
swiftly acting upon their instructions, one quickly gives rise to all roots of goodness and increases the mind of wisdom, like a lotus born from within the water.
One should extensively listen to and receive the Dharma; thus, what is wholesome will increase swiftly.
By increasing the mind of wisdom, one is able to sever all outflows (*āsrava*).
Possessing great majesty and fearlessness, with great wisdom and great diligence—
Desiring to benefit others, one brings great benefit to oneself.
A householder should renounce the beating and striking of sentient beings;
setting out to seek awakening, one shall attain non-retrogression in the Dharma.
Free from illness and most upright, all people love and respect him.
If one cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, one abandons the various evil realms;
in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, one shall enjoy oneself with the five desires.
When their life in heaven comes to an end, they do not fall into the three evil realms;
instead, they are born into the human world within a noble and wealthy family.
Their physical form is most upright and majestic, such that no one can disparage them.
Guarded by devas and nāgas, practicing correctly in accordance with the Dharma,
one dwells in a most excellent place, is loved and respected by others,
sleeps in peace and security, and awakens with a mind at ease.
Thinking that they are protected by Heaven, they ultimately harbor no heart of fear;
such is the supreme characteristic of this vast Dharma.
Whether at home or having left the home life, there is further great benefit.
Causing many people to awaken and remember their various roots of goodness;
granting peace through giving to those who are afraid,
they proceed toward the fruit of Bodhi and no longer serve other deities, except for the All-Knowing One.
This person attains the right path, with all wisdoms in harmonious accord.
By means of these roots of goodness, they abandon the three evil realms;
they attain wisdom and achieve the three insights, having trained well in the three trainings.
According to the merits one has performed, and according to the reverence one has shown, one becomes uniquely honored among sentient beings; many people pay homage with deep respect.
Those who pay homage to the Tathāgata are the most supreme among the multitude.
"Even if one dwells on the level of a householder, if they give rise to the bodhicitta,
you should listen as I speak these words of Dharma for them,
as well as other matters. Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
A lay bodhisattva should accomplish three dharmas. What are these three?

They should avoid worldly amusements, negligence, mutual gift-giving, and the selection of auspicious days and favorable times; they should always remain pure and refrain from receiving many offerings; furthermore, they should diligently cultivate learning through extensive study.
A bodhisattva should accomplish these three dharmas.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas that should be received and practiced. What are these three?
One should not create obstacles for those who preach the Dharma; rather, one should exhort such preachers and constantly provide lamps and candles.
One should always practice these three kinds of conduct.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there are three kinds of actions that one must never perform; if one performs them, one will receive a female body.
What are these three?

One should not obstruct one’s mother from hearing the true Dharma or seeing bhikṣus; one should not obstruct one’s wife from seeing bhikṣus or hearing the true Dharma; nor should one commit an improper act with one’s own wife.
"These three things must never be done; should one do them, one will receive a female body. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One should always, with a faithful heart, Light lamps of radiant brilliance;
One shall then obtain the stainless, Pure eye of a Buddha."
By relying on this eye, one comprehends all knowable phenomena.
If one can comprehend what is knowable, one knows past phenomena;
knowing the present is likewise so, while one does not conceptualize the future.
There are no three kinds of marks;
by relinquishing the third, the mark itself is called "markless," for both share the same single meaning.
Yet phenomena have no fundamental basis; by giving rise to conceptual discrimination regarding them, one loses the supreme enlightenment.
To realize all phenomena directly—this very phrase is enlightenment.
As has been revealed above,
there is likewise no one who can disparage it; all phenomena are like space,
and for this reason they have been revealed.
If one, while still a householder, constantly burns lamps and candles,
one will attain the clarity of the Buddha-eye.
Following the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas, one shall never again go to the three miserable realms.
May they not suffer the fruit of being born blind;
by proclaiming the most supreme teaching, through the power of these roots of goodness,
may they turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Having created obstacles to the Dharma, one receives the body of a lowly woman;
blind, hunchbacked, and burdened by many sins,
one has never beheld various forms nor heard many sounds, dwelling instead in profound darkness.
Just like a bat, she will create conditions that obstruct the Dharma; from this point on, her life will swiftly end,
and she shall become an extremely ugly woman with yellow hair and green eyes.
Dark-skinned and blind, with crippled feet and a venomous heart, deaf and garrulous—
may they swiftly receive such bodies of manifold evils, always due to the causes and conditions of desire.
The husband became jealous.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are three kinds of things that a lay bodhisattva should not do."
What are these three?

If another person offers an object—whether it be a small amount of ghee or clarified butter, or even many items that are difficult to give—one should not bestow them as a gift unless the owner requests it.
One should not create obstacles for another who wishes to leave the household life; rather, one should encourage those who have not yet left the household life and cause them to do so.
When one sees the construction of a stūpa or temple for the Tathāgata, one should assist in its repair and building, but one should not, on this account, take possession of its wealth.
These three things are what a lay bodhisattva should not do.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When one bestows the wealth of merit upon others, It should not be given to an improper recipient;
If it is given to such a heavy [burden], one incurs guilt, And what has been bestowed cannot be withheld."
When a faithful person approaches the place of almsgiving, they stand solemnly with palms joined.
If there are few people present for the task, and one wishes to serve the monks,
they should follow the donor’s instructions and assist where manpower is scarce.
Water, juices, soups, drinks, and other such light items—
provided they do not contradict the donor’s intention and do not cause resentment in others—
if there is one who wishes to go forth, whether it be a son or a relative, [one should grant permission].
Within this, the bodhisattva should not create obstacles.
May sentient beings be at peace and happy; may they attain realization of nirvana.
Such is my superior intention: may I preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
Having recognized these faults, one should not defile oneself;
do not lament for long nights, being stained by afflictions.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
There are three kinds of practices that a lay bodhisattva should not engage in.
What are these three?
One should not trade in men or women; furthermore, one should not give what is not medicine to others; and if there are those who do so, one should not associate with them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One should abstain from selling men, And likewise abstain from selling women.
Do not give anything to others that is not medicine; If one gives such things, one should abstain."
For the sake of sentient beings suffering, they are censured alike by the gods and others;
wherever they go—in the cardinal or intermediate directions—they are struck and harmed by the arrows of sorrow.
Through the long night, their afflictions increase, and manifold sufferings press upon their bodies.
Premature death and longevity naturally perish; therefore, one should not commit such acts.
Having fully understood the causes of these faults and other failings, I have briefly explained a small portion of them for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are three kinds of things that a lay bodhisattva should not do.
What are these three?
One should not go to the houses of courtesans, one should not associate with go-betweens, and one should not dwell in places where cattle, sheep, or other animals are slaughtered.
These are the three things that ought not to be done.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One who does not go to the houses of courtesans, yet exclusively practices defiled desires,
will quickly incur the world’s reproach, because he frequents base lusts."
The Venerable One, knowing of his departure, immediately rebuked him with disdain;
this invited illness that harmed his body and thereby brought his life to its end.
One should never associate with those who act as go-betweens for men and women.
He marries a woman and, upon approaching her, is slandered.
One should likewise not visit those who are butchers;
such people are not praised by the Bodhisattvas, the supreme refuge for beings.
These profound faults and perils, the Tathāgata fully understands;
for those who practice incorrectly, I now speak according to reality.
All the teachings of the World-Honored One, my disciples are able to know.
Such a person, before the Buddha, is able to reach the place where practice leads.
When sentient beings abide in the Noble Path, they will swiftly arrive at Nirvana;
for such people as these, the Buddha speaks, not for those of evil conduct.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva should accomplish three dharmas.
What are these three?

While living at home, one should regard one’s own body and life as those of a passing guest; one should regard the things already given away as a mere accumulation; one should regard those who have not yet received gifts as being a hundred yojanas distant from oneself; and one should not form the thought of accumulating wealth for the sake of wife or children.
“A lay bodhisattva should accomplish these three dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Constantly cultivate the perception of death, Thinking: ‘My life shall soon come to an end.’”
Regarding the wealth one has accumulated, one should cultivate the acquisition of what is solid and enduring.
This wealth is not for the sake of wife or children, nor is it for one's own self;
rather, one should swiftly attain firm stability in both life and material possessions.
Seeking the Buddha-way with earnest devotion, one should not give rise to a haughty mind;
if one abandons the gateway of benefit, one will constantly encounter various harms.
It is like children at play, who taste only a little and are never satisfied.
The flavor of the Dharma is still slight; though one has faith, it is not yet secure.
If one’s practice lacks fierce diligence, the distance remains truly vast.
If one propagates it without ceasing, this is called the ultimate Dharma.
Kāśyapa, I now proclaim these various Dharma gates;
whoever can understand them is called "All-Knowing.
Through wisdom, one skillfully observes and gives rise to weary detachment toward the body.
"Always maintain right reflection, contemplating [the Buddha] as if he were present before me. Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva who accomplishes three dharmas will attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
What are these three?

To cause parents who lack faith to abide in faith; to exhort parents who violate the precepts to abide in the precepts; and to exhort parents who are stingy and greedy to abide in relinquishment. One praises unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and teaches the Dharma to others;
this is the first way of attaining non-retrogression from unsurpassed enlightenment.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a lay bodhisattva knows who is worthy of offerings and who is not.
One who is worthy of offerings they shall offer to; one who is not, they shall not offer to. Nevertheless, they cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward that person.
By accomplishing this second dharma, one attains non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva diligently amasses wealth through arduous effort.
Do not let it be wasted, nor let it be lost!

Do not give it away recklessly to others; rather, hold it firmly and bestow it equally upon those who observe pure precepts—śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all sentient beings—and grant it to fellow practitioners of the Dharma without hindrance.
By accomplishing this third dharma, one attains non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If a bodhisattva living at home Seeks unsurpassed enlightenment,
And gives rise to the three fundamental wisdoms, This constitutes the supreme awakening."

If one's father or mother possess evil wisdom and lack faith, one should exhort them to give rise to faith and joy, causing them to abide in the sublime Dharma. If they are stingy, one should establish them in generosity;
if they violate the precepts, one should establish them in morality; and for those lacking wisdom, one should teach them so that they may attain wisdom.
One should also constantly encourage others in this, as it is the supreme dharma for awakening.
One should travel to the four directions to seek out those who preach the Dharma;
by teaching others through the gift of Dharma, one increases wisdom thereby.
Those who have broken the precepts are established in the precepts; those without faith are made to have faith;
those without wisdom are taught to attain wisdom, so that they may achieve the stage of non-retrogression.
If one encounters a wise bhikṣu who upholds the precepts and is of great learning—
Reverently approach and draw near to them, going repeatedly to consult and inquire;
by this method, those living at home shall attain non-retrogression from bodhi.
Know that such persons of superior virtue are widely learned and endowed with all forms of wisdom.
One who possesses wisdom and understanding is worthy of respect; such a person may be given even their own flesh and body as an offering.
This is the mark of faith, as I have previously stated:
without faith, one cannot give rise to the great mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
The wise perceive superior matters and swiftly accomplish profound benefit;
regarding all sublime and wondrous dharmas, it is not difficult for them to attain realization.
Knowing this supreme advantage for both themselves and others, they act accordingly.
Being associated with renunciation, one thereby increases wisdom.
All the various provisions that have been constantly accumulated from the beginning are stored together with the observance of precepts as resources for the future.
These words are not different from the truth; they are not spoken in vain.
Through courageous progress and steadfast generosity, one shall realize the fruit of a Tathāgata.
Easy to dwell with due to the observance of precepts, the valiant attain profound compassion.
Gathering sentient beings through generosity is no different whether done first or last.
This pure and supreme giving is free from all longing;
whether it be gold or silver, there is nothing that he does not give.
Bravely bestowing everything, he practiced the giving of alms in past lives;
seeking the unsurpassed vehicle, the most profound and supreme state,
he made offerings to all devas and humans in accordance with what is not of the Dharma.
It is not as good as being able to accord with the Dharma by making offerings to even a single sentient being.
One who is courageous and diligent in seeking the Dharma can, through the Dharma, fully comprehend the Dharma;
through the supreme path, one becomes wise and attains unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
once a lay bodhisattva has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are three dharmas by which they attain parinirvāṇa within the Śrāvaka vehicle.
What are the three?

There is a certain class of people who fear the three evil realms and perceive great awakening as a heavy burden. Although they have accumulated roots of goodness, they do not apply themselves with focused mindfulness nor do they delight in seeking the good; being harmed by their own minds, they give rise to perceptions of suffering.
Because they have established such a primary condition, they fall away from awakening and instead attain parinirvāṇa through the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there is a certain class of people who do not give rise to a joyful mind regarding the practice of giving; having practiced generosity, they immediately feel regret, and furthermore, they do not dedicate the merit toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
Because they have established this second dharma, they fall away from bodhi and quickly enter parinirvāṇa within the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there is a certain class of people who do not apply themselves with diligent effort to seek extensive learning, yet, by means of inferior roots of goodness, they quickly attain parinirvāṇa;
because they have established this third dharma, they fall away from bodhi and quickly proceed toward the Śrāvaka vehicle to attain parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Having already resolved upon the Bodhicitta, If one does not practice in accordance with it,
One will fall away from the Buddha-vehicle And enter the path of the Śrāvakas."
Enlightenment is not attained through lack of faith, nor by a mind of indolence;
for one who lacks wisdom and clings to stinginess and greed, there will be obstacles.
One who recognizes kindness, abides in pure precepts, and always delights in practicing generosity extensively—[for such a person, enlightenment is near].
Enlightenment is not difficult to attain;
if the mind also practices generosity well, and if the minds of sentient beings are firm,
they shall become stupas for the world.
With the mind directed toward great enlightenment, one shall become a venerable one for the world and an unsurpassed Arhat.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
A lay bodhisattva who possesses three qualities falls away from awakening and attains parinirvāṇa within the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
What are these three?
There is a certain class of persons who, although they have already set out toward the mind of great awakening, are stingy with respect to the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another class who are addicted to gazing and divining, as well as grasping at the signs of worldly fortune and misfortune.
Again, there is another class who have resolved their minds on enlightenment, yet because of indolence, they are unable to seek out the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) in their entirety.
"Because they have established these three kinds of dharmas, each is able to fall away from bodhi and enter parinirvāṇa through the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Being stingy with the true Dharma, One does not instruct or admonish others."
Having attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, one falls away from the unsurpassed path.
Due to these two conditions, one loses the benefit [of the path] and various sufferings arise;
though one draws near to practice, one harbors doubts regarding the path to enlightenment.
To contemplate the Mahāyāna teachings while seeking auspiciousness and avoiding misfortune is not true faith; such a person is forsaken by the Buddhas.
Those who can focus their minds with joy and resolutely direct themselves toward Bodhi—
One shall never pay homage to other honored ones, except for the stupas of the world.
If one possesses pure faith and does not serve other deities, this constitutes the supreme accomplishment; such a person is called the God among Gods.
"If there are those who delight in bodhi and do not serve other deities,
in every place where they are born, their physical form and strength will always be complete.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
A lay bodhisattva receives a body of darkness by virtue of three dharmas.
What are these three?
Taking the lamp-light from a stūpa of the Tathāgata; manifesting anger during disputes with others; and groundlessly slandering other dark-skinned people who are not involved in one's own affairs.
"By these three things, one's body becomes dark.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The lamp-light burning at the stupa— one cuts off this blazing flame; [and likewise, one extinguishes the light of wisdom. By these three things, one's body becomes dark."
The body then becomes dark, like the wool of a black carpet.
By reviling those with dark skin, saying, "I am white and your body is black," because of that disparagement of others, one receives a body that is dark.
"One should guard one's speech well; karma will never perish.
According to the karma one has created, one shall become a vessel for that very karma.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:
A lay bodhisattva who commits three types of karma will be born into a family of artisans. What are these three?

If a bodhisattva personally observes the five precepts, yet when relatives come from afar, he gives them alcohol to drink or encourages others to drink it, he shall be born into that family of artisans.
This is called the foremost dharma.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,

if a lay bodhisattva practices pure conduct himself while inciting others to engage in impure desires, because he has accumulated this karma through such conditions, he will be born into the family of a craftsman.
This is called the second dharma.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
when a bodhisattva sees another diligently engaged in recitation and study, yet begins to undertake construction and labor within his own household, he immediately says to that person:
“Cease for now your practice of recitation and study; you should instead prepare what I require at this time.
Because of the accumulation of such karmic conditions, one will be born into the family of a craftsman;
this is the third dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Giving wine to others and to one’s own kinsmen,
In order to bring about excessive drinking, One becomes a master of idle chatter.”
He does not understand how to forge knives or needles, nor any other craft;
he can do nothing but sit and wave his hands, blowing the bellows before the furnace.
While he practices the holy life for himself, he praises sexual indulgence to others.
When this karma ripens, he shall become a master of flowery speech.
He does not understand how to make knives or needles, nor can he operate a bellows;
he only knows how to brandish a long hammer and forge iron before the anvil.
Having caused others to abandon the Dharma, they pass away from this life and are swiftly reborn into a family of artisans; their consciousness is perpetually dull and obscured.
They never see moneybags or purses, nor do they see tongs or hammers.
Such is the karmic retribution; it utterly destroys all vessels.
Kāśyapa, you should guard your mind and well protect your speech;
never teach others any unwholesome dharmas.
The suffering of saṃsāra arises and increases because of craving;
one should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and censure all that is unwholesome.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa:

When a lay bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas, they shall be born into the social class of a wealthy kṣatriya family, possessing a handsome and dignified appearance that is loved and respected by others; they will be intelligent, skillful, and free from laziness.
What are these three? They are:

upon seeing a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa never seen before, one immediately gives rise to faith and makes offerings with reverence, declaring them to be a field of merit; then, with a pure mind, one invites them to accept all necessities—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and so forth.
When a lay bodhisattva accomplishes this first dharma, they shall be born into the social class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of a noble kṣatriya family.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva remains steadfastly established in their original vow, practicing as they have spoken and never uttering falsehoods.
By accomplishing this second dharma, one will be born into the common lot of a noble kṣatriya family.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
when a lay bodhisattva practices making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the aggregate of ethical discipline, they are able to grasp the firm dharma.
