"By accomplishing such a third dharma, one shall be born into the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of a noble Kṣatriya family.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who possess wisdom and the like, Who see [the value of] upholding the precepts and extensive learning..."
One should give rise to a heart of joy and go there to request [the Dharma].
Having already made the request, one should provide offerings according to the Dharma,
without any sense of weariness or regret, and bestow gifts without obstruction.
This is the grasping of the firm dharma; that which is practiced through intimacy accords with various forms of wisdom and is swiftly attained even amidst difficulties.
With such a mind of profound faith, one proceeds toward great enlightenment.
This is the sphere of activity of wisdom; the Buddha-way is not difficult to realize.
Always making one’s livelihood supreme, one should receive the most excellent wealth;
seeking the sublime Dharma, one realizes unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
One shall be born into a noble family, with a most upright and dignified countenance;
obtaining exquisite garments, one shall realize the supreme Nirvana,
as praised by the Buddha.
By means of the Buddha-vehicle one can realize the cool and wondrous nirvāṇa;
this is the most supreme fruit.
The attainment of this fruit is also a natural outflow, even if it takes ten billion kalpas.
This karma can never be destroyed.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva who accomplishes three dharmas plants all roots of goodness and, until the realization of unsurpassed bodhi, shall never again experience the worldly pleasures of the five desires."
What are these three?

A lay bodhisattva who upholds the five precepts does not praise the pleasures of the five desires to others; they diligently attend to their own duties and do not employ women, nor do they give rise to this thought:
"I shall refrain from associating with any woman until I realize unsurpassed bodhi; may I never encounter the worldly pleasures of the five desires."
"Because he has accomplished such an initial dharma, he shall not experience the five desires until he attains bodhi.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, when a lay bodhisattva hears sūtras such as these and develops deep faith, seeking to proceed toward nirvāṇa, even if they uphold such teachings but conceal them and do not practice them, there are those who can expound and promote them; if anyone hears them, they should immediately abandon all bases for unwholesome actions."
By means of these roots of goodness, they shall attain unimpeded eloquence and unattached eloquence; whether in the present life or at the time of death, they shall swiftly behold the Buddha.
After their lives end, they will be reborn in the heavens and, before long, realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By accomplishing this second dharma, one shall not experience the five desires until reaching bodhi.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a lay bodhisattva dedicates all roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi; they take no pleasure in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, dharmas, wealth, estates, or nobility, nor do they cherish their retinue. With a mind of non-action and its non-active fruition, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi.
"By accomplishing this third dharma, one shall not experience the five desires until reaching enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Cultivating the five precepts while at home, Firmly maintaining and well-guarding them,"
Do not associate with women, but cultivate a sense of revulsion toward them;
diligently seek such Dharma-gates without weariness,
and whatever constitutes a basis for unwholesome action, one should swiftly abandon it.
All wholesome dharmas whatsoever, I dedicate entirely toward Bodhi;
by these roots of goodness, may I swiftly leave behind the five desires.
May I always attain superior and abundant learning, and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Giving rise to a mind of great compassion, one seeks unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, hearing of these benefits, one should generate a noble and virtuous mind;
staying far from all desires, one shall swiftly turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what name shall this Dharma of the sutra be known?"
"How should we now receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This sutra is named 'The Exposition of the Threefold Restraint,' it is also named 'The Proclamation of the Bodhisattva Precepts,' and it is also named 'The Common Entry into All Dharmas.'"

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the great assembly—including all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others in the world—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Three;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
2. The Second Assembly: The Assembly on Boundless Adornments Chapter 1: The Supreme Dhāraṇī, Part One of One Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and immeasurable, innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
These bodhisattvas were all in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), having gathered from various buddha-fields.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat surrounded by a great assembly, who honored and revered him while he preached the Dharma for them.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Anantavyūha. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I have a slight doubt that I now wish to consult you about; I only pray that the Tathāgata will, out of compassion, grant me permission to do so.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantavyūha, saying: "Good son!"
“Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, please allow you to ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it according to your doubts so as to bring you joy.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
World-Honored One, I have donned the armor of diligence in order to seek boundless wisdom.

This applies to those bodhisattvas who seek the stage of great skillful means, who proceed toward the skillful mastery of the knowledge of boundless meanings, who are the first to initiate definitive great wisdom, and who are already established upon the path to enlightenment. World-Honored One!

I inquire of the Tathāgata for the sake of such bodhisattvas, and also for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. With a mind beyond compare, they contemplate the profound meaning of the great wisdom and skillful means of the pure knowledge of all phenomena; having attained discernment and mastery in the infinite meanings, they seek to ascend the lion-throne of the Great Teacher and the lion-throne of omniscience. Having correctly initiated courageous and diligent practice to attain non-retrogression, these are those who possess eloquence, have accumulated diligence, and have donned the armor—on account of such bodhisattvas, I inquire of the Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva who aspires to transcend and reach the other shore for the sake of all sentient beings, and further seeks with resolve the unobstructed and fearless state, abiding in fearlessness to skillfully expound the meanings of all dharmas according to their capacities, discerning them with expertise without adding or subtracting, and proclaiming the original nature and intrinsic nature of all dharmas as they truly are.”

"Bhagavān! Furthermore, because they have attained mastery over the mind that enters into the peerless and incomparable, the most excellent, and the unsurpassed, they inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such matters as these."
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who seek spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) and teacherless wisdom (*aśikṣita-jñāna*), shatter the shell of ignorance, and transcend both gods and humans—being most supreme, rare, and bringing benefit and happiness to all the world—and who desire to pursue great wisdom and fearlessness while setting aside [other] spontaneous wisdom; who desire to demonstrate boundless knowledge and skillful means, and intend to preach immeasurable, definitive teachings, wishing to illuminate the world with light for the sake of gods and humans.”

Furthermore, for the sake of those sentient beings who desire [the truth], who have been shown the skillful means of supreme and unimpeded great wisdom, who wish to practice the ultimately pure knowledge and vision, and who seek the stage of skillfulness in all-knowledge—I now wish to question the Tathāgata on their behalf.

"Bhagavān! If bodhisattvas abide in this stage, they will swiftly be able to perfectly fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata and realize the inconceivable perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*), thereby maturing sentient beings with little effort."

Manifesting before them, one is able to attain such wisdom as causes all sentient beings to abandon unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas; it reveals the path to bodhi and the lineage of the Buddhas, and is able to establish immeasurable sentient beings in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* so that they never regress.
"Blessed One!
Those bodhisattvas are able to open the path to awakening and cause their minds to rejoice within the Buddha-dharma; for their sake, I inquire of the Tathāgata."
World-Honored One!
This great assembly has now fully gathered; this is precisely the time to preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

We only pray that the Tathāgata will reveal and expound such a Dharma-gate, bestowing it upon all Bodhisattvas so that they may attain the fulfillment of their inconceivable vows and all the roots of goodness pertaining to the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood.

"Bhagavān! Such skillful gateways of dhāraṇī should be bestowed by the Tathāgata at the appropriate time, so that all bodhisattvas may maintain the skillful certainty of the principles and methods of immeasurable dharma-gates, and may expound their various meanings through words; furthermore, so that they may possess the aspiration to realize bodhi, abide in the activities of boundless great supernormal powers, mature immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, and receive the skillful wisdom of the Tathāgata."
I pray that you will reveal such a Dharma gate, so that sentient beings may realize the path to Bodhi.
In the long night of the past, the World-Honored One already made a great vow to cause countless sentient beings to dwell securely in the Buddha-wisdom and self-arisen wisdom.

This dharani gateway should be expounded so that all bodhisattvas may perfect their own roots of goodness and, through the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic empowerment, uphold those unsurpassed and inconceivable vows.
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already realized immeasurable skillful means and attained the inconceivable ground of fearlessness; he understands the differences in the inclinations and dispositions of all sentient beings, having accumulated all-encompassing wisdom throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas.
“World-Honored One!

This great assembly gazes upon the Tathāgata, never for a moment ceasing to do so; they seek all-knowledge and the treasury of all dharmas with tireless resolve and insatiable desire, wishing to hear the definitive meaning of the Tathāgata.”
The World-Honored One abides in the realm of all-knowledge and has already fully understood these skillful means of the bodhisattvas' vows and their setting forth toward awakening.
World-Honored One!

These dharma-gates and dharani-gates are the perfection of words and meanings, the definitive skillfulness regarding all dharmas. Such dharma-gates as these should be taught by the Tathāgata, so that those bodhisattvas who are not yet mature may all reach maturity, and those who are already mature may swiftly attain supernatural powers, all-knowledge, and the wisdom and vision of liberation of mind.
“World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas dwell in the stage of non-fixity, these bodhisattvas, upon first hearing the Dharma, shall achieve the realm of all-knowledge.”
"World-Honored One!
For this reason, I venture to pose these great questions; I only pray that Your Great Compassion will bestow protection and sustain all bodhisattvas by preaching such a Dharma.
World-Honored One!"

In the future final age, when disputes arise and sentient beings, out of attachment, further harm one another, and the three poisons increase to corrupt and disrupt the True Dharma—may all Bodhisattvas, through great compassion, endure these matters during that time and propagate this Dharma without dispute.
By conforming to the state of non-contention (*araṇā*), one is able to embrace great loving-kindness and great compassion, as well as accumulate the power of all roots of goodness.
World-Honored One!
I now venture, on account of this meaning, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the definitive meaning of the unimpeded Dharma-gate.
“World-Honored One!
How do those bodhisattvas initiate the immeasurable dharma-gates, the gates of the radiance of dharma, and the skillful means regarding all dharmas?

Furthermore, we pray that the Tathāgata will expound the dharma-gate of quiescence that is indestructible, while also unfolding the boundless and subtle treasury of the Dharma, fully accomplishing unceasing power of mindfulness, subduing Māra’s enemies and all heterodox disputants, and remaining unsubdued by them.”

I only pray that the Tathāgata will expound the True Dharma, so that all sentient beings may accumulate roots of goodness and also accumulate boundless skillful means; so that they may manifest the arising of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and through recollection, compile immeasurable essential teachings; so that they may attain pure and perfect eloquence, with a continuous and unconfused succession of peerless phrases and meanings, desiring that they realize immeasurable dharma-gates and the true expedient means of dhāraṇīs.

Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to generate the aspiration [for awakening] and, for their sake, explain the practices of the two limits of past and future; they reveal the seeing of all phenomena of the past, future, and present, [showing that] one has mastery over causes and that phenomena abide nowhere.

May all bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the past deeds of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; may they traverse all buddha-fields with their supernormal powers and fearlessness, bestow upon sentient beings the pure eye of Dharma, reveal to them the inconceivable Dharma, and bring to maturity the skillful means of buddha-wisdom.
Based on this meaning, I venture to make a request.

I pray that the World-Honored One will expound the profound Dharma of the vast skillful means of the Tathāgata-ground, which constitutes all-knowledge and encompasses all skillful, immeasurable, and inconceivable principles of the Dharma, so as to bring to perfection the vows and skillful means of those bodhisattvas.

Having heard this Dharma, all these bodhisattvas attained the illumination of the Great Dharma, accomplished the sublime skillful means of awakening, and brought their great vows to complete fulfillment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantavyūha,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Anantavyūha!”

Now, because you dwell in the skillful means of pure vows for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and also out of compassion for all sentient beings, you have questioned the Tathāgata with definitive wisdom; your merit is immeasurable.

Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect according to reality; I shall now analyze and explain for you, so that all bodhisattvas may give rise to immeasurable and manifold merits within the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Anantavyūha said:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We would delight to hear it.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Anantavyūha:

"If bodhisattvas seek the aspiration for boundless skillful means, they should understand the secret speech of the Buddhas, receiving, upholding, contemplating, and investigating it according to reality."
How should one observe this, Anantavyūha?
The wisdom of the Tathāgata encompasses all skillful means; whatever he proclaims is not without purity. These bodhisattvas should diligently cultivate these essential teachings.
All that is spoken by the Buddhas is entirely equal; abiding in great compassion, they universally [work for] all living beings, decisively bringing all classes of sentient beings to maturity.

Whether one aspires to liberation through the Lesser Vehicle, or seeks the true and most supreme *nirvāṇa* on the path of the *śrāvaka*, through the fulfillment of their great vows, they shall achieve all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

I now abide in unsurpassed liberation, far removed from the inferior dharmas of other vehicles; I have skillfully entered the secret language of all Buddhas and speak the incomparable words and phrases of the Tathāgata, which are vast, pure, and encompass all phenomena, thereby causing all sentient beings to attain liberation and maturation according to their respective capacities.

However, all these phenomena are entirely equal, neither increasing nor decreasing, without deficiency and without leakage; even unto formlessness and the peerless form, they are boundless, limitless, and pure by their very nature.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have expounded that one should understand self-nature and intrinsic nature as they truly are; yet, there is no dharma that is either understood or not understood. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are merely spoken of by the Tathāgata as provisional designations.
If those phenomena exist only by way of provisional designation, then they cannot be established as real dharmas, nor can they be manifested.

Because there is no manifestation, all that the Tathāgata has taught is the true ultimate meaning; it accords with the Dharma and enters equally into all phenomena, neither dwelling in conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena, nor not dwelling therein.
By means of both the discrimination of phenomena and non-discrimination, one realizes all phenomena as they truly are—equal and without distinction.
Phenomena have no arising, because such arising phenomena do not exist;
phenomena have no intrinsic nature, because they are produced by the pervasive conceptualization of false discrimination.
Phenomena have no arising, because they lack self-mastery;
phenomena have no dependence, because they are perfected in relinquishment;
phenomena have no activity, because they neither come nor go.
Dharmas have no intrinsic nature, for they transcend all dharmas that possess an intrinsic nature;
dharmas are fundamentally equal and without differentiation, for they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Whatever dharmas one performs, if one gives rise to sublime vows, there is nothing that will not be accomplished; yet within this, there is no agent, nor is there even the slightest dharma to be attained—all return to emptiness.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said that all dharmas are like illusions and like dreams, and possess no high or low.
When I gather in sentient beings with these pure and great vows, there is truly not the slightest dharma to which I may become attached.
Anantavyūha! This is the gateway to the light of the Dharma for all bodhisattvas.
By means of this gateway, their sublime vows increase and flourish, just as when the sun appears, its radiance shines everywhere.
"In this way, noble sons who are able to have faith and understanding in this Dharma-gate act as a light of the Dharma for all sentient beings. Anantavyūha!"

If bodhisattvas correctly contemplate within and remain undistracted without, abiding in that which can sever all obstacles, and if they recollect the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Universal Radiance and are able to have faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, they should investigate these various Dharma-gates.
The Tathāgata fully knows all phenomena and reveals and proclaims them through the gateway of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Thus, this dependent origination is false and unreal; its self-nature and essential nature are entirely empty and quiescent, and even this nature of dependent origination is not ultimately real.

It can cause sentient beings to transition from defilement to purity; yet, when sought throughout the ten directions, it is entirely unobtainable. Because it is unobtainable, there is no grasping; because there is no grasping, even that which I have taught should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma.
That which is called "renunciation" does not exist as a thing; it is without anything to be grasped and without effortful application, for its intrinsic nature is pure.
All phenomena are devoid of discrimination, because one realizes the true nature of discrimination as it is.
All phenomena have no place of abiding and cannot be perceived, because they lack any distinct nature.

Therefore, all phenomena neither abide nor rely; they exist only as conventional designations through names. They are all empty and quiescent, devoid of intrinsic nature, abiding in a state of non-abiding.

Therefore, all phenomena have no place of abiding; because such a place does not exist, because they are exhausted, because they are extinguished, and because they undergo transformation, the Tathāgata merely proclaims them by different names.
This underlying intention should be understood; one should not cling to what is wholesome or unwholesome.
If one clings to wholesome dharmas, one will likewise cling to those unwholesome dharmas.
Because of grasping at such unwholesome dharmas, various sufferings and afflictions arise; the Buddha has therefore taught this under another name as the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Because of non-attachment to both wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas], those cravings are extinguished; the Tathāgata has taught this cessation of wholesome dharmas under another name as the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering].

Because the second noble truth is thoroughly understood, because it is ceased, because it is exhausted, because it is free from conceptualization, because it is observed through the contemplation of non-existence, and because it is free from the conceptualization and feeling of joy, the Tathāgata designates this by another name as the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

Because one fully understands the third noble truth of cessation, one enters into the ground of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-bhūmi*) as it truly is through the path sought; one transcends the sphere of all conceptualization, discrimination, and proliferation (*prapañca*), and practices the eightfold path from right view through to right concentration. Having understood the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, the Buddha has proclaimed this by another name as the fourth truth.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have established herein the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path;
that is, suffering, its origin, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to its cessation.
This suffering does not exist; it is provisionally designated by way of worldly convention.
These factors, such as ignorance and so forth, are all merely the grasping of non-cognition. Why is this so?

In that state, there is neither ignorance nor even the slightest object of perception to be grasped; there is nothing realized, no radiance, nothing that can be known, and nothing that can be attained—what, then, could possibly exist therein?
All things are false and subject to disintegration; they possess no solidity or substance.
If one were to designate them as real entities, one would consequently become attached to the notion of permanence.
If one were to have attachment through non-discriminative grasping, one would consequently have attachment toward cessation.

Therefore, one should not engage in discrimination regarding suffering; rather, through wisdom, one should understand that the nature of ignorance is itself the nature of suffering. Because it is associated with ignorance, ignorance neither associates nor dissociates with any entity, for even that [ignorance] does not exist.
Because they are dissociated from one another, ignorance is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization; it is neither produced nor destroyed, and there is no agent.
Since an agent cannot be found through conventional designation, O Anantavyūha!
This is the gateway of the Dharma that accords with illumination, through which all bodhisattvas thoroughly understand and enter into the intrinsic nature of ignorance.

By means of this gateway, they are able to abandon all the darkness of ignorance, directly realize the Dharma that accords with illumination, skillfully cultivate the factors of enlightenment, and skillfully comprehend the noble truths.

These bodhisattvas are able to attain purity within this Dharma-gate: that is to say, suffering is purified through non-arising; origination is purified through non-objectification; cessation is purified through total extinction; and the path is purified through cultivation. Because they have faith in equality, the path itself is equal.
One should understand these various distinctions of the different names for such phenomena.
Having understood them, one should abandon, realize, and cultivate them.
If one can understand the words of the Tathāgata, then that person fully knows, abandons accordingly, realizes, and cultivates.
Therefore, having known this, the Noble One neither grasps nor rejects any phenomena, and thus attains abiding in the Dharma-gate of the Four Truths. "O Anantavyūha!
All phenomena are without discrimination; they neither increase nor accumulate.

Because the noble ones have thoroughly understood them as they truly are, they do not give rise to discrimination nor engage in conceptual proliferation; they are able to see things as they truly are, neither deprecating nor clinging to them.
Because they are severed by the Path, one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination or engage in proliferation regarding any wholesome dharmas, much less unwholesome ones.
Due to being conjoined with this non-discrimination, one likewise does not abide in the cessation of either dharma or non-dharma.
If they are fully understood and abandoned, there will be neither fetters of phenomena nor fetters of non-phenomena.
They are able to realize that the phenomena of fettering are illusory; these illusory phenomena are empty and non-existent. This is the gateway to the truth entered by them.

By means of this gateway, one is without attachment or aversion; having realized the perfection of equanimity, one is able to sever all fetters, abides securely in the right path, reaches the further shore, and realizes the self-nature of phenomena, which is without entering or exiting.

“Anantavyūha! You should now observe that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is empty, their self-nature is quiescent, and there is no agent; phenomena are neither truly associated with fetters nor dissociated from them.”
Within those phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, one should not form attachments; nor should one give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding existence or non-existence.
Being able to understand the purity of causes and conditions, one should not engage in frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
All phenomena that arise through causes and conditions are empty of the nature of those conditions and are ultimately pure; thus, these causes and conditions do not correspond with one another.

All phenomena are successively devoid of agency, devoid of activity, and devoid of functional operation. Contemplating all phenomena in this way, because they are mutually empty, they lack intrinsic nature and are without support or abiding.
Anantavyūha! You should enter into this; by doing so, you will be able to increase the pure dharma-gate of indestructible, universal radiance.

Through embracing [the teachings], one shall attain purity; through the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one shall become luminous and transcend the fetters (*saṃyojana*); through non-attachment, one shall achieve liberation.
“Anantavyūha! All dharmas are merely names and signs that are revealed and proclaimed.
What are these names and signs?
"Characteristics" (*nimitta*) refer to all material forms (*rūpa*) derived from the four great elements; "names" (*nāman*) refer to all non-material aggregates (*skandha*).

Such names and characteristics are entirely false and unreal. Due to inversion, there arises attachment—thinking "form is the self" or "form belongs to the self"—and through the discrimination of characteristics, there is the designation and expression of names.
Thus, both name and form are equally unreal; everything is a deceptive and disintegrating phenomenon, like an illusion or a dream.
The substance of form is as insubstantial as what is seen in a dream, and even the other four aggregates are not real, being merely designated by conventional words and letters.

Knowing thus at that time, one does not perceive suffering; because of the ultimate truth, there is no objective referent (*ālambana*); because there is no objective referent, the mind has nothing [to grasp]; and since it has nothing, how could there be any association with such a referent?
By means of this, one is able to transcend the sphere of nirvāṇa and attain the cessation of perception and the knowable. "Anantavyūha!
The three realms arise from perception and mental attention; therefore, it is said that the three realms are illusory, and that perception and mental attention are likewise not real."
Whatever perceptions he has are attachments to form; whatever mental attentions he has are all associated with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is neither associated nor dissociated, even to the point of being neither perception nor mental attention; the intrinsic nature of both perception and mental attention is empty.
All verbal expressions are likewise illusory; they are merely provisional designations intended to bring about the tranquility of intrinsic nature.
O Anantavyūha! Because the fundamental nature of all phenomena is established by way of conventional names, that which is thus spoken is also entirely equal.

Anantavyūha! Within this Dharma, those bodhisattvas who have realized the ultimate truth should understand that because all Tathāgatas have abandoned every fetter, whatever they proclaim is never in vain.

You should reflect well upon this so as not to give rise to attachment; do not produce conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena, but remain free from all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet give rise to thoughts of compassion for sentient beings. Contemplate and enter into this Dharma-gate, and for the benefit of all, reveal and expound it.
What is the Dharma-gate?

It refers to the thorough understanding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) such as ignorance, and the awakening to all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) such as wisdom and insight. One should universally purify and realize entry into all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena through non-conceptualizing wisdom (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*), which is neither a numerical entry nor a numerical abiding.

By conforming to such non-enumerated phenomena (*apratisaṃkhyā-dharma*), they enter the gate of unconditioned purity (*asaṃskṛta-viśuddhi-dvāra*). They attain the wisdom of pervasive retention and illumination (*samantadhāraṇī-prabhā-jñāna*), which gathers and sustains all phenomena so that they are not lost or destroyed. Through the skillful means of awakened wisdom (*bodhi-prajñopāya-kauśalya*), they extensively expound all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings.
Anantavyūha! This is the entrance to the dhāraṇī-gate for all bodhisattvas.
By means of this gate, they give rise to vast and differentiated awakening-wisdom, as well as the skillful wisdom capable of initiating the exposition of the meanings of all dharmas.
“Anantavyūha! What herein is that *dhāraṇī* gateway,
by means of which a bodhisattva attains the skillful means of total retention (*dhāraṇī*) regarding all phenomena?”

Anantavyūha! Herein, the bodhisattva dwells in the practice of eloquence through the wisdom of universal purity, and by means of the awakening intelligence of meaning, he contemplates the fundamental nature and intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

However, all phenomena have no abiding in their own nature; they are without name, without mark, and without anything established. Their boundless establishment cannot be proclaimed, yet it is expounded merely through conventional expressions.
The fundamental nature and intrinsic nature of all phenomena are inherently ineffable; they neither come nor go and are devoid of syllables. These syllables are pure and functionless.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is equal to empty space.
All phenomena are likewise thus: they are without action, without arising, and pure in their signlessness. To reveal and expound them by means of empty space is the gateless gate of all phenomena.
Because the gates are pure, they are ultimately unstained and do not follow after stains. Why is this?
All phenomena are ultimately unproduced and unarisen; their intrinsic nature likewise does not arise.

Therefore, you should know that all dharmas spoken throughout the three periods of time are by nature devoid of self-nature; yet one should not cling to the idea that dharmas are devoid of self-nature. This is the *dhāraṇī* gate of non-attachment for all bodhisattvas.
For the sake of purifying the gateways of all bodhisattvas, he thus reveals and teaches all phenomena.

As for those that have form and characteristics, the form and characteristics spoken of are themselves not form and characteristics; they are neither created nor destroyed, neither cherished nor resented.
Therefore, one should know that the gate of form and characteristics is, in fact, no-gate.
Because the gate is pure, by means of this one is able to enter the pure Dharma-gate of formlessness.

Because one wishes to thoroughly understand that this gateway of forms is non-existent, one does not proclaim it as having the meaning of existence; since there is nothing to be done, one enters into the signless.
"Anantavyūha! This gateway of formlessness thus described functions for the sake of the purification of dhāraṇī. Anantavyūha!"
That which is called a "gate" is like empty space.

All phenomena arise and cease in dependence upon empty space; that which arises and ceases is equal in nature. When one contemplates in this way, there is neither arising nor ceasing, and nothing to be grasped. One should understand all phenomena in this manner.
All dharmas are neither grasped nor ungrasped, neither equal nor unequal; indeed, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended.
By means of this, one can thoroughly understand this gateway of forms; it is for the sake of attaining the purity of the signless gateway that this is revealed and expounded. O Anantavyūha!
That which is called "signless" refers to the absence of body and the designation of a body, the absence of names, the absence of phrases, and the absence of manifestation.
One should understand this teaching and its meaning: that which is formless is equal to space.
As for what is called "space," there is neither space nor even the designation of "emptiness."
This is the dharma-gate of the accumulation of power through the wisdom that accords with clarity regarding ignorance.

A bodhisattva is able to realize the principle and skillful means of the dhāraṇī-gates; by virtue of this realization and entry, they are free from dispute and free from forgetfulness, and they enter the dhāraṇī-gate of secret language that follows along without interruption.
It is like a dragon named Anavatapta, who pours down great rain in an unceasing flow.
O Anantavyūha! As for what is called "dhāraṇī," what is the meaning of this term?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, ‘dhāraṇī’ is a conventional designation for the secret skillful means that accord with all dharmas; it is the activity of universal retention through recollection; it is the phrases of speech used in expounding the Dharma.”
By means of the power of wisdom-gathering, one attains entry into such dhāraṇīs.
With the wisdom of excellent awakening, one should uphold the immeasurable and boundless power of bodhi.
World-Honored One!

As I understand it, this exposition of the skillful means of boundless wisdom is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; you have revealed and disseminated it so that the Dharma shall not be interrupted.
"World-Honored One!
This dharani-gate is the great void and the great vaipulya; for this reason, it is able to be extensively proclaimed.
Because it can encompass through the teaching of equality, it is called the 'Teaching that Follows the Dharma'."
Because he has attained perfection in the differentiation of syllables, he skillfully reveals and widely disseminates [the teachings], thereby achieving mastery in eloquence.
Because he skillfully explains through the investigation of meaning, he attains perfection in the eloquence of meaning.
Because he definitively and skillfully elucidates all phenomena, he has attained perfection in the eloquence regarding the Dharma.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, he is able to gather them in through great kindness and mercy; by means of this gathering, he gradually tames them and brings them to purity, preaching the Dharma of equanimity that is free from all conceptual proliferation.
When the World-Honored One spoke this chapter on the Secret Skillful Means of the Dhāraṇī, immeasurable and boundless meanings of skillful means issued from the Buddha’s mouth.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantavyūha:
“What is called a ‘gate’ is a synonym for the gate of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.”
Within this gateway, all phenomena are expounded by means of language.
The Tathāgata, abiding in boundless, ultimate, and naturally pure wisdom and vision, without dwelling anywhere and without establishing anything, pours forth the vast and profound Dharma.
Anantavyūha! The Tathāgata has said that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; for one who is able to thoroughly understand and know all dharmas is said to possess the Buddha-dharma.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is equal to the Buddha-dharma; therefore, all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma.
Because one is able to discern what is dharma and what is non-dharma, it is said that one is able to discern all phenomena.
One who is able to comprehend is one who can comprehend the gateways of dhāraṇī.
This dhāraṇī is capable of universally entering into all phenomena, namely: speech, exposition, and discourse.
All speech, discourse, and conversation are expressed and proclaimed through written characters; among these characters, the letter *A* is the first and the letter *Ha* is the last.

Just as entering the womb, taking up the womb, and maintaining the womb are preceded by the mother; just as the growth and nourishment of a seed are preceded by the father; and just as the accumulation of the aggregates is preceded by birth, followed by the establishment of subsequent distinctions, such that the six sense bases and faculties mature in succession.
With these syllables as the precursor, all distinctions of written characters are combined.
With these syllables as the precursor, light is emitted and nurtured.

That is to say, with the letter *A* as the beginning and the letter *Ha* as the end, all other characters are situated between them; they proceed by combining in accordance with their respective correspondences. This is the dhāraṇī gateway for entering into and expounding upon speech and language.

Furthermore, one should understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are subject to disintegration and cessation, just as written characters, once the study of calligraphy is completed, are subsequently erased.

In this same way, the establishment of all factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) must likewise perish; just as these conditioned phenomena arise through combination, one should know that they perish when they no longer combine.
When these two types of conditions are thus conjoined, they establish the fetter of craving for all forms of existence;
likewise, through the conjunction of these same two types of conditions, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are established.

Observing in this manner, one is gradually able to purify the dharma-gate of non-conditioned phenomena; by means of this, one can enter the dhāraṇī-gate that expounds arising and ceasing, causing all bodhisattvas to swiftly attain the perfection of skillful means.

Just as the letter *a* is the first and the letter *ha* is the last among the syllables, having acted in this manner, one should discourse and converse using speech, skillfully entering into all secret terminology.
Furthermore, Anantavyūha, you should understand that the unobstructed Dharma is revealed and proclaimed as follows:

it is like beginning with the letter *a* and continuing through all other letters until they are fully differentiated; once one has formed them and applied the mind in a continuous stream to the act of writing, after the letter *ha*, there is no further letter that can be established.
Through these two types of mental attention, all conditioned activities are produced; yet those two forms of conceptualization lack any true reality.

Because within reality there is not even a slight word or letter, and because the fundamental nature and intrinsic nature are neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized, there is furthermore not the slightest thing to be done therein.
“Anantavyūha! All phenomena are known through wisdom, and this wisdom arises by being established through syllables.
Since these syllables are not ultimately established, that wisdom likewise has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended.”
Why is this? Because in ultimate reality there are no forms or characteristics.
By entering into such formlessness, one abandons all conditioned activities.
Because there is nothing to be done, one abandons all conditioned activities.
O Boundless Adornment!
This is the dharma-gate of the skillful means of the pure dhāraṇī that universally upholds.

When bodhisattvas train in this, they are able to initiate all activities free from delusion and proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, ensuring it is not deficient; they do not dwell in the obscurations and attachments of various conceptualizations, and they are able to distance themselves from both conceptualization and mental attention.
By means of the awakened wisdom that enters into all phenomena, one realizes the skillful mastery of the principle of boundless knowledge.
"O Boundless Adornment!
If bodhisattvas have thoroughly grasped names, they understand that all phenomena are merely names arising from various accumulations of verbal designations, and possess no reality."
One who knows thus should enter into skill in the principles of the dharanī-gates.
How should one enter into skill in the principles of the dharanī-gates?

One knows that all names have no abiding place; they do not abide within, without, between, or at the extremes of any phenomena (*dharma*). They are entirely unobtainable in any location, being merely provisional designations based upon the accumulation of various expressions. To realize, as it truly is, the nature of these designated names is the "phrase of reality" (*tathatā-pada*); by means of this phrase of reality, one should understand that all phenomena are nameless and ineffable.
This is the stage of the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas.
Regarding all phenomena, one should reveal and expound them by means of this gateway.
All phenomena taught by the Tathāgata are neither of a single nature nor of diverse natures, because phenomena possess neither a single nor a diverse nature.
All these phenomena are neither born nor existent; thus it is proclaimed that all phenomena are also empty.
If phenomena are empty, they are signless; if they are signless, they are wishless.
If a dharma is empty, signless, and wishless, it cannot be known and cannot be fully understood; one should not say of it that it exists or that it does not exist.
To speak of existence or non-existence is merely conventional expression; one should not give rise to attachment therein.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has constantly taught that if one does not cling to any phenomena, that is the true ultimate meaning;
if there is clinging, then by virtue of that clinging, one will give rise to further attachment toward various phenomena accordingly.
Thus, all such attachments are empty; they are phenomena subject to decay, being nothing but false conceptual proliferation and discrimination. Anantavyūha!
You should contemplate the exposition of all dharmas, yet realize that in those dharmas there is truly nothing to be shown or taught.
"How could there be anyone here capable of explaining this to others? O Anantavyūha!
This pure Dharma has been brought forth by all the Tathāgatas; those who are able to understand it are exceedingly rare."

“Anantavyūha! Although many among you who have now heard such a Dharma before me are able to understand it well, abide in pure faith, and give rise to superior resolve, they will be rare in future ages—beings who can fully comprehend this Dharma. The only exception is those who, at this very time, have personally made a great vow before me, saying:
‘For the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings in future lives, we shall uphold the teachings of the Tathāgata.’”

If there are those who, having in the past served and made offerings to the Tathāgatas, have developed deep faith and understanding, and who, delighting in and aspiring for the profound principles of the Dharma, wish to hear them skillfully explained—these bodhisattvas shall be able to attain the dhāraṇī-dharma.

O Anantavyūha! Because they have made offerings to Tathāgatas in the past and have further encountered and served immeasurable Buddhas, these individuals possess deep faith and understanding in the principles of the causal nature of the profound Dharma; they are skillful seekers of the Dharma with great resolute conviction, and they proceed toward the vast and profound path seeking the Mahāyāna.
Even those followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle who have grown weary of the triple world and diligently practice the profound Dharma—none of these people have ever heard this most profound Dharma before.

Anantavyūha! For the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to these sentient beings, and so that they may realize the profound, vast, immeasurable, and difficult-to-see, difficult-to-understand awakening of the knowledge of all modes, the Tathāgata further proclaims this profound Dharma.
This is not the domain of those foolish, unlearned individuals who cling to their attachments and do not seek the Dharma;

rather, it is the place of reliance for those who practice according to reason, who are fully endowed with roots of goodness, who feel great dread toward even the slightest transgression, and who seek liberation from all fears.

“Anantavyūha! The Tathāgata now constantly expounds the Dharma for you and the world of gods and humans without ever becoming weary. This is because when the Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he diligently cultivated and studied this profound Dharma for immeasurable billions of kalpas; having completed his cultivation and study, he dedicated it through skillful means, thinking:

‘How may I turn the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings, and how may I manifest supreme great wisdom for the sake of sentient beings, so that the lineage of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge shall never be interrupted?’”

"Anantavyūha! This is due to the power of the Tathāgata’s former vows, in order that all lineages of spiritual potential (*gotra*) may not be interrupted; and by the majestic empowerment of these dhāraṇī phrases, he has revealed and expounded this profound Dharma so that it may spread widely, enabling all sentient beings to gain entry into the Buddha-dharma, ensuring that the lineage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-gotra*) remains unbroken, and illuminating and proclaiming these teachings of the Dharma."

Anantavyūha! You who now wish to follow and learn from the Tathāgata, when there are sentient beings who long for the Dharma, you should reveal and expound it to them without giving rise to weariness or fatigue.

“Anantavyūha! Just as the Bodhisattvas have heard the Dharma, they shall extensively expound all dharmic practices within the great assembly; by means of this, they shall draw near to the Buddha’s wisdom and be able to swiftly realize and attain the gateways of dhāraṇī.”
By virtue of realizing the dhāraṇī, one is able to receive and uphold this "Radiant and Pure Dharma-gate" with little effort. O Anantavyūha! The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure;

if the intrinsic nature of phenomena is neither associated nor dissociated, neither abiding in combination nor not in combination, then among all phenomena there is no phenomenon whatsoever. If there is nothing that exists, then there is no locus that can be pointed out or explained, except for the exhaustion of causes. Because causes are exhausted, there is detachment; because of detachment, there is cessation.
For the sake of bringing sentient beings to full understanding, I teach that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is their fundamental nature.
In that state, there is no cause, and thus no exhaustion of causes; because there is no exhaustion of causes, there is neither departure nor cessation.
Anantavyūha! Behold how the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is thus pure; if there were anyone who perceived the Tathāgata by means of the Dharma, they would have an impure vision of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? The Tathāgata is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
The Tathāgata does not abide even in the slightest dharma, much less in what is non-dharma.
It is impossible for one who abides in what is not the Dharma;
for the Tathāgata transcends all indicative phenomena and is inexpressible, because all speech is utterly pure.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is most profoundly deep, vast, and immeasurable. "Anantavyūha!
Thus, the Tathāgata cannot be represented by form, nor can he be represented by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
The Tathāgata is neither liberated through the exhaustion of form, nor liberated through the exhaustion of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Consequently, the Tathāgata transcends all designations; he is neither associated with nor dissociated from phenomena such as form, yet he is universally liberated from all conditioned and unconditioned things. He gives rise to no discrimination and is free from conceptual proliferation.

The Tathāgata does not associate with the grasping of form, nor does he associate with the grasping of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he has forever severed the root of all aggregates of grasping, and is likewise detached from the root of all phenomena.

This means being without conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), neither entering nor exiting, having transcended the torrential flood; it is not abiding in the supreme cognitive realm of the Buddhas, yet it is also not non-abiding.
One should say that the Tathāgata does not abide in even the slightest phenomenon, neither grasping nor relinquishing.
As it is with the Tathāgata, so it is with the teaching of the Dharma.
Because the Tathāgata is non-associated, the Dharma of the Tathāgata is also non-associated.
As it is with the Dharma of the Tathāgata, so it is with all phenomena.

In accordance with the principle of reality as it is, all dharmas are suchness; therefore, the World-Honored One has taught that all dharmas are entirely true suchness (*tathatā*). The suchness of all dharmas and the true suchness of the Buddha are neither two nor distinct, neither identical nor different.
The Tathāgata abides in the dharma of non-conceptualization, for he is not subject to false imagination. Anantavyūha!
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he never transcends all dharmas.
Why is this? Because there is not even the slightest dharma that can be transcended.
O Boundless Adornment!

At that certain time, the Tathāgata realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet at that time, there was truly no dharma whatsoever that could be apprehended, because all dharmas and their attendant phenomena are unapprehendable. He gave rise to no conceptual discrimination, nor did he give rise to thoughts of dharma or non-dharma, or of mental construction. He neither dwelt upon nor established himself within that intrinsically pure nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
When one thus understands and discerns phenomena, there is neither an understanding nor a discerner. O Anantavyūha!
These words of the ultimate truth that have been proclaimed are the "non-word" word of the Tathāgata, because the word is utterly pure.

For this reason, all bodhisattvas attain the wisdom that purifies all phrases; by means of this, they are able to enter the dharani-door of boundless principles, yet there is not even the slightest dharma to be realized or entered, for it neither comes nor goes.
“Anantavyūha! As for what is called a ‘phrase,’ no phrase can be apprehended, because it is not a phrase; thus should one understand all phrases.”
These phrases are phrases of wearying detachment; if they are phrases of wearying detachment, they are phrases of falsity, and if they are phrases of falsity, they are phrases of wearying detachment.

All those phrases are phrases of cessation; if they are phrases of cessation, they are phrases of *tathatā* (suchness), and if they are phrases of *tathatā*, they are phrases of the ultimate. If they are phrases of the ultimate, they are phrases of exhaustion, detachment, and cessation; and if they are phrases of exhaustion, detachment, and cessation, they are phrases of *nirvāṇa*.
If the term "nirvāṇa" were not conventional, there would be no designation of terms nor any teaching or exposition. Anantavyūha!
What is called "a single phrase" enters with equanimity into all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
What is the single phrase?
It is the so-called "phrase of detachment.
Within detachment there is not even the slightest phrase; all phrases are like the phrase of detachment.
Nor are they phrases, because phrases are pure.
If phrases are pure, then nirvāṇa is pure; if nirvāṇa is pure, then phrases are pure.
Thus, all such phrases are inexpressible.
If one attempts to declare or indicate this through words and phrases, those very words cannot be found even when sought throughout the worlds of the ten directions; who, then, would speak to whom?
Therefore, all verbal expressions are entirely empty.
If that were empty, it would have no meaning; one should not engage in conceptual proliferation or discrimination regarding it.
All such phrases and meanings as these that arise are entirely phrases of non-discrimination and phrases free from conceptual proliferation.
Therefore, when a practitioner of meditation seeks and examines all phrases, they should know that these are all for the sake of nirvana as cessation and transcendence.
Such phrases are not different from nirvana, yet they cannot be said to be so; however, it is not that they are not different.

Because all conventional expressions are false, they constitute the phrase of purity; it is taught that skillful designations are not actual designations, and that which is neither a designation nor a non-designation abides in the Middle Way.
If one abides in the Middle Way, there is no conceptual discrimination, because within this state all discrimination has been severed.
When entering into the equality of this dharmatā, one does not engage in even the slightest unwholesome conduct, for nothing can be apprehended.

Thus, one does not practice, nor does one practice universally, nor does one practice with partiality. If one practices in this manner—when the Buddhas declare that for those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle there is not even the slightest dharma to be practiced—it is because they practice the stages of a bodhisattva while abiding in the unsurpassed, pure dhāraṇī.
“Anantavyūha! I shall now proclaim the dhāraṇī phrases.
By means of these phrases, may all bodhisattvas attain dhāraṇīs and be able to reveal the boundless treasury of the Dharma.”

It should be said that these abide in the stage of non-contention (*araṇā-bhūmi*) because they are able to crush the arguments of others, because they are utterly tranquil, and because they extensively expound the Dharma.
Among these, what are the dhāraṇī-phrases of those dharma-gates?
Tadyathā jaye vijaye ukye.

These are the phrases that define and explain the dhāraṇī.

By means of these phrases, all bodhisattvas are able to recollect the entire Dharma-treasury of immeasurable Tathāgatas; they are also able to reveal and expound it for the sake of all sentient beings while abiding in the stage of non-contention (araṇā-vihāra); furthermore, they are able to enter into the skillful methods of all meanings, phrases, and principles, and are well able to comprehend immeasurable, vast, and diverse wisdom-awakenings, such that all their aspirations are fully realized.
