Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Second Part of the First Chapter on the Unsurpassed Dhāraṇī from the *Anantavyūha-parivarta*.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Anantavyūha, saying:

“I shall now explain the distinctions of the principles and the skillful wisdom of those dhāraṇī-gates, so that all bodhisattvas may attain the skillful means of dhāraṇīs; by realizing this, they shall be able to understand the skillful principles of the secrets that accord with the Dharma.”
How is this thoroughly understood? O Anantavyūha!
It is through the dhāraṇī of forms seen by the eye, up to the dhāraṇī-gate of phenomena known by the mind.
Anantavyūha! What is the dhāraṇī gate of the external phenomena that are grasped by the six internal phenomena? Anantavyūha!

If bodhisattvas, having seen forms with their eyes, through the power of wisdom that cannot be eclipsed and through skill in mindfulness, are neither deluded nor forgetful, they thoroughly understand and maintain that all forms are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, unstable, and entirely exhausted, detached, and ceased.
By means of this, one is further able to refrain from clinging to a self or non-self regarding the internal eye-element, skillfully abiding in the purity of the sense-base of the eye.

Because one does not grasp at forms as objects of perception, one is able to purify the gateways of dhāraṇī; through skillfully observing exhaustion, weariness, detachment, and cessation, one is free from conceptual proliferation.

Through skill in the dhāraṇī of non-proliferation, they abide in the absence of false conceptualization and the lack of accumulation; within the path they traverse, they are able to relinquish the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena known by them, remaining free from discrimination.

Because they attain purity through seeing things as they truly are, they are also able to recollect all phenomena as being like illusions; when they attain mastery over the purity of both subject and object consciousness and achieve dhāraṇī, they are well able to grasp the vast aggregate of wisdom that is uncommon to the world.

Thus, to speak briefly, this extends even to the dharma-dhāraṇī-gate of what is known by the mind. Having understood dharmas with the mind, the bodhisattva—by virtue of an invincible power of wisdom and skill in mindfulness that prevents confusion or forgetfulness—is able to retain all dharmas: their impermanence, arising and ceasing, non-abiding, exhaustion, weariness, detachment, cessation, and extinction.

Abiding in the internal sense-base (*manāyatana*) through dhāraṇī, one does not cling to either self or non-self; being skilled in abiding within the sphere of mental consciousness, one is able to skillfully contemplate the dexterity of dhāraṇī, and subsequently becomes well-established in the purity of the sense-base of mind.
Because one does not grasp at external phenomena, one is able to attain the gateways of pure dhāraṇī.

Since internal and external phenomena, as well as other fetters and afflictions, are no longer associated with one, one is able to contemplate them according to their nature as exhaustion, weariness, detachment, and cessation, and thus refrains from engaging in conceptual proliferation.
Through skill in the *dhāraṇī* of non-proliferation, one abides in the path of conduct that is free from false conceptualization and without accumulation, thereby being able to relinquish it.

Regarding the mind, mental consciousness, and all cognizable phenomena, there is no proliferation and no arising of discrimination; because one attains purity through seeing things as they truly are, one is able to recollect all phenomena as being like illusions. Furthermore, by means of the skill in the purity of consciousness and its objects, one is able to maintain the *dhāraṇī* and to gather the extraordinary merit and wisdom that are superior to those of the world.

Furthermore, one is thus able, regarding all phenomena—past, future, and present, as well as internal and external—to grasp skillful means through the power of wisdom that accords with the meaning of things; thereby, one does not give rise to the view of causelessness regarding even the slightest phenomenon.

They do not give rise to the view of conditions regarding causes, nor do they give rise to the view of causes regarding conditions; they understand that all phenomena are mutually non-associated and enter into the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as it truly is. This intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure and successively quiescent.

If all phenomena were to abide by virtue of being mutually supported, maintained according to their respective categories, and through universal support and common association, one should know that those phenomena do not abide by means of mutual support or common association; they are unarisen and unproduced, do not undergo transmigration, and the meaning they possess cannot be attained through verbal expression.

All phenomena are each of a different nature; they are neither associated nor dissociated. Because all phenomena lack an agent who acts as a creator, they are devoid of a life-principle (*jīva*), devoid of a sentient being (*sattva*), and devoid of a person (*pudgala*). These words of the Dharma are neither according to reality nor not according to reality, for all phenomena are not grasped; they are identical to *nirvāṇa*, free from attachment, having severed attachment, and being far removed from attachment.
Anantavyūha! This is the skillful mastery of the various distinctions in the exposition of dhāraṇīs by all bodhisattvas.
Just as with internal and external phenomena, one should understand all phenomena in this way.

When this was said, those bodhisattvas abandoned internal designations and did not grasp at external ones; they were able to observe that there is neither beginning nor end, and yet they remained mounted upon the wheel of birth and death, fallen into the world, entering the chamber of ignorance and dwelling within the shell of ignorance, wandering throughout all realms.
Although they thus revolve in the cycle of birth and death, within it neither birth and death nor a truly real wheel of birth and death can be found.

Even though they follow along with the revolution of the cycle of birth and death and are found to have fallen into the world, because sentient beings cannot understand these phenomena, they wander and run about throughout the cycle of birth and death; furthermore, being unable to comprehend their own delusions and inversions, they conceive the notion of "sentient beings" where there are no sentient beings.

If sentient beings are bound by the perception of a self, they are unable to understand all phenomena; they follow and enter into states of destruction and utter destruction, becoming attached through the grasping of emptiness.
The Buddha told Anantavyūha:

"If bodhisattvas are able to understand this Dharma, they will swiftly attain the gateway to the Dharma that accords with the light of wisdom, purify their eloquence, cultivate patience, and be able to diligently give rise to great compassion. With a mind free from weariness, they will skillfully abide in it; they will expound secret words and skillful means, and will also be able to comprehend the various names, distinctions, and most excellent expressions of all dharmas."

According to whatever he recalls, he can skillfully expound upon his former abodes without the slightest contradiction, causing all sentient beings to abide in non-contention and enabling him to destroy all the doctrines of external paths.

When he teaches the Dharma to destroy the various darknesses of sentient beings, he is praised by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of immeasurable worlds in the ten directions; he emits the light of the Dharma as an inconceivable donor of the Dharma, skillfully revealing the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas without confusion, and is able to embrace sublime great vows, fulfilling them all according to his aspirations, and attaining inconceivable skillful means.

It causes the inclinations of all sentient beings to be awakened and enables the manifestation of the causes of the past and future limits, as well as the manifestation of the skillful means of going and coming.

Boundless Adornment: herein, a bodhisattva should diligently cultivate the samādhi-gates that can give rise [to these qualities]; having cultivated them, they are able to realize and enter the dhāraṇī-gates.

Having attained mastery over the gates of dhāraṇī, they are able to expound upon all secret, vast, and diverse names, as well as enter into the wisdom regarding these diverse names. They are able to accord with and enter profound principles, skillfully understanding the manifestations of verbal expression so that not the slightest doubt arises anywhere. Without relying on the instruction of others, they abide in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).

Anantavyūha! If bodhisattvas are able to skillfully arouse courageous and vigorous diligence, desiring out of compassion for all sentient beings to seek the knowledge of all dharmas and attain realization and penetration, it will not be difficult for them to achieve all vehicles without exception, to obtain the great wisdom of a Buddha that transcends all worldly wisdom, and to attain the ultimately pure wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

“Anantavyūha! Regarding all the dharmas contained within this chapter on the Profound Expedient Means of the Dharani-Gate, which have been revealed and initiated for the sake of gathering in all bodhisattvas, I shall now speak so as to bring about universal awakening in all bodhisattvas, enabling them to skillfully grasp secret teachings, to fully comprehend the meaning of all speech and sounds in whatever they do, and further to realize the wisdom of skillful means regarding the various levels of discerning insight.”
"What are those dharmas possessed by them? O Anantavyūha!

These bodhisattvas, possessing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and abiding in the power of the empowerment of the true reality (*satya*), are able to increase the skillful means of giving; they seek the dharma that is without 'mine' and without grasping, and they cultivate skillful means to realize the true principle of all dharmas. They attain the non-retrogressive dharma and dwell securely on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*); they swiftly become fully endowed with unimpeded eloquence (*apratihata-pratibhāna*), and their wisdom expands like the great ocean."

Anantavyūha! In future times, there will be no other persons capable of reverently receiving and upholding this Dharma, except for those bodhisattvas who seek the profound and true Dharma; those who, with a superior mind of aspiration and desire, wish to reveal the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma; and those whose intentions are disciplined and who engage in right reflection. Such individuals, by diligently training in this profound Dharma and entering this principle, will be able to understand its explanations through various synonyms, and they will also be able to understand the self-nature and fundamental nature of all phenomena.
“Anantavyūha! Even if the Tathāgata were to expound all dharmas by means of various names, he would not contradict the fundamental nature and intrinsic nature of those dharmas.”
The Tathāgata reveals that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-contradictory, teaching that all phenomena are without fabrication.
In whatever he proclaims, there is neither that which is spoken nor a speaker.

Anantavyūha! The Tathāgata has attained the supreme perfection of skillful exposition; yet, for the Tathāgata, there is not even the slightest dharma to be obtained, nor is there anything subsequently obtained, nor is there anything obtained universally.
The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma not for the sake of abiding in even the slightest phenomenon, nor for the sake of abandoning it, nor for the sake of its arising.
Furthermore, it is neither for the sake of attaining even a small portion of phenomena, nor for the sake of not attaining them; the Tathāgata acts through non-attainment.
The Tathāgata neither acts nor does not act, nor should it be said that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, act in accordance with reality.
Why is this? Because there is not even the slightest dharma that can be called a "Tathāgata."
This is the Tathāgata abiding in such an abiding and practicing such a practice.
If that Tathāgata is called "Tathāgata" by way of a name, then the Tathāgata is neither different from the name nor not different from it.
Because they are neither different nor not different, one should not say that the Tathāgata comes or goes.
The Tathāgata is not one who engages in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); he has transcended conceptual proliferation, yet there is no transcending.
The Tathāgata does not transcend [the Tathāgata-nature], nor does the Tathāgata exist apart from transcendence.
Thus, the Tathāgata and the Tathāgata-nature are neither identical nor separate; the same applies to the non-false nature and the unchanging nature.
Thus, while praising the essential nature of the Tathāgata, there is not even the slightest dharma that is revealed, expounded, or manifested.
The Tathāgata has realized the true intrinsic nature of all dharmas; yet the intrinsic nature of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed, because all dharmas are non-existent.
In this way, the Tathāgata teaches that all dharmas have no activity and no transformation; they are neither born nor extinguished, neither emerge nor depart, because all dharmas are ultimately pure.

It is neither non-attainment nor universal attainment; regarding all phenomena, there is nothing to be attained. Because there is nothing to be attained, there is nothing to be realized. Thus, not even the slightest phenomenon can be found.
If a phenomenon were obtainable, there would have to be a recipient among all phenomena.
Since there is no recipient, one should know that because all phenomena are unarisen, there is no one who obtains them.

The name of the Tathāgata is also a conventional designation established by the holy teaching; because the nature of such verbal expression is pure, the noble ones do not apprehend even the slightest phenomenon therein.

However, even for a noble one (ārya), there is neither dharma nor non-dharma; there is no dharma called "noble" or "non-noble," nor is there even the slightest dharma that is associated with them or will be associated with them.
One should understand all that the Tathāgata has spoken herein, and furthermore, one should not follow along with worldly conventions.
The Tathāgata is able to speak of both the Dharma and the non-Dharma, yet he does not establish the existence of either Dharma or non-Dharma.
The Tathāgata can speak of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, yet he does not establish the existence of wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas].
The Tathāgata can speak of all dharmas, yet he does not establish the existence of all dharmas.
The Tathāgata is able to teach the Dharma as being without representation, nor does he establish the representation of existence or non-existence. "Anantavyūha!
This profound Dharma taught by the Tathāgata cannot be understood by those who lack pure karma."
If there are those who aspire to seek unsurpassed bodhi and seek liberation within the cycle of birth and death, they should awaken to and understand the Dharma taught by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

Anantavyūha! If bodhisattvas can comprehend this Dharma, they should be free from hesitation, neither grasping nor rejecting; they should not perceive even the slightest dharma arising or ceasing; they should be neither characterized by conceptual proliferation nor devoid of it—then they will be able to expound this true Dharma.
Within this exposition of the true Dharma, one should likewise not cling to it.

Anantavyūha! It is, for example, like Sumeru, the king of mountains, which serves as a basis for the palaces used by sentient beings who possess merit and roots of goodness, and within which those beings experience joy.

In this way, in this way, those bodhisattvas who have cultivated roots of goodness are able to hear and receive this teaching on the accumulation of the treasury of Dharma; by means of this treasury of Dharma, bodhisattvas are able to attain the wisdom of all-knowledge.

Anantavyūha! This dharma of the sūtra is able to accord with and enter into the supreme knowledge of dharmas; it is for the purpose of revealing the dhāraṇī of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-treasury that this dhāraṇī is thus disseminated, for it is capable of encompassing all vast and true dharmas.
All the dharmas taught by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, flow forth from this boundless dharanī-gate; because this dharanī is intended to purify all dharma-gates, the Tathāgata reveals and expounds it.
This dhāraṇī can encompass all dharmas such as the sūtras; it is neither formed nor destroyed, and it is without beginning, middle, or end.
This dhāraṇī is protected by the mindfulness of the Tathāgatas, pervading the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, and is able to perform immeasurable and boundless buddha-works.
Anantavyūha! Within this first chapter on dhāraṇīs, in the section on the meaning and the section on the principles, all dharmas are able to be subsumed. Anantavyūha!

Those bodhisattvas therein who wish to awaken to and understand this teaching; who wish to cause the flow of the Dharma to remain uninterrupted; who wish to enter the seal of non-abiding in all phenomena; who wish to awaken to and understand the secret gateways that are without obstruction; who wish to give rise to and apply themselves toward great diligence in practice; and who wish to awaken to and understand the nature and characteristics of all phenomena by expounding this Dharma—should uphold the verbal teachings proclaimed by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Having already received and upheld [this teaching], one should accordingly understand all secret terminology.

For those who wish to enter into the wisdom of explaining words according to their general characteristics; for those who wish to awaken to and understand the principles of the distinctions among all phenomena as they are explained; and for those who wish to recollect the wisdom that discriminates all phenomena—[the Buddha] establishes the ultimate truth for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, skillfully bestowing it upon them according to their individual faculties and dispositions so that they may obtain benefit.

Whether praising the Dharma, circulating the Dharma, or expounding the Dharma, they do so with a mind of provisions, out of compassion and for the benefit of others, seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, and they do not give rise to attachment toward even the slightest phenomenon.

Because they do not cling, there is nothing to be grasped; nor do they contemplate the non-dual wisdom of phenomena, nor do they manifest internal or external wisdom. They do not give rise to complacency regarding even the slightest dharma, nor should they seek superior wisdom through inferior diligence.
Diligently cultivate all profound dharmas and explain all difficult questions according to their true meaning.
One should abide in both self-benefit and the benefit of others, skillfully observe the notions of self and other, and enter into the realization that all phenomena are entirely without self.

Once I am purified, I accordingly enter into the purity of all phenomena; I delight in revealing and expounding the verbal teachings, and whether questioned or unasked, I harbor no stinginess regarding even the slightest dharma.
A bodhisattva should cultivate these four immeasurable minds:
"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I shall provide them with superior gifts and the most excellent gifts—namely, the treasury of the unsurpassed Dharma-jewel."

I shall now cause all sentient beings to be endowed with the dharma-treasure of the ineffable; even if sentient beings commit various grave evils, I shall never give rise to a mind of stinginess regarding the Dharma toward them, but shall remain free from all parsimony and be able to practice relinquishment as a master of the Dharma-gift.
I shall now perform the work of a Tathāgata and the work of omniscience, causing all sentient beings to cast off their heavy burdens.
Amidst the great torrent, I shall ferry across the multitudes with the ship of Dharma, enabling sentient beings to obtain all requisites for peace and happiness.

A bodhisattva should, by means of such compassion, give rise to awakened wisdom and swiftly realize the sublime Dharma. Within this gateway of dhāraṇīs of the sūtra, they should expound the various distinctions of the dhāraṇīs of all phenomena; thus they shall achieve the transcendence of birth and death, not be subsumed by the treatises of others, be able to shatter all the arguments of external paths, and subdue the armies of Māra. Desiring to destroy the nature of contentious debate, they should abide in this manner.
“Anantavyūha! This dharanī gateway is sustained by all Tathāgatas and skillfully brings about mindfulness.

It is, for example, like a bodhisattva in his final birth who dwells among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens; there, all the gods in the Tuṣita palace serve and make offerings to him, and all sentient beings give rise to love and joy, thereby maturing their roots of goodness and gathering supreme merit.”

With only one more birth remaining, his aggregates of merit from generosity and ethical discipline are fully perfected and pure; he has accomplished all supreme aggregates of wisdom that cannot be equaled by any sentient being within this trichiliocosm. He outshines all the roots of virtue possessed by all sentient beings and is honored and praised by all beings, attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) before his very eyes.

When that Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven to Jambudvīpa, he manifests his birth within a great city in the central land, a most excellent and wondrous place free from fear, amidst a vast assembly of all sentient beings, so that all beings may gaze upon him, prostrate before him, and offer him worship and respect.
This gateway of the dhāraṇī sūtra is likewise: it enters into all phenomena and dwells therein; all phenomena arise from this and also cease within this.

Once the bodhisattva has attained stable abiding in this, they mature and increase in all dharmas and attain stable abiding therein; they attain mastery over all dharmas because they act as their sovereign.

When a bodhisattva receives their final body and is born among human beings, by means of the power of the samādhi of the seal that non-contemplatively perceives all phenomena, they universally observe all sentient beings and thoroughly examine the entirety of the trichiliocosm.

Having attained the flavor of the supreme essence (*amṛta*) of the *dhāraṇī* of the Dharma, they abide well within the sphere of vast wisdom with a magnanimous mind; they never crave any sensual pleasures, amusements, or articles of utility, nor do they seek after any defiled phenomena characterized by beauty or continuity.

By means of the awakening that dwells in that samādhi of emptiness, one is able to skillfully examine all phenomena; accordingly, one attains the skillful means of signlessness and remains without attachment to anything whatsoever.

They are able to thoroughly understand that all conditioned phenomena within the three realms are nothing but faults and afflictions; they are not to be clung to with craving, but should instead seek liberation, swiftly attaining the realm of peace and supreme tranquility, as well as the realm of sublime deliverance and transcendence.

Yet, they do not dwell upon nor cling to that consciousness; they observe its arising and ceasing, its accumulation and dispersal, and its dissolution and decay. Toward all sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion; for the sake of their maturation, they develop the awakening of renunciation. Through the principles of awakening and appropriate skillful means, they are able to enter into accord with the most supreme wisdom.
Mindfully recollecting all sentient beings, they attain mastery through skillful means, and accordingly obtain the skillful method of the *dhāraṇī* that is unimpeded regarding all phenomena.
With skillful wisdom, he discerns and examines all sentient beings, and thoroughly investigates the definitive principles of inconceivable phenomena.
Although he is young, handsome, and beautiful, he has never felt attachment toward the objects of sensual desire.

Having renounced all possessions, treasures, articles of enjoyment, kinsmen, and relatives, he reflects and contemplates, seeking tranquility with a mind of weary detachment; having departed from the household life, he proceeds toward the homeless state.

Having already left the household life, he was able to accomplish inconceivable awakening and profound skillful means; according to his actions, he accumulated the provisions for enlightenment and proceeded toward the site of supreme bodhi. In accordance with his vows, he adorned himself and attained the supreme crown of the most excellent ones—the profound skillful means of the unsurpassed dharani-seal.

By means of this skillful method of the gateway of the pure dhāraṇī, one attains the wisdom of the self-nature of all phenomena, as well as the skillful mastery of the unimpeded knowledge of all-knowledge that universally sustains them.

Having attained the dhāraṇī-door of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and having subsequently attained the definitive and thoroughly purified knowledge of all modes of knowledge, they abide in the power of the empowerment of the unsurpassed knowledge of all modes of knowledge; they are able to turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma, and they are also able to attain, in accordance with that, all the dharmas of the skillful speech and terminology of the knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharmajñāna*).
Just as the brilliant light of the midday sun shines forth, so too does the light of the sound of this Dharma illuminate all classes of gods and humans.
Boundless Adornment!
When a bodhisattva dwells in the dhāraṇī of the knowledge of all-knowledge, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The distinctions in the meanings of the phrases of this dhāraṇī-gate are such that they cannot be known by other bodhisattvas.
Only when a bodhisattva in his last birth sits at the site of enlightenment does he attain the manifestation of this dhāraṇī through pure awakening, self-realized without a teacher.

It is just as when a bodhisattva, for the sake of awakening, accumulates roots of goodness throughout immeasurable eons; having practiced the holy life for a long night and attained profound dharma-patience, the mind of great compassion finally manifests before him out of pity for all sentient beings.
“Anantavyūha! By means of this dhāraṇī, a bodhisattva shall sit at the site of enlightenment and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.”
I cannot now show or explain this to you; it is when you have attained the wisdom of a bodhisattva that manifests before you and you are able to realize that dharma.
At that time, all bodhisattvas will naturally understand it for themselves.
At that time, the Bodhisattva attained the gate of boundlessness, the gate of immeasurability, the gate of causes, and the gate of the incomparable, all of which appeared before him.

These gates he attained cannot be fully described; they transcend the world and are not shared by any devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas. He has reached the most supreme and pure dharmas: the knowledge of all-knowledge and spontaneous wisdom.

By means of this, the bodhisattva is able to enter the pure, spontaneous wisdom and turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma, gradually causing immeasurable sentient beings to attain the unsurpassed wisdom of omniscience.

Because they have attained purity regarding all gateways of dharmas and the gateway of nirvāṇa, they reveal and expound immeasurable varieties of skillful principles; they are able to give rise to skill in maintaining the aggregates (*skandha*), and can also manifest the wisdom of skill in purifying the aggregates. It is the same for the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to give rise to and enter the Dharma-gate of the Noble Truths, and are also able to manifest the wisdom of skillful means regarding the purity of the Noble Truths.

They can also cause the arising of the distinct skillful means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharmas*), and are also able to manifest the wisdom of the purity of these factors of enlightenment.
They are able to initiate and maintain the skillful wisdom of śamatha and vipaśyanā, and they are also able to manifest the pure skillfulness of maintaining śamatha and vipaśyanā.

Furthermore, they are able to give rise to the wisdom of skillfulness regarding the dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and samāpattis, and they are also able to manifest the purity of skillfulness regarding dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis.

Furthermore, they are able to initiate the skillful wisdom that maintains non-delusion so that its merit is not in vain, and they are also able to manifest the pure wisdom that maintains non-delusion so that its merit is not in vain.

Furthermore, they are able to initiate the wisdom that maintains the knowledge of weariness, exhaustion, and non-arising; they are also able to manifest the wisdom of skillful means that maintains the purity of weariness, exhaustion, and non-arising.
Furthermore, one can give rise to the wisdom of skillfulness regarding the liberation of the Vidyādharas, and can also manifest the pure skillfulness of the liberation of the Vidyādharas.

One can expound upon the gateway to Great Nirvāṇa and maintain the meaning of all phrases and sentences. Having abandoned [attachment to] skillful means, one proclaims and expresses the conditioned and unconditioned, the out-flowing and non-out-flowing, and the mundane and supramundane dharmas through immeasurable names; this is because the Dharma-gate is pure.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he reveals the unsurpassed, definitive Dharma and maintains the causes for pure and subtle wisdom. "Anantavyūha!

The Tathāgata has taught this great dhāraṇī of universal retention as a skillful means, so that by the power of the expertise of the dhāraṇī of omniscience, one may abide securely; and in accordance with the original vows of all sentient beings, he demonstrates such practices, causing them to enter the various distinctions of the principles of realization."

He is skillfully able to reveal the unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of the power of dhāraṇīs, and can pour down and sprinkle the rain of Dharma to moisten and satisfy all withered sentient beings, bestowing the sublime Dharma upon them all so that they may be fully satisfied.
You all should follow the training of the Tathāgata; you must not oppose this profound and definitive Dharma.

Regarding this Great Dhāraṇī of the Knowledge of All-Knowledge, before long you shall attain the Dhāraṇī of Universal Retention and Sovereign Abiding, and you shall bring about such immeasurable benefit for all sentient beings as I do now.
"You all should reveal and expound this dhāraṇī of the profound wisdom that definitively establishes all phenomena through immeasurable alternative names. Anantavyūha!"
In this regard, one should aspire for resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and must not abandon the accumulations for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
How should one aspire for resolute conviction?

It means that bodhisattvas should understand that all phenomena are unborn and unceasing, unmoving and non-abiding, neither coming nor going, and empty and quiescent by nature; they should not even cling to that emptiness, let alone give rise to thoughts of clinging to signs (*nimitta*).
Within that emptiness, there is no perception of signs.

If within that emptiness there were no signs, one would be able to enter into what the Tathāgata has taught: that conditioned phenomena are empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self, and free from all notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.

Thus, this emptiness is neither stained nor unstained, neither defiled nor undefiled, neither deluded nor undeluded, neither desirable nor undesirable; it does not abide in emptiness, nor does it pervade it, nor is it established therein.

If one is weary of and detached from emptiness, that is itself cessation, free from discrimination; it is without pervasive discrimination, without superior discrimination, without universal discrimination, and without effort, such that there is not even the slightest dharma to be grasped.

Intrinsic purity is the very nature and essence of all phenomena; the intrinsic nature of all conditioned things is empty, and this applies likewise to all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, the conditioned and the unconditioned, and the mundane and the supramundane.

When a bodhisattva embraces such resolute conviction, they attain entry into liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and are able to gather the provisions for enlightenment that constitute the locus of universal, pure, and stainless liberation.
What are called the provisions for enlightenment? They are:

purity of ethical discipline, purity of wisdom, purity of samādhi, purity of liberation, and purity of the knowledge and vision of liberation; as well as the purity of the perfection of giving, the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline, the purity of the perfection of patience, the purity of the perfection of diligence, the purity of the perfection of meditation, and the purity of the perfection of wisdom.
If that is pure, it is universally pure; if it is universally pure, it is the stainless Dharma-gate.

The mind of intrinsic purity shines with radiance and is free from afflictions; yet that mind abides eternally in its original nature of emptiness and stillness, and thus lacks even such radiance. The three types of defilement caused by adventitious secondary afflictions are all unreal, empty, and non-existent.
Thus, the nature of the mind is not associated with either afflictions or purity.
Why is this? Because this mind is non-dual and lacks any division; its intrinsic nature is pure.

If one can thus understand the nature of the mind—that it is not defiled by the afflictions, that it is neither internal nor external nor in between, and is entirely ungraspable, existing only through the combination of the causes and conditions of deluded thought—then one has truly understood.
Although the arising of the mind occurs, it cannot be seen; even when sought throughout the ten directions, it is utterly unobtainable. Furthermore, there is no mind that can see the mind.
Thus, the object of perception and the mind do not conjoin, nor does the mind conjoin with the object of perception.
Nor are causal conditions associated with the mind, nor does the mind associate with causal conditions.
It is solely by virtue of the mind that all those phenomena are associated with the mind.
All phenomena that are associated with the mind do not know one another, nor can they be seen; how much more so those phenomena that are not associated with the mind?
When contemplating and investigating through the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is not even the slightest thing that can be said to be either associated or dissociated.
Why is this? There is not even the slightest dharma that is associated with or dissociated from another dharma; all dharmas are quiescent by their very nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, self-nature itself is neither associated with nor dissociated from any thing whatsoever. The self-nature of all dharmas is precisely their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*); and that which is the fundamental nature is devoid of self-nature.
You should now know this: it is impossible to attain the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena through verbal expression.

Among all phenomena, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be called the fundamental nature or intrinsic nature of phenomena; the fundamental nature of all phenomena is entirely empty, and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is a non-nature. That which is empty and a non-nature is a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*); because it is signless, it attains purity.

If emptiness is without intrinsic nature, it cannot be indicated by means of signs; just as emptiness, being without intrinsic nature, cannot be indicated by signs, so it is with all phenomena as well.
This emptiness is without intrinsic nature; it is neither defiled nor pure, yet it is the fundamental nature of all phenomena.
If it is the fundamental nature of all phenomena, it is not established by means of defilement or purity; it is without abiding and without arising.
“Anantavyūha! You should now contemplate all phenomena as being without abiding and without arising, without anything established, and pure by their very nature.”
How is it that sentient beings are deluded therein?
It is because they ride upon the wheel of falsehood in this world and are thus deluded by that wheel of falsehood.

As for what is called "riding," there is neither a vehicle nor is there no vehicle; yet this world rides upon the wheel of space and is bound by that wheel of space, though the wheel of space itself is non-existent.
These sentient beings are deluded by great ignorance, yet within this there is neither ignorance nor delusion. O Anantavyūha!
“Observe, Anantavyūha, that because sentient beings are deluded, they are unable to understand this Dharma and remain stuck in contentious debate.
To remain stuck in contentious debate, Anantavyūha, is itself to remain unestablished.”
However, because all worldly beings are deluded, they are unable to realize that this very state is pure.
That which is non-abiding is itself called abiding; thus, it is the non-abiding of pure roots of goodness.

Anantavyūha! Thus, this secret Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; it can be realized only by those like you who have practiced wholesome dharmas throughout the long night.
“Anantavyūha! The Tathāgata has said that one who dwells in contentious debate does not truly dwell.
What, then, constitutes dwelling?

That which is called "unwholesome" is, in fact, non-existent. If, within this non-existence, one cannot discern the lack of distinction between abiding and not abiding, this is what is meant by dwelling in contentious debate.
Furthermore, if one dwells in pure roots of goodness, that is not called "dwelling"; if one does not dwell [in such a state], there is no fault.
Because there is no fault, one is able to understand this Dharma-gate; it is impossible for it not to be pure.

If sentient beings lack wisdom and are shrouded by great afflictions due to their lack of wisdom, they cannot understand even a slight, clear, and conformable teaching; how much less so a secret teaching that is not conformable? If one does not dwell [in such views], then there is purity.
What is meant by "not abiding"?
It means not abiding in wholesome dharmas or the realm of renunciation. Why is this?
There is no realm of departure nor any designation of a realm.
If one does not abide even in the realm of nirvāṇa, this is called attaining nirvāṇa.
This name "nirvāṇa" is merely a conventional designation; such nirvāṇa is nothing that can be attained, nor is there anyone who attains nirvāṇa.
If there were one who attained [it], then after parinirvāṇa there would still be a Tathāgata; if there were no one who attained it, then after parinirvāṇa there would be no Tathāgata.
If, after parinirvāṇa, one says that there is a Tathāgata or that there is no Tathāgata, both are inexpressible. This very inexpressibility is also a provisional designation of the Tathāgata.

There are sentient beings who, failing to diligently practice the profound Dharma, give rise to doubt and confusion. Some may say that if the Tathāgata possesses form, then the Tathāgata must exist after his parinirvāṇa;
others may say that if the Tathāgata is formless, then the Tathāgata must not exist after his parinirvāṇa.
This applies equally to the view that after his passing, the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist.
If a phenomenon is neither born nor extinguished, then after its extinction, one should not say that it exists or that it does not exist.
In the same way, the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished; therefore, even after his extinction, one should not say that he exists or that he does not exist.
Regarding such matters as finitude and infinitude, the Tathāgata says that both are ineffable.
If one speaks of finitude, then there is no middle; if one speaks of a middle, then there is no finitude. That which is called the "middle" is neither existent nor non-existent.
If, moreover, within this [reality] there were both truly existent and truly non-existent, it would then contradict dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

If, furthermore, there were a phenomenon that neither arose from conditions nor was not dependently originated, that phenomenon would be indestructible; whether it be existent or non-existent, neither would be contradictory.
All phenomena that arise from conditions and the very nature of dependent origination are without center or periphery, neither existent nor non-existent.
If they are neither existent nor non-existent, how can they be described?

“Anantavyūha! The Tathāgata dwells therein by means of great skillful means, in order to shatter the shell of ignorance for all sentient beings, revealing and expounding that which does not contradict dependent origination.”

All phenomena enter into dependent origination; if they enter into dependent origination, there is no discourse of middle or extremes. If one is free from verbal expression, there is not even the slightest dharma to be apprehended.

Anantavyūha! You should now observe that the non-existence of phenomena and the absence of limits are called the Middle Way. Because of skillful means, it is said that there is awakened wisdom capable of upholding all phenomena; yet, even that which upholds the phenomena cannot be apprehended. Because it cannot be apprehended, there is no verbal expression.
Anantavyūha! You wise ones should understand it thus:

the true characteristic of all dharmas neither comes nor goes; they are without division and without interruption; they are neither of a single nature nor of different natures. They reach the supreme further shore of all dharmas, such that there is not even the slightest dharma that does not reach that further shore. To reach that further shore is itself nirvana.
All dharmas possess the characteristic of nirvāṇa; therefore, one should know that they cannot be expressed in words, except for the conventional designation of them as the "Middle Way.
This Middle Way is the path leading toward Great Nirvāṇa, yet there is no nirvāṇa that serves as its destination.
If there were a nirvāṇa that was a destination toward which one proceeds, then all phenomena would necessarily have coming and going.
Since the nature of all phenomena is entirely equal, nirvāṇa is therefore called "having no destination."
Anantavyūha! This is called the Middle Way;
yet this Middle Way is not the Middle Way.
Why is this? Because there is neither increase nor decrease, and because it is boundless and without grasping.
If phenomena are boundless, how could they have limits?
That which has no location is the boundless Dharma.
Ordinary beings grasp at what has no location as being a finite place; because they perceive such finite places, they do not attain liberation, for in reality there is no location.
“Anantavyūha! Observe how the Tathāgata, through skillful means and definitive awakened wisdom, is able to expound such a Middle Way. Anantavyūha!”

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have no doubt regarding any phenomenon and possess no loss of mindfulness. The hearts of these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are always in meditative concentration; having attained unimpeded mastery in samādhi, they constantly observe with skillful wisdom. Abiding in the most supreme samāhita, they utter speech that does not dwell in improper places, yet possesses immeasurable knowledge and vision. They preach the pure Dharma, the ultimate Dharma, and the tranquil Dharma; there is nothing left unsaid in what the Tathāgata proclaims.

Anantavyūha! It is like a precious gem named "Various Colors" that exists within the great ocean; although immeasurable and vast currents of water flow into the great ocean, by the fiery power of the gem, the water is consumed and does not overflow.

In this same way, once the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized awakening, he is able to cause the afflictions of sentient beings to be消滅 (extinguished) by the power of his wisdom; it is just like this.

Anantavyūha! If there are further beings who, day after day, proclaim the merit of the Tathāgata’s name, these sentient beings will be able to leave behind darkness and shall gradually attain the burning away of all afflictions.
Thus, for one who recites "Namo Buddha," the vocal karma is not in vain; such vocal karma is called grasping a great torch capable of burning away afflictions.
Furthermore, if there are those who hear the name and title of the Tathāgata or a Buddha, they will be freed from all darkness and become causes for *nirvāṇa* for those sentient beings.
Anantavyūha! For the sake of those who have faith in the Tathāgata, in sentient beings, and for the extinction of the afflictions of all sentient beings, I pour down the rain of Dharma. Anantavyūha!
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is true; because it is true, there is not the slightest dharma that is revealed or expounded, yet in this Dharma there is neither reality nor unreality.
Anantavyūha! The Tathāgata is a speaker of truth; abiding in the Dharma of reality, he is able to expound this dharanī gateway. Anantavyūha!
Who will be able to comprehend this true Dharma?
None other than those bodhisattvas who see according to reality, who possess complete vision, and who perform wholesome deeds; regarding this profound Dharma, no others are capable of comprehension.
“Anantavyūha! Within this meaning, you should conform accordingly.
You yourself should maintain mindfulness toward these dharmas so that they are present before you; do not find pleasure in anything else, nor derive knowledge from others.”
Desiring to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, one should give rise to compliance within this Dharma.
If one gives rise to the patience of compliance within this, then one does not abide in non-compliance.
Anantavyūha! Those beings who have not heard [the Dharma] lack the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) and are unable to understand this teaching of the Dharma.

Furthermore, there are others who follow different views, who travel by divergent paths, who head toward evil destinies, who do not perform wholesome deeds, and who associate with those who practice other divergent ways; they are unable to enter this Dharma-gate.

Anantavyūha! You should now observe this: when this Dharma-light of the Unobstructed Treasury is being proclaimed, all those sentient beings who have not heard it—because their ordinary minds have not been well-tamed and they lack dignified deportment—will, for this reason, remain far removed from such a teaching of the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who are able to cultivate the body, even if they do not possess the patient acceptance that accords with this Dharma, they will still not be separated from it; how much more so for those who can give rise to untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) and, being free from attachment, turn the unobstructed and unhindered wheel of Dharma within this assembly?
Why is this? Because they all abide on the stage of non-obstruction, O Anantavyūha!

For the sake of sentient beings who have perfected roots of goodness, and for those sentient beings sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgata, because I perceive the purity of unimpeded dharmas, and also desiring to benefit and compassionately pity all, I shall expound this gateway of dhāraṇī.

Anantavyūha! If there are those who are able to gain entry into this dharma-gate, you should know that they have already established themselves upon the bodhisattva stages; they will swiftly realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and before long shall receive the prediction of their future enlightenment (bodhi-vyākaraṇa).
Anantavyūha! You all should give rise to resolute conviction in this profound Dharma-gate. Anantavyūha!

You should now know that this Dharma-gate takes as its ground those who are without attachment and those who have attained patient endurance. If there are those who have made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, who have diligently practiced with a devoted mind throughout the long night, who are well-regulated in physical deportment, well-guarded in verbal karma, and well-subdued in mind; who possess equal wisdom that accords with mindfulness, whose minds dwell nowhere, and who skillfully uphold this Dharma—disregarding even their own bodies and lives—such persons will be able to propagate this sutra.

In the future, if there are sentient beings who, for the sake of hearing this Dharma, diligently practice it, such persons will already be difficult to find; how much more so those who are able to write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it until they master it, explain and disseminate it, and expound it extensively for others? Such a person will before long obtain the gate of pure dhāraṇī, swiftly attain pure wisdom, and shall be able to enter the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Anantavyūha! Observe how the Tathāgata, for the sake of enabling all bodhisattvas to attain the knowledge of all modes, reveals and expounds this treasury of Dharma; yet within it, there is not the slightest dharma that he does not expound.
Thus, what has been spoken is spoken without speaking; it can give rise to purity and reveal the gateway to the pure Dharma, wherein all phenomena are equal to the characteristics of empty space.
What is meant by "equality"?
It is because all phenomena are equal to space; yet this space is neither equal nor unequal, and all phenomena are likewise so.

Just as space is boundless, so too are all phenomena; the limits of all phenomena cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they have no boundaries; because they have no boundaries, they are said to be boundless.
If one can abide in this manner within it, this is precisely what is called abiding in the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
To abide in the Dharma of the Tathāgata is to have nothing to say.
If there is nothing to say, one should understand all phenomena according to their provisional names and signs as they correspond; one should not give rise to attachment therein.

If one does not cling, one does not fall into extremes; if one does not fall into extremes, one does not fall into the middle. For if one falls into extremes, one falls into the middle; therefore, one should remain free from both the middle and the extremes.

If one is free from the middle and the extremes, one is free from all things; if one is free from all things, there is nothing to be spoken. By means of this, one attains pure wisdom, remaining without attachment to any phenomena, wherein neither the grasped object nor the grasper exists.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self, and because they are non-apprehendable; for the nature of the self and its own-being do not exist.
It is thus, thus, Anantavyūha!
As the Buddha has taught that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, so he expounds upon the meaning of non-alteration and non-correspondence.
As the Buddha has taught the meaning of suffering inherent in all existence, so he expounds upon the meaning of nirvana and the meaning of weary detachment.

As the Buddha has taught that nirvāṇa is tranquility, so too does he expound upon the meaning of relinquishing all conditioned phenomena—whether by way of their impermanence, their suffering, their selflessness, or their nature as nirvāṇa.
Through such gateways as these, this has been expounded by the Tathāgata; it also reveals the fundamental nature and intrinsic nature of all phenomena. "O Anantavyūha!

The Tathāgata expounds all dharmas through various names, various gateways, and various languages; yet the Tathāgata does not, apart from the intrinsic nature of all dharmas, designate them as being either identical or different. All dharmas are neither identical nor different, for they cannot be seen; thus one swiftly realizes and enters the self-nature of space, proceeding toward the mark of non-existence in all dharmas.
“Anantavyūha! This dharani gateway is initiated because it is the natural purity of all bodhisattvas and their self-natured discipline.”

As for what is called "subduing," it is for the purpose of subduing greed, hatred, and delusion; it is for the purpose of subduing ignorance, and for causing entry into such equanimity. Since that which could subdue greed, hatred, and delusion is itself unapprehendable, this very non-apprehension is subduing.

Anantavyūha! Whether it be greed, hatred, or delusion, when sought through correct reasoning, they cannot be found; for greed, hatred, and delusion are empty, non-existent, false, and unreal. They deceive the foolish and have no place of abiding; likewise, they too have no place of residence and cannot be found.
This greed, hatred, and delusion arise from that and cease within that; their intrinsic nature is empty and quiescent—one should know it thus.
How should one know this?

Just as they do not arise, so they are neither real nor inverted. This greed, hatred, and delusion all have the darkness of ignorance as their primary cause; arising from it and produced by it, they are all entirely false and unreal.
This greed, hatred, and delusion are pure by nature; one who perceives them thus can give rise to the gate of inconceivable purity and can attain the gates of dhāraṇī.

If there are those who are able to contemplate and examine such a Dharma as this, it is called attaining the karma of dhāraṇī and the karma of wisdom; it is called the knowledge of equal realization; it is called the pure provisions for bodhi; it is called the stage of diligence and non-negligence; it is called the stage of subduing arrogance and negligence; it is called the unbreakable precepts, views, and deportment; it is called the purity of the actions of body, speech, and mind; it is called conforming to the characteristics of the wisdom of non-self; it is called that which can sever and extinguish the notion of separation; and it is called the production of immeasurable and boundless skillful means.

“Anantavyūha! You should now observe that within this dharma of liberation through faith and understanding, the intrinsic nature and specific characteristics of all phenomena are revealed and expounded; furthermore, these very gateways of the Dharma reveal that the equality of all phenomena is like the nature of space, such that neither the speaker of the Dharma can be spoken of, nor can the object for which it is spoken of be apprehended.”

Anantavyūha! I now proclaim these gateways of phrases for the entry into awakening of all bodhisattvas; if bodhisattvas train in these, they will be able to attain ocean-like wisdom that is profoundly deep, such that no other treatises can ever overcome them.
They attain the conduct that accords with the destination of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and skillfully expound the essential points of the Dharma without depending on the instruction of others.

They attain inconceivable, impartial wisdom; by virtue of this wisdom, they are free from all attachment and are able to expound these nameless and signless gateways to all dharmas. They draw near to the names and titles of the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) and the self-arisen wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*) of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and they attain the purity of all names and signs. They realize and swiftly master a universal voice, obtaining a pleasing voice, an exquisite voice, and a pure voice. Their speech is trusted and accepted by all sentient beings who approach them to inquire; with decisive wisdom, they are able to provide skillful answers.

That is to say: speech that is timely, speech that is according to principle, speech that is beneficial, speech that is gentle, and speech that is definitive in meaning; by expressing a single meaning, it enables sentient beings to understand many meanings.

Anantavyūha! You should now observe that when bodhisattvas practice in this way, they are able to awaken to the bodhi of all buddhas and attain such immeasurable merit; they sever all craving, hatred, grief, affliction, and delusion, and are able to accomplish what must be done and attain discerning wisdom.

Having thoroughly trained in all things, they have attained the perfection of patience and the quality of non-retrogression; with pure intention, they abide in great vows and address all sentient beings with kind words of greeting.

“Anantavyūha! If bodhisattvas have not diligently practiced, do not diligently practice, or will not diligently practice within this Dharma, they shall possess not even a fraction of the sublime qualities of the Tathāgatas.”

Anantavyūha! If there are bodhisattvas who, within this Dharma, are able to diligently practice and aspire for all things—fulfilling them according to their vows, their practices, their resolute advances, and their inclinations—they will be few, exceedingly few, and most difficult to find.

If there are those who, within this profound Dharma, are able to abide, endure, observe, and discern, they shall realize inexhaustible supernormal powers and great wisdom of supernormal powers, surpassing all mundane knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, boundless knowledge, and immeasurable knowledge.

Anantavyūha! This dhāraṇī gateway of the dharma of renunciation—if there be those who diligently practice and study it—they shall draw near to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and for the sake of all sentient beings, they shall abide in and give rise to great loving-kindness and great compassion, performing the deeds of a Buddha.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Five;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Two: The Dhāraṇī of Renunciation, from the *Anantavyūha-parivarta*. Chapter Two: The Dhāraṇī of Renunciation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, what is called the ‘Dhāraṇī-gate of Renunciation of All Dharmas’?”
The Buddha said:
"Anantavyūha! This is the seal-dharma that transcends all words; all dharmas are entirely contained within it."
What is meant by "entering"?
It is because of equality.
All phenomena enter into equality, yet one does not perceive any phenomenon entering into equality, for it cannot be cognized and cannot be apprehended.
When one does not conceptually differentiate the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as they truly are, all phenomena are entirely subsumed therein, because one is free from both non-action and action.
Because both the written characters and the vocal activity used to expound all phenomena are not, in themselves, real;
since their nature is equal, all written characters and vocal activities are entirely equal.
Among all phenomena, every verbal expression is not in accordance with reality; this is the meaning of the phrase "the suchness of all phenomena.
Both written characters and vocal activity are non-existent; because they do not exist, there is no true revelation or exposition.

That which is called "letters" and "vocal action" is without reality; it is the phrase of non-differentiation among all phenomena, the phrase of non-excellence, and the phrase of non-establishment. This profound dharma cannot be proclaimed.
All phenomena are neither real nor unreal. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena cannot be proclaimed, seen, or attained through words or verbal activity; all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
These dharmas are neither created nor uncreated, neither equal nor unequal, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent; yet they abide in both quiescence and non-quiescence within all dharmas.
That which is called "abiding" neither abides anywhere nor undergoes transformation; furthermore, it does not abide even in the state of non-transformation. Why is this?

Because dharmas have no abiding, they do not enter into numerical calculation; it is not by means of establishing teachings through calculation that one can cause dharmas to enter into numerical calculation.
All verbal activities consisting of written characters and speech cannot be apprehended; they do not abide in any location or in all locations.
Thus, these written characters and verbal activities come from nowhere and go nowhere; they abide neither in the middle nor at the extremes.

Regarding all letters and vocal actions, because action is not action and is not a functional exertion, and because the intrinsic nature of all letters and vocal actions is empty, letters and vocal actions are likewise entirely empty.
Furthermore, because the vocal karma of syllables is empty of other-nature, other-nature is also empty.
Up to: because self-nature and other-nature are empty, self-nature and other-nature are also empty.
Because both self and other are empty, they are quiescent; that which is quiescent is extinguished; and that which is extinguished is the gate of extinction of all phenomena.

The designation "Dharma" is attained through various gateways—whether one speaks of written characters or of vocal action—but none of these gateways can be apprehended, because the gateways are pure and because they are non-existent.

Expounding all phenomena through various gateways, one attains ultimate purity within these gateways and is able to enter all phenomena with equanimity; thus, one becomes weary of and detached from them.
What is weary detachment?
It is the intrinsic nature of craving.
That which is the intrinsic nature of craving is pure; that which is pure is ultimate; and if it is ultimate, how could there be craving?
"What is this so-called teaching? 'O Anantavyūha!
Thus, in brief, is explained the pure dhāraṇī gateway of the dharma-door that is free from conceptual discrimination and free from conceptual proliferation.'"

By entering this gate, one is able to shatter the heavy obscurations of the darkness of ignorance; one is able to recollect, in accordance with mindfulness, the luminous lineage of the Dharma; one attains the dhāraṇī gate of the pure Dharma-eye that enters into the light of all phenomena; and one is able to realize the dharma-gate of expounding the distinctions of syllables.
By means of this gateway, one enters into the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) and draws near to all the Tathāgatas.

Among all phenomena, one becomes courageous and valiant, capable of shattering the heterodoxies and subduing the armies of Māra. One causes all sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness, enters the secret Dharma of the Tathāgata, and accordingly attains the gateways of Dharma and the gateways of dhāraṇī.
By means of this Dharma-gate, one obtains the great light of the Dharma within the ten powers and swiftly accomplishes the powers of a Tathāgata. O Anantavyūha!
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, take the ten powers as their power and their unsurpassed power; surpassing all worldly powers, they are able to let out the lion’s roar amidst the assembly.
What are called the ten powers of the Tathāgata?

O Anantavyūha! By means of the supreme, unsurpassed knowledge of all-knowledge, the Tathāgata understands, as they truly are, what is possible and what is impossible, regarding the possible and the impossible.
This is the first power of the Tathāgata.
By virtue of this power, he abides in the station of the Great Sage, expounds the True Dharma for all sentient beings, and is able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Except for the Tathāgata, there has never been anyone in the world of devas and humans who has been able to turn [the wheel of Dharma] in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, by means of his non-conceptualizing omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, all past, future, and present karmas, as well as the immeasurable modes of conduct—the causes that grasp karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome, without attachment or obstruction.
This is the second power of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, by means of his non-conceptualizing omniscient wisdom, which is unattached and unimpeded, the Tathāgata is able to thoroughly understand the infinite modes of conduct of all sentient beings.
This is the third power of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, by means of his unsurpassed, supreme knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various inclinations, immeasurable inclinations, and individual inclinations, along with all their conceptualizations and false imaginings.
This is the fourth power of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is able to know, as they truly are, the infinite realms, the various realms, the infinite conditions, and the various conditions by which the world abides.
This is the fifth power of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is able to know, as they truly are, the causes and conditions, as well as the paths leading to various destinations and insights.
This is the sixth power of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge-vision of the divine eye and the unsurpassed knowledge of all-knowledge, the Tathāgata knows, in accordance with reality, the wisdom regarding the birth and death of all sentient beings.
This is the seventh power of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti); he possesses the knowledge of entering and emerging from them with detachment and purity.
This is the eighth power of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses the analytical knowledge of recollecting past lives as a basis for realization, knowing them as they truly are.
This is the ninth power of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata, through the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows,
understands things as they truly are. This, Anantavyūha, is the tenth power of the Tathāgata.

Because he has fully accomplished such immeasurable and unsurpassed powers of all-knowledge, and in order to provide all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings with the support of the Buddhas' wisdom, and to realize the purity of the wisdom of all phenomena, he reveals and expounds this boundless treasury of Dharma.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantavyūha, saying: "Good son!

You should now contemplate that because the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes is thus profound, thus difficult to comprehend, and pure, all dharmas are designated as the 'Tathāgata' and the 'Tathāgata's powers'; yet those dharmas cannot be seen, nor can they be described."
Anantavyūha! That which is called "power" is the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed dharma-gate that cannot be overcome; abiding therein, one reveals and expounds this principle of the Dharma.
By virtue of establishing this principle, one is able to expound upon the non-establishment of all phenomena; this serves as the power.
Thus, these powers are without arising, lack intrinsic nature, and are devoid of self-nature.
Thus, with the ten powers of a Tathāgata fully perfected, he is able to reveal immeasurable and boundless, most profound meanings.
O Anantavyūha! This is the unsurpassed Dharma-gate of all Buddhas.

Having dwelled in this gateway, one is able to expound the ten powers of the Tathāgata, as well as to explain this gateway of the purity of those powers and the gateway of universal purity. O Anantavyūha!
I shall further speak a dhāraṇī for the sake of all bodhisattvas so that they may attain purity in this dharma-gate;
you should listen and receive it. The dhāraṇī is as follows: "Tadyathā | Pramukhane ||"
Nirmuñce nirmuñce vibhramanti.

What is called the phrase of supreme transcendence?
