These are the dhāraṇī phrases of supreme transcendence.
If there is a bodhisattva who diligently practices within this Dharma, they will be able to increase their wisdom like the ocean and, with great compassion, console sentient beings, saying:..."

"I bestow upon you the vast medicinal elixir of the Dharma to destroy the dark ignorance within you, to extract the poisonous arrows of birth, death, affliction, and sorrow that have no beginning or end, and to cause the bonds of craving to be severed, so that you may transcend the torrential flood of all saṃsāra."
They produce the great light of the Dharma so that the roots of goodness in all sentient beings may grow and flourish, enabling them to attain ultimate and eternal liberation.

Such virtuous persons serve as the foremost of skillful guides, capable of leading others into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), and ensuring that not even a single sentient being shall fall away from this unsurpassed, supreme wisdom.

They are able to pervade all things with great compassion, causing all sentient beings to attain unimpeded eloquence regarding the gateway of the wisdom of non-arising—which accords with the meaning [of the teachings] even before they have been heard—and which leads to tranquility and weary detachment.
Anantavyūha! When bodhisattvas wish to preach the Dharma, how should they apply their mindfulness to these dharani phrases so that they remain present before them and the Dharma is never interrupted?
This refers to bodhisattvas seated upon the lion throne, contemplating the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata through unimpeded eloquence;
for by means of skillful means and vast wisdom, they cause the stage of excellence to become utterly purified.

When sentient beings gather like clouds at the place where the Dharma is being heard, one should give rise to great compassion for them and arouse a mind of great loving-kindness toward all beings; then, through the definitive principles of vast wisdom, one should reveal the truth as it is, without addition or subtraction.

Knowing the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings, they extensively proclaim the teachings through speech and written characters that are skillfully clear, definitive, and composed of well-ordered phrases.
By means of such exposition, they are able to cause their own roots of virtue to increase and to gather in sentient beings through the pure Dharma.
The Tathāgata is able, through immeasurable parables, to reveal and expound such a dhāraṇī gateway of the collection of dharmas.
If you are able to proclaim this unsurpassed true Dharma in this manner, you will abide in the work performed by the Buddha and swiftly fulfill the four fearlessnesses.

“Anantavyūha! In this way, a bodhisattva, through great skillful means and pure wisdom, is well able to cultivate the arising of supernormal powers, thereby being able to grasp all dharmas as a vast accumulation of knowledge.”
In this regard, what is the activity that gives rise to supernormal powers? O Anantavyūha!

If bodhisattvas abide in the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they are well able to analyze the accumulation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) by means of the thought of non-reliance, which is like space.

The Tathāgata has accomplished unimpeded wisdom and vision, boundless wisdom and vision; by the power of this wisdom and vision, he attains skillful knowledge regarding all phenomena and is able to determine them with certainty. There is not the slightest phenomenon that can be known, for he dwells in non-apprehension and dwells in the unequaled, yet he does not associate with these states.

He dwells in the araṇya, dwells in non-attachment, and dwells in pure wisdom; there is not the slightest phenomenon that he does not know or see. Having distanced himself from darkness and being without obstruction, he abides well in immeasurable and boundless wisdom and vision.

Therefore, the Tathāgata perceives and awakens to all phenomena as being equal, like illusions and like dreams, and is able to reveal that there is no conceptualization of dharmas devoid of names; for this reason, we should follow the Buddha’s example and train accordingly.

The Tathāgata’s wisdom is unimpeded; he can skillfully discern the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings, causing all bodhisattvas to abide in equanimity and give rise to the activity of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-karma*). Through this, they achieve the manifestation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

By the power of this empowerment of the supernormal bases (*ṛddhipāda*), one is well able to abide in the purification of the knowledge of phenomena regarding ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Through this, one attains true empowerment and masters immeasurable varieties of miraculous transformations (*vikurvita*).
Having attained mastery in the Brahma-world, he sits upon the lion throne and beats the great Dharma drum, causing all those in the assembly to rejoice and bringing great benefit to sentient beings.

“Anantavyūha! Just as the great Cakravāḍa mountain king, through the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings, stands encircling this world so that sentient beings do not smell the fragrance of hell, hear the sounds of hell, or see hell.”
When a bodhisattva has thus well trained in this Dharma, they eliminate all obstructive dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings and bestow upon them all unobstructed dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva, through the skillful means of embracing adamantine wisdom, gains profound insight into these teachings and abides in the nectar-sprinkling of non-apprehension.
What is meant by "attaining the sprinkling of ambrosia"?

It means being incapable of being harmed by the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), or the celestial demon (*devaputramāra*); even at the time of death, although the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*) may exist, one attains mastery and does not give rise to the perception of death.

Why is this? Because those noble beings abide in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena; they are neither born nor extinguished, neither falling away nor arising, neither coming nor going, neither staying nor abiding; they are neither defiled nor pure, and they are neither timid nor weak. Being without obstruction and without anything to be attained, they have abandoned pride and their minds are humble. Internally free from delusion, they clearly understand that which is external, such that they cannot be encompassed by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Having realized that all phenomena are entirely equal, they enter the Dharma of the Tathāgata as it truly is, abiding in suchness which is non-deceptive and immutable.
This is called the gateway to the perfection of wisdom entered by all bodhisattvas.
Having dwelled therein, they are able to accomplish boundless wisdom.

By the power of this wisdom, one is able to enter into inconceivable knowledge and the secret teachings of all Tathāgatas; one is able to thoroughly understand all phenomena and realize them as being equal to uninterrupted enlightenment (*bodhi*); thus, one realizes that which is uninterrupted and inconceivable, and realizes its equality with the inconceivability of enlightenment.
He realizes that there is no interval and nothing to be discriminated; he is equal to bodhi because there is nothing to be discriminated.

Because he understands that both the state of non-interval and the dharmas of bodhi are unattainable, he does not create a distinction regarding the state of non-interval, nor does he form a conceptualization of the equality of bodhi.

In the state of uninterrupted awakening, there is neither creating nor destroying, neither accumulating nor dispersing. Regarding this meaning, one who is capable of acting does not cling to this taught dharma-gate of tranquility, nor does he discriminate among the fruits of karma; he is able to thoroughly understand the equality of karma and its fruit. Because of this equality, he does not obtain karma or its fruit, nor does he discriminate or cling to them.

Why is this? Because they have attained pliancy regarding afflictions and karmic obstructions, thereby distancing themselves from the causes of bondage; they are able to illuminate all dharma-gates and attain radiance within this chapter on dhāraṇī.

Because he dwells in such a gate of purity, he is able to travel and transform beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions; possessing pure conduct, he is without attachment or dwelling, and is not defiled by worldly dharmas. Among all the devas and humans of the world, he is worthy of being a field of merit, to be approached, honored, and supported.
Anantavyūha! I say that the merit of those good sons who dwell in the eighth stage through making offerings is immeasurable; how much more so for a bodhisattva who practices such a Dharma as this!

If one does not apprehend, nor differentiate, nor engage in conceptual proliferation regarding awakening and sentient beings, the dharmas of sentient beings, and even the dharmas of the world, then that person can understand these dharmas and practice according to what has been taught; they can digest the vast offerings of the world and should be honored with the same honor accorded to a Tathāgata.

“Anantavyūha! If bodhisattvas practice and study this Dharma, they will be fully endowed with all requisites for making offerings, free from all fears, and even capable of relinquishing their own bodies and lives.”
He does not grasp at any phenomena, yet he is able to embrace the vast Dharma.
Seated upon the fearless throne, he utters the lion’s roar;
he subdues non-Buddhists and their doctrines, destroys Māra and his hosts, and is able to eliminate all obscurations for sentient beings.

I shall ferry all sentient beings across with the ship of Dharma; I shall show all sentient beings the path to omniscience; I shall be able to establish all sentient beings upon the path of conformity; I shall be able to cause all those sentient beings to conform to the Noble Truths without contradiction; I shall reveal and explain all the factors of enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings; I shall console and encourage sentient beings through the gift of Dharma; and I shall enable sentient beings to attain the joy of the Dharma.
Anantavyūha! If there are those who are able to endure, believe in, and accept this dharani-gate, they are no different from those who have received the prediction of enlightenment.
Having heard the Dharma, they shall receive their own prediction of enlightenment within their very own bodies.
The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, has established this Dharma and opened this treasury of the Dharma; he is able to settle this seal of dhāraṇī and establish these various Dharma-gates to gather us in.
"He is our father and the one who has compassion for us.
O Anantavyūha! If there is a bodhisattva who, with a superior intention, can conceive of me as their father, that person shall enter the number of the Tathāgatas, no different from myself."
O Anantavyūha! Within this Dharma-section of the gate of dhāraṇīs, this is the second exposition of the treasury of teachings through the seal of the dhāraṇī of renunciation.

3. Chapter on the Pure Dhāraṇī, Part One of Three. At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the four quarters and performed various kinds of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). By means of these supernormal powers, he caused all the bodhisattvas in this assembly to see the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions and hear the Dharma preached by those Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Anantavyūha:
"Observe how the Tathāgata, regarding all phenomena, has nothing to be done; through the countless, the numberless, and the quiescent number, he is able to exercise such sovereign supernormal powers.
Such are the powers and fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata."

Anantavyūha! The nature of the Tathāgata is neither one nor different, yet not non-one and non-different; because it is non-existent, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it has no intrinsic nature, yet it is not without intrinsic nature. One should know the nature of the Tathāgata in this way, such that not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Even for one who sees in this way, there is not the slightest dharma that can be seen; if it cannot be seen, then it is non-existent and there is nothing to be grasped. O Anantavyūha!
The nature of the Tathāgata is such that there is not the slightest bit of reality nor the slightest bit of unreality.
If there were even the slightest bit of reality or the slightest bit of unreality, then one could say that there both is and is not the nature of a Tathāgata.
The nature of the Tathāgata is free from existence and free from non-existence, yet it is never apart from them. Anantavyūha!
The self-nature and fundamental nature of all phenomena are like empty space.
This Dharma-gate has never before been taught by any Buddha-Tathāgata since they appeared in the world.

Anantavyūha, if Bodhisattvas understand this Dharma in such a way, they will be able to give rise to immeasurable eloquence; they will be able to illuminate all dharmas and act as a radiance within the fearlessness of the Buddhas.

Anantavyūha! As for the term "fearlessness," it refers to attaining the supreme fearlessness of the Tathāgata, because one does not grasp at even the slightest phenomenon, does not cause it to increase, does not find it, does not find it pervasively, and does not find it through following after it.
Whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, phenomena neither increase nor decrease, nor do they universally increase or decrease.
The self-nature and original nature of all phenomena are eternally abiding; it is the abiding nature of the dharma-realm and the fixed nature of the dharma-realm.
Anantavyūha! All dharmas abide in the fixed nature of dharmas, for they are thus non-existent and unobtainable.
All dharmas are merely false conceptualizations and are not accomplished through karmic retribution; therefore, one can enter the gate of all dharmas being without karmic retribution.

Because these phenomena lack intrinsic nature and do not exist as they appear, various karmas are not the cause for the arising or ceasing of results, nor are they the cause for the path leading to cessation.

The Tathāgata merely speaks of all phenomena as having causes or being causeless through worldly convention; this is because he possesses mastery over causes and because there is no [intrinsic] cause.
This is the ground of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness; for the Tathāgata, being endowed with immeasurable eloquence, is able to enter the great ground of fearlessness.
“Anantavyūha! What is fearlessness?
It refers to the four kinds of fearlessness of all Tathāgatas.”
These four fearlessnesses are not possessed even by pratyekabuddhas, let alone by śrāvakas or others in the world.
What are the four? First, he proclaims:
"I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the knower of all, the seer of all.
Yet there may be some among the world of devas and humans who establish a thesis against me, saying that I have not fully awakened to all phenomena."
"Such a thing is impossible.
By this, he attains supreme fearlessness and, amidst the assembly, rightly roars the lion’s roar: "I am able to expound the unsurpassed, most profound, and vast Dharma teaching."
Second, he proclaims:
"I am one who has exhausted all outflows (āsrava).
Should anyone in the world of devas and humans establish a thesis against me that my outflows are not yet exhausted," [he remains unshaken].
"Such a thing is impossible.
By means of this, one is able to abide in peace and happiness; I have revealed this unsurpassed treasury of Dharma accumulated over immeasurable koṭis of kalpas.
Third: "The liberation and awakening that I have proclaimed is practiced for the sake of the complete cessation of suffering.
Or, if there are those in the world of gods who establish a thesis against me, claiming that the path to the end of suffering does not lead to liberation."
"That is impossible.

I do not perceive such signs; when I do not perceive such signs, I abide in peace and happiness, manifesting this dharma-lineage for all sentient beings and uttering the lion’s roar amidst the assembly.

Fourth: "Regarding the various obstructive dharmas that I have proclaimed, there may be among the assembly of devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas those who establish a thesis against me, yet they are unable to find any obstacle in their practice of them."
"That is impossible.

When I perceived this sign, I attained a superior dwelling in peace and security; I let out a true lion's roar in the midst of the assembly, saying: "I am able to turn this unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, which no outsider, deity, or anyone in the world can turn."
Anantavyūha! These are the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata.
When a bodhisattva diligently trains in these, they swiftly attain the stage of fearlessness and become most preeminent among gods and humans.
“Anantavyūha! If bodhisattvas, through the thorough cultivation of the characteristic of space, are able to give rise to the inconceivable gate of universal purity.
By means of this gateway, one first realizes all phenomena, seeing that all phenomena are equal to the characteristics of space—non-dual and undifferentiated—and all dharmas are likewise so.
Yet, regarding space as well, they do not engage in conceptual discrimination nor in frivolous proliferation, thereby attaining skillfulness in meaning.

Not even the slightest dharma-realm is brought from anywhere, nor is it taken away, nor is it accumulated; thus they are able to observe that all phenomena have no accumulation, neither coming nor going. Regarding all phenomena, they practice non-practice, lighting the great Dharma-torches to serve as illumination for all sentient beings.
Anantavyūha! Observe how much benefit and how many activities this Dharma can bring about for bodhisattvas!
This refers to the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Buddha; yet, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended, nor is it non-apprehensible. O Anantavyūha!

All dharmas have the same characteristic as space. For the sake of attaining meaningful benefit, they reveal and expound upon the basis of activity and the causes of that activity; yet within them, no meaningful benefit can be apprehended.
Anantavyūha! This profound Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe.

All the world is characterized by destruction and established upon falsehood; therefore, they are unable to have faith in and accept this Dharma-Vinaya, nor can the world understand that the world is entirely devoid of true reality.

Due to attachment, one speaks of a "world" and a "place of abiding"; yet even if there were attachment to the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), there would be no phenomenon whatsoever that could be attached to.

Because they give rise to attachment through what is not in accordance with the Dharma, they engage in disputes with the Tathāgata and the teachings he has proclaimed; furthermore, they fail to comprehend the self-nature and intrinsic nature of all phenomena and contradict such principles as the dharma of non-arising. For these reasons, they are unable to understand and realize this profound teaching of the Dharma.
“Anantavyūha! I am trusted by all gods and humans;

I am one who speaks according to reality and one who is free from disputation. Because the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has stilled all disputes and relinquished the aggregates, he has revealed and expounded such a teaching, in which there are neither aggregates nor the exhaustion of aggregates.”

Anantavyūha! As for all that exists—namely, all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas—within them there are no wholesome or unwholesome dharmas at all. Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are entirely quiescent; wholesome and unwholesome dharmas do not know one another, nor do they obscure one another. Because of the causes and conditions of attachment to wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas], the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because those truly existent dharmas of good and non-good cannot be apprehended, if they cannot be apprehended, they are without designation (*avyākṛta*).
Why is this? Because within them there is no cause, and no cause can be perceived.
Anantavyūha! You should now observe that all dharmas are entirely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If bodhisattvas awaken in this way, even the verbal expression "indeterminate" regarding all dharmas cannot be found.

This Dharma gate is for the sake of bodhisattvas who, by seeing unwholesome phenomena as they truly are, attain the perfection of relinquishment and do not dwell upon phenomena, entering all dharmas through the gateway of the indeterminate.

That which is an indeterminate gate is not a gate; that which is not a gate cannot be apprehended. That which cannot be apprehended is pure. This is the Dharma-gate of the purity of dhāraṇīs entered by all bodhisattvas.

By means of this gateway, one attains the radiant illumination of all phenomena; within all phenomena, there is no longer any ignorance, delusion, or hesitation, and one is able to obtain the pure eye of wisdom regarding unimpeded dharmas.
“Anantavyūha! Within this Dharma, you should give rise to aspiration and joy.
What is meant by aspiration and joy?

This means that because there is nothing to be grasped among all phenomena, there is no attachment; one is ultimately free from relinquishing and transcends hoarding; because there is no seeking, one does not depend upon anything virtuous or non-virtuous, nor upon any conditioned or worldly phenomena.

This is the unsurpassed stage of heedfulness, the stage free from objective referents; it abides in nothing among all phenomena, neither coming nor going, and established nowhere. This is called the ultimate purification and complete detachment of the eye of wisdom.
Because there is nothing to be grasped, one is well able to observe and relinquish all intrinsic natures and essences; this is called the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
What is termed the wisdom-eye is the nature of knowledge that is characterized by total cessation, weariness, and detachment.

Such a nature of wisdom is unborn and unconditioned, inherently quiescent, yet it does not correspond with quiescence because it has severed all correspondence; it is neither severed nor non-severed, without deficiency or diminution—this is called the path of non-conceptual proliferation of the pure eye of wisdom.

Because the eye of wisdom is thus accomplished, one gathers all sentient beings through great compassion, causing them to resolve their minds upon and abide in inexhaustible, sublime practices directed toward sentient beings, and enabling them to realize that all phenomena are devoid of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.

When he realizes great enlightenment, he will certainly be able to reveal and expound the unsurpassed treasury of Dharma and purify the gateways of dhāraṇī; therefore, one should establish the seal of Dharma so that the lineage and teachings for all sentient beings shall never be interrupted or exhausted.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantavyūha, saying:
"This dharma-gate of the pure dhāraṇī is constantly protected, remembered, sustained, and expounded by all Buddhas."

The Buddhas dwelling throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time also all proclaim this Dharma-gate, revealing the nature of phenomena that is equal across the three periods of time for the sake of all bodhisattvas.

By means of this, one can truly awaken to and enter this dharma-gate regarding all phenomena of the three periods of time, thereby accomplishing the bodhisattva’s pure wisdom of the dhāraṇī of the three periods of time.

Those bodhisattvas are free from worldly conceptions; they understand that the wholesome and the unwholesome are non-dual, yet they are able to cultivate various roots of goodness. Their actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely pure, and they are able to universally purify immeasurable Dharma-gates.

In order to attain the wisdom of pure dhāraṇī, they are also able to expound the teachings on the pure nature of non-arising; furthermore, they can reveal that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent like space, and they can manifest the vast light of wisdom.
Furthermore, for the sake of revealing pure wisdom, he is also able to reveal that all phenomena and awakening are of the same nature as space.
Moreover, for the sake of manifesting the purity of the path to omniscience, he is further able to reveal that the dharma of the pure path is itself awakening.

Because they attain fulfillment according to their aspirations, they are able to correctly understand and skillfully manifest the means for realizing the ultimate truth, thereby proclaiming the non-conceptual truth; because they accord with the awakening to all meanings, they are able to skillfully reveal the wisdom of all Buddhas.

Anantavyūha! If bodhisattvas skillfully cultivate and study within this Dharma, they will be able to swiftly purify the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), abide in enlightenment without distance or proximity, and not be in conflict with even the slightest phenomenon. Furthermore, they do not perceive distance or proximity regarding these explained dharmas, nor do they view enlightenment through the lens of either dharma or non-dharma.
Thoroughly penetrating bodhi transcends all manifestations; one can understand bodhi through the meaning of equality and non-manifestation.

Furthermore, when contemplating the meaning of the quiescence of all phenomena, one does not discriminate bodhi, nor does one perceive the meanings of quiescence or non-quiescence. One does not see non-quiescence apart from quiescence; there is not even the slightest conceptualization of observation or perception.
In all places, one is able to purify one’s vision, yet there is not even the slightest thing that can be purified.
This is the gateway to the pure wisdom of all bodhisattvas.

By means of this gateway, they are able to recollect the dhāraṇī gateways of the boundless Dharma-treasuries of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas; they are able to fully comprehend the self-nature and fundamental nature of all classes of sentient beings, and for the sake of those sentient beings, they reveal and expound these treasuries of Dharma.

They are able to completely purify all activities of wisdom and all aspirations; having manifested perfect awakening in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, their superior resolve never regresses, and they are able to recollect their well-purified vows, swiftly attaining mastery over all phenomena and practicing accordingly.
The great kindness and compassion of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as well as the treasury of skillful dharmas of all Tathāgatas, are all manifest before them.
Furthermore, they are able to manifest the immeasurable and boundless light of the Great Dharma, their bodies eternally dwelling in the realm of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
“Anantavyūha! Of whom is this ‘immeasurable and boundless dharma-gate’ a designation? Anantavyūha!”

"Immeasurable and boundless" means that all phenomena—the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—are immeasurable; and because the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, and the realms of all sentient beings are without measure. Yet, not even a slight portion of the realms of sentient beings can be apprehended, for sentient beings do not exist.
In this way, in this manner, this realm of sentient beings is ungraspable and unknowable, because no such realm exists.
Therefore, all phenomena are equal to the realm of nirvāṇa and enter into nirvāṇa.
All phenomena enter equally into the ineffable realm, for within the realm of nirvāṇa there is not even the slightest thing that can be described.
Within the realm of nirvāṇa there is no obstruction and no obscuration, because obstructions and obscurations are eternally purified; therefore, the realm of nirvāṇa is pure and supremely pure.

This is the realm of nirvāṇa; yet this realm is also not a realm, because it is far removed from realms, because there is no realm, and because it transcends all realms. Nevertheless, it is explained through the skillful means of appearing as a realm.
What is called a "realm" (dhātu) abides neither in non-realm nor in non-non-realm; even within verbal expression there is no realm, yet one merely uses language to manifest and explain all phenomena.
All speech and all speakers are unobtainable and cannot be fully known.
All speech is not speech; thus, all such speech enters into space, being equal in nature to space itself.
Because of this, the earth element cannot speak and lacks the power of speech; this extends even to the space element, which cannot speak and lacks the power of speech.

As for what is called the consciousness element, it merely uses language to manifest and explain all phenomena; yet that consciousness element is neither an element nor a non-element—it does not enter into the elements, it is neither associated with the elements nor dissociated from them, and it arises from space and enters back into space.

Thus, this element of consciousness is neither internal, nor external, nor in between; it is encompassed by its own spatial dimension and enters into space, being impossible to designate and impossible to perceive.

If it cannot be designated as having no activity, then through the conjunction with other conditions, one speaks of the existence of the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*). This is the entrance for Bodhisattvas.

The fundamental nature and intrinsic nature of all phenomena are like space; they are revealed and expounded by relying upon the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), yet there is no realm of phenomena, because the realm is not a realm.
All phenomena are like space; therefore, the Tathāgata says that all phenomena are empty, because their measure is difficult to apprehend.
To reveal that all phenomena possess the nature of emptiness—since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like space—he merely employs language to open up, indicate, and expound upon them.
“Anantavyūha! Behold how pure is that which is expounded by the Tathāgata’s wisdom; therein, no dharma can arise, nor is any dharma bestowed.”
Such is the teaching of the pure Dharma; this is the non-erroneous wisdom of all bodhisattvas.

Therefore, you should aspire to it: through wisdom not dependent on others, one attains non-conceptualization and does not increase conceptualization, thereby purifying the ineffable principle of the Dharma-gate, because the wisdom regarding all phenomena is pure.
The Buddha said to Anantavyūha,
“Where do the various species of flying birds travel?
Anantavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I travel through space.
The Buddha asked again:
"What does space, moreover, travel? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, space has no movement. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
All dharmas are like space and have no movement; one cannot find a dharma of 'moving without moving. Therefore, all dharmas have no movement, nor do they move."

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is such that there is nothing to be practiced and nothing to be spoken; yet this Dharma-gate is turned for the sake of purifying the space-like wisdom of all bodhisattvas.
This is the Dharma-gate of Boundless Radiance, which universally illumines the immeasurable and boundless, just like space; even that radiance which universally illumines cannot itself be seen.
Once the Bodhisattva has attained this gate, they are able to universally observe the worlds of the ten directions and perceive all worlds as they truly are.
This is the ground known by the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas, the ground of penetrating wisdom; it is not the ground of any other proponents, for they are unable to explain it.
This principle of the Dharma is the seal of the ineffable, because linguistic expression cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, all phenomena are neither sealed nor increased by a seal.
Through the skillful cultivation of knowing that there is no seal, one seals all phenomena with the seal of space.

By means of the seal of signlessness, one can manifest that space is signless—devoid of conditioned characteristics and devoid of the characteristic of speech—and it is because of this emptiness and absence that this is called "space."
That which is called "space" is said to be empty because it lacks substantial reality.
By way of the true ultimate meaning, one should know that all phenomena are beyond words. O Anantavyūha!
In this regard, I shall explain the dhāraṇī-seal of the phrases capable of purification, which are the phrases of space because wisdom is pure.
Just as space has no phrases, so too are the phrases pure.
"In this way, one should understand that there are no phrases at all.
What, then, are these phrases?
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

These various dhāraṇī seals are phrases capable of purifying; they expound the phrases of the divisions of space. Being without division, they are universally without division; because there is no division, there are no phrases within them.
The purity of non-words arises from the purity of all dharma-words.
For those who have set out and abide in the Great Vehicle and who long for the profound and pure Dharma, these mantra-words are made to circulate through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power.

O Anantavyūha! "Good son! I shall now further speak the phrases for subduing those who lack faith.

“*Pratīyabhas-ta-ṇe.*” (25) The Buddha said: “Anantavyūha! This is the phrase for subduing those who lack faith;
by means of it, one prevents them from committing various transgressions and evils.”
Even toward wholesome dharmas as they are, there is much hatred and envy; how much more so regarding this unsurpassed teaching of the Dharma!
Therefore, these mantra-words revolve for the purpose of extinguishing all faults and evils, and for the purpose of severing all afflictions.
Anantavyūha! I see sentient beings who, lacking pure faith in their hearts, approach the Tathāgata with the intent to quarrel, to cause harm, or to create disturbance.

Knowing the movements of their minds, he awakens them through various Dharma-gates according to their respective dispositions, causing them to abandon unwholesome thoughts and to give rise to the causes of all roots of goodness.

“Anantavyūha! The Tathāgata, dwelling in the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), is able to thoroughly understand the mental activities of sentient beings, as well as the phenomena subsumed within the mind.”
Anantavyūha! What are called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? Anantavyūha!

It is said that from the time the Tathāgata, during a certain night, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), until his entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, in the interval between those two moments, he was without error, without harsh sounds, without loss of mindfulness, without indeterminate equanimity, without diverse perceptions, and without unconcentrated mind; his diligence did not decline, his mindfulness did not decline, his aspiration did not decline, his meditative concentration did not decline, his wisdom did not decline, his liberation did not decline, and his knowledge and vision of liberation did not decline.

The physical actions of all Tathāgatas are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom; the verbal actions of all Tathāgatas are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom; the mental actions of all Tathāgatas are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.

The Tathāgata’s wisdom and vision are unattached and unimpeded regarding the past; the Tathāgata’s wisdom and vision are unattached and unimpeded regarding the future; the Tathāgata’s wisdom and vision are unattached and unimpeded regarding the present.

Anantavyūha! Because the Tathāgata has accomplished these eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and has fully realized immeasurable powers of wisdom and vision, he is able to expound this chapter on the pure Dharma of the *dhāraṇī* gateway.
It is for the sake of generating pure faith in all sentient beings who lack it, and for the sake of enabling those with pure faith to attain pure wisdom regarding this Dharma-gate. O Anantavyūha!

Although the Tathāgata, according to his inclinations and desires, may analyze and explain this gateway of dhāraṇī through all manner of immeasurable and diverse languages, he could not express even one hundredth part of the principle of severing doubt within this gateway of dhāraṇī, nor even a fraction as small as a koṭi of hundreds of thousands of calculations or metaphors.
Why is this? Because these dharma-gates are immeasurable gates and inconceivable gates; all these gates are able to bring about the turning of the wisdom of all-knowledge.
"Furthermore, Anantavyūha!

By means of these immeasurable alternative names, the Tathāgata now reveals and expounds these various Dharma-gates for you all, desiring that you universally understand immeasurable Dharma-gates and attain dhāraṇīs."
Then he spoke the mantra, saying: "Tadyathā | Ārye | Āryavati |"

Anuṣaṇe luḍadapramiṃ sarvarajñepane naraśeṇi. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Anantavyūha, saying:

"These dhāraṇī seals are phrases for purification and phrases spoken with diverse names. By receiving and upholding this dharma-gate of dhāraṇīs, one realizes the distinctions of the sublime wisdom of the bodhisattva stages with little effort and draws near to great compassion; by awakening to the meaning according to its principles, one attains the realization and entry into the knowledge of all phenomena."
Anantavyūha! These dhāraṇī phrases are a great medicine, for they are able to eliminate and destroy all grave illnesses.
Furthermore, they can eradicate the extremely dark obscurations of ignorance and lack of wisdom, as they accord with the luminous Dharma and bring it to perfect fulfillment.
He proceeds with the perfection of whatever illuminating dharma turns forth, because his knowledge of the illuminating dharma is perfected;
and he is able to realize the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, because of his skill in the knowledge that accords with the illuminating dharma.
And one attains the light of knowledge of the divine eye, because of conforming to and abandoning all afflictions.

One is able to directly realize the light of knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; by means of this, one further attains all the perfections of training, unsurpassed wisdom-vision, the vision of the knowledge of all-knowledge, and the stage of the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Anantavyūha! Behold how the Tathāgata is well able to expound such vast teachings, being perfectly accomplished in all skillful means. Anantavyūha!
The Tathāgata, having thus accomplished great wisdom, is able to dwell securely in the powers of all-knowledge, the powers of the Tathāgata, the fearlessnesses, and so forth.
This unsurpassed treasury is the accumulation of roots of goodness cultivated over immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.

For this reason, being able to dwell skillfully within these dharma-gates, I now bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity for you all; having given rise to expertise in the principles of the Dharma, I shall reveal and expound this chapter on the pure dharma of the dhāraṇī.

If sons or daughters of good family who have resolved to seek and attain great enlightenment wish to follow and correctly practice my teachings; those who wish to protect my Dharma-instructions; and those who wish to receive and uphold the immeasurable Dharma-treasuries of all Tathāgatas—these individuals should diligently cultivate and apply themselves with zeal to this Dharma. They should abide in heedfulness, remain unattached to the three realms, and maintain their minds through the excellent empowerment of the aspiration for omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). They should skillfully and thoroughly cultivate purity regarding the conditions of form (*rūpa*); they should diligently cultivate skill in purity regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*); and they should diligently cultivate purity in the arising of the phrases of true reality (*bhūtārtha-pada*). Within all phenomena, they should joyfully seek all forms of pure knowledge.

Anantavyūha! Because the internal is pure, all phenomena are pure; because the internal is tranquil, all phenomena are tranquil; because the internal is extinguished, all phenomena are extinguished; because the internal is without grasping, all phenomena are without grasping; because the internal does not abide, all phenomena do not abide; because the internal is ceased, all phenomena are ceased; because the internal is without activity, all phenomena are without activity; because the internal has no coming or going, all phenomena likewise have no coming or going.

Anantavyūha! These phrases of the gates cause all bodhisattvas to turn toward internal purity; because they are non-conceptual regarding external intrinsic nature, they do not give rise to discrimination, yet they are able to uphold the pure dhāraṇī-gates.

Having abandoned greed and anger, with a mind free from arrogance, you will be praised by all Tathāgatas; as the most excellent among all sentient beings, you shall act as their unsurpassed sovereign. You will be able to realize unimpeded wisdom and preach with eloquence that brings joy; you will attain pure knowledge regarding the past and future limits, be able to universally record and recollect the nature of the Middle Way, and realize the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). You will realize the excellence of the vow for dependent origination and achieve universal purity in all vows. You shall be able to fully maintain the skillful mastery of all unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), such that the words you utter will be received with faith by all, and you will be able to rain down the great Dharma-rain in the future.

Anantavyūha! Because a bodhisattva has attained dhāraṇī, they will certainly realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), attain the pure wisdom of all phenomena, and be able to give rise to such wisdom of phenomena as that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.
Furthermore, one realizes such knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), namely: that which arises through falsehood does not achieve birth.
That which is unachieved is immediately dispersed and destroyed; as for phenomena that are dispersed and destroyed, they have no destination. All these phenomena are gates of dissolution.

This gate of dissolution is identical to the characteristic of non-arising; if there is no arising, then there is no cessation. When one observes all phenomena as they truly are and becomes detached from their characteristics, one then neither clings nor engages in conceptual proliferation.

Anantavyūha! This is the skillful observation of the gate of non-arising wisdom of all bodhisattvas, by which they are able to enter these dhāraṇīs; through this, they are swiftly able to attain the patience of non-arising and become fully endowed with eloquence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If phenomena arise falsely, Having arisen, they must perish;
All phenomena are devoid of existence— To whom could they be fully entrusted?"
Since all phenomena do not exist, there is nothing existent or nonexistent to be grasped;
if phenomena cannot be apprehended, what is there to be universally maintained?
If one does not understand all phenomena, their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
He then courses in signs and does not attain dhāraṇī.
All phenomena are like space; it is for this reason that they are taught and revealed.
Both space and the teaching are entirely non-existent.
These two are free from existence, and all phenomena are likewise empty and non-existent;
one who understands phenomena in this way can attain dhāraṇī.
Realizing that there is no beginning, they do not discriminate between middle and end.
All phenomena are free from conceptual construction; everything is entirely empty and non-existent.
Since that which abides therein lacks solidity, and what is unreal does not exist, how can one universally uphold [the teachings] based on the true principle of all phenomena?
Thus understanding all phenomena, Their intrinsic nature is non-existent;
I have now briefly explained this, Attaining the pure dhāraṇī.
All phenomena are like space, And are equal to the vast void.
By constantly observing with wisdom, one can attain dhāraṇī.
All phenomena are non-existent; they are neither born nor arisen.
Being without existence and without anything to be grasped, how could these be universally maintained?
All phenomena are signless; their intrinsic nature is free from conceptual proliferation.
All are devoid of characteristics, and the teaching of the Dharma is non-existent.
If one can understand in this way, all phenomena accord with reality.
He is without conceptual discrimination, yet is able to attain universal retention.
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended;
by understanding that there is no objective referent, he accomplishes dhāraṇī.
If one observes in this way, all phenomena remain unstained;
with wisdom that does not conceptualize emptiness, one is able to uphold all dharmas.
The meaning of impermanence, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of suffering, and the meaning of weary detachment—[these are upheld].
If one understands through wisdom, that knowledge will increase.
To teach and demonstrate the meaning of nirvāṇa as it truly is— without grasping—
one maintains a firm, non-conceptual mind and does not discriminate among phenomena.
By this, one is able to uphold that all phenomena are not solid,
that they neither exist nor can be grasped, and that they are tranquil, empty, and difficult to perceive.
If one understands the Dharma as it has been taught, one does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding that teaching.
Without attachment and without conceptualization, one can uphold this Dharma-gate.
Having understood characteristics, one is able to comprehend the signless;
such a person likewise does not give rise to the thought of abandoning all phenomena.
He who can understand this meaning, as taught by the Perfectly Awakened One,
and who skillfully explains the secret [teachings], can follow my awakening.
If one investigates all immeasurable phenomena according to reality, [one will realize them].
Having abandoned all means of valid cognition, one can awaken to this principle.
If one can contemplate phenomena as being without name and without mark,
and can thoroughly understand this meaning, one will be able to increase in patience.
All vows and excellences, as well as correct contemplation,
the aspirations and all forms— abiding not therein, one can oppose them.
Understanding the meaning of this Dharma-gate, one is able to contemplate correctly.
Regarding the principles of all phenomena, they likewise have no doubt.
If one observes the characteristics of all phenomena with wisdom and attains definitive understanding, one then enters the signless.
One who can thoroughly understand and dwell securely in this principle,
such a fearless one, will swiftly realize the Buddha-dharma.
Not engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding phenomena, they remain equanimous and free from discrimination.
Having fully understood the correspondence of phenomena, one is free from doubt regarding disenchantment.
Without conceptualizing cessation, one realizes the meaning of the tranquility of the exhaustion of the aggregates;
being thus equanimous toward all phenomena, one attains eloquence in accordance with reality.
Those who are able to cultivate loving-kindness and compassion, benefiting all sentient beings,
and who dwell well in meditative correspondence, they awaken to the unsurpassed.
If they are free from the mark of a sentient being, they can realize the selflessness of phenomena.
The Dharma is free from conceptual proliferation; one should not proliferate according to the nature of reality.
If, having heard this Dharma, one can swiftly attain pure faith, that person shall behold the Perfectly Awakened One, Maitreya, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings.
He brings me joy; whoever among this assembly hears this Dharma will be able to act as a virtuous friend.
Those who revere the Tathāgata will never suffer division.
Having heard this Dharma, one will be beloved by the virtuous and noble.
If, within this Auspicious Aeon (Bhadrakalpa), one wishes to behold all the Tathāgatas,
by practicing and studying this Dharma-gate, one can bring joy to all the Buddhas.
If one wishes to behold the majestic radiance of Amitāyus or the great renown of Akṣobhya,
one should study this Dharma-gate. If one wishes to realize bodhi,
the most supreme and tranquil dharma, [one should study this Dharma-gate].
Or if one seeks the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, one should study this dharma-gate.
If one delights in seeking the supreme, the skillful gate of dhāraṇī,
one should study this dharma and always remain heedful.
If one wishes to accomplish vast and most supreme aspirations,
and seeks to realize awakening, one should study this Dharma gate.
This which is taught in the sutra is the Dharma gate of dhāraṇī.
It can reveal all phenomena; this seal is most unsurpassed.
The inner reality of all phenomena is revealed through dhāraṇī;
this dharma-gate of space skillfully resolves boundless meanings.
The various gateways of goodness that have been taught— this Dharma is able to reveal them.
Through skillfulness in the meaning of dhāraṇī and by the power of dhāraṇī,
it is said that dhāraṇī is wisdom, for it is able to uphold all phenomena.
Skilled in the meaning of the dhāraṇīs, he understands them through wisdom.
Regarding these various many explanations, he has already well expounded the Buddha-dharma;
having correctly revealed it through its meaning, [he teaches] the factors of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Skillful in the wisdom of distinctions, you provide this correct exposition;
if one studies this Dharma, they shall realize unsurpassed enlightenment.
Within this teaching, you reveal the unsurpassed gateway to the sublime Dharma.
Having attained the wisdom of skillful means, one should preach this Dharma.
Never before have all dharmas been spoken; this is the unsurpassed lineage.
One should study this meaning and reveal the words of the nectar of immortality.
If a wise person seeks the unimpeded wisdom of all Buddhas,
And studies this meaning, they shall attain the supreme knowledge.
In times past, throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, I...
If one does not study this Dharma, one will not realize the path of tranquility.
Because I have made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
I am able to understand and thus proclaim this unsurpassed Dharma.
For the sake of all sentient beings, I have brought about boundless benefit;
you all should likewise act so as to obtain this dhāraṇī.
If one can thoroughly understand this seal of the gateway to the dhāraṇī, [one shall attain it].
Through a single phrase, the wise can enter this Dharma gate.
My wisdom is unsurpassed and beyond all measure;
because I possess the aggregate of wisdom, I am able to reveal this Dharma.
The wise seek herein; following the realization of the meaning of bodhi, they should diligently study this fearless gateway of the Dharma.
If the wise desire to seek the nature of vast wisdom, [they should do so here].
One who wishes to conceive reverence for the Buddha should study this Dharma-gate.
If one desires to turn the wheel of Dharma and blow the great conch of the Dharma,
the wise person should, in accordance with reality, study this Dharma-gate.
If you wish to emit radiance that universally illuminates the boundless,
and when seeking the Buddha-dharma, study this according to the principle.
If you wish to be the foremost in the world of gods and humans, [study this].
They should study this sutra, which definitively establishes all phenomena.
Those who seek vast wisdom, who wish to give rise to all merits,
and who delight in seeking the Buddha’s insight— these should follow and study herein.
If one wishes to reveal the Dharma-gate, And seeks with joy the most supreme,
non-conceptual Buddha-wisdom, One should train in this meaning.
If one desires to joyfully reveal that which is spoken by unimpeded wisdom, [one should train in this meaning].
Having trained in this Dharma, one should proclaim the words of nectar.
If one wishes to illuminate millions of infinite and boundless realms,
those individuals should train well in this teaching.
This unsurpassed Dharma gate can purify all phenomena;
that all phenomena are pure is taught within this sutra.
The Honored One among Two-legged Beings, possessing the knowledge of all modes, has expounded this vast Dharma.
"For those who are bodhisattvas, this sūtra is the most unsurpassed. The Buddha told Anantavyūha:

"Therefore, once bodhisattvas have conceived a sense of love and joy for this Dharma teaching, they should write it down, receive it, uphold it, read it, and recite it, both in order to ensure that this Dharma teaching remains for a long time and out of compassion for all sentient beings."

Anantavyūha! Furthermore, if there are people who, during that time, hear this Dharma and constantly contemplate it with a heart of love and joy toward the Tathāgata, those individuals shall attain the various dhāraṇīs of the Tathāgata’s boundless treasury of Dharma; they shall be endowed with eloquence, swiftly attain mastery over all phenomena, and be able to fully embrace and sustain the inconceivable adornments of Buddha-fields, as well as the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas therein.

Anantavyūha! If bodhisattvas abide in the non-conceptualization of all phenomena, then by means of the gateway of the purification of dhāraṇīs, these gateways of the Dharma will constantly manifest before them, and they will be able to embrace immeasurable and inconceivable, supreme merits.
Anantavyūha! This is the third chapter on the purity of the dhāraṇī-gates. Anantavyūha!

In the future, if there should be any bodhisattvas who wish to follow and study this dharani dharma-gate, they should draw near to virtuous friends and distance themselves from evil friends. To provide universal protection for all these dharma-gates, they should sacrifice their bodies and lives to uphold this pure dharma-seal of the dharani.
For example, when the moon of the month of Kārttika is full, its radiance shines brilliantly, being the most preeminent among all the stars.

In this same way, these three sections of the dhāraṇī-seal encompass all dharma-gates; likewise, among all the sūtras, the light of this Dharma is the most preeminent. All bodhisattvas hold it in great respect, and thus it is able to give rise to immeasurable eloquence.
This immeasurable eloquence should be understood as the stage of non-negligence (*apramāda-bhūmi*).
What is this stage of non-negligence?

It refers to the mental attention and contemplation of this Dharma, observing it according to reality so that false thoughts do not arise; in this way, one is able to bring about the complete purification of patience.
If there are bodhisattvas who diligently and resolutely seek non-negligence, they should skillfully cultivate this Dharma-gate.

In order that this Dharma may endure for a long time, their minds should always be humble and respectful toward the Dharma; they should keep the written scrolls of the sutras upon their own persons, never parting from them. Upon seeing those who possess the aspiration and longing for the Dharma, or those who have resolved to advance toward great enlightenment, they should for their sake reveal, disseminate, instruct, recite, and transcribe the sutra scrolls, even explaining them according to their meaning.

Just as we should not conceal any Dharma-gates that we uphold, we vow that all sentient beings may obtain the benefit of this unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma; we shall cause all sentient beings never to lack or diminish in any of the Buddha-teachings.

In this way, the bodhisattva is without stinginess regarding the Dharma and always delights in bestowing it upon others; they do not conceal its meaning but explain it all completely, leaving no dharma-gate unexpounded.

Anantavyūha! For the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, you should receive and uphold this dhāraṇī-gate from the chapter on the Dharma-door, which is the phrase for complete purification.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold this chapter on the Dharma-gate.
My disciples who serve me should likewise receive and uphold such a sutra."
Then Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“By the Buddha’s spiritual power, I have already received and upheld it.
Because I have accomplished this dharma-gate, immeasurable dharma-gates have all become manifest before me.”
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! It is so, it is so; it is just as you have said."

By the power of the Buddha and because this Dharma gate is universally pure, all those who uphold this Dharma gate, as well as those who personally serve me and are able to uphold it, shall have immeasurable Dharma gates manifest before them.
"Therefore, Ānanda! You should receive and uphold the Tathāgata’s teaching, the immeasurable treasury of Dharma.
When this Dharma was being spoken, immeasurable bodhisattvas within the assembly immediately attained the great light of the Dharma."

Because they have attained the light of the Dharma, all the dharma-gates taught by immeasurable Buddhas appear before them; furthermore, they draw near to the wisdom of all-knowledge, and all the magnificent adornments of their supreme vows, as they have joyfully sought, are fully accomplished.

Ānanda! Behold how the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is profoundly deep. Thus, the Tathāgata is able to apply names and signs to phenomena that are nameless and signless, and he is also able to reveal the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, purifying them so that they may be seen as pure. Although he speaks of all phenomena, there is no phenomenon to be spoken of, nor is there anyone who speaks.
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! If one can contemplate the nature of all phenomena in this way, one will give rise to immeasurable wisdom.”

When this Dharma was being taught, countless Bodhisattvas realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and were destined to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment after incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*); furthermore, they were able to produce immeasurable eloquence.
At that time, the World-Honored One empowered this dharani-gate and emitted a great radiance; its light shone universally throughout immeasurable and boundless buddha-worlds.
By means of this radiance, all bodhisattvas in those various worlds shall hear this dhāraṇī; having heard this Dharma, they will be able to fully mature the factors of the qualities of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sentient beings therein who all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, all sentient beings attained peace and happiness.
At that time, there were also various devas who rained down *pāṭala* flowers upon the great assembly among the bodhisattvas, proclaiming these words:
"May all sentient beings attain the wisdom of the Buddha."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Eloquence addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What should this Dharma-gate be named?"
"How should I receive and uphold it?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Eloquence, saying:
"This Dharma-gate is named 'Dhāraṇī King,' and is also named 'Dhāraṇī Seal,' and is also named 'Skillfulness Subsumed within the Three Categories. You should receive and uphold it."
This is the Dharma-gate of Boundless Eloquence, which skillfully encompasses all meanings.
By means of this Dharma-gate, one is able to illuminate all phenomena and sever all doubts; therefore, all Bodhisattvas should receive, uphold, and maintain this Dharma-gate.
At that time, the entire great assembly, in order to make offerings to the Dharma, scattered five-colored flowers over the Buddha.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the entire assembly, and the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

3. The Chapter on the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, Part One of Three.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of forty-two thousand bhikṣus and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.

All the great sages have attained mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and have gathered here from various Buddha assemblies throughout the ten directions. They have all attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), reached the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), and are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Having attained *dhāraṇī* and unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇapratibhāna*), they roam through countless Buddha-lands in the ten directions, delighting in their own supernatural powers. They have abandoned all external teachings, subdued the hosts of Māras, and eliminated all enemies. With an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, they perceive the source of all things and understand the fundamental nature of sentient beings within the three realms, universally entering into all the *pāramitās*.
He constantly dwells in seclusion and tranquility, and his skillful means and expedients are such that there is nothing he does not master.

All Buddhas praise and proclaim his virtue; having cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva for incalculable eons, he has accumulated merit and virtue for billions of years. Throughout infinite lifetimes, his mind has remained as level as the earth, and the realms of all Buddha-lands are beyond measure.
Their conduct is pure; they have cast off all hindrances and eliminated the various veils (*āvaraṇa*).
Their bodies are as firm and strong as linked chains, having attained a diamond-like resolve and reached the noble nature of the Way.

He lets out the great lion’s roar, walking alone amidst the assembly; having realized the truth of what he has entered, he attains fearlessness. His radiance eclipses the sun and moon as he proclaims the true Dharma.
Equal toward the three periods of time—past, future, and present—he awakens others from delusion and resolves their doubts.

He penetrates deeply into the subtle and profound, descending through dependent origination to transform those who are stubborn and rigid, causing them to relinquish the notions of annihilationism and eternalism.
He protects and brings to full realization all meditative contemplations, samādhis, and states of correct reception, entering into every sphere of attainment.

Hearing the sounds from the ten directions, they receive no further questioning; they do not sever the instructions and teachings of the Three Jewels, accumulate immeasurable merit, and cause the treasure of the Way to flourish, surpassing the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Practicing inexhaustible kindness and observing boundless compassion, he embraced the four Brahma-vihāras and universally relieved others through the four debts of gratitude; according to the time, he opened the way for their deliverance, passing through the three gates of liberation to reach the three types of supernormal knowledge.

He circulates through the three realms like the sun and moon; he travels to and fro across the four quarters like a Wheel-Turning Sage King. With courageous wisdom, he delivers beings from birth, old age, and death; his coming and going among the five destinies is like a torch illuminating the darkness. His mind is free from attachment, like a lotus born from the mud; his conduct neither increases nor diminishes, like space which possesses no increase or craving.

He proclaims the Tripiṭaka like a wise sovereign of a nation bestowing seals and insignia and conferring official titles; yet he remains unmoved by joy or sorrow regarding the eight worldly dharmas that transcend the mundane. He enters the eight difficult conditions to transform those in peril and distress, achieving wisdom and turning the non-retrogressive wheel. He resolves the confusion and disorder of the masses, manifesting the true and correct Dharma of original non-being.
He issues forth training that transcends all categories to reach omniscience, shaking the three realms.

With the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he instructs all who are ignorant and obscured; he parts from the three poisons as one blows away floating clouds. Using the vessel of the Dharma, he goes to ferry sentient beings across; he exhorts those in the twelve oceans to escape the wheel of birth and death, rescuing them from the twelve causes within the cycle of coming and going through the three states of existence.
The bodhisattvas assembled there were endowed with perfected merit; their names were:

Bodhisattva Candradatta, Bodhisattva Candracchattra, Bodhisattva Śānticchattra, Bodhisattva Mūrdhacchattra, Bodhisattva Prabhācchattra, and Bodhisattva Prabhāmūrdhan, as well as Mūrdhakūṭa, Mūrdhaśānti, Śṛṅkhalā, and Nāga.
Nandi, Nāgadatta, Bimba-dhara, Varuṇa, Varadatta, Nityotkṣiptahasta,
Nityanikṣiptahasta, Ratnamudrāhasta, Ratnapāṇi, Viśvabhū, Jyotiṣprabha, Vajramati, Vajrapada, Acalagatipracāra, Traikalokottīrṇa, Amitapada, and Ananta...
Mātr̥neta, Sāgaranetra, Dṛḍhamati, Uttaramati, Dhāraṇīmati, Vardhamānamati,
Sadāprarudita, Sadāpramukta, Nandendriya, Suprabhāsa-tejas, Vimala, Apagatāpāya,
Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, Atitejas, Jñānakūṭa, Nityodyukta, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Śikhin (Mountain Peak), Gaganagañja (Treasury of Space), Animiṣa (Unblinking), Anabhirati (Not Delighting in Pleasure),

Ratnottama (Supreme Jewel), Ratnacitta (Jewel-Minded), Sucintita (Well-Considered), Sucintitārtha (One Who Has Well-Considered the Meaning), Maṇigranthiśekhara (Crest of the Pearl-Knot), Śrīrāja (Glorious King), Vimalarāja (Stainless King),

Kṣetravyūha (Adorned Realm), Ratnakāra (Jewel-Maker), Varada (Bestower of Boons), Indradeva (Lord of Gods), Varuṇadeva (Lord of Waters), Īśvara (Sovereign), Prabhāketu (Luminous Banner), and Upendradeva (Lord of the Secondary Gods).
Accumulated Joy, Virtuous Arm, White Elephant, Fragrant Hand, Many-Fragrant Hand, Lion,
Universal Excellence, Sharp Intellect, Wondrous Charioteer, Great Charioteer, Tranquil Mind, Maitreya,
Universal Head, and Youthful Truth— these were the names of each of those eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.

At that time, in this trichiliocosm Buddha-field, the Great Honored Ones—the exalted Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings; as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and gandharvas—along with their kings and retinues, all assembled together.

The Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Sāgara, the Dragon King Mānasa, the Dragon King Tāṭaka, the Dragon King Himavarṇa, the Dragon King Anantavarṇa, the Dragon King Susīma, and countless hundreds of thousands of other dragon kings, together with their officials and retinues, all came to the assembly.

The Āsura King Kṣāntivāsa, the Āsura King Sumati, the Āsura King Vaitaraṇī, the Āsura King Vṛkṣānuga, the Āsura King Mālādhāra, the Āsura King Unmāda, the Āsura King Chinnabandhana, and the Āsura King Graha-grahaṇa—each surrounded by countless retinues—all came to this assembly.
King Bimbisāra of Magadha, along with his palace ladies and retinue, all came to the assembly.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; the lords of the earth and gods, the gods of the desire realm, the gods of the form realm, and the Śuddhāvāsa gods—all came to the assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of followers as he preached the sutra, proclaiming the deeds of the Bodhisattvas, the Great Beings; the name of that Dharma was "The Extensive Propagation of the Meaning of the Path of Pure Deliverance."
What is called the karma of a bodhisattva?
It is to practice giving in order to transform sentient beings and rescue them from peril and distress;
and to cultivate the karma of the precepts so as to fulfill all aspirations through the ten virtuous deeds.
Practicing the karma of patience, one fully perfects all the primary marks and eighty minor characteristics to adorn one's own body;
practicing the karma of diligence, one brings to complete fulfillment all roots of virtue created, leaving nothing deficient or omitted;
practicing the karma of meditative reflection, one’s disposition becomes peaceful and stable, achieving the inconceivable.

They practice the karma of wisdom, severing all worldly afflictions and achieving holy illumination to transform those who have not yet attained understanding; they practice the karma of extensive learning, attaining unimpeded eloquence such that their speech flows like a stream and listeners immediately receive it;
they practice the karma of merit, exhorting and benefiting sentient beings with limitless blessings;
and they practice the karma of holy illumination, whereby they attain immeasurable and ultimate true eloquence.
They practice the karma of tranquility, giving rise to that which is inconceivable to the multitudes;
they practice the karma of right contemplation, abandoning perverse conduct and unbeneficial matters;
they practice the karma of a compassionate mind, constantly cultivating benevolence and harmony without ever harboring malice.
They practice the karma of compassion, desiring to rescue sentient beings without weariness from beginning to end;
they practice the karma of joy, delighting in the bliss of the Dharma for their own amusement, while also transforming sentient beings to cause them to yearn for the Way and the Dharma;

they practice the karma of protection, severing immeasurable transgressions and demonstrating both faults and blessings through the Dharma to benefit all, and attending Dharma assemblies to remove the various veils of the aggregates so that they do not become conceited.
They practice the vocation of renunciation, relinquishing the worldly habits of affection, attachment, resentment, and longing;
they practice the vocation of dwelling in seclusion, ensuring that the essential principles they establish do not lose their single-minded focus;
they practice the vocation of aspiration, attaining *dhāraṇī* so that they may remember the Dharma without forgetfulness and thereby transform the multitudes.
He practices the karma of mindfulness, his mind being clear and understanding such that nothing remains unpenetrated;
he practices the karma of purposeful movement, comprehending the direction of meanings so that they are beneficial and not detrimental;
he practices the karma of the foundations of mindfulness, observing the body, sensations, the mind, and all phenomena.
Practicing the karma of the right exertions (*samyakprahāṇa*), they sever all sinful and evil dharmas, universally cultivating the meaning of the Path and the sublime dharmas of all practices;
practicing the karma of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they make their bodies and minds light, coming and going to reach those in distress and rescue the lowly and inferior;
practicing the karma of the faculties (*indriya*), they are fully endowed with tranquility, causing the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind to be concentrated and undisturbed.
They practice the karma of the various powers, eliminating the faults of all worldly afflictions and impurities, constantly being able to exercise self-restraint while transforming the multitudes;
they practice the karma of the factors of enlightenment, elucidating the natural Dharma to achieve rectitude within themselves;
they practice the karma of the Path, transcending the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths.
One practices the karma of true correctness, thereby accomplishing deeds of benevolence and righteousness without feelings of anger or joy;
one practices the karma of liberating eloquence, perceiving the minds of sentient beings and elucidating the Dharma for them;
one practices the karma of self-reliance, attaining realization within oneself without depending on others.
They practice the karma of spiritual friends, penetrating the gateway of merit and saving others through wisdom and virtue;
they practice the karma of pure nature, universally harmonizing the three periods of time without deception or delusion;
they practice the karma of timely response, being able to fully accomplish the transcendence of all difficulties.
They practice the deeds of the noble and wise;
wherever they go, they are distinguished and far surpass the multitude;
they practice the deed of serene sitting, constantly upholding and practicing the Dharma as it has been heard.
They practice the karma of the four debts of gratitude, gathering the assembly to expound the Dharma;
they practice the karma of the true Dharma, following the teachings of the Three Jewels so that they shall not be interrupted;
they understand the karma of exhortation and assistance, diligently transforming sentient beings and adorning and purifying the Buddha-lands.
The activity of skillful means universally fulfills all compassionate wisdom.
Thus, the World-Honored One extensively proclaimed for all the bodhisattva activities, which are called "Purity."
Thereupon, the Vajrapāṇi named Guhyapada, who stood to the right of the World-Honored One holding a vajra in his hand, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly unprecedented that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, has so excellently expounded the essential sūtra entitled 'The Pure and Saving Acts of Bodhisattvas.'"
As the Great Sage has proclaimed this Dharma, I observe and contemplate that all these activities enter into the bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom-activities. Why is this so?
All these sublime merits are that which all bodhisattvas enjoy and through which they manifest transformations; by means of these delights, they gather and guide sentient beings.
As for their activity of wisdom, the bodhisattvas’ elegant words bring great joy and satisfaction.

If there is a bodhisattva who thoroughly understands the meritorious karma of the essential points and cultivates the karma of clear wisdom, this is the foremost practice of true sincerity. Why is this so?
That meritorious karma is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), through which he fulfills the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) and is endowed with auspicious blessings.
That wisdom-karma is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), in which all various practices are fully perfected.

By means of these two karmas, they universally fulfill all bodhisattva paths and provide vast relief through their benevolence; no followers of Māra can withstand them, as they have transcended the realm of Māra.
When a bodhisattva thus reaches the stage of non-retrogression, they shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path by reckoning the fundamental nature of all dharmas.

Those who have reached non-retrogression draw near to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and all attain the Tathāgata’s secret and essential treasury, which they may proclaim at will without ever concealing it.
Then, the Bodhisattva Silent Intent addressed the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada: "Guhyapada!
That which is called the two types of practice brings one close to the wisdom of the Tathāgata."

O Benevolent One, you are able to joyfully abide in and proclaim the secret activities of the Tathāgata, which are beyond the reach of the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone those of other ordinary worldlings!
At that time, Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, remained silent and gave no reply.
Then the Bodhisattva Śāntamati came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Could it be that the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapāda would deign to lower his dignity and, for the sake of this assembly, expound at this opportune moment the secrets of the bodhisattvas and the esoteric essentials of the Tathāgata?"
The entire assembly universally yearned with thirsting aspiration to hear it;

upon hearing what was spoken, their minds became serene, and they rejoiced with great delight, vowing to practice the bodhisattva path, fully accomplishing these essential and secret matters, harmonizing their mental natures, and entering into boundless compassion.
The Buddha addressed Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi:

"You are capable of undertaking this great responsibility to explain for this assembly the Bodhisattva’s esoteric teachings and the secret essentials of the Tathāgata; the thousand Buddhas commend and praise you."
“You, O Minister, shall proclaim the various practices and the stages of the bodhisattva path; the assembly longs to hear them.
Then Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I am somewhat capable of proclaiming for this assembly the secrets of the bodhisattvas and the essential mysteries of the Tathāgata.”

If the Tathāgata were to assist with his majestic spiritual power and provide support, and if I were to ride upon the light of great wisdom and receive the Buddha’s holy mandate, I would then dare to proclaim the secrets of all bodhisattvas and the essential mysteries of the Tathāgata.
It is just as, World-Honored One, when it is dark at night,
by relying on the light of a lamp, one is able to see forms and colors, comings and goings, beauty and ugliness, and the east, west, south, and north, as well as what should be advanced or retreated.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Having seen that which was established in accordance with the Buddha’s holy intent, I have briefly raised up and praised what I know.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Speak it when the time is right.
Then, the Māṇibhadra Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"O Benevolent One, listen for a moment; and you who have gathered here, upon hearing this secret of the Bodhisattvas and the profound mystery of the Tathāgata, do not be afraid, do not be terrified, and harbor no fear."
Then the Bodhisattva Silent Intent addressed those gathered:
"The Tathāgata has proclaimed four inconceivable things; by means of these, he attained the path of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment, reaching supreme, perfect awakening."
What are these four?
