The karma they perform and establish is inconceivable; their resolve is like that of a dragon king and their conduct is incalculable; their single-minded meditative concentration is beyond measure; and the practices of the Buddhas are boundless.
These are the four matters.

Virtuous one, you should know that these four are inconceivable: the practice of the Buddha-way is inconceivable; having attained supreme sovereignty, one achieves perfect enlightenment. For these reasons, they are called the four inconceivables.

Virtuous ones, when gathered here, if you hear of the inconceivable nature of the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, you should not be terrified or harbor fear; rather, you should increase your exultation and redouble your reverence, thereby attaining the Great Way.

At that time, Śāntamati entered the samādhi known as "Just as It Is" (yathāvat), causing all those in the assembly to hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata. None among them felt revulsion; instead, each was filled with joy in their heart. All who had gathered at the site of the assembly were present, and the heavens rained down various kinds of flowers—flowers corresponding to the diverse thoughts in their minds—which they scattered over the Buddha and the entire assembly as an offering.
Thereupon, the Malla Guhyapāda said to Śāntamati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
I shall now proclaim the secrets of the bodhisattvas and the essential mysteries of the Tathāgata; you should practice with serene detachment day and night in profound stillness."

The words of the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas are most sincere; having reached a definitive resolution free from discrimination, they bestow the distinction of the Way. From this point onward, one follows and accords with the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva of the Five Practices is without flattery or deceit, does not harbor concealment or hypocrisy, and is not self-exalting;
when the time for manifestation arises, he exercises mastery over transformations.
With a mind of mastery, they do not calculate the karma of the wicked, the sycophantic, or that which is contrary to the Dharma;
they are prudent in their physical conduct, maintaining dignified deportment and ritual propriety to transform sentient beings, while their speech remains free of idle talk and false words;
the majestic demeanor of a Bodhisattva is immeasurable.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!

In accordance with the conduct of sentient beings, he employs all manner of majestic deportment and ritual propriety as means for their transformation. He causes them to train in various modes of learning, meditative contemplation, and etiquette, ensuring that they clearly understand numerous sounds, resonances, and modes of speech.

Regarding the conduct, movements, deportment, and ritual etiquette of both men and women, each should act according to their station; those who are to be transformed by seeing infants at their breasts should each be careful in their dignified demeanor.

Whether among the elderly, those of middle age, or the young; whether in matters of transformation through teaching, dignified deportment, or ritual propriety; and whether concerning the conduct of the noble or the lowly, the wealthy or the poor, the wise or the ignorant, or their various states of openness, obstruction, penetration, or delusion.
According to the extent of their conduct and their observance of dignified decorum and ritual etiquette, he transforms those who are ready to be delivered by relying upon his instructions.

He guides and leads those who should be transformed—beings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and whether they be humans or non-humans.

He should instruct and admonish bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the great, sublime devas—whomever is fit to be transformed and taught.

The Bodhisattvas fully know the depth and shallowness, the thickness and thinness, and the difficulty or ease of transforming others; they administer medicine according to the ailment and preach the Dharma accordingly, causing those who are greedy and lustful to cease their craving for wealth and worldly affairs, and to establish dignified deportment in accordance with proper etiquette.

The Bodhisattva abides therein in the unconditioned and profound stillness; practicing with his very body, he does not abandon silent contemplation while manifesting the majestic deportment of his form. Should there be those possessed by greed or envy, he manifests himself before each of them, never sparing his own body or life as he provides timely salvation and succor.

With physical conduct purified, his body radiates light; for all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals who suffer the afflictions of diligent toil and hardship, he rescues them from their perilous distress, establishing them in a place of peace so that they are free from all calamities.

If there are sentient beings who possess much karma of stinginess, [the Bodhisattva] manifests various kinds of rare treasures and wealth according to their inclinations, so that each may find what they need.

Whether it be his head, eyes, flesh, bones, joints, limbs, marrow, or brain; or his wife, children, attendants, chariots, horses, slaves, servants, robes, or furs—he gives all these away in accordance with their desires and whatever brings them joy.
If they seek sweet delicacies or superior garments and bedding, may all have their desires fulfilled and each find what they need.
Assuming the countless bodies of all sentient beings, throughout the infinite Dharma-realm, he establishes them all in peace and satisfies everyone completely.
The wisdom of the Way is inexhaustible, manifesting its bodies throughout the ten directions without limit; the skillful means of causes and conditions are likewise endless.
By manifesting its essence through innumerable bodies according to the times, it transforms and enlightens sentient beings, each leading them to their proper place.

If there are sentient beings who have much greed for desire, lustful thoughts, and passion for form, [the Buddha] manifests the appearance of a woman, upright and exquisite. When those people see her, they rejoice and turn toward her with reverence; they delight in her company and gaze upon her without weariness, as if she were a precious luminous pearl. Suddenly, however, she becomes foul-smelling and loathsome, her complexion becoming extremely hideous.

Beholding these transformed states of mind, he felt weary and disgusted; he then manifested death to further increase their sense of revulsion, and subsequently preached the Dharma on impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, explaining that all within the three realms is like an illusion or a transformation, wherein not a single thing possesses true reality.
Upon hearing this, they attained penetration and immediately gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, true enlightenment, reaching the stage of non-retrogression.

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas were able to cover this trichiliocosm with a single precious canopy such that no part was left uncovered, and yet they could also place it within a single mustard seed.
If at the time of the kalpa-conflagration, one were to take up all [the burning worlds] and place them upon a single palm, this body would neither expand nor diminish.

This body makes offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions; furthermore, it transforms flowers as large as Mount Sumeru, holds them in its lap, and forms them into flower canopies to present as offerings to the Tathāgatas.

He transforms a single incense burner so that it becomes like a thousand buddha-fields and creates a single lamp-torch as large as Mount Sumeru; he offers these to the Tathāgata, illuminating buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to present as offerings to the Buddha.
Wrapping his body in fine silk and cotton, he used sesame oil as fuel for a lamp; naturally, his own body emanated light that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm of Buddha-fields.
If sentient beings perceive the reason for this marvel, they may attain the contemplation of the bodhisattva realm.
Beholding these countless transformations, all give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, attaining a state of joy that fills them with contentment and satiety.

Clad in the armor of the great vow, manifesting the form of a Hārītī and wielding infinite power, he held a vajra in his hand as a Vajrapāṇi attendant to the Buddha, shining forth with brilliance; all people were struck with awe and took refuge, prostrating themselves in worship.

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva listens to and receives the Dharma of the sutras, he manifests as a great strongman in a charnel ground, gathering a vast multitude of people by manifesting his own death.

His body, broad and tall, is cast into a great cemetery; furthermore, various birds and beasts devour his flesh, and four-footed and two-footed creatures feed upon his body. After his life has ended, they all attain rebirth in the heavens.
From this as the basis up to final nirvāṇa, all of these are brought about by the extraordinary power of the bodhisattva’s original vows.
Why is this so? When that bodhisattva first resolved his mind [on awakening], he made a solemn vow within his own heart:

"Suppose there were humans, beasts, or flying birds who, upon seeing my body dead, came to devour my flesh; by the end of their lives, they would be reborn in heaven, transcend the world, and attain the Way, for they have upheld the prohibitive precepts and obtained whatever they wished for."
"Thus it is, Śāntamati! You should contemplate in this way:
the conduct of a bodhisattva consists of transforming beings according to the appropriate ritual conventions for each occasion.
Thus spoke the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada to the Bodhisattva Śāntamati.

"In the distant past, long ago, this Jambudvīpa was a vast, unified realm consisting of eighty-four thousand kingdoms, with countless hundreds of thousands of additional districts, counties, villages, and hamlets, where the population was so flourishing it could not be measured."
At that time, there was an abundance of wealth, treasures, clothing, and food, naturally filling every place; various wondrous jewel-trees entwined the dwellings.

Among these sentient beings, there were many who suffered from various ailments, distressing afflictions, and were emaciated by weakness; they had golden wounds, sores, abscesses, and painful, malignant diseases, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of conditions that even the most skilled physicians could not cure.
This multitude has suffered from this illness for many years; unable to find peace, they have come to me seeking refuge in their distress.

While these people encounter such calamity, they find no protection; each laments their own plight, crying out to the heavens, the nāgas, the devas, the gandharvas, the kinnaras, the mahoragas, humans, and non-humans:
"Who can heal me and eliminate my suffering and misfortune?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva was the foremost of all; appearing as a skilled physician, he treated the illnesses of the multitude. He constantly employed a compassionate heart, diligently serving and following behind them like a slave, providing whatever was required to repay their kindness and rescue them from peril and distress.
Therefore, Śāntamati!
In ages long past, during that very time, this present World-Honored One was the Lord of Devas, named Suśīla.

While in the heavens, he saw from afar many people afflicted by various diseases and suffering from hardships beyond description; with his divine ear, he heard the groans and lamentations of those in distress. Having seen and heard this, he gave rise to great compassion and thought to himself:
"Now these many people are abandoned to great distress and hardship, with no one to turn to for refuge.

It is now fitting that I should rescue these people from their suffering: for those without rescue, I shall provide a virtuous savior; for those without reliance, I shall establish a multitude of refuges; and for those without a place of return, I shall create a destination for them."

At that time, within Jambudvīpa under heaven, there was a great kingdom and city named Kuru. Not far from that city, the Celestial Emperor Bodhisattva transformed himself into a beast called Renliang (Kind and Good), spontaneously manifesting by transformation within the borders of that kingdom.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was in the sky and addressed the people of Jambudvīpa in the world with these verses:
"Not far from this land, there is an insect named Renliang (Benevolent and Good).
Whoever eats the flesh of this insect shall obtain deliverance and escape from all calamities."
Do not be afraid, do not harbor fear; behold this insect’s body and take its flesh as you please.
It harbors no anger and is free from loathsome impurity; it is a divine, wondrous, and excellent medicine.
Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, further addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"At that time, all those who were afflicted by illness—the inhabitants of that great kingdom, its cities, districts, counties, villages, hamlets, and settlements—upon hearing this sound, all gathered together and came to the great kingdom of Kuśāvatī."

He went to where the insects were, took pieces of their flesh, and brought them back to treat his illness; each part was healed, yet the body-flesh of the insects remained as it was before, without any diminution.
At that time, an insect in the wilderness within the borders of that country spoke this verse:
"By means of these essential words, May the multitude attain the Buddha-way;
May my wondrous wisdom Ultimately reach inexhaustibility."
"Having repeatedly practiced and studied the prohibitions and precepts, and having offered even his own flesh and muscles as a gift,
by means of these words of utmost sincerity, he has swiftly attained the True and Right Path.
Thus spoke the Vajrapāṇi Mārṣa Guhyapada.
"Thus it is, Śāntamati!

All those in the world of Jambudvīpa who are afflicted by illness shall go and take the flesh of this benevolent and excellent insect and consume it entirely; there is no bodily ailment that will not be healed."

At that time, those insects, out of compassion for sentient beings, kept their bodies as they were, neither increasing nor decreasing in size; though each was cut off, it grew back as before, their bodies remaining whole and complete without any deficiency.

In all commanderies, kingdoms, counties, towns, cities, and great states, wherever there are those suffering from afflictions, may those who dare to come and eat the flesh of these benevolent insects all attain peace and security.

Within seven days, let the people of the world no longer suffer from the hardships of disease or various calamities; however, let only the physical ailments be removed, while the mental maladies of lust, anger, and delusion remain undissolved.
At that time, all the people of the world—men and women, great and small—attained peace and security, and their physical ailments were no more.

Each thought to themselves: "By what means may we now repay the benevolent care and compassionate nurturing provided by this virtuous one, who has enabled us to be relieved of our many illnesses and attained peace and security, forever free from all suffering?"

All those whose illnesses had been cured gathered together and went to the land of Kiu-liu to the abode of the benevolent insect. They all joined their palms and addressed this verse to the benevolent insect:
“You are our protector; Your body is the medicine of a skilled physician.
May you cause us all to be freed from affliction; How shall we repay your nurturing kindness?”
At that time, the insect Renliang submerged its own body and manifested in the form of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"Just as my body today, It does not rely on various worldly occupations,
Nor is it sustained by food and drink, Nor by gold, silver, or precious jewels."
They do not use fine elephant-drawn chariots, nor swift horses or elegant carriages.
Men and women, great and small alike, all share a single heart in harmony;
they all reform their past ways and cultivate the future, personally practicing the ten wholesome deeds.
Each facing one another with a heart of loving-kindness, they take turns feeling compassion for one another;
seeing each other as their own flesh and bone, just like a parent and child,
they harbor no thoughts of malice in their hearts, thereby repaying the kindness of their upbringing.
Guhya-pāda, the Vajrapāṇi, said to the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"At that time, having heard his instruction and being transformed by their past merits, all those people together practiced these ten wholesome actions; they were fully pure and free from any deficiency."
Thus it was, Śāntamati!

At that time, the men and women, great and small, of the world practiced the ten wholesome deeds; throughout their lives and even after death, they did not fall into the evil realms or the perils of the three calamities, and upon the end of their lives, they naturally attained rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of Devas, expounded the Dharma for them and revealed the great enterprise; they all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and immediately established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression.

Śāntamati, you should understand that this is the secret practice cultivated by Bodhisattvas: to maintain the purity of their bodies while not begrudging their own lives, giving themselves as alms to transform and rescue countless sentient beings, leading them to the Great Way.
The Buddha told Śāntamati:
“The multitude of secrets practiced by the body of a bodhisattva is firm, solid, and strong; it is indestructible, like a vajra.
Because his body is dispersed through the discipline of the vows according to the aspirations learned by all people, even if one wishes to destroy it, one cannot break it.”
Sentient beings, through study, abide in the unbreakable state of all dharmas by following the Dharma of study.
The teachings they proclaim cannot be burned by fire nor harmed by the sword;
their bodies are firm and strong, essential and indestructible. It is just so, Śāntamati!
As for the body of that bodhisattva, it accords with the Dharma and Vinaya to discipline and transform sentient beings.
As for the mind of that bodhisattva, it does not dwell in quiescence nor harbor delusive thoughts.
The bodies of all sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent; one’s own self is likewise so, being fundamentally empty.
By realizing that the self is fundamentally non-existent, one understands that all dharmas are likewise fundamentally non-existent.
Since all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, one further realizes that the self returns to this fundamental non-existence, and thus all dharmas are likewise fundamentally non-existent.
All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; one's own body, being natural, likewise returns to fundamental non-existence.
Since the self is fundamentally non-existent, the dharmas of the past, future, and present are likewise fundamentally non-existent.

One realizes that the phenomena of the past, future, and present are fundamentally non-existent; furthermore, one's own body is also fundamentally non-existent. One understands that the past is fundamentally non-existent and the future is fundamentally non-existent, without any confusion.

The fundamental non-existence of the future does not contradict the fundamental non-existence of the past; the fundamental non-existence of the past does not contradict the fundamental non-existence of the present; and the fundamental non-existence of the present does not contradict the fundamental non-existence of the past.

The present non-existence does not contradict the past and future non-existences; the past and future non-existences do not contradict the present non-existence; and that future non-existence does not contradict the present non-existence.
The fundamental non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*) of the past, future, and present is not in contradiction with the fundamental non-existence of the present.

For one who practices the fundamental non-existence of the past, future, and present, there is never any contradiction between the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), various decays, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Suppose that both saṃsāra and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are by nature originally non-existent. Since saṃsāra is originally non-existent, it is by nature originally non-existent because there is nothing therein to be practiced.
Since non-practice is originally non-existent, it does not contradict original non-existence; thus all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature originally non-existent.
Furthermore, son of good family!

That which is called "original non-existence" (prakṛti-nirvāṇa) is equal and without distinction; it does not depart from desire, nor is there anything established therein. Original non-existence is without contention;

that which contends with various forms of contention does not contend at all. Because there is no contention, that which is originally non-existent likewise has no contention. This is what is termed the "original non-existence of the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata has no form; returning to this fundamental non-existence is what is called the "form and image" of the Tathāgata.

He universally manifests all manner of forms and images; therefore, these forms and images—the forms and images of the Tathāgata—are fundamentally empty in every respect, and this is what is called the "image of the Tathāgata."
Therefore, while the Bodhisattva manifests all forms, the Tathāgata has never created or manifested any form.
Being without form and without contention, he then universally manifests all manner of images, yet this is not established by means of an original non-existence.

Based on the fundamental non-existence of karma, one contemplates one's own body; all bodies are fundamentally non-existent. One examines the Dharma-body and all other bodies, finding that they are all without a body.

Contemplating the body of the Tathāgata, one understands that all bodies arise from causes and conditions; by comprehending the original course of the Dharma-body, the causal factors and the Dharma-body together constitute the Dharma-body.
When there are no aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*), it is said that the Dharma-body performs impartial action.
It eliminates the conditions of what sentient beings perceive; whether there is something heard or experienced, coarse or subtle—it is just so, O Śāntamati!

The physician-king Jīvaka gathered various medicines and fashioned them into the form of a youth, exquisite and beautiful, a rarity in the world. His every action was composed and perfect, displaying transformations of such incomparable excellence that whether walking, wandering, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, or pacing, there was no deficiency in the miraculous deeds he manifested.

There may be great and powerful kings, crown princes, ministers, officials of high rank, those of noble lineage, or elders who come to the presence of Jīvaka, the King of Physicians. There, they watch as he plays and sings with the young attendant who prepares his medicines; by observing their facial expressions, Jīvaka diagnoses their ailments so that all illnesses are eliminated, leading them immediately to a state of peace, tranquility, and freedom from desire.
Śāntamati, observe this: the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, treats those in the world in a manner that no other physicians can equal.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!

If a bodhisattva practices in accordance with the Dharma-body, even if sentient beings abound in lust, anger, and ignorance, and men and women, great and small, desire to cherish and delight in one another and thus enjoy each other's company, their greedy desires and worldly afflictions shall all find rest.

Because they have attained rest within the perception of inhalation and exhalation—meaning they are free from the causes of feverish desire and thereby receive transformation—all of these are the fulfillment of the Bodhisattvas' vows.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
If Bodhisattvas practice and cultivate the Dharma-body, these Bodhisattvas are themselves the Dharma-body.

They manifest the filling of this body with food and drink, yet they do not consume solid food to sustain their physical form, having severed all desire for such meals. Out of compassion for sentient beings, they manifest eating again; however, the food does not enter into the interior of the body nor adhere within the body, and thus the power of their Dharma-body neither increases nor diminishes.
The Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva is such that its origin is unknown and it is without death; it has no end and no beginning, yet it manifests birth and death in accordance with worldly conventions.
Although it manifests passing away, it understands that all phenomena are entirely without activity.
Manifesting birth, they expound that all dharmas are unconditioned and without assembly.

Although all dharmas appear to have birth, they are in fact without birth; they clearly understand that all conditioned phenomena manifest their own bodies. Though their faculties may be deficient, their conduct does not destroy the Dharma-body. Thus, by means of the power of the Dharma-body, the food of the Dharma, and the power of the Dharma, they take refuge in the Dharma itself and realize the body of the Tathāgata.

"Śāntamati! If you wish to know the body of the Tathāgata, it is the body of empty space, without equal. Abiding within the triple world as the most supreme, he bestows upon sentient beings a body that has no place of return; it cannot be illustrated by analogy and has no counterpart."

His body is pure, having cast off defilement and being free from dust; his body is fundamentally pure and unstained, naturally radiant and forever devoid of the darkness of impurity; its original nature is harmonious and benevolent, entirely without arising.
His body is tranquil, not bound or constrained by mind, thought, or consciousness.
His body is spontaneous, like a magical illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water.
His body has already transcended emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
His body pervades the void of the ten directions; his mind is entirely equanimous, having realized the fundamental nature of the triple world, wherein all sentient beings are devoid of selfhood.
His body is bottomless and immeasurable, without action and without thought.
This body is without attachment and free from all thought; abiding in the ultimate truth, it reaches the point of non-retrogression.

This body has no form, yet naturally manifests forms; it has no sensation, yet manifests sensations; it is naturally without perception, yet manifests perceptions; it has no consciousness of birth and death, yet naturally manifests all consciousnesses of birth and death; it lacks the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, yet through them it manifests the body of the four great elements.

One understands that all phenomena appearing in the world are empty and unreal: the eye sees nothing, the ear hears nothing, the nose does not smell fragrances, the tongue does not dwell on flavors, and the body does not rely upon tactile activity; thus, all consciousnesses are forever extinguished.
The mind has nothing to receive; the consciousness does not shift. Being without mind, thought, or consciousness, one understands the ultimate truth without ever advancing or retreating.
"At that time, O Śāntamati!..."
Regarding the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, if there is a bodhisattva who is able to attain this equal body of the Tathāgata, there are no bodhisattva practices that they do not universally uphold.

Within this trichiliocosm—in all the regions of the four quarters, the prefectures, kingdoms, counties, towns, cities, and great states—they manifest their bodies everywhere. All demons are unable to perceive or know the deeds performed by the bodhisattva; whether manifesting or remaining unmanifest, they are fully able to comprehend these subtle and wondrous karmas.

Although there is nothing manifested, he universally manifests all things; yet he never conceives thoughts of seeing, hearing, knowing, or perceiving, nor does he have anything to practice for the sake of transforming sentient beings, and he does not lose the four foundations of mindfulness through his physical conduct.

For the sake of sentient beings, he manifests his body to demonstrate the principles of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, so that they may understand and penetrate how the fundamental nature of all bodies is entirely quiescent.

He manifests his body to sentient beings as subject to decay and ruin; those who seek the body through the pursuit of karmic retribution thereby turn back from the truth, for such seeking for retribution follows the four inversions.

Those who understand and perceive that there is neither action nor seeing, and who clearly know that their own bodies are like grass, trees, walls, or bricks and stones, manifest pure bodies for the sake of all sentient beings.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
Since the time he was first granted the prediction by Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the Bodhisattva has attained a secret body of pure essence.
Even when the Bodhisattva utters words from his mouth, they are entirely devoid of verbal expression.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!

That which the Tathāgata has spoken is appropriate to the occasion; according to their conceptualizations, he speaks of the quiescence of the secret body of the bodhisattva. From this, they progress further and attain deliverance, reaching the boundless.
What is called the secret of the Bodhisattva’s body is attained through mastery.

The Bodhisattva, in proclaiming the profound mystery of his own person, has briefly set forth its essentials; were he to wish to explain it in full detail, even eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not suffice to exhaustively elucidate it.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati: "What is meant by 'mystery' (guhya)? His speech is pure;

according to the various classes of sentient beings—even those who have fallen among the animals in their respective numbers—the Bodhisattva likewise manifests as many sounds and languages. Examining those sounds, he manifests various expressions, conforming to the chapters, phrases, and languages of those beings to expound his teachings. He proclaims them at the appropriate times, engaging them in conversation, and speaks of the places of suffering and joy, and of good and evil."
The voice of that Bodhisattva enters everywhere and reaches all places without exception.

Whether manifesting songs, plays, illusions, transformations, anger, or joy, he utters his words and phrases, entering into the training and instruction of sentient beings by following their respective languages and sounds.
"According to all that is believed by their bodies and minds, and what is cherished by their hearts, the Bodhisattva fully understands and discerns it, causing each to hear and comprehend.
The Bodhisattva Silent Intent (Śāntamati) asked the Vajrapāṇi Mārṣa:
"What is the nature of the sounds and voices emanated by the Bodhisattva?"
Guhyapada replied: "It follows all the sounds and voices of sentient beings.

Furthermore, the resonance of a bodhisattva is boundless; just as the mental inclinations of sentient beings differ according to their place of birth, and the languages and sounds of the five destinies are each distinct and beyond calculation."

In this way, the Bodhisattva issues forth from each sound and word yet remains without words; this is called following the voices of sentient beings without failing to reach them, while understanding that they are non-existent.

One should contemplate in this way: all the words and phrases proclaimed by every resonance are ultimately inconceivable and their expressions are inexhaustible; this is the bodhisattva’s transformative teaching according to the occasion, which cannot be fully illustrated by analogy.

He freely proclaims an immeasurable resonance; sometimes he manifests the voices of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, and at other times he freely proclaims the voices of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. Following the voices of sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior, coarse or subtle, beautiful or ugly—he emanates these sounds and resonances to bring joy to all.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"By means of such words and phrases, he resolves many matters; he expounds and disseminates the countless teachings he has proclaimed."
He heals with a heart of loving-kindness, penetrating into compassion; he proclaims and expounds widely, his mind protected by joy.
The Lord of Devas gathers [the assembly] with gentleness and harmony; whoever hears this eclipses all other sounds.
Following from the musical performances, the sorrowful sounds produced therein proclaim the teachings of these sūtras.
These tones are like this, universally complete in every way; hearing them causes desire to cease.
No lustful thoughts arise.
All the mountain deities delight in music; throughout the desire realm, there are all manner of wondrous sounds.
The sounds of all musical instruments and the voices of the devas arise entirely from this; they are truly lovely and pleasing.
These sounds of the Dharma, through skillful means according to the occasion, proclaim verses that eliminate anger and desire, and remove ignorance, pride, and the conduct of self-aggrandizement.
Having clearly distinguished and fully understood, one knows the destination toward which one’s conduct leads.
Because of proclaiming this, all the devas within the realm of form (rūpadhātu) are able to find delight; such is the intention of these devas.
Because they have been able to hear these extraordinary teachings, those who have resolved their minds while in the world shall attain the Buddha-way.
The nāgas, gandharvas, mahoragas, and all varieties of musical instruments and performances—
When the ocean of virtue proclaims its subtle and wondrous teachings, all sentient beings rejoice, their hearts leaping with joy.
Entering into countless varieties of sounds, [he reaches] throughout Jambudvīpa, to all the people who dwell therein.
That sound is all-pervasive, entering these sentient beings; those who hear it shall all attain liberation.
Its resonance reaches everywhere, extending to those distant realms, so that all may hear the teaching.
There was none who did not rejoice; all together they resolved their doubts and were filled with heartfelt joy.
The cries of the mourning pheasant, the crane, and the wild goose; the voice of the red-beaked crow;
the mountain birds, the peacock, the parrot, the *kūṭa*, and the *kukkuṭa*; the various extraordinary birds, the *śirīṣa* and the ruddy sheldrake—[all sang in harmony].
If they hear this sound, all shall find joy in their hearts.
Bears, cubs, and monkeys; fawns, deer, mules, and donkeys; wild foxes and various rabbits;
elephants, horses, dogs, and bitches; oxen, sheep, and swine—when these kinds of creatures hear its sound, [they too rejoice].
They are content and filled with joy;
those with many limbs and those without limbs all delight in hearing this.
Understanding its sounds, they proclaim and receive the teachings, abandoning all unwholesome deeds.
Within these three thousand worlds, wherever there are sounds—from those of the highest, the intermediate, and the noble or the lowly;
from those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and down to the species of animals;
from the devas and human beings—all these various sounds and resonances are perceived by him without false views.
They contemplate only the Ultimate Truth;
they harbor no thoughts of seeking, never engage in dispute, carry out their assigned tasks, and keep their resolve fixed upon the mind of the Way.
Proclaiming the command to manifest, one should act according to the proper season; with single-minded concentration, one should endure the disputes of sentient beings.
Teaching through the sound of the Dharma to ten billion lands, one attains penetration from this point onward, reaching as far as the sands of the Ganges;
not relying on wealth or worldly affairs, the mind has no place for activity.
In all the Buddha-lands, wherever there are various Māras, upon hearing this great harmonious voice,
they will be moved by compassion and provide protection; those thus rescued, whether entering or departing,
walking or standing, shall all perform acts of reverence.
Even if there were hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings, each harboring various thoughts and inclinations in their minds,
upon hearing these words, they would not be obstructed or hindered; with their ten fingers joined in prayer,
they would bow their heads in prostration.
Though lying in sleep, deaf, or mute, unable to speak, or lame and footless, afflicted by various great diseases;
may they always keep in mind these subtle and virtuous words, which proclaim gentleness and harmony, and this most excellent teaching of the voice.
Having undergone eons of worldly toil, those who are able to hear this pure sound of the Dharma shall transform even the crows and birds,
leading them to the state of cool serenity.
All sentient beings hear the sūtras and teachings of all Buddhas, as well as the noble Saṃgha;
they hear of the dharma of giving and the precepts, the practice of patience, diligence and single-mindedness,
and the dharma of wisdom.
To describe the intentions harbored in his mind, and the multitude of meritorious deeds performed over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, could not fully exhaust them.
His fundamental limit is bottomless and his intent is immeasurable; he proclaims the Buddha’s voice, reaching everywhere without end.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 8;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 9.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
In the third assembly of the *Guhyakapāda-vajrapāṇi-parivarta*, part two,
Guhyakapāda Vajrapāṇi addressed the bodhisattva Śāntamati:
"Regarding what the Bodhisattva speaks, his mouth has never uttered defiled or evil words, nor unkind expressions."
His speech is free from anger, hatred, and delusion, and likewise devoid of flattery, rigid or contentious words, frivolous jests, and useless rhetoric.
His speech is not characterized by false laughter, slander, or double-tongued talk; he does not disregard the distinction between men and women, nor is he harsh or rigid.
He possesses no coarse language or a nature prone to sudden violence, and is entirely without such faults.
Free from malice, with a mind devoid of grasping or rejecting, one does not lose proper decorum nor harbor knots of resentment in the will.
One is without attachment, without words of contention, without dependence, without defilement, without what is raised up,
without frivolous negligence, without self-indulgence, without improper conduct lacking principle, and without untimely speech.
He is free from greed, free from non-virtue, and free from attachment; he has no fixed abode, nor is there anything impure about him.
He does not act out of season, nor does he violate the proper measure. His faculties are unimpaired, his voice is flawless, and his mind harbors no malice nor any partiality.
There is no license or negligence, no concealment, no contentious speech, no resentment or dislike, and no harbored hatred; one does not falsely accept what is deviant or wrong.
There is no self-refuge, no calculation of "I" or "mine," no harassment of others, and no vexation of oneself or others.
He does not proclaim harm; he is free from the laws of calamity and transgression.
He does not fail in his speech; there is nothing he does not practice, nothing that is not in accordance with his karma, and nothing he cannot endure; all that he proclaims is harmonious.
There is no matter of lacking the spiritual lineage; there is no teaching of frivolousness, and one abandons unrighteous conduct.
One does not destroy the practice of the Dharma, does not transgress the proper seasons, does not violate what is appropriate and measured, and does not proclaim [the truth] for a mere moment.

One does not disparage one's own kind, nor does one disrupt the companionship of others; one does not rejoice when receiving praise for oneself, nor feel distressed or agitated upon seeing others praised.
One guards one’s integrity with vigilance and does not treat others with contempt; one does not speak what is inappropriate, does not disparage what is appropriate, and does not slander secret words.

Always protect yourself according to the occasion; do not slander those of clear wisdom, do not revile the noble and holy ones, let your speech not be false, do not disparage those who bear witness to the truth, do not impute guilt to others, and do not seek out the shortcomings of others.
What is called "turning the teaching" does not involve injuring one's sinews or bones, nor does it consist of proclaiming the evils of others.

One’s aspiration is for the unsurpassed; one does not judge by outward appearances, does not seek out a different faction, does not harbor thoughts of convenience regarding karma, does not perform rebellious acts, and the mind is always gentle and compliant.
The Vajrapāṇi Mārṣa said to Śāntamati:

"This is what it means for a bodhisattva’s words and deeds to correspond. Taking emptiness, the void, and spiritual valor as their power, they bring forth the fruits of their actions through the retribution of merit, proclaiming sincere speech in accordance with the results of what they have done."
Suppose there were a person who went to a great tree, or perhaps stood there and observed the tree, and having observed it, asked another person: "O man!..."
"Can one know how many leaves grow upon this tree?

There was a man of great wisdom who, without examining the trees nor calculating them, knew the number of those leaves and spoke of their quantity as it was, even while sitting with his companions without having counted them himself.

Since they have not yet attained the realization of the Way and its Virtue, they know only their numerical calculations; though they appear among all beings and manifest in various ways, the words and expressions of these individuals are no different from one another.
If someone were to come and ask, "How many grains of sand are there in the great rivers and sands?
If one were to calculate each one individually, how many grains, how many hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, billions, trillions, quadrillions, and quintillions would there be?"

The water has a measure in liters, pecks, bushels, and gallons that cannot be grasped by ordinary calculation; yet, without observing its limits nor counting them, one knows the exact number of billions, trillions, and quadrillions of grains of sand in the rivers, and knows the precise measures of every liter, peck, bushel, and gallon of water, expounding upon each of these with various kinds of discourse.

Only the Great Sage knows; the devas cannot testify to it, nor can the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas—none of them can provide testimony. Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to know it.

Viewed in this light, the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is immeasurable; he proclaims ten billion voices, which all sentient beings hear, and each attains understanding and liberation.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
"In the distant past, during a long-elapsed eon, there was a seer named Lohitya."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Śānta.
In that kingdom, there was a great tree named Bhadra, whose branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were lush and abundant.
The deity Lohitya constantly dwells beneath it; for twelve full years, he has been counting its leaves and observing them.
On a later day, the tranquil brahmin emerged from the city and went to the site of the Rṣipatana tree, where he spent his time in contemplation day and night.
After finishing his meal, he counted the stems and leaves of several trees, again employing his sagely wisdom with single-minded concentration.
He further asked, "What is meant by 'informing the divine immortals'? I shall count them to know how many there are."
At that time, the brahmin Śānta did not look at the tree nor count its leaves; he immediately spoke this verse:
“There are eight thousand *nayutas* and eight thousand *koṭis* of leaves; The joints number nine thousand six hundred and twenty;
There are five sections, each consisting of two hundred and fifty.”
Six thousand and six hundred and sixty boils and rashes—
O Holy Teacher, if you wish to know, how many leaves are there?
By counting the trunks of the trees and their distribution throughout the land, as well as what I have understood, I report it to you thus.
"Now, being free from negligence, count them whenever you have doubts.
The seer Luyi sighed and said: "Excellent are these ultimate words;
they are truthful and without deception."
"I have sat in meditation for twelve years, counting the limits of my practice; I have even counted the leaves upon those trees, knowing exactly how many leaves there are from root to tip.
I only wish that you, O Brahmin, would explain to me: of what nature is the movement of his voice?"
Jiran then said: "Immortals, listen! It is neither Heaven that does not aid me, nor am I a man of this world;
it is because of my utmost sincerity that I transmit these Great Righteous Practices, all of which are based on true purity and freedom from contention."
The divine seer Lohitya was Śāriputra; the brahmin Śamaṇa was Śākyasiṃha.
You should uphold this teaching of the Ultimate Truth, abiding in utmost sincerity in accordance with what is appropriate for the Dharma.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed Śāntamati:
"This is the most secret activity of the bodhisattva, the source of purity.
His boundless wisdom penetrates deeply into the immeasurable; it is lofty and limitless, manifesting itself according to the occasion. It is the ultimate truth, formless and beyond description."
Guhyakapāṇi, the Vajrapāṇi, again addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
"What is meant by the 'secrecy of the mind'?

It is when the activities of the mind are pure and one does not lose supernormal powers; when one establishes the karma of wisdom and delights in supernormal powers; when one manifests as required and dwells correctly within supernormal powers; and when one establishes the karma of infinite great compassion."

Through supernatural powers, they manifest countless transformations that appear everywhere; taking truthful penetration and wisdom as their dwelling, they perceive all phenomena directly before their eyes—this is the true and correct Dharma of the bodhisattva.
Wisdom penetrates the infinite and universally governs all things; its supernormal wisdom manifests all forms, yet it clearly understands that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of inherent form.

Through its supernormal powers, it universally enters all sounds, equating them to their original resonance, and is able to observe the mental activities and conduct of all sentient beings as being fundamentally pure from the very beginning.
Constantly perceiving all beings and transforming them according to the times, he always maintains mindfulness of this, never allowing it to be forgotten.

Having severed the mind of coming and going, he universally manifests spiritual powers without hindrance; he walks alone through the three realms without being constrained, realizing that all things are non-existent and thus not establishing any conditioned practices.

His supernormal powers and clarity exhaust all outflows; he understands the proper timing and never loses his seasonal measure; he manifests the difficulties of birth and death to demonstrate the work of transcending the world; what he examines is profound and far-reaching.

Their supernormal powers and insights all surpass those of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they penetrate deeply into the subtle and wondrous, sit beneath the Bodhi tree to subdue the hosts of Māra, and fully comprehend and expound all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas. They turn the holy wheel of the timely path-dharma in accordance with the seasons, transforming and enlightening all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, leading them into the Dharma and Vinaya until they reach the stage of *avaivartika* and turn all dharmas.
Śāntamati, you should know that this is the secret activity of the bodhisattva’s mind, the purity of mental conduct.

If the mind is truly pure, it has no ultimate destination and yet there is nothing it does not delight in. Its nature is peaceful, harmonious, and its practice is exceedingly excellent; thus, through the concentration of the Samādhi of Universal Wisdom, it enters right meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). It does not enter final extinction, nor does it loathe the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); even if born therein, it is without attachment and is not bound by it. Whatever birth it manifests, it is never fettered by the knots of affliction.

Why is this so? Because they have transcended all delusive thoughts regarding empty space and have resolved the various fetters of dust and the inverted perceptions through which [beings] receive [existence]; their minds are without attachment, and by virtue of this, they attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Although there is that which arises, it is entirely without arising; for the Great Vehicle fundamentally accomplishes all the dharmas of the Buddhas' paths, and these Buddha-dharmas protect and deliver the ten directions.

Seeking it everywhere, it cannot be found; yet one thereby realizes that all the dharmas of the Buddhas, all dharmas whatsoever, are entirely subsumed within the Buddha-dharma, and that these dharmas of the Buddhas are themselves all dharmas.
All these phenomena, as well as the Buddha-dharmas, are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this? Because when one seeks the origin, the end, or the location of all phenomena, they cannot be found.

If one seeks all phenomena and finds them to have no location, then they are without number; transcending all numerical designations for abiding, one knows all phenomena and thus does not rely upon any phenomena.
Because he does not rely upon any phenomena, his pursuit of gain and benefit leads instead to great decline.
Being without thought or seeking, he has neither gain nor decline; as he advances further in his studies and encounters gain and benefit, his mind is neither sorrowful nor delighted.

When the mind is free from sorrow and the will is without obstruction, there is no place of abiding. This absence of abiding is the absence of fragmentation; this absence of fragmentation is the absence of direction. Such being the absence of direction, it is truly a state of direction; yet such a state of direction is itself without direction. This absence of direction is the absence of self; this absence of self is the absence of grasping. This absence of grasping is the absence of contention; this absence of contention is the absence of strife and disorder. This absence of strife and disorder is the Dharma of the śramaṇa.
Their mind is equanimous like space; abiding in that equanimity like space, they do not follow the desire realm, do not dwell in the form realm, and do not cling to the formless realm.
If one regards all things as entirely without attachment, there is neither praise nor blame.
This absence of praise and blame refers to all dharmas.
Those who understand these profound meanings in such a way are truly liberated.
Because one is able to know the activities of these six matters, the proclamation and analysis are likewise so.
For what reason are they explained and analyzed?
It is because all dharmas are unattainable.

To be able to thoroughly understand and discern that all dharmas fundamentally have no place of abiding and that the three realms are entirely empty, and thereby to thoroughly understand and discern them all—this is the secret of the mind.
Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, again addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"The secrecy of his mental conduct arises because he practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*) without reckoning a self (*ātman*); his practice of compassion (*karuṇā*) arises because there is no sentient being (*sattva*);
his practice of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) arises because there is no life-principle (*jīva*); and his ability to provide protection arises..."
Because he has realized the absence of a life-span; because his mind is free from stinginess as he practices the four kinds of giving;

because he upholds the prohibitions and precepts to harmonize his mind; because this practice of patience exhausts the activities of the mind; because if he cultivates diligence, he contemplates tranquility;
because that tranquil single-mindedness abandons the location of the mind; and because his knowledge of the noble mind is without any object.
Because of practice, the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are without intention and without thought;

because the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) bring the mind to full comprehension through neither arising nor ceasing; because the bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda) cause the flying mind to be vast and boundless;
because practicing with earnest faith results in a mind free from obstruction; and because cultivating diligence results in the tranquility of mental activity—such is his intention.
Because he has attained mastery over mental activities through mindfulness; because his concentrated mind is equanimous and free from differentiation;
because his faculty of wisdom is free from conceptualization; and because his power follows the fundamental nature of the mind.

If one discriminates with a mind of awakening through wisdom; if one practices the path of deeds with a mind free from conceptualization; if one is tranquil through serene and quiet contemplation; if the mind observing phenomena perceives non-attachment; if one practices the cultivation of the ultimate liberating mind of the noble ones; if the mind mindful of the Buddha possesses clear wisdom and is free from delusive thoughts; if the mind contemplating the Way has an immeasurable resolve; if the mind recollecting the Dharma is impartial; and if the mind recollecting the Sangha dwells nowhere while instructing sentient beings.

Because their minds are profoundly pure as they protect the True Dharma; because their minds are unimpaired across all realms as they uphold that Dharma; because their minds are equal to space as they purify the Buddha-fields; because their minds have no distinct forms as they are endowed with all marks; because their minds are free from inversion as they attain patience; because their minds do not regress as they reach the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*); because their minds do not fall [into error] while being adorned within the triple world at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); because their minds gather in sentient beings as they subdue the works of Māra; because their minds awaken to the equality of all phenomena as they receive the instructions of the Way; and because their minds do not return as they turn the wheel of Dharma, wherein all dharmas are without turning.
He manifests great parinirvāṇa to resolve the origin of birth and death, because the mind is naturally equal.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada said to Śāntamati:
"If a bodhisattva attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), his mind becomes profoundly secret and his mind also becomes pure."
Once the mind is purified, one understands that the minds of all sentient beings are pure; there is nowhere among the minds of these beings that one does not enter.
Entering the mind of the Way, the minds of all sentient beings as they incline toward the mind of the Way are illuminated.
Just as space is universally and entirely equal, so too does the path-mind (bodhicitta) pervasively enter all that is formed and formless.
In this same way, it enters the mental activities of all sentient beings.

When Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi Māhārājika, had spoken these inconceivable secrets of the body, speech, and mind of the bodhisattvas, seventy-two thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas; fourteen thousand people’s eyes were purified of all dharmas, becoming free from dust and defilement; and eight thousand bhikṣus attained the liberation of the mind through the outflow-free state.

This trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great radiance shone universally throughout the ten directions. From the void above, the heavens rained down various flowers, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. Amidst these musical sounds, this was proclaimed:

"Should there be those who hear the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, and if they have faith and joy, such people shall attain the prediction of enlightenment. They shall cherish and delight in the sūtras, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting them; they shall explain them extensively for others without losing their resolve for the Way. Having accumulated the roots of merit, they shall never be in vain.
Having once made offerings to countless Buddhas and planted many roots of virtue, they shall benefit sentient beings, and there shall be none who do not receive salvation."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Śāntamati:
"Did you hear the sounds and words emanating from those musical instruments? He replied:
"I have heard it,
World-Honored One!
Indeed so, Great Sage!"
"By whose majestic spiritual power [is this]?
The Buddha said to Śāntamati:

"There is a bodhisattva named Ghoṣadatta who has set out from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ghoṣarāja—whose land is named Ubhayajāti—and has come to this Sahā world-system. He desires to see my body, prostrate himself in worship, and inquire about the essentials of the Dharma; he wishes to hear me preach this secret and essential teaching of the Tathāgata."

Remaining in the void without manifesting their physical forms, they made offerings to the Tathāgata and to this sutra; therefore, they rained down celestial flowers and performed various musical performances, and from those instruments issued forth these kinds of sounds.

Not long after the Buddha had spoken, the Bodhisattva Thunder-Sound descended from the void, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times, and standing before the Buddha, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One!”
"May Tathāgata Ghoṣarāja inquire after you with great respect: Are you free from ailment, light in movement, and dwelling in peace?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Ghoṣa:
"Welcome, noble son!"

"How wonderful! Out of regard for the righteous purpose, we have come to offer our presence; we truly desire to hear and receive the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s secret and essential sūtras. Now, Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, shall proclaim them by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power."
Thereupon, some among the assembly of bodhisattvas thought to themselves:
"In what world did this Guhyapāda Vajrapāṇi accumulate these roots of manifold merit?"
"Under which Buddha did you first resolve to attain the Way?
By what original vow was such vast, infinite, and magnificent eloquence as this attained?
At that time, the Buddha, knowing fully the thoughts in the minds of these bodhisattvas, addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"In the distant past, incalculable and inconceivable kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Immeasurable Merit Jewel-Scarf Pure King (*Anantaguṇaratnapaṭṭaviśuddharāja*). He was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, a Buddha, a World-Honored One."
The world was named Adorned, and the eon was called Good Vision.

That Buddha-land possessed extraordinary majesty and virtue; its inhabitants were numerous and all attained peace and security. The five grains ripened in abundance, the land flourished greatly, and all together experienced joy and happiness.

Devas and humans were flourishing in abundance; the ground was entirely level, like the palm of a grindstone, free from dust, filth, thorns, shards, or stones. Only lapis lazuli, crystal, moon-bright pearls and jade, coral, amber, tridacna shell, and agate covered the earth.

The ground is as soft as celestial raiment, possessing a sweet fragrance and a most excellent luster; it grows fine grass like heavenly tapestries, such that when one treads upon it, the ground sinks four inches beneath the foot, returning to its original state once the foot is lifted.
That land is blissful, with neither extreme cold nor excessive heat.
Its inhabitants are benevolent and their natures are harmonious; their bodies, speech, and minds are tranquil, and the ground is fragrant and the color of deep blue lapis lazuli.

The people of that land have all attained mastery; they all receive instruction such that their lust, anger, and delusion are diminished. They dwell in peace and tranquility, all possessing majestic power; when they hear the words of the Dharma being preached, they all understand and discern its principles.
At the time of that Buddha-World-Honored One, there were twelve koṭis of śrāvaka disciples and three thousand two hundred million bodhisattvas.
The lifespan of that Buddha was three hundred sixty million years.
There are none who die prematurely.
This adorns the kingdom; within it are four cities named Kṣemadarśana, which are exceedingly vast and extensive.
Wind and rain fall in their proper seasons, the five grains are abundant, and the people are peaceful and secure; the strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds their rightful place.
Each of these square cities measures eighty thousand li in both width and length, with a distance of four hundred li between them.
There is one great kingdom, and each of these great kingdoms contains a thousand districts, counties, villages, hamlets, and settlements.
The people of that land were four *li* in height.

At that time, there was the great city of Sudarśana (Joyous Vision) on all four sides; furthermore, there was another great city named Viśuddha (Pure), the seat of the king’s governance. Its territory was vast and extensive: the city was two thousand five hundred and sixty *li* long from east to west, and one thousand two hundred and eighty *li* wide from south to north, with ten thousand districts, states, counties, and towns.
They were endowed with perfect happiness. There were ten thousand pleasure gardens, each exceedingly pure and composed of the seven treasures.

At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named King Śūra; he possessed the seven treasures: first, the golden wheel; second, a white elephant with six tusks; third, a dark-blue horse with crimson mane and tail; fourth, the divine moon-pearl; fifth, a jade-like queen as his consort; sixth, a noble minister who presided over the treasury; and seventh, a great general who commanded the army. He ruled over the four continents under heaven. Having made offerings to past Buddhas and planted many roots of virtue, his majestic spiritual power was immeasurable; he had resolved upon the path of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment and had attained the stage of non-retrogression.

In the center of the city, he erected a residence that was vast, long, and high; it measured six hundred and forty *li* both in length and breadth. It was constructed with seven precious substances, featuring sevenfold walls, railings, sevenfold intersecting roads, sevenfold jeweled canopies, and sevenfold deep moats.

Within the interior of that residence were four great fruit gardens where various flowers grew: the first was named Wondrous Flower, the second Merit-Abundance, the third Mountain River, and the fourth Spring Peace.

There is a pond filled with water, twenty li in both width and length, all surrounded by railings made of various jewels. The pond is of purple gold, with a bed of sand made of purple gold and lapis lazuli. It is filled with water of eight virtues and produces various precious lotuses; ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and birds of diverse species sport within it.
There were four bathing pools: the first was named Bestowing Wealth, the second Supreme Cave, the third Supreme Fragrance, and the fourth Wondrous Chariot.

Within the inner palace were seventy-six thousand court ladies, like celestial jade maidens; each possessed excellent marks, being upright and exceptionally beautiful in a way that does not exist in the world.
The king’s principal consort, the Woman-Jewel, and all the court ladies all conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

The king had a thousand sons, who were endowed with valor and were far superior to others; they were exceptionally handsome and adorned their bodies with twenty-eight marks. Their natures were gentle and harmonious, and they likewise united in mind to conceive the aspiration for the Great Way.

"At that time, that Buddha was traveling through the great kingdom of Qingjing (Pure). Its king, Yongjun (Valiant Army), made offerings for a full hundred million years to the Tathāgata Wuliangxunbaoji Jingwang (Immeasurable Merit-Jewel-Clean-King) and his assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. He provided them with all necessities for their well-being: clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine; as well as gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, residences, lecture halls, chambers, vihāras, high terraces, and multi-storied towers. To each bhikṣu, he assigned two attendants to provide whatever was required."

The sons of that king were of peaceful and harmonious disposition, free from heedless conduct; with a sincere heart, they constantly made offerings to the Tathāgata and listened to the reception of the sūtras. They took no pleasure in sensual desires, frivolous laughter, or unwholesome deeds. Listening to and receiving the sūtras without negligence and without generating [discursive] thoughts, before long they attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Having attained supernormal powers, he leaped into the void, flying with sovereign ease and without obstruction like a king of geese; proceeding from one monastery to another, from one district to another, and traveling from one kingdom to another, he journeyed and observed throughout every world-system.
With these essential verses, he spoke to the great assembly:
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world Is profound, remote, and extremely difficult to encounter;
That a person is born into this world Is likewise very difficult to meet."
All these people share the same aspiration; together they believe, rejoice in, and listen to the sutras—a thing most difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Now, this hero among men has appeared in the world.
Desiring to bring about tranquil concentration, he thus expounded the meaning of the sutras and dharmas.
Following the World-Honored One who dwells in peace, he received his instructions and admonitions;
seeking the great sage’s brilliance, he respectfully presented the Buddha’s ultimate words.
By hearing and receiving the scriptural teachings, one abandons the evil realms;
by attaining the hearing of the True Dharma, one gains a seat in the place of ultimate peace;
by attaining the hearing of the True Dharma, one eliminates all worldly afflictions.
Because they have heard and received this wisdom, they shall attain the True and Right Dharma.
At that time, as the teachings were proclaimed and this sweet fragrance was spread,
by virtue of this auspicious response, the earth shook in six ways.
He universally proclaimed this to devas and humans;
all the devas raised their voices in praise, and immediately rained down celestial flowers of many varieties.
Sentient beings all gathered there, beyond all calculation or measure.
The most supreme transformation brings all to enter the Way and its Dharma.
Bowing their heads at his feet, they pay homage to the Honored One among gods and men;
with palms joined together, they stand respectfully and reverently.
That most supreme and holy teacher, having attained this mind,
explains the Dharma according to the principles of the times.
Such companions as these, upon hearing it, abide securely in the Dharma.
Together with thirty-six billion beings, they all resolved their minds upon the Great Way.
Among those three hundred billion followers, not one was lacking;
they had all attained the pure and most supreme Dharma-eye.
With hearts weary of and disgusted by worldly household affairs,
they all together left that world, renounced their homes, and practiced the Way.
There were countless multitudes of people— billions, trillions, and tens of billions of men.
All received the sutras and precepts, and became lay followers of pure faith.
Having heard the Dharma, they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet;
each took their leave and departed, returning to their respective homes.
The Buddha told Śāntamati:

"At that time, the prince, together with his father the king, constructed a multi-storied pavilion out of sandalwood; it was vast, pure, and beautifully adorned. They fashioned windows made of various jewels, and by burning one *śuṅga* of ox-head sandalwood incense, its fragrance pervaded the entire world with a sublime scent."

He constructed a multi-storied pavilion out of this sandalwood, vast, long, and high, reaching four hundred li in height; it was magnificently adorned and decorated, its majestic spiritual power manifesting in boundless grandeur.
It was perfectly square, with four excellent corners and four pillars; its construction was level, upright, and stable, without any leaning.

That king, Yungjun, wishing to go to the presence of the Tathāgata Wuliangxunbaoji Jingwang (Infinite Merit Jewel Pure King), to pay his respects, prostrate himself, inquire after his well-being, and listen to and receive the sūtras, exhorted the king’s retinue:
"Human life is difficult to obtain, and the appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter; it occurs but once in hundreds of millions of years, and the Way of the Sūtras is difficult to hear."
"You should go to attend upon him and receive the sūtras from him.

Thereupon, the king, the crown prince, the queen, the court ladies, the ministers, the officials, and the people, both great and small, all entered the jeweled pavilions and high towers of the open-air hall. They sat upon hundreds of thousands of exquisitely adorned precious thrones, using various flowers, incense, blended perfumes, garments, precious canopies, banners, and streamers, and playing all manner of music. With hearts of reverence and devotion, they served and honored him, offering up the jeweled pavilions and high towers of the open-air hall as a tribute.

With hearts of universal harmony and benevolence, they rose into the void like the king of phoenixes; together with their retinue, they moved without any obstruction, flying swiftly to the place where the Buddha was.
Those precious, adorned, high towers and pavilions proceeded to the Great Assembly; they went before the Buddha’s dwelling, circled the Buddha seven times, and then withdrew to stand at one side.

The King and the great assembly each descended from their vehicles and emerged; they went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and pay homage to the assembly of noble ones. Having circumambulated the Buddha seven times, they stood before him and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For a long time we have revered your holy voice, yet due to the many affairs of state, we were unable to come to attend upon you. We are filled with shame and have no face to show ourselves."
"Today, at long last, my feelings of hunger and emptiness have been fulfilled.

At that time, the Great Sage Buddha, perceiving the king’s sincere heart and seeing that his palace ladies and retinue had come specifically to hear the Dharma, observed their minds according to their fundamental dispositions and, like administering medicine to suit an illness, proclaimed the teachings of the sutras.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"There are four dharmas for establishing the will in the Mahāyāna; by practicing them, one's conduct becomes extraordinary and does not deviate from the Great Way. What are these four?"
If one studies the Mahāyāna with sincere faith and reverence, their conduct will be extraordinary and never deviate from the intent of the Way.
What is meant by "faith"?
It is to joyfully revere all the worthy sages and never to engage in that which ought not to be done.

Great King, if you practice with reverence, you will study the Mahāyāna; your conduct will be extraordinary and never deviate from the Great Way. If you listen to the sutras of the worthy sages with humility and respect, entering them with a sincere heart and receiving them upon hearing, you shall uphold them.

Without conceit, he trains in the Mahāyāna; his conduct is extraordinary and does not deviate from the Great Way. Without conceit, he beholds the various sages, prostrating himself in worship and taking refuge with a single-minded devotion.

If one honors diligence and studies the Mahāyāna, their sphere of activity will be extraordinary and not contrary to the Great Way; through the application of diligence, they render the body, speech, and mind light, making their movements and conduct appropriate, and thus their practice transcends all other practices.
"These are the four matters.
The Buddha told the king:
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one sees non-negligence and is protected by what is seen."
What are the four? They are:

guarding the sense faculties; seeing the peril in sensual desire; understanding that all feelings and perceptions are impermanent; and obtaining the life-faculty through the Dharma, which is foremost.
These are the four matters.
A bodhisattva possesses four qualities by which they are called a Dharma King. What are these four?
First, not abandoning the mind of enlightenment;
second, likewise exhorting and transforming others to resolve their minds upon it;
third, using the roots of all virtues to assist the mind of enlightenment, so that the scope of what one hears becomes infinitely vast.

The fourth is that all Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings, as well as all the śrāvakas and those on the stage of pratyekabuddhas, [attain] karma that is infinite, indestructible, vast, and inexhaustible.
These are the four matters.

Therefore, Great King, you should practice heedfulness and constantly cultivate firm faith; delighting in the meaning of the immeasurable dharmas of the Path, you should always receive the True Dharma and find self-delight in the joy of the Dharma.
If one seeks the Dharma through diligence, Great King, your conduct shall not be covetous of sensory realms. Why is this?
Great King, you should understand that craving is insatiable, like drinking salt water; it is only upon seeing the brilliant wisdom of the noble ones that one comes to know moderation.

Human life is exceedingly short; there is little peace and much suffering. Birth inevitably ends in death, and one must proceed to the next world; one is constantly apprehensive of what lies ahead, for the mind cannot be relied upon.
Today, Your Majesty has made offerings to the Buddha; by virtue of this root of merit, you have been encouraged and assisted through the fulfillment of four matters.
What are these four?

In life after life, their wealth and resources shall be immeasurable; their meritorious rewards and blessings shall be inexhaustible; their sagely and brilliant wisdom shall be boundless; and their eloquence and intellectual insight shall be entirely without end.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters that one should encourage and assist. What are these four?

Purifying the conduct of the body through deeds of merit; purifying the conduct of speech through the fulfillment of precepts and prohibitions; purifying the conduct of the mind through insatiable pursuit of extensive learning; and purifying the Dharma through the company of the noble and wise.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters that encourage and assist the roots of virtue. What are these four?
Through skillful means and expedient methods, they cultivate pure conduct and instruct sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom;
by means of pure karma, they subdue the hosts of Māra;
their vows are pure and their words correspond to their deeds, such that all the dharmas of the Buddhas are entirely pure.
“By accumulating merit and virtue, one reaches the point of beholding the Buddhas;
this is the fourth.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the profound meaning through the discernment of wisdom within a sutra for the sake of the Cakravartin King Vīrabhūti. The king’s mind was awakened, and he immediately rejoiced. He then untied from his neck a magnificent pearl necklace composed of countless hundreds of thousands of rare pearls and offered it to the Buddha. He dedicated the entire kingdom to serve the Buddha with all that was required, observed the five precepts, and throughout the remainder of his life, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring.

The king’s ladies of the inner court and maidservants, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, felt joy in their hearts; according to their dispositions, they conceived a mind of gentleness and a mind free from the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), and they removed their own garments and extraordinary jeweled necklaces to drape over the Buddha.
Jie addressed the King, saying:
"I wish to leave the household life to become a śramaṇa, purely cultivating the Brahma-faring, and upholding the prohibitive precepts for as long as my life lasts.
The King immediately granted his permission.
"Thus it was, Śāntamati!

That King Vīrabhadra, having received the Dharma of the Infinite and attained the wealth of the Dharma, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him seven times. Together with his inner court, female attendants, and official retinue, he entered a great high-storied pavilion adorned with canopies; then, surging upward, he ascended into the void, and in a mere moment, returned once more to his pure and great kingdom."

Thereupon, on the full moon of the fifteenth day, when the moon was at its peak, the Holy King went out to his pleasure garden accompanied by various kinds of flowers; there, the ladies of the inner palace and their retinue beheld a beautiful site.
