At that time, the noble king was in his pleasure garden enjoying various musical performances.

His two principal queens—one named Aprakramaṇī and the other named Avandhyā—had emerged from the palace to bathe their bodies; having just returned from their ablutions, they sat upon a most excellent couch and lotus pedestal, wearing garments perfumed with incense.

Two young children spontaneously came and sat upon the lady’s lap in the full lotus posture; they were upright and exceptionally beautiful, unlike anything seen in the world, their bodies adorned with the twenty-eight marks of a great man, which appeared there quite naturally.
Immediately, hundreds of thousands of devas in the void raised their voices in praise, saying:
"These two children are truly divine and sagely; one is named Dharmamati and the other is named Dharmasmṛti."

As these two children appeared spontaneously, the child named Dharmasmṛti sat unmoving upon the lady’s lap, while the child Dharmacitta was born by transformation without injury upon the lady’s lap. As soon as he sat cross-legged, they spoke in verse with one voice:
“If there are those who guard their own bodies And are able to give rise to the bodhicitta, Such practitioners of learning Shall attain excellent merit and auspicious blessings.”
Thinking that he had once beheld him, and that the Lion’s Roar had appeared in this world,
he always served the Buddha with a joyful heart and single-minded devotion.
Through these great deeds of supernatural power, he swiftly attained the blessing of protection.
One attains the dissolution of the wheel of birth and death, swiftly extinguishing that which is unarisen.
If one gives rise to the bodhicitta and never forgets it for even a moment,
using it to rescue and gather sentient beings, one shall shatter the perils of birth and death.
In the realm above, beyond incalculable buddha-fields,
there is a Buddha whose name is Season (Kāla).
Having come from that buddha-field, he has been raised up for the sake of the Dharma.
They also wished to see his meritorious achievements and all that belonged to the kingdom.
At that time, the two children each rose from their seats;
they then moved down from their mother’s knees and set themselves upon the ground.
Together they set out upon the road, traveling to where the Honored One among gods and men dwells.
Arriving before him, they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to stand with palms joined:
"Proclaiming the Buddha’s virtues in the four directions, we have now come specifically to hear the sutra."
The Buddha-dharma is exceedingly difficult to attain; even hearing and receiving it is rare to encounter.
Having now heard this Dharma, one should exalt the Honored One of Men and, with utmost sincerity, apply oneself to the unsurpassed, truly authentic practice of the Buddha-way.
The path and Dharma of all Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter;
those who delight in the meaning of the sutras are likewise even more difficult to meet.
Today, through this leisure and tranquility, I shall cultivate the Dharma dear to my friends.
In accordance with the majestic standard, one reverently honors and believes the teachings of the Dharma.
Yearning for excellence through diligence, one acts without negligence;
having thus become a śramaṇa, one dwells in such seclusion.
Abiding thus with compassion, simple and pure in measureless ways,
always harboring a sense of shame and remorse, they know that extensive learning is difficult to encounter.
Their kindness is universally complete as they take pity upon all sentient beings.
Because they are able to penetrate the profound Dharma, they can attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Considering all their majestic power and influence, their minds are neither timid nor weak;
they gather in and rescue all sentient beings, transforming and enlightening all who face difficulties.
If one dwells in solitude, performing inconceivable deeds,
because they do not crave their own body, nor their life-span or faculties;
never tiring of the training in prohibitions, I contemplate the Dharma of the Path.
By this one can attain clear understanding, reaching such meritorious achievements as these.
If one can train in this manner, it is the foremost and most difficult to obtain;
the work of the Dharma King is praised as supreme.
This is the essence of all dharmas, wherein retribution and response are fully perfected;
one should set forth and arrive together at the place where the Sages, the Abiders in Peace, the Buddhas, reside.
Those of such clear wisdom receive the practice of the Bodhisattva path.
Practicing the pure and white dharmas, he proclaims and spreads the teaching.
At all times remaining tranquil and secluded, he attains the five supernormal powers.
Through his consciousness, he is mindful of all things; the dharmas he practices are serene and detached.
The two crown princes of that king, together with their consorts and court ladies—
these two of wise intelligence— practiced the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
Having attained supernatural powers and wisdom, they traveled through the midst of the void.
They went to where the World-Honored One was, that ocean of merit and wisdom.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they took refuge in the Honored One among Men;
all together in harmony, they approached and paid homage with palms joined.
Dharmamati stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, as well as the entire assembly:
"I pray only that the Great Holy One will expound the Dharma for me.
You, the Most Victorious One, know all that is being thought within our hearts."
Then he shall provide a detailed exposition of the profound and wondrous meaning of the Dharma:
that all these phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
originally there is no master or teacher, for they manifest through the process of transformation.
Understanding that what is internal is empty, and that what is external lacks causes and conditions,
all these dharmas are, in their fleeting nature, entirely void.
By being able to examine both the beginning and the end, one attains the vision of purity through non-action.
When reckoned, it is like empty space, Constantly beyond being maintained or protected.
The Buddha, through countless skillful means, Proclaims this for their sake;
He analyzes and expounds upon this Profound, ultimate, and true reality.
Seventy-six *koṭis* of people, along with a multitude of two hundred million, all simultaneously attained the patient acceptance of the Dharma that accords with reality (*anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King Yǒngxùn, the ladies of the inner palace, the crown prince, his retinue, and the common people circumambulated the Buddha, paid homage, and made offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of sages; after seven days and nights had passed, they finally returned to their own palace.
Thereupon, King Śūradatta, the Wheel-Turning Sage-King, sat alone in quietude upon a pure, high, open pavilion, and thought to himself:
"All these sons of mine have resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment."
"Now we shall test this: which of the princes will first attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to become a Most Perfectly Awakened One?

He then commanded a master craftsman to fashion seven-jeweled vases, exquisitely round and perfect; he also had him create a seven-jeweled stand, manifesting in subtle beauty, forty-nine feet high with seven spans of height. He had each of the thousand princes write down their names on seven-jeweled tally-sticks and place them into the vases. The vases were then lifted and set upon the stand. For seven days and nights, they all together made offerings, using celestial flowers and incense, powdered incense, blended fragrances, flower canopies, banners, and streamers, and performing various kinds of music as offerings to the names inscribed upon the jeweled vases.
Ten thousand devas came to assist and encourage the offering of these names.

After seven days had passed, the Wheel-Turning King took these seven precious jars and, before the ladies of the inner palace, the court ladies, and the assembly of his princes, placed them upon a table of purple gold. He then ordered attendants to lift the jars and commanded each of the princes to draw a lot.

There was a crown prince named Viśuddhamati who obtained the first tally. As soon as he obtained this tally, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; at that moment, all the palace ladies, court beauties, and musical instruments sounded spontaneously without being struck.
What do you think, Śāntamati?
Was the Prince Viśuddhamati at that time someone else?
Do not conceive such a view.
Why is this so? Because he was Krakucchanda Tathāgata.
Next, the crown prince named Vigatasaṃśaya-vīra was Kanakamuni Buddha.
Next was a crown prince named Śāntamūla, who was Kāśyapa Tathāgata.
Next was a crown prince named Sarvaduḥkhahara, who was my own self.
Next was a crown prince named Varṣagṛha, who is none other than Maitreya Tathāgata.
Next was a crown prince named Candramaṇivāsas, who will later become a Buddha named Siṃha.
Next, there was a crown prince who will attain Buddhahood in a future age, named Miaoying (Wondrous Brilliance).
Next, there was a crown prince named Xianshi (Virtuous Lineage), who will attain Buddhahood in a future age, named Gongyang (Offering).
Next there was a crown prince named Prabhāvamati, who later became a Buddha known as Supuṣpa.
Next there was a crown prince named Padmagarbha, who later became a Buddha known as Upasthāyaka.
Next was a crown prince named Vimalaprabha, who later became a Buddha known as Sunetra.
Next was a crown prince named Śākyamuni, who later became a Buddha known as Laghupāṇi.
Next was a crown prince named Yimiao (Exquisite Intention), who later became a Buddha named Yan'guang (Flame Light).
Next was a crown prince named Jingfujing (Pure and Further Pure), who later became a Buddha named Yanwei (Flame Flavor).
Next there was a crown prince named Puṇyavanta, who later, upon attaining Buddhahood, was named Anivartita.
Next there was a crown prince named Vimalaviśuddha, who later, upon attaining Buddhahood, was named Guṇadhara.
Next there was a crown prince named Dṛḍha, who later attained Buddhahood under the name Ratnakāra.
Next there was a crown prince named Ratnayaśas, who later attained Buddhahood under the name Avimānita-loka.
Thus, Śāntamati! To state the essentials briefly, and then to elaborate fully:

there was a prince named Madhukavarmasamalaṃkṛta, the ninth-hundred-and-ninety-ninth—falling one short of a thousand—who, when he later attains Buddhahood, shall be known as Amitaguṇaratnayaśas, appearing in this Bhadrakalpa during the future world.
The Buddha said, “It is so, Śāntamati!
There is a prince named Amitamati who has received the final tally; this prince shall be the very last to achieve the path of awakening.”
At that time, the various princes treated him with contempt and mocked him repeatedly, laughing at him. Each of them said:

"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall subdue the hosts of Māra, turn the Wheel of Dharma, and through my teaching and transformation, deliver immeasurable sentient beings, leading them to final Nirvāṇa."
"If all sentient beings were to be exhausted, what would be established thereafter?
How could there be any further salvation?

Subsequently, the Prince named Amitamati personally witnessed that he had obtained the final tally and reached the ultimate limit of attaining Buddhahood; at that moment, he was overcome with grief and distress.
"How is it that I alone, having committed such faults, have reached the depths and obtained this strategy?
He prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground like the collapsing of Mount Tai, and declared aloud:
"The Way and Dharma of all Buddhas are immeasurable; the realms of sentient beings are likewise limitless; my aspiration is extraordinary and inconceivable."
He immediately established all his vows:

"May the number of disciples taught and those delivered by my thousand brothers after they have attained Buddhahood, as well as the length of their lifespans—when these lifespans are all calculated together—be exactly equal to the duration of my own lifespan when I attain the Way of the Buddha."
"O virtuous ones, all you noble assemblies shall be my exclusive assembly when I attain Buddhahood.

The proclamation of the Dharma and the deliverance of all sentient beings through it shall likewise be so; the merit and majesty of you thousand people shall be equal and no different, being immeasurable."

"If what I have spoken with utmost sincerity is indeed true and not false, may this trichiliocosm manifest auspicious signs for me: let it tremble in six ways, let the heavens rain down various flowers, and let musical instruments such as the *konghou* sound of their own accord without being struck."

At the moment Prince Anantamati of King Arthavatsa had made this vow, the trichiliocosm immediately shook in six ways; the heavens rained down various flowers, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
In the sky above, hundreds of thousands of devas uttered this eulogy:
"May you fulfill your vow and become the final Buddha, named Luyou (Ratna) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The Buddha said: "Śāntamati!
For what reason is he named Luyou?"

At that time, overcome with grief, he threw himself upon the ground; having taken up the counting-sticks, he accumulated his vows, and for this reason the World-Honored One named him Luyou—Luyou being the Jin translation for "weeping."
At that time in that world, having fulfilled his vow, the Prince spoke these verses:
“The Dharma of the Buddhas is equal to space;
The awakening of the mind is like an illusion, Yet sentient beings can never be exhausted.”
May my vows be auspicious, and may my observance of the precepts be purified.
Listen now, O virtuous ones, to this vow I desire to make:
gather together, O noble lords, for the lifespan allotted to us is limited.
I have seen all those venerable and holy kings;
calculating the names of these Buddhas, they are equal in number to my own lifespan.
He who attained Buddhahood was named Luyou, and his assembly of bhikṣus was likewise.
The Crown Prince was moved, and thus he uttered these words;
the devas stood in the void and raised their voices in praise, saying:
"Now that this person is so pure, whatever he aspires to shall surely be accomplished."
"Because of sentient beings, I have gathered together to fulfill my essential vows.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Silent Intent:
"Do you wish to know who that Prince Immeasurable-Mind was at that time?"
He replied, "I am not equal to him.
The Buddha said:

"In this Bhadrakalpa, the last Buddha to attain enlightenment shall be named Ruciraketu. Among all the Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa, he will be less than one thousandth of their number; yet the sentient beings he delivers, the bodhisattvas in training, and the assembly of noble bhikṣus will surpass those delivered by all other Buddhas. As the final Buddha of this kalpa, his lifespan shall be half a kalpa, and the total number of sentient beings, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and all noble assemblies he delivers will, by the end of this Bhadrakalpa, be exactly equal to what was delivered by the nine hundred and ninety-nine other Buddhas, without any difference."
The Buddha told Śāntamati:

"Furthermore, observe how the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) accomplish the precepts with such distinction; he fulfills his vows, walking alone and sitting alone, traversing the three realms without ever ceasing."

Why is this so? Because although Louyou, the Tathāgata, alone with his single body, transforms and enlightens sentient beings, it is no different from what is accomplished by the appearance of a thousand Buddhas; the benefit bestowed is thus limitless and as magnificent as this.
Thus it was, Śāntamati!
Subsequently, the two youngest of the king’s thousand princes each thought to themselves:
"What are the aspirations of you noble beings?"
Prince Dharmamati said: "I make this solemn vow:

when all these people attain Buddhahood, I shall become a Vajrapāṇi, always remaining in close attendance upon the Buddhas, maintaining majestic deportment outside their presence, examining all the secret essentials of the Tathāgatas, and being constantly entrusted with their reliance; I shall universally hear of the secret and esoteric matters of all Buddhas, receiving them with faith and joy, never harboring doubt or resentment."
Prince Dharmasmṛti said: "Listen, all you noble ones!

I make this vow in my own heart: when you, sirs, attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall personally provide encouragement and assistance so that you may turn the wheel of Dharma; as soon as I see you being exhorted, I shall immediately turn the wheel of Dharma."
“Śāntamati! Do you wish to know who that Universal Monarch Vīrakṣetra was at that time? He replied:
"It was not equal," the Buddha said.
"It was none other than the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara of the past."
At that time, those sons were the thousand Buddhas who appeared during this Bhadrakalpa;
beginning with Krakucchanda as the first to attain Buddhahood and ending with Roca, they comprise the thousand Buddhas.
The Prince Dharmamati is none other than the present Vajrapāṇi, known by the name Guhyapada;
the Prince Dharmasmṛti is the present Viśvabhū Brahmā.
The queens, consorts, and court ladies of that noble king’s inner palace at that time are these very ones who have now gathered here.

Those princes of the king whom he exhorted to leave the household life to become śramaṇas, as well as those he instructed and transformed, are all those in this Bhadrakalpa who have gradually received their predictions of enlightenment and shall successively attain supreme perfect awakening.

Śāntamati! Observe, moreover, that within the twelve links of dependent origination, one does not disturb the roots of virtue and thereby attains the fruit of retribution; whatever intentions are generated do not lose their efficacy, and these true persons, fully equipped with the ten powers, realize all their aspirations.
Therefore, Śāntamati!

If there are bodhisattvas who wish to swiftly attain and perfect the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to become the most perfectly awakened ones, they should study the practices of these various righteous beings (satpuruṣas), diligently cultivating and practicing them so as to remain fully established in the Buddha-way.
What is called the Buddha-way?

It is to harbor no harmful intent toward sentient beings, to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, and to practice the Perfection of Giving; to cultivate the four debts of gratitude, constantly practice pure conduct, and follow the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment; to fully advance in spiritual powers, employ skillful means, and accomplish the roots of virtue—this is the Buddha-way.
The Buddha again addressed Śāntamati:

"Their path is pure in mind, whereby their nature attains thorough penetration; their path is harmonious and elegant, whereby their will and nature are tranquil and secure; their path is simple and unadorned, free from flattery and deceit; their path is vast and universal, without any obstruction; their path is impartial, with no partiality or favoritism in the heart; their path is fearless, not committing any evils; their path is wealth and abundance, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); their path is richness and sufficiency, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); their path is beyond consultation, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); their path is detached from dwelling places, the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); their path is undisturbed, the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); their path is skillful discernment, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). The path returns to one's own wisdom and honors great kindness (*maitrī*); the path does not distort the intent, reaching toward great compassion (*karuṇā*); the path receives joy, practicing through great sympathetic joy (*muditā*); the path returns to wondrous mastery, reaching toward great equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
That Way removes the afflictions of manifold sufferings and eliminates thoughts of greed, harm, and anger.
That Way leads to a peaceful mind that harbors no attachment to form; the Way transforms those difficult to tame by cutting away the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
The Way subdues the hosts of Māra, causing them to transform and abandon mental arrogance and the various thieving enemies. This is the Way.
Eliminating the seeds of the aggregates and being entirely unattached to the sense bases; the Way abandons demonic activities while attaining mastery amidst the various defilements;
the Way returns to the supreme mind, remaining free from the thoughts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the Way practices all past and future conduct to reach the realization of equal enlightenment; the Way governs the great treasure, accords with omniscience, and is eternal.

The path clarifies the unimpeded wisdom of discernment; the path gathers virtuous deeds through association with good friends; the path fills the moats and ditches that cause ruin, dissolving all fetters and attachments;
the path abandons worldly toil and transcends the ground of anger and contention; the path returns to peace and security, casting off all that is non-virtuous and evil;
the path leads to auspiciousness and proceeds toward the karma of *nirvāṇa*.
These are the thirty-two matters of the bodhisattva’s practice of the Buddha-way.
Abiding in these, the bodhisattva swiftly accomplishes the unsurpassed, right, and true path and attains supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Nine;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
The Third Part of the Third Assembly on the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada.
At that time, Śāntamati again asked the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada:
"How many secret essentials does the Tathāgata possess that are beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone the common folk who are shrouded in darkness?"
"Excellent, Guhyapāda!
We wish that you would graciously grant us leave to proclaim the secret essentials of the Tathāgata for universal entry; all those gathered here desire to hear them.
Guhyapāda the Malla said to Śāntamati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall now expound the secret essentials of the Tathāgata.
There are three matters. What are these three?"
The first is the secret of body, the second is the secret of speech, and the third is the secret of mind.
What is meant by the secret of body?
The Tathāgata has no conceptual thoughts nor deliberations regarding this; he universally manifests all dignified postures and ritual decorum.
There were some devas and humans who delighted in walking meditation; when they saw the Tathāgata walking in meditation, those devas and humans thought to themselves:
"The World-Honored One is supreme."

These beings attain the vision of the Tathāgata’s secret body; they neither conceive thoughts nor harbor expectations regarding what the Buddha contemplates, yet all sentient beings behold the Tathāgata’s supreme, true, and wondrous virtue and majestic deportment.
If the devas and humans prefer sitting, they see the Tathāgata sitting;
if the devas and humans prefer lying down, they see the Tathāgata lying down;
if they prefer listening to the sutras, they see the Tathāgata preaching the sutras.
If they delight in tranquility, they see the Tathāgata in silence.
If they delight in meditative reflection, they see the Tathāgata in samādhi.
If there are gods or humans whose eyes do not blink, they see the Tathāgata’s eyes never blinking.
If one’s mind is at ease and delights in light, one will see the Tathāgata’s light as being without obstruction.
If one delights in the purple-gold color, one will likewise see the purple-polished gold color.
If gods and humans take pleasure in the colors of silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, yellow conch-shell, pure white pearl,
pure red, pale yellow, crimson, or purple; or if they take the color of the moon-pearl,
the color of a turbulent storm, or the blazing light of the sun and moon, [the deities] of the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra [manifest in these forms].
The color of Brahmā or the Asuras; or the color of the intermediate realm, the color of Mount Sumeru flowers, or the color of exquisite thoughts;
or the color of medicinal herbs, or the color of azure stone; or the color of the aśoka flower or the campaka flower;
or the color of blue, red, yellow, or white lotuses; or the color of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Some have the countenance of King Vaiśravaṇa, some the form of the Four Heavenly Kings; their heads conceal the Blue Emperor, the Yellow Emperor, the Red Emperor, and the White Emperor;

some are as pure as space; and according to the immeasurable varieties of the mental dispositions of devas and humans, each with its distinct colors, they likewise perceive the Tathāgata’s various kinds of meritorious virtues and radiant colors.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!

Suppose all the sentient beings and living creatures filling as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges were to love one another and give birth to one another in succession; and suppose they were all to exhaust their karmic offenses and attain human form, born from thought.
Even if one among them were to give rise [to thoughts], it would be just like that of all sentient beings.

The Tathāgata likewise perceives their various types of physical forms, as well as their immeasurable deportment, etiquette, and mental inclinations; he likewise desires to fully examine and know the origins and ends of their speech and conduct.

The Tathāgata, the Ultimate Reality, by virtue of these conditions, manifests the image of a Tathāgata before each sentient being, such that his majestic demeanor, etiquette, and verbal conduct appear thus.

It is just as when one person attains liberation of mind; this is not something shared in common with a second person. He desires to proclaim the ultimate truth so that they may attain liberation of mind and reach the Way.

The Tathāgata, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, is indeed able to gladden all sentient beings; he manifests physical forms to gladden them, and his majestic demeanor, etiquette, and conduct are likewise so.

It is just as, Śāntamati, when a pure and bright mirror reflects various forms and appearances, their images appear therein without losing their original characteristics; they are displayed equally and without distinction, never undergoing change or alteration, and yet the bright mirror reflects these forms without any conceptualization.

The Tathāgata is thus: although he saves all sentient beings through the Dharma, he is free from conceptualization and has no desire for gain or offerings. He can gladden the mental activities of all sentient beings, and according to their superior, middling, or inferior capacities and the depth or shallowness of their faculties, he opens the way for them, transforming and liberating those deluded within the three realms; this is the secret essential of the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada again addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

“The secret essentials of the Tathāgata do not differentiate the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*); they do not revert to sin or merit, do not give rise to worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), and do not constitute father or mother; they possess neither the womb of the four great elements nor flesh and bone.”

Regarding the merits one hears of, there are no ointments, flowers, or incense; they are entirely non-existent, unattached to form, without inhalation or exhalation, and with the exhaustion of life-span.

If one wishes to know the Buddha-body, it is the Dharma-body; this body has no form and is free from all delusive thoughts. The physical forms and appearances that are manifested are for the sake of sentient beings who crave, long for, and seek noble and honorable positions, so that he may manifest a physical form for them to behold with their eyes.
The characteristics of dharmas are tranquil and still; for the sake of honoring wisdom, all sentient beings are led toward the divine eye.
Guhyapāda further addressed Śāntamati:
“If there are sentient beings gathered together in a single assembly, each perceives the Buddha’s body by observing it through the conditions of their own minds.”
When one dwells far away observing the basis of dwelling, one does not see that basis of dwelling.
To see the dwelling from afar yet not see it is because there is no intentional object; to see it yet not see it is because the observer uses a distracted mind as the intentional object.
If one cannot see by means of mental objects, yet can perceive them by examining with one's own body, it is because one sees others that one does not see [them].
Furthermore, if one is able to see again by seeing others, it is because one sees one's own mind that one does not see [them].
Whatever is seen within a dream is no longer seen once one has awakened from that dream. What is seen through concentrated mind arises as non-seeing;

what is seen upon arising from concentration is definitively non-seeing. What is seen in empty stillness is not seen by one who is not still; yet for one who abides in empty stillness, there is nothing that is not seen.

When one perceives that there is no karma, one is free from the perception of "no-karma"; yet, in being free from "no-karma," there is still something perceived—namely, the total absence of anything perceived.
Guhyapāda further said to Śāntamati:

"The body of the Tathāgata manifests according to countless conditions; its physical conduct and the conduct of the gods are serene, and its majestic demeanor and etiquette are such that the mind is naturally settled before it becomes disordered again."
This body of the Tathāgata is without limit or boundary; it is neither obstructed nor subject to delusive thought, and cannot be conceptualized in terms of joints.
This body of the Tathāgata cannot be grasped as finite; it does not possess manifold forms. The body of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Just as empty space is devoid of conceptual construction, so too the Tathāgata is forever free from thought.
Just as empty space pervades all forms and colors, so too the Tathāgata universally illumines all sentient beings.

Just as empty space universally enters into all forms and interpenetrates their interiors, so too is the body of the Tathāgata; it universally illumines sentient beings, reaching everywhere without exception.
Just as empty space nurtures all the hundred grains, grasses, and trees, so too is the Tathāgata; the body of the Truly Real One nurtures the roots of virtue.

Just as empty space does not calculate whether there is permanence or impermanence, nor has day or night, so too is the Tathāgata; his body is neither permanent nor is it said to be impermanent, and its crown cannot be seen.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
Among all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the heavens, the world, the Māras, and the Brahmās, there is none who dares to face the Buddha or behold the crown of his head.

Neither the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, nor non-humans—nor śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas—are able to bear the sight of the Tathāgata’s crown.
Why is this? Not long after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he turned the wheel of Dharma and traveled to Vārāṇasī.
To the east of this world, at a very great distance, one finds the buddha-field of the Buddha Siyehua; that world is called Huaitiao.
There was a bodhisattva named Yingchi (Upendra) who came to the Sahā world to pay homage to the World-Honored One; he prostrated himself in greeting and made offerings.
Having bowed at the Buddha’s feet, he circumambulated the Buddha seven times and then stood before him.
The Bodhisattva Yingchi, while in his mind, thought:
"I wish to know the limits of the Tathāgata’s body.

He transformed his own body to a height of three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*, and observed the Tathāgata’s body to be five hundred forty-three million *zhao-hai* (10^24) and twenty trillion *li*.
Then he thought to himself:
"I have attained the power of spiritual travel and delight in my own supernormal faculties.
Why should I not further investigate how the Buddha’s body enters [into various states]?"

By means of his majestic virtue and supernatural power, the Buddha traveled upward from here through buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers to a world named Lotus Adornment. In that land dwells a buddha named Lotus Superior Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Yingchi went before him but could not behold him.

Standing above and looking from afar, he never succeeded in seeing the crown of the head of the World-Honored One, the Great Sage, the Buddha Śākyamuni; though he desired to see the mark of the uṣṇīṣa, he could never see it. He did not know how many thousands of billions of Ganges-sands of Buddha-fields the height, length, and breadth of the Buddha’s body extended.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Time-Holder went to the presence of the Buddha Padmottara, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and standing before the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"How far is it from here to where I have come?"
The Buddha said,
"A hundred billion Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands away from here, noble son, you have come from there to this place.
Yingchi Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have traveled upward through various Buddha-lands, yet I have been unable to see the crown of Śākyamuni Buddha’s head; I do not know how many hundreds of thousands of billions of Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands it rises above."
That Buddha replied:

"Even if a son of good family were to employ such skillful means and sagely, enlightened wisdom, as well as this power of spiritual footprints (*ṛddhi-pāda*), and were to travel upward from here for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, suddenly surpassing those worlds to reach a buddha-field beyond compare, he would still be unable to see the crown of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni’s head, nor could he find the limits of his body."
Furthermore, son of good family, you should know that the Buddha’s body is thus infinite, sublime, and beyond all analogy; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot be fully described or measured.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Because it is without peer, it is called "incomparable.

The Tathāgata’s prohibitive precepts are likewise beyond analogy; his samādhi, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the aggregate of knowledge and vision, as well as his physical, verbal, and mental actions, and his physical marks and minor signs, are all entirely incomparable.

For all sentient beings, by means of various categories of inductions, parables, and metaphors, they extol the Tathāgata’s infinite precepts, his concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; as well as his physical and verbal actions, mental karma, and the excellence of his physical marks and majestic appearance—which, like space, have no perceivable limits.
“The body of the Tathāgata is thus boundless.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāraṇa, having heard what the Tathāgata Padmottara had said, was filled with joy and experienced a state never before known. He immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Sage seven times, and vanished from that buddha-field. By receiving the Tathāgata’s holy command and relying upon his own spiritual power, he reached this buddha-land in the mere interval of a thought.
He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself before the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and then stood before the Buddha, speaking in verse:
“Desiring to understand and penetrate the Buddha’s body, which is like the metaphor of empty space, I wish to know its limits, having abandoned all conditioned constructs.”
Passing beyond hundreds of thousands of billions, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers,
and ascending above many lands, he desired to see the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Having passed through infinite lands, he arrived at the realm of the Buddha Padma.
Delighting in the boundaries of body and mind, they do not behold the crown of the Buddha’s head.
In that land, the Buddha is named Padmottara;
perceiving what my mind contemplates, he then explains it through detailed analysis.
Even if one were to cite numerous analogies to expound upon the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
it would not accord with the Buddha’s teaching and would constitute slandering the Sages.
If one wishes to understand analogies, the Dharma of all Buddhas is equal.
Proclaiming the limits of space, yet in truth it has no boundaries;
even as space itself, so too are the Buddha’s precepts.
Such are the activities of concentration and wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of deliverance.
Just as space is boundless, so too is the form-body (rūpakāya).
If one wishes to behold the crown of the Protector of the World, it is equal to space;
as far as space extends, so does the Buddha’s body pervade.
Just as space pervades all, so too does the radiance of light shine;
wherever that light reaches, there are words such as these;
and just as those words reach everywhere, so too does the mind pervade all.
Just as the mind reaches everywhere, so too is the mind of loving-kindness spread;
just as the mind of loving-kindness pervades, so too does wisdom extend equally without distinction;
just as wisdom extends everywhere, so too does the body reach everywhere in this same way.
Merit is likewise so; the mind of the Way is without duality.
As is the merit of the mind of the Way, so too is the understanding of form;
it fills all of empty space, and that which is delivered exceeds even this.
Just as all sentient beings possess their respective portions of merit,
the merit of one person who has resolved to attain the Way is likewise;
and just as that person who has resolved to attain the Way possesses their own karma of merit and renown, so too is it for all.
If one receives the True Dharma, their merit shall surpass that [of the former].
Even if all Buddhas were to appear and proclaim for ten billion eons,
they could not reach the limit of praising the merit of upholding the True Dharma.
If one gives rise to the mind of the Way and protects all the True Dharma,
yet delights only in the understanding of emptiness and non-existence, one will not obtain even one-sixteenth [of the merit].
By delighting in the understanding of emptiness and non-existence, one does not lose the mind of the Way.
Upholding the most sublime Dharma, this wisdom is then harmonious;
having attained this course of the Dharma, the bodhisattva is courageous,
achieves the merit of a Buddha, and reverently practices the conduct of the Buddha-way.
When these verses were spoken, a billion Buddha-lands shook;
hundreds of thousands of billions of devas played billions of musical instruments,
and countless billions of people all resolved their minds upon the Great Way.
Because of hearing the Great Dharma, that which is praised by those who uphold it is inconceivable; it is unsurpassed and limitless,
the sovereign secret activity universally manifested by all Buddhas.
The Vajrapāṇi Malla said to Śāntamati:
"This is the secret essence of the Tathāgata’s body; even if all those sentient beings were gathered in a single assembly, some would be able to see the Tathāgata’s body while others would not."
Those who are able to see him gaze upon him with joy; those who do not see him observe him in silence.
Although the Tathāgata does not eat, all sentient beings perceive the Tathāgata partaking of food.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
There was a deva named *Tejas* who, having been first transformed and received the Way, took the Tathāgata’s food and received it in a vessel to relieve those in poverty and distress.
All the people saw the Tathāgata eating; they saw the Tathāgata lift the food and place it in his mouth, whereupon it would naturally return to the vessel.

The sons of the gods take the roots of merit planted by the Tathāgatas in past lives that still have residual karmic consequences; wherever they are born, they encounter weakness and inferiority, being forced to consume [the fruits of their karma]. To those who are famished, destitute, and in distress, unable to find food, the Tathāgata, out of compassion for them, bestows food.

After these sentient beings have eaten this meal, their bodies become tranquil and secure, the dust and toil of afflictions are eliminated, all discursive thoughts come to rest, and their mental nature becomes harmonious and gentle; with their wills set upon the Unsurpassed, they give rise to inconceivable awakening through equanimity.
For this reason, one should form this contemplation: the Tathāgata does not eat; the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, takes the Dharma as his food.
Why is this so? The body of the Tathāgata is formed as a linked chain, like a vajra—resonant, firm, and indestructible.

The body of that Tathāgata has no stomach for raw food nor any for digested food; furthermore, it is neither solid nor soft, and it is free from the impurities of excrement, urine, coughing, or spitting.
Furthermore, the body of the Tathāgata is like the color of purple gold; it is neither timid nor weak, and possesses no fear.
Śāntamati, observe the body of the Tathāgata for a moment.
Vast and boundless, it is exceedingly wondrous and firm like a vajra, yet the body is supple like the finest celestial raiment.

At times, when this sublime and manifest subtle body appears, gods and celestial maidens prostrate at its feet; they pay homage to the Tathāgata’s body and touch his feet, which are so soft and exquisitely fine that they are beyond all analogy, causing them all to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, forever free from the dust of the world.

If a person of lustful desire, anger, or delusion—whether possessing these individually or in equal measure—should behold the body of the Tathāgata upon encountering it with their own eyes, all their physical actions characterized by lust, anger, and delusion, as well as their various defilements, will be entirely eliminated and no longer remain.

If there are those who possess stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, anger, indolence, distraction, or ignorance, [the Tathāgata] causes them to practice giving, maintaining the precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom.
To state the essential point: if anyone departs from unwholesome states and beholds the body of the Tathāgata, they cast off all unwholesome thoughts and cultivate the roots of virtue.
To contemplate the Tathāgata without conceptualization is called the True Path; this, O Śāntamati, is the secret essence of the Tathāgata’s body.

If there is giving, it is the sovereign transformation through the auspicious response of the Tathāgata. By means of the Vinaya, he transforms sentient beings so that they do not undergo further growth or accumulation; he dissolves the perceptions of sentient beings and proclaims and establishes for them that which accords with their capacity for deliverance.
The Tathāgata contemplates therein that there is no karma and no activity.
The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has never thought:
"I shall manifest a transformed body."
Regarding those who are to be transformed, if they are currently being transformed, their minds naturally think thus.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, whom they observe through transformation, appears before them; even throughout the lands described in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, wherever the Tathāgata goes and comes in his transformations, the Tathāgata remains there observing without any conceptualization.
That Tathāgata emits from his body various kinds of light—countless colors and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of radiant hues.

Wherever that light shines upon Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, its radiance reaches afar, and all sentient beings who encounter it are transformed and awakened through the practice of the path they have undertaken.
Because there is no karma and no activity performed, therefore, Śāntamati,

the secret essence of the Tathāgata’s body consists of all his mental activities, all that he proclaims and teaches, and all that he accomplishes by generating the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
"Furthermore, the secret of the Tathāgata’s body is beyond measure or calculation.

When this essential secret of the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct was being spoken, ten thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, and eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The devas, humans, asuras, and people of the world praised Guhyapada, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!
The musical instruments of the devas resounded spontaneously without being struck, and celestial flowers rained down.
The World-Honored One raised his right hand, which was the color of purple-polished gold, and placed it upon the crown of the head of Guhyapada, the Vajrapāṇi Mahāpuruṣa,
and praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Guhyapada!"
"Excellent, Excellent! This is the secret and essential teaching on the body of the Tathāgata.
What has now been proclaimed is in perfect accord with the Buddha’s instructions and is without duality.
Thus spoke the Mārṣa Guhyapāda to Śāntamati:
"What is meant by the secret essentials of the Tathāgata’s speech?

From the night the Tathāgata attained the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path and realized supreme enlightenment, until the day and night of his parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder—in that interval, he bestowed but a single word, yet was able to proclaim it with detailed analysis, expounding and disseminating infinite principles for countless billions of years."
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata is eternally in meditative concentration.

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has no inhalation or exhalation; he has no mental recollection, nor does he engage in any activity, nor does he harbor further discursive thoughts. He is entirely without engagement; though he utters words with his mouth, there is neither conceptualization nor activity therein.
The Tathāgata’s practice is neither appropriate nor inappropriate; it is without speech and without discourse, and he does not conceive of there being a person.
All that the World-Honored One has taught—transcending all samādhis and meditative attainments—is explained through the differentiation of words and letters.

They proclaim written words and rely upon them as their own; all sentient beings thus circulate and come and go, thinking, "The Tathāgata has preached the Dharma for me. This is called the Tathāgata being present there yet remaining without any conceptualization.
The Tathāgata observes and knows contentment; from his mouth, sounds are proclaimed by his tongue, and there are none who do not rejoice upon hearing these proclaimed sounds.

He expounds the teachings of the Tathāgata’s speech, and with a single voice, he pervades everywhere throughout the thoughts and mental inclinations of all sentient beings; this is how the Tathāgata unfolds [the teaching] from his mouth.
The Tathāgata’s speech issues forth in sixty qualities, each with a distinct resonance.
What are these sixty? They are:
the auspicious sound, the gentle sound, the delightful sound, the pleasing and pure sound, and the stainless sound... [and so forth].
The sound, the resplendent sound, the subtle and wondrous sound, the clear and audible sound, the unconfused sound, the unagitated sound,
the sound of a master and teacher, the sound free from harshness, the sound free from coarseness and rudeness, the well-accordant sound, the steady and grave sound,
the auspicious and harmonious sound of the body, the sound that accords with the timing of the mind, the empty and joyful sound, and the bestowing [sound].
The sound of loving peace, the sound free from affliction and fever, the square and upright sound, the sound of penetrating knowledge, the sound of intimacy,
the sound pleasing to the mind, the sound of joy, the sound of harmonious instruction, the sound of clear understanding, the sound of diligent effort, the sound of patient harmony,
the sound of profound realization, the sound whose resonance removes defilement, and the sound corresponding to that of a lion.
The sound of the dragon’s roar; the sound of pleasant rain; the sound of the ocean-thundering Dragon King; the sound of the *kiṃnara* musicians;

the sound of the plaintive *luán* bird; the sound of the soaring falcon; the sound of the crane’s cry; the sound of the *jīyù* bird; the sound of the exquisite bird; the sound of thunderous resonance;
the sound that is not abrupt; the sound that is not violent; the sound of universal penetration; and the sound that eliminates what is erroneous.
Voice of timely sound; voice free from deficiency; voice free from timidity; voice of joy and delight; voice of clarity and fluency; voice of moral discipline and restraint;
voice of sweetness and beauty; voice of progress; voice of vast universality; voice of complete perfection; voice with flawless sense faculties;
voice that is neither light nor hurried; voice that does not dwell; voice whose resonance pervades the entire assembly.
...proclaiming all sounds of virtue.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
“These are the sixty qualities of the Tathāgata’s voice.”
The voice of that Tathāgata pervades all Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, capable of gladdening the mental dispositions and conduct of all sentient beings.
In the Tathāgata’s contemplation, there is no delusive thought; the Tathāgata’s mind of the Way does not form such a notion as:
"I shall proclaim the Dharma of the sutras for their sake with my own mouth."
They are thoroughly versed in the Sūtras of Hearing, the Sūtras of Virtue, the Sūtras of Exposition, the Sūtras of Analysis, the Sūtras of Verses and Poetry, and the Sūtras of the Pitakas.

Furthermore, they are proficient in the Sūtras of Accordance, the Sūtras of Birth, the Vaipulya Sūtras, the Sūtras of Unprecedented Dharmas, the Sūtras of Parables, and the Sūtras of Chapters and Phrases. Whether they speak ancient parables or provide illustrative metaphors, whether they deliver proclamations, discourses, and conversations, or discuss all manner of supreme matters, they expound upon various events and unfold manifold affairs. They appropriately distribute these teachings far and near, opening up their fundamental principles so that others may understand them clearly; they proclaim their meanings to bring about transformation and enlightenment.

Furthermore, within this assembly—the Dharma scriptures proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—there are those who sit near the Buddha, having entered the community of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; as well as the multitudes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. According to the faculties, conduct, and diligence of each being, and in accordance with the Dharma they delight in, he causes them to enter the Path.
Entering the Path in accordance with this, they seek to transform sentient beings without seeking their own causes; their delight in the resonance of the Dharma is likewise so.
These sentient beings think to themselves:
"It issues from the mouth of the Tathāgata."

Not by preaching the Dharma to each individually, but by responding appropriately to their diverse mentalities through speech and action suited to the occasion, so that each hears the Dharma and attains understanding—this is called the essential secret of the Tathāgata’s mouth.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

There are countless sentient beings whose conduct is immeasurable; their speech consists of eighty-four thousand dark and inferior states. To lead and advance these beings of ignorance, they enter the Dharma of the Tathāgata and receive transformation and enlightenment."

Furthermore, the conduct of sentient beings is immeasurable; if there are those who harbor lustful desire, [the Bodhisattva], according to the time and following the conduct of those beings, enters into their midst and thereby delivers them.

For the sake of sentient beings who are dominated by anger or delusion, as well as those whose conduct is equally divided among the three poisons and thus obscured by them, he—according to their respective conceptualizations within the triple world—adorns and uproots [these afflictions], causing them to abide nowhere.
Yet, without harboring any divergent thoughts, he enters among the classes of sentient beings to discern their actions of merit and demerit.

He manifests a lifespan for the Tathāgata that appears limited and finite, and, unaware of the specific merits and demerits practiced by sentient beings, he preaches various distinct teachings through skillful means.
The Tathāgata’s skillful means and sentient beings are infinite and immeasurable; as their practices differ, he accordingly proclaims various categories of Dharma.

Furthermore, because sentient beings encounter him face-to-face in my presence, all that the Tathāgata speaks enters their hearts completely. According to their original conduct, he proclaims the work of the Path so that each may understand and enter it—this is called the secret essence of the Tathāgata.

If there are bodhisattvas who enter the secret essentials of the Tathāgata, they do not understand this: namely, that while the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, expounds the gateway of the conditioned, all dharmas of the Tathāgata are in fact unconditioned.

Furthermore, when a Tathāgata proclaims a single tone, sentient beings each imagine that he is speaking to them; those who delight in recollecting the Tathāgata’s voice merely perceive what they imagine him to be saying.
One should not form such a view;
for the Tathāgata’s mouth has never uttered a word. Why is this?

There are some sentient beings who, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s voice, perceive the mark between his eyebrows as being at the crown of his head; if they have the perception of hair, they know it to be deep blue, standing upright from the center of his head, with eyes that are exceptionally bright and beautiful—beings are unable to bear gazing intently upon the Tathāgata.

The reason for this giving is to eliminate all that is non-virtuous and to abandon the gateway of contention; it is to be free from a harmful mind. Whether by means of the neck, shoulders, or arms to remove the various aggregates of suffering;

whether by means of the fingers; whether by means of the torso or the flanks; whether by means of proclaiming verses from the back down to the feet; whether by means of the abdomen, the navel, or the male organ; whether by means of the knees or calves—through these, one rests in freedom from anger. Furthermore, by means of the marks and the eighty minor characteristics, one becomes supreme in the world.

If there are those who perceive and know the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, upon hearing his voice, he shall transform and guide them according to their inclinations and the varying degrees of their faculties, delivering this instruction so that they all enter the discipline.
Even so, the Tathāgata’s contemplation and transformation of beings is likewise free from the notion of characteristics.
It is like this, Śāntamati!

For example, it is as when musical instruments are tuned; when struck by hand, their sounds are harmonious and moving, yet there is no one present who actually produces those sounds. All arise through the convergence of skillful means and conditions, resulting in these extraordinary, harmonious, and moving tones.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!

The words of the Tathāgata transform the minds of sentient beings by providing them with the conditions for his teaching. Whatever the Tathāgata proclaims therein is without partiality; these are all established through the specific practices formed by past conditions. The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, stands supreme and exalted among sentient beings because of his original distinction.
It is just as with the sound of a call, Śāntamati! Its resonance reaches far and wide; yet the source of that sound does not exist within, nor does it abide without, nor is it found in between.

The Tathāgata is likewise; when he proclaims sounds to instruct and transform the minds of sentient beings, his words and teachings do not issue from the body, nor from the mind, nor from within, nor from without, nor from between them.

It is like the wish-fulfilling jewel within the great ocean, which radiates its brilliance for the sake of all beings; or like a precious jewel fastened to the top of a banner that illuminates the entire city. According to the desires and aspirations in the minds of sentient beings, that moon-bright jewel produces treasures so that everyone obtains what they wish for, yet this precious jewel has no thoughts or perceptions.

The Tathāgata is thus: possessing a jewel-like mind, his resolve abiding in purity as he upholds the banner of great compassion, he accords with the dispositions and faculties of sentient beings without exception, causing each to attain awakening and understanding; yet, though he manifests these teachings, he remains free from conceptual thought—this is the secret essence proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada further addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"I have now surveyed universally all the Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, and human beings in the heavens and the world, yet none at all can limit the sounds, resonance, or phrasing proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

Why is this? As I recall, when the World-Honored One was on Vulture Peak Mountain surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas, there was a Dharma scripture titled "The Field of Pure Sound," which he extensively proclaimed for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, established by the Bodhisattva Maitreya,
the worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"I wish to test and know how far the resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice can penetrate."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana suddenly vanished from his seat and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru; there he heard the voice of the Tathāgata as if it were right before his eyes.

By means of his own supernormal power, he traveled to the very edge of this trichiliocosm, passing beyond all the Mount Sumers, the various four quarters, and all the Cakravāḍa mountains, until he stood upon the summit of the Great Cakravāḍa at the extreme limit. There he heard the voice of the Tathāgata, no different than before, neither near nor far.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"This Mahāmaudgalyāyana wishes to test the Tathāgata’s field of pure sound.
I should now manifest my supernormal powers for him."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One manifested his supernormal powers. At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command and relying upon his own supernormal powers, traveled toward the western direction. Though it was an immense distance from here, he passed through as many buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in ninety-nine Ganges Rivers, until he reached a buddha-world named *Prabhāketu*.
Furthermore, in that land there is a Buddha named Prabhāsarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.
When Maudgalyāyana arrived there and stayed in that buddha-field, he heard the voice of the Buddha as clearly as if one were standing face-to-face listening to someone's words.

In that Buddha-land of Prabhāsa-dhvaja, there is a great radiance; the Buddha’s body is forty li in height, the bodies of the bodhisattvas are twenty li in height, and the bowls from which those bodhisattvas eat are one li in height.
As Maudgalyāyana walked along the rim of his almsbowl, the bodhisattvas addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, Great Sage!
From where has this insect come, that it wears the robes of a śramaṇa and walks upon the rim of the almsbowl?"
At that time, the Buddha said:
"O sons of noble family!
Be careful not to give rise to a mind of contempt for this worthy one."
Why is this? This venerable elder named Mahāmaudgalyāyana is one of the great disciples among the śrāvakas of Śākyamuni Buddha, foremost in supernatural powers.
Then, the Buddha King of Radiance told Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in my land all see that your body is small and have consequently conceived feelings of contempt."
"Virtuous one, you should manifest your own supernormal powers, sustained by the majestic virtue and holy authority of Śākyamuni Buddha.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to the place of the Buddha King of Radiance, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood before him. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Furthermore, with this very body, I wish to sit cross-legged upon this ground; would it be permissible?"
The Buddha said to him,
"As you wish. Thereupon,
Mahāmaudgalyāyana leaped into the air to a height of hundreds of millions of fathoms and, within that precious realm, fashioned a couch and sat upon it cross-legged.

From his seat hung hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of necklaces made of various precious jewels; from each individual necklace and from every single jewel within them, a hundred thousand rays of light were emitted. Within each ray of light there was a lotus flower, and upon every lotus flower appeared the body of Śākyamuni sitting amidst the blossoms. The sound of what he preached was like the voice of Śākyamuni—pure and resonant as he proclaimed the sūtras, being exactly the same without any difference.
When Mahāmaudgalyāyana had thus manifested his supernormal powers, he returned before the Buddha.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, having attained what they had never experienced before, marveled at the reason for this and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"For what purpose has this Mahāmaudgalyāyana come to this world?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"He has come to this land because he wishes to test how far the resonance of Śākyamuni Buddha’s voice can penetrate.
Then, the Buddha King of Radiance addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Virtuous one, you should not test [the Tathāgata]. The sound of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, is infinite and has neither distance nor proximity; how could you wish to know its limits?
You have made a very great error."

"Suppose, O Maudgalyāyana, that you were to travel westward with your supernormal powers without ceasing for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; even then, you would not be able to know the extent of what is heard of the Tathāgata’s voice.
The voices of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are vast and far-reaching, transcendent and limitless; they are sublime, immeasurable, and beyond all analogy."
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, standing before that World-Honored One at his own feet, confessed his transgression:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
My person was not quick-witted."
"The Buddha’s voice is immeasurable, yet you have conceived the thought to know its limits and how far it can be heard.
The King of Radiance said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Although you have come from afar, passing through as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in ninety-nine Ganges Rivers to reach this Buddha-land."
Again he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is exceedingly far, exceedingly far,
O God among Gods!"
"My body is utterly exhausted, and I am unable to return to my own land.
The World-Honored One said,
"What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?"
"Do not hold the view that you have reached this world by means of your own supernatural power.

Rather, it is through the majestic authority established by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha that you have arrived here. You should from afar take refuge in him, prostrate yourself, and pay homage to Śākyamuni Buddha; by that Buddha’s holy will, he shall lead you back to your own native land."
Even if you, by means of your own supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), were to wish to return to your native land, you would not arrive for an entire eon (*kalpa*).
Since you have not yet arrived, you will not witness the time when the Buddha Kāśyapa enters parinirvāṇa.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
From which direction did I come—
from the east, the south, the west, or the north?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "I do not know which direction it is.
Now, being utterly bewildered, I do not know where my native land is located; in which direction does it lie?"
The World-Honored One told Maudgalyāyana:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is in the eastern direction.

Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the eastern direction where Śākyamuni Buddha was located, and took refuge in him. At that time, he spoke in verse:
“O Honored One among gods and humans, you who look upon us with compassionate power;
your majestic virtue is most lofty and sublime, revered by both gods and men.”
"Their resonance penetrates the immeasurable, and their wisdom is boundless;
I pray that you reveal your land, for I now wish to return to this realm.
Thus it was, O Śāntamati!
The voices of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are boundless and immeasurable.
At that time, when Śākyamuni Buddha was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Venerable Śāriputra heard the Honorable Mahāmaudgalyāyana proclaiming with a great voice and wondered at its cause.
The worthy Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Who is it that now proclaims this great sound from afar, seeking refuge?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"The elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana is currently in a western region, ninety-nine *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* buddha-fields away from here. That world is named Light Banner (*Prabhāketu*), and the Buddha there is named King of Light (*Prabhārāja*) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma."
"The elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana reached that Buddha-land and, desiring in his mind to return to this land, has therefore proclaimed this great, far-reaching sound.
Ānanda asked again:
"By what causes and conditions did he go to that Buddha-land?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“When Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrives, you shall ask him about his intention.
At that time, the members of the great assembly each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to behold the world-system *Prabhāsa-dhvaja* and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha *Prabhāsa-rāja*, and to see Mahāmaudgalyāyana wandering therein."

At that time, the World-Honored One, perceiving the intent of the assembled multitude to offer encouragement and support, emitted from the mark between his eyebrows a great radiance named "Universally Received. This light illuminated worlds as numerous as the sands of ninety-nine Ganges Rivers, reaching as far as the Buddha-land of Radiant Banner.

A great radiance pervaded the entire assembly, and everyone beheld the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, King of Light of that land; seeing this, Mahāmaudgalyāyana threw himself to the ground and proclaimed it with a loud voice.
At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Follow this radiance and return to this land.

Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana, relying upon the Buddha’s radiance, returned to this land in the mere twinkling of an eye. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood before the Buddha to repent and take refuge, severely reproaching himself:
"I have been greatly deluded.
The resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice is immeasurable, yet I sought to test it.

The distance I have traveled is exceedingly vast; yet wherever I have gone, the sound I heard was exactly the same as when I was near, and I did not realize it was distant. The resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice is majestic and boundless."
The Buddha said: "So it is, Maudgalyāyana!
It is just as you have said."
The resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice penetrates to such great distances that it is beyond all analogy.
To wish to know the limits of the Tathāgata’s resonance is like seeking the boundaries of empty space. Why is this so?
"Just as empty space is all-pervasive and boundless, so too do the words of the Tathāgata resound through the infinite and the far-reaching.

"Śāntamati! When this Chapter on Maudgalyāyana’s往返 (Coming and Going) was being preached, ten thousand people in that assembly immediately conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment."
"This is the secret essential of the Tathāgata’s speech.
Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, said: "What do you understand, Śāntamati?"
"Can the various thoughts in the minds of all sentient beings ever be known? Śāntamati replied:

"The thoughts and reflections of a single person's mind are difficult to limit; even if all the sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to collectively calculate and observe them for an entire kalpa, they could not know them. How much more so the thoughts and reflections of all sentient beings—they are truly beyond measure and limit."
"I now speak to you with earnestness and entrust this to you: consider that the sounds produced by the mental conceptions of all sentient beings are as infinite as this.
How much more so the nature of the minds of all sentient beings, which is formless and beyond all comparison!"
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“If all sentient beings in the three thousandfold world system were to become pratyekabuddhas,
the mind-thoughts of even a single person within a single kalpa could not be known.”
All that is conceived by the mind, the Buddha fully knows their intentions and thoughts;
with a mind free of conceptualization, the Buddha thoroughly understands these thoughts.
Whatever all sentient beings have conceived throughout the three periods of time, [the Buddha knows them all].
Whatever the World-Protector utters with his mouth, each who hears it attains understanding.
According to the thoughts of beings, the Buddha proclaims sounds and lectures on the sūtras;
these resonant sounds dwell within the heart, and thus he expounds what is appropriate for their path.
Just as all sentient beings conceive of various names and forms,
so too is the light emanated from a single pore of the Hero of the World.
Just as all sentient beings possess names, forms, and mental conceptions, [so too is the light].
The Tathāgata’s resonant voice surpasses all those conceptualizations.
The Buddha proclaims everything, employing metaphors to calculate all thoughts;
his voice never ceases, for one cannot reach the limit of the Buddha’s words.
Who can attain the formless? Out of compassion for those who lack words, one realizes that the formless is beyond speech; thus, the defilements of the formless are extinguished.
If even the defilements were formless, nothing at all could be apprehended.
Because these are formless objects, they can ultimately not be apprehended.
To say that they are empty and lack reality, being neither internal nor external—
since afflictions and empty space are equal— it is said that they have no interior or exterior.
Even if one were unable to find words, the Buddha’s speech pervades the ten directions;
though the afflictions are boundless, this is the locus where he establishes himself.
All the speech of sentient beings—words of superior, middling, and inferior quality—[are likewise encompassed].
Without the activities of body, speech, or mind, they do not abandon anything nor do they establish themselves anywhere.
Their manifestations are like those of a dancer;
even the music of the devas lacks body or verbal expression, yet its resonance pervades everywhere.
Thus, the fundamental nature is utterly pure; the minds of sentient beings are likewise so.
The Buddha proclaims this for all, yet that mind is devoid of conceptualization.
It is like an echo produced by a call: it exists neither within nor without.
The Honored One among Men speaks thus: there is neither internal nor external.
His thoughtlessness is like a wondrous jewel; what he teaches delights all sentient beings.
His words are free from delusive conceptualization and are suitable for all classes of living creatures.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada said to Śāntamati:
"This is the secret essential of the Tathāgata’s speech.
Furthermore, through the Tathāgata’s secret essentials, he preaches the Dharma to sentient beings for their transformation and edification in accordance with their voices."

In this trichiliocosm, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, proclaims his instructions through various means; according to their respective languages and innumerable names and titles, he establishes them in ultimate sincerity, such that they proceed toward the state where karma ceases. This is called the Noble Truths of Suffering, its Origin, its Cessation, and the Path; it is called the Earth Deity protecting their minds so that their fundamental intentions remain firm.
Thereupon he spoke this incantation:
"Abhe, Apamūle, Kāhane, Akayute. This protects all; this divine spell is called the Path to the Cessation of Suffering through the Understanding of its Origin.
All the devas in the void sighed in admiration of these words and each proclaimed a mantra, saying:
“Jīvañjīve, ajīvañjīve, ajīvatakāme, āhaniṇire. To save all beings—this is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering through the Path.”
The devas of the Four Great Kings further recited this mantra:
"Ini mini, tave duttave, vilu. "To save all sentient beings—this is what is called the Dharma of the Suffering, its Origin, its Cessation, and the Path."
The devas of that Trāyastriṃśa Heaven recited this mantra:
“This mantra protects all; its turning, its thorough practice, its mastery, its extinction, and its being exhausted—this is the essential summary.
The devas of the third heaven, Yāma, further recited this mantra: “Śūli, dāra, sahanī, dāra, siṣyaya, darsiṣyaya, pihani. The fourth heaven, Tuṣita, recited this mantra:
“Duk-fan-mien-chu, Gu-zhuan-zhong-chu-ye; these mantras protect all. This is the fifth mantra spoken by the gods of the Heaven of No-Arrogance (Nirmāṇarati):
“So-tu, Ju-so-tu, Hu-so-tu, Chu-du-nü; these mantras protect all. The sixth, the mantra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, says:
“He-hu-she-yeh, Hu-he-ni-yi, A-lo-ni-han; this mantra protects all. The seventh, the mantra of the Brahmā gods, says:
"Karmic activity, the seed of karmic activity, the tree of causes and conditions—by means of causes and conditions, this mantra protects all.
The eighth, the mantra of the Brahmakāyika devas, says: "Pure clarity, creating purity, the pure wind, moving with purity—this divine mantra protects all.

The ninth, the mantra of the Brahmapurohita devas, says: "O Infinite One, lead them all away; O Lord of the Path, remember the firm essentials—this divine mantra protects all. The tenth, the mantra of the Mahābrahmā devas, says:
"Hana hana sande, hana hahana, hana kumana; this divine mantra protects all. The eleventh, the mantra of the Mahābrahmā devas, says:
"Mukim, mukim, piṅga piṅga piṃśi; this divine mantra protects all. The twelfth, the mantra of the Ābhāsvara devas, says:
"Ihe he, jaṃ he gatu, upasaṃkrama; this divine mantra protects all. The thirteenth, the mantra of the Parīttābha devas, says:
"Taking this away, not carrying it away, not causing it to go, reaching nowhere—this divine mantra protects all. (14) The mantra of the gods of Immeasurable Light says:
"Guṇi, guṇiguṇi, guṇakṣaya, guṇāpramāṇa—this divine mantra protects all. (15) The mantra of the gods of Radiant Sound says:
"Severing the end, mastery in severing, compliant harmony, ever-pure—this divine mantra protects all. (16) The mantra of the gods of Purity says:
"Wherever one goes, wherever one returns, and the place one approaches—by means of that which is approached, this divine mantra protects all.
(17) The mantra of the Śuddhāvāsa devas says: "Pure! O Pure One! Pure again, pure! Return to purity! This divine mantra protects all. (18) The mantra of the Apramāṇaśubha devas says:
"O Selfless One! O One Without 'I'! Not arrogant, yet returning to self-majesty! This divine mantra protects all. (19) The mantra of the Śubhakṛtsna devas says:

"Emancipation through cessation; the trace of liberation is the root of proximity to liberation. This divine mantra protects all. (20) The mantra of the Deva of the Fruit of Arhatship and the 21st, the Deva of Governing Words, says:
"By non-action and non-doing, one eliminates doing and what is done; it is ultimate. This divine mantra protects all. The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada said:

"This is called the Truth of Suffering, its Origin, its Cessation, and the Path. It is that which should be practiced, that which should be cultivated for transformation, and that which follows the teachings of the Vinaya, manifesting the subtle and infinite karma."

The twenty-second are the Vītarāga-devas; the twenty-third are the Śakra-devas; the twenty-fourth are the Sudarśana-devas; the twenty-fifth are the Ekottara-devas; and the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) consist of four heavens, namely: the Abhāsvara-devas who have attained certainty through the practice of a single point, the Atapa-devas, the Avṛha-devas, and the Sudṛśa-devas.
This, Śāntamati, is the assembly of the gods who have established the wisdom of their sincere vows.
Likewise, the yakṣas, bhūtas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kālaka-ghosts, and flower-holding ghosts— each of their modes of speech and instruction is distinct.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
This Jambudvīpa continent consists of one thousand great nations, each with its own major districts.
These sixteen great nations govern and protect one another, each praising the others.
All humans and non-humans have diverse languages and differing sounds, with expressions ranging from light to grave.
The Tathāgata’s holy wisdom enters according to their respective voices and tones, transforming them all and establishing them in the correct and true karma.
