Each has its own distinct name: the Śākya clan, Anxi (Parthia), Yuezhi, Daqin (Roman Empire), Jianfu, Rǎodòng, Qiuci (Kucha), Yutian (Khotan), Shale (Kashgar), Chanshan (Tashkurgan), Wugqi (Uḍḍiyāna), and the various kingdoms of the past and present such as the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Wu, Shu, and the region of Qin; the various Mleccha barbarians, the ignorant folk of Tarata, and the wild men; as well as those who recite the *Sūmanya* mantras; the countries of women, the country of Moutoutuo (Multaka), the country of Yin-yuan (Nepal), the country of Vārāṇasī, the country of Shushu (Śrughna), the country of Jinben (Jambudvīpa), the country of Pilaben (Pīlava), the country of Yispi-sha (Viśākhā), the country of Yiben (Ayodhyā), the country of Shangben (Uttarapāṭha), the country of Tantan (Takṣaśilā), the various foreign lands of the north, and the countries maintained in the west.
The various deities within the ocean, the multitude of insects, fish, and turtles;

the deities among the mountains, and all classes of embodied, sentient beings—such as the Akrūras, Makūras, and Anasans; the various sheep-herders and wild beasts; and all those with crooked dispositions whose minds are not upright, whether they were born in the past or currently dwell in this world.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
These thousand lands are filled around about, with each person in Jambudvīpa dwelling separately.
Furthermore, these humans and non-humans have various languages, different dispositions, and distinct voices.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, enters into their respective languages and voices to transform them and establish them in the True and Right Path.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying:
"In this trichiliocosm, there are eighty-four billion hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings, each with different modes of speech."
In reckoning, all these converge upon a single meaning: the wisdom of ultimate truth, which is utterly sincere and free from anger.
Thus, Śāntamati! This is the secret essence of the Tathāgata’s speech.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
The words of the Tathāgata decisively sever the net of doubts of all sentient beings, leaving no remaining fetters.

All sentient beings throughout the ten directions—whose species are more numerous than the dust of the earth—each have different modes of conduct and origins; [the Tathāgata] causes their transgressions to be fully exhausted so that they may attain human bodies.
Having obtained this human body, which arises from thought, may all these sentient beings attain wisdom, eloquence, sageliness, and heroic vigor like that of Śāriputra.

If the wisdom of all these were combined into a single sage, and if, by such analogy, all sentient beings were to universally obtain wisdom each equal to that of the aforementioned one sage’s brilliance.
This noble clarity may persist for one kalpa or even beyond a kalpa; through wisdom and meditative contemplation, one examines all perceptions to seek their origin and end.

Just as one person’s wisdom and meditation do not require further instruction, so too those from the second person onward all receive verbal teachings, each possessing the great illumination of wise and sagely penetration.
By means of such analogies, the Tathāgata, in the mere twinkling of an eye,
fully explains from beginning to end all the various doubts held by these sentient beings as they approach him.

The Great Sage is thus: with a single mind, he constantly enters into the mental activities of all sentient beings, being able to discern through his wisdom and clarity the location of their insights. With a single word, he completely resolves their webs of doubt; he establishes each one in the fundamental seat of wisdom, causing them all to rejoice and find their proper place. Regarding the Tathāgata’s wisdom and penetrating clarity that they have heard, the Tathāgata causes them all to understand it fully.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
The Tathāgata completely resolves all the doubts of sentient beings regarding their past and future lives, leaving no remaining fetters; this is the secret essential of the Tathāgata’s speech.
"The sounds they enter and their verbal teachings are beyond description; the Tathāgata’s speech is immeasurable and can have no analogy.

When these secret and essential words of the Tathāgata were spoken, twenty-two thousand sentient beings all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and right path. The entire assembly experienced what they had never known before. Having heard the secret and essential deeds regarding the Tathāgata’s speech proclaimed by the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, each felt great joy; they rose from their seats and, bowing their heads, took refuge in the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ten [and] Volume Eleven,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Third Assembly on the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, Part Four.
Again, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
“What is called the secret essence of the Tathāgata’s mind?”

Their karma is pure; by reason of these causes and conditions, they are born among all the devaputras. Possessing a single consciousness and wisdom, their lifespan lasts eighty-four thousand kalpas. Furthermore, their spiritual consciousness does not shift or change, yet through the power of other consciousnesses up to the state of meditative concentration, they regain their life-span.
When they eventually pass away from that realm, they receive a body and are born again according to their past conduct.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
From the night the Tathāgata attained the Way of the Buddha until the day of his parinirvāṇa, during that interval, the Tathāgata was without doubt and without turning back;
his mind was without volitional activity, his mind was without wandering, and his mind was without...
The mind is not solid; the mind has no point of conjunction; the mind has no dispersion; the mind is not distracted; the mind does not shift; the mind does not wander;
the mind has nothing to protect; the mind is not stilled; the mind does not miss its timing; the mind is not deluded;
the mind does not seek principles; the mind is not obscured; the mind is not born; the mind is not joyful; the mind...

Without timidity; with a mind that does not dwell, a mind that does not go forth, a mind without conceptualization, a mind without expectation, a mind without seeking, a mind without extinction, a mind without observation, a mind without directing consciousness, a mind without a place of abiding, a mind without observing others; with eyes that see nothing and ears that hear nothing.
The nose, mouth, body, and mind are free from conceptualization; the mind does not rely on forms, nor are there sounds, fragrances, tastes, or tactile sensations.
The mind does not rely on dharmas; the mind has no place of attachment, nor does it have any aversion.

The mind does not abide within, nor does it abide without; the mind does not enter into dharmas, nor does the mind transcend wisdom; the mind does not contemplate the past, the mind does not contemplate the future, and the mind does not contemplate the present.
The mind of the Tathāgata is noble and sublime; his mind is pure and majestic.

His mind does not create the karma of either sin or merit; regarding all phenomena, his wisdom is without obstruction. Having universally manifested the purity of his own mind, he perceives no impurity in the minds of others.

That which is seen is also without an object of observation; if there is an object of observation, it is likewise free from deluded thought. Examining without negligence, one beholds that which is observed and seen without any further wandering; observing what is seen, one ultimately finds nothing to be seen.

That which the Tathāgata perceives is not seen with the fleshly eye, nor beheld with the divine eye, nor examined with the wisdom-eye, nor viewed with the Dharma-eye, nor observed with the Buddha-eye.

It is not appropriate to listen with the divine ear; it is not appropriate to observe the minds of others; it is not appropriate to recognize the affairs of past lives through distracted thoughts; it is not appropriate to perform transformations by relying on the bases of psychic power; and it is not appropriate to depend upon anything that exists.

With all outflows extinguished, they have no conjunction with any phenomena; they should be without obstruction regarding all phenomena, being without auspiciousness, without manifold karma, and forever without any activity.
The dwelling of that wisdom is as if originally non-existent, yet it fully knows the mental activities of all sentient beings.
The ten powers of action, the wisdom of the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise such.

Whether advancing or retreating, they are without fixed activity; having relinquished mind, intellect, and consciousness, they abide in the samādhi of the Tathāgata without departing from it. They universally perform all the works of the Buddhas' path, and regarding all dharmas, their wisdom is unimpeded and entirely free from attachment.
It is just as with Śāntamati!

When a Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, manifests an emanated image of a Tathāgata, that emanated Tathāgata possesses no mind, consciousness, body, speech, or mental activity. Yet, wherever it acts, the Truly Realized One manifests it so that it can perform Buddha-work according to the occasion; and this emanation is without conceptualization and without seeking thoughts.
Thus it is, Śāntamati! The mind of the Way is like this:
it is just like a transformation created by the Tathāgata, being equal and without any difference.

That which is transformed has no thoughts, no body, speech, or mind; yet through causes and conditions, its advances and retreats are seen with the eyes as performing the work of a Buddha, while nevertheless nothing exists therein—for that which is called "a transformation" performs no action at all.
All dharmas are like transformations; it is by understanding this that the Tathāgata attained supreme perfect enlightenment.

Having attained perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata’s wisdom-consciousness does not abide in the five aggregates, nor in the eighteen elements, nor in the twelve bases. It does not abide in the internal or external; there is neither good nor evil, neither the present world nor the world beyond, neither outflows nor the absence of outflows, and no weariness with the strife of afflictions. It does not abide in the unconditioned, nor in the conditioned or the uncountable; it has no activity regarding the three periods of past, future, and present, nor does it circulate back and forth. It does not abide in the conditioned where there is observation, nor does it abide in the unconditioned where there is contemplation.
His wisdom is likewise such that it abides nowhere at all.

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, dwells within the mental dispositions of all sentient beings, manifesting benevolent compassion and wisdom, remaining free from harm, and rescuing them from peril and distress.
Śāntamati, you should know that this is the secret essence of the Tathāgata; whatever he enters into, there is nothing of what he proclaims that does not reach everywhere.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
"The secret essentials of the Tathāgata are immeasurable; the secrets he proclaims cannot be fathomed.

When the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada spoke this "Chapter on the Secret Essentials of the Tathāgata," countless Buddha-worlds shook in six ways, and a great radiance illuminated the ten directions. One beheld the infinite Buddha-lands of the ten directions; the heavens rained down various flowers, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

Innumerable people all resolved their minds upon the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; incalculable bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and limitless people attained the patience of compliance with the Dharma (anulomika-dharma-kṣānti).

Twofold more incalculable were the bodhisattvas who attained the stage of being "born once more" (ekajātipratibaddha), their roots of virtue pure and refined; by these causes and conditions, in all the buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, each before the various Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, the multitudes of bodhisattvas within this Bhadrakalpa purified themselves in the Brahma-faring.
These bodhisattvas, making offerings of the Dharma, each scattered flowers as a tribute to serve and present them to the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada.

The flowers they scattered transformed into flower canopies; through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all these flower canopies came together before the Buddha, circumambulated the Buddha and the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada three times, and spread over the entire assembly.
Furthermore, that jeweled canopy remained suspended in mid-air directly above the Buddha, and from within the canopy issued forth such excellent and wondrous sounds as these:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"

The Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa have sent us here to make offerings to the Great Sage and to Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi; to present this Dharma-offering and to proclaim these secret essentials spoken by the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, which are all brought about by the Buddha’s majestic transformations.

At that time, when the entire assembly that had gathered heard this Dharma being preached, they were filled with joy and delight; all together they joined their palms in reverence and bowed their heads in prostration to Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi Māhārakṣa. Increasing their respect, they manifested various transformations and proclaimed these words:
"We, O World-Honored One!"

Having attained excellent benefit and secured boundless joy, they were able to behold the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada and encounter the hearing of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable, secret, and essential teachings.

If there are sentient beings who, having encountered this essential sūtra, believe in it with joy, they will draw near to the work of the Path; free from doubt and never wavering, they shall enter the Buddha’s instruction. One should regard them as non-retrogressive and destined to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is well said; it is truly as you have expressed."
He further addressed the Bodhisattva Silent Intent: "O Mahasattva!
The Tathagata’s meritorious achievements are most marvelous and true; he possesses the four fearlessnesses."
This sutra is that which the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada has praised; it is a swift exposition of the ultimate instruction.
Such are these true men, and such is the majesty of the noble Dharma and the wisdom of the Way of all Buddhas.

If one hears this Dharma and is neither terrified nor frightened, nor harbors any fear, but understands its meaning and its purpose; and if one further upholds it, is able to recite and study it, and explains it extensively for others, such a person will receive the prediction of enlightenment before long.
"You should contemplate in this way; you shall swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.

At that time, in the very center of that assembly’s gathering place, before the World-Honored One, the earth suddenly split open to a depth of six million eight hundred thousand yojanas. Water spontaneously gushed forth from it in droplets as large as carriage axles, rising into the void of space as high as the Brahma Heaven, and sprinkling throughout the trichiliocosm.
The Buddha told Śāntamati:
"Do you see these great drops of water being sprinkled upon the earth of the trichiliocosm from within the midst of space?"
He replied: "I have seen them,
O God among Gods!"
"Indeed, Great Sage!
Out of compassion, please tell us what these preliminary omens signify.
The Buddha told寂意 (Ji-yì):

“O Benevolent One, you should know this: just as these drops of water now emerge spontaneously from the earth—without the earth having any thought or intention, and without it being torn asunder—the various Dharma masters are likewise so. If they uphold the essential core of this sutra and abide by the aforementioned teachings to practice the Dharma, they shall all tear asunder the sixty-two views and the net of various false doubts. They will attain this inexhaustible wisdom of eloquence regarding the luminous Dharma, and these true sons of the Buddha will joyfully expound the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, universally gladdening their hearts.”
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
Those who know this sutra will be completely liberated from all evils and the hardships of the three miserable realms.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Among the assembly of bodhisattvas in this present Bhadrakalpa who are now purely cultivating the brahma-faring in the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, why is it that this Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi will serve as their hand-bearer, holding a vajra and attending them from behind when all these bodhisattvas later attain Buddhahood?"
The Buddha said: "Stop, Śāriputra!
"This is inconceivable.
When the devas and people of the world hear these words, they will likely be bewildered and perplexed, and may fail to believe in the conduct of the Bodhisattva.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there are practitioners who plant the roots of various virtues, you should believe in and rejoice in them; we shall all accept the Tathāgata’s command.
The Buddha said, “Do you see this Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi, the Māravijayin, standing in attendance behind the Buddha?”
He replied, “I have seen it.
The Buddha said:

"By the power of my supernormal faculties and through the fulfillment of my original vows, I shall always provide offerings to the assembly of bodhisattvas; and when they attain Buddhahood within this Bhadrakalpa, the Mārṣa Guhyaka Vajrapāṇi shall always attend upon them, just as he attends upon me."
Śāriputra, these Vajrapāṇi Guhyapatis shall always serve and protect all the bodhisattvas throughout the Bhadrakalpa.
This is due to the supernatural power of the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, which arises from their original vows of sovereign mastery made in past lives.
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra!

Even if all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were to come and become Buddhas, they would all require your service; and when they attain the Way of Buddhahood, you shall likewise hold the vajra to guard and attend them from behind as a manifestation of yourself.”
"Despite such transformations, this noble being’s virtue of supernormal power (ṛddhi) and his established holy majesty have never diminished. Śāriputra,
do you see Maitreya Bodhisattva, whom the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada now constantly attends from behind?"
He replied, “I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
"For this reason, having received the Buddha’s sacred command, I have never heard of such a thing since ancient times.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You have constantly attended Maitreya; you simply do not see him."
Furthermore, bodhisattvas coming from the Buddha-lands of other directions, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, saw the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada attending behind Maitreya Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, at that time, during the remaining portion of this Bhadrakalpa, Maitreya Bodhisattva and other bodhisattvas will manifest as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva assemblies; all shall follow behind them to attend upon these manifested beings, opening the way for and delivering sentient beings.

Because this true person has established such inconceivable majestic power through supernormal transformations, and is thus so lofty and magnificent, he is fully endowed with manifold virtues and the power of the six superknowledges, which are immeasurable.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, saying:

"Would you be so kind as to deign to proclaim how the Tathāgata practiced austerities with diligent effort, adorned the tree of enlightenment, subdued the hosts of Māra, and turned the wheel of Dharma to establish the ultimate truth?"
“O Benevolent One, please explain clearly the meaning of what you have clarified. Vajrapāṇi, the Guhyapada Mārṣa, said to Śāntamati:

“The merit and achievements of his virtue are immeasurable; even if one were to live for an eon praising his supreme virtue, one could not fully proclaim or discuss its meaning. Relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall briefly set forth its essentials.”
He continued: "Śāntamati!

The practices of a bodhisattva do not consist of cultivating ascetic hardships through a single method alone. A bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma is for the sake of those who follow external heterodox teachings; desiring to rescue them from peril and distress, he manifests these meanings according to what is appropriate for each, clearly proclaiming his majestic demeanor to whatever extent necessary, thereby transforming the assemblies of heterodox and evil followers."
He manifests as the most supreme, honored, and noble being, difficult to approach; his diligent practices and austerities are utterly beyond compare.
He displays the majestic deportment and etiquette of a bodhisattva, which none among those of external paths or heterodox practices can ever attain.
The Bodhisattva, dwelling therein, explains the immeasurable meanings within a single chapter or phrase; he may manifest in the zenith, or appear as the sun and moon revolving back and forth,
or manifest as a transcendent being (ṛṣi) with supernormal powers traveling through the air, or manifest as a member of the Confucian academy,
a national preceptor, or a lay devotee (gṛhapati), or manifest as a patriarch, a sage emperor, one of the Four Heavenly Kings, or Śakra Devānām Indra.
Whether as Brahmā or as a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King, he may manifest his own conduct as incomplete;
he may manifest his body lying upon thorns, or lying upon straw, or lying upon the earth;
he may manifest himself as being afraid or fearless regarding where he lies; he may manifest his place of rest, or manifest sitting and eating fruit.
He manifests wearing tattered robes, or lying upon a pool of foam, or appearing in ochre garments,
or appearing naked as he dwells and travels among others; or he appears eating and drinking like the filial son Śyāma,
or appearing to eat foul food, or appearing to eat beans and grains, or appearing to eat sesame and rice, or appearing to eat radishes, taro, or turnips.
They may feed on grain, or eat vegetables and tubers; they may eat thorns, or consume leaves, flowers, and fruits;
or they may appear to eat dates and other fruits. They may eat once a day, or twice a day, or appear to eat constantly;
or they may appear to eat once every seven days, or once every fifteen days, or once every month.
Sometimes they consume a single drop of ghee, or a single drop of oil, or a single drop of honey,
or a single drop of water, or a single drop of milk; sometimes they appear not to eat, or they appear to remain standing,
or they appear to remain seated.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
These and other practices, beyond measure and calculation, consisting of dignified deportment and ritual propriety, constitute the ascetic practices manifested by the Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva manifested these arduous practices for a full six years; not only did he perform a single form of deportment and ritual propriety, but he manifested various kinds of demonstrations in their entirety, further surpassing them all through his steadfast cultivation of diligence.
Furthermore, sentient beings do not perceive the various forms of the Tathāgata’s majestic deportment and ritual propriety, nor can they know the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas.

If there are sentient beings who are able to practice the Way, [the Buddha] transforms and delivers them according to their own conduct, movements, progressions, halts, majestic deportment, and ritual propriety.
If one beholds the majestic deportment and ritual decorum of a bodhisattva, one is then able to perceive the conduct of a bodhisattva as being free from deluded thoughts.

This constitutes the diligent practice of a bodhisattva; having fully brought sixty *koṭis* of people and three million devas and humans to spiritual maturity, they all enter the path of practice. At that time, the bodhisattva performs subtle and wondrous deeds.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s practice resides within his place of birth; while seated upon a high pavilion adorned with precious lattices, he manifests birth, yet remains free from all afflictions and calamities, forever attaining peace and security, and constantly abiding in samādhi. Nevertheless, he further manifests six years of ascetic practice and is seen again rising and departing.

At that time, the devas seek the joy of the Dharma; if their resolve is set upon the scriptures and they do not long for worldly things, dwelling in the presence of Bodhisattvas, having no other occupation but the proclamation of the Dharma—this is what constitutes a Bodhisattva.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmagotra, who delighted in the Mahāyāna and entered into great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

There was also a Dharma scripture titled "Entering the Inconceivable Dharma Gate," also known as "Universal Gathering," which subdues all heterodoxies and all māras, enters the wisdom of suffering and difficulty, and forever attains great peace.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

“After the Bodhisattva had completed six years of diligent practice, he rose from his seat with the same majestic deportment of exertion as he had manifested. He proceeded to the banks of the secluded Nairañjanā River; following the worldly custom, he reached the river’s edge in that secluded place, washed his body for purification, crossed the river, and went to another spot where he stood alone.”

There was a Māgadhī woman named Supraticchannā who milked a thousand cows; she passed the milk from one vessel to another until she obtained the final thick cream, which she used to make a milk porridge that leaped up from the cauldron to a height of several tens of feet.
The woman wondered at the reason for this.
A Brahmin divined it, saying, "Only one who is about to attain Buddhahood should consume this.

At that time, the woman took the food and went to where the Bodhisattva was, as did sixty thousand devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, each bringing extraordinary and delicious delicacies to the Bodhisattva’s presence, and each addressed him, saying:
"May you deign to show compassion and accept this offering.

At that time, the Bodhisattva accepted the milk-gruel from the maiden Sujātā and consumed it; he also took the food of all sixty thousand wives of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, manifesting that he ate them all as well.
Each of those who came to offer alms saw only themselves receiving the food and did not see others; nor were they aware of one another.
At that time, each person thought to themselves:
"The Bodhisattva is thinking only of me and taking my offering; he shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become a most perfectly awakened Buddha."
Through this joy, he resolved upon the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-citta) and immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika-bhūmi).
This is what is meant by "accepting the offering of food": for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifested six years of arduous ascetic practice.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada said to Śāntamati:
"This is how a bodhisattva partakes of offerings according to worldly custom, so that his physical strength becomes fully restored and harmonious."
As he was proceeding toward the foot of the tree, a terrestrial deity named the Son of Heaven Good Ground (Sudhara) addressed the various sons of heaven and other earth-dwelling deities, saying:
"Hold the earth steady and do not let it tremble; sever all cravings and fetters of attachment, for the Bodhisattva has already arrived beneath the King of Trees."

He purified that ground and made successive offerings; the three thousandfold world system became spontaneously pure, as flowers were scattered, incense burned, and fragrant water sprinkled upon the earth. The Kāruṇika-devas and the spirits holding flowers descended from their celestial palaces and remained in mid-air; seeing the Bodhisattva, they joyfully rained down various kinds of flowers.

The Four Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues, went to the four quarters and, using canopies of exquisite purple-gold netting, completely covered the three thousandfold world-systems as an offering to the Buddha.
Before Śakra, Lord of Devas, and Brahmā, there were great supernormal powers that adorned them according to their wishes and extolled the trichiliocosm.
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Yāma Heaven each displayed canopies of purple-golden sandalwood, while lapis lazuli canopies covered the Buddha-fields of the trichiliocosm as an offering.

In the Tuṣita Heaven, they adorned and offered pavilions decorated with jewels to the majestic and magnificent Tathāgata; the various heavenly kings were exquisitely beautiful like purple-polished gold, their hearts filled with great joy as they made offerings to the Tathāgata by raining down fine pearls.

The Celestial King Śubhavikrāmin, with a white jade and silver canopy shimmering with the brilliance of bright moon pearls, emanated a harmonious sound that spread throughout the ten directions, causing all within the trichiliocosm to rejoice.
Even the various heavens possess pure and exquisite jewels, their majestic spiritual power immeasurable, stainless, and brilliantly radiant.
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven fashioned a single canopy composed of many jewels, universally offering service to the Buddha.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas each manifested adornments through their supernormal powers and noble might, cultivating and purifying the entire realm of desire.
The Malla said to Śāntamati:
"At that time, there was a Great Brahmā King named Īśvaraprabhāva, who was the most honored and immeasurable sovereign over the trichiliocosm."
As that Bodhisattva proceeded to behold the Bodhi tree, the Heavenly King addressed the Brahmā gods, saying:

"Virtuous ones, you should know that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has cultivated correct practice under past Buddhas and planted the roots of all virtues. He has prostrated and taken refuge in countless Buddhas; his great vows are unshakable, his resolve is firm, and his will is free from weariness. He has brought forth all Bodhisattva practices and has reverently cultivated the various perfections (pāramitās) to reach the infinite. In all these stages, he has attained mastery."

Their resolve and nature are universally harmonious and well-cultivated in purity; they penetrate the very root of all sentient beings, master all the secret essentials of the Tathāgatas, and completely transcend all demonic activities.

The foundation of these manifold virtues does not rely upon others; for the sake of all Tathāgatas, he skillfully cultivates and establishes the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Way. Acting as a great guide to rescue and deliver sentient beings, he proclaims the scriptures so that all beings may unite in courageous vigor to extricate themselves from the realm of Māra, forever free from demonic karma and clearly understanding the Dharma of the Path.
Acting as a Great Physician-King to heal the illnesses of sentient beings, wearing the Crown of Liberation as a Great Dharma King, he manifests the light of wisdom as an Infinite Holy Emperor.

Unrestrained by the eight worldly concerns, he is like a lotus flower unsullied by dust or water; upholding all dharmas without ever neglecting them, his wisdom is as boundless as the rivers and seas, and as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
They cleanse their minds as one washes away grime with water; they never become conceited, but always practice humility.
Like a bright moon-jewel that dispels darkness and all turbidity, they attain mastery over all phenomena.
Having accumulated the roots of all virtues, he was like Brahmā, the foremost in the heavens.

He proceeded to the foot of the tree and subdued the hosts of Māras; he attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and became the Most Perfectly Awakened One. He was fully endowed with the ten powers of the Buddhas, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas. He turned the great wheel of Dharma, roared the lion’s roar, and filled all things, moistening them with the gift of the Dharma.

Desiring to purify the path-eye of all sentient beings and to encompass all dharmas, they cast aside the ninety-six kinds of external heterodox practices; they fulfill their original vows and delight in beholding the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions; through the majestic virtue of the Great Sage, they attain sovereign mastery, and by means of the foremost perfections, they provide infinite salvation.
"You virtuous ones, you should always be humble and reverent toward all Bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Īśvara spoke these verses before the gods:
"Purified in right conduct, Resolute in the sublime Dharma, Compassionate toward the world,"
Grief extends even to the devas.
Now the Great Sage departs, proceeding beneath the Bodhi tree;
there he shall subdue Māra and his retinue, attain perfect enlightenment, and achieve all-knowledge.
Having fully perfected all delights and the deeds of supreme perfect enlightenment,
he then turns the wheel of the True Dharma.
With inexhaustible great wisdom and the roar of a great lion, he brings joy to the hearts of all sentient beings.
Because of its purity, he attained the sublime Dharma-eye; the Teacher proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Having subdued and cast down all Māras and extinguished the heterodox teachings of outsiders, he fully realized his original vows from past lives.
Possessing the Dharmakāya of perfect enlightenment, he never grew weary of what he beheld.
At that time, the Guide went to the place where the Buddha was; "Excellent!
they all said in unison, "We shall adorn the lands of the three thousandfold world-system well;
therefore, let us decorate it throughout the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm."
The adornment is thus.
Excellent, Brahmā! Your mind is harmonious and gentle; this trichiliocosm is entirely adorned and purified.
Thus, in this realm of desire, with its purity and excellence, the offerings seen there surpass even those [of the former].
With famous fragrant aloeswood, various flowers of auspicious meaning, the radiance of these jewels,
and the sounding of manifold musical instruments, there is no one who beholds them who does not rejoice.
And the Brahmā King, throughout the entire trichiliocosm— from the realm of Brahmā down to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—
each Brahmā heaven was level, upright, and pure, suspended in mid-air;
the divine Honored One, most venerable among the venerable.
There is a God among Gods, pure and further purified.
For sixty billion years, the various devas have gathered to adorn the Vajra Site for the sake of the Bodhisattva.
They rained down offerings— various fragrant waters used to sprinkle the ground—
and prepared various seats with exquisite jeweled couches, adorned and purified,
as he sat beneath the Buddha-tree.
"Our Teacher, praised by all, wherever he dwells, causes that place to be purified.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada said to the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
"When the Bodhisattva went and sat beneath the tree, the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel appeared on the soles of his feet, from which light radiated forth."

That light shone everywhere throughout this Buddha-land, reaching every corner without exception; the suffering and affliction of all beings in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and among all people were brought to rest.

Furthermore, a great light shone upon the Kālasūtra Hell. At that time, the Kālasūtra Hell was bathed in the light of the World-Honored One; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, the multitudes gathered like clouds.
Then all the devas spoke these verses:
“The light of purple-golden hue Emerges from between the brows of the Deva.”
Shining upon our bodies, it causes our hearts to rejoice.
Having encountered the Buddhas of the past, we have beheld these auspicious omens;
there is no doubt that the Great Hero will appear in the world, for the Buddha is surely about to manifest in this realm.
Excellent are the variously adorned garlands, scented flowers, and fragrant ointments;
fashioned from gold, purple, and bright pearls, they hold robes in their right hands,
play exquisite music, and receive variegated banners and canopies.
They also raised their great banners as an offering to the World-Honored One.
Those within the various hells were universally purified by receiving his light;
thus they made offerings to the Buddha and served the Great Sage.

At that time, Kṛṣṇakarṇī, the king of the Great Black-Ear Hell, together with his inner court and the entire assembled multitude, each holding flowers, incense, blended perfumes, fragrant oils, robes, banners, parasols, streamers, and musical instruments, emerged from his palace and manifested a precious cloud in the sky above. They rained down bright moon pearls, famous incense, *mukhaka* wood, sandalwood, various flowers, and pearls. Relying on the supernatural transformations of the great deity Nāga, they proceeded to where the Bodhisattva was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and together with their retinue, each offered the implements they held as worship, performing music for the Bodhisattva.
With these verses, he praised the World-Honored One:
"Just like a precious ground, Adorned with various and abundant wonders,
The Buddha-tree flourishes with flowers and fruit, As he sits upon his site of enlightenment."
Like a river that no longer flows, or as the moon abiding in the void,
having attained Buddhahood for the sake of all, you have subdued the hosts of Māra.
O World-Honored One, the radiance of the Benefactor of the Multitudes is like the intense brilliance of the sun.
If one were to weigh the six supernormal powers, they would be like the harmonious sounds proclaimed by the king of bees;
he manifests the light of wisdom like the *ūrṇā* on the brow of Brahmā.
Today the Benefactor of the Multitudes appears, filling the infinite treasuries.
The light of the sun, moon, jewels, and fire, And the radiance of Śakra, Brahmā, and the gods—
As soon as the Light of the Capable One appeared, They were all eclipsed by its brilliance.
When the light manifested in my palace, I knew that a Buddha had arisen in the world.
Manifesting auspicious omens and filled with joy, they knew that a Buddha had now appeared.
Having seen and heard of Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni,
and Kāśyapa approaching the tree of enlightenment, they have just now heard his voice and made offerings to him.
Beholding one without equal, whose auspicious signs are identical to those [of the past], my heart gives rise to joy and gladness; surely a Buddha must now appear.
O World-Honored One, it is my great benefit to have obtained the opportunity to make extensive offerings to the Buddha.
With four matters, one serves the Light of the World, Offering faith, practice, and reverence.
The merit and blessings thus accumulated Are fully offered to the Eye of Wisdom;
This radiance of the world’s light Attains Buddhahood, peerless and beyond compare.

At that time, the Bodhisattva went to the realm where the Dragon King Kāliṅga resided. Upon seeing the Buddha, the Dragon King was filled with joy in his heart; he emerged from his abode, approached the Tree of Enlightenment, and stood to the Buddha’s right.

Furthermore, there was a man named Kṣema who stood at a distance watching the Buddha; seeking fine grass, he held it in his hand and observed the Bodhisattva approaching the tree of enlightenment. The devas proclaimed words that were gentle, subtle, and exquisite, extolling the virtuous sound of his majesty—tranquil, sublime, pleasing, and unsurpassed—and they circled him as he proceeded forward.
The fragrance of those grasses was exquisite, and a fragrant breeze spread abroad; they were magnificent, lustrous, fine, and immeasurable, like celestial robes.

Taking such excellent grasses at the proper time, he went to where the Bodhisattva was and offered them to him. He prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and with a mind of benevolence and harmony, attained the stage of non-retrogression and resolved upon the inconceivable, unsurpassed, and truly correct path.
He thought to himself:
"I must not perform such improper actions.
When one observes things in this way, nothing auspicious will come."
"Furthermore, when Kṣemaṅkara bestows upon the Bodhisattva the grass at the proper time, he shall resolve his mind toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Why is this? It is due to the power of his original vow."
Śāntamati, you should know that this was the original vow made by Śrīgupta in his past lives.
Why is this? Śāntamati Bodhisattva, I recall and remember it thus: [it was so].

In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, ninety-one kalpas prior, the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, World-Honored One.
During the time of that Buddha, there were a thousand bhikṣus who purely cultivated the brahma-faring.

At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed upon these thousand bhikṣus the prediction that, within this Bhadrakalpa, they would attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become most perfectly awakened Buddhas.
At that time, there was an elder in the assembly named Zhìyǒu (Vīrya) who, upon hearing that the Bodhisattva had been granted the prediction of enlightenment, thought to himself:

"It would not be improper for me to become a Tathāgata and attain supreme perfect enlightenment during this Bhadrakalpa; in that world, I shall offer excellent grass and at that time spread it as a most wonderful, pure, harmonious, and serene lion throne, and by means of this, I shall resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
"Śāntamati! If you wish to know who the householder Chih-yi was at that time, it is none other than the present Kṣemaṅkara.
For this reason, you should form this contemplation: act in accordance with his original vow to bring about the practice of peace and auspiciousness."

Because he offered excellent grass at that opportune moment, by which he was subsequently named, when he later attained Buddhahood, he was called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaviśuddhasiṃha.

At that time, the Bodhisattva took the excellent grass and spread it beneath the Bodhi tree; furthermore, from the tree deity up to ten thousand celestial maidens in the void, each holding fine celestial flowers in the folds of their robes, took fragrant flowers, various incenses, and perfumed oils to go forth and welcome the Bodhisattva. They prostrated themselves in salutation and each offered the Bodhisattva various flowers, incense, banners, and canopies.
He praised him with these words:
“Fearless and without dread, unhesitant and free from anxiety;
established in that which is difficult to encounter, unstained and devoid of delusion or evil.”
Free from the guilt of calamity, without stinginess, envy, or folly,
liberated through the renunciation of desire— may I bow my head to the Great Sage.
Those who were transformed by the Vinaya and thereby attained deliverance, including those who were coarse, wild, and of evil conduct.
A virtuous and noble sage for the world, he heals the ailments of all suffering.
Seeing those who are without protection and have no lamp-light to which to turn for refuge,
the Buddha has now arisen in the world to deliver and liberate beings throughout the three periods of time.
The great assemblies of devas each harbored hearts of leaping joy;
they all rained down flowers everywhere, of many different kinds.
The offerings fashioned by the devas included garments and exquisite fabrics.
When he shall attain the Way of the Buddha, may all give rise to a heart of joy.
Sitting beneath the King of Trees, his mind harbors no fear;
with the flavor of the nectar of immortality, he shatters the net of worldly toil.
Awakening to the state of profound stillness, he attains the most honored path of Buddhahood;
like all Buddhas of the past, he clearly understands the supreme Dharma.
Regarding the essentials of his practice, he has cultivated them for incalculable eons.
Through the accumulation of ascetic practices, you sought to deliver all sentient beings.
Your ancient vow has now been fulfilled; this is precisely the time.
Having attained the supreme path of Buddhahood, please spread forth your compassion.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"The Buddha took the grass at the appropriate time and went to the Tree of Enlightenment; there he spread this fine grass beneath the tree, prostrated himself in worship, and circumambulated it seven times to the right."

Just as he had finished laying out the seats, eighty-four thousand sons of gods beheld the Bodhisattva arranging them; their hearts filled with joy, they immediately prepared eighty-four thousand lion thrones.

The seat was exceedingly subtle and wondrous, diverse and extraordinary; it was extremely high, vast, and long, composed of many jewels. It had railings made of rare treasures, with canopies erected all around, adorned with purple gold and hung with strings of pearls interspersed therein. Moon-bright gems and nocturnal luminaries were set out in alternating patterns, and exquisite jewels were used to fashion bells that hung down and chimed most resonantly; their sound was harmonious and elegant, blending in infinite melodies.
Countless celestial robes were spread upon them.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva transformed his own body so that it pervaded all eighty-four thousand lion thrones.
These sons of gods did not see one another, nor were they aware of each other’s presence; yet, each son of a god thought to himself:
"The Bodhisattva shall sit alone upon my lion throne and attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
With such a joyful heart, they will reach the stage of non-retrogression, and thereafter all shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
The Vajrapāṇi Malla said to Śāntamati: "At that time, the Bodhisattva established his majestic spiritual power so that Māra would know it.

Accompanied by incalculable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of spirits and deities, he set forth surrounded by his retinue. All were clad in armor and displayed great supernormal powers, exerting supreme force. Leading an army of ghosts for three hundred and thirty-six thousand li, their appearances were each different and their origins varied; they each manifested countless formidable and difficult-to-withstand forms. Their weapons were strictly arrayed, their leaders were each distinct, and their aspirations were each separate. Their dietary habits, conduct, and principles differed; their voices were each distinct and their speech and accents varied. They all approached the Bodhisattva."

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, accompanied by a vast and most terrifying retinue, acted with great injustice, contrary to benevolence and righteousness. He incited rebellious acts that were unspeakable and unheard of, having no regard for the Way or its virtue. Each brandishing weapons, they cried out and shouted at the top of their lungs; the sound they raised shook the three realms. Should any ordinary person who had not yet transcended desire hear this sound, their blood would immediately boil and gush from their faces, or they would die of terror.

At that time, the Bodhisattva was neither afraid nor hindered by these difficulties; instead, the Bodhisattva gave rise to great compassion, and the terrifying sounds naturally vanished, their destination unknown.
Why is this? It is because he desires to bring peace to sentient beings so that they are not disturbed and are free from harm and affliction.

When the Bodhisattva has attained and upholds the pure mind of the Way and its skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), even upon hearing these sounds, he realizes they are fundamentally empty and fundamentally without sound; thus, his hair does not stand on end.

Seeing the hosts of Māra approaching, his countenance became even more radiant and majestic; he manifested great brilliance and proclaimed the four deeds with a mind free from fear. Employing sixteen matters to arouse his own eloquence and wisdom, he subdued the great calamities according to their inclinations and addressed Māra, saying: "Cease, Pāpīyan!"

Why do you harbor poisonous anger for the sake of undertaking such useless matters as these displays of form, thereby endangering yourself and remaining restless throughout the long night? Why is this so?

Pāpīyān! Today you have resolved to destroy the Bodhisattva; yet the Bodhisattva possesses vast benevolence and great valor, and with inexhaustible great compassion and boundless loving-kindness, he subdues you, the evil and rebellious one who seeks to disturb the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva is fundamentally pure, having eliminated the dust of defilement, weakness, obstruction, and evil; today, Pāpīyān has instead become a Bodhisattva.

He wishes to surpass the light of the sun and moon with the glow of a firefly, yet the Bodhisattva has already transcended the bottomless abyss and proclaims the great, gentle, profound, and wondrous flavor of the nectar of the True Awakening.
Just as small insects and beasts wish to frighten a lion, so now does Māra seek to topple the Great Tree of Infinite Excellence in order to break it and uproot its very foundation.

It is like attempting to compare the water in a cow’s footprint to the great ocean; instead of achieving anything, he only fosters a city of long-standing enmity and gives rise to a mind of malevolent hostility.

Today, the King of Māra shall be delivered from his enmity; though he may raise perverse calamities through speech and discourse, we shall eliminate such delusions by taking the evil spirits as our peers. We shall cause those who take us as companions on the Path to reach a state of equality without distinction, casting aside the King of Unrighteousness and returning to the Noble Path—rigorous, pure, subtle, and wondrous. We shall give birth to supreme wisdom and the flavor of benevolence and righteousness, abandoning all crookedness and depravity to make the mind simple and sincere.
Today, Pāpīyān, you should reflect upon this: having traversed the vast wilderness and reached the ultimate end of the source of birth and death, you instead gallop back into the great ocean.

One should board the great vessel to cross the current of beginning and end. Now that you have encountered this training, even if you meet with the conflagration at the end of an eon and the calamities that burn trees and various medicinal herbs, do not let the Great Vajra Art be destroyed. You shall surely return to the Great Way and thereafter attain Buddhahood, delivering and liberating all sentient beings and persons throughout the ten directions.
The Mārṣa Guhyapāda said to Śāntamati:
"At that time, the devas praised and extolled the Buddha’s virtues, which were so majestic and peerless.
When Māra Pāpīyas heard these sixteen matters in praise of the Buddha—things he had long cherished and admired—his mind became intent upon the Great Way."
Then the Malla Guhyapāda said to the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
"The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

'My meritorious deeds have been universally manifest for incalculable kalpas; through the accumulation of merit and virtue over countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas, all of these are the fundamental dharmas of my past lives, generation after generation.'"

In every birth, he disciplines himself and takes pity on the suffering of sentient beings within the three realms; therefore, he performs actions that are gentle, upright, and luminous, leading to pure karma.
Who would dare to destroy this, which is uniquely witnessed and certified?

At that time, the Bodhisattva drew forth his purple-gold hand from within his kāṣāya robe and stroked his entire body; without abandoning his great compassion, his nature was harmonious and balanced as he desired to deliver all sentient beings. Always acting with calm and composure, he raised his right hand toward the worlds of the ten directions.
As soon as he saw himself arrive at the ground, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a spontaneous sound arose, its resonance penetrating throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.

When Māra Pāpīyān heard this sound, and his demonic retinue in the void likewise heard this resonance, they all reproached themselves together, becoming hungry for the precepts and delighting in diligent cultivation.

Furthermore, at that time, the Great Sage bestowed fearlessness upon them and took pity on sentient beings; accordingly, eighty *koṭis* of Māras and spirits bowed toward the Bodhisattva, falling prostrate to the ground of their own accord and taking refuge in him with all their hearts, seeking only his protection. Those among the assembly who were followers of Māra were shattered and fled away, naturally bewildered and not knowing where to go.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva radiated a great light, out of compassion for them all, causing each to be free from fear and to return to their celestial palaces.

By means of this, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifested the subduing of the Māra king and his retinue; eighty billion *koṭis* of spirits and deities all resolved upon the unsurpassed, true, and right path. Ninety-two billion people established themselves in non-retrogression with hearts of benevolence and harmony, while eighty-four thousand sons of gods, having planted roots of virtue in past lives, attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Vajrapāṇi Mārṣa said to Śāntamati:

"By means of such manifestations, the multitudes of Māras were subdued; gods and worldlings beyond measure received transformation and attained salvation, while those gods and humans pursued the Māra Pāpīyān."

If people see the conduct of a bodhisattva—whether seeing him seated upon a pure jewel lotus lion-throne, or on the ground, or in the void upon a lion-seat, or again seeing him beneath a peepal tree (*pāṭali*), or seeing him beneath the Day-and-Night Tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or seeing him beneath various jewel trees, or universally seeing him beneath the seven-fathom Buddha-trees of all people;
or if gods see him seated beneath a Buddha-tree on a lion-seat half a fathom high, or seven fathoms high, or ten *li*, or twenty *li*, or forty *li*;
or if gods and humans all see him seated beneath a Buddha-tree eighty-four thousand *yojana*s high, or again see him presently seated on a lion-throne forty-two thousand *yojana*s high.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!

The spheres of the bodhisattvas are incalculable and their limits difficult to fathom; by means of this, the assembly of bodhisattvas returns to that which is extraordinary at the site of enlightenment.
The practices performed by Bodhisattvas consist of eight hundred thousand types of joyful deeds.

The manifestations of Bodhisattvas vary, as they each transform beings according to their respective natures, inspiring them toward the aspiration of the noble ones so that they may achieve supreme perfect enlightenment and reach all-knowledge. In accordance with the sounds and voices of the times, they proclaim the Dharma and provide the offerings that should be revered.
Whatever praises the Bodhisattva offers there through various modes are all the practices he performed in his past lives.
All those whom the Bodhisattva has inspired, delighted, and instructed in the meaning of the Dharma come to praise him and make offerings to him.

Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva’s mind remains unattached; free from the obstacles of Māra and able to abandon all harms, they universally attain the path and Dharma of all Buddhas. In the mere instant of a single thought-moment, through the equal practice of wisdom, they shall fully know this and reach the Buddha-way as the Most Perfectly Awakened One.

Having attained all-knowledge and reached supreme perfect enlightenment, they dwell throughout all worlds in the ten directions, where they behold immeasurable and infinite Tathāgatas; placing their right palms in [the Buddhas'] hands, they inquire exhaustively about the Buddha-way and consult regarding the source of eternal peace and the Way and its Virtue.

The wisdom of the Way is subtle and wondrous, free from weariness or aversion; in expounding the ultimate wisdom of the Way, one attains mastery. Proclaiming equality, one enters into non-perverse karma and distinguishes and demonstrates for the multitude countless practices. Discerning and analyzing the Three Jewels so they shall not be severed, one elaborates upon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and attains mastery over all dharmas, entering into the inexhaustible karma of noble power.
If there are sentient beings whose faculties are mature, they are all able to fully comprehend the conduct of this bodhisattva;
if their faculties are distracted, they do not know where he is headed.

As soon as the bodhisattva had perfected the path and dharma of a Tathāgata, for seven days and nights he remained entirely absorbed in the joy of the Dharma, gazing at the Bodhi tree without weariness, his eyes never blinking.

Hundreds of thousands of billions of devas came to offer praise and make offerings; they presented hundreds of thousands of jade trays laden with sweet delicacies. All of them resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of enlightenment, beholding the majestic deportment and ritual etiquette of the Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had already attained the Buddha-way, the Four Heavenly Kings each went to present their alms bowls to the Tathāgata.

In such a land, within each of the four directions of a trichiliocosm—the central world-system—there are ten billion great thousandfold world-systems; in each of these, the four great heavenly kings of the four directions, numbering forty billion in total, all went individually with their alms bowls to offer them to the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata accepted them all.
The Buddha manifested his majestic spiritual power, causing the various heavenly kings not to see one another;
each thought to himself, "The Buddha shall accept my bowl for the purpose of eating.
Because of this joy, their minds became serene, and they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, most true path of enlightenment, reaching the stage of non-retrogression.
When the Buddha had attained the Way, he wished to deliver the five hundred merchants, Trapusa and Bhallika.
He manifested a place where their carriage and horses could rest; however, the merchant party and the others were not at ease and wondered at the reason for this.
A deity in the void proclaimed:
"The Buddha has appeared in the world; you should go to make offerings.
Hearing this, they were filled with joy, and each offered honey-cakes and clarified butter.
An assembly of eighty-four thousand devaputras also presented offerings of food.
The Tathāgata accepted them; for in a previous life, he had established this supreme vow:
"When the Tathāgata attains enlightenment, we shall be the very first to present him with offerings of food."
Wishing to fulfill their original vows, they did not see one another and were unaware of each other's whereabouts.
Each thought to themselves:
"I alone am making offerings to the Buddha; there is no one else who has made an offering."

"By means of this, one joyfully anticipates attaining the stage of non-retrogression; thereafter, one shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path to become a Most Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha) and deliver the multitude from their perils and distress."
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eleven;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twelve.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Third Assembly of the Guhyapāda Vajrapāṇi, Part Five.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapāda addressed Śāntamati, saying:
"The Bodhisattva proceeded to the Tree of Enlightenment and attained the Way of the Buddha."

When the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, had not yet turned the Wheel of Dharma, his guidance and instruction of sentient beings was already so sublime that those he transformed were immeasurable—far exceeding the number of beings saved when he first resolved to practice the Way or while sitting beneath the Bodhi tree; how could this be disparaged?
Therefore, know this: one should cultivate this contemplation.
If there is a bodhisattva seated upon the Dharma-throne, they will swiftly approach the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and the number of sentient beings they deliver will increase manifold.

Just as he had attained the Way of the Buddha, the Brahma King Miaoshi, surrounded by a retinue of sixty-eight trillion *ya* and hundreds of thousands of followers, went to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood to one side before the Buddha, exhorting the World-Honored One:
"Please, out of great compassion, turn the Wheel of Dharma and proclaim the transformation of the Way."
"There are many sentient beings who ought to be vessels for the Dharma; having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, they would be able to understand, receive, and practice it. Thus, Śāntamati!

The Brahma King Subhakṛtsna exhorted and assisted the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma, remaining thus earnestly before the Buddha because he had attained his vision of the World-Honored One through his original vows made in past lives.
One celestial king, named Dhṛtarāṣṭra—translated into Chinese as Yǒnghù (Valiant Protector)—together with his sons, courageously brought forth this original vow:
"I shall universally exhort all the Tathāgatas of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa to turn the wheel of Dharma."
"If you wish to know whether it was solely the Brahmā King Miàoshì who exhorted and assisted the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, do not hold such a view. Why is this? Because..."
Together with a retinue of one billion Brahmās, one billion Śakras, and ten trillion bodhisattvas, they exhorted and assisted the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is now the right time; you should turn the wheel of Dharma."

The Brahma King Subhakṛtsna went to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, the grove where the ṛṣis roam, and there he arranged a lion throne three thousand two hundred and eighty li high, exquisitely adorned with various kinds of exquisite ornaments and arrayed with a multitude of rare jewels.

As soon as the Brahma King Wondrous Ritual had laid out the lion throne for the Tathāgata, ten billion Brahmās, ten billion Śakras, and ten trillion koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas likewise laid out lion thrones for the World-Honored One, all equal in height and breadth.
Each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata shall sit upon my lion throne and turn the wheel of Dharma.
Then the Mārṣa Guhyapāda addressed Śāntamati, saying:
At that time, the Tathāgata went to the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, the haunt of seers, and sat upon the lion throne.
Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and all the bodhisattvas each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata sits alone upon my lion throne."
Once the Tathāgata had sat cross-legged upon the lion throne, at that moment the infinite Buddha-lands of the ten directions shook in six ways.

Then, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi of the Boundless Realm; immediately, this trichiliocosm became entirely level and even, like the palm of a hand. Within this trichiliocosm, those in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, as well as those in the heavens and among humans, all attained universal peace and security.

All sentient beings are free from lust, anger, and delusion; having eliminated the maladies of the three poisons, they are pure and stainless, regarding one another with compassion as if they were father and son, or mother and daughter.
Countless bodhisattvas from the infinite Buddha-worlds of the ten directions came to listen to the Buddha’s preaching of the sutra.

Great deities of the trichiliocosm—including limitless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all went to where the Buddha was, desiring to hear the Dharma of the sutra.

All those who had gathered filled this trichiliocosm to its utmost extent; there was not even a space as small as a hair’s breadth that was not occupied. With one mind, they were all parched with a thirst for the Dharma, desiring to bow their heads in prostration to inquire about and receive the Great Way.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the great assembly had all gathered like clouds to request the turning of the wheel of Dharma, so that he might proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of the śramaṇas, the heterodox brahmins, the devas, Māra, the Brahmā kings above, and all worldly beings.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!

At that time, when the Tathāgata had just turned the wheel of Dharma, he acted according to what was appropriate for the occasion, causing each sentient being to attain understanding according to their own mind.

Because they had gathered like clouds, he proclaimed for each of them the practices they had cultivated in past lives, causing their minds to open and reach realization so that they might all follow the practice of the Dharma.
As soon as the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, had spoken this Dharma, he further analyzed it for them, saying:
"Kauṇḍinya, you wish to know that the eye is entirely impermanent; by understanding the impermanence of the eye, one follows the discipline of karma.
To reckon the eye as permanent and take no pleasure in its impermanence, yet to hear that the eye is impermanent and that the eye is suffering and painful."
To calculate the eye as "self" is not to be fond of the bodiless state where there is no self at all;
by hearing that the eye has no self, one then follows the disciplinary teachings to understand their resonance.

The eye is like a magical illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water; it is like a dream upon awakening, or like a form and its shadow, or an echo in the mountains. Following these disciplinary teachings, one practices the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of dharmas; thus, the eye is without activity, tranquil, and utterly still.
Hearing that the eye is tranquil and silent, one understands that the eye arises from conditions;
through understanding dependent origination, one sees that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise all subject to impermanence.
By hearing of impermanence, one understands that the mind is suffering; by beholding the absence of self, one becomes tranquil, detached, and realizes emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Because of failing to penetrate this, one arises from causes and conditions as the five aggregates, which are impermanent; thus, one reckons that the aggregates exist, failing to realize that there are no aggregates.
Although it is taught that all elements ultimately revert to impermanence, by hearing this teaching on the impermanence of all elements, the mind remains unattached.
Having heard the teaching that the five aggregates are impermanent, the mind understands them entirely as empty.
There are various sense bases (*āyatana*); yet, not understanding the meaning of the impermanence of these sense bases, one hears that the sense bases ultimately revert to impermanence.
It is the same for the five aggregates (*skandha*), the various sense bases, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

They hear of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
Having heard of these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they understand impermanence and emptiness.
If one hears of tranquility, they proclaim the Dharma in accordance with the Vinaya teachings.

If one hears of what is to be contemplated, they may be a śrāvaka who does not delight in the pratyekabuddha path, or they may delight in hearing of the pratyekabuddha path while having no aspiration for the śrāvaka path; or they may yearn for the two vehicles and not speak of the Mahāyāna.
"If he proclaims the Mahāyāna, they hear its meaning and purpose, yet do not find pleasure in the terminology of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Thus it is, Śāntamati!
The Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma according to what is pleasing and delightful to the minds of sentient beings, so that each may obtain their due.
The Tathāgata preaches for the sake of sentient beings by means of this, turning the wheel of Dharma.

At that time, the elder Śāriputra contemplated the path, its principles, and the spheres of entry for a hundred thousand years, yet he could not fathom or know their limits; how much less so for other sentient beings, who are bottomless?

When the Buddha spoke thus concerning this bodhisattva’s ascetic practices, his adornment of the tree of enlightenment, his subduing of the hosts of Māra, and his turning of the wheel of Dharma, eighty-four thousand people all resolved their minds upon supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, O Great Sage!

Regarding the secret essentials of the Tathāgata that I have just proclaimed, have I perhaps failed to convey them correctly, or have I slandered the Tathāgata by not being in accord with the Dharma?"

The secret essentials of the Tathāgata are profoundly mysterious, vast, and boundless; they cannot be believed by anyone in the world. Although those of inferior capacity may speak of these secret essentials of the Tathāgata, they should inwardly reflect: "It is the Tathāgata’s supreme wisdom that has entered my body; it is not through my own power or my own saintly might."
The Buddha said:
"It is so. It is as Guhyapada has spoken."
In all places reached by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the Path, there are none who do not receive peace and security.

Whenever the disciples of the Buddha propagate the scriptures, they do so entirely by relying on the majestic spiritual power and sacred intent of the Tathāgata; thus, they enter the body of the Tathāgata’s dharma of emptiness, and there is nothing of the profound and wondrous wisdom of the Path that they do not fully comprehend.

Why is this? It is because there has never been anyone who could cause sentient beings to respectfully uphold and establish the noble intent of the Tathāgata, proclaiming the meaning of compliant harmony.
You have examined the true reality and inherited the wisdom of the Tathāgata to attain fearlessness; the "true reality" spoken of when you now expound this Dharma refers precisely to this teaching.

Why is this? It is because what is called the Right Truth is that which the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have universally proclaimed throughout the world, such that there are none who do not sincerely delight in it; it is the practice of the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way.
If one were to proclaim this essential sūtra in accordance with the Dharma without contravening it, all shall attain Buddhahood.
As for those who, upon hearing this sūtra of the Tathāgata’s secret and essential dharma, believe in and delight in it—they too belong to this same category.
All in the world believe in and revere them.
Even if someone were to carry Mount Sumeru upon their head or shoulders while in mid-air, such a thing would be possible.

A person of no virtue cannot endure hearing this sutra; having heard it, they do not believe it and cannot take delight in it, let alone receive, uphold, recite, or explain it—such a thing has never occurred.

If one hears this sutra, receives and upholds it, recites it, and explains it for others, it is because in past lives they have already made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

"These true persons have planted the roots of manifold virtues; their resolve is set upon the Mahāyāna, and they receive the prediction of enlightenment without doubt—how much more so those who can actually practice the Way of the Truly Realized One.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Silent Intent (Śāntamati) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, Great Sage!"
"What is the meaning of what you call 'serene stillness and pure detachment'?
The Buddha told Śāntamati:
"The meaning of what is called 'serene stillness and pure detachment' refers to the elimination of worldly afflictions and the detachment from all impurities."

By thus eliminating worldly toil, one is then said to have departed from greed, desire, manifold conceptions, and expectations. By departing from these desires and conceptions, there is no longer anything to which the mind is directed;

by having nothing to which the mind is directed, one does not cling to the realms of existence (*dhātu*); by not clinging to the realms, there is no longer the correspondence of retribution and causal conditions; by the absence of the correspondence of retribution and causal conditions, there is no longer ignorance or the craving that belongs to it; by eliminating ignorance and its associated craving, one eliminates the notion of a self (*ātman*); by the absence of a self, one eliminates name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); by the absence of name-and-form, one eliminates the karma of nihilism and eternalism; and by the absence of the karma of nihilism and eternalism, one eliminates attachment to the body.
The Buddha told Śāntamati:
"All karmic retributions arising from causal conditions follow upon the karma of inverted views and thus become afflictions; all these calamities arise from craving the body."

By means of a body free from greed, one abandons all sixty-two views and doubts; by means of a body free from greed, one brings all conditions to stillness; by means of a body free from greed, all craving naturally subsides into tranquility; by means of a body free from greed, all aspirations are peacefully extinguished.
It is just as, Śāntamati, when the roots, stumps, trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a tree are all pulled out at once, the tree is forever gone.

In the same way, the practitioner who eliminates attachment to the body is free from all views and the sixty-two doubts; because they are free from attachment to the body, they depart from all perceived phenomena—the afflictions of the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and worldly toil—and because they are free from attachment to the body, the afflictions of the five aggregates and worldly toil no longer exist.
“Indeed, Great Sage! It is because one does not sever the body of greed that there is a self.
The Buddha told Śāntamati:
"Because one abides in the notion of a self, one does not sever craving for the body; because one abides in the notions of persons and life-span, one does not sever craving and attachment.
As for what is perceived, one does not abide in either the internal or the external; since all views have no locus, there is ultimately nothing to be seen in any state reached."
To see with wisdom that there is no dwelling because there is nothing to dwell upon is called severing the view of a self-body and realizing that the body is entirely empty.

By being able to understand emptiness, one complies with the patience of conforming to the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*) and does not accept those views. When one’s own body is without conceptualization and entirely without activity—neither arising nor originating, and having nothing further produced—this is called the patience of conforming to the Dharma. Not accepting any views is what is meant by severing the craving for the body.
Śāntamati! If you wish to know: if one does not crave the body, one is liberated from the body and becomes bodiless.
What is meant by "bodiless"?

The four great elements that constitute the body are fundamentally nameless; because one who understands this realizes through mental comprehension that they are false and illusory, it is said that they are not real and cannot be apprehended.
All arise from unreal conceptualization; if there is nothing sought and no harboring of conceptualization, one will neither be deluded nor confused, and will neither act nor dwell.
If there is no dwelling, then there is no anger or contention; this absence of anger and contention is called "tranquility.
What is it that is extinguished which is termed "tranquility"?
The extinguishing of all causes and conditions is called "quiescence.
Why is this so? Because it is through those causes and conditions that the mind becomes inflamed; in the absence of causes and conditions, there is no inflammation.
It is just as, Śāntamati, fire arises from the encounter of its conditions:
when two pieces of wood are rubbed together, fire blazes forth; but where there is no encounter, there is no fire, and thus it does not blaze.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
Through the presence of conditions and objects, the mind burns with fervor; through the absence of conditions and objects, it does not burn with fervor.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through skillful means, clearly understands how to pacify causes and conditions according to the occasion, yet does not extinguish the roots of all virtues;
he does not give rise to the opposition of the causes and conditions of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), yet he brings forth all forms of distraction and the various *pāramitās*;
he abandons the works of Māra and all evil deeds, yet does not abandon the causal karma of the practices of the Buddhas' path.
They relinquish the causes of nirvana, yet do not abandon the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that constitute the path;
their minds take no pleasure in the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they forsake the bodhisattva’s resolve for the path of the truly real.

By contemplating emptiness, one gives rise to great compassion; by examining the various causes and conditions, one proclaims the supreme virtue through the condition of signlessness, never losing the mind of the Way through false conceptualization.
Through the condition of wishlessness, one becomes weary of the triple world; by confronting all objects of encounter, one contemplates only the condition of non-arising.
