Without abandoning what has arisen, through the condition of non-hesitation, one cultivates the roots of virtue through all activities and enters into the practice of the path.
This is the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom entering purity and attaining mastery.
Alas for the conditions of impermanence! Because they do not weary of birth and death, they attain freedom, being without fear.
It is because of the condition of suffering that he establishes sentient beings in extinction and peace, so that they may attain stability.
It is because of the condition of non-self that he establishes a mind of compassion and peace for sentient beings, practicing great pity.
It is devoid of conditions, for the mind attains the eightfold sameness as the pure body of the Tathāgata.
It takes desire as its condition, for it serves as the purifying medicine for the disease of all craving and attachment.
He proclaims the Dharma so that the mind may abide firmly;
he relies upon anger so that he may administer the medicine of a compassionate heart to those who act with wrath, his own will abiding in health.
It is because they are deluded and ignorant; by means of the twelve links of dependent origination as medicine, one treats their mental illness so that it may not shift or move.

It is because they are conditioned by the equal distribution [of the three poisons]; by means of the three matters, one transforms the conduct of sentient beings and establishes their minds, preaching the medicine of impermanence.
It is because of freedom from desire that the mind is established to transform and open the way for the śrāvakas.
It is because of freedom from hatred that the mind is established to attain the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
They are free from ignorance and delusion, for they have opened and transformed their minds, establishing them in the Mahāyāna.
They take form and appearance as their condition, for their minds abide in equanimity and they attain the body of a Tathāgata.
It is by reason of sounds that the mind dwells upon the vocal teachings of the Tathāgata;
it is by reason of various fragrances that the mind remains established in the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s precepts.
It is because of the manifold flavors; for the mind abides in the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Way.
It is because of the marks of a great man; for the mental conduct abides in attaining adornment.
It is because of the subtle and smooth [skin] that the mind is established in attaining the softness of the Tathāgata’s hands and feet;
it is because of the sūtras and the Dharma that the mind dwells in attaining the Tathāgata’s state of non-arising.
It is because of giving that the mind dwells upon the perfection of the marks and signs;
it is because of upholding the precepts that the mind exists for the sake of the adornment and purity of the Buddha-lands.
It is because of patience that the mind dwells upon attaining the resonance of the Brahma-voice;
it is because of diligence that the mind remains established in the deliverance of sentient beings.
It is because of meditative concentration that the mind abides and gives rise to great supernormal powers;
it is because of wisdom that the mind remains established in severing the causes of all false views, the sixty-two doubts, and all obstructions.
It is because of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), for the mind dwells in equanimity toward all sentient beings and harbors no malice.
It is because of the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), for the mind is established in the rescue and deliverance of sentient beings.
How joyful it is to rely upon! For the mind dwells with delight in the hearing of the Dharma.
How protective it is to rely upon! For the mind establishes itself in the relinquishing of all fetters and the perils of affliction.
It is because of the four debts of gratitude that the mind exists to guide and lead sentient beings;
it is because of greed and anger that the mind exists to bestow all that one possesses as instruction and gifts upon sentient beings.
It is because of the transgression of evil that the mind abides in the pure practice of the Tathāgata’s precepts;
it is because of the defilement of contention that the mind dwells in the Tathāgata’s patience toward dispute.
It is because of enmity and harm that the mind establishes itself through the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses;
it is because of disorder and confusion that the mind abides and attains the Buddha-samādhi.
It is because of false wisdom that the mind establishes itself in order to bring sentient beings to fulfillment through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that is free from all obstructions.
It is because of the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) that the mind dwells in the accumulation of merit and virtue, for its aspiration is set upon the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna).
It is a favorable condition, for the mind thereby maintains a firm resolve that is harmonious and serene, as it refrains from all evils and everything improper.
It is a condition for the evil realms, for the mind thereby abides in the protection of all sentient beings from falling into the evil realms and the eight difficulties.
"O all you devas, may your minds be established in the realization that all unions must inevitably end in separation.
O all you people, may your minds abide in all that is wondrously good."
One contemplates the Buddha because one has habitually beheld the various Buddhas.
One contemplates the Dharma because the mind establishes itself in the practice of the path of the Dharma, abandoning what is unbeneficial and adhering to what is appropriate.
They take mindfulness of sentient beings as their object, because they have attained and abide in the dharma of non-retrogression.
They take generosity as their object, because their minds dwell upon never abandoning sentient beings.
One relies on the precepts because they fulfill all aspirations;
one relies on mindfulness of the heavens because the mind establishes and perfects the merit of being in the stage of "one birth remaining" before Buddhahood.
It is by relying on bodily conduct, for it leads to the attainment of the Buddha-body;
it is by relying on verbal speech, for the mind abides therein to bring about the various sūtras of the Buddha’s teachings;
it is by relying on the mind, for the mind remains established to realize the intent of the Buddha.
It is conditioned by the conditioned, for the mind abides in the accumulation of merit and virtue through self-discipline.
It is conditioned by the unconditioned, for the mind abides in the perfection of noble wisdom.

Thus, Śāntamati, one does not attain the vehicle of the Way through transformation without conditions; rather, it is by means of conditioned mind that one attains the Buddha-way and guides toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

If there are bodhisattvas who, by virtue of conditions, guide toward all-knowledge, this constitutes the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva, for they see all dharmas and thereby bring forth guidance.

It is just as the trichiliocosm contains within it all lands, the sentient beings of the ten directions, grasses, trees, the five grains, all rivers, seas, and even the forms of hairs; there is nothing that is not encompassed by it, and all depend upon it for their livelihood.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
All conditions arise from the Bodhisattva’s skillful means; by practicing the most supreme and foremost of all deeds, one reaches omniscience.
Just as all colors and various forms possess the four great elements, so too does the Bodhisattva employ skillful means; thus, all actions and conditions he creates lead to the path of Buddhahood.

Why is this? Because all sentient beings commit calamities and transgressions and act without gratitude or reciprocity, the Bodhisattva, by taking these as conditions, practices the Perfection of Giving and is thereby able to fully accomplish the Perfection of Precepts.

If a person harbors a mind of anger and malice, at that time the Bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and immediately becomes fully endowed with the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

If he sees sentient beings in a state of agitation and unable to settle their minds, for this reason the Bodhisattva practices the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) and suddenly achieves the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

If there are sentient beings existing amidst various obscurations, established in the calamities of a dark, profound, and obscure chamber, the Bodhisattva acts to sever their bonds, hindrances, and the net of all fetters.
If there are sentient beings who can diligently cultivate their practice, they shall eliminate all attachments.
Those who seek [the Way] will praise and prostrate to them, regarding them as their own teachers.
Even toward those who delight in slander, he acts in accordance with their inclinations so that they do not give rise to such thoughts.

When he sees those undergoing toil and hardship, afflicted by countless vexations, the Bodhisattva then gives rise to great compassion for them; seeing those who abide in peace, he embraces and protects them with great joy.

When a bodhisattva encounters those who are stubborn and difficult to transform at any given time, they provide instruction, guidance, and exhortation to inspire them toward awakening; seeing them as kind and harmonious people, the bodhisattva cultivates supreme practices in their presence and arouses the mind of the Way.
If there are sentient beings whose power and influence reside in conditions, the Bodhisattva accordingly manifests and protects their resolve for enlightenment.

If there are those with the karmic retribution of great physical strength, the Bodhisattva immediately accords with them, gathering them in, instructing and admonishing them, and causing the aspiration for the Way to arise.
This is called attaining mastery by following conditions.

The Bodhisattva, in accordance with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), understands sentient beings and proclaims the Dharma at the appropriate time through the power of karmic retribution; he inspires their aspirations and affection, transforming and discerning them so that each may attain tranquility and diligently advance toward the Great Way.

The Noble Wisdom expounds upon the profound and unfathomable meaning; the Retentive Wisdom extensively unfolds and disseminates the Way of Ultimate Truth, gradually proclaiming and revealing the causal basis of this Way.
He discerns and distinguishes chapters and phrases, using a single phrase of the Dharma to elucidate manifold wisdom.
For those who delight in tranquility, he accordingly provides analytical exposition to universally contemplate all things.

For those who prefer contemplation, he uses the meditative concentration of the liberation-samādhi to explain that the prohibitions and precepts are inexhaustible, and further proclaims them for their sake.
When those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals hear this Dharma, they come to understand impermanence and the lack of refuge, leading them to seek the protection of the Path.

If there are those with concentrated minds, he will discourse upon the perfection of wisdom for them, causing them to aspire to dwell in seclusion; through such practice, he transforms them so that their body, speech, and mind become tranquil.
One who knows contentment with limits manifests the noble and sagely practice of the faculty of wisdom.
Toward those dwelling in the darkness of self-conceit and ignorance, one should proclaim the necessity of diligent study and broad learning.
To those who are fond of greed and desire, he demonstrates the afflictions of impurity and futility.
To those who delight in anger and hatred, he exhorts them to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and to harbor no malice.
If they persist in delusion and ignorance, he reveals and transforms their minds through the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination and the cycle of birth and death.
For those who dwell in the state of equilibrium, he expounds impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
For those who zealously pursue form and desire, he transforms them through the contemplation of impurity, extending his benevolence to the utmost limit.
To those who are ignorant and mired in darkness, he instructs on the defilements and the principle of dependent origination.
Some may give rise to various views, yet through the wisdom that definitively realizes emptiness and non-existence,
they resolve their aspirations and expound the practice of signlessness (*animitta*).
With their will set upon essential vows, they instruct others in the state of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
He trains in yearning for the various coverings (*āvaraṇa*) and analyzes the various aggregates (*skandha*), perceiving them as like illusions and transformations—false and unreal.

Regarding attachment to the various elements (*dhātu*), he understands that the four great elements and the eighteen elements appear like forms and shadows manifesting through their mutual interaction.

Relying upon the sense bases (*āyatana*), he expounds that all twelve internal and external bases are not "mine," just as one who has awakened from a dream cannot find where what was seen therein remains.
Relying upon the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), he analyzes and clearly explains for others that all phenomena return to impermanence.
If one relies on the realm of form, one proclaims that all practices are fundamentally rooted in suffering and affliction.
Even if one takes refuge in the formless realm, one proclaims the Way of the Teachings—that all dharmas are devoid of self.
Those who are difficult to transform should always be encouraged to diligently practice the Dharma of the sages and saints.
For those who are easily pacified and transformed, one should reveal the words of the infinite.
Those whose aspirations lie in the realms of devas and humans, yet whose minds are anxious as they seek to proceed, should be made to sigh in admiration for the precepts that are pure and stainless.
For those who delight in the Śrāvaka vehicle, he points out the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
If they aspire to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he then reveals the twelve links of dependent origination, which have ignorance as their root.
Awakening to the karma of the Mahāyāna, one instructs and guides others by means of the dissemination of the six pāramitās, the four immeasurables, and the four debts of gratitude.
For those who have first resolved their minds, one observes their aspirations and dispositions and provides them with instruction and exhortation.
Fully comprehending all practices, they do not weary of birth and death; by demonstrating that there is no difficulty, they cause others to establish themselves so as not to regress.
For those who are non-regressive, they explain the purity of the Buddha-fields through analytical discourse.
A great being, a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood, manifests the true Buddha-tree at the site of enlightenment.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!

If there is a Bodhisattva who has attained mastery, the Dharma he proclaims through his transformative influence is free from fault or transgression, and he gladdens sentient beings with his skillful speech.

When these words were spoken, ten thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and five hundred bodhisattvas all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.
At that time, there were bodhisattvas in that assembly who each thought to themselves:
"How long will it be before the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path and becomes a most perfectly awakened one?"
What will be your title when you attain the Way of the Buddha?
What will be the nature of the merits and adornments of your buddha-field?
And how will the assembly of bodhisattvas achieve perfection?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the beginning and end of the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattvas, immediately smiled. Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light issued from the Buddha’s mouth, illuminating infinite worlds in the ten directions, eclipsing the light of the sun and moon and overshadowing the palaces of Māra. The light then circled the Buddha countless times and entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Silent Mind rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha with verses,
inquiring about the meaning of the smile: "Sublime as refined gold, With wondrous light casting off all defilements,
Your mind is tranquil and firmly established, Like the sun in the midst of space."
Its radiance is vast and brilliant, completely dispelling all darkness;
that which is now manifested has been proclaimed by the Honored One among Men.
Serene as a lotus flower, he grows and stands amidst the mud.
Its stem and roots are in the water; as it grows, it remains free from defilement.
Its merit is most fragrant, and its thoughts become increasingly vast and far-reaching.
Pray, dwell in peace and tell us: for what reason do you rejoice?
His intention and wisdom are eternally secure; he is tranquil and gentle.
His compassion increases day by day, eliminating all defilements and impurities.
With the radiance of wisdom, he dispels all darkness.
Abiding like a lotus flower, he has cast aside all doubts.
Increasing his compassion, he cultivates the site of enlightenment;
practicing with mastery, his mouth and face radiate light, drying up all cravings and desires.
He transforms and enlightens sentient beings, causing their eyes to become pure;
he establishes them in the cessation of the rebellious thieves and removes all their blemishes.
He clearly understands that birth and death do not exist, as well as the nature and conduct of sentient beings.
To instruct and awaken all— the devas, the people of the world,
and the entire universal assembly— who gaze upon the countenance of the Great Sage,
please now explain the meaning of this manifested smile.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Silent Intent (Śāntamati):
"Do you see the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada? He replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"This Guhyapāda Vajrapāṇi has already made offerings to the assembly of all Tathāgatas of the Bhadrakalpa; he shall protect the true sutras, receive and uphold them, and bring benefit and advantage to immeasurable sentient beings through the Way."
Having passed away from here, they will be born in the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya.

Being born in that land of Wondrous Joy, the Buddha Akṣobhya will proclaim eighteen hundred seals (*mudrā*) for the sake of the bodhisattvas; they shall all attain these and return to the meaning of the Way through repeated cycles of coming and going. Thereafter, in future lives, they shall behold immeasurable and incalculable Tathāgatas, prostrate themselves in self-refuge, and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*). Thus it shall be in future lives.

After accumulating the roots of virtue through these kalpas, he attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path, achieving supreme perfect enlightenment and becoming a Buddha. He appeared in the world with the name Vajrapada (Golden Stepping), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The world is called Universal Purity (*Samantaprasanna*), and the eon is called Adorned Purity (*Vyūhaprasanna*).
Furthermore, O Silent One!

That world Universal Purity is divinely wondrous, abundant, flourishing, and peaceful. The five grains are so plentiful that they are naturally priceless; the populace is thriving, and gods and humans are exceedingly numerous. Its city is constructed from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, coral, and pearl—and it has eight crossroads as level as the palm of a hand.
The ground is soft and supple, like celestial silk.
It is like the Tuṣita Heaven, with garments, food, drink, palaces, mansions, gardens, groves, bathing pools, and ornate pavilions.
The Buddha-land is as magnificent as this.

The gods and people naturally manifest splendor like celestial music; they hang various colorful banners, erect fine pennants and canopies, burn many kinds of famous incense, and rain down a profusion of precious flowers that scatter throughout the land. In the sky above, numerous parasols are arrayed, accompanied by harmonious and elegant music.

In that Buddha-land, there are no evil realms nor the poisons of the three types of suffering; furthermore, there are no places of the eight difficulties or lack of leisure. All its karmic manifestations are like those of Tuṣita Heaven, such that its clothing, food and drink, palaces, gardens, pavilions, and towers are no different from those found there.
There is no distinction between devas and humans; all the gods and people alike admire the subtle and wondrous, aspiring solely to the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, in that buddha-field there are no two vehicles; even the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not exist. It is composed entirely of bodhisattvas, and the Honored Tathāgata proclaims for them the great Dharma of non-retrogression.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas surrounding the World-Honored One Vajrapada is incalculable, immeasurable, and spans hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
In that Buddha-land, there are no people of evil lineage or those who act with malice and envy; there are none who violate the precepts or fall into false views.
The people of this land have all reached the ultimate state and cherish the Buddha-dharma with great devotion.

There are none who are blind, deaf, mute, or afflicted by goiters or swellings; they are gentle and refined in character and conduct, and their bodies are all adorned with the twenty-eight marks of excellence.
Furthermore, when that Tathāgata is present in the world, his lifespan shall be eight minor kalpas.

When those devas and humans are about to reach the end of their lives, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, will constantly preach the Dharma for them, and he will manifest bodily radiance that illuminates the entire trichiliocosm.
At that time, all the devas and humans, having been graced by this radiance, had all their doubts resolved; they praised the Dharma and followed the Buddha, each thinking in their hearts:
"We should go to the Buddha to inquire about and receive the sutras."
Some went to the Buddha’s abode by means of their own supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), while other practitioners went to the Buddha’s abode in accordance with the Buddha’s holy command.

The Buddha remained suspended in space a hundred thousand fathoms above the ground; at a great seat set out at the crossroads of that world, he addressed the ten directions to gladden all the assembled multitudes. Using the words of a Tathāgata, he expounded the path of the sūtras for the sake of the bodhisattvas, proclaiming only the Mahāyāna, the unsurpassed Great Way.

In that Buddha-land, there is not a single person who opposes the World-Honored One’s teaching, nor is there anyone who slanders, reviles, or insults him; all sentient beings possess keen and sharp faculties, and their wisdom is thoroughly penetrating.
That land has no king; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, serves as its Dharma King.

The people of that land have no sense of self and no basis for the accumulation of karma; they possess nothing as "mine" and hold no ownership over fields or houses. It is exactly thus for all the devas and human beings alike.

When the Tathāgata Vajrapada, the Arhat, desired to receive food out of compassion for him, he manifested the form of a Buddha at the hour of late afternoon on the previous day, wearing his robes and holding his alms bowl, standing before the man's gate.
The family, realizing this, thought to themselves:
"The Buddha, out of compassion for us, wishes to come and eat with us.
That very night, they prepared and adorned a seat, providing pure bedding and various kinds of delicious, flavorful food.

Early the next morning, at the appointed hour, the Buddha and his assembly of noble ones went to his house. When the meal was finished and the water for washing had been offered, the Buddha preached the Dharma to the donor according to their needs. That person attained the stage of non-retrogression; once it was explained that they would surely attain supreme, perfect enlightenment, the Buddha rose from his seat and returned to the monastery.

If the Buddha is seated in meditative repose within a quiet chamber, at that time the various bodhisattvas each cultivate themselves through the samādhis attained by their respective original practices.
Thus it is, Śāntamati!
The merits and virtues of that Buddha-world are so immeasurable, lofty, extraordinary, and sublime; its lands are adorned, pure, universally level, vast, and beautiful, beyond measure.

When the Buddha spoke this sutra and bestowed the prophecy upon the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, twenty thousand people in the assembly at that time all resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Each of those gathered there thought in their hearts that they wished to be born in that land.
The Buddha then gave this prediction:
"When Vajrapada attains the Way of the Buddha, all who have desired to see him shall be born in that land."
"That Buddha shall also bestow upon them the prediction that they too shall all attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become Most Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, having heard from the Buddha this bestowal of predictions, leaped for joy and cast his vajra into the void.

Just as it was cast into the air, at that very moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; light illuminated the ten directions; the heavens rained down a profusion of flowers like falling snow; and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
In every assembly, various kinds of flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and ornaments spontaneously appeared in their right hands, which they each held as they proceeded.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, with precious flowers, incense, banners, canopies, silken streamers, and pennants, circumambulated the Buddha and praised him in verse:
"The vast Dharma is universally sovereign; The treasury of Dharma is inexhaustible."
Thoroughly understanding and discerning all phenomena, you lead and benefit sentient beings.
Entrusting me with this meaning, you always delight in the gift of Dharma;
most excellently upholding the True Dharma, you dwell in the Way—may I take refuge in you.
Wisdom can purify, clearly illuminating all actions performed;
its fame resounds through the three worlds—this is the perfection of merit.
His wisdom penetrates the three realms; the Benevolent One remains unattached.
Having delivered them from all obstacles, he proclaims the Dharma to swiftly relieve their distress.
Pure as the clarity of the moon, his countenance is exceedingly radiant;
this brilliance shines forth to the furthest reaches, comparable to the light of the sun and fire.
His voice is exceptionally sublime and beautiful, with a harmonious resonance like that of Brahmā;
he proclaims compassion—homage to the Jewel among sentient beings!
He manifests his own body, displaying a physical form and a lifespan.
I only pray that you will proclaim the Dharma, Expounding it through the sounds of written characters.
Though you preach and explain the sutras and the Dharma, You harbor no conception of a "Dharma.
In delivering and liberating sentient beings, You likewise harbor no conception of a "person."
Who can repay the Buddha’s kindness, as transformed and enlightened by the World-Honored One?
Even if all sentient beings were to accumulate meritorious practices for immeasurable eons,
receiving and accepting only the Buddha’s teachings with a resolve set on no other task, [they could not repay it].
"One is able to practice and uphold it oneself, and furthermore transform and guide others.

At that time, Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, circumambulated the Buddha and the assembly seven times; then, holding various flowers and precious canopies in his hands, he offered them by scattering them over the Buddha.

To provide offerings for the Buddha’s dispersal, at that moment, throughout all regions of the four continents, various kinds of flowers were spontaneously produced by transformation, adorning and embellishing the eightfold crossroads and the pools of the eight-flavored water; sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they pervaded everywhere in a manner so magnificent it was beyond measure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Silent Intent (Śāntamati) asked the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada:
"The Tathāgata has bestowed upon you, O Benevolent One, the prediction of the Way. He replied:
“Son of good family!
Because one sees that the prediction of enlightenment and the path-prediction received are naturally like a dream.
He asked again:
“Virtuous one, what have you attained by receiving this prediction? He replied: “Noble son!”
"One who has received the prediction of enlightenment has nothing to attain.
He asked again: "What is it that is not attained?"

He replied: "One does not grasp at a self, nor does one obtain a person, a life-span, or a soul; one does not obtain the five aggregates, the six sense-fields, or the four great elements. One does not perceive the karmic actions of this world or the world beyond. One does not grasp at any offenses or non-offenses, the outflow-free or the with-outflows, worldly afflictions and resentment, the conditioned or the unconditioned, or birth-and-death and the unconditioned—none of these are grasped."
"This, son of good family,
is what is called receiving the prediction [of enlightenment]. Śāntamati asked again:
"If there is nothing attained, who is it that receives the prediction of enlightenment?
He replied, "That which has no attainment is what is called 'attainment'."
He asked again:
"If there is no self, who is it that receives the prediction?
And who is it that grants the prediction?"
He replied, "Those who receive the prediction and those who bestow the prediction are both equally identical; in the ultimate limit, they are non-dual.
He then asked Guhyapāda again:
"If there is no fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), who is it that receives the prediction [of enlightenment]? He replied:
"The fundamental limit is neither born nor extinguished; there are not two limits."
"It is by means of this primordial limit that one receives the prediction today.
He asked again:
"Abiding in what primordial limit does one receive the prediction?"
“Abiding in spontaneity, there is no dual limit, no limit of self, and no person, life, or lifespan.
To abide in spontaneity is called receiving the prediction of enlightenment.”
He asked again:
"Where does the original limit of the self abide? He replied:
"The abode of the Tathāgata.
He asked again:
"What is known by that which has no cognition?"
He replied: "That which is known and cognized is itself without anything known.
He spoke again:
"If there is nothing to be told, it constitutes not speaking.
He asked again:
"If there is nothing spoken, what is being taught?"
He replied: "The teaching has nothing to be taught.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'teaching that there is nothing to teach'? He replied,
"All dharmas are entirely without anything to be taught."
He asked again:
"Since you say there is nothing to be taught, how is this known? He replied:
"If there is nothing to be taught, that which is known is like this.
He asked again:
"How does one teach what is known?"
He replied, “I do not ask about what is known.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'not questioning what is to be known'?
He replied: "It means that consciousness is free from negligence."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'consciousness being without negligence'? He replied:
"The essential meaning of taking refuge.
He asked again:
"What is meant by the essential meaning of taking refuge?"
He replied, "I do not see any lack of righteousness.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'not seeing the non-meaningful'?
He replied: "To neither regard it as meaningful nor as non-meaningful—this is called 'the meaningful.'"
He asked again:
"What is meant by that which is neither in accordance with principle nor contrary to principle, yet is called 'principle'? He replied:
"It is neither by means of righteousness nor by the absence of righteousness that one advances in righteousness.
He asked again:
"If it is by means of the absence of righteousness, does this not fail to establish the meaning of the Dharma?"
He replied: "Regarding that which is called 'the meaning of the Dharma,' what is its meaning? Why is this so?"
As for the meaning of its inclination, it is non-Dharma and does not constitute Dharma.
He asked again:
"What is meant by Dharma?"
He replied, "The Dharma is without sound; this is what is called 'the Dharma'.
He asked again:
“The Dharma has no sound; what, then, is meant by ‘Dharma’?
He replied, “That which is without syllables within that Dharma is called ‘Dharma.’”
"That which is non-attainable is that dharma which has no sound and no words.
He further asked Guhyapada:
"What is meant by 'that which is attained'?"
He replied: "Son of good family!
That which can be attained is precisely what is called 'all non-attainment,' being free from anything to be acquired."
He asked Guhyapāda again:
"This is what I have attained; it is by practicing all dharmas that the Tathāgata is able to attain it.
He asked once more:
"How could one possibly quiet the mind that clings to a self?
All the illumination of wisdom that is proclaimed uses written words to declare the deeds of the Tathāgata; it is neither through non-attainment nor through future attainment."
He asked again:
"What is it that cannot be attained by those who have reached this state? He replied:
"What is spoken by the mouth is 'not so'.
He asked again:
"If what is spoken by the mouth relies upon written characters, then it is 'not so'."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'acceptable'? He replied:
"That which has nothing to attain has nothing to teach.
That which has nothing to teach or know does not know itself, nor does it know others.
When one neither knows oneself nor knows others, that is called being 'sufficient' (ke)."
He asked again:
"Which of these cannot be considered the root?
Which of these can be considered the root?"
He replied, "That which is received is the fundamental.
He asked again:
"Who is the basis for that which is received?
He replied: "That upon which one relies is the basis."
He asked again:
"Upon what does that which you rely upon depend?
What is its root? He replied:
"False conceptualization is its very root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of false conceptualization?"
He replied, "Falsehood,
delusive conceptualization, and the dust of affliction are the root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of these false conceptualizations and the dust of affliction? He replied,
"Attachment is the root."
He asked again:
"What is the fundamental basis of this attachment? He replied:
"Form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility—attachment to these is the root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of attachment?"
He replied: "The accumulation of affectionate attachments is called the root of clinging.
To be free from longing for these various clingings is called non-attachment."
This, Śāntamati, is why all the Buddhas,

the World-Honored Ones, proclaim the Dharma and repeatedly teach this teaching: that among the fetters of affection and craving, one seeks that which is attached to, yet ultimately finds nothing to which one is attached.

When the prophecy was bestowed upon the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, five hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind, and two hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twelve;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Third Assembly on the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, Part Six.

At that time, having fulfilled his vows and received the Buddha’s prophecy, and with all his aspirations completed, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada was filled with joy and delight. Joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Sage, may you deign to come to my realm in the wilderness, to the kingdom of the King of Ghosts, and accept my invitation to stay for seven days in the palace of Guhyapada."
May all the Bodhisattvas and great Śrāvakas look upon us with compassion and not neglect us.

Whether at the place where the Buddha resides, in the wilderness lands of the *kumbhāṇḍa* kings, or within our humble dwellings, may you deign to accept a small meal. May you transform the hosts of ghosts and spirits, the *piśācas*, the *gandharvas*, the *mahoragas*, and all other sentient beings who inhabit these places, so that they may behold the Honored Tathāgata and hear this Dharma of the sutra. Thus, throughout the long night, they shall be secure and free from all afflictions, remaining steadfastly without calamity; they shall then abandon their poisonous malice and harbor no rebellious thoughts.

When the Four Heavenly Kings and all their retinues roam within the realm of the yakṣa kings in the wilderness, if they behold the Tathāgata or hear the Dharma he preaches, they will always attain peace and harmony and never encounter peril or distress.

At that time, the Buddha remained silent and accepted Guhyapada’s invitation for seven days of offerings; out of compassion, and wishing to transform and enlighten countless sentient beings so that they might plant the roots of virtue.

At that time, Guhyapada, seeing that the Buddha had accepted his request by remaining silent, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew in reverence.
Suddenly vanishing from sight, he returned to the kingdom of Āṭavī and entered his palace.
At that time, the Māṇibhadra Yakṣa thought to himself:

"I shall adorn the palace for the Great Sage so that the gods of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm may experience what they have never known before, and all the Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions shall rejoice."
He thought to himself:
"I recall that in the past, at one time during the night, I harbored a vow of aspiration; the Dharma of the Way I revere is inconceivable, and it must be so now as well."

Immediately, as he entered into samādhi, an immeasurable proclamation was made; at that time, countless billions of trillions of lion thrones appeared spontaneously, with legs fashioned of jewels and railings of rare treasures, covered upon them with hundreds of thousands of celestial garments.
Pure and wondrous flowers and pearl necklaces were placed at the eight intersections, with precious lotus flowers covering them above.

Having entered the samādhi of right reception, [he saw that] "to the east of here, past as many buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a world named Immeasurable Jewel Virtue Purity; the Buddha there is named King of Purity."
He proceeded to the adorned and pure lion-throne of the Tathāgata King of Purity, desiring to bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon ten thousand bodhisattvas.
The splendor and purity seen in that Buddha-field surpassed all the adornments and purities of countless devas and humans.
"I shall now go to that buddha-field to adorn the high seat.
At that time, the Mārapramardaka Vajrapāṇi entered the samādhi of the King of Pure Jewels.

As soon as he had attained this samādhi, a magnificent high seat spontaneously appeared, adorned and pure, equal in height, breadth, beauty, and purity to the lion throne in the Buddha-field of Immeasurable Jewel Virtue and Purity, without any difference. Suddenly, it arrived at the land of the wilderness and the realm of the yakṣas.

The high seat bestowed was as majestic as this: exceedingly tall, broad, and long, measuring two thousand four hundred and eighty *li* from east to west and one thousand two hundred and eighty *li* from south to north. Its ground was composed of dark-blue lapis lazuli, crystal, and *musāragalva*; it was perfumed with the auspicious-treasury jewels and immeasurable varieties of renowned and blended incenses. Countless censers made of various jewels were erected, burning exquisite and wondrous fragrances. Flowers of the heavens and various kinds of articles were scattered about; their supreme beauty and majesty, and their radiant, brilliant colors, were such as to delight the human heart and bring peace and harmony to the body.

Acting according to the Dharma of Bodhisattvas in accordance with the mind and the occasion, they do not lose their proper timing; their meritorious achievements are boundless, and the wondrous virtues they extol are without limit or bottom.

Furthermore, the high seats for transformation appear spontaneously, consisting of hundreds of thousands of billions of incalculable lion thrones, with legs made of jewels and railings made of jewels, upon which countless celestial garments are spread.

Pure jewel lotuses, adorned with pearls, stand at every intersection of the eightfold paths; they are spread over the ground with various jewels, established upon the earth and fully complete in every respect.

At that time, the Mārṣa Guhyapuruṣa, manifesting such inconceivable forms, prepared various high seats—lofty, broad, pure, and exceptionally magnificent lion-thrones beyond measure—and then rose from samādhi with calm composure and dignified grace.
That very night, he prepared various kinds of sweet foods and drinks, honoring the Bodhisattva’s harmonious nature and conduct, and manifesting the fruits of the Tathāgata’s retribution.
When the various offerings had been prepared and the night was not yet turning to dawn, he addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"All you people should know that today the World-Honored One shall come to my palace for a meal; having invited him for seven days, all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas shall likewise assemble."

May you all be reverent and diligent, free from negligence; for a Great Sage is difficult to encounter, appearing but once in ten million ages. Therefore, with single-minded devotion, renounce the secular world and aspire to the Way, serving with reverence to eliminate birth and death through the vast compassion of the Ultimate Path.

This time is difficult to encounter and this Dharma is difficult to hear; in the three realms there is no refuge, and only the Path can be relied upon. It is universally pervasive like space and free from all further obstructions; do not harbor a distracted mind or engage in heedless conduct.

You and your retinue—wives, children, and servants—should provide offerings for seven days without relying on body or mind; take only the Way as your foundation. Do not follow other worldly pursuits that would harm or contravene the teachings of the Way, but with single-minded devotion, offer worship to the Tathāgata, always maintaining a humble heart and redoubling your reverence without duplicity.

He caused the spirits dwelling in the wilderness, the kings, the local deities, the *yakṣas*, the *rākṣasas*, the *pratilomacara* demons, the *gandharvas*, and all others to take refuge in the Buddha and secretly deliberate upon the Dharma.
The Four Heavenly Kings and all other sentient beings shall, without missing their appointed time, universally receive deliverance.

You virtuous ones should understand this: having invited the Celestial Honored One, prostrated yourselves in homage, and made offerings to the Buddha, you must diligently listen to the scriptures and proclaim them throughout the eight directions, so that all may receive benefit; this is how you repay the Buddha’s kindness.
At that time, the son of the Mārṣa Vajrapāṇi, named Guhyasena, addressed him, saying:

"Go, and cause the earth deities and space deities to announce throughout to the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and up to the Māra Heaven, so that each may know: 'Today the World-Honored One is in the realm of the King of the Wilderness Ghosts, having accepted the invitation of the Mārṣa Vajrapāṇi to his palace, and shall partake of food;
the same applies to the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.'"
"If you wish to see the Buddha and hear the teachings of the Way, all must go there.
Prince Vajrasena received these instructions and proclaimed the command, which was made known everywhere in an instant.
His second son was named Shanfen (Good Share). He addressed him, saying: "Son! You must now go yourself;

by means of your own power and spiritual foot, inform all the Brahmā gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Vṛhatphala gods, the Avṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the Akaniṣṭha gods, making it known to them all everywhere."
Today the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of the Ghost-King in the Wilderness and had accepted an invitation to the palace of Guhyaka Vajrapāṇi.
Desiring to see him, all the people went together to the assembly.
Having received the instruction, Śubhakṛtsna issued the proclamation.

In a mere moment, the gods of the Heaven of Desire and the gods of the Form Realm all assembled together in the void; it extended forty thousand *li* in width and likewise forty thousand *li* from top to bottom, with the various gods seated everywhere in their respective order.
Thereupon, Guhyapada, the Vajrapāṇi, adorned the site of the assembly; once the meal was prepared, he joined his palms toward where the Buddha was and addressed him from afar, saying:
"The time has now arrived."
"May the Buddha, the Great Sage, deign to shed his light and turn his mind [toward us].
He then spoke in verse:
"The Honored Hero among Men has condescended; O Supreme One among humans, we pray you look upon us."
The Lotus-like Noble Being has set forth; the Great Sage’s time has arrived.

The Honored One among Two-Legged Beings has deigned to visit; the object of worship for devas and humans, the Honored One among Men, has humbled himself to come. The Holy and Wise One has reached this moment.
Precepts are like a flourishing lotus; diligence increases ever further.
Guarded by supreme shame and remorse, the most excellent is mindfulness alone.
Established in the Noble Truths, one bestows the great grace of compassion and pity.
Without self and without anything to give, you who look back like the most excellent lion;
with the practice of precepts and the karma of vast learning, bearing the flourishing flowers of the factors of enlightenment;
possessing the fruit of complete liberation—O Supreme Tree, may you come!
The ocean of meritorious deeds is solely without error; its intent is profound and vast.
With pure water as its resolve, it performs the blazing work of diligence and the work of the compassionate site of enlightenment, adorned with the necklace of wisdom.
The enlightened one clarifies the fundamental wisdom and awakens it; the sage, having attained realization, looks down upon those who harbor enmity.
He is the foremost light, immovable, healing the sick with the medicinal tree.
Whether they have studied or not, he brings forth abundant clarity; most supreme, he alone bends his divine spirit.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, seeing that the time had arrived for Guhyapada the Vajrapāṇi, addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you, prepare yourselves early; put on your robes, take up your bowls, and command the temple guards to attend."
When the time arrived, Guhyapada, the Vajrapāṇi, came forward to announce that the seven-day period had begun and that they were invited to attend.
Among the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, those who possessed the power of supernatural faculties (ṛddhi) used their own spiritual powers to go and follow and attend upon the Buddha.
"Those who lack the supernormal powers shall enter the light of the Tathāgata and receive its majestic brilliance; out of compassion, the Buddha will cause them all to proceed there.

At that moment, as the World-Honored One set forth on his journey, the bodhisattvas all led the way before him, while the assembly of śrāvakas followed behind in attendance. Devas, nāgas, and spirits hovered in the void with flowers, incense, and music; celestial maidens praised the Buddha, uttering these verses:
"Joyfully he emits radiance, And musical instruments sound spontaneously."
The Buddha-fields tremble and quake, and the heavens rain down myriad flowers.
Such is the Buddha’s great majestic power; his supernormal powers are infinite, his holy transformations are boundless, and his gladdening of beings is inexhaustible.
The Buddha’s auspiciousness is boundless; the Buddha’s divine sanctity is immeasurable;
the Buddha’s majestic demeanor is bottomless; the Buddha’s meritorious achievements are limitless.
He roams Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and dwells among the eight mountains.
"In the sky above, he is unimpeded like the king of hawks.

At that time, the devas of the desire realm and the devas of the form realm saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, coming through the void, like the sunlight appearing upon the water, like the full moon shining alone among the host of stars, like Śakra, the lord of gods, most honored among the deities, or like Brahmā illuminating the great assembly. Seeing this miraculous manifestation, they were greatly delighted and joyful; they rained down various lotus flowers—blue, red, yellow, and white—as offerings, scattering them over the Buddha.

There are *manojña* flowers, *mahāmanojña* flowers, *mṛduka* flowers, *mahāmṛduka* flowers, and *ahorātra-vṛkṣa* flowers; there are fruits with large kernels, as well as the stainless flowers of the various Cakravartin kings—hundred-petaled, thousand-petaled, and even a hundred-thousand-petaled varieties—and all manner of fragrant flowers that arise from joy and delight, possess exquisite flavors, and emit light that illuminates everything.

With exquisite fragrances, constant perfumes, and *uśīra* incense; with the constant joy of flowers and the delight of the eyes—such various flowers rose like clouds and brought forth rain, raining down a multitude of diverse scents and sounding the sublime music of the heavens.

Accompanied by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens and their retinues, they arrived in an instant at the kingdom of the *kumbhāṇḍa* king Vemacitrin in the wilderness, within the palace of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

Surrounded by a retinue of all the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as soon as the Buddha descended and took his place upon the ground, the earth shook greatly and light illuminated the ten directions; it was peaceful, harmonious, and gentle, not disturbing any sentient beings.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, seeing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had arrived in the realm of the yakṣa king Mahāraṇya, quickly, very quickly, together with their palace ladies and retinues, took various flowers, blended incenses, and fragrant oils, as well as silken banners, canopies, music, and rows of conch shells, each carrying these offerings to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to stand to one side, presenting the offerings they had brought to the Buddha.

Upon seeing the Buddha, they were greatly delighted and their hearts were filled with joy; having scattered offerings before the Buddha, they withdrew to one side and joined their palms in self-surrender.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the Four Heavenly Kings, proclaimed the Dharma according to their capacities and the times. Thereupon, thirteen thousand classes of ghosts, spirits, goblins, and malevolent demons all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and ten thousand jade maidens likewise gave rise to this supreme and great resolve.

At that time, Guhyapāla the Malla, together with palace ladies, court dancers, sons, and his retinue, taking flowers, blended incenses, powdered incenses, banners, parasols, and musical instruments, departed from his own palace for the residence of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and each offered what they held as a scattered offering upon the Buddha.

They sat in succession within the palace of King Vaiśravaṇa; as various musical instruments were played, they themselves entered a state of pure mind free from attachment, while their respective attendants took their seats.

The Tathāgata’s high seat alone appeared majestic, pure, and supremely wondrous; the secret sons of Mārīcī lifted the adorned and decorated canopy and lion throne from the void and set them down upon the earth, remaining silent and motionless.
The assembly of bodhisattvas and the śrāvakas returned to their original seats.

At that time, the devas of the desire realm and the devas of the form realm, beholding the arrangement of the seats—so high, vast, and magnificent—attained what they had never experienced before; struck with wonder at such an unprecedented sight, they thought to themselves:
"By what means has the Malla Vajrapāṇi obtained this precious, high, and vast lion throne?"
"It is profound, wondrous, and infinite; its excellence is beyond comparison.
At that time, through the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, a voice spontaneously resounded from the void:

"O Benevolent One, if you wish to know: to the east, passing from this world-system across lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a world named Kṣemāvatī. There, the Buddha is named Śuddharāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, has previously beheld that land as subtle, wondrous, and pure; now, for the sake of the Dharma, he has sent this exquisite, magnificent, and lofty throne.

At that moment, as the Buddha ascended the high and broad lion throne, the kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, pādakānta spirits, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas from the realm of the Kumbhāṇḍa King Āṭavika immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side with palms joined in homage to the Buddha.
At that time, Guhyapāda the Vajrapāṇi addressed the Four Heavenly Kings and the entire assembly:

"Worthy ones, please exert yourselves and with one mind prepare the food and drink; each of you should serve it by hand and diligently make offerings to the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, and the holy multitude."

Why is this? As the Buddha has taught, if one can joyfully assist in performing meritorious deeds and make offerings, one will receive blessings and obtain immeasurable merit; the merit of the original donor is not diminished thereby.
"Virtuous ones, by thus encouraging and assisting his acts of giving, you shall receive immeasurable merit and blessings.

Thereupon, Guhyapada, the Vajrapāṇi, together with his palace attendants, maidservants, all his sons, and his retinue, personally served hundreds of kinds of delicacies of incalculable flavors. With hearts intent on assisting the Bodhisattva in seeking the blessings of a Tathāgata, they made offerings to the Great Sage with profound humility and reverence; the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas were all fully satisfied.
When the meal was finished and the water for washing had been served, Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi Yakṣa, took a small seat and sat before the Buddha, addressing the World-Honored One:

"May Your Great Compassion be extended to expound the Dharma at this opportune moment and proclaim the gateway into the Dharma, so that all classes of sentient beings may understand the path and the origins from which their mental activities arise;
and for those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment, may they give rise to this aspiration for the Way."
Having already resolved their minds on the Way and attained the stage of non-retrogression,
may these spirits, demons, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, and others find eternal peace throughout the long night, being freed from all afflictions and brought to great tranquility and harmony.
"Out of great compassion for the gods, humans, and all sentient beings of the three realms, he has attained a most extraordinary vow that transcends the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, and the entire great assembly:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well."
If sons or daughters of noble family enter this Dharma-gate and abide firmly therein, they will reach the extraordinary vow, remaining free from discrimination and without undergoing depletion.
The Mārṣa Guhyapāla and the great assembly received the instruction and listened. The Buddha addressed the Mārṣa Guhyapāla:

"If sons of good family or daughters of good family should maintain sincere faith and follow the Dharma well, being compliant with many appropriate practices; if they desire to see the noble ones and delight in hearing the Dharma; if their minds are free from stinginess and envy, and they do not withhold their wealth or resources; if they extend their hands in giving, renouncing worldly habits; if they take pleasure in the merit of giving without expecting a reward; if their minds harbor no malice and their resolve is pure; if they are single-mindedly diligent without turbulence or distraction; if they believe in the fruits of retribution and cherish the true practice of goodness; if they do not entertain doubt or hesitation; and if, seeing the principle of purity, they know that actions do not perish without fruit, such that they would rather lose their own body and life than commit an unrighteous act."

Being compassionate, one does not kill; one does not take what is not given; one does not engage in sexual misconduct; and one does not commit false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech, nor harbor envy, ill will, or delusion.
They do not commit the ten evil deeds; they personally practice the ten wholesome actions and also exhort others to do so. They constantly uphold impartial faith.

Seeing various śramaṇas who observe the precepts, possess the Dharma, and diligently cultivate their practice, they set their will upon contemplating the Way and always act in accordance with righteousness and propriety. They are tranquil and harmonious, their minds abiding in detachment. They accept nothing with attachment and do not receive false speech. Their nature is benevolent and compassionate; they cast away evil dharmas and their conduct is free from violence. They are as bright as a torch and not as ignorant as beasts; their speech is without slander and their mind-nature is peaceful and harmonious.

Having cut off sleep, abandoned the mind of negligence, and cast off heavy burdens, one should practice frequent giving and always act with reverence toward all virtuous friends, all Buddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha.

In this manner, they constantly follow and attend upon śramaṇas and brahmins, showing humility and paying them homage; they practice associating with them without losing their intent, always honoring such virtuous friends.

Out of love and joy, he further employs the Dharma to rescue those in peril; he proclaims the Dharma to exhort and transform others, expounding upon retribution—how giving leads to great wealth, how upholding the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven, and how extensive learning leads to great wisdom.

Cultivating practice in accordance with the Way, each receives their respective retribution: those who give great wealth become hungry ghosts of stinginess and greed; those who maintain the precepts, practice patience, exert diligence, concentrate the mind, and cultivate wisdom gradually enter the source of the Way.
Violating the precepts leads to hell; anger results in ugliness; laziness causes one to abandon the Path; a distracted mind leads to falling into transgression; and folly casts one into darkness.
These are the retributions for evil conduct of body, speech, and mind; they are the fruits of good and evil in body, speech, and mind.
Committing these three matters leads to long-term unrest, casting one into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
By guarding these three karmas, one is born among gods and humans before the Buddhas of the ten directions, enjoying eternal peace for all time and free from all afflictions.
For each, he reveals the retribution of sins and blessings and the destinations of good and evil.

If he perceives one who is a suitable vessel, he expounds for them the profound Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; that there is nothing to be practiced and no place to be reached; and that there is no self, no person, no life-span, and no vital principle.
One discerns the profound and subtle twelvefold dependent origination: if one relies upon these factors, then there is birth; if one does not rely upon them, then there is no birth.
From this, that arises; from non-this, that does not arise.

From ignorance arise volitional formations; from volitional formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises clinging; from clinging arises becoming; from becoming arises birth; from birth arise old age and death, and the great mass of suffering, which constitutes the four great elements of the body.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, and this entire mass of great suffering cease. One does not receive the four great elements, and thus one is forever at peace, eternally free from all afflictions.
That which is extinguished is non-existent.
Why is this so? Because that which arises and that which is born—when these are absent, they do not exist.

It is just as when a tree is planted, it first produces sprouts, roots, stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; if the tree were uprooted and there were no sprouts, from what could these stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit arise?
When one understands that there is no ignorance, the mind has nothing to which it is attached, and thus there is no entanglement.

The twelve links of dependent origination all arise from conditions and oppositions; where there are no conditions, there is no opposition. All things within the three realms are fundamentally non-existent, for they all arise from non-arising.

Because one dies from existence and fails to reach non-existence, it is said that there is birth through causation and that one does not know emptiness; by relying on the notion of "self," one consequently meets death.

To understand that non-existence does not give rise to birth and to realize that existence does not lead to death, one is pursued by transgressions and overtaken by the afflictions (*kleśa*). Being inverted, suffering, deluded, and unreal, for such a person the True Dharma is proclaimed according to its proper ritual sequence. When one contemplates all phenomena in accordance with the Dharma and performs no conditioned action (*saṃskāra*) toward them, and because no such action is obtained, there is neither regression nor non-regression, and no difficulty of coming and going or circling in saṃsāra.
If one’s mind and mental objects are without attachment, and one accepts with faith that all things are fundamentally empty, then all fundamental natures will be entirely pure and serene.

As for such a person—if they are a bodhisattva mahāsattva—they shall always behold the Buddhas and never be far from them; they shall not fail to hear the Dharma and shall not go against the assembly of sages; wherever they are born, they shall always see the Buddhas.
Although they take birth, they do not arise in lands where there is no Buddha.
Their birth is for the purpose of seeing the Buddha; they practice without negligence, yearning for and seeking the Dharma of true and correct diligence.

Having diligently cultivated this, one need not attend to household affairs but should properly uphold pure conduct; one need not concern oneself with wife, children, male or female slaves, servants, or the protection of the home, but should swiftly uphold the Dharma, without indulging in play, negligence, or self-indulgence in sensual desires.
Having placed firm faith in the verbal teachings bestowed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one renounces the household life to follow the Path.
Having faithfully renounced the household life, one becomes a virtuous friend and a true companion.

Having received the true practice, their nature and conduct are subtle as they hear the profound and wondrous Dharma; taking practice as essential, they do not return to outward adornment; their awakening of mind is supreme, and they never grow weary in their quest for extensive learning.

One should extensively expound the Dharma as it has been heard for the sake of others, without harboring expectations for sustenance or gain, nor relying upon one's own words as an object of veneration.

When lecturing on the sutras, one should do so according to the wisdom one has heard; following the conduct and abiding of the listeners, one explains them for their benefit, causing those who hear the Dharma to give rise to great compassion.
Yet he gives rise to inexhaustible compassion for all sentient beings, thereby attaining broad learning without any stinginess or attachment.

He does not crave his own body or life, having few desires and seeking little, knowing contentment and sufficiency. Through the weight of his wholesome deeds, he provides most joyful offerings; he delights in dwelling in seclusion, remaining single-mindedly focused and guarding his integrity.
Contemplating the meaning and intent of the Dharma as it is heard, one takes refuge in the true principle and practices it through reflection, rather than seeking mere outward adornment.

In guiding both the heavens and the world, one does not act solely for one's own sake, but seeks the supreme Mahāyāna for the sake of all sentient beings; thus, with a profound aspiration for the Buddha-way—the vehicle of sovereignty—one achieves non-laxity.
What is meant by non-negligence?

It is to penetrate the sensory realms such that the eye does not perceive forms, does not undergo delusive thoughts, and does not cling to ornamental appearances, thereby fully understanding the difficulty regarding form.
Although one may abandon them out of longing and pleasure, one understands that they are fundamentally non-existent.

It is the same for the ear hearing sounds, the nose perceiving fragrances and various perceptions, the tongue craving delicious flavors, the body contacting tactile objects, and the mind engaging with mental phenomena.

What is called "freedom from negligence" means that one's own mind is non-arising, that one protects the minds of others, that one abandons the pleasure of craving and enters into the joy of the Dharma, that one does not engage in thoughts of desire, that one is without thoughts of anger or thoughts of harm, and that one is free from the karmic actions of greed, anger, and delusion.

Without this root of evil, one does not commit evil with the body, does not speak what is wrong with the mouth, and does not harbor impurities with the mind; one does not engage in contrary thoughts and does not transgress any unwholesome dharmas.
This is called non-negligence.
Through non-negligence, one should always act with moderation, clearly understanding existence and non-existence, and knowing that there is no "non-existence" apart from "existence.
What is meant by "existence"?
What is meant by "non-existence"?
Those who practice equanimity possess the liberation of the noble ones (ārya), whereas those who cultivate deviant practices lack the liberation of the noble ones.
Furthermore, there are both retributions for transgressions and merits, as well as cases where there are no such retributions for transgressions or merits.
Some possess eyes, while others do not;
some possess ears, noses, tongues, or bodies, while others possess minds, or have no minds.
Furthermore, they are able to discern that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and subject to separation.
This is called "existence.
One who is intent on studying the Path calculates that form is permanent, eternally enduring, and eternally established, being subject to no law of separation.
Because they dwell without equanimity and possess this notion, there arise feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
There exist the phenomena of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and separation;
furthermore, from ignorance as a condition, unwholesome states arise, and if there were no ignorance, then there would be no volitional formations.
Because of the condition of birth, there are old age, sickness, and death; if the condition of birth were absent, there would be no old age, sickness, or death.
Generosity brings about great merit, while poverty results from a lack of relinquishment; those who are destitute possess greed and envy, whereas the stingy possess no great wealth.
To serve the Dharma and the Ultimate Way, if one does not accord with its meaning, one will not reach the stage of the Way.
A Bodhisattva who practices with diligence attains Great Wisdom; a Bodhisattva who is indolent does not attain the Way.
Those who are not arrogant have truly attained the extraordinary resolution; those who are haughty do not reach *nirvāṇa*.

If one enters universally into quiescence and reaches emptiness and non-existence, yet still calculates in terms of self, person, and others, or craves the body and the duration of life, one will not attain the wisdom of the Way.
"Such a person should act in accordance with the proper timing and decorum.
The Buddha said:

"If sons or daughters of good family cultivate universal wisdom or attain that which is known—whether they exist in the world or do not exist in the world—universal wisdom reckons that there is nothing therein to be known."
They have celestial food yet are without attachment; even if there were no celestial food, they would still be without attachment.
All Tathāgatas expound this so that one may enter into all dharmas according with the meaning, for the Tathāgatas have clearly realized the four lower dharmas.

What are these four? First, all things in the universe ultimately revert to impermanence; second, all forms of existence are entirely bitter suffering; third, all dharmas are devoid of a self; fourth, all that has form reaches the state of emptiness, non-action, and the tranquility of Nirvana.

Therefore it is said: all phenomena return to impermanence, yet sentient beings, deluded and ignorant, imagine them to be permanent; the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma to sever all such attachments to permanence.
All that exists is entirely bitter poison; yet sentient beings are shrouded in darkness and deludedly conceive of pleasure, so I preach the Dharma for them to sever all notions of pleasure.
All dharmas are devoid of self, yet the minds of sentient beings conceive of a "self," so I preach the Dharma for them to sever all conceptions of selfhood.

All that has form ultimately returns to emptiness; yet sentient beings dwell in darkness and, through inverted perceptions, imagine all things to exist. Therefore, I preach the Dharma to sever their attachments and conceptualizations, leading them to the tranquil state of Nirvana.
For all sentient beings who harbor self-importance, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma so that those who are conceited no longer remain arrogant and abandon their attachments.
By hearing about impermanence and understanding that all sounds are entirely empty, they will then clearly comprehend the true meaning of impermanence.
What is the meaning of this?
That which is fundamentally unarisen, non-increasing, neither arising nor ceasing—this is called entering eternal impermanence.
Hearing the sound of suffering and entering the realm of one's vows, such that the five aggregates are empty and nothing arises—this is called the meaning of suffering.

By hearing the sound that all phenomena are without self, one upholds the gate of emptiness and liberation; therein, the dualistic marks of "self" and "non-self" do not exist—this is the meaning of non-self.

By hearing of the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*, one sets the mind upon the realm of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*); neither burning nor extinguishing, it is the concentration of universal cessation, without beginning or end. This is what is called understanding the meaning of emptiness, yet not taking non-conceptualization as a basis for realization.
Thus it is, worthy one!
If there is a bodhisattva who can practice in this way, they will never fail or lose any of the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) of all paths.
By practicing through non-conceptualization (asaṃjñā-caryā), they will universally and completely fulfill the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma) of all buddhas.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in the palace of the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, expounding the Dharma according to the needs of those present. Immediately, twenty thousand devas and humans in that assembly all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and incalculable numbers of people all received the five precepts.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Out of compassion for us, please tell us: how should we protect the world?
The Buddha told the Four Heavenly Kings:
“Virtuous ones, you should protect the beings of the world by practicing these ten dharmas that ought to be followed.

What are the ten? First, do not harm any living beings; second, do not steal the wealth or treasures of others; third, do not violate the wives of others; fourth, do not engage in double-tongued speech to cause strife and discord among people; fifth, do not speak falsely or deceive others; sixth, do not use harsh words to wound others; seventh, never speak with frivolous ornamentation; eighth, do not harbor jealousy or give rise to thoughts of ‘self’ versus ‘other’; ninth, do not give way to anger regarding good or evil karma; tenth, always cultivate right view and do not follow false doubts.”
"These are the ten.
O worthy ones, by means of these ten matters you shall protect the world, and thus accord with the Dharma teaching.
The Buddha again addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"Furthermore, O worthy ones, there are eight dharmas that protect the world. What are these eight?

First, the correspondence between speech and action, never being at variance; second, honoring and respecting elders and superiors without harboring contempt or arrogance; third, using gentle and soft words, never proclaiming what is coarse or harsh; fourth, being humble and submissive, always maintaining a spirit of deference; fifth, constantly practicing sincerity and simplicity, never engaging in flattery or deceit; sixth, constantly cultivating benevolence and harmony without affectation or hypocrisy; seventh, refraining from committing any evil whatsoever; and eighth, following along with the world by means of the roots of all virtues."
"These are the eight.
The Buddha told the Four Heavenly Kings:
"Furthermore, there are six matters by which one protects the world."

What are these six? First, the body constantly practices compassion and does not harm sentient beings; second, the mouth proclaims benevolence and kindness and does not utter evil words; third, the mind maintains a compassionate heart and harbors no thoughts of increase or decrease; fourth, one governs one's actions with equanimity regarding gains and offerings; fifth, one equally guards the prohibitions and precepts without transgression; sixth, one uses right view with equanimity to guide those who are crooked and perverse. These are the six.
The Buddha addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"Furthermore, there are four matters that always serve as the foremost principles for protecting the world. What are these four?"

First, to establish a course of conduct that is never marked by greed or envy; second, not to harbor anger or inflict harm upon others; third, not to use the darkness of ignorance to obstruct those who have not yet attained realization; fourth, to be free from fear wherever one goes while practicing these deeds—these are the four matters.
The Buddha addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"Furthermore, there are two matters by which one protects the Dharma and the people of the world. What are these two?"

The first is a sense of shame for having failed to accord with the Dharma throughout incalculable eons; the second is a sense of remorse and self-reproach for not penetrating deeply into the Dharma to rescue and protect all beings.
These are the two.
The Buddha said:
"O virtuous ones!
You should practice this Dharma to protect the world."
“Because one can establish such a practice of the Dharma, one is able to protect the world.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada offered a jeweled canopy to cover the Buddha and again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva, through the dharma of being free from anger, reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path?”
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! There are ten things by which a bodhisattva practices the dharma of non-anger and attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path.”

What are the ten?
