First, constantly practicing a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and refraining from harming others; second, never wearying of the various hardships and constantly cultivating great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); third, being always diligent and energetic in all undertakings so that they become extraordinary; fourth, constantly upholding the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to attain samādhi; fifth, giving rise to wisdom through causes and conditions and entering into it; sixth, universally entering into all things by means of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); seventh, understanding and penetrating the three periods of time to purify the past, future, and present; eighth, seeing with the vision of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) without any obstruction; ninth, reverently following the path of practice to enter into all phenomena (*dharma*); tenth, realizing that all phenomena ultimately return to emptiness. These are the ten.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By how many dharmas is a bodhisattva endowed so that, upon hearing the inconceivable dharma of the Buddha, they do not feel fear?”
The Buddha said,
“Son of good family!
A bodhisattva possesses eight qualities by which, upon hearing of the inconceivable [powers] of a Buddha, his mind remains free from fear.”

What are the eight? First, that the merits one has cultivated are always brought to ultimate completion; second, that single-minded meditative reflection is thorough and undisturbed; third, that one takes virtuous friends as guides and follows their lead; fourth, that the mind is constantly firm in faith and delights in the subtle and wondrous Dharma; fifth, that one understands all phenomena to be entirely like illusions and transformations; sixth, that one comprehends all phenomena to be inconceivable; seventh, that one realizes all phenomena cannot be established, being like entering empty space; eighth, that one thoroughly understands the characteristics of all phenomena as being delusive, heedless, and false. These are the eight.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining mastery over all activities and the dharmas of a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva attains mastery through four dharmas. What are these four?
First, to practice the illusion-like samādhi to master all dharmas, entering the five supernormal powers with particular transcendence;
second, to surpass the four dhyānas by means of the three gates of liberation;
third, to cultivate the four brahma-vihāras through the perfection of wisdom.
"The fourth is to practice skillful means and be endowed with the six pāramitās;
these are the four.
Guhyapada, the Vajrapāṇi, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How many dharmas does a bodhisattva possess that lead to entry into the Dharma-gate?
The Buddha said, “Noble son!”
There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva enters the gateways of the Dharma. What are these four?
First is entering the gateway of meditative contemplation, fully and clearly understanding the fundamental nature of all sentient beings.
Second, entering the gate of wisdom, they analyze the meanings and principles of all chapters and phrases and expound them for the multitude;
third, entering the gate of dhāraṇī, they constantly maintain mindfulness of everything they have grasped without forgetting;
fourth, entering the gate of eloquence, they are able to gladden the minds of all sentient beings through their skillful means.
"These are the four.
Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many powers does a bodhisattva possess to bring about the practices of an ārya?"
"Furthermore, why is it that the power of this Way cannot be matched by any,
and it subdues all Māras? The Buddha said, "Noble son!"
A bodhisattva possesses eight powers, which none can withstand, and by which they subdue all Māras.

What are these eight? First is the power of the mind of the Way, whose nature and conduct are pure; second is the power of diligent practice, which does not regress; third is the power of extensive learning, which reveres infinite wisdom; fourth is the power of patience, practiced for the sake of protecting sentient beings; fifth is the power of non-arising, which harbors no anger; sixth is the power of non-falsity, which is fully endowed with liberation; seventh is the power of practicing the Way, which completely perfects wisdom; and eighth is the power of great compassion, which transforms and enlightens sentient beings.
"These are the eight.
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada and his five hundred sons all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Having attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), he came before the Buddha and said:
"I only pray that the Great Sage will cause these eight dharmas, the essentials of this sutra, to flow throughout the world out of compassion for us;

may the palace of Guhyapada be naturally expanded by this root of virtue and its radiance universally shine forth, so that even after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, it may be widely disseminated everywhere without ever perishing."
At that time, the World-Honored One, perceiving the thoughts in the minds of Guhyapada’s sons and others as they urged and encouraged him to address the Buddha, spoke to the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada:
“Guhyapada, you are capable of bearing these verses and phrases.”

"When I go beneath the Bodhi tree, you, together with the bodhisattvas, shall encounter the armies of Māra; at that time, you must use your majestic power to come and protect me so as to subdue those demonic forces, and you should immediately bring to mind, recite, and master [this teaching]."

Now, you must further protect the future age of decadence, causing the Dharma to spread throughout Jambudvīpa and pervade the ten directions; ensure that the teachings you have imparted endure for a long time, and restrain all those of various external heterodox schools.

At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, observing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had given this exhortation, rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and immediately spoke these words and verses, proclaiming the mantra:

“Hiri | Hūlu hūlu | Kiṅkiṇī-jāla | Akṣi-vidhūna-nivartana | Kṣānti-bala-bala-kṣaya | Śānta-bhīta-śṛṅga-gṛdhra-ilikha-khu-khu-lī-kha-lī | Rakṣa avīci | Tiṣṭha jaya-janma-gati-avakra | Maitryā parigṛhṇa saṃskṛta-siddhi | Dhāraya. “O devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, piśācas, whether humans or non-humans: may there always be peace, auspiciousness, and protection! You shall move the king of mountains, shake heaven and earth, and stir the king of waters!”
"By reciting this mantra, one subdues the non-Buddhists; it is that which the Lord of Dharma saves, the radiant blaze of the Dharma, and the phrase in which we place our deep faith.
Having heard this mantra, the hosts of devas each raised their voices and exclaimed:
"The True Dharma shall abide for a very long time, shaking the three thousand buddha-fields!"
The entire assembly together, Came before the King of Men and prostrated themselves.
"Take refuge in us so that we may be free from transgression; Grant us this freedom from fear and hardship.
Those who uphold these teachings Shall cause the True Dharma to endure forever.

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted offerings for seven days from the palace of the Kṣetrapāla king Pāñcika and the Vajrapāṇi Mārīci, thereby converting and transforming countless sentient beings.

Within seven days, he suddenly vanished from the palace in the wilderness and leaped into the void. Together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, all the devas above universally made offerings to the Buddha and the holy multitude. The hosts of jade maidens all joined in praise as they manifested a great radiance; the various celestial musicians played a hundred kinds of instruments spontaneously, flowers rained down from the sky, and the buddha-field shook violently, manifesting the Buddha’s great transformation.
The Buddha departed from the palace of the Mārṣa Guhyapada and returned to dwell on Vulture Peak Mountain, just as the King of Phoenixes returns to its abode.
While the Buddha was at Vulture Peak Mountain together with a multitude of bhikṣus, he was surrounded by his retinue of bodhisattvas, each of whom contemplated the Way and its teachings.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru departed from the great city of Rājagṛha together with a multitude of faithful and devoted elders and brahmins. When the people of the entire kingdom heard that the Buddha had returned to the country, they each gathered at the hour of *bhūta* (the afternoon) and likewise left the city, proceeding to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The king approached the Buddha and said:
"I was previously sitting and deliberating on certain matters when the bhikṣus came to the prince's location and declared aloud:"
"Today the World-Honored One went to the realm of the kingly ghost Kāntāra to visit the abode of Guhyaka Vajrapāṇi for a meal.
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Having heard this, I find it strange, difficult to fathom, and truly unprecedented."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are inconceivable; they are able to manifest great compassion and extend pity to all sentient beings.
The Tathāgata practices loving-kindness to universally rescue sentient beings, just as space is impartial and without partiality toward any one, for it serves all.
He traveled to the realm of the King of the Wilderness Ghosts and went to the residence of Guhyaka Vajrapāṇi to partake of food.
The Buddha’s great and expansive resolve was beyond all analogy; no words could fully express it.
If there are those who receive the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma, the proclamation of the Way’s instructions, and the rules for resolving doubts, none fail to attain peace.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
How many matters must the Mārṣa Guhyapada fulfill to abide in equanimity and attain perfect enlightenment?
"Only by being most profoundly reverent and planting the roots of manifold virtues can one possess such wondrous and great eloquence?
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"This matter is ultimate and cannot be surpassed; its supreme root of virtue is such that none can exceed it.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying, "Truly it is most authentic; because one plants the roots of virtue, one obtains this fruit."
"If there are those who have faith, what will their merit be like?
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Suppose that in each of the ten directions there were as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges River; even the limit of each individual grain of sand could still be known."

The Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi has seen incalculable numbers of Buddhas; having reached the very limits of his capacity, he has made offerings to and served them all. By virtue of these practices, he has accumulated great eloquence.
"You should contemplate this: all things have their beginning and their end.
The Buddha said to the king:

"In the distant past, incalculable and immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Śāntamati Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The world was called Selection of Lords, and the eon was named Immovable.

That Buddha Śāntamati exclusively transformed all the assemblies of bodhisattvas, causing them all to be diligent; he taught that in practicing the Dharma of a bodhisattva, there should be no indolence and no weariness of mind, casting aside body and life without stinginess, aspiring only to the Way and the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Courageous Strength (Vīryabala) who rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha Śāntamati was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Great Sage has proclaimed, I have received and understood its meaning."
If there is a bodhisattva who thinks to himself,
"I shall swiftly attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become a most perfectly awakened one," such a bodhisattva is said to be indolent.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva does not employ diligence and feels weary of birth and death, they do not join this mind with the Great Path to Buddhahood.
If a bodhisattva perceives birth and death as difficult, they perceive them as fetters and will not reach extinction.
Only by transforming sentient beings does one achieve perfect enlightenment. Why is this so?
It is because, World-Honored One, it is thus.

The Dharma of the Bodhisattva is to practice with universal diligence; wherever they may be within the cycle of birth and death, they guide and benefit immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain liberation, yet without any sense of teaching.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices, they should value birth-and-death and not revere extinction (nirvāṇa).

Once a bodhisattva has practiced with a primary focus on birth-and-death, they honor infinite Buddhas, guide and transform immeasurable sentient beings, hear countless teachings, and enter into the thoughts of sentient beings. Yet, if their practiced disposition comes to revere the practice of nirvāṇa and values the various meditative observations, they will then fall away and sink into minor attachments.
If there is a bodhisattva who fears birth and death, harbors dread and difficulty, and delights in the practice of nirvāṇa, they should reflect thus:
such a bodhisattva has fallen; by failing to practice, they have lost the conduct of a Tathāgata and thereby incurs fault toward all sentient beings.
What is meant by a bodhisattva who does not practice in accordance [with the path] and delights in the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Although they observe their own conduct with the desire to transform sentient beings, for this reason they are said to lack the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Their practice is that of the śrāvakas and not the practice of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because all śrāvaka practices involve a fear of the suffering of birth and death.
"A Bodhisattva wanders through immeasurable births and deaths without being constrained by them.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śāntamati praised the Bodhisattva Vīryabala, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Noble One!
You have eloquently spoken these words of pure and wholesome teaching.
When a bodhisattva practices the path, he relinquishes the security of his own body but does not relinquish others; he constantly examines himself and does not seek out the faults of others."
He asked again:
"What is meant by the conduct of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:

"Noble son! Rectify your own conduct and proclaim to sentient beings the matters of success and failure, as well as the hardships of birth and death; endure the sufferings of immeasurable births and deaths without fear;
take no pleasure in the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, but practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva."

Without dwelling near meditative contemplation within the triple world, they clearly understand dhyāna-concentration; they discern the evil realms and practice skillful means, exhausting the merits of dhyāna-wisdom and the noble insight that is inexhaustible.

They give rise to the wisdom of non-arising and proclaim for others that all things are fundamentally non-existent, that wisdom is without birth, and that they know what is received by all sentient beings as being without self. By means of wisdom, they transform and enlighten all sentient beings; they understand the stillness of all dharmas and protect them through liberation, and they master all Buddha-lands, realizing that the Buddha-lands are naturally empty and pure.
His wisdom is brilliant and clear; through this sagely wisdom, he realizes that all phenomena are non-existent, thereby augmenting his primary and secondary marks to enter into sublime adornment.

His wisdom has no objective sphere of activity, yet because he reverently upholds all roots of virtue without ever forgetting or abandoning them, he experiences little affliction and few worldly affairs.
He constantly acts to rescue sentient beings from conditioned existence;

his body and mind are serene and tranquil, accumulating merit and the Dharma without any sense of defilement or weariness, giving rise to meditative reflection and clearly realizing eternal stillness.

Through the skillful means of single-minded right concentration, one awakens to and realizes the profound and subtle Dharma. By proclaiming various categories of teachings, one distinguishes the various contemplations to protect the fruits of virtue, opens and transforms the disciplines of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, delights in the karma of liberation as understood by the Tathāgata, and manifests the fundamental conduct practiced by the Tathāgata while descending into the bodhisattva path.
"This, noble son, is the activity practiced by the Tathāgata.
"The King should know that at that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryabala, having heard this teaching on the purity of practice from that Tathāgata, further addressed that Buddha:"
"Most difficult, World-Honored One!
It is truly unprecedented.
Now, through the words of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, you have proclaimed that which a bodhisattva ought to practice."
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, according to my examination and understanding, these Bodhisattvas employ skillful means such that all dharmas arise from their own practice. It is just as the World-Honored One observes space, which contains all things; the myriad phenomena of the ten directions manifest their own essence as all forms in incalculable numbers, encompassing all categories of existence. Yet the activity of space remains entirely unimpeded.
"So it is, World-Honored One!

These bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), attain mastery over all dharmas; whether they be dharmas already studied or those not yet studied, the dharmas of ordinary beings, or the dharmas of supreme perfect enlightenment—all proceed from them."
"Just as, World-Honored One,
whatever grasses, woods, or hundred-grains encounter fire are all consumed by it;
so too does the Bodhisattva, acting with mastery over all dharmas, burn away all the darkness of ignorance within the triple world with the flames of wisdom until no smoke remains."
"Just as, World-Honored One, a man in a great rage,
his anger blazing intensely, might harm another person without regard for difficulty or consequence;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who, through skillful means and the mastery of his own wisdom-perfection (prajñāpāramitā), cuts away all the afflictions of sentient beings."
"Just as, World-Honored One,
a precious gem placed in turbid water immediately makes it clear and transparent,
so too does the Bodhisattva, through skillful means, eliminate all dust, the three defilements, and impurities."
It is just as, World-Honored One,
there is a medicine of great power called "Eliminator," which, when applied to poison, eliminates all poisons so that none remain.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva, by means of skillful expedients, wanders through the perils of the entire triple world, wielding the work of skillful wisdom to extinguish the afflictions and sensual desires of sentient beings.
For this reason, World-Honored One, one should cultivate this contemplation of skillful means: that all these bodhisattvas exercise mastery over all dharmas in their own practice.
"Thus it was, Great King!
When the Bodhisattva Vīryabala spoke these words, incalculable numbers of people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
If you wish to know, Great King, who else could the Bodhisattva Vīryabala have been at that time?"
Do not form such a view.
Why is this? It is because he is none other than the present Vajrapāṇi, the Mysterious Trace (Guhyapada) Vajra-wielding Malla.

This noble being’s body is firm and his vigor is resolute; he has donned the lofty, great armor of the infinite virtue of the great vow. His offerings to the Buddhas are beyond measure, and his radiant splendor is such that it can have no comparison.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru thought to himself:
"How heavy is this vajra wielded by the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada? Is it because he possesses such great power that he is able to grasp and hold it?"
At that time, Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, knowing the thoughts in King Ajātaśatru’s mind, took up his vajra and set it upon the ground.
As soon as it was placed on the earth, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada said to King Ajātaśatru, "Your Majesty, please try to lift this.
Then King Ajātaśatru, exerting all the strength of a great athlete, attempted to lift it; yet he could not move it from the ground even by as much as a hair's breadth.
At that time, the king marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and approached the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I have a great strongman who wears most extraordinary armor; he can seize a large elephant by its trunk and hurl it wherever he wishes without any hindrance."
"Today, though I lift this small vajra scepter, I cannot move it even as much as a hair's breadth.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru became all the more suspicious and asked:
"For what reason, World-Honored One?"
"Is it truly so? The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"This vajra resides within profound merit; it cannot be lifted or moved by the power of armor or the strength of elephants.
At that time, Guhyapada said to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"O Benevolent One, your title is Vajrapāṇi Kauśika; today, may you first lift this vajra from the ground."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, exerting his boundless supernatural power and fully manifesting his divine foot, attempted to lift that vajra but was utterly unable to do so.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came forward and addressed the Buddha:

"When our bodies and those of all the devas joined together to fight with the Asuras, I could lift the Asura Vemacitrin with a single finger and hurl him like a round ball, causing them all to flee in terror, not knowing where to go."
"Furthermore, is it because this vajra is so small that it cannot move?
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!"
This vajra enters into profound virtue; it cannot be compared to the body of an asura, even one three million three hundred and sixty thousand li in height, wherever it might be cast.
Kausika, what do you think? What is known by your mind?
"Is Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, heavy?
He replied, "It is exceedingly heavy."
“World-Honored One!
It is beyond measure and beyond analogy.
The Buddha said:

“Kauśika! Suppose there were a valiant hero of great and infinite power who took this vajra and held it in his right hand; he might place this vajra beside Mount Sumeru, hide it within it so that only its form is barely visible, and then lift both forms together. Even then, King Sumeru would still be lighter than the vajra.”
If, Śakra Devānām-Indra!
the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada were to strike Mount Cakravāḍa, Mount Mahācakravāḍa, and Mount Vajra with this vajra, he would cause them to shatter into dust.
"Even so, O noble son, you have not yet exhausted the manifestation of your power;
it cannot be fully compared. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 13 [and] Volume 14.
The Third Assembly of the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, Part Seven, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Elder Maudgalyāyana! You are praised by the World-Honored One as foremost in supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
You should now lift this vajra from the ground."

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana raised the vajra before him; with his boundless strength, he used the waters of the four great oceans to drench the sun. Its momentum further drew him as far as the Wild Horse World (Haya-loka), reaching everywhere without exception.

The power of the Way manifests transformations; he exerts his supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) and desires to move it, yet while this trichiliocosm trembles from top to bottom, he cannot shake the vajra even as much as a hair’s breadth.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, marveling at what had never occurred before, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the World-Honored One,
saying: “I pray only that the Great Sage would praise me as foremost among the śrāvakas in supernormal powers.”
I have personally tested my supernormal powers, shaking this trichiliocosm as if picking up a small bowl to cast it toward another Buddha-field.
I have converted and subdued the Nanda and Upananda Dragon Kings, who can consume great boulders as large as Mount Sumeru; how could they fail to move this small vajra?

In the mere instant of forming this thought, he grasped the sun and moon, causing them to halt and cease their movement; though he rubbed them with his hands, they could not be moved—this was a small vajra-pestle as fine as a hair.
"What is the meaning of this?
Could it be that my own body has lost its power of psychic flight?
The Buddha said:
“Maudgalyāyana! You have not lost your supernormal power.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!”
This is brought about by the power of the Bodhisattva’s supernormal faculties, which no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can attain.

Even if all the Mount Sumerus in as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to merge into a single Mount Sumeru, it might still be shaken; yet this vajra-pestle cannot be moved.
"The conduct established by the majestic spiritual power of a bodhisattva is inconceivable and as lofty as this.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having attained what he had never experienced before, declared with his own mouth:
"It is difficult to reach!"
"Great Sage!
Is it through the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that this Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada wields the vajra-pestle?
Furthermore, is the strength currently possessed by this Guhyapada the strength inherited from his parents' physical body?"
"Is it the power of the divine feet?
The Buddha said,
"It is the power of the physical body inherited from one's parents."
"Suppose a bodhisattva were to exercise the power of the divine feet (ṛddhipāda), being able to manifest everywhere and achieve success throughout both the heavens and the world.
The Buddha said to the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada:
"You yourself lift up this vajra."

Then Guhyapāda shook the trichiliocosm; with his right hand, he took up a vajra and hurled it into the void, where it circled seven times in the sky before returning to rest in the right hand of the Māhapuruṣa Guhyapāda.
At that time, the entire assembly that had gathered attained what they had never experienced before; with palms joined, they all took refuge in him and paid homage, speaking with one voice:
"Unsurpassed! Unsurpassed!"
"The power of the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada is truly so wondrous!
May all sentient beings likewise attain such great strength and inexhaustible momentum.
Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How many dharmas must a bodhisattva practice to attain such power and infinite majesty?
The Buddha said,
“A bodhisattva possesses ten great dharmas to attain such elephant-like, infinite great power.”
What are the ten? First, one should rather sacrifice body and life than fail to diligently receive the True Dharma;
second, one should never be arrogant, but remain humble and reverent, bowing in respect toward all sentient beings.
Third, upon seeing sentient beings who are stubborn and difficult to transform, one establishes them in patience;
fourth, upon seeing those suffering from famine, one provides them with excellent and delicious food as an offering;
fifth, upon witnessing those who are terrified, one encourages, consoles, and brings them peace.
Sixth: if there are sentient beings afflicted by severe illness, to treat them with excellent medicine;
seventh: if there are those who are weak and inferior and thus held in contempt by others, to regard them with reverence and affection so that they are not treated with neglect or disdain;
eighth: to apply pure mud and water to the temples of the Tathāgata to repair their dilapidated or deficient parts.
Ninth: To see those who are solitary, suffering, impoverished, and in distress, constantly bearing heavy burdens, and to cause them to be freed from their hardships and most grievous calamities;
Tenth: If there are those who are unprotected and have no one to rely upon, to always provide for them, and to ensure that what is spoken is as it is said, without deviation or failure.
"These are the ten dharmas.
The King again asked the Buddha:

"How many dharmas does a Bodhisattva possess that are characterized by benevolence and harmony, such that in all his comings and goings and movements, he always remains gentle and refined, never giving rise to coarse thoughts?"
The Buddha said:
“There are eight dharmas of benevolence and harmony for a bodhisattva. What are these eight?

First, their disposition is upright and straightforward, free from flattery and deceit; second, their conduct is harmonious and elegant, always devoid of sycophancy or hypocrisy; third, their minds are pure and mature, forever free from falsehood; fourth, their mental actions are firm and essential, never weak or inferior; fifth, they are without delusion, their will being fixed upon benevolence and harmony; sixth, as benefactors of the world, they receive extraordinary virtuous qualities; seventh, their mental actions are thoroughly realized and free from attachment; eighth, in contemplating sin and merit, their minds harbor no conceptualizations.
"These are the eight matters.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one's will and nature become matured as they come and go and circulate through the world."
What are the four? First, being among humans as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin), one encounters the appearance of various Buddhas and does not abandon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Second, being in the heavens as Śakra, Lord of Devas—the god among gods—one constantly beholds the Buddhas and does not deviate from the Way of the Sūtras.
Third, even if one becomes a Brahmā King and attains sovereign mastery, one plants the seeds of the path and does not allow the resolve for enlightenment to be destroyed;
fourth, one is constantly born in pure Buddha-lands and personally beholds the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as they preach the Dharma.
"These are the four matters.
King Ajātaśatru again asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'relying on faith'?"
The Buddha said,
"Great King, it is where a virtuous friend sits."
He asked the Buddha again,
“On what does the donor sit?
The Buddha said:
“Great King! The field of giving lies in great wealth, abundant resources, and many treasures;
those who uphold the precepts attain rebirth in the heavens.”
Those who dwell in patience have countenances that are pure and joyful, and they are always upright and handsome;
those who practice diligence cultivate with vigor and achieve penetration, excelling above the masses;
those who practice meditative concentration always attain tranquil stillness, and their faculties remain undisturbed.
Those with wisdom sever the afflictions of all worldly dust and defilements;
those who are widely learned give rise to great insight, resolving doubts in every matter so that no residual fetters remain;
and those who are diligent in study gather together to enter the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
"To observe impermanence, non-self, and tranquility, and to eliminate all inversions while remaining seated—this is called 'sitting in faith.
He asked again:
"What is the seat for the mindfulness that accords with the seasons?"
The Buddha said: “Great King!

Contemplate impermanence, suffering, and stillness while seated in right view; do not follow wrong actions, and with body and mind purified, sit in meditative contemplation to give rise to supernormal powers.”
He asked again:
"Where does the Way reside? He replied:
"Abiding in non-liberation while seated, one accomplishes the fruit of the Way, free from the hardships of the three realms.
He asked again:
"In what place does this non-liberation reside?"
He replied: "Those who have no liberation sit within the very liberation from the manifold afflictions of birth and death.
He asked again:
"What does the Buddha sit upon when he appears? He replied:

"He sits upon the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that he has practiced; he turns the wheel of Dharma without causing destruction, and he ensures that the teachings of the Three Jewels are never severed."
He asked again:
"Who shall bring forth the Buddha? He replied:
"Great King! One who is able to give rise to profound faith understands that which is fundamentally non-existent.
He asked again:
"Who gives rise to profound faith?
He replied, "It is whoever is able to resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva."
He asked again:
"Who is it that gives rise to the bodhicitta? He replied:
"He is one whose will and nature are settled and undisturbed.
He asked again:
"Who is it whose will and nature are settled and undisturbed?"
He replied: "It is that his practice of great compassion has never ceased.
He asked again:
"Who does not sever great compassion?
He replied, "It is one who does not abandon any sentient being."
He asked again:
"Who does not abandon sentient beings? He replied:
"It is one who brings peace to oneself and brings peace to all.
He asked again:
"Who is it that brings peace to oneself and to all sentient beings?"
He replied: "It is one who causes the Way to flourish and ensures that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
He asked again:
"Who does not sever the Three Jewels? He replied,
"One who abandons worldly defilements (kleśa) does not sever the Three Jewels."
King Ajātaśatru stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is truly unprecedented,
World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata proclaims and enters into the laws and regulations;

the Tathāgata disseminates the teachings and the dharmas he proclaims until they reach gentle compliance. He abandons the karmic activities of nihilism and eternalism, yet does not forget or lose the fruits of retribution.

One enters into the established practices of conditioned formations without confusion; there is no karma that is neither good nor evil, nor pure nor impure; one diligently cultivates the fruits of realization without any transgression or loss.
Indeed, World-Honored One!
Who will enter this vow to resolve the doubts of the multitude and accord with the Tathāgata’s teaching of the true and correct Dharma?
Who, upon hearing this Dharma, will give rise to hesitation?
Only those who have failed to plant the roots of virtue in past lives.
"Following evil friends, we lacked faith and slandered [the Dharma]. World-Honored One!

In our past lives, we have planted roots of virtue; it was not that we were without merit or blessings. Now that we have been granted the opportunity to hear the True Dharma, we wish to repay this grace, yet our sincere intentions cannot suffice."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and Mañjuśrī, whose virtue is compassion, have resolved our manifold doubts and manifested great radiance for us.
The World-Honored One’s excellent words fully encompass the Brahma-conduct; he is the most virtuous friend who has attained the compassion of a Great Man, being a supreme companion.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Silent Intent (Prashantamati) stepped forward and questioned the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, saying:
"You, sir, have established this Dharma of the sutra so that it may be propagated throughout all future ages."

He replied: "I shall establish the essentials of this sutra so that, in the final age after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, it may be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa, ensuring that all Dharma-preachers and noble sons (satpuruṣa) receive its illumination."
Guhyapada spoke again:
"Now, son of good family!
The Buddha has established this essential sūtra, and all Buddhas protect it."
Why is this? Those who are able to protect it have well studied the Dharma; they do not give rise to written characters, their speech is inexhaustible, and nothing can interrupt them.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, does not abandon any phenomena. Why is this?
Because they are without arising.
That which is unarisen cannot be destroyed; for this reason, the Tathāgata has said:
"The Tathāgata appears as one who is unarisen.
The Tathāgata abides established in the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the Dharma abides according to the Dharma."
"Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the Buddha-dharma remains eternally as it was.
Abiding in this way, the twelve links of dependent origination are not erroneous;
one does not confuse dependent origination, nor does one confuse the True Dharma.
Furthermore, observing that this Dharma is eternally beyond verbal expression, it is said that the True Dharma is characterized by non-verbal expression.
Jiyi asked: “Guhyapāda! What do you mean?”
"He who protects the True Dharma dons the armor of the great vow; it is by means of this armor that he is so called.
He further asked Śāntamati:
"One who dons the armor of the great vow intends to protect the True Dharma and not to confuse the various dharmas, yet does not do so by means of these dharmas."
Why is this? Because this True Dharma is such that all phenomena are entirely without confusion; he protects the True Dharma.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'disturbing the True Dharma'? He replied:
"To rely upon fear and dread constitutes confusion."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
To be ultimately undisturbed regarding what is called 'disturbance of meaning'—this is what is termed 'protecting the True Dharma.
He then asked the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada:
"Is there a skillful means by which one may protect the True Dharma amidst all the turmoil of the world?
He replied, "Noble son!"
They protect it because of confusion. Why is this?
It is because they rely on the sixty-two views of worldly heterodoxy and doubt.
The conduct of a bodhisattva takes emptiness as its foundation; therefore, it is in conflict with all worldly things.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Those of the mundane world rely on various calculations of permanence and establish a dependence upon a self, regarding it as pure and secure.

The Bodhisattva constantly realizes that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; for this reason, it is said that he contends with the world and follows along with its current.
Yet, through skillful means, the Bodhisattva flows against the current to its very source, turning back from the stream of birth and death to manifest within the heavy world of the present.
The Bodhisattva reveres the accumulation of merit and the gathering of virtue; for this reason, he contends with the world's turmoil.
Worldly people rely upon the aggregates (skandhas), the sense-fields (āyatanas), and the eighteen elements (dhātus).
Practicing the deeds of a bodhisattva with a mind free from attachment, one therefore contends with and disturbs the world.
Why is this? Because one does not conform to the defilements of the world.
"Therefore, Śāntamati!
When a bodhisattva protects all the true Dharma, they will come into conflict with the world.
He asked again:
“Guhyaka! How does a practitioner protect the True Dharma? He replied:

“Noble son! By receiving the True Dharma, one protects one’s own person, and likewise protects the life-span and physical forms of sentient beings; one protects all dharmas by means of non-protection.”
He asked again:
"How does one receive it? He replied:
"When the self is tranquil, sentient beings are serene.
When sentient beings are tranquil, the three periods of time become silent.
When the three periods of time are silent, the Buddha-dharma becomes silent."
When the Buddha-dharma has become silent, the Buddha-field becomes tranquil.
When the Buddha-field has become tranquil, all dharmas become tranquil.
To have no place of resort within all dharmas is what is called "protecting and upholding the true Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
This is indeed what is called 'protecting and upholding the True Dharma.'"
Their protection of all dharmas consists in having nothing to protect and nothing to forget.
Furthermore, those who protect the True Dharma receive everything, yet they remain free from deluded thoughts regarding all perceptions.

Having already attained the absence of conceptualization, one does not engage in heedlessness regarding all delusive thoughts; this is called being without heedlessness regarding all dharmas, and it is precisely what is termed the Dharma of the Path.
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named King of Worthiness (Bhadrarāja), who stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
The speech of all Buddhas is exceedingly tranquil; what is it that is seen by those who behold it?"
The Buddha said: “The meaning of correct teaching through speech is the principle of tranquility; all that is joyfully practiced is simply tranquility.

Because one applies patience, and having already applied patience, one is able to kindle [the flame]; because one has already kindled it, it is called radiance; because one has already become radiant, it is called tranquility, which constitutes the state of detachment (*śānta-prasrabdhi*). This is how the Tathāgata protects the True Dharma, and this is what is called the *dhāraṇī* of the assembly of all Tathāgatas.”
"The way of the Buddha is sustained in this manner: neither grasping at the Dharma nor abandoning the Dharma, one proclaims such practice.

When he had spoken these words as a response to the realization of the Devaputra Bhadrapāla, the minds of a full thousand bhikṣus were liberated through the exhaustion of outflows, and in a thousand devaputras, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye arose regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Devaputra Bhadra-rāja, saying:
"From where have you obtained this eloquence?
The Devaputra replied:
"If one can sever all hindrances and attain nothing at all, thereby realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then because there is no dependence, this is called eloquence (*pratibhāna*)."
To understand this for oneself—wherein the spiritual consciousness does not shift, does not pass through other consciousnesses, and has no fixed point—is called eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
When the mind is not distracted and wanders within that which is grasped, if one can practice and uphold the dharma of non-attachment, one attains this eloquence.
If one contemplates all dharmas and understands that their coming and going are but manifestations, and if the consciousness attains faith and rest, one will then attain eloquence.
O son of good family!

A practitioner who acts in this way attains eloquence (*pratibhāna*); being without any abiding and having no course of action to be performed, they cross over the perils of the waves and the four great rivers.
That which is unarisen and does not originate likewise does not cease; that which cannot be extinguished is what is called "crossing over" and attaining eloquence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Silent Intent (Śāntamati) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From where has this Bodhisattva Worthy King (Bhadrarāja) come to reach this land, such that he possesses such eloquence?"
The Buddha said:
"They have come from the land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
Having passed away there and been reborn here in this world of Wondrous Joy (Sukhāvatī), they all desire to see and hear the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata as his secret essentials."

Śāntamati, you should know that this Devaputra, King Bhadra, has entered the chamber of the Dharma and mastered his mind through dhāraṇī; even if one were to proclaim his merits for an eon, or even longer than an eon, the limits of his eloquence could not be exhausted.
He again asked the Buddha:
"What is meant by the 'Dharma-chamber Dhāraṇī,' which this son of heaven has attained and by which he follows the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! That which is called ‘attaining the dhāraṇī of the Dharma-chamber’ means entering into the inexhaustible syllables of wisdom; all phenomena enter this chamber.”
Regarding all phenomena, one performs no action whatsoever; one understands the chamber of the Dharma and practices within the chamber of the Dharma.

Through the sounds of syllables, that which is spoken by the mouth, one neither perceives the act of constructing a dwelling nor the act of not constructing one; rather, one proclaims all matters of sound. This is called the practice of the dhāraṇī for entering the chamber of the Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
That which is said to "enter" the Dharma is, moreover, that all dharmas are unattainable.
This is what is called "entry."
As for the words of the wisdom that emerges, they do not come from anywhere nor enter into an inner chamber.
Furthermore, those words do not appear within the inner chamber, nor do they appear as they emerge; they have no destination and no direction.

Furthermore, regarding the convergence of these successive characters, one does not form conceptual thoughts; the characters do not conform to dharmas, nor are they non-dharmas, and there is no such conceptualization.
These characters are entirely without speech, nor are they without speech; they are without increase or decrease.
Furthermore, regarding syllables, they are not seen to arise, nor do they cease; there is no creating of syllables, nor is there any loss.
Moreover, Śāntamati!
Just as with the enumeration of syllables, so too is the enumeration of mental states; all such enumerations of dharmas have a point of convergence.
If there were any enumeration of dharmas, they would then be non-enumerable. Why is this?
Because that which does not resort to the enumeration of dharmas and possesses no enumeration is called the "enumeration of dharmas."
In accordance with the enumeration of dharmas, it is thus called "entering the chamber of dharmas.
One does not enter the past; one enters the non-arising of dharmas that have no origin.
Since there is nothing produced, and since there is no arising, what is there to enter?

By means of non-entry—if one enters into these various enumerations—in this very way, one is able to reach the Dharma-gate and personally behold original non-existence; thereupon, one attains stable abiding and enters the practice of the dhāraṇī within the chamber of the Dharma, entering the minds of sentient beings.
By entering the minds of sentient beings and following their inclinations, one should preach the Dharma to those who are ready to be saved.
If one receives this dhāraṇī, it is called "Quiescent Intent" (Śāntamati).
Quiescent Intent!

The Bodhisattva’s mind is free from defilement; his mind is pure, majestic, harmonious, and exceedingly luminous. His nature transcends all that he dwells within, remaining serene and composed. His wisdom is without error and his vows are firm. Those whom he is destined to deliver cannot be destroyed by Māra; he subdues all external and heterodox practices without exception, extinguishes the dust of afflictions, and eliminates all enemies and thieves.
His physical strength is flourishing and his mind is free from timidity; his eloquence is inexhaustible, what he speaks is immeasurable, and that to which he turns is limitless.

His wisdom is unimpeded as he enters the state of awakening; his brilliance extends far and wide as he proclaims profound, wondrous, and authentic words. His vast learning is like the rivers and seas.
This samādhi is like Mount Sumeru situated within the great ocean, and like a lion amidst the great assembly.
It does not rely on worldly dharmas, just as a lotus flower is unsullied by dust or water.
He is free from feelings of hatred or attachment; like the earth, he causes the hundred grains, grasses, and trees to grow, and brings peace to all the people.
He washes away all defilements like clear water; he transforms and enlightens sentient beings and burns away all poisons and hardships, just as a blazing fire consumes all grasses and trees.
He universally instructs sentient beings, just as a great wind blows upon everything without exception.
He practices a mind of equanimity, like the full moon illuminating the stars.
He eliminates lust, anger, and delusion, just as the sunlight dispels all darkness.
Subduing the mind, intellect, and consciousness is like a valiant general crushing a formidable enemy.
Harmonizing the mind is like a dragon king.
Maturing it according to the occasion is like rain falling after a deep, dark cloud has thundered.

In this way, the Bodhisattva harmonizes his mind, spreading the rain of Dharma to moisten the three realms; he proclaims the water of ambrosia to purify the defilements of the mind, just as heavenly rain washes away all wind-blown dust. He cures the various maladies of lust, anger, and ignorance, just as a skilled physician treats the illnesses of all people.

To set one's will upon non-action and practice the True Dharma is to serve as a Dharma King who instructs the ten directions; it is like a secular king governing his myriad subjects, protecting and transforming all beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Just as the Four Heavenly Kings rule over the four continents, and just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, dwells in the Trāyastriṃśa palace to instruct and guide the devas and humans, so too does the Bodhisattva dwell within the realm of desire to transform the various classes of sentient beings.
Through the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and fine touch—which are as pure as bright pearls—he is able to subdue the mind and attain mastery.
If one is like Brahmā, lord over the celestial beings, whose mind is pure and free from all dependence or attachment;
who is like a flying bird soaring through the void, unimpeded by anything and maintaining its course with ease and composure.
Just as a leader of deer, having emerged from his herd, respectfully receives the teachings of the Dharma and cherishes true practice;
like a mother who loves her child, ensuring their safety and well-being while instructing them in all arts and skills.
It is like a stern father who guides his descendants, causing them to hear and turn toward all dharmas.

Like King Śāntamati, he is adorned by his own virtues, embellished with the thirty-two marks of a great man and graced by the various qualities of the eighty minor characteristics, whom all the world collectively honors and looks up to.

They are not bound by false views; they are fully endowed with the seven riches and free from the karma of poverty; they are protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions and praised by all the wise; they are universally esteemed by all assemblies and lauded by the higher devas; they are remembered and rescued by virtuous friends; they are the most eminent among those who preach the Dharma, possessing the six supernormal powers and attaining mastery.

Furthermore, they universally enter into the nature and conduct of sentient beings and pervasively penetrate all their faculties; they proclaim the scriptures without ever becoming weary or indolent, and never set their hearts on seeking gain or offerings.

He delights in disseminating the teachings of the Dharma without stinginess; his resolve is pure and free from transgression or failure; he is patient and clear-sighted, never erring or losing his way; whatever deeds he undertakes, he brings them to completion; through pure diligence, his mind-nature is peaceful and harmonious; with single-minded purity, he eliminates all defilements; his awakening-mind is serene and his wisdom is pure; he cultivates the four Brahma-vihāras without negligence; he accomplishes the world-transcending dhyāna, samādhi, and right concentration (samyaksamāpatti); he attains the unsurpassed path of the bodhisattva and the path of the Buddha; he is universally able to fulfill all appropriate practices without ceasing midway, until he reaches the stage of *avaivartika*.
This, Śāntamati, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the emptiness of phenomena and attains dhāraṇī; their meritorious achievements are thus immeasurable and sublime.

Śāntamati, you should know that even if a bodhisattva were to dwell in the world for a hundred thousand years without attending to any other matters, merely extolling this dhāraṇī practice, they could not exhaustively describe the dhāraṇī practices or the virtues of all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Silent Intent (Śāntamati) said to the Devaputra Worthy King (Bhadrarāja):
"O Benevolent One, you possess great benefit, boundless goodness, and auspicious celebration, for now the Tathāgata has praised your virtues with such radiant glory."
The devaputra replied:
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Within these dharmas, there is no place where a true, ultimate attainment can be found."
To praise his meritorious achievements, O son of noble family!
Since he is without form, without appearance, and without physical manifestation, even one who practices in this way can never fully exhaust the praise of his meritorious achievements.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Bhadrapāla came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All dharmas cannot be grasped or taken up; they are devoid of self and have no ownership. For this reason, they cannot be bestowed upon others, nor can they be taken away."

"Indeed, Great Sage! If there should be a person who practices and delights in this, they should practice equanimity; if they diligently uphold and practice the training in equanimity, they will attain this Dharma-gate."
"It is just as, World-Honored One,
this great earth appears with its soil upon the water and the water upon the wind.

Even if the element of earth were to spread these soils throughout the world, and if someone were to dig into that earth and remove the dust and soil until, through the utmost exertion of effort, they finally reached the water."
He does not abandon those who have gone far away, but provides water for the thirsty.

The Tathāgata’s noble wisdom universally enters the nature and conduct of all sentient beings; thus, those liberated by the Tathāgata proceed toward the Dharma-gates and cultivate diligence. Through these skillful means, they attain the light of great wisdom, and such diligent ones are never deceived or harmed.
It is just as when one digs the earth very deeply, removing the soil, and thereby finds water;
likewise, if there is someone who practices with diligence during the lifetime of a Tathāgata, this gives rise to the great radiance of wisdom.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
If sons of good family and daughters of good family desire to seek the Buddha-way, they should constantly practice diligence.
By what kind of diligence?
One should, by means of this, approach the gateways of all dharmas through the gateway of dharmas.
It is just as, World-Honored One,
a man born blind who has never seen form since birth.
If there were someone who does not practice diligence, they would be called a companion of the ignorant, dark, and blind, failing to see the beginning and end of the arising of all phenomena.
It is just so, World-Honored One!
Those with eyes behold objects when they encounter light, yet see nothing when no light emerges in the dark night; the celestial eye of external seers is likewise.
Without the guidance of virtuous friends, there is no transformation or enlightenment, and one remains ignorant of all contemplations regarding the phenomena one experiences.

Just as with the divine eye, if there is a man who possesses innate wisdom, he does not rely on external light to achieve vision; because he possesses the virtue of great knowledge, his practice is such as this.
"Just as, World-Honored One, when birds fly through a vast wilderness and roam across a wide expanse of marshland, they see no increase or decrease in that empty wild;
so too is the practice of diligence of all bodhisattvas: they see no increase or decrease in the Buddha-way as they enter the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment."
It is just as, World-Honored One, when trees grow from snow and rain upon that Himālaya mountain, they cannot be harmed by any winds.

In this same way, a bodhisattva should act according to the occasion, generating the radiance of wisdom to illuminate all things; he does not engage in calculating or discriminating among sentient beings, and there is nothing lost or forgotten regarding his sphere of activity.
It is just as, World-Honored One,
when a Wheel-Turning Sage King is born into a noble lineage, the seven treasures appear. What are these seven?

First is the purple-gold wheel with a thousand spokes; second is the white elephant with six tusks; third is the dark-blue divine horse with a black head and crimson mane; fourth is the bright moon transformation pearl with eight facets; fifth is the jade maiden queen, whose mouth has the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus and whose body the fragrance of sandalwood; sixth is the holy minister who presides over the treasury; and seventh is the great general who presides over the army, commanding the forces of the four regions.
Thus it is, Great Sage!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests the seven treasures in the world, the treasure of the Way naturally appears in the world.
What are these seven?

The first is the treasure of the perfection of giving; the treasures of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, wisdom, and skillful means appear in the world to deliver and save all beings.
Just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King travels through the four quarters of the realm, there are countless people with various thoughts, so it is with the Bodhisattva:

by means of the four methods of benevolence, they rescue and gather in sentient beings; yet they do not conceive of sentient beings as having various categories, for they understand them to be fundamentally non-existent.

It is just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King undertakes a task and sits upon his rightful throne; there being no strife or contention, and no need for arguments regarding right or wrong, the people naturally submit to his commands.

In this way, when a bodhisattva occupies the seat of the Buddha-dharma, there is no one from whom conflict could arise; even though the various officials and retinues of Māra harbor evil intentions, they are naturally subdued.
It is just as, in this trichiliocosm, there first stand the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
Thus it is, O Great Sage!

A bodhisattva who is a seeker of the Way is likewise: first they establish the Great Vehicle, next they establish great compassion, and their nature and character are most perfectly settled in benevolence and harmony.
It is like when the sun first rises: its great radiance first illuminates the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains and Sumeru, the King of Mountains, and only then does it illuminate the rest.

In this way, the Bodhisattva manifests the brilliance of the sun of wisdom, universally illuminating the three realms; with a mind of benevolence and harmony, he first shines upon sentient beings, and through the radiance of the Mahāyāna, he dispels the darkness of the three poisons so that all attain supernormal powers.
It is just as, World-Honored One!

All trees, cities, states, districts, and villages rely upon the earth for their sustenance; all that is produced—the hundred grains, grasses, and woods—all look up to the earth, so that the myriad things that arise attain their autonomy.
"In this way, for a bodhisattva, all roots of virtue arise because of the mind of the Way; they nurture holy wisdom and lead to the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Bodhisattva King Worthy, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O son of noble family!
To explain and draw upon this analogy to describe the meritorious deeds with such great clarity is truly wonderful.
Furthermore, O son of noble family!

Just as with the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm, so too is the noble wisdom of the bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī; he is fully capable of employing analogies and explaining characteristics regarding how all things ultimately return to impermanence.
To state the essential point: it is likewise with never becoming weary or disheartened, such that one is able to fully expound upon all that has been taught. Why is this?
Because there is neither speech nor anything to be spoken.
If there is a bodhisattva who has not yet attained dhāraṇī, they lack the causal conditions for verbal instruction.

Furthermore, such a bodhisattva is not free from hindrances and does not give rise to eloquence; other śrāvakas, lacking this eloquence, do not contemplate the fundamental source when preaching the Dharma.
Why is this so? Because this assembly of bodhisattvas has attained unimpeded eloquence; their speech is inexhaustible, free from obscuration, and without pause or interruption.
With analytical eloquence, they preach the Dharma before the honored presence of all Buddhas, neither timid nor weak.
In this way, the bodhisattva, having been established by the Buddha and having attained the gate of dhāraṇī, speaks with confidence and without any sense of inferiority.
Thus, the bodhisattva attains the three kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
What are the three?
First is the dhāraṇī that is without obstruction; second is eloquence that is without obstruction; third is the Dharma of the Path that is without obstruction.
These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three matters by which one enters into pure karma. What are these three?
First is natural purity; second is primordial non-existence purity; third is the purity of the ultimate limit (*koṭi*).
These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three matters by which one may enter the inexhaustible.
What are these three?
First, the Dharma of the sutras is inexhaustible; second, the meaning of the words is inexhaustible; third, the instructions and admonitions proclaimed are inexhaustible—these are the three.
Furthermore, one enters the three abodes of non-abiding.
What are these three?
First is noble wisdom that has no abode; second is speech and literary adornment that also have no abode; third is the establishment of what is cultivated that likewise has no abode.
These are the three.
Furthermore, one attains three forms of decisive response. What are these three?
The first is the wisdom proclaimed through censure; the second is the eloquence that arises spontaneously; the third is timely wisdom—these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three ways to swiftly attain the wisdom of return.
What are these three?

First, resolving doubts so that no further fetters remain; second, severing hesitation so as to eliminate lingering indecision; third, being able to gladden the minds and hearts of all sentient beings.
These are the three.
When these words were spoken, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the *dhāraṇī*.
Thereupon, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that the World-Honored Buddha will establish the Dharma scriptures, so that at the time of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final age, they may be spread throughout Jambudvīpa, remaining for a long time without being extinguished."
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the four directions; having completed his observation, he spoke in verse:
"The senses subdued, naturally victorious; The faculties stilled, free from harm.
Without basis, severing non-existence; Subduing the hosts of Māra’s armies."
Liberated, pure, and stainless, Fearless and free from dread,
Having cast off the heavy burden, The physician, the master of divine spells—
He who subdues external heterodox teachers And gathers them in through the Dharma.
To protect those who practice the Dharma, this divine mantra was spoken by the Buddha.
Through non-self one eliminates the self; its meaning should be understood as liberation.
Regarding these four great kings, he spoke these words on the absence of moisture.
The merit of courageously upholding these verses is pure and perfectly equal;
Brahmā, Śakra, and the Lord of Devas—such is the vehicle they have created.
Maitreya has attained that patient endurance, observing and examining all with compassion.
With love and reverence one beholds Brahmā; herein there is nothing to transgress.
Leaving the wilderness for the open space, the rootless Dharma is called purity.
Having subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials, this divine mantra is therefore proclaimed.
The Honored One among Men established this sutra of excellent meaning and phrasing;
at that time, it was widely disseminated according to the capacity of those able to receive it.
When this dhāraṇī-vidyā was spoken, the earth shook greatly.
All the Māras came together, each proclaiming these words with their own mouths:
"We shall protect the head and leader; such a one is called a Dharma Master.
If one receives this sutra in hand, they shall return to what was spoken by the Buddha."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Guhyapada, the Vajrapāṇi:
"Because you have established the essentials of this sutra;
now that you have established it, none shall be able to disturb it."

Why is this so? The Buddha recollects and remembers that in a past life there was a Buddha named Ratnacandra who appeared in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The world was called Wu-yue (Joyless).
During the time of that Buddha, there were two bhikṣus who served as Dharma masters: the first was named Zhiji (Wisdom-Quiescence), and the second was named Chizhicheng (Upholder of Sincerity).

His majestic spiritual power and transformations were of boundless and supreme virtue; he was a Great Honored One of towering sublimity who received these chapter-verses and mantras from that Tathāgata and upheld them.

For half an eon after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he maintained the Dharma, whereby hundreds of thousands of billions of Māras throughout the trichiliocosm were all converted and enlightened, and they embraced the unsurpassed, right, and true Way.
Guhyapada! If you wish to know who those two bhikṣus were who served as Dharma masters at that time, could they possibly have been anyone else?
Do not entertain such a thought.
Why is this so? That which is the quiescent Dharma is none other than my own body.
The bhikṣu who upholds the Dharma with utmost sincerity is the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada.
"These verses and passages shall cause this Dharma of the sutra to bring great benefit and to protect the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire assembly on all four sides and declared aloud:
"You noble sons are capable and able to undertake this task."

In this regard, the Tathāgata, having accumulated merit and virtue over countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, has mastered the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way, and by means of this mastery, he protects and sustains it without any hindrance.
"From that time until now, we have been sustained by this; it is from this that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present arise.
Thereupon, thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly rose from their seats, stood with palms joined, bowed their heads in prostration to the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Abandoning body and life, They contemplate the sublime tranquility."
To uphold this sutra-dharma is praised by the Protectors of the World.
This sutra is like medicine, which cures all illnesses;
by upholding its spoken teachings, one brings forth the intention of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the five hundred devaputras, including the Devaputra Bhadrapāla, spoke these verses:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, We shall accumulate merit through such intention;
By upholding this sutra, It is most supreme, extraordinary, profound, and wondrous."
Thereupon, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada spoke these verses:
"This discourse is without letters, yet it is proclaimed through words;
That which was performed by the Honored One among Men— I shall uphold and disseminate it."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahmā Viśvabhū:
"The Tathāgata possesses three immeasurables, and the merit of his unsurpassed offerings is without limit."
What are these three?

First, to cultivate a sincere, harmonious, and benevolent mind and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; second, having given rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, to protect the True Dharma; third, to explain the Dharma as one has heard it for others and to act accordingly in one's own conduct.
These constitute the most incalculable merit.

Brahmā, you should know that the Tathāgata has accumulated meritorious deeds through these three matters; even if his lifespan were to remain in the world for an eon, he could not fully explain them in detail.
Therefore, Brahmā, you should serve the Tathāgata, the Arhat, with compliance and reverence.
These are the three matters, Brahmā!

By making offerings to the Tathāgata and receiving even a four-line verse, one upholds and protects that which has been taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Why is this so? Because all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are born from this Dharma; therefore, one should make offerings to the Dharma.

One does not offer to the Dharma with food or clothing; rather, offering through the Dharma is the most honored among all forms of sustenance, for it is supreme, foremost, peerless, and without equal.
Therefore, Brahmā! You should honor one another with the True Dharma; this is the nourishment of the ultimate truth, not with food or clothing.
Thus did the Buddha himself recollect, O Brahmā King!
In the past, he was once born as the crown prince of a king, named Iṅgitakārin.
Having been born into a royal family, he was thus instructed and took sincere delight in the Dharma.

Once, while lying in a dream, he heard these four lines of verse: "Fundamental conduct that is heedless has no path to liberation; for the sake of sentient beings, one sets the mind upon the Way; with the mind dwelling in the seclusion of the mountains, following mindfulness, there is nothing craved or received, for all is fundamentally at peace."
The Buddha said to Brahmā:

"At that time, having heard these verses of instruction and awakened from the dream, he contemplated them with perfect clarity; he was filled with great joy, and his mind felt liberated and expansive."
Immediately, he praised with a verse, saying:
"How wonderful is this supreme peace and bliss! Having attained the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma, I shall fill all sentient beings— The poor among gods and humans."
The Buddha told the Great Brahma Heaven, Shan'an:
"At that time, the Prince obtained the Treasury of Peaceful Composure (*anāvilakośa*). Understanding that letters are non-existent, he thought to himself:
'May the meaning of these verses fill the poverty and destitution of sentient beings.'"
He went and said to his parents:
"Do you have any store of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, mother-of-pearl, agate, or bright pearls?
I wish to relieve the poor and destitute with these, so that they may rejoice."
The parents replied:
"All wealth and possessions are not true treasures; they are merely shared among the five families: water, fire, thieves, enemies and creditors, government officials, and wicked sons."
"The wisdom of extensive learning, which seeks neither clothing nor food, is extremely difficult to find.
His parents said, "Excellent!"
"Let it be as you have resolved.
He then took the extensive gifts and bestowed them upon those in need,
causing them to realize the emptiness of the three realms and attain the difficult-to-attain, inexhaustible wisdom.

For this reason, Brahmā, having heard this single four-line verse, transformed eight thousand people by encouraging them to resolve their minds on the Way, and countless sentient beings were destined to be born in the heavens.
For this reason, O Brahmā!

Should there be anyone who receives this profound and wondrous Dharma, upholds, recites, reads, and explains it extensively for others; and should they hear it with joy and practice it accordingly, their merit shall be immeasurable, reaching the treasury of the infinite.
"Furthermore, Brahmā!
There are three dharmas of practicing the Mahāyāna path that greatly benefit bodhisattvas.
What are these three?"
First, to establish oneself through hearing and practice, receiving the teachings without weariness;
second, to establish oneself through hearing with practice as the essential, guarding the mouth as foremost, and not adding harm to sentient beings with a malicious mind;
third, not abandoning great compassion.
These are the three.
Therefore, Brahmā!
For the benefit of sentient beings, you should provide encouragement and assistance for this essential sūtra.
Furthermore, there are two matters by which the practices and vows one has undertaken will not be forgotten or lost. What are these two?
The first is when the Buddha first attained enlightenment.
First, to exhort and assist the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma;

second, for Brahmā to exhort and assist the future thousand Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of this Bhadrakalpa to turn the wheel of Dharma, causing them to transform those who have left the household life so that they may perform the practices of Bodhisattvas.
Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the Sovereign Dharma King, whose skillful instruction and admonition few can equal and none can easily attain;
for this reason, Brahmā!
through such manifestations, he establishes many beings, leading all people to eliminate old age, sickness, and death, and to reach the karma of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Being unattached to form, through thorough understanding, one is able to endure all sufferings and endure without seeking anything; such a person presides over gods and humans and establishes the three types of patience.
To uphold the True Dharma and to receive, recite, and read it is exceedingly difficult.

Those who receive this sutra should form this contemplation: "May I receive this body for hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, cultivate pure conduct, adorn and purify Buddha-lands, protect the true Dharma, and swiftly attain perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha told the venerable Ānanda:
"Receive this sutra, uphold it, recite it, read it, and explain it to others. Ānanda said:
"Yes. I shall receive and uphold it so that it remains firm.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do not transmit this Dharma to those who are not vessels for it; do not bestow it upon evil associates. You should give it to virtuous friends and those who aspire to and delight in learning.
Having transmitted this sutra-Dharma, you must always uphold and protect it."

Ānanda! This sutra does not lead to what is contrary to the Dharma; it shall lead to those who are worthy vessels, who are able to practice and uphold the Dharma, and who always maintain a heart of loving-kindness toward the assembly.

Furthermore, this sutra is free from delusive thoughts; its auspicious responses manifest before one as the result of diligent effort. To practice this scripture brings forth such meritorious retribution.
Ānanda said: “I shall receive this sutra and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, cause it to flow everywhere.
If one receives this Dharma, being sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, its radiance will shine afar, and such a person will not follow the karma of those who are unworthy vessels.”
Furthermore, what is the title of this sutra?
How should it be practiced and upheld?
The Buddha said:
"This sutra is titled 'The Buddha’s Instruction. Ānanda!
It is also known as 'The Meaning Proclaimed by the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada'; you should uphold and practice it."
It is also titled "The Retribution for the Merits of the Tathāgata," which you should uphold;

furthermore, it is titled "The Chapter on the Secret Essential Dharma of the Tathāgata," which distinguishes [the teachings] for others without seeking self-nourishment, returning to immeasurable merit and acceding to the laws and regulations—this you should uphold.

Why is this? If there are those who uphold this sutra and its Dharma, they shall be enabled by the Buddha-eye to see universally the Buddha-lands and the lands of the ten directions, from the earth upward as high as the Heaven of the Thirty-three and the Yāma Heaven, filled with the seven treasures and a hundred kinds of fine foods, offered as gifts to the Tathāgata.
If there are those who receive this sutra, study, uphold, and practice it, and who preach it for others without seeking sustenance, their merit will be greatest.
Furthermore, by providing offerings of food and clothing to this essential scripture and proclaiming the virtues of the Tathāgata, one shall attain immeasurable blessings beyond compare.

When this sutra was being preached, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the Great Way; incalculable bodhisattvas attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and furthermore, countless bodhisattvas reached the stage of being born only once more before attaining buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).
The Buddha spoke thus.

The venerable Ānanda, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, and the entire assembly of great śrāvakas, as well as the devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, and all people of the world, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with joy; they bowed their heads in prostration and departed.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume 14;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume 15.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
4. The Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras, Part One of Four.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of sixty thousand bodhisattvas and bhikṣus, all of whom were established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and were well-known among the community of śrāvakas.
At that time, after the midday meal, the World-Honored One entered into samādhi; by the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi, the trichiliocosm was shaken.

At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, the Four Great Kings, and others came to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet and stood to one side, joining their palms toward the Buddha.
