By the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi, at that time the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven—the Joyful Devaputra, the Well-Joyful Devaputra, the Great-Joyful Devaputra, the Virtuous-Joyful Devaputra, and the Well-Receptive Devaputra—as well as those of the Tuṣita Heaven, the Īśvara Heaven, and the Maheśvara Heaven, along with the entire great assembly of devas and the Śuddhāvāsa deities, each approached the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, and stood to one side with single-minded devotion.
At that time, the assembly of Śuddhāvāsa devas addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!

We pray that you will expound upon and clearly distinguish the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s practice and the encompassing of all dharmas as taught by the Buddhas of the past—for the benefit and happiness of many sentient beings, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, peace, and happiness of gods and humans."

For the sake of future bodhisattvas, so that those who hear this Dharma after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa may give rise to a mind of aspiration and joy, may know for themselves as it truly is regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may not give rise to doubt or regret, may ultimately abide securely in heedful practice, and may not fall back even when encountering suffering.
At that time, the assembly of Śuddhāvāsa deities and the Tuṣita devas, having spoken these words to the World-Honored One, remained silent.
Then there was a son of heaven named Vajrapramardin, who, on behalf of the assembly of devas, requested the World-Honored One and spoke in verse:
"Because the hundred merits are fulfilled, he asks this; Because he is revered and loved by humans and devas, he asks this."
Because you abide in heedfulness, you ask this; because you are the King of Physicians for a great multitude, you ask this.
May you clearly proclaim these faultless verses of Dharma, O Supreme among all voices, World-Illuminating Wisdom!
You are able to sever hundreds of thousands of doubts and regrets; because you can radiate manifold light, you ask this.
Just as the sun can dispel all darkness, And as the moon’s pure radiance removes the stifling heat;
Giving rise to equanimity toward both enemy and friend, Enduring what is difficult to endure like the earth,
And like pure water washing away dust and grime, Like fire that can burn away the net of afflictions.
Because his mind is pure, he is questioned regarding this; with unimpeded wisdom and eloquence, he looks toward its proclamation.

Like a physician who treats the illnesses of the multitude, like Vaiśravaṇa with his vast treasures providing for the destitute and the poor, and like clouds that can extinguish the three kinds of heat.

This phrase is most supreme; I pray you, speak it! If one can shatter the arrows of manifold afflictions and sufferings, the defilements, stains, guile, and deceit, and skillfully tame them to bestow peace and happiness—for the sake of sentient beings, I ask this.

Possessing shame, remorse, clear wisdom, and firm mindfulness; being most venerable, free from guile, and devoid of crookedness; because you are a mass of merit characterized by signlessness, I ask this of you.
Hatred, resentment, and malice are forever extinguished; you abide in patience for the sake of the peace and happiness of all sentient beings.
You look upon sentient beings with a gentle countenance and a joyful expression, always speaking with words of kindness before they have even thought of it.
Regarding all sentient beings with the thought of them as kinsmen and friends, he leads all beings to the further shore;
with palms joined in reverence and single-minded devotion, he entreats the One of Ten Powers, the Sugata, the Jewel among sentient beings.
I only pray that you will speak in due time to sever the doubts of the multitude;
once gods and humans have heard this practice of the Path, they shall behold the foremost of all signs and thereby come to know the Great Man.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapramardana, saying:
“Vajrapramardana! Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall explain for you all the characteristics so that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may come to know them as such.”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapramardana said:
"I have heard and received this causal connection.
The World-Honored One spoke these words:
“There are one hundred and eight marks, O Vajrapramardana!
Those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle should know them.
What are these one hundred and eight?
Among those seen in dreams, there is first the dream of seeing the body of the Tathāgata, conversing with him, and beholding his wondrous form;
second, the dream of seeing the Tathāgata remaining silent;
and third, the dream of seeing the Tathāgata sitting with his head covered.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing the Tathāgata seated with his back turned;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the body of the Tathāgata as red in color;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the body of the Tathāgata painted in various colors.
Furthermore, one dreams of the Tathāgata departing;
furthermore, one dreams of the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma for others;
furthermore, one dreams of the Tathāgata traveling through the sky by means of supernatural powers.
Furthermore, one dreams of the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa;
furthermore, one dreams of cremating the body of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, one dreams of obtaining the relics of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one dreams of obtaining the hair of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing a stūpa of the Tathāgata never seen before;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing a stūpa of the Tathāgata adorned with jewels.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing a stupa of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the light of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, one dreams of hearing the voice of the Tathāgata without seeing his body.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing the body of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, one dreams that flower garlands and fragrant ointments cover the Tathāgata;
furthermore, one dreams that the Tathāgata is wearing soiled and greasy garments.
Furthermore, one dreams of hearing a Dharma that has never been heard before;

furthermore, one dreams of preaching a Dharma never heard before to others, yet upon waking, there is nothing to demonstrate and not even a memory of it; furthermore, one sees a Dharma teacher never seen before;
furthermore, one dreams of sitting upon a Dharma seat and preaching the Dharma for others.
Furthermore, one dreams of attaining fearlessness;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the Tathāgata walking in meditation (caṅkrama).
Furthermore, he dreams of the Tathāgata turning the wheel of Dharma;
furthermore, he dreams of the stūpa of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa;
furthermore, he dreams of obtaining the robe of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one dreams of obtaining the Tathāgata’s almsbowl;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing a single Tathāgata alone;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the Tathāgata surrounded by many people.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing the Tathāgata’s parasol;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the Tathāgata’s leather sandals;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the Tathāgata seated.
Furthermore, one dreams of personally offering food to the Tathāgata;
furthermore, one dreams of personally offering robes to the Tathāgata;
furthermore, one dreams of personally offering flowers to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one dreams of entering a mountain;
furthermore, one dreams of being naked;
furthermore, one dreams of traveling toward the four intermediate directions.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing a region never before seen;
furthermore, one dreams of walking through turbid water;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing clouds and rain.
Furthermore, one dreams that the earth is spinning;
furthermore, one dreams of walking among jackals, wolves, and wild dogs;
furthermore, one dreams of being ill.
Furthermore, one may dream of falling from a mountain with nothing to rely upon;
furthermore, one may dream of being bound and led away to be executed;
furthermore, one may dream of walking amidst swords and blades.
Furthermore, one dreams of traveling through the void of space;
furthermore, one dreams of holding a torch in one's hand;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing a bodhisattva leap over the palace walls and depart from the city.
Furthermore, one dreams of receiving a sutra;
furthermore, one dreams of hearing the sound of a dhāraṇī;
furthermore, one dreams of hearing the sound of samādhi.
Furthermore, one may dream of hearing the sound of the Vaipulya sutras;
furthermore, one may dream of the voice of a certain Dharma Master;
furthermore, one may dream of receiving verses within a dream.
Furthermore, one may dream within a dream that one has obtained a sutra;
furthermore, one may dream that one hears the sound of the Dharma-treasury;
furthermore, one may dream that one hears the names of Tathāgatas in other worlds.
Furthermore, one dreams of hearing the name of a certain bodhisattva in another world;
furthermore, one dreams of entering the ocean;
furthermore, one dreams of gathering jewels.
Furthermore, one dreams that one is already at the summit of Mount Sumeru;
furthermore, one dreams that one is climbing the mountain;
furthermore, one dreams that one has ascended to the summit of the mountain.
Furthermore, he dreams of climbing a tree;
furthermore, he dreams of seeing a dragon-elephant;
furthermore, he dreams of riding a dragon-elephant.
Furthermore, one dreams of riding a horse;
furthermore, one dreams of making a vow of truth;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing fruit trees.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing flowering trees;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing a city never seen before;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing the great Anavatapta Lake.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing a deva-son;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing a nāga;
furthermore, one dreams of departing for another Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, one dreams of oneself wearing white garments;
furthermore, one dreams of a jeweled garland upon one's head;
furthermore, one dreams of a flower garland upon one's head.
Furthermore, one dreams of picking up scattered flowers;
furthermore, one dreams of beating a drum while others perform music;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing an eclipse of the sun or an eclipse of the moon.
Furthermore, one dreams of smearing oneself with impurities;
furthermore, one dreams of becoming a king;
furthermore, one dreams of being a royal minister walking among a great assembly.
Furthermore, one dreams of riding in a vehicle and going toward a grove;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing regions, villages, monasteries, dwellings, and crowds of people never seen before;
furthermore, one dreams of obtaining a parasol.
Furthermore, one dreams of oneself preaching the Dharma to many people;
furthermore, one dreams of oneself entering a village;
furthermore, one dreams of oneself providing gifts such as building bridges.
Furthermore, one dreams of gathering boats;
furthermore, one dreams of seeing clouds, thunder, and lightning;
furthermore, one dreams of gaining strength and donning armor and weapons.
Furthermore, one dreams of obtaining vessels and utensils;
furthermore, one dreams of showing the path to sentient beings;
furthermore, one dreams of entering a grove of trees.
Furthermore, one dreams of seeing heaps of various grains;
furthermore, one dreams of curing the illnesses of many people;
furthermore, one dreams of hearing the voice of receiving a prophecy.
Furthermore, it is the path of awakening from one's own dream;
furthermore, it is obtaining a full flask in one's own dream.
Thus, O Vajrapramardin!
These are called the one hundred and eight signs.

"If one sees the Tathāgata sitting with his head covered, this person has seen an obstacle created against the causes and conditions for a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) practicing and preaching the Dharma; they should, with an unobstructed mind, cultivate and gather what is required for preaching the Dharma."
This explains the first sign.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardaka!

If one sees the Tathāgata sitting with his back turned in a dream, it indicates that obstacles have been created for those who have gone forth as monastics or for those who listen to the Dharma. Such a person should always provide Dharma seats and exhort many sentient beings to listen to the Dharma; in this way, they shall eliminate their karmic obstructions.
This is the initial sign of the seventh stage, and it is also the sign of each respective stage from the first stage through the seventh.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If one sees in a dream a clay image of the Tathāgata, this is the sign of the Bodhisattva’s first stage.

Because this person previously disparaged a Dharma teacher, they should, before a sutra or an image, or before a stupa of the Tathāgata, honorably receive and offer lamps with an unobstructed mind; in this way, they shall purify their karmic obstacles.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
When a bodhisattva sees an image of the Tathāgata in a dream, this bodhisattva is seeing the signs of various places within the fifth bhūmi."
This person should offer flowers and incense to an image of the Buddha; this is the sign seen at various stages of the sixth bhūmi of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata walking in a dream, this person should diligently cultivate vigor and should zealously practice receiving instruction, study, and recitation; this is the sign seen at the third bhūmi of a bodhisattva.
This person should constantly practice the gift of Dharma and should also sweep the stupas of the Tathāgata, thereby destroying arrogance and purifying their karmic obstructions.
What is the significance of seeing other bodhisattvas approaching the presence of the Tathāgata?
Seeing the Tathāgata heading toward the place where he eats is the sign of the first stage.
Seeing the Tathāgata heading toward the place where he walks in meditation is the sign of the second stage.
Seeing the Tathāgata heading toward the place where he teaches the Dharma is the sign of the third stage.
Seeing the Tathāgata sitting in silence is the sign of the fourth stage.
Seeing the Tathāgata sitting in a secluded place is the sign of the fifth stage.
Seeing the Tathāgata performing a hymn of praise is the sign of the sixth stage.
To see the Tathāgata walking swiftly is the sign of the seventh stage.
To see the Tathāgata performing supernatural powers is the sign of the eighth stage.
To see the Tathāgata manifesting transformations and departing through those transformations is the sign of the ninth stage.
To see the Tathāgata walking away, turning back to look, and conversing about emptiness is the mark of the tenth stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
When a bodhisattva in a dream knows himself to be preaching the Dharma for sentient beings but does not know what he is saying, this is the mark of the second stage.
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, such a person disparages the Dharma-preachers while remaining unaware of their own faults.

This person should seek out spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to make offerings to and listen to the sublime Dharma, without seeking their faults; in this way, they shall purify their karmic obstructions.

Hearing the Buddha speak of giving is the mark of the first stage. Hearing him speak of precepts is the mark of the second stage. Hearing him speak of patience is the mark of the third stage. Hearing him speak of diligence is the mark of the fourth stage. Hearing him speak of dhyāna is the mark of the fifth stage. Hearing him speak of prajñā-wisdom is the mark of the sixth stage. Hearing him speak of great compassion is the mark of the seventh stage. Hearing him speak of non-obstruction is the mark of the eighth stage. Hearing him speak of samādhi is the mark of the ninth stage. Hearing him speak of the accomplishment of powers is the mark of the tenth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva sees in a dream the Tathāgata traveling through the sky by means of supernatural powers (ṛddhi), this is the sign of the seventh stage, wherein one hears and receives the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa)."
This person should constantly cultivate respectful silence and practice until they achieve profound patience;

in this way, they will swiftly attain perfect enlightenment. Seeing the Tathāgata in the midst of the void is the sign of the first stage; seeing the Tathāgata eating is the second stage; seeing light is the third stage; seeing him preaching the Dharma is the fourth stage; seeing him manifest supernatural powers is the fifth dwelling stage; seeing him enter samādhi is the sixth dwelling stage; and seeing him emit light and travel through the void is the seventh dwelling stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa in a dream, this person previously slandered the Dharma and, having gone forth, practiced with deceit and crookedness in pursuit of gain."

One should diligently make offerings to the Triple Gem and provide gifts to those who preach the Dharma; with single-minded devotion, one should practice with vigor during the three periods of the day.
In this way, one purifies karmic obstructions and perceives the signs of each stage up to the fifth bhūmi.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees in a dream the cremation of a Tathāgata, this person has had evil associates and has seen the destruction of the Dharma with approval.

This bodhisattva is at the first stage (*bhūmi*); this person has not long since resolved their mind toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). This person should, for seven days and seven nights, hold a lamp before a Dharma-preacher or before a stūpa of the Tathāgata and repent with single-minded devotion. During the three periods of the day, they should exhort the multitude to listen to the Dharma, thereby purifying their karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
When a bodhisattva obtains the relics of a Tathāgata in a dream, this is said to be the third stage of the bodhisattva.
To personally attend upon a Tathāgata in a dream and hear the prediction of his future attainment of enlightenment is called 'crossing over.'"

If one obtains the relics of the Tathāgata while dwelling in another stage, such signs indicate the stages as follows: obtaining the hair of the Tathāgata is the first stage; dreaming of obtaining the nails of the Tathāgata is the second stage; dreaming of obtaining the relics is the third stage; dreaming of obtaining the teeth is the fourth stage; dreaming of obtaining the tusks is the fifth stage; dreaming of obtaining the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft) is the sixth stage; dreaming of obtaining the hands is the seventh stage; dreaming of obtaining the crown is the eighth stage; seeing the complete body of the Tathāgata being cremated without dispersal is the ninth stage; and seeing the complete body of the Tathāgata is the tenth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
When a bodhisattva dreams that they obtain the hair of a Tathāgata without it being scattered, this is the ninth stage of the bodhisattva.
Dreaming that the Buddha bestows the prediction of enlightenment before them signifies the removal of the karmic obstacles of birth and death."

The hair obtained while at home represents the first stage (*bhūmi*); the hair obtained upon leaving home represents the second stage; obtaining hair in the marketplace is said to be the third station (*vihāra*); obtaining it within the city is the fourth station; obtaining it at the city gate is said to be the fifth station; obtaining it outside is the sixth stage; obtaining it in a garden or park is the seventh stage; obtaining it atop a vehicle is the eighth stage; obtaining it in the midst of space is the ninth stage; and obtaining it within samādhi is the tenth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!

If a bodhisattva sees a stūpa in a dream, this bodhisattva has few karmic obstructions and little demonic activity; if they draw near to virtuous friends, they will well understand the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti) and attain dhāraṇī."

These are the characteristics of all ten stages (*bhūmi*). Seeing a stupa of clay for the Tathāgata is said to be the first stage of the bodhisattva; seeing a stone stupa is the second stage; seeing a stone or clay image is said to be the third dwelling stage (*vihāra-bhūmi*); seeing a stupa with railings is the fourth dwelling stage; seeing a stupa surrounded by stone pillars is said to be the fifth dwelling stage; seeing a stupa covered in gold is said to be the sixth dwelling stage; seeing a jeweled stupa is the seventh stage; seeing a stupa covered with a network of bells is the eighth stage. If one sees these at the beginning of the seventh stage, it is recognized as the work of Māra; however, if they are seen at the ninth or tenth stages, it is non-perverted vision.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees a stūpa adorned by the Tathāgata in a dream, they will before long awaken to the path of enlightenment and be remembered by the devas."
This is the eighth dwelling of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees a stūpa of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers in a dream, they shall purify their karmic obstructions in this very life.
This is the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva.

If a Bodhisattva keeps this in mind, they should distance themselves from evil associates. They should cultivate faith in the first stage, wisdom in the second stage, cultivate resolute understanding extensively in the third stage, practice for a long duration in the fourth stage, cultivate pure resolute understanding in the fifth stage, cultivate an impartial mind in the sixth stage, cultivate the understanding of the ultimate truth in the seventh stage, cultivate the adornment of Buddha-lands in the eighth stage, receive and uphold [the teachings] in the ninth stage, and abide in non-perversion in the tenth stage.
If one dwells in any stage other than the first dwelling, know that this is the work of Māra.
If a person is at the seventh dwelling, they cannot be deceived and possess no skillful means.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva hears the voice of the Tathāgata in a dream but does not see his form, this is the fourth stage of the bodhisattva.

Because they abide in the stage of self-mastery, they destroy the views of those who claim to have seen the Buddha, as well as the renunciation and the crooked preaching of the Dharma by others. Such a person should cultivate a pure mind during the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night; in this way, they shall purify their karmic obstructions.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

When a bodhisattva makes offerings to the Tathāgata within a dream, this is said to be the bodhisattva’s first stage through to the ninth stage. Such a bodhisattva is able to accomplish dhāraṇīs, and such a bodhisattva is held in the mindful regard of all Buddhas."

This bodhisattva should cultivate a mind of equanimity; in this way, they will swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed path. If, in a dream, they dwell in making offerings to the Tathāgata, this is said to be the mark of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

If they give while seated, this is said to be the second stage. If they give while adorned, this is said to be the third stage. If they give together with their own retinue, this is said to be the fourth stage. If they give together with many others, this is said to be the fifth stage. If they give to their own retinue as well as to many others together, this is said to be the sixth stage. If they give all manner of perfected adornments, this is said to be the seventh stage. If they give while offering praise, this is said to be the eighth stage. If they give by performing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), this is said to be the ninth stage, wherein one awakens to all demonic activities.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva sees himself in a dream making offerings of flower garlands, incense powder, and sandalwood to a stūpa of the Tathāgata, this is the bodhisattva seeing the first through the fifth bhūmis; it indicates that he has previously practiced the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) to a small degree."

Having awakened, one recollects this sign; the cultivation and growth of the mind of giving is said to be the sign of the first stage (*bhūmi*). The cultivation and growth of the mind of ethical discipline is said to be the second stage. The cultivation and growth of patience is the third stage. The cultivation and growth of diligence is the seeing of the fourth stage. The cultivation and growth of meditative concentration is the seeing of the fifth stage. The cultivation and growth of the unimpeded mind that swiftly pervades all things is the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata wearing soiled and greasy garments in a dream, this bodhisattva has many obstacles to the Dharma; this pertains to the initial stage at various points.

To see exclusively those objects of dedication with feelings of aversion is the vision of the first bhūmi; to dedicate while free from both aversion and attachment is the vision of the second bhūmi; if one sees them in the body, it is the third bhūmi; if one sees them in the mind, it is the fourth bhūmi; if one sees them in dreams, it is the fifth bhūmi; and if one has accomplished the state of a bodhisattva, there will be few dreams of perceiving such retributions.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva hears in a dream a Dharma never heard before, this bodhisattva has made offerings to many Buddhas and has served as a Dharma teacher throughout many lifetimes."

This explains that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, one sees [the truth] through various points. If one practices according to what has been taught, this is the swift awakening to *bodhi*. If, upon hearing various teachings, one sees the first stage;

if, having a mind of doubt, one still desires to hear more, this is seeing the second stage; if, having heard [the teaching], one’s doubts are severed, this is seeing the third stage; if one hears the explanation of *dhāraṇī*, this is seeing the fourth stage; if one hears the explanation of the marks of a Buddha (*buddhalakṣaṇa*), this is seeing the fifth stage; if one hears the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), this is seeing the sixth stage; and if one hears the explanation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), this is seeing the seventh stage.
Thus one knows each stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva, within a dream, attains a dharma never before studied, having studied it, they do not forget it, do not lose it, and do not fail to see it.

If one has forgotten or lost [the teachings], this bodhisattva should, because in a previous life he gave the Dharma with a mind seeking gain and an impure mind, now purify that karma by providing pure offerings to attract students; seeking all things with a mind free from flattery and crookedness, he should provide for those who preach the Dharma and study, thereby purifying his karmic obstructions.
If, while on the first or second bhūmi, one hears the Dharma without losing it, this is seeing the first bhūmi; if one perceives a loss, this is seeing the second bhūmi.
This perception of loss is the work of Māra and an obstacle to karma. Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees in a dream a Dharma teacher never seen before, this bodhisattva is remembered by all bodhisattvas and has few karmic obstructions.
Upon awakening, they attain the vision of clarity; this bodhisattva’s teaching refers to the first through the sixth bhūmis.

If one speaks in verse but not in prose, this refers to the first stage; if one speaks in prose, this refers to the second stage; if one speaks both in prose and verse, this refers to the third stage; if one speaks of various matters, this refers to the fourth stage; if one speaks of the profound, this refers to the fifth stage; if one speaks of the unimpeded, this refers to the sixth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva dreams that he himself is on a Dharma seat preaching the Dharma, this bodhisattva, in a previous life, prepared a Dharma seat for a Buddha; this bodhisattva is a vessel for the profound patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and this is the first sign of seeing the eighth stage (*bhūmi*)."

If one joyfully preaches in a dream, it refers to the first stage; if one does not preach with joy, it refers to the second stage; if one preaches with patient endurance, it refers to the third stage; if one preaches without eloquence, it refers to the fourth stage; if one speaks of the realm of ordinary beings, it refers to the fifth stage; if one speaks of the realm of śrāvakas, it refers to the sixth stage; if one speaks of the realm of bodhisattvas, it refers to the seventh stage; and if one speaks of the realm of buddhas, it refers to the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!

If a bodhisattva knows for themselves within a dream that they have attained fearlessness, this bodhisattva has transcended all karmic obstacles and has passed beyond the eighth stage to see the various places of the ninth stage."
If in a dream one attains fearlessness and what one says is joyfully heard by the multitude, this bodhisattva sees the first stage.
If in a dream one attains fearlessness and gains wealth while preaching the Dharma, this bodhisattva sees the second stage.
If one attains fearlessness regarding the benefit of the Dharma, this bodhisattva perceives the third stage.
If one attains fearlessness regarding the sight of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), this bodhisattva perceives the fourth stage.
If one contemplates with a virtuous mind and is fearless, this bodhisattva sees the fifth stage.
If one attains physical peace and happiness and is fearless, this bodhisattva sees the sixth stage.
If the mind delights in fearlessness, this bodhisattva sees the seventh stage.
If they attain the fearlessness of supernormal powers, this bodhisattva sees the eighth stage.
If they attain the fearlessness of receiving the prediction [of enlightenment], this bodhisattva sees the ninth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva sees a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in a dream, this bodhisattva possesses a purely virtuous mind directed toward the Way and is non-retrogressive; this is seen at every stage of the ten bhūmis."
If one sees the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) but does not see the tree, this is said to be the first stage (bhūmi).
If one sees the tree but does not see the Bodhisattva, this is said to be the second stage.
If one sees many trees surrounding it, this is said to be the third stage.
If one sees the leaves fully perfected, this bodhisattva is said to be on the fourth bhūmi.
If one sees both flowers and leaves fully perfected, this bodhisattva is seen to be on the fifth bhūmi.
If one sees the fruit accomplished, this bodhisattva sees the sixth bhūmi.
If one sees a seat spread out, this bodhisattva sees the seventh bhūmi.
If one sees people surrounding him, this bodhisattva sees the eighth bhūmi.
If one sees oneself surrounded by nāgas, this bodhisattva sees the ninth bhūmi.
If one sees oneself surrounded by devas scattering flowers and hears the sound of joyful voices, this bodhisattva sees the tenth bhūmi.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata walking in meditation within a dream, this bodhisattva should diligently cultivate vigor and diligently practice the gift of Dharma, comforting their kin and not seeking out their faults."
If a bodhisattva sees this in various places throughout the seventh stage:
if they see the Tathāgata walking upon an impure ground, this bodhisattva is on the first stage;
if they see him walking upon a pure ground, this bodhisattva sees the second stage.
If he sees them spreading out seats and walking in meditation, this bodhisattva sees the third bhūmi.
If he sees them sitting, this bodhisattva sees the fourth bhūmi.
If he sees them surrounded by trees, this bodhisattva sees the fifth bhūmi.
If one sees scattered flowers, this bodhisattva sees the sixth stage.
If one sees a high seat covered above, this bodhisattva sees the seventh stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!

If a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata turning the wheel of Dharma in a dream, this bodhisattva is non-retrogressive; they are at the first stage or the seventh stage, seeing the purity of each stage and being free from karmic obstructions.
If one sees a seat, this bodhisattva sees the first bhūmi.
If one sees a seat being spread, this bodhisattva sees the second bhūmi.
If one sees a seat of variegated colors being spread, this bodhisattva sees the third bhūmi.
If one sees flowers scattered upon the seat, this bodhisattva is seeing the fourth bhūmi.
If one sees various jewels covering the high seat, this bodhisattva is seeing the fifth bhūmi.
If one hears the sound of songs and praises resounding from the air, this bodhisattva has seen the sixth bhūmi.
If one sees a white parasol covered above with a net of jewels, this bodhisattva has seen the tenth bhūmi.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!

If a bodhisattva sees in a dream a stūpa of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, this bodhisattva has seen it at various stages from the first bhūmi to the eighth bhūmi; they are close to the unsurpassed path and have few karmic obstructions."
If he sees dust and soil covering the stupa, this bodhisattva sees the first stage (bhūmi).
If he sees it pure and free of dust, this bodhisattva sees the second stage.
If grass grows upon it, this bodhisattva sees the third stage.
If one sees green grass covering the ground, this bodhisattva is seeing the fourth bhūmi.
If one sees various kinds of flowering trees surrounding [the scene], this bodhisattva is seeing the fifth bhūmi.
If one sees flower and fruit trees surrounding and covering [the bodhisattva] from above, this bodhisattva is seeing the sixth stage.
If one sees various beings of diverse castes surrounding [the bodhisattva], this bodhisattva is seeing the seventh stage.
If one sees a gathering of banners and canopies, this bodhisattva is seeing the eighth stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin Bodhisattva!

If a bodhisattva obtains the robe of a Tathāgata in a dream, this bodhisattva is seeing the signs of each of the stages from the first to the eighth; this bodhisattva should diligently cultivate and accomplish the wisdom of mindfulness of the Buddha.
This bodhisattva has few karmic obstructions.
If they obtain a soiled garment of the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva sees the sign of the first bhūmi.
If they obtain a pure garment of the Tathāgata, this is seeing the second bhūmi.
If one obtains the dyed robe of a Tathāgata, this bodhisattva sees the signs of the third bhūmi.
If one obtains the beaten robe of a Tathāgata, this bodhisattva sees the signs of the fourth bhūmi.
If one obtains a robe from which the Tathāgata has emitted light, this bodhisattva is seeing the sign of the fifth bhūmi.
If one obtains a single robe of the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is seeing the sign of the sixth bhūmi.
If one obtains the three robes of a Tathāgata, this is a sign of the seventh stage of a bodhisattva.
The signs of diligence and the signs of non-diligence eliminate demonic activities; yet, such a bodhisattva may still harbor doubts.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva obtains the bowl of a Tathāgata in a dream, this bodhisattva is remembered by the Buddhas; this is the vision of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
This bodhisattva is a vessel for the clear hearing of the Dharma, cultivates the patience of being free from karmic obstructions, and thus advances toward the unsurpassed path."
If he obtains a bowl that is soiled and impure, this bodhisattva is at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
If he obtains an empty and pure bowl, this bodhisattva is at the second stage.
If he obtains a bowl full of flavors, this bodhisattva is at the third stage.
If one obtains a full bowl of flowers, this bodhisattva is at the fourth stage.
If one obtains a full bowl of fruits, this bodhisattva is at the fifth stage.
If one obtains a full bowl of food, this bodhisattva is at the sixth stage.
If one obtains a full bowl of incense, this bodhisattva is at the seventh stage.
If one obtains a full bowl of flower garlands and incense, this bodhisattva is at the eighth stage.
If one obtains the Tathāgata’s robe and bowl, this bodhisattva is at the ninth stage.
If one obtains the Tathāgata’s bowl from within the void, this bodhisattva is at the tenth stage.
This bodhisattva should recognize demonic activities (*mārakarma*) and eliminate them, with the exception of the first activity, which does not require diligent cultivation.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees a Tathāgata in a dream, they should diligently cultivate the samādhi of emptiness in a quiet place.
This bodhisattva has mixed karmic obstacles pertaining to the eighth bhūmi; they should diligently cultivate a pure mind."
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata in a dream, or sees the body of the Tathāgata amidst a great multitude of people, he should joyfully accept and embrace that great multitude."
This Bodhisattva is seen in every stage and at every location, corresponding to diligent progress in the cultivation of the path.
If one sees a householder surrounded by people of various castes attending upon the Tathāgata, this Bodhisattva is in the first stage (bhūmi).
If one sees the Tathāgata surrounded by a multitude of kings, this bodhisattva is on the second stage.
If one sees the Tathāgata surrounded by brahmins, this bodhisattva is on the third stage.
If one sees the Tathāgata surrounded by kings, this bodhisattva is at the fourth stage (bhūmi).
If one sees the Tathāgata surrounded by nāgas, this bodhisattva is at the fifth stage.
If one sees the Four Great Heavenly Kings surrounding the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at the sixth stage.
If one sees Śakra surrounding the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at the seventh stage.
If one sees the Brahmā deities surrounding the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at the eighth stage.
If one sees the Śuddhāvāsa deities surrounding the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at the ninth stage.
If one sees a bodhisattva surrounding the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and has eliminated demonic activities (*mārakarma*).
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva obtains a parasol of the Tathāgata in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the final stage, seeing the ground in all places; they understand demonic activities and mixed activities, and while seeking gain and offerings, they swiftly advance toward [enlightenment].
If one sees a canopy made of grass and leaves, this bodhisattva is at the first stage (bhūmi).
If one sees a bamboo canopy, this bodhisattva is at the second stage.
If one sees a canopy made of birch bark, this bodhisattva is at the third stage.
If one sees a great canopy, this bodhisattva is at the fourth stage.
If one sees an iron-layered canopy, this bodhisattva is at the fifth stage.
If one sees a copper canopy, this bodhisattva is at the sixth stage.
If one sees a golden canopy, this bodhisattva is in the seventh stage.
If one sees a canopy of the seven precious jewels, this bodhisattva is in the eighth stage.
If one sees a canopy with hanging nets of bells, this bodhisattva is in the ninth stage.
One should recognize the demonic activities of the sixth stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees the leather sandals of a Tathāgata in a dream, they see all ten stages.
This bodhisattva should diligently cultivate and apply effort toward this; this bodhisattva has received the prediction [of enlightenment] and is bound within the realm of prediction.
If, while traveling through a village, they see a leather sandal, this bodhisattva is at the first stage (bhūmi).
If one sees leather sandals within a monastic dwelling, this bodhisattva is at the second stage.
If one sees leather sandals within a garden or grove, this bodhisattva is at the third stage.
If one sees leather sandals at the place of walking meditation (caṅkrama), this bodhisattva is on the fourth stage (bhūmi).
If one sees leather sandals within the dwelling, this bodhisattva is on the fifth stage.
If, while practicing dhyāna, one sees leather sandals, this bodhisattva is at the sixth stage.
If, within river water, one sees leather sandals, this bodhisattva is at the seventh stage.
If one sees leather sandals on a mountain, this bodhisattva is at the eighth stage.
If one sees leather sandals in the air, this bodhisattva is at the ninth stage.
If, through supernormal power, one sees leather sandals, this bodhisattva is at the tenth stage.
This eliminates demonic activity.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata seated in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the first or sixth stage (*bhūmi*).
This bodhisattva should delight in cultivating tranquility and have few karmic obstructions; they have not yet perfected their karma.
If there is no spreading of a seat, this bodhisattva is on the first stage.
If there is the spreading of a seat, this bodhisattva is on the second stage.
If there is the manifesting of the spreading of a seat, this bodhisattva is on the third stage.
If they arrange various seats for sitting, this bodhisattva is on the fourth stage.
If they ultimately arrange the seats, this bodhisattva is on the fifth stage.
If they skillfully arrange excellent seats, this bodhisattva is on the sixth stage.
One should recognize these as the works of Māra. Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva, in a dream, offers food to a Tathāgata, this bodhisattva has attained the vision of the first bhūmi while on the seventh bhūmi; they diligently cultivate vigor and advance toward the Path, and this bodhisattva has few karmic obstructions.
If one sees the Tathāgata entering a house and standing while receiving food, this bodhisattva is on the first stage (bhūmi).
If one sees him sitting in the house while receiving food, this bodhisattva is on the second stage.
If one gives food to a bodhisattva standing outside a gate, this bodhisattva is on the third stage.
If one gives food to a bodhisattva in a marketplace, this bodhisattva is on the fourth stage.
If one gives food to a bodhisattva at a city gate, this bodhisattva is on the fifth stage.
If one gives food within a communal monastic dwelling, this bodhisattva is at the sixth stage.
If one gives food within a private room, this bodhisattva is at the seventh stage,
having eliminated demonic activities.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva, within a dream, knows for themselves that they have offered a robe to a Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at either the sixth or the first stage."
This bodhisattva should diligently cultivate the signless samādhi and advance toward enlightenment.
If one offers robes to the Tathāgata with a mind of reverence, this bodhisattva is at the first stage (bhūmi).
If one gives white robes to the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the second bhūmi.
If one gives dyed robes, this bodhisattva is on the third bhūmi.
If one gives variegated robes to the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the fourth bhūmi.
If one gives a golden robe to the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the fifth stage.
If one gives a robe of various jewels to the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the sixth stage.
If one gives a robe of physical form to the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at the seventh stage.
If one gives a celestial robe to the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva, in a dream, knows for himself that he has offered flowers to a Tathāgata, this is a sign of the sixth bhūmi.
Such a person has many karmic obstructions, and it is difficult for roots of goodness to arise."
If, in a dream, one offers *mandārava* flowers to a Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the first stage (*bhūmi*).
If one offers by scattering flowers, this bodhisattva is on the second stage.
If one offers various kinds of multicolored flowers, this bodhisattva is at the third stage.
If one places flowers upon the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is at the fourth stage.
If one places flowers with one’s own hands into the hands of the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the fifth bhūmi.
If one offers celestial flowers to the Tathāgata, this bodhisattva is on the sixth bhūmi, having eliminated the activities of Māra.
"Except for two kinds of people: those who are beginners and those who have many doubts and regrets.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin Bodhisattva!
If a bodhisattva dreams of entering a mountain and gives rise to doubt or slander, you should know that they have many karmic obstructions, much physical illness, and little wisdom."

This person should give rise to a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings; by means of this mind, they advance toward Bodhi. This Bodhisattva is seen at the first stage of the fifth ground.
This bodhisattva should, for seven years, arouse a pure mind during the six periods of day and night.

This corresponds to the clear wisdom of the first stage (*bhūmi*). One should diligently provide all requisites for comfort; for the second and third stages, one should make offerings to the Triple Gem; for the fourth stage, one should diligently cultivate the profound patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*); and for the fifth stage, one should do likewise.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees himself naked in a dream, one should know that he is free from karmic obstructions and that he has seen the first stage (bhūmi)."
If one sees oneself naked within a city, this is seeing the second bhūmi.
If one sees a naked body in an araṇya (wilderness), this is seeing the third bhūmi.
If one sees a naked form in the mountains, this is seeing the fourth bhūmi.
One should know this to be the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!
If a bodhisattva dreams that they go toward the four intermediate directions, this bodhisattva has abandoned their spiritual friends; this is the vision of the first bhūmi.

Lacking wisdom, they are indolent, full of anxiety and affliction, ridiculed by many, plagued by much illness, and frequently subject to mental derangement; though they seek ordination for the sake of roots of goodness, they return once more to secular life.

Being impoverished, lacking wealth and possessions, and afflicted by many illnesses, they slandered the Dharma Master for the sake of gain and offerings; they slandered the Dharma, neither believing nor understanding it. They shall now return to a state of upright mind, draw near to the Dharma Master, diligently practice all forms of giving with an unobstructed mind, and advance toward Bodhi.
This bodhisattva continues until they attain understanding in the sixth bhūmi; this bodhisattva eliminates harmful transgressions through the lower, middle, and superior levels of mind.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva, in a dream, sees themselves heading toward a direction never seen before, this is a demonic activity and an obstacle of karma.
This bodhisattva perceives various grounds throughout the third stage; they should diligently cultivate the purification of their faculties.

By making offerings to the Triple Gem, one purifies the first stage; by diligently cultivating the view of emptiness, one attains the second stage; by cultivating the patience of dharmas, one attains the third stage, and so on up to abiding in the sixth stage.
This bodhisattva knows for himself that upon seeing the first stage (*bhūmi*), his emergence and entry [into states] involve many roots of goodness as well as many roots of unwholesomeness.

He does not give rise to grief or affliction when casting off his life; he abandons evil associates and draws near to those who possess faith and understanding and know the Dharma. Being free from guile and deceit, he thus purifies his karmic obstructions.
Because he has stolen the Dharma with a deceitful and fraudulent mind, he should draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This Bodhisattva dreams that he is departing from turbid water; this is the vision of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
If one sees oneself walking amidst turbid water and foam, this is the vision of the second bhūmi.
If one sees oneself walking while surging and submerging in the water, this is the vision of the third bhūmi.
If one dreams of walking upon dried-up water, this indicates the fourth bhūmi.
If one dreams of walking upon clear water, this indicates the fifth bhūmi.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardaka!
If a bodhisattva sees clouds and rain in a dream, this bodhisattva has much demonic activity.

This bodhisattva is seen at the first through the seventh stages; by the power of their mastery, they disturb the dharma-preacher before they have left the household life, and for the sake of gain and offerings, they revile the dharma-preacher.

If a Dharma teacher instructs and exhorts according to the Dharma, yet you constantly contravene the teacher’s words, you should diligently cultivate patience and give rise to a mind of faith and understanding; remain detached from gain and offerings, and act solely for the benefit of others, thereby purifying these karmic obstacles.
If one sees clouds of dust and rain, this bodhisattva is at the first stage.
If one sees black clouds, this bodhisattva is at the second stage.
If one sees turbulent clouds, this bodhisattva is at the third stage.
If one sees thunderclouds, this bodhisattva is at the fourth stage.
If one is startled and terrified by lightning clouds, this bodhisattva is at the fifth stage.
If one sees rain and hail, this bodhisattva is at the sixth stage.
One should know that these are the stages of demonic activity for each ground. Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees the earth tremble in a dream, this bodhisattva is on the first ground; they have long practiced the initial deeds extensively.

For those who have many karmas from previous lives and many beings who are terrified by the obstacles of such karma, they should practice the giving of fearlessness to sentient beings and guard their three types of action; thereby, they shall purify and eliminate their karmic obstacles.
If he constantly perceives the earth shaking, this is the first stage for one engaged in the preliminary practice.
If he sees cities and moats destroyed and multitudes of people burned, this Bodhisattva is at the second stage.
If the earth shakes persistently, this is the third stage.
Making true vows is the fourth stage;
the activities of Māra are the fifth and sixth stages;
and diligently cultivating dhāraṇī is the seventh stage.
When all the devas of great majesty gather together, this is the eighth stage (bhūmi).
When the nāgas come to augment his strength, this is the ninth stage.
When the Brahmā devas come, this is the tenth stage.
Upon hearing the secret words of the Tathāgata, the earth shakes; this should be recognized at each respective stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees himself in a dream amidst strife and litigation, that bodhisattva is at either the fourth or the first bhūmi.
If one perceives the higher stages as the work of Māra, up to the seventh stage;

if one does not diligently practice to gather and subdue those who follow non-Dharmic persons; if, for the sake of gain and offerings in the past, one has contradicted those who preach the Dharma; or if one preaches the Dharma with deceit and craftiness for the purpose of self-sustenance.
One should study skillful means and cultivate the six pāramitās with a virtuous mind, thereby purifying karmic obstructions.
If one feels startled or fearful when rebuked or scolded, this is the first stage (bhūmi).
If one dreams of being struck with a sword, this is the second stage (bhūmi).
If one is struck with a clod of earth or a staff, this is the third stage.
If one is subjected to harsh abuse, this is the fourth stage.
The Māra does not understand and does not diligently practice.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees himself ill in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the second bhūmi; this is the sign seen in various places on that bhūmi.

In both the mundane and supramundane realms, many find it difficult to practice; those who wish to give much of the Dharma gift find it repeatedly interrupted, and those who wish to give much of material wealth find it likewise interrupted.

One should provide for those who practice the Dharma, cultivating an unobstructed mind, cultivating non-negligence and freedom from pride, and cultivating the absence of self-conceit, thereby purifying karmic obstacles.

If one sees oneself suffering from illness in another location, this is an awareness of the work of Māra. Furthermore, Vajrapramardin! If in a dream a bodhisattva falls from a mountain with no support;

if previously, regarding a virtuous mind, they were consistently deceitful and lacked faith and understanding; if hindrances of karma and the works of Māra have greatly increased; if body and mind are weak and inferior; if upon receiving the Dharma they quickly forget it; if they give up midway while desiring pleasure; if they see wealth and possessions and abandon them, or see the Buddha-Dharma and abandon it; if they abandon patience; if they associate with those of evil conduct and do not approach wholesome dharmas; or if, in the presence of those with deep faith and understanding, they do not produce faith and understanding—[these are all works of Māra].
This bodhisattva sees both the second and the first stages.
If he sees himself walking through a mountain of knives, this is seeing the first stage;
if he knows himself falling from a mountain of stones, this is seeing the second stage.

Abiding in other stages, one is free from karmic obstructions and demonic activities; one should give rise to faith and, for three months, perform repentance during the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night. One should contemplate the law of dependent origination in the world and practice making offerings; in this way, one eliminates karmic obstructions.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifteen;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Fourth Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras, Part Two:
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees himself bound and about to be executed in a dream, this indicates that his demonic activities (*mārakarma*) are flourishing, not an obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*)."
He should cultivate the unimpeded samādhi and practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to purify his karmic obstacles through these means.
This bodhisattva sees from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage.
If, in a dream, he is bound among corpses, this indicates the fifth stage.
If one is bound and surrounded by kinsmen and relatives, this is the sixth stage.
This is a demonic activity; because one does not diligently practice and is weak and inferior at the first stage, one should cultivate superior progress for the sake of the unsurpassed path.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!

If a bodhisattva knows in a dream that they are amidst blades, this bodhisattva is at the first through the fifth bhūmis. They will have many evil associates and encounter many hardships; they should remain tranquil, free from anger and obstacles, and single-mindedly strive to benefit others, thereby purifying their karmic obstructions."
In a previous life, one occupied a position of authority and harassed those who maintained the precepts.
Now, seeing others holding various kinds of knives, one perceives oneself among them; this is what a bodhisattva on the first stage (prathamabhūmi) sees.
If one sees a person holding a single sword in the center, this is the second stage.
If one sees a person grasping a staff in the center, this is seeing the third stage.
If one sees a person grasping a stone in the center, this is seeing the fourth stage.
If one sees [the deity] standing amidst a multitude of empty-handed beings, this is the fifth bhūmi.
It eliminates the activities of Māra. Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees himself in a dream as being in the air, this bodhisattva is on the stage of faith and has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This bodhisattva is mindful of by the various devas; he should cultivate excellent deportment, should constantly practice diligence, and should exhort sentient beings to seek the unsurpassed path. He should not remain fixed in one place; in this way, he is pure.
This bodhisattva perceives these stages from the first stage through the seventh stage.
If one sees them practicing giving within the empty sky, this is the first stage.
If one sees sages within the sky, this is the perception of the second stage.
If one sees a śramaṇa, this indicates the third bhūmi.
If one sees a nāga, the fourth bhūmi.
If one sees a deva, the fifth bhūmi.
If one sees Brahmā, this is the sixth stage.
If one sees a bodhisattva or a Tathāgata, this is the seventh stage.
This excludes the activities of Māra.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees himself holding a torch in a dream, he should diligently cultivate clear wisdom.
This bodhisattva is at the first through the fifth stages."
This bodhisattva should disregard body and life and pay no heed to food or drink; they should practice dhyāna without giving rise to doubt or regret, proceeding in this manner.

Abiding in the first stage, they delight in practicing the remedies; abiding in the second stage, they delight in practicing dhyāna; abiding in the third stage, they delight in practicing loving-kindness; abiding in the fourth stage, they delight in practicing compassion; and abiding in the fifth stage, they delight in practicing equanimity.

One dwelling in the first stage should practice mindfulness of the Buddha to achieve clear vision; one dwelling in the second stage should practice relinquishment and liberation; one dwelling in the third stage should practice hearing; one dwelling in the fourth stage should practice upholding; and one dwelling in the fifth stage should practice emptiness.
In this way, one should attain clarity.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!

If a bodhisattva sees in a dream a bodhisattva departing from the palace, this is seen at every stage from the first to the sixth bhūmi; such a person increases their diligence, attains non-retrogression, and, within the realm of the prediction of enlightenment, swiftly approaches the unsurpassed path.
If one sees him go out on foot, this is seeing the first stage.
If one sees him go out riding in an ox-cart, this is seeing the second stage.
If one sees him go out riding in a horse-drawn carriage, this is seeing the third stage.
If one sees [the Bodhisattva] departing by riding an elephant chariot, this is seeing the fourth stage.
If one sees him departing by riding a human-drawn carriage, this is seeing the fifth stage.
If one sees him departing by riding a vehicle through the air, this is seeing the sixth stage.
Eliminating the deeds of Māra.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva obtains a sūtra in a dream, this bodhisattva is seen in the first, third, or various other stages."
This person will encounter many causes and conditions, much slander and defamation, and frequent hardships; they should single-mindedly practice repentance and constantly cultivate diligence.
If one dreams of obtaining worldly treatises or the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas, this is the first bhūmi.
Dreaming of obtaining sūtras corresponding to dāna is seeing the second bhūmi.
Dreaming of obtaining those corresponding to the profound is seeing the third bhūmi.
If one does not diligently practice up to the seventh stage, whether it be the celestial deities, the bodhisattvas, or the Tathāgata who bestow the treasury of the Dharma—
furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva, within a dream, hears the sound of the merit of attaining the Dharma, this bodhisattva is one who perceives the stages from the first through the sixth; having previously attained the Buddha’s dhāraṇī.
This bodhisattva has few karmic obstructions but an abundance of demonic activities; they should bestow eloquence upon others without seeking out their faults, and thus they become pure.
Upon hearing the sound of the *Udgata-gandha* dhāraṇī, this bodhisattva is at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Hearing the *dhāraṇī* of syllables is the second stage (*bhūmi*).
Hearing the *dhāraṇī* of transcription is the eighth stage, the first stage, and seeing all stages everywhere.
One should not be attached to the triple world, but diligently practice dwelling in solitude.

That person has little karmic obstruction and little demonic activity, yet their afflictions are flourishing; they should listen to various teachings and cultivate many contemplations, practicing in such a manner accordingly.
The samādhi with vitarka and vicāra is the first stage.
That which is without vitarka and has little vicāra is the third stage.
That which is without vitarka and without vicāra is the fourth stage.
The samādhi of the Brahma-abode and the sphere of infinite space is the fifth stage of abiding.
The samādhi of manifesting a single body is the sixth stage of abiding.
The samādhi of great penetration is the seventh stage of abiding.
The birth of the Buddha-ornament samādhi is the eighth stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva hears the sound of the Vaipulya sūtras in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the first stage of the sixth stage; they should cultivate the resolute patience regarding the dharma of faith and understanding.

This bodhisattva has few hindrances and proceeds slowly toward the unsurpassed path; they should diligently inquire about the characteristics of upholding the precepts and respect their teachers and elders, thus advancing toward enlightenment.
Hearing the sound of the *Dānapāramitā-sūtra* is the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Hearing the sound of the *Śīla-sūtra* is the second stage.
Hearing the sound of the *Kṣānti-sūtra* is the third stage.
Hearing the sound of the *Vīrya-sūtra* is the fourth stage;
hearing the sound of the *Dhyāna-sūtra* is the fifth stage;
hearing the sound of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the sixth stage.
“Excluding those who do not practice diligently and those who possess a virtuous mind sustained by the Buddha.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva hears the name of a bhikṣu preaching the Dharma in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the first or fourth stage; they should rely upon a spiritual friend.”

This bodhisattva encounters many hardships and many doubts and regrets, and possesses little wisdom; they should cultivate an unobstructed mind and skillfully encourage all sentient beings to cultivate a mind free from doubt and regret, whereby they will thus become pure.
If one sees the name of the Dharma Master previously heard, this is the first stage.
If one hears [the name] but does not see the Dharma Master's name, one sees the second stage.
If one hears the name of a Dharma Master from another world-system, this is the third stage.
If one hears of a bodhisattva who is in his last birth before buddhahood, or hears the sound of delighting in the higher stages, this is the fourth stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva attains eloquence born of faith within a dream, this bodhisattva is in either the first or the third stage.
This bodhisattva is a vessel for eloquence; if they distance themselves from three things, they will swiftly attain clarity.
What are these three?
Seeing others obtain gain, their hearts give rise to envy; and for the sake of profit and offerings, they approach others with guile and deceit.
One should distance oneself from these three dharmas and then proceed; the recitation of brief verses is the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Being able to speak various kinds of verses is the second stage.
To speak verses of profound depth is the third stage;
to speak many verses concerning the higher stages is [the fourth].
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!
If a bodhisattva attains eloquence regarding the sūtras in a dream, this is a vision of the first through the eighth bhūmis.

Because there are many causes and conditions for such merit, one should diligently rely upon and cultivate the precepts, practice supreme offerings, and make offerings to those who practice purity; one should not cultivate pride regarding wisdom.
In this way, while experiencing karmic obstacles within a dream, one receives only a slight retribution for suffering.
This marks the emergence from the first stage (*bhūmi*).
To preach the Vaipulya sutras through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) constitutes the teaching of the second stage.
To expound various sūtras is the third stage.
To expound prior causes and conditions is the fourth stage.
To expound the three periods of time is the fifth stage.
To speak of the *pāramitās* is the sixth stage;
to speak of profound sutras is the seventh stage;
to speak of all certainties is the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!
If a bodhisattva hears the sound of a dhāraṇī in a dream, they are at the seventh stage.

This bodhisattva experiences various afflictions and has few karmic obstructions; they should inquire of the wise regarding the cultivation of a place of silent seclusion for the sake of attaining liberation, and thus proceed toward it."
Dreaming of being in a village is the first stage;
being in a house is the second stage;
being in a monastic dwelling is the third stage.
Sitting in an araṇya (forest hermitage) corresponds to the fourth stage;
if sitting in a dream, it is the fifth stage;
if in a garden or park, it is the sixth stage.
Dreaming of being on a mountain peak is the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!

If a bodhisattva, in a dream, hears the name of a Tathāgata never before heard in another world-system, this bodhisattva has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) for the first through the eighth stages.
Because they are dominated by pride, they do not incline toward the Path and engage in many demonic activities;
for the sake of making offerings, they cultivate impure deportment and only then proceed toward it.

Cultivating equanimity is the first stage; pride regarding precepts in dreams is the second stage; pride regarding what has been heard is the third stage; pride regarding skillful means is the fourth stage; pride regarding doubt is the fifth stage; pride regarding wisdom is the sixth stage; pride regarding what is taught is the seventh stage; and pride regarding upholding [the teachings] is the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva hears the voice of a certain bodhisattva in a certain world within a dream, this bodhisattva is at the fifth stage or the first stage."
This bodhisattva is remembered by other bodhisattvas; with few afflictions, they should abandon arrogance, encourage many people to cultivate wisdom, and through such correspondence, attain dhāraṇī.

Hearing this is the first stage; dreaming of leaving home is the second stage; dreaming of ascetic practice is the third stage; dreaming of subduing Māra at the site of enlightenment is the fourth stage; and dreaming of awakening to the Way is the fifth stage.

Hearing and seeing much, yet with indeterminate and weak wholesome minds, is the first stage; abiding in a state of doubt is the second stage; a regressive mind and negligence are the third stage; increased negligence is the fourth stage; and abundance of meditative concentration is the fifth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva dreams that they are in the midst of the ocean, this bodhisattva’s diligence pertains to the eighth stage; they should cultivate extensive learning, diligence, wisdom, and liberation across all stages."

If in a dream there is no place of reliance, this is the first stage (*bhūmi*); if at the edge of the ocean, the second stage; if on a ship or vehicle, the third stage; dreaming of departing, the fourth stage; dreaming of boarding a ship, the fifth stage; dreaming of sitting in water, the sixth stage; sitting within a ship, the seventh stage; and dreaming of sitting upon a ship full of jewels with the intent to sail out to sea, is the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva gathers jewels in a dream, this bodhisattva is seen to be on the first, third, or various stages (*bhūmi*).

This bodhisattva will encounter much suffering and affliction; they should joyfully cultivate pure karma and not seek out the faults of others. They should recognize the kindness of those who preach the Dharma and proceed in such a manner."

Dreaming of digging in the earth and finding treasure represents the first bhūmi; finding treasure in mixed soil represents seeing the second bhūmi; finding treasure among weeds represents seeing the third bhūmi.

This lack of diligent progress is a demonic activity (*māra-karman*); whether it be the sixth or the fourth bhūmi, such lack of diligent application is a demonic activity and an obstacle (*karmāvaraṇa*).
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva dreams that they are on the summit of Mount Sumeru, this person has not regressed; this is the vision of the first through the fifth bhūmis."

Although he possesses some slight merit, he has associated with evil friends, and due to the causes and conditions of deceit and fraud, he lacks faith in associating with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Now, he should cultivate non-deceit and extensively cultivate faith and understanding; in this manner, he should proceed.
If one dreams of being on Mount Sumeru, one should know that this corresponds to the sixth stage (*vihāra*).
Dreaming of dwelling on Mount Sumeru is the seventh stage.
Dreaming of looking around in all four directions is the eighth stage.
Dreaming of sitting represents the ninth stage (*bhūmi*).
Dreaming of a mountain shaking represents the tenth stage.
From this first stage up to seeing the fifth stage, diligently cultivating a virtuous mind while remaining under the guidance of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) constitutes the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
When a bodhisattva sees himself climbing a mountain in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the first through the fifth stages (*bhūmi*).

Although he has destroyed all afflictions and karmic obstructions, he does not give rise to reverence for those who preach the Dharma. He should cultivate freedom from deceit and crookedness to purify these karmic obstructions; in this way, he shall advance toward enlightenment."

On the first stage, one increases diligent progress during the three times; on the second stage, one diligently cultivates mindfulness of the Buddha; on the third stage, one cultivates emptiness; on the fourth stage, one cultivates great compassion; and on the fifth stage, one cultivates wisdom.

Dreaming of ascending a mountain is the first stage; being on the mountain is the second stage; being at the summit of the mountain is the third stage; dreaming of surveying the view is the fourth stage; and sitting there is the fifth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva dreams of ascending a mountain, this bodhisattva sees [the progression] from the first bhūmi to the seventh bhūmi.

This bodhisattva has little karmic obstruction, yet demonic activity (*māra-karman*) is flourishing; he should relinquish all cherished possessions to make offerings to those of wisdom, and in the presence of wise persons, he should personally subdue his pride."
If one dreams of crossing the seven great mountains up to Mount Sumeru, this is the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, Vajrapramardaka!

If a bodhisattva dreams of climbing a tree in a dream, this bodhisattva is seen in each of the stages from the first to the fourth; they should awaken to their karmic obstacles and the works of Māra, and should draw near to and rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to attain the light of wisdom. From time to time, they should decisively determine the meaning of the Dharma through awakening and awareness, proceeding in this manner.

Seeing tree branches and leaves fully provided with cool shade is the first stage; seeing fragrant trees is the second stage; seeing flowering trees is the third stage; and seeing fruit-bearing trees is the fourth stage.
This is the mark of diligent exertion; if one is not diligently exerted, it is the work of Māra.
If one sees a high place where tree branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are fully present, this excludes [the influence of] karmic retribution.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees a dragon-elephant in a dream, this bodhisattva is at one of the stages from the first to the sixth;
this bodhisattva practices giving but does not practice wisdom, their roots of goodness are exhausted, and they should cultivate faith.
One should cultivate wholesome mindfulness in this manner.

Therein, on the first stage, one sees impure elephants; on the second stage, one sees white elephants; on the third stage, one sees six-tusked white elephants; on the fourth stage, one sees adorned elephants; on the fifth stage, one sees elephants holding banners and parasols; and on the sixth stage, one sees elephants frolicking in joy.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva dreams that he is riding upon a dragon-elephant, this bodhisattva has seen the first through the seventh bhūmis and shall, in one lifetime, attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat.

There is an entry into the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) characterized by much aspiration; one should cultivate reverence and exhort bodhisattvas to remain free from illusion, falsehood, and deceit. One should practice contentment in all circumstances and perform appropriate giving; in this way, one becomes pure.

Dreaming of mounting an elephant is the first stage; dreaming of oneself wearing white robes while mounting an elephant is the second stage; if one dreams of dyed robes, it is the third stage; if one dreams of robes of various colors, it is the fourth stage; if one dreams of robes dyed with fragrances and fully adorned, it is the fifth stage; if one dreams of wearing a crown, it is the sixth stage; and if one dreams of grasping an adorned parasol, it is the seventh stage.
"Excluding the activity of Māra, one does not fail to apply oneself with diligence; the signs of the higher stages are seen in their entirety.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva dreams of mounting a horse, this bodhisattva is at the first or fourth stage; they should cultivate reliance upon the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā)."
When those demonic activities increase and obstacles to karma are few, one should extensively cultivate the wisdom of emptiness and diligently practice to give rise to faith;

in this way, one becomes pure. If in one's own dreams one mounts a standing horse, it is the first bhūmi; dreaming of mounting a walking horse is the second bhūmi; dreaming of mounting a galloping horse is the third bhūmi; and mounting a decorated horse is the fourth bhūmi.
Excluding the demonic activities of the higher stages, these are the demonic activities of the bodhisattva’s overweening pride.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva makes a vow of realization within a dream, this bodhisattva will see it in every stage, from the first stage through the tenth stage.

For him, demonic activities will greatly increase within the obstacle of karma; he will employ many various arts and practices, skillfully cultivate the samādhi of manifestation, correctly practice dignified deportment, and refrain from excessive accumulation—thus purifying the obstacle of karma.

The accomplishment and implementation of the vow is the first stage; for the sake of liberation from bondage it is the second stage; for the sake of liberation from illness it is the third stage; for the sake of a citadel it is the fourth stage; for the sake of a king it is the fifth stage; for the sake of Jambudvīpa it is the sixth stage; for the sake of the four continents it is the seventh stage; for the sake of a thousand-world system it is the eighth stage; for the sake of a three-thousandfold world system it is the ninth stage; and when the sun rises, wandering upon the earth and raining down celestial flowers, it is the tenth stage.
This excludes the demonic activities of the first and sixth stages.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!

If a bodhisattva sees a medicinal tree in a dream, this bodhisattva is seeing the first through the seventh stages, wherein they fulfill and achieve the dharma of receiving the prediction of enlightenment."
One should practice giving without expectation of reward and remain upright without seeking out the faults of others;

such is purity. To see a small fruit tree in a dream is the first stage (*bhūmi*); if one sees a large fruit tree, it is the second stage; if one sees a tree with bitter fruit, it is the fourth stage; seeing a medicinal tree is the fifth stage; seeing a celestial tree is the sixth stage; and seeing a tree with sweet fruit is the seventh stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!
If a bodhisattva sees flowering trees in a dream, this bodhisattva is at either the seventh or the first bhūmi.
They should cultivate various roots of goodness and not associate with the four assemblies; in this manner they should proceed."

Seeing many flowering trees without fragrance is the first bhūmi; seeing fragrant flowering trees is the second bhūmi; dreaming of many fragrant flowering trees is the third bhūmi; seeing trees with various flowers and fruits is the fourth bhūmi; seeing flowering trees without leaves is the fifth bhūmi; seeing celestial flowering trees is the sixth bhūmi; and if one sees a Bodhi tree, that is the seventh bhūmi.
"Except for those in the hands of evil associates, those who are negligent and lack diligent perseverance—the demonic activities of these are all seen as accomplished in the higher stages.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!"
If a bodhisattva sees in a dream a city never seen before, this pertains to the first stage of the sixth bhūmi.

This bodhisattva has karmic obstructions; yet, regarding this patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they have previously cultivated the firm samādhi and the samādhi of emptiness, and through unimpeded mind and extreme ascetic practices, they have thus become purified.

Seeing the initial construction of a city is the first stage; seeing the city completed is the second stage; seeing the streets and markets within the city completed is the third stage; seeing the pleasure grounds completed is the fourth stage; and seeing the ponds and waters completed is the sixth stage.
"Except for those in the hands of evil associates, those who are negligent and lack diligence—the works of Māra—and those who possess the vision of the higher stages.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!"
