If a bodhisattva sees the pool of the Dragon King Anavatapta in a dream, this indicates the first stage of the eighth bhūmi;
with few afflictions, they will swiftly give birth to clear illumination.
If one is free from deceit and practices with diligent progress, disregarding even body and life, and fulfills all needs to satisfy the intentions of others, such is purity.

If one sees the bank of Lake Anavatapta, this is the first stage (*bhūmi*); if one sees within the lake, it is the second stage; if one sees everything [within the lake], it is the third stage; if one touches the water with the hand, it is the fourth stage; if one washes [in the water], it is the fifth stage; if one sits on the bank, it is the sixth stage; if one sees the Naga King Anavatapta, it is the seventh stage; if one enters the Naga palace and increases one’s strength, it is the eighth stage; and the removal of demonic activities is the ninth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!
If a bodhisattva sees a devaputra in a dream, this bodhisattva has attained the fifth stage among the higher stages.

His minor karmic obstructions and minor demonic activities are like mere droplets; he should diligently practice tranquility for three months, whereby he will eliminate his karmic obstructions and attain clarity and purity."
Such a person should keep the Buddhas of the ten directions in mind and should cultivate freedom from anxiety and distress.

If they see the assembly of the Four Great Heavenly Kings, this is the sixth stage; seeing the Heaven of the Thirty-three is the seventh stage; seeing the Tuṣita Heaven is the eighth stage; seeing the assembly of the Brahma Heavens is the ninth stage; and seeing the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Heavens is the tenth stage.
Corresponding to the first bhūmi, one perceives all demonic activities; having accomplished the virtuous mind, one perceives all ten bhūmis.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees a nāga in a dream, this is the perception of the eighth bhūmi in various places.

One should achieve careful patience; even if one’s diligent application is repeatedly interrupted by delays, and one’s diligent cultivation of skillful means is again and again abandoned, all of one’s wealth and possessions should be provided for the Dharma teacher, and even one’s most beloved things should be relinquished and given away before proceeding.

If one sees a dragon on a mountain, this is the first stage; if one sees it in a wilderness, this is the second stage; if one sees it on the bank of a pond, this is the third stage; if one sees it in a forest, this is the fourth stage; if one sees it among a multitude of people, this is the fifth stage; if one sees it within a royal city, this is the sixth stage; if one sees it surrounded by a great crowd of people, this is the seventh stage; if one sees it in the sky, this is the eighth stage.
The karmic obstacles of demonic activities are eliminated from the first to the sixth bhūmi.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardaka!
If a bodhisattva dreams that they themselves are traveling toward other regions of Jambudvīpa, this indicates the first through the sixth bhūmis.

If one attains patience, one will have few obstacles; if one does not diligently practice, one will not attain clarity; if one is indolent or associates with the deceitful, yet gives rise to faith, one will thus become pure.

If one does not delight in seeing Jambudvīpa, this is the first stage; if one delights in seeing it, this is the second stage; if one sees villages, towns, and cities as delightful, this is the third stage; if one sees gardens and groves with various flowers, this is the fourth stage; if one sees a great assembly rejoicing, this is the fifth stage; and if they amuse themselves together, this is the sixth stage, wherein demonic activities are eliminated.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
When a bodhisattva dreams that they are wearing white robes, this bodhisattva sees [visions] from the first to the eighth bhūmi.

Their karmic obstructions are purified, yet demonic activities increase; their inclination toward the Dharma arises, but their mental factors repeatedly diminish in merit, and they encounter many hardships."
One should not be stingy or begrudge any material thing; in this way, one is pure.
If one personally perceives all necessities and all bedding that are pleasing to others, one should not spare even body or life, but rather cultivate roots of goodness through extensive learning.

If one sees fine clothes worn for a long time, this is the first stage; if one sees a new robe with a long collar, this is the second stage; if one sees a robe with a long collar, this is the third stage; if one sees a beaten and pressed robe, this is the fourth stage; if one sees a beaten and polished robe, this is the fifth stage; if one sees a dyed robe, this is the sixth stage; if one sees an elephant-colored robe, this is the seventh stage; if one sees a celestial robe, this is the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva dreams of obtaining a jeweled garland, this pertains to the first through the ninth bhūmis.

Such a person has no karmic obstructions and no demonic activities; they should reproach their own faults rather than blaming others, seek to cultivate the hearing of the Dharma rather than engaging in strife or litigation—thus they are pure."

If one type of jewel garland represents the first stage (*bhūmi*), then two types up to seven types of jewel garlands represent the seventh stage; if one obtains the *maṇi* jewel garland of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), it is the eighth stage; and if one sees the celestial jewel garland, it is the ninth stage, wherein demonic activities (*mārakarma*) are eliminated.

This is the mark of initiating activity in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). If one associates with those who joke, are indolent, or fail to reflect upon their own conduct, one should recognize this.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees someone with a flower garland upon their head, this indicates the first or eighth bhūmi; yet there is truly an obstacle of karma (karmāvaraṇa) present.
If, from beginning to middle to end, they give rise to a mind of certain goodness, relinquish all things without giving rise to sorrow or affliction, they are thus purified.

If one obtains a garland of a single color, this is the first stage; if one obtains a garland of unattractive colors, this is the second stage; if one obtains a garland of various colors, this is the third stage; if one obtains garlands of all flowers, this is the fourth stage; if one obtains a garland of nāga flowers, this is the fifth stage; if one obtains a garland of celestial flowers, this is the sixth stage; if one obtains a garland of various celestial flowers, this is the seventh stage; if one obtains a garland of miscellaneous flowers from both devas and humans, this is the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva dreams that they obtain scattered flowers, this bodhisattva is seeing the first through the sixth bhūmis.
This bodhisattva should encourage other bodhisattvas; if they possess sovereign power and influence, they must not oppress or wrong others."

If one takes flowers that have color but no fragrance, this is the first stage; if one takes flowers that have both color and fragrance, this is the second stage; if one takes golden-colored flowers, this is the third stage; if one takes flowers of various colors, this is the fourth stage; if one takes flowers from both water and land, this is the fifth stage; and if one takes various mixed flowers from both water and land, this is seen as the sixth stage.
Thus, one should diligently cultivate such signs of vigor.
Whether it be the works of Māra, the higher stages, or the four stages, all that is pleasing will be brought forth by the nāgas.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardaka!

If a bodhisattva beats a drum and performs music in a dream, this is a vision of the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*). It indicates that karmic obstructions and the activities of Māra are increasing; therefore, one should diligently cultivate extensive learning and vigor, and give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings. In this way, it becomes purified.

If one sees a drum being beaten in the sky in a dream, this is the first stage; if seen on level ground, the second stage; if seen in a village, the third stage; if seen in a great city, the fourth stage; if seen among a great assembly, the fifth stage; if seen atop a house, the sixth stage; if seen in the mountains, the seventh stage; if seen on the summit of Mount Sumeru, the eighth stage; and if seen in the void of space, the ninth stage.
This excludes the demonic activity of one who diligently cultivates wisdom. Furthermore, Vajrapramardaka!

If a bodhisattva sees an eclipse of the sun or moon in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the first or sixth stage (*bhūmi*). Having destroyed wholesome dharmas, possessed many afflictions, and accomplished evil karma, they should give away all their possessions without expecting karmic retribution; in this way, they shall be purified.

Seeing the sun and moon just beginning to rise signifies the first and second bhūmis; seeing clouds signifies the third bhūmi; seeing massed clouds signifies the fifth bhūmi; and seeing them free from dust and mist signifies the sixth bhūmi. When one sees the sun and moon at their full intensity, the karmic obstacles of māra-activity are eliminated.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees themselves with their body smeared with impurities in a dream, this bodhisattva is seeing the first through the third bhūmis.
This refers to a bodhisattva who, in a previous life, reviled and insulted the worthy ones and sages, and practiced evil conduct."

This bodhisattva should diligently practice repentance during three periods of the day and night for three years; thereafter, they shall no longer give rise to thoughts of contempt toward other beings, but should cultivate faith and understanding extensively, thereby becoming thus purified.
Smearing one's body with blue mud signifies the first stage; if half the body is smeared, it is the second stage; if it is smeared everywhere, it is the third stage.
One should recognize these as demonic activities up to the sixth stage.

"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin! If a bodhisattva sees himself as a king in a dream, this bodhisattva perceives all ten stages (*bhūmi*) at every stage; there are both thick roots of goodness and thick difficulties. He should not place hope in others, nor should he offer worship to others with deceitful intent. He should practice straightforward giving, share his observance of the precepts with others, neither praising himself nor disparaging others; in this way, he awakens to the Path."

If one is in a village where there is fear, this is the first stage; if in a monastic dwelling, it is the second stage; if in a garden or park, it is the third stage; if in a temple of the gods, it is the fourth stage; if in a great city, it is the fifth stage; if in the mountains, it is the sixth stage; if acting as a king of Jambudvīpa, it is the seventh stage; if acting as a universal monarch (cakravartin), it is the eighth stage; if upon the ocean, it is the ninth stage; and if upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, it is the tenth stage.
Except for the activity of Māra, one should not fail to be diligent and energetic; rather, one should keep the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a Bodhisattva dreams of being before a king, before a high minister, or in the midst of a great assembly, this Bodhisattva is seen to be at the eighth stage."
These are the various afflictions; he should teach and transform sentient beings, cultivate offerings, and personally practice purity—such is purity.

In the first bhūmi, giving is mixed with various afflictions; in the second, morality; in the third, learning; in the fourth, meditative concentration; in the fifth, retention; in the sixth, supernormal powers; in the seventh, preaching the Dharma; and in the eighth, the accomplishment of a retinue.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva dreams of riding [a mount] within a grove, this bodhisattva is one who sees [visions] from the first to the ninth bhūmi.

This bodhisattva does not recognize worldly gain, offerings, food, or drink, and is led and bound by Māra; yet they have few karmic obstructions. They should provide for the Dharma teacher and supply what is required for his offerings, and should practice silent seclusion; in this way, they shall proceed toward that goal."

In the first stage, there is no practice of wisdom; in the second stage, no wisdom; in the third stage, no definitive wisdom; in the fourth stage, no dhyāna-wisdom; in the fifth stage, no unimpeded wisdom; in the seventh stage, no wisdom of production; in the eighth stage, no wisdom of adornment; and in the ninth stage, no wisdom of aspiration.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees in a dream villages, monasteries, and assemblies of people that they have never seen before, this bodhisattva is at the first through the sixth bhūmi."
When one encounters many hardships, one should practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*); thus it becomes pure.

To cultivate the giving of faith and to cultivate all forms of faithful understanding—seeing such signs of practice is the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). If there is a sudden undertaking of activity, it is the second stage; if there is adornment, it is the third stage; if the completion of the adornment is seen, it is the fourth stage; if the assembly of the fourfold community is seen, it is the fifth stage; and if the assembly of devas is seen, it is the sixth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva obtains a parasol in a dream, this is seen as belonging to the first through the seventh stages. They are sustained by the Buddhas; though they encounter many hardships, they are not overcome by them. They should not give rise to ill will toward those who preach the Dharma. In this way, they are purified."

If one sees a flower canopy, it is the first stage; if one sees a lapis lazuli canopy, it is the second stage; if one sees both flowers and a canopy, it is the third stage; if one sees a material canopy, it is the fourth stage; if one sees a canopy with painted stalks, it is the fifth stage; if one sees a canopy with a network of bells, it is the sixth stage; if one sees a canopy with a jeweled net draped over it, it is the seventh stage.
This excludes the failure to diligently apply oneself to eliminating demonic activities.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana Bodhisattva!

If a bodhisattva dreams that they are preaching the Dharma to many people, this bodhisattva perceives all ten stages; in each of those stages, they should recognize these as demonic activities and karmic obstructions.

If one wishes to attain decisive eloquence, one should investigate and emerge from it; one should not be attached to any objects, should give rise to pure faith toward those who seek the Dharma, and should cultivate the precepts of the six points of concordant respect. In this way, one becomes pure.
If in a dream it is asked, "How does one practice giving? this is the first stage (bhūmi).
"What are the ten wholesome dharmas? is the second stage.
"What is hearing [the Dharma]? is the third stage.
What is the virtue of dhūta? It is the fourth stage.
What is the teaching on emptiness? It is the fifth stage.
What is the teaching on the reproval of habitual tendencies? It is the sixth stage.
Why is it said that the seventh stage is "freedom from attachment"?
Why is it said that the eighth stage is "adornment of concentration"?
Why is it said that the ninth stage is "adornment of the Buddha"?
What is meant by "speaking of the sublime at the proper time"? These are the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

In the first stage, there is the wealth of giving material goods; in the second, the wealth of ethical discipline; in the third, the wealth of skillful means; in the fourth, the possession of the seven riches; in the fifth, the wealth of providing service; in the sixth, the wealth of decisive judgment; in the seventh, the wealth of certainty; in the eighth, the wealth of unhindered penetration; in the ninth, the wealth of practice; and in the tenth, the wealth of attainment.

In that first stage, the roots of goodness are predominant; in the second, ethical discipline; in the third, skillful means; in the fourth, what is to be accomplished; in the fifth, the twelve links of dependent origination; in the sixth, profound patience; in the seventh, the wisdom of destruction; in the eighth, the destruction of [obstacles to] teaching and transforming sentient beings; in the ninth, subduing; and in the tenth, the purification of buddha-fields.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva sees himself in a dream establishing a city and its walls for the first time, this bodhisattva is at the eighth stage and has received the prediction of non-retrogression."

One should approach and make offerings to those who possess profound faith and understanding; for those with many doubts and regrets face obstacles to the Dharma, they should make offerings to a Dharma teacher to eliminate their doubts and regrets, thereby attaining such purity.

Dwelling therein, the doubt regarding whether one will attain Buddhahood or not upon abiding in the first stage is the second stage; the doubt regarding the wisdom for teaching and transforming sentient beings is the third stage; the doubt regarding the production of meditative concentrations is the fourth stage; the doubt regarding the wisdom of what ought to be done is the fifth stage; the doubt regarding the fruit of the path is the sixth stage; the doubt regarding birth is the seventh stage; and the doubt regarding the playful mastery [of the dharmas] is the eighth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!

If a bodhisattva dreams of crossing turbid waters by means of a bound raft, this pertains to the transition from the seventh ground to the first. In such a state, karmic obstructions and demonic activities flourish; therefore, one should give rise to a superior resolve that is firm, indestructible, harmonious, and corresponding, characterized by the luminous purity of non-arising."

If wisdom and skillful means are difficult, this is the first stage; if one desires to cultivate diligence but the body is indolent, this is the second stage; if the mind is untimely, this is the third stage; if at times it is clear, this is the fourth stage; if there is little fearlessness, this is the fifth stage; if teaching and transforming others is difficult, this is the sixth stage; if the Buddha-dharma is difficult, this is the seventh stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva dreams of gathering boats, this bodhisattva is at the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*).
If there are difficulties in practicing the six *pāramitās* with equanimity, one should practice the six *pāramitās* without dependence; in this way, they become purified."

If one dreams of making a boat that is not yet finished, it is the first stage (*bhūmi*); if the boat is finished, it is the second stage; if one dreams of two boats side by side, it is the third stage; if one ties the two boats together, it is the fourth stage; seeing a great multitude board the boat is the fifth stage; and seeing them enter the boat and depart is the sixth stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardaka!
If a bodhisattva sees clouds, thunder, and lightning in his own dream, this bodhisattva is at either the fifth or the first stage.

His demonic activities will increase, yet he will have few karmic obstructions; he should frequently contemplate wholesome thoughts, relinquish what he holds dear, and gather dhāraṇīs—thus he shall become purified."

If one is startled and terrified by seeing clouds, rain, and lightning, this is the first stage; if one is not startled or terrified, this is the second stage; if one recollects the Dharma, this is the third stage; if one recollects while staying on a mountain peak, this is the fourth stage; if one recollects in mid-air, this is the fifth stage.
It eliminates demonic activities.
If dragons from the higher realms come to assemble and perform acts of service, one will not give rise to fear or alarm.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva dreams of receiving a sword while adorned with ornaments, this bodhisattva is at the first or third stage (*bhūmi*).

This is an activity of Māra and an increase in karmic obstructions; they should cultivate the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) to become thus purified.
If it is a stained and greasy blade, this is the first stage; obtaining a stainless blade is the second stage; obtaining a sharp blade is the third stage.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva obtains utensils in a dream, this bodhisattva is at the seventh stage; they should practice in accordance with this correspondence.

Although they may not necessarily encounter demonic activities or karmic obstructions, they should diligently practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); in this way, they will become purified.
"One should purify the sixth stage; through the dharma of retrogression, one attains the superior seventh stage.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva, in his own dream, shows the path to sentient beings, this is the sign of all ten stages."

This is the first application: awakening to the obstacle of karma and the obstacle of afflictions, one should honor and attend upon Dharma masters, relinquish all possessions, and diligently cultivate vigor; thus one proceeds.

If one sees a vehicle moving along a road, this is the first stage; showing the way to a garden is the second stage; showing the way to a city is the third stage; showing the way to an araṇya (forest hermitage) is the fourth stage; showing the way to a mountain is the fifth stage; showing the way to the sea is the sixth stage; showing the way to the heavens is the seventh stage; showing the way of the śrāvakas is the eighth stage; showing the way of the bodhisattvas is the ninth stage; and showing the way of the Buddhas is the tenth stage.

Having finished the exposition of the Path, he now reveals the first stage (*bhūmi*). One awakens to the activities of Māra and awakens to the activities of afflictions (*kleśa*); up to this point, there is no fault in the first six stages.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!..."
If a bodhisattva enters a grove or park within a dream, this bodhisattva is at the first stage of the eighth bhūmi.

If, in that dream, they experience the karma of Māra or the karma of afflictions, and upon waking from the dream's terror, they give rise to sorrow and suffering, they should practice emptiness and listen to the profound Dharma; they should remain silent and distance themselves from sleep, and they should associate with those who definitively proclaim the path of the Dharma—in this way, they will be purified.

If one dreams of losing the royal throne and feels fear in one's heart, this is the first stage; dreaming of breaking the precepts and feeling fear is the second stage; dreaming of the extinction of the Dharma and feeling fear is the third stage; dreaming of the death of a Dharma master and feeling fear is the fourth stage; if one dreams of being burned by fire and feels fear, this is the fifth stage; dreaming of being terrified is the sixth stage; dreaming of falling from a mountain and feeling fear is the seventh stage; and dreaming of seeing the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa and feeling fear is the eighth stage.
Lacking diligence in the sixth stage, one awakens from the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees a heap of the five grains in a dream, this bodhisattva dwells on the eighth stage or above.
In the first and second stages, one sees thus and does not exert oneself; one sees the works of Māra and does not concern oneself with discussing them.

Having previously made offerings to various Buddhas in former lives, one encounters many hardships; one does not rely on anything in the world, and does not regard the abandoning or guarding of the three karmas—thus is one pure.

Dreaming of a heap of grain signifies the seventh bhūmi; dreaming of a heap of grain filling the trichiliocosm signifies the eighth bhūmi; if one dreams of the five grains gathered and ripened, it is the ninth bhūmi; and if one dreams of harvesting the grain, it is the tenth bhūmi.
"Furthermore, Vajrapramardana!
If a bodhisattva sees in a dream the healing of the illnesses of sentient beings, this bodhisattva is at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

Although their karmic obstructions are slight, demonic activities (*mārakarma*) are flourishing; they should cultivate great compassion and diligently exhort others to conversion without giving rise to doubt or regret. In this way, they will be in accord."

Dreaming of treating children is the first stage; dreaming of treating women is the second stage; dreaming of treating adults is the third stage; dreaming of treating fever is the fourth stage; dreaming of treating white leprosy is the fifth stage; dreaming of treating self-inflicted wounds is the sixth stage; dreaming of treating wasting diseases is the seventh stage; and dreaming of treating demonic afflictions is the eighth stage.
To eliminate demonic activities, one should cultivate and accumulate the practice of patience, thereby accomplishing the bodhisattva’s mind of great compassion and goodness.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva hears for themselves the bestowal of the prophecy of enlightenment, this bodhisattva is one who has seen the tenth stage.
Regarding this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), one should be aware of the demonic activities and karmic obstructions involved in receiving the prediction for the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

One receives the prediction of the Path at the first stage; the prediction of Bodhisattva conduct at the second stage; the prediction of patience (*kṣānti*) at the third stage; the prediction of vows (*praṇidhāna*) at the fourth stage; the prediction of samādhi at the fifth stage; the prediction of wisdom (*prajñā*) at the sixth stage; the prediction of skillful means (*upāya*) at the seventh stage; the prediction of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) that transcends the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas at the eighth stage; the prediction of being in the final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) at the ninth stage; and the prediction of the Buddha’s consecration (*abhiṣeka*) at the tenth stage.
He cultivates the perfection of wisdom of great compassion and approaches it through skillful means;
such is his course. Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva awakens to the path even within a dream, this bodhisattva is at the first stage (bhūmi).
One should awaken to great compassion, diligently cultivate vigor, and have faith in a virtuous mind; thus one proceeds.

To be aware of this is the eighth stage (*bhūmi*); to cause the trichiliocosm to tremble is the ninth stage; and to dream of emitting light, with various devas singing praises and joyful whistling in a great voice, is the tenth stage.
From the first bhūmi to the seventh bhūmi, such are the signs of the demonic activities of those who do not exert themselves in diligent progress.
Furthermore, Vajrapramardin!
If a bodhisattva obtains a full vessel in a dream, this bodhisattva perceives all ten bhūmis; it should be known in this way.

If one attains this in a village, it is the first stage; if in a gateway, it is the second stage; if on a road, it is the third stage; if under a tree, it is the fourth stage; if while standing, it is the fifth stage; if while sitting, it is the sixth stage; if on a mountain peak, it is the seventh stage; if in mid-air, it is the eighth stage; if at the time of eating, it is the ninth stage; and if while riding in a decorated carriage or visiting a garden, it is the tenth stage.
"In these stages, one should be aware of the demonic activities and karmic obstacles of each stage; thus purified, one proceeds.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Such characteristics as these are attained, Decisively, without any doubt."
A Great Being should act thus: do not look for the faults of others, for human virtue is difficult to measure.
Water might arise from fire; each of these things possesses its own characteristics.
That one would ever fall back from bodhi— such a thing is absolutely impossible.
Even if one were to carry Mount Sumeru upon both shoulders,
traveling throughout the ten directions across worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
Such appearances as these may still occur;
yet this bodhicitta shall never regress. The great earth might be turned upside down, but the bodhicitta shall not turn back.
This is ultimately impossible.
If there is a person of virtuous mind who is directed toward the unsurpassed path,
they possess four immeasurable qualities.
The realm of space is difficult to know, and likewise is the realm of sentient beings;
yet the Buddha knows the bodhicitta.
The foolish should understand that they ought not to give rise to contempt for the conduct of the Bodhisattvas.
One might measure the great ocean with a single blade of grass,
but the conduct of sentient beings cannot be conceived.
Even if the waters of the great ocean were all melted into molten bronze, [it would still not equal their deeds].
For the sake of one's own life, one might still be able to drink it all up;
yet regarding the practices of the Bodhisattvas, one must never disparage or destroy them.
Like drinking molten copper, its suffering is beyond counting.
Whether there be obstacles of karma, or they be disturbed by Māra,
in whatever place those people are reborn, they shall never have sorrow or regret.
If a person, for the sake of pleasure, is deluded regarding foul forms, [they will suffer].
One who breaks the precepts is loathsome and not to be revered;
yet toward such persons, one should not give rise to contempt.
The conduct of sentient beings is exceedingly difficult to comprehend.
Just as Śāriputra, Entering silent meditative concentration,
Is able, within a single moment of mind, To know only fifty moments of mind;
Yet just as the World-Honored Ones, Know the immeasurable in a single thought.
One should not give rise to doubt regarding the Buddhas.
Just as an Arhat does not know his own realm, how much less could he possibly know the realm of sentient beings?
Therefore, no person at all should speak these words:
"I can know what is being thought in the minds of sentient beings.
I see one wearing dyed robes who, in an instant, puts on white garments.
Thus, in every moment of thought, there is change and transformation;
how much more so for one who can know the truth? Such a person is afflicted by folly.
It is like Ajātaśatru, who murdered his own father.
Furthermore, if one conceives a mind of malice and rebellion toward the Tathāgata,
yet within a single thought-moment deeply repents of that transgression,
one can immediately eliminate the retribution for the sin and be liberated from the suffering of the evil realms.
How much more so for one who can give rise to a pure and wholesome mind of their own accord?
This mind is sometimes bound and this mind is sometimes liberated;
this body is indeterminate (avyākṛta) and possesses no object of cognition.
How can this body be subject to faults and evils? This body should not be attached to bodily form,
nor should it ever commit the act of killing another’s body.
Just as pure gold, though fallen into impurity,
Is eternally pure by its very nature and cannot be defiled by that impurity; so too,
although such a person may indulge in desires and engage in worldly ways, [they remain untainted].
That person possesses true merit, and their virtuous mind never diminishes.
Whether as a prince or the son of a householder, they bring laughter and joy to the assembly;
all the great kings who behold them find delight.
Moving among these sentient beings, some dwell among gods and humans;
some eat poison without dying, and some grasp fire without being burned—
how much more so for one who possesses true awakening!
The ignorant cannot take away [the merit of] practice; even Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas do not equal the giving to a Bodhisattva.
Being equal like the Buddha, the Bodhisattva is equal to the Buddha.
Behold how profound is the virtuous mind!

It is like the sands of the Ganges; even if one were to fill all the worlds of the Buddhas with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, if one were to write out and uphold this sutra, should one wish to compare its merit [to that offering], [the latter would far surpass it].
Its manifold benefits are beyond comparison; one gains excellent benefit for one's life and does not lose the bodhicitta.
If a person, for the sake of wealth, enters the great ocean, they will surely obtain great profit.
If one upholds all the sutras and is able to expound them for many people,
yet has not heard this sutra, one will not know the conduct of sentient beings.
For these reasons, one should understand its superiority.
Do not praise your own virtues, nor should you slander or disparage others;
practice with a virtuous mind and pure conduct.
This is the foremost path to enlightenment: delighting in forest hermitages.
Constantly guarding the sensory faculties, diligently practicing vigor,
remaining far removed from kinsmen, and cultivating the supreme compassion of ultimate truth—
in this way, one shall swiftly attain the path to enlightenment.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this sutra, sixty thousand devas and humans attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
eighteen nayutas of devas and humans who had not yet resolved their minds were inspired to give rise to the bodhicitta.

By hearing this sutra, one eliminates the offenses of birth and death for eighty kalpas; therefore, those who do not wish to abandon bodhi should receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and contemplate it well, applying themselves diligently to skillful means, enduring with patience, and joyfully practicing its teachings.

At that time, ten thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly were about to withdraw from the resolve for enlightenment, giving rise to doubt and regret; they wished to return home, unaware of the obstacles and the transgressions of demonic activities.

Upon hearing this sutra preached, they shall abandon their transgressions and, having conceived even a small measure of faith before the World-Honored One, shall attain Buddhahood simultaneously with Maitreya Bodhisattva in this world.

Having purified the demonic activities of twenty kalpas, they shall not rise from this seat but will dwell in the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha). They shall be reborn in other worlds and, at the time when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, they shall all attain Buddhahood simultaneously; for they have eliminated the demonic activities and afflictions of twenty kalpas.
If even merely hearing this sutra can bring about such great benefit for a bodhisattva, how much more so for one who receives, upholds, reads, recites, and explains it clearly!
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the devas, humans, and asuras rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixteen;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Fifth Assembly of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, Part One: The Holy Assembly at the Dharma Gathering, Number One. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were renowned among the great śrāvaka community. Their names were as follows:

The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāman, Bhadrika, Vimala, Subhadra, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Gavāmpati, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahācunda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Aniruddha, Revata, Rājakarṇin, Tīrṇapāra, Makula, Nanda, Prabhasa, Svāgata, Rāhula, Ānanda, and others, were his chief disciples.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, namely the bodhisattvas Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and Maitreya, as well as the assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, surrounding him in front and behind.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by a group of sixteen great beings, including the Bodhisattva Skillful Contemplation of Meaning, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Eloquence, the Bodhisattva Contemplating Non-abiding, the Bodhisattva Skillful Transformation of Supernatural Powers, the Bodhisattva Light Banner, the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Tranquil Faculties, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Vow, the Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, and the Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, who served as their leaders. Together they all followed and cultivated the path of Samantabhadra, fulfilling all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, dwelling securely within all dharmas of merit, and reaching the ultimate further shore of all Buddha-dharmas.

May I attain equal and perfect enlightenment within all worlds; furthermore, may I be born in that Tuṣita Heaven, and at the end of my lifespan there, descend to be born from the right side [of my mother], take seven steps, emit great radiance, cause the entire Buddha-world to quake in six ways, and proclaim:
"I am the most noble and honored among all the worlds."
Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas came to personally attend upon him.

Furthermore, he was seen practicing and studying writing, calculation, calendrical science, grammar, the arts, medicine, hygiene, and the casting of seals; as well as other games and diversions, in which he excelled and surpassed others.

Dwelling within the royal palace, he grew weary of all sensual realms; seeing old age, sickness, and death, he realized the impermanence of the world. Renouncing his royal station, he scaled the city walls to study the Way.

Unbinding his various necklaces and Kāśika silks, he donned the kāṣāya robe and practiced austerities for six years, being able to manifest such demonstrations within this world-system of five turbidities.

In accordance with worldly custom, he bathed in the Nairañjanā River and proceeded toward the site of enlightenment. There, the dragon king welcomed and praised him, while the assembly of bodhisattvas circumambulated him to the right and extolled his virtues.
At that time, the Bodhisattva accepted the grass and spread it himself beneath the Bodhi tree, where he sat down cross-legged.

Furthermore, seeing the hosts of Māra surrounding him and about to inflict harm, the Bodhisattva, through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, subdued the demonic adversaries and attained supreme enlightenment.

At the request of Brahmā to turn the Wheel of Dharma, the Buddha—courageous and fearless—roared with his voice, beating the drum of Dharma, blowing the conch of Dharma, erecting the great banner of Dharma, and kindling the torch of the True Dharma. He embraced the True Dharma and all meditative absorptions; he rained down the great rain of Dharma to nourish all living beings, and thundered the great roar of Dharma to awaken everyone.

A great light shines universally throughout all Buddha-fields; within these worlds, the earth quakes everywhere, the palaces of Māra are destroyed, and Pāpīyān is struck with terror. The city of afflictions is shattered, the net of false views is cast down, dark dharmas are abandoned, and all pure dharmas are brought forth.
They are able to receive and digest the food offered to the Buddha, proclaiming the sublime principles to discipline sentient beings.

Sometimes they see him smile and emit hundreds of thousands of rays of light, ascending the stage of empowerment and receiving the prediction of enlightenment; or they see him attain the Way of Buddhahood and enter Nirvana, causing immeasurable sentient beings to all achieve the exhaustion of outflows and bringing to maturity the boundless roots of goodness of bodhisattvas.
In this way, they are able to manifest and display all such Buddha-fields.
It is like a master illusionist who, being well-versed in the arts of illusion, can manifest the appearances of men, women, and so forth, yet within those appearances, nothing real can be found.

In this way, because these bodhisattvas have well studied the merit of boundless illusory arts, they are able to manifest transformations in accordance with reality; and because they have thoroughly understood the path of transformation, they manifest great compassion throughout all buddha-fields, universally benefiting all living beings.
The bodhisattva’s vows and practices achieve boundlessness; they penetrate the equality of immeasurable gateways of meaning and fully cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
They enter impartially into all buddha-fields and are constantly exhorted and empowered by all buddhas.
Recognized and certified by all Tathāgatas, he acts as an ācārya for the instruction of bodhisattvas.

He constantly practices and accords with boundless deeds, attains mastery over the conduct of the entire dharma-realm, is well able to understand sentient beings and their lands, and always exerts himself to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.

They perceive various bodies as being like reflections; having skillfully mastered the Indra’s Net, they are able to shatter the net of Māra, destroy the net of all views, and enter the net of sentient beings. They are able to transcend the retinue of afflictions, as well as the factions and followers of Māra.

Having distanced themselves from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they enter the gateways of the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet are able to abide securely in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

From the outset, they take no pleasure in entering the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles; they attain various samādhis that are without arising or ceasing, as well as all the gateways of dhāraṇī. Their faculties, eloquence, and resolve are vast and definitive, and they are thoroughly proficient in understanding the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Entering awakening into the Buddha-flower Samādhi according to the occasion, they possess all kinds of profound meditative concentrations; all Buddhas appear before them, and within a single thought-moment, they travel throughout all Buddha-lands, circling back and forth without the passage of time differing.

They are able to discern all extremes regarding what is difficult and what is not difficult; they skillfully understand and expound the distinctions of the *bhūtakoṭi*; they attain the eloquence of the Buddhas and abide in the practices of Samantabhadra.
They are well able to distinguish the languages of sentient beings, transcend all worldly phenomena, and skillfully know all supramundane dharmas.
Having attained the perfection of mastery over requisites, they shoulder the burden of sentient beings as uninvited friends.
They are able to uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Tathāgatas and abide in the uninterrupted lineage of all Buddhas.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he is able to open the Dharma-eye, closing the gates to all evil realms and opening the doors to the happy realms.
He universally regards all sentient beings with the thought that they are his parents and brothers, and furthermore, he views all living beings as being like his own body.
Having realized all praiseworthy virtues, they are well-versed in the *pāramitās* and can eloquently praise all the virtues of the Tathāgata, as well as other dharmas worthy of praise.
In this way, an immeasurable and boundless assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered together.

Then, at that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "O Great Virtuous World-Honored One! [This concludes] the second request made by Ānanda. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robes, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
The color of his body and all his faculties are utterly pure; his majestic radiance is brilliant, like a mass of molten gold, and like a bright mirror reflecting a concentrated glow.
Never having seen such a sight since time immemorial, I am filled with joy at being able to behold him and give rise to a sense of rare wonder.

The World-Honored One has now entered the Great Samādhi of Quiescence; his practice of the Tathāgata’s deeds is entirely perfected, and he is well able to establish the conduct of a Great Man as he contemplates the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you dwell in this contemplation?
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
“How can you now understand this meaning?”
“Did various devas come to inform you?
Or did you see me and know it yourself?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!”
"I conceived this thought because I saw the Tathāgata’s rare and auspicious radiance, not because of the devas and others.
The Buddha granted his permission for the proclamation and addressed Ānanda with these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
It is well that you have asked this now.
You possess subtle eloquence and are most skillful in discernment to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning as this.

It is because you are a Great Being who has appeared in the world—rare as the udumbara flower—for the sake of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and for the benefit of all living beings through abiding in great compassion, that you ask about this meaning.
Furthermore, out of compassion and for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, you are able to inquire about such a matter as this from the Tathāgata.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is well able to reveal immeasurable knowledge and vision.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are without obstruction. Ānanda!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, desiring to remain in the world for as long as he wishes, can abide for immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, or even exceeding such numbers, yet there is no increase or decrease in the Tathāgata’s body or his sense faculties.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has attained mastery over samādhi and reached the further shore, possessing supreme mastery over all dharmas. Therefore, Ānanda!
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
This was the fourth instance of an ancient Buddha's appearance. At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In the past, beyond incalculable and countless great kalpas, a Buddha appeared named Dīpaṃkara."
Beyond an incalculable number of eons prior to that Buddha, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Duṣkaracaryā.
Prior to the Buddha Duṣkaracaryā, there was another Tathāgata named Candrānana.
Beyond countless Buddhas before the Buddha Candramaṇḍala, there was the Buddha Candanagandha.
Before that Buddha was the Buddha Sumerusamcaya, and before the Buddha Sumerusamcaya was the Buddha Merukalpa.
In this manner, through successive succession, there appeared the Buddha Vimalamukha,
the Buddha Asaṃkliṣṭa, the Buddha Nāgadeva, the Buddha Parvataśvararāja, the Buddha Sumerusaṃcaya, the Buddha Suvarṇagarbha,
the Buddha Prabhāsvara, the Buddha Tejorāja, the Buddha Mahāpṛthivīgotra, and the Buddha Vairocanaprabhā-vaiḍūryasuvarṇakāñcana.
Candrapratibimba-buddha, Vikasitakusumavyūhaprabha-buddha, Sāgaravarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña-buddha,
Vajraprabha-buddha, Mahāgadakṣagandhaprabha-buddha, Vigatasaṃkleśacitta-buddha, Ratnavardhana-buddha,
Parākramasaṃcaya-buddha, Jayasaṃcaya-buddha, and Mahāguṇadhara-buddha.
Dharma-Gift Supernatural Power Buddha, Outshining the Sun and Moon Light Buddha, Radiant Lapis Lazuli Buddha, Mind-Awakening Flower Buddha,
Moonlight Buddha, Sunlight Buddha, Flower-Garland Color-King Fully Blossomed Supernatural Power Buddha,
Water-Moonlight Buddha, Destroyer of the Darkness of Ignorance Buddha, and Pearl-Coral Canopy Buddha.
Buddha Tiṣya, Buddha Victorious Flower, Buddha Dharma-Wisdom Roar, Buddha Possessing the Lion’s Roar and Goose’s Cry,
and Buddha Brahma-Voice Dragon-Roar.
Buddhas such as these appeared in the world, with the intervals between their appearances exceeding all measurable kalpas.
Countless eons before that Buddha Nāgarāja appeared in the world, there was a Buddha named Lokendra.

Countless eons prior to the time of Lokendra, a Buddha appeared in the world named Lokendrarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
The Fifth Chapter: Praising the Buddha Dharmodgata. “Ānanda!

Within that Buddha’s teaching, there was a bhikṣu named Dharmodgata. He possessed superior conduct, vows, and the power of mindfulness and wisdom; his mind was firm and unshakable, and he was distinguished by merit and knowledge, with a most majestic and handsome appearance.”

Ānanda! That bhikṣu Dharmasthiti went to where the Tathāgata Lokendrarāja was, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable and boundless light; Throughout the entire world, no light can serve as a metaphor for it.”
The light and majesty of all suns, moons, and mani-jewels are entirely eclipsed by the Buddha’s radiance.
The World-Honored One can manifest a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind;
he can also manifest a single wondrous form-body, enabling all beings to see it according to their respective types.
In ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, diligence, and extensive learning, you are peerless among all sentient beings;
with a mind-stream of awakened insight like the great ocean, you are well able to comprehend the most profound Dharma.
With delusions exhausted and faults extinguished, you are worthy of receiving offerings; such noble virtue belongs only to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha possesses extraordinary and great majestic radiance, universally illuminating immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions.
I now praise all your virtues, hoping that my merit and wisdom may equal those of the Tathāgata,
so that you may save all the worlds from the manifold sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
May you abide steadfastly in samādhi, And expound the various Dharma-gates of generosity and morality,
As well as patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, So that you may attain Buddhahood and deliver all sentient beings.
In pursuit of the unsurpassed Great Bodhi, they made offerings to the wondrously awakened ones of the ten directions—
hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, may I obtain great divine radiance, Shining doubly upon billions of Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
And through boundless power of supreme progress, May I attain a distinguished, vast, and pure abode.
Thus, within these peerless Buddha-fields, they shall dwell and bring benefit to all sentient beings;
those most excellent Great Beings of the ten directions shall all be born there with joyful hearts.

Only the noble wisdom of the Buddha can realize and know this; now I seek the power of firmness, so that even if I were to sink into the various Avīci hells, my resolve for such a vow shall never retreat.
"The unimpeded wisdom regarding all worlds— One should understand such a mind in this way.
[Chapter Six: Receiving a Pure Land] "Furthermore, Ānanda!..."
Having praised the Buddha’s virtues, the bhikṣu Dharmasthāna addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now resolve my mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. I only pray that the Tathāgata will expound for me such teachings as these, so that I may attain the peerless great bodhi within the world and fully encompass the pure adornments of a buddha-field.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu,
"You should personally purify your own buddha-field.
Dharmasthiti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We lack the power and capacity to undertake this task of reception; we only pray that the Tathāgata will describe the pure adornments of other buddha-fields, so that having heard them, we may vow to bring them to fulfillment.”

At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded for him the twenty-one billion pure buddha-fields and their complete adornments; when he preached this Dharma, one hundred million years passed.

Ānanda! The bhikṣu Dharmasthiti fully embraced all the matters of adornment and purity within those twenty-one billion buddha-fields; having embraced them, he contemplated and practiced them for the full duration of five kalpas.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is the lifespan of that Tathāgata Lokendrarāja?"
The World-Honored One said:
"The lifespan of that Buddha shall be a full forty kalpas, Ānanda!"
The buddha-fields of those twenty-one koṭis of buddhas were surpassed by the buddha-field encompassed by the bhikṣu Dharmodgata.

Having taken possession of it, he went to the place where the Tathāgata Lokêśvararāja was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and standing to one side, addressed him:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I have already taken possession of and fully perfected a pure Buddha-field endowed with all virtues.
The Buddha said, "Now is the very time; you should explain this in detail to bring joy to the assembly, so that the great multitude shall likewise take possession of and perfect a Buddha-field."
The Seventh: Making the Great Vow. Dharmasthāna addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, will grant me his hearing; I shall now declare a most excellent vow.”
"If I should attain unsurpassed bodhi, yet there remain those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals within my land, I shall never take up unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any sentient beings in my land who fall into the three evil realms, may I never attain perfect enlightenment.
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land should not all be of the same golden hue, may I never attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any difference in the physical appearance or features of the sentient beings in my land such that some are handsome and others ugly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land should fail to recall their past lives, even to the extent of being unable to know events of a hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of kalpas ago, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings within my land should lack the divine eye, such that they cannot see even hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings within my land do not obtain the divine ear, such that they cannot hear the Dharma being preached by Buddhas even as many as hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of yojanas away, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings within my land lack the knowledge of others' minds, such that they do not even know the mental activities of sentient beings within hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

“If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, the sentient beings within my land do not attain the perfection of sovereign supernormal powers such that they can, in a single thought-moment, traverse hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddha-fields, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
"If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings within my land who give rise to even the slightest notion of 'I' or 'mine,' may I not attain Bodhi.
"If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings within my land who do not resolutely achieve Equal and Perfect Enlightenment or realize Great Nirvana, may I not attain Bodhi."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, my radiance should be limited such that it does not extend downward to illuminate even hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of buddha-fields beyond calculation, may I not attain bodhi."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, my lifespan were limited—even to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas or any number that can be calculated—I shall not take hold of Bodhi."

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the number of śrāvakas in my land shall be such that none can know it—even if all sentient beings and pratyekabuddhas throughout the trichiliocosm were to exhaust their intellectual calculations for hundreds of thousands of years, they still could not know it;
if there were anyone who could know it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings within my land have a limited lifespan, may I not attain Bodhi—
except for those who take birth through the power of their vows."
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any being in my land who bears an unwholesome name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the countless Buddhas within those immeasurable lands do not collectively praise and extol my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I realize unexcelled enlightenment, sentient beings in other buddha-fields, having heard my name, dedicate all their roots of goodness with every thought toward the vow to be born in my land—even if they do so for as few as ten recitations—if they should not be born there, may I not attain bodhi;
excepting only those who have committed the evil karma of the immediate retributions, or who slander the true Dharma and the noble ones."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings in other lands who resolve their minds on Bodhi, and who conceive pure thoughts of me, further dedicating their roots of goodness with the vow to be born in Sukhāvatī; yet, if such beings should not be reborn there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
"When that person is on the verge of death, I, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, shall appear before them.
If this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
'If, when I become a Buddha, all sentient beings in immeasurable lands who hear my name and dedicate their own roots of goodness toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss..."
If these do not arise, I shall not attain awakening.
"If, when I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas in my land do not all achieve the thirty-two marks, I shall not attain awakening."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, all bodhisattvas in that land shall reach the stage of being 'born only once more' before attaining great enlightenment—

except for those bodhisattvas who have made great vows to don the armor of diligence for the sake of all sentient beings, who zealously practice for their benefit and cultivate great nirvana, who traverse all Buddha-lands performing the bodhisattva conduct, who make offerings to all Tathāgatas, who establish sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in unexcelled awakening, whose practiced deeds are even more sublime than before, and who depart by traversing the path of Samantabhadra."
"If it were not so, I would not attain enlightenment.

'If, when I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas in my land shall every morning make offerings to as many Buddhas as there are in other directions—even up to immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands—and by the power of those Buddhas, they shall return to their own land before the meal is finished.'"
"If it were not so, I would not attain enlightenment.

'If, when I become a Buddha, the various kinds of requisites required by the assembly of bodhisattvas in that land, as well as the roots of goodness planted in the presence of the Buddhas, were not of such a nature as to be perfectly complete, I would not attain enlightenment.'"
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who preach the essentials of all dharmas do not skillfully and harmoniously enter into omniscience, may I not attain bodhi."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas born in that land do not possess the firm strength of Nārāyaṇa, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be no sentient being capable of fully describing all the ornamental features throughout the land, nor even those with the divine eye able to comprehend all the various forms, colors, and radiant signs thereof."
"If there were anyone capable of knowing [these trees] and fully describing them, I would not take up bodhi.

'If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land possesses immeasurable colored trees a hundred thousand yojanas high, and if among the bodhisattvas there were those with inferior roots of goodness who could not understand them, I would not attain perfect enlightenment.'"
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land who read, recite, teach, and expound the scriptures should not obtain supreme eloquence, may I not attain Bodhi.”
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any bodhisattvas in my land who do not achieve boundless eloquence, may I not attain Bodhi.

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land is so radiant and pure that it is peerless throughout, illuminating immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds, like the reflection of one's face appearing in a clear mirror."
"If it were not so, I would not attain enlightenment.

'If, when I become a Buddha, within the lands of my realm there shall be infinite varieties of incense in both the earth and the void, and furthermore, hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of precious incense burners, the fragrance of which shall universally permeate the entire realm of space—its scent being so sublime as to surpass the treasures of humans and devas—and this be offered to the Tathāgata and the assembly of Bodhisattvas.'"
"If it were not so, I would not attain enlightenment.

'If, when I become a Buddha, all sentient beings throughout the infinite, countless, inconceivable, and incomparable realms of the ten directions who are touched by the illumination of my Buddha-majesty shall have their bodies and minds find peace and happiness exceeding that of humans and devas.'"
"If it were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment.

'If, when I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas in immeasurable, inconceivable, and incomparable Buddha-fields, upon hearing my name, should not realize the stage of non-retrogression and obtain dharanis, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'"

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, all women throughout the countless, inconceivable, and immeasurable Buddha-lands, upon hearing my name, shall attain pure faith, resolve for Bodhicitta, and grow weary of their female bodies."
"If, in a future life, I do not relinquish the female body, may I not attain bodhi.

'If, when I have become a Buddha, the assembly of bodhisattvas in immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and peerless buddha-fields, having heard my name, should attain the state of non-arising yet fail to practice the sublime brahmacarya until they reach great bodhi, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'"

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, all the Bodhisattvas throughout the measureless Buddha-fields of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, shall prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva with a pure mind."
"If any devas or humans do not pay me homage, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
"If, when I become a Buddha, the clothing required by the sentient beings in my land arrives as soon as it is thought of, just as the Buddha [said]: 'Welcome, bhikṣu.'"
“Dharma robes shall naturally appear upon my body; if this were not so, I would not attain bodhi.

‘If, when I become a Buddha, all classes of sentient beings who are born within my land do not all obtain the necessities of life and achieve pure hearts and peaceful bliss, as do bhikṣus who have attained the destruction of outflows, I would not attain bodhi.’”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings in my land who wish to see the various Buddhas and the sublime adornments of their pure lands shall all appear within the jeweled trees, just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a clear mirror."
"If it were not so, I would not attain enlightenment.

'If, when I become a Buddha, there are sentient beings in other buddha-fields who, upon hearing my name, should have any deficiency in their faculties or lack the full breadth of spiritual qualities and functions until they reach enlightenment, may I not attain enlightenment.'"

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are bodhisattvas in other Buddha-fields who, upon hearing my name, do not all skillfully distinguish the names and terminology of the supreme samādhis, such that while dwelling in those samādhis they cannot, in a single moment of speech, make offerings to immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and peerless Buddhas, and furthermore do not directly realize the six samādhis, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be bodhisattvas in other buddha-fields who, upon hearing my name, do not—after the end of their lives—attain birth into noble and wealthy families, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in other Buddha-fields who hear my name do not, at the appropriate time, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, attain pure joy, dwell in equanimity, and become fully endowed with all roots of goodness, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, bodhisattvas from other realms, upon hearing my name, shall all attain the gate of samādhi of equality; dwelling within this concentration, they shall constantly make offerings to immeasurable and peerless Buddhas, never regressing until they reach bodhi."
"If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
'If, when I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas in my land shall, according to their aspirations, spontaneously hear whatever Dharma they wish to hear.'"
"If it were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment.
'If, when I have realized unsurpassed bodhi, any bodhisattvas in other buddha-fields who hear my name should regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'"

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, any bodhisattvas in other Buddha-fields who hear my name should not, at that very moment, obtain the first, second, or third stage of patience (*kṣānti*), and should not be able to realize for themselves the state of non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas, may I not attain enlightenment."
8. Thus, having spoken these verses as a self-imposed vow, at that time the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"After that Bhikṣu Dharmasthiti had made this vow before the Tathāgata Lokendrarāja, he, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, spoke in verse:
'I now, before the Tathāgata, have made this great vow: On the day when I shall realize unsurpassed Bodhi, ...'"
If I do not fulfill these supreme vows, I shall not become the peerless Honored One endowed with the ten powers.
If my mind cannot endure practicing giving constantly, to extensively relieve the poor and destitute and free them from all suffering,
to benefit the world and bring it peace and happiness, I shall not become the Dharma King who saves the world.
If, when I have realized bodhi while seated at the site of enlightenment, my fame does not pervade the ten directions throughout immeasurable and boundless diverse buddha-fields,
may I not attain the state of the World-Honored One endowed with the ten powers.
While he was setting out for supreme, great enlightenment, he left the home life seeking only the objects of desire;
lacking mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct therein, he did not become a Tamer, a Teacher of Gods and Men.
May I obtain the immeasurable light of the Tathāgata, Which universally illumines all Buddha-lands in the ten directions;
May it be able to extinguish all greed, anger, and delusion, And likewise sever all evil destinies within the world.
May I obtain the light that opens the eye of pure wisdom, Shatter the darkness within all realms of existence,
Extinguish all hardships without remainder, And establish all in the Greatly Majestic One, among devas and humans.
Having purified his fundamental practices through cultivation, he has attained immeasurable and supreme majestic radiance;
the brilliance of the sun, moon, devas, and mani-jewels is all eclipsed by it.
Having completed his practice, the Supreme Man becomes a hidden treasure for those in poverty;
possessing peerless perfection in wholesome qualities, he lets out a lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
In the past, you made offerings to the self-arisen wisdom; Through many eons, you diligently practiced various asceticisms.
Seeking the most supreme aggregate of all wisdoms, O Honored One among gods and humans, you have fulfilled your original vow.
The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are unimpeded; he fully comprehends all conditioned phenomena.
May I likewise become one who is peerless, a supreme knower and true guide.
If I shall indeed realize great enlightenment, And this vast vow be truly fulfilled,
May the trichiliocosm tremble, And the hosts of devas rain down flowers from the sky.
At that time, the great earth shook everywhere; celestial flowers and music filled the void, while fine sandalwood powder rained down as they proclaimed: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha."
9. Cultivating the Bodhisattva Practices. The Buddha told Ānanda:

“That Bhikṣu Dharmodgata, in the presence of the Tathāgata Lokêśvararāja, as well as before gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, extensively made such great and vast vows; all have already been accomplished, being rare wonders in the world.”
Having made this vow, he dwells in accordance with reality within various meritorious qualities, fully adorning a vast, pure buddha-field of majestic power.

While practicing such bodhisattva conduct, throughout immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and incomparable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he never once gives rise to greed, hatred, or delusion, nor thoughts of desire, harm, or malice; he does not give rise to perceptions of form, sound, smell, taste, or touch. Toward all sentient beings, he always delights in love and respect as if toward his own kin; his nature is gentle and easy to dwell with.

When others come to seek something, he does not oppose their intentions; with kind words and exhortations, there is none who does not follow his heart’s desire. He provides whatever necessities are required to sustain their physical lives.
Having few desires and being content, he always delights in seclusion and tranquility; endowed with sharp intelligence, he is free from artifice and falsehood.
His nature is disciplined and compliant, free from violence or malice; he constantly harbors compassion and patience toward all sentient beings.
His mind is neither deceitful nor fickle, nor is it indolent; he skillfully uses virtuous words to exhort himself to seek all pure dharmas.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he is courageous and never retreats; his great vows for the benefit of the world are fulfilled.
He serves his teachers and honors the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; he constantly dons the armor of bodhisattva conduct and delights in tranquility, remaining free from all defilements and attachments.

To cause sentient beings to constantly cultivate pure dharmas and to be preeminent among all wholesome qualities, they abide in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; in non-action, non-arising, and non-ceasing; and remain free from pride.
When that noble being practices the bodhisattva path, he always guards his speech; he does not harm others or himself through words, but always uses vocal karma to benefit both himself and others.
If he enters a royal city or various villages, although he sees various forms, his mind remains unstained; with a pure mind, he feels neither attachment nor aversion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having initiated the practice of the *dānapāramitā* himself, is further able to cause others to practice giving.
Regarding the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they bring both of the aforementioned practices to complete fulfillment.

By virtue of having perfected such roots of goodness, immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of treasuries spontaneously emerge wherever they are born; furthermore, they cause immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, peerless, and boundless classes of sentient beings to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In this way, the boundless assembly of bodhisattvas gives rise to various sublime practices to make offerings to and serve all World-Honored Ones until they attain buddhahood; all of these cannot be known through the conceptual discrimination of language.

Or they may become wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), Śakra, Suyāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, or Mahābrahmā; in all these states, they are able to serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, and are able to entreat the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

If they become kings of Jambudvīpa, or various elders, officials, brahmins, kṣatriyas, and others among the various castes, they will all be able to respect and make offerings to the Buddhas, and furthermore, they will be able to expound immeasurable Dharma gates.
From this point on, they will forever leave the world behind and attain unsurpassed enlightenment.

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas are able to provide all Tathāgatas with the finest clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal requisites for as long as they live, enabling them to dwell in peace and happiness.
Such various and perfected roots of goodness cannot be fully described by words.

From his mouth there constantly issues the wondrous fragrance of sandalwood, which pervades immeasurable, incalculable, and even hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of worlds; furthermore, from all his pores issues a sublime fragrance surpassing that of humans and devas, like the scent of the utpala lotus.
In whatever place they are born, their physical marks and signs will be upright, dignified, and supremely perfect.
Furthermore, they shall attain the perfection of mastery over all requisites, such that all articles of use are universally provided without lack.

All manner of precious incense, flowers, banners, pennants, silken canopies, exquisite garments, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, as well as hidden treasures, rare curiosities, and all necessities, naturally flow forth from the palms of the Bodhisattva’s hands; furthermore, from all the pores of his body, issue forth every kind of music for humans and devas.
By these causes and conditions, they are able to cause immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable multitudes of sentient beings to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Ānanda! I have now explained the places where Bodhisattvas originally practiced their cultivation.
This was the tenth [chapter], "The Places at the Time of Attaining Buddhahood. At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for that Bodhisattva Dharmasthiti who attains enlightenment, does he belong to the past,
or does he belong to the future?”
"Is it currently in another world elsewhere?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"To the west of here, beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-fields, there is a world named Sukhāvatī."
The bhikṣu Dharmasthiti attained buddhahood there, named Amitāyus; he currently dwells there preaching the Dharma, surrounded by a respectful assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Chapter Eleven: The Infinite Radiance "Ānanda!

The radiance of that Buddha shines universally throughout immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable Buddha-fields. I shall now describe it briefly: his light illuminates lands in the eastern direction equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River; likewise, it is so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. Except for those places empowered by the majestic spiritual power of the original vows of other Buddhas, all are completely illuminated."
These rays of light from the Buddhas may extend one fathom, or one yojana, or even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of yojanas, or they may illuminate the entire Buddha-field.

Ānanda, for this reason, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life has further alternative names, namely: Immeasurable Light, Boundless Light, Unattached Light, Unobstructed Light, King of Radiant Majesty Light, Beloved Light, Joyful Light, Wondrous Light, Inconceivable Light, Peerless Light, Incommensurable Light, Outshining the Sun’s Light, Outshining the Moon’s Light, and Surpassing the Light of Both Sun and Moon.

That radiance was pure and vast, universally causing the bodies and minds of sentient beings to experience joy and bliss, and further causing all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others in all other buddha-fields to attain great delight.
"Ānanda! I now reveal the light of that Buddha; even if one were to speak for an entire kalpa, one could not exhaustively describe it.
The twelfth [chapter]: 'Furthermore, Ānanda, the assembly of noble ones is immeasurable.'"
The assembly of śrāvakas of that Tathāgata Amitāyus is immeasurable, and its limit cannot be known.

Suppose there were bhikṣus numbering in the hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis, all possessing mastery in supernatural powers like Mahāmaudgalyāyana; and suppose they were to traverse the great trichiliocosm at dawn and return to their original place in a mere instant. Even if they were to spend hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of years attempting to calculate the number of śrāvakas in the first assembly of the Buddha Amitāyus, exhausting all their supernatural power until their final nirvāṇa, they would not know even one part in a hundred, nor one part in a thousand, nor one part in a hundred-thousand, nor even one part in an *upaniṣad* fraction.
Ānanda! It is like the great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, whose limits cannot be known even when gazed upon with the eyes.
Suppose there were a man who split the tip of a single hair into fifty parts, and with one of those parts, he took up a single drop from within that great ocean.
