Even if an ordained bodhisattva stays in the home of a layperson, I say there is no fault, and they may remain there as permitted. Why is this?
Because those good men and good women desire that this Dharma shall not disappear after their lives have ended.

Śāriputra! Even if those villages and towns are far away, these bodhisattvas should still go there, and while residing therein, they should receive, uphold, read, recite, reveal, and expound [the teachings].

Śāriputra! Those sons or daughters of good family, regarding this Dharma-gate that has already been disseminated and praised, or wherever else such a scripture may exist with another person, should go to them and transcribe it.

If that person has any aspiration or request, you should observe a fast, or engage in walking meditation, sitting, standing, or whatever else is required; you should comply with their instructions and transcribe this sutra.

If one cannot find it in that village, one should go to a neighboring region to transcribe it, receive it, uphold it, read and recite it until it is mastered, and furthermore, explain and expound it for others.
If one goes to other regions and diligently seeks it but does not obtain it, that person should give rise to this vow:
"I shall not give rise to any sign of regression regarding unsurpassed bodhi."
"Because I have heard the name and the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, this person wishes to benefit me by causing me to hear it. Śāriputra!
"Such praise of this Dharma-gate—that there are those who can expound it and those who may hear it—is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"After the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, by whose power shall this be heard? "Śāriputra!
After my parinirvāṇa, it shall again be heard through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya."
Alternatively, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, and others shall diligently provide protection so that these Dharma-preachers may proclaim this teaching.
Furthermore, as the fundamental karma of those bodhisattvas matures, the Four Heavenly Kings and others will exert their majestic power to encourage them, enabling the bodhisattvas to hear it.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A dharma-gate such as this is able to accomplish vast and great merit.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said, Śāriputra.”

If within the kingdom there is the calamity of rain and hail, untimely thunderbolts, or various other terrifying events, those sons and daughters of good family should single-mindedly recollect the Tathāgata Acalamati and invoke his name; then all such disasters shall be eliminated.

Because that Tathāgata, in the past, extensively rescued hundreds of thousands of nāgas and liberated them from all suffering; and because his compassionate original vow is true and not in vain, having dedicated these roots of goodness with the firm resolve for its fulfillment, the calling of his name causes afflictions and misfortunes to vanish of their own accord—except where the karmic retribution of sentient beings has already reached maturity.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those bodhisattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed bodhi in their present bodies should cultivate vows and practices just as the Tathāgata Akṣobhya did in the past.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“So it is, so it is, just as you have said. Śāriputra!”
Śāriputra, there are few bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already been able to thus fully cultivate a pure land and shall purify it like that of the Tathāgata Acala.

All those bodhisattvas shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they will be entirely equal in their buddha-nature, their omniscience, and their mastery over the adornment of buddha-lands.
"While there is no lack of distinction between Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, they are not different regarding liberation.
At that time, the devas of the desire realm and the Brahmakāyika devas all joined their palms toward the Tathāgata, prostrated themselves, and thrice proclaimed:
"Namo to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya! This is most rare!"
Furthermore, I take refuge in the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni of this world-system, who is well able to expound that Dharma-gate of praise.

At that time, the devas of the desire realm scattered *mandārava* flowers and various celestial incenses over the Buddha; the scattered incense and flowers combined in the air to form a canopy, and they further scattered celestial flowers and incense from afar upon that Buddha as an offering.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"This assembly of my fourfold followers and the various devas of the desire realm all wish to see that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that Śakradevendra, sat cross-legged and dwelt peacefully in mid-air.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, this great assembly also remained in the air, and they all beheld from afar the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and his assembly of śrāvakas in the world-system of Abhirati.
Having seen this, the assembly all knelt with their right knees upon the ground before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Acalo.
At that time, the people of this world all thought to themselves:
"Could it not be that the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have gathered here to see that Buddha, to pay homage, and to make offerings?"
At that time, Śakra thought to himself:
"The gods of that realm dwell with human forms; I observe that the clothing, ornaments, and articles of those humans are not in the slightest degree inferior to those of the gods."
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers and addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas, saying:
"All those people are enjoying celestial bliss; you should rejoice in this."

Those people who behold that Tathāgata and who delight in receiving celestial requisites—all those sentient beings, after passing away from their lives in other worlds, shall attain rebirth in the buddha-field of Akṣobhya.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Śakra:

“Since you have seen Śākyamuni Buddha and the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, by this very cause you have attained great and wholesome benefit in this body, let alone the fact that you have already attained superhuman dharmas.”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
“If those sentient beings gain such excellent benefit merely by hearing this Dharma-gate, how much more so will they who are born in the buddha-field of Akṣobhya!”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Those persons of the Bodhisattva vehicle who shall be born in that buddha-field will also obtain excellent benefit. Why is this?"
Because all those bodhisattvas should attain the stage of non-retrogression.
It should be known that if other bodhisattvas vow to be born in that Buddha-land in their current bodies, they are all already established in non-retrogression.
When the Buddha taught this Dharma-gate, five hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of mind through the outflow-free dharmas;
five thousand bodhisattvas, six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, eight thousand upāsakas, ten thousand upāsikās, and immeasurable devaputras from the desire realm all made vows to be reborn in that buddha-field.
At that time, the Tathāgata grants them all the prediction of enlightenment, that they shall attain rebirth in that buddha-field.
If there are other sentient beings who wish to be born there, the Tathāgata shall likewise grant them the prediction of birth in that buddha-field.

At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways—namely, it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere—due to the empowerment of this Dharma-gate.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Śāriputra and the others, as well as all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Dharma-Flower Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty, and Volume Twenty-One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
7. The Chapter on the Armor and Adornment, Part One of Seven.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom had gathered there from various buddha-fields.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by and venerated with respect by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands.

Within that assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Anantamati, who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated himself in homage, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have a slight doubt and wish to question the Tathāgata; I pray that you will deign to grant me your hearing and explain it for my sake.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati spoke in verse:
"The Great Hero, the Great Man, To whom none in the world is equal,"
For the sake of sentient beings, I ask my questions with little doubt.
Without rising from the lion throne, you manifest your body throughout the ten directions;
among all rival doctrines, none are able to shake you.
The treasury of wisdom is boundless, and the various powers are immeasurable;
with each of his powers, the World-Honored One is able to deliver the world universally.
He dwells well in all-knowledge and dwells well in the ten powers.
The fearless Great Lion, the most supreme and unsurpassed Honored One,
possesses the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata;
illuminating the world, he subdues all those of external paths.
Having fully understood all phenomena, you are therefore unsurpassed;
O Great Teacher, free from error, I shall ask you to resolve my doubts.
You possess boundless, stainless wisdom and the ocean-like, immovable wisdom.
Regarding the unimpeded knowledge of the spheres of experience, I have doubts that I shall ask you to resolve. O World-Honored One,
who has skillfully cultivated and gathered [wisdom], who is free from doubt regarding the Path,
the secure and great Guide— I have doubts that I shall ask you to resolve.
Having crossed over all violent floods, Having severed all fetters and bonds,
Able to extract the many poisoned arrows— I ask you, who have dispelled my doubts.
Having shattered the shell of ignorance, Having stilled the fever of the afflictions,
Calmly and securely abiding, I ask my doubts of you.
You who possess fearless, unsurpassed wisdom; you who possess unattached and unimpeded wisdom;
the ocean of Dharma, the omniscient one—O Tathāgata, you have already realized this.
The Buddha’s immeasurable merit and wisdom are all perfectly fulfilled;
he has exhausted all outflows and shattered all afflictions and views.
The World-Honored One has extensively accumulated immeasurable and great merit.
Inconceivable Dharma King, I shall ask my doubts of you.
World-Honored One of supreme wisdom, who universally illumines the world,
you who expound the radiance of the Dharma, an ocean of boundless merit.
Because the Teacher Dharmaprabha universally illuminates the world,
the light of the Buddha-dharma appears within this world.
He is the ocean of Dharma and the one of all-knowledge, whose eloquence is unsurpassed.
His diligence is inconceivable, pure and free from all views.
Because the Buddha-eye is boundless, the realm of his wisdom is likewise boundless.
To the World-Honored One, peerless in the world, I shall ask my doubts.
The Dharma King, the Great Sage, who can sever the delusions of sentient beings—the Guide—I shall now question him; may he act according to his own inclination.
I have surveyed every place, both in the heavens and among humans.
There is no one equal to the Tathāgata, the one who illuminates everywhere.
Firmly established in all virtues, adorned as a Great Man,
the inconceivable Dharma King, the radiant one among sages.
Just as the Great Snowy Mountains are a place of exquisite beauty adorned with myriad jewels,
so too is the World-Honored One seated upon the Dharma-throne, equally majestic and sublime.
With wondrous voice and great diligence, he is able to proclaim sounds that gladden the mind.
If sentient beings should hear it, their roots of goodness will all be purified.
The World-Honored One, supreme among men, now radiates the light of the Dharma;
by this means, all these sentient beings shall awaken according to their inclinations.
Knowing the time and the assembly, the Great Teacher who knows all men,
you spread forth the radiance of the Dharma; O possessor of timely wisdom,
with your Brahma-voice and great diligence, we pray that you grant us pure words.
Just as rain falls upon the great earth, The Dharma-moisture pervades and saturates all.
When the World-Honored One dwells amidst the assembly And universally proclaims the rain of Dharma,
All sentient beings who aspire to this Dharma Attain complete fulfillment.
Abiding in the most supreme and secure state, like a king atop Mount Sumeru,
he bestows gifts upon all sentient beings and is able to bring joy to the multitude.
The Great Hero, the Honored One among bipeds, dwells in an inconceivable realm.
Among all sentient beings, there is none who can know [this].
The Great Mahāsattva, having gathered the assembly in harmony,
relies upon the Great Muni and aspires to seek the realm of the Buddha.
I have come together here because I am intent upon the Buddha’s realm;
how may the Teacher, with his unimpeded wisdom, swiftly bring about awakening?
Following my own inclinations, I gaze upon his countenance, desiring to inquire.
World-Honored One, we pray that you will reveal [the truth], so as to sever all doubts.
If we hear this unsurpassed Dharma, our hearts will immediately find joy;
with rapture pervading our entire bodies, we shall be able to cut through the web of all uncertainties.
The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, Possessing all-knowledge and fearlessness,
the one who perceives all— I shall ask my doubts to you.
In all phenomena, the Buddha has not the slightest doubt.
Great Guide of Diligence, I shall ask you of my doubts;
O Unsurpassed One who severs doubt, you who have no uncertainty regarding the Dharma,
ocean of boundless merit, I shall ask you of my doubts.
Boundless great radiance, Boundless great merit,
Boundless pure wisdom— I ask you, who are free from doubt, about these.
Boundless wisdom of diligence, Boundless wisdom of the objective realm.
O World-Honored One of boundless wisdom, I have doubts that I shall now ask you to resolve.
O World-Honored One of boundless knowledge, who has transcended both extremes and the limitless, you are able to sever all doubts; I have doubts that I shall now ask you to resolve.
Inconceivable Dharma King, deign to listen to my inquiry with compassion;
having granted me permission to ask, O Muni, please proclaim the answer.
I inquire of the All-Knowing One, Śākyamuni, the Honored One of renowned fame.
"If you would deign to listen to me, I pray that you resolve my web of doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying: "Anantamati!..."
"You now look up to me with thirsty longing and seek with resolve; what do you wish to ask of the Tathāgata?
If there is anything to be asked, I shall explain it for you.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Tell Anantamati: ‘What do you wish to ask? You may ask anything, and I shall explain it.
According to what is asked, I will clarify each point; following your inclination, I shall swiftly provide the teaching.’”
I shall speak for you; have no doubt at all. According to your aspiration and in accordance with your inquiry, I will explain.
Since you ask now at the proper time and on the proper subject, because of this timely questioning, I shall give a definitive teaching.
According to your inclination, ask whatever you ought to ask; I shall comply with all of it and explain it for you.
You ask now at the proper time, and I too shall speak at the proper time; I will sever the net of your doubts, so that you may attain freedom from uncertainty.
I am the Dharma King; having realized the ultimate definitive meaning, I have attained freedom from doubt regarding all phenomena.
Having attained the inconceivable perfect awakening to all dharmas, I shall explain them according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, in response to their questions.
Regarding all dharmas, I have no doubts whatsoever; whenever one asks at the proper time, I shall quickly explain them for that person.
At such times, I explain for them without any uncertainty, resolving their doubts according to their inclinations.
I always clearly understand the time and the assembly, as well as the common inclinations of all sentient beings.
I also constantly observe all sentient beings—whether they possess desire or are free from desire—and perceive them all with perfect clarity.
If there are those with wisdom who are able to practice well, I shall, at the proper time,
awaken them through the True Dharma.
If there are those without wisdom, who are foolish and deluded, lacking the light of insight, they do not respect the Dharma.
If one lacks reverence and does not seek the Dharma, though one hears this Dharma, one will have no great wisdom.
One who is skillful in the Dharma seeks it with longing; if such a person hears this Dharma, they will attain great wisdom.
Those who delight in the Mahāyāna and seek the Honored One among men, having heard this Dharma, shall attain great and clear wisdom.
Those who set out toward the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom and inconceivable wisdom shall all find their hearing fully satisfied.
Delighting in unimpeded wisdom and seeking the most supreme Honored One, they who hear this Dharma obtain great benefit.
Those possessing the nature of wisdom and seeking the inconceivable, they who hear this Dharma attain unsurpassed knowledge.
If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha’s place of enlightenment, turning the unsurpassed wheel and attaining joy in the Dharma;
who delight in diligence and revere the Dharma, leaping for joy upon hearing the stainless teaching.
If there are sentient beings who delight in wholesome practice, through the light of the Dharma they shall proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma.
Bearing heavy burdens and striving with boundless diligence, once they have heard the Dharma, they will be filled with joy.
If you have aspirations and contemplate wholesome dharmas, I shall explain them to you with compassion.
Out of pity for you, I am able to provide a definitive resolution according to your questions; I shall sever your doubts.
For many thousands of years I have practiced skillful means; my doubts have been eliminated, and I know your intentions.
If you have any doubts, ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you and sever all your uncertainties.
If there be any who have doubts, let them ask whatever they wish; according to their desire, I shall explain it to them.
If there be any who have doubts, let them ask whatever they wish; I abide in the Dharma, having attained immovability.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I have a slight doubt concerning the Bodhisattvayāna; I shall now ask about it.”

What is the noble being who, free from fear and with single-minded right mindfulness, dons the great armor for the sake of all sentient beings, adorns himself with that great armor, gives rise to great love and joy, and honors it; who, through heedfulness, mounts this Great Vehicle and proceeds by the path of great purity, evenness, and correctness—a path devoid of mounds, tiles, stones, thorns, and all manner of evil impurities; free from the dense forests of various views, as well as poisonous thorns, the pits of suffering and affliction, and the hardships of bondage and fear?

Is it by means of a path that is upright and without crookedness, a path that accords with reality and is level, an unobstructed path—one that cuts through all dense thickets, tears asunder all nets, distances oneself from darkness, eliminates attachment, and abandons all associations—that you set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
World-Honored One!
It is for the sake of this meaning that I, regarding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, have posed this question:
Who is the virtuous man?
What is this great armor?
Clad in this armor and mounted upon the Great Vehicle, one should set forth by means of this Great Way.
World-Honored One!

One should explain the armor and adornment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: they abide securely in the path and abide securely in skillfulness regarding the principles of all dharmas; because they dwell in skillfulness regarding the principles of dharmas, they are able to give rise to the light of skillfulness regarding the principles of all dharmas.

Because of the light of the Dharma, they do not cast off their armor; riding upon the Great Vehicle, through the power of non-regressive diligence, the faculty of non-forgetfulness, and the power of continuous wisdom, they are swiftly able to achieve mastery in the clear and skillful principles of the Dharma-realm. They proceed to the site of enlightenment to turn the wheel of Dharma, preaching the teaching for the sake of all sentient beings, so that all sentient beings may, according to their aspirations and according to their respective inclinations, be liberated from birth and death.
World-Honored One!
Regarding this Great Vehicle of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I ask about this meaning for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings.
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is the all-knowing one and the all-seeing one. By what dharma do you bring about the accomplishment of the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal of All Dharmas for all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? And by means of this samādhi, how do you cause these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not to fall back, even until they have realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has accomplished the knowledge and vision of unprecedented dharmas and is skilled in the medicinal wisdom for all sentient beings;
therefore, I have asked this. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati spoke in verse:
"For the sake of all bodhisattvas, I ask the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings,
the All-Knowing and All-Seeing One, about the meaning of the profound Dharma of the Buddha:
regarding the practices cultivated in the Mahāyāna, by what concentration can one set out upon it?"
I now ask all these questions for the benefit of all sentient beings:
How does a virtuous man don the armor of the infinite?
Having thus donned the armor, how should he set forth?
How does one give rise to joyful aspiration?
How does one love that [state]?
And how does one possess great diligence?
What is non-negligence?
How do the bodhisattvas Mount this Great Vehicle?
Having mounted it, what then?
This matter should be explained:
how does one mount the Great Vehicle and set out upon the path of a bodhisattva?
I pray only that the World-Honored One, our Teacher, will swiftly proclaim this for me.
What is the path of the straight way, by which one proceeds with equanimity?
How does one tirelessly clear away the dense forest of all views?
And within the midst of all sensory objects, how does one achieve transcendence?
How, through equanimity, can one tear asunder the net of craving?
How can one dispel the darkness and attain the radiance of great wisdom?
How should those bodhisattvas set forth upon the path?
How can one observe so as to be far removed from all fetters?
How do the bodhisattvas dwell securely, free from bondage? How do the bodhisattvas transcend great terror?
Skillful in the meaning of all dharmas, how do they set out for the unsurpassed?
With what kind of boundless great armor is the bodhisattva clad?
Having donned this armor, they mount this Great Vehicle.
How do the bodhisattvas set out upon the level and correct path?
This is what I now ask; O World-Honored One, you should explain it.
How does a bodhisattva obtain the adornment of the great armor?
How does one adorn the Unsurpassed Vehicle?
World-Honored One, you should explain this.
How does one abide in this path, as well as adorn that path?
O World-Honored One, you should expound the skillfulness regarding all phenomena.
How can one come to understand the principle of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—
the light of skillfulness regarding phenomena?
World-Honored One, you should expound this:
how do all bodhisattvas attain this light of the Dharma and reach the ultimate realization of all phenomena?
World-Honored One, you should explain this:
how is it that all bodhisattvas, having attained the light of the Dharma,
do not cast off their great armor and thereby set forth?
How do the bodhisattvas, riding upon this Great Vehicle, advance with diligence and without regression? By what means do they set forth?
How do the bodhisattvas maintain constant firmness in their resolve and mindfulness?
By what power of wisdom can one achieve perfect self-mastery?
How does one attain skillfulness regarding the principles of the Dharma-realm?
O inconceivable King of Dharma, World-Honored One, we pray that you will proclaim this for us.
How can one travel swiftly to reach the site of enlightenment and turn the Great Brahma-wheel, which no one in the world can turn?
How is it that, remaining unmoved, one expounds all dharmas?
For the sake of all sentient beings, in accordance with their former vows, you expound all dharmas; thus, how can they be liberated from birth and death?
How may you cause sentient beings to ultimately attain peace and happiness?
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I ask the Teacher of the World,
the one who possesses all knowledge and vision: I pray that you will proclaim for me by what dharmas the various bodhisattvas are brought to fulfillment.
The great ocean of all phenomena, the seal of all that is done, and the samādhi—
those who joyfully seek the Buddha-dharma and thirst for the great bodhi will have their entire bodies suffused with delight upon hearing this teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, Anantamati!"

In the past, you made offerings to and served immeasurable Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness and accumulating merits beyond measure. You have long sought and yearned for this profound Dharma, and with great resolve and joy, you have brought sentient beings to maturity; thus, out of great compassion, you have questioned the Tathāgata.
Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall, for your sake, explain how all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through the fulfillment of their merits, set forth toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying:

“Anantamati! Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who don the armor for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi don the great armor because they desire to gather in all sentient beings; they practice giving for the sake of all sentient beings.”
Because of purity, they don the great armor; for the sake of the pure ethical discipline of all sentient beings, they don the great armor;
for the sake of the pure patience of all sentient beings, they don the great armor; for the sake of the pure diligence of all sentient beings, they don the great armor;
for the sake of the pure meditative concentration of all sentient beings, they don [the great armor].

Great Armor! One dons this great armor for the sake of purifying the wisdom of all sentient beings; one dons this great armor for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness;
one dons this great armor for the sake of giving rise to a mind that accords with the performance of beneficial deeds for all sentient beings;
and one dons this great armor for the sake of providing remedies for the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion among all sentient beings.
He dons the great armor because he is skillful in performing great merit; he dons the great armor because he brings supreme wisdom to perfect completion;
he dons the great armor because he acts as a protector for all sentient beings from the terrors of birth and death;
he dons the great armor because he desires to manifest the perfect completion of unequaled wisdom.

He has donned the great armor because he engages in battle against all the Māras in this trichiliocosm, whether they be the retinues of Māra, the messengers of Māra, or those who abide in the karma of Māra; and against those who travel the perilous paths of the dense forest of various views, including all the *cārikas* among the non-Buddhists, the Vaidika-Umārikas, the Lokāyatas, and those belonging to such non-Buddhist factions. Thus, for the sake of combat, he has donned the great armor.

Once all these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have thus donned the great armor, they do not cast off that armor but give rise to great diligence; they are able to enter into the realms of all sentient beings, abiding in patience and remaining far removed from fear, neither startled nor terrified, neither shaken nor disturbed, while further donning the boundless armor.

These are the armor for rescuing and protecting all sentient beings; the armor for cutting through the dense forest of all views; the armor for destroying the armies of Māra; the armor capable of bestowing wisdom; the armor of boundless ferries and bridges; the armor for crossing over heavy burdens; the armor for increasing pure faith; the armor for abiding securely in ethical discipline (*śīla*); the armor for purifying the storehouse of karma; the armor of the storehouse of all powers of purity; the armor of the storehouse of the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); the armor capable of severing all attachments; and the armor of wisdom that is non-retrogressive and free from regret.

Having donned such great armor as this, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not abandon it; until the very limit of existence, they never waver from their power of firm diligence as they set forth toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva dons the armor To gather in all sentient beings;
Because sentient beings are boundless, The armor he dons is likewise boundless.”
Because their generosity is pure, they cause all to be fully satisfied;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, they don these armor-like vows.
Because their ethical discipline is pure, they bring great benefit to the world.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one dons this armor;
because of the purity of forbearance, one dwells with courageous stability.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one dons this armor.
Because their diligence is pure, they achieve non-retrogression;
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they don these armor-like vows.
Because their meditative concentration is pure, the spheres of their activity are likewise so.
To benefit all sentient beings, he has donned this armor;
because his wisdom is pure, it is untainted and unsurpassed.
To benefit all sentient beings, he has donned this armor.
To all sentient beings, one should provide every means of happiness;
because of knowing this meaning well, one donned these armor-like vows.
Toward sentient beings, the Bodhisattva is able to perform acts of benefit.
By means of the four pure means of integration, he pervades all realms of existence.
If beings are afflicted by the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion, he acts as their remedy;
bestowing medicinal herbs upon all sentient beings, he causes their ailments to be eliminated.
By this, these bodhisattvas are well able to don their armor;
regarding the equipment of merit, they attain boundless skillfulness.
As for the suffering of birth and death that oppresses sentient beings, leaving them in a state of unrest—
I shall act as their protector, donning boundless armor;
the infinite sufferings of birth and death, I am able to bring them to liberation;
those bound by the net of craving and views—all these shall be severed.
Regarding this web of afflictions, those who are able to sever it all do so through the power of firm diligence, donning their armor with valor.
They cause all sentient beings to abide upon the path of peace and happiness.
By this one proceeds to nirvāṇa, peaceful and unsurpassed.
Through the power of great diligence, one donned this armor;
together with all Māras, one shall engage in battle without ever growing weary.
If one dwells amidst various views and wanders through the dense forest,
then for those such as the Lokāyatas who wear armor against them,
as well as for other immeasurable multitudes who practice all manner of heterodox paths, [this teaching] is beneficial.
Because they benefit all therein, they don the armor that is boundless.
Having thus donned the armor, they do not cast off their mail;
exerting the power of great diligence, they don the armor that is supremely firm.
Entering the realm of birth and death, one dwells in peace through patience;
having perfected steadfast patience, one dons the armor that is unsurpassed.
Free from all fear, one likewise remains without alarm or dread.
Donning the armor of the boundless, they diligently cultivate all practices.
Firmly established in this armor, they are always able to understand correctly;
serene and unmoving, they are neither distracted nor regressive.
Having donned such armor, the wise one should further don the armor that protects and saves sentient beings, the armor that destroys the armor of all Māras,
and the armor of the boundless bridge; all these should indeed be donned.
The person of courageous and supreme wisdom, having donned [the armor], dwells in peace.
Because it is a great and heavy burden, this unsurpassed armor is donned to deliver all sentient beings and cause them to be entirely freed from the burden of suffering.
Increasing pure faith, dwelling well within the six sense faculties,
and attaining harmony with the precepts— this armor is unsurpassed.
Accomplishing courageous wisdom, the bodhisattva is able to abide securely therein.
In accordance with the precepts of majestic deportment, Clad in armor, he remains unshakable.
Having purified his various karmas Amidst the assembly of the Victorious Ones of the past,
He therefore dons this armor And is never timid or weak.
With wisdom that cherishes sentient beings, they benefit all the worlds;
having mastered skillful means, they don their armor and dwell securely.
In the wisdom of skillful means, the bodhisattva is able to attain thorough penetration.
Having thus donned the armor, one severs all fetters and bonds;
remaining free from all attachments and possessing right faith without contradiction,
the wise person who has donned the armor sets out for the unsurpassed.
The Bodhisattva is able to be decisive regarding both self-benefit and the benefit of others;
through the power of virtuous diligence, they remain steadfast and without regression. Furthermore, Anantamati!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, throughout immeasurable eons, bear heavy burdens and don the great armor; this armor cannot be seen by Māras, the retinues of Māras, or the messengers of Māras, nor by those sentient beings who wander in the dense forests of false views or the treacherous deserts.
Why is this? Because it has no form or color and cannot be manifested; it is non-obstructive, signless, having abandoned signs, detached from signs, and nameless.
O Boundless Wisdom!
Even if flying arrows as large as Mount Sumeru were launched with their points bristling together, none could strike him.

Suppose every single sentient being in the trichiliocosm were to become a Māra, each accompanied by a host of Māra-armies and retinues, who all simultaneously discharged sharp arrows; even so, like Mount Sumeru, he would ultimately remain unharmed.
This armor of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot damage even a single hair-tip.
It cannot cause even a single divergent thought to arise in the minds of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, let alone affect their bodies.

If all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with a single-minded resolve, subdue them, they can cause all Māras to retreat, disperse, and be extinguished; they are well able to abide in such armor without wavering, such that no sentient being whatsoever can destroy them.
Why is this? Because it is signless (*animitta*), it is not within the range of perception for sentient beings; thus, all sentient beings are unable to see or know it.

Yet, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are able to comprehend all phenomena (*dharma*) as they truly are, they don the great armor (*mahā-saṃnāha*) through their knowledge and vision in accordance with reality, desiring to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
They have no attachment to any phenomena because they desire to benefit all sentient beings;
yet they also find nothing to be apprehended in any phenomena, and for this reason, sentient beings are unable to see or know them.

Because this armor has no form, no manifestation, and no verbal expression, it is not associated with form; it is not associated with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It is not associated with the internal, not associated with the external, not associated with both the internal and the external, and not associated with that which is neither internal nor external. It is not associated with the elements (*dhātu*), nor is it associated with the sense bases (*āyatana*).
It is not associated with the earth element, nor with the water element, nor with the fire, wind, or space elements.
It is not associated with the desire realm, nor with the form or formless realms.

It is not associated with volitional activity (*abhisaṃskāra*), nor is it associated with non-volitional activity; it is not associated with both volitional and non-volitional activity, nor is it associated with neither volitional nor non-volitional activity.
It is not associated with the stage of the śrāvaka, not associated with the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and not associated with the stage of the Buddha.
It is not associated with the path of verbal expression.

It is neither associated with the cause of form nor with the characteristics of form; it is neither associated with the causes of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor with the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is neither associated with characteristics nor non-characteristics; and it is neither associated with all phenomena nor dissociated from them.
There is no bondage and no liberation, nor can it be known through calculation or analogy, for all phenomena transcend all numbers.

Such armor is such that the perception of any phenomenon is unattainable; the perception of form is unattainable, the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unattainable, and so on, until not even the slightest perception of a phenomenon can be found.

Such armor is neither associated with nor dissociated from any phenomena; it is neither associated with nor dissociated from form; it is neither associated with nor dissociated from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Regarding all phenomena, whether associated or dissociated, he remains detached from them all.
Such armor is likewise without action, because there is no agent.
Furthermore, there is no characteristic, because characteristics do not exist.
There is no characteristic of location, no characteristic of combination, no conceptual differentiation, no fluctuation, no object of apprehension, and no nature that can be perceived.
The one who dons the armor is likewise unobtainable, and thus the act of donning the armor cannot be seen. Why is this?

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas don the armor, they do not see anyone who dons it, nor where they don it, nor from where they don it; nor do they see a "self" that dons the armor, nor a "mine" that is donned by the armor; nor do they see this place being donned as opposed to another place being donned; nor do they see any sentient beings for whose sake the armor is donned. This is because they do not engage in any phenomena and because all things are non-existent.
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don such armor, they don the armor donned by the Tathāgata; therein, body is unapprehendable, mind is unapprehendable, and thought is unapprehendable."
Because they are unattainable, they are free from conceptual discrimination.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in even a slight dharma or attain even a slight dharma—whether they are currently donning the armor or will don it in the future—they should not be said to be "donning the great armor."
If the mind transcends this, it may be said that one has donned the inconceivable great armor.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not don the great armor for the sake of a few sentient beings, nor do they don the great armor for the sake of sentient beings of a single kalpa; nor do they don the great armor for the sake of sentient beings of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of kalpas. Rather, they don the great armor for the sake of all sentient beings throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas; therefore, it is called donning the immeasurable great armor.

"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don their armor, they don the armor of not dwelling on the notion of sentient beings; they don the armor of not giving rise to the notion of a self; they don the armor of being detached from the notion of sentient beings; they don the armor of extinguishing the notion of a self; they don the armor of knowing the nature of sentient beings; they don the armor of knowing the nature of the self; they don the armor of transcending perception and feeling; they don the armor of knowing that all phenomena have the characteristic of non-action; the armor of the characteristic of emptiness; the armor of the characteristic of signlessness; the armor of the characteristic of wishlessness; the armor of knowing that all phenomena have the characteristic of non-arising; the armor of the characteristic of non-cessation; the armor of knowing the characteristic of the distinct natures of all phenomena; the armor of the characteristic of non-distinct natures; the armor of knowing the characteristic of the activities of all phenomena; and the armor of the characteristic of non-activity."
“Anantamati! If one dons the armor while dwelling in phenomena (*vastu*), it is never called donning the great armor.
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not dwell in phenomena when seeking great wisdom, it is therefore called donning the great armor.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Throughout immeasurable thousands of kalpas, I have donned the great, boundless armor,
Desiring to cause all sentient beings To be liberated from all suffering and affliction."
Such a great armor cannot be seen by the eyes of Māras, their emissaries, or those who perform the deeds of Māra;
nor can it be seen by other sentient beings who wander through the dense forest of views.
The armor is inconceivable, and it is not seen by them.
It has no color and no form; it is without resistance and without dependence.
The armor is inconceivable, and therefore it is not seen by the eye.
Without name and without mark, far removed from all marks, his armor is boundless; therefore, no one can perceive its form.
Even if one were to take Mount Sumeru as an arrow and, with a drill, fire it from afar, [it could not pierce him].
This inconceivable armor causes arrows to break of their own accord.
Even all the Māras in the world, with arrows as large as Mount Sumeru,
come together in competition to shoot at this great armor.
Yet within this great armor, not even a hair’s breadth is diminished;
this inconceivable armor cannot be destroyed by any means.
By virtue of this, the bodhisattvas undergo no transformation or change in body or mind.
This armor is inconceivable; who could possibly shake it?
If, with a single thought-moment, one subdues all the hosts of Māra, the Bodhisattva’s power is inconceivable, and the demonic armies shall all retreat and scatter.
Such is this great armor, which has never known movement;
among all sentient beings, there is none who can see it.
All sentient beings do not know the characteristics of this armor.
Therefore, all sentient beings cannot see them with their eyes.
The Bodhisattva acts as their refuge; able to know all phenomena like a supreme vajra, such a one is well-armored.
Not grasping at any phenomena, yet rescuing and protecting all sentient beings;
because they accord with the teachings of all Buddhas, they are those who have properly donned the armor.
Their armor is without grasping, as they accord with all phenomena.
This inconceivable armor is that which is well donned.
This armor has no manifestation; it purifies all phenomena.
Since all phenomena are beyond verbal expression, there is nothing that can be manifested.
Not associated with form, not associated with feeling, nor with perception, mental formations, or consciousness; neither in association nor in combination.
Not associated with the internal, not associated with the external.
Neither with the internal nor the external, Neither in association nor in conjunction.
Not associated with the elements (*dhātu*), Nor associated with the sense bases (*āyatana*);
Within either the elements or the sense bases, There is likewise no conjunction.
It does not correspond with earth, nor does it correspond with water;
it does not correspond with fire, wind, or space, nor does it correspond through their combination or conjunction.
It does not correspond with desire, nor does it correspond with form.
It does not correspond with or unite with the formless realm;
all things are unapprehendable. It does not engage in conditioned existence, nor does it engage in the unconditioned, nor does it correspond with or unite with them.
The armor is inconceivable: it neither abides nor is it a composite;
it is neither bound nor liberated, and yet there is nothing with which it is not in accord.
The armor is without limit; it is not shared with the stage of the śrāvakas.
It is not shared with the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas, nor is it associated with or conjoined to them;
even up to the stage of the Buddhas and all phenomena,
it is entirely dissociated and entirely unconjoined.
By all paths of language, none can reach it;
The armor is boundless, for it is without substance and inconceivable.
It neither corresponds nor does not correspond with any phenomena whatsoever.
The armor is inconceivable, transcending all numbers.
This armor is unsurpassed; it is neither bound nor unbound.
It possesses no characteristics of form, nor does it possess the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It does not correspond with nor unite with those various marks;
it does not correspond with nor unite with the marks of all phenomena,
nor does it correspond with nor unite with the markless.
This armor is unsurpassed; it is neither bound nor liberated.
Among all phenomena, it does not fall within the category of even a single phenomenon.
Within all phenomena, this armor cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, it is unsurpassed, and is called "inconceivable.
This armor has no form, no sensation, and no perception;
it has no mental formations and no consciousness, and is not comprised within the aggregates.
Thus, the courageous one, donning this great armor,
finds nothing to be apprehended in body or mind, nor does he perceive even the slightest phenomenon.
Because he has transcended all conceptual analysis, his pure mind abides in tranquility.
Always free from timidity, it is called "inconceivable.
Firmly donning the armor of resolve, with a mind that wavers not and no calculation of the duration of kalpas, it is called "inconceivable."
The armor is immeasurable; It does not grasp at dharma or non-dharma.
Because it is without temporal measure, It is called "immeasurable.
It gives rise to no notion of sentient beings, Nor is there any notion of a self.
Because one is able to know this perception, no perceptions whatsoever arise.
One also knows that all phenomena are devoid of marks;
thus donning this armor is called "inconceivable."
"Furthermore, Anantamati!
This great armor is called 'Adornment with the Ornaments of the Sublime Dharma';
it is also named 'Supreme,' because it is indestructible."
It is also called the non-differentiation of all phenomena, because no differentiation is made regarding even the slightest phenomenon.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas don this armor and maintain the power of great wisdom, they mount the Great Vehicle, the Supreme Vehicle, the Peerless Vehicle, the Vehicle of Great Gathering, the Vehicle of Boundless Gathering—the vehicle upon which all sentient beings ride. Within this vehicle, there is nothing that is not accommodated; yet, this vehicle neither increases nor decreases. It enables sentient beings to dwell in peace and happiness, and it also enables sentient beings to emerge from it in peace and happiness.
If there are sentient beings who mount this vehicle of certain peace and bliss, they shall experience no physical or mental fatigue or hardship.
O Boundless Wisdom!
This vehicle outshines all the worlds of devas, humans, asuras, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all other vehicles, and by means of it, one shall attain liberation.

This vehicle neither comes nor goes; it has no abiding, no seeing, and no knowing. Its prior limit is unattainable, its posterior limit is unattainable, and its middle is unattainable. It is equal throughout the three periods of time, like space, untainted by dust or defilement. It is without mutual dependence, without obstruction, and without attachment; by means of this vehicle, one shall attain liberation.
This vehicle is immeasurable because it cannot be measured;
it is fundamentally characterized by non-obstruction because it does not abide in any marks;
it is the most supreme and foremost.
Those who mount this vehicle possess no timid or weak mind as they set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Boundless Wisdom!
This vehicle is like a lamp, like the orbs of the sun and moon, providing great illumination for all sentient beings.

This Great Vehicle is likewise so: its light illuminates the trichiliocosm, such that nothing can obscure it and nothing can obstruct it; by means of this boundless ocean of great merit, one sets out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Anantamati! This vehicle is free from darkness; it can eliminate all the ailments of the world and transcend all worldly dharmas.
It gathers in the great multitudes of sentient beings and cannot be mounted by those who are inferior, except for those who are able to don the great armor.

As I have taught, this vehicle is that which can be mounted by those who, through the purification of the provisions of various roots of goodness gained from protecting sentient beings and making offerings to the Buddhas over immeasurable kalpas, are [worthy]. As for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others who are bound by inferior worldly attachments and associated with the world, or those overcome by overweening pride and arrogance, and all the faithless followers of external paths—they do not even wish to hear the name of this vehicle, let alone be able to mount it.
If there are sentient beings who sport within inconceivable realms, having mounted this vehicle, they shall proceed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in accordance with their supreme vows.
“Anantamati! This vehicle is without limit; its beginning, middle, and end cannot be discerned.
The limits of this vehicle are severed and no limits can be found; the infinite limit is the limit of this vehicle, and the immeasurable limit is the limit of this vehicle.”
Anantamati! This vehicle has neither a limit at the end nor a limit in the middle; there is not even the slightest limit that can be severed.

When one speaks of "severing limits," it is because there is no slight limit that it is called the severing of limits, and it is by not discriminating a limit that it is called the severing of limits. This is what is meant by the severing of limits of this vehicle.
The non-existence of limits is called the middle limit; the non-existence of limits is called the extreme limit. Because limits are non-existent, they are spoken of by way of limits.

Within those limits, neither a middle limit nor an extreme limit can be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, the extreme limit, the middle limit, and the absence of limits are without interruption as one enters the gateway of limits. By entering this gateway of limits, this vehicle transcends; yet even in that transcendence, nothing is apprehended.
Anantamati! What is the limit? It refers to the limits of annihilation and permanence.
Because it enters into linguistic expression, the limit (*koṭi*) is not a limit.
That limit of annihilation and permanence has no boundary, for the characteristics of that limit are themselves boundless.
What is called a "limit" is without discrimination; because discrimination is severed, one transcends the limit and remains far removed from annihilation and permanence.
Anantamati! Those who possess the view of a self rely upon the gateway of limits; if one is without the view of a self, one has no attachment to the gateway of limits.
Because they are without attachment, they are able to transcend the extremes of annihilation and permanence.
O Boundless Wisdom!
These extremes of annihilation and permanence have no reality; they are merely deceptive words.
Within the three realms of existence, one discriminates between two extremes; if one neither grasps at nor conforms to those two extremes, one is able to transcend them.
By severing the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one has no attachment toward the gateway of these two extremes.

Anantamati! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet abandoned the view of a self-identity, they cannot be said to be clad in the great armor and mounted upon the Great Vehicle; rather, they are attached to that gateway of limits.
If one intends to sever the limits and conceives the thought of severing the limits, one engages in discrimination regarding the prior and subsequent limits.

If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have already abandoned the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they are then said to be clad in the great armor and mounted upon the Great Vehicle; regarding those gates of the limits, they harbor no attachments.
Having transcended the two limits, they set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the vehicle of peace and bliss.
"O Boundless Wisdom!

By the power of great wisdom, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to neither sever nor destroy any phenomena that abide within the limits. Through skillful means, they embrace śamatha and vipaśyanā; practicing the signless and attaining the realization of the signless, they are then granted the light of the Dharma by all Buddhas."

Because of the light of the Dharma, all limits are severed; regarding that severance of limits, there is no grasping, nor is there even the slightest limit within those gates of limits—whether in association or non-association, whether in recollection or non-recollection. By skillfully abiding in śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding all phenomena, one then attains the boundless great light of the Dharma.

Because of the light of the Dharma, he is far removed from the darkness that causes fear and makes one’s hair stand on end; he raises the great banner of the Dharma, utters the great Brahma-sound, and lets out the great lion’s roar, addressing sentient beings:

"Come quickly! Set forth toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment within this Great Vehicle, the Vehicle of Great Peace and Bliss, the Great Vehicle of the Great Tamer, the Vehicle of Great Resolve."
"For the sake of all sentient beings, he expounds the light of the Dharma; because of this light of the Dharma, he enables sentient beings to don the great armor and mount this Mahāyāna.
O Boundless Wisdom!"

May all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not give rise to stinginess regarding this Great Vehicle and this great armor; they should instead vow that all sentient beings may resolve upon bodhicitta, don this armor, and mount this Great Vehicle.

Regarding this Mahāyāna and this great armor, do not be stingy; rather, you should successively exhort all sentient beings, further aspiring that they may don this armor and mount this Mahāyāna to achieve transcendence.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this practice, they take up the purification of buddha-fields and take up the perfected merits of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; by means of this boundless ocean of great merit, they set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Anantamati! This Great Vehicle is equal to the *dharmadhātu*; neither this shore nor the other shore can be apprehended therein. Nevertheless, it is able to transport all sentient beings from here to within the *dharmadhātu*, through correspondence with no-place, correspondence with the *dharmadhātu*, and correspondence with the armor.
“If one diligently practices this vehicle, which is equal to the dharma-realm, they shall set out toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. O Anantamati!
For example, the dharma-realm is free from the defilement of dust; it cannot be destroyed, nor can it be stained.

This Great Vehicle is likewise: it is neither destructible nor stainable. Because it is free from destruction and staining, one should proceed toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); therefore, this vehicle is called the "Great Vehicle."

This vehicle is unimpeded; no gods, humans, or asuras in any world can cause it to regress. Because it is free from attachment, it shall lead toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); therefore, this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna.
"What is called the Mahāyāna refers to the Great Adornment; there is no adornment whatsoever that does not enter into this Mahāyāna.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In this vehicle, how could there be any conditioned adornments?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying: "So it is, so it is."
Anantamati! Following worldly convention, within this vehicle I also speak of the adornments of all conditioned phenomena. Anantamati!
Whether it be a Wheel-Turning King, Śakra, or Brahmā, there are none who do not emerge from this Mahāyāna.

Whether they have already emerged or are yet to emerge, although they may dwell in the exalted positions of a Wheel-Turning King, Śakra, or Brahmā, they are not defiled by the faults of birth-and-death or afflictions. They are able to weigh each and every desire; having so weighed them, they then grow weary of and abandon them, and are thus able to understand the path of renunciation.

Anantamati! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas mount this vehicle, although they undergo birth and death, they are not defiled in any place; they are able to perceive its faults and are able to know the way of transcendence.

If there are any dharmas or adornments that I have not yet explained here, by means of these characteristics of the vehicle, one will be able to understand those dharmas and adornments as well, and thus set out toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Great Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle—this vehicle is inconceivable.
Whoever mounts this vehicle shall all attain liberation.”
This is the great place of reliance; this vehicle is inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna.
All sentient beings who mount this vehicle—
This vehicle neither diminishes nor increases.
All sentient beings who mount this vehicle proceed with peace and joy; therein they find no suffering or affliction.
If there are bodhisattvas who set out upon this vehicle,
advancing directly without other courses of action, their bodies and minds never weary;
they illuminate the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
One should set out for this unsurpassed Great Vehicle;
it outshines all vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas,
and one likewise sets out for this unsurpassed Great Vehicle.
Neither coming nor going, neither abiding nor having a prior limit, nor a posterior limit, nor a middle limit; there is nothing attained and nothing perceived.
The three periods of time are entirely equal, just like the pure void.
This vehicle is likewise so: it remains far removed from all afflictions.
This vehicle is without dependence on others; it is unobstructed and free from hindrance.
It is able to save all beings, and wherever it goes, there is no attachment.
This vehicle is immeasurable, And it is devoid of all marks;
Its intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended, It is fearless and inconceivable.
If there are those who mount this vehicle And attain fearlessness, [they shall be so].
Thus, within the Buddha-dharma, one is without obstruction or hindrance.
Setting out by means of this vehicle, one illuminates the world universally,
like the hundred-thousandfold light of the sun, which never fails to shine.
This vehicle is indestructible; none can obscure it.
With immeasurable stores of merit, one sets out for the unsurpassed.
This vehicle transcends the world and surpasses the three realms.
Far removed from all darkness, it leads to the state beyond outflows.
This vehicle embraces only all bodhisattvas;
as for other classes of sentient beings, there is no room for them within it.
If there are those possessed of wisdom who, throughout immeasurable thousands of kalpas,
have diligently practiced with skillful means, they shall then mount this vehicle;
it is not for the assembly of śrāvakas, nor for the pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the various non-Buddhist paths can indeed mount this vehicle.
Yet if there are sentient beings who have entered onto wrong paths,
such people possess meager merit and are unable to hear this vehicle.
If there are sentient beings who skillfully sport within the inconceivable Dharma,
abiding in this vehicle according to their established and most excellent vows,
Abiding within this true path, one sets out for the unsurpassed.
This vehicle is without limit, nor is there a middle limit;
neither the limit nor the middle can be apprehended in any way.
Because limits cannot be apprehended, this vehicle has no limit;
since all limits are severed, one sets out with peace and joy.
This vehicle is boundless; the boundless is the limit of this vehicle.
This vehicle has no limit; the limit of this vehicle is immeasurable.
This vehicle is severed from limits; it is through the absence of limits that limits are severed.
One does not discriminate regarding limits, and even "severance" cannot be apprehended.
The limit of the vehicle is a boundless limit; there is neither a middle limit nor a limit of no-limit.
The nature of limits is non-existent. Within limits, there is the characteristic of no-limit; that which is not a limit is the characteristic of a limit.
Within those various limits, the characteristics of limits do not exist at all.
By means of the gateway of speaking of limits where there are no limits, this vehicle has already transcended them;
regarding that which has been thus surpassed, no corresponding [reality] can be found.
I speak of the limits of annihilation and permanence, The limits of finitude and infinity—all such limits Are, in their very nature, no limits at all.
All limits are boundless; The characteristic of a limit does not exist.
The intrinsic nature of all limits is such that no discrimination is made therein.
Within these various limits, by severing discrimination,
one is able to sever everything— both the finite limit and the infinite limit.
If one possesses the view of a self-identity, one speaks of the various limits;
clinging to these limits, such a person is without refuge.
If one is free from the view of a self-identity, one does not cling to the gates of these limits.
Not grasping at any limit, one is a true illuminator.
All limits are no limits; all limits are not real.
As for the nature and characteristics of all limits, they are entirely non-existent.
Not grasping at any limit, one completely transcends all limits;
by not clinging to the gates of limits, one is able to sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
If one neither severs nor distances oneself from the view of a self-identity, [one remains bound].
Not donning the great armor, not riding the Great Vehicle;
because they grasp at the various limits (*koṭi*), they discriminate the characteristics of those limits—
the prior limit and the posterior limit— discriminating them all.
If one has already been able to sever all views of a self-existent body,
then one is clad in the armor of the boundless and mounts the unsurpassed vehicle.
Unattached to the gates of the extremes, such a person is a wise one in the world.
Able to transcend all various extremes,
thereby proceeding with ease within the Buddha-dharma; the Bodhisattva,
through skillful observation, is able to employ the power of great wisdom.
There is not even the slightest dharma that can be severed or extinguished;
always by means of skillful expedients, one skillfully sustains both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Because the single characteristic is thoroughly understood, all characteristics are thoroughly understood.
Abiding securely in the True Dharma, one attains the great light of the Dharma.
By means of this light of the Dharma, one decisively realizes all those limits;
seeing not even the slightest limit—neither a limit nor a non-limit.
Being able to act in accordance with that, being entirely without attachment, if one sees suffering sentient beings, one should comfort and address them, saying:
"Come here to this vehicle; you shall attain peace and liberation."
In all places of rebirth, one can manifest the light of the Dharma;
donning the armor and mounting the Great Vehicle, one likewise reveals it through this.
Regarding this vehicle and this armor, do not be stingy with them toward others.
They also cause all sentient beings to don armor and mount the Great Vehicle;
mounting this vehicle of peace and bliss, they set out for the unsurpassed state.
Thus do these bodhisattvas dwell securely in this practice.
One is able, within the Buddha-dharma, to swiftly set forth;
to purify the buddha-fields and to gather in all śrāvakas as well as bodhisattvas and others, through the adornment of meritorious qualities.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-one;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Seventh Assembly on the Adornment of Donning the Armor, Part Two: "Furthermore, Anantamati!

I recall that in the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I donned such armor and mounted such a Great Vehicle as this. It transcends all limits, can extinguish darkness, and can eliminate fear. Through great diligence, I heard this 'Adornment of the Armor of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva' and the 'Adornment of the Great Vehicle' from immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas."
When one observes this Dharma with leaping joy and great delight, one should maintain reverence and respect for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and not entertain such thoughts as:
"I am clad in these armor-like vows," "I possess these armor-like vows," "I have attained this Dharma," "I possess this Dharma," or "I possess this kind of Dharma."

At that time, I was devoid of the notion of a self; I had abandoned the view of a body and discarded egoism. My mind was free from highs and lows and devoid of discrimination. Desiring to embrace all sentient beings, to protect and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and to bring to maturity immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings, I never for a single thought-moment felt weariness or fatigue.

At that time, I did not cast off my armor and mounted the boundless vehicle; throughout my successive births, I was able to shatter the armies of Māra, causing his retinue to retreat, be defeated, and perish; the messengers of Māra fled in terror and dispersed; and as for all those of heterodox paths—the Carakas, Lokāyatas, Pārivrajakas, and other such followers of external paths—I subdued them all to bring about peace and security. All rival doctrines have been utterly crushed, all externalists have been brought under submission, and sentient beings on wrong paths have been established in this vehicle through the yoke of manifold virtues.

For the sake of all sentient beings, he reveals the armor and the adornment of armor; he also expounds for sentient beings such dharmas as the blissful Mahāyāna. Those who abide in this vehicle obtain all requisites of bliss, namely: the requisites of conditioned bliss, the requisites of bliss of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), the requisites of bliss of Śakra and Brahmā, and the attainment of the requisites of unconditioned bliss.

When preaching this Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, may they cause those beings to enter into this Dharma and give rise to the noble lineage, erect the great banner of the Dharma, let out the lion’s roar, and set forth toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Anantamati! Having donned such great armor as this, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should examine and select it according to principle; toward what dharma should they then set forth?”
They are able to know and see all phenomena exhaustively, without any discrimination. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the right path and understand things according to reality.
One sets out upon the right path because of seeing according to reality.

When one is purified through seeing according to reality, one neither discriminates nor does not discriminate; rather, one possesses equal knowledge and vision regarding both discrimination and non-discrimination.
If one perceives any phenomenon as something to be sought or pursued, it is unbalanced; one does not abide in the pure knowledge and vision that accords with suchness.
Because there is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization, one has no grasping within that conceptualization and non-conceptualization;
through this lack of grasping, one remains far removed from both conceptualization and non-conceptualization.
Within this path there is no compassion and no purposeful action; there is neither augmentation nor grasping or rejecting.
Abiding in the straight and correct path, one does not differentiate between the past, present, and future, yet is universally able to comprehend all conceptualizations.

“O Unbounded Wisdom! All latent dispositions (anuśaya) that abide in the state of equality regarding all phenomena and possess the meaning of non-perversion are said to be those who abide in this path.”
What is the path and the purification of the path?
It refers to what is called the Noble Eightfold Path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Right view can sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and transcend the entire sphere of activity of all views; it attains complete purification regarding all views in all respects, and is able to fully comprehend all conceptualizations—whether superior conceptualization or pervasive conceptualization—such that there is no conceptualization, no superior conceptualization, and no pervasive conceptualization.

Not dwelling in wrong thoughts and severing wrong reflection, one is able to see right livelihood, perceive the notion of right livelihood, see the purity of livelihood, and abide in a pure livelihood.
One is able to see, in accordance with reality, pure bodily action, pure verbal action, and pure mental action.

Abiding in right action and possessing right view regarding verbal action, one is fully able to see and know all that is spoken; abiding in right speech, one is able to purify its counteractive measures.

With right effort, one perceives well-governed effort; abiding in right effort, one possesses right view and mindfulness, yet is without recollective thought, without mental engagement, and without grasping.

By means of pure mindfulness, one abides in right mindfulness, right view, and samādhi; within that samādhi, being without any dependence, one is able to purify the view of samādhi and abide in right concentration.
Anantamati! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive things in this way, they attain pure right view in all respects and abide in the path of purity.

This path of purity is practiced by noble beings; it is honored by the wise, approved by the multitude of sages, and praised by the Tathāgatas. It is not the domain of any Māras, their subjects, their emissaries, the celestial Māras, or their great assemblies. Nor is it the domain of any who are attached to external paths, who rely on contentious debate, who wander through the dense forest of views, or who follow wrong paths such as those of the Lokāyatas. Furthermore, it is not the domain of any who merely crave nirvāṇa.

Why is this? One who dwells in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) makes a conceptual distinction regarding nirvāṇa; when there is a conceptual distinction regarding nirvāṇa, there is a conceptual distinction regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Why is this?
Within the realm of nirvāṇa, one transcends all movement of thought and discrimination; therein, even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist, let alone the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This path can purify all discrimination such that there is not even the slightest discrimination of the unconditioned—how, then, could there be any discrimination of the conditioned?
If one harbors conceptual discrimination regarding the Noble Path, one cannot be said to dwell in the Noble Path.

If one cuts off all stirring thoughts and discriminations, this is called dwelling in the Noble Path, dwelling in the path of fearlessness, dwelling in the path of tranquility, and dwelling in the path of bliss.

This path leads to the place where there is no aging, death, sorrow, or suffering; this path leads to the place that is devoid of intrinsic nature and transcends all natures; this path leads to the place far removed from all existence and non-existence; this path leads to the place where there is no manifestation of signs and no realm of form; like space, this path pervades all places and leads to the unsurpassed Great Palace.
Thus, the one who has departed does not return, and immediately attains manifold peace and happiness.

That great palace cannot be manifested; it is devoid of all phenomena and signs, possessing nothing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and nothing of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Having extinguished the conditioned and relinquished the unconditioned, it bestows neither conditioned nor unconditioned peace and happiness upon sentient beings.
“Anantamati! Those who take delight in conditioned nirvāṇa do not even seek conditioned happiness, much less could they dwell within the Great Palace?”

Within the Great Palace there is no artificial construction; because it is cool and tranquil, it is called *nirvāṇa*. It is called *nirvāṇa* because it extinguishes greed, hatred, and delusion; severs all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); tears apart the net of craving and views; dries up the stream of ignorance; extracts the many poisoned arrows; and brings an end to all unwholesome phenomena.
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it is far removed from all diseases of pride and the afflictions of manifold sufferings;
it is called *nirvāṇa* because it is not the domain of mind, intellect, consciousness, or mental factors.
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it quiets all disputes, all fetters (*saṃyojana*), and even the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it severs all inclinations and their objects of pursuit, and is devoid of both conceptualization and the characteristics of that which is conceptualized.
Anantamati! This is the essential nature of the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is boundless and cannot be fully described; if there were a destination toward which it moves, it would not be the Way. The Way, moreover, is beyond words and cannot be fully described.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas proceed toward the great palace of nirvāṇa by means of this path, they also cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to abide upon this path.

“Anantamati! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out upon this path, they experience neither fatigue nor distress. According to their desires and aspirations, and according to their desired adornments, they provide every kind of adornment wherever it is required. They gather in sentient beings and preach the Dharma for them, causing all sentient beings to attain joy.”
Why is this? Because this path is peerless, capable of purifying and counteracting [afflictions], and brings all that is to be done to ultimate completion.

All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas set out upon this very path without contradiction; until they reach that stage, and as long as their vows remain unfulfilled, they never depart from it.
What constitutes the ground?
It is the ground of nirvāṇa, the ground of the great palace.
Just as space cannot be used as a metaphor for itself, save that one uses space to metaphorize space.

That which is vast, empty, and tranquil is called space; the palace of Nirvana is likewise so, being a great emptiness and tranquility, without a sovereign and without anything belonging to a self. Even if all sentient beings were to enter therein, they would be unable to grasp even as much as the tip of a single hair.
Vast, empty, and tranquil, vast and immeasurable, it is called Great Nirvāṇa and called the Great Palace.
"O Boundless Wisdom!
This supreme path of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas does not belong to the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."

Those who abide in this path accomplish all the provisions of merit and attain non-retrogression; they bring great benefit to all sentient beings, adorning themselves with sublime conduct, and it is for the sake of this path that they set out toward it.
Such adornments as these do not belong to the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this path, if they act as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), they are without attachment or parsimony; possessing great majesty, virtue, and supernormal transformations, they are able to fully comprehend both the mundane and supramundane realms.
