If they become Śakra or Mahābrahmā, they will be free from attachment and far removed from arrogance; they will delight in seeing all Buddhas and delight in hearing the True Dharma, bringing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas to maturity and leading them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva’s supreme path Is unsurpassed in all the world;
All sages and those of the two vehicles All proceed upon this very path."
All bodhisattvas who have set out for great enlightenment,
in order to attain the adornment of the path, reveal this path.
Those who have already entered this path, or those who are entering it now—
They all, by means of right view, abide securely on this path.
All bodhisattvas who dwell in the vision of equality travel within this path, proceeding toward it with peace and joy.
This path is most excellent; this path is unsurpassed.
It can truly lead one forward, yet within it there is nothing to grasp.
If one abides in this path and walks upon this path, [one shall attain liberation].
All those who possess true wisdom, their minds are unshakable.
They do not speak of this path to those who are even slightly wavering;
because they themselves are unmoved, they remain forever distant from all agitation.
I say that in this path there is no movement and no activity, nor is there any augmentation;
for this reason, this path is unsurpassed. All Bodhisattvas dwell well within this path.
This path has no attachment, nor does it have any aversion.
This path is not of the past, nor is this path of the future;
without discriminating between those limits, one practices in this way.
This path is free from afflictions; this path is free from discrimination.
Without contradicting the meaning, one dwells in peace in this way.
Abiding in the most supreme path, non-abiding is true abiding.
Those who abide in this path can attain the nature of purity.
I have taught the Eightfold Path, the practice of all the Noble Ones;
those who abide in this path will find enlightenment not difficult to attain.
The Bodhisattvas, the Protectors, dwelling thus upon this path,
are able to attain the purity of the Way, advancing step by step.
This most supreme path is that which the virtuous ones practice.
This wisdom, praised by the Tathāgata, is unsurpassed.
It is not the domain of Māra and his hosts, nor of those possessed by Māra,
nor of outsiders or other sentient beings.
Those who conceptualize nirvāṇa do not abide on this supreme path;
harmed by their own conceptualization, the deluded are unable to proceed toward nirvāṇa.
Those who have transcended conceptualization are without ideation and without discrimination.
Within this Great Path, one proceeds by means of this;
it is the supreme path of all the Sages, which fools keep far away.
If one practices this Dharma, this path shall be unsurpassed.
This most supreme path can lead to the unsurpassed state;
therein is no decay or affliction, no fear and no calamity.
This unsurpassed path is without color and without form.
It cannot be manifested through the marks of physical form;
this path of peace and security is upright and fearless.
By setting out upon this path, one reaches the ultimate great nirvana.
This supreme path of purity is like the great void;
Free from all obstructions, it constantly leads toward Nirvana.
Once one reaches Nirvana, there is no returning again.
This Great Nirvana is the supreme and most excellent peace and bliss.
The great palace of Nirvana is empty, quiescent, and immeasurable;
therefore it is named Great Nirvana, and is also called the Great Palace.
Within this Great Nirvana, the afflictions of the three poisons are extinguished;
those who reach its midst neither regress nor undergo rebirth.
This Nirvana is great emptiness and stillness, just like the vast void of space.
Because it is vast, empty, and tranquil, there is no obstruction within it.
This great palace of nirvāṇa is forever free from suffering and distress;
this realm of boundless scope is what is called "nirvāṇa."
Nirvāṇa is without measure; its measure cannot be found.
Its nature is quiescent and cool; it is called nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is without designation, and the path leading to it is likewise unsurpassed.
Immeasurable and non-conceptual, wherein conceptualization cannot be found—
I have revealed this path for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Those who abide upon this path draw near to nirvāṇa.
If one abides in this path, all the supreme peace and happiness in the world shall be attained;
such a person is called one who possesses fearlessness.
Abiding well in this path, their mind remains unstained.
Because this path is pure, he is called one who possesses fearlessness.
Having seen the level and right path, he is able to awaken to everything;
amidst all requisites for life, he is entirely free from attachment.
The Bodhisattvas, the protectors, Upon the supreme and true path,
Which benefits all sentient beings, Valiantly set forth.
If they attain the unsurpassed path, Adorned with the most sublime path,
Causing the whole world to rejoice, one sets out upon this path.
This path is most excellent; it can purify the mind.
According to what each seeks and desires, all should set out upon it.
If one attains the rank of a noble king, with a great army as a wheel-turning monarch,
yet can renounce the position of a great sovereign to leave the household life and practice the Way;
or if one attains the rank of Śakra, Lord of Devas, or the position of Mahābrahmā, the King of Gods.
To have no attachment therein is to be well-aligned with the Path.
One who clearly understands all the training rules of the world and abides within this Path is a speaker of truth.
"Furthermore, Anantamati!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out upon this path, they practice a single dharma in order to embrace the Eightfold Noble Path; that is to say, the non-performance of all unwholesome dharmas."
Furthermore, in order to fully embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices two methods:
first, to inwardly reflect upon any wholesome phenomenon according to reason; second, to outwardly inquire about any wholesome phenomenon according to reason.
Furthermore, in order to embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices two dharmas:
first, to understand all phenomena as they truly are; second, to understand that there are no phenomena, no abiding, and nothing to be discriminated.
Furthermore, in order to embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices two dharmas:
first, internal conformity with awakening and awareness; second, non-attachment toward external objects.
Furthermore, in order to embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices two dharmas:
first, to have self-confidence that is free from discrimination;
second, if sentient beings have not yet attained faith, to cause them to dwell securely within this path.
Furthermore, in order to embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices two dharmas:
first, being able to know and see the actions one performs as they truly are; second, being able to remain without attachment to the actions one performs.
Furthermore, in order to fully embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices three dharmas:

first, to thoroughly understand each of the aggregates of grasping that are characterized by suffering; second, to diligently seek supreme bliss within those aggregates of grasping that are free from suffering; and third, to cultivate detachment exclusively toward all conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, in order to embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices three dharmas:
first, proclaiming the most supreme Dharma with speech that is not contradictory, and having no contentious debate regarding the meaning of the teachings as they are explained;
second, not being attached to any words or letters.
Third, it is the gathering of all dharmas.
Furthermore, for the sake of gathering the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices four dharmas:

first, the practice of correct application regarding the meaning; second, the practice of correct application that accords with the meaning; third, the practice of correct application that observes in accordance with the Dharma; and fourth, the practice of correct application that gives rise to no attachments whatsoever.
Furthermore, in order to embrace the Eightfold Noble Path, one practices four dharmas:

first, being able to maintain oneself through firm vows and acting according to what has been taught; second, being able to skillfully direct the six sense faculties toward the path; third, being able to purify one's intentions; and fourth, being able to abide in heedful conduct.

“Anantamati! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas embrace the path through this practice of the Dharma, they may be called those who accord with the path. By contemplating that the nature of all dharmas is empty, nameless, signless, wishless, unarisen, unconditioned, wearying, detached, ceased, and transcendent, they attain the radiance of the Dharma.”

When observing the exhaustion of arising, one does not give rise to the perception of arising regarding non-arising; at that moment, one transcends and leaves behind birth, surpasses what is not the Dharma, attains the purity of the Path, and realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

Because the Way is pure, one transcends all perceptions; not dwelling in non-perception, one extinguishes the perception of the Way. Detached from the perception of dharmas, one emerges from the net of ignorance and, through the cultivation of clarity, attains all dharmas that ought to be attained.
What kind of dharmas are obtained through the cultivation of clear knowledge?

It means that through the cultivation of clear knowledge, one obtains the cessation of perception and feeling, obtains definitive skillfulness regarding all dharmas, and attains accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in conformity with the secret [teachings].

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this path, they do not abide in any location nor are they obscured by signs; they know that all phenomena are identical to space, their arising is like the arising of space, and their nature is like the nature of space, such that there is not the slightest sign to act as an obstruction.

This path is pure and fearless toward calamities; donned in the great armor, one is not bound by attachments; riding upon the Great Vehicle, one is free from delusion; and being detached from all obstacles and difficulties, one is like empty space.
One sets out upon this path and acts as a great light for all sentient beings.
O Boundless Wisdom!
This is the sublime path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which is not traversed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"To encompass the Eightfold Noble Path, I expound the practice of all dharmas.
If one abides within this path, This is called great diligence."
One who practices wholesome dharmas, being able at all times to refrain from unwholesome dharmas, has their conduct encompassed by the Path.
A Bodhisattva who practices thus reflects correctly within.
Seeking instruction from others, this practice is subsumed within the Path.
When a Bodhisattva who observes examines things as they truly are,
abiding in accordance with reality and the Dharma, this practice is subsumed within the Path.
The Bodhisattva, the Protector, internally awakens to awareness while remaining unattached to the external; this practice is subsumed within the Path.
The Bodhisattva, free from fear, possesses self-confidence and non-discrimination.
Causing others to abide in pure faith—this practice is subsumed within the Path.
The Bodhisattva who reflects thus purifies all karmic actions;
being without attachment to karma—this practice is subsumed within the Path.
The Bodhisattva who is unattached always understands the aggregates of grasping as suffering and seeks the aggregates free from grasping; such practice is subsumed within the Path.
The Bodhisattva of skillful wisdom cultivates conduct that is detached from all conjunctions.
Able to remain detached from conditioned combinations, this practice encompasses the Path.
The Bodhisattva who contemplates meaning is able to understand it according to its true sense;
expounding it without contradiction or dispute, this practice encompasses the Path.
The Bodhisattva endowed with wisdom does not cling to words and letters;
by upholding all dharmas, this practice is encompassed within the Path.
The Bodhisattva who practices the Dharma is able to be in accord with the Dharma.
Furthermore, acting in accordance with the meaning, this practice encompasses the Path.
The Bodhisattva who follows the Path abides correctly in firm vows;
practicing exactly as taught, this practice encompasses the Path.
The Bodhisattva path is pure; with a thoroughly purified intention, dwelling in the Dharma without negligence, these practices encompass the path.
At all times, the Bodhisattva diligently cultivates these various practices.
Body and mind attain peace and bliss; this practice is subsumed within the Path.
The Bodhisattva of right mindfulness abides in the pure path, thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are empty and devoid of marks.
The Bodhisattva who observes can cause his vows to be pure;
yet he does not dwell in wishlessness, remaining far removed from all signs.
The Bodhisattva contemplates according to reality, for the nature of reality is entirely equal.
Regarding all phenomena as unarisen, they harbor not the slightest doubt.
The Bodhisattva of wondrous wisdom is able to contemplate all phenomena;
because of their weary detachment and realization of cessation, they see clearly and proceed toward liberation.
When a bodhisattva contemplates phenomena, they see the arising of phenomena in accordance with reality;
they do not perceive arising as arising, nor do they perceive cessation as cessation.
When a bodhisattva is thus diligent in such observation,
Departing from what is not the Dharma, they ascend into the state of correctness.
For the Bodhisattvas of sublime wisdom, this path is pure;
swiftly reaching great peace and security, they achieve unsurpassed patience.
The Bodhisattva of sublime wisdom, observing all phenomena in accordance with reality,
transcends all conceptualizations and dwells eternally in the state of non-conceptualization.
The Bodhisattva of sublime wisdom is able to purify this path.
Distant from the notion of a path, And likewise not dwelling on the notion of dharmas,
The Bodhisattva of wondrous wisdom, Because he purifies this path,
Emerges from the net of ignorance And attains the great light of the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva of wondrous wisdom, through the cultivation of illumination, instructs all sentient beings; from this they set forth.
By cultivating the Bodhisattva’s illumination, one attains all dharmas.
The profound meaning is definitive; it is the skillful great expedient.
When Bodhisattvas clearly cultivate this, through expedients they leave behind all conceptualizations.
By acceding to the secret Dharma, they are able to know the definitive meaning.
The Bodhisattva of sublime wisdom, by means of the light of the Great Dharma, is able to extinguish perception and sensation; from this, he sets forth.
The Bodhisattva of sublime wisdom does not abide in this path.
Because they do not abide in this path, they set out upon the path.
The fearless Bodhisattvas are able to know all phenomena as being like the pure void, unobscured by any signs.
The Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena have a nature identical to space;
because all phenomena are like space, they are pure and stainless.
Abiding thus, the Bodhisattva is not obstructed by signs.
Swiftly for the sake of all sentient beings, you expound and instruct them.
The Bodhisattva of wondrous wisdom purifies all paths;
being free from calamities on the path, he advances with unimpeded resolve.
This path of purity leads swiftly to great enlightenment;
it enables one to realize the unconditioned and proceed toward equality.
It is the great armor of the bodhisattva, the Great Vehicle, and the Great Path.
Like space, unimpeded, they set forth in purity;
Entering this vehicle and this path, they are like entering the great void.
Far removed from all signs, they set forth in signlessness.
The Mahāyāna is the vehicle of equality, as vast as space;
toward this pure path, one should set out upon this vehicle.
All Bodhisattvas hold this Dharma in the highest respect.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they courageously set forth.
If one approaches great enlightenment and abides in this supreme path,
those of the two vehicles and the like cannot set forth upon it.
The Bodhisattva, through right mindfulness, is able to purify the path;
by means of this purified path, they set out toward the supreme goal.
"Furthermore, Anantamati!..."

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out in this manner, they are able, through skillful means, to correctly understand the immeasurable foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, liberations, meditative concentrations, attainments, bases of psychic power, and calm abiding and insight—adorned with the excellence of immeasurable merits. Desiring to subdue all the worlds, they don the great armor; desiring to transcend the three realms, they mount the Great Vehicle; and desiring to gather in devas, humans, and asuras, they abide in this path and set out for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Anantamati! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the great armor, mount the Great Vehicle, and abide upon this path, they do not universally illumine sentient beings with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, nor do they cherish sentient beings as they do themselves.
Such armor and such Mahāyāna Great Path are beyond what the great earth can bear, and all sentient beings are incapable of approaching them.

Yet, out of compassion and for the benefit of sentient beings, one dons this great armor and mounts the Mahāyāna to abide upon this path. This armor and this Mahāyāna Great Path cannot be traversed by any in the world—gods, humans, or asuras—and it cannot even be seen by any foolish persons who are attached to the world and dwell within the world.

Furthermore, because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have compassion for all sentient beings, they don the great armor. By means of the empowerment of this armor, they are able to stabilize the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element, so that this earth element does not collapse and all sentient beings do not give rise to fear; they can cause the water, fire, and wind elements to perform whatever functions are appropriate for them.

Furthermore, from the time Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas first don the armor of setting out upon the path at their initial resolve, until they now don this great armor and mount this Great Vehicle, proceeding by way of the pure path toward the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and arriving at the foot of the Bodhi tree to sit upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Within this trichiliocosm, even this adamantine ground, firm and solid as it is composed of vajra, would not remain stable—leaping up, sinking down, or tilting over—if it were not empowered.
Though it is composed of solid vajra, it is incapable of bearing the weight of this great armor, this Great Vehicle, and this Great Path.

Furthermore, because all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have made vows in the past to direct compassion toward all sentient beings, and because they are collectively praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, even if there were the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains of Vajra, Mount Sumeru, all mountains of jewels, and other kings of mountains, were it not for their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one would be unable to bear this great armor of the Mahāyāna or this Great Vehicle path.

Furthermore, by the power of the original vows of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and by the power of the original vows of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, they do not cause affliction, harm, injury, enmity, hostility, arrogance, or oppression toward sentient beings. Rather, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain peace and happiness, they don the great armor, mount the Great Vehicle, abide upon this path, and set forth toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Anantamati! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don their armor, they don the armor of wisdom, wield the weapons of wisdom, and perform the great dedication of wisdom. Riding the vehicle of dedication, they give rise to the radiance of wisdom and abide in the path of radiance; with the clear eye of wisdom, they observe all phenomena and thereby initiate the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).”

Desiring to encompass the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), they practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), and the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) for the sake of all sentient beings; all of these are preceded by wisdom, cultivated through wisdom, and sustained by wisdom, as they are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
The various wisdoms of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas pervade all places and are able to sustain them all, thereby accomplishing the immeasurable dharmas of all Buddhas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying: “Anantamati!
It is so, it is so, just as you have said.”

The various wisdoms of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas encompass all phenomena throughout all places; donning the great armor and mounting the Great Vehicle, they abide upon this Great Path, each and every one of them proceeding toward it with wisdom as their precursor.
Anantamati! If one possesses wisdom that is not preceded by wisdom, one cannot set out upon this path.

If one possesses wisdom that is preceded by wisdom, such that it functions and proceeds throughout all places—sustained by wisdom and guarded by wisdom—then one is said to be clad in the great armor, mounted upon the Great Vehicle, and dwelling on this Great Path. By means of the dharma of peace and security, one benefits the world; one can open the eye of wisdom and observe with that eye, the body of wisdom shining brightly and emitting great radiance as one sets out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Anantamati! This is the armor and the adornment of armor of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is the Great Vehicle and the adornment of the Great Vehicle; this is the Great Path and the adornment of the Great Path, by which they set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Anantamati! The armor-adornment of all noble beings, the adornment of the Great Vehicle, the adornment of the Great Path, and the various adornments of all merits—if I were to describe them in detail, they could not be exhausted even in immeasurable kalpas.

In order that you may fully understand this, and for the sake of future noble sons who will be adorned with the armor of the Great Vehicle, adorned with the Great Way, adorned with the equipment of boundless merit, I shall now briefly explain a small portion of it here.
If those good men hear my Dharma, they too shall don the great armor, mount the Great Vehicle, and abide upon this Great Path, adorning themselves with merit as they set forth toward it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I teach the severance of all [defilements], And I also teach the four foundations of mindfulness;
All skillful means Arise from heedfulness."
Fully endowed with right mindfulness, skillfully corresponding with the Dharma,
and emerging through courageous exertion— all this arises from non-negligence.
Clad in the armor of the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, one mounts the Great Vehicle.
With these as his retinue, the bodhisattva should set forth.
With meditative concentration, the supreme liberations, samādhi,
and meditative attainments as his retinue, the bodhisattva should set forth.
Great compassion, joy, and equanimity— Donning the armor and mounting the Great Vehicle,
with these as one's protection, A bodhisattva should set forth.
Accomplishing calm abiding and insight, As well as the bases of psychic power and miraculous transformations,
Taking these as his retinue, the Bodhisattva should set forth.
Clad in the armor of immeasurable virtues and mounted upon the Great Vehicle,
tireless on the path, the Bodhisattva should set forth.
With diligence and heedfulness, donning the armor and mounting the Great Vehicle,
and thoroughly understanding those foundations of mindfulness, the Bodhisattva should set forth.
With the great armor of radiant light, they subdue all worlds.
Having donned these armor-like robes, one is then called a wise person.
Rightly proceeding toward all-knowledge and transcending the triple world,
having mounted this Great Vehicle, one is then called a wise person.
The Great Way is the path of purity, Outshining all the worlds;
Among devas, humans, and asuras, He is thus named the One of Universal Renown.
Such bodhisattvas likewise, For the sake of all sentient beings everywhere,
At all times, they don the armor of diligence;
yet if a bodhisattva does not cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy,
and great equanimity, the Great Earth cannot bear them.
If a bodhisattva does not cultivate the practice of knowing the proper time to benefit those sentient beings, the great earth will be unable to bear him.
If a bodhisattva does not cultivate the practice toward those sentient beings...
One who loves others as oneself— the great earth cannot bear such a weight.
If a bodhisattva does not cultivate this, yet rides the Great Vehicle with loving-kindness,
then even all the mountains and the great ocean— the great earth cannot bear such a weight.
If a bodhisattva does not cultivate the compassionate mindfulness of all sentient beings,
though they ride upon this Great Vehicle, sentient beings will not draw near them.
If one dons these armor-like vows, yet the light of compassion does not illuminate, [they shall not attain awakening].
Sentient beings do not approach that great armor;
if one is clad in this armor, the ocean of merit is boundless.
It empowers the four great elements, and thus one is able to bear the burden.
Because of gathering in sentient beings, he universally illuminates them with the light of compassion;
by sustaining the four great elements, he is thus able to bear the burden.
Because of gathering in sentient beings, he brings great bodhi to fulfillment.
Empowering the four great elements, they are then able to bear the burden.
Without reviling or vexing sentient beings, clad in this great armor, they transcend by means of the Mahāyāna; such a person is called a wise one.
Skillful in great expedient means, they empower all things;
having attained the unsurpassed transcendence, such persons are called the wise.
Because of this, this great earth neither sinks nor tilts.
The elements of water, fire, wind, and so forth, can perform their respective functions;
yet the great Bodhisattvas don armor that is boundless,
mount this Great Vehicle, and set out upon the Path.
Having accomplished the state of a single birth and reached his final body,
he went beneath the King of Trees and sat upon the firm ground.
At this site of enlightenment, he remained steadfast like a vajra.
With body and mind free from weariness, he realizes all-knowledge.
If the fearless Bodhisattva did not provide his sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), that earth would collapse; once destroyed, it could never be restored.
If the entire realm of the great earth were not sustained by empowerment,
even if it were composed of vajra, there would be nothing that would not collapse.
Through the adornment of his great vows in the past, the Bodhisattva [remains steadfast].
Toward all sentient beings, you have already given rise to thoughts of great compassion.
Throughout the present worlds of the ten directions, within all the Buddha-fields, the All-Knowing Ones,
the Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings, protect and mind you all.
Even if there were other stone mountains— the Sumeru mountain of jewels,
the Vajra-circled mountains— standing firm and majestic,
a Bodhisattva of wisdom would not remain [unmoved] unless sustained by empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna).
Regarding this great armor, none but those sustained by the supernatural power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
neither sentient beings nor the great earth— are able to approach it or bear its weight.
Donning this great armor, one does not afflict sentient beings;
this armor is unsurpassed, and by means of it, one should set forth upon the vehicle.
Donning this great armor, one does not harm sentient beings.
The armor is inconceivable; one should set out by means of this vehicle.
Having donned this great armor, one does not act as an enemy toward sentient beings, but rather sets out by means of this vehicle for the sake of eliminating the diseases of all beings.
Fully endowed with the sublime path, the unsurpassed and most pure purification,
free from affliction, enmity, and resentment, they dwell securely without harming others.
Clad in the great armor of wisdom, they mount the vehicle of dedication through wisdom.
The armor is indestructible, and the dedication is unsurpassed.
The Bodhisattva, the protector, abiding in the light of the wisdom of the path,
observes all phenomena with wisdom and proceeds toward the Unsurpassed.
The bodhisattva’s sublime path, the armor, and the Great Vehicle—all arise from the light of wisdom; therefore, the mind is pure.
Riding upon the various pāramitās, one proceeds toward the Buddha’s great enlightenment.
Wisdom encompasses wisdom and purifies wisdom; with wisdom as its precursor, all perfections take this wisdom as their guide.
Wisdom encompasses wisdom and purifies wisdom, and is thus able to bestow supreme knowledge.
The Bodhisattva, inconceivable, is able to give rise to the radiance of wisdom and can kindle the lamp of great insight; thus he proceeds toward peace and bliss.
Because he gives rise to the radiance of wisdom, the eye of insight is thereby opened.
Regarding the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha, they see it clearly and set forth toward it.
These courageous Bodhisattvas possess armor that is truly boundless;
because their adornments are boundless, it is called the "Great Armor."
The Bodhisattva of great wisdom, Greatly adorned by the Mahāyāna,
Advances toward the Buddha’s omniscience Without being defiled.
The Bodhisattva of great wisdom, Greatly adorned by the Great Path,
Exquisite, inconceivable, and pure, he sets forth.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-two.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Seventh Assembly: The Adornment of Donning the Armor, Part Three.
"Furthermore, Anantamati!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out toward the boundless realm of armor, the boundless realm of the Great Vehicle, and the boundless realm of the Great Path.
Why is this? Because they are able to penetrate accordingly into all places.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas don the great armor because they wish to penetrate accordingly into all phenomena; they mount the Great Vehicle because they wish to penetrate accordingly into all phenomena; they abide in this Great Path because they wish to penetrate accordingly into all phenomena; and they set out toward it because they have attained equanimity regarding all phenomena.

However, regarding this armor, one does not apprehend even the slightest phenomenon—whether internal or external, coarse or subtle, distant or near, past, present, or future, conditioned or unconditioned, or abiding or non-abiding.
If this armor cannot discern, cannot resolve, cannot fully know, cannot enter into, cannot realize, and cannot transcend all phenomena, it cannot be called "donning the great armor."

If one can discern all phenomena, can decisively comprehend them, can fully know them, can enter into them accordingly, can realize them, and can transcend them, only then can one be said to be clad in the great armor.

Furthermore, in this Mahāyāna there is not even the slightest dharma—whether internal or external—that is not fully known, entered into, realized, transcended, and dedicated toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). For this reason, this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna, the vehicle of skill in dharmas, the vehicle that reaches nirvāṇa, the unsurpassed supreme vehicle, and the unequaled vehicle.

Furthermore, this Great Path contains not even the slightest phenomenon, whether internal or external, such that one might set out upon it; yet, regarding this level and upright Great Path, there is not the slightest phenomenon that is not fully known. For this reason, this path is called the Unsurpassed Path, the Immeasurable Path, and the Peerless Path.

“Anantamati! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the great armor; they are able to universally enter into the mental activities and mental concomitants of all sentient beings; they are able to universally purify the defilements and afflictions of all sentient beings; riding upon the Mahāyāna, they increase all the roots of goodness in sentient beings; abiding in this Great Path, they exhort and transform sentient beings toward all wholesome dharmas.”
Anantamati! For the sake of each and every sentient being and each and every mental activity,

these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek the joy of wisdom through long periods of transmigration until the very end of saṃsāra, never casting off their armor, and are thus able to firmly don the great [armor].
The armor, the immeasurable armor, the inconceivable armor, the pure armor, the boundless armor, the armor of non-appropriation,
the armor of knowing the perceptions of sentient beings, the armor of knowing the non-existence of sentient beings, the armor of knowing selflessness,
the armor of knowing the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, and the armor of awakening to sentient beings according to their needs.
The armor of intrinsic nature; the armor of knowing one’s own intrinsic nature; the armor of following and awakening to one’s own intrinsic nature;
the armor of knowing internal intrinsic nature; the armor of following and awakening to internal intrinsic nature;

the armor of knowing external intrinsic nature; the armor of following and awakening to external intrinsic nature; the armor of knowing both internal and external intrinsic nature; and the armor of following and awakening [to it].
The armor of the intrinsic nature of both internal and external; the armor of knowing the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
the armor of awakening to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; the armor of knowing that all phenomena are unattainable;
the armor of knowing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unattainable; the armor of thoroughly understanding all phenomena; and the armor of the infinite.
The armor of non-existence, the armor of neither middle nor extremes, the armor that is not of the past,
the armor that is not of the future, the armor that is not of the present, the armor of non-action, and the armor of the absence of an agent.

“Anantamati! Regarding this armor, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas neither don it, nor do they follow its realization, nor do they resolve upon it, nor do they depart by means of it, nor do they realize it through direct manifestation. Because there is no armor, they don the armor; because there is no following of realization, they are able to follow realization; because there is no resolution, they are able to resolve; because there is no departure, they are able to depart; because there is no direct manifestation, they are able to manifest directly. Because there is no vehicle, they ride the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*); yet they do not establish any designation within the Great Vehicle, nor do they establish a designation where there is no designation. Nevertheless, there is not even the slightest designation in the Great Vehicle; if there were a designation, it would not be a designation, for that designation is unobtainable and invisible.”

Furthermore, there is no vehicle by which one dwells securely; rather, one dwells in the Great Vehicle through non-apprehension. Being far removed from any directed movement, one neither reaches the ultimate nor arrives at nirvana; because it is unobtainable, that which is not the path is taken as the path.
Because one sets out upon the path by means of its levelness and correctness, this level and correct path is not something established;
who establishes it? Where is it established? From what is it established?
There is neither action nor an agent; it is neither a combination nor a non-combination; one is weary of and detached from all things and seeks nothing at all. Why is this?
This path of equanimity is neither different from nor identical to all phenomena, for it does not correspond with them.

It gives rise to no conception of phenomena; it is free from all phenomena, being neither defiled nor pure. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise neither defiled nor pure. Therefore, this path is called the "unstained path" (*asaṃkliṣṭamārga*); it proceeds by way of that which cannot be proceeded toward, and it gathers by way of that which cannot be gathered.

This path is profoundly deep: it is without arising and without origination, without emergence and without fabrication, without attainment and without practice, without location and without abiding, without obstruction and without objective referent; yet it can clearly manifest all phenomena and remains undifferentiated amidst all phenomena. It does not revolve according to phenomena, and because it is without objective referents, it reaches the unsurpassed state.
Anantamati! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand this armor, this vehicle, and this path in this way.
Yet, this armor, this vehicle, and this path are not to be seen and are not to be known, because they are ungraspable.
Who is it that dons the armor?
Who is it that mounts this vehicle?
Who is it that traverses this path?
"It is neither visible, nor knowable, nor obtainable. 'O Boundless Wisdom!

If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having heard this Dharma, are not startled and not terrified, but read, recite, and proclaim it; if they do not deviate from the principles of the Dharma, but practice in accordance with them, giving rise to love and joy and entering into resolute conviction, they should apply themselves with diligent vigor for the sake of this Dharma."

If there are those who possess the capacity for skillful means regarding the definitive principles of this Dharma, and who don these armor, mount this vehicle, and travel this path—because they do not apprehend anything within this profound Dharma—they set out toward it to reach the far shore of birth and death as perfectly awakened ones, and are able to appear in the world adorned with boundless merit.
Anantamati! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to love and joy toward this Dharma, exerting great diligence and remaining free from negligence.

If there are sentient beings who, upon merely giving rise to love and joy for this profound Dharma, I say that such persons obtain great benefit; how much more so those who are able to apply themselves with diligence, remain free from negligence, and set forth with pure conduct of precepts.

Anantamati! Observe how this Dharma is so vast, so sublime, and so pure! I praise this Dharma with earnestness, desiring that sentient beings may conceive a joyful attachment toward it, so that they may obtain benefit and happiness for a long night, for the sake of wearying detachment, for the sake of cessation, and for the sake of universal knowledge.
Anantamati! You should further observe that this Dharma is able to bestow upon the world both mundane and supramundane, complete peace and happiness.

Because those sentient beings who suffer from various deprivations have fallen away from this profound Dharma, they remain far removed from all mundane and supramundane, abundant, and complete peace and happiness.

Anantamati! You should further observe how this profound jewel of the Dharma is presently manifested by the Tathāgata—how abundant it is and how easily it may be obtained; you should now diligently cultivate and practice this most profound Dharma.
When I am preaching this jewel of the Dharma, foolish people do not even wish to hear it; how much less could they receive and uphold the abundant jewel of the Dharma present before the Tathāgata?
They take no pleasure in hearing [the Dharma] and have no desire to inquire about it.

If, during the final five hundred years of the latter age when the True Dharma is extinguished, the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and those who uphold the Dharma do not appear before them, how could they possibly wish to hear it, delight in it, or inquire about it?
Anantamati! However, in a future time, if one is well-sustained by the Tathāgata, this profound jewel of the Dharma can also be attained. Anantamati!

At that time of fear, this profound jewel of the Dharma will truly suffer neither diminution nor extinction; however, there will be none to hear it and none to uphold it, except for those before me who, thirsting for and yearning to hear it, have donned the armor—only they shall be able to love, delight in, and receive this Dharma at that time.

At that time, when sentient beings hear this Dharma, they are able to give rise to pure faith; I say that such persons shall achieve the accomplishment of this vast Dharma, let alone those in the present age who can give rise to pure faith within this Dharma and practice it with diligence.
“Anantamati! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the unsurpassed armor, the immeasurable armor, and the great armor, they should form this thought:

‘For the sake of all sentient beings who are destitute—namely, those destitute of ethical discipline, destitute of learning, destitute of wisdom, destitute of liberation, and destitute of the knowledge and vision of liberation—I shall bring them full abundance through this Great Dharma.’”
Because of this abundance of the Great Dharma, all forms of deprivation are caused to be abandoned.

The wealth of ethical discipline, the wealth of learning, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of liberation, and the wealth of the knowledge and vision of liberation are all made to be rich and abundant.

The fires of greed, hatred, and delusion are all extinguished; all manner of illnesses are healed; and the unsurpassed excellent medicine is administered to all. By taking this medicine, all illnesses are eliminated, and they attain great peace and happiness, forever departing from the remainder of existence (*saupadhiśeṣa*). They realize the nature of coolness, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, and no longer engage in further conceptualization or observation, nor do they seek anything conditioned or unconditioned.
For what reason?
Because this nirvana is the supreme peace and bliss; because there is nothing further to be sought among all that is desired, and because all seeking has forever ceased and been extinguished.
Anantamati! Having donned such great armor, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further mount this Great Vehicle for the sake of compassionately gathering in and embracing all sentient beings.
This Great Vehicle is that by which the Buddhas of the past have already departed, by which the Buddhas of the future shall depart, and by which the Buddhas of the present are now departing.
There is no one who goes, nor is there any vehicle, nor is there any departure. Why is this?
Because of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and the absence of an agent; it is not that one has already departed, nor is one departing now, nor will one depart in the future.
Those who ride this vehicle transcend in this manner; they achieve a sublime transcendence free from attachment.
Regarding all phenomena, there is neither conjunction nor non-conjunction, neither coming nor going.
When one departs by means of this vehicle and this path, it is neither a composite entity, nor does it come or go.

When one departs by means of this vehicle and this path through the great armor, it is neither a composite entity nor a non-composite entity, for it neither comes nor goes, being ultimately unapprehendable.
Anantamati! It is with this armor, this vehicle, and this path that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set forth.
Furthermore, when setting forth with this armor, this vehicle, and this path, they do not form such a thought:
"Whether it be the dharmas of ordinary persons, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, or the dharmas of the Buddhas—those dharmas are neither distant nor near to me."
Nor does he form the thought:
"Whether emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, or non-conditioning, those dharmas are distant from me or near to me.
Nor does he form the thought:
“Whether it be weariness, detachment, or cessation, up to and including great parinirvāṇa— if those dharmas are distant or near to me, O Anantamati!”

This great armor, this vehicle, and this path cannot be shaken by any bodhisattvas, any śrāvakas, any pratyekabuddhas, or any sentient beings; they set out toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of it.
Anantamati! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, having attained immovability regarding this armor, this vehicle, and this path, enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are immovable; because the nature of all phenomena is devoid of the characteristics of a nature, because its characteristics are pure, and because it is universally pure.
One cannot engage in observation, superior observation, or universal observation by means of characteristics;
for the nature of the characteristics of all phenomena is such that one cannot engage in observation, superior observation, or universal observation by means of that nature.
All dharmas are without intrinsic nature and without marks; they cannot be displayed and cannot be spoken of—this is the true nature and mark of all dharmas. Anantamati!
The true nature of this armor, this vehicle, and this path cannot be displayed, nor can it be expressed in words; it is likewise inexpressible.
Nevertheless, in order to enable sentient beings to understand them and to increase the radiance of all phenomena, these armor, vehicle, and path are provisionally designated and briefly explained.

If you now wish to practice according to the meaning of this armor, this vehicle, and this path, you should practice according to the meaning without relying on conceptual designations, without relying on manifestation, and without relying on verbal expression.
One who acts in accordance with the meaning has nothing whatsoever to practice and nothing whatsoever to follow.
That which is not meaningful should not be followed; that which is meaningful should be followed.

When practicing in accordance with the meaning, one does not practice in accordance with the sound, does not practice in accordance with the letter, and does not practice in accordance with the speech; because one does not practice in accordance [with these], one does not turn along with them.
What is meant by "meaning"?
This refers to the secret teaching.
Regarding the secret teaching, one should awaken to it accordingly and should practice with faith.
One who practices with faith does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding this meaning; rather, one should follow the practice within that state of non-discrimination.
"One who should follow practice" is, in fact, one who neither practices nor follows practice.

Why is this? Because within this meaning there is not the slightest practice, not the slightest following of practice, and not the slightest universal practice; for it is the transcendence of practice.

One should not act accordingly; one should not act in accordance with what corresponds to awakening, nor act in accordance with what corresponds to saṃsāra. Since both such correspondence and non-correspondence are neither objects of mental attention (*manasikāra*) nor objects of right mindfulness (*smṛti*), and because mindfulness is pure, one should not act accordingly.
“Anantamati! Regarding this meaning, you should practice accordingly and not act otherwise; if you practice otherwise, it will lead to delusion and loss.
To follow after sounds, to follow after letters, and to follow after speech, one is unable to relinquish that speech.”
Thoroughly knowing sounds, transcending syllables, and awakening to language as it is, one does not follow after them, nor does one circulate.
In this meaning, practicing accordingly and entering accordingly, there is no slight practice whatsoever, because all practice has come to rest.
Anantamati! When practicing for the sake of the meaning, do not practice the meaning by means of further practice.
If one does not practice the meaning by means of practice, then one neither comes nor returns.

If one attains the state of non-returning and does not regress further, then by means of this armor, this vehicle, and this path, one proceeds in accordance with *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and brings great benefit to all sentient beings.

“Anantamati! If one speaks thus regarding this Dharma, practices in accordance with its meaning, and is able to enter into it accordingly, their mind will not be inverted, they will be free from doubt, and they will achieve resolute conviction.”
Regarding this armor, this vehicle, and this path, those who have not yet embraced them shall quickly embrace them and swiftly set forth;
those who have not yet donned this armor shall quickly don it;
and those who have not yet mounted this vehicle shall quickly mount it.
If there are those who have not yet established themselves in this path, they will be able to do so swiftly.
O Boundless Wisdom!

Those sentient beings shall gather a vast store of merit and provisions; they will be protected and remembered by the Buddha, the World-Honored One; they will not contradict the Dharma and will practice together with the Saṃgha.

Anantamati! You have already gathered immeasurable roots of goodness; in the future final age, you shall gather all sentient beings through this Dharma and bear their heavy burdens for them. The measure of the merit you will obtain is difficult to describe.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When a fearless Bodhisattva dons the armor in this manner,
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he donnes the boundless armor."
If sentient beings are impoverished, suffering from the lack of the wealth of the Dharma—
lacking ethical discipline, extensive learning, wisdom, and liberation—
may they don these boundless armor-clad robes so that the Dharma may become abundant.
Because the Dharma is abundant, all obtain peace and happiness.
To relinquish all poverty and suffering, he expounds the unsurpassed Dharma;
those who hear it are all freed from defilement and abide upon this path of peace and happiness.
With the aggregate of ethical discipline fully perfected, and with great learning like the great ocean, one attains the supreme wisdom; by this, one is able to sever the fetters.
There is the universal illumination of liberation and the correct knowledge and vision of liberation.
If one can realize this directly, all shall obtain peace and happiness.
The great fires of greed, hatred, and delusion constantly burn and blaze everywhere;
because of these, sentient beings suffer, and I shall extinguish those fires for them.
Bestowing the medicine upon all sentient beings, all illnesses are entirely removed;
once the illnesses have been eliminated, one attains the realm of nirvana.
Having forever abandoned all else, one proceeds to the place of peace and bliss.
From that state of peace and bliss, none shall ever fall back.
Among all conditioned pleasures, they seek nothing more;
in that supreme, great bliss, they shall all realize it.
By means of the dharma free from conceptual proliferation, one brings all sentient beings to maturity;
they shall all ultimately attain great peace and happiness.
Those who set out in this manner will go forth once and never return.
Transcending the path of striving, one always attains supreme peace and happiness.
Within this great bliss, both desire and non-desire,
striving and non-striving— all these must be severed.
Having thus donned the armor, one should mount this vehicle;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, one shall embrace them all.
The Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past have already departed by means of this vehicle.
The future Samyaksaṃbuddhas shall depart by means of this vehicle;
The present Buddha, the World-Honored One, departs by means of this vehicle now.
Therefore, regarding this Mahāyāna, there is no one who does not ride it.
All those Most Victorious Ones, the great refuges of the world, have attained liberation by means of this vehicle; yet they do not give rise to the notion of a "vehicle.
That which is not a vehicle they take as a vehicle, and that which is not a path they take as a path.
That which is not an emergence is taken as an emergence;
because it is an emergence through transcendence, it is unsurpassed.
When this vehicle emerges, there has never been even the slightest emergence, for it is empty, signless, wishless, and unconditioned.
Neither a vehicle nor an escape, it is called the Great Vehicle;
all things are entirely equal, and from this one sets forth.
This vehicle has no conjunction, nor does it have non-conjunction.
Setting out upon the unsurpassed path, one realizes the great bliss of manifest awakening.
This vehicle is neither associated nor dissociated;
it has no location and no basis—by means of this, one sets forth.
This path has no coming, and this path has no going;
those who practice this true path proceed with tranquility.
I speak of this path, this vehicle, and this armor.
Having no dependence on any phenomena, it is the most supreme tranquility.
All phenomena of ordinary beings, all phenomena of śrāvakas,
and all phenomena of pratyekabuddhas— all are unattainable.
Regarding all the dharmas of the Buddha, the stainless and unsurpassed dharmas, they are neither distant nor near; all are unobtainable.
Regarding the dharmas of emptiness and signlessness, they are wishless and unconditioned.
Neither far nor near, all things are unattainable.
Regarding the dharma of wearying detachment and cessation, and the dharma of the tranquility of nirvāṇa—
neither far nor near, all things are unattainable.
This vehicle, this armor, and this path are without grasping;
they are unsurpassed, immovable, and ultimately unattainable.
The self-nature of all phenomena is a truly marvelous characteristic.
It cannot be established by means of conceptual designation, for the nature of all phenomena is empty.
This vehicle, this armor, and this path are not to be manifested;
as is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, so too is that nature.
Among all phenomena, their characteristics and intrinsic natures cannot be apprehended;
regarding these phenomena that are without characteristics or nature, I shall briefly provide an exposition.
Among all phenomena, all characteristics of intrinsic nature—
Regarding what I have thus taught, there is ultimately nothing at all.
This vehicle and this path, as well as the intrinsic characteristics of the armor—
when one seeks verbal expressions for these, they too ultimately do not exist.
Because verbal expression does not exist, this is a mark of rarity;
within that verbal expression, even the characteristic of speech does not exist.
All phenomena are immeasurable, without superior or boundless measure.
All things are unfathomable; therefore, the Dharma is unsurpassed.
This vehicle, this armor, and likewise this path—within that signlessness, one should enter accordingly.
To cause all sentient beings to know thoroughly and practice with diligence, so that they may swiftly attain the light of the Dharma, I have spoken thus:
All phenomena are beyond words; nothing at all can be expressed.
Within all those phenomena, one should enter into them all accordingly.
Because phenomena are ineffable, one should practice accordingly therein;
yet in practice there is not even the slightest practice, for all phenomena are without practice.
Seeking that which is not to be sought, practicing that which is not to be practiced—
those who practice in such a manner do not discern the true meaning.
You should now practice everything in accordance with the ultimate truth.
Regarding sounds and speech, do not follow after them. If one does not follow after sounds and speech,
but instead acts in accordance with their meaning, such a person is one who seeks the meaning.
What is called "meaning" should be known as the secret teaching;
through faith and non-conceptuality, one follows that meaning.
Having clearly understood such meaning, one is able [to understand] the secret teaching.
Without grasping and without attachment, one does not act nor follow along.
If there were one who followed along, that person would then follow with grasping and attachment;
if there is no one who follows along, then nothing whatsoever follows along.
Through this right mindfulness, one remains far removed from that which follows after;
both awakening and saṃsāra are neither conjoined with it.
Therein, even mindfulness is absent; this absence of mindfulness is true mindfulness.
Because mindfulness is pure, it is called "pure.
If one practices otherwise, one will be far removed from the unsurpassed Dharma;
you should practice this meaning exactly as it has been taught.
If one follows speech, one follows sounds;
not transcending them, one is the same as worldly phenomena.
One should not allow oneself to be turned by sounds or words.
One should know the true meaning by practicing in accordance with non-practice.
The true meaning has no sound and possesses no letters;
because it transcends all speech, it is called the "true meaning."
This meaning should be followed in practice; in following it, there is nothing [to be grasped].
Because practice comes to rest, it is called the true meaning.
Within this true meaning, non-practice is itself practice.
This is non-retrogression, not casting off the armor.
Following the great armor, the Great Vehicle, and the Great Path,
one proceeds toward the place of peace and happiness to benefit all sentient beings.
These dharmas of peace and security, I now declare to you;
you should practice according to their meaning, and thus be able to sever your doubts.
If one mounts this vehicle, having mounted it, one should set forth.
Swiftly proceeding to great enlightenment, one realizes unsurpassed awakening.
Regarding this supreme vehicle, it is a "swift vehicle" for those who do not ride [it];
the same meaning applies to the path and the armor.
Those sentient beings who diligently practice this unsurpassed Dharma shall be protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha.
In a future time of fear and dread, you should reveal this Dharma.
Acting as a benefactor for all sentient beings,
if one is able to reveal this Dharma during a time of future fear,
the unsurpassed merit thus produced will be immeasurable in its number.
“Anantamati! The armor donned by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is called ‘Greatly Victorious,’ and it is also called ‘Boundlessly Victorious’ and ‘Great Adornment.’”
The vehicle he rides is named the Great Merchant; it is also named Boundless Light and Sublime Adornment.
The path he traverses is named the Requisite of Immeasurable Adornments, and it is also named the Requisite of Immeasurable Skillful Means.
By means of this path, all noble beings set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Anantamati!..."

In the distant past, beyond immeasurable kalpas—and even twice that number—there appeared in the world a Buddha named Candanagandhaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The kalpa was named Lightning Flash, and the land was named Radiance.

At that time, the ground of that buddha-field was as level as the palm of a hand, free from all impurities, rubble, pebbles, and thorns; it was strewn with heaps of gold and silver sand, arranged along the boundaries of the realm, bringing joy to all who beheld it.

At that time, each of the four continents under heaven was two hundred million yojanas in extent; within each continent, there were furthermore forty-eight thousand great cities. Each of these cities was ten yojanas wide and twenty yojanas long, with surrounding walls that were magnificent, lofty, and most formidable.
In each city dwell eight koṭis of people, surrounded and adorned by ten thousand villages and one thousand parks.
Furthermore, this realm is interspersed and embellished with various kinds of flowering trees, fruit trees, fragrant trees, clothing trees, trees of supreme flavors, and diamond trees.

The ponds and streams have banks with straight edges, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities; blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), yellow lotuses (*kumuda*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) of various colors shine in mutual reflection, pervading everywhere without exception.
The lifespan of that Tathāgata Candanagandhaprabha was sixty-eight koṭi-nayuta years, and he had a retinue of sixty koṭi-nayuta śrāvakas.

At that time, the people were handsome in appearance and lived in peace and happiness; with diminished greed, hatred, and delusion, they were easily instructed, and through slight exhortation, they were able to fully comprehend the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
"Anantamati! Furthermore, at that time there was a universal monarch named Sarvārthasiddha, who possessed the seven treasures and over whom the four continents were converted.
In that Jambudvīpa, there was a great city; the city measured forty yojanas in length and breadth, and its inhabitants were numerous, living in peace, security, and abundance."
The interior of the palace city was five yojanas wide, adorned with the seven treasures; exquisite tāla trees hung with bells, and nets of pure gold covered it from above.

The king’s main hall was made of pure, deep-blue lapis lazuli; it was one yojana wide with a thousand pillars on each of its four sides. Above the hall were another thousand towers, lofty and magnificent, adorned with various precious gems.

Before that palace was a great fragrant pond, its waters clear and limpid all around; beside it were sixteen smaller ponds of fragrant light, composed of the seven treasures, arrayed in a surrounding circle.
Between each of the ponds, irrigation channels flow and surge, producing wondrous sounds like the performance of various musical ensembles.

Each small pond has eight stairways, while the Great Pond of Fragrant Light has thirty-two; every single stairway is composed of pure gold. Rows of jewel trees stand in alignment, covered overhead by jeweled nets, and exquisite fragrances pervade the entire city; therefore, that pond is named Fragrant Light.
“Anantamati! That wheel-turning king had four consorts:
the first was named Anantaghoṣā, the second Bhadraghoṣā, the third Citraghoṣā, and the fourth Haṃsarājaghoṣā.”
Each of the queens had two sons:
the first was named Akāśavijaya, the second Bhadravijaya, the third Nāgavijaya, the fourth Jayaghoṣa, the fifth Sughoṣa, the sixth Brahmaghoṣa, the seventh Jayamegha, and the eighth Meghaghoṣa.
He had six hundred million court ladies and ten thousand sons.
At that time, while the king was sporting and playing with his retinue within the inner palace, he suddenly beheld in the sky the wondrously beautiful body of a Tathāgata.
Then that Tathāgata addressed the king, saying: "Great King!

You should don the unsurpassed armor and mount the unsurpassed vehicle to set forth toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; bestow the medicine of wisdom upon all sentient beings, and do not become greedily attached to the five desires of humans and devas."
This great armor is able to encompass unsurpassed peace and bliss; this unsurpassed vehicle is able to lead one into the unsurpassed garden, and those who enter it shall never again fall back.
"O Anantamati! All the various desires of humans and devas are phenomena that are impermanent and subject to decay; their power does not endure for long, but perishes in an instant."
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King Sarvārthasiddha addressed that Tathāgata, saying:
"Who is able to show this great armor, so that one may don it as that armor is arrayed?"
Who is able to show this Great Vehicle and ride it as that Great Vehicle is ridden?
Who is able to show this Great Path and set out upon it as that Great Path is traversed?
Then that Tathāgata addressed the Great King Sarvārthasiddha, saying:

"Great King, you should know that there is a Tathāgata named Candanagandhaprabhāsa. You, O King, should go to him; he shall expound this Dharma for you, so that you may don the great armor, mount the Great Vehicle, and proceed upon the Great Path."
When that Tathāgata had thus spoken, he suddenly vanished. "O Anantamati!

At that time, having witnessed this event, the Great King Sarvārthasiddha was struck with awe and his hair stood on end; he conceived a sense of rare wonder and gave rise to fear. He no longer took pleasure in the various sensual delights of humans and devas, but grew weary of and renounced all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). Seeking the great armor and the Great Vehicle’s Great Path, he immediately set out for the dwelling of the Tathāgata Candanagandhaprabhāsa together with his eight sons, four consorts, as well as his other sons, court ladies, and attendants."

Having arrived there, he and his retinue paid respectful homage, prostrating themselves at the feet of the Buddha; they then scattered one hundred *tandulana* measures of flowers made of the seven precious gems over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Furthermore, they offered immeasurable *jīvapala* to the Tathāgata and the assembly of śrāvakas, and for ten thousand years, they provided them with every kind of requisite for peace and happiness as an act of worship.
From that time forward, he renounced his royal throne and his retinue, and went forth into homelessness within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Candanagandhaprabhāsa. O Anantamati!

At that time, the Tathāgata Candanagandhaprabha, knowing the heart of supreme joy belonging to the bhikṣu Sarvārthasiddha and his retinue, revealed for them the armor-adornment and the Mahāyāna-adornment.

Having heard this, he gave rise to a firm and resolute mind; for the sake of the profound Dharma, he would exhaust his very life, sitting upright in contemplation with diligent effort and without retreat, always remaining close to the Tathāgata, and attaining a state of immovability regarding all worldly desires.
"O Anantamati! At that time, the Tathāgata asked the bhikṣu Sarvārthasiddha: 'Noble son!'"
At this time, have you donned the great armor and set out upon the Great Vehicle by means of this path,
so that you may accomplish the knowledge of all modes and the unequaled knowledge?
"You should practice with diligent application according to the truth.
Then, that bhikṣu Sarvārthasiddha addressed the Tathāgata Candanagandhaprabhāsa, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

At this time, I do not perceive a dharma called "armor," nor do I perceive one who can don armor, nor do I perceive that from which the armor proceeds, nor do I perceive the place where the armor is donned.
“World-Honored One!
I do not see a dharma called ‘vehicle,’ nor do I see one who rides the Great Vehicle, nor do I see a place from which one departs by vehicle, nor do I see a place where one rides the Great Vehicle.”

"Bhagavān! I do not see any dharma named 'the path,' nor do I see anyone who has already set out or is currently setting out by means of this path. Furthermore, I do not see the origin from which the path comes, nor do I see the location where the path resides."
World-Honored One!
Regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, whether it be distant or near, or whether it pertains to the past, future, or present, there is neither attainment nor seeing.
As I now engage in this contemplation, there is truly not even the slightest dharma that can be approached or realized.
If I have nothing to realize, how could the World-Honored One ask me:
"Have you donned the great armor, mounted the Great Vehicle, and set out upon the Path?"

The World-Honored One is the All-Knowing One and the All-Seeing One; regarding our practice of the Dharma as we do, only the Tathāgata can fully comprehend it, for it is not within the realm of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"Anantamati! When that bhikṣu Sarvārthasiddha spoke these words before the Tathāgata, he and his retinue immediately attained the bodhisattva’s endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); because they had attained this endurance of phenomena, they all became non-retrogressive."
At that time, the Tathāgata Candanagandhaprabha bestowed prophecies upon them all, declaring that after five hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they would realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Upon hearing this prophecy, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; ascending into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, he immediately praised the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
“O One of immeasurable and great renown, Exalted and preeminent like the King of Mountains, World-Honored One, Possessor of All-Knowledge, Able to expound all merits.”
The Buddha’s eye perceives all clearly, Like the sun shining down from above;
Amidst this majestic great assembly, I pay homage at the Tathāgata’s feet.
With immeasurable stores of merit, The Buddha’s wisdom is already perfected.
We, too, shall attain the unsurpassed wisdom of the World-Honored One;
the supreme, great radiance that universally illumines humans and devas,
revealing the treasury of all dharmas— the ocean of boundless merit.
Wisdom ever without loss, Perfectly Awakened and free from afflictions,
With the great light of wisdom and vast diligence— I pay homage to you of profound merit.
Great Dragon, Greatly Adorned, with manifold marks adorning your body.
Abiding as steadfast as Mount Sumeru, you lead the multitude without peer;
able to act as a guide for the world, you outshine the hosts of humans and devas.
Expounding the Dharma with fearlessness, I pay homage to the Supreme Man.
The World-Honored One, the Great Muni, ocean of boundless merit,
has been able to open my Dharma-eye and cause me to don the armor.
Thus, at all times, I shall be one who rides the Mahāyāna.
Always upon this supreme path, setting out with no other destination;
the Muni, the courageous Honored One, who has awakened to all phenomena—
there is none in the world who surpasses him— to him we all pay homage.
“Anantamati! When that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candanagandhaprabhāsa preached this Dharma, he brought immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to maturity.”

From that time forward, the bhikṣu Sarvārthasiddha, together with his retinue, made offerings to and served immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. After five hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas had passed, he realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and was named the Tathāgata Transcending the Boundless Realm King.

The characteristics of the vast and extensive merits of that buddha-field are no different from those of the world of Radiance belonging to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candanagandhaprabhāsa; the assembly of śrāvakas there is likewise immeasurable in number.
The king’s consort, his sons, and their retinue also, after the passage of more than five hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, all realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Anantamati! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, donning the great armor and mounting the Great Vehicle, within this path uphold the great Dharma-torch, produce the great Dharma-illumination, radiate the great Dharma-light, erect the great Dharma-banner, beat the great Dharma-drum, and board the great Dharma-ship; they set forth by means of gathering in the Great Dharma.

These noble beings sport and play with skillful means; raining down the rain of Dharma, they moisten all sentient beings and cause them all to rejoice, applying themselves with diligent vigor as they set forth toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Anantamati! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this path, they attain the illumination of the Dharma. By means of this illumination, they are able to see the dependent origination of all phenomena (*dharmas*), [realizing that] their intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, their intrinsic nature is without marks, and their intrinsic nature is without arising. They do not perceive form within form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. They do not perceive consciousness within consciousness as something distinct from the dependent origination of consciousness. They thoroughly understand that the characteristics of consciousness are fundamentally empty by nature, without marks by nature, and without arising by nature; they see them only as belonging to a multitude of conditions, appearing through the conjunction of conditions. Furthermore, these conditions themselves are empty, without marks, and without arising.

When one forms this vision, one does not see the eye within the eye; it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—one does not see the mind within the mind. Rather, one perceives that which arises through conditions distinct from the mind, understanding that the characteristics of the mind are by nature fundamentally empty, by nature signless, and by nature unarisen.
Even as far as the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, there is no agent and no experiencer.

One does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as arising from conditions distinct [from itself]; rather, it belongs to a multitude of causes and conditions. Its intrinsic nature is without marks and without arising, and the nature of conditions is likewise empty, without marks, and without arising.

“Anantamati! This is how all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on this path contemplate dependent origination; having made such contemplation, they are able to realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) within dependent origination by means of wisdom.”

By means of this illumination of all dharmas, the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as all the dharmas of all Buddhas, will swiftly be brought to full perfection.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The fearless Bodhisattva, Abiding thus, brings forth the great light of the Dharma And advances with wondrous wisdom.”
They erect the great banner of the Dharma; this banner is unsurpassed.
Amidst all the Buddha-dharmas, they advance with right mindfulness.
Skillfully sporting in wisdom, they bestow the gift of Dharma upon all sentient beings.
They pour down the great rain of the Dharma, Advancing with fearlessness;
Moistening sentient beings with the Dharma, Causing them all to attain joy.
By means of this, these bodhisattvas Advance with sublime excellence.
Thus these bodhisattvas, having attained the great light of the Dharma,
are able to dwell with courageous stability within the True Dharma.
By means of this light of the Dharma, they thoroughly understand all phenomena.
Arising through a multitude of conditions, all things lack any solid reality.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; their intrinsic nature is without characteristics, their intrinsic nature is without arising, and their intrinsic nature is without essence.
All phenomena arise together through the harmony of manifold conditions;
because they arise from the harmony of manifold conditions, they possess no intrinsic nature.
When Bodhisattvas are able to observe this, they realize that the manifold conditions themselves are also empty.
The nature of all conditions is empty; their intrinsic nature is devoid of marks.
There is no arising, nor is there anything produced.
One who observes in this manner should diligently practice regarding all phenomena.
Since all that arises has no intrinsic nature, even the various conditions are not [true] conditions.
Observing in this way according to reality, one can know all phenomena.
One observes form, sensation, and perception; the same applies to mental formations and consciousness.
All arise through a multitude of causes and conditions; from these, the various aggregates (skandhas) emerge.
These aggregates have no reality; their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is originally empty.
Because their nature is empty, they are signless (animitta), and thus nothing whatsoever arises.
The aggregates are characterized by detachment; being detached from characteristics, they are without arising.
Being without arising, they are without cessation—such is the nature of the aggregates.
Where there are no characteristics, one falsely perceives characteristics; from what source could those characteristics arise?
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic substance, these aggregates likewise lack self-nature.
The elements and sense-bases are also thus; everything arises from conditions, its self-nature is originally empty, signless, and without essence.
Among all phenomena, the intrinsic nature of phenomena cannot be apprehended;
one who understands all phenomena as such is a thinker of names and meanings.
Within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, everything arises from conditions.
The intrinsic nature is primordially empty; it is signless and without essence.
When one contemplates this observing wisdom, how can it know that object?
This wisdom and that object are by their very nature eternally detached.
That which arises and its various conditions—both of these are devoid of agency.
To know them as such is the true characteristic.
Though signless, it is described by means of signs; through this, the bodhisattva enters [into reality].
Yet they do not discriminate between signs and signlessness.
Such wise ones are able to see the true nature;
within the realm of all phenomena, they do not construct even the slightest conceptual mark of a dharma.
If phenomena and the dharma-realm—these two are both signless;
all phenomena are far removed from signs, and thus they are called the dharma-realm.
That which is called the dharma-realm has neither realm nor non-realm.
Although it is called the "Dharma-realm," in reality it cannot be apprehended.
When contemplating this meaning, one does not even think of its unapprehendability;
because all conceptual discriminations are abandoned, one attains the great light of the Dharma.
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, Radiance likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
Through such contemplation, One further attains the radiance of the Dharma.
