When the wisdom that contemplates is not seen, Even this seeing is not seen.
Because one sees that phenomena are illusory, this is called "contemplation.
Its radiance is inconceivable, boundless and immeasurable;
seeing that all phenomena are empty is called "non-conceptualization."
If phenomena possessed various characteristics, And there were never anyone who realized them,
Upon hearing this sound of the pure Dharma, One should give rise to great joy.
If phenomena have no arising, And there is always no conceptual differentiation,
Hearing this sound of the pure Dharma, they attain tranquil peace and joy.
If, in a future age at the end of time, one hears this unsurpassed Dharma,
one should know that those sentient beings have long accumulated all manner of merit.
If, in the final age of the future, one hears this unsurpassed Dharma,
one should swiftly set out toward it within this very Dharma.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-three.
The Great Ratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume Twenty-Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The Seventh Assembly: The Array of Armor, Part Four.

"Furthermore, Anantamati! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe all phenomena in this manner, they attain the light of the Dharma regarding all phenomena. They do not perceive emptiness within emptiness, nor do they perceive emptiness apart from emptiness. They do not see even the slightest phenomenon as being associated with or dissociated from emptiness. They do not perceive emptiness by means of the emptiness of emptiness, nor do they perceive non-emptiness; furthermore, they do not contemplate all phenomena through such perceptions."

When one forms this vision, one does not perceive the signless within the signless, nor does one perceive the signless as something distinct from the signless; furthermore, there is not even the slightest dharma that is either associated with or dissociated from the signless.

One does not perceive the signless as signless, nor does one perceive the characterized as characterized; one neither perceives it as characterized nor perceives it as signless. It is likewise with the unarisen and the unconditioned.

One does not perceive extinction within extinction, nor does one perceive extinction as something other than extinction. One does not perceive even the slightest dharma as being associated with or dissociated from extinction. One does not perceive extinction by means of extinction, nor does one perceive extinction by means of non-extinction; it is neither the perception of extinction nor the perception of non-extinction.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hold such a view, there is not the slightest dharma that can be seen or cannot be seen, that can be manifested or cannot be manifested, that can be entered into or cannot be entered into, or that can be cognized or cannot be cognized.

Anantamati! This is the great light of the Dharma by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide securely on this path. Because of this light of the Dharma, they see that all phenomena are entirely without limit; they harbor no attachment to extremes or to the middle. Because they harbor no attachments, they set out toward the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One does not see emptiness within emptiness, Nor does one see emptiness as something other than emptiness.
To be able to see in this way Is called 'seeing emptiness.'"
Not dwelling in even the slightest phenomenon, nor perceiving even the slightest phenomenon, one is in accord with that emptiness, as well as its non-correspondence.
Emptiness is empty of its own intrinsic nature; within emptiness, there is nothing to be grasped.
Because there is nothing to be grasped, one is able to know all phenomena.
Having no grasping in seeing and no attachment in contemplation,
one is able to know seeing and contemplation, yet does not accept either of these two.
In vision, all is utterly pure; in contemplation, nothing can be apprehended.
Contemplating all phenomena in this way, one ultimately has no attachments.
One does not see by means of signlessness, nor does one contemplate by means of signlessness.
Nor does one practice the contemplation of signlessness within signlessness.
Since signlessness has nothing to be manifested, and wishlessness is unattainable,
there is not even the slightest essence of a dharma that can be cultivated.
One does not dwell on signlessness, nor does one dwell on wishlessness;
thus, being without conceptual discrimination, one clearly realizes both signs and signlessness.
One does not proceed toward signlessness, nor does one enter into signlessness.
Without destination and without entry, one abides in the manifestation of equality.
The wise person perceives no marks, nor do they perceive the markless;
they neither see nor conceptualize, for all things are without manifestation.
If a person constantly contemplates that there is neither thought nor manifestation, they abide in perfect equanimity regarding both thought and manifestation.
Thus it is with the signless; the same applies to the unconditioned.
Although there is manifestation, there is nothing manifested, for it is understood through contemplation.
Non-arising is likewise: not even the slightest dharma has ever arisen;
its self-nature is non-existent, manifest yet without essence.
Whether arising or non-arising, whether conditioned or unconditioned, there is not the slightest thing to be grasped; the wise do not engage in conceptual discrimination.
With mindfulness and wisdom unmoving, they clearly perceive without discursive deliberation.
Existence and non-existence are equal, transcending all natures.
One does not perceive exhaustion within exhaustion, nor does one perceive non-exhaustion;
manifesting the state where nothing is seen, this knowledge of exhaustion is unsurpassed.
Whether regarding exhaustion or non-exhaustion, one does not differentiate between the two;
because there is no differentiation, one dwells in equanimity free from thought.
Regarding the view of exhaustion and non-exhaustion, there is likewise no view of non-exhaustion.
When one thus perceives exhaustion, one does not cling to either exhaustion or non-exhaustion.
If one has no clinging whatsoever toward either exhaustion or non-exhaustion,
then through this absence of clinging, the knowledge of exhaustion shall become manifest.
"The realm of the knowledge of exhaustion, attained through fearlessness—because this Dharma is thus clearly revealed, the Bodhisattva dwells well therein.

At that time, there was another Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the assembly named Jñānavijaya (Victorious Wisdom). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to practice with the desire to grasp the wisdom of all dharmas that they are able to attain this great light of the Dharma.”

Within the radiance of the Dharma, not even the slightest thing is visible; yet, by means of this radiance of the Dharma, one thoroughly understands all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane, conformable or contrary, and whether accompanied by conceptual proliferation or free from conceptual proliferation.
“World-Honored One!
Could this light of the Dharma be attained by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas without practicing?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Vijñānaketu, saying:

“Jñānottara! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of no slight practice, no superior practice, no conforming practice, and no pervasive practice, are able to attain the light of the boundless Great Dharma.”
Since even the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves cannot be apprehended or seen, how much less can the bodhisattva practices be apprehended or seen?
How, then, could one see that the practice over various eons can result in attaining the light of the boundless Great Dharma?

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having stilled all conditioned activities and purified their sphere of practice, attain the light of the Dharma. This practice of the light of the Dharma is neither a practice of numerical measure nor a practice that follows signs; from what, then, could all conditioned activities be designated?
However, the practice one cultivates is neither a practice of conceptual designation nor is it apart from it.
O Victorious Wisdom!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this practice, they relinquish all practices without any grasping.

"One who practices in this manner does not practice with quantitative measures, nor does one practice by following signs; being signless and without practice, one is then able to attain the radiance of this Great Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva has no place of practice, And yet there is no practice at all."
Having attained the state of non-action, one advances with fearlessness.
There is no superior practice, nor is there any universal practice;
being without practice and without superior practice, one advances in equanimity.
This practice is without manifestation; it demonstrates that no signs exist.
That which is signless and without activity—this is the characteristic of practice.
The bodhisattva’s signless practice does not abide in any phenomena.
Without activity and without abiding, the wise achieve accomplishment.
Without activity there is no movement; this practice is unsurpassed.
Able to practice the practice of non-movement, they advance with courageous resolve.
The Bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, nor can their practice be seen;
nor is a physical body perceived—one who is thus is a true follower.
Being without color and without form, they are therefore devoid of all conditioned activities.
In seeing, there is nothing to grasp; this is the peerless practice.
The supreme conduct of a Bodhisattva does not fall into conceptual designations, nor is there any transition or change; therein, there is no attachment.
Because practice is without conceptual designation, it is the supreme practice;
if one attains such practice, one obtains the great light of the Dharma.
The practice cultivated by Bodhisattvas is ineffable and beyond the measure of kalpas.
Able, throughout immeasurable eons, to clearly expound all conditioned phenomena;
the bodhisattva’s practice is pure, abiding in pure and wondrous stillness,
having completely relinquished all conditioned activities, never grasping at anything whatsoever.
The Bodhisattva constantly abides in equanimity, guarding all conditioned phenomena;
having relinquished all formations, they dwell in sublime equanimity.
The Bodhisattva’s boundless conduct is free from both extremes and the absence of extremes.
That practice is unmoving, and is thus called the "unexcelled practice.
The bodhisattva’s signless practice—this practice is unexcelled;
when one cultivates this practice, one transcends all realms of Māra.
The Bodhisattva practices the signless, clearly understanding the signless;
whether regarding signs or the signless, they have no dependence on anything at all.
Abiding in this wisdom, the Bodhisattva brings this practice to perfect accomplishment.
There is not the slightest thing practiced; such is called one who does not practice.
The Bodhisattva is ever pure, fearless regarding practice;
proceeding with right mindfulness, this is to be well-established.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānavara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
The various practices of these good sons are exceedingly profound; few among the foolish who practice with signs and conditioned phenomena are able to carry them out.”
"Blessed One!
There is not even the slightest dharma that enters into this practice; therefore, this practice is the practice of equality of the true man (satpuruṣa).
Blessed One!"
"The conduct of a virtuous man cannot be measured by the limits of any number.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānavatī praised the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
"Great Hero, Perfectly Enlightened One, Unsurpassed Honored One among two-legged beings,"
He expounds the profound practice, Benefiting all bodhisattvas.
The World-Honored One’s wondrous eloquence Is difficult to fathom in its measure;
Possessing boundless eloquence, He is the most supreme Great Being.
The Dharma King stilled all censure; this arose from his perfect and universal knowledge.
He then expounded for the sake of all bodhisattvas this unsurpassed practice.
The World-Honored One was able to proclaim the skillful means for extinguishing conditioned activities.
Having completely transcended all conditioned activities, the wise person should set out upon this path.
The Great Dragon of inconceivable power, whose sphere of wisdom is boundless—
the All-Knowing One, the Honored One among bipeds— has skillfully opened up these sublime practices.
That which was revealed by the Blessed One, the immovable practice of the Muni—
this practice cannot be shaken, and is therefore called the peerless practice.
That which was practiced in the past by the Great Hero, the Great Muni, [is this very same practice].
Even if one were to practice for many eons, no one could reach its limit.
When a bodhisattva hears this Dharma, although they remain in the world,
they shall before long realize all-encompassing wisdom.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, we shall, in the midst of the final age,
be able to act as protectors and upholders of this unsurpassed Dharma.
Having heard this teaching, we shall, in the midst of the final age, [uphold it].
For the sake of all sentient beings, you are able both to practice and to teach.
By means of our radiance, we shall, in the final age,
bring about great benefit for those who seek the Dharma.
We have made this vow: in the final age, for the sake of all sentient beings, we shall protect, uphold, and establish [the Dharma].
We constantly reflect that in the final age...
Making offerings to the ocean of the Buddha-dharma, we vow to uphold the unsurpassed Dharma.
Within this treasury of the Dharma, may we become supreme men;
we vow to uphold this dharma-gate, guarding it so that it remains for a long time.
We vow that we shall be able to drink from the water of the Dharma;
regarding this Dharma-gate, we shall act as its protectors.
Having heard the Dharma, we shall, during the final age, [uphold it].
May we become great beings and uphold the Buddha’s true Dharma.
We would rather lose our lives than abandon the unsurpassed Dharma;
may we, within this Dharma, become its upholders.
We who uphold this Dharma have never known contentment;
we thirst to hear this profound and definitive sūtra.
In the final age, for the sake of those seeking all dharmas, [we shall teach it].
When this True Dharma is expounded, it can cause all to rejoice.
The Dharma King is inconceivable; he is able to act as a great refuge.
I pray that you will grant me your protection and mindfulness of me, who upholds the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānottara,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Jñānottara!”
In the future final age, you have donned the great armor for the sake of protecting and upholding these teachings.

You are no different from the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past who, at the most excellent sites, made offerings and served [the Buddhas], planted various roots of goodness, long cultivated pure conduct, and donned the great armor to protect and uphold the Dharma of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In a future time of fear, you shall uphold this Dharma;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, you shall reveal and teach it."
In the final age of the future, you shall uphold the most supreme Dharma;
whoever hears this Dharma will all give rise to love and joy.
In the final age of the future, you shall be a holder of the Dharma.
I shall preach the profound Dharma; you should receive and uphold it all.
Regarding these secret sūtras, once you have heard them, you should keep them in mind;
within this principle, do not harbor any further doubt.
You should remember the profoundly deep meaning you have heard,
so as to benefit all sentient beings and become a keeper of the treasury of the Dharma.
Bestow the Dharma upon all, universally moistening all sentient beings.
Having heard this, they are filled with satisfaction, their bodies and minds pervaded by joy.
This is because they have ultimately received and upheld the principles of practice for the path of all bodhisattvas, as well as those sūtras.
You shall be able to deliver extensively immeasurable sentient beings—
those who cannot be delivered by anyone within all the worlds.
Because you uphold this Dharma, you will bring benefit to all the worlds.
Having attained this victorious mass of merit, one proceeds by means of it.
I now proclaim this Dharma; you should receive and uphold it all, and in the future age of decline, expound it for the sake of those who are wise.
In the present and future worlds, those who are able to uphold this Dharma shall thereby receive and maintain the true Dharma of the thousand Buddhas.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they shall protect and sustain this Dharma-gate.
In the final age of the future, they shall bring about great benefit.
Those who are able to protect and uphold this Dharma in the final age will not have merely approached and served a single Buddha.
If one is able, in this final age, to protect and uphold this Dharma,
that person has already served for long those who have well expounded this Dharma.
Within this Dharma, they shall harbor not the slightest doubt.
Those who protect and uphold the Dharma in the final age are the truly wise.
Clad in the great armor of boundlessness, they are supreme in the battle against adversaries;
thus, within this final age, they are able to maintain this Dharma.
"He has completely removed the web of doubt regarding the Buddha’s true Dharma;
hearing the Dharma without fear, he is thus able to uphold this teaching.
Therefore, O Victorious Wisdom!"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who diligently seek the most supreme and great merit, they should, for the sake of the profound Dharma in the final age, don the armor of practice and uphold, recite, and explain its meaning.
"Furthermore, Jñānottara!

I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas and even twice that number, a Buddha appeared in the world named Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Damyaśārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The kalpa was named Transcendent Excellence (Abhyudgata) and the land was named Free from Defilement (Vimala).
Its ground was level, vast, expansive, majestic, and pure, composed of the seven treasures.
At that time, that great continent extended for seventy thousand yojanas in breadth and length, and within it there were sixty thousand great cities.

Each of these great cities was sixteen yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal; they were surrounded by walls and adorned with watchtowers and battlements. Their gates and arches were so magnificent that all who beheld them rejoiced; they were encircled by rows of exquisite tala trees and graced by hundreds of thousands of gardens and groves.

Within the various gardens, terraces, seats, and couches were arranged everywhere in solemn array; the ponds, pools, and canals were each filled to the brim; their banks and steps were adorned with various jewels, and they were level and even all around, providing safe passage for those entering and exiting.
Along its banks, various fragrant trees such as *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *candana*, and *tamāla* stand in dense, spreading rows.

Within each of those cities, ten thousand *koṭis* of people reside; because all those beings have fully accomplished the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), they all enjoy such peace and happiness.
At that time, that Tathāgata appeared having transcended two hundred kalpas from the beginning of the first kalpa; therefore, that kalpa was named "Transcendently Victorious" (Abhyudgata).
Within that kalpa, five hundred Tathāgatas appeared in succession, and each of their buddha-fields was composed of the seven precious jewels.
After the parinirvāṇa of each of those Buddhas, the True Dharma remained in the world for ten thousand years.

In this manner, five hundred Tathāgatas appeared in the world, and in their many assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, there were in each assembly countless bodhisattvas—numbering in the hundreds of millions and billions—who entered the path of the One Vehicle and attained the realization of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
“At that time, in that kalpa, there was a wheel-turning king named Śūrasena, who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents.

In Jambudvīpa there was a great city; the city was sixty yojanas in circumference, and eighty thousand koṭis of people resided within it. It was peaceful, happy, abundant, and flourishing, adorned by a great city surrounded by sevenfold moats and ditches, sevenfold rows of trees, sevenfold streets, sevenfold flagstaffs, and sevenfold nets of bells, all encircled by a thousand gardens.

Each garden and grove is exactly twenty yojanas in length and breadth; within each, there are seven layers of walls and seven layers of nets, adorned in various ways, with every exquisite jewel and precious plaything like those of the devas.

Each of these, moreover, has one hundred ponds with embankments made of lapis lazuli and steps fashioned from agate and various jades; they are filled with blooming flowers and lined with rows of precious trees.

Within the great city, the king’s principal palace measured seven yojanas in size; it was constructed from gold interspersed with blue jewels, surrounded by jeweled pillars and adorned with lapis lazuli, with nets of maṇi pearls covering its summit, all further embellished by the radiant splendor of many tala trees.

It is encircled and girded by twenty deep pools; their bottoms are spread with pure gold and covered with golden nets, while various lapis lazuli jewels form the causeway bridges, and exquisite, refined gold constitutes the stairways and paths.
In that pond, blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*kumuda*), and white water lilies (*puṇḍarīka*) were in full bloom, covering it entirely.

There, the wheel-turning king, together with his two thousand court ladies and sixty thousand sons, along with their retinue, enjoyed the five sensory pleasures within that garden. He then had this thought:
"All desires are impermanent and will soon change and perish; I shall resolutely seek the Buddha-dharma."
"If, having heard the Dharma, I practice according to the teaching, it will bring me long-lasting benefit and peace.
As soon as he had thought this, a deity suddenly appeared in the sky and addressed the king, saying:
"Excellent, O noble man!"

Now there is a Tathāgata named Samantaprabha who has appeared in the world, proclaiming the True Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; Your Majesty should go quickly to that Buddha’s presence to hear the True Dharma, which will bring you benefit and peace for a long night, and cause you to accomplish and perfect the Buddha-dharmas.
Upon hearing the words of the deva, the king leaped for joy and, surrounded by his retinue and attendants, immediately went to the place where the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa was.
Prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"By what dharma can one skillfully encompass all dharmas, such that the holy life may be swiftly brought to fulfillment?
This is what I shall practice.
Having asked this, the Tathāgata then extensively revealed it to him.

Having heard the Dharma, the king, together with his retinue, renounced all their comfortable means of livelihood and venerated and made offerings to the Tathāgata Samantaprabha and the great assembly for twenty thousand years; they then left the household life within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha to practice the True Dharma.

By virtue of hearing the Dharma, he at that time attained the roots of goodness for receiving the Dharma, the roots of goodness for upholding the Dharma, and the roots of goodness for expounding the Dharma. He reflected upon whatever Dharma he heard without forgetting it, and through diligent cultivation of immeasurable merits, he made this vow:
"May I uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata throughout the three periods of time and proclaim it in various ways for the sake of all sentient beings."
Having made this vow, he personally approached, made offerings to, and served each of the Tathāgatas throughout the *vijaya* (Victorious) eon.

He was able to receive and uphold the True Dharma of those Tathāgatas during their appearance, during the intermediate period, and during the final period. He taught and brought to maturity forty-eight thousand *koṭi-nayuta* of sentient beings, leading them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and through skillful means, he disciplined immeasurable sentient beings so that they dwelt in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"In that kalpa, the final Tathāgata was named Vidyutprabha.
When the bhikṣu Vīrasena heard the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata Vidyutprabha, he attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti)."
The Tathāgata Vidyutprabha then bestowed upon him this prophecy: "O Viryasena!

In a future age, you shall make offerings to immeasurable thousands of Buddha-Bhagavats; you shall uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas during the three periods; you shall benefit immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings; you shall establish hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and immeasurable sentient beings shall abide in the Śrāvaka-yāna."
Thus, after passing through incalculable kalpas, he realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and was named the Tathāgata Boundless Diligence Radiance Merit Transcendent Victor King.
That buddha-field has accumulated immeasurable pure merits; it is peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, filled with people, and abounds in assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.

The lifespan of that Buddha shall last for five minor kalpas; after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for one minor kalpa. His teachings shall spread throughout the realms of gods and humans, who will uphold them, and stupas and temples containing his relics shall be established throughout all buddha-fields.
"Therefore, Jñānottara!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, regarding this pure and profound Dharma, respect, uphold, and practice it; they should adorn their bodies with the ornaments of the Dharma. Because of this adornment by the Dharma, they realize the adamantine, great Nārāyaṇa-like, firm body accomplished by the Tathāgata."

Even if all sentient beings throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to exhaust their physical strength in an attempt to destroy this firm and solid body, none would be able to subdue or crush it.
Among all the multitudes of worldlings, devas, and asuras, there is no one capable of opposing his radiance of Dharma when he expounds it.

If there are sentient beings who receive, uphold, read, recite, and diligently practice this profound Dharma, they will, according to their inclinations, be born into pure and noble families, and even until they sit beneath the Bodhi tree, they will possess full renown in wondrous worlds that are unmixed with heterodox paths; therein, even the name "Brahmin" or "Cāṇḍāla" does not exist, let alone those of evil views and perverse seeking.
Even the names of unwholesome dharmas have never been heard by them, much less could there be anyone among them who practices the unwholesome roots.

They are able to emit great radiance from their toes, which universally illumines all boundless worlds; all sentient beings who encounter this light shall attain peace and happiness and shall realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, Jñānottara!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice within my Dharma, they shall obtain such supreme merits as these.
"If I were to explain it in full detail, it would be impossible to exhaust.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying: "Anantamati!"

If there are those who abide in this bodhisattva path and diligently cultivate such pure and profound dharmas, which accord with emptiness and accord with tranquility, they will attain the light of the Dharma.

By means of the light of the Dharma, one perceives that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is without differentiation; because their nature is undifferentiated, what is seen is pure. Because what is seen is pure, there is no perception of phenomena, nor is there any phenomenon apart from the perception of its own nature. When the perception of phenomena is pure, even that purity does not exist. In the absence of purity and the absence of a time of purity, one is able to attain the sphere of pure wisdom.

One perceives that all dharma-realms are neither realms nor non-realms; the vision of the realm is purified, and one becomes remote from the various conceptualizations of the nature of realms. Because one is free from such conceptualizations of nature, one is able to awaken to and comprehend the secret terminology regarding the principles of the realms. Furthermore, one can universally know that all dharmas are not realms, because one perceives that the dharma-realm is without differentiation, indestructible, and immutable. Thus, one attains skillful means in the principles of the entire dharma-realm.

By means of skillful expedients, they are able to thoroughly understand the principles of the dharma-realm; by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are able to accord with and enter into the various differentiated principles of all dharma-realms.

While abiding in this practice, through skillful means regarding all phenomena, one neither dwells nor clings to any phenomenon; because there is no clinging, one is able to manifest various teachings according to what is appropriate for each case within the principles and modes of the entire realm of phenomena.

By the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are further able to give rise to the dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations, and attainments (*samāpatti*); they sport with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), transforming one into many and many into one, and traveling through mountains, rocks, and walls with sovereign ease and without obstruction.

Being skillful, they are able to know the combination of the four elements while not dwelling within those elements; they know that all elements are conjoined with the space-element, remaining without attachment or bondage to the space-element by virtue of their skillful wisdom regarding the combination of elements.

Through skillful cultivation regarding all elements, by virtue of such cultivation, they definitively comprehend the water element; they can cause smoke to rise within the water element, or cause flames to burst forth, or even cause both smoke and flames to blaze together therein, manifesting immeasurable and diverse transformations to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.

By means of skillful means that abide securely in the principle of the *dharmadhātu* without wavering, they follow their own inclinations and, in whichever Buddha-field they may be, are able to transform their form from a womb-born state into a body of miraculous birth within all realms of existence, constantly beholding all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the worlds in the ten directions.
He fully discerns and knows all those Tathāgatas—their names, their clans, their assemblies, and their teachings of the Dharma—just as they are.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Anantavijaya, who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what dharmas do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide so that they may obtain such supreme merits as those spoken of by the Buddha?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantavijaya, saying:
"Anantavijaya! Those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who do not dwell upon any phenomena, as I have taught, are able to attain such supreme merit."

Anantavijaya! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; or dwell in the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, or space element; or dwell in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—I do not say that they possess these merits in this sūtra.
However, because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not abide in any phenomena and neither enter nor emerge from them, I say that they shall attain an infinite ocean of great merit.

Why is this? Because for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there is not the slightest dharma that can be obtained or dwelt upon, nor is there the slightest dharma that enters or exits; they are well able to abide securely in the fundamental principles of all dharmas without being moved.

Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have no dwelling and no movement; because they are without movement, they have neither high nor low. Because there is neither high nor low, they remain far removed from height and do not dwell in lowness. Because they do not dwell [in such states], they are said to dwell in the "excellent place" (*susthāna*). Those who dwell in the excellent place dwell in the "placeless" (*asthāna*); those who dwell in the placeless do not dwell in any place at all.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not establish or accumulate even the slightest dharma; they have no location, no dwelling, no arising, and no activity.
Why is this? Because a location cannot be apprehended.
Since there is no location, there is no conceptual differentiation; since there is no conceptual differentiation, one dwells unmoving in the state of non-abiding, abiding as the dharma-realm.
When there is no abiding in a place, there is no abiding at all; to have no attachment to either a place or a non-place is called "abiding well.
O Boundless Victor!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the principles of the Dharma, they are thus established in non-abiding.
Dwelling in non-abiding, one perceives all phenomena as being without discrimination and abides in such non-discriminative practice.

Through such practice, one perceives all phenomena without being moved; thus, one accords with dwelling in accordance with reality, accords with immovability in accordance with reality, and accords with non-appropriation in accordance with reality.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva who maintains right mindfulness, Who reflects well upon the meaning,
And does not dwell within any phenomena— Such a person is called a wise one.”
There has never been even the slightest dharma that can be established;
because there is no establishment, they proceed with fearlessness.
They do not establish themselves in any form, nor do they establish themselves in any sensation.
All perceptions and all volitional formations, as well as consciousness and the rest, are likewise thus.
They do not abide within the aggregates, nor within the elements or the sense bases;
whether in what is possible or what is impossible, they likewise never abide anywhere.
Not abiding in the earth element, nor abiding in the water element,
the fire element, or the wind element, they likewise always abide nowhere.
Not abiding in the desire realm, nor in the form realm or the formless realm.
Because they have attained non-abiding, they do not dwell within the three realms, nor even in the realm of empty space;
having no place of abiding therein, they proceed with equanimity.
Therefore, there is not even the slightest dharma in which one may dwell;
if one attains this non-dwelling, such a person is a wise one of wondrous insight.
With wondrous insight dwelling nowhere, one who dwells nowhere is a bodhisattva.
One who is able to abide in this way, Then abides within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Because of the correspondence with non-abiding, They are always able to abide well;
Without abiding and without reliance, They attain stable dwelling in the Dharma.
If one attains non-reliance, then one is forever unmoving;
neither entering nor emerging, one dwells well in equanimity.
Abiding in the Dharma in this manner is what constitutes a courageous one.
All phenomena are without high; all phenomena are without low.
Thus, being unmoved, one dwells well within the dharma-realm.
Because of dwelling there without movement, one attains the unsurpassed abode.
Abiding in non-abiding is the mark of the courageous;
not dwelling in a place of dwelling, they remain unmoved within that place.
Having accomplished the state of no-abode, they attain sublime and secure abiding.
Whether in what is appropriate or what is inappropriate, there is no movement whatsoever.
Abiding in the state of non-movement is what is called "immovable.
If one abides in the state of non-movement, there is no abiding in anything at all.
Not dwelling on what is possible or impossible, always abiding in non-discrimination,
because one does not abide in any location, there is nothing by which one can be moved.
Being unmoved within any location, all things attain non-abiding.
If one attains the state of non-abiding, one is unmoved by what is possible and what is impossible.
If one is unmoved regarding what is possible, one then dwells well within that possibility.
Dwelling securely in such a possibility, one abides in non-abiding.
Able to see all phenomena, one dwells in the dwelling of accordance with the Dharma.
Seeing all phenomena in this way, they are manifold yet have no place of abiding;
being without abiding and without a fixed dwelling, one is skillful in the dwelling of the Dharma.
Abiding eternally in all phenomena, yet without conceptual discrimination;
because they are free from all conceptualization, these are the immovable ones.
If one can abide in this immovability, there will be no conceptual discrimination regarding conditioned activities.
One who remains far removed from what is possible and what is impossible is a true observer.
If one can contemplate with unwavering mind, then all things remain unmoved;
as all phenomena are eternally equal, one should thus set out upon the path.
"Abiding in accordance with reality and in union with it, remaining unmoving in accordance with reality—
those who have attained the state of immovability dwell eternally in the placeless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantavijaya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
You are able to establish all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the principle of the Dharma, wherein there is neither bondage nor liberation.”

“World-Honored One! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are skillfully established in the principles of the Dharma; they do not associate with, nor dissociate from, any dharma whatsoever; they neither harmonize with nor disharmonize with it; they neither grasp at it nor let go of it; they neither have a point of reliance nor lack one; and they neither cling to it nor are free from clinging. They neither harbor hatred toward it nor are free from hatred.”

"Bhagavān! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are skillfully established within the principles of all phenomena, even if there are sentient beings who offer them worship and respect, they do not give rise to craving or attachment; nor do they give rise to anger when subjected to insult or affliction. They are free from diverse perceptions and remain detached from all phenomena."
One does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that could be associated or dissociated with another phenomenon, because one has transcended association and dissociation.
One is free from the conceptualization of association and dissociation, yet fully understands the conceptualization of association and dissociation.
Transcending all cognition, one does not engage in mental correspondence with respect to even the slightest phenomenon—whether advancing or retreating, or having a destination or no destination.
Within the principles of all phenomena, there is neither deluded thought nor grasping; through skillful means, one does not destroy the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
“World-Honored One!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in all phenomena in this manner, they are able to skillfully proclaim the principles of the entire dharma-realm, and all buddha-dharmas will swiftly reach fulfillment.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying:

"Anantamati! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have no establishment and no dwelling within the Buddha-dharma, they then see that the Buddha-dharma has no establishment and no dwelling; it has neither superior dwelling nor pervasive dwelling. Because they see the Buddha-dharma abiding without being shaken, without transmigrating, and without changing, they abide in correspondence with the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); this is called skillful establishment in the principle of the entire dharma-realm."

Anantamati! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, within the Buddha-dharma, neither abide nor do not abide; neither have a superior abiding nor a pervasive abiding; neither abide in a place nor abide in a non-place; and are likewise unmoving, without conceptualization, without superior conceptualization, and without pervasive conceptualization—this is called skillful establishment in the principle of the entire dharma-realm.

Anantamati! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as being able to establish another phenomenon, nor do they perceive any locus of all phenomena as a superior establishment. Being without conceptualization, without superior conceptualization, and without pervasive conceptualization, this is called skillful establishment in the principle of the realm of all phenomena.

Anantamati! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as abiding or departing; they have no conceptualization, no superior conceptualization, and no pervasive conceptualization. They see all phenomena as pure space, luminously radiant and far removed from afflictions. Because they illuminate all phenomena with such light, this is called attaining skillful means regarding the principle of the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-naya*), observing the dharma-realm without establishing any fixed positions.
Why is this? Because there is not even the slightest establishment within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
For example, just as space and the wind-element have no location, are neither visible nor established anywhere, have no place of dependence, and cannot be demonstrated.
The dharma-realm is likewise: there is no place of entry, no place of visibility, no place of establishment, and no place of reliance; furthermore, there is neither cognition nor manifestation.
Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are without manifestation, they dwell in accordance with the realm of suchness (tathatā-dhātu). O Anantamati!
The entire dharma-realm is without birth, without life, without aging, and without death; it is without rising, without sinking, and without a realm of manifestation—this is the dharma-realm.
The unchanging realm is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm pervades all places.
Boundless Wisdom!
The dharma-realm neither departs nor has a place of departure; because it has no place of departure, it is called abiding in accordance with the dharma-realm.
In suchness and the dharma-realm, there is neither place nor non-place.
Why is this? Because suchness, the dharma-realm, and the intrinsic nature of suchness are all non-existent.
“Anantamati! When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear this teaching of mine, they shall obtain the boundless light of the Great Dharma regarding the principles of all dharma-realms.”

Through the light of the Dharma, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and are swiftly able to fulfill the Tathāgata’s ten powers, eighteen unique qualities, and all Buddha-dharmas.

For the sake of maturing the vast roots of goodness and supreme provisions of all sentient beings, and so that the lineage of the Tathāgatas may never be severed, they quickly proceed to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to turn the wheel of Dharma. They eclipse the palaces of Māra, subdue heterodox arguments, and act as virtuous men and great lion-roarers. For the sake of all sentient beings, they expound the sublime Dharma, so that according to their inclinations, their aspirations, and their directed efforts toward right liberation, all may be led toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All Bodhisattvas do not abide in any phenomena; Within the Buddha-dharma, they have no fixed establishment."
Because all bodhisattvas have no fixed establishment, they proceed with fearlessness within the Buddha-dharma.
All bodhisattvas see that all Buddha-dharmas are established in wondrous goodness, being without abiding and without location.
All bodhisattvas do not abide in any place; they are able to see all phenomena as neither abiding nor regressing.
All bodhisattvas, seeing that phenomena have no abiding, do not move from the Buddha-dharma, nor do they seek the Buddha-dharma.
All bodhisattvas perceive phenomena as non-different; they do not stir from the Buddha-dharma, nor do they seek it out.
All bodhisattvas perceive phenomena in this way, being skillful in the Dharma and dwelling in expedient means.
Not abiding in the Buddha-dharma, yet not non-abiding; always without a place of abiding, yet not without a place;
always without discrimination, yet not without discrimination;
amidst various discriminations, there is always nothing at all.
All Bodhisattvas are in accord with non-abiding; at all times and in all places, they remain unmoved.
When all Bodhisattvas abide in equanimity regarding the principles of the Dharma, this is called "abiding well."
All bodhisattvas, regarding the principles of phenomena, do not perceive even the slightest dharma that could be dwelt upon with equanimity.
They are able to see that all dharmas have no location, yet they do not depart from location;
thus they attain immovability and remain without attachment.
One who is skillful in the principles of all phenomena, who dwells securely through expedient means,
and who abides in non-abiding— such a person is called a bodhisattva.
Not abiding through conceptualization regarding even the slightest phenomenon— whether coming or going—
at that time one truly abides in the fundamental principle of all phenomena.
Abiding in various ways within the principles of the Dharma, they are able to give rise to the boundless light of the Great Dharma.
They perceive all phenomena and the principles of the Dharma as being like the pure void.
Like a shadow, like a reflection, they are equal and stainless.
All bodhisattvas perceive and understand them, yet there is no understanding, for they are far removed from intrinsic nature.
All bodhisattvas, observing in this manner, abide in the principle of all phenomena;
they are able to cultivate with firm diligence within the dharma-realm,
and this is called the skillful means of the principle of the dharma-realm.
All Bodhisattvas do not abide in the dharma-realm; they contemplate all dharma-realms as ultimately non-existent.
All Bodhisattvas definitively resolve the dharma-realm and see all phenomena as being like the wind in space—without any established foundation, yet pervading all places.
The dharma-realm is likewise: it pervades all places; the dharma-realm is inconceivable and cannot be manifested.
That realm which is without manifestation is the dharma-realm; it has no place of abiding.
That which is called "abiding" is the non-arising of the dharma-realm; it has no life, no aging, no death, and no sinking, nor is there any departure from it.
Without coming and without going, the dharma-realm is not the aggregates;
it is neither the elements nor the sense bases, yet it is not apart from the sense bases, remaining utterly unmoving.
The dharma-realm is suchness; its self-nature is non-existent.
All bodhisattvas, understanding it thus, realize that the dharma-realm is inconceivable and attain the light of the Dharma.
Having proceeded to the site of enlightenment, they harbor no doubts or perplexity regarding the Buddha-dharma and remain unshakable;
through the radiance of the Dharma, they cause all sentient beings to attain great peace and happiness.

“Anantamati! Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to diligently practice such profound dharmas as these attain the great illumination of the Dharma; by means of this wisdom, they set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume Twenty-Four (and Volume Twenty-Five),
translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Seventh Assembly on the Adornment of Donning the Armor, Part Five: "Furthermore, Anantamati!

I recall that in the past, beyond two asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīparāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The eon was named Amṛta, and the land was named Viśuddha.

That Buddha-world was composed of crystal, and a constant radiance always illuminated its realm; if any sentient beings encountered this light, they became pure, wondrous, and dignified. For this reason, the world was named Viśuddha.
There were no other names for cities or villages; the crossroads were exquisite, adorned with boundaries of golden cords, and the distance between each pair of crossroads was exactly half a krośa.
Between each path, there are numerous jewel pillars with *tāla* trees, eighty-four of each standing in radiant rows; furthermore, they are surrounded by four ponds with embankments.

The people dwell within palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems, covered with nets of bells and suspended with various silk streamers; adorned with flowers and rare treasures, they are like those in the heavens.

The sentient beings in that realm are tranquil and at peace, having fully accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action. They are handsome and dignified in appearance, possess long lifespans, and have but slight greed, hatred, and delusion, making them easy to enlighten; through minimal expedient means, they gain extensive knowledge of all dharmas.
That Buddha’s lifespan was one thousand koṭis of years, and after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for one koṭi of years.

He preached the Dharma in ten assemblies; in each of these assemblies, there were twenty koṭi-nayutas of śrāvakas who were still on the stage of training, while the number of bodhisattvas who had set out toward the Single Vehicle was immeasurable.

“Anantamati! That precious Bodhi tree of the Tathāgata Candraprabharāja was fifty yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height; its roots were of coral, its trunk of lapis lazuli, its branches of gold, and its leaves of agate. The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) was one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.”
The base was encircled by a surrounding balustrade, with rows of exquisite *tāla* trees planted in orderly lines; golden bells and jeweled nets covered it all in magnificent adornment.

The Great Bodhi Seat stood three *yojanas* high, spread over with fine and soft coverings, decorated with hundreds of thousands of exquisite garments hanging down in intervals, and twenty banners and streamers were set up in rows beside it.

When the Buddha Candrasūryapradīparāja attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon this very seat, at that time there were no three evil destinies nor even the names of evil destinies in that realm, nor were there any calamities nor even the names of calamities.
The Buddha Candrasūryapradīparāja constantly manifests his body throughout all worlds and turns the wheel of Dharma.
"O Anantamati! That Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīparāja has two bodhisattvas:
The first was named Cloud Sound, and the second was named Boundless Sound.
These two bodhisattvas addressed that Tathāgata, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain skillful means for establishing themselves within the principles of all dharmas?

At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to cause the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain skillful means for establishing themselves within the principles of all dharmas, extensively expounded this Dharma for the two bodhisattvas.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had heard this Dharma, they attained skillful means for establishing themselves within the principles of all dharmas.

From that time forward, these two bodhisattvas remained for twenty thousand years without sleep, free from desire, anger, or affliction; they did not give rise to thoughts of food or thoughts of lying down, nor did they have any thoughts regarding the causes of illness or medicinal decoctions, nor did they take pleasure in worldly excursions, spectacles, or idle chatter.
At the time when that Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma, he attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) while still upon the Dharma-seat. Then, that Tathāgata asked him:
"O son of good family!..."
"Within the principles of all phenomena, you have thus established them through skillful means;
do you now seek [enlightenment]?
Those two bodhisattvas then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I do not even perceive the name ‘skillful establishment of the principles of all dharmas,’ nor do I perceive the dharma of ‘skillful establishment of the principles of all dharmas,’ let alone the skillful means for the establishment of the principles of all dharmas.”
World-Honored One!
I also do not apprehend any dharmas, nor do I apprehend the establishment of dharmas; regarding all dharmas, there is neither abiding nor non-abiding.
"Bhagavān! This is how I see it.
Furthermore, regarding this skillful means established within the principles of all phenomena, is it for the sake of seeking or for the sake of not seeking?"

"Bhagavān! Within the principles of all phenomena, I do not see anyone who, through such skillful means, establishes themselves as a seeker; nor do I see anyone, whether internally, externally, or in between the two."
If all phenomena are established through skillful means according to the principles of the Dharma, one does not perceive any phenomenon as being internal, external, or in between the two.
"O Bhagavān, regarding all phenomena, or any rational principle (*nayayukti*) established through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*),

I do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon— whether internal, external, or intermediate— that can be established by a rational principle or skillful means such that it could be approached or cultivated."
"Bhagavān! Since there is not even the slightest dharma that can be approached or cultivated, how should I establish myself therein? Bhagavān!"
I do not perceive any basis for establishment in the past, present, or future; if there is no basis for establishment, wherein could I possibly be established?
World-Honored One!
Because there is no establishment, it is neither associated with abiding nor associated with non-abiding; it is associated with the inexhaustible and associated with the unarisen.
World-Honored One!
I do not perceive from whom, by whom, from where, or at what time my mind, intellect, and consciousness arise or cease.
How, then, could I say that the mind, intellect, and consciousness are established through skillful means in the principles and methods of all phenomena?

"Anantamati! When these two bodhisattvas spoke thus before the Tathāgata, one thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), and a thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas resolved their minds upon awakening (bodhicitta)."
At that time, the Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīparāja further addressed him, saying:
"Son of good family!
You abide by means of non-abiding in the placeless, abiding in the skillful means established in the principles and methods of all dharmas."
"Good son! All dharmas are likewise thus.
It is by conforming to the conventional path that the Tathāgata manifests the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
It is likewise with the Tathāgata’s realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which does not follow worldly convention.

Good son, all dharmas have no location, nor are they without location; whether as a location or a non-location, they both follow worldly convention. If one follows worldly convention, then within it there is not even the slightest dharma that can be produced or that can be realized.
"Therefore, son of good family!
You should apply yourself with even greater diligence so that you may swiftly attain liberation in all dharmas.
Having heard this teaching before the Tathāgata, these two bodhisattvas soared into the air and praised the Tathāgata with these verses:
“The Dharma King is inconceivable; having attained the unprecedented Dharma, the All-Knowing One, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, possesses a Buddha-Dharma unsurpassed.
Because this Dharma is supreme, the Tathāgata is peerless in the world.”
All phenomena are unborn; I have now attained this patience.
I never make distinctions between what is born and what is unborn;
likewise, I do not dwell upon them, for all things are without discrimination.
Dharma-King, Great Sage, whose merit transcends words and thought,
I pray you speak the pure Dharma so that all may rejoice.
Regarding the Buddha’s supreme virtues, those who wish to know their limits—
Even if one were to pass through immeasurable eons, it could not be attained;
because its merit is boundless, it is most supreme and unsurpassed.
All phenomena are unborn, and I likewise do not discriminate them.
Within the Buddha-dharma, I have never caused any destruction.
Yet I do not say that the various roots of goodness cannot be attained.
All phenomena are without manifestation; they are unborn and without marks.
Thus, this patience of signlessness has also been fully realized herein.
The patience I have now attained is ultimately irreversible;
therefore, regarding all-knowledge, I feel great joy on account of this.
Regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata, I am resolute and free from hesitation;
likewise, regarding all phenomena, I have distanced myself from all doubts.
Within this unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma, I have now attained this patience (kṣānti).
“I, too, do not engage in conceptual discrimination, nor am I without non-discrimination.

“O Anantamati! After these two bodhisattvas had spoken this verse, they circumambulated the Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīparāja three times to the right and scattered divine, exquisite flowers and sandalwood powder as incense upon the Buddha.”
Then that Tathāgata bestowed upon them a prophecy, declaring:
"You, Cloud-Sound and the others, shall realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after twenty thousand kalpas have passed."

Upon hearing the Tathāgata’s prophecy, these two bodhisattvas leaped for joy and gazed intently upon the Tathāgata; they entered various dhyānas and sported with supernormal powers, appearing and disappearing at will as smoke and flames radiated forth.
Furthermore, they preached the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, instructing and revealing it so that twenty-four koṭis of humans and devas were led toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

These two bodhisattvas diligently practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) until the end of their lives, and throughout both the period of the True Dharma and the period of the Semblance Dharma of that Tathāgata, they were able to protect and uphold it entirely.
Furthermore, at that time, they taught and matured four koṭis of sentient beings, leading them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

These two bodhisattvas successively made offerings to, drew near to, and served many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; they received and upheld each of the samādhis and the true Dharma of those Tathāgatas. After twenty thousand kalpas had passed, they again encountered the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, who turned the wheel of Dharma for them, teaching and maturing immeasurable sentient beings and leading them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The buddha-field of Ratnastambha Tathāgata is pure; it is devoid of śrāvakas and contains only bodhisattvas who are in their last birth before enlightenment (ekajātipratibaddha).
When Ratnastambha Tathāgata was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he bestowed this prophecy:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Meghasvara shall next realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and his name shall be Sūryapradīparāja Tathāgata."
That buddha-field will be perfectly adorned and have accumulated immeasurable and boundless merit.
It will be filled with a complete assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Sūryapradīparāja, the bodhisattva Anantaghoṣa shall next realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
"Anantamati! Because this Dharma-gate is non-apprehendable and beyond verbal expression, it cannot be demonstrated; it is without arising and without cessation.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice it according to the principle."

If there is a bodhisattva who abides in the skillful means of the well-established principles of all phenomena, who attains the patience of non-arising through non-apprehension, and who adorns themselves with the immeasurable merits of the Buddha-dharma, they set out toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Anantamati! I have never said that there is any other dharma, apart from these, by which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas can swiftly accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If there are those who diligently practice this profound dharma of emptiness, which is neither born nor extinguished, they will swiftly attain skillful means and dhāraṇīs regarding the principles of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-realm, as well as eloquence and supreme methods for gathering and transforming others. They will be praised by all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and adorned with the ornaments of the Dharma. They will be able to fulfill generosity, abide in pure ethical discipline, attain pure patience, supreme diligence, and objectless meditative concentration, and through great wisdom, they shall set out toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Among all victors, he is the most preeminent; he will swiftly be named the All-Knowing One.

Seated at the site of enlightenment, the Four Great Heavenly Kings will come bearing parasols to request him to turn the wheel of Dharma, acting as a great light for all humans and devas, leading them all toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Anantamati!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently cultivate the Ocean-Seal Samādhi regarding all phenomena, they perceive all phenomena as identical to the dharma-realm."

When seeing in this way, one does not see all phenomena within the dharma-realm, nor does one see the dharma-realm within all phenomena. One practices with diligence through the skillful means of the harmonious integration of all phenomena and all realms; thus, regarding the harmonious integration of all phenomena and all realms, one is without attachment and without movement. Regarding the skillful means of the harmonious integration of all phenomena and all realms, one is likewise without attachment and without discrimination. One is able to see the integration of all phenomena within the integration of a single phenomenon, and to see the integration of a single phenomenon within the integration of all phenomena. One does not approach the integration of a single phenomenon by departing from the integration of all phenomena, nor does one approach the integration of all phenomena by departing from the integration of a single phenomenon.

Because one is able to thoroughly understand this single dharma, one is also able to thoroughly understand all dharmas; because one is able to thoroughly understand all dharmas, one is also able to thoroughly understand this single dharma at the point where it should be understood, without approaching the single dharma by means of the various dharmas.

Within the aggregation of all appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), they are able to fully comprehend them; they do not give rise to attachment regarding the various natures and characteristics of these appropriated aggregates, whether in their state of aggregation or non-aggregation.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice in this manner, they are able to fully comprehend all phenomena that arise through the conjunction of various causes and conditions, as well as all phenomena that are established through the conjunction of various causes and conditions.

If there are various phenomena that arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions and correspond with diverse natures, one is able to understand those phenomena without attachment. One understands in accordance with the conventional designations of all phenomena; one is also able to understand whether they have signs or are signless. One is able to understand the distinctions between the elements (*dhātu*) and the differences in the various natures and characteristics of those elements. One is able to understand by what cause [phenomena arise], and does not approach the laws of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through the intimacy of afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, one does not contradict worldly or world-transcending (*lokottara*) phenomena, but understands all worldly and world-transcending phenomena in accordance with them, thoroughly comprehending the seals of all worldly characteristics.

By means of a single dharma-gate, one is able to comprehend all dharma-gates; by means of all dharma-gates, one is further able to comprehend the gate of a single dharma. One does not approach the gate of a single dharma by means of the gates of all dharmas, nor does one approach the gates of all dharmas by means of the gate of a single dharma.
Such a Dharma gate is able to completely purify and treat [all things].
O Boundless Wisdom!

Those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who diligently practice within this Dharma will, through the gateway of teaching based on a single principle, be able to understand that the nature of all dharmas is of one single flavor. They will attain supreme non-contention regarding all dharmas, remaining in accord with reality, tranquil, and without contradiction. They will be able to praise and expound this Dharma in great assemblies, and through diligent cultivation, they will attain the Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) of all dharmas.

Practicing in this manner, whether there is dispute or no dispute, one causes all to become tranquil and abides in accordance with the Dharma; one follows the path of severing pride and negligence, is well able to receive and uphold the definitive teachings, is capable of awakening to the distinctions of conventional terminology, and diligently cultivates the skillful means of the principles of the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding all dharma-gates, one should contemplate them with thorough tranquility; considering which dharmas correspond or do not correspond to one another, one should be able to abide in pure mindfulness regarding their definitive meaning through skillful means.

Anantamati! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this dharma-gate in such a manner, they attain the Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) of all dharmas with minimal application of effort; by means of this immeasurable Sea-of-Dharmas Samādhi, they set forth toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Observe all phenomena as they flow into the Dharma-realm;
All dharmas are identical to the Dharma-realm, And their underlying principles are entirely equal."
Again, one contemplates the dharma-realm as it flows into all phenomena;
the dharma-realm is identical to all phenomena, and its underlying principle is likewise equal.
One does not observe all phenomena apart from within the dharma-realm.
Nor does one see all phenomena apart from the dharma-realm;
nor does one observe the dharma-realm within phenomena.
Nor does one see the dharma-realm apart from all phenomena.
Thoroughly knowing the various realms and the manifold natures of the dharma-realm, all phenomena are in harmony; through skillful means, they abide nowhere.
At all times and in all places, the various natures are in harmony.
Without abiding and without basis, there is likewise nothing to be grasped.
Regarding the nature of both synthesis and differentiation, and both conceptualization and non-conceptualization—these two are equally absent; the wise perceive them with equanimity.
By knowing one conjunction, one knows all conjunctions; by knowing all conjunctions, one knows one conjunction.
Conjunction and non-conjunction, the nature of unity and the nature of differentiation—these are all thus.
Neither approaching nor discriminating, without grasping and without attachment;
thoroughly understanding all phenomena— that those phenomena have no combination,
nor does one even conceive of combination— without grasping and without attachment.
Fully understanding all aspects, The characteristics of the designations of those phenomena,
They do not even think of associating with them, Being without grasping and without attachment.
Karma and the retribution of karma— All of these they are able to know completely.
One who does not contradict that [reality] is a practitioner of diligence.
Both action and the agent of action— knowing these two to be of a combined nature,
yet understanding their nature to be signless, such a one is a practitioner of diligence.
Regarding the conjunction of the various elements (*dhātu*) and the distinct natures of those elements,
one who knows them to be eternally equal is a person of diligence.
One who is able to fully understand that all things are interconnected through cause and effect is a person of diligence.
Regarding those various conditioned phenomena, one dons the armor and abides according to the Dharma.
Being able to know the supramundane Dharma, one has not the slightest contradiction with any mundane phenomena; thus one abides in equanimity.
He also knows the worldly dharmas, and with respect to all supramundane dharmas, there is not even the slightest contradiction; thus he abides in equanimity.
Regarding what should be done in the world, he possesses the seal of all characteristics.
Following along, one is able to observe; through universal knowledge, one abides in equanimity.
By means of a single dharma-gate, one thoroughly understands all dharma-gates;
likewise, by means of all dharma-gates, one thoroughly understands a single dharma-gate.
One does not approach all dharma-gates by means of a single dharma-gate,
nor does one approach a single dharma-gate by means of all dharma-gates.
Within all dharma-gates, there is universal purity and equality.
One who perceives no marks of difference within phenomena is an observer.
One who can speak with equanimity regarding the teachings on all phenomena,
abiding eternally in the state of equality, is an observer.
Regarding the verbal teachings on all phenomena, one who can know and see them according to reality attains skillful correspondence;
such a person is one who possesses expedient means.
They do not give rise to contentious debate, nor do they create the causes and conditions for contention.
To be in no way contradictory is what it means to be one who is in accord.
Constantly giving rise to non-contention, through non-contention one attains accord;
to be impartial and without contradiction is what it means to be one of wisdom.
Within the principles of the Dharma, one forever brings all disputes to rest;
donning the armor of practice according to the truth, such a person is truly courageous.
Observing thus in every way, there is pure unity and no conflict.
Within the assemblies of the Dharma, they are able to praise and expound the unsurpassed Dharma.
Such bodhisattvas have accomplished all dharmas;
through the ocean-seal samādhi, they are those who possess right mindfulness.
By practicing with such diligence, being purely singular and free from conflict,
and corresponding to the cessation of disputes, one accomplishes this samādhi;
abiding therein according to the principle, one is able to understand the secret teachings.
Knowing "I" and the conceit of "I," one cuts off pride and severs arrogance.
Within the definitive teachings, having accomplished skillful means and also knowing the various designations— one is a wise person.
Within the principles of all phenomena, If one diligently practices according to the truth, One will be able to see all the gateways of the Dharma; Such a person is one who sees the Dharma.
By practicing diligently in this way, One can come to know all phenomena.
Which phenomena are associated?
Which phenomena are dissociated?
Among all phenomena, those whose karma is purified through mindfulness—
One who is able to attain skillful means regarding the definitive meaning,
and who, among all phenomena, meditates with diligence,
will thoroughly understand all dharmas and thereby obtain this samādhi.
"Furthermore, Anantamati!
For those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who diligently practice within this Dharma,
there is further a method for mastering the samādhi that encompasses all."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall explain it.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying: “Anantamati!

There are gateways of the light of the Dharma for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which can give rise to skillful means regarding the principles of all dharmas, and can also give rise to all dharma-seals. They can enter the gates of all dharma-seals; they can understand and enter into all that ought to be done regarding all dharmas; they can attain and expound the light of the Dharma, entering into the gateways of all dharma-terms in accordance with that light of the Dharma.”
What is called the "Dharma-gate of Radiance" that is able to give rise to skillful radiance?

It refers to being able to thoroughly understand the gate of synonymous terminology, the gate of secret terminology, the gate of synonymous phenomena, the gate of encompassing phenomena, and the gates of various distinctions.

How does one come to understand that which enables the emergence of the gateways of samādhi and the gateways of the principles of the entire dharma-realm, so as to enter into the single meaning and be able to follow and comprehend the radiance of all phenomena?

“Anantamati! Regarding these skillful means in the principles of the profound dharmas, whether Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are currently practicing or will practice them in the future, or are currently seeking them or will seek them in the future—upon hearing this Dharma-gate, they shall attain great illumination with minimal application and enter into all dharma-gates; from this Dharma-gate, further illumination shall arise.”

By means of this radiance, according to whichever dharma-gate or whichever practice it may be, one should enter and practice in accordance with its underlying principle. Through the power of samādhi, one contemplates all dharma-gates; through the gate of samādhi, one gives rise to wisdom and attains thorough understanding. By virtue of the power of samādhi regarding the true principle, by contemplating the dharma-gates, and by the arising of wisdom, one uses the gate of samādhi to understand the dharma-realm and abide in skillful means. One is able to give rise to the radiance of all dharma-gates and attain the Ocean-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas.
“Anantamati! What is the Dharma-gate?

It is the seal of the letter A that seals all dharmas produced by ignorance; it is the perfection of formative action (saṃskāra) with the letter A as its foremost, because ignorance is stilled and there is nothing further to be done.”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of signlessness (*animitta-mudrā-dvāra*). They should seal all phenomena with the seal of the syllable *a* (pronounced as *ā*); because they thoroughly understand the conditions for the convergence of karma and its fruit—the maturation of karma, that which is to be performed by karma, and the union of karma and its fruit—all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of no-karma, no-fruit, no-convergence, and no-conditions.

One seals all phenomena with the seal of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), because it gives rise to the light of wisdom regarding all phenomena within the various karmas and the tasks to be performed by karma.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of skillfulness in all conditioned formations.

One seals all phenomena with the seal of the syllable *ḍa*; one employs the syllable *ma* as an auxiliary to establish designations and names, bringing them into correspondence with various phenomena. Because one understands how *ḍa* and *ma* assist one another, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal that is without conjunction, without assistance, and without name.

Sealing all phenomena with the seal of the boundless, no conceptualization whatsoever can be apprehended; because they are free from conceptualization, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-conceptualization.

Because the seal of the limitlessness seals all phenomena such that their limits do not conjoin, for the sake of exhausting all limits, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-investigation, non-discernment, and ineffability.

By sealing all phenomena with the seal of the absence of manifold intrinsic natures—thereby severing the perception of manifold intrinsic natures through the characteristic of arising from a single intrinsic nature—all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of manifold intrinsic natures.

By means of the seal of union corresponding to desire, one seals all phenomena so that the arising of conditioned formations is perfected; yet because desire is abandoned, there is tranquility and no union. Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-union, which is the wisdom and vision that exhausts desire.
Anantamati! This is the seal-gate of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas that seals all dharmas.
By means of this seal-gate, one should enter into all dharmas.
“Anantamati! Furthermore, there are the gate of non-obstruction and the gate of non-conjunction, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should accordingly awaken to and enter.
What are the gate of non-obstruction and the gate of non-conjunction?
