It means that all phenomena are sealed by the seal of space; therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-attachment.
All phenomena are sealed by the seal of emptiness and solitude; therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-duality.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of tranquility, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of cessation.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of no-gateway, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of immovability.
Sealing all dharmas with the seal of non-abiding, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-defilement.
Sealing all dharmas with the seal of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-attainment.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of signlessness, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of skillful cultivation of expedient means.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of wishlessness, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of the light of vows of sublime tranquility.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of non-attachment, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of reality that distinguishes universal knowledge.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of non-arising, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of non-arising through the arising of correct wisdom and vision.
Sealing all dharmas with the seal of quiescence, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of detachment from the aggregates (*skandha*).
Sealing all dharmas with the seal of the characteristic of exhaustion, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of the exhaustion of birth.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-mudrā*), bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the skillful seal that manifests the dharma-realm.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra-mudrā*), bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of true non-discrimination and equality.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of the nature of detachment, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of universal knowledge of all intrinsic natures.
Sealing all phenomena with the seal of nirvāṇa, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should enter the gateway of the seal of true tranquility and conformity with cessation.

Anantamati! This is the gate of non-obstruction and the gate of non-conjunction for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regarding all phenomena; it transcends all gates of the views of annihilationism and eternalism, the gate of infinite limits, and the gate of the prior and posterior limits, by means of wearying detachment, cessation, quiescence, and coolness.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in and entering this gateway of the seal of all dharmas, and by skillfully practicing these various dharma-gateways, attain the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal of All Dharmas.

This samādhi is the skillful means of wisdom that, through its accord with reality as it is, can encompass all dharmas; therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should skillfully cultivate this gateway of the seal, abide in the Sea-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas, and contemplate all dharmas, thereby being able to produce the immeasurable and boundless radiance of the Great Dharma.

"Anantamati! For example, the waters of the great ocean are immeasurable, and there is no one who can fathom their measure; all dharmas are likewise, for ultimately there is no one who can fathom their measure."

Furthermore, just as all rivers flow into the great ocean, so too do all phenomena enter into the Dharma Seal; therefore, it is called the "Ocean Seal" because it seals all phenomena, such that they all enter into the Ocean Seal of all phenomena, and within this seal, one perceives all phenomena as being identical to the Dharma Seal.
Furthermore, it is like the great nāgas and their hosts, those beings of immense bodies who are able to possess the great ocean, enter the great ocean, and take up residence within that great ocean.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise; having skillfully cultivated all karmas throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they are able to enter this gateway of the seal of samādhi. Taking that gateway of the seal as their dwelling place, for the sake of realizing all Buddha-dharmas and for the sake of skillfully perfecting all-knowledge, they accomplish such gateways of the seals of all dharmas.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice and study this dharma-gate, they are able to study all dharma-gates; because they see that all dharma-gates are contained within this gate, they are able to give rise to the light of all dharmas and enter into the ocean of all dharmas. For this reason, this dharma is called the "Samādhi of the Ocean-Seal of All Dharmas."
Furthermore, just as the great ocean is a place where great treasures are accumulated, so too is this samādhi: it is a place where all dharmas and skillfulness regarding dharmas are accumulated.

“Anantamati! If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge and vision, have sought, will seek, or are currently seeking this samādhi, they shall be able to seek the perfect wisdom of the ocean of all dharmas.”
For this reason, I entrust this Dharma-seal to you.
In the final age, during the last fifty years when the True Dharma is extinguished, you shall seal all sentient beings with this Dharma-seal.

Those who seal themselves with this Dharma-seal shall all attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they shall accomplish the Buddha-dharma and swiftly proceed to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), turning the unsurpassed wheel and perpetuating the lineage of the Buddhas; they shall dwell in accordance with the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*) and be able to enter parinirvāṇa in the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa, causing all devas and humans to uphold the True Dharma.
Anantamati! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to embrace such immeasurable and sublime merits, they should diligently delight in this profound Dharma and remain free from negligence.
"Furthermore, Anantamati!

I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and even twice that number, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Sumeruprakampaprabharāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The kalpa was named Susthita, and the land was named Manojña.
During that kalpa, the lifespan of sentient beings was immeasurable; they dwelt in peace, security, and abundance, abiding in all wholesome dharmas. For this reason, that kalpa was called Susthita.

That Buddha-land is vast, magnificent, and adorned with many exquisite beauties; those who see it feel harmony and joy in their hearts, and fragrant scents circulate everywhere. For these reasons, that land is named "Joyful" (Ramaṇīya).

At that time, among the four continents, three of them were equal in size, each measuring eighty thousand yojanas; within each continent there were twenty thousand cities, and each city measured ten yojanas in extent.
Only the single continent of Jambudvīpa exists, measuring ten million yojanas in extent, with eighty thousand cities, each city being twenty yojanas in size.

Adorned with multi-storied pavilions, flagstaffs, and surrounding walls, it is further embellished by various trees of clothing, various trees of flavors, diverse flowering trees, and precious tārā trees; the realm is peaceful and blissful, and filled with people.
Within it, moreover, was a preeminent capital city measuring one hundred *yojana* in circumference, surrounded by twenty thousand gardens.

Within these gardens, clear ponds and flowing streams filled and poured everywhere; flowers and buds, as well as sweet fruits, each flourished in lush abundance. Famed incenses wafted everywhere, bringing joy to all who smelled them, while birds and beasts sang in harmony, their voices elegant and resonant.
At that time, that Buddha was dwelling in a garden, preaching the Dharma to the assembly. Anantamati!
The lifespan of the Tathāgata Sumeruprabharāja exceeded ten minor kalpas, and after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for a full minor kalpa.

At that time, that Tathāgata taught the Dharma in four assemblies; in each of these dharma assemblies, there were five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* of śrāvakas who were still on the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), and fifty *koṭi-nayuta* each of arhats and bodhisattvas.
At that time, that Tathāgata had two bodhisattvas:
the first was named Śūramgama (Valorous Army), and the second was named Śūrabala (Valorous Power).
These two bodhisattvas were fully endowed with supernatural powers and had attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; they came before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what dharmas does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplish the ocean-seal samādhi (sāgaramudrā-samādhi) of all dharmas?
At that time, the Tathāgata extensively expounded this for him through the gateway of these phrases.

When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and these two bodhisattvas realized the ocean-seal samādhi (*sarva-dharma-samudra-mudrā-samādhi*) as well as all bodhisattva samādhis.

Because he had realized the Sea-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas and realized the various samādhis of a bodhisattva, he was able to manifest great spiritual transformations and radiate great light within all buddha-fields, producing sublime Brahma-sounds to expound the True Dharma for all sentient beings, thereby bringing eight koṭis of people to maturity and leading them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then that Tathāgata bestowed upon them this prophecy:
"After one hundred kalpas have passed, you shall all realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

During those hundred kalpas, in each and every kalpa, you shall make offerings to and serve five hundred Tathāgatas; within the teachings of those Tathāgatas—both during the period of the True Dharma and the period of the Semblance Dharma—you shall be able to receive and uphold them, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings."

In each and every kalpa, his mind remains undistracted; in each and every place of birth, he undergoes transformational birth; in each and every lifetime, he does not regress from samādhi, employing spiritual transformations and preaching the Dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
After passing through more than a hundred kalpas, he again encountered the Tathāgata Boundless Merit (*Anantaguṇa*), whom he served and attended upon.
He was skillfully able to sport within the transformations and liberations of immeasurable samādhis.

These two bodhisattvas were in the presence of that Buddha—one named Vigataśoka and the other named Supratiṣṭhita—and were able to turn the wheel of Dharma following the Tathāgata, teaching and transforming immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to abide in the three vehicles.
Then that Tathāgata further bestowed upon him a prediction:
"After my parinirvāṇa, Viśoka shall realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and be known by the name Tathāgata Anantapratibhāna."
After his parinirvāṇa, Shan-zhu shall realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and be named Most Victorious Radiance Tathāgata.
His lifespan shall last for one kalpa, and his buddha-field shall be accumulated with immeasurable merit.
"After these two bodhisattvas have received this prediction in the presence of the Tathāgata, they will successively realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Anantamati!"

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [seek] the Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) of all dharmas, they should give rise to love and joy, exert great diligence, and practice with heedfulness, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva mahāsattva in that assembly named Huiyi (Wisdom-Meaning), who rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"

He is now able, for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, to expound the Sea-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas, so that they may attain skill in the knowledge of all dharmas and realize the all-knowledge of the Tathāgata.

"Bhagavān! If one attains the Sea-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas, one will certainly attain skillful means regarding the principles of all dharmas and swiftly proceed to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

By means of this boundless great ocean of merit, one sets out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, constantly beholding the Buddhas, diligently practicing the True Dharma, and walking together with the Saṅgha; one is able to consume the supreme offerings of the Tathāgata and transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Huiyi, saying:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said, Huiyi!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain the Sea-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas, they obtain immeasurable and supreme merits.
If they abide in the Sea-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas, they can, through the skillful means of the Sea-Seal Samādhi of all dharmas, resolutely proceed toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"O Huiyi! Just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, composed of various jewels, rises from the great ocean to a height of eighty-four thousand yojanas, standing majestically and abiding in supreme radiance;

so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Because they have skillfully set out by means of this samādhi, they emerge from the great ocean of the treasury of all dharmas, eclipsing all the devas and humans of the world, abiding in unsurpassed and supreme radiance."

Furthermore, just as the full moon is surrounded by a multitude of stars, so too are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are able to produce great radiance amidst all the assemblies of gods and humans in every world.
Huiyi! Observe this Dharma: who would not give rise to love and joy for it, and fail to arouse diligence while falling into negligence?
Only those inferior beings of meager merit are excluded.
If there are sentient beings who possess great wisdom, they will be able to accomplish this vast Dharma.
This vast Dharma is endowed with merit and is embraced by all noble beings.
As I have taught, if one can grasp this vast wealth of Dharma, they will be attended by devas and humans, and protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying:

“Anantamati! If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas diligently practice and study this Dharma, they will be able to bring great benefit to sentient beings; they will eliminate all doubts and resolve all fetters, abandon all habitual tendencies and sever all latent proclivities, transcend all craving and delight, and cross the ocean of existence. They will forever extinguish darkness and forever leave behind fear, and through skillful means, they will swiftly be able to know the minds of all sentient beings.”
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he emitted a great radiance; that light shone throughout countless worlds, eclipsing the brilliance of all suns and moons.
Having emitted this light, he again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying: "Anantamati!

If all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas can diligently cultivate the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi), they too shall likewise manifest great supernormal transformations, emit great radiance, and utter the Great Lion’s Roar to expound this Dharma, transcending the three realms and providing great illumination, no different from what I do today."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that the Tathāgata will empower this Dharma, so that if there are sentient beings in the future final age who hear the name of this Dharma, they shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to empower this Dharma-gate, again emitted rays of light and moved the entire trichiliocosm with a single finger, causing all sentient beings to attain great peace and happiness.

At that time, within the assembly, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and such multitudes as these scattered celestial wonderful flowers and celestial wonderful robes, while celestial music and dance were performed simultaneously.
Immeasurable devas held celestial robes in their hands, fluttering and billowing throughout the void, and with one voice they proclaimed:
"How marvelous, how marvelous! The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable!"
"If there are those who receive, uphold, and maintain this profound Dharma, you should know that they are worthy of receiving the respect and prostrations of all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, saying: "Anantamati!"
In the future, at the end of the age, sentient beings of meager merit will not be able to hear this Armor-Adornment Samādhi Adornment.
Only those sentient beings who possess skillful means and have gathered a great store of provisions will hear this Dharma in the future, at the end of the age.
Those who diligently practice this Dharma shall be taken into the care of the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Boundless Wisdom!
In the future final age, during a time of great terror, I entrust this Dharma-gate to you all.

Over countless koṭis and nayutas of kalpas, I have accumulated the unsurpassed treasury of all Dharma-jewels, endowed with merit and boundless peace and happiness; you have now attained them all, and you have now abandoned the entire aggregate of suffering.
"By means of this great ocean of boundless merit, you shall swiftly proceed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantamati, together with five hundred Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas and the lay devotees headed by the merchant leader Bhadrapāla, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"According to our capacity, we shall uphold the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Great Bodhi and bring great benefit to all sentient beings in the future final age.

At that time, the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas each rose from their seats, scattered various flowers over the Tathāgata, removed their exquisite robes to offer as an act of worship, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!"

By means of these roots of goodness, I dedicate them all to all sentient beings, wishing that all beings may fully perfect the factors of enlightenment and achieve the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom of all phenomena.
"In the future final age, may all the roots of goodness of all sentient beings be fully accomplished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to inspire joy in all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, spoke these verses:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, You should bring about great benefit."
Upholding my Dharma of enlightenment, the Dharma King roars the lion’s roar.
In the final age of the future, should there be those who seek the Dharma,
upon hearing this vast teaching, they shall all attain peace and happiness.
As I have taught, if there are those who behold this vehicle and hear the Dharma of this sūtra, they shall attain whatever they desire.
If there are those possessed of wisdom who cultivate skillful means, [they shall likewise attain their goal].
Hearing this supreme Dharma, their bodies and minds are filled with great joy.
Those who are present in this assembly and see me before them,
having heard this Dharma, are well able to cherish and delight in it.
In the final age of the future, you shall give birth to a great mass of merit—
incalculable, immeasurable, vast, and boundless.
In the final age of the future, if one is able to receive and uphold this,
The Dharma taught by the Dharma King is sustained by the Buddha’s empowerment.
In the final age of the future, those who uphold my Bodhi-Dharma shall become immeasurable Buddhas; they are the final upholders of the Dharma.

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, immeasurable bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and immeasurable sentient beings brought their roots of goodness to maturity.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantamati and all the other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, along with the devas, humans, asuras, and others of all worlds, having heard what the Buddha preached, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-five;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-six.
Translated by the Liang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Mandaraka.
Chapter Eight: The Non-differentiation of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm (Part One) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus.
There were twelve thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered there from immeasurable buddha-fields;
furthermore, there were thirty-two thousand devaputras, all of whom were oriented toward the Mahāyāna.
At that time, within the great assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named the Youth Mañjuśrī, as well as the Devaputra Ratnottama.
Then, the Devaputra Ratnottama had this thought:

“If, now, the World-Honored One were to command Mañjuśrī to expound the Dharma, and having so commanded him, were to cause all the palaces of Māra to be completely shrouded in darkness so that they no longer possess majestic power; were to cause Māra Pāpīyān to be distressed and displeased; were to cause all the hosts of Māras to be thoroughly subdued; were to cause those with overweening pride to break their pride; were to cause those who have well practiced to realize the fruits of śramaṇaship for themselves, and those who have already attained the fruits to advance further; were to cause the lineages of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha to continue without interruption; were to cause many people to resolve upon Bodhicitta; and were to cause the Bodhi accumulated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas to endure for a long time—[then this would be most excellent].”

"If one constantly hears this Dharma being taught, whether while the Tathāgata is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, one will swiftly attain parinirvāṇa according to whichever vehicle one is inclined toward.
At that time, the World-Honored One, mindful of the thoughts of the Devaputra Ratnavyūha, addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"You may briefly expound the Dharma within this assembly; this great multitude now wishes to hear it from you."
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what Dharma should you preach?”
The Buddha said:
"I shall explain the causes and conditions for the essential nature of the dharma-realm. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
The essential nature of the dharma-realm of all dharmas is the dharma-realm itself, World-Honored One!
Outside of the dharma-realm, there is nothing to be heard.”
“World-Honored One, why do you say that one expounds the Dharma by means of the dharma-realm? The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!”
“World-Honored One, if arrogant sentient beings were to hear this Dharma, they would give rise to alarm and wonder. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!”
The essential nature of the dharma-realm is devoid of any marvel.
World-Honored One!
That which is marvelous is itself the essential nature of the dharma-realm.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the youth Mañjuśrī: “Mañjuśrī!
If all phenomena are of the very nature of the dharma-realm, where could there be defilement or purity for sentient beings?”
"Because the essential nature of the dharma-realm is neither defiled nor pure. Mañjuśrī said,
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
These sentient beings possess the inversion of the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and abide in the notions of "I am superior" and "mine is superior.

These ordinary persons give rise to the notion of a self; these sentient beings cling to the notion of a self and cling to the notion of another, thereby giving rise to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*). Through these minds and mental factors, they perform various karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome. Because of these karmic actions as causes, these sentient beings obtain their retributive fruits.
Venerable Śāriputra! If there is birth, there is defilement; this defilement is the very essence of the dharmadhātu. Venerable Śāriputra!

If one knows that defilement is the very essence of the dharma-dhātu, this is called "purity"; yet, in the ultimate sense, there is neither defilement nor purity, whether it be defiled dharmas or pure dharmas.
When Mañjuśrī spoke this Dharma, one hundred bhikṣus emerged, having completely severed all outflows and attained the outflow-free mind.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the youth Mañjuśrī:
"The Dharma realm you have explained is without error; having spoken this Dharma, more than one hundred bhikṣus have completely severed all outflows and attained the outflow-free mind."
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Śāriputra! As for this dharmadhātu, was it originally bound that it has now attained liberation?"
Śāriputra said: "Mañjuśrī,
is this dharmadhātu something that was originally bound and has now attained liberation?"
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Where have these bhikṣus now attained liberation of mind?
Śāriputra replied:
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata has subdued a great many śrāvakas, all of whom have severed their outflows and attained liberation of mind. Mañjuśrī replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra! Are you not a śrāvaka of the World-Honored One? Śāriputra replied:
“Mañjuśrī! It is so, it is so. As you have said, I am a śrāvaka of the Blessed One.”
Mañjuśrī said, “Venerable Śāriputra,
have you severed all outflows and attained the mind of untainted liberation?”
Śāriputra said, "I have attained the mind of untainted liberation. Mañjuśrī said:
"Venerable sir, by means of what kind of mind do you attain liberation?
Is it by means of a past mind, a future mind, or a present mind?"
"Venerable One!
There is the perception that the mind of the past has already ceased, the perception that the mind of the future has not yet arrived, and the perception that the mind of the present does not abide."
"How does the Venerable One’s mind attain liberation? Śāriputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"Neither is liberation attained by a mind of the past, nor is liberation attained by a mind of the future or the present. Mañjuśrī said,
"Venerable One!"
"How can you say that the mind attains liberation? Śāriputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"Abiding in conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one speaks of the mind attaining liberation; however, in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is absolutely no mind that is bound or liberated.
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Śāriputra!"
"Do you wish to have the essential nature of the dharma-realm exist within the conventional truth or the ultimate truth? Śāriputra replied, "Mañjuśrī!"
"The essential nature of the dharma-realm possesses neither the conventional truth nor the ultimate truth. Mañjuśrī said,
"Virtuous One!"
"How can you say that one attains liberation of mind while abiding in conventional truth? Śāriputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"Is it not possible to attain liberation without having a mind? Mañjuśrī replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra!"
If the mind had an interior, an exterior, or a middle, it would attain liberation;
however, Venerable Sir, this mind has no interior, exterior, or middle, and thus there is neither bondage nor liberation.
At that time, there were two hundred bhikṣus in the assembly who, upon hearing what Mañjuśrī had said, rose from their seats and spoke these words:
"If there is no liberation and no mind of liberation, for what purpose have we left the household life to practice the Way?"
"If there is no transcendence of the world, why practice the Path?
Having spoken these harsh words, those bhikṣus turned their backs on the assembly and departed.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, wishing to subdue these bhikṣus, knew the path upon which they were traveling and manifested a bhikṣu before them.
Those bhikṣus went to where the transformed bhikṣu was and, standing before him, asked him thus:
"Venerable sir,
from where have you come?"
The transformed bhikṣu replied to the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!
Regarding what Mañjuśrī has spoken, I do not understand it, I do not know it, I do not believe it, and I do not incline toward it; for this reason, I have come from that assembly."
Those bhikṣus then spoke again to this manifested bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir! We are likewise;
we do not understand, we do not know, we do not believe, and we do not incline toward it. For these reasons, we have come from that assembly."
The transformed bhikṣu said: "Virtuous One!
Why did you depart from the assembly, finding the Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī unsuitable and contrary to your own inclinations?"
The bhikṣus said: "Venerable sir!
Mañjuśrī has taught that there is no fruit of the path toward which one is directed, no fruit of realization, and furthermore, no liberation."
Having heard this, we thought to ourselves:
"If there is no fruit of the path, no realization of the fruit, and no one who attains liberation, for what purpose do we practice the holy life?"
"If there is no emergence, for what purpose does one cultivate the path?
Thinking on this meaning, he came forth from that assembly.
Thus spoke the transformed bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
Because you do not understand, and for the sake of slandering and reviling, you have departed from that assembly. The bhikṣus said:
"We neither slander nor revile you; we have merely come out from among that assembly because we do not see liberation.
Then the transformed bhikṣu praised those bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
"Venerable sir!
We should now deliberate together well upon this:
that which is not reviling is not contention; that which is not contention is the ultimate Dharma of the śramaṇa."
"What are the characteristics of your minds? Are they blue, yellow, red, white, purple, or the color of crystal?
Are they real or unreal?"
"Is it eternal, or is it impermanent?
Is it form, or is it non-form?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Venerable sir!
The mind is non-material and invisible; it has no form or manifestation, nor does it possess tactile resistance; it has no location and no instruction.
The transformed bhikṣu said:
"Venerable Sir!
This mind is truly not form and cannot be seen; it has no shape or appearance, nor does it possess tangibility; it has no location and no teaching.
Does this mind abide internally, abide externally, or abide both internally and externally?"
Those bhikṣus replied, "No. The transformed bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sir!

Your mind is not form and is invisible; it has no shape or manifestation, no contact or resistance, no location or instruction, and is neither internal, external, nor in between—is this correctly accomplished?"
Those bhikṣus replied, “No. The transformed bhikṣu said:
“Venerable sir!

Your mind is not form and is invisible; it has no shape or manifestation, no resistance, no location, and no instruction; it is neither internal, external, nor in between—is this rightly accomplished?”
The bhikṣus replied, “No. The transformed bhikṣu said:
"Venerable Sir!
If the mind is unreal and lacks accomplishment, how can there be liberation?
To this, those bhikṣus replied:
"No," replied the transformed bhikṣu,
"O Venerable One!"
For this reason, Mañjuśrī, he teaches that the essential nature of the Dharma-realm is undefiled and pure.

Venerable sir, because you are an ordinary person under the influence of inversion, you grasp at a self and what belongs to a self, giving rise to the mind; you engage with various objects, giving rise to a mind of攀缘 (pān-yuán—clinging/conditioning). This [teaching] is able to utterly extinguish all such clinging and the dharmas of arising and ceasing, non-abiding, and transformation.

If the mind takes as its object the renunciation of household life, the reception of full ordination, the cultivation of the path, and the attainment of the fruits, the essence of that mind is empty and lacks reality, arising from deluded thoughts. If it is unreal deluded thought, then it is neither born, nor abiding, nor ceasing.
If it were not subject to arising, abiding, and ceasing, there would be neither bondage nor liberation, neither progress nor attainment.
Venerable One!
For this reason, Mañjuśrī teaches that the essential nature of the dharma-realm is undefiled and pure, and that therein there is no progress, no attainment, and no liberation.
When the transformed bhikṣu had spoken thus, the bhikṣus attained untainted liberation (*anāsravavimukti*).
Having attained liberation, they immediately returned to where Mañjuśrī was.
Having arrived, each removed his *uttarāsaṅga* robe to offer it to Mañjuśrī, saying these words: "Mañjuśrī!
You have now skillfully protected us."
"Because we do not have faith in or incline toward this profound Dharma of discipline, we have distanced ourselves and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked them thus:
"O Venerable Ones!..."
"For what reason have you attained this, and for what reason have you realized this, that each of you has set aside your *uttarāsaṅga* robes as an offering to Mañjuśrī?
The bhikṣus replied, "Venerable Subhūti!"
We have neither attainment nor realization; for this reason, we offer worship to the youth Mañjuśrī. Venerable Subhūti!
Because we harbored the notion of attainment, we rose from our seats and departed from this assembly.
"We have already been able to abandon the perception of attainment;
for this reason, we have returned here. Subhūti said, "For what reason do you speak these words?"
The bhikṣus said: "Venerable Subhūti!
To give names is called agitation and attachment; if there is agitation and attachment, there is neither orientation nor attainment."
"Venerable Subhūti!
If there is no movement toward attainment, then at this very point one is able to sever all agitation and attachment. Subhūti said:
“Who has tamed you? The bhikṣus replied, “Venerable Subhūti!”
To have nothing attained and nothing realized is to subdue the self.
Such a person is neither born nor does they enter parinirvāṇa; they are neither in meditative concentration nor in a distracted mind.
Subhūti asked, "Who has tamed you? The bhikṣus replied:
"You may ask the youth Mañjuśrī. Then, the Venerable Ānanda asked Mañjuśrī:
"By whom have these bhikṣus been disciplined?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Ānanda!

That which is without aggregates, elements, or sense bases is neither an ordinary person, nor a pratyekabuddha, nor a śrāvaka, nor a bodhisattva, nor a Tathāgata; it is not associated with body, nor associated with speech, nor associated with mind."
Ānanda said: "Mañjuśrī! To whom do you refer?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Ānanda! If it is a transformation created by a Tathāgata, does that transformation possess any correspondence [with reality]?"
Ānanda said: “Mañjuśrī!
An emanation has no dharma with which it could be associated or dissociated.”
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Ānanda! The essential nature of all phenomena is an emanation."
Ānanda said: “Mañjuśrī! As you have said, the essential nature of all dharmas is illusory transformation.”
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Ānanda, it is this emanation that has subdued these bhikṣus."
Venerable Ānanda! Just as those who are tamed through transformation, so too are all śrāvakas. Venerable Ānanda!
"To tame in this way is true taming;
those who do not understand such taming should be known as those of overweening pride.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Mañjuśrī! Can such bhikṣus of overweening pride be recognized? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Venerable Ānanda! That the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is pure is itself a fluctuation; you should know that this is overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

That the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*) are pure is itself a fluctuation; you should know that this is overweening pride.”
"I have attained my realization"—to think thus with such wavering and deluded conceptualization, know that this is precisely overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

To be startled and afraid of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), thinking it is as empty as space, and to enter the single path, thinking it too is empty—this is called "speaking correctly," yet know that this is precisely overweening pride.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, if a bhikṣu understands that the view of a self-identity is empty, up to entering the emptiness of the single path—such emptiness is the emptiness of equality.
You should know that this is precisely overweening pride (adhimāna).
Why is this? Venerable Ānanda!
The view of a self is distinct from emptiness; because they are distinct, the view of a self is itself emptiness.
Emptiness is not different from the Path, and the Path is itself emptiness.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda!
If one feels fear toward ignorance and craving for existence, yet delights in clarity and liberation, you should know that this is precisely overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Why is this?
If there are two characteristics, it is not liberation.

Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda! If there is a bhikṣu who fears greed, hatred, and delusion, yet delights in the three liberations; who is terrified of the four inversions, yet delights in the four marks; who is terrified of the five hindrances, yet delights in the five faculties; who is terrified of the six sense bases, yet delights in the six supernormal powers; who is terrified of the seven stations of consciousness, yet delights in the seven factors of enlightenment; who is terrified of the eight wrong paths, yet delights in the eightfold noble path; who is terrified of the nine abodes of sentient beings, yet delights in the nine successive attainments; who is terrified of the ten unwholesome actions, yet delights in the ten untainted wholesome actions; and who is terrified of the conditioned realm, yet delights in unconditioned dharmas—know that this person possesses overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Why is this? Venerable Ānanda!
For all these things are in constant flux and are mere conceptual proliferation.
Venerable Ānanda!
If there is agitation or conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the mind becomes self-exalting.

To grasp at things with autonomy, relying on and enduring through the accomplishment of false imaginings (*vikalpa*)—such dharmas as these are called "autonomy" (*svatantra*); because of this autonomy, arrogance arises.
Venerable Ānanda!
Such a bhikṣu should be known as one who possesses overweening pride (adhimāna). Why is this so?
"Venerable Ānanda,
how can the conditioned realm be empty?
This monk who enters emptiness into emptiness should be known as one possessed of overweening pride."
The Venerable Ānanda asked Mañjuśrī,
“How does a bhikṣu become free from overweening pride? Mañjuśrī replied:

“Venerable Ānanda! If a bhikṣu is inwardly tranquil, he is outwardly tranquil; regarding all objective realms—whether equal or unequal, existent or non-existent, conditioned or unconditioned—he is without agitation. He is without conceptualization and without non-conceptualization; without duality and without unity; without adornment and without non-adornment. Free from frivolous proliferation and without attachment, he first perceives the equality of all dharmas, yet there is neither equality nor inequality.”

There is not a single dharma that can be made equal or unequal; thus it is immovable and unshakable, without conceptualization and without non-conceptualization, neither clinging nor perceiving conceptualization—how much less could there be any movement or shaking in the realization of the fruit of wisdom? Such a thing is impossible.
Venerable Ānanda!

Such a bhikṣu has no companions of overweening pride and is free from frivolous proliferation; he distances himself from both self and others as companions, relinquishing all attachments, because all attachment is non-attachment.
Free from all objects of perception, observation, and reflection, one reflects upon liberation and the path leading to liberation; there is no grasper, and all is utterly tranquil.

By reason of this tranquility, I have reached the further shore regarding my body and what belongs to my body, seeing no dharma whatsoever that can be liberated, directed toward, severed, or realized.

If there is a bhikṣu who practices in this way without conceit, because of the equality of emptiness, he understands that all dharmas are equal and devoid of high or low—whether wholesome or unwholesome, what may be done or not done, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned. Regarding such fluctuations of high and low, there is nothing that is not a false conceptualization, nor does he perceive or know them as such.
Thus, all these phenomena are seen as equal, like space.
Venerable Ānanda!
If there is a bhikṣu who understands in this way, he is called "well-liberated"; such a bhikṣu is free from overweening pride.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has said: "If there is a bhikṣu who understands that all phenomena are equal, like space—just as when one moves within space, there is nothing with which to come into contact."
"The Dharma of the śramaṇa is also like this.
When these words were spoken, two hundred bhikṣus completely severed all outflows (āsrava) and attained the dharma of outflow-free liberation (anāsrava-vimukti).
At that time, the Celestial Son Ratnottama asked Mañjuśrī,
“How does a bodhisattva become free from overweening pride?
I pray that you will explain this according to reality.”
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses the mind of omniscience, the unequaled mind, and the mind that is supreme within the triple world—surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and who dwells with a mind that transcends all external objects, yet still cultivates all roots of goodness for the sake of preeminence, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, and for the sake of upholding the true Dharma; and who, for the sake of other sentient beings and others, explains this mind of omniscience, understanding this mind as it truly is as fundamentally and originally equal."
Just as they understand the essential nature of their own minds according to what they have heard, they understand the essential nature of all sentient beings;
because they understand the essential nature of all phenomena, they understand the essential nature of all roots of goodness;
and because they understand the essential nature of all roots of goodness, they understand the essential nature of the exposition of the bodhisattva.
"O Devaputra!
This Bodhisattva speaks of the prophecy of enlightenment as it truly is.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!"
When a bodhisattva practices giving, whether it be that which is given, that which is given according to one's vows, or any other forms of giving, all are without obstruction.
This giving is without dependence, without attachment, without conceptualization, and without liberation; because there is no liberation, it is emptiness.

If one can understand the essential nature of giving in this way, by understanding the essential nature of giving, one understands the essential nature of the primordial beginning as it truly is; by understanding the essential nature of the primordial beginning as it truly is, one understands the essential nature of all phenomena; by understanding the essential nature of all phenomena, one understands the essential nature of all sentient beings; and by understanding the essential nature of all sentient beings, one explains the essential nature of the bodhisattva.
"O Son of Heaven!
This is called the purity of a bodhisattva’s giving; therefore, the prediction of enlightenment is proclaimed.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"

If there is a bodhisattva who understands the body, they understand precepts; if they understand the mouth, they understand precepts; if they understand the mind, they understand precepts. Understanding the body and mouth, they understand awakening and tranquility. Because they understand awakening and tranquility, they understand the tranquility of sentient beings. Because they understand the tranquility of sentient beings, they understand the tranquility of all phenomena (*dharma*). Because they understand the tranquility of all phenomena, they understand the primordial tranquility of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*). Because they understand the primordial tranquility of reality as it is, they attain the dharma of tranquility. With tranquility as its cause and tranquility as its condition, whatever all phenomena they hear, they are able to explain them as tranquil.
"O Son of Heaven!
This is called the purity of the Bodhisattva precepts; therefore, I speak of the bestowal of the prediction of enlightenment according to reality.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"

If there is a bodhisattva who knows that the nature of phenomena is ultimately empty and knows that the nature of phenomena is ultimately sovereign, they will be able to endure all evils from sentient beings; their mind does not give rise to [a concept of] patience, they do not contemplate external objects, and they do not turn away from sentient beings, thereby being able to extinguish all evils.
Just as the nature of patience in all sentient beings is such, so too is its essential nature.
Just as the essential nature of patience is such, so too is the nature of bodhi.
Just as the nature of bodhi is such, so too is the essential nature of all phenomena.
Just as one knows the essential nature of all phenomena, so it is in accordance with reality and the Dharma.

Just as that which is heard likewise exhausts the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the realm of dharma-nature is ultimately empty—this ultimate emptiness of the dharma-nature is called practicing the patient acceptance of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti).
"O Son of Heaven!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s truly pure patience; it is the bestowal of the prediction of enlightenment.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"

The Bodhisattva knows how to be cautious regarding all dharmas and practices, remaining free from all discursive thought; without any adornments, they achieve the practice of relinquishment and progress. As if there were something to be done, yet there is nothing actually done; their knowledge is firm and capable of renouncing everything, while their inner nature is tranquil as they transform sentient beings externally.

Because one knows that diligence is quiescent, one knows that awakening (*bodhi*) is quiescent; because one knows that awakening is quiescent, one also knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are tranquil; because one knows that all phenomena are tranquil, one knows the beginning as it truly is, according to the Dharma as it has been heard; and because the nature of diligence is quiescent, one is able to expound everything.
"O Son of Heaven!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s pure diligence that knows the bestowal of prophecy as it truly is.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"

If a bodhisattva enters the meditative concentration of the equality of all phenomena, which is without increase or decrease, by the power of that concentration his mind dwells in peace; because the mind dwells in peace, consciousness has no place of abiding; because consciousness has no place of abiding, the seven factors of enlightenment are equal; because the seven factors of enlightenment are equal, he attains the equality of meditative concentration; because he attains the equality of meditative concentration, he knows the equality of bodhi; because he knows the equality of bodhi, he knows the equality of all sentient beings; and because he knows the equality of all sentient beings, he knows the equality of all phenomena.
If one knows all phenomena to be equal in this way, one is able to explain the equality of the essential nature of all phenomena according to whatever Dharma has been heard.
O Devaputra!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s pure meditative concentration that explains the prediction of enlightenment as it truly is.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

If there is a bodhisattva whose eye of wisdom is pure, who knows and sees all dharmas as they truly are, then according to those dharmas as they are seen, there is nothing seen and no movement. Such a one attains unmoving wisdom, a practice that is without activity, without cause, and without conditions; yet they do not practice the various rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), nor do they fail to practice them. They know that all dharmas are equal, and thus they neither rescue nor fail to act.
Why is this? If one does not engage in [such activity], there is no conceptual discrimination; one severs all deluded thoughts, expectations, and attachments.

This Bodhisattva is detached from all that exists, yet they also practice within the spheres of activity of all sentient beings, for the sake of teaching and transforming all sentient beings, for the sake of gathering all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), for the sake of upholding the True Dharma, and for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never interrupted.

As for the practice of the Tathāgata: regarding the pure essence of all phenomena, there is no conceptual differentiation. Because the essence of this *prajñā* is pure, one knows that the essence of *bodhi* is pure; because one knows the essence of *bodhi* is pure, one knows that the essence of sentient beings is pure; because one knows the essence of sentient beings is pure, one knows that the essence of all phenomena is pure; because one knows the essence of all phenomena is pure, one attains the knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) regarding the essence of all phenomena; and because one has attained the knowledge of reality, one teaches the nature of the *dharmadhātu* without conceptual differentiation in accordance with whatever matters have been heard.
“O Son of Heaven!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s pure eye of wisdom speaking truthfully regarding the prediction of enlightenment.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!”

The Bodhisattva contemplates the body through the application of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*): he knows that the past body has no limit; he knows that the future body has no destination; and he knows that the present body is like grass, trees, tiles, stones, walls, or fences—the body is likewise so. If one can thus contemplate the body and its activities, then the nature of this body is the stillness of deluded activity; both reflection and concurrent action are without arousal. This non-reflection and non-arising mastery is called "being free from self. Consciousness has no place of abiding as he practices the application of mindfulness of the body; furthermore, there is no dharma that can be practiced, nor is it a case of not practicing.

Knowing that all phenomena have no intrinsic nature, yet are not without nature; thus observing the body and practicing bodily conduct, observing the mind as an illusion and knowing the mind as an echo; knowing the mind as it truly is—when experiencing pleasure, one does not crave it; when experiencing pain, one does not suffer; when experiencing neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one does not lose right mindfulness; not clinging to ignorance, one remains detached from feelings and is not led astray by them. This is called the correct knowledge and vision of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).

If one can contemplate feelings and formations in this way, the mind has no objective engagement with any phenomena of feeling and does not dwell upon them; yet, one does not abandon these mental states, nor does one lose mindfulness of the bodhicitta or become separated from it. This is called the application of mindfulness to the contemplation of the activities of the mind.

Skillfully knowing the Dharma, knowing and seeing the Dharma, and practicing the Dharma; being without recollection or discursive thought, one enters the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) where there is no body, sensation, or mind. It is not by contemplating the characteristics of phenomena that one initiates views and practices to enter the nature of phenomena; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the practice of observing phenomena.

All these phenomena are the union of their essential natures; they are a collection of nothingness, like empty space. Regarding all things as they have been heard, one is without recollection or conceptualization; this is the natural application of mindfulness to dharmas.
"O Son of Heaven!
This is called explaining the bestowal of the prediction [of enlightenment] through the mindfulness of pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"
Furthermore, this bodhisattva attains mastery over the mind of omniscience; as instructed, they dwell correctly without attachment, distraction, or loss.
They remain mindful of their initial aspiration for all roots of goodness and practice with an immaculate mind.
Wherever they go, they are able to relinquish everything; they censure the mind that violates precepts yet do not rely on the precepts themselves, practicing patience without contention.
In the context of *sòng* (litigation/conflict), one does not give rise to anger toward sentient beings through body, speech, mind, or intention;
one does not initiate the diligence of the vehicles of the *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*; one does not dwell upon or contemplate any wholesome dharmas;

one does not rely on the successive stages of the various *dhyānas*; the mind has no place of activity and does not perceive the activities of various views; and one does not practice various dharmas, but enters into the One.
Regarding all phenomena, just as the various noble ones have no engagement with any objects of experience, although they may be near those who are not noble,
their bodily, verbal, and mental actions are never censured; nor do they seek wholesome dharmas out of mere faith, but practice alone without a companion,
desiring to transcend the world through the practice of vigor, in order to forever sever the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because their minds are free from afflictions and they do not break the precepts;
because they do not associate with those who practice evil, as they are free from flattery and their inner conduct is pure;
because they have no distracted speech, as their verbal karma is pure; and because they have no cravings, as they are content with their own wealth.
They are not driven by others because they do not live by wrong livelihood; they have no accumulations because they are content with whatever they obtain;
they have no expectations because they are free from the desires of the three realms; they are content because they are free from evil seeking;
they are tranquil because they understand that all phenomena are inherently tranquil; they manifest anger and delusion because they [have abandoned...].
Because he acts for the sake of the world; because he who is free from conceptual proliferation has severed all proliferations;
because he who is a non-returner has severed desire, hatred, and delusion; because he who delights in the Dharma has subdued pride; because he who is easy to understand has well-disciplined his mind;
because he who is a good guardian protects the aggregate of precepts; and because the one whose mind is well-liberated purifies the aggregate of wisdom.
Therefore, they do not abandon because they practice the noble lineages; they do not regress because they have brought the arousal of the bodhicitta to ultimate completion;
they have nothing to employ because all worldly activities [are transcended]; they are without dispute because they treat all sentient beings with equality;
they skillfully protect themselves because they protect others; and they discipline their own minds because they do not seek [external things].
Because he has transcended [the world], he guards pure precepts by being free from all expectations; because he extensively expounds the Dharma, he is without parsimony;
because he is a protector, he guards the minds of all sentient beings; because he has first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he gathers all wholesome dharmas;
because he is without divergent practice, he attains the single flavor in all dharmas.
The "unwavering" is so called because it severs all fluctuations; the "non-contemplation of lineage" is for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
the "equality toward sentient beings" is for the sake of gathering in all sentient beings; the "initial contemplation of emptiness" concerns all phenomena;

the "taming of all views" is for the sake of skillful teaching and transformation; and the "absence of conceptual practice" is for the sake of taming those who harbor conceptualizations regarding practice.
Because of sentient beings, one knows that those who have no vows have their aspirations fulfilled through excellent self-discipline;
because the All-Knowing One contemplates the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*); because those who practice virtue are never satisfied;
because those who contemplate the non-substantiality of things manifest what is not a thing as being a thing; because those who contemplate beyond thought are themselves tranquil; there is no...
The self is that which observes the transformation of sentient beings through non-self;

there is no practice that is not the Way, for it transforms all sentient beings so they may leave behind the fetters and proclivities; the mind of skillful means attains the ultimate through the cultivation of prajñā;
and being firmly established without departing, one ultimately does not realize or touch the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—this is the departure from the [limited] Way.
It is non-path because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); it is free from both practice and non-practice because all ordinary beings realize right practice;
it is neither adorned nor unadorned because there is no lack of aspiration for all phenomena;
it is one who does not praise self because it does not engage in frivolous discourse regarding others; it is the peerless wisdom because it is endowed with the Buddha-qualities; it is unborn.
"O Son of Heaven! Because the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) is the patience regarding the fact that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished,
this is called a bodhisattva attaining mastery."

“Devaputra! Wherever a bodhisattva is born, it is not because of ignorance that they are born, but because of knowledge that they are born. For this bodhisattva has grasped birth-and-death (saṃsāra) and attained mastery over it; thus, they also fully accomplish and perfect the Buddha-dharma.”

Yet this bodhisattva does not undergo the cycle of birth and death; by the power of their vows, they attain sovereign wisdom wherever they are born. This is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of sovereign wisdom.
A bodhisattva does not attain the wisdom of mastery by reaching a limit; rather, it is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the wisdom of mastery when they do not sever any roots of goodness.

A bodhisattva is called one with mastery of wisdom because they do not "acquire" various roots of goodness; they are called one with mastery of wisdom because they never feel satiety regarding those roots of goodness.

A bodhisattva is not called one with mastery by virtue of not being born within the three realms; rather, it is by intentionally taking birth within the three realms for the sake of transforming sentient beings that they are named one with mastery.

A bodhisattva does not attain the name "sovereign" merely by being free from his own fetters; rather, it is because he diligently cultivates vigor in order to sever the fetters and latent tendencies of all sentient beings that he is said to have attained sovereign wisdom.

A bodhisattva does not attain the name "sovereign" for the sake of his own body; rather, he is called sovereign because of [his concern] for all the sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings in their quest for tranquility.
A bodhisattva does not attain mastery by means of renunciation; rather, they are called "masterful" because they embrace and transform sentient beings.

A bodhisattva does not attain the name of "mastery" by severing their own greed, hatred, and delusion; rather, they are called "masterful" because they sever the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion in all sentient beings.
A bodhisattva does not attain mastery by personally realizing the dharma of cessation; rather, they attain mastery by causing all sentient beings to realize the dharma of cessation.

A bodhisattva does not attain mastery by personally severing outflows (*āsrava*); rather, a bodhisattva attains mastery by ensuring that the dharmas of severed outflows do not cease as their roots of goodness increase.

A bodhisattva does not attain mastery by realizing the three gates of liberation; rather, it is because a bodhisattva thoroughly understands the three gates of liberation that they are called "mastery.

A bodhisattva does not attain mastery by entering the quiescent extinction of the five aggregates; rather, it is for the sake of laying down the heavy burden of all sentient beings that they are called "mastery."
A bodhisattva does not attain mastery by means of extinguishing the six sense faculties; rather, it is called mastery because of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings.
A bodhisattva does not attain mastery by means of exhausting the factors of birth; a bodhisattva does not call mastery the severance of birth.

The Bodhisattva does not attain mastery by attaining a liberation that exceeds that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; rather, because he attains the fruit of liberation at the Bodhimanda and enjoys it for the sake of all sentient beings, it is called mastery.
When this "Chapter on Sovereignty" was thus expounded, thirty-two thousand devaputras within that assembly all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent! You have well explained the prediction of enlightenment for all bodhisattvas.”

Mañjuśrī! If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing such an account of a bodhisattva receiving a prediction, believe and understand it with single-minded resolve and do not give rise to alarm or fear, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall bestow upon them the true prediction of the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the Devaputra Ratnottama said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
“You should now expound upon the prediction of enlightenment. Mañjuśrī replied:

“Son of Heaven! When I say that I have received a prediction of enlightenment, it is because I possess this Dharma and there is one who has fully realized it; such a person, Son of Heaven, I say has received a prediction.
But now, I do not perceive even a single dharma, nor is there anything for me to fully realize. How, then, could I speak of receiving a prediction?”
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, not attain the fruit without having directed their understanding toward it?”
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not attain the fruits through the path of liberation.”
"Son of Heaven!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not preach the Dharma for those who have already attained liberation or the fruits [of the path].
The Son of Heaven said:
“Mañjuśrī! How do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not preach the Dharma by discriminating the intrinsic nature [of phenomena].

There is no arising and no ceasing; no cause and no condition; no going and no coming; neither the existence of sentient beings nor the non-existence of sentient beings; neither defilement nor purity; neither birth-and-death nor nirvana. Devaputra!”
"The Buddha-Bhagavāns teach the Dharma in this way.
The devaputra asked Mañjuśrī,
"If the Buddha-Bhagavāns do not teach the Dharma for the sake of nirvāṇa, for what reason is it said that a Buddha has appeared in the world?"
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Twenty-Six;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Twenty-Seven.
Translated by the Liang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Mandaraka.
In the eighth assembly, "The Non-differentiation of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm," Part Two, Mañjuśrī said:
"O Son of Heaven!
Because he has fully awakened to the essential nature of the view of a self-body, O Devaputra, it is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

He manifests the essential nature of ignorance and craving, which is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world; because he has fully awakened to the essential nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, it is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
"O Son of Heaven!
To manifest the equality of the essential nature of perversion is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
O Son of Heaven!"
Because he has fully awakened to the essential nature of all views, it is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world,
O Son of Heaven!
To demonstrate the essential nature of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and the realm of phenomena is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
"O Son of Heaven!

When a Buddha appears in the world, the fact that all phenomena are without arising is what is called 'expounding the dharma of non-arising. This dharma of non-arising is entirely devoid of both birth-and-death and nirvana."
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! You should preach for the sake of sentient beings the dharma that adorns the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
Why is this? Mañjuśrī! The appearance of the Buddhas in the world does not bring about any increase.
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!
One who knows gratitude and repays kindness. The Devaputra said:
"One who has performed a service should know how to repay that kindness. Mañjuśrī said, "O Devaputra!"
"You wish to cause the Tathāgata to perform some action.
The devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"The Tathāgata has nothing that is performed.
All Buddha-Tathāgatas have reached the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); in the path of the unconditioned, there is nothing that is performed. Mañjuśrī said:
“Devaputra! You who have realized the unconditioned neither repay a debt of gratitude nor fail to repay it.
The Devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! This Dharma should not be taught to those who have newly resolved their minds. Why is this?
"If one hears this Dharma and gives rise to alarm and fear,
they will immediately regress. Mañjuśrī said,
"O Devaputra!..."
"If there is a bodhisattva who, having first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, becomes startled, fearful, and regresses, that person dwells in regression.
The devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"For what reason do you say this? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Son of Heaven!"
If a bodhisattva, having first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, is startled by or fears the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they will then regress.
If, however, they are stingy, violate the precepts, harbor anger, succumb to indolence, distraction, or delusion, they will abide in non-retrogression.
The devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī! How does one abide?"
Mañjuśrī said, “Devaputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment and dwells securely within the equality of the dharmadhātu, this is called a ‘well-established bodhisattva who has first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment’; this is what is meant by ‘dwelling.’”
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! To what extent is a bodhisattva said to have 'first resolved' their mind [on awakening]?"
Mañjuśrī said, "Devaputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment and practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, understanding that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation— this is called the initial resolution of a bodhisattva."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! In what way is a bodhisattva called one who has long practiced?”
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! All ordinary beings are called 'those who have practiced for a long time,' because within saṃsāra they do not know its beginning."
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, why is a bodhisattva called one who has long practiced?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who practices amidst passion and attachment for the sake of transforming those sentient beings who are attached, yet does not dwell together with that passion and attachment, this is called a bodhisattva who has long practiced."
He practices in the midst of anger, yet does not dwell with anger, for the sake of transforming all sentient beings who are prone to anger;
he also practices in the midst of delusion, yet does not dwell with delusion, for the sake of transforming all sentient beings who are prone to delusion;

he also practices in the midst of the three poisons in equal measure, yet does not dwell with any fetters whatsoever, for the sake of transforming all sentient beings whose natures are equally divided among the three poisons.
"O Son of Heaven!

If there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, contemplates all marks yet does not discriminate the essential nature or characteristics of the dharma-realm, such a one is called a bodhisattva who has long practiced."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī, in what way is a bodhisattva called ‘irreversible’?”
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates all phenomena as being neither calamitous nor non-calamitous, and contemplates the essential nature of the dharma-realm as being neither calamitous nor non-calamitous, this is called the non-retrogression of a bodhisattva."
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
If there is a bodhisattva who both regresses and does not regress, this is called the non-regression of a bodhisattva. Why is this so?
"Regressing" means retreating from the various wholesome states of the desire realm.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
A bodhisattva regresses because of lack of knowledge and lack of understanding; because of knowledge and understanding, there is no contention, which is called non-regression.
Why is this? Because one understands the dharma-nature of all phenomena.
Since I have been able to understand the dharma-nature of all phenomena and shall no longer regress, this is called "non-retrogression."

To have no doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma and not rely on the words of others; to transcend the duality of "is" and "is not"; to possess pure initial resolve, free from envy and unshakable; to have wisdom that illuminates all phenomena and attains mastery over them; and to thoroughly comprehend the Buddha-dharma—this is called the non-retrogression of a bodhisattva.
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! In what sense is a bodhisattva called 'one who has but one more birth'?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!

If a bodhisattva knows that all births are in fact non-birth, and likewise knows the birth and death of all sentient beings, he is able to skillfully preach the Dharma among those births to teach and transform sentient beings. He takes no grasping toward the places where beings are born, yet he takes up those births while remaining free from the grasping for birth and death. He neither goes nor comes, neither ascends nor descends, because all dharmas are entirely equal."

They also know that through the conjunction and growth of causes and conditions, the body, speech, mind, and intentions of all sentient beings are entirely equal; that all sentient beings have no fixed realm, yet abide in the realm of the Buddha and enter the Dharma-realm.

Because the dharma-realm is equal, one equally understands the minds of sentient beings; skillfully understanding and knowing the proper time, one reaches the site of enlightenment—this is called "one life," O Son of Heaven!
"This is what is called a 'Bodhisattva of one birth'.
At that time, the Devaputra Ratnottama asked the youth Mañjuśrī,
"What is meant by a Bodhisattva who is 'unborn,' yet attains mastery over all things?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Son of Heaven!
If there is a bodhisattva who understands that karmic actions are not due to arrogance, this bodhisattva does not arise, and yet attains mastery over all things."
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
When a bodhisattva is able to relinquish all that they possess for the sake of the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) and never regresses, this is called “non-arising.
If they dwell without being joined with the fetters of envy and jealousy, this is called “attaining mastery over all things.”
If there is a bodhisattva who fully accomplishes the practice of the rules of dignified conduct and all meritorious precepts, this is called "non-arising";
dwelling without transgressing the precepts, this is called "attaining mastery over all."
The mind does not abandon or turn its back on any sentient being; this is called "non-arising.
It does not dwell together with any ignorance, anger, or fetters; this is called "attaining mastery over all."
To remain firm and unshakable in all roots of goodness is called "non-arising";
to arouse diligent effort and courageous resolve within those roots of goodness is called "attaining mastery over all."
To enter into various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) is called non-arising;
not to relish the bliss of meditation is called attaining mastery over all things.
To apply diligent effort in seeking the wisdom of *prajñā* and to study without weariness is called non-arising.
To dwell without cohabiting with delusion is called attaining mastery over all things.
To be without anger, vexation, or contention is called non-arising;
to dwell without cohabiting with anger, vexation, or any disputes is called attaining mastery over all things.
If one speaks according to reality, this is called non-arising;
if one abides according to reality, this is called attaining mastery.
If there is inner tranquility, this is called non-arising.
If one is not defiled by external objects, this is called attaining mastery.
If one can bring the mind of omniscience to ultimate fulfillment, this is called non-arising;
if one does not seek the Lesser Vehicle, this is called attaining mastery.
To realize the fruits of all karmic actions is called non-arising;
to subdue the activities of Māra is called attaining mastery.
To attain the light of the world is called non-arising.
To be unstained by worldly dharmas is called attaining mastery;
not to oppose that in which one dwells is called non-arising;
not to fall into what is done is called attaining mastery.
If one is free from the power of all forms of pride and negligence, this is called "non-arising";
if one’s wisdom-consciousness achieves noble bliss, this is called "attaining mastery.
Not retreating from one's vows is called "non-arising."
The vow to transcend the world is called attaining mastery.
To follow the process of dependent origination is called non-arising;
not to cling to phenomena of dependent origination is called attaining mastery.
If one contemplates all things as empty through the wisdom of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), this is called non-arising;
to be endowed with all roots of goodness is called attaining mastery.
If one initiates activity through skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and cultivating diligent progress, this is called non-arising.
If one can abide securely in all dharmas of liberation, it is called attaining mastery.
If one is not defiled by any dharma, it is called non-arising.
If one severs all views and preaches the Dharma, it is called attaining mastery.
If, through correct contemplation, one does not perceive any phenomena, this is called non-arising;
if one attains power yet does not realize any phenomena, this is called attaining mastery.
If one contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is empty, this is called non-arising.
If one does not abandon all sentient beings, this is called attaining mastery.
If one does not dwell within the triple world, this is called non-arising;
if, for the sake of sentient beings, one does not enter nirvana, this is called attaining mastery.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
If there is speech, it is speech of agitation, speech of false conceptualization, speech of attachment, and it involves origination."
"O Son of Heaven!

Within all dharmas there is no speech; they do not proceed nor do they move, being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One neither abandons sentient beings nor enters parinirvāṇa, for there is nothing to be spoken."
"O Son of Heaven!
If there were neither speech nor letters, then there would be nothing to be expressed; if they are employed, then there is the initiation of speech and letters.
O Son of Heaven!"

For this reason, the practice of a bodhisattva cannot be described through function nor can it be conceived through action; this is called the mind of loving-kindness, this is called non-killing, and among all the noble ones, one attains the name of mastery.
When he had spoken this Dharma, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
He skillfully expounded for the bodhisattvas the mastery over non-arising.
Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva practices such dharmas with mastery and without obstruction, that bodhisattva will swiftly receive from all Buddhas the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Upon hearing this Dharma, five hundred bodhisattvas among the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately bestowed upon them the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, each for a distinct buddha-field and each with a specific name, such as "Tathāgata So-and-so."
At that time, there was among the assembly a son of heaven who thought to himself:
"When will this noble son of heaven, Ratnottama, attain the unsurpassed path?
What shall be the name of the Buddha?"
"What is this Buddha-field like?
Then, by the power of the Buddha, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"At what time will this Bodhisattva Ratnottama attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path?
What will his Buddha-field be like?
And after he has attained the path, what will that Buddha be named?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
