“This Devaputra Ratnaśikhin shall, after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path, and be known as the Tathāgata Ratnavyūha.”
To the east of here, there is a buddha-field named Ratnavyūha, and its eon is named Ratnāgama.

Ānanda! This buddha-field of Ratnavyūha is prosperous, joyful, and most delightful; it abounds in wealth and treasures and is populated by many people. It is free from all calamities and has no evil realms.

Ānanda! In this buddha-field, there are no tiles, stones, sand, soil, thorns, mountain valleys, or mounds; the ground is as level as the palm of a hand, composed of the Three Jewels—Jāmbūnada gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal—which are interspersed with one another and are most delightful, covered above by a net of gold.

Ānanda! Just as the palaces, gardens, ponds, and garments of the gods in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations are abundant, and they move about and travel back and forth, so too are the people of this Jewel-Adorned Buddha-field.

In that land, there are no names for the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; there are only bodhisattvas who enjoy various dharma-pleasures, enter various meditative concentrations as adornments, and amuse themselves with various supernormal powers. There is no other pleasure except for the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of the preliminary stages; therefore, the world is named "Adorned with Jewels."
That Buddha’s lifespan was six hundred and sixty billion years.
There were six hundred and sixty billion monastic bodhisattvas, and the lay bodhisattvas were immeasurable and boundless.

When that Tathāgata, Adornment, preached the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he ascended into the void to a height of eight billion *tāla* trees and sat cross-legged, filling a thousand lands. He emitted a thousand rays of light that illuminated those buddha-fields, raining down celestial flowers, celestial incense, and powdered incense. There were hundreds of thousands of varieties of celestial music, and the sound of his preaching the Dharma was heard throughout the buddha-fields as he expounded the Dharma of the *Dhāraṇī* of the Lord of the Inexhaustible.
What is the Dharma of the *Akṣayamati-dhāraṇī*?
It is because it is the sovereign of the tranquility of all dharmas.
It manifests the perception of the tranquility of body and mind, for it is the sovereign that contemplates all dharmas.
He manifests discernment regarding all phenomena, for he is the master of the skillful contemplation of all dharmas.
He manifests the tranquility of all phenomena, for he is the master of the skillful practice of all dharmas.
It manifests the radiant illumination of all conditioned phenomena, for it is the sovereign of equality illuminated by the light of wisdom regarding all dharmas.
It manifests that all dharmas neither increase nor decrease, for it is the sovereign of certainty regarding all dharmas.
It manifests the increase of all phenomena, for it is the master of wisdom regarding all phenomena.
It manifests that all phenomena are free from contention, for it is the master of skillful observation regarding all phenomena.
It demonstrates that all phenomena are without anger, for all phenomena have right mindfulness as their master.
It demonstrates that all phenomena do not lose mindfulness, for all phenomena have guidance as their master.
It reveals the meaning of the characteristics of all phenomena, for it is the master of the wisdom that discriminates all phenomena.
It reveals the pure intention of all phenomena, for it is the master of the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena.
It reveals that all phenomena sever the paths of all views, for it is the master of the signlessness of all phenomena.
It reveals that all phenomena are quiescent, for it is the master of the wishlessness of all phenomena.
It reveals that all phenomena sever the various paths, because all phenomena lack a master of action.
It reveals that all phenomena are free from an agent, because all phenomena lack a master of emergence.
It demonstrates that all phenomena have no emergence, for it is the master of the non-arising of all phenomena.
It demonstrates that all phenomena are inexhaustible, for it is the master of the detachment from desire of all phenomena.
It demonstrates that all phenomena are without error, because all phenomena have no dual master.
It demonstrates the present-knowledge of all phenomena, because all phenomena have no dual master.
It reveals that all phenomena are free from duality, because all phenomena lack a master;
it reveals that all phenomena are immovable, because all phenomena lack a sentient being as a master.
It reveals the equality of all phenomena and sentient beings, for it is the master of the quiescence of all phenomena.
It reveals that all phenomena are unchanging, for no phenomenon can be grasped as a master.
It demonstrates that all phenomena are without activity, because all phenomena lack a presiding master.
It demonstrates that all phenomena are free from location, because all phenomena lack a fixed master.
It demonstrates mastery over all phenomena, because all phenomena arise from causes and conditions.
It demonstrates transcendence beyond all phenomena, because it is the heroic sovereign of all phenomena.
It demonstrates that all phenomena do not emerge, because all phenomena have no master;
it demonstrates that all phenomena are unarisen, because all phenomena are like a master.
It reveals that all phenomena are without non-suchness, because all phenomena have the Suchness of the Primordial Jewel Lord as their beginning.
It reveals that all phenomena are indestructible, because all phenomena have the Dharma-nature Lord as their master.
He manifests that all phenomena are of one flavor, for he is the master of all phenomena as they truly are.
He manifests that all phenomena are equal throughout the three periods of time, for he is the master of the ineffability of all phenomena.
It demonstrates non-attachment to the verbal discourse concerning all phenomena, for it is the master of meditative concentration regarding all phenomena.
It demonstrates the quiescence of all phenomena, for it is the master of the *dharmatā* of all phenomena.
It reveals that all phenomena are devoid of a person, for all phenomena have awakening as their master.
It reveals that all phenomena are equal, for all phenomena have the vow as their master.

Ānanda! While the Tathāgata Ratnavyūha remains seated in the air and has not yet arisen, this *Dhāraṇī* of the Lord of the Inexhaustible, the Mistress of Dhāraṇīs, is being extensively expounded for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
"In that land, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have all attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"It is truly marvelous!
If all Tathāgatas are spontaneously effortless, they attain unimpeded wisdom regarding the phenomena of the past, future, and present.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! I shall now explain for you how all Tathāgatas, being spontaneous and effortless, attain unimpeded wisdom regarding the phenomena of the past, future, and present.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Devaputra Ratnaśikhin: "Devaputra!
You have attained great benefit."
“The Tathāgata has prophesied for you the unsurpassed path.
The devaputra said: “Venerable Ānanda!
There is no dharma whatsoever that is not explained as receiving the prediction. Why is this?
Form is not the bodhisattva; it is not by explaining form that one gives the prediction.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the bodhisattva; it is not by way of designating consciousness that one speaks of the bodhisattva.
The earth element is not the bodhisattva; it is not by way of designating the earth element that one speaks of the bodhisattva.
Likewise, the water, fire, and wind elements are not the bodhisattva; it is not by way of designating the wind element that one speaks of the bodhisattva.
The eye is not the bodhisattva; it is not by speaking of the eye that one gives a prediction.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not the bodhisattva; it is not by speaking of the mind that one gives a prediction.
Name-and-form is not the bodhisattva; it is not by speaking of name-and-form that one gives a prediction.
The past, future, and present are not the bodhisattva; it is not a prediction concerning the equality of the three times.
Because seeing is not the bodhisattva, it is not a prediction concerning seeing.
Arising and ceasing are not the Bodhisattva; nor is it a teaching that records arising and ceasing. Venerable Ānanda!
That which is called "Bodhisattva" is merely a provisional name; it is a word for tranquility.
If a phenomenon were ultimately quiescent, there would be no prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). Venerable Ānanda!
One who receives a prediction encompasses all phenomena that are expressed through speech.
Venerable Ānanda!
There is no dharma whatsoever that a bodhisattva can grasp—whether internal or external, wholesome or unwholesome, conditioned or unconditioned—and yet still receive a prediction of enlightenment.

Venerable Ānanda, regarding the Bodhisattva’s prediction (vyākaraṇa): that all dharmas have no point of attachment is called the prediction; that one does not grasp at any dharma is called the prediction; that all dharmas have no location is called the prediction; that all dharmas have no abode is called the prediction; that all dharmas have no emergence is called the prediction; and that all dharmas are free from false conceptualization is called the prediction.
"Venerable Ānanda! Such is the manner in which a bodhisattva receives this prediction.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Devaputra Ratnaśikha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, O Devaputra!
Because the Bodhisattva has thoroughly realized all these dharmas, he is thus able to speak of his prediction of enlightenment.”
"Just as the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have prophesied regarding the path to unsurpassed bodhi.
When this Dharma was being spoken, Māra Pāpīyān, together with his retinue, each riding their respective mounts, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he stood to one side and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason do you bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas, yet not upon śrāvakas?"
When Pāpīyān had finished his question, the Buddha replied: “Pāpīyān!
All the devas and humans throughout the lands of the trichiliocosm know this bodhisattva well; for this reason, I bestow upon him the prediction of enlightenment.”
Śrāvakas are not recognized by humans or devas; therefore, they are not granted the prediction (vyākaraṇa) that is spoken for bodhisattvas.
Because many sentient beings have resolved their minds toward bodhi, for this reason the prediction of the bodhisattvas is spoken.
"Because it was said that a bodhisattva who receives a prediction as a śrāvaka would fall back, for this reason it was not spoken.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī said to Pāpīyas:
"For what reason have you come to this assembly now?"
Pāpīyān replied: "Mañjuśrī!
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has bestowed the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment upon the Devaputra Ratnaśikhi:
"You shall become a Buddha, named Ratnavyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He did not utter a prediction for the śrāvakas.
From my palaces, towers, railings, jewel trees, groves, and pleasure grounds, as they touched one another, such sounds issued forth, saying:
"I have heard this voice: 'The Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has bestowed the prediction of supreme enlightenment upon the Devaputra Ratnottama.
Furthermore, I hear this sound: 'Pāpīyān!'"
"Now go to where the assembly is, and do not allow any other bodhisattvas who have received their prediction to be born in your palace.
Mañjuśrī said to Pāpīyas, "Do you not rejoice now that the predictions for the bodhisattvas have been proclaimed?"
Māra said: "Mañjuśrī! I truly do not rejoice."
To preach the prediction of Arhatship for all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa causes me no grief or affliction;
yet to preach the prediction of the unsurpassed path for even a single Bodhisattva causes my grief and affliction to be beyond description.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
When the prediction of the unsurpassed path for a bodhisattva is proclaimed, my various māra palaces become shrouded in darkness and lose their brilliance.
Yet this bodhisattva, by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, delivers immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings and others, causing them to emerge from the triple world. Mañjuśrī!
"Because of this matter, I am experiencing various sorrows and afflictions. Mañjuśrī said, "Pāpīyan!"
Return to your dwelling.
You lack the power or strength to obstruct or hinder those who are ultimately directed toward the path of enlightenment and who practice the perfection of wisdom endowed with skillful means.
"Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have severed the bonds of Māra and accomplished ultimate practice; they skillfully know the expedient means and practice the prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, by the Buddha's spiritual power, he caused Māra Pāpīyān to question Mañjuśrī:
“How does a bodhisattva practice ultimate conduct and, being well-versed in skillful means,
practice the perfection of wisdom? Mañjuśrī replied, “Pāpīyan!
If a bodhisattva is free from all practices of limited scope, this is called a bodhisattva accomplishing ultimate practice.
If, upon seeing all fetters and the works of Māra, they are able to bring benefit to the unsurpassed path, this is called a bodhisattva who skillfully knows expedient means.
To act without being conjoined with any of the fetters (saṃyojana) is called a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, Pāpīyan!
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of ultimately delivering all sentient beings, adorns himself with the great adornments, this is called the ultimate mental practice of a bodhisattva.
If one gathers all sentient beings through the four means of integration, this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of expedient means.
If one ultimately contemplates that the essential nature of all sentient beings is quiescent extinction, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Pāpīyān!

If there is a bodhisattva who relinquishes all internal and external things that can be given, and whose mind of awakening is ultimately perfected, this is called the ultimate mental practice of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of a recipient for the sake of all sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding both the beggar and the recipient, knows them as they truly are and practices the conduct of equality from the very beginning, this is called a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñā-pāramitā*.

Furthermore, Pāpīyan, if there is a bodhisattva who, regarding all wholesome dharmas, never regresses from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the end, this is called the bodhisattva’s ultimate practice of the mind of awakening.
If there is a bodhisattva who, without being coerced by others, is able to relinquish self-interest, this is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of means (*upāya*).
When a bodhisattva contemplates the meaning and does not dwell on the words, this is called a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Pāpīyan!
If one sees a beggar and does not turn away from them, this is called the ultimate mental conduct of a bodhisattva.
If there is a bodhisattva who gathers all roots of goodness and aspires for omniscience, this is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of means.
“A Bodhisattva who thoroughly knows the essential nature of all phenomena is said to be practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, the Devaputra Ratnottama said to Mañjuśrī, “The retinues and mounts of this Māra Pāpīyān could be brought inside his belly by means of supernatural power; or perhaps he might create obstacles for those sons and daughters of good family who are oriented toward the Mahāyāna.”
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! It is not as you say—that the internal Māra Pāpīyān is placed within the belly of a bodhisattva."
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

You who uphold the foremost bliss of the Buddha’s marks and adornments shall cause Māra Pāpīyas to sit upon the lion throne; by the power of the Buddha, the Buddha shall expound the Dharma with his eloquence.
At that time, having heard these words, Pāpīyān wished to conceal his body and leave the assembly, but he was unable to do so because he was sustained by Mañjuśrī.

Then, after Mañjuśrī had formed this thought, the Māra Pāpīyān assumed the physical marks of a Buddha and sat upon the lion throne; at that moment, the entire great assembly perceived and recognized him as the Māra Pāpīyān.
Mañjuśrī spoke again: "Pāpīyān!
Have you now attained the path of all the Tathāgatas?"
"How can one become a Buddha and sit upon a lion throne?
Because he was sustained by the power of Mañjuśrī, Māra Pāpīyān said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
Even the World-Honored One did not attain bodhi; how much less could I attain it?
Why is this? Bodhi is the mark of repaying kindness; it is not attained by the departure from desire, nor is it attained by turning toward liberation.
Furthermore, bodhi is the attainment of the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*);
because it attains the characteristic of the unconditioned, the realization of the characteristic of emptiness is called bodhi, not because one awakens to emptiness by means of emptiness.
To realize the markless mark is called bodhi; it is not by means of a markless [subject] realizing a markless mark.
To realize the wishless mark is called bodhi; it is not by means of a wishless mark realizing a wishless mark.
To awaken to the essential nature of the dharma-realm is called bodhi; it is not because one awakens to the essential nature by means of the essential nature.
To awaken to suchness as being free from the marks of conceptual discrimination is called bodhi; it is not because one awakens to suchness by means of suchness.
Awakened awareness abides in the beginning of reality as it is; therefore, it is called bodhi. It is not that one abides in the beginning of reality as it is by means of awakened awareness.
Awakening is the absence of self, the absence of sentient beings, the absence of life, and the absence of persons; its essential nature is bodhi, because there is no knower.

Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing such an exposition of the characteristics of bodhi, is able to remain without any conceptual discrimination regarding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, they are then called a Buddha.
When the Buddha, through his eloquence, preached this Dharma, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī:
"It is unprecedented!

"Because you sustain him with your power, Māra Pāpīyān has manifested in the form of the Tathāgata, endowed with all the physical marks, sitting upon a lion throne, and preaching this profound Dharma. Mañjuśrī said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
All grasses, trees, and forests are mindless, yet they can manifest the physical marks of a Tathāgata in their entirety and preach the Dharma.
I can also cause the Venerable Śāriputra to become the body of a Tathāgata, endowed with all the physical marks, and to preach the Dharma with the eloquence of a Buddha.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:

"I should now vanish from within this assembly; perhaps Mañjuśrī will cause me to manifest the body of a Tathāgata, complete with all its physical marks, thereby mocking me by making a śrāvaka appear in the likeness of the World-Honored One."
Because Mañjuśrī sustained him through his supernatural power, Śāriputra could not remain hidden.

Then, knowing what the venerable Śāriputra was thinking in his mind, Mañjuśrī transformed the venerable Śāriputra into the body of a Tathāgata, complete with all the physical marks, seated upon a lion throne; the entire assembly likewise saw and recognized this.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"You may speak with Māra Pāpīyān just as you would speak with the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked in this way:
"Pāpīyan! What is the essential nature of bodhi?"
Pāpīyān replied: “To realize that all phenomena are equal is the essential nature of bodhi.
To realize these two dharmas is the essential nature of bodhi.”
The nature of bodhi is the contemplation of omniscience; it is not a lack of nature.

It is neither practice nor non-practice, having forever severed all practices and non-practices; it is neither the path nor the non-path—this is called the bodhi of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Pāpīyān asked: "Venerable Śāriputra!
Where do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, abide?"
Śāriputra said: “One dwells in the equality of saṃsāra;

one dwells unmoving in nirvāṇa; one dwells in the true nature of all views; one dwells in the fetters and afflictions of all sentient beings, and likewise dwells in the root of all dharmas; one dwells in the two dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned—dwelling in non-dwelling, because there is no dwelling.”
"Pāpīyān! Thus do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, abide.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pāpīyān:
"Where should one seek enlightenment?
Pāpīyān replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!..."

One seeks bodhi from the root of the view of a self; one seeks bodhi from ignorance, existence, and craving; one seeks bodhi from the arising of perverted views and fetters; one seeks bodhi from obstacles and obscurations.
Śāriputra said: “Pāpīyan! For what reason and by what causes do you speak thus?”
Pāpīyān replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
To realize and know such dharmas as they truly are is called bodhi."
When this Dharma was being taught, eight hundred bhikṣus completely severed all outflows and attained the outflow-free mind.
Because the sons of the gods had faith in Śāriputra and Māra Pāpīyān, thirty-two thousand sons of the gods resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In order to subdue the various devaputras, the youth Mañjuśrī caused Māra Pāpīyas and the Venerable Śāriputra to manifest the body of a Tathāgata, complete with all its physical marks.
Mañjuśrī withdrew his supernormal powers, and the bodies of the Venerable Śāriputra and Māra Pāpīyān returned to their original forms.

At that time, a thousand bodhisattvas emerged from the four directions, traveling through the air from various buddha-fields to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Tathāgata to the right, and having stood to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
Having heard this *Dharmadhātuprakṛtyasambhedanirdeśa-sūtra*, we have come here to protect the True Dharma.
World-Honored One!
We shall uphold and protect this sutra, recite it until we have mastered it, explain it extensively for others, and thereby embrace the True Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
from where have these bodhisattvas come?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These bodhisattvas have each gathered from their respective buddha-fields; all these bodhisattvas were originally taught by the youth Mañjuśrī, who constantly instructed and transformed them by preaching this *Dharmadhātusvabhāvanirvikalpaprakāśana-sūtra*."

These bodhisattvas have come here because they know how to repay the kindness of this sutra; furthermore, they have come to see the Tathāgata, pay him homage, and circumambulate him, and also because they wish to make offerings to and prostrate before the youth Mañjuśrī, and out of their aspiration to protect this sutra.
Ānanda! After my parinirvāṇa, these bodhisattvas shall widely disseminate and protect this true Dharma here in Jambudvīpa. Ānanda!
"These bodhisattvas, under hundreds of thousands of buddhas, have maintained courageous resolve to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
At that time, among the assembly were Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and various celestial kings, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

"Whosoever among us, whether here or there, are protectors and upholders of the Dharma—those virtuous men, sons, and daughters—we shall guard and provide for them, ensuring that they remain free from suffering and affliction."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting Heavenly Kings, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

That you are able to courageously protect these good men who cherish and uphold the True Dharma is itself an offering to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as a protection of the True Dharma."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"You shall uphold this sutra and, in the future age of the final dharma, cause it to be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa."
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
When the calamity of fire arises, this space neither sustains anything nor is it burned.”
“World-Honored One!
Just as the nature of space is such, so too are all dharmas; these dharmas are neither born nor extinguished.
If a dharma is without birth and without extinction, it is also without anything to be upheld.”
"Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena has nothing to be grasped or maintained, it is like the intrinsic nature of reality itself;
the grasping and maintaining of all phenomena is likewise so.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will uphold this sutra for the sake of planting roots of goodness in good sons and good daughters.
If those who honor the Dharma desire and delight in this sutra, World-Honored One!”

In this way, by upholding this sutra, one will subdue all enemies such as pride and ill-will, so that no obstacles can arise; thus, in future ages, it shall be widely circulated and propagated throughout this Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from his body; this light shone everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm, the Buddha-world, turning it all the color of gold.
Then the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"The radiance of the Tathāgata shines universally upon all things, and this sutra is likewise."
"Those whose mental activities are unimpeded shall reach the ultimate realization of the Buddha-dharma; these sons and daughters of good family shall hold this sutra in their hands.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda!"
If you uphold this sutra, recite it until you have mastered it, and explain it extensively for others, Ānanda,
you will thereby be making offerings to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of this sutra?”
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You should receive and uphold this sutra; its name is 'The Non-differentiation of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm,' it is also named 'The Questions of the Devaputra Ratnaśikhi,' and it is also named 'The Discourse of the Youth Mañjuśrī. Uphold it well."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the youth Mañjuśrī, the Devaputra Ratnajyotis, and all the bodhisattvas who had come from various buddha-fields, as well as the devas, nāgas, asuras, and the people of the world, were all greatly rejoiced; they received it upon their heads and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-seven;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
9. The Ninth Assembly on the Ten Dharmas of the Mahāyāna.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus who were all great arhats, and with immeasurable, boundless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja. He rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee upon the lotus pedestal. Approaching the Tathāgata, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“World-Honored One, how does a bhikṣu who practices the Mahāyāna and dwells in the Mahāyāna practice the Mahāyāna? How does he dwell in the Mahāyāna?”
"For what reason is this Great Vehicle called the 'Great Vehicle'?
Furthermore, for what reason is it said to be 'abiding in the Great Vehicle'?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Vimalaratnacandraprabha! O noble son!”
"You have asked well about this profound meaning.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha heard the Buddha’s permission, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We receive the holy teaching upon our heads.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he is one who practices the Mahāyāna and dwells in the Mahāyāna. What are these ten?

First, accomplishment in faith; second, accomplishment in practice; third, accomplishment in nature; fourth, delighting in the bodhicitta; fifth, delighting in the Dharma; sixth, contemplating the practice of the true Dharma; seventh, practicing the Dharma and being cautious regarding the Dharma; eighth, abandoning pride and great arrogance; ninth, skillfully understanding the Tathāgata’s secret teachings; tenth, the mind having no desire for the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva achieve the perfection of faith?”
The Buddha said:

"Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices non-deceptive conduct, he attains supple conduct; that bodhisattva has faith in the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Tathāgatas, the Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones."
One has faith that all Tathāgatas, within a single thought-moment, expound the events of the three periods of time;
one has faith that the Tathāgatagarbha is neither aging nor dying, immeasurable and boundless, neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor discontinuous;

and one has faith in the Buddhas' reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the all-knowledge (sarvajñā) and the power of the all-knowing one (sarvajña-jñātṛ), the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
One has faith in the Tathāgatas’ mark of the invisible crown of the head;
one has faith that the bodies of all Tathāgatas are adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks and possess a halo;
and one has faith in what is spoken by Śrāvakas, what is spoken by Pratyekabuddhas, and what is spoken by Bodhisattvas, as well as in all those who speak virtuous words.
He has faith in this world and the world beyond;
he has faith that those who practice rightly abide in right practice, whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas;
and he has faith in the fruits of wholesome karma, which are exceedingly delightful, subtle, and supreme—namely, those of the gods and their lords, or of humans and their lords.
He believes that the fruits of unwholesome karma are undesirable, bringing immeasurable suffering and affliction, whether in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, or as animals.
Having gained such faith, that bodhisattva becomes free from three things:
first, doubt; second, delusion; and third, indecisiveness.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such faith, it is called the ‘accomplishment of faith.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
“Faith is the supreme vehicle; those with faith are the children of the Buddha.
Therefore, the wise should always draw near to faith.
Faith is the greatest in the world; those with faith never suffer from lack.”
Therefore, the wise should always draw near to those who have faith.
If one lacks faith, no wholesome qualities (*śukladharma*) will arise,
just as a burnt seed cannot produce roots, sprouts, and the like.
“Good son! What is the accomplishment of the practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? Good son!”
Because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva has accomplished their practice, they shave off their hair and beard, don the robes of the True Dharma, and leave the home life for homelessness.
Having gone forth, they cultivate and study the practices of the Bodhisattva precepts, the practices of the Śrāvaka precepts, and the practices of the Pratyekabuddha precepts.
Having trained as a bodhisattva in this way, all unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind is completely extinguished.
What is called unwholesome karma of the body?

It refers to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; using tiles, stones, knives, or staves to deceive or strike others, injuring their hands or feet, and committing acts of bullying whether coming or going.
Good son, such as these are called bodily unwholesome karma. Good son,
what is called verbal unwholesome karma?

What are called false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words—unwholesome modes of expression; slandering the profound sūtras of the true Dharma; and speaking of the faults and shortcomings of one's preceptors, ācāryas, and others who abide in the true Dharma—all such things as these are termed unwholesome verbal karma.
"Good son! What is called unwholesome mental karma? It refers to envy, stinginess, and wrong views; excessive jealousy and avarice;

delighting in profit, delighting in praise, and delighting in intimacy; pride regarding one's family, pride regarding one's physical appearance; pride in being young and strong, pride in being free from illness, pride in longevity, pride in extensive learning, and pride in spiritual practice; thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of malice, and thoughts of ill-will; as well as thoughts of one’s country, thoughts of clothing and other such things; attachment to dwellings, vehicles, and bedding; attachment to drink and food, as well as attachment to children, oxen for plowing, farming, and various activities; and anxiety over slaves, servants, laborers, grain, silk, storehouses, and all manner of wealth."
Once that bodhisattva has become thus attached, if he loses even a single one of the various matters previously described, his mind will give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
That bodhisattva, with a mind moistened by craving, thereby gives rise to the seed of the sprout of future existence.
Son of good family!
Briefly stated, mental karma is like a revolving wheel; such is called unwholesome mental karma.

That bodhisattva, having set aside physical and other such actions, conceives the notion of a preceptor toward his preceptor, the notion of a preceptor toward his ācārya, and maintains respectful conduct toward others, whether they be old or young.
That bodhisattva, dwelling in solitude, reflects thus:

"I ought not to act in such a way—for I have already given rise to the mind to deliver all sentient beings, to rescue all sentient beings, and to establish all sentient beings within the practice of right concentration."
That bodhisattva reflects thus:
"At present, my own self has not disciplined its faculties, has not applied itself diligently to practice, has not guarded its faculties, and has not tamed its faculties."
That bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Now that I have practiced in this way, as soon as these sentient beings see me, their minds are immediately tamed and they comply with my teaching; all Buddhas rejoice, and all devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and others likewise rejoice."
"Good son! Such practices as these are called the 'shame' (hrī) of a bodhisattva.
That bodhisattva reflects in this way:"

"May neither monastics nor laypeople reproach me for my bodily, verbal, or mental actions, or for my various modes of conduct—namely, by accusing me of violating my ethical discipline, or of engaging in wrong views, or of engaging in improper conduct, or of practicing a wrong livelihood."
Having cultivated such a sense of shame, that bodhisattva binds his mind day and night to observe the practice of the precepts.
Having observed the practice of the precepts, he is free from all regret and anxiety, and is liberated from all obstacles.
When a bodhisattva has thus practiced correctly, they cultivate various practices within the true Dharma of all Tathāgatas.
Son of good family!
Such practices as these are called the "shame" (hrī) of a bodhisattva.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, it is called ‘the accomplishment of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
“The Vehicle of the Superiority of Action is that of all Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others;
therefore, the wise cultivate those subtle matters.
The Bodhisattvas of great renown have accomplished the practice of fearlessness.”
Therefore, the realization of Bodhi is what all Buddhas have fundamentally taught. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva achieve perfection of nature?"

"Good son! By their very nature, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have little desire, little anger, and little delusion; they are not stingy, nor harsh, nor coarse; they are free from pride and lack of sudden violence; they are harmonious and gentle, speaking with kind and soft words, and are easy to dwell with."

That bodhisattva practices giving with a mind that seeks all supreme and excellent offerings; he relinquishes and bestows upon others all things, such as clothing and food. Having given in this manner, joy arises and pervades his body and mind, continuing even until he gives away his own limbs.
"Good son! When that bodhisattva practices such conduct, whether he sees a Tathāgata or a śrāvaka, upon seeing them, he immediately gives rise to a heart of joy."
"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes such dharmas as these, it is called 'accomplishment of nature.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
“From smoke one knows there is fire; seeing a ruddy sheldrake, one knows there is water.
From distinctive marks one knows a Bodhisattva, the great wisdom of a Bodhisattva.
Not harsh and not vexing the multitude, he abandons all crooked and deceitful conduct.”
Because they have faith in sentient beings who are virtuous, this is called the nature of a bodhisattva. "Good son,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s delight in the bodhicitta?"

"Good son! Because there is the characteristic of bodhi, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva resolves upon the mind of bodhi; even before he has resolved upon the mind of bodhi, either the Tathāgatas or the Śrāvakas may exhort him to resolve upon the mind of bodhi."
"Good son! This is the mark of a bodhisattva’s initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta). Good son!"

When that bodhisattva hears that there is awakening, hears that the bodhicitta possesses great merit, and hears of the arousal of the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is the second characteristic of the arousal of the bodhicitta by a bodhisattva.

"Good son! When that bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have no master and no kin, no savior and no protector, and no one capable of ferrying them to the other shore, the bodhisattva immediately arouses a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward those sentient beings and speaks these words:
'I shall act as a savior and protector for all those sentient beings who have no master and no kin, no savior and no protector.'"
For that cause and condition, one resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the third characteristic of a bodhisattva’s resolution for enlightenment.

"Good son! That bodhisattva, by beholding the Tathāgata’s body endowed with the marks of perfection, gives rise to a heart of joy and a heart of courageous delight. With this cause and condition, he resolves his mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is the fourth characteristic of a bodhisattva’s arousal of the bodhicitta."

"Good son! For the sake of causing those sentient beings to obtain benefit, peace, and happiness, that bodhisattva practices generosity, ethical discipline, patience, effort, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice giving? Good son!"
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"How should I practice generosity?
and immediately gives rise to this thought:

"To those who need food, give food; to those who need drink, give drink; to those who need bedding and mats, give bedding and mats; to those who need clothing, give clothing; and whatever else they require, such as signet rings, armlets, or jeweled crowns, give all such things to them."

"Good son! A bodhisattva may even cut his own flesh to give to sentient beings; practicing such giving while aspiring for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet without grasping at the recipient or the material object, and without dwelling on the phenomena involved—this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of generosity."
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice and maintain the precepts? Good son!"

That bodhisattva first disciplines his own physical actions, disciplines his verbal actions, and disciplines his mental actions; he completely abandons all unwholesome physical actions, completely abandons all unwholesome verbal actions, and completely abandons all unwholesome mental actions, maintaining the precepts without deficiency, without leakage, and without admixture.

When a bodhisattva has thus maintained the precepts and dedicated them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet their mind never grasps or clings to those precepts, this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation and maintenance of the precepts.
Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice patience? Good son!

Whether it be from those of the religious path or the laity, even when subjected to abuse and insults, or hearing reports of their own misdeeds, or being beaten, imprisoned, or having their hands and feet severed, a bodhisattva is able to endure all of this and gives rise to a mind of patience toward those individuals.

When a bodhisattva has thus practiced patience and dedicated it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, without giving rise to a mind of pride on account of that patience, this is called a bodhisattva’s practice of patience.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice diligence? Good son!"
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Just as the realm of space is immeasurable and boundless, so too is the realm of sentient beings immeasurable and boundless; yet I alone am without equal or peer, and I shall cause them all to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder."

"In this way, for the sake of those causes and conditions, the bodhisattva arouses diligent effort and first maintains the body; having maintained the bodily practice, they contemplate feelings, mind, and phenomena. Having thus correctly contemplated feelings, mind, and phenomena, they practice the maintenance of the mind; once the bodhisattva has practiced the maintenance of the mind, they next further cultivate the practices of seeing phenomena and so forth."

When the bodhisattva has thus maintained the mind and mental factors, he arouses desire, effort, and diligence so that unarisen evil and unwholesome states may be abandoned and not arise; he arouses desire, effort, and diligence so that unarisen wholesome states may arise.
In this manner, the bodhisattva next practices the first base of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and likewise practices the second, third, and even the fourth bases of psychic power.
To cultivate such practices without giving rise to a conceited mind is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of diligence.
Good son, how does a bodhisattva cultivate meditative concentration?

Good son! A bodhisattva practices giving without attachment to desire, without attachment to cessation, without attachment to the departure from desire, without attachment to one’s own body, without attachment to the bodies of others, without attachment to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; without attachment to the realm of desire, without attachment to the realm of form, without attachment to emptiness, without attachment to signlessness or wishlessness, and without attachment to this world or future worlds.

Not relying on generosity, not relying on ethical discipline, not relying on patience, not relying on diligence, and not relying on meditative concentration—practicing meditative concentration in this way and dedicating it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without making conceptual distinctions is called a bodhisattva’s practice of meditative concentration.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice prajñā? Good son!"
The Bodhisattva constantly reflects in this way while transforming sentient beings; having transformed them, he further thinks:
"I have led immeasurable and boundless realms of sentient beings into the realm of nirvana without remainder, yet not a single sentient being has entered the realm of nirvana."
Why is this? As the Buddha has taught, all dharmas are without self, without sentient beings, without life, without nourishment, and without a person (pudgala).

Thus cultivating wisdom and dedicating that wisdom toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making such a vow while not giving rise to discrimination regarding that wisdom—this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of *prajñā*.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva generates the bodhicitta in this manner, it is called the ‘bodhisattva’s delight in the bodhicitta.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"Just as a genuine jewel never parts from its radiance,
and just as gold within ore becomes increasingly bright once refined,
so too does the nature of awakening become ever more luminous through the bodhicitta."
When both extremes are purified, Māra finds no opportunity.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva delight in the Dharma?"

"Good son! The nature of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is to naturally delight in the Dharma, to be moistened by the joy of the Dharma, and to be nourished by the Dharma. If they see a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa who accords with the Dharma, they offer whatever goods they possess, giving all things such as food and drink, and even joining their palms to give rise to a mind of reverence. Having given rise to reverence, they hear from them the Dharma never heard before; having thus sought the True Dharma, the bodhisattva practices it according to reality."
Regarding those who are vessels for upholding the Dharma, the Bodhisattva conceives of them as venerable ones, as preceptors (upādhyāya), and as teachers (ācārya), giving rise to this thought:
"Since long ago, I have been deprived of a guide; now, suddenly, I have encountered one."
He conceived the thought of [the Buddha] as a guide. Furthermore, he thought:
"I have long been bound in the prison of the world, without release, without rescue, and without anyone to seek me out; now, suddenly, I have encountered him."
He gave rise to the thought of seeking and investigating. Furthermore, he thought:
"For a long time I have slept in this world, deluded and blind; suddenly now, my eyes have been opened."
He immediately gave rise to the thought of awakening and the thought of revealing [the truth].
Furthermore, he thought:
"For a long time I have been submerged in deep mud with no one to rescue me; now, suddenly, I have encountered such a person."
He conceived the thought of being rescued.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"For a long time I have been lost, lacking a guide to lead sentient beings; now, suddenly, I have encountered one."
One should conceive of him as a guide.
Furthermore, one should think:
"For a long time I have been confined within this world, living in poverty and suffering where there was no one to provide aid; now, suddenly, I have encountered him."
"Therefore, he immediately conceived the thought of one who would rescue and receive him. He further thought:
'For a long time I have encountered a difficult-to-cure illness, and there was no skilled physician able to treat it; now, suddenly, I have met one.'"
"Thus one should conceive the thought of him as a skilled physician.
Furthermore, one should reflect:
'For a long time I have been scorched by the fire of craving and have not received the rain from the clouds; now, suddenly, I have encountered it.'"
"Therefore, he immediately gives rise to the perception of a great cloud and rain.

For such causes and conditions, the bodhisattva endures various painful afflictions such as cold and heat, as well as those things that can harm sentient beings—such as mosquitoes and gadflies—and he is likewise able to endure hunger, thirst, and other such matters."
Seeing sentient beings who delight in pleasure, they do not give rise to a mind of attachment; that bodhisattva reflects thus:
"Although I may experience worldly happiness, if I hear even a single phrase of the Dharma, I shall be able to achieve the wisdom born of hearing."
Thus, they give rise to the perception of wisdom derived from hearing.

Because the bodhisattva possesses these causes and conditions for delighting in the Dharma, they practice giving without giving rise to sorrow, and even without experiencing such matters as grief or suffering.
Thus, having distanced himself from all matters of sorrow, suffering, and the like, the bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:

"For the sake of hearing even a single phrase of the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, I would enter even the Avīci Hell for a lifespan of one kalpa, or even a hundred thousand kalpas, without weariness."
"Once free from weariness, he practices the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and enables those who have not yet attained the Buddha’s true Dharma to attain it. "Good son!"
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva delights in the Dharma in this manner, it is called 'the Bodhisattva’s delight in the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"The seekers of the Dharma with great wisdom, That is to say, all the Bodhisattvas..."
Seeking the Dharma without weariness, out of a mind of reverence;
one should seek the True Dharma—this is called the mark of a bodhisattva.
Having heard it, one should always remember and uphold it, and further practice in accordance with the Dharma.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the practice of the true Dharma? Good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this way, they see that all phenomena are like illusions because they deceive ordinary people;
their minds are shrouded by ignorance because they lack correct wisdom;
and all phenomena are false and dreamlike because they consist of nothing but mental recollection.
All phenomena are like the moon in water, for they have no substantial reality;
all phenomena are like reflections in a mirror, for there are no sentient beings;
all phenomena are like echoes, for they arise from empty sounds.
All phenomena arise and perish because they are established through causes and conditions;
all phenomena do not arise because their nature is true suchness;
all phenomena do not perish because they are without arising.
All phenomena are without action, because there is no agent;
all phenomena are like space, because they are undefiled;
all phenomena are quiescent, because their essential nature is undefiled.
All phenomena are free from defilement, because they are apart from all stains;
all phenomena are eternally extinguished, because afflictions have been fundamentally extinguished;
all phenomena are formless, because they cannot be seen.
All dharmas are free from mind, thought, and consciousness, because they lack a body;
all dharmas are without abiding, because they have extinguished the ālayavijñāna;
all dharmas are without seeking, because they are free from attachment to this and that.
All phenomena are without attachment, because they are free from the sphere of all afflictions;
all phenomena are like snakes, because they lack the power of skillful mantras and spells;
all phenomena are like plantains, because they are insubstantial.
All phenomena are like foam on water, for their nature is devoid of power.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the practice of the true Dharma in this manner, it is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the practice of the true Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"All phenomena are like illusions, For they obscure the minds of sentient beings;
They are false and delusive, just like dreams— One should accept and uphold them in this way."
"All dharmas are like the moon in water, because they arise as reflections;
all dharmas are like images in a mirror—why does wisdom not perceive them? "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the dharmas in accordance with the Dharma?
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates form as impermanent, yet does not realize the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) by means of the cessation of form. By means of the wisdom of suchness, having realized the characteristics of all phenomena within the dharma-realm exactly as they are, he skillfully memorizes and skillfully cultivates all the characteristics within that dharma-realm. Whatever is spoken, whatever is cultivated, and whatever is remembered, he naturally enters the practice of the dharma-realm in this manner.

In this way, one proceeds even unto feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; having observed them with suchness and having correctly examined them, one does not extinguish consciousness nor does one feel revulsion toward consciousness, but realizes entry into the dharma-realm.

All phenomena within the entire dharma-realm are realized as they truly are through authentic wisdom; within those phenomena there are various names, which are well-spoken, well-known, well-cultivated, and well-remembered. Because of this thorough knowledge, thorough cultivation, and thorough recollection, one naturally enters the practice of the dharma-realm in this manner.
Just as one knows impermanence, so too does one know suffering, non-self, and impurity in the same way.
By contemplating the impermanence of form and knowing it correctly as it truly is, one no longer gives rise to thoughts of fear regarding that form.
Why is this? Because they know, as it truly is, that form arises falsely; thus, the bodhisattva knows well according to reality.

They know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent, suffering, selfless, impure, and so forth; consequently, within that consciousness, they no longer give rise to thoughts of fear.
Why is this? Because they know, as it truly is, that consciousness is illusory.
The bodhisattva thus knows well according to reality.

"Good son! It is like a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s disciple who conjures various things such as the fourfold army—namely, elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and a wise person, having seen this, does not give rise to fear."
Why is this? Because they well understand that these are produced by false illusions, manifested to delude and mislead sentient beings. Good son!
In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates that form is impermanent; having contemplated its impermanence, he does not give rise to thoughts of fear within it.
Why is this? Because he knows, in accordance with reality, that form arises falsely; thus the bodhisattva knows well in accordance with reality.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent; having contemplated their impermanence, one does not give rise to fear regarding consciousness.
Why is this? Because one knows consciousness as it truly is—as arising from falsehood—the Bodhisattva thus understands it correctly and thoroughly.
“Good son! A bodhisattva contemplates phenomena and accords with phenomena in this way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva contemplate form as impermanent, yet without departing from form speak of the dharma-realm, realize the dharma-realm, and train in the dharma-realm, such that all dharmas are realized and known as they truly are through the power of wisdom?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja, saying:
"Good son! Because of your question, I shall now speak a parable for you."
Good son! It is like a wise person in the world who possesses various poisonous drugs.
Having taken these poisonous drugs, he either decocts them, roasts them, or combines them with other medicines.
Having compounded it with other medicines, he sells it for the sake of profit and does not consume it himself.
Why is this? That person reflects:
"May my life not be cut short on account of this cause.
Son of good family!

Although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s mind inclines toward Nirvāṇa, his mind is moistened by Nirvāṇa, his mind flows toward Nirvāṇa, and his mind correctly grasps Nirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not realize Nirvāṇa.
Why is this? The Bodhisattva reflects:
"May my person not, by reason of these causes and conditions, regress from bodhi."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
I shall speak another parable.
Son of good family!"
For example, suppose there is a person who serves fire.
Having served it, he honors, respects, complies with, and carefully protects it, yet he does not give rise to such a thought as:
"Because I have made offerings to the fire, honored and praised it, and carefully protected it, I shall grasp it with both hands."
Why is this? That person thinks:
"May my body not suffer physical pain and mental distress on account of these causes and conditions."

"Good son! Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mind inclines toward nirvāṇa, his mind is moistened by nirvāṇa, his mind flows toward nirvāṇa, his mind correctly directs itself toward nirvāṇa, and he inclines toward the shore of nirvāṇa, that bodhisattva does not realize nirvāṇa."
Why is this? The Bodhisattva reflects:
"May my own person not, on account of these causes and conditions, regress from the wisdom of bodhi."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, a bodhisattva should always abide in the world.”
The Buddha said, “Good son! So it is, so it is!”
“A bodhisattva should always abide in the world.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“How does a bodhisattva dwell in the world without being defiled by worldly phenomena?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
I shall now speak to you by means of an analogy. Good son!

Suppose there were a person skilled in expedient means who, by the power of mantras, would play with various venomous snakes, grasping them, holding them in his mouth, rubbing them, and performing all manner of antics with them, yet never, on account of playing with snakes, be harmed or lose his life.
Why is this? It is because they possess the power of skillful incantations.
O son of good family!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the world and practices worldly dharmas, by virtue of the power of skillful great wisdom and expedient mantras, they play with the poisonous medicines of the various afflictions and dally with the snakes of the afflictions, yet they do not retreat from bodhi on account of those afflictions.
"Why is this? It is because Bodhisattvas have accomplished the power of skillful means and wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How extraordinary is the World-Honored One! How marvelous is the Sugata! How most rare is the World-Honored One! How most rare is the Sugata!
World-Honored One!”
Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas incline their minds toward nirvāṇa, they do not realize nirvāṇa; although they remain in the world, they are not defiled by worldly dharmas.
World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One!
If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing of such bodhisattva practices, give rise to a heart of joy, those people have planted various roots of goodness in the past.
Why is this? World-Honored One, if any sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, give rise to a sense of rare wonder for even the duration of a finger-snap,
they have already received a prediction of enlightenment from the Tathāgata.
"Why is this? Because they have heard this Dharma-gate and listened with a sincere and attentive mind.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent son! It is so, it is so!
When this Dharma-gate was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus attained the mind free from outflows (anāsrava-citta).
Having attained the untainted mind, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
“World-Honored One, the bodhisattvas may rightly revere the Sugata, and they may pay homage to the bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said, “O bhikṣus!”
"So it is, so it is. Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates phenomena and accords with phenomena in this manner, it is called 'the bodhisattva’s contemplation of phenomena and accordance with phenomena.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"One should revere those of great wisdom; One should revere those of great fearlessness;
One should revere those who wear the proper robes; One should revere those born from the Buddha."
By the power of skillful means and through the excellence of wisdom,
the Bodhisattva’s great wisdom transcends the stage of the Śrāvaka.
He thoroughly understands that the aggregates (skandhas) are empty, for they are subject to arising and ceasing and are unstable.
"Seeing the fires burning in the world, for this reason he does not realize cessation.
'O son of good family!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of phenomena and conformity with phenomena.'"
Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abandon pride and great pride? Good son!
Regarding what is called pride (*māna*), one gives rise to such a thought:

"That which I now possess—whether my family, my clan, my physical appearance, or various kinds of gold, silver, rare treasures, and treasuries, as well as my elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—is not inferior to that of others."
"If a person gives rise to such a mind of arrogance, this is called pride (māna), because they do not give rise to a mind of reverence.
Good son! What is great pride (mahāmāna)?"
"Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who thinks thus:
'Only I, in terms of family, clan, physical appearance, or stores of gold, silver, and treasures; or in terms of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—surpass others.'"
"For this reason, one does not give rise to a mind of reverence; this is called great pride (mahāmāna). Good son!
Such is conceit (māna) and great pride."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have completely abandoned them. Good son!
In this way, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are free from pride and free from great pride.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"Free from pride and free from great arrogance, Always practicing a heart of loving-kindness and compassion,
Because the mind is moistened by these, One does not become negligent in the world."
"Though they perform the act of begging for food, this is the great task of the bodhisattvas:
to explain the meaning and benefit of the teachings to gods and humans.
O son of good family!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully understand the secret teachings of the Tathāgata?
Noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all the profound and hidden meanings contained within the various sūtras, understands them as they truly are within those explanations.
"Good son! What is this secret teaching of the Tathāgata? Good son!"
That I have predicted that the śrāvakas will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is not possible;
it would be as impossible as saying, "Ānanda, I am suffering from back pain."
He said to the bhikṣus, "I am now old and infirm; you should seek out an attendant for me. This should not have been said.
He said to Maudgalyāyana, "You should go and ask Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, what medicine I should take for my ailment. This should not have been said.
"Good son! It is not appropriate for the Tathāgata to pursue various non-Buddhist teachers in various places to debate and compete for victory. Good son!"
"That the khaṭvāṅga thorn pierced the Tathāgata’s foot—this should not have been so.
Son of good family!
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said that Devadatta was my宿怨 (long-standing enemy), who constantly followed me about seeking an opportunity for harm—this should not have been so."

"Good son! When the Tathāgata entered the city of Śrāvastī in the past, he went on almsround throughout the village of the brahmin Śāleyya and returned with an empty bowl; this should not have been so."
"Good son! When Ciñcā Mānavikā and Viśvantarī slandered the Tathāgata by joining wooden vessels against their bellies,
they likewise should not have done so."

"Good son! When the Tathāgata was formerly in the country of Vairaṇtī, he accepted the invitation of the brahmin Vairaṇya and remained in the three-month summer retreat eating barley; this was not the case."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one grasp what has just been explained?”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you prophesy that the śrāvakas shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! My prediction that śrāvakas shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is because I see that śrāvakas possess buddha-nature.”
Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These śrāvakas have severed all outflows (āsrava) and departed from the three realms of existence (tridhātu). Since their rebirth has been cut off yet they possess the nature [for enlightenment], how is it that the Tathāgata bestows upon them the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? How can this be?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! I shall now speak a parable for you.”
"Good son! It is like a consecrated universal monarch who possesses a thousand sons; he bestows the royal throne upon the eldest among them.

Yet, because that wheel-turning king perceives that his son’s faculties are dull, he teaches those things that should be taught first to him later, and those things that should be taught later to him first—namely, all matters of craftsmanship, incantations, and arts."
However, because this prince has dull faculties, he studied what should have been studied by beginners before studying what should have been studied by those of intermediate capacity. Good son!
"What do you think?
Having trained in this way, would that Prince Cakravartin not truly be the legitimate son of the king?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha replied:
"No, World-Honored One! It is not so, Sugata!
He is truly the prince."
The Buddha said: “Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Because his faculties are dull, he should study what is to be studied at the beginning, and study what is to be studied in the middle only after that. In this way, by observing the five aggregates of sentient beings, he extinguishes all afflictions; once the afflictions are extinguished, he then attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Good son! What do you think?
Since those śrāvakas attain perfect enlightenment through these causes and conditions, can it be said that śrāvakas cannot attain perfect enlightenment?"
Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja said:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Among all these assemblies—whether humans, devas, Māras, or Brahmās—I have never seen anyone who could say that a śrāvaka cannot attain perfect awakening."
"If there were anyone capable of saying that this is not possible, it would be except for an icchantika.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha, saying: "Good son!
I shall now provide you with another analogy,
son of good family:
it is like a bodhisattva of sharp faculties dwelling in the tenth stage, who has eliminated the two kinds of selflessness and sits at the site of enlightenment.
"Do you sit because you have removed [the afflictions], or do you sit without having removed them?
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja spoke:
“World-Honored One!
We have already removed our old seats. World-Honored One!
We have already removed our old seats. Sugata!”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! Since those of sharp faculties possess these causes and conditions, how could they not attain perfect enlightenment?”
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja said:
“It is accomplished, World-Honored One!
It is accomplished, Sugata!”
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja, saying: "Good son,
it is likewise in this place."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja said:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason did the Tathāgata formerly tell Ānanda, 'I am suffering from back pain'?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!

Observing future generations and out of compassion for sentient beings, I have made this statement, saying that my back aches, so that those who are ill may understand: ‘If even the Buddha’s adamantine body still suffers from back pain, how much more so will it be for us and others?’”
It is for this reason that I have spoken these words.
Yet foolish people take them literally, claiming that the Buddha was ill or suffered from back pain; thus they ruin themselves and cause others to be ruined as well.
The Tathāgata again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja, saying:
“Good son, in the past I told the bhikṣus: ‘I am now old and infirm; you should seek out an attendant for me.’”
"Good son! I spoke these words out of compassion for future generations; it was for this purpose that I said such a thing.
To ensure that my śrāvaka disciples in future ages who have grown old and infirm will receive proper attendance, I said: 'I am now old and infirm, and must seek an attendant.'"

So that those in future generations, having understood this, may not give rise to regression; for this reason I have spoken these words: "I am now old and infirm; you may seek out an attendant for me."
Yet foolish people take this literally, thinking that because the Tathāgata is aged and infirm, he must have an attendant.
"Good son! How should you understand this?"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "Go to Jīvaka, the Great King of Physicians, and inquire about the method for taking medicine.
Good son! This too was spoken by me out of compassion for future generations."
There are some śrāvakas who sustain their bodies by means of medicine; they should reflect that even our Buddha’s adamantine body still requires medicine, let alone ourselves and others.
It was for this reason that I spoke these words: "Go to Jīvaka, the great king of physicians, and ask him about the method of taking medicine.
Yet foolish people took them literally, claiming that the body of the Tathāgata is a body afflicted by illness.
"Good son! In the past, the Tathāgata instructed the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana to question Jīvaka regarding medicine.
Because Jīvaka had no room for hesitation, he did not answer directly, but said only this: 'One should simply take ghee; one should simply take ghee.'"
However, this is the Tathāgata demonstrating the retribution of karmic fruits, so that his disciples, upon hearing it, shall remember and understand it and not regress.
"Good son! The Tathāgata has gone everywhere to debate and challenge non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others regarding their doctrines."
What is the meaning of this? Good son!

Out of compassion for sentient beings in future ages, I contemplate them and perform these deeds so that those beings may come to know: "If even the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, the perfectly and truly awakened ones, still have enemies, how much more so must it be for us and others?"
Yet foolish people grasp at this literally, claiming that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, truly has enemies. Good son!
Even a Wheel-Turning Sage King, by virtue of his meager merit, has no enemies; how much less so the Tathāgata, who has accomplished immeasurable and boundless merit?
“Good son, as for the matter of the *khadira* thorn piercing the Tathāgata’s foot, what does it mean?

Good son, it is because the Tathāgata manifests the retribution of karma so that those in future ages may understand this: if even the Tathāgata, who has accomplished immeasurable merit, still possesses karmic retribution, how much more so must it be for us and others?”
By these causes and conditions, I cause them to cease their evil; furthermore, for this reason I declare that such karmic retribution exists.
Yet foolish people grasp at this as literal truth, [as when] the *khaṭvāṅga* thorn pierced the Tathāgata’s foot.
Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja said:
“World-Honored One!
Devadatta was the Buddha’s long-standing enemy, seeking an opportunity against the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! If it were not for the spiritual friend Deva, you would never have come to know that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merit.”

"Good son! Devadatta is a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Although he contended with me for supremacy and acted as my enemy in the present, he has served to manifest the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata."

"Good son! The good friend and spiritual mentor Devadatta, while within the palace, spoke to King Ajātaśatru, inciting him to harm the Tathāgata. At that time, the king intentionally released the elephant king Dhanapāla to destroy the Tathāgata."
"Good son! When the Tathāgata saw the elephant, he immediately tamed it.

At that time, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, seeing the elephant tamed, conceived a sense of wonder and gave rise to right faith, taking refuge in the Three Jewels—namely, the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel—thereby manifesting the Three Jewels."
"Good son! Such matters should be understood in this way:
Devadatta was a spiritual friend who, for a long time, followed [the Buddha] while manifesting as an enemy."
Yet foolish people grasp it according to its literal meaning and speak thus: "Devadatta is the one who harmed the Buddha; he is his enemy.
O son of good family!

Even throughout five hundred past lifetimes, wherever he was born, Devadatta was his spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); the display of enmity and domestic affairs was entirely a manifestation intended to reveal the various bodhisattvas and to manifest the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.
Yet foolish people grasp this according to its literal meaning, thinking that Devadatta was one who harmed the Buddha and was his enemy.
Because of these causes and conditions of grasping the meaning incorrectly, they fall into the three miserable realms—the various places of suffering known as hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Why is this? Good son!

Devadatta, as a spiritual friend, has well cultivated immeasurable and supreme merits; he has well cultivated roots of goodness, drawn near to the Buddhas, and planted the seeds of virtue in past lives. His mind is directed toward the Mahāyāna, he accords with the Mahāyāna, and he is heading for the further shore of the Mahāyāna; he is close to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! Because they have corrupted their minds, in future ages they shall be born within the various evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha said:
“World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata entered the city of Śrāvastī in the past, he went on almsround throughout the brahmin village of Śālīya and returned with an empty bowl. How can this be so?”

“Good son! This which I have done was also for the sake of compassionately regarding sentient beings of future generations; I manifested this matter so that those in future ages might understand thus: ‘If even the Tathāgata, who is fully endowed with immeasurable merit, goes forth with an empty bowl, how much more so should we and others do the same?’”
"Good son! Furthermore, there are those who say that this Māra Pāpīyān exhorted the brahmins, elders, and householders, causing them to be unwilling to make offerings to the Tathāgata."
This is not so either. Why? Good son!
Because the Māra King lacked the power to persuade the elder not to offer food to the Tathāgata.
Good son! This matter should not be understood in such a way.

Why is this? It is because the Māra-king lacks the power to obstruct the offerings made to the Tathāgata; rather, it is the Tathāgata who exhorts and influences the Māra-king to command the householders, brahmins, and others not to make offerings.

"Good son! The Tathāgata has already extinguished all obstacles and accomplished immeasurable, supreme merits; therefore, it is impossible for there to be anything that can obstruct offerings made to the Tathāgata."

The Tathāgata has no actual karma or karmic retribution; rather, for the sake of enabling those sentient beings to attain the Path, the Tathāgata manifests such various matters through skillful means.

"Good son! If the Tathāgata were to cease taking even a single meal, he would cause all the śrāvakas, Māra Pāpīyas, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others, as well as the sons of gods, to think thus:
'Let not our kinsmen give rise to sorrowful thoughts or perform such acts for his sake.'"

For this reason, the Tathāgata manifests such matters day and night to cause even a single thought of unwholesomeness to arise; yet this is precisely how the Tathāgata severs all forms of existence (*bhava*). As he manifested previously, so shall he do hereafter.
This was intended to cause those in future ages to understand that if even the Tathāgata, having severed existence, still possesses such matters, how much more so for us and others.
When this matter was manifested, seventy thousand celestial beings conceived a pure mind toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata, having known their minds, taught the Dharma in various ways; upon hearing the Dharma, they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
