Son of good family!
I have observed future generations and thus displayed this matter; the Tathāgata has no such karmic retribution.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja said:
“World-Honored One,
regarding the matter of Cāṇāmā Kāpilavastunī, who slandered the World-Honored One by joining her wooden bowls against her belly— how was this?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, this is also not so.”
The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable merit and is free from the affliction of karmic retribution. Good son!
It is by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata that he is able to place Cañcā, Mānava, Viśvantarī, and others beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers.
Those who are slandered are, in fact, the Tathāgata manifesting the retribution of karmic results through the power of skillful means.
Because my disciples possess meager merit, once they have left the household life to enter my Dharma, they may fall away from my Dharma due to such slander.
Because we have spoken thus without reflecting upon the Tathāgata’s teachings, we have now been slandered and should no longer be permitted to remain within the Buddha’s True Dharma.

May those people, upon hearing this teaching, remember that even though the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have fully accomplished all pure dharmas and extinguished all unwholesome dharmas, they were still subjected to such evil opposition and slander; how much more so for us and others?
Having realized this, they no longer regress but cultivate the pure Brahma-faring. Good son!

When Ciñcā Mānavikā, Viśvantarī, and others gave rise to evil intentions, it was through the power of the Buddha that they were awakened in their dreams, [realizing]: "I have indeed slandered the Buddha; if I cast off this body, I shall surely fall into the three evil realms."
"Good son! If the Tathāgata knows that something can be guarded against, he will certainly guard against it; for this reason, he manifests such an event. Good son!"
“There is not a single sentient being whom the Tathāgata abandons; therefore, he manifests this matter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja said, “World-Honored One!
"How was it that in the past, when the Tathāgata was in the country of Vairaṇtī, he accepted the invitation of the brahmin Vairaṇya and ate barley?
What does this mean? The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
I have manifested this matter out of compassion for sentient beings of future generations.

The Tathāgata truly knows that although various brahmins and householders invited him, they failed to provide offerings; nevertheless, he accepted their invitations and entered the rains retreat in those places.
Why is this? Good son!
At that place of retreat there were five hundred horses; all the barley they consumed was given to the community of monks to sustain them for three months.
"Good son! Those horses were all great bodhisattvas who, having planted roots of virtue in the past, encountered evil friends and committed various evil deeds, thereby being born among the animals."
"Good son! That horse-tamer among the five hundred horses was the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha; by the power of his vows, he was born in that place. Good son!"
On that day, the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha exhorted five hundred horses to resolve upon bodhicitta; he was born in that place for the purpose of enabling them to attain liberation.
Son of good family!
By the power of that well-trained horse king, those five hundred horses all remembered their past lives, attained bodhicitta, and recovered their original minds.

"Good son! Out of compassion for those five hundred horses, the Tathāgata accepted their invitation and entered the rains retreat at that place. The horse trainer gave barley to the Tathāgata as food, while the five hundred horses' barley was given to the disciples."

"Good son! That horse-tamer used the sounds of horses to train five hundred horses, causing them all to repent and exhorting them to resolve their minds for enlightenment; he further caused those horses to give rise to a heart of reverence toward the Buddha-dharma and the Triple Gem."
"Good son! After three months had passed, those five hundred horses cast off their bodies and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
While they were still among the animals, they obtained such benefit; at that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for them, causing them to receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Good son! As for those who were the trainers and guardians of the five hundred horses there, the Tathāgata has prophesied that they shall achieve the path of a pratyekabuddha, which consists in the self-subduing of the mind."
"Good son! There is nothing in the world that can be eaten which, when consumed by the Tathāgata, does not become a subtle and exquisite flavor. Good son!"
Even if the Tathāgata were to eat such things as clods of earth, shards of tile, or stones, he would never fail to experience the most subtle and exquisite flavors.
Son of good family!
Whatever the Tathāgata eats becomes a supreme flavor; there is nothing within this world-system of three thousandfold great thousands that can be compared to it.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has attained the supreme flavor among all flavors, has attained the supreme taste in food, and has attained the various marks and signs of a Great Man,
O son of good family!
"You should now correctly perceive that the food consumed by the Tathāgata is entirely of subtle and exquisite flavor, beyond all comparison.
Good son! It was out of compassion for me that the bhikṣu Ānanda spoke these words:"
"How is it that the Tathāgata, having been born into the family of a Cakravartin king and having renounced his royal throne to leave the household life, can eat barley?
Having understood Ānanda’s thoughts, the Tathāgata gave him a grain of barley and said: "Ānanda!"
"You should know this: what kind of flavor is this?
Having eaten, Ānanda conceived a sense of wonder and immediately said to me:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I was born into a royal family and raised in a royal household, yet I have never before experienced such a superior flavor.
Son of good family!
Because of the taste of that food, the Bhikṣu Ānanda attained peace in body and mind and did not eat for seven days.
"Good son! For this reason, you should know that the Tathāgata has no karmic retribution.

However, when those householders and brahmins invited virtuous and pure bhikṣus but failed to provide them with offerings, the bhikṣus accepted the invitations and went to them; their failure to receive offerings was a manifestation of karmic retribution."

"Good son! You should observe the supernatural power of the Tathāgata: although that brahmin invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha but failed to provide offerings, the Tathāgata prophesied that he would not fall into the evil realms."

"Good son! Among the five hundred bhikṣus who, together with the Buddha, accepted the invitation to observe the rains retreat at that place, there were forty bhikṣus who possessed much greed and were unable to contemplate the practice of impurity; consequently, whenever they obtained exquisite food to their liking, they all fell back from their resolve."
Because he ate horse fodder, no desire arose in him; after seven days had passed, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Son of good family!
The Tathāgata skillfully knows the minds of sentient beings; therefore, he accepted their invitation in order to deliver them.

"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully accomplishes such profound secret teachings and manifests these matters, if one knows them in this way, it is called being well-versed in the Tathāgata’s secret teachings."
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
“Skillfully knowing the gradual dharma-gate, as well as that which is taught all at once,
with internal skillful knowledge— this is what the Bodhisattvas manifest.”
“Skilled in knowing the secrets, / Far removed from all doubts and delusions,
/ Well-knowing the teachings of all Buddhas / Regarding all secret instructions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is within the various evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, although they undergo there the most grievous sufferings that cannot be fully described, their mind does not seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor does it have the intention to seek liberation for themselves alone. They do not dwell on few desires, nor do they dwell on doing little; they do not practice few desires, nor do they perform deeds of doing little.”

"Good son! A bodhisattva engages in the same activities as those sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds; yet, that bodhisattva skillfully exhorts and transforms those beings, causing them to practice and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Good son, because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such dharmas as these, they do not seek the enlightenment of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
“Constantly transforming all sentient beings, Their minds never give rise to weariness.”
Regarding unsurpassed enlightenment, they are firm and non-retrogressive;
their minds cannot be shaken, like the wondrous King of Mountains.
They cultivate the mind of loving-kindness and compassion, seeking no path of the two vehicles.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has already explained how a bodhisattva accomplishes such dharmas as these; for this reason, they are called one who practices the Great Vehicle and abides in the Great Vehicle.”
"But for what reason does the Tathāgata not explain why this Great Vehicle is called the 'Great Vehicle'?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
"Good son! What do you think?
By what name is the road traveled by a wheel-turning sage king—the path traversed by him while accompanied by his fourfold army—described?"
Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja said:
“World-Honored One!
This is called the royal path; this is called the great path. It is the path of fearlessness, the unobstructed path, and the royal path that surpasses all other kingdoms.”
The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja: “Good son!

The path practiced by all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, that vehicle is called the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), the Supreme Vehicle, the Wondrous Vehicle, the Victorious Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Unsurpassed-Surpassing Vehicle, the Unequaled Vehicle, the Non-evil Vehicle, and the Vehicle Equal to the Unequaled.”
“Good son! For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One! Excellent, Sugata!
Excellent, World-Honored One!”
"Quickly explain such names and meanings of the Mahāyāna.
When the Tathāgata was speaking this Dharma-gate of the ten dharmas, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"Today, the śramaṇa Gautama has transgressed my realm."
"If I were to afflict that Gautama with my fourfold army, he would be unable to preach this Dharma-gate.
Having formed this thought, Māra Pāpīyān immediately assembled his fourfold army and went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja saw from afar that Pāpīyān, accompanied by an army of the four divisions, was coming here with the intent to harass the Tathāgata and prevent him from preaching this Dharma-gate.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha immediately manifested supernatural powers. Having manifested these powers, he caused Māra Pāpīyas to go to the crossroads of Rājagṛha and proclaim these words:

"All you people of Rājagṛha, you should know that today the śramaṇa Gautama is at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha, expounding the true Dharma for the fourfold assembly. It is good in the beginning, middle, and end; its words and meaning are both profound; it is pure, complete, and perfect in the holy life."
"You all should go to that śramaṇa Gautama and listen to his teaching of the Dharma; it will bring you great peace, happiness, and beneficial matters for a long night."

At that time, within the great city of Rājagṛha, the various brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, elders, and householders, having been exhorted by Māra, took in their hands incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, precious banners, and precious parasols. They departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to the place where the Tathāgata was. There they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid him honor and offered praise, and then withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, also accompanied by his fourfold army, departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to where the Tathāgata was. Having manifested māndārava flowers and scattered them over the Tathāgata, he withdrew with his fourfold army and sat to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha, knowing that Māra Pāpīyas was seated to one side, addressed Māra, saying: "You, Māra Pāpīyas!
For what reason have you led these fourfold armies to harass the Tathāgata and obstruct him from preaching this Dharma-gate?
You should now give rise to a sense of shame and remorse before the Tathāgata and offer repentance, lest you suffer no benefit for a long night and incur the retribution of great suffering.

At that time, having heard the words of the Bodhisattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja, Māra Pāpīyān immediately joined his ten fingers and palms together, touching the ground as he prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata. Feeling a sense of shame and remorse toward the Tathāgata, he gave rise to a mind of repentance and spoke these words:
“I am now deeply afraid of the Tathāgata.”
"How marvelous, O Sugata!
I pray only that you, in your great compassion, accept my confession.

I was exceedingly foolish and lacked wisdom; lacking skillful means and having no regard for my own life, I gave rise to an evil mind toward the Tathāgata and further sought to cause this Dharma-gate to be extinguished."
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
Please accept my repentance once more.
The Buddha said:
“Pāpīyan! Excellent, excellent! You have nurtured roots of goodness.”
"If there are sons or daughters of good family within my Dharma who give rise to the thought of repentance to seek purity,
how excellent, Pāpīyān! At that time,
Māra Pāpīyān went to where the Buddha was, stood before him, and said:
“World-Honored One!
Do all the sūtras of the Tathāgata sever evil speech and unwholesome speech?
The Tathāgata replied:
"So be it, so be it," said Māra Pāpīyān. "How is it that the Tathāgata,
the Dharma King and Lord of Dharma who has attained mastery over all dharmas, addresses me by the name 'Pāpīyān' and calls me thus?"
The Buddha said,
“Pāpīyān! I shall now speak a parable for you.”

Good son! It is like a wealthy householder whose riches are inexhaustible, who has but one son whom he loves dearly; he cannot bear to be out of his son's sight, for his very life is bound up in that son.

However, because that only son’s faculties were undisciplined and he was exceedingly wicked, deceitful, and crooked, the elder householder—out of a heart of affection—struck him with a staff, or used a tile or a stone, desiring to cause this son to cease such behavior.
"Good son! What do you think?
Does this elder householder have an evil mind when he beats his son?"
Māra Pāpīyān said: “No, World-Honored One!
It was because he wished to bring about the fulfillment of his affection for his son that he performed such an act.”

The Buddha said, “Pāpīyan, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, thoroughly understands the mental natures, faculties, and desires of sentient beings. Therefore, he observes them: for those who are to be delivered by harsh words, he speaks harsh words; for those who are to be delivered through silence and non-discourse, he remains silent; for those who are to be delivered by being sent away, he sends them away; for those who are to be delivered by the teaching of the Dharma, he teaches it to them; for those who are to be delivered by being taken into his care, he takes them into his care; for those who are to be delivered by seeing his physical body, he manifests his physical body so that they may see it; and for those who are to be delivered by hearing sounds, smelling scents, tasting flavors, or touching tangibles, he manifests sounds and teaches the Dharma to them, even manifesting scents, flavors, and tangibles to bring about their deliverance.”
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān rejoiced and leaped for joy; he again joined his ten fingers and palms together in homage, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!

In whatever place—whether a village, a city, or a royal capital—this Dharma-gate is preached, I shall go to those places for the sake of hearing and receiving this Dharma-gate, and I shall protect this Dharma-gate as well as those vessels who uphold it.”

"Bhagavān! When I reach that time, there will surely be various signs: the assembly will be tranquil and composed, free from the hindrance of drowsiness; furthermore, superior and excellent vessels from all directions will come to inquire about the Dharma. Whether reading, reciting, or upholding it, my body and mind shall both be at peace, and without giving rise to pride, I shall explain this Dharma accordingly."
Whether explained in detail or in brief, they give rise to a heart of joy toward the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata gives rise to a heart of joy toward all sentient beings; once those sentient beings have their hearts filled with joy, their roots of goodness increase and unwholesome dharmas are extinguished.

At that time, among the great assembly there were various non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others who, hearing Māra Pāpīyān repent in this manner, were filled with immense joy and exultation beyond measure, and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions did these various non-Buddhists attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas when this Dharma was being taught?”

The Buddha said, “Ānanda! In the distant past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, on Vulture Peak Mountain in this city of Rājagṛha, there was at that time a Buddha named Upendrabala, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, who was preaching the Dharma here.”

After the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) came toward the Buddha, desiring to vex the Tathāgata and wishing to obstruct the preaching of this Dharma-gate; thus they arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Having heard the Dharma, his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately said:
"World-Honored One!
You have excellently expounded this Dharma."
He conceived a sense of wonder toward the Tathāgata.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, for sixty kalpas he did not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; he was born only among humans and devas, and in every place of birth he recollected that Buddha. Although he recollected the Buddha, however, he lacked virtuous friends.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Are those non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others anyone other than [myself]?
Those among this assembly who are non-Buddhists are they. Why is this?
Because at that time, these sons of good family were possessed of evil views, desiring to vex the Tathāgata and to obstruct this Dharma.

Having heard the Dharma, they gave rise to great joy; by this cause and condition, they now receive the Buddha’s prediction that these non-Buddhists shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, let alone having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in the present.

When this Dharma-door was being taught, twelve thousand sentient beings were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; twenty thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should give rise to even a single thought of faith in this Dharma-gate, their merit would be immeasurable; how much more so for those who read, recite, receive, uphold, protect it, and extensively explain it to others!”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! If there are sons or daughters of good family who exhort all sentient beings without exception to resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;”

Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who conceive even a single thought of faith in this Dharma-gate, and whether they read it, recite it, or explain it extensively for others, the merit obtained by these people exceeds that of those previously mentioned.
Why is this? Ānanda! Because this Dharma-gate is the locus of the path to the knowledge of all modes of knowing.
Ānanda! If any man or woman hears this Dharma-gate and, upon seeing a Dharma-preacher who upholds this Dharma-gate, gives rise to an evil mind, they will commit a transgression greater than before.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabha said:
"If there are men or women who slander this sutra, the Tathāgata has already stated that their transgression is greater than the former."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaratnacandraprabharāja, saying:
"If a man or a woman were at once to gouge out the eyes of all sentient beings;
yet if another man or woman were to give rise to a single evil thought toward this Dharma-gate and those who uphold it, the latter would incur a transgression greater than the former."
Why is this? Ānanda! This Dharma-gate is named "Light," for it is able to bestow the eye of wisdom upon all sentient beings.
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma-gate should not be spoken before men or women who lack faith.”
For what reason?
Because one must protect sentient beings,
World-Honored One!
"I have seen that through such karmic conditions of slandering the Dharma, one is born within the evil realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You should preach this Dharma-gate; you should not fail to preach it."
"Why is this? Because this name serves as the cause for that, enabling those who practice it to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what name should this Dharma-gate be called?
How should it be upheld?”
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!

Ānanda, you should know that because these ten dharmas are taught, it is called the ‘Dharma-gate of the Ten Dharmas. You should uphold it thus; it is also called ‘The Questions of the Bodhisattva Vimalacandraprabharāja,’ and you should uphold it thus.”

When the Buddha had spoken this Dharma-gate, the Venerable Ānanda, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pure Stainless Jewel Moon King Radiance, along with the great bodhisattvas in the assembly, as well as the multitude of śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they received it upon their heads and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-Eight;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
10. The Universal Gate Chapter of Mañjuśrī. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of eight hundred bhikṣus and forty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbha who, surrounded by a retinue of ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas, came through the air with respectful devotion.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:

"Those bodhisattvas have been exhorted by the Tathāgata Samantakusuma of the world-system Sarvapariśuddhacaryā to come to this Sahā world, so that they may hear and receive from me the Dharma-gate of Universally Entering the Inconceivable."
"All those bodhisattvas shall likewise assemble.

Having spoken these words, immeasurable and boundless assemblies of bodhisattvas from other directions and this world-system all came together at Vulture Peak Mountain; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, holding a seven-jeweled thousand-petaled lotus flower, approached the Tathāgata, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Samantakusuma from the world-system Sarvavyūhapariśuddhacaryā offered these precious flowers to the World-Honored One.
He extended greetings of immeasurable concern, asking whether he was free from illness and affliction, whether his daily life was light and easy, and whether he dwelt in peace and happiness.
Having spoken these words, he immediately ascended into the air and sat cross-legged.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee upon the ground, he joined his palms in reverent salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that in the distant past, during a long-elapsed age, I once heard the teaching of the ‘Dharma-gate of Universally Entering the Inconceivable’ from the presence of the Buddha Samantapradīpa.”
At that time, I immediately attained eight thousand four hundred billion nayutas of samādhis, and was further able to comprehend seven million seven hundred billion nayutas of samādhis.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will deign to show compassion and expound this Dharma-gate for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Listen attentively now, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mañjuśrī replied, “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said,
"If bodhisattvas wish to study this Dharma, they should cultivate and practice the various gates of samādhi."
These are: the samādhi of the mark of form, the samādhi of the mark of sound, the samādhi of the mark of fragrance,
the samādhi of the mark of taste, the samādhi of the mark of touch, the samādhi of the mental realm, the samādhi of the female mark, the samādhi of the male mark,
the samādhi of the male youth mark, the samādhi of the female youth mark, the samādhi of the celestial mark, and the samādhi of the nāga [mark].
The samādhi of the form of devas, the samādhi of the form of yakṣas, the samādhi of the form of gandharvas,
the samādhi of the form of asuras, the samādhi of the form of garuḍas, the samādhi of the form of kiṃnaras, the samādhi of the form of mahoragas,
the samādhi of the form of hell-beings, the samādhi of the form of animals, and the samādhi of Yama.
The *samādhi* of the desire realm, the *samādhi* of the characteristic of greed, the *samādhi* of the characteristic of hatred, the *samādhi* of the characteristic of delusion,
the *samādhi* of unwholesome dharmas, the *samādhi* of wholesome dharmas, the *samādhi* of the conditioned, and the *samādhi* of the unconditioned.
Mañjuśrī! If bodhisattvas have thoroughly mastered all such samādhis as these, they have already trained in this Dharma.
Mañjuśrī! What is called the samādhi of the marks of form?
He then spoke in verse:
“Contemplating form as being like a mass of foam, wherein there is no solidity or substance,
and which cannot be grasped— this is called the samādhi of form. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!”
What is called the Samādhi of the Characteristics of Sound?
It is explained in verse:
"Contemplate sound as being like an echo; its nature cannot be apprehended."
"All dharmas are likewise thus: without marks and without differentiation;
to realize that they are all quiescent—this is called the Sound Samādhi. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"
What is called the Samādhi of the Characteristics of Fragrance?
It is explained in verse:
"Even if for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, One were constantly to smell all kinds of fragrances..."
Just as the ocean receives all streams without ever being satiated,
if this fragrance were real, it should likewise be capable of satisfaction;
yet it possesses only a provisional name, for its reality cannot be grasped.
Because it cannot be grasped, the nose also does not exist;
realizing that its nature is empty and quiescent is called the *gandha-samādhi*. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"
What is called the samādhi of the characteristic of taste?
It is stated in verse:
"That which is received by the faculty of the tongue— The various tastes such as salty, sour, and so forth."
All arise from a multitude of conditions; their nature is non-existent.
If one can know them thus—arising through the harmony of causes and conditions—and fully comprehend this inconceivability, this is called the Samādhi of Taste.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the samādhi of the characteristic of contact?
It is stated in verse: [Verse follows]"
"Contact exists only as a name; its intrinsic nature cannot be found.
The various phenomena such as smoothness and so forth all arise from conditions.
If one can understand that the nature of contact arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions,"
"Ultimately non-existent— this is called the samādhi of contact. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
what is called the samādhi of the mind-element?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"Even if all the sentient beings of the three thousandfold world system were to gather together and seek with a single mind, the realm of mind could not be found."
It exists neither internally nor externally, nor can it be gathered together;
it is only through conventional designations that various characteristics are said to exist.
Just like a magical illusion, it has no abiding and no location.
To thoroughly understand that their nature is empty— this is called the samādhi of the mind. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
what is called the samādhi of female characteristics?
Then he spoke in verse:
“The four elements are falsely conceived as a woman; Within them, nothing exists at all.
The deluded minds of ordinary people Grasp at them and take them to be real.”
Women are like illusions and transformations; the foolish cannot comprehend this.
Because they falsely perceive the marks of a woman, they give rise to a mind of defiled attachment.
They are like illusory women created by magic; they are not actual women.
The ignorant are deluded, and thus give rise to thoughts of desire.
Having understood this, one sees that all women are without marks;
these marks are entirely quiescent—this is called the "Woman Samādhi."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Samādhi of Male Characteristics'?
It is stated in verse: [Verse follows]"
"One considers oneself a man, yet perceives another as a woman;
from this discriminating mind, the thought of desire arises.
Yet desire has no inherent existence from the start, for the characteristics of the mind cannot be apprehended."
Due to false conceptualization, one gives rise to the notion of "male" regarding the body.
In reality, there is no male therein; I say it is like a mirage.
Knowing that the characteristic of "male" is quiescent—this is called the Samādhi of the Male.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Samādhi of the Appearance of a Youth'?
It is explained in verse as follows: [Verse follows]"
"Just as when a tree has no roots or branches, flowers cannot be found;
because the flowers do not exist, its fruit likewise does not arise.
Since that woman does not exist, the young man likewise does not exist."
Following conceptual discrimination, such names are provisionally designated.
To understand that both that woman and the young boy do not exist,
and to be able to observe in this way— this is the *kumāra-samādhi*.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Samādhi of the Maiden's Mark'?
It is stated in verse: [Verse follows]"
"Just as when a *tāla* tree is cut down, it never grows again;
what wise person would seek fruit from it?
If there is one who can understand that all phenomena are without arising,"
One should not give rise to conceptual discrimination that a young girl is capable of giving birth;
just as a parched grain seed will never produce a sprout,
so it is with women— this is the samādhi of the young girl.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Samādhi of Celestial Marks'?
It is stated in verse: [Verse follows]"
“Due to pure faith and various virtuous deeds, one receives the superior retribution of the devas: a body of exquisite and wondrous beauty.
Their precious palaces are not produced by artificial construction;”
The wondrous flowers of the maṇḍala have no one who plants them;
likewise, this inconceivable realm arises entirely through the power of karma,
manifesting various forms like pure lapis lazuli.
Such a wondrous body, as well as the various palaces and so forth, all arise from falsehood; this is called the Celestial Samādhi.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
What is called the "Dragon-like Samādhi"?
It is explained in verse:
"Having received these various dragon bodies, It is due to not having cultivated patience."
Raising great clouds and rain, they fill Jambudvīpa;
Neither from the past nor the future, Nor yet in the present interval,
Yet they are able to produce this water, Which then returns once more to the great ocean.
Thus these various nāgas and others, through the differentiation of their accumulated habitual tendencies, give rise to manifold karmas; yet karma itself has no arising.
All things are not real, yet the foolish claim they exist.
To be able to understand in this way is called the Dragon Samādhi.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the Yakṣa-mark Samādhi?
Then he spoke in verse:
"This body of a great yakṣa Arises from one's own mind;
Within it there is no reality, Yet out of delusion fear is born."
Yet they have no mind of fear, nor do they give rise to dread.
Because they contemplate that phenomena are not real, they are signless and unattainable;
in emptiness and the state of quiescence, they manifest this yakṣa form.
To know things thus as false and illusory is the yakṣa-samādhi.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the gandharva-lakṣaṇa-samādhi?
Then he spoke in verse:
"In reality, there is nowhere to go; Names and terms are merely provisional designations.
To fully understand going and non-going— This is the Gandharva Samādhi."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Asura-mark Samādhi'?
It is stated in verse: [Verse follows]"
"Sealed by the marks of the asuras, those marks are fundamentally unarisen;
because they are unarisen, they do not cease—this is the asura-samādhi. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"
What is called the *garuḍa-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*?
It is explained in verse:
"Taking that which is bodiless as a body, Names are merely provisional designations."
"The non-existence of names and signs is the Garuḍa Samādhi. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
what is called the Kiṃnara-mark Samādhi?"
Then he spoke in verse:
“The Dharma is without action yet acts; it is called the Kinnara.
To realize that this is unarisen is the Kinnara Samādhi.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Mahoraga-mark Samādhi'?
It is stated in verse: [Verse follows]"
"Because they rely on names, they establish them according to worldly convention;
yet within this, no phenomenon exists, and so they falsely give rise to conceptualization.
Understanding that these conceptualizations have no inherent nature whatsoever,"
Because those signs are quiescent, it is the Mahoraga Samādhi. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
what is called the Hell-Sign Samādhi?
Then he spoke in verse:
"The hells are empty and signless; their nature is utterly pure.
Within them there is no agent; they arise from one's own conceptual discrimination."
When I sat at the site of enlightenment, I realized this mark of non-arising;
because it is without marks and without arising, its nature is like empty space.
All such marks are utterly quiescent—this is the samādhi of hell.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Samādhi of the Characteristics of Animals'?
It is stated in verse: [Verse follows]"
"Just as clouds manifest various forms, yet within them there is no reality,
so they cause ignorant people to give rise to delusions regarding them;
thus, in the realm of animals, they receive all manner of bodies."
Just as clouds appear in the void, manifesting all manner of forms,
One understands that karma is like an illusion and does not give rise to a deluded mind;
Those signs are fundamentally quiescent— this is the samādhi of animals.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'Yama-realm Samādhi'?
He then spoke in verse: [Verse follows]"
"Those who perform purely black karma, as well as mixed karma,
wander through the realm of Yama and undergo various sufferings.
In truth, there is no realm of Yama, nor is there anyone who wanders."
"Self-nature is fundamentally without arising; all sufferings are like dreams.
If one can contemplate in this way, that is the Samādhi of the Realm of Yama. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī:
What is called the samādhi of the mark of greed?
It is explained in verse:
"Greed arises from conceptual discrimination, And conceptual discrimination, too, does not exist."
Without arising and without marks, its locus cannot be found.
The nature of craving is like space; it is likewise without establishment.
It is through the false discrimination of ordinary beings that the defilement of craving arises.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally unstained, Pure as the empty sky;
Though one searches throughout the ten directions, Its nature cannot be apprehended.
Because they do not understand that its nature is empty, They perceive desire and give rise to fear.
If those who are fearless perceive fear, how can they find peace?
They are like foolish people who are terrified of empty space;
struck with alarm, they run about, seeking to avoid and not behold the void.
Space pervades all things; from what could it be separated?
Because fools are deluded, inverted conceptualizations arise.
Greed has no inherent nature; yet they falsely give rise to a mind of revulsion and detachment.
Just as one who wishes to avoid space can never escape it;
The nature of all phenomena is inherently detached, just like nirvāṇa.
All Buddhas of the three times thoroughly understand that the nature of greed is empty.
Abiding within this state, one never departs from it;
for those who fear and dread desire, contemplate and seek liberation.
Thus, the very nature of desire is ultimately and eternally pure.
When I realized awakening, I understood all things to be equal.
If one clings to greed as being existent, one should abandon it;
yet, because of false conceptualization, one speaks of "abandoning greed."
This is merely the discriminating mind; in reality, there is nothing to be abandoned.
Its nature is ungraspable, and it is without cessation or destruction.
Within the equality of the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), there is no discrimination regarding liberation.
If one is liberated from desire, one is also liberated from emptiness;
space and desire are inexhaustible and without distinction.
If one perceives a distinction between them, I say that such a person must abandon it.
Greed truly has no arising; it is through delusion that conceptualization arises.
That greed is empty of intrinsic nature and exists only as a provisional name;
one should not give rise to attachment based on this name.
Because one realizes that desire is without defilement, this is ultimate emptiness;
it is not by the destruction of desire that one attains liberation.
The nature of desire and the Buddha-dharma are equal, and this is nirvana.
The wise one should know that, having realized the stillness of craving, they enter the realm of tranquility; this is called the samādhi of craving. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
What is called the samādhi of the characteristics of anger?
It is explained in verse:
"Through false causes and conditions, One gives rise to anger."
Grasping at what is selfless as a self, and through harsh words,
one gives rise to a fierce mind of anger; yet just as with a virulent poison,
both sound and anger ultimately have no existence whatsoever.
Just as fire is produced by drilling wood, it requires the power of various conditions;
if the conditions do not harmonize, the fire will never arise.
These unpleasant sounds are ultimately non-existent.
Because one knows the nature of sound is empty, anger no longer arises.
Anger does not reside in the sound, nor does it dwell within the body;
it arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and apart from those conditions, it never arises.
Just as when conditions such as milk combine, butter and curd are produced,
so too does anger arise from harsh and evil sounds; yet the foolish do not understand its nature,
and they burn themselves with the heat of their own afflictions.
One should understand it thus: ultimately there is nothing at all.
The nature of anger is fundamentally quiescent; it exists only as a provisional designation.
Anger itself is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), for it arises based upon suchness (*tathatā*).
To understand [all things] as being like the dharma-realm is called the samādhi of hatred.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the samādhi of the characteristic of delusion?
Then he spoke in verse:
“The nature of ignorance is empty; It is fundamentally without arising.
Within it there is not the slightest dharma That can be described as delusion.”
Ordinary beings give rise to deluded thoughts regarding that which is free from delusion, and produce attachment toward that which is unattached, as if they were binding empty space.
How strange are these ignorant people! They do what ought not to be done.
All phenomena are non-existent; they arise from the conceptualization of afflictions.
It is like attempting to grasp space and place it in a single location;
even if one were to pass through ten million eons, there would never be any accumulation.
From the very beginning, for inconceivable eons,
the delusive fetters that have arisen in fools have not increased by even the slightest degree.
Just as when one grasps at space, there is ultimately no increase or decrease.
Having accumulated delusion over many eons, its increase and decrease are likewise so.
Just as a bellows receives wind without limit or end,
the fool who clings to sensual pleasure never knows satiety.
This delusion is non-existent; it has no root and no place of abiding.
Because its root does not exist, there is likewise no delusion to be exhausted.
Since delusion is inexhaustible, its limit cannot be found.
Therefore, I am unable to bring all sentient beings to their end. Even if,
within a single day, I were able to deliver all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm and cause them all to enter nirvana, [the cycle would still not cease].
Furthermore, throughout inconceivable and immeasurable thousands of millions of kalpas,
he transforms beings in this manner day after day, yet the realm of sentient beings is never exhausted.
The realm of ignorance and the realm of sentient beings— these two are both devoid of marks.
All these are like illusions and transformations, and thus cannot be brought to an end.
The nature of delusion and the Buddha-nature are equal and without distinction;
if one discriminates regarding the Buddha, one remains in ignorance.
Ignorance and all-encompassing wisdom— Their nature cannot be apprehended;
yet all those sentient beings Are entirely equal to ignorance.
Sentient beings are inconceivable, And ignorance is likewise inconceivable.
Because it is inconceivable, one should not engage in conceptual discrimination.
When the mind is contemplated in this way, it cannot be apprehended through deliberation;
even delusion cannot be measured, for it is without limit.
Since there is no limit, from what could it arise?
Because its intrinsic nature is non-arising, its characteristics are likewise unapprehendable.
Having realized that delusion has no characteristics, one views the Buddha in the same way.
One should know thus: all phenomena are non-dual.
The nature of delusion is fundamentally quiescent; it exists only as a provisional name.
When I realized awakening, I likewise understood the equality of delusion.
To be able to contemplate in this way is called the samādhi of delusion.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the 'unwholesome samādhi'?
Then he spoke in verse:
"Knowing that greed, hatred, and delusion, And all various afflictions,
As well as the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena, Are false and devoid of reality."
To be able to observe in this way is the non-virtuous samādhi. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
what is called the virtuous dharma samādhi?
Then he spoke in verse:
“You should all know that those with virtuous inclinations,
though their mental activities differ individually, are all identical in their single practice.”
Because one understands through the single characteristic of renunciation that all things are entirely quiescent, this is called "skillful samādhi. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
What is called the conditioned samādhi?
It is stated in verse:
"You all should know that all conditioned phenomena..."
It is not something created, nor is it capable of being measured.
I have realized that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are by nature without accumulation;
they are entirely quiescent—this is called the conditioned samādhi.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what is called the unconditioned samādhi?
He then spoke in verse: [Verse follows]"
“The unconditioned nature is quiescent; within it there is no attachment, nor is there any departure, for there are only provisional names.
For the sake of sentient beings who cling, those names are spoken.”
"To be able to understand in this way is called the unconditioned samādhi.

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these inconceivable and subtle verses, ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); thirty-six thousand bhikṣus attained liberation of mind from all outflows (*āsrava*);

and seventy-two trillion nayutas of devas, along with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, one million eight hundred thousand upāsakas, and two thousand two hundred upāsikās, all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound for the sake of all bodhisattvas the names of various samādhis, so that those who hear them may have their faculties sharpened and become keen, attain the light of wisdom regarding all dharmas, and not be overcome by any sentient beings with false views; furthermore, may they realize the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence, such that within a single syllable they can understand various syllables, and within all syllables they understand a single syllable."

Furthermore, with boundless eloquence, he skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma for all sentient beings, enabling them to realize the profound patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) and to comprehend all modes of conduct in a single instant.
"All these conditioned phenomena each possess further infinite modes of manifestation, all of which he is able to fully comprehend. The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"
There is a samādhi called Boundless Freedom from Defilement; if a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they can manifest all pure forms.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi called Terrifying Face; if one attains this samādhi, they possess great majestic radiance that eclipses the sun and moon.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Emanating Blazing Light"; having attained this samādhi, one can eclipse all the majestic radiance of Śakra and Brahmā.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Renunciation"; having attained this samādhi, one causes all sentient beings to renounce all greed, anger, and delusion.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Unobstructed Light; having attained this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all buddha-fields.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Non-Forgetfulness; having attained this samādhi, one is able to uphold the teachings spoken by all Buddhas and can also expound their meaning for others.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Thunder Sound; having attained this samādhi, one is well able to manifest all vocal sounds, reaching upward as far as the Brahma world.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Joyful Delight; having attained this samādhi, one causes all sentient beings to be fulfilled with joy and delight.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Inexhaustible Joy"; having attained this samādhi, those who see or hear it can never be satiated.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Inconceivable Merit of Single-Pointed Focus"; having attained this samādhi, one is able to manifest all manner of spiritual transformations.

Furthermore, there is a samādhi called "Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings. Having attained this samādhi, one is well able to proclaim all languages; within a single syllable, one speaks all syllables, and understands that all syllables are identical to a single syllable.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Surpassing All Dhāraṇī Kings"; having attained this samādhi, one is able to thoroughly understand all dhāraṇīs.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Adorned with All Eloquence"; having attained this samādhi, one is well able to discern all characters and various sounds of speech.

Furthermore, there is a samādhi called "Accumulation of All Wholesome Dharmas. Having attained this samādhi, one can cause all sentient beings to hear the voice of the Buddha, the voice of the Dharma, the voice of the Saṃgha, the voices of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the voices of the pāramitās; thus, when a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they cause the voices of all sentient beings to be heard without interruption.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One will exert his majestic power and grant his protective mindfulness, so that I may attain unimpeded eloquence to proclaim the sublime merits of this Dharma-gate."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! It shall be according to your wish.”
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are bodhisattvas who receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma-gate without any doubt or hesitation, you should know that such persons will, in their present bodies, certainly obtain four kinds of eloquence: namely, swift eloquence, vast eloquence, profound eloquence, and inexhaustible eloquence. They will constantly protect and mindfully attend to all sentient beings; and regarding those who would seek to destroy whatever they practice, they are able to awaken them so that no destruction occurs."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are able to skillfully discern this meaning: just as a donor obtains great wealth, so one who upholds the prohibitive precepts will certainly be reborn in heaven.”
If one is able to receive and uphold this sutra, the eloquence attained in the present will certainly not be in vain.

Just as the rising sun can dispel all darkness, and just as it is certain and beyond doubt that a Bodhisattva seated upon the seat of enlightenment will attain perfect awakening, so too is it for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra: they shall attain eloquence in the present.

Mañjuśrī! If there should be anyone who, in this present body, desires to seek eloquence, they should give rise to faith and joy toward this sutra, receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it to others, without giving rise to doubt or hesitation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, have no doubt or hesitation regarding this Dharma-gate, and receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it for others, I shall sustain them and augment their eloquence.”
At that time, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, overcome with grief, affliction, and distress, came weeping and shedding tears to where the Buddha was, and addressed him, saying:
"When the Tathāgata previously realized unsurpassed bodhi, I already harbored sorrow and affliction at that time."
Furthermore, now that this Dharma-gate is being preached, they experience a redoubled great suffering as if pierced by a poisoned arrow.
If sentient beings hear this sutra, they will certainly never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will enter parinirvāṇa, thereby leaving my realm entirely empty.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is able to cause all sentient beings suffering to attain peace and happiness, we pray that you will deign to show compassion and great loving-kindness, bestowing your majestic protection and mindfulness upon this sutra, so that I may be secure and all my anxieties and sufferings removed.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pāpīyān, saying:
"Do not harbor grief or distress.
I shall not bestow my protective empowerment upon this Dharma, nor shall all sentient beings enter parinirvāṇa."
Upon hearing these words, the Māra Pāpīyān was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; his anxieties and distress were entirely dispelled, and he suddenly vanished from before the Buddha.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What hidden intention does the Tathāgata have now that he tells Pāpīyān, ‘I shall not provide protection for this Dharma’?”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! Because this Dharma is protected by the protection of non-protection, for that reason I speak these words to them."

Because all phenomena are the equal limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), they all return to suchness and are identical with the dharma-realm; since they are free from all verbal expression and possess the characteristic of non-duality, there is nothing further to be protected or guarded.
"By virtue of these words of mine being truthful and free from falsehood, may this sutra be widely circulated and propagated throughout Jambudvīpa.
When the World-Honored One had finished speaking these words, he addressed Ānanda, saying:

"This sutra is named 'The Universal Entry into the Inconceivable Dharma-Gate. If one can receive and uphold such a scripture as this, it is no different from receiving and upholding the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates."
Why is this? Because only after I have thoroughly mastered this sutra am I able to expound the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates for those sentient beings.
"Therefore, Ānanda! You should skillfully protect and uphold this Dharma; read, recite, and circulate it so that it is not forgotten or lost.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Vimalagarbha Bodhisattva, the Venerable Ānanda, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Twenty-nine;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Thirty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
11. The Assembly on the Manifestation of Radiance, Part One of Eleven.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom had attained great mastery.
Furthermore, there were eighty nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), with the Bodhisattva Maitreya as their leader;
additionally, there were forty nayutas of great bodhisattvas, with the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī and others as their leaders.

At that time, there was a youth in the assembly named Candraprabha. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
What kind of karma did the Tathāgata cultivate in the past that he was able to attain such definitive light,
encompassing light, initiating light, manifesting light, light of various colors, unmixed-colored light, narrow light, vast light, and pure light?
All-pure radiance, stainless radiance, utterly stainless radiance, defilement-free radiance,
progressively increasing radiance, fresh and pure radiance, extremely fresh and pure radiance,
boundless radiance, extremely boundless radiance, immeasurable radiance, and extremely immeasurable radiance.
immeasurable light, extremely immeasurable light, swift light, extremely swift light,
non-abiding light, placeless light, blazing light, illuminating light, delightful light, light that reaches the other shore, and unobstructed light.
The light of clarity, the light of immovability, the light of rectitude, the light of abiding in the sphere of infinite space,
the light of physical forms, the light of various physical forms, the light of immeasurable physical forms,
the light of physical forms in blue, yellow, red, and white, the light of crimson physical forms, and the light of crystal-colored physical forms.
The luminous marks of the void and such various kinds of light as these all manifest in combination with the five-colored lights;
even phenomena such as blue, yellow, red, and white each likewise manifest in combination with immeasurable and boundless varieties of colored light?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Candraprabha:
"By means of inconceivable And the causal conditions of virtuous karma,
I have distanced myself from all delusions And accomplished various kinds of light."
Furthermore, through various practices, they abide securely in the Buddha-way;
by means of the wisdom of emptiness and non-action, they manifest light in harmonious union.
Just as within external phenomena, there are various distinct characteristics and differences, [so too is this].
Within this, there is emptiness, no self, no action, and no mind.
Just as within the internal body there is emptiness, no self, and no action,
yet from within it various kinds of sounds can be manifested.
Through such non-action, he manifests boundless rays of colored light;
according to their respective inclinations, he causes them all to attain fulfillment.
Or, within a single ray of light, he brings forth two kinds of colors.
Each possesses the superior, the middling, and the inferior, appearing with distinct differentiation.
Or, within a single ray of light, three kinds of colors are produced,
each possessing the superior, the middling, and the inferior, appearing with distinct differentiation.
Or within a single ray of light, four kinds of colors are produced,
each distinguished as superior, middling, or inferior, manifesting in their differences.
Or within a single ray of light, five kinds of colors are produced.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior [qualities], arising from pure karma.
Or within a single ray of light, six kinds of colors are produced;
each has its superior, middling, and inferior, arising from skillful means.
Or within a single ray of light, seven kinds of colors are produced,
each having superior, middling, and inferior qualities, all arising from virtuous karma.
Or within a single ray of light, eight kinds of colors are produced.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from supreme goodness.
Or, within a single ray of light, nine kinds of colors are produced;
each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from the accumulations.
Or within a single ray of light, ten kinds of colors are produced, each having superior, middling, and inferior qualities; these arise from the practice of giving.
Or within a single phenomenon, twenty colors are produced.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from the observance of precepts.
Or within a single matter, thirty forms are produced, each with its superior,
middling, and inferior aspects, arising from the practice of patience.
Or within a single phenomenon, forty forms arise, each with its superior, middling, and inferior qualities; these are born from diligence.
Or within a single phenomenon, fifty forms arise.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Within a single phenomenon, sixty colors may arise, each with its superior,
middling, and inferior aspects, born from wisdom (*prajñā*).
Or within a single object, seventy colors arise, each having superior, middling, and inferior qualities; these are born from a mind of loving-kindness.
Or within a single object, eighty colors arise.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from a mind of compassion.
Or, within a single object, ninety colors may arise, each with its superior,
middling, and inferior aspects, arising from a mind of joy.
Or from within a single object, one may produce a hundred kinds of forms,
each having superior, middling, and inferior qualities, all arising from a mind of equanimity.
Or from within a single object, one may produce a thousand kinds of forms.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from a thousand merits.
Or, within a single phenomenon, it gives rise to ten thousand kinds of forms;
each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from the provisions of merit.
Or within a single object, one may manifest ten million colors,
each having superior, middling, and inferior qualities, arising from pure faith.
Or within a single object, one may manifest twenty million colors.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Or, within a single phenomenon, three koṭis of colors appear, each with its superior,
middling, and inferior aspects, arising from pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Or within a single object, he manifests four koṭis of colors, each having superior, middling, and inferior qualities; these arise from honoring the Buddha.
Or within a single object, he manifests five koṭis of colors.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from honoring the Dharma.
Or, within a single object, six koṭis of colors appear, each with its superior,
middling, and inferior aspects, arising from honoring the Saṅgha.
Or within a single object, he manifests seven koṭis of colors, each with its own superior, middling, and inferior qualities;
these arise from his reverent observance of the precepts.
Or within a single object, he manifests eight koṭis of colors.
Each has its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from the concentration of reverence.
Or, within a single object, he manifests nine koṭis of forms,
each with its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, arising from universal compassion.
Or within a single object, they manifest ten koṭis of colors, each with superior, middling, and inferior qualities; these arise from non-negligence.
Furthermore, from a single pore, all manner of radiances are manifested.
The various names of those lights shall now be explained for you.
I possess a single light named Cloud-Pure-Illumination;
that light arises from the accumulation of immeasurable roots of goodness.
In times of yore, seeing sentient beings afflicted by various and manifold illnesses and distresses,
you gave rise to a heart of compassion and bestowed all manner of medicines upon them, causing them all to be healed and restored.
By these causes and conditions, I have attained such radiance.
Furthermore, I possess another light called "Purity of the Eye," which was born from my offering of lamps to the Buddha.
I have another light, named "Purity of the Ear," which arose from making offerings through sound.
I have another light, named "Purity of the Nose."
Because I made offerings with fragrant water, I was born from this cause.
Furthermore, I possess a light called "Pure Tongue," because I made offerings with the most excellent flavors, I was born from this cause.
I possess yet another radiance, named "Purity of Body," which arose because I made offerings of robes;
I possess yet another radiance, named "Purity of Mind."
Because I always had faith and joy in the Buddha, I was born here for this reason.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance called "Pure Color," which arose because I painted images of the Buddha.
I have another light, named Pure Sound;
because I constantly praised the Dharma, I was born from this.
I have another light, named Pure Fragrance;
I was always respectful toward the Saṃgha; because of this, I have been born here.
Furthermore, I possess a light called "Pure Flavor," which I bestow according to everyone's wishes; because of this, I have been born here.
I have another radiance, named "Purity of Touch," which arose from making offerings of fragrant ointments;
I have another radiance, named "Purity of Dharma."
Because I gathered and upheld all dharmas, I was born from this cause.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named "Pure Earth," which arose because I swept and cleansed the grounds of the Buddhas and the Saṅgha.
I also possess a light named "Water Purity," which arose from making offerings of wells and springs; for this reason, it was born.
I also possess a light named "Fire Purity."
I offered a lamp by holding it aloft; from this, that [light] was born.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named "Wind-Purity," which was born because I offered a fan by holding it aloft.
I also possess a radiance, named "Purity of the Aggregates" (skandha-viśuddhi),
which arose from making offerings to the Buddha with my body.
I also possess a radiance, named "Purity of the Elements" (dhātu-viśuddhi).
I constantly cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, and by this means I was born here.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named "Utterly Pure," for I always remained free from false speech; it is by this that I have been born here.
I have another light, named "Pure Realm," Which was born from my constant practice of giving.
I have another light, named "Pure Sound," And so forth.
Because I praised all the Buddhas, I was born from this cause.
Furthermore, I possess a light named "Pure Mindfulness," because I praised samādhi, I was born from this cause.
I also possess a light, named "Pure Eloquence," which was born from praising the dhāraṇī; therefore it came into being.
I also possess a light, named "Harmony with the Sun."
Because it reconciles discord, it is born from this;
I also possess a light named "Manifesting Meaning," which arises because it penetrates the nature of emptiness.
I further possess a radiance, named the "Blue-Colored Mark," which arose from making offerings of blue lotuses; thus was it obtained.
I further possess a radiance, named the "Yellow-Colored Mark."
Because I made an offering of campaka flowers, I was born from this cause.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance called "Red Appearance," which arose because I made an offering of pearls.
I also possess a light, named "White Appearance," which arose from making offerings of golden lotuses;
I also possess a light, named "Supreme Merit."
Adorned with various colors, it was from this that I attained birth.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named Dragon Power;
because I made an offering of a dragon-bannered pennant, it was from this that I attained birth.
I have another light, named Elephant Power;
because I made offerings with elephant banners, I was born from this cause.
I have another light, named Lion King.
I made an offering of a lion banner; by virtue of this, I was born here.
Furthermore, I have a radiance named "Bull King";
I made an offering of a bull king banner, and by virtue of this, I was born here.
I have another radiance, named Moon-Purity;
because I swept and cleansed the Buddha’s stūpa, I was born by virtue of this.
I have another radiance, named Subduing the Dragons.
I offered a silk band as a gift; by virtue of this, I attained birth.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named "Subduer of Yakṣas";
because I was able to observe with clear discernment, by virtue of this, I attained birth.
I further possess a light named Awakening Woman;
because she is free from the characteristics of womanhood, it is from this that she is born.
I further possess a light named Awakening Man.
Because of being free from the mark of masculinity, I was thus born.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named Vajra-Power;
because of the purity of karmic wisdom, I was thus born.
I further possess a light named "Manifesting Emptiness," which reveals the retributions of the world; from this it arises.
I further possess a light named "Awakening to Reality."
Because it is free from inversion, it is born from this;
I also possess a light named "Revealing the Buddha’s Words," which praises the dharma-realm, and it is born from this.
I further possess a light named "Free from All Faults," which arose because I praised resolute conviction.
I further possess a light named "Adorned Universal Radiance."
Because I praised the offering of lamps, I was born here by virtue of that cause.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance called "Free from Affection," which arose because I praised meditative concentration and wisdom; it is by virtue of this that I was born.
I have another radiance, named "Free from All Habitual Tendencies," which arises because I praised the wisdom regarding the prior limit.
I have another radiance, named "Free from All Attachments."
Because I praised the knowledge of non-arising, I was born from this cause.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named "Departing from All Destinies," because I praised the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, I was born from this cause.
I have another light, named "Abandoning the Place," which arises from praising the wisdom of suffering; for this reason, it is born.
I have another light, named "The Buddha’s Supernatural Transformation."
Because I praised the power of supernormal knowledges, I was born here for this reason.
Furthermore, I possess a radiance named "Transcending Conceptual Proliferation," because I praised all-knowledge, I was born here for this reason.
I possess another radiance, named Manifesting All Colors;
because I praised the supernormal powers, I was born from this.
I possess another radiance, named Delighting in Good Friends.
Because I praised the nature of awakening, I was born from this;
I also possess a light named "The Limit of the Eye," and because I praised the limit of the eye, I was born from this.
I further possess a light, named "Limit of the Eye's Exhaustion," which arises from praising that which is inexhaustible.
I further possess a light, named "Limit of Existence."
Because I praised non-existence, I was born from this;
I also possess a radiance named "Indestructible," because I praised the nature of cessation, I was born from this.
I possess another radiance, named "The Boundless," which arose from praising that which is without limit;
I possess another radiance, named "The Characterized."
Because I praised the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I was born from this;
I also possess a light named "Unchanging," because I praised non-differentiation, I was born from this.
I further possess a radiance named "Non-Entry," Which praises non-attachment; It is from this that it arises.
I further possess a radiance named "Non-Emergence."
Because it praises non-arising, it is thereby born.
I also have a light called "Non-arising," because it praises non-manifestation, it is thereby born.
"I possess a light named 'Non-indication,' which is able to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
I possess a light named 'Dharma-nature,' whose radiance can shake billions of lands."
I have a light named "Subduing Māras," its majestic power strikes terror into Māra.
I have a light named "Banner of Merit"; those who hold its name shall be freed from peril and distress.
I have a light named Banner of Power; those who hold its name are freed from adversaries.
I have a light named Banner of Tranquility; those who hold its name are freed from craving.
I have a light named Banner of Meditative Concentration; those who hold its name leave behind unwholesome conduct.
I have a light named Banner of Renown; those who hold its name attain praise.
I have a light named Banner of Delight; those who hold its name shall be free from sorrow and affliction.
I have a light named Banner of Pure Precepts; those who hold its name shall be free from the violation of prohibitions.
I have a light named "Exquisite Fragrance Banner"; those who hold its name shall be free from foul odors.
I have a light named "Profound Dharma"; those who hold its name shall be free from doubt and confusion.
I have a light named "Non-abiding"; those who hold its name leave all states of existence behind.
I have a light named "Free from Discrimination"; those who hold its name are without grasping.
I have a light named Sumeru; those who hold its name cannot be moved.
I have a light named Secret Conduct; those who hold its name are free from attachment.
I have a light named "Liberating Conduct"; those who hold its name shall be free from bondage.
I have a light named "Excellent Subduing"; those who hold its name shall attain gentleness.
I have a light named "Unwavering"; those who hold its name are free from the defilement of greed.
I have a light named "Well-Subdued"; those who hold its name are perfected in ethical discipline.
I have a light named "Multitude of Wholesome Deeds"; those who hold its name shall be unstained.
I have a light named "Great Benefit"; those who hear its name shall be free from all faults.
I have a light named "Victorious Knowledge and Vision"; those who hear its name shall be free from delusion.
I have a light named "Seeking Benefit"; those who hear its name shall be free from anger.
I have a light named "Mental Joy," by hearing its name one attains peace and happiness.
I have a light named "Free from Heat and Affliction," by upholding its name one realizes the nature of emptiness.
I have a light named "Emptiness and Lack of Self-Nature"; those who hold its name transcend conceptual proliferation.
I have a light named "Non-Reliance"; those who hold its name remain unshakable.
I have a light named "Free from Delusion"; those who hold its name shall have no hesitation.
I have a light named "Without Abiding Place"; those who hold its name shall be free from the darkness of ignorance.
I have a light named "Disgust for the Fleshly Body"; those who hold its name shall not undergo rebirth.
I have a light named "Nothing to Be Grasped"; those who hold its name transcend all words and letters.
I have a light named "Free from Delusion"; those who hold its name transcend all verbal expression.
I have a light named "Without a Place of Departure"; those who hold its name know the future.
I have a light named Universal Limit; those who hold its name know the past.
I have a light named Peerless; those who hold its name realize the outflow-free.
I have a light named "Realizing the Holy," and those who hold its name shall know the supreme.
I have a light named "Free from Defilement," and those who hold its name shall be detached from all attachments.
I have a light named "Free from Dust"; those who hold its name shall have no darkness or obscuration.
I have a light named "Free from Attachment"; those who hold its name shall be liberated from all dependence.
I have a light named Most Supreme; those who hold its name shall defeat the arguments of others.
I have a light named Youthful Vigor; those who hold its name shall accomplish the six practices.
I have a light named Most Victorious Honored One; those who hold its name possess unimpeded wisdom.
I have a radiance named Swift; those who hold its name become the supreme Saṅgha.
I have a light named "Possessing Characteristics"; those who uphold its name realize the profound Dharma.
I have a light named "Characteristics-less"; those who uphold its name are free from conceit.
I possess a radiance named "Non-arising"; those who uphold its name shall attain non-attainment.
I possess a radiance named "Recollection of the Buddhas," praised by all Tathāgatas;
having cultivated various practices in the presence of many Buddhas, one then succeeds in accomplishing such light.
The various rays of light manifested from the Buddha’s body are as numerous as the atoms within a thousand koṭis of lands;
such immeasurable koṭis of lands are as many as the sands of the great ocean.
Within each and every atom, there are rays of light, each with its own vast retinue of attendants.
That light pervades all Buddha-fields where no Buddhas dwell, Manifesting the pure bodies of Tathāgatas,
Proclaiming the profound and subtle Dharma, And establishing sentient beings in the practice of patience.
I possess a radiance named "Buddha," which causes all sentient beings to abide in the Buddha-way.
I possess a radiance named "Dharma," which is pure, brilliantly illuminating, and free from all blemish or defilement.
I possess a light named Saṃgha, praised by all the Tathāgatas;
I possess a light named Viśuddha, a radiance that is supreme and exceedingly rare to obtain.
I have a light named "Flower," which benefits sentient beings and brings them to maturity.
I have a light named "Brahmā," or named "Śakra," or named "Deva";
It is named "Moon," named "Nāga," and named "Yakṣa"; It is named "Asura" and "Garuḍa."
Some are named kings or named women, some are named maidens or named boys;
through such various kinds of radiance, each transforms their own kind by means of wholesome dharmas,
enabling countless koṭis of beings to all achieve enlightenment.
I possess a radiance named Wisdom; some are named Discipline or named Compassion;
some are named Joy or named Lamp; some are called Ointment or named Music—such various kinds of radiances are each designated according to their original practice.
They gather in all immeasurable classes of sentient beings; from this, they achieve this radiance.
I possess a radiance named "Venerable," praised by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
always showing reverence for the Buddha’s teachings, from this, they achieve this radiance.
As many sentient beings as are seen by the Buddha-eye, From a single pore he manifests manifold rays of light;
Each and every one of those lights Is surrounded by its own retinue.
According to what sentient beings think in their minds, They are all brought to maturity by the Buddha’s radiance.
If there are those who, upon hearing this discourse on light, can give rise to joy and profound delight,
such persons have in the past already heard such a sūtra from the presence of various Buddhas.
I possess a light named Most Supreme, with a retinue numbering eighty koṭis;
