because I once praised the Buddha with a single verse, I have thereby accomplished this light.
I possess a light named "Sorrowless," with a retinue of eighty nayutas;
because I uphold the Dharma taught by a single Tathāgata, I have thus accomplished this light.
I possess a radiance named Supreme Purity, with a retinue numbering eighty koṭis;
if one can receive and uphold even a single samādhi, one shall therefore achieve this radiance.
"In the past there was a Buddha named Most Victorious; that Buddha dwelt in the world for an immeasurable lifespan.
When he first attained the Way, within his assembly of the Dharma, there were eighty nayutas of followers."
At that time, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Rāvaṇa.
That king also had five hundred princes, whose countenances were upright and handsome,
bringing joy to all who beheld them.
At that time, the father-king, possessing sovereign majesty and virtue, conceived deep faith and joy toward the Triple Gem.
All the king’s most excellent and wondrous gardens and groves were entirely offered as gifts to that Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Within this garden, in the places for walking meditation,
there were furthermore immeasurable *campaka* trees, *kovidāra* trees, *cāmpeya* trees, *udumbara*, *pāṭala*, as well as *śirīṣa* trees.
The *aśoka* trees and others, each numbering eighty *koṭis*,
all these trees flourish throughout both winter and summer; their flowers, fruits, branches,
and leaves are radiant and lush, emitting a subtle fragrance that perfumes the body of the Tathāgata.
There were bhikṣus whose bodies were of true golden color;
each sat beneath the trees of this forest, valiant and diligent, having attained dhāraṇīs.
At that time, that Buddha, out of compassion for his father the king,
as well as for the princes and the rest of the great assembly, expounded this Sūtra of Resolute Radiance.
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he praised the Tathāgata with immeasurable verses.
The king further offered eighty koṭis of exquisite jeweled parasols to the Buddha.
Each individual jeweled canopy is adorned all around with mani-jewels set within its latticework.
Each of these mani-jewels is worth eighty koṭis of Jambūnada gold.
Each of these canopies is adorned with eighty *koṭi* of maṇi jewels serving as necklaces.
These maṇi jewels are of brilliant and pure color; they have neither day nor night, for they constantly emit radiance.
Each individual ray of light shines for a hundred yojanas; its brilliance outshines both the sun and the moon.
There are eighty koṭis of lion-jewel girdles and jeweled garlands of golden thread.
Its four sides were magnificently adorned;
furthermore, it was decorated with various exquisite colors and rare wonders, interspersed with nets of genuine jewels.
Encompassing the gardens and groves, upon them there are furthermore *sumanā* flowers, *atimuktaka*, *mucilinda*, *udumbara*,
blue lotuses, and other such varieties— countless flower canopies of every kind.
Each and every one was adorned in accordance with its jeweled net.
Furthermore, canopies made of golden thread and *kūṭāgāra* cloth were fashioned as silk awnings to cover them above.
Furthermore, there were golden pedestals and sandalwood jewel beds,
numbering eighty koṭis.
These beds were further adorned with eighty koṭis of silk brocades and cushions.
All classes of sentient beings, even up to the Summit of Existence,
have all gathered together in the presence of the Tathāgata to listen to this sutra.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharva kings, mahoragas, asuras, and so forth—
Having heard this sutra, they gave rise to a heart of joy and praised the Tathāgata with hundreds of thousands of verses;
all of them then brought forth the great vow for Bodhi.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits, as well as the asuras, with profound and pure hearts,
rained down māndārava flowers, pearls, and other jewels as an offering.
At that time, there were also eighty koṭis of devas of great majesty who,
having heard this sutra, felt joy in their hearts and made the vow for bodhi,
so that in future ages they might obtain this radiance.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing their inclinations, immediately bestowed upon them the prediction that they would become Buddhas.
Then there were also eighty koṭis of Śakras, Indras, along with the hosts of Brahmās, who,
having heard this exposition of the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, [were likewise inspired].
They too gave rise to joy and resolved upon bodhicitta; all received the prediction that they would become Buddhas in the future.
Having heard this sutra, nayutas of nāgas also resolved upon bodhicitta.
All received their predictions of enlightenment.
Having heard this sutra, the King of the Golden-Winged Birds also maintained the five precepts and was likewise granted his prediction.
The Gandharva King, having heard this sutra, performed a thousand kinds of music,
producing subtle and wondrous sounds to make offerings to the Buddha, and thereby received a prediction of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there were eighty nayutas of yakṣa kings who,
having heard this sutra, conceived deep and pure faith in the Buddha’s wisdom;
they all received the prediction of their future enlightenment.
At that time, was the King of Music, who made all manner of offerings to that Tathāgata,
anyone else? It was none other than you yourself.
Because you heard this sutra in the past, you now once again inquire about it.
If there should be someone who, after my parinirvāṇa, at the time when the Wheel of Dharma is about to perish, gives rise to pure faith within this teaching—
Then one will be able to expound extensively such a sutra as this:
"If, in the future, one speaks this sutra, one thereby protects and upholds my Dharma;
like a skilled guide for a multitude of merchants, one is also called a protector of the treasure-store."
If, in the final age, one hears this sutra and gives rise to joy for even as long as a finger-snap,
know that this is entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the protection bestowed by Mañjuśrī.
Such a person shall behold all Buddhas, who will bestow secret teachings upon them to make them wise.
If a person is upright, their mind supple, and they constantly and diligently make offerings to all Buddhas;
if they practice non-self and give rise to compassion and patience—such a person will love and delight in this sutra.
If a person constantly harbors unwholesome thoughts, greedily seeking gain and honor without satiety,
and feels no admiration for tranquility, such a person will not delight in this sutra.
If a person makes offerings to all Tathāgatas, Is well able to understand the profound and wondrous Dharma,
And gives rise to pure faith in the Buddha’s right wisdom, That person will love and delight in this sutra.
If a person is distracted and lacks a pure mind, constantly acting as an executioner and difficult to tame,
serving as a slave to the realms of desire— such a person does not delight in this sutra.
If a person always delights in the araṇya, dwelling alone in seclusion with a tranquil mind,
unattached to gain and kin, such a person will love and delight in this sutra.
If a person follows evil companions, they will destroy all wholesome dharmas for themselves and others;
such a person will greatly fall away from ethical discipline and meditative concentration, and will take no delight in this sutra.
If a person’s aspiration is utterly pure, And they constantly contemplate all phenomena with wisdom,
Being protected by virtuous spiritual friends, Such a person will love and delight in this sutra.
If a person is bound by attachment to the homes of relatives and friends, giving them flowers and fruits to please them,
and whose mind lacks uprightness while harboring deceit and crookedness— such a person will not delight in this sutra.
If a person constantly keeps in mind the kindness of all Buddhas, And gives rise to love and joy for supreme roots of goodness,
Dedicating them toward Bodhi without guile or crookedness— Such a person loves and delights in this sutra.
If a person is attached to women, adorning themselves with various fine garments and ornaments,
and constantly desires to sport with them, such a person will not delight in this sutra.
If a person’s profound mind has no dependence, And is never stained by the objects of desire,
Nor gives rise to flattery for the sake of food or drink— Such a person loves and delights in this sutra.
If a person instructs all living beings, saying that sexual desire is free from fault, they slander the Buddhas of the three periods of time; such a person does not delight in this sutra.
If a person’s faith and delight are always firm and steadfast, And they initiate diligence to seek all dharmas,
Without giving rise to weariness or contempt, Such a person will love and delight in this sutra.
If a person is bound by attachment to women, constantly harboring thoughts of sensual objects,
and fails to cultivate wisdom for the sake of broad benefit, such a person will not delight in this sutra.
If a person dwells in seclusion within mountain forests, cultivating wisdom until it is entirely pure,
and does not crave any of the necessities of life, that person will love and delight in this sutra.

If a person is constantly deluded regarding the past and future limits of the present, and cannot comprehend them, that person is a fool caught in the snare of Māra; such a person does not delight in this sutra.

If a person, regarding the past and future limits of the present moment, always penetrates them without delusion, they shall be liberated from the snares of all Māras; such a person delights in this sutra.

If a person regards the eye as being infinite, yet remains constantly deluded and unable to comprehend it, that person is a fool caught in the snare of Māra; such a person takes no delight in this sutra.
If a person perceives the eye as being boundless, And always penetrates it without delusion, They shall be liberated from the snares of all Māras; Such a person delights in this sutra.

If a person is constantly deluded regarding the marks of the eye’s formation and disintegration and cannot comprehend them, that person is a fool caught in the snare of Māra; such a person does not delight in this sutra.

If a person, regarding the eye’s characteristics of formation and disintegration, Always penetrates them without delusion, they shall be liberated from the snares of all Māras; Such a person will love and delight in this sūtra.
Even unto the ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, And forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena;
Earth, water, fire, and wind, along with their essential natures, Objects, sentient beings, and suffering;
The aggregates, elements, worlds, birth, sounds, names, and truths; Greed, hatred, delusion, pride, craving, concealment, and arrogance—
Avarice, envy, flattery, deception, as well as anger and the like—know that each of these is likewise [to be understood].

If a person, regarding the limit of the exhaustion of the eye, remains constantly deluded and unable to comprehend it, they will fall into the conduct of ordinary worldlings; such a person does not delight in this sutra.
If a person constantly penetrates the limit of the exhaustion of the eye without confusion, they will then depart from all the practices of ordinary beings; such a person delights in this sutra.

If a person, when the eye perishes and dissolves, remains constantly deluded and unable to comprehend it, they will fall into the conduct of ordinary worldlings; such a person does not delight in this sūtra.

If a person, regarding the destruction of that eye, Is always thoroughly penetrating and without delusion, They will then be free from all the conduct of ordinary beings; Such a person loves and delights in this sutra.
If a person is constantly deluded and unable to comprehend the quiescence of that eye, they will fall into the conduct of ordinary worldlings; such a person does not delight in this sūtra.

If a person, regarding the cessation of that eye, Is always penetratingly realized and free from delusion, They have then departed from all the practices of ordinary beings; Such a person loves and delights in this sutra.

If a person perceives no coming or going within the eye, yet remains constantly deluded and unable to understand it, they fall into the conduct of ordinary worldlings; such a person does not delight in this sutra.

If a person perceives no coming or going in the eye, And always penetrates it without confusion, Then they have departed from the conduct of ordinary beings; Such a person loves and delights in this sutra.

If a person does not understand that the eye is without self, and remains constantly deluded regarding the nature of the eye’s exhaustion, they will fall into the conduct of ordinary worldlings; such a person does not delight in this sutra.

If a person can perceive that the eye is without self, and constantly penetrates the nature of the eye’s exhaustion, they will then depart from the conduct of ordinary beings; such a person delights in this sutra.
If a person does not understand that the eye is without self, they will remain constantly deluded regarding the sphere of patient endurance;
such a person falls into the conduct of ordinary worldlings and takes no delight in this sutra.

If a person can perceive that the eye is selfless, And always attains mastery in the practice of patience, They will then depart from all the practices of ordinary beings; Such a person shall love and delight in this sutra.
If a person does not understand the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, they do not accomplish the refuge-less precepts;
because they do not accomplish the refuge-less precepts, such a person does not delight in this sutra.
If a person can perceive the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, they will then achieve the precepts of non-reliance;
by achieving the precepts of non-reliance, such a person will love and delight in this sutra.
If a person does not understand the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, they do not accomplish untainted precepts;
because they do not accomplish untainted precepts, such a person does not delight in this sutra.
If a person can perceive the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, they will then achieve the outflow-free precepts;
because they have achieved the outflow-free precepts, such a person delights in this sutra.
If a person does not understand the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, they do not achieve untainted wisdom;
because they do not achieve untainted wisdom, such a person does not delight in this sutra.
If a person can realize the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, they will then achieve untainted wisdom;
because they have achieved untainted wisdom, such a person delights in this sutra.

If a person does not understand the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, and is constantly deluded regarding the emptiness of the eye, they will be unable to give rise to the wisdom of dhāraṇī; such a person does not delight in this sutra.

If a person can realize the nature of the eye’s exhaustion, And constantly penetrate the emptiness of the eye, They will be able to give rise to the wisdom of dhāraṇī; Such a person delights in this sūtra.

If a person thoroughly understands the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, they will then achieve the wisdom of dhāraṇī, up to the unsurpassed and unattached wisdom; such a person shall love and delight in this sutra.
If a person does not delight in this sutra, they will remain perpetually deluded regarding the nature of the exhaustion of the eye;
such a person will then fall away from all meditative concentrations, and it will truly be difficult for them to realize unsurpassed wisdom.
If a person loves and delights in this sutra, they will thoroughly penetrate the nature of the exhaustion of the eye;
such a one will then accomplish all meditative concentrations, and it will not be difficult for them to realize unsurpassed wisdom.
If a person thoroughly understands the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, and is able to penetrate the mark of non-self,
they will constantly hear such a Dharma as this, giving rise to profound faith and understanding, free from doubt.
If a person contemplates the nature of the exhaustion of the eye, Diligent day and night without weariness,
They will then achieve dhāraṇī and eloquence, And shall always be able to expound this sutra.
If a person contemplates this sutra, they will achieve the wisdom that manifests radiant light;
they shall then reveal all Tathāgatas and thoroughly penetrate the empty nature of the eye.
Even if one were to erect hundreds of thousands of stupas And make offerings to all the World-Honored Ones,
If a person contemplates this sutra, The merit obtained shall exceed that even more.
Even if one were to offer hundreds of thousands of musical performances as an offering to the relics of the Tathāgata,
the merit obtained by anyone who hears this sutra would surpass that even more.

If one were to see all sentient beings perceived by the Buddha-eye and offer them worship equal to that offered to the Tathāgata for more than immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, it would not be as meritorious as upholding this sutra.
If a person receives, upholds, and expounds even a single four-line verse from this sūtra,
one should show them reverence as if they were the Most Victorious One, the Honored One of Great Compassion.
In the past, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, while transmigrating through the cycle of birth and death within the three realms of existence,
I have made offerings at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas for the sake of this sutra.

Or perhaps they light immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lamps, each wick equal in size to a yojana, in order to attain mastery over this sutra; for this reason, they make offerings to the Great Teacher.
Or with campaka and paribhadra flowers, sumana and aśoka flowers— with such flower garlands,
banners, and canopies, they made various offerings at the stūpas of the Tathāgata.
In the past, throughout the cycle of birth and death, whenever anyone came to me seeking something, I was able to give it all:
I gave flowers, fruits, and various groves; I gave bridges and wells;
I gave white elephants and qilin; and I gave precious horses along with beautiful women.
Some offered golden couches and precious jeweled canopies; others offered necklaces and various flower garlands.
In this manner, each [offering] reached hundreds of thousands, yet their minds never grew weary for the sake of this sutra.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Tang Dynasty.
The Eleventh Assembly on the Appearance of Radiance,
Part Two: "In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I upheld the pure precepts,
Constantly cultivated meditative concentration and wisdom, And practiced giving to all sentient beings."
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, when wicked people came to revile and abuse me,
I gave rise to compassion at that time and did not inflict harm upon them.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I bestowed everything upon those who sought it.
Each according to their own inclinations, may they all attain joy.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I offered various palaces adorned with nets of many jewels as an offering to the Buddhas.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I gave up all manner of rare treasures and mani-jewels to make offerings to the Buddhas. In the past,
for the sake of this sutra, I constantly remembered those who had shown me kindness.
Even upon hearing a single verse, I have always held them in high esteem.
For the sake of this sutra, I have in the past revered those who uphold the precepts;
even at their place of walking meditation, I have always shown them constant respect.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, whether dwelling in the cycle of birth and death or even receiving a small kindness from others, I have always harbored the intent to repay them.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I did not seek profit nor did I slander the Dharma.
Out of compassion for my kin and friends, and even for all sentient beings,
I formerly studied this sutra; possessing great learning and eloquence,
I was unattached to the Dharma and never begrudged my kin and friends.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, if unwholesome thoughts arose in my mind,
I quickly repented so as to eliminate them, never allowing them to increase.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I was the crown prince of a king.
Whatever precious jewels, unguents, and powdered incense I obtained,
I then gave rise to a pure mind and dedicated them as offerings to all Buddhas.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, out of compassion for those in prison,
Undergoing various forms of torture and poison, I took them upon myself in their stead.
For the sake of this sutra in the past, I renounced all the pleasures of the five desires;
constantly, during the six monthly fast days, I observed and upheld all the prohibitive precepts.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I constantly practiced patience;
even toward my own wife, I never gave rise to greed or stinginess.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I caused those who were impoverished...
All have attained peace and happiness, And are abundantly provided with all manner of wealth and treasures.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, I gathered in and sustained all beings—
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, And all varieties of living creatures.
In the past, for the sake of this sutra, To benefit all beings,
I was always a great donor, Never withholding my heart from those who sought;
Whether planting flowers or fruit trees, I never allowed others to prune or cut them down.
I universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, satisfying them all according to their wishes.
When I practiced giving in the past, my mind was always impartial;
I maintained the precepts and possessed merit, while those who broke the precepts were devoid of shame and remorse.
Whether they had realized great supernormal powers or were as lowly as ordinary fools,
all conceived a sense of wonder and provided them with respectful offerings.
When I practiced giving in the past, my mind was free from any sense of superiority or inferiority.
Seeking not rebirth in the happy realms, they set their resolve and delight in this sutra;
they cause all within the realm to be free from enemies,
subdue the hosts of nāgas, and cause sweet rain to fall in due season.
Candraprabha, you should know: for the sake of seeking this sutra, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have practiced various ascetic austerities;
even if one were to expound them for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one could never exhaustively describe them.
Since you have already established yourself in pure faith, when the future age of the final dharma arrives,
you should give rise to a mind of right mindfulness and expound this sutra.
With the Buddha-eye I observe and clearly see the future world.
He fully understands all their various modes of conduct.
If there are bhikṣus who, seeking supreme wisdom,
are able to expound this sūtra with a pure and faithful mind,
These persons and their locations, all are fully known.
If, in the final age, one hears this sutra and takes joy in it,
their aspirations and skillful means— all are fully known.
If there are those of inferior capacity who have not heard this sutra and slander its expounder, may they all come to full understanding.
If there are bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, [who likewise...]
Those who hear this sutra and weep with feelings of sorrowful inspiration—
I shall grant them all the prediction of enlightenment so that they may behold the Most Victorious Honored One.
Candraprabha, you should know that such is the supernormal power of the Buddhas.
Whether a person’s mind is pure or impure,
even down to their faith and understanding, he knows them all completely.
If there are sentient beings whose aspirations always delight in tranquility, [he knows them all completely].
Abiding securely in all meditative concentrations, they do not cling within the cycle of birth and death;
even their habitual tendencies are ultimately and forever severed.
Such merits as these, they fully comprehend them all.
There are some sentient beings who are attached to illusory phenomena,
while there are others who feel joy and devotion toward the Buddha;
such future events as these he knows them all completely.
If there are sentient beings who, being stained by and attached to worldly pleasures,
are unable to properly cultivate the seeds of the Buddha’s bodhi,
for this reason they fall away from all skillful means.
If there is one who can thoroughly understand the seeds of the Bodhi of all Buddhas,
that person shall obtain pure and boundless light.
Candraprabha, you should observe that such radiance and the like—
Each and every causal condition has its own distinct differences;
by the power of your wisdom, you should understand them all.
If you abandon evil associates and draw near to virtuous friends, [you shall attain liberation].
Maintain the pure precepts and accomplish the radiance of the Buddha.
You should guard your sense faculties, abandon shamelessness and lack of remorse,
practice wholesome dharmas, and protect all sentient beings accordingly.
You should abandon contention and strife, realize the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and not be greedily attached to gain and offerings; you should possess great learning and speak well.
You should regard gain and offerings as being like excrement and filth.
Do not let the defilement of gain and offerings Pollute your pure mind;
always seek luminous liberation, And you shall constantly attain the unsurpassed benefit.
You should cultivate the Buddha-way, Contemplating the Buddha as identical to the Dharma-nature.
Constantly kindle the great torch of the Dharma, Shining universally throughout the world.
You should be like the king of mountains, Your mind peaceful and unmoving;
Whether reviled, abused, or beaten, Be able to endure it all.
You should act as a true and virtuous friend for all sentient beings;
you should abandon inferior states of mind and constantly cultivate pure deeds.
With a steadfast mind, you shall expound the unsurpassed Dharma.
This subtle and wondrous sūtra should be bestowed upon those with a compassionate heart.
Those who seek supreme wisdom need not fear birth and death;
by abandoning all evils through this, they shall attain great victory.
For example, a person of wisdom who is skilled in using fire can ripen various flavors without being burned by that fire.
But those who are foolish and lack skillful means—
If one places fire upon the palm, one is immediately burned by that fire.
It is like a person who has been poisoned; when they are dazed and their mind is deranged, they may use fire for cauterization therapy, and through this, they attain recovery.
Candraprabha, you should know that the wise are likewise thus:

relying on the mind, they realize the emptiness of the mind; therefore, while abiding within birth and death, by relying on the eye, they realize the emptiness of the eye, and have no attachment to the eye.
If one can understand in this way, Abiding in the eye, there will be no affliction.
If one realizes that the nature of the eye is empty, One accomplishes true wisdom;
By means of this true wisdom, One shall attain the manifestation of light.
If one realizes that the nature of the eye is empty, Craving and desire will be forever extinguished.
Because there is no craving or desire, One shall attain the manifestation of light.
The same applies to hatred and delusion, As well as self-grasping and the afflictions of concealment and resentment.
Avarice, envy, lack of shame and lack of remorse, intolerance and arrogance,
pride and overweening conceit, as well as flattery, deception, and negligence—
even up to hypocrisy and the like— are each to be explained in the same manner as greed.
If one attains true wisdom, one understands that the eye is quiescent;
because of knowing its quiescence, one shall attain the manifestation of light.
If one attains true wisdom, one abides within the principle of the Buddhas.
By abiding in the principle, one shall obtain the light of manifestation.
If one attains true wisdom and abides within the Buddha’s skillful means,
by abiding in those skillful means, one shall obtain the light of manifestation.
If one does not cultivate true wisdom, one will never be free from obscurations and afflictions;
though the light of manifestation may be accomplished, such as I have never before heard or seen.
If one diligently cultivates true wisdom, one will forever be free from obscurations and afflictions.
One who can accord with this practice shall attain the manifestation of light.
If one seeks the most supreme practice, one should study this sutra;
by making offerings to all Tathāgatas, one attains the skillful means of true wisdom.
If one cultivates true and real wisdom, one should make offerings to all Buddhas;
then the manifestation of light will be accomplished as easily as a fruit held in the palm of the hand.
If one is deluded regarding the eye of selflessness, one falls away from the dharma of a śramaṇa.
That person cannot obtain such an emerging radiance.
But if one perceives that the eye is selfless and accomplishes the dharma of a śramaṇa,
that person shall realize such an emerging radiance.
If one understands the limit of the eye’s exhaustion, And likewise understands the boundary of the ear’s arising—
By understanding the boundary of the ear’s arising, This is the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa.
If one does not thoroughly comprehend The ultimate limit of the nature of the eye,
If one cannot fully comprehend the limit of the eye’s arising,
that person shall not obtain such an appearance of light.
If one can fully comprehend the limit of the nature of the eye, [one shall obtain it].
One who can fully comprehend the limit of the eye’s arising shall realize such an appearance of light.
If one does not properly comprehend the limit of the nature of the eye, [one remains bound].
If one cannot properly understand the limit of the eye's arising,
that person shall not obtain such an appearance of light.
If one can thoroughly comprehend the limit of the nature of the eye, [one shall obtain it].
One who can also thoroughly understand the limit of the eye’s arising,
that person shall realize such an appearance of light.
If one does not clearly understand the limit of the nature of the eye, [one cannot realize it].
If one cannot directly know the limit of the eye’s arising,
that person will not attain such an emerging radiance.
If one can directly and fully realize the limit of the nature of the eye, [one will attain it].
One who can also clearly and fully understand the limit of the eye’s arising will,
in that way, realize the manifestation of light.
If one does not clearly understand the limit of the nature of the eye, [one will not attain this].
If one cannot fully comprehend the limit of the eye’s arising,
that person shall not obtain such an appearance of light.
If one can thoroughly understand the limit of the nature of the eye, [one shall obtain it].
One who can also clearly understand the limit of the eye’s arising shall realize the manifestation of such light.
If one does not clearly understand the purity of the nature of the eye, [one will not attain this].
If one cannot properly understand the purity of the nature of the ear,
that person will not obtain such an emerging radiance.
If one can thoroughly comprehend the purity of the nature of the eye, [one shall attain it].
Regarding the purity of the nature of the ear, one who is also able to understand it well shall realize such an appearance of light.
This applies even to the ear, nose, and tongue, as well as the body, mind, forms, and sounds.
Odors, tastes, and tangibles; earth, water, fire, and wind;
the nature of things and worldly suffering; the aggregates, elements, and the arising of the world;
as well as sounds, names, and so forth—all are like this.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying:
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who set out upon the Mahāyāna..."
For one who wishes to fully accomplish such an emergence of light,
there are eighty kinds of provisions of roots of goodness.
What are these eighty?
What is called "protecting and mindful of sentient beings" means having no intent to harm in one's mind; upholding the pure precepts without deficiency;
maintaining a mind of equanimity free from flattery or crookedness; being devoid of stinginess, envy, greed, or deceit;
having deep faith in the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras; not being addicted to wealth, honor, pride, or indulgence; and possessing the power of patience.
Endowed with these qualities, his aspirations are unshakable and his intention is pure;
dwelling in an araṇya, he does not rely on followers, gain, or fame. Abiding in the various dhyānas, he manifests the Samādhi of Radiance.

Toward those who possess ethical discipline, he serves them without guile; toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he gives rise to a superior intention, always [acting] out of reverence for the Dharma.
He conceives deep respect for his preceptors and ācāryas; he thoroughly understands the sūtras and is skillful in proclaiming them;
his words are truthful and sincere; he abides in right reflection, diligently plants roots of goodness, and constantly practices the giving of wisdom;
he recognizes the activities of Māra, closely guards his sense faculties, is calm and deliberate in speech, and is well-versed in the truth.
He also clearly understands the specific characteristics of each stage (*bhūmi*), seeks inexhaustible forms, and does not spare his own body or life.
He instructs the fourfold assembly, severs worldly thoughts, and abandons all false views. He holds that there is no dharma of a future world;

he does not falsely manifest the signs of one who has already studied when he has not yet studied, but always reveals the teachings according to his capacity for those who have already studied. Previously...
They do not praise the sounds of song and chant, nor do they extol the adornment of material requisites;
they realize and enter into the truths, possess extensive learning, abandon slothful sleep, and diligently seek the True Dharma.
They revere the Buddha, resolve upon Bodhicitta, renounce worldly occupations, cultivate the various precepts, and cherish the Dharma.
Therefore, relying upon superior friends, they seek all roots of goodness with a mind never weary of seeking;
they delight in leaving the household life and uphold the Buddha-dharma; they do not give rise to evil karma and harbor no doubts regarding the teachings;
they skillfully explain parables and reveal the secrets; they aspire toward great Bodhi without weariness, and as for the sūtras they have received, they have never...
Free from forgetfulness, not abandoning one's own training, subduing the arguments of others, seeking the path to liberation,
and practicing immeasurable deeds, his mind is resolved in the knowledge of those dharmas; clearly seeing the continuity of cause and effect within saṃsāra,
he is unattached to the three realms of existence and free from overweening pride, establishing remedies for those who have faith, and fully understanding.
He attains the distinctions of future karmic retributions, thoroughly understands the past without depending on external conditions,
diligently cultivates practices of seclusion, and is fully adorned with the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha.
These constitute the eighty.
Furthermore, Candraprabha,
these eighty dharmas are subsumed within five dharmas.
What are these five? They are:
knowledge of birth and death, knowledge of nirvāṇa, knowledge of the exhaustion of afflictions, knowledge of the supreme, and knowledge of the fruits of merit.
Furthermore, Candraprabha!
In this way, these five dharmas enter into two dharmas. What are the two?
They are the adornment of the purity of mind and the adornment of the purity of form.
Furthermore, Candraprabha!
These two dharmas enter into one dharma. What is that one?
This refers to that which can accomplish the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Candraprabha!
There are another eighty kinds of dharmas that skillfully accomplish the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas."
What are the eighty? They are:

the provision of generosity, vast wisdom, the cultivation of pure precepts, freedom from the heat of afflictions, the subduing of pride, gentle speech, and knowing the proper time for all various matters.
Furthermore, they know well those virtuous friends who have set out upon the Mahāyāna, who are clad in the armor of diligence, whose majestic deportment benefits all beings,
who cause those fallen into afflictions to sever their doubts, who disparage all that is unwholesome, who practice pure dharmas, who do not associate with evil people,
who plant various roots of goodness without ever feeling weary or satisfied, and who have resolved upon Bodhi.
Holding the mind with courageous diligence, one recognizes the deeds of Māra, realizes the various truths, and makes offerings of true reality with definitive certainty and without doubt.
One keeps sentient beings in mind, constantly cherishing their deliverance, and remains unattached to the realms of existence.
Arousing the Great Mind, one reveals the faults and evils of those who are unwholesome, causing them to abandon greed, hatred, and delusion. Do not...
Seeking benefit and profit, they bring sentient beings to maturity, repair and adorn Buddha-stūpas, show respect and reverence toward all noble ones,
and draw near to and serve those who abide in the Mahāyāna; they never praise those of the inferior vehicles,
distance themselves from śrāvakas, subdue enemies, and make vast offerings to the World-Honored One.
By making various offerings with a distinguished mind, one attains unimpeded wisdom and is endowed with eloquence;
through various parables, one reveals the True Dharma without contradicting the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Seeking the Dharma without laziness, one elucidates profound meanings, possesses great dhāraṇī, and preaches the Dharma without defilement, being able to cause it to flow widely.
He transforms and guides others without weariness; he brings all practices to perfection and possesses great majestic power.
His eloquence is unimpeded, and he has achieved extensive learning. He does not praise evil persons, cultivates wholesome deeds, and thoroughly understands the aggregates (*skandhas*).
Having abandoned all views, he penetrates the nature of causes, transcends the sphere of conditioned activity, and remains far removed from what is not his proper domain.
Giving rise to pure faith, abiding in the Right Path, delighting in the Mahāyāna, and impartially embracing all beings;
they do not cling to non-self, nor do they weary of birth and death, but joyfully seek nirvāṇa.
Because of having few desires, they dwell in araṇya hermitages and constantly practice alms-gathering without weariness, giving rise to a mind of contentment with whatever they obtain.
Contentment; freedom from shamelessness and lack of conscience; drawing near to the Buddha; dwelling with virtuous friends;

abandoning those of dissimilar character; having compassion for ordinary worldlings; acting in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings; pure faith in the Buddha; avoiding those who are not suitable vessels;
not engaging in conversation with those who oppose him; and not providing instruction to those who do not come seeking it.

If there are those who come seeking [something], one should explain it to them as appropriate; one should be equanimous regarding food, constantly practicing equal giving and opening one's doors for great generosity.
Thus it is, young man!
"These eighty dharmas can bring about the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas.
At that time, the youth Candraprabha, having heard this Dharma, gave rise to great joy and immediately praised the Buddha before him in verse:
"The Tathāgata fully knows the limit of the exhaustion of the eye; Therefore, he is able to manifest pure wisdom."
Because he can manifest pure wisdom, He is endowed with the Tathāgata’s pure radiance.
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that the eye is without self; Therefore, he can manifest pure sounds.
Because he can manifest pure sounds, He is endowed with the Tathāgata’s mark of the Brahma-voice.
In the past, the Buddha benefited sentient beings; Thus he was able to achieve purity of speech.
By achieving this purity of speech, He brought benefit to immeasurable worlds.
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that the nature of the eye is empty; Therefore, he is able to accomplish the wisdom of dhāraṇī.
By accomplishing the wisdom of dhāraṇī, He manifests the immeasurable light of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the distinctions of the eye, And the names for the eye are likewise infinite;
Because he knows that names are boundless, He manifests the immeasurable light of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha knows the gateway of the distinctions among syllables; thus he knows that the eye is empty and free from syllables.
Because he knows the eye is empty and free from syllables, he manifests the immeasurable light of the Tathāgata.
If a person contemplates that the eye is without self, they will immediately understand the Buddha’s words to be true;
because they can know the truth of the Buddha’s words, the definitive light of the Tathāgata appears.
The Tathāgata has accomplished supreme supernormal powers, And thus understands the destruction of the boundless eye;
By being able to understand the destruction of the eye, He brings benefit to all worlds.
The Great Compassionate One, Supreme among Two-legged Beings, has fully realized the arising of the boundless eye;
just as the Buddha knows the arising of the eye, may I likewise attain this before long.
In this way, the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects,
And even the world, birth, sounds, names, and so forth— One should know that all these are to be performed accordingly.

I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all beings throughout the world.

I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Thoroughly understanding the practice of meditative concentration;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Thoroughly understanding the conduct of liberation;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Thoroughly understanding the conduct of those who follow the path of equal proportions;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Thoroughly understanding the conduct of meditative attainments;
I too vow to accomplish such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands birth and death, That their cyclic flow arises entirely from afflictions;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata fully understands all things; In benefiting the world, none is his equal.
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata dwells skillfully in meditative equipoise, And gives rise to supreme wisdom of skillful means;
I too vow to accomplish such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Thoroughly comprehending the infinite past abodes, conduct, and dwellings;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Thoroughly understanding that birth and death are boundless;
I too vow to accomplish such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Having fully realized that all afflictions are exhausted;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Having accomplished unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
I too vow to accomplish such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Free from all afflictions and their habitual tendencies;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Fully understanding that the defilement of desire obstructs bodhi;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Thoroughly knowing the dharma for transcending birth and death;
May I also accomplish such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the meaning of all phenomena and awakens immeasurable sentient beings;
may I also attain such wisdom to benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata has thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena, Which are like illusions, dreams, and mirages;
I too vow to attain such wisdom To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands all the worlds, All written characters and spoken words;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all the worlds.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme eloquence, Revealing the profound and subtle Dharma;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata has well disciplined his body, speech, and mind;
all his actions follow wisdom. May I also accomplish such wisdom, to benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the three periods of time, Without grasping, without attachment, and without obstruction;
I too vow to accomplish such wisdom, To benefit all worlds.
The Tathāgata has skillfully cultivated morality, concentration, and wisdom, And in all these matters, he never regresses;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, And become a Greatly Compassionate Honored One for the three realms.
The Tathāgata has skillfully cultivated liberation, And his knowledge and vision of liberation are non-retrogressive;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To become a Great Compassionate Honored One of the triple world.
The Tathāgata has skillfully cultivated right contemplation; Among gods, humans, and the world, there is none his equal.
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, To become a Greatly Compassionate Honored One of the three realms.
The Tathāgata is endowed with supreme wisdom, Untainted by any worldly phenomena;
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, And become a Great Compassionate Honored One of the three realms.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the world, clearly perceiving all its various realms of existence;
may I also attain such wisdom, and achieve unimpeded mastery over those realms.
The Tathāgata has thoroughly understood the limit of birth; therefore, he is free from delusion regarding it.
May I also attain such wisdom, and may I reach certainty concerning the nature of the exhaustion of birth.
The Tathāgata has thoroughly realized the limit of tranquility; therefore, he is free from delusion regarding it.
May I also attain such wisdom, so that I may reach certainty concerning that tranquility.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the limits of saṃsāra; therefore, he has no delusion regarding it.
May I also attain such wisdom, so that I may reach certainty concerning that saṃsāra.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the past and future limits; therefore, he is fully endowed with teacherless wisdom.
I too vow to accomplish such wisdom, so that I may attain freedom from doubt regarding the past and future limits.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the limits of rebirth; therefore, he is endowed with teacherless wisdom.
May I also attain such wisdom, so that regarding the turning away from those births, I may reach certainty.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the past and future limits; regarding the eye, he has no attachment to permanence or annihilation.
I too vow to achieve such wisdom, so that I may attain freedom from doubt concerning the past and future limits.
The Tathāgata has thoroughly realized the limit of the exhaustion of birth; regarding the eye, he harbors no attachment to permanence or annihilation.
May I also accomplish such wisdom, and attain freedom from doubt concerning the nature of the exhaustion of birth.
If a person does not understand the past and future limits, they will give rise to grasping and attachment toward desire;
the Tathāgata can realize and know this, and therefore remains unstained by desire.
If a person does not understand the limits of existence and non-existence, they will give rise to grasping and attachment toward desire;
the Tathāgata can realize and know this, and therefore remains unstained by desire.
If a person does not understand exhaustion and boundlessness, they will give rise to grasping and attachment toward desire;
the Tathāgata is able to realize and know this, and therefore remains unstained by desire.
If a person does not understand transformation and non-transformation, they will give rise to grasping and attachment toward desire;
the Tathāgata can realize and know this, and therefore remains unstained by desire.
Hatred, delusion, anger, concealment, as well as envy and deceit, Crookedness, arrogance, pride, and conceit— In giving,
ethical discipline, and patience, And likewise in meditative concentration and wisdom, it is thus.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep thoughts in the mind of the youth Candraprabha, smiled serenely and emitted golden light. That light shone universally upon immeasurable and boundless Buddha-lands; having brought benefit to those realms, it circled the Buddha three times and returned to enter through the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, praised him with verses and asked:
“With the roar of clouds and thunder, The voice of the kalaviṅka bird,
And the sound of the great Dharma drum— For what reason do you manifest a smile?”
Surpassing hundreds of thousands of suns, with pure and wondrous sounds, your merit is most rare; for what reason do you manifest this light?
Adorned with the perfections of giving, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom—
All things are perfectly complete; for what reason does this light appear?
The Tathāgata’s voice is supple and gentle, always free from harsh speech;
it skillfully heals the ailments of sentient beings—for what reason does this light appear?
The Greatly Compassionate One, Honored among Two-legged Beings, knowing that the eye is eternally empty and quiescent,
proclaims this for the sake of sentient beings with a pure Brahma-voice.
So too are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as sound, name, and so forth.
And likewise for the truths of cessation and the path, so too are the knowledges and patiences.
The Greatly Compassionate One, the Honored One among bipeds, knows that the eye reaches its limit at the end of birth;
both quiescence and saṃsāra are entirely empty and still.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and even names and sounds— All things are thus.
Furthermore, it is taught that the law of dependent origination Is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence.
Not created by self, nor created by another, it arises from a multitude of conditions.
By various gateways, he reveals the root of suffering;
by various meanings, he extols the radiance of the Buddha.
With immeasurable words and phrases, you have expounded the Dharma of quiescence:
that there is no person and no life-span, no self and no sentient being.
The countless Buddhas of the past likewise, through inconceivable means, [taught this same truth].
With hundreds of thousands of verses, he expounded such a Dharma.
That which the Tathāgata has expounded is the Dharma of true merit;
therein is neither the teaching nor the teacher, and the Dharma taught is likewise non-existent.
The Buddha has preached the most supreme Dharma, awakening all living beings;
the devas and yakṣas who hear it are all able to understand it,
and all the asuras have already purified their intentions.
The nets of doubt of immeasurable multitudes of people were entirely removed.
They came to understand the intrinsic nature of greed, and destroyed hatred and delusion,
as well as craving, pride, ignorance, flattery, envy, and conceptual proliferation.
Even unto the aggregate of suffering and so forth, all are completely relinquished;
such meanings of these phrases are ultimately and entirely pure.
Regarding a single dharma, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands its manifold names.
Numbering in the hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands, even unto the inconceivable;
having well studied such a Dharma under immeasurable Buddhas,
they expound it without end within a single teaching.
The Tathāgata has thoroughly mastered all various Dharma-gates,
and is likewise able to discern and know the superior, middling, and inferior aspects of names and phrases.
He has cultivated and studied every kind of diverse terminology.
Skillfully proclaiming the subtle and supreme ultimate truth—
such pure sounds arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
they do not depend upon the throat or tongue, nor even upon the body or mind.
The earth shook in six ways, and the multitudes from the ten directions all assembled;
with palms joined, they gazed up at the Buddha, wishing for him to dispel their doubts.
The Tathāgata clearly understands the limit of the eye’s arising and its exhaustion.
The intrinsic nature is eternally empty and quiescent; There is neither going nor coming.
Without abiding and without location, One deeply enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
With the Buddha-eye free from all obstruction, I therefore now pose this question.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the nature of the eye— its past and future limits,
its exhaustion and non-exhaustion, and its cyclic flow— knowing that its self-nature is eternally empty and quiescent.
He reveals the meaning of all phenomena, causing the world to rejoice.
O Muni of exquisite voice, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows the limits of the past and future; the nature of the eye is eternally empty and quiescent, free from conceptualization and verbal expression—for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that the eye is immeasurable, And proclaims it through various words;
Its original nature is eternally empty and quiescent— For what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows the limit of all births; The nature of the eye is eternally empty and quiescent.
Having abandoned all afflictions and realized the Buddha’s wisdom of enlightenment, you possess supreme renown; for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Having long practiced and studied, the Tathāgata now expounds the inconceivable.
Thoroughly realizing that the nature of the eye is empty, Free from defilement and eternally pure,
He understands all immeasurable mental activities In a single thought-moment;
His radiance illuminates the world— What auspicious sign is this?
The Great Sage, the Truly Enlightened One, the most supreme among two-legged beings, has completely eliminated all afflictions; his mind is ever tranquil.
With the Tathāgata’s transcendent wisdom, he has profoundly penetrated the ultimate limit of the eye.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do you now manifest a smile?
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the six sense objects and the four great elements;
even sounds, names, and so forth—all are exactly like this.
The Buddha knows that the eye is without self, And has likewise realized that the ear is impermanent;
Having understood that the nature of the nose is empty, For what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that the tongue is without self, And has likewise realized that the body is impermanent.
Having realized that the nature of mind is empty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that form is without self, and has also attained the realization that sound is impermanent;
having realized that the nature of fragrance is empty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that taste is without self, And has likewise realized that touch is impermanent;
Having understood that the nature of phenomena is empty, For what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that earth is without self, And has likewise realized that water is impermanent.
Having realized that the nature of fire is empty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that wind has no self and also understands its nature to be impermanent;
having realized that the nature of things is empty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Knowing that the world is without self, And likewise realizing suffering and impermanence,
As well as understanding that the nature of the aggregates is empty— For what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that the elements are without self, And likewise realizes that the world is impermanent.
Having realized that the nature of birth is empty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that sound is without self and has also mastered that names are impermanent;
having realized that the nature of the Path is empty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that wisdom is selfless, He realizes tranquility and impermanence,
As well as the emptiness of the nature of sentient beings— For what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha knows that nature is without intrinsic being, And he also knows that the self is not a self.
Having realized that mental intentions are empty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Observing that birth and death are without self, and having also attained the realization of permanence and impermanence,
as well as the emptiness of nirvāṇa— for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Tathāgata’s mind is liberated, and his fame fills the three realms;
Śakra, kings of men, nāgas, and spirits all make offerings to him.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the limit of the eye's arising and its exhaustion.
Even unto the state of tranquility, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Immeasurable sons of the Buddha have gathered together in this assembly;
born from the mouth of the Buddha, they are born through transformation from the Dharma.
They all came before the Buddha and stood there, joining their palms in reverence;
for the sake of that assembly, they asked about the cause and conditions of this light.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands that the nature of the eye is empty and without self.
Surpassing all those who practice as householders,
the Buddha, through his wisdom of equality, realizes that phenomena are without distinction;
this is known through the Tathāgata’s intentional resolve, not through the vision of supernatural powers.
The Buddha knows that the eye is without self, Its nature is empty, with neither coming nor going;
His pure wisdom is boundless— For what reason do you manifest a smile?
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-One.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Thirty-Two, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Tang Dynasty;
The Eleventh Assembly: The Manifestation of Radiance, Part Three.
“The Tathāgata has already reached the end of the realm of birth; his great compassion universally covers all worlds.
O Dharma King, most supreme among those honored by men, we pray you tell us for what reason you manifest this smile.”
Immeasurable and boundless great bodhisattvas, along with other hosts of majestic devas, all held exquisite parasols in the air; meanwhile, this great earth shook throughout.
Who, in the presence of the Tathāgatas of the past, practiced various wholesome dharmas through the long night?
O Honored One of Great Compassion, who brings equal joy to all, I pray you tell us for what reason you manifest this smile?
Who in the past made offerings to the Buddhas, That upon hearing this Dharma, they give rise to such joy?
O Guide, most supreme among the honored ones of men, I pray you tell us for what reason you manifest this smile?
The World-Honored One’s voice delights the minds of all, Like the exquisite and beautiful cry of the king of geese;
Spontaneously and immeasurably harmonious and elegant— I pray you tell us, for what reason have you emitted this light?
With immeasurable tens of millions of verses, words of praise, exhortation, and encouragement,
and with a voice as exquisite as the *kucira* bird— pray tell us, for what reason have you emitted this light?
The sound of the Dharma being preached is like the deep resonance of thunder, heard throughout boundless billions of realms;
whether with words of compassion, harsh speech, or gentle discourse—why does he manifest this golden light?

Having realized birth and non-birth, exhaustion and non-exhaustion, and knowing that the nature of the eye is detached and devoid of coming or going, you illuminate the world as the extinction of ambrosia; for what reason do you manifest this golden light?
Knowing that the arising of the eye is eternally empty and quiescent, Without going, without coming, and without a place of abiding,
Like a mirage, water, or foam— For what cause and condition do you manifest a smile?
So it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; With forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects;
And even with sounds and names— Know that all things are likewise thus.
The Vajra-Eternal Body is an indestructible body, Complete with hundreds of thousands of supreme marks;
Though its substance has no mechanical joints, it moves— I pray you tell me, for what cause and condition do you smile?

Your thighs and shoulders are well-filled, and your heels are long; your abdominal form is unmanifest like that of a lion, your navel is deep and wondrously beautiful, and your waist is perfectly rounded. I pray you tell me: what is the cause and condition for this smile?
Your golden, pure body is free from dust and defilement;
each hair is deep blue-black, curling to the right and flowing upward with a fragrant scent. I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for your smile.
His wondrous body is perfectly complete and dwells eternally in peace, Like the king of trees, the nyagrodha;
Adorned with all meritorious virtues, His voice delights and gladdens all beings.
His arms are long and his shoulders are well-rounded and exquisite; his neck is perfectly full with the marks of whorled curls appearing.
He wanders through boundless hundreds of thousands of lands, showing all sentient beings the paths of both the heterodox and the correct.
The teeth are white and stainless like jade or snow; the tongue is broad and long, covering the face.
The jaw is like that of a lion and the nose is straight and prominent—all arise from a mind purified through skillful means.
The fragrance of the utpala lily issues from his mouth, and the scent of sandalwood pervades his body;
having extensively cultivated loving-kindness in the past, his pure intention continues in constant succession.
The soles of the Tathāgata’s feet are perfectly level and even; wherever his feet tread, the ground is never uneven or sloped.
Like the gait of a lion or a lordly elephant, he transcends all worlds.
The mark of the thousand-spoked wheel is wondrously sublime; its extraordinary radiance and patterns are ever resplendent.
He acts for the benefit and welfare of all beings, so that all who behold him give rise to pure faith.
A single finger can emit hundreds of thousands of rays of light, Universally illuminating the boundless buddha-fields;
Having diligently cultivated myriad virtuous deeds in the past, One attains these various marks of adornment.

Having accomplished a physical form beyond compare, with a countenance so dignified and most excellent, you manifest supernormal transformations to benefit all worlds; pray tell us, for what reason do you manifest this smile?
The shoulders are rounded and level like those of a deer king; the body is not bent, like that of a lion.
Having appeared in the world to act as a lamp, we pray you tell us for what reason you manifest a smile.
The horse-king’s hidden marks are free from dust and defilement; his palms are level and full, and his hands reach below his knees.
O rare and most supreme Lion among Men, pray tell us: what is the cause and condition for this smile?
Boundless light emanates from his body, its wondrous colors serene and ever-shining;
his mind is pure and constantly continuous, as he expounds boundless sūtras.
Those who abide in the views of nihilism or eternalism cannot purify and cultivate such a Dharma;
yet, if one can abandon all extreme views, one will swiftly achieve the pure body of a Tathāgata.
The sound of celestial drums and thunderous clouds resounds afar; the majestic cry of the Kalaviṅka is pure and penetrating.
With the sounds of celestial music in thousands of varieties, we pray that you tell us why this light has appeared.
The Guide proclaims the Dharma with a single voice, causing those who violate the precepts to sever their continuity;
the wondrous sounds uttered by the Tathāgata are all profound and rare teachings.
The white tuft of hair between the brows of the Bull-King extends throughout hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields;
his wondrous eyes are like the color of deep blue sapphire, and the mark of his crown cannot be seen even by the empty sky.
His teeth are white, even, and closely set—forty in number—resembling pure crystal jewels.
All arise from immeasurable wholesome karma; pray tell us, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Tathāgata’s body of perfected merit has accomplished boundless, subtle, and wondrous form, emitting rare and pure radiance;
pray tell us, for what reason do you manifest a smile?

O Great Compassionate One, Supreme among Two-legged Beings, You who thoroughly understand the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, And have attained unimpeded, wondrous eloquence— I pray you tell us: for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Tathāgata has already reached the further shore, Possessing the three types of knowledge and the six supernormal powers;
He manifests boundless, pure radiance— I pray that you tell us for what reason he smiles.
In the past, throughout immeasurable eons, you made offerings to hundreds of thousands of World-Honored Ones;
since such causes and effects do not perish, we pray that you tell us for what reason you manifest this smile.
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, you dwelt peacefully in subtle and wondrous samādhis;
knowing the limits of the eye’s arising and its exhaustion, we pray you tell us for what reason you manifest this smile.
Regarding the past, future, and present worlds, the Guide fully comprehends them all;
with pure wisdom that is unimpeded and inconceivable, we pray you tell us for what reason you manifest this smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, stroked the crown of Candraprabha’s head with his golden hand and spoke these verses:
“Listen attentively, young man! I now entrust to you this Dharma of Bodhi, The Sutra of the Appearance of Light.”
In the future evil age, when the Dharma is about to perish, you shall open up and expound it for the sake of sentient beings.
Seeing the future world, you shall fully comprehend whether [beings] take pleasure in or do not take pleasure in this subtle and profound sūtra.
If there are sentient beings who aspire to seek the Buddha-way and constantly keep the Buddhas in mind, you should bestow this sutra upon them.
If they have impaired pure faith, delight in clamor and bustle, and remain in a state of long-term drowsiness and sleep,
they will not take pleasure in this sutra.
One who feels no joy or delight in the Dharma of Nirvana— such a deluded person consumes the offerings of the faithful in vain.
One who remains attached to the world and feels no sense of alarm or dread— such a deluded person [consumes the offerings of the faithful in vain].
The wise reproach him: though he wears the dharma robes, he lacks wisdom.
Regarding the true words spoken by the Muni, if one who lacks wisdom hears them, he cannot believe or accept them. One should not dwell together with such a fool.
If there are those who, upon hearing this most excellent Dharma, do not give rise to joy or a heart of love and delight— such persons as these are censured by me;
though they have obtained a human body, it has been spent in vain.
This profound Dharma can give rise to joy and a heart of love and delight;
such a person has already encountered the various Buddhas in the past and will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
One’s life of wisdom is severed, and one is far removed from Bodhi;
therefore, one should abandon evil associates and instead draw near to and revere those of clear wisdom.
In all the worlds, there are immeasurable afflictions; sentient beings are constantly submerged within the three evil realms. All these arise from the causes and conditions of delusion and confusion;
following the flow of such confusion, they find no autonomy.
Abandoning the True Dharma and practicing what is contrary to the Dharma— for this reason, one should distance oneself from such foolish and petty people.
Just as a charioteer who breaks his own axle, having committed evil karma,
is reborn in the hells.
Uttering evil words from the mouth, one constantly brings harm upon oneself, like holding a sharp axe to hack at one’s own body.
Not knowing that all phenomena are produced through causes and conditions, and that one receives retribution according to karma, there is no one who can save them.
They draw near to world-transcending sages and take them as virtuous friends, yet they claim for themselves that they are practicing emptiness.
Having realized the unconditioned, they give rise to the view of annihilation, thinking that when the vessel of the body breaks, the mind likewise perishes along with it.
One who delights in much talk and embellishes their speech with flowery words, becoming attached to such tastes, will ultimately find no benefit or profit.
Though one might be bitten and harmed by a venomous snake, it will never cause a person to fall into the evil realms.
The fool preaches the Dharma, destroying the roots of goodness in others and causing immeasurable multitudes to fall into hell.
You should observe that this youth before me has, in the past,
already made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, practice with steadfast resolve, seeking unsurpassed wisdom; their minds do not rely upon any form of existence.
Knowing that the arising limit of the eye is ultimately pure, free from all conceptual proliferation, and without any attachment,
he expounds this unsurpassed Sūtra of Manifesting Light for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings.
The fool is unable to cultivate and study this Dharma; instead, he perceives only the faults in those who practice it.
Therefore, one should abandon such foolish people and not associate with them while cultivating and studying this Dharma.
Foolish people delight in contentious debate; they are unable to diligently cultivate the practice of non-contention.
Such individuals lack a mind that accords with reality; therefore, one should neither revere nor praise them.
Lax and indolent, they constantly perform unwholesome deeds;
their actions of body, speech, and mind lack pure precepts, wisdom, and extensive learning. They always contemplate objects of desire and delight in the clamor of the crowd.
Their lineage and bodies are both utterly base and evil; they are full of anger and stubborn perversity, and their physical appearance is ugly.
Clinging to the notion of a self, they are deluded regarding the true principle and lack wisdom.
Discriminating speech— having heard that the nature of phenomena is empty— one does not give rise to attachment or delight.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has long since distanced himself from all worldly speech and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Ordinary people, regarding this, develop deep attachment; throughout their entire lives, they are unable to understand it.
They do not cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet they speak of the Dharma with their mouths while their bodies perform what is contrary to the Dharma.
Claiming themselves to be followers of the Vinaya, they constantly act contrary to the Vinaya, even though they are disciples of the Buddha’s teaching.
Wearing robes of a ruined color, yet being one who breaks the precepts—
to don these garments while increasing arrogance and a mind of negligence is like swallowing fierce fire with the alms-food offered in faith.
Furthermore, regarding the Buddha-dharma, they find no supreme and wondrous joy;
they delight in mixed practices and do not leave behind the two extremes; all their underlying intentions are entirely impure.
Such a foolish person, though situated among the great assembly like a jackal entering a pride of lions,
may speak of the Dharma of tranquility in this way, yet cannot understand the true meaning of emptiness.
Praising themselves before the assembly, they give rise to a mind of arrogance; they do not think of the Great Teacher’s sense of shame and humility.
Receiving impure things, they rejoice as if obtaining a *maṇi* jewel, grasping them with delight and never letting go for even a moment.
Maintaining dignified deportment and carrying the robes and bowl, yet possessing only outward form without true wisdom—
though one has shaved the head, if one does not abandon an evil mind and falls into inverted views, this is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
On the path to nirvāṇa, there is likewise no śramaṇa; as for the fruit realized,
ignorance and afflictions have not been extinguished even by a mote’s breadth, yet they wander through villages,
claiming to be tranquil.
The foolish person lacks wisdom and does not know the right path; whatever they desire in their hearts is entirely unwholesome.
For the sake of gain and support, they dwell in an araṇya, yet this is not for the purpose of cultivating the causes of nirvāṇa.
Lax and fond of sleep, they think only of physical comfort; though they always delight in such practices as cultivation,
because of their inverted views, they lose the path to nirvana and shall ultimately never attain it.
The śramaṇa’s fruits of the path:
destroying right view, violating the prohibitions and precepts, and delighting in clothing to adorn the body.
Constantly giving rise to lustful attachments, when entering cities or towns,
they manifest signs of arrogance and abandon themselves to physical misconduct, failing to abide in dignified deportment.
Sometimes entering cities and towns, he wanders about speaking of himself: "That aranya, within the mountain caves—
know that it is where I dwell"— walking slowly with downcast eyes,
his every movement composed and serene.
Causing the assembly of laypeople to say to one another, "The forest-dwelling bhikṣu is a true noble one.
When he sees someone coming, he immediately points it out, saying, "In this place, I..."
They practice walking meditation day and night; some provide soft grass for places of quiet sitting.
Or they enter villages and go to the homes of laypeople, feigning earnest devotion as they inquire after their well-being.
Or, with a defiled mind, before women, he uses various skillful means to praise his own virtues, saying:
"I am able to act as a great field of merit for the world;
I have renounced the royal throne to leave the household life and cultivate the Way; my palace ladies and maidservants..."

Clinging to delicious flavors, you do not recognize their peril; you have given the Māra an opportunity, like a turtle that has fallen into a net.
Among the assembly in the forest hermitage, they are arrogant regarding gain and offerings, and they disparage and slander the bhikṣus who practice with diligence.
Their minds are deluded by fame and profit, and they give rise to further craving and attachment.
For the sake of their livelihood, they constantly practice deception, increasing the unwholesome karma of body and speech.
If there is a donor who makes offerings with a pure mind, yet due to indolence causes that merit to diminish—

"If one can avoid such faults within my teaching,
And diligently practices without negligence, It will not be difficult to attain this Dharma.
Regarding gain and loss, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure, and so forth,"
If one cannot be moved by worldly dharmas, attaining this Dharma is not difficult.
Contemplating the body as impure, contemplating the aggregates as sores and tumors,
and contemplating food as an ointment for sores— if one does these, attaining this Dharma is not difficult.

for the sake of concealing shame, attaining this Dharma is not difficult.
Without flaunting one’s physical strength, one remains without craving or attachment toward food.
For the sake of preserving one's life, it is not difficult to obtain this Dharma.
Thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are empty, having neither attachment nor aversion toward desires,
and constantly practicing the conduct of emptiness and stillness— it is not difficult to obtain this Dharma.
Going one *yojana* from the mountain, sitting alone to practice meditative concentration,
observing that conditioned phenomena are without self— it is not difficult to attain this Dharma.
One observes the eye’s limit of arising and its characteristic of flux.

It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
and even for sounds and names—all are like this.
In this way, in future ages, all those immeasurable bhikṣus—

the exhaustion of the paths of the faculties, and their cultivation or non-cultivation.

Even if one should at times fall away from it, one may yet regain pure faith.

though they initially give rise to faith, they will later abandon it.

bound by the five desires, they greedily pursue all worldly affairs.

When one falls into the Avīci Hell, one shall never again be born in heaven.

Filled with joy, he gave rise to a pure mind; with palms joined, he made this vow:

The Māṇava and the youth Both heard and received it at that time.
I myself, in a former life, With *utpala* flowers,

The foolish do not apply themselves diligently; they slander me in this life.

I constantly cultivate the power of patience to bring benefit to all the world.
Through the accomplishment of the power of patience, the body is adorned with the marks and signs.

When I press the earth with my toe, Boundless lands tremble and shake;

From a single pore, I emit Hundreds of thousands of rays of light.
Purely illuminating all things, it is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
Even the rākṣasas, who are most fearsome and who suck the vital essence of humans, always regard me with a compassionate heart; this is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
