do so entirely through the power of supreme patience.
Amidst the great assembly, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resound everywhere.
Praising the Buddha’s virtues is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
The hundreds of thousands of dragon kings, whose poisonous wrath was most fearsome, saw the Buddha and gave rise to joy; this too is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
Rākṣasas, yakṣas, and others, bearing hundreds of thousands of flower garlands, all come to make offerings to me;
this is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
In immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lands, the Tathāgatas currently residing there—
That they praise my merits is entirely due to the power of supreme patience;
that eight thousand kumbhāṇḍas and aṭavakas scatter flowers as an offering to me is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
Sixty hundred koṭis of yakṣa kings and others have all come to make offerings to me;
this is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
Furthermore, there are a thousand nāga kings, such as Mānasa and Sāgara.
The offering of red pearls to me was entirely due to the power of supreme patience.
The hundreds of thousands of Dhumarās and Śikhis provided musical offerings to me; all was due to the power of supreme patience.
A hundred thousand kumbhāṇḍas, Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and others,

The Dragon King who Sustains the Great Earth manifested his body to half its height.
That they join their palms in reverence to me is all due to the power of supreme patience.
That hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodiless Rāhus and others make offerings to me with pure hearts is all due to the power of supreme patience.
"Young man, you should observe: those whom the light of the Tathāgata illuminates leave suffering behind and attain peace and happiness; all this is due to the power of supreme patience.

Observe the Buddha’s supernormal powers: the sound of his teachings on generosity and ethical discipline is heard everywhere; this is entirely due to the power of supreme patience.

“Greed, hatred, delusion, anger, concealment, envy, jealousy, flattery, deception, arrogance, pride, and so forth— the detailed explanation is likewise. At that time,
having heard this most supreme Dharma being taught, the youth Candraprabha rejoiced, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Tomorrow I wish to invite the Tathāgata along with the great assembly; I only pray that you will compassionately accept my meal.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the boy’s intention was pure and that he would bring benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, gave rise to a heart of great compassion and silently accepted the invitation.
At that time, the youth rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and returned home with joy.
Together with his retinue, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others, they all collectively adorned the great city of Rājagṛha.

At the crossroads, he spread out ornamental canopies; these canopies were so high and wide that they covered everything, with golden cords interlaced and pearl tassels hanging down, adorned with lion banners, golden medicinal hooks, and garlands in hundreds of thousands of varieties.

Furthermore, there were precious flowers of extraordinary colors, interlaced and intertwined to form flower garlands—garlands of *campaka* flowers and garlands of *mucilinda* flowers. In such infinite and incalculable varieties, they hung down all around within the jeweled canopies, universally adorning the entire great assembly.

Furthermore, beneath it, various seats were spread, and many precious incenses were burned—Bhṛṅgāra incense, Tamāla incense, sandalwood, and saffron, pure and pleasing to the mind; with such diverse and harmonious, wondrous fragrances, they made offerings.
Furthermore, they sprinkled fragrant water everywhere upon the streets, and various flowers covered the ground, filling every place.

At that time, countless celestial maidens, asura maidens, and mahoraga maidens, their hearts filled with joy, came together to adorn the most excellent great city for the sake of accomplishing the causes of Bodhi.
Knowing that this city was everywhere adorned and purified, and that the time for the meal had arrived, the youth Candraprabha came before the Buddha and said,
"I pray that you enter this city for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."

At that time, as the Tathāgata entered the city gate together with his great assembly, the moment he set foot down, the great earth within the city shook everywhere, and throughout the hundreds of thousands of billions of lands in the ten directions, all likewise trembled.

At that time, the blind were able to see, those suffering obtained happiness, the deaf were able to hear, those with inferior complexions obtained exquisite beauty, those without wealth obtained wealth, those without children obtained children, those without clothing obtained clothing, those without gold and jewels obtained all manner of gold and jewels, those without relatives obtained relatives, and those lacking any articles for adorning the body were all provided with such ornaments.

Furthermore, there were various birds—cuckoos, parrots, peacocks, and śārikas; when these flocks of birds saw the Tathāgata, they gave rise to hearts of joy and uttered sublime and wondrous sounds, such that those who heard these sounds had their minds gladdened.

Furthermore, by the power of his supernatural penetrations, the Tathāgata manifested immeasurable campaka trees; hundreds of thousands of sentient beings took those pure flowers along with other exquisite incenses and scattered them over the Buddha as an offering.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of asura maidens and Maheśvaras who, holding red pearls and sandalwood powder, joyfully scattered them over the Tathāgata.
The hosts of asuras and the other devas held precious parasols, all adorned with gold and silver, which covered the Tathāgata from above in the midst of the sky.

The World-Honored One further employed his power of spiritual transformations to manifest immeasurable sandalwood trees, hundreds of thousands of vajra trees, and such trees as those of precious vessels and robes, in infinite and boundless numbers. Adorned with rare jewels, their flowers and leaves were lush and flourishing; the fruits of the merit of all sentient beings ripened together upon them. As a gentle breeze stirred them, a most supreme and wondrous fragrance wafted forth, overflowing and pervading immeasurable Buddha-lands, while hundreds of thousands of sentient beings together held them to scatter over the Buddha.
Thus, these immeasurable sentient and non-sentient beings are all transformations produced by the power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal knowledges.
If there are those who have aspirations, through his miraculous powers, he causes them all to be fully satisfied according to their inclinations.

The power of supernormal knowledges, merit, wisdom, and abiding; The power of skillful means, physical form, renown, and fame;

With loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity, patience, and freedom from affliction— just so with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
the Holy Lord of Ten Powers, Honored One among Devas, whose merit and fame are beyond compare,

In the past, within the three realms of existence, you cultivated pure deeds, increasing the various wholesome practices of the devas;
all the worlds universally revere and honor you, and hearing these words of mine, they all rejoice.
As the Tathāgata entered the city and set foot upon the ground, the towns and the great earth all shook;

The World-Honored One entered the city, bringing vast benefit; the hearts of the great assembly of humans and devas rejoiced.
Throughout the three realms of existence, both on earth and in the air, all praised the Tathāgata for his excellent peace and happiness.
When the World-Honored One first set the wheels of his feet upon the earth, a pure light shone everywhere in an unprecedented manner;

That the deaf, the blind, and the disabled have regained their faculties— All these are the extraordinary fruits of the Tathāgata.

The Buddha’s wisdom thoroughly understands the conduct of others; In accordance with the world, he brings about benefit.

through the continuity of pure faith, this arises from contemplating the limit of the exhaustion of the eye.

In the continuity of pure faith, by contemplating the limit of the eye’s exhaustion;
if one loves the limit of the eye’s exhaustion, one attains precepts without grasping.
In the continuity of pure morality, by contemplating the limit of the eye’s exhaustion.

The continuity of bodhi-wisdom arises From contemplating the limit of the eye’s exhaustion.
This extends even to the limit of the eye’s arising, Its boundaries and its cyclic flow.
Quiescence and non-existence, non-arising and cessation—
through such gateways as these, all are explained by the exhaustion of the eye.
If one takes delight in the limit of the eye’s exhaustion, they will forever be free from doubt.
Because they are free from doubt, they immediately attain the supernormal powers of a Buddha.

The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and even sounds and names—all are thus.
Knowing that the eye arises boundlessly, one gives rise to boundless wisdom.
Because wisdom is boundless, this Dharma is likewise said to be so.
Knowing that the exhaustion of the eye is boundless, one encounters no obstruction regarding the eye;
because there is no obstruction, one attains the unimpeded wisdom of a Buddha.
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
even sounds and names—all are thus. When the World-Honored One entered the city, hundreds of thousands of classes of sentient beings [were transformed].
Hearing the voice from the void preaching the Dharma, one has no doubt regarding the Buddha’s virtues.
Some, though they give rise to desire, do not impair their wisdom of the Buddha;
others, however, give rise to desire and thereby fall away from the Buddha’s merits.
Or though they give rise to desire, they seek unsurpassed wisdom;
diligently cultivating the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), they take no pleasure in the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Fools practice meditation, finding delight in the bliss of dhyāna-concentration.
They then give rise to overweening pride, claiming to have attained the fruits of the śramaṇa.
These fools practice meditation, yet lack the eye of knowledge regarding the limit of exhaustion;
even in a hundred thousand kalpas, they will never attain liberation.
All those who undergo birth are stained by attachment therein;
if one realizes that the nature of birth is empty, what is perceived is eternally pure.
Furthermore, even if one cultivates the four dhyānas, without the wisdom that reaches the limit of the eye’s exhaustion, [one cannot attain liberation].
Even if one were to pass through hundreds of thousands of eons, If one's meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is not pure,
And even if one attains equipoise (*samāpatti*), If one lacks the knowledge that reaches the limit of exhaustion,
Because one does not know the realization of exhaustion, One will constantly practice within the realization of outflows (*āsrava*).
If one clings to perceptions, lacking the knowledge of the limit where perceptions end,
one does not know the exhaustion of perceptions and thus constantly dwells within the taints of perception.
If one delights in and clings to the world, lacking the knowledge of the limit where the world ends, [one remains bound].
Because they do not know the exhaustion of the world, they constantly engage in worldly outflows (*āsrava*).
If one dwells with a mind possessed of outflows, there is no wisdom regarding the limit of the mind's exhaustion;
because they do not know the exhaustion of the mind, they constantly engage in mental outflows.
If one dwells in tainted phenomena, there is no knowledge of the limit of the exhaustion of phenomena;
because one does not know the exhaustion of phenomena, one constantly acts within the taints of phenomena.
If one possesses the dhuta practices, yet lacks the knowledge of the limit of the exhaustion of the eye—
Because they do not know the exhaustion of the eye, they are not true dhūta practitioners.
Though they wear robes of dyed color, lacking the wisdom of the limit of the exhaustion of the eye,
because they do not know the exhaustion of the eye, their dharma robes are not truly in accordance with the Dharma.
Though born into a noble family, if one lacks the wisdom that reaches the limit of the eye’s exhaustion,
and because they do not know the exhaustion of the eye, their lineage is not pure. Though they may maintain many dependents,
if they lack the wisdom that reaches the limit of the eye’s exhaustion, [they are not truly noble].
One will swiftly fall into the miserable realms, where even one's kinsmen cannot provide rescue.
Though one may be skilled in the treatises on grammar (*śabdavidyā*), if one lacks the wisdom that reaches the limit of the eye’s exhaustion,
and does not know that limit of the eye’s exhaustion, one is not a master of grammar.
Though one may be skilled in various crafts, if they lack the wisdom that reaches the limit of the eye's exhaustion,
and because they do not know the exhaustion of the eye, they are not true craftsmen.
Though they may provide extensive analysis of a single word in response to many difficult questions, [they remain unskilled].
One who lacks the wisdom regarding the limit of the exhaustion [of suffering] does not speak in accordance with the meaning.
Though they may speak as learned ones do, they do not know the secret from the non-secret;
lacking the wisdom regarding the limit of the exhaustion, they find nothing attained within the Dharma.
Though one may understand various words— worldly treatises and all phenomena—
without the eye of the knowledge that reaches the limit of exhaustion, it is like falling from a precipice while clutching at a vine.

Even if they have mastered all written characters, phonology, recitation, and chanting,

So it is with the arising of the eye, its limits, its transmigration,

The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; even sounds and names—all are thus.

even if they recite the four Vedas and have mastered all incantations;

and its transmigration, up to its cessation, one should know it is likewise so. It is the same for the ear,
nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
Even down to sounds and names, all are thus.

Because one can thoroughly understand the limit of the exhaustion of the eye, one can then thoroughly understand the merits of all Buddhas.
Regarding the arising of the eye, there is no dependence;
regarding the stillness of the eye, there is no movement of thought. Such a person is one who sees the Tathāgata.
Regarding the arising of the eye, there is no conceptual differentiation;
regarding the limit of the eye, there is no mental construction; regarding the destruction of the eye, there is no indication.
Such a person is one who sees the Tathāgata.
Without defiled attachment, with no arising regarding the eye, without grasping,
and with the cessation of the eye, being free from all clinging— such a person is one who sees the Tathāgata.
Because one knows the limits of the eye, one is certain regarding the faculties;
because one knows the arising of the eye, one attains mastery over the faculties. Such a person is one who beholds the Tathāgata.
Knowing that the eye does not exist, one thoroughly understands forms;
knowing that the eye is subject to destruction, one contemplates phenomena;
knowing that the eye is unborn, one cultivates the Path—such a person is one who beholds the Tathāgata.
Because of the limitlessness of the eye, one is also able to fully understand the distinctions among karmas;
because one is able to fully understand these distinctions among karmas,
such a person is said to see the Tathāgata.
One is also able to understand the distinctions among sufferings;
because one is able to understand these distinctions of suffering, such a person is said to see the Tathāgata.
Knowing it as it truly is— that because the eye perishes and disintegrates,
one can also know that suffering perishes and disintegrates— by being able to know that suffering perishes and disintegrates,
such a person is one who sees the Tathāgata.
Because the eye does not exist, one is free from all marks; by being able to understand this,
and because of that understanding which is free from all marks,
such a person sees the Tathāgata.
One is also able to understand that which is free from habitual tendencies;
because one is able to understand that which is free from habitual tendencies, such a person is said to see the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, knowing as it truly is that the eye is impermanent by nature,
one is also able to understand its freedom from obstruction. Because of this understanding of its freedom from obstruction,
such a person is said to see the Tathāgata.
The eye has no words or letters, yet it can also fully comprehend the Buddha’s power of wisdom;
because it can thus comprehend the Buddha’s power of wisdom, such a person is said to behold the Tathāgata.
One who is detached from all desires is also able to understand;
because they are able to understand detachment from all desires, such a person is one who has seen the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, knowing things as they truly are, one cultivates meditative concentration;
one is also able to understand the freedom from afflictions. Because of this understanding of freedom from afflictions, such a person is said to behold the Tathāgata.
Having accomplished such as these: the wisdom of the eye’s limit, the wisdom of the eye’s non-abiding, the wisdom of the eye’s non-arising,
the Buddha’s supernormal power wisdom, the wisdom of the eye’s inferiority, the wisdom of the eye’s excellence,
the wisdom of the inferiority of wisdom, and the wisdom of the purity of wisdom.
Knowledge of the purity of ethical discipline; knowledge of bodily restraint; knowledge of the purity of sound; knowledge of vocal restraint;
knowledge of the purity of the mind; knowledge of the distinctions between bases;
knowledge of all mental factors; knowledge of the defects of the mind; and knowledge of the purity of karma.
Knowledge of the rhythm of the heart, knowledge of the faults of wisdom, knowledge of the purity of sound,
knowledge of the differentiation of the aggregates, knowledge of the causal conditions of the aggregates, knowledge of the full comprehension of the eye,
knowledge of the arising of suffering, knowledge of untainted morality, and knowledge of the causal conditions of morality.
Knowledge of the causes and conditions of suffering, knowledge of the exhaustion of the causes of suffering, knowledge of all conditioned phenomena,
and knowledge of the exhausted and the inexhaustible; furthermore, knowing as it truly is the twelve links of dependent origination,
knowledge of that which has an object of activity, knowledge of that which lacks an object of activity, and the characterized and the uncharacterized.
Conditioned and unconditioned, their establishment and inclusion, and the knowledge of the minds of oneself and others; furthermore,
knowing as it truly is the limit of the eye’s exhaustion and arising,
its ultimate quiescence, and even its cyclic flow— therein is neither existence nor non-arising, the very nature of cessation.
May all sentient beings attain pure wisdom, the wisdom of all powers, and the wisdom of diligence.
Furthermore, may they know reality as it is: the wisdom of the various categories of unity and difference, and the wisdom of the inclinations of all sentient beings.

All sentient beings possess: The superior intention; The wisdom of the purity of mind, the wisdom of the maturation of karma, The wisdom of the faculties and elements, the wisdom of the transformations of the mind, The wisdom of liberation through insight, the wisdom of universal liberation, And the wisdom of supreme eloquence.
Furthermore, knowing as it truly is that there are sentient beings who commit evil and do not delight in the Dharma,
he causes them to thirst for and yearn for wisdom.
Moreover, knowing as it truly is the various principles and methods, he possesses the wisdom of knowing the proper time for cultivation and being free from indolence.
Furthermore, knowing as it truly is the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), the analytical discernment of all phenomena,
and unobstructed wisdom; likewise, knowing as it truly is the vast meaning and the verbal teachings,
possessing the wisdom that understands them accordingly.
Furthermore, one knows as it truly is: the wisdom of moderation in clothing, food, and drink when dwelling together with virtuous friends;
and furthermore, one knows as it truly is: the wisdom of diligent cultivation regarding the dhāraṇī-dharmas of all that is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Furthermore, knowing reality as it is, with no faults in body or mind, and remaining far removed from increase or decrease,
one seeks unsurpassed wisdom. Within the void of space, one manifests transformation bodies, accomplishing the immeasurable.
May hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all be made joyful, giving rise to pure faith and wisdom.
Regarding all Tathāgatas, may they delight in the wisdom of reverence; regarding the Dharma of detachment from desire, may they delight in the wisdom of cultivation.
The wisdom that delights in making offerings to the assembly of noble ones; the wisdom that delights in dedicating [merit] toward great enlightenment;
and the wisdom that delights in expounding upon dhāraṇīs.
Regarding all intentions, it is the wisdom of skillful observation;
regarding the meditative concentrations of the noble ones, it is the wisdom of thorough understanding;
regarding all forms of protective mindfulness, it is the wisdom of definitive certainty.
The wisdom that skillfully enters into the boundless mind;
the wisdom capable of expounding upon boundless verses;
the wisdom capable of awakening from the fetters of all desires.
The wisdom that does not fall into inferior realms;
the wisdom that should abandon evil associates;
and the wisdom that is able to draw near to virtuous friends.
The wisdom capable of discerning through all questions and answers;
the wisdom capable of understanding what is possible and what is impossible;
the wisdom capable of knowing what constitutes a ground and what does not.
Regarding the superior, middling, and inferior, one possesses the wisdom that can discern them.
There is the wisdom of the conditioned, the wisdom of the unconditioned, the wisdom of phenomena,
the wisdom of non-phenomena, the wisdom of grasping, and the wisdom of non-grasping.
The wisdom of cultivation, the wisdom of non-cultivation, the wisdom of the eye and the non-eye, the wisdom of the common characteristics of the eye,
the wisdom of the specific distinctions of the eye, and the wisdom of the intrinsic nature of the eye;
[the same applies to] the ear, nose, tongue, body, and even down to name and so forth— these are the twenty-five dharmas.
It is likewise so:
truly empty and quiescent, ultimately without self; such a person is then able to accomplish this kind of true and definitive mental samādhi.
If a person contemplates that the eye arises through causes and conditions,
and definitively understands that the eye has the characteristic of impermanence, then that person will be able to understand, as it truly is,
that both the eye and its causes and conditions are ultimately non-existent.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and even [the mind] with its objects such as names—these twenty-five factors are likewise so.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was entering the city, he pressed his foot upon the ground and manifested a rare wonder;
I shall now briefly describe a small portion of his merit.
Universally causing all sentient beings, Who hear it, to rejoice.
From a single pore, There appear immeasurable Hundreds of thousands of rays of light;
each ray of light Pervades immeasurable lands, For the sake of all sentient beings.
They perform the work of a Buddha.
Having practiced for a long night through generosity and the observance of precepts, those people,
upon hearing such teachings as these concerning miraculous transformations, will feel joy and delight.
If one can understand that the miraculous transformations of all Buddhas are not within the sphere of experience of the śrāvakas, that person, upon hearing of such miraculous transformations,
shall give rise to faith and understanding, and conceive a sense of rare wonder.
By inconceivable power, manifesting such various supernatural transformations,
they enable immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to draw near to and make offerings to the Tathāgatas.
He expounds immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sūtras, causing all sentient beings who hear what he says to be able to believe and accept it, their hearts filled with joy.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was entering the city, by means of his supernormal powers,
he spoke thus from mid-air: "Knowing the limit of the exhaustion of the eye,
up to its cessation— regarding the causal nature of the eye, it neither goes nor comes."
Ultimately empty and quiescent.
The ears, nose, tongue, and body, up to and including name—these twenty-five dharmas—are likewise so.
"At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter the city,
a subtle and wondrous sound issued from the midst of space, extolling the various names and titles of the Tathāgata,
causing the great assembly to give rise to a mind of faith and understanding."
The Lion among Men, known as the Vanquisher, the Dharma King who subdues the armies of Māra—
whosoever hears such a name as this shall be able to overcome all hosts of the heterodox.
He is named the Destroyer, the Dharma King who subdues craving;
if anyone should hear such a name, they will be able to abandon all craving.
Now in the present age, the lion among men, known as the Dharma King who crushes and destroys anger— if anyone hears such a name,
they will be able to abandon all anger.
The Lion among Men is named Destroyer; he is the Dharma King who dispels ignorance.
If anyone should hear such a name as this, they will be able to abandon all folly.
Named "The Destroyer," he is the Dharma King who subdues pride.
If anyone should hear such a name as this, they will be able to destroy all forms of pride.
Now in the present world, the lion among men, known as the Dharma King who Crushes and Extirpates Anger—
whosoever hears such a name as this shall be able to abandon all anger.
The Lion among Men, named Destroyer, the Dharma King who subdues envy— whosoever hears such a name as this shall be able to abandon all envy.
Named "The Destroyer," he is the King of Falsehood; if anyone should hear such a name as this, they will then be able to abandon all falsehoods.
Now, in the present world, there is a Lion among Men named Crusher,
the Dharma King who subdues all views. If anyone should hear such a name as this,
they will be able to abandon and leave behind all views.
The lion among men, named Destroyer, the Dharma King who plays with all phenomena—
if anyone hears such a name as this, they will be able to abandon all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is called the True Dharma, the Dharma King of Purity; if anyone should hear such a name, they will then be able to understand and realize the pure Dharma.
In the present world, the Lion among Men, known as Tongda (Thoroughly Penetrating),
is the Dharma King of all karmic actions. If anyone should hear such a name,
they will be able to understand and comprehend all karmic deeds.
The Lion among Men, named "Endowed with All," is a Dharma King of supernormal powers;
if anyone hears such a name, they shall be able to accomplish majestic virtue and supernormal powers.
Named "Endowed with," the Dharma King of all perfections; if anyone should hear such a name, they will then be able to accomplish the six pāramitās.
Now, in the present world, there is a Lion among Men named Liao-da (The Thoroughly Penetrating),
the Dharma King of all conditioned phenomena. If anyone should hear such a name,
they will then be able to thoroughly penetrate all conditioned phenomena.
The Lion among Men, named Pure Birth, possesses the light of dhāraṇī;
if anyone hears such a name, they shall be able to achieve a most excellent rebirth.
The purity of name-and-form, the light of the dhāraṇī— if anyone should hear such a name as this,
they shall be able to accomplish a most excellent and wondrous form.
Now, in the present world, the Lion among Men, whose name and body are pure and who possesses the dhāraṇī of radiance— if anyone hears such a name,
they shall be able to achieve a most excellent physical form.
The Lion among Men, named Pure Nature, possesses the light of dhāraṇī;
if anyone hears such a name as this, they shall be able to achieve a most excellent lineage.
Named Renown, the Dhāraṇī of Radiance: If anyone should hear such a name as this, They will be able to achieve Vast and far-reaching renown.
Now, in the present age, there is a Lion among Men named Dānaśūra (Giving Hero),
who maintains ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration,
wisdom, and dhāraṇī. If anyone should hear such a name as this, they will be able to achieve accomplishment.
Generosity and ethical discipline, up to and including wisdom and the gateways of dhāraṇī—
those who can uphold the name of the Lion among Men in the present age, known as the Dharmarāja Accomplished in Emptiness, [shall attain these].
Then one will be able to expound the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena.
This lion among men is named "Accomplished," the Dharma King who is without self.
If there is anyone who can uphold such a name, they will then be able to expound [it].
The meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing is called the purity of the eye. It is the Dharma King’s dhāraṇī;
if there is anyone who can uphold such a name, they will then be able to expound upon the meaning of the limit of the eye's exhaustion.
The ears, nose, tongue, and body, up to and including names and so forth—
these twenty-five dharmas, along with flower garlands, incense, lamps, parasols, and robes, are all likewise thus.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Thirty-three;

The Eleventh Assembly on the Manifestation of Radiance, Part Five:
"At that time, when the World-Honored One was entering the city, by means of his inconceivable power of supernatural transformations,
a subtle and wondrous sound issued forth from the midst of the sky:"
He expounded various dhāraṇī practices, causing the great assembly to hear these words:
"The limits and boundaries of existence, the tranquil flow of saṃsāra, and even its ultimate cessation."
Thus, one is able to penetrate all these dharmas and dwell in ultimate tranquility.
By the power of generosity, one ultimately gathers [beings]; by the power of ethical discipline, one ultimately achieves perfection; by the power of patience, one ultimately adorns oneself.
By the power of diligence, one brings about ultimate arousal; by the power of wisdom, one brings about ultimate proclamation.
Free from all written characters, speech, and sounds, and even from form and mind, it is ultimately pure.
Whether with outflows or without outflows, whether in meaning or in benefit, all are entirely empty and quiescent, ultimately pure.
Without relying upon any forms of existence, they dwell ultimately in the samādhi of dhāraṇī.
Even up to the indeterminate, in benefiting oneself and others, all such characteristics are ultimately pure.
Neither śrāvakas nor ordinary beings, nor even the dharmas of the Buddhas, abide therein.
At the limit of the exhaustion of the eye, one gives rise to the boundary of limits;
even unto cessation, such conditioned phenomena are ultimately quiescent.
Whether arising or not arising, whether suffering or pleasure, praise or blame—having completely relinquished all these, one is ultimately pure and ultimately illuminated.
This is the thorough understanding of the *śūnyatā-dhāraṇī*; this is precisely dwelling in the sphere traversed by the Buddhas.
This is the dwelling place where the Buddhas sport; this is the abiding in the supernormal powers of all Buddhas; this is the abiding in the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Abiding thus in the power of the limit of the exhaustion of the eye; abiding thus in the power of the limit of the arising of the eye;
abiding thus in the power of the boundary of the eye, and so on, up to abiding in the power of cessation, [and likewise] for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Even so it is with the twenty-five dharmas, including names and the rest.
This dhāraṇī accomplishes the sublime power of the Tathāgata.
This dhāraṇī accomplishes such majestic power.
It enters into all the spheres of activity of the Tathāgatas and abides within all the realms of the Tathāgatas.
Free from a rigid mind, abiding in the conduct of Brahmā, they are able to cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣas and kumbhāṇḍas to all give rise to joy.
Furthermore, they cause immeasurable hosts of gandharvas, along with all rākṣasas, to delight in and be tamed by it.
As for its phrases and meanings, they cannot be fully proclaimed; it is not a phenomenon of the mind.
That which is conceptualized by the mind is not a mental dharma, nor is it that which is grasped and maintained. This dhāraṇī is not obtained by the eye;
this dhāraṇī does not reach the body; this dhāraṇī is not obtained by the eye.
Nor do they reach the domain of the eye;
the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and even the twenty-five factors such as "name" (nāman) and so forth.

Furthermore, it is said regarding the eye: from its limit of exhaustion to its limit of arising, throughout the cycle of transmigration up to its final cessation—therein is no self and no person, no sentient being and no life-span; indeed, there is not even a *pudgala*.
Signless and unconditioned, neither coming nor going—such characteristics as these he fully understands.
Furthermore, he explains that he has understood the eye of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, it is said that one fully understands the eye accomplished through the Dharma: the eye of knowledge (*jñāna-cakṣus*), the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the Brahma-eye (*brahma-cakṣus*), and the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).

There is the eye obtained through birth as a Brahmā, the eye obtained through birth as a deva, the eye that is the maturation (*vipāka*) of being a Brahmā, and the eye that is the maturation of being a deva;
there is the eye produced by the cause of being a Brahmā, and the eye produced by the cause of being a deva.
The divine eye, the eye of celestial diligence, the eye born of the inferior,
the eye born of the sublime, the eye that abandons Yama, the worldly eye,
the eye of nāgas and yakṣas, the eye of kumbhāṇḍas, and the eye of burning affliction.
The eye free from feverish affliction, the pure eye, the non-pure eye, the wide and narrow eye,
the eye of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the eye of meditative concentration,
the eye of samādhi, the eye of objective spheres, and the eye born of conceptualization.
The eye born of craving, the eye of renunciation of craving; the eye born from causes, the eye not born from causes; the eye that is associated, the eye that is dissociated;
the eye born from a gateway, the eye not born from a gateway; the eye born from causes and conditions.
The eye arises from causes; it is not formed of flesh. It is the eye of pure wisdom, the eye of non-existence, the eye that cannot be apprehended.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and even name and so forth— these twenty-five dharmas are likewise thus.
At that time, from the midst of space, the World-Honored One further produced immeasurable,
subtle, and wondrous sounds, expounding the supreme dharma of *dhāraṇī*.
All these are transformations manifested by the Tathāgata.
The dhāraṇī says: "Such a dhāraṇī as this is that which has been attained by all Buddhas."
Endowed with great majestic power, his wisdom is boundless.
Free from all attachment, the foundations of mindfulness are entirely pure.
Without form, without coming or going, it is neither a direction nor a location.
Signless and beyond verbal expression, transcending all conceptual proliferation—
by diligently practicing this, the Bodhisattva ultimately attains cool serenity.
Even if one were to use hundreds of thousands of nayutas of verses,
Though one were to expound upon a single phrase, one could never reach its limit.
Praised by all the sages, pure and free from attachment,
all those gathered in the assembly develop a sense of profound respect.
Such is this dhāraṇī, through the majestic power of wholesome dharmas,
capable of crushing and extinguishing afflictions and causing one to attain supreme victory.
Its merit and wisdom are as vast as the great ocean.
Having accomplished the power of patience, their minds remain unshakable.
Bodhisattvas constantly cultivate this, which is praised by the wise;
they abandon poverty and shall obtain great wealth and treasure.
This dhāraṇī increases all merits; it is always adorned with the words of truth such as emptiness (śūnyatā).
Because it relinquishes all syllables, it is called "emptiness."
By relinquishing mind and consciousness, it is termed the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Such a dhāraṇī is free from defilement and eternally pure;
abiding in true wisdom, it manifests various benefits.
Causing all sentient beings alike to rejoice and give rise to pure minds;
the immeasurable hosts of yakṣas, as well as the kumbhāṇḍas—
such kings of ghostly hordes likewise gave birth to great joy.
This dhāraṇī is tranquil and free from conceptual proliferation;
it loves all sentient beings and bestows peace and happiness upon them all.
Throughout many hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it remains constantly within the various realms of existence.
Performing immeasurable benefit, pure and unstained by defilement;
sometimes using hundreds of thousands of verses, they expound the nectar-like Dharma,
causing immeasurable sentient beings to all give rise to great joy.
In the past, immeasurable Buddhas, with pure intention,
constantly contemplated the nature of phenomena within this dhāraṇī.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the hosts of devas, as well as the nāga kings and asuras, [all paid homage].
Upon hearing this dhāraṇī, the mind gives rise to great joy.
Wherever this dhāraṇī passes through various lands,
there shall always be no calamities, nor the suffering of illness, nor any distress.
May all sentient beings, each and every one, rejoice;
may this dhāraṇī abide forever within my heart.
May this dhāraṇī likewise abide wherever my body and mind are located.
From the throat, palate, lips, and tongue, immeasurable merit is born.
If one can constantly receive and uphold it, one will obtain immeasurable merit,
benefiting many sentient beings and causing them all to attain joy.
This dhāraṇī abandons all faults and evils,
expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma, and attains inexhaustible eloquence;
it causes hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to sever all doubts and delusions.
Crushing all arrogance, one attains immeasurable merit.
Such a dhāraṇī, this most profound and subtle dharma—
wise ones should constantly contemplate it and practice it with courageous diligence.
Donning the armor of wisdom, one destroys all afflictions;
having increased merit, one finds joy in it without satiety.
Such is this dhāraṇī, possessing vast renown.
Able to comprehend both the finite and the infinite, as well as the limit of birth and the limit of non-birth;
with such wisdom, they adorn themselves in manifold ways and are revered and made offerings to by hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas.
This dhāraṇī has clear conduct as its two feet;
relying upon supreme concentration, it proceeds toward the path of bodhi,
accords with śamatha and vipaśyanā, and penetrates untainted wisdom.
By the power of the faculty of pure faith, the two hands are perfected;
by diligence and patience, the two breasts are perfected;
and the perfection of wisdom constitutes the mark of the crown protuberance.
With the sūtras as the thread, one strings together the garland of the four analytical knowledges;
the various merits practiced in the past,
along with immeasurable parables, all serve as its adornments.
Such a dhāraṇī possesses immeasurable merit;
regarding the past, present, and future limits of the eye, it is both finite and infinite.
Whether in arising or non-arising, it is both a limit and not a limit.
Quiescence and non-quiescence, Transmigration and non-transmigration,
Non-existence and non-arising, Cessation and selflessness, The absence of a person,
the absence of a life-span, And even the absence of sentient beings.
In this way, through immeasurable gateways, all things are fully understood:
the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the six sense objects and the four great elements;
even worldly birth and names—all are exactly like this.
As praised above, this subtle and wondrous dhāraṇī possesses the supreme merit of tranquility; it is the domain of all Buddhas.
The true meaning of the dhāraṇī cannot be expressed through written words.
"Conforming to worldly convention, I speak only by means of provisional names.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, went to the youth’s house, spread out his seat, and sat down.

At that time, having known that the Buddha was seated, the youth Candraprabha personally brought exquisite offerings and presented them to the Tathāgata and the great assembly; these offerings were matured solely through the inconceivable power of the supreme roots of goodness arising from meditative concentration and merit.

When giving in this manner, one does not do so for oneself alone, but rather causes all immeasurable sentient beings to set out toward Bodhi and obtain great, wholesome benefits, such that the offerings are universal and all are fully satisfied.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he addressed the youth Candraprabha within the assembly, saying: "Young man!
If sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna practice the provisions for giving, there are eighty kinds of supreme merits."
What are the eighty? They are:
maturing sentient beings by gathering them through virtuous speech; the perfection of the excellent marks; the absence of deficiency in the sense faculties;
the relinquishing of birth and death; the realization of nirvāṇa; the exhaustion of all fetters and afflictions; and the attainment of supreme mastery.
Endowed with merit, they adorn Buddha-fields; their retinues are pure, and they possess great majestic power.
They are complete in wisdom, have accomplished the most supreme and excellent practices, and have perfected the unsurpassed and unequaled conduct.
They eliminate habitual tendencies and increase the Tathāgata’s conduct of all-knowledge, as well as their own bodies and...
The relics are venerated by all the world’s śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

they crush the wicked and enable human kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asura kings, garuḍa kings, and even Brahmā kings to give rise to pure faith. Possessing great majestic power, they proclaim the sūtras.
Whether it be *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, or even *upadeśa*,
they should uphold and expound them with a mind free from weariness; being without stinginess regarding the Dharma,
they abide securely in the Buddha-way, the most supreme in all worlds— this is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Pure, they realize the Dharma-body and attain fearlessness; having accomplished merit and virtue, they eclipse all non-Buddhists, possess the qualities of virtuous persons, and abandon the conduct of the wicked.
Believing in the causes of merit and wisdom, they harmonize with the Buddha-dharma, subdue all Māras, and are free from doubt regarding the peaceful and blissful teachings spoken by the Buddha.
Having crushed and destroyed evil desires, possessing great majestic power, practicing the bodhisattva path,
attaining supreme supernormal powers, abandoning birth and death, bringing sentient beings to maturity, praising boundless conduct, gathering in merits,
consoling and encouraging sentient beings, enjoying the bliss of the Dharma, practicing generous giving, and entering the gateway of great wisdom.
Abiding in the stage of *uṣmagata*, their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is determined; they practice the patience for the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) and dwell securely in the Buddha-way. O Youth!
"If good sons and good daughters cultivate the provisions of giving, they will fully accomplish these eighty kinds of sublime merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattvas of great wisdom, Fully endowed with the provisions of giving..."
There are eighty victories, which I have now briefly explained.
Furthermore, there are other merits, immeasurable and inconceivable, all born from generosity; these I shall now proclaim in brief.
"You should give with equanimity, extending it universally throughout this great assembly;
such a provision of giving is what the wise should cultivate.
Through this giving, one can accumulate an inconceivable mass of merit."
The body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks, all of which are perfectly complete.
His place of birth, lineage, country, and household,
as well as his reputation, physical form, and mind— all are utterly pure.
The various supernatural transformations of the devas, as well as their palaces and celestial maidens,
and pure, unimpeded eloquence— all these arise from generosity.
Generosity is the supreme provision, praised by all the Buddhas.
This is itself awakening, the primordial abiding ground.
Bodhisattvas who are diligent have no doubt regarding giving;
abiding in a mind of certainty, they practice generosity with diligence.
With such a mind of giving, one accomplishes supreme merit;
the Bodhisattva who diligently practices this shall realize the Buddha’s enlightenment.
Through the power of giving, one accomplishes sublime supernormal faculties.
He causes millions of worlds to tremble, yet does not harm any sentient beings.
Through the power of giving, he is able to induce pure ethical discipline,
extensive learning, right faith, diligence, meditative concentration, and untainted wisdom.
Through generosity, one can bring forth the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment,
the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power, thereby distancing oneself from all habitual tendencies.
Through generosity, one can bring forth pure and wondrous speech.
In hundreds of koṭis of lands, he reveals boundless teachings.
By practicing generosity with pure faith, one swiftly attains all supernormal powers;
to accomplish these supernormal powers, one should diligently cultivate generosity.
Immeasurable hosts of devas, hundreds of thousands of asuras,
nāgas, spirits, and yakṣas, together with their retinues, all surround [him];
they ride upon exquisite pavilions, sporting with sovereign ease.
When such kings as these see one who diligently practices giving,
they shall all rise to welcome them from afar, prepare seats, and offer them sustenance.
Such a person who practices giving in this way will be endowed with great majesty and virtue.
By the power of his sovereign spiritual penetrations, he gathers and sustains all the celestial kings;
the kumbhāṇḍas and yakṣas all come to submit to him,
as do the hosts of gandharvas, who likewise present various musical offerings.
May compassion arise toward those who would harm; may one stay far away from wicked people.
May precious wealth never diminish, and may storehouses be entirely filled.
By practicing generosity, one accomplishes the supreme provisions for enlightenment.
Even unto the wisdom of the Buddha, they do not practice the teachings of external paths.
Such persons are free from illness and affliction;
by guarding the dhāraṇī, they attain all manner of supreme powers—all of which arise from generosity.
Such a person who practices giving, cultivating the path to enlightenment,
does not encounter evil associates but attains virtuous friends of like kind.
Furthermore, there are other bodhisattvas who accumulate the provisions for giving.
They achieve inconceivable dhāraṇī-wisdom;
with immeasurable verses and stanzas, they expound the total retention (dhāraṇī),
remaining entirely unimpeded and never losing the original meaning.
With the vast mind of enlightenment, may your aspirations always remain firm;
Possessing pure ethical discipline, abandon all demonic activities.
Unattached to the pleasures of the five desires, apply yourself with diligence to seeking right mindfulness.
The mind is always free from delusion, nor does it give rise to craving or attachment.
All afflictions, such as anger and hatred, are understood exactly as they are;
regarding all sensory objects, one is neither attached nor deluded.
This person thoroughly understands that all such afflictions,
through the convergence of causes and conditions, are able to give rise to various faults;
even regarding the Buddha-dharma, whether it be the cause or the cause of the cause.
Thus, through the operation of causes, one can thoroughly understand all things.
Such a person is able to realize the causal nature of the limit of the eye;
free from all delusions, they remain unstained by the eye.
This person is able to thoroughly understand the arising and the limits of the eye,
its tranquility and its flux, its non-existence and its non-arising,
up to its cessation; such are the natures of these causes.
Far removed from all delusions, they have no attachment to the eye.

Such persons are able to understand that the discourse regarding the "prior limit" of the eye is a conventional designation established in accordance with the world; therein, there is no reality whatsoever.

This person is able to understand that the discourse regarding the posterior limit of the eye is a conventional designation established in accordance with the world, and that within it there is no reality.
This person is able to understand the boundary and limit of the arising of the eye.
Quiescence and saṃsāra, non-existence and non-arising,
even up to nirvāṇa— such expressions are provisionally established in accordance with the world; therein, there is no reality whatsoever.

This person is able to understand that the conventional designations regarding the prior limit of the eye arise merely from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and thus they have no attachment therein.
This person is able to understand the conventional designations regarding the posterior limit of the eye.
Yet through the conjunction of causes and conditions, one remains unattached therein.
Such a person is able to understand the limits and boundaries of the eye’s arising—
its tranquility and its flux, its non-existence and its non-arising.
Even up to the discourse on "extinction," such expressions as these arise merely from the conjunction of causes and conditions; therein, one remains unattached.
Such a person is able to understand that even the discourse concerning the prior limit of the present is likewise so.
The intrinsic nature is inexpressible; therein, there is no defilement.
One who can understand this understands that the discourse regarding the posterior limit of the eye is inexpressible in its intrinsic nature; therein, there is no defilement.
This person is able to understand the limits and boundaries of the eye’s arising,
its stillness and its flux, its non-existence and its non-arising,
and even its cessation; such are the expressions [they comprehend].
The intrinsic nature is without representation, and therein is no defilement.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, the six sense objects and the four great elements,
even down to worldly birth and names— all are exactly like this.
This person is able to understand that desire itself is the Buddha-way;
since their intrinsic nature is without distinction, they remain unstained by desire.
One should seek the path of all Buddhas within the afflictions.
Knowing that their nature is without distinction—this is entering the gateway of dhāraṇī.
To say that desire is dhāraṇī, and that dhāraṇī is itself desire;
knowing that their nature is without distinction—this is training in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to greed is itself making offerings to the Buddha;
by making offerings to the Buddha, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Such a person is able to understand that hatred is itself the path of the Buddha.
In their intrinsic nature there is no distinction; they are unstained by anger.
Anger itself is the dhāraṇī, and the dhāraṇī is itself anger.
Knowing that their natures are without distinction is to train in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to anger is also making offerings to the Buddha;
because of making offerings to the Buddha, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Such a person is able to realize that ignorance is itself the path of the Buddha.
Intrinsic nature is without distinction, and thus one is unstained by delusion.
If one understands, as it truly is, the ultimate limit of the nature of delusion,
then one cultivates the Buddha-way and accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Delusion is itself the dhāraṇī, and the dhāraṇī is itself delusion;
knowing that their natures are without distinction is to study the gateway of the dhāraṇī.
To thus make offerings to delusion is to make offerings to the Buddha.
For the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, by making offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to the Dharma;
for the sake of making offerings to the Dharma, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is itself making offerings to the Saṅgha;
by making offerings to the Saṅgha, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is itself making offerings to the precepts.
By making offerings to the precepts, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, by making offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to diligence;
by making offerings to diligence, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
To thus make offerings to delusion is to offer praise;
because of offering praise, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
To thus make offerings to delusion is to offer to the Buddha-dharma.
Because one makes offerings to the Buddha-dharma, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, by making offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to the dharma-nature;
because one makes offerings to the dharma-nature, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
To make such an offering to delusion is to make an offering to True Suchness (tathatā);
by making an offering to True Suchness, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
To make such an offering to delusion is to make an offering to non-arising (anutpāda).
Because one makes offerings to that which is unborn, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, by making offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to that which is unceasing;
because one makes offerings to that which is unceasing, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to the inexhaustible;
because one makes offerings to the inexhaustible, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to non-existence.
Because there is no object of offering, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus, by offering to delusion, one offers to the infinite;
because one offers to the infinite, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to the three realms of existence;
by making offerings to the three realms of existence, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to tranquility.
Because one makes offerings to tranquility, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, because one makes offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to saṃsāra;
and by making offerings to that which revolves, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to the non-turning;
because one makes offerings to the non-turning, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to non-existence.
Because there is no offering, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Thus, by offering to delusion, one offers to non-arising;
because one offers to non-arising, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to quiescence;
by making offerings to quiescence, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Thus making offerings to delusion is to make offerings to the non-coming.
Because offerings do not come, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus, by offering to delusion, one offers to non-action;
because one offers to non-action, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to ignorance is to make offerings to the conditioned;
because one makes offerings to the conditioned, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to ignorance is to make offerings to suffering and the like.
By making offerings to suffering and the rest, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, by making offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to the knowledge of suffering;
because one makes offerings to the knowledge of suffering, one accomplishes the gate of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to delusion is itself making offerings to the wisdom of origination;
by making offerings to the wisdom of origination, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Thus, making offerings to delusion is itself making offerings to the wisdom of cessation.
Because one makes offerings to the knowledge of cessation, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, by making offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to the knowledge of the path;
because one makes offerings to the knowledge of the path, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
To make such an offering to ignorance is to make an offering to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna);
by making an offering to the knowledge of phenomena, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
To make such an offering to ignorance is to make an offering to subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
By making offerings to subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, by making offerings to ignorance (*moha*), one makes offerings to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);
because of making offerings to non-arising, one accomplishes the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Thus, by making offerings to delusion, one makes offerings to the knowledge of exhaustion;
because of making offerings to the knowledge of exhaustion, one accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Likewise, regarding the right efforts, the foundations of mindfulness, and the bases of psychic power, [one should offer in this same way].
The five faculties and the five powers, the seven factors of awakening and the eightfold path,
together with śamatha and vipaśyanā— among these nine kinds of dharmas, all are thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying: "Good son!
If there are sentient beings who abide in the Mahāyāna and desire to accomplish the dhāraṇīs as described above, they should keep themselves far away from eighty kinds of persons."
What are the eighty? They are:

killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, killing an arhat, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha with a murderous intent, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, living as a thief while ordained, being without sexual organs, having both sexual organs, and holding wrong views.
Wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration;
lack of knowledge regarding the proper place, the proper time, the proper dharma, the proper path, the proper measure, and the distinction between self and others;
and an inability to show respect toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the various precepts of training.
They neither revere heedfulness nor exalted objects; they do not know the Dharma, they do not know the Vinaya, and they do not know the training rules.
They do not know whether an offense is heavy or light, nor do they know whether their precepts are broken or deficient.
Furthermore, they do not know whether their conduct is subtle or coarse, nor do they know of future karma.
Now, they lack understanding even regarding inferior matters; they praise the Śrāvaka-yāna and disparage the Tathāgata’s Dharma;
they exhort and instruct others in the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, causing them to distance themselves from and abandon the unsurpassed Right Path;
they violate the precepts, violate right view, and violate all dignified conduct; they practice what is not the Way, and they speak of a self and a person.
There are sentient beings who assert the existence of a life-principle (*jīva*) and assert the existence of a person (*pudgala*);
they are of inferior resolve, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion; they hold views of nihilism and eternalism, views of emptiness and causelessness;
they do not perceive existence, do not perceive non-existence, do not perceive karma, and do not perceive diligence; they do not understand karma, nor do they understand...
They do not know karma as a cause; they do not know maturation, nor do they know the cause of maturation.
They do not know the faculties, nor do they know the cause of the faculties. They do not know the realms, nor do they know the cause of the realms.
They do not know liberation, nor do they know the cause of liberation. They do not know the path, nor do they know the cause of the path. They do not know the afflictions...
They know the cause of afflictions, yet they do not know giving; they do not know the cause of giving; they do not know the past limit nor the future limit;
they do not know the cause of the past limit nor the cause of the future limit; they do not know birth and death; they do not know the cause of birth and death;
they do not know outflows; they do not know the cause of outflows; they do not know exhaustion or non-exhaustion.
They do not know existence or non-existence; they do not know the limit or the absence of a limit; they do not know tranquility or the absence of tranquility;
they do not know transformation or the absence of transformation; they do not know nature or the absence of nature; they do not know arising or the absence of arising;
they do not know cessation or the absence of cessation.
"O Youth! If good sons or good daughters wish to accomplish the dhāraṇīs as described above, they should abandon these eighty kinds of unrighteous persons."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If one does not understand the eye, the limit where birth is exhausted, such a person is deluded regarding the dhāraṇī; the wise should keep far away from them."
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, That it is without self and without sentient beings, Such a person dwells in the dhāraṇī; The wise should draw near to them.
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, Birth is exhausted and transcends all words.
This person abides in dhāraṇī; the wise should draw near them.
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, being tranquil and dwelling nowhere, this person abides in dhāraṇī; the wise should draw near them.
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, That its intrinsic nature abides nowhere, Such a person dwells in dhāraṇī; The wise should draw near to them.
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, That it neither revolves nor possesses the mark of form,
This person dwells in dhāraṇī; the wise should draw near them.
If one can understand that the eye is of an unarisen and quiescent nature, this person dwells in dhāraṇī; the wise should draw near them.
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, Its self-nature being free from names and signs,
Such that even all Buddhas have nothing to say, Neither to praise nor to designate—
This person dwells in dhāraṇī; The wise should draw near to them.
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, Its self-nature being free from names and marks,
There is nothing that can be conceptualized, Nor anything to receive, uphold, or proclaim;
Such a person dwells in dhāraṇī, And the wise should draw near to them.
Such is the nature of this dhāraṇī: it cannot be expressed or explained by words;
it has no location or direction, nor can it be reached by the mind.
This Dharma is free from joy and likewise does not abide in anger.
Immovable like the king of mountains, though it is said that there is nothing to be attained;
the dhāraṇī is truly non-existent, even to the extent that "I" do not exist.
If my own self-nature is empty, the dhāraṇī likewise does not exist.
The dhāraṇī is empty of intrinsic nature, yet the foolish reckon it to exist;
through such false discrimination, they do not hear [the truth] and give rise to distress.
If one discriminates the nature of greed as well as the emptiness of the dhāraṇī, [one remains deluded].
These two kinds of conceptualization are ultimately unfindable.
If one realizes that emptiness itself is empty, then even the dhāraṇīs do not exist;
likewise, up to the factors of enlightenment, even samādhi is empty.
If one is able to understand dhāraṇī and emptiness,
up to and including samādhi, one understands the eye as well.
If one thoroughly understands the limit of the exhaustion of the eye as it truly is, [one is liberated].
Then, regarding the gateway of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection. If,
regarding the arising-limit of the eye, one understands it well as it truly is,
then, regarding the gateway of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
If one thoroughly understands, as it truly is, the limit of the eye,
then one will ultimately achieve mastery over the gateways of dhāraṇī.
If one thoroughly understands, as it truly is, the tranquility of the eye, [one will likewise achieve this].
Then, regarding the gateways of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
If one thoroughly understands, as it truly is, the shifting of the eye, then,
regarding the gateways of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
If one thoroughly understands, as it truly is, that the eye does not exist,
Then one will ultimately achieve accomplishment in the gateways of dhāraṇī. If one thoroughly understands,
as it truly is, that the eye is unarisen, [Then one will ultimately achieve accomplishment in the gateways of dhāraṇī.]
Then, regarding the gate of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
If one thoroughly understands the quiescence of the eye as it truly is, then,
regarding the gate of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
If one knows, as it truly is, the limit of exhaustion regarding the transformation of the eye,
then one will ultimately achieve mastery over the gateways of dhāraṇī.
If one knows, as it truly is, the limit of arising regarding the transformation of the eye...
Then, regarding the gateways of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection. If,
regarding the transformations of the eye, one knows their limits as they truly are,
then, regarding the gateways of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
If one knows, as it truly is, the stillness within the transformation of the eye,
then one will ultimately achieve mastery of the gateways of dhāraṇī.
If one knows, as it truly is, the flux within the transformation of the eye, [one will likewise achieve mastery].
Then, regarding the gateway of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection. If,
regarding the transformations of the eye, one knows them as they truly are— namely, that they do not exist— then,
regarding the gateway of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
If one knows, as it truly is, that the eye is subject to transformation and is without arising,
then one will ultimately achieve mastery over the gateways of dhāraṇī.
If one knows, as it truly is, that the eye is subject to transformation and is utterly quiescent, [then one will ultimately achieve mastery over the gateways of dhāraṇī].
Then, regarding the gateway of dhāraṇī, one will ultimately achieve perfection.
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the six sense objects and the four great elements;
even worldly birth and names—all things are thus.
If, regarding the prior limit of the eye, there is no change and no mark of difference,
no grasping and no conceptualization— this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the ultimate limit of the eye, there is no change and no mark of difference...
Without grasping and without conceptualization— this is dwelling in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the limit of the eye’s arising, there is no change and no mark of difference,
without grasping and without conceptualization— this is dwelling in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the limit of the eye, there is no change and no mark of difference,
no grasping and no conceptualization— this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the tranquility of the eye, there is no change and no mark of difference...
Without grasping and without conceptualization— this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the activity of the eye, there is no change and no mark of difference,
without grasping and without conceptualization— this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the eye, there is no existence, No change, and no characteristic of difference,
No grasping, and no conceptual differentiation— This is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the eye, there is no arising, No change, and no characteristic of difference...
Without grasping and without conceptual differentiation, one dwells in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If, regarding the cessation of the eye, there is no change and no mark of difference,
without grasping and without conceptual differentiation, one dwells in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, The six sense objects and the four great elements,
Even down to worldly birth and names— All are exactly like this. Greed, hatred,
delusion, anger, pride, Envy, deceit, stinginess, sorrow, and affliction—
Faults, stains, and the poison of arrows; the violent floods and black-and-white karmas—
these are neither born nor extinguished, neither departing nor arriving,
neither moving nor changing, and neither created nor conditioned.
Neither light nor darkness, neither flowing nor abandoning the torrent;
neither exhaustion nor abiding, neither proceeding nor not proceeding;
neither syllables nor objects of perception, neither emerging nor entering.
Conceptual constructions, delusions, and so forth— The sixty-two various gateways— Each follows its own principles; All things are exactly like this.
If one knows the limit of the past, And likewise the upper and lower limits, [one attains liberation].
Without grasping and without conceptualization, this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows the limit of the exhaustion of the eye, and so on up to the zenith and nadir,
without grasping and without conceptualization, this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows the limit of the eye’s arising, And so on up to its upper and lower bounds,
Being without grasping and without conceptual discrimination, This is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows the boundary of the eye, And so on up to its upper and lower bounds...
Without grasping and without conceptualization— this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows that the eye is quiescent, and so on up to the upper and lower [senses],
without grasping and without conceptualization— this is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows the流转 (saṃsāra) of the eye, And so on up to its upper and lower limits,
Being without grasping and without conceptual discrimination, This is abiding in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows that the eye does not exist, And so on up to its upper and lower limits,
Without grasping and without conceptualization, one dwells in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows that the eye is unborn, and likewise for everything up to the zenith and nadir,
without grasping and without conceptualization, one dwells in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one knows that the eye is quiescent, And likewise for all things from the highest to the lowest,
Being without grasping or conceptual discrimination, One dwells in the gateway of dhāraṇī.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, The six sense objects, and the four great elements—
Even unto the names of worldly births, all are thus.
Unchanging within the ground, without grasping or conceptualization—
those who understand in this way achieve the gateway of dhāraṇī.
In the stages there is no characteristic of arising; Without grasping and without conceptualization— One who understands thus Accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
In the stages there is no characteristic of cessation; Without grasping and without conceptualization—
One who understands in this way, accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Regarding the signs of entering the stages, there is no grasping and no conceptual differentiation;
one who understands in this way, accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Regarding the earth, its characteristic of renunciation is without grasping and without conceptual differentiation;
one who understands it thus accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Regarding the earth, its characteristic of wishlessness is without grasping and without conceptual differentiation.
One who understands in this way achieves the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Regarding the stages, there is no characteristic of abiding; there is neither coming nor going, neither the boundless nor the inexhaustible, neither correspondence nor non-correspondence.
Free from conceptualization based on names, it is observed as both flowing and ceasing;
it is without attainment and involves cultivation, being ineffable and beyond representation.
It is tranquil and without dependence, consisting of the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts.
The bases of supernormal power, the faculties and powers, the factors of awakening, the fearlessnesses, and the path—
these dharmas of the stages are without grasping and without conceptual differentiation.
One who understands them thus accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one does not enter into a self, Is without grasping and without conceptualization,
One who understands in this way Accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one does not emerge from a self, Is without grasping and without conceptualization,
One who understands in this way accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one regards me as signless, without grasping and without conceptual differentiation—
one who understands in this way accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one has no aspiration for a self, no grasping, and no conceptual differentiation—
one who understands in this way achieves the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one does not dwell upon a self, has no grasping, and no conceptual differentiation,
One who understands in this way accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one realizes that the self is unborn, without grasping and without conceptual differentiation—
one who understands in this way accomplishes the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one perceives that in "self" there is no cessation, no grasping, and no conceptual differentiation,
one who understands in this way achieves the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If one perceives that in the words for "self" there is no grasping and no conceptual differentiation,
One who understands in this way achieves the gateway of dhāraṇī.
If I am free from words and letters, without grasping and without conceptualization—
one who understands in this way achieves the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Knowing the past and future limits of the eye, one remains far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;
that the self-nature of causes and conditions is empty is what the Guide has taught through skillful means.
When expounding the Dharma, if one discriminates the characteristics of the eye, [one fails to see its true nature].
This person engages in false conceptualization; it is not called the true teaching of the Dharma.
If, when contemplating the Dharma, one discriminates the characteristics of the eye, this person engages in false conceptualization; it is not called the contemplation of the Dharma.
If, when practicing the Dharma, one discriminates the characteristics of the eye,
that person is engaging in false discrimination and is not said to be practicing the Dharma.
If one realizes the emptiness of the eye, one does not [conceptually] approach Bodhi.
The Buddhas always appear before such a person and preach the Dharma.
If one does not understand the eye, one will also not understand forms;
if one can understand the eye, one will also understand forms.
If one can thoroughly understand the eye, one will also thoroughly understand forms;
if one thoroughly understands forms, one will also be able to thoroughly understand the eye.
This applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the six sense objects and the four great elements.
Even down to the names for the worlds and their births, all are thus. If,
when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates the characteristics of causes,
such a person is engaged in false discrimination and is not said to be preaching the Dharma.
If, when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates the characteristics of tranquility,
such a person is engaged in false discrimination and is not said to be expounding the Dharma.
If, when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates the characteristics of the Path...
Such a person engages in false discrimination; this is not called preaching the Dharma.
If, when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates the characteristics of emptiness, such a person engages in false discrimination; this is not called preaching the Dharma.
If, when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates regarding the accumulation [of merit],
such a person is engaged in false discrimination and is not said to be expounding the Dharma.
If, when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates regarding phenomena, [one is likewise not expounding the Dharma].
Such a person engages in false discrimination; this is not called preaching the Dharma.
If, when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates by grasping at the eye, such a person engages in false discrimination; this is not called preaching the Dharma.
If one does not understand the eye, then desire arises; if one can understand the eye, desire will not arise.
This applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the six sense objects and the four great elements.
Even down to the names for the worlds and their births, all are like this.
If, when expounding the Dharma, one discriminates among various fruits,
such a person is engaged in false discrimination and is not said to be preaching the Dharma.
Not retreating from their aspiration, they thoroughly realize the emptiness of nature;
