having attained the gates of all samādhis, they are able to skillfully expound the Dharma.
Not retreating from their aspiration, they remain free from conceptual discrimination regarding the eye.
Because they are free from conceptual discrimination, they are able to skillfully teach the Dharma.
Those who do not understand that the nature of the eye is empty, and are likewise deluded regarding the self-nature of the eye—
because they lack such understanding, they should not teach the Dharma.
If one understands that the nature of the eye is empty, One then knows the self-nature of the eye;
because of this understanding, Such a person should preach the Dharma.
Failing to understand that the nature of the eye is empty, One is likewise deluded regarding the self-nature of words.
Because they do not understand this, they should not preach the Dharma.
If they realize that the nature of the eye is empty, they will know the intrinsic nature of words;
because they are able to understand this, such a person should preach the Dharma.
Not understanding that the nature of the eye is empty, And being likewise deluded regarding the self-nature of letters,
Because of this lack of understanding, One should not preach the Dharma.
If one understands that the nature of the eye is empty, Then one knows the self-nature of letters.
Because they are able to understand this, such persons should preach the Dharma.
Those who do not understand that the nature of the eye is empty, and who are likewise deluded regarding the intrinsic nature of names—
because they lack such understanding, they should not preach the Dharma.
If one understands that the nature of the eye is empty, Then one knows its own intrinsic nature;
because of this understanding, Such a person should preach the Dharma.
If one does not understand that the nature of the eye is empty, One is likewise deluded regarding the intrinsic nature of form.
Because they do not understand this, they should not preach the Dharma.
If they realize that the nature of the eye is empty, they will know the self-nature of form;
because they are able to understand this, such persons should preach the Dharma.
Failing to realize that the nature of the eye is empty, one discriminates based on worldly appearances;
unable to skillfully accord with them, one cannot subdue sentient beings.
If one realizes that the nature of the eye is empty, one does not rely on appearances for discrimination.
One who can thus skillfully accord with others and subdue all sentient beings,
yet does not understand whether the eye exists or not while preaching the Dharma among the assembly—
such a person craves gain and honor, and no one will have faith in or accept their words.
If one understands the existence and non-existence of the eye, and preaches the Dharma while amidst the assembly,
such a person will not be greedily attached, and all will believe and accept it.
But if one does not understand that the nature of the eye is empty, yet occupies the Dharma seat, [they will be unable to lead others].
Though many parables are spoken, none will believe or accept them.
But if one realizes the emptiness of the nature of the eye and sits upon the Dharma-seat,
then all the parables spoken will be believed and accepted by all.
"The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, The six sense objects and the four great elements, Even down to worldly birth and names— All are exactly like this.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the youth Candraprabha and the great assembly—including all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others in the world—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Thirty-Four;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Thirty-Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
12. The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, Part One of Twelve. Chapter One: The Conversion of the Householder.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavat was observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in Śrāvastī. When the three months had passed and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) had been performed, and he had finished making his robes, he traveled through various countries together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

This Bhagavān has accomplished vast and sublime renown and appeared in the world, being praised by all devas and humans, namely: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Worthy One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Bhagavān.
Deeply abiding in self-realization and fully endowed with supernormal powers, his majestic virtue eclipses that of all devas, worldly beings, māras, brahmās, and asuras.

He constantly expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma for sentient beings, revealing its excellence in the beginning, the middle, and the end—its phrasing and meaning being skillful, singular, perfect, and pure, constituting the holy life of Brahma.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, kings, ministers, various non-Buddhists, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as elders, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, offered to the Tathāgata immeasurable and most excellent offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various kinds of requisites.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a great assembly who offered him worship, respect, reverence, and praise, traveled by stages until he reached the kingdom of Magadha, where he went to the great city of Rājagṛha and stayed on Vulture Peak Mountain.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great elder named Bhadrapāla. Having personally attended upon past Buddhas in former lives, he had cultivated roots of goodness whose meritorious influence extended everywhere; he belonged to a noble clan and possessed great wealth, with assets and treasures in full abundance.

At that time, the elder heard that the Great Śramaṇa had left the palace of the Śākyas and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; that he had come to travel through this country with a great assembly of followers; and that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possessed such vast renown as to have appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles, having accomplished supernormal wisdom and preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma, even unto the fulfillment of the pure and white holy life.
At that time, the elder thought to himself:
"I shall now go to Vulture Peak, the King of Mountains, desiring to behold that Tathāgata; if I see him, I will surely obtain great benefit."
Having formed this thought, he departed from Rājagṛha with five hundred elders, intending to go to where the Buddha was.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One donned his saṃghāṭī robe and took up his bowl and robes. Surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣu monks, he proceeded before the great assembly with majestic and disciplined deportment. His every movement was calm and composed, proceeding with right mindfulness; his glances, his bending and stretching were dignified and extraordinary. To transform sentient beings, he manifested the manner of seeking alms, and as he was about to enter the city, he was on the middle road.

At that time, the five hundred elders, including Bhadrapāla, saw the Tathāgata from afar; his majestic and towering presence was a sight for all to behold with joy. He had attained a golden-hued body endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). His faculties were tranquil and settled, and his mind was serene and calm. Having reached the supreme state of discipline, compliance, and stillness, he guarded his sense-faculties like a great elephant. He was pure and undisturbed like a clear spring. With his feet treading upon hundreds of thousands of billions of red lotuses made of the seven precious gems, he was honored by countless devas, humans, and yakṣas, who rained down great celestial flowers over the Tathāgata; these flowers fell like flowing streams, covering the entire ground.

When the elders beheld the World-Honored One approaching from afar, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits, they marveled at such an unprecedented sight. With pure hearts, they went to the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the five hundred elders, including Bhadrapāla, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is unprecedented!”

The Tathāgata’s supernatural power eclipses the auspiciousness of devas, asuras, Māras, and Brahmās; the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue possesses great renown, and his radiant halo and wondrous color outshine the entire assembly.
The physical form of the World-Honored One is like a great mountain of gold; his countenance is upright and majestic, peerless and unequaled.
The World-Honored One has accomplished all the most rare and marvelous dharmas of the world.
"I contemplate how the World-Honored One’s majestic virtue is such as this; observing what signs did he abandon the ways of the household life to awaken to Great Bodhi?
At that time, the elder Bhadrapāla spoke in verse before the Buddha:
"In the past, I heard of the Most Victorious Honored One, Of auspicious and wondrous form, of great renown."
Now beholding this majestic radiance, it surpasses all that was heard; like an image of pure gold, it is endowed with every virtue.
The Tathāgata’s physical form is like a mountain of gold—lofty, vast, adorned, and pure, such that one never tires of gazing upon it.
His majestic virtue adorns the assembly of bhikṣus, just as the full moon shines amidst the host of stars.
The World-Honored One’s crown-mark cannot be seen; lofty and radiant, it surpasses the king of mountains.
His usnīṣa is perfectly rounded and gradually tapers upward, its surface level and even like a celestial canopy.
His dark hair is soft, glossy, and curls to the right; Like an añjana or indranīla gem, its fresh purity and radiance surpass the neck of a peacock; I now gaze upon it with never-tiring devotion.
His countenance is dignified and his brow is level and straight; The shape of his eyebrows is bright and pure like a celestial bow.
The white tuft of hair shines through with perfect clarity, free from all blemish; Its brilliant luster illuminates like the king of stars.
The pure eyes you have developed are most subtle and wondrous; all who behold them give rise to hearts of joy.
Now I gaze upon them, never for a moment turning away; I prostrate to the One with Pure Eyes, the Refuge of the World.
The features of the nose are high, level, long, and straight; they gradually broaden and become rounded like cast gold.
The features of the lips are crimson and exceedingly pure, comparable to the bimba fruit or mani jewels.

His wondrous teeth are fresh white, imbued with radiant luster; Equal to a crane’s beak, cow’s milk, or the root of a lotus, They are firm, dense, even, and exceedingly clear and pure— The result of the harmony of śamatha.
The teeth and their sockets are deep and firm; the upper and lower gums are perfectly even.
The Buddha’s teeth are radiant white and most preeminent, like the king of geese standing in the center of the flock.
The Sugata’s broad and long tongue covers his face, thin and pure like a lotus flower.
The mani-jewel of ruddy copper color, Containing radiance as clear as a mirror, like the rising sun;
The Blessed One’s ear-features are most exquisite and dignified, Unheard of or unseen by the gods and humans of the Brahma world.
Born of the Gautama clan with a jaw like a lion’s, He is fearless, just like the lion king.
I contemplate the marks of the Sugata’s throat, Which can draw forth the nectar-flavor of the world;
Pure, translucent, and free from blemish, Possessing great supernormal power and inconceivability.
The front of his neck is girt with a horizontal line, long and straight; in its center there is not the slightest speck of blemish.
Manifesting as the most excellent among men, the God among Gods, he always partakes of the foremost flavor among all flavors.
His shoulders are full and perfectly rounded; his chest is powerful and majestic in its grandeur.
Such a mark of a World-Honored One among men has never been heard of before; it is like the radiance of the sun streaming from the peak of a mountain.
The two hands, feet, shoulders, and the back of the neck—these seven places are radiant, pure, and always perfectly full;
his long arms are smooth and rounded like the trunk of an elephant king, and his two palms hang down, reaching to his knees.
The upper body is broad and thick like that of the king of beasts; the *goda* tree-mark is perfectly complete.
His body is formed through the power of Nārāyaṇa, endowed with great strength and the power of forbearance.
The hairs on his stainless body all point upward; as each pore appears, a single hair grows from it.
Unstained by smoke or dust like a lotus flower, they curl to the right and are fine and soft.
In the past, I heard of his secret marks: his private organ was concealed as deeply as that of the king of celestial horses;
his thighs and calves were rounded and tapered in succession, their appearance like that of the king of celestial deer;
his feet were thick with high arches and long, rounded heels; and the webbing between his fingers was like that of the king of geese.
The twenty fingers are even, full, slender, and long; The copper-colored nails are like lotus flowers.
Both soles bear the mark of the thousand-spoked golden wheel, Radiant, pure, subtle, and exquisitely adorned.
The Tathāgata wanders through the world; his gopāla-hair marks do not touch one another.
Four finger-widths above the ground, he treads upon the void as he walks. Precious red lotuses appear beneath his feet with every step.
His gaze is steady and his gait is calm, like that of a lordly elephant king; his dignified progress is like that of the Lord of Devas.
The Great Sage’s majestic and awe-inspiring presence is fearless; amidst the assembly, he surpasses the lion king.
His wondrous form outshines Vaiśravaṇa, and his radiant splendor exceeds a hundred thousand suns.
Even the devas of the Brahma world have no equal to him, let alone anyone who could surpass the Tathāgata.
Whether walking, standing, preaching the Dharma, or delivering sentient beings, celestial immortals, devas, and nāgas all pay him homage;
some scatter heavenly flowers and play celestial music, gathering in such profusion that they fill the void.
Now that I behold the Great World-Honored One’s great spiritual transformations, I have secretly harbored a mind of doubt:
what supreme merits did you originally perceive that led you to leave the household life and pursue the Unsurpassed Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder Bhadrapāla, saying:
"Elder, you should know that I observe all sentient beings in the world as being oppressed by ten kinds of suffering."

What are the ten? First, being oppressed by the suffering of birth; second, being oppressed by the suffering of aging; third, being oppressed by the suffering of illness; fourth, being oppressed by the suffering of death; fifth, being oppressed by the suffering of grief; sixth, being oppressed by the suffering of resentment; seventh, being oppressed by the sensation of pain; eighth, being oppressed by the sensation of sorrow; ninth, being oppressed by the suffering of anguish; and tenth, being oppressed by the great suffering of the cycle of birth and death.
"O Householder!

Seeing these ten kinds of suffering afflicting sentient beings, and desiring to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in order to escape such afflictions, I have, with pure faith, renounced the household life of the Śākyas to pursue the Unsurpassed Way."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse: "I observe all ordinary beings, Confined within the prison of saṃsāra,
Constantly oppressed by birth, old age, and sickness, And tormented by a multitude of sufferings."
"Drawn by sorrow, grief, resentment, and the suffering of death and the like, you are led toward the terrors of the prison;
therefore, to remove this fear, I shall cause you to rejoice in the Dharma of renunciation.
Furthermore, householder!"
I observe that all sentient beings in the world harbor mutual hatred and jealousy due to ten kinds of afflictive harms. What are these ten?
First, they have previously caused me harm and conceived a mind of malice; second, they do so now...
First, they have caused me harm and given rise to thoughts of malice; second, they will cause me harm and give rise to thoughts of malice;
third, they are currently causing me harm and giving rise to thoughts of malice; fourth, they have caused harm and given rise to thoughts of malice toward those dear to me;
fifth, they are now causing harm and [giving rise to thoughts of malice] toward those dear to me.
Sixth, one gives rise to malice and harm when those who are dear to me do something unbeneficial;
seventh, one gives rise to malice and harm when those whom I did not love previously did something beneficial;
eighth, one gives rise to malice and harm when those whom I do not love now do something beneficial; ninth...
First, to cause harm and give rise to a mind of malice toward those whom one does not love;
tenth, to cause harm and give rise to a mind of malice toward those who commit transgressions.
"O Householder!

I have seen these ten kinds of afflictions and harms that afflict all sentient beings in the world. In order to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to escape from such matters of affliction and harm, I have, with pure faith, renounced the household life of the Śākyas to pursue the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Sentient beings harbor mutual hatred and jealousy, All arising from the ten afflictions.
Toward myself and my kin, They cause harm throughout the three periods of time.”
Or toward those who are not my kin, one gives rise to perceptions of benefit;
from this, enmity and hatred are born, causing affliction and harm throughout the three times.
This tenth fault gives rise to and grows the suffering of enmity and hatred.
"Observing such faults as these, I became weary of them and left the household life.
Furthermore, householder!
I observe that all sentient beings in the world have entered a dense forest of ten kinds of evil views; because of their divergent views, they are unable to emerge from it on their own."

What are the ten? First, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view of a self; second, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view of a sentient being; third, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view of a life-force; fourth, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view of a person who undergoes rebirth; fifth, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view of annihilationism; sixth, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view of eternalism; seventh, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view that there is no action; eighth, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view that there is no cause; ninth, the thicket of evil views consisting of the view of an unequal cause; and tenth, the thicket of evil views consisting of false views.
"O Householder!

I see sentient beings entering the dense forest of ten kinds of evil views and being unable to emerge from them. In order to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to forever sever such evil views, I have, with pure faith, renounced the household life of the Śākyas and set out upon the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"All ignorant ordinary beings Enter the dense forest of evil views:
The view of a self, the view of sentient beings, And the view of a life span."
"Having severed the views of annihilationism and eternalism, and relying on the view of non-action and so forth,
I have gone forth in order to establish right view.
Furthermore, householder!"

I observe that all sentient beings in the world, throughout incalculable eons, have committed hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of transgressions and are constantly pierced by ten kinds of great poisonous arrows.

What are the ten? First, the poisoned arrow of craving; second, the poisoned arrow of ignorance; third, the poisoned arrow of desire; fourth, the poisoned arrow of greed; fifth, the poisoned arrow of transgression; sixth, the poisoned arrow of delusion; seventh, the poisoned arrow of pride; eighth, the poisoned arrow of views; ninth, the poisoned arrow of existence; and tenth, the poisoned arrow of non-existence.
"O Householder!

I see sentient beings struck by ten kinds of poisonous arrows; seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in order to forever sever such poisonous arrows, I have, with pure faith, left the household of the Śākyas to pursue the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The poison of the arrow of craving afflicts sentient beings;
For more than a hundred million great kalpas, blinded by ignorance, They pass from darkness into darkness."
The arrows of desire pierce the aggregates; the arrow of craving is named "sucking in the defiled";
the arrow of the fault of agitation and confusion, the arrow of ignorance as one's raiment, the arrow of pride that soars aloft, and the arrow of views arising from contention.
Because of existence and non-existence as arrows, they fall into existence and non-existence.
All foolish worldlings have swords at their mouths;
they provoke disputes with one another, saying, "This is true, this is not true."
"To extract the poisoned arrow, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world to rescue those pierced by arrows;
he has left the household life and realized the Noble Path.
Furthermore, householder!"

I observe that all sentient beings in the world establish their foundation through ten kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). What are these ten? They are: because of craving, there is seeking; because of seeking, there is acquisition;

because of acquisition, there arises the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*); because of the notion of "mine," there arise various fixed attachments; because of fixed attachments, there arises sensual desire (*kāmarāga*); because of sensual desire, there arises deep clinging; because of deep clinging, there arises stinginess; because of stinginess, there arises the accumulation of possessions; because of accumulation, there arises the guarding of them; because of guarding, one wields weapons and staves, engages in disputes and litigation, and incurs various sufferings such as slander; and furthermore, because of this, there arises speech of separation, which nurtures all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
"O Householder!

I see that sentient beings, established by these ten dharmas rooted in craving, seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of attaining that which is rootless and without any basis for reliance; thus, with pure faith, they renounce the household life of the Śākyas to enter the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Sentient beings swallowed by craving, They pursue all manner of desires;
Having gained profit, they give rise to the notion of 'mine,' And from this, fixed attachments arise."
I shall perform what is to be done; for the bonds of sensual desire increase, and through attachment, stinginess, and the like, they arise in continuous succession.
The fault of stinginess defiles the world and is able to give rise to firm accumulation.
Because they amass wealth, they guard it; this guarding arises everywhere without interval.
Such guarding belongs to the fool, who inflicts harm with blades and weapons, planting various unwholesome karmas, and thereby giving rise to manifold sufferings.
Having contemplated the causal conditions of craving, manifold sufferings do not arise;
this awakening, rootless and without abiding, is the most supreme among all awakenings.
"Furthermore, householder!
I observe that all sentient beings in the world establish themselves in wrong determination (*mithyā-niyata*) due to ten kinds of evil and perverse natures.

What are these ten? First, wrong view; second, wrong thought; third, wrong speech; fourth, wrong action; fifth, wrong livelihood; sixth, wrong effort; seventh, wrong mindfulness; eighth, wrong concentration; ninth, wrong liberation; and tenth, wrong knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Householder!

I observe that sentient beings establish themselves in false certainty due to these ten kinds of false natures. Desiring to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to escape from all such false natures, I have, with pure faith, left the household life of the Śākyas to enter the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Sentient beings who harbor wrong views, Whose objects of thought are perverted,
Who proclaim perverse speech, And who perform various perverse deeds.”
Wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration;
they achieve wrong liberation and proceed toward wrong knowledge and views.
This group of those fixed in wrong nature is that upon which fools rely.
In order to cause them to abide in the right nature, I have set out upon the unsurpassed path.
"Furthermore, householder!
I observe that all sentient beings in the world, by means of the ten unwholesome paths of action, establish themselves in and remain within wrong paths, and mostly fall into the evil destinies."

What are the ten? First, taking life; second, taking what is not given; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, divisive speech; sixth, harsh speech; seventh, frivolous speech; eighth, covetousness; ninth, malice; and tenth, wrong view.
"O Householder!

I see that because of these ten kinds of unwholesome karma, sentient beings ride upon false paths, tending toward many destinations and frequently falling into evil realms. Desiring to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to transcend all such false paths, I have, with pure faith, renounced my home in the Śākya clan to enter the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Those sentient beings who take life, Who plunder the wealth and property of others,
And who engage in various forms of sexual misconduct, Shall swiftly fall into hell."
Harsh speech, divisive talk, Falsehood that violates tranquility,
And frivolous chatter— these bind the ordinary person, Ensnared by ignorance.
Clinging greedily to the wealth of others, They repeatedly give rise to anger.
Giving rise to various wrong views, such a person goes to the evil realms.
Three types arise from the body, four are born of vocal karma, and the mind can accomplish the three evils;
therefore, they are called those who perform evil deeds.
"Having committed various evil deeds, one is dragged toward the miserable realms;
I now appear in the world to rescue and deliver them from them.
Furthermore, householder!"
I observe all sentient beings in the world who, due to ten kinds of defiled dharmas, dwell amidst afflictions and fall into the stains of affliction.
What are these ten?

First, defilement by the stain of stinginess; second, defilement by the stain of immoral conduct; third, defilement by the stain of anger; fourth, defilement by the stain of laziness; fifth, defilement by the stain of distraction; sixth, defilement by the stain of faulty wisdom; seventh, defilement by the stain of failing to follow the noble teachings; eighth, defilement by the stain of wrong doubt; ninth, defilement by the stain of lack of faith and understanding; tenth, defilement by the stain of lack of respect.
"Householder!

I see that sentient beings are defiled by these ten kinds of defiled dharmas; therefore, in order to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to realize the undefiled, unsurpassed Dharma, I have, with pure faith, renounced the household life of the Śākyas to enter the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Most beings in the world Are oppressed by the ten defilements;
Delighting in conditioned phenomena and afflictions, They never give rise to weary detachment.”
Defiled by the stain of stinginess, all foolish worldlings violate the precepts and lack tranquility; they do not practice samādhi,
turn their backs on patience due to the stain of anger, and fall away from right effort through indolence.
Those whose minds do not dwell with single-minded focus, who possess evil wisdom and are dull-witted,
do not honor the instructions of their parents and teachers;
caught in the net of doubt and views, they do not seek the Awakened One who illuminates the world.
Slandering the profound and sublime Dharma spoken by the Buddha,
Clad in the aggregates of ignorance, they harbor contempt for the Noble Ones.
Having observed such defilement, who would delight in dwelling within the conditioned?
"One should diligently realize cessation, which is unconditioned and untainted.
Furthermore, householder,
I observe that all sentient beings in the world are bound by ten kinds of fetters."

What are these ten? First, being bound and fettered by the net of stinginess and envy; second, being shrouded and obscured by the film of ignorance; third, being intoxicated by afflictions and falling into the pit of folly; fourth, being swept away and submerged by the swift current of craving and desire; fifth, being struck by the crooked arrows at the vital points (*marmāṇi*) of death; sixth, being scorched and suffocated by the dense smoke of anger and resentment; seventh, being burned by the blazing fire of greed and lust; eighth, being distressed and disoriented by the poisonous drugs of transgressions; ninth, being obstructed and hindered by the poisonous thorns of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); and tenth, constantly dwelling within the cycle of birth and death, weary and exhausted in the wilderness of famine.

"Elder! Having observed that sentient beings are bound by these ten kinds of fetters, I sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in order to realize the dharma that is without fetter or bond; thus, with pure faith, I left the household of the Śākyas to enter the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Old age devours the vigor of youth; Old age destroys pure and wondrous beauty;
Old age impairs mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; In the end, one is swallowed by death."
Sickness can destroy one's power and plunder the courageous mind;
it ruins the collection of the sense faculties, leaving one weak, inferior, and without refuge.
Death is like a rākṣasī demoness—fierce, powerful, and utterly terrifying.
Constantly pursuing the world, it drinks dry the life-force of all beings.
I have grown weary of this world, oppressed as it is by old age, sickness, and death;
seeking freedom from aging and death, I have gone forth into the Dharma of purity and peace.
The world is scorched by the three fires; seeing none to offer rescue, I shall rain down the nectar-like Dharma rain to extinguish the flames of the three poisons.
Beholding those who have lost their way—those born blind, the ignorant, and the sightless—[I shall lead them forth].
I have gone forth to act as the eye for the world and to provide guidance;
Sentient beings are nurtured by doubt and obscured by the veils of the aggregates;
To eliminate their remorse and affliction, I have gone forth to preach the Dharma.
Fools act in mutual opposition, seeking every opening to inflict harm;
it is for the sake of reconciling enmity and for the benefit of the world that one leaves the home life.
Yet toward parents and teachers, they show forceful arrogance and lack respect.
To topple the banner of arrogance, I have gone forth from home.
Observing that greed obstructs the world through the harm caused by the pursuit of wealth,
I seek to attain the seven noble riches and sever the poverty of all dharmas.
Some even bring about mutual injury and mutilation; though it benefits oneself, in the end it is no true benefit.
I observe that one must certainly relinquish the body to seek liberation from the prison of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Regarding the truly beneficial matters of the three realms, which were previously unknown, [I now understand them].
To open the door to true benefit, I have thus gone forth from home.
Observing those heading for hell, whose causes of evil karma burn fiercely as they undergo boundless,
heavy suffering, I have gone forth in order to liberate them.
Observing the realm of animals, where they inflict harm and slaughter upon one another,
he left the home life out of compassion to provide refuge for those who have no refuge.
Observing the realm of hungry ghosts and hell-beings, oppressed by the great suffering of hunger and thirst, [he left the home life].
To realize sublime enlightenment, he bestowed the ambrosia of immortality.
Seeing that the human realm suffers from the pursuit of desires and the celestial realms suffer from the loss of life—
observing that suffering pervades all three states of existence— he went forth into homelessness for the sake of liberation.
I observe those who indulge in desire; they are far removed from all sense of shame and modesty.
They oppress their elders and kin; their wild lust exceeds even that of pigs and dogs.
Furthermore, I observe these foolish men, devoured by the seductive charms of women.
Those who, through negligence, create what is meaningless have gone forth into homelessness for the sake of abandoning it.
Observing the sentient beings of this age of decadence (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), who are afflicted by evil dharmas and the emissaries of Māra,
I have set out to attain supreme enlightenment in order to subdue them.
"The household life is fraught with faults; / Having gone forth, one proceeds toward Bodhi.
/ Therefore, one renounces the great earth and all else, / To reach the very limit of saṃsāra.
At that time, the five hundred elders, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, attained what they had never experienced before, and only then realized that the Tathāgata is the Truly Awakened One.
Then, before the Buddha, they spoke in verse with one voice:
"We are terrified, oppressed by old age and death; We pray that you proclaim the sublime Dharma to its ultimate end."
Blessed One, you who are purified of all realms of existence, whose nature is pure and who have transcended all existences—
may you uproot those in the realms of existence so that they no longer exist, as well as those confined within the home of existence.
Hero of the World, free from defilement and most liberated, Far removed from dust and grime, with a pure mind,
Great Tamer among those who tame through the Dharma— I pray that you open the subtle and wondrous gate of ambrosia.
Equipped with the most sublime form, the supreme among men, Unequaled in the world of gods and humans,
the peerless and most honored one— We pray that you will proclaim the wondrous Dharma to deliver all living beings.
The three stains are eternally extinguished and all faults cast out; the eye of wisdom is pure as obscurations vanish.
With dust cleansed and darkness departed, the web of delusion is torn asunder; may the Peerless Honored One proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
Sentient beings are a mass of suffering, without refuge; Drowned in the great pool of existence, they have no savior.
I pray you will give rise to a heart of compassion and vast salvation, Swiftly pulling them out and elevating them to the shore of peace and security.
There is a river of pride, delusion, and turbulence, With surging waves of strife, litigation, sickness, and suffering;
Sentient beings drift and sink with no refuge or rescue— I pray you arouse a heart of compassion to save those in the stream of existence.
A thousand million suns illuminate the mountain of gold, yet the radiance of the Buddha’s body surpasses them all;
we pray that with your sublime and wondrous Brahma-voice, you shall proclaim the upright, majestic, and supreme Dharma.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally pure; its essence and appearance are transparently penetrating like a bright pearl.
There is no agent and no recipient; without hearing it from another, one awakens to universal illumination.
Spontaneously endowed with the powers and fearlessnesses, Practicing wondrous, pure conduct beyond measure,
With boundless wisdom and understanding like roaming through space, I pray that the Great Dharma King shall proclaim the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"The roots of goodness of these five hundred elders have already matured and they are capable of being transformed by the Dharma. I shall now preach the Dharma to them as is appropriate, so that these elders may immediately cast off their worldly appearances here and go forth into homelessness out of faith, severing all afflictions and attaining the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows."
Having formed this thought, he immediately ascended into the air and sat cross-legged.
When the elders beheld this miraculous manifestation, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and conceived a redoubled sense of reverence and faith toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elders:
"Listen well, all of you.

There are ten kinds of oppressive sufferings in the world, namely: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, the suffering of resentment, painful sensation, sorrowful sensation, affliction, and the cycle of birth and death. These ten kinds of oppressive sufferings oppress sentient beings."
"Do you now wish for liberation? Furthermore, O householders! There are ten matters of affliction and harm in the world, namely:

'He has done me harm in the past,' 'He is doing me harm now,' 'He will do me harm in the future'; 'He has done harm to those I loved in the past,' 'He is doing harm to those I love now,' 'He will do harm to those I shall love in the future'; 'He has done benefit to those I disliked in the past,' 'He is doing benefit to those I dislike now,' 'He will do benefit to those I shall dislike in the future'; and furthermore, giving rise to affliction and harm toward the mind regarding all such harms and benefits."
Regarding these ten kinds of afflictive harms, do you now wish to be liberated from them?
Furthermore, householders!

There are ten kinds of dense forests of heterodox and evil views in the world, namely: the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of a person, the view of annihilationism, the view of eternalism, the view of non-action, the view of causelessness, the view of inequality, and wrong view.
"Is it that you now wish to be liberated from these ten kinds of dense forests of evil views?

Furthermore, householder, the world is pierced by ten kinds of great poisoned arrows, namely: the poison of craving, the poison of ignorance, the poison of desire, the poison of greed, the poison of transgression, the poison of delusion, the poison of pride, the poison of views, the poison of existence, and the poison of non-existence."
"Do you now wish to be liberated from these ten kinds of great poisonous arrows? Furthermore, O householders! There are ten dharmas that are the roots of craving in the world:

namely, conditioned by craving there is seeking; conditioned by seeking there is acquisition; conditioned by acquisition one gives rise to the notion of 'mine'; conditioned by the notion of 'mine' one gives rise to fixed attachments; conditioned by fixed attachments one gives rise to sensual desire; conditioned by sensual desire one gives rise to deep attachment; conditioned by deep attachment one gives rise to stinginess; conditioned by stinginess one gives rise to hoarding; conditioned by hoarding one gives rise to guarding; and conditioned by guarding, one grasps at weapons and staves, engages in slander and litigation, utters divisive speech, and various forms of suffering, evil, and unwholesome dharmas all arise because of this."
"Are you now desirous of being liberated from these ten kinds of dharmas that are the root of craving?
Furthermore, O householders!

There are ten kinds of wrongness in the world, namely: wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong liberation, and wrong knowledge and vision of liberation."
"Are you now desirous of being liberated from these ten kinds of wrong nature?
Furthermore, O householders!

There are ten unwholesome courses of action in the world, namely: taking life, taking what is not given, engaging in sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view."
"Are you now desirous of liberation from these ten kinds of unwholesome courses of action? Furthermore, householders, there are ten kinds of defiled and impure dharmas in the world, namely:

the stain of stinginess, the stain of immoral conduct, the stain of anger, the stain of laziness, the stain of distraction, the stain of faulty wisdom, the stain of not following the instructions of the Honored One, the stain of doubt, the stain of lack of faith and understanding, and the stain of disrespect."

"Are you now desirous of liberation from these ten kinds of defiled and impure dharmas? Furthermore, householders! There are ten kinds of great terrors of the cycle of birth and death in the world, namely:

the net of entanglements, stinginess, and envy; the film of obscuration that is ignorance; the deep pit into which one falls through folly; the swift current of craving in which one is swept away; being struck by the false arrows of the *marmans*; the dense smoke of smoldering anger and resentment; the blazing fire of intense greed; the poisonous drug of delusion and error; the poisonous thorns of the hindrances that obstruct; and wandering through the wilderness of famine."
"Are you now desirous of being liberated from these ten kinds of great terrors of the cycle of birth and death?
At that time, the five hundred elders, with one mind and in unison, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

We now wish to be liberated from the ten kinds of oppressive sufferings that have been described—namely, birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, resentment, sorrow, pain, affliction, and the cycle of birth and death—and as extensively explained up to the various oppressions of wandering through famine-stricken wildernesses; we all pray that we may attain liberation from these.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed these five hundred elders, saying:
"Listen well, all of you; I shall now expound the essentials of the True Dharma. O elders!
The eye does not seek liberation.
Why is this? Because the eye is without agency and without function; the eye cannot think and cannot discern. Therefore, O householders, the eye is not the self.
One should maintain it in this way.
Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: the mind does not seek liberation. Why is this?
Because the mind is inactive and without function, the mind cannot think and cannot discern; therefore, O householders, the mind is also not the self.
You should hold this view.
"Furthermore, O householders!
Form does not seek liberation. Why is this?
Because form is inactive and without function, form cannot think and cannot discern; therefore, O householders, form is also not self.
You should hold this view.
In this same way, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena do not seek liberation. Why is this?
Because phenomena are without agency and without utility; phenomena cannot think and cannot discern.
Therefore, O householders!
The Dharma is also not the self.
You should uphold it in this way.
"Furthermore, O householders!
The aggregate of form does not seek liberation. Why is that?
Because the aggregate of form is without agency and without purpose, the aggregate of form cannot think and cannot discern; therefore, O householders, the aggregate of form is not self.
You should hold this view.
In this same way, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness do not seek liberation. Why is this?
Because the aggregate of consciousness is without agency and without function; the aggregate of consciousness cannot think and cannot discern. Therefore, O Householders!
"The aggregate of consciousness is not-self;
you should hold it thus.
Furthermore, O householders!"
The earth element does not seek liberation.
Why is this? Because the earth element is without agency and without purpose; the earth element cannot think and cannot discern. Therefore, O householders, the earth element is not the self.
It should be maintained in this way.
Likewise, regarding the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element—the consciousness element does not seek liberation. Why is that?
Is it because the element of consciousness is without action and without function?
Is it that the element of consciousness cannot think and cannot discern?
Therefore, O householders!
"The element of consciousness is not-self;
you should hold it thus.
Furthermore, O householders!"
All phenomena are unreal, arising from conceptual construction and depending upon various conditions; they possess neither capacity nor power, but revolve according to those conditions.
If there are various conditions, one provisionally designates all phenomena; if there are no various conditions, then there are no provisional phenomena.
"O householders!

All phenomena are merely provisional designations; herein there is absolutely no one who is born, ages, dies, passes away, or arises. There is only the eternal cessation of all realms of existence—the pure and tranquil nirvana—which can serve as a refuge. Therefore, you should understand it thus."
Therefore, O householders!
All phenomena arise from unreal conceptualization; depending upon various conditions, they are weak and powerless, turning according to those conditions.
If there are various conditions, then all phenomena are provisionally established; if there are no various conditions, then there are no provisional phenomena. O Householders!

All phenomena are merely provisional designations; herein there is absolutely no one who is born, ages, dies, passes away, or arises. There is only the eternal cessation of the various realms of existence—a purity and tranquility that can be taken as a refuge.
Thus, O householders!

If there is unreal conceptualization, then there is the adventitious establishment of improper attention; if there is no unreal conceptualization, then there is no adventitious establishment of improper attention.

If there is improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), then there is the designation of ignorance (*avidyā*); if there is no improper mental attention, then there is no designation of ignorance.
If there is ignorance, then there is the designation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*); if there is no ignorance, then there is no designation of formative forces.
If there are formations, then there is the conventional designation of consciousness; if there are no formations, then there is no conventional designation of consciousness.
If there is conventional consciousness, then there is the conventional designation of name-and-form; if there is no consciousness, then there is no conventional designation of name-and-form.
If there is name-and-form, then the designation of the six sense bases exists; if there is no name-and-form, then the designation of the six sense bases does not exist.
If there are the six sense bases, then the designation of contact exists; if there are no six sense bases, then the designation of contact does not exist.
If there is contact, there is the designation of feeling; if there is no contact, there is no designation of feeling.
If there is feeling, there is the designation of craving; if there is no feeling, there is no designation of craving.
If there is craving, there is the conventional designation of grasping; if there is no craving, there is no conventional designation of grasping.
If there is grasping, there is the conventional designation of becoming; if there is no grasping, there is no conventional designation of becoming.
If there is existence, then there is the conventional designation of birth; if there is no existence, then there is no conventional designation of birth.
If there is birth, then there is the conventional designation of old age and death; if there is no birth, then there is no conventional designation of old age and death.
Thus it is, O householders! What is aging?

It is that which is characterized by the dulling and senility of consciousness, the whitening of hair and its falling out, the sagging of skin and the wrinkling of the face, the diminution of the life-span, the maturation and decay of the faculties, and the withering of all conditioned formations; this is called aging.

What is death? It is that which is called passing away and transmigrating, ceasing and falling away, the dissolution and disintegration of the aggregates, being cast down upon the earth, and the relinquishing of the homogeneous class; this is termed death.
Whether it be aging or death, these together are termed "aging-and-death.
"O householders! If birth exists, there is the conventional designation of aging-and-death."
If birth were non-existent, there would be no basis for aging and death. What, then, is birth?

That which is called birth is the arising of the various aggregates (*skandha*), the manifestation of the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the acquisition of the assembly of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*); this is termed birth.
"O householders!
If existence exists, then there is conventional birth; if existence does not exist, then there is no conventional birth.
What constitutes existence?"
That which is called existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm; merit, non-merit, and immovable karma—these are what is termed "existence.
O Householders!
If grasping exists, then there is conventional existence; if grasping does not exist, then there is no conventional existence.
What is grasping? It refers to the grasping of sensual desire, the grasping of views, the grasping of precepts and observances, and the grasping of a self; therefore, it is called grasping.
O householders!
If craving exists, then grasping exists; if craving does not exist, then grasping does not exist. What is craving?
That which is called craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena—this is termed craving. Householders!
If feeling exists, then there is conventional craving; if feeling does not exist, then there is no conventional craving.
What is feeling? It refers to the feelings produced by eye-contact, and the feelings produced by ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact; these are called feeling.
"O householders!
If contact exists, then there is the designation of feeling; if contact does not exist, then there is no designation of feeling. What is contact?"
What are called eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—these are termed "contact.
O householders! If the six sense bases exist, then conventional contact exists; if the six sense bases do not exist, then conventional contact does not exist.
What are the six sense bases?
They are the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base; these are called the six sense bases. O householders!
If name-and-form exists, there is the designation of the six sense bases; if name-and-form does not exist, there is no designation of the six sense bases.

What is name-and-form? It refers to sensation, perception, volition, contact, and attention, as well as the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements; this is called name-and-form.
"O householders!
If consciousness exists, there is the conventional designation 'form'; if consciousness does not exist, there is no conventional designation 'form.
What is consciousness? It refers to eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; this is called consciousness."
O householders! If volitional formations exist, then there exists conventional consciousness; if volitional formations do not exist, then there does not exist conventional consciousness.
What are volitional formations?

What are called the volition regarding forms, the volition regarding sounds, the volition regarding odors, the volition regarding tastes, the volition regarding tangibles, and the volition regarding phenomena—these are termed formations (*saṃskāra*). O householders!
If ignorance exists, then there are provisional formations; if ignorance does not exist, then there are no provisional formations.
What is ignorance? It is said to be:

lack of knowledge regarding the past, lack of knowledge regarding the future, and lack of knowledge regarding both the past and the future; lack of knowledge regarding the internal, lack of knowledge regarding the external, and lack of knowledge regarding both the internal and the external; lack of knowledge regarding suffering, lack of knowledge regarding its origin, lack of knowledge regarding its cessation, and lack of knowledge regarding the path; and lack of knowledge regarding conditions and lack of knowledge regarding dependent origination.

Regarding dependently arisen phenomena—whether black or white, with conditions or without conditions, with radiance or without radiance, faulty or faultless, approachable or unapproachable—to lack knowledge and vision, to lack contemplation, and to lack penetrating understanding regarding such characteristics as these is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

"O householders! If there is improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), then there is the designation of ignorance (*avidyā*); if there is no improper mental attention, then there is no designation of ignorance."
What is called improper mental attention?
It is as follows: "In the past, what was my nature?
In what place did I exist?"
What kind of category am I?
What is my nature in the past and the future?
In what state do I abide?
What kind of being is this?
Furthermore, he gives rise to much doubt regarding his own internal body, wondering:
"What is called 'self'? Who is this self?"
Is it existent or non-existent? Is it empty or real?
What is its nature?
In what place was this? Of what kind was it?

In what location did I formerly dwell when I gave rise to such improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), whereby from among the six views one view arose—either the view of grasping at a self, the view of grasping at non-self, or observing a view of self based on a self, or observing a view of self without being based on a self?
Furthermore, they give rise to such false views as: "Am I the world? Or shall I arise through conditions?
Am I permanent, eternal, unchanging, and immutable, remaining forever fixed and stable?"
Such views as these are called improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). "O householders!
If unreal conceptualization exists, then there is the designation of improper mental attention; if unreal conceptualization does not exist, then there is no designation of improper mental attention."
What is called unreal conceptualization?

It refers to the self, the sentient being, the life-principle, the person, the one who undergoes rebirth, the one who is born, the mind-born, the manava, the agent, and the experiencer; these are called unreal.

However, because unlearned ordinary persons falsely give rise to such conceptual constructions as the construction of a self, the construction of a sentient being, the construction of a life-principle, the construction of a person, the construction of a "one-who-takes-up-aggregate," the construction of a "born-being," the construction of a "mind-born," the construction of a "manava," the construction of an agent, and the construction of an experiencer, these are considered unreal conceptual constructions.
"O householders!

If such unreal conceptualization exists, then there is the adventitious designation of improper attention; if such unreal conceptualization does not exist, then there is no adventitious designation of improper attention."
O householders!
If there is improper mental attention, there is the designation of ignorance; if there is no improper mental attention, there is no designation of ignorance.
If ignorance exists, then there is the conceptual designation of formative forces; if ignorance does not exist, then there is no conceptual designation of formative forces.
In this way, up to and including: if birth exists, then there is the conceptual designation of aging and death; if birth does not exist, then there is no conceptual designation of aging and death.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elders:

"You should now know that all phenomena arise from unreal conceptualization; they depend upon a multitude of conditions, being weak and powerless, and proceed by turning according to those various conditions."
If the various conditions exist, then there are provisional phenomena; if the various conditions do not exist, then there are no provisional phenomena. O Householders!

All phenomena are merely provisional designations; herein, there is absolutely no one who is born, ages, dies, passes away, or arises. There is only the eternal cessation of all realms of existence—the pure and tranquil nirvana—which can be taken as a refuge.
"O householders! What do you think?
For example, by what power do the various fish and aquatic creatures born in a great pond abide?"
The householder said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One!
These fish and others dwell by depending upon the power of water."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, O householders!"
“Does this water possess the power of thought?
The householder replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"This water is powerless and incapable; what can it possibly contemplate?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
O householders!
All phenomena arising from unreal conceptualization are likewise; they are merely provisional designations, lacking power or capacity, and proceed only through the turning of various conditions.
If the various conditions exist, then there are provisional phenomena; if the various conditions do not exist, then there are no provisional phenomena. O Householders!

All phenomena are merely provisional designations; herein there is absolutely no one who is born, ages, dies, passes away, or arises. There is only the eternal severance of all realms of existence—the pure and quiescent nirvana—which can be taken as a refuge.
Therefore, O householders!
You should correctly observe these various conditions as being no place of security and difficult to maintain; you should give rise to deep fear and flee far away from them.
Furthermore, you should examine: what dharma is this?
Out of fear for what dharma have you come here?
When you observe correctly in this manner, no dharma can be found; there is neither fear nor abandonment.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are unattainable, as they cannot be found when sought in every way;
because all phenomena are selfless, being free from defilement and dust.
All phenomena are without sentient beings, for they are far removed from a self;
all phenomena are without a life-principle, for they transcend birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction;
all phenomena are without a person, for the three periods of time are severed.
All phenomena are without letters, for they cannot be expressed by any speech or sound;
all phenomena are without attachment, for they have no objective referent;
all phenomena are quiescent, for they possess the characteristic of cessation.
All phenomena are universal because they have the nature of space;
all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature because they lack fixed attributes;
all phenomena are immovable because they have no basis of reliance.
All phenomena abide well within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for they are in accord with immovability;
all phenomena cannot be opened or explained, for they are free from the waves of marks;
all phenomena cannot be displayed, for they are without marks, without form, without light or shadow, and are detached from all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*).
All phenomena do not belong to a self, for they are free from the notion of "mine";
all phenomena are indivisible, for they are free from mind, intellect, and consciousness;
all phenomena possess no attachment or hoarding, for they transcend the paths of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
All phenomena cannot be lifted or moved, for they are free from arising, abiding, and ceasing;
all phenomena are without action or utility, for they are free from mind, intellect, and consciousness;
all phenomena depend upon conditions, for their nature is weak and inferior.
"O householders!

I declare that this eye is composed of the four great elements; it is impermanent, unstable, lacking constancy, and not a solid dharma. It is frail, quickly decaying, and difficult to rely upon with confidence; it is the locus where all sufferings accumulate, full of disease and many harms."
"You householders!
The eye is thus; you should not rely upon it.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise; you should not rely upon them."
One should contemplate in this way.
Furthermore, O householders!
The eye is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped; the eye is like a floating bubble that cannot endure for long; the eye is like...
The eye arises from the thirst of karma and delusion like a mirage; the eye is as insubstantial in nature as a plantain tree; the eye arises from inversion like a magical illusion;
this eye is like a dream, being nothing but false perception; this eye is like an echo, dependent upon various conditions;
the eye is like a reflection of light, appearing through the light of karma; the eye is like a floating cloud, characterized by gathering, disorder, and dispersal.
The eye is like a flash of lightning, ceasing in an instant; this eye has no master, being like the earth; this eye has no self, being like water;
the eye is not a sentient being, being like fire; the eye is not a life-force, being like wind;
the eye is not a person (pudgala), being like space; the eye is unreal, being a repository for the great elements. This is...
The eye is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self; this eye is insentient like grass, wood, earth, or stone;
this eye is inactive, turning only by means of the wind of mechanisms; this eye is a false aggregation of decay and impurity;
this eye is a phenomenon that is frivolous, deceptive, subject to disintegration, destruction, and extinction; the eye is like a ruined well, constantly assailed by old age; the eye is without...
That which abides in its limits ultimately returns to destruction. O householders!
You should contemplate the eye as having many faults; this applies likewise to the mind and all phenomena.
"Furthermore, O householders!

All phenomena consist of nothing but false desire. Because ordinary, foolish worldlings do not understand this false desire, they falsely claim it is the eye, they falsely claim it is the ear, and so on, up to falsely claiming it is the mind."

O householders, there is only false desire; because foolish worldlings do not understand false desire, they say, "This is form," and "This is sound," and it is the same for odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
"O householders!

There is only delusive desire; because ordinary, foolish worldlings do not understand delusive desire, they conceive of this aggregate of form, they conceive of this aggregate of feeling, and the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so."
"O householders!

There is only false desire; because foolish worldlings do not understand that it is false desire, they speak of this earth element, and likewise of this water element, fire, wind, space, and consciousness."
"O householders!

All phenomena consist solely of false desire; because foolish ordinary beings do not understand this false desire, they claim 'this is conditioned' or 'this is unconditioned,' and so it is for all phenomena without exception."
"O householders!
You should now abandon false desires and proceed toward desirelessness; you must deeply realize that wives, children, homes, and wealth are all illusory and should not be clung to."
Because they are without attachment, they renounce the life of a householder with pure faith and go forth into the homeless state; thus they shall attain freedom from desire.
Householders! What is meant by "going forth into the homeless state and being free from desire"?

This refers to abiding in the śīla of the Prātimokṣa precepts, fully maintaining dignified deportment and spheres of conduct, perceiving even minor transgressions with great dread, and training in the vows to accomplish the aggregate of ethical discipline.
"O householders!

If you are able to uphold the precepts, and having done so, deeply understand that these six faculties, six objects, five aggregates, and six elements are all false and deceptive, and thus do not cling to them—because of this non-clinging, it is called the dharma of renunciation and desirelessness."
O householders!
If one does not cling to the eye, and so on up to the element of consciousness, then because of this non-clinging, one does not protect them.
What is it that is not protected?

The eye is not protected; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not protected. Visible forms are not protected; sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are not protected. The aggregate of form is not protected; the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are not protected. The earth element is not protected; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are not protected.
Because there is no protection, there is no affliction; if there is no affliction, it is called "lightness.
What is meant by lightness?
It refers to being without views.

If there is nothing perceived, one does not give rise to a mind of anger or malice toward objects; because of the absence of anger and malice, one does not harm oneself, does not intend to harm others, and does not intend to harm both. Because there is no harm, one then enters into and realizes the realm of great *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
"O householders! You should know this: who is it that enters into the realization of cessation?
O householders!"

The eye does not enter into quiescence, nor do the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind enter into quiescence; yet, based upon the eye, various false attachments arise—either conceiving of it as a self or as belonging to a self—and if one distances oneself from these, that is quiescence.
By distancing oneself from what does one attain cessation?

If one distances oneself from greed, that is cessation; if one distances oneself from hatred, that is cessation; if one distances oneself from delusion, that is cessation; if one distances oneself from ignorance, that is cessation.
Furthermore, O householders!
Ignorance of the past cannot be abandoned; ignorance of the future cannot be abandoned; ignorance of the present cannot be abandoned.
Nevertheless, it is precisely by means of abandoning ignorance that right knowledge arises.
"O householders!
What is wisdom? It is what is called the knowledge of exhaustion."
What is the knowledge of exhaustion?
It is not the knowledge of exhaustion in the past, not the knowledge of exhaustion in the future, and not the knowledge of exhaustion in the present.
Nevertheless, O householders!
This wisdom arises because of being free from ignorance;
this wisdom is not separate from wisdom. Furthermore, householders, this wisdom arises because of being free from ignorance regarding the eye.
Moreover, householders!
The eye is not mine; if it is not mine, then one does not grasp at it. If one does not grasp at it, that is the supreme state; if it is the supreme state, that is liberation.
From what is one liberated?
One attains liberation from the locus of the grasping at a self;

from the locus of the grasping at a sentient being, the locus of the grasping at a life-force, the locus of the grasping at a person, the locus of the grasping at annihilationism and eternalism, and from all forms of grasping, up to and including the locus of the grasping at conceptual discrimination.

If a practitioner can be liberated from grasping, they do not engage in conceptual differentiation; if they do not engage in conceptual differentiation, they neither differentiate nor do they not differentiate.
What is this non-differentiation?
This refers to not discriminating between "self" and "what belongs to self.

At that time, the practitioner, regarding all phenomena, disperses them without accumulating, relinquishes them without grasping; through relinquishment, they are stilled, liberated, and eliminated—this is the supreme liberation, free from all fetters.
In what place is there that which is called "dispelling"?
It is in all places of suffering that dispelling is attained. O householders!
If you seek liberation, do not give rise to grasping or attachment toward even a single phenomenon. Why is this?
If there is grasping, there is fear; if there is no grasping, there is no fear.
"Furthermore, O householders! The eye is not quiescent;
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also not quiescent. Visible forms are not quiescent, and so on, up to the element of consciousness, which is also not quiescent."
However, O householders!
It is because of the element of consciousness that one gives rise to unreal attachments, either conceiving it as a self or as belonging to a self; to be free from this is itself nirvana.
By distancing oneself from what does one attain tranquility?
It means that by distancing oneself from greed, one attains tranquility; by distancing oneself from hatred, delusion, and ignorance, one attains tranquility.
Furthermore, householders!
Ignorance of the past cannot be avoided; ignorance of the future cannot be avoided; ignorance of the present cannot be avoided.
Nevertheless, by departing from ignorance, wisdom arises.
"O householders!
What is wisdom? It is what is called the knowledge of exhaustion."
What is the knowledge of exhaustion?
It is not the knowledge of exhaustion in the past, not the knowledge of exhaustion in the future, and not the knowledge of exhaustion in the present;
yet, O householders!
Through the departure from non-knowledge, knowledge arises.
This knowledge does not depart from knowledge; through the departure from the non-knowledge of consciousness, knowledge arises.
Furthermore, this element of consciousness is not "mine. If it is not mine, one does not grasp at it; if one does not grasp at it, that is supreme; if it is supreme, that is liberation.
From what is one liberated?
One attains liberation from the grasping at a self, and liberation from the grasping at sentient beings, life-force, and even all conceptual discriminations.

If a practitioner can be liberated from grasping, they do not engage in conceptual discrimination; if they do not engage in conceptual discrimination, they neither discriminate nor do they not discriminate.
What is this non-discrimination?
That is to say, one does not discriminate between "self" and "what belongs to self.

At that time, the practitioner disperses and does not accumulate; he relinquishes and does not grasp. Because of this relinquishment, there is quiescence, liberation, and elimination; it is the supreme liberation, free from all fetters.
Wherein are they dispelled?
They are dispelled in all places of suffering. O you elders!
If you seek liberation, do not give rise to attachment toward even a single dharma. Why is this?
If there is attachment, there is fear; if there is no attachment, there is no fear.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Grasping and attachment give rise to fear; Because of them, one goes to the evil realms.
Observing that there is such a place of fear, The wise person should not grasp.”
As you cultivate the various noble paths, you should observe them skillfully;
by observing in this way, you will attain [realization], for otherwise it is impossible.
All places are empty; they are fleeting and unstable, lacking any solidity.
Craving deludes and deceives the world; do not let your mind be disturbed in this life.
I have already realized the dharma of emptiness and understood that all phenomena are not solid.
Having attained profound tranquility and peace, I have realized the wondrous bliss of immovability.
If one understands in this way that all phenomena are merely empty,
they will be liberated from all suffering and extinguish all disputes;
yet they will wish to gather in and protect those who give rise to all manner of calamities and misfortunes.
Through grasping, one clings; through clinging, one gives rise to the various realms of existence (*bhava*).
From existence arises birth; because of birth, one is far removed from peace.
For one who is born, there are old age, sickness, and death—thus one is oppressed by such great suffering.
Because there is no desire, there is no grasping; because there is no grasping, there is no becoming;
because there is no becoming, there is no birth—and likewise for old age, sickness, and death.
Having gathered the requisites for life, one must at once abandon them all.
Having renounced both beloved wife and children, one should adopt the deportment of a bhikṣu.
Do not covet kin or wealth; alas, practice contentment!
Do not come and go with the mind of a lowly Caṇḍāla.
Do not rely on your own observance of the precepts to despise those who violate them;
to pride oneself on one's discipline and look down upon others is called true breaking of the precepts.
It is like a deer caught in a snare—whether it be bound or brought to its death.
Those who dwell within the snares of Māra and pride are likewise bound and harmed by them.
Pride can destroy a virtuous mind and further diminish the goodness of both oneself and others;
therefore, do not treat the precepts with contempt or ruin them, much less the pure conduct of one who upholds them.
One who aspires to be a great sage should always dwell in secluded places;
disregarding body and life, one should proceed toward tranquil liberation.
One should abandon the root of what is meaningless and follow the teachings of the world-renouncing Nirgranthas.
With love and reverence, I shall expound the profound and wondrous Dharma associated with emptiness.
Regarding the twelve internal and external bases, I declare that the mind is their root;
they, in turn, arise from karma, and karma persists through volition.
With both the eye and form as conditions, consciousness arises;
when conditions are lacking, it does not arise, like a fire without fuel.
Thus all phenomena arise, mutually producing one another through their conjunction.
There is no agent and no experiencer; Manifest activity is like an illusion.
All internal and external phenomena— I have already known them to be empty and illusory.
Fools, through their inverted attachments, Discriminate between "self" and "mine."
Within the eye there is no sentient being; the same applies to all external sense bases.
It is not created by a self or a life-principle; one should understand that all categories of phenomena are thus.
The eye does not conceive of liberation; the ear, nose, tongue, and likewise the others are the same.
Body and mind are equally without action; all phenomena are to be viewed in this way.
Just as in the great ocean, where surging waves form a mass of foam, one with clear vision perceives it and examines it to find it lacks any solid substance.
Thus, regarding the nature of these five aggregates, the realized one knows them to be not solid;
they shall be liberated from birth and old age, from sorrow, grief, calamities, and misfortunes.
Having gone forth within my Dharma, they know all phenomena to be like illusions.
"To not make that gift of faith in vain is itself called making offerings to all Buddhas.

At that time, having heard this Dharma, the five hundred elders immediately became free from dust and defilement right there, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena. Just as a clean black cloth placed in a dye-vat quickly takes on the color, so too was the Dharma-eye of these elders purified.
At that time, the World-Honored One further proclaimed the sublime Dharma for the elder, instructing, exhorting, and praising him: "Elders!
I declare that this eye is by its very nature suffering and is moreover ablaze."
What is meant by "blazing"?

It refers to being set ablaze by the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion; it refers to being set ablaze by such phenomena as birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, sorrow, distress, pain, and unease.
Thus it is, O householders!
I declare that this self-nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is suffering and, moreover, ablaze.
What is it that is ablaze?

What are called the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion—these are what burn with the phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and unease.
O householders!
I say that this form has suffering as its intrinsic nature and is moreover ablaze.
What is it that blazes?
It is ablaze with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; and so it is for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena as well.
"O householders!
I say that the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form is suffering and, moreover, ablaze.
What is it that is ablaze?

That which is said to be ablaze with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion—this applies even to the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. O householders!
I say that the intrinsic nature of the earth element is suffering and yet it is ablaze.
What is meant by "blazing"?

It refers to being set ablaze by the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion; likewise, even up to the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness, their very nature is suffering and yet they are further set ablaze.
What is meant by "blazing"?

It refers to the blazing of the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion, as well as the blazing of such phenomena as birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and unrest.
Therefore, O householders!
I now do not grasp at the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; you too should train yourselves accordingly.
