I now do not grasp at forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor even at the aggregates such as form, the elements such as earth, this world, or the other world; you too should train yourselves accordingly.
"O householders!
If you do not cling to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, then you will not dwell in dependence upon the eye, nor will you dwell in dependence upon the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
When you do not rely on form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena, you will not abide by relying on any phenomena whatsoever.

When you do not abide by relying on the aggregate of form, up to and including the aggregate of consciousness, then you do not abide by relying on the aggregate of form, up to and including the aggregate of consciousness.
When you do not rely upon the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness, you will not abide by relying on the element of earth up to the element of consciousness.
When you do not abide by relying on this world, the other world, or any world at all, and when you thus do not grasp at any phenomena, you will not abide by relying on any phenomena.
If one can abide without relying on any phenomena, this is called neither that which will exist nor that which will not exist.
If you all awaken to that which neither will exist nor will not exist, I declare that you are liberated from the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The raging fires of birth and death Burn all the worlds;
Suffering is endured with no one to save, And the Noble Path is lost.”
The Tathāgatas who illumine the world appear but once in an age;
they are never absent for even a single moment. One should therefore arouse firm diligence, cultivate right practice, and examine all with the insight of wisdom.
As it is to be attained through the vision of wisdom, it cannot be obtained otherwise.
If one practices in this way, one should know that all things are empty;
having thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness, one understands that bodhi is not a mind that is empty.
Greed, hatred, and delusion— these three poisons are a great fire that burns all the fools of the world, who sleep long and do not awaken.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death, along with grief, lamentation, and all such sufferings—
"Having understood the world's oppression, do not dwell relying upon any phenomena.
At that time, five hundred elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We now wish to go forth under the Buddha, receive full ordination, and cultivate pure conduct.
We do not yet know whether the World-Honored One will compassionately grant us permission.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu. By this very name, he was ordained with full precepts and became a Bhikṣu according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Once they had accepted the saṃghāṭī robes, their hair fell away naturally;
all of them took up their alms bowls and became arhats right on their seats.
Knowing they had attained arhatship, [the Buddha] stood before the assembly of bhikṣus."
And in response to the various devas and others, the Great Teacher has already asked and declared:
"In the past, when relying upon the Protector of the World, one practiced extensive acts of giving;
wherever one was reborn accordingly, one always experienced abundant peace and happiness."
Having now beheld me, he has again given rise to a pure mind;
because his mind is pure, I have preached the sublime Dharma for him.
Upon hearing the teaching, he attained arhatship and was forever freed from the view of a self.
"Realizing emptiness manifests before one, and one is liberated from all birth and death.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll 35; *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll 36.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva-piṭaka Assembly, Part Two. Chapter Two: The Prophecy of the Deity Kumbhīra.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained in that very place without moving, causing all those elders to establish the fruits of the noble path.
Entering the city of Rājagṛha by the majestic power of the Tathāgata, he was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, his deportment composed and dignified.
At that time, there was a great benevolent king of spirits named Kumbhīra, a yakṣa who protected the city of Rājagṛha, who thought to himself:
"The physical form and appearance of the Tathāgata now are extraordinary; he is the most supreme and difficult to encounter in all the world, worthy of receiving the offerings of gods and humans."
"We should now present various kinds of supreme and exquisite offerings to the Tathāgata.
Having formed this thought, they immediately presented to the Buddha the most excellent food and drink, complete with fragrance, flavor, and perfect color.
At that time, out of compassion for the offering presented, the World-Honored One graciously accepted it.
Then, the sixty-eight thousand great yakṣas led by King Kumbhīra, dwelling in the midst of the void, all gave rise to sympathetic joy and proclaimed in clear and far-reaching voices:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Then Kumbhīra addressed his assembly with these words:

"I have already presented the most sublime offerings to the Buddha; you all should likewise offer various gifts to the community of bhikṣus, so that you may enjoy benefit and happiness throughout the long night."
Having received the King’s instructions, the host of yakṣas immediately presented the superior offerings to the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the assembly of monks compassionately accepted the offerings.
Then, for the sake of alms, the World-Honored One entered the city of Rājagṛha; having obtained food, he was returning to his dwelling.

At that time, there were immeasurable thousands of assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, as well as immeasurable thousands of humans and non-humans, and furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings, all following behind the Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata went to that most excellent and vast place, spread out his usual seat, and sat upon it.

Then Kumbhīra, together with his retinue, took various celestial *mandārava* flowers, *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *pundarīka* flowers; furthermore, they took various celestial sandalwood powders and other articles of offering and scattered them over the Buddha—namely, the "Victorious Scattering," the "Great Victorious Scattering," the "Exquisite Scattering," and the "Great Exquisite Scattering."
Having thus performed these offerings with great earnestness, he stood before the Buddha with palms joined in reverent salutation.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing the thoughts in the minds of Kumbhīra and his great assembly, smiled.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they manifest a smile, various immeasurable rays of light issue from their faces—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, silver, and crystal-colored. These rays illuminate infinitely and boundlessly all worlds, such that the majestic radiance of the sun and moon is eclipsed and made invisible. They shine downward into the hells, bringing joy to those beings, and even surge upward as far as the Brahma-world.

Having completed what was to be done, they returned and circumambulated the World-Honored One seven times, then vanished either into the crown of the World-Honored One’s head, or from his two shoulders, or from his two knees.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon a being in the hells, the light then vanishes beneath both soles of their feet; when they bestow it upon an animal, the light vanishes from their back; when they bestow it upon one in the realm of hungry ghosts, it vanishes from the front of their body; when they bestow it upon a human, it vanishes from their left side; when they bestow it upon one in the realm of devas, it vanishes from their right side; when they bestow it upon a śrāvaka, it vanishes from their two knees; when they bestow it upon a pratyekabuddha, it vanishes from their two shoulders; and when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows a prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the light then vanishes from the crown of their heads.

At that time, the Elder Ānanda, having beheld the radiance of the World-Honored One’s smile, covered his left shoulder with his seven-strip robe, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in salutation at the Buddha’s feet, and asked in verse:
“O Refuge and Protector who illumines the world, For what reason do you emit this radiance?”
O Honored One who benefits the world, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Who now plants the noble seeds that serve as the cause for the Buddha’s enlightenment?
To whom do you grant a prophecy today?
Who should dwell in liberation?
O Great Hero, courageous Teacher, you do not smile without cause;
I pray that the Muni will explain the purpose of this manifestation of light.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Ānanda in verse:
"Kimbila, with a pure mind, Presents these various offerings;
For the sake of the Savior and Protector of the world, I have manifested this smile."
Having relinquished the retribution of a divine king, he went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
when his celestial merit there was exhausted, he ascended to be born in the Yāma Heaven,
and again in Tuṣita, where he experienced the various sensual pleasures of the devas.
When his merit is exhausted, he is born among humans, arising as a wise king;
a sovereign ruler of the four continents, a powerful Wheel-Turning Emperor.
Having later relinquished his status as a human king, he is then born in the Brahma world.
In the heavens and among humans, he traveled back and forth without ceasing for twenty koṭis of kalpas,
constantly experiencing all manner of sublime joys.
Finally, he relinquished his royal throne, left the household life, and sought the path of the Buddha.
When all conditions were fully met, he attained ultimate enlightenment.
Thirty thousand yakṣas, by serving and honoring the Buddha,
cast off their yakṣa rebirths and were born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Later, they shall behold the Honored One Maitreya and again attain arhatship;
having received his instruction and transformation, they will each make offerings to all Buddhas.
A full thousand yakṣas, for the sake of abiding in great bodhi, [shall do so].
By virtue of these roots of goodness, they shall not be born in the various evil realms.
There may be a thousand yakṣas who, in order to benefit sentient beings, shall make offerings to the Buddha, the Guide, seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
Some, numbering two or three thousand, holding incense, flowers, garlands, and the like,
shall make offerings to the Buddhas in order to attain the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Others, numbering a thousand koṭis, having made offerings to the Buddhas, [shall likewise attain it].
Cultivating the purity of one’s own essence, One subsequently realizes and enters into bodhi.
Kimbila and Śaila, Possessing great supernormal powers, Also gave rise to the mind of great aspiration: "I shall attain equal enlightenment."
Having made offerings to all Buddhas and universally aroused great vows,
you now again make offerings to me, your mind directed toward the unsurpassed path.
By the power of these roots of goodness, you shall abandon all wretched and evil realms.
When he beholds the Honored One Maitreya, he shall further offer ten million parasols;
having offered ten million parasols, he shall again offer ten million robes;
having offered ten million robes, at that time he shall immediately renounce the household life.
For a full five hundred years, he exclusively practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya),
seeking the supreme enlightenment for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
In order to fulfill that vow, he practiced generosity, ethical discipline, and the other perfections.
For as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they practice with constant diligence and never cease.
Know this: it is for the sake of manifestation that I speak thus;
their cultivation of supreme conduct increases even beyond such numbers.
As previously described by way of analogy, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one shall behold those Buddhas and perform great offerings.
How marvelous is this supreme, wondrous wisdom! How marvelous is this unsurpassed mind!
The Great Teacher of all multitudes, whose name cannot be fully expressed—
In the future, he shall attain perfect enlightenment as the Honored One of all sentient beings;
His title shall be "King of Physicians," renowned throughout the realms of the ten directions.
For seventy koṭis of years, that World-Honored One among bipeds shall preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; before long, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
In twenty great assemblies, he will subdue the minds of sentient beings.
The final great assembly lasted for two hundred billion years.
As described for that great assembly, it delivered immeasurable śrāvakas;
as was the number of śrāvakas, so too was the number of the bodhisattva multitude.
Having brought benefit to sentient beings, the Tathāgata will then enter parinirvāṇa;
the True Dharma shall remain in the world for a hundred thousand years.
Within five hundred kalpas, this bhikṣu shall attain Buddhahood.
In each and every one of those eons, a thousand Tathāgatas appear.
Those who possess wisdom should contemplate being sprinkled with the water of the Dharma;
they should give rise to a courageous mind and practice the principles of extensive learning.
Stay far from what is not the right principle, And always practice the Dharma of the right principle.
One should cultivate extensive learning, For by this, wisdom increases.
The four fundamental dharmas and meanings Rescue and deliver all bodhisattvas.
The dharmas of giving, precepts, learning, and relinquishment, The noble and virtuous path to enlightenment—
He taught these dharmas for the sake of the multitude, The most supreme Mahāyāna vehicle;
He expounded the path of the śrāvakas, Skillfully severing the net of all doubts.
"To all who come to inquire, I now grant full permission;
for those who can preach the profound and wondrous Dharma, such illuminators of the world are difficult to encounter.
At that time, Vaira, the son of Kimpira, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy before him, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented experience, and he thought to himself:
"Now the World-Honored One is about to depart for Vulture Peak Mountain, the King of Mountains; I too should plant some small roots of goodness before the Tathāgata.
Having formed this thought, he addressed his assembly, saying:

"You all should know that the Tathāgata shall depart from the great city of Rājagṛha to ascend Vulture Peak Mountain. You should all arouse courageous minds and provide various offerings according to your respective capacities."

Then Viśvantara, together with his officials, cleared away the weeds, filth, bricks, tiles, pebbles, stones, stumps, and thorns from the road between Rājagṛha and Vulture Peak Mountain, making it utterly pure like the surface of a bright mirror. He further sprinkled the ground with scented water and spread exquisite cloths throughout the middle of the path. He scattered famous flowers as high as a person’s height, burned wondrous and enduring incense so that its fragrance pervaded the road, and set up rows of banners and streamers with various precious canopies suspended from them. In the sky above, he unfurled and displayed silken fabrics, arranging them in distinct sections and spreading them across the expanse.
Furthermore, various celestial musical instruments were played, filling the air before and behind.
The road was exceedingly wide, spanning the distance of a single arrow-shot, and was entirely covered with various water-born flowers, namely the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*.
Furthermore, with the most excellent ruddy sheldrakes interspersed among the flowers, they were arranged in rows along the sides of the road.
Upon that path, brocades of golden thread were spread out, and above them, exquisite nets made of the seven precious gems were suspended, covering the entire road.
At that time, after Vessavaṇa had thus performed such great adornments along the path to the Buddha, he transformed his own body to be exceedingly beautiful and vast;
together with his various officials and subordinates, he leaped for joy, feeling redoubled delight and giving rise to sublime states of mind, namely:
a mind of exhilaration, a mind of harmony and goodness, a mind of suppleness, and a mind of purity.
A pure mind, a mind free from hindrances, a magnificent mind, a mind taking refuge in the Buddha,
a mind taking refuge in the Dharma, a mind taking refuge in the Saṃgha, the immovable bodhicitta, the non-retrogressive mind,
the incomparable mind, the peerless mind, a mind that transcends all the three realms, and the arousal of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
They give rise to the mind of great compassion, the mind of great joy, and the mind of great equanimity; they give rise to the mind that is a vessel for all Buddha-dharmas,
a firm mind, a steadfast mind, an indestructible mind, an imperishable mind,
a mind that has abandoned the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and a mind established in all the stages of the bodhisattvas.

Having established himself in these supreme states of mind, he went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
“I have prepared this unsurpassed offering for the Refuge of the World;
The Buddha is the Honored One of the world, the expounder of the most sublime Dharma.”
Having fully accomplished the ten powers, you dwell securely in the fearlessnesses;
your deeds for the benefit of sentient beings are like those performed by a Great Guide.
You possess the thirty-two marks and the eighty secondary characteristics.
The Protector of the World is like the sun, whose radiant light pervades the world.
He turns the wondrous Wheel of Dharma through the twelve most excellent modes,
proclaiming the profound and subtle teaching for the benefit of all living beings.
Displaying various miraculous transformations according to the protocols of a Buddha,
they perform deeds for the benefit of many koṭis of beings.
The Great Heroes of the future shall likewise grace the world like the sun.
Proclaiming that noble Dharma, he awakens to and achieves unsurpassed wisdom.
He is a shelter and a rescue; he is the path and the refuge.
For the multitude who are born blind, he guides them and bestows the eye of insight.
Of the classes of beings in the five destinies, I shall become their refuge;
I shall liberate them from the mass of all sufferings, just as the former Buddhas have transcended them.
I am the Honored One among two-legged beings, the Sun and Moon among gods.
The devas, nāgas, and asuras pay him homage and respect.
Among all the offerings presented, none in the world can equal them;
the sublime deeds I have performed have no peer.
"Just as the World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, is fully endowed with the thirty-two supreme and subtle marks of merit, there is no one in the world who can equal him.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Śaila, the son of Kumbhīra:
"Those who make offerings to the Great Master create the supreme cause for the Dharma;
among all sentient beings, they are most excellent, and for them, Bodhi is not difficult to attain.
They honor the Illuminator of the World, the Light-Natured One, the Refuge of the World."
Worthy of offerings by all devas, nāgas, and humans,
Awakening to the supreme and wondrous Bodhi, Sitting beneath the most excellent tree of enlightenment,
He subdues all evil Māras and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of sentient beings; the Buddha sat at their very head in the midst of this assembly.

By virtue of the Tathāgata’s great majesty, his great supernormal powers, his great sovereign authority, and his various great transformations of mastery, he emitted a great radiance that shook the great earth, rained down great lotuses that filled the void of space, and caused hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of celestial musical instruments to resound.
At that time, the great assembly marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; beholding these miraculous transformations, their reverence increased all the more.
Then the Tathāgata, his feet treading upon lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels, proceeded along the adorned path toward Gṛdhrakūṭa, the King of Mountains.
Having arrived there, he addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying:

"Prepare for the Tathāgata a supreme seat—a most excellent seat, a Dharma-seat, a subtle and wondrous seat, a seat surpassing all those of the triple world, a preeminent seat, a Buddha-seat, a Tathāgata-seat. Seated upon this, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I shall proclaim the Mahāyāna sūtra that serves as the basis for the bodhisattva practices, titled the *Sublime and Auspicious Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka*."

This sutra can cause the mountain of doubt of all sentient beings to collapse; this sutra can cause the net of doubt of all sentient beings to be severed; this sutra can cause the root of doubt of all sentient beings not to arise. Because this Mahāyāna sutra benefits and brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and out of compassion for the great assembly as well as for devas and humans, the Tathāgata now reveals and expounds it.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda, following the Buddha’s instructions, prepared and arranged the Dharma seat.
Then, among that assembly, there were sixty-eight koṭis of devaputras, each of whom cast off his upper robe and spread it upon the Dharma seat for the sake of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha sat upon it as usual, having spread his seat, and looking toward the sons of the gods, he spoke these verses:
"The garments spread by the devas Are most excellent, supreme, and subtle;
The Great Teacher, Savior of the World, Is seated comfortably upon this Dharma-throne."
Having reached the further shore of all dharmas, the Tathāgata ascended his seat;
the great earth shook in six ways, causing all beings to rejoice.
He emitted light that illuminated the Buddha-fields and shone upon all the kings of mountains.
The World-Honored One manifests supernormal powers to deliver those who delight in the Dharma.
Devas, nāgas, and humans, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas,
and the multitude of pūtanas— all see one another without obstruction.
Hundreds of thousands of nayutas and koṭis of devas and others beheld the Buddha emitting light; such a time is extremely difficult to encounter.
King Bimbisāra was surrounded by his various ministers.
They came into the presence of the World’s Protector, to where the Most Victorious Tathāgata was.
Knowing that the great assembly of devas, nāgas, and humans were all seated, the Buddha,
for the benefit of all sentient beings, gazed out toward the four quarters.
"I address all who have doubts: you should question the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
I shall lead the world and skillfully sever the net of all doubts.
At that time, all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm gathered together to hear the Dharma.
Having heard the Tathāgata speak this Dharma, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, they stilled external conditions and dwelt with their minds fixed on a single object, maintaining mindfulness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should now know: there are bhikṣus staying in distant places who have not yet come to join the assembly; you must summon them and bring them together."

At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa was dwelling on the southern side of the Great Snow Mountains. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having known this through his recollection, traveled there by means of his supernormal powers and said to him:

"The Tathāgata is currently at Vulture Peak Mountain; before a great assembly, he shall preach the sublime Dharma for the sake of the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, humans, asuras, and others."
"We are now waiting for you, O Venerable One, so that we may go there together; do not let us encounter obstacles regarding the Dharma.
Then Mahākāśyapa said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly after."

Having spoken these words, Mahākāśyapa did not rise from his seat; through the power of his supernormal transformations, he entered the city of Rājagṛha, leading a multitude of followers from the four assemblies, and went to the summit of Vulture Peak to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet, sitting among the great assembly not far from the Buddha.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having witnessed this transformation, arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling by means of his supernormal powers; there he saw Kāśyapa already seated upon his throne.
He addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"Venerable One!"
"Only by having accomplished the portion of swift and great supernormal powers can one manifest such spiritual transformations without rising from one's seat.
Mahākāśyapa said, "The World-Honored One has declared that you are foremost in supernormal powers."
"I have now manifested but a slight portion; it is not yet possible to exhaustively describe it.

**Chapter Three: Testing the Bodhisattva** At that time, the Elder Śāriputra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over his left shoulder, bared his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee upon the ground. Facing the Buddha, he joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I now wish to ask a few questions; I only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will compassionately grant me leave to explain them for my sake.
The Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying:
"Ask whatever you wish."
"The Tathāgata shall now explain it for you, so as to bring joy to your heart.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become free from error in bodily action, free from error in verbal action, and free from error in mental action?
By accomplishing how many dharmas do their bodily action, verbal action, and mental action become pure?

By accomplishing how many dharmas does one become immovable in bodily action, immovable in vocal action, and immovable in mental action; not being disturbed or swayed by the celestial Māra or his hosts of armies; and from the initial generation of the mind of omniscience, practicing the correct path, increasing skillful means more excellently at each stage, acting as a supreme guide for all sentient beings—acting as a universal guide, a great illuminating torch, a great ladder, a bridge, a boat, a savior, one who has reached the other shore, a shelter, a rescue, a refuge, and a destination—while never abandoning the mind of omniscience?
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
“For what purpose does a bodhisattva Abide in great enlightenment?”
What are called virtue and the Dharma, by which one awakens to the Unsurpassed?
Furthermore, what kind of practices does one perform to benefit all sentient beings?
Having cultivated what Dharma does one become a Buddha, the most excellent among men?
How does one subdue the evil Māra, abide in supreme bodhi,
shake billions of lands, and awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
What is the meaning of "bodhisattva"?
What are such phrases?
What constitutes enlightenment and the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma?
How does one move through the world to benefit the multitudes of sentient beings?
Untainted like a lotus flower, how do you liberate millions of beings?
How is it that you are honored by devas, nāgas, non-humans, and others?
Regarding all that I have asked, I pray that out of your compassion you will explain it for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent!
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.”
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes one dharma, they will be able to encompass the dharmas you have asked about, as well as other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas.
What is this single dharma?
It is the bodhicitta and the possession of faith and aspiration. Śāriputra!
"This is called the single dharma which, when accomplished by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enables them to fully embrace the boundless Buddha-dharmas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by being fully endowed with faith and aspiration?
Furthermore, in what sense is it called the bodhicitta?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"One who is fully endowed with faith and aspiration is said to be solid because they are indestructible; they are said to be firm because they are immovable.
To be immovable means to be free from stumbling; to be free from stumbling means to be well-established;
to be well-established means to be non-retrogressive; and to be non-retrogressive means to contemplate sentient beings. Contemplating sentient beings...
Because it is the root of great compassion; because one who has great compassion as their root does not grow weary;
because one who is not weary brings sentient beings to maturity; because one who brings sentient beings to maturity well understands their own happiness;

because one who well understands their own happiness is free from expectation; because one who is free from expectation is not stained by material requisites; [because one who is] unstained by material requisites...
One who possesses [these qualities] acts as a refuge for sentient beings; acting as a refuge for sentient beings is for the sake of regarding those of inferior capacity;
regarding those of inferior capacity is for the sake of providing rescue and relief; providing rescue and relief is for the sake of being a place of resort;
being a place of resort is for the sake of not being impetuous; and not being impetuous is for the sake of skillful observation.
Because one who observes well is free from resentment; because one free from resentment is well-disciplined in faith and aspiration;
because one well-disciplined in faith and aspiration has no attachments; because one without attachments is well-purified; because one who is well-purified is exquisitely bright and white;
because one who is exquisitely bright and white is inwardly free from defilement; as for being inwardly free from defilement—
"Because it is externally well-purified. Śāriputra,
that which is thus solid and difficult to destroy, even to the point of being internally free from defilement and externally well-purified— this is called being endowed with faith and aspiration."
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
“What are the characteristics and what is the appearance of the bodhicitta? Śāriputra!”
The bodhicitta is without fault, for it is not defiled by any afflictions.
The bodhicitta is an uninterrupted continuity, for it is not something realized within other vehicles.
The bodhicitta is firm and difficult to move, for it cannot be led astray or seized by heterodox arguments.
The bodhicitta is indestructible, for no celestial Māras can cause its downfall or ruin.
The bodhicitta is eternal and unchanging, for it is accumulated through the provisions of the roots of virtue.
The bodhicitta is immovable, for it is certain to realize all the Buddha-dharmas independently.
The bodhicitta is wondrously and virtuously established, because it is well-established upon the bodhisattva stages.
The bodhicitta is uninterrupted, because it cannot be countered by any other phenomena.
The bodhicitta is like a vajra, for it is well able to penetrate the profound Dharma of the Buddhas.
The bodhicitta is supreme goodness and equanimity, for it is without partiality toward the various inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings.
The bodhicitta is supremely pure, for its nature is unstained.
The bodhicitta is free from dust and defilement, for it brings forth illuminating wisdom.
The bodhicitta is vast and unimpeded, for it encompasses the nature of all sentient beings.
The bodhicitta is vast and boundless, for it is like space.
The bodhicitta is without obstruction, for it causes unimpeded wisdom to pervade all things and ensures that objectless great compassion never ceases.
The bodhicitta should be cultivated, for it is praised by all the wise.
The bodhicitta is like a seed, for it is able to give rise to all the qualities of a Buddha.
The bodhicitta is that which establishes, for it establishes all matters of joy and happiness.
The bodhicitta gives rise to all vows, by virtue of the purity of ethical discipline.
The bodhicitta is difficult to destroy because it abides in patience;
the bodhicitta is invincible because of right effort;
the bodhicitta is supremely tranquil because it relies upon all great meditative concentrations.
The bodhicitta is without deficiency, because it is perfectly fulfilled by the accumulation of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra,

the bodhicitta is the root of the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhis-kandha*), the aggregate of transcendent wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).
"Furthermore, the bodhicitta is the very root of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra said: "As for 'bodhicitta,' it is called bodhicitta because this mind takes awakening (bodhi) as its essential nature of arising."
“In this way, Śāriputra!

Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the bodhicitta of faith and aspiration, they are called ‘bodhisattvas,’ they are called ‘vast sattvas,’ they are called ‘most wondrous sattvas,’ they are called ‘sattvas who have transcended the entire triple world. They are called those whose bodily actions are without fault, whose verbal actions are without fault, and whose mental actions are without fault; they are called those whose bodily actions are pure, whose verbal actions are pure, and whose mental actions are pure; they are called those whose bodily actions are unmoving, whose verbal actions are unmoving, and whose mental actions are unmoving.”

Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with such purity of all karmas, they cannot be disturbed or turned aside by celestial Māras or the hosts of Māra’s armies. From the initial generation of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), they practice right conduct, increasing their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) at each successive stage (*bhūmi*). Unmoved by any worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*), they are able to act as great guides for sentient beings—supreme guides, universal guides; as a great illuminating torch, a great ladder, a bridge, and a boat; as a savior, one who has reached the other shore, a shelter, a rescue, a refuge, and a destination.
"Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thus give rise to the mind of omniscience, Māra and his hosts cannot shake them.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such pure faith and aspiration, once they have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, their minds are filled with pure faith; they delight in beholding the noble ones, delight in hearing the true Dharma, and delight in being free from stinginess. With open hands and hearts, they practice great giving, rejoicing in great renunciation and delighting in impartial and universal bestowal.”

Toward all sentient beings, their minds are free from obstruction, free from defilement, free from agitation, and free from distraction. They deeply revere karma and its retributions with a sincere heart, remaining free from doubt or hesitation; they know that the fruits and retributions of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are never destroyed, and even at the cost of their lives, they do not commit any evil. They are forever detached from killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and deluded wrong views.

In order to sever such unwholesome courses of action, one should undertake and practice the ten wholesome courses of action. Because of being endowed with faith, toward all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have reached the goal, who practice rightly, who possess virtue and precepts, whose minds are purely clean and have become disciplined, who are possessed of much learning and diligently engage in inquiry, who cultivate right attention and are well-tamed and tranquil, who associate with those seeking cessation and do not initiate disputes, who do not speak unpleasant words, who well understand faith and aspiration rather than lacking such understanding, who are associated with wholesome dharmas and remain far from unwholesome dharmas, who are neither fickle nor arrogant and by nature free from agitation, who by nature avoid coarse speech and lack frivolity, who maintain mindfulness and dwell in right presence with the mind settled in sublime concentration—one thoroughly severs the root of existence, is not pierced by the poisoned arrow, lays down the heavy burden, and transcends doubt and hesitation.

Furthermore, in the future, there will be various Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas; having realized [the truth] as it truly is under such virtuous spiritual friends, they shall personally attend upon, revere, serve, and encounter them.

In this way, the practitioner serves the physical needs of a virtuous friend and further gathers them through the gift of Dharma, proclaiming the sublime Dharma to instruct, admonish, and gladden them; that is to say: by practicing *dāna* one obtains great wealth; by practicing *śīla* one obtains the joy of rebirth in heaven; by being fond of hearing much one obtains great wisdom; and by cultivating various meditative concentrations one becomes free from bondage.
Furthermore, he reveals and elucidates various subtle, pure, and sublime dharmas: "This is generosity; this is the retribution for generosity. This is stinginess;
this is the retribution for stinginess. This is ethical discipline (*śīla*); this is the retribution for ethical discipline. This is the violation of precepts;
this is the retribution for violating precepts. This is patience (*kṣānti*); this is the retribution for patience. This is...
"This is ill will and this is the retribution for ill will; this is right effort and this is the retribution for right effort;
this is laziness and this is the retribution for laziness; this is meditative concentration and this is the retribution for meditative concentration;

this is a distracted mind and this is the retribution for a distracted mind; this is wisdom and this is the retribution for wisdom; this is faulty wisdom and this is the retribution for faulty wisdom."
This is bodily wholesome conduct and this is the result of bodily wholesome conduct; this is bodily unwholesome conduct and this is the result of bodily unwholesome conduct;
this is verbal wholesome conduct and this is the result of verbal wholesome conduct; this is verbal unwholesome conduct and this is the result of verbal unwholesome conduct;
this is mental wholesome conduct and this is the result of mental wholesome conduct; this is mental unwholesome conduct and this is the result of mental unwholesome conduct.
"This is wholesome, this is unwholesome; this should be done, this should not be done;

if this is performed, it will result in benefit, welfare, and happiness for a long night; if this is performed, it will result in what is not beneficial, not advantageous, and not happiness for a long night."

“Śāriputra! When a practitioner has thus explained, taught, instructed, praised, and gladdened this Dharma for the sake of spiritual friends, and perceives that they are a fit vessel for the Great Dharma, he then reveals to them the profound and subtle Dharma corresponding to emptiness—namely, the dharma of emptiness, the dharma of signlessness, the dharma of wishlessness, the dharma of non-activity, the dharma of non-arising, the dharma of non-origination, the dharma of selflessness, the dharma of no person, the dharma of no life-span, and the dharma of no sentient being.”
Furthermore, he revealed for them the profound principle of dependent origination: namely, because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.

With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
In this way, there arises this entire mass of pure suffering.
Furthermore, because this does not exist, that does not exist;

because this ceases, that ceases. That is to say: because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; and so on, until because birth ceases, aging and death cease; and in this manner, the entire mass of pure suffering ceases.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, you should explain that herein there is not a single dharma that exists which can be apprehended or extinguished. Why is this?

Because all those phenomena arise from causes and conditions, they have no master, no agent, and no experiencer; they proceed from causes and conditions, and furthermore, there is not a single phenomenon that undergoes transmigration or returns, nor is there anything that follows in its movement.
Due to delusion and falsehood, the three realms are provisionally established; their circulation from afflictions and suffering is merely a conventional designation.
When a practitioner thus observes delusion and falsehood as they truly are, there is not a single dharma that can act upon another dharma.

If within this there is no agent, because an agent cannot be apprehended, then there is not even a single dharma that undergoes transmigration or returns, because such transmigration and returning cannot be apprehended.

Śāriputra! If a practitioner, having heard such a profound Dharma, is without doubt or hesitation and skillfully enters into the unobstructed nature of all phenomena, that person does not cling to form, nor do they cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. They do not cling to the eye, forms, or eye-consciousness; nor do they cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, phenomena, or mind-consciousness, because all these are ultimately ungraspable.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith in and accepted this dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they do not regress from seeing the Buddha, do not regress from hearing the Dharma, and do not regress from serving the Saṅgha. In every place where they are born, they are never separated from seeing the Buddha, never separated from hearing the Dharma, and never separated from serving the Saṅgha; they are born in the presence of the Buddhas, exerting fierce and diligent effort with a mind intent on seeking the wholesome Dharma."

Once this person has established themselves in right effort, they no longer cherish their household, male and female relatives, servants, laborers, or various possessions. Untroubled by sensual desire, they quickly renounce the pleasures of their prime in this very life and, with pure faith, leave the home life to enter the path within the Buddha-dharma.
Having gone forth, he obtains virtuous spiritual friends, good companions, and good associates; he abides well in reflection and abides well in faith and aspiration.

Because he abides well in faith and aspiration, he listens to the Dharma well and steadfastly practices it according to the teachings; he does not take mere verbal expression as his ultimate goal, but achieves realized wisdom, delighting in seeking extensive learning without ever being satisfied.

According to the Dharma as it has been heard, one should expound it extensively for others with a mind free from defilement; having no longing for gain, honor, or reputation, one does not abandon the true meaning to speak falsely to others, but teaches the Dharma exactly as it was heard and exactly as it is realized.
One should give rise to great loving-kindness toward the assembly listening to the Dharma, and give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Śāriputra, because the practitioner thus possesses much learning, they disregard body and life, have few desires and are content, delight in tranquility, are easy to satisfy and easy to support, and take pleasure in dwelling in seclusion. They contemplate the meaning of the Dharma as it was heard, relying on the true meaning rather than the literal words.

They serve as the refuge for the realms of devas, humans, and asuras; they do not seek the Great Vehicle solely for themselves, but for the sake of all sentient beings—that is, the Buddha-knowledge, the unequaled knowledge, the knowledge equal to the unequaled, and the knowledge that transcends the entire triple world.
"Śāriputra! I say that such a person has attained the foremost dharma of heedfulness. Śāriputra!"
What is called the dharma of heedfulness?
It is the tranquility of the sense faculties.
What is meant by the tranquility of the sense faculties?
That is to say: when the eye sees forms, one does not grasp at their appearances, but realizes as they truly are the gratification of forms, the danger of forms, and the escape from forms.

Likewise, regarding sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the mind, one does not grasp at their appearances, but realizes as they truly are the gratification of phenomena, the danger of phenomena, and the escape from phenomena.
Śāriputra! This is called non-negligence of the mind. Furthermore, one who is non-negligent subdues their own mind and skillfully protects the minds of others;

they abandon delighting in afflictions and turn toward delighting in the True Dharma. They do not engage in thoughts of desire, thoughts of malice, or thoughts of harm; they do not engage in the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, or the unwholesome root of delusion; they do not engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, or misconduct of mind; they do not engage in improper mental attention, nor do they engage in any evil or unwholesome dharmas. This is what is meant by non-negligence.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Since these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are not negligent, they are able to diligently cultivate appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*). If a phenomenon exists, they know it as it truly is to exist; if a phenomenon does not exist, they know it as it truly is to not exist. They investigate within this: "What is existent? What is non-existent?"
By the power of wisdom, one is able to know things as they truly are:
for those who practice correctly, noble liberation exists; for those who practice erroneously, noble liberation does not exist.
For those without karmic retribution, this [liberation] exists; for those with karmic retribution, this [liberation] does not exist.
Furthermore, the eye exists, but the one who possesses the eye does not exist.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind exist, but the one who possesses the mind does not exist.
Furthermore, that form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this exists; that form is permanent, unchanging, and indestructible—this does not exist.

That feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is existence. That feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, unchanging, and indestructible—this is non-existence.
Furthermore, with ignorance as a condition, volitional formations come to be; if there were no ignorance, volitional formations would not exist.
This continues until: with birth as a condition, old age and death come to be; if there were no birth, old age and death would also not exist.
Furthermore, it is a fact that giving results in great wealth, whereas it is a non-fact that giving results in poverty.
It is a fact that observing the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven, whereas it is a non-fact that violating the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven.
To hear [the Dharma] and give rise to great wisdom is existence; for those of evil wisdom to be able to give rise to great wisdom is non-existence.
Cultivating meditative concentration to become free from bondage is existence; cultivating meditative concentration while remaining bound is non-existence.

Furthermore, if it were the case that there is bondage through correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and liberation through incorrect mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), then both of these would not exist.
If bodhisattvas initiate right effort (*samyak-vīrya*), then awakening (*bodhi*) exists; if they give rise to laziness (*kausīdya*), then awakening does not exist.
If one who has gone forth without pride receives a prediction [of enlightenment], this is called "existence"; if one possesses pride, then even in the state of cessation, there is none.
Furthermore, emptiness exists pervading all places; whereas the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, or a soul exist pervading all places—this is "non-existence."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

If bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice heedfulness and are able to skillfully cultivate appropriate mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra), those wise ones of the world collectively recognize what is designated as existent as being existent, and those wise ones of the world collectively recognize what is designated as non-existent as being non-existent.
Śāriputra, if one definitively asserts that [the self] exists, this is not correct understanding;
if one definitively asserts that it does not exist, this likewise is called incorrect understanding. Why is this?
"Because they are able to realize and understand the true meaning taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, possessing the power of great wisdom, encompass all dharmas and establish them within the four types of *udāna*."
What are these four? They are:
all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all dharmas are without self; and nirvana is quiescent extinction. Śāriputra!
When the Tathāgata teaches that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, it is for the sake of severing the notion of permanence in sentient beings who perceive things as permanent.
When he teaches that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, it is for the sake of severing the notion of pleasure in sentient beings who perceive things as pleasurable.
As for the teaching of all dharmas as being without self, it is because the Tathāgata seeks to sever the notion of self in sentient beings who possess such a notion.
As for the teaching of the dharma of quiescent nirvāṇa, it is because the Tathāgata seeks to sever the mind of grasping and inversion in sentient beings who dwell in grasping and inversion.
Śāriputra! If these bodhisattva mahāsattvas hear the Tathāgata say that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
they will be able to skillfully enter ultimate impermanence.
If one hears it said that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering," one will then be able to give rise to a sense of weary detachment and the aspiration for renunciation.
If one hears it said that "all phenomena are without self," [one will likewise develop such resolve].
Then one is able to cultivate the sublime gate of liberation that is samādhi.
If one hears the teaching of tranquil nirvāṇa,
one is then able to cultivate the signless samādhi without entering the limit of reality at an improper time.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to skillfully cultivate such dharmas as these, they will never fall away from any wholesome dharmas and will swiftly bring all Buddha-dharmas to full perfection.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 36 and Volume 37,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Four: The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata, Part One The Third Session of the Twelfth Chapter:
The Bodhisattva Piṭaka At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well established themselves in such pure faith, they are further able to believe and accept the ten kinds of inconceivable dharmas of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. They reverently uphold them with purity, free from delusion or doubt, and without divergent conceptualization; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound delight and a sense of wonder.”
Śāriputra! What are called the ten inconceivable dharmas of the Tathāgata? Śāriputra!

First, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable body; second, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable voice; third, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom; fourth, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable light; fifth, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable ethical discipline (*śīla*) and equanimous contemplation; sixth, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); seventh, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable powers (*bala*); eighth, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); ninth, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); and tenth, faith and acceptance of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Śāriputra! These are called the ten kinds of inconceivable dharmas.

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, arouses right diligence—neither cowering nor retreating, and not giving rise to renunciation—they should give rise to such a thought:

"I have not yet attained the inconceivable Dharma; rather than that, I would let my skin, flesh, sinews, and bones be subjected to great suffering by the wind, or even let my blood and flesh wither away until they are completely exhausted, but I must certainly practice with diligent vigor without ceasing for even a moment."

"In this way, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already attained faith and understanding hear these ten inconceivable dharmas of the Tathāgata, they accept them with conviction, revere them with sincerity, and remain pure and free from doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound delight and a sense of wonder."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddha-body is inconceivable; It manifests as the true Dharma-body.
Being signless, it cannot be perceived; Only the sons of the Buddha can believe in it."
The various types of beings in all realms of existence have inconceivable voices;
according to their voices, he preaches the Dharma, for they believe in the domain of the Buddhas.
Among all classes of living beings, the faculties of those in the three periods of time differ.
The Buddha is able to awaken to and comprehend all; faith in this is inconceivable.
The boundless light of all Buddhas, an inconceivable net of light, pervades the worlds of the ten directions throughout the oceans of infinite buddha-lands.
The Buddha’s precepts transcend the world; they do not rely on worldly dharmas.
With inconceivable supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva is able to believe and accept them.
Sentient beings cannot know the realm of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is ever in meditative concentration, His liberation is inconceivable.
The Dharma-realm is unmixed; Only the power of a Buddha can know it.
The various powers of knowledge of the Great Sage Are like space, without limit.
For the sake of benefiting even a single sentient being, They remain for an ocean of boundless eons until that being is tamed; Such is the nature of the Great Compassionate Mind.
Toward all living beings, Regarding the ocean of their various questions and challenges,
With a single sound, they bring joy and understanding; Fearless and inconceivable, they achieve all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Awakening to all phenomena according to their nature, As well as the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), Their universal wisdom perceives them all.
"All things are inconceivable; such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
Those who are able to accept and believe this are said to be well-established in faith.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the inconceivable body of the Tathāgata, accept it with faith, revere it with truth, and be pure and without doubt; how does he leap for joy all the more, give rise to deep gladness, and conceive a sense of wonder?”
Śāriputra! That which is called the body of the Tathāgata has forever severed all evil and unwholesome dharmas. Why is this?
Because he is able to accomplish all subtle and sublime wholesome dharmas,
the body of the Tathāgata is free from all impurities, such as mucus, saliva, phlegm, sputum, pus, blood, feces, and urine.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has long since been liberated from all bones, flesh, sinews, and veins.
The body of the Tathāgata is by its very nature pure and transparent.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has long since distanced himself from all afflictions and defilements.
The body of the Tathāgata transcends the world.
Why is this? Because it is not defiled by worldly dharmas. The body of the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merit;
having long since accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom, it is the refuge for the life-force of wisdom of all sentient beings.

The body of the Tathāgata is cultivated by immeasurable pure precepts, and it is cultivated by immeasurable equanimity, as well as immeasurable wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The body of the Tathāgata is adorned with the flowers of all meritorious virtues.
The body of the Tathāgata is like a subtle and wondrous image within a pure mirror, like the bright and full moon reflected in clear water, and like the radiance of light and shadow.
The body of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, equal to the realm of empty space and reaching the ultimate nature of the Dharma-realm.
The body of the Tathāgata is pure and unstained, far removed from all defilements and turbidities.
The body of the Tathāgata is unconditioned, being utterly remote from all conditioned characteristics.
The body of the Tathāgata is the body of space; it is the unequaled body, the body equal to the unequaled, and the body with which nothing in the entire triple world can be equaled.
The body of the Tathāgata is a body beyond analogy, a body without peer.
The body of the Tathāgata is pure and stainless, free from all afflictions, and by its very nature, it is utterly transparent.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought in the past, nor can it be sought in the future, nor can it be sought in the present; it cannot be sought in terms of its place of birth or its lineage.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through form, cannot be sought through marks, and cannot be sought through excellence.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through the mind, cannot be sought through the intellect, and cannot be sought through consciousness.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through sight, cannot be sought through hearing, cannot be sought through thought, and cannot be sought through discernment.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought within the aggregates, cannot be sought within the elements, and cannot be sought within the sense bases.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through birth, nor can it be sought through abiding, nor can it be sought through destruction.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through grasping, nor can it be sought through relinquishing, nor can it be sought through renunciation, nor can it be sought through conditioned activity.

The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through manifest color, nor can it be sought through physical marks, nor can it be sought through shape or form, nor can it be sought through coming, nor can it be sought through going.

The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through the mental application of pure precepts; it cannot be sought through the mental application of equanimity; it cannot be sought through the mental application of right wisdom; it cannot be sought through the mental application of liberation; and it cannot be sought through the mental application of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through marks, nor can it be sought through the absence of marks, nor can it be sought through the marks of all phenomena.

The body of the Tathāgata cannot be sought through the augmentation of powers, nor through the augmentation of fearlessnesses, nor through the augmentation of unimpeded eloquence, nor through the augmentation of supernormal powers, nor through the augmentation of great compassion, nor through the augmentation of the unique qualities of a Buddha.

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who seeks the body of a Tathāgata should seek the body of a Tathāgata by way of its intrinsic nature as being like an illusion, like a flame, and like the moon reflected in water.

“Śāriputra! The body of the Tathāgata is the body of liberation—empty, signless, and wishless; it is a body without transformation, a body without movement or decay, a body without discrimination, a body without dependence, and a body without thought.”
The body of the Tathāgata is the body that abides in peace, abides securely, and has attained immovability.

The body of the Tathāgata is the body whose intrinsic nature is formlessness regarding form; it is the body whose intrinsic nature is the absence of sensation regarding sensation; it is the body whose intrinsic nature is the absence of perception regarding perception; it is the body whose intrinsic nature is the absence of mental formations regarding mental formations; and it is the body whose intrinsic nature is the absence of consciousness regarding consciousness.
Śāriputra! The body of the Tathāgata is without non-arising and without a body composed of the four great elements; the body of the Tathāgata is precisely this rare and marvelous Dharma-body.
The body of the Tathāgata does not arise from the eye; it is neither within form nor without it.
It does not depend on the ear; it is neither within sound nor without it.
It is not known by the nose; it is neither within fragrance nor without it.
It is not manifested by the tongue; it is neither within tastes nor outside them. It does not conjoin with the body;
it is neither within tactile sensations nor outside them.

The body of the Tathāgata does not turn in dependence upon the mind, does not turn in dependence upon the intellect, and does not turn in dependence upon consciousness. It abides immovably; it is not something that revolves, nor does it follow along with anything.

Śāriputra! The body of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space; the body of the Tathāgata extends to the limit of the Dharma-realm; the body of the Tathāgata pervades the entire realm of empty space.
"Śāriputra! This is called the first inconceivable body of the Tathāgata.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that the inconceivable body of the Tathāgata is like space, they accept it with faith, uphold it with truth, and remain pure and free from doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Throughout koṭis and nayutas of eons, Practicing immeasurable great deeds,
Thoroughly purifying the three karmas of the body, One attains the peerless Buddha-body.”
With a mind of loving-kindness pervading the ten directions, Arising great compassion and practicing giving,
Always remaining free from the conduct of sexual misconduct, One attains a supreme body like space.
Toward the World-Honored One, the field of merit, The sons of the Buddha practice giving extensively.
He renounced pure and precious garments and the like, as numerous as the sands of the immeasurable Ganges;
he upheld the pure precepts as a yak protects its tail,
and even when his body was shattered in suffering, he gave rise to great patience toward his enemies.
Through the perfection of right effort, practicing with extreme toil and hardship,
one gives rise to vast and great vows, seeking the eternally abiding Buddha-body.
One delights in contemplating the states of various meditative concentrations and rejoices in the expansion of wisdom and skillful means.
Contemplating the Dharma-realm with joy, may my body be equal to the Dharma-realm.
Having performed wholesome deeds for the Buddhas, may I attain incomparable, wondrous enlightenment;
may I obtain a great void-body, pure and white, free from the stains of dust.
Selfless and empty of human nature, signless and ineffable—this is the body of the Muni realized; it transcends the realm of all eyes.
With a mind pure and free from form and sound, it is fundamentally empty and without arising or activity.
One who perceives the body of True Suchness sees the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Just as various magical illusions— such as elephants, horses, and madmen—
deceive and delude the ignorant and the perverted, so too should one contemplate the ten directions.
"The Buddhas of the three periods, immeasurable in number, Dwell together in the body of the dharma-nature,
Unequaled like empty space, The utterly pure realm of phenomena.
"Thus it is, Śāriputra!"
This is called the inconceivable body of the Tathāgata.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas believe in, accept, and reverently uphold this with purity and without doubt, they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the inconceivable voice of the Tathāgata, accept it with faith, revere it with sincerity, and remain pure and free from doubt, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder?”

Śāriputra! When the Tathāgata appears in the world out of compassion for all sentient beings, he expounds the transformative teachings of the Dharma, and the sound he utters reaches the entire assembly.
By the power of his ability to discipline sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s voice pervades the infinite worlds of the ten directions, causing the hearts of all sentient beings to rejoice.
Śāriputra! Although the sounds produced by the Tathāgatas pervade the entire world, they do not form such thoughts as:

"I am teaching the Dharma for the assembly of bhikṣus; I am teaching the Dharma for the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs; I am teaching the Dharma for the assembly of upāsakas, the assembly of upāsikās, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of householders, the assembly of devas, or the assembly of Brahmās—and so forth—for these various assemblies."
Nor does he form this thought:
"I am now expounding the twelvefold teachings, such as the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, avadānas, and upadeśas."
"From the very beginning, he has never had the thought to elaborate upon it for their sake. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata, according to the various assemblies—whether they be bhikṣus or even the assembly of Brahmās—teaches the Dharma by means of various forms of right effort, in accordance with what they have heard."
Because these sentient beings delight in hearing the Dharma, each thinks that the sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma issues from his face.

Yet, regarding the Dharma-sound as it is spoken, the various types of words and phrases do not obstruct one another; each understands the specific Dharma they have perceived for themselves. This is what is called the inconceivable.
Śāriputra! The sounds resulting from the karmic fruition of the prior merit of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are immeasurable in their characteristics.
These are known as: the sound of compassionate moisture, the agreeable sound, the pleasing sound, the pure sound, and the stainless sound.
A voice that is melodious, a beautiful voice, a pleasant-to-hear voice, a distinct voice, a non-harsh voice, a non-grating voice,
a voice that brings physical comfort and joy, a voice that causes the heart to leap with excitement, a voice that gladdens the mind, a voice that arouses delight,
a voice that is easy to understand, a voice that is easy to recognize, a straightforward voice, and a lovely voice.
A voice that is pleasant, delightful, joyous, heart-gladdening, like the roar of a lion king, like the crashing of a great thunderclap,
like the surging of the great ocean, like the song of the *kiṃnaras*, like the call of the kalaviṅka bird,
like the voice of Brahmā, like the sound of celestial drums, auspicious, supple, and clearly articulated.
The sound of great thunder deep and far-reaching; the sound that gladdens the faculties of all sentient beings;
the sound that is pleasing to all assemblies; and the sound that accomplishes all subtle and wondrous marks.
Śāriputra! Such voices of the Tathāgata as these are fully endowed with such supreme merits, as well as being adorned by other immeasurable and boundless merits.
“Śāriputra! This is called the second inconceivable voice of the Tathāgata.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear this inconceivable voice of the Tathāgata, they become endowed with immeasurable, supreme merits; they accept it with faith, uphold it with truth, and remain pure and free from doubt. They leap for joy all the more, giving rise to deep gladness and a sense of wonder.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Guide utters wondrous sounds, namely, the voice of Brahmā;
because he is fully endowed with these dharmas, he causes all Brahmās to rejoice.”
The Muni utters wondrous sounds, flowing forth from great compassion;
they are said to be associated with loving-kindness, and likewise with sympathetic joy and equanimity.
Possessing such perfect sounds, he extinguishes the fire of craving in sentient beings.
Extinguishing the poison of hatred, Tearing asunder all the darkness of delusion.
Even if one were to hear every kind of human voice Throughout the entire continent of Jambudvīpa, One would never thereby awaken to liberation.
The sounds of heaven, earth, and space—failing to awaken to them is likewise so;
yet if one hears the voice of the Holy Lord, one will surely realize nirvana.
Whether they have two feet, four feet, many feet, or no feet at all—
He utters sounds identical to all of them, awakening them to the dharmas of good and evil.
Within the three thousandfold world system, through the lower, middle, and superior sounds,
he transforms beings according to their respective types of speech, leading them to realize liberation.
He utters sounds free from conceptual discrimination, unbound and without grasping;
abiding in meditative concentration, he reveals the true reality, so that those who hear him find their afflictions stilled.
Boundless sentient beings hear the sounds of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
As well as generosity, ethical discipline, learning, and patience—the voice of the Tathāgata is like this.
That voice is not of limited measure; both the sound and its wisdom are boundless.
Only the wise bodhisattvas, free from doubt, place their faith in the Buddha’s voice.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having with faith accepted, sincerely revered, and purified himself of doubt regarding the inconceivable great wisdom of the Tathāgata, leaps for joy even more, gives rise to profound gladness, and conceives a sense of wonder?”
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom and vision are inconceivable, arising in dependence upon all phenomena.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to believe in, accept, and reverently uphold them, even to the point of conceiving thoughts of wonder.

Śāriputra! In order to inspire faith, the Tathāgata extensively expounds parables based on the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom (jñānapāramitā), whereby those who possess wisdom attain understanding and liberation.

Śāriputra! Suppose there were a person who took all the grasses, trees, trunks, branches, and leaves within as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, stacking them into a great heap reaching at least four finger-widths in height, and burned them with fire until they were turned into ink. He would then cast this ink into the oceans of as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in other directions, and for a hundred thousand years, he would grind it down until it was entirely reduced to ink-juice.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has accomplished such unimpeded knowledge and vision.

By means of this wisdom, he takes a single drop of ink from within such a great ocean; by the power of his wisdom, he analytically discerns and fully knows that it originated from such a tree in such a world—its roots, its trunk, its branches, its twigs, its flowers, fruits, and leaves—and he thoroughly understands all their distinct characteristics and formations.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because the Tathāgata has thoroughly mastered the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), he is able to know in this way that this ink came from such-and-such a world and from such-and-such a tree.
Thus it continues in sequence, as explained at length. Śāriputra,

this is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, being endowed with such great power of supernormal knowledge, endowed with such great power of majestic virtue, and endowed with such great power of sovereign authority.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, with great wisdom, receive and believe in the Tathāgata’s purity, and who give rise to a heart of love and reverence toward the Buddha, the extent of those roots of goodness belonging to such sons and daughters of good family cannot be known; they shall swiftly reach the end of suffering.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because the Tathāgata has thoroughly and skillfully realized the dharma-realm.

"By virtue of this penetration, Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who give rise to even a slight root of goodness toward the Tathāgata, they will reach the end of suffering and never again be destroyed."
I shall now speak another parable for you, so that those of wisdom may understand the meaning by means of this analogy.

Śāriputra, suppose there were a man with a lifespan of a hundred years; this man takes a single hair-tip and divides it into one hundred and fifty parts, taking one part of that hair to moisten a single drop of water, and then comes to me and says:
"I venture to entrust this drop of water to you; should you require it later, please return it to me.

At that time, the Tathāgata took the drop of water and placed it within the Ganges River, where it was caught in the swirling eddies of the river's current, mingled with the flow, and carried onward until it reached the great ocean.
After a hundred years have passed, this person comes to me and says to me:
"I previously entrusted you with a drop of water; I now request it back. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata has accomplished inconceivable wisdom; by means of this wisdom, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows that drop of water is within the great ocean, and he then takes a single hair-tip from within the great ocean, dips it into that original drop of water, and returns it to that person.
Śāriputra! What is the meaning of this analogy?

It means that sentient beings have once entrusted even a single drop of the water of subtle goodness into the hands of the Tathāgata’s field of merit, and it remains there for a long time without being lost.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, with pure faith and acceptance, give rise to a heart of love and reverence toward the inconceivable wisdom of the Tathāgata; who, recollecting the Tathāgata, offer various forms of worship; and who further scatter famous flowers into the air as an offering—the extent of all such roots of goodness belonging to these persons cannot be known, and they shall swiftly reach the end of suffering.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because the Tathāgata has thoroughly and skillfully realized the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
"If any person gives rise to even a single thought of a wholesome mind toward the Tathāgata, they will reach the end of suffering and shall never again be destroyed.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great wisdom function apart from consciousness? The Buddha said, “No.”
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If it is thus, what constitutes wisdom?"
"What is consciousness?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!..."
There are four stations of consciousness; because consciousness abides by depending upon them, they are called "stations of consciousness.
What are the four? They are as follows:

regarding the station of consciousness in form, consciousness takes form as its object and abides within form. Because of this, it gives rise to delight and becomes attached, further increasing, strengthening, and expanding.

Regarding those who dwell in consciousness through feeling: consciousness takes feeling as its object and dwells within feeling; because of this, joy arises and they become attached, whereby [the consciousness] further increases, becomes firm, and expands.

Regarding the station of consciousness in perception (*saṃjñā-vijñānasthiti*): consciousness takes perception as its object and dwells within perception; because of this, joy arises and one becomes attached, whereby [consciousness] further increases, becomes firm, and expands.
