Regarding the station of consciousness in formations: consciousness conditions formations, and as consciousness dwells within formations, through this it gives rise to delight, abiding with attachment; thus it further increases, becomes firm, and expands.
Śāriputra! Such characteristics as these are called consciousness (vijñāna).
Furthermore, by what is it called wisdom (jñāna)?
That which is called "wisdom" (jñāna) refers to not dwelling within the five aggregates of clinging and thoroughly comprehending the aggregate of consciousness.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the ability to discern the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element; this is what is called consciousness.

As for what is called "wisdom": if one does not abide within the four great elements and is able to skillfully penetrate the fact that consciousness and the dharma-realm are inseparable, this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

That which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the ability to discern forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, odors known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, tangibles known by the body, and mental phenomena known by the mind; this is termed consciousness.

What is called "wisdom" (jñāna) is that which is inwardly tranquil and does not operate externally; relying solely upon wisdom, it gives rise to no conceptualization or manifold conceptualizations regarding even a single phenomenon—this is what is termed wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That which arises from objects is called consciousness; that which arises from mental attention is called consciousness; that which arises from discrimination is called consciousness.
To be without grasping, without clinging, without an object of perception, without discernment, and without conceptualization—this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That which is called consciousness abides in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Why is this?
Because consciousness cannot function within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
If one can thoroughly comprehend the unconditioned dharma, this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which abides in arising and ceasing is called consciousness.
That which is neither born nor extinguished and has no abiding place is called wisdom.
Śāriputra, these characteristics—
whether they be consciousness or wisdom— are called the Tathāgata’s third inconceivable great wisdom.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear of this inconceivable great wisdom—unobstructed and unimpeded, which arises based upon all phenomena—and receive it with faith, accept it as truth, and follow it with pure minds free from doubt, they will leap for joy, experience profound gladness, and conceive a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse: "Countless sands of the Ganges, The grasses and trees of the worlds in the ten directions—
All burned to ashes and turned to ink, Ground for billions of years within the ocean."
The wisdom of the Ten Powers is profound and subtle; taking up a single drop, he shows it to all living beings.
As he discerns and knows them according to reality, he says, "This is such-and-such a realm, a tree, and so forth.
In this way, throughout the realms of the ten directions, he takes up particles of dust and water to show them to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha’s wisdom is equal to space, universally illuminating all things without doubt or obstruction.
He knows, exactly as they are, the minds of sentient beings throughout the ten directions as they give rise to the activities of greed, hatred, and delusion;
he possesses liberation that is free from increase or decrease.
"The wisdom of the World-Honored One, endowed with the ten powers, illuminates the dharma-realm;
free from discrimination and beyond conceptual thought, the sons of the Buddha are able to believe and accept it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the inconceivable great light of the Tathāgata, accept it with faith and venerate it with truth, being pure and free from doubt, and further, leaping for joy, generating profound gladness, and giving rise to a sense of wonder?"
Śāriputra! Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have thoroughly mastered the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), they are inconceivable.
By virtue of this mastery, all Tathāgatas emit great radiance that illuminates the entire trichiliocosm of Buddha-worlds without obstruction.
Śāriputra! It is, for example, as when there are no clouds or mists in the sky, and the sun’s orb, blazing intensely, emits great radiance that shines everywhere throughout the world.
In the same way, Śāriputra!
In the same way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha emits a great radiance that universally illuminates all things.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, just as the light of oil-lamps in the world is more extensive and vast than the light of fireflies, being brilliant, clear, and surpassingly superior in its illumination; so too is it with the Tathāgata.

The brilliance of a torch surpasses that of a lamp; a cluster of fire from a courtyard brazier surpasses a torch; the radiance of medicinal herbs exceeds that of the fire clusters; the light of the stars is twice as great as that of the herbs; the flowing light of the full moon surpasses the splendor of the stars; and the blazing light of the sun exceeds that of the moon. The light emitted from the bodies of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, as well as the light of their palaces, walls, and ornaments, is many times greater than the former and beyond all comparison.

In this manner, it continued successively until the bodies, palaces, walls, and bodily ornaments of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations all emitted radiance, which was twice as great as that of the previous levels.

The light of the Brahmakāyika devas, the light of the Brahmapurohita devas, the light of the Brahmakāyika-parṣadya devas, and the light of the Mahābrahmā devas; likewise, the light of Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, up to Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Saṃjñisattva, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha—heavenly bodies—all such bodily radiance, palace radiance, wall radiance, and radiance from ornaments, are the most supreme when compared to the aforementioned lights.

Thus, compared to the light of the Tathāgata, the Perfectly All-Knowing One, the radiance of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is surpassed; the Tathāgata’s light is more subtle, brilliantly illuminating, most supreme and pure, vast, foremost, and beyond all comparison.
Why is this? Śāriputra, the light of the Tathāgata is inconceivable;

it arises from an immeasurable mass of ethical discipline, from a mass of meditative concentration, from a mass of wisdom, from a mass of liberation, and from a mass of the knowledge and vision of liberation. It arises from such immeasurable qualities as these.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

All the lights existing within the trichiliocosm, compared to the light of the Tathāgata, do not equal even one hundredth part of it; they do not even equal one *upaniṣad* (fraction) part of it. Thus, they cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is like placing Jambūnada gold among ordinary gold; it causes that ordinary gold to appear like a heap of ink, losing its brilliance.
In this way, Śāriputra!
All the light that exists within this trichiliocosm is likewise unable to shine brightly in the presence of the Tathāgata’s radiance.
Furthermore, compared to the light of the Tathāgata, all the lights existing in the entire world cannot be said to possess light, purity, excellence, superiority, or unsurpassedness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

You should know now that if the Tathāgata did not intentionally sustain this light so that it extends for only one fathom out of compassion for sentient beings, then by means of a single portion of light produced by his karma, he could illuminate the entire trichiliocosm of the Buddha-world, causing the light of the sun and moon to no longer appear."
If it were thus, one could not distinguish between day and night, nor distinguish between months, half-months, seasons, or the divisions of years;
yet, out of compassion for all sentient beings, he manifests a height of one fathom.
Śāriputra! If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha intends to pervade immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds with light, he is able to illuminate them all.
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because the Tathāgata has attained the foremost *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra! I shall now provide you with another analogy to further clarify this meaning, so that those who possess wisdom may understand it all the more clearly. Śāriputra!

Suppose there were a person who reduced this trichiliocosm into fine motes of dust, placed them in the fold of their garment, and traveled toward the eastern direction, dropping a single mote of dust after passing as many worlds as there are motes of dust; if one proceeded in this manner until all these motes of dust were exhausted, the limit of all the worlds in that eastern direction would still not have been reached.
In the same way, it is also thus in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions,
and above and below. Śāriputra, what do you think?
"Is there anyone who can reach the boundaries of this world-system? Śāriputra replied, "No."
"Bhagavan! No, Sugata!"
“Śāriputra! All the lights existing in these worlds are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, yet the light of the Tathāgata is the foremost of all.”
That universal radiance does not equal even one hundredth part of the Tathāgata’s radiance; it does not even equal one *upaniṣad* part, nor can it be reached by any such calculation or analogy.
Śāriputra! When the Tathāgata intends to illuminate all worlds with his radiance, he is able to illuminate them everywhere. Why is this?
Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata has attained the foremost perfection of wisdom, the light of the Tathāgata is without obstruction.

No walls, nor trees, nor timber, nor the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Gandhamādana Mountains, Mucilinda Mountains, Mahāmucilinda Mountains, Īśādhara Mountains, Snowy Mountains, Black Mountains, or Sumeru, King of Mountains—none of these can obstruct it. The Buddha’s radiance penetrates them all, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm.

Śāriputra! Sentient beings of meager wisdom cannot believe in or understand the light of the Tathāgata. Some sentient beings see the light of the Tathāgata illuminating only one *vyāma*; next, those of greater wisdom see the light of the Tathāgata illuminating two *vyāmas*; next, those of further wisdom see the light of the Tathāgata illuminating a *krośa*; and finally, those of great wisdom are able to see the radiance of the Tathāgata pervading and illuminating the trichiliocosm.
Śāriputra! Even the Brahmā kings, lords of a hundred thousand worlds, can see the Tathāgata’s light illuminating those hundred thousand worlds.
In this manner, progressing further, even the great Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who have ascended to the higher stages can see the Tathāgata’s light illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Śāriputra! Out of a desire to have compassion for all sentient beings, the Tathāgata again emits light that shines universally throughout all realms of sentient beings, as vast as space.
“Śāriputra! This is called the fourth inconceivable light of the Tathāgata.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear the Tathāgata speak of this great light as being inconceivable and like space, they accept it with pure faith, free from confusion or doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to deep gladness and a sense of wonder.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse: "The light of the sun and moon, And that of Śakra, Brahmā, and others,
Even reaching up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven— None of these lights can equal the Buddha."
The light of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven Shines everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm;
Compared to the light from a single pore of the Buddha, It does not equal even a sixteenth part.
The light emitted by the Tathāgata Pervades and fills the realm of empty space.
Only those sentient beings of great wisdom Are able to see it in this way.
The Buddha’s light is boundless, Its measure equal to the nature of space;
Yet according to the beings to be transformed, They perceive differences in the light.
Just as one born blind does not see the light of the sun,
and failing to see its radiance, claims that sunlight does not exist;
so too do inferior sentient beings, failing to see the Buddha’s radiance, [conclude it does not exist].
Some do not see the light shining, claiming that the Buddha’s light does not exist;
others see it at a distance of one fathom, or one krośa,
or even one yojana, or filling the entire trichiliocosm.
Having already dwelt upon the great stages, the Bodhisattvas of Great Wisdom and Radiance—
those dwelling on the eighth or ninth stages, up to those who have reached the tenth stage—
the Tathāgata transcends those stages; his circle of light is without limit.
The inconceivable Buddha-lands perform all the works of the Buddhas;
the Buddhas are inconceivable, and the Buddha-light is inconceivable;
those who have faith and the merit they obtain are likewise difficult to conceive.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the Tathāgata’s inconceivable assembly of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the assembly of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), accepts and reverently upholds them with purity and without doubt, and further leaps for joy, giving rise to deep gladness and a sense of wonder?”

Śāriputra! You should know that this is the correct teaching: if sentient beings in this world uphold the precepts (śīla) purely and without defilement, then by virtue of that purity, you should know that such persons have accomplished pure bodily action (kāyakarman), accomplished pure verbal action (vākkarman), and accomplished pure mental action (manaskarman).
Although such a person constantly dwells within the world, they are not defiled by worldly dharmas.

You should know that this person is a brāhmaṇa, one who has abandoned all evils, a śramaṇa, and one who is tranquil; they are called the foremost practitioner of dhyāna and the one who has attained the foremost perfection of samādhi.
Śāriputra! Such a sentient being is the Tathāgata.
To speak thus is called speaking correctly.
Why is this? Śāriputra, from the very beginning,

I have not seen anyone in the world of gods— whether Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, or any other beings such as devas and asuras— who possesses such immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable purity of ethical discipline (śīla), meditative concentration (samādhi), and the assembly [of qualities] as a Tathāgata.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because the Tathāgata has attained the foremost perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-samādhi-pāramitā).
“Śāriputra! Do you now wish to hear the Buddha’s teaching on the parables for the Tathāgata’s perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)? Śāriputra replied:
"Now is the very time, Blessed One! Now is the very time!"
"Sujāta! World-Honored One!
If the bhikṣus hear this parable of the Tathāgata’s śīlapāramitā spoken by the Buddha, they shall, having heard it as it was taught, together receive and uphold it."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Excellent, excellent!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
"Śāriputra, what do you think?
Between the realm of sentient beings and the realm of the great earth, which is more numerous?"
Śāriputra said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the realm of sentient beings is vast; it is not the realm of earth.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Śāriputra! The realm of sentient beings is vast; it is not like the realm of earth."

Śāriputra! Suppose there were all the sentient beings in the trichiliocosm—those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form or without form; those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all such sentient beings as these.
Suppose all those sentient beings were, in a single kṣaṇa, or a single muhūrta, or a single lava, simultaneously to obtain human bodies.
Śāriputra! Suppose all those sentient beings, having attained human bodies, were simultaneously to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single kṣaṇa, or even within the duration of a lava.

Each of these Tathāgatas further emanates as many Tathāgatas as there are; each of these emanated Tathāgatas has a thousand heads, each head has a thousand mouths, and each mouth has a thousand tongues.

At that time, all those emanated Tathāgatas fully accomplished the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges; furthermore, they accomplished the Buddha’s unobstructed, unhindered, and inexhaustible eloquence.

Śāriputra! With as many tongues as there are, these Tathāgatas employ unimpeded and inexhaustible eloquence to offer countless praises for the śīla-pāramitā of a single Tathāgata; yet, even if such praises were uttered for hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta great kalpas, they would still be unable to exhaust the mass of that Tathāgata’s ethical discipline.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline is immeasurable, boundless, inexhaustible, and inconceivable. Likewise, the unsurpassed wisdom of all Tathāgatas, as well as their unimpeded, unobstructed, and inexhaustible eloquence, are also inexhaustible and inconceivable.
Even until all the emanated Tathāgatas have simultaneously entered great parinirvāṇa, one could not exhaustively praise and describe the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*).

Why is this? Because both the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline and the unsurpassed wisdom and unimpeded eloquence of all the World-Honored Ones are inconceivable; they are immeasurable and innumerable, equal and coextensive with the realm of empty space.
Śāriputra! Let alone all the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm.

Suppose there were as many sentient beings in worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to the east; likewise, suppose there were as many sentient beings in worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—in all ten directions. If all those sentient beings were, in a single kṣaṇa, or even in a lava, simultaneously to obtain human bodies and together attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Thus it is explained in detail, up to the point that the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline, as well as the unsurpassed wisdom and unimpeded eloquence of all Tathāgatas, are all inconceivable, immeasurable, and innumerable, equal in parity to the realm of empty space.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because the Tathāgata has realized the foremost perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Do you now wish to hear the Buddha’s exposition of analogies for the Tathāgata’s perfection of samādhi? Śāriputra replied:
"Now is precisely the right time.
If the bhikṣus hear this analogy for the Tathāgata’s perfection of samādhi as taught by the Buddha, they should, having heard it, together uphold it."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Suppose there comes a time when this world-system is about to be consumed by fire; on the seventh day, because that sun rises, the trichiliocosm is simultaneously set ablaze—thus burning intensely, burning all over, and burning with a great conflagration."

Śāriputra, you should know that within this world-system of great conflagration, in whichever place the Tathāgata may be— whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down— it should be known that ten kinds of most rare and marvelous, inconceivable qualities are accomplished in that location.
Śāriputra! What are the ten marvelous phenomena? They are as follows:
wherever the Tathāgata dwells or stays, the ground becomes naturally level and even, without the application of effort, just like the palm of a hand.
"Śāriputra! This is called the first most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Even if the world above were thus completely ablaze with fire, wherever the Tathāgata might walk, stand, sit, or lie within it, that place would naturally rise up, becoming elevated, spacious, and free from any debris such as tiles or stones.
"Śāriputra! This is called the second most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Even if the worlds above were thus entirely ablaze with great fires, wherever the Tathāgata might walk, stand, sit, or lie within them, that place would naturally become level, vast, majestic, and pure, serving as a dwelling for the Tathāgata’s use.
“Śāriputra! This is called the third most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

Even if the worlds above, up to those that are completely ablaze, were such that the Tathāgata were therein walking, standing, sitting, or lying down according to the sūtras, at those places various fragrant herbs would naturally grow—vibrant green in color, curled and soft, turning to the right, and possessing a fine, smooth texture like that of kācalindika cloth.
"Śāriputra! This is called the fourth most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Even if the worlds above were thus completely ablaze with fire, wherever the Tathāgata might walk, stand, sit, or lie within them, there would naturally appear from the earth water endowed with the eight qualities: namely, first, lightness; second, coolness; third, softness; fourth, clarity and stillness; fifth, absence of impurity; sixth, purity; seventh, pleasantness when drunk; and eighth, no harm from drinking in excess.
"Śāriputra! This is called the fifth most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Even if this world above were to become completely engulfed in flames, wherever the Tathāgata walks, stands, sits, or lies within it, that place naturally gives rise to cool, harmonious, and gentle breezes; this is the result of the Tathāgata’s past karma.

Śāriputra, it is as if, during the height of the summer heat, there were a man in the afternoon who, driven by the heat, rushed toward the Gaṅgā River. Casting himself into the water, he bathed his body; once his exhaustion from the heat had subsided, he felt cool, refreshed, and joyful. He then went back and forth, playing and sporting, crossing to the other shore and walking to and fro.
Seeing from afar, not far away, a great forest with lush, verdant foliage and thick, dense shade, he proceeded into the woods.

There he saw that exquisite couches and seats had been prepared, spread with superior woolen rugs, topped with cotton mattresses, and covered with *kācalindika* cloths; over these were layered light, fine, and fresh fabrics, and soft pillows were arranged at both ends of the beds.
When that Great Being ascends this couch, whether sitting or reclining, a gentle breeze stirs from the four sides of the couch, providing a continuous, light fanning.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Just as the Tathāgata walks, stands, sits, and lies within this great world-system that is ablaze with fire, so too does a natural cool breeze fan gently and continuously in the same manner.
"Śāriputra! This is called the sixth most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Even if the world above were thus entirely ablaze with great conflagrations, wherever the Tathāgata might walk, stand, sit, or lie within it, that place would naturally manifest various water-born flowers upon rivers, streams, ponds, and marshes—namely, the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers. These flowers would be fragrant, their radiance shining forth, bringing joy and delight to all who behold them.
"Śāriputra! This is called the seventh most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Even if the worlds above were thus entirely ablaze with great conflagrations, as the Tathāgata walks, stands, sits, or lies therein, that place naturally becomes level ground and hills where various wonderful flowers appear. These are the *adhimuktaka*, *campaka*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *aśoka*, *pāṭala*, *kaṇikāra*, *tālī*, and *gotālī* flowers; such flowers bloom in full splendor, endowed with exquisite colors and fragrances, such that sentient beings who see them experience what they have never known before.
"Śāriputra! This is called the eighth most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Even if the aforementioned worlds were to become completely ablaze with fire, the place where the Tathāgata walks, stands, sits, or lies down would naturally become adamantine in substance, firm and indestructible.
"Śāriputra! This is called the ninth most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Suppose that at the time when the kalpa of this aforementioned trichiliocosm is about to end, and it is burning, intensely burning, and universally intensely burning; blazing, intensely blazing, and universally intensely blazing; and completely ablaze—within these worlds, wherever the Tathāgata may walk, stand, sit, or lie down, one should know that such places are the sacred shrines of the Buddha, revered by the devas and the world, and honored, venerated, and respected by Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, humans, asuras, and others.
"Śāriputra! This is called the tenth most marvelous and extraordinary quality accomplished in this place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
You should now know that these ten kinds of most rare and marvelous phenomena are all accomplished through the power of the Tathāgata’s past karma. Why is this so?
Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata has thoroughly mastered the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), through that mastery, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha enters this samādhi.

Relying on this concentrated mind, he experiences bliss without regression; even though he remains for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the Tathāgata never regresses from the state of this samādhi-mind.

Śāriputra! Based on this concentrated mind, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha may remain for the duration of a single meal, or for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or a hundred thousand kalpas; or he may remain for one koṭi of kalpas, a hundred koṭis of kalpas, a thousand koṭis of kalpas, or a hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas, or even beyond these numbers.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished the foremost perfection of samādhi.

By virtue of this accomplishment, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with such great power of supernormal knowledge, fully endowed with such great power of majestic virtue, and fully endowed with such great power of sovereign authority.

Śāriputra! Just as when those devaputras born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception give rise to consciousness that takes a single object as its condition and remains for eighty-four thousand kalpas, until their lifespan in samādhi has not yet expired, this consciousness is not displaced or shifted by any other objective consciousness.

Śāriputra! If those sons of the gods can remain for such a duration by the power of worldly meditative concentration, how much more so could the Tathāgata remain for a long time through the perfection of samādhi?
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

From the night the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha first realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, until the night he entered the realm of great parinirvāṇa without remainder, during that interval, the mind of the Tathāgata never arose from samādhi."

Therefore, this concentration is so named because it is a state devoid of a mind that turns back, a mind that engages in activity, a mind that observes, a mind that wavers in deliberation, a mind that wanders, a mind that gathers a multitude, a mind that is distracted, a mind that is uplifted, a mind that is depressed, a mind that guards, a mind that conceals, a mind that exults, a mind that resists, a mind that withers, a mind that is agitated, a mind that is startled, a mind that is dull, a mind that discriminates, a mind that differentiates, and a mind that conceptualizes extensively.

Furthermore, this concentration does not follow the mind of consciousness; it does not rely on the mind of the eye, nor on the minds of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or intellect; it does not rely on the mind of forms, nor on the minds of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; it does not tend toward the mind of all dharmas, it does not give rise to the mind of wisdom, and it does not contemplate the past, the future, or the present mind.

Śāriputra! When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha abides in samādhi, he is thus detached from the mind; there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended, and unimpeded wisdom and vision arise regarding all dharmas because they are effortless.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata does not arise from samādhi; yet, being free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, he is able to perform all the works of a Buddha because he is without effortful application (*anābhoga*).
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Having heard of the inconceivable ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the Tathāgata, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accept them with faith and venerate them with truth, pure and without doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“For immeasurable and peerless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, In former existences, he practiced the conduct of awakening;
Through precepts, learning, concentration, patience, and heedfulness, The Guide was able to cultivate the causes of sublime awakening.”
The purity of the fruit of the most supreme karma is thus; the wondrous, vast, and pure precepts transcend all realms of existence.
The precepts of the Honored One of Ten Powers are as pure as space; their stainlessness is difficult to describe, being like the void.

From the night the Buddha first attained enlightenment, until the night he later entered into parinirvāṇa, the Buddha’s mind was without activity and without differentiated activity; his great meditative absorption never once arose [from its state].
The aggregate of the ten powers is free from any part of decline; liberation and spiritual power are likewise so.
Abiding with single-mindedness for immeasurable eons, the Great Sage is without thought and without divergent thought.
The Buddha’s wisdom is like space, not a realm of thought; Its clear penetration shines upon the three periods of time without conditions.
Free from mental volition and without change, Only the sons of the Buddha can believe and accept it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having faith in and sincerely revering the inconceivable spiritual power of the Tathāgata with pure and doubtless conviction, leaps for joy, gives rise to profound gladness, and conceives a sense of wonder?”
Śāriputra! The supernormal powers attained by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, are inconceivable and ineffable; I shall now skillfully reveal them to you.
"Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has always declared that among my assembly of śrāvakas, the one who has attained supernormal powers is foremost, namely the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
Śāriputra! If one were to examine with critical assessment the supernormal powers thus attained by śrāvakas, one would not find any that are equal to the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.

If one were to weigh and examine the supernormal powers attained by śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, one would not see any that are equal to the supernormal powers of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. Śāriputra!
This is called the inconceivable supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize the supernormal power of the Tathāgata should, with redoubled effort, arouse superior-grade right diligence (*samyag-vīrya*), and they will then be able to attain realization.
"Śāriputra! Do you now wish to hear from the Tathāgata an inconceivable analogy regarding supernormal powers? Śāriputra replied:
"Now is the very time.
If the bhikṣus hear this discourse by the Buddha on supernatural powers and parables, having heard it, they should together receive and uphold it.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall speak for your sake.
Śāriputra said, “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "What do you think?"
“Does the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana possess great supernormal powers?
Śāriputra replied, “In the past, I received and upheld these words from the Buddha: ‘Among the assembly of śrāvakas, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in supernormal powers.’”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!"
I shall now provide you with a detailed analogy.
Suppose the trichiliocosm were filled with śrāvakas, all of whom had attained supernatural powers like those of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as dense as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, or hemp.

When these śrāvakas manifest their supernatural transformations through the power and swiftness of their right efforts, if one were to compare them to the supernatural transformations of a Tathāgata, they would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part; they would not equal a *koṭi*-th part, a hundred-*koṭi*-th part, a thousand-*koṭi*-th part, or a hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-th part. Likewise, they would not equal a *saṃkhyeya*-th part, a *kalā*-th part, a *gaṇanā*-th part, an *upamā*-th part, or an *upanisad*-th part.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the supreme perfection of supernatural powers and transformations.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:

Suppose the Tathāgata were to cast a single mustard seed upon the ground; even when that assembly of śrāvakas manifests great supernatural transformations through the power of their right efforts and swift spiritual penetrations, they would ultimately be unable to move that cast mustard seed by even as much as the tip of a hair.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the foremost supernatural powers and transformations.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Setting aside the trichiliocosm for a moment,

suppose all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges from the eastern direction, and likewise all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions— from those born from eggs or from wombs, up to those in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception— were all śrāvakas who had attained the foremost supernatural powers and transformations, just like the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

Thus, even when the śrāvakas manifest great supernatural transformations through the swift power of their right efforts, they cannot move so much as a single mustard seed or a hair-tip from where it was placed.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has attained the foremost perfection, the perfection of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāramitā*). Śāriputra!

This is called the Tathāgata’s possession of such great power of supernatural faculties, his possession of such great power of majestic virtue, and his possession of such great power of sovereign authority.
At that time, the Bhagavān again addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!
Have you ever heard that when the kalpa of wind arises, there is a great wind in the world named Saṃghāta?"

If that wind were to blow, would it not lift this trichiliocosm—including Sumeru, the king of mountains, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, as well as the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, the great mountains, and the great oceans—lifting them from their original locations by more than a yojana and crushing them into powder?
Śāriputra said, “In the past,
I personally heard and received such matters in the presence of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Śāriputra! Furthermore,
when the calamity of wind arises, there is another great wind named Saṃghāta."

Blown by that wind, this trichiliocosm—including Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and so forth, as well as all the great oceans—is lifted up to a height of one hundred yojanas and ground into dust.

Or again, having lifted [a mass] two hundred yojanas high, or four or five hundred, even up to a thousand yojanas high, or three or four thousand yojanas high, they crush it into dust; or even having lifted it up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas high, they crush it into dust.
These particles of dust, scattered and extinguished by the wind, become utterly unfindable; how much more so would any mountain or rock remain?

This wind rises further, striking and dispersing the palaces of the Yama Heaven until they are destroyed and extinguished; even the finest particles are scattered and vanish, so how could any palace remain?

In this manner, proceeding successively upward, they strike, scatter, shatter, and destroy all the palaces of the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Māra-kāyika devas, the Brahmakāyika devas, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven; even down to their atoms, all are dispersed and extinguished so that nothing can be found, let alone the palaces or their walls that might remain.

Śāriputra! Even if a great wind such as described were to suddenly arise and destroy the world-system, that very wind could not move even a single hair-tip on the Tathāgata’s robe, let alone its hem or the garment as a whole.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished inconceivable supernormal powers, inconceivable deportment, inconceivable sublime conduct, and inconceivable great compassion.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
suppose great wind-circles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River were to arise in worlds throughout the ten directions, intending to blow these worlds into ruin.

At that time, the Tathāgata took this world upon the tip of a single finger and traveled to another place; he could even render the wind-circle powerless to blow, causing it to suddenly return, yet there was no diminution whatsoever in the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations or his all-encompassing power.

"Śāriputra! The supernormal powers of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, difficult to hear, and difficult to believe. Only the great Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to accept them with faith, to revere them with sincerity, and to maintain purity without confusion or doubt; they leap for joy, experience profound delight, and conceive a sense of wonder."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Suppose all sentient beings within the three realms Were entirely transformed into the assembly of śrāvakas,
And all attained the perfection of supernatural powers, Just like the Venerable Maudgalyāyana."
The Tathāgata Huode Dashentongli (Obtainer of Great Supernatural Power), Taking a single mustard seed and casting it upon the ground,
Caused all the śrāvakas to manifest their supernatural powers, Yet they could not move it even by the measure of a hair-tip.
Even if, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as many great and violent Vairambha winds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to blow and shatter all such worlds.
Though such winds as these are exceedingly fierce, they shall blow upon the robes of the Omniscient One;
yet, even with all their power exhausted, they cannot move them so much as the breadth of a single hair-tip.
The Great Muni, with a single hair, can obstruct that wind so it does not arise;
the Buddha possesses such great supernormal power, equal to space and without limit.
"In this way, Śāriputra,
this is called the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power of great supernormal knowledge.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas receive it with faith, accept it as true, and follow it with pure minds free from doubt, they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound delight and a sense of wonder."
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Thirty-seven;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Thirty-eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Bodhisattvapiṭaka Assembly, Volume Twelve, Part Four: Chapter Four, Part Two, "The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata, accept it with faith, revere it with sincerity, and remain pure and free from doubt; how does he leap for joy, give rise to profound gladness, and conceive a sense of wonder?"

Śāriputra! The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are fully endowed with these ten powers. Because they have achieved them, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, declaring: "I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel, which no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, or Brahmas in all the world can turn in accordance with the Dharma."
Śāriputra! What are called the ten powers of the Tathāgata? They are: the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible;

the power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma; the power of knowledge regarding the various elements; the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations; the power of knowledge regarding the various faculties; the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere; the power of knowledge regarding the defilement and purification of meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis; the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past lives as a direct realization; the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth as a direct realization; and the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows as a direct realization.
Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata has accomplished these ten powers, he is able to turn the Brahma-wheel amidst the great assembly—a wheel that no one in any world can turn.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible? Śāriputra!"

The Tathāgata’s unsurpassed power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible means that he knows, as it truly is, what is possible as possible, and knows, as it truly is, what is impossible as impossible.
Śāriputra! What is the possible? And what is the impossible?

Śāriputra, that which is called "impossible" (asthāna) is not to be accepted; namely, that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct could result in a retribution that is desirable, pleasant, lovely, and agreeable—such a thing is impossible.

Regarding what is called "a possibility": there is the taking up of things, namely, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, which can bring about retribution that is undesirable, unpleasant, unlovely, and disagreeable—this is indeed possible.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called "impossible" (asthāna) is that which cannot be accepted as true: namely, that there could be an instance where excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind results in a retribution that is undesirable, unpleasant, unlovely, or disagreeable—such a thing is impossible.

Regarding what is called "a possible case," it refers to that which is embraced: namely, that bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct—which can bring about a result that is desirable, pleasant, lovely, and agreeable—is indeed a possible case.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called "impossible" (asthāna) refers to that which cannot be realized. That is to say: it is impossible for one who is miserly to attain great wealth; for one who violates the precepts to be reborn among humans or gods; for one who harbors malice to attain physical beauty; for one who is indolent to attain meditative insight; for one whose mind is distracted to enter the path of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma); or for one with faulty wisdom to forever sever all habitual tendencies of the continuum (*saṃtati-vāsanā*). To speak in such a manner is impossible.

Regarding what is called "a possible case," there is that which is encompassed by it: namely, that through stinginess one brings about poverty; through violating the precepts, one brings about rebirth in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; through malice, one brings about an ugly retribution; through laziness, one fails to attain direct contemplation; through mental distraction, one does not enter right concentration; and through faulty wisdom, one does not sever all continuous habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). To speak in this manner is indeed a possible case.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

That which is called "impossible" (asthāna) is that which cannot be accepted as true; namely, that one might experience poverty through giving, fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts through upholding the precepts, experience ugliness through patience, fail to attain insight through right effort, fail to enter right concentration through one-pointedness of mind, or fail to sever all habitual tendencies of continuity through noble wisdom—to speak thus is impossible.

To say that there is a possibility [of such results] means that there is what is grasped; namely, that through giving one can bring about great wealth, through observing the precepts one attains birth among humans or devas, through maintaining patience one brings about physical excellence, through right effort one is able to attain contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), through one-pointedness of mind one enters into the certainty of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and through noble wisdom one forever severs all latencies (*vāsanā*) of the continuum—to speak thus is indeed possible.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called 'impossible' (asthāna) refers to that which cannot be accepted as true: namely, that one who kills will experience a long life; that one who takes what is not given will attain great wealth; or that one who engages in sexual misconduct will obtain a chaste and virtuous wife—to speak thus is impossible.

Regarding what is called "a possible case," it refers to that which is subject to causal determination: namely, that one who kills will experience a short lifespan; one who takes what is not given will experience poverty; and one who engages in sexual misconduct will have an unchaste wife—to speak thus is indeed a possible case.

Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that one who abstains from killing could experience a short lifespan, that one who abstains from taking what is not given could experience poverty, or that the wife of one who abstains from sexual misconduct could be unchaste—no such thing can occur. To say otherwise is impossible.

To say that there is such a possibility means that there is something to be grasped: namely, that one who abstains from killing will experience long life; one who abstains from taking what is not given will experience great wealth; and one who abstains from sexual misconduct will obtain a chaste and virtuous wife—to speak thus is indeed possible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Regarding all such wholesome and unwholesome paths of action, whether they are possible or impossible, I shall now briefly explain and reveal their essential points."
It is impossible for one who speaks falsely not to incur slander; it is possible that they may incur it.
It is impossible for one who abstains from false speech to incur slander; it is possible that they do not incur it.
Regarding divisive speech: it is impossible that one who engages in divisive speech could obtain an undivided retinue; it is possible that they could not obtain one.
It is impossible that one who abstains from divisive speech could obtain a divided retinue; it is possible that they could obtain an undivided retinue.
Regarding harsh speech: it is impossible that one who engages in harsh speech should constantly hear agreeable sounds; it is possible that they should hear disagreeable sounds.
It is impossible that one who abstains from harsh speech should hear disagreeable sounds; it is possible that they should not hear them.
If one harbors frivolous speech, it is impossible that the words and teachings spoken would cause others to believe and accept them; it is only possible that they would not believe and accept them.
If one is free from frivolous speech, it is impossible that the words and teachings spoken would not be accepted by others; it is only possible that they would believe and accept them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is impossible for one who is attached to greed to experience wealth that does not disperse; it is only possible for such wealth to be dispersed.
It is impossible for one who is free from attachment to greed to experience the dispersal of wealth; it is only possible that they do not experience such dispersal.
It is impossible that one whose mind is full of hatred should not go to hell; it is only possible that they should go there.
It is impossible that one who is free from hatred should not be born in a happy realm; it is only possible that they should be so born.
If one who gives rise to wrong views and undergoes the causes of wrong views could attain the Path, such a thing is impossible; that they cannot attain the Path is the case that is possible.
That one who possesses right view and undergoes the causes of right view should fail to attain the Noble Path is impossible; that they can attain the Noble Path is the case that is possible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is impossible for one who has committed an act of immediate retribution to find peace and stability of mind; it is only possible that they do not find such stability.
Moreover, Śāriputra!"
If one whose precepts are pure does not have a mind that dwells in peace, such a thing is impossible; if they do attain such peaceful dwelling, such a thing is possible.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if one who dwells in the view of apprehending something can attain compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*), such a thing is impossible; if they do not so attain it, such a thing is possible.
If one who has faith and understanding of emptiness were unable to attain the patient acceptance of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*), such a thing is impossible;

if there are those who do attain it, such a thing is possible. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if one who dwells in remorse were to attain peace of mind, such a thing is impossible; if they cannot so attain it, such a thing is possible.
If one who binds the mind cannot attain peace of mind, such a thing is impossible; if one can so attain it, such a thing is possible.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a woman were to become a Wheel-Turning King, a Lord of the Śakras, or a Brahmā-Svayambhū, such a thing is impossible; if a man were to do so, such a thing is possible.

If there were such a thing as a woman appearing in the world to become a Buddha, it would be impossible; however, if she were to transform her female body and then appear in the world to become a Buddha, that would be possible.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is impossible for a person at the eighth stage who has not yet realized the fruit to emerge from existence; it is possible only after they have realized the fruit.
It is impossible for one who has entered the stream of the Noble Ones to undergo an eighth existence; it is possible only that they attain parinirvāṇa within these very aggregates.
It is impossible for a once-returner to undergo a third existence; it is possible that they attain parinirvāṇa within these very aggregates.
It is impossible for a non-returner to return here again; it is possible that they attain parinirvāṇa in that very place.
It is impossible for an Arhat to continue into further existence; it is only possible that they do not continue into further existence.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is impossible for any noble one to seek out a false teacher or adopt false insignia; it is only possible that they do not seek out a false teacher or false insignia.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

It is impossible for a bodhisattva who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) to fall back; it is certain that they will attain enlightenment without falling back—this is indeed possible.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called 'impossible' (asthāna) is that which cannot be accepted as true: it is impossible for a bodhisattva who is seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to rise from there without having realized awakening (bodhi)."
Regarding what is called "possible": there is such a case where, if bodhisattvas sit at the site of enlightenment and, having realized the Buddha-way, then arise, this is indeed possible.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That which is called "impossible" (asthāna) is this: to claim that the Tathāgata possesses a continuity of habitual tendencies (vāsanā)—such a thing is impossible.
That which is called "possible" (sthāna) is this: that all Tathāgatas have eternally severed their habitual tendencies—this is indeed possible.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is impossible that the wisdom of the Tathāgata should be obstructed; it is only possible that the Buddha’s wisdom is unobstructed.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is impossible for anyone to behold the crown of the Tathāgata’s head; it is possible that no one can do so.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is impossible for anyone to know where the mind of the Tathāgata abides; it is possible that no one can know it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

It is impossible that one could find a Tathāgata with an unconcentrated mind; it is only possible that the minds of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are always in a state of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is impossible for the Tathāgatas to speak words that are not true; however, it is entirely possible that the Tathāgatas are speakers of truth, speakers of reality, speakers of what is certain, and speakers of that which does not differ from the facts.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is impossible for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, to have any error or transgression; because they are free from all error, it is indeed possible to call them "Buddha" and "Bhagavān."
Śāriputra, these four fearlessnesses and eighteen unique qualities of a buddha should likewise be explained in detail through such analysis.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

To say that there is no such possibility—that the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision could function with obstruction or impediment in the present world—is impossible; it is not a case where such a thing can occur.

Regarding what is called "a possible case," it is indeed possible that the Buddha, the Blessed One, exercises unobstructed and unhindered knowledge and vision regarding the present world. This is a possible case.
Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), which is inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless.
Just as space is limitless and boundless, so too is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible limitless and boundless.
If there were anyone who sought the limit of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible, it would not differ from someone seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears that the Tathāgatas possess the inconceivable power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible, which is like space, they accept it with faith, uphold it with truth, and are pure and free from doubt; they leap for joy all the more, give rise to deep gladness, and conceive a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The space of the ten directions is boundless, And the wisdom regarding what is possible and impossible is likewise boundless.
Having known, as they truly are, what is possible and impossible, He proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma extensively for the sake of the multitudes."
The Buddha knows those who have attained the vessel for the path of liberation and teaches them according to their conduct;
if one is not a vessel for the path of liberation, he recognizes this unsuitable case and simply leaves them aside.
Even if space could be moved, And the great earth of the ten directions were to split asunder at once,
The Great Holy Honored One of the mundane and supramundane worlds Possesses the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, all according to reality.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s first power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible.

By virtue of its accomplishment, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the true lion’s roar in the great assembly, declaring: ‘I occupy the supreme seat of the Great Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel; no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, or Brahmās in all the world can turn it in accordance with the Dharma.’”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma? Śāriputra!"

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of his unsurpassed power of wisdom, is able to know, in accordance with reality, the karma of the past, future, and present, as well as the experience of that karma; he fully understands its causes, its locations, and all its various karmic retributions.
Śāriputra! How does the Tathāgata know things as they truly are?

It is that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows as they truly are the experiences of past karma: how one attains wholesome causes and distances oneself from unwholesome ones, such that these shall serve as causes for wholesome roots in future lives.
If, regarding past karma and its retribution, one acquires unwholesome causes and distances oneself from the wholesome, such that in future lives these will serve as the cause for unwholesome roots—
the Tathāgata knows all such characteristics as they truly are.

If there are karmas that will result in a lowly portion in future lives, or if there are karmas that will result in a superior portion in future lives—the Tathāgata knows such characteristics as these exactly as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are karmic experiences that are of an inferior nature in the present life but will be of a superior nature in future lives; or if there are karmic experiences that are of a superior nature in the present life but will be of an inferior nature in future lives; or if there are karmic experiences that are of an inferior nature in the present life and will also be of an inferior nature in future lives; or if there are karmic experiences that are of a superior nature in the present life and will also be of a superior nature in future lives—the Tathāgata knows such characteristics as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are karmic experiences that involved limited means in past lives but will involve vast means in future lives; if there are karmic experiences where a small amount of activity results in great advancement, or where extensive activity results in little advancement—one should know such characteristics as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are karmic experiences that will serve as the cause for attaining the nature of a śrāvaka, the cause for attaining the nature of a pratyekabuddha, or the cause for attaining the nature of a buddha—the Tathāgata knows such characteristics as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are karmas that involve suffering in the present life but can bring about a pleasant ripening in the future; if there are karmas that involve pleasure in the present life but can bring about a painful ripening in the future; if there are karmas that involve suffering in the present life and can bring about a painful ripening in the future; and if there are karmas that involve pleasure in the present life and can bring about a pleasant ripening in the future—the Tathāgata knows such characteristics as these exactly as they are.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata is able to know, as they truly are, all the karma, causes, various retributions, states of union and separation, and those factors that are concordant and non-differentiated regarding all sentient beings of the past, future, and present. Having known such characteristics, the Tathāgata proclaims them to sentient beings in accordance with reality."

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s knowledge of the causes, locations, and diverse retributions of the karma of the past, future, and present, as well as the experience of that karma, is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Just as space is boundless and limitless, so too is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the diversity of karmic results boundless and limitless.

Should anyone seek the limit of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s power of knowledge regarding the diversity of karmic results, it would be no different from someone seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears that the Tathāgatas’ power of knowledge regarding the diversity of karmic retributions is like space and inconceivable, they receive it with faith, accept it with devotion, and follow it with purity and without doubt; they leap for joy all the more, give rise to deep gladness, and conceive a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata thoroughly knows causes and their diverse retributions; With clear vision, he understands all karmas as they truly are.
Supreme and unimpeded throughout the three periods of time, He knows the various actions of sentient beings according to reality.”
All sentient beings within the five realms of existence shall come to experience the causes of various sufferings and joys;
if one can transform the causes that produce suffering, the Sugata perceives this clearly and knows it as it truly is.
All karmic actions, whether black or white, yield their respective retributions according to their causes;
like a wish-fulfilling gem held in the palm of the hand, the Sugata perceives and knows them exactly as they are.
Though the causes of various karmic retributions may be slight, the fruits obtained in the future shall be immeasurable;
or when immeasurable causes produce but a small fruit—the Sugata is able to know all such things exactly as they are.
Whether one is to realize the fruit of a śrāvaka, or is to realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha,
or is capable of attaining the power of unsurpassed, wondrous wisdom— the Sugata knows all such things truly and without remainder.
If an action is matured such that it is painful at the time of its cause, one should know as it truly is: this action will yield a pleasant fruit.
If an action is matured such that it is pleasant at the time of its cause, one should know as it truly is: it will yield a painful fruit.
Whether karma and its fruit both abide in suffering, or whether karma and its fruit both abide in happiness,
or whether the nature of the karma itself is the nature of the cause— the Sugata knows these as they truly are.
The fruits of suffering circulate through the three periods of time, and sentient beings transmigrate within the five destinies;
yet the most excellent and perfect wisdom of bodhi knows them all as they truly are, without any discrepancy.
“Śāriputra! This is called the second power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the diverse results of karma.

By virtue of its accomplishment, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the true lion’s roar in the midst of the great assembly, declaring: ‘I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel; among all the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, or Brahmas in all the worlds, none can turn it in accordance with the Dharma.’”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations of beings? Śāriputra!"

By means of the power of unsurpassed wisdom, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to know those classes of sentient beings and those individuals as they truly are: that their inclinations and understandings are not uniform, but diverse; and the Tathāgata is able to comprehend them all simultaneously.
Śāriputra! I shall further explain this to you in detail.

Whether those who undergo repeated existence dwell in desire and give rise to the understanding of hatred, or dwell in hatred and give rise to the understanding of desire, and so on up to dwelling in delusion and giving rise to the understanding of desire and hatred—the Tathāgata is able to know all such characteristics as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Whether a person subject to grasping dwells in unwholesome states and gives rise to unwholesome understanding, or dwells in wholesome dharmas and gives rise to wholesome understanding—the Tathāgata knows this as it truly is.

If a person of frequent rebirth abides in inferior means yet gives rise to a vast understanding, or abides in vast means yet gives rise to an inferior understanding; or if, by virtue of this understanding, they should abide in superior progress through inferior means, or by virtue of this understanding, they should abide in inferiority through superior means—the Tathāgata knows all this as it truly is.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Whether by means of such an understanding one will plant the seeds of wrong determination, or by means of such an understanding one will plant the seeds of right determination, or by means of such an understanding one will plant the seeds of right liberation—this too the Tathāgata knows as it truly is.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If by means of this understanding one is destined for the desire realm, or the form realm, or the formless realm; or if by means of this understanding one is destined for all three realms—this too the Tathāgata knows as it truly is.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If, through this understanding, one who is inclined toward the inferior portion should attain superior progress, or if one who has attained superior progress should abide in the inferior, the Tathāgata knows this also as it truly is.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If, by virtue of this understanding, one shall undergo various births and experience various kinds of enjoyments in future lives, the Tathāgata knows this as it truly is.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Whether by means of this understanding one will fall back from the summit, or by means of this understanding one plants the seeds of liberation—this too the Tathāgata knows as it truly is.
Having understood them thus, he extensively expounds the Dharma to sentient beings as is appropriate for each.
In this way, Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various understandings of others— which is inconceivable, boundless, limitless, and equal to space— is not a single [power].

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas heard that the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations of beings is like space and inconceivable, they accepted it with faith, revered it with sincerity, and were pure and free from doubt; they leaped for joy all the more, gave rise to profound gladness, and conceived a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The various understandings in the world, Past and present, are immeasurable;
The minds of those various understandings— The Teacher is able to comprehend them all.”
If there is one who understands through desire, they should further abide in aversion;
or appearing to abide in aversion, they should know the understanding through delusion as it truly is.
Abiding in delusion while giving rise to the understanding through desire, their mind is focused on the inconceivable.
The Teacher fully knows those who arise through various mixed and wandering courses;
he fully knows those who, through inferior means, give rise to vast understanding, or those who employ superior means.
Entering into false natures, and further entering into those states that are not [proper] destinations—
the liberation from the three realms and its understanding— the Tathāgata is able to know them all.
The various births and species, as well as the differences in their enjoyments, [he knows].
If one falls back from the summit, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings can know it.
Having known their various inclinations, the Guide teaches according to the Dharma;
this is the third power of a Buddha, which the most excellent sons of the Victor can believe in.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s third power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations of beings.

Because he has accomplished this, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the true lion’s roar in the midst of the great assembly, declaring: ‘I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel; no śramaṇas, brahmins, celestial Māras, or Brahmas in any world can turn it in accordance with the Dharma.’”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various elements? Śāriputra!"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of his unsurpassed power of wisdom, knows as they truly are all the various elements (*dhātu*) of the world.

Because of these elements, sentient beings in the world accumulate meritorious formations, accumulate non-meritorious formations, or accumulate immovable formations; or, because of these elements, they plant the seeds of renunciation. The Tathāgata knows such elements as these exactly as they are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element. How does he know such elements?
That is to say, knowing things as they truly are by means of internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness;
and so on, until one knows as they truly are the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
How are such elements as these to be known?
It is by knowing them as they truly are, through internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness.
Furthermore, it is by knowing the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element as they truly are.
How are such realms as these to be known? They are to be known as they truly are, because they are like the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*).

In this way, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are understood as they truly are, because they arise from pervasive conceptualization.

Furthermore, one knows the conditioned realm as it truly is because its characteristic is volitional construction; the unconditioned realm because its characteristic is the absence of volitional construction; the defiled realm because its characteristic is being led by afflictions; and the pure realm because its characteristic is natural luminosity and purity.

Furthermore, one knows as they truly are that the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dhātu*) has the characteristic of ignorance because it is contrary to principle, whereas the realm of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-dhātu*) has the characteristic of clear knowledge because it accords with principle;
thus, one can clearly comprehend all such realms.
Therefore, Śāriputra! If an element (*dhātu*) can establish the world, this element is that upon which the world relies and dwells.

Likewise, if an element can project [rebirth], if an element can bring about establishment, if an element can give rise to skillful means, if an element can produce desire, if an element can cause fervent application, or if an element can serve as a basis—Śāriputra! [all these are such elements].
Such realms as these are immeasurable and boundless, and the Tathāgata understands them exactly as they are.
Having understood them clearly, he extensively expounds the Dharma for sentient beings according to their needs and in accordance with the truth.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the single realm and various realms is inconceivable, boundless, and equal to space.
Should anyone seek the limit of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various realms, it would be no different from a person seeking the limit of space.

In this way, Śāriputra, when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various elements (nānādhātu-jñānabala) is like space and inconceivable, they accept it with faith, reverently uphold it with purity and without doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"All sentient beings in the world, Depending upon various realms,
As they wander according to their course— The Most Victorious One knows them all."
Meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable, as well as those conducive to renunciation—
having established oneself within such realms, one realizes the peace of nirvāṇa.
Whether it be the eye-element, the form-element, or the eye-consciousness-element...
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind— He fully knows all these elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, he knows the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) And the realm of mental consciousness;
That the internal and external realms are entirely empty— The Buddha knows this according to reality.
The earth element and the water element, the fire element and the wind element—these four elements share the same characteristic as space; thus one can know them all.
Whether it be the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, [one knows them all].
The Buddha knows, according to reality, that which arises from pervasive conceptualization.
Just as space is boundless, so too are the realms boundless;
the Buddha illuminates them all, yet he does not think, "I am able to know."
The various elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally without arising, and likewise there is no one who undergoes cessation;
this is called the realm of nirvāṇa, which the supreme person is able to know.
Just as the measure of space is boundless, so too is the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Through wisdom one understands the transformations within the various elements;
having known these diverse elements, one tames all sentient beings.
This is the fourth power of the Buddha, which the most excellent sons of the Buddha are able to believe in.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s fourth power of knowledge: the power of knowing various elements rather than a single element.

Because he has accomplished this power, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the true lion’s roar before the great assembly, declaring: ‘I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deity, Māra, or Brahmā in all the world can turn.’”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the various faculties rather than a single faculty? Śāriputra!"

By means of his unsurpassed power of wisdom, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to know things as they truly are; whether they be other sentient beings or persons subject to rebirth (*pudgala*), the Tathāgata can discern and fully comprehend all the various distinctions among their faculties.
Śāriputra! How are such characteristics as these to be known?
They are known by means of the thorough and universal discernment of faculties—namely, dull faculties, medium faculties, sharp faculties, superior faculties, and inferior faculties.

He is able to know when sentient beings give rise to extremely heavy greed, extremely heavy hatred, or extremely heavy delusion; such faculties as these are also known by the Tathāgata exactly as they are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

By virtue of following and discerning the faculties (*indriya*), the Tathāgata is able to know whether they give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion through conventional designation; or whether they give rise to subtle greed, hatred, and delusion; or whether they give rise to perverted greed, hatred, and delusion; or whether they give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion that have been subdued. Such characteristics as these are also known by the Tathāgata exactly as they are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Whether they be faculties produced from unwholesome causes, faculties produced from wholesome causes, faculties produced from immovable causes, or faculties produced from causes of renunciation—the Tathāgata knows these all as they truly are.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata knows as they truly are the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, and mind faculty; the female faculty, male faculty, and life faculty; the faculty of pleasure, faculty of pain, faculty of grief, faculty of joy, and faculty of equanimity; the faculty of faith, faculty of right effort, faculty of mindfulness, faculty of wisdom, and faculty of concentration; and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known. Such distinctions among these various faculties—the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata knows those faculties as they truly are: that because of the eye faculty one will abide in the ear faculty and not in the nose, tongue, or body faculties; or because of the ear faculty one will abide in the nose faculty; or because of the nose faculty one will abide in the tongue faculty; or because of the tongue faculty one will abide in the body faculty; or because of the body faculty one will abide in the eye faculty. The Tathāgata knows such faculties as these exactly as they are.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if there are sentient beings who abide in the faculty of generosity while practicing the means of ethical discipline, at that time the Tathāgata, by means of his knowledge of superior and inferior faculties, teaches them generosity."
If one abides in the faculty of ethical discipline and practices the skillful means of generosity, I teach them the precepts.
If one abides in the faculty of patience and practices the skillful means of diligence, I teach them the Dharma of patience.
If one abides in the faculty of right effort and practices the skillful means of patience, I teach them right effort.
