For those who abide in the faculty of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and employ the skillful means of cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*), one should teach them meditative concentration.
For those who abide in the faculty of wisdom and employ the skillful means of cultivating meditative concentration, one should teach them right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*).

In this manner, one should extensively explain how all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are to be understood according to reality through the distinctions among the faculties.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if there are sentient beings who abide in the faculties of a śrāvaka yet instead cultivate the skillful means of a pratyekabuddha, the Tathāgata, through his knowledge of the faculties, teaches them the inferior vehicle.
For those who abide in the faculties of a pratyekabuddha yet cultivate the skillful means of śrāvaka wisdom, he teaches the Middle Vehicle by means of the knowledge of their faculties.
For those who abide in the faculties of the Mahāyāna yet cultivate the skillful means of the wisdom of the two vehicles, he teaches the Mahāyāna by means of the knowledge of their faculties.
Those who abide in inferior faculties yet cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna are taught the two vehicles by means of the wisdom of their various faculties.
If sentient beings possess neither the capacity nor the signs of capacity, the Tathāgata knows them as they truly are—lacking capacity and being unfit vessels—and thus sets them aside.

If sentient beings possess capable faculties and the signs of capability, and the Tathāgata knows according to reality that they are capable vessels for the Dharma, he then earnestly and respectfully teaches the Dharma so that they may realize and enter it.
In this way, Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata thoroughly knows the ripening and non-ripening of the faculties of all sentient beings, as well as their transcendence and non-transcendence of the faculties.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata knows all the faculties of sentient beings as they truly are: he knows them as they abide in such characteristics, such skillful means, such faith and understanding, such original causes, such objects of focus, such continuities, and such ultimate consummations.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s various knowledges of the faculties are inconceivable, boundless, and limitless, equal to space. Should anyone wish to seek the limits of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the faculties, it would be no different from a person seeking the limit of space.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard that these faculties and powers are like space, they receive them with faith, uphold them with truth, and remain pure and free from doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound delight and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Honored One among all sentient beings has reached the further shore of the faculties; He thoroughly understands the mentalities, natures, and conducts of living beings.
According to what each being’s faculties can bear, The Lion among Men preaches the Dharma.”
Capable of being sustained by those of inferior, middling, and superior faculties, the Sugata’s supreme wisdom arises within those faculties;
having observed their minds as vessels for liberation, he who possesses the knowledge of conduct and wisdom teaches the Dharma.
If there is a person whose faculties are capable of being aroused, even down to the most subtle and continuous afflictions,
one who thoroughly understands all such faculties of that person will know their conduct and teach the Dharma accordingly.
If there are noble beings who possess roots of virtue, I shall extensively reveal [the Dharma] according to their diligence, faith, and aspirations;
furthermore, in accordance with the distinctions of their faculties, conduct, and characteristics, I shall explain the various supreme meanings, such as meditative concentration and wisdom.
If a person gives rise to faith and desire, the wise one teaches the path of purity according to their faculties;
having understood the various practices they undertake, he teaches them the supreme Dharma that transcends all suffering.
There are those who are firmly established in the roots of a Buddha’s bodhi, yet whose śrāvaka wisdom has been led astray by delusion;
for their sake, he teaches the Mahāyāna so that they may achieve perfect awakening—this is the fifth power of the Buddha, which is difficult to overcome.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s fifth power, the knowledge of the various faculties (*nānādhātujñānabala*).

By virtue of accomplishing this power, the Tathāgata rightly roars the lion’s roar in the great assembly, declaring: ‘I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, or Brahmā in all the world can turn according to the Dharma.’”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere? Śāriputra,"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by virtue of his unsurpassed power of wisdom, knows all pervasive conditioned phenomena as they truly are.
Śāriputra, how are such characteristics known?

This refers to being able to fully understand the nature of sentient beings, namely: the nature of those fixed in the right [path], the nature of those not fixed, and the nature of those fixed in the wrong [path].
Śāriputra, what is meant by "the nature of those fixed in the right [path]"?

This means that because they are born from the power of causes—the skillful means of previous lives—and from the opening of wisdom and the possession of sharp faculties, whether the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma for them or do not preach it, the Tathāgatas know those sentient beings as they truly are, including their past-life causes and conditions and their fitness as vessels for the Dharma; accordingly, they teach the Dharma so that these beings may swiftly attain liberation.
Śāriputra! What is meant by the nature of being indeterminate?

It is characterized by maturation through the power of external conditions; if one receives appropriate instruction and admonition, one may attain liberation, but if one does not receive appropriate instruction and admonition, one does not attain liberation.

The Tathāgata taught them the Dharma that accords with conditions and causes; having heard this true Dharma, those sentient beings practiced according to the principle and realized the fruit of liberation.
It is for the sake of such beings attaining their welfare and benefit that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world. Śāriputra,
what is meant by the nature of those fixed in the wrong way?

It refers to sentient beings whose nature is obscured by afflictions and who do not cultivate pure karma; whose consciousness is weak and whose ignorance is profound; who dwell within the net of false views and are not vessels for the True Dharma.
Whether the Tathāgata were to preach the Dharma for them or not, they would ultimately be incapable of realizing liberation.
The Tathāgata, knowing those sentient beings as he truly is—that they are not vessels for the Dharma—simply sets them aside.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

Out of compassion for these sentient beings and for the sake of benefiting them, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the armor of the great vow and enter the army of false views to teach, transform, and subdue them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, three types of greedy conduct:
greedy conduct arising from the perception of purity and beauty, greedy conduct arising from the perception of endearment, and greedy conduct arising from causes in previous lives.
Furthermore, one can discern three types of conduct arising from aversion:

conduct arising from aversion due to the perception of harm, conduct arising from aversion through detailed investigation, and conduct arising from aversion due to latent tendencies from previous lives.
Furthermore, one contemplates and understands three types of deluded conduct:
some deluded conduct arises from ignorance; some deluded conduct arises from the false view of a self-body; and some deluded conduct arises from doubt.
In this way, all Tathāgatas understand things as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata understands all conditioned phenomena as they truly are.
Both the painful and pleasant modes of practice can lead to swift penetration because the faculties are sharp.
Both the painful and pleasant modes of practice lead to slow penetration because the faculties are dull.
Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that the slow mode of practice leads to slow penetration because the object of focus is abandoned.
Slow progress with rapid penetration occurs because the path does not cease.
Rapid progress with slow penetration occurs because of courageous and decisive advancement.
Rapid progress with rapid penetration occurs because it is not of that [ordinary] nature.

Furthermore, as he knows them truly: there are some formations for which the power of discernment is perfected but not the power of cultivation; there are some formations for which the power of cultivation is perfected but not the power of discernment; there are some formations for which both the power of discernment and the power of cultivation are perfected; and there are some formations for which neither the power of discernment nor the power of cultivation is perfected.
The Tathāgata is able to understand all such characteristics exactly as they are.

Furthermore, he knows things as they truly are: there are some formations that are complete in faith and aspiration but incomplete in skillful means; there are some formations that are complete in skillful means but incomplete in faith and aspiration; there are some formations where both faith, aspiration, and skillful means are incomplete; and there are some formations where both faith, aspiration, and skillful means are complete—he is able to discern all such cases.

Furthermore, one knows things as they truly are: there are some formations whose bodily action is pure but not so their vocal or mental actions; there are some formations whose vocal action is pure but not so their bodily or mental actions; there are some formations whose mental action is pure but not so their bodily or vocal actions; there are some formations that are neither bodily, vocal, nor mental; and there are some formations that attain purity through body, speech, and mind.

Śāriputra! In this way, even regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of all sentient beings—whether they arise from transmigration, from non-transmigration, or from both transmigration and non-transmigration—the Tathāgata, by virtue of his unimpeded knowledge and vision, acts with respect to all such instances.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge in teaching the practice of all paths is inconceivable, boundless, limitless, and equal to space. When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that this power of knowledge is inconceivable like space, they accept it with faith, uphold it with truth, and remain pure and without doubt; they leap for joy even more intensely, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"The Sugata has realized all conditioned phenomena as they truly are; He can know the determinate causes within the nature of sentient beings, As well as the signs of maturation for those who are indeterminate, And the factors corresponding to the causes of their faculties."
All conditioned phenomena are associated with the three kinds of greed, as well as combined with the three kinds of hatred and delusion;
these formations are associated with boundless and vast afflictions—the Great Teacher knows them truly as they are, through their conditions and causes.
Those who practice asceticism with sharp faculties, and those who practice this same path with dull faculties;
those who practice the path of ease with both sharp and dull faculties—the Great Refuge of the World knows them all as they truly are.
Some possess dull faculties and dull cultivation; some have dull faculties but sharp cultivation;
some have swift faculties but slow cultivation; and some possess both swiftness, yet it is not their inherent nature.
Some formations arise through discernment, not produced by the power of cultivating the path;
some arise through cultivation, not through discernment; they arise together, distinct yet mutually associated.
Some conditioned phenomena proceed through faith and aspiration, being pure yet not purified by skillful means;
some are the reverse, or neither, nor both—O Buddha, the Omniscient One, clearly understands them all.
Furthermore, there are those who purify their physical actions, yet neither their speech nor their mental actions are pure;
or again, there are those whose speech and bodies are pure, yet the essence of their minds is not pure.
Some have minds that are always pure, yet their two activities of body and speech are not pure;
others have pure speech and pure minds, yet their activity of body has never been pure.

Whether body, speech, or mind be pure or impure, and whether conditioned phenomena be in flux or in cessation—the All-Knowing One perceives them as they truly are; this is the sixth power of the Tathāgata.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s sixth power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere.
By virtue of this power, the Tathāgata, abiding in the exalted position of a Sage, turns the Great Brahma-wheel, such that no one can turn it in accordance with the Dharma as he does.”

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the defilement and purification of the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), samādhis, and samāpattis? "

Śāriputra! By means of his unsurpassed power of wisdom, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows as they truly are all the dharmas of defilement and purification involved in the arising of the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), samādhis, and samāpattis, whether belonging to himself or others.
Śāriputra! How are such characteristics as these to be known?
They are to be known as they truly are: that it is by means of causes and conditions that all sentient beings are made subject to defilement.
Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that all sentient beings can be purified by means of causes and conditions.
Śāriputra, what are the causes and what are the conditions that bring about defilement?
Śāriputra! Due to improper mental attention as the cause and ignorance as the condition, sentient beings give rise to affliction.

Thus, with ignorance as the cause and volitional formations as the condition; with volitional formations as the cause and consciousness as the condition; with consciousness as the cause and name-and-form as the condition; with name-and-form as the cause and the six sense bases as the condition; with the six sense bases as the cause and contact as the condition; with contact as the cause and feeling as the condition; with feeling as the cause and craving as the condition; with craving as the cause and clinging as the condition; with clinging as the cause and existence as the condition; with existence as the cause and birth as the condition; with birth as the cause and old age and death as the condition; with afflictions as the cause and various karmas as the condition; with various views as the cause and craving as the condition; and with latent tendencies as the cause and the various fetters as the condition.
Śāriputra, it is through such causes and conditions as these that sentient beings give rise to defilement.
The Tathāgata understands these characteristics exactly as they are.
Śāriputra! By what cause and by what condition can one bring about purification? Śāriputra!

There are two causes and two conditions that can bring about the purification of all sentient beings: namely, the compliant voice of others and internal correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), as well as *śamatha* focused on a single object and the skillful means of *vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, there are two causes and two conditions that can bring about purification: namely, the knowledge of non-coming and the knowledge of non-going.
Furthermore, there are two causes and two conditions that can bring about purification: namely, the contemplation of non-arising and the realization of right concentration.
Furthermore, there are two causes and two conditions that can bring about purification: namely, the fulfillment of practice and the realization of liberation from both knowledge and ignorance.
Furthermore, there are two causes and two conditions that can bring about purification: namely, the cultivation of the doors of liberation and the wisdom of natural liberation.
Furthermore, there are two causes and two conditions that can bring about purification, namely: the realization of the truths and the attainment of the truths.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata knows as they truly are these various causes and conditions by which all sentient beings may be purified.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the defiled spheres of sentient beings and the purified spheres of sentient beings; he knows those whose defiled spheres enter into purified spheres, and those whose purified spheres enter into defiled spheres—all such things are due to his observation according to reality."
Some enter into defiled realms from defiled realms, while others enter into pure realms from pure realms; all such occurrences arise from the grasping of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
The Tathāgata turns the wheel of knowledge therein as it truly is.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, through knowing things as they truly are, the Tathāgata turns [the wheel] amidst the various distinctions of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), such as: being free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, possessing directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful, he fully attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

The Tathāgata, having dwelt in the first dhyāna, emerges from the meditative absorption of cessation; likewise, he even enters the meditative absorption of cessation and emerges from the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata, through knowing things as they truly are, enters the eight liberations either in direct order, or in reverse order, or in both direct and reverse order, or in an alternating manner.
Śāriputra! What are these eight liberations? They are as follows: perceiving forms while possessing form is the first liberation;

with the internal perception of no form, perceiving external forms is the second liberation; attaining the liberation of purity, or arising in the liberation of purity regarding the nature of purity, is the third liberation; the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space is the fourth liberation; the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness is the fifth liberation; the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness is the sixth liberation; the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the seventh liberation; and the cessation of perception and feeling is the eighth liberation.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

By means of their knowledge of reality as it is, the Tathāgatas may abide in a single samādhi and yet manifest other samādhis and samāpattis, and further manifest various modes of contemplation; yet, the Tathāgatas never become confused regarding these meditative concentrations.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not enter samādhi by taking a specific samādhi as their object; rather, they may accomplish all other samādhis by relying upon a single samādhi, or they may enter all samādhis universally without even arising from a single samādhi.

Furthermore, the minds of all Tathāgatas abide eternally in meditative concentration without shifting to successive objects of perception; moreover, no state of non-concentrated mind can be found in any Tathāgata.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, dwell in a profound and subtle concentration such that no one is able to observe the samādhi attained by a Tathāgata.

Śāriputra! The samādhis attained by śrāvakas are eclipsed by the samādhis of pratyekabuddhas; the samādhis attained by pratyekabuddhas are eclipsed by the samādhis of bodhisattvas; the samādhis attained by bodhisattvas are eclipsed by the samādhis of all buddhas; yet the samādhis attained by the Tathāgata are beyond being eclipsed.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgatas possess a wisdom that cannot be eclipsed, which is constantly manifest and active. Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata understands this as it truly is; through such instruction and such admonition, he is able to give rise to the various samādhis of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, by means of such instructions and admonitions, they are able to give rise to the sublime samādhis of the bodhisattvas.
Having known this as it truly is, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, provide these instructions and admonitions.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the origination of the defilement and purification of dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti is inconceivable, boundless, limitless, and equal to space. Should anyone wish to seek the limit of the Tathāgata’s power of concentration, it would be no different from someone seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that these powers of concentration and wisdom are inconceivable like space, they accept them with faith, uphold them with truth, and remain pure and free from doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"It is from this that sentient beings give rise to defilement, and it is from this that sentient beings attain purification.
Having understood this, the Great Hero extensively proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma."
Due to that cause of irrational attention, defilement arises with ignorance as its condition;
furthermore, with ignorance as the cause, volitional formations arise as conditions, and so on, proceeding through successive stages until all sufferings are produced.
Improper mental attention and ignorance are the roots from which the factors of existence arise;
having realized this as it truly is, the Buddhas proclaim the sublime Dharma according to what is appropriate for each being.
The root of all defilements is what is called karmic activity and ignorance;
from these conditions, the various consciousnesses arise, and thus, through this succession, all forms of suffering are produced.
Through the sounds spoken by him which accord with reality, and through the internal cultivation of correct contemplation—
by virtue of these two causes and two conditions, all sentient beings realize purity.
Through the cause of śamatha according to reality, and through the condition of vipaśyanā,
the Great Teacher understands exactly how these sentient beings realize liberation.
The practitioner dwells securely in pure ethical discipline, observing that all phenomena are empty and quiescent;
having well cultivated the gates of liberation, they remain far removed from the suffering of confinement within the realms of existence.
All these pure practices of all sentient beings, As well as the gates of liberation—
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— The Sugatas know as they truly are, And reveal them according to the faculties [of beings].
The Pratyekabuddhas, the most excellent, and the Śrāvakas traverse the meditative absorptions in both forward and reverse order;
the Tathāgata has declared their realization to be like a poisonous thorn or an enemy.
The concentration and liberation realized by all Buddhas are ultimately free from enmity and the thorns of affliction;
know that this seventh power of the Tathāgata cannot be overcome by any other realization.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s seventh power of knowledge regarding all meditative absorptions.

By virtue of attaining this power, the Tathāgata himself claims to occupy the exalted position of a Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel, such that no one can turn it in accordance with the Dharma as he does.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the realization of the recollection of past lives? Śāriputra,"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by virtue of his unsurpassed power of wisdom, knows all things exactly as they are according to what he recollects. Śāriputra,

the Tathāgata thus knows exactly as it is the immeasurable past lives of all sentient beings, whether himself or others— be they one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, or even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of births— all of which he knows through recollection.

Furthermore, through recollection, they know the dissolution of an eon, the formation of an eon, or both the formation and dissolution of an eon; or they know immeasurable eons of dissolution, immeasurable eons of formation, or immeasurable eons of both formation and dissolution; or again, through recollection, they are able to fully comprehend a hundred koṭis of eons, up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons.

Furthermore, he is able to recollect: "In previous lives, in such and such places, I had such a name, such a clan, such a lineage, such food and drink, such a complexion, such marks, such features, such a lifespan, such a duration of stay, and such experiences of suffering and pleasure."
"In such and such places I passed away and was reborn in such and such places; again, from such and such places I passed away and was born here.
In this way, whether concerning myself or others, including all their physical forms, characteristics, locations, and lineages, I am able to recollect and know all these immeasurable past lives.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, that all sentient beings come to be born here according to their past causes; having known these causes, he teaches the Dharma to them accordingly.

Furthermore, one is able to discern the mental continuums of all sentient beings throughout past lives: how, following this mind, another mind arose in relation to such an object; and how, due to the incompleteness of those conditions, that mind ceased.
All such things, the Tathāgata knows through recollecting them exactly as they are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a single sentient being were to produce a succession of thoughts, following one after another in immediate sequence with such characteristics, even various explanations for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not exhaustively describe them.

Just as the mental characteristics of one sentient being are such, so too are the minds of all sentient beings; the Tathāgata, according to all those various mental characteristics, is able to know them all truly and accurately through mindfulness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Even if the Tathāgata were to speak, based on the successive states of mind of all sentient beings, for as many *koṭi* eons as there are until the end of time, he could not exhaustively describe them; yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata remains inexhaustible.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past lives is inconceivable, peerless, equal to the unequaled, immeasurable and innumerable, and beyond description; moreover, it cannot be said that it has any limit or end."
"Śāriputra! By means of the Buddha’s spiritual power, the Tathāgata empowers sentient beings to recollect their past lives and addresses them, saying:

'You should now recollect your past lives; you have already planted the roots of these various wholesome dharmas—whether before a Buddha, a śrāvaka, or a pratyekabuddha, or by planting roots of goodness within the True Dharma. You must recollect all such roots of goodness.'"
"Those sentient beings, through the power of the Tathāgata, know all this by recollecting it. Śāriputra!

Thus, the Tathāgata, having empowered those sentient beings with his Buddha-magical power so that they may know the objects of their immeasurable roots of goodness from past lives, then preaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate."

Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who have attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and who seek liberation according to their inclinations and understandings—whether they rely on the Śrāvaka-yāna, or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are through his power of the knowledge of recollecting [past lives].
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the realization of the recollection of past lives is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless, equal to space. Anyone who seeks the limit of the Tathāgata’s recollection of past lives is no different from a person seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that this power of knowledge regarding past lives is inconceivable like space, they accept it with faith and revere it with truth, free from confusion or doubt, even to the point of leaping for joy and conceiving a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Throughout inconceivable nayutas of koṭis of eons, The bright lamps that illuminate the world follow all thoughts;
They also recall past lives of themselves and others, As clearly as one observes five myrobalan fruits in the palm of the hand."
Recalling names, clans, forms, and distinctions, Abiding through the end of their lifespans across all realms of birth,
Seeing that sentient beings possess such causes, He knows the proper time and teaches the Dharma accordingly.
All the infinite past ages, and all the mental states and mental factors of sentient beings—
how these minds arise in immediate succession and how they are produced— the Supreme One of Great Wisdom fully understands them all.
The Sugata thoroughly knows the mental continuum of a single sentient being throughout the succession of past lives;
even in tens of millions of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could not exhaustively describe its limits.
Even throughout billions of kalpas until the end of time, They expound the past deeds of all sentient beings;
Yet their equalizing wisdom remains inexhaustible— This is called the ocean-like measure of the Buddhas' wisdom.

All sentient beings possess virtuous faith and aspiration; having already made offerings to all the World-Honored Ones, they are empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual strength, causing them to take the past as their object and cultivate pure conduct.
The Great Master, recollecting what they have received— The various meritorious deeds practiced in the past;
And recollecting the wisdom of the Three Vehicles in which they abide— The ground upon which they rely for non-retrogressive liberation.
The Sugata praises the wisdom of the past, which is boundless; the realm of all sentient beings is inconceivable.
With boundless renown, the eighth power is that which the eldest son of the Most Victorious One is able to believe and accept.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s eighth power of knowledge regarding past abodes.

By virtue of attaining this power, the Tathāgata declares himself to occupy the position of the Honored One among Sages and turns the Great Brahma-wheel, which no one else is able to turn in accordance with the Dharma.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge resulting from the realization of the supernormal power of the divine eye? Śāriputra!"

With the power of unsurpassed wisdom, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a pure divine eye that transcends that of humans; he observes sentient beings as they die here and are born there—whether inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly—and according to their habitual karma, whether they go to a happy destination or a miserable destination. Such signs as these the Tathāgata perceives clearly and understands as they truly are.

Furthermore, he is able to know, as they truly are, the karmic actions performed by all sentient beings: that such-and-such a sentient being has accomplished misconduct of body, accomplished misconduct of speech, and accomplished misconduct of mind; that they have slandered the noble ones and given rise to various wrong views. Because they have taken up the causes and conditions of such karma born of wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the evil destinies—either being reborn in hell, or among animals, or in the realm of hungry ghosts.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows that there are sentient beings who have accomplished excellent conduct of body, accomplished excellent conduct of speech, and accomplished excellent conduct of mind; who do not revile the noble ones and cultivate right view. Because they have taken up such karma and causes based on right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, they go to the various happy realms, or are reborn in the blissful worlds of the heavens.

Furthermore, with his pure divine eye, the Tathāgata beholds the various appearances of the Buddha-worlds in the ten directions—worlds that cannot be described, exceeding in number the sands of the Ganges, reaching to the limits of space, and exhausting the measure of the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, he may see some Buddha-fields that are ablaze with fire; or he may see fields that are currently being destroyed; or he may see fields that are currently being formed.
Furthermore, he clearly perceives all sentient beings at the time of death and the time of birth.

He may also clearly perceive great bodhisattvas descending from Tuṣita Heaven into their mothers’ wombs; or he may clearly perceive them emerging from the womb; or he observes them walking seven steps in each direction; or he clearly perceives them entering the inner palace; or he sees them renouncing the world and practicing asceticism; or he sees the Buddhas awakening to great bodhi; or he clearly perceives them turning the great wheel of Dharma; or he clearly perceives them relinquishing the formations of life and entering great parinirvāṇa.

Or again, they may see the entire assembly of śrāvakas ultimately entering parinirvāṇa; or again, they may see all pratyekabuddhas manifesting various supernormal powers and entering nirvāṇa as a reward for the merit of pure giving.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cannot be seen by ordinary sight, yet they are seen by the Tathāgata’s divine eye; they cannot be seen by the eyes of those non-Buddhist seers possessing the five supernormal powers, nor can they be seen by the eyes of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas; all such beings are fully visible to the divine eye of every Tathāgata.

In this way, there are subtle beings of invisible form, the size of a chariot wheel; when the Tathāgata observes them with his divine eye, they exceed in number all the humans and devas in the trichiliocosm.
All such things, being immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, the Tathāgata is able to see clearly and exactly as they are.
Śāriputra, with his pure divine eye, the Tathāgata observes the natures of all sentient beings in immeasurable Buddha-fields: which sentient beings are those to be transformed by the Tathāgata?
What kind of sentient beings are those who are tamed only after having seen the Tathāgata?

At that time, the Tathāgata, perceiving their capacity for benefit according to their needs, causes them to attain realization while standing before them; this is something that other sentient beings cannot know.
In this way, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting of the realization through recollection by means of the divine eye is inconceivable, limitless, and equal to space. Anyone who seeks the limit of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting of the divine eye is no different from a person seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When the bodhisattva mahāsattvas hear that these powers are thus inconceivable and like space, they believe, accept, and reverently uphold them, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

“The Sugata’s divine eye is pure and stainless; Through the cultivation of pure karma for immeasurable eons, The Most Victorious One thereby beholds the ten directions, And all the stainless, inconceivable Buddha-lands.”
Whether destroying or forming, or both forming and destroying, even until the arising and abiding of blazing fires;
whether there is a Buddha dwelling therein or no Buddha, the Eyes of the Self-Existent Honored One can see them all.
The nature of sentient beings is vast and inconceivable, Including those with form and those without form;
Whether they fall into the evil realms or are born in the happy realms, The eyes of the Self-Arisen Honored One can see them all.
Whether many koṭis of Buddhas are currently present, or whether Tathāgatas manifest entry into nirvāṇa,
as well as pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas— the Sovereign of Self-Arisen Wisdom can see them all with his eyes.
Whether they be bodhisattvas acting for the benefit of sentient beings, or those practicing the sublime conduct near perfect enlightenment,
dwelling in the unobstructed state of all Tathāgatas— the natural Teachers can see them all.
The Sugata’s eye is thus stainless, able to see all sentient beings, however subtle;
this ninth power of vision is inconceivable, understood and believed only by the most supreme and wise.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s ninth power of knowledge, the divine eye.
By virtue of this power, he declares of himself: ‘I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel, which no one in any world can turn in accordance with the Dharma.’”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the realization of the exhaustion of the outflows? Śāriputra!"

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of his unsurpassed power of wisdom, knows as it truly is that the outflows are exhausted and he is free from outflows; with mind liberated and wisdom liberated, he has personally realized and dwells in the fulfillment of spontaneous super-knowledge.
He knows it as it truly is: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows is pure, stainless, radiant, and perfectly illuminating, having forever severed all habitual tendencies of continuity.
Although those of the Śrāvaka vehicle have exhausted the outflows (*āsrava*), they can only eliminate a small portion of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Although those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle have likewise exhausted the outflows and can also eliminate a small portion of their habitual tendencies, they remain devoid of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and various forms of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

Only the Tathāgata has forever exhausted all outflows and possesses all aspects of the subtle and wondrous Buddha-dharma; having severed all habitual tendencies of continuity, he is observed by fearless eloquence embraced by great compassion, which no sentient beings in any world can eclipse or surpass, remaining in constant, perfect, and non-differentiated correspondence within a single moment of mind.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has no karma and no afflictions, and is free from the habitual tendencies of lapsing in dignified deportment. Śāriputra!

Just as the pure void does not coexist with any smoke, dust, clouds, or mist, so too the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows does not coexist with any afflictions or habitual tendencies.

Śāriputra! After the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have dwelled in such knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, they are further able to teach the dharma of the exhaustion of outflows and the dharma of the permanent severance of all grasping to all sentient beings who possess outflows and grasping.

All the outflows and grasping of all sentient beings arise from false and pervasive conceptualization. Having observed this as it truly is, the Tathāgata—desiring that these no longer arise for anyone—teaches the Dharma through various appropriate parables so that they may know the outflows to be false. By knowing this, they do not grasp at phenomena; because they do not grasp, they are able to enter parinirvāṇa ultimately.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the arising and ceasing of all outflows (āsrava) of all sentient beings, and the course of those outflows; having known this, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.

In this way, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the realization of the destruction of the outflows is inconceivable, boundless, and equal to space. Were there anyone who sought the limit of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows, it would be no different from a person seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge in realizing the exhaustion of outflows is inconceivable like space, they accept it with faith and venerate it with truth; their minds become pure, free from confusion and doubt, and they leap for joy with even greater intensity, giving rise to a sense of wonder and deep gladness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Guide’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is stainless, Immeasurable, vast, pure, and unobstructed.
Because he has accomplished such a tenth power, He proclaims the sublime Bodhi of tranquility."
The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows of the śrāvakayāna followers is bound by limited habitual tendencies;
the Great Teacher, supreme among men, has reduced immeasurable fetters and habits to ashes.
There are those who have realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, yet they are devoid of great compassion, talent, and eloquence;
only the Bhagavān, whose outflows are exhausted, possesses great compassion, talent, and eloquence that are immeasurable.
The Buddhas abide in the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, fully understanding that sentient beings grasp at the signs of outflows—
all of which arise from false dharmas— and that these beings have not yet realized the course of this true principle.
The Tathāgata, arising from compassion, has expounded the dharmas of impermanence, impurity, and non-self;
those who contemplate all dharmas as empty and devoid of intrinsic nature shall realize the tranquil ground of the Tathāgata.
There is no self, no life-principle, no person, no individual, no manava, and no experiencer;
these are false notions that pervade all phenomena. Arising with great compassion, he teaches so that they may be liberated.
The Sugata’s compassion is free from weariness; his true wisdom flows constantly without loss.
By means of these most excellent and perpetual skillful means, he reveals the sublime Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings.
The tenth power, which can subdue the arguments of others, is boundless and equal to space;
because the World-Honored One eternally abides in these ten powers, he constantly turns the peerless Wheel of Dharma in the world.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s tenth power, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.

By virtue of accomplishing this power, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, declares of himself: ‘I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage; amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar and turn the Great Brahma Wheel, which no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, or brahmās in all the world can turn in accordance with the Dharma.’”

In this way, Śāriputra, because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that the qualities of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, they accept and faithfully uphold the ten powers of the Tathāgata; their minds are pure, free from delusion and doubt, and they leap for joy with profound gladness, conceiving a sense of wonder.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 38 [and] Volume 39.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Twelfth Assembly of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Part Five: Chapter Four, Part Three, "The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the inconceivable fearlessness of the Tathāgata, accept it with faith and veneration, such that his mind is pure, free from delusion and doubt, and he leaps for joy with deep gladness, conceiving a sense of wonder?"
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses four kinds of inconceivable fearlessnesses.

Because he has accomplished these four fearlessnesses, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, declares himself to occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage amidst the great assembly; he truly roars the lion’s roar and turns the Great Brahma-wheel, which no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, or brahmās in all the world can turn in accordance with the Dharma.
Śāriputra! What are called the four fearlessnesses? Śāriputra!
Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained unsurpassed power of knowledge, he declares himself among the great assembly to be a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Within this world, including its gods, no one is seen who can stand before the Tathāgata and maintain such a proposition as:
"You have not attained perfect enlightenment regarding these dharmas."
"Śāriputra! Why is the Tathāgata called 'Perfectly Awakened One' (Samyaksaṃbuddha)? Śāriputra!"

The Tathāgata is able to attain perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena as equal; there is nothing that is not equal. Whether they be the phenomena of ordinary beings, the phenomena of the noble ones, the phenomena of the Buddhas, the phenomena of those in training, the phenomena of those beyond training, the phenomena of the solitary realizers, or the phenomena of the bodhisattvas—they are all equally equal.

Whether they be mundane dharmas or supramundane dharmas, whether they be with fault or without fault, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—all such dharmas as these the Tathāgata is able to perfectly awaken to with equanimity; for this reason, he is called the Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
Śāriputra! What is called the nature of equality? Śāriputra!

The intrinsic nature of all views is equal in essence to emptiness; the intrinsic nature of all marks is equal in essence to signlessness; the intrinsic nature of the three realms is equal in essence to wishlessness; the intrinsic nature of arising phenomena is equal in essence to non-arising; the intrinsic nature of conditioned formations is equal in essence to the unconditioned; the intrinsic nature of originating phenomena is equal in essence to non-origination; the intrinsic nature of the essence of craving is equal in essence to non-craving; the intrinsic nature of the three times is equal in essence to suchness; the intrinsic nature of ignorance and the craving for existence is equal in essence to clear knowledge and liberation; and the intrinsic nature of the cyclic flow of birth and death is equal in essence to the tranquility of nirvana.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata is able to attain perfect enlightenment regarding the equality of all phenomena; therefore, the Tathāgata is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

This fearlessness of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; furthermore, taking great compassion as its skillful means, it is the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of true reality, not a nature that is otherwise, an unchanging nature, a nature without concealment, a nature without fear, a nature without retreat, and a nature without contention. Because of these qualities, it illuminates the great assembly, causing them to be joyful, with their entire bodies feeling at ease and comfort, and giving rise in their minds to pure faith, leaping with exuberant joy.
Śāriputra! Among the sentient beings of the world, there is none who can give rise to opposition or contention against the Tathāgata’s fearlessness. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s fearlessness cannot be contested, it is equal in nature to the dharmadhātu;
it flows forth and pervades all worlds, such that nothing can obstruct or harm it.

Śāriputra! Just as the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment regarding all extremely profound, subtle, and difficult-to-know phenomena with fearlessness, so too does the Tathāgata, abiding in great compassion, reveal the sublime Dharma to those sentient beings through various vocal expressions and various Dharma gates; if they can rely upon this to practice the conduct of seclusion, they will swiftly reach the end of suffering.

If there are sentient beings who are not actually Great Teachers yet claim to be Great Teachers, or who are not Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones yet claim to be Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones, they shall all be eclipsed by the inconceivable fearlessness of the Tathāgata; he shall cause their arrogance to shatter and drive them to flee far away.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s fearlessness is inconceivable, boundless, and limitless, like space. Should anyone wish to seek the limits of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness, it would be no different from a person seeking the limits of space.

Śāriputra! When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear the Tathāgata speak of this inconceivable fearlessness, they receive it with faith, accept it with truth, and follow it with purity and without doubt; they leap for joy and conceive a sense of wonder.
Śāriputra! This is called the first fearlessness of a perfectly awakened one.
Because the Tathāgata has achieved this fearlessness, he utters the true lion’s roar in the great assembly and turns the Great Brahma Wheel, which no one in all the worlds can ever turn.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the power of unsurpassed wisdom, he declares within the great assembly: 'I have now exhausted all outflows (āsrava). Within this world of gods and humans, no one is able to establish a discourse in accordance with the Dharma before the Tathāgata, saying:
"You still possess such outflows that have not been exhausted. "
"Śāriputra! What is the nature of the Tathāgata’s exhaustion of outflows? Śāriputra!"
The Tathāgata is perfectly liberated in mind from the flood of desire, because he has forever severed all habitual tendencies of greedy conduct;
the Tathāgata is perfectly liberated in mind from the flood of existence, because he has forever severed all habitual tendencies of hateful conduct;
the Tathāgata is perfectly liberated in mind from the flood of ignorance, because he has forever severed all habitual tendencies of deluded conduct.
The Tathāgata is well-liberated in mind from the flow of views, because he has forever severed all afflictions, activities, and habitual tendencies.
For this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata’s outflows are exhausted.

Śāriputra! Such a teaching of the Dharma relies upon conventional truth and is not the ultimate truth. Within the ultimate truth, there is not a single dharma that stands before noble wisdom which can be fully known, permanently abandoned, cultivated, or realized.

Why is this? Śāriputra, that which is called "exhaustion" is never anything other than the ultimate exhaustion of the nature of exhaustion itself; it is not designated as "exhaustion" by virtue of being a counteragent.
The nature of reality as it is is exhausted.

Because the nature of reality as it is is exhausted, there is no dharma that can be exhausted; because no dharma can be exhausted, this is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Being unconditioned, there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor is there any abiding.

Therefore it is said: whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains eternally constant, and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) remains eternally constant.
Within this very state, noble wisdom functions; though it functions in this way, there is neither functioning nor returning.
Śāriputra! Because of this Dharma-gate, there are no outflows (*āsrava*), nor is there any exhaustion of outflows to be found.
Thus, having abided in great compassion, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the exhaustion of outflows to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s fearlessness is inconceivable.

Furthermore, taking great compassion as his skillful means, he is true suchness, equality, the nature of reality, the nature of suchness, not the nature of non-suchness, unchanging nature, the nature of having no concealment, the nature of having no fear, the nature of having no retreat, and the nature of having no contention. Because of these qualities, he illuminates the great assembly, enabling them to be joyful and physically refreshed, their minds giving rise to pure faith, and leaping with exultation."
Śāriputra! Among the sentient beings of the world, there is none who can give rise to opposition or contention against the Tathāgata’s fearlessness. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata’s fearlessness cannot be contested, it abides in the equality of true suchness within the nature of the dharma-realm; it is disseminated and pervades all worlds, and nothing can obstruct or harm it.

Thus, having accomplished these inconceivable, immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sublime dharmas, the Tathāgata—with a mind perfumed by great compassion—teaches the dharma for the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*) to all sentient beings, desiring that they forever sever those outflows.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s fearlessness is inconceivable, boundless, and limitless, like space. If there were anyone who sought the limit of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness, it would be no different from a person seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear the Tathāgata speak of this inconceivable fearlessness, they accept it with faith, reverently uphold it with purity and without doubt, even giving rise to thoughts of its wondrous rarity.
Śāriputra! This is called the second fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of the outflows.

Because he has accomplished this fearlessness, the Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, rightly roars the lion’s roar, declaring: "I occupy the supreme position of the Great Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel, which no one in any world can ever turn."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the power of unsurpassed wisdom, he proclaims these words in the great assembly:
'I declare that obstructive dharmas will certainly constitute obstructions.'"
"In this regard, no one in the world of gods and humans is able to establish a discourse in accordance with the Dharma before the Tathāgata, saying:
'The obstructive dharmas you have described are incapable of acting as obstructions.'"
"Śāriputra! What are called the dharmas that act as obstacles? Śāriputra!"
It is said that there is one dharma capable of acting as an obstacle.
What is this one dharma?
It is the lack of purity of mind.
Furthermore, there are two things that can act as obstacles, namely: lack of shame and lack of dread of blame.
Furthermore, there are three things that can act as obstacles, namely: misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.

Furthermore, there are four factors that act as obstacles: acting what should not be done out of desire, acting what should not be done out of hatred, acting what should not be done out of delusion, and acting what should not be done out of fear.
Furthermore, there are five things that can act as obstacles: namely, killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants.

Furthermore, there are six things that can act as obstacles: namely, lack of reverence for the Buddha’s enlightenment, lack of reverence for the Dharma, lack of reverence for the Saṅgha, lack of reverence for the discipline (vinaya), lack of reverence for meditative concentration (samādhi), and lack of reverence for established designations.
Furthermore, there are seven factors that act as obstacles: namely, pride, superior pride, supreme pride, overweening pride, false pride, inferior pride, and the pride of "I am."
Furthermore, there are eight factors that can act as obstacles. What are these eight?
They are: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
Furthermore, there are nine things that can act as obstacles. What are these nine? They are:

performing acts that are unbeneficial, distressing, and harmful toward my own person in the past, future, and present; performing acts that are unbeneficial, distressing, and harmful toward those dear to me in the past, future, and present; and performing acts that are beneficial, distressing, and harmful toward those not dear to me in the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that can act as obstacles, namely the ten unwholesome paths of action.

Therefore, these ten kinds of dharmas are briefly described as being able to act as obstacles; and because he wishes to bring them to rest, to pacify them, and to permanently sever such obstructing dharmas, the Tathāgata expounds the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

Śāriputra! All fetters associated with mental engagements that contravene the Dharma, whether they arise from dwelling in the contemplation of the relish of phenomena, being associated with perversions, turning away from renunciation, attachment through craving and views, or clinging to flavors, as well as all bodily, verbal, and mental actions based upon such things—all these signs the Tathāgata fully knows to be obstacles.
Having understood this, they describe it as a phenomenon that acts as an obstacle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, this fearlessness of the Tathāgata is inconceivable;

with great compassion as its skillful means, it is true suchness, equality, the nature of reality, the nature of suchness, not otherwise than suchness, unchanging, unrevealed, fearless, undaunted, and non-contentious. Because of these qualities, it illuminates the great assembly, causing them to be joyful, their entire bodies to feel at ease, and their minds to give rise to pure faith, leaping with exultation and delight.
Śāriputra! Among the sentient beings of the world, there is none who can oppose or dispute the Tathāgata’s fearlessness. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s fearlessness cannot be contested,
it abides in the nature of equality within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), pervading and filling all worlds, such that no one can oppose or harm it.

Thus, although he has accomplished the wondrous Dharma—which is immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, peerless, and inexpressible—the Tathāgata, with great compassion permeating his mind, teaches the obstructive dharmas to all sentient beings, desiring to cause them to cease, become tranquil, and forever sever those obstructive dharmas.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s fearlessness is inconceivable, boundless, and limitless, like space. Should anyone wish to seek the limit of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness, it would be no different from a person seeking the limit of space.

Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear the Tathāgata speak of this inconceivable fearlessness that is like space, they accept it with faith, revere it with sincerity, and are pure and free from doubt, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
Śāriputra! This is called the third fearlessness regarding the teaching of obstructive dharmas.
Because the Tathāgata has accomplished this fearlessness, he rightly roars the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Great Brahma Wheel, which no one in any world can ever turn.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the power of unsurpassed wisdom, he proclaims these words amidst the great assembly:
'I declare that this is the noble departure, the cultivated path that leads to the complete exhaustion of suffering;'"
"If sentient beings practice this path, they will certainly attain liberation.
Regarding this, no one in the world of gods and humans is able to establish a formal argument before the Tathāgata, saying:
"The path you have taught cannot lead to liberation."
"Śāriputra! What is called the noble path of deliverance? Śāriputra!"
What is called the one path leading to the right goal is that which can bring sentient beings ultimate purity.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that can bring sentient beings ultimate liberation: namely, śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas that can lead to deliverance, namely: the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Furthermore, there are four dharmas that can lead to deliverance, namely: the application of mindfulness directed toward the body, the application of mindfulness directed toward feelings, the application of mindfulness directed toward the mind, and the application of mindfulness directed toward phenomena.

Furthermore, there are five factors that can lead to liberation: namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Furthermore, there are six factors that can lead to liberation: namely, mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment, and mindfulness of the devas.

Furthermore, there are seven factors that lead to deliverance: namely, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

Furthermore, there are eight factors that lead to liberation, namely the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Furthermore, there are nine kinds of fundamental factors of gratification that can lead to renunciation: namely, gratification, joy, tranquility, bliss, samādhi, knowledge and vision according to reality, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that can lead to deliverance, namely the ten paths of wholesome action.
In this way, the Tathāgata has revealed to all sentient beings the noble path of deliverance as it truly is.

Śāriputra! All the various factors conducive to enlightenment that are correct and wholesome—whether they correspond to the aggregate of ethical discipline, or to the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, or correspond to the noble truths—these are called the practices capable of leading to deliverance.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which is capable of leading to transcendence is called "right practice.
As for what is meant by "right practice," within this Dharma there is not a single phenomenon that increases or decreases, comes or goes, or is grasped or abandoned.
Why is this? One who practices correctly does not practice a single type of awakening.
If one can know and see all phenomena as they truly are—possessing a non-dual nature—this is called the noble path of transcendence.

Śāriputra! This fearlessness of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; taking great compassion as its means, it is true suchness, equality, the nature of reality, not a non-nature, unchanging, without concealment, without fear, without retreat, and without contention. Because of these qualities, it illuminates the great assembly, causing them to be joyful, their entire bodies to feel at ease and comfortable, and their minds to give rise to pure faith, leaping with exultation and joy.
Śāriputra! Among the sentient beings of the world, there is none who can raise opposition or dispute against the Tathāgata’s fearlessness. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s fearlessness cannot be contested, it is equal in nature to the dharmadhātu;
it flows forth and pervades all worlds, such that nothing can obstruct or harm it.

Thus, this noble practice of renunciation—which is immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, peerless, and an accomplishment of the wondrous Dharma that cannot be fully described—is revealed and expounded by the Tathāgata for the sake of all sentient beings, his mind being suffused with great compassion.
If there are sentient beings who understand reality as it is and practice the right path, they will certainly be able to transcend and swiftly exhaust all suffering. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s fearlessness is boundless and limitless, like space. If anyone were to seek the limits of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness, it would be no different from a person seeking the limits of space.

Śāriputra! Having heard of these inconceivable fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas believe, accept, and reverently uphold them with pure minds free from doubt, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
Śāriputra! This is called the fourth fearlessness, the teaching of the noble path of transcendence.

Because the Tathāgata has accomplished this fearlessness, he utters the true lion’s roar and turns the Great Brahma Wheel amidst the great assembly; no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, or brahmās in any world can turn it in accordance with the Dharma.
Śāriputra! These four kinds of fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata are thus boundless and limitless, like space; no sentient beings can reach their limit.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that the Tathāgata’s inconceivable fearlessness is thus like space, they accept it with faith, reverently uphold it with purity and without doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Spontaneously and perfectly awakened to the equal nature of all phenomena,
Therefore the Tathāgata, seeing them everywhere, Is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Whether they be the dharmas of ordinary worldlings, the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training,
or the dharmas of the most supreme Pratyekabuddhas— all such Buddha-dharmas are entirely equal.
All mundane dharmas of the world, as well as all supramundane dharmas, [are likewise equal].
Wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable— The path to nirvāṇa is equal.
Whether empty or signless, Whether free from all aspirations and delights,
Without arising and without conditioned existence— One perceives their entirely equal nature.
Having realized the nature of equality, as he has taught, he liberates all sentient beings; the Great Muni is fearless.
Having himself been liberated from the three realms of existence, he further reveals the path to liberation.
O Holy One, honored by gods and humans, you manifest the second fearlessness:
that there is no obstruction to the supreme awakening. You declare that those who practice [the path] fail to realize liberation;
they are neither pure nor inferior, for they lack all sense of shame and dread of blame.
Never having practiced restraint of body, nor restraint of speech and mind;
driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, and out of fear, they take life,
plunder the wealth of others, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, drink alcohol, and show no reverence.
The seven types of pride and the eightfold wrong path are not at all places of liberation;
the nine grounds for resentment involve many faults, and the ten unwholesome courses of action stem from improper reflection; through such folly, there is no liberation.
Practicing all conditioned activities with perversion, clinging to the false and being heedless—the Buddha knows these and teaches them as obstructive dharmas; this is the third fearlessness.
There are immeasurable gates of purity through which one cultivates and realizes enlightenment.
The Buddha, having spontaneously attained mastery, proclaims the Dharma that leads to the deathless nectar.
Furthermore, all those various and wondrously virtuous dharmas that assist pure bodhi are praised by the Most Victorious One.
If one has practiced well, yet does not realize the various liberations, such a thing is impossible;
this is the truthful word of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
If one contemplates according to reality, the vast afflictions will be stilled.
Contemplating the equality of all phenomena, One skillfully cultivates the noble conduct.
Without clinging to any signs— Whether they be dharmas or non-dharmas—one is liberated from all sorrow and fear; This is what the Great Purifier has taught.
Skillfully knowing the various phenomena, which are as vast and empty as the pure sky,
and like illusions or dreams, one is liberated from the ocean of all existences.
Yet, if one is heedless and creates karma, one will wander through the realms of existence in saṃsāra.
Out of great compassion for sentient beings, desiring to lead them to realize liberation,
the Honored Muni of Ten Powers dwells within birth and death to transform through the Dharma;
this is the fourth fearlessness, pure and equal to space.
“In this way, Śāriputra,
this is called the inconceivable fearlessness of the Tathāgata.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas believe in, accept, and faithfully uphold it with purity and without doubt, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva believe in, accept, and faithfully uphold the inconceivable great compassion of the Tathāgata, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder?"
Śāriputra! The great compassion of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is constantly active. Why is this?

Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not abandon any sentient beings, and because they act at all times to bring all sentient beings to maturity, it should be known that their great compassion constantly arises without ceasing.

Śāriputra! This great compassion of the Tathāgata is thus immeasurable, thus inconceivable, thus unequaled, thus boundless, thus ineffable, thus fierce and sharp, and thus long-enduring; yet even in accordance with all the verbal activities of sentient beings up to those of the Tathāgata himself, this great compassion remains difficult to fully describe.
Why is this? Just as the Tathāgata’s realization of bodhi is inconceivable, so too is the Tathāgata’s arousal of great compassion toward all sentient beings likewise inconceivable.
Śāriputra! How does the Tathāgata realize awakening? Śāriputra!
Just as the Tathāgata entered suchness by way of being rootless and non-abiding,
he realized awakening. Śāriputra,
what is meant by "root"?
What is "abiding"? Taking the body as a root and false discrimination as abiding—these are the two dharmas.
The Tathāgata understands these two dharmas with equanimity; therefore it is said: "Just as the Tathāgata enters into that which is rootless and non-abiding, he realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

All sentient beings are unable to understand these two dharmas; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I must now certainly reveal and instruct them so that they may understand such rootless and non-abiding dharmas."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, awakening (bodhi) is by nature quiescent.
What are the two dharmas that are called 'quiescent'? "
Śāriputra! It is quiescent within and tranquil without. Why is this?
The nature of the eye is empty, free from "I" and "mine"; likewise, the natures of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, free from "I" and "mine.
To know it thus is called tranquility.

Having realized, as it truly is, that the nature of the eye is empty, one does not pursue forms; likewise, having realized, as it truly is, that the nature of the mind is empty, one does not pursue mental objects.
To know in this way is called tranquility.

All sentient beings are unable to understand these two dharmas of tranquility; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I must now certainly reveal and instruct them so that they may understand these two dharmas of tranquility."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, I have realized that the self-nature of bodhi is pure.
What is meant by 'self-nature purity'? "

Śāriputra! The essence of bodhi is inherently undefiled; the essence of bodhi is equal to space; the essence of bodhi is the nature of space; the essence of bodhi is identical to space; bodhi and space are perfectly equal, being ultimately pure in their fundamental nature.
Foolish ordinary beings do not awaken to such intrinsic purity and are defiled by adventitious afflictions.

All sentient beings fail to understand this intrinsic purity; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I must now definitively reveal and cause them to understand this intrinsic purity."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the awakening I have realized is without entering and without exiting.
What are called the two dharmas of entering and exiting? "
Śāriputra! What is called "entering" refers to grasping at all phenomena; what is called "emerging" refers to non-grasping at all phenomena.

The Tathāgata clearly perceives the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as being without entering or emerging, just as the Tathāgata clearly perceives that there is neither distance nor a further shore.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are by nature remote from both this shore and the other shore; one who is able to realize these dharmas is therefore called a Tathāgata.

All sentient beings, however, cannot awaken to this dharma-nature that is neither entering nor emerging. For their sake, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion, thinking: "I shall now definitively reveal and instruct them so that they may awaken to such a dharma-nature that is neither entering nor emerging."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, I have realized enlightenment that is signless and objectless.
What is meant by 'signless and objectless'? "
Śāriputra, the non-apprehension of visual consciousness is called "signlessness"; the non-contemplation of forms is called "objectlessness.
This extends up to the non-apprehension of mental consciousness being called "signlessness," and the non-contemplation of phenomena being called "objectlessness."
Śāriputra! The signless and objectless is that which is practiced by the noble ones.
What is it that they practice?
This refers to the fact that foolish ordinary beings within the three realms are unable to practice what the noble ones practice, and thus cannot realize the signless and the objectless.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I must now certainly reveal and instruct them so that they may realize such a dharma that is signless and objectless."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is neither past, future, nor present; it is the equality of the three times and the severance of the wheel of the three marks.
What is meant by the severance of the wheel of the three marks?
Śāriputra! In the past, the mind does not turn back; in the future, consciousness does not move toward anything; in the present, the intellect does not arise or act.
This mind, consciousness, and mentation have no fixed abode; they do not conceptualize the past, do not cling to the future, and do not engage in proliferation regarding the present.

All sentient beings are unable to awaken to the equality of the three periods of time and the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*). Therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I must now definitively reveal and cause them to awaken to this equality and purity of the three periods of time and the three spheres."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, I have realized an unconditioned and essence-less bodhi.
For what reason is it called 'unconditioned and essence-less'? "
Śāriputra! This nature of bodhi is not cognized by visual consciousness, nor is it cognized by any consciousness up to and including mental consciousness.

That which is called "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding; because it is eternally free from these three characteristics, it is named "unconditioned."
Śāriputra! One who knows the nature of the unconditioned should awaken to the conditioned. Why is this?
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself the absence of nature.

That which is the absence of nature is, in its essence, non-dual. Because all sentient beings are unable to awaken to this absence of nature and the unconditioned, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I must now definitively reveal and cause them to awaken to such an absence of nature and the unconditioned."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, I have realized the path of non-differentiation regarding awakening.
For what reason is it called the path of non-differentiation?

Śāriputra! Both *tathatā* (suchness) and *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) are termed "traces"; because their nature is without differentiation and their nature is without abiding, they are called "undifferentiated.
The *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality) of all phenomena is termed a "trace"; because its nature is without movement or fluctuation, it is called "undifferentiated."
The emptiness of all phenomena is called a "trace," and because their nature cannot be apprehended, it is called "non-differentiation.
The signlessness of all phenomena is called a "trace," and because their nature cannot be sought, it is called "non-differentiation."
The wishlessness of all phenomena is called a "trace"; their nature being without origination, they are without differentiation.
The absence of a self-nature in sentient beings is called a "trace"; as for their essential substance, it is without name and without differentiation.
This characteristic of space is called a "trace," while its nature being unattainable is called "non-differentiation.
That its nature is without arising is called a "trace," and that its nature is without cessation is called "non-differentiation."
Its nature is unconditioned; this is called the trace. Its nature has no going or staying; this is called non-differentiation.
It serves as the characteristic of bodhi; this is called the trace. Its nature is quiescent; this is called non-differentiation.
That which has the characteristic of nirvāṇa is called the "trace," and its nature of non-arising is called "non-differentiation. Śāriputra!
