Because all sentient beings are unable to awaken to this trace of non-differentiation, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion toward them, thinking: "I must now definitively reveal and cause them to awaken to such a trace of non-differentiation."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) cannot be realized by means of the body, nor can it be realized by means of the mind. Why is this?
The nature of the body is devoid of cognition and lacks functional activity, like grass, trees, walls, or the light reflected from carved stone; the nature of the mind is likewise.
Just as with illusions, mirages, or the moon reflected in water—if one can awaken to the body and mind in this way, it is called bodhi.

Śāriputra! It is only by means of conventional worldly discourse that we provisionally designate "bodhi. The true nature of bodhi is ineffable; it cannot be attained through the body, nor through the mind, nor through dharmas, nor through non-dharmas; it cannot be attained through reality, nor through unreality; it cannot be attained through truth, nor through falsehood.
Why is this? Because the nature of bodhi is beyond verbal expression and is also free from the characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, because bodhi has no form or substance that can be communicated through speech—just as space has no form or location and thus cannot be described.
Śāriputra! When one seeks all dharmas as they truly are, they are found to be beyond verbal expression. Why is this?
Because within all phenomena there is no verbal expression, and within verbal expression there are likewise no phenomena, all sentient beings are unable to awaken to such a principle of phenomena.

Therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I shall now definitively reveal the principles of all phenomena so that they may awaken to the meaning of such true reality."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called 'bodhi' is without grasping and without storing.
What is meant by 'without grasping and without storing'? "
Śāriputra! Because one thoroughly understands the eye, it is called "without grasping"; because one does not contemplate forms, it is called "without storage. Śāriputra!

Because the Tathāgata has realized this bodhi without grasping or storing, he does not grasp at the eye, does not store away forms, and does not dwell upon consciousness; and so on, up to not grasping at the mind, not storing away phenomena, and not dwelling upon consciousness.
Although he does not abide in consciousness, he is able to discern the abodes of the minds of all sentient beings.
How does he discern them?
It is said that the minds of all sentient beings abide in four dharmas.
What are these four?
The minds of all sentient beings abide in consciousness, their minds abide in sensation, their minds abide in perception, and their minds abide in mental formations.

The Tathāgata thus knows, in accordance with reality, both abiding and non-abiding; yet all sentient beings are unable to awaken to the non-abiding limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I must now definitively reveal and cause them to awaken to this Dharma of the non-abiding limit of reality."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is another name for emptiness. Because emptiness is empty, awakening is also empty; because awakening is empty, all phenomena are also empty. Therefore, the Tathāgata awakens to all phenomena according to their emptiness; it is not by means of emptiness that he awakens to the emptiness of phenomena, but rather through the wisdom of a single principle that he awakens to the emptiness of the nature of phenomena."
Emptiness and the nature of awakening are non-dual; because they are non-dual, one cannot say, "this is awakening" and "this is emptiness.
If there were duality, then one could speak of this as awakening and that as emptiness.
Because phenomena are non-dual and lack dual characteristics, they are without name, without mark, and without activity; they ultimately do not function, nor do they manifest.

That which is called "emptiness" is the distancing from grasping and attachment; within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), no phenomenon can be apprehended, and it is termed "empty" because its nature is empty.
As it is said that the great void is called "space," yet the nature of the great void is ineffable;
so too, this dharma of emptiness is called "empty," yet that emptiness-nature is ineffable.
Thus one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are truly without name, yet names are provisionally established and spoken for them; however, the names of phenomena have no direction and no location.
Just as names designate all phenomena, so too these phenomena have no direction and no location.

The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that all phenomena have been unborn and unarisen from the very beginning; having known this, he realizes liberation, yet their actual nature is neither bound nor liberated.

Ordinary, deluded worldlings are unable to awaken to this nature of bodhi; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I shall reveal and cause them to awaken to such reality-nature of bodhi."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the nature of bodhi is equal to the great void; yet the nature of the great void is neither equal nor unequal.
Bodhi is likewise neither equal nor unequal; just as the nature of all phenomena has no reality, it cannot be said to be either equal or unequal."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata awakens to the fact that the nature of all phenomena is equal and without anything unequal; he awakens to reality such that there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be called equal or unequal. In this way, the measure of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of reality as it is exhausts the measure of all phenomena.
What is called "knowledge in accordance with reality"?

It means knowing that all phenomena are originally non-existent yet arise, and having arisen, they disperse; they arise without a master and disperse without a master. Whether arising or dispersing, they revolve according to various conditions. Within this, there is not a single phenomenon that revolves, returns, or revolves accordingly. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata, in order to sever all paths, has taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

All sentient beings are unable to awaken to and sever the dharmas that lead to various paths; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I shall reveal and teach so that they may awaken to these dharmas that sever the various paths."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called 'bodhi' is the very expression of suchness (tathatā).
What is the characteristic of this expression of suchness?

Śāriputra! Just as the characteristic of bodhi is, so too are all forms; they are identical to that suchness (tathatā), without regression and without not being omnipresent. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise; just as that suchness is, there is nothing to which they do not pervade.

Śāriputra! Just as the characteristic of bodhi is identical to that true thusness (tathatā), so too is the nature of the four great elements; like that true thusness, it does not regress and there is nowhere to which it does not pervade.

Just as the nature of bodhi is identical to that true thusness (tathatā), so it is with the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind element, the phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Just as the characteristic of bodhi is merely a conventional designation, so too are all dharmas—the aggregates, elements, bases, and so forth—merely conventional designations.
To know such characteristics is called the "phrase of thusness."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata’s awakening is entirely according to reality and is an unerring awakening; as it was in the past, so it is in the middle and the future. Why is this?

The prior limit is non-arising, the posterior limit is non-destiny, and the middle limit is detached; all such things are called "the word of suchness. As it is with one such phrase, so it is with all; as it is with all, so it is with one single phrase. Within the nature of suchness, neither oneness nor multiplicity can be apprehended.

Because all sentient beings are unable to awaken to this suchness-phrase, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I shall reveal and cause them to awaken to such a phrase of the true thusness-dharma."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which is called 'bodhi' refers to entering into practice and entering into non-practice.
What are meant by 'practice' and 'non-practice'?
Śāriputra! To initiate wholesome dharmas is called "practice"; that all dharmas are ultimately unattainable is called "non-practice.
To abide in a mind that does not abide is called "practice"; the liberation door of the signless samādhi is called "non-practice."
Śāriputra! What is called "practice" refers to weighing, calculating, and examining the mind; what is called "non-practice" transcends such weighing and so forth.
What is meant by "transcending weighing and so forth"?
Because in all places there is no activity or function of the various consciousnesses, Śāriputra!
What is called "action" refers to the observation of the conditioned in those places; what is called "non-action" refers to the realization of the unconditioned in those places.

Foolish ordinary beings are unable to awaken to and enter into the practice of what is not the path; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking, "I shall reveal and cause them to awaken to such dharmas of entering into the practice of what is not the path."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, awakening (bodhi) is without outflows and without grasping.
Why is it called 'without outflows and without grasping'? "
Śāriputra! Because it is free from the nature of the four floods, it is called "without outflows" (anāsrava). What are these four?

It is the nature of being free from the flow of desire, the nature of being free from the flow of existence, the nature of being free from the flow of ignorance, and the nature of being free from the flow of views.
Śāriputra, it is called "without grasping" because it is free from the nature of the four graspings.
What are the four? They are:

being free from the nature of grasping at sensual desire, being free from the nature of grasping at existence, being free from the nature of grasping at views, and being free from the nature of grasping at precepts and observances. Śāriputra!

Thus, these four types of clinging all arise from ignorance; being shrouded by the blinding darkness and confined within the moats and ponds of the waters of craving, one undergoes the aggregates, elements, and sense bases due to the grasping at a self.
The Tathāgata understands this as it truly is: that the root of self-grasping is intrinsically pure, and he causes sentient beings to likewise realize this purity. Śāriputra!
Because the Tathāgata has realized this purity, he makes no conceptual distinctions among all phenomena.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

From this conceptualization arises improper mental attention; because this is only associated with what is correct, ignorance does not arise. Because ignorance does not arise, one cannot give rise to the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). If the twelve links of existence are not given rise to, this is non-arising (*anutpāda*). If there is non-arising, this is definitiveness (*niyama*). If it is definitive, this is the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*). If it is the explicit meaning, this is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). If it is the ultimate meaning, this is the meaning of no person (*anātman*). The meaning of no person is the meaning of the ineffable (*anabhilāpya*). The meaning of the ineffable is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). All meanings of dependent origination are the meaning of phenomena (*dharma*). All meanings of phenomena are the meaning of the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra! One who can contemplate dependent origination in this way is contemplating the Dharma; one who contemplates the Dharma is contemplating the Tathāgata.
For one who contemplates in this manner, there is nothing to be contemplated apart from True Suchness (tathatā).
In this context, what constitutes "that which exists"?
It refers to characteristics (*nimitta*) and conditions (*ālambana*).
If one can observe these two factors as being without characteristics and without conditions, that is true observation.

Because the Tathāgata has awakened to the equality of all such phenomena, he is equal; yet foolish ordinary beings cannot awaken to this nature that is free from outflows and free from grasping. Therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them, thinking: "I shall reveal and cause them to awaken to this nature that is free from outflows and free from grasping."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for bodhi, its nature is pure, stainless, and without grasping.
What is meant by 'pure,' 'stainless,' and 'without grasping'? "
Śāriputra! Because it is empty, it is pure; because it is signless, it is stainless; because it is wishless, it is without grasping.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Because it is unarisen, it is pure; because it is unconditioned, it is stainless; because it is without grasping, it is without attachment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is pure by virtue of its intrinsic nature, stainless because it is universally pure, and without attachment because it is luminously radiant.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is pure because it is free from conceptual proliferation; it is stainless because it is detached from conceptual proliferation; it is without grasping because conceptual proliferation is stilled.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is pure because it is suchness (*tathatā*); it is stainless because it is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); it is without grasping because it is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is pure because it is void and tranquil; it is stainless because it is unimpeded; it is without grasping because it is empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Because of thorough knowledge of the internal, there is purity; because of non-engagement with the external, there is stainlessness; because the internal and external are both unapprehendable, there is non-attachment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

It is pure because of the thorough knowledge of the aggregates (*skandha*); it is stainless because of the intrinsic nature of the elements (*dhātu*); it is without grasping because of the elimination of the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is pure because of the knowledge of exhaustion regarding the past; it is stainless because of the knowledge of non-arising regarding the future; it is without grasping because of the knowledge of abiding in the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) regarding the present.
Śāriputra! Such a nature—pure, stainless, and non-clinging—is unified in a single phrase; that which is called a single phrase is the phrase of tranquility.
All that is tranquil is supreme tranquility; that which is supremely tranquil is universal tranquility; and that which is universally tranquil is named the Great Muni.

Śāriputra! Just as the great void is, so too is bodhi; as is the nature of bodhi, so too are all phenomena (dharmas); as is the nature of all phenomena, so too is reality (bhūtatā); as is the nature of reality, so too is the land (kṣetra); as is the nature of the land, so too is nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said that the equality of all phenomena with nirvāṇa is also called the ultimate.

Because they have the characteristic of being boundless, they have no antidote; because they are free from the characteristic of an antidote, these dharmas are thus primordially pure, stainless, and without grasping. Śāriputra!

Regarding all phenomena, such as these forms and formless states, the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are and contemplates the nature of sentient beings; sporting in purity, stainlessness, and non-attachment, he gives rise to great compassion, thinking: "I must now certainly reveal and cause them to awaken to this dharma of purity, stainlessness, and non-attachment."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
such inconceivable great compassion of the Tathāgata proceeds spontaneously and effortlessly, pervading and filling the worlds of the ten directions without any obstruction."

Śāriputra! The great compassion of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, boundless, and limitless, just like space. Should anyone wish to seek the limits of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, it would be no different from a person seeking the limits of space.

Śāriputra! Having heard that the inconceivable great compassion of the Tathāgata is equal to space, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accept it with faith, uphold it with truth, and follow it with purity and without doubt, even giving rise to thoughts of its marvelous rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Buddhas realize enlightenment, Rootless and without abode;
Having realized it as the Buddha has, They speak of it for the sake of all sentient beings.”
The Buddhas realize awakening, which is tranquil and utterly tranquil;
they perceive the internal emptiness of the eyes and so forth, and the external emptiness of form and so forth.
Sentient beings do not awaken to this tranquility and utter tranquility.
The Tathāgata understands the meaning of words and gives rise to great compassion for them.
The nature of awakening is luminous and pure, as vast and clear as space;
because sentient beings do not realize this, he gives rise to great compassion for them.
The Buddhas realize enlightenment, Without coming, going, grasping, or rejecting;
Because sentient beings do not understand this, The Buddhas give rise to great compassion for them.
The Buddhas realize enlightenment, Which is signless and without objective realm.
This is the path traversed by the multitude of sages, not the one walked by foolish men.
Ordinary worldlings do not know it; though they may know it, they lack clear realization.
Toward such beings, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
The intrinsic nature of the unconditioned is without arising and without ceasing;
therein it also has no abiding, and the three spheres are forever liberated.
Fools cannot awaken to this, nor to the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena.
Arising great compassion for them, he reveals such a principle:
awakening is not realized by the body, nor is it realized by the mind;
the nature of the body is insentient, and the mind is like an illusion and so forth.
Fools cannot awaken to the intrinsic nature of body and mind;
toward them, I give rise to great compassion and reveal such a sublime principle.
The Buddhas have spontaneously realized the vast and supreme bodhi.
Sitting serenely beneath the King of Trees, he observed the nature of sentient beings;
ascending the wheel of birth and death, they circulate through various realms of existence.
Having seen them thus, the Tathāgata gave rise to fierce and powerful great compassion.
Ruined by pride, they are perpetually entangled in the net of views;
they conceive the notion of pleasure within suffering, and the notion of permanence within impermanence.
They calculate purity, self, and a sentient being, destroyed by the view of a life-principle.
Having observed them thus, the Tathāgata gave rise to fierce and powerful great compassion.
The nature of all sentient beings is shrouded by the film of ignorance;
lacking the light of wisdom, they are like the sun obscured by heavy clouds.
When the Tathāgata beholds them, he gives rise to fierce and powerful great compassion;
with the light of stainless wisdom, he shall illuminate them.
Having entered the various evil realms, they are constantly lost and confused regarding the right path.
Some fall into the realm of hell, or into the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
The Buddhas of the past already knew this and opened the path of the former rectitude;
now the Buddha, having seen them, gives rise to fierce and powerful great compassion.
The Buddha knows all phenomena— true suchness and their actual nature—
as pure as space, having realized true liberation.
Yet all sentient beings do not know these such pure and wondrous dharmas.
When the Tathāgata beheld them, he gave rise to fierce and powerful great compassion.
"In this way, Śāriputra, this is called the inconceivable great compassion of the Tathāgata."

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard of this inconceivable great compassion, they accept it with faith and venerate it with truth, pure and without doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to deep gladness and a sense of wonder.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 39 [and] Volume 40.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Bodhisattvapiṭaka Assembly, Volume Twelve, Part Six: Chapter Four, Part Four, "The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the inconceivable and unique buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata, accept them with faith and reverence, remaining pure and free from doubt, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder?"

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has accomplished the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma). By virtue of having accomplished them, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, declaring: "I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and turn the Great Brahma-wheel, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, or brahmā in any world can turn in accordance with the Dharma."
Śāriputra! What are called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? Śāriputra!
What is meant by the Tathāgata dwelling in the world without any errors? Because he is without error, he is called the Tathāgata.
What is meant by being without error? Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s bodily actions are free from error; because they are without error, no one in any world—whether foolish or wise—is able to establish a discourse in accordance with the Dharma claiming that the Tathāgata’s body possesses error.
Why is this? Because the physical actions of the Buddha, the Bhagavān, are ultimately free from error. Śāriputra!

As the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, move through the world—whether gazing straight ahead, turning their bodies to look back, bending or stretching, donning the saṃghāṭī robe, or taking up and holding the robes and bowl; whether advancing or retreating, coming or going, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—in all these actions, the Tathāgata never loses his dignified deportment, remaining solemn, majestic, and composed.

Śāriputra! Whether the Tathāgata is departing for a city or returning from it, his two feet tread upon the air, and the thousand-spoked wheels appear upon the surface of the earth; delightful and wondrous fragrant padma flowers spontaneously spring up to receive the Tathāgata’s feet.

If any sentient beings of the animal realm are touched by the feet of the Tathāgata, they shall experience supreme happiness for a full seven nights; after their lives end, they will be reborn in the happy world of the higher realms.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s robes do not adhere to his body even to the extent of four finger-widths, and the Vairambha winds cannot ruffle them. Śāriputra!
The light of the Tathāgata’s body shines most intensely even into the Avīci hell, touching those sentient beings and causing them to experience feelings of joy. Śāriputra,
because all parts of his body are free from any mark of fault, it is said that the Tathāgata’s body is without error or transgression.
Just as his own realization is free from error regarding the body, he likewise teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings, causing them to forever sever errors regarding bodily karma. Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata’s verbal karma is free from error; because it is without error, no one in any world, whether foolish or wise, can lawfully seek out any error in the Tathāgata’s verbal karma.
Why is this? Śāriputra, the Tathāgata speaks at the proper time;

the Tathāgata speaks words that are real, speaks words that are true, speaks words that are timely, acts in accordance with his words, is skilled in explaining terminology, speaks words that gladden sentient beings, does not repeat himself, adorns his speech with both letter and meaning, and ensures that every single sound he utters inspires faith, understanding, and joy.
Śāriputra! Because all such speech is characterized by the absence of fault, it is said that the Tathāgata’s verbal karma is without error.
Just as his own realized speech is free from mistake, he likewise teaches the Dharma to sentient beings so that they may forever sever errors in their verbal karma.

Śāriputra! The mind of the Tathāgata is free from error; because it is without error, no one in the world—whether foolish or wise—is able to observe, in accordance with the Dharma, any lapse in the mental activities of the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because the Tathāgata does not abandon the profound state of meditative concentration, yet is able to initiate all buddha-activities without exerting mental effort; his unimpeded wisdom and vision regarding all phenomena proceed spontaneously. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s mind is free from error.
Because his own mind, as realized by him, is free from error, he also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings, causing them to forever sever errors in their mental karma. Śāriputra!
Because his physical, vocal, and mental actions are thus without error, this is called the Tathāgata’s first unique Buddha-dharma:
that all his actions are free from mistake. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!
How is it that the speech and voice of the Tathāgata are free from abruptness?

Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata speaks with a voice free from abruptness, neither Māra nor his retinue, nor other sons of gods, nor various non-Buddhists, can find an opportunity to exploit a vulnerability in the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
the speech and sounds of the Tathāgata are fundamentally free from abruptness and free from following after abruptness.

Why is this? Because he has long since forever departed from all craving and hatred; thus, although all sentient beings may treat him with reverence, his mind does not become elated, and although they may treat him with contempt, his mind does not become dejected.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

For the Tathāgata, there is no action performed at an improper time or that is not brought to completion; nor does he give rise to regret on account of such matters, nor does he utter harsh or impulsive sounds concerning past events.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata has no disputes with the world; therefore, the Tathāgata has no harsh or violent sounds.

The Tathāgata always abides in the profound samādhi of non-contention and is free from the grasping of "mine"; he is without appropriation and has distanced himself from all fetters. Therefore, the Tathāgata has no harsh or violent sounds.
Śāriputra! Such immeasurable sounds are free from abruptness, and the Tathāgata has fully realized and entered into them all.
Just as the sounds realized by the Buddha are free from abruptness, he also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings in order to cause them to forever sever all forms of abruptness.
"Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s second unique Buddha-dharma, which is that his speech is never abrupt or violent.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is the Tathāgata’s mindfulness free from forgetfulness? Śāriputra,
because the Tathāgata’s right mindfulness is free from forgetfulness, he does not give rise to confusion regarding even a single dharma.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata dwells within the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis without delusion or forgetfulness; because he observes the mental movements and activities of all sentient beings without obstruction; because he proclaims the sublime Dharma as is appropriate without loss or error; because he is without loss or error regarding the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of meaning, phenomena, terminology, and eloquence; and because he possesses such immeasurable, unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past, future, and present without loss or error.

Just as he himself has realized unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past, future, and present without any loss of mindfulness, so too does he teach such a Dharma to sentient beings, causing them to realize non-forgetful mindfulness.
"Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s third unique Buddha-dharma: mindfulness without forgetfulness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is meant by saying that the Tathāgata has no state of non-concentrated mind that can be apprehended? Śāriputra,

whether the Tathāgata is walking or standing, sitting or lying down, eating or drinking, speaking or remaining silent, he always dwells in profound meditative concentration without ever emerging from it.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has realized the most supreme perfection of profound samādhi, having accomplished unobstructed and unhindered deep meditative concentration (dhyāna).

Śāriputra! Among the class of sentient beings, there is no being—whether of fixed or unfixed destiny—who can perceive the mind and mental factors of a Tathāgata, except through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s own majestic power by which such knowledge may be attained.

Just as he himself has realized and constantly dwells in a concentrated mind, he likewise teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings based on samādhi, so that they may forever sever their distracted minds.
"Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s fourth unique Buddha-dharma of non-lapsing mental stability.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How is it that the Tathāgata has no diverse conceptions? For what reason? Śāriputra!
Because of divergent perceptions, one may abide in an unbalanced mind;
however, since the Tathāgata’s mind always abides in equanimity, he has no divergent perceptions regarding anything whatsoever.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata has no diverse conceptions regarding the various Buddha-fields, for those Buddha-fields are like space.
The Tathāgata has no manifold conceptions regarding sentient beings, because the nature of those sentient beings is selfless.
The Tathāgata has no notion of diversity regarding all Buddhas, because of his equalizing wisdom in which that dharmatā is without differentiation.
The Tathāgata has no notion of diversity regarding all phenomena, because the dharmatā of the state free from desire is equal.

The Tathāgata has no attachment toward those who uphold the precepts and no resentment toward those who violate them; he does not fail to repay kindness received, nor does he harbor malice toward those who bear him enmity; he is never partial toward those he seeks to discipline, nor does he treat with contempt those whose minds are fixed in wrong concentration; he dwells in equanimity regarding all phenomena. For these reasons, the Tathāgata is said to be free from diverse perceptions.

Because he has no notion of difference regarding what he has realized for himself, he also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings, causing them to forever sever various notions of difference. Śāriputra!
This is called the Tathāgata’s fifth unique Buddha-dharma, which is free from all divergent thoughts.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the Tathāgata’s equanimity that is without discrimination?
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because the Tathāgata has already cultivated the noble path and realized this equanimity; it is not that he has realized it without having cultivated the path.

The Tathāgata has already cultivated the mind, has already cultivated ethical discipline, and has already cultivated wisdom to realize this equanimity; it is not that he realizes what he has not previously cultivated.

Śāriputra! The equanimity of the Tathāgata follows the course of wisdom and does not follow the course of delusion; the equanimity of the Tathāgata is supramundane and does not fall into the mundane; the equanimity of the Tathāgata is noble and is renunciation, being neither ignoble nor non-renunciatory; the equanimity of the Tathāgata is able to turn the Brahma-wheel, out of compassion for sentient beings never abandoning them; and the equanimity of the Tathāgata is spontaneously accomplished because it does not depend on antidotes.

Śāriputra! The relinquishment of the Tathāgata is neither high nor not high, and it is without inferiority; it abides in immovability, remains far removed from the two extremes, and transcends all conceptualization and discrimination.

In relation to time, it does not transcend its proper moment; it is without movement, without thought, without conceptualization, without discursive differentiation, without cultivation, without diminution, without arrogance or negligence, and without manifestation. It is the nature of reality, the nature as it is, the non-false nature, and the nature that is not otherwise—thus it is immeasurable.

Śāriputra! It is because the Tathāgata has thus accomplished such great equanimity, and for the sake of bringing the perfection of relinquishment to all sentient beings, that he teaches this Dharma. Śāriputra!
This is called the Tathāgata’s sixth unique Buddha-dharma: equanimity without discrimination.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the Tathāgata’s lack of decline or diminution in his aspiration?
Śāriputra! What is the aspiration that is without decline?
It is the aspiration for the wholesome dharmas of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "aspiration" (*chanda*)? Śāriputra, the aspiration of the Tathāgata’s great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) does not diminish;

the aspiration of the Tathāgata’s great compassion (*karuṇā*) does not diminish; the aspiration of the Tathāgata to teach the Dharma does not diminish; the aspiration to discipline sentient beings does not diminish; the aspiration to bring sentient beings to maturity does not diminish; the aspiration to give rise to seclusion (*viveka*) does not diminish; the aspiration to instruct bodhisattvas does not diminish; and the aspiration to perpetuate the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it is never severed does not diminish.
All Tathāgatas do not act according to their own desires; rather, for the Tathāgatas, wisdom is the precursor to their aspirations.

Just as their own realized aspirations never diminish, they likewise teach such a Dharma to sentient beings, so that those beings may realize the aspiration for the perfect, unsurpassed knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s seventh unique Buddha-dharma, the non-decline of his resolve.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How is it that the Tathāgata’s right effort never declines?
Śāriputra, what is this right effort that does not decline?
This refers to the right effort of not abandoning sentient beings who are to be converted, and the right effort of harboring no intention to exclude those in the assembly who listen to the Dharma.
Because there is no such decline or regression in these matters, it is said that the Tathāgata’s right effort does not diminish.

Śāriputra! Suppose the Tathāgata encounters such an assembly that delights in hearing the Dharma and is a fit vessel for the teaching; if they can listen to the Dharma without weariness for the duration of an eon, the Tathāgata likewise remains seated without rising for the duration of that eon, and without regard for food or drink, he continuously preaches the Dharma without even a moment’s interruption.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

For the sake of sentient beings, even if there were only a single sentient being remaining to be converted by a Buddha throughout all Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, at that time the Tathāgata would personally go to that place to preach the essential Dharma for them, causing them to awaken and enter it with tireless and right diligence.
Śāriputra! The body of the Tathāgata is free from fatigue, and his speech and mind are likewise free from fatigue. Why is this?
Because the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata are ever at peace, Śāriputra,

the Tathāgata has for long eons initiated diligence and praised diligence, teaching such a Dharma to all sentient beings so that they may diligently cultivate this diligence and thereby realize noble liberation.
"Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s eighth unshared Buddha-dharma, the non-deficiency of right exertion.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How is it that the Tathāgata does not experience any decline or diminution regarding all single dharmas, all their aspects, or any of his recollections? Why is this?
Because the recollections of all Tathāgatas are without decline.

Śāriputra! Having realized unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata observes the continuous succession of the minds of all sentient beings throughout their past and future lives; having known them, the Tathāgata possesses ultimate and thorough knowledge of them, such that there is no lapse of mindfulness therein.
Furthermore, having known the conduct of sentient beings as it truly is, the Tathāgata no longer exerts his wisdom regarding them, yet the Tathāgata’s mindfulness never declines.
Moreover, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata, having thoroughly examined the faculties, modes of awakening, inclinations, and courses of action of sentient beings categorized into the three groups, no longer recalls them, does not engage in further reflection, and does not observe them again; yet he constantly proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings without interruption.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s mindfulness is without decline or diminution.

Just as his own realization is characterized by undiminished mindfulness, he likewise teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings, causing them to forever sever all decline and diminution of mindfulness.
"Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s ninth unshared Buddha-dharma, which is mindfulness without decline or diminution.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How is it that the Buddha’s samādhi is without decline?
Śāriputra, the nature of the Buddha’s samādhi is equal to all phenomena; there is nothing that is not equal.
Why is this? Because there is no lack of equality among all single dharmas and all manifold dharmas. Śāriputra!
For what reason does the Buddha’s samādhi not undergo further decline?
Śāriputra, because true suchness (tathatā) is equal, samādhi is equal; because samādhi is equal, the Tathāgata is equal.
Because one is able to realize and enter into such equality, this samādhi is called "Equal Concentration" (Samatā-samādhi).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if the limit of desire is equal, it is the equality of being free from the limit of desire; if the limit of hatred is equal, it is the equality of being free from the limit of hatred; if the limit of delusion is equal, it is the equality of being free from the limit of delusion; if the limit of the conditioned is equal, it is the equality of the unconditioned limit; and if the limit of birth and death is equal, it is the equality of the limit of nirvāṇa.
Because the Tathāgata has realized and entered into such equality, he does not regress or diminish in his samādhi. Why is this?
Because the nature of equality is without regression or diminution.
Śāriputra! This Buddha-samādhi is not associated with the eye, nor is it associated with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Why is this?

However, because that Tathāgata’s faculties are without deficiency, furthermore, the Tathāgata’s samādhi does not rely on the earth element, nor does it rely on the water, fire, or wind elements; it does not rely on the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; it does not rely on this world or other worlds.
Why is this? Because being without dependence, there is neither regression nor diminution.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, like the various samādhis he has realized for himself, is without regression or diminution; furthermore, he teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings so that they may also realize those various samādhis.
"Śāriputra! This is called the thirteenth unshared Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata: the meditative absorption (samādhi) that is without decline or diminution.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How is it that the Tathāgata’s wisdom never undergoes decline? Śāriputra,
what is called the Tathāgata’s wisdom?

That is to say: the knowledge that realizes all phenomena without depending on others for understanding; the knowledge of eloquently expounding the sublime Dharma for other sentient beings and others; the knowledge of inexhaustible skillful means and unimpeded analytical comprehension (*pratisaṃvid*); the knowledge that discriminates all phrases; the knowledge of entering into a single phrase to explain it inexhaustibly throughout hundreds of thousands of great eons; the knowledge that cuts through the web of doubt exactly as one has heard; the knowledge that is without obstruction in all places; the knowledge that proclaims and establishes the noble Three Vehicles; the knowledge that thoroughly and universally understands the mental activities of eighty-four thousand sentient beings; and the knowledge that appropriately reveals eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma.

Śāriputra! This wisdom of the Tathāgata is boundless, limitless, and inexhaustible. Because this wisdom is inexhaustible, that which is spoken in accordance with it is likewise inexhaustible; therefore, it is said that the wisdom of the Tathāgata never declines or diminishes.
Just as his own realized wisdom does not diminish, he also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings, so that they may realize inexhaustible wisdom. Śāriputra!
This is called the Tathāgata’s eleventh unique Buddha-dharma,
the non-deficiency of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how is it that the Tathāgata’s liberation is without decline?
Śāriputra! What is called the liberation of the Tathāgata? Śāriputra!

The Śrāvakayāna attains liberation by awakening to sounds; the Pratyekabuddhayāna attains liberation by awakening to the conditions of dependent origination; and the Buddha, the Bhagavān, attains liberation by remaining far removed from all attachment to the two extremes. Therefore, it is called the liberation of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
such liberation is unbound in the past, does not transition in the future, and does not abide in the present.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There is liberation from the dualistic grasping of the eye and forms; likewise, there is liberation from the dualistic grasping of the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, and the body and tangibles, because one relies upon liberation through non-grasping and the gathering-in of that non-grasping.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The mind and wisdom are luminous by nature, their essence being free from defilement; therefore, by means of the wisdom associated with the mind in a single moment, all Buddhas realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, according to what he has realized and awakened to, also teaches such a Dharma to sentient beings, so that they may realize and awaken to this very Dharma. Śāriputra!
This is called the Tathāgata’s twelfth unshared Buddha-dharma: liberation that is never diminished.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, how is it that all the bodily actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom?
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because he is able to accomplish such bodily karma, all sentient beings are immediately tamed upon seeing the Tathāgata, or they are likewise tamed upon hearing him preach the Dharma.

Therefore, the Tathāgata may manifest silence to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest eating and drinking to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest various dignified postures to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest various supreme marks to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest the secondary signs to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest the invisible crown of the head to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest the gaze of his eyes to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest the touch of his divine light to discipline sentient beings; he may manifest the lifting and lowering of his feet as he walks to discipline sentient beings; or he may manifest traveling to and from cities and villages to discipline sentient beings.

Śāriputra! To speak in brief, there is no mode of conduct of the Buddha Bhagavān that does not discipline sentient beings; therefore, it is said that all bodily actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. Furthermore, he teaches such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may realize and enter into this very wisdom.
“Śāriputra! This is called the thirteenth unique Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata: physical action guided by wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
In what way is it that all verbal actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom?
Why is this so, Śāriputra?

Because the Buddha, the Bhagavān, teaches the Dharma without falsehood, he is preceded by wisdom; all his prophetic declarations are perfectly complete, and every word he proclaims is manifest and sublime.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s speech manifests and proceeds in an inconceivable manner; I shall now explain it briefly. Śāriputra!
The speech of the Tathāgata is speech that is easy to understand, speech that is easy to recognize, speech that is neither haughty nor base,
speech that is not inferior, speech that is not crooked, speech that is not stammering, speech that is not confused or disordered,
speech that is not harsh or dull, speech that is not coarse or rugged, and speech that is not obscure.
Speech that is gentle and soft; speech that is delightful and pleasing; speech that is not empty or feeble; speech that is not frivolous or fickle;
speech that is not hurried or rash; speech that is not burdensome or redundant; speech that is not rapid or impetuous; speech that is well-delimited and concise;
speech that is well-composed and explanatory; speech that is supremely exquisite and harmonious; speech with a sublime and wonderful resonance; and speech that is skillfully exhortative and guiding.
The speech of great clarity, the speech of the great thunderclap, the speech that leaves nothing omitted, the speech that drinks the nectar of immortality,
the speech possessing profound meaning, the speech worthy of being approached and relied upon, the speech that is vast and expansive,
the speech that is lovely and cherished, the speech free from defilement, the speech detached from turbidity, the speech free from impurity, and the speech free from stain and murkiness.
...speech that is not dull, speech of majestic intensity, unobstructed speech, instructive speech,
pure speech, upright speech, fearless speech, flawless speech, speech that is neither frivolous nor hurried,
speech that gives rise to joy and happiness, speech that brings physical well-being, and speech that gladdens the mind...
Speech that causes leaping joy; speech that pacifies desire; speech that pacifies hatred; speech that destroys delusion; speech that devours Māra; speech that subdues the wicked;
speech that crushes heterodox arguments; speech that conveys meaning; speech with the resonance of a celestial drum;
speech that delights the wise; speech with the voice of the kalaviṅka bird; and speech with the voice of the supreme deity.
The voice of Brahmā; the voice of the ocean tide; the voice of clouds and thunder; the voice of the earth and mountains resounding;
the voice of the king of swans; the voice of the king of peacocks; the voice of the oriole; the voice of the kalaviṅka bird;
the voice of the king of geese and wild ducks; the voice of the king of deer; and the voice of the vīṇā lute.
...speech with the resonance of a drum, speech with the resonance of a *paṇava* drum, speech with the resonance of a great lion’s roar,
speech with the resonance of a long flute, speech that is easy to understand, speech that is easy to discern, speech that is clear and lucid,
speech that is pleasing to the mind, speech that is worth hearing, speech with a deep and far-reaching resonance, speech free from muteness, and speech that is delightful...
Speech that may be whispered; speech that generates roots of goodness; speech with flawless phrasing; speech with well-expressed phrasing;
speech consistent with the meaning of phrases; speech consistent with the Dharma-phrases; speech appropriate to the occasion;
speech with swift response to the occasion; speech that does not exceed the proper time; speech that knows the superiority or inferiority of faculties; speech that adorns giving; pure speech.

Speech regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*), speech regarding the instruction in patience, speech regarding the refinement of right effort, speech regarding the delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), speech regarding the entry into right wisdom,
speech regarding the accumulation of loving-kindness and compassion, speech regarding tireless compassion, speech regarding pure joy,
speech regarding the realization of equanimity, speech regarding the establishment of the three vehicles, and speech regarding ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed.
The speech that establishes the three groups; the speech that purifies the three doors of liberation; the speech that universally cultivates the truths; the speech that universally cultivates wisdom;
the speech that is not disparaged by the realized ones; the speech praised by the noble ones; the speech whose measure is equal to space;
and the speech that perfectly accomplishes all aspects.

Śāriputra! Because such words of the Tathāgata are immeasurable, boundless, subtle, and pure, it is said that all verbal actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Just as his verbal activity is realized by himself, he likewise teaches the Dharma to sentient beings in accordance with them, so that they may realize and enter into such speech. Śāriputra!
This is called the fourteenth unique Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata: that his verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and guided by wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, how is it that all the mental actions of the Tathāgata are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom?
Śāriputra! This is because the mind, the intellect, and consciousness of a Tathāgata are all inexpressible. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata should be sought through wisdom; because wisdom is supreme, he is called the Tathāgata. This wisdom of the Tathāgata reaches the minds of all sentient beings, enters the intentions of all sentient beings, and does not depart from the consciousness of all sentient beings.

It incinerates all phenomena and all *samādhis*; it does not depend on other conditions and transcends all objective spheres of reference. It remains far removed from the three realms of existence born of dependent origination and cessation, surpasses all seeds of pride, liberates one from the works of Māra, and is free from all flattery and deception. Having abandoned the notions of "I" and "mine," it eradicates the film of ignorance and the darkness of delusion. It skillfully cultivates the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), is equal to space and without differentiation, and is non-distinct from the realm of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata enters into such mental activity, with such-characteristic wisdom as its precursor, preaching the Dharma in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, so that they may enter into the mental activity of the Tathāgata.
"Śāriputra! This is called the fifteenth unique Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata: mental action guided by wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How does the Tathāgata exercise unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past? Śāriputra,
for what reason is this knowledge called "turning"?

Śāriputra! By means of unimpeded wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know all the Buddha-lands throughout such immeasurable and boundless past ages—whether they were forming or decaying—and all those matters, being immeasurable and innumerable, the Tathāgata can skillfully enumerate and know them all.
In this way, even all things within the Buddha-fields—including all grasses, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs—the Tathāgata is able to fully know them all.
In this way, even throughout the lands of all Buddhas, he is able to fully comprehend all the signs of the provisional designations of "sentient beings" applied to the bodies of those beings.

Furthermore, he is able to fully comprehend the various dispositions and various complexions of all the numerous sentient beings therein; as it is explained at length, the Tathāgata is able to fully comprehend all of this.

Śāriputra! In this manner, regarding all the Buddhas who appear in the world therein, the Tathāgata is able to correctly discern and understand, exactly as they are, the true Dharma proclaimed by each and every one of those Tathāgatas.

In this way, even as many sentient beings as there may be who have been disciplined in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, or those disciplined in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or those disciplined in the Mahāyāna—all these the Tathāgata is able to fully know.

Furthermore, regarding the distinct characteristics of various Buddha-fields, such as the lifespan and duration of the Dharma of the bhikṣu-saṃghas, their inhalation and exhalation, and their consumption of food and drink—the Tathāgata is able to fully know all such distinct characteristics.
Śāriputra! Regarding the characteristics of all sentient beings in past lives—whether death or birth, whether realm or destiny—the Tathāgata is able to discern and know them all exactly as they are.
Furthermore, he is able to fully comprehend the various faculties, various temperaments, and various inclinations of all sentient beings; such immeasurable qualities he knows completely.

He is also able to discern the continuity of all minds—namely, that following such and such a mind, such and such a mind arises—and through his skillful means, the Tathāgata is able to calculate and know all these diverse mental characteristics, which are manifold and not one.

Śāriputra! Whether by means of direct knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) or subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdhajñāna*), the Tathāgata has realized the continuity of such past minds that have already ceased and passed away.
Having himself realized this knowledge in its entirety, he teaches the Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings, desiring to lead them to realize and enter into such knowledge as well.
"Śāriputra! This is called the sixteenth unique Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata: the unimpeded knowledge of the past.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How does the Tathāgata exercise unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding future worlds? Śāriputra,
for what reason is this knowledge called "turning"?

Regarding all Tathāgatas in future ages—whether they are yet to appear or have already entered parinirvāṇa, whether they will exist or will not exist—the Tathāgata fully understands all such characteristics.

In this way, even regarding the future fire calamity that will burn, the future water calamity that will destroy, and the future wind calamity that will destroy, as well as the various differences in the duration of stay and other such factors across all Buddha-lands of the future, the Tathāgata is able to know them all completely.

In this manner, even regarding all the lands of future buddhas—the various atoms of their earth elements, as well as all grasses, trees, forests, medicinal herbs, and other such things, up to the diverse and manifold colors and forms of the future constellations—the Tathāgata is able to know them all completely.

In this manner, even throughout each and every Buddha-field, the Tathāgata is able to know, exactly as they truly are, all the infinite characteristics of the future Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Bodhisattvas who appear in the world—including their enjoyments, whether food or drink; their inhalations and exhalations; and their modes of conduct, such as walking and standing.

In this way, even down to the specific differences in the transformative activities of each individual Tathāgata—observing the nature of sentient beings so that they may realize liberation, whether by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna—the Tathāgata is able to fully know them all.

In this manner, throughout all future worlds, in every single buddha-field, and regarding the distinctions among the birthplaces of as many sentient beings as there may be, the Tathāgata is able to fully comprehend all the minds and mental factors of those sentient beings.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata understands this thus according to reality: there is no future existence through the continuity of a distant mind; yet, by means of his observation of the future, the Tathāgata understands it according to reality.
Having realized it for himself, he also expounds this Dharma to sentient beings, desiring to cause them to realize and enter such wisdom.
Śāriputra, this is called the seventeenth unique Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata: unimpeded knowledge of the future.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does the Tathāgata exercise the unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present world?
Śāriputra, [it is as follows...]"
Why is this wisdom called "transformation"?

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata, within all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions in the present world, knows by means of three kinds of skillful means; he fully understands and comprehends the various distinctions among the present Buddhas, the assemblies of bodhisattvas, the assemblies of śrāvakas, and the assemblies of pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, he can thoroughly discern, within the present world, the colors and forms of the stars, as well as the various medicinal herbs, shrubs, and forests; even down to the minute dimensions of every atom within the entire earth-element throughout the ten directions of the present, the Tathāgata knows them all through his skillful means with perfect accuracy.

Śāriputra! The entire realm of water in all lands throughout the ten directions is inconceivable; yet the Tathāgata can lift every drop with a single hair-tip until none remains, and he is able to clearly understand and calculate such immeasurable quantities through his skillful means.
Furthermore, regarding the various manifestations of the flames arising from all fire realms throughout the lands of the ten directions, the Tathāgata knows them through skillful means.
Moreover, regarding all wind realms throughout the lands of the ten directions that arise based on the sphere of form, the Tathāgata is likewise able to know them through skillful means.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the various great voids of the lands in the ten directions, as numerous as the tips of hairs and not merely one, the Tathāgata knows by means of his skillful means exactly as they truly are. Śāriputra!

In this way, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands the three types of realms of sentient beings in the present, even unto the realm of hell-dwelling sentient beings in the present, as well as their causes for arising and their causes for emergence.
Furthermore, he knows the realm of present animal beings, being able to fully comprehend both the causes of their birth and the causes of their emergence.
It is likewise with the hosts of the realm of Yama.
He is also able to fully comprehend the realms of present human beings, being able to fully comprehend both the causes for their birth therein and the causes for their death and passing away.

Furthermore, they are able to discern the realms of sentient beings currently in the celestial destinies, understanding both the causes for their birth there and the causes for their death and passing away.
They are also able to discern the mental continuums of present sentient beings, whether they possess the nature of afflictions or are free from the nature of afflictions.

Furthermore, regarding the differences in the faculties of the sentient beings currently being transformed, as well as those who are not yet to be transformed—the differences in the faculties of all such immeasurable sentient beings—the Tathāgata is able to know them all exactly as they are.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata thus understands all phenomena of the present; it is not that the wisdom of the Tathāgata functions according to dualistic consciousness. For the sake of enabling all sentient beings to awaken to and enter into non-duality, he teaches this Dharma, so that they may realize such wisdom.
"Śāriputra! This is called the eighteenth unique Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata: the unimpeded knowledge of the present.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Because the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have accomplished these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are perfectly complete without exception throughout the worlds of the ten directions, their radiance streaming forth to illuminate the entire great assembly.
Furthermore, by virtue of this dharma—its rare and extraordinary majesty, renown, and meritorious qualities—it eclipses all the assemblies of the celestial Māras. Śāriputra!

The unique Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, boundless, and limitless, like space. Should anyone wish to seek the limits or measure of all the unique Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata, it would be no different from a person seeking the edge of space.

Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear that the unique buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata are inconceivable and like space, they accept them with faith and reverence, maintaining a mind of pure devotion, free from confusion or doubt; they leap for joy all the more, giving rise to profound gladness and a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The physical, verbal, and mental actions of the Guide Are free from error and without wavering;
By means of these very dharmas he guides sentient beings— This is the unique quality of the Tathāgata."

His mind is neither elated nor depressed; having ultimately transcended both hatred and attachment, he dwells eternally in non-contention where all strife is forever extinguished—this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
The Teacher is unforgetful regarding the Dharma and wisdom, Regarding liberation and his sphere of activity;
He likewise never loses the analytical knowledges— This is the unique quality of a Tathāgata.
Whether standing, eating, or walking, whether sitting or lying down, his mind is always concentrated;
free from distraction and devoid of the notion of a sentient being—this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
The Sugata, regarding all buddha-fields, sentient beings, and Buddhas, has no notion of difference;
abiding in the great realization of the nature of equality—this is the unique quality of a Tathāgata.
The supreme equanimity free from all discrimination arises from the thorough cultivation of the excellent path of definitive certainty;
being devoid of conceptualization and discursive differentiation, this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
The Great Master’s noble aspiration never declines; He is ever accompanied by compassion and skillful means.
Taming sentient beings on a vast and immeasurable scale— This is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.

The Sugata’s diligence never diminishes; observing the infinite number of beings to be converted, he disciplines all sentient beings through his three karmas—this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
The great mindfulness of all Buddhas has never diminished; seated upon the bodhi throne, they attain perfect awakening.
Having already awakened to the fact that all phenomena require no further awakening, this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
Without conceptualization or discursive differentiation, naturally abiding in the samādhi of equanimity,
and with no dependence on any dharmas of dhyāna— this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
The Guide’s wisdom is most auspicious; He thoroughly understands the conduct of all sentient beings.
He expounds the sublime Dharma according to their inclinations; This is the unique quality of a Tathāgata.
Hearing according to sound, the solitary realizers, and the supreme liberation of all Buddhas are unimpeded,
stainless, and like space; the Great Equanimity of the Sugatas is inconceivable,
for the Buddhas have originally no mind, their mental continuum being liberated by its very nature.
To preach the Dharma of liberation for the sake of the multitude— this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
When sentient beings behold with their own eyes the Buddha’s majestic deportment— whether he stands or walks as he enters a city—
the various manifestations of his marks, signs, and radiance cause all who see them to be tamed and to cultivate goodness.
The True Being emits rays of light, bringing peace and happiness to many koṭis of beings;
there is no sentient being whom these lights do not deliver—this is his supreme, uncommon quality.
The Sage spontaneously proclaims the sound of the Dharma, Which all beings hear and understand according to their own inclinations;
The sound of the Dharma they hear resonates like an echo— This is called the supreme, unique quality.
The Sugata, the Guide, has no mental karma; all the turning of karmic actions proceeds from wisdom.
That wisdom enters the minds of all sentient beings—this is called the supreme unique quality (āveṇika-dharma).
All samādhis and dhyānas, well-cultivated and perfected, free from conceptual proliferation,
abiding in the state of equality like space— this is called the supreme, uncommon quality.
Regarding all phenomena of the past, the wisdom that liberates from the various realms of existence—the Sugata’s sublime wisdom turns without obstruction; this is called the supreme unique quality.
Regarding those future worlds— whether they shall exist or not—
and their sentient beings, lands, and supreme ones, the Buddhas possess perfect clarity without exception.
As the Sugatas contemplate the future, their minds remain tranquil, never for a moment distracted.
To know sentient beings and phenomena as they truly are—this is called the supreme, unique quality (āveṇika-dharma).
Whatever exists flowing in the present world, the Supreme One knows all without obstruction;
the Guide’s sphere of activity is equal to space—this is called the Tathāgata’s unique quality.

The uncommon dharmas of the Tathāgata, These eighteen supreme, inconceivable qualities, Are like true suchness and reality itself, equal to space; Only the wise Bodhisattvas can believe and accept them.
“Śāriputra! This is called the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).

Because he has accomplished them, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, utters the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, declaring: ‘I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, or Brahmā in all the world can turn in accordance with the Dharma.’”

Śāriputra! Thus, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in pure faith, regarding the ten inconceivables of the Tathāgata and the ten kinds of inconceivable dharmas, accept them with conviction and venerate them with truth; their minds are pure, free from confusion or doubt, and they leap for joy, giving rise to deep gladness and a sense of wonder.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Forty;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Forty-one.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five: The Four Immeasurables, Part Seven of the Twelfth Assembly of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, Section on the Immeasurables.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in such pure faith, the Buddha Bhagavān knows that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is a vessel for the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka. Having known them to be true vessels for the Dharma of all Buddhas, he goes in person to their place to reveal and manifest the path of the bodhisattvas.”
Śāriputra! You should now understand these distinct characteristics of the Dharma-gate.

That is to say, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in pure faith, the Buddha Bhagavān recognizes that this bodhisattva is a vessel for the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; having recognized them as a true vessel for the Dharma of all Buddhas, he personally goes to their location to reveal the path of the bodhisattvas.

Śāriputra! In the past, beyond incalculable, vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Mahāskandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. Abiding in self-realization and endowed with supernormal powers, he proclaimed and expounded the sublime Dharma for a great assembly of immeasurable beings—including gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and asuras—making it clear, manifest, and thorough; excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; skillful in phrasing and meaning; pure, complete, and leading to the holy life.

Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha had seventy-two nayutas of śrāvaka disciples assembled together to hear the Dharma. They were all great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they had attained mastery over their minds and reached the supreme, ultimate shore.
Śāriputra! At that time, there was a king named Jyeṣṭhāyus who ruled the world with righteousness; he was known as King Dharmadhara.
His capital city was named Jyeṣṭhadhvaja, which was vast, magnificent, peaceful, prosperous, and exceedingly delightful. It was filled with people and teemed with bustling activity.

Śāriputra! At that time, King Jīvasena had a son named Vīryaprabhūta. He was of tender age, with a handsome and dignified appearance, endowed with the most perfect and pure physical form, and was a joy for all sentient beings to behold. He had already made offerings to and served hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas, attending upon them with reverence and planting the roots of all manner of goodness.

Śāriputra! At that time, the youth Vīryadatta went out with the ladies of the inner palace to visit the pleasure gardens. Then the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha, knowing that this youth was a vessel for the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and a vessel for the true Dharma of all Buddhas, proceeded to those gardens where Vīryadatta was.
Having arrived there, he ascended into the air and, for the sake of this youth, opened the way of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, he praised and spoke of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, saying: "Youth, you should know: what is called the 'way of the bodhisattva'?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivating the four immeasurable minds toward all sentient beings?
What are these four?
They are the perfection of great loving-kindness, the perfection of great compassion, the perfection of great sympathetic joy, and the perfection of great equanimity.
Furthermore, he diligently applies himself with vigor to training in accordance with the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Youth!
If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, it is called "opening the bodhisattva path."
"Furthermore, young man,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivate and train in the immeasurable perfection of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings?"

It is said that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they pervade the entire realm of sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness.
By what measure is the realm of sentient beings defined?
It is said that the entirety of the realm of empty space is the measure of sentient beings.

Young man, you should know that just as the realm of empty space pervades everywhere without exception, so too is the immeasurable great compassion of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; there is no kind of sentient being or conscious creature that it does not pervade.
Young man, you should know that just as the realm of sentient beings is without limit, so too is the loving-kindness cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva without limit.
Because space is boundless, sentient beings are boundless; because sentient beings are boundless, loving-kindness is also boundless.
Young man, you should know that the realm of sentient beings is vast, exceeding the realm of earth, and likewise exceeding the realms of water, fire, and wind.
I shall now explain a parable for you in detail, so that you may understand the meaning of the infinite extent of the realms of sentient beings.

Young man, you should know: suppose that in each of the ten directions there were as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and all of them simultaneously merged to form a single great ocean, filled with water.

Furthermore, suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River gathered together, who divided the tip of a single hair into one hundred and fifty parts, and together used one part to take up the very first drop of water from the great ocean.

Furthermore, there are other sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who assemble together as before and, using a single strand of hair, take up the second drop of water from the ocean.

Again, there are other sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who assemble together as before and, using a single strand of hair, take up the third drop of water from the ocean.

"Young man, you should know that even if one were to use this method of dipping with a hair-tip, it might be possible to exhaust all the water of this great ocean; yet the limit and measure of the nature of sentient beings are inexhaustible."
Therefore, you should know, O youth, that the nature of sentient beings is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, yet the compassion of the bodhisattva pervades them all.
"What do you think?
Is it possible to reach the limit of such immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness cultivated through loving-kindness and compassion?
The youth Vīryadatta replied to the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, young man! In the same way,
the roots of goodness cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva through loving-kindness pervade the realm of sentient beings and are thus immeasurable."
Furthermore, young man! I shall now further explain the characteristics of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

Young man, you should know that this immeasurable loving-kindness can protect one's own person; this loving-kindness thus gives rise to the benefit of others; among all forms of non-contention, loving-kindness is supreme; loving-kindness can sever the roots and sprouts of anger and resentment; loving-kindness can eternally extinguish all faults; and loving-kindness can distance one from the entanglements of craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*).
This loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is such that it perceives only the pure and superior virtues of sentient beings, without seeing their faults or transgressions.
Loving-kindness can transcend the affliction of burning distress; loving-kindness can cause the growth of happiness in body, speech, and mind.

The power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is such that one is not afflicted or harmed by any other; its nature is peaceful and secure, free from all fears. Through the power of the wholesome root of loving-kindness, one accords with the Noble Path. Loving-kindness can cause sentient beings who are full of anger, violence, and intolerance to give rise to pure faith; loving-kindness can rescue and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
By the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one does not grasp at the nature of weapons or staves; loving-kindness can lead all sentient beings toward liberation.

This loving-kindness can extinguish all evil and malice; it keeps one far removed from feigning dignified demeanor, flattery, hypocrisy, and coercive solicitation, while being able to increase gains, honor, and reputation.
By the power of loving-kindness, one is honored and revered by the celestial kings Brahmā and Śakra; by loving-kindness, one’s body is adorned with all majestic virtues.
Those who practice loving-kindness are praised together by the wise, and loving-kindness can protect all foolish beings.
By the power of this loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), accords with the path of Brahmā, and opens the way to liberation.

Loving-kindness serves as the foremost guide at the head of the Mahāyāna; it is able to encompass and direct all vehicles (*yāna*). Loving-kindness is able to accumulate an untainted mass of merit (*puṇya-skandha*); by the power of the excellence of loving-kindness, all beings have a reliance that no other meritorious deeds can equal.

Loving-kindness can adorn the thirty-two primary marks and the eighty secondary signs; loving-kindness can cause one to leave behind that which is base, contemptible, inferior, and characterized by impaired faculties; loving-kindness serves as a level path, a virtuous way, and the destination for returning to nirvana.

This loving-kindness can distance one from all evil realms and the eight difficult conditions; by the power of this loving-kindness, one finds joy in the bliss of the Dharma, and does not crave any wealth, noble rank, sovereignty, or objects of enjoyment.
By the power of this loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one practices giving with an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;

this loving-kindness can eliminate various kinds of false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*). Loving-kindness serves as the gateway and path by which all training in ethical discipline (*śīla*) proceeds; it can rescue and protect those who have transgressed the prohibitions. This loving-kindness can manifest the power of patience (*kṣānti*); it can distance one from all forms of pride, arrogance, and self-aggrandizement. It can initiate unshakable diligence (*vīrya*); it can cause the cultivation of correct skillful means (*upāya*) to reach swift completion. Loving-kindness can serve as the fundamental basis for all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis.
Loving-kindness enables the mind to transcend the afflictions and the blazing fires of existence; loving-kindness is the cause for the arising of all wisdom.
Because one is capable of hearing and retaining through immeasurable loving-kindness, all categories concerning oneself and others become entirely certain.
