Loving-kindness can dispel the afflictions that accord with Māra; by the power of this loving-kindness, one dwells together in peace and happiness.
Loving-kindness enables people to maintain their dignified deportment whether rising, standing, sitting, or reclining; loving-kindness can diminish all restless desires.

This loving-kindness is like a sublime fragrance anointed upon the body; this loving-kindness can clothe one in the raiment of shame and remorse; this loving-kindness can dispel all calamities, afflictions, and the evil destinies.

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can rescue and deliver all sentient beings; immeasurable great loving-kindness relinquishes one’s own happiness and is able to bestow peace and joy upon all sentient beings.
Such characteristics of immeasurable and inconceivable great loving-kindness, I shall now briefly explain.
"O Youth! This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s immeasurable perfection of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has accomplished this immeasurable great loving-kindness, they regard all sentient beings with constant benevolence and compassion, diligently seeking the True Dharma without weariness."
"Young man, you should know that the compassion of the śrāvakas can only save themselves, whereas the compassion of the bodhisattvas ultimately delivers all sentient beings.
Young man, you should know that the compassion directed toward sentient beings is that which is attained by bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon the Great Mind."
The compassion that takes phenomena as its object is attained by Bodhisattvas who are progressing toward noble conduct.
The compassion that is without an object is attained by Bodhisattvas who have realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. O Youth!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s immeasurable perfection of great loving-kindness.
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of great loving-kindness, their mind of loving-kindness pervades all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Vīryārambha-kumāra!
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s immeasurable perfection of great compassion?

Kumāra, you should know that because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva desires to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they must take great compassion as their guide, just as for a person, the out-breath and in-breath are the primary life-faculties."
In this same way, young man, it is also thus for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has realized the Great Vehicle: he must take great compassion as his guide.
Young man!
Just as all the treasures possessed by a wheel-turning monarch are preceded by the golden wheel,
so it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva, O youth! All the true dharmas of all Buddhas have great compassion as their guiding head.
"Furthermore, O youth!
For the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices great compassion (mahākaruṇā) to deliver all sentient beings, never ultimately abandoning any of them."
"O youth! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings? O youth!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice great compassion, they observe that all sentient beings are bound by the false view of a self and concealed by various evil views.

Having contemplated in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, thinking: "I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that they may forever sever the various fetters of the false view of a self-body and all such evil views."

"Furthermore, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that all sentient beings dwell in unreality, falsehood, and perversion; they falsely give rise to the notion of permanence amidst impermanence, the notion of pleasure amidst suffering, the notion of self amidst non-self, and the notion of purity amidst impurity."

"O youth! Having observed in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, thinking: 'I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that they may forever sever all false, unreal, and inverted views.'"
"Furthermore, O youth!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that sentient beings are deluded, inverted, and addicted to sensual desires; they even give rise to violence and oppression toward their own mothers and sisters, let alone toward other sentient beings."
Having observed these matters, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:
"Alas for the world! It can tolerate the assembly of the unholy, filled with those who commit evil deeds without shame."
He further thought: "Alas, what suffering!
How can these beings, who once dwelt in the mother’s womb, lay there in rest, and were born by emerging from the birth canal, now act in such a way without shame?"
Such sentient beings have suffered a profound and great loss and are most pitiable; their manifold faults and afflictions are utterly reprehensible. Why is this?

Because they are harmed by greed, hatred, and delusion, and further afflicted by ignorance, they abandon the True Dharma and dwell in what is not the Dharma; practicing evil dharmas, they fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Thus, because these sentient beings are led by their evil karma, they travel by improper paths wherever they go. Young man!

It is like a jackal in a cemetery, being chased and driven away by a pack of dogs; fleeing and seeking refuge, it comes upon a steep precipice, and being driven to its wits' end, it howls in the middle of the night.
In this way, young man!
Those sentient beings are likewise just like jackals.
Furthermore, young man!
It is like a person born blind who is pursued by a pack of dogs toward a great pit or ravine.
In this way, young man,
those sentient beings are just like one born blind.
Furthermore, young man!
It is, for example, like a pig in a latrine that wanders through filth and dung, eating it without ever feeling revulsion.
In this same way, young man!
Those sentient beings are likewise like pigs in a latrine. Such beings are most pitiable;

oppressed by the affliction of lust, they direct it toward both kin and strangers. Harmed by various defilements, they act as partisans of Māra, bound by Māra’s snare, enveloped in the net of delusion, and submerged in the mire of desire.

"O Youth! Having contemplated these matters, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion toward those sentient beings, thinking: 'I shall proclaim the sublime Dharma for them so that they may forever sever all desires and afflictions.'"

"Furthermore, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that all sentient beings are shrouded by the five hindrances and pierced by the arrows of desire; they are greedily attached to the six sense bases. Having seen forms with the eye, they cling to their appearances and cannot relinquish them. Likewise, regarding sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, and tangibles felt by the body, they cling to their characteristics and are unable to let go of them."

These sentient beings are mostly full of anger and mutual enmity; when they obtain what is beneficial, they call it their "good friend," but when they encounter what is not beneficial, they inflict harm upon one another.
These sentient beings are for the most part overcome by lethargy and drowsiness; they are weak, dull, and stupid, shrouded and obstructed by the film of ignorance.
These sentient beings are bound and fettered by unwholesome restlessness and regret, and their minds are constantly defiled by various evil afflictions.
These sentient beings are entangled by a web of doubt and are unable to reach certainty regarding the profound Dharma. Child!

Having observed this, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, thinking: "I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that they may forever sever all hindrances and coverings."

"Furthermore, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that sentient beings are afflicted by pride, afflicted by over-pride, afflicted by the pride of 'I', afflicted by overweening pride, and afflicted by false pride; they consider themselves superior to those who are inferior, and consider themselves the most excellent among their equals."

There are some sentient beings who conceive of form as the self, or even up to conceiving of consciousness as the self; regarding what they have not yet realized, they claim, "I have already realized it.

Relying upon this conceit, they fail to offer greetings when they ought to greet, and fail to prostrate when they ought to prostrate. They harbor no respect or compliance toward their elders and seniors, show no veneration or admiration for their honored teachers, and do not inquire of the wise: "What is wholesome? What is unwholesome?"
What should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated?
What should be done and what should not be done? What is with fault and what is without fault?
What is the path? What is samādhi? What is liberation?
Such dharmas as these they have never clearly understood, yet they merely reckon themselves to be superior and venerable.
Young man!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has observed this, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings, thinking: "I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that they may forever sever all seeds of arrogance."

"Furthermore, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that all sentient beings are bound by the fetters of craving; they are completely entangled by the servants, wives, concubines, sons, and daughters of craving; they are surrounded by what is meaningless and disadvantageous; they are shackled by various misfortunes and calamities; and they are obstructed by the pivotal gates of birth and death, such that they are unable to escape the realms of hell, animals, and the world of hungry ghosts and asuras."
Bound by the fetters of existence, they are unable to attain freedom and self-mastery. Young man!

Having observed this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, thinking: "I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that they may attain freedom and self-mastery, moving according to their will toward nirvāṇa."

"Furthermore, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that sentient beings are far removed from virtuous friends and are ensnared by evil associates. Because they draw near to such evil companions, they become addicted to all manner of unwholesome deeds—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, greed, malice, and wrong views—and thus establish themselves in these immeasurable evil karmas with blazing intensity."

"O Youth! Having observed in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, thinking: 'I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma to them, so that they may be gathered by virtuous friends, abandon the ten paths of unwholesome action, and come to fully uphold the ten paths of wholesome action.'"

"Furthermore, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that all sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and obscured by the darkness of nescience; they are inverted in their attachments, and regarding their own bodies, they hold fast and do not relinquish these infinite and immeasurable views: that there is a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, a person, a youth, a man, a transmigrator, an agent, an enjoyer, a self, and what belongs to a self."

"O Youth! Having observed thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, thinking: 'I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that their noble eye of wisdom may become pure, and so that they may forever sever all views.'"

"Furthermore, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he observes that all sentient beings delight in and are attached to the incessant flow and turning of birth and death; they are the executioners of the five aggregates, constantly and perpetually pursuing the prison of the three realms, never distancing themselves from their shackles and fetters, and not thinking of their release."

Having observed this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, thinking: "I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, so that they may be liberated from the executioner of the five aggregates, cross over the wilderness of birth and death, and emerge from the bonds of confinement within the prison of the three realms."
"Furthermore, young man,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he contemplates all sentient beings as arising from non-virtue, like a ball or a wheel, revolving in a circle without fixed direction."
Due to this karma, one transmigrates swiftly from this world to that world and from that world back to this world, rushing toward the five destinies and turning away from the path to Nirvāṇa.

"O Youth! Having contemplated these matters, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, thinking: 'I should preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them; I shall open the gates of the palace of Nirvāṇa and cause them to enter.'"
Thus it is, young man!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices great compassion, he contemplates the nature of sentient beings and gives rise to ten kinds of immeasurable great compassion.
Furthermore, young man:

Furthermore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten further modes of the transformation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). They are as follows: such great compassion arises because of being free from deceit, just as space is eternally transcendent.
Such great compassion arises from non-deception, for it emerges from the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Such great compassion is not initiated through hypocrisy or falsehood, for it emerges from a mind made upright by the path of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-mārga*).
Such great compassion arises because it is born from being free from crookedness, as it emerges by dwelling perfectly in a mind that is without crookedness.
Such great compassion arises because it is free from arrogance and timidity, as it skillfully brings about the transcendence of all sentient beings' pride and despondency.
Such great compassion arises from protecting others, for it emerges from the purity of one's own mind.
Such great compassion arises through firm wisdom, for it is forever free from all moving and unmoving minds, abiding excellently in the mind and being perfectly renounced.
Such great compassion arises by relinquishing one's own happiness, for it is the excellent renunciation that bestows happiness upon others.
Such great compassion arises out of a desire to bear the burden of all sentient beings, for it is the excellent renunciation of firm diligence.
"Furthermore, young man, the great compassion of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is immeasurable and possesses ten such modes of transformation.
That is to say, all departures via the Mahāyāna result from great compassion; for this reason, it is called 'great compassion. "
In this way, great compassion establishes all forms of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; for this reason, it is called "great compassion."
In this way, great compassion establishes the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

In this way, great compassion establishes the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the recollections (*anusmṛti*), the factors of awakening associated with common dharmas, as well as the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), the fundamental karma of joy, the successive stages of meditative concentrations, the ten paths of wholesome action, and even all the marks (*lakṣaṇa*)—all are explained in this manner. For these reasons, it is called "great compassion."
In this way, great compassion establishes the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom; for this reason, it is called "great compassion.

Young man, you should know that such great compassion performs its own function, performs its function well, and performs its function without deviation, acting as that which ought to be done for all sentient beings.
In this way, Great Compassion fulfills the wishes of all sentient beings; O Youth!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s immeasurable perfection of Great Compassion.

Because they have accomplished this perfection of great compassion, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas observe sentient beings situated in such a state, they give rise once again to profound pity and compassion toward them.
"Furthermore, Vīryacārin, what is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s immeasurable perfection of great joy? Young man,
you should know that when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva seeks unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, they practice great joy."
Such joy has immeasurable characteristics.
Young man, you should know that the joy of a bodhisattva is called the pure, sublime joy of recollecting all wholesome dharmas with gladness.
Why is this? Because regarding all wholesome dharmas, it possesses no nature of dejection, no nature of despondency, and no nature of weariness.
This joy is called being far removed from all worldly attachment to pleasure.
Why is this? Because it abides in the nature of delighting in all dharmas of bliss.
This joy causes the body within to be filled with gladness, making its strength courageous and sharp.
Why is this? Because wisdom brings awakening, which gladdens the mind and causes the heart to leap with joy.
This is the delight in the body of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because they delight in seeking signs and take pleasure in fine adornment;
thus, they take joy in hearing the Dharma without ever becoming weary.
Why is this? Because one delights in practicing correctly according to the Dharma.

Through this joy, one is enthusiastic toward the Dharma; one’s mind harbors no malice toward sentient beings; one delights in Bodhi and is able to have faith and understanding in the vast Dharma; and one gives rise to a mind that distances itself from the Lesser Vehicle.
This joy is called the joy of subduing stinginess. Why is this?
Because one practices giving to all who seek it.

Because of this joy, one embraces those who have transgressed the precepts with a heart of loving-kindness, maintains a mind that is always pure toward those who uphold the precepts, and furthermore, is able to purify one's own ethical discipline (*śīla*).

This joy is called the joy of security that transcends all fear of the evil realms; this joy is called the joy of the path of enduring the various evil words and vulgar speech of others; this joy is called the joy of non-retaliation.
Why is this? Because when encountering the gouging out of eyes, the cutting off of hands, the amputation of feet, or the severing of limbs, the mind is able to endure it.
This joy is called the joy of reverence and respect.
Why is this? Because toward all elders and seniors, he fully cultivates dignified deportment, bowing his body with reverence and prostrating himself with solemnity.
This joy is called "the constant expansion of a joyful countenance."
Why is this? Because their minds are harmonious and serene, they are free from frowning and are the first to speak in greeting others.
This joy is called the joy that is far removed from all feigned deportment, flattery, deceit, and forced solicitation.
Why is this? Because this joy is the path that leads toward the firm and authentic Dharma.
By means of this joy, one gives rise to profound affection and delight for all bodhisattvas, regarding them as if they were the Great Teacher, and [toward] the True...
One should give rise to a heart of love and joy toward the Dharma as toward one’s own body;
toward the Tathāgata, a heart of love and joy as toward one’s own life; toward the venerable teacher, a heart of love and joy as toward one’s parents;
toward all sentient beings, a heart of love and joy viewing them as an only child; and toward the ācārya and upādhyāya...

One should give rise to a heart of love and reverence for them as one does for one's own eyes; one should give rise to a heart of love and reverence for all correct practices as one does for one's own body and head;
one should give rise to a heart of love and reverence for the *pāramitās* as one does for one's own hands and feet;

one should give rise to a heart of love and reverence for the Dharma-preachers as one does for a multitude of precious treasures; and one should give rise to a heart of love and reverence for the sought-after True Dharma as one does for excellent medicine.
One should give rise to a heart of affection and joy toward those who point out one's faults and those who remind one of them, regarding them as if they were skilled physicians. Thus, young man,
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of immeasurable great sympathetic joy.
Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this perfection of great joy, they practice the bodhisattva path with constant gladness, diligently seeking the true Dharma without weariness or fatigue.
"Furthermore, Vīryacārin, what is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s immeasurable perfection of great relinquishment? Young man,
you should know that once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of sentient beings, they must practice great relinquishment."
It should be known that this equanimity is of three kinds.
What are these three? They are:
equanimity regarding afflictions, equanimity in protecting oneself and others, and equanimity regarding the timely and the untimely.
What is called the relinquishment of afflictions?

Young man, you should know that for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the mind does not become haughty when faced with honor and service, nor does it become dejected when faced with lack of honor and service;
if one receives offerings and sustenance, the mind does not become arrogant, and if one does not receive them, [the mind does not become dejected].
Nurturing the mind without any distress or agitation, one gives rise to the awakening of equanimity toward both those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them;
one attains excellent reputation without craving for it, and remains free from sorrow or grief when subjected to slander;
if reviled or censured, one’s resolve does not waver or retreat, and in the face of praise, one abides well within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); and regarding all matters of suffering...
The power of discerning wisdom (*prajñā*) possesses the force of contemplation upon impermanence and suffering regarding all pleasant things;
it abandons craving and desire, severs all ill-will, maintains equanimity toward both enemies and kin, remains without duality of mind toward both good and evil deeds,
harbors no conceptual observation regarding feelings of attachment or aversion, and remains impartial toward both pleasant and unpleasant reports.
Without giving rise to attachment, their minds are free from affection or aversion toward well-spoken or ill-spoken words;
they weigh equally the flavors of sensual desires and their underlying defects; they give rise to a mind of impartial faith and aspiration toward themselves and other sentient beings;
they have no lingering attachment to body or life; and [they treat] all beings—whether inferior, middling, or superior—with equanimity.

Arising from birth, it illuminates with equanimity; regarding phenomena that are hidden or manifest, it gives rise to the nature of equality; and regarding what is truth or not truth, its own essence is pure.
Thus it is, young man!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can naturally give rise to superior remedies, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s relinquishing of afflictions.
"Furthermore, young man!"
What is called "equanimity that protects both self and others"?

Young man, you should know that when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is having his body cut limb from limb and his skin and flesh sliced away by another, he constantly observes his own mind and abides in great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*). Although his limbs and flesh are being dismembered and cut, his inner mind dwells solely in equanimity without any expectation or pursuit. Even if various transformations arise in his body or speech, he is able to endure them all; this is what is called "equanimity that protects both self and others."
At that time, the Bodhisattva further contemplates two kinds of minds that are free from harm.
What are these two? They are:

not giving rise to a harmful mind through the characteristics of the eye and forms, and so on, up to not giving rise to a harmful mind through the characteristics of the mind and mental phenomena, but instead abiding in equanimity.
Why is this? To be without harm and without injury is what is called the equanimity of protecting oneself and others.
Furthermore, what is meant by the equanimity of protecting oneself and others?
Because one does not retaliate against those who have caused harm, being able to endure it both toward oneself and others, this is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Applying equal means toward all, whether they have been kind or unkind, is called equanimity.
This equanimity is called the equanimity of non-contention, the equanimity of extinguishing one's own mind, the equanimity of contemplating one's own nature, and the equanimity of not harming others.
Regarding various meditative objects, the Bodhisattva is able to practice this equanimity; however, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not permit Bodhisattvas to cultivate equanimity alone.

Why is this? A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should still cultivate all modes of conduct and activity, constantly maintaining mindfulness day and night to initiate diligence in seeking all wholesome dharmas; it is only at times that are neither [opportune nor inopportune] that they should practice equanimity.
"Furthermore, young man, what is meant by 'renunciation at the proper time and at the improper time'?

"Young man, you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, possessing great wisdom, is skillfully able to practice at the proper and improper times. This means: one should maintain equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward those sentient beings who are not vessels for the Dharma; one should maintain equanimity toward those who do not show respect; one should maintain equanimity toward those who cause harm through slander and affliction; and one should maintain equanimity toward those of the Śrāvaka vehicle who have attained the certainty of right resolve. When practicing generosity, one should set aside the cultivation of ethical discipline; when practicing ethical discipline, one should set aside the cultivation of generosity; when practicing patience, one should set aside the inducement of generosity, ethical discipline, and diligence; when practicing diligence, one should set aside the cultivation of ethical discipline; when practicing meditative concentration, one should set aside the perfection of generosity; and when cultivating wisdom, one should set aside the conditions that give rise to the other five perfections."
"O youth! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s relinquishing at the proper time and the improper time. Why is that?"
Because there is a nature of non-activity regarding that which should not be done, the bodhisattva deeply understands this and practices equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward what is unbeneficial.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the practice of the perfection of great equanimity while performing the bodhisattva conduct, they are then able to exercise great equanimity toward all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
"O youth, such characteristics as these are called the great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If any bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in these four immeasurable perfections, you should know that they are vessels for the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and furthermore, they are vessels for the true Dharma of all Buddhas."
"Thus it was, Śāriputra!

After this Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahāskandha, had extensively expounded these four immeasurables for the youth Vīryacaryā, he further explained the six pāramitās and the various means of integration (saṃgrahavastu), causing the youth to practice and study them accordingly."
"Śāriputra! This youth Vīryaprabha diligently practices the Dharma as he has heard it, in detail as will be explained below.
Chapter Six: The Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā) At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, diligently practice the perfections and carry out the conduct of a bodhisattva?”
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of a bodhisattva, they diligently train in these six pāramitās; this is what is called practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra! What are called the six pāramitās? Śāriputra!

They are: the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Śāriputra! These are called the six pāramitās.
It is by relying on these six pāramitās that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the bodhisattva path by relying on the perfection of dāna?
Śāriputra, [it is as follows:]..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they act as a donor for all beings.

Should śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others come seeking anything, they give it all away: to those who need food, they give food; to those who need drink, they give drink; and there are no rare delicacies or exquisite dishes that they do not give in full.

In this way, whether they seek vehicles, clothing, flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense; or seats, beds, recliners, couches, mats, bedding, medicines for illness, lamps, music, or male and female slaves; or they seek gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and other such treasures; or they seek elephants, horses, chariots, gardens, groves, ponds, men, women, wives, concubines, wealth, grain, and storehouses; or they seek sovereignty over the four great continents with all their instruments of pleasure and various objects for play and entertainment; or there are those who come seeking hands, feet, ears, noses, heads, eyes, flesh, blood, marrow, or limbs—the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, upon seeing such seekers, is able to joyfully bestow everything upon them.

Śāriputra! To state it briefly, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice great giving, they give everything that is required by all in the world; whenever they see someone come to beg, there is nothing they do not bestow.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), there are ten further types of pure giving.
What are these ten?
First, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice giving by seeking wealth through improper means;
second, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice giving by coercing sentient beings;
third, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice giving out of fear; fourth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon...
Fifth, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives gifts without looking at the faces [of the recipients];
sixth, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives gifts with no discriminatory thoughts toward sentient beings;
seventh, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives gifts without a mind of greedy attachment.
Eighth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without giving rise to anger;
ninth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without seeking a buddha-field;
tenth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva conceives of all sentient beings as fields of merit and practices giving without treating them with contempt.
Śāriputra! These are called the ten kinds of pure giving practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the purpose of fulfilling the perfection of dāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna, there are ten further types of pure giving.
What are the ten? First, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without disparaging the retribution of karma;
second, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without a crooked mind; third, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [is without...]
1) Giving while lacking faith and understanding; 2) giving while lacking faith and understanding; 3) giving while lacking faith and understanding;
fourth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives while free from weariness; fifth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives while free from manifesting signs;
sixth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives with courageous and fervent exertion; seventh, the bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva practices giving without regret or remorse; eighth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not practice giving out of partiality toward those who uphold the precepts;
ninth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not practice giving with contempt for those who violate the precepts; tenth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not...
They practice giving with the hope for a karmic reward. Śāriputra,
these are called the ten kinds of pure giving practiced by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of dāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna, there are ten further ways of practicing pure giving."
What are the ten? First, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice giving with disparagement;
second, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice giving with averted face; third, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has no...
Fourth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without manifesting signs of anger;
fifth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without manifesting signs of envy;
sixth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without manifesting signs of malice; seventh, the bodhisattva...
Eighth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva never fails to practice giving with profound reverence;
ninth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva never fails to give with his own hands;
tenth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give little after having promised much; and eleventh, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not seek [rewards] in future lives.
He practices giving.
Śāriputra, these are called the ten kinds of pure giving practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of dāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna,
there are ten further ways of practicing pure giving."
What are the ten?
First, the bodhisattva mahāsattva never fails to give constantly; second, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives without attachment;
third, the bodhisattva mahāsattva... [text continues]

1. Giving without discrimination. 2. The bodhisattva mahāsattva gives without external conditions. 3. The bodhisattva mahāsattva gives without meager intent. 4. The bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without desiring wealth, beauty, or power. 5. The bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without seeking rebirth among the great devas such as Śakra, Brahmā, or the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). 6. The bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without dedicating [the merit] toward the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. 7. The bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving so as not to be censured by the wise. 8. The bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without failing to dedicate [the merit] toward sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Śāriputra! These are called the ten kinds of pure giving practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of dāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), there are ten further ways of practicing pure giving.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
among the ten kinds of dharmas previously mentioned, there is the renunciation of the conditioned and the realization of the unconditioned.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice giving in this manner, they are able to attain ten kinds of praiseworthy, beneficial, and sublime merits. What are these ten?

First, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give food, they obtain longevity, eloquence, peace and happiness, exquisite physical form, and heroic strength and vigor, all of which they possess in full measure.
Second, by giving drinks, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas obtain the permanent departure from all thirst of afflictions, such that nothing is incomplete.
Third, by giving various vehicles, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas obtain all matters of benefit and peace, such that nothing is incomplete.
Fourth, by virtue of giving clothing, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the perfection of shame and modesty; his skin becomes pure like the color of gold, and nothing is lacking.

Fifth, by virtue of giving fragrant garlands, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas obtain pure ethical discipline, extensive learning, all samādhis, and the holy practice of ointments and perfumes, such that none are incomplete.

Sixth, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the giving of powdered incense and unguents, they shall attain the holy conduct of pervasive bodily fragrance and purity, which will be fully perfected in every respect.
Seventh, by virtue of giving superior flavors, the bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains the supreme flavor of ambrosia and the marks of a great man, all of which are fully perfected.

Eighth, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the giving of houses and dwellings, they shall become a shelter, a home, a refuge, an island, a resort, and a destination for all sentient beings, possessing these qualities in their entirety.

Ninth, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas compassionately bestow medicine upon the sick, they shall attain freedom from old age, illness, and death, and achieve the perfect, ambrosial, and deathless wondrous medicine, lacking nothing.

Tenth, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice giving with various kinds of life-sustaining requisites, they attain all perfectly complete requisites for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), none of which are lacking.

Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of this giving for the sake of attaining awakening, by which they obtain these ten kinds of praiseworthy, beneficial, and sublime merits; all of these are for the purpose of fulfilling the dānapāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and cultivates generosity, they further attain ten kinds of praiseworthy, beneficial, and sublime merits."
What are the ten?
First, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives the gift of lamp-light, they obtain the Tathāgata’s five pure eyes, all of which are fully perfected.
Second, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give music, they obtain the Tathāgata’s pure divine ear, which is fully perfected without exception.

Third, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give gold, silver, maṇi-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and all manner of rare treasures, they bring forth the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, which are fully perfected without exception.

Fourth, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice giving various kinds of miscellaneous jewels and many varieties of famous flowers, they obtain the eighty minor marks in their entirety, without anything being incomplete.
Fifth, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the giving of elephant and horse carriages, he obtains a vast multitude of followers and numerous retinues, all of whom are fully complete.

Sixth, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give away gardens, groves, and palatial towers, they attain and perfect meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis, such that none are incomplete.
Seventh, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives away wealth, grain, and treasuries, he attains the perfect accomplishment of the treasury of all dharmas, such that nothing is lacking.
Eighth, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives away slaves, servants, and laborers, he attains the perfection of sovereign physical and mental ease, such that nothing is lacking.

Ninth, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives away sons, daughters, wives, and concubines, he attains the perfect, lovely, delightful, and pleasing state of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is entirely complete.

Tenth, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives away all royal thrones of sovereignty over the four continents, he attains the subtle, perfect, and complete knowledge of all modes—the knowledge of all-knowledge—without anything being lacking.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving in this way, it is called the gathering of ten kinds of praiseworthy, beneficial, and sublime merits, all for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of dāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna for the sake of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they cultivate giving and further obtain ten kinds of praiseworthy benefits."
What are the ten?

First, because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives away the five excellent sensual desires, they obtain the pure aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, all of which are fully complete.
Second, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give exquisite musical instruments as gifts, they obtain pure joy in the play of the Dharma, which is entirely complete and without deficiency.

Third, because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the giving of their feet, they attain the perfection of legs that embody the meaning of the Dharma; proceeding toward the seat of enlightenment, there is nothing they lack.

Fourth, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the giving of his hand, he attains the perfection of pure Dharma-hands to rescue and deliver sentient beings, such that nothing remains incomplete.
Fifth, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives away his ears and nose, he attains the perfection of all sense faculties, such that none are incomplete.
Sixth, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives away his limbs and joints, he attains the pure, unstained, and majestic body of a Buddha, such that none of its features are incomplete.

Seventh, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the gift of his eyes, he attains the pure Dharma-eye that beholds all sentient beings, which is free from obstruction and fully perfected in every respect.

Eighth, because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the giving of flesh and blood, they obtain a firm and enduring body and life, and they fully possess the true and skillful means that gather in, sustain, and nourish all sentient beings.
Ninth, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives marrow and brain as a gift, he obtains a perfect, indestructible, adamantine body that is fully endowed with all qualities.

Tenth, because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives away his head as an offering, he realizes and attains the perfect, unsurpassed, and supreme head of all-knowledge that transcends the three realms, which is entirely complete and without deficiency.

Śāriputra! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice such giving for the sake of attaining bodhi, they embrace such characteristics and fulfill the Buddha-dharmas—those praised, beneficial, and sublime merits—all for the purpose of bringing the dāna-pāramitā to completion.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna, his nature is sagacious and his wisdom is profoundly deep. He practices giving through immeasurable skillful means, seeking the wealth of the noble kings—the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—by means of worldly wealth; seeking the immortal wealth of the sages—the nectar of immortality—by means of the wealth of saṃsāra; and seeking the firm and substantial wealth of the noble ones by means of deceptive wealth. It is for these reasons that he extensively practices giving."

Śāriputra! For the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa, when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice giving with worldly wealth and goods, there are no worldly riches or objects of enjoyment that they do not relinquish entirely.
Why is this? Because they all rely upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Śāriputra!

Just as a worldly farmer, having plowed the earth with his oxen, sows the seeds; so too does this farmer, relying on the implements of the plow and through immeasurable effort, successively obtain gold, silver, mani-jewels, and all manner of precious objects, as well as various kinds of exquisite garments.
Why is this? Because there are no material goods in all the worlds that equal [the value of] grain and the like.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
It is likewise, Śāriputra, that at certain times and on certain occasions, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening by relying upon worldly wealth.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:

For example, just as a dairy cow—whether eating dry grass or wet grass, or drinking cold water or warm water—is able to produce milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and even the finest cream (sarpis).
In this way, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the giving of worldly wealth based on unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they are able to obtain, according to their aspirations, the retribution of a wheel-turning monarch as well as the superior retribution of Śakra or Brahmā.

By accomplishing these three kinds of retributions, the Bodhisattva’s ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are swiftly brought to fulfillment; likewise, through this giving, the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*daśabala*) and four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) are swiftly fulfilled. Furthermore, one fulfills the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) arising from a thousand karmas; one also possesses the sixty kinds of perfect, wondrous voice arising from a thousand karmas; one possesses each of the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) arising from a hundred karmas; one possesses the mark of the invisible crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*) arising from two hundred karmas; one surpasses this by a hundredfold in the perfect accomplishment of the mark of the great Dharma-conch of the Tathāgata; and one surpasses it by a hundred-thousand *koṭi*-fold in the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s mark of white teeth that are even, complete, without gaps, and perfectly aligned.

Such characteristics as these are composed of immeasurable meritorious deeds; they all arise from the Tathāgata’s performance of acts that result in karmic retribution, through which they are swiftly brought to full perfection.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna, they give gifts while giving rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward those who beg; this mind continues to arise until it is fulfilled after as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, during which time the Buddha-samādhi remains uninterrupted."

Śāriputra! Having dwelt in this samādhi, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to produce one hundred samādhis from each and every pore, attaining mastery such that they flow forth unceasingly like the great river Gaṅgā.
Therefore, you should know that all the supernatural powers and transformations of the Tathāgata are for the most part accomplished through the practice of giving. Śāriputra,
all such Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata are encompassed by the worldly gifts of material wealth given while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past.

Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the gift of material wealth. When seeking the nectar of immortality, seeking the solid and enduring, seeking awakening, and seeking nirvāṇa, one should understand the distinctions within this Dharma gateway in this way.
It is said that because a bodhisattva mahāsattva relies on the giving of worldly wealth and accords with the dānapāramitā, they realize the awakening of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna,
its aspects are immeasurable; I shall now explain them."

In the past, incalculable, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, at that time there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Paṅkajirasi Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Śāriputra, that Buddha remained in the world for a lifespan of ten thousand years, and he was joined by an assembly of one hundred thousand bhikṣus who were great śrāvakas; all were arhats, free from all afflictions, possessed of great power, and had attained mastery over their minds, reaching the ultimate excellence.
"Śāriputra! At that time, there was a spinner in that world named Weft-Weaver (Tantravāya), whose physical appearance was upright and handsome, such that all who beheld him found him pleasing.

His place of work was not far from the Buddha; every day at dusk, when he was about to return home, he would go to the Buddha’s dwelling and habitually offer a single fine thread to the Tathāgata, then address the Buddha, saying:"
“May the Bhagavān, out of compassion for me, accept these threads as an object of his grace.
By this root of goodness, may I, in a future age, attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and be able to gather all beings.”
Then that World-Honored One accepted it.
Thus, he offered one thread each day until fifteen hundred had been fully gathered as a virtuous offering.

By virtue of this merit, for fifteen *koṭi* kalpas he did not fall into the evil realms; furthermore, for a thousand *koṭis* of times he became a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), and for another thousand *koṭis* of times he became Śakra, Lord of the Devas.

By means of these roots of goodness—consisting of such activities as gentleness, subtlety, and joyful affection—he was able to attend upon and behold a thousand koṭis of Buddhas. At the abodes of those Buddhas, he made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise; furthermore, he presented to the Tathāgatas all manner of things, including various flowers, unguents, powdered incense, fragrant garlands, silk canopies, banners and pennants, clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for illness.

After this, having appeared in the world once again after the passing of one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, he realized the awakening of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He was named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān, known as Śubhasaṃgraha. He remained in the world for a lifespan of twenty *koṭi* years, and he had a community of twenty *koṭi-nayuta* great śrāvakas, all of whom were great arhats.

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, having established and settled five koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and having expounded the sublime Dharma for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, has now entered parinirvāṇa.

After that Blessed One has passed into parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for a full one thousand years; his relics shall be widely distributed and offered everywhere, just as they are now after my own parinirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! You should now observe that by giving a single thread and generating the great resolve, one successively and progressively brings the Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment. Śāriputra!
One should know that this generosity arises from the vastness of the mind and not from the thread itself. Why is this?
If generosity were vast without being due to the mind, then as in the previous case where a donor gave a tiny thread, one would not attain the ultimate purity of mind.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
You should observe that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dāna, by relying upon the gift of worldly wealth, they attain all perfect merits.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), his nature is sagacious and his wisdom is profoundly deep; through a small gift he accomplishes much. By the power of his intellectual strength, his accomplishments are superior; by the power of his wisdom, his accomplishments are vast; and by the power of dedication (pariṇāmanā), his accomplishments are boundless.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"One who practices giving does not seek exquisite forms or wealth, nor does one wish to be reborn in the realms of devas or humans;
seeking instead the unsurpassed, supreme Bodhi, even a small gift brings forth immeasurable merit."

One practices generosity without seeking fame or renown, nor for the sake of pleasure or a following, nor for the retribution of various births and deaths; though the gift be small, one obtains a great fruit.
Giving food, drink, and clothing, one does not seek existence in any realm or destiny;
seeking instead to open the gateway to the nectar of liberation, the merit of such giving is as immeasurable as the tip of a hair.
Free from agitation and arrogance, and likewise devoid of deceit, hypocrisy, stinginess, and envy,
having completely abandoned all causes for indolence, he exerts himself solely in the practice of giving for the benefit of the world.

Wealth, grain, royal sovereignty, and even one’s own life—having joyfully relinquished these with an unchanging mind, one who practices such noble giving attains vast merit; for them, awakening and liberation are not difficult to achieve.
He loves all who come to beg, regarding them as his father, mother, or wife;
whatever wealth he acquires, he constantly practices giving, and seeing others obtain riches, he feels no envy.

When practicing generosity, the crowd was vast and tumultuous; though they came to inflict harm with clods of earth, staves, and wooden clubs, he never gave rise to a heart of anger even upon seeing them, but spoke with loving words as before, his mind filled with joy.
If one gives to those enemies as if to kin, bestows fearlessness upon those who are terrified,
and is able to relinquish all possessions, yet the mind never gives rise to stinginess or parsimony.
Always delighting in the constant pursuit of the unsurpassed Dharma, they have severed all longing for worldly sovereignty;
having departed from the fineries of the world, they always diligently practice the giving of the Dharma.
Aside from those who seek after defiled desires, who could possibly seek the sovereignty of the world of gods?
Therefore, the wise do not crave the pleasures of desire, nor the rank of kingship, nor the bliss of rebirth in heaven.
The practice of giving by those of great renown is always sought for the sake of unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment;
by relinquishing body, life, and all other things, they are swiftly able to bring forth abundant peace and happiness.
The wise Bodhisattva practices all forms of giving, never departing from supreme enlightenment;
they do not seek exquisite forms or worldly wealth, nor do they desire the pleasures of rebirth in heaven.
Though seeking nirvāṇa, one has no dependence; having distanced oneself from all hopes and desires, if one can thus practice skillfully, one is called a knower of the Way and an opener of the Way.
“Śāriputra! The wise bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully accomplished this perfection of giving, is well able to practice the sublime conduct of a bodhisattva without any doubt.”
Śāriputra, this is called the dānapāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If all bodhisattva mahāsattvas, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, diligently practice these bodhisattva deeds, then no māras, nor the māra-subjects, nor the sons of gods will be able to disturb them; furthermore, they cannot be defeated or overthrown by the heterodox paths or the doctrines of others.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 41;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 42.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 7: The Perfection of Ethical Discipline (Śīlapāramitā). Section Twelve of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Part Eight.
Chapter Seven, Part One: The Perfection of Ethical Discipline. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"What is the śīlapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
relies upon this to diligently practice the bodhisattva path. Śāriputra!
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), there are three kinds of sublime conduct. What are these three?
First, sublime conduct of body; second, sublime conduct of speech; and third, sublime conduct of mind.
Śāriputra, what are called the sublime conduct of body, the sublime conduct of speech, and the sublime conduct of mind?
Śāriputra, they are as follows:
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct, this is called the sublime conduct of body.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva stays far removed from false speech, stays far removed from divisive speech, stays far removed from harsh speech, and stays far removed from frivolous speech, this is called excellent conduct of speech.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is entirely devoid of all attachment, ill will, and wrong views, this is called sublime conduct of the mind.
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are fully endowed with these three kinds of sublime conduct, this is called the Śīla-pāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they reflect in this way:
"What are the sublime conduct of body, the sublime conduct of speech, and the sublime conduct of mind?"
"Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:
'If one does not engage in the bodily actions of killing, taking what is not given, or sexual misconduct, this is called excellent conduct of the body.'"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus:
"If one refrains from the karmic actions of lying, divisive speech, harsh words, and frivolous chatter, this is called excellent conduct of speech."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus:
"If the mind does not create karma characterized by greed, hatred, or wrong views, this is called excellent mental conduct."
Because he possesses such right reflection, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they form this thought:
"If an action is not performed by means of body, speech, or mind, can that action be established?"

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva investigates in this manner according to reality, if an action were not created by body, speech, or mind, that action could not be established as being blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, or crystal-colored."
Furthermore, this karma is not cognized by the eye, nor cognized by the ear, nor cognized by the nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Why is this so? Śāriputra!

Because this karma is neither the producer nor the produced, nor has it been produced; because it cannot be grasped and there is absolutely no one capable of cognizing this karma, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands that the nature of this śīla is non-actionable. If it is non-actionable, it cannot be established; if it cannot be established, we should not harbor attachment toward it.

In this way, by the power of contemplative understanding, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive sublime conduct or ethical discipline (śīla), nor does he perceive one who possesses ethical discipline, nor does he perceive the destination to which ethical discipline is dedicated.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has contemplated in this way, they ultimately do not give rise to the false view of a self-existent body.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Because of the existence of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), there can be observation: "This is the observance of precepts; this is the transgression of precepts.

Having observed in this way, one acts with full situational awareness (saṃprajanya) regarding both conduct and its objects, as well as in the protection [of the senses] and in formal decorum. Because one acts with such full situational awareness, one is called a "precept-keeper" (śīlavat).
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices by neither grasping at a self nor grasping at others; he practices by neither violating the precepts nor grasping at the precepts.
If one grasps at a self, one then grasps at ethical discipline (*śīla*); if one does not grasp at a self, one does not grasp at ethical discipline.
If one knows that ethical discipline is unapprehendable, one will not transgress any of the vows of restraint.
If one does not commit any transgression against the discipline, one is neither said to have violated the śīla, nor is one said to be grasping at the śīla. Śāriputra!
For what reason is one not grasping at this ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
It is because all phenomena are known to have the characteristic of otherness (*paralakṣaṇa*).
If, by virtue of the characteristic of otherness, there is no self (*ātman*), then if the self is non-existent, what is there to be grasped?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke in verse: "If one’s body, speech, and mind are pure, If one constantly cultivates all purities while acting,
And always abides in the pure prohibitions and precepts— This is called a bodhisattva endowed with śīla."

The wise and sagacious bodhisattvas, who are able to skillfully uphold the ten paths of action, do not perform them through body, speech, or mind; such is what the wise call ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If it is neither conditioned nor born, Neither grasped, formless, nor manifest—
Because it lacks form and manifestation, It can never be apprehended or established.

Śīla is unconditioned and without action; it cannot be seen by the eye nor heard by the ear, nor can it be perceived by the nose, the tongue, or the body, nor can it be cognized by the mind or consciousness.
If it is not cognized by the six sense faculties, then there is no one capable of designating it;
observing ethical discipline (*śīla*) in this way, one has never relied upon or clung to ethical discipline.
Do not rely on the observance of precepts to give rise to arrogance; do not harbor the notion of a self while guarding the śīla.
Guarding the śīla well without the thought of "precepts," one fulfills the śīla and practices the path of awakening.
The false view of a self has already been dispelled; neither the seeing nor the seer ever exists.
There is no one who sees, nor is there any place [of seeing]; one does not observe those who keep or violate the precepts.
Skillfully entering the principle of the dharma that is without protection, Possessing inconceivable perfection of dignified conduct,
Able to guard through wondrous goodness and correct awareness— Apart from this, there is no one else who possesses the precepts.

One who lacks the perception of self has no ethical discipline; one who relies on the precepts without a basis of "I" is said by me to be ultimately and eternally fearless, for they do not cling to a body, a self, or ethical discipline.
Those who preach non-self do not grasp at precepts; those who preach non-self have no reliance on precepts;
those who preach non-self do not hope for precepts; those who preach non-self have no mind toward precepts.
Not violating the precepts, yet not clinging to them; Nor conceiving of a self that gives rise to the precepts.
Free from any dependence on notions of self or precepts, One practices the profound wisdom and the conduct of awakening.
Such ethical discipline is fearless; this person never violates the precepts.
If one can refrain from grasping at the existence of phenomena, such ethical discipline is praised by the Noble Ones.
If foolish people dwelling in the view of self reckon that they possess the precepts and are able to maintain them,
once they have exhausted the fruits of receiving and guarding those precepts, they will remain perpetually bound within the three evil realms.
If one has completely severed all views of a self, Therein exists neither "I" nor "mine";
Because they truly uphold the precepts without such views, They shall no longer fear falling into the various evil realms.
If one can understand the practice of ethical discipline in this way, there is no one who can see a transgression of the *śīla*;
since one does not even perceive a self or the three realms of existence, how much less could one see the observance or the violation of ethical discipline?
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) performs the bodhisattva conduct of pure morality, they possess ten kinds of extremely profound and deep resolve."

What are these ten? First, to give rise to a profound resolve and have faith in all practices; second, to give rise to a profound resolve and apply oneself with diligent vigor; third, to be fiercely determined and delight in the true Dharma of the Buddhas; fourth, to extensively possess reverence for all karmic actions; fifth, to deeply cherish and have faith in all karmic fruits and retributions; sixth, to develop a heart of deep respect toward all noble ones and sages; seventh, to serve one’s venerable upādhyāyas and ācāryas with pure devotion; eighth, to offer worship to those who are noble and saintly; ninth, to earnestly seek and request the true Dharma; and tenth, when seeking bodhi, to disregard both body and life.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices ethical discipline (*śīla*) in this manner possesses these ten qualities of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
Abiding in the profound mind, the bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
What are called all wholesome dharmas?
They are the three kinds of excellent conduct:
excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech, and excellent conduct of mind.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these three kinds of sublime conduct, it is because they desire to diligently seek the subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka. Why is this?
"Because by relying on this Dharma-gate, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to proceed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"From the body one initiates The wholesome karma praised by the Buddhas."
In order to hear the Dharma, one makes offerings to all the worthy and noble ones.
Toward the Dharma and the sages, one rouses fierce diligence and reverence;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, one maintains a heart of loving-kindness free from envy.
One should speak as a wise person speaks; do not utter words that are unpleasant.
What is said should be characterized by joy, and one's speech should never be coarse or vulgar.
One’s mental karma should always abide in goodness, never taking pleasure in various evils.
Constantly observing the nature of phenomena, Dwelling with reverence and a mind of loving-kindness;
Toward the holy teaching of the Tathāgata, Listening to the Dharma with a respectful heart;
Having cultivated reverence for the Dharma, One will swiftly awaken to great bodhi.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they abide in these ten supreme dharmas. Because they diligently seek the Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they apply themselves with great reverence to honoring, serving, and making offerings to all noble ones and their teachers, even to the extent of giving them vessels for storing water.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they should possess these ten kinds of mental resolve. What are the ten?

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates this diseased body as a collection of various elements like venomous snakes that are constantly at odds and harmful to one another; it is filled with manifold sufferings and afflictions, and abounds in calamities and misfortunes, being a gathering place for insanity, boils, carbuncles, scabs, malignant sores, and the various diseases of wind, heat, and phlegm.

Furthermore, this body is like a disease, like an ulcer, like being pierced by an arrow, like a torrential flood, and like an executioner; it vibrates without ceasing, arising and perishing with great speed.

Furthermore, he contemplates this body as false and deceptive, frail and weak, worn out by old age and subject to decay; it remains for but a brief moment, difficult to find pleasure in, resembling a cemetery.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflects:
"Although this sickly body of mine has endured such suffering, I have never before encountered a field of merit such as this."

Having now encountered this opportunity and having further obtained such a body through wholesome karma, I shall rely upon the fields of merit to nourish my life of wisdom; I shall relinquish this non-solid body to attain a solid body.

Desiring to diligently seek the subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one should serve and make offerings to those noble masters—upādhyāyas and ācāryas—even providing them with water vessels for their use.
“Śāriputra! This is called the first production of the thought of enlightenment by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The various elements are like violent, venomous snakes, Mutually dependent upon one another;
If even one stirs with increased agitation, Its arising brings about great calamity.
These are what are called the eye, ear, and nose, The tongue, teeth, and the internal organs."
All such afflictions and distresses arise entirely dependent upon the body.
Boils, abscesses, and insanity; carbuncles, scabs, and great epidemics—among all these various ailments, there are none that do not arise dependent upon the body.
This body is like a disease, like an abscess, like one struck by an arrow;
such a body, poisoned and harmful, quickly decays and stays but for a moment.
Like approaching a cemetery, it is entirely characterized by impermanence.
This body is like a rattle-drum, decaying and falling apart; all manner of diseases swiftly arise and perish.
I shall cultivate the Buddha-body through the causes of noble and wholesome karma;
for this body is withered, rotten, and decaying—an aged and impermanent form.
It is transformed into the Buddha-body and the inconceivable Dharma-body.
By means of such a decaying body, one that is constantly pervaded by impurities,
one shall realize such a body that is free from outflows and free from defilement.
If a person fears cold and heat, And shields themselves with firm protection,
In the end they are still tormented by the suffering Of old age,
sickness, and death. But if a person, regarding cold and heat, Is able to endure them throughout the body, [they are not harmed].
Adorning the deeds of a Great Being, may I swiftly achieve the Unsurpassed Body.
I shall diligently make offerings to those honored by the world,
exchanging this unsubstantial body for that which is substantial.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated such supreme states of mind as these, they—desiring to diligently seek the subtle dharma-gates of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka—serve and provide diligent offerings to the Dharma-preachers even more extensively, up to and including the gift of water vessels.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:
'The body is of an unstable nature and is not solid; it must be provisionally covered, washed, and massaged, yet it ultimately returns to the state of destruction, dispersion, and extinction.'"
"Śāriputra! It is just as when a potter fashions earthenware vessels from clay; whether large or small, they all ultimately end in destruction.
In the same way, Śāriputra!"
Being inherently unstable, they ultimately perish, just like a clay vessel.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is like the flowers, leaves, and fruits that depend upon the branches of a tree; they all eventually fall away.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The body is unsubstantial and subject to inevitable fall; its momentum cannot endure for long, like a ripe fruit, for example.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as dewdrops and frost gather upon the tips of blades of grass and must inevitably vanish when struck by the scorching rays of the sun,
so too, Śāriputra, this body is insubstantial; like those drops of dew and frost, it does not endure for long.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is like the great ocean and its many rivers, where there are masses of foam that are entirely insubstantial; their nature is so fragile that they cannot withstand being touched.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This body is insubstantial, like a mass of foam; its nature is likewise frail and weak.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as when it rains heavily from heaven, bubbles surge and drift about, slowly rising and slowly vanishing; even so, Śāriputra,
this body is unsubstantial like a bubble upon the water, and its nature is likewise light and fragile.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva deeply contemplates his own body and perceives this matter, he further reflects:
"Throughout the long night, I have obtained such an impermanent body, yet I have never before encountered such a field of merit."

Having now encountered this opportunity and having further attained such a body as this, I shall rely upon the fields of merit to nurture my life of wisdom. Trading this non-durable body for a durable one, and desiring to diligently seek the subtle Dharma-gates of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall serve and make offerings to the Dharma-preachers, even down to giving them vessels for holding water.
"Śāriputra! This is called the second production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Just as the various potters of the world, Fashioning clay into vessels,
Must all eventually meet with destruction, So too is the life of sentient beings.
It is like the leaves, flowers, and fruits That depend upon the branches of a tree."
All things return to the law of decay; the life of a human being is just like this.
Like a drop of dew hanging from the tip of a blade of grass when struck by the rays of the sun, it does not remain for even a moment; the life of a human being is just like this.
Like foam gathered on a river or sea, its nature is inherently frail;
this body, lacking solidity, is likewise hollow and buoyant.
Just as when it rains heavily from the heavens, water bubbles arise.
Momentarily and swiftly they perish; so too is this unsubstantial body.

To conceive a notion of substantiality in what is unsubstantial, or to perceive unsubstantiality in what is substantial—this is the sphere of false discrimination, by which one cannot realize the solid reality.
Perceiving the solid as solid, and knowing the non-solid as non-solid,
one who correctly discerns the sphere of practice can realize the solid reality.
To cultivate the perception of solidity, even a small offering of water in a vessel [yields great merit].
"Therefore, with this non-durable body, one trades for that which is durable and substantial. "Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated this second thought, they—desiring to diligently seek the subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka—serve and provide diligent offerings to the Dharma-preacher even more extensively, even to the point of giving vessels for storing water."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:

'For a long night I have been far removed from virtuous friends and have been held fast by evil associates. By nature I am indolent and do not cultivate diligence; I am base, dull-witted, and possessed of many false and evil views. I have falsely given rise to such deluded and unwholesome thoughts, being without generosity, without love, and without meritorious offerings; I have neither performed good deeds nor avoided evil deeds, thereby increasing the karmic fruits and retributions of my actions.'"
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:
"I have been deluded and distracted by desire, wandering through the long night and committing various kinds of evil and unwholesome karma."

Due to the power of these unwholesome and evil karmic actions, he has brought about the retribution of a foul and loathsome physical form; born in the realm of hungry ghosts, he lacks the necessities of life and finds no supreme field of merit whatsoever.

Furthermore, I was once born among the hungry ghosts, where I constantly consumed burning coals for immeasurable years; moreover, throughout many hundreds of thousands of years, I did not even hear the name of water, let alone experience it with my body.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:

"I have now encountered such a most supreme field of merit, and I have obtained this excellent body as a karmic fruition, complete with many provisions for life. I shall rely upon these fields of merit to extensively cultivate virtuous deeds; disregarding even my own body and life, I shall serve my teachers—the *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*—and, desiring to diligently seek the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall honor and make offerings to the Dharma-preachers, providing even vessels for storing water."
"Śāriputra! This is called the third generation of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"By constantly associating with and revering such spiritual friends, one comes to possess such a nature; therefore, one should associate with them frequently.
Being held fast by evil companions, one distances oneself from virtuous and noble friends."
