Laxity and contempt for diligence, stinginess, envy, and much crookedness;
lack of generosity and other such false views—denying all things.
I was once born in the realm of hungry ghosts, receiving a wretched and evil physical form.
Within the long night of birth and death, amidst terrifying and vast darkness,
they are tormented everywhere by hunger and thirst, undergoing manifold sufferings for many hundreds of thousands of years, never even hearing the name of water.
Not seeing a pure field of merit, one cannot avoid these hardships.
Now I am moved by this rare world, and having further encountered the wise and enlightened,
I have obtained the fulfillment of being free from such hardships.
Furthermore, having distanced myself from evil associates, I have encountered virtuous and noble friends;
vowing never to regard my own body or life, I shall surely realize Bodhi.
With a pure and wholesome mind, I shall reverently serve my honored teachers and elders.
"One should also make offerings to all Buddhas for the sake of realizing bodhi. Śāriputra,

when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having thus generated this third thought, they— desiring to diligently seek the subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka— redouble their reverence and respect for the Dharma-preacher and provide diligent offerings, even down to the gift of a water vessel."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:

'For a long night, I have been far removed from virtuous friends; I have been held fast by evil associates, characterized by indolence, laziness, inferior diligence, lack of wisdom, and folly. By such views and such tolerances, when there are sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and distresses, weeping and wailing in this manner, I have furthermore used my body and hands to falsely inflict blows and various forms of harm upon them.'"
Due to these causes and conditions, they give rise to such immeasurable evil views, saying: "There is no evil karma, nor is there any retribution for evil karma.

Furthermore, because their minds are shrouded by hatred and anger, they commit various kinds of evil and unwholesome deeds. By the retribution of such karma, they obtain a defiled and loathsome body, are born among the animals where the means of subsistence are lacking, and find no supreme field of merit whatsoever.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought:

"In those realms of rebirth, I may become a camel, an ox, a donkey, or the like, eating only coarse fodder while being subjected to the blows of sticks, lashes, and the terror of shouting commands; though my heart finds no joy in it, I am forced to carry heavy loads."
He further thought to himself:
"In the past, although I underwent such sufferings, I never encountered a field of merit such as this.

Now that I have encountered one, and having further obtained such a body through good fortune, I shall rely upon these fields of merit regardless of my own body or life. Trading this non-durable body for a durable one, I shall serve my teachers and elders. For the sake of diligently seeking the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall honor, serve, and make offerings to the Dharma-preacher, even providing vessels for storing water."
"Śāriputra! This is called the fourth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"In that long night, I did not know how to ascend the Noble Path;
I fell among camels, oxen, and donkeys, and underwent much toil and suffering.
Now that I have obtained this human body, I shall cultivate the deeds of the virtuous and good."
By this one realizes enlightenment; this is the mark of the wise.
I shall arouse reverence and establish the teachings of all Buddhas, attending upon the Dharma-preachers for the sake of attaining enlightenment.
In inconceivable kalpas of the past, you have circled the wheel of birth and death;
coming and going has brought no righteous benefit, as you sustained your life without a field of merit.
You remained far removed from virtuous friends and constantly associated with evil companions.
Following their instructions, I repeatedly fell into various evil realms.
Once, while among the animals, I was confined, bound, driven, beaten, and reviled;
due to such evil karma, I experienced undesirable bitter fruits.
Consequently, one falls into evil realms, becoming a camel, an ox, or a donkey;
bearing heavy loads while still being struck with whips, all because one did not associate with virtuous friends.
Now that I have obtained what is difficult to obtain—the human body and virtuous friends—[I must not let them go to waste].
Having been born in a favorable realm and having encountered no hardships,
like a turtle dwelling long in the ocean who joyfully meets the hole of a floating log,
one should guard body and speech well, with diligence and a powerful mind.
Without guile, serve virtuous friends, Nourishing the body of the life of wisdom.
If there is a revered teacher Who awakens the mind of wisdom within me,
A great master who can proclaim The supreme and wondrous path to enlightenment—
I shall reverently offer to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings:
various unguents, powdered incenses, diverse garments, and flower garlands.
To the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present, who constantly reveal the ultimate truth—
The boundless golden sun— One should practice making offerings to it.
Wandering through all buddha-fields, Extensively making offerings to the Tamer of Men,
To purify the path to bodhi, One shall ascend the seat of great awakening.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated such fourth thoughts as these, they—desiring to diligently seek the subtle Dharma-gates of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka—serve and provide offerings to the Dharma-preachers with redoubled devotion, even providing them with vessels for storing water.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:

'In the long night of the past, I was far removed from virtuous friends and held fast by evil associates; I was indolent, lazy, and possessed inferior diligence; lacking wisdom and being deluded, I gave rise to wrong views, and with such faith, acceptance, and inclination, I falsely conceived these thoughts.'"

If one were to take the flesh of all sentient beings and all living creatures, either boiling them together in a single cauldron or mincing their bodies into sashimi, even though such acts were committed, they would not be called non-meritorious.
Furthermore, they give rise to evil views, claiming that one does not incur evil because of this, nor is evil produced because of this.
Due to such false views, even if they were to provide all manner of gifts to satisfy every sentient being on this side of the great ocean, though they act in this way, it is not called non-offensive.
They give rise to false notions, claiming that one does not bring about merit because of this, nor does merit arise because of this.

Due to such false views, they further claim that even if one were to slaughter all sentient beings on the other shore of the great ocean, one would neither bring about evil because of this, nor would evil arise because of this.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus:

"In the past, having acted in such a manner, I was unable to discern what was sinful and what was not sinful, or what was meritorious and what was not meritorious; obscured by ignorance and associating with wrong views, I committed many unwholesome and grave evil karmas."

Due to this karmic retribution, one receives a body in the low, base, and foul hell; therein, one may be made to swallow iron balls or be dismembered with saws, undergoing various kinds of harsh and bitter suffering that flows in an uninterrupted succession of pure misery for many hundreds of thousands of years, during which time one does not even hear the sound of joy, let alone experience physical touch.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again had this thought:
"Although I have undergone such suffering in the past, I never before encountered a field of merit such as this.

Now that I have encountered it, and having further attained such a body through wholesome karma, I shall rely upon these fields of merit to nurture my life of wisdom. Trading this non-enduring body for an enduring one, disregarding my own body and life, I shall serve my teachers and elders. For the sake of diligently seeking the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall serve and make offerings to the Dharma-preacher, even providing them with vessels for storing water."
"Śāriputra! This is called the fifth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I have associated with evil friends, Deceived by their malicious intent;
Relying on various wrong views, I have pointlessly created evil karma.
Throughout this entire shore of the great ocean, All sentient beings who dwell therein—"
To provide food and drink until they are fully satisfied, yet claim it does not produce merit;
to go to the very far shore of the great ocean and kill every sentient being dwelling there,
yet claim it does not produce evil karma.
Thus, by repeatedly practicing and constantly associating with these various evil views,
one falls into the most agonizing hells, where one’s body and head are crushed.
In the past, within the three miserable realms, one has pointlessly exhausted hundreds of thousands of bodies.
I have never before seen the Buddhas, the foremost guides of the world.
Even the fame of these virtuous friends of the world is difficult to hear;
yet, having fortunately obtained this human benefit, I shall cultivate noble and wholesome deeds.
To obtain a human body is extremely difficult; having obtained it, a long life is difficult.
To encounter and hear the True Dharma is difficult; for Buddhas to appear in the world is difficult.
I have already obtained a human body, yet I am subject to this precarious and fragile life.
Having encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world and having entered the true teaching of the Tathāgata,
I shall no longer commit evil deeds of body, speech, or mind; may I not,
in the future, experience the fruits of suffering that I do not desire.
With a pure mind, I shall cultivate pure deeds;
through body, speech, and mind, I shall perform what is difficult for the world to do.
I shall never transgress my teacher or the instructions authorized by the assembly.
Furthermore, one should offer worship for the sake of the Buddha’s bodhi.
Because I am free from flattery and deception, and possess a mind devoid of guile and falsehood,
I shall open and cultivate the direct path for the sake of the path to the Buddha’s bodhi.
The Great Bodhisattva Abhaya, having already resolved his mind in this way, offered a water vessel;
he was fully endowed with wisdom and skillful means. "Śāriputra!..."

When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated this fifth mind, they—desiring to zealously seek the subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka—serve and diligently make offerings to the Dharma-preacher with redoubled intensity, even providing vessels for storing water.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:

'Throughout the long night, I have been far removed from virtuous friends and held fast by evil associates; I have been indolent, lazy, and possessed of inferior diligence, lacking wisdom and being foolish. Due to such evil views, such convictions, and such inclinations, I have falsely conceived this notion, denying the karmic retribution of wholesome deeds—such as welcoming and receiving others, bowing and prostrating, and joining the palms in greeting—and, obscured by pride, I have committed many unwholesome actions.'"
"Due to the retribution of evil karma, I have received a base and defiled form within the human realm, and I have never nurtured the life-force of pure wisdom within the fields of merit.
Thus the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects:

"I recall that in the past, I was among those who were orphaned, destitute, lowly, and base; I was among the class of slaves and servants bound to others; furthermore, I was among sentient beings who indulged in sensual desires, being greedily attached to all forms and marks of desire. I dwelt among those of unwholesome conduct, giving rise to various evil and false views; I violated ethical discipline (*śīla*) and violated right view. I dwelt within the three unwholesome roots and dwelt in the four improper courses of action. I was shrouded by the five hindrances, lacked reverence for the six objects of respect, and failed to conform to the seven dharmas. I followed the fixed course of the eightfold wrongness, was tormented by the nine causes of resentment, and constantly trod upon the ten paths of unwholesome action."

The path that leads to hell constantly appears before them, while they turn their backs on the path that leads to the heavens; they remain far removed from all virtuous spiritual friends and are held fast by evil associates; following the influence of Māra and his enemies, they act according to their own will, distancing themselves from all wholesome dharmas and manifesting every kind of unwholesome dharma.

"Furthermore, they are subjected to such things as being struck with whips and canes, scolded, and terrified; unable to bear it in their hearts, they are forcibly suppressed, driven into service, and made to provide for others.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:
"In the past, because I did not encounter such a field of merit, I underwent all manner of evils."

Having now encountered this opportunity and further having been fortunate enough to perceive the body of a Tathāgata, I shall rely upon the fields of merit to exchange this non-durable body for a durable one. Furthermore, I shall nourish my own life of wisdom, disregarding my own body and life to serve my teachers and elders; and for the sake of diligently seeking the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall serve and make offerings to the Dharma-preachers, even down to giving them vessels for storing water.
"Śāriputra! This is called the sixth production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"By associating with evil friends, one increases arrogance; For immeasurable oceans of kalpas, one takes birth in the human realm in the body of a slave, Wandering through the long night of the various streams of existence."
I have now attained what is difficult to attain: The supreme, courageous human body;
Furthermore, I have been born in a wondrous land, Encountering a Buddha in a pure realm free from all hardships.
Those who are virtuous, excellent, and supreme friends, Who can proclaim the path of the bodhisattva—
The jewel of the mind that increases all bodhisattvas— Are encountered only now after many koṭis of kalpas.

The body is impermanent, unstable, and hollow; it is like a bubble on water or a mass of foam, and resembles a magical illusion or a theatrical performance, as well as what is seen in a dream or spoken in sleep.
Life is like a cloud or lightning, not remaining for long; in this world, it perishes moment by moment.
Since this life will pass away in a mere instant, one should exchange this non-durable life for a durable one.
I recall that in times long past, I fell into the deep and perilous ravines of the mountain of pride;
having been deceived therein, I remained for an inconceivable ocean of hundreds of kalpas.
I now completely renounce attachment to the body, And harbor no lingering longing for my life;
I shall swiftly abandon pride and arrogance, And deeply revere and serve my honored teacher.
Furthermore, toward those universally honored as elders in the world— namely one's parents, elder brothers, and so forth—
one should swiftly abandon arrogance and pride, and instead hold them in the highest esteem and profound veneration.

Those bodhisattvas who are near to sublime enlightenment and who, like me, practice the conduct of awakening—toward them you should give rise to firm love and respect; you should delight in making offerings and devotedly serve them.

In the past, heavy pride was fully developed and increased; Not knowing the Dharma for subduing and severing pride, One shall now use the vajra of unsurpassed wisdom To forever shatter the mountain of arrogance.
Having perfected the sublime conduct of bodhi, And being firmly seated upon the most excellent bodhi-throne,
You shall subdue the hosts of the Māra-armies of strife and contention, And deliver all sentient beings from the four torrents.
All those afflicted by illness throughout the ten directions, Lying in their own excrement and loathed by all,
Toward them he arouses a mind of compassion, Acting as their savior and refuge.
Abiding securely in the perfection of great generosity, they are able to protect the majesty of the Buddha;
fully cultivating and perfecting the practice of patience, they arouse right diligence to bring it forth before them.
Having attained the perfection of pure contemplation (*śubha-vipaśyanā-pāramitā*), at this time one tames the mind and causes it to abide;
dwelling securely in great wisdom and skillful means, one shall become a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) honored by all.

Thus does the power of flourishing merit increase; through inconceivable and virtuous wisdom, if one attains the foremost sovereign knowledge, one shall even offer a water vessel at the appropriate time.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated this sixth mind, they—desiring to diligently seek the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka—serve and provide diligent offerings to the Dharma-preacher even more extensively, even to the point of giving them vessels for storing water.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:

'Throughout the long night, I have been far removed from virtuous friends and held fast by evil associates; I have been indolent, lazy, of inferior diligence, and devoid of wisdom and intelligence. Due to such evil views, with such convictions and such inclinations, I have falsely conceived this notion: that there is no black karma and no retribution for black karma; there is no white karma and no retribution for white karma; there is no black-and-white karma and no retribution for black-and-white karma; and there is no karma that is neither black nor white and no retribution for karma that is neither black nor white.'"
Furthermore, they do not inquire of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas: "What is wholesome?
What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy?"
What is faultless? What should be cultivated?
What should not be cultivated?

What should be done? What should not be done? Furthermore, they do not inquire about what kind of practices should be cultivated that, throughout the long night, would result in what is meaningless, disadvantageous, and various forms of suffering.
"Furthermore, what kind of practice can bring about meaningful results, benefit, and various forms of peace and happiness throughout the long night [of saṃsāra]?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus:

"In the past, because I was obscured by this pride and the pride of superiority, I committed many unwholesome and evil karmas. Due to the retribution of these karmas, I have obtained a human body with impaired faculties, and I have failed to nourish my life of wisdom within the supreme field of merit."

Though dwelling among human beings, they act like overturned vessels; being childish, playful, foolish, dull-witted, deaf, and blind, they lack the power or capacity to comprehend, realize, or proclaim the meaning of good and evil.
He further thought to himself:

"In the past, because I had not encountered such a supreme field of merit, I committed various evils. Now that I have met him, and furthermore, having fortunately obtained this body endowed with all its faculties, I shall rely upon these fields of merit to increase my life of wisdom. Moreover, disregarding even my own body and life, I shall seek the various powers to thoroughly comprehend the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings, and I shall inquire of the Dharma-preacher: 'What constitutes the good?'"
What is unwholesome?
What is blameworthy? What is blameless?
What should be cultivated?
What should not be cultivated?
What should be performed?
What should not be done? What kind of practice brings the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas before one?
What kind of practice brings the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of the bodhisattvas before one?

"Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas desire to diligently seek the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva by relying on the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā). They exchange their non-durable bodies for durable ones, serving and making offerings to the Dharma-preachers, even to the extent of giving them vessels for storing water."
“Śāriputra! This is called the seventh production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the distant past, across many hundreds of eons, I remained far removed from those kind and virtuous friends who could have instructed me on what is wholesome and unwholesome,
or on the karmic fruits of actions that are blameworthy and blameless."
Through the sovereign power of overweening pride, they fall into the realms of hell and hungry ghosts;
taking evil thoughts as their companions, they plummet into the miserable paths for many hundreds of eons.
Or having practiced among the human realms for many thousands of kalpas, one may still wander in saṃsāra with impaired faculties;
unaware of what is virtuous and what is non-virtuous, nor of the karmic fruits of actions that are blameworthy or blameless.
I have obtained this human body of vigorous strength, With all faculties complete and dwelling in purity;
Having distanced myself from all hardships, I have attained freedom from obstacles, Like a turtle stretching its neck to meet a floating log with a single hole.
When the World was served by a Lamp of Illumination, I heard the holy teachings on the transcendence of desire;
At that time, I questioned the Honored One of the World concerning the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
How does one possessed of stinginess fall into the various realms of existence?
How does one free from stinginess become a donor?
How are greed and deceit defilements of ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
How does one fully protect the wealth of ethical discipline?
How does one become a person agitated by anger and resentment?
And how does one possess the power of patience free from anger?
What is a mind that is indolent and distracted?
What is diligence and delight in meditative concentration?
What is evil wisdom, muteness, and folly?
How does one possess the wisdom that delights in reality?
How does one practice bodhi with single-minded devotion, fully seeking the conduct of the noble ones?
How does one let compassion flow throughout the world?
How does one deliver others from the evil realms?
How does one possess a mind that delights in the Dharma without weariness, capable of seeking the treasury of all practices for awakening?
How does one travel to the lands of the ten directions and appear before the currently dwelling Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?
How does one pay homage and cultivate meritorious deeds?
How does one inquire about the conduct of Samantabhadra?
Now, I should diligently make these inquiries; the Dharma Master is as venerable as the Buddhas themselves.
How does one delight in honoring and supporting the teacher?
How does one cause the teacher’s mind to be joyful?
When a son of the Buddha has given rise to such a mind, he is able to accumulate the power of vast and sublime merit.
"And with the power of supreme sovereign wisdom, they joyfully offer gifts as far as the water vessel. "Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) and have thus generated this seventh mind, in order to diligently seek the subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, they serve and provide diligent offerings to the Dharma-preacher even more abundantly, even to the extent of giving vessels for storing water."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:

'For a long night, I have been far removed from virtuous friends and held fast by evil associates; I have been indolent, lazy, and of inferior diligence; I have been dull-witted and ignorant like a mute sheep; and I have abandoned all phrases corresponding to the true meaning, phrases corresponding to the true Dharma, phrases corresponding to tranquility, phrases corresponding to cessation, phrases corresponding to perfect awakening, and phrases corresponding to the parinirvāṇa of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.'"

Having abandoned such passages as these, one instead takes up, retains, recites, and contemplates them, even coming to master all those passages that are inconsistent with the meaningful, inconsistent with the Dharma, and even inconsistent with nirvāṇa and so forth.

Because of this, they falsely give rise to such views, saying: "There is no power, there is no diligence, there is no fruit of the person (*puruṣakāra*), there is no might, no valor, no activity, and no majesty; or, simultaneously with these thoughts, they conceive that there is neither activity nor majesty."

Furthermore, he gave rise to this thought: "There can be no cause and no condition that causes sentient beings to become defiled; sentient beings do not become defiled through causes and conditions. Again, he gave rise to this thought:
"There can be no cause and no condition that enables sentient beings to attain purity; sentient beings do not attain purity through causes and conditions."
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects:
"Throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], because I relied upon such views of unequal causes and causelessness, I have committed many various kinds of evil and unwholesome karma."
Due to the retribution of this karma, in my past existence within the human realm, I was deficient in the various physical marks; I had not cultivated the life of wisdom within the fields of merit.

Although I dwelt among humans, I was like an overturned vessel—childish, playing in ignorance, foolish, deaf, and blind. I lacked the power and ability to receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, or thoroughly penetrate the words and phrases corresponding to the true meaning, even those corresponding to Nirvana.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:

"In the past, because I had not encountered such a supreme field of merit, I gave rise to false views. Now that I have encountered it, even at the cost of my own body and life, I shall seek the power and capability to comprehend those phrases and sentences corresponding to the true meaning, corresponding to the True Dharma, corresponding to tranquility, and even corresponding to Nirvāṇa—all such phrases of the True Dharma which are subsumed within this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka."

I shall now receive, uphold, read, recite, and contemplate this to its ultimate conclusion; I will certainly arouse the most supreme diligence and serve the Dharma-preacher for as long as my life lasts.

Now, relying upon the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), I practice the bodhisattva conduct in order to be able to receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, and make offerings to this Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
He further reflects:
"I shall exchange this non-durable body for a durable body; I shall skillfully cultivate and accumulate the two kinds of provisions, namely merit and wisdom."
"By means of these two powers, one shall constantly and perpetually draw near to the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Having reflected thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva serves and makes offerings to the Dharma-preacher, even providing him with vessels for storing water.
"Śāriputra! This is called the eighth production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“If a teaching accords with the true meaning, And one practices the factors of the path accordingly,
It will lead to the realization of cessation And enable the path to Nirvāṇa to flourish.”
In the past, I abandoned such teachings as these, Instead further flowing into the practice of various evils;
They were neither Dharma, nor meaningful, nor tranquil, And were entirely inconsistent with Nirvana.
There is no diligence and no strength; there is no fruit of the heroic man and no majestic power.
Denying the existence of all conditioned phenomena, one lacks valor; everything is utterly empty and nothing can be attained.
There are no Buddhas and no dharmas, Nor are there parents in the world;
There are no dark dharmas and no white dharmas, And neither fruit nor retribution exists at all.
Regarding such evil views as these, which have been habitually practiced since beginningless time,
one falls thereby into the hells, where one undergoes nothing but extreme suffering for a long duration before emerging.
Thus they undergo rebirth among the animal realms, Or fall into the evil world of Yama;
At times they may be born within the human realm, But are foolish, witless, and mute,
Childish in their play, blind, and deaf, Dull-witted, stubborn, and ignorant.
From this, one falls again into hell, Enduring various heavy sufferings that increase delusion and darkness.
Since time immemorial, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have never yet obtained such a pure body;
Now that I have encountered it with all faculties complete, It is right at this time to swiftly apply diligent effort.
Corresponding to the true meaning of all phenomena, Aiding toward tranquility,
leading to the path and the awakening of Bodhi— I ought to seek this Dharma at once, while there is still time.
The secret and profound treasury of all great Bodhisattvas, corresponding to the most profound and true meaning—
were one to hear it even after hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, it would be a rare occurrence indeed.
Thus, as well as all other Buddha-dharmas— immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable—
I shall diligently receive and uphold them in order to realize the bodhi of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, one should apply oneself with right diligence and arouse reverence, serving and making offerings to the Dharma-preachers—
namely, the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas— from whom one should hear the unsurpassed Dharma.
All you great Bodhisattvas, free from fear, Have generated such courageous resolve;
Having perfectly accomplished wisdom and skillful means, They even give away water jars for storage.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated this eighth mind, they—desiring to diligently seek the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka—serve and provide offerings to the Dharma-preacher with redoubled diligence, even to the extent of giving them vessels for storing water.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:

'All sentient beings are bound and constrained by unwholesome conduct; they cherish their bodies and lives and are attached to unwholesome conduct, such that they are unable to exert their minds to cultivate what is meaningful and beneficial.'"
"Śāriputra! What is meant by 'clinging to meaningless conduct'?

It refers to having attachment and longing for one's body and life, having no aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), taking the notion of 'self' and 'what belongs to self' as a guide, and constantly guarding, covering, bathing, regulating, adorning, and protecting that body. This is what is called clinging to meaningless conduct."

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is the practice of attachment to what is meaningless, which refers to being preoccupied with one’s body and life, having no aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), and being led by the conceit of "I" and "mine. To protect, shield, and conceal one's wives, concubines, sons, daughters, brothers, friends, retinues, and kinsmen, and even to be attached to all manner of requisites, treasures, and playthings—this is called the practice of attachment to what is meaningless.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is the practice of attachment to what is meaningless, which refers to being attached to one’s body and life, having no aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), and taking the conception of "I" and "mine" as the precursor to guarding, employing, shackling, and protecting servants, slaves, and laborers; this is called the practice of attachment to what is meaningless.
Śāriputra! What is meant by "exclusively cultivating what is meaningful"?

It means having no attachment or longing for one's body or life, having aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), taking the sublime mind of awakening (bodhicitta) as the guide, and exclusively cultivating superior wholesome actions of body, mind, and speech; this is what is called exclusively cultivating what is meaningful.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is the cultivation of meaningful benefit, which means having no attachment or longing for one’s body or life, maintaining hope for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), taking the sublime mind of awakening (bodhicitta) as the precursor, and single-mindedly cultivating the elicitation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). This is what is called the cultivation of meaningful benefit.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is the exclusive cultivation of meaningful benefit, which means having no attachment or longing for one's body or life, while maintaining aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma). With the sublime mind of awakening (bodhicitta) as the guide, one exclusively practices generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation to gather and transform all sentient beings; this is what is called the exclusive cultivation of meaningful benefit.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is the cultivation of meaningful benefit, which means having no regard or attachment for body or life, while maintaining aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma). With the sublime mind of awakening (bodhicitta) as one's guide, one single-mindedly cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment—these branches of the path are what is called the cultivation of meaningful benefit.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is the dedicated cultivation of what is meaningful: namely, having no regard or attachment for one’s own body or life, while maintaining aspiration for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma); with the sublime mind of awakening (bodhicitta) as one's guide, one single-mindedly cultivates the offering, honoring, and prostration toward parents and all teachers and elders; bowing with palms joined, acting with humility, inquiring after their well-being, welcoming them, attending to their needs, and performing acts of harmony and compliance—this is called the dedicated cultivation of what is meaningful.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is the practice of dedicated cultivation for the sake of meaningful benefit: namely, having no regard or attachment for one's own body or life; harboring aspirations for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma); taking the sublime mind of awakening (bodhicitta) as one's guide; and single-mindedly cultivating respectful service toward the Three Jewels in accordance with their Dharma teachings.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

"All sentient beings are single-mindedly attached to what is meaningless; they are bound and constrained by meaningless conduct, and they are negligent and indolent, cherishing their own bodies and lives."
I shall now exclusively cultivate what is meaningful and beneficial, being protected by that which is meaningful and beneficial.

I shall apply myself with diligent vigor, serving the Dharma-preachers with my body, exchanging this non-enduring body for an enduring one. I shall cultivate the two accumulations of merit and wisdom; by cultivating the accumulations of merit and wisdom, I shall draw near to unsurpassed, sublime Bodhi.

"Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, serves and makes offerings to all Dharma-preachers in order to seek such a Bodhisattva-piṭaka, even to the extent of giving them water vessels."
“Śāriputra! This is the ninth production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Foolish ordinary beings always look after their own bodies and lives;
they do not aspire to seek awakening, but give rise to the three types of defiled karma.
They constantly act for the sake of benefiting themselves, as well as their wives, children, and kinsmen.”
To take pleasure in what is meaningless is called being a foolish worldling;
To employ servants and the like, and to keep many four-footed beasts,
While remaining attached to what is meaningless, is called being one without wisdom.
Accumulating great stores of wealth and grain, yet neither giving nor consuming them,
one who is attached to what is meaningless is called a fool who guards a hoard.
All such ignorant worldlings are solely attached to what is meaningless.
The Bodhisattva Endowed with Sublime Wisdom, Diligently seeks all manner of beneficial aims,
Disregarding even body and life, Rejoicing in assisting toward enlightenment;
Arising in various kinds of wholesome karma— This is called being dedicated to what is beneficial.
Skillfully cultivating through skillful means generosity, ethical discipline, patience, right effort,
meditative concentration, and sublime wisdom— this is called being dedicated to what is meaningful.
To make offerings to one’s parents and to serve one’s teachers and elders;
To reverently honor the Triple Gem with deep devotion is called being dedicated to the meaningful benefit.
To recite, uphold, and expound the wondrous treasury of all Bodhisattvas,
which encompasses all dharmas, is called being dedicated to the meaningful benefit.
Thus devoted solely to what is meaningful, praised by all Buddhas,
and perfectly endowed with diligence— such is the supreme son of the Fearless One.
Having formed such a thought, with pure faith,
"Reverently supporting and honoring the teacher, even to the point of offering vessels for water. Śāriputra,

when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated this ninth mind, they— desiring to diligently seek the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka— serve and provide offerings to the Dharma-preacher with redoubled diligence, even to the extent of giving them vessels for storing water."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives rise to this thought:
'The sentient beings of the world are dominated by perversity; they instead cling to the teachings of their teachers and thus achieve nothing.'
What is it that they do not obtain?
It is what is called the noble wealth (*ārya-dhana*). What is this noble wealth?
That is to say: faith, ethical discipline, learning, shame, dread of blame, equanimity, and wisdom—such dharmas as these are called the noble wealth.
Because those sentient beings have not obtained them, they are said to be utterly impoverished.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus:
"I should now cultivate sublime and virtuous mastery, receiving the teacher's instructions with compliance and reverence."
Why is this so? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, through their sublime mastery, respectfully receive and comply with the instructions of their teachers, thereby attaining certain realizations.
What is it that they attain?
This refers to the noble wealth.
What is called the noble wealth of a bodhisattva?
It refers to the various distinctions within the Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Knowing the sublime mastery of the bodhisattvas, one likewise knows the sublime mastery of the Dharma teacher; regarding the distinctions within the Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they extensively proclaim, expound, analyze, establish, elucidate, differentiate, reveal, and disseminate them for the sake of sentient beings.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell securely in this Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they acquire the wealth of the noble Dharma, forever severing poverty, and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of a bodhisattva by relying on the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated this mind with sublime goodness and mastery, they respectfully receive the teacher’s instructions in accordance with them. Furthermore, they form this thought:

'I shall trade this non-solid body for a solid body; for the sake of diligently seeking the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall serve and make offerings to the Dharma-preacher, even to the point of giving away my water vessel.'"
"Śāriputra! This is called the tenth generation of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The inferior beings of this world, Deceitful, delusive, and full of guile and falsehood,
Perverse, biased, and irrational, Devoted to evil, self-willed, and contrary to the Teacher’s instructions.”
Having deeply understood this and followed the teacher’s instruction, one is able to discern and extensively expound it;
through this, one obtains the wealth of the sages and saints: faith, ethical discipline, renunciation, learning, shame, dread of blame, and wisdom.
These seven treasures are an inexhaustible treasury; do not reveal them to those known to be unfit vessels.
There are many virtuous beings in the world who are capable of serving as pure Dharma-vessels for all Buddhas.

Free from flattery, they come with beautiful words to inquire; Exquisite, virtuous, self-possessed, and serene, They always give rise to courageous and diligent effort, Revering the True Dharma and delighting in hearing it constantly.
To realize the wondrous Bodhi of all Buddhas, they disregard their own cherished bodies and lives;
knowing that such persons are capable vessels for the True Dharma, they are further able to receive and uphold its profound and subtle principles.

The Teacher, having aroused great compassion, Expounds for them the unmixed true Dharma-realm, The wondrous treasury of Dharma of all the great Bodhisattvas; Relying upon that, supreme enlightenment is established.
Furthermore, therein he extensively reveals the firm and holy treasures of the Buddhas:
that all phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness, and likewise the characteristic of signlessness and the characteristic of selflessness.
There is no life-span and no transformation; there is no conceptual proliferation and no storehouse of sensation.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is not born of conditions and is without marks.
Never having an initial arising nor a final cessation, it is manifested as signless *tathatā*.
Those who are skillful, self-possessed, and gentle will not hold perverted views regarding the Teacher’s instructions.
The Most Victorious One naturally reveals the gateways to liberation that are the objects of one's original training:
pure faith, ethical discipline, shame and dread of blame, correct hearing, renunciation, and wisdom.
For their sake, he has extensively expounded and revealed the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the seven riches;
the Buddha-sons, gentle, harmonious, and wondrously sovereign, follow the instructions of their spiritual friends.
I shall serve these teachers of the Dharma in order to realize unsurpassed bodhi.
As soon as the Bodhisattva has given rise to this mind, he conceives compassionate love for those who suffer from thirst;
he even goes so far as to prepare clean earthenware vessels, fills them with clear water, and bestows them at the appropriate time.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having generated this tenth mind, they—desiring to zealously seek the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka—serve and diligently make offerings to the Dharma-preachers even more extensively, even to the extent of giving them water vessels.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 42;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 43.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Bodhisattvapiṭaka Assembly, Part Twelve, Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Śīla, Part Two of Seven.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of śīla, by virtue of accomplishing such power of roots of goodness, they attain four kinds of vast and sublime states.”

What are the four? First, one is able to swiftly enter into all wholesome dharmas; second, one is praised by Dharma teachers; third, one’s practice reaches fulfillment without transgression; and fourth, one firmly upholds the Buddha’s true Dharma without allowing it to decline.
Śāriputra! These are the four kinds of vast and supreme dharmas attained by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
By virtue of this power, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, while dwelling among human beings, further attain four kinds of vast and superior dharmas.
What are these four? First, they cause many sentient beings to follow and train in their practice, becoming ultimately established in all pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*).
Second, by constructing well-built and secure guesthouses along level roads, one swiftly causes sentient beings to obtain joy;
third, because one attains the benefits of the Dharma throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], the mind of serenity and peace never diminishes;
fourth, at the time of death, the mind will not be entangled by delusion, and one will be reborn in a happy realm and a world of bliss.
Śāriputra! These are the four kinds of vast and superior states that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains while dwelling among human beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
By virtue of this power, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while dwelling among the devas, further attains four kinds of vast and superior states.
What are these four? First, by means of the maturation of merit, they are able to gather the assembly of devas.
Second, the assemblies of devas gaze upon his face, thinking:
"What will the Bodhisattva now proclaim?
Having heard it, we shall surely attain awakening."
Third, although he is visited by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and other sons of gods who request the Dharma and seek to resolve their doubts, this bodhisattva does not go to their abodes.
Fourth, he manifests great palaces for the enjoyment of the bodhisattva.
Śāriputra! These are the four kinds of vast and superior states that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains while dwelling among the gods. Śāriputra!

In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), whether they are in the heavens or born among humans, they further attain immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sublime Dharma-gates, all for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva sits upon a high seat, Reverently honored by all the devas.
Gazing up at his venerable countenance, What Dharma will he proclaim?”
All paid him reverent homage; endowed with wisdom, he removed their stinginess.
Dwellings in palaces of joy, Śakra came to invite him to resolve his doubts.
When his life in the heavens had ended, he was reborn in the human realm.
He becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King, possessing great power and free from stinginess.
If his life in the human realm comes to an end, he returns once more to birth in the heavens;
he has never again experienced manifold sufferings because he served and supported the Dharma Master.
One will constantly obtain such as these— four kinds of vast and sublime states—
because one has no inferior mind and reveres the teacher of the Dharma.
If, with a heart of reverence and love, one offers a vessel for water, [one shall likewise attain these fruits].
Then devas, nāgas, and humans should personally make offerings to them.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), because they have accomplished such roots of goodness, they further obtain four kinds of dharmas among the devas."
What are the four? First, knowing the karma created and experienced in previous lives;
second, knowing that one has been born in the heavens because of these wholesome deeds, as well as being able to know when one falls away from those wholesome dharmas.
Third, they clearly know that upon passing away from this life, they shall be reborn in a certain place;
fourth, they proclaim the sublime Dharma to the assembly of devas, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, and having thus benefited them, they relinquish their celestial bodies.
Śāriputra! These are the four dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains upon being born among the devas, all of which result from the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), because they have accomplished such roots of goodness, they further attain four kinds of perfectly accomplished supreme dharmas."
Śāriputra! What are these four?
First, having relinquished the celestial palaces, a bodhisattva mahāsattva returns to the human realm and is born together with the precepts.
Second, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell among human beings, they obtain five kinds of dharmas that bring about an excellent rebirth.

What are these five? They are: obtaining birth in an excellent family; obtaining excellent and wondrous physical form; obtaining excellent and pure precepts; obtaining an excellent retinue; and cultivating excellent loving-kindness toward all sentient beings. These are called the five kinds of dharmas that bring about an excellent rebirth.
Third, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell among human beings, they further attain five kinds of indestructible qualities (*abhedyadharma*).

What are these five? They are: attaining spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) that cannot be destroyed; the body one receives never meeting with untimely death; not suffering any loss or decline regarding the wealth and status one has attained; having the bodhicitta that no one can destroy; and being personally abundant and self-sufficient during times when the Dharma is in scarcity. These are called the five kinds of indestructible qualities obtained.
Fourth, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells among human beings, they further obtain five kinds of rare and perfect qualities.
What are these five?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva places empty vessels within his dwelling, as soon as they reach the range of the bodhisattva’s hand, they all become filled with every kind of precious jewel.
This is called the first attainment of a rare and perfect dharma.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters thirst, a pond endowed with the eight qualities spontaneously appears before them; this is called the second attainment of a rare and perfect dharma.

The body of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, sustained by merit, cannot be harmed by external things—namely, whether by poison, knives, fire, water, or those who suck vitality; nor can it be damaged by yakṣas or various evil spirits. This is called the third attainment of the marvelous and perfect dharma.

When the various calamitous kalpas arise in Jambudvīpa—namely, the kalpa of weapons, the kalpa of famine, the kalpa of disease, the kalpa of fire, the kalpa of water, the kalpa of wind, the kalpa of thirst, the kalpa of scorching heat, or the kalpa of yakṣas—the bodhisattva-mahāsattva [acts as follows].

Śāriputra! When such an intermediate kalpa arises, the Bodhisattva is not born therein, but instead dwells in the heavens, experiencing supreme happiness and manifold great bliss; this is called the fourth attainment of the marvelous and perfect Dharma.

By the power of such roots of goodness, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva never again takes birth in places of adversity or in the evil destinies; if the mind becomes entangled in regret, they are able to perceive it and swiftly distance themselves from it. This is called the fifth attainment of the rare and perfect dharma.

Śāriputra! This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s attainment of four kinds of rare and perfectly accomplished supreme dharmas by virtue of practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), by virtue of accomplishing such power of roots of goodness, they are never separated from four kinds of sublime dharmas."
What are the four?
First, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives sentient beings who are subject to suffering, they immediately attain the mind of great compassion.
Second, all the sons and daughters of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva revere and comply with that bodhisattva.
Third, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to subdue aging so as not to be invaded by it;
fourth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gains a hundredfold profit from his livelihood and labor, or even more than this—twofold or threefold.

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), accomplishes these four kinds of sublime dharmas and remains forever undetached from them.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), because they have accomplished such roots of goodness, they cannot be robbed by three things."
What are these three?
First, not being plundered by greed; second, not being plundered by anger; and third, not being plundered by delusion.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā),
remains far removed from the three kinds of plundering dharmas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), by virtue of accomplishing such roots of goodness, they obtain four kinds of states of health."

What are the four? First, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not afflicted or oppressed by chronic illness. Second, a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s limbs and body are fresh and lustrous, never emaciated or withered. Third, a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s requisites for life are never diminished. Fourth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not subjected to harm or affliction by kings, thieves, evil persons, or other sentient beings.
"Śāriputra! These are the four dharmas for achieving freedom from illness that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains by practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), by virtue of accomplishing such roots of goodness, they attain the four marks of noble status.

What are the four? First, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a wheel-turning king (cakravartin), whose majesty extends over the four regions; he governs the world by means of the Dharma and is thus called a Dharma King, and the seven treasures appear in response to him, all of which he fully accomplishes.
What are the seven?
They are the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the woman-treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure.
He possesses a full complement of a thousand sons, whose forms are dignified and handsome, and who are fierce and powerful enough to subdue all enemies.

This Wheel-Turning King is venerated, admired, and brought into submission by the inhabitants of the four great continents; he is further honored and respected by his ministers, officials, guards, the assembled populace within his realm, and all the minor kings.
Śāriputra! This is the mark of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the foremost rank.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become stained by or attached to the pleasures of the five sublime desires—namely, forms cognizable by the eye, sounds cognizable by the ear, odors cognizable by the nose, tastes cognizable by the tongue, and tangibles cognizable by the body.

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is unstained by and unattached to these five desires, they renounce the household life for the path with pure faith and swiftly attain the five supernatural powers, receiving the reverence of both humans and non-humans.
Śāriputra! This is the mark of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the second stage of honor. Śāriputra!
Wherever a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born,
they naturally and constantly attain the most supreme awakening, the most supreme wisdom, and the most supreme eloquence, and are revered by all great kings.

Just as in the past the great Ummada was held in high esteem by the king, so too this Bodhisattva was likewise honored by the king, who invited him to ascend the royal throne; furthermore, he was protected by ministers and officials, and was universally revered and looked up to by the assembly and the people within the realm.
Śāriputra! This is the mark by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the third rank of honor.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Once the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has awakened to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), his majestic virtue becomes supremely excellent and perfect; he becomes the object of refuge and veneration for all sentient beings, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.

Why is this? Because by means of these, the bodhisattva accomplishes the categories of supreme morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the categories of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, thereby realizing purity within these dharmas.
Śāriputra! This is the mark of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the fourth honorable station. Śāriputra!

This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s attainment of four marks of noble status while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), all for the sake of bringing the perfection of ethical discipline to full completion.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) with a pure mind, by offering a water vessel to his two honored teachers— the upādhyāya and the ācārya— he attains such immeasurable, boundless, and sublime dharmas of merit."

It is said that when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks the Dharma, they follow their teacher in coming, going, advancing, and halting; they never contravene what the teacher says. By virtue of accomplishing such power of roots of goodness, they further obtain four kinds of most excellent provisions.
What are the four?
First, wherever a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born, they obtain the wealth and resources used by great kings, rather than the inferior requisites of other beings.

Second, wherever a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born, they receive the dharma of detachment and obtain the wealth of the rishis; by means of pure faith, they leave the household life to enter the path, which is called the wealth of the noble Dharma.
Third, wherever a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born, they attain the recollection of past lives; this is called acquiring the wealth of mindfulness.
By virtue of this mindfulness, in every place of birth, they never forget or lose the bodhicitta.

Fourth, once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are called "the wealth of enlightenment" and are constantly surrounded by the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
"Śāriputra! This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s attainment of the four kinds of supreme wealth by virtue of practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they follow the instructions of the Dharma teacher—even regarding one who merely upholds a four-line verse—by complying with their coming and going and every movement, namely: what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, and what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated.
Furthermore, regarding such instructions as these, up until the completion of this action, they may lead to states of suffering that are meaningless and disadvantageous throughout the long night;
yet if one performs this [action], it may lead to states of peace and happiness that are meaningful and advantageous throughout the long night.
Following such instructions as these, as directed by the teacher, they do not commit unwholesome deeds and cultivate wholesome dharmas without opposition or contravention.
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have accomplished such power of roots of goodness, they further attain four kinds of methods for achieving high excellence.
What are these four?

First, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and accomplishes the most exalted dharmas; second, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s manifested physical form has all its limbs and members entirely complete; third, the bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains great wisdom, surging wisdom, lofty wisdom, vast wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, rapid wisdom, profound wisdom, and the wisdom of discernment; fourth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is reborn in the happy realms among the worlds of the devas.

“Śāriputra! These are called the four kinds of dharmas that bring about loftiness and excellence which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), by virtue of accomplishing such power of roots of goodness, they further attain four kinds of unobservable dharmas.
What are these four? Śāriputra!

Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such power of roots of goodness, in whatever place he is born, he attains the mark of the concealed male organ; this is called the first dharma that cannot be observed.

Śāriputra! Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such power of roots of goodness, from the moment of birth, neither mother nor father, nor other kinsmen, nor gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans—among all sentient beings, whether with pure minds or defiled minds—none are able to see the crown of the bodhisattva’s head. This is called the second dharma of being unable to be observed.

Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such power of roots of goodness, from the moment of birth, whether it be his mother, father, or even humans and non-humans—among all sentient beings, whether their minds are pure or defiled—none are able to alter the countenance of the bodhisattva.
If anyone who beholds him should give rise to the thought,
"I shall gaze upon and adorn the face of the Bodhisattva," then a reflection of his face will appear upon his two feet. Why is this?

Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished such extraordinary qualities, they are called "noble beings" (satpuruṣa); furthermore, they have accomplished the foremost eloquence of the most excellent beings. This is called the third dharma that cannot be scrutinized.

Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such power of roots of goodness, at the time of his birth, without anyone to support him, he stands up by himself upon the ground and gazes in all four directions, immediately attaining clear and sharp wisdom.
Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, in past lives, sought to hear the Dharma with a mind free from guile.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has obtained eyes free from guile; by virtue of possessing these guileless eyes, his pure divine eye surpasses that of humans, even to the point of being able to observe all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains swift and vast wisdom; by virtue of having accomplished this vast wisdom, he is able to know the minds accumulated by all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.

Why is this? Because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were seeking the Dharma in the past, they applied their minds and concentrated their thoughts with diligent reverence; regarding the true Dharma, they conceived the thought of it as a potent medicine, the thought of it as a rare treasure, the thought of its being difficult to encounter, and the thought of its being sublime and virtuous. Accordingly, they sought to hear the true Dharma, and having heard it, they received and upheld it.

Furthermore, because of this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva also attains swift and discerning wisdom; by virtue of accomplishing this discerning wisdom, he is well able to weigh the ethical discipline of all sentient beings, and even well able to weigh their correct hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are well able to weigh the commonality of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of all sentient beings, and even well able to weigh the commonality of right hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are well able to weigh the outflows of the precepts of all sentient beings, and even well able to weigh the outflows of right hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is well able to weigh the characteristics of the excellence of the outflows of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of all sentient beings, and even well able to weigh the characteristics of the excellence of the outflows of right hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is well able to weigh and discern the movements, deportment, cultivation of right conduct, and courageous characteristics of all sentient beings. Śāriputra!
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has thus successively weighed and reflected upon all the virtues of all sentient beings, he forms this thought:

"Whatever precepts and learning these sentient beings possess, up to their liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation—these are of the same nature as the morality (*śīla*) of these sentient beings, and so on, up to the same nature of right hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation."

These are the outflows of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of all these sentient beings, up to and including the outflows of correct hearing, concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).

These are the marks of the preeminent outflow of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of all these sentient beings, up to and including the marks of the preeminent outflow of their correct hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

All the modes of movement and stillness, the dignified deportment, the practice of right conduct, and the signs of valorous effort belonging to these sentient beings—all such signs as these are the merits possessed by sentient beings.
"I have now weighed and observed among them, yet I do not see anyone who is my equal.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected:
"When I compare all sentient beings—who are fundamentally and firmly established—to myself, I do not see anyone at all who is my equal."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
At the moment of his initial birth, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to swiftly give rise to the sublime wisdom regarding the retribution of karma within a single kṣaṇa.
By means of this wisdom, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he is well able to thoroughly understand the thousandfold mental characteristics of all sentient beings."
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva uses wisdom to investigate all these minds and does not perceive anything equal to his own.

Thus correctly knowing, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva thinks: "I now dwell alone in the most supreme and honored position, abiding fearlessly like a lion king, possessing great majestic power like a great nāga king."
Without treading upon the ground, he took seven steps in each direction; mindful of the subtle and wondrous karmic retribution of the Bodhi seat, he stood before it and proclaimed these words:
"I am the most honored and supreme in the world."
I am the most preeminent in the world.
I shall now realize the end of birth, old age, and death.
I shall deliver all sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"I shall proclaim for the sake of all sentient beings the vast, subtle, most excellent, and unsurpassed True Dharma. Śāriputra,
when the bodhisattva mahāsattva utters these words, without any interval, their voice reaches and fills this entire trichiliocosm Buddha-world.
When the sentient beings therein heard this sound, they were struck with terror and their hair stood on end; the celestial drums rattled and repeatedly emitted great sounds.
This entire world-system trembled violently, yet only the area where the Bodhisattva dwelt remained as immovable and tranquil as a chariot wheel.
Furthermore, even this earth-disk resting upon the mass of water below is not shaken by those great winds.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, observing his own body, sees immeasurable light pervading his entire body; having thus realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he becomes an object of veneration for all sentient beings. This is called the fourth "unobservable dharma."
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of the four kinds of unobservable dharmas. Why is that?

All of these are because, in past lives, when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas followed the movements and conduct of the Dharma masters, respectfully receiving their instructions and commands without any opposition or contravention.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having accomplished such roots of goodness, they further attain four kinds of swift qualities.
What are these four?

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Buddhahood, they are fully endowed with such qualities: the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is without deficiency, and the words of the Dharma they teach are never in vain.
This is called the foremost method of swiftness.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Buddhahood, he is fully endowed with such qualities that whenever the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have a command, they speak these words:
"Come forward, Bhikṣu!"
At that time, the sentient beings proceeded to the Buddha’s presence; their hair fell away of its own accord, they were clothed in *kāṣāya* robes, and they held *pātra* bowls.
This is called the second swift method.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains Buddhahood, he is fully endowed with this quality: all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, thoroughly know the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
This is called the third dharma of swiftness.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains Buddhahood, he is fully endowed with such wisdom as the Tathāgatas possess—the wisdom that skillfully knows the medicine appropriate for the ailments of sentient beings.
This is called the fourth swift dharma.
Śāriputra! These are called the four kinds of swift dharmas attained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Why is this?

This is because, in the past, while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he offered vessels for water with a pure mind to his upādhyāyas, ācāryas, and various Dharma-preachers.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because a bodhisattva mahāsattva relies on the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and is endowed with such power of roots of goodness, at the time of attaining buddhahood, they further obtain four kinds of dharmas that cannot be harmed by others.
What are the four? Śāriputra,
the body of the Tathāgata is without dependence and without grasping.
Why is this? It is impossible, Śāriputra, that the body of a Tathāgata could be harmed by fire, weapons, poison, or any other external object.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, at the time of attaining buddhahood, possesses the śīla and thereby acquires four kinds of non-harming dharmas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

By relying on the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the power of such roots of virtue, further attains four qualities beyond reproach by others at the time of becoming a Buddha.
What are these four?
First, all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without dependence and without grasping. Why is this so?
There is no sentient being who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, could utter these words:
"I have heard from the Tathāgata a Dharma not heard before," even so much as a single phrase.
If one were able to speak thus, it would be impossible.
Second, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without dependence and without grasping. Why is this?
Because there is no sentient being who can establish a discourse in accordance with the Dharma before the Tathāgata, even for a single phrase.
If one were to establish such a thesis, it would be impossible.
Thirdly, all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without dependence and without grasping. Why is this so?
There is no sentient being capable of attaining even a minute fraction of a Tathāgata’s indeterminate mind.
If such were possible, it could not be. Why is this?
Śāriputra! The minds of all Buddha-Tathāgatas are constantly in meditative absorption, because they abide in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Fourth, all Buddha-Tathāgatas are without dependence and without grasping.
Why is this? There is no sentient being capable of grasping the various marks of the Tathāgata’s physical form.
Were such grasping of marks possible, it would be impossible for it not to exist.
Śāriputra! Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are endowed with ethical discipline (śīla), they attain four qualities that others cannot surpass.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have accomplished such power of roots of goodness, they attain the fulfillment of five immeasurable qualities.

What are these five? First, the immeasurable ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; second, the immeasurable correct hearing (*samyag-śruta*) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; third, the immeasurable correct concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; fourth, the immeasurable correct wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; and fifth, the immeasurable liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

Śāriputra! These five immeasurable qualities of the Tathāgata all arise from his practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) in the past, when he followed the instructions of his preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya), never acting in opposition to them in coming, going, advancing, or withdrawing.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, are fully endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) and have accomplished such power of roots of virtue, they attain four kinds of unobstructed knowledge."
What are the four? They are:
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, exercise unobstructed and unhindered knowledge and vision regarding the past;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, exercise unobstructed and unhindered knowledge and vision regarding the future.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, turn the wheel of unhindered and unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding the present world.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are well able to give rise to a mind of equanimity; because they give rise to such a mind of equanimity, they are able to know the nature of equality throughout the three periods of time.
"Śāriputra! It is because the Tathāgata is endowed with ethical discipline (śīla) that he attains these four kinds of unobstructed knowledge.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are well able to accomplish right wisdom; by virtue of this right wisdom, they do not depend on others and are able to fully know all dharmas.

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are further able to accomplish inconceivable wisdom; by virtue of accomplishing this inconceivable wisdom, they are able to fully understand the signs of all winds and rains.

"Śāriputra! The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that there is a great wind in the world named Ulūpaka, because all sensations and perceptions experienced by sentient beings are moved and stirred by this wind."
This wind-circle is three krośas in height; above this wind, within the void of space, there arises another wind called the Cloud-Wind (megha-vāyu), and this wind-circle is five krośas in height.
Above this wind, in the midst of space, another wind arises called Cāpaka; this wind-wheel is ten yojanas in height.
