Above this wind, in the midst of space, another wind arises called Vaiśravaṇaka; this wind-wheel is thirty yojanas in height.
Furthermore, within the space above this wind, another wind arises called "Coming and Going" (*gatyāgatī*); the measure of this wind-wheel is forty *yojana*s in height.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying upon his great wisdom, is able to fully know the characteristics of the sixty-eight thousand koṭis of wind-circles that arise in successive succession.

Śāriputra! The supreme wind-circle is named "Pervasive" (Samantataḥ), which serves as the support for the water-circle of the upper realm; the height of that water measures six million eight hundred thousand yojanas, serving as the support for that great earth.
The extent of that ground is sixty-eight thousand yojanas.

Śāriputra, upon the surface of that ground lies a trichiliocosm; therein dwells a Buddha named Mahāskandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there, remaining in the world to bestow his transformative teachings.

The lifespan of that Buddha was thirty koṭis of years; he had thirty koṭi-nayutas of śrāvaka disciples, all of whom were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, having even attained the supreme pāramitā of mastery over all minds.
At that time, that Buddha was gathered together with such a great assembly of śrāvakas.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom had fully realized the Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; they were perfectly certain regarding all principles and meanings, were oceans of learning, were great Dharma-preachers, and dwelt in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Śāriputra! A full thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, that Buddha shall likewise enter parinirvāṇa; his True Dharma shall remain in the world for a full thousand years, and his relics shall be distributed everywhere to benefit the world—just as the manner of the distribution of my relics to benefit all occurs after my parinirvāṇa today.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom can also fully comprehend the circular forms of the immeasurable and boundless wind-wheels that lie beyond those Buddha-worlds, as well as the complete circular forms of all the Buddha-lands.
Śāriputra! Furthermore, beyond this, there is another world where no Tathāgata currently resides, but where hundreds of thousands of pratyekabuddhas dwell.
The sentient beings therein all plant roots of goodness with these pratyekabuddhas.

Śāriputra! By virtue of that wisdom, the Tathāgata further knows that upon this world-system, there are Buddhas, Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who have appeared in the world, and who are currently dwelling there, delivering all sentient beings.

In this way, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and incalculable—who have appeared in the world throughout the ten directions, and who currently dwell there delivering all sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom is fully able to know them all.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is further able to know that the aforementioned Buddha-worlds manifest infinite and boundless signs of formation and destruction, such as being consumed by fire; the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata clearly understands them all.
When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “Blessed One,
by virtue of having accomplished what roots of goodness has the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, been able to obtain such immeasurable, inconceivable, and unobstructed wisdom?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Because the Tathāgata abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he possesses sublime mastery and gives rise to thoughts of reverence and respect toward the True Dharma; he conceives of it as a potent medicine, as a precious jewel, as something difficult to encounter, as a root of virtue, and as that which is appropriate to be so conceived; he generates thoughts of profound veneration and is further able to abide securely in the thought of gathering the True Dharma."
Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) and reveres the Dharma, he has attained such clear and sharp great wisdom.
Furthermore, this great wisdom is able to comprehend immeasurable and innumerable things that exceed all prior measures.
Śāriputra! The wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is uninterrupted; its characteristics of coming and going are immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and ineffable.
Śāriputra! Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are endowed with ethical discipline (śīla), they further attain such sovereign power.
Therefore, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, the Tathāgata travels to Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and returns again to his original dwelling place.

Śāriputra! Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have pure faith and understanding toward this perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) within the true Dharma, they hear, receive, and uphold it; by means of this, they attain swift liberation, and through that liberation, they are well-liberated.
From what phenomena does one attain liberation?
It is said: one attains excellent liberation from all forms of suffering.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having heard this Dharma regarding these four modes of dwelling in reverence, attains pure faith and, by practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), gives rise to such a thought:
"I dwell thus; I dwell in this."
"Because I thus abide constantly, I am never separated from the true Dharma of all Buddhas.

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds the words and phrases of this sūtra-dharmaparyāya, by the power of such roots of goodness, they further attain four kinds of dharmas accomplished through wisdom.
What are the four?
First, by virtue of possessing wisdom, one is able to give rise to great wisdom.
Second, by virtue of possessing wisdom, one encounters and personally attends upon all Buddhas.
Third, because they possess wisdom, they renounce the household life and enter the path with pure faith;
fourth, because they possess wisdom, they swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Śāriputra! These are called the four kinds of dharmas performed by wisdom that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), by virtue of accomplishing the power of these roots of goodness, they further attain four kinds of activities that are of great benefit.
What are the four? First, having attained a human body is called "having done much.
Second, encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world is called "having done much."
Third, to leave the household life and enter the path with pure faith is called "doing much.
Fourth, to swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called "doing much."
"Śāriputra! These are called the four kinds of activities that bring about great benefit which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), by virtue of accomplishing the power of these roots of goodness, they further attain four kinds of constituent dharmas.
What are the four? First, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the factors of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), meaning he becomes a wheel-turning king among human beings.
Second, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the Brahma-world as a Great Brahma King (*mahābrahman*).
Third, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells among the hosts of devas as the Lord of Devas (Śakra).

Fourth, having realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva becomes fully perfected in all dharmas and is titled the Dharma King; dwelling in the world, he bestows transformation and further attains the auspicious powers, the pure wisdom for purifying sentient beings, and the sphere of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*). Being able to thoroughly understand all such marks, he serves as the eye for all the devas and humans of the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The bright eye that saves the world, The most supreme among all living beings,
Thoroughly understanding all medical arts, By means of these, one realizes nirvana."
Coming and going in accordance with the teacher’s instructions, such is the karmic retribution received:
one never undergoes manifold sufferings nor falls under the power of the unwholesome.
One swiftly is reborn in the heavens and swiftly returns again among humans.
May they swiftly behold all Buddhas, And swiftly attain liberation from all hardships.
Possessing great wealth and abundant riches, May they behold all hidden treasures with their own eyes;
Whatever their hands may reach, May they be filled with every kind of jewel.
He manifests a wondrous pond, ever filled with water of eight virtues;
never having experienced sorrow or affliction, this is the fruit of mastery in doing good.
His hands and feet are not crooked, nor does he possess any mark of ugliness or deficiency.
His limbs are neither withered nor emaciated, nor are they diminished;
he is not hunchbacked, nor does he have deformed eyes; his fingers show no increase or decrease.
His head differs from that of an elephant—this is the fruit of mastery in virtue.
His physical features are all perfectly complete, Substantial and heavy like a mass of gold;
Majestic and dignified, he is a joy for all to behold, Every aspect of his countenance is fresh and wondrous.
Whether they be devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits, Or even the people of the world, [they all gaze upon him].
Making offerings and showing reverence constitutes the virtue of sublime mastery;
Being far removed from all evil realms and proceeding to the auspicious destinies of humans and gods,
one swiftly awakens to great bodhi— this is the fruit of excellent mastery.
If a person can fully comprehend the minds of all sentient beings, and having taken seven steps, proclaims throughout the world with a wondrous voice:
"This person’s wisdom is supreme; this person’s insight is supreme."
Liberation is also supreme; it is the most supreme among sentient beings.
Wisdom purifies wisdom; wisdom is established upon knowledge.
Both wisdom and knowledge, along with liberation, all rely upon the realization of the Buddhas.
Arising from the intrinsic nature of wisdom, the objects of knowledge are realized through cognition;
if one possesses such wisdom, there is nothing sought that will not be fulfilled.
Thus, I have briefly explained this profound meaning for you.
How could a person lacking wisdom and possessing few desires accept this teaching?
Deluded by ignorance and oppressed by manifold evils,
they give rise to anger and show no reverence for the True Dharma.
If beings with few desires do not show reverence for such a true Dharma,
but instead give rise to various other matters;
those beings who do not respect the Dharma are deluded and gripped by anger and resentment.
One who constantly harbors a defiled mind should not be taught [the Dharma].
As for those who have reached old age, the decrepit mahallakas—
when they approach the end of their lives, they dwell in future existence with empty words.
When one has reached the state of old age, being decrepit and a mahallaka,
yet recklessly consumes the offerings intended for an arhat, one will swiftly fall into hell.
Since even the possession of precepts is difficult to obtain, how much more so the fruit of arhatship!
Those who have faith may build temples for the spirits, yet they still fall into the evil realms. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā):
In this way, one should diligently practice the conduct of the precepts!
For the sake of seeking the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
one should serve and attend upon spiritual teachers who practice correctly with one's own body!
One shall obtain the merits described above,
and furthermore, one shall obtain immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable benefits and merits that exceed the former by many times over.

Śāriputra! You should know that because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they practice the various bodhisattva deeds of the excellent, sovereign, and wondrously pure precepts.
Śāriputra! What is called the purity of sublime ethical discipline? Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), obtain ten kinds of pure ethical discipline;
you should know them. What are these ten?
First, never to cause harm to any sentient being;
second, not to commit robbery or theft of another's property;
third, to distance oneself from all defiled attachments toward the wives and concubines of others.
Fourth, one does not engage in deception toward sentient beings.
Fifth, one maintains harmony within one's family and retinue, free from discord or estrangement.
Sixth, one does not utter harsh words toward sentient beings, because one is able to endure their abusive speech.
Seventh, he is far removed from frivolous speech, because whatever he says is spoken with careful deliberation.
Eighth, he is far removed from covetous attachment, because he has no sense of "mine" regarding the enjoyments of others.
Ninth, they remain far removed from malice, for they are well able to endure coarse words and insults.
Tenth, they remain far removed from wrong views, because they do not show reverence to other celestial seers, gods, or spirits.
Śāriputra! These are the ten kinds of pure ethical discipline that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
One should train in this way.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), there are ten further forms of pure ethical discipline that you should now know."
What are the ten? First is unimpaired ethical discipline (*śīla*), because it is not realized through a lack of wisdom.
Second is unpierced ethical discipline, because it is far removed from the conditions of unequal birth.
Third is unblemished ethical discipline (*śīla*), because it is not intermingled with any afflictions (*kleśa*).
Fourth is unstained ethical discipline, because it is increased solely by pure qualities (*śukladharma*).
Fifth is the ethical discipline of being worthy of offerings, because one acts with mastery according to one's wishes.
Sixth is the ethical discipline that is praised, because it is not censured or disparaged by the wise.
Seventh is non-censuring śīla, because it does not tolerate any faults or evils.
Eighth is well-guarded śīla, because it is well able to protect the gates of the sense faculties.
Ninth is the ethical discipline of being well-guarded, because right knowledge naturally and constantly manifests before one.
Tenth is the ethical discipline of the good destination, because the vow for great enlightenment serves as its companion.
Śāriputra! These are the ten kinds of pure ethical discipline that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
One should train in this manner.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), there are ten further types of pure ethical discipline; you should now know them."
What are the ten? First is the precept of few desires, because one knows the proper measure according to the Dharma and is pure.
Second is the precept of contentment, because one has forever severed all forms of greedy attachment.
Third is the morality of correct practice, which enables both body and mind to remain far removed from defilements.
Fourth is the morality of dwelling in tranquility, which involves abandoning and distancing oneself from all forms of clamor and distraction.
Fifth is the śīla of the dhūta virtues that eliminates craving, for it is accomplished through the mastery of wholesome roots.
Sixth is the śīla of contentment with the noble lineages, for it disregards the countenances of others and is free from expectations.
Seventh is the precept of acting according to what one has taught, for one upholds and restrains oneself in both the hidden and the manifest, never deceiving humans or devas.
Eighth is the precept of self-examination regarding one's own faults, for one constantly uses the mirror of the Dharma to illuminate and understand one’s own mind.
Ninth is the ethical discipline of not deriding the faults of others, because it protects their minds.
Tenth is the ethical discipline of maturing sentient beings, because it does not abandon the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Śāriputra! It is for this reason that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), obtain these ten kinds of pure ethical discipline.
You should train yourselves in this way.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā),
there are ten further kinds of pure ethical discipline."
You should now know:
what are the ten? First is the ethical discipline of pure faith in the Buddha, because it is free from the stumps and sprouts of the mind.
Second is the morality of pure faith in the Dharma, because it protects the true Dharma.
Third is the morality of pure faith in the Saṃgha, because it reveres the noble assembly.
Fourth is the śīla of humble application, because one does not depart from the contemplation of the Buddha’s bodhi.
Fifth is the śīla of associating with virtuous friends, because the provisions for the factors of awakening are well-accumulated.
Sixth is the ethical discipline of distancing oneself from evil associates, because it involves abandoning all unwholesome dharmas.
Seventh is the ethical discipline of the perfection of great loving-kindness, because it brings all sentient beings to maturity.
Eighth is the śīla of the perfection of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-pāramitā*), because it brings liberation to sentient beings who are in distress.
Ninth is the śīla of the perfection of great joy (*mahāmuditā-pāramitā*), because it gives rise to joy and delight toward that sublime Dharma.
Tenth is the śīla of the perfection of great equanimity (*mahopekṣā-pāramitā*), because of the relinquishing of both attachment and aversion toward all things. Śāriputra,
these are the ten kinds of pure śīla obtained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the śīla-pāramitā.
"You should train in this way. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), there are ten further forms of pure ethical discipline that you should now know."
What are the ten? First is the śīla of dāna-pāramitā, for the sake of skillfully bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
Second is the śīla of kṣānti-pāramitā, for the sake of skillfully protecting the minds of all sentient beings.
Third is the śīla of the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), because it does not regress from any correct practice.
Fourth is the śīla of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā), because the provisions for meditative concentration are well fulfilled.
Fifth is the śīla of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because one never tires of hearing the fundamental [teachings].
Sixth is the śīla of delighting in seeking to hear the Dharma, because one constantly delights in requesting the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Seventh is the ethical discipline of not cherishing the body, because one constantly observes it with the perception of impermanence.
Eighth is the ethical discipline of not esteeming life, because one constantly contemplates the mind as being like an illusion.
Ninth is the morality of complete satisfaction of all intentions, because it is perfectly pure from the first generation of the mind of awakening.
Tenth is the morality of harmony with the Buddha’s precepts, because it is dedicated toward all the precepts of the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), attains pure ethical discipline.
One should train in this manner.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), because they are fully endowed with such pure morality,
there is no sublime happiness of gods or humans that these bodhisattvas do not experience."
There is no worldly craft or field of activity that these bodhisattvas do not know;
there is no worldly requisite for the enjoyment of sentient beings that these bodhisattvas do not obtain;
and there is no ordinary person with whom they have not been at odds, yet toward such beings, these bodhisattvas have never harbored anger.
There are no beings in the world who speak with false and deceptive words whom the Bodhisattva does not trust and accept;
there are no sentient beings in the world toward whom the Bodhisattva does not conceive the thought of them as a mother;

there are no sentient beings in the world toward whom the Bodhisattva does not conceive the thought of them as a father; there are no sentient beings in the world [who are not thus regarded by the Bodhisattva].
The Bodhisattva does not give rise to thoughts of reliance or intimacy toward them;
nor does the Bodhisattva give rise to thoughts of impermanence, arising, or ceasing regarding any conditioned phenomena.

Śāriputra! Having realized that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, the bodhisattva mahāsattva disregards body and life to cultivate pure ethical discipline and practices the correct conduct of all bodhisattvas, all for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"With exquisite form and exquisite voice, Able to deliver those who delight in the Dharma—
This is not difficult for a bodhisattva, Because they abide in pure ethical discipline."
With faces and features all perfectly pure and clean, Never born blind, lame, or hunchbacked;
All parts of the body upright and well-proportioned— All arise from pure precepts.
Possessing great strength and great power, Radiant with magnificent and great majestic light.
Furthermore, through diligence and wisdom, he causes the evil Māras to tremble with fear.
All kings offer him worship; he is revered by devas and nāgas.
He skillfully severs the net of all doubts and practices great compassion with a profound mind.
Abiding firmly in the aggregate of ethical discipline, possessing great renown for practicing the Dharma,
they feel no fear when oppressed by suffering and shall never fall into the evil realms.
While all sentient beings are mired in a deep slumber, the Bodhisattva is able to awaken them.
Never resting for even a moment, he sought the Dharma throughout the four quarters.
Abiding steadfastly in the mass of precepts, he sought the path to Bodhi;
he renounced his most precious jewels, as well as his wife, children, and even his own flesh.
Seeking the most excellent Dharma teachings and the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma,
which serve as the refuge for the world, one should practice various forms of veneration.
Even if one is reviled, scolded, harmed, or subjected to malevolent conduct, [one should remain steadfast].
They receive compassion and praise because they abide in patience;
practicing according to what has been taught, their words are never false or deceptive.
Having sat peacefully at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they cause the great earth to tremble.
Free from doubt regarding the Buddha’s Dharma, they abandon the hosts of false deities and constantly serve the one honored by the gods— the Buddha, the Bhagavān.
Toward all sentient beings in the world, even when subjected to such things as blades and staves, [they remain steadfast].
To be able to bring them into harmony is the mark of one who is wise and alert.
Though sentient beings undergo heavy suffering for many hundreds of koṭis of kalpas and do not come to see him or seek him out, if he beholds them, he never abandons them.
Through discourse with virtuous friends, benefit and profit are thereby obtained;
yet sentient beings do not seek this, but instead inflict harm upon one another.
With Jambudvīpa and all the Buddha-fields, I [bestow them].
Even if there were a heap of precious jewels filling the world, used only to support the quest for a virtuous friend;
even if one were to use a sharp blade to sever my limbs and joints,
I would always maintain a mind of equanimity toward all such sentient beings.
Abandoning the deeds of foolish people, one creates the causes and conditions for the Buddha-dharma;
always maintaining pure śīla, one dwells securely in the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Cultivating the practice that accords with the Dharma, one performs the sublime conduct of bodhi.
Seeking the Buddha’s bodhi— the nectar of the wisdom of the three knowledges—
Abiding securely in the aggregate of precepts and training in all the Buddha-dharmas,
Such a person is truly wise; gods and humans alike should offer them worship.
Free from doubt regarding all phenomena, skillfully proficient in all arts and crafts,
deeply understanding the intentions of sentient beings, he propagates the sublime and beautiful Dharma.
With the aggregate of ethical discipline already purified, he sits serenely beneath the Bodhi tree.
Having subdued the armies of Māra, he awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
His radiance fills the world like the light of the sun and moon;
the Bodhisattva, honored among sentient beings, is able to open the eye of noble wisdom.
He reaches out his hand to lead all living beings, revealing the Way to all who inquire;
he always speaks first with joyful laughter, never harboring jealousy or anger.
He has sacrificed countless bodies of his own and bestowed vast wealth and treasures.
There has never been a separation from the supreme Buddha-bodhi.
Having fully perfected faith and precepts, dwelling well in truthful speech,
being utterly free from illusion and deceit, one abides securely in the mass of ethical discipline (śīla).
To the various bodhisattvas who come, even if they should utter false words, all who hear them will believe and accept them; yet [the bodhisattva] always relies on truthful speech.
If there are those who promise a bodhisattva the gift of clothing or food through false pretenses, [the bodhisattva remains steadfast].
Ultimately there is no benefit to be gained; the Bodhisattva has no mind of anger.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 43 [and] Volume 44.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, at the Imperial Command.
Chapter Twelve, Part Ten of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka:
The Chapter on Śīlapāramitā, Part Three. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they are fully endowed with such pure ethical discipline; they constantly and perpetually give rise to the perception of non-delight toward all conditioned formations (saṃskāra); they conceive of all sentient beings as their own parents; they perceive those sentient beings as being difficult to protect; they regard the five exquisite sensual desires as not being exquisite; and they conceive of the apprehension and discernment [of objects] as being without consciousness.
Śāriputra! Having made this contemplation, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to thoughts of equality or inequality. Why is that?
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such contemplation, if they give rise to a mind of equanimity, they should transcend the mind and enter into cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
If they give rise to a mind of non-equanimity, they should cause that defiled mind to transform into non-equanimity.

Thus, with the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; the arising and ceasing of the defiled mind occurs due to latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), whereby that mental substance is produced and the deluded mind falsely conceives the objects of perception to be pure.
If one can thoroughly understand that it is irrational and its essence is impure, having known this, one attains liberation; if one is liberated from that, then one has exhausted it.
What is it that is exhausted?
It is the exhaustion of greed, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion.
Such exhaustion is, in fact, not the exhaustion of greed, not the exhaustion of hatred, and not the exhaustion of delusion.
Why is this? If there were a cessation of craving within a single moment, then craving would have to be distinct from its cessation.
If that were the case, then craving would be real and its cessation would also be real.
If greed were real, it should not be extinguished.
However, Śāriputra,
all sentient beings give rise to greed because they do not engage in correct mental attention and improper reflection.

Desire arises from conceptual discrimination; if there is no discrimination, such clinging is severed. If clinging is severed, then there is no reality. Because there is no reality, there is nothing to crave within the middle way. Because there is no craving, this is the ultimate truth.
If it is true, there is no suffering within it; because there is no suffering, there is no burning affliction; and because there is no burning affliction, it is the ultimate truth.
If it is true, there is no heat within it; because there is no heat, it is cooling, and it is nirvāṇa.
Within nirvana there is no craving. Why is this? Śāriputra!
Now, Nirvana is devoid of thought and deliberation; it is the thought, "I shall eliminate such craving," and because craving is exhausted, one is said to have attained Nirvana.
If this were the case, then the subject who craves would be distinct, the object of craving would be distinct, and Nirvana itself would be yet another distinct entity.
If this were different from that, then it would be "that" in relation to "that.
If it were "that" in relation to "that," the wise person should investigate its reality.
Having sought it in this way and not finding any solid substance, if there is no solid substance, it is empty; if it is empty, it is quiescent; if it is quiescent, it is void.
What dharma is empty and non-existent?
It refers to "self" and "what belongs to self.
Whether it be permanent, eternal, abiding, or subject to change, there is no sentient being and no life-principle.
Because of this, greed, hatred, and delusion do not arise. Śāriputra,
for what reason is there "I" and "mine"?

Calculating "this is I" and "this is mine," one gives rise to the notions of "I" and "mine. Because of this inverted calculation of a self, one clings to what belongs to a self; because of clinging to what belongs to a self, there is then purposeful activity, and within that activity, four types of conduct arise.
What are the four? They are:

actions of the body, actions of speech, and actions of the mind; specifically, the utterance of coarse and evil speech prompted by mental volition, from which follows the physical act of inflicting harm.
Śāriputra! Because all foolish ordinary beings give rise to the notion of a distinction between self and other, they are seized by conceptions and bound by conceptions.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they recognize such matters as being inverted and do not associate with or become intimate with conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
Why is this? Because through habitual association, fear arises.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
"I now seek to deliver all sentient beings for the sake of attaining fearlessness; it is not fitting that I should give rise to fear toward them. I shall instead treat them with mutual affection."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
by relying on the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), give rise to the perception of all sentient beings as their parents?
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he reflects thus:
"Among sentient beings, it is not easy to find anyone who, throughout the vast expanse of the past, has not been one's father or mother."
Why is this? All sentient beings have certainly been my father or my mother in the past.

Yet, because of giving rise to a mind of greed toward them, one abandons the perception of them as a mother; because of giving rise to a mind of anger, one abandons the perception of them as a father. Thus, one wanders through birth and death without being able to sever [this cycle].
"Therefore, Śāriputra, because of this matter,
after reflecting deeply, a bodhisattva mahāsattva conceives the notion of all sentient beings as their own kin."

Śāriputra! In the past, beyond incalculable, vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable eons, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Jina-vara (Most Victorious One)—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Men, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
That Buddha’s lifespan lasted ninety million years, and he was gathered together with an assembly of nine hundred billion great śrāvakas.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Smṛtilabdha, born into a royal palace; his appearance was upright and majestic, a sight all delighted to behold, and he had perfected the foremost, perfectly pure physical marks.

Now, at the time of this bodhisattva’s birth, his parents each bestowed upon him eighty-four thousand young maidservants; his kinsmen and retinue further presented him with eighty-four thousand exquisite female musicians; and his parents’ friends and acquaintances likewise offered eighty-four thousand female musicians to the bodhisattva, desiring to raise him and always attend to him as his followers.

Śāriputra! At that time, the Bodhisattva’s father constructed three seasonal palaces for the Bodhisattva—for the hot season, the rainy season, and the cold season—so that the Bodhisattva might dwell within these magnificent halls at all times as the seasons changed. Furthermore, he had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of musical performances surround the Bodhisattva to provide him with entertainment.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva heard the sounds of music, as he was about to raise his voice, the perception of arising and ceasing manifested before him.
When the music momentarily ceased, he then reflected: "Upon what does this sound depend for its arising?"
From where does it arise?
Upon what does it depend for its subsistence? Where does it cease?

At that time, when the Bodhisattva engages in this contemplation, he does not give rise to the perception of distinctions between day and night; rather, he constantly gives rise to the perception of impermanence and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in.

Śāriputra! At that time, for forty thousand years, the Bodhisattva Smṛtilābha never gave rise to attachment toward pleasure, nor for forty thousand years did he ever become defiled by craving for sensual desires.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, dwelling within the deep inner palace, entered the four dhyānas and gave rise to the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Thereupon, by means of his power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi*), he rose from the inner palace into the air and proceeded to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Bhagavān Most Victorious Assembly was.
Having arrived there, he questioned that Buddha, and having acquired a small measure of wholesome dharmas, he returned to his own palace. Śāriputra,
on the day that Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Smṛtilābha again went to the place where the Tathāgata resided and asked the bhikṣus:
"Where are the most excellent Buddhas now?
I wish to see, pay homage to, and make offerings to them.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to Smṛti:
"Good son! Do you not know? The Tathāgata has now entered parinirvāṇa."

At that time, having learned that the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva immediately cast his entire body to the ground at that spot; weeping and sobbing, he fainted for a long while before finally regaining consciousness.
Then he spoke in verse:
“Thus illuminating the world, Having reached the further shore of all dharmas,
How can I, dwelling on the ground of negligence, Deceive myself?”
Only once in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons does a Tathāgata appear;
yet I have not served him—whom else shall I take as my refuge and protector?
As I reflect upon myself, I realize that my mother was no true kinswoman or benefactor.
Why do you not praise the Tathāgata, so that I may behold him upon my first birth?
My father is neither a kinsman nor a benefactor; he has cast me into the midst of various desires.
Now that I am thus bound and constrained, I have turned away from serving the World-Honored One.
Not hearing the sixty kinds of wondrous sounds spoken by the Buddha, one is born having lost a great benefit; this is because one did not serve the Buddha.
He who has reached the other shore of all dharmas and possesses great compassion for the world—
Held fast by pride and negligence, I did not serve the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
Throughout billions of nayutas of kalpas, it is extremely difficult to behold the Buddhas;
yet I failed to practice offerings, arriving only after their parinirvāṇa.
Now I reflect deeply: my parents were not virtuous;
when I was first born, why did they not praise the Buddha for me, so that I might behold the Most Victorious Honored One and dwell forever in the presence of the Tathāgata?
Extensively practicing various offerings and hearing the True Dharma—
those sixty kinds of wondrous sounds proclaimed by the Tathāgata,
which I had never heard before— I have only now arrived after his parinirvāṇa.
"I have now lost a great benefit, coming only after his parinirvāṇa,
when he will expound the wondrous Dharma of the unconditioned, just as the former Buddhas have taught. "Śāriputra!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Smṛtiprāpta arose from that spot weeping and went to the bed of parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Varagana.
Having arrived there, he wailed and sobbed with grief; he circumambulated the Tathāgata to the right one hundred thousand times, then withdrew to stand to one side and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha is the true Honored One for all living beings, Who has proclaimed the unsurpassed, subtle, and wonderful Dharma.”
I now arouse a heart of utmost sincerity, for the sake of attaining supreme bodhi.
I now pay homage at the feet of the Tathāgata, the Greatly Wise One of the world’s mantras;
may I attain such wisdom as that which the Most Victorious Honored One has obtained.
In the past, I was weak and lacked wisdom; I fell among the ranks of Māra.
Dwelling at home, I was beset by many constraints, and so I could not serve the Supreme among Men.
I have already cultivated supreme and wondrous merit, By which I have briefly gained the opportunity to behold the Tathāgata;
Yet the Buddha has not deigned to reveal the True Dharma, And thus I now undergo extreme suffering.
Today, before this assembly of nāgas and others, I utter these words of sincere truth:
if my original aspiration is indeed as it was, may all that I have spoken be fulfilled without fail.
May I, in a future age, when the Buddhas, the Honored Ones among Men, appear,
behold their profound meaning and vast activity, and proclaim the unsurpassed, true Dharma.
At that time, no obstacles arose for me; having arisen, I did not indulge in various desires.
Mastering the charms of women, I was not led astray by them, and I shattered the prison of Māra.
In every life they shall always behold the Buddhas, And hear the unsurpassed True Dharma manifest before them;
From beholding the Buddhas, pure faith arises, And having given rise to pure faith, they cultivate all practices.
If the sincere words I have uttered are indeed true and not false,
by this power may the Tathāgata rise from his seat, suddenly awakening as if from a deep sleep.
As soon as the Bodhisattva had uttered these sincere words, the Tathāgata rose from his seat at that very moment;
hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devas then offered and scattered exquisite garments upon him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with joy; he rose up from his body and leaped into the void.
Having established himself securely in the sky, he praised the Most Victorious One with sublime verses.
With a compassionate mind that benefits the world and shines with great brilliance, the foremost teacher of great supernormal powers,
the awakened one who pities and takes pity upon the world, proclaims the unsurpassed True Dharma.

“Śāriputra! At that time, after the Bodhisattva Smṛtilabdha had proclaimed these verses of praise, wishing to cause the great assembly to rejoice all the more, he further spoke these verses before the Buddha:
‘In the future I shall become a Buddha, Manifesting the bestowal of prophecy, O Honored One among Men.’”
You, the great assembly, should follow and learn this, And offer worship to the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One is inconceivable; Who would not give rise to faith in him?
"Out of compassion for us and all sentient beings, you who have already entered nirvāṇa have now arisen once more.

"Śāriputra! This Bodhisattva Smṛtiplāvin made grand offerings within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Varasundara and planted various roots of merit. By the power of such roots of goodness, at the end of his life here, he was reborn in that realm of the gods in a happy destination. For twenty koṭis of great kalpas, he did not fall into the evil destinies; furthermore, for another twenty koṭis of great kalpas, he did not experience sensual pleasures."

Śāriputra! At that time, the Bodhisattva Smṛtiprāpta personally attended upon and served seven thousand Buddhas, making extensive offerings at the abodes of those Buddhas and constantly practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya) for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

In the final kalpa of the future age, through the power of his own roots of goodness, he will attain the supreme body and manifest complete and perfect enlightenment, appearing in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Śālarāja.

Śāriputra! The lifespan of that Buddha, King of Śālas, was twenty koṭis of years. He held two assemblies with his disciples to preach the Dharma. In the first great assembly, there were twenty koṭis of śrāvaka disciples; in the second great assembly, there were forty thousand. All of them were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions. They had attained great power and reached the supreme shore of mastery over all mental states.
Śāriputra! After that Blessed One entered parinirvāṇa, his relics were widely distributed and numerous stupas were erected; his True Dharma remained in the world for a full ten thousand years.
At that time, the Bhagavān, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Śāriputra, you should know: This Bodhisattva Pratiṣṭhitasmṛti Has never fallen into the evil realms For twenty koṭis of kalpas.”
Furthermore, throughout such kalpas, he did not cultivate any greedy desires;
during that intervening time, seven thousand Buddhas passed into parinirvāṇa.
Delighting in all Buddha-dharmas, he constantly practiced pure conduct.
Finally awakening to bodhi, he was named Śālarāja Buddha.
For thirty thousand koṭis of years, he dwelt in unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
having awakened to supreme bodhi, he benefited all sentient beings.
For twenty koṭis of years, he extensively proclaimed the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
twenty koṭis of followers, along with another forty thousand,
all completely exhausted their outflows— these were all the Buddha’s assembly of sages.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his relics were widely distributed,
and stupas were fully established, numbering sixty thousand koṭis.
After his passing, the Dharma remained in the world for ten thousand years.
Hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the True Dharma, all give rise to pure faith.
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the wise harbor no doubt;
they shall never fall into the evil realms and will swiftly realize nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), their aggregate of pure morality gives rise to the perception of all sentient beings as one's own parents."
Why is this? Because in the past, due to the arising of a mind of desire, I abandoned the perception of my mother; due to the arising of a mind of anger, I abandoned the perception of my father.
Now, as I practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and abide in pure morality, I constantly give rise to a mind of revulsion and opposition toward those various desires.

In order to eliminate greed, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, through correct mental attention (*samyak-manasikāra*), gives rise to a perception of genuine revulsion toward all sensual desires. Śāriputra!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such correct reflection, he is able to personally understand the characteristics of all desires, and he is also able to understand the repulsiveness and aversion associated with all desires.
Śāriputra! What is meant by "understanding all desires" and being able to understand the aversion to and repulsion toward all desires? Śāriputra!

What is called "desires" refers to craving and attachment; that is, craving for the various forms cognized by visual consciousness is called desire, and craving for the various sounds cognized by auditory consciousness is called desire.

In this way, craving for the various fragrances cognized by the nose-consciousness, the various flavors cognized by the tongue-consciousness, and the various tangibles cognized by the body-consciousness—this is called desire.
Śāriputra! Where there is craving, there is attachment; that which is attachment is called a fetter (*saṃyojana*).
A fetter is called an undertaking; an undertaking is called bondage, and it is also termed unreal conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

In this way, Śāriputra, all sentient beings are bound, ensnared, thoroughly fettered, and intensely and universally bound by the unreal bonds of conceptual proliferation; thus, they do not attain liberation.
Śāriputra! By what are all sentient beings bound that they are called "bound"?
It is because they are bound by the bondage of form that they are called "bound," and so on, up to being bound by the bondage of sound, odor, taste, and touch that they are called "bound."
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the "bondage of form" (*rūpa-bandhana*)?

It refers to the false arising of the notion of a self, the notion of a life-principle, the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of permanence, the notion of constancy, the notion of immutability, the notion of reality, the notion of wholeness, and the notion of a unified whole with respect to all forms obtained within one's own body; such notions as these are called the bondage of form.
Śāriputra! What is meant by being bound by the fetters of form?

It refers to deeply cherishing and valuing the self-nature and characteristics that have arisen, extensively giving rise to self-love, and never ceasing to be attached to all forms of women, such as wives and concubines; this is what is meant by being bound by the fetters of form.
Śāriputra! Once these sentient beings have enjoyed various sensual desires, they commit unwholesome karma, failing to know the faults of those desires as they truly are.
What are called the faults of sensual desires?
Śāriputra, there is not a single sensual desire that is not a fault.
Therefore, a wise person should not give rise to desire for any faults.
Yet, to head toward the evil realms is a grave fault rooted in desire; I shall now reveal its characteristics to you.
Śāriputra! What are called the grave faults of sensual desires that lead to rebirth in the evil realms? Śāriputra!
When I say that one who indulges in all sensual desires does not fail to commit even the slightest evil,
it means there is no small suffering that such a person will not experience when those actions ripen.
Therefore, Śāriputra!
When I observe all the thousandfold world systems, I see that among sentient beings, no greater enemy exists than the desires for wives, concubines, and female forms. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Those who possess wisdom are the Tathāgata; those spoken of as lacking wisdom are the multitudes of sentient beings.
That which is censured and rejected by the wise is called the truth; that which is embraced by the ignorant is not the truth.
Śāriputra! What do those who lack wisdom grasp at?
That is to say, they grasp at all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and they grasp at wives, concubines, female beauty, various sensual desires, as well as sons, daughters, and the like.
Furthermore, that person of little wisdom is captivated by his wife, children, and various forms of female beauty.
As they thus become mutually entangled and bound to one another, they fail to embrace the Noble Path.
Śāriputra! Because those who lack wisdom are bound by men and women, wives and concubines, and all forms of female beauty, they create many obstacles to wholesome dharmas.
What are these obstacles? They are:

that which obstructs leaving the household life, obstructs ethical discipline (śīla), obstructs meditative concentration (dhyāna), obstructs the heavenly realms, and obstructs nirvāṇa; furthermore, they can obstruct all sublime and wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If those who lack wisdom should take possession of men, women, wives, concubines, and various female forms, in brief, this is to take possession of enemies; it is to take possession of the realms of hell, animals, and the world of hungry ghosts and asuras.
Śāriputra! To speak of such appropriation in brief, it is the appropriation of all evil and unwholesome dharmas, which obstructs all the dharmas of the noble and holy ones.
Furthermore, if one indulges in the company of men and women, wives and concubines, and various female forms, it will even obstruct one from all kinds of fine food, let alone other superior matters.

Śāriputra! To speak briefly of such hindrances: they are what obstructs seeing the Buddha, obstructs hearing the Dharma, and obstructs serving the Saṅgha; they obstruct the pure faith gained from seeing the Buddha, the pure faith gained from hearing the Dharma, and the pure faith gained from serving the Saṅgha.

To speak briefly, it obstructs the attainment of the perfection of being free from calamities, and it obstructs the wealth of faith, the wealth of ethical discipline, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of shame, and the wealth of dread of blame.

Śāriputra! If one embraces sons, daughters, wives, concubines, and various forms of sensual desire, one thereby embraces lack of faith, immoral conduct, false learning, stinginess, and corrupt wisdom; furthermore, one embraces shamelessness, lack of remorse, as well as diseases, abscesses, poisonous arrows, masses of fire, and venomous snakes.

Śāriputra! If there are those who delight in living at home, becoming addicted to it and unable to renounce it, you should know that this is precisely to delight in dwelling among graves. Therefore, I say that delighting in living at home is like staying among graves; furthermore, to be in a wilderness with no one to whom one can turn for refuge is to lose all pure and wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are sentient beings who relish and become attached to the various female forms of desire—men, women, wives, concubines, and daughters—you should know that they are relishing gravel and hailstones; they are relishing the edge of a sharp sword; they are relishing a great hot iron ball; they are relishing sitting upon a hot iron bed; and they are relishing a hot iron stool.

Śāriputra! If one takes pleasure in garlands, perfumes, and ointments, it is the same as taking pleasure in garlands of glowing red-hot iron, or taking pleasure in smearing one's body with excrement and urine.
Śāriputra! If one appropriates a dwelling or house, know that one is appropriating a great, heated iron cauldron.
If one appropriates slaves or laborers, know that one is appropriating the cruel wardens of hell.

If one takes possession of elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, oxen, sheep, chickens, or pigs, know that one is taking possession of the black and brindled dogs within the hells, and furthermore, one is taking possession of the guards stationed over a hundred *yojanas*.

To state the essential point: if one takes possession of wives, concubines, sons, daughters, or any objects of female desire, you should know that this is precisely to take possession of the entire mass of all sufferings, sorrows, griefs, and afflictions.

Śāriputra! It would be better to rely upon an iron bed a thousand yojanas in size, intensely hot, thoroughly heated, and ablaze with fierce flames, than to even look at the wives, concubines, or daughters provided by one’s parents with a mind of defiled attachment, let alone to draw near to or embrace them.

Why is this? Śāriputra, you should know that a woman is the root of all suffering, the root of obstacles, the root of slaughter, the root of bondage, the root of sorrow, the root of enmity, and the root of congenital blindness; you should know that a woman extinguishes the noble eye of wisdom.
One should know that women are like hot iron flowers scattered upon the ground, which one treads upon with one's feet.
One should know that women cause all manner of perverse natures to spread and increase.
Śāriputra! For what reason is she called a "woman"?
That which is called a "woman" is named the bearer of a heavy burden.

Why is this? Because it causes sentient beings to bear heavy burdens; because it causes sentient beings to wear out heavy burdens; because it causes sentient beings to undergo heavy burdens; because it causes sentient beings to carry heavy burdens as they go about their affairs; because it causes sentient beings to travel everywhere while laden with heavy burdens; because it causes sentient beings to experience mental exhaustion and suffering due to these heavy burdens; because it causes sentient beings to be tormented and oppressed by heavy burdens; and because it causes sentient beings to be harmed by heavy burdens.
Śāriputra! Furthermore, for what reason is she called a "wife"? That which is called a wife is the place where all sentient beings entrust their burdens;

it is the place where slaves of craving sink and drown; it is the place where those who obey their wives pay their taxes; it is the place where those infatuated by a wife’s charms are deluded; it is the place where those dominated by their wives seek refuge; it is the place where those subjugated by their wives rely for support; it is the place where those who are masters over their wives indulge in negligence; it is the place where those who are slaves to their wives suffer exhaustion; and it is the place where those who revolve according to their wives look up with longing.
Śāriputra! For these and other such reasons, these various places are designated as "wives.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Sentient beings in the world do not cast off their heavy burden on account of women.
What is this heavy burden that they do not cast off?
It is the so-called five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
What are the five aggregates?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. Śāriputra!
Worldly women cause sentient beings not to abandon this heavy burden of the five aggregates; therefore, the five aggregates are designated as "wives. Śāriputra!
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do people in the world call a wife "the second [self]"?

Śāriputra, it is because such a woman is the second companion in the violation of ethical discipline (śīla); she is the second companion in the violation of dignified conduct (vṛtta); she is the second companion in the violation of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi); she is the second companion at the time of eating; she is the second companion in going to the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; and she is the second companion who can obstruct noble wisdom, hinder the bliss of nirvāṇa, and encompass all suffering. For these reasons, she is called "the second."
Śāriputra! Furthermore, for what reason do people of the world refer to women as the "mother-folk" (mātṛgrāma)? Śāriputra!
All women give rise to many faults and are characterized by boundless illusion and deception; therefore, they are called the "multitude of mothers.
If one follows after this multitude of mothers and falls under their sway, know that one has fallen into the hands of Māra and is at his disposal to commit evil.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

You should know that all women in the world give rise to many faults and boundless illusions and deceptions; their minds are largely fickle and restless, and their hearts wander, overturn, and fail to abide.
Their minds are like mountain langurs, their minds are like monkeys; they are skilled at manifesting illusory and deceptive arts.
Because of such characteristics, women are called the "multitude of mothers."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

What is called the "multitude of mothers" is the illusory village of mothers; it is also named the illusory city, the capital of the illusory king, the pavilion for illusory guests, the hall of illusory people, the illusory country and illusory village, the illusory place and illusory region. It is this illusory world, this illusory universe, this boundless illusion, this vast illusion, this immeasurable illusion, and this inconceivable illusion.
Śāriputra! Because such heavy faults as these regarding sensual desires lead one toward the evil destinies, women are called "the mother’s village of illusion. Śāriputra!
For example, it is like a master illusionist who has well studied the arts of illusion and manifests various deceptive illusions before a great assembly.

Śāriputra, the village of women is just like this; they have well studied the arts of feminine deception and are able to bind men—whether they see them, hear them, touch them, or come into contact with them.

Furthermore, women are skillfully adept at seduction and charm; because they possess such charm, they exercise power and autonomy. Whether they are engaged in singing, dancing, playing, laughing, weeping, coming and going, or remaining in a state of standing, sitting, or lying down, at all times they are able to deprive men of their self-mastery, binding them to follow the woman's lead and subjecting them to her commands.
Śāriputra! It is just as when a field of ripening rice in the world is severely damaged by a great hailstorm.
In the same way, Śāriputra!
This mother’s illusory village is like a great hailstorm falling upon a man’s field, destroying all the sprouts of the white dharmas and annihilating them entirely. Śāriputra!

All such heavy transgressions of craving that lead to the evil realms, worldly fools and ordinary people are deluded by them and fail to realize their nature; furthermore, they cling to the beloved wives, concubines, and various women, becoming intoxicated and infatuated by sensual desire.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the wise bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having deeply understood the faults of these various desires, he gives rise to two kinds of perceptions based on the true Dharma: namely, the perception of ordinary fools as wicked persons, and the perception of Buddhas and bodhisattvas as virtuous persons."
Having made this contemplation, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects to himself:
"I should now proceed toward the destination of virtuous beings; it is not fitting for me to go toward that destination of wicked beings."

I should not go to the realms of hell-beings, animals, or the hungry ghosts and asuras; I should not go to the realm of those who have destroyed their ethical discipline, nor to the abodes of those who violate the precepts;
I should now go to the most excellent, unsurpassed, and unobstructed realm that is free from all such states, and I should now go to the realm of the great wisdom of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, he forms this thought: "I shall proceed against the current, not with the current; I shall utter the lion’s roar, not the jackal’s cry; I shall manifest the great power of the king of golden-winged birds, and should not manifest the power of a minute insect; I should now act as a virtuous and noble person, not as a person who is treacherous, evil, or vulgar; I should now consume the pure food of virtuous and superior men, and should not consume the impure food of those base and unworthy men; I should practice subtle meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supreme meditative concentration, extraordinary meditative concentration, and the meditative concentrations belonging to the category attained through the foremost *samādhi*, and I should not practice meditative concentrations that do not belong to that category, nor inferior or meager meditative concentrations."
"Śāriputra! Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
'I should sport in the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) of all Buddhas; I should not sport in the meditative concentrations of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or any foolish ordinary beings.'"
I shall practice the meditative concentration that is independent; I should not practice the meditative concentration that relies on form.

Furthermore, I should not rely on the meditative concentrations of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor should I practice the meditative concentration that relies on the earth element.

Furthermore, they do not rely on the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) based on the element of water, the element of fire, or the element of wind; nor do they practice the meditative absorptions based on the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

Furthermore, they do not rely on the meditative absorptions based on the form realm (rūpadhātu) or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); nor do they practice the meditative absorptions based on this world or other worlds.
"Furthermore, he does not rely on such meditative concentration as that which has been seen, heard, thought, cognized, attained, touched, or realized. Śāriputra,
this bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects, saying:
"I shall cultivate the supportless meditative concentration; by cultivating it, I shall neither harm myself, nor harm others, nor harm both.
I shall pursue the perfect attainment of Buddha-wisdom; why should I further seek the various desires of the world?"

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a wise bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), having performed such correct contemplations as these, he should further give rise to four kinds of disenchantment."
What are the four? They are:

being able to give rise to weary detachment toward all sensual desires; being able to give rise to weary detachment toward all states of existence (*bhava*); being able to give rise to weary detachment toward those sentient beings who are ungrateful; and being able to give rise to weary detachment toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and their various sufferings and afflictions.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s arousal of four kinds of thoughts of revulsion by virtue of practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
One should train in this way.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he should contemplate sentient beings who, while situated in the evil realms, give rise to lustful thoughts upon seeing beautiful women, and should cultivate four kinds of thoughts of revulsion.
What are these four?
They are the perception of decline, the perception of falling into ruin, the perception of a walking latrine, and the perception of pus, festering filth, and impurity.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Śāriputra, if those sentient beings with consciousness dwelling in the evil realms should still give rise to these four perceptions upon seeing the exquisite form of a woman, how much more so should this be the case for humans? Śāriputra!

When sons of noble family who are firmly established in the Mahāyāna and weary of all conditioned phenomena see the exquisite form of a woman, they give rise to four perceptions: that it is subject to decline and loss, that it is a precipice from which one falls, that it is a latrine, and that it is festering pus and foul excrement.

If, despite forming these perceptions, a mind of desire still arises, one should further cultivate three kinds of perceptions of kinship: namely, regarding those of the mother’s class, one should form the perception of them as a mother; regarding those of the sister’s class, one should form the perception of them as a sister; and regarding those of the daughter’s class, one should form the perception of them as a daughter.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who, upon hearing what I have spoken, is able to understand it well, should accordingly follow the śīlapāramitā of such a sūtra.”
Why is this? Because there is no sentient being who can be easily found who has not been my parent over the course of the long, distant past. Why is that?
All these sentient beings have once been my parents.
If one associates with wives, concubines, or women, it is as if one is associating with one's mothers of the past.
"Śāriputra! Having heard what I have said, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of purification, should thus exert themselves in diligent cultivation and study.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
All the ignorant, ordinary worldlings oppose and do not believe that True Dharma;
the Bodhisattva is not so, for he accords with the True Dharma without opposition.

If, while practicing such contemplations, one is still pursued by a mind of craving, the bodhisattva should further observe according to reality: from what does the arising craving see that it is produced?
If one should give rise to a mind of craving toward the eye, the bodhisattva should again contemplate it correctly according to reality:
"As for me who gives rise to defiled attachment toward the eye, who is it that can see the eye?"
Does the eye see the eye?
Would that mean the self-substance sees its own self-substance? Why is this so?

That is also the eye, and this is also the eye; since both are produced by the four great elements and arise from the primary elements, one does not give rise to defiled attachment toward this very self-body by means of that self-body, nor does one give rise to defiled attachment toward one's own self-body.
Why is this? Because that is precisely this.
If one were to give rise to defiled attachment toward that, one would likewise have to give rise to defiled attachment toward this, for there is no distinction between them.
All the foolish worldlings of the entire world dwell without distinction; I must now seek the Dharma of distinction.
Why is this? Because all thoughts of sensual desire possess no merit whatsoever.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Successively they share the same meaning, Entirely lacking any nature of differentiation;
Yet through deviant attachments that contradict the principle, This craving and affection arise."
How can that which is produced from the four great elements further defile those very elements?
All phenomena are like illusions; there is no basis for giving rise to craving and attachment.
It is through our own false discrimination that we falsely give rise to a mind of craving and attachment.
The unworthy give rise to craving, while the virtuous and good have no attachment.
Throughout the realms of the ten directions, there is no real craving to be found;
it is only through false conceptualization that this craving and attachment arise.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), even after having made such an observation, if they are still pursued by a mind of craving, they should—by virtue of the power of the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) from hearing the teachings spoken by the Buddha—further conform to such sūtras as this, which say: 'The eye is like a mass of foam; it cannot be grasped.'"

Why is this? Because all these phenomena, such as the mass of foam and so forth, are fundamentally without a self and without a sentient being; they have no life-principle, no person, no manava, no individual, no spirit-born, no agent, and no experiencer.
In such things as these, which are without action and without recipient, among all dharmas, who could be subject to defiled attachment?
And toward what object could such defiled attachment arise? Śāriputra!
The eye is like a floating bubble; its nature is not solid. Why is this?

Because all phenomena, such as those bubbles and the like, are fundamentally without a self and without a sentient being; they have no life-principle, no person, no manava, no individual born of mind, no agent, and no experiencer.
Within such phenomena that are unconditioned and purposeless, who could conceive of attachment or craving?
And toward what object could such attachment and craving arise? Śāriputra!
The eye is like a mirage, arising from karma, delusion, and craving. Why is this?
Because all phenomena, such as that mirage, are fundamentally without a self and without sentient beings; who, then, could be subject to defiled attachment?
In what does one find defiled attachment?
Śāriputra, the eye is like a plantain tree; its substance is not solid or enduring.

Why is this? Because all phenomena, such as the plantain tree and others, are fundamentally without a self and without sentient beings; even who could be subject to defiled attachment, and toward what could there be defiled attachment?
Śāriputra! This eye is like a dream; it does not see according to reality. Why is this?

All these phenomena, such as that empty dream, are fundamentally without a self and without sentient beings; even so, who could be subject to defiled attachment, and toward what could they be attached?
Śāriputra! The eye is like an echo, dependent upon a multitude of conditions. Why is this?

All those dharmas, such as echoes and the like, are fundamentally without a self and without sentient beings; even so, who could be subject to defiled attachment, and toward what could they be attached?
Śāriputra! The eye is like a reflection of light, appearing as a shadow dependent upon karma. Why is this?
All these phenomena, such as reflections and shadows, are fundamentally without a self and without sentient beings; who, then, could be subject to defiled attachment?
Toward what could one be defiledly attached?
Śāriputra! The eye is like a drifting cloud, appearing as a scattered and disordered phenomenon. Why is this?

In those dharmas such as clouds and so forth, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient being; even down to the question of who could be subject to defiled attachment, or toward what could one be attached? Śāriputra!
The eye is like a flash of lightning, perishing in the very moment it arises. Why is this?
For in phenomena such as lightning, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient being; indeed, who could possibly be subject to defiled attachment?
In what is there attachment or craving? Śāriputra,
this eye is like space, devoid of self and what belongs to self.

Why is this? Because in those dharmas such as emptiness, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient beings; even down to the question of who could be subject to defiled attachment, or toward what could they be attached?
Śāriputra! The eye is devoid of cognition, like grass, wood, earth, or stone. Why is this?
In phenomena such as ignorance, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient being; even so, who could be subject to defiled attachment?
Toward what could one be attached? Śāriputra!
The eye has no agency; it turns according to the mechanism of the wind. Why is this?
Because in phenomena such as non-action, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient being; even so, who could possibly be subject to defiled attachment?
In what does one find defiled attachment? Śāriputra,
the eye is a deceptive accumulation of impurity and decay.
Why is this? Because in phenomena such as falsehood, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient being; who, then, could be subject to defiled attachment, and toward what could they be attached?
Śāriputra! The eye is a phenomenon that is deceptive, subject to destruction, disintegration, and total extinction. Why is this so?
In phenomena such as falsehood, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient being; even so, who could be subject to defiled attachment, and toward what could one be attached? Śāriputra!
The eye is like a well on a mound, constantly beset by old age. Why is this?
In phenomena such as the well on a mound, there is fundamentally no self and no sentient being; even so, who could possibly be subject to defiled attachment?
In what does one find attachment?
Śāriputra, the eye does not endure for long; it ultimately ends at the threshold of death.

Why is this? Because all phenomena do not abide for long; fundamentally, there is no self and no sentient being; there is no life-principle, no person, no individual, no manava, no spirit, no agent, and no experiencer.
Within such phenomena produced by the convergence of conditions—which are without agency and without purpose—who could be subject to defiled attachment?
And toward what object would one practice such defiled attachment?
In this way, it is extensively taught that all internal and external phenomena, including the sense faculties and their objects,
are likewise so. Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes correctly in this manner, it is impossible for them to be led astray by any craving or attachment.
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who contemplates in this manner, you should know that they have forever abandoned craving and attachment regarding all phenomena.
Śāriputra, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) with ultimate purity, extinguishing all craving and attachment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who thus practices the pure conduct of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) does not perform any action that harms sentient beings; even at the cost of his own life, he never inflicts harm upon any living being.”
He does not engage in any act of taking what is not given; even at the cost of his life, he never steals the possessions of others.
He does not practice any form of sexual misconduct or debauchery; even at the cost of his life, he never becomes attached to or pursues women.
He does not utter any deceptive or false speech; even at the cost of his life, he does not practice falsehood toward any sentient being.
He does not speak any harsh or rude words; even at the cost of his life, he never reviles or insults any sentient being.

One does not utter any words of divisive speech, nor even at the cost of one's life does one engage in slander toward sentient beings, because one has developed contentment regarding one's own kinsmen.
He does not propagate any frivolous or ornate speech; his words are always measured by the facts. Even at the cost of his life, he never uses flowery embellishments or artfully adorned phrases.
He does not give rise to covetous attachment toward the wealth and property of others; even at the cost of his life, he remains forever free from craving for any objects of enjoyment.
They possess the perfection of patience toward all forms of affliction and insult; they are well able to endure harsh and evil words, and do not give rise to anger even at the cost of their lives.
Among all phenomena, they do not give rise to wrong views; even at the cost of their lives, they never place faith in other celestial deities, but take refuge with a pure mind in the Buddha alone.
"Śāriputra! This is called the purity of ethical discipline (śīla) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he fully accomplishes the immeasurable and boundless true dharmas of all Buddhas. Śāriputra!

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they fully accomplish and perfect unimpaired ethical discipline, as they do not associate with those lacking wisdom.
He fully accomplishes the integrity of unbroken *śīla*, because he is able to distance himself from rebirth in unequal states.
He fully accomplishes the integrity of unstained *śīla*, because he does not associate with evil persons or the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
They fully accomplish the unadulterated ethical discipline (*śīla*), because it is increased solely by wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*).
They fully accomplish the ethical discipline worthy of offerings, because they act with mastery according to their wishes.
He is fully accomplished in the praised morality, for he is not censured or reviled by the wise.
He is fully accomplished in well-guarded morality, for he is endowed with perfect mindfulness and clear comprehension.
He is fully accomplished in non-reproachable ethical discipline (*akṣata-śīla*), because he does not give rise to any faults.
He is fully accomplished in well-guarded ethical discipline (*susaṃvṛta-śīla*), because he is well-restrained at the gates of the sense faculties.
They fully accomplish lofty and expansive ethical discipline (*śīla*), because they are remembered by all Buddhas.
They fully accomplish ethical discipline characterized by few desires, because they know the measure of purity.
He fully accomplishes the morality of contentment because he delights in renunciation;
he fully accomplishes the morality of right conduct because his body and mind are secluded;
he fully accomplishes the morality of dwelling in stillness because he is weary of clamor and bustle.
He is fully accomplished in the noble lineage of ethical discipline characterized by wholesome joy, because he disregards the countenances of others and is free from expectations.
He is fully accomplished in the ethical discipline of the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*) and fewness of affairs, because he freely cultivates all roots of goodness.
