They fully accomplish the ethical discipline of acting according to what has been taught, so as not to deceive the world of gods and humans;
they fully accomplish the ethical discipline of great loving-kindness, so as not to harm any living being.
They fully accomplish the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of great compassion, because they are able to endure all forms of suffering and affliction.
They fully accomplish the ethical discipline of great joy, because they never regress from that dharma-bliss.
They are fully accomplished in the śīla of great equanimity, because all attachment and aversion have been utterly severed.
They are fully accomplished in the śīla of constantly examining one's own faults, because they perpetually and skillfully investigate and illuminate their inner minds.
He fully accomplishes the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of not disparaging the faults of others, because he skillfully protects the minds of sentient beings.
He fully accomplishes the ethical discipline of maturing sentient beings, because he is ultimately able to reach the perfection (*pāramitā*) of generosity.
They are fully accomplished in the well-guarded śīla, for they are ultimately able to reach the further shore of ethical discipline.
They are fully accomplished in the śīla of a mind free from malice and harm, for they are ultimately able to reach the further shore of patience.
They fully accomplish the morality of non-retrogression, because they are ultimately able to reach the further shore of right effort.
They fully accomplish the morality of the perfection of the factors of concentration, because they are ultimately able to reach the further shore of meditative absorption.
They are fully endowed with the ethical discipline of insatiable hearing of the true Dharma, because they are ultimately able to reach the further shore of great wisdom.
They are fully endowed with the ethical discipline of associating with virtuous friends, because they have skillfully cultivated and accumulated the provisions for the factors of enlightenment.
He is fully accomplished in the ethical discipline of distancing oneself from evil friends, because he has abandoned all uneven paths.
He is fully accomplished in the ethical discipline of non-attachment to the body, because he constantly observes it with the perception of impermanence.
They fully accomplish the ethical discipline of non-attachment to life, because that which they value is not constantly maintained.
They fully accomplish the ethical discipline of being free from remorse, because their minds are thoroughly purified.
He fully accomplishes the precept of not feigning hypocrisy, because it is thoroughly purified through skillful means.
He fully accomplishes the precept of freedom from affliction and feverish distress, because his superior intention is thoroughly purified.
They fully accomplish the precept of being neither conceited nor fickle, because they have forever abandoned all craving and attachment.
They fully accomplish the precept of being free from arrogance, because they are gentle, supple, and straightforward.
He is fully accomplished in the morality of being free from harshness and perversity, because his nature is virtuous and gentle.
He is fully accomplished in the morality of being well-disciplined, because he is free from anger and resentment.
They are fully accomplished in the morality of tranquility, because their nature is peaceful and collected.
They are fully accomplished in the morality of virtuous speech, because they do not contradict what they have said.
They are fully accomplished in the ethical discipline (*śīla*) that matures sentient beings, because they never abandon the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
They are fully accomplished in the ethical discipline that protects the true Dharma, because they do not themselves corrupt the noble wealth of the Dharma.

Śāriputra! A wise bodhisattva mahāsattva, possessing such a pure aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and fully accomplishing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), is well able to practice the sublime conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksambodhi*).
Śāriputra! This is called the śīla-pāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

If all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice this bodhisattva conduct, no māras, māra-folk, or sons of gods will be able to disturb or confuse them, nor can they be defeated or overwhelmed by the heterodox doctrines of others.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Forty-Four and Volume Forty-Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight: The Perfection of Forbearance (Kṣānti-pāramitā), Part Eleven of the Twelfth Assembly, the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"What is called the perfection of forbearance (kṣānti-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
For the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently studies and practices such dharmas while performing the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), they are endowed with the power of endurance and possess a nature that is firm and upright. They are able to voluntarily endure all contacts such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, snakes, scorpions, mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, and sun; furthermore, they can endure harsh and abusive speech, vulgar expressions, and even those intense, swift, piercing, and agonizing physical pains arising from the body—ranging from life-threatening to fatal. All such sufferings, they are able to endure.
“Śāriputra! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to possess these qualities, this is called the pāramitā of kṣānti.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
"In the distant past, during the long night before I attained Buddhahood, I practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva and constantly cultivated patience.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How did the Blessed One, while practicing as a bodhisattva, cultivate and accumulate the practice of patience, the bodhisattva conduct?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“I recall that in the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva conduct, many sentient beings came repeatedly to revile and abuse me, and in my very presence they uttered various unlawful, wicked, and evil words.”
Śāriputra! At that time, because I was practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), I subdued my mind so that no anger, stinginess, or burning affliction arose. I thought only this:

"Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is not even the slightest thing that can be easily obtained which surpasses being reviled and rebuked; therefore, I should now cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
Furthermore, I should give rise to compassion for them.

Why is this? Most beings in the world dwell in reviling and censuring; by virtue of such karma, they in turn experience the retribution of being reviled and disparaged, and in every place where they are born, they constantly obtain an ugly and loathsome body.
I do not now delight in things that are ugly; how could I take pleasure in practicing slander, abuse, or reproach? Why is this?

Such evil deeds as reviling and slandering are called discordant karma, irrational karma, and the karma of fools; they are inferior karma, the karma of non-virtuous persons, and the karma of those who are not noble or holy.
Due to this karma, one falls into the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, and the world of Yama. Furthermore, by this karma, one becomes an associate of those in the evil destinies;

by this karma, one obtains the body of a poor yakṣa, and by this karma, one obtains the fundamental retribution of a poor yakṣa. By this karma, one obtains the body of a poor preta, and by this karma, one obtains the fundamental retribution of a poor preta. By this karma, one obtains the body of a poor human being, and by this karma, one obtains the fundamental retribution of a poor human being. Moreover, due to such censurable karma, one obtains the lower destinies and the fundamental retributions of those lower destinies.
I should not now seek an inferior rebirth.
Why is this? If I were to pursue such a course of action, what difference would there be between me and all other sentient beings?
"However, those sentient beings do not accord with reason; since I do accord with reason, I should not act like them. Śāriputra!
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) should follow my example and train in this Dharma.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
when these bodhisattvas are reviled, abused, or rebuked by others, they are able to rely upon this true Dharma, apply their attention to it, and endure it with patience.
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained such power of patience, they further acquire immeasurable and wondrous roots of goodness.
Even if one were to fill the four great continents of a Buddha-world with various precious jewels and offer them as a gift, it could not equal even a fraction of the merit mentioned previously.
Why is this? This practice of patience can only be cultivated by those who are truly superior men.
For what reason?
All sentient beings are for the most part constrained and bound by reviling, abuse, and reproach; because of this, the cycle of birth and death continues to flow on without interruption.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the pāramitā of kṣānti, they should exert themselves and observe with careful discernment, forming this thought:
"If I am reviled or disparaged by others, am I able to contemplate the Buddha, Bodhi, and the Dharma and Saṅgha?"
"If one can contemplate this, it is virtuous; if one cannot contemplate it, it is not called virtuous.
Furthermore, by means of other immeasurable skillful methods, he contemplated the Buddha, contemplated Bodhi, and contemplated the Dharma and the Sangha.
Śāriputra! Having formed this thought, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate: "What distinguishing characteristics or differences exist between me and all sentient beings?"
Why is this? Those sentient beings who manifest anger and malice toward my person have never contemplated the Buddha, Bodhi, or the Dharma and Sangha.
If I were like them and did not engage in reflection, what difference would there be between me and all sentient beings? What extraordinary or marvelous distinction would there be? Śāriputra!
Furthermore, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects:

"If, when others manifest anger toward me, my mind immediately gives rise to equanimity (*upekṣā*), and I fail to maintain mindfulness of the Buddha, Bodhi, and the Dharma and Sangha, this is not appropriate for me."
Again, he thought: "If I were to give rise to anger toward him, I would be lacking in wisdom and the power of patience, and I would also abandon my original vow."
Why is this? If one gives rise to anger, then one has no such thought as:
"I shall embrace all sentient beings; I shall not abandon any sentient being."
If I were to give rise to anger toward even a single sentient being, it would not be called the bodhisattva’s method of gathering and transforming others.
Who requested that I practice the bodhisattva path?
Moreover, in the past, I made such a vow:
"Once I have swiftly realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), I shall extensively proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
At the very moment he made such a great vow, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, collectively bore witness to him, and I thought:

"This son of good family has resolved his mind and established himself in this unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he shall extensively proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
Furthermore, at this moment, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, with their unobstructed wisdom and unobstructed vision, directly perceive and know me.

Therefore, when others revile, abuse, or reproach you, you should not give rise to anger; nor should you harbor thoughts of abandoning the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. You must not dwell upon such thoughts.

Why is this? Because in the present, in as many Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there currently dwell and maintain themselves Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, has likewise witnessed and known that my mind has conceived this right vow.
It is the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
When I uttered this right vow, all the Buddhas praised my power of forbearance with one voice; therefore, having already let out a lion’s roar, I ought not to make the sound of a jackal again.
The "lion's roar" refers to my realization of the power of great patience;
the "jackal's cry" refers to the manifestation of anger, reviling, and so forth toward sentient beings.
"Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects:

'If worldly beings only benefit others after they have first obtained benefit for themselves, and I likewise only benefit them after obtaining benefit for sentient beings, then what difference would there be between me and the world?'"
"What extraordinary and marvelous signs are there?
He further thought: "If sentient beings in the world cause harm to one another, they in turn cause harm to each other."
I am also like this: if sentient beings do me harm and I in turn do them harm, then what extraordinary distinction or difference is there between me and these sentient beings?
"Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this Dharma.
Furthermore, they should form this thought:"
"Sentient beings in the world act as mutual enemies; if they obtain benefit from another, they regard that person as a good friend, but if they do not obtain such benefit, they kill one another.
Seeing these profound faults, I should not observe whether sentient beings bring me various benefits and joys, nor whether they cause me harm and disadvantage."
One should simply form this thought:
"I must now certainly benefit all sentient beings, for the sake of fulfilling the pāramitā of kṣānti."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Even if they bring me no benefit, Throughout many hundreds of koṭis of kalpas,
Seeing those sentient beings undergoing manifold sufferings, I shall never abide in a mind of equanimity."
If they mutually obtain worldly wealth and profit, they praise one another as good friends;
if they do not mutually obtain worldly wealth and profit, they become mutual enemies and harm one another.
Even if one were to fill this Jambudvīpa, or even the three thousandfold world-system,
with precious jewels to bestow upon me, they would constantly seek me out as a virtuous and good friend.
Even if someone were to take up a sharp sword and come to sever the various limbs and joints of my body,
I would maintain a mind of impartial benefit toward all those sentient beings, without any duality.
I shall endure all insults and abuse, and likewise endure every hardship and suffering;
for the sake of sentient beings, I shall praise the power of patience, and I myself shall abide securely within great patience.
When sentient beings in this world are violent and cruel, Harming one another with weapons, poison, and the like,
To be able to harmonize them and act as a virtuous friend— This is the mark of the wise and noble.
I shall not follow the ways of worldly fools, for I must differ from them;
there is a distinction between the conduct of ordinary beings and that of the noble ones, due to the difference between cyclic existence and nirvana.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they should train in the true Dharma in this manner."
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects:

"Even if for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of great kalpas, all sentient beings were to constantly inflict upon me various harms with swords, staves, tiles, stones, and clods of earth, as long as I can preserve even a moment of my fragile life, I should still rejoice and think thus:"
"How marvelous it is that these noble beings, such as these sentient ones, do not see my life entirely severed!
Thereafter, this bodhisattva mahāsattva increases his practice and training even further, and reflects again:

"Even if sentient beings were to sever my head and other limbs as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River while I am walking for the duration of seven steps, I would never give rise to anger or malice toward them."

Why is this? For one who is prone to anger can swiftly destroy the roots of goodness accumulated over hundreds of thousands of great eons; if my roots of goodness were destroyed by anger, I would have to undergo another hundred thousand great eons before I could begin to diligently practice the Noble Path.
If this is so, then Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is extremely difficult to attain; therefore, I shall don the armor of patience and, with steadfast power, crush the army of anger and resentment.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the Great Vehicle gives rise to a mind of anger and resentment, Māra gains an opportunity; having gained that opportunity, he is able to create obstacles to their *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Śāriputra! A mind of anger and resentment can disturb the path to enlightenment; a disturbed mind can give rise to all the demonic activities of Māra.
In this context, what is called "the work of Māra"?
If a bodhisattva’s mind dwells upon robes and alms bowls and cannot relinquish them, one should know this is the work of Māra;
if the mind dwells upon begging for food and cannot relinquish the households of donors, one should know this is the work of Māra.
If the mind dwells upon fame, respect, and gain such that one cannot relinquish them, know this to be the work of Māra;
if one constantly feels weariness and aversion toward the dharma of renunciation, know this to be the work of Māra;
if one frequently treats pure and wholesome dharmas with contempt, know this to be the work of Māra.
One should recognize as the work of Māra the lack of aspiration for the state of empty stillness;
one should recognize as the work of Māra the lack of delight in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and one should recognize as the work of Māra the constant seeking and practicing of other forms of wisdom.
Furthermore, one should recognize as the work of Māra any failure to cultivate a mind of reverence, respect, and deference toward one's two superior teachers, the upādhyāya and the ācārya.
Śāriputra! Such states of mind as anger and resentment can cause disturbance to bodhi. Śāriputra!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells with a distracted mind, acting as an agent for all evil māras and performing all manner of demonic deeds.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they form this thought:
"Throughout the long night, all sentient beings have been sought out by evil māras for an opportunity to harm them—namely, through anger."
"Śāriputra! I shall now explain this matter to you in detail.

I recall that in the past, when I was a great seer named *Caryāsthita*, there was an evil Māra who manifested as five hundred fierce revilers. They constantly pursued me, launching various insults day and night—whether I was coming or going, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether I was in a monastic cell, a quiet chamber, a village, or a lay home; whether on the streets or in secluded places—they followed wherever I sat or stood. These manifested māras reviled, abused, and censured me with coarse and wicked words for a full five hundred years, never ceasing for a moment."

Śāriputra! I recall that during five hundred years in the past, I was reviled and slandered by various Māras; yet I never gave rise to even a slight heart of resentment toward them, but always maintained a compassionate and salvific observation of them.
Śāriputra! At that time, I further had this thought:

"If there are sons of good family who guard the precepts (śīla), possess all wholesome dharmas, and have but slight and minor tendencies toward greed, hatred, and delusion, I shall not only provide them with various benefits, but also declare myself to be one who practices what is difficult to practice."
Furthermore, one does not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment merely by performing acts of benefit for them.

Why is this? If there are sentient beings who are stubborn and difficult to subdue, who violate the precepts, who possess all manner of evil dharmas, and whose natures are turbid, heavy, and full of greed, hatred, and delusion—if I perform acts of benefit for such as these, then I am said to be a practitioner of what is difficult to do.
"Because I have brought about various benefits for them, I shall swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so that I may first cause them to realize nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas find a mind of anger and resentment manifesting before them, they should give rise to such great and correct mindfulness.
If they give rise to this mindfulness, all beneficial matters will swiftly reach fulfillment.
Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata practiced such bodhisattva conduct of the perfection of kṣānti (patience) in past lives, he realized unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who seeks unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment must always fully accomplish the power of patience (*kṣānti-bala*). They must be able to endure all contacts of cold and heat, hunger and thirst, wind, sun, mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, and scorpions; furthermore, they must be able to endure harsh and abusive speech, vulgar expressions, and the intense, piercing, and agonizing sufferings arising from the body—ranging from life-threatening pain to death—and thus be able to endure all such painful sensations.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in this patience, for it enables them to swiftly accomplish the pāramitā of kṣānti.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
What is the *kṣānti-pāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is that by relying upon which the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and fully accomplishes the characteristics of the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*).
Śāriputra! As for the patience of a bodhisattva: the absence of malice is the patience of a bodhisattva; the absence of resentment is the patience of a bodhisattva;
the absence of anger and harm is the patience of a bodhisattva; and the non-arising of enmity and contention is the patience of a bodhisattva.
To be free from all afflictions is the patience of a bodhisattva; to be well able to protect oneself is the patience of a bodhisattva;
to be well able to protect others is the patience of a bodhisattva; to well protect one’s body is the patience of a bodhisattva; to well protect one’s speech is the patience of a bodhisattva;
to well protect one’s mind is the patience of a bodhisattva; and to investigate according to reality is [the patience of a bodhisattva].
The patience of a bodhisattva is the patience that involves wearying detachment from all desires; it is the patience that relies upon the retribution of pure karma;
it is the patience that consists in the thorough purity of body; it is the patience that consists in the thorough purity of speech;
it is the patience that consists in the thorough purity of mind; and it is the patience that experiences the perfect, pure bliss of devas and humans.

Patience: the Tathāgata’s physical marks and signs being perfectly complete and adorned is the patience of a bodhisattva; the Tathāgata’s speech being the subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice is the patience of a bodhisattva;
practicing the bodhisattva path to gather all roots of goodness so they are not lost or destroyed is the patience of a bodhisattva;
emerging from the oppression and affliction of sentient beings is the patience of a bodhisattva; and its eradication—
All evil adversaries are the patience of a bodhisattva. Śāriputra!

To speak briefly, you should know that all the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-qualities of the Tathāgatas, as well as the immeasurable and perfect sublime dharmas of all Buddhas—great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity—are all accomplished by the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they should fulfill all correct practices of patience."
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is reviled, he never retaliates, for he thoroughly understands that speech is like an echo.
If he is struck, he never retaliates, for he thoroughly understands that the physical body is like a reflection.
If one is met with anger, one never retaliates, for one skillfully contemplates that the mind is like an illusion because it is illusory.
If one is met with praise or blame, one never feels attachment or aversion, for one skillfully knows that one's own virtues are already perfected.
They do not give rise to joy or sorrow regarding gain or loss, for they have tamed their minds and abide in tranquility.
They do not long for a fine reputation nor fear an evil name, for they are well able to observe with vast wisdom.
He does not disparage others nor praise himself with arrogance, for his virtuous qualities are securely established and unshakable.
He never feels aversion toward any form of suffering, for he harbors deep compassion for sentient beings who suffer.
He has never felt delight or attachment toward any marks of pleasure, for he knows that the nature of conditioned happiness is impermanent.
He cannot be defiled by the eight worldly concerns, for he does not rely on birth within any realm of existence.
They are well able to endure all their own sufferings, for they never cause others to experience suffering and distress;
they never retreat from the supreme mind of enlightenment, for they have perfectly fulfilled the provisions for the factors of awakening.
They are well able to endure being dismembered limb by limb and even having their heads severed, because they aspire to the Tathāgata’s adamantine body.
They are well able to endure the cutting and carving of their own flesh, for the sake of seeking the Tathāgata’s wondrous marks and signs.
They are well able to endure all adverse and evil circumstances for the sake of planting the power of all wholesome karmas. Śāriputra,
such characteristics as these are called the accomplishment of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
One should train in this way.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the characteristics of all forms of patience are as follows: that is to say, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, this is called ultimate endurance.
Why is this? If one thinks, "I am capable of enduring insults," and then gives rise to patience, this is called innate patience; such patience is not ultimate patience.

If one thinks, "Who is it that can initiate the abuse, and what is it that is being abused? and yet gives rise to patience, this is called the patience of analytical deliberation (*tulanā-dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*).
If one thinks, "Is it this eye that can abuse the eye? and yet gives rise to patience, this is called the patience of contemplating the sense bases (*āyatana-pratyavekṣaṇa-kṣānti*).
If one maintains patience therein without perceiving either an agent of abuse or an object of abuse, this is called the patience that realizes the non-existence of all sentient beings. Śāriputra!
Such forms of patience are not the ultimate patience of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if one considers that the sound of abuse consists merely of syllables, this is called the patience of an echo; such patience is not ultimate patience.
If one says that both the other and oneself are impermanent, this is called the patience of awakening to impermanence.
If one says that the other possesses inversion while oneself is free from inversion, this is called the patience of high and low.
If one claims, "That is not the correct principle, whereas this is the correct principle," it is called the patience of conformity and non-conformity.
If one claims, "That person abides in a wrong path, whereas I abide in the right path," this is termed the patience of distinguishing between two paths; such patience is not ultimate patience.

"Śāriputra, if one were to say: 'I tolerate emptiness but do not tolerate the inclinations toward views; I tolerate signlessness but do not tolerate discursive thoughts; I tolerate wishlessness but do not tolerate aspiration; I tolerate the unconditioned but do not tolerate conditioned formations; I tolerate the exhaustion of delusion but do not tolerate afflictions; I tolerate all that is wholesome but do not tolerate what is unwholesome; I tolerate the faultless but do not tolerate the faulty; I tolerate the outflow-free but do not tolerate the with-outflows; I tolerate the supramundane but do not tolerate the mundane; I tolerate purity but do not tolerate defilement; I tolerate nirvāṇa but do not tolerate saṃsāra'—[such a person does not understand my teaching]."
Such forms of patience are merely termed "patience for subduing and severing"; they are not the ultimate patience of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), cultivate the ultimate patience of a bodhisattva?"

Śāriputra! If one accords with emptiness without diminishing any views, and does not superimpose anything upon that emptiness either—such forbearance is called the ultimate forbearance of a bodhisattva.
If one accords with emptiness without diminishing aspiration, there is no augmentation regarding the nature of wishlessness;
if one accords with emptiness without diminishing formative activities, there is no augmentation regarding the nature of non-action;
if one accords with emptiness without diminishing afflictions, there is no augmentation regarding the nature of the exhaustion of delusion.
If one accords with emptiness, one does not diminish unwholesomeness, nor does one increase the nature of wholesomeness;
if one accords with emptiness, one does not diminish that which is blameworthy, nor does one increase the nature of blamelessness;
and so on, until: if one accords with emptiness, one does not diminish saṃsāra, nor does one increase the nature of nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! When such signs as these give rise to patience, it is called the ultimate patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!

All phenomena are neither the producer nor the produced; they have not been produced, nor are they being produced now. There is not a single phenomenon that can be brought into existence; because there is no arising, there is no exhaustion.
If there is one who can know this inexhaustibility, that is called the ultimate patience (*atyanta-kṣānti*) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Śāriputra! All dharmas are neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); they have no addition and no subtraction, no increase and no nourishment, no waxing and no waning. They have no agent and no originator; because they have no origin, they also have no exhaustion.
Such forbearance is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva conduct for the sake of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), if they fully accomplish such forbearance, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s fulfillment and accomplishment of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) and diligently trains in the practice of a bodhisattva, they will not be disturbed by Māras or the sons of gods belonging to the hosts of Māras, nor can they be overcome by the heterodox views and false arguments of other paths.
Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Vigor (Vīrya-pāramitā), Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva by relying on the perfection of vigor?”
Śāriputra! In this perfection of right exertion, the bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently trains and practices the conduct of a bodhisattva. Śāriputra!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva fully accomplishes non-retrogressive right diligence, they are able to disregard even their own cherished body and life, giving rise to great vigor to seek the subtle Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. They listen with profound respect, receive and uphold them, read and recite them, thoroughly investigate and penetrate their meaning and intent, and extensively expound and reveal them to others; or alternatively, they transcribe and maintain them, practicing and studying them according to the principle. This is called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the Bodhisattva conduct.
Śāriputra! What is meant by "disregarding body and life"? Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of right effort (*samyag-vīrya-pāramitā*), even if another person should inflict terror upon them by saying:

"If you uphold, recite, or even extensively explain, transcribe, and practice this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra according to the principle, I shall pierce your body with a hundred spears and arrows and take your life."

"Śāriputra! At that time, although the bodhisattva mahāsattva hears these words, they do not enter his mind; he is without fear, without terror, without alarm, and without dread. He generates four kinds of firm, courageous, and majestic power, increasing his diligence toward the subtle dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, neither abandoning nor forsaking them, neither distancing himself from nor departing from them, and fully accomplishing sharp and keen faith-and-understanding, firm faith-and-understanding, firm endurance, and firm right effort."

Śāriputra! I shall now speak to you of the analogies for firm patience and firm right effort, so that bodhisattvas may attain firm patience and firm right effort, practicing the bodhisattva path regardless of body or life.

Śāriputra! Suppose all sentient beings included within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; whether visible or invisible—all these beings were to simultaneously attain human bodies for even a single moment and collectively bind themselves in hundreds of thousands of most grievous enmities toward a bodhisattva.
Those enemies said to the Bodhisattva:

"If you receive, uphold, read, recite, or even extensively explain, transcribe, and practice according to the principle the various textual passages of this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra for others, we shall all bind you simultaneously and cut off your life."

"Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), at that time, although they hear these words, they do not give rise to even a single thought of fear. Rather, they fully uphold the four kinds of true Dharma and devote themselves exclusively to seeking the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka."
Śāriputra! This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s fulfillment and accomplishment of the perfection of non-regressive right effort (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, he accomplishes boundless power and heroic diligence; his right effort is heroic and robust, his mind is heroic and robust, his pure ethical discipline is heroic and robust, his great patience is heroic and robust, his meditative concentration is heroic and robust, his great wisdom is heroic and robust, and his correct practice and supreme knowledge are all entirely heroic and robust.

Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of right effort, because they are endowed with such great power of patience, even if immeasurable sentient beings from the ten directions were each vying to seize and brandish hundreds of thousands of swords and blades to inflict harm and violence upon the bodhisattva;
At that time, the bodhisattva never gives rise to even a single thought of anger toward sentient beings. Śāriputra!

Because such a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the power of patience, they are like the Great Brahmā King, like Śakra Devendra, and like Sumeru, the king of the four precious mountains—unshakable. Constantly dwelling in loving-kindness and compassion, they perpetually give rise to the intention to rescue and heal sentient beings, never regressing in any of their practices.

Furthermore, the mind of this bodhisattva is like the great earth, like great water, like a great fire, like a great wind, and like space; moreover, they are well able to cultivate the remedies for the roots and stumps of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Śāriputra! Suppose there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who filled immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with all manner of priceless jewels, and offered them as gifts to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the *vīrya-pāramitā*; having heard this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, and having heard this sūtra, they go to a secluded place, focus their mindfulness to contemplate such a Dharma, and diligently cultivate and study it, so that all bodhisattvas who have not yet practiced may come to cherish, delight in, and engage in its cultivation.

Śāriputra! Because such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice right effort, they gather and uphold immeasurable, wondrous roots of goodness, which cannot be equaled by those who merely practice generosity.
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because such roots of goodness are bound to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should listen to, receive, uphold, read, and recite this subtle dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; furthermore, they should transcribe it, explain it extensively to others, and cultivate it with the initiation of right diligence and heroic vigor.
“Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has initiated the perfection of right effort should practice the non-practice of places of practice.”
Śāriputra! What is meant by "the sphere of non-practice"? Śāriputra!
The state of non-practice is what is called nirvana.
It is called "non-practice" because it is not a place where various evil celestial māras can practice.
It is called "practice" because it is the practice of those who are rightly diligent and virtuous.
Those called "virtuous persons" (satpuruṣa) refer to the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because all virtuous persons who have ascended the noble path, as well as the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are all oriented toward parinirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! All sentient beings mostly practice in three spheres.
What are these three spheres?
That is to say, they would conform to the evil realms, tend toward the evil realms, and be on the verge of falling into the evil realms.
Therefore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never conform to defiled phenomena, but seek only the transcendence of them through precepts, patience, extensive learning, purity, and other such dharmas.
Śāriputra! The sentient beings of the world mostly abide in non-action, yet they constantly reckon themselves as abiding in action.
The sentient beings of the world are mostly indolent, yet they constantly claim to have initiated right effort.

Therefore, Śāriputra, a wise bodhisattva mahāsattva never associates with those who are unindustrious and lack diligence, nor does he fall into their company; rather, he associates only with fellow great bodhisattvas who have likewise initiated right effort.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
there is no sentient being who can give rise to pure faith and understanding regarding that most supreme, untainted, and pure mark of Great Parinirvāṇa as a bodhisattva does.

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who has initiated the perfection of right diligence does not exert himself merely for the sake of realizing nirvāṇa for himself; rather, he exerts himself in right practice in order to gather in all sentient beings and bring them benefit and happiness. Because he instructs, guides, and establishes sentient beings upon the noble path, he is called a "virtuous man" (satpuruṣa).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Exerting right effort without slackness, Always endowed with great vigor,
Regarding the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, The wise shall always receive and uphold them."
One who skillfully contemplates the meaning of the Dharma, Regarding the inconceivable Buddha,
And strives only to seek the pure Dharma, Is therefore called a Bodhisattva.
The one of right diligence and great wisdom Sits beneath the wondrous Bodhi tree.
Subduing the terrifying armies of Māra through the vigor of prajñā,
manifesting the protection of the precepts and sustaining all worlds,
one exerts constant and limitless vigor for the benefit of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This subtle and wondrous sūtra of the Mahāyāna Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, as it circulates in the world, can cause sentient beings to give rise to great joy; it can further induce the production of merit and wisdom, bring about great wealth and cause it to increase, elicit the sublime happiness of the devas, and bring about all forms of perfection and fulfillment. It can generate the powers, fearlessnesses, unimpeded knowledge and understanding, and the unique Buddha-dharmas—great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity—of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas."

To speak briefly: it can lead one to all the dharmas of the Buddhas, crush and terrify the demonic adversaries so as to purify the mind, give rise to fierce wisdom that exhausts the root of the life-process, and reach the limit of suffering so as to draw near to Nirvana.

Śāriputra! In a future age, after my and your parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there will be many beings of little merit who will not give rise to faith or reverence for this sūtra, but will instead destroy and abandon it.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable sentient beings of great merit who revere this sutra and practice its teachings according to principle with diligent vigor. This is for the sake of seeking unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; for the sake of seeking ethical discipline (*śīla*); for the sake of seeking extensive learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; for the sake of seeking all Buddha-dharmas to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; for the sake of abandoning false views and practicing right view; for the sake of abandoning the cycle of birth and death and cultivating the Noble Path; for the sake of wishing to proclaim the True Dharma and subdue the celestial Māras; and for the sake of wishing to abandon craving, tame the mind of hatred, destroy delusion, eliminate ignorance, and give rise to the light of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
In a future age, if there are sentient beings who, having heard this Dharma, shall give rise to superior, courageous, and right diligence for the sake of seeking all wholesome dharmas."
Because they have heard such a subtle and wondrous Dharma, they shall be without obstruction regarding all Buddha-dharmas, possessing certainty and freedom from doubt. Śāriputra!

At that time, there will also be immeasurable sentient beings who, sustained by the fruits of their merit, abide in the superior resolve; for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they shall listen to this sutra. Having heard it, they shall attain vast and great joy, thoroughly study the subtle Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and practice according to the teaching.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

At that time, there will be those who delight in hearing the Dharma within the teaching of the Tathāgata. Those sentient beings, by whatever specific causes and conditions they may encounter, shall have the opportunity to hear such a sūtra as this. Having heard it, they shall obtain vast joy; having given rise to joy, they shall exert firm diligence and be able to take even a small portion of the jewel from this subtle and wondrous Dharma-treasure of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Śāriputra! It is as if there were immeasurable varieties of ripe fruits floating upon the waters of the great ocean, all fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor.
Suppose there were a man who, exerting the power of courageous and great diligence, entered the sea and moved his hands and feet to grasp two or three of those fruits.

However, this man took hold of this fruit, emerged from the sea, and went to a certain place where he picked it up and tasted it. Upon realizing its flavor was pure, exquisite, and rare, he thought to himself:

"This wondrous fruit possesses color, fragrance, and taste; since my birth, I have never eaten such a thing. I shall exert further diligent effort and enter the sea once more, moving my hands and feet to gather the remaining fruits."
Having had this thought, he went to the seashore and searched everywhere, but could not see them at all. He felt deep regret and was overcome with great distress, thinking:
"Why did I not gather more before? I have now caused me to lose these immeasurable, wondrous fruits."
"In this way, Śāriputra!

In the five hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, at the time when the unsurpassed True Dharma is about to perish, there will be immeasurable sentient beings who possess little faith, little generosity, little ethical discipline, little wisdom, and little cultivation or diligence; yet, through whatever various causes and conditions they may encounter, they shall happen to hear and receive such a jewel of a sutra."

Having heard the Dharma, they grasp only a small portion of its subtle and shallow meaning within this sutra, even if it be as little as a single four-line verse; furthermore, being harassed and obstructed by evil Māras, they are not honored, questioned, provided for, praised, or faithfully followed by the multitude.

Because those who uphold this sutra know that the people there do not respect it, they maintain an attitude of equanimity toward this sutra. Retaining even a small portion of the subtle meanings of the phrases from the sutras previously heard, they go to a secluded place to contemplate and observe them. Their hearts give rise to joy, yet they also feel regret, saying:
"Alas, how marvelous! How extraordinary!"
"I have now greatly lost the opportunity for wholesome benefit.
How could I not have listened to and received more of the unsurpassed, correct teaching of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
Furthermore, he conceived a profound and deep respect for the Tathāgata, doubling the degree of right mindfulness he had previously developed.

Śāriputra! At that time, there will be certain bhikṣus who, because they are possessed by Māra, shall hear this sūtra and then give rise to slander before the assembly, saying: "This sūtra was composed by those fond of flowery rhetoric; it was certainly not spoken by the Buddha."
"For this reason, there are some bhikṣus who do not hear or receive this sūtra at all.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Having heard this Dharma, one shall be without obstruction regarding all the Buddha-dharmas."
This is supreme and beyond doubt.
Those with little merit shall not hear it; those with great merit shall hear this sutra.
Those with little merit do not believe even when they hear [the teaching]; those with great merit, having heard it, wear it upon their heads like a garland.
Those with little merit declare it to be no holy teaching; they shall fall into the evil realms, like the blind falling into a pit.
Those of great merit, upon hearing this, give rise to joy; they shall go to the happy realms, like a drop of water falling into ghee.
Those of little merit, upon hearing this, give rise to distress; they shall suffer through the long night, never escaping the darkness.
"Though they have gained some learning, they are further tormented by Māra;
slandering the Buddha’s bodhi, they will swiftly enter hell. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are fully endowed with and have perfected pure, wondrous wisdom, such that they are even able to know the minds of the fourfold assembly.

Whether it be a single bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā who, at the time when the True Dharma is extinguished in the future, either hears and receives such a sūtra in accordance with its meaning, or having heard it, slights, disparages, or reviles it, or whether there are sentient beings who do not hear it at all—all such things the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata is fully able to comprehend.

Śāriputra! If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all other sentient beings who, having heard and received such a sūtra as this, practice it with diligence, they shall achieve the four kinds of unobstructed, pure dharmas.

What are these four? First, the accomplishment of the purity of unobstructed ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, the accomplishment of the purity of being endowed with the absence of obstacles; third, the accomplishment of the purity of unobstructed meeting, serving, and making offerings to all Buddhas; and fourth, the accomplishment of the purity of unobstructed beholding Maitreya Buddha upon first seeing him.
Śāriputra! Once those sentient beings have heard this sutra, they shall, through various skillful means, certainly attain all the aforementioned sublime and wholesome roots.
Śāriputra! This is called the accomplishment of the four kinds of unsurpassed pure dharmas by a bodhisattva mahāsattva through practicing the perfection of right effort.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the future age when the True Dharma is about to perish, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in the Mahāyāna and practice the perfection of right effort. They will apply themselves diligently to the study of this sūtra, exerting great vigor to hear, receive, and uphold it; to copy, read, and recite it; to thoroughly investigate its essential meaning; and to extensively explain, propagate, and elucidate it for others."

At that time, ten obstructive dharmas will appear in the world; those who possess wisdom should deeply recognize them and not follow along with them, but should instead rouse courageous diligence to receive and uphold this sutra.
Śāriputra! What are the ten kinds of obstacles that the wise should recognize and not follow? Śāriputra!
There were certain bhikṣus who exerted diligent effort, seeking to hear, recite, and practice this sūtra.
At that time, Māra the Evil caused those who held the sūtra to have their mouths clamped shut so they could not speak, whereby they were unable to establish this sūtra.
This is called the first obstructive dharma.
All who possess wisdom should deeply recognize this and must not follow it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There were certain bhikṣus who exerted diligent effort, seeking to hear, recite, and study this sūtra.
At that time, Māra caused those who held the sūtra to suffer afflictions of the eyes, so that they could not establish themselves in this sūtra.
This is called the second obstructive dharma.
All wise ones should deeply recognize this and must not follow after it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There were certain bhikṣus who exerted diligent effort, seeking to hear, recite, and study this sūtra.
At that time, Māra the Evil caused all the limbs and joints of those who held the sūtra to fall ill simultaneously, so that they were unable to establish themselves in this sūtra.
This is called the third obstructive dharma.
All who possess wisdom should deeply recognize this and must not follow after it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There were certain bhikṣus who exerted diligent effort, seeking to hear, recite, and study this sūtra.

At that time, Māra the Evil One caused those who held the sūtra to feel no joy in their place of residence and to desire to abandon it immediately, so that they could not establish themselves in this sūtra.
This is called the fourth obstructive dharma.
All who possess wisdom should deeply recognize this and must not follow after it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There are some bhikṣus who exert diligent effort, seeking to hear, recite, and study this sūtra.

At that time, Māra causes those who uphold the sūtra to give rise to mutual anger; with their minds ruined by anger, they inflict harm upon one another, and thus they are unable to establish themselves in this sūtra.
This is called the fifth obstructive dharma.
All who possess wisdom should deeply recognize this and must not follow after it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There were certain bhikṣus who exerted diligent effort, desiring to seek out the recitation and study of this sūtra.

At that time, Māra the Evil One caused those who held the sūtra to give rise to disputes, to litigations, to insults, to estrangements, and to angry reviling. Because of these matters, sharp spears arose within their mouths as they mutually accused one another, harmed one another, and contended with one another. Due to the occurrence of such strife and contention, obstacles were produced; thus, this sūtra could not circulate, and they set their minds to performing various other worldly tasks.
This is called the sixth obstructive dharma.
All those who possess wisdom should deeply recognize this and must not follow after it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There were certain bhikṣus who exerted diligent effort, desiring to study and recite this sūtra.

At that time, Māra the Evil One, intending to destroy them, assumed various forms—either the form of a layperson or the form of an ordained monk—and came to their place to disturb their minds, causing them to be unable to receive and uphold this sūtra, instead leading them to slander it and further giving rise to thoughts of delighting in other worldly activities.
This is called the seventh obstructive dharma.
All those who possess wisdom should deeply recognize this and must not follow after it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In a future age when the True Dharma is about to perish, there will be young bhikṣus who give rise to pure faith in these sūtras and develop a sense of love and joy for them. Within my Dharma and Vinaya, they shall exert diligent effort in order to practice the pāramitā of vīrya (diligence), deeply abiding their minds in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and respectfully listening to these sūtras; having heard them, they will experience great rejoicing.
At that time, the young bhikṣus were obstructed by their two teachers, the upādhyāya and the ācārya, such that they did not develop a desire for their own Dharma.
At that time, the two teachers said to him:
"The scripture you hold is not the word of the Buddha, it is not the Bodhi of the Buddha, it is not the True Dharma, it is not the Vinaya, and it is not the teaching of the Great Teacher."
Then those bhikṣus, having heard the instruction of their teachers, accepted it with faith and understood it; they immediately abandoned the Buddha’s bodhi.
At that time, the two teachers spoke again to the bhikṣus:
"You should practice and study with diligence according to what I have taught regarding the Dharma and the Vinaya."

At that time, having accepted and received [the teaching] with faith, the bhikṣus had all the superior roots of goodness they had previously cultivated destroyed and utterly eradicated by their teacher, Śāriputra. Śāriputra.

Once those bhikṣus have severed their roots of virtue, they are further deceived and deluded by Māra, the Evil One. Because of this deception, they create karma that obstructs the Dharma within the Buddha’s true teaching. At the time of death, as malevolent objects appear before them, they become dazed, deluded, and confused; even premature death manifests in its entirety, and they further give rise to karma that brings about rebirth in the hells.
Śāriputra! Thus, regarding all such unwholesome matters that will arise in the future, the Tathāgata is fully able to know them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In future ages, there will be certain young bhikṣus who give rise to various evil views regarding this sūtra, slandering it and lacking faith; wherever they travel, walk, or come and go, they will constantly engage in slander and defamation with all manner of words.
The Tathāgata fully understands this. Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has aroused diligent vigor and dwells in the Great Vehicle should, at that time, give rise to four perceptions.
What are the four? First, one should give rise to the thought of self-discipline;
second, one should observe the deeds performed by oneself, rather than observing the various affairs of others.
Third, one should give rise to thoughts of compassion toward those sentient beings;
fourth, dwelling in a secluded place, one should give rise to thoughts of protecting the minds of both oneself and others. Śāriputra!
These four perceptions should be aroused by those dwelling in the Mahāyāna if they are subjected to slander.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, in future ages, there will be immeasurable sentient beings who embrace various false views; among them, few bhikṣus who preach the true Dharma will have followers who accept it with faith. They will not harbor respect or inquire about the meaning of the sūtras, nor will they make offerings, draw near, or visit them. Instead of serving them, they will even treat them with contempt and disdain.

Among those who preach what is not the Dharma, there are many who receive it with faith; they gain great power and are collectively revered by all sentient beings, who inquire about the meaning of the scriptures, make offerings to them, and praise these proponents of what is not the Dharma.
For this reason, they further slander and mock this sutra. Śāriputra!
At that time, those sentient beings who did not take delight in this scripture will, upon hearing such slander, become all the more displeased.
Because those who take delight [in worldly things] are subjected to slander and defamation, they abandon their desire for this sutra; thus, it teaches the relinquishing of such desire.
Consequently, the bhikṣus become even more fervent in their opposition, causing those who recite this scripture to be unable to expound it before the assembled congregation.
This is called the eighth obstructive dharma.
All who possess wisdom should recognize it and not follow after it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
In a future age, there will be certain bhikṣus who, obscured by craving and greed, will frequently commit acts of robbery and theft, taking delight in three kinds of base worldly dharmas.
What are these three?

First, delighting in the pursuit of worldly robes and alms bowls; second, delighting in the pursuit of worldly food and drink; third, delighting in the pursuit of worldly frivolous discourse and ornate verses.
These three dharmas are called the ninth obstructive dharma.
All those who possess wisdom should recognize them and must not follow after them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In a future age, when the True Dharma is on the verge of extinction, there will be bodhisattvas who, dwelling securely in the Mahāyāna and practicing the pāramitā of vīrya, shall apply themselves with diligent, heroic, and superior energy toward this sutra—copying it, receiving and upholding it, investigating and reciting it, and extensively explaining and expounding it for others.

Those people will be possessed by various Māras and shrouded by the obscurations of afflictions and karma; they will delight in worldly activities, take pleasure in worldly activities, and diligently seek after worldly undertakings through skillful means. Their fondness for worldly discourse will increase further, as they diligently seek worldly discourse through skillful means. They will delight in sleep and diligently seek it through skillful means; they will delight in the turmoil of crowds and take pleasure in the turmoil of crowds, diligently seeking attachment to such turmoil through skillful means.
Śāriputra, they will be unable to receive and uphold this sutra, nor will they recite it or investigate its meaning, nor will they extensively expound and reveal it to others.
Within the Buddha's teaching, there is nothing else that can cause such internal harm, and nothing else that can so swiftly bring about destruction, except for the indolent and wicked bhikṣus.
"This is called the tenth obstructive dharma.
All those who possess wisdom should recognize it and must not follow after it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"When the True Dharma is extinguished, obstacles will be many;
various demonic deeds shall arise, and one will neither practice the pure and white dharmas nor seek the supreme Nirvāṇa."
Possessing meager wisdom and harboring evil thoughts, they do not seek to abide securely in the True Dharma;
having fully engaged in various unrighteous practices, there is no doubt that they will wander through the evil realms.
When those sentient beings approach the end of their lives, there is no one able to provide them with protection;
furthermore, even their preceptors and instructors, at the end of their own lives, shall fall into the three evil realms.
For hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons, they have undergone all manner of sufferings in pursuit of worldly gain;
constantly burned by the three fires, how can one cause them to be swiftly liberated?
I have realized peerless awakening and turned the subtle, sublime Wheel of Brahma, which neither gods nor the world can turn; I now turn it for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
Thus, at that time, those multitudes of living beings, having abandoned the Dharma so difficult to find in this world,
will associate with various classes of evil Māras and undergo boundless, most grievous suffering.
They obstruct the practice of giving, morality, and so forth—the causes and conditions for the noble path to enlightenment;
if one exerts oneself in the Buddha's teaching, they shall cause confusion regarding that correct path.
When those who hear such a Dharma— the teaching on the principles of selflessness and emptiness—
abide in the correct practice of this Dharma, Māra, the Evil One, shall create obstacles for them.

Claiming that this is supreme and this is the truth, while harboring notions of supremacy and truth regarding what is not supreme or true, they instead slander the Buddha’s authentic teaching; know that such persons will swiftly fall into hell.
If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of the Buddha, give rise to deep, firm love and reverence,
and having heard such true Dharma, rejoice, comply with it, and offer praise.
When Māra knew that he had already given rise to joy, he and his retinue became equally sorrowful and terrified;
they then manifested various signs of alarm and fear, creating obstacles for that person.
Some may transform themselves into the form of bhikṣus, feigning intimacy while secretly deliberating:
"This is not the true path to bodhi; why do you hasten toward it?"
There are sentient beings who, regarding this sutra, have begun to develop firm resolve and abide in right diligence;
yet they are further enticed and led astray by others, treated with contempt and mockery, whereby they abandon it and fail to practice or study it.
Once deluded and confused by Māra, they follow his will and become bound by it;
they then declare that this sutra is not the true Dharma, and thus forever abandon the state of tranquil extinction.
Having abandoned that Great Guide, and failing to diligently seek the unsurpassed Dharma,
they further give rise to self-love and swiftly hasten toward those hells.
At that time, there will be some sentient beings who delight in and diligently seek this teaching of emptiness;
unable to practice it together in harmony, they shall instead disperse to other lands.

Such is this unsurpassed, most supreme Dharma; all who hear it shall revile and disparage it, and those who uphold the Dharma will fear it and flee far away—such conditions shall arise in future ages.
In this land, there are none at all who uphold the Dharma; though there may be some from distant regions, they are not many.
Even if there are those who receive and uphold this sutra, they have all abandoned it and no longer seek instruction.
Within the holy teachings, the refuge of the world, such profound and unsurpassed dharmas—
though immeasurable obstacles lie in the future— remain as clearly manifest as if they were present now.
At that time, there were those who upheld the Dharma and were virtuous;
disregarding their own bodies and lives, they dwelt in secluded places, practicing and proclaiming such a Dharma, and swiftly ascended to the happy realms.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 45 [and] Volume 46,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Twelfth Assembly of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Part Twelve:
Chapter Nine, Part Two on the Perfection of Vigor (Vīryapāramitā).

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, in a future age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will again be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the Mahāyāna and practice the perfection of vigor. Having seen such evil beings slandering and destroying this True Dharma, they will redouble their courageous, right exertion and the power of great diligence. They will zealously listen to, receive, write down, uphold, read, and recite these sūtras—the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates of the Great Bodhisattvapiṭaka—and extensively explain and expound them for others."
Śāriputra, at that time, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to four perceptions.
What are these four? Śāriputra!

It is said that my father’s treasure storehouse will soon perish; for this very reason, the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, through diligent cultivation of difficult and ascetic practices over hundreds of thousands of nayuta-koṭi incalculable great kalpas, has finally attained this treasure storehouse of the True Dharma.

Therefore, I shall arouse diligent effort to uphold this treasury and master it completely; I shall thoroughly master and widely disseminate this treasury, desiring that the Jewel of the Dharma may endure for a long time without perishing.
Śāriputra! It is as if there were a man who had an only son, whom he cherished, loved, and held dear, possessing marks of great merit that he could never tire of beholding.

Later, when this man wished to travel somewhere and took his son along to cross through a place of peril and difficulty, fearing he might fall or tumble, he grasped him with his hand, holding him firmly and all around, and holding him most perfectly and all around, thinking: "May my son not fall into a place of danger and hardship."

In this way, Śāriputra, it is the same for that son of good family: he harbors deep faith and reverence for me, does not abandon such an unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma, and his resolve constantly aspires toward pure cessation; thus, even though he passes through an evil age, he is able to uphold the most excellent True Dharma.
Śāriputra! I now entrust this unsurpassed true Dharma, which is the causal condition for my enlightenment, to such a person.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

For example, when a great army engages in battle in the world, there are few beings who stand at the vanguard for the sake of protecting the multitude; rather, it is only a courageous and heroic man, capable of leading the brave to resist a powerful enemy, who stands before the great army, manifesting his majesty, in order to protect his own troops.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

In a future age, at the time when the True Dharma is perishing and those who destroy the True Dharma appear before us, there will be sentient beings who give rise to a profound resolve and take delight in cessation, and who are able to receive and uphold even a small portion of the essential meaning of this unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.

One should know that this person is likewise so: having donned the firm armor of right effort and exerting the great power of courageous and heroic diligence, they shatter all the military arrays of Māra.
Why is this? Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who,

regarding even a single four-line verse of this sutra, do not give rise to slander but instead rejoice in it and praise it, saying, "This sutra is truly the word of the Buddha," and proclaim and reveal it extensively before many people, you should know that such a person is rejoicing in and praising the teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

"Śāriputra! The Tathāgata does not say that such a person merely attains a small portion of the fruit of merit; I declare that such a person is able to accomplish a great mass of merit as vast as space."
Why is this? Śāriputra!
I declare that such persons as these are called "virtuous people."
Such virtuous persons are extremely rare to find—namely, those who recognize kindness and those who repay it. Śāriputra!
You should know that such individuals who recognize and repay kindness are the true jewels among humanity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In the future age when the True Dharma is extinguished, and when the power of various evil Māras manifests, if there are sentient beings who place their trust and respect in the Tathāgata without forsaking him, and who receive, uphold, and never distance themselves from this sutra—I declare that such persons are the foremost of men, virtuous men, superior men, courageous men, and great men.

You should know that such a person is a true companion to the Tathāgata’s sublime Dharma, not one who falsely pretends to be a partisan of evil; you should know that this person is a practitioner of genuine conduct.
In this way, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate firm and correct practice without ceasing for even a moment until the end of life.
They should diligently protect and serve all Buddhas without ceasing for even a moment until the end of life.
One should diligently embrace the True Dharma, never ceasing for even a moment until the end of life.
One should diligently cultivate faith and understanding in the profound dharma of emptiness, never ceasing for even a moment until the end of life.
Śāriputra! These are the four dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva will bring forth in the future evil age.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these four dharmas, then when the Dharma is about to perish in a future age—when the true Dharma is being slandered, when the true Dharma is being extinguished, when factions of those who violate the precepts are exceedingly powerful, when the pursuit of worldly paths and evil incantations is rampant, during the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of lifespan, the turbidity of afflictions, and the turbidity of views—the bodhisattva mahāsattva should, at such a time, abide in three places as their refuge.
What are these three? They are:
one should dwell in an araṇya (forest hermitage); one should dwell in a place where disputes have been extinguished; and one should dwell in the state of a Buddha’s bodhi (awakening). Śāriputra!

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in three places during the future evil age; they should maintain this practice, for it is by means of this that they fulfill the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Remaining never distant from the most supreme Dharma, To exhaust the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death,
Always exerting diligent effort without deluded thoughts— One shall swiftly accomplish the benefit of oneself and others."
If there are those who, having heard this well-spoken Dharma, abide in right reflection,
know that I am their great teacher, and they are my true disciples.
If one does not hear such a Dharma, or if having heard it, one does not abide in right reflection,
that person shall proceed toward the various evil realms, just as all rivers flow toward the great ocean.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons, the appearance of the Buddhas is exceedingly rare;
though one may briefly encounter them, if one does not serve them intimately, one will surely fall under the sway of the evil Māra.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Śāriputra! Within that Buddha-dharma there were six bhikṣus who constantly followed one another in practicing various evil deeds:
the first was named Sudarśana, the second Suśīla, the third Nanda, the fourth Vinīta, the fifth Suyodhana, and the sixth Agnidatta.

"Śāriputra! These six bhikṣus constantly preach what is not the Dharma, asserting that there is a self and there are persons, and that there is permanence or annihilation. They remain closely bound together, circulating among one another with mutual trust and reliance. They frequent secluded places to hold secret consultations, saying:
'We should each go out and convert others, gathering a hundred households for each person to serve as our followers.'"
Furthermore, he caused a hundred households to inform their own kin, and in this manner, it was passed on through relatives and kinsmen until it reached perhaps fifty or a hundred families.

Having made this plan, he went forth to teach and transform others—whether in villages, cities, wildernesses, or marketplaces; whether reaching royal capitals or other kingdoms—he visited every single household.
Having arrived there, they did not preach the True Dharma, but instead first slandered the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Śāriputra,
how did those wicked bhikṣus slander him?
Śāriputra! Those wicked bhikṣus say to the multitude:
"In this world, there definitely exists a self, there exist sentient beings, there exists a life-principle, and there exists a person who undergoes rebirth."

If, in all the worlds, there were definitely no self and no phenomena, who would go and who would come? Who would sit and who would lie down? Who would speak and who would remain silent? Who could practice giving, who is the recipient, who could experience [objects], who would undergo suffering and pleasure, and who would be able to experience neither-suffering-nor-pleasure?
If someone were to come and say to you:
"In this world, there definitely is no self, no sentient being, no life-span, and no person who grasps at aggregates."
"You should know that such a person is your enemy and not your virtuous friend.
Śāriputra, at that time,
those wicked bhikṣus would again entice and convert women, men, boys, and girls, speaking to them in this way:
"If there be anyone who says that dharmas such as non-self do not exist, you should know that such a person is unwholesome and violent; they are your evil friend, not your virtuous friend."
Again, he transformed them further, saying:
"You all are wise and are deeply able to comprehend the meaning of what I have taught.
From this day forward, if any evil friends or those who are not true friends should come, they will preach to you the doctrine that in the world there is definitively no self and so forth."
"You should not hastily become intimate with one another, looking toward each other, visiting, or serving and making offerings.
Śāriputra, these wicked bhikṣus employ such methods of conversion; within half a month, they have individually enticed five hundred families to follow their views.

Śāriputra! At that time, there were certain bhikṣus who were arhats, forever free from all defilements and impurities, and true disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jinaśāsanadarśin. For the sake of various causes and conditions such as seeking alms, they went to the homes where those wicked bhikṣus had converted [the families].

Upon arriving at their gate, he was immediately subjected to verbal abuse, irrational rebukes, and personal insults from women, men, and various boys and girls. Addressing the bhikṣus with harsh and offensive words, he spoke these verses:
“You do not understand the True Dharma; You have lost your way on the Noble Path.
You have abandoned the Pure Teaching; You shall all fall into hell.”
"Śāriputra! After those people had spoken these words, they reviled the arhats even more intensely.
Having reviled them, they further insulted the Buddha with various kinds of speech."
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
"What the Tathāgata has spoken is not false: That all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent;
And that all dharmas are without self, As well as being neither constant nor unchanging."
All conditioned phenomena are utterly devoid of solidity; they are all deceptive, false, and subject to loss.
Like the flowers in the sky of which one speaks, they possess no reality at all, serving only to delude and mislead the foolish.
"Śāriputra! After those people had spoken such words in contempt of the Buddha, their indignation redoubled, and they further spoke these verses before the Buddha:
'All phenomena taught by the Tathāgata Are definitively without self and without sentient beings;'"
There is no life-span and no person who grasps; there is neither an agent nor a recipient.
Yet now we see in all the worlds those who can practice giving and those who receive, as well as various other users of enjoyments, and those who perceive vast sensations and the like.
"You should know that those who proclaim that there is certainly no self will all fall into the evil realms. "Śāriputra!

At that time, when those unwholesome people spoke these words of what is not the Dharma with one voice, there were sixty-eight *koṭis* of thousands of sentient beings—men and women, both great and small—who, having been led astray by wicked bhikṣus, committed such evil deeds."

After their lives have ended, they are reborn together in the Avīci Great Hell, where they receive a massive body in the form of a fish with a human head; their tongues are so long and wide that they spread across the ground, with nails driven all over them like a field of ginger, and many iron plows constantly till upon their tongues.
Each of those bodies is further devoured by a hundred extremely wicked conch-eaters (*śaṅkha*).
