Moreover, from the sky, great hot iron balls—blazing with fierce flames and radiant with intense light—fall from above, raining down constantly upon their bodies.
"Because of their evil karma, these transgressors undergo such various forms of torment and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Iron balls with fierce flames like streaks of lightning, In countless hundreds of thousands of terrifying forms, Constantly fall upon their bodies;
Blazing intensely, they perpetually undergo various sufferings.”
Furthermore, it circulates throughout the interior of the body; blazing with fierce intensity, it is difficult to approach.
Its flames surge upward for a hundred yojanas, and flowing fire issues forth from every pore of the body.
Furthermore, each and every tongue of those sentient beings is plowed by countless iron plows;
all parts of their tongues are split asunder, and such agonizing sensations constantly envelop them.
This arises from having associated with evil friends, which can evoke such a great mass of suffering;
furthermore, by staying far away from those possessed of full precepts, one causes oneself to fall swiftly into the evil realms.
“Śāriputra! At that time, those six unrighteous and evil bhikṣus, due to their evil teachings, will all be reborn in the Great Avīci Hell after their lives have ended.”

Each individual body they receive is thirty *yojana* in length and breadth. From each of those bodies, a thousand mouths are produced; within each mouth, two tongues are produced. Each tongue is four *yojana* in width and length. Upon each tongue are five hundred iron plows, which iron oxen pull to plow the tongues.
Although these sinners undergo suffering and pain, they are so overwhelmed by great agony that they have no leisure to cry out.

Furthermore, upon each of their heads there are ten billion hell-wardens, who hold instruments of harm—swords, saws, spears, and lances—with which they hack, pierce, tear, and shatter their bodies and heads.
In this hell, they live for ten trillion years; thus, passing from one to another, they go on to other great hells, where they fully undergo all manner of bitter and agonizing torments.
Why is this? Because they have, out of anger, slandered the holy teaching of the Buddha. Śāriputra!

At that time, there was a great elder named An-yin (Peaceful Security), whose wealth was immeasurable and whose assets were complete; he possessed many rare treasures, including gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, mani-jewels, pearls, conch shells, and jade, none of which were lacking.
Furthermore, he had many servants and slaves, and his treasuries of wealth and grain were all completely full.
At that time, the elder was taught by wicked bhikṣus; having accepted their words, he gave rise to the view of nihilism.
The elder had a wife named Jvālāmati, whose complexion was radiant and beautiful, and whom all people held in high esteem.

She gave birth to a son whose physical appearance was so dignified and handsome that no one ever grew weary of beholding him; he possessed a supreme, perfect, and pure form, having planted the roots of virtue under hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddhas in the past.
At the time of his birth, he smiled three times and spoke these words:
"How marvelous, how marvelous!
Why has he now been born into a family that holds the view of annihilationism?"
Upon hearing this, his mother was struck with terror and alarm; her hair stood on end, and she fled together with the other women, abandoning him. Śāriputra!
Then those women, wishing to ascertain the truth, returned to stay nearby and observed what kind of being this child was.
Is he a deva? A nāga? Or is he a yakṣa?
Are you a gandharva? Are you an asura?
Or are you a garuḍa?
Are you a kinnara? Are you a mahoraga?
Or are you a kumbhāṇḍa?
"Are you piśācas or non-human beings?
Śāriputra, at that time the infant spoke these words again, addressing the women:
"Though you flee in fear, I am very at ease.
Then the infant spoke these verses to the women:
"You should delight in what is beneficial; do not fear that which is beneficial."
I shall deliver you all, causing you to escape from the wrong path.
Be at peace and do not fear; rather, you should fear your former evil companions.
I shall deliver you all, causing you to escape from false views.
"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the infant, his parents and the rest of the great assembly went to where the child was.
Then the infant spoke this stanza to his parents:"
"Whatever is within the house, all the vast wealth and grain—
bring it quickly here and give it to us, to offer to the Buddha and his śrāvakas."
That great assembly of śrāvakas, the World-Illuminating Honored One of Supreme Vision—
within the circle of the three realms, there is none at all who is his equal.
That great assembly of śrāvakas, the World-Illuminating Honored One of Supreme Vision...
Extensively expounding the sublime Dharma, he benefits all classes of beings.
That assembly of great śrāvakas and the World-Illuminating Honored One of Supreme Vision possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
“The śrāvaka assembly of that Buddha is like the udumbara flower;
his name is extremely difficult to hear even after passing through billions of koṭis of kalpas. “Śāriputra!...”
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the child’s parents took twenty koṭis of the finest treasures from their home, went to where the child was, and said to him:
"These treasures are the property belonging to your parents; you should take them and, according to your own inclination, offer them as a gift to those in whom you have placed your faith."
At that time, the parents spoke these verses for the child:
"These are your parents, And the various treasures we have provided;
According to what you respect and believe in, You should take them and practice giving."
Whether it be gold or precious jewels, accumulated in great abundance within your home,
you should take whatever your heart reveres and trusts and bestow it quickly as a gift.
Likewise, garments, bedding, and seating, as well as flower garlands and scented ointments— take these and give them away.
According to what your heart reveres and trusts, you should joyfully offer gifts.
To the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha— the supreme field of merit—
for the benefit of all living beings, you ought to practice giving.
"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard the verses spoken by his parents, the infant spoke these verses in return for them:
'I shall now go to the Abhirati world, To where the Refuge of the World resides.'
One should extensively arrange offerings for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Those who desire to seek the joys of the heavens and the human realm should follow where I go— to the presence of the Tathāgata Abhirati.
“Śāriputra! At that time, the infant, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, surveyed the four directions and said to his parents:
‘Parents, you should know that I must now go to the presence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.’”
Thereupon, when the multitude heard these words, they were all greatly astonished and asked:
"How is it that this infant, on the very day of his birth, is already able to converse and debate with others?"
"Furthermore, how can he travel on foot to such a destination?
At that time, eighty-four thousand sentient beings, hearing of this marvel, all gathered like clouds and said:
"We shall observe what kind of being this infant is."
"Are you a deva?
Are you a nāga?
Or are you a yakṣa?"
"Or even a piśāca or a non-human being?
Śāriputra! At that time, the infant, surrounded by a great assembly of eighty-four thousand beings in front and behind, proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata Abhirati resided.

As this infant was proceeding toward the Buddha’s dwelling, ten thousand jeweled parasols spontaneously appeared in the sky above him to shield his body from being harmed or distressed by the wind and sun, through the power of his merit.

Furthermore, along the path traversed by the infant, golden nets were spread throughout the void, raining down exquisite flowers and fine powdered incense that surpassed those constantly scattered by the devas.
A cool, refreshing breeze blended with celestial fragrances, circulating and dispersing in an unceasing succession.
Furthermore, the devas in the void sprinkled various scented waters along the path and covered it with golden gauze and various kinds of precious garments.
Furthermore, those devas rained down flowers that were spread along the path, their radiance shining brilliantly and accumulating up to the knees.

Beside the path, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of pure ponds appeared spontaneously, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues, and producing various exquisite flowers—namely, utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers—which, fresh and flourishing, filled the interior of the ponds.
Furthermore, there were various species of birds, such as ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, sporting upon the water. Śāriputra!

At that time, along the path by which the infant traveled, railings made of the seven precious gems lined both sides of the way; and the celestial music, numbering in the thousands, produced profound and wondrous sounds spontaneously.

On both sides, rows of precious trees stand in solemn array; further, flower paths are laid out across the great road, appearing before his body as an offering, awaiting the infant’s treading upon them.
Upon that flower-path, the flowers beneath his feet would naturally vanish as he lifted them, and reappear as he was about to set them down.
While the infant traversed this path of flowers for a brief moment, he turned back to look at the great assembly and spoke these verses:
"Your ways are irrational and should not be practiced; This path of mine is unique; any other is unrighteous."
I constantly travel within this correct principle, and thus proceed to the most supreme state of reasoned existence.
Having passed through immeasurable nayutas of eons, one encounters a human body by virtue of a single merit;
at such a time, a Buddha appears in the world, and at such a time, one diligently cultivates pure faith and wisdom.
“Śāriputra! At that time, after the infant had spoken these verses for the great assembly, eighty-four thousand great devaputras in the sky praised him with one voice, saying:
‘Excellent, excellent!’”
He then spoke a verse in praise of the infant, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! What you have proclaimed accords with the correct principle.
O benevolent one, those who look back possess no principle; those who possess the correct principle move forward.”
"Śāriputra! At that time, the infant again addressed the devas with these verses:
'The reasoned and unreasoned correct words That you, O devas, have proclaimed—'
"I now ask you; you should answer me regarding the true meaning of what is logical and what is illogical. "Śāriputra!
At that time, the devas again addressed the infant in verse, saying:"
"If one delights in dwelling amidst various wealth and treasures, and does not delight in the sphere of practice that leads to renunciation—
such irrational, foolish commoners abide upon the path leading to hell."
If one delights in renouncing the home for the homeless life, they should abandon desire and discard wealth;
such a person possesses right principle in this world and will before long open the gate of liberation.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the infant again addressed the devas in verse, saying:
'Whether what you have said is logical or illogical, upon examination, it is clear that you have not yet understood it at all.'"
"In this way, regarding the meanings of what is logical and what is illogical, I have attained profound and correct awakening herein. "Śāriputra!
At that time, having spoken these words, the infant immediately stepped forward and approached the great assembly of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin."

Having arrived there, he prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side. Filled with deep reverence and admiration for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, he praised him with these verses:
“Ever acting for the benefit of all worlds, Vipaśyin, you bestow the nectar of the Three Knowledges;
Like a great nāga-elephant or a mighty lion, Therefore, I now constantly pay you homage.”
The illuminator of the world is exceedingly difficult to encounter, Like the udumbara flower;
as the refuge and light for the world, His form and color are subtle, wondrous, and perfectly complete.
Oppressed by the manifold sufferings of the world, they cannot comprehend the true path of the noble ones;
straying from the correct road and fleeing in all directions, they are like those born blind dwelling in this world.
May I attain Buddhahood in this very life, just like the Supreme among Men, Vipaśyin;
may I uproot the immeasurable sufferings of sentient beings and rescue those burning with the three fires.
Thus, these boundless hundreds of thousands of beings have all followed me here;
I only pray that you will proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma, so that they may all dwell securely in supreme Bodhi.
"Śāriputra! At that time, having spoken these verses, the infant addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vijayadarśin, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"

May I, in a future life in this world, become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, just as the present Tathāgata Vipasyin extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the great assembly.
At that time, there were eighty-four thousand sentient beings in the assembly who again addressed the Tathāgata Vijaya-darśana, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We too vow that in a future age we shall attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and for the sake of sentient beings, proclaim the True Dharma, just as the present Tathāgata Vijaya-darśana and others do, without any difference.”
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vijaya-darśana, having fully understood the exalted resolve of these eighty-four thousand people, smiled.

Śāriputra, it is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they smile, various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal-colored—spontaneously issue from the Buddha’s face. These lights pervade immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds, reaching upward as far as the Brahma-world and eclipsing the radiance of all suns and moons.

Having universally illumined all that was to be done with its light, it returned once more, circumambulated the Tathāgata Vipaśyin one hundred thousand times to the right, and entered through the uṣṇīṣa of the Bhagavat.

Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata Abhirati had an attendant who, having witnessed the Buddha’s miraculous transformation and the manifestation of his smile, rose from his seat, bared his left shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, bowed in prostration and addressed him in verse:
"I now question the Honored One, Abhirati, Whose majestic and rare appearance brings joy to all beings."
For what cause and condition, O Great Sugata, refuge of the world, do you manifest a smile?
Since the World-Honored One, supreme among bipeds, manifests a smile, there must be a cause and condition for this mark.
Pray, explain the fundamental cause and condition of this smile, out of compassion for the benefit of the world.
Now there are hundreds of thousands of koṭis of beings currently standing before the Muni, the World-Honored One;
with ears pricked and minds focused, they joyfully desire to hear. We pray that the Refuge of the World will, out of compassion for these beings, speak.
The Buddha is the eye for all sentient beings; he is their shelter, their rescue, and their refuge.
He is able to sever all doubts within the realms of existence for sentient beings; he is the one who pities the world and brings it benefit.
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows all that has passed, And can also penetrate the future;
He harbors no doubt regarding any phenomena, Nor concerning the buddha-fields of the present.

O Dharma King, master of the treatises on penetrating wisdom, Transcendent Tathāgata, wondrous beyond the three times, I now inquire of you, the refuge of the world: By what causes and conditions do you manifest a smile?
The Buddha can forever sever the net of others' doubts, Being himself free from doubt regarding all phenomena;
With an eightfold voice, he proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma, Skillfully extracting the poisoned arrows of suffering from sentient beings.
My heart leaps with joy beyond description; with palms joined in reverence, I venture to ask the Great Holy Honored One, the Master of Dharma: by what causes and conditions do you manifest a smile?
"Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin addressed his attendant, saying: 'Bhikṣu!'"
"Do you now see this infant before me? He replied, "Indeed, I do."
"I have now seen it.
The Buddha Vijaya said:

"This infant, in the distant past, made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise to sixty-four *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Having presented them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other necessities, he did so in order to advance toward *sambodhi*. Furthermore, in the past, he practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*) under ten *nayuta* of Buddhas, dedicating his merit toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"O Bhikṣus, you should know that these eighty-four thousand people in the great assembly whom this infant leads were all, in past lives, the infant's own parents."
Why is this? This infant once made such a vow in the past:
"May all my parents, wherever I may be born throughout the course of my lives, be established securely in the Buddha's bodhi."
Furthermore, I have caused those mothers never again to undergo a second birth in a female body.

By virtue of this vow, those sentient beings follow after the infant to my presence even until this day, and by following and training together with him, they have given rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata Abhibhū, wishing to reiterate this meaning for the sake of his attendant bhikṣu, spoke these verses:
“Bhikṣu, you should observe this infant, And the many thousands of beings gathered before him;
With hearts leaping with joy, he utters a sincere vow: ‘May I in the future become a Lord of Dharma like this.’”
One should know that in past lives, they have reverently made offerings to Great Guides as numerous as those mentioned above—
those who bring benefit to devas, humans, and the world.
In the presence of ten nayutas of Buddhas, he followed those Buddhas to leave the household life and uphold the True Dharma,
constantly practicing the most supreme conduct for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
Behold these eighty-four thousand beings, now all standing before the Tathāgata;
in ages long past, they were all the parents of this infant.

Furthermore, this infant had previously made a vow: "May all those who have been my parents throughout successive births be universally established in supreme, perfect enlightenment, and may they never again receive a female body."
They all followed and learned the conduct of infants, and gave rise to the bodhicitta in my presence;
now I shall bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon them all, for they are soon to become the Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings in the world.
For this reason, I manifest a smile; I know his past sublime conduct, as well as all that he shall do in the future—he shall realize the state of a Great Holy Lord among men.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and humans— immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas—
hearing the Buddha bestow predictions upon them, gave rise to great joy toward the Honored One of Supreme Vision.

“Śāriputra! At that time, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, the infant felt immeasurable joy and exultation; his mind was serene and he experienced what he had never known before. He quickly went to where his parents were and spoke these verses:
‘These many thousands of beings Were my parents in my previous lives.’”
"All have already established themselves in enlightenment; what is the destination of our parents' hearts? "Śāriputra!
At that time, the parents replied to their son with these verses:"
"As the direction of your resolve, so too shall mine;
I shall attain all-knowledge—of this there is no doubt."
“Now that you have been born into my family, I pray that you will not forsake me hereafter;
may you always remember me and cause me to quickly realize Bodhi. “Śāriputra!
At that time, the infant again addressed his parents in verse, saying:
"May all those whom I have guided through my various deeds and transformations first attain Buddhahood;
may I become the final one to achieve it, illuminating the world as a Tamer of Men."
“Śāriputra! You should now consider: was that infant in the Dharma of the Tathāgata Abhibhū of the past anyone else?
Do not harbor any other doubt; it is none other than the present Great Maheśvara Devaputra.”

From this point forward, he will pass through further *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas without ever falling back. After those kalpas have elapsed, he will be born into the noble lineage of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). His future father shall be named Yaśas, just as my current father is the Great King Śuddhodana;
his future mother shall be named Vigatatamas, just as my current mother is Mahāmāyā;
and his future son shall be named Aśoka, just as my current son is Rāhula.
Śāriputra! Having left the household life and awakened to bodhi, he became a Buddha named Mahākāruṇika Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.

The lifespan of that Buddha was a full hundred thousand koṭis of years; the constant radiance of the Buddha’s body pervaded ten yojanas, and the great assembly at the place where the Buddha preached the Dharma filled a hundred yojanas.
The Tathāgata of Great Compassion dwells in the world to teach and transform beings, preaching the Dharma at three assemblies to deliver the śrāvakas.

At the first great assembly, he delivered one hundred koṭis of disciples; at the second great assembly, he delivered nayutas of koṭis of disciples; and at the third great assembly, he delivered hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of disciples.

Śāriputra! Among his disciples, there were a full one koṭi who were all great arhats; their outflows were exhausted and they were free from further afflictions; they had attained sovereign wisdom and were endowed with the eight liberations; they had accomplished meditative concentration and the six supernormal powers.

Śāriputra, the number of the assembly of śrāvaka arhats liberated by the Tathāgata Mahākāruṇika is equal to the quantities of the three assemblies mentioned above; the number of his bodhisattva assembly is likewise equal, and all of them were his parents in previous lives.
After that Buddha, the World-Honored One, had proclaimed the sublime Dharma and benefited countless sentient beings, he subsequently entered parinirvāṇa.

Following the Buddha’s passing, the True Dharma remained in the world for a full *koṭi* of years; his relics were distributed to benefit sentient beings, exactly as they will be after my own parinirvāṇa, with no difference in their dissemination or veneration.

Śāriputra! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who abides in right effort: when practicing the pāramitā of vīrya, for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are able to practice this sūtra with correct conduct, further increasing their courageous and right effort of great diligence to deliver immeasurable sentient beings.

I declare that such a person is a virtuous man (satpuruṣa), who reflects and examines with tireless and non-regressive diligence, and who applies courageous effort with clear mindfulness fixed in the heart. Śāriputra!
What is the tireless diligence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
"Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks awakening for the sake of sentient beings, they should not limit their seeking by means of numerical measures."
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such a thought as:
"I shall wander through transmigrations for so many kalpas."
"I shall not wander through saṃsāra for as many eons as that.
For this reason, when a bodhisattva dons the inconceivable armor and dwells within birth and death, they form this thought:

"Even if I were to undergo the same amount of hardship and experience birth and death as I did throughout my past limits, or even double that amount, I would never grow weary or cease in my quest for bodhi."
"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such firm and great vows, they are said to have accomplished untiring diligence.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice courageous diligence?

Śāriputra, suppose the trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire; yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has initiated courageous and right effort, desiring to go and behold that Tathāgata, would pass through that blazing fire by the power of diligence, neither cowering nor retreating.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who exerts courageous and right effort, for the sake of seeking to hear this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, shall pass straight through even such a fire by the power of his diligence, without fear or retreat.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire; yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva of courageous and right diligence, desiring to proclaim the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, would pass straight through that blazing fire by the power of his vigor, without fear or retreat.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose the trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire; yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva of courageous and right diligence, desiring to give rise to the causes and conditions for roots of goodness, would pass straight through that blazing fire by the power of his vigor, without fear or retreat.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire, a bodhisattva mahāsattva of courageous and correct diligence, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, would be able to pass through it by the power of their vigor.
Thus, because he desires to cause others to attain tranquility and to attain discipline, even when encountering such fire, he passes through it without fear or retreat.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has initiated courageous and tireless right effort, desiring to lead others to parinirvāṇa, is able to pass through such a fire by the power of diligence, remaining free from fear or retreat.
"Śāriputra! This is called the mark of the heroic vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vīrya.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has initiated courageous and tireless right effort practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), because they are permeated by the unsurpassed great compassion arising from roots of goodness that are firm and non-retrogressive due to being untiring, they constantly exert the power of courageous and great diligence, always acting to transform and guide all sentient beings.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who thus initiates courageous and tireless right effort never, at any time, abandons the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*) while lifting or lowering a foot. He constantly maintains a state of reverence for the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, keeping them ever-present before his mind. For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he constantly and universally observes them, wishing not to allow them to be overcome or stripped away by the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has initiated courageous and tireless right effort dedicates all already-arisen excellent roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment, he causes these roots of goodness to be ultimately inexhaustible.
For example, if a small amount of water is poured into the great ocean, it will not be exhausted even until the end of the kalpa when the world is consumed by fire.

Śāriputra, it is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: by dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment, they too are inexhaustible. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of great diligence that is courageous and tireless.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is courageous and untiring in diligence accumulates roots of goodness through the practice of equanimity; he accumulates roots of goodness by giving rise to the practice of equanimity toward all sentient beings; he accumulates roots of goodness out of a desire to bring forth the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); and he accumulates roots of goodness for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Śāriputra! Such immeasurable great roots of goodness are all produced through the power of the great, tireless, and courageous diligence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who thus applies himself with courageous and tireless right effort should always diligently train in this Dharma; the mass of merit he thereby acquires will be immeasurable and boundless."
I shall now explain at length the characteristics of the mass of merit. Śāriputra!

I observe that the mass of merit possessed by all sentient beings in the world is immeasurable and boundless; likewise, the mass of merit of all those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as the mass of merit of all pratyekabuddhas, is even more immeasurable and inconceivable.

If all these aforementioned masses of merit were placed within a single pore of a sentient being, and if every single pore of such a sentient being likewise contained such a mass of merit—immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.

Suppose, for instance, that all the merit contained within every single pore of all sentient beings were gathered together and placed within a single great dharma sanctuary, free from any obstruction.
Śāriputra! The mass of merit and blessings from such a Dharma-sacrifice is multiplied a hundredfold, resulting in the attainment of a single mark of the physical form of a Tathāgata, a Great Man.
Each one of these marks of a great man is accomplished by such merit as this.
All the masses of merit contained within all the marks of a great man upon the bodies of all Tathāgatas combine to form a single mark of the tuft of hair between the eyebrows (ūrṇā-kośa).

The mass of merit required to produce even a single tuft of hair between the eyebrows is such that, multiplied by a hundred thousand times its full measure, it forms the Great Man’s mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, which is invisible to the gaze of others.

Thus, by entering into this single mass of great merit of the *uṣṇīṣa*, and further exceeding this by a full hundred thousand *koṭi* times greater mass of merit, the mark of the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-conch (*dharma-śaṅkha*) is formed.

Śāriputra! Because this mark of the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-conch is an accumulation of immeasurable kinds of merit, for this reason, the Tathāgata, according to his will, emits a great sound that reaches all infinite and boundless worlds, extensively preaching the sublime Dharma for all sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice through faith and understanding according to their respective faculties and natures.
Why is this? It is because they have all been cultivated and studied through diligence. Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:

"Although this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain, I shall not cast off the armor of diligence and shall summon great courage; it will certainly not be difficult for me to swiftly awaken to unsurpassed enlightenment."

Having attained Buddhahood, according to my wish, I shall produce a great sound from the mark of the conch shell, universally proclaiming it throughout all infinite and boundless worlds; for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, causing them all to rejoice according to their faculties, inclinations, and understandings.
"Śāriputra! This is called the mark of the courageous and tireless right effort of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The bodhisattva mahāsattva who is courageous and untiring in diligence, by relying upon the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), should always practice and train in this manner; through such training, they will fully accomplish all wisdom.

Śāriputra! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to achieve the wisdom of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); even with this wisdom, if one were to compare it to the wisdom of a single person who has achieved the wisdom of those who follow by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), it would not equal a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor a *saṃkhyā* part, nor a *kalā* part, nor a *gaṇanā* part, nor an *upamā* part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to achieve the wisdom of one who practices in accordance with the Dharma; if one were to compare this to the wisdom of a single person on the eighth stage, it would not equal even a hundredth part of it, nor even a fraction as small as an *upaniṣad*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to achieve the wisdom of the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*); if one were to compare this to the wisdom of a single stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), it would not equal even a hundredth part, nor even a fraction as small as an *upaniṣad*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to achieve the wisdom of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), and one wished to compare that to the wisdom of even a single candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*)—and likewise, from the wisdom of the fruit of once-returning up to the wisdom of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and so on, up to the wisdom of an arhat, the wisdom of a pratyekabuddha, the wisdom of a bodhisattva who has passed a hundred kalpas, the wisdom of a bodhisattva who has attained the stage of non-retrogression, and even the wisdom of a bodhisattva bound to only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*)—all these should be explained extensively as being immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
In this way, Śāriputra!

Suppose all sentient beings in all the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions were to fully accomplish the wisdom of a bodhisattva who is bound to only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*); yet, if they were to desire to compare it with even a single portion of the Tathāgata’s ten powers—specifically the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthānajñāna*)—they would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, nor a *koṭīśatasahasra*th part; they would not equal a *saṃkhyā*th part, a *kalā*th part, a *gaṇanā*th part, an *upamā*th part, or an *upaniṣad*th part; indeed, they could not be reached by calculation or analogy.

Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), when hearing of such profound wisdom and understanding of the Tathāgata, his mind is not startled and he has no fear. This person of wisdom gives rise to a heart of joyful aspiration, initiates right effort (*samyak-vīrya*) without any abandonment, and forms this thought:

"I shall now practice with courageous diligence; even if my body’s skin, flesh, bones, blood, tendons, veins, marrow, and brain were all to become parched, decay, and perish without remainder, until I have attained the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), I will in the meantime exert great courage and firm vigor, never becoming weary or desisting."
"Śāriputra! This is called the mark of the firmness of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of right effort that is courageous and tireless.
One should train in this way."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), they give rise to great courage and tireless right effort, and should always train with such diligence.
Through cultivation and study, one is able to extinguish the fires of affliction of all sentient beings. Śāriputra!
Suppose that all the minds of all sentient beings throughout the past were to enter and revolve within the single mind of one sentient being.
In this way, each and every mind of a single sentient being—and even all such minds possessed by every single sentient being—is immeasurable, manifold, and difficult to comprehend.
In this way, within the individual mind of each and every sentient being, there exist immeasurable and manifold afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
All the afflictions possessed by all these sentient beings enter and revolve within the single mind of one sentient being.
"Śāriputra! Even if one were to examine all sentient beings in succession, they would all possess such immeasurable afflictions that they are difficult to fully comprehend.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:"

"I shall exert myself with vigor and arouse diligent perseverance to seek such provisions of wisdom; according to the power of my right effort, I must cause the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all other fevers and afflictions, to be extinguished in sentient beings without remainder; I shall cut off their poisonous harms, shatter and destroy them until they are like ashes, and swiftly establish sentient beings upon the path to nirvana."
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of right effort that is courageous and tireless.
One should train in this way."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, by relying on the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in courageous and tireless diligence; they should always train with correct application in this manner."

Because of this cultivation and study, all virtuous physical actions are never ceased or abandoned; all virtuous verbal actions are never ceased or abandoned; and all virtuous mental actions are never ceased or abandoned. Furthermore, every form of right effort serves as a skillful means to stimulate and advance the bodhisattva’s physical, verbal, and mental actions.

Śāriputra! However, those in the world speak only of the bodhisattva’s diligence in the two activities of body and speech as being foremost, but they do not speak of the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s mental diligence.
Śāriputra! The signs of mental diligence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immeasurable and boundless; I shall now briefly explain them.
What are called the signs of mental diligence?
It means that when a bodhisattva’s mind practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), whether advancing or ceasing, such is its characteristic. Śāriputra,
what is meant by the advancement and cessation of right effort?
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva who practices great diligence exerts himself with vigor for the sake of awakening.
What is called "vigor" is the arousal of great compassion toward all sentient beings; what is called "cessation" is the patience of non-self.
What is called "advancing" is gathering in all sentient beings; what is called "stopping" is not grasping at dharmas.
What is called "advancing" is being untiring amidst birth and death; what is called "stopping" is not attaining the three realms.
What is called "advancing" is the relinquishing of everything; what is called "stopping" is not being weary of giving.
What is called "advancing" is the undertaking of pure precepts; what is called "stopping" is not being weary of *śīla*.
What is called "advancing" is the endurance of all sufferings; what is called "stopping" is that the mind is not destroyed.
What is called "advancing" is the arising of all wholesome dharmas; what is called "stopping" is that the mind is always detached.
What is called "exertion" is the cultivation of meditative concentration; what is called "tranquility" is the constant quiescence of the mind.
What is called "exertion" is insatiability in hearing the Dharma; what is called "tranquility" is skillfulness in accordance with reality.
What is called "advancing" is listening to the Dharma without weariness; what is called "stopping" is the absence of frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).
What is called "advancing" is seeking the provisions for wisdom; what is called "stopping" is severing all frivolous discourse.
What is called "advancing" is the increase of pure faith; what is called "stopping" is truly knowing equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is called "advancing" is possessing the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); what is called "stopping" is the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
What is called "progress" is the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness; what is called "stopping" is mindfulness free from effort.
What is called "progress" is the application of the right efforts; what is called "stopping" is the relinquishing of both good and evil.
What is called "advancing" refers to the elicitation of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*); what is called "stopping" refers to spontaneous functioning.
What is called "advancing" refers to the skillful means of the faculties (*indriya*); what is called "stopping" refers to observing that which is not of the nature of a faculty.
What is called "advancing" is the gathering of the powers; what is called "stopping" is wisdom that is not subject to subjugation.
What is called "advancing" is the arising of the factors of enlightenment; what is called "stopping" is wisdom that discriminates phenomena.
What is called "progress" refers to seeking the provisions for the Way; what is called "stopping" refers to the nature of being without coming or going.
What is called "progress" refers to seeking śamatha; what is called "stopping" refers to the mind abiding in tranquility.
What is called "progress" (vīrya) is that which assists superior insight (vipaśyanā); what is called "stopping" (śamatha) is the investigation of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
What is called "progress" is the sequential awakening to all causes; what is called "stopping" is the thorough knowledge of all causes.
What is called "advancing" is hearing the sounds from others; what is called "stopping" is practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
What is called "advancing" refers to the adornment of the body; what is called "stopping" refers to the Dharma-nature body.
What is called "advancing" refers to the adornment of speech; what is called "stopping" refers to the nature of noble silence.
What is called "advancing" refers to the gate of liberation through faith; what is called "stopping" refers to the absence of any arousal [of thought].
What is called "advancing" is to remain far removed from the four māras; what is called "stopping" is to abandon the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
What is called "advancing" is skillful means; what is called "stopping" is the observation of profound wisdom.
What is called "progress" is the observation of conditioned objects; what is called "stopping" is effortless contemplation (*anābhoga-vipaśyanā*).
What is called "progress" is the observation of conventional designations (*prajñapti*); what is called "stopping" is the thorough realization of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).
Śāriputra! All such signs of movement and stillness are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s diligence of mind-only.
If bodhisattva mahāsattvas hear of such signs of mental diligence, they should arouse courageous and tireless right effort.

Śāriputra! This is called the characteristic of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of right effort, which is free from weariness and characterized by courageous and vigorous diligence.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Forty-Six;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Forty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka Assembly, Volume Twelve, Part Thirteen:
Chapter Nine, Part Three, on the Perfection of Vigor.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus courageous and untiringly diligent in right effort accomplishes five methods of progress, they are able to swiftly awaken to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Śāriputra! What are the five dharmas that constitute progress? They are: encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world is a dharma of progress;

finding proximity to virtuous friends is a dharma of progress; obtaining the possession of the absence of obstacles is a dharma of progress; never losing or destroying any wholesome dharmas one has cultivated and accumulated is a dharma of progress; and following and training under those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in their vows and ethical discipline is a dharma of progress.

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), accomplishes five dharmas that lead to progress and non-retrogression, swiftly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
is it possible for a bodhisattva to suffer a decline in these five dharmas?"
The Buddha said, "There are. He asked:
"What do you mean? O Great Virtuous Blessed One! What is it?"
"Venerable Sugata. The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There are five things that, when accomplished by a bodhisattva, lead to their decline."

What are these five? They are: not encountering a Buddha in the world; not maintaining intimacy with spiritual friends; possessing the conditions of no adversity yet failing to obtain them; having much ruin and failure in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas; and lacking the resolve to follow and train in the minds of bodhisattvas who abide in the vows of discipline.
Because they possess such factors that lead to diminution, they do not swiftly awaken to unsurpassed bodhi. Śāriputra,
what five dharmas do bodhisattvas accomplish?

Śāriputra! A lay bodhisattva may act as a counselor or teacher to a king, using his power and influence to intimidate sentient beings, thereby inducing them to seek his protection for various affairs; if he succeeds in accomplishing such matters, they offer him substantial rewards in gratitude.
However, because these bodhisattvas perceive worldly gain, their minds lack integrity as they act for such ends; whatever words they utter are nothing other than for the sake of profit. Śāriputra!
By such dharmas, the wholesome paths are diminished; by such dharmas, the absence of calamities is diminished.

Thus, a lay bodhisattva who performs various unwholesome deeds for the sake of maintaining the body will not encounter a Buddha-world, nor will they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Śāriputra! This is called the first dharma that brings about decline for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
A lay bodhisattva dwells in the dharma of destroying cities.
What is meant by dwelling in the dharma of destroying cities? Śāriputra!

If Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world, they teach the Dharma to gods, humans, Māras, and Brahmās, revealing and proclaiming the holy life that is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, with exquisite phrasing and meaning, pure, singular, complete, and pristine.
At that time, four assemblies shall appear: namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Then, for the sake of guarding the precepts, the bhikṣuṇīs shall dwell within villages, cities, outskirts, lodgings, kingdoms, districts, and royal capitals, relying upon them for support.
Those lay bodhisattvas who come to this dwelling place defile the assembly of those who uphold the precepts; because they have violated the precepts, they are said to dwell in a ruined city.
Having committed such an offense, they will not encounter the era of a Buddha, nor will they be able to swiftly awaken to unsurpassed bodhi.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the second dharma of diminution.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a lay bodhisattva sees those who rely on the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya preaching the True Dharma, they create an obstacle to the Dharma for their parents, brothers, sisters, wives, concubines, sons, daughters, retinues, and all sentient beings.

Śāriputra! Once a lay bodhisattva has committed these obstructing dharmas, they will for a long night constantly encounter many obstacles within the Dharma and Vinaya themselves; they will not meet a Buddha in the world, and may even fail to swiftly awaken to unsurpassed bodhi.
“Śāriputra! This is called the third dharma that causes the decline of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

When a householder bodhisattva hears the Tathāgata’s praise in the Buddha’s sūtras regarding the dharma of few desires and contentment, which corresponds to renunciation and consists of dwelling alone and in stillness within mountain forests to leave suffering behind, they give rise to a lack of faith, treating it with contempt and slandering it, and they also teach others to hold such views.
These lay bodhisattvas who are unwholesome, having reviled the Tathāgata’s pure teaching, will once again sink into the states that are subject to revilement.
What are these states called that are subject to revilement?
That is to say, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or the world of Yama; or they are born in borderlands among the Mlecchas with evil and heterodox views.
Because the householder bodhisattva performs such deeds, he does not encounter the era of a Buddha, nor does he awaken to unsurpassed bodhi.
"Śāriputra! This is called the fourth dharma of diminution accomplished by a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Householder bodhisattvas who rely upon kings, ministers, and even those who are wealthy, noble, and powerful, may engage in wicked conduct and, relying on their influence, revile, scold, insult, despise, and mock countless sentient beings.

Śāriputra! Because a householder bodhisattva accomplishes such verbal misconduct, they will swiftly gather the retributions of the evil destinies; they will not encounter the era of a Buddha, nor meet with virtuous friends; they will not obtain the absence of obstacles, will ruin their roots of goodness, will not follow the training in the true Dharma of bodhisattvas who abide in the vows of discipline, and will be unable to quickly awaken to unsurpassed bodhi.
“Śāriputra! This is called the fifth dharma that causes the decline of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes five kinds of dharmas, such wisdom will not increase;
neither will they swiftly see the Tathāgata, nor will they encounter and serve the Supreme among Men."
Or acting as a great preceptor to kings, they deceive and delude all sentient beings;
because they have accumulated such unwholesome karma, they do not encounter the Protector of the World.
Causing many sentient beings to give rise to fear, whether by accepting bribes or by inflicting harm—
having committed such evil deeds as these, one will never encounter the Honored One among Men.
Or if they cause the assembly of pure precepts of the nuns to be broken, destroyed, and annihilated, giving rise to sorrow and suffering,
they shall be separated from immeasurable billions of Tathāgatas and will be unable to achieve the state free from all obstacles.
Regarding one's parents, wife, children, and others, they create obstacles that prevent the practice of the Dharma and further hinder the hearing of the True Dharma;
these swiftly bring about the fruit of being shrouded by ignorance and delusion.
If a person, weary of worldly pleasures, leaves the home life, yet falls into attachment and is hindered by lingering obstacles,
they shall depart from the immeasurable, most supreme Honored One and be unable to achieve the state free from all difficulties.
If there are those who, upon hearing such a teaching— namely, this praise of dwelling in seclusion—
give rise to a mind of intolerance and anger, slandering it as an unrighteous teaching.
Having slandered and reviled such a true Dharma, one will dwell eternally in the great agony of being born blind;
among all heavy obstructions and sinful karmas, even the most severe does not approach even a sixteenth part of this.
It is difficult for them to behold the Tathāgatas; even if they do see them, they cannot conceive faith or reverence.
They receive the bodies of women, eunuchs, and those born blind, and further, they receive the forms of camels, donkeys, pigs, dogs, and the like.
If there are those who, toward the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, Give rise to a heart of profound, earnest love and respect,
Having distanced themselves from all obstacles, They shall continuously cultivate the path of the noble ones.
May parents, wives, children, and kinsfolk always delight in peace and diligence within the True Dharma;
may sentient beings who weary of the world seek to leave the household life, and may they be praised, encouraged, and assisted so that their goal is realized.
If one dwells within the true Dharma and its retinue, one shall swiftly ascend to the noble and auspicious realms;
those who are able to praise and encourage others to leave the household life will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are five further dharmas for a bodhisattva who has gone forth; if they are accomplished, one will not encounter the age of a Buddha, will not associate with virtuous friends, will not possess the absence of obstacles, will lose and destroy the roots of goodness, and will not follow or train in the true Dharma of bodhisattvas who abide in the vows of discipline, nor will one swiftly awaken to unsurpassed bodhi."
Śāriputra! What are the five dharmas that a renunciant bodhisattva fulfills?

First, violating the precepts (śīla); second, slandering the true Dharma; third, being greedily attached to fame and profit; fourth, stubbornly adhering to the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi); and fifth, giving rise to much stinginess and jealousy toward the households of others.

Śāriputra! These are called the five dharmas that a renunciant bodhisattva accomplishes, by which they do not encounter the era of a Buddha and so forth, until finally failing to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Śāriputra, it is like a starving dog that, wandering along a road in a state of panic and distress, encounters a fragment of bone from which the flesh and marrow have long since vanished; seeing only the red coating, it thinks it is a rich flavor and proceeds to seize it in its mouth.

In a place where many people gather, at a crossroads, because of their craving for flavor, they let saliva flow over their bones and falsely imagine them to be sweet; they gnaw, lick, bite, or suck, clinging with affectionate attachment without ever letting go.
At that time, there were kṣatriyas, brahmins, and various elders, all of great wealth and status, who came traveling along this road.
When the starving dog saw them approaching from afar, his heart was filled with distress, and he thought to himself:
"Will these people coming not take away the precious, delicious food I hold dear?"
"Thereupon, he gave rise to great wrath toward that person, let out a deeply venomous cry, glared with malevolent eyes, bared his teeth, and proceeded to bite and harm him. Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
That person who has come must have some other business; would he truly seek this skeleton of bare bones smeared with blood?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"No, World-Honored One! No, World-Honored One!"
"No, Sugata. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“If that is so, for what reason does that stingy, hungry dog emit such a deeply venomous sound, baring its teeth and barking?

Śāriputra replied, “As I understand it, he fears that the person coming here, being greedily attached to fine food, will surely seize my excellent flavor of ambrosia; it is with this intention that he bares his teeth and barks.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”

In the future, at the end of the age, there will be bhikṣus who diligently cultivate stinginess toward the households of other donors; they will be attached to excrement and urine, falsely wrapping themselves in them. Although they encounter such times where all conditions for practice are complete and free from calamity, they will instead cast them aside and fail to practice proper restraint.
"Śāriputra, I say that the conduct of this bhikṣu is like that of the foolish dog mentioned before. Śāriputra,

having now appeared in the world out of compassion for sentient beings and desiring to bring them to rest, I have reflected deeply upon this matter and have spoken this parable for the sake of such evil bhikṣus."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, seek the wisdom of a Buddha and practice the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā)."

Since those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the giving away of even their own flesh, how much less would they harbor thoughts of stinginess or jealousy toward other households over imaginary, unwholesome meat?

Śāriputra! Because those bhikṣus are stingy toward the families of others, I declare that such persons are deluded men; they are those who live merely for their own livelihood; they are slaves to wealth, grain, and possessions; they are those bound by the heavy fetters of worldly riches and playthings; they are those who hold only food and clothing in high esteem; and they are those who give rise to stinginess and envy out of a craving for the "flesh" of false conceptualizations.
Śāriputra! I shall now further explain this true Dharma.
When those bhikṣus have first arrived at another's home, they should not give rise to envy upon seeing other bhikṣus.
If there is a bhikṣu who violates my Dharma teachings and, seeing another bhikṣu, should speak thus:
"This donor's household was previously known to me; from where have you come to be here?"
"I am extremely close to this family; we share jests and mutual regard.
From where have you come to thus intrude upon and seize [what belongs to us]? O Śāriputra!
For what reason does that stingy bhikṣu give rise to particular jealousy toward those who come later?
Śāriputra, it is because various donors have promised him robes, alms-bowls, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other such articles for his personal livelihood.
He thinks to himself:
"I fear that the donor will give the previously promised items to those who arrive later.
Because of this, that bhikṣu incurs three kinds of faults regarding the donor's household:
First, the fault of arising from one's dwelling place: seeing another bhikṣu, one gives rise to words of resentment, saying, "I shall now depart from this place.
Second, regarding whatever one associates with, one should say that one does not yet know whether it is appropriate or inappropriate.
Third, they falsely impute various faults to those of indeterminate status. Śāriputra,
that stingy bhikṣu utters three kinds of evil words toward latercomers:
First, they speak of the faults of the dwelling place, exaggerating its various evils to make future bhikṣus unwilling to reside there.
Second, they turn the truthful words of future bhikṣus into falsehoods.
Third, they falsely manifest signs of virtue to flatter and attach themselves to such a person, waiting for even a slight opening to publicly accuse and expose them before the assembly. Śāriputra!

A bhikṣu such as this, who gives rise to stinginess and envy toward the families that provide alms, will swiftly extinguish all his wholesome dharmas (śukladharma), exhausting them completely until nothing remains.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there is a bhikṣu who dwells in the stinginess of householders, I declare that such a person is unwholesome; he has abandoned the provisions for enlightenment and is unable to follow those bodhisattvas who dwell in accordance with the correct Dharma and abide in the observance of discipline."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I shall further explain these characteristics of the lineage.

In the past, beyond incalculable, vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Jayasudarśanarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.

That Buddha’s lifespan lasted ninety *koṭi* years, and his assembly of śrāvakas numbered ninety *koṭinayuta*. All were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, and who had attained the supreme perfection of mastery over the mind.

Śāriputra! At that time, there was a great elder named Sunetra, whose family was immensely wealthy and possessed abundant riches and treasures; his assets and servants were so numerous that they filled every quarter.
He had two sons:
the first was named Vinaya, and the second was named Vinayasthita.
They were of tender age, with handsome features and perfect complexions, such that all who saw them were filled with joy.

Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jina-abhyudgatarāja, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, was followed on both sides by a great assembly of bhikṣus. With the World-Honored Buddha at the head of the Saṅgha, for the sake of merit and benefit, he manifested the practice of begging for alms and entered the great city where the elder resided.

His deportment was dignified and orderly, his faculties were tranquil and stilled, and his mind was serene and composed. He had attained disciplined *śamatha*, as well as the foremost discipline of *śamatha*. He restrained his faculties like a great elephant, was clear and undisturbed like a deep spring or pond, possessed towering and magnificent virtue like a golden pavilion, and his physical appearance was preeminent like a mountain of purple gold.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, he is like the great ocean filled with all manner of jewels; like Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by the gods; and like Mahābrahmā, whose mind and thoughts are tranquil. Śāriputra!
That Bhagavān was adorned with such majestic marks and signs.

At that time, the two sons of the elder were on an upper terrace; from afar they beheld the Buddha Śrīsaṃdarśanarāja approaching from the distance, his countenance majestic and his physical form supreme, and they felt a heart of joy, exclaiming at this unprecedented marvel.
"Śāriputra! Because the youth Vinīteśvara had previously beheld the Buddha, his heart leaped with joy, and he said to his elder brother:
'Since the time of our birth, has my brother ever before seen such a majestic King of Beings?'"
The elder brother replied to his younger brother,
"Since my birth, I have truly never seen such a majestic king among sentient beings.
The younger brother said to his elder brother:
"As I reflect upon it, he will certainly become the king among all sentient beings in a future age. Śāriputra,
at that time, the youth Vinayadhara spoke these verses for his elder brother:
"Just as my elder brother, Vinīta, now beholds, so shall it surely be for me in the future:
surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus, it shall be even more magnificent than it is today."
For the sake of seeking the causes and conditions for the path to Bodhi, I vow never to consume food or drink;
since my elder brother delights in dwelling within the prison, my resolve is firm that I shall surely transcend it.
Such is the Honored One among all sentient beings, comparable to the full moon amidst the multitude of stars;
who, upon seeing this, would not give rise to faith, yet delight in the household life instead of renouncing it?
"Śāriputra! At that time, the youth Vinaya immediately replied to his younger brother in verse:
'Brother, you should stop for now and not raise your voice; it is not by mere words alone that one's purpose is accomplished.'"
"How could I possibly utter worldly speech? Let us test who shall first attain perfect enlightenment! "Śāriputra!
At that time, the youth Vinayadhara again addressed his elder brother in verse:"
“‘Such a path to unsurpassed enlightenment is not realized by a base and stingy mind;
I shall utter the great and noble sound, and I shall certainly become a Buddha, supreme among men.’”
Such are the characteristics of those who harbor stinginess: they do not wish for others to know their assets.
Why should I now maintain such silence? I would even give up my body and life, let alone my wealth and treasures.
I have given away my family’s entire fortune as an expedient cause for seeking the path to Bodhi;
likewise, I have offered all the wealth and treasures that were my elder brother’s share, out of deep reverence for the Field of the Buddha.
Who, upon seeing such a most supreme Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two wondrous marks,
would not resolve to proceed toward Bodhi, except for those possessed of inferior views?
All my homes and treasures, my parents and all my kinsmen—
I shall renounce them all and quickly go to the presence of the Sugata Tathāgata.
Acting as a refuge for the world and creating illumination, the Compassionate Honored One who lights up the world is extremely difficult to encounter;
even in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, such sublime signs are very difficult to hear.
I saw the World-Honored One enter the royal capital, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus;
like the full moon in a clear sky, his radiance shone forth, illuminating all that rests upon the earth.
I see the World-Honored One wandering through the four crossroads, Universally adorning all things;
like that sun endowed with a thousand rays, He alone fills the void, constantly shining everywhere.
I behold the World-Honored One at the head of the assembly, Adorning and illuminating the community of bhikṣus;
Like that King of Mountains, Sumeru, He outshines all other jeweled mountains with his sublime beauty.
The Tathāgata’s majestic radiance is most blazingly intense, Pervasively illuminating all sentient beings in this land;
The Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, perfected in wondrous marks, His glorious light adorns and embellishes the entire great assembly.
The Tathāgata abides in great supernormal power, skillfully guiding devas, nāgas, and non-human beings;
manifesting again in immeasurable varieties of transformations, he enters the royal capital for the sake of sentient beings.
Who, having seen such a Lord of the True Dharma, so magnificently adorned with the thirty-two marks,
would yet aspire to an inferior vehicle?
Only those who are unworthy, foolish, and ignorant.
Now I joyfully behold the Honored One among Men, And have given rise to rare and pure faith;
To benefit all sentient beings and advance toward Bodhi, I must surely go to visit the Tathāgata’s abode.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the youth Vinaya again addressed his younger brother in verse, saying:
'I am not indolent on this journey, yet I do not hasten to the presence of the Tathāgata.'"
Once I have descended from these lofty galleries, I shall go outside and contemplate with earnest attention.
I should renounce the notion of a self and disregard even my own body and life, seeking the supreme wisdom of the Great Being; only then shall I proceed to the place where the Tathāgata dwells.
My parents, home, and wealth—toward all such things I have felt deep attachment;
now I renounce them all at once, and only then shall I go to where the Tathāgata dwells.
If there are those who desire and vow to attain Buddhahood, And who deeply love and delight in the Tathāgata,
They should swiftly relinquish their heaps of precious jewels And, abandoning the ways of the household, go forth into the homeless life.

"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard these words, the youth Vinayadhara immediately descended the stairway from the pavilion and proceeded toward the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jinaśrīrāja."
Before he had even arrived, his elder brother, Vinaya, descended swiftly from the multi-storied pavilion and hurried to the Buddha’s presence;
having completed his acts of reverence, he stood behind Vinaya before finally arriving himself.
At that time, the youth Vinīteśvara immediately offered ten billion priceless robes to the Tathāgata and, before the Buddha, spoke these verses:
"I now do not seek for marvelous marks; I offer these priceless robes to the Tathāgata.
May the retribution I obtain in the future Be no different from that of the World-Honored One today."
Most supreme among all sentient beings, Perfectly abiding in all sublime dharmas,
I pray that the retribution obtained in the future May be no different from that of the World-Honored One in this present life.
Fully endowed with the unsurpassed treasury of wisdom, Perfectly established in the powers and right efforts,
Sustained by a body possessed of the thirty-two marks— May you swiftly become the supreme among men.
May they accomplish the ten powers of all Buddhas And dwell securely in the four fearlessnesses;
I pray that the retribution they shall obtain in the future Be no different from that of the World-Honored One today.
Just as the Buddha knows the truly pure Dharma, Only the Buddha dwells well within it and illuminates it all;
I pray that you will grant an exposition of such a Dharma, So that I may swiftly awaken to supreme Bodhi.

I now do not seek for exquisite physical marks; I offer this priceless, supreme upper robe to the Buddha, desiring only the wondrous Bodhi of tranquility for the sake of benefiting all the devas and the world.
The subtle and wondrous Dharma in which the Tathāgata dwells cannot be shaken by any heterodox arguments;
now, seeking such a Dharma as this, I venture to offer you this priceless, supreme upper robe.
All phenomena are without birth, aging, or illness, And likewise free from sorrow, grief, and lamentation;
I pray that you will reveal this quiescent Dharma To guide and benefit the devas and the world.
If there are no phenomena of greed, hatred, or delusion, Nor any forms of pride or craving,
I pray you speak of bodhi and buddha-nature, The unconditioned, cool, and nectar-like Dharma.
If there is a dharma in which the Tathāgata dwells, To which devas, nāgas, and others pay profound homage—
Whether they possess thought or are without thought— I pray that you will reveal this tranquil dharma.

Abiding in this place, the Buddha is able to illuminate universally the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the four directions, like a great flame breaking forth in deep darkness; may he realize such nectar as this.
If all things, whether loved or unloved, are by nature never dependent upon the desire realm,
nor do they depend upon the form or formless realms— may you please expound such a supreme and wondrous Dharma.

"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard his elder brother Vinīta recite these verses, the youth Vinīta then offered a pair of new and exquisite jeweled sandals to the Tathāgata Jina-abhyudgata, and spoke this gāthā before the Buddha:
‘May I become for all living beings A savior, a refuge, and a shelter;’"
Never again shall they tread upon the crooked paths, but always guide the deluded multitudes by preaching the true way.
May they never practice any forms of greed and desire, which are the conduct of the foolish;
may they forever remain detached from all conditioned phenomena and always encounter the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
Having encountered the one who illuminates the world, you should immediately make offerings to the Honored One among two-legged beings;
strive diligently for unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment for the sake of benefiting all living beings.
With immeasurable incense, flowers, and garlands, And sublime banners, pennants, and various jeweled canopies,
I offer these to the Great Dragon among dragons, For the sake of benefiting all living beings.
Furthermore, with various kinds of superior robes, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal herbs,
they all brought these as offerings to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for the sake of benefiting all living beings.
Beating large and small drums and blowing conch shells, as well as performing on flutes and pipes with pure songs—
all these are offered together to the World-Honored One for the benefit of all living beings.
Various flavors, most rich and intense, The subtle and exquisite things prized by the world—
I offer them all together to the World-Savior, For the sake of benefiting all living beings.
Having extensively performed such offerings and benefited immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings,
I then went forth into homelessness and diligently cultivated the holy life with vigor.
May I abide in these eight sublime paths, and further establish immeasurable billions of sentient beings;
may I be a refuge for all who possess consciousness, and never tread upon the crooked and deviant ways.
The multitude of noble ones censure and revile that which is most base and inferior—namely, sensual desire—which I am able to abandon;
furthermore, I shall cast off all forms of heedlessness and constantly practice and train in heedfulness.
May I never encounter any obstacles, And always be born into families of pure faith;
In every life, may I behold the Honored One among Men, And upon seeing him, may I give rise to deep faith in the Buddha.

Having already given rise to faith, they practice reverence; having made offerings with exquisite flower garlands, ointments, and various kinds of music, they do so in pursuit of the profound wisdom of all Buddhas.
Thus extensively performing various offerings for immeasurable koṭis of kalpas,
he forever severed the dharmas of desire, left his home, and diligently cultivated pure conduct.

“Śāriputra! At that time, after the youth Vinayadhara had spoken these verses, he established a bodhimanda for the Tathāgata Suprabha, whom he had praised, using red sandalwood. It was four yojanas in height, adorned with exquisite flowers, and its length and breadth were magnificently decorated with every kind of refined beauty.”

At that time, having established the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and completed its adornment, the youth offered it to that Buddha, the World-Honored One, and further spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“The four kinds of abidings in which the Buddhas dwell, Praised by the Most Victorious Ones of the past— I now joyfully seek such abidings;
I only pray that the Sugata will compassionately grant his permission.”
If there are those who dwell securely in this dwelling, Whose minds always understand immeasurable beings,
And who know births in the past and future— I now joyfully seek such a dwelling.
If one abides in this dwelling until reaching the ultimate, The four bases of power, the four foundations of mindfulness,
And the four supreme, unimpeded analytical knowledges— Such a dwelling is what I now joyfully seek.

"Śāriputra! At that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Jina-saṃdarśana-rāja, out of compassion for this youth, accepted the supreme and excellent site of enlightenment he had offered, and together with the community of bhikṣus, entered and resided therein."

At that time, having witnessed the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus receiving his offerings, the youth was filled with immense joy and leaped for boundless delight. He further made offerings with various kinds of exquisite requisites, redoubling his reverence, respect, and praise without ceasing for the duration of half a month.

After this, he shaved off his beard and hair before the Buddha, donned the kashaya robes, and with pure faith abandoned the life of a householder to go forth into homelessness, applying himself with single-minded diligence to seek all wholesome dharmas.
"Śāriputra! At that time, having sought the sublime Dharma, the two youths attained correct understanding in their minds and together made a great vow for the Buddha’s bodhi.
Their elder brother, Vinaya, made this solemn vow:”
"May I be the very first to attain equal and perfect enlightenment; that Buddha shall be named 'World-Reliance Emitting Great Radiance' (Lokanātha-prabhāsa-mahāraśmi).
His younger brother, who abided in the precepts, further made this vow:

"May I be the very first to attain equal and perfect enlightenment; that Buddha shall be named 'Great Guide, Caravan Leader, Honored One among Gods and Humans' (Mahānāyaka-sārthavāha-devamanuṣya-guru)."

"Śāriputra! At that time, after the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kṣāntivādī had made this vow, he stood before the Tathāgata Jina-pratyakṣa with palms joined, adorned by his great resolve, and spoke these verses:
'I shall no longer sit down again, Nor shall I ever lie down to sleep with my body relaxed.'
I shall single-mindedly and diligently seek the path to enlightenment for the sake of benefiting all living beings.
I shall disregard both body and life, constantly casting off sloth and exerting diligent effort;
I shall resolve to seek the supreme and wondrous path of enlightenment for the sake of benefiting all living beings.
Even if my flesh and blood should completely dry up, and my skin, bones, sinews, and veins all wither away,
I shall renounce indolence as well as body and life, applying myself with diligent effort to attain supreme enlightenment.

"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard his elder brother, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vinīta-kumāra, utter this vow, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vinīta-vihārin was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He then spoke these verses before him:
'Now we shall together pledge our harmony and friendship, And practice the conduct of unsurpassed bodhi.'"
I shall arouse the most supreme diligence and vigor for the sake of benefiting all living beings.
Now I will sustain my body and life with but little care;
even as my flesh and blood wither away, I will exert a thousandfold vigor to follow my elder brother’s example, seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
I shall dwell alone in secluded places, Exerting diligent effort amidst mountains, wilds, and forests;
Constantly seeking the subtle, wondrous, and most supreme wisdom, I shall abide wherever I am, as an adornment of the Great Dharma King.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"In the past, during the Dharma of the Tathāgata King of Supreme Manifestation, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vinayadhara and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vinayasthita made great, far-reaching vows before that Buddha. Because they were practicing the pāramitā of vīrya (diligence), they cultivated the right path with tireless and earnest application."
