Śāriputra! When those two bodhisattvas practiced diligence, throughout a thousand years they were never for even as long as a finger-snap seized by sleep.
During those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of wishing to lie down to rest his mind;
during those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of wishing to sit at ease;
during those thousand years, he never once bent his body to squat, except when attending to the calls of nature or when eating and drinking, at which times he would simply remain standing.
During those thousand years, he never ate a second time; he took but one meal per day, consisting of but a single morsel, and drank but a single vessel of water.

Throughout the thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of delighting in food, nor did any such thought as "I am now extremely hungry and thirsty; may I quickly obtain [food]" ever arise within him from the very beginning.
During those thousand years, he never once consumed food or drink in excess.

Throughout that millennium, he never gave rise to the thought of weighing or evaluating his food and drink; whether it was salty or bland, sweet or bitter, pungent, sour, delicious, or unpalatable, he never entertained such considerations from the very beginning.
During those thousand years, whenever he went for alms, he maintained single-minded right mindfulness and never looked at the face of the person giving him food, nor did he give rise to the thought:
"Who is giving me this food?"
"Is he a man? Is she a woman? Thus they did not even look upon the boys or the girls.
For a thousand years he dwelt beneath a tree, never once looking up to observe the appearance of the tree.
During those thousand years, the garments he wore were never changed even once.
During those thousand years, he never for a single moment gave rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of harm.
During those thousand years, he never once gave rise to thoughts directed toward relatives—whether father, mother, brothers, sisters, or other kinsmen—and he did not dwell upon them at all.
During those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of longing for his home or conceived any discursive thoughts regarding it.
During those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of looking up at the sky to gaze upon the sun, moon, stars, constellations, clouds, or mists.
During those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of leaning his body against a wall or a tree;
during those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of anointing his limbs with various kinds of ghee or oil.
During those thousand years, he never once gave rise to a thought of physical or mental alarm or fear;
during those thousand years, he never once gave rise to a thought of physical or mental fatigue;
and during those thousand years, he never once gave rise to a thought of indolence, laziness, or heedlessness.
He gave rise to this thought alone:
"I am now practicing for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; when shall I realize it?
When shall I attain it?"
During those thousand years, he never once experienced physical or mental pain or distress.

Throughout that millennium, he never even entertained the thought of wishing to shave his hair, except when the Four Great Heavenly Kings came to his head and, by means of their supernatural power, stroked it with their hands and took it away to erect a stūpa in their celestial palaces, adorning it with various jewels as an offering.
During those thousand years, although the celestial kings came and went, his mind was entirely devoid of any thought of coming or going.
Throughout that millennium, he never once gave rise to the thought of moving from a place of shadow to a place of light, or from a place of heat to a place of coolness.
During those thousand years, even in times of severe cold, he never once gave rise to the thought of covering himself with thick, warm clothing to seek physical comfort.
During those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the thought of engaging in worldly talk that is devoid of benefit.

"Śāriputra! These two bodhisattvas practiced such firm and diligent perseverance for a thousand years. At that time, there was an evil Māra named Mūḍhacintin, just as there is now an evil Māra-rāja named Mūḍhacintin who has appeared in the world."
Śāriputra! At that time, because the evil Māra was intent on causing ruin and disorder, he spread sharp blades upward across the entire path traversed by the Bodhisattva Vinayavīra.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vinaya, having slightly lost his original resolve on that path of blades, conceived the thought of sharp-edged weapons; as soon as this thought arose, he immediately felt remorse and raised a great voice, crying out once more:
"Alas, how strange! How is it that I now dwell in negligence?"

"Śāriputra! At that time, the sound uttered by that bodhisattva resounded throughout the trichiliocosm. In the sky above, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of celestial Māra followers, hearing this bodhisattva’s voice of mindfulness, simultaneously spoke to the bodhisattva, saying:
'This voice of yours which now proclaims everywhere is most excellent in its teaching; it is most excellent in its teaching.'"

"Śāriputra! Such celestial sounds are heard only by those who abide in the code of discipline (vinaya). Those who abide in the code of discipline do not hear these celestial sounds, nor do they hear this great sound of the Bodhisattva’s universal proclamation at the outset."

At that time, having heard the words of the deva, the Bodhisattva Vinaya exerted firm and great vigor, wishing to proceed again with his walking meditation, and once more turned his mind away from the blade.

Śāriputra! At that time, having subdued the Māra-enemies, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in such majestic deportment, practice such sublime conduct, cultivate such tracks of the Path, give rise to such great compassion, and exert such courageous diligence, never ceasing or abandoning them.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Because those two great beings practiced the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) within that Dharma, they both accomplished this majestic conduct, track, and courageous great compassion; moreover, for a thousand years, they dwelt in forest retreats cultivating the recollection of the Buddha."
After this had passed, the Tathāgata Śreṇikarāja was finally about to enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the devas came and addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"Do you not know? The Tathāgata has now entered parinirvāṇa.
When the two great beings heard this announcement from the deva, they immediately went to the site of the forest where the Tathāgata Śrīdarśanarāja had entered nirvāṇa.
Having arrived there, he stood with palms joined, gazing up at the Tathāgata without ever averting his eyes; filled with profound longing and deep reverence, he thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata who has appeared in the world is one of great compassion, who protects all sentient beings as if they were his own home."
"How can you so suddenly enter parinirvāṇa, leaving us without refuge or protection?

Śāriputra, these two great beings stood before the Tathāgata with deep longing and veneration; for seven days and seven nights they did not move from their place, and overcome by unbearable grief, they passed away and were reborn in the Brahma world.

Having received the body of a Brahmā and attained the power of recollecting past lives, he descended from above by means of great supernormal powers to the assembly at the site of his parinirvāṇa. For the sake of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śreṇya-abhyudgata-rāja, he erected a stūpa for all his relics, adorned with the most exquisite jewels and worldly ornaments. It took forty thousand years to complete, and upon it were placed various wheels and parasols.

"Śāriputra! At that time, after the two bodhisattvas had erected a stūpa for that Tathāgata, their hearts were filled with great joy; they stood with palms joined, gazing upon his marks of merit with redoubled celebration."

In this manner, after another seventy thousand years had passed, they finally paid their respects; thereupon they passed away and were both reborn in the womb of the Queen Mother within the family of a great universal monarch (cakravartin) on Jambudvīpa.
Śāriputra! Having been born, he immediately recalled all the events of his past lives and spoke these words:
"I shall now abide in the supreme and foremost dharma of heedfulness."
He further admonished himself with these verses:
"Born now in the house of a universal monarch, With vast wealth and food all at my disposal as I wish,
I must renounce this extreme indulgence And strive diligently for the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha."
Wealth, treasures, sensual desires, and royal power—impermanence sweeps them away in a mere instant;
the wise find no delight therein, but diligently seek the supreme and wondrous enlightenment of the Buddha.
If you do not take pleasure in wealth and treasures, but seek to realize bodhi for the benefit of all sentient beings,
you should swiftly abandon desire and seek to go forth from the household life, practicing the supreme and wondrous pure conduct.
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I was addicted to the five desires, regarding them as meritorious deeds;
whether born among the gods or among humans, I never once felt weary of or detached from them.
Therefore, one should renounce desire and royal sovereignty, parents, kinsmen, and all wealth and treasures;
having abandoned the kingdom, cities, and great armies, one should leave the household life and diligently seek to realize awakening.

“Śāriputra! At that time, the physical appearance of that bodhisattva was as upright and handsome as that of a sixteen-year-old youth. Taking no pleasure in the worldly net and constantly contemplating its faults and perils, he immediately shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and with pure faith abandoned the household life for the homeless state, diligently practicing the holy life for twenty thousand years.”
After his life there had ended, he was reborn in the Brahma world; when his lifespan there was exhausted, he returned to be born in Jambudvīpa. Śāriputra!

At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world in Jambudvīpa, named Sugandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At that time, having encountered the Buddha, that bodhisattva immediately shaved off his hair and beard within the Dharma and donned the saffron robes; with pure faith, he renounced the life of a householder to enter the homeless life, practicing the holy life for a full hundred million years.

In this manner, ten thousand Tathāgatas appeared in succession in the world, all of whom the Bodhisattva Vinaya encountered; in the presence of these Buddhas, he planted many roots of virtue and constantly practiced the holy life with diligent vigor.

That Bodhisattva Viniyamasthita always lived in the same place as his elder brother, practicing the various noble paths; he was the only one among them who did not practice the holy life under a single Buddha. For this reason, the Bodhisattva Viniyamasthita first attained Buddhahood and appeared in the world, named Tīvravīrya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavat.
He remained in the world to teach and transform for ninety *koṭi* years, and a great assembly of ninety *nayuta* śrāvakas gathered together to hear him preach the Dharma. Śāriputra!

When the Tathāgata Jvalanatejas appeared in the world, that Bodhisattva Viniyata was a universal monarch (cakravartin) whose majesty extended over the four quarters. Empowered by his merit, he conceived profound faith in the Tathāgata Jvalanatejas and, with various excellent garments, delicacies, food and drink, medicinal requisites for illness, and diverse household articles, he made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise to the Buddha, as well as to the community of bhikṣus, for a period of three months.

Śāriputra! At that time, although the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jvalantavīrya received such offerings, in order to awaken that wheel-turning king and cause him to remember [his past vows], he spoke these verses:
“If one wishes to realize all the Buddha-dharmas, Vigorous and courageous diligence is supreme.”
Sentient beings who are greedily attached to the five desires find it difficult to achieve whatever they seek.
If one seeks profit and benefit within the five desires, the wise should know that no such profit or benefit exists;
you now dwell in what is meaningless, and thus cannot obtain the supreme benefit.
In the past, I was your brother; together we made a great vow to attain Bodhi.
At that time, we vied with one another in uttering words of sincerity, asking: "Who shall first and most swiftly achieve Perfect Enlightenment?"
Now you see me realize enlightenment and turn the supreme Brahma-wheel before the great assembly,
yet you still wallow in the house of the five desires, constantly guarding your lustful indulgence in female beauty.
The Buddhas of the past have always proclaimed: "The wise should not cling to base desires.
Therefore, I have constantly and diligently distanced myself from them, never seeking after them or acting with negligence.
You embrace unwholesome wisdom and act without purpose; you constantly abide in meaningless deeds.
Your desire for dharmas leads to suffering and long-lasting delusion; freedom from desire is purity, praised by the Noble Ones.

"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard the verses spoken by the Tathāgata Dīptavīrya, the wheel-turning monarch attained great awakening, deeply perceived the faults of desire, and yearned for renunciation."

Ultimately, without taking leave of his wives, children, kinsmen, elders, ministers, or kings of high and low rank, and without looking back with longing at his kingdom, cities, people, wealth, or treasuries, he rose from his seat and went before the Tathāgata. With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms and spoke these verses:
“I shall completely renounce my home and kingdom, Vowing to go to a secluded place until the end of my life;
I would rather let my flesh and blood wither away entirely For the sake of the causal conditions for the Buddha’s Bodhi.”
Furthermore, one should exert great and courageous diligence to benefit immeasurable sentient beings;
having renounced the ways of the household for the homeless life, one should dwell in the state of empty stillness and non-action.
They take no delight in the five desires to which they cling; these base and evil things deceive and delude those foolish men.
Because of me, they have sunk into the mire of desire, and thus they cover their faces as they follow behind.
All desires, wealth, treasures, and royal sovereignty— He renounced them all at once;
Then, within the holy teaching of the Tathāgata, He devoted himself exclusively to the diligent cultivation of the unsurpassed path.
Who is the wise one whom I should approach?
Who practices the study of the treasury of conditioned phenomena?
Having practiced with diligence, why do I not swiftly attain Buddhahood instead of lingering in various desires?
Therefore, I have renounced all sensual pleasures, and have utterly severed my attachment to kingship and wealth;
I shall go forth from the home-life into the Buddha’s teaching for the sake of the causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood.

"Śāriputra! When the Wheel-Turning King had finished speaking these verses, he immediately shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saffron robes in the presence of the Buddha Jvalantavīrya. With pure faith, he renounced the life of a householder to enter the homeless path and went to a secluded place to diligently cultivate the holy life."

At that time, there were again sixty hundred thousand *koṭis* of sentient beings who, upon hearing that the wheel-turning monarch had left the household life to study the Way, likewise conceived pure faith, cast off their worldly appearances, and followed the king forth from home to cultivate the various holy practices (*brahmacarya*).
"Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata Jvalanavīrya remained in the world to transform sentient beings for a long duration before finally entering parinirvāṇa.

When the bhikṣu Cakravartin saw that the Buddha had passed away, he was overwhelmed with grief and sorrow. He received the Tathāgata’s remains and śarīras, erected a stūpa, and made offerings to it with elaborate adornments."
Not long thereafter, he passed away and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
When his celestial retribution was exhausted, he returned to be born in Jambudvīpa.

Within that very kalpa, he attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), becoming known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Subhūti.

That Buddha remained in the world for a full *koṭi* of years, and his assembly of *śrāvaka* disciples numbered in the hundreds of billions (*koṭi-nayuta*). They were all great *arhats*, whose outflows (*āsrava*) had been exhausted, and who had attained mastery over all their minds, having reached the ultimate, foremost shore.

The Tathāgata Subhacaryā abides with hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them never again to regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, while also proclaiming the sublime Dharma for immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
Having performed what was to be done, he will enter parinirvāṇa.

His True Dharma shall remain in the world for the remainder of one kalpa, and his relics shall be disseminated to benefit sentient beings, no different from the widespread distribution of my own relics after my parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the pāramitā of vīrya (diligence), they abide in right effort while practicing the bodhisattva path; they should follow and train in the pāramitā of courageous, tireless diligence according to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in ethical discipline, and they should not rely upon those stingy beings who dwell among skeletons of dry bones to train."
Śāriputra! If there are bodhisattvas who joyfully seek awakening, they should not give rise to stinginess regarding the households of others.
Furthermore, if they should lose mindfulness and give rise to stinginess, they should joyfully observe three kinds of fear.
What are the three? They are:
frequently visiting other families, whether for the purpose of begging for alms or for conversation; becoming entangled in these interactions without ceasing, and thereby forming close personal ties.

Seeing that second virtuous bhikṣu, he gave rise to stinginess and jealousy due to his attachment; at times, he even briefly conceived a thought of malice and failed to act in accordance with him. By reason of these conditions, you should know that he has taken up the karmic paths of the various sufferings of hell; you should know that he has sown the seeds of being born blind in the field of his own mind; and you should know that he has fully taken up the karma for being born in a borderland.
Śāriputra! I shall now further explain their characteristics for you.

It is when those bodhisattvas, upon seeing virtuous and pure bhikṣus come to their presence, immediately give rise to thoughts of envy and malice; though harboring internal resentment and knots of anger, they outwardly manifest purity. When engaging in conversation with them, their minds are stingy and parsimonious, yet they constantly provide material offerings according to circumstances. Or, in private and secluded places, they glare at them with angry eyes, or they use false matters to slander and defame them.

Śāriputra! By these causes and conditions, you should know that such a bodhisattva has taken up the karmic path of the hells; the seed of congenital blindness has been planted within his heart. Although he is born into the human realm, he remains in a remote borderland, encounters various forms of suffering, and undergoes the retribution of being blind from birth. He is frequently subjected to slander and is made a servant by others, laboring day and night without a moment’s rest.
“Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas should give rise to stinginess or envy toward the households of others, they should contemplate these three kinds of fear.
When the Tathāgata had spoken these words, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Most marvelous, World-Honored One!
It is unprecedented.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare indeed, for they have been able to encounter the Tathāgata’s teaching of this Dharma that is the essential method for transcending stinginess regarding one's home.”
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain for us, the assembly of śrāvakas, the essential points of the True Dharma regarding the characteristics of abandoning attachment to the household life. Why is this?

Within the Buddha-dharma, it is not that we do not wish to be liberated from the retributions of hell, birth-blindness, and the borderlands of slander; rather, we constantly aspire to be born in the human realm of the Central Land.

"We, the śrāvakas, deeply desire to hear the Dharma on being free from the stinginess of the household life; we only pray that the World-Honored One will set aside his causeless resentment and not abandon us, but will surely proclaim it for our sake."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!”
This is most rare!
That you are able to dwell without vanity or flattery and inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning—
listen attentively, listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you.
Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who wish to follow the Tathāgata and study the Buddha-dharma, I shall explain it to them as is appropriate. Why is this?
Because all sentient beings are able to follow and learn from the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not oppose their intentions, but necessarily manifests before them to preach the Dharma for them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are sentient beings who do not delight in following the Buddha to cultivate and study the True Dharma, and one were to preach it to them, such persons, having heard it, would establish the very root of contention.

Śāriputra! Thus, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has accomplished pure faith practices the pāramitā of vīrya, they generate vast pure faith in all the Buddha-dharmas. Throughout the long night of saṃsāra, they constantly delight in contemplation; and for the sake of rescuing sentient beings who are drowning, they go to the presence of the Tathāgata, earnestly and respectfully inquiring about the meaning of the teachings, and they delight in hearing whatever is expounded.
Having heard the Dharma, they further attained vast and pure deep faith; with joyful exultation, they redoubled their diligence, upholding the True Dharma and practicing according to its teachings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In future ages, among my disciples, there will be few bhikṣus who, with a profound mind, aspire to the dharma of the peace and stillness of parinirvāṇa; rather, most will take three matters as their constant practice.
What are these three?

First, constantly delighting in the pursuit of worldly fame and profit; second, greedily enjoying the company of factions and pursuing constant social visits with families for meals; third, delighting in the pursuit of decorating rooms with flowers and accumulating wealth, provisions, and material requisites.
This is called relying upon and pursuing three matters. Śāriputra!
Because these bhikṣus rely upon these three kinds of matters, they will ultimately not be liberated from the three evil destinies.

Śāriputra! Such bhikṣus do not delight in liberation from the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or asuras; instead, they take pleasure in diligently cultivating the path and dharmas that lead to the exhaustion [of existence]. Furthermore, they constantly and diligently engage in matters of physical appearance, speech, quarreling, litigation, sarcasm, slander, and contentious debate. Moreover, they delight in associating with evil friends who possess impure faith in their hearts; they abandon empty, quiet forests to dwell among villages, taking laypeople and householders as their companions and supporters.
Śāriputra! Those householders speak thus:

"This venerable one comes to my house often and shares my interests; I shall provide for him by giving him robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines for the treatment of illness, and all other necessary requisites."
"Since those elders who dwell in secluded retreats have never before had any social interaction with laypeople, how can we engage them in conversation?
For this reason, these bhikṣus became increasingly intimate with householders, and they conversed with one another only about worldly affairs, trivial matters, and idle chatter.

Śāriputra! These wicked bhikṣus delight in dwelling and traveling together with those who are unwholesome; they remain long in their residences without ever moving on, frequently seeking out factions and families that provide food, repeatedly visiting them to personally offer congratulations or condolences, and because of these matters, they harbor secret feelings of intimacy and affection.
When visiting bhikṣus arrive, they receive no hospitality at all; instead, [the resident bhikṣus] first utter disparaging and unrighteous words.
Yet these visiting bhikṣus are actually noble and holy, and those evil bhikṣus do not even say of them:
"You are learned, possessed of the precepts, and pure."
"You are a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or one who has attained the fruit of arhatship"—
such words as these were not mentioned at all. Śāriputra!
"Śāriputra, these evil bhikṣus do not cultivate my Dharma within my teaching; they have no other concern but to take pleasure in ceaselessly slandering and reviling."
Those laypeople who formed factions further spoke thus:

"The visiting bhikṣus have never lived with us for long, nor have they associated with us or traveled with us; however, the resident bhikṣus have lived among us for a long time, and we have entrusted our affairs to them, relying on them to deliver messages and manage our various business matters."
"For this reason, I shall protect and cherish the resident bhikṣus and provide them with a semblance of authority.
Śāriputra, for these reasons,
whether they understand this sūtra or not, all those wicked bhikṣus will at all times slander, revile, and refuse to believe it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are those who hear the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata and constantly delight in hearing such diverse dharma-gates of words and phrases, and upon hearing them, believe and understand them without doubt or hesitation, they will surely be able to abandon such sentient beings and relinquish the karma that leads to rebirth in the evil destinies.

In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices with tireless diligence, having heard of such signs as stinginess and envy that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies, will not personally engage in acts of domestic stinginess and the like; how much less would he teach such a dharma to others?
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s diligent and tireless cultivation of the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
One should train in this way.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Forty-Seven;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Forty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka Section, Chapter Twelve: The Ninth Part of the Vīrya-pāramitā Section, Part Four.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) with diligent effort and without weariness, they conceive of all sentient beings as being like those who are ill."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are constantly ill, perpetually scorched and tormented by the three kinds of feverish afflictions. Śāriputra!
What are called the three kinds of feverish affliction?
They are the feverish affliction of desire, the feverish affliction of hatred, and the feverish affliction of delusion.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"We should now apply this unsurpassed, true Dharma *agada* ointment to these sentient beings who are afflicted by such feverish distress. Why is this?..."

Because this supreme, true Dharma—this cooling and subtle medicinal ointment—is applied as an anointing, all the diseases of feverish affliction, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, of all sentient beings are entirely eliminated.

"Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas apply this excellent medicinal drug of the True Dharma to sentient beings to extinguish the three poisons, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) with untiring and correct diligence."
One should train in this way. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the characteristics of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) are immeasurable.
I shall now speak.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects in this way:
"It is said that all sentient beings are ill. Why is this?
Because they are constantly afflicted by the feverish distress of the three poisons."
If there are sentient beings born in the hells, they too are tormented by such greed, hatred, and delusion.
Likewise, among those born as animals, in the realm of Yama, among humans, or in the heavens—all sentient beings therein are without exception tormented by these three poisons.
"If there are sentient beings who have formed doubts, wrong views, and other such afflictions, they too are constantly tormented by greed, hatred, and delusion.
Thus spoke Śāriputra.

These sentient beings are afflicted by the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*); no other skilled physician nor any superior, wondrous medicine—whether applied as an ointment or a plaster—can cause the feverish distress of greed, hatred, and delusion to subside. Only the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed and supreme Great Dharma-Physician King, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have realized the Dharma-body and, through the power of their great vows, have adorned and sustained their own bodies as the excellent medicine, are able to eliminate all the diseases of feverish distress, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, in all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, you should understand this Dharma gate:

namely, that the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion of all sentient beings cannot be cured by any other medicine; they can only be eliminated by the unsurpassed King of Physicians, the Tathāgata, and by Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body through the power of their great vows."
"Śāriputra! What do you think? Which is more numerous:
the realm of sentient beings or the realms of earth and so forth?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the sublime meaning spoken by the Buddha, the realm of sentient beings is vast; it cannot be compared to the earth element, nor can it be compared to the water, fire, or wind elements.”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
It is just as you have said."
The realm of sentient beings is vast; it is not the realm of the great earth.
And so on, up to: the realm of sentient beings is vast; it is not that realm of wind. Śāriputra!
I shall now further explain such signs. Śāriputra!

There are sentient beings whose physical forms are so subtle that they are difficult to perceive; they are beyond the reach of the eyes of the various seers outside the Buddha-dharma, nor do they fall within the range of the divine eye of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they can only be clearly perceived by the pure divine eye of the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra! With his pure divine eye, the Tathāgata clearly perceives as far as the distance of a chariot wheel.
There are immeasurable numbers of subtle sentient beings, more numerous than those born among the realms of humans and devas within a trichiliocosm.

Śāriputra! Thus, throughout this immeasurable and boundless realm of sentient beings—even all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, whether born from eggs, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient; whether visible or invisible—and indeed, throughout the entire realm of sentient beings established by conventional designations, should they all, in a single kṣaṇa, or a single lava, or a single muhūrta, simultaneously and without succession attain human bodies.

Those people all became excellent physicians; with a lifespan of one kalpa, they were thoroughly proficient in medical arts, well-versed in the path of healing, and served as great masters of medicine, skillfully treating all manner of ailments just like the present-day King of Physicians, Jīvaka.
"Śāriputra! Those physicians gathered together and deliberated, saying:
'There is a sentient being who harbors the disease of the feverish affliction of greed, hatred, and delusion; as we are physicians, we shall apply diligent effort to eliminate it.'"
"In this way, Śāriputra!

Suppose each and every one of those physicians were to hold a sublime, cooling medicine, as high and vast in measure as Sumeru, the king of mountains, and furthermore, were to apply diligent effort with the intent to extinguish the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion within a single sentient being."
Furthermore, suppose those physicians were to grind this mountain king of cooling medicinal ingredients into powder and, throughout the duration of an entire eon, apply it to a single sentient being;

even if all the kings of physicians exhausted their skills and arts until they were utterly weary, and even if they used up the entire mountain king of medicinal ingredients as powder to apply to them, they would still be unable to extinguish the afflictions and feverish diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion within that single sentient being.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world, they see that sentient beings are afflicted by the disease of the defilements.

The Tathāgata teaches only this single, unsurpassed, true Dharma—the *agada* medicinal ointment of the contemplation of impurity—to be applied as a salve; thereby, the feverish afflictions of desire of immeasurable sentient beings are all extinguished without exception.

In this way, by hearing even a single instance of the contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), the feverish affliction of desire is simultaneously stilled for immeasurable hundreds of beings, immeasurable thousands of beings, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings, immeasurable *koṭi* of beings, immeasurable hundreds of *koṭi*, immeasurable thousands of *koṭi*, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭi* of beings, immeasurable *koṭī-nayuta* of beings, immeasurable hundreds of *koṭī-nayuta*, immeasurable thousands of *koṭī-nayuta*, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭī-nayuta* beings; likewise for immeasurable *gaṅgā-kalā* of beings, immeasurable *vibhara* of beings, and so on, up to immeasurable unspeakably unspeakable numbers of beings.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata teaches only this single supreme, right Dharma—the cooling, wondrous medicine of the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion—which, when applied as an ointment, causes the heat and affliction of hatred in immeasurable sentient beings to be entirely extinguished.
Even for unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings, the elimination of their malice is likewise so. Śāriputra,

the Tathāgata teaches but a single causal contemplation— the supreme, right Dharma, a sublime and cooling medicine— and by applying it as an ointment, the ignorant delusions and burning afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings are all brought to rest.
Even unto unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings, the cessation of their ignorance is likewise so.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have realized the Dharma-body also adorn and sustain their own bodies through great vows as a sublime medicine for the Dharma; they are well able to extinguish the feverish afflictions of the three poisons of immeasurable sentient beings, even unto extinguishing the various afflictions and fevers of greed, hatred, and delusion of unspeakably unspeakable, immeasurable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

As I have previously taught, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has realized and attained the Dharma-body maintains a body through the power of his vows as a supreme medicine, used to extinguish the feverish diseases of affliction of immeasurable, ineffable sentient beings."
Regarding such signs as these, I shall now speak further; you should listen attentively. Śāriputra!

I recall that in the past, beyond incalculable kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara conferred upon me the prediction of enlightenment, speaking these words: 'O Māṇava!'"
In a future age, after incalculable eons have passed, you shall attain buddhahood, known by the name Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to Buddha, Bhagavān.
"Śāriputra! After that Buddha Dīpaṃkara had bestowed this prediction upon me, I immediately realized the attainment of the Dharmakāya.

Following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I became Śakra, named Subhūṣita, among the Trāyastriṃśa devas; there I attained great mastery, possessed great supernormal powers, exercised great majestic virtue, and my lineage flourished."

Śāriputra! At that time, in Jambudvīpa there were eighty-four thousand great cities, with immeasurable thousands of villages, towns, settlements, and marketplaces; furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of all sentient beings dwelt in such places, where people and things were so densely crowded that it was exceedingly prosperous.

Śāriputra! At that time, a great intermediate kalpa of pestilence will appear, and many sentient beings will encounter severe illnesses: their bodies will become putrid and ulcerated; they will suffer from carbuncles, boils, pustules, scabies, and malignant sores; and their bodily humors—wind, heat, and phlegm—will fall into mutual conflict.
In short, every form of illness and suffering gathered there without exception.

At that time, there were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of physicians and pharmacists who, desiring to cure such illnesses and sufferings, applied themselves with diligent effort until they reached the limit of exhaustion; yet, the diseases of the multitude remained incurable.

"Śāriputra! Those immeasurable sentient beings suffering from illness, having failed to encounter a skilled physician, are oppressed by their ailments; lacking protection and lacking a refuge, they all together lament, wailing aloud with tears streaming down, speaking thus:
'We now endure this immeasurable, grievous sickness.'"
Where could there be gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or rākṣasas—humans or non-humans—who, out of great compassion, would be able to see me and remove my illness?

"If there be anyone who can eliminate the suffering of my illness, I shall not begrudge any of my wealth or treasures in generously repaying their kindness, and I shall follow whatever instructions they give. Śāriputra!

At that time, with the pure divine eye that surpasses that of humans, I saw various sentient beings whose bodies were oppressed by manifold epidemics; they were entangled in distress and resentment, with no one to provide them relief.

Furthermore, with his divine ear, purified and surpassing that of humans, he heard the voices of sentient beings crying out in lamentation—voices of extreme sorrow, resentment, and bitterness, so painful as to be almost unbearable to hear. Śāriputra!
At that time, having seen and heard this, I gave rise to profound great compassion for these sentient beings and immediately thought:
"How bitter is their suffering!

Thus, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings have encountered this grave illness; they have no shelter and no home, no rescue and no protection, no refuge to turn to, and no one able to heal them."

I now resolutely act as a shelter and a dwelling for all sentient beings; as a savior and a protector; as a place of refuge; and as a physician, ensuring that their illnesses and afflictions are entirely healed and restored.

"Śāriputra! At that time, I then concealed my vast and lofty form as Śakra and, not far from the great city of Kurujāṅgala in Jambudvīpa, underwent transformational birth as a great being named Soma."
Having taken birth, he remained in mid-air and addressed all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa with a verse, saying:
"The great city of Kuru is not far away; there dwells one of great stature named Soma.
If any sentient being eats his flesh, all their ailments and afflictions shall be completely cured."
Free from anger, resentment, and malice, he has appeared as a healing medicine for Jambudvīpa;
you should rejoice and not be startled or doubtful, cutting off your flesh at will to dispel the afflictions of the multitude.

"Śāriputra! At that time, all the cities, eighty-four thousand villages, and market towns within Jambudvīpa, as well as immeasurable thousands of all sentient beings afflicted by illness, having heard this sound, went simultaneously to the great city of Kuru to the place where the Bodhisattva Suma’s great body lay, vying with one another to cut or slice off pieces of his flesh with sharp knives."
"Śāriputra! When the Bodhisattva Soma was practicing the conduct of diligence, as he was being cut, a great sound issued from within his body, and he spoke these verses:
'If this [practice] can truly realize awakening, And if the treasury of wisdom shall become inexhaustible, then by this truth, may my limbs be restored.'"
"By the power of my truthful and sincere words, may my body and flesh likewise never be exhausted.
Śāriputra, at that time, because all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa were oppressed by illness, they cut the Bodhisattva’s body into pieces, either carrying them away or consuming them on the spot.
Although he was subjected to such harm, by the power of his vow, his flesh grew back as it was cut away, leaving no deficiency. Śāriputra!
Once these sentient beings had eaten the flesh of the Bodhisattva Soma, all their illnesses were completely eliminated.
Once their illnesses have been cured, they further cause the minds of sentient beings to attain peace and happiness, with no change in their physical forms.
These sentient beings, with both body and mind at ease, spread the news from one to another until it reaches throughout Jambudvīpa.
After they had eaten the flesh, their illnesses were all cured without relapse, and their bodies and minds became peaceful and joyful. Śāriputra!

At that time, among all the people of Jambudvīpa—whether men or women, boys or girls—those who had their illnesses cured by eating the Bodhisattva’s flesh deeply felt his kindness and wisdom, and they vied with one another in reflecting upon it:
"This Soma has bestowed upon me most profound kindness; he has removed my suffering from illness and granted me peace and happiness that shall not change.
How should I provide offerings to repay such great bounty?"
Having formed this thought, they all gathered together and went to the place where the Bodhisattva Soma lay with his great body in the great city of Kuru.
Upon arriving there, they all surrounded him; overwhelmed by gratitude for his kindness, they could not contain themselves and spoke these verses:
“You are our home and our protection; You are our skilled physician and our wondrous medicine.”
"Only pray that you will take pity on us and grant us instruction: how should we practice our offerings?

"Śāriputra! At that time, for the sake of this great body, I rescued sentient beings from such suffering of illness. Knowing that these immeasurable sentient beings had taken my profound kindness to heart and sought refuge in me, I then extinguished the manifested Soma-great-body and resumed the form of Śakra, standing before the assembly. With majestic light shining brilliantly, I addressed them, saying:"
"You should know this: if you have been cured of your illness through the flesh of my body and you cherish this kindness and intend to repay it,
you should know that I originally did not practice giving my own flesh out of pity for your suffering on account of villages,
cities, hamlets, royal capitals, kingdoms, fields, houses, dwellings, or places of residence."
As for giving, I do not practice the gift of my own body and flesh for the sake of gold, silver, mani-jewels, lapis lazuli, pearls, conch shells, jade, coral, or other such treasures;
nor do I practice the gift of my own body and flesh for the sake of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, livestock, or herds;
nor do I practice it for the sake of women, men, boys, girls, slaves, or servants.
I do not practice the gift of my own flesh for the sake of delicacies, food and drink, clothing, bedding, or medicinal requisites for illness;

nor do I practice the gift of my own flesh for the sake of other provisions. I practice the gift of my own flesh out of compassion for your suffering from disease, not for the sake of gardens, groves, ponds, palaces, or towers.

"You ministers should know that the reason I previously took pity on you for your suffering from illness and gave the flesh of my own body as an offering was to cause sentient beings to abandon unwholesome karma.

You should simply be able, for my sake, to forever sever and forever leave behind the karma of killing; to forever sever and forever leave behind the karma of taking what is not given; and to forever sever and forever leave behind the karma of sexual misconduct. Likewise, you should forever sever and forever leave behind the karma of false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, as well as the karma of covetousness, malice, and all views of wrong attachment."
"For you to forever sever and abandon this is what constitutes true benefit and the repayment of gratitude. Śāriputra,
at that time, Śakra again spoke these verses for the great assembly:
“I do not seek a heap of precious jewels, vast and high as Mount Meru;
nor do I seek celestial jade maidens, nor the necessities of food, clothing, and bedding.”
Those who wish to uphold the Great Body of Soma should simply revere harmony and unity;
with mutual compassion and respectful regard, they should single-mindedly cultivate the ten pure and wondrous paths of action.
"You all should, regarding the ten paths of karmic action, always remain in harmony and maintain firm defense;
this is called the great offering of the Dharma, for Bodhisattvas do not seek worldly wealth."
I do not require the various worldly treasures, Fragrant delicacies, food and drink, or exquisite garments;
Nor elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, sheep, and the like, Nor couches, bedding, court ladies, or articles for daily life.
You all should simply remain united and in harmony, skillfully upholding the ten paths of pure action;
mutually inspiring great compassion, you should cultivate within yourselves the intent to benefit and bring peace to one another.

"Śāriputra! At that time, immeasurable people within Jambudvīpa, having heard me speak these words of exhortation, prostrated at my feet out of gratitude for my virtue and all undertook the ten kinds of pure and excellent paths of wholesome action."

"Śāriputra! At that time, I extensively proclaimed the True Dharma to that great assembly, instructing, teaching, encouraging, and gladdening them; I then concealed my celestial body and did not appear in the world."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
As I recall in times past, among all the people in Jambudvīpa who ate the flesh of the Bodhisattva Soma, not a single one has ever since fallen into the evil destinies.
After their lives there had ended, they were all reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; by the power of their past karma, they were born together with the precepts. Śāriputra!

At that time, I further expounded the Dharma for those devas according to their needs, instructing, teaching, exhorting, and gladdening them, causing them all to dwell securely in the vehicle of the śrāvaka, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, or to dwell in the vehicle of unsurpassed omniscience (anuttara-sarvajñatā-yāna).
Because these multitudes have heard my Dharma, some have already attained parinirvāṇa, some are currently attaining parinirvāṇa, and some will attain parinirvāṇa. Śāriputra!

Observe how these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, abiding thus in the Dharma-body and practicing the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), have achieved such great power of supernormal knowledges, such great power of majestic virtue, and such great power of influence that they are able, by the wisdom of relinquishing even a single body, to bring infinite sentient beings to full maturity, causing them all to abide in the Three Vehicles and attain the stage of non-retrogression.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), diligently cultivate and attain the characteristics of the dharma-body?"
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain this for us.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The mark of the Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is without birth and without death; it is firm and indestructible like a vajra, inconceivable.

Yet, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body manifest a decaying body in order to transform and deliver sentient beings whose bodies are subject to decay, and they manifest an indestructible body in order to transform those whose bodies are not subject to decay. Nevertheless, this Dharma-body is perfectly accomplished and complete; it cannot be burned by fire nor can it be cut by a blade, for it is as firm and indestructible as that vajra.”

Śāriputra! Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva established in the Dharma-body practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), their tireless diligence is effortless and requires no deliberate application. Merely by means of that body, they are able to bring immeasurable sentient beings to maturity, without relying on mental deliberation or discrimination. This Bodhisattva’s own body naturally knows and realizes that all bodily characteristics accord with and enter the *tathatā* (suchness) of its own true nature.
One's own suchness enters into the suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of all phenomena enters into one's own suchness.
One's own suchness enters into the suchness of all Buddhas, and the suchness of all Buddhas enters into one's own suchness.

The *tathatā* (suchness) of one's own self enters into the *tathatā* of the past, future, and present; the *tathatā* of the past, future, and present likewise enters into the *tathatā* of one's own self.
Furthermore, the *tathatā* of the past does not conflict with the *tathatā* of the future, nor does the *tathatā* of the future conflict with the *tathatā* of the past.
Furthermore, the suchness of the past does not contradict the suchness of the present, nor does the suchness of the present contradict the suchness of the past.
Moreover, the suchness of the future does not contradict the suchness of the past, nor does the suchness of the past contradict the suchness of the future.
Furthermore, future suchness does not contradict present suchness, nor does present suchness contradict future suchness.
Moreover, present suchness does not contradict past suchness, nor does past suchness contradict present suchness.
Furthermore, the suchness of the present does not contradict the suchness of the future, nor does the suchness of the future contradict the suchness of the present.

Moreover, the suchness of the past, future, and present is itself the suchness of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). Furthermore, the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases is itself the suchness of defilement and purification. Moreover, the suchness of defilement and purification is itself the suchness of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the suchness of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is itself the suchness of preparatory application (prayoga). Moreover, the suchness of preparatory application is itself the suchness of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are themselves suchness (*tathatā*), and this suchness is itself all conditioned phenomena.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is suchness is the nature of reality, it is the nature of thusness; it is not a non-thus-nature, it is a non-separating nature, it is a non-activating nature, it is a non-disturbing nature, it is a non-contradictory nature, and it is a non-contentious nature."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) is free from conflict; because it is free from conflict, it is named *tathatā*, yet the Tathāgatas speak of it by the name "conflict."
Śāriputra! True suchness (tathatā) is said to be "conformable inclusion.
For what reason and by what causal conditions does the Tathāgata speak of it as being "contentious"?
Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata is free from all contention, for this reason,
the Bodhisattva constantly manifests all forms of contentious opposition.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas are fundamentally free from conflict and have never given rise to it.
Why is this? Because being without conflict and without contention is what defines a Tathāgata; yet they constantly manifest various forms that appear to involve conflict and contention.

It is not only the Tathāgata who is subject to movement and disturbance; rather, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate the body of the Tathāgata with the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), they perceive the equality of the Dharma-nature within the Tathāgata’s body as the equality of the Dharma-nature within their own bodies. Furthermore, they observe the equality of the Dharma-nature within their own bodies as the equality of the Dharma-nature within the Tathāgata’s body. Moreover, within the equality of the Dharma-nature of their own bodies, they observe all bodies and non-bodies, and within all bodies and non-bodies, they observe that inconceivable body.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands all bodies within dependently arisen phenomena, and having so understood them, draws forth and gathers the dharma-body (dharmakāya), Śāriputra,
at the very moment a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws forth and gathers this dharma-body, I declare that they have realized the dharma-body.
Having attained such realization, one is further able to manifest the bodies of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; you should know that these bodies are manifested by the Dharma-body.

Therefore, Śāriputra, if any sentient beings encounter such a Dharma-body—whether seeing it or hearing it—they are all immediately tamed; and when they touch that body, it enables them to accomplish all manner of beneficial purposes.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Just as the great physician-king Jīvaka gathers various medicines and blends them into a physical form, transforming it into the image of a woman—elegant, beautiful, and of such pure complexion that it delights the beholder."
Because this King of Physicians is skilled at performing [these acts], he has perfectly accomplished and beautifully adorned them. Śāriputra,
although this image of the Medicine Woman is without thought or discrimination, she can manifest coming and going, staying and resting, whether sitting or lying down.
Whenever noble kings, princes, ministers, elders, or minor rulers suffer from illness, they go to the great physician-king Jīvaka.
At that time, the King of Physicians, observing those he was treating, bestowed the medicinal women upon them as consorts.

Once these people had received such a gift, they took hold of the medicinal women and briefly touched their bodies; immediately, all their ailments and sufferings were naturally eliminated, and they became healthy, peaceful, and free from any further change.

"Śāriputra! At that time, the great king of physicians, Bhaṣaja, possessed the wondrous wisdom that cures all the diseases of the world; among all other physicians in the world, there was none who could equal him."

In this way, Śāriputra, it is also thus for the bodhisattva mahāsattva manifested from the dharmakāya: even for all sentient beings—whether men, women, boys, or girls—who suffer from the feverish afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, if they come into the presence of the bodhisattva and briefly touch his body, all their painful illnesses will be extinguished, and they will further perceive their bodies freed from all such feverish afflictions.
Why is this? It is because the bodhisattva mahāsattvas have originally made great vows that are thoroughly purified.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Dharma-body Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not rely on the consumption of solid food for their bodies to remain sustained.

Although they thoroughly understand that all food and drink are fundamentally non-existent, they manifest the acceptance of food out of compassion for sentient beings; though they manifest the act of eating, their minds have no attachment, and they never harbor any lingering concern for their own bodies.
Why is this? Because the power of the Dharma-body neither recedes nor diminishes; it does not maintain the body through food and drink.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The Dharma-body Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are difficult to comprehend within the cycle of birth and death, yet they manifest having birth and death.
Why is this? Because they desire to bring sentient beings to maturity, they manifest an end; however, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas understand that all phenomena have no end.
He manifests birth, yet he understands that all phenomena are without arising or activity;
though he manifests birth, he understands that all phenomena are ultimately unborn.

Furthermore, this Dharma-body takes the Dharma as its sustenance and is sustained by the power of the Dharma; because it relies upon the power of the fundamental vows inherent in the Dharma, it matures sentient beings without any deliberate effort.

Śāriputra! These and other such characteristics of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body are all realized through the diligent practice of the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor) with tireless perseverance.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The body is like a vajra, indestructible; Knowing the proper time, he manifests birth through expedient transformation.
Poison, evil weapons, and fire cannot burn or harm him; Those who appear to be burned or harmed are the beings he transforms."
To those who are ill, it appears as a potent medicine; to hungry and thirsty sentient beings, it appears as food and drink.
Because the nature of all phenomena is non-discriminatory, one realizes the single principle that the Dharma-body is bodiless.
To understand that all phenomena arise from conditions— there being no such thing as a "manava" or a "mind-born"—
and that because of the presence of various conditions the web of suffering is set in motion, while because of the absence of various conditions the web of suffering is severed.
One should understand that form is as unsubstantial as a mass of foam; contemplate all feelings as being like bubbles on water;
perceive perceptions as flickering mirages in the heat; and one should examine volitional formations as being like the core of a plantain tree.
Just as a skilled worldly illusionist can manifest all manner of forms in an instant, so too should one understand the functioning of consciousness; the wise have no longing for them.
Knowing that worldly wealth is like an arrow released from a bowstring, Or like lightning flashing or a mountain torrent,
Gathering for a moment before dispersing like clouds in the sky— The wise have no desire for any of it.

Among all that exists, there are no sentient beings at all who have not failed to enjoy the various pleasures of the heavens, only to fall again into hell and suffer further poverty and misery; having observed this, the sons of the Buddha do not seek rebirth in the heavens.
That mind has no support, like one wandering in space; it is neither existent nor non-existent, free from dependence.
Though it arises within the various realms of existence, it is without birth-and-death, for it realizes the Great Self that is free from aging and death.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is untiring in vigor practices the pāramitā of vīrya, they should train with a rightly directed mind in this manner."
Śāriputra! Although there are physicians in the world who fill the universe, they are unable to comprehend the three great afflictions. Why is this?
Because they are all unwholesome and lack wisdom, they are unable to recognize the three great afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Śāriputra! Those ignorant physicians not only fail to recognize these three great afflictions, but they also do not understand the three great excellent medicines that serve as the remedies for those three afflictions.
What are these three? They are:
being unable to understand that sensual desire is a great affliction and that the medicine of impurity is its antidote;
and being unable to understand that ill will is a great affliction and that the medicine of loving-kindness is its antidote.
Ignorance is a great affliction, for which dependent origination serves as the excellent medicine of remedy.
Śāriputra, such physicians can only treat one or two specific ailments; they cannot universally cure all diseases.
"This can only provide temporary relief for a short time; it does not constitute the complete eradication of the disease or its ultimate cure.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
"Since I am now practicing the *vīryapāramitā* while cultivating the bodhisattva path, how could I ever follow and learn from such physicians?"
I shall follow the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have thoroughly mastered all dharmas as supreme great physicians; they ultimately heal and treat all who are ill.
These great physician-kings—I now follow, rely upon, and train under them.
Having already completed my training, I ought to universally treat all suffering from illness; how could I merely treat individual ailments one by one?
I ought to ultimately eliminate the root of all diseases; how could I merely provide temporary relief without removing the root of the disease?
"Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects:

'I should accumulate such unsurpassed, true Dharma as this Ajaṭa medicinal ointment, so that once all sentient beings have heard the sound of this medicine, their most grievous and great afflictions—greed, hatred, and delusion—will naturally be extinguished.'"

Therefore, Śāriputra, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices with untiring diligence cultivates the pāramitā of vigor (vīryapāramitā), he accumulates such unsurpassed, true Dharma as the medicinal ointment of the Ajaṭa, which he applies to all sentient beings who are afflicted by illness.

This is not shared with the dharmas of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, except for the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed King of Great Physicians who is thoroughly proficient in all dharmas; he takes the supreme, correct Dharma *ājñāta* ointment and anoints the great Dharma conch shell, and having thus anointed it, he proceeds to blow it.

That sound resounded throughout the trichiliocosm, and all the various sentient beings therein, upon hearing this sound, had all their great and heavy illnesses—namely greed, hatred, and delusion—completely eradicated.

In this way, they eliminate not merely one hundred beings, nor one thousand beings, nor one hundred thousand beings; in this way, they eliminate not merely one *koṭi* of beings, nor one hundred *koṭis*, nor one thousand *koṭis*, nor one hundred thousand *koṭis* of beings; in this way, they eliminate not merely one *koṭī-nayuta* of beings, nor one hundred *koṭī-nayutas*, nor one thousand *koṭī-nayutas*, nor one hundred thousand *koṭī-nayutas* of beings, nor even one *gaṅgā-kalā* of beings.
In this way, the great afflictions of the three poisons belonging to as many as unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings are all eliminated.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
For example, within the Great Snow Mountains there is a great medicinal king named Vigama; if its sound is heard, all the fierce poisons and fevers of the world are completely extinguished.
If this medicine remains within a range of one hundred *yojana*, its majestic power will cause all malevolent poisons to lose their potency.

If this King of Medicines is applied to a great conch or drum, whether it is struck or blown, all sentient beings within the reach of that sound—be they those who have ingested poison, been bitten by venomous creatures, been smeared with poison, pierced by poisoned thorns, or afflicted by various poisons—if such sounds from the conch or drum merely briefly reach their ears, all their poisons shall be entirely eradicated.
Śāriputra! Thus, this great and wondrous medicinal king, Vigama, cannot be recognized by any physicians of the world; only the great physician-king Jīvaka knows its nature and color.

In this way, Śāriputra, it is also so for the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is untiring in diligence. Because he practices the *vīrya-pāramitā*, he accumulates such unsurpassed, true Dharma *agada* (antidote) ointment, which is not shared with the dharmas of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Except for the Tathāgata, the supreme king of physicians of the unsurpassed true Dharma, who can extinguish all the diseases of sentient beings, [the bodhisattva] uses the unsurpassed true Dharma *agada* ointment to anoint the conch of the Great Dharma; having anointed it, he blows it, and its sound proclaims throughout the trichiliocosm. All sentient beings therein, even those numbering as many as the unspeakably unspeakable, having heard this sound, find that all their heavy and great afflictions—greed, hatred, and delusion—are completely extinguished without remainder.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
From where does this unsurpassed, true Dharma *agada* ointment come and gather here? Śāriputra!"
You should know that such medicinal ointment comes from the vessel of great bodhi.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
from where does that vessel of bodhi come?
You should know that they come from the casket of the jewels of the Dharma of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
from where does such a precious casket of the bodhisattvas come?
You should know that this has emerged from no other source than the Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices with tireless diligence, desiring to cultivate the *vīryapāramitā*, should seek out such a sūtra of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka with the utmost sincerity; having heard it, they should receive and uphold it, read and recite it, investigate its meaning and principles, and extensively proclaim and reveal it to sentient beings.
Śāriputra! You should further understand that such are the characteristics; I shall now speak again to further elucidate their meaning.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are untiringly diligent in practicing the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) hear what I have said, they should, with the utmost sincerity, investigate the principles of this sūtra and reveal them to others.

“Śāriputra! In the distant past, beyond incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, and difficult to fathom—even exceeding such numbers and such measures—at that time, a Buddha appeared in this world named Raktapadma-vijaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Śāriputra! In a single great assembly of that Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples, their number reached a full eighty koṭis; they were all great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, and who had even attained the most supreme pāramitā of mastery over the mind.

Śāriputra! That Buddha’s lifespan will be a full eighty years, after which he will enter parinirvāṇa; the True Dharma will remain in the world for five hundred years, and the Semblance Dharma will likewise remain for five hundred years, with his relics being widely distributed.
"Just as I now manifest the signs of the distribution of my relics after my parinirvāṇa,
so it shall be, Śāriputra.

One hundred years after that Buddha has passed away and entered parinirvāṇa, there will be a bodhisattva who, having ended his life in another world-system, will be born here in the family of a great king."
Immediately upon being born, he uttered these words:
"How extraordinary!
Today I have been born in an improper place."
He further spoke these words:
"How extraordinary!
Today you have been born in an improper place."
Having spoken thus, he further said:
"I shall now practice the Dharma; I shall now practice the Dharma."
At that time, the multitude all gave rise to doubt and wonder; because of what he had recounted, they collectively named him Dharmacārin.
Śāriputra, as Prince Dharmacārin gradually grew up, his faculties reached full maturity at the age of twenty, and with pure faith, he left the household life to pursue the unsurpassed path.
Having already gone forth, he dwelt alone in a secluded and empty forest, staying in a quiet chamber.
At that time, a great celestial deity appeared in the void and addressed him, saying:

"Bhikṣu, you should know this: if you now seek the fruit of Buddhahood of the Tathāgata—the renown of which is lofty and far-reaching, and the Dharma of which is most supreme—you should simply apply yourself diligently to studying the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka."
"If you have not yet attained it, do not abandon your diligence; apply yourself single-mindedly to seeking it so that it may not remain unfulfilled.

Śāriputra, when the bhikṣu Dharmacara heard these words from that deva, his heart was filled with great joy and he leaped up immeasurably, his body and mind overflowing with delight. He immediately set out to search for the Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, traveling personally through villages, cities, royal capitals, provinces, and even to roadside inns, searching everywhere in succession, yet finding nothing at all.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmacārin again traveled through various monasteries; whenever he saw a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, he would go to them and speak these words:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"

Where is there a subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, by relying upon which bodhisattvas mahāsattvas may practice and train, thereby giving birth to the immeasurable sublime Dharmas of all Buddhas?
He then replied: "Bhikṣu, you should know that previously I had not heard what is called the subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It is only now, because of your explanation, that I have heard the name of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka Dharma-gate enter my ears."
"Śāriputra! At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmacārin reflected again to himself:
'Such a Dharma-gate, the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas, should not have been spoken falsely by a celestial deity.'"

From this moment forth, I shall certainly not relinquish my courageous diligence; until I have heard this Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall never allow myself to become weary or negligent in the interim.
He then further questioned those bhikṣus:
"At what location was the site where the Tathāgata Padmottara entered parinirvāṇa and his body was cremated?"
"You should show me the direction of this place; I shall go there to practice the deeds of diligence.
Those bhikṣus then said to him: "Bhikṣu, you should know that in this very direction lies the site where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Padmottara-rakta-padma, underwent the cremation of his body."

At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmacārin went to that place. Having arrived, he prostrated himself, circumambulated him to the right countless times, and withdrew to one side where he sat cross-legged. With single-minded concentration and mindfulness directed toward that Buddha, he made this vow:

"I sit here in the cross-legged posture; until I have heard from the presence of the Tathāgata Raktapadma-vijaya the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Mahābodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall certainly not break this posture nor rise from this place."

"Śāriputra! At that time, the rishi-monk Dharmacārin, with firm and steadfast diligence, made such a vow and sat in the full lotus posture. After seven days had passed, there was a Bhagavān in the eastern world named Ratnagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who, for the sake of the rishi-monk Dharmacārin, came from that realm and appeared before him, expounding and revealing to him the Dharma of the eight-gated phrases."
He further addressed him, saying: "Rājarṣi Bhikṣu!

You should now diligently practice the subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka according to the method of the eightfold formula; then the realization of all Buddha-dharmas will not be difficult to attain."

When the rishi-monk Rājarṣi had heard the Buddha’s teaching, he applied himself with diligence to practicing the Dharma of the eightfold phrases; before long, he attained the inconceivable and unsurpassed mastery of vast learning.

He immediately rose from the ground, leaving his original seat, and for the sake of extensively practicing the *vīryapāramitā*, with courageous and correct diligence, he traveled to various villages, cities, royal capitals, provinces, and even to pavilions and guest houses; moving from one place to another, he successively proclaimed and disseminated this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka for a full sixty years.

At that time, he taught and transformed sentient beings, and a multitude of devas, humans, and others, numbering in the hundreds of millions (koṭi), all attained stable abiding within the Three Vehicles. “Śāriputra!
After that royal seer bhikṣu had converted sentient beings, at the time of his death he made this aspiration:
"May I be reborn among humans in this Buddha-world, where I shall practice the Dharma."
Having made this vow, he passed away.
By the power of that vow, he was reborn in this world in the continent of Jambudvīpa within the family of a householder.
On the very day of his birth, he uttered these words:
"I shall now practice the Dharma. Again, he says:
"I shall now practice the Dharma."
At that time, the multitude established his original name based on what he had related, calling him Dharmacārin once more.
Śāriputra! This youth Dharmacārin, appearing as if eight years of age, with pure faith left the home life and set out upon the unsurpassed path.
Not long after he had gone forth, due to his past habitual practice, the subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka and its unsurpassed, profound meaning spontaneously manifested before him.
The Bhikṣu Dharmacārin dwelt securely in this Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka and extensively propagated the transformative teachings of the Dharma for sixty years.

He traveled in person to villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, cities, and even to pavilions and lodgings, teaching and transforming beings everywhere, revealing this Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

For sixty years, he taught and transformed gods and humans, bringing a full *koṭi* of beings to maturity within the three vehicles: some abiding in the Śrāvaka vehicle, some in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and others in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
“Śāriputra! At that time, after the bhikṣu Dharmacārin had transformed sentient beings, as his life was coming to an end, he spoke these words:
‘May I, in the future, obtain human birth, leave the household life, and hear the Dharma.’”
After his life had ended, by the power of his vows, he was born into a royal family here in Jambudvīpa.
On the day of his birth, the devas in the sky above proclaimed:
"In this realm of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva Dharmavijaya has appeared in the world."
Again, he proclaimed these words:
"In this realm of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva Dharmavijaya has appeared in the world.
At that time, having heard the celestial announcement, the multitude of people named the prince Dharmavijaya.
Śāriputra! In this way, as Prince Dharmodgata’s faculties gradually matured, at the age of twenty, with pure faith he left his home for the homeless life.
Once he had gone forth, the multitude named him the Bhikṣu Dharmodgata. Śāriputra!

Because the Bhikṣu Dharmodgata was sustained by the power of great mindfulness and wisdom, the subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka appeared spontaneously before him; through diligent cultivation, he was able to skillfully and forever sever the doubts and delusions of sentient beings.

For sixty years, he personally engaged in the work of wandering and transforming others, traveling through villages, cities, royal capitals, provinces, and even to pavilions and lodgings, to reveal and teach this Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
During those sixty years, he brought millions of devas and humans to spiritual maturity, causing them all to dwell securely in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Śāriputra!..."
When the bhikṣu Dharmodgata was about to pass away, he made this aspiration:
"May I, in a future life, be born among human beings and leave the household life with right faith.
As soon as he had made this vow, he passed away and was reborn in this world in the home of a wealthy householder in Jambudvīpa.
When he was first born, there were again celestial deities who proclaimed in a loud voice:
"In this world, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara has appeared today!
This was repeated a second time.
At that time, having heard the proclamation of the deva, the multitude all collectively named him Smṛti.

Śāriputra, this Bodhisattva Smṛti’s faculties were fully developed; appearing as strong as one in the prime of youth at twenty years of age, he, with pure faith, renounced his home to go forth into the homeless life.

As soon as he had gone forth, by the power of his past habitual practice, he immediately attained the accomplishment of an inconceivable, most supreme, unsurpassed, and unforgetting dhāraṇī, becoming fully endowed with great learning.
