For sixty years, he traveled through villages, cities, royal capitals, provinces, and even waystations, personally guiding and transforming beings. Everywhere he went, he spread the transformative influence of the Dharma, proclaiming the True Teaching to sever the doubts of sentient beings and reveal such a subtle and wondrous Dharma gate as this Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
After sixty years have passed, he establishes one *koṭi* of devas and humans, causing them to abide either as śrāvakas, or as pratyekabuddhas, or else to dwell in the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
"Śāriputra! After this Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati had transformed sentient beings, at the time of his death he spoke these words:
'May I, in the future, be born among humans and leave the household life with right faith.'"
After his life there had ended, he was reborn in this world into the family of a great king.
At the time of his birth, a celestial deity again proclaimed with a loud voice:
"In this realm of sentient beings, a Dharma-following Bodhisattva has appeared in the world."
Thus it was repeated a second time.
At that moment, having heard the proclamation of the deva, the multitude named the prince "Dharmasena" (依法律). Śāriputra!
In accordance with the Dharma, the Bodhisattva thus gradually brought his faculties to full maturity; at the age of twenty, out of faith, he left the household life for the homeless state.

As soon as he had gone forth, by the power of his past habituation and because of the sustaining power of his uninterrupted moment-to-moment mindfulness, the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka spontaneously appeared before him.

Śāriputra! Acting as a bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, this Bodhisattva traveled for fifty years to teach and transform others, going from one village to another, from one hamlet to another, from city to city, from inn to inn, from kingdom to kingdom, and from one royal capital to another royal capital, revealing such teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka to all sentient beings and severing their doubts.
During his fiftieth year, he caused four koṭis of devas and humans to abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed Mahāyāna of the Buddhas.
“Śāriputra! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmatā will, at the end of this life, be reborn in the world-system of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha in the eastern direction.”

At the very moment of his birth, he immediately attained inconceivable and unsurpassed great learning; he taught, transformed, and guided sixty-eight koṭis of devas and humans, causing them all to achieve fulfillment and dwell securely in the Three Vehicles.

Śāriputra! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmayukta, having transformed sentient beings within the Dharma of that Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, at the end of his life returned to this world, to Jambudvīpa in the Buddha-field of the Victorious One Padmottara, and was born into the family of a great king.

When he was first born, the sixty-eight koṭis of devas and humans whom he had taught and brought to maturity all passed away there and were reborn in this buddha-field following the Bodhisattva, becoming his retinue.

Śāriputra! At that time, in this world-system, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Paramavikrāmin (Highest Conduct), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Men, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavat.
The lifespan of that Buddha will be a full eighty *koṭi* years, and at that time, the lifespan of human beings will be equal to that of the Buddha.
Śāriputra, while the Tathāgata, Arhat,

Samyaksaṃbuddha Supreme Conduct dwells in the world preaching the Dharma, there shall be one great assembly each year, and in each of these great assemblies, there will be eighty *koṭi* of śrāvaka followers.
That Buddha had eighty *koṭi* assemblies of śrāvakas, all of whom were great arhats.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva was a prince named Vīradatta, he had accomplished extensive learning, wisdom, and sublime insight; accompanied by a retinue of sixty-eight *koṭis*, and surrounded before and behind by such a great multitude, he proceeded to the place where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Paramavikrāmin resided.
Having arrived there, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and withdrew to sit to one side. "Śāriputra!

At that time, the Tathāgata Supreme Conduct, having thoroughly understood the prince Vīradatta’s superior faith and devotion, immediately revealed to him the subtle and supreme Dharma corresponding to his past conduct."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s exposition of this Dharma, Prince Vīradatta attained sudden and clear understanding and gained pure faith.
Because his mind was purified, he immediately renounced the home life for the homeless state with a retinue of sixty-eight koṭis, out of faith.
Having gone forth, he purified his holy life (brahmacarya) until the end of his lifespan. Śāriputra!
At that time, Prince Vīradatta practiced the bodhisattva path with diligence through walking meditation within that Buddha’s Dharma, his mind intent on realizing unsurpassed bodhi.
Then the Tathāgata Supreme Conduct bestowed a prophecy upon him, addressing the great assembly:

"This bhikṣu, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vīradatta, after my parinirvāṇa, shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and appear in the world with the name Tathāgata Mahāvīrya, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān."
"Śāriputra! After the Tathāgata Paramavikrāmin had bestowed this prediction upon him, he entered parinirvāṇa.

Upon seeing the Buddha’s passing, the Bodhisattva Vīradatta was filled with even greater longing and devotion; he reverently made offerings to the Tathāgata’s relics, extensively erected sacred shrines for the benefit of sentient beings, and upheld the True Dharma to transform and enlighten immeasurable numbers."
Not long thereafter, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and was named Mahāvīrya.

Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Tathāgata Mahāvīrya was half an eon; that Buddha’s Dharma assemblies were immeasurable in number, and in each assembly there were twelve *nayuta* of śrāvaka disciples, all of whom were arhats.

“Śāriputra! Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva of tireless diligence, desiring to practice the *vīryapāramitā*, earnestly and with great devotion seeks this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka. He hears it, receives and upholds it, reads it, recites it, contemplates and investigates it, analyzes its principles, and extensively proclaims and expounds it for all sentient beings. Through his unceasing efforts, he eventually attains Buddhahood, becoming the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Mahāvīrya (Great Diligence), appearing in the world to widely proclaim the Dharma and benefit sentient beings, as described above.”
Therefore, Śāriputra!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who abide in the subtle and sublime right practice of the Mahāyāna and wish to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), they should exert themselves with courageous and vigorous diligence, earnestly and respectfully seeking such Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; thereby they shall encounter it, reverently hear and receive it, and even extensively proclaim and expound it for all sentient beings.
Why is this? Śāriputra,

it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is courageous and diligent must necessarily seek the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka before they can fully accomplish the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s courageous diligence in assiduously practicing the pāramitā of vīrya, performing the bodhisattva conduct for the sake of sentient beings.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice this bodhisattva conduct, all Māras, their followers, and the sons of gods will be unable to disturb or harass them, nor can they be overcome or defeated by the heterodox paths or the arguments of others.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume XLVIII and XLIX.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Ten: The Perfection of Meditative Concentration. Chapter Twelve of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, Part Fifteen.
Chapter Ten, Part One: The Perfection of Meditative Concentration. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently training in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) and practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of sentient beings? Śāriputra!
For the sake of sentient beings, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully and diligently cultivate the four types of dhyāna.
What are these four? Śāriputra!

Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva is detached from desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, there is applied thought and sustained thought, born of detachment, accompanied by joy and bliss; this is called the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the first complete dhyāna.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva has stilled directed thought and evaluation, his mind becomes inwardly purified, unified, and single-pointed; free from directed thought and evaluation, he experiences the joy and happiness born of concentration. This is called the bodhisattva’s abiding in the second complete dhyāna.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva has become free from joy, he dwells in equanimity; with right mindfulness and right awareness, he experiences bliss in the body. That which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in bliss through equanimity and mindfulness, being free from joy"—this is called the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the third complete dhyāna.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

for the sake of abandoning pleasure, first abandons pain, and with the disappearance of both sorrow and joy, dwells in a state that is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and pure mindfulness— this is called the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the fourth complete dhyāna.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), their concentrated mind is pure and free from defilement; being detached from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), they do not abandon deep concentration, yet are able to initiate all the various activities of meditative concentration. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivating these four kinds of meditative concentration by relying on the perfection of concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the activity of the meditative concentration of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is that the bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of the wisdom-activity of supernormal powers."
Śāriputra! What is called the supernormal power (abhijñā) of a bodhisattva?
Furthermore, what constitutes their activity of wisdom (jñānakarma)?

Śāriputra! Regarding what is called "knowledge of the supernormal powers" (abhijñājñāna), bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve this knowledge of the supernormal powers by being fully endowed with five kinds. What are these five?

These are the supernormal power of the knowledge of realization through the divine eye, the supernormal power of the knowledge of realization through the divine ear, the supernormal power of the knowledge of realization through the knowledge of others' minds, the supernormal power of the knowledge of realization through the recollection of past abodes, and the supernormal power of the knowledge of realization through the various modes of the bases of psychic power.
"Śāriputra! These are called the five supernormal knowledges of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; therein, the bodhisattva fully accomplishes the perfection of the activity of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal knowledge of the realization of the nature of the divine eye?
And how is the activity of the wisdom of these supernormal knowledges perfected? Śāriputra!
Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), he attains the perfection of the knowledge and activity of the divine eye (divyacakṣus).

Since his mind of samādhi is thus pure, lucid, free from turbidity and defilement, and devoid of secondary afflictions (upakleśa), his mind enters skillfully into the supernormal power of the knowledge that realizes the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

Śāriputra! Thus, the divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is purified, luminous, and surpasses that of humans; it perceives all sentient beings—whether dying or being born, of beautiful or ugly appearance, in happy or miserable realms, or whether inferior or superior—and understands them all according to the karma they have accumulated.

Thus, with the purified divine eye, he sees sentient beings who have accomplished evil conduct of body, accomplished evil conduct of speech, and accomplished evil conduct of mind; who revile the noble ones and give rise to wrong views. Because they experience the causes and conditions of karma resulting from those wrong views, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the miserable realms and are born in hell.

In this way, those beings who have accomplished virtuous conduct of body, accomplished virtuous conduct of speech, and accomplished virtuous conduct of mind; who do not revile the noble ones and have given rise to right view—because of that karma and the cause of their right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the world of the devas.
Śāriputra! This is called the pure divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, which surpasses that of humans and is able to clearly perceive all the karmic accumulations of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), the divine eye they obtain is lucid and most excellent, surpassing the divine eyes obtained by all other sentient beings."

Śāriputra! Because the divine eye attained by this bodhisattva is exceedingly clear and luminous, he perceives and manifests all forms and appearances—whether coarse or subtle, superior or inferior, distant or near—and is able to see all such objects clearly as if they were directly before his eyes.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
by means of this eye, all forms and images that are obstructed are seen clearly and transparently through the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s eye, such that there is no obstruction whatsoever.
Therefore, Śāriputra, the divine eye attained by this bodhisattva mahāsattva is the most supreme among all the gods. Compared to the eyes obtained by all nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras,

those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the divine eye attained by the bodhisattva is the most excellent, the highest, the most venerable, the most superior, the most sublime, and the most luminous— transcendently pure and foremost.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), the divine eye they obtain is produced by the various paths of renunciation."

Because this divine eye is extremely clear and penetrates all that is manifested, one sees all forms—whether coarse or subtle, superior or inferior, near or far—as they truly are, throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions.

Furthermore, with this eye, one is able to know and see clearly and in accordance with reality all classes of sentient beings born in any of the destinies throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, with the exception of those in the formless realm.

Furthermore, with this eye, one skillfully knows all the causes of karma and the karmic retributions of sentient beings; moreover, one thoroughly understands all the faculties of those sentient beings, as well as the causes of those faculties and their various distinctions, being able to discern and know them all exactly as they are.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of dhyāna, they are able to observe with this eye the meritorious adornments of the infinite and boundless buddha-fields of the ten directions, seeing them all clearly before their eyes as if present."

Having thus directly perceived this, one purifies and cultivates the aggregate of ethical discipline that constitutes one's practice, and dedicates it toward the adornment of the pure merit of the buddha-field one is to achieve.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fulfillment of the divine eye and the dedication of the perfection of abiding in ethical discipline (śīla).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The divine eye of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is clear and bright, surpassing that of humans; he perceives all Buddhas and the assembly of bodhisattvas as they truly are.

Having seen them directly, he clearly perceives, exactly as they are, all the modes of conduct, the exemplary practices, the faculties and mindfulness, the correct wisdom and majestic deportment, the noble dharmas, and the knowledge of liberation belonging to those true beings (satpuruṣa). He also perceives their abiding in the attainment of dhāraṇīs and supreme wisdom, their skillful wisdom, and their excellent expedient means (upāya-kauśalya). Regarding all such sublime and wondrous dharmic practices, the bodhisattva is able to see them as they truly are, and thus applies himself with diligent resolve to bring them swiftly to perfection.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they attain the pure divine eye (divyacakṣus) that transcends that of humans, which is accomplished through immeasurable merits."
Why is this? Because this eye is unobstructed, for it is able to see all forms;
because this eye is unattached, for it has no clinging to any forms.
This eye is liberation, for it is liberated from all latent tendencies and views;
this eye is pure, for its nature is transparently clear.
This eye is without dependence, because all objective spheres have nothing upon which to depend;
this eye is without grasping, because the latent tendencies of affliction are not clung to;
this eye is without obscuration, because it is free from doubt and confusion.
This eye is unbound, because it is free from obstructive dharmas;
this eye is lucid, because it realizes the illumination of the Dharma;
this eye relies upon wisdom, because its activity is not that of consciousness.
This eye is without defilement, without hatred, and without delusion, for it is far removed from all turbidity of affliction;
this eye accords with the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), for it serves as the root of noble practice;
this eye has the characteristic of non-obstruction, for it radiates divine light equally upon all sentient beings.
This eye is clear and bright, because it is free from the turbulence of aggregation;
this eye is stainless, because its nature is luminously pure.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
This bodhisattva’s eye can lead to the Buddha-eye; its nature is like empty space, with nothing to be lost or abandoned.
This bodhisattva’s eye is without attachment or bondage, and is entirely free from all craving and aversion.

This Bodhisattva’s eye operates within the sphere of meaning; it practices the path of pure wisdom that is equal in its application to the True Dharma, and is well able to abide in high and vast great compassion for all sentient beings.

This Bodhisattva’s eye harbors no resentment or obstruction toward those who come seeking; this Bodhisattva’s eye never censures or disparages those who violate the precepts; this Bodhisattva’s eye is able to protect and guard against all transgressions; this Bodhisattva’s eye bestows diligent exertion upon those who are indolent; this Bodhisattva’s eye reveals the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to those whose minds are distracted; this Bodhisattva’s eye grants the eye of right wisdom to those with faulty wisdom; this Bodhisattva’s eye opens the way to the correct path for those traveling on deviant paths; this Bodhisattva’s eye manifests the vast Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata to sentient beings of inferior faith and inclination; this Bodhisattva’s eye ultimately leads to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), bringing before one lofty and expansive supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wondrous awakening, such that there is no regression even unto the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Śāriputra! This is called the perfection of the knowledge of realization through the supernormal power of the divine eye, attained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva by relying upon the dhyāna-pāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
by practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), attain the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the nature of the divine ear (divyaśrotratā)?”
Furthermore, by what supernormal knowledge and activity is he fully perfected?

Śāriputra, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), he diligently cultivates and attains this divine ear (divyaśrotra). His hearing is utterly pure and transcends that of humans; he hears both kinds of sounds—those of humans and non-humans alike—whether distant or near, as they clearly manifest.

Śāriputra! By means of the nature of the divine ear, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to hear all sounds throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions—namely, the voices of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans and non-humans—as well as the voices of the preaching of noble ones, the voices of Tathāgatas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas.
All such sounds and voices as these, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears and knows them all through the power of the celestial ear’s penetrating hearing.
Furthermore, they are able to discern all the sounds within the various wretched and evil realms: the sounds of the hells, the sounds of animals, and the sounds of the realm of Yama.
All such infinite and boundless sounds and voices, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to hear them all clearly through the power of the divine ear’s penetrating hearing.

Furthermore, regarding the sounds produced by various small creatures—mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, ants, and even the most minute living beings—the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of the nature of the divine ear, is able to hear them all clearly.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the divine ear of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is purified; if sentient beings, based on mental objects, give rise to verbal karma that is either wholesome or unwholesome, he is able to fully comprehend it all through the nature of his divine ear.
Furthermore, one is able to discern whether various karmas are embraced by wholesome causes or whether various karmas are embraced by unwholesome causes; all such things can be fully understood.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to discern that some verbal karma arises from anger due to underlying tendencies of greed, while other verbal karma arises from desire due to underlying tendencies of anger.

Furthermore, one can discern that some verbal karma arises from ignorance due to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed and hatred, while other verbal karma arises from greed and hatred due to the underlying tendency of ignorance.

Furthermore, one can discern that some verbal karma arises from greed because of the underlying tendency toward greed; some verbal karma arises from hatred because of the underlying tendency toward hatred; and some verbal karma arises from delusion because of the underlying tendency toward delusion.
All such things manifested through the sounds of speech, he is able to fully comprehend.

Furthermore, he can discern whether there are vocal actions where the mental resolve is pure while the skillful means are defiled and obstructed, or vocal actions where the skillful means are pure while the mental resolve is defiled and obstructed. Regarding all such sounds, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of the great supernormal power of unimpeded divine hearing, knows them all as they truly are, regardless of distance.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration, his knowledge of the supernormal power of the divine ear becomes pure, clear, and penetrating; he hears all sounds, whether of the noble or the non-noble, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and is further able to distinguish them without error."
Although they have heard and listened, they do not give rise to delight or attachment toward noble sounds, nor do they produce aversion or envy toward non-noble sounds.
Furthermore, by hearing and knowing noble sounds, they attain great loving-kindness; by hearing and knowing non-noble sounds, they attain great compassion.

Furthermore, although the various sounds throughout the ten directions are simultaneously infinite, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the power of wisdom that discerns the limits of the past and future, knows them all as they truly are through his unconfused divine ear.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, with the purified divine ear, the bodhisattva mahāsattva hears extensively and universally; reaching as far as all the worlds in the ten directions, he hears every sound of the Dharma teachings spoken by the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, in the lands where the Tathāgatas travel and transform beings."

Having heard it, they maintain it in their minds without forgetting; they are able to uphold everything so that it does not leak away or disperse, remaining firmly established like water contained within a vessel.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears the voice of the Tathāgata, it is likewise thus: they are able to fully comprehend all phenomena, whether stable or unstable.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not selectively receive the sounds of the Dharma spoken by one Buddha while being bound and obstructed by the sounds of the Dharma spoken by a second Buddha.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never tire of hearing the Dharma;
thus, they listen to the sounds of the Dharma taught by all Tathāgatas, both past and present.
They are all able to maintain them without error or confusion.
Furthermore, by means of their purified divine ear, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to hear all sounds—
both wholesome and unwholesome— throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Among these various sounds, there are those that express speech appropriate to the occasion and those inappropriate to the occasion; all such immeasurable instances he knows as they truly are.
Śāriputra, what is meant by speech that is timely and untimely?

Śāriputra! The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are skilled in knowing the appropriate timing; at times they expound the essential teachings extensively for the assembly, and at times they expound the essential teachings concisely for the assembly.
After the bodhisattva mahāsattva has heard all such sounds, he expounds them extensively or concisely through a single voice, according to what is appropriate for each being.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to thoroughly understand that there may be matters truly worthy of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); yet, if explaining them would cause distress to others, they do not provide a prediction.

Alternatively, there may be matters truly unworthy of a prediction because they lead to what is meaningless; however, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, being skillful in immeasurable and excellent means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that effectively benefit others, purify their own minds and then grant a prediction.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), through the power of his purified divine ear that penetrates all sounds, he knows the characteristics of various sounds. If at any time there are sounds possessing such characteristics that ought to be heard with sympathetic joy, the bodhisattva mahāsattva immediately hears those sounds of such characteristics."
If at times there are sounds possessing such characteristics that one ought not to rejoice in hearing them, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva then does not listen to such sounds.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells among a great assembly and preaches the Dharma, if the ear-consciousness of sentient beings is not pure, he shall empower them with his supernormal powers so that they may understand the sound of his preaching.
If there are sentient beings who desire to comprehend all dharmas, they cause them to hear such sounds of the Dharma.
If there are sentient beings who do not delight in the dharmas and have no desire for comprehension, they cause them not to hear such sounds of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they attain such knowledge of the supernormal power of the divine ear (divyaśrotra-abhijñā-jñāna), through which they hear sounds that are immeasurable and boundless."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
As for the nature of the divine ear, it is that which causes all phenomena to become luminous and pure.
As for the nature of the divine ear, it is that which causes the nature of wisdom to become clear and transparent.
The nature of the divine ear enables the bodhisattva to attain self-purification.
The nature of the divine ear enables the nature of sentient beings to be purified.

The nature of the divine ear is characterized by supreme and thorough discernment; it allows one to hear with clarity and fluency the sounds and words as they are expressed in their respective scripts. Furthermore, it enables one to penetrate the various distinctions in speech and sound among all conscious beings born within the five destinies, such that the bodhisattva can preach the Dharma using a voice identical to that of each particular class of being.

Śāriputra! This divine ear of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, through its supernormal power, can only proceed toward the divine ear of a Tathāgata; it will certainly not proceed toward the practices of any other vehicles.

Śāriputra! This is called the perfection of the wisdom-action of the supernormal power of clairaudience attained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva through practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of dhyāna, attain the supernormal power of the knowledge that realizes the minds of others?
Furthermore, what is meant by the perfection of the cognitive activity of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others?

Śāriputra, by means of this pure supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, a bodhisattva mahāsattva clearly perceives and fully understands, exactly as they are, all the infinite mental characteristics of sentient beings throughout all the worlds in the ten directions. A bodhisattva is thus able to know them all in accordance with reality.

Śāriputra, if there are the mental characteristics of sentient beings in the past, the mental characteristics in the future, and the mental characteristics in the present, the bodhisattva is able to understand them all therein. Śāriputra!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with such supernormal knowledge of others' minds, by means of the wisdom of the past mind, they are able to thoroughly understand and enter into the causal factors and the various distinctions of those causes of all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they are able to discern that such sentient beings possess the mental causes produced by vast causes;
and that such sentient beings possess the mental causes produced by middling causes.
Such sentient beings have minds produced by inferior causes;
all such things he knows as they truly are.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to discern that such sentient beings possess faculties associated with the inclination for generosity, such sentient beings possess faculties associated with the inclination for ethical discipline, such sentient beings possess faculties associated with the inclination for patience, such sentient beings possess faculties associated with the inclination for diligence, such sentient beings possess faculties associated with the inclination for meditative concentration, and such sentient beings possess faculties associated with the inclination for wisdom.
In this way, the Bodhisattva is able to clearly understand all such associations with the faculties as they truly are.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to know that such sentient beings possess the faculty for the practice of loving-kindness, such sentient beings possess the faculty for the practice of compassion, such sentient beings possess the faculty for the practice of sympathetic joy, and such sentient beings possess the faculty for the practice of equanimity; he is able to know them all and distinguish them according to reality.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to discern that such sentient beings possess the roots for the practice of the Buddha-vehicle, such sentient beings possess the roots for the practice of the pratyekabuddha-vehicle, and such sentient beings possess the roots for the practice of the śrāvaka-vehicle; he is able to discern all such things in this way.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows as it truly is: that such sentient beings possess the power of strong causes and are thus accomplished in the wholesome causes for proceeding toward the Mahāyāna;
and that such sentient beings possess the power of strong conditions and are thus accomplished in the conditional causes for proceeding toward the Mahāyāna.
They are all able to discern and understand them as they truly are.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows as it truly is: "This sentient being possesses the power of strong causes and has accomplished the wholesome causes for proceeding toward the Great Vehicle; nevertheless, due to the cause of skillful means, this sentient being is born into a lowly family."

Thus, there are sentient beings who possess the power of strong skillful means; although they do not accomplish vast roots of goodness, these beings nonetheless plant the power of causes that give rise to a vast household.
All such things he is able to fully understand. Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva can also fully understand:

that such sentient beings have pure intentions and aspirations but lack purity of means; that such sentient beings have purity of means but lack purity of intentions and aspirations; that such sentient beings have both purity of intentions and aspirations and purity of means; and that such sentient beings have neither purity of intentions and aspirations nor purity of means.
"Śāriputra! By means of this supernormal power, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fully comprehend all such things as these.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they attain the knowledge of the superknowledge of others' minds (paracittajñānābhijñā). Consequently, all the knowledge regarding the causal faculties and mental activities of the past of all sentient beings, as well as the knowledge of teaching the Dharma in accordance with those various activities—these are all termed the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the superknowledge of others' minds.

Śāriputra, because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess this wisdom, they are able to fully comprehend through the supernormal power of knowledge by means of their minds directed toward the future limit: that such sentient beings will have the cause for ethical discipline in future lives, while possessing the cause for generosity in the present life.
Such sentient beings will have the cause of giving in future lives, while possessing the cause of ethical discipline in the present life.
Such sentient beings will have the cause of diligence in future lives, while possessing the cause of patience in the present life.
Such sentient beings will possess the cause for patience in future lives, while possessing the cause for diligence in the present life.
Such sentient beings will possess the cause for wisdom in future lives, while possessing the cause for meditative concentration in the present life.

Thus, he knows with reality as his standard and understands with clarity and penetration all such immeasurable courses of action, wherein sentient beings possess the causes for meditative concentration in future lives and the causes for wisdom in the present life.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to discern that such sentient beings will possess the causes for supramundane conduct in future lives, while possessing the causes for mundane conduct in the present life.
Thus, he is able to fully comprehend how these sentient beings will have causes for worldly conduct in future lives, yet possess causes for supramundane conduct in the present life;
all such things he knows completely.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to discern that such sentient beings will, in future lives, produce roots of merit through the causes of the Mahāyāna, while in the present life they possess roots produced through the causes of the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
Such sentient beings will possess faculties produced by the causes of the Pratyekabuddhayāna in future lives, yet possess faculties produced by the causes of the Mahāyāna in the present life.
Such sentient beings will, in future ages, possess faculties produced by the causes of the Mahāyāna, while in the present age they possess faculties produced by the causes of the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Thus, there are sentient beings who possess faculties produced by the causes of the Śrāvaka vehicle in future lives, yet possess faculties produced by the causes of the Mahāyāna in the present life.

Thus, there are sentient beings who possess faculties produced by the causes of the Pratyekabuddhayāna in future lives, yet possess faculties produced by the causes of the Śrāvakayāna in the present life.

In this way, there are sentient beings who possess faculties produced by the causes of the Śrāvaka vehicle in future lives, yet possess faculties produced by the causes of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle in the present life.
In this way, Śāriputra!

Regarding the various causal activities and conditions for existence as previously described, there will be such faculties among all sentient beings in future ages; by means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to discern and understand them all, whether as causes, activities, or conditions, exactly as they truly are.

Śāriputra! You should know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, toward sentient beings who have not yet matured, arouse right diligence and employ skillful means to guide and transform them without ever becoming weary; according to the minds of those sentient beings, they are able to penetrate their dispositions and preach the true Dharma for them.

Why is this? Because once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has well understood such a person as a vessel for the true Dharma, they immediately preach that true Dharma to them; since their activity of preaching the Dharma is always free from error, they are all called "those who preach the Dharma not in vain."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they attain the supernormal knowledge of the activity of the minds of others (paracittajñāna-abhijñā). They fully comprehend, in their entirety and without limit, the successive arising of all the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings in the present world."
Śāriputra! What is meant by knowing how the mind and mental factors arise in successive succession? Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the minds of all sentient beings, knows as it truly is a mind with greed as a mind with greed; knows as it truly is a mind free from greed as a mind free from greed; knows as it truly is a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; knows as it truly is a mind free from hatred as a mind free from hatred; knows as it truly is a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; and knows as it truly is a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion.
Furthermore, he is able to know that by means of such and such afflictions and delusions, the minds of such and such sentient beings are obscured and hindered.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands all these matters as they truly are; having understood them, he teaches the Dharma of renunciation in accordance with those very afflictions.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has acquired such supernormal knowledge of others' minds, when he intends to preach the Dharma and goes among the great assembly, he should first observe the various characteristics of the differences in the faculties, conducts, and so forth of all those in the assembly."
Having understood this, he teaches the Dharma according to the conduct appropriate for those sentient beings. Śāriputra,

you should know that by means of the wisdom that understands the superior and inferior faculties and mentalities of sentient beings, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fully comprehend the nature of the superior and inferior faculties and mentalities of sentient beings.
Śāriputra, you should know that such a bodhisattva does not falsely disparage the characteristics of their own mind or the characteristics of the minds of others. Why is this?

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of wisdom, discriminates and collects the continuity of the mind; thus, through mindfulness, through awakening, through inclination, through insight, and through awareness, they discriminate and collect the continuity of the mind. Consequently, they are free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions, their continuity is severed, and they are pure, stainless, translucent, untainted, unclouded, and unperturbed. They discern and illuminate all phenomena and enter into accordance with all the mental activities of sentient beings, because they thus discriminate and collect the continuity of the mind.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus awaken to and enter into the knowledge of all such mental phenomena, this is called the dharma of the accomplishment of the perfection of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, attained through the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), attain the perfection of the knowledge and activity of the supernormal power of realizing the recollection of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñājñānakarmaparipūri)?”

Śāriputra! Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses such power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, they are able to recollect all the various matters of past lives—of every single kind—for all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the worlds in the ten directions.

In this way, they are able to know one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, or even hundreds of thousands of births—not merely a hundred, not merely a thousand, nor merely a hundred thousand—but to understand them all in such successive order.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to thoroughly understand the kalpa of destruction, the kalpa of formation, and the kalpas of both formation and destruction; he understands that these are not merely a single kalpa of destruction, nor a single kalpa of formation, nor a single kalpa of both formation and destruction—he thus thoroughly understands all such immeasurable kalpas.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that such sentient beings, having previously been in such a place, with such a name, such a lineage, such a class, such physical characteristics, such appearance, such features, such food and drink, such a lifespan, and having experienced such matters of suffering and pleasure—all these the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to recollect through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to recollect, discern, and fully understand all such modes of activity and locations—whether for themselves or others—including how these sentient beings pass away from this place and are reborn in that place, or pass away from that place and are reborn here, and how they die and take birth in such various ways across many different lifetimes. They can thus know all such diverse past abodes in their entirety.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because this bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), through the power of recollecting past lives, he is well able to recollect all his own past existences in the prior limit; he is fully able to comprehend them and also to recollect them."
He is able to recollect and know all the various, manifold, and immeasurable past lives of other sentient beings and other individuals throughout the prior limit of time.

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to recollect, in accordance with their mindfulness, the causes for the arising of their own roots of goodness from the past; they are also able to recollect, in accordance with their mindfulness, the causes for the arising of the roots of goodness of all sentient beings from the past. In this way, they thoroughly understand all such recollections.

Śāriputra! By means of the power of knowledge regarding past lives and immeasurable skillful means, this bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates his own roots of goodness toward awakening, enabling sentient beings to each remember and recognize all their own roots of goodness, and further causing sentient beings to diligently practice the gathering of the bodhicitta; thus, he knows all such things through recollection.

Furthermore, he is able to recollect all the causes of suffering and happiness from his previous lives, and he thoroughly understands that these causes all lead to impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth. Śāriputra!

Once this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has understood this, he is free from pride and arrogance regarding the bodhisattva practices; he is free from pride and arrogance regarding material wealth, free from pride and arrogance regarding retinues, and free from pride and arrogance regarding sovereignty. He is free from pride and arrogance regarding the desire to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, free from pride and arrogance regarding the desire to become Śakra, Lord of the Devas, free from pride and arrogance regarding the desire to become a Brahmā, Lord of the World-Spheres, and free from pride and arrogance regarding the desire to become a World-Protecting Heavenly King. He is free from pride and arrogance regarding attachment to rebirth in various realms, and free from pride and arrogance regarding the pursuit of the riches and pleasures of a king of desires. He only accepts existence through the power of his vows for the sake of maturing sentient beings.

Śāriputra! Thus, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands that all things ultimately lead to impermanence, suffering, and non-self, they are well able to censure, despise, and feel revulsion toward the afflictions and conditioned formations of the past. In the present life, they do not admit such afflictions any further; even for the sake of life-threatening or severe suffering, they will never commit unwholesome dharmas or various evil deeds.

Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates all previously accumulated roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, causing those roots of goodness currently being accumulated to increase and expand. This is because he wishes to embrace all sentient beings and remain far removed from all forms of unequal dedication.

Having perfected such roots of goodness as these, this bodhisattva mahāsattva succeeds to the lineage of the Triple Gem, ensuring that it remains unbroken, all for the sake of dedicating [the merit] toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"Śāriputra! You should know that it is through the power of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mindfulness and concentration that they are thus able to accomplish immeasurable, subtle, and sublime wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they attain this recollection of the wondrous conditions of past lives, as they dwell with supreme stability within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Thus, mindfulness is firm and unshakable because it is gathered through the skillful means of discernment;
thus, mindfulness is free from agitation because the work of meditative concentration has been well-cultivated.
Thus, mindfulness is free from agitation because it is well-sustained by sublime śamatha;
thus, mindfulness is free from delusion because it is well-aided by vipaśyanā.
Thus, through such recollection, one is free from coarseness, because one has well-realized purity and manifests sublime wisdom.
Thus, through such recollection, one is able to maintain mindfulness skillfully, because one does not forget any thoughts from the distant past.
Thus one recollects the great treasure-store of jewels, because the provisions of merit have been well accumulated;
thus one recollects without depending on others, because the provisions of wisdom have been well accumulated.
Thus, by means of such recollection, one has reached the further shore, for the provisions for the perfections have been well accumulated.

In this way, Śāriputra, you should know that all immeasurable and boundless sublime and wholesome dharmas are sustained by the power of mindfulness; thus, in both the past and the present, one gives rise to recollection and the quality of non-forgetfulness.

Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, based upon the perfection of meditative concentration, through which the wisdom of his activities is fully perfected.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s supernormal knowledge of the realization of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*),
and what is called the perfection of the activity of the knowledge of the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power?

Śāriputra! By relying on the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting in the accomplishment of the cultivation of the meditative absorption of desire and the formations of abandonment; likewise, they attain the basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the cultivation of the meditative absorptions of diligence, mind, and investigation, along with the formations of abandonment.

Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon such factors that assist and inspire—namely, desire, diligence, mind, and investigation—and because he has thoroughly cultivated, perfectly established, and attained mastery over them, he is able to skillfully practice the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Śāriputra! Once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they realize the supernormal power of mastery over their own will (*kāma-vaśitā*) according to their aspirations, and are able to manifest various kinds of miraculous transformations.
Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations, they cultivate them all for the sake of liberating all sentient beings. Śāriputra!

If there are sentient beings who should be tamed by seeing such supernatural transformations and miraculous manifestations, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accordingly displays such infinite supernatural transformations as may be appropriate for them—whether manifesting physical forms, manifesting majestic power, or bestowing secret empowerment—and through these means, those sentient beings attain liberation and deliverance.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery (*ṛddhipāda*), manifest various physical forms to discipline sentient beings? Śāriputra!"
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe that sentient beings can only be tamed after seeing or hearing such various manifestations.

The bodhisattva then manifests these forms according to what those beings think of, whether manifesting as the form of a Tathāgata, or the form of a pratyekabuddha, or the form of a śrāvaka, or the form of Śakra, Lord of Devas, or the form of Brahmā, King of the Brahmā World, or the form of a Lokapāla Heavenly King, or the form of a Cakravartin Universal Monarch; in this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to manifest all such other forms as required for the sake of transforming and delivering beings.

Even unto those who are to be tamed by manifesting the physical forms of animals or by any other means whatsoever, he immediately manifests such forms and expounds the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva manifest various powers through the supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery? Śāriputra!"

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perceive that sentient beings possess excessive pride in their strength, along with anger, arrogance, and negligence, and that those who are deeply steeped in such traits can be tamed by means of power, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest such spiritual powers according to what is appropriate for them. They may manifest the power of Mahānagna, or one-quarter of the power of Nārāyaṇa, or half of the full portion of the power of Nārāyaṇa, or the complete and full portion of the power of Nārāyaṇa; in this manner, they gradually increase it even to double its amount, thereby taming, transforming, and delivering those sentient beings.

Śāriputra! By the power of the supernormal knowledge of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) derived from the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva can lift up Sumeru, the greatest king of mountains, with two fingers and turn it about with ease, just as if picking up a single *āmra* fruit.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, this king of mountains was cast away to other boundless worlds.

This king of mountains rises sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas in height and measures eighty-four thousand yojanas in breadth; composed of the four precious substances, it is supreme in both height and width.

Because the bodhisattva dwells in the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), even if he were to cast [this world] to another direction, there would be no impairment or diminution of the bodhisattva’s power. Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the bases of psychic power, he can take this trichiliocosm— extending as far as its limits in length and breadth, from the mass of the water-circle up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)— and hold it in his palm for the duration of an eon, manifesting all manner of dignified postures (*īryāpatha*) without any hindrance.
Śāriputra! In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to manifest miraculous transformations according to the needs of beings, all of which are immeasurable and inconceivable.

Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas achieve such great power through their emanations so that sentient beings who possess excessive pride in their strength, anger, arrogance, and negligence may see and hear the bodhisattvas manifest these miraculous transformations; thereby, all their reliance on strength, their conceit, anger, arrogance, and negligence are utterly destroyed.
Once the Bodhisattva has understood that [the beings] have been tamed, he teaches them the essentials of the Dharma as is appropriate for each.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attain the wisdom of empowerment through the supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery?
Śāriputra! By means of such empowered wisdom-power, whatever the bodhisattva mahāsattva brings to mind through this empowerment is immediately accomplished. Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to apply his mindfulness so that the deep and vast great ocean becomes like a cow’s footprint, he can, by the power of that very thought, cause this great ocean to be as large as a cow’s footprint.

Furthermore, if one wishes to conceive of a shallow, minute cow's footprint as being like the great ocean, then by that very thought, he causes the dimensions of that cow's footprint to become equal to the great ocean.
Moreover, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to transform the great fires that consume the kalpa into a mass of water through focused intention, it shall immediately become a mass of water according to that intention.
If he focuses his intention on transforming the calamity of water into the calamity of fire, the calamity of fire shall immediately arise according to that intention.
Śāriputra! To state it briefly, regarding all gateways of the supernormal power of mental application, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains accomplishment in whatever they apply their mindfulness to.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva applies their focused attention such that lower, middling, or superior dharmas are mutually transformed, they shall achieve success in accordance with that very intention.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Whatever objects a bodhisattva-mahāsattva empowers with his focused attention through supernormal powers become steadfast and difficult to destroy, remaining unalterable; nothing in any world can cause them to waver or vanish.

Neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas, nor the various devas such as Śakra, nor Māra, nor Brahmā, nor any other beings in the world are able to shake or cause the disappearance of this [teaching] in accordance with the Dharma, except for the Lords of the Dharma, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Śāriputra! You should know that it is through the power of such mindful sustenance and empowerment that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest majestic spiritual power for the sake of proclaiming the true Dharma to those sentient beings who possess various vast, extraordinary, and marvelous transformations, solely out of respect for them.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā), they attain such sovereign mastery over the supernormal power of psychic transformation (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna) that it is never lost; they transcend the realms of all māras and afflictions, and enter into the realm of all Buddhas.

The accumulation of all roots of goodness and provisions for skillful means that do not afflict these sentient beings cannot be interrupted by any Māras, hosts of Māra’s armies, or gods of majestic power.

Śāriputra! This is called the perfection of the knowledge and activity of the supernormal power of realization through the bases of psychic power, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain these supernormal powers by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration?
What is the meaning and principle of these supernormal powers?"
Furthermore, by what means is it called "wisdom"?

Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates forms and images, this is called "supernormal power" (abhijñā); if they can thoroughly understand that forms and images are subject to the law of exhaustion, yet do not realize that exhaustion, this is called "wisdom."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To be able to hear all sounds and voices is called supernormal power (abhijñā); to be able to know that the prior limit of sounds and voices is fundamentally inexpressible is called wisdom (jñāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If one can thoroughly comprehend the mental activities of sentient beings, this is called supernormal power (abhijñā); if one can thoroughly comprehend that the nature of the mind is quiescent, yet does not realize that extinction, this is called wisdom (jñāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one can recollect the limits of the past, this is called supernormal power; if one can understand the three periods of time without obstruction, this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To come and go among the various buddha-fields is called supernormal power (abhijñā); to know that these fields have the same nature as empty space is called wisdom (jñāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Because of the thorough understanding of the arising of phenomena, it is called supernormal power (abhijñā); because of the contemplation of the equality of phenomena, it is called wisdom (jñāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Because it clearly penetrates all worlds, it is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*); because it does not mingle with any worldly things, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, because its majestic power outshines all the gods—Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors—it is called supernormal power; because it thoroughly understands that the realization of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is inferior, it is called wisdom.

Śāriputra! Such powers and wisdom as these are immeasurable and inconceivable in their merit; this is called the perfection of the karma of supernatural powers and wisdom attained through the diligent application of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize boundless, profound, and wondrous states of meditative absorption."
Why is this? Śāriputra,

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes a mind accumulated with countless afflictions, to that same extent he also abides in a mind endowed with countless merits of the provisions for meditative concentration (dhyāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

To whatever extent all those sentient beings give rise to various forms of distraction through their afflictive minds, to that same extent the bodhisattva mahāsattva should also accumulate the merit of the provisions for meditative concentration (dhyāna-sambhāra) toward them.

Śāriputra! These are called the meditative concentrations realized by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are immeasurable and boundless, all being initiated by the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the concentration realized by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly profound and subtle; when a bodhisattva dwells within it with equanimity at the appropriate time, this state is called *samāhita*.
Śāriputra! What is meant by "equanimous gathering"? Śāriputra!
As for *samāhita*, it is so named because this meditative concentration draws forth and gathers the nature of equality of sentient beings;
Śāriputra, *samāhita* is so called because it draws forth and gathers the equality of the mind.
Furthermore, *samāhita* refers to the drawing forth and gathering of the equality of aspiration and resolve.
Furthermore, *samāhita* refers to the drawing forth and gathering of the equality of skillful means.
Furthermore, *samāhita* refers to the drawing forth and inclusion of the equality of superior aspiration and resolve.
Furthermore, *samāhita* refers to the drawing forth and inclusion of the equality of *dāna*; it can also draw forth and include the equality of *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñā*.
Furthermore, *samāhita* refers to the fact that it draws forth and encompasses the equality of all phenomena. Śāriputra,
this is called the *samāhita* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, because profound and wondrous meditative concentration draws forth and encompasses the nature of equality of all phenomena.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, by virtue of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s reliance on the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), the subtle, secret, profound, and wondrous meditative concentration he attains can be entered only by wisdom; it is also termed samāpatti."
Śāriputra! What is called *samāpatti*? Śāriputra!
Such sublime meditative concentration and other dharmas are of this nature. Why is this?

If the equality of bodhi is the equality of all sentient beings, and if the equality of all sentient beings is the equality of all dharmas, then the ability to equanimously realize and enter into this equality is what is called *samāpatti*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If the equality of emptiness is the equality of all phenomena, then the ability to realize and enter into this equality is what is called *samāpatti*.
Thus, the nature of signlessness, wishlessness, and non-activity are all equal; this is the equality of all phenomena. If one can realize and enter into this equality, it is called *samāpatti*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If the nature of the mind is equal, then all phenomena are equal; if one can realize and enter this state of equality, it is called samāpatti.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of the state of equality regarding these dhyānas and samāpattis, all of which are due to the perfection of dhyāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this sublime and equanimous meditative concentration, giving rise to a mind of equality toward all sentient beings— whether they have been beneficial or harmful— without any partiality or discrimination."

Therefore, the bodhisattva maintains an equanimous mind toward earth, an equanimous mind toward water, an equanimous mind toward fire, an equanimous mind toward wind, and an equanimous mind toward space; without distinction of high or low, nor any sense of dejection, they abide securely and firmly, realizing immovability. Their minds remain constantly in meditative concentration throughout all modes of conduct, yet they do not discriminate among the modes of conduct in which they abide.

With a mind matured in nature, he delights in dwelling in profound meditative concentration; he is neither agitated nor elated, and is free from wavering. Far removed from all dullness, his speech is without confusion; he understands meaning and the Dharma, and skillfully discerns all appropriate times—namely, *kāla*, *velā*, and *samaya*. He is adept at conforming to all worldly ways, yet his nature remains unmixed with the world. Having transcended the eight worldly concerns such as gain and loss, he cannot be defiled by any afflictions or delusions.

They remain far removed from places of confusion and clamor, always dwelling peacefully in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) which is equal and impartial; without relinquishing profound meditative concentration, they manifest all worldly activities.

Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s entry into such immeasurable merits by relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); you should know that these are all initiated through skillful means and sublime wisdom (prajñā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), realize this sublime wisdom and skillful means?
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva binds the mind to its object through the power of great compassion in order to deliver sentient beings, this is called skillful means (upāya).
To realize and enter into tranquility and ultimate quiescence is called wisdom (prajñā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one is able to realize and enter the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddha, this is called skillful means (*upāya*).
That there is not a single dharma that can be conceptually apprehended or known is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one is able to realize and enter the contemplation that encompasses all phenomena, this is called skillful means (upāya).
If one contemplates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without confusion, this is called wisdom (prajñā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To equanimously realize and enter the adornments of the Buddha-body so that they manifest before one is called skillful means (upāya).
To observe that the nature of the Dharma-body has no location is called wisdom (prajñā).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To equanimously realize and enter into the words, phrases, and Brahma-like voices uttered by all Buddhas is called skillful means.
To observe that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is ineffable is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To enter into equanimity with a mind that abides in the diamond-like samādhi (vajropamasamādhi) is called skillful means.
To maintain mindfulness without distraction and contemplate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one thus abides in meditative concentration to bring sentient beings to maturity through their original vows, this is called skillful means.
To observe that all sentient beings are devoid of a self-nature is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one generates all superior roots of goodness by taking those superior objects as the focal point of concentration, this is called skillful means.
If one is able to observe that there is neither root nor abiding, this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one cultivates and purifies a buddha-field so that it manifests before one, this is called skillful means.
To contemplate that the land is equal to space, this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one brings forth meditative concentration to adorn the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
this is called skillful means (upāya).
If one dwells in meditative concentration and knows all phenomena,
this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one definitively initiates the turning of the wheel of the Dharma, this is called skillful means.
If one contemplates that the wheel of the Dharma being turned has no arising, this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Thus, the immeasurable factors of enlightenment and their provisions are equally realized, observed, and manifested before one;

this is called skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, the immeasurable afflictions are extinguished and the feverish distress is eliminated. The sublime bliss of the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) does not correspond with any phenomena; it is free from all signs (*nimitta*), yet fully knows all signs; it is far removed from all objects of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*). In this way, Śāriputra, they all enter the meditative concentrations belonging to the correct samādhi of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus fully cultivate such observation, this is called wisdom.

Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes such inexhaustible meditative concentration (dhyāna) is endowed with the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), no evil Māras can find an opportunity [to harm them]; they are then said to be securely established as a vessel for the teachings of all Buddhas.

Śāriputra! Such skillful means and such sublime wisdom are called the perfection of meditative concentration fully accomplished by a bodhisattva mahāsattva; all of these are initiated by sublime wisdom and skillful means.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), the bodhisattva mahāsattva fully accomplishes non-retrogressive supernormal powers (abhijñā). He is well able to establish the activities performed through wisdom; these are not initiated by the power of pride. Playing with supernormal powers, he manifests in the world; all his actions abide in supernormal powers, as he initiates all great deeds of the world."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these supernormal powers (abhijñā) are the mark of great wisdom, for they are fully endowed with the subtle and wondrous functions of both the mundane and the supramundane.
These supernormal powers are the mark of great insight, for they directly perceive all phenomena of both the mundane and the supramundane.
This supernormal power has the characteristic of inexhaustibility, for it pervades all things everywhere like space.
This supernormal power views all forms with equanimity, for it perceives them with equality within both the realm of form and the formless realm.
This supernormal power is well able to enter the dharma-gate of sounds, because the equality of sounds throughout the past is realized.
This supernormal power is able to observe all mental activities of sentient beings, because their nature is directly perceived.
This supernormal power is well able to recollect all kalpas, because it discerns and understands the limits of the past and the future.
This supernormal power is well able to manifest immeasurable miraculous transformations ever present before one, because it is free from the characteristics of volitional application.
This supernormal power consists in the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows, because it observes the *kāla* and *samaya* without missing the proper time.
This supernormal power is noble and supramundane, because it constitutes the stage of definitive discernment regarding all phenomena.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Such supernormal powers are subtle, wondrous, and profoundly deep, such that they cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Such supernormal powers possess great majestic virtue and are well able to subdue all sentient beings.
Such supernormal powers possess great merit and activity, for they realize the empowerment of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the sovereign mastery over all phenomena.

Thus, Śāriputra, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of these non-regressive, supreme supernormal powers by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). They are well able to establish the activities performed through wisdom; they are not initiated by the power of pride.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Forty-nine;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Bodhisattvapiṭaka Assembly, Part Twelve, Chapter Sixteen: The Perfection of Dhyāna, Part Two.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of dhyāna, they attain such non-retrogressive supernormal powers!"
They are well able to establish the activities performed by wisdom. Śāriputra,
you should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained this supernormal knowledge!

From a pure mind, a bright white mind, a luminous mind, an unclouded mind, a mind free from secondary afflictions, a well-tamed mind, a well-peaceful mind, and a well-cultivated mind—such characteristics of the mind arise, and they are initiated by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, and samāpatti.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the world through intentional rebirth; it is not a birth born of bondage, nor does he pass away and take rebirth through the power of bondage.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are liberated from all false conceptualizations, liberated from the bonds of all unreal afflictions, and liberated from the basis of all inverted and deluded attachments.
Therefore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, in accordance with the worlds he appears in, is born from liberation, passes away in liberation, and takes birth in liberation. Śāriputra!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having manifested birth and already accomplished the Great Vehicle, fulfills all the true teachings of the Buddhas and travels throughout the ten directions to extensively seek the Buddha-dharma. Although his will seeks that which is sought, he is without grasping and without attainment; entering into the Buddha-dharmas, they immediately become all dharmas, and entering into all dharmas, they immediately become the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, the bodhisattva enters into the Buddha-dharma and all phenomena, yet does not act in accordance with those phenomena or non-phenomena. "Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when seeking all phenomena as they truly are, abides in non-appropriation and non-attainment, then there is not a single phenomenon that can be reckoned by calculation."
Why is this? Because all phenomena transcend the path of calculation.
If one can thoroughly comprehend the equality of phenomena, then one does not cling to what is dharma or what is non-dharma.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is without grasping.
If one calculates that there is meaning within them, one will instead obtain vast meaninglessness.

If there is one who is skillfully able not to conceptualize "meaning," then because both meaning and non-meaning do not manifest before them, the one who does not perceive meaning possesses unimpeded awakened wisdom in all places.
If this bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus awaken to non-obstruction, they will obtain unobstructed awakening;
if there is unobstructed awakening, then one has no attachment toward anything;
if there is no attachment, then there is no dwelling; if there is no dwelling, then there is no lack; if there is no lack...
When one is devoid [of craving], there is neither delusion nor seeking; if there is neither delusion nor seeking, there is neither confusion nor doubt;
if there is neither confusion nor doubt, there is no sense of "mine"; if there is no sense of "mine," there is no grasping;
if there is no grasping, there is no attachment; if there is no attachment, there is no contention; if there is no contention, this is...

Thus, there is the dharma of the śramaṇa who is without contention; if one possesses this dharma of the śramaṇa who is without contention, then one is entirely unimpeded, unobstructed, and equal to space in one's seeking.

If one can seek in a manner equal to that space, then one is not bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If one is not bound to any of these realms, then there is no [suffering].
Regarding color-appearance and dimensional form, if these color-appearance and dimensional form do not exist, then one can thus follow and awaken to them;
if one can thus follow and awaken to them, then one can thus penetrate and realize them.
Śāriputra! How is it called "thoroughly awakening to and penetrating"? Śāriputra!
