Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus awaken to and penetrate the fact that not even the slightest dharma is to be found therein, this is called awakening to and penetrating. Śāriputra!

Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into equality through such realization, awakening, and thorough penetration, it is said that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), achieve marvelous and unprecedented qualities.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is meant by 'a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishing marvelous and unprecedented dharmas'? Śāriputra!"

By virtue of relying on the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he constantly contemplates selflessness;

although he practices great compassion (*karuṇā*), he knows there are no sentient beings (*sattva*); although he practices great sympathetic joy (*muditā*), he knows there is no life-principle (*jīva*);
although he practices great equanimity (*upekṣā*), he knows there is no person (*pudgala*); and although he extensively practices great giving (*dāna*)...
The mind is ever harmonious and compliant; though it takes pure precepts as its object, the mind remains eternally tranquil;
though it follows the practice of patience under insult, the mind is boundless; though it exerts itself with diligence, the mind is able to discern and gather;
though it enters the various meditative concentrations, it observes with a correct mind; and though it pervasively employs wisdom, the mind has no place of activity.
Although they practice the four foundations of mindfulness, their minds are without objective referents and without mental engagement;
although they practice the four right efforts, their minds are without arising or ceasing; although they practice the bases of psychic power, their minds are without conceptual proliferation;
although they practice pure faith, their minds are without attachment; although they practice right diligence, their minds are always detached; although they practice...
While maintaining mindfulness, the mind is ever-sovereign; though abiding in samādhi, the mind realizes equanimity;
though practicing prajñā, the mind is fundamentally rootless; though practicing the powers, the mind is indestructible;
though practicing the factors of enlightenment, it analyzes bodhi; though practicing the factors of the path, the mind has nothing to cultivate; and though...
While practicing śamatha, the mind remains eternally quiescent; though practicing vipaśyanā, the mind is free from fixed contemplation;
though cultivating the Noble Truths, there is ultimate and universal knowledge; though maturing sentient beings, the mind is fundamentally pure;
though upholding the True Dharma, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not impaired; and though purifying buddha-fields...
Yet their minds are equal to space; though they realize the dharma of non-arising, their minds have nothing to be attained;
though they practice on the stages of non-retrogression, the nature of their minds never regresses; though they obtain all the wondrous marks, they know that the nature of phenomena is markless;
though they adorn the site of enlightenment, their minds roam through the triple world while constantly abiding in the wheel of universal transformation; and though they subdue the armies of Māra...
Yet among all sentient beings, there is nothing that can subdue or overcome them; though they know that all phenomena are the nature of Bodhi, their minds follow through with clear realization;
though they turn the wheel of Dharma, their minds abide in the Dharmatā without returning or turning;
and though they further manifest Great Parinirvāṇa, their minds remain ever equal toward the nature of birth and death.
In this way, Śāriputra, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s equal realization, awakening, and thorough penetration.
Know that such a marvelous and unprecedented phenomenon is accomplished through the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the characteristic of a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the bodhisattva meditative concentration by relying on the perfection of meditative concentration?
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva’s meditative concentration does not abide in its own nature, for the sake of fulfilling such samādhi.
A bodhisattva’s meditative concentration is without relish, for it is not for the sake of attachment to one's own peace and happiness.
The meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of a bodhisattva takes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its object, for the purpose of severing all the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.
The meditative concentration of a bodhisattva is certainly non-retrogressive, because it takes the nature of aspiration and the nature of supremacy as its objects.
The bodhisattva’s meditative concentration polishes and brings forth supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because it thoroughly understands the mental activities of all sentient beings.
The bodhisattva’s meditative concentration is joyful and delightful, because it is well able to manifest mastery over the mind (*citta-vaśitā*).
The meditative concentration of a bodhisattva thoroughly understands all *samāpattis*, for it outshines all realms of form and formlessness.
This meditative concentration of a bodhisattva is quiescent, supremely quiescent, and proximate to quiescence, for it outshines the concentrations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of a bodhisattva is free from conceptual discrimination, for it is utterly perfected and supremely pure.
The category of practice (*caryā-pakṣa*) of a bodhisattva’s meditative concentration is most excellent, for the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) has been eternally eliminated.
The bodhisattva’s meditative concentration transcends through wisdom, for it transcends all worlds.
The bodhisattva’s meditative concentration serves as the foremost guide for the inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings, for it is well able to deliver and liberate them.
The meditative concentration of a bodhisattva perpetuates the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it remains uninterrupted, because the meditative concentration of a Buddha is inexhaustible.
The meditative concentration of a bodhisattva is most exalted, because *samāhita* (equipoise) is constantly present before them.
The bodhisattva’s meditative concentration proceeds with mastery, because all that he undertakes is perfectly fulfilled.
This meditative concentration of the bodhisattva constitutes the Great Self, for it takes sublime wisdom as its Great Self.

Śāriputra! Such immeasurable meditative concentrations of bodhisattvas are all brought forth by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through reliance upon the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what dharmas serve as the precursors to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s perfection of meditative concentration? Śāriputra,"
Regarding the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*): it is preceded by the wisdom of mental quiescent observation;
it is preceded by the mind abiding on a single object; it is preceded by the mind being free from distraction and agitation;
it is preceded by the mind being firmly established; it is preceded by the mind of *śamatha*; and it is preceded by the mind of *samādhi*.
Guidance: it is preceded by the faculty of concentration, preceded by the power of concentration,
preceded by the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, preceded by right concentration,
preceded by the meditative absorptions and liberations, preceded by the nine successive attainments, and preceded by the nine cessations.
Taking the Dharma as the precursor; taking all wholesome dharmas as the precursor; taking the subduing of the enemy of afflictions as the precursor;
taking the complete fulfillment of the aggregate of samādhi as the precursor;
taking the various samādhis of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as the precursor; and taking the various samādhis of the Buddha Bhagavāns as the precursor.
They serve as the precursors. Śāriputra!
Such immeasurable meditative concentrations are all dharmas that serve as precursors to the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless dharmas that realize tranquility, all of which are preceded by the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā). Śāriputra!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
For the sake of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply diligent effort within this, fully training in and practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Having reached the further shore through meditative concentration and liberation, They have diligently practiced these deeds for oceans of many eons.
Their minds are pure and free from turbidity or defilement; Untainted by worldly dharmas, they are like lotus flowers."
There is a great meditative concentration named "Universal Illumination"; by practicing this concentration, one reaches the other shore.
It is also called "Pure Adornment of Moonlight," and it is further named "Adorned with Lightning Light."
Some were named Noble Conduct or Courageous Mind; some were named Stainless Light in Samādhi, or Virtue Accomplished in Precepts, or Free from Sorrow;
some were named Sovereign Turn of All Dharmas, or Dharma Torch, or Dharma Hero; some were named Mountain Majesty Sovereign in Dharma.
Some naturally transcend through the knowledge of the True Dharma; some uphold the True Dharma with sublime purity;
some are named for the concentration that observes the minds of others; and some are named for the Radiance of the Jewel of the True Dharma.
Also named the Banner of Victory Adorned by the Extinction of Delusion, there is a samādhi named Crushing the Power of Māra;
or it is named Severing Doubt and Non-attachment, or a samādhi named Lamp of Tranquility;
or the Power of Exalted Victory, or the Ten Powers, or named Reverent Hand of Great Renown.
Some are named Sustainer of Mountains, Well-Abiding; some are Sumeru, the Great Bright Lamp;
some are named Invincible, Victorious over the Victorious; some are named Wisdom-Torch or Wisdom-Practice;
some are Boundless Wisdom or Sovereign; some are named Awakening Wisdom, Tranquil Samādhi.
Some are named Moon-Pure Sun-Sound, Or Nārāyaṇa Who Crushes Arrogance,
Or Well-Subduing-Lion’s-Roar; Some are named Far-Removed-from-Diverse-Conceptions,
Or Revolving, or Returning, Or Unblinking-Eye-Pure-Power.
Some name this concentration "Mindfulness of the Buddhas," Others name it "Mindfulness of the Dharma" or "Mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
Some name it "The Turning of Wisdom" or "Entry into Emptiness," Others name it "Signlessness" or "Wishlessness.
Some call it the "Vajra-like" or the "Peaceful Ground," Others the "Vajra Ground" or the "Exalted and Supreme."
Some are named King of Mountains or Unblinking; some are Boundless Turning or Pure Sound;
some are Free from Affliction or Observation; some are Wondrous Void or Like Space;
some give rise to vast and manifold merits; some are Inclined toward Awakening Wisdom or Mindfulness Wisdom.

Either inexhaustible in debate or continuous; Either boundless in speech with words that never end, or indestructible in performing what is well-done; Or called "Investigation," or "Delighting the Multitude";
Or called "Manifesting Loving-kindness," or "Extensive Compassion"; Or "Entering into Joy," or "Rejoicing."
Some abandon or release two kinds of hindrances; some are named Dharmaprabha or Dharmārtha;
some are Vajradhvaja or Jñānasāgara; some are Vimuktisāra or Saṃpraharṣa;
some are named Jñānolkā or Acalasamādhi; and some samādhis are named Vijayapadma.
Some are named Dharma-Selecting or Immovable; some are named Wisdom-Supreme or Tranquility;
some are named Boundless Light or Buddha-Ocean; some are named Liberation or Bestowing Wisdom;
some are named Tathāgata’s Sublime Adornment; and some are named Boundless Supreme Radiance.
Some call it the Land Adorned with Joy, others the Land that Delights the Minds of Beings.
There is a samādhi named "At All Times," the samādhi of the Path Accordant with Bodhi;
there is a samādhi named "Reaching the Other Shore," and the Samādhi of the Jewel-Crest Adorned with the Flowers of the Factors of Enlightenment.
Some bestow the firm liberation of ambrosia; some are like wind, unmoving yet radiating intense light;
some are named Sea-Tide, Ditch, or Treasure-Treasury; others possess the power of the peaks of Mount Nārāyaṇa.
It is called the meaning of the vastness of supernormal powers, The sublime and excellent samādhi of gathering-in.
Or this concentration is named Great Pervasive Illumination, The realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Having realized such tranquil samādhi, And countless other billions beyond measure, The Bodhisattva practices dhyāna to reach the further shore; Their merit is vast and immeasurable.
Whether walking or standing, he constantly dwells within the sphere of meditative concentration; his mind is undisturbed and ever serene.
Whether sitting or reclining, he remains within stillness and absorption; there is no posture in which he is not in samādhi.
Abiding in meditative concentration, one can emit great sounds;
for the nature of all phenomena is eternally quiescent, free from discursive differentiation and lack of mastery, devoid of self, life-principle, and conceptualization.
Thus, together with other boundless and incalculable oceans of merit,
the wise Bodhisattva, out of compassion for all sentient beings, practices meditative concentration and reaches the further shore.
11. The Chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), Part One of Eleven. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
For the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon this and diligently practices the bodhisattva conduct.

Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they diligently and reverently listen to and uphold the subtle dharma-gates of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; whether reading or reciting them, they investigate their meanings and principles. Having attained thorough mastery themselves, they further extensively proclaim, expound, and reveal their essentials to others.

Śāriputra! If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having heard what I have taught, practice in accordance with the Dharma, and who—regarding this subtle dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka—listen to it with earnest gravity, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, investigate and study it, penetrate its meaning, and having explained and extensively revealed it to others, should know that such persons realize the marks of this inexhaustible wisdom.
Śāriputra, what are the characteristics of such wisdom?
How does one enter into its realization? Śāriputra!
What is called wisdom has hearing as its characteristic; because Bodhisattvas realize and enter into it according to reality, it is therefore described as the characteristic of inexhaustible wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Such characteristics as these I shall explain in detail. To wit, these characteristics are:
the characteristic of the desire and aspiration for the true Dharma; the characteristic of the desire and understanding [for it];
the characteristic of skillful means; the characteristic of virtuous friends; and the characteristic of being free from pride.
It has the characteristic of reverence toward those who are learned; the characteristic of honoring them; the characteristic of circumambulating them;
the characteristic of humble respect; the characteristic of attending upon them; the characteristic of listening attentively; the characteristic of serving them; the characteristic of reflection;
the characteristic of non-distraction; the characteristic of regarding them as precious jewels; and the characteristic of regarding them as excellent medicine.
...the characteristic of pacifying all notions of illness; the characteristic of mindfulness toward the vessel; the characteristic of inclining toward awakening;

the characteristic of delighting in great wisdom; the characteristic of entering into realization; the characteristic of insatiability in hearing the Dharma; the characteristic of relinquishing increase [of afflictions];
the characteristic of being disciplined and free from the fuel [of craving]; the characteristic of associating with those who have heard much; regarding all...
It has the characteristic of delighting in purposeful activity, the characteristic of physical well-being, and the characteristic of mental vigor.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it has the characteristic of listening to the Dharma without weariness and the characteristic of hearing the true meaning.
It has the characteristic of listening to the sublime Dharma; it has the characteristic of listening to right conduct; it has the characteristic of listening to realized wisdom;
it has the characteristic of listening to the *pāramitās*; it has the characteristic of listening to the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
it has the characteristic of listening to the methods of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*); it has the characteristic of listening to skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Listening...

Hearing that the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are its characteristic; hearing that supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are its characteristic; hearing that right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samyaksmṛti-samprajanya*) are its characteristic;

hearing that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are its characteristic; hearing that the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are its characteristic; hearing that the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) are its characteristic;

hearing that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is its characteristic; hearing that impermanence (*anityatā*) is its characteristic; hearing that suffering (*duḥkha*) [is its characteristic].
The Dharma has the characteristic of being a sign; it has the characteristic of hearing non-self; it has the characteristic of hearing tranquility;
it has the characteristic of hearing emptiness; it has the characteristic of hearing signlessness; it has the characteristic of hearing wishlessness;
it has the characteristic of hearing the absence of effort; and it has the characteristic of hearing the application of roots of goodness.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, it has mastery as its characteristic; hearing the Dharma as its characteristic; counteracting defilement as its characteristic; subduing all conceptualizations of affliction as its characteristic; praising the wise as its characteristic; attending upon the noble ones as its characteristic; distancing oneself from those who are not noble as its characteristic; listening to the noble ones as its characteristic; listening to the faculties as its characteristic; listening to the cultivation of mindfulness as its characteristic; listening to the factors of enlightenment as its characteristic; listening to the Noble Eightfold Path as its characteristic; and listening to the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, unimpeded eloquence, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as its characteristic.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
You should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this, they understand it; when they understand it, they practice it correctly.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the characteristics of the subtle dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka upon hearing them, their skillful means are immeasurable.
I shall now briefly explain forty-one kinds.
Śāriputra, what are these characteristics?

First, if there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to a desire for joy toward this Dharma-gate, it should be known that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already heard it and understood it upon hearing; having understood it, they then practice the correct conduct.

Second, if there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to aspiration and understanding toward this Dharma-gate, it should be known that such a person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
Third, if there are bodhisattvas who skillfully enter this Dharma-gate, it should be known that such persons have heard, understood, and practiced the correct conduct.
Fourth, if there is a bodhisattva who associates with virtuous friends, this person will listen to, understand, and practice the correct conduct.
Fifth, if there is a bodhisattva who has no pride regarding extensive learning, this person will listen to, understand, and practice the correct conduct.
Sixth, if there is a bodhisattva who reveres those who are learned, this person will listen, understand, and practice the correct conduct.
Seventh, if there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to a mind of respect toward those who are learned, this person will listen, understand, and practice the correct conduct.
Eighth, if there is a bodhisattva who circumambulates and reverently honors those who possess great learning, this person thereby listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
Ninth, if there is a bodhisattva who maintains a humble mind toward those who possess great learning, this person thereby listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
Tenth, if there is a bodhisattva who associates with those of great learning, that person thereby listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
Eleventh, if there is a bodhisattva who, regarding those of great learning, lends an ear and listens attentively, that person thereby listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
12. If there is a bodhisattva who serves, greets, and receives those who possess great learning, this person thereby listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

13. If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the meaning and intent of what has been heard from those possessing great learning with a concentrated and undistracted mind, this person thereby listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
14. If there is a bodhisattva who conceives the thought of rare treasure toward extensive learning, this person listens to, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
15. If there is a bodhisattva who conceives the thought of excellent medicine toward extensive learning, this person listens to, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

Sixteenth, if a bodhisattva can give rise to the thought that extinguishes greed, hatred, and delusion regarding what has been heard, this person is one who listens, understands, and practices the right conduct.
17. If there is a bodhisattva who, having heard much, is able to retain what has been heard, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
18. If there is a bodhisattva who attains awakening regarding the Dharma, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
19. If there is a bodhisattva who delights in wisdom through extensive learning, this person listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
20. If there is a bodhisattva who, having heard through extensive learning, attains awakening, this person listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
21. If there is a bodhisattva who hears [the Dharma] without weariness, this person is one who listens, understands, and practices right conduct.
22. If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching of *dāna*, increases their renunciation, this person is one who listens, understands, and practices right conduct.
23. If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching on śīla, guards the precepts, this person has heard, understood, and practices the correct conduct.
24. If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching on kṣānti, is able to cultivate patience, this person has heard, understood, and practices the correct conduct.

Twenty-fifth: If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching on *vīrya*, gives rise to right exertion and tireless diligence, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

Twenty-sixth: If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), enters into meditative concentration with an undistracted mind, this person is one who listens, understands, and practices the correct conduct (*samyakpratipatti*).

Twenty-seventh: If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching of *prajñā*, develops a resolute mind and cultivates wisdom for the sake of exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*), this person is one who listens, understands, and practices the right path.
28. If a bodhisattva gives rise to great joy toward what has been heard, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the right conduct.
29. If a bodhisattva, having heard the Dharma, finds their body to be well-adjusted, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the right conduct.
30. If a bodhisattva, having heard the Dharma, possesses a courageous and keen mind, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
31. If a bodhisattva, upon hearing a Mahāyāna sūtra, gives rise to faith and aspiration, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.
32. If a bodhisattva, having heard the teachings on the gathering of dharmas, enters into them with their mind, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

33. If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, immediately applies themselves to the body, feelings, mind, and dharmas, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

34. If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching on the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), turns away from or abandons unwholesome dharmas—whether already arisen or not yet arisen—and does not relinquish the cultivation of wholesome dharmas—whether already arisen or not yet arisen—then this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the right conduct.

Thirty-fifth: If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the teaching on the supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda), is able to practice them by generating lightness of body, lightness of mind, and lightness of desire, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the right conduct.

36. If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching on meditative concentration (dhyāna), reflects tranquilly and their mind enters into it, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

37. If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing that one should not practice contempt toward any phenomena, gives rise to great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sentient beings, great compassion (*karuṇā*) toward those entering suffering, great sympathetic joy (*muditā*) toward the true Dharma, and great equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward what is unwholesome, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

38. If there is a bodhisattva who, having heard the teaching on the faculties, directs his mind toward those faculties—namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, and the faculty of meditative concentration—then this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

Thirty-ninth: If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the teaching on the factors of enlightenment, directs his mind toward entering into the realization of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

Fortieth: If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the explanation of the factors of the path, directs his mind toward the true path to nirvana, this person is one who hears, understands, and practices the correct conduct.

Forty-first: If there is a bodhisattva who, having heard the exposition of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as unimpeded eloquence, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other immeasurable true dharmas of all Buddhas, enters into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with their mind; such a person, having thus heard the Dharma in accordance with the truth, is able to comprehend it upon hearing it, and having comprehended it, practices the correct conduct.
Śāriputra! I have already explained these forty-one dharmas that lead to the entry into the characteristics of hearing, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study. Śāriputra!
This is called the fundamental characteristic of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who acts as a bodhisattva practitioner should, with great reverence, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, and contemplate the meaning of this subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, thereby mastering the subtle dharma; furthermore, they should extensively analyze and explain it for others—this is the provision for practice."
Śāriputra! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva engage in correct practice regarding such dharmas? Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva engages in correct practice regarding the Dharma, it means establishing and abiding in practice exactly as taught; this is called engaging in correct practice regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, if one is able to not grasp at anything at all, this is called engaging in correct practice regarding the Dharma.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
if one grasps at dharmas, it is called wrong practice.
There is no possibility, nor any basis for it, that a person who clings to phenomena could attain liberation through such phenomena. Why is this?

Even for one who does not cling to a practitioner and has no engagement with phenomena, doubt should still arise because of the absence of functional activity; how much more so for one who clings to the practice of phenomena—is that not indeed a perverse practice?
Therefore, one should practice the right path without grasping at any phenomena.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which is without obstruction regarding all phenomena is called the right path.
If one does not disparage any phenomena, this is called right practice.
If one neither grasps nor rejects, neither gives rise to nor extinguishes any phenomena, this is called right practice.
Furthermore, if one neither joins with nor disperses from any phenomena, this is called right practice.
Moreover, Śāriputra, regarding what I have said:

if there were such a case where not even the slightest phenomenon could be seen or heard, nor could it be spoken of—in this way, all phenomena are neither obtainable through vision nor capable of being grasped.
Why is this? Because all phenomena possess but a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being signless.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The nature of all dharmas is fundamentally without marks.
If there were a bodhisattva who spoke of "marklessness," then marklessness itself would still be something that could be spoken of. Why is this?
Because both the signless and the signed are signless, one cannot say that "this is the signed" or "this is the signless.

Śāriputra, if there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who can realize that all such dharmic signs are themselves signless— being invisible, ungraspable, and understood according to the Dharma— this is called right practice.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has diligently practiced such right Dharma conduct, they shall realize and enter into the wisdom of unobstructed illumination regarding all phenomena.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
"This is called the characteristic of the correct practice of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The wise one who abides in correct practice Is well-established in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;..."
This person does not give rise to attachment toward phenomena; such is the characteristic of practice free from grasping.

They realize that all phenomena are not for the sake of emptiness, nor do they dwell in a state of equanimity regarding the emptiness of phenomena, nor do they grasp at empty phenomena as having any existence; such is the characteristic of correct practice free from grasping.
In regard to phenomena, there is neither grasping nor abandoning; nor is it that one takes phenomena as being phenomena.
This absence of grasping is called the characteristic of all phenomena; such is the characteristic of right practice without grasping.
If one’s knowledge regarding all phenomena is unimpeded, this wisdom burns away nothing that remains;
in this wisdom of burning away, there is no grasping—such is the characteristic of the correct practice regarding all phenomena.
The wise abide in the virtue of seclusion; they should arouse diligent effort toward the Dharma.
If they can act in reliance upon the rules of conduct, at that time they shall enter the gate of purity.
This gate of purity penetrates all phenomena, and likewise understands the various inclinations and understandings of sentient beings;
though the wise know there is nothing to be observed, they are nonetheless able to proclaim such a Dharma.
Having realized the ultimate truth within the profound Dharma, you constantly engage in the supreme discernment of its deep meaning;
you manifest boundless conduct of merit, your wisdom and vast learning being like the great ocean.
Regarding the words and meanings spoken therein, no one at all can ever fully realize them;
for both those words and meanings are boundless, and true, correct practice is eternally unmoving.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having reverently heard the subtle Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and even having explained them to others in accordance with the Dharma, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained illumination regarding all phenomena, capable of destroying all the darkness of ignorance and all cataracts."
Śāriputra! Such radiance is itself wisdom. Why is this?
Because they are able to clearly and accurately know all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas as they truly are,

these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having cultivated such dharmas and attained clear wisdom, will resolutely refrain from committing any unwholesome dharmas even at the cost of their lives or due to the causes and conditions of various sufferings.

Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to eternally extinguish unwholesome dharmas, he thoroughly penetrates whatever dharma he hears; having thus penetrated it, he is then called a Muni, one who is tranquil.
"Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This is called the characteristic of correct practice when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as when a person enters a dark room, Where all light is shrouded and cut off,
Though many forms and images are present, They are not seen by one without clear vision.
In this way, though a person exists Who internally possesses all clarity and understanding,"
Without hearing the True Dharma, how can one distinguish between good and evil?
Through much learning, one understands the Dharma; through much learning, one does not commit evil;
through much learning, one abandons what is meaningless; through much learning, one attains Nirvana.
Listen well to increase your learning; learning can increase wisdom.
Wisdom can cultivate the pure meaning, and attaining that meaning can bring forth happiness.
Having attained the meaning through keen wisdom, one realizes *nirvāṇa* in this very life.
In accord with the Dharma of pure awakening, they realize the supreme bliss.
Having heard the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they dwell securely in the True Dharma;
as great luminaries for the world, they practice the wondrous conduct of bodhi.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should give rise to a heart of profound respect and regard those who correctly practice the Bodhisattva-piṭaka sūtras as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)."

Having already given rise to this thought, he further seeks out the subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka even more intensely, causing this Dharma-gate to become increasingly bright and pure. Śāriputra!

For the sake of seeking the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to faith and aspiration, exerts right diligence, and restrains and collects his mind so that it remains settled in concentration.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having cultivated and perfected the skillful means of the four right endeavors, attains non-obstruction regarding all phenomena.
Thus, Śāriputra, this is called the characteristic of the correct practice of the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"One who expounds the Dharma is indeed a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Respectfully listening to the Dharma, one abides securely in right practice."
Desiring liberation, always without regression; with diligence ever lofty and courageous;
refining pure wisdom constantly; and always abiding securely in knowledge.
Spontaneously penetrating all phenomena, they do not follow the path of faith-based practice.
To observe phenomena with wisdom is what the Buddhas have taught.
The wise analyze the words, skillfully training in their meaning;
regarding the categories of the white and the black, they constantly practice cultivation and constant distancing.
The mind never grows weary, nor does it recede from the Dharma;
body and desire are both tranquil, and one swiftly attains mental diligence.
Through hearing the Dharma, wisdom increases; as wisdom increases, there is no decline in mindfulness.
Wisdom always relies upon the foundations of mindfulness, To discern the nature of pure and impure phenomena.
Training in the unsurpassed Dharma, One advances toward the power of sublime mindfulness and wisdom;
Understanding the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings, One trains oneself throughout the long night.
Having already ascended through the training in the Dharma, with supreme progress and pure wisdom,
he understands the desires and dispositions of sentient beings, and according to that understanding,
he reveals and teaches them. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they seek and penetrate such awakened insight into the subtle dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; relying on these gates of illumination consisting of pure and wholesome dharmas, the bodhisattva should always train in this manner.
Śāriputra! If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in the Dharma, they should form this thought:
"Two causes and two conditions can give rise to right view."
"What are the two?
They are hearing the voice from another and internal appropriate mental attention.
He then reflected further:
"What are the characteristics of hearing sounds from others and applying the mind correctly?
Thus he reflected and pondered again:

"If there are bodhisattvas who delight in meditative concentration and practice the corresponding conduct, yet have never heard this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, nor have they heard the teachings of the Noble Law and Discipline, but instead give rise to a sense of contentment within their samādhi alone."

You should know that because of the power of pride, such a person gives rise to overweening conceit; I say that this person cannot be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and all such burning afflictions.
Since they have not yet escaped the sufferings of various fevers and afflictions, how could they escape the cycle of birth and death through the five gates?
They remain submerged within it, transmigrating without ceasing.

These sentient beings are truly not liberated, yet they claim to themselves, "I am already liberated"; they are truly not free from suffering, yet they claim to themselves, "I have transcended all suffering."

Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying upon such persons, teaches the Dharma in accordance with reality; if they can listen to it from another in a compliant manner, they will be liberated from old age, death, and all other such sufferings.
He further spoke these words:
"As I have previously heard the Blessed One say:
'The one who is learned understands the Dharma; the one who is learned does not commit evil.'"
The learned abandon what is meaningless; the learned attain Nirvana.
Listen well to increase your learning; learning can increase wisdom.
Wisdom can cultivate pure meaning; attaining that meaning brings forth happiness.
"Having attained the meaning through wisdom, one realizes nirvana in the present life;
having heard the Dharma, with pure and keen intelligence, one attains the supreme bliss. "Therefore, Śāriputra!"

After the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have reflected in this way, they should reverently listen to, receive, uphold, read, and recite the subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, as well as the teachings of the noble Dharma-Vinaya, and extensively expound and reveal them to others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if sentient beings,

although they have heard this subtle Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, do not apply their attention through appropriate skillful means, you should know that such persons are unable to practice correctly upon that noble path."

Therefore, for the sake of such persons, the Tathāgata has taught the essential points of the True Dharma, saying: "If you wish to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, you should cultivate internal reflection in accordance with reality."
All bodhisattvas should train in this manner.
Śāriputra, what is called "skillful means according to principle"?
What kind of bodhisattva is able to practice and train through correct mental attention? Śāriputra,
for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses skillful means in accordance with reality, there is not a single dharma that is either joined or separated.
Why is this? Because skillful means that accord with reality are not [mere] means.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in skillful means and mental attention that accord with reality, one should know that these signs are merely sounds; yet the nature of these sounds neither arises nor evolves, and it is only by virtue of them that sounds are produced.
Why is this? Because all of them are unattainable.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates this sound regarding its prior limit and its posterior limit: from where does it arise, and where does it perish as it passes away?
Having observed in this way, one realizes that it is ultimately unfindable.
Furthermore, one further investigates such sound: does it exist in what has already been spoken, in what is currently being spoken, or in what will yet be spoken?
Furthermore, one should again investigate such a sound: is it that which has already been spoken, that which is being spoken now, or that which will be spoken?
Is such a sound spoken for the sake of abandoning [afflictions] in the past, spoken for the sake of abandoning them in the present, or spoken for the sake of abandoning them in the future?
Regarding such sounds: have they been spoken for the sake of realization, are they being spoken now for the sake of realization, or will they be spoken in the future for the sake of realization?

When this bodhisattva thus searches for all sounds and finds nothing at all, he further examines them—whether as past characteristics, future characteristics, or present characteristics—and having observed them in this way, finds that none can be apprehended.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus correctly observes, this is called "mental attention through skillful means in accordance with reality.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who employs skillful means in accordance with reality should cultivate and train in such observation.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate according to reality? How should the bodhisattvas train?"
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is extinguished; to contemplate in this way is called contemplation according to reality.
To contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent is called correct contemplation according to reality.
If one contemplates all phenomena as ultimately empty and quiescent, this is called correct contemplation according to reality.
If one contemplates all phenomena as entering into the state of equality, this is called correct contemplation according to reality.
If one contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, this is called correct contemplation in accordance with reality.
If one contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately non-arising, this is called correct contemplation in accordance with reality.
If one contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately non-arising, this is called correct contemplation according to reality.
If one contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately quiescent, this is called correct contemplation according to reality.
Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva performs such contemplation, he does not perceive any one who contemplates.
He should contemplate in this way: namely, because it is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation.
If there is a bodhisattva who practices such contemplation, it is called contemplation according to principle; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called contemplation contrary to principle.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in such skillful means according to principle?"
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses skillful means in accordance with reality does not have delusion regarding even the slightest phenomenon.
One who possesses skillful means in accordance with reality does not give rise to obstacles regarding even the slightest phenomenon.
Regarding skillful means in accordance with reality, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not a gateway to liberation.
Regarding skillful means in accordance with reality, one does not exert diligent effort for the sake of abandoning even a fraction of phenomena.
Regarding skillful means in accordance with reality: one does not exert right effort for the sake of realizing a limited dharma.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should, by means of such right view in accordance with reality, correctly contemplate all dharmas just as they are seen.
Śāriputra! What is meant by "correctly contemplating all phenomena just as they are seen"? Śāriputra!
It is said that "not seeing anything" is what is meant by contemplating all phenomena. What is this "not seeing anything"? Śāriputra!
That which has nothing to be seen is called "non-arising"; that which is non-arising is called "non-origination"; that which is non-origination is called "that which has no illumination.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on this true Dharma, speaks these words: "If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates all conditioned phenomena and perceives their non-arising, this is precisely entering into the certainty of the right nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*)."
Now, right view refers to being able to enter into the certainty of the correct nature. Śāriputra!
That bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects as follows:
“For what cause and condition shall one enter into the certainty of the right nature? “Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way: if one contemplates the view of self as being equal, then all dharmas are equal.”
If one contemplates in this way, it should be known that one is entering into the certainty of the right nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Therefore, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to enter into the certainty of the right nature, they should, with earnest respect, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, and investigate the meaning and intent of this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka; furthermore, they should explain it extensively for others in accordance with the Dharma, and they should then practice and study this Dharma-gate through appropriate skillful means and mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Śāriputra! This is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the bodhisattva conduct for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-one.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Eleventh Chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom, Part Two, within the Twelfth Assembly of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Section Seventeen: "Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, in order to seek such profound, supreme, wondrously good, pure, and white awakened insight, they enter into contemplation of the words of reality through appropriate means and diligent application, by way of this gate of illumination of the wondrously good and pure dharmas."
Śāriputra! What is called "entering through realization in accordance with reality"?
Furthermore, what constitutes a "phrase in accordance with reality"?

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters [reality] according to the principle, it means: entering by relying on *śamatha*; entering through *vipaśyanā*; entering through correct practice; entering according to the principle; entering through physical seclusion; entering through mental pliancy; entering through non-annihilation; entering through non-permanence; entering through causes and conditions; entering through dependent origination; entering through the absence of a sentient being, a life-principle, and a person who grasps at aggregates; entering through the future and the past, and whether things exist or do not exist; and entering through the absence of transference and the indestructibility of cause and effect.

Although they cultivate and realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), they do not grasp at the realization of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Although they enter into meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), they do not take birth through the power of such realizations.
Although they enter through the realization of the wisdom of supernormal powers, they do not realize the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they enter through the observation of non-arising, they do not correctly proceed toward definitive realization.
Although they realize the entry into the selflessness of sentient beings, they do not abandon the realization of great compassion;
although they realize the entry into the dreadfulness of all existence, they nevertheless take up all forms of existence.
Although he enters into the realization of cessation and detachment from desire, he does not realize the state of detachment itself as a final goal.
Although he enters into the abandonment of the bliss of sensual desires, he does not abandon the bliss of the Dharma.
Although one enters into realization by relinquishing all conceptual proliferation and discursive thought, one does not relinquish the realization of skillful means.
Śāriputra, this is called entering into realization in accordance with reality.
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to attain such reasoned realization and entry should practice and study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how should they train in these words of the true Dharma according to reality? Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it thus: the phrase "in accordance with reality" is the phrase of origination, the phrase of entering into reality, the phrase of the Dharma-gate, the phrase of the gateway, the phrase of the cause, the phrase of accumulation, the phrase of non-contradiction, the phrase of non-contention, the phrase of relinquishment, the phrase of non-grasping, the phrase of non-abandonment, the phrase of non-proliferation, the phrase of non-rejection, the phrase of non-slander, the phrase of non-contempt, the phrase of contentment, the phrase of non-contention, the phrase of non-retrogression, and the phrase of non-antidote.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the phrase "according to reality" is the phrase of true nature, the phrase of suchness, the phrase of not being otherwise than suchness, the phrase of true thusness, the phrase of accord with reality, the phrase of the equality of the three times, and the phrase of freedom from conceptual discrimination.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! As for the phrases that accord with reality: they are the phrase that form-consciousness has no basis or dwelling; the phrase that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no basis or dwelling; the phrase that the nature of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness has no basis or dwelling; the phrase that the nature of the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness has no basis or dwelling; the phrase that the nature of the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness has no basis or dwelling; the phrase that the nature of the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness has no basis or dwelling; the phrase that the nature of the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness has no basis or dwelling; and the phrase that the nature of the mind, phenomena, and mind-consciousness has no basis or dwelling.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A phrase that accords with reality is called a phrase based on meaning; it is called a phrase based on the Dharma; it is called a phrase based on wisdom; and it is called a phrase based on the definitive meaning.
Śāriputra! Such immeasurable dharma-gates as these are called "sentences that accord with reality.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained right effort through realization in accordance with reality performs such contemplation, they do not perceive a subject who contemplates; this is because one should contemplate in accordance with reality by means of neither contemplating nor non-contemplating.
If there is a bodhisattva who practices this contemplation, it is called contemplation according to principle; if they contemplate otherwise, it is called contemplation contrary to principle.

Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva who employs skillful means according to principle, there is no delusion regarding even the slightest phenomenon, nor does any slight phenomenon arise as an obstruction. There is not the slightest phenomenon that is not a gateway to liberation. They do not exert diligent effort for the sake of abandoning even the slightest phenomenon, nor do they apply courageous and earnest diligence for the sake of realizing even a minor dharma.
One should possess such right view in accordance with reality and correctly contemplate all phenomena as they are seen.
What is correct contemplation?
It is the absence of anything to be seen.
That which is without seeing is precisely non-arising; that which is called non-arising is precisely non-origination; that which is called non-origination is termed non-illumination. Śāriputra!
The successive transformation of these dharmas is as extensively explained before, up until it is called "because the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how should they train in correct contemplation according to reality?

Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice such correct contemplation of all phenomena: that is to say, because the self is according to reality, one contemplates all phenomena as being entirely according to reality; because the self is non-self, one likewise contemplates all phenomena as being non-self; and because sentient beings are non-self, one likewise contemplates all phenomena as being non-self.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who performs this contemplation is said to practice correct contemplation. Śāriputra!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice skillful means in accordance with reality?

Śāriputra, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the nature of saṃsāra in accordance with reality as being intermingled with the nature of nirvāṇa in accordance with reality; to engage in such contemplation is what is called skillful means in accordance with reality.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva contemplates that the nature of afflictions and the nature of nirvāṇa share a single, unified characteristic without any difference; nor does he discriminate between them as being either conjoined or opposed. To contemplate in this manner is called "skillful means according to reality" and is also termed "correct contemplation according to reality."

Śāriputra! You should know that all the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that accord with reality arise from the realm of immeasurable sentient beings. If one does not abandon the realm of sentient beings and does not destroy the nature of all phenomena, this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means that accord with reality.

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that such characteristics, such hearing, such reasoned entry, such reasoned observation, and such reasoned right view as their natural outflow constitute what is called a bodhisattva’s rightly directed correct wisdom.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice right conduct in this manner, all for the sake of bringing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to full completion.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the nature of that wisdom is pure and does not coexist with any conditioned phenomena."
Śāriputra, with which phenomena does it not coexist?
Śāriputra, it is as follows:

this prajñā does not coexist with ignorance; it does not coexist with volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and so on, as explained at length, up to its not coexisting with old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Śāriputra! Thus, this prajñā does not coexist with the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), nor does it coexist even with the sixty-two types of speculative views rooted in the view of a self-body; likewise, this prajñā does not coexist with arrogance, nor does it coexist with inferiority, nor does it coexist with the eight worldly dharmas (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*).

Śāriputra! Thus, this prajñā does not coexist with the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases, nor does it coexist with any object of focus or mental attention, up to and including all such things.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with pride; it does not coexist with inferiority-complex or false pride, nor does it coexist with the twenty-one secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and so forth.
In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with subtle, inferior, medium, or superior grades of greed, nor does it coexist with any afflictions whatsoever.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with ignorance, darkness, cataracts, hindrances, coverings, or the various fetters; it does not even coexist with any dharmas that accord with the factors leading to decline.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with the defilements of desire, contention, and the māra of affliction; it does not coexist with the māras of the aggregates, death, or the celestial māra; indeed, it does not coexist with any of the activities of the māras.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with the grasping at a self; it does not coexist with [the notions of] a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, or a manava; and so on, up to its not coexisting with those who abide in the view of a self.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with the obstacle of karma; it does not coexist with the obstacle of afflictions, the obstacle of phenomena, the obstacle of views, the obstacle of retribution, or the obstacle to knowledge; indeed, it does not coexist with any habitual tendencies that conform to worldly conventions.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with discursive thought and conceptualization; it does not coexist with signs, objects of focus, seeing, hearing, recollecting, or cognizing; and it does not even coexist with any fetters, bonds, or accumulations.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with stinginess or generosity; it does not coexist with observance or violation, patience or anger, diligence or indolence, tranquility or agitation, or ignorance or wisdom; indeed, it does not coexist with any phenomena that are either the antidotes or the objects to be countered within the perfections, nor with their cognitive natures.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with detachment; it does not coexist with non-detachment, nor with the nature of error or correctness, nor with the wholesome or unwholesome, nor with the blameworthy or blameless, nor with saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; indeed, it does not coexist with any phenomena that serve as mutual antidotes.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with various forms of differentiation; it does not coexist with the differentiation of realms, the differentiation of Buddhas, the differentiation of sentient beings, or the differentiation of all phenomena, nor indeed does it coexist with any form of differentiation whatsoever.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with ignorance; it does not coexist with consciousness, the conventional, the ultimate, nor even with the mental attention toward the characteristics of any sentient being.

In this way, such prajñā does not coexist with the non-manifestation of wisdom; it does not coexist with that which is bodiless, formless, signless, or unconditioned; and it does not even coexist with any phenomena associated with the dwelling of thought, mind, or consciousness.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, all that subtle and pure wisdom does not coexist with such immeasurable and boundless conditioned phenomena.
Śāriputra! This is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the application of wisdom in this manner.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the Great Vehicle, the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, practices the perfection of wisdom, they attain skill in the discernment of wisdom."
It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of this very dharma, attains clear understanding, thorough penetration,
and skillfulness regarding all dharmas. Śāriputra, what is meant by such skillfulness in the discernment of prajñā?
Śāriputra! Such skillfulness is immeasurable and boundless; I shall now briefly explain ten kinds of skillfulness. What are these ten?

That is to say: skill in the phenomena of the aggregates, skill in the phenomena of the elements, skill in the phenomena of the sense bases, skill in the phenomena of the truths, skill in the analytical knowledges, skill in the reliances, skill in the provisions, skill in the phenomena of the path, skill in dependent origination, and skill in all phenomena.
Śāriputra! These ten kinds of subtle and skillful discernments—those who penetrate them are said to possess the discernment of *prajñā*. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in these skills.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, attain mastery in the skillful analysis of the phenomena of the aggregates?
Śāriputra! One who is skillful in the dharmas of the aggregates is one who gives rise to verbal expressions based upon those very aggregate-dharmas.
What are these verbal expressions?

Śāriputra, such discourse is like a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, an echo, a reflection, or a shadow; therefore, the Tathāgata, with unimpeded eloquence, teaches this Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Śāriputra! I say that this form is like a mass of foam. Why is that?

Śāriputra! This very mass of foam is fundamentally without a self, and likewise without a sentient being, without a living soul, without a life-principle, without a person, without a nourisher, without a mind-born being, and without a manava. Because the nature of the mass of foam is itself the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva who skillfully understands such phenomena is said to be "skillful in the phenomena of the aggregates."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
I say that this feeling is like a water bubble. Why is that?

Śāriputra! These very water bubbles are fundamentally without a self, and likewise without a sentient being, without a living soul, without a life-principle, without a person, without a nourisher, without a mind-born being, and without a manava. Because the nature of the water bubble is itself the nature of sensation, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully understands such phenomena, this is called skillfulness regarding the phenomena of the aggregates.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I say that this perception is like a mirage. Why is that?

Śāriputra! This very mirage is fundamentally without a self, and likewise without a sentient being, without a living soul, without a life-principle, without a person, without a nourisher, without a mind-born, and without a manava; for the nature of a mirage is the very nature of perception (*saṃjñā*). When a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully understands such phenomena in this way, it is called "skillfulness regarding the phenomena of the aggregates."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
I say that this practice is like a plantain tree. Why is that?
Śāriputra! This plantain tree is fundamentally without a self;

it is also without a sentient being, without a living soul, without a life-principle, without a nourisher, without a person, without a mind-born being, without a manava, without an agent, and without an experiencer. Because the nature of the plantain is itself the nature of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), when a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully understands such phenomena, this is called skillfulness regarding the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
I say that this consciousness is like a magical illusion. Why is that?

Śāriputra! This very illusory phenomenon is fundamentally without a self, and likewise without a sentient being, without a living soul, without a life-principle, without a nourisher, without a person, without a mind-born being, without a manava, without an agent, and without an experiencer. Because the nature of the illusory phenomenon is identical to the nature of consciousness, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully understands such phenomena, this is called skillfulness regarding the phenomena of the aggregates.

Śāriputra! That which is called the aggregates (skandha) is designated as the world; the phenomena of the world possess the characteristic of decay and disintegration. Therefore, you should know that the nature of all worlds is the very self-nature of the aggregates.
Śāriputra! What is called the nature of the world?

It refers to the nature of impermanence, the nature of suffering, and the nature of non-self; such natures as these are called the nature of the aggregates (skandha), and this nature of the aggregates is precisely the nature of the world.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful knowledge regarding this, it is called skillfulness in the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha-dharma-kauśalya*). Śāriputra,
if there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, desiring to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), diligently cultivate skillfulness in the phenomena of the aggregates.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, become proficient in the skillful means regarding the dharmas of the elements?"
Śāriputra! One who is skillful in the dharmas of the elements (dhātu) understands that the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is itself the earth element. Why is this?
Because that dharmadhātu does not possess the characteristic of solidity.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is itself the water element. Why is this?
Because that dharmadhātu does not have the characteristic of moisture.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is itself the fire element. Why is this?
Because that dharmadhātu is not a characteristic of maturation.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is itself the wind element. Why is this so?
Because that dharmadhātu is characterized by immovability, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands this as it truly is, this is called skillfulness regarding the dharmas of the elements.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which is called the dharma-dhātu is the eye-consciousness element. Why is this?
Because that dharmadhātu does not possess the characteristic of illumination.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is itself the ear-consciousness element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*). Why is this so?
Because that dharmadhātu is not characterized by the perception of sound.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is itself the olfactory consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*). Why is this?
Because that dharmadhātu does not have the characteristic of smelling odors.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is the tongue-consciousness element (jihvāvijñānadhātu). Why is this?
Because that dharmadhātu does not have the characteristic of being tasted.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is the body-consciousness element (kāyavijñānadhātu). Why is this?
Because that dharmadhātu is not characterized by the contact of cognition.
Furthermore, the dharmadhātu is the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu). Why is this so?
Because that dharmadhātu is not a characteristic of conceptual discrimination. Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands this therein as it truly is, this is called skillfulness regarding the dharma of the elements (dhātukuśala).

Furthermore, Śāriputra! Thus, the realm of self (*ātma-dhātu*) is equal to the realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*); the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*) is equal to the realm of phenomena; the realm of desire (*kāma-dhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), and the realm of formlessness (*ārūpya-dhātu*) are equal to the realm of phenomena; the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra-dhātu*) and the realm of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-dhātu*) are equal to the realm of phenomena. In this way, even up to the realm of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*), the realm of phenomena, and all realms of phenomena, they are entirely equal.
Śāriputra! For what reason is there equality?
It is because all phenomena are equal by virtue of the equality of emptiness; all phenomena are equal by virtue of the equality of non-alteration.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If there were any teaching regarding the realization of the conditioned realm or the realization of the unconditioned realm, such would be immeasurable and boundless.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas engage in such discernment and thereby enter into the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), this is called skillfulness regarding the dharmas of the realms.
Śāriputra, in this way,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should diligently cultivate skillfulness regarding the dharmas of the realms.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), attain mastery in the skillful means regarding the bases of phenomena (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya)?"
Śāriputra! One who is skillful in the dharmas of the bases understands, as they truly are, that the eye is empty and devoid of self or what belongs to a self;
likewise, up to the mind, it is empty and devoid of self or what belongs to a self. A bodhisattva mahāsattva understands the nature of the eye in this way, and so forth, up to the mind.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands the nature of this mind as it truly is. Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not accumulate unwholesome states in any sphere but accumulates wholesome ones, they do not give rise to dualistic marks regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome. To understand in this way is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the dharmas of the spheres.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva achieve thorough penetration and skillful understanding of the sense base of the eye and the sense base of forms? Śāriputra!
This refers to observing and seeing the detachment from forms perceived by the eye, yet not personally realizing that detachment.
To understand in this way is called a bodhisattva’s skill in the methods of abiding.

In the same way, regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena: one contemplates these very mental phenomena as being free from desire, yet one does not personally realize that state of freedom from desire.
To understand in this way is called the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the dharmas of abiding.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma; they may speak of the noble abodes or of what is not the noble abode.
What is called a "noble place" is one where the Dharma of the Path can be received; what is not a noble place is one that is remote from the Dharma of the Path.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in the Path; toward those sentient beings who dwell apart from the Path, he attains great compassion and does not abandon the station of the Path.

If there is a bodhisattva who understands in this way and has attained thorough mastery, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the stations of phenomena (*dharmasthāna-kuśala*). Śāriputra,
because bodhisattva mahāsattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should diligently train in skillfulness regarding the stations of phenomena.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, become proficient in the skillful means regarding the Dharma of the truths?
Śāriputra! You should know that there are four kinds of practices by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into skillfulness regarding the truths. What are these four?
These are the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path. Śāriputra,
what is meant by the knowledge of suffering up to the knowledge of the path?
The wisdom that realizes the fundamental non-arising of the aggregates is called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
The wisdom that brings about the eternal cessation and eradication of all defiled craving is called the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
That which realizes that all things are without arising and without destruction—such wisdom is called the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
That which, at all times, neither diminishes nor augments any object of cognition—such wisdom is called the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands these four truths through such wisdom as this, although they clearly comprehend them, they do not realize them [as a final cessation].
Why is this? It is because they desire to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
Thus, being fully endowed with these qualities is called skill in the truths.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are three kinds of skill in the truths for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these three?
First is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), second is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and third is the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*).

Śāriputra, you should know that the conventional truth refers to all worldly speech, written characters, sounds, and provisional designations; such characteristics as these are called the conventional truth.

As for the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it refers to those phenomena where even mental activity does not operate, let alone the ability to express them through words; such phenomena are called the ultimate truth.

Regarding the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*): what are called various characteristics are in fact a single characteristic; this single characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). To speak in this way is termed the truth of characteristics.

Śāriputra! For the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva never tires of teaching according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he realizes it within himself without falling back. Regarding the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), he profoundly penetrates its fundamental nature and understands it to be signless (*animitta*).
Śāriputra! This is called the skill in the Dharma of the truths, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices and studies for the sake of cultivating the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who diligently trains in skillfulness regarding the truths should know, as it truly is, that there is one further truth and no second.
What is the single truth?
It is the truth of cessation, Śāriputra.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, clearly understand and penetrate this single truth without any superimposition; having attained such penetration, they proclaim this Dharma of the single truth for the sake of all sentient beings who dwell in superimposition, so that by practicing it, those beings may realize the absence of superimposition.
"Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva possesses such knowledge as this, he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva skilled in the dharmas of truth.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate and study skillfulness regarding the truths (*satya*). Śāriputra,
skillfulness regarding the truths means being thoroughly proficient in penetrating all the noble truths (*āryasatya*).
What is called "thoroughly penetrating the noble truths"?
Śāriputra, the noble truth of suffering refers to the five aggregates of clinging; their nature is truly suffering, and this is called the truth of suffering.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva penetrates these truths, they realize that the five aggregates are all characterized by suffering; since the characteristic of suffering is itself the characteristic of emptiness, this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Śāriputra! The noble truth of origination is the cause of the five aggregates of clinging; latent tendencies, craving, and views—these are called the truth of origination.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding these causal phenomena, neither increases craving nor views, and is without grasping, without delusion, clearly and thoroughly penetrating them, this is called the noble truth of origination.
Śāriputra! As for the noble truth of cessation: the ultimate exhaustion of the five aggregates of clinging is called the truth of cessation.
