When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates this dharma of truth—neither losing the past limit, nor proceeding to the future limit, nor dwelling in the present—but clearly understands and penetrates it, this is called the noble truth of cessation.

Śāriputra! As for the Noble Truth of the Path: if, by relying on that path, one realizes the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, and the knowledge of cessation, and there is no second knowledge, this is called the Truth of the Path.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva clearly understands and penetrates these truths in such a way as to be free from conceptual discrimination, this is called the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes these truths with wisdom and also causes sentient beings to observe and understand them, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skill in the dharma of the truths.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding these dharmas of the truths, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should further observe and know these four truths in this way.
What is the truth of suffering?
All that is capable of being felt and all that is felt constitute the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Within this, one should skillfully exercise discernment; this very nature of wisdom—skillful discernment, awakening, clarity, and thorough penetration—is called the Bodhisattva’s Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is the noble truth of origination?
Whatever arising of the aggregates occurs from this cause is the noble truth of origination.
To understand such a cause as it truly is—this is called the bodhisattva’s noble truth of the origination of suffering.
What is the noble truth of cessation?
The eternal subsiding of all sensations, such that there is no further perception or experience of them, is called the noble truth of cessation.
To penetrate this in such a way—observing the cessation of sensation yet not personally realizing it—is called the bodhisattva’s noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
What is the Truth of the Path?
If one skillfully cultivates the Noble Path that is free from grasping, this is called the Truth of the Path.
For example, like a boat or raft, neither seeking grasping nor seeking the path—this is called the Bodhisattva’s Noble Truth of the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
In this way, Śāriputra,
if there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who thus realizes through direct insight and, relying on a tranquil concentration, gives rise to four kinds of views, these four views are not ultimately pure.
If one can thoroughly penetrate such dharmas as these, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skill in the dharma of the truths.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has thoroughly penetrated skill in these dharmas of the truths, if they realize cessation, then suffering does not arise; the wisdom that contemplates non-arising is called the knowledge of suffering.
"Śāriputra! When one observes that conditioned arising is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both, such wisdom is called the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna). Śāriputra!"
"All that is born is unborn; because one realizes this, there is nothing at all to be extinguished. This wisdom of non-extinction is called the wisdom of the exhaustion of extinction. Śāriputra!"
If this path is such that it cannot be measured, cannot be sought after, and cannot be scrutinized, it is called vast wisdom; such wisdom is termed the knowledge of the path.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is well-established in these dharmas of the truths, yet dwells without attachment to the wisdom of those truths, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the dharmas of the truths.
"Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they diligently cultivate skillfulness in these dharmas of the truths.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skill in the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) obtained by practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)? Śāriputra,
because the bodhisattva mahāsattva has fully studied and practiced the perfection of wisdom, they are endowed with the four kinds of unobstructed analytical knowledges.
What are the four?
They are the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of expression, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence. Śāriputra!
What is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*)?

Śāriputra, it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that bodhisattvas attain this analytical knowledge of meaning; namely, the knowledge regarding the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena. To contemplate this knowledge is itself the analytical knowledge of meaning.
Thus, there is the wisdom of various awakenings, the wisdom of causes, the wisdom of conditions, the wisdom of conjunction, the wisdom of universal concomitance,
the wisdom of the vast dependent origination, the wisdom of the unmixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),

the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s entry [into reality], the wisdom of abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the wisdom of contemplative observation in accordance with empty phenomena, and regarding signless phenomena as they are...

The wisdom of contemplation; the wisdom that gives rise to the practice of aspiration toward phenomena that are wishless; the wisdom that gives rise to application toward that which is without application;
the wisdom of contemplative entry and realization into the single principle; the wisdom of contemplative entry and realization into the absence of sentient beings;
the wisdom of contemplative entry and realization into the phenomena that are selfless; the wisdom of exclusive entry into the absence of a life-principle; and the wisdom of the non-existent...
The wisdom that perceives the ultimate truth; the unimpeded wisdom that perceives the past; the boundless wisdom that perceives the future;
the wisdom that perceives all locations in the present; the wisdom that perceives all aggregates as being like illusions and transformations;
the wisdom that perceives all elements as being like venomous snakes; and the wisdom that perceives all sense bases as being like...
The wisdom of empty embers; the wisdom that contemplates the tranquility of all internal phenomena; the wisdom that contemplates the absence of activity in all external phenomena;
the wisdom that contemplates the non-existence of all objective spheres; the wisdom that contemplates abiding in the foundations of mindfulness;
the wisdom that contemplates following along with those various realms of existence; and the wisdom that contemplates direct perception of dependent origination.
The wisdom that penetrates through contemplation of all the truths (*satya*); the wisdom that contemplates all suffering as non-arising;
the wisdom that contemplates all origins as being without volitional application (*anabhisamskāra*); the wisdom that contemplates all cessations as being free from signs (*animitta*);

the wisdom that contemplates all paths as being deliverance; the wisdom that contemplates the analysis of phrases within all phenomena (*dharma*); and [the wisdom] regarding the factors of the faculties (*indriya*).
The wisdom that observes and realizes entry; the wisdom that observes the qualities of the powers (*bala*) as being without defeat or subjugation;
the wisdom that observes the basis of *śamatha*; the wisdom that observes the illumination of *vipaśyanā*; the wisdom that observes all illusory phenomena as being gathered through emptiness;
the wisdom that observes all mirages as being delusive confusion; and the wisdom that observes the contents of dreams as being empty visions.
The wisdom that contemplates resonance as it echoes from those [objects]; the wisdom that contemplates the union of conditions as a reflection of light;
the wisdom that contemplates diverse characteristics as a single characteristic; the wisdom that contemplates all fetters as freedom from fetters;

the wisdom that contemplates all continuities as the absence of continuity; the wisdom that contemplates the knowledge of the śrāvakas as entering in accordance with sounds; and regarding the pratyekabuddha...
Śāriputra, it is the wisdom of awakening that contemplates the vast dependent origination and enters into the single-object wisdom;
it is the wisdom that, through contemplating the Buddha’s Mahāyāna, knows how to accumulate all the provisions of the roots of virtue. Śāriputra!
All such observational wisdoms as these are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses yet another unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning.
The meaning of "that which is relied upon" refers to that which is the basis for the nature of all phenomena. Why is this so?
Because all phenomena are universally empty, and the meaning of emptiness is what is designated as "the meaning."
Because all phenomena are universally signless, that which is signless is explained as their true meaning.
Because all phenomena are universally wishless, that which is wishless is explained as their true meaning.
Because all phenomena are universally and utterly secluded, that which is the meaning of seclusion is called "the meaning.
Because all phenomena are universally devoid of a sentient being, a life-principle, a nourisher, or a person, that which is the meaning of this absence is called "the meaning."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus enter into the meaning of such characteristics, this is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

Śāriputra, if there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who explains this meaning, you should know that he is explaining the dharma of non-abiding, explaining the inexhaustible dharma; he is explaining all that is manifested by expression, and he is explaining the meanings discerned by the unimpeded analytical knowledges of all-knowledge.

One should know that such a person is approved and rejoiced in by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; one should know that this wisdom is true wisdom, is real wisdom, is non-dual wisdom, and is the wisdom that discerns all spheres without obstruction.
"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way, it is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*)?

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they attain this unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena; that is to say, it is the knowledge that enters into realization in accordance with all phenomena.
What is called the wisdom of entering in accordance with realization? Śāriputra,
it refers to that which is realized and entered within all phenomena.
What are these phenomena? They are:
wholesome and unwholesome; blameworthy and blameless; with outflows and without outflows; mundane and supramundane; conditioned and unconditioned; defiled and pure.

If one can, in accordance with all such phenomena—whether they accord with saṃsāra or nirvāṇa—realize the equality of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the equality of awakening (bodhi), such a nature of wisdom is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid).

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of such an understanding of the mind, realizes and enters into such conduct of desire (rāga-carita); he realizes and enters into the conventionally designated conduct of desire, or again, realizes and enters into the conduct of desire through skillful means (upāya), or again, realizes and enters into firm conduct of desire, or again, realizes and enters into subtle and thin conduct of desire, or again, realizes and enters into improper conduct of desire, or again, realizes and enters into conduct of desire involving seeking and striving, or again, realizes and enters into conduct of desire from past lives, or again, realizes and enters into conduct of desire with infinite diverse characteristics, or again, realizes and enters into conduct of desire through present conditions."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands such characteristics of craving in sentient beings as follows: namely, there are some sentient beings who have internal craving but not external craving; some sentient beings who have external craving but not internal craving; and some sentient beings who have craving for both the internal and the external.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave forms but do not crave sounds; there are some sentient beings who crave sounds but do not crave forms; and there are some sentient beings who crave both forms and sounds.
Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who crave form but not fragrance; some who crave fragrance but not form; and some who crave both form and fragrance.
Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who crave form but not taste; some sentient beings who crave taste but not form; and some sentient beings who crave both form and taste.
Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who crave form but not touch; there may be sentient beings who crave touch but not form; and there may be sentient beings who crave both form and touch.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave sounds but not fragrances; there are some sentient beings who crave fragrances but not sounds; and there are some sentient beings who crave both sounds and fragrances.

Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who crave sounds but not flavors; there may be sentient beings who crave flavors but not sounds; and there may be sentient beings who crave both sounds and flavors.
Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who crave sound but not touch; there may be sentient beings who crave touch but not sound; and there may be sentient beings who crave both sound and touch.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave fragrance but not flavor; there are some sentient beings who crave flavor but not fragrance; and there are some sentient beings who crave both fragrance and flavor.
Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who crave fragrance but not touch; some sentient beings who crave touch but not fragrance; and some sentient beings who crave both fragrance and touch.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave flavors but not tangibles; there are some sentient beings who crave tangibles but not flavors; and there are some sentient beings who crave both flavors and tangibles.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave forms and sounds but not odors; there are some sentient beings who crave odors but not forms and sounds; and there are some sentient beings who crave forms, sounds, and odors all together.

Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who crave forms and sounds but do not crave flavors; some sentient beings who crave flavors but do not crave forms and sounds; and some sentient beings who crave both forms, sounds, and flavors.

Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who crave forms and sounds but do not crave touch; some sentient beings who crave touch but do not crave forms and sounds; and some sentient beings who crave forms, sounds, and touch alike.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave sounds and fragrances but not tastes; there are some sentient beings who crave tastes but not sounds and fragrances; and there are some sentient beings who crave sounds, fragrances, and tastes all together.

Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who crave sounds and odors but do not crave tactile objects; some sentient beings crave tactile objects but do not crave sounds and odors; and some sentient beings crave sounds, odors, and tactile objects alike.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave odors and flavors but do not crave tangibles; there are some sentient beings who crave tangibles but do not crave odors and flavors; and there are some sentient beings who crave odors, flavors, and tangibles alike.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave forms, sounds, and odors but do not crave tastes; there are some sentient beings who crave tastes but do not crave forms, sounds, and odors; and there are some sentient beings who crave forms, sounds, odors, and tastes all together.

Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who crave form, sound, and fragrance but do not crave touch; some sentient beings who crave touch but do not crave form, sound, and fragrance; and some sentient beings who crave form, sound, fragrance, and touch all together.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave sounds, odors, and tastes but do not crave tangibles; there are some sentient beings who crave tangibles but do not crave sounds, odors, and tastes; and there are some sentient beings who crave sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles all together.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are some sentient beings who crave form, sound, odor, and taste, but do not crave touch; there are some sentient beings who crave touch, but do not crave form, sound, odor, or taste; and there are some sentient beings who crave form, sound, odor, taste, and touch all together.
Śāriputra! Thus, these and other immeasurable sentient beings each give rise to such immeasurable marks of greed and enter into greedy conduct.

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva realizes and enters this gateway, he enters the twenty-one thousand gateways of greedy conduct, the twenty-one thousand gateways of hateful conduct, the twenty-one thousand gateways of deluded conduct, and the twenty-one thousand gateways of equal-part conduct among all sentient beings.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into these eighty-four thousand gateways to the conduct of afflictions, you should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the vast wisdom of the mind, as well as the wisdom of teaching in accordance with conduct, the wisdom of teaching without increase or decrease, the wisdom of teaching at the appropriate time, the wisdom of discerning differences in faculties, and the wisdom of establishing speech that is not in vain.

Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with such supreme wisdoms as these, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of language?
Śāriputra, [it is as follows...]"

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are fully endowed with this analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid), which is the wisdom that realizes and enters into all verbal expressions.

Having attained this wisdom, he is able to fully understand the speech of devas, the speech of nāgas, the speech of yakṣas, the speech of gandharvas, the speech of asuras, the speech of garuḍas, the speech of kiṃnaras, the speech of mahoragas, the speech of humans, and the speech of non-humans; indeed, regarding all the words, sounds, and deliberations of every conscious being within the five realms of existence, the bodhisattva is able to enter them all through his wisdom, and furthermore, he can use those very same words and sounds to proclaim the True Dharma for those beings.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of language.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Furthermore, there is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which means that bodhisattvas are skillfully able to understand that such words should only manifest such dharmas;
that such words should only be used to explain such dharmas;
and that such words should conceal such dharmas by means of these specific syllables.
Furthermore, by means of this understanding, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thoroughly comprehend that these are designations for "one," designations for "two," and designations for "many.
They should also be able to thoroughly comprehend that these are designations for "female," designations for "male," and designations for "neither male nor female."
Furthermore, one is able to discern which conventional expressions are abbreviated, which are extensive, which are excellent, and which are inferior.
One is also able to discern past conventional expressions, future conventional expressions, and present conventional expressions.
Furthermore, one can discern such characteristics as the augmentation by a single syllable and the augmentation by multiple syllables.
If bodhisattvas are able to thoroughly understand these, this is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There is also the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid), which consists of the speech uttered by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, being collectively integrated from immeasurable merits.
What are these? Śāriputra, the speech uttered by all bodhisattvas is never feeble;

rather, this speech is skillfully contrived, neither prolix nor hurried. Its words are extremely clear, its phrasing and meaning are perfectly complete, and it accords with and gladdens the great assembly. It displays various kinds of exquisite profundity, adorned with both the conventional and the ultimate truths. Their own mental wisdom and vision penetrate all things without obstruction, and it is approved by all Buddhas as that which delights sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! Being thus endowed with these qualities is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s analytical knowledge of language.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence? Śāriputra,
the eloquence of a bodhisattva refers to the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Therefore, one attains these: the eloquence of unimpeded speech, the eloquence of unhindered prophetic declaration,
the eloquence of fluent and uninterrupted exposition, swift eloquence, rapid eloquence, unshakable eloquence, eloquence free from stammering or dullness,
responsive eloquence that answers according to questions, eloquence free from timidity, non-contradictory eloquence, and eloquence free from contentious debate.
...the eloquence of the dharma of joy, the eloquence of abiding in the power of patience, the eloquence of the wondrously profound,
the eloquence of various distinctions, the eloquence of various subtleties, the eloquence of the conventional and the ultimate, the eloquence of establishing all generosity,
ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and the eloquence of establishing all the foundations of mindfulness and right [efforts]...
The eloquence of the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the branches of the path, calm abiding, and insight;
the eloquence of establishing all meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis, as well as the truths and vast wisdom;
the eloquence of the vehicle upon which all noble ones ride; the eloquence regarding the mental activities of all sentient beings; and the eloquence of speech that is free from stammering.
...eloquence free from obstruction; eloquence free from frivolity; eloquence free from coarseness;
eloquence with affectionate and moistening tones; pure eloquence; unrestrained eloquence; unattached eloquence; eloquence of instruction;
eloquence of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*); eloquence of sublime correspondence; and eloquence free from impediment...

The eloquence of speech that is expansive, the eloquence of speech with beautiful and exquisite tones, the eloquence of speech with smooth and supple tones, the eloquence of speech that incurs no reproach,
and the eloquence of speech praised by all the noble ones.
Śāriputra! By means of such eloquence as this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva proclaims throughout all boundless buddha-fields; the sounds and voices he utters surpass all Brahma-like tones and speech.
Such speech is clear, lucid, and pure, and is certified by all Tathāgatas. These Bodhisattvas possess perfect eloquence;

with this speech, they compassionately address all sentient beings and persons subject to rebirth, extensively proclaiming the subtle and sublime True Dharma, enabling them to transcend birth and death and completely exhaust all suffering.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid). Śāriputra!
This is called skill in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
By means of this skill in the analytical knowledges, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and diligently cultivates skill in the analytical knowledges.

The Twelfth Assembly of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, Section Eighteen;
Chapter Eleven on the Perfection of Wisdom, Part Three:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skill in reliance?"
Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are well able to fulfill the four reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni). What are these four?

That is to say: relying on the meaning and not on the letter; relying on knowledge and not on consciousness; relying on sūtras of definitive meaning and not on sūtras of interpretable meaning; and relying on the Dharma and not on the person.
Śāriputra! What is meant by relying on the meaning and not relying on the letter?
Furthermore, what constitutes the letter and what constitutes the meaning?
Śāriputra! What is called "letter" refers to the conventional expressions and linguistic conventions through which the functions of all worldly phenomena are transmitted and practiced.
What is called "meaning" refers to the supramundane phenomena that have been fully realized.
What is called "phrasing" refers to the words that proclaim what is delightful: generosity, discipline, and tranquility.
What is called "meaning" refers to the wisdom that definitively realizes the imperishability of that which is given, disciplined, and tranquil.
What is called "letter" refers to the verbal expressions that revile and reject the discrimination of birth and death.
What is called "meaning" refers to the unsoiled state within birth and death, which penetrates to the full vision of the dharma-nature.
What is called "letter" refers to the eulogies and praises of the merits of nirvāṇa.
What is called "meaning" refers to the nature of all phenomena as nirvāṇa, which is the nature of non-discrimination.
What is called "letter" refers to the establishment of verbal expressions in accordance with the various vehicles.
What is called "meaning" is the wisdom that thoroughly penetrates the single principle of reality (*ekayāna-dharma*).
What is called "letter" is the proclamation of relinquishing all phenomena.
What is called "meaning" refers to the ultimate purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi*).
What is called "phrasing" refers to the proclamation of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*), and the discipline of body, speech, and mind.
What is called "meaning" refers to the fact that body, speech, and mental actions are all unapprehendable, such that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is purified not through deliberate effort (*prayoga*).

As for what is called "letter," it refers to the proclamation and patient endurance of anger, resentment, arrogance, pride, and negligence; one who is able to practice such patience is called a "noble person" (*satpuruṣa*).
As for what is called "meaning," it refers to the excellent realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What is called "phrasing" refers to the manifestation of all roots of goodness and the arousal of diligence.
What is called "meaning" refers to diligence that is without grasping, without abandoning, and without dwelling.
What is called "phrasing" refers to the proclamation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
What is called "meaning" is the wisdom of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
What is called "letter" is the root of all wisdom for retaining what has been heard.
What is called "meaning" is the meaning that is ineffable.
What is called "letter" refers to the sublime Dharma of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble path that is capable of revealing [the truth].
What is called "meaning" refers to the fruit of correct practice, which is the realization of the factors of enlightenment.
What is called "phrasing" refers to that which can reveal the truths of suffering, its origin, and the path.
What is called "meaning" refers to the realization of cessation.
What is called "phrasing" refers to the revelation of everything from ignorance as the beginning up to old age and death.
What is called "meaning" refers to the cessation of ignorance and, consequently, the cessation of everything up to old age and death.
What is called "letter" refers to the teaching of the true Dharma that serves as the provision for śamatha and vipaśyanā.
What is called "meaning" refers to the wisdom of liberation.
What is called "letter" refers to the teachings that proclaim the dharmas pertaining to the temperaments of greed, hatred, and delusion.
What is called "meaning" refers to the non-conceptual wisdom of the liberated mind.
What is called "letter" (vyañjana) refers to the teaching that reveals all obstructive phenomena.
What is called "meaning" (artha) refers to the wisdom of unobstructed liberation.
What is called "letter" refers to the teaching that reveals the meritorious qualities praised in the Three Jewels.
What is called "meaning" refers to the practice of the unconditioned and unattached merit of the dharma-nature that is free from desire.

What is called "letter" refers to the proclamation of the bodhisattva’s practice of initiating meritorious cultivation, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment up to the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
What is called "meaning" refers to the realization and awakening to the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) through momentary mental engagement.
Śāriputra, to state it briefly:

all the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma consisting of vocal teachings expounded by the Tathāgata are called "letters"; that which is free from all sounds, voices, and written characters, and which cannot be expressed in principle, is called "meaning."
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s reliance on the meaning rather than the letter, by virtue of practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva rely upon wisdom and not rely upon consciousness? Śāriputra!"

By relying on the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully understands the meaning of "person" (pudgala) as it appears in all verbal teachings; this is called consciousness, and one should not rely upon it.
The meaning of "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) as it appears in all verbal teachings is itself wisdom; this is what one should rely upon.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
by means of skillfulness in two dharmas, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). What are these two?
It refers to consciousness and wisdom. Śāriputra, what is consciousness?
What is wisdom? Śāriputra,
that which is called "consciousness" refers to the four stations of consciousness.

What are the four? First, the basis for consciousness in the realm of form; second, the basis for consciousness in the realm of feeling; third, the basis for consciousness in the realm of perception; and fourth, the basis for consciousness in the realm of mental formations.
Such stations of consciousness are called "consciousness," and one should not rely upon them.
That which is called "wisdom" is the non-abiding of consciousness within the five aggregates of clinging.
Thorough knowledge of all aggregates is called "wisdom," and this is what one should rely upon.

What is called "consciousness" refers to the ability to discern the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element; such discernment is termed consciousness and should not be relied upon.
If there is one who says that consciousness does not abide within the four stations of consciousness, this is called the dharma-nature of consciousness.
If one possesses non-confused wisdom regarding this dharma-nature, it is called wisdom, and it is upon this that one may rely.

Furthermore, as for consciousness (*vijñāna*), it refers to the discernment of forms cognized by the eye, sounds cognized by the ear, odors cognized by the nose, tastes cognized by the tongue, tangibles cognized by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the mind; such discernment is called consciousness.

As for what is called "wisdom": if the mind is tranquil within the internal sense bases, and if discursive thought and investigation do not arise regarding external sense bases; if one relies upon wisdom and does not give rise to conceptual discrimination toward even a single phenomenon—such characteristics as these are termed "wisdom."

Furthermore, as for consciousness: consciousness arises from its objective referent, consciousness arises from various acts of attention (*manasikāra*), and consciousness arises from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*); such characteristics as these are termed "consciousness."
That which is called "wisdom" (jñāna) is without grasping, without attachment, without objective conditions, without discernment, and without conceptual differentiation; this is termed wisdom.
Furthermore, as for "consciousness" (vijñāna), that which serves as the basis and the resort for consciousness regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-dharma) is termed consciousness.
As for what is called "wisdom" (jñāna): it is the wisdom regarding unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) that is capable of functioning within the unconditioned; this is what is termed wisdom.
Furthermore, as for "consciousness" (vijñāna), it is consciousness that has arising, cessation, and abiding; therefore, it is termed consciousness and should not be relied upon.
That which is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding—this is called wisdom; this is what one should rely upon.
Śāriputra, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom that they rely upon wisdom and do not rely upon consciousness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva not relying on sūtras of provisional meaning (neyārtha) but relying on sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha)? Śāriputra,"

The bodhisattvas are well able to penetrate this: that which was previously described as extensive wording is called a sūtra of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), and such extensive wording should not be relied upon;
whereas that which was previously described as extensive meaning is called the limit of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and such extensive meaning may indeed be relied upon.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
In which sūtras are they considered definitive (nītārtha),
and in which sūtras are they called non-definitive (neyārtha)?

Śāriputra! By relying on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are well able to discern: those teachings among the sūtras that proclaim the path are called "of provisional meaning" (neyārtha);
those teachings among the sūtras that proclaim the fruit are called "of definitive meaning" (nītārtha).
If, among the various sūtras, those that teach conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are called of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*);
those that teach ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) are called of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
If, among the various sūtras, those that proclaim the performance of actions and the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*) are called of provisional meaning;
If there is a teaching that proclaims the exhaustion of afflictions and karma, this is called definitive (nītārtha).
If, within various sūtras, there is a teaching that censures defiled phenomena, it is called non-definitive (neyārtha);
if there is a teaching that explains the cultivation and purification [of phenomena], such teachings are called definitive.
If, within the various sūtras, there is that which proclaims aversion toward saṃsāra and delight in nirvāṇa, it is called "of incomplete meaning" (neyārtha);
if there is that which proclaims no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, it is called "of complete meaning" (nītārtha).
If various sūtras proclaim diverse distinctions of words and phrases, they are called "of incomplete meaning" (neyārtha);
if they speak of what is profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize, these are called "of complete meaning" (nītārtha).
If the words and phrases in various sutras are extensive and cause the minds of sentient beings to leap with joy, they are called of incomplete meaning (neyārtha);
if there is an exposition in which both words and mind are said to be like ashes, this is called of complete meaning (nītārtha).

If, within various sūtras, it is taught that there exists a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a nourisher, a person, a soul, a human, a man, an agent, or an experiencer; and if it further teaches the establishment of various aggregates of sensation while asserting that no sovereign master exists—such verbal teachings are called "of incomplete meaning" (neyārtha) and should not be relied upon.

If, within various sūtras, it is taught that there is emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-origination, and non-manifestation; and that there is no self, no sentient being, no life-principle, no nourisher, no person, as well as the three doors of liberation—such teachings are called definitive (nītārtha) and may be relied upon.
Śāriputra! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom by relying on the definitive meaning and not relying on the non-definitive meaning.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva relying on the Dharma and not relying on the person (pudgala)? Śāriputra,"

By relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is well able to distinguish among all scriptural teachings: those that proclaim sutras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) are for the sake of the person (*pudgala*), and such verbal instructions should not be relied upon;
whereas those that are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) concern the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and such verbal instructions should be relied upon.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
By what is it called "relying on the Dharma"?
And what is meant by a "person" (pudgala)?

Śāriputra! If there is one who relies upon the views of a person subject to grasping (pudgala-dṛṣṭi) regarding all objective phenomena (ālambana-dharma), such a characteristic is called "a person subject to grasping.
The nature of these objective phenomena relied upon by the view of a person subject to grasping—the very dharmatā of phenomena—is what is called "Dharma" when characterized in this way.
Regarding the term "repeatedly taking up" (*pudgala*), it refers to the so-called ordinary person who repeatedly takes up [existence].

It includes the virtuous ordinary person who repeatedly takes up; those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) who repeatedly take up; those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) who repeatedly take up; the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*) who repeatedly takes up; the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) who repeatedly takes up; the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) who repeatedly takes up; the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who repeatedly takes up; the arhat (*arhat*) who repeatedly takes up; the pratyekabuddha who repeatedly takes up; and the bodhisattva who repeatedly takes up.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there appears in the world another person subject to rebirth who benefits and brings peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings; out of compassion for the world, he acts for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
These are the various designations for what is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Śāriputra,
all such names and designations are spoken by the Tathāgata for the sake of sentient beings based upon conventional truth.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to attachment toward these teachings, such types as these should not be relied upon.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata desires that they rely correctly; thus the Buddha, the Bhagavān, has taught this Dharma: "You all should rely upon the true nature of all phenomena; it is not appropriate to rely upon those who are subject to grasping at a self."
Śāriputra! What is the true nature of all phenomena? Śāriputra!
That which is without change, without increase, without action or non-action, without abiding, and without root—such characteristics are called the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Furthermore, it universally illuminates equality in all places; it abides well in equality amidst all things that are equal, and it abides well in equality amidst all things that are unequal. It is wondrously and perfectly equal within both the equal and the unequal. Such characteristics as these are called the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).

Furthermore, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without conceptual differentiation and without an object of cognition; it is the realization of the definitive, ultimate essence and characteristic of all phenomena. This is called the true nature of all phenomena.
Śāriputra! If there is one who takes refuge in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), then there is no phenomenon that does not take refuge in that nature.
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter through such a gateway, they take refuge in the nature of all phenomena within all phenomena.
Śāriputra! These are called the four reliances of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who can thoroughly penetrate these dharmas, they are said to be skilled in the reliances.
Śāriputra! This is called skillfulness in the reliances; for the sake of practicing the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivates skillfulness in the reliances.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the provisions?
Śāriputra, [it is as follows:]..."
It should be known that because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are well able to master two kinds of provisions (sambhāra). What are these?
That is to say: merit and wisdom.
Śāriputra, what is called the "provision of merit"?

That which is called the meritorious activity whose essential nature is giving, the meritorious activity whose essential nature is ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the meritorious activity whose essential nature is various cultivations, as well as the meditative concentration of great loving-kindness and the skillful means of great compassion—because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these meritorious activities, they can, with diligent resolve, give rise to all roots of goodness, whether their own or those of others, and fully confess all evils accumulated throughout the three periods of time.

Furthermore, regarding all the merits of all sentient beings, all the merits of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all the merits of all pratyekabuddhas, and all the merits of all bodhisattvas mahāsattvas—from their initial generation of the mind of awakening through their extensive cultivation of various practices until they attain non-retrogression and are bound to only one more birth—the bodhisattva universally gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward all such infinite and boundless merits.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding all roots of goodness in all the Bhagavān Buddhas of the past, future, and present, the bodhisattva also gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward them all. Śāriputra!

Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is well able to perform the deeds of merit arising from sympathetic joy; he is further able to perform the deeds of merit arising from exhortation by requesting all Buddhas to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma and requesting all noble ones to expound the supreme Dharma; and he is further able to perform the deeds of merit arising from dedication by dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see bodhisattvas who have not yet resolved to attain great enlightenment, they employ skillful means to instruct them so that they may resolve their minds on enlightenment.
If there are those who have already resolved their minds on enlightenment, they teach and guide them by preaching the Dharma so that they may reach maturity.

They gather in the poor with material wealth; to those who are ill, they provide medicine and diligent care, serving them with reverence; toward those who are violent and wicked, they give rise to patience; regarding any transgressions of the precepts, they do not conceal them, but openly confess their faults, thereby effectively eliminating their offenses.
One should constantly practice offerings to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have already entered parinirvāṇa.

One should revere one’s *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* as if they were the Great Master himself. One should apply diligent effort toward the True Dharma, seeking it out and inquiring about it; and one should honor and venerate a teacher of the Dharma with love and respect, just as if serving the Buddha.

There are assemblies for the preaching of the Dharma; even if they are many hundreds of *yojanas* distant from oneself, one must go to them to hear the True Dharma without ever feeling weary or satiated.
Or there may be sentient beings who come to request clarification regarding their doubts and obstructions, to whom one proclaims the pure Dharma with a mind free from defilement.
They receive and cultivate offerings toward their parents, recognizing and repaying their kindness without any change of heart or regret.
They accumulate all pure merits and establish their practice with a mind free from weariness.
By means of the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*), one guards the body so that the body is free from deceit;
one guards speech so that the words spoken are harmonious and elegant;
one guards the mind so that the mind is free from flattery and delusion.
In order to encompass the merit of Brahma, he constructed caityas for all the Tathāgatas;
and in order to bring the marks of a Great Man to full perfection, he accumulated the dharma-assembly of the unobstructed great sacrifice.
In order to manifest the characteristics [of a Buddha] and bring them to perfection, one accumulates the various provisions of the roots of goodness.
To adorn the body, one abandons arrogance;
to adorn speech, one distances oneself from all faults of speech.
In order to adorn the mind, they remain far removed from all thoughts of malice and envy.
In order to greatly adorn the Buddha-fields, they manifest supernatural powers and transformations with sovereign mastery.
In order to adorn the characteristics of all phenomena, their unsurpassed, wondrous wisdom is excellently victorious and pure.
In order to adorn the great assembly of the Dharma, they remain far removed from all divisive, harsh, and destructive speech.
In order to avoid grasping at or becoming attached to any phenomena, one should abandon false conceptualization.
To ensure that the teacher of the Dharma is free from sorrow and distress, one should joyfully bestow upon them words of praise, saying, "Excellent! (Sādhu).
To ensure that those who preach the Dharma do not labor in vain, they listen to the Dharma with reverence, remaining free from all hindrances.
To adorn the Bodhi tree, they offer pure groves and gardens to the Buddhas.
In order to adorn the Buddha’s site of enlightenment, they cultivate roots of goodness thoroughly and without regression.
In order to purify and eliminate the phenomena of birth and death, they remain unstained by any karma or afflictions.
Desiring to obtain hands that hold precious jewels, one practices the giving of all manner of treasures.
Desiring to obtain inexhaustible wealth and inexhaustible treasuries, one first practices the giving of those things most cherished and valued.

In order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to pure faith upon merely seeing him for a moment, he displays a gracious countenance and asks after them first, remaining far removed from any frown.
In order to obtain the mark of palms as level as a basin, he directs his impartial gaze toward all sentient beings.
In order to radiate infinite nets of light, he does not treat those sentient beings who lack learning and knowledge with contempt, nor does he abandon them.
In order that his future births may be pure, he constantly maintains and accumulates the merit of pure ethical discipline.
In order to purify the womb, they are well able to purify all transgressions.
Desiring to be born among gods and humans, they cultivate and purify the ten paths of wholesome action.
Because they are far removed from ignorance regarding coming and going, advancing and withdrawing, they harbor no false discrimination toward any instructions.
Because they have attained mastery over the wealth of the Dharma, they harbor no stinginess or concealment regarding the profound nature of phenomena.
Because they are to be looked up to by all the world, they cultivate and purify a superior aspiration and resolve.
Because they seek to attain a vast and great resolute belief in the Dharma, they do not practice for or realize minor or limited deeds.
In order to gather all merit, they constantly contemplate the Omniscient One with their minds.
To bring the seven noble riches to fulfillment, they take faith in the Buddha’s true Dharma as their guide.
In order to embrace and sustain all pure dharmas, they have never looked back upon or cherished their own bodies or lives.
Because they are entrusted with the affairs of the world, they ensure that whatever was previously promised is necessarily brought to fruition.
In order to bring the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas to full perfection, they cultivate all Buddha-dharmas to completion.
Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with such characteristics as these, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the accumulation of merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the equipment of the wisdom-merit? Śāriputra!"
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they gather up wisdom by abiding in such and such causal dharmas; therefore, this is called the equipment of the merit of wisdom.
Śāriputra! By what dharma does such gathering of wisdom have its cause and its condition? Śāriputra!

It should be known that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is free from weariness and seeks with diligence the nature of wisdom and its practice; they draw near to virtuous friends, incline toward the wisdom of the Buddhas rather than the wisdom of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and maintain a heart free from pride toward those virtuous friends, honoring and cherishing them as they would a great teacher.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva knows that those spiritual friends possess all the necessary inclinations and understandings; there is not even the slightest word of discourse in accordance with wisdom that he does not consult and receive from them.
Furthermore, having recognized that these bodhisattvas are vessels for the Dharma, he immediately proclaims it to them without even a moment’s interruption.
Having heard this teaching on the practice associated with the provisions for the True Dharma, these bodhisattvas diligently investigate and cultivate it through skillful means.
Śāriputra! These various characteristics are called the correct practice associated with the provisions for the merit of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s correct practice associated with the provisions for the true Dharma?

Śāriputra, as for the provisions for the true Dharma, it means that because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices correct conduct, they are well able to exercise moderation and frugality regarding their cravings and gluttony; they are well able to reduce and simplify their worldly affairs and activities; they are well able to distance themselves from idle talk and conversation; they are well able to renounce all sounds; and throughout the first and last watches of the night, they remain without sleep, diligently cultivating the correct practice associated with them.
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva weighs and deliberates upon the principles and meanings with gravity; because his mind is free from turbidity and defilement as he subdues the hindrances;
because he well understands the way out of transgressions and manifests the removal of remorse without guile or deceit;
and because he pursues nothing else but firmly cultivates right practice, he accords with the true Dharma and advances toward the correct goal.
One should look down upon the True Dharma with reverence; one should always be courageous regarding the Dharma, as if one’s head or clothing were ablaze;
one should diligently seek sublime wisdom without even momentary rest, so as not to dwell in the darkness of ignorance; one should be free from laxity and never abandon the noble yoke;
one should distance oneself from clamor and always delight in solitary dwelling; and one should contemplate in silent seclusion, knowing the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Because they are complete; because they do not abandon the merits of the *dhūta* practices and delight in the joy of the Dharma;
because they always delight in seeking supramundane dharmas and do not think to treasure or play with mundane literature or incantations;
because they have accomplished right mindfulness and are free from forgetfulness; because they are equipped with profound meaning and practice it well; and because they are endowed with excellence.
Because it accords with the path of wisdom; because it is firm and courageous in guarding against external conditions;
because it is adorned by the internal cultivation of shame and remorse; because it follows the course of the Buddhas and remains free from non-wisdom;

because it casts off the film of delusion so that the eye of wisdom is pure and well-awakened; and because its enlightened insight is vast and expansive, never becoming narrow or inferior in such awakening.
Because he has clearly realized and manifested the wisdom of wondrous enlightenment.

Śāriputra, all the merits of this bodhisattva mahāsattva do not depend on others; he is free from overweening pride regarding his own merits, and he neither envies nor disparages the merits of others. He skillfully practices his deeds and does not slight the ripening of karma. It is because of these qualities that he fully accomplishes the pure wisdom of karma.
“Śāriputra! When such characteristics as these are fully and perfectly complete, this is called the skillful practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accumulation of the merit of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess skillful means regarding the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and virtue; that is, by being able to fulfill four kinds of giving, they successfully accomplish the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and virtue.
What are the four?
First, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees such a sūtra being transcribed, they provide and bestow upon it all necessary materials, such as leaves, paper, pens, and ink.
Second, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas request those who preach the Dharma to expound profound and wondrous meanings.
Third, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas offer all manner of material benefits, respect, fame, praise, and eulogies to those who preach the Dharma.

Fourth, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva encounters a Dharma teacher who upholds the true Dharma, they should not act with flattery or crookedness to please that person's mind, but should instead offer these words: "Excellent! Excellent!"
Śāriputra! If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice these four kinds of pure giving, you should know that they are skillfully able to accumulate the provisions for wisdom and merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are four kinds of inexhaustible accumulations of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom and merit.
What are these four?
First, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is skillfully able to protect the body of the Dharma-preacher;
second, he is skillfully able to protect all wholesome qualities;
third, he is skillfully able to protect his dwelling place.
Fourth, they are skillfully able to protect the retinues of those who preach the Dharma.
Śāriputra, these are the four kinds of accumulation of the provisions for the merit of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are four kinds of skillful means regarding the accumulation of wisdom and merit that sustain the bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these four?
That is to say, a bodhisattva mahāsattva supports those who preach the Dharma by means of the Dharma, by means of wisdom, by means of material wealth, and by means of the merit of awakening.
"Śāriputra! These are the four kinds of sustenance for the wisdom-merit provisions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five kinds of superior powers that serve as skillful provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and virtue.
What are these five? They are:
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s possession of the power of faith, for the purpose of accomplishing a mind of resolute belief;
They possess the power of vigor, seeking spiritual friends in order to achieve great learning;
they possess the power of mindfulness, ensuring that the bodhicitta is never forgotten;
and they possess the power of meditative concentration, discerning and observing the state of equal enlightenment.
He is endowed with the power of wisdom, due to having long cultivated the power of extensive learning. Śāriputra,
this is called the skillful practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accumulation of the merit of the five powers of knowledge.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

there is another skillful means regarding the equipment of wisdom and virtue for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, namely, possessing the four kinds of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), by which they are able to skillfully accumulate the equipment of wisdom and virtue."
What are the four? They are:

the ethical discipline of delighting in the Dharma, the ethical discipline of seeking the Dharma, the ethical discipline of contemplating the Dharma, and the ethical discipline of dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these four kinds of pure ethical discipline (śīla), they will be able to skillfully accumulate the provisions of wisdom and merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

there is another skillful means regarding the equipment of the wisdom-virtue of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, namely, being able to fulfill the four kinds of patience, which serves as skillful means for the equipment of the wisdom-virtue."
What are the four?
First, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seeks the Dharma, they are well able to endure all coarse, evil, and unrighteous speech.
Second, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seeks the Dharma, he is well able to endure all winds, sun, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.
Third, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seeks the Dharma, he receives with the highest reverence whatever instructions are given by his two superior teachers, the ācārya and the upādhyāya.
Fourth, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seeks the Dharma, they are well able to have faith and understanding in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness,
and wishlessness. Śāriputra,
these four kinds of patience that embrace the Dharma serve as the practice for the provisions of wisdom and merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses another skillful means regarding the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and virtue, namely, the ability to fulfill four kinds of diligence, which serves as a skillful means for the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and virtue."
What are these four? They are:

the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s firm diligence in hearing the true Dharma, firm diligence in upholding the true Dharma, firm diligence in expounding the true Dharma, and firm diligence in practicing the right conduct.
"Śāriputra! These four kinds of firm diligence serve as the practices that constitute the provisions for wisdom and virtue.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means regarding the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and merit; that is to say, by being fully endowed with the four dhyānas and practicing them within the Dharma, they are able to serve as skillful means for the provisions of the accumulation of wisdom and merit.
What are these four?

First, a bodhisattva always delights in practicing the dharma of seclusion; second, they delight in dwelling alone and exclusively in the quietude of mountain forests; third, they always delight in seeking out supernormal powers and meditative concentration; fourth, they constantly and diligently cultivate the vast wisdom of a Buddha.
“Śāriputra! These four kinds of meditative concentration on the true Dharma serve as the practice that provides the provisions for the merit of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

Furthermore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means regarding the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and merit; that is to say, they are able to fulfill the four kinds of light of wisdom regarding the sublime Dharma, thereby serving as skillful means for the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and merit.
What are these four? They are:

when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices such light of wisdom, they do not abide in nihilism, do not propound eternalism, do not contradict dependent origination, and have faith and understanding in non-self.
“Śāriputra, these four kinds of light of wisdom constitute the correct practice that serves as the provision for the accumulation of knowledge and virtue.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses further skillfulness regarding the provisions for the accumulation of knowledge and virtue; that is to say, they are able to accomplish four kinds of unsurpassed skillful means of the true Dharma, which serve as skillfulness regarding the provisions for the accumulation of knowledge and virtue.”
What are these four? They are:
because the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they accord with the world, accord with the scriptures, accord with the sublime Dharma, and accord with pure knowledge.
"Śāriputra! These four kinds of skillful means regarding the true Dharma constitute the correct practice for the accumulation of the provisions of knowledge and merit.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means regarding the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and virtue; that is to say, they are able to advance upon four kinds of dharma-paths, which serve as skillful means for the provisions of the accumulation of wisdom and virtue.
What are the four? They are:

by relying on the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattva fully practices the path to the further shore, the path of the seven factors of enlightenment, the path of the eightfold noble path, and the path leading toward the wisdom of omniscience.
"Śāriputra! These four kinds of paths of the true Dharma constitute the correct practice for the accumulation of the provisions of wisdom and virtue.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means regarding the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and merit; that is to say, by possessing four kinds of insatiable dharmas, they are able to properly accumulate the provisions for the accumulation of wisdom and merit.
What are these four? They are as follows:

because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they uphold the true Dharma without ever being weary of hearing it; they preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude without ever being weary; they contemplate the principles and meanings without ever being weary; and they employ wisdom and skillful means without ever being weary.
"Śāriputra! These four kinds of insatiable dharmas can accumulate the right practice of the provisions for wisdom and merit.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, through such skillfulness in the provisions of wisdom and virtue, enters universally into all spheres of conduct.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

One should know that generosity is accomplished through the equipment of wisdom; likewise, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and right wisdom are also accomplished through the equipment of the virtue of wisdom, and even all wholesome dharmas—compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity—are accomplished by means of the equipment of the virtue of wisdom.
Why is this? Śāriputra, all the firm and correct practices initiated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely upon right knowledge; in all those practices, knowledge serves as the precursor.

Because these bodhisattvas possess great wisdom, they become the refuge for all who lack it; no evil māras can find an opportunity against them, and they are collectively protected by all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as they are about to enter into the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Śāriputra! This is the skillful practice of the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the provisions for wisdom and merit.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such skillfulness in these two types of accumulations—merit and wisdom—it should be known that they obtain this power of skillfulness in the accumulations by virtue of practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the foundations of mindfulness? Śāriputra,"

It is said that because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they fully cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and thereby achieve skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
Śāriputra! What are these four?

First, the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness by observing the body as the body; second, the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness by observing feelings as feelings; third, the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness by observing the mind as the mind; and fourth, the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness by observing phenomena as phenomena.
Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he cultivate the application of mindfulness by observing the body in the body?
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva dwells in mindfulness of the body, observing the faults of this body from its prior limit. This bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
"Such a body as this is produced by the causal conditions of inverted karma; fundamentally, it has no master and nothing that appropriates it."
Just as those flowers, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs arise from causes and conditions, having originally no sovereign and nothing that appropriates them;
so too is this body like a dwelling that has arisen, being a composite formed through a multitude of conditions such as grasses, woods, walls, and moats.

This body is likewise; it is merely sustained by the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, yet its fundamental nature is empty, devoid of a self or what belongs to a self, impermanent, non-eternal, lacking any stable endurance, and not a phenomenon that remains unchanging.
I should not now falsely conceive of this body as having any substantiality; therefore, I shall now use this unsubstantial body to exchange for a substantial body.
What kind of body is called "solid and substantial"?
It is the body of the Tathāgata that is the solid and substantial body.
I observe this [present] body to be utterly deceptive; I must surely accomplish the body of a Tathāgata.
For what reason?
The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, the vajra-body, the indestructible body, the firm and solid body, and the most supreme body that transcends the triple world.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"This body of mine is defiled by immeasurable faults; I shall seek to realize the body of a Tathāgata, which is free from all such faults and defilements."

"Śāriputra! By the power of discernment through various forms of awakening wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that this body is comprised of the four great elements and serves as a dwelling place and cave for all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Therefore, I shall now employ this body to serve and attend upon all sentient beings."

Why is this? It is because, for example, the four external great elements of the world—namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element—benefit and nourish all sentient beings through various means and immeasurable varieties of implements and resources.

I am now likewise so; using this body composed of the four great elements, and with the various gateways, immeasurable distinctions, objects, and resources, I shall serve as that which is enjoyed by sentient beings.

Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates this body by relying on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and because it possesses such great purpose and function, although he contemplates that the nature of this body is suffering, he does not feel weary of or distressed by such a suffering body; although he contemplates that this body is ultimately of the nature of exhaustion, he does not feel weary of the cycle of birth and rebirth; although he contemplates that the nature of this body is selflessness, he does not become weary or indolent in maturing sentient beings; although he contemplates that the nature of this body is the tranquility of cessation (nirvāṇa), he does not fall into the extreme of permanently abandoning that cessation; and although he contemplates that the body is empty, signless, and detached, he does not fall into the extreme of detachment.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to this physical body, observing that this body is without reality and without solidity.
Furthermore, dwelling in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal body, he follows it internally and no longer allows any room for the afflictions.
Furthermore, he dwells observing the external body, following it as it moves externally, and does not cohabit with any afflictions.

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such mindfulness of the body, his body is pure and free from defilement; he is endowed with all pure bodily actions and attains a body adorned with pure marks.
Because he has thus become endowed with such a body of adornment, he is one toward whom all gods and humans look for refuge and veneration. Śāriputra,
this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness by means of observing the body as it follows the body while practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he practice the application of mindfulness by observing feelings as they arise?
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:
"All sensations whatsoever are entirely suffering."

Now that I am endowed with the power of awakened wisdom, I shall thoroughly discern these feelings through discernment by means of knowledge, discernment by means of wisdom, and discernment by means of skillful means.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has thus attained such superior power of discernment, even while experiencing pleasure at the moment of contact with that pleasure, they immediately give rise to great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings in the happy realms, and are not afflicted by the latent tendencies of desire.

Even when experiencing suffering at the moment of contact with pain, they immediately give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings in the evil realms, and are not afflicted by the latent tendencies of anger.
Even when experiencing various feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant, at the moment of contact and sensation, they are not afflicted by the latent tendencies of ignorance. Śāriputra!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely on the perfection of wisdom and possess such power of contemplative understanding, they act in accordance with whatever they experience, cultivating the foundations of mindfulness regarding all sensations—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—and are well able to observe the transcendence of all sensations; furthermore, they enable all sentient beings to realize the dharma of universal knowledge and the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"These sentient beings, because they are possessed of afflictions, lack wisdom and are unable to understand the transcendence of all sensations. Why is this?"
When experiencing pleasure, one gives rise to craving; when experiencing pain, one gives rise to aversion; and when experiencing neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one gives rise to delusion.

How much more so for us bodhisattvas who act in accordance with wisdom—since all faulty states resulting from sensation have already been extinguished, how could we ever again give rise to afflictions regarding sensation?
I should now fully arouse skillful means and great compassion to gather in all sentient beings, causing them to attain the cessation of all sensations.
"Śāriputra! For what reason does such a bodhisattva say that they are able not to follow after any sensations? Śāriputra!"
It means that through wisdom one discriminates among all feelings, such that they lead to happiness and do not lead to suffering. Śāriputra,
by what kind of wisdom does one further discriminate?
This means that the bodhisattva observes that within this there is no one who can experience—neither a self, nor a sentient being, nor a life-force, nor a person who takes up rebirth.
Upon completing this observation, there is ultimately no one who experiences; there is only the experiencing itself.
What kinds of feeling are there?

They are: feeling as appropriation, feeling as grasping, feeling as taking up, feeling with acquisition, perverted feeling, discriminative feeling, feeling associated with the latent tendencies of views, feeling produced by the perception of the eye up to feeling produced by the perception of the mind, feeling produced by the perception of forms up to feeling produced by the perception of phenomena, and those various feelings produced by eye-contact.

Thus, in detail, all phenomena whether internal or external, up to and including the feelings produced conditioned by contact—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—such characteristics as these are called feeling (*vedanā*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, distinguish the various gateways and differentiated characteristics of all feelings. Śāriputra!"
The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of a single sensation, namely, the mind’s discernment of various objects.
Sometimes he speaks of two sensations, namely, the internal and the external.
Sometimes he speaks of three sensations, namely, the discernment of the past, the discernment of the future, and the discernment of the present.
Some speak of four feelings, namely the distinctions between the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Some speak of five feelings, namely the contemplation of these five aggregates.
Some speak of six feelings, namely the discrimination of these six sense bases.
Some speak of seven feelings, namely the seven stations of consciousness.
Some speak of eight feelings, namely the characteristics of the eightfold wrong means.
Some speak of nine feelings, namely the abodes where the nine classes of sentient beings dwell.
Some speak of ten types of feeling, namely the ten paths of wholesome action and so forth.

Śāriputra, in this way, to speak extensively, up to all immeasurable feelings— according to their respective objects and according to their respective mental orientations, there are such specific measures and limits of those feelings.
Nevertheless, the Tathāgatas have taught that feelings are immeasurable. Why is this?
Because sentient beings are immeasurable; as there are sentient beings, each possesses such immeasurable feelings.
Śāriputra! In this way, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell observing feelings in accordance with feelings? Śāriputra!

This refers to bodhisattvas who, by means of pure wisdom and skillful means, thoroughly comprehend all sensations—whether arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing—of all sentient beings, as well as their knowledge of the sensations of all sentient beings, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
If bodhisattvas contemplate in this manner, it is called the thorough observation of feeling. Śāriputra,
this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the foundation of mindfulness through the cultivation of observing every feeling as it arises while practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he cultivate the application of mindfulness by observing the mind in accordance with the mind?

Śāriputra! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess no forgetfulness; they guard and protect themselves in secret, remaining free from all distraction. They observe that the arising and ceasing of the mind is momentary and unstable, neither abiding nor revolving within or without. This is called the bodhisattva’s correct contemplation of the mind.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects: "I recall the initial mind that was first generated;
once such minds have arisen, they immediately cease, disperse, and undergo transformation, so that it is impossible to know to what destination they go."

Furthermore, all the immeasurable roots of goodness accumulated by my various minds arise and immediately perish; they are dispersed, subject to transformation and decay, and possess no fixed location.
Moreover, although the immeasurable mental characteristics of mine are dedicated toward Bodhi, the essential nature of the mind cannot cognize itself.
How can this mind give rise to such a thought as,
"I shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment"? For what reason?
"Because this essence of mind cannot comprehend the mind, cannot contemplate the mind, and cannot penetrate its own nature. Śāriputra,
that bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects thus:
