"If the bodhicitta is not lost through the mind of roots of goodness, then the mind of roots of goodness is not lost through the mind of dedication.
If the mind of dedication is not lost because of bodhi, then Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi itself will be without loss."
Having made this contemplation, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is not confused, nor does he feel fear or terror.
He further reflects:

"In this law of dependent origination, cause and effect are indestructible. Although these mental phenomena lack intrinsic nature, lack functional activity, and lack a sovereign master, nevertheless, all these dharmas arise by depending upon causes and conditions."
"I shall accumulate roots of virtue according to my desire; having accumulated them, I shall practice the corresponding conduct, never abandoning this nature of the mind's dharmas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva accumulate [merit] therein?

Śāriputra, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas contemplate the nature of accumulation in this way: the intrinsic nature of this mind is like a magical illusion; there is not a single dharma that can be given as a gift.

This nature of the mind is able to practice giving to all sentient beings and dedicate the merit toward the accumulation of adornments for the Buddha-lands; this is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The intrinsic nature of this mind is like that which is seen in a dream; its characteristics are quiescent. This dharma-nature of the mind is able to accumulate and maintain ethical discipline (śīla), all of which is dedicated toward the functioning of supernormal powers (abhijñā); this is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The intrinsic nature of this mind is like a mirage, ultimately extinguished and ceased. Yet, the dharma-nature of this mind is able to cultivate all forms of delightful power of patience, dedicating and accumulating them to adorn bodhi; this is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The intrinsic nature of the mind is like the moon in water, ultimately free from the characteristics of accumulation. This dharmic nature of the mind is able to initiate all right efforts and dedicate them toward the maturation of immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; this is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the mind cannot be grasped and cannot be seen. This dharmic nature of the mind is able to cultivate all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis, and dedicate them toward the supreme samādhi of all Buddhas; this is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, contemplate that the nature of this mind is fundamentally not a form, being invisible, non-obstructive, and unknowable. Yet, this dharma-nature of the mind is able to cultivate all distinctions of the phrases of wisdom, dedicating the knowledge of these diverse teachings toward the perfection of the wisdom of all Buddhas; this is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The mind has no object of focus; it is unborn and unarisen. Yet, this very nature of the mind (*cittadharmatā*) is able to establish immeasurable wholesome dharmas and assume physical forms (*rūpalakṣaṇa*). This is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the mind has no cause and is not produced; yet this nature of the mind (dharmatā) is able to encompass the causes of the factors of awakening (bodhipakṣa-dharma). This is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The nature of the mind is remote from the six sense objects and does not arise; yet this dharmic nature of the mind can give rise to the mind produced by the causes of the bodhi-realm. This is what is called the accumulation of roots of goodness.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness by means of observing the mind in accordance with the mind, based upon the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with all thoughts observing the mind as it arises; for the sake of seeking to realize the supreme supernormal powers, he binds his mind and trains in the knowledge of those powers."
Having attained the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one is able to thoroughly know the characteristics of all minds through single-minded concentration.
Once this has been fully understood, one proclaims all phenomena based on the intrinsic nature of the mind itself.

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who abides in this manner, observing according to the mind, employs the power of great compassion to govern his own mind, maturing sentient beings without weariness.

Because this bodhisattva dwells in the contemplation that accords with the mind, he does not dwell upon the exhaustion of the mind nor its cessation, but dwells within the mind solely for the purpose of causing the mind to distance itself from the fetters of the continuous succession of birth and death.

Furthermore, by means of the power of wisdom regarding mental recollection, they abide in the correct certainty that all phenomena are unarisen and unproduced, and thus do not fall back into the stages of the two vehicles.

Furthermore, by means of this power, one sustains the continuity of the mind until all Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected; through the sublime wisdom associated with a single moment of mind, one awakens to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, Śāriputra, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness by relying on the perfection of wisdom, observing all thoughts in accordance with the mind.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he cultivate the foundations of mindfulness by observing phenomena in accordance with the Dharma?

Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives all phenomena with the noble eye of wisdom; from that point until sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there is no loss of direction or confusion in the interval between.

This bodhisattva dwells in the contemplation of phenomena according to the Dharma regarding all phenomena; they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that is apart from emptiness, apart from signlessness, apart from wishlessness, apart from non-arising, apart from non-origination, or apart from non-exertion.
Furthermore, he observes again and finds that not even the slightest phenomenon exists apart from dependent origination. Śāriputra,
because this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells thus in the contemplation of phenomena according to their nature, he does not perceive either phenomena or non-phenomena.
In this context, what is that which has meditative concentration as its dharma?

It refers to the meaning of selflessness, which is called the meaning of dharma; the meaning of the absence of a sentient being, the meaning of the absence of a life-principle, and the meaning of the absence of a person—such meanings as these are called dharma.
Furthermore, what constitutes the meaning of non-Dharma?

It refers to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a person, the view of annihilationism and eternalism, and the views of existence and non-existence; such views as these are called non-Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To state the essential point: all dharmas are either called "dharmas" or called "non-dharmas. Why is this so?
If one can thoroughly understand that all such phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless, then all phenomena are collectively termed "Dharma.
If there is attachment to the views of "self" and "mine," along with their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), then all phenomena are collectively termed "non-Dharma."

Śāriputra! Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the contemplation of phenomena in accordance with reality by relying on the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive even a single dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma, not the Buddha, not the Path, not liberation, or not transcendence.

Having realized that all phenomena are characterized by transcendence, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva further attains unobstructed great compassion; he observes that all afflictions of sentient beings arise from false conceptualization and knows that the intrinsic nature of these afflictions is itself detached from them.
Why is this? These afflictions and so forth lead toward the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); there is not the slightest affliction that can be accumulated or gathered.
Such awakening is itself bodhi; the nature of afflictions is itself the nature of bodhi.

In this way, although the bodhisattva dwells in mindfulness, he dwells nowhere; neither recollecting nor forgetting, he is nonetheless able to fully understand that which mindfulness rests upon. Why is this?

The mindfulness in which one dwells is itself called the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); if one dwells in the dharma-realm, one dwells in the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*); if one dwells in the realm of sentient beings, one dwells in the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*). Because it is thus, these phenomena are said to be equal to space.

Śāriputra! Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the contemplation of phenomena according to the Dharma relies upon the Buddha-dharma; therefore, they have faith and understanding that all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma.
Although they have thus aroused the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they are able not to realize the unconditioned dharma of cessation.

Although they have aroused the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they manifest birth out of compassion for all sentient beings, yet they do not abandon the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of non-arising.
Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with mindfulness amidst all phenomena, he is able to fully embrace the dharmas of both vehicles.

Although he dwells in mindfulness regarding all conventionally designated phenomena, this right mindfulness is neither distracted nor lost; even unto the future limit, he cultivates the foundations of mindfulness by observing phenomena according to their nature among all dharmas. He is able, through the expressions of immeasurable discourse, to enter into the equality of all Buddha-dharmas within the context of unequal objects, to gladden the minds of all sentient beings, and to crush all the firm armies of Māra; by means of this, he realizes spontaneous great wisdom.

Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness by means of observing all phenomena in accordance with the Dharma, as he practices the perfection of wisdom.
This is called the skillful method of the four foundations of mindfulness. Thus, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should cultivate skill in the foundations of mindfulness.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-Two;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Bodhisattvapiṭaka Section XII-19, Prajñāpāramitā Chapter XI-4: "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the four right efforts?"
Śāriputra! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there are four kinds of paths.
What are these four?

First, for the sake of not giving rise to unwholesome and evil states that have not yet arisen, one generates desire and delight, exerts oneself with vigor and diligence, and maintains the mind with equanimity and stability.

Second, for the sake of permanently abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire and delight, exerts oneself with vigor and diligence, and maintains the mind with focused composure, dwelling in equanimity.

Third, for the sake of giving rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one generates desire and interest, exerts oneself with vigor and diligence, and maintains the mind with focused application, dwelling in equanimity.

Fourth, for the sake of causing already arisen wholesome states to endure, not be forgotten, and reach fulfillment through cultivation, one generates desire and delight, exerts oneself with vigor and diligence, and maintains the mind in balanced composure.
"Śāriputra! These four kinds are also called the four right strivings (*samyakprahāṇa*). Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is meant by "for the sake of not producing unarisen evil and unwholesome states," and so forth, up to "maintaining the mind and dwelling in equanimity"? Śāriputra!

Regarding the statement: "In order that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, one generates desire, joy, vigor, and exertion"—this is called appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
To exert diligent effort means not abandoning appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
To maintain the mind and abide in equanimity is what is called appropriate investigation (*yoniśaḥ-pratyavekṣā*).
Why is this? Because through skillful means that accord with reality, unwholesome and evil dharmas no longer manifest. Śāriputra!
"What are called evil and unwholesome dharmas?
Furthermore, by what principle do evil and unwholesome dharmas no longer manifest? Śāriputra!"

There are evil and unwholesome dharmas, namely those counteracted by ethical discipline (*śīla*), those counteracted by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and those counteracted by wisdom (*prajñā*).
What is meant by "counteracted by ethical discipline"?

Śāriputra! That which is called the "antidote" refers to the violation of the precepts and all other factors that give rise to the transgression of ethical discipline (śīla); it is the antidote to the entire collection of sublime precepts, and is thus termed the "antidote to ethical discipline."
Śāriputra! What is called that which is counteracted by meditative concentration?

It refers to violations of the rules of conduct, as well as all other factors that lead to mental distraction; these factors counteracted by the collection of sublime concentrations are what is called that which is counteracted by meditative concentration.
Śāriputra! What is that which is counteracted by wisdom?

It refers to the violation of views, as well as all other factors—such as the fetters, hindrances, and obscurations—that lead to various views; these are what the collection of sublime wisdom counteracts. This is called that which is counteracted by wisdom.
Śāriputra! All such things as these are termed evil and unwholesome dharmas.
If any form of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) prevents such evil and unwholesome dharmas from arising, this is termed the non-occurrence of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
"Śāriputra! This is called the first right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is meant by "for the sake of permanently abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen," up to "maintaining the mind and dwelling in equanimity"? Śāriputra!

If various evil and unwholesome dharmas accumulate in the mind without direction or location, and if these evil and unwholesome dharmas manifest within the cognizing mind, they arise by depending upon causes, conditions, and objective referents.
What is meant by "arising in dependence upon objects"?

It refers to the arising of a mind of attachment due to pure and exquisite signs, the arising of a mind of aversion due to harmful signs, and the arising of a mind of delusion due to signs of ignorance.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwelt in such reasoned reflection:
"Through the sign of impurity, sensual desire is stilled; through the sign of loving-kindness and compassion, hatred is stilled; through the sign of dependent origination, delusion is stilled."

"Although these afflictions are conventionally designated as 'quiescence' because they are permanently extinguished through mental attention (*manasikāra*), in reality no separate quiescence can be found. Rather, one realizes all phenomena (*dharmas*) for the sake of the equality of their cessation; it is precisely by means of this dharma that they are called the 'Right Efforts' (*samyakprahāṇa*)."
"Śāriputra! This is called the second right effort of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is meant by "for the sake of generating unarisen wholesome dharmas," and so forth, up to "maintaining the mind and abiding in equanimity"?
Śāriputra, the words and phrases for such meanings are immeasurable.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva should accumulate immeasurable wholesome dharmas; it is by virtue of these that the phrases are immeasurable. Śāriputra!
It should be known that for a bodhisattva, aspiration is the root of all roots of goodness; through diligence, one is then able to accumulate all roots of goodness. Why is this?
Because they are sustained and established by such dharmas, all roots of goodness attain ultimate perfection.
Śāriputra, this is called the third right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is meant by 'arousing the desire for the sake of maintaining, not forgetting, cultivating, and perfecting those wholesome dharmas that have already arisen, and so forth, until one maintains them within the mind and dwells in equanimity'? "
Śāriputra! You should know that such a meaning is precisely dedication toward bodhi. Why is this?
Because all roots of goodness are never again lost or destroyed due to being dedicated toward enlightenment.
Why is this? It is because those bodhisattvas do not give rise to the mind of awakening while relying upon the three realms.

Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas cultivate roots of goodness without relying on the three realms, and further dedicate them toward omniscience, you should know that all such wholesome dharmas will ultimately be inexhaustible.
Śāriputra! This is called the fourth right effort of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!
In order to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivates skillfulness in these four kinds of factors of the path (mārgāṅga).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the fivefold path? Śāriputra,"
What are these five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; these are called the five. Śāriputra!
What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s faculty of faith while practicing the perfection of wisdom?
Śāriputra, such a person of faith has faith in four kinds of dharmas.
What are the four? First, one has faith in and accepts such mundane right view within the cycle of birth and death.
Because of this faith, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the law of karmic retribution, will never conceive the intention to commit any evil deeds, even at the cost of losing their life.
Second, they have faith in and accept these various bodhisattva practices;
by virtue of this faith, they practice the correct conduct and never give rise to the intention to realize any other vehicle.
Third, they have faith in and accept such profound dependent origination, which is of ultimate meaning and definitive import.

All phenomena are without self and without sentient beings; they are merely established through conventional expression, possessing only the characteristics of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
By virtue of this faith, the views and inclinations of sentient beings, as well as their underlying tendencies, no longer increase.
Fourth, one has faith and acceptance in all Buddha-dharmas, such as these powers and fearlessnesses.
Having already attained faith and acceptance, one becomes free from doubt and confusion, cultivating and gathering all existing Buddha-dharmas.
Śāriputra! Such characteristics as these are called the faculty of faith of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!
What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) in the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
It refers to the fact that the dharmas which are objects of faith arise by means of the faculty of diligence; it is for this reason that these dharmas are termed the faculty of diligence.
Śāriputra! What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?

It is that all dharmas, having been accumulated through diligence, are not lost or destroyed by the power of the faculty of mindfulness; it is precisely by means of these dharmas that one constitutes the faculty of mindfulness.
Śāriputra! What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) within the perfection of wisdom?

It is that all phenomena, by the power of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛti-indriya*), are not lost or destroyed; because those very same phenomena are gathered and held upon a single object by means of the faculty of concentration, it is called the faculty of concentration.
Śāriputra! What is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom? It is as follows:

because all phenomena are gathered and held upon a single object by means of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), those very phenomena are then perceived and clearly understood through the power of the faculty of wisdom; therefore, it is called the faculty of wisdom.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses these five superior faculties and practices the correct path with uninterrupted continuity, they will be able to swiftly perfect all Buddha-dharmas and quickly enter the stage of receiving the prediction of enlightenment.

Śāriputra! For example, it is like a non-Buddhist practitioner endowed with the five supernormal powers who, so long as the male or female characteristics within a womb have not yet emerged, would never falsely bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon that being.
The Tathāgata is likewise; if bodhisattvas have not yet fully accomplished these five faculties in uninterrupted succession, he will never bestow upon them a prediction of enlightenment.
Śāriputra! Such characteristics as these are called the fivefold path-dharma of a bodhisattva.
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas desire to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to cultivate skillfulness in these fivefold paths.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā, there are five further divisions of skill in the path.
What are these five?
They are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom; these are called the five. Śāriputra!
What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of faith?

Śāriputra, it is the purity of these bodhisattvas’ resolute conviction, their acceptance and certainty, which is firm, indestructible, and invincible. Even if an evil Māra were to manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to the bodhisattva to create obstacles, seeking to cause that bodhisattva to distance himself from the wisdom of the true Dharma and from the desire for supreme liberation, making him feel no joy or inclination toward them, and even saying these words:
"Such a teaching is not the true doctrine of the Buddha.

Śāriputra! Even if the natures of the four great elements were to undergo mutual transformation, they could never cause a bodhisattva who has achieved the power of faith and resolute conviction to have that power of faith shaken by being deluded by Māra.
“Śāriputra! This is called the power of faith of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of diligence? Śāriputra,

it refers to the bodhisattva’s exertion of diligent effort and skillful means in cultivating all wholesome dharmas, thereby attaining the power of firm maintenance and sustenance in those various states.

By the power of this, until the task to be performed at that place is finally completed, throughout that interval, there is not a single deity or being in the world who can cause the Bodhisattva to move from his station or prevent him from remaining in his original place.
"Śāriputra! This is called the power of diligence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is the power of mindfulness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra, it is when bodhisattvas,
through abiding in mindfulness regarding various dharmas, cause the mind to abide securely, such that nothing can cause it to be moved or distracted.
By the power of mindfulness and retention, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is well able to destroy all afflictions, and no one is able to subdue this mindfulness. Śāriputra!
This is called the power of mindfulness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the power of samādhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Śāriputra! Bodhisattvas, dwelling securely in seclusion and the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*), may indeed observe all sounds, all paths of vocal action, and the thorns of sound, yet they cannot obstruct their initial meditative concentration.
Although these bodhisattvas investigate and examine immeasurable dharmas through all such wholesome dharmas by means of vitarka and vicāra, they are not able to obstruct the second dhyāna.
Although these bodhisattvas abide in the joy born of that [first dhyāna], it does not obstruct their third dhyāna.
Although these bodhisattvas, for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, do not abide in equanimity while upholding the true Dharma, it does not obstruct their fourth dhyāna.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in these four kinds of dhyāna, no phenomena that are the opposites of dhyāna can overcome them.
Furthermore, although this bodhisattva remains steadfastly established in samādhi without relinquishing it, he does not undergo rebirth according to the power of that concentration. Śāriputra,
this is called the power of samādhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the power of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra,"
This power of wisdom is firm and difficult to subdue, meaning it cannot be overcome by any worldly or world-transcending phenomena.

Such intellectual power is the very birthplace of the Bodhisattva; even regarding the various worldly practices, crafts, and occupations that are difficult to perform or understand, the Bodhisattvas clearly comprehend them all through direct realization without relying on a teacher’s instruction.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, regarding all supramundane dharmas—those which are able to deliver all worlds—the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by the power of their wisdom, are fully able to embrace them and cannot be overcome by any worldly devas or humans.
Śāriputra! This is called the power of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Such characteristics as these are termed the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the fivefold path.
Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they diligently cultivate skillfulness in these fivefold paths.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice skillfulness regarding the factors of enlightenment while cultivating the perfection of wisdom? Śāriputra,"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
What are the seven? They are:

the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. These are called the seven factors of enlightenment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Śāriputra! What is called the awakening factor of mindfulness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

It refers to the fact that, by relying on the power of such right mindfulness, bodhisattvas awaken to all phenomena, observe all phenomena, investigate all phenomena, comprehend all phenomena, discern all phenomena, and illuminate all phenomena.
By the power of mindfulness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
Śāriputra, what is called the wisdom that thoroughly penetrates the self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena?
This means that by the power of mindfulness, one realizes that the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
If bodhisattvas thoroughly penetrate this, it is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s factor of awakening of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga)?

It refers to the bodhisattvas being fully endowed with the wisdom that discriminates the eighty-four thousand treasuries of dharmas, and according to those dharmas, they should perform such investigation. Such investigation is what is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha). This definitive meaning is understood by means of the non-definitive meaning (neyārtha); the non-definitive meaning is understood by means of the conventional meaning (saṃvṛtyartha); the conventional meaning is understood by means of the ultimate meaning (paramārthārtha); the ultimate meaning is understood by means of provisional designation (prajñapti); and provisional designation is understood by means of supreme discernment (viniścaya). This supreme discernment is called 'investigation.'"
“Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas accomplish this, it is called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the bodhisattva’s non-retrogressive aspiration for joy, vigor, power, and resolve, which embraces such wisdom regarding mindfulness, the investigation of phenomena, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; it is the right exertion that encourages and rouses one to not abandon the noble yoke, and the right exertion generated for the sake of the clear realization of the path.
"Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas accomplish this, it is called the awakening-factor of diligence.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It means that because the bodhisattva gives rise to joy toward the Dharma, he takes delight in the Dharma; because he takes delight in the Dharma, his mind does not sink; because his mind does not sink, pure joy arises; and because his joy is pure, his body and mind become tranquil and free from all afflictions.
"Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas accomplish these, they are said to possess the factor of awakening known as joy.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It is as follows: because the bodhisattva possesses physical tranquility, they attain mental tranquility; because they possess mental tranquility, they pacify all afflictions and distance themselves from all hindrances and obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). Their mind dwells securely upon the object of focus, and thus they enter into samādhi.
"Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas accomplish this, it is called the dharma of the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s awakening factor of samādhi?
It refers to the bodhisattva’s realization of phenomena through this concentrated mind, and not through a non-concentrated mind.

Why is this? If the mind attains concentration and realizes all phenomena, it will never give rise to the fetters and obstacles of craving, views, and so forth, nor to false awakening; rather, with the exception of the equal and true nature of phenomena, the mind will resolutely enter into and awaken to the equal nature of all phenomena.
"Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas accomplish these, they are said to possess the factors of enlightenment pertaining to samādhi.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s factor of enlightenment of equanimity?

It refers to the bodhisattva having no attachment in the mind toward factors conducive to sorrow or joy; not grasping at worldly phenomena with the mind; abiding in a state that is neither high nor low and remaining unmoving; being without elation or aversion, without craving or anger; and being able only to practice in accordance with the Noble Path.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these, this is called the dharma of the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Thus, Śāriputra,

because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to attain skillful mastery in these seven factors of awakening, they delight in practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and diligently cultivate skillfulness in the factors of awakening.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice skillfulness in the factors of the path that constitute the perfection of wisdom? Śāriputra,"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are fully endowed with these eight factors of the noble path.
What are the eight? They are:

right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi. These are called the eight factors of the noble path for all bodhisattvas and others.
Śāriputra! What is called the right view of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra!
This refers to the supramundane vision of the various noble ones.

Such a vision does not arise from the view of a self, nor does it arise from the view of a sentient being, nor from the view of a life-principle, nor from the view of a person, nor from the view of annihilationism, nor from the view of eternalism, nor from the view of existence, nor from the view of non-existence, nor from the view of the wholesome, nor from the view of the unwholesome, and so on, up to and including not arising from the view of nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas distance themselves from these views, this is called the right view of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What is the right reflection of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Śāriputra, if there is any reflection by which a bodhisattva might give rise to all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, such a reflection they never initiate.

If, by means of such reflection, bodhisattvas are able to cultivate and increase the accumulations of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, then bodhisattvas should constantly initiate this kind of reflection.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva accomplishes this dharma, it is called the factor of right reflection.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What is called the right speech of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Śāriputra, it refers to the speech of bodhisattvas that does not harm or afflict themselves, does not harm or afflict others, and does not lead to mutual contention with sentient beings.
Because by means of this, the bodhisattva accomplishes this speech and is able to enter the noble path, it is called "right speech" (*samyagvāc*) of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called the 'right action' (*samyakkarmānta*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
Śāriputra! It means that bodhisattvas never perform actions that result in dark and dark retribution;
rather, they skillfully initiate those actions which can bring about pure and white fruits of retribution, or those actions which can exhaust all karma.

Śāriputra! These bodhisattvas take these very actions as pure actions; relying upon such actions, they apply themselves with skillful means to cultivate impartial action. This is called the right action of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the right livelihood of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra!"

This refers to all the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*), and merits of the bodhisattvas: they are without guile, without deceit, and free from hypocrisy; regarding their begging for alms, they are by nature free from distress, easy to satisfy, and easy to support; they respectfully practice those rules of conduct without becoming lax or negligent; they do not give rise to envy toward the gains and offerings of others; they feel contentment with their own gains and offerings; and regarding what is permitted by the Noble Ones, they are not deeply attached, but always maintain a pure livelihood through self-restraint.
“Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas accomplish these, this is called the right livelihood of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
What is the right diligence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva exerts diligent effort toward those things— such as the latent tendencies of afflictions like greed, hatred, and delusion, or various wrong practices— which are not permitted by the noble ones, that bodhisattva does not delight in practicing such diligence.

If the various right efforts are subsumed within the Noble Truths, lead to entry into the Noble Path, enable one to reach Nirvana, and induce correct practice—such diligence is what all Bodhisattvas joyfully cultivate and study; it is by means of this dharma that it is termed "right effort."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the right mindfulness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra!"

This means that there are various forms of mindfulness that are extremely well-established by nature and not inferior; the mind is upright and free from crookedness, capable of contemplating all the faults and afflictions of birth and death, and serving as the path leading to the great nirvana.
If bodhisattvas constantly and correctly maintain such mindfulness so as not to lose sight of the noble path, this very practice is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the right samādhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra!"
Regarding samādhi: if one is equal within the state of true reality (bhūtatā), then one is equal toward all phenomena.
Once bodhisattvas and others are established in such a samādhi, they enter into the state of true reality for the sake of liberating all sentient beings.

Such right concentration is the inexhaustible path; it has been proclaimed and revealed by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present for the sake of bodhisattvas to realize clear observation (*abhisamaya*). This is what is called the right concentration of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra! These are called the eight branches of the noble path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If any bodhisattva mahāsattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should diligently cultivate skillfulness in these eight branches of the noble path.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they possess skill in the path.
This skill in the path is further of two kinds."
What are these two? They are śamatha and vipaśyanā; these are called the two. Śāriputra!
What is called the path of śamatha? Śāriputra!

It refers to those bodhisattvas whose minds are tranquil, profoundly tranquil, and supremely tranquil; who are without distraction; whose faculties are serene, neither agitated nor uplifted; who are free from all turbulence and lethargy; who are peaceful, guarded in secrecy, and free from all guile; who are disciplined, capable, and delight in always dwelling alone; who avoid clamor and delight in the practice of seclusion; whose bodies are free from defilement and whose minds are free from confusion; who contemplate and attend to the gate of tranquility; who are free from evil desires and have no expectations; who distance themselves from great cravings and find joy in contentment; whose livelihood is pure and whose right conduct is perfected; who guard their deportment in secrecy, knowing the proper time and measure; who are easy to support and easy to satisfy, well-knowing the proper limit; who always delight in discernment, being neither haughty nor base; and who are by nature able to endure coarse and vulgar speech.

He fixes his mind in meditative application, delights in dwelling in a secluded chamber, and directs his attention toward the objects of concentration associated with the stages of dhyāna. He gives rise to great loving-kindness and evokes great compassion; he abides in great sympathetic joy and cultivates great equanimity, successively entering the meditative absorptions from the first dhyāna up to the eighth.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these, this is called the path of śamatha.
Śāriputra, furthermore,
there are immeasurable practices that serve as the provisions for the śamatha of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
When bodhisattvas enter into these provisions and skillful means in this manner,
it is also called the path of śamatha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called the path of vipaśyanā?

It refers to how bodhisattvas cultivate the noble path within the domain of sublime wisdom, giving rise to the non-conceptualizing contemplative knowledge regarding all phenomena; furthermore, they give rise to the contemplative knowledge of selflessness, the absence of sentient beings, the absence of life-principles, and the absence of persons; they give rise to the contemplative knowledge of phenomena regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), the contemplative knowledge of the dharma-realm regarding the elements (*dhātu*), and the contemplative knowledge of an empty village regarding the sense-bases (*āyatana*); they give rise to the contemplative knowledge of illuminating discernment regarding the eyes, the contemplative knowledge of non-contradiction regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the contemplative knowledge of detachment regarding various views; they give rise to the contemplative knowledge of karmic retribution regarding causes and effects, the contemplative knowledge of realization regarding the fruits to be attained, and the contemplative knowledge of entering regarding the correct nature (*samyaktva*).

Śāriputra! What is called vipaśyanā is the arising of a view that accords with reality regarding all phenomena, the arising of a view of truth regarding all phenomena, the arising of a view of non-alteration regarding all phenomena, the arising of a view of emptiness regarding all phenomena, the arising of a view of signlessness regarding all phenomena, and the arising of a view of wishlessness regarding all phenomena.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for vipaśyanā, it does not contemplate by way of a cause that exists, nor does it contemplate by way of a cause that does not exist; it does not contemplate by way of the causes of arising, ceasing, or abiding, nor does it contemplate by way of a cause that is something to be attained.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva observes here without observing anything at all; he sees without seeing, and does not see while seeing. Śāriputra!
If bodhisattvas practice such contemplation, it is called "contemplation according to reality," "true vision," and is also termed "attaining the skillful means of vipaśyanā."

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such contemplative understanding within this observation, they do not fall into that state of non-action, nor do they distance themselves from the application of roots of virtue.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these, it is called the vipaśyanā of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Śāriputra,
because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they diligently cultivate skillfulness in the dharmas of the paths of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, such is the mark of the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If I were to explain the bodhisattva path in brief, it would consist solely of skillfulness regarding the single vehicle."
Śāriputra! What is this?

It refers to the Bodhisattva who is solitary and peerless among the masses, having no equal and requiring no assistance from others; for the sake of realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he exerts the power of his own gathered diligence, possesses pure aspiration and resolve, and dons the firm armor.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas do not awaken through another nor rely upon another; they establish their own positions and exert themselves by their own power, thus fully equipping themselves with such firm armor.
"Śāriputra! These bodhisattvas give rise to this thought:
'Such armor as this cannot be donned by any sentient beings; I alone now don such armor.'"
"This armor has never been donned by any of the worthy and holy ones, nor by those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds but have not yet entered the stage of certainty;
I alone now don it. At that time, the bodhisattva further thought:
"I am now so fully equipped; how could I allow the mastery of giving to surpass me?"
I shall freely transcend that generosity.
Likewise, how could I allow morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom to freely transcend me?
"I shall exercise mastery and deliver them first.
Furthermore, he thought:
"How could it be that the pāramitās should now cause me to arise?"
"I shall initiate the pāramitās.
Thus, it is explained at length that all roots of virtue shall be initiated because of me, and not that the roots of virtue shall initiate themselves within me.

"Śāriputra! If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, regarding such dharmas, are able to establish themselves without relying on companions—thinking, 'I am alone and without equal'—they shall sit upon the firm and supreme Vajrāsana, personally subduing the armies of Māra through their own power, and by means of the wondrous wisdom corresponding to a single kṣaṇa, they shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Śāriputra, if bodhisattvas give rise to such aspirations, understandings, skillful means, and definitive observations, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness in approaching the single path.
Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they cultivate such skillfulness in the single path that leads to it.

Śāriputra! Such are the characteristics of skillfulness regarding the path; for the sake of practicing the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate such skillfulness in the dharmas of the path.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding dependent origination? Śāriputra,"
This refers to those bodhisattvas who, relying on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), cultivate dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
Secluded in a quiet chamber, they reflect thus: "From what source does this entire mass of suffering in the world arise?"

Having reflected thus, he came to understand for himself: "This mass of suffering arises because of the accumulation of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*). Because of the accumulation of ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise; because of the accumulation of volitional formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises; because of the accumulation of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises; because of the accumulation of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise; because of the accumulation of the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*) arises; because of the accumulation of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises; because of the accumulation of feeling, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises; because of the accumulation of craving, clinging (*upādāna*) arises; because of the accumulation of clinging, existence (*bhava*) arises; because of the accumulation of existence, birth (*jāti*) arises; and because of the accumulation of birth, old age, death, lamentation, grief, suffering, and despair all arise."
Śāriputra! Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:
"Although those phenomena arise through accumulation, they are without agency, without utility, and without a sovereign."

In this way, all these phenomena have wholesome states as their cause, the immovable as their cause, and nirvāṇa as their cause; that all such phenomena arise from conditions, and that they likewise lack a sovereign master, is also thus.

If sentient beings have inferior faculties as their cause, middling faculties as their cause, superior faculties as their cause, or various karmas as their cause, the flow and revolution of cause and effect are likewise thus.

"Śāriputra! All such phenomena that involve grasping arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions; the Bodhisattva is able to fully comprehend them all. This is what is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination."
Śāriputra! Furthermore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
"By the cessation of what do those phenomena cease?"

Having reflected thus, he understood for himself: "Through the cessation of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases; through the cessation of ignorance, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) cease; through the cessation of the formative forces, up to the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering."
Śāriputra! If one can thoroughly understand such knowledge of phenomena, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination. Śāriputra!
These bodhisattvas further reflect:
"One cultivates all virtues by relying on the true Dharma, depending upon various conditions, and depending upon their conjunction.

If these dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and depend upon various conditions, then these dharmas do not rely on a self, do not rely on a sentient being, do not rely on a life-principle, and do not rely on a person; thus, these dharmas are immeasurable."
“Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas can investigate in this manner according to the principle, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, they observe that all Buddha-dharmas are the marks of awakening arising from conditions, and they observe that all dependent originations are the marks of total cessation. Because they are able to regard all sentient beings, they do not enter into ultimate quiescence; this is also called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.”
Śāriputra! These bodhisattva mahāsattvas, desiring to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), cultivate such skillfulness regarding dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding all phenomena? Śāriputra,"
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they universally encompass all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned.
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should cultivate skillfulness regarding all such phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned.
Śāriputra! What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the conditioned?
It refers to excellent physical conduct, excellent verbal conduct, and excellent mental conduct; this is called skillfulness regarding the conditioned.
What is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

It is to dedicate such sublime and virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind toward ultimate unconditioned enlightenment, to dedicate it toward the sublime contemplation of unconditioned enlightenment, and furthermore, to dedicate it toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); this is what is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which constitutes the skillfulness regarding conditioned phenomena for a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the accumulation of the five pāramitās. What are these five?
What are called the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration are termed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
However, by virtue of the unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*) of the perfection of insight (*prajñāpāramitā*), these five perfections are not to be disparaged or rejected.

Furthermore, when such sublime wisdom can accumulate the virtuous dharmas that serve as the provisions for the various pāramitās, and when it resolves with faith upon untainted, unsurpassed bodhi and dedicates [the merit] toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), this is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta-kauśalya).

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is as follows: namely, illuminating all sentient beings with unimpeded light and gathering all sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); this is called the conditioned."

If one contemplates all phenomena as being without self, without sentient beings, without grasping, and without attachment; if one is skillful in means regarding the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); if one delights in, has faith in, and accepts unconditioned perfect enlightenment (*asaṃskṛta-abhisambodhi*); and if one dedicates [these merits] toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), this is called skillfulness in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtakauśalya*).

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which constitutes the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-kauśalya*) is as follows: namely, not severing the fetters that cause the continuity of birth and death, yet permanently severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) that cause the continuity of birth and death; maintaining the continuity of the fetters of enlightenment (*bodhi-bandhana*) so that the partial fetters no longer manifest—this is called skillfulness regarding the conditioned."

Furthermore, if one cultivates the correct wisdom regarding all phenomena—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and through skill in clear realization attains unsurpassed enlightenment without depending on others, thereby personally realizing unconditioned phenomena, this is called "skill in the unconditioned."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillfulness regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it means that although these bodhisattvas act within the three realms, they are not defiled by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of those three realms; this is called skillfulness regarding the conditioned."

Although one possesses thorough mastery of all dharmas for transcendence from the three realms, one does not fall into the realm of transcendence itself; this is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Śāriputra! That which is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding all phenomena is precisely what is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
If bodhisattvas fully realize and enter this knowledge of all modes, they possess skillful wisdom at all times; this is precisely what is called skillfulness regarding all phenomena.
Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they cultivate skillfulness regarding all such phenomena.
In this way, Śāriputra,

if there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who relies upon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka to practice the perfection of wisdom, and for the sake of practicing the perfection of wisdom, relies upon discernment through wisdom to skillfully and thoroughly master these ten kinds of skillful means, they shall cultivate them in such a manner.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What is called the 'sublime wisdom' of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
And what is the meaning of 'reaching the other shore'?"
Śāriputra! That which is called wisdom is the ability to understand and realize all wholesome dharmas.
It is the wisdom of direct perception, for it accords with and penetrates all phenomena.
This is the wisdom of true measure, for it penetrates all phenomena as they truly are.
This is the wisdom of penetration, for it is not obstructed by any fetters or views.
This is the wisdom of detachment from aspiration, because it is forever free from all desires and longings.
This is the wisdom of peace and joy, because it eternally stills all feverish afflictions.
This is the wisdom of rapture, because its reliance on the joy of the Dharma is uninterrupted.
This is the wisdom of reliance, because it directly perceives all knowledge regarding meanings.
This is the wisdom of establishment, because it establishes all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This is the wisdom of realization, because it realizes the fruit according to the vehicle one has mounted.
This is the wisdom of discerning characteristics, for it is well able to illuminate and realize the nature of this knowledge.
This is the wisdom of deliverance, for it rescues and delivers one from all the torrents.
This is the wisdom of entry, for it is able to enter into the correct nature of the non-arising of phenomena.
This is the wisdom of exertion, for it rouses and brings forth all wholesome dharmas.
This is the pure wisdom, for it is free from the turbidity of previously latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).
This is the supreme wisdom, for it ascends to the pinnacle of all dharmas.
This is subtle wisdom, for it awakens to phenomena through spontaneous knowledge (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
This is wisdom free from activity, for it is further untainted by any phenomena of the three realms.
This is inclusive wisdom, for it is embraced by all noble ones and sages.
This is the wisdom that severs aspiration, for it dispels all conceptualization of signs.
This is the wisdom that abandons negligence, for it remains far removed from all the darkness of ignorance.
This is the wisdom of skillful means, for it is accomplished by those who abide in all the stages of yoga practice.
This is the wisdom of setting forth, for it abides in the path of all noble knowledge.
This is the wisdom of illumination, for it eliminates the cataracts and darkness of the torrent of all ignorance.
This is the wisdom of illumination, for it guides all beings like the eye;
this is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), for the eye of wisdom transcends the paths of deviation;
this is ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-prajñā*), for it clearly perceives such great noble truths (*āryasatya*).
This is non-dual wisdom, because it is well-tamed and compliant.
This is luminous wisdom, because it is the gateway to all forms of knowledge.
This is inexhaustible wisdom, because it shines forth in accordance with everything everywhere.
This is the wisdom of non-extinction, because it constantly perceives extensively.
This is the wisdom of the path of liberation, because it forever severs all bonds of grasping and attachment.
This is the wisdom that does not depart from its locus, because it does not coexist with any dharmas that constitute afflictive hindrances.
Śāriputra! These characteristics of wisdom have now been briefly explained by me.
You should know that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess further immeasurable and boundless forms of wisdom.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Just as there are all such mental activities of all sentient beings, you should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise possesses an equal measure of wisdom-action and cognitive practice.

In this way, up to and including all the inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings, one should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise possesses as many forms of wisdom-observation as there are.

In this way, up to and including all the gateways of affliction possessed by all sentient beings, one should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise possesses as many gateways of vast wisdom as there are.

In this way, up to and including all the universal knowledge of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and perfectly awakened ones, one should know that the sphere of activity of the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise extensive.
Śāriputra! In all such bases of wisdom, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice and study; this is what is called the sublime wisdom of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the meaning of the 'perfection' (pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Śāriputra,"

In this way, it should be understood that all excellent and wholesome dharmas among all objects of knowledge that enable one to reach the further shore possess the meaning of "reaching the further shore.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
As extensively explained above, all terms for wisdom (*prajñā*) should be understood as having the meaning of "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it should be known that the meaning of the various distinctions in the cultivation and fulfillment of the bodhisattvas' practices is likewise the meaning of "reaching the other shore."
One should know that all meanings concerning the perfection of the knowledge of all modes are meanings of reaching the other shore.
One should know that all meanings concerning non-attachment to any phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, are meanings of reaching the other shore.
One should know that the ability to skillfully awaken to the meaning of the immeasurable great faults of birth and death is entirely the meaning of reaching the other shore (*pāramitā*).
One should know that the existence of any dharma capable of awakening those who have not yet awakened is entirely the meaning of reaching the other shore.
One who is able to reveal the meaning of the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma-treasure should be known as having reached the further shore.
One who possesses the meaning of unobstructed liberation and perfection should be known as having reached the further shore.

One should know that the meaning of awakening to the equality of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is the meaning of reaching the other shore (*pāramitā*).
One should know that the meaning of skillfulness in supreme discernment is the meaning of reaching the other shore.
The meaning of pervading the realm of all sentient beings is what is called the meaning of reaching the other shore.
The meaning of the perfection of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is what is called the meaning of reaching the other shore.
The meaning of the ultimate fulfillment of the stage of non-retrogression is what is called the meaning of reaching the other shore.
The meaning of purely cultivating and adorning all Buddha-fields is what is called the meaning of reaching the other shore.
The meaning of maturing all sentient beings is precisely what is called the meaning of reaching the other shore.
The meaning of proceeding to the site of enlightenment and ascending the seat of bodhi is precisely what is called the meaning of reaching the other shore.
The sense of ultimately subduing all demonic armies is precisely what is meant by the sense of reaching the other shore.
The sense of the complete fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas is precisely what is meant by the sense of reaching the other shore.
To be correctly established in the meaning of the various dharma-gates within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka is what is called the meaning of reaching the other shore (*pāramitā*). Śāriputra,
if one has correctly trained in such a subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, I declare that such persons have attained the ultimate consummation of all the *pāramitās*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna, they should all earnestly request this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, receive, uphold, read, recite, and master its meaning and principles, and extensively explain and reveal it to others."
Why is this? Śāriputra, if there are those who, with deep reverence,

hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra, and even analyze and explain it for others, you should know that such persons will certainly obtain ten kinds of meritorious qualities, praises, and benefits.

What are these ten? First, in every place of rebirth, one attains ultimate mastery in all subtle and refined fields of craft and industry; second, in every place of rebirth, one always dwells in a noble clan with honor and renown in the world; third, in every place of rebirth, one possesses great majesty, power, and sovereignty; fourth, whatever one says is followed by all, who never fail to believe and submit; fifth, in every place of rebirth, one is endowed with great wealth and prosperity; sixth, in every place of rebirth, one is constantly cherished and respected by gods and humans; seventh, when born among humans, one always becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and attains great sovereignty; eighth, in every birth, one always becomes Śakra, the Lord of Devas; ninth, if born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), one becomes a Great Brahmā King; tenth, in every place of rebirth, one is never separated from the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).
"Śāriputra! Those who uphold this sutra shall obtain ten kinds of meritorious qualities, praises, and benefits.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

It should be known that these sons and daughters of good family who uphold this sutra, listen to it with earnest reverence, read and recite it, understand its meaning, and even extensively explain and reveal it to others, shall further obtain these ten kinds of meritorious virtues, praises, and benefits.

What are these ten? First, not mixing with the heterodox doctrines of the Nirgranthas; second, not giving rise to the view of a self; third, having no view of a sentient being; fourth, having no view of a life-principle; fifth, having no view of a person who grasps at aggregates; sixth, not giving rise to the view of annihilationism; seventh, not giving rise to the view of eternalism; eighth, having no emotional attachment or concern for any worldly affairs; ninth, constantly generating the superior resolve to delight in leaving the household life; and tenth, being able to quickly receive, uphold, and realize the profound meaning upon hearing the sutras.
Śāriputra! These are called the ten kinds of meritorious benefits and praises obtained.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When these sons and daughters of good family uphold this sutra, listen to it with earnest reverence, read and recite it, understand its meaning, and even explain it in detail for others, you should know that such persons further obtain these ten kinds of meritorious virtues, praises, and benefits.
What are the ten? First, the accomplishment of right mindfulness;
second, the accomplishment of right awakening.
Third, accomplishment of the right course;
fourth, accomplishment of courageous resolve;
fifth, accomplishment of right wisdom.
Sixth, one attains the possession of being free from obstacles;
seventh, one remembers past lives;
eighth, one’s nature is characterized by a thinness of craving and lacks intense greed, such that one is not tormented by heavy desire.
Ninth, their nature is characterized by a thinness of anger and an absence of intense malice; they are not tormented by heavy anger.
Tenth, their nature is characterized by a thinness of delusion and an absence of intense folly; they are not tormented by heavy delusion.
"Śāriputra! These are called the ten kinds of meritorious benefits and praises obtained.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If these sons and daughters of good family uphold this sutra, listen to it with profound reverence, read and recite it, understand its meaning, and even explain it in detail for others, you should know that such persons further attain these ten kinds of meritorious virtues, praises, and benefits.
What are the ten? First, the accomplishment of the wisdom of swift capacity;
second, the accomplishment of the wisdom of rapid eloquence.
Third, they achieve sharp and penetrating wisdom;
fourth, they achieve swift and rapid wisdom;
fifth, they achieve vast and extensive wisdom.
Sixth, they achieve profound wisdom;
seventh, they achieve penetrating wisdom;
eighth, they achieve unattached wisdom.
Ninth, they constantly behold all Tathāgatas before them, and having beheld them, they praise them with pure and beautiful verses;
tenth, they are well able to inquire of the Tathāgatas in accordance with the principle, and are likewise able to resolve doubts and difficulties in accordance with the principle.
Śāriputra! These are called the ten kinds of meritorious benefits and praises obtained.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When these sons and daughters of good family uphold this sutra, read and recite it, explain its meaning, and even expound it extensively for others, you should know that they further obtain these ten kinds of meritorious qualities, praises, and benefits.

What are the ten? First, always delighting in staying far away from all unwholesome friends; second, always delighting in drawing near to all virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); third, being able to loosen all the bonds of Māra; fourth, destroying all the military arrays of Māra; fifth, being well able to revile and loathe all afflictions (*kleśa*); sixth, constantly relinquishing the mind toward all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*); seventh, turning away from all paths leading to the evil realms; eighth, turning toward all paths leading to nirvāṇa; ninth, skillfully explaining all the pure grounds for transcending birth and death (*saṃsāra*); and tenth, being skillfully able to follow and learn all the rules of conduct practiced by Bodhisattvas, as well as being able to carry out the instructions and commands of all Buddhas.
These are called the ten kinds of meritorious benefits and praises.

Śāriputra, if there are sons or daughters of good family who are able to reverently hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka; who investigate its meaning and penetrate it with clarity; and who further extensively explain and reveal it to others—know that such persons shall obtain the aforementioned meritorious benefits and praises.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Those who are wise possess boundless insight; They are skillfully able to penetrate both the Dharma and its meaning.
Their sublime and excellent phrasing is perfectly complete, Because they uphold such a great king of sutras.”
One shall constantly obtain the abundant treasury of the Dharma jewels, Always joyfully practicing the gift of Dharma with a delighted mind,
And giving rise to the most supreme and excellent joy, By upholding such a king of great sūtras as this.
When many sentient beings hear this teaching of the Dharma, they realize these vast and supreme merits;
how then shall I explain this Dharma so that others may obtain what those who uphold this sutra have attained?
Having realized such supreme wisdom, one shall never be destroyed regarding the True Dharma;
through mindfulness, one gives rise to subtle and wondrous knowledge, capable of expounding the locus of unsurpassed wisdom.
Diligently seek the well-spoken verses of the True Dharma, which are praised by the most excellent assembly of noble ones;
constantly hear and initiate transcendent practices by upholding such a great king of sutras as this.

Having heard it, the wise uphold its profound meaning; they harbor no false attachments to words and phrases, but constantly contemplate according to the underlying principle, thereby increasing their sublime wisdom to boundless measure.
Boundless wondrous wisdom and boundless meanings— The understanding of the ultimate truth is truly inconceivable.
Wandering throughout the ten directions, you praise it extensively; The benefits of hearing this sutra are inexhaustible.
With greed, hatred, and delusion rendered extremely subtle and thin, one attains the foremost purity of mind;
by hearing such a king of great sūtras, the merit and benefits are boundless.
Though one has acquired excellent wealth, do not be negligent; who is firm in weighing the true meaning of wealth?
Having deeply realized that worldly wealth lacks substantial reality, one should have no attachment to wealth and depart for the homeless life.
He went forth to dwell in a secluded grove within the forest;
there he remained ever free from sloth, never weary of hearing the pure Dharma, and was without stinginess regarding the teachings on meditative concentration.
I ask the Teacher of the World about difficult points; having heard [the answers], he explains them extensively for others.
Through this, subtle wisdom increases, and one never regresses from the pure, white dharmas.

"In this way, Śāriputra, because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas desire to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they diligently study and train in this sūtra while performing the conduct of a bodhisattva; this is called the essential method for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to skillfully study and train in the true Dharma within the perfection of wisdom."
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume 53 and Volume 54.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twelve: The Prophecy of Maheśvara, Part Two of the Twelfth Assembly: The Bodhisattva Piṭaka. Chapter Twelve:
The Prophecy of Maheśvara. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"In the distant past, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha, having extensively expounded these four immeasurable dharmas and the six pāramitās for the youth Vīryacaryā, at that time the Buddha further addressed the youth Vīryacaryā:"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva engage in the practice of gathering through the dharmas?

Young man, you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the four dharmas of attraction (saṃgraha-vastu) of the Tathāgata; by means of these dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells throughout the long night gathering all sentient beings."
What are the four? They are giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation; these are called the four methods of integration, young man.
What is meant by "thus gathering the Dharma"?
Young man, that which is called giving is of two kinds:
The first is the gift of material wealth, and the second is the gift of the Dharma; these constitute giving (*dāna*).

As for "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*), it means that toward all who come to beg or those who wish to hear the Dharma, the Bodhisattva is always able to speak with loving words to comfort and encourage them.
Beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) refers to being able to fulfill all the aspirations of both oneself and others.
Common purpose (*samānārthatā*) refers to teaching and establishing all sentient beings according to one's own wisdom and merit, causing them to abide securely in either wisdom or the Dharma.
Furthermore, young man!
What is called "generosity" (dāna) is a pure state of mind toward all sentient beings who come to beg.
What is called "kind speech" (priyavāditā) is the comforting of those sentient beings who come to beg with virtuous words.
Regarding beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), it means causing all the aims and benefits of sentient beings to reach maturity according to their needs.
Regarding common purpose (*samānārthatā*), it means acting with a mind of equanimity toward those sentient beings who come to beg, thereby accomplishing their aims and benefits.
Furthermore, young man!
What is called "generosity" refers to the bodhisattvas' resolve to practice relinquishment.
What is called "loving speech" refers to uninterrupted skillful means.
Regarding beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), it is a profound mind free from regret.
Regarding common purpose (*samānārthatā*), it is the dedication [of merit] toward the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, O youth!
What is called "giving" (dāna) refers to practicing relinquishment in accordance with a compassionate mind.
What is called "loving speech" (priyavāditā) refers to never abandoning a heart of joy.
What is called "beneficial conduct" (arthacaryā) refers to accomplishing great compassion, such that the mind always delights in the work of benefiting sentient beings.

Regarding "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*): one cultivates equanimity through relinquishment, free from high or low, with a mind constantly dedicated toward the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Furthermore, young man, regarding "generosity" (*dāna*):
one seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and constantly contemplates practicing relinquishment to rescue and relieve the poor and destitute.
Regarding "loving speech," it means that after having bestowed material gifts, one further establishes others in the meaning of the Dharma.
Regarding "beneficial conduct," it means impartially embracing both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Regarding "common purpose" (samānārthatā): it is because one desires to benefit all sentient beings that one ultimately gives rise to the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta).
Furthermore, young man, regarding "generosity" (dāna): it is the complete relinquishing of all internal and external phenomena whatsoever.
Regarding "loving speech," it means not being secretive or stingy with one's merits and wisdom concerning any dharma.
Regarding "beneficial conduct," it means relinquishing self-interest and devoting oneself exclusively to the benefit of others.

Regarding "sameness of purpose" (samānārthatā): it means gathering all wealth and property as if placing them in the palm of one's hand, bestowing gifts according to circumstances without any feeling of grief or regret. "Furthermore, O youth!
Regarding "Dharma-giving," it means extensively expounding the Dharma to others just as one has heard it.
Regarding "loving speech," it means explaining and revealing [the teachings] with a mind free from defilement.
Regarding "beneficial conduct," it refers to reciting the scriptures for others and even teaching the Dharma without weariness.
Regarding "common purpose" (samānārthatā): it means not abandoning the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), and establishing all sentient beings within the True Dharma.

Furthermore, young man, as for what is called the "gift of Dharma" (dharma-dāna): if there are those who come and go seeking to hear the Dharma, one should proclaim it without confusion, in accordance with the Buddha’s authentic teaching.
"Kind speech" refers to revealing the True Dharma with a subtle and wondrous voice.

"Beneficial conduct" refers to providing robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessary utensils and requisites to those who seek the Dharma and those who preach it whenever they are in need or lacking anything.
Regarding "common purpose," it means constantly giving rise to a profound mind and teaching the Dharma without interruption.
Furthermore, young man,
regarding "Dharma-giving," it is because this bodhisattva understands that among all forms of giving, Dharma-giving is supreme, and thus they constantly practice the giving of the Dharma.
"Affectionate speech" refers to the discourse that expounds matters of benefit.
