"Beneficial conduct" refers to elucidating the meaning rather than relying on the literal text.
"Common purpose" refers to the desire to bring all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment, constantly manifesting transformative teachings for sentient beings according to their needs.
Furthermore, young man!
That which is called "generosity" refers to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
That which is called "loving speech" refers to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) and the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Beneficial conduct refers to the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
Common purpose refers to the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Furthermore, young man!
That which is called "generosity" refers to all bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment].
That which is called "kind speech" refers to all bodhisattvas who have already set forth in practice.
Regarding "beneficial conduct," this refers to all bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive.
Regarding "common purpose," this refers to those great bodhisattvas who are bound to only one more birth (ekajātipratibaddha).
Furthermore, young man!
What is called "generosity" is for the purpose of strengthening the root of bodhi.
What is called "loving speech" is for the purpose of bringing to fruition the sprout of bodhi.
"Beneficial conduct" refers to the desire to cause the wondrous flower of bodhi to bloom.
"Common purpose" refers to the desire to bring the supreme fruit of bodhi to maturity.
Thus it is, young man!
These are called the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to practice for the sake of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they employ these four methods of attraction throughout the long night to gather in and sustain sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s turning according to the methods of attraction.
"O youth! These methods of gathering [beings] are thus immeasurable and boundless; all are called the path to enlightenment. "Śāriputra!"

At that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha, revealed this path to great enlightenment to the youth Vīryaparamita. Having heard this Dharma from the Buddha, and further hearing the praises of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, the youth was filled with great joy. He then took excellent garments, delicacies, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various household requisites, and offered them to the Tathāgata Mahāskandha and his assembly of śrāvakas.
In this manner, for ninety-six koṭis of years, he made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise; furthermore, he gave rise once more to the great vow for bodhi.
Although he performed such immeasurable meritorious deeds, the Tathāgata Mahāskandha did not yet bestow upon the youth the prediction of his attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! Do you think that the youth Vīryaprabha at that time was anyone else?
Do not harbor any other doubt; it was none other than myself.
At that Buddha’s place, I made offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha for as many years as those; furthermore, I gave rise to the great aspiration for enlightenment.
Yet, that Tathāgata did not grant me this prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

"Śāriputra! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Mahāskandha, after the passage of incalculable kalpas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Ratnagotra, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān."

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata Ratnagotra had an assembly of eighty nayutas of śrāvaka disciples who gathered together to hear the Dharma; all were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, even to the point that their minds were autonomous and they had realized the foremost pāramitā.

At that time, there was a wheel-turning sage king in that world named Sudarśana, to whom the seven treasures appeared, namely the accomplishment of the golden wheel up to the treasure of the general of the army.

King Śubhavyūha, by means of the majesty of his precious wheel, brought the four continents under his sway; ruling the world with the True Dharma, he was known as a Dharma King. His benevolence and virtue nurtured all beings, whom they all esteemed and revered, and the lands and people within his realm dwelt in vast abundance.

The capital city ruled there was named Pūrṇa; it was twelve yojanas long from east to west and seven yojanas wide from south to north. It was secure, prosperous, and joyful, with a flourishing population that was most delightful to behold, and it abounded in various treasures and provisions.

At that time, there was a great elder in the city named Śrīmati; his family was immensely wealthy with abundant treasures and riches, and he had already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, planting many roots of virtue.
Śāriputra! At that time, the Bhagavān Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, observing the profound resolve and aspiration of this elder, reflected thus:
"This great elder’s roots of goodness have already ripened; he is a fit vessel for such a Dharma-door of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and also a vessel for the true Dharma of all Buddhas."

Having understood this, he went to that place and manifested great supernormal powers, dwelling in the air with his legs crossed in the full lotus posture. For the sake of that elder, he opened the path to bodhi and further praised and spoke of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

Śāriputra! At that time, having heard the Buddha’s exposition of the path of the great bodhisattvas and having heard the praise of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, Sudhana attained vast joy and pure faith; he then offered exquisite garments, delicacies, food and drink, and other requisites to the Tathāgata Ratnagotra and his assembly of disciples.
For a thousand years, he made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise; furthermore, he gave rise once more to the subtle and wondrous great vow for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Although he thus extensively performed these manifold practices, that Tathāgata did not yet bestow upon him a prophecy.
Śāriputra, do you think that at that time the elder Suprajñā was anyone other than this person?
Do not harbor any further doubts; it was I myself who was that person.

At that time, although I made various offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha and gave rise to vast and supreme vows for enlightenment, that Tathāgata did not bestow upon me a prophecy, saying, "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

Śāriputra! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Ratnagotra, after the passing of incalculable kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Prabhāsa-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Men, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Śāriputra! For what reason is the Buddha named "Emitting Light"? Śāriputra!
At that time, there was a king born into the world named Jayasena.

His capital city was named Prabhūtapadma; it was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with a flourishing population and an abundance of wealth, treasures, and all manner of necessities overflowing in every direction.
The king had a minister of Brahmin descent named Prabhāpāla; his family was immensely wealthy, with their treasuries and granaries fully stocked and overflowing.
This minister was especially cherished and highly esteemed by King Jayasena, who admired his virtue and never grew weary of meeting him or encountering him.
Śāriputra! At that time, King Jayasena divided his kingdom into four parts and granted one quarter to this great minister, enfeoffing him as a king.
Meanwhile, King Prabhūtaratna ruled over a small kingdom, governing the world with the Dharma and never practicing injustice or corruption.

Śāriputra! At a later time, King Prabhāpāla gave birth to a crown prince whose physical appearance was upright and pleasing for all to behold; he possessed the foremost, perfect, and pure complexion, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Furthermore, light radiated from every part of the prince's body, shining like the orb of the sun; therefore, he was given the name Prabhāsa, "Radiant Light."

Śāriputra! At that time, King Jyotiṣprabha summoned all the brahmins within his realm who were skilled in reading physiognomy; once they had all assembled, he presented the prince to them and commanded them to examine his marks.
When the brahmins had observed these signs, they spoke thus:
"This prince shall certainly become a Buddha.
Thereupon, King Prabhāpāla entrusted the prince to various foster mothers.
Not long thereafter, his physical form grew large and he became wise, intelligent, and far-sighted.

At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, residing in the palace of Akaniṣṭha, knew through the power of supernormal knowledge that this prince was about to attain perfect enlightenment. He then vanished from that place and came to where the Bodhisattva Prince Emitting Light (Prabhāsa) was staying. Having circumambulated the Bodhisattva to the right, he stood before him and spoke these verses:
"It is not by dwelling in the palace of a great king That one can give rise to pure and supreme merit; [...]"
Relying upon the signs of the celestial banner and the *kāṣāya* robe, one realizes the fruit of unsurpassed, wondrous *bodhi*.
Vigorous youth flows away in an instant; it passes more swiftly than a great, violent wind.
One must not take pleasure in this wretched old age, which destroys all that is beloved in the world.
Old age can cause one's strength to diminish, making it difficult to find joy in the path leading out of the home;
Great Sage, now that you are in the prime of your years, you ought to exert yourself with diligence at this very time.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Excellent, excellent, O one of great transcendent realization!
Excellent, excellent, that you have so swiftly gone forth; You shall certainly attain the firm, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Śāriputra! At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Emitting Light had been awakened by the gods of the Pure Abodes, he went forth into the homeless life with pure faith.”
On the very night he left the household life, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the World-Honored One appeared in the world with such vast renown, being titled the Tathāgata Emitting Light (*Prabhāsa*), fully endowed with the ten epithets, and praised by all devas and humans.

At that time, King Jayasena, hearing that Prince Prabhāpāla had left the household life to practice and attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, named Prabhāsa, went at once to inform King Prabhāpāla, saying:
"I have heard that your son has left the household life to become a Buddha; I wonder if, out of great compassion, the World-Honored One might deign to come down to us?"
"If you do not show compassion by coming here, I shall prepare a fourfold army and go to the place where the Tathāgata resides to personally serve and pay him homage. O Śāriputra!
King Kālarāja immediately assembled his ministers and the military guards and fully explained this matter to them.
The ministers said:
"Your Majesty should now go in person to the Tathāgata Prabhāsa to inquire about this matter."
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, will the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One go to the place of King Jitaśatru, or will He not? Thereupon,
King Prabhāpāla immediately prepared his carriage and, accompanied by his ministers, attendants, and retinue, proceeded to where the Tathāgata was.
Having arrived there, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata Emitting Light said to the King, his father:
“Great King, you should know that I am now going to the place of King Vijitāvin for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings.”

"Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa, according to his wish, stayed separately in a certain place within the royal capital of Jayasena; he then set out for that country together with twenty koṭis of great arhats."

At that time, the father-king also prepared a fourfold army of powerful forces to follow behind the Buddha, and provided various kinds of exquisite garments, delicacies, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha. He followed the Tathāgata all the way to the border of his own kingdom, where he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, and returned home after bidding farewell with tears and choked sobs.

At that time, when King Jayasena heard that the Tathāgata Prabhāsa was coming with a great assembly to this city of Padmavati, he immediately adorned his capital city; he removed all gravel, shards, and stones, making the streets and roads pure, level, and smooth, sweeping and repairing them until they were exceedingly magnificent.

Furthermore, he again sprinkled fragrant water profusely and scattered famous flowers to a height level with a person's knees; he arranged exquisite incense jars along the path to perfume it, spread various kinds of subtle and wondrous precious garments, and suspended banners and canopies in the empty space above, while the sounds of music and song rose up in a dense, pervasive abundance.

Śāriputra! When King Jayasena had thus completed the magnificent adornments and decorations of the great royal capital, the city of Padmavatī, he issued a strict decree by beating the drums to proclaim: "Within and without this royal capital, no one shall at all take for their own use or sell any flower garlands, ointments, or perfumes; all such items must be offered as an act of worship to the Tathāgata Prabhāsa-raśmi.
Should anyone violate this command, they shall be subject to severe punishment."

Śāriputra! At that time, King Jayasena took with him various flower garlands, ointments, powdered incenses, exquisite robes, banners, and precious parasols; he played various kinds of wonderful music and prepared a grand ceremonial procession with great military array. Out of a desire to behold that Tathāgata, and to pay homage and present offerings, he set out from his capital city with his fourfold army and all the Brahmins, elders, householders, and nobles within the royal city to go to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived there, King Vijitāvin was the first to prostrate at the feet of that Tathāgata; he further made offerings to the Tathāgata with various flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, exquisite robes, banners, pennants, and precious parasols.

Having made offerings himself, he further caused the princes, ministers, and the various attendants—brahmins, householders, and lay devotees—to likewise perform extensive offerings, just as the Great King had done.

Śāriputra! Having made this offering, King Jayasena—possessing a mind of joy, a mind of sublime goodness, a mind free from hindrances, and a mind of serene delight—followed behind the Buddha together with his ministers.

Śāriputra! At that time, there was a brahmin named Ratna who dwelt beside the Great Snowy Mountain King (Himavat). He had five hundred young scholars as his disciples; he was honored by all people, his fame and virtue spread afar, and he was skilled in the arts and sciences. He had reached the further shore of the three Vedas and was thoroughly proficient in the following treatises: the Nirgrantha scriptures, the Kīrapa-śāstra, the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra, the Itihāsa-śāstra, the Pañcavidha-jñāna-śāstra, the Lokānuvartana-śāstra, the Yajña-mantra-śāstra, and the Puruṣa-lakṣaṇa-śāstra. Furthermore, regarding the great teachings of the Three Vedas of his own tradition and those of his preceptors, he understood their underlying principles and possessed subtle discernment regarding what was to be practiced and what was to be avoided.

"Śāriputra! This brāhmaṇa has a young disciple living in close attendance named Mṛga, who has received instruction in the precious [sciences], fully mastered their profound principles, and attained clear understanding in both the arts and the sūtras and śāstras; his wisdom is equal to that of his teacher and he is fit to be a leader."
Then Migāra addressed his teacher, saying:
"Great Master, you should know that I have thoroughly mastered all the sūtras and śāstras you have taught; I shall now return to my native land."
"How, then, may one repay the great master’s kindness?
At that time, the master said: "Vatsamitra!"
Now, a disciple who wishes to repay the kindness of their teacher should express this profound sentiment through material wealth and treasures.
What is meant by this?
If one can provide five hundred *kārsāpaṇas*, it will sufficiently manifest a deep heart.

"Śāriputra! At that time, having received his teacher’s instructions, the youth Megha paid his respects, circumambulated him to the right, took his leave, and departed. He traveled extensively through villages, cities, pavilions, towns, provinces, and royal capitals, searching everywhere for the wealth and treasures to repay his teacher."

Having gathered them all together and being about to present his offerings, he gradually proceeded toward the city of Pundravardhana. From afar, he saw the royal capital adorned in various ways, brilliantly radiant and magnificent, exceedingly delightful to behold. He then asked those nearby:
"What great event is occurring in this royal capital today, such that these honors and decorations are spread so extensively and it is adorned in this manner?"
A bystander replied, "Do you not know?

Today the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Raśmipramokṣa, together with eighty koṭis of great arhats and eighty-four thousand great bodhisattvas, will enter this city. The people therein shall practice great giving and generate great merit."
"It is because of this matter that such adornments have been brought forth.
At that time, the youth Megha suddenly heard the sound of these names of the Buddhas; he attained vast joy and pure faith, and reflected to himself:

"The appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world is extremely rare. It is even more difficult to encounter them than the udumbara flower, and harder to meet than a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating yoke; they may appear but once in hundreds of thousands of great kalpas."

"It is most rare that I have now been granted this audience; I must certainly use these five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to purchase flowers to scatter as an offering to the Tathāgata Emitting Light, and I shall seek further wealth to repay my teacher's kindness."
"Śāriputra! At that time, there was a woman who, carrying seven utpala flowers, came from the marketplace.
Megha said to her:"
"From where did you obtain these water-born flowers?
The woman replied,
"I purchased these flowers for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas at a flower-garland shop in such-and-such a place."
Miga said, "Now that the original price has been paid, can you give me the flowers?
The woman replied:
"Not so," he replied. He spoke again:
"If you do not permit it, here are five hundred *kārsāpaṇas*; you should take these seven stalks of flowers alone, while we two shall share [the money] together—is this acceptable?"
The woman asked,
"What do you intend to do with these flowers? He replied:
"I shall use it to scatter as an offering to the Tathāgata Emitting Radiance.
The girl said, "As you have spoken."
"From this day forward, may she who is always able to descend into all realms of existence and become my husband accept this flower as a token of our mutual commitment.
Then Migā replied to the woman,
saying, "Stop, stop, O woman!"
Do not speak thus. Why is this?
Because you women are by nature fickle, volatile, and prone to many forms of negligence; what you have said is not worthy of being accepted or adopted.

Furthermore, throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I shall cultivate and gather the Buddha-dharmas and extensively practice giving: whether it be gold, silver, rare treasures, coral, *maṇi* gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, oxen, sheep, and various domestic animals; or even the relinquishing of the great throne of a king, chariots, carriages, and finery, as well as the ladies of the inner palace, queens, sons, daughters, and retinues; or the relinquishing of hands, feet, ears, noses, skin, flesh, marrow, and bones, the bright jewel from the topknot, eyes, and head.
To speak in general terms, there is not a single thing, whether internal or external, that I have not relinquished through the gate of giving.
Furthermore, there may come a time when I shall relinquish you as well, entering the Buddha-dharma to go forth with faith from the household life into homelessness.
"Your nature is fickle, volatile, and negligent; at such a time, it may well become an obstacle to my great equanimity.
The girl replied, "Truly, as you have said, this shall be of great benefit to me."
Even if you were now to sell this body of mine, even to the extent of providing a single *kārsāpaṇa*, I would never harbor any contrary thought or obstruction regarding such giving.
Or, if my body were again cut into pieces and given away as alms, I would certainly have no hesitation in cultivating and accumulating the Buddha-dharma.
Miga replied, "If it may be so, then this is acceptable; you should give me the flowers quickly.
At that time, the woman took the flowers and handed them to him. Miga took the flowers and immediately went to the place where the Buddha Prabhāsa was.

From afar he saw the Tathāgata surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings; with dignified and composed deportment, he led the multitude forward, arriving from that direction adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits.

In the presence of the Blessed One, he gave rise to pure faith; with immeasurable kinds of pure joy and deep, respectful love, he approached the Buddha, prostrating himself in reverence, his heart overflowing with boundless celebration.
Furthermore, he saw many people using various expensive and exquisite garments, which they had spread upon the path as an offering to the Buddha; he then thought to himself:
"Although I currently possess no superior or exquisite garments, I have only this worn deerskin robe that I am wearing; I shall spread it across the path to serve as a mat for the Tathāgata’s feet."
Having formed this thought, he stripped off his garment and spread it upon the ground.
Thereupon, the people vied with one another to seize the deerskin robe and cast it far away to another place, all expressing contempt and reproach:
"How can one who is a jewel among sentient beings spread out such a wretched deerskin robe?"
Then Migāra immediately hurried to a muddy spot at a crossroads, took a deer-skin garment and spread it there, thinking to himself:

"May the Tathāgata Emitting Light, the Greatly Compassionate One, take pity on me; may he look upon my actions with his all-illuminating eye and all-illuminating wisdom, and I pray that he will step upon this garment of mine with his feet."
At that time, the Tathāgata, out of compassion for his thoughts, stepped upon the deerskin garment with his toe.
When Miga saw this, his heart was filled with joy; leaping up in exultation, he immediately took the utpala flowers he held and scattered them over the Buddha.

At that time, there were also immeasurable sons of gods dwelling in the void who scattered celestial mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, as well as celestial sandalwood powder, over the Buddha. They played celestial music and sang celestial pure songs, filling the void and performing a grand offering.

At that time, the flowers scattered by Vigaya remained suspended in mid-air; they then transformed into thousands of *utpala* lotus petals, which hung down to form a floral canopy that followed behind the Buddha as he walked.

Upon seeing this, Megha was filled with even greater joy and pure faith arose in his heart. Before the Tathāgata, he untied his twelve-year-old golden topknot and spread it upon the ground, then made this great vow for unexcelled bodhi:
"If it is certain that I shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in a future life, I pray that the present Radiant Light Tathāgata will extend his hand to comfort me."
Furthermore, he made a firm and powerful vow of great resolve, speaking these words:

"If the Tathāgata does not step upon my golden hair with his foot and comfort me by taking my hand, and if he does not grant me the prediction of enlightenment, I shall never rise; I will die right here on this spot, my body withered and dried up."

"Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Emitting Light possessed the all-illuminating eye and all-illuminating wisdom; there was nothing throughout the three periods of time that he did not penetrate. Having known the intention of that Miga, he then lifted his toe and stepped upon his hair."
Even as he turned his gaze to the right like a dragon or an elephant, he addressed all the śrāvakas and the great assembly:
"O bhikṣus, do not tread upon these hairs. Why is this?
This youth, after the passing of incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa), shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, named Śākyamuni.

"Śāriputra! At that time, Migāra, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and realized hundreds of thousands of *nayuta-koṭi* immovable meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). Furthermore, by the power of his supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), he perceived that immeasurable Buddhas in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were all bestowing prophecies upon him, saying:
'O Youth, you should know that after an incalculable number of eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) in a future life, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.'"

"In this way, throughout the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—pervading the ten directions—there are immeasurable Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of whom grant prophecies just as the Buddhas of the eastern direction have done."

Śāriputra! Once the youth Megha had received the consolation of the Buddhas’ prophecy, he descended from the sky to the place where the Buddha was. Out of faith, he left his home for the homeless life and practiced the firm and pure holy life.
Śāriputra! You should now have no doubt or uncertainty regarding this: that the youth Mṛga in a former age was someone else.
Do not view it so; I myself was that Bodhisattva, the youth Mṛga.

At that time, I offered these five stalks of blue lotuses to that Buddha and further untied my golden hair, spreading it upon the path; by performing such an act, I received the prediction of enlightenment.

Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to swiftly receive the Tathāgata’s prediction of enlightenment, they should, with earnest gravity, listen to, uphold, read, recite, and thoroughly clarify the meaning and intent of this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, extensively explain and elucidate it for others, and furthermore, practice the correct conduct of signlessness.
Why is this? I recall that in the past, before I had encountered the Buddha Emitting Light, there was no pure and wholesome practice that I did not cultivate.
Although he exerted himself with such immeasurable toil and hardship, he did not receive a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha.
Why was this? It was because all the practices he cultivated were characterized by signs (*nimitta*).
From that time forward, I have dwelt in right practice according to what I have heard from this subtle Dharma-gate of the Mahābodhisattva-piṭaka.

Such a practitioner practices the signless practice, the effortless practice, and the non-apprehending practice; having practiced such signless practices as these, the Tathāgata Raśmipramokṣa then bestowed upon me a prophecy.

"Śāriputra! I recall that when I first beheld the Buddha Prabhūtaratna in the past, I immediately transcended all conditioned phenomena and all practices involving effort. Furthermore, upon first seeing the Buddha, I was able to realize the nature of all dharmas and attained penetration into the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena."
From that time onward, the Tathāgata Emitting Light bestowed upon him a prophecy,
speaking these words: "O Mṛga, the Youth!"
In a future age, after incalculable eons have passed, you shall become a Buddha, known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Śāriputra! At the time I was given this prediction, I realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Śāriputra!"
What kind of patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is realized?

It is the realization of the patience of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena of form; the realization of the patience of non-apprehension regarding the phenomena of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and the realization of the patience of non-apprehension regarding the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Śāriputra! That which is called "attaining patience" is defined as the patient endurance of all dharmas, wherein nothing at all is apprehended. Why is this?

When one has realized such patience, worldly phenomena no longer manifest; nor do the phenomena of ordinary beings, the phenomena of those in training, the phenomena of those beyond training, the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, the phenomena of bodhisattvas, or the phenomena of buddhas manifest again.

Why is this so? Because all phenomena do not manifest, it is called "attaining patience" (*kṣānti*); because all phenomena are ultimately neither attained nor obtainable, it is called "attaining patience."
Furthermore, this "Patience" (kṣānti) is so named because, in a single instant, it exhausts all marks (nimitta) and all objects of cognition (ālambana).
Moreover, this "Patience" is so named because it does not tolerate the eye, nor does it destroy the eye and its objects; thus, it is called the attainment of Patience.

Not being impatient with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and not destroying the mind—such patience is the inexhaustible realm; such patience is the non-rebirth realm; therefore it is called "attaining patience."

Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to swiftly receive the Tathāgata’s prediction of enlightenment and realize this patience, they should, with profound reverence, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, and master the meaning and intent of this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka. They should extensively explain it to others, analyze and reveal it, and abide in right practice—namely, the practice of signlessness, the practice of effortlessness, and the practice of non-apprehension. Such dharmas as these are called right practice.

At that time, there was among the great assembly a son of a householder named Naradatta. Having heard from the Blessed One this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and having further heard the praise of the supreme merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he immediately rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddha, prostrated himself and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, previously you extensively expounded for the sons of householders and others the various dharmas in their continuous succession; thus did you reveal and thus did you instruct them, causing them all to realize the fruit of Arhatship and reach the end of old age and death within this very life. Yet, we have not heard you speak of this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, nor have we heard the praise of the merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
I am fortunate to have now heard this great benefit in its entirety, and I have privately conceived this thought:
"Such a Mahāyāna is honored, supreme, foremost, exquisite, and unsurpassed; there is nothing superior to it—namely, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

"I have now personally heard the Buddha’s teaching in his presence; I have received, upheld, understood, and elucidated all dharmas. Such dharmas as these involve the discernment of all phenomena as being without basis or attachment, without self or what belongs to a self, and without grasping."
"Bhagavān! I have had this thought:
'Such a sublime Dharma is honored, supreme, excellent, wondrous, and unsurpassed; there is nothing beyond it. Such a Dharma as this, I shall cultivate and gather.'"
"World-Honored One!
As I now contemplate, that which is supreme among all vehicles is what is called the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna).
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, likewise proclaim this vehicle, establishing it as the foremost and the most unsurpassed."

From this day forth, I arouse the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to bring benefit and peace to many sentient beings, out of compassion for all the world, and to benefit, bring peace, and bring happiness to immeasurable devas and humans. Just as the Buddha has established the training precepts of all great bodhisattvas, I shall now follow and train in them all.
When he had spoken these words, the World-Honored One then addressed the son of the elder:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
“Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is extremely difficult to realize and believe in, and extremely difficult to cultivate; yet you are now able to give rise to such a profound aspiration.
At that time, the son of the elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Although unsurpassed bodhi is extremely difficult to realize, believe in, and cultivate, I shall now arouse such fierce vigor and diligence that I will certainly cultivate and gather anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, regarding it as no difficulty at all.
Furthermore, regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall cultivate it with firm and steadfast concentration, never regressing.
World-Honored One!

I now make this great and solemn vow: even if one must generate the mind of *bodhicitta* as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges before attaining unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I shall increase my diligence toward this matter all the more. Even if each successive generation of the mind of *bodhicitta* must pass through as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and even if the generation of that *bodhicitta* requires the severing of as many limbs and heads as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, though I must undergo such diligent suffering, I shall redouble my diligence therein and never abandon unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Why is this? Even when encountering such various hardships and difficulties, one should still cultivate and accumulate [merit and wisdom], for by virtue of these conditions, one will certainly realize Bodhi; how much more so should one practice and study while experiencing various forms of peace and happiness for the sake of realizing unsurpassed Bodhi?

Why is this? Because the nature of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is lofty and vast; it is fully endowed with the great and unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas, being inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless, and inexpressible. Even though the Buddhas possess unobstructed wisdom, were they to spend hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas speaking of this bodhi through various sounds and voices, it would not be easy to exhaustively describe it.
At that time, the elder’s son Naradatta spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Only after hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas Does one first give rise to the bodhicitta;
Though pressed by manifold sufferings, One does not abandon the realm of sentient beings.”
In accordance with my arousal of the bodhicitta, I am able to endure even if I must sever as many heads and bodies as would form a heap as high as Mount Meru;
for I abide in enlightenment to bring benefit and happiness to all living beings.
May I, in future lives, be like the World-Honored One of this day;
may I distance myself from the Śrāvaka vehicle while simultaneously delivering those of the lower vehicles.
May I, in future lives, be like the World-Honored One of this day.
This vehicle is the Mahāyāna, praised as supreme by the Buddhas;
seeing that nothing is equal to it, I rejoice in Bodhi.
To rescue those in peril and distress, and to liberate them from the three evil realms.
"In order to seek such a Tathāgata, he has appeared in the world and manifested the attainment of Buddhahood.
At that time, after the elder’s son Naradatta had spoken these verses, he reflected to himself:
"I have now clearly realized the vast Dharma of the Buddha; why should I not use it to transform my wife, children, and all my kinsmen?"
"This is not appropriate for me.
Having thought this, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and quickly returned home.

He prepared various kinds of offerings, including seven wives, seven sons, seven daughters, and seven male and female servants; he brought with him a thousand pairs of exquisite garments and various flowers, perfumes, and other articles for worship. Accompanied by five hundred musicians, he swiftly departed from the great city of Rājagṛha, desiring to pay homage to and behold the Bhagavat.
At that time, there were many people in Rājagṛha who saw the son of the elder and his retinue rushing out in haste, and they asked:
"What is the cause of your great urgency now?"
"Where are you going with your retinue?
The son of the elder replied, "Noble sons, do you not know?"

Now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, resides on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded before and behind by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, employing countless skillful means to analyze and reveal the vast Buddha-dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

I shall now lead my retinue to the presence of the Buddha, in order to seek such vast and extensive Buddha-dharma, in order to accomplish the inconceivable and immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas, and in order to plant the roots of goodness for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If you wish to accomplish the vast dharmas of the Buddhas, you should all go together to the place where that Tathāgata resides; there, you shall together plant these unsurpassed roots of goodness for the vast dharmas of the Buddhas.
At that time, when the people of Rājagṛha heard these words spoken by the son of the elder, ten thousand people were all delighted to follow him to the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, the elder’s son Naradatta, together with his retinue and ten thousand followers, simultaneously beheld the Buddha; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the son of the elder, together with the entire assembly who had come with him, brought flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, robes, parasols, banners, and streamers; they performed music and sang hymns of praise to make offerings to the Tathāgata, and further covered the Buddha with a thousand pairs of pure and exquisite precious garments.
At that time, having made this offering, the son of the householder was filled with immeasurable joy and spoke a verse of praise before the Buddha.
The stanza said:
"O Supreme among sentient beings, most subtle one, Who has perfected pure conduct and attained unsurpassed enlightenment."
Able to give rise to boundless, supreme wisdom and vision, Thus do I now practice this offering.

Having practiced extensively throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, Seeking great enlightenment for the benefit of sentient beings, You have realized mastery over the Dharma and manifested as a Buddha; Thus do I now practice this offering.
Together with my wife, my kinsmen, and my retinue, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings and seeking bodhi,
as well as for the sake of thousands of other people, we all together take refuge in the Great Awakened One.
At that time, having praised the Buddha with these verses, the son of the elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I and all these sentient beings have now come before the Tathāgata and have all firmly established ourselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on them and preach the Dharma for them once more, so that they shall never again regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

Furthermore, I now wish to plant various roots of goodness before the Buddha; I only pray that the World-Honored One will appear as my witness. By the power of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings equally and swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and likewise attain immeasurable and vast Buddha-dharmas, just as the present World-Honored One does now.
Then the son of the elder, together with his retinue, five hundred musicians, and a multitude of ten thousand people, spoke to the Buddha with one mind and a single voice, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We now, before the Tathāgata, together with one mind and utmost sincerity, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. We pray only that the World-Honored One will remember us as upāsakas; from this day forth until the end of our lives, we would rather sacrifice our bodies and lives than abandon our refuge in pure faith.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, may you hold us in your mindfulness; from this day forth until we reach enlightenment, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, we shall give rise to a mind of supreme vigor and courage.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, please keep us in mind; we only pray that you will swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and proclaim the True Dharma for all sentient beings, no different from what the Tathāgata does now.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, please keep us in mind: we pray that when we attain Buddhahood in a future life, we shall be surrounded by a great assembly no different from the present one.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, please keep us in mind: we pray that in a future life we shall deliver and liberate immeasurable sentient beings oppressed by suffering, no different from the present.

Then the son of the elder, along with the assembled multitude and the five hundred musicians, having made this vow, further offered various kinds of exquisite music as an offering to the Tathāgata and circumambulated him three times to the right.
At that time, out of compassion for them, the World-Honored One ascended into the air and sat cross-legged.
When the five hundred musicians beheld the Tathāgata manifesting this supernatural transformation, their pure faith in the World-Honored One redoubled.

By the Buddha’s majestic power, all the musical instruments, without being held or supported, spontaneously rose upward and remained suspended in mid-air without any physical basis, performing a vast array of music that resounded in profusion as they circled the Tathāgata to the right.

At that time, the assembly, including the son of the elder, all witnessed these miraculous transformations and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Their hearts were filled with joy and they leaped for gladness; together they joined their palms in reverence toward the Tathāgata.

At that time, throughout the entire circumference of one *yojana* in the sky, there further appeared immeasurable hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, manifesting spontaneously without being held by anyone; like beehives suspended in the void, they performed music and produced subtle, wondrous sounds.

At that time, the son of the elder, together with his retinue, five hundred musicians, ten thousand city-dwellers, sixty thousand people from among the previous assembly who had come to hear the Dharma, and the community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus—all leaped into the air through the Buddha’s majestic power.
Furthermore, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, five hundred musical pavilions spontaneously appeared in the sky above; within these pavilions, the sublime Dharma was being preached.
Additionally, four great musical pavilions manifested before the Buddha, adorned with carvings and decorations of such exquisite beauty that they surpassed all wonders of the world.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devaputras stood arrayed in the air, scattering celestial māndārava flowers over the Buddha.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the scattered flowers were transformed in mid-air into eighty thousand exquisite and sublime flower pedestals.
At that time, the great assembly,

beholding such vast and magnificent adornments within the upper terrace, conceived a redoubled sense of pure faith, love, and reverence toward the Tathāgata, and marveled at this unprecedented wonder.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the minds of the great assembly were pure and further perceiving the superior resolve of Narada and the multitude who had come with him, manifested a smile as previously described in detail, until the light returned and vanished into the crown of his head.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda, having witnessed the smile, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha in respectful salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition do you manifest this smile?
I consider that the divine manifestations displayed by the Tathāgata are never without cause or condition.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You should know now that these thirty-six people—the son of this elder, Naradatta; his seven wives; his sons and daughters; and his male and female slaves—by the power of the roots of goodness from making offerings to me, shall not fall into the evil realms for a thousand koṭis of kalpas in future ages, but will instead pass through the realms of humans and devas, experiencing all manner of happiness."

After this kalpa has passed, he will encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world named Śreṣṭhin (Lord of Merchants), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. Under that Buddha, he will make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise, extensively cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*). From that time forward, he will pass through twenty koṭis of kalpas without falling into the evil realms.

Ānanda, you should know that these seven wives, seven daughters, and seven maidservants of the elder’s son, upon the end of their lives here, shall cast off their female bodies and become men. They will never be separated from Naladatta as they practice the bodhisattva path, and in a future age, dwelling together in the same kalpa, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Ānanda, you should know that when the bodhisattva mahāsattva Naladatta, the son of a householder, attains buddhahood, he shall appear in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Samacitta, fully endowed with the ten titles.
When this great bodhisattva attains buddhahood, all his retinue shall bear the same name: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ājñātamānya, fully endowed with the ten titles.

By the power of the roots of goodness from having made offerings to me, these five hundred musicians shall not fall into the evil realms for another incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and they shall serve as attendants to a full thousand *koṭi* of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) during that time.

Ānanda, you should know that, speaking in general terms, these five hundred musicians encountered ten thousand Buddhas during this kalpa; they were all able to personally serve and make offerings to them, with none of their efforts being in vain.
From this time forward, within the same kalpa, they shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all shall be named Melodious Sound (Surūpa).

Because of the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through making offerings to me, four hundred of these ten thousand people shall encounter the Tathāgata Maitreya; under that Buddha, they shall purely cultivate the Brahma-faring and, having exhausted all outflows (āsrava), they shall enter Parinirvāṇa.

As for the remaining persons, they shall not fall into the evil realms for as many great kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in the future; gradually, they will encounter a thousand koṭis of buddhas, cultivate all manner of practices extensively under those buddhas, and thereafter all shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all bearing the same name: "Most Rare."

Ānanda, you should know that among these sixty thousand people, there will be a full thousand who, after my parinirvāṇa and the exhaustion of the True Dharma, and further beyond that intermediate kalpa of weapons, at the time when the lifespan of sentient beings is gradually increasing before the appearance of Maitreya Tathāgata, will see eighty thousand pratyekabuddhas appear in Jambudvīpa. These one thousand people shall all encounter them, make offerings, and cultivate goodness; later, they will again encounter Maitreya Tathāgata and once more make offerings. From that point forward, for twenty-five koṭi-nayuta kalpas, they will not fall into the evil realms. Finally, through the awakening power of their various roots of goodness in their last human body, they will develop pure faith, leave the household life for the homeless state, and immediately realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Ānanda, you should know that among this assembly there are ten thousand people who have fully given rise to the noble vision;
the remaining thousand people likewise resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, sixty nayutas of devaputras, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Thus, Ānanda, who that sees such extraordinary and superior benefits would not give rise to pure faith, affection, reverence, and a sense of wonder toward the Buddha?
This excludes only those who are foolish and unworthy. Why is this?
Because such people, by cultivating even these subtle roots of goodness toward the Tathāgata, are able to attain the Great Self of the Tathāgata or enter into unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"By performing various offerings to the Buddha, One obtains such supreme merit as this.
If there are those who seek lofty and great fruits, They should perform offerings to the Teacher."
Whether making offerings while the Buddha is present in the world, or after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa,
one who makes an offering to a *dhātu* even as small as a mustard seed will always be able to serve all the Tathāgatas.
If one further wishes to practice various forms of offering, whether the Tathāgata remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa,
by making an offering to the *dhātu* the size of a mustard seed, one will attain equal results through the practice of an impartial mind.
If one fully cultivates a mind of equanimity and makes offerings to those who are equal and supreme among men,
one shall attain the sublime retribution of equality and realize the wondrous Bodhi of equality.
If one wishes to gather all those in the happy realms, To block, sever, and eliminate all evil paths,
And desires to proceed along the path to nirvāṇa, Such attainment will not be difficult.
The Buddha is endowed with the most supreme pure śīla; The Buddha is endowed with the most supreme samādhi.
If one gives rise to the most supreme pure faith, One shall attain the most supreme fruit of the Tathāgata.
If one practices the most supreme offerings, one will swiftly ascend the most supreme path of goodness;
having realized the most supreme and honored right view, one can proclaim the most supreme and subtle Dharma.
If one among humans delights in wisdom, And personally upholds the pure Dharma of the Buddhas,
One should cultivate fierce and keen right aspiration, And engage in extensive learning and correct reflection according to principle.
Some shall become noble Wheel-Turning Monarchs, Or serve as Śakra or Brahmā, King of Gods;
Having extensively cultivated immeasurable and supreme merit, They will certainly proceed to the great nirvāṇa without remainder.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Śāriputra:

“If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna and wish to swiftly realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), they should, regarding this subtle Dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva-piṭaka, give rise to a fierce, pure aspiration and joy; they should listen with earnest reverence, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, penetrate its meaning and intent, and extensively explain and reveal it to others.”

Why is this? If one receives, upholds, reads, recites, and even explains this sutra in detail for others, one will be able to ensure that the Three Jewels are never severed; one will never be separated from the four immeasurable practices; one will constantly and diligently cultivate the six perfections (pāramitās); and one will always employ correct skillful means to gather and transform sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastus).
Śāriputra! You should know that this subtle Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka is itself the path of all bodhisattvas. Why is this so?
This sutra is well able to uphold and maintain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Śāriputra!

This sutra is the noble treasury of jewels for all bodhisattvas; having relied upon this sutra to practice correctly, I have ultimately realized the eternal cessation of birth and death, and have also realized all the *pāramitās*.
Because he has realized this, he is designated as the "Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata has reached the ultimate consummation in all perfections (pāramitās); the Tathāgata has brought all that was to be done to rest; the Tathāgata has already attained all the immeasurable stages (bhūmis), and furthermore, he has realized yet further boundless stages.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has realized these *pāramitās*, he is able to dwell ultimately in all the dharmas that reach the further shore.
Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice this subtle dharma-gate of the Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka, just as I have realized it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One should understand karma as karma, And one should understand its retribution as retribution.
Where there is neither karma nor retribution, That is the peace of Nirvana."
"All conditioned phenomena are suffering; within them there is no wisdom.
Therefore, once wisdom has arisen, one is liberated from all conditioned phenomena.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the Venerable Śāriputra, the great bhikṣus, and all sentient beings—including devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-Four and Volume Fifty-Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
13. The Thirteenth Assembly: The Buddha’s Discourse to Ānanda on Dwelling in the Womb.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

In the late afternoon, the Venerable Ānanda arose from meditative concentration and, together with five hundred bhikṣus, went to where the Buddha was. With palms joined in reverence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda and the bhikṣus:

"I have an essential teaching, good in the beginning, middle, and end; its meaning is subtle and profound, pure and unadulterated, fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life (brahmacarya). This is the Sūtra on Entering the Womb."
"You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well;
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who wish to enter the womb, they will receive a body once the causes and conditions are complete; if they are not complete, they do not receive a body.
What is meant by 'incompleteness of conditions'? "

That is to say, when the parents give rise to a mind of passionate attachment and the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) appears seeking a place of rebirth, yet the father’s semen and the mother’s blood do not unite simultaneously—whether the one precedes or follows the other—and furthermore, if there are various ailments within their bodies, then [the being] does not enter the womb.

If the mother’s womb is afflicted by wind, bile, or blood disorders resulting in blockage; or if the womb is obstructed, or there are fleshy growths and knots; or if she suffers from salty diseases, wheat-belly disease, or "ant-waist" disease; or if the womb is shaped like a camel's mouth, or curved like a wagon-pole, or like a wagon-axle, or like the hub of a wheel, or like a tree leaf; or if it is twisted and coiled like a vine or bamboo sprout; or if the interior of the womb is like the awn of a grain of wheat; or if the semen and blood are discharged in excess and do not remain for even a moment; or if there is dysentery with watery discharge, or the passage of the womb is rough; or if it is pointed at the top or bottom, or curved, or shallow, or perforated and leaking; or if it is elevated, or depressed, or short and small—due to such various ailments, one cannot enter the womb.

If the parents are noble and possess great merit while the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is lowly, or if the intermediate state being is noble and possesses great merit while the parents are lowly, or if both lack the karma of mutual affinity, then in such cases, conception does not occur.
When the intermediate state being (antarābhava) is about to take conception in this manner, it first gives rise to two kinds of inverted thoughts. What are these two?

That is to say, at the time of the union of the parents, if the being is male, it conceives love for the mother and hatred toward the father; when the father’s seed is emitted, it considers it to be its own.
If it is to be female, she conceives affection for the father and aversion toward the mother; when the mother discharges the seed, she also claims it as her own.
If these feelings of aversion and affection do not arise, then conception does not occur.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
How does one enter the mother’s womb?

It is said that when the father and mother give rise to a mind of passionate attachment, the mother’s menstrual cycle is in order, and the intermediate state being (antarābhava) appears before them; provided there are none of the many aforementioned defects and the karmic conditions are complete, one then enters the womb."
Thus, when the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is about to enter the womb, there are again two types. What are these two?
First, those who lack merit; second, those who possess great merit.
Those lacking merit, when thoughts of discursive reflection arise, perceive their surroundings and think:
"I am now beset by wind, cold, and damp rain; the great assembly is tumultuous, and the power of the multitude is pressing upon me."
He then became terrified and thought:
"I should now enter a grass hut or a leaf hut, or hide at the base of a wall, or go into the mountains, marshes, thickets, or caves."
Furthermore, various perceptions arise once more, and according to what he perceives, he enters the mother’s womb.
One of great merit also gives rise to this thought:
"I am now encountering wind, cold, mist, and rain; a great crowd is clamorous and the majesty of the multitude presses upon me."

Feeling likewise terrified, he immediately ascends a high tower or climbs a great pavilion, or enters a hall or a chamber upon a couch; giving rise to various other thoughts as well, he enters the mother’s womb according to what he perceives.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In this way, when the intermediate state (antarābhava) first receives the womb, it is called the kalala; it acquires its body entirely by depending upon the impurities of the parents and past karma."
In this way, karma, parents, and various conditions do not each arise independently; rather, through the power of their combined forces, a body is received.

It is like using a vessel to hold curd and a person’s rope to produce butter: the butter cannot be found within any of the individual conditions, yet through the power of their combined forces, the butter is produced.
The kalala body is also like this; by the power of causes and conditions, it receives conception in the womb.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

It is as if, depending upon green grass, cow dung, dates, and curd, various worms are born; within each of these, no worm can be found, yet by the power of causes and conditions, the worms come to be born."
When this worm is born, it appears blue, yellow, red, or white, each taking on its color according to that upon which it relies.

Therefore, one should know that this body is produced from the impurities of the parents; though it cannot be found when sought among the various conditions, nor is it separate from them, yet through the power of their harmonious convergence, it enters the womb.

When this body is born, it is no different from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of its parents: namely, earth has the nature of solidity, water has the nature of moisture, fire has the nature of heat, and wind has the nature of motion.
If the *kalala* body possessed only the earth element and lacked the water element, it would be like a person grasping dry flour or ash, which can never cohere.
If it possessed only the water element and lacked the earth element, it would be like oil or water, whose nature is moist; lacking solidity, it would immediately flow away and disperse.

If there were only the elements of earth and water without the element of fire, it would be like a mass of flesh in the shade during the summer months; without the light of the sun, it would rot and decay.

If there were only the elements of earth, water, and fire without the element of wind, there would be no growth; it is like a man and his disciple who are skilled at refining sugar, yet whatever they produce has its interior made entirely hollow—if there is no force of wind, it will never reach completion.

In this way, the four great elements support one another to establish their existence; therefore, one should know that the kalala body, which arises due to the karmic winds of the four great elements of the parents, is likewise so: it cannot be found within any of the individual conditions, yet through the power of their combined force, the body is received.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like fresh, pure seeds that have been well stored away, not eaten by insects, and free from decay, withering, or holes."

Furthermore, suppose there were someone who selected a fertile field of rich, moist soil and sowed these seeds therein; would they not, within a single day, produce sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves that grow luxuriantly and provide shade, while fruits and flowers flourish and reach full maturity?
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The *kalala* body is also like this: it grows and develops through causes and conditions in successive stages, and the sense faculties cannot be fully formed all at once.

Therefore, you should know that although this body arises from a father and mother, it cannot be found within any of the individual conditions; rather, it takes birth through the power of their harmonious conjunction.”
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

It is like a person with clear vision who takes a sun-crystal gem and places it in the sunlight, suspending dried cow dung above it; not far from the gem, fire is produced. Neither the cow dung nor the sunlight can produce fire individually, yet they are not separate from one another; through the power of causes and conditions, fire is produced."

The body born from one's parents is likewise thus: the *kalala* stage is called "form" (*rūpa*), while feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called "name" (*nāma*). This body, composed of the five aggregates of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), undergoes suffering moment by moment; I do not praise it even for this brief duration, much less for the long-term wandering through the various realms of existence.
For example, even a small amount of excrement is foul and stinking; how much more so a large amount!
In this same way, who would find delight in the five aggregates of this *kalala* body?
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"
Such a body, remaining within the mother’s womb, emerges only after passing through thirty-eight weeks.

During the first week while in the womb, it is called *kalala*; the physical characteristics first appear like fresh curd, and within those seven days, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) gradually form as they are boiled by internal heat.
"In the second week of dwelling in the mother’s womb, there arises a karmically induced wind called 'Pervasive' (*vyāpaka*).

This subtle wind blows against the mother’s left and right flanks, causing the physical characteristics of the *kalala* stage to gradually manifest; it resembles thick curd or solidified butter. Through internal heat and boiling, it is immediately transformed into the *arbuda* stage, and thus the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) gradually achieve completion."
During the third seven-day period while dwelling in the mother’s womb, there arises again a karmic wind called "Treasury-Mouth" (kośamukha).
By the power of this wind, the embryo gradually coagulates; that *aṇḍa* (oval stage) transforms into the *peśī* (lump stage), which resembles a medicinal pestle but is shorter and smaller.
Within that womb, it is boiled by internal heat, and thus the four great elements gradually increase.
During the fourth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind called "Appropriation" (saṃgraha).
By the power of this wind, it is able to cause the closed hand to transform into a *gaṇa*, resembling a warm stone; internally heated and boiled, the four great elements gradually increase.
During the fifth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named "Sustaining" (*saṃdhāraṇa*).

By the power of this wind, the *ghana* is transformed into the *praśākhā*; the various swellings split open, and the two thighs, the two shoulders, as well as the body and head, emerge, just as the branches and twigs of trees sprout when the seasonal rains fall during the spring months.
By the power of the winds of karma, when the various blisters appear, it is likewise thus.
During the sixth seven-day period while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named "Fragrance" (Bhaktā).
By the power of this wind, four signs appear. What are these four?
They are the two knees and the two elbows; these are called the four signs.
"In the seventh week of dwelling in the mother's womb, there arises again a karmic wind called 'Revolution.
By the power of this wind, four characteristics appear, namely the webbed membrane between the hands and feet; these characteristics are as soft as a mass of foam."

In the eighth week of dwelling in the mother’s womb, there arises again a karmic wind called "Turning Over. By the power of this wind, twenty signs appear—namely, the twenty fingers and toes of the hands and feet—and he is then born.
Just as the branches and twigs of trees gradually grow when rain falls from the heavens, so too do the various marks manifest through the power of karmic winds.
During the ninth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named "Dispersal."
By the power of this wind, nine types of manifestations appear. What are these nine?
They are the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and the openings for the large and small excretions; these are called the nine manifestations.
"On the seventeenth day of dwelling in the womb, another karmic wind called 'Hardening' arises; by the power of this wind, the fetus immediately becomes firm and solid.
Furthermore, there is a wind called 'Universal Gate' which blows upon the fetal body, causing it to expand and fill out entirely, like a floating air-bladder."
"In the eleventh week of dwelling in the mother’s womb, there arises again a karmic wind called Vajra.
By the power of this wind, [the fetus] moves upward or downward within the womb, causing all the apertures of its body to become thoroughly permeated."

Furthermore, by the power of the wind, the one who is pregnant may experience alternating states of grief and joy while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; her temperament changes from its usual state, and she moves her hands and feet, causing the orifices of the fetal body to gradually expand, resulting in black blood issuing from her mouth and foul, impure fluids issuing from her nose.
After this wind has circulated through the various sense faculties, it then subsides.
During the twelfth seven-day period of remaining in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named "Curved Mouth."

By the power of this wind, the large and small intestines arise between the left and right sides, like lotus fibers or tightly spun threads laid upon the ground; they revolve eighteen times and abide supported by the body.
Furthermore, there is another wind named Veṇīvedhana (Hair-Parting); by means of this wind, three hundred and twenty joints and one hundred and one apertures are produced within the body.
During the thirteenth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named Kṣutpipāsā (Hunger and Thirst).
Due to the power of this wind, the fetal body becomes emaciated and weak, giving rise to sensations of hunger and thirst;
whatever flavors the mother consumes in her food and drink are then sustained and nourished within the cavity of the fetus and at its navel wheel.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The child has been in the mother’s womb for thirteen weeks;
his body already feels weak and emaciated, and he immediately gives rise to thoughts of hunger and thirst."
Whatever food and drink the mother consumes nourishes that which is within the womb;
by this, the life-force of the body is sustained and it gradually grows.
During the fourteenth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, there further arises a karmic wind called "Thread-Mouth" (Sūtramukha).
By the power of this wind, nine hundred sinews are produced, which interlace and bind the front, back, left, and right of the body.
During the fifteenth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named "Lotus."
By the power of this wind, twenty channels are produced; the flavors of food and drink flow into these channels to moisten and benefit the body. What are the twenty?

There are five channels each on the front, back, left, and right of the body. Each of these channels has forty branch-channels (sūkṣma-nāḍī), and each of these branches further has one hundred sub-branches. Thus, these channels each have one hundred sub-branches.

The twenty thousand [beings] in front of his body are named Śaṅkha, which in this language means "conch"; those behind his body are called Bala; those on his left side are named Sthira; and those on his right side are named Balavat.
In this way, eighty thousand major and minor channels arise within this body.
These channels further possess various colors, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of ghee, curd, or oil.

Of these eighty thousand channels, each channel has a single root; upon that root there arises one opening, or perhaps two, up to seven openings, each of which is connected to the pores of the skin, just as the roots of a lotus produce various perforations.
"At sixteen weeks and seven days while dwelling in the mother’s womb, there arises again a karmic wind named Amṛta.

By the power of this wind, it causes the nine apertures—the locations of the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, chest, and the four sides of the heart organ—to all open and develop, so that the inhalation and exhalation of breath pass through above and below without obstruction."
If there is food and drink that moistens and nourishes the body, and there is a place where it collects, it can further be digested and transformed, flowing out from below.

It is like a potter or his apprentice who, being skilled at tempering clay and arranging the wheel and cord, causes them to rotate up and down so that the vessels he fashions are successfully completed.
This is likewise so; it is all due to the power of the winds and the influence of wholesome and unwholesome karma that the eyes, ears, and other faculties gradually become complete.
During the seventeenth seven-day period while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named "Ox-Face."
By the power of this wind, his two eyes become clear and bright, and his sense faculties, such as those of the ears and nose, gradually reach full development.
It is like a mirror covered by dust and grime, which is then polished clean using brick powder and oil-based ash.
Therefore, one should know that the power of the karmic winds blowing upon the eyes and other organs to make them clear and pure is likewise so.
During the eighteenth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, there is further induced a karmic wind named "Great Firmness" (mahā-dṛḍha).
By the power of this wind, their sense faculties gradually reach maturity and become clear and pure.
It is like the sun and moon, which are shrouded by clouds and mist; when a fierce wind suddenly arises and blows them apart in all directions, the sun and moon instantly shine with great brilliance.
Just as before, by the wind of karma, his sense faculties become even more clear and pure.
"In the nineteenth week while dwelling in the mother's womb, through the power of the aforementioned winds, the four faculties of the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are fully formed."
At the very moment of entering the womb, one already possesses three faculties:
first, the body faculty; second, the life faculty; and third, the mind faculty.
Thus, all these faculties are fully complete.
During the twenty-seventh day of remaining in the mother’s womb, there arises again a karmic wind called "Solidification.

By the power of this wind, various kinds of bones are produced within the body: twenty bones are produced in the left leg, and likewise twenty in the right leg; four bones in the heels, two in the ankles, two in the knees, two in the thighs, three in the waist and hips, eighteen in the spine, twenty-four in the ribs, thirteen in the chest, twenty bones each in the left and right hands, four in the forearms, two in the shoulders, two in the jaws, four in the skull, and thirty-two in the roots of the teeth and so forth.

For example, it is like a sculptor and his disciples who first use hard wood and subsequently wrap it with cords to fashion various forms; even though the clay has not yet been applied, at such a time it is called the "bone-stage" (asthi-saṃsthāna).
The generation of the various bones by the power of the karmic winds is likewise so.
Therefore, one should know that within seven days, excluding the minor bones, the number of major bones that arise is two hundred.
"In the twenty-first week while dwelling in the mother's womb, there arises again a karmic wind called 'Arising.
By the power of this wind, it is able to cause the formation of flesh on the child's body."
Just as a master mason and his disciples are skilled at preparing clay to plaster walls, so too is it that the wind of karma can produce the flesh of the body.
"At twenty-two weeks while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind called *phulla*.
By the power of this wind, bodily blood is produced.
At twenty-three weeks while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind named *viśuddhadhara*."
By the power of this wind, the skin of the body is produced.
During the twenty-fourth week while dwelling in the mother’s womb, one further encounters a karmic wind called "Cloud-Sustainer" (Dhāraṇamegha).
By the power of this wind, the skin becomes perfectly even and its complexion becomes lustrous and moist.
"In the twenty-fifth week of dwelling in the mother’s womb, there arises again a karmic wind called *Dhāraṇī-nagara* (Holding the City).
By the power of this wind, the flesh and blood of the child’s body increase and gradually become moistened."
"In the twenty-sixth week of dwelling in the mother’s womb, there arises again a karmic wind called 'Generation.
By the power of this wind, hair, body hair, and nails are produced, each of which is connected to the various channels."
"In the twenty-seventh week of dwelling in the mother's womb, there arises again a karmic wind called 'Curved Medicine.
By the power of this wind, the physical characteristics of the body gradually attain completion."

Alternatively, having created various evil karmas in previous lives, they were stingy and greedy regarding their possessions and refused to practice charity; or again, they failed to accept the instructions of their parents and teachers. Due to such karma, they obtain various bodies that are contrary to their wishes.
If one considers a body that is tall, large, fat, white, and soft to be handsome, one will instead receive a body that is short, small, thin, black, and hard;
if one considers a body that is short, small, thin, black, and hard to be handsome, one will instead receive a body that is tall, large, fat, white, and soft.

If one considers the limbs and members of the body to be beautiful based on their height, depth, quantity, or density, then one will instead receive a body that lacks these qualities and is neither high nor low, neither sparse nor dense, and thus incomplete.

Or again, they may be born deaf, blind, mute, or with hands and feet cramped and crippled, their sense faculties incomplete; whatever sounds they produce, people do not wish to hear, and their bodies are as hideous as hungry ghosts.
Due to evil karma, one receives various kinds of undesirable bodies; even one's parents and relatives do not wish to see them, let alone others.
