Furthermore, you are possessed by various divine maladies—namely, being seized by the eight classes of spirits such as devas and nāgas, as well as by ghosts and spirits, even up to the kaṭapūtanas and other animal-demons, or being afflicted by the sun, moon, and stars.
"These spirits and ghosts cause various illnesses that afflict both body and mind; it would be difficult to describe them all in detail.
The Buddha told Nanda:

"Who would take pleasure in the cycle of birth and death as to enter a mother’s womb, undergo such extreme suffering, and be thus born and thus grown? Drinking the mother’s milk and blood, as well as various foods and drinks, they falsely conceive notions of deliciousness until they gradually reach maturity."
Even if one’s body were to attain peace and freedom from illness, and one were to enjoy food and clothing at will for a full hundred years, half of this life would be spent in sleep.

Furthermore, beginning as an infant, then as a child, and gradually reaching adulthood, one is beset by sorrow, grief, calamities, and various diseases; immeasurable hundreds of sufferings afflict the body, such that they can hardly be fully described.
When the various sufferings within the body become unbearable, one no longer desires to live and instead seeks death.
Such a body has much suffering and little joy; though it may endure for a time, it must inevitably perish.
Nanda! All who are born must die; there is nothing that remains forever.
Even if one sustains life through medicine and food and manages to extend one's years, in the end one cannot escape being slain by the King of Death and sent to the empty field.
Therefore, you should know that birth is not to be relished.
You ought to diligently accumulate the provisions for future lives; do not be negligent, cultivate the holy life with vigor, and do not be indolent.
One should always delight in cultivating beneficial conduct, dharmic conduct, meritorious conduct, and purely wholesome conduct.
One should constantly observe one's own two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—and keep them fastened in mind, so as not to give rise to great regret at a later time.
One must part from all things that are cherished; according to one's good or evil karma, one proceeds to the next world. "Nanda!
A lifespan of a hundred years consists of ten stages:
The first refers to the stage of infancy, lying swaddled in a cradle.
The second refers to childhood, delighting in children’s play.
The third refers to youth, experiencing various sensual pleasures.
The fourth refers to being young and vigorous, possessing great strength and courage.
The fifth refers to being in the prime of life, possessing wisdom and the ability for discourse.
The sixth refers to being fully accomplished, capable of careful deliberation and skillfully devising strategic plans.
The seventh refers to gradual decline, being well-versed in ritual propriety.
The eighth refers to decrepitude, wherein all faculties have weakened.
The ninth refers to extreme old age, being incapable of performing any action.
"Ten" refers to a hundred years; this is the stage of impending death.
Nanda! Such is the general outline of the major stages, explained in brief.
Calculating four months as one season, there are three hundred seasons within a hundred years, with one hundred each for spring, summer, and winter.

A year consists of twelve months, totaling one thousand two hundred months; if calculated by half-months, there are a total of two thousand four hundred half-months, with eight hundred half-months in each of the three seasons, totaling thirty-six thousand days and nights.
Eating twice a day amounts to a total of seventy-two thousand meals; even those occasions where one does not eat due to specific circumstances are included in this count.

The circumstances for not eating include: not eating out of anger or resentment, not eating when encountering suffering, not eating because one cannot obtain what is sought, not eating due to sleep, observing a fast, restlessness, playfulness, or being preoccupied with affairs.
Whether eating or not eating, they gather together in such numbers;

including the drinking of mother’s milk, I have already fully explained the number of years, months, days, nights, and meals throughout a human life of a hundred years. You should give rise to a sense of weary detachment.

"Nanda! Thus one is born, grows, and reaches maturity, yet the body is subject to manifold ailments—namely, those of the head, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, teeth, throat, chest, abdomen, hands, and feet; such as scabies, leprosy, insanity, dropsy, coughing, disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as various types of malaria and pain in the limbs and joints."
Nanda! The human body is subject to such sufferings of illness.

Furthermore, there are one hundred and one wind disorders, one hundred and one bile disorders, one hundred and one phlegm disorders, and one hundred and one combined disorders; in total, there are four hundred and four illnesses that arise from within.
Nanda! The body is like an abscess or an arrow, composed of manifold ailments; it does not pause for even a moment, nor does it abide from one thought-moment to the next.
Its nature is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is constantly near death and subject to decay—a thing that cannot be cherished or protected.

Nanda! Furthermore, all sentient beings undergo such sufferings at birth as these: namely, having their hands, feet, eyes, ears, noses, tongues, heads, and limbs severed; furthermore, undergoing imprisonment, shackles, fetters, whippings, and tortures; suffering from hunger, thirst, exhaustion, cold, heat, rain, snow, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, wind, dust, wild beasts, and various harmful contacts. These manifold afflictions are immeasurable and boundless, and difficult to describe in full.

Beings of this world constantly delight in and sink into such harsh suffering; whatever they desire is rooted in suffering, yet they do not know to renounce it but instead pursue it further. Day and night they are tormented and their bodies and minds are afflicted; burning from within, they find no rest.

Thus there is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.

Among the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all are suffering. If one constantly walks without standing, sitting, or lying down, one experiences suffering and lacks joy;

if one constantly stands without walking, sitting, or lying down; or if one sits without walking, standing, or lying down; or if one lies down without walking, standing, or sitting, one experiences extreme suffering and finds no peace or happiness.

Nanda! All these are the abandonment of suffering and the seeking of suffering; they are merely the arising of suffering and merely the cessation of suffering, which proceed in continuous succession through the causes and conditions of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

The Tathāgata, having fully understood this, has declared that the phenomena of birth and death for sentient beings are characterized by the impermanence of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); they are not ultimately real, are subject to transformation and decay, and cannot be maintained.
One should seek contentment, cultivate a deep sense of weary detachment, and strive diligently for liberation. Nanda!

Among the classes of sentient beings in the happy realms, the impurity of their birthplaces and the intensity of their suffering are such that their various deceptions could never be fully described; how much more so, then, regarding the unbearable, agonizing torments experienced by sentient beings in the three miserable realms—the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the hells?
"Furthermore, Nanda!
There are four ways of entering the mother's womb.
What are these four?
First, there are sentient beings who enter with right mindfulness, abide with right mindfulness, and emerge with right mindfulness.
Second, there are those who enter with right mindfulness, abide with right mindfulness, but emerge without right mindfulness.
Third, entering with right mindfulness and abiding with wrong mindfulness;
fourth, all three being with wrong mindfulness.
Who is it that enters, abides, and exits with right mindfulness?

Suppose there is a certain class of ordinary sentient beings who, by nature, delight in upholding the precepts, frequently practice wholesome qualities, take pleasure in sublime deeds, perform various meritorious actions, and are extremely well-restrained; they constantly contemplate integrity and refrain from negligence, possess great wisdom, and at the time of death experience no regret before being reborn—whether as a *saptakṛdbhava-parama* stream-enterer, a *kulamkula*, a *sakṛdāgāmin*, or an *antarāparinirvāyin*.

Because this person has previously cultivated wholesome conduct, at the time of their passing, although they are oppressed by suffering and undergo various pains and afflictions, their mind remains undistracted; they die with right mindfulness and, returning to right mindfulness, enter the mother’s womb, clearly understanding that all phenomena arise from karma and are produced through causes and conditions, serving as a dwelling place for all demons.

Nanda, you should know that this body is at all times a dwelling place for every kind of impurity; its nature is not permanent, and it is a delusive object used by the ignorant to entice and deceive people.

This body is a mechanical device constructed of bones, with sinews and veins connecting the various apertures; fat, flesh, marrow, and bone are bound together, covered over by skin so that its faults remain unseen. Within this hot cave, it is filled with impurities; hair, fur, nails, and teeth are differentiated in their positions. Because of clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," one is constantly pulled and dragged about, never attaining autonomy.

It constantly emits tears, saliva, filth, and sweat; it is filled with yellow fluid, phlegm, putrid fat, and the loathsome excrement and urine of the kidneys, gallbladder, liver, lungs, large intestine, and small intestine; it is pervaded everywhere by various types of worms, and its upper and lower orifices perpetually flow with foul impurities.
The two receptacles, the raw and the cooked, are covered with a thin skin; this is what is called a walking latrine.

You should observe that when you eat, as the food is chewed by the teeth and moistened by saliva, it is swallowed down the throat, where the marrow and brain mingle and their fluids flow into the belly.
It is like a dog gnawing on a dry bone, falsely imagining it to be delicious; as it eats until the food reaches its navel, it vomits it back up, only to swallow it down again.

Nanda! This body originally grows from impure and foul substances—kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā—and flows through the stages from infancy to old age and death. Its cyclic existence and bondage are like a dark pit or a foul, decaying well.
It is constantly sustained by the flavors of salty, bland, bitter, sour, and pungent food.
Furthermore, the body-sense organs are scorched and boiled by the fire within the mother’s womb, perpetually beset by the suffering of heat in this impure cauldron of excrement.

"Nanda! When a mother walks, stands, sits, or lies down, it is as if she were bound by five fetters; moreover, it is like being scorched by fire, such that it is difficult to endure and beyond all analogy."
Although that fetus is within such a pit of excrement and filth and is tormented by manifold sufferings, because its faculties are sharp, its mind does not become distracted.

Furthermore, there is a class of sentient beings with meager merit who, while in the mother’s womb, remain either transverse or inverted. This occurs due to the power of the causal conditions of their prior karma; or because the mother’s food—whether cold, hot, salty, sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, or acrid—is not properly balanced; or because she drinks excessive amounts of liquids; or because she engages excessively in sexual desire; or because she is afflicted by many illnesses; or because she harbors grief and distress; or because she falls to the ground at times; or because she is beaten or struck. Due to these various conditions, the mother’s body becomes intensely feverish.
Due to the heat of the body, the fetus is also scorched; because it is scorched, it experiences various sufferings and afflictions; because there is suffering, it immediately begins to move and turn;
and because it moves and turns, its body may become transverse or inverted, making it impossible to emerge.

There was a woman skilled in such matters who, having smeared her hands with ghee and oil, inserted them into the mother’s womb and gently touched the fetus to settle it back into its original position.
At the moment her hands touched it, the fetus immediately experienced great suffering and distress.
Nanda! It is like a young boy or girl whose skin and flesh are sliced open by someone with a sharp knife, and ashes are scattered upon them; from this, great suffering and affliction arise.
The agonizing suffering of the fetus is likewise thus.
Although it undergoes this pain, because its faculties are sharp, right mindfulness does not scatter. Nanda!

Thus the fetus dwells within the mother’s womb, undergoing such suffering; furthermore, at the time of birth, it emerges with great hardship, and driven by the winds of karma, its hands are joined together and its limbs and joints are clenched in a state of intense agony.

As he emerges from the mother’s womb, his body is bluish and bruised, like a fresh swelling that is difficult to touch; oppressed by hunger and thirst, with a mind in a state of suspended anxiety and burning distress, he is pushed out by the wind through the conditions of karma.

Once he has emerged from the womb, he is touched by the external wind as if being cut, smeared with charcoal, or immersed in fire; when his hands or clothing touch him, he experiences extreme suffering.
Although he undergoes this suffering, because his faculties are exceptionally sharp, his right mindfulness remains undisturbed.
"Nanda! Within the mother's womb, one knows that entering, abiding, and exiting are all entirely suffering.
Nanda! Who would take pleasure in entering such a womb? "Nanda! [he said].
Who is it that enters and dwells in the mother’s womb with right mindfulness, yet departs without right mindfulness? Nanda!

It is like a certain class of ordinary beings who by nature delight in observing the precepts, cultivate wholesome qualities, constantly engage in superior deeds, and perform meritorious actions; whose minds are upright and not given to negligence, who possess a modicum of wisdom, and who have no regrets at the time of death—such as those who are stream-enterers bound to seven more births, or "family-to-family" practitioners, or once-returners, or those separated from nirvana by only one interval.

This person, having previously cultivated wholesome conduct, though assailed by suffering and undergoing various pains and afflictions at the time of death, does not have their mind distracted; instead, returning to right mindfulness, they enter the mother’s womb with full awareness that all phenomena arise from karma and are produced through causes and conditions.

As explained in detail above, even though he undergoes such extreme sufferings until his emergence from the womb, because his faculties are of medium-sharp capacity, he enters and dwells with right mindfulness, but emerges without right mindfulness.
The detailed explanation is as above, up until: "Who, indeed, would take pleasure in entering such a womb?
"Nanda! Who is it that enters the womb with right mindfulness, but dwells and emerges without right mindfulness?"

Nanda! Suppose there is a certain class of ordinary sentient beings who, by nature, delight in observing the precepts, cultivate wholesome qualities, constantly engage in superior deeds, and perform various meritorious actions.

As explained in detail above, up until the point that they have no regrets at the time of death—such as those who are stream-enterers destined for seven more births—even when various sufferings press upon them at the moment of passing away, although they experience pain and affliction, their minds do not become distracted; rather, returning to right mindfulness, they enter the mother's womb.
Because of these inferior faculties, one is aware at the time of entering the womb but unaware during the periods of staying and emerging.
As explained in detail above, this continues until: "Who would take pleasure in entering such a womb?"
"Nanda! Who is it that is unwholesome in mindfulness regarding entering, abiding in, and emerging from [the meditative state]?

It is like a certain class of ordinary beings who delight in violating the pure precepts, do not cultivate wholesome qualities, constantly engage in evil deeds, and perform various misdeeds; whose minds are not upright and who practice much heedlessness; who lack wisdom, are greedy for wealth and stingy, with hands always clenched and unable to be extended; who are ever full of expectations when bestowing gifts upon others; whose minds are not disciplined and compliant, whose views and conduct are inverted, and who feel regret at the time of death as all their unwholesome karmas manifest before them."
At the time of death, when one is oppressed by intense, sharp, and agonizing suffering, the mind becomes distracted;
due to these various afflictions, one does not remember or recognize who one is.
From where have you come?
Where are you going now, Nanda?
This is called being without right mindfulness at all three times.
The detailed explanation is as above. Nanda!
Although these sentient beings born among humans experience such immeasurable suffering and affliction, this is nonetheless a superior state.
Within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, a human body is difficult to obtain.
If one is born in the heavens, one is constantly fearful of falling back down and suffers from the pain of separation from those one loves.
When life is about to end, other devas will say to them:
"May you be reborn in a favorable realm within the world."
What is the worldly happy destination?
It refers to humans and devas.
A human rebirth is difficult to obtain; to be far removed from unfavorable conditions is even more difficult.
What are the evil destinies?
They refer to the three miserable realms.
As for the destiny of the hells, one constantly undergoes suffering that is agonizing and utterly disagreeable; its fierce and piercing torment is beyond easy comparison.

As for those in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), their nature is dominated by anger and they lack a gentle heart; they are deceitful, treacherous, and murderous, smearing their hands with blood. Devoid of compassion, their appearance is hideous, striking terror into those who behold them;
even when they draw near to humans, they suffer from hunger and thirst and are constantly beset by obstacles.

As for those in the realm of animals, they engage in immeasurable and boundless unwholesome conduct, meritless conduct, unrighteous conduct, non-virtuous conduct, and conduct lacking sincerity; they devour one another, with the strong bullying the weak.
There are various animals—whether born, growing, or dying—all of whom dwell in darkness amidst impure excrement, filth, and stench.
Occasionally they experience a brief moment of light, such as bees, butterflies, mosquitoes, ants, fleas, lice, maggots, and the like.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless others who have grown up in perpetual darkness.

Because they were foolish people in their previous lives—failing to listen to the sutras and the Dharma, indulging unrestrainedly in body, speech, and mind, being greedily attached to the five desires, and committing various evil deeds—they are born among this class to undergo the suffering of ignorance and delusion.

Nanda! Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings among the animals who are born, grow, and die entirely within the water—namely, those such as fish, turtles, crocodiles, alligators, cicadas, leeches, clams, oysters, and frogs.
This is due to the evil deeds of body, speech, and mind committed in previous lives, as explained extensively above. Nanda!

Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings among the animals who, upon smelling the scent of excrement and urine, quickly go to those places to consume them as food and drink—namely, such species as pigs, sheep, chickens, dogs, foxes, weasels, vultures, eagles, crows, flies, dung beetles, and various other beasts.
All of this is summoned by the evil karma of previous lives, resulting in such retribution. Nanda!

Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless classes of animals that constantly subsist on grass, wood, and various impurities for their food and drink—namely, those belonging to the species of elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, mules, and the like.
"Thus, until the end of his life, due to his prior evil karma, he receives such retribution.
Furthermore, Nanda! The ocean of birth and death is suffering; how painful it is!"
Fierce flames burn with extreme intensity, such that not a single sentient being remains unscorched or unbosomed.

All this is due to the blazing, fierce fires of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which greedily crave the objects before them: forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Nanda! What is meant by "blazing, fierce fires"? They are the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion;

the fires of birth, old age, sickness, and death; and the fires of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—fires of poisonous harm that constantly burn of their own accord, from which not a single person can escape.
Nanda! Those who are indolent undergo much suffering; ensnared by afflictions, they perform unwholesome deeds, cycling through saṃsāra without rest and without end.

Those who apply themselves with diligence enjoy abundant peace and happiness; they rouse a courageous mind to sever the afflictions and cultivate wholesome dharmas, never abandoning the yoke of virtue nor resting for even a moment.
Therefore, you should now contemplate this body—its skin, flesh, sinews, bones, blood vessels, and marrow—which will soon disintegrate and perish.
You must always maintain a single-minded focus and not be indolent; strive diligently to realize that which has not yet been realized.
"You should train yourself in this way, Nanda!
I do not engage in disputes with the world, yet the world forcibly engages me in disputes."
Why is this so? Those who know the Dharma do not dispute with others; being free from "I" and "mine," with whom would they engage in debate?
Because false attachments arise from views and misconceptions, I have realized perfect enlightenment and speak thus: regarding all phenomena, there is nothing that I do not fully understand.
"Nanda! Is there any discrepancy in what I have said? Nanda replied:
"No, World-Honored One! What the Tathāgata speaks has no difference."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Nanda!"
What the Tathāgata speaks is invariably without discrepancy.

The Tathāgata is one who speaks truthfully, one who speaks reality, one who speaks according to suchness, one who does not speak otherwise, and one who does not speak deceptively; he desires to bring long-term peace, happiness, and great benefit to the world.

He is the knower of the path, the one who recognizes the path, the one who proclaims the path, the one who reveals the path, the Great Guide—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

People of the world lack knowledge and faith; they constantly act as slaves to their sense faculties. They look only at what is in the palm of their hand and fail to perceive the great benefit; they do not cultivate what is easy to do, yet they constantly engage in what is difficult.
Nanda! Let us set aside such a sphere of wisdom for a moment.
You should now observe with what is seen by the physical eye; knowing that all that is seen is entirely false and illusory is itself called liberation.
Nanda! Do not trust me; do not follow my desires; do not rely on my words; do not observe my physical marks; do not follow whatever views the śramaṇa holds; do not conceive reverence for the śramaṇa;
and do not speak these words: "The śramaṇa Gautama is my teacher."
"However, regarding the Dharma realized through my own direct realization, you should dwell alone in a quiet place, reflecting and examining it, and constantly practice its cultivation extensively.

Following whatever Dharma you observe with your mind, you should dwell in right mindfulness by contemplating and realizing that very Dharma. Make yourself an island and make yourself a refuge; make the Dharma your island and make the Dharma your refuge.
There is no other island, and there is no other refuge."
Nanda! How is it that a bhikṣu makes himself his island and makes himself his refuge; makes the Dharma his island and makes the Dharma his refuge;
having no other island and no other refuge?
In this way, Nanda!

If there is a bhikṣu who dwells contemplating his own internal body, being diligent, resolute, and mindful, attaining right understanding, and constantly intending to subdue all resentment and affliction within the world—this is called "contemplating the internal body as suffering."
If one contemplates the external body and the internal-external body, it is likewise so. Nanda!

Next, one dwells contemplating the body in terms of the phenomenon of origination, dwells contemplating the body in terms of cessation, and further dwells contemplating the body in terms of both the phenomena of origination and cessation. Thus, regarding this very body, one is able to maintain right mindfulness; there may be only wisdom, or only vision, or only mindfulness, dwelling without dependence, knowing that in this world there is nothing to be grasped.
Thus, Nanda! This is called a bhikṣu dwelling in the contemplation of his own internal body.
It is the same for the external body and for both the internal and external bodies.

Next, one dwells contemplating internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings; one dwells contemplating the internal mind, the external mind, and both internal and external minds; one dwells contemplating internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena.

Through diligent effort and focused mindfulness, one attains correct understanding; one constantly contemplates the subduing of all anger and afflictions within the world, abiding in the contemplation of the phenomena of origination and abiding in the contemplation of the phenomena of cessation. Furthermore, one abides in the contemplation of the phenomena regarding both the dharma of origination and the dharma of cessation; thus, one is able to maintain right mindfulness toward this very body—possessing either wisdom alone, or vision alone, or mindfulness alone—and realizes that there is nothing in this world to be grasped.
Thus it is, Nanda!
This is called a bhikṣu making himself an island, making himself a refuge; making the Dharma an island, making the Dharma a refuge;
having no other island, having no other refuge.

"Nanda! If there is a man of upright nature who is free from flattery and deceit, and comes to me in the morning, I shall instruct him in the wholesome Dharma according to his capacity; by evening, he will report what he has attained.
If I instruct him with the Dharma in the evening, he will report what he has attained by dawn."

"Nanda! My wholesome Dharma is realized through direct experience here and now; it can eliminate feverish afflictions, is well-suited to the times, easy to practice as a skillful means, and is a self-realized teaching that provides excellent protection."
"Venerable sir, I have heard the Dharma taught before me, which accords with tranquility and leads toward enlightenment;
this is what I know.
Therefore, you should now constantly practice and study such dharmas as those that bring benefit to oneself, benefit to others, and benefit to both."

Practice the Dharma of renunciation with diligence so that it does not pass in vain; you shall thereby attain the supreme fruit of unconditioned peace and happiness. By receiving from others the offerings of clothing, food, bedding, medicine for illness, and other necessities, cause those donors to obtain great benefit and merit, and to receive a noble and vast reward of the highest fruition.
Thus it is, Nanda!
You should practice and train in this way. Furthermore, Nanda!
There is no such thing as a form that is lovely and delightful yet remains unchanging and undecaying at a later time; such a case does not exist.
Nor is there any such thing as one who does not give rise to sorrow and lamentation, yet does not produce afflictions; such a case also does not exist.
Nanda! What do you think? Is this form permanent?
"Is it impermanent? "Venerable sir,
its nature is impermanent."
“Nanda! Since the body is impermanent, is it suffering? “Venerable Sir!”
"This is suffering.
"If it is impermanent and suffering, and subject to change and decay,
would my many-hearing noble disciples regard form as self, or hold that 'I have form,' or that 'form belongs to me,' or that 'I am within form'?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"What do you think? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent? "Venerable sir!"
"All are impermanent. "Nanda! Since the body is impermanent, is it suffering?"
“Venerable sir, it is suffering.
“If it is impermanent and suffering, then it is a phenomenon subject to change and decay.”

"Do you consider that for my many-heard noble disciples, feeling and so forth are the self, or that 'I have feeling and so forth,' or that 'feeling and so forth belong to me,' or that 'I am within feeling and so forth'?"
"No, World-Honored One!

Therefore, one should know that as for all forms—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; superior or inferior; far or near—all such forms are not the self, the self does not possess form, form does not belong to the self, and the self does not exist within form."
In this way, one should examine with right mindfulness and right wisdom:

whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; far or near—none of these are the self, the self does not possess these, nor does the self exist within them.
In this way, one should examine with right mindfulness and right wisdom.

If my well-learned noble disciples thus contemplate form with revulsion, and likewise give rise to revulsion toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; having become revulsed, they are no longer attached; being without attachment, they attain liberation; and having attained liberation, they know for themselves that they are liberated, declaring:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

When the Blessed One had spoken this Dharma, the Venerable Nanda was far removed from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and the minds of five hundred bhikṣus were liberated from all outflows (āsravas).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse, addressing Nanda:
"If a person lacks a concentrated mind, They will lack pure wisdom;
Being unable to sever all outflows, Therefore, you must practice with diligence."
You have constantly cultivated sublime contemplation, knowing the arising and ceasing of all aggregates;
as you are pure and perfect, all the devas rejoice.
Friends and kin share in your joy, coming and going with mutual affection and remembrance.
Abandon greed for fame and gain, Nanda; you should renounce them.
Do not associate with householders or those who have gone forth from the home life.
Mindful of transcending the ocean of birth and death, bring an end to the limits of suffering.
First from the kalala, next the arbuda is born;
from the arbuda the peśī is born, and from the peśī the ghana is born.
When the ghana undergoes a brief transformation, the head and the four limbs are produced.
A multitude of bones aggregate to form the body, all arising from the causes of karma.
The skull consists of nine pieces joined together; the jaw is connected by two bones.
There are thirty-two teeth, and their roots are likewise.
The auditory canals and the cervical vertebrae, the palate bone and the bridge of the nose,
the chest and the throat— these together comprise twelve bones.
The eye sockets consist of four bones, and the shoulder joints likewise form two pairs.
The two arms and the fingers together have fifty bones;
behind the neck there are eight bones, and the backbone has thirty-two.
Each of these has its own foundation, and their number is likewise divided into four parts.
On the right side of the ribs, there are thirteen connected together;
on the left side they likewise grow in connection, numbering thirteen bones.
These various skeletal chains are linked together in groups of three.
The two pairs of bones are hooked together, while the remaining ones do not connect.
The left and right legs and feet together contain fifty bones;
totaling three hundred and sixteen, they support the flesh of the body.
The joints are linked together, forming the body of sentient beings;
this is what those who speak truth have declared, and that which the Perfectly Awakened One knows.
From the feet to the crown of the head, it is a collection of impurities, lacking any solidity.
By these [elements] together a body is formed, as fragile and precarious as a reed hut;
with no roof but standing only on bones, smeared all over with flesh and blood,
it is like a wooden automaton or a conjured phantom.
One should contemplate this body: Tendons and sinews further entwine it, Moist skin envelops it from all sides, And at nine locations there are orifices of sores.
From these, impurities such as feces and urine Constantly flow and overflow everywhere.
Just as granaries and baskets hold various grains and wheat,
so too is this body: filled with impurities within,
a mechanism of moving bones, precarious and fragile rather than solid.
Fools always delight in it, while the wise have no attachment;
It constantly flows with the filth of mucus and spittle, And is forever filled with pus and blood.
Yellow fat mixed with breast milk, And brains fill the skull.
Phlegm and mucus flow within the chest and diaphragm; inside lie the organs of digestion, both raw and cooked.
Fat, grease, skin, and membranes, along with the five viscera, the abdomen, and the stomach—such foul and putrid things as these dwell together in this place of impurity.
This body of sin is deeply fearsome; it is indeed an enemy.
Yet those ignorant people who indulge in desire foolishly protect it at all times.
Such a foul and filthy body is like a dilapidated city wall.
Day and night oppressed by afflictions, it flows on without a moment’s rest.
The body-city has bones for its walls and flesh and blood for its plaster;
greed, hatred, and delusion serve as the painted colors, adorning it everywhere.
This loathsome city of bone, with its flesh and blood joined together,
is constantly tormented within and without by evil associates.
Nanda, you should know this as I have described it.
Day and night, always maintain mindfulness; do not dwell upon the realm of desire.
If you wish to distance yourself from it, constantly practice such contemplation;
diligently seek the state of liberation, and you shall swiftly transcend the ocean of birth and death.
When the Blessed One had thus spoken this Sūtra on Entering the Womb, the Venerable Nanda and the five hundred bhikṣus were all greatly rejoiced; they faithfully accepted and practiced it.

The Bhikṣu Nanda, having crossed the perilous and difficult waters of birth and death, reached the secure state of ultimate Nirvāṇa and attained the fruit of Arhatship. He spoke this verse of self-congratulation:
"By respectfully offering a bath, Pure water and fragrant ointments, And by cultivating various fields of merit, I have obtained this most excellent reward."
When the great assembly heard this teaching, they were all filled with doubt. To sever their doubts, they requested of the Great Master:
"Venerable One!

What karma did the bhikṣu Nanda previously create, such that by its retribution he obtained a golden-colored body, adorned with the thirty marks, which was only four finger-widths shorter than the body of the World-Honored One?"

He conceived an extreme attachment toward the objects of sensual desire; out of compassion, the Great Master forcibly pulled him from the ocean of birth and death and, through skillful means, established him in ultimate nirvana.
"I only wish that you would explain this for us.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"The karma previously committed by the bhikṣu Nanda has reached its fruition; the ripening of its results has now all manifested before him."
The full explanation is as in other [passages].
Then he spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish."
"When the causes and conditions meet, the fruit of retribution is received by oneself. "Listen attentively.

Ninety-one eons ago in the past, when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavān—appeared in the world. Accompanied by sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, he traveled through the human realm and arrived at the capital city of Bandhumatī, where he went to the Bandhumatī Grove and stayed there."
At that time, that Blessed One had a half-brother who was extremely attached to the objects of sensual desire.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin exhorted him to leave the household life within the ocean of birth and death, and through skillful means established him in ultimate nirvāṇa.

At that time, there was a king named Upajyoti who ruled the world according to the Dharma; the population was flourishing, prosperous, and at peace, free from all deceit, theft, and pestilence, while cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane abounded everywhere.

The king’s half-brother was excessively addicted to sensual lust. When the king heard that the Buddha and his assembly were residing at the Kāṣṭhavāṭa Forest, he took his princes, personal attendants, ministers, women of the inner palace, and the common people as his retinue and went to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One proclaimed the sublime Dharma for the assembly of kings, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them so that they attained a distinguished understanding.
However, the younger brother, being addicted to sensual desires, was unwilling to leave his door. Then, the son of a high minister and other friends of similar standing went to him and said:
"Good friend, do you not know?"

The king, along with the princes, the ladies of the inner court, the ministers, and the multitude of attendants, went to the presence of Vipaśyin Buddha; they personally performed acts of reverence, listened to and received the sublime Dharma, and attained a most excellent understanding.
"A human body is difficult to obtain, yet you have already obtained one; why now do you indulge so deeply in lustful desires that you refuse to leave your door?
Having heard this reprimand, he felt shame and humiliation in his heart, and with a reluctant air, he followed along with him as they went together.
At that time, the Buddha’s younger brother, a bhikṣu, saw his companions departing together and asked,
"For what reason are you all traveling along with this one man as your companion?"
Then his companion reported the matter in full to the bhikṣu, saying:
"I am the younger brother of the Buddha.
In the past, when I was at home, I was deeply attached to the objects of sensual desire; fortunately, the Great Master forcibly led me out and brought me safely toward ultimate nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, there are others like me who are likewise ignorant; it would be truly excellent if you, out of compassion, were to take us along by force.
We shall now proceed to the Unsurpassed Great Teacher; upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, we will surely give rise to profound faith.
Then his companions went together to where the Buddha was; the Buddha, observing their kind, expounded the Dharma to them in accordance with their faculties, inclinations, and dispositions.
Having heard it, they conceived a profound faith.
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!
I pray only that the Great Master and the assembly of noble ones will come to my home tomorrow morning to enter the warm bathhouse and bathe."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing he had been accepted, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
He then went to the king’s residence, offered his respects, and said:

"Great King! Having gone to the Buddha’s dwelling and heard the Dharma, faith was born in me; I conceived a sense of weary detachment toward the objects of sensual desire and invited the Buddha and the Sangha to come to my home tomorrow to bathe in the warm bathhouse. The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, accepted my invitation."
"The Buddha is one who should be honored by devas and humans; Your Majesty should now sprinkle and sweep the streets and adorn the city walls.
The King thought to himself:
"When the Buddha enters the city, I shall adorn it."
"However, my younger brother was addicted to sensual desires and difficult to admonish; that the Buddha has now tamed him is truly rare.
He replied, "Excellent!"
"You may now go and prepare the requisites for the bath; I shall, according to my ability, adorn the city walls and moats.
The younger brother was filled with great joy, took his leave of the king, and departed.
The King addressed his ministers, saying:
"An edict shall be proclaimed to inform all people that tomorrow the World-Honored One will enter the city.

All of you—both those who have long resided here and those who have come from afar—should each adorn the city walls and streets to the best of your ability, sweep the thoroughfares, and carry various incense and flowers to welcome the Great Master as he enters."
The minister, having received the king’s command, issued a general proclamation to inform all, fully conveying the royal decree.

At that time, the multitude within the city cleared away rubble and debris, sprinkled scented water everywhere, burned various exquisite incenses, hung up many banners and canopies, and scattered flowers as offerings, so that it resembled the Joyful Garden of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
At that time, the king’s younger brother prepared various fragrant decoctions, scented oils, and other requisites, and adorned the bathhouse by arranging seats and couches.

As the Buddha Vipaśyin gradually approached the city, the king, his ministers, the crown prince, the queen, the palace attendants, the court ladies, and the general populace all came out to welcome him; they paid homage from afar at the Buddha’s feet and followed him into the city.
Then the king’s younger brother led the Buddha, the World-Honored One, into the heated chamber and offered fragrant water and other substances for his ablution.

Seeing that the body of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was like the color of gold, fully adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, he rejoiced upon seeing him and gave rise to deep faith.
Having finished bathing and put on his robes, he immediately prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and made this vow, saying:
"I have now had the good fortune to encounter the supreme field of merit and have offered it a small measure of worship."
By this root of merit, may my body in future lives attain a golden hue no different from that of the Buddha.
Just as the World-Honored One’s younger brother, who had developed deep attachment to the realm of desire, was forcibly pulled out and led to the secure and ultimate state of *nirvāṇa*.
"May I, in a future life, become a younger brother to the Buddha, and may I likewise obtain a golden body.
When I give rise to attachment toward the objects of desire, may he forcibly lead me out of the deep river of craving and enable me to reach the secure place of Nirvana."
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts. That younger brother of King Bandhumat who was addicted to sensual pleasures was none other than the bhikṣu Nanda.
Because in the past he invited the Buddha Vipaśyin to enter the bathhouse and bathe in fragrant water, he made a vow with a pure mind."
Due to those roots of goodness, he is now the younger brother of the Buddha, his body being the color of gold.

Because I forcibly extracted him from his attachment to the realm of sensual desire, causing him to renounce the world and leave the household life, he has reached ultimate nirvana and the state of peace and security.
At that time, the great assembly again had doubts and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
What karma did the bhikṣu Nanda previously perform, such that in this present life he has attained the thirty marks of a Great Man?"
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"The karma he performed is explained at length as before.
Long ago, in a certain village, there was an elder who was immensely wealthy with abundant riches and provisions for life."
There was a garden where flowers and fruits flourished, with flowing springs, bathing pools, and dense groves of trees, serving as a fitting place for renunciants to dwell in seclusion.

At that time, a Pratyekabuddha appeared in the world; out of compassion for sentient beings, he dwelt in quietude, for when no Buddha is present in the world, such a field of merit is the only one available.
At that time, a certain Pratyekabuddha, wandering through the human realm, arrived at this village; after traveling about and observing his surroundings, he reached the garden.
When the gardener saw the venerable one, he said to him, "Welcome; here, rest from your fatigue."
The Venerable One remained there and entered the fire-light concentration during the middle watch of the night.
When the park keeper saw this, he thought to himself:
"This Great Virtuous One has accomplished such a sublime practice."
He immediately rose during the night and went to his father, saying: "O Great One!
You should now give rise to a heart of joy."

In the garden, there was a great virtuous one who came to seek lodging with me; he had perfected sublime conduct and was endowed with supernormal powers, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the entire garden.
Having heard this, the householder went quickly to the park; after prostrating at his feet, he spoke thus:
"Noble One! You seek food, and I seek the cause of merit. I pray that you will dwell in this park, and I shall constantly provide you with food."
Seeing his earnestness, he accepted the invitation and, remaining within this grove, entered into the bliss of liberation through the sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
He further thought:

"This foul body of mine has transmigrated through birth and death; that which was to be accomplished has already been attained. It is fitting that I enter parinirvāṇa and forever realize the state of non-arising."

Having formed this thought, he immediately ascended into the void and entered the fire-light samādhi, manifesting various supernatural transformations and emitting a great radiance; above, it shone with crimson brilliance, and below, it flowed as clear water. Having cast off this body, his consciousness was not reborn, and he forever realized the wondrous realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.

Then that elder took the remains and cremated them with fragrant wood; he then extinguished the fire with milk, collected the remaining bone fragments and placed them in a new jar, and erected a stūpa, hanging banners and canopies there while giving rise to profound faith and reverence.
He sprinkled thirty kinds of exquisite perfumed waters and made great vows to seek the various marks and signs of excellence.
Listen attentively and do not harbor doubts: the elder of that time was none other than Nanda.
"Because of his karma of offering supreme and exquisite worship with reverence and faith, he now experiences the fruit of retribution by attaining thirty extraordinary and sublime marks.
At that time, the great assembly again had doubts and once more requested the World-Honored One:
"Venerable Sir!"
"What karma did the bhikṣu Nanda create in the past such that, had he not gone forth and abandoned the secular world, he would certainly have succeeded to the rank of a Cakravartin King?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The karma created by Nanda in previous lives must necessarily be experienced by him in person when its retribution ripens."
As explained in detail above:

in the past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, endowed with the ten titles, and dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a king in that city named Kṛkī, who ruled the world according to the Dharma as a great Dharma-king, as described at length above.
The king had three sons, namely the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
When that Buddha Kāśyapa had finished his work of transforming beings, he entered Great Parinirvāṇa like an extinguished fire.

The king, with faith and reverence, took the Buddha’s remains and, using various fragrant woods—such as sandalwood, aloeswood, *udumbara*, and celestial *gośīrṣa*—burned them until they were consumed; he then extinguished the embers with fragrant milk.

Having collected his relics and placed them in a precious golden jar, he constructed a great stūpa made entirely of the four jewels, measuring exactly one yojana in length and breadth and half a yojana in height, and was equipped with a *cakra* pinnacle.
At that time, the king’s middle son personally offered the middle parasol.
Monks, do not harbor doubts; the king’s middle son at that time was none other than Nanda.

Because of this wholesome karma of offering the middle parasol with a respectful heart in the past, he became a powerful Wheel-Turning King for two thousand five hundred lifetimes, bringing transformation to one continent.
"If he had not gone forth into homelessness during this life, he would have become a Wheel-Turning King and attained great sovereignty.
At that time, the great assembly again harbored doubts and questioned the World-Honored One:
"Venerable Sir!..."
“What karma did the bhikṣu Nanda perform in the past such that he is foremost among the disciples of the Buddha for being most thoroughly guarded in the doors of the sense faculties?
The Buddha said,
“This was due to the power of his aspiration.”

The bhikṣu Nanda left the household life for homelessness during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. His preceptor was renowned as the foremost among those who well-guarded the doors of the sensory faculties within that Buddha's teaching; he maintained the holy life (brahmacarya) for the duration of his entire lifespan, yet throughout his present existence, he ultimately attained no realization.
At the time of his death, he made this vow:
"I have maintained the holy life under the Buddha for as long as this body lasted, yet during my present existence, I have attained nothing at all."

"By these roots of merit from my practice, may I—just as this Buddha, the World-Honored One, has prophesied that there shall be a young brahmin in a future age who will attain perfect enlightenment under the name Śākyamuni—go forth from home into homelessness within his teaching and destroy all afflictions to realize arhatship. Just as my preceptor was foremost among those who well-guarded the doors of the sense faculties in the presence of this Buddha, may I likewise be foremost among those who guard the doors of the sense faculties within that teaching."
"By the power of that vow, he is now foremost among my disciples in guarding the doors of the sense faculties.

Thus, monks, if one performs purely black karma, one receives a purely black retribution; if one performs purely white karma, one receives a purely white retribution; and if one performs mixed karma, one shall receive a mixed retribution."
"Therefore, you all should abandon purely black and mixed karma and cultivate purely white karma.
In this manner, you should practice.
— *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll 57.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-Eight, translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Fifteen: The Prediction for Mañjuśrī. Part One of Chapter Fifteen: The Prediction for Mañjuśrī.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha,
together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, headed by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, he was accompanied by seventy-two billion hosts of devas, all of whom were intent upon the path of the bodhisattva.

Additionally, he was accompanied by the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, and Brahmā-deva, along with their retinues, each numbering fifty-two thousand, all of whom likewise were intent upon the path of the bodhisattva.
There were four asura kings, each accompanied by an immeasurable multitude of followers.

They were also joined by seventy-two thousand great nāga kings, headed by such leaders as the nāga king Nanda, the nāga king Upananda, Varuṇa the nāga king, Sāgara the nāga king, Mahīdhara the nāga king, Anavatapta the nāga king, Abhyudgatarāja the nāga king, Mārapramardana the nāga king, Jayanta the nāga king, and Candrābha the nāga king. Such beings as these were their chiefs.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by immeasurable yakṣa kings, of whom the foremost were: the yakṣa king Kumbhīra, the yakṣa king Aṭavaka, the yakṣa king Suciloma, the yakṣa king Sumati, the yakṣa king Subuddhi, the yakṣa king Sulakṣaṇa, the yakṣa king Viśvarūpa, the yakṣa king Akṣobhya, the yakṣa king Balin, and the yakṣa king Mahābala. These and others served as his leaders.

At that time, the kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly of Rājagṛha, along with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, each offered robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various requisites to the Tathāgata, honoring and respecting him with worship.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl, surrounded before and behind by a multitude of bhikṣus and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, proceeding toward King Ajātaśatru’s palace in Rājagṛha.

Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, hundreds of thousands of kinds of wondrously colored light rays were emitted; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played in unison, and a rain of various exquisite flowers fell—blue utpala flowers, pink padma flowers, yellow kumuda flowers, and white puṇḍarīka flowers descended in profusion.

At that time, by the power of his supernormal faculties, the Tathāgata caused jewel lotuses to emerge wherever he traveled; they were as large as chariot wheels, with stems of white silver, petals of pure gold, and filaments of lapis lazuli. Within the calyx of each flower sat a manifested bodhisattva, seated in the full lotus posture.
These bodhisattvas, together with the precious lotuses, circumambulated the city of Rājagṛha seven times, keeping it to their right, and spoke these verses:
"The Śākya, the Worthy One, the Great Caravan Leader, Who brings benefit and joy to sentient beings and grants them peace;
Possessing great majesty and a tranquil mind, The refuge of the world is now entering the city."

If you wish to distance yourself from the suffering of old age and death, or if you delight in sporting within celestial palaces, or if you desire to shatter the armies of Māra, you should draw near the Lord of Men, possessed of wondrous eloquence.
His name is difficult to hear, yet now he has appeared; having cultivated myriad practices for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he stands before us.
Wandering through the world with a heart of great compassion, this Honored One shall now enter the city.
Having practiced immeasurable and boundless renunciation—giving away sons, daughters, wives, and royal thrones;
heads, eyes, ears, noses, as well as hands and feet; even clothing and food and drink were likewise surrendered.
Having cultivated immeasurable merit through giving, he has realized the unsurpassed, all-encompassing wisdom;
with a mind tamed by generosity, he makes his conduct firm.
A Great Man whose precepts are pure and without flaw, having perfected immeasurable merit through patience, his mind is ever serene as he enters the city.
Having practiced supreme diligence for koṭis of eons, Forgetting weariness as he contemplates the suffering of sentient beings,
And possessing immeasurable, incomparable dhyāna— That one with the Brahma-voice shall now enter the city.
His wisdom is immeasurable and peerless, like the infinite expanse of space;
the supreme Honored One among men is likewise in his precepts. Having fully cultivated all practices, his wisdom is pure;
he destroys the armies of Māra and is able to deliver others. He abides in the state of sorrowlessness and immovability.
The Peerless Dharma King turns the wheel of Dharma; that Lion of the Śākyas shall enter the city.
If you wish for a Buddha to arise in the world, adorned with the thirty-two marks, you should give rise to the peerless bodhicitta and offer worship to the Tathāgata.
If you wish to forever abandon greed, anger, and delusion, And to distance yourself from all afflictions,
You should swiftly draw near to the Lion of the Śākyas And perform various kinds of offerings.
If one desires to swiftly become a Śakra or a Brahmā king, with each accompanied by a thousand retinues constantly following them,
and to eternally enjoy all the pleasures of the celestial palaces, they should draw near to the Lion of the Śākyas.
If you wish to become a supreme Wheel-Turning King over the four continents, with all seven treasures perfectly accomplished and a thousand most excellent sons,
all valiant and strong, you should make offerings to that Most Victorious Honored One.
If you wish to become a wealthy elder and lord of a town, with resources and wealth expanding beyond measure,
and with a retinue and physical appearance that surpass all others, you should make offerings to the Lion of the Śākyas.
Those who have already attained liberation and those who shall attain it, all do so by hearing the Buddha’s teaching on tranquility;
for that Supreme Honored One is difficult to encounter, one should listen to his nectar-like words free from sorrow.

At that time, immeasurable beings—men and women, old and young—from within the city of Rājagṛha, upon hearing these verses, immediately attained awakening. Each brought incense, flowers, precious parasols, banners, and pennants, along with immeasurable music, and proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata was. With single-minded devotion they gazed up at him, leaping for joy and offering worship with reverence.

Thereupon, as the World-Honored One was about to enter the city, his foot stepped upon the threshold, and the ground within the city shook in six ways; a rain of various exquisite flowers fell, accompanied by the sounds of all manner of music.

The sentient beings within the city who were blind regained their sight; those who were deaf regained their hearing; those who were insane regained their sanity; those who were naked obtained clothing; those who were hungry obtained food; and those who were poor obtained wealth. At that time, those sentient beings were no longer oppressed by greed, anger, ignorance, or pride; they looked upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness, like a father and son.
Within those musical sounds, a verse was spoken:
“The Great Man of Ten Powers, the most supreme Lion among Men, Enters the city to benefit all beings;
may all living creatures obtain peace and happiness.”
The blind shall see forms; the deaf and mute shall hear sounds;
the insane shall regain their original minds; the naked shall be clothed;
those who hunger and thirst shall encounter exquisite food; and the destitute shall obtain wealth.
Furthermore, in the void of space, hundreds of billions of devas together made offerings to the Buddha, vying with one another to play various musical sounds.
"The Honored One of Ten Powers, endowed with all virtues, now enters this city."
The city shook in six ways, namely the universal shaking and so forth;
yet the sentient beings felt no fear, but all attained great joy.
Now, within this city, all living beings—
Untroubled by greed, anger, or delusion, nor vexed by stinginess or envy,
their bodies filled with joy, they face one another with thoughts of loving-kindness.
May the Buddha quickly enter the city and bring peace and happiness to all living beings.
When the World-Honored One entered the city, he radiated great light everywhere;
humans and devas all played music, their hearts and minds filled with joy.
Such wonders as these were manifold and beyond measure.
“Devas, humans, and asuras—there are none who do not gaze upon and revere him. At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a son of a bodhisattva householder named Dūṣaṇasūdana.

From within the lanes and alleys, he beheld from afar the World-Honored One, whose appearance was marvelous, extraordinary, upright, and serene; whose faculties were profoundly tranquil, such that those who gazed upon him could never tire; who dwelt in the supreme self-mastery of *śamatha*; who guarded his sense-faculties like a well-trained elephant; whose right mindfulness was undisturbed like a pure, deep pool; and whose body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

Having seen this, that bodhisattva gave rise to a mind of supreme reverence and pure faith; he then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings went together to the place where the Buddha was, while countless devas remained in the air, joining their palms in reverence and respectfully prostrating themselves.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Faults addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and, according to his vows, adorn and purify a buddha-field?”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, desiring to discipline all sentient beings and out of compassion to crush their transgressions, went to the marketplace and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O sons of good family!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes one dharma, they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and, according to their vows, adorn and purify a buddha-field. Good son!
What is this one dharma?
It is that this bodhisattva, practicing great compassion toward all sentient beings, gives rise to the bodhicitta through superior aspiration and joy.
What is meant by giving rise to the bodhicitta through superior aspiration and joy?
It should be stated thus: if there are those who have already resolved upon bodhicitta, they shall never again commit even the slightest evil.
What is it that they do not do? It refers to greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the worldly deportment and frivolous play of householders—all of which they completely abandon.
Once one has gone forth, one no longer hopes for fame, profit, or honor, but dwells securely in the dharmas practiced by those who have gone forth.
What are these dharmas practiced by those who have gone forth?
This refers to penetrating all phenomena (dharmas) as they truly are.
What are these phenomena that are to be realized?
They are the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), bases (āyatanas), the conditioned (saṃskṛta), and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
How does one awaken and enter [this state]?

It means observing that the five aggregates are quiescent, like illusions, empty, and non-existent. When awakening in this way, one perceives neither an act of awakening nor an entry; there is no cognition and no thought, and all conceptual discrimination is entirely stilled.
If one thus gains insight into the aggregates, one thereby gains insight into all phenomena.
This is called the dharma practiced by those who have gone forth.
When a bodhisattva practices this way, they do not abandon any sentient beings.
Why is this? This bodhisattva explains to sentient beings according to what he himself has observed, yet he remains unattached to both phenomena and sentient beings. Good son!
This is the one dharma that a bodhisattva accomplishes to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and also causes the buddha-field to be fully perfected.

When this Dharma was being taught, the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Faults attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena; filled with joy and exultation, he ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees.
Within that assembly, two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon bodhicitta;
fourteen thousand devas and humans became free from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance, and from his mouth he emitted rays of light of various colors that illuminated immeasurable worlds.
Having shone upon them, they returned, circled the Buddha three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes so as to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and spoke these verses before the World-Honored One:
"O Guide of sovereign power, Who has reached the further shore of all dharmas,
Venerable One of all-knowledge, For what reason do you manifest a smile?"
The Sugata, Honored One of the Ten Powers, who is able to bring about all benefits and has fully realized the three periods of time— by what cause do you manifest a smile?
You understand the mental activities of sentient beings and their distinctions as superior, middling, and inferior.
Knowing that all perceptions are unimpeded, we pray that the Buddha will proclaim this for us.
Billions of nayutas of devas have all come to prostrate before the Buddha;
we pray that you will emit a subtle and wondrous sound to satisfy all who look up to you with longing.
Having reached the further shore of supreme concentration, and likewise with wisdom, you are far removed from all error; for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Hundreds of thousands of devas have gathered here for the sake of the Dharma.
Immeasurable bhikṣus, with palms joined, all wish to hear;
they play various kinds of music as an offering to the Tathāgata.
"Excellent, World-Honored Buddha! We pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see this Bodhisattva Destroyer of Faults ascending into the void? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, I have seen it. The Buddha said, “Good son!
After this, having eliminated faults and passed beyond sixty-two thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood in this world, with the name Śāntavinayasvara.
The eon was named Free from Heat and Affliction.

The meritorious adornments of that Buddha-field, as well as its assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, were equal to and indistinguishable from those of the World of Wondrous Joy belonging to the Tathāgata Acala.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, arrived at the palace of King Ajātaśatru and sat down, each taking his place according to seniority.
Then the king, with his own hands, served various kinds of food and drink to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, providing for them all until they were fully satisfied.
Furthermore, he offered exquisite garments to the Tathāgata and, sitting upon a low seat before the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
From what do anger, resentment, hatred, and vexation arise?"
"By what means is delusion and lack of wisdom extinguished?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Anger, resentment, and the affliction of hatred arise from the notions of 'I' and 'mine'."
If one cannot discern merit and fault, as well as "self" and "what belongs to self," this is called ignorance.
If one knows that "self" and "what belongs to self" as they truly are, this is neither knowledge nor ignorance.
Great King, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) come from nowhere and go nowhere; if there is no coming or going, then there is no arising or ceasing.
If there is no arising or ceasing, then both wisdom and non-wisdom are likewise entirely absent.
Why is this? There is not the slightest dharma that can cognize arising or non-arising.
To be free from the cognizer is itself knowing.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is rare indeed that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has so well expounded this. I would rather meet an untimely death while hearing the Dharma than wish for the mere continuation of a life lived in vain.”

At that time, having exhorted, enlightened, and gladdened Ajātaśatru, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed for Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. Having washed his feet, he spread out a seat and sat down, entering into samādhi.

At that time, for the sake of the gift of Dharma, the Tathāgata arose from samādhi during the late afternoon; all the great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas likewise emerged from their meditative concentration.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with forty-two thousand devaputras who had set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle; Maitreya Bodhisattva, together with a multitude of five thousand bodhisattvas; and Vīrabhānu-rasita-ghoṣa Bodhisattva, together with a multitude of five hundred bodhisattvas—all such bodhisattvas as these, along with the śrāvakas and King Ajātaśatru, each surrounded by their respective retinues, approached the place where the Tathāgata was. They prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the city of Rājagṛha who all went together to Vulture Peak Mountain; having arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

Thereupon, Śāriputra, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Previously, in the marketplace of Rājagṛha, the Tathāgata briefly expounded for the sake of subduing faults the adornments and purity of the buddha-fields of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
Excellent, World-Honored One!

We pray that you will explain in detail how bodhisattvas practice the non-retrogressive path to enlightenment, pacifying all afflictions, adorning and purifying buddha-fields, fulfilling great vows, and fully practicing the various pāramitās; how they remain far removed from the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, tread upon the tracks traversed by the Tathāgatas, subdue all māras and restrain all heterodox teachers, and, endowed with all-knowledge, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
In this way, even before a bodhisattva has attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to definitively bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
Now, within this assembly, those sons and daughters of good family who seek awakening, having heard this Dharma, will joyfully practice it.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"What I have now spoken is not intended merely for this present assembly; therefore, it is fitting that I should manifest a supernatural transformation."

Having formed this thought, he emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light of wondrous colors; each ray of light universally illuminated hundreds of thousands of millions of lands in the ten directions, such that all the light of the suns, moons, devas, nāgas, maṇi-jewels, lightning, and fire within those Buddha-lands was eclipsed and no longer appeared.

Furthermore, all those great and small surrounding mountains, Sumeru the king of mountains, and all other mountains, groves, and trees were so completely penetrated by the Buddha’s radiance that none could cast a shadow.
At that time, the Tathāgata again manifested the majestic sound of his coughing, and that sound was heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

At that moment, eighty-four *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-fields away from here to the east, there was a world named Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*), where a Buddha currently resides, known as King of Accumulated Auspiciousness (*Saṃbhavaraśmīśvara*).

Furthermore, in that buddha-field there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is filled solely with bodhisattvas, and each bodhisattva has ten billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas as their retinue.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva among that assembly named Dharmottara.
For what reason was he named Dharmottara?

It was because, having heard the Dharma being preached before the great assembly, that bodhisattva ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, concealed his own body, and expounded the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka called the "Vajrapada Dhāraṇī."
At that time, the entire assembly thought to themselves:
"All phenomena possess only their sounds. Why is this so?"

It is just as when the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata did not perceive the marks of the body but heard only its voice; this voice has no substance, just like those bodily marks. Since it is free from both seeing and hearing, it is the dharma-nature.
When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable bodhisattvas who had attained patience within the assembly saw from afar the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata in that land.
They also saw the Buddha of this world-system emitting rays of light, and they heard his voice reaching as far as that realm.
Those bodhisattvas immediately went together to the place where the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition has this unprecedented auspicious sign appeared?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

To the west, passing from here through Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of eighty-four Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā. There currently dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni; wishing to assemble the bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions, he has emitted this light and the sound of his coughing from all his pores.
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage, visit, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata and all the bodhisattvas, and I also wish to listen to the Dharma.”
The Buddha said, "You may go;
now is precisely the right time."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata had this thought:
"By what supernatural transformation shall I now go there to pay homage and visit the Tathāgata Śākyamuni?
Having had this thought, he immediately entered the Samādhi of the Body Adorned with All Ornaments.

By the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi, this great trichiliocosm was filled with exquisite flowers piled up to the knees; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played simultaneously, adorned with various precious banners, streamers, and canopies; and it was further suffused everywhere with exquisite fragrances, becoming like the celestial palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata had manifested these supernatural transformations, he was surrounded by a retinue of sixty-three billion great bodhisattvas, and in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, they vanished from that land and appeared within this world-system.
Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Then, according to the direction from which they had come, they manifested lotus flowers through the power of their vows and sat upon them.

At that time, to the south, passing beyond ninety-six billion nayutas of Buddha-fields, there was a world named Free from Dust. There currently dwells a Buddha named Lion’s Valiant and Swift Prowess, who is respectfully surrounded by a vast assembly of great Bodhisattvas.
Within that assembly there was a bodhisattva named Ratnapāṇi.
For what reason was he named Ratnapāṇi?

It was because when that bodhisattva was transforming sentient beings in various buddha-fields and wished to touch as many buddha-worlds as he desired with his right hand, he could accomplish it exactly as he wished. From his hand issued forth the sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; the sounds of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; and such sounds of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of dharma-jewels.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, seeing a great radiance and hearing the sound of a cough, went to the place where that Buddha was and said to him:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen appeared?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!

To the north of here, passing beyond ninety-six billion nayutas of buddha-fields, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is titled Śākyamuni. Desiring to expound the Dharma-gate of the Adornments of the Merits of a Buddha-field, and wishing to assemble all bodhisattvas so that they may hear this teaching and thereby receive its merits, he has manifested this auspicious sign.”
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage to, visit, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata and the various bodhisattvas, and we also wish to hear the Dharma.”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, why would you need to go?”
"Why is this? Because that Sahā world is a gathering place for sentient beings who are fully possessed of the afflictions of the three poisons.
