Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what purpose and benefit did that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, abandon a magnificent and pure land to manifest within this defiled world-system?”
The Buddha said, “Good son! That Buddha-Tathāgata,
in the distant past, spoke these words during the long night:”
"May I swiftly attain the accomplishment of great compassion, and always manifest perfect enlightenment and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma among sentient beings who are corrupt and evil.
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
That Śākyamuni Tathāgata was indeed able, in the past, to conceive this great compassion and difficult-to-conceive vow to appear in such a world of evil.
Such a Compassionate Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter; I shall now go to pay him homage, visit him, and make offerings to him.
The Buddha said,
"So be it. Now is precisely the right time."
However, son of good family!
When you go to that land, you should examine it with care so as not to harm yourself. Why is this?
"Although the bodhisattvas born in that world are difficult to encounter, other sentient beings there have minds and conducts that are treacherous and crooked,
making them difficult to tame. Ratnapāṇi replied,
"Even though there may be anger, resentment, and enmity in that land, it shall do no harm to me."

Even if all sentient beings were to harbor hatred and revile me until the end of the future, or even strike and pelt me with swords, staves, tiles, and stones, I would be able to endure it all and never retaliate in return.
At that time, the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmin addressed all those bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!
If you are able to be like Ratnapāṇi, you may go together with him."
When these words were spoken, seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas in that assembly spoke with one voice, saying:
"We shall go together to the Sahā world."
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi then had this thought:

"By what kind of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) may I now go there to pay homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and furthermore, how may I bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately covered this trichiliocosm with his right hand and rained down various foods, drinks, garments, vehicles, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, conch shells, coral, jade, and precious stones. He was able to completely satisfy the hopes and aspirations of all sentient beings according to their minds: those who delighted in hearing the Dharma were enabled to hear it, and furthermore, he caused immeasurable sentient beings who heard the Dharma to realize the truth, while also causing countless sentient beings afflicted by illness and suffering to receive supreme and wondrous bliss.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi had manifested these supernatural transformations, he and the assembly of bodhisattvas vanished from that land in a single thought-moment and appeared within this realm.
Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times to the right.
According to the direction from which they came, by the power of their vows, they manifested lotus flowers and sat upon them.

At that time, seventy-two billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields away to the west from here, there was a world named Maṇigarbha; there currently dwells a Buddha named Maṇicayendrarāja.

That Buddha-field is composed of pure lapis lazuli; it contains no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only a multitude of pure great bodhisattvas who come, go, sit, and stand upon the lapis lazuli ground. All clearly behold the Tathāgata manifest before them, as if seeing the reflection of one's own face in a bright mirror.

In that same manner, those bodhisattvas see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, within that stage; having seen him, they request the Dharma, and the Buddha then explains for them his past great vows. Upon hearing this Dharma, those bodhisattvas attain patience (*kṣānti*).

At that time, from within the maṇi-jewel of the ūrṇā-kośa between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated that land in its entirety; therein, the light of the sun and moon was eclipsed and did not appear, and day and night were distinguished by the opening and closing of flowers.
In that land, there was a bodhisattva named Vijñānapraṇidhi; having encountered this light, he went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“By what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen appeared? The Buddha said, “Good son!

To the east, passing from here through seventy-two billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is titled Śākyamuni; it is for the purpose of summoning all the bodhisattvas that he has manifested this auspicious sign.
At that time, having heard these words, Jñānottarapraṇidhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage to, visit, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata and the various bodhisattvas, and we also wish to hear the Dharma.”
The Buddha said, "You may go.
Now is precisely the right time."
At that time, Jñānottarapraṇidhi thought to himself:
"By what supernatural transformation (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) shall I now go there to pay homage and visit the Tathāgata Śākyamuni?

Having had this thought, he immediately entered into samādhi, causing the sufferings of the three evil realms within this trichiliocosm to be entirely extinguished and all beings to attain unsurpassed bliss, just as a bhikṣu attains the various dhyāna-concentrations.

At that time, all devas, humans, and non-humans were no longer oppressed by greed, hatred, and delusion; nor by various views, pride, resentment, anger, malice, stinginess, envy, arrogance, flattery, or hypocrisy; they all gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Jñānaprasthāna had manifested these supernatural transformations, he and forty-two thousand bodhisattvas vanished from that land in a single moment of thought and appeared within this realm; arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.
According to the direction from which they came, by the power of their vows, they manifested lotus flowers and sat upon them.

At that time, sixty-three thousand Buddha-fields away to the north from here, there was a world named Constantly Adorned; there currently resides a Buddha there, titled King Arisen from the Śāla Tree.
In that buddha-field, the very name "woman" had never been heard before; all beings were born through transformation from lotuses, with monastic robes appearing spontaneously upon their bodies.
At that time, the Buddha expounded for the assembly of bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of the Seal of the Buddha-lineage.
What is called the seal of the Buddha-lineage (*buddhagotra-mudrā*)? It is the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

From this point on, one possesses the bodhisattva precepts and enters the bodhisattva-piṭaka; one attains dhāraṇī with a mind free from distraction, remains inseparable from equanimity (*upekṣā*), and realizes emptiness (*śūnyatā*). One correctly cultivates signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), is by nature free from the defilement of greed, and is able to realize the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*). One acts in accordance with awareness, joyfully seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, and truly understands the nature of non-arising (*anutpatti*). One realizes all phenomena (*dharma*) without discrimination, is endowed with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and severs deluded thoughts. For these reasons, it is called the seal of the Buddha-lineage.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva among that assembly named Lakṣaṇavyūhatārakāsaṃcayarāja, whose original vow was sublime: if any sentient beings were to see his body, they would certainly attain the thirty-two marks of a great man.

At that time, that bodhisattva, encountering the Buddha’s radiance and hearing his voice, proceeded to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition has this auspicious omen appeared? The Buddha said, "Good son!

To the south of here, beyond sixty-three thousand buddha-fields, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni; he has manifested this auspicious sign in order to summon all the bodhisattvas.
That bodhisattva asked,
"For what reason is this world called Sahā?
The Buddha said:
“Because that realm endures greed, anger, ignorance, and all manner of suffering and affliction, it is therefore called the Sahā world.
That bodhisattva asked:
“Do all the sentient beings in the Sahā world truly endure insults, beatings, and various disturbances?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
In that realm, sentient beings rarely achieve such merit; rather, they mostly follow along with greed, anger, ignorance, resentment, and the fetters of attachment.”
That bodhisattva said:
"If that were so, that realm should not be called Sahā.
The Buddha said:

“Lakṣaṇavyūha-tārāgaṇarāja! In that buddha-field there are also sons and daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva vehicle; they have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, have accomplished patience, protect sentient beings, and have skillfully disciplined themselves.”
If there are sentient beings who come to inflict harm with various sufferings and afflictions, one is able to endure them all, never succumbing to negligence, greed, anger, or delusion. Good son!
Because there are such virtuous beings, that realm is called Sahā.

Furthermore, within that realm, there are also sentient beings who are fully possessed of various evils and have little capacity for repentance; their minds are coarse and violent, devoid of shame or remorse, and they do not revere the Buddha, do not honor the Dharma, and do not love the Saṅgha—they are destined to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.

That Śākyamuni Tathāgata, amidst these inferior sentient beings, is able to fully endure insults, contempt, resentment, slander, harassment, malicious speech, and intimidation; his mind is like the great earth, unshakable and beyond opposition.
Whether he receives offerings or does not receive them, his mind is without fluctuation, neither exalting nor disparaging, and free from both hatred and affection.
For this reason, that realm is named Sahā.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Constellation Cluster Adorned with Marks addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have now attained a great and wholesome benefit.”
"One shall not be born among those wretched, evil, and inferior sentient beings. The Buddha said, "Good son!
Do not speak thus. Why is this?
To the northeast there is a world named Adorned with Sublime Patience; therein currently resides a Buddha named Mahesvararaja.
The sentient beings in that land are all fully endowed with unswerving peace and happiness, just as a bhikṣu has entered the meditative absorption of cessation; their bliss is likewise so.

If there were sentient beings in that buddha-field who practiced various pure conducts for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, it would not equal the merit obtained by one who, in this Sahā world, gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings for even the duration of a finger-snap; how much more so if they can abide in a pure mind for a single day and night!
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Constellation Cluster of Adorned Marks addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage to, visit, and serve Śākyamuni Tathāgata and all the bodhisattvas, and we also wish to listen to the Dharma.”
The Buddha said: "You may go;
now is precisely the right time."
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Constellation Cluster of Adorned Marks thought to himself:
"By what power of supernormal knowledge shall I now go there to pay homage and visit the Tathāgata Śākyamuni?"

Having formed this thought, he manifested a precious canopy in the void that covered this trichiliocosm, with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of pearl tassels and jeweled banners draped all around it.
From within that canopy, various kinds of flowers rained down, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played spontaneously.

Furthermore, they caused the monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others in this assembly to each see their own bodies, endowed with the thirty-two marks, appearing within the precious canopy.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva King of the Constellation Cluster of Adorned Marks had manifested these supernatural transformations, he and ten billion bodhisattvas vanished from that land in a single moment of thought and appeared in this realm. Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him three times to the right.
According to the direction from which they came, by the power of their vows, they manifested lotus flowers and sat upon them.

In this manner, throughout the ten directions, in each of the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas—having seen the great radiance and heard the sound of the clearing of the throat—questioned their respective World-Honored Ones and came to this land.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each sat to one side; it was likewise so for all others.

Furthermore, within this world-system, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, gods of great majesty and power, as well as nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others—all beheld the radiance and came before the Buddha to prostrate at his two feet, then withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had manifested these supernatural transformations, all the bodhisattvas who had gathered from immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields in the ten directions beheld the adornments of merit in this land, as well as the dimensions of the Buddha’s body, the bodhisattvas, the śrāvakas, and their requisites; all were exactly equal to those in their own original lands. Nevertheless, they knew that the various fields remained distinct and without confusion.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke in verse:
"Your fame resounds throughout the ten directions, and your wisdom is immeasurable; You emit great radiance that illuminates the world.
Though all sentient beings together attempt to measure it, No one can fathom the supreme wisdom of the Honored One among Men."
Bodhisattvas from the ten directions, numbering in the hundreds of millions, have all gathered here for the sake of seeking the Dharma;
they all have faith and delight in the various Dharma-gates, and pray that the Buddha will expound them so that they may rejoice.
The Tathāgata’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom, His fame is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions;
He expounds the Dharma fearlessly like a lion, His light pervades the void as the sun shines.
All devas, nāgas, and rākṣasas, as well as bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs,
upāsakas and upāsikās, join their palms and joyfully desire to hear the Tathāgata speak.
The Blessed One fully understands all things—past, future, and present;
by the power of his supreme resolve, he uproots the delusions of the masses. We pray that you will sever our doubts and bring us to clear understanding.
How does a bodhisattva practice wisdom to adorn and purify buddha-fields so that they are radiant and immaculate?
How are all vows swiftly fulfilled?
We now entreat the Tathāgata to explain this for us.
How does one possess the precept of non-avarice without flaw, Able to endure insults and all manner of hardships,
Practicing with diligence without weariness, And liberate immeasurable suffering beings?
With single-minded devotion, you delight in entering the gates of samādhi; You dwell and move within the pure palaces of dhyāna.
Benefiting the world while remaining untainted— Are you not like a lotus flower that is not wetted by water?
How does one’s wisdom transcend the world, Expounding the profound and subtle Dharma?
How does one subdue all hosts of Māras And swiftly become fully endowed with śamatha?
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 58;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 59.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The Fifteenth Assembly: The Prediction of Mañjuśrī, Part Two.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

“You should now prepare a Dharma seat for the Buddha; having ascended it, I shall proclaim the various practices cultivated through my past aspirations and delights, as well as the skillful means for generating the meritorious adornments of all Buddha-fields and the gateway to the true Dharma.”
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One now command me to prepare the seat, rather than having Ānanda, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the others do so?"
Why does he set aside those śrāvakas? Is this not taught solely for the sake of the bodhisattvas?
Or is it because those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not vessels for this dharma-gate? For these reasons, the World-Honored One has had me prepare the seats.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested for the Tathāgata a lion throne made of various jewels, forty thousand yojanas in height, adorned with exquisite beauty on all sides, and spread upon it with soft celestial garments.
From his seat, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated this trichiliocosm.
At that time, once the Tathāgata had ascended the seat, he caused this world to shake in six ways.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to fulfill all their aspirations. What are these four?
First, to generate a superior aspiration; second, to give rise to a mind of compassion for all sentient beings; third, to initiate diligent effort; and fourth, to serve spiritual friends.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes one dharma, it will cause his vows not to regress and will purify the Buddha-fields.
What is this one dharma?
This bodhisattva should joyfully study the great vows originally established and practiced by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya when he was a bodhisattva:
"In whatever place I am born, at the time of my first birth, if I do not go forth into homelessness, I would be deceiving the Buddhas of the ten directions."
"In this way, Śāriputra!

These bodhisattvas should train in accordance [with this]: whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, they shall all, in every place of birth, resolutely renounce the household life to go forth as monastics."
Why is this? Because for all bodhisattvas, the most supreme benefit is what is called "leaving the home life. Śāriputra!
Those who delight in leaving the household life are able to acquire ten kinds of merit. What are these ten? First, they are not attached to various desires;

second, they delight in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages); third, they practice what the Buddhas have practiced; fourth, they distance themselves from the conduct of ordinary worldlings; fifth, they are not attached to wives, children, or property; sixth, they distance themselves from the causes of the evil realms; seventh, they cultivate the dharmas that lead to happy rebirths; eighth, their roots of goodness from past lives are never diminished; ninth, they are constantly praised and envied by the devas; and tenth, all ghosts and spirits respectfully protect them.
If a bodhisattva always delights in leaving the household life, they will obtain these ten kinds of merit. Therefore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva who aspires to seek awakening and desires to deliver sentient beings should always leave the household life.
This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of one dharma. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes two dharmas, they cause their vows not to regress and purify the buddha-field.
What are these two? They are as follows:

a bodhisattva does not delight in the stage of the śrāvaka, does not seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, does not take pleasure in teaching the vehicle of the śrāvaka, does not associate with those of the śrāvaka vehicle, does not train in the precepts of the śrāvaka, does not delight in proclaiming dharmas associated with the shared vehicle of the śrāvaka, nor does he encourage others to practice the vehicle of the śrāvaka. It is likewise regarding the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha. He encourages sentient beings solely for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, so that they may achieve the supreme, unsurpassed *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These are called the two.
Śāriputra, if there is one who encourages others to enter the Buddha-vehicle, this bodhisattva will be able to acquire ten kinds of merit.

What are the ten? First, attaining a pure buddha-field devoid of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; second, attaining a community of exclusively pure bodhisattvas; third, being protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; fourth, constantly having one’s name praised by the Buddhas as they preach the Dharma for one; fifth, all aspirations made being entirely vast; sixth, if born in the heavens, becoming Śakra or a Brahmā King; seventh, if born among humans, becoming a Cakravartin King; eighth, constantly seeing the Buddhas; ninth, being beloved by gods and humans; and tenth, gathering immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits.

Why is this? Śāriputra, if there were one who could cause all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm to attain the fruit of arhatship, or even establish them in the stage of a pratyekabuddha; yet, if there were another who could establish a single sentient being in the bodhi of a Buddha, the merit of the latter would far exceed that of the former.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
It is not by means of the appearance of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas that the lineage of the Buddhas remains unbroken.
If there were no Buddha in the world, there would be no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra, it is because the Buddha appears that the lineage of Buddhas remains unbroken, and furthermore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are brought forth.
Therefore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva causes others to abide in the Buddha-vehicle, they obtain these ten kinds of merit and attain a pure buddha-field.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra," [he said].
When a bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas, they cause their vows not to regress and enable them to embrace the meritorious adornments of a buddha-field. What are these three?

First, to respect and delight in dwelling in an araṇya; second, to practice the gift of Dharma without any attachment; and third, to be firm and securely established in the discipline of pure precepts.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva firmly abides in the precepts, they attain ten kinds of fearlessness. What are these ten?

First, fearlessness in entering a village; second, fearlessness in preaching the Dharma among the assembly; third, fearlessness regarding food and drink; fourth, fearlessness in leaving a village; fifth, fearlessness in entering a monastery; sixth, fearlessness in eating within a great assembly; seventh, fearlessness in instructing others; eighth, fearlessness in attending upon one’s preceptors and ācāryas; ninth, fearlessness in teaching and admonishing one’s own kinsmen with a mind of loving-kindness; tenth, fearlessness in using robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, and in having all one’s speech accepted with faith by others who abide in the Vinaya.
Śāriputra! These are the ten kinds of fearlessness of a bodhisattva. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma with a mind free from attachment, they are able to embrace ten kinds of merit.

What are these ten? First, not giving rise to evil desires; second, not seeking to be recognized by others; third, not giving rise to a mind for fame and reputation; fourth, the mind being unattached to the households of donors; fifth, not monopolizing or guarding over other families; sixth, feeling joy and contentment even when receiving the four requisites of the most inferior quality; seventh, teaching the Dharma so that others believe and accept it; eighth, being protected by benevolent deities; ninth, not giving rise to false thoughts; and tenth, giving rise to the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.
These are called the ten.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva respectfully honors, cherishes, and delights in dwelling in an araṇya, they accomplish these ten kinds of meritorious benefits.

What are these ten? First, distancing oneself from worldly discourse; second, devoting oneself exclusively to quietude; third, focusing the mind on the objects of meditative concentration; fourth, relinquishing all worldly affairs; fifth, loving and delighting in all Buddhas; sixth, constantly experiencing the joy and bliss of dhyāna-concentration; seventh, being free from obstacles when practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya); eighth, attaining samādhi with little exertion of effort; ninth, never forgetting the teachings one has received; and tenth, fully understanding all the meanings of the Dharma one has heard.
These are called the ten.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will cause their vows not to regress and will purify the Buddha-fields."
What are these four?

First, being able to practice according to what one preaches and preaching according to how one practices; second, constantly remaining humble and self-effacing; third, distancing oneself from stinginess and envy; and fourth, giving rise to a heart of joy upon seeing others obtain benefit.
These are called the four.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva is able to teach in accordance with their practice, there are four kinds of benefits.

What are the four? First, the mouth constantly emits the fragrance of blue lotuses; second, the vocal karma is pure and free from error or confusion; third, one is universally trusted and accepted by all the world; and fourth, one masters the perfect voices of all Buddhas.
These are called the four.
Śāriputra, there are four kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva who practices humility.
What are these four?

First, one is far removed from rebirth in the evil destinies, such as the bodies of animals; second, one experiences sublime happiness; third, neither secret plots nor violent bandits can cause harm; and fourth, one is worthy of receiving the respect and prostrations of humans and devas.
These are called the four.
Śāriputra, there are four kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva who remains far removed from stinginess and envy.

What are the four? First, not forgetting the mind of giving; second, acting as a great donor during times of famine; third, seeing those who uphold the precepts approach, one goes out to welcome and receive them; and fourth, whether receiving gifts from others or giving to others, there is not a single person toward whom one feels envy.
These are called the four.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva sees others obtain benefit and gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, there are four kinds of benefit.

What are the four? First, one constantly gives rise to this thought: "I shall gather in sentient beings and provide them with benefit and happiness; since they have now attained these for themselves, I feel joy.
Second, all one's wealth and possessions cannot be plundered by kings, calamities, water, fire, bandits, enemies, or relatives.
Third, wherever he is born, he will be fully endowed with wealth, treasures, and sons; even kings will not feel jealousy toward him, much less others.
Fourth, his accumulated resources and expenditures shall both be inexhaustible.
These are called the four.
Śāriputra, it is by accomplishing these four dharmas that a bodhisattva is perfected.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes five dharmas, they cause their vows not to regress and purify the Buddha-fields. What are these five?
First, that bodhisattva approaches the teacher of the Dharma and asks him:
"By practicing what kind of conduct can one attain the pure adornment of a buddha-field?
Having heard this, he practices according to what was taught.

Second, because of their pure upholding of the precepts and the power of their vows, Bodhisattvas are born in the Buddha-lands. Having been born in those lands, they observe the various adornments and manifold precious requisites of that realm, as well as the subtle and wondrous characteristics of the great assemblies of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, and they show reverence and respect toward the Tathāgata.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!
What practices must a bodhisattva cultivate to attain the vast purification and adornment of a buddha-field?"
That Tathāgata, knowing that this bodhisattva’s aspirations and inclinations were exceptionally sublime, immediately proclaimed for him the accomplishment of such meritorious buddha-fields.
Having heard this, he practiced in accordance with the Dharma.
Third, a bodhisattva possesses both wisdom and practice; they should purify their wisdom and advance their practice.
What is the purification of wisdom?
It refers to being free from the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas regarding both the subjective perceiving mind and the objective perceived phenomena.
How does one progress?
It means practicing with certainty according to what has been heard, because of being free from non-practice.
Fourth, the bodhisattva skillfully knows that which has causes and knows the discourse on transcendence.

That which has a cause refers to improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), for it is the basis upon which the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) rely and serves as the cause of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

That which is called "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*) refers to correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*); because one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) regarding any phenomena, it constitutes renunciation.

Fifth, the bodhisattva thoroughly understands that both the essential nature of the Buddhas and the nature of their buddha-fields are merely names, and that these names are themselves quiescent; having understood this, they do not give rise to the conceptualization of "knowing."
These are called the five.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes six dharmas, they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will also be able to take possession of the most supreme buddha-fields in all worlds."
What are the six? First, this bodhisattva acts as a great donor, joyfully bestowing all his precious playthings and delightful objects without any stinginess or attachment.
Furthermore, he thinks:

"I shall practice great giving to fulfill the Great Vehicle; that is to say, when seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I will relinquish everything without attachment and fully accomplish the provisions for enlightenment."
"I would not give rise to regret even at the sacrifice of my own life, much less regarding property, wife, children,
and so forth. Śāriputra,
for what reason is the Tathāgata named "All-Knowing One" (Sarvajña)?
This means that when practicing the bodhisattva path, one relinquishes everything belonging to oneself; for this reason, once awakening (bodhi) is attained, one is called "Omniscient" (sarvajña).

Second, whether a bodhisattva is a householder or has left the home life, they would rather sacrifice their own body and life than ever break the precepts; thus, they dedicate this observance of the precepts together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Thus, maintaining the precepts, he experiences joy through self-awakening; delighting in the cultivation of the holy life, he dwells in peace and happiness day and night. He increases his efforts in seeking the Dharma and abides in correct practice, feeling weary of and fearful toward the three realms while yearning for liberation.
Although they perceive the way of transcendence, they look back with compassion upon sentient beings, thinking:
"As I suffer, so do they all; I shall take up this heavy burden and gather in sentient beings, establishing them in the state of nirvana and peace."

"Maintaining the precepts in this manner, when one experiences joy through self-awareness, one attains the mind of great compassion; furthermore, until one has attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not relinquish diligence, as if one's head were on fire."
Third, the bodhisattva dons the armor of patience; free from arrogance, they attain the power of great forbearance.
When encountering verbal abuse or physical assault, they perfect the mind of patience and give rise to no resentment.

Even if there were a staff as large as Mount Sumeru, and someone were to hold it and constantly strike and revile one throughout billions of kalpas, one would still not give rise to a heart of resentment.
Why is this? [Because one thinks:
"Those sentient beings have not yet followed the Buddha’s teachings, whereas I am now about to follow the Buddha and practice.
For this reason, when one receives beating or abuse from them, it is able to increase one's great compassion accordingly.
"I shall don the armor of the great vow for the sake of all sentient beings to gather them in, enabling them to attain liberation and enter nirvana.
Therefore, I should not harbor anger or resentment now."
When a bodhisattva dwells correctly in such patience, they achieve ten kinds of perfections.
What are these ten? First, noble lineage;

second, wealth and property; third, retinue; fourth, physical appearance; fifth, skillful relinquishment; sixth, virtuous friends; seventh, hearing the true Dharma; eighth, practicing according to the teachings; ninth, seeing the Buddhas at the time of death; and tenth, having seen the Buddhas, giving rise to pure faith.
These are the ten kinds of perfection of merit.
Fourth, the bodhisattva, desiring to accomplish wholesome dharmas, initiates diligence through firm self-exhortation.

Furthermore, for the sake of each and every sentient being, throughout the entirety of the future until the end of saṃsāra, they practice various forms of diligent conduct in succession without weariness. Through this work of self-exhortation and this great compassion for all sentient beings, they circulate within saṃsāra for that duration of time without abandoning sentient beings.

Śāriputra! If there were a bodhisattva who, in every moment of thought, offered to the Tathāgatas the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions, continuing this practice without interruption until the end of the future;

and if there were another bodhisattva who, having given rise to the mind of great compassion and donned the armor of diligence, [practiced accordingly]—the merit of the latter would be far greater than that of the former.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva is endowed with this diligence, they attain ten kinds of superior aspirations and dharmas of joy. What are these ten?

First, distancing oneself from the conduct of the foolish; second, embracing the conduct of the Buddhas; third, perceiving the faults of birth and death; fourth, abiding in a mind of great compassion; fifth, not retreating from one's original vows; sixth, having few illnesses; seventh, conforming to the teachings of all Buddhas; eighth, attenuating lust, anger, and delusion; ninth, understanding the definitive meaning according to the texts; and tenth, achieving perfection in practice.
These are called the ten.
Fifth, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
"The minds of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are always in meditative concentration and have never lost mindfulness; I should follow the conduct of the Buddhas."

If the mind is distracted, one will ultimately be unable to realize the sphere of the Buddha’s activity; therefore, one should abandon all mental attachments, as well as all gain, honor, villages, cities, food, drink, means of subsistence, and kinsmen. Yet, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one does not abandon them; instead, one delights in dwelling in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) in a place of tranquility, wandering alone without companion like the single horn of a rhinoceros.

Having dwelt in a place of stillness, one gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness; first pervading one direction, it gradually extends to the ten directions until it encompasses all sentient beings. Once the mind of loving-kindness has pervaded them, one attains entry into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

"Śāriputra! If there were a lay bodhisattva who, with all manner of articles of pleasure, made offerings to as many Buddhas and their assemblies of bhikṣus as there are grains of sand in the Ganges for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

and if there were a renunciant bodhisattva who, having taken seven steps toward a forest hermitage in a state of quietude, the merit of this latter would far exceed that of the former, because they are able to swiftly attain great Bodhi."
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva who delights in dwelling in tranquility and enters meditative concentration attains ten kinds of meritorious benefits. What are these ten?

First, attaining mindfulness; second, attaining wisdom; third, practicing cultivation; fourth, possessing swift eloquence; fifth, attaining dhāraṇī; sixth, skillfully knowing the arising of phenomena; seventh, skillfully knowing the cessation of phenomena; eighth, being without transgression regarding the aggregate of ethical discipline; ninth, receiving offerings from the devas; and tenth, not coveting the excellence of others.
These are called the ten.
Sixth, the bodhisattva skillfully understands that wisdom is the outflow [of the path], thinking:
"Wisdom has ethical discipline as its foremost; the increase of pure dharmas has wisdom as its foremost. Therefore, a bodhisattva should study wisdom."

He thoroughly studied all that is difficult to perform and difficult to accomplish in this world—all crafts and all medical arts; yet, with this wisdom, he was unable to realize or enter into the tranquility of detachment, nor could he proceed toward Bodhi, nor toward the state of a śramaṇa, nor toward that of a brāhmaṇa, nor toward nirvāṇa.
"Therefore, I should now further seek everywhere for the skillful means of the medicine of the Dharma, so that through such wisdom I may attain ultimate quiescence.
Thus, that bodhisattva seeks the root of all dharmas and does not perceive even the slightest dharma capable of giving rise to another dharma.

Because they do not perceive [anything], they abide in quiescence; because they abide in quiescence, they are free from feverish affliction; being free from feverish affliction, they thoroughly understand birth and death, and thus take on rebirth for the sake of sentient beings in order to cause all sentient beings to eliminate suffering.
These are called the six.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes seven dharmas, their vows do not regress and they purify the Buddha-fields."
What are the seven?
First, giving by relinquishing all of one's own possessions because nothing can be apprehended.
Second, maintaining precepts without deficiency or transgression because of non-attachment to those precepts.
Third is the practice of patience and gentleness, because sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Fourth is the arousal of diligence, because body and mind cannot be apprehended.
Fifth is the accomplishment of meditative concentration, because one does not abide in concentration.
Sixth is the perfection of wisdom, because it is free from conceptual discrimination.
Seventh is the recollection of all Buddhas, because it is far removed from signs.
These are called the seven.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, their vow will not regress and they will adorn and purify a buddha-field.
What are these eight?

First, not delighting in nirvāṇa; second, giving ornaments and finery; third, having a vast mind; fourth, honoring and respecting the Dharma teacher; fifth, not practicing wrong livelihood; sixth, bestowing gifts with equanimity; seventh, not being self-conceited; eighth, not treating others with contempt.
These are called the eight.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes nine dharmas, their vows will not regress and they will adorn and purify buddha-fields."

What are the nine? First, possessing restraint of the body; second, possessing restraint of speech; third, possessing restraint of the mind; fourth, extinguishing all covetousness; fifth, extinguishing all ill-will; sixth, extinguishing all delusion; seventh, not practicing deception; eighth, being a steadfast friend; ninth, not treating spiritual friends with contempt.
These are called the nine. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will cause their vows not to regress and will adorn and purify Buddha-fields."
What are the ten? First, upon hearing of the sufferings of the hells, one gives rise only to great compassion and does not give rise to fear.
Second, upon hearing of the sufferings of animals, one gives rise only to great compassion and does not give rise to fear.
Third, upon hearing of the sufferings of the hungry ghosts, they give rise only to great compassion and do not experience fear.
Fourth, upon hearing of the decline and afflictions of the devas, they give rise only to great compassion and do not experience fear.
Fifth, upon hearing of famine, bandits, enemies, or killings among human beings, he gives rise only to great compassion and does not experience fear.
Sixth, the bodhisattva forms this thought:
"At this time, I shall arouse diligence; until I have attained a pure buddha-field, I will never be indolent."
"Seventh: 'May food and clothing in my buddha-field be obtained simply by thinking of them.
Eighth: 'May the lifespans of all sentient beings in my buddha-field be immeasurable.'"
"Ninth, 'In my buddha-field, all sentient beings shall be free from the notions of "self" and "other.
Tenth, 'All sentient beings in my buddha-field shall resolutely advance toward unsurpassed bodhi.'"
These are called the ten.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva takes beautiful flowers and goes to the presence of the Tathāgata or to a Buddha-stūpa to perform an offering, they make this aspiration, saying:
"These exquisite flowers possess such superior color and fragrance that all who see them rejoice.
When I attain Buddhahood, may my buddha-field be strewn everywhere with various such wonderful flowers, and may it be adorned on all sides by trees made of many jewels."

"Furthermore, when offering powdered incense, ointments, clothing, food and drink, precious canopies, banners and streamers, and treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and pearls, one should likewise dedicate these merits toward the adornment of the Buddha-field."
Because that bodhisattva abides in the precepts, whatever his heart desires is all accomplished.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva does not seek his own pleasure but rejoices in others obtaining pleasure; therefore, when that bodhisattva attains bodhi, all sentient beings within his buddha-field are fully endowed with exclusive happiness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva should always universally embrace the ten paths of wholesome action and dedicate them all toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For this reason, when that bodhisattva attains awakening, all sentient beings within that buddha-field will, upon their first birth, be endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action as well as the wisdom of renunciation."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, wherever a bodhisattva goes, they exhort all sentient beings to aspire toward unexcelled bodhi; they praise only the Buddha-vehicle and do not speak of the two vehicles or the shared dharmas."

Therefore, when that Bodhisattva attains enlightenment, all sentient beings within that Buddha-field will certainly attain unsurpassed enlightenment; they shall forever be free from the states of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and the land shall be filled with immeasurable Bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva never obstructs the gains and offerings of others; seeing others receive benefit, they always give rise to joy.

Therefore, when that bodhisattva attains bodhi, all sentient beings within that buddha-field will have their requisites for sustenance constantly and without interruption, and they will fully obtain the great light of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva sees a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who has committed an offense, he shall never expose it, but shall instead abide solely within the True Dharma."
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment, there shall be no mention whatsoever of faults within that Buddha-field.
Why is this? Because all those in the great assembly have attained the dharma of purity free from fault.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva delights in the Dharma and seeks the Dharma without giving rise to feverish distress; they dwell correctly in the practice of the Dharma as it has been heard.

Therefore, when that bodhisattva attains awakening, the beings born within that buddha-field who seek the Dharma and delight in the Dharma shall all be free from feverish distress, practicing in accordance with the Dharma as it has been heard."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva makes offerings to a Buddha stūpa with various musical instruments such as stringed lutes, songs, drums, and wind instruments, they dedicate these roots of goodness toward the adornment of the merits of a Buddha-field."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva attains enlightenment, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments in that buddha-field will resound spontaneously without being struck.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have lost mindfulness, he causes them to attain right mindfulness."
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment, he causes his disciples to obtain the food of dhyāna-joy.
Śāriputra, such are the merits of this Buddha-field; even if one were to speak for an eon or more than an eon with the eloquence of a Tathāgata, one could not exhaustively describe them.

Śāriputra! However, I now provide this brief exposition according to the inclinations of these bodhisattvas; those of superior resolve who hear it and apply themselves toward it shall attain the perfection of the merits of a buddha-field.
“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas, they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all the Buddha-fields they seek shall be fully realized.”
What are the three?
First, the excellence of the great vow; second, abiding in heedfulness; and third, initiating correct practice in accordance with the Dharma as it has been heard.
"These are called the three.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata has most wonderfully and skillfully expounded this Dharma.

World-Honored One, by abiding in heedfulness, you have attained the factors of enlightenment; by abiding in practice, you have attained great bodhi; and by abiding in supreme vows, you have accomplished the meritorious adornments of the Buddha-field.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"So it is, so it is, just as you have said.
Just as I, in the past, accomplished a buddha-field through the power of great vows, and attained awakening because of non-negligence."

Śāriputra! If one merely engages in verbal discourse while dwelling in negligence and fails to practice, such a person cannot even reach the stage of a śrāvaka, let alone attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Therefore, if a bodhisattva wishes to know for themselves that they are a true bodhisattva, they should train in accordance with how a bodhisattva is to train.
At that time, forty thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and said with one voice:
"We shall train according to the bodhisattva precepts as taught by the Buddha; we shall dwell in heedfulness, accomplish our practice, fulfill our great vows, and purify the buddha-fields."
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance.
Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and condition do you manifest this smile?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Do you see these sons of good family making the lion’s roar?"
Śāriputra said, “Indeed, I have seen it.
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! After hundreds of thousands of kalpas, these sons of good family will each attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in different lands, all sharing the same name, Praṇidhāna-vyūha (Adorned by Vows). They will be just like the future Buddha Siṃha and others; their lands will be as pure as the land of Amitāyus, with the sole exception of the lifespan.”
Śāriputra asked, “What is the lifespan of those Tathāgatas?
The Buddha said:
“Each of those Buddhas has a lifespan of ten kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
“This Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva is constantly praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; how long will it be before he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
"What will the buddha-field he attains be like?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
“You should ask Mañjuśrī yourself. Then Siṃhavikrama asked Mañjuśrī,
“Virtuous one, when will you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
He replied: "Good son!
Why do you not ask me whether I am proceeding toward enlightenment, but instead ask me whether I have attained enlightenment?"
"Why is this? I do not even incline toward awakening, much less shall I attain it. He asked:
“Mañjuśrī! Do you not, O Noble One, proceed toward enlightenment for the sake of benefiting sentient beings? He replied:
"No. Why is this? Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended."
If sentient beings were existent, one could strive for enlightenment for their benefit;
however, since sentient beings, life-span, and the *pudgala* are all non-existent, I now neither strive for enlightenment nor do I regress from it.
Siṃhavikrama said: "Mañjuśrī!
Do you, O Noble One, proceed toward the dharmas of all Buddhas?"
He replied, "No, good son!"
All dharmas tend toward the Buddha-dharma. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are without outflows, without fetters, formless, and signless; as they tend toward the Buddha and as they are like tending toward the Buddha, so too are all dharmas.
"Good son! Regarding your question concerning the approach to the Buddha-dharma, I shall now question you; answer according to your own understanding.
What do you think?"
Is it for the sake of form that you seek awakening?

Is it for the sake of the intrinsic nature of form, the suchness of form, the self-essence of form, the emptiness of form, the detachment of form, or the dharma-nature of form that you seek awakening?
"Good son! What do you think?
Is it by means of form that one attains bodhi, or even by means of the dharma-nature of form that one attains bodhi?"
He replied, “No, Mañjuśrī!”
Form does not seek awakening, nor does the dharma-nature of form seek awakening.
Form does not attain awakening, nor does the dharma-nature of form attain awakening.
Mañjuśrī said: "What do you think?
Is it by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that one seeks awakening, or even by means of the dharma-nature of consciousness that one seeks awakening?"
"Is it by cognizing bodhi, or even by cognizing the dharma-nature, that one attains bodhi? He replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not seek awakening; even the dharma-nature of consciousness does not seek awakening.
Consciousness does not attain awakening; even the dharma-nature of consciousness does not attain awakening.
Mañjuśrī said: "What do you think?
Apart from the five aggregates, is there a self or what belongs to a self?"
He replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"So it is, so it is, son of good family!
By what further dharma could one seek awakening or attain awakening?"
Siṃhavikrama said: “Mañjuśrī! What you have spoken is sincerely believed by all;
yet now you say that one neither seeks nor attains bodhi. Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved upon enlightenment will surely give rise to alarm and fear upon hearing these words.”
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son! All dharmas are devoid of fear; even within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), there is no fear."

The Tathāgata expounds the Dharma for those who are without fear; if one is fearful, they will give rise to revulsion; if revulsion arises, they will become free from desire; if they are free from desire, they will attain liberation; if they are liberated, there is no awakening (*bodhi*); if there is no awakening, there is no abiding; if there is no abiding, there is no going; if there is no going, there is no coming, and thus there is no seeking or aspiration; if there is no seeking or aspiration, there is no regression; and if there is no regression, that is itself regression.
From what phenomena does one regress?

It refers to the attachment to a self, a sentient being, a life-span, or a person (pudgala), as well as all conceptualizations that grasp at signs of either annihilationism or eternalism—from these one entirely regresses.
If he were to regress, he would not regress.
From what dharma would he not regress?
It is from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the reality-limit, and all the Buddha-dharmas that he does not regress.

What is meant by the Buddha-dharma? It refers to that which is neither departing nor clinging, and is without any object of focus; it has no entering and no exiting, and there is nothing therein to be practiced. It cannot be expressed, existing only as a name; it is empty and without arising. It is without going and without coming, without defilement and without purity, without dust and free from dust, without self and without discrimination, without combination and without grasping. To be equal and without contradiction—this is the Buddha-dharma.
Good son! These dharmas of the Buddhas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. Why is this?
Because all Buddha-dharmas have no place of arising,
if a newly resolved bodhisattva, upon hearing this teaching, should experience alarm or fear, they will swiftly attain bodhi.
If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination and thinks thus:
"The bodhi that we have now accomplished is attained by following the arousal of the mind and abiding in manifest realization;
if one does not arouse the mind, one will ultimately never attain it."

Because such conceptual discriminations do not arise at all, both awakening and the mind are unattainable; because they are unattainable, there is no conceptual discrimination; and if there is no conceptual discrimination, there is no manifest realization.
Why is this? Because the cause for manifest realization cannot be apprehended. Good son!
"What do you think? Can space attain bodhi? He replied:
"No," he replied. He spoke again: "Good son!
“Does the Tathāgata not realize that all phenomena are identical to empty space?
He replied, “So it is, so it is.”
He further said:
"Good son! Just as space is, so too is bodhi."
As is awakening, so too is space.
Space and awakening are non-dual and without distinction.
If a bodhisattva knows this equality, then there is neither knowing nor not-knowing, and neither seeing nor not-seeing.

When this Dharma was being taught, fourteen thousand bhikṣus were completely freed from all outflows (āsrava), their minds attaining liberation; twelve nayutas of bhikṣus became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; ninety-six thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta; and fifty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Virtuous One, how long has it been since you first resolved to attain bodhicitta?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Stop, son of good family!"
Do not give rise to deluded thoughts.
If anyone, regarding the dharma of non-arising, should speak these words:
"I have resolved to attain bodhicitta."
"To say, 'I am practicing the bodhisattva conduct,' is a great false view. Good son!..."
"I do not perceive any mind that sets out toward bodhi.
Because I do not perceive either the mind or bodhi, there is therefore no setting out. Siṃhavikrama said:
“Mañjuśrī! What is the meaning of the phrase ‘not perceiving the mind at all’? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! This total non-seeing is what is called ‘equality.
He asked again:
“How is it said to be equal? He replied: “Good son!
Thus, because all various natures are non-existent through such equality, it is said that all those phenomena are of one flavor.

This "teaching of one flavor" means that they are detached; they are neither defiled nor pure, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither arising nor ceasing, without self and without what is received, and neither grasped nor abandoned.
When teaching the Dharma in this way, one does not think "I am speaking" nor does one engage in discrimination.
Son of good family!
To understand and practice within this equal Dharma is called "equality."
Furthermore, son of good family!

If a bodhisattva enters this equality, they do not perceive any various realms as being either one or many. Within equality, they do not perceive equality; within contradiction, they do not perceive contradiction, because their primordial nature is pure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Mañjuśrī is unwilling to speak for himself regarding how long it has been since he first resolved his mind upon enlightenment.”
"This great assembly all desires to hear it.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
Mañjuśrī, this profound patience is such that within this profound patience, both awakening and the mind are unapprehendable; because they are unapprehendable, they are not spoken of.
Nevertheless, son of good family!
I shall now speak of how long it has been since Mañjuśrī first resolved his mind [on enlightenment].
Son of good family!

In the distant past, more than seventy million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vāsava-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
To the east, passing from here through seventy-two nayutas of buddha-fields, there is a world named Unborn; therein, the Tathāgata Thunderous Sound preaches the Dharma.
The assembly of śrāvakas numbered eighty-four billion nayutas, and the assembly of bodhisattvas was twice that number. Good son!

At that time there was a king named Samantacchadana (Universal Canopy), who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents; he governed through the True Dharma and was a Wheel-Turning King.

For eighty-four thousand years, he reverently made offerings to the Tathāgata Thunder Sound and the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, providing them with clothing, food and drink, palaces, towers, and pavilions, as well as servants and attendants, each of which was exquisite and sublime.
Among the king’s kinsmen, palace ladies, princes, and ministers, they devoted themselves solely to making offerings and did nothing else; though many years passed, they never grew weary.
After this had passed, the king remained alone in a quiet place and reflected:
"I have now accumulated vast roots of goodness, yet I have not yet determined where they should be dedicated; shall I seek to become Śakra, Mahābrahmā, or a Cakravartin King?"
"Is it for the sake of seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha?
Having had this thought, the devas in the sky addressed him, saying: "Great King!
Do not give rise to such narrow and inferior thoughts. Why is this?
The merit accumulated by the King is vast; he ought to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son! At that time, having heard these words, King Universal Cover (Samantacchadana) thought with joy:
'I am now certain not to regress from this.'"
"Why is this? The deva knew my thoughts and has come to inform me.
"O son of good family!"

At that time, the king, together with a great assembly of eighty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, went to the place where the Buddha Thunderous Sound was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and with his body bent in reverence and palms joined toward the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
“I now ask the Most Victorious One; I pray that you will speak for me.”
How may one achieve accomplishment as the most supreme among men,
the refuge of the world? Although I have made extensive offerings,
with a mind that was not yet resolved, I did not know where to dedicate [the merit].
Having already cultivated vast merit, toward what should it be dedicated?
Is it for the sake of seeking the station of Brahmā, or that of Śakra or a Cakravartin king;
or is it for the sake of seeking the state of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha?
When I gave rise to this thought, a deity in the sky addressed me:
"Great King, do not give way to such a narrow and inferior resolve for dedication;
for the sake of all sentient beings, you should instead arouse vast aspirations."
For the sake of benefiting the world, one should resolve to attain bodhicitta.
I now entreat the World-Honored One, the Sovereign of the Dharma:
may you explain bodhicitta and the skillful means for its arousal.
"Having generated the bodhicitta, one shall become like a Muni.
I pray only that the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings will fully expound this for me.
At that time, the Tathāgata Thunder-Voice spoke in verse to King Universal-Cover:
“Great King, listen attentively; I shall explain this in due order.
All phenomena arising from causes and conditions proceed according to one’s faculties, desires, and conduct;
whatever one’s aspirations may be, such is the retribution one obtains.”
In the past, I too gave rise to the bodhicitta;
for the sake of all sentient beings, I vowed to bring about their benefit.
Just as I have made this vow, and just as I originally resolved my mind, so shall it be.
Having attained non-retrogression from enlightenment, may your aspirations be swiftly fulfilled.
Great King, you should remain firm and cultivate all practices;
thus you shall attain the vast, unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha.

At that time, King Samantacchadana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented experience. Before the assembled multitude, he let out a great lion’s roar and spoke in verse:
“Now, before this entire assembly, I give rise to the mind of great bodhicitta.”
For the sake of each and every sentient being, I vow to endure immeasurable births and deaths until the end of the future, bringing great benefit to all,
fully cultivating the bodhisattva practices, and rescuing all beings from their suffering.
From this day forth, if I violate my vow, giving rise to a mind of greed and desire,
or to stinginess, envy, resentment, and hatred, then I shall have deceived the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, from this day forth, until I attain Bodhi,
One should always learn from the Buddhas, practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and following the pure precepts and discipline, remaining far removed from all faults.
Furthermore, regarding enlightenment, I do not wish to realize it too quickly.
Throughout the limits of the future, may I extensively benefit all living beings and purify the buddha-fields, immeasurable and inconceivable;
may my name be heard everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
I now bestow this prediction upon myself: I shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
With a resolve for supreme purity, I am firm and have no doubt in this.
I shall purify my three karmas and never allow any evils to arise.
By this truth, may I become a Buddha, the Honored One among men.
If this mind is true, let the earth tremble in six ways;
if my words are sincere and free from falsehood, [may this be so].
May music play spontaneously in the midst of the void.
If I am free from deceit and crookedness, as well as from a heart of resentment,
by virtue of this truth, may mandārava flowers rain down.

When King Universal Cover had spoken these verses, because his mind was sincere and true, billions of lands in the ten directions shook in six ways; celestial music resounded in the void, and mandārava flowers rained down.
At that time, the twenty billion sentient beings who followed the king were all filled with great joy and congratulated themselves, saying:
"We shall attain the most supreme bodhi."
"He then followed that king’s example and resolved to attain bodhicitta.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"At that time, was King Universal Cover anyone else?"
This is none other than the present Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.

In the past, after the passing of seventy million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he first resolved his mind upon Bodhi. Subsequently, after the passing of sixty-four *Ganges*-sands of kalpas, he attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). He was able to fulfill the ten stages of a bodhisattva and the ten powers of a Tathāgata; all the dharmas of the Buddha-ground were completely perfected, yet he never gave rise to a single thought, thinking:
"I shall become a Buddha."

"Good son! At that time, the twenty billion sentient beings who followed that king to the presence of Thunder-Sound Buddha and resolved their minds on Bodhi did so entirely through the exhortation of Mañjuśrī, who led them into the practices of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. They have all now realized Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, turned the Great Wheel of Dharma, performed the work of a Buddha, and entered Parinirvāṇa."
Mañjuśrī made offerings to all those Tathāgatas and likewise upheld and protected all their Buddha-dharmas.
There was only one Buddha named Dharanimdhara-giri, located forty Ganges-sands of world-systems below here; that Buddha’s world is called Dharanimdhara.
There are also countless assemblies of śrāvakas, and the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and continues to the present day.
When this account of Mañjuśrī’s past causes and conditions was spoken, seven thousand beings among the assembly resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Fifty-nine;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The Fifteenth Assembly: The Prediction for Mañjuśrī, Part Three.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Virtuous One, you have already fulfilled the ten stages and the ten powers of a Tathāgata; all the Buddha-dharmas are entirely perfected. For what reason do you not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son, there is no such thing as having already perfected all the Buddha-dharmas and then further realizing bodhi."
"Why is this? Because it has already been perfected, it should not be realized again. Siṃhavikrama said:
“How does one bring the qualities of a Buddha to fulfillment? He replied:

“The fulfillment of the qualities of a Buddha is like the fulfillment of suchness; the fulfillment of suchness is like the fulfillment of space. Thus, the qualities of a Buddha, suchness, and space are not two.”

"Good son! Regarding what you have asked about how to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas: just as there is the fulfillment of form up to the fulfillment of consciousness, so too is the fulfillment of the Buddha-dharmas."
Siṃhavikrāmin asked, "What is the perfection of form and so forth? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! What do you think?
Is the form that you perceive permanent?”
"Is this impermanent? He replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son, if a phenomenon is neither permanent nor impermanent, could it have increase or decrease?"
He replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
“Good son! If a phenomenon neither increases nor decreases, it is called ‘perfection. What is perfection?
If one cannot thoroughly understand all phenomena, then conceptual discrimination arises; if one can thoroughly understand them, there is no conceptual discrimination.
If there is no conceptual discrimination, there is neither increase nor decrease; if there is neither increase nor decrease, this is equanimity.
Therefore, noble son!
If one perceives the equality of form, that is the perfection of form; the same applies to the perfection of feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and all phenomena.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminirghoṣa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:

“Virtuous One, since you attained the patience of dharmas (kṣānti), not a single thought-moment has arisen in you wishing to achieve perfect enlightenment; why then do you now exhort others to turn toward bodhi?”
Mañjuśrī said: "I have never actually exhorted a single sentient being to aspire toward bodhi. Why is this?"
Because sentient beings do not exist and because the nature of sentient beings is inherently detached;
if sentient beings could be apprehended, one would cause them to turn toward bodhi, but since they cannot be apprehended, there is nothing to exhort.
Why is this? Because it is equality and non-discrimination; one does not seek equality by means of equality, nor is there anything that arises.
Therefore, it is constantly said: one should contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as having no place from which they come and no place to which they go; this is called equality.
This is the emptiness of nature; within the emptiness of nature, there is nothing to be sought.
Good son! Regarding your question as to whether, since I attained patience (*kṣānti*), there has ever been a single thought-moment that "I shall attain bodhi"—good son!
"Do you see that mind?
Is it by means of this mind that one attains bodhi? Siṃhavikrama replied:
"No, Mañjuśrī! Why is that? Because..."
Because the mind is not form and is thus invisible, bodhi is likewise; it is merely a name and a concept.
Whether it be the name "mind" or the name "bodhi," both are non-existent.
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son! As for your statement that you do not give rise to even a single thought of attaining bodhi, this was spoken with intentional meaning."
Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally without arising, it is therefore unarisen.
Since there is no arising, what could be attained and what could be realized?
Siṃhavikrama asked, "What is meant by 'equanimous realization and entry'? He replied:
"To be without attachment toward any phenomena is called 'equal realization.

As for what is termed 'entering realization,' even that subtle wisdom neither arises nor ceases; it is no different from *tathatā* (suchness) and is beyond all conceptual differentiation—this is called entering realization."
If a practitioner of right view finds not a single dharma to be obtained within equality, and being free from manifold natures, does not cling even to the one, this is called "realization and entry."

If one personally realizes that all phenomena are signless, clearly understanding that their characteristic is precisely "signlessness," and yet remains without attachment even to body and mind, this is called the perfect realization and entry.
Siṃhavikrāṇḍa asked: "What is meant by 'attainment'? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! It is by means of worldly convention that it is called ‘attainment’; that which is attained by the noble ones cannot be expressed in words. Why is this?
Dharmas have no basis, for they are beyond verbal expression.
Furthermore, son of good family,
taking non-attainment as attainment— neither attainment nor non-attainment— is what is called "attainment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent!”
“I pray that you will describe the Buddha-field attained by Mañjuśrī. The Buddha said, “Good son!
"You should ask Mañjuśrī yourself.
Then that bodhisattva addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "Virtuous one,
what kind of meritorious adornments of a buddha-field will you attain?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son! If I were seeking bodhi, you may ask about the buddha-field that would be attained."
Siṃhavikrāmin said: "Virtuous one, do you not seek awakening? Mañjuśrī replied:

"No, it is not so. Why is that? If there is something sought, there is attachment; if there is attachment, there is craving; if there is craving, there is birth; if there is birth, there is desire; and if there is desire, one will ultimately never find liberation from within it."
Good son! For this reason, I do not seek bodhi. Why is that?
Because bodhi is unattainable;
since it is unattainable, one does not seek it. Good son!
However, as for your question regarding which Buddha-field you shall attain, I am unable to say.
Why is this? To speak of the merits and adornments of one’s own Buddha-field before the Tathāgata, the Omniscient One, would constitute a Bodhisattva praising his own virtues.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“You may now speak for yourself regarding what kind of vows you have used to adorn this buddha-field, so that when all bodhisattvas hear them, they will become determined to fulfill these very vows.”
Then Mañjuśrī, having received the instruction of the Tathāgata, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall now, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, proclaim this for you.
All those who seek great enlightenment should listen with focused attention; having heard this vow, they should study it according to reality so as to bring it to fulfillment.
When Mañjuśrī touched his right knee to the ground, the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shook in six ways.
Then Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas past, I have made this vow:

‘If, among all the Tathāgatas in the infinite and boundless Buddha-fields of the ten directions whom I behold with my unimpeded divine eye, there are any whom I have not inspired to resolve upon bodhicitta through exhortation and instruction, nor taught and admonished to cultivate giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, up to and including attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—then I shall never realize bodhi myself.’”
"I must fulfill this vow of mine before I can realize unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bodhisattvas within that assembly all had this thought:
"How many Tathāgatas does Mañjuśrī perceive with his unimpeded divine eye?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara, saying: "Good son!
Suppose this trichiliocosm were ground into fine dust; what do you think?
Could one calculate and know the number of these particles?
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

Mañjuśrī possesses unimpeded divine vision; he sees immeasurable Buddhas in the eastern direction, exceeding even this number, and it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.”
Then Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have this vow: that I shall take as many buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges and make them a single buddha-field, adorned with the intermingling of immeasurable wonderful jewels; if it is not so, I shall never realize unsurpassed bodhi.”
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I have another aspiration: that within my buddha-field there shall be a bodhi tree equal in size to ten great trichiliocosms, and that the radiance of that tree shall pervade this entire buddha-field.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I have another vow: once I have sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* up until my entry into *nirvāṇa*, I shall not rise from this seat during that interval; yet, by means of emanations, I shall pervade the immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, expounding the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I have another vow: that in my land there shall be no name for "woman," but only a multitude of bodhisattvas who are free from the defilements of affliction and possess pure brahmacarya; at the moment of birth, they shall suddenly appear seated in the full lotus posture with the *kāṣāya* robe already upon their bodies.

In this manner, bodhisattvas fill that buddha-field, such that even the names "śrāvaka" and "pratyekabuddha" do not exist, except for those emanated by the Tathāgata who travel to the ten directions to preach the Dharma of the three vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagajagarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What shall be the name of Mañjuśrī when he attains Buddhahood in the future?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! When this Mañjuśrī attains Buddhahood, his name shall be Samantadarśin.”
For what reason is he named "Universal Vision"?
Because that Tathāgata causes him to be seen everywhere throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields in the ten directions.
If any sentient beings see that Buddha, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Although the Tathāgata Samantadarśin has not yet attained Buddhahood, those who hear his name—both during my present lifetime and after my parinirvāṇa—will likewise all certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, with the sole exception of those who have already entered the stage of "separation from birth" (*avivartika*) and those of narrow and inferior minds.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have another vow: just as in the land of Amitābha Buddha, where the Dharma-joy serves as food, so too in my land, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the thought of eating, a hundred flavors shall immediately fill their bowl and appear in their right hand; thereupon, they shall think thus:”
