"If I have not yet made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, nor bestowed gifts upon impoverished and suffering sentient beings, such as those of the preta realm, to satisfy them, I must certainly not eat myself."

When he formed this thought, he attained the five supernormal powers and traveled unimpeded through the air to immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-fields in the ten directions. There, he offered food to the Tathāgatas and their assemblies of śrāvakas, and he also provided for all beings who were poor and suffering. Furthermore, he preached the Dharma for them so that they might be freed from craving and thirst, and in a single moment of thought, he returned to his original location.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I have another vow: when the bodhisattvas in my land are first born, whatever clothing they require shall emerge from their hands at will as various kinds of precious garments—fresh, clean, fitting their bodies, and appropriate for the robes of śramaṇas.
He then thought: "If I have not yet made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, I should not use this for myself.

In a single moment of thought, he traveled to immeasurable Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions; having offered these robes and jewels to all the Buddhas, he returned to his original location before finally using them himself.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I have another vow: that whatever wealth and requisites are obtained by the assembly of bodhisattvas within my buddha-field must first be shared and bestowed upon all Buddhas and śrāvakas; only after making universal offerings to them shall they themselves enjoy them.

Furthermore, within my buddha-field, one is far removed from the eight difficulties and unwholesome dharmas; since there are no faults, there are also no prohibitions or precepts, nor are there any sufferings or unpleasant things.
Then Siṃhavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of that buddha-field?”
The Buddha said:
"That land is named 'Pure and Perfect Accumulation of Wishes'. Siṃhavikrama said:
“World-Honored One!
In which direction does that buddha-world lie?
The Buddha said:
"It is in the southern direction; this Sahā world shall likewise be situated within that Buddha-field.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have another vow: my Buddha-field shall be composed of an accumulation of immeasurable wonderful jewels, further adorned with the interspersed ornamentation of immeasurable mani-jewels."
This maṇi jewel has never before existed within the worlds of the ten directions and is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Even if one were to speak for billions of years, one could not exhaustively describe the names of such jewels.

According to the inclinations of the bodhisattvas who wish to see that land as having gold for its substance, they see it as gold; those who wish to see it as having silver for its substance see it as silver; yet, the appearance of gold is never diminished.
They joyfully behold immeasurable jewels such as crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, and red pearls; each sees according to their own inclination, and none obstructs another.
Likewise, regarding the substance of sandalwood, agarwood, and even red sandalwood, it is the same: each sees according to what they delight in seeing.

Furthermore, in that land, things are not illuminated by the light of the sun, moon, mani-jewels, fire, or stars; rather, those bodhisattvas all illuminate billions of nayutas of lands with the radiance of their own bodies.

Furthermore, in that land, the blossoming of flowers constitutes day and the closing of flowers constitutes night; these follow the seasons as desired by the bodhisattvas, yet there is neither cold nor heat, nor old age, sickness, or death.

If bodhisattvas, according to their own inclinations, desire to realize awakening, they immediately proceed to other realms, where they exhaust their lifespan in Tuṣita Heaven, descend to be born, and realize awakening.
In this buddha-field there is no nirvana.

Although hundreds of thousands of kinds of music do not manifest their forms in the void, their sounds are heard; these instruments do not produce sounds that accord with craving and attachment, but rather produce the sounds of the perfections, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as the sounds of the dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Whatever sublime dharmas the bodhisattvas understand, they hear them all.

Furthermore, if bodhisattvas wish to see the Buddha, wherever they may go—whether walking, sitting, or standing—they shall behold the Tathāgata Samantadarśin seated at the Bodhi tree as soon as they bring him to mind.

"If bodhisattvas have doubts regarding the Dharma, merely by seeing that Buddha, their nets of doubt are severed and they fully comprehend the meaning of the Dharma without waiting for an explanation.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas in the assembly spoke with one voice, saying:
"If anyone should hear the name of the Buddha Universal Vision, that person will obtain the most supreme and beneficial merit; how much more so for those who are born in that Buddha-field!"
If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate of Mañjuśrī’s prophecy, as well as those who hear the name of Mañjuśrī, they are said to have beheld all the Buddhas face-to-face.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.
O sons of good family!

If there were one who upholds the names of hundreds of billions of Buddhas, and another who recites the name of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the latter would possess greater merit than the former; how much more so for one who recites the name of the Buddha Samantadarśin?
Why is this? The benefit to sentient beings achieved by those hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddhas does not equal the benefit performed by Mañjuśrī in a single eon.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others within the assembly, cried out with one voice:
“Homage to the Youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī!”
"Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantadarśin!

Upon these words being spoken, eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* of sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable sentient beings brought their roots of goodness to maturity, attaining non-retrogression within the three vehicles.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have another vow: may all the meritorious adornments of the buddha-fields belonging to the immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, whom I have seen, be placed entirely within my own single buddha-field—excepting only those of the two vehicles and the five corruptions."
"Bhagavān! If I were to describe myself the various adornments and merits of my buddha-field, I could not exhaust them even in kalpas exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
As for my vows, only the Buddha can know them."
The Buddha said: "So it is, Mañjuśrī!"
"The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are without limit or obstruction throughout the three periods of time.
At that time, there were bodhisattvas in the assembly who thought to themselves:
"Is the merit and adornment of the Buddha-field attained by Mañjuśrī equal to that of Amitābha Buddha’s field?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that bodhisattva, addressed Siṃhavikrāmin, saying: "Good son!
It is as if there were a person who divided a single hair into one hundred parts, and with one part of that hair, took a single drop of water from the great ocean."

This single drop of water is a metaphor for the adornments of Amitābha Buddha’s buddha-field; the waters of that great ocean are a metaphor for the adornments of Samantadarśin Tathāgata’s buddha-field, which surpasses even this.
"Why is this? It is because the adornments of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin’s buddha-field are inconceivable.
At that time, Siṃhavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are there perhaps other such adornments of Buddha-fields throughout the Buddha-fields of the three periods of time?
The Buddha said:
“There is, son of good family! To the east of here,
passing beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named Abiding in the Supreme Vow.”
In that land there is a Buddha named Universal Radiance, Constantly Abounding Merit Ocean King.
That Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and boundless, and he constantly expounds the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas.
"Good son! The meritorious adornments of that buddha-field are equal to those of the buddha-field of Samantadarśin, without any difference. Good son!"

There are four bodhisattvas who have donned the armor of inconceivable and vast vows; they shall certainly fulfill these aspirations and likewise attain the adornment of this buddha-field just like that of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin.

Then Siṃhavikrama said: "I pray that the Buddha will proclaim the names of those bodhisattvas and their dwelling places, and further reveal the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-nityabahuguṇasāgararāja, so that this great assembly may receive much benefit."
"For what reason?
If these bodhisattvas see or hear this, their aspiration shall be fulfilled.
The Buddha said:
“Good sons! Listen attentively; I shall speak for you. Good sons!
One of those bodhisattvas was named Prabhāketu; he resided in the buddha-field of Aśokaguṇa in the east.
The next was named Jñānottara; he resided in the buddha-field of Jñānarāja Tathāgata in the south.
The next is named Śāntendriya (Tranquil Faculties), residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Prajñākūṭa in the west.
The next is named Praṇidhijñāna (Vow-Wisdom), residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Nārāyaṇa in the north.

At that time, by means of his supernatural powers, the World-Honored One manifested the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Constantly Abounding Merit-Ocean King, causing this great assembly to see that Tathāgata and the host of bodhisattvas, as well as the meritorious adornments of that buddha-field—all of which had never been seen or heard before, and all of which were inconceivable.

Adorned with the intermingled splendor of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of jewels, even if one were to describe its merits for an entire kalpa, they could not be exhausted; all beheld it clearly, as if looking at an amala fruit in the palm of their hand.

That Bodhisattva was forty-two thousand yojanas in height, while the Buddha’s body was eighty-four thousand yojanas in height; his radiance shone brilliantly like a mountain of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with the accomplishment of vast and magnificent merit.

Seated beneath the Great Bodhi Tree, surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas who pay him respectful homage, he manifests hundreds of thousands of billions of miraculous transformations and proceeds to the worlds of the ten directions to expound the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
Do you see the adornments of that Tathāgata’s buddha-field and the assembly of bodhisattvas?"
Then the great assembly spoke with one voice, saying:
"Indeed, we have seen it.
We shall train in this bodhisattva practice just as Mañjuśrī has practiced; we, too, shall accomplish such adornment of a buddha-field."
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with serene joy, emitting rays of light of various colors from his face, which illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Having shone upon them, the light returned, circled the Buddha three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do you manifest this smile?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"Within this great assembly, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, having seen the adornments of that buddha-field, have all resolved their minds, desiring to accomplish such a buddha-field."

Nevertheless, among them there are sixteen great beings who possess superior aspirations and have resolved upon the Great Mind; they will be able to fulfill the great vows undertaken by Mañjuśrī, and the other bodhisattvas shall also swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, with the merits and adornments of their buddha-fields being like those of the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Maitreya, you should know that for all bodhisattvas, since their aspirations and inclinations are superior, what they accomplish is likewise great.
As for those with superior aspirations and inclinations, they say: "I shall achieve a buddha-field adorned in the manner of Mañjuśrī."

As for those of lesser capacity, even though they utter these words with mere faith, by this karmic action of speech they are still able to abandon the cycle of birth and death for sixty billion hundred thousand nayutas of kalpas, and they also attain the fulfillment of the five pāramitās.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva saw four great bodhisattvas—the Banner of Radiance and others—from the four directions, each seated within a lapis lazuli radiant pavilion. They were surrounded by hundreds of thousands of billions of devas who rained down flowers and played music, manifesting great supernatural transformations that shook the great earth as they approached this place.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I ask to be informed of this matter.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! These four bodhisattvas have been sent from the Tathāgatas of the four directions to come here for the sake of seeing me.

When those bodhisattvas arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side; the radiance of those four bodhisattvas illuminated this entire great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Good sons! The aspirations and destinations of these four great virtuous men are all inconceivable; you should honor them and request their essential teachings."
Furthermore, that aspiration is the most supreme among all those of bodhisattvas.

Any good man or good woman who beholds him will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, shall abandon twenty billion kalpas of wandering in birth and death, and will fully perfect the five *pāramitās*.
"If any woman hears the name of this bodhisattva, she shall swiftly attain liberation from her female body.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal power, and that buddha-field suddenly vanished from sight.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
All dharmas are entirely like illusions."
Why is this? It is like a magician who creates illusions that appear and disappear; the arising and ceasing of all phenomena is likewise so.
Yet this arising and ceasing is itself without arising or ceasing, for that which is without arising or ceasing is equality.
"When a bodhisattva cultivates this equanimity, they are able to realize unsurpassed bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Jñānottara addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "How is this bodhi realized?"
Mañjuśrī said: "This bodhi is not something that can be attained, nor is it something that can be destroyed, nor is it something to which one can become attached. Jñānottara replied:
"Furthermore, this bodhi is not attained through abiding, nor is it attained through non-abiding.
Why is this? Because that dharmatā is originally unborn; it has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and is also indestructible. Therefore, there is no attainment."
Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattvas, headed by Jñānottara, saying:
"What is called the Dharma-gate of Teaching the Single Characteristic?
Maitreya Bodhisattva replied:

"If there is neither seeing of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, nor non-seeing; no conceptual discrimination, and no seeing of their gathering or dispersal—this is called the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the single characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrānta-ghoṣa said:

"If one does not engage in various conceptual discriminations—such as 'this is the dharma of ordinary beings' or 'this is the dharma of those of the Two Vehicles'—then one does not contravene the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and enters into the single characteristic, which is the so-called 'characteristicless. This is called the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Delight-to-See said:

"If one practices the conduct of true suchness (tathatā) yet does not form the conceptualization of 'true suchness,' remaining without discrimination regarding this profound depth—this is called the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the single characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Unhindered Eloquence said:
"If one can thoroughly exhaust all phenomena and also expound these phenomena for others, this is called the Dharma-gate of preaching the single characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Sucintita said:
"If one enters the inconceivable by means of the conceivable, then even this inconceivability cannot be apprehended; this is called the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the single characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Sublime Detachment from Dust said:

"If one is unstained by any signs, neither stained nor unstained, without opposition or compliance and without delusion, neither one nor two and not manifold, neither grasping nor abandoning—this is called teaching the Dharma-gate of the single sign."
The Bodhisattva Sāgara said:

"If there is one who can enter the extremely profound Dharma that is as difficult to enter as the ocean, yet does not discriminate within this Dharma; and though they teach it to others, they have no notion of 'teaching'—this is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Candrottara said:

"If one maintains equanimity toward the mental activities of all sentient beings, like the full moon, and is free from the notion of 'sentient beings,' this is called teaching the Dharma-gate of the single characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Vigatāśoka said:
"How does one extract the arrow of sorrow from sentient beings?
It is this notion of 'I' and 'mine' that constitutes the root of that sorrow."
"If one can abide in the equality of 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' this is called teaching the Dharma-gate of the single characteristic.
The Bodhisattva Without Object said:

"If one does not take as an object of focus the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, nor the teachings of the śrāvakas, the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas, or the teachings of the Buddhas, this is called teaching the Dharma-gate of the single characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Universal Vision said:

"When preaching the Dharma, one should preach the Dharma of equality—namely, the equality of the dharma of emptiness—and yet have neither the notion of emptiness nor the notion of equality; this is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Pure Three Circles said:

"When preaching the Dharma, one should purify the three circles: namely, that the sentient beings for whom one preaches cannot be apprehended as 'self,' nor does one discriminate oneself as being a Dharma teacher, and one has no dwelling or attachment toward the Dharma being preached. Preaching the Dharma in this way is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Accomplished Practice said:

"If there is one who can explain that for all phenomena one cultivates the practice of equanimity, such that what is known is according to reality and not explained by means of words—because all phenomena are beyond verbal expression—this is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
The Bodhisattva Profound Practice said:

"If there is one who can explain and thoroughly understand all profound dharmas, yet does not perceive the speaker, the spoken, or that for which it is spoken—this is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic."
In this manner, immeasurable bodhisattvas each expounded the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic through their own eloquence.

While this Dharma-gate was being taught, thirty-seven *koṭis* of bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand *nayutas* of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; seven thousand bhikṣus, no longer grasping at any phenomena and having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), attained liberation of mind; and ninety-six *nayutas* of devas and humans attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How long will it be before this Mañjuśrī attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
“Virtuous man, how long is that Buddha’s lifespan, and how many are the number of his assembly of bodhisattvas?
The Buddha said: “Virtuous man!”
“You should ask Mañjuśrī yourself. Then Siṃhavikrama said to Mañjuśrī,
“Virtuous One, how long will it be before you attain bodhi?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son! If the realm of empty space were to become a physical body, only then would I attain unsurpassed bodhi."
If an illusory person were to attain bodhi, then I would attain it.
If an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted were itself bodhi, then I would attain it.
If a dream, an echo, a shadow, a reflection, or a magically conjured person were to attain bodhi, then I would attain it.
"If the moonlight were to become day and the sunlight were to become night, only then would I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son! What you have asked should be asked of those who seek bodhi."
Siṃhavikrama said: "Virtuous one, do you not seek awakening? He replied:
"No. Why is this? Mañjuśrī is himself bodhi, and bodhi is itself Mañjuśrī."
Why is this so? Mañjuśrī, both "name" and "bodhi" are merely names; these names are detached and empty because they are unconditioned, and that very emptiness is bodhi.
At that time, the Buddha said to Siṃhavikrama,
"Have you ever seen or heard of the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Amitābha?"
“Yes, I have heard and seen it.
The Buddha asked,
“How many are their number?”
He replied, "It is beyond the reach of calculation or conceptual thought.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! Suppose there were a *śata* of sesame seeds from the kingdom of Magadha; taking up a single seed represents the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in the land of Amitābha Buddha, while the remaining seeds not taken up represent the assembly of bodhisattvas when Mañjuśrī attains *bodhi*, which exceeds even that number.”

"Good son! If one were to compare eons as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm to the number of eons comprising the lifespan of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin, it would not approach even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation, analogy, or metaphor."
It should be known that the lifespan of that Tathāgata Samantadarśin is beyond calculation and without limit.
Suppose there were one person who ground a trichiliocosm into atoms, and a second and a third person likewise ground a trichiliocosm into atoms.

Furthermore, suppose there were a person who took those atoms and, traveling eastward from here, dropped one atom after passing as many worlds as there are atoms; then, having passed another as many worlds, he dropped another atom. In this manner, he proceeded in succession until all the atoms were exhausted.

Furthermore, there is a second person who likewise takes that same number of subtle atoms and travels south from here, dropping one atom as before, proceeding in succession until the atoms are exhausted.
In the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, there is likewise one person in each, with the number of particles they cast down being exactly the same.
Good son! Is it possible to know the number of all these worlds?
He replied, “No. The Buddha said:
“Good son! Suppose all those worlds through which these people have passed in the ten directions—whether they are covered by atoms of dust or not—are ground entirely into powder to become dust.”
"What do you think?
Can the number of these atoms be calculated so that their quantity is known? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
If one were to attempt to calculate it, the mind would become confused and unable to comprehend it."
The Buddha said:
“Good son! All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are fully able to know the number of those atoms; even if it exceeds this, the Tathāgata likewise knows it.”
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For the sake of seeking such great wisdom as this, bodhisattvas undergo all manner of extreme suffering in the great hells for immeasurable billions of kalpas; they should never abandon such great wisdom.”
The Buddha said, "Maitreya! So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."
"How could anyone not give rise to a longing for this great wisdom?
Only those who are base and indolent would fail to do so.
When he spoke these words regarding this wisdom, ten thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Siṃhavikrama, saying: "Good son,
what do you think?"
Just as those ten people [could reduce] the worlds of the ten directions to a total of atoms, Mañjuśrī, you shall practice the bodhisattva path for as many eons as there are those atoms.

Why is this? Mañjuśrī’s great vows are inconceivable; his course of practice is also inconceivable; having attained bodhi, the span of his life is also inconceivable; and his assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise inconceivable.
At that time, Siṃhavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Mañjuśrī’s resolve is most great, and the practice he cultivates is likewise vast; yet he does not give rise to weariness throughout as many eons as there are atoms in those lands.”
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is. Good son!"
It is as you have said.
What do you think?
Does the realm of space have such a thought as to pass through days and nights, seasons, years, months, kalpas, and so forth?
He replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"In this way, noble son!

If one realizes that all phenomena are equal to space, that subtle wisdom is free from conceptual differentiation, and there is no thought of passing through days, nights, seasons, months, years, or the enumeration of kalpas."
Why is this? Because they have no conceptualization regarding all phenomena. Good son!
Just as the realm of space is free from weariness and the perception of heat and affliction, why is this?
Even if an eon longer than the sands of the Ganges were to pass, the realm of space would neither arise nor be consumed by fire, nor could it ever be destroyed.
Why is this? Because the realm of space is non-existent.
Thus it is, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena are non-existent, they will likewise experience no feverish distress, nor weariness and the like.
Son of good family!
Even the name of that space is without burning, destruction, feverish distress, or weariness; it is also neither moving nor shaking, neither arising nor aging, neither coming nor going.
"The name Mañjuśrī is likewise; it is free from feverish affliction, fatigue, and the like. Why is this?
Because the nature of names is detached [from such qualities].
When this Dharma was being taught, the Four Great Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Devānām Indra, and other sons of the gods of great majesty and virtue raised their voices in unison, declaring:

“If these sentient beings obtain such great and virtuous benefit merely by hearing this Dharma-gate, how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it? You should know that the roots of goodness they cultivate will be exceedingly vast.”
“World-Honored One!
We shall receive, uphold, read, recite, and widely propagate this Dharma-gate, desiring to protect and maintain this profound Dharma.
At that time, Siṃhavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who hear such a Dharma-gate as this, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it, and give rise to the mind that adorns a Buddha-field with such meritorious qualities, how much merit will they obtain?”
The Buddha said,

“Good son! Whatever Buddhas and their lands are seen by the Tathāgata with his unimpeded Buddha-eye— if there were a bodhisattva who filled those various lands with exquisite seven treasures and offered them as gifts to each and every Tathāgata, continuing this for as long as the future endures, causing this bodhisattva to abide securely in pure precepts and attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.”

If there should be a bodhisattva who, having received, upheld, read, and recited this Dharma-gate of the Array of Meritorious Buddha-fields, further gives rise to the resolve and practices for seven paces according to what Mañjuśrī has learned;
These two merits, compared to the merit of the previous gift of the seven treasures, do not equal even one hundredth part; indeed, they cannot be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this Dharma-gate be named?”
"How should we uphold it?

The Buddha said, "This Dharma door is named 'The Play of All Buddhas,' and it is also named 'The Fulfillment of All Vows,' and it is also named 'Mañjuśrī’s Adornment of the Buddha-field with Merits,' and it is also named 'Causing Bodhisattvas Who Have Aroused the Bodhicitta to Rejoice,' and it is also named 'The Prediction of Mañjuśrī. You should uphold it thus."
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions, desiring to make offerings to this Dharma-gate, rained down various flowers and praised it, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
"How rare, World-Honored One!
We have now been able to hear this inconceivable Dharma-gate of Mañjuśrī’s Lion’s Roar Adornment.
When the bodhisattvas had finished speaking these words, they each returned to their own lands.

When this Dharma was being taught, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the stage of non-retrogression, and the roots of goodness of immeasurable sentient beings reached maturity.
At that time, Mañjuśrī entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi called "The Birth of Radiance Universally Illuminating Like an Illusion."

Having entered into samādhi, he caused this entire assembly to see all the Tathāgatas within the infinite and boundless Buddha-fields of the ten directions; before each and every Buddha, there was a Mañjuśrī proclaiming the meritorious adornments of his own Buddha-field.
Having seen this, the assembly conceived a sense of wonder toward Mañjuśrī’s sublime and great vows.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all those bodhisattvas, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty, and Volume Sixty-One,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Nālandiyayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
16. The Chapter on the Bodhisattvas Beholding Reality (Bodhisattvadarśanabhūtasamaya-parivarta) Chapter One:
The Introduction Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Grove, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. Their names were as follows:

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, Mahā-Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, and Mahā-Maudgalyāyana—all were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; their minds were autonomous, being well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom; like great dragon-elephants, they had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, and brought an end to all fetters of existence.
Having attained excellent understanding of the true teaching within one's heart, with a mind unimpeded regarding all phenomena, one reaches the further shore and attains liberation for oneself;
having attained liberation, one attains self-subjugation for one's retinue; having attained subjugation, one attains tranquil concentration for one's retinue;
having attained tranquil concentration, one attains deliverance for one's retinue; and having attained deliverance, one has reached the goal.
The further shore; those belonging to the further shore have already reached dry land; those belonging to dry land have attained peace and security for themselves;
those belonging to peace and security have attained nirvana for themselves; those belonging to nirvana have destroyed their afflictions for themselves;

those belonging to the destruction of afflictions have attained the state of a śramaṇa for themselves; those belonging to the state of a śramaṇa have attained the cessation of evil for themselves; [those belonging to] the cessation of evil...

The retinue of the Brahmins consists of those who have abandoned unwholesome dharmas; the retinue of those who have abandoned unwholesome dharmas consists of those who thoroughly understand all dharmas;

the retinue of those who thoroughly understand all dharmas consists of those who are able to attain liberation; the retinue of those who are able to attain liberation consists of those who possess all virtues;
the retinue of those who possess all virtues consists of those who are free from afflictions; [the retinue] of those free from affliction...

When those in his retinue are free from affliction, they themselves become free from the five hindrances; when those in his retinue are free from the five hindrances, they themselves become free from obstacles;

when those in his retinue are free from obstacles, they themselves attain tranquility of mind; when those in his retinue have attained tranquility of mind, they themselves possess the six supernormal powers;

when those in his retinue possess the six supernormal powers, they themselves become liberated by being free from hatred and attachment; and when those in his retinue are liberated by being free from hatred and attachment, they themselves guard their single-mindedness.
The retinue of guarding the single mind is self-possessed of the perfection of the gates of mindfulness;
the retinue of the perfection of the gates of mindfulness relies upon itself on the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*); the retinue of the four reliances is itself free from various views;

the retinue of being free from various views is itself abandoned of all expectations; the retinue of abandoning all expectations attains for itself the practice of exhaustion; [the practice of] exhaustion...
When the practice of the retinue has accomplished its own task, the task being accomplished, the retinue practices for itself;
when the retinue practices for itself, the retinue is naturally free from turbid thoughts; when the retinue is free from turbid thoughts, the retinue naturally severs discursive thought;

when the retinue severs discursive thought, the retinue naturally relies upon bodily conduct; when the retinue relies upon bodily conduct, the retinue naturally attains unmoving bliss; as for the retinue of unmoving bliss...
One’s own mind is well-liberated; with a well-liberated mind, one’s retinue is well-liberated through their own wisdom;
with well-liberated wisdom, one’s retinue attains the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Such noble ones and their retinues are like this: having shed the branches and leaves and removed the bark, they abide solely in the heart-wood, which is firm and solid.
At that time, during the latter part of the night, the World-Honored One sat upon the open ground, surrounded on all sides by the assembly of bhikṣus.
Then the World-Honored One remained silent for a while, observing the assembly of bhikṣus, and addressed them:
"Among you, seek out one person capable of going to convert King Śuddhodana."

At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, paid homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Shall I go to convert King Śuddhodana?
The Buddha said, "Stop, Kauṇḍinya!"
"You now possess the virtues of a Great Teacher; you should not go there.
At that time, the Venerable Vāṣpa, Mahānāman Yaśoda, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We are capable of going to convert King Śuddhodana.
The Buddha told Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Cease for now."
"You all are fully endowed with the qualities of a revered Great Teacher; you should not go to convert him.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Whom does the World-Honored One now wish to send to convert King Śuddhodana?"

At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately entered the samādhi of suchness; adorning his mind with the power of this samādhi, he perceived the Buddha’s intention: that his thoughts were directed toward the Venerable Kālodāyin, wishing for him to go and transform King Śuddhodana.
For example, just as when the sun enters through a window of a multi-storied pavilion from the east, its light illuminates the western wall;
so too was it with Maudgalyāyana’s vision of the World-Honored One’s mind being focused solely on Kāḷodāyin, desiring to transform the king.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana arose from his meditative concentration and went to where Kālodayin was.
Having arrived, he said to him:
"The World-Honored One, knowing with his mind, considers you capable of going to convert King Śuddhodana."
“Kālodāyin! You should now rouse great courage and go quickly to convert the king.
After Maudgalyāyana had spoken these words, the venerable Kālodāyin addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Ordinary commoners are difficult to transform, how much more so a king.
Why is this? Because a Great King of the Kṣatriya caste who has been consecrated possesses sovereign power, making him difficult to transform."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
It is like a heap of gathered firewood, whether two or three pieces, or even as many as a thousand years old; such a pile of wood, having passed through many years, becomes exceedingly dry.
Suppose at that time someone were to set fire to it, creating a great mass of flames.
What do you think?
Would this mass of fire be considered large?
Maudgalyāyana said, "Very great. [The Buddha asked:
"If another person were to further douse this fire with immeasurable quantities of ghee and oil, would this fire not blaze even more intensely?"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said,
"It blazes even more fiercely.
[The Buddha asked,] "What do you think?"
"Can one approach this fire?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"It is difficult to approach."
"Even so, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
A great king of the Kṣatriya caste who has been consecrated is likewise difficult to convert and impossible to approach."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
For example, could one touch the tusks of a mad elephant?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"It cannot be touched. "It is even so, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
A consecrated Kṣatriya is likewise difficult to convert."
Then the Venerable Maudgalyāyana spoke again to Udāyin:
“The World-Honored One, knowing with his mind, understands that you are capable of going to convert King Śuddhodana.
Udāyin replied to Maudgalyāyana:
“World-Honored One, do you truly intend to look upon me with favor, thinking that I am capable of going to convert King Śuddhodana?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“The World-Honored One truly and sincerely thinks of you, believing that you are capable of teaching and transforming your father, the King.”
At that time, the World-Honored One personally addressed Udāyin, saying: "Udāyin!
You may enter the city to convert our father, the King."
Why is this? Only you and I are capable of teaching and transforming King Śuddhodana. Udāyin!
"Among all my śrāvaka disciples, you are the foremost in being able to teach and transform the various towns and villages.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Udāyin with these verses:
"Listen attentively, Udāyin!"
"You are capable of providing excellent instruction and will surely bring joy to the Śākya clan; go and convert the most eminent king.
Now is the time for the king to receive awakening, which will benefit both gods and humans alike, ensuring he reaches the further shore. You should go quickly to convert him."
King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan now harbors resentment and is mired in confusion;
his mindfulness remains fixed while wisdom fails to function, as if he had fallen from a high precipice.
Yearning for his son’s high station, his heart of wisdom is utterly lost in delusion.
Like a merchant who has lost a precious treasure, He pursues it with remembrance, giving rise to great suffering.
Like a celestial being falling from his palace, He yearns for the pleasures of the five desires;
Not yet knowing the Buddha’s True Dharma, He is filled with sorrow and great turmoil.
Thinking to himself that he had lost the seven treasures, as well as the four paths for men, and remembering this position of a holy king, words of unrighteousness issued from his mouth.
At that time, the king spoke in grief and agitation; unaware of both himself and others, he lamented.
Just as a spirit that seizes the vital essence holds a person's body,
so that while still on Mount Kīla they see nothing at all;
likewise, the obstruction of vexation and resentment prevents one from seeing what ought to be seen.
Just as one who has fallen asleep or died does not perceive their own mind, so too, King,
you do not recognize your own joy due to the obstacles of grief, resentment, and delusion.
Like a wife whose husband has passed away, she weeps in sorrow and gives rise to regret.
The King is now bewildered and distressed, giving rise to great suffering through his longing;
you, who possess skillful means, should go to transform King Śuddhodana,
topple the banner of false pride, and establish the lamp of the True Dharma.
There is no one else capable of converting the Great King Śuddhodana;
it is only you, Udāyin, who have practiced together with him in the past.
Udāyin, you should know that there was once a great king.
His name was Vardhamāna-satya; his fame resounded throughout the ten directions.
Acting as the sovereign of the land in accordance with the Dharma, all submitted to his transformation.
Governing by means of the True Dharma, the King ruled over the four continents.
The cities and towns were entirely filled with gardens of flowers and fruits fragrant with incense;
they were inhabited by many hosts of sages and saints, and no base or evil persons were found there.
The fragrant groves were exceedingly dense, and the ground was pure and free of thorns.
Abounding in pure and exquisite things, the flower ponds are beautifully adorned.
The people are vast and prosperous; they abandon evil and dwell constantly in goodness.
Having closed the gates to the evil realms, they will surely ascend to the sublime celestial paths.
That king had a son in the past who once made extensive offerings to the Buddha;
having fully cultivated all roots of goodness and perfected all merits,
he was named Miaojianhui (Subtle Firm Wisdom), and was honored by billions of beings.
Constantly seeing the faults of form and desire, he abandoned his home to delight in tranquility.
His father, the king, commanded his son, saying:
"Let the court ladies amuse themselves; go and enjoy yourself in the jeweled palaces and ponds."
I have now prepared these for you; enjoy them without lack.
Why do you not find delight?
You should explain your intention.
Knowing that all realms of existence are excellent and sublime,
you dwell within a precious palace surrounded by the jewel of women; though such wondrous scenes are most delightful,
even the seers dwelling in secluded forests have abandoned them to return home.
You have experienced all manner of sensual pleasures; how much more so now that you lack for nothing?
Surrounded by a host of court ladies and followed by kings and ministers, with palaces like celestial mansions, you ought to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
These women are exceedingly beautiful, as lovely as celestial maidens;
they are skilled at performing song, dance, and music, capable of delighting one’s own mind.
Their eyes are like *utpala* flowers, and their lips are red as if stained with vermilion.
His face is full with broad, dark eyebrows; his forehead is even and his throat is beautiful.
His chest is level and his collarbones are hidden; his arms are like the trunks of elephant kings.
His palms are the color of lotus flowers; his fingers are round, smooth, slender, and elegant.
The tongue is thin, broad, and crimson; his eloquent speech is like nectar.
His teeth are white, sharp, even, and closely set. He wears necklaces of pearls and precious garments.
His navel is deep, yet his abdomen does not protrude. His spine is like a vajra scepter.
Your thighs and hips are firm, round, and straight; your calves are like those of the eneya deer king.
Your gait is like that of the king of geese; all gaze upon you.
In the prime of youth, you are most lovely and capable of preserving the lineage.
"You and your many beautiful women are like spring flowers in full bloom;
while your prime and beauty have not yet faded, you should quickly enjoy pleasures.
Resolute Wisdom addressed his father, the King:
The King said, "Your words are not in accord with right principle; if there were speech that conformed to the Dharma, I would not dare to disobey your command.
O King, listen now to what I say: I delight in wholesome and truthful speech, and even in my dreams, I do not give rise to thoughts of lust."
"Father King, these words of yours are not approved by the wise;
the foolish delight in such things, while the enlightened always loathe them.
Why, then, would one with clear vision envy a blind guide?"
How could there be one standing on the shore who would instead delight in drowning?
How could there be one who has attained liberation who would again take pleasure in prison?
How could there be one who possesses peace and happiness who would envy those amidst manifold sufferings?
In my view, I regard the Father King as one who is blind and drowning in hell;
like one experiencing the five desires in a dream, he is once again submerged by desire.
The Father King is like one in blinding darkness, while I see with eyes what is most excellent.
The King was swept away by desire; I now loathe and despise it deeply.
Desire is like a vessel of poisonous medicine, like the head of a venomous snake, like a sharp sword or spear, and like a great, fierce fire.
When the king and his ministers exhorted him, Dṛḍhamati would not consent to anything;
abandoning his kin and his kingdom, he cast off desire and went forth into homelessness.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, or like discarding mucus and spittle, he left it all behind.
Having distanced himself from faults and evils, he renounced the world forever out of despair.
When Dṛḍhamati left the secular life, his ministers and sons followed him into homelessness.
One of them was named Candadatta; having abandoned desire, he followed Dṛḍhamati.
Once the youth had gone forth, together with the sons of the great ministers,
they accomplished the four Brahma-abodes and were endowed with the five supernormal powers.
Deeply perceiving the faults of the five sensory objects, they transcended the realm of desire.
He turned the sublime and wondrous Wheel of Dharma and was reborn directly in the Brahma Heaven.
After the youth had left the household life, his father the King gave rise to resentment;
Candradatta went to the King’s presence and skillfully transformed him so that the King rejoiced.
Udāyin, you should know that he who was formerly named Dṛḍhamati,
who remained far removed from the five desires, is none other than my own self today.
Udāyin, you should know that he who was King Vardhamāna at that time—
Could this have been anyone else?
It was King Śuddhodana.
Udāyin, you should know that those who followed me in leaving the household life—
Candapradyota was your body in that life, And he was once also transformed by Udraka Rāmaputra.
Therefore, Udāyin, you should now transform your father, the king;
There will surely be great benefit, for he was previously transformed by you.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, having received the Buddha’s instruction, silently gave his consent.
Then, when the night had passed and dawn had broken, at the hour for eating, Udāyin put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, more than a thousand members of the Śākya clan gathered at the king’s gate, each having some request.
King Śuddhodana, hearing that the Buddha Tathāgata had arrived at Kapilavastu and was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove, conceived a feeling of resentment, thinking:
"This son has left the household life and deprived my clan of its wealth, nobility, and great pleasures."

If he had remained a householder, he would have succeeded as a Wheel-Turning King over the four continents, ruling them according to the Dharma so that the people did not disobey his commands, and possessing the seven treasures.
What are these seven?

First is the wheel-treasure (cakraratna); second is the elephant-treasure (hastiratna); third is the horse-treasure (aśvaratna); fourth is the mani-jewel-treasure (maṇiratna); fifth is called the woman-treasure (strīratna); sixth is the minister-treasure of the treasury (gṛhapatiratna); and seventh is called the counselor-treasure (pariṇāyakaratna).
He possessed a full thousand sons, valiant and invincible, with exquisite countenances, capable of crushing powerful enemies and protecting the four continents.
He governed the realm not by means of the sword or staff, but through righteous law; thus, the land was naturally and spontaneously at peace.
"I have attained the sovereign happiness of a Wheel-Turning King; he ought to honor and make offerings to me.
Because my son has gone forth into homelessness, everything that was rightfully mine has fallen away."

Having formed this thought, he commanded all the Śākyas: "None of you shall go to my son’s place to pay respects, have faith, or listen to the Dharma; should anyone violate this, his head shall be severed."
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Priyamukha who was not among the assembly and had not heard the king’s command; seeing Udāyin, he went to him, prostrated himself, and said:
"Welcome, Venerable One!"
"Are you at peace? Is the World-Honored One well, free from illness and affliction, light and agile in his movements, not fatigued on the road, and provided with an abundance of offerings?
Then Udāyin replied to Nandika, saying:
"The Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction; his movements are light and agile, he is not fatigued on the road, and his food and drink are not lacking.
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Sujāta, who saw Nandamukha conversing in private with Udāyin. He also approached them and said, "Venerable sir!"
Having come from afar, how have you been, Kauṇḍinya?
Is the World-Honored One living in peace and comfort, with little illness and little affliction? Are you not fatigued by the journey, and is there no lack of provisions for your meals?
Udāyin replied, "The Tathāgata’s holy person is at ease; he is not fatigued on the road, nor does he lack anything.

At that time, there were two other Śākyas, one named Aśoka and the other named Vigatāśoka, who saw Nandamukha and Sujāta together with Udāyin in a secluded place. They too left the crowd and approached them, saying to Udāyin:
"Welcome here; are you well and strong?
Is the World-Honored One living in peace and comfort?
Having traveled such a long distance, I hope you have not been fatigued?"
Udāyin replied, "The Tathāgata’s holy person is at ease; he is not fatigued by the journey.
Then the two Śākya clansmen spoke again, saying:
“Why is it that the Tathāgata’s journey lacks for nothing?
Udāyin replied, “Because the Four Heavenly Kings,
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the various Brahmā Kings constantly come to make offerings, he lacks for nothing.”
Then the Śākyas all said to Udāyin:
"We now wish to go to the Buddha, to the place where the World-Honored One is, to make offerings and listen to the Dharma; we fear we may not succeed."
Why is this? Because King Śuddhodana has recently issued a decree commanding that none of the Śākyas shall be permitted to go to the Buddha’s presence to make offerings or listen to the Dharma.
Should anyone violate this, their head shall be severed.
"Because I fear the King's punishment, I am unable to pay homage, make offerings, or listen to and receive the True Dharma.
When Udāyin heard these words, he knew that his father the King harbored great resentment.
"What skillful means can I employ now to reach the king's presence?
Having had this thought, he resolved: "I shall rise to a height of seven *tāla* trees and, sitting cross-legged in mid-air, proceed to the king's presence."

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin entered the samādhi of suchness; adorning his mind with that samādhi, he further used his supernormal power to rise to the height of seven *tāla* trees and sat cross-legged in mid-air, flying through the sky to the place where King Śuddhodana was.

At that time, the king saw from afar Udāyin approaching through the air, sitting cross-legged by means of his supernormal powers. Rising from his seat, he joined his palms in reverence and addressed Udāyin in verse:
"Great Master in dyed robes, from where have you come?"
"To you who have accomplished such majestic deportment and are so difficult to behold, if you have any need, please speak quickly;
with a sincere heart, I shall surely provide it. Then the Venerable Udāyin replied in verse:
"I am the son of the Great Prince; the Great King is my grandfather."
I have gone on alms-round for the Tathāgata, and having obtained food, I offer it to the Great Sugata.
Today the Great King has gained a sublime benefit; the King’s son is the most honored among gods and men, his majestic radiance illuminating the ten directions like the autumn moon at midday.
Like the sun in the sky, free from clouds and mist, Its brilliant radiance shines forth, illuminating all;
So too does this most excellent prince, the son of a noble king, His majestic virtue and light manifest, heard throughout the ten directions.
Just as when the autumn sun first rises, it eclipses the light of all fireflies and shines everywhere;
so too does this most excellent son of a king subdue all non-Buddhists and alone manifest his brilliance.
Just as at midday, when the sun is at its peak and blazing, the stars do not appear because they are overwhelmed by it;
so too, this most excellent King and Noble Son, having subdued the non-Buddhists, causes his own light to shine forth.
Just as the brilliance of the moon is eclipsed at midday by the sun, causing it to lose its luster and remain unseen;
so too has the noble son of this king subdued the non-Buddhists, like the bright moon hidden when the sun is in full splendor.
Just as when beasts hear the lion’s roar, those moving in water, on land, or through the air scatter back to their lairs,
fleeing in terror and losing their way in all directions, for the sound of the lion is unbearable to them.
When the Great Sage Tathāgata roars his lion’s roar, the heterodox followers of false paths hear the sound of "no-self.
Even those who are ignorant and have reached the Peak of Existence, upon hearing this teaching of no-self, are all struck with terror.
Among the blind, deluded, and ignorant among gods and humans, the Tathāgata with eyes reveals the torch of illumination;
acting as a bright lamp to dispel the darkness of folly, he raises aloft the wheel of supreme wisdom-light.
Revealing the false and the correct, the equal and the unequal, He instructs the world on what is the path and what is not the path;
For those who have lost their way, he shows them the road, And pulls them from the mire of desire to place them upon the shore.
Just as rising clouds cover a parched pond, and falling rain fills the plains and marshes to their capacity,
so too does the Great King, the Son of Sages, raise the rain of Dharma to moisten humans and devas.
Just as water moistens the earth, the mountains, and the rivers, as well as the myriad flowers, thickets, and trees—
the medicinal herbs, stalks, stems, branches, and vines— so too do the various blossoms flourish luxuriantly, beautifying the entire mountain.
Thus, with the ten powers and four fearlessnesses, Fully endowed with the tree of the eighteen unique qualities,
Adorned with the flowers and fruits of omniscience— Such is the subtle and wondrous body of the Royal Sage, the Son of the Holy One.
Just as Mount Sumeru stands in the great ocean, Majestic, unmoving, and the joyous abode of the gods,
So too is this Great Prince of the Sugatas, The foremost among the ocean of śramaṇas.
The Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the husband of Śacī, is most extraordinary and wondrous among the celestial hosts;
even so, the World-Honored One, the Great Prince, is the most preeminent among the assembly of śramaṇas.

He roars forth the secret and most profound Dharma; with the lightning of his garland of compassion pervading all, the Tathāgata dragon-king lets fall the rain of Dharma, as the waters of the pond of the foundations of mindfulness flow down in fine streams.
The majesty of his precepts is like the orb of the sun; by the power of samādhi, he dispels the darkness of affliction.
With the light of wisdom, he extinguishes the craving of the defilements; the Great Muni shines upon the world like the sun.
Fully endowed with the mani-jewel of the foundations of mindfulness, they cross to the other shore by means of the boat and raft of precepts and concentration;
their treasuries of the factors of enlightenment are filled with dhyāna, and they further seek *vikṣa* to enter the ocean of the Buddhas.

The root of pure precepts is firm and difficult to shake; The leaves are samādhi, the branches are the foundations of mindfulness, The flowers are the seven factors of enlightenment, and the trunk is the emptiness of the solid tree; With the solidity of non-self, it is the tree that becomes a Buddha.
A powerful one who wanders within the forest of precepts, Relying on the mountain of virtue tamed by samādhi,
Taking the three gates of liberation as his sphere of activity— The Buddha’s ten powers are the fangs of this prince.
The Muni, the Honored One, possesses right view and is free from attachment; he is the bull-king who can subdue powerful adversaries.
Terrifying all manner of non-Buddhists, this Great Prince utters the roar of fearlessness.
Adorned with the wondrous array of the treasury of śīla, Clad in the immeasurable robes of dhyāna and nirvāṇa,
The Muni, endowed with wisdom, dwells in the realm of liberation, Able to bestow wealth and goods like a great householder.
Distant from all evils, he has gathered all virtues; Having extinguished all afflictions, his faculty of wisdom is excellent.
Bestowing wisdom upon devas, humans, asuras, and others, The light of this prince, the son of a king, shines brilliantly.
The cloud of precepts has the wisdom of emptiness as its lightning; the fine rain of the eightfold path can provide nourishment.
The Muni can bestow [this] upon the seeds of the supreme crop, just as a prince is like a great dragon’s rain.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked in verse:
"O Noble One, have you arrived in peace and well-being?
Is there no lack of food and drink? Are you free from physical fatigue regarding your bedding and seating? Are you like a flower on the bank, not withered?"
At that time, Udāyin replied with a verse:
“Possessing the power of spiritual faculties within the realm of meditative concentration, His body and mind are filled with pervasive peace and joy;
The Sage’s divine contemplation rests in tranquil stillness, Like a golden lotus, never withering.”
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked in verse:

"In the past, you were awakened by the sounding of banners and drums; You delighted yourself with the beautiful sounds of zithers, flutes, and lutes, And with exquisite female musicians for your own amusement."
"Do you not feel suffering now, being alone in the forest?
At that time, Udāyin replied in verse:
"With meditative concentration and profound stillness as his domain, He is skillfully able to cultivate the bliss of samādhi."
"In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, he relies upon all that is wholesome; his mind is always joyful and free from suffering.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked in verse:
"He always lies peacefully upon a priceless jeweled couch, and when he sleeps, a multitude of beautiful women are at his side."
"With bright lamp-trees set out all around, how could one lie in darkness without being distressed?
At that time, Udāyin replied in verse:
"When the Muni sleeps, he lies upon the noble bed; compassion is his mattress and kindness his pillow."
"The Buddha dwells in a mind of joy, ever serene and glad; having abandoned the three realms of existence, he is free from sorrow.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked in verse:
"Surrounded by the ever-valiant Śākyas, with those of vast learning as his companions,"
"You were nurtured within palace halls and celestial mansions;
why do you now delight in the forest?
At that time, Udāyin replied in verse:
A son born according to the Dharma is ever present before him; practicing śamatha together, he stays by his side.
With a mind fond of the forest, he cultivates various meditative concentrations; the Teacher, free from fear, delights in the mountain forests.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked in verse:
"When the youth was formerly in the palace, He bathed in celestial bathing pools And likewise anointed his body with fragrant unguents;
Now he has entered this forest, How shall he bathe?"
"Now that you are in the forest, who is it that washes you?
At that time, Udāyin replied in verse:
"The waters of the pool of all dharmas, with the shore of virtue and precepts— The Muni bathes himself and bathes others therein."
"I and my sons float without getting wet; we have crossed over ourselves and reached all living beings.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked in verse:
"In the past, various fragrances constantly perfumed your body, And golden threads and pearls adorned your person."
"You were always clothed in the exquisite garments of a celestial son;
now that you are in this forest, with what do you adorn yourself?
At that time, Udāyin replied in verse:
Adorned with the garland of merit and perfumed by the fragrance of precepts, With the necklace of meditative concentration and the robe of shame and remorse,
Self-adorned with supernormal powers, clarity, and liberation, His radiant majesty shines forth within the forest.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked in verse:
"In the past, you were constantly guarded by heroic men wielding swords, spears, bows, and arrows;
you were also perpetually sheltered by precious parasols."
"Now who alone protects you within the forest?
At that time, Udāyin replied in verse:
"Compassion and patience guard me of their own accord; The power of the Śrāvaka disciples is my retinue."
"By means of his merit and dharmas, he is certainly free from fear; The Ten Powers are his heroic might and the Four Fearlessnesses.
At that time, King Śuddhodana praised him with these verses:
"Excellent! Well-spoken is the description of my son’s virtues; Having long cultivated wholesome dharmas, he does not regress."
"Once you have finished eating, take the food and depart; I too shall go to visit the King of Munis.
At that time, Udāyin again addressed the king, saying: "Great King!"

The Bhagavān is the Teacher of the Great Assembly who skillfully guides all living beings; he is the Great Sage who dwells securely amidst the community of śramaṇas as the King of Śramaṇas, his radiance shining everywhere.
Just as on the night of the fifteenth day the pure full moon, surrounded by the host of stars, shines with such intense radiance that it illuminates all things, so too is the World-Honored One;
amidst the assembly of śramaṇas, his radiant splendor shines forth in just this same way.
Just as the autumn sun is present in the sky free from all clouds and obscurations, so too is that Blessed One; he likewise shines with radiant light amidst the great assembly.
Just as Śakra, the king of the gods, sits in the Hall of Good Dharma and his radiance is most brilliant among all the devas,
so too is the Bhagavat’s radiance resplendent when he is amidst the assembly.

For example, just as the kings of the Suyāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven possess radiant brilliance and preeminent majesty when among the hosts of devas.

The majestic splendor of that Blessed One amidst the assembly of śramaṇas was likewise manifest in this way; he was like Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, surrounded by ten billion Brahmā hosts, his radiance dazzling and his majesty uniquely supreme.
“That Blessed One, amidst the assembly of śramaṇas, is likewise resplendent with light and supremely majestic in his power.
At that time, having heard this account of the Blessed One’s moral excellence, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
“If even these śrāvaka disciples of the World-Honored One possess such great supernormal powers, such great majesty, and such great merit, how much more so must it be for the Tathāgata himself!”

He further reflected: "When the Prince was originally born, the great earth shook in six ways and eighteen modes: it shook, shook everywhere, and shook equally everywhere; it leaped, leaped everywhere, and leaped equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; it stirred, stirred everywhere, and stirred equally everywhere, emitting a great radiance."
Without anyone to support him, he walked seven paces; from the sky, two streams of water poured down to bathe his body.
Spontaneously, a sacred throne of pure gold appeared, and a celestial canopy manifested in mid-air as the various devas prostrated in worship.
Even until the time he left the household life, he was not deluded by the five desires.
Whatever he undertook, he was resolute and never retreated; as he spoke, so he acted.
At all times, possessing firm and great strength, he did not speak falsely nor did he violate his conduct of faith.
He had previously made this vow:
"Once I have attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and have finished delivering myself, I shall further deliver the King."
At that time, the King, recollecting the original vows made by the Buddha when he was a bodhisattva, spoke this verse: “If there is one who,
from the very moment of birth, possesses clear wisdom whose words are not false and whose speech never deviates from the truth— who among the wise would not believe such a person?”
If at the moment of birth, the World-Honored One declared him peerless,
destined to become a Sovereign of Gods and Men— who among the wise would not believe it?
If one cannot cherish even a heap of jewels as vast as the Snowy Mountains, [how much less so this supreme treasure].
Who among the wise would not believe one who is free from greed and stinginess?
If one can refrain from false speech even in dreams,
practicing exactly as they speak, who among the wise would not believe them?
Like words from a sword or blade, they cannot cause distress or provoke anger;
having abandoned all matters of wrath, who among the wise would not believe this?
There is no one able to deceive them, nor are they stained by greed or hatred.
Who that is wise would not believe in the King who is fully endowed with wisdom?
Who that is wise would not believe that none can bind him, whether by all the exquisite five sensual pleasures or by various karmic retributions?
Regarding various rare occurrences and manifold wonderful things,
who among the wise would not believe that nothing can cause fear?
Through exquisite words, the sagacious one speaks with skillful artistry.
Who that is wise would not believe that there is nothing capable of deluding or binding?
Since one cannot be bound by words of agreeable meaning or by definitive phrases regarding desires, who that is wise would not believe this?
With the power of his military forces and various forms of protection, he was able to depart from the wondrous city; who among the wise would not believe this?
Having renounced exquisite sensual pleasures, he set out to seek the practice of the Deathless.
Who among the wise would not believe that he aspired to enlightenment?
Who among the wise would not believe that for six years he practiced austerities,
possessing such courage that none could withstand him, as he sought supreme enlightenment?
For six years he ate coarse and meager food, seeking supreme enlightenment for the benefit and peace of all the world; who among the wise would not believe this?
For six years he was disturbed by Māra, who incessantly sought his vulnerabilities.
Unable to find any opportunity [to harm them], who among the wise would not believe this?
Having distanced themselves from the faults of the five desires and seeking no other things, they constantly benefit the world; who among the wise would not believe this?
Without hearing the Dharma from another, he spontaneously attained Bodhi;
his tranquil concentration is difficult to perceive—what wise person would not believe this?
Brahmā himself exhorted him, earnestly entreating the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Who that is wise would not believe when you have preached as requested?
Out of compassion and pity for me, you have come to the Nyagrodha Grove;
who that is wise would not believe that you have come to deliver the Śākyas?
The Tathāgata, having himself crossed over, has ferried me across the ocean of existence;
remembering his original vow, who that is wise would not believe?
Now is the very time to gain benefit; know that the Buddha possesses all-knowledge.
"Who that is wise would not believe this out of compassion for me?
I shall now go forth to behold the body of the Teacher of Men.
While he was reflecting thus, he recognized himself as a king of men.
At that time, after King Śuddhodana had reflected for a long while, he said to the venerable Udāyin:
"Bhikṣu! Now that you have arrived here, what further do you require?"
Then Udāyin replied in verse:
"Originally, for the sake of benefiting the Great King, I have now come here by means of supernormal power.
If one gives rise to even a single faith in the One of Ten Powers, Both men and women shall attain the path of goodness."
The merit of the Ten Powers is boundless; the Great Sage has come for the sake of the Śākya clan.
This joyful event is now at hand; the Lord of Men should give rise to faith.
The Great King’s fame shall surely increase, pervading the entire trichiliocosm.

Your son is indeed the treasury of the king of men; Fully endowed with the ten powers and a heart of compassion, He wanders through the ten directions with an unimpeded mind, Like a lotus in water, unstained by attachment.
Having crossed over the four floods and all states of existence yourself, you have likewise delivered gods and humans from the four torrential rivers;
having established them upon the shore of the island of fearlessness, Great King, you should place your faith in the Teacher.
He has pulled out the arrows of the four floods and the three poisons;
he is the supreme physician who subdues all living beings, the most honored and exalted among all healers—Great King, you should regard him with deep reverence and faith.
He is also able to subdue all military hosts, the Māra kings, their retinues, and evil kinsmen;
having realized the wondrous Bodhi of tranquil extinction, Great King, you should regard him with deep reverence and faith.
All the kings of gods and men together entreat you: To deliver sentient beings, preach the sublime Dharma;
Unfold and expound the unsurpassed nectar-medicine— O Bull-King among Men, you should grant this with faith.
Obscuring all the hosts of external paths, He turns the wondrous Wheel of Dharma beyond all measure;
Transforming and delivering immeasurable billions of sentient beings— The Great Hero, King of Men, should be believed.
Amidst the darkness thickly shrouded by ignorance, you purify your own eyes and further purify those of others;
through preaching the Dharma, you can remove all cataracts of blindness—O Great Hero, King of Men, you should be believed.

To those oppressed by the fears of old age, sickness, and death, he teaches the Dharma that removes aging, illness, and death, causing the multitudes of the world to ascend to the happy realms; the Great Hero, King of Men, should be believed.
The multitudes of the world are burned by the three fires;
just as a blazing earth is extinguished with water, the Noble Eightfold Path is taught for humanity—O Great Hero, Bull among Men, you should have faith.
Having severed the three impurities and vomited forth all evils, Able to leave behind the three turbid stains of the world,
Wandering through the ten directions most wondrously— This valiant Bull-King should be believed.
Like a father who loves his son, he pities the world; With the ten powers and a heart of great compassion, he universally moistens all.
Arousing great pity and mercy, he delivers sentient beings; This valiant Bull-King—one should place faith in him.
The Blessed One who can tame those difficult to tame, who has now fully delivered all those who were to be delivered,
and who can extinguish the blazing afflictions— O Great King, you should place your faith in this valiant one.
Sentient beings have fallen into the ocean of the three realms of existence;
Like a ship capable of delivering them across, The One of Ten Powers, with great compassion, rescues the world; One should place faith in this valiant Bull King.

With a body of immeasurable merit and sublime form, The Greatly Compassionate One wanders through the world to transform it, Causing long-turbid minds to attain purity; O Great King, you should place your faith in him with valor.
Like a mani jewel that clarifies turbid water, it wanders through the world to purify sentient beings;
it cuts off the confusion, strife, and defilement of the masses—O Great King, you should have faith in this with valor.
Like a mani jewel whose nature is pure, it causes the hearts of the wise to rejoice;
the World-Honored One, free from evil and resplendent, causes all enlightened ones to admire and delight in him.
He inspires the highest faith in the world and enables devas and humans to cast off the burden of suffering.
Having abandoned all realms of existence, one attains peace; O valiant Great King, you should have faith.
This collection of merits is here described but in small measure, like a single bird’s track in the sky.
I do not know the further shore of the Buddha’s merits; O Great King, you should regard them with deep reverence and faith.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard the Venerable Udāyin’s excellent account of the merits cultivated by the World-Honored One while he was a bodhisattva, immediately recalled the Tathāgata’s original vow:
"Once I have attained liberation, I shall surely deliver the King."
Having reflected thus, he conceived deep reverence and faith, and spoke again to the Venerable Udāyin: "Bhikṣu!
You are now indeed the son of my son."
"You may finish eating and quickly return to the Buddha's presence to offer this food to him.
I, too, shall now go to see the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, knowing that King Śuddhodana had attained faith and reverence, finished his meal and immediately took the delicacies to present them to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Udāyin has converted King Śuddhodana and caused him to attain right faith. O bhikṣus!"
"Today, the gods and the people of the world have gained great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Udāyin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Today you have attained great merit because King Śuddhodana has gained faith and reverence.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If the merit obtained by Kālodāyin through his conversion of King Śuddhodana were to take physical form, the world-systems of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, would not be able to contain it, for this mass of merit is vast and immeasurable."
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-One;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter 16, Part 2: King Śuddhodana Visits the Buddha; Chapter 2 of the *Bodhisattvadarśanavastu-saṃnipāta*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal and washed his hands and bowl, manifested a portentous sign.

At that moment, King Vaiśravaṇa, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nāyakas, vanished from his celestial palace and appeared before the Buddha in a single thought-instant, as swiftly as a strong man might bend or extend his arm. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to the north, amidst a great assembly of nāyakas surrounding him in the air, joining his palms in reverent salutation toward the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of gandharvas, vanished from his celestial palace as swiftly as a strong man might bend or extend his arm. He appeared before the Tathāgata, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and remained in the eastern sky, paying reverent homage to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kumbhāṇḍas, vanished from his celestial palace as swiftly as a strong man might extend or contract his arm. He appeared before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood in the southern quarter in the midst of space, joining his palms in reverent salutation toward the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa of the western quarter, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of nāgas, likewise vanished from his celestial palace in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, and appeared before the Tathāgata. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and remained in the western quarter, standing in mid-air with palms joined in reverence toward the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus.
