Śakra, the Devānām Indra, was likewise surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas; vanishing from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he stood before the Buddha, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and remained in mid-air showing reverence to the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus.

The King of the Yāma Heaven, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, the King of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the King of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the King of the Bṛhatphala Heaven, and the Kings of the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens—each surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of celestial hosts—disappeared from their respective heavens and stood before the Buddha, prostrating with their heads at his feet. They likewise remained in the air, paying respectful homage to the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, surrounded by a retinue of sixty nayutas, vanished from his own palace and appeared before the Buddha in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, manifested an air of reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.

The King of the Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda), likewise surrounded by a retinue of eighty-six thousand Garudas, vanished from his own palace and stood before the Buddha, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet.
Furthermore, there were eight hundred million non-Buddhists who came from various directions and spoke these verses:
“In the pure, empty sky, The full moon of the fifteenth night Surpasses the multitude of stars;
Its radiance alone shines forth brilliantly.”
The Buddha is like the pure lunar disk; extinguishing darkness and removing the three defilements, he is able to transcend all non-Buddhist paths, just like the moon in the sky.
Like the autumn sun with its thousand rays of light, he is able to dispel all obscurity.
Surpassing the light of the bright moon, he spreads forth a lotus pond;
the Buddha’s radiance exceeds that of the sun, universally illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
The Tathāgata is able to reveal and manifest the forest of lotuses of the śrāvakas.
The Lord of Devas, Kauśika, dwelling in the Hall of Good Dharma, stands preeminent above the great assembly; his vajra radiates brilliant light.
A mountain of merit possessing the ten powers, the supreme king among those with two feet.
Surpassing all non-Buddhists, he is like the King of the Śakras;
Like the King of the Suyāma Heaven, honored by the celestial hosts,
He dwells amidst the assembly of gods, Radiant and majestic as he sits upon his jeweled throne.
With the boundless majesty of the ten powers, he has transcended the paths of evil;
possessing the virtue of fearless radiance, he clearly proclaims the Eightfold Noble Path.
Like the King of Tuṣita Heaven, surrounded by his retinue in his palace, he sits amidst the assembly.
Surpassing the hosts of devas, radiant with past merit,
the Tamer and Teacher of Gods and Humans is venerated by the eight classes of beings;
transcending all worlds, he fearlessly proclaims the Dharma.
Just as the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Dwelling within his celestial palace,
Surpasses all the hosts of devas, His merit alone shining with brilliance;
So the Buddha transcends all worlds, Free from turbidity and emerged from the triple realm.
He who can tame those yet untamed, a king endowed with the radiance of the ten powers,
is like the Sovereign Lord of Devas dwelling within his celestial palace;
surpassing all the hosts of gods, he shines brilliantly through his past merits.
Thus the Buddha’s radiance, Perfecting the ten powers and practices,
Surpasses the multitudes of devas and humans, Due to his fundamental roots of goodness and merit.
Just as the Great Brahmā King Surpasses all the hosts of Brahmās,
The Radiant One speaks with sweetness, manifesting the Eightfold Noble Path.
The Tathāgata, superior even to Brahmā, the King among the assembly of śramaṇas,
his light illuminating the three realms, turns the Dharma of the Four Truths.
Having perceived that the assembly had gathered—gods, humans, and nāgas listening to the Dharma—the King Supreme among Men uttered the words of the Eightfold Path.
The sky might be measured; the ocean might be exhausted by measuring it with jars.
“Mount Sumeru may be weighed, but the Buddha’s virtue is difficult to know.
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Śākyas, saying:
“O people, it is like when the sun is about to rise and its auspicious signs first appear; that is to say, when the morning star emerges, one should know that the sun will not rise long after.”
Kālodāyin was also like this; prior to the Tathāgata’s attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), auspicious signs first appeared.
What the bhikṣu has spoken regarding the merits of the Tathāgata is precisely the mark of omniscience.
"O virtuous ones!
Quickly prepare excellent vehicles; I shall go to where the Tathāgata resides.
Then the Śākya ministers said:
“Excellent, Great King!
Now is precisely the right time.
All the requisites you require have now been fully prepared.”
At that time, the Great King commanded his ministers, saying:

"From the city of Kapilavastu to the Nyagrodha Grove, clear and prepare the road in the interval between them. Cover the ground with fine, soft sand, scatter various kinds of flowers, hang silken banners, and perform various songs, music, dances, and performances."
At that time, the Great King mounted a fine carriage and departed from the city of Kapilavastu, proceeding to the Nyagrodha Garden.
Behind his carriage followed eighty thousand white elephants, adorned with various jewels interspersed as ornamentation.
Upon each of the elephants stood a pavilion made of the seven treasures, most marvelous and subtle.
Behind each elephant were arrayed eighty thousand precious horses, and upon each horse was a golden banner.
The horses and banners were each adorned with the seven treasures, being of the most exquisite and supreme quality.
At that time, there were immeasurable people within the city who had decorated their carriages and mounts.

Their various accoutrements consisted of blue horses and blue chariots, adorned with blue canopies; they brandished blue swords, their garments were all blue, and the saddles, stirrups, cruppers, and reins were likewise entirely blue. Each held a blue banner, and behind every chariot was a retinue of one hundred blue-clad attendants.

Furthermore, there were members of the Śākya clan, each of whom had adorned various excellent chariots with blue, yellow, white, red, and multicolored ornaments; these multicolored chariots and horses were likewise decorated in various colors. Each chariot and horse was further embellished by a hundred attendants in multicolored finery, all in the same manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw King [Śuddhodana] approaching from afar and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to see the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods sporting and playing, you should observe the Śākya clan as they depart from the city of Kapilavastu."
"For what reason?
Because the Śākyas roam about no differently than the gods.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In that wondrous city of Kapilavastu, King Śuddhodana and his retinue—this most excellent of kings—is now arriving; listen closely, listen closely, for I shall speak."
Elephants, horses, and chariots exceeding hundreds of thousands, adorned in various ways with exquisite beauty,
were led out from Kapilavastu— the royal treasure-trove of the king and his various vehicles.
The horse is blue, the chariot is blue, and the adornments are blue;
the retinue’s clothing is entirely blue, as are their boots, hats, swords, and fly-whisks.
The blue whips, blue reins, and blue bells and nets are present, while blue-clad attendants hold blue banners and parasols; both men and horses are blue, most exceptionally wondrous.

Yellow horses, yellow chariot, and yellow ornaments; the attendants' clothing was entirely yellow, as were their boots, hats, swords, and whisks. Yellow whips, yellow reins, and yellow bells and nets;
yellow-clad men held yellow banners and canopies. Both men and horses were yellow, most exceptionally wondrous.
Red horses, a red chariot, and red ornaments; the clothing of the retinue is entirely red in color.
Boots, hats, swords, and whisks are all likewise red; red whips, red reins, and red bells and nets.
A person in red robes holds a red banner and parasol; both man and horse are red, most exceptionally wondrous.
White horses and white chariots with white adornments; the retinue’s clothing is entirely white, as are their boots, hats, swords, and fly-whisks. White whips, white reins, and white bells and nets;
men in white robes hold white banners and parasols. Both men and horses are white, most exquisite and wondrous.
The chariots and horses were of various colors, adorned with diverse ornaments;
the garments of the retinue were all multicolored, as were their boots, hats, swords, and fly-whisks. The whips and bridles were of variegated hues, along with bells and nets;
men clad in many-colored robes carried banners and parasols. Both men and horses were of diverse colors, most exquisitely beautiful.
Behind those chariots were adorned elephants, numbering a full eighty thousand;
with golden saddles, golden trappings, and golden ornaments, each elephant’s back bore a pavilion made of the seven treasures.
There were eighty thousand exquisite dragon-horses, adorned with various ornaments;
embellished with the seven treasures, they were most wondrous and beautiful, followed by a multitude of fine trappings behind the chariot.
They scattered exquisite flowers along the royal road and perfumed the ground with five kinds of incense;
hanging various fragrant jars and silken banners, they adorned the path everywhere with athletes, performers,
and those skilled in song and dance, while musicians played their instruments following behind the King.

At that time, King Śuddhodana and his attendants arrived at the Nyagrodha Grove; they alighted from their carriage and entered on foot, surrounded by the multitude of followers leading and following them.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the heart of his father, the King, was filled with deep resentment, and in order to deliver the King, transcended the human realm and traveled freely through the void of space.

As the Tathāgata proceeded, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, stood to the Tathāgata’s right, and Śakra-devendra stood to his left; the kings of the Suyāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens each held various celestial parasols as offerings to the Tathāgata.

At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa and the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra were on the eastern side of the Buddha; with their right shoulders bared and their right knees touching the ground, they joined their palms toward the Buddha, manifesting an attitude of reverence.

King Virūḍhaka and King Virūpākṣa stood to the west of the Buddha; they also bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees upon the ground, and joined their palms toward the Buddha, manifesting an air of reverence.

At that time, the sons of the gods from the realms of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin rained down celestial *utpala* flowers, sandalwood powder, and *mandārava* flowers from the midst of the sky; they performed celestial music, as well as song and dance.

Furthermore, from the midst of the sky, they rained down various fragrant waters—*utpala* flowers and sandalwood incense powder such as had never before been seen or heard of since ancient times—to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested supernatural powers; by means of this power, he caused people to see the distinct appearances of the devas.
When King Śuddhodana saw the sons of the gods making offerings to the Tathāgata, he conceived a sense of rare wonder.
Furthermore, he saw multi-storied pavilions adorned with the seven treasures filling the void of space; having seen this, he spoke these words:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata was a youth, he felt no lingering attachment to his status as a Wheel-Turning Sage King over the four continents."
For what reason? Now, within this trichiliocosm, he acts as the Great Dharma King, ruling over devas and humans with sovereign wealth and power.
Now this World-Honored One is the True Dharma King; whereas I am currently surrounded by human beings, the World-Honored One is attended by devas and humans.

At that time, King Śuddhodana bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke these words:
“World-Honored One, when you were first born, without anyone to support you, you walked seven steps and surveyed the ten directions, saying:
‘I am the most honored and supreme in the world; I shall attain liberation from the limits of old age, sickness, and death.’”
At that time, I prostrated my head at the feet of the World-Honored One.

Later, I went to a village near a field and sat beneath a Jambu tree in the cool shade; although the sun moved toward the west, the shadow did not shift at all. Furthermore, six celestial youths appeared before the Tathāgata, joining their palms in reverent salutation.
"At that time, I prostrated with my head at the feet of the Great Muni.
Now, for a third time, I again prostrate with my head at the feet of the World-Honored One.
Then King Śuddhodana spoke these verses:
"When the World-Honored One with two feet was first born, without anyone to support him, he took seven steps and declared himself the most supreme in the world;
at that time, I paid homage to the one of brilliant wisdom."
When the Muni left the city and reached the village of fields, the shadow of the Jambu tree remained unmoving over him;
while the youths of the six heavens performed offerings, I then again paid homage to the World-Honored One, the Worthy of Offerings.

Now this is the third prostration, In reverent homage to the World-Honored One, who is compassionate toward the world, Worthy of receiving the exquisite offerings of devas and humans; In the world there is none like the Buddha—how could there be any superior?
The World-Honored One’s original name was Siddhārtha; His title was one cherished by his parents.
Only now do we know that the Tathāgata’s renown is true: His vows have been fulfilled, and he has attained the nectar of immortality.

At that time, the devas of the desire realm prepared a lion throne for the World-Honored One; they spread celestial, exquisite garments upon the throne and throughout the Nyagrodha Garden, and further covered the void with celestial karpāsa-tree garments.
At that time, the World-Honored One descended from the air and sat cross-legged upon the lion throne.
Then King Śuddhodana and his retinue prostrated themselves at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The sons of the gods from both the desire and form realms also prostrated with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side in mid-air.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"King Śuddhodana and his retinue Have come to the World-Honored One to present offerings."
Emerging from the wondrous city of Kapilavastu, he proceeded toward the delightful Nyagrodha Grove.
The Buddha was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude, including the Asura King and the Naga King,
the Kumbhanda King and the Garuda King, as well as the Gandharva King and his retinue.
The great yakṣa kings and their hosts of spirits, the kinnara kings—all have assembled;
the celestial kings of the desire realm and their sons likewise, all give rise to hearts of joy.
The gods of the six heavens of desire are thus; so too are the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities,
along with the Śubhakṛtsna gods and their retinues, up to the Bṛhatphala and Śuddhāvāsa deities,
as well as the great assembly of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and Nirgranthas.
As well as all other various non-Buddhists and practitioners of diverse heterodox arts—
all such groups gathered from every direction.
The Tathāgata manifested his own supernormal powers, causing King Śuddhodana and the Śākya clan to attain faith and achieve great joy.
The Tathāgata, for the sake of all beings, with subtle words and well-expressed meanings,
directed his intention toward King Śuddhodana and manifested various supreme supernormal powers.
The King originally did not permit the Buddha to leave the home life; yet in the past, the physiognomist examined the boy and said:

"If he remains at home, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning King, receiving the offerings of immeasurable billions of beings, possessing the seven kinds of treasures of a noble king, and furthermore being endowed with the four supernormal powers."
Ruling the kingdom according to the Dharma, you are a Kṣatriya king over the four continents.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these words:
"For immeasurable nayutas of kalpas in the past, I have always spoken the truth at all times; Great King, listen attentively as I now speak."
"Great King, from the past until now, you have truly never possessed a heart of faith or reverence toward me;
you wished to make me a Wheel-Turning Monarch, out of attachment and longing for the four continents."
For example, in the distant past there was a divine tortoise that followed the ebb and flow of the ocean tide onto dry land;
when the tidal waters receded and returned, the tortoise fell into a deep well.
An old turtle from within a well questioned a sea tortoise: "From where did you originally come to reach this place now?
The wise sea tortoise answered the well-turtle: "I encountered a rising tide and fell into this well;
when the tidal waters returned to their source, I traveled too slowly and could not keep up."
"Because of this, I have now lost my opportunity and fallen into this small well to dwell with you.
The turtle in the well asked the sea turtle again, "How much is that ocean compared to the water in this well?
Could it possibly be more vast and wide than this?"
"Whether you are great or small, please speak quickly.
The tortoise of the vast ocean of wisdom answered the turtle in the well: 'You who lack wisdom dwell in a place of human excavation;
I reside within the waters of the great ocean, having lived there for many years.'"
They do not even know that the ocean lies within them, let alone understand how to reach its further shore.
Thus, Great King, you are entirely unaware of the power of my supernatural faculties and majestic virtue;
you desire the four continents as a Wheel-Turning King, clinging with worldly ambition and pride to me.
I now manifest as the Wheel-Turning King, ruling over the trichiliocosm;
governing according to the Dharma and free from weapons, I receive the most supreme offerings from the eight classes of beings.
I now recite the words spoken in the past, And have thus appeared before this great assembly.

Cultivating their minds through supernatural powers, And summoning the multitude with thoughts of compassion, All beings from every realm have gathered like clouds; There is none who has not gained pure faith in the King.
Chapter Three: The Prophecy of the Asura King. At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a portentous sign. Because of this sign, the Asura King Vimalacitra thought to himself:
"I shall now be the very first to make offerings to the World-Honored One."

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, together with his retinue of sixty nayutas and his assembly of sixty nayutas of celestial maidens, gathered priceless jewels from the ocean and other treasures not found elsewhere in the sea to present as offerings.

At that time, the Asura King manifested sixty nayutas of chariots made of the seven precious gems. From each chariot, he further manifested sixty nayutas of well-trained horses. Upon each trained horse, he manifested decorative nets of bells made of the seven precious gems; furthermore, he manifested genuine golden bells and bracelets to adorn the horses' legs. Each horse was also transformed to have a topknot and tail wrapped in the seven precious gems. Each trained horse was further provided with bridles of genuine gold, and the horns of all those trained horses were made of the seven precious gems.

Those chariots for taming horses were adorned with the seven treasures; their canopies were likewise made entirely of the seven treasures and followed the movement and stationing of the chariots through the void.
Suspended from each canopy were tassels of seven-jeweled streamers and bells, and above each canopy was manifested a jeweled net that completely covered it.

The chariots, horses, canopies, and bell-nets were blown by the wind, producing subtle and wondrous sounds that captivated both sight and hearing; they were like a hundred skilled musicians performing various melodies, bringing joy to people and stealing their hearts and minds.

Each jeweled chariot was suspended in mid-air sixty yojanas above the ground; behind each chariot various musical instruments were played, and upon each chariot sat asura maidens, adorned with every kind of ornament.
Among these women, some danced while standing, some danced while seated; some sang songs, some moved their bodies about;

some scattered powdered sandalwood incense, some scattered powdered *utpala* flowers, some rained down powdered aloeswood, some rained down *tamālapatra*, and some rained down various celestial powdered incenses.
They scattered powdered incense of the asuras, or rained down gold powder; or they rained down *māndārava* flowers,
*mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers,
*pāruṣaka* flowers, *mahāpāruṣaka* flowers, and *karkarava* flowers, *mahākarkarava* flowers.
Kakāravā flowers, pāṭalī flowers, mahāpāṭalī flowers, citrapāṭalī flowers,
and mahācitrapāṭalī flowers were all miraculously manifested to serve as offerings to the Buddha.
Some scattered flowers of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, agate, and musaragalva; others held the seven precious jewels and scattered them over the World-Honored One.

Some scattered garments; others scattered hand-rings, armlets, anklets, breastplates, bracelets, jeweled crowns, and jeweled garlands—ornaments for adorning the body; gold chains, silver chains, and strings of pearls, both long and short; some scattered neck-turbans made of the seven jewels and various necklaces, gold and silver earrings, or pouches for holding hair made of the seven jewels, all as offerings to the Buddha.

Some wore crests on their heads with arm-bells and bracelets that jingled as they moved; some wore crests inlaid with the seven precious gems and adorned with gold; and some wore crests inlaid with gold and adorned with the seven precious gems.

Some held golden nets; some grasped golden *sūtras*; some held *maṇi* *sūtras*; some held pearl *sūtras*. Some held golden canopies or silver canopies; some held lapis lazuli canopies; some held canopies made of the seven treasures. Some held various jeweled banners, or various colored pennants, or rained down fragrant water—all for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha.
Some, with palms joined, spoke these verses in praise:
"Homage to the Great Man, the Teacher who tames; Homage to the Great Man, the most excellent being;
Homage to the Great Man, the Honored One among two-legged beings; Homage to the Great Man, who is without equal."
I take refuge in the one who illuminates the world; I take refuge in the supreme ocean of great wisdom;
I take refuge in the forest of perfected merit; I take refuge in the most excellent and subtle mountain.
I take refuge in the one who possesses the full assembly of merit; I take refuge in the one who has extinguished all afflictions;
I take refuge in the teacher who cultivates all pure practices; I take refuge in the uninterrupted continuity of pure conduct.
I take refuge in the one who is without dependence and free from cowardice; I take refuge in the one who is without indolence and free from agitation;
I take refuge in the one who resolutely exerts diligence; I take refuge in the one who resolutely attains fulfillment.
At that time, the asura king likewise manifested sixty nayutas of pavilions made of the seven precious gems, which were most wonderful, subtle, and adorned with various colors.

Beneath each and every floating pavilion, there were likewise transformed sixty nayutas of great earths made of the seven treasures; upon those grounds, there were likewise transformed sixty nayutas of watchtowers and battlements, composed of the seven treasures, most subtle and supreme.
Each defensive wall was further transformed into sixty nayutas of multi-storied halls and pavilions, adorned with the seven treasures.
Within each hall and pavilion, there were again sixty nayutas of doors, windows, and casements, decorated with the seven treasures.
Each door had golden frames and silver panels adorned with various precious gems; every threshold was made of lapis lazuli, and every door pivot was made of musaragalva.
Furthermore, the pillars were made of musaragalva; upon each pillar, red pearls formed the capitals and arches, while the floor was made of agate.

As for the silver gates, they all used golden panels, lapis lazuli for the thresholds, musaragalva carved and inlaid with agate for the pivots, red pearls for the columns, white jade for the arches, and crystal for the floors.
The gates were made of vaidūrya, with panels of crystal; the door-sills were of gold, the pivots of silver, the pillars of white jade, the arches of agate, and the floor of red pearls.

The doors and frames were made of crystal; the panels were of lapis lazuli, the thresholds of agate, and the pivots of red pearls. The pillars were of gold, the beams and brackets of silver, and the floor was of white jade.

The doors and windows were made of agate and adorned with white jade; the lintels and panels were made of red *cintāmaṇi* jewels, the door pivots were of silver, the pillars were of lapis lazuli, the base rafters were of gold, and the floor was of crystal.

The doors were made of red pearls and adorned with agate; the doorframes and panels were of white jade, the pivots were of silver, the pillars were of lapis lazuli, the bases and brackets were of crystal, and the ground was of gold.

The gates are made of white jade and adorned with agate; the door-frames and panels are of gold, the pivots are of lapis lazuli, the pillars are of silver, the floor is of crystal, and the architraves and rafters are made of red *cintāmaṇi* jewels.
In each of those gateways, he manifested sixty nayutas of lion thrones made of the seven precious substances.
These were completely covered with the garments of devas, humans, and asuras; some were spread with kācilindika cloth, and others with kauśeya silk.
At both ends of those seats were placed crimson pillows.

Before each of those seats stood a footstool made of the seven precious substances; upon each footstool were six hundred million garments of various kinds belonging to the asura kings, namely: garments from the celestial trees, kṣaumalaka garments, kauśeya garments, and kāśika garments.
Upon each and every lion throne, there were two asura maidens adorned with various precious jewels; each woman held a fan made of *tāla* leaves from the seven treasures.
Within each seat, there was a transformed son of an asura seated upon it, attended on both sides by two women who held fans made of the seven precious gems.

At those various gateways, sixty nayutas of banners and canopies made of the seven precious gems were likewise manifested: at the golden gateways, blue banners with yellow handles were manifested, interspersed with crystal; at the silver gateways, yellow banners with red pearl handles were manifested, interspersed with white silver; at the lapis lazuli gateways, red pearl banners with golden handles were manifested, interspersed with crystal; and at the crystal gateways, multicolored jewel banners with golden handles were manifested, interspersed with white silver.

The blue banners had yellow tops; the yellow banners had blue tops; the red banners had white tops; the white banners had red tops; and those of variegated colors had tops made of the seven precious jewels.

Those various jeweled canopies and halls circled the Buddha three times in mid-air, just as the elephant-king Airāvaṇa of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven travels through the sky, carrying both Pītalaka and Śirīṣa trees as offerings for the devas.
Those various canopies likewise circled three times clockwise through the air in the same manner.

Within those jeweled curtains and defensive enclosures, as well as upon the ground, in the multi-storied pavilions and halls, there were various gateways, lion thrones, and adorned jeweled canopies, banners, and flowers. There rained down celestial sandalwood powder, celestial *utpala* powder, and aloeswood powder; furthermore, there rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, *karkarava* flowers, *mahākarkarava* flowers, *pāṭali* flowers, *mahāpāṭali* flowers, *citrāpāṭali* flowers, *mahācitrāpāṭali* flowers, golden flowers, silver flowers, *vaiḍūrya* flowers, *musāragalva* flowers, and flowers made of all kinds of precious jewels.
Gold rained down, silver rained down, and celestial tree-garments rained down.
All those asura princes held such precious jewels in their hands; by the power of these jewels, they were able to cause whatever they desired to rain down at will.

At that time, outside each of the four gates of the city of Kapilavastu, the area extending sixty yojanas in length and breadth was illuminated everywhere for sixty yojanas by the majestic spiritual power of the asura king; the light shone upward for sixty thousand yojanas, and all around were filled with articles of offering.
Those floating canopies hovered around the Buddha.
At that time, the *mandārava* flowers piled up within the city of Kapilavastu reached a height of seven zhang, and the celestial fragrant water formed a mire.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the fragrance was made to pervade the trichiliocosm.

Within this trichiliocosm, all those who dwell in the Mahāyāna—those sentient beings who, upon smelling that fragrance, even those who have only just first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—attained the stage of non-retrogression, let alone those who have long practiced.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, riding in a chariot made of the seven precious gems, circumambulated the Buddha three times. He scattered exquisite, natural sandalwood powder over the Buddha and spoke this praise:
"I now take refuge in the Bhagavān, Who bestows fearlessness upon devas and humans;
I take refuge in the most supreme and immovable One, Aspiring to unsurpassed, wondrous Bodhi."
I now take refuge in the Bhagavān; with a joyful heart, I shall not fall into the three evil realms.
Therefore, I now take refuge in the Buddha, aspiring for the peerless, wondrous Bodhi.
I now take refuge in the Bhagavān, Who can eliminate the great ocean of suffering of birth and death;
Who can sever the wilderness and is pure, free from affliction; The Teacher capable of guiding all sentient beings.
I now take refuge in the Bhagavān; through this refuge, I seek no further rebirth.
Oppressed by old age and death and beset by great suffering, the World-Honored One is the refuge for all devas and humans.
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra praised the Buddha with verses and circumambulated him three times to the right.

Then, the various horse ornaments, the various chariot decorations, the various adornments of the asuras and asura maidens, and the various banners, flags, jeweled canopies, and bell-nets were stirred by the wind, producing deep and wondrous sounds that were pleasing to the mind and captivating to the ear.

It is like a musician fully endowed with a hundred arts who, through skillful playing and striking, produces a profound and wondrous sound; this agreeable voice is so exquisite that it is worth listening to and captivates both the ears and eyes of others.

Thus, the various ornaments and necklaces upon these horses, even down to the nets of bells, produce subtle and wondrous sounds when stirred by the wind, like the exquisite performance of a hundred kinds of musical instruments, most delightful to hear.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra circumambulated the Buddha three times, raining down powdered sandalwood from the heavens, powdered blue lotuses, powdered aloeswood, powdered tamāla, and various kinds of powdered Asura incense, all descending from the sky.

It rained mandārava flowers, mahāmandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, pāruṣaka flowers, mahāpāruṣaka flowers, karkarava flowers, mahākarkarava flowers, pāṭala flowers, mahāpāṭala flowers, citrapāṭala flowers, and mahācitrapāṭala flowers.
Furthermore, there were various kinds of transformed flowers—flowers of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and even flowers made of the seven precious gems—which rained down from the sky.
Raining down fragrant waters from the heavens and fragrant waters from the asuras, they descended from the sky.

Because of these fragrant waters, the city of Kapilavastu, both inside and out, spanning sixty yojanas in length and breadth, was entirely transformed into fragrant mud. The fragrance of this mud pervaded the entire trichiliocosm; all bodhisattvas who smelled it attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the asura king Vemacitra circumambulated the Buddha three times; by the Buddha’s spiritual power, he produced celestial music and the sounds of asuras in the midst of the sky.

Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the sounds of those various musical instruments pervaded the entire trichiliocosm so that all could hear and know them; and upon hearing these sounds, all those who dwell in the Mahāyāna attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Countless hundreds of thousands of asura maidens sang or danced, played musical instruments, or moved their bodies in various ways; furthermore, they scattered powdered celestial sandalwood, blue lotus powder, aloeswood powder, *tāmarasa* incense, *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, *pāruṣaka* flowers, *mahāpāruṣaka* flowers, *karkarava* flowers, *mahākarkarava* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, *mahāpāṭala* flowers, *citrataru* flowers, *mahācitrataru* flowers, golden flowers, silver flowers, *vaiḍūrya* flowers, and various flowers made of many jewels; they also rained down transformed flowers, scattering them over the Buddha.
Furthermore, they scattered various celestial garments, arm-bells, and leg-bracelets over the Buddha.

They offered waist-garlands, arm-garlands, finger-rings, neck-turbans, wreaths of the seven jewels, golden and silver chains, strings of pearls, *maṇi* necklaces, and crescent-moon pearl necklaces. Upon their two shoulders, they offered necklaces of seven-jeweled robes and various precious necklaces. They offered earrings of *śukti* shells, jeweled hair-pouches, and crowns that adorned the head. There were various hanging tassels—tassels of various scents, tassels of various pearls, and tassels of various *maṇi* gems. Some rained down various jeweled parasols, powdered gold, and fragrant water.

Furthermore, an asura maiden held red pearls in her hand and scattered them over the Buddha; others held various jewels to scatter, and still others held diverse kinds of pearls to scatter—all for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha.
The Asura King Vemacitra and his retinue, all in harmony with one another, spoke these verses:
"With such a mind as this, we have encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
because we take refuge in the Tathāgata, we shall constantly make offerings in the future."

At that time, the offerings presented by the asura king Pāratas were also no different from those of the asura king Vemacitra; mounting a chariot of the seven precious gems, he circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right and praised the Buddha with these verses:
"I pay homage to the one who has attained true power, the ten-fold strength; I also pay homage to the one who is free from fear and possesses fearlessness.
Having definitively attained the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), I take refuge in the guide of all worlds."
I pay homage to the one who has severed all fetters; I also pay homage to the one who has departed from the path of birth and death.
I pay homage to the one who has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground, the Teacher who leads the destitute masses of sentient beings.
I pay homage to the one of profound and inconceivable wisdom, who remains harmonious with the multitude without wavering;
whose mind is liberated amidst all realms of existence, just as a lotus is unstained by water.
The Muni fundamentally cultivated all dharmas of emptiness; Free from all conceptual discrimination, he attained the signless;
In all places, he harbors no aspirations; I pay homage to him who is like space, without dependence.

At that time, the offerings presented by the Asura King Subāhu were vast and immeasurable, no different from those of the Asura King Vemacitra. Mounting a palanquin adorned with various jewels, he circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, scattered golden grains, and praised him in verse:
"The Great Muni is peerless; In the heavens above and the world below, there is none his equal.
The Buddha knows sentient beings to be like a mirage— Not truly existent, but merely the shifting of conceptualization."
In this, there is no agent and no experiencer; there is also no person, for it is empty and selfless.
Free from all conditioned activities and devoid of intrinsic nature, it teaches the dharma of universal quiescence.
Having attained faith and understanding in the Dharma of the Sugata, and perceiving all phenomena as entirely equal,
they shall become sons of the Teacher, following the Buddha’s instructions just as a father speaks them.
The merit obtained from my present praise can only be fully perceived through the wisdom of a Buddha;
by means of this merit in its entirety, I dedicate it so that all sentient beings may become Buddhas.

At that time, there was also the asura king Vajra-vairocana, whose offerings were likewise no different from those of the asura king Vemacitra. Riding a chariot made of the seven treasures, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and scattered silver flowers, then spoke these verses in praise:
"I now pay homage to the Buddha’s wondrous and excellent marks, Who has crossed the ocean of birth and death to reach the other shore.
Having attained liberation himself, he delivers others as well, Establishing them on the fearless shore beyond."

Only the Buddha’s great wisdom knows all living beings: those with forest-like thickets of inverted views and lacking wisdom, who are deluded by mirages and reckon them as real—all this is known by his peerless compassion.
The World-Honored One, the Sublime Person, beholds sentient beings As being like illusions, mirages, and reflected images;
The Muni gives birth to virtuous sons according to the Dharma, Moving through the three realms of existence without being defiled.
The Great Sovereign Person knows they are not real; He knows the nature of all phenomena is empty of self and other.
Fools, like those in a dream, experience sensual pleasures; Having realized this, the Buddha’s heirs cultivate all practices.

At that time, the offerings presented by Rāhu, the Asura King, were also like those presented by Vemacitra, the Asura. Mounting a chariot made of the seven precious gems, he circumambulated the Buddha three times, scattered *citrāpāṭalī* flowers over the Buddha, and spoke this verse in praise:
"The divine and wondrous body of the Great Seer, the Tathāgata, Surpasses all devas and humans;
It is as if Mount Sumeru were compared to a mustard seed, Or as if the great ocean were likened to a cow’s footprint."
The Tathāgata’s countenance is most upright and handsome; adorned with the various marks, he is foremost and supreme.
Surpassing all that exists within the realm of form, he is like the rising sun, while the glow of fireflies fades away.
The World-Honored One is a mass of immeasurable majesty and virtue, surpassing all who possess majesty and virtue;
he causes all such powers to be unable to manifest, just as the glow of fireflies vanishes when the sun rises.
The ocean of wisdom of the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, transcends and pervades the three realms of existence;
it eclipses all non-Buddhists so they do not appear, just as the intense light of the sun causes the moonlight to vanish.
At that time, the offerings presented by the asura king Śambhala were also like those of the asura king Vemacitra.

Having completed his offerings, he mounted a chariot made of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He scattered mahāpāṭalī flowers over the Buddha and spoke this verse in praise:
“Those who delight in śamatha and wisdom Are able to eliminate the three poisons: greed, hatred, and delusion.”
He leads sentient beings out of the mundane world, Just as sweet rain extinguishes the flames of dust.
The World-Honored One’s blazing Eye of the True Dharma Is like clarified butter poured onto a great, raging fire;
It can sever the entire web of afflictions and doubts, Just as a fire consumes a vast wilderness.
His countenance is upright and exceedingly subtle; adorned with the marks of excellence, he is foremost among all.
He surpasses every exquisite form, just as the glow of fireflies vanishes when the sun rises.
The Tathāgata upholds all roots of goodness through immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas;
he is able to eliminate afflictions and evil karma, just as consuming nectar removes poison from the body.
He blows away all the darkness of ignorance, like a bright torch illuminating the night’s gloom;
the Tathāgata manifests the eye of the True Dharma, just as a master jeweler reveals the value of a gem.
At that time, the offerings presented by the Asura King Rāvaṇa were also like those of the Asura King Vemacitra.
Having completed his offerings, he mounted a chariot made of the seven treasures, circumambulated the Buddha three times, scattered various precious flowers, and praised him with these verses:
“The Buddha can tame the unruly and evil mind, Just as a valiant warrior subdues a superior enemy.”
Having well attained mastery over a supple mind, I pay homage to the one whose mind is disciplined and fearless.
Able to discipline all faculties and remain free from enmity, he is free from fear, fearless, and has attained peace.
O World-Honored One, afflictions no longer arise; you have utterly extinguished and subdued all poison and harm without exception.
With the strength of Nārāyaṇa, he has well-cultivated loving-kindness; his mind remains impartial toward both the beloved and the hateful.
The Tathāgata knows the characteristics of all sentient beings, and thus they are not encompassed by the six realms of existence.
Detached from all perceptions, with the mind’s craving for existence exhausted, He radiates the light of wisdom to shatter all darkness;
With no attachment in his mind toward any phenomena, The Muni transcends all, beyond compare.
At that time, the offerings presented by the asura king Sunetra were also like those of the asura king Vemacitra.

Having completed his offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven treasures, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and offered a treasury of various jewels to the Buddha, praising him with this verse:
"The Great Hero has long since known The true nature of all phenomena."
That which is called a "dharma" is a mere conventional designation formed by the combination of various factors.
The essence of all dharmas cannot be found when sought in any way whatsoever;
what is referred to as "this dharma" is said to be nothing but a provisional name.
Detached from names, the nature of names is empty; all characteristics are likewise so.
Without characteristics, there is no name; thus one is already detached from these three kinds of phenomena.
As for that which is called "explanation," in reality, there is nothing to be revealed or expressed.
The speaker has no speech, and the listener is likewise so.
Knowing the Dharma in this way, the sons of the Unsurpassed Muni do not cling to any phenomena, practicing with great renown.
At that time, the offerings presented by the Asura King Subduer of the Three Realms were also like those of the Asura King Vemacitra.

Having completed his offerings, he mounted a chariot of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. He then offered a necklace of genuine pearls to the Tathāgata and spoke these verses in praise:
"I now praise the Buddha, who has transcended all enemies, Whose countenance is upright and handsome, and who possesses the power of wisdom and the precepts."
In all the worlds there is none like the Buddha, who subdues adversaries with his peerless body.
His physical power and radiance illuminate the three realms; through the cultivation of various wholesome deeds, he attained such perfect countenance.
By the power of his generosity, he acquired the [major] marks, and the eighty minor characteristics are all perfectly adorned and pure.
The power of his pure observance of the precepts cannot be shaken; it is beyond the reach of the deliberations of wise men.
Because the Buddha’s mind of ethical discipline is pure, this Lion among Men has accomplished what he set out to do.
The Tathāgata’s power of wisdom is peerless; through fearlessness, he triumphs over the three realms.
Like a lion king roaring amidst the herd, he transcends all those of the external paths.
At that time, the offerings presented by the asura king Vairocana were also like those of the asura king Vemacitra.

Having completed his offerings, he mounted a chariot made of the seven precious gems and circumambulated the Buddha three times. Holding various jewels in his hands, he scattered them over the Tathāgata and further praised him with these verses:
"The multitudes have all gathered at the abode of the Muni; With pure hearts, they gaze upon the face of the Tathāgata."
All behold the World-Honored One present before them; this is an uncommon mark of the Tathāgata.
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, each understands it according to their own various inclinations;
the World-Honored One speaks in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings—this is an uncommon mark of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind;
they comprehend its meaning as they desire—this is the unique characteristic of the Tathāgata.
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, some cultivate progress, some achieve subduing, and some attain the fruit of no-more-learning; this is the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the offerings presented by the asura king Mucilinda were also like those of the asura king Vemacitra.

Having completed his offerings, he mounted a chariot made of the seven treasures and circumambulated the Buddha three times. Holding red pearls in his hand, he scattered them over the Buddha and spoke these verses of praise:
"With a joyful and pure mind, I revere and trust the Buddha; Free from arrogance and devoid of false views."
Following the Buddha’s Āgamas and practicing heedfulness—this is the peerless practice of a son of the Buddha.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena cannot be apprehended; like one who dreams of indulging in desire, they are entirely empty.
They arise merely according to the movement of thought and do not truly exist; the World-Honored One knows all phenomena in this very way.
Like autumn clouds or the moon reflected in water, they may delude ignorant and foolish sentient beings,
but they cannot confuse or attach the wise person who deeply delights in the Buddha-dharma and exerts diligence.
The wondrous person, most wondrous and unerring in awakening, Is heedful within the Buddha-dharma;
Discerning all phenomena as being like a dream, They attain the wondrous samādhi that perceives reality as it is.

At that time, sixty nayutas of asuras, including the asura king Vemacitra and others, having made their offerings, all joined their palms in prostration and stood there. Elated and leaping with joy, their hearts were filled with delight and satisfaction, and the bodhicitta flowed through them without interruption.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that those asuras had made offerings with faith, manifested a smile in accordance with the dharmas of all Buddhas. From his face, he emitted light of immeasurable colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, crystal-like, as well as gold, silver, and various other hues. Having issued from his mouth, the light circled the Buddha three times and re-entered through the crown of his head.

At that time, the venerable monk Aśvajit rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, paid homage to the Buddha, and questioned him in verse:
"The heroic and courageous Muni has manifested auspicious signs; The Compassionate One who pities the world does not act without cause.
O Supreme among Men, we pray you explain The causes and conditions for what the Great Sage has manifested."

Out of compassion for the world, you manifest auspicious omens; seeing the superior offerings of the asuras, you wish to bestow upon them the definitive prediction of enlightenment, so that we and our like may attain great joy.
In the morning, they possess a resolute mind free from doubt; among this assembly, there are those who have awakened the aspiration for enlightenment.
Knowing that their faculty of faith is mature, the World-Honored One, the Lion among Men, manifests these auspicious signs.
Who at dawn has awakened a pure mind?
Who among men has given rise to supreme faith?
Knowing that their faculty of faith is mature, the World-Honored One manifests this most wondrous and sublime omen.
Now this great assembly all harbors doubt, seeing the Tathāgata manifest a smile;
who else could it be that this morning subdued the Māra-enemies?
For whose sake has this auspicious sign been manifested?
Excellent, Great Sage who has subdued all enmity! We pray that you will sever the doubts in the minds of this great assembly.
We pray that the Honored One will speak swiftly without hesitation, and cut through the web of doubt of this multitude.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered the bhikṣu Aśvajit with a verse:

“Excellent is the meaning you have asked, bhikṣu! The auspicious sign I have manifested for the benefit of the world— I shall explain its fruit and retribution without omission; Now listen with single-minded attention.”
The asuras made offerings to the Buddha, seeking supreme and unsurpassed bodhi;
their minds were free from dependence, like a hand in space, unobstructed.
Having thus made these offerings to the World-Honored One, the assembly of asuras attained purity of mind;
with great wisdom, they all abandoned the path of asuras and enjoyed happiness for a long time among humans and devas.
In a future age, these shall encounter as many Lion-like Teachers of Men as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
they shall attain Buddhahood during the eon named *Kalyāṇanāman*, and all such Tathāgatas shall be known by the name *Kalyāṇa*.
Having completed sixty nayutas [of lifetimes], his fame resounded throughout the ten directions, illuminating the world;
he expounded the Dharma that is independent and unattached, extensively delivering multitudes of superior devas and humans.
Those buddha-fields are exceedingly adorned and pure; The Buddha knows that the world is free from the five turbidities.
He purifies buddha-lands throughout the trichiliocosm, Fulfilling sixty nayutas of them.
That land is devoid of the three evil realms; with a joyful mind, its soil is pure.
That Buddha, heroic and fierce, eliminates all calamities and expounds the unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma.
Those Buddhas attained a lifespan, remaining in the world for sixty nayutas of kalpas;
they expounded the Dharma that is without dependence, and each and every Guide was likewise so.
After those Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa and all the wise ones of the world have likewise passed away,
for sixty nayutas of kalpas, the True Dharma of those Buddhas shall remain in the world.
Each of these Tathāgatas individually delivers multitudes of sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
those Tathāgatas are all immeasurable, and their lands, lifespans, and the duration of the Dharma are likewise so.
Those Sugatas were able to bring to maturity sixty nayutas of sentient beings,
causing them all to dwell securely within the Mahāyāna, so that each might successively inherit the lineage of the Triple Gem.
"Now this prophecy for the asura, which benefits the world, has been spoken by the Great Sage.
Having heard this prophecy, the devas and humans leaped with joy in body and mind, attaining pure faith.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Two;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi.
Chapter Four: Past Deeds, Part Three; Chapter Sixteen: The Assembly Where the Bodhisattva Saw Reality.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having seen the various asura kings make offerings to the Buddha, gave rise to a sense of wonder and reflected thus:
"What roots of goodness did the World-Honored One cultivate when he was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, such that he obtained this karmic fruit?"

Then Kāśyapa immediately entered the *yathābhūta-samādhi*. By means of the power of the mind adorned by that samādhi, he recollected all the merits cultivated by the Tathāgatas throughout incalculable upon incalculable *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas. He clearly remembered all the roots of goodness cultivated in various paths and various births, which had all served to fulfill unsurpassed bodhi; through these roots of goodness, they had attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), and he came to know and remember all those roots of goodness.
At that time, as Kāśyapa recollected the Tathāgata’s great roots of goodness, he thought to himself:
"The roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddha are vast and expansive.

If every single sentient being within all the world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions were to attain a human body, and if those beings, having attained human bodies, were to provide offerings to the Sugata for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; and if each and every one of those beings were likewise to provide offerings to the Tathāgata for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—even after such offerings, they would still be unable to repay the Tathāgata for a single root of goodness arising from one moment of his resolve."
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa arose from samādhi and praised him in verse:
"Each and every Tathāgata, the Honored Muni, Has resolved his mind upon the vast awakening of Bodhi.
The offerings made by these asuras and others Do not equal even a single *kalā* of the Buddha."
The World-Honored One, the Arhat, supreme among men, is like Mount Sumeru or a mass of pure sandalwood;
he is the most excellent among gods and humans, worthy of offerings, because he has crossed to the further shore of merit.
The Lion among Men, who deserves offerings surpassing those given to as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—
just as one might offer an ocean filled to the brim with water, blended with fragrant perfumes.
Endowed with all virtues and worthy of offerings, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
one might heap up flowers to make offerings to them until they reach the height of Mount Sumeru.
The Great Being, naturally worthy of offerings, is like a lamp with a wick upon Mount Sumeru;
taking the great ocean as a vessel for fragrant oil, he makes this lamp-offering to all the Victors.
Worthy of receiving offerings and possessing great majesty, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
because they have crossed to the further shore of merit, they establish stupas and temples to make offerings.
The steadfast one among men, worthy of offerings, was honored with vast and supreme jeweled parasols that completely covered the trichiliocosm for the duration of nayuta eons.
The Honored One among men, who has compassion for the world, Whose boundless merit merits offerings—
May he be honored with various jeweled banners, Pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Throughout inconceivable billions of eons, one makes offerings with vast banners,
filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for immeasurable billions of eons.
Having made offerings to the Tathāgata, the Lion among Men, he has arisen through discernment to compose this analogy;
O sons of lions among the great masters, all you devas and humans, listen attentively, listen attentively!
Myself and all those gathered here in this assembly, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and all beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions— may they all attain Buddhahood.
The Lion among Men, endowed with the ten powers, has as many heads as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
each head likewise possesses as many heads as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and upon each of those heads are as many [eyes] as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Each possesses mouths as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
within each of those infinite mouths, there are tongues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with which they praise the Tathāgata.
Those Tathāgatas cannot exhaustively describe them; The further shore of their merit cannot be reached;
The wisdom of omniscience is immeasurable, Because they have crossed to the further shore of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, bhikṣus!"
My śrāvakas abide uprightly; possessing wisdom and the Dharma, they are like the Brahmā gods, and are thus able to enter the ocean of my merits. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is endowed with immeasurable merit; he is endowed with inconceivable merit.
O bhikṣus! The accumulation of the Tathāgata’s merit is inconceivable.

"O Bhikṣus! If the mass of the Tathāgata’s merit were to have form, the merit obtained from each single arousal of the thought of enlightenment would not be contained even within worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Why is this? O bhikṣus!

The merit of each single thought-moment of the Tathāgata, which is the object of omniscience, cannot be measured even by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; it is impossible to describe it exhaustively.

Why is this? When the Tathāgata originally cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, there was not a single arousal of the mind that was not for the benefit of all sentient beings and those included within the category of sentient beings; there was not a single arousal of the mind that was not for the sake of all sentient beings.
The realm of sentient beings is boundless, and the sentient beings therein are likewise boundless.
As the realm of sentient beings is boundless, so too is the merit of each single thought-moment generated by the Tathāgata boundless.

Why is this? Just as the realm of sentient beings is boundless and just as the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable, so too the mass of merit from each single thought of enlightenment of the Tathāgata cannot be exhausted; it is for the sake of pitying, benefiting, and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings that he thus resolves his mind.
Even if all sentient beings were to make offerings at such a time, they could not repay even a single portion of the merit of the Tathāgata’s initial resolve. Why is this?
It is because those sentient beings who offer to the Tathāgata do so out of a desire for worldly rewards, such as various forms of food and material gain.

When a bodhisattva first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment, they abandon the mind that seeks worldly rewards through various forms of sustenance; rather, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, they desire to cause sentient beings to turn their backs on birth and death and proceed toward nirvana.
"When the Tathāgata was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he acted for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, abstaining from mixed foods and seeking no worldly retribution.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the past, during immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable aeons of beginningless worlds—within an unspeakable number of kalpas of cyclic existence—there appeared in the world a Buddha named Indradhvajarāja, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
That Buddha-Tathāgata, with each single thought of enlightenment, has generated the resolve to bring benefit and peace to sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Monks! When that Tathāgata Indradhvaja became a Buddha, worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges formed a single buddha-field.
The land of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Indradhvaja was adorned and pure, being free from the evil destinies and the eight difficulties."
In the buddha-field of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Indradhvaja, all sentient beings abide in the group of those destined for rightness (samyaktva-niyāma).

There are absolutely no sentient beings of wrong determination (mithyātva-niyāma) or those with overweening pride (adhimāna); there is a total absence of impure physical action, impure verbal action, and impure mental action; furthermore, there are no afflictions leading to the miserable realms, nor any karma that produces rebirth in the miserable realms.

Why is this? The Tathāgata Indradhvaja instructed these sentient beings, causing them to resolve their minds on awakening and to cease all evil, and he bestowed upon them wholesome dharmas, commanding them to practice and study them.

Within the buddha-field of Tathāgata Indradhvaja, five kinds of bliss were once attained: namely, first, the bliss of desire; second, the bliss of renunciation; third, the bliss of dhyāna; fourth, the bliss of samāpatti; and fifth, the bliss of unsurpassed bodhi.
Although those sentient beings experience that pleasure, they do not become greedily attached to it.
Just as a honeybee takes only its flavor and does not take the flower's color, so too are those sentient beings; although they experience that pleasure, they do not grasp at or become attached to it.
Just as a flying bird moves through the air without clinging to that air, so too it is with sentient beings who experience pleasure without grasping or attachment; it is exactly like this.

In the buddha-field of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Indraketu, all sentient beings have no sorrow or suffering, but only joy and bliss; nor do they experience sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant.
Because ignorance is absent, there is only joy that accords with the mind. Why is this?
Because those sentient beings have fundamentally cultivated wholesome deeds.

When that Tathāgata Indradhvaja was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he manifested various marks and signs to cause those sentient beings to refrain from all evil, establishing them in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas. They gradually departed from all evil realms and were settled in wholesome states; thus, they became entirely and completely free from all kinds of unwholesome karma.
When the karmic results of the actions they have performed are realized, their minds do not rejoice.
It is impossible for them to experience painful sensations, because one who has not committed evil deeds does not undergo the fruit of suffering.
Because ignorance is absent, neither painful nor pleasant sensations are also absent.
In that buddha-field of the Tathāgata Indradhvaja, at all times there are never fierce winds or torrential rains, nor is there any poisonous heat.
For those sentient beings, the suffering caused by the changes of the seasons is entirely non-existent.

When that Tathāgata Indradhvaja was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, all the physical actions of the sentient beings within his buddha-field were governed by wisdom; they proceeded according to supreme wisdom, and he expounded, revealed, and clearly manifested this for them.

In this way, all forms of knowledge regarding vocal karma—the foremost knowledge that proceeds accordingly, is expounded, elucidated, and correctly revealed—are likewise [the same as] all forms of knowledge regarding mental karma—the foremost knowledge that proceeds accordingly, is expounded, elucidated, and correctly revealed.

When those sentient beings have heard this from that bodhisattva, all their physical actions, all their verbal actions, and all their mental actions—guided by wisdom and directed toward supreme wisdom—are transformed and dedicated; because of these wholesome deeds, the retribution of delusion does not arise.
Because of their ignorance, they experience sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant;
however, among those sentient beings in that Buddha-field, painful sensations and sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant are entirely absent, because they have abandoned ignorance.
When those beings are born in that land and have been taught by the Tathāgata Indraketu, they will revere the Dharma.
As they travel about, they will contemplate the Dharma, cherish the Dharma, and be deeply attached to the Dharma.

Their minds were stained by the defilement of sensual desire; while moving about for the sake of the Dharma, they experienced no painful sensations, nor did they suffer any discomfort regarding their deportment—whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, or waking.
Those sentient beings within that land have no evil to which they might conform; because there is no evil, no suffering can arise.
They have no attachment to the wholesome; by this cause and condition, those sentient beings lack the suffering of change because they do not conform to evil.
They do not give rise to craving or attachment toward any phenomena; therefore, the suffering of disintegration does not arise.
Nor is there the suffering of association with the disliked. Why is this?
Because those beings abide in a state where an impartial mind toward all sentient beings is manifest; therefore, there is no suffering of association with the disliked.
Nor is there the suffering of being separated from what one loves. Why is this?

Because those sentient beings do not cling to any phenomena; since the suffering of separation from what one loves arises from attachment, they are thus without the suffering of being separated from what one loves.
Suffering as suffering also does not exist. Why?
Because one does not give rise to attachment toward pleasant feelings.
There is only the suffering of conditioned formations, which is to say, the suffering of impermanence. Why is this?
Because that Buddha teaches only the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

That Buddha remained in the world for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; in that buddha-field, not a single sentient being who would challenge the Buddha in debate was born in his land. Why is this?
"This is because that Tathāgata, when he was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, brought sentient beings to maturity.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?"

Can one, by means of inferior roots of goodness, scanty roots of goodness, roots of goodness that have been poorly cultivated, roots of goodness associated with non-virtue, roots of goodness lacking great diligence, roots of goodness not leading to happy rebirths, roots of goodness not well-initiated, or roots of goodness not well-dedicated, truly benefit such sentient beings and grant them happiness while removing their suffering?
"Is it possible to purify such a vast land and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha spoke again to the bhikṣus, saying:
"What do you think?"

Can a mind that is dejected, associated with the unwholesome roots of cowardice and weakness, lacking in diligence, not having well-cultivated the faculties, not tending toward the wholesome, not having well-activated the wholesome roots, and not being well-dedicated, be able to benefit such sentient beings by contemplating the granting of happiness and the removal of suffering?
"Is it possible to purify such a vast Buddha-field and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“What do you think?”

Can a faith that is inferior, meager, feeble, timid, associated with unwholesomeness, lacking in diligence, not having well-accumulated roots of goodness, not tending toward the wholesome, not having well-aroused roots of goodness, and not well-dedicated—can such a faith benefit these kinds of sentient beings by removing their suffering and bestowing happiness?
"Can one purify such a vast Buddha-field and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?"

Can a precept that is inferior, meager, weak, lacking in diligence, lacking in the thorough accumulation of roots of goodness, lacking in a wholesome rebirth, lacking in the wholesome arousal of roots of goodness, or lacking in wholesome dedication, be able to benefit such sentient beings by removing their suffering and bestowing happiness?
"Can one adorn and purify such a vast Buddha-field and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“What do you think?”

Could one with inferior diligence, meager diligence, feeble diligence, cowardly diligence, uncorresponding diligence, non-diligent diligence, diligence that has not well accumulated roots of goodness, diligence that does not lead toward excellence, diligence that has not well aroused roots of goodness, or diligence that is not well dedicated, be able to benefit such sentient beings as these by removing their suffering and bestowing happiness?
"And can you purify such a vast Buddha-field and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
"Bhagavān. The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think?"

Could a thought that is inferior, meager, feeble, timid, a thought not associated with roots of goodness, a thought lacking diligence, a thought not well-accumulated in roots of goodness, a thought not directed toward the good, a thought not well-aroused in roots of goodness, or a thought not well-dedicated, be able to benefit sentient beings or contemplate bestowing happiness upon them?
"And can you purify such a vast Buddha-field and bring many sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
“World-Honored One.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “What do you think?”

Can one who possesses a concentration that is inferior, meager, feeble, timid, a concentration of roots of goodness that is not associated [with wisdom], a concentration lacking diligence, a concentration in which roots of goodness are not well-accumulated, a concentration that does not lead to a good destination, and a concentration in which roots of goodness are not well-aroused, truly benefit sentient beings by contemplating the bestowal of happiness?
"Can one purify such a vast Buddha-field and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "What do you think?"

Could one with inferior wisdom, meager wisdom, feeble wisdom, timid wisdom, wisdom that is not associated with roots of goodness, wisdom that is not diligent, wisdom that has not well accumulated roots of goodness, wisdom that is not well-directed, or wisdom that has not well aroused roots of goodness, be able to benefit sentient beings by contemplating the bestowing of happiness upon them?
"Are you able to adorn and purify such a vast Buddha-field and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “Bhikṣus! ”

It is indeed so; one cannot benefit sentient beings, contemplate their happiness, or bring them freedom from suffering by means of meager roots of goodness, meager morality, meager faith, meager diligence, meager mindfulness, meager concentration, or meager wisdom; nor can one purify a vast Buddha-field and bring such a multitude of sentient beings to maturity through these alone.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Do you know who that Tathāgata Indradhvaja was at that time?"
After the Tathāgata had thus questioned them, the bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, to the east, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there was a world named Moonlight Adornment.
In that land there is a Buddha named Ghaivideharāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells in the world.
Mañjuśrī, being among that assembly, immediately understood the thought in the mind of Śākyamuni and addressed the Buddha Ghaivideharāja, saying:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is currently preaching the Dharma in the Sahā world."
“World-Honored One!
I shall now go there to see Śākyamuni Tathāgata, to pay homage, listen to the Dharma, and offer worship and respect.
Having made this request, the Tathāgata King of High Majesty and Virtue addressed Mañjuśrī:
"You may depart as you wish;
now is precisely the right time.

At that moment, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata King of High Majesty and Virtue, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Just as it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, at that moment Mañjuśrī vanished from that world-system called Moonlight Adornment and reappeared before Śākyamuni Buddha.
He bowed his head to the Tathāgata’s feet in prostration, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Indradhvaja of former times was none other than the World-Honored One himself.”

Why is this? Because the World-Honored One is fully endowed with inconceivable skillful means, capable of maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-lands, remaining forever free from weariness and never satiated; thus, the World-Honored One establishes sentient beings in the Bodhisattva Vehicle without ever feeling weary or satisfied.

If there is a person who speaks the truth and utters correct speech—one who is the most excellent among the excellent, the most sublime among the sublime, the foremost among the excellent, and the most supreme among the most supreme—and says, "The Buddha is such," you should know that Śākyamuni Buddha is truly and without exception so.
Then Mañjuśrī spoke these verses: “Heroic and skilled in expedient means, Out of compassion for all the worlds,
He manifests great majestic spiritual power For the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity.”
In past ages, you have already served eight hundred million buddhas;
yet, possessing your own spiritual power, you had no intention of attaining perfect enlightenment.
You purified sixty-one sets of three thousandfold world systems as your pure buddha-fields.
Those of shallow understanding do not know the Buddha, The skillful means of the Muni.
Without abandoning his initial resolve, He manifests in various places;
Furthermore, in future ages, He will manifest as immeasurable Buddhas.

Chapter Five: The Prophecy of the Garuḍa Kings At that time, there were also eight hundred and sixty million kings of the garuḍas. Having seen the asuras making offerings to the World-Honored One and receiving their prophecies, they conceived a peerless, reverent faith toward the Tathāgata. Leaping for joy and filled with delight, they manifested eighty-six million palaces for the sake of making offerings, adorned entirely with the seven treasures of the devas, which were most marvelous, subtle, and exquisite.

Each hall has seven tiers of railings made of the four precious substances, which are the most exquisite and sublime, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. As for the golden railings, gold is used for the lintels and the various pillars, while silver is used for the curved crossbars.
Regarding the silver balustrades: the horizontal beams and the various pillars were made of silver, while the curved crossbars were made of gold.
As for the beryl balustrades, the beams and pillars were made of beryl, and the crossbars were made of crystal.
The railings were made of crystal, as were the beams and pillars, while the crossbeams were of lapis lazuli.

Around those halls on all four sides hung bells made of the seven treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, musaragalva, and agate—which were exquisite, marvelous, subtle, and unsurpassed.

These halls were further covered above with nets made of the seven treasures—namely, nets of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musāragalva, and agate—which were of the most exquisite and supreme quality.
Furthermore, he further manifested eighty-six million canopies made of the seven treasures, subtle and extraordinary, namely gold, silver, and so forth, up to agate.

He further manifested eighty-six million exquisite banners made of the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, and so forth, up to agate: blue banners with yellow tops, yellow banners with blue tops, red banners with white tops, white banners with red tops, multicolored banners with solid-colored tops, and solid-colored banners with multicolored tops.
Furthermore, he further manifested eight hundred and sixty million exquisite banners made of the seven treasures, adorned with various colors, the most pure and magnificent of all.

He further manifested eight hundred and sixty million canopies made of the seven treasures—namely gold, silver, and so forth up to agate—woven from precious threads, the most subtle and exquisite of all.
