At that time, the various Garuḍa kings took these eight hundred and sixty million palaces made of the seven treasures, eight hundred and sixty million canopies made of the seven treasures, eight hundred and sixty million banners made of the seven treasures, eight hundred and sixty million pennants made of the seven treasures, and eight hundred and sixty million curtains made of the seven treasures, and offered them all to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
Having made this offering, those bird-kings and their articles of worship circled the Buddha three times in the air.
It was like the elephant king Pāṇḍaravaṇa in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, who carries the gods upon his head and travels through the sky to the Pārijātaka tree.
Those bird-kings, carrying these celestial palaces, canopies, banners, and curtains, soared through the air and circled the Buddha three times, just as before.
At that time, having respectfully circumambulated the Buddha, those bird-kings withdrew to stand to one side; bowing with palms joined, they praised him in unison with a single voice in verse:
"Homage to the one who has transcended birth and death! Homage to the one who delivers beings from birth and death!"
I take refuge in the peerless and steadfast Hero; I take refuge in the unsurpassed and incomparable Sage.
May I attain a steadfast body, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and further graced by the eighty secondary characteristics; may we become just like the Teacher.
May my halo be endowed with majestic power, And may my physical form and meritorious qualities all be perfected;
May I attain the foremost dignity of a Buddha, Causing the minds of others to be purified and realize nirvana.
May they fully uphold the precepts and samādhi, and likewise attain the supreme wisdom of all Buddhas;
may they all become Buddhas to deliver all beings, just as the Buddha now acts as the Guide of the world.
World-Honored One, I vow to be endowed with the ten powers, And likewise reach the shore of the eighteen unique qualities;
May I attain the Buddha’s wisdom that transcends the world, Just as the Tathāgata now is, the most supreme among the supreme.
He also knows that sentient beings have no inherent nature, Like illusions and dreams, they have no basis;
He proclaims them to be like echoes and like space, Just as the Buddha speaks for the assembly today.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the various bird kings had attained respectful faith, manifested a smile.
Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, seeing the Buddha’s smile, questioned him with a verse:
“O Supreme Guide, unsurpassed among men, You do not manifest a smile without cause.”
O Compassionate One who pities the world, please speak for me: what is the cause and condition for manifesting this smile?
Those kings of birds have already made offerings to the Buddha, and jeweled palaces, banners, and streamers appear in the sky, causing wonder among these gods and humans;
O Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, I pray that you explain this meaning.
The entire great assembly stands with palms joined, their profound minds pure and all filled with joy;
they wish to hear of the future fruits for the Golden-Winged One, and pray that the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings will explain this meaning.
Once the Supreme among Men has spoken, the entire great assembly is free from doubt;
having abandoned doubt, the assembly attains fearlessness, for the Tathāgata’s wisdom brings them joy.
The great assembly rejoiced and attained fearlessness; free from all faults and evils, their minds were pure.
That assembly delighted in hearing the Tathāgata speak, just as disciples receive the words of their teacher.
May you sever the doubts in the minds of the great assembly; may the Buddha accept them so that they may rejoice.
As the multitude gathers together in delight, may you proclaim the future fruits of the Golden-Winged One.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered the Venerable Aśvajit with these verses:
“The One of Ten Powers is truly transcendent beyond all; He is fully endowed with the eightfold Brahma-voice.
Having subdued his faculties for the sake of Aśvajit, He speaks of the future fruit of the garuḍa.”
Excellent, Aśvajit, that you ask about this meaning; out of compassion for the world, I manifest a smile.
Listen attentively as I explain it with delight; let your heart rejoice and cast away the net of doubt.
The King of Birds made sublime offerings to me, seeking the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi;
having attained those dharmas—the ten powers of knowledge and the four fearlessnesses—he became a Teacher.
Furthermore, they seek the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), and with these offerings of golden-winged garuḍas,
they present them to the Sugata; they also seek a firm and indestructible body, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
the pure precepts and samādhis of a Buddha, and the great wisdom of the Buddhas' realm.
Having accomplished the Pure Land to deliver the world, the Golden-Winged One seeks this [offering] to make offerings to me.
Once they have offered with faith to me, the wise shall be able to leave the realm of animals;
they will surely be born in the heavens—this is their final body in the evil paths.
Thereafter, for as many eons as the sands of the Ganges, they shall constantly be born among humans and in the heavens;
having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, they shall attain Buddhahood and subdue all their faculties.
In that Buddha-land there are no evil realms; beings possess complete physical marks and are free from the eight difficulties.
That Buddha is named Samantavyūha (Universally Handsome), and the eon is called Sumeruketu (Sumeru Banner).
For eighty-four million years, he remained in the world out of compassion for the sake of the world;
at that time, the lifespan and the buddha-activities of all those Sugatas were entirely the same.
That Buddha has transcended fever and crossed over afflictions;
in each of his eighty assemblies, there are eight hundred million people who, free from pride and arrogance, have attained mastery.
Because he originally possessed a golden body and always harbored great pride due to his immense power,
when he later attained Buddhahood for the sake of sentient beings, he severed that pride and turned the wheel of Dharma.
In the past, they were a multitude of sages who had practiced extreme austerities;
numbering eight hundred and sixty million, all their practices were for the sake of supernatural powers.
When those seers attained supernatural powers, they marveled at their own ascetic practices as rare;
though they were unbroken in their prohibitions and precepts and possessed merit, they gave rise to arrogance while dwelling in the forest.
Due to pride, one is born among the garuḍas; through mental mastery, one possesses supernormal powers;
because of pure precepts, one attains the vision of the Buddha; yet due to pride, one forgets the bodhicitta.
Thus the Buddha bestowed the prophecy of enlightenment and spoke of the original birth of the Golden-Winged Bird;
having heard this, the great assembly was filled with joy, and through that joy, they all became vessels for enlightenment.

Chapter Six: The Prophecy for the Dragon Maidens At that time, nine hundred and sixty million dragon maidens, having witnessed the various asuras and garuḍas making offerings to the World-Honored One and receiving their prophecies, felt great joy arise within their hearts.

Filled with joy and exceeding delight, he conceived a heart of devotion toward the World-Honored One and manifested nine hundred and sixty million parasols, all fashioned from the seven precious gems.

It was covered above by nets of vaidūrya, with borders made of red *cintāmaṇi* jewels; the stems of the canopies were of gold, and the canopy tops were of vaidūrya jewels, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, with tassels of various gems hanging down on all four sides.

He manifested nine hundred and sixty million horses; they were blue horses with blue complexions, blue forms, and blue light, all their ornaments being entirely blue, with reins and bridles made of *vaiḍūrya* gemstone.

In the space above, he manifested a great and majestic maṇi-jewel chariot; upon that chariot was a jeweled palace, sixty yojanas in length and breadth, which completely covered the entire assembly of those who had gathered.

On the four sides of that palace, nine hundred and sixty million banners made of various jewels were magically manifested; they hung down everywhere, most marvelous and subtle, their radiance so dazzling that it captivated the hearts and eyes of all.
He manifested a jeweled net that completely covered the palace hall, and further, precious bells were suspended from the four sides of the hall.
He also manifested seven-jeweled cranes, egrets, and white doves, which flew in succession around the four sides of the hall.
Furthermore, he manifested nine hundred and sixty million varieties of nāga music.
At that time, the nāga maidens, riding upon those blue horses, each cast up a precious parasol and traveled naturally through the void of space.

These nāga maidens each took up musical instruments and played various melodies; they circumambulated the Buddha three times and scattered divine sandalwood powder, divine aloeswood powder, *tamarā* leaf powder, pure celestial gold powder, and various nāga flowers—furthermore, having magically transformed them into diverse kinds of blossoms—over the Buddha.

Furthermore, they scattered *utpala* flower garlands, various multi-colored garlands of diverse flowers, and garlands of various immeasurable mixed incenses; they also offered various immeasurable garments of diverse colors and various immeasurable necklaces of diverse colors as offerings to the Buddha, just as those asura kings had done.
At that time, when nine hundred and sixty million nāga girls performed music, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the sound pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, the world-system of the Buddha.
Among those sentient beings who hear this sound, they shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Within the great and majestic pavilions made of various jewels, and amidst the rows of jeweled tassels and flocks of birds, nets of precious bells are struck by gentle breezes, producing exquisite sounds that are harmonious, elegant, and most delightful.
Just as the sounds produced by a person skilled in a hundred musical arts and well-trained in performance are harmonious, elegant,
and lovely, so too are the sounds produced by the great and majestic palace, even from its network of bells.

This sound also pervades the Buddha-worlds of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system; among those beings who hear this sound, none shall regress from their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, those nāga maidens again rained down various celestial flowers and various celestial incenses, which fell together with the water; the fragrance of these flowers and incense could reach everywhere—whether with the wind, against the wind, or neither with nor against the wind.
Because of the fragrant water, the city of Kapilavastu—extending sixty yojanas in both length and breadth—was entirely transformed into fragrant mud.
The scent of this fragrant mud pervaded the entire trichiliocosm; when the sentient beings therein smelled this fragrance, they also attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, after those nāga daughters had made offerings to the Buddha—with nine hundred and sixty million parasols, nine hundred and sixty million horses, nine hundred and sixty million musical instruments, and all manner of precious ornaments and ritual implements—they bowed their heads to the Buddha in the air, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side.
With bodies bent and palms joined, they praised him in verse: "The wives of the nāgas possess wisdom; Their hearts leap with joy and gladness.
They make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, Seeking the peace of great bodhi."
He manifested nine hundred and sixty million precious parasols and exquisite adornments,
making offerings to the Sugata of well-tamed mind, thereby departing from all obstacles.
Furthermore, he manifested nine hundred and sixty million exquisite horses along with their decorative trappings;
both the horses and their ornaments were all blue in color, and there were also blue banners.
Those horses all traveled through the air, proceeding to where the Buddha was to present their offerings;
the nāga women, all possessing hearts of faith and reverence, prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata.
Within the dragon palace, he manifested music, which he brought here for the sake of making offerings;
having arrived, he presented it to Śākyamuni, the Great Teacher who is worthy of receiving offerings.
The Sugata caused the sound of those musical instruments to pervade the trichiliocosm;
having heard it, immeasurable sentient beings all became irreversible from the bodhicitta.
Those nāga maidens, in mid-air, magically transformed a great palace of many jewels,
sixty yojanas in length and breadth, completely covering all the multitudes throughout the ten directions.
The jewel named Blazing Light of Majestic Virtue Shines universally throughout the great trichiliocosm;
Before that assembly of nāga maidens, With pure hearts and joyful minds, they made offerings to the Buddha.
Giving rise to a heart of peerless joy and exultation, they sought the fruit of peaceful enlightenment, saying:
"May we all become Buddhas for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."
We vow that among immeasurable multitudes, we shall preach the Dharma to deliver them from the entanglements of all afflictions,
just as the Great Guide of Ten Powers manifests to rescue sentient beings who suffer in distress.
All phenomena are like illusions and mirages, And like bubbles on water, lacking solidity;
They are also like the foam produced by falling rain— One should know that all phenomena have no master.

Sentient beings are like images and like shadows; having thus observed the world, we pray that you will explain for the sake of the multitude the nature of phenomena, true suchness, and the limit of reality.
Just as the Buddha is faultless and has clearly perceived the Dharma, so too do false and deceptive appearances delude the ignorant;
like a magical illusion, they have no reality, serving only to confuse and bewilder ordinary worldlings.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding phenomena and lack wisdom; they do not know the true nature of all phenomena.
The Guide has already seen each and every phenomenon, and is further able to cause other sentient beings to understand them.
Clouds arise in the void and spread to cover the earth; yet one sees those clouds in the sky as being like reflections.
They have no substantial essence and nothing upon which they rely; likewise, they are like shadows, devoid of reality.
Thus sentient beings have no intrinsic nature; they can only deceive the gates of the sense faculties.
The Buddha’s wisdom perceives the realms of existence in this way: they can only deceive those who lack wisdom.
The World-Honored One, through this karma, brings benefit to those of wisdom;
the Tathāgata manifests as having no intrinsic nature, for the sake of the true reality of all sentient beings.
Only by means of the true Dharma do I gladden my sons, acting as a bridge over the mire of birth and death;
the true Dharma is not the domain of the foolish, for they cling to the sound and do not seek its meaning.
I take refuge in the Buddha, who is boundless, The one who fully manifests reality,
Who acts as a close savior for the ignorant, And serves as a home and a spiritual friend.
Thus, seeking great enlightenment, we make offerings to the Honored Teacher;
may we attain Buddhahood to awaken others, and benefit the world just as the Buddha does.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the dragon maidens had attained deep faith, manifested a smile.
Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya asked in verse:
"O Supreme Knower among those wise in the world, The Most Excellent Guide has manifested a smile."
One who honors the firm virtue that is like a mountain now manifests a smile; it cannot be without cause.
O Supreme Lord, most excellent among men, pray tell us the reason for this smile.
Should devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits hear it, they will all give rise to great joy toward the Buddha.
The Guide of the World is renowned throughout the world; he always knows all phenomena of causes and conditions.
There is not a single dharma that the Buddha does not understand; the Buddha fully knows every variety of causal condition.
I only pray that the Sugata will deign to explain it; may the Buddha reveal the cause and condition of his smile as he knows it.
If the entire great assembly should hear it, they will all give rise to joy and cast off the net of doubt.
The Tathāgata’s sublime Dharma brings great benefit; this great assembly shall surely obtain it.
If this assembly attains a mind of tranquil concentration, it will be due to the benefit of the flavor of the sublime Dharma.
Once the Buddha’s power has caused all conceptual discrimination to cease, they will delight only in Bodhi and listen to the Buddha’s teaching;
if they hear the causes and conditions for his smile, they shall surely achieve the path of Buddhahood.
If a person harbors doubt regarding the Dharma, their mind becomes restless and gives rise to suffering;
those present in this great assembly today are such people, for they do not know the cause and condition of this smile.
The great assembly is capable of severing the web of doubt; we pray only that the Guide will cause it to be extinguished.
Quickly speak for the sake of the multitude to deliver us: by what causes and conditions did you manifest this smile?
Who today has a mind of pure clarity?
Who today has subdued the enemies that are Māra?
Who has given rise to reverent faith toward the Buddha?
Who today makes offerings to the Buddha?
We pray that the Teacher will proclaim before this great assembly who possesses such power;
having heard it, we shall give rise to a joyful heart, and having given rise to a joyful heart, we shall attain peace and happiness.
This entire great assembly bows in reverence; all possess minds shrouded by the net of doubt.
We pray that you explain the cause of your smile to bring forth joy, and that the World-Honored One alone shall sever the doubts of the multitude.
Once these devas and humans have heard this, the great assembly shall be freed from the net of doubt;
if they hear what the Tathāgata speaks, all shall attain a heart of joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Aśvajit in verse:
“Excellent, excellent, wise Aśvajit! You are able to ask the Tathāgata about the cause and condition of my smile.
Having seen the nāga maidens present their offerings, I smiled out of compassion for the world.”
I shall now declare that fruit for you; listen with a sincere mind, free from all faults and evils.
As for the reason why I have manifested this smile, you, Aśvajit and the others, listen to my words.
These nāga maidens have minds free from attachment; seeking great bodhi, they practice and progress.
Cultivating the emptiness of the world through wisdom, they are firmly established on the path to bodhi.
In this, there is no agent and no experiencer, nor is there any one who gives birth or nurtures;
there are only phenomena and nothing else, and these phenomena are likewise false, like a mirage.
Because they recognize my kindness, they make offerings to me; they are able to know reality through wisdom.
Excellent is the Buddha’s understanding of all worlds—that which is called seeing them as empty and without a master.
Delighting in this cultivation of emptiness, though they provide offerings, they regard them as like an illusion;
regarding the vows they have made for supreme enlightenment, they contemplate that enlightenment itself as being without attachment.
Having made peerless offerings to the Buddha and having contemplated that sentient beings are empty and quiescent,
they forever leave behind the bodies of the dragon realm and evil destinies, and dwell together with Śakra among the devas.
Having experienced supreme bliss in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, when his lifespan as a devaputra there has ended,
no one can disparage his reputation, and he is reborn again in that Yāma Heaven.
While dwelling in the palace of the Yāma Heaven, they fully experience the supreme and wondrous pleasures of that celestial realm;
the sons of the Buddhas who reside therein remain until the very end of that heaven’s lifespan.
These sons of the Buddha, having fully experienced such bliss and completed their lifespan in the Yāma Heaven,
shall again attain rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven, where they will become of the same class as the devas of that place.
Constantly surrounded by celestial maidens, he fully experiences the supreme and wondrous pleasures of that heaven;
his mind remains unattached as he dwells in the good path, like a lotus flower unsullied by water.
That deity, by means of great wisdom, observes that all worlds are empty;
just as letters carved upon stone do not perish, so too his mindfulness is never lost.
Those sons of gods dwelling in that heaven, fully experiencing the supreme and wondrous pleasures therein,
when their lives in that auspicious realm have ended, shall proceed once more to be reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.
He attains a good reputation that none can disparage, and receives supreme offerings from the celestial maidens;
though he dwells in the celestial palaces, his mind remains unattached until the very end of his lifespan in those heavens.
Within that celestial palace of the Nirmāṇarati devas, he fully experienced the superior rewards of heavenly bliss;
once that wise one’s life had ended, he attained the ultimate realization regarding all phenomena.
Reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, Acting as a great caravan leader with pure faith,
Dwelling in that heaven with a mind free from defilement, One dwells thus, delighting in the Dharma.
Dwelling in those celestial palaces, they experience the most exquisite pleasures of the five senses;
free from delusion, they abide in the wholesome path until the full exhaustion of their allotted lifespan.

Though they experience celestial desires, they perceive their faults; seeking joyfully in tranquility and nirvana, they practice and attain meditative concentration, and at the end of life, they are reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
In the Brahma palace, he was well-versed in dhyāna; Receiving the fruit of that meditation, he enjoyed the bliss of quiescence.
With peerless wisdom, he remained for one kalpa, Vowing to seek the unsurpassed, great bodhi.
Dwelling in that Brahma palace for the duration of an eon, He abides well in majestic deportment while seeking wisdom;
Through skillful means he benefits the world, Extensively performing deeds that are boundless and immeasurable.
The wise abide in the Brahma-palace and delight in dhyāna; yet they do not cling to dhyāna, remaining in nirvāṇa.
Knowing that attachment to the bliss of dhyāna is also a fault, they quiet the sense-faculties and seek bodhi.
With a mind of faith and resolve toward all things, they abide securely in all bodhisattva practices;
knowing that all meditative concentrations possess the characteristic of being deceptive, they seek only the quiescence of great nirvāṇa.
Those sons of the Buddhas therein seek the fruit of peaceful enlightenment;
dwelling in those Brahma palaces with pure minds, they contemplate the benefit of the world and skillfully discipline their hearts.
The various Brahmās and others teach naturally, yet what they preach as the Brahma-teaching does not transcend the world;
only the path to Bodhi of the Buddhas can ultimately lead one beyond the mundane world.
When Brahmā had thus conceived faith, he resolved his mind to abide securely in the Buddha-dharma;
he realized that the original teachings of Brahmā were merely natural laws and not the ultimate path for transcending the world.
In accordance with the Dharma of the Sugata, he speaks this Dharma for the sake of the world;
just as the fruit described by the Eye of Dharma, may those who hear it quickly come to understand it.
While they dwell in those Brahma palaces, having performed various benefits for the world,
they are able to establish immeasurable nayutas of billions of beings upon the path to enlightenment.
Throughout immeasurable nayutas of kalpas, he shall make offerings to all Buddhas;
later, in the future Star-Constellation Kalpa, with his faculties stilled, he shall become a Buddha.
The devas, humans, nāgas, and asuras, The garuḍas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, The kumbhāṇḍas,
pretas, and kiṃnaras— The entire great assembly was filled with joy.
All of them were converted by the Buddha; having gained mastery within the Buddha-dharma, they all joyfully joined their palms and prostrated themselves, bowing their heads at the Buddha’s feet.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-three;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi.
Chapter Seven: The Prophecy of the Dragon Kings; Chapter Sixteen: The Bodhisattvas’ Realization of Truth, Part Four.

At that time, Nanda, Upananda, and the other nine hundred million dragon kings, having seen the dragon maidens present such exquisite offerings and having heard that the dragon maidens had received their prophecies, gave rise to a sense of wonder and unprecedented amazement, and reflected as follows:

"Furthermore, it is rare and unprecedented for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, World-Honored One, to possess such qualities as these. Because the Tathāgata knows the faculties and the deep faith of all sentient beings, there is not the slightest portion of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma that they do not see, hear, or realize. This is his excellent teaching, which enables the great assembly to know it directly upon hearing it; there is no time when this does not occur. According to their capacities, he bestows the Dharma so that they must attain the fruit, enabling all wise ones to realize and know it in the present."

Even women, who are fickle and restless and possess shallow wisdom, are still able to understand the profound Dharma taught by the Buddha; how much more so, then, the other wise ones—the assembly of disciples who are well-established in the Dharma of the Tathāgata.

"Just as women, even when their desire, anger, or delusion are predominant, are still able to understand what the Tathāgata has taught, so too the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, along with all the other dragons, gave rise to a sense of rare wonder and a sense of unprecedented devotion toward the Tathāgata. For the sake of making offerings, they raised clouds that covered the entire world—including all the mountains and great oceans of Jambudvīpa—and rained down fragrant water everywhere to form a bed of fragrant mud."

The fragrance of that fragrant mud pervaded the trichiliocosm Buddha-field; all sentient beings therein who smelled the fragrance did not regress from their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In the city of Kapilavastu, which was sixty yojanas square, red pearls rained down, completely covering the ground; furthermore, various kinds of priceless jewels covered the entire circumference of the Nyagrodha Garden.
Furthermore, he transformed the Dragon Flower into a wondrous hall, sixty yojanas in length and breadth, with rafters, pillars, beams, and walls all fashioned from the seven treasures.
He further manifested immeasurable musical instruments, which, for the sake of making offerings, produced sublime sounds when struck.

Within that subtle and wondrous Hall of Nāga-flowers, he manifested nine hundred million various multicolored flower tassels suspended from the ceiling; he covered the precious pillars with lapis lazuli nets and spread priceless jewels across the floor beneath the hall.

That jewel is soft and supple, like the *pañcakaṣāya* stone of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; its color is like lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), and its touch is as soft as *kācalindikā* cloth—subtle, delightful, and captivating to the eye, causing all devas and humans to cherish it with longing and constant mindfulness.
Those various jewels are likewise so.

Among those various kinds of maṇi jewels, some emit cool, refreshing flames; some emit blue water, some emit red water, some emit white water, and some emit yellow water; others emit water of variegated colors, and yet others emit cool and pleasant breezes.

There were some precious jewels that produced whatever things all sentient beings required; others produced rich, fertile lands; and there were *maṇi* gems that served as clear mirrors, within which the entire great assembly appeared. Furthermore, among the people born within the great city of Kapilavastu, whether few or many, they all appeared within those jewels.
The entire assembly beheld the Buddha and his śrāvakas performing these various supernatural transformations.
By the power of those maṇi jewels, various multicolored precious canopies, various multicolored precious banners, and various multicolored precious streamers emerged from within the ground.
Furthermore, there emerged various kinds of flower tassels, as well as various kinds of incense tassels, various kinds of jewel tassels, and various kinds of pearl tassels.
Furthermore, various multi-colored dragon banners emerged, and various nets of bells made of many kinds of jewels emerged.
Additionally, various multi-colored fine horses emerged; all that was produced was through the power of the dragons.

At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, along with nine hundred million dragons, drove those fine horses and followed on foot, circumambulating the World-Honored One three times to the right, scattering exquisite, soft *kācilindika* jewels over the Blessed One.
The various kinds of precious jewels that emerged from the ground beneath that hall ascended into the void and rained down upon the Tathāgata and the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, with the immeasurable musical instruments of the nāgas, exquisite and subtle sounds spontaneously issued forth in the sky as an offering to the Buddha.

At that time, nine hundred million nāgas circumambulated the Buddha three times; standing before the Buddha with palms joined, they remained silent as they recollected the Buddha’s merits, gazing up at the Tathāgata without ever averting their eyes for a moment.
They took delight in the Buddha’s merits, for their profound minds were firmly established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

After they had silently recollected the Buddha’s merits with palms joined for a short while, they bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, prostrated themselves before him with their five limbs touching the earth. Then, with one voice, the assembly praised him in verse:
“Having long cultivated majestic deportment and the marks of a hundred blessings, Your compassionate mind is free from defilement and your conduct is perfected.”
Having renounced the inexhaustible ground of manifold jewels, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Kapilavastu.
For six years he practiced austerities; though the Tathāgata did not yet attain the path of the Deathless, the mind of the Sugata did not falter or despond, for he had long cultivated wisdom.
The Tathāgata is truly the Teacher of Gods and Humans; for the sake of the world, he practiced austerities.
Even when people hear of them, they cannot endure it, let alone behold them with their own eyes.
The Muni of the past gave away his head and eyes; as for the bodhicitta thus gathered by the Sage, we feel no joy upon hearing this, because of having heard of the Tathāgata’s ascetic hardships.
When the Buddha was formerly the Seer Kṣāntivādin, King Kali severed his hands and feet, and cut off his ears and nose;
yet he felt no anger. Hearing of this, we are unable to endure it.

As the Buddha placed his body upon the scale-pan, And did not abandon the bird that sought refuge in him, We too, having heard this, find no joy; The Tathāgata underwent such great hardship in the past.
Why is it that our hearts find no joy?
Because the World-Honored One has undergone such extreme suffering; and when those who have committed evil against the Tathāgata fall into the evil realms, the Buddha again feels compassion for them.
Great Guide endowed with noble wisdom, how can one practice a mind of non-harming?
Cultivating the path of practice free from blemish—O Buddha, we pray that you will teach the practice of peace and bliss.
Now these hosts of nāgas have resolved their minds, seeking the bodhi-practice of the Sugata;
they are able to practice everything as the Buddha has taught—only pray, quickly speak the path to bodhi.
These hosts of nāgas are filled with deep longing, seeking only the state that is neither born nor dies;
may you explain the Tathāgata’s practice of peace and security, so that these sentient beings may easily be transformed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the assembly of nāgas making their offerings and hearing them make their vows, and knowing their profound faith, manifested a smile.

It is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they manifest a smile, they emit immeasurable rays of light of various colors from the gateway of their faces; these rays shine everywhere, reaching up as far as the Brahma Heaven, and having shone, they return and enter through the crown of the Buddha’s head.
At that time, the venerable monk Aśvajit asked in verse:
“Excellent, O Śramaṇa, Great Muni! It is not without cause that you manifest a smile.
O Compassionate Teacher, I pray that you will explain the reason for this peerless, virtuous smile.”
The great assembly gazes up with longing to hear of the World-Honored One’s immeasurable meritorious deeds;
having conceived doubt upon seeing his smile, they find no joy. We pray only that the Dharma King will sever the doubts of the multitude.
Who within the Dharma of Śākyamuni has now given rise to reverent faith and joy?
Who has caused Māra Pāpīyas today to have a confused mind and no delight?
Who today is able to serve with reverence the Great Teacher, the Father of Dharma endowed with merit?
Who shall perform the foremost and most excellent offering?
May the Lion of the Śākyas explain this supreme matter.
This great assembly joins their palms together, all gazing up at the Buddha with reverence;
we pray that the Guide will dispel our web of doubts and explain to the multitude the cause and conditions for his smile.
Having heard this, the great assembly was filled with joy; they were able to understand the World-Honored One’s teaching of the True Dharma.
The Greatly Wise World-Honored One gladdened the multitude, who, in accordance with the True Teaching, dwell in perfect peace.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya with these verses:
“The Great Teacher of the assembly, possessed of profound and vast wisdom, Speaks with the eightfold Brahma-voice when teaching.
With a pure mind free from all defilement, Listen attentively as I explain the cause and conditions for my smile.”
These dragon kings, with hearts of reverence and faith, have made offerings to me that surpass all others;
they do so for the sake of seeking the Buddha’s bodhi and for the benefit of the entire world.
With compassion as my primary motive, I observe sentient beings; how can there be joy when there is no guide?
How may I attain great enlightenment and bring sentient beings to maturity without weariness?
Deeply delighting in tranquil concentration and endowed with wisdom, Riding the vehicle of peace and bliss with a pure mind,
Regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, They have practiced these for immeasurable eons.
With a mind of equanimity, he contemplates the world, Just as the Buddha perceives the marks of wisdom;
His thoughts of loving-kindness, compassion, and joy are all impartial, For the sake of bringing peace and security to the world.
Those who possess the first compassion and are filled with pity shall attain Buddhahood according to their wish;
having surveyed the world, they shall become Teachers known by the name "The One Without Enmity."
When they attain the nectar of immortality, there shall be no Māra-enemies nor any others;
they will constantly proclaim the Dharma of non-self, never uttering a single worldly word.
Those Tathāgatas, endowed with great compassion, cause all sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s wisdom;
when these Sugatas preach the Dharma, all sentient beings believe and understand it.
When they cultivate the path throughout successive lifetimes, it is not difficult for them to bring sentient beings to maturity;
once those matured beings have heard the Dharma, they shall attain liberation and realize the nectar of immortality.
All who hear the Dharma attain liberation; all these sentient beings are upright and majestic.
All sentient beings are able to understand the teachings spoken by those Tathāgatas;
among all ghosts, spirits, and animals, there are none who do not comprehend the Buddha’s words.
Once all have attained mindfulness of the Dharma, they will be able to understand the Tathāgata’s nectar-like Dharma.
There is no sentient being who, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, would not then give rise to a heart of love and joy;
those who love and rejoice in what that Buddha has taught shall all attain the nectar of immortality.
At that time, all those who were to be transformed shall attain liberation from birth, old age, and sickness, as well as liberation from death, grief, lamentation, and suffering;
having heard the Buddha’s teaching, their minds will be free from defilement.
Thus did Śākyamuni Buddha, speaking the intentions of the nāgas to answer the sons of the Buddha,
turn them according to their firm wisdom in their minds, for the sake of attaining peerless bodhi.
The Tathāgata bestowed predictions upon those nāgas; having heard this, the great assembly was filled with joy.
Once the assembly rejoiced, they took refuge in the Buddha, and all became completely serene in mind.

Chapter Eight: The Prediction for the Kumbhāṇḍas At that time, there were further one hundred and eighty million kumbhāṇḍas who, seeing the asuras, garuḍas, nāga girls, and nāga kings making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing their predictions, were deeply satisfied in their hearts. They leaped for joy with great delight, conceiving a sense of rarity and experiencing what they had never before encountered, thinking:

"The merit and wisdom of the World-Honored Tathāgata are subtle, wondrous, and supreme. That he receives such rare offerings without being surprised or elated is because the Buddha’s wisdom is the most honored and victorious among all forms of wisdom."
It is, for example, like the great ocean, which neither increases nor decreases. Why is this?
Because it is profound and vast.
In this same way, the World-Honored One’s mind neither increases nor decreases when receiving superior offerings;
it is likewise so. Why is this?
Because he harbors no doubts regarding any phenomena.

At that time, one hundred and eighty million kumbhāṇḍas, for the sake of making offerings, manifested one hundred and eighty million parasols, all of which were fashioned from the seven precious jewels: parasols with cords of gold, parasols with cords of silver, parasols with cords of lapis lazuli and various jewels, parasols with cords of crystal beads and various jewels, parasols with cords of red pearls and various jewels, parasols with cords of agate beads and various jewels, and parasols with cords of musāragalva beads and various jewels.

Those *kumbhāṇḍas* [adorned] the various jewel canopies with suspended jewel tassels of diverse colors: there were jewel canopies with golden threads and silver-threaded tassels, silver-threaded jewel canopies with golden-threaded tassels, lapis lazuli canopies with crystal tassels, crystal jewel canopies with lapis lazuli threads for their tassels, red pearl canopies with *śaṅkha* (conch-shell) tassels, *śaṅkha* jewel canopies with red pearl threads for their tassels, and agate jewel canopies with crystal tassels.

Furthermore, he further manifested one hundred and eighty million chariots made of various jewels, also of diverse colors and most wonderfully exquisite, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, musaragalva, and agate.

Upon that chariot, he further manifested one hundred and eighty million canopies made of various jewels, which were connected to the chariot; each jewel canopy had a hundred children, and the shafts of all those canopies were made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.

Upon that jeweled canopy, he further manifested various kinds of jeweled flower tassels to adorn it—namely, tassels of golden flowers, silver flowers, *vaiḍūrya* flowers, crystal tassels, red-jewel tassels, dragon-gem tassels, and red pearl flowers—and further covered its surface with a net of red pearls.
Furthermore, he further manifested the music of kumbhāṇḍas, producing various sounds to delight the Buddha.
He further manifested one hundred and eighty million horses of myriad precious colors, tamed and swift, to draw his chariot.
At that time, the kumbhāṇḍas each mounted a precious chariot and circumambulated the Buddha three times, scattering flowers made of the seven treasures over him.

Then those kumbhāṇḍas descended from their chariots and approached the presence of the Buddha; having prostrated with their heads at his feet, they again circumambulated him three times. Bowing with palms joined, they stood to one side and praised him in verse:
“Neither increasing nor decreasing, the Great Muni is like Sumeru, the king of all mountains.”
He who receives this unsurpassed offering is the Tathāgata, for he has attained fearlessness.
He contemplates all sentient beings as being merely names and merely functions, without grasping or attachment;
because the Guide has cultivated the samādhi of cessation, the wise one is free from arrogance.
The Muni knows the world to be like an illusion, And like the enjoyment of desires within a dream;
Furthermore, it resembles the moon reflected in water or a mirage in springtime— Thus he observes it, leaving nothing unexamined.
For example, a city of the gandharvas has no reality; though sought throughout the ten directions, it cannot be found.
That city has no substance and exists as a name alone; the Buddha perceives all worldly phenomena to be exactly like this.
Worshipped by all humans and devas with jeweled chariots, jeweled canopies, and music, with banners,
flowers, tassels, incense, and palms joined in reverence— the World-Honored One perceives these as being like echoes and shadows.
Having made these offerings, we pray that in the future we may become Buddhas;
may we also realize that the world is like a dream, and having realized this, may we preach the Dharma just as the World-Honored One does.
We behold those afflicted by suffering, oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death;
may we know the deathless Bodhi of the Buddha and preach it so that all who hear may attain liberation.
Among all sentient beings who lack wisdom, may I attain Bodhi and preach the Dharma for them;
may I expound the stainless and untainted Dharma, acting as a guide for those who have no path.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the kumbhāṇḍas and others had conceived deep faith, manifested a smile.
Then, the venerable monk Aśvajit asked in verse:
"The Buddha does not manifest a smile without cause; Nothing is rare that he does not find wondrous."
The Tathāgata does not smile without cause; I now wish to hear the reason for this.
All devas and humans have doubts upon seeing the smile appear from the Buddha’s mouth.
We pray that you will sever the web of all our doubts and proclaim, O World-Honored One, the matter of this smile.
Who has attained deep faith in the True Dharma?
Who is able to see the Compassionate Father according to the Dharma?
Who practices the offerings praised by the Buddha?
O Supreme among Men, I pray that you hear me:
who today, amidst conditioned phenomena, perceives their faults and is able to relinquish them?
Who today is able to abide in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
I wish to hear from those with pure minds:
who is able to subdue Māra and his retinue?
Who is able to cause the Buddha’s heart to rejoice?
Who is able to reach the profound bottom of conditioned existence?
I vow to hear [this] so as to sever my doubts.
The entire great assembly stands with palms joined, desiring to hear the causes and conditions for the Tathāgata’s smile.
"May you sever the doubts of all sentient beings; O Most Honored of the Two-Legged, please grant them this prophecy.
Then the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya in verse:
"Excellent, Kauṇḍinya, that you ask about this meaning; you bring great benefit to the world."
Because you ask about the cause and conditions for my smile, listen attentively, Aśvajit, as I now explain.
The hosts of kumbhāṇḍas have made offerings to me; their minds abide in the dharma of cessation.
Seeing me, they were not startled or alarmed; with hearts filled by a sense of wonder, they gave rise to aspirations.
Today they have made offerings to me; their minds discern the Dharma of tranquility.
With deep-seated faith, they give rise to great compassion, acting as a path for those who have lost their way.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, they made offerings to me; For those who had lost their way, they gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness.
Having performed such deeds, these wise and noble ones Shed their ghostly bodies and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Lord of Devas, with a heart of constant compassion, repeatedly instructs him while in heaven;
having attained freedom from doubt regarding all dharmas, he becomes a kinsman of Śakra.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have practiced the Buddha-way in every single land,
donning the firm armor of great and vast vows, and making offerings to those who possess the Great True Dharma.
Throughout immeasurable lands, his mind shall never grow weary as he purifies them;
acting as a guide to benefit the great masses, he shall attain Buddhahood under the name Adbhuta.
When he travels through various lands, the people of those countries will surely know that he will attain Buddhahood;
by this skillful means, even as he delivers sentient beings in future ages, they will harbor no feelings of strangeness or suspicion.
Seeking the unsurpassed path of peace and security, they purify all buddha-fields without ever feeling weary;
their minds remain unattached to whatever they do, and it is the same regarding great enlightenment.
The reason for my smile has been answered; the doubting minds of all sentient beings have been severed.
The great assembly, freed from doubt, has attained joy, and through meditative concentration they know that he is worthy of offerings.

Chapter Nine: The Prophecy for the Gandharvas At that time, there were also thirty-six million hosts of gandharvas who, seeing the asuras, garuḍas, nāga girls, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, and others making offerings to the World-Honored One and hearing his prophecy, were filled with joy and delight in their hearts. They felt a sense of wonder and attained what they had never experienced before, exclaiming:
"How rare! How unprecedented!"

Even though the dharma-realm as taught by the Tathāgata is without change, he demonstrates the growth of roots of goodness through purposeful action; and although there is no agent, he demonstrates the performance of deeds.
When those gandharvas had thus understood this Dharma, they conceived a heart of reverence toward the Tathāgata and resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having rejoiced, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, he manifested thirty-six million great nāga-elephant kings named Airāvaṇa, each possessing six tusks.

Upon each tusk, seven ponds were manifested; within each pond, seven lotus flowers were manifested; each lotus flower was transformed into one with a thousand petals; upon each petal, seven jade maidens were manifested; and between each petal, seven handmaidens were manifested. They were adorned with ornaments made of various celestial jewels, and they further held celestial incense as an offering.

Furthermore, upon the head of each of the *pīlavaṇa* elephant kings, he manifested three hundred and sixty million canopies; tassels of the seven treasures hung from the four sides of the canopies, and nets of the seven treasures covered them above.

Furthermore, upon the head of each of the Pāṇḍara-vāhana elephant kings, he manifested three hundred and sixty million canopies, all fashioned from the exquisite incenses of the devas, with silken streamers and tassels hanging from their four sides.

Having manifested as three hundred and sixty million *Airāvaṇa* elephant kings, those gandharvas each mounted their elephants and played celestial music as they circled the Tathāgata thirty-six times through the air. They scattered divine sandalwood powder, divine aloeswood powder, divine *tamāla* leaf powder, divine pure gold powder, *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, *pāruṣaka* flowers, *mahāpāruṣaka* flowers, *karkarava* flowers, and *mahākarkarava* flowers; furthermore, they manifested flowers made of the seven precious gems and scattered them over the Buddha.
When those gandharvas and others scattered the fragrant flowers, the scent of these flowers spread in all directions—against the wind, with the wind, and across—without exception.

Furthermore, they rained down various kinds of sublime celestial perfumed water; as this perfumed water fell, it formed a fragrant mud throughout the city of Kapilavastu, covering an area of sixty yojanas in both length and breadth, perfectly equal on all sides.
The fragrance of that fragrant mud pervaded the trichiliocosm; all sentient beings within it who smelled the scent never regressed from their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When the music was performed, its sounds filled the trichiliocosm; all sentient beings therein who heard these sounds also attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In this manner, each of the gandharvas individually made offerings upon the heads of three hundred and sixty million elephant kings, causing the jade maidens to perform music, some to sing, and some to dance.
When those jade maidens performed songs and dances, they caused the entire great assembly to gaze upon them with single-minded attention.

Furthermore, there were jade maidens who moved their hands and bodies, some scattering powdered candana and others scattering powdered agallochum; they extensively made offerings that were no different from the rites prepared by the asuras.

At that time, the gandharvas each mounted the head of the great elephant king Airāvaṇa and, having circled the Buddha thirty-six times in the air, descended from their elephants and circled him three more times. Prostrating with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, they bowed with palms joined and stood to one side, praising him in verse:
“The World-Honored One’s supreme wisdom transcends the Peak of Existence; Having himself emerged, he further delivers others.
In all the world, none is equal to the Buddha; His marks and signs, his radiant countenance, are most upright and handsome.”
The most wondrous among men, of boundless renown, manifests inconceivable displays within the world;
yet seeing not even a single dharma as differing in nature or characteristic, he causes sentient beings to abide in goodness.
The dharma of suchness is devoid of change; it consists merely of verbal expression and possesses no further meaning.
There is neither an object of action nor an agent of action; yet, nevertheless, the Buddha transforms all sentient beings.
Neither coming nor going, and likewise unborn—thus the Buddha can expound such a Dharma;
though he teaches that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, the Hero of the World causes beings to cultivate the Path.
There is not a single dharma that can act of its own accord; yet the wise of the world speak of action.
While all dharmas are individually devoid of self-awareness, the World-Honored One manifests all activity.
Just as a chariot is assembled from many parts, yet those parts do not know their own capacity to act,
and the functioning of the chariot is visible to all— so too, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are.
All phenomena do not instruct one another, nor do they mutually awaken each other;
all things likewise do not rely upon one another, for dharmas are fundamentally neither born nor do they die.
The Buddha speaks thus according to worldly convention; In worldly convention, all phenomena are not entirely non-existent.
Just as the essential nature of worldly phenomena abides, Having understood this, he teaches it for the sake of the multitude.
Thus has the World-Honored One spoken of all dharmas; the deeds performed by his great compassion are most extraordinary.
The essential nature of all dharmas cannot be seen, yet the Tathāgata, through skillful means, explains their nature.
May we become those of boundless renown, great guides endowed with the marks of a hundred merits;
through great compassion benefiting all worlds, may we become protectors of the world just like the present Buddha.
We pray that for those obscured by darkness, who follow the swift current of greed and desire,
and who are entangled by craving and beset by a hundred sufferings, you may rescue and deliver them, just as the World-Honored One has done.
We pray that for those who suffer amidst manifold pains, who do not see the further shore and are bound by Māra,
and who run about as restless as monkeys— may you rescue and deliver them, just as the World-Honored One does.
We pray that for those who are blind and ignorant, for those weary from wandering through the six realms of existence,
and for those whose own karmic fruits have brought about their ruin— may you rescue and deliver them, just as the World-Honored One has done.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that those three hundred and sixty million gandharvas had conceived deep faith, manifested a smile.
Then, the venerable monk Aśvajit asked in verse:
“You of boundless majesty manifest a smile; O Guide, such as this is never without cause.”
We pray that the Buddha will swiftly explain these causes and conditions, To sever the net of doubts of all sentient beings.
Now that we have seen the World-Honored One smile, The entire great assembly is caught in a web of uncertainty.
All wish to hear the meaning of this smile; We only pray that the Great Compassionate One will sever our doubts.
Who has conceived respectful faith in the Buddha-dharma and is able to escape the net of all doubts?
Knowing that sentient beings have deep faith, the Buddha— the supreme among gods and humans— manifests a smile.
Who possesses the wisdom to accord with the true nature (*tathatā*) as taught by the Tathāgata,
having understood their mindfulness, wisdom, liberation, and practice?
For this reason, you manifest a smile amidst the great assembly.
The entire assembly was of one mind, desiring only to hear the discourse of the Hero;
with palms joined and placed upon their heads, they gazed single-mindedly at the face of the Tathāgata.
Free from all defilement and free from anxiety, you rejoice because the Eye of the World is present;
to dispel all doubts in our minds, we pray that the Great Compassionate One will explain the cause and conditions of your smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered the Venerable Aśvajit with these verses:
“The smile I have manifested is for the sake of the world; Excellent is your question, for it is indeed the right time.
The roots of goodness of this great assembly shall increase; I shall grant a prophecy regarding my subtle smile.”
Aśvajit, listen attentively to what I say: the reason why the Teacher has manifested this smile, I shall now explain correctly; you should listen with joy to my words.
The Gandharva King, with reverence and faith in the Buddha, His mind pure and filled with joy,
Having entered the Dharma by relying on the true Dharma, He conceived a sense of wonder toward the Buddha’s True Dharma.
All phenomena are quiescent, peaceful, and immovable; this great assembly proceeds toward the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Entering as one would a city of the Gandharvas, they make offerings to me that are beyond compare.
Thus all these phenomena have no arising, and none of them ever undergo extinction;
the great assembly contemplates that they abide like illusions, yet being unable to fully comprehend this, they give rise to doubt and confusion.
That which cannot be spoken is taught through skillful means;
because I act out of truth, they enter my True Dharma and, mounting great dragon-elephants, make offerings to the Buddha.
Observing that bodhi is without arising or ceasing, the Gandharva King made offerings to me;
out of compassion for ignorant and deluded sentient beings, he therefore sought the great all-knowing wisdom.
They made the vow to become Buddhas, so that all those who are deluded and lost in ignorance might enter the true Dharma,
abide therein, and attain the deathless state of nirvāṇa.
Having made these offerings, they abandon their ghostly bodies and minds filled with joy;
they will certainly attain rebirth in the celestial palaces, where they shall always remain in close proximity to Śakra.
Having encountered many billions of nayutas of stainless Sugatas,
they travel from one buddha-field to another, hearing the Dharma from all those Buddhas.
Having cultivated the pure conduct of a Buddha, the buddha-fields they attain will likewise be pure;
they transform immeasurable multitudes, causing them to resolve upon the Way and thereby increase the seeds of Buddhahood.
Having realized that the nature of all worlds is empty, they likewise teach this Dharma to others,
causing all beings to abide in omniscience and remaining in the world for immeasurable nayutas of eons.
Those Buddhas were all named Anantamati; each of those Buddhas remained in the world for immeasurable nayutas of kalpas, expounding the Buddha-way so that others might hear it.
Thus Śākyamuni Buddha, having explained the retribution for the gandharva’s offering,
granted him a prophecy so that he might hear it, as well as the causes and conditions for his smile as asked by Aśvajit.

Having heard this, the great assembly was filled with joy; knowing that the Buddha’s prophecy was most delightful, and having heard this peerless prophecy from the Buddha, they all took refuge in Śākyamuni.

The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: The Prophecy for the Yakṣas; Part Five of the Sixteenth Assembly, "Bodhisattvas Beholding Reality. Chapter Ten: The Prophecy for the Yakṣas.

At that time, there were also eight hundred million yakṣas who, having witnessed the asuras, garuḍas, nāga girls, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, and others making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing their prophecies, were filled with joy and exultation, their hearts' desires being fully satisfied. They conceived a sense of rarity and attained what they had never experienced before.

Knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses inexhaustible wisdom—most honored, most supreme, unimpeded, and inconceivable—and further hearing the sequence of the Dharma-gates, one forms the perception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as a Teacher, and further forms the perception of the Buddha as one of inexhaustible wisdom.
Having realized that the Buddha’s wisdom is inexhaustible, those yakṣas conceived a heart of love and joy for the Buddha’s True Dharma.
Having developed such deep love and joy for the Buddha’s Dharma, they exerted diligent effort for the sake of making offerings and praised him with these verses:
“We now praise the Benefactor of the World, Because he is fully endowed with the power of the Buddha’s wisdom.”
Inexhaustible and immeasurable like the great ocean, the body of the Lion among Men is thus peerless.
One might be able to know the weight of Mount Sumeru, or one might be able to know the breadth or narrowness of space;
yet the power of wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata cannot be measured by anyone at all.
Knowing the reverent and faithful minds of all sentient beings, he has accordingly received them all across;
knowing the destination of those he has delivered, the Buddha is peerless and without equal.
According to the realms of good and evil cultivated by them, he takes on a body in every place of birth;
knowing their faculties, faith, and what they should receive, the Buddha is thus peerless and without equal.
The Buddha fully knows the conduct of greed, the conduct of hatred, and likewise the conduct of delusion;
he also knows pride and envy in this same way. Therefore, the Buddha is peerless and without equal.
Sentient beings lose much in this regard; the Tathāgata well knows their paths of karma.
The World-Honored One knows them with extreme swiftness and sharpness; therefore, the Buddha is peerless and without equal.
The Sugata clearly perceives all worlds; whatever is lost in any direction, and whatever is forfeited through speech—the World-Honored One beholds all of that without exception.
For how long one dwells within the six realms of existence, The extent of the suffering experienced therein,
And the various bodies that are received— The World-Honored One knows and sees them all.
The Teacher fully understands all that arises through the power of afflictions— the contrivances and karmic actions performed,
and the various sufferings experienced according to those karmas.
According to the path of liberation sought by each, they have already gone forth within the Buddha-dharma;
having diligently practiced and studied the Noble Path, the Buddha fully knows that all their afflictions are exhausted.
Within the Buddha’s Dharma there are worldlings who, though they have gone forth as monastics, do not understand its meaning;
they revile the subtle Dharma of the Wise One, yet the World-Honored One perceives them clearly as well.
The various sufferings obtained through the karmic actions of those who slander the Dharma of the True Person,
and how long they shall dwell in the hells according to their duration— this the Tathāgata knows fully and completely.
Having gained profound reverence and faith in the Buddha, he left the household life to uphold the treasury of the True Dharma;
observing that all phenomena are entirely empty, he severed the path of all existence.
They do not desire bodies in any of the realms of existence;
observing this body as being like an illusion, they know all sounds to be like echoes—the Buddhas, who firmly abide in the Way, know them as well.
I have praised the Peerless Great Teacher; by this mass of merit now obtained, may I attain Buddhahood, and may all sentient beings likewise become self-arisen ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the assembly of yakṣas had developed deep faith in their hearts, manifested a smile.
Then the venerable monk Aśvajit asked in verse:
“The Lion among Men has manifested a smile; I pray only that you will explain the cause and condition of this smile.”
All Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause, O Moon among Men;
now this great assembly all harbors doubt because they have seen the Guide smile.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will dispel their doubts and cause this entire assembly to attain joy.
Those who have now attained faith in the Buddha, and those who understand the subtle and wondrous True Dharma,
whose minds are firm and unshakable— I pray that the Buddha will proclaim it so that they may hear it.
This great assembly all harbors doubts; everyone gazes upon the face of the Tathāgata.
What matter will there be today? We only pray that the World-Honored One will sever their doubts.
Who today manifests such great supernormal power? Who today exerts such great diligence?
With whom is the Buddha now a close friend? We pray that you will reveal this to this great assembly.
Excellent, O Muni, who takes pity on the world! We pray that you will sever all our doubts;
if the great assembly of devas and humans hears this, they shall surely rejoice greatly today.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered the Venerable Aśvajit with these verses:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, is what you have asked; It shall now bring great benefit to all the world.
Because you were able to ask about the cause and conditions of my smile, I therefore praise you for your skillful understanding of my intent.”
I shall now fully answer that meaning; you should listen with single-minded attention.
Having understood the intentions of all the yakṣas, I manifest a smile for the sake of the world.
The hosts of yakṣas, their minds filled with reverence and faith, because they understood that bodhi is quiescent,
having praised the Buddha’s true merits, resolved their minds to advance toward great bodhi.
In order to know that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, They eliminate all existing signs;
having vowed to renounce all realms of existence, They resolve their minds to advance toward great enlightenment.
Through the power of meditative concentration, they know the aggregates to be merely conventional truth and do not grasp them;
unattached to all phenomena like a lotus, they resolve their minds to advance toward great enlightenment.
Regarding the obstacles within all states of existence, because they see them as empty, they are not bound;
having realized that the Buddha’s bodhi is unsurpassed, they are able to cultivate the practices of awakening.
Birth, old age, and death are all entirely empty; this is the unsurpassed path to bodhi.
Having realized that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is empty and quiescent, one is able to attain the secure and great bodhi.
Having realized that the self-nature of the aggregates is empty and quiescent, the nature of bodhi is likewise difficult to fathom;
the practices cultivated for bodhi are also empty—this wisdom can know, which is not within the comprehension of ordinary beings.
The nature of the wisdom that can observe is itself empty; The objects observed are all quiescent and extinguished.
Knowing that the knower is likewise empty— Such a person is able to cultivate the path to Bodhi.
One should know that emptiness is also empty by its very nature; characteristics and aspirations likewise lack any intrinsic substance.
If there is one who can understand in this way, that person is able to cultivate the practice of true reality.
When the great assembly of devas and humans heard this, their hearts were filled with joy and they attained benefit.
Having conceived reverent faith in the Buddha, their minds dwelt in the state of bodhi and tranquility.
Now that this sublime offering has been made, the hosts of yakṣas have purified their minds;
these wise ones will abandon the realm of ghosts and enjoy happiness for a long time within the happy destinies.
In the future, amidst many billions of buddhas, he shall, by the power of his supernormal faculties,
perform acts of worship within a single thought-moment across many buddha-fields, and thereby attain the stage of patience (kṣānti) in the presence of those buddhas.
Not giving rise to signs regarding any world, the wise are able to travel there by means of supernormal power;
viewing this world as like a magical illusion, the wise wander about without attachment.
These valiant ones, having made offerings to all Buddhas, shall attain supreme, great Bodhi;
they shall also attain supreme, pure Buddha-fields, wherein they shall deliver immeasurable multitudes of beings.
They shall become knowers of the world, all sharing the same name, Boundless Wisdom;
their fame shall reach the ten directions and their lifespan shall last for a thousand kalpas, equal in duration to their wisdom of cessation.
All those who are their disciples, like the various stars in a tranquil night sky, shall all easily attain great enlightenment; none among them shall encounter any suffering or hardship.
Having heard this, the great assembly of devas and humans rejoiced in the bodhicitta;
their minds became firm and they exerted themselves with diligence, sustaining all practices through the power of their vigor.

Chapter Eleven: The Prophecy for the Kiṃnaras At that time, there was also a multitude of eight hundred million kiṃnaras, with the great tree-king Kiṃnara as their leader. Having seen the asuras, garuḍas, nāga maidens, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and others making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing his prophecy, they were filled with a sense of rare and unprecedented wonder, and reflected thus:
"This is truly a rare and unprecedented event."

Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended; because there is no life-principle, no being born, no person, no manava, no nourisher, no life-span, no self, and likewise no "mine"; it is only by way of the aggregates that they are called "sentient beings."
All the aggregates (*skandha*) are likewise unapprehendable; it is because of their elements (*dhātu*) that they are called "sentient beings.
All the elements are likewise unapprehendable; it is because of their sense-bases (*āyatana*) that they are called "sentient beings."
All sense bases (*āyatana*) are likewise unattainable; yet, because there is karma, there is the attainment of its retribution.
Furthermore, those karmic actions are unattainable, unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is unattainable, all bodhisattvas are unattainable, and all buddhas are unattainable.

World-Honored One, although this is so, you nevertheless bestow predictions upon the bodhisattvas. For what reason does the Tathāgata bestow predictions upon the bodhisattvas, revealing their names, manifesting their karmic retributions, and declaring what they shall become in the future?

The great assembly of bodhisattvas further manifested the supernatural powers of all Buddhas and spoke of the power of the True Dharma; they also manifested the adornment of Buddha-lands and proclaimed that sentient beings possess karma and its retribution. Furthermore, they spoke of pure Buddha-fields, demonstrating how bodhisattvas travel through various Buddha-lands, proceeding from one Buddha-field to another.

Furthermore, he recounted how the Bodhisattva had gone there to make offerings, and also described the sublime, miraculous transformations of those offerings, as well as listing the exquisite and rare implements used for worship.

Moreover, he prophesied that after a certain number of kalpas, he would attain Buddhahood; that this Buddha would remain in the world for a certain number of kalpas; that this Buddha would have a certain number of śrāvakas; and that after this Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma would remain in the world for a certain number of kalpas.
"Why has the Tathāgata abandoned all sentient beings and entered parinirvāṇa?

At that time, having conceived this doubt, the Great Tree Kinnara King rose from his seat together with a retinue of eight hundred million kinnaras. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, questioned him in verse:
"Having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, we have given rise to great doubt and confusion."
O Great Wisdom!
You have spoken of the bestowal of prophecy and yet spoken of emptiness; I cannot comprehend these two teachings.
You have said that all is empty and quiescent, devoid of intrinsic nature, and that the dharma-realm is equal and unchanging.
Furthermore, that the Tathāgata accepts offerings— how can this be so,
O Moon among the Assembly?
Since the Buddha has taught that there is no arising, yet he has also spoken of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Regarding the two-fold teaching on immeasurable wisdom, I do not understand this secret statement:
how can you say that cessation is unattainable, yet the Lion among Men speaks of death?
I pray that you explain this according to reality, severing my doubts so that none remain.
Why does the Buddha say that all is like an illusion, yet again manifest rebirth in the heavenly realms?
Regarding what the Lion of the Śākyas has thus spoken, I do not understand this secret teaching.
The Buddha says that all phenomena have no basis, yet he further says they depend upon a spiritual friend;
this is the secret speech of the World-Honored One, which I truly do not understand, O Hero among Men.
Why do you speak of being incapable of anything, yet further teach sentient beings to cultivate various karmas?
O Honored One among Gods who subdues enemies, I do not understand this secret teaching.
Why does the Buddha say that nature is inherently empty, yet further state that by contemplating emptiness one attains liberation?
I am currently unable to understand this; I pray that your boundless wisdom will sever my doubts.
Why does the Buddha say that phenomena are extinguished, and yet further say that the nature of all dharmas is quiescent?
I now pray only that the Peerless One will reveal and clarify these secret teachings.
How is it, O upright Sugata, that you reveal all phenomena to be like space,
yet foolish people slander the Dharma and will surely fall into the great hells after death?
The Great Hero constantly speaks of the various heavenly realms, and further speaks of the other destinies;
having stated that these arise from the performance of karma, he further declares that there is no agent who performs it.
That which is proclaimed by the Invincible One is of such diverse distinctions that it cannot be known;
I now harbor doubts regarding this, and I pray only that the World-Honored One will sever them for me.
Since you have stated that wholesome karma cannot be accumulated, yet further declare that one attains enlightenment through practice—
the Śramaṇa, the Dharma King, speaks thus, and this too we are unable to comprehend.
How can it be that the Dharma you preach is inexhaustible, yet those who slander it have their sins brought to an end?
O You of Immeasurable Wisdom, please grant us an explanation; I have great doubts concerning this matter.
Since the Tathāgata has spoken of the dharma of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and further of inversion, giving, and so forth—
[how] for one with pure eyes free from cataracts who has extinguished all sins, this meaning, I pray, may you explain to me.
There is no one else capable of explaining and resolving such doubts for us;
only the Tathāgata can sever them. Therefore, I revere the Omniscient One.
At that time, having heard the questions regarding various doubts posed by the Great Kinnara King Druma and the others, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"You speak of emptiness and yet grant a prediction; you cannot comprehend these two matters."
If all phenomena were not empty, the Buddha would not have bestowed upon them a prediction of enlightenment.
For what reason was it said thus?
If phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature, they would all be eternally abiding and unchangeable; they would neither decrease nor increase.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is originally empty, Like a level, upright, and pure mirror that can manifest all forms and images; In this way, one should understand all dharmas.
The Dharma-realm has no characteristic of change; you should examine each and every part of all these offerings: in which part does a characteristic exist?
The Dharma-realm is eternally abiding and without change; the wise should contemplate it thus.
All ordinary beings are utterly deluded; because they lack wisdom, they cannot understand it.
You say that the Buddha taught there is no arising, yet you also say that the arousal of the mind is difficult to understand;
you all should now listen with a single mind to the secret meaning spoken by the One of Ten Powers.
Ordinary beings drown in the river of birth and death, And likewise bind their minds with attachment to that place;
Their minds constantly harbor inverted perceptions, Therefore they undergo the various sufferings of birth and death.
Since time immemorial, they have never heard the Dharma; if I were to definitively explain it to them, ordinary and foolish people would only further increase their doubts regarding this teaching.
Hearing of the supreme benefits of enlightenment, his mind is focused intently upon that fruit;
his mind further develops a deep attachment to it, such that no superior wisdom can surpass it.
As for your words that there is death even without cessation—these two things I cannot now know;
listen attentively with a single mind, and I shall speak the truth to you.
For the sake of those sentient beings who reckon things as permanent, the Tathāgata therefore taught cessation;
for he constantly sees that all states of existence are subject to decay and ruin, and there is not a single dharma that is permanent.
You say that all phenomena are like illusions, yet you further express doubt regarding rebirth in the heavens;
learners, ordinary worldlings, those in the happy realms, and so forth—these states are not fixed, and therefore they are like illusions.
As you have said, there is no basis; yet you also speak of relying upon a spiritual friend.
Because you wish to abandon all reliance, the virtuous friend has taught you that there is nothing to rely upon.
You say that ultimately there is no capacity, yet you further say that there is action; this I do not understand.
One should observe that a chariot is composed of many parts, and one should also observe that the chariot performs its function.
If there are those who cling to a self, and likewise grasp at what belongs to a self, for such as these I teach that [the self] is incapable; yet even though it is thus, it is not without activity.
You say that all natures are empty by themselves, yet you further doubt that liberation is attained through the contemplation of emptiness;
those who are inverted, deluded, and lacking wisdom are unable to understand that the essential nature is empty.
Arising from the conceptualization of false imagination, beings are bound by clinging to what is unreal;
to transform such sentient beings, the Sugata taught that intrinsic nature does not exist.
As you have said, all things are utterly extinguished, and the nature of all phenomena is likewise extinguished;
yet deluded and ignorant sentient beings give rise to craving through their false conceptualizations.
Just as a thirsty person sees a mirage, Whose thirst increases through conceptualization,
So too are fools harmed by the false, Giving rise to discrimination regarding that which does not exist.
The thirsty person falsely conceives the notion of water; yet where the mirage appears, water is fundamentally non-existent.
So too are all sentient beings harmed by their own deluded thoughts, perceiving purity within that which is impure.
