Foolish worldlings are bound by craving; that which is foul and impure has no purity within its nature.
It is like a mirage appearing with the mark of water, yet in its essential nature, there is truly no water therein.
Thus, within this body there is no pure form; the nature of the body’s color is likewise not pure.
Foolish ordinary people hold perverted views, falsely conceiving it to be pure and thereby remaining bound.
Although it is taught that all phenomena are like space, it is also taught that those who slander them fall into hell;
when fools hear this, they give rise to fear, but though the wise hear it, their minds remain at peace.
The nature of the world is inherently empty and quiescent; yet out of folly and lack of wisdom, they give rise to the notion of a self.
When such people hear the teaching on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they become terrified and fear that they will no longer be able to take rebirth.
They revile the sublime Dharma of emptiness, all because they are attached to the view of a self;
like one who attempts to bind the sky, these ignorant people fall into hell.
The various happy realms that I have previously taught, as well as the other paths I have explained for the world—
by teaching that actions performed do not perish, I also strip away their attachment to the existence of a creator.
All realms of existence are like a dream; I have taught you to know them as such.
Within a dream there is no characteristic of coming or going; it is those with perverted views who cling to coming and going.
I have already explained that there is the performance of action, yet when one searches throughout the ten directions, no agent is found;
it is like a fierce wind blowing through various trees, and when those trees strike one another, fire is produced.
Neither the wind nor the tree conceives the thought, "We are able to produce fire.
Yet, despite this being so, fire arises; one should know that while there is karma, there is no agent.
"You say that merit cannot be accumulated, yet you also claim to have well attained the fruit of Bodhi.
I shall now speak to you with absolute truth; you should listen with focused attention and a sincere heart."
For example, as when people in the world attain long life, their lifespan reaching over a hundred years;
yet those years do not accumulate as a mass, and all conditioned aggregations are likewise so.
You say that all phenomena are inexhaustible, yet you also say that I claim karma can be brought to an end.
For one who contemplates the emptiness of phenomena, there is no exhaustion; it is only in accordance with worldly conventions that karma is said to have an end.
Although I speak of the dharma of the limit of reality, inversion is not outside the limit of reality;
yet those beings who are inverted and deluded are unable to comprehend the true limit of reality.
King of the Kiṃnaras, listen attentively: for those who possess wisdom and exert diligent effort, all characteristics are but a single characteristic;
one should know that this is what is called "the characteristic of non-existence."
If one can understand and enter into a single syllable, I shall explain awakening for that wise person:
all phenomena are without action; this is the teaching on the dhāraṇī gateway of the syllable A.
I have already explained the boundless characteristics of all the practices of the bodhisattvas;
these also enable entry into all phenomena, namely, the dhāraṇī gate of the letter A.
All phenomena are utterly quiescent; The gateway of the letter A is shown to enable entry.
Kinnara Druma, you should know this: This too is the dhāraṇī gateway of the letter A.
All phenomena are without discrimination; having entered this dharma-gate, it has been proclaimed.
King of the Kiṃnaras, you should know that this too is the dhāraṇī-gate of the letter A.
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; The gateway of the letter A is shown so that one may enter.
Kinnara Druma, you should know this: This too is the dhāraṇī gateway of the letter A.
All phenomena are without limit; they are explained through the gateway of the syllable A.
O King of Kinnaras, you should know that this too is the dhāraṇī-gateway of the syllable A.
I have already taught the dharmas of exhaustion and non-exhaustion; one should teach that all dharmas are inexhaustible.
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions have already taught the gateway of the inexhaustible dhāraṇī.
All phenomena have no gate; because things do not exist, they appear as non-existent.
This itself is the gateway of dhāraṇī, by which one can enter the gateway of the letter A.
Regarding all inconceivable dharmas, the Buddhas are able to manifest them according to reality;
Druma Kinnara, you should know that this too is the A-syllable Dhāraṇī.
All dharmas have no destination; for the sake of the wise, I proclaim bodhi.
This is also the gateway of the dhāraṇī; one should enter through this letter A-gate.
All phenomena have no coming; if one does not cultivate them, they cannot be attained.
This too is a gateway of dhāraṇī; this is the gateway of the letter A, which one should enter.
All dharmas exist as mere provisional names; when their intrinsic nature is sought, it cannot be found.
This too is a gateway to the dhāraṇī; one should enter this gateway of the letter A.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; when one investigates that intrinsic nature, it cannot be found.
This too is a gateway to dhāraṇī, a dhāraṇī spoken by the Buddha.
All phenomena are unattainable, for they are thus because their intrinsic nature is non-existent;
this too is a gateway to dhāraṇī—this is the gateway of the letter A, which one should enter.
Kinnara, you should listen: all dharmas are free from conceptual thought;
this too is a gateway to dhāraṇī, as taught by the Sugata.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have already revealed that because phenomena lack substantial reality, they are without obstruction;
this too is a gate of dhāraṇī, wherein one should enter the *akṣara* dhāraṇī.
All dharmas are without obstruction; there is nothing that can obstruct any dharma.
This too is a gate of dhāraṇī; I have already explained the entry into the letter A-gate.
All phenomena are without arising; the wise should know they have but a single characteristic.
That all phenomena are without arising—know that these phenomena have no name.
All phenomena are without arising; their arising is fundamentally unattainable.
This too is a gate of dhāraṇī; one should enter this gateway of the letter A.
If phenomena are without reality and without arising, they cannot be seen and cannot be shown;
since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unattainable, there is therefore no one who can see them.
All dharmas have no counterpart; therefore, they are of one mark, which is the markless.
Just as space has no equal, so too it is with all dharmas.
All phenomena are without increase or decrease; they are neither one nor two, nor are they affliction.
They are neither cold nor hot; because they do not exist, they cannot be seen.
There is no mark of crookedness nor mark of straightness, Nor is there any mark of light or darkness;
Furthermore, there are no marks of seeing, hearing, or any other perceptions— This is the *Dhāraṇī* of Non-existence.
It is neither crooked nor upright; it possesses no characteristics such as contraction or expansion.
It is free from both anger and joy, and likewise devoid of arising activity or cessation.
There is no characteristic of entering nor of exiting; there is no advancing, no retreating, and no coming or going.
Furthermore, there is neither sleep nor waking; one should know that it is free from the association of cognitive awareness.
It is neither this eye nor yet blind; there is no one who can see, nor any obscuration of darkness.
There is neither the appearance of opening nor the appearance of closing; it is neither disciplined nor undisciplined.
Neither agitation nor stillness, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa;
neither real nor unreal—thus should one know the realm of the Buddha.
In order to subdue the world, I have severed your doubts; I am without doubt.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), no one is able to sever the entire web of others' doubts except me.
At that time, when the Great Kinnara King Druma heard the Buddha speak upon the gateways of dhāraṇī, his heart was filled with great joy.
Having rejoiced, he gave rise to a courageous mind and immediately manifested eight hundred million multi-storied pavilions.
These multi-storied pavilions were situated either upon trees, or upon lotuses, or upon mountains; all were adorned with the seven precious gems.

Those pavilions were further embellished with various canopies made of manifold jewels and various jeweled banners, as well as with tassels of diverse precious flowers and tassels of variegated colored silks.

At that time, the Great Kinnara King Mahādruma, together with a multitude of eight hundred million kinnaras, took all the flowers from both water and land found within Mount Gandhamādana and scattered them over the Buddha.

Having finished scattering [the flowers] before the Buddha, each one ascended a multi-storied pavilion made of the seven precious gems and circumambulated the Buddha three times; they then again scattered all the various flowers available on land and in water upon the Tathāgata, and once more circumambulated him three times.

At that time, the Great Kinnara King Mahādruma, together with a multitude of eight hundred million kinnaras, descended from the multi-storied pavilion and circumambulated the Buddha three times more. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they joined their palms with single-minded devotion, gazing up at the World-Honored One without averting their eyes for even a moment. They withdrew to stand to one side, contemplating the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata in the past and present.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep-seated aspiration of the Great Tree Kinnara King and his assembly of eight hundred million beings, manifested a smile.
Then, the Venerable Aśvajit Bhikṣu asked in verse:
"The Sugata does not smile without cause; O one worshipped by gods and humans, please speak according to reality."
The assembly, beholding the Buddha’s smile, all harbored doubts; seeing the Most Victorious One like the new moon, they wondered:
"O World-Honored One of wondrous form, who today has given rise to supreme wisdom regarding the non-dual Dharma?"
Today I harbor doubts; I pray only that the Honored Among Men will dispel my uncertainty.
Who has attained a pure mind in the Buddha’s Dharma, that the Tathāgata manifests a smile because of them?
I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me a prophecy, That supreme among all speech, to sever my doubts.
At that time, the entire great assembly, Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, will all rejoice;
May you remove their various uncertainties, So that they may practice everything according to the Buddha’s instruction.
Therefore, the Most Victorious One, Honored Among Two-Legged Beings,
has severed all doubt and granted this prophecy for the sake of the Kinnara King and others, as well as for all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered Aśvajit in verse:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, you who know the proper time to ask! I shall now explain it to you in detail.
Because of your inquiry, I reveal this, so that all people may attain the merits of a Buddha.”
You should listen with a pure and single-minded focus, without distracting thoughts, to this rare occurrence:
namely, the supreme wisdom of the Sugata, his unimpeded and vast knowledge and vision.
The Kinnara King has posed this question for the benefit of all sentient beings;
I shall now declare its future fruit—listen attentively, and I shall sever your doubts.
The eight hundred million *kiṃnaras* led by Druma, along with the king, ministers, subjects, and all their retinues—
having made offerings to me, they passed away from this life and were reborn in the heavens.
From this point onward, for nine hundred million kalpas, they will transmigrate among humans and devas,
fully cultivating the five supernormal powers, and attaining mastery over wisdom and mastery over the mind.
In those nayutas of Buddha-fields, this Lion among Men undergoes miraculous birth;
though his body remains unmoving within celestial palaces, he constantly experiences the peaceful joy of meditative rapture.
After wandering through the realms of humans and devas for ninety million *koṭis* of eons,
they shall each, within their own Buddha-fields, attain the unsurpassed path.
That eon shall be named Constant Illumination; within that eon they will attain the Way of the Buddha.
All these are persons in their final birth before Buddhahood; those wise ones shall surely become Buddhas.
In that Buddha-land, there is not a single person who is not one whose practice is fully matured;
they are all those in their final birth before Buddhahood, and none among them seek the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
All are great bodhisattvas; as illuminators of the world, they are all born there.
All are those in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and hereafter they shall all attain the path of Buddhahood.
The great assembly of Bodhisattvas in that land dwells securely within their vast vows and great aspirations;
throughout immeasurable Buddha-fields, they have all cultivated and purified them.
Those bodhisattvas have made most vast vows; having reflected well throughout the long night, with hearts of pure faith and joy, each has cultivated and purified their own buddha-field.
Those buddha-fields are wondrously adorned, Far removed from all afflictions;
Throughout their lands are various palaces and groves, Liberating all from the evil realms.
All faults and the eight difficulties are entirely absent in that Buddha-land;
having cultivated such a pure buddha-field, sentient beings become easily disciplined.
Thus the World-Honored One, the God among Gods, bestowed this prophecy for the sake of the kinnaras;
at that time, the entire great assembly, having heard it, were all filled with great joy in their hearts.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Five;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Prediction for the Sky-Traveling Devas; Chapter Sixteen of the Bodhisattva-Darśana-tattva Assembly, Part Six.

At that time, there were eighty thousand sky-traveling devas who, seeing the asuras, garuḍas, nāga maidens, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and others making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing their predictions, all rejoiced with immeasurable exultation and leaped for joy. They conceived a profound heart of love and delight for the Buddha-dharma.
To make offerings to the Buddha, they gave rise to a courageous mind.

Those devas who travel through space rained down māndārava flowers for sixty yojanas in every direction around the city of Kapilavastu, covering the ground until it reached the height of a person's knees.

Having rained down *mandārava* flowers until they covered the ground, he presented them as an offering to the Buddha, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then praised the Buddha with these verses:
“Your faculties are serene, your face bears a smile; You rescue and protect all sentient beings.
Sugata, you are fully endowed with great compassion; Therefore, you are the World-Honored One, the Lion among Men.”
The Tathāgata and his great assembly all dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma and in nirvāṇa;
to the World-Honored One, the Guide with supreme and wondrous feet, I now prostrate with my head at his feet.
Just as on the fifteenth day the moon is full, and all people in the world pay homage to the moon among the stars,
so too do all the hosts of devas, beholding the Buddha’s smiling face, pay him their respectful salutations.
Having accumulated a vast mass of immeasurable merit, And likewise having perfected the body of wisdom,
Possessing immeasurable and great majestic power, I therefore prostrate to the Kinsman of the World.
Fully endowed with the mountain of merit of the ten powers, fearless regarding the truths and free from the three stains, you have accomplished the eighteen unique qualities;
seeing clearly without doubt, you are the most excellent among those who teach.
Fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, Adorned by the eighty minor characteristics, Your mind is supreme like the banner of Indra; Therefore, I prostrate to the Peerless One.
Having already perfected the power of ethical discipline, and with the power of dhyāna remaining resolute and unshakable, he wields the supreme sword of wisdom;
most victorious and valiant, he subdues the celestial Māras.
Having reached the further shore through the power of wisdom, he trains the minds of śrāvakas without stinginess;
with a mind of profound tranquility, he wanders through all directions, delivering all devas and humans.
The World-Honored One, supreme lion among men, has attained the most excellent dharma of quiescence;
we pray that you, endowed with the ten powers, may likewise cause us to attain this sublime and wondrous dharma.
May I likewise become one among gods and humans, Admired and cherished by all the world;
May I be equal to the World-Honored One without distinction, Fully understanding the inclinations and desires of sentient beings.
May I bring benefit to all the world; with a heart of compassion and great pity for sentient beings fallen into the ocean of birth and death, may I be able to deliver them all to liberation.
May I become a supreme, unsurpassed Great Teacher among all devas and humans;
may I liberate all beings from the various realms of existence who are oppressed by a hundredfold sufferings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the deva Ākāśagāmin’s heart was filled with profound faith and joy, smiled.
Then the bhikṣu Aśvajit questioned the Buddha in verse, saying:
"The Buddha, King of Munis, does not smile without cause; Illuminating the three realms, you manifest this smile."
I pray that the One of Ten Powers will explain to me: for what sentient beings do you manifest this sign of joy?
Having beheld the Tathāgata’s most supreme countenance, you manifest a smile that brings delight to the multitude.
All in the great assembly harbor doubts; we wish to hear the Buddha speak of the causes and conditions for your smile.
I pray that the Great Guide will swiftly explain the causes and conditions for this smile and its beneficial purpose;
may you sever the web of doubts for all beings and proclaim it, O King among Śramaṇas.
Who is able to cause the Buddha to manifest a joyful smile?
Who has presented supreme offerings to the Buddha?
And who is able to reach the bottom of birth and death?
May the Lion among Men dispel my doubts:
Who today has shaken the palace of Māra, causing Māra to become frantic and his mind uneasy?
Who today has caused the hosts of devas to all rejoice and leap for great joy?
I only pray that you will swiftly proclaim it for me, severing the net of all worldly doubts;
when the great assembly hears the Buddha’s teaching, they shall all be filled with immense joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Aśvajit with these verses:
“Aśvajit, you have now questioned me regarding the prophecy concerning the deva who travels through space.
Your inquiry of me brings great benefit to immeasurable people and devas throughout the world.”
If the Lion of the Ten Powers were not questioned, he could not bestow the prophecy upon the Son of the Buddha;
today you have questioned the Tathāgata for the sake of the vast benefit of all the world.
This goddess of the empty space made offerings to me with a joyful heart;
after the passing of incalculable eons, she will extinguish all afflictions and attain Buddhahood.
Having passed away from this world, they are immediately reborn in a superior celestial realm;
in the presence of immeasurable billions of Buddhas, they fully understand how to cultivate offerings of incense and flowers.
Having resolved upon the mind of enlightenment in the presence of that Buddha, they further advanced their bodhicitta,
praising the self-arisen wisdom of the Lion among Men with immeasurable, sublime verses.
In future ages, before immeasurable and boundless Buddhas,
they shall make offerings with supreme fragrant flowers and likewise praise the Buddhas with sublime verses.
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇakāya and the others, having made offerings and praised all the Buddhas,
shall attain supreme, unsurpassed wisdom in the future world of the Joyful Eon.
That Buddha shall be named Puṣpadhvaja, his fame renowned everywhere without reproach;
those eighty thousand hosts of devas shall all become Buddhas within the same eon.
In that Buddha-field there are no hells, nor are there hungry ghosts or animals;
that land also has no realm of asuras, and none of the eight difficulties whatsoever.

When this Ākāśagarbha attains Buddhahood, all the people of that land and those sentient beings shall have immeasurable lifespans, and their karmic rewards will be like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
In that land, even the names of evil realms are unheard of, let alone anyone who commits evil deeds;
at that time, all sentient beings are in accordance with the Dharma, and everyone is a disciplined assembly.
That Buddha delivered immeasurable billions of people, their number exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
for them he preached the Dharma of non-reliance and non-attachment, liberating those sentient beings through the ten powers.
After that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, his relics were widely distributed and stūpas were erected;
within each of those relics, the physical marks of a Buddha’s body were all manifested.
With a reputation for irreproachable physical form, he displays miraculous transformations for those sentient beings;
countless billions of sentient beings all resolve their minds upon unsurpassed bodhi.
The Guide, with such wisdom and skillful means, bestowed this prophecy upon that sky-faring goddess;
having heard the prophecy, the entire great assembly was filled with joy and leaped for great exultation.

Chapter Thirteen: The Prophecy of the Four Heavenly Kings At that time, ninety-four thousand devas of the Four Heavenly Kings, seeing the asuras, garuḍas, nāga maidens, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and others making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing the prophecy granted to the devas who travel through the air, were all filled with immeasurable joy and exultation. They conceived a profound heart of faith and delight in the Buddha-dharma.
For example, suppose there is a person who boards a boat made of clay and enters a river, thinking to himself:
"This clay boat will soon break apart; before it sinks, I must quickly reach the opposite bank to escape this peril of the water."

In this same way, ninety-four thousand gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings likewise beheld the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; for the sake of attaining the Buddha-dharma, they gave rise to deep faith and joy, and with courageous resolve, made offerings to the Tathāgata.

At that time, the gods of the Four Great Kings, together with the Four Great Kings themselves, manifested ninety thousand exquisite canopies made of the seven precious jewels. They were of various colors, wonderful, rare, vast, and magnificent; among them were many canopies of red pearls, fire-jewel pearls, lapis lazuli, celestial gold, and diamond pearls.
Having manifested these ninety-seven thousand canopies made of the seven treasures, they circled the Buddha three times through the air.
Furthermore, they manifested ninety thousand celestial musical instruments, which likewise revolved through the air, circling the Buddha three times.

Furthermore, he manifested *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, *karkarava* flowers, and *mahākarkarava* flowers. Holding these manifested flowers, he scattered them over the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and then praised the Buddha with these verses:
“Nine hundred million devas, All before the Guide, With single-minded palms joined, Long for the Buddha’s virtues.”
Neither agitation nor depression, neither greed nor regret, neither elation nor dejection—
therefore I pay homage to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
Having severed the seeds of all existence and extinguished the darkness of ignorance, [I pay homage].
He has pulled out the thorns of affliction and can shatter the mountain of self-conceit.
The Buddha skillfully extracts the poisoned arrows and can extinguish all sores and blemishes.
Having well-cultivated the practice of non-negligence, his body is perfect and without deficiency.
Having extinguished all afflictions, liberated from every bond,
severed all fetters and latent tendencies, and emerged from all turmoil—
emptiness and the signless dharma: these are the practices of the Buddha.
Within all states of existence, their mind has no longing or delight.
Having severed the root of craving and abandoned the darkness of ignorance,
they are able to distance themselves entirely from the four inversions.
The Buddha can know the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet none in the world know it;
when ordinary beings hear of it, they give rise to fear, like deer terrified of a hunter.
Sentient beings who have fallen into the view of a self cannot understand emptiness.
Enshrouded by ignorance, they cling to worldly fetters.
Seeing *tathatā* as it truly is, they perceive the world as an empty fist.
To reveal true wisdom to the world, they thereby obtain the pure eye.
It is shown that the aggregates are empty, and name-and-form are likewise so;
the essential nature of the elements does not exist, and the sense-bases are also thus.
These dharmas and other dharmas are spoken of by means of names.
These names and all phenomena, the Buddha has taught to be entirely empty.
Just as a great master of illusion conjures various forms,
there is no establishment of a sentient being, nor is there a life-principle, nor a person.
Thus these aggregates, elements, sense faculties, and twelve bases— All arise from illusory transformations; so the Tathāgata has taught.
It is like a skilled painter Who paints the body of a white elephant.
The branches and joints are all alike, and their heights and depths are likewise so.
In reality, there is no characteristic of high or low; it merely deludes the eyes of the ignorant.
This Dharma-realm is equal, yet the ignorant are themselves deluded.
The Buddha reveals all things for them, as clearly as an *āmra* fruit held in the palm of his hand;
the wise are not deluded, having well studied the teachings of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgata’s great wisdom serves as the lamp of knowledge for the world.
Turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma, you teach and transform all living beings;
may you likewise awaken me to the unsurpassed, tranquil Bodhi,
turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma just as the Buddha has now turned it.
"For us who are lost on the path within this world, you should preach the sublime Dharma, just as the Buddha has now spoken.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep thoughts in the minds of those Four Heavenly Kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately smiled; from the Buddha’s mouth issued various rays of light of five colors.
At that time, Aśvajit addressed the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
“The Buddha does not manifest a smile Without cause or condition.
O Great Hero, World-Honored Buddha, I pray you will explain the reason for this smile.”
Beholding the Buddha manifest a smile, all those gathered in the assembly harbor great doubt; O Honored One among Men, you should know:
who is it now that destroys the hosts of Māra?
Who now has attained the removal of doubt?
Who has reached certainty regarding the Dharma?
We pray only that the Honored One among Men will explain.
Who now attains the offering to the Buddha?
Who follows the practice of the Buddha’s teaching?
All in this assembly harbor doubts; we pray that the Guide will explain this for us.
The Honored One among Two-legged Beings has delivered this prophecy;
if sentient beings hear it, they shall all cast off the net of doubt.
We pray only that the Guide will speak further, so that all sentient beings may rely upon the path of omniscience.
"One shall swiftly attain Bodhi; therefore, you should grant a prophecy.
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered Aśvajit in verse:
"Excellent, you, Aśvajit!"
For the sake of the multitude, I request the Buddha to explain the cause and condition for his smile.
Listen attentively as I speak for you.
Out of compassion for all the world, you should listen with single-minded concentration.
Ninety thousand devas in all, All stood before me.
With pure faith, They had already made offerings to the Buddha;
Furthermore, they praised him with verses, Thoroughly understanding all dharmas as empty.
Having attained certainty in the Dharma, they dwell securely within my teaching.
These hosts of devas have made offerings to eight hundred million Buddhas in the past,
and in future ages as well, they shall do so before immeasurable billions of Buddhas.
Making offerings to those Buddhas, they seek the unsurpassed path.
If one does not make offerings to immeasurable billions of Buddhas,
they will never sit beneath the Bodhi tree to realize enlightenment.
In a future age, they shall attain the path of Buddhahood;
known by the name Mahādhara, they will be supreme in the world.
Those lamps of the world will each have their own assembly of śrāvakas.
An assembly of eighty thousand will gather there, their knowledge and vision free from obstruction.
Once they have attained Buddhahood, all the sentient beings in that land shall have a lifespan of eight hundred million years.
That Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable, and his countless billions of bhikṣus have all distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, all dwelling in their final bodies.
After that Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, for the sake of those who possess such merit,
Adorning that buddha-field, they caused immeasurable stupas to be built.
Those countless thousands of beings, as well as hundreds of nayutas,
made offerings to those shrines, bringing benefit to the people of the world.
Some gave rise to the bodhicitta, while others realized nirvāṇa.
After that Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for eighty million years and immeasurable nayutas.
Those sons of the Dharma Kings, because they uphold and protect the Dharma,
were prophesied by that Buddha; as hosts of the Four Heavenly Kings,
they act for the benefit of the world and for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Having heard this, the great assembly was filled with immense joy;
they leaped for joy beyond measure and respectfully followed the Tathāgata’s teaching. Chapter 14:

The Prophecy for the Gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven At that time, there were also eight hundred million gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, with Śakra, the Lord of Devas, as their chief. Seeing the asuras, garuḍas, nāga girls, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and the gods who travel through space, up to the gods of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, all making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing his prophecy, they were all filled with immense joy and leaped for joy beyond measure. They conceived a deep-seated faith and delight in the Buddha-dharma.
Having developed deep faith and joy, Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven then gave rise to a courageous mind to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

They immediately manifested eight hundred million multi-storied pavilions made of the seven precious gems, adorned with various colors, dignified, extraordinary, exquisite, and marvelous; all were draped with necklaces of red pearls, necklaces of lapis lazuli, mixed necklaces, and necklaces of fire-jewel beads.

Each multi-storied pavilion has one hundred tiers of ornate banner-gates; within each tier there are further four small multi-storied pavilions, adorned with windows, lion thrones, banners and streamers, canopies, jeweled bells, and jeweled nets.
There were celestial maidens, foremost in their exquisite beauty, who attended the multi-storied pavilion and the lion throne, playing various celestial musical instruments.
Furthermore, they manifested eighty million well-trained horse-drawn chariots, adorned with celestial ornaments such as jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, and various musical ensembles.

Throughout the entire great city of Kapilavastu, extending sixty yojanas in length and breadth, he scattered mandārava flowers, mahāmandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, karkārava flowers, mahākarkārava flowers, pāruṣaka flowers, and mahāpāruṣaka flowers, covering the ground until they reached the height of a person’s knees.

At that time, Śakra again manifested eight hundred million *airāvaṇa* dragon-elephants; each elephant had eight hundred million heads, and each head had six tusks. Upon every tusk were seven lotus ponds, and within each pond were seven lotuses. Each lotus had a thousand petals, and within each petal were seven celestial maidens, each of whom was attended by seven handmaidens adorned with various ornaments.
Between the tiers of the multi-storied pavilions, dragon-elephant jeweled chariots were stationed in succession to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

From atop the celestial pavilions, they rained down celestial sandalwood powder, celestial aloeswood powder, and celestial pure gold powder; they rained down celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, *pāruṣaka* flowers, *mahāpāruṣaka* flowers, *karkarava* flowers, *mahākarkarava* flowers, golden flowers, silver flowers, *vaiḍūrya* flowers, and various multicolored *pāṭali* flowers. Thus, they magically produced all manner of exquisite and wondrous jewel flowers and scattered them over the Buddha.
Those celestial maidens may play music, sing, or dance, or move their bodies, as described in detail among the asuras.
Furthermore, they manifest eight hundred million well-trained horse-kings, adorned with various ornaments, and ride upon them.
Furthermore, they scattered various celestial offerings over the Buddha.
Additionally, eight hundred million celestial musical instruments spontaneously played in the midst of the void.

Furthermore, upon each of the eight hundred million precious chariots, there was a single emanated celestial maiden; those eight hundred million celestial maidens either sang or danced, played music, or moved their bodies, as described in detail in the *Asura* section.
The celestial maidens emanated from within the head of that Ilā Dragon King all performed music, as described in detail in the account of the offerings made by the Asuras.
At that time, eight hundred million celestial maidens all made offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, those eight hundred million devas had this thought:
"These manifested celestial maidens make offerings to the Tathāgata; all dharmas are likewise thus, just as the Buddha has taught."
Having realized that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, he was free from the net of doubt regarding all phenomena.
Once he had attained this state of non-doubt within all phenomena, he circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Having realized that all phenomena are like illusions, they also realize that their own bodies are identical to illusory transformations; they know that those offerings and the Tathāgata are likewise identical to illusions, and the Dharma taught by the Buddha is also thus.
Having attained freedom from doubt regarding all illusory phenomena, he then praised the Buddha with these verses:
"These transformed beings who present offerings, And all other people as well,
Śakra, the gods, and all dharmas— All are entirely like illusions and transformations."
The Tathāgata, the Guide, is likewise like an illusion; The assembly of śrāvakas is born through transformation from the Dharma.
They have no doubt whatsoever regarding what the Buddha has taught, And are able to understand the prophecies spoken by the Tathāgata.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cannot be understood by foolish ordinary beings;
all the dharmas spoken of by the Tathāgata are entirely like illusions.

Whether they be those in training or those beyond training, the disciples of the Buddha who have been disciplined—all these, too, are like magical illusions; regarding this Dharma, I have attained freedom from doubt.

World-Honored One, if there are those who delight in silence, solitary and without affliction like a *kiṇṇara*, all such beings are entirely identical to an illusion; regarding this Dharma, I have no doubt.

If one practices the conduct of Buddhas and the conduct of Bodhisattvas, benefiting sentient beings without negligence, such a person is a Bodhisattva, a child of the Tathāgata; all things are entirely like illusions and transformations.
The Sugata, the Guide, possesses self-arisen wisdom; With the ten powers and great compassion, his wisdom is immeasurable.
He is sovereign in wisdom, the most supreme in the world; That Buddha is likewise like an illusion.
Just as the Dharma taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is cool, tranquil, and without dependence—
both the attainment of the dharma of nirvāṇa and nirvāṇa itself— are likewise like an illusion.
The Sugata is in accordance with the Dharma and possesses nothing; all things are like the nature of illusions and transformations.
Regarding this Buddha-Dharma and its wisdom, we have no doubts whatsoever.
We constantly aspire to become like the Buddha, seeing all phenomena as being like illusions;
practicing this realm of the Buddha, we vow to attain Buddhahood without doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the eight hundred million devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven possessed deep faith and joy in their hearts, immediately smiled.
Thereupon, the Venerable Aśvajit questioned the Buddha in verse, saying:
"Your fame is peerless and you are endowed with all virtues; The Tathāgata manifests a smile not without cause."
For what reason does the Tathāgata smile today?
We pray that you will explain this for us and dispel our doubts.
Seeing the Tathāgata manifest a smile, the assembly all harbors uncertainty.
We pray that you will dispel these many doubts, so that the assembly may no longer harbor a web of uncertainty.
All these hosts of devas are filled with joy; they praise and make offerings to the Tathāgata.
For whose sake has the Tathāgata manifested this smile?
May the Buddha speak for the sake of the assembly’s joy.
You whose virtues are pure like the moon, O Worthy of Offerings, pray speak;
if they hear what the Tathāgata has spoken, these beings will rejoice and attain Buddhahood.
All these great assemblies of devas, knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, practice and study without hindrance;
we pray only that the One of Ten Powers will explain this matter.
If the entire great assembly dispels all doubt, Cultivates bodhi with a joyful mind,
And gives rise to a superior aspiration that is not inferior, The multitude, upon hearing this, will immediately develop a courageous heart.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Aśvajit in verse:
“Aśvajit, what you have now asked the Tathāgata Is well-suited to the occasion and of great benefit.
Knowing that the host of devas is filled with joy, I shall now explain the reason for my smile.”
Since you, for the sake of the assembly of devas, have asked about the cause of my smile, you now bring great benefit to all sentient beings;
I shall now explain the cause of my smile to you—listen with a pure mind and with careful attention.
Thus these great assemblies of devas, Knowing all phenomena to be like illusions,
With immeasurable, unimpeded wisdom, vision, and insight, Shall in the future leave behind darkness and attain Buddhahood.
Throughout the past, while wandering through birth and death, you have made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
under those Buddhas, you have repeatedly cultivated the realization that all phenomena are like illusions.
Now you have again made an excellent offering to me; You also know that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations.
Because you have deep faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, In a future age, you shall surely attain Buddhahood.
The merit created within this Buddha-dharma is subject to neither loss nor obstruction;
having made offerings to me, the hosts of devas further realize that all phenomena are like illusions.
In the future, during the Upāsaka-kalpa, they shall attain the state of the most supreme among those who preach the supreme;
all those of such preeminent merit shall share the same name: Indra-dhvaja-rāja Buddha.
That Buddha proclaimed the dharma that is like an illusion, Delivering immeasurable billions of sentient beings;
Therefore, you all should abandon negligence And cultivate all dharmas as being like illusions.

These non-indolent ones are my disciples; for the sake of fulfilling the factors of enlightenment, they exert themselves with vigor as if their heads were on fire, swiftly seeking the supreme enlightenment of peace.

Chapter Fifteen: The Prophecy for the Yāma Heaven Devas At that time, there were also four hundred million assemblies of Yāma heaven devas who, seeing the asuras, garuḍas, nāga maidens, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, the devas who roam the sky, the Cāturmahārājika devas, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, and others making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing their prophecies, were all filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for joy.

At that time, the assembly of the Yāma devas, knowing that the Buddha Tathāgata had bestowed the prediction upon them with unimpeded wisdom, immediately conceived a heart of faith and joy toward the Buddha-dharma.
Having conceived such faith and joy, they thought:
"This Buddha-dharma is most wonderful and subtle."

If one realizes the Buddha-dharma, there is nothing not known, nothing not seen, nothing not discerned, and nothing not realized. Regarding karma and its retribution—whether already arisen, yet to arise, or presently arising; or already ceased, yet to cease, or presently ceasing—one knows them all as they truly are.

How marvelous it is that the Tathāgata is able to know both conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and knows these two well such that there is nothing further beyond them.

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, is well-able to know and see the dharma of emptiness, well-able to discern it, and has well-realized its correspondence; therefore, he is named Sarvajña (the Omniscient One).
What is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
It refers to all worldly activities within birth and death; one is able to fully understand and know all these phenomena.
As for ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is beyond verbal expression, there is no knower, and it is not within the sphere of the mind.
Because of this lack of knowledge, there is no one who can speak, no one who reveals, no one who explains, and no one who hears.
Because there is no speaking, there is likewise no one who knows.
There is no arising and no manifestation; there is no one who sees.

There is no establishment, no grasping, no cognition, no one who can arrive nor anything to be arrived at, no one who can approach, no one who can fathom, no establishing, no abandoning, no action nor anyone who acts, and neither praise nor blame, neither gain nor loss, neither renown nor infamy, neither suffering nor pleasure.

It is neither form nor non-form; neither number nor non-number; neither light nor non-light; neither possessed of afflictions nor free from afflictions; neither the world nor nirvana; neither applied thought nor sustained thought; neither advancing nor retreating; it is unmoving and without activity.
There is no conceptual proliferation; it transcends all conceptual proliferation.
The characteristics of form cannot be apprehended, nor can sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be apprehended.
The characteristic of the eye cannot be apprehended, and the same applies to the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The characteristic of form cannot be apprehended; the characteristics of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena cannot be apprehended.
The characteristic of visual consciousness cannot be apprehended, nor can those of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness.
The characteristic of eye-contact is unapprehendable; the characteristics of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are likewise so.
The sensation produced by eye-contact is also unapprehendable; the sensations produced by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are likewise so.

The characteristics of the perception and conceptualization of form (*rūpa*) are likewise unattainable; even so it is for the characteristics of the perception and conceptualization of phenomena (*dharma*).

The characteristic of the mind (*manas*) is unattainable, the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is unattainable, and the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) are also unattainable.
The characteristics of the desire realm cannot be apprehended; the characteristics of the form realm cannot be apprehended; the characteristics of the formless realm cannot be apprehended.
The characteristics of the conditioned cannot be apprehended; the characteristics of the unconditioned cannot be apprehended.
If there are no speakers for the verbal expressions of such various phenomena, then those phenomena are called "ineffable dharmas.
The Buddha-dharma is supreme because ignorant, ordinary beings who have not heard it are unable to know it.
Having heard this, they are struck with alarm and fear; they develop dread toward the Buddha’s Dharma and immediately fall away from the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
All devas and worldlings should feel compassion for such beings, who dwell perpetually within birth and death and are constantly tormented by suffering.

At that time, the gods of the Yāma Heaven, having observed the sentient beings in the world afflicted by defilements, gave rise to a courageous mind for the sake of attaining the Buddha-dharma and to make offerings to the Tathāgata. The ritual implements they prepared surpassed those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as they made their offering to the Buddha.
Having made offerings to the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Yāma devas praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
"The Buddha perceives that all aggregates (skandhas) are empty and quiescent; The same is true for the elements (dhātus) and sense bases (āyatanas).”
The aggregates of the sense faculties are all devoid of marks; the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
Regarding the true dharma, the wise of the world understand it spontaneously without hearing it from another:
namely, the conventional truth and the ultimate truth; apart from these, there is no third dharma.
The Tathāgata, out of compassion for all, speaks of conventional truth for the benefit of the world;
the Tathāgata proclaims it to the world, revealing the six realms of existence for the sake of all sentient beings.
The denizens of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; the paths of humans, devas, and asuras;
lowly families and noble families; all poor households and wealthy households;
the class of male servants and female attendants; and those of both sexes and those with dual sexual organs—[all these are encompassed].
The Buddha’s peerless body has fully described all the six realms of existence in the world.
Having observed all phenomena according to conventional truth, the Buddha proclaimed them for the benefit of the world;
yet sentient beings take pleasure in and cling to birth and death, unable to free themselves from the eight worldly concerns.
What are called gain and loss, as well as defamation and praise, All instances of honor and censure, and suffering and pleasure:
Upon gaining profit, one immediately gives rise to joy; Upon losing profit, the mind immediately gives rise to anger and affliction.
The rest should be understood as previously explained.
The world follows these eight dharmas; those who speak of "truth" within conventional reality should be known as possessing inverted wisdom.
They speak of purity and pleasure within what is impure and suffering;
they speak of a self within what is non-self, and of permanence within impermanent phenomena, remaining attached to these characteristics.
Having heard the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, they are terrified, slander them, and do not accept them;
having slandered the Tathāgata’s true teaching, they fall into the hells of extreme suffering.
Because these foolish and ignorant ones greedily seek worldly pleasures, they undergo hundreds of boundless kinds of suffering.
If there are those who, within this Buddha-dharma, observe reality as it is without inversion,
they abandon all states of existence and enter nirvāṇa, just as a snake sheds its old skin.

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent; emptiness, signlessness, and the ultimate truth— if one hears this Dharma and gives rise to love and joy, one will surely attain unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment.
The Tathāgata has taught this Dharma as it truly is, Eliminating all doubts and delusions among the assembly of devas;
They have all resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta For the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
Once this assembly of devas had thus resolved their minds, they were all filled with joy and their hearts became pure;
having heard the most supreme Buddha-dharma, all these devas shall attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the assembly of four hundred million Yāma devas possessed deep-seated faith and joy, smiled.
Then, Aśvajit questioned the Tathāgata with these verses:
“The Buddha manifests a smile for the sake of the world; All those present in the assembly have given rise to doubt.”
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the cause of his smile, so that this entire assembly may be filled with joy.
Having heard the predictions for the various devas, all have leaped for great joy;
those possessed of wisdom have aroused valorous resolve and shall practice according to the teachings within the Buddha-dharma.
This assembly of the Tathāgata’s supreme followers is fully endowed with the vessels for the Buddha’s merit;
well done, you who proclaim these exquisite words in order to gather such a great multitude.
Hearing of the Buddha’s virtues, their hearts are filled with joy; this great assembly shall surely attain it.
Having heard the Tathāgata’s prophecy, they shall diligently cultivate practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Excellent is the teaching of the Honored One among men, supreme among all;
for this assembly of those with doubt and divided minds, we pray that the World-Honored One will quickly explain it, for the entire congregation now desires to hear it with one mind.
The Yāma devas have received this supreme prediction; may the Lion among Men quickly explain it!
This entire great assembly is filled with joy, and all have resolved their minds upon Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Aśvajit with these verses:
“I manifest a smile for the benefit of the world; Aśvajit, you have asked well at this opportune moment.
It brings benefit to the immeasurable great assembly, Because they shall hear of the merits of the Buddha-Tathāgata.”
Sentient beings who are attached to and crave lust and anger have no inclination for the Buddha’s virtues;
their minds, deluded and distracted by ignorance, shall sink into the great ocean of birth and death.
Those who have deep faith and joy in the Buddha’s Dharma, who have previously posed questions to former Buddhas,
and who are endowed with a heart of great compassion— such persons are able to attain the qualities of a Buddha.
When a superior person sees others oppressed by decay and distress, they give rise to compassion for them;
those sentient beings, hearing of the Buddha’s virtues, receive the Buddha’s teachings upon their heads like a garland of flowers.
My assembly is exceedingly pure; having cultivated merit under previous Buddhas, they receive upon their heads the Tathāgata’s virtues, as if wearing a garland of vārṣika flowers.
The hosts of the Yāma Heaven, having previously been in the presence of Buddhas, practiced the precepts and eliminated greedy attachment;
with minds purified through wearying detachment from afflictions, they gave rise to compassion for defiled sentient beings.
They have personally attended immeasurable Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
they have practiced immeasurable virtues in order to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
Knowing that sentient beings have sunk into afflictions, he gives rise to compassion for those suffering beings;
toward the Lion among Men, the benefactor of the world, he asks about the immeasurable gateways to all dharmas.
I, the Guide, now preach for them; all who hear shall attain the path to Buddhahood.
Knowing that sentient beings are caught by the hook of afflictions, I preach for them the most supreme and wondrous Dharma.
That supreme man, the Great Guide, expounds the Dharma of emptiness for those sentient beings;
having heard what the Buddhas have taught, they all come to fully realize that all phenomena are empty.
That which is called emptiness is the absence of all dharmic characteristics; it is taught as the dharma of selflessness and signlessness.
Thus understanding all the Buddha-dharmas, they abide entirely within the virtues of the Buddhas.
Having made these supreme and wondrous offerings to me, each shall receive a prediction according to the Dharma;
in a future age, during the Nakṣatra Kalpa, they shall all attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Thus, there were no more and no fewer Tathāgatas, their number being a full forty billion;
those Buddhas were all named Honored One of Pure Wisdom, awakening immeasurable sentient beings.
The Great Sage, who has subdued all enemies, Answers the inquiry posed by Aśvajit;
Fulfilling the aspirations of the Yāma devas, The great assembly of gods and humans all rejoice.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Six;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Sixteen: The Prediction for the Tuṣita Heaven, Part Seven of the Sixteenth Assembly on Bodhisattvas Perceiving Reality. Chapter Sixteen:

The Prediction for the Tuṣita Heaven. At that time, eight hundred million devas of the Tuṣita Heaven, having seen the asuras, garuḍas, and even those up to the yāmas making offerings to the Tathāgata and having heard his prediction, were filled with joy and exultation, and they thought thus:
"In what dharma has the World-Honored One bestowed upon us the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

"Is it by means of form that one receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or is it by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that one receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Those devas then further thought:
"It is not by means of form that the prediction is given, nor is it by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is given."
Why is this? Since form is unarisen, awakening (bodhi) is also unarisen.
How can unarisen form awaken to unarisen awakening?
In this way, even consciousness does not arise; how can non-arising consciousness awaken to non-arising bodhi?
Since form is neither extinguished, nor is bodhi extinguished, how can unextinguished form awaken to unextinguished bodhi?
In this way, even consciousness does not cease; how can that which is unceasing consciousness awaken to unceasing bodhi?
Form is without discrimination, and bodhi is also without discrimination; how can form, which is without discrimination, awaken to bodhi, which is without discrimination?
In this way, even consciousness is without discrimination; how can non-discriminating consciousness awaken to non-discriminating bodhi?
Since form is non-dual, bodhi is also non-dual; how can non-dual form awaken to non-dual bodhi?
In this way, even consciousness is non-dual; how can non-dual consciousness awaken to non-dual bodhi?
Since form is without action, bodhi is also without action; how can form, which is without action, realize bodhi, which is without action?
In this way, even consciousness is without activity; how can non-active consciousness awaken to non-active bodhi?
Since form cannot be apprehended, bodhi likewise cannot be apprehended.
How can one who cannot apprehend form awaken to an unapprehendable bodhi?
Likewise, up to the aggregate of consciousness, which is unapprehendable, and bodhi, which is also unapprehendable—how can one who cannot apprehend consciousness awaken to an unapprehendable bodhi?
Thus, within those dharmas that are non-apprehendable, what is the Buddha?
What is bodhi? And what is the bodhisattva?
What is this prediction?
The aggregate of form is empty; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise all empty. Why is this so?
Because their nature is inherently empty.
Thus, the Buddha is empty, awakening is empty, the bodhisattva is empty, and the prediction of enlightenment is empty. Why is this?

Because their intrinsic nature is empty, within all phenomena whose nature is thus empty, that which is called "Buddha" is merely a name and a function; it is merely conventional truth, merely verbal expression, and merely a conceptual designation.

The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise merely names and functions, mere worldly expressions and conceptual designations. A wise person should not grasp at or become attached to these.

For example, suppose there is a person who experiences the pleasures of the five senses within a dream; once that person has awakened, they no longer see those pleasures, and because they cannot recall the pleasures of the five senses, they give rise to suffering and distress.

Thus, those who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, if they harbor attachments and do not encounter bodhi, will not realize bodhi; because they do not realize it, they do not obtain its flavor, and because they do not obtain its flavor, their minds give rise to suffering and affliction.
Why is this? Because all such phenomena are unreal, like dreams.
Although the meanings of those phenomena differ, foolish ordinary beings grasp and understand them in various ways; all phenomena should be known in this manner.
Which dharmas are the Buddha?
Which dharmas are the bodhisattva?
Which dharmas are awakening (bodhi)?
All those Buddha-dharmas are unattainable.
Ordinary beings are unattainable, and the dharmas of ordinary beings are also unattainable.
Śrāvakas are unattainable, and the dharmas of śrāvakas are also unattainable.
Pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha be apprehended.
Bodhisattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharmas of a Bodhisattva be apprehended.
The Buddha cannot be apprehended, nor can the Buddha-dharma be apprehended.
Bodhi cannot be apprehended, nor can nirvāṇa be apprehended.
Within these dharmas, we have attained understanding and are free from doubt.

At that time, the gods of Tuṣita Heaven, having no further doubts or hesitations regarding this Dharma, delighted in practicing offerings to the World-Honored One; the offerings they performed were superior to those of the Yāma Heaven.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side. He then praised the World-Honored One with these verses:
"To all who abide in the virtues of a Buddha, The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of practice;
They attain the three gates of liberation And cultivate themselves within the peerless realm."
In the formless there is no feeling, perception, or mental formations; there is no one who feels, nor is there mind.
This is the realm of unimpeded wisdom, where the Lion among Men delights in being free from the aggregates of desire.
Those wise and sublime beings do not grasp at the thought of awakening;
having transcended the aggregates, they have attained supreme roots of goodness and harbor no doubts regarding the Buddha’s virtues.
Aspiring to the unsurpassed Great Bodhi, yet remaining free from attachment to that Bodhi, one thus has neither sorrow nor joy within the mind;
such a person is called a Son of the Buddha practicing the Noble Path.
Seeing that all phenomena are equal to the Buddha, they thus have no fear regarding the Dharma;
wise ones, dwelling in this world, seek the Buddha’s virtues and initiate their practice.
Discerning the characteristics of form without attachment, Abandoning all minds that perceive signs,
One does not give rise to aspirations for those three realms of existence, Observing that all states of being are entirely empty.
One who can know that each of the five aggregates is unarisen, That the Tathāgata’s prediction and bodhi are likewise unarisen,
And that the bodhicitta and so forth are also without arising— One who speaks thus is not deluded or confused.
The merits of the Tathāgata as well as birth and death—these dharmas of the Buddha are all unarisen.
One who knows thus is the most excellent among men; such a person is a true son of the Tathāgata.
If one can know that these aggregates do not perish, And that the elements, the sense bases,
and the dharmas of the Tathāgata, As well as the Buddha, awakening, and the prediction of enlightenment— All such dharmas are likewise imperishable.
If there are those who practice for the sake of Bodhi, you should know that they too are imperishable;
because they know that all worlds are imperishable, their quest for Bodhi will not be difficult.
The five aggregates, elements, and sense bases, as well as awakening, the Buddha, and the bodhisattvas—all are without action.
One who understands this thus is a child of the Buddha; such a person can uphold the true Dharma of the Buddha.
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all devoid of awakening;
enlightenment, the Buddha, and the bodhisattvas, as well as the bestowal of prophecy—all are entirely devoid of awakening. One who knows thus is a child of the Buddha.
The five aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases are empty and quiescent in nature;
the Buddha, as well as enlightenment and the prediction of awakening, and even the true sons of the Tathāgata who practice the path—all these are likewise empty of intrinsic nature.

The aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all false; the two-legged World-Honored One and awakening, as well as the practitioner’s prediction of enlightenment, are likewise false. To understand them thus is to be a child of the Buddha.
Neither relying nor not relying, neither existent phenomena nor non-existent phenomena,
neither conditioned nor unconditioned— one who understands thus is a child of the Buddha.
The World-Honored One perceives the world in this way; we likewise understand the Buddha’s mind.
This itself constitutes the most sublime and wondrous offering to the Buddha and to the entire assembly of worthy sages.
The merit we have gained from praising the Buddha can only be fully known by the World-Honored Buddha himself;
by dedicating this merit to all living beings, may they all attain Buddhahood and be endowed with all the marks of perfection.
At that time, having heard the praise from those devas of Tuṣita and knowing their profound faith, the World-Honored One manifested a smile for the sake of the assembly of devas.
Then the Venerable Aśvajit asked in verse:
“O Unsurpassed One of Great Power, By the force of its cause, you manifest the light of a smile.”
May the Buddha explain the cause of this smile, so that all who hear it may rejoice.
Because they have seen the Tathāgata smile, this great assembly is filled with doubt;
the multitude gazes up at him with earnest devotion, all with one mind desiring to hear.
Just as a person in the world who is ill thinks only of a physician and excellent medicine,
so too this great assembly, in the presence of the Buddha, yearns with joy to hear the proclamation of their prediction.
All these possess profound wisdom; with their minds set on seeking Bodhi, they are free from attachment.
With all reverence, they gaze up at you, desiring only that the Tathāgata grant them a prediction of enlightenment.
The World-Honored One gives rise to great compassion herein; With the power of a Buddha’s wisdom, he cuts through the net of doubt.
Therefore, the great assembly attains joy, And all together aspire to seek the virtues of a Buddha.
World-Honored One, now is the very time for you to bestow the prophecy; we pray that you will eliminate all doubts and delusions.
Since long ago the Tathāgata has been free from all enemies, we pray that you will sever the various heterodox arguments of the outsiders.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Aśvajit with these verses:
"You have now requested the meaning from the Tathāgata; To ask about this smile is precisely the right time.
Because you have asked for the benefit of the world, You shall surely bring great advantage to all sentient beings."
Knowing the inclinations and desires of the assembly of devas, I have manifested this light of a smile;
because they know the excellence and wondrousness of the Buddha-dharma, they have rendered supreme offerings to me.
They all perceive the world as it truly is; Following the noble teaching, they have realized the Dharma.
Having reached the three gates of liberation, they cannot be known by those in the world.
In the past, he made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas And also inquired about this profound significance;
Having long cultivated emptiness under those Buddhas, He now reveals the meaning of emptiness here.
Therefore, at this very place, I have now encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
with emptiness I praise the Unsurpassed One, who benefits all worlds.
Just as this world is entirely without arising, so too are the Buddhas, their awakening, and the predictions of enlightenment;
all those who practice for the sake of awakening are likewise entirely without arising.
All sentient beings equally possess this Dharma; having known it thus, they attain Bodhi.
Those who have previously trained in the bodhicitta are able to understand this meaning.

Thus, this world is neither extinguished; these hosts of devas have attained excellent penetration, their brilliant wisdom illuminating all things without doubt, and for this reason, those devas shall all become Buddhas.
One will certainly attain the state of non-reliance; not grasping at phenomena, one is free from conceptual construction.
All worlds are without activity—such is the meaning that he is able to understand.
The essence of all phenomena is devoid of intrinsic nature; The minds of the celestial hosts are pure and free from doubt.
Both awakening and the mind of awakening— All are empty and lack intrinsic nature.
The gods of Tuṣita possess firm wisdom; They all dwell securely in non-reliance.
Therefore, attaining bodhi is not difficult for them; They shall surely and swiftly accomplish unsurpassed knowledge.
In the future Star-Constellation Kalpa, they shall deliver and liberate boundless multitudes;
all those devas will attain Buddhahood, sharing the same name: King Who Selects the Dharma.
The Tathāgata, regarding this assembly of devas, knows their hearts' inclinations and provides them with a prophetic teaching;
having heard his discourse, all the devas and humans are filled with joy, and it accords perfectly with their wishes.

Chapter Seventeen: The Prediction for the Gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven. At that time, the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, together with his retinue of seven hundred million gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, saw the asuras, garuḍas, and even the gods of the Tuṣita Heaven and others making offerings to the Tathāgata. Having heard the prediction, they were filled with joy and exultation; all attained their hearts’ desire and dwelt in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), free from doubt regarding suchness (*tathatā*).

Rising from their seats, they bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees upon the ground, and prostrated themselves before the Buddha with their heads at his feet. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they addressed him with one voice, saying:
"World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, all dharmas are the true limit (bhūtakoṭi), the boundless limit, the unobstructed limit, the non-abiding limit, the inexhaustible limit, the non-dual limit, and the limit that is no-limit.
World-Honored One!
That which is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi) is so called because it is non-perverted.
That which is "without limit" is so called because it is immeasurable.
The limit of non-obstruction is because it is free from antidotes;
the limit of non-abiding is because it is free from intrinsic nature;
the limit of inexhaustibility is because there is no arising.
The non-dual limit refers to the fact that it is of a single flavor.
That which is called "not a limit" refers to the fact that it does not exist.
World-Honored One!
That reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) pervades all places; there is not a single dharma that is not the reality-limit.
World-Honored One!
That which is called bodhi is also the reality-limit.
"Bhagavān! What is bodhi? All dharmas are bodhi, because they are devoid of intrinsic nature."
Even the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) are awakening (*bodhi*). Why is this?
Awakening has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the five deeds of immediate retribution also have no intrinsic nature; therefore, even the deeds of immediate retribution are awakening.
World-Honored One!
That which is called bodhi is like the nature of nirvana without remainder, and it is also like the nature of the karma of immediate retribution. Why is this so?
All dharmas are the nature of nirvana without remainder and also the nature of immediate retribution; therefore, the realm of nirvana without remainder is itself bodhi.
World-Honored One!

If there were sentient beings dwelling in birth and death, one might seek nirvana; however, within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no one who dwells in birth and death while seeking nirvana. Why is this?
"Because the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is non-dual,
O Bhagavān! We understand this and have no doubt."
If one has no doubts or hesitations regarding this Dharma, it should be known that such a person has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from various Buddhas in the past.

At that time, having heard the words of the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the seven hundred million devas of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven regarding their predictions, the World-Honored One smiled, wishing to bring joy to the hearts of the great assembly.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit asked in verse:
“The Compassionate One for the World has manifested a smile, Yet he does not declare the cause and condition of that smile.
The Teacher of Gods and Humans does not act without cause; He manifests this extraordinary mark of a smile.”
Having seen the light of the World-Honored One’s smile, the entire great assembly now harbors doubts;
we pray that you will explain the cause of this smile and sever all webs of uncertainty.
If these beings are taught by the Tathāgata, having heard it, they will all give rise to a sense of wonder;
for the sake of that assembly, it shall purify the true path and serve as the causal condition for proceeding toward Bodhi.
If there are sentient beings who harbor doubts and suspicions, such people will find it difficult to attain the wondrous Bodhi;
I only pray that the One of Great Wisdom will sever their delusions and doubts, so that they may diligently and swiftly realize the Unsurpassed Way.
"World-Honored One, this great assembly, having set their will upon seeking Bodhi and being free from all evils,
shall surely become Great Dharma Kings once they have heard the predictions granted by the devas."
Therefore, World-Honored One, we pray that out of compassion,
you will sever all hearts of doubt and bestow upon these devas the prediction of bodhi, so that the entire great assembly may rejoice.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya with these verses:
"Out of compassion for the world, I have manifested this smile; Kauṇḍinya, you have now asked me about its meaning.
I shall grant predictions to all those devas; All of you, listen each with a pure mind."
These hosts of gods from the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, having themselves declared that they shall receive the prediction of attaining bodhi,
have let out a lion’s roar amidst the assembly, able to destroy the various false views of the non-Buddhists.
Just as when a shower of stones falls from the sky, they will surely fall upon the great earth without doubt;
so too, the Son of the Buddha, free from all uncertainty, knows for himself that he shall certainly attain the Way of the Buddha.
Just as when the sun has set and night has fallen, one knows that the sun will surely rise before long;
so it is with a Son of the Buddha who is equipped with all practices—one can be certain that he will surely possess the ten powers.
Furthermore, just as when the sun is at its zenith, All forms and images are seen with perfect clarity,
So too the Son of the Buddha, endowed with all practices, Knows for himself that he will surely attain *sarvajñā*.
Just as when the sunlight reaches its setting, all people know that the sun is no longer seen;
so too do these sons of the Buddha know for themselves that they will certainly attain the most supreme wisdom.
Just as all streams flow downward, the wise should know they return to the great ocean;
so too, the sons of the Buddha who possess clear wisdom are certain to attain supreme enlightenment.
Just as when a person hurls a stone into the sky, it will certainly fall to the ground without doubt;
so too do these sons of the Buddha know for themselves that before long they shall attain the state of a Knower of the World.
It is the natural law for the wise to hold this view; because they know the Dharma, they harbor no doubt.
Knowing that they themselves possess a share of the Buddha’s merit, they are certain to draw near to spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
Even if there were tens of millions of māras appearing as Buddhas and saying,
"You shall not become a Buddha," they could not thwart his resolve, for he has already attained a thorough understanding of the true Dharma.
Having definitively realized those buddha-qualities, they each spoke of having received their prediction;
regarding these predictions granted to the devas, the Tathāgata gave rise to a heart of sympathetic joy.
The bodhisattva practices cultivated by these devas, they fully understand by themselves without depending on others;
having declared for themselves that they shall become Sugatas, the World-Honored One rejoices in them all.
Therefore, Aśvajit, if there is anyone who wishes to attain unsurpassed enlightenment, they should diligently seek this Dharma;
they will surely obtain the most supreme state of peace and security.

Having attained self-enlightenment, one awakens to this principle; by understanding it according to its meaning as it truly is, and by drawing near to and making offerings to spiritual friends, the realization of Bodhi will not be difficult.
If one were to practice asceticism for a thousand eons, Without attachment or regret for skin, fat, blood, or flesh,
Yet if one can understand the true meaning and intent of this, This merit would be vast and superior to that.
All Buddhas of the past, those who compassionately regard sentient beings in the future,
and all World-Honored Ones of the present— every one of them has attained the path of Buddhahood by relying entirely upon this Dharma.
Having made offerings to me, these transformed devas all thoroughly understand the ultimate truth;
having once made offerings to the Tathāgatas of the past, they shall awaken to this principle and attain Buddhahood.
The supreme samādhis possessed by all Buddhas, as well as the concentration in which they currently abide—
the devas have deeply attained these Buddha-realms through long-term cultivation in previous lives.
"Aśvajit! The gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven have no doubt regarding that samādhi; having thoroughly studied the pure Buddha-dharma, they now manifest its practice upon the path of the Buddha."
Therefore, having conceived faith and understanding in this principle, one should rightly and diligently seek the end of suffering;
by constantly drawing near to those of great learning, one will surely attain unsurpassed, great bodhi.
Having heard the sublime Dharma spoken by the Buddha, the assembly of gods from the Nirmāṇarati heaven were all filled with joy;
their nets of doubt were cleared away, and they flowed toward Great Nirvāṇa.

Chapter 18: The Prophecy for the Gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations At that time, the King of the Gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations, together with his retinue of eighty nayutas of devas, saw the asuras, garuḍas, nāga girls, nāga kings, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, hārakalpa devas, the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and others making offerings to the Tathāgata. Having heard the prophecy, they were filled with joy and exultation, their hearts satisfied, and with one voice they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Regarding the 'reality-limit' (bhūtakoṭi) spoken of by the gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, we do not even perceive reality, much less perceive its limit. Why is this so,
World-Honored One?"
If one were to see reality, one could be said to see the limit.
Why is this? Because such a person acts within two spheres.
For those sons or daughters of good family who abide in such a vehicle, one should explain these two kinds of dharmas to them.
These two dharmas are not the true realm.
“World-Honored One!

If a son or daughter of good family does not believe in and enter the Dharma of non-duality, even though they may thus resolve their minds with the hope of attaining bodhi, you should know that this person is traveling upon a wrong path.”
Why is this? Because this is not the practice of the path toward enlightenment,
World-Honored One.
If there are sentient beings who seek bodhi, such persons do not perceive even a single dharma that can be awakened to.
Why is this? Because there is not the slightest dharma that can be awakened to as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!
