That dharma is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is not to be cognized, not to be known, not to be abandoned, not to be cultivated, and not to be realized.
That which is called "enlightenment" (bodhi) does not serve as an antidote to other phenomena, nor do other phenomena serve as an antidote to it. Why is this?
Those dharmas are neither associated with afflictions nor free from afflictions; the essence of these dharmas cannot be apprehended, for their nature is inherently detached.
These dharmas do not act as antidotes to those dharmas, nor do those dharmas act as antidotes to these dharmas.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are devoid of all marks.
Therefore, those phenomena cannot be known, cannot be cognized, cannot be abandoned, cannot be cultivated, and cannot be realized.
World-Honored One!

Because the arising of form is free from the characteristic of arising, it cannot be known, nor can it be attained, up to and including being realized; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
World-Honored One!
Because the cessation of form is free from the characteristics of form, it is neither knowable nor even realizable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
World-Honored One!
Because the past is devoid of the characteristics of the past, it is neither knowable nor even realizable;
because the future is devoid of the characteristics of the future, it is likewise neither knowable nor even realizable.
Because the present is devoid of the characteristics of the present, it is likewise neither knowable nor even realizable.
World-Honored One!
Because the conditioned is devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned, it is likewise neither knowable nor even realizable.
Because the unconditioned is free from the characteristics of the unconditioned, it is neither knowable, nor cognizable, nor abandonable, nor cultivatable, nor realizable.
World-Honored One!

In this manner, up to and including those subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*), or subsumed under the past, the present, or the future, or subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), none of these phenomena can be apprehended.
Because they cannot be apprehended, those dharmas are neither knowable nor cognizable, neither to be abandoned nor to be cultivated, nor to be realized. World-Honored One,
if there are good sons or good daughters who thus resolve their minds and practice for the sake of seeking bodhi, they are all said to abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
At that time, after all the devas of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations had each spoken the Dharma they knew, they praised him in verse:
"The World-Honored One has well explained the end of existence; He shall never again, even for a moment, receive a body within the six realms.
The world lacks wisdom and fears birth and death; He has resolved his mind to ferry others across the shore of saṃsāra."
The essence of those aggregates cannot be apprehended, for the nature and characteristics of the aggregates are fundamentally empty;
all phenomena are empty and devoid of marks, and therefore all phenomena are free from antidotes.

The self-nature is itself empty and devoid of substance; there is nothing to be known, nor anything to be cultivated or relinquished, nor is it a dharma that can be realized. What the Tathāgata says exists is precisely non-existence.
Seeking bodhi through its characteristics is unattainable; all dharmas that assist the path are likewise so.
Seeking a Buddha by grasping at the mind is unattainable; seeking a Bodhisattva through characteristics is also unattainable.
Those foolish people who are stubbornly attached to various signs hope to awaken to bodhi;
yet, practicing by grasping at signs within inverted realms, they lack wisdom and do not walk the path of bodhi.
Entering the realm of the Buddha and departing from all marks is called the practice of the wise according to the Dharma;
it is to remain far removed from both marks and the markless, and likewise to be free from both emptiness and non-emptiness.
He is able to awaken to and understand the unsurpassed path;
it is not within the realm of the various non-Buddhists, nor is it something that śrāvakas can know, nor is it the destination of pratyekabuddhas.
The mind that has attained liberation, pure and stainless— this is not the domain of the wisdom of those Arhats who are harmonized with the Dharma, nor of all the Pratyekabuddhas.
That phrase is not known by a mind that grasps at signs, nor is it understood through the limited cultivation of emptiness;
yet if there is one who understands emptiness and speaks of emptiness, they also speak of all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature.
He who receives the Buddha’s teaching without disparagement is said to have well-cultivated emptiness and tranquility;
he can awaken to the path of Bodhi that is so difficult to awaken to—the World-Honored One is his true guide.
Having praised the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings, may the immeasurable merit thus obtained be dedicated to all living beings,
so that they may attain Buddhahood and awaken those who have not yet awakened.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that those eighty nayutas of gods from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations and the heavenly kings had attained profound faith, manifested a smile in order to cause the great assembly to further increase their roots of goodness.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit asked in verse:
"The World-Honored One among bipeds manifests a smile, Because he knows the profound faith of the gods who control others' emanations.
He has never before explained the cause and conditions for his smile; I only pray that the Tathāgata will provide an exposition."
Great Sage, it is not without cause that you now manifest this rare smile;
we pray that the Buddha will reveal the meaning of its causal conditions and dispel the various doubts of the great assembly.
Because we have seen the World-Honored One smile, this entire assembly now harbors doubts;
O Compassionate One who pities all the world, we pray that you will explain and analyze it for us.
This assembly has all turned their backs on birth and death; with palms joined in reverence, they seek nirvana.
Among them, none are without lingering doubt; O Unobstructed Speaker, we pray that you will sever it.
All have developed right faith in the Dharma of the Sugata; their minds are liberated and free from grasping.
With pure faith and a heart of reverence, they exclaim, "Excellent, O Muni! We pray that you will explain it."
Bravely and with diligent effort in the Buddha-dharma, One leaves behind the net of doubt and ascends the path of the sages;
All Buddhas traverse this path, Therefore, I pray that you dispel the doubts of the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya in verse:
“Out of compassion for the great assembly, you have asked me this very question in verse at the appropriate time.
Possessing perfect eloquence and skillful means, you are indeed able to inquire about the meaning of this smile.”
Because you ask the Tathāgata why he has manifested a smile, there will surely be benefit for immeasurable multitudes;
therefore, all those in this assembly shall dwell in supreme bodhi.
Knowing that they have deep faith in the other-transformed [heaven], I therefore manifest this light of a smile;
all of them follow the Tathāgata’s teaching and cultivate sublime practices in pursuit of enlightenment.
Contemplate worldly phenomena as being devoid of all marks, like seeing a mirage that is not real;
the fool sees the mirage and calls it water—those who seek bodhi should not be like them.
Ordinary beings grasp at signs and crave the pleasures of their realm; lacking wisdom, they are perpetually terrified of signlessness.
Out of folly, they cling to signs and abandon the true path; yet by being free from signs, one can attain sublime bodhi.
Deluded thoughts and calculations are but false dharmas; Following whatever one discriminates, one is immediately bound.
The wise observe that all signs are entirely empty, And thus attain the dharani of supreme tranquility.
Ordinary fools who grasp at signs dwell in evil minds; lacking wisdom, they all return to the six realms of existence.
Oppressed by the cycle of saṃsāra, they undergo manifold sufferings, all because they dwell upon signs out of ignorance.
Sentient beings who cling to signs perceive the aggregates, as well as the Buddha, bodhi, and bodhisattvas;
but the wise, having abandoned signs and seen emptiness, are able to attain unsurpassed great bodhi.
Those who dwell upon signs increase their afflictions; by being able to contemplate signlessness, one attains the removal of fetters.
What are called "fetters" are themselves signs; by contemplating that these fetters are signless, they are severed and eliminated.
If there are those who seek the Way through conceptual discrimination, such discrimination becomes an obstacle to the Way;
yet for the wise, even though they may engage in desire, that very desire becomes practice of the signless.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are unattainable; by discerning all phenomena, one speaks of them as empty.
If one is free from such discernment, one attains the signless; that itself is bodhi, with nothing else remaining.
Having heard these words spoken by the Sugata, the great assembly was freed from doubt and attained fearlessness;
they received the Dharma taught by the Muni upon their heads, just as the wise wear the *campaka* flower upon their crowns.
These hosts of devas have attained fearlessness; having made the most unsurpassed offerings to me, and knowing all dharmas as the realm of the Buddha, they shall become great teachers of the world.

Chapter Nineteen: The Prediction for the Brahmā Devas and Others At that time, six million Brahmā deities, having witnessed the asuras, garuḍas, and even those up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas making offerings to the Tathāgata, and having heard their predictions, were filled with joy and exultation, their hearts satisfied beyond measure.

Regarding worldly dhyāna, he takes joy as his sustenance; furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, he has attained the light of wisdom. Because he has planted roots of goodness in past lives, because he has personally attended upon and made offerings to various Buddhas, and because of his profound and pure faith, he has attained the patient acceptance of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) regarding the most profound teachings.

Those devas know that all dharmas are without action and not without action; neither arising nor non-arising; neither existent nor non-existent; neither originating nor non-originating; neither ceasing nor non-ceasing; neither dependent nor non-dependent; neither clear nor turbid; neither hateful nor loving; neither wise nor foolish; neither knowing nor not knowing; neither seeing nor not seeing; neither receiving nor not receiving; neither compassionate nor non-compassionate; neither non-existent nor not non-existent; neither a thing nor not a thing; neither obtainable nor unobtainable; neither departing nor coming; neither proceeding nor not proceeding; neither empty nor non-empty; neither characterized nor non-characterized; neither aspiring nor non-aspiring.

Those Brahmā devas have no mental attachment to any phenomena and do not dwell upon them; they do not form the notion of "non-utility" regarding what is not useful, nor do they form the notion of "not non-utility" regarding what is not useless.
Within speech, there is no perception of speech; within that which is not speech, there is also no perception of non-speech.
Within the conditioned, there is no perception of the conditioned; within the unconditioned, there is also no perception of the unconditioned.
One does not form the notion of "ordinary person" regarding an ordinary person, nor does one form the notion of "non-ordinary person" regarding a non-ordinary person.

One does not form the notion of "phenomena of an ordinary person" regarding phenomena of an ordinary person, nor does one form the notion of "phenomena of a non-ordinary person" regarding phenomena of a non-ordinary person.
One does not form the notion of "śrāvaka" regarding a śrāvaka, nor does one form the notion of "non-śrāvaka" regarding one who is not a śrāvaka.
One does not form the notion of "śrāvaka-dharma" regarding the dharmas of a śrāvaka, nor does one form the notion of "non-śrāvaka-dharma" regarding the dharmas of one who is not a śrāvaka.
One does not form the notion of a pratyekabuddha regarding a pratyekabuddha, nor does one form the notion of a non-pratyekabuddha regarding one who is not a pratyekabuddha.

One does not form the notion of pratyekabuddha-dharmas regarding pratyekabuddha-dharmas, nor does one form the notion of non-pratyekabuddha-dharmas regarding those that are not pratyekabuddha-dharmas.
One does not form the notion of a bodhisattva with respect to a bodhisattva, nor does one form the notion of a non-bodhisattva with respect to a non-bodhisattva.
One does not form the notion of bodhisattva-dharmas with respect to bodhisattva-dharmas, nor does one form the notion of non-bodhisattva-dharmas with respect to non-bodhisattva-dharmas.
One does not form the notion of "Buddha" regarding the Buddha, nor does one form the notion of "non-Buddha" regarding what is not the Buddha.
One does not form the notion of "Buddha-dharma" regarding the Buddha-dharmas, nor does one form the notion of "non-Buddha-dharma" regarding what are not the Buddha-dharmas.
One does not form the notion of nirvana regarding nirvana, nor does one form the notion of non-nirvana regarding what is not nirvana.
One does not form the notion of saṃsāra regarding saṃsāra, nor does one form the notion of non-saṃsāra regarding what is not saṃsāra.
Thus, all those devas were entirely free from conceptual discrimination, their concentrated minds pure.
Having attained such purity of mind, they praised the Buddha with verses on the dharma of cessation:
“The Great Sage possesses the profound wisdom of cessation; Through the practice of cessation, he has reached the further shore.”
He proclaims the teaching of quiescence to deliver sentient beings, And he himself constantly practices the dharma of quiescence.
Enlightenment is quiescent and perfectly pure; This dharma is the domain of the Muni.
Swiftly attaining the supreme nectar of quiescence, By this, he has now brought all existence to an end.
He constantly proclaims the subtle path of quiescent extinction, which is the sphere of action for those wise ones;
this Eightfold Path extinguishes affliction and turbidity, delivering all living beings from suffering.
Skillfully cultivating cessation to realize enlightenment is the practice of the Buddhas of the past;
by practicing this, one can reach the city of peace, as realized and known by all the Buddhas of the past.
These Tathāgatas practiced and studied this Dharma; thus the Teacher transforms the world.
If a person can practice the Dharma of those still in training (śaikṣa), they will attain the supreme enlightenment of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

With single-minded devotion, you have pursued the path of quiescence; having long cultivated the tranquility of the sense faculties, you shall become a Buddha, a knower of the world, who with the power of Nārāyaṇa delivers all living beings.
One who knows the nectar of tranquil extinction can exhaust all marks of existence;
such a person is a true son of the Tathāgata, for tranquil extinction can remove the fears of the world.
The offerings they prepared for the Buddha were supreme, rare, and most extraordinary;
the teaching of the cessation that exhausts all afflictions is the foremost among all signless dharmas.
The world is quiescent and free from all signs; what is called quiescence is precisely nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings transmigrate and undergo various sufferings because they distance themselves from quiescence and grasp at signs.
The inconceivable dharmas of the Muni are themselves the bodhi of omniscience;
having crossed the mire and reached the further shore, the Buddha has no doubts or anxieties regarding this.
If one seeks liberation apart from the aggregates, And takes no delight in the Buddha’s Mahāyāna,
Desiring instead to seek bodhi through the thought of extinction, Such a person gives rise to fear toward the five aggregates.
Seeking nirvāṇa with a mind purified of desire— such discerning wisdom regarding phenomena as being within the domain of grasping at signs is what the Tathāgata has taught.
If one grasps at quiescent extinction, that is bondage; because of this, one does not attain omniscience.
If there are those who perceive the characteristics of the five aggregates, they should not give rise to a mind of grasping or attachment.
He is able to benefit the Dharma of Śākya; this is called the practice of joy and bliss without signs.

He can attain the nameless state of peace and security, reach the realm of Bodhi and the Buddhas, subdue Māra and contentious disputations, extinguish the afflictions, and swiftly achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
The merit we have gained from praising the Unsurpassed One, and the qualities of peace therein, can only be fully known by the Buddha’s great wisdom;
we dedicate it to all sentient beings, vowing that they may attain Buddhahood.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, knowing that the various Brahmās had finished praising the Buddha, stood upright before the Buddha and praised him with verses of true merit, saying:

"The Dharma King has already known all dharmas; They are unreal, deceptive, and like an empty fist, Like autumn clouds and flashes of lightning; Therefore, the Great Sage is free from the mind of grasping."
Just as a hungry person in a dream Eats a hundred flavors of sweet and delicious food,
The hunger and eating of the dreamer are both unreal— The Tathāgata’s vision of phenomena is likewise so.
Furthermore, it is like a person suffering from parching thirst in a dream who obtains to drink pure, cool, clear water;
the thirst in the dream and the drinking of water are both empty and false—so too does the Buddha perceive all phenomena.

There is no agent, no recipient, and no sentient being; there is no action performed nor any resulting retribution, nor is there anyone who receives the fruit of retribution—of this, the World-Honored One has no doubt.
Just as pleasant words win the affection of others, yet those words have nothing to be grasped,
and there is neither speaker nor listener— the Great Sage understands that all are unreal.
Just as when one hears the exquisite sound of a lute, that sound likewise lacks any true reality;
so too does the World-Honored One view the aggregates, knowing that the aggregates have no essence and are ungraspable.
Just as a mani jewel is pure by its very nature, yet changes according to the colors of the cloth upon which it is tied, so too the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally pure;
it is only through false conceptualization that delusive defilements increase.
Just as a stainless, fresh white cloth changes according to whatever dye it receives,
so too are all phenomena pure by nature, yet they become defiled according to how they are conceptualized.
Just as someone who hears the sound of a conch shell seeks to find from where that sound comes,
yet the sound has no nature of its own nor of another— so too does the Great Sage perceive all phenomena.
Just as a person thinks of eating a delicious meal, That meal is composed of a combination of many conditions;
When observing that each part lacks intrinsic nature, The Tathāgata sees all phenomena in this same way.
For example, a city is designated based on various conditions; yet when its substance is examined, it lacks intrinsic nature.
Thus all such conditions are entirely empty, and the Dharma King perceives phenomena in this very same way.

Just as when someone strikes a drum, Though its sound can bring joy to the hearts of men, The sound and all its contributing conditions are entirely empty; The Great Sage’s vision of phenomena is likewise so.
For example, when someone beats a drum, its sound does not come from the ten directions;
when the sound ceases, it likewise does not go toward any direction. The World-Honored One perceives all phenomena to be just like this.

Thus, after that person has struck the drum, the drum gives rise to neither aversion nor attachment, nor does it discriminate among the nature of various conditions; the Buddha perceives all phenomena to be just like this.
Furthermore, just as when a person strikes a wondrous drum, The sound does not arise with a mind [of its own] yet brings joy to others;
So too it is with all conditions— The Teacher perceives all phenomena in this very way.

Just as when a person strikes a fine drum, the drum itself gives rise to neither the perception of suffering nor pleasure, nor does it examine the nature of its various conditions; so too does the Tathāgata perceive all phenomena.
Just as when someone strikes a fine drum, the sound neither follows its conditions nor is it separate from them;
and so it is with the conditions of the musician—the Muni’s vision of all phenomena is likewise thus.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the various Brahmā deities, the Great Brahmā King, and others possessed deep-seated reverence and faith, and having heard their eulogies of the Buddha regarding the state of cessation, and further seeing that the great assembly desired to give rise to roots of goodness, immediately smiled.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit asked in verse:
“Having seen the stainless, pure light of a smile issue from the mouth of the Tathāgata,
the great assembly of gods and humans in the world all have conceived a sense of wonder.”
Because they saw the World-Honored One smile, the entire assembled multitude was filled with doubt;
all gazed up at the Tathāgata’s face, earnestly longing to hear his teaching.
I pray that the Buddha will reveal the cause and conditions of his smile, dispelling the hearts of doubt among the great assembly;
for the Most Victorious Muni does not manifest this rare sign of a subtle smile without a reason.
The light of the smile manifested by all Buddhas Is surely for the benefit of all worlds;
For whom has this smile now appeared?
I pray that you will explain it in detail.

The great assembly, having heard this, will surely rejoice; because they know the cause and condition for the smile, all these members of the assembly join their palms, gazing with single-minded devotion, desiring to hear it.
Therefore, we pray that the Buddha will provide an explanation; he shall surely sever all our doubts.
For the sake of this assembled multitude, O Guide, we pray that you graciously expound the cause of your smile.
If the assembly hears this, they will surely rejoice, for by it they shall wash away the net of doubt;
their minds will become firm and entirely pure, as they single-mindedly contemplate and yearn for the virtues of the Tathāgata.
The great assembly gazes upon the World-Honored One’s countenance, As if beholding the newly risen moon;
Possessing the eight wondrous tones like Brahmā, They look up with single-minded longing, wishing to hear him speak soon.
When the hosts of devas and humans hear the Buddha’s teaching, they will surely eliminate their doubts and abide in the True Dharma.
As he proclaims with the Brahma-voice, his meaning accords with reality; having heard this profound supramundane Dharma, they shall attain realization.
The Buddha’s wisdom is skillful and able to bring joy; thus it causes the great assembly to increase their exultation.
This assembly, with pure minds free from the knots of doubt, is able to delight in the Tathāgata’s omniscience.
Only those of courageous diligence and great power can aspire to seek the unsurpassed path;
therefore, O Guide, out of compassion for the world, we pray that you explain it so that all may rejoice.
Excellent is the World-Honored One’s impartial mind, Which has compassion for all sentient beings;
May it cause the great assembly to increase their roots of goodness, And settle their minds unmovingly as they seek the Buddha-wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Aśvajit with these verses:
“Out of compassion for all the worlds, I have manifested this light of a smile.”
You should listen attentively as I explain the cause, these verses of profound and subtle meaning.
If this assembly hears them, they will rouse diligent effort to cultivate wholesome deeds;
they shall bring benefit to all sentient beings and undertake supreme practice within the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma.
All these assemblies of Brahmās are filled with joy; within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, they have no doubts at all.
Having practiced for nayutas of kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
They are entirely unattached to any sensory objects; their minds are like space, free from obstruction.
Though they delight in constantly practicing the bodhisattva path, they do not hastily realize the fruit of enlightenment.
Furthermore, in future ages, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
these hosts of devas, pure and free from defilement, shall attain great power and abide in the world.
Thereafter, one shall attain all-knowledge, becoming a Great Dharma King of majestic power;
endowed with all merits, exhausting all realms of existence, one contemplates all worlds as entirely empty and quiescent.
That Buddha, having practiced for a long time as originally intended, has a lifespan of equal measure;
these Sugatas, while remaining in the world, are able to deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction.
That Buddha-land is without peer; its world is adorned, pure, and most flourishing.
Throughout immeasurable nayutas of eons, the Tathāgata could not exhaustively describe it.
The adornments and purity of that Buddha-field could not be fully exhausted even by the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas;
those Buddhas all share the name Great Intellectual Power (Mahā-jñānabala), and their lands are all named Most Victorious (Parama-jaya).
For the sake of the multitude, he expounds the immovable Dharma, Inconceivable and without dependence;
the sentient beings in that Buddha-world All together cultivate and purify all roots of goodness.

Not a single sentient being undergoes further existence; among those who are reborn within the cycle of birth and death, they experience suffering at that time, which then manifests within that world.
Fearing only that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, he causes all sentient beings to give rise to weary detachment;
at that time, the beings of that land will be free from the various marks of suffering such as old age, illness, and death.
All rely upon this single teaching; together they weary of impermanence and cultivate sublime practice.
At that time, those sentient beings no longer hear any other sounds, but hear only impurity, impermanence, suffering, non-self, tranquility, emptiness, and signlessness.
The nectar of nirvāṇa and bodhi, The secure, cool, and unsurpassed bliss—
May such sublime and wondrous sounds as these Be heard constantly and repeatedly.
At that time, no other sounds shall exist, Whether from trees, walls, or open spaces.
Furthermore, whether in the air or within temples, they hear only such subtle and wondrous phrases.
Having heard them, all attain the Way and are immediately liberated from birth and death;
this is entirely due to the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, which possesses the eight qualities of sublime sound.
At that time, there was no mind of mixed poison— namely, being free from desire and hatred—
and neither was there the delusion that produces harsh sounds or coarse words that come to pierce the ear.
All shall turn their backs on birth and death, And proceed toward the great, correct path of Nirvāṇa;
That land will then become entirely empty, For both the Buddha and sentient beings have all attained parinirvāṇa.
This is the great supernatural power of that Buddha, who gave rise to inconceivable and vast vows;
in the past, throughout nayutas of eons, he practiced the path in pursuit of bodhi.
All sentient beings in that land shall all become Buddhas;
these Brahmā devas have made such vast vows, all through contemplating the state of cessation.
They have fully realized and known the profound meaning, And understood the auspicious path of the Tathāgata;
In all that they practice and study, they have attained mastery, And serve as guides for all the worlds.
They are able to contemplate the emptiness of sentient beings, Without giving rise to weariness or indolence;
Therefore, they skillfully enter the nature of all phenomena, Cultivating and accumulating the supreme and wondrous practices of a bodhisattva.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-seven;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: The Light-Sound Heaven Receiving Prophecy; Chapter Sixteen of the Bodhisattva-Dr̥ṣṭatattva Assembly, Part Eight.

At that time, fifty-eight million devas from the Light-Sound Heaven (*Ābhāsvara*), seeing the asuras, garuḍas, and even those up to the Brahmā heavens making offerings to the Tathāgata, and having heard their prophecies, were filled with joy and exultation, their hearts being fully satisfied. They bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees upon the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha in reverent salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

There is a samādhi called "Illuminating All Dharmas. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies this samādhi, they will attain radiance within all dharmas and gain entry into the dharma-gate of the bodhisattvas.

Having understood and realized this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains boundless eloquence, unimpeded eloquence, continuous eloquence, manifold eloquence, exquisite eloquence, truly virtuous eloquence, corresponding eloquence, liberative eloquence, subtle eloquence, unique eloquence, and profound eloquence, even unto the eloquence of a Tathāgata.
"World-Honored One!
What is called the Samādhi that Illuminates All Dharmas?

Because a bodhisattva enters these gateways of all dharmas, they contemplate all mental explorations (*vitarka*) and examinations (*vicāra*), knowing that all dharmas are without exploration and free from exploration. This state of non-exploration pervades all places; there is not a single dharma that can perform the act of exploring."
Why is this? Because their nature is inherently detached.
If dharmas lack intrinsic nature, how can they perceive all dharmas?
Having ceased that cognition, one enters the gateway of the letter A and attains supreme eloquence.
Once that bodhisattva has entered the gateway of the letter A, they attain boundless eloquence.
The letter A is boundless; the letter A is not pervasive; the letter A is unconditioned; the letter A is non-existent.
The letter A is not an accomplishment; the letter A is not an activity; the letter A has no basis;
the letter A is without movement or change; the letter A is not concise; the letter A is not extensive;
the letter A is not conceptualization; the letter A is not produced by a collection of things; the letter A cannot be pierced; the letter A is not form; the letter A—
The letter A cannot be shown; the letter A cannot be observed; there is no one who can see the letter A;
the letter A is not an object of thought; the letter A does not abide fixedly; the letter A is not knowable;
the letter A is not that which knows; the letter A is not measurable; the letter A cannot manifest itself; and the letter A...
It cannot be shown to others; the syllable A is beyond thought; the syllable A does not go; the syllable A does not come;
the syllable A is not near; the syllable A is not far; the syllable A is not speech; the syllable A is also not that which can be spoken;
the syllable A is not a name; the syllable A is not a function; the syllable A is not manifest before one.
The letter A is not an obstruction; the letter A is not a transmigration; the letter A is not subject to change;
the letter A is not differentiated; the letter A is non-dual; the letter A is not born;
the letter A is not false; the letter A is not real; the letter A is ineffable; the letter A is neither arising nor ceasing.
The syllable A is not pure; the syllable A is also not a dharma that can be purified; the syllable A is not grasped; the syllable A does not encompass others;
the syllable A is not abandoned; the syllable A does not act for the sake of other dharmas;
the syllable A also does not produce other dharmas; the syllable A is unarisen; the syllable A is unceasing; the syllable A is not...
It can neither produce other dharmas nor extinguish any dharmas; the letter A is neither produced nor unproduced.
The letter A does not act as a productive cause for dharmas that are produced, nor does it act as a condition for those that are unproduced.
The letter A is neither dependent nor non-dependent; it is neither provisional nor non-provisional; it is neither excluded nor non-excluded.
The letter A is neither permitted nor prohibited; the letter A is neither obtainable nor unobtainable;
the letter A is neither empty nor non-empty; the letter A is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization;
the letter A is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic; the letter A is neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas have such a characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
All dharmas are of one and the same reality, namely, the reality of being without reality.”
All share the same destination, which is called having no destination.
All share the same entry, which is called having no entry.
All share the same designation, which is called having no designation.
All share the same function, which is so-called non-functioning.
All dharmas are explained by the same teaching, which is so-called non-teaching.
World-Honored One!
All phenomena are without arising, because they cannot be apprehended.
All phenomena do not exist, because they have no existence.
All phenomena are without birth, because they are unborn.
All phenomena are without cessation, because they do not cease.
As for unconditioned phenomena, O World-Honored One, they are so called because they are without activity.
All dharmas are identical in their suchness; it should be known in this way.
World-Honored One!
Regarding these dharmas that are non-arising, how can one know their functional activity?
World-Honored One!
Just as the actions performed by someone in a dream, you should know that all phenomena are likewise so. Why is this?
The activities performed in a dream do not arise, do not originate, and do not exist as substantial entities;
yet, although the dream is unreal, it is not without conventional designation, and thus one speaks of "dream-activities.
All phenomena are likewise thus.
World-Honored One!
For example, an echo exists only as a provisional name; all phenomena are likewise merely provisional.
World-Honored One!
"Just as a phantom person is merely a provisional designation, one should know that all phenomena are likewise so.
World-Honored One!
For example, like a mirage which is merely a provisional name, the provisional names of all phenomena are likewise so."
“World-Honored One!
Just as an image in a mirror exists only as a name and a function, one should know that all phenomena are likewise so,
World-Honored One.”

To gladden the ordinary and the ignorant, one speaks of the occurrence of dreams; yet whatever is done within a dream is not real. Echoes, illusions, mirages, and reflections are likewise so: they possess only provisional names and lack any actual activity.
“World-Honored One!
We understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata in this way.
At that time, the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven praised the Buddha with these verses:
“The World-Honored One well understands the meaning of this Dharma, as well as other various and boundless teachings;
all the sons of the Tathāgata obtain their father’s inheritance and constantly sport with it.”
Those of little wisdom in the world cannot enter [this truth], because they constantly cling to the notion of a self.
Though one seeks "me" throughout the ten directions, it cannot be found; the essence of the self is originally empty by its very nature.
Just as a mirage in the sky is not real water, yet the deluded perceive it and conceive the thought that it is water—

this is entirely due to confusion arising from a lack of wisdom; by falsely and perversely reckoning "self" and "person," those who are ignorant and deluded regarding the Tathāgata’s teaching fail to understand its profound meaning.
The mind-consciousness of ordinary beings is like a mirage; they cannot understand the true meaning of the aggregates.
Their minds delight in birth and death and are pierced by the arrows of suffering, drifting and drowning in the swift current of the sense-faculties.
These beings ultimately lack intrinsic nature, yet, obscured by ignorance, they undergo suffering in vain;
having lost their wisdom and their minds being deranged, they conceive the notion of pleasure amidst all manner of suffering.
The mind is constantly inverted and follows the three poisons; these afflictions are truly terrifying.
Greed, hatred, and delusion—these fetters and latent tendencies always pursue one.
Because they deeply delight in sensation, craving arises; because they are ignorant and lack discernment, they suffer.
Lacking wisdom, they follow along with all afflictions, like a fool walking while carrying an enemy on his back.
Hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the gate of emptiness, they instead fear emptiness and lose their liberation;
like a coward grasping a sword, they should attain security but instead give rise to fear.
The Dharma taught by the World-Honored One of Great Wisdom Is called this subtle and wondrous gateway of the letter A;
It can give rise to true and supreme wisdom, Just as a great tree grows from level ground.
Having subdued the myriads of māras and adversaries, you were able to awaken to the peaceful and wondrous Bodhi;
by means of that great raft of the Eightfold Noble Path, you ferry all sentient beings across the ocean of existence.
All the sons of the Buddhas under the World-Honored One, Thoroughly understanding the supreme teaching of the Tathāgata,
Swiftly extinguish the enemies that are the afflictions, And quickly realize the unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
Having already attained liberation for oneself and freed the mind from poison, one sees others who are poisoned and bestows the medicine of wisdom;
having reached the fruit of the ultimate further shore, one attains the state of great peace and bliss that is unconditioned.
All phenomena are entirely empty; the various other external treatises are but false discriminations.
The wise person abandons evil and follows the correct path, all because they have long practiced and studied from the very beginning.
When the mind has no attachments, it is liberation; the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself thus.
One who can understand this in such a way becomes a Buddha of great power, a Nārāyaṇa.
There is neither bondage nor one who binds; the nature of all phenomena is empty and likewise non-existent.
Suchness is quiescent and beyond likeness; it is neither defiled nor pure.
Afflictions have no marks and are not to be severed, for their primordial nature is itself empty;
one who can thus know the true Dharma shall attain all-knowledge.
Having realized liberation for oneself, one further delivers others;
these [phenomena] are neither born nor extinguished, yet gods and humans in the world are all deluded, like birds and beasts in springtime seeing a mirage as water.
False conceptualization gives rise to a thirsting mind; Perceiving men and women, one undergoes suffering and affliction.
Through various karmas, one is born into the various realms of existence; Because they are produced by the mind, there are distinctions.
Karma is created, and there is its retribution and its experiencing; Yet that karma has no creator.
We understand the Buddha-dharma in this way: it is the sublime realm of all Tathāgatas.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s mind is disciplined, his faculties are tranquil, and he is capable of patience.
The World-Honored One receives offerings in accordance with the Dharma; pure and stainless, he has exhausted all defilements.
Endowed with every virtue, he is free from darkness; only the Buddha can bestow the eye upon the three realms.
The merit I have now gained by praising the Buddha can only be known by the Great Teacher who has transcended the world,
the World-Honored One among two-legged beings, the mass of all virtues, who understands the retribution we have obtained.
By means of these subtle, wondrous, and supreme roots of goodness, I dedicate them to all living beings;
may they, in future worlds, fully attain the realization of omniscience.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the profound faith of the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven and their perfection in the eloquence of practice, and desiring to cause the roots of merit and virtue of the great assembly to further gradually advance and increase, the Tathāgata then manifested a smile.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
"The Great Compassionate Sugata does not manifest this rare smile without cause;
O Unsurpassed Being who benefits the world, your Perfectly Awakened wisdom transcends all living beings."
O Blessed One among bipeds, mass of merit, out of compassion for sentient beings, please explain:
for whose sake have you manifested this smile, which radiates such sublime light throughout the world?
If all sentient beings should hear it, their minds will become resolute and filled with great joy;
by practicing wholesome deeds, they shall realize the fruit of Buddhahood, leaving birth and death behind to reach nirvana.
These multitudes of worldlings, devas, and humans, Pressed by the sufferings and afflictions of birth and death,
I pray you deliver all beings from the ocean of existence By expounding the path of the great eightfold vessel.
Having thus heard the Great Sage’s teaching on the supreme path endowed with the eight qualities, the world was filled with joy;
delighting in the cultivation of all virtues, they aspired to attain Buddhahood.
Brave, diligent, and possessed of great strength, with a pure inner mind free from all doubt, you shall transmit the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata;
such a one is a true son of the Buddha who follows the holy teaching.
This entire assembly is free from other thoughts, gazing with single-minded devotion upon Mahāgautama;
we pray only that you will expound the prophecy of our future attainment, so as to bring final resolution to our hearts of doubt.
With palms joined in reverence and dwelling in right mindfulness, all are filled with joy and desire to hear;
how excellent it would be if you would preach the flavor of the nectar, so that all who thirst for the Dharma may drink of it.
All these members of the assembly, their minds pure and delighting in supreme merit,
gaze upon the Tathāgata’s most excellent countenance, just as an infant looks upon its mother’s face.
O Mahāmati, we pray that you grant this deity a prophecy and reveal the causes and conditions for your smile;
having heard the Tathāgata’s prophecy, the world shall obtain great benefit.
Whoever has increased their roots of goodness toward the Muni, and whose aspirations have been fulfilled,
thereby attaining a treasury of subtle and wondrous merit— I now desire to hear their prophecy.
The great assembly will surely give rise to hearts of joy, Because they hear the Buddha’s teaching of the prophecy;
They shall certainly be endowed with the power of mindfulness and wisdom, And attain the practice of samādhi-concentration.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse to the Venerable Aśvajit:
“Excellent is the matter asked by Aśvajit; Your eloquence is timely and appropriate for this very moment.”
This is indeed the supernatural power of the Tathāgata; by this means, you have now given birth to wisdom.
For the sake of benefiting the world, your eloquence has increased, and thus you are now able to pose this question.
I now bestow upon them this prophecy; listen with tranquil faculties and a single mind.
These gods of the Light-Sound Heaven of Supreme Wisdom have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past;
seeing that this world is orphaned and without refuge, they have resolved their minds to abide in the aspiration for Buddhahood.
Cultivating true and subtle practices, you will certainly attain all-encompassing wisdom;
for the sake of all sentient beings seeking the Buddha-way, you teach the correct path to those who have lost their way.
Having thus heard the teaching of the World-Honored One— whose voice is most supreme and peerless—
the person who delights in the Buddha’s merit, virtue, and wisdom will surely attain the ultimate state and reach the other shore.
Possessing the power of wisdom, he discerns good and evil; He is certain to attain the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Having rejoiced, he has made the vow for Bodhi, Like a woman who gives birth to a son to her heart's content.
This deva, for the sake of those seeking enlightenment, Reveals the true path that transcends the world;
Throughout unspeakable nayutas of eons, He has cultivated the supreme and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva.
Having established the sentient beings to be converted— more numerous than the stars— in the Bodhi of the Buddha,
they shall in the future become fully endowed with the knowledge of the world and spontaneously achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
Those wondrous lands are unspeakable; the worlds are vast, numbering ten billion.
These exquisite realms are exceedingly pure, adorned with immeasurable varieties of supreme ornaments.
In that Buddha-land, all sentient beings have no three evil realms nor eight difficult conditions;
they all resolve upon Bodhicitta and each dwells in the stage of non-retrogression.
Within the lands of those Tathāgatas, there is likewise no Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle;
all sentient beings seek the Buddha-way and thereby attain progress toward the stage of non-retrogression.
The classes of sentient beings in all these lands have lifespans that are entirely equal;
for ten billion kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have all encountered various Buddhas.

If one were to teach the beings of ten billion lands so that they all attained the lesser nirvāṇa, yet another person were to transform a single individual—whether male or female—and lead them into the Mahāyāna; [the latter would generate far greater merit].
Compared to this mass of merit, the initial merit cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy;
therefore, those who abide in the Mahāyāna should convert and transform others.
"Āśvajit! For these reasons, it is extremely rare for a Tathāgata to appear in the world; he is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower. Thus speaks the one of boundless great wisdom."
One who possesses skillful and profound wisdom, who is a true spiritual friend,
well-versed in expedient means to show the right path toward the secure and unsurpassed supreme enlightenment— such a person should be approached by those who seek it.

Having heard such words from the Buddha’s own mouth, Complete with subtle, wondrous, and profound meaning, The entire great assembly was filled with joy; They leaped for gladness, their hearts overflowing with satisfaction.
Nayutas of devas dwelling in the air all scattered celestial garments as they descended in swirling circles;
voices of joyful praise filled the void:
"Homage to the one of incomparable great power, who with pure and wondrous wisdom delivers the world and can extinguish the fever of sentient beings' afflictions."
The Buddha has taught that ambrosia extinguishes the three poisons, Just as agada medicine eliminates all toxins;
By hearing this wisdom, one severs all fetters.
The world is deluded and full of suffering and affliction, Yet from within the realms of existence, one shall attain liberation, Because of having heard the supreme Dharma from the Buddha.

Chapter 21: The Prophecy of the Śubhakṛtsna Devas. At that time, twelve nayutas of Śubhakṛtsna devas, having seen the asuras, garuḍas, and even the Ābhāsvara devas making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing their prophecies, were filled with joy and exultation, their hearts’ desires fulfilled. Manifesting their own majestic power, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
There is a samādhi called "Transcending All Dharmas.
Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained this samādhi, regarding all objects of perception and all phenomena, they give rise only to pleasant sensations and no painful sensations.
Even if, within the affairs of the hells, they experience all manner of suffering and affliction, they conceive the notion of pleasure;
or again, within the realm of animals, even while receiving the retribution of an animal, they likewise conceive the notion of pleasure.
Furthermore, within the realm of hungry ghosts, they experience the suffering of hunger yet still give rise to the perception of pleasure;
likewise, within the realm of the asuras, they also give rise to the perception of pleasure.
Furthermore, regarding the various sufferings experienced among human beings, they likewise give rise to the perception of pleasure rather than the perception of suffering.

Even if their hands are severed and their feet are cut off, or their ears are sliced and their noses are cut away; or if they are whipped, beaten, or pierced with staves until the wounds enter the body;
or if they are imprisoned and confined, or even suspended upside down, or subjected to dismemberment as if—
They may be clothed in silk, or further wrapped, bound, and fettered; or they may be minced like meat, or pounded like sugarcane;
or they may be trampled and crushed like reeds; or they may be burned with fire like a wick of ghee and oil;
or they may have their bodies set ablaze like bright torches; or they may be made prey to lions, tigers, and wolves.
They may be made to eat [filth], or have their mouths and noses doused with pungent vinegar and spicy liquids;
they may be steamed, boiled, or roasted over fires; they may be trampled by mad elephants, or have their eyes gouged out;
or they may be impaled on spears and lances and hoisted high, even if one were to come in a fit of rage and sever their head—all such things as these.
They all give rise to the perception of pleasure. Why is this?
Because when that bodhisattva was practicing the bodhisattva path throughout the long night, he made such a vow:
“If there are sentient beings who give me food, may they all attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.

If there are those who bathe my body, prostrate to me, welcome me, respect me, or make offerings to me; if there are sentient beings who revile and insult me, or others who praise me; if there are sentient beings who whip, strike, or stab me, even taking my life—may they all attain the bliss of nirvāṇa, and ultimately awaken to unsurpassed bodhi.”

That bodhisattva, having accomplished such a mind, being endowed with such karma, and likewise being endowed with such vows, gives rise to the perception of joy toward all sentient beings, constantly able to cultivate and accumulate [these qualities] without interruption or cessation.
By virtue of this karmic retribution, he attains the samādhi called "Skillfully Grasping the Joy of All Dharmas.
When that bodhisattva attains this samādhi, he cannot be shaken or destroyed by any māras, nor can he be bound by any demonic activities.
It should be known that this bodhisattva attains five kinds of mastery.

What are these five? First, mastery over lifespan; second, mastery over birth; third, mastery over karma; fourth, mastery over applied and sustained thought; and fifth, mastery over the fruits of requisites and retribution.

If that bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to transcend one more birth and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he shall be able to attain it immediately through the power of that samādhi.
If one does not seek to swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi, one can remain for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas to deliver and liberate sentient beings. Why is this?
It should be known that such a bodhisattva dwells in the Mahāyāna, constantly acts as a guide for all bodhisattvas, and gathers in and sustains all other bodhisattvas.

These great bodhisattvas have developed weary detachment from all realms of existence, yet for the sake of sentient beings, they are born again within all such realms. They have brought to ultimate completion all that is to be studied by bodhisattvas; they are sustained by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), are fully endowed with the power of all skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), recognize the activities of Māra, and have attained the ultimate realization of the Dharma.
"By virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, those bodhisattvas have attained complete knowledge of all dharmas.
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas praised the World-Honored One with these verses:
"We, all the Śuddhāvāsa devas, Have fully understood all the Buddha-dharmas."
I bow my head in reverent homage to the Teacher of Gods and Humans, whose faculties are tranquil and who knows the state of cessation.
He has understood all meanings and is honored by wisdom; having already crossed over birth and death, he is the Honored Muni.
I now praise the Great Guide, who is able to skillfully lead others, rather than being led by them.
The nature and characteristics of all phenomena are not ultimate, nor do they have any place of dependence or abiding;
the Tathāgata thoroughly understands these matters of false conceptualization, just as a magician knows his own illusions.
The wise understand the sounds of speech to be like echoes in a deep valley;
the World-Honored One thus possesses excellent knowledge and vision regarding all the world’s devas and humans.
There are no sentient beings nor life-force, Nor is there a person or a soul.
With great wisdom one observes all perceptions, And realizes that all such conceptions ultimately return to emptiness.
The World-Honored One among bipeds possesses peerless compassion; He constantly practices loving-kindness, never abandoning it for even a moment.
All the devas and humans in the entire world Cannot fathom or know the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

The Teacher proclaims for the sake of sentient beings: That which is called the cultivation of a compassionate mind Is to understand that among all sentient beings, There is no sentient being and no life-principle.
We are here, free from defilement and turbidity; our minds are pure and devoid of doubt.
Therefore, toward the Buddha’s supreme wisdom, we shall offer worship to the one worthy of offerings.
Within the worlds of the ten directions, suffering cannot ultimately be found;
the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed God among gods, speaks of giving rise to a mind of compassion for sentient beings.
This is indeed the teaching of the World-Honored One; I have now attained understanding just as the Buddha did.
Therefore, I am one who understands the world, and I now offer worship to the Worthy of Offerings.
Since there are neither sentient beings nor suffering, there is consequently nothing to be delivered;
having already dispelled the mind’s distress, one immediately attains great joy and exultation.
Thus we have come to know, as it truly is, the inconceivable teaching of the Buddha;
therefore, we now make offerings to the Buddha, wishing to attain the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha perceives no suffering within the various realms of existence, nor can nirvana be apprehended;
having transcendentally relinquished birth and death, he thereby benefits all the worlds.
There is no suffering, no realm of rebirth, and no sentient beings; there is likewise no nirvana upon which to rely.
Having thus understood the Buddha’s Dharma, we now offer this worship.
The Buddha, endowed with compassion, joy, and equanimity, constantly expounds them for the sake of the world;
yet, seeing no sentient beings whatsoever, he dwells in the four immeasurable minds.
I see no one who is negligent, nor do I see anyone who is not negligent;
having thus understood the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, I now make offerings to the Great Teacher.
Regarding the body, he is detached from the body, a Supreme Being;
He contemplates that the body is ultimately unobtainable, Yet he does not say it is non-existent, For he speaks of those who possess mindfulness and those who have lost it.
The Sugata has always taught the cultivation of mindfulness, namely, the foundation of mindfulness that contemplates the body;
thus have we understood the Buddha’s Dharma, and now we are able to make offerings to the Savior.
The World-Honored One observes that sensation cannot be apprehended, because sensation lacks any intrinsic nature;
he likewise examines the one who feels, and finds that ultimately no such reality exists.
Furthermore, when one observes that practitioner of mindfulness, even the ultimate [state] cannot be apprehended;
we, knowing the Buddha-nature in this way, now offer worship to the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Contemplating the mind and its mental factors, one finds they ultimately lack substance and cannot be apprehended;
likewise, one does not perceive any cultivation of mindfulness, nor any who abides correctly in the foundations of mindfulness.
The Buddha taught that mindfulness is in harmony with the mind; those who seek liberation should practice and learn this.
Thus we understand the Buddha’s teaching, and now we offer worship to the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Tathāgata perceives no phenomena, nor does he perceive one who cultivates the Dharma;
that which the Great Sage taught as the cultivation of mindfulness—its nature, too, is inherently empty.
Furthermore, it is said that mindfulness is conjoined with the Dharma; those seeking liberation should practice it.
Thus we understand the Buddha’s teachings, and now we offer worship to the All-Knowing One.
Since even a single foundation of mindfulness cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be three or four?
Regarding those foundations of mindfulness, all such foundations of mindfulness are entirely non-existent.
Therefore, when sought in truth, it cannot be found; ultimately, there is no one who experiences suffering or pleasure.
Having understood the Noble Teaching in this way, we now offer worship to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The four right efforts taught by the Muni— if a bhikṣu practices them with single-minded devotion—
these shall serve as the path to liberation, and he shall emerge from the ocean of birth and death.
There is neither liberation nor one who is bound; there is no Buddha, no teaching, and no enlightenment.
Yet, without destroying the utility of conventional designations, I now make this offering to the Great Sage.
The Buddha taught the four bases of psychic power, The supreme, wondrous, peaceful path to liberation;
Those beings who have stilled their faculties Practice this path and attain Nirvana.
For the practitioner who possesses the power of mastery and the feet of practice, True observation finds nothing to be grasped;
yet, without falling into nihilism, they manifest purposeful action. The realm of wisdom is invisible to the eye.
Thus, within the teaching of the World-Honored One, we have all come to full understanding;
our minds are pure and free from defilement, and we have all distanced ourselves from every doubt and uncertainty.

This itself constitutes the supreme offering; by making offerings to the One worthy of receiving the most excellent offerings, I have now fully attained the practice of worship, for which reason my wondrous wisdom is peerless.
The Knower of the World has taught the five faculties, which lead to the supramundane path of liberation;
be careful not to be negligent, but always practice diligently—this is the way leading toward Nirvāṇa.
There are no faculties, nor those who cultivate the faculties; there is neither liberation, nor one who is liberated.
We have no doubt whatsoever regarding this, and for this reason we now offer worship to the Buddha.
The five kinds of powers taught by the Teacher cannot be subverted by what is false;
they lead toward the city of Nirvāṇa, can utterly extinguish the bonds of affliction, and cause those who are bound to attain liberation.
The essential nature of those powers is itself empty; both afflictions and Buddhas are likewise non-existent.
We have no doubts or anxieties regarding this, and for this reason we now offer worship to the Tathāgata.
The sevenfold goodness taught by the Great Sage is the supreme path of the factors of enlightenment;
it can untie the bonds of all sentient beings and lead them toward the great, correct road to Nirvana.
There is neither bondage nor liberation, nor is there anyone who is bound or attains release;
we have no doubt regarding this, and for that reason we now offer worship to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One has taught this Eightfold Noble Path, revealing it to all living beings:
that these afflictions are the root of suffering, and by practicing and training in the Noble Path, one can sever them.
These two dharmas are free from opposition—namely, the Noble Path and the afflictions;
the devas have no doubt regarding these, and thus they now make offerings to the One Worthy of Offerings.
By cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā, this path can bring all suffering to its ultimate end;
the World-Honored One has already washed away the habitual tendencies and defilements that cause one to undergo various sufferings throughout vast eons.
The fruits of śamatha and vipaśyanā— All these are entirely empty.
O hosts of devas, free yourselves from the net of doubt herein; Therefore, we now make this offering.

The Buddha taught that impurity is the remedy for lust, Loving-kindness is the remedy for hatred, And insight (vipaśyanā) is the remedy for delusion; Thus the Tathāgata reveals it to all sentient beings.
All these are without action and do not abide for even a moment; therefore, they are neither defiled nor pure.
We have no doubts whatsoever regarding this, and we always delight in making offerings to the Great Teacher.
The ten unwholesome actions taught by the Tathāgata are designated as the paths of karma:
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; false speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech;
frivolous speech, covetousness, and malice; and finally, the tenth, which is called wrong view.
The Buddha has taught that these are unwholesome; they are the paths of evil karma for all sentient beings.
Since there are no sentient beings and no harm, the same applies to the remaining nine karmas.
There is no antidote for any good or evil, because their intrinsic nature is empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, it is not that the teaching of the Ten Powers does not exist;
because the intrinsic nature of phenomena is indestructible, I have no doubt regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, and for this reason, I now make offerings to the Unsurpassed Intelligence.
If there are those who cultivate this Dharma of the Tathāgata, they are truly the sons of the Buddha;
such persons shall experience happiness everywhere and remain forever free from all suffering and affliction.
Thus, the Sugata’s supreme wisdom safely guides all living beings;
we are free from doubt regarding this, and now we make offerings to the One Worthy of Offerings.
At that time, after the Śubhakṛtsna devas had praised the Buddha with verses, they all remained silent and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the World-Honored One, seeing that the assembly of devas stood in silence and knowing their profound faith, manifested a smile.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit asked in verse:
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One of supreme wisdom, Manifests a smile for the benefit of the world.
The Hero of the World with ten powers transcends all, And is able to transform and subdue the great assembly."
Great Guide who thoroughly understands all phenomena, The smile you have manifested is not without cause;
O Knower of the World whose mind lacks nothing, I pray that you will explain the meaning of this smile.
This entire great assembly is single-minded; free from distracted thoughts, they abide in right mindfulness.
With hearts of joy, they gaze upon the Mountain of Merit, desiring only to hear [the teaching] as they dwell in reverent attention.
Upon hearing the teachings of the Buddha, the Sovereign Great Master of Treatises, one will surely rejoice;
having attained the definitive wisdom that skillfully understands all phenomena, one shall become a Buddha and guide all living beings.
If a person conceives pure faith in the Buddha, they will surely become a supreme being of great wisdom in the world;
having fathomed the subtle and wondrous words of nectar, such a person is able to behold the ten directions.
Who, in the kalpas of future ages, shall attain Buddhahood to compassionately pity the world?
O Great Guide of subtle and wondrous speech, we pray that you will speak of them so as to bring joy to the assembly.
If one gives rise to a heart of reverence, faith, and respect toward the Noble Hero, the Śramaṇa,
and likewise abides in the True Dharma with faith and wisdom, no māras whatsoever shall be able to move them.
If one can give rise to faith and attain certainty, they are a child of the Buddha born from the mind;
we pray only that the World-Honored One will expound this for them, so that this great assembly may have their doubts dispelled.
If one directs a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, universally covering the entire world,
and possesses firm wisdom, they shall attain Buddhahood and abide securely in omniscience.
O Unsurpassed One, adorned with a hundred blessings, we pray that you will expound the teaching to dispel the net of doubt;
for whom among those who wish to uphold the World-Honored One’s Dharma has the Tathāgata manifested this smile?
May I be granted the opportunity to hear the Buddha’s skillful teaching, his subtle and wondrous voice endowed with the eight qualities;
may I first attain the path of virtue for myself, and thereafter be able to guide all living beings.
Thus, within the subtle Dharma of the Sugata, the sons of the Buddha dwell;
the seed of the Buddhas, O World-Honored One, shall not be severed, and it will surely abide long in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya with these verses:
“Kauṇḍinya, you have now asked about the light of my smile; For the benefit of all the worlds, I have spoken.
You shall obtain merit according to your heart’s desire; This merit is immeasurable and inexhaustible.”
The Sublime Being is able to inquire at the opportune moment;
for the great benefit of all sentient beings, you and this entire assembly should listen with joyful and single-minded attention as I speak.
These hosts of Śuddhāvāsa devas have no doubts whatsoever regarding my Dharma;
with all joy and pure faith, they praise my virtues in verse.
In past lives, this deva once made offerings to a thousand billion nayutas of Buddhas;
he also inquired about this meaning under those Buddhas and has attained freedom from doubt regarding all dharmas.
Due to those causes and conditions from the past, they now praise me with verses;
likewise, with a pure mind, they shall also praise all the Tathāgatas of the Bhadrakalpa.
During the Utpala eon, you shall become the Buddha Mahābalanārāyaṇa;
you will teach and transform inconceivable *nayuta*s of beings, leading them into the city of nirvāṇa.
When those great seers attained Buddhahood, the renown they acquired was most subtle and wondrous;
I shall now speak of those Buddhas for you—listen with a single-minded tranquility and hear it well.
Within that same eon, they all became Buddhas, Known by the name Dharmadhvaja, the Perfectly Awakened Ones;
Together they rescued and delivered inconceivable numbers, Leading nayutas of beings into nirvana.
After those Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, they cremate their bodies and widely distribute their relics;
stupas are erected for all these relics, filling the Buddha-fields like scattered flowers.
At that time, the relics of all Buddhas were each widely distributed;
after each of those Buddhas entered parinirvāṇa, they all brought great benefit to the world.
Countless nayutas of sentient beings, having made offerings to the relics of that Buddha,
shall attain the wondrous nirvana of ambrosia, which is praised by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
If there are those who recite the names of those Buddhas, The subtle, wondrous,
and supreme roots of goodness they obtain Shall lead to the accomplishment of the path of the learner (śaikṣa), And meeting a Buddha, they shall further attain the most excellent fruit.
Just as an immeasurable and inconceivable multitude, All of whom have planted roots of goodness within me,
With joyful faith, delight, and a pure mind, Shall encounter the Buddha Maitreya.

Thus those śrāvakas of that Buddha, proceeding from one Buddha to the abodes of other Buddhas, always encounter Buddhas and enter their assemblies; all this is due to having made offerings to those relics.
Having heard such words of the Buddha, the entire great assembly was struck with wonder;
possessing supreme and wondrous merit and majestic spiritual power, the gods of the Pure Abodes, the lay devotees of pure faith,
and the entire multitude were filled with universal joy, and all flowed toward Bodhi.
Having realized the great power of the Tathāgata, they all prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
*The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra*, Fascicle Sixty-Eight;
*The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra*, Fascicle Sixty-Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-two: The Prophecy of the Gods of the Bṛhatphala Heaven. The Ninth Part of the Sixteenth Assembly: Bodhisattvas Beholding Reality. Chapter Twenty-two:
The Prophecy of the Gods of the Bṛhatphala Heaven. At that time, eight hundred million gods of the Bṛhatphala Heaven saw the various asuras and...
The kumbhāṇḍas, nāgas and nāga maidens, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, hārakagajadevas, the devas of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa devas,
the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas...
Having made offerings to the Tathāgata in the heavens of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Ābhāsvara, and Śubhakṛtsna devas,
and having heard their prediction of enlightenment, they were all filled with joy and exultation, their hearts’ desires fulfilled. They entered each and every dharma-gate,
and from each dharma-gate they perceived immeasurable dharma-gates, attaining infinite eloquence regarding all dharma-gates.
...uninterrupted eloquence, corresponding eloquence, liberating eloquence, unattached eloquence, unimpeded eloquence,
subtle eloquence, profound eloquence, manifold eloquence, exquisite eloquence, and continuous eloquence.
Having fully understood all forms of eloquence, he paid homage with reverence and respect to the Tathāgata and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

There is a dhāraṇī named ‘Infinite Gateways. If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates and gathers this dhāraṇī, it should be known that they will attain uninterrupted eloquence and the like, such that their mind is never deluded regarding any object of experience.”

Among all these realms, there is not a single dharma that is not a dhāraṇī; when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain this dhāraṇī, they fully attain the dhāraṇī of understanding and unhindered eloquence regarding all dharmas.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this dharani of the immeasurable Dharma-gates, they attain indestructible eloquence regarding all such spheres: the entry into the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements; the entry into the faculties, the four truths, and the twelve links of dependent origination; the entry into sentient beings and non-sentient beings; the entry into existence and non-existence; the entry into grasping at signs and non-grasping at signs; the entry into dependence and non-dependence; the entry into emptiness; the entry into the self; the entry into signs and non-signs; the entry into vows and non-vows; and the entry into the conditioned and the unconditioned. In all these instances, they attain indestructible eloquence.
This bodhisattva attains dhāraṇīs regarding the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas). That which is called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is not established as such.
Why is this? Because there is not even the slightest dharma of form that can be established.
Why is this? Because the nature of the earth element is not established;
likewise, the natures of the water, fire, and wind elements are also not established.
Why is this? Because the nature of earth is devoid [of intrinsic being]; if a phenomenon lacks an essential nature, it is said to be unestablished.
Likewise, because the natures of water, fire, and wind are themselves devoid [of intrinsic being], and because phenomena lack an essential nature, they are unestablished.
In this way, form is not established; because it is not established, it cannot be described as past, present, or future. Why is this?
Because form is not an existent dharma, it is therefore unattainable.
If form (*rūpa*) does not arise, it is then non-ceasing; because it is neither arising nor ceasing, it cannot be described.

Furthermore, there is this teaching: all past, present, and future forms—this collection is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Since the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that form is also unattainable, how can there be past, present, or future?
Therefore, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is not something that can be described;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Thus, the aggregates and sense bases (āyatana) are themselves the entrance into dhāraṇī.
Because they are the entrance into dhāraṇī, the aggregates cannot be apprehended.
Because the aggregates (*skandha*) cannot be apprehended, the *dhāraṇī* also cannot be apprehended.

Because the entry into the *dhāraṇī* cannot be apprehended, it is merely a name, merely a function, and merely a designation; it is merely conventional, merely a verbal expression, and merely a conceptual construct. It is neither an aggregate nor form, nor is it the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), nor can the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the *dhāraṇī* be apprehended.

Why is this? It is because what are called the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are not conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); since they are not conditioned phenomena, there is no accumulation (*caya*), and it is precisely because of such accumulation that they are designated as "aggregates."

For example, when many materials are gathered together in the world, they are conventionally designated as houses, dwellings, palaces, multi-storied pavilions, towers, gatehouses, windows, railings, city walls, parapets, battlements, and watchtowers; when these are fully provided all around, it is called a "city."
That nature of form is unobtainable and lacks any accumulation; because it lacks accumulation, there is no form, nor is there an aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise: their nature is unobtainable and they lack any accumulation; because they lack accumulation, there is no consciousness, nor is there an aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Those aggregates and bases should be understood in this way:
"Of what is that eye-base the base?
It is the base of suffering."
What is the eye? It is that which is called the eye, being a form derived from the four great elements.
What are these four great elements?
This refers to the pure earth element and the elements of water, fire, and wind.
Because that pure earth element is by nature self-detached, and because its essential substance cannot be apprehended, it is not established.
In this way, the essential natures of the elements of water, fire, and wind are inherently detached; because the substance of phenomena cannot be apprehended, they are not established.
Likewise, the sense-base of the eye is not established; therefore, one cannot speak of it as past, present, or future.
Why is this? The sense-base of the eye is not a substantial entity.
Because it is not a substantial entity, it is neither born nor extinguished; that which is neither born nor extinguished is ineffable.
In this way, the eye is neither arising nor ceasing, and its entry is likewise neither arising nor ceasing; because it is neither arising nor ceasing, it is ineffable.
One should understand it in this manner.
These are merely names, merely functions, and merely designations; they are merely conventional and merely verbal expressions.
Even the essence of those names is devoid of intrinsic nature. Why is this so?
There is not a single dharma that can be named "eye," named "entrance," or named "suffering.
Because names are unattainable, the eye-entrance is likewise unattainable; this very unattainability of the eye is itself the entrance of dhāraṇī.
This dhāraṇī cannot be apprehended even in its entry. Why?
Because its nature is inherently detached; it is merely a name, merely a function, merely a conventional designation, and a worldly expression.
In this way, by entering through the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), one attains dhāraṇī; having attained dhāraṇī, one then attains eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
One should know that it is likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
“In those realms and sense bases, one attains the dharani-eye; yet the essence of the eye is unattainable, and the essence of the realms is unattainable.
Why is this? Because the eye is devoid of the nature of an eye, and the realms are devoid of the nature of realms.”
Because the essence of phenomena cannot be apprehended, they are not entities.

Because they are not entities, they are not established. That which is not established is neither born nor extinguished. Because it is neither born nor extinguished, it is neither past, nor present, nor future; it is merely a name, merely a function, merely a designation, merely conventional, merely a verbal expression, and merely a conceptual construct.
That which is called "name" is devoid of the intrinsic nature of names, up to and including designations; it is also devoid of the intrinsic nature of designations.

If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended, it is not a substantial entity (*avastu*). Because it is not a substantial entity, it is not established (*asiddha*).
