That which is not established neither arises nor ceases. Because it neither arises nor ceases, it is neither past, nor present, nor future.

That which is not subsumed within the three periods of time is called neither sign nor perception, neither function nor designation, neither conditioned nor expressible, neither coming nor going, neither capable of being told to others nor capable of being demonstrated, neither cognizable nor identifiable, neither black nor white; because it is free from abodes, it is neither an abode nor the departure from an abode; because it is neither arrival nor that which can be arrived at, neither attainment nor that which can be attained, neither realization nor that which can be realized; it is neither an ordinary person nor the stage of an ordinary person, neither a śrāvaka nor the stage of a śrāvaka, neither a pratyekabuddha nor the stage of a pratyekabuddha, neither a bodhisattva nor the stage of a bodhisattva, neither a Buddha nor the stage of a Buddha, and it is neither a ground nor a non-ground.
This is precisely suchness (tathatā), not different from suchness, and not non-suchness; it is quiescent and signless, being merely functional and merely conventional.
As for what is called the "Tathāgata," he is designated as such only because of worldly convention; in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because those dharmas are unattainable, there is no Tathāgata.
Regarding those realms and bases, one should enter thus into the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind realms, as well as the dharma realm and the mental consciousness realm.
In this same way, one should know that all other realms are likewise; thus should one extensively enter the dharma-realm.
“World-Honored One!
When that dharma-realm is spoken of as the aggregates (skandhas), it does not destroy the intrinsic nature of that dharma-realm.”

When speaking of entry, when speaking of the realms, when speaking of the Four Noble Truths, and when speaking of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, one does not destroy the essential nature of the fundamental Dharma-realm.
Wherever that dharmadhātu is spoken of, all phenomena are established by names, yet none of them destroy the essential nature of that dharmadhātu.
World-Honored One!
It is like the earth element, which receives various names according to its location, yet does not destroy its original nature as the earth element.
"World-Honored One!
Thus, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) receives various names according to its location, yet it does not destroy the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm.
The same is true for the realms of water, fire, and wind."
“World-Honored One!
It is as if space, according to its various locations, performs different functions, yet does not destroy the essential nature of that space.
World-Honored One!”
In this way, although the Dharma-realm manifests through various names and functions according to its location, it does not destroy the essential nature of that Dharma-realm.
World-Honored One!
To enter the various faculties is precisely to enter the Dharma-realm.

Regarding the "faculties" (indriya), they are: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, and mind faculty; the male faculty, female faculty, and life faculty; the faculty of pleasure, pain, joy, grief, and equanimity; the faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known.
That eye is not found as a substantial entity (mūla), nor is the substantial entity of the root found.
Why is this? Because this eye is devoid of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of an eye.

Because phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they are not substantial entities; because they are not substantial entities, they are not established; that which is not established does not arise; and that which does not arise does not cease. Because they are neither arising nor ceasing, it cannot be said that they belong to the past, the present, or the future.
If it neither arises nor ceases throughout the three periods of time, then it is neither the eye nor the visual faculty; how, then, could it have any function?
One should understand it in this way, World-Honored One!

For example, an empty fist is deceptive and devoid of substance; it exists only as a name and even as a verbal expression, yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), even the empty fist does not exist.

In this same way, the eye and the visual faculty are like an empty fist—false and unreal, manifesting illusory appearances that deceive ordinary people, existing only as names and even as verbal expressions.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), both the eye and the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) are unapprehendable.
Thus, after the Blessed One had attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he spoke of them as "faculties" for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Since those sense faculties are by their very nature detached from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the essence of the faculties is entirely empty.

As for that dharma-essence which is empty, its function is likewise illusory; it is neither existent nor real, deceiving the ignorant and foolish. Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is neither born nor extinguished. That which is neither born nor extinguished cannot be said to belong to the past, present, or future.

If that which does not exist within the three periods of time is without name and without characteristic, it cannot be spoken of nor can it be explained to others; it is neither arisen nor capable of arising; it is neither already known nor to be known; it is neither already heard nor to be heard; it is neither cognized nor capable of being cognized; it is neither already realized nor to be realized; it is neither already attained nor to be attained; it is neither already seen nor to be seen; it is neither already reached nor to be reached.
For what reason?
Because they do not exist,
World-Honored One!
For example, suppose there is a person who, within a dream, experiences pleasure, laughs, chats, and plays.
After this person has awakened from sleep, they recall the pleasure and play experienced in the dream; having recalled them, they seek them but do not see or find them.
Why is this? Even the pleasure, laughter, chatter, and play experienced by that person in a dream lack any reality; how much more so is it impossible for anything to be seen or obtained upon waking?
World-Honored One!
These faculties are like the enjoyment of pleasure and play within a dream, which are truly unattainable.
In this same way, the essential nature of all phenomena is also unattainable; because they are unattainable, it cannot be said that they belong to the past, the present, or the future.
"If that which cannot be found within the three periods of time is thus ineffable, all the sense-faculties (*indriya*) should be known in this same way.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
If one enters the Dharma-realm, one enters all phenomena; to enter all phenomena is precisely to enter the Dharma-realm.
World-Honored One!
To enter the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is precisely to enter the Dharma-realm.
What are the four? They are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The World-Honored One has also taught that all phenomena are entirely empty—neither sentient beings, nor life, nor persons (*pudgala*), nor perceptions, nor characteristics.
We have no doubts or hesitations regarding this Dharma.
World-Honored One!
Because there are no sentient beings, there is likewise no suffering.

Why is this? Because sentient beings do not exist, the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) does not exist either; because suffering does not exist, the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) also does not exist. Why is this?
"There is no fruit where there is no such cause.
"World-Honored One!
Because there is no origination, the truth of cessation is also non-existent."

Why is this? Because there is no truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), there is also no abandonment of origination; because there is no cessation (*nirodha*), the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) likewise does not exist. Why is this?
"There is no such path that does not sever accumulation.
World-Honored One!
The fruit of the path refers to the Truth of Cessation."
Those afflictions cannot be found to be severed, nor can the cessation of afflictions be found.
Because cessation cannot be found, the Path also cannot be found; there is no such Path that is without its fruit.
These Four Noble Truths are merely conceptual constructions and are not real.
Because they do not exist, they cannot be said to belong to the past, the present, or the future.

If it cannot be apprehended within the three periods of time, then it is neither arising nor ceasing; it is neither characteristic nor perception; it is neither that which is designated nor that which can be designated;
it is neither that which is shown nor that which can be shown; it is neither that which is manifested nor that which can be manifested;
it is neither language nor that which can be expressed in language; it is neither terminology nor that which can be described by terminology; it is neither speech nor that which can be spoken.
It is not speech, nor is it that which can be seen; it is not knowledge, nor is it that which can be known; it is not consciousness, nor is it that which can be cognized;
it is not fathomed, nor is it that which can be fathomed; it is not realized, nor is it that which can be realized; it is not attained, nor is it that which can be attained;
it is not heard, nor is it that which can be heard; it is not seen, nor is it that which can be seen; it is not an object of opposition, nor is it that which can be opposed.
It is neither subject to realization nor realizable; neither white nor black; neither light nor dark;
neither going nor coming; neither shallow nor deep; neither clear nor turbid; neither fearful nor secure; neither bound nor liberated;
neither hateful nor loving; neither afflicted nor pure; and neither wisdom nor non-wisdom.
Neither path nor non-path, neither destruction nor non-destruction, neither grasping nor non-grasping,
neither birth-and-death nor non-birth-and-death, neither obtainable nor unobtainable,
neither sentient being nor non-sentient being, neither life nor non-life, neither one who lives nor non-one who lives.
I am neither non-self nor self; neither a thing nor a non-thing; neither empty nor non-empty;
neither characterized nor non-characterized; neither aspiring nor non-aspiring; neither dependent nor non-dependent;
neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither annihilated nor eternal; neither false nor correct; neither real nor illusory; and neither conceptual construction nor non-conceptual construction.
It is neither non-delusion, nor place, nor non-place; neither house, nor non-house; neither knowledge, nor non-knowledge;
neither relinquishment, nor cultivation; neither birth-and-death, nor nirvana; neither awakening, nor non-awakening;
it is not the realm of ordinary beings, nor the realm of śrāvakas, nor the realm of pratyekabuddhas.
The realm of the bodhisattva is not the realm of the Buddha; it is neither a realm nor a non-realm, neither something created nor something uncreated.
To enter into such truth is to enter the dharma-realm; having entered the dharma-realm, one attains dhāraṇī; having attained dhāraṇī, one attains eloquence.

"To enter into the twelve links of dependent origination is to enter the Dharma-realm: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress—this is the great mass of suffering."
Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair— the great mass of suffering ceases. World-Honored One,
that ignorance has no essence of ignorance that can be apprehended.
Why is this? Because their nature is inherently detached.

If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is not a substantial entity; because it is not a substantial entity, it is not established. That which is not established neither arises nor ceases. That which neither arises nor ceases is neither past, nor present, nor future.

If it cannot be found within the three periods of time, it is without name, without form, without characteristics, and without conceptualization, nor is it differentiated; it is merely a name, merely a convention, merely a function, merely the conventional, and merely a verbal expression, for the sake of teaching and transforming all ordinary sentient beings.
That ignorance, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), is truly unobtainable; that which is unobtainable is neither a differentiated function nor can it be described.
World-Honored One!

If it is merely a name, or even merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), then it is not real; it is nothing but false speech, conceptualization (*vikalpa*), discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and non-concentration—it is merely idle proliferation (*prapañca*).
If that ignorance were without intrinsic nature, how could it give rise to volitional formations?
Since ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not arise either.
Because they do not arise, they do not age, do not fall ill, do not die, and do not undergo transmigration; that is, they are non-arising.
Why is this? If there is no birth, how could there be aging?
Because there is no aging, there is likewise no birth, and so forth.

That which is neither born nor dies is the bodhi of all Buddhas of the past, present, and future; it is merely a conventional name and not the ultimate truth (paramārtha). What is called ignorance is itself bodhi.
One should know that all the links of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga*) are likewise so.
Entering the twelve links of dependent origination in this way, one should know that it is precisely entering the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is unarisen, and all dharmas are likewise unarisen; therefore, all dharmas are the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is undestroyed, and all dharmas are likewise undestroyed; therefore, all dharmas are the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is without marks, and all dharmas are likewise without marks; therefore, all dharmas are the Tathāgata.
To speak briefly, such marklessness is unapprehendable: it is neither defiled nor pure, neither loved nor hated; the dharma-realm cannot be cognized and is likewise unknowable.
World-Honored One!
True Suchness is the Tathāgata.
All dharmas are True Suchness; therefore, all dharmas are the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
That which is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is the Tathāgata; all dharmas are the limit of reality. Therefore, all dharmas are the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
Within whatever dharma there is, there is the Tathāgata; within those dharmas, there are all dharmas. Therefore, all dharmas are themselves the Tathāgata.
"Blessed One!
If there are beings who say that the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, those sentient beings possess views of clinging."
Why is this? The Tathāgata is non-dual, and bodhi is also non-dual; that which is non-dual cannot awaken to the non-dual.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, if there are those who say,
"The Tathāgata turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma," those sentient beings possess views of attachment.
For what reason?
The Tathāgata neither advances nor retreats,
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, if there should be someone who speaks thus:
"The Tathāgata brings immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," all such persons are merely clinging to views.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are in reality devoid of sentient beings; therefore, there is no one who attains parinirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, if there are those who say,
"The Tathāgata benefits immeasurable sentient beings," all such [statements] are views of grasping and attachment.
Why is this? The Tathāgata does not appear in the world for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, nor for the sake of not benefiting sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, if there are people in future ages who speak thus:
"The Tathāgata has relinquished his life-span," all such sentient beings are clinging to false views.
Why is this? Because the dharma-realm is neither grasped nor abandoned,
World-Honored One!
If there are those who speak thus:
"The Tathāgata has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder," those sentient beings possess a view of conceptual attachment.
Why is this? World-Honored One, the dharma-realm is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
Furthermore, if there are beings who can definitively understand the Dharma I have taught, those sentient beings shall all never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One!

Even if the dharma-realm were subject to change, these sons and daughters of good family who are able to have such faith will certainly awaken to unsurpassed bodhi without any alteration or regression.

At that time, eight hundred million devas of the Bṛhatphala heaven, having heard the World-Honored One expound the Dharma they themselves had realized, prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side. With palms joined, they praised the Buddha in unison with these verses:
"Homage to the Sugata, the Knower of Dharma, The Great Guide with the strength of Nārāyaṇa!
O Supreme Muni who compassionates all, You skillfully manifest the ultimate reality."
Having personally realized all phenomena, you manifest them to the world exactly as they are;
I prostrate to the one of immeasurable merit-body, the supreme and unsurpassed being of wisdom.
Such is this true and subtle Dharma, As taught by the Sage, consistent and without variation;
The World-Honored One, the peerless King of Physicians, Is able to purify the Dharma-eye of sentient beings.
Expounding the eightfold path of the true sages, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, great bodhi;
I take refuge and pay homage to the one of immeasurable merit-body, the supreme and unsurpassed being of wisdom.
Revealing the straight path to enlightenment, Leading definitively toward great nirvāṇa,
One attains peerless, supreme bodhi— Tranquil, secure, and most steadfast.
Having delivered many billions of nayutas of sentient beings suffering in the cycle of birth and death,
I prostrate to the one of immeasurable merit-body, the Supreme Unsurpassed Being of wisdom.
Observing that the five aggregates are entirely empty and non-existent, the essence of the aggregates is ultimately unattainable;
those aggregates are themselves the essence, free from all conceptual observations, and serve only to deceive deluded and ignorant sentient beings.
Ordinary beings are all bound by this, Just like a monkey stuck in glue;
The wise attain liberation therein, Wandering without obstruction like the wind in space.
The various elements are empty by their very nature; thus has the Omniscient One taught.
That emptiness itself is empty and lacks intrinsic nature; when sought to the ultimate end, it cannot be found.
Ordinary beings are all bound by this, entirely because they do not know true reality;
the wise, through contemplation, attain liberation, remaining unattached to the three realms.
The sense bases have no intrinsic nature and are by nature empty and quiescent; thus has the Omniscient One declared.
Like an empty fist, they are void and not real, yet they delude and deceive the ranks of ignorant sentient beings.
Ordinary beings give rise to deluded minds of grasping and attachment; all this stems from harboring doubts regarding the Dharma.
They fall into the cycle of birth and death and are utterly destroyed, just like merchants who have sunk into the great ocean.
Those sense faculties are empty by their very nature; ultimately, they cannot be found when sought.
They are like the reflection of a face appearing in a mirror; that reflection has no reality and is ultimately empty.
Fools lacking wisdom become attached to this, precisely because they do not know the true Dharma;
they are like flocks of birds entering a net, or like fish caught on a hook in a deep pool.
Sentient beings have no substance and are devoid of the marks of birth; Seeking them within the Truth, they cannot be found.
They are like painted images upon a wall; Ultimately, there is no real nature of sentient beings.
Ordinary beings, lacking wisdom, grasp and cling, all because they do not know the true meaning;
when the wise contemplate them, they attain liberation, just as a creature born from an egg emerges from its shell.
All phenomena born of causes and conditions are impermanent; they are entirely empty and quiescent, free from objective grasping.
Like the pleasures experienced within a dream, they are not real, yet they delude foolish worldlings.

The fool, lacking wisdom, is bound by them; Due to failing to reflect and engaging in false conceptualization, The wise person, through observation, attains liberation, Just like a flying bird escaping from a cage or net.
As the Buddha’s virtues are inconceivable, so too are all phenomena;
all phenomena are signless like the Muni, their essential nature quiescent like nirvāṇa.
All phenomena are without support, like the Tathāgata; they are not grasped or clung to within the three realms.
Therefore, all who attain Buddhahood do so by virtue of understanding this meaning.
All phenomena are without fear, just as the World-Honored One is; one does not give rise to thoughts of self or others.
All phenomena are inconceivable, just as the Teacher is; only the Buddha can know how to guide all living beings.
Dharmas are non-conceptual like the Sugata; they are not within the range of the minds of ordinary beings.
They are the sublime sphere of all Tathāgatas, known only by the Great Sage, the Buddha.
If there is one lacking wisdom who speaks thus: "The Buddha has realized the peerless Great Enlightenment," or if another person should speak thus:
"The World-Honored One has already turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma."
If there should be someone who says: "The Sugata has already delivered millions of beings," they are all bound by views, for they do not know the true nature of reality.

If one were to say that the Buddha spoke thus: "Having destroyed the aggregate of formations and life itself, and having brought immeasurable sentient beings to benefit, the One of Ten Powers has entered nirvana."
Those people all cling to views and enter the bonds of Māra;
unable to understand the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), because they do not know it, they do not know the Buddha.
If there are those who well understand right and wrong, they shall all be able to know the Great Teacher;
they will obtain the unsurpassed mass of merit and become Buddhas who have compassion for the world.
This is indeed suchness, free from change; all dharmas are devoid of doubt.
To the Unsurpassed and Most Victorious Honored One among men, we have now understood this meaning.
Thus the assembly of gods from the Vast Fruit Heaven, having all attained exhaustive knowledge of the Dharma,
spoke forth of their own accord before the Teacher, the Buddha, manifesting the pure faith and understanding within their own minds.
All rejoice without doubt, each seeing for themselves that they shall become Buddhas;
this is the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata, and thus they receive the prophecy of the Teacher.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the devas of the Vast Fruit Heaven were fully endowed with deep faith and possessed certainty free from doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma, manifested a smile in order to cause the great assembly to plant roots of goodness.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit questioned the World-Honored One in verse:
"O Guide of Wisdom, Mountain of Merit, It is not without cause that you manifest a smile.
I have heard directly from the Sugata That the World-Honored One’s manifestation of a smile must surely have a cause."
The Tathāgata displays this sign of a smile, Causing all beings to receive the bliss of refreshing coolness.
O Great Teacher of devas, humans, and asuras, We pray only that you will explain the causes and conditions of this smile.
Now we see the Tathāgata from his face-portal; The smile he manifests is most refreshing.
All those in this assembly harbor doubts, And with single-minded devotion gaze upon the Tathāgata’s countenance.
O Great Compassionate One, supreme among the highest of men, I pray you will explain the cause of this rare smile;
if the world were to hear it from the Buddha, they would certainly and surely eliminate their hearts of doubt.
"Bhagavān! Those hosts of devas have all proclaimed their own predictions of enlightenment; by what merit did they obtain these fruits?
We pray that you will explain the matters of their attainment of Buddhahood and their supernormal powers."
He unfolds the subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice; we pray that he will universally sever all doubts.
When the entire great assembly hears the Buddha’s teaching, they all leap for joy with profound delight.
All these, with palms joined and minds unified, dwell in reverent worship, gazing up with pure faith;
the sons of the Buddha and the hosts of devas each contemplate, aspiring for supreme, great bodhi.
These assembled multitudes harbor doubts; we pray only that the Tathāgata will sever them for us.
They shall surely attain the power to discern right from wrong, and fully accomplish all-encompassing wisdom.
Having heard the eightfold voice of the Tathāgata, the hosts of devas are all without exception filled with joy;
they shall uphold the teaching of the Tathāgata and practice in accordance with the True Dharma as it has been taught.
Having observed and known the thoughts of those devas, the One of Unsurpassed Great Wisdom desires to explain them;
thereby these great beings will rejoice and attain faith and understanding within the Buddha-dharma.
Now, before the Guide, we pray to hear of the practices performed by the celestial hosts in the past;
if we are granted this explanation by the Tathāgata, all our aspirations shall be fully satisfied.
The gods of the Bṛhatphala heaven who practice according to the Dharma will surely attain the realization of all-knowledge;
they shall deliver all sentient beings in the world and manifest the true nature of the essence of Suchness.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Venerable Aśvajit with these verses:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, you know the proper time; that you now question me is indeed most appropriate.”
For the sake of the gods of the Vast Fruit Heaven, I manifest a smile here before this great assembly.
Now I shall explain it to you in detail; listen all with one mind.
Regarding the meaning of the causes and conditions for this manifested smile, you and the entire assembly shall hear it all.
The Tathāgata, endowed with all-encompassing wisdom, observes that there are three kinds of causes and conditions;
having correctly contemplated the mass of virtues of the two-legged ones, he manifests a smile to show the world.
Some delight in dwelling in nirvāṇa; possessing little wisdom and shallow aspirations, they seek the state of a śrāvaka.
Others delight in dwelling in silence; their resolve is set on seeking the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, there are those who joyfully seek a Teacher of the World and become Buddhas with the great power of Nārāyaṇa;
having observed their profound faith, I deliver them according to their aspirations.
One who manifests for the sake of seeking the state of a śrāvaka should know that this is the lowest form of smile;
one should know that my middle-grade smile is manifested for the sake of seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Aśvajit, you should know that this smile above was for the sake of bestowing a prophecy upon the assembly of devas;
I have thus explained these three reasons for the smile, namely: the lowest, the middle, and the highest.
The Supreme Guide, who thoroughly understands the world, manifests auspicious signs with a smile;
the Buddha knows that sentient beings desire the three vehicles and joyfully seek to realize the holy fruits.
When a smile is manifested for those seeking the vehicle of the Śrāvaka, the light of that smile vanishes into the soles of the feet;
when it is manifested for those seeking the Pratyekabuddha, you should know that the light of the smile enters the navel wheel.
For one who is to receive the unsurpassed ten powers, the light enters through the crown of the Buddha’s head;
Aśvajit, you should now know that there are three causes for a smile.
The light of the smile I have manifested has vanished into the crown of my head;
you should know that this previously manifested smile is entirely a prophecy of unsurpassed enlightenment.
I shall now further explain for you that there are three causes for a smile.
Excellent, Aśvajit and the great assembly; listen all with single-minded attention and tranquil minds.
If a smile first appears as a sign of Buddhahood, its light enters through the crown of the head;
if the light remains upon the body or waist for a short while and vanishes after a brief moment, it indicates a Pratyekabuddha.
I now manifest a smile and emit a radiance that dwells for a moment before my feet;
this light manifests according to their respective vehicles—know that these are the śrāvakas.
Now I shall further explain the cause of the smile; listen attentively, Aśvajit, for there are three kinds.
The various rays of light emitted by the Guide, having gone forth, encircle the One of Ten Powers.
Once these rays had issued forth, they all dispersed; then they quickly gathered back together, encircling his waist.
Gradually turning, they expanded even further, and likewise circled the Tathāgata to the right.
There was light that first rested and then expanded; gradually it circled my body to the right.
That light completely pervaded the form of the World-Honored One, being equal to his body without any difference.
That light adorns the marks of the Buddha’s body, Resplendent like a mass of pure gold;
The smiling radiance emitted by the Muni— Know that this light prophesies the buddha-field.
Light emerged and became like a canopy, completely covering the body of the World-Honored One from above;
light appeared like flowers abiding in the air, their radiance illuminating the Guide.
All those rays of light turned to the right, circling the body of the Tathāgata three times;
know that these rays signify his lifespan, as this great world-transcending wisdom manifests such an auspicious sign.
These three kinds of smiling radiance, the Sugata manifests according to the differences in faculties;
Aśvajit, you should now know that these are the causes for the three kinds of smiles.
The signs manifested by the Guide of the World, who well understands the deep faith and inclinations of sentient beings—
now, within the teaching of the Tathāgata, you shall hear these and have your doubts dispelled.
These hosts of the Bṛhatphala devas, numbering a full eight hundred million, extensively expounded the subtle and wondrous gate of the True Dharma; each has attained Buddhahood in a different land.
His lifespan is fully endowed and immeasurable, Abiding in the world throughout many kalpas;
Therefore, the Tathāgata manifests this auspicious sign, The vast radiance of five colors.
Throughout thirty-six *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past, this assembly of devas constantly encountered various World-Honored Ones,
personally receiving their teachings, making offerings, and practicing all manner of virtues.
Furthermore, for thirty-six asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they practiced extensively;
these great beings dwelling in the world made offerings to the Tathāgatas without ever growing weary.
Reflecting upon the salvation of sentient beings, they repeatedly and diligently practice making offerings to the Buddhas;
honoring the World-Honored One in a manner befitting him, they aspire to the unsurpassed Great Bodhi.
Those hosts of devas in future ages shall become Nārāyaṇa Buddhas, forming sublime mountains of merit as sages; that kalpa shall be named Supreme Golden Banner.
These Tathāgatas each dwell within their own pure and adorned lands;
those Buddhas are all named Sūryamaṇḍala, fully possessing a multitude of immeasurable merits.
Each and every Tathāgata remains in the world for immeasurable nayuta kalpas;
the assemblies gathered by these Sugatas are infinite, boundless, and incalculable.
When each and every Teacher attains Buddhahood, all his śrāvaka disciples shall dwell for *nayuta* eons in the possession of the ten powers; their number cannot be exhausted by calculation.
If all mathematicians were to gather together, they could not exhaustively calculate that multitude;
at that time, the bodhisattvas present were twice as numerous as the assembly of śrāvakas.
All have resolved their minds to abide in the Buddha-vehicle, vowing to attain the realization of omniscience;
within those pure lands, they shall all become Buddhas, endowed with the ten powers.
The practices cultivated by these bodhisattvas are in every way identical to those of their original teacher, without any difference;
after those Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall flourish and remain long in the world.
Having passed through twelve nayutas of kalpas, protected by all the sons of the Buddhas,
during this time when the Dharma of these Buddhas flourishes, there are those who resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi.
Their number exceeds that of the sands of the Ganges; all have diligently cultivated the bodhisattva practices.
After those Sugatas have entered parinirvāṇa, there remain all their assemblies of śrāvakas.
This entire assembly has all attained nirvāṇa, surpassing in number the sands of the great ocean;
thus shall the True Dharma of those Buddhas be fully manifested and exalted in the world.
Benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, their teaching shall flourish greatly in accordance with the Dharma.
Having heard what the Buddha has spoken, the entire great assembly gains faith and understanding;
they shall surely attain Buddhahood as World-Honored Ones and be able to extensively benefit all living beings.

At that time, the entire assembly was filled with joy; they bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, paying incomparable honor to the Sugata and making offerings to the Teacher of Gods and Humans in accordance with the Dharma.
Therefore, leap for joy and exert diligence, as if someone were extinguishing a fire on their own head;
one should always draw near to virtuous friends and diligently cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā.
This is the superior practice for seeing reality; you, monks, should cultivate it.
You shall become the Unsurpassed Honored Ones among two-legged beings, with merit like a mountain benefiting the world.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Sixty-nine;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Seventy.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter 23: Verses of Praise by the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras, Part One The Sixteenth Assembly:

Bodhisattvas Realizing Reality At that time, the various devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, knowing that immeasurable sentient beings had attained abiding in bodhi and were free from doubt and hesitation regarding the Buddha-dharma, were filled with joy and satisfaction. Each, with exquisite verses, praised the merits of the Buddha.
At that time, the Devaputra Śraddhādatta praised him with these verses:
"Giving away one's beloved wife and children, And renouncing even the body one holds dear,
Even unto kingship and wealth— I pay homage to those who practice the perfection of generosity."
At that time, the devaputra Delight-in-Holding-the-Morality praised him with these verses:
“The Tathāgata originally maintained the precepts, Unattached to anything whatsoever;
Having attained the fruit and reached the further shore, I pay homage to the one who has crossed over by means of morality.”
At that time, the Devaputra Ratinandana praised him in verse:
"The Buddha formerly cultivated patience, Enduring even when his limbs were severed;
From the beginning, he had no heart of regret or vexation— I pay homage to the one perfected in the perfection of patience."
At that time, the Devaputra Rativīrya praised him with a verse:
"Unretreating leader of the valiant, Possessing great power through diligence,
Having already attained supreme enlightenment, I pay homage to the one perfected in vigor."
At that time, the Devaputra Rata-dhyāna praised him in verse:
“The Buddha originally cultivated meditative concentration, Which the world does not know;
Having attained equality across the three periods of time, I pay homage to the one perfected in the perfection of dhyāna.”
At that time, the Devaputra Tejodhipati praised him in verse:
"The Great Hero, through the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā in continuous succession, has attained inexhaustible wisdom;
I pay homage to the one perfected in the Perfection of Wisdom."
At that time, the Devaputra Dhātumati praised him in verse:
"Through generosity and kind words, through beneficial conduct and shared purpose, you deliver sentient beings by these means; I pay homage to the Great Teacher."
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhamati praised him with a verse:
"In great compassion and joy, You have constantly practiced throughout the long night;
By means of these, you rescue all living beings— I take refuge in the Great Captain."
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhacitta praised him with a verse:
"By means of the practice of non-contention, the Great Muni has tamed his own mind;
Able to tame those who are yet untamed, I pay homage to the Teacher of Men."
At that time, the Devaputra Vimalamati praised him in verse:
"With a vast mind and a supple mind, With a disciplined mind and all his faculties,
Knowing the minds of all sentient beings— I pay homage to the All-Knowing One."
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhamati praised him with these verses:
"Endowed with right mindfulness, Abiding securely within firm wisdom,
Thoroughly understanding and clearly realizing all— I pay homage to the Awakened One who awakens others."
At that time, the Devaputra Adhyāśaya-vyūha praised him with these verses:
"The Buddha’s mind has long been pure, And he has purified the buddha-fields, as well as the wisdom of all sentient beings; I pay homage to the Pure Dharma King."
At that time, the Devaputra Anabhibhū praised him with these verses:
“Your aspirations cannot be thwarted; You have subdued the power of Māra’s enemies.
Having fulfilled all great vows, You bring joy and satisfaction to the hosts of devas.”
At that time, the devaputra Kṣiprakārya praised him with a verse:
"The Tathāgata swiftly knows the Dharma And also rapidly purifies sentient beings;
Having seen the Dharma that is difficult to see, I pay homage to the one who accomplishes things with speed."
At that time, the Devaputra Dṛḍhavīrya praised him with these verses:
“Liberated in every respect, Free from delusion and devoid of outflows,
Having crossed to the further shore and dwelling there— I pay homage to you of steadfast power.”
At that time, the Devaputra Priyavinīta praised him with these verses:
"Free from desire and devoid of all faults, Having dispelled darkness and attained the exhaustion of outflows,
The supreme field of merit for the world— I pay homage to the one worthy of offerings."
At that time, the Devaputra Susthita praised with a verse:
“The World-Honored One abides in the True Dharma, Worshipped by those in the three realms;
He practices the single path of peace and security— Therefore, I pay him homage.”
At that time, the Devaputra Acala praised him with a verse:
"The Buddha is like a firm mountain, Unmoved by the wind;
In praise and blame he is always equanimous— Therefore, I now pay homage."
At that time, the devaputra Samatāprāpta praised him with these verses:
“The Great Hero’s form is most excellent, Endowed with the thirty-two marks;
Possessing great and profound wisdom, I pay homage to the one of upright intelligence.”
At that time, the Devaputra Gambhīramati praised him with these verses:
"One who is without body yet possesses the Great Body, Who dwells securely in the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā),
And clearly proclaims the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi)— In the world, there is none equal to you."
At that time, the Devaputra Anupamāpratihatamati praised him with a verse:
"Ultimately identical and non-dual, Valiant and capable of subduing Māra,
Without doubt regarding the profound meaning, Illuminating the Dharma, you have reached the other shore."
At that time, the Devaputra Priyadarśana praised him with a verse:
"Priyadarśana was originally courageous and steadfast; In all that he studied, he attained mastery.
He has cast off this triple world, Just as a snake sheds its old skin."
At that time, the Devaputra Samāhita-mati praised him with a verse:
"Just as a lamp in a dark room, Its light extinguished when the oil is spent,
So too does the wise one bring [defilements] to an end, By virtue of hearing the Buddha’s Dharma."
At that time, the devaputra Śamathasthita praised him with a verse:
“The Tathāgata observes all beings who are bound by the fetters of desire;
the Buddha is able to sever those snares because he wields the sword of wisdom.”
At that time, the devaputra Viśeṣamati praised with a verse:
"With a concentrated mind and concentrated conduct, With concentration in deportment and objective sphere, The Buddha is able to extinguish the afflictions; I pay homage to the Subduer of Enemies."
At that time, the devaputra Abhayaśamatha praised with a verse:
"By training in the Buddha’s śamatha, The Bodhisattva gains renown;
Because he is guided by right concentration, He accomplishes the Buddha of concentrated mind."
At that time, the Devaputra Niyata-bhojana praised him with a verse:
"All phenomena are quiescent; this is what the Great Hero has proclaimed.
Those of great wisdom who understand this shall swiftly become Tathāgatas."
At that time, the Devaputra Constantly Observing praised him with a verse:
“Constantly observing all sentient beings, They all follow the teachings of the Tathāgata;
Having attained supreme bodhi, They fulfill great wisdom.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dhṛtiguṇa praised him in verse:
"The Tathāgata’s wisdom has reached the further shore; Because Bodhisattvas practice and study it, They achieve great majesty and virtue in the world, And are able to perceive immeasurable dharmas."
At that time, the Devaputra Nirmāṇaprabha praised him in verse:
"He shall attain inconceivable light, And obtain stainless bliss;
In the presence of the Tathāgata who illuminates the world, He shall hear the realm of wisdom."
At that time, the Devaputra Vimalaprabha praised him with these verses:
"All phenomena are without discrimination; By means of skillful expedients, One cultivates such wisdom, And thus becomes a sublime Great Being."
At that time, the Devaputra Anihśrita praised with a verse:
“Without dwelling and without contact or affliction, All dharmas are without anything to be perceived;
One perceives neither self nor other— The Buddha relies upon this vision of reality.”
At that time, the Devaputra Gṛhamedhin praised him with these verses:
"All phenomena have no dwelling place; The Guide perceives them thus.
Yet, for the sake of teaching sentient beings, He conforms to them by grasping at the marks of phenomena."
At that time, the Devaputra Anāśrita-mati praised him in verse:
"All phenomena are without dependence, Transcending both self and other;
The Tathāgata reveals the reality As clearly as an āmalaka fruit in the palm of the hand."
At that time, the Devaputra Ākāśagāmin praised him in verse:
"Knowing that phenomena are like space, Neither arising nor ceasing—
The Buddha perceives phenomena thus, And is therefore able to transcend the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Anupacaya praised with a verse:
"Without seeking and without pride, without awakening and without non-awakening,
relying on the truth that lacks intrinsic nature— this is how the Buddha perceives the world."
At that time, the devaputra Bhāvanāmati praised him with these verses:
"Just as a skilled illusionist Manifests all manner of things through illusion— Though they are unreal, they appear as real; Therefore, the Buddha has no equal."
At that time, the Devaputra Xiwu (Joyful Awakening) praised him with a verse:
"Just as an image in a mirror, Though seen, is not real;
So the Buddha perceives all phenomena, And is not deluded by the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Vimatisamudghātin praised him in verse:
“The Buddha is like an echo; all phenomena are likewise so.
Both speaking and hearing are not real—this is how the Buddha perceives the world.”
At that time, the Devaputra Unobstructed Eloquence (Anāvaraṇapratibhāna) praised him in verse:
"Those who dwell securely in the True Dharma Speak with eloquence profound and wondrous;
The World-Honored One has long realized the Dharma, And is therefore fully endowed with eloquence."
At that time, the Devaputra Unobstructed Wisdom (Anāvaraṇajñāna) praised him in verse:
"Relying on the truth that there is no self-nature, All phenomena are thus;
The Tathāgata knows them as they truly are, And is therefore able to dispel the darkness."
At that time, the Devaputra Aśoka praised him with a verse:
“Without sorrow and without affliction, Without stillness and without turbidity;
All phenomena are free from defilement— The Buddha perceives their true nature.”
At that time, the Devaputra Caritrasampanna praised with a verse:
"Neither coming nor going, All phenomena are non-existent;
The Tathāgata perceives reality as it is, And thus speaks for the sake of the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Jñānavatī praised him with these verses:
"Neither defiled nor pure, Neither foolish nor wise;
All phenomena lack subject and object— The Buddha perceives them according to reality."
At that time, the Devaputra Anāvaraṇaprāpta praised him with a verse:
Neither light nor darkness, Neither form nor non-form,
Neither bound nor liberated— The Buddha’s wisdom perceives reality as it is.
At that time, the Devaputra Vīranetra praised with these verses:
Neither restricted nor pervasive, Neither existent nor non-existent;
Like one experiencing the five desires in a dream— Thus does the Buddha perceive phenomena as they truly are.
At that time, the Devaputra Animiṣa praised him with a verse:
"Neither born nor extinguished, Nor abiding in between;
Those of unwise minds are deluded by this, But only the Buddha perceives the reality."
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in Emptiness praised him with a verse:
"Not a person, not a sentient being, Not utility, nor worldly wealth;
Yet through conventional designation it has use— The Buddha is able to see this as it truly is."
At that time, the Devaputra Dwelling in the Signless praised him with these verses:
"All phenomena employed, They are all entirely signless;
The nature and characteristics of all dharmas are detached— Thus does the Guide perceive."
At that time, the Devaputra Apraṇihita praised him with these verses:
"Because phenomena are empty and signless, One does not give rise to aspiration through this.
If one were to falsely assume the seeking of an aspiration, Only the Buddha knows it as it truly is."
At that time, the Devaputra Samayapravāha praised with a verse:
"Having attained the gate of liberation, there is no one who liberates;
The root of afflictions is likewise non-existent— The Buddha perceives the nature of reality."
At that time, the Devaputra Adūṣya praised him in verse:
"Having abandoned all evil and accumulated a multitude of merits,
the Buddha is beyond reproach, nor is there anything in him to be censured."
At that time, the Devaputra Vidyutmegha praised him in verse:
"Just as thunder and lightning clouds Send down rain that fills the great earth,
So the Buddha pours down the rain of the True Dharma, Bringing fulfillment to all living beings."
At that time, the Devaputra Adhṛṣyapraṇidhi praised him with these verses:
“The World-Honored One’s words are unsurpassed; He is able to turn the wheel of the True Dharma.
He clearly realizes the profound principles of the Dharma And is fully endowed with all-encompassing wisdom.”
At that time, the Devaputra Endowed with Wisdom praised him in verse:
“Without arising and without ceasing, Such is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Because the Tathāgata understands this well, He likewise turns the teaching over to others.”
At that time, the Devaputra Siṃhanāda praised him in verse:
"When the Tathāgata roars the lion’s roar And proclaims the Dharma of emptiness,
The non-Buddhists are all struck with fear, Just as wild beasts fear the lion."
At that time, the devaputra Karma-apramāda praised him in verse:
"Free from negligence before his eyes, the Buddha cultivated and attained enlightenment;
The Teacher, regarding the True Dharma, reached the further shore through diligence."
At that time, the devaputra Abiding in Heedfulness praised him with these verses:
“Abiding securely in heedfulness, He increases the Buddha’s True Dharma;
The Ten Powers and other practices— The Buddha-dharma is inconceivable.”
At that time, the devaputra Apramāda-ja praised him with these verses:
"By abiding in heedfulness, The factors of enlightenment grow and flourish;
Through this, he delivers all beings, And the Buddha himself is likewise liberated."
At that time, the devaputra Accomplished in Heedlessness (Anati-māda-siddha) praised him in verse:
"Through the attainment of non-heedlessness, all those who rely on existence—
whether Śrāvakas or Bodhisattvas— achieve liberation by training in this very way."
At that time, the Devaputra Apramādavihārin praised him with a verse:
"All those sons of the Buddhas Who always practice heedfulness Are able to attain all-knowledge Because they skillfully observe the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Anatiṣaṇḍa praised him in verse:
"When the Buddha cultivated bodhi, He guarded against negligence;
Having attained supreme bodhi, It was because of the adornment of great compassion."
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in Heedfulness praised him with these verses:
"If one abides in heedfulness, Discerning the dharma of a single characteristic,
The Son of the Buddha, great in valor and strength, Shall obtain the inheritance left by his father."
At that time, the devaputra Delight-in-Heedfulness praised him in verse:
"The valiant ones who delight in heedfulness Can shatter the mountain of afflictions;
By means of the Buddha’s wisdom, They swiftly extinguish the mass of arrogance."
At that time, the devaputra Firmly Maintaining Non-Negligence praised him in verse:
"Guarding against negligence, In the past he sought all-knowledge;
For incalculable billions of eons, The Buddha’s mind never grew weary."
At that time, the devaputra Śamathābhimukha praised with a verse:
“The nature of phenomena is thus quiescent; this is the domain of all Buddhas.
The wise who abide in reliance upon it are able to proceed toward supreme enlightenment.”
At that time, the devaputra Śamathāśrita praised him in verse:
"The Buddhas rely upon śamatha; Relying upon it, they do not grasp at anything.
The afflictions of sentient beings are extinguished, Like rain soaking away all dust."
At that time, the devaputra Śamathasthita praised him in verse:
"The Buddhas abide in śamatha, Immovable like a great mountain;
Even the celestial Māras cannot destroy them— Because their minds are tranquil, I take refuge."
At that time, the Devaputra Śamathavinīta praised him in verse:
"Subdued by śamatha, the Son of the Buddha is beyond reproach;
Even billions of Māras cannot move him; He is free from desire, like an Arhat."
At that time, the devaputra Śamathābhāvanīya praised him in verse:
"When the Great Hero formerly practiced The samādhi of śamatha,
No one could know the Buddha’s mind— Upon what did he rely to attain such meditative concentration?"
At that time, the Devaputra Śamathottama praised him in verse:
“The Buddha turned the wheel of the True Dharma, Exerting himself to attain śamatha;
All other dharmas depend entirely upon it, And by means of this, he attained bodhi.”
At that time, the devaputra Śamatha praised with a verse:
“The Buddha has taught *śamatha*; It is the cage and net for the mind.
Sentient beings fall into the prison of delusion; The Buddha teaches the subduing of the mind.”
At that time, the Devaputra Śamathaviṣaya praised with a verse:
“The sublime realm of all Buddhas Is this very śamatha;
By practicing this one attains non-obstruction And becomes a Great Guide.”
At that time, the devaputra Pūrṇaśamatha praised him in verse:
"Having filled the mind with dhyāna, And further cultivating and accumulating wisdom,
The Buddha attained bodhi, And is thus able to bring peace to all sentient beings."
Then, the devaputra Gauravaśamatha praised him in verse:
"Seeing no other path, Only within the Buddha’s Dharma Does one obtain great wisdom And become an Unsurpassed One."
At that time, the devaputra Prītivipaśyana praised with a verse:
“The Buddha, relying on vipaśyanā, Is able to perceive all phenomena;
The bodhisattva follows and learns accordingly, Accomplishing spontaneous wisdom.”
At that time, the devaputra Jātipratiśaraṇa praised him in verse:
"Because you have reached the further shore of wisdom, You have become the accomplished Great King of Physicians;
That you reveal the Four Noble Truths Is entirely due to vipaśyanā."
At that time, the devaputra Vipaśyanastha praised him with a verse:
"Abiding in vipaśyanā, Knowing all phenomena as they truly are,
The valiant one realizes bodhi And is able to become a great guide."
At that time, the devaputra Bhāvitakṣayavipaśyanā praised him in verse:
"The Great Being, through wisdom, Cultivated supreme bodhi;
Not giving rise to the sphere of consciousness, He has become a great guide."
At that time, the devaputra Priyavipaśyanā praised him in verse:
“The wise one relies upon reality; observing this Dharma in such a way, he is able to attain the peerless fruit, becoming a Buddha named the Teacher.”
At that time, the devaputra Vīryavibhāṣana praised him in verse:
“Because he diligently cultivates wisdom, He is able to establish all ascetic practices;
Having achieved that which is difficult to subdue, He cannot be destroyed by false paths.”
At that time, the devaputra Viśeṣamati praised with a verse:
"All those sons of the Buddha, Because they contemplate the characteristics of phenomena,
Having realized those characteristics of phenomena, They become accomplished Teachers who Subdue."
At that time, the devaputra Vibhāṣana praised with a verse:
“The Tathāgata, throughout the long night, Cultivated supreme wisdom;
He was able to accomplish all-knowledge And deliver immeasurable multitudes.”
At that time, the Devaputra Viśeṣacārin praised him in verse:
“The Buddha has cultivated all-knowledge and become a perfected Great Guide;
By means of the Dharma he rescues the world, Crossing over the swift-flowing stream.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vipaśyanāvihārin praised him with a verse:
“Abiding in vipaśyanā, He observes all phenomena;
The Buddha-dharmas are born from him, Just as the nyagrodha tree grows from the earth.”
At that time, the devaputra Vipaśyanadhara praised with a verse:
“The World-Honored One and all sons of the Buddha,
Having embraced supreme wisdom and attained unsurpassed enlightenment, Are able to deliver all sentient beings.”
At that time, the devaputra Vikrīḍita-vipaśyana praised him in verse:
"Sporting amidst all dharmas, You have attained the fearlessnesses of a Buddha;
Without timidity and without dread, O Great Muni of supreme wisdom."
At that time, the devaputra Anuvilokita praised with a verse:
“The Great Hero, regarding all phenomena, Has fully realized vipaśyanā;
Observing their lack of intrinsic nature— This is the awakening of the Buddha.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vipaśyanā-dṛḍha praised him in verse, saying:
“The wisdom of all Buddhas is firm; They have no fear regarding the Dharma.
Observing the suffering of all living beings, They are able to give rise to great compassion.”
At that time, the devaputra Viśeṣamati praised him in verse:
"By means of wisdom one approaches enlightenment; One who possesses wisdom can learn well.
Such a person attains supreme enlightenment And delivers all sentient beings."
At that time, the Devaputra Śūnyatābhāvanīya praised him with a verse:
"Cultivating the dharma of emptiness, The wise awaken to bodhi;
They are able to destroy all prisons And deliver those bound by fetters."
At that time, the Devaputra Understanding Emptiness praised with a verse:
"Because the World-Honored One understands emptiness, He perceives neither body nor life;
Being without conditions and without intrinsic nature, He relies upon this to speak for the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Śūnyatāviṣaya praised him with a verse:
"The realm of all Buddhas— The nature of all phenomena is inherently empty.
The Great Hero trains within this, Out of compassion to deliver all sentient beings."
At that time, the Devaputra Śūnyatāśraddha praised him with a verse:
“The Tathāgata is free from foulness and impurity, And has long since transcended all fear.
He does not cling to any phenomena, Like the wind, he has no place of dependence.”
At that time, the Devaputra Delight-in-Emptiness praised with a verse:
“Those who cultivate the dharma of emptiness Are able to delight in the realm of the Buddha;
They thereby make offerings to the Buddha, And also accomplish the unsurpassed offering.”
At that time, the devaputra Śūnyatā-vyavasthāpana praised him in verse:
"Because he has cultivated the dharma of emptiness, The Guide has attained firm establishment;
Having mastered the dharma of emptiness, He has become the kinsman of the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Ākāśābhimukha praised him with a verse:
“The Buddha knows that there is not a single dharma That is not nirvāṇa;
all dharmas tend toward nirvāṇa— This is the awakening (bodhi) of the Buddha.”
At that time, the Devaputra Ākāśasaṃpatti praised him with a verse:
“Having attained the samādhi of emptiness and tranquility, The sons of the Buddha have achieved perfection;
They make offerings to the Buddha, For they are practitioners of the dharma of emptiness.”
At that time, the Devaputra Gaganagañja praised him with these verses:
"Those who take refuge in emptiness possess wisdom and are not deluded;
Unattached, they sever the afflictions; free from defilement, they attain Bodhi."
At that time, the Devaputra Pūrṇa-śūnya praised him with these verses:
"The Buddha-dharma has been brought to fulfillment; He has achieved that which is difficult to subdue.
All those who cultivate emptiness Are able to benefit the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in Emptiness praised him with these verses:
“Those who dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma And are able to cultivate the wisdom of emptiness—
Even immeasurable hosts of Māras Cannot cause them to waver.”
At that time, the Devaputra Nairātmyarata praised him with a verse:
"Delighting in the signless, Not clinging to that which has signs,
Having discerned all phenomena, The Buddha is able to transcend the world."
At that time, the Devaputra Nimitāpagata praised with a verse:
"When practicing the signless, one cultivates the conduct of pure quiescence;
Sentient beings who have abandoned signs—Māra does not know their destination."
At that time, the Devaputra Realm of Signlessness praised him with a verse:
"The realm of the signless Buddha— The Tathāgata cultivates within it.
The signless is difficult to realize; I pay homage to the practitioner of meditative concentration."
At that time, the Devaputra Thirsting for the Signless praised him with a verse:
"All these multitudes thirst and long for the signless Dharma;
Seeking the father’s inheritance, they make offerings to the Teacher of Gods and Men."
At that time, the devaputra Cultivating Formless Practice praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata, regarding the formless, Constantly practices day and night;
Gods, humans, and spirits alike Do not know where the Buddha goes.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vimokṣa-nirnimitta praised him with a verse:
“The Great Hero abides in the signless, Contemplating all phenomena;
That which the Guide has practiced and studied— Therefore, I pay homage to him.”
At that time, the Devaputra *Nirnimitta-vikrīḍita* praised him with a verse:
“Great Compassion manifests as play, Always relying upon the dharma of signlessness;
For the sake of maturing sentient beings, You abide within the wisdom of the Buddha.”
At that time, the Devaputra Niḥsanimānasaṃpanna praised him in verse:
"One who has well cultivated the departure from signs Is able to attain the Bodhi of the Buddha,
And is also able to make offerings to the Buddha, Just as a son reveres his father."
At that time, the Devaputra Long-Enjoying the Signless (Ciranirābhāsa) praised him with these verses:
"He who loves the Buddha’s True Dharma Is a stūpa for all sentient beings;
All those who have abandoned signs Abide in the presence of the Teacher."
At that time, the devaputra Nirnimittamārga praised with a verse:
“The destination for all sentient beings, Relying on the Way they attain deliverance;
The practice of non-attachment and quiescent extinction— The Tathāgata is most supreme.”
At that time, the Devaputra Śraddhā-nimitta praised with a verse:
"To those who have faith and understanding in the signless, Who are tranquil, extinguished,
and free from all enmity— I pay homage to all Buddhas, Those who have crossed over themselves and deliver others."
At that time, the devaputra Nirāśa praised with a verse:
"The aspirations of the World-Honored One cannot be found by seeking;
they are free from all conditioned activity—thus has the Buddha appeared in the world."
At that time, the devaputra Bhāvanāpraṇihita praised him with these verses:
“Not giving rise to wishes for existence, Cultivating a mind of tranquil extinction,
Severing the bonds of craving— This Buddha has transcended the world.”
At that time, the devaputra Anabhisaṃskāra praised him with these verses:
"They have attained great diligence, And are free from attachment to existence;
These sons of the Tathāgata All pay homage to their own father."
At that time, the devaputra Praṇidhānajanman praised him with these verses:
“They do not give rise to aspirations; they destroy existence within existence.
Those who are able to sever craving—such sons of the Buddha are free from reproach.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vimuktipraṇidhāna praised him with these verses:
“Through wishlessness one attains liberation; Seeking nothing, one is freed from all bonds.
Relinquishing all and not giving rise to wishes— Such is the majestic power maintained by the Son of the Buddha.”
At that time, the Devaputra Niryāṇa praised with a verse:
"Having emerged from the wilderness of sorrow, And having uprooted the source of craving’s defilement,
They pay homage to the Tathāgata, The one who has attained the removal of hunger and thirst."
At that time, the Devaputra Niyata-apraṇihita praised him in verse:
“Those who well know the existence of suffering, And who likewise know worldly pleasure to be illusory— The Buddha is the father of such as these; They are the sons of the Guide.”
At that time, the Devaputra Abhimukha praised him with a verse:
"To those who perceive suffering within existence, That person attains subduing;
I pay homage to the Well-Subdued One, The Tamer of Beings who has shattered existence."
At that time, the Devaputra Atikrāntapraṇidhāna praised him with a verse:
"Having crossed over the wilderness of existence, He dwells securely in a place of peace;
I prostrate universally to the Great Teacher, Who has already subdued the enemy of afflictions."
At that time, the Devaputra Clad in the Armor of Wishlessness praised him with these verses:
"Victorious in battle, having shattered the enemy host, Most powerful and difficult to subdue,
Having already subdued the multitudes of Māras, The courageous one seeks no further existence."
At that time, the Devaputra Anabhilāṣabala praised with a verse:
"With great power regarding liberation, They are able to sever all the bonds of Māra.
These sons of the Buddhas regard Māra As mere grass in a net."
At that time, the Devaputra Kāyadarśin praised with a verse:
"Those who contemplate this body Are able to delight in the Buddha-dharma;
Being without self and without an agent, Such as these accord with the Dharma."
At that time, the devaputra Smṛtikāya praised him with a verse:
"Regarding all mindfulness of this body, Which is foul, loathsome, and impure—
Having known the body as it truly is, I pay homage to the Great Teacher."
At that time, the devaputra Nivṛttakāya praised him with a verse:
“Fixing mindfulness upon the internal body, He contemplates the signs of impurity;
Thus he attains liberation from bodily suffering— To you, the Tamer, I pay homage.”
At that time, the Devaputra Śarīratyāga praised him with a verse:
"Having cast off this body of pus and blood, Like a snake shedding its old skin,
I pay homage to the non-body, The great body of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the devaputra Nivṛttakāya praised him with a verse:
“Disgusted by this body of pus and blood, Impure, most foul and filthy—
Having abandoned this impure body, I take refuge in and revere the Teacher of Gods and Humans.”
At that time, the Devaputra Troubled by Bodily Fatigue praised him with a verse:
“The body that is afflicted and decaying— The Son of the Buddha seeks its purification;
He shall fully pay homage to the Buddha, The true Dharma-body that he cultivates.”
At that time, the devaputra Bhayadarśin praised him with these verses:
"Observing and knowing these four great elements To be like venomous serpents, He has transcended them within his body; I pay homage to the Great Teacher."
At that time, the devaputra Seeing the Faults of the Body praised him with a verse:
"Seeing the faults of the body before one's eyes Is the attainment of the eye of wisdom;
It illuminates all these three realms of existence, For the wise rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom."
At that time, the devaputra Anabhirati praised him with these verses:
"All those who find no delight in the body, Who do not abide by the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*),
And who are unattached to any fetters (*saṃyojana*)— To them, the Tamer (*Vināyaka*), I pay homage."
At that time, the devaputra Vairāśaya uttered these verses in praise:
“Regarding existence as an enemy, One cultivates insight to destroy all forms of becoming.
A son of the Buddha trains in this way; Wisdom arises and he awakens to Bodhi.”
At that time, the devaputra Bhavavigama praised him with a verse:
"Having perceived the faults of existence, He is able to know its cessation and is fearless;
The Son of the Buddha diligently seeks the Path, And obtains the inheritance left by his father."
At that time, the devaputra Abandoning Existence (Tyaktabhava) praised him with a verse:
"You have cultivated the abandonment of all existences, And delight in dwelling in great nirvāṇa;
With a pure mind free from all fetters, I pay homage to the Great Teacher."
At that time, the devaputra Chinnabhava praised with a verse:
“Having severed the root of existence, He illuminates the three thousandfold world system.
The sons of the World-Honored One Have mastered all that they study.”
At that time, the devaputra Dūyavī praised him with these verses:
“Having crossed the ocean of existence, You rescue those who are solitary and alone;
Within these three realms, They are not even counted among the living.”
At that time, the Devaputra Bhavavidhvamsin praised him in verse:
“The sons of the Buddha who cultivate the Way Are able to shatter the three realms of existence;
They are those who make offerings to the Buddha, For the sake of transforming sentient beings.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vimukta praised him with a verse:
"Having attained liberation from the flow of existence, Abiding ultimately at the final limit, The Great Hero has appeared in the world; I pay homage to the one who has severed existence."
At that time, the devaputra named Extinction-of-Existence (Nirbhava) praised him with a verse:
"You have eradicated the root of existence, Crossed over existence to reach the further shore, And severed the future limit; In this world, there is none like the Buddha."
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in the Future Limit praised him with a verse:
“The Tathāgata abides in the future limit, Having reached the further shore of quiescence;
Possessing omniscience, he has crossed over all, Awakening those who have not yet awakened.”
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in the Subsequent Limit (Pacchimakoti) praised him with a verse:
“The Buddha abides in the subsequent limit, And explains the cause of those three realms of existence.
Seeing no fetters within existence, He is thereafter unable to give rise to further existence.”
At that time, the devaputra Nirodhaprāpta praised him with a verse:
"Having realized that existence is empty and quiescent, You are able to understand the causes of the three realms of existence.
With diligence and without cowardice, I pay homage to you, the Equanimous One."
At that time, the Devaputra Tūitpāragata (Having Crossed Over Existence) praised him with a verse:
"Having crossed over existence to the other shore, You have uprooted the very source of existence;
You deliver all living beings— O Guide, you have compassion for all."
At that time, the devaputra Untroubled by Feeling praised him with these verses:
"Free from arrogance regarding feeling, Without thought and without deliberation,
Fully understanding and comprehending all matters of dhyāna, He contemplates feeling as being like a bubble."
At that time, the devaputra Vijñāpti praised with a verse:
“The Tathāgata knows all sensations (vedanā) To be fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
That which ordinary beings cling to Is like experiencing sensual pleasure in a dream.”
At that time, the devaputra Avalokita-vedanā praised him in verse:
"The wise one observes all sensations (*vedanā*), And is able to take up the path of goodness;
He does not give rise to future sensations— Thus do I behold the Teacher."
At that time, the devaputra Vigatarāga praised with a verse:
“Feeling and that which is felt, The Buddha saw as being without intrinsic nature;
He was able to explain this for the sake of the assembly— A phrase profound and difficult to know.”
At that time, the devaputra Niyatajñānavedanā praised him with these verses:
"All sensations exist only in conventional truth; In the ultimate sense, they do not exist.
The Tathāgata speaks the reality That cuts through the doubts of the world."
At that time, the devaputra Sujñāptavedanīya praised with a verse:
“The World-Honored One well understands sensation, Like clouds in the sky.
Who among the ignorant is deluded? Only the Buddha can truly comprehend it.”
At that time, the devaputra Pratividdhavedanā praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata has realized all sensations; He understands sensation and has reached the further shore.
Knowing that sensation is devoid of ‘mine-ness,’ His teaching of the Dharma is supreme.”
At that time, the devaputra Duśruta praised with a verse:
"The World-Honored One has long since crossed over The most difficult sea of the three sensations;
Having abandoned the mire of evil, The Buddha’s wisdom is called unsurpassed."
At that time, the devaputra Chinnasrava praised him in verse:
"The Guide has fully understood all sensations as transcending the world;
Having surpassed and left behind the mire of defilement, He does not cling to any state of existence."
At that time, the Devaputra Cintitavedanīya praised with a verse:
“The Tathāgata contemplates all sensations; Because the world suffers through sensation, Sentient beings are bound by afflictions, Yet the Buddha knows their true nature.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vimati-citta praised with a verse:
“The Buddha’s mind subdues afflictions, And likewise overcomes all Māras and enemies;
Relying on the truth, there is nothing to be destroyed— Therefore, the Buddha is named Muni.”
At that time, the Devaputra Vijñānacitta praised with a verse:
"The Buddha has long understood the characteristics of consciousness, Like a skillful magician who conjures various forms; Therefore, the Buddha is named Arhat."
At that time, the devaputra Citta-carita praised him in verse:
“The Great Hero has already completed his practice; He is able to sever the objects of the mind.
Throughout billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, The nature of the mind cannot be apprehended.”
At that time, the Devaputra Samāhita-citta praised him with these verses:
"Restless and difficult to subdue, Formless yet dwelling in its lair— The Buddha has severed this swift-moving mind;
Therefore, he is able to receive supreme offerings."
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhacitta praised with a verse:
“The Buddha has already discerned the mind; Sentient beings are bound by the mind.
The Buddha knows it truly, Just as a magician instructs his son.”
At that time, the Devaputra Realm of Cultivating the Mind praised him in verse:
"The realm of the mind as it is practiced, the Teacher perceives with certainty;
like experiencing the five desires in a dream, those who are deluded therein are ignorant."
At that time, the Devaputra Cittavasu praised with a verse:
"Having completed the work of subduing, The mind is free from conceptualizing objects;
The Tathāgata perceives the characteristics of the mind, Which the world does not know."
At that time, the Devaputra Sūramati praised him in verse:
"One called 'Courageous in Mind' Is able to shatter the hosts of Māra;
One who sees the mind with the mind Contemplates the mind without weariness."
At that time, the devaputra Jianli praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata observes sentient beings And establishes them in the Dharma;
One who can know the mind with the mind Is truly a son of the Buddha.”
At that time, the Devaputra Samāhitacitta praised him with these verses:
“Those who have subdued their minds are able to practice tranquility;
such as these are freed from all bonds and are not troubled by Māra.”
At that time, the devaputra Mṛdumati praised him with a verse:
“With a courageous and gentle mind, you tame the multitudes of sentient beings;
those who delight in the Buddha-dharma do not cling to any desires.”
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhamati praised him in verse:
"With a virtuous mind delighting in purity, He performs actions with careful reflection;
Having heard the Buddha’s True Dharma, He has no doubt regarding its profound meaning."
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in the Dharma praised him with these verses:
"Those who possess a mind directed toward the Dharma, Deeply delighting in it without falling back—
They are true sons of the Buddha, Having already reached the stage of self-mastery."
At that time, the Devaputra Contemplating the Dharma praised with a verse:
"Contemplating the dharma-realm, Its spheres of experience are none other than one;
The entire dharma-realm is pure— The place where all Buddhas train."
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātuvyūha praised with a verse:
"That which is established in the Dharma-realm Is the mind of great compassion;
One who can abide within the single mark Is a true son of the Buddha."
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātugocara praised with a verse:
“The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma-realm; This is the realm of all Buddhas, The sphere of practice for Great Beings— This wisdom is inconceivable.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātujāta praised him with these verses:
"Born from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), this wisdom is inconceivable;
He does not doubt the profound Buddha-dharma, And he also knows the nature of all faculties."
At that time, the Devaputra Entering the Dharma Realm praised him with these verses:
"One who enters the profound Dharma realm Understands that dharmas have no equal;
This power is inconceivable, And they also attain all wondrous vows."
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātuvaiśāradya praised him in verse:
“Having attained the state of fearlessness, He dwells in a place of peace and security;
With all the power of his eloquence, None can equal him.”
At that time, the Devaputra Well-Understanding the Dharma-Dhātu praised him in verse:
“The Tathāgata understands the dharma-dhātu And has also attained all-knowledge;
He manifests the characteristics of the dharma-dhātu As clearly as an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand.”
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in the Dharmadhātu praised with a verse:
“The World-Honored One abides in the dharmadhātu, Perceiving the true nature of phenomena;
Neither relying nor departing, Neither grasping nor abandoning.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātucārin praised him with these verses:
“The Tathāgata traverses the realm of phenomena, Tranquil as empty space.
O Great Muni, whose sphere of experience is such, I pay homage to you, the Father of Compassion.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātvanugata praised with a verse:
“In accordance with their various gateways, The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma-realm;
Within each and every such gateway, There is neither mind nor form.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātu-vīrya praised with a verse:
“The World-Honored One speaks of diligence, Which enables one to know the dharma-realm;
Because of practicing diligence, Awakened wisdom reaches the other shore.”
At that time, the Devaputra Dharmadhātuparipūrṇa praised him with these verses:
"With great compassion and the true Dharma, He fills and satisfies all worlds;
One who can know the dharmadhātu Shall attain the state of awakening."
At that time, the Devaputra Chèfǎjiè (Thoroughly Penetrating the Dharma-realm) praised him in verse:
"The World-Honored One has thoroughly penetrated the profound Dharma; Therefore, he is able to contemplate the world.
Having fully known the entire dharma-realm, I pay homage to the Teacher of Gods and Humans."
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding in the Sphere of Wisdom praised him with these verses:
"This sphere is supreme among men, attained through the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
it is the realm of the Dharma and the ten directions—the sphere traversed by the Guide."
At that time, the Devaputra Abiding-Place praised with a verse:
“The Dharma-realm is the place of abiding; It is the path traversed by all wisdoms.
All phenomena of every existence Are entirely understood as having a single characteristic.”
At that time, the Devaputra Jñānavāsī praised him with these verses:
“The World-Honored One knows the Dharma-realm; Having cultivated the single characteristic, The various desires and natures of sentient beings— The Buddha likewise understands them all.”
At that time, the Devaputra Source of Emergence praised with a verse:
"One who can grasp all-knowledge is called a son of the Buddhas;
regarding this locus of the Dharma-realm, it can be known only by wisdom."
At that time, the Devaputra Śikṣāpada praised him with these verses:
