His hair is yellow and his eyes are wide with anger as he stares straight ahead. He is constantly fond of hunger and thirst, stingy, greedy, and envious. He delights in an abundance of food and drink, enjoys slandering others behind their backs, and has much body hair. His pupils are bloodshot and bright; he thinks much of various foods and greedily delights in hoarding them, having no desire to give them away. He takes no pleasure in seeing virtuous people and covets the wealth he sees. Even upon obtaining a small amount of property, he is immediately filled with joy. He constantly seeks profit and gain, delights in impure food, and feels envy and jealousy whenever he sees another’s assets. Furthermore, he regards the wealth of others as his own; when he sees others using it, he feels stinginess. Upon hearing of fine food, his heart is displeased; even seeing fallen fruit or the five grains on a street, he gives rise to a greedy mind to pick them up and collect them.
"O non-Buddhists!
There are such immeasurable varieties of signs; I have now briefly described these signs for you—these are called those who pass away from among the hungry ghosts and are reborn in the human realm."
The wise can know this, but the foolish cannot fathom it.
"Heterodox practitioners, listen well: if one passes away from among the asuras and is reborn among humans, there shall be these signs; the wise should know them."
Arrogant and conceited, he is constantly prone to anger and delights in strife. He harbors grudges without forgetting them and gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

His body is massive and powerful; his eyes are as white as those of a dog, and his long teeth protrude prominently. Brave and possessing great strength, he always takes pleasure in battle arrays. He also enjoys using double-tongued speech to destroy others. With sparse teeth and a haughty mind, he looks down upon the treatises composed by others. Although he knows that others possess subtle and refined eloquence, as well as the power of wisdom and the power of afflictions (*kleśa*), he merely delights in nourishing his own body.
"O non-Buddhist!
There are such immeasurable varieties of signs; I have now briefly described these signs, which are called those who, having passed away from among the asuras, are reborn in the human realm."
The wise can know this, whereas it is beyond the comprehension of the foolish.
"O non-Buddhists, listen attentively: if one who has passed away from among humans is reborn again among humans, there will be these signs; the wise should know them."

That person is virtuous and upright; they associate with good people and disparage evil ones. They cherish their family reputation, are sincere and faithful to their word, and delight in fame and renown. They take pleasure in the arts and crafts, revere wisdom, and possess a sense of shame and modesty. Their nature is gentle, and they recognize kindness and support. Toward virtuous friends, their mind is compliant and free of opposition; they delight in giving and charity. They discern the status of others and skillfully observe whether a person will be beneficial or not. They are adept at responding to questions and grasping the meaning of what is said. They are skilled at reconciling differences as well as separating those who should be parted. They are capable of acting as a messenger to convey messages, and they are able to master various forms of speech, retaining them in memory without forgetting.
Furthermore, one is also able to know what is possible and what is impossible. O outsider!
There are such immeasurable varieties of signs; I have now briefly described these signs, which are called "passing away from among humans and being reborn again among humans."
The wise are able to know this; it is not something the foolish can fathom.
"Listen attentively, O non-Buddhists: if one passes away from among the devas and is reborn in the human realm, there shall be these signs; the wise should recognize them."

He is upright in character and delights in purity; he rejoices in wearing flower garlands and being perfumed with incense, and takes pleasure in anointing his body with fragrant unguents and bathing frequently. Regarding the five sensory desires, he discriminates for the best and takes no pleasure in what is inferior. He delights in music, song, and dance, and forms friendships exclusively with superior persons rather than associating with those who are base. He is fond of pavilions, lofty halls, and private chambers; he finds joy in compassion as his path, smiling without anger. His speech is graceful and eloquent, bringing delight to others. He enjoys necklaces, fine garments, and ornaments for adorning the body, and always delights in moving about with a steady, unhurried gait. In all that he does, he is diligent and never indolent.
"O non-Buddhists!
There are such immeasurable varieties of signs; I have now briefly described these signs, which are called 'passing away from among the devas and being born in the human realm.'"
"This wisdom can be known; it cannot be fathomed by the ignorant.
'O non-Buddhists!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to transcend these marks, they should draw near to virtuous friends and follow their will; whatever those virtuous friends do, they should likewise do. Those virtuous friends will cause them to cross over by preaching the Dharma for them.'"
"O non-Buddhist!

Those who pass away from hell and are reborn among humans did so because, while they were previously in human form before falling into hell, they committed various transgressions and evils and gave rise to anger, thereby committing acts of killing; it was by the牵引 (karmic pull) of those deeds that they fell into hell."
Having undergone various kinds of suffering in that hell, they still retain residual habits (*vāsanā*) when later reborn among humans.
Once such a person has recognized these signs, they must know for themselves: "I have come from the hells to be born among humans."
Such a person, in order to abandon the causes and conditions for hell, should seek out a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Having encountered such a virtuous friend, that friend, for the sake of eliminating the karma of anger, teaches loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*), as well as the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) associated with loving-kindness and compassion.
By means of these practices, one can eliminate that person's remaining habitual tendencies and the causal conditions for hell.
That spiritual friend may, for this person’s sake, teach the *śīlapāramitā* associated with loving-kindness and compassion, thereby severing the faults and evils of their anger.
When such a person cultivates loving-kindness and compassion, they shall fulfill the six *pāramitās* and increase their merit and virtue.
O outsider!
One who passes away from the animal realm to be born among humans must have, while previously in a human body, practiced and accumulated the dharmas of ignorance.
Due to the habituation of delusion, one performs unwholesome karma; by having committed such karma, one is born among animals.
Because that person previously took an animal body and dwelt for a long time with other animals, they now perform the rituals and behaviors of animals.

Having passed away from the animal realm, because of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for the conduct of animals, once this person has obtained a human body and hears such a teaching and observes his own past conduct, he should know for himself: "I must have previously passed away from among animals to be born here in the human world."
Because this person wishes to abandon the conduct of animals, they should seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

That spiritual friend, in order to eliminate this person's karma of ignorance, teaches the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); by means of this Dharma, their ignorance is eliminated.

That spiritual friend may explain the *prajñāpāramitā* to that person; having heard the *prajñāpāramitā*, the person’s nature of ignorance naturally departs, and when they engage in this contemplation, wisdom arises.
"O non-Buddhist!

Those who pass away from the realm of hungry ghosts and are born among humans did so because, while they were previously human beings, they practiced and habituated themselves to the ways of stinginess and greed."

Because this person practiced the dharma of stinginess and greed, they held fast to it and did not relinquish it; by the power of that karma, they were born among the hungry ghosts (preta), and because they have long dwelt with those hungry ghosts, they perform the actions of hungry ghosts.

Having passed away from among the hungry ghosts, because they still possess the habitual tendencies and the conduct of hungry ghosts, once such a person has obtained a human body, upon hearing this Dharma and observing their own past conduct, they should know for themselves: "I must have previously passed away from among the hungry ghosts and been reborn here in the human realm."
Because such a person seeks to abandon the conduct of hungry ghosts, they should seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

That spiritual friend, in order to eliminate that person's karma of stinginess and greed, teaches them the practice of giving (*dāna*); by means of this Dharma, their stinginess and greed are eliminated.
That spiritual friend may explain to them the factors conducive to awakening associated with generosity, causing their stinginess and greed to be completely severed.
That spiritual friend may also explain the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) to that person; because this person practices the perfection of giving, they will fulfill all six perfections.

That spiritual friend may explain to that person that all phenomena are entirely equal; because this person practices the equality of phenomena, they will fulfill the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Because they cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, they flow toward and incline toward the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
O non-Buddhists!

Those among the asuras who are eventually reborn in the human realm did so because, in their previous lives as humans, they performed many roots of goodness while practicing arrogance. Due to that pride, they committed various karmic actions; having cultivated and accumulated the karma of arrogance, they were born among the asuras by the power of that karma.
Because they have dwelt for a long time among the asuras, they perform the karma of asuras;
even after their lives as asuras have ended, they still possess the habitual tendencies of asura conduct.

Having obtained this human body, when such a person hears this Dharma and observes their own conduct, they must realize for themselves: "I have certainly come from death among the asuras to be born here in the human realm."
Because this person wishes to abandon the conduct of the asuras, they should seek out virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Those virtuous friends, in order to eliminate that person’s karma of arrogance, will explain the noble abodes (*āryavihāra*); by means of these teachings, they cause that person to eliminate the karma of arrogance.

Or he may preach the Dharma-gate of emptiness to that person; by means of this teaching on emptiness, he causes that person's karma of arrogance to be eliminated, and further eliminates the grasping at a self so that they attain the realization of non-self.

Or he may explain to them that all phenomena exist because of the conjunction of causes and conditions; that because of this conjunction there is activity, and if there were no conjunction, there would be no activity.
Having performed this contemplation, the latent tendencies of pride and their corresponding karma are entirely severed.

Alternatively, for the sake of those persons, one may explain that all dharmas have a single characteristic; by practicing accordingly, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is brought to fulfillment.
Having fully cultivated the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one swiftly realizes all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) and never regresses.

O outsider! Those among humans who are ultimately reborn as humans did so because, in their previous lives as human beings, they practiced and accumulated the ten paths of wholesome action (daśakuśalakarmapatha). Having performed those deeds, they practiced them repeatedly; by the power of that karma, they are reborn again among humans.
In the past, when he was a human being, he lived among people for a long time and practiced their customs and rituals;

now, having returned to the state of a human, because of these residual habits (*vāsanā*), once this person has heard such a Dharma teaching, they should know for themselves: "I must have previously passed away from among humans and have now been reborn among humans."
Because this person seeks to transcend those habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they should seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
That spiritual friend will explain the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) to that person, using the perception of impermanence to eliminate their habitual tendencies.

That spiritual friend may explain to this person the faults of birth and death and the supreme bliss of nirvana; having heard this Dharma, the person is able to become weary of the faults of birth and death and rejoice in the bliss of nirvana.
That spiritual friend may explain the six pāramitās to this person; having heard them, the person is able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.

That spiritual friend may also explain skillful means to this person; by means of these skillful means, the person is then able to firmly uphold the six pāramitās, swiftly realize all-knowledge, and never regress.
"O non-Buddhist!

Those who pass away from the heavenly realms and are reborn among humans did so because, while they still possessed human bodies prior to their existence as gods, they practiced the holy life, gave alms, and observed the precepts with the hope of receiving a future reward."
When this person has thus completed their long-term cultivation and accumulation of karmic actions, they are born in the heavens by the power of that karma.
Having been born in heaven, they dwell there for a long time and perform the rituals of the devas.

Having passed away from the heavens, due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the practices of the devas, this person, having obtained a human body, hears such teachings and observes their own past conduct; they should then know for themselves: "I must have previously passed away from among the devas to be born here in the human realm."
In order to transcend the habitual tendencies within the heavens, that person should seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

That spiritual friend instructs the person to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) without expecting a future reward, explaining that seeking a reward is a fault; rather, they clearly teach that by practicing the pure holy life without any dependence or attachment, one attains immeasurable merit.

He teaches the practice of giving without expecting a reward in return, explaining that seeking a reward is a fault; rather, he clearly proclaims that by practicing giving without any dependence or attachment, one attains immeasurable merit.

He teaches the practice of observing the precepts without expecting a future reward, explaining that seeking such retribution is a fault; he does so only to clearly demonstrate that the merit of upholding the prohibitive precepts without any dependence or attachment is immeasurable.

That spiritual friend may explain skillful means to them; by means of these skillful means, this person is able to practice the six pāramitās. Having practiced the six pāramitās, they gradually bring the six pāramitās to fulfillment, swiftly realize all-knowledge, and never regress.
“O non-Buddhists!
Those who, having passed away from hell, obtain a human body, should rely upon a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Having relied upon such a friend, they should listen to the impartial Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.”

Having heard the Dharma of equality, one should arouse diligent vigor and dwell together with the great assembly in cities and villages. Within the fourfold community, they should engage one another in discussing, weighing, and debating the Buddhist teachings and inquiries. Thus, the equality of the dharmas of the three times will manifest before them; understanding that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature, and by cultivating this understanding, their afflictions will gradually be eliminated.
"O outsider!

One who passes away from among the animals and is reborn as a human being should rely upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and draw near to those who are learned; by drawing near to those who are learned, one shall sever ignorance."
Although this person seeks out those who possess great learning as well as various sūtras and śāstras, they form the conception that these do not exist.
Having observed that they do not exist, this person spontaneously realizes and attests to the dharmas that lack intrinsic nature.
Because this person realizes the equality of these dharmas of the three periods of time as they naturally manifest before them, they will swiftly realize all-knowledge and never regress.
O outsider!

Those who pass away from the realm of hungry ghosts and are reborn among humans should rely upon spiritual friends to practice generosity, eliminate their stinginess and greed, and perform various meritorious deeds; because they cultivate relinquishment, their minds do not accumulate possessions.

This person, through these dharmas of the three periods of time being equal and spontaneously manifest before them, forms the understanding of the single characteristic; that which is called the single characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics (*animitta*).
Because this person cultivates this understanding of the absence of characteristics, they swiftly realize all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and never regress.
"O outsider!
Those who pass away from the realm of the asuras and are reborn among humans should rely upon virtuous friends to battle the māra of afflictions.
What is the māra of afflictions?"
Regarding what is called pride:
at that time, that person should investigate—what is this pride?
Who is it that is proud?
Who experiences this conceit?
Who, by means of this conceit, gives rise to the afflictions and latent tendencies?
Who abandons this conceit?
When this person investigates in this manner, no pride can be found, nor does he see anyone who grasps at pride.

Because that person observes the meaning in this way, no pride can be found and no one who gives rise to pride exists; even the objective sphere associated with pride cannot be found, nor does he see anyone capable of abandoning pride.
Having observed in this way, not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Again, one performs this observation: by grasping at evil, one deceives oneself, and others do likewise.
When one contemplates in this way, one is able to see that all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because one sees that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, one sees that phenomena do not exist.
Because they do not exist, one knows them to be unestablished.
Because it is not established, one knows that it is unborn.
If it is unborn, one knows that it does not cease.
That which is neither born nor ceasing cannot be described.
If one understands that which is ineffable, then it is neither past, nor present, nor future; the three periods of time cannot be apprehended.
If a dharma cannot be apprehended within the three periods of time, one should know that there has never been anything gained or lost.
"O outsider!
You should know that this is the equality of all dharmas.

By means of this equality of all dharmas, you should know that all dharmas are suchness—unchanging and undifferentiated—and that the Tathāgata is likewise suchness—unchanging and undifferentiated. Since all dharmas are themselves suchness, it is through the contemplation of pride that this is known."

Such a person, having passed away from among humans, is reborn among humans; because they possess the power of the habitual tendencies of pride, even after passing away from that hell, they are reborn among humans, and through the habituation of pride, they are able to recognize these signs.
If there were no habitual tendencies of pride, one could not say that this person comes from such-and-such a place, even down to saying they come from the hells.

O outsider! This is called the wisdom that is free from pride; its characteristics can only be known by one who possesses skillful means, and furthermore, it is only through the empowerment of the Prajñāpāramitā that this person may come to know it.
At that time, when the eight thousand non-Buddhist practitioners heard this teaching of the Dharma, they attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, they rose from their seats and prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.
They withdrew to stand to one side.
Once those various non-Buddhists had withdrawn to stand to one side, they spoke in unison with a single voice, reciting these verses of praise:
"Established by the power of the Guide’s wisdom, He knows the destinations of all paths without depending on another."
He knows all sentient beings wandering through the various realms of existence, as clearly as seeing an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand.
Because the world is turbid with various views and inclinations, it is like the sky obscured by clouds and mist;
thus these masses of fools constantly transmigrate, like the blind who have lost their way.
The world is eternal, or it is non-eternal; again, they say it is both eternal and non-eternal, or that it is neither eternal nor non-eternal—like a blind elephant walking through a city.
They say the world is finite, or else infinite; they say it is both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite. Thus they wander about like birds in a cage.
Again, some say that the body itself is the self (ātman), while others say that the self exists apart from the body;
thus bound by the fetters of false conceptualization and discrimination, they suffer in their minds like birds caught in a net.
Some say they are created by Īśvara; others say they are not born from causes.
All sentient beings are shrouded by views and grasping, just as clouds and mist obscure the moon.

Just as a bird born from an egg within a cage constantly seeks to escape through its various openings, so too are sentient beings deluded by views and grasping; they fail to attain liberation, like that caged bird.
Again he prostrates to Brahmā and the Lords of the World, and prostrates to Kumāra and Vaiśravaṇa;
he also prostrates to the directional oceans and Vaiśravaṇa, like a thief caught in the act who seeks refuge with various deities.
Just as a poor man encounters a creditor and seeks to find a guarantor for the debt, so too do those in the world who cling to views;
out of folly, they seek rebirth in heaven, hoping for sensual pleasure.
The Buddha beholds sentient beings relying on the truth, as if seeing the five fingers of one's own palm;
they undergo a hundred sufferings within the various realms of existence, like a band of thieves entering a prison.

The World-Honored One gave rise to compassion for them; having cultivated the various paths of practice and known all realms of existence, the World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma for release from prison, like a king who, upon the birth of a son, grants a great amnesty.
Out of compassion for the world, throughout inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he practiced various austerities and attained *bodhi*;
seeing those foolish ones ruined by grasping at views, the Buddha causes them to attain liberation.
Because you, O Sugata, Lion among Men, have attained mastery over all phenomena,
we who were lost on the wrong path due to our clinging to views have been pulled out from that clinging by the Buddha.
Because the World-Honored One possesses great power, Is fully endowed with fearlessness and has no adversaries,
And roars amidst the assembly like a lion, We too wish to attain that Dharma.
Because he is able to move throughout the three realms, And because he universally illuminates with that Dharma,
And because he bestows predictions of enlightenment upon all sentient beings, May we also encounter him.
The World-Honored One, knowing that those non-Buddhists had attained deep faith, manifested a portentous radiance by smiling.
At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya asked the Buddha in verse:
“The Buddha, out of compassion for the world, manifests a smile; This is because he has beheld this assembly of non-Buddhists.”
I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain its cause: what is the meaning of this manifested smile?
One who well understands causes does not manifest a smile without reason, yet you have displayed these auspicious rays of light.
How excellent is this manifestation of smiling radiance; the entire great assembly gazes up at the Buddha.
The entire great assembly of the World-Honored One harbors doubt, having seen the Sugata manifest the light of a smile;
all gaze upon him as if beholding the full moon, looking to the Buddha and praying that he explain the cause of his smile.
Who today has prepared this supreme offering?
Who today has gladdened the Compassionate Father?
Who today has attained the virtues of the Buddha?
Excellent! O One of Great Wisdom, please expound this;

when the great assembly hears it, they will surely rejoice. Since all these followers of external paths have received their predictions, we pray that the Guide will explain for us all: by which vehicle did they attain the Way?
Excellent is the Muni who has removed the delusions of the mind; for those who were in doubt, he has severed the net of uncertainty.
Because of this, the great assembly has attained joy, and they proceed single-mindedly toward the Buddha without turning back.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Aśvajit in verse:
“Excellent, Aśvajit, you who skillfully know the right moment! You are able to question the Tathāgata, the Vanquisher of Enemies.
Out of compassion for the world, you have made this speech; You are able to question the Guide, the Self-Arisen One.”
I shall now explain the reason for my smile; listen with single-minded attention to the cause of what has been done.
You should listen with joy as I speak of the meaning and purpose of this smile.
All these non-Buddhists have been subdued; having abandoned all evil views, they abide in right view.
Beholding the afflictions of this world’s adherence to views, they all give rise to compassion and seek enlightenment.
All clinging to views is completely relinquished, for they have attained unclouded right view;
having heard from me this unhindered prophecy, they all joyfully seek omniscience.
Having received the prophecy from the Buddhas of the past, he made offerings to the Greatly Compassionate Honored One among bipeds;
he dwelt for twenty million eons in the presence of various Buddhas, seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
The giving practiced by the Buddha was not slight; he also purely maintained the precepts and cultivated meditative concentration.
He purified his cultivation of wisdom and exerted diligent effort, practicing patience toward all sentient beings.
He constantly cultivated the six *pāramitās*, and through the discernment of wisdom, he sought awakening.
Aśvajit questioned the Vanquisher of Enemies, who had resolved his mind to seek the awakening of a Buddha.
Those who were afflicted by suffering due to evil factions and who relied upon base views and grasping have now beheld the Supreme Guide; they have abandoned all evil views without exception.
Having attained true understanding of the Tathāgata’s teaching, they follow the Buddha-dharma and give rise to deep faith;
in the future, they shall all make offerings to many billions of Buddhas as they seek awakening.
In the future Star宿 Kalpa, they shall all attain Buddhahood with one and the same name, known as Universal Renown of Exalted Fame; these ones of great wisdom shall deliver the world.
That Buddha-land is exceedingly pure, its manifold adornments peerless;
it is free from beings with evil views and is a place where the noble ones solely seek enlightenment.
The sentient beings of that land are free from the evil realms, and at that time there are no difficulties whatsoever;
those Buddhas attain a lifespan, all of which is exactly eighty thousand years.
Sentient beings who hear the name of that Buddha shall all never regress from supreme enlightenment;
if there are women who hear the Buddha’s name, they shall all obtain male bodies.
Thus the World-Honored One, the Vanquisher of Enmity, bestowed this prophecy upon the various non-Buddhists;
when all devas and humans heard that prophecy, there was none who did not rejoice and give rise to reverent faith.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Seventy-Two and Volume Seventy-Three,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi Dynasty.

Chapter 25: The Differentiation of the Elements (Dhātu-vibhaṅga-parivarta) Section 13 of the Sixteenth Assembly: The Bodhisattvas Beholding Reality The Differentiation of the Six Elements (Ṣaḍ-dhātu-vibhaṅga-parivarta)

25.1 At that time, King Śuddhodana and his retinue saw the asuras, garuḍas, nāgas and nāga maidens, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the Hāragajas devas, the Cāturmahārājika devas, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, the Brahmāpurohita devas, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, and even up to the Bṛhatphala devas. They witnessed their offerings and heard the bestowal of predictions. Furthermore, they heard the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens reciting verses in praise of the Buddha, and they also heard that the non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) had likewise received predictions.
King Śuddhodana then reflected: "This matter is rare and inconceivable."
“The World-Honored One has thus well expounded this; having heard it, all in the world are filled with joy.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, out of his deep affection for his son, was moved by the most earnest and sincere sentiments.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the King, his father, saying:

"The Dharma I teach is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. Its meaning is profound, its flavor is excellent, and it is pure and unadulterated. It is a clear exposition of the holy life (brahmacarya), stainless and untainted."
What is the holy life?
It is the Dharma-gate of the analysis of the six elements.
Your Majesty, listen now attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you.
The king said: "Excellent!
I shall now listen attentively; I only pray that you will speak."
The Buddha said,
“Great King! What is the Dharma-gate of the analysis of the six elements?”
"Great King!
That which is called the six elements is the person; the six bases of contact are also the person; and the eighteen spheres of mental consciousness are also the person."
"Great King!
For what reason do I say that the six elements are themselves the person?
Great King!"
What are the six elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
Great King!
These are called the six elements.
That which is referred to as the "six elements" being the person (*puruṣa*) is precisely this.
I say that the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*) are what constitutes the person.
For what reason is it said thus?
Great King! What is that which is called the sense-base of contact (spraṣṭavyāyatana)?
This means that because the eye-contact base sees various forms,
and likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body, and because the mind-contact base cognizes phenomena, when I say that the six contact bases constitute the person (*puruṣa*), it refers to this.
When I say that the eighteen spheres of mental consciousness are the "person" (puruṣa), for what reason do you speak thus?
Great King!
What are these eighteen spheres of mental consciousness?
That is to say, when the eye sees a pleasing form, one gives rise to volitional thoughts through recollection and conceptualization;
likewise, after seeing an unpleasing form, one also gives rise to volitional thoughts through recollection and conceptualization.
Having seen forms that are objects of equanimity, one also gives rise to volitions and perceptions through recollection and conceptualization.

It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind cognizes mental phenomena (*dharma*), having cognized those phenomena that are agreeable, one gives rise to recollection and conceptualization; having cognized those phenomena that are disagreeable, one also gives rise to recollection and conceptualization; and having cognized those phenomena that are objects of equanimity, one also gives rise to recollection and conceptualization.
"Great King!
When I speak of the eighteen consciousnesses and their objects as being the 'person' (puruṣa), it is this that I mean. Great King!"
The earth element is of two kinds:
there is the internal and there is the external, Great King!
What is the internal earth element?
It refers to whatever exists within one's own body.

Whatever exists within that body which is acquired, possessed, solid, or firm—namely: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, dirt, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, spleen, kidneys, liver, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, feces, bladder, membranes, brain, and skull.
"Great King!
These are called the internal earth element of the body.
Great King!"
What is the external earth element of the body?
It refers to whatever exists externally to the body that is not grasped, not appropriated, and is hard and solid.
Great King!
This is called the external earth element of the body.
Great King!
The internal earth element of the body, when it arises, comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
"Great King!
There are times when a woman discriminates for herself, 'I am a woman.
Having discriminated thus for herself that she is a woman, she then perceives an external man and further gives rise to discrimination, thinking, 'He is a man.'"
Once this woman has discriminated that he is a man, she immediately gives rise to thoughts of desire.
Having given rise to thoughts of desire, she delights in union and conceives passionate attachment toward that man.
That man also makes this discrimination, thinking, "I am a man.
Having discriminated for himself that he is a man, he sees an external woman and further gives rise to discrimination, thinking, "She is a woman."
After this man has made such a conceptualization, he gives rise to lustful attachment toward that woman.
Once both the man and the woman have given rise to lustful attachment, they unite; because of their union, the *kalala* comes into being.
"Great King!
That man and the object of his conceptualization—both are unobtainable.
A woman and the nature of a woman are likewise unobtainable; a man and the nature of a man are likewise unobtainable."
Because they do not arise in a continuous succession, such conceptualization is produced; yet that conceptualization is also unfindable in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Just as conceptualization is unfindable in its intrinsic nature, so too are conjunction and the nature of conjunction unfindable.
Just as a combination and the nature of combination cannot be apprehended, so too the *kalala* and the nature of the *kalala* cannot be apprehended.
If its intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended, how could it produce something solid?
"Great King!
You should know that it is due to conceptual discrimination that there arises what is solid and what is strong.
When that solidity and strength arise, they come from nowhere."
"Great King,
there comes a time when this body ends and becomes a corpse in a cemetery.
When that corpse’s perception of solidity undergoes transformation and decay, it does not go toward the east, nor toward the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below."
"Great King!
In this way, you should understand it as the internal earth element of the body. Great King!"
At times, when the dwellings of the world are entirely empty, there arises a palace of the seven treasures in the Brahma Heaven.
When that palace manifests with its solid and firm characteristics, it comes from nowhere.
In this way, when the seven-jeweled palaces of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations arise with their solid forms, they come from nowhere.

Likewise, when all the seven-jeweled palaces of the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and the Heaven of the Four Great Kings arise with their solid forms, they come from nowhere.
The Cakravāḍa Mountains and the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains are firm, solid, and of one substance with diamond; when these strong formations arise, they come from nowhere.

Likewise, when Sumeru, Nimindhara, Vinataka, Aśvakarṇa, Īṣādhara, Khadiraka, Viniataka, Aśvakapāla, Cakravāḍa, Mahācakravāḍa, Sudarśana, Mahāsudarśana, Yugandhara, Himavat, Gandhamādana, and all other Black Mountains, as well as the trichiliocosm, are formed and all these strong formations arise, they come from nowhere.
This great earth, one million six hundred thousand yojanas in thickness, arose and remains thus.
Great King!
When that solidity arose, it came from nowhere.
Great King!
Furthermore, at times this world undergoes destruction.
When this world is about to be destroyed, this great earth is either consumed by fire, swept away by water, or blown apart by wind, until it is entirely dispersed and extinguished.
When that earth is consumed by fire, not even so much as smoke or ash remains to be seen.
Great King!
It is just as when ghee or oil is burned by fire, leaving nothing behind.
"Great King!
When this trichiliocosm has been thus consumed by fire, not even its ashes will remain visible.
Later, when it is swept away by water, there will likewise be nothing left that can be seen."
Great King!
It is like throwing salt into water, which dissolves until nothing remains.
Great King!
In this way, in this manner, the trichiliocosm, having been submerged by water, would leave nothing behind.
Great King!
In this way, when the trichiliocosm is destroyed by wind, there remains nothing at all.
"Great King!
It is like the fierce Vairambha wind blowing against flying birds; those birds are scattered and destroyed, leaving nothing behind.
Great King!"
In this way, in this manner, this trichiliocosm is blown apart by the fierce Vairambha winds; everything is dispersed and extinguished, leaving nothing behind.
"Great King!
When that earth element is formed, it comes from nowhere; when it is destroyed, it goes nowhere.
Great King!"
In this way, and in this way, when the earth element arises within the internal body, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere.
Great King!
That earth element is empty when arising and empty when abiding; during both the times of arising and abiding, its essential nature is entirely empty.
“Great King! That water element also has two kinds:
there is the internal and there is the external.

"Great King! This is the internal water element within one's own body. It refers to whatever exists internally within one's own body, as well as whatever is obtained and contained within the bodies of others—whether it be water, the nature of water, or the substance of water; whether it be moisture, the nature of moisture, or the substance of moisture. That is to say: the tears, sweat, nasal mucus, saliva, pus and blood, pus from sores, fat, marrow, milk, bile, and urine within this body."
"Great King!
Such things as these are called the internal water element.
Great King!"
What is the external water element?
It refers to that which is not obtained or grasped by the body: water and its watery nature, the substance of water; moisture and its moistening nature, the substance of moisture.
"Great King!
This is called the external water element.
Great King!"
When that internal water element arises within his body, it comes from nowhere;

when it ceases, it goes nowhere. Great King! It is like seeing a beloved person and tears flowing from one’s eyes; being oppressed by suffering and distress, one likewise sheds tears; hearing the Dharma with reverent faith, one likewise sheds tears; encountering wind and cold, one likewise sheds tears; and when the eyes are red and painful, one likewise sheds tears.
"Great King!
When those tears emerge, they come from nowhere; when they cease, they go nowhere.
Great King!"

Furthermore, at times the water element within the body increases; having increased, it benefits that water element and is able to extinguish the fire element within the body. When that fire element is extinguished, it departs without going anywhere.
"Great King!
Those internal and external elements of the body, at the time of their arising, come from nowhere; at the time of their ceasing, they go nowhere.
Great King!"
That internal water element is empty when it arises and empty when it ceases; its nature as a water element is itself empty.
Great King, there are times when that internal fire element becomes intense, and having become intense, it is able to dry up the internal water element of the body.
When that water element is consumed by fire and dried up, it goes nowhere. Great King!
When that internal water element arises within the body, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it likewise goes nowhere.
Great King!
That internal water element is empty when it arises and empty when it ceases; its essential nature is itself empty.
Great King!
Furthermore, at times this world undergoes destruction.
Great King!
When this world is about to be destroyed, thirty-two layers of clouds arise in the sky and remain there.
Having arisen as thirty-two layers of clouds and remained thus, they completely covered the trichiliocosm.
Once the trichiliocosm was entirely covered, for five intermediate kalpas, the heavens sent down a great rain that flowed in an unceasing stream like the urine of an elephant king.
Thereafter, during another five intermediate kalpas, a coarse great rain fell. At that time, the accumulated water rose up as high as the Brahma-heaven.
Great King! When that great realm of water first arose, it came from nowhere.
"Great King!
Furthermore, at the time when the abodes of this world are being destroyed, a second sun appears in this world.
When the second sun appears, all the small rivers and springs completely dry up."
"Great King!
Furthermore, at another time, a third sun appears in this world.
When the third sun appears, the great ponds, rivers, and streams all completely dry up."
"Great King!
Furthermore, at another time, a fourth sun shall arise in this world.
When the fourth sun arises, even the sources of the four great rivers will completely dry up and vanish."
"Great King!
At another time, a fifth sun shall arise in the world.
Once the fifth sun has arisen, the waters of the great ocean—whether one yojana, two yojanas, three yojanas, four, five, or even ten yojanas deep—all shall utterly dry up and vanish."
The seawater dries up over an area of twenty-three, twenty-four, twenty-five, and fifty yojanas;
it dries up over one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred, and even up to one thousand yojanas;
and it likewise dries up entirely over two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, and even up to ten thousand yojanas.
The waters of the great ocean, measuring twenty thousand, thirty thousand, and even up to forty-four thousand yojanas, are all completely dried up.
Great King! Furthermore, at that time, there remains a residue of water in the great ocean, with forty thousand yojanas of residual water still remaining.

When thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand yojanas of water remain, it subsequently gradually diminishes further until nine thousand, eight thousand, down to one thousand yojanas; then nine hundred, eight hundred, down to one hundred yojanas of water remain.

Ninety yojanas, eighty-seven, eighty-six, eighty-five, eighty-four, eighty-three, seventy, sixty, and even down to ten yojanas; ninety yojanas, eighty yojanas, and even down to one yojana—only this much water remains.

Descending five *li*, there were ten *tāla* trees; then nine *tāla* down to one *tāla*; ten people down to one person. The remaining water stood at the height of a person's throat, then reached the armpits, the navel, the waist, the hips, the knees, and the ankles; the remaining water persisted until there was only as much as a cow’s footprint.
"Great King!
At that time, there will be only a slight sign of moisture within the great ocean, like when coarse rain falls and the ground is alternately wet and dry.
Great King!"
For example, O Great King, it is like coarse rain where each drop is distinct and the moisture has not yet spread everywhere;
the waters of the great ocean are likewise.
O Great King!
Furthermore, at that time, among all the moist places within the great ocean, only the surface of a single finger remains damp. Great King!
When that water element gradually ceases, it goes nowhere; it does not depart for the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below.
"Great King!
That water element is empty when it arises, empty when it abides, and empty when it ceases.
It is thus, Great King!"
The nature of that water element is unattainable; there is only its mere function, and yet that mere function is neither male nor female.
"Great King! The fire element is likewise of two kinds:
First, the internal; second, the external.
Great King!
What is the internal fire element?
Great King!

Whatever exists within one's own body and whatever is taken from within another's body—namely fire, the essence of fire, the characteristics of fire, the essence of heat, the characteristics of heat—that which is able to digest food and drink, and all the warmth and internal heat within the body that belongs to the category of heat.
"Great King!
This is called the fire element within the body.
Great King!"
What is the external fire element?
It refers to all that is external to the body which is neither grasped nor appropriated—namely, fire, the substance of fire, the characteristics of fire, and warmth or heat.
"Great King!
This is called the external fire element.
Great King!"

Furthermore, at times within the kalala stage of the womb, the fire element within the body increases while the water element gradually diminishes; for this reason, the kalala becomes increasingly thick and increasingly solid.
"Great King!
It is like when molasses is boiled in an iron vessel; by the power of the fire, it gradually becomes thick and solid.
Great King, in just this way, by the power of the fire, the *kalala* gradually becomes thick and gradually becomes firm."
Because the *kalala* gradually becomes thick and solid, it is called the *arbuda*.
Because the *arbuda* is formed through the power of heat, it is called the *peśī*.
Because the *peśī* is formed through the power of heat, it is called "solid" (*kaṭhina*).
Because it is solidified by fire, it arises as five branches. In this way, Great King,
that water element is matured by the fire element.
In this way, in this manner, because that water element gradually becomes thick and solid, it forms a mass of flesh.
Great King!
When that fire element arises, it comes from nowhere, yet it is able to burn and destroy that water element.
"Great King!
Furthermore, there will come a time when a patient’s internal fire element (tejo-dhātu) is completely extinguished.
Once the internal fire element within that patient’s body has been extinguished, the food they have consumed can no longer be digested."
Because that patient was unable to digest it, he could not eat any more thereafter.
Due to his inability to eat, the fire element within his body was completely extinguished.
Because that person is unable to take food and the internal fire is extinguished, they will inevitably meet their end.
Great King!
When the fire element is extinguished, it does not go to the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below.
"Great King!
When that fire element arises, it is empty; when it ceases, it is also empty. Moreover, from its very origin, the essential nature of that fire element is itself empty.
Great King!"
At times the world is destroyed.
When the world is being destroyed, the external fire element increases and blazes intensely; having blazed intensely, it completely burns the trichiliocosm.
"Great King!
When that external fire element arises within the body, it comes from nowhere.
Great King!"
Furthermore, at that time, after that great mass of fire has completely burned the trichiliocosm, it returns to being extinguished.
Great King!
When that fire is extinguished, it does not go to the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above or below.
"Great King!

That external fire element is empty when it arises and empty when it ceases. The essential nature of that great fire element is itself empty; it does not exist and cannot be apprehended. It is merely a functional activity (*vyavahāra*), yet that mere activity is neither male nor female."
"Great King! The wind element is also of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external."
Great King!
What is the internal wind element?

It refers to all that constitutes the wind element within one's own body and within the bodies of others—whatever is experienced or grasped as wind, the substance of wind, the designation "wind," swiftness, the substance of swiftness, and the designation "swiftness."

That which is called the wind residing in the four limbs of the body is wind; that which resides in the stomach is wind; that which moves through the five limbs is wind; that which moves through all the minor branches is also entirely wind; that which pervades the major and minor branches is also wind; and the inhalation and exhalation of breath is also wind.
To speak briefly, all movements throughout the body are entirely wind.
Great King! This is called the internal wind element within the body.
"Great King!
Furthermore, at times the wind element within the body becomes excessive and accumulates.
When it becomes excessive and accumulates, it can dry up the water element and also diminish the fire element."

At that time, once the water element has become parched and the fire element has diminished, it causes the human body to lose its moisture and warmth; the abdomen becomes distended, the four limbs become stiff and rigid, the vessels swell profusely, and the tendons and joints become cramped and tense.
At that time, that person experiences great suffering and affliction, or perhaps their life comes to an end. Great King!
When that internal wind element arises within the body, it comes from nowhere.
"Great King!

Furthermore, at another time, that patient encountered a skilled physician. Having examined the patient, the physician prescribed medicine appropriate to the condition; because he administered the medicine according to the illness, the wind disorder was cured."
"Great King!
When that wind element ceases, it likewise has no place to go.
Great King!"
When that internal wind element arises, it is empty; when it ceases, it is also empty. The intrinsic nature of the internal wind element is itself empty.
Great King! What is the external wind element?
Whatever exists outside the body, which the body does not grasp or receive—namely, wind, the substance of wind, the name "wind," swiftness, the substance of swiftness, and the name "swiftness."
"Great King!
This is the external wind element.
Great King!"

Furthermore, at times that external wind element becomes intense; because it is so intense, the wind element gathers together. When it gathers, it causes leaves to fall, branches and twigs to break, trees to be uprooted, mountain peaks to crumble, and great mountains to collapse and be destroyed. It breaks them apart into sections, gradually dispersing and destroying them down to the level of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
And this trichiliocosm is blown by the wind and revolves in a circular motion.

Great King, it is just as when a potter turns his wheel with a staff; the trichiliocosm is turned by the wind in exactly the same way. It is like a small amount of barley flour that, when blown by the wind, is reduced to fine dust so subtle that it is difficult to see.
In this way, Great King!
When this trichiliocosm has been blown apart and pulverized by the wind until it becomes fine dust,
once it has become fine dust, it can no longer be seen.
"Great King!
It is, for example, like a great and violent wind-circle arising; if one were to scatter a handful of earth against that wind, even its finest particles would become invisible.
In this same way, Great King!"
This trichiliocosm, blown by the wind, would be analyzed and reduced to powder; once analyzed and reduced to powder, not even a single remaining minute particle would be visible.
"Great King!
When that external wind element arises, it comes from nowhere.
Great King!"
Furthermore, at the beginning of summer, that external wind element entirely subsides and ceases.
Because it has subsided and ceased, there is no wind and the heat is intense; consequently, there is no dew upon the grasses and trees.
Because there is no dew, all grasses and trees lack any moisture.
"Great King!
When that external wind element ceases, it likewise has no place to which it goes.
Great King!"
When that wind element arises, it is empty; when it ceases, it is also empty. The intrinsic nature of that wind element is itself empty.
Great King!

Both that internal wind element and the external wind element are both empty; their intrinsic natures are themselves detached, their characteristics are themselves detached, their essence cannot be apprehended, and even the characteristic of cessation is detached.
Why is this? That wind element is unconditioned, for there is no agent. "Great King!
What is the space element?
The space element is also of two kinds:
internal and external.
Great King!
What is the internal space element?
It is that which is received and grasped within one’s own body or within the bodies of others—namely, space, the essence of space, and the designation "space."

"O Great King, whatever internal cavities and apertures are produced within this body— those which are included among the aggregates (*skandha*), those included among the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and those included among the elements (*dhātu*)—
this is called the internal space element (*ākāśadhātu*)."
"Great King!
What is the external space element?
Whatever exists externally that is non-material, down to even a space as small as a hair's breadth where there is no form—this is called space."
"Great King!
This is called the external space element.
Great King!"

Furthermore, at times, due to the causal conditions of karma, the various sense bases (*āyatana*) arise; once those sense bases have arisen, they surround the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), and at that time, it is designated as being included within the category of the internal space element.
"Great King!
When one thus investigates each and every phenomenon, not even a single eye-base can be found; there is only mere functioning.
Great King!"
Why is it empty? Because the earth element is pure.
Just as the earth element is empty because it is pure, so too are the water, fire, and wind elements empty because they are pure; they come from nowhere.
Great King!
Furthermore, at times all forms are entirely destroyed and transformed into empty space. Why is this?
"Because the realm of space is inexhaustible, Great King!
Only the internal realm of space remains abiding and unmoving."
"Great King!
Just as the unconditioned realm of nirvāṇa abides immovably, you should know that the realm of space likewise pervades all places.
Great King!"
Suppose, for example, there were a person who, in a desolate wilderness or vast marshland, dug a spring, a pond, a reservoir,
or a well. Great King, what do you think?
“From where do all those spaces come?
The King said,
“World-Honored One!”
"It has come from nowhere.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
If that person were to fill it back up with earth again,
Great King, what do you think?
"Where does that realm of space go?
The King replied, "It goes nowhere."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
That realm of empty space neither comes nor goes.
"Why is this? Because that realm of space is neither male nor female.
The Buddha said:
“Great King! The external realm of space is likewise immovable, its nature being without change.
The realm of space is empty; it is not a functional entity.”
Why is this? Because the realm of empty space is neither male nor female. "Great King!
What is the element of consciousness?

Just as the eye serves as the primary faculty that apprehends form, visual consciousness arises because it cognizes form; it can cognize blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated colors, and it also cognizes long, short, coarse, and fine.
All such things as visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth that can be perceived by visual consciousness are called the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).

Likewise, whether it be the cognition of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects (*dharma*), or the cognition of what is known through the objects of the six sense faculties, this is called the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
"Great King!
Furthermore, this consciousness-element does not rely upon the sense-faculties, nor does it rely upon the elements. Why is this?"
"Great King!
It is not the purity of the earth element that constitutes the eye-base; nor is it the purity of the water, fire, or wind elements that constitutes the eye-base. Why is this so?"
It is not the purity of the earth element, nor any other phenomena, that constitutes the eye-base or one who possesses the eye-base.
Likewise, it is not the purity of the water, fire, or wind elements, nor any other phenomena, that constitutes the eye-base or one who possesses the eye-base.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are without cognition, without discernment, and without capacity; they are neither beginning, middle, nor end; and they are neither internal, nor external, nor in between.
"Great King!
Thus, once this element of consciousness has cognized a preceding object, it immediately passes away and ceases, never to arise again.
When that consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere."
Great King!
What is called the eye-base?
It refers to the translucent matter derived from the four great elements.
If the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself empty,
what is clear and what is turbid?
Since there is neither purity nor defilement among all phenomena, how can one perceive purity or defilement therein?
Thus it is, Great King!
Therefore, you should know that the essential nature of the sense-base of the eye is ultimately empty and quiescent; neither its prior limit nor its subsequent limit can be apprehended. Why is this?
Because the future has not yet arrived, it cannot be apprehended; because the past has already ceased, it cannot be apprehended; and future future phenomena cannot be apprehended.
That eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) likewise cannot be apprehended, for it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If the essential nature cannot be apprehended, then neither male nor female can be apprehended.
Since there is no male or female, how could there be a self or what belongs to a self?
Great King!
If there is "self" and "what belongs to self," that is the realm of Māra; if there is no "self" and "what belongs to self," that is called the realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are free from "self" and "what belongs to self."
Great King!
One should know, as it truly is, that the eye-base is empty; the intrinsic nature of the eye-base is empty. Why is this?
This characteristic of the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) is unattainable; therefore, the essential nature of this eye-base is empty and quiescent.
This emptiness, which is free from the characteristic of the eye-base, is called signlessness (animitta). Because there is no seeking within signs, it is called wishlessness (apraṇihita).
"Great King!
This is called the manifestation of the three gates of liberation within emptiness regarding the eye-base. Great King!"
"What is the ear-entrance element (*śrotra-āyatana*) up to the body-entrance element (*kāya-āyatana*)?
Great King!

All these dharmas manifest before the three gates of liberation; they are definitively directed toward the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), ultimately pervading all of space. They cannot be named, cannot be described, cannot be employed, and cannot be demonstrated. They are without dispute, without speech, and immeasurable."
"Great King!

Such objects are the domain of the mind and are traversed by the mind; therefore, they are called "objects of the mind.
Great King!
When that mind encounters agreeable forms, it gives rise to desire; when it encounters disagreeable forms, it gives rise to anger; and when it encounters neutral forms, it gives rise to ignorance.

In the same way, regarding the objects of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*), one likewise engages in three activities that give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion: when the mind conditions agreeable mental phenomena, greed arises; when the mind conditions disagreeable mental phenomena, hatred arises; and when the mind conditions neutral mental phenomena, ignorance arises, giving rise to folly.
"Great King!

Great King!"
