Chapter Sixteen of the Sixteenth Assembly: The Bodhisattva’s Realization of Reality—The Chapter on the Four Universal Monarchs.
Part Two of Twenty-Six: “Great King!
In the past there was a king named Bhūmideva, who ruled according to the Dharma and was thus called a Dharma King.

He was possessed of the seven treasures, namely: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure; these are known as the seven treasures.”
"Great King!
The father of that Earth-Ruling Heavenly King was named Earth-Born (Dharaṇīja).
When that King Earth-Born was approaching the end of his life, this Earth-Ruling Heavenly King was his eldest son."

When his life there comes to an end, he shall be consecrated upon the crown of the head by the ministers and high officials as the Great King of the Earth; he thus becomes a consecrated Kṣatriya Great King.

At that time, having been consecrated as a Kṣatriya king by the King of the Earth Devas, on the fifteenth day of the month when the moon was full and perfect—the day for observing the fast—he bathed and washed his head, trimmed his beard, hair, and nails, and donned fresh, clean garments. Adorning his body with various flower garlands, diverse necklaces, celestial crowns, armlets, bracelets, and conch-shell earrings, he sat upon a high terrace surrounded by court ladies.

Then, in the eastern direction, there appeared the precious golden wheel, with its thousand spokes complete and lacking nothing, together with its hub and rim; it was brilliantly radiant, seven cubits in length and breadth, and made entirely of pure gold.
"Great King!
At that time, having witnessed these events, King Mahārāja Pṛthivīdeva had this thought:

'In the past, I heard ancient people say that when a Kṣatriya consecrated king, on the fifteenth day of the month when the moon is full, on the day he observes the fast, bathes his head, shaves his beard and hair and trims his nails, puts on unstained garments, and adorns his body with various flower garlands, diverse necklaces, celestial crowns, armlets, bracelets, rings, and conch-shell ornaments, while standing upon a high tower surrounded by court ladies—'"

If, from the eastern direction, there should appear a precious golden wheel, complete with hub and rim and possessing no fewer than a thousand spokes, coming to attend him, it should be known that this king will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
Again, he had this thought:
"How could I possibly be a wheel-turning monarch?
I shall put this to the test now."

"Great King! At that time, the Heavenly King Earth immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the wheel, and addressed the celestial wheel, saying:
'O precious wheel, descend to the earth and remain there.'"
Having spoken these words, the divine jewel-wheel descended from the sky to the ground and came to rest before the king.

At that time, the Heavenly King of the Earth immediately smeared his hands with exquisite incense and wiped the precious wheel with a most excellent and fine cloth; he then took the jewel-wheel with his right hand and placed it within his left hand.
Again, he rubbed and wiped the wheel with his right hand and spoke these words:
"You should now subdue the eastern direction.
Having spoken thus, the precious golden wheel then soared into the void, circling to the left and right, and proceeded toward the east, reaching the former royal path of a wheel-turning monarch.
The road was level and straight, strewn with various flowers that were most delightful.
Wherever the wheel passed, the ground was entirely level and even, without any elevations or depressions.
By the power of the king’s merit, places where rivers, ponds, wells, and springs had run dry were all filled to the brim with water possessing the eight qualities.
All trees, forests, flowers, and fruits that had withered all flourished and bloomed; those already in bloom became even more lush and verdant.
Great King!
At that time, the Cakravartin King Bhūmideva, together with his fourfold army, followed the wheel as it moved along.
When the wheel-treasure comes to a halt, the king likewise halts there.

In whatever territory the king arrives, the various kings—both great and small—together with their ministers and subjects, each take a golden platter filled with silver grain or a silver platter filled with golden grain to welcome the Great King, each saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
"Welcome, Great King!
These lands are peaceful, prosperous, and abundant, with a flourishing population.
We pray that Your Majesty will accept these territories to govern and transform the people; we shall all serve you as your attendants. We only wish for you to take up residence here."
At that time, the Cakravartin King Bhūmideva addressed those kings, ministers, and citizens, saying these words:
"I have no need for the kingdom or its treasures; you may enjoy them yourselves."

If you now wish to follow me, you should abstain from taking life; likewise, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, do not speak divisively, do not speak harshly, do not engage in frivolous speech, do not harbor covetousness, do not harbor ill will, and do not hold wrong views.

"You all should abide yourselves in the ten wholesome actions and also teach others to abide in the ten wholesome actions. Then I shall know that you have taken refuge in me and accepted my instructions; I regard you all as my own children."

You should always make offerings to your parents, teachers, elders, and all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; do not commit unlawful, unwholesome, or evil deeds, and also exhort others to practice the wholesome Dharma.
"If you can do this, I know that all the people in all your lands will surely submit to and follow me.
He further declared:

"You should always filially support your parents and respectfully serve your teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; do not commit unlawful, unwholesome, or evil deeds, and likewise exhort others to practice the wholesome Dharma."
"If you can do thus, I know that all the people in every land shall surely submit to and become my subjects.
At that time, the Holy King and his fourfold army gradually crossed the great ocean and conquered Pūrvavideha; once they had passed beyond the entire human realm, the wheel-treasure came to a halt.
In this manner, he proceeded until he had completely subdued the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as Uttarakuru.

Having crossed the northern sea and traversed the entire human realm, the king and the wheel-treasure returned to the gate of his palace in Jambudvīpa, where they remained suspended motionless in mid-air.
At that time, after the Cakravartin King Bhūmideva had thus subdued the four continents, he returned to Jambudvīpa and took up residence there.
When King Bhūmideva and the wheel-treasure returned to this Jambudvīpa, those four continents were transformed into the seven treasures, becoming magnificent and exceptionally beautiful.
What are the seven treasures?
They are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musāragalva, red pearls, and agate.

At that time, after the wheel-treasure has circled throughout the four continents, all hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and the eight difficulties are extinguished; all evil sounds of unwholesome deeds throughout the four continents are entirely eliminated—how much more so for those who actually commit various evil karmas.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the original vows of the Holy King, the Deva of the Earth.
Furthermore, as the wheel-treasure revolves, throughout the four continents, without the need for planting, natural non-glutinous rice grows everywhere, pure and free from husks and chaff.
Furthermore, as the wheel-treasure revolves, celestial trees and precious garments spontaneously appear throughout the four continents.
Moreover, as the wheel-treasure revolves, all illnesses within the four continents are completely healed and cured, with the sole exception of three types of afflictions.
What are these three?
First, the pursuit of desire; second, edible food; and third, senescence.
Furthermore, when the wheel-treasure revolves, all the people within the four continents have a lifespan of ten million years.
Furthermore, as the precious wheel turns in every direction, all the sufferings and afflictions of the people throughout the four continents naturally vanish.
In this manner, immeasurable, boundless, rare, and inconceivable events such as these appear in the world.
At that time, King Mahārāja Bhūmideva again, after a long period, thought to himself:
"While I now enjoy these various pleasures here, is there perhaps another place where the requisites for the five desires are more excellent than this?"
He further reflected to himself:
"In the past, I have heard that on the summit of Mount Sumeru there are the Trāyastriṃśa gods; what are the objects of their five desires and their various provisions?"

At that time, King Mahārāja Bhūmideva had not yet eliminated his craving and desire; he loathed all the five sensual pleasures and the requisites for wealth found in the human realm, and instead took delight in the sublime and exquisite joys of that celestial world.
"I shall now go to that heavenly realm.
Having formed this thought, King Mahīndra and his fourfold army suddenly arrived at the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven in an instant.
At that time, Śakra, seeing King Bhūmideva from afar, spoke these words:
"Welcome, Great King! Well done, Great King!"
He immediately divided his seat in half and invited the king to sit;
the king then took his seat.
At that time, the Earth Deity had governed his station in that celestial realm for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years.
At that time, after a long period, King Mahārāja Bhūmideva again gave rise to a great covetous mind and thought to himself:
"I should now displace that Lord of Devas and become the sole King of Devas myself."
Having formed this thought, he immediately fell from half of Śakra’s seat, together with his fourfold army, and arrived at the city of An-yin (Anvaya) in Jambudvīpa.

At that time, King Bhūmideva had long enjoyed supreme and wondrous pleasures in the heavens, and his mind was so deeply attached to them that when he suddenly reached the human realm, he could not endure the necessities of human life. His body and mind sank into despondency; it was as if a portion of *sarpis* (clarified butter) were placed in hot sand—it melted away instantly, leaving no trace of its whereabouts known.
The Great King Bhūmideva’s body and mind likewise became submerged and overwhelmed; he was unable to endure the essence of food and drink possessed by human beings.
At that time, the Great King Bhūmideva, his body and mind exhausted and weary, spoke these verses:
“Though a great king with sovereign power, I cannot eliminate this thirst and craving.”
Like dry grass meeting fire, one should therefore abandon desire.
Constantly engaging in sexual indulgence never brings satisfaction;
it is like drinking salt water when thirsty—it can never quench the thirst.
Just as the myriad streams flow toward the sea and are never satisfied, so too it is with sensual desire; there is never a time when it is satiated.
Like fire consuming grass and wood, it knows no moment of weariness or contentment.
Desire is also like this: it is never satisfied.
Just as an echo in a deep valley follows a sound without ceasing, so too is the hearing of sounds; there is no time when it rests.
It is also like a casket filled with incense, which receives the fragrance without discrimination;
smelling the fragrance is likewise such that there is never any satiety.
It is like a ladle stirring fine food, which never knows when to stop.
The tongue craves delicious flavors and likewise knows no contentment;
just as a mirror reflects the image of a face and never tires of it,
so too does one who pursues sensual desires never reach satiety with those desires.
Just as space receives the wind and is never satiated,
the body constantly receives various tactile sensations and never reaches a time of satiety.
Like drinking water in a dream, it can never truly quench thirst.
Regarding all phenomena received by the mind, there is likewise no satiety.
For those who greedily crave sensual desires, their craving increases further;
observing all sensory objects, one never finds a time when craving is satisfied.
"Seeing that the increase of desire brings suffering and affliction, just as fire consumes wood,
one should extinguish all cravings, just as water extinguishes fire.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Great King! Do you know who that Great King Bhūmideva was at that time?
Great King, you should know that you must not view him as anyone else; the Great King Bhūmideva was none other than myself.”
"Great King, you should know that in the past, the Great King Bhūmideva was wealthy and possessed of great power; yet, because his greed and craving were insatiable, he eventually met his end.
For what reason?"
The sense faculties are never satiated, and no objects can ever satisfy them;
the sense faculties are like mirrors, and objects are like reflected light and shadows;
the sense faculties are like illusions, and objective realms are like dreams.
"Great King!
You should settle your mind in this Dharma, observe it deeply within yourself, and do not follow the teachings of others.
Great King!"
This Dharma is the unsurpassed enlightenment of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Great King!

You should distance yourself from all worldly power and nobility; you should dry up the ocean of craving, overturn the mountain of arrogance, and remain far removed from all calamities and misfortunes.

It is equal toward all phenomena; it is not the domain of any ordinary person, nor is it what can be practiced by Śrāvakas, nor is it the sphere of any Pratyekabuddha. Rather, it is the practice of all Bodhisattvas and that which is realized by the perfect awakening of all Buddhas.
"O King, you should settle your mind and not allow it to become distracted;

you should form this thought: 'How may I, in future ages, among all the worlds of devas and humans, become a lamp, a torch, a light, a ship, a guide, a teacher, a caravan leader, a chief, and one who is unsurpassed—crossing over myself and crossing others over, liberating myself and liberating others, bringing peace to myself and bringing peace to others, and attaining nirvana for myself and leading others to nirvana?'"

"O Great King! Do not look back upon the wealth, power, and sovereignty you experienced in the past. Great King, you should know that the sense faculties are like illusions; they can never be satiated, nor can they be fulfilled.
Sense objects are like dreams; they cannot bring fulfillment."
The Buddha said, "Great King!
In the past, there was a king named Mūrdhaja, who possessed great majesty, great supernormal power, and great authority; he was born from the crown of his father, King Upoṣadha."
Having long accumulated roots of goodness, he had previously beheld immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas and cultivated various roots of virtue.
Having reverently made offerings to those World-Honored Ones, he accumulated the foundations of goodness and attained noble power and sovereignty over the four continents.
"Great King!
Seven days after King Mūrdhaja had been consecrated and ascended the throne,
he came to possess the seven treasures in their entirety and became a Wheel-turning Monarch."
What are the seven?

First is the precious golden wheel, with its thousand spokes complete and lacking nothing, together with its hub and rim; it appears spontaneously, measuring seven cubits in length and breadth, and comes to attend him.
Second is the white elephant treasure, complete with six tusks, its seven limbs touching the ground, as white as the snow mountains, which arrives spontaneously.
Third is the horse treasure, of a deep blue hue, which comes forth in response.
These elephants and horses travel from dawn until mealtime, circling the four continents and the eight directions as far as the limits of the great ocean, before returning to their original place.
Fourth is the jewel-treasure, as large as a human thigh, made of pure blue lapis lazuli; its radiance shines throughout the eight directions for one yojana on each side.

Fifth is the Treasure of the Householder (*gṛhapati-ratna*): possessing abundant wealth and immeasurable riches, he can accomplish whatever the King thinks of, providing it spontaneously and as required.

Sixth is the Treasure of the Jade Woman (*strī-ratna*): her appearance is upright and exquisite, the foremost in beauty; she is neither tall nor short, neither too pale nor too dark. From every pore of her body issues the fragrance of *candana* sandalwood, and her breath is pure like a blue lotus. Her tongue is broad and long, capable of covering her face; its color is fine and thin like a sheet of red copper. Her body is supple as if boneless, warm in winter and cool in summer. Her mind is compassionate, and she always speaks gentle words. When she touches the King with her hand, she immediately knows the place where his mind is directed.

Seventh is the Treasure of the Military Commander, who appears spontaneously. He is preeminent in valor, strategy, and martial arts; he can anticipate the King’s thoughts for seven days in advance, possesses expert knowledge of the methods of warfare for the four types of troops, and is able to assemble those not yet gathered and disperse those already assembled.
He was endowed with a thousand sons who were brave, robust, handsome, and capable of subduing enemies.
Great King!

At that time, the Wheel-turning Sage King Mūrdhaja possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents, transforming the world according to the Dharma. He caused the four continents to be abundant, joyful, peaceful, and secure, and the population flourished; cities and villages were so close together that a rooster could fly from one to the next.

At that time, the entire great earth was free of sand, gravel, and thorns; it abounded in many precious gems and was fully endowed with immeasurable gardens, groves, springs, and ponds—exquisite, beautiful, and most delightful.
Why is this? It is entirely due to the power of the Dharma in which the noble King Mūrdhaja dwells securely.
At that time, whether among gods or humans, they experience the foremost of all sensual pleasures.
"Great King!
At that time, the city where King Mūrdhaja resided was named Ayodhyā; that city was twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas long from south to north."
That city was made of the seven treasures, with nets of various jewels covering it from above and bells of various jewels suspended therefrom.

Its interior and exterior were adorned in every manner, being entirely identical to the City of Immeasurable Renown Adorned with Jewels of King Anantayaśas, and no different at all; it was also like the Hall of Victory in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
"Great King! King Mahāsudarśana constructed three palaces:
the first was named Candrodaya Palace, which the king occupied during the heat of the summer."
The second palace is named Vaiḍūryagarbha, in which the king resides during the spring months;
the third palace is named Sūryatejo'bhyudgata, in which the king resides during the cold winter months.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja, surrounded by the Jewel of the Woman and his various court ladies, entered the Moon-Rising Palace.
At that moment, his body felt cool and refreshing, as if his limbs had been anointed with gośīrṣa sandalwood.

When the king, surrounded by his retinue in front and behind, enters that Vaiḍūrya palace, his body and mind become harmonious and well-adjusted, as if his body were anointed with the fragrance of *tamarā* leaves.
"Great King!

When that Great King Mūrdhagata entered the Hall of Solar Splendor, surrounded by his retinue and court ladies, his body was warm and pleasant, as if his body had been anointed with aloeswood incense; when he entered that hall, his body was likewise warm and pleasant."
"Great King!

This King Māndhātṛ possessed sovereign mastery over his desires; he caused all the palaces and other structures to produce pleasant tactile sensations according to the seasons, and winds and rains issued forth at will. Various kinds of music arrived as he wished, and all necessities for life also appeared according to his intent."
"Great King!
At that time, within his palace, rain fell as gold and silver for seven days.
When the seven days had passed, he thought to himself:"

"How truly marvelous, rare, and inconceivable! The fruit obtained from such pure karma manifests according to one's wishes, fulfilling my heart's desire; this is the unfailing result brought about by merit."
"Who, having witnessed such a karmic fruition, would ever become complacent regarding the cultivation of merit?
Great King! After the noble King Mūrdhaja had ruled over Jambudvīpa for a hundred thousand years, he thought to himself:
"Right now, this continent of Jambudvīpa is peaceful, prosperous, and joyful; its people are flourishing and all have come under my dominion;
within my palace, there has been a rain of jewels for seven days."
"I shall now go to Aparagoyānī.
Having formed this thought, King Mūrdhaja immediately ascended into the air with his fourfold army and proceeded from Jambudvīpa, arriving gradually at that Aparagoyānī.
Once the King had arrived there, he remained under the rule of that king for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years.
Great King, although the sovereign reward of King Mahāsammata surpassed that of humans, he had not yet attained the rewards of the devas. Great King!
The noble King Mūrdhagata caused a rain of jewels to fall at will upon Godānīya, filling his palace so that it was no different from that of Jambudvīpa.
Great King!
At that time, at a later period, King Mūrdhaja again had this thought:
"I rule over Jambudvīpa, which is prosperous, peaceful, and secure, with its population flourishing; furthermore, within my palace, treasures rain down according to my will."
This continent of Aparagoyānī is likewise peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with its population flourishing; moreover, within its palaces, treasures rain down at will.
I now also know that there is a great continent to the east named Pūrvavideha, and I shall go there now.
Having formed this thought, he immediately ascended into the air with his fourfold army and proceeded gradually from Godānīya toward Pūrvavideha.

Once the king arrived there, he established his royal domain in Pūrvavideha and enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses for immeasurable thousands of years; his conditioned rewards surpassed those of ordinary men, though they had not yet reached the level of celestial retribution.
"Great King!
The noble king Mūrdhagata caused rainfalls of jewels at will within his palace in Pūrvavideha, just as in Jambudvīpa; there was no difference between them.
Great King!
At that time, at a later period, King Mūrdhaja again had this thought:
"My Jambudvīpa is prosperous, peaceful, and secure, with its population flourishing; furthermore, within my palace, treasures rain down according to my will."
Goddhaniya is likewise peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with its population flourishing; there too, within the palace, treasures rain down at will.
This Pūrvavideha is entirely peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with its population flourishing; there too, within the palace, treasures rain down at will.
I now also know that there is a great continent to the north named Uttarakuru, where the people have no sense of "I" or "mine.
Even though this is so, I shall go there myself to test my retinue.
Having formed this thought, Great King Mūrdhagata ascended into the air together with his fourfold army and proceeded gradually from Pūrvavideha toward Uttarakuru in the north.
Once the King had arrived there, he instructed his retinue for immeasurable thousands of years in Uttarakuru.
After a long time, he thought to himself:

"My Jambudvīpa is prosperous, peaceful, and secure; it has rained down the seven treasures. Likewise, in Aparagoyānī, the people are flourishing and secure, and the rain of treasures has fallen. In Pūrvavideha, it is also exactly thus, with treasures raining down at will. This Uttarakuru is likewise entirely secure."
"I have heard that there are the Thirty-three Heavens dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru; I shall now go there to behold them with my own eyes.
Having formed this thought, King Mūrdhaja immediately ascended into the air together with his fourfold army and took his place atop the summit of Mount Sumeru.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, had assembled in the Sudharmā Hall to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.
Then, seeing King Mūrdhaja approaching from afar, Śakra went out to meet him and spoke these words:
"Welcome, Great King!"
"Welcome here. He then divided his seat in half and bade the king to sit;
the king immediately took his place.
When King Mūrdhagata sat upon half of the throne, ten superior qualities immediately eclipsed those of the devas.

What are these ten? First, his lifespan surpassed that of the devas; second, his physical appearance surpassed theirs; third, his renown surpassed theirs; fourth, his enjoyment of pleasure surpassed theirs; fifth, his sovereign dominion surpassed theirs; sixth, his physical form surpassed theirs; seventh, his voice surpassed theirs; eighth, his fragrance surpassed theirs; ninth, the flavor of his food surpassed theirs; and tenth, the quality of his tactile sensations surpassed theirs.
"Great King!

At that time, Māndhātṛ and Śakra were indistinguishable in their physical appearance, movements, and deportment; they were entirely without difference in their food, drink, clothing, or articles of livelihood, with the sole exception of their blinking."
Yet the various devas distinguish and recognize the difference between these two types: the celestial kings and the human kings.
The Buddha said, “Great King!
"How most marvelous and rare!
Although Śakra and Māndhātṛ are distinct—one celestial and one human—their physical forms and appearances are identical and without difference.
Great King, you should know that such is the power of merit."
"Who could ever be satisfied with merit? Great King!
At that time, Mūrdhaja dwelt in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, exercising supreme sovereignty for immeasurable thousands of years."
"Great King!

At that time, Mūrdhaja possessed sovereign wealth and power over the four continents, and he likewise possessed sovereign wealth and power in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Yet, even while ruling as a co-sovereign with Śakra, he was not satisfied; he further thought:
'I would rather be the sole Lord of Devas myself—what need have I for Śakra?'"
"It would be appropriate to retreat. Great King!
Having formed this thought, at that time King Mūrdhaja descended from the heavens and returned to Jambudvīpa, to the supreme garden within the city of Ayodhyā.
When the King descended, his majestic radiance shone throughout Jambudvīpa, eclipsing the light of the sun in all directions.
It was as if the moon had lost its brilliance when the sun rose, or as if the sunlight in the sky were no longer luminous.
The King’s radiance eclipsing [others] was likewise so.
Just as the emergence of the solar disk eclipses the lunar disk, so too did the majestic radiance of Mūrdhaja eclipse that solar disk.
"Great King!
At that time, the people of the city of Ayodhyā went out of the city to sightsee, and they saw that Mūrdhaja, together with his fourfold army, had descended from heaven and fallen into their park."
Having seen this, the man marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; he immediately entered the city and proclaimed to all the citizens:
"Now a son of heaven, together with his fourfold army, has descended from the sky and landed in the king’s most excellent garden."

"Great King! At that time, the king, his ministers, and the citizens within the city prepared various kinds of song, dance, and music; they brought scented ointments, powdered incense, precious banners, flags, and canopies, as well as flower garlands and necklaces. Having purified their bodies and clothing, they quickly departed the city and proceeded to that garden."
"Great King, at that time when Mūrdhaja fell from heaven, the entire earth shook in six ways.
At that very moment, all the human ornaments and the most excellent, wondrous perfumes used for anointing the body came together in the garden to where King Mūrdhaja was."

At that time, Māndhātṛ became so attached to the exquisite wealth of the heavens that he could no longer endure the fragrances of human possessions; he fell into a stupor and lay prostrate upon the ground.

It was like fresh butter or clarified butter cast into extremely hot sand, unable to remain there; at that time, King Mūrdhaja’s sinking into a stupor and his inability to remain conscious was just like this.
Then, the king, ministers, subjects, and the multitudes of people inside and outside the city, seeing King Mūrdhaja lying unconscious on the ground in that garden, immediately asked:
"Your Majesty, who is this?"
At that time, Mūrdhaja immediately addressed the king and the people, saying:
"Have you ever heard of the Great King Mūrdhaja?
Then the king and all the people replied together:

"I have previously heard from the elders that there was once a great king named Mūrdhaja, who, without relinquishing his human body, ascended to the heavens together with his retinue and the fourfold army."
At that time, Mūrdhaja addressed the people, saying:
"The one who was formerly Mūrdhaja is my very self.
I and my fourfold army have fallen from heaven."
At that time, the king and all the people within and without the city immediately addressed King Mūrdhaja in verse:
"I have heard from those of old Of a majestic and virtuous king Named Mūrdhaja, Who possesses supreme renown."
"Having ascended from here to the heavens with my own body and the fourfold army,
together with all my retinue, I shall rule as a Dharma King according to the Dharma.
Thus spoke the Supreme King of Humans and Gods.
"Harmed by the power of impermanence, I have fallen from celestial bliss to suffer; I am he who was born from the crown of the head.
All the people joined their palms and prostrated at the Great King’s feet, saying:
"What extraordinary event has occurred that shall be proclaimed for all time?"
To those who have descended from the heavens, King Duḥkha said:
"Listen to this rare occurrence; rejoice and do not be heedless."
The Great King Mūrdhaja ruled over the four continents;
his enjoyment of pleasure surpassed that of gods and humans, yet his desires remained insatiable until they brought about his death.
Within his inner palace, for seven days, precious jewels rained down.
Though he ruled the world according to the Dharma, he died with desires unsatiated.
Sharing half the throne with that Lord Śakra, he was disturbed by evil thoughts; because of his great desire, he fell away.
In the ocean of birth and death, one sinks due to a lack of wisdom;
those who delight in and cling to the five desires find no satiety even with celestial pleasures,
yet die like one who dreams of drinking water in thirst but cannot thereby quench that thirst.
The same applies to the enjoyment of the five desires; one is never satisfied.
Those sentient beings possessed of wisdom cut off the darkness of ignorance;
those wise ones are content and correctly contemplate all realms of existence.
With wisdom one observes the realms of existence; with insight one perceives old age, sickness, and death.
By severing all craving, one abandons the realms of existence without attachment.
Viewing contact as like a burning fire, one then relinquishes craving.
Contemplating feeling is also like this: one knows that feeling is not wholesome.
Just as when various musical instruments are struck, so it is with the sense faculties and their objects;
through training within the Noble Teaching, one is able to relinquish the intrinsic nature of the faculties.
All five kinds of sense-bases arise from name-and-form;
consciousness discriminates within them, and thus volitional perceptions arise.
When the noble ones contemplate in this way, they do not cling to the realms of existence.
The wise one, his wisdom fulfilled, realized cessation as if fuel were exhausted.
Having spoken thus to the king, the crown prince,
and the ministers and subjects regarding the impermanence of all conditioned existence, he immediately met his end.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Do you know that King Mūrdhaja of that time? Could he have been anyone else?
Do not view him as another, nor give rise to doubt or confusion; it was I myself."
"In the past, when I was King Mūrdhaja, I ruled over humans and devas with sovereign power and noble status; yet, insatiable in my greed and desire, I met my end.
Therefore, O Great King!"
One should abandon the pride of wealth and power, as well as self-indulgence, and abide in heedfulness.
If one can abide in the practice of heedfulness, that person is then able to cultivate all roots of goodness.
"Great King!
If one is not negligent, one can further enter into the equality of the dharma-realm.
Great King!"
If a person can remain free from negligence, they will achieve benefit.
Great King!
The conditioned and unconditioned realms are neither male nor female; they are not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present.
"Great King!
You should establish your own mind in this Dharma and not follow the teachings of others.
Great King!"
This Dharma is the unsurpassed enlightenment of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Great King!
You should distance yourself from all worldly power and nobility, dry up the ocean of craving, topple the mountain of arrogance, and remain far removed from all misfortunes and calamities.

It is equal toward all things; it is not the stage of any ordinary person, nor is it that which can be practiced by Śrāvakas, nor is it the sphere of any Pratyekabuddhas. It is the practice of all Bodhisattvas and that which is realized by the perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas.
"Your Majesty, you should settle your mind and not allow it to become distracted; you should reflect thus:

'How may I, in future ages, among all the worlds of devas and humans, become a lamp, a torch, a light, a ship, a guide, and a teacher? How may I become a caravan leader, a chief, and one who is unsurpassed—crossing over myself so as to ferry others across, liberating myself so as to liberate others, bringing peace to myself so as to bring peace to others, and attaining nirvana for myself so as to lead others to nirvana?'"

"O Great King! Observe the wealth, power, and sovereignty experienced in the past; O Great King, you should know that the sense faculties are like illusions—there is no satiety, and nothing can satisfy them;
objects of perception are like dreams—they cannot bring fulfillment."

"Great King! In the past there was a king named Nimi, who understood all phenomena and ruled as a king in accordance with the Dharma; he valued non-negligence, and whatever actions he performed were free from all negligence."
"Great King!

This King Nimi constantly contemplates the equality of the three periods of time; furthermore, he contemplates all phenomena as being equal to the three periods of time. He contemplates that all phenomena of the past are devoid of intrinsic nature, he contemplates that all phenomena of the future are devoid of intrinsic nature, and he likewise contemplates that present phenomena are also devoid of intrinsic nature."
"Great King!
Having contemplated the equality of all phenomena across the three periods of time, King Nimi no longer gave rise to grasping or attachment toward any phenomena.

King Nimi observed that the entire world is inverted by the four perversions: conceiving the notion of purity within impure phenomena, the notion of pleasure within suffering phenomena, the notion of permanence within impermanent phenomena, and the notion of self within selfless phenomena."
Seeing the world in this way, he then thought:
"The world is ruined, utterly devastated.
Such sentient beings do not realize that all phenomena are by their very nature empty and quiescent."
"Great King! At that time, King Nimi again had this thought:
'I shall gather all sentient beings through the four methods of attraction.'"
"If I were to gather sentient beings through the four methods of attraction, these sentient beings would follow me and accept my instructions.
At that time, after King Nimi had first employed this skillful means, he immediately gathered all sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction.
Having gathered all sentient beings together, King Nimi then taught the people that all phenomena are equal, speaking these words:
"O sentient beings, all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature."
If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then those phenomena are neither past, nor future, nor present.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of those phenomena lacks reality.
"If a phenomenon is devoid of intrinsic nature, that phenomenon cannot be described as past, future, or present. "Great King!

At that time, after King Nimi had taught those sentient beings this Dharma of the equality of the three times, eighty *koṭi-nayuta*—that is, immeasurable hundreds of thousands—of sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
"Great King!
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were gathered and seated in the Sudharmā Hall, where they deliberated, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
The people of the kingdom of Videha have gained great and wholesome benefit.

This King Nimi understands all phenomena according to the Dharma as he rules; being fully endowed with skillful means, he uses those very means to demonstrate the non-perverted Dharma to sentient beings who are subject to perversion.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra was in another place far from the Sudharmā Hall; having heard those devas speaking with his divine ear, he immediately came to the Sudharmā Hall, took his seat, and sat down.
Having taken their seats, he asked those devas:
"What were you discussing while in the Sudharmā Hall?
When he had thus questioned them, the devas replied to Śakra:
"So be it, Lord of Devas!
Listen to what we have been discussing while assembled in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).
We have spoken of how the people of the kingdom of Videha have attained great benefit."

This King Nimi understood all phenomena as they truly are and acted as king in accordance with the Dharma; being fully endowed with skillful means, he used those very means to demonstrate the non-perverted Dharma to sentient beings who are subject to perversion—namely, by revealing the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
After those devas had spoken these words, Śakra then replied to the sons of the gods, saying:
"This King Nimi is fully endowed with inconceivable skillful means."
"Do you all, who are here in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, wish to see that King Nimi?
At that time, all the devas spoke with one voice, saying:
"Indeed, O Lord of Devas!"
"We wish to see that Great King Nimi here.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed his charioteer named Mātali, saying: "You should come forward;
quickly prepare the divine precious chariot drawn by a thousand horses and proceed to the kingdom of Videha in Jambudvīpa, to where King Nimi resides."
He spoke these words:
"This is the thousand-horse chariot of the devas, sent to welcome Your Majesty.
We pray that Your Majesty will mount this precious chariot and feel no fear; all the inhabitants of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven long to behold Your Majesty."
Once he had mounted the carriage, he spoke these words:
"Great King! By which path shall I now lead Your Majesty from here to that celestial realm?"
"Is he departing by the path of sentient beings who dwell in perverted views,
or is he departing by the path of sentient beings who dwell in non-perverted views?
At that time, Mātali replied to Śakra:
"Very well, I shall receive your instructions.

Having heard these words, he immediately prepared a chariot drawn by a thousand well-trained horses, ascended it himself, and descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa, arriving at the palace of King Nimi in the kingdom of Videha.
He spoke thus to King Nimi:

"The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have now sent a chariot drawn by a thousand well-trained horses; Your Majesty may ascend the chariot and feel no fear, for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven long to behold you."
At that time, Great King Nimi, with a fearless mind, immediately ascended it.
Once he had mounted the chariot, Mātali spoke these words:
"By which path shall I now lead the King?"
"Are you departing by the path of sentient beings who abide in perverted views,
or are you departing by the path of sentient beings who abide in non-perverted views?
The King then replied:
"You may take me from between those two paths and depart.
Thereupon, Mātali immediately led King Nimi away from both the realm of beings who dwell in an inverted state and the realm of beings who dwell in an un-inverted state.
"Great King! At that time, King Nimi said to Mātali:
'You should halt the chariot for a short while; I shall observe the dwelling place of those beings who live in perversion.'"
Then Mātali, immediately receiving the King’s command, briefly halted the chariot.
At that moment, King Nimi caused eighty million sentient beings to dwell securely within the Samādhi of Seeing Reality.
For what reason? Because this king, in a short period of time, has caused such a multitude to abide in the Samādhi of Seeing Reality;
this is because the king has well practiced the conduct of heedfulness.
Those sentient beings who were established in samādhi all subsequently attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Mātali was entirely unaware of what the king had done.
At that time, Mātali again led the king to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Then, King Nimi saw from afar a lush and verdant forest and said to Mātali:
"That forest must surely be the dwelling place of beings who are not subject to delusion."
Mātali said: "Great King!
This is the Hall of Good Dharma belonging to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; the assembly of those Trāyastriṃśa gods has gathered in this hall desiring to see you, O King."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will not give way to fear, but shall ascend this hall.
At that time, King Nimi, his heart free from dread, ascended the hall.
Then Śakra, seeing King Nimi approaching from afar, spoke these words:
"Welcome, Great King!
he said, and then offered half of his seat, commanding the king to sit.
Thereupon, King Nimi took his place upon half of Śakra’s seat.
At that time, Śakra addressed him with gracious words of consolation, saying:
"Great King! You have swiftly attained a sublime benefit, being able to cause the Buddha-dharma to blaze forth and flourish."
At that time, Śakra addressed the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:
"This King Nimi has accomplished and perfected inconceivable skillful means."
"In a short period of time, this king was able to establish eight hundred million sentient beings within the Buddha-dharma, yet Mātali did not perceive it at all.
At that time, King Nimi extensively expounded various kinds of sublime and wondrous dharmas for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having benefited the assembly of devas, he addressed Śakra, saying:
"I now wish to return to Jambudvīpa.
For what reason?"
"In Jambudvīpa, it is for the sake of protecting and upholding the Buddha’s true Dharma. Śakra replied,
"Now is precisely the right time."
He further commanded his charioteer, Mātali, saying:
"You must return with the chariot drawn by the thousand well-trained horses and escort King Nimi back to Jambudvīpa.
Once King Nimi had arrived in Jambudvīpa, he perfected great compassion and skillful means, causing immeasurable sentient beings to dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma.
Great King!
Do not harbor doubts, nor give rise to misconceptions.
The King Nimi of old was none other than myself.
"Great King!
You should contemplate that the power of heedfulness is inconceivable.
Even when Great King Nimi ascended the throne of Śakra, he remained free from any attachment!"
Therefore, Great King!
Within the Buddha-dharma, you should practice with diligent vigor and cultivate heedfulness.
Great King!
"What is meant by 'the Buddha-dharma'? Great King!
All dharmas whatsoever are the Buddha-dharma."
At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, then all sentient beings should also be Buddhas."
The Buddha said:
"O Great King, one who perceives sentient beings without inversion is himself a Buddha."
What is called "Buddha" is the seeing of sentient beings as they truly are.
To see sentient beings as they truly are is to see the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The limit of reality is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Great King!

The dharma-realm cannot be demonstrated; it is merely a name, merely conventional, merely a worldly enumeration, merely verbal expression, and merely a provisional designation. It should be viewed in this way."
"O Great King!
All dharmas are unarisen; this is the gateway of dhāraṇī. Why is this so?"
This is called the gateway of dhāraṇī; herein, all phenomena are unmoving and unshakable, without grasping and without relinquishing—this is called the gateway of dhāraṇī, Great King!
The non-extinction of all phenomena is a dhāraṇī gateway. Why is this?
Because non-extinction is a dhāraṇī gateway; within it, all phenomena are without movement, without fluctuation, and without grasping.
It is without relinquishment; that dharani-door is without characteristics, without intrinsic nature, and cannot be designated;
it is without action or agency, without coming or going, without sentient beings, without life-force, without a person, and without a nourisher;
it is not an antidote, without form or shape, and without entanglement or liberation.
Neither defiled nor pure; neither loving nor hating; neither bound nor liberated; no living being; neither emerging nor receding;
neither attainment nor abiding; neither fixed nor distracted; neither knowledge nor non-knowledge; neither seeing nor not seeing;
neither precept-keeping nor transgression; neither remorse nor lack of remorse; neither joy...
It is not non-joy, neither reliance nor non-reliance; it is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither concentration nor non-concentration;
it is neither reality nor perversion, neither nirvana nor non-nirvana;
it is neither craving nor freedom from craving, neither seeing nor non-seeing, neither liberation nor non-liberation, and neither wisdom nor non-wisdom.
It is neither seeing nor not seeing, neither karma nor non-karma, neither the path nor non-path.
Great King!
One should enter into all phenomena by means of these sixty-seven dharma-gates.
"Great King!

This very essence of form has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present. Likewise, the essential nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also thus: it has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present."
"Great King!
Just as a reflection in a mirror is neither existent nor non-existent, so too is the essential nature of form: it has never existed, it will not exist, and it does not exist now."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so: they have not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and do not exist in the present.
Great King!
They are like an echo, which has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present.
"Great King!

In this same way, the essential nature of form is likewise: it has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this: they have not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and do not exist in the present."
Great King!
It is like a mirage, which has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present.
The essential nature of this form is likewise: it has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present.
"Great King!
For example, a mass of foam has no solidity; it did not exist in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present.
The essential nature of this form is likewise so: it did not exist in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present, Great King!"

In this same way, the essential nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise: it has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present.
Great King!

For example, if one were to see the most excellent woman in the kingdom within a dream, that which is seen in the dream has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present.

The essential nature of this form is likewise thus: it has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present. Likewise, the essential nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise thus: they have not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and do not exist in the present.
"Great King!
It is like a barren woman who dreams of giving birth to a son; that which is seen in the dream has never existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present."

The essential nature of this form is likewise thus: it has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus: they have not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and do not exist in the present.
"Great King! Form has no basis, and so on, up to consciousness, which also has no basis.
Great King!"
Just as space has nothing upon which it depends, so too, Great King!
Form has nothing upon which it depends, and even consciousness likewise has nothing upon which it depends.
Great King!
Form has no arising, and even consciousness likewise has no arising.
Great King!
Form has no cessation, and even consciousness likewise has no cessation.
"Great King!
Just as the realm of nirvāṇa has neither arising nor cessation,
so it is, Great King!"
In this way, form is also without arising and without cessation, and so on up to consciousness, which is also without arising and without cessation.
Great King! It is, for example, like the dharma-realm, which is also without arising and without cessation.
"Great King!
In this way, form is neither born nor extinguished; even up to consciousness, it is neither born nor extinguished.
Thus it is, Great King!"
All phenomena are the domain of the Tathāgata.
That which is inconceivable is also the domain of the Tathāgata, as are the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), because they are not shared with the domains of any ordinary beings.

Therefore, for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is neither disparaged nor praised; neither attained nor lost; neither awakened nor unawakened; neither known nor unknown; neither cognized nor uncognized; neither relinquished nor unrelinquished; neither cultivated nor uncultivated; neither spoken nor unspeakable; neither realized nor unrealized; neither manifested nor unmanifested; and neither audible nor inaudible.
Why is this? Great King!
Those dharmas possess no such quality by which they could be supported or by which they could be overturned.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature,
Great King!
"Now you may settle your mind within this Dharma; contemplate this Dharma deeply and do not rely on others.
At that time, King Śuddhodana had this thought:
"Among all dharmas, no dharma can be apprehended; there is no such dharma by which one could realize it and be called a Buddha."
"All dharmas are truly unattainable; the Buddha speaks of them for the sake of sentient beings merely by way of conventional designation.
When the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, King Śuddhodana and seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Śākyas had attained deep faith, manifested a smile.
Then the venerable monk Aśvajit asked in verse:
“Great Hero, Honored Guide, For the sake of the world you have manifested a smile.”
I pray that the Lamp of the World will expound upon the matter of this smile.
O One of Ten Powers, Possessor of All-Knowledge, for what cause do you manifest a smile?
I pray you tell the reason for that smile, severing the net of all doubts in the world.
For the sake of the Śākya assembly, the Buddha manifested the auspicious sign of a smile;
for the sake of the multitudes of humans and devas, may he swiftly remove the net of all doubts.
Having heard the Great Hero’s teaching, the world shall be freed from all uncertainty.
Their minds were all filled with joy as they dwelt securely within the Buddha-dharma.
These sons of the World-Honored One, having understood the cause of the smile, remain steadfast in their vows;
their wisdom shall surely reach full penetration.
“May the Honored One, the Great Guide, sever the doubts of this assembly;
once the multitude has had their doubts removed, they shall surely attain vast bliss.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Aśvajit in verse:
“I now manifest this smile of quiescence; Aśvajit, you should listen attentively.
I shall now speak according to reality, the definitive wisdom of the Śākya clan.
That all phenomena are ungraspable—this the Śākyas have fully realized.”
Therefore, within the Buddha-dharma, one should decisively abide with a settled mind.
You, of great renown among the Śākya clan, by relying on non-apprehension,
shall attain supreme enlightenment and thoroughly understand all phenomena.
Having ended their lives among humans, these members of the Śākya clan will certainly be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, where they shall personally attend upon Amitāyus.
Having dwelt in the Land of Peace and Bliss, they will fearlessly attain awakening.
They are able to travel to the realms of the ten directions to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
while dwelling securely in a single Buddha-land, they are able to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, they seek the unsurpassed path.
Traveling through the lands of all Buddhas, They have all arrived by means of their spiritual powers To offer worship to those Buddhas and others, Following wherever the Buddhas appear.
Throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, They have made offerings to all the Teachers.
With various kinds of sublime offerings, they shall later attain the Buddha-way.
Having each attained Buddhahood, they will be able to deliver immeasurable multitudes,
causing them to attain the Buddha-way, and further transform all sentient beings.
The sentient beings of that land shall all attain the Buddha-way;
those World-Honored Ones therein will not deliver a multitude of śrāvakas.
Each and every one of those Buddhas shall have a lifespan of one kalpa.
The True Dharma of that Buddha shall remain for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
After that Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, a multitude of Bodhisattvas of great wisdom will uphold the Dharma and transform the world for a hundred million asaṃkhyeya years.
Those sons of the Buddhas teach and transform immeasurable multitudes,
establishing them in the unsurpassed path; they preach the Dharma that is entirely empty and quiescent,
causing them to abide in heedfulness and cultivate the accumulation of the dharmas of emptiness and stillness.
One can attain all-knowledge by delighting in the practice of heedfulness.
Having heard this account of the Śākya lineage as spoken by the World-Honored One,
gods and humans alike rejoice, setting their will upon seeking the Buddha-way.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra!
This is the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Seeing Reality; you should explain it to those bodhisattvas who are of non-retrogressive wisdom.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, this samādhi cannot be described.

Yet, within that samādhi, the Tathāgata does not apprehend a single dharma. That which is not apprehended cannot be awakened to; that which cannot be awakened to cannot be explained; that which cannot be explained cannot be known. That which cannot be known is precisely the Dharma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Śāriputra! I now entrust this to you: this is the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Seeing Reality. You should receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it for others.
Śāriputra! If there are sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna and practice the five pāramitās for ten kalpas while remaining apart from the prajñāpāramitā;
yet, if another person were to hear of this Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Seeing Reality, the merit they obtain would surpass that of the former.
Furthermore, if there is another son or daughter of good family who briefly hears of the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Seeing Reality;

or if there is someone who, having heard of this Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Seeing Reality, explains it to even a single person—the merit gained by this latter person is even more superior than that of the former.
Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family were to spend ten eons hearing this and then explaining it to others;
yet if another person were to practice this Bodhisattva Samādhi of Seeing Reality for even a single kṣaṇa, the merit obtained by the latter would exceed that of the former.
Therefore, Śāriputra, you should use this *Bodhisattvadarśanatatvasamādhi-sūtra* to teach, instruct, and guide the practice of all bodhisattvas. Śāriputra!
If one cultivates this Bodhisattva Samādhi of Seeing Reality, one shall attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Śāriputra!
All those bodhisattvas within this assembly whom I have granted the prediction of the unsurpassed path have all come to dwell securely within this Bodhisattva Samādhi of Seeing Reality.

At that time, all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, humans, and the entire great assembly—including asuras, gandharvas, humans, non-humans, and others—having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

17. The Chapter on Pūrṇa, Part One of Seventeen: Chapter One, On the Bodhisattva Practice.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and an immeasurable number of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I wish to ask a few questions; I only pray that the Tathāgata will look upon me with compassion and grant me permission.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa, "Ask whatever you wish."
"I shall provide an explanation to bring you joy. Pūrṇa said,

"I now have a request to make for the sake of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who possess supreme merit among all conditioned phenomena, whose fame is lofty and far-reaching, and who constantly seek the peace and happiness of sentient beings."
At that time, Pūrṇa spoke in verse:
"Practicing the supreme merit, Your fame is most lofty and far-reaching;
To you who delight in the Dharma through pure precepts, I ask about your conduct."
How does one cultivate and purify the mind?
How does one extensively practice giving?
And how does one deliver sentient beings?
"How does one constantly practice the path with a mind of joy?
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
It is for the sake of these great beings that I now ask about such matters:
How does a bodhisattva cultivate and accumulate extensive learning so that it is like the great ocean, inexhaustible?
"How can one gather the treasure-trove of extensive learning, attain definitive meaning regarding all phenomena, and skillfully understand the words and phrases of all languages?
He then spoke in verse:
"How does a bodhisattva seek Extensive learning like the great ocean?"
How does one attain certainty regarding the Dharma and become well-versed in the Buddha-way?
How can one understand immeasurable meanings within a single word,
and through the power of wisdom, penetrate all phenomena?
"His extensive learning is inexhaustible; his mind remains unshaken when questioned or challenged.
Out of compassion, he teaches the Dharma to sever the doubts of sentient beings.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Following my power of wisdom regarding the stages, I now inquire of the Tathāgata: how can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas avoid falling back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
And he spoke in verse:
"How may one leave behind all hardships and encounter the Buddhas?
Having encountered the Buddhas, how may one swiftly attain pure faith?"
Having attained unsurpassed faith, you are able to relinquish what is difficult to give up;
having cast aside everything, how do you practice the unimpeded path?
Why do you delight in leaving the household life, dwelling in seclusion to cultivate the wisdom of emptiness?
"What is meant by 'not opposing the Dharma'?
I pray that you will answer this matter in full.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We all know that the Buddha has already perfected all wisdom and has already crossed to the other shore of all supernormal powers. He is the most supreme and honored one within the triple world, having attained peerless, subtle, and great knowledge, and he moves through all phenomena without obstruction.”
"Therefore, I now inquire about this matter.
He praised him in verse, saying:
"The Buddha abides in supreme merit, Having already crossed to the shore of supernormal powers."
Having attained unobstructed wisdom, I ask you, O valiant one.
You have well-mastered all dharmas; your merit is most supreme.
You destroy darkness and give rise to the light of wisdom, causing all beings to rejoice.
Neither hating enemies nor loving kin, free from sorrow and free from deception,
he has conquered the King of Death in great battle and shattered the hosts of Māra’s army.
Without grasping at sword or staff, he has subdued all adversaries.
Always possessing a heart of compassion, firmly abiding in pure precepts;
the World-Honored One is free from flattery and crookedness, without pride or frivolity;
having attained realization and liberation, he is the most supreme among all merits.
"The path you originally practiced, and the supreme wisdom you have attained—may you now explain this to me: how does one practice to become a Buddha?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇa, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! It is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this matter.

Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain for you the practices undertaken by Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment], as they cultivate and accumulate all the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I shall now speak of the bodhisattva Who has first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Always with courageous power, He delights in practicing the bodhisattva path."
The various practices undertaken by all bodhisattvas, And their diverse deeds of profound resolve—
Having received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha, These matters shall now be briefly explained.
Their profound resolve and their joy in the Dharma Are immeasurable and boundless.
Various forms of conduct manifest, yet they are not accomplished by a single cause.
With a heart filled with joy within, one practices giving;
having given, the mind feels no regret, and the spirit becomes even more glad.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"Sentient beings are constantly impoverished, lacking the wealth of extensive learning; I shall seek it for their sake.
Sentient beings are constantly impoverished because they are all characterized by indolence."
I shall apply myself with diligent vigor; from this, I shall attain Bodhi.
For the sake of sentient beings, I shall cultivate patience in my mind;
even when faced with foul words, abuse, or physical blows, I shall receive them silently without retaliation.
"One should reflect: 'Who is it that reviles me?
The reviler cannot be found.
Those who revile, those who harbor anger and hatred—all these are entirely empty matters."
Having reflected thus, with a mind free from anger and resentment, one constantly practices patience and thereby attains the path of Buddhahood.
"Sentient beings lack a virtuous mind; I shall act as a lamp for the world."
I shall cause them to find refuge; though they lack wealth, I shall provide for them with wealth.
Sentient beings are pitiable, for they all together follow the wrong path;
I shall deliver them and cause them to abide in nirvāṇa.
All sentient beings are impoverished, lacking the wealth of wisdom;
having attained all-knowledge, I shall cause them to be fully satisfied.
Thus do these Bodhisattvas act for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
"Generating the aspiration for Bodhi, they practice such vows as these.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"The various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest their minds through manifold causes and conditions, yet they do not abide in any single dharma."
Why is this so? Because all bodhisattvas study all dharmas before attaining the Way.
There are four great and rare matters concerning bodhisattvas, and they do not see any other dharma that surpasses these.
What are the four?
That a bodhisattva is able to practice diligence toward indolent sentient beings is called marvelous.
That they are able to practice patience among violent and wrathful sentient beings is called marvelous.
To see all sentient beings walking upon deviant paths while one personally exerts oneself in the right path is called rare.
To give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a profound resolve for the sake of delivering sentient beings from the cycle of birth and death is called rare.
"Pūrṇa! These four rare qualities are called the greatest rarities of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Seeing sentient beings who are indolent, one should arouse diligence with a resolute mind:
'I ought not to emulate them by performing various unrighteous deeds.'"
One should not emulate anger; anger is not the path of the Buddha.
Constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, for Bodhi arises from this.
Sentient beings delight in deviant paths and rely upon those deviant paths.
The Bodhisattva seeks the Right Path, Causing all beings to abide in the Right Path.
Seeing the faults and afflictions of birth and death, He single-mindedly seeks the Buddha’s wisdom.
Having attained the unsurpassed treasure, He shall deliver all sentient beings.
Such a rare occurrence as this, none other can surpass;
for this reason, you should know that one has attained freedom from obstructing dharmas.
Even if one’s body and robes were to burn, or even if one’s head were on fire, one would not seek to extinguish it.
"If a mind of indolence arises, one should immediately and swiftly eliminate it.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"A bodhisattva has four dharmas that can give rise to a joyful mind."
What are the four?

Seeing that sentient beings dwell securely within birth and death and are unable to exert diligence, while seeing oneself situated upon the Buddha-way and practicing with diligence, one gives rise to a heart of joy.
Seeing that all sentient beings are constantly indolent in mind, while seeing oneself diligently practicing with vigor within the Buddha-dharma, one gives rise to a heart of joy.
Seeing that all sentient beings harbor anger, resentment, and jealousy, while seeing oneself free from malice and envy and always maintaining compassion, one gives rise to a heart of joy.
"Seeing no other person who practices the Buddha-dharma with diligence equal to my own, I give rise to a heart of joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Seeing sentient beings indolent, I myself practice with vigor."
Therefore, this bodhisattva attains a heart of joy within;
seeing the faults and afflictions of birth and death, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Fearing the prison of the triple world, he strives with diligence to seek liberation from it.
While sentient beings delight in anger and resentment, the Bodhisattva abides in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion;
for this reason, the Bodhisattva gives rise to joy and gladness. "Whatever sentient beings may do, none of it should be done."
Therefore, I shall seek the unsurpassed path of the Buddhas.
This is called true wisdom, praised by all Buddhas;
I shall study this wisdom so that sentient beings may find a refuge.
"Therefore, this bodhisattva always attains a mind of joy;
from existence, non-existence, emptiness, and falsehood, he shall give rise to the true Dharma.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:

“Bodhisattvas possess four dharmas by which they escape all calamities and encounter places free from calamity; having encountered them, they do not lose them and are able to cultivate the Buddha-dharma. What are these four?

First, the Bodhisattva is humble and their mind is supple; whenever they see sentient beings, they always say, "Welcome," with a serene and joyful countenance, greeting them before they have spoken, and always smiling as they converse with them.
Second, one should single-mindedly seek the Dharma, always delighting in inquiry and questioning, and diligently pursue wholesome benefits without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Third, one should take pleasure in empty and quiet places, remaining secluded and dwelling alone.
Fourth, one personally abides in the path of the Buddha’s bodhi and also transforms sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Buddha’s path.

When a bodhisattva possesses these four dharmas, they attain freedom from all difficulties and encounter places free of difficulty; having encountered them, they do not lose them, and are able to cultivate the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Endowed with a supple and gentle mind, Always delighting in practicing loving-kindness and compassion,
When speaking with sentient beings, One should be humble in heart and harmonious in expression."
Constantly seeking the profound and subtle Dharma praised by the Buddha,
Always upholding the pure precepts, and delighting in the practice of dhūta austerities.
Though practicing the dhūta methods, one also practices profound and wondrous wisdom.
Therefore, this bodhisattva, having left behind hardships and encountered a state free from difficulty,
constantly inquires about the profound dharmas in the presence of all Buddhas;
thus their wisdom increases, and they are not born in places of hardship.
Always delighting in secluded places, practicing the pure dhūta austerities—
for this reason, these bodhisattvas leave behind hardships and encounter no difficulties.
All those possessed of wisdom who draw near to these four dharmas [shall likewise attain such results].
They are able to leave behind all hardships and encounter the various Buddhas.
Having encountered the various Buddhas, they possess indestructible faith and are able to give rise to supreme diligence in order to seek the Buddha’s wisdom.
Therefore, those who seek wisdom Should study the True Dharma;
If one can study the True Dharma, Attaining the Way of the Buddha will not be difficult.
Chapter Two: On Much Learning (Bahuśruta-varga) The Buddha addressed Pūrṇa:

"If a bodhisattva possesses four dharmas, they will be able to cultivate and accumulate extensive learning so that it is like the great ocean, inexhaustible; they will constantly be able to cultivate and accumulate the treasure-trove of extensive learning, attain definitive meaning regarding all phenomena, and skillfully understand the phrases and sentences of all languages."
What are the four?
The Bodhisattva seeks the Dharma, namely the twelve divisions of the scriptures:
Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, Avadāna, and Upadeśa.
Having sought it, one recites and studies it; having recited and studied it, one maintains right mindfulness; having maintained right mindfulness, one acts according to what has been taught.
Pūrṇa, when a bodhisattva possesses this first dharma, they are able to cultivate and accumulate great learning, which is like the great ocean that can never be exhausted.

He is always able to cultivate and accumulate the treasure-trove of extensive learning, attains definitive meaning regarding all phenomena, and is skilled in understanding the phrasing and sentences of all languages. "Furthermore, Pūrṇa!
The Bodhisattva has no point of reliance among all phenomena; although they enter meditative concentration, they have no reliance.
Because they have no reliance, they attain the wisdom of non-abiding amidst all phenomena.
Having attained non-abiding wisdom, one attains unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all dharmas.
Why is this? Pūrṇa!
There is no dharma that can be craved or that acts as an obstacle.

When a bodhisattva possesses these three dharmas, they are able to cultivate and accumulate extensive learning (bahuśruta) such that it is like the great ocean, inexhaustible; they are able to constantly cultivate and accumulate the treasure-trove of extensive learning; they are able to attain definitive meaning regarding all dharmas; and they are skilled in understanding the phrases and syllables of all languages.

"Furthermore, Pūrṇa! A bodhisattva recollects the Buddha and recollects the Buddha-dharma by means of the causal conditions of the Dharma. When such a person recollects the Buddha and recollects the Buddha-dharma by means of the causal conditions of the Dharma, they do not perceive any dharma that can be greedily grasped or accepted."
Because this person does not greedily grasp at sensations, their mind has no attachment to any phenomena.
Because this person has no attachment to any phenomena, they respond to all questions and challenges according to what is asked, without any hindrance.

When a bodhisattva possesses these three dharmas, they are able to cultivate and accumulate extensive learning, which is like the great ocean that can never be exhausted; they are able to constantly cultivate and accumulate the treasure-trove of extensive learning, attain definitive meaning regarding all phenomena, and skillfully understand the phrasing and sentences of all languages.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇa! A bodhisattva who accomplishes the compassion of non-apprehension is unimpeded in his practice.
This compassion of non-apprehension does not grasp at any phenomena."
Why is this? Pūrṇa!
Those who dwell upon these signs may give rise to desire, or give rise to hatred, or give rise to delusion.
Those who dwell upon signs may give rise to desire, or give rise to hatred, or give rise to delusion.

Those who dwell upon the signs of things, the signs of objects, the signs of the aggregates (*skandha*), the signs of the sense bases (*āyatana*), the signs of the elements (*dhātu*), the signs of dharmas, or the signs of non-dharmas, may likewise give rise to desire, or give rise to hatred, or give rise to delusion.
Therefore, Pūrṇa! All characteristics of sensation are termed false views; the bodhisattva completely extinguishes all such characteristics and cultivates the accumulation of a compassionate mind.

Because sentient beings are subject to decay, their characteristics also decay; because characteristics decay, their phenomena also decay; because phenomena decay, their views also decay. At that time, the bodhisattva destroys all dharmas and cultivates the accumulation of compassion.

Such loving-kindness is called "loving-kindness of non-apprehension"; such loving-kindness of non-apprehension is called "Dharma-loving-kindness"; and such Dharma-loving-kindness is called "Buddha-loving-kindness."
Pūrṇa! What is called the Buddha’s compassion?
That which is unconditioned and indestructible is called the Buddha’s compassion.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇa!
To penetrate all dharmas as they truly are—this is called the Buddha’s compassion.
"World-Honored One! [Pūrṇa replied.]
"What is meant by 'thoroughly penetrating all dharmas as they truly are'?
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"That which is thoroughly penetrated is not called a dharma, nor is it called a non-dharma."
For what reason?
Pūrṇa! If one says that there is a dharma, that is itself a non-dharma.
If there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, then within that there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); the absence of conceptual proliferation is called nirvāṇa.
Examine this thoroughly, whether from the furthest distance or the closest proximity.
Pūrṇa said: "Neither far nor near. Why is this?"
“World-Honored One!
Such a principle has no direction and no location; it is neither internal nor external.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, Pūrṇa, one makes a calculation regarding dharmas.
"World-Honored One! [Pūrṇa replied.]
"In what kind of dharmas does he calculate?
"Pūrṇa! Regarding the dharmas to which ordinary people are attached, the Tathāgata neither acquires them, nor cultivates them, nor realizes them, nor penetrates them."
To establish a numerical reckoning for such dharmas,
Pūrṇa, is not for the sake of differentiating those dharmas. Pūrṇa!
I shall now explain this for you: this foremost dharma of quiescence is able to encompass the Buddha-way.
Pūrṇa! In the future, there will be those who eagerly pursue worldly gain; if they hear this sutra, they will not delight in hearing or receiving it.
Pūrṇa! Of this bodhi of mine, you all know only a little by means of sounds and phrases; its underlying meaning and intent remain unknown to you.
"This meaning is profound and remote, beyond the reach of words; it can only be known within by the wise.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who cannot understand this meaning, Hear the Buddha's Dharma with sorrow and distress."
If one can understand the meaning, the Tathāgata acts as their teacher.
If a person takes the Buddha as their teacher, they seek nirvāṇa;
free from a contentious mind, they are able to contemplate the Dharma correctly.
In this, no dharma arises, nor does any dharma cease;
being without arising and without cessation, such is the true nature of all dharmas.
If a dharma has no arising, then there is no production or origination.
Neither identity nor difference—within this Dharma, neither exists.
