This is called nirvāṇa; within it, there is no one who attains extinction.
Whether one speaks of it as extremely distant or near, both of these are empty.
"If one can know emptiness, they are called one who knows nirvāṇa;
if one knows nirvāṇa, they are called my disciple. "Pūrṇa!..."

When a bodhisattva possesses these four qualities, they are able to cultivate and accumulate extensive learning that is inexhaustible like the great ocean; they are able to constantly cultivate and accumulate the treasure-trove of extensive learning; they are able to attain definitive understanding of the meaning of all dharmas; and they are skilled in discerning the words and phrases of all languages.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Always desiring to seek much learning, Praised by all Buddhas, One is able to attain the definitive, true meaning; Therefore, one is like the great ocean."
Within a single syllable, and even within the meaning of a single phrase, one could speak for billions of kalpas without exhausting it.
Therefore, one should seek the True Dharma; having sought it, one should contemplate it correctly.
Do not greedily grasp at the marks of phenomena, nor crave that which is praised by the Buddhas.
Mindfully recollect all Tathāgatas and keep the True Dharma in mind;
do not seek the Teacher with a heart of greedy competition.
Always toward all sentient beings, he practices a mind of loving-kindness and compassion,
yet does not cling to sentient beings, dispersing and extinguishing all phenomena.
The Bodhisattva of Great Renown cultivates such dharmas as these.
One quickly attains dhāraṇī, and from this, great learning arises.
Just as the nature of space neither increases nor decreases, so too is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā): it neither increases nor decreases.
By the power of my wisdom, I have preached the Dharma for immeasurable eons;
though what has been spoken is incalculable, it is still not called "fully preached.
Even if all sentient beings were to exhaust their natures and all were to attain human form, [they would still not be able to fully comprehend it].
All together they practice the life of renunciation, possessing vast learning like Ānanda.
These dhāraṇī-holding bodhisattvas, for the sake of all these people,
preach the Dharma for a thousand billion kalpas, yet their wisdom remains inexhaustible.
The Buddha’s wisdom is peerless, equal to the immeasurable void;
as the void has no arising, so too is wisdom.
Just as a dragon does not draw from water yet can rain down great floods, so it is with this.
This water has no place of abiding, yet the rain it pours down is inexhaustible.
So too it is with the Bodhisattva who has attained this dhāraṇī:
all phenomena have no place of abiding, and the explanations based upon them can never be exhausted.
Therefore, one should seek extensive learning; having sought it, one should engage in right reflection.
By taking the Dharma as the object, one recollects the Buddha, and from this, extensive learning arises.
With universal compassion covering all sentient beings, one disperses and eliminates the perception of a self in beings.
Furthermore, one extinguishes all marks of dharmas; Much learning arises from this.
Chapter Three: On Non-Retrogression The Buddha addressed Pūrṇa:
“If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to remain non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are the four?
When a bodhisattva hears a teaching not previously heard, they contemplate its meaning and principles rather than immediately declaring it wrong.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes this first quality, they will not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Hearing a Dharma never heard before, One’s mind attains non-opposition;
Contemplating its meaning and principles, One does not immediately declare it to be non-Dharma."
If one hears the Dharma of emptiness and constantly seeks its underlying principles,
wisdom will thereby increase, and the Buddha-way arises from this.
Upon hearing the Dharma never heard before, one should seek its underlying principles.
Not regressing from awakening, one’s wisdom increases.
Hearing the Dharma never heard before, one does not follow a mind of evil pride;
one does not give rise to flattery or crookedness—for if such things arise, that is not awakening.
When hearing a Dharma one has never heard before, one should seek to understand its meaning;
though it was previously unheard, one should contemplate it with a single mind.
When such a person seeks the Dharma, they will be able to hear the True Dharma.
They constantly encounter all Buddhas and never regress from Bodhi.
Having seen the Buddhas, they are able to pose questions correctly;
when the śrāvakas hear this, they all rejoice.
This person is most rare and extraordinary, able to pose such a question;
even we have no [such] intent, much less could we hear of this matter.
The Śrāvakas call it rare, and the devas all rejoice.
The Buddhas proclaim his name; this is the fruit of much learning.
Whenever there is a question, the Buddha answers that which is asked, so that the immeasurable great assembly all obtains vast benefit.
Having heard these many teachings on the questions and answers of the Bodhisattvas,
immeasurable multitudes have all attained the unsurpassed Dharma-eye.
The Buddha addressed Pūrṇa:

"For this reason, you should know that when a bodhisattva hears the Dharma not previously heard, they accept it with faith and do not oppose it; they contemplate it with right mind and do not immediately declare it wrong. Thus, they are able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings."

Pūrṇa! In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Sarvaguṇaprabhāsarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Pūrṇa! The lifespan of that Buddha, Sarvaguṇaprabhāsa-rāja, was eight billion years. In a single assembly of that Buddha, the śrāvaka disciples who were free from outflows through the exhaustion of all dharmas and attained liberation were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, beyond calculation; all these arhats had attained the liberation common to all.
The number of the assembly of bodhisattvas was likewise so.
Pūrṇa! After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma remained for sixty thousand years.

When he was about to enter nirvana, he bestowed supernatural powers upon ten billion bodhisattvas; for the sake of protecting the Dharma, they were sent throughout the ten billion Jambudvīpas, with one bodhisattva in each Jambudvīpa.

Pūrṇa! After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Sarvaguṇaprabhāsarāja, his assembly of disciples gradually became indolent and no longer recited or upheld such profound sūtras as the Sūtra on the Emptiness of All Dharmas and the Sūtra on Pure Precepts and Dhūta Practices; these were gradually extinguished because they could not be read, recited, or explained.

That Dharma is vast and extensive, consisting of eight hundred and forty thousand dharma-treasuries (*dharmakośa*). Within each dharma-treasury are sixty-eight million *nayuta* of sūtras; within each sūtra are thirty-six thousand udānas; and within each udāna are seven hundred and sixty *koṭi* of verses.
Pūrṇa! At the end of the final age, when the Dharma is about to perish, among all these treasuries of the Buddha’s teachings, there will remain only a single sūtra, an udāna.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu-dharma-master named Nārāyaṇa within this Jambudvīpa.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, this Dharma-master Nārāyaṇa was one of vast and extensive learning who was skilled at preaching the Dharma; his phrasing was elegant and his principles were clear, and he constantly delighted in expounding teachings never heard before.
When the Dharma was being taught, many people opposed and rejected it.
The Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa then thought to himself:

"These multitudes have not heard the Dharma before; having heard it, they cannot believe it, nor do they delight in listening to or receiving it. Even if they listen, they do not understand and their minds do not accord with it. Having heard it, they oppose and destroy it, finding fault with it, and speak thus:"
"This is not the word of the Buddha; it is not the teaching of the Great Master. Why is this so?
Because we have never heard such a sutra from our teachers or preceptors."
Furthermore, the elder bhikṣus also do not say that they have heard this transmitted from their teachers or preceptors in succession.
Now, the bhikṣus possess only a single remaining Sūtra and Udana; why should I not dwell alone in a quiet and secluded place?
"Pūrṇa, after the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa had formed this thought, he entered the deep mountains alone.

At that time, within Jambudvīpa, there were sixty-eight thousand great cities that had existed since the beginning of the kalpa; each city was twelve yojanas long and seven yojanas wide, magnificently adorned with streets and alleys aligned in order, filled with people who lived in abundance, joy, and peace."
Subsequently, he constructed eighty-four billion small cities, each seven yojanas wide, or six, five, four, three, or two yojanas; the smallest among them was one yojana wide.
Pūrṇa! At that time, in Jambudvīpa there was a great city named Anurādhapura. In it lived an elder named Janaka, who had a son named Mahānāman.
While this son of a householder was in a secluded place, a deva came to him and spoke these verses:
“You should diligently seek the Dharma; having sought it, contemplate it correctly.
The Tathāgata Guṇarāja has already prophesied that you shall become a Buddha.”
"Pūrṇa! After the deva had spoken this verse, he suddenly vanished.
Thereupon, the son of the elder went to his father's place, prostrated himself at his feet, and spoke these words:"
"I wish to leave the household life and practice the holy life within the Buddha-dharma of the King of All Merit and Radiance.
At that time, the elder Śāṇaka replied in verse:
"My household possesses abundant wealth and treasures; gold and silver are beyond measure.
What does not exist in Jambudvīpa, my household has it all."
"The wealth and treasures I seek are for my son to enjoy sensual pleasures;
why do you practice renunciation, only to be held in contempt by the world?
At that time, the elder’s son answered his father in verse:
"I delight in constantly seeking the Dharma; having sought it, I practice right reflection.
I take no pleasure in receiving worldly wealth or enjoyments; I shall become a Buddha for the sake of the world."
I have no need for family wealth or treasures; desiring few desires, I seek the spiritual riches that arise from the Dharma, and shall now go forth into homelessness.
Rare is the appearance of a Buddha in the world, and rare is the teaching of the Dharma by a Buddha.
"Now that I have encountered the Buddha-dharma, how could I ever abandon it?
Pūrṇa, at that time, the son of the elder prostrated himself at his father's feet, circumambulated him, and departed, speaking these verses:
"Even if there were a hundred million fathers and a billion mothers,
they still could not obstruct my resolve to leave the household life."
"I shall relinquish my body and life, my parents, kinsmen, and wealth;
I alone will not relinquish the Buddha-dharma, and I shall practice the seeking of the homeless life. "Pūrṇa!"
When the son of the elder had spoken these verses, he left the household life to pursue the Way.
He then went to the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa, seeking to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa expounded for him sūtras that he had never heard before.
At that time, having heard a sutra never before heard, the bhikṣu Mahānāman addressed the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa, saying:
"I have not previously heard this sutra."
"Who reads and recites these various sutras? Who receives and upholds them?
From whom were they heard? Nārāyaṇa replied:

"By virtue of the causes and conditions of my roots of goodness from past lives, and by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha Sarvaguṇālokārāja, this profound sūtra has naturally arisen in my mind."
"Pūrṇa! After the bhikṣuṇī Madhā had heard this teaching, she applied her mind with focused reflection, and the power of wisdom immediately arose within her.
By virtue of the power of great wisdom and skillful means, she posed difficult questions to the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa."
Having answered according to the meaning, Nārāyaṇa spoke these words:
"In the time of the Buddha Sarvaguṇaprabhāsa-rāja, there was a bhikṣu who asked the Buddha this same matter, just as you have now asked; the Buddha answered him in this way."
At that time, having heard this, the bhikṣu was filled with joy. Pūrṇa!
This bhikṣu Mahānāman then questioned the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa again.
Nārāyaṇa said: "In the time of the Buddha Sarvaguṇaprabhāsa-rāja, there was a bhikṣu who asked such a question as you have just now; the Buddha answered him in this very way."
When that bhikṣu heard this, he rejoiced.
"Pūrṇa! At that time, the bhikṣu Madhā said to the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa:
“O Noble Being!
In the past, what such questions and answers did you hear from the Buddha? Nārāyaṇa replied:
"Set this aside and do not ask.
This matter is difficult to believe; it would likewise be difficult for other people whose bodies have not yet realized the superior dharma to believe.
He asked this a second and a third time, and the reply was the same each time.
Mahānāman asked: "Virtuous One!
On what occasions in the past did you hear from the Buddha these various questions and answers?"
Nārāyaṇa said: "Set this aside and do not ask.
Since you insist, I shall now provide you with an analogy and explanation, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through analogies."
"Monks! At the place of the Buddha Sarvaguṇaprabhāsarāja, I heard that the nature of sentient beings is more abundant than the element of earth. Monks!"

Suppose all sentient beings in the entire trichiliocosm—whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception—were all to exhaustively attain human bodies endowed with the power of wisdom, and each of these beings were able to pose questions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, with each question being distinct from the others.

"Monks! In this manner, proceeding by succession, even if all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, without exception, were to raise these various questions for an eon or more than an eon."
Furthermore, suppose there were another person who, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, could raise as many distinct and varied questions as those aforementioned people.

Suppose such a single person were to continue doing so for an entire eon, or even slightly less than an eon, until every single sentient being without exception had been addressed with these various questions.
"What do you think? Are these questions that have arisen many or not? He replied:
"It is exceedingly much; it cannot be reached by any analogy.
Nārāyaṇa said to the bhikṣu Mātaṅga:
"I now tell you clearly: do not give rise to doubt or regret."

Whatever doubts and questions all those sentient beings without exception might raise throughout an eon or less than an eon, what I have heard from the Buddha as answers within a single dharma-gate is more numerous than those.
"Monks! In this way, there are two gates, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of gates. Monks!
I shall briefly describe all the names for calculation—immeasurable, inexhaustible, and inconceivable—and I have fully memorized and mastered all such numbers."

"Monks! All these answers are collectively contained within a single Dharma-gate, which I fully know. That is to say, the Tathāgata Sarvaguṇaprabhāsarāja has spoken of this as the phrase of the path, the phrase of the gate, the phrase of the seal, the phrase of the original basis, the phrase of the vajra, the phrase of the weighty, the phrase of the immovable, and the phrase of the unfathomable depth."
"Monks! Within a single gate all dharmas are subsumed; that is to say, the gate of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra).
All dharmas and all phrases take this gate as their basis and all enter into this gate."
All sūtras and udānas enter the gateway of the single syllable; by discerning one syllable, one can enter many syllables. Bhikṣu!
In this way, one can enter the seventy-eight thousand dhāraṇīs, within which there are ninety-two thousand distinctions of the faculties (indriya).

Within this gateway of the practices of sentient beings, there are eighty trillion forms and colors differentiated across the various realms of existence; I know the names of all these forms and colors.
Within each single color, I know one hundred names, and likewise two hundred names, three hundred names, up to knowing a thousand names, all of which exist within Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, beyond these Buddha-lands of the ten directions, I know all their respective conditions and their respective names. To state it briefly:

regarding all the powers of the Buddhas—the various distinctions among phenomena and the distinctions in their questions and answers—I know them all; this is entirely through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Sarvaguṇaprabhāsarāja.
"Pūrṇa! At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mādhā said to the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa:
'I pray only that you, O Righteous One, will return to the villages and cities to continue turning the wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata Sarvaguṇaprabhāsarāja.'"
"I pray that you accept my invitation; I shall act as your protector and serve as a recipient of the Dharma.
Nārāyaṇa said, "Let it be; do not speak of this."
"The bhikṣus of the present age are all indolent; they lack deep aspiration within the accumulation of wholesome dharmas.
Māthā replied again, "From this day forward, I shall give rise to a deep aspiration for wholesome dharmas; for the sake of seeking this Dharma, I dare not be indolent."
"Pūrṇa! The bhikṣuṇī Mādhā then invited Nārāyaṇa to return to the village to preach the True Dharma, pledging to follow and protect him while listening to what she had not heard before."

“Pūrṇa! At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Māthā was widely honored and revered by the multitude of people. At that time, everyone said that she was supreme in her observance of the precepts, wisdom, and extensive learning, and that her merit was immeasurable.”

At that time, the bhikṣu Māta entered cities and villages to praise the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa, in order to lead sentient beings into the True Dharma and to cause the Buddha-dharma to be widely disseminated.
Pūrṇa! At that time, the bhikṣu Mādhā led a great multitude of people to provide offerings to and reverently protect the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

Pūrṇa! Thereafter, once the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa had been protected by the bhikṣuṇī Mātā, he entered cities and villages and extensively expounded in various ways the bodhi cultivated by the Tathāgata Sarvaguṇaprabhāsarāja over incalculable kalpas, causing it to spread everywhere.
Thus it was, Pūrṇa!
For a hundred years, the bhikṣuṇī Mādhā constantly followed the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa; all the dharmas she inquired about were always novel and unprecedented, never having been repeated.

Pūrṇa! Because the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa has obtained the protection and assistance of this Bhikṣuṇī Mātā, he causes immeasurable sentient beings to abide in the noble Dharma, and immeasurable sentient beings to abide in the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Pūrṇa! Do you think that the Dharma Master Nārāyaṇa at that time—the protector of the Dharma and the skillful expounder of the Dharma—was anyone else?
He was none other than the Bodhisattva Maitreya.

Pūrṇa! The bhikṣuṇī Mātā protected this Dharma Master, assisted him, and exhorted him; by the power of these merits, after the end of his life, he was immediately reborn in the presence of the Buddha Worldly Multitude (Lokasattva) on the tenth world below, where, before that Buddha, he inquired about the Sūtra for Severing All Doubts of Sentient Beings.
At that time, the Buddha praised him with hundreds of thousands of "Excellent! and immediately expounded for him the Sūtra on Severing All Doubts of Sentient Beings.
While this sūtra was being preached, immeasurable sentient beings first resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and immediately entered the stage of certainty.
Pūrṇa! After the bhikṣuṇī Mādhā passed away, she again encountered the Buddha Sumeru; before that Buddha, she inquired about the *Sarvadharmasaṃgrahanirhārasūtra*.
At that time, the Buddha praised him with hundreds of thousands of "Excellent! and immediately expounded for him at length the *Sarvadharmasaṃgrahaniḥsaraṇasūtra*.
While this sutra was being preached, immeasurable sentient beings became fixed in their attainment of *anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*.
After his life ended, he again encountered Śailendra-rāja Buddha, before whom he inquired about the *Sarva-dharmamukha-sūtra*.
At that time, the Buddha praised him with hundreds of thousands of "Excellent! and immediately expounded for him at length the *Sarva-dharmamukha-sūtra*.
While this sutra was being spoken, immeasurable sentient beings became fixed in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After their lives ended, they again encountered the Buddha Brahmāsvara and, in the presence of that Buddha, requested the *Sarvadharmasaṃgraha Sūtra*.
At that time, the Buddha praised him a hundred thousand times with "Excellent! and immediately expounded for him at length the *Sarvadharmasaṃgraha Sūtra*.
While this sūtra was being preached, immeasurable sentient beings became fixed in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Pūrṇa! In this manner, as the bhikṣuṇī Mādhā proceeded from one to another, she encountered various buddhas; having encountered them, she inquired about the sūtras and brought the sentient beings she saved to abide in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If I were to speak the names of the Buddhas and those sentient beings who dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for an eon, or even more than an eon, I could not reach their end.
Pūrṇa! The number of Tathāgatas whom this bhikṣuṇī Mātā has protected and upheld throughout the True Dharma is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These Buddhas—whether currently in the world or already passed into parinirvāṇa—are beyond all calculation.
Therefore, Pūrṇa! You should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears the Dharma not yet heard and contemplates its meaning and principles, they obtain such great benefits and merits as these.

Pūrṇa! Do you think that the bhikṣu Mahānāmadatta, who at that time heard the Dharma never before heard from the Dharma-master Nārāyaṇa and followed its meaning and intent, was anyone else? It was none other than myself.
He was none other than the Bodhisattva Pāyāsi.

At that time, the bhikṣu Mahānāmadatta protected the True Dharma and heard what he had never heard before; following its underlying meaning rather than clinging to the literal words, he encountered immeasurable Buddhas through these causes and conditions, and having encountered them, he heard various profound and wondrous sūtras.
By virtue of these causes and conditions from past roots of goodness, you now inquire before me regarding the *Sūtra of the Ocean-like Dharma-Gate that Encompasses All Dharmas*.
As I expound it for you, immeasurable sentient beings will obtain great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter once more, spoke in verse:
"When a bodhisattva hears what they have not heard before, they should contemplate its meaning and principle;
they should not say such words as: 'I have never heard this before.'"
Hearing the Dharma never heard before, one contemplates its meaning with right mindfulness;
thus wisdom increases, like the ocean receiving all streams.
As much learning increases further and further, so too does wisdom.
He is able to inquire about the affairs of all Buddhas and extensively benefit all sentient beings.
His accumulation of learning is like the ocean; his wisdom is inexhaustible.
He is well able to understand chapters and verses, being foremost among those who discern distinctions.
"Therefore, you should hear the Dharma never heard before;
by seeking the Dharma never heard before, you shall obtain such a fruit and reward. Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to a profound desire for seeking extensive learning, gives rise to a profound joy for dwelling in secluded places, and with single-minded diligence seeks Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Having made this request, he cultivated the contemplation of loving-kindness to sever hatred, cultivated the contemplation of impurity to sever desire, and cultivated the contemplation of dependent origination to sever ignorance. Pūrṇa!
"What is the vigor of a bodhisattva?
How does a bodhisattva cultivate and accumulate vigor? Pūrṇa!"
If there is a bodhisattva who, for an entire kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, constantly exerts diligence whether walking or sitting—
Pūrṇa, such as this is not called true diligence.

If there is a bodhisattva who practices pure precepts for an eon or slightly less than an eon, performing asceticism and difficult practices while fully observing the dhūtas, yet gives rise to a deep desire for objects of perception and thereby departs from the true reality of all phenomena—this is not called genuine diligence.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the true diligence of a bodhisattva?”
"Praised by all Buddhas and not disparaged by those wise in the world," the Buddha told Pūrṇa:

"When a bodhisattva encounters profound sutras on the emptiness of phenomena that have never been heard before—sutras that lack even the slightest mark and accord with the ultimate truth (paramārtha)—he does not oppose or resist them, but clearly understands their meaning. Diligently exerting his vigor, his mind neither regresses nor sinks; he listens to, receives, reads, recites, and explains them for others. This is called the true vigor of a bodhisattva."

This means that upon hearing profound sutras, one penetrates their meaning without opposition or contradiction; such diligence is praised by all Buddhas and cannot be censured by the wise of the world.
Therefore, Pūrṇa! A bodhisattva should give rise to such an adornment:
"The worldlings cannot reach its bottom; within this, I shall exhaust its very depths."
Wherein worldly beings may sink, I should not sink therein;
wherein worldly beings may fear, I should not be afraid therein.
Why is this? I have resolved upon adornment that does not accord with the world; I resolve upon adornment for the sake of departing from worldly dharmas.
I do not resolve upon adornment by practicing worldly dharmas; I resolve upon adornment for the sake of not practicing worldly dharmas.
One does not cultivate adornment for the sake of conforming to worldly dharmas, but cultivates adornment for the sake of transforming worldly dharmas. Pūrṇa,
this is called the true diligence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"When a bodhisattva accomplishes this second dharma, they shall not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The bodhisattva seeks the profound Dharma, And constantly exerts diligent vigor."
Contemplating its underlying meaning, one does not follow the sounds.
The Bodhisattva does not follow words, knowing them all to be false and deceptive;
because they know all phenomena are empty, they seek only that which is wholesome speech.
If, throughout thousands of myriads of kotis of immeasurable kalpas,
one constantly practices walking and sitting day and night, exerting the mind to perform ascetic austerities,
yet does not believe in sutras previously unheard, that is not true diligence.
One who can reach the bottom of the profound meaning is not called indolent.
Such a person of diligence is praised by all Buddhas;
while the world cannot reach its bottom, the Bodhisattva reaches its bottom.
The world fears submergence, but the Bodhisattva does not fear submergence;
with a diligent mind, he constantly seeks the true, wondrous Dharma of emptiness and stillness.
Within the Dharma of emptiness there is no fear, nor is there any falling away or submergence.
Abiding in the notion of a self and the notion of phenomena, one thus gives rise to fear and sinks.
To disperse and destroy all phenomena is called the path to bodhi;
with a diligent mind and the arousal of vigor, one will swiftly become an ocean of great learning.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

A bodhisattva thoroughly understands the five aggregates, thoroughly understands the twelve bases, thoroughly understands the eighteen elements, and thoroughly understands the twelve links of dependent origination. Because they thoroughly understand the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination, they are able to accomplish the wisdom that is without dependence."
Because they have attained the wisdom of non-reliance, they do not think of or differentiate any phenomena.
Preaching the Dharma for sentient beings through this non-thinking and non-differentiation, they shatter all views so as to uproot the view of a self.
"When a bodhisattva accomplishes this third dharma, they shall not regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The bodhisattva knows the five aggregates, And that the twelve bases are all empty;..."
Discerning the eighteen realms and penetrating the twelve links of dependent origination,
they do not follow after the five aggregates; knowing the body to be deceptive,
they realize that the nature of all internal and external sense bases is empty.
Knowing all phenomena in this way, and having known them, explaining them for others—
therefore, this bodhisattva’s wisdom becomes increasingly vast and sublime. Furthermore, Pūrṇa!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva is well able to train in accordance with the precepts as they are formulated and as they are proclaimed, without any deficiency or transgression.
What is this training in the precepts of a bodhisattva?
To study all dharmas is the bodhisattva’s training in the precepts.
Why is this? Pūrṇa!

The bodhisattva studies all dharmas and attains knowledge of all dharmas; by means of this knowledge of dharmas, he attains non-conceptual wisdom, and by means of this non-conceptual wisdom, he is able to know all things.
How does one know all things?
A bodhisattva fully knows all internal things, all external things, and all internal-external things. Pūrṇa!
Why is it called "internal"?

That which is called "internal" refers to all that is felt and can be clung to; this refers to the internal body produced from the twelve links of dependent origination. Within this, there are only conventional designations, namely: "this eye," "this ear," "this nose," "this tongue," "this body," and "this mind."
Pūrṇa! This is called "internal.
Because ordinary people are greedily attached to these phenomena, they are termed "internal."
They speak thus:
"I shall obtain such eyes and not such eyes; I shall obtain such ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and not such ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
In this context, that which arises solely from the conditions of karmic activity and gives rise to retribution is therefore called "internal.
Within this, ordinary people become attached to its distinctions, referring to the eye, ear, body, nose, tongue, and mind as "internal."
Furthermore, Pūrṇa! That which is called "internal" constitutes duality.
This matter is false and deceptive; yet ordinary worldlings greedily cling to it, grasp at it, and thereby give rise to disputes.
Pūrṇa! Regarding this, the Tathāgata has known it as it truly is from the very beginning and does not cling to it.
How does the Tathāgata know it as it truly is and not cling to it?
The Tathāgata does not take refuge in this dharma.
Who does not take refuge?
It is namely the fetter of craving.

This eye does not constitute a refuge, nor does that which is apart from the eye constitute a refuge; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not constitute a refuge, nor does that which is apart from the mind constitute a refuge. Why is this?
Pūrṇa! The Tathāgata does not apprehend the Dharma internally, nor does he apprehend it externally; therefore, the Tathāgata does not take refuge in this Dharma.
The Tathāgata is a speaker of truth, and he says this:
"Monks! The eye is not yours, nor does it belong to others. Why is this?
Because its essential nature cannot be apprehended,
what dharma is the eye?
To whom does this eye belong?
What dharmas are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
To whom does this mind belong?
For what reason?
"Because its essential nature cannot be apprehended. Pūrṇa!
One should now investigate the eye; one should now investigate the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, so that there is no craving or grasping toward phenomena.
Why is this? If there is the grasping of dharmas, then suffering and affliction arise; because suffering and affliction arise, there is no joy. Therefore, Pūrṇa!
Regarding phenomena, wherever there is grasping, there is suffering; if one suffers, one does not escape suffering. Pūrṇa!
This is called examining the eye, and examining the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—there is no point of entry.
Why is this? Pūrṇa! If there is a point of entry, then there is a point of exit.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said in the sūtras: "The eye is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self;
its intrinsic nature is thus.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; their intrinsic nature is thus."
This nature is non-nature; thus, this non-nature is without creation and without destruction.
Pūrṇa! Such is the nature of dharmas: whether Buddhas arise or Buddhas do not arise, this nature remains eternally abiding.
The Tathāgata knows that all phenomena arise as non-arising; therefore, the Tathāgata is a speaker of truth. He declares:
"Whether a Buddha arises or a Buddha does not arise, this nature remains eternally constant."
“Pūrṇa! What is called ‘non-arising’? What is called ‘knowledge of non-arising’?”
Pūrṇa! The equality of all dharmas is called non-arising; the Path is called the wisdom of non-arising.
The exhaustion of suffering is called non-arising; the Path is called the wisdom of non-arising.
This is what the Tathāgata calls the teaching of two truths: namely, the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.
Pūrṇa! That which the Tathāgata describes as the characteristic of suffering is precisely the teaching of signlessness.
What is called the characteristic of suffering?
It is the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the unconditioned is itself the signless (*animitta*).
The wise know that the unconditioned is signless.
Pūrṇa! How does the wise one know that the unconditioned is signless?

It means knowing that unconditioned dharmas are empty, knowing them to be quiescent extinction, knowing them to be the place of refuge, knowing them to be the supreme benefit, and knowing them to be free from feverish affliction.
The wise one knows the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in this way, and within this wisdom, they do not give rise to signs (*nimitta*).
Pūrṇa! The wise one, free from all signs, attains the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is without fabrication and without destruction.
Pūrṇa! If a person has activity, there is destruction; if there is no activity, there is no destruction.
This mark of non-destruction is emptiness; this mark of non-destruction is signlessness; this mark of non-destruction is wishlessness.

Pūrṇa! In the dharma of emptiness, there is no person who creates it and no person who destroys it; in signlessness and wishlessness, there is likewise no person who creates them and no person who destroys them.
Pūrṇa! This is called the indestructible characteristic of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas.
What is this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas?
"It refers to that which cannot be apprehended by all Tathāgatas.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What kind of phenomena are those which all Tathāgatas do not apprehend? The Buddha said, “Pūrṇa!
"All dharmas are that which cannot be apprehended by the Tathāgatas.
"World-Honored One!
For this reason, are all dharmas the bodhi of the Buddhas?"
The Buddha said: “It is so, Pūrṇa.”
All phenomena are the bodhi of all Buddhas, yet that bodhi is not designated as "all phenomena.
To say that all phenomena are the bodhi of all Buddhas is merely spoken by means of conventional, provisional names; it is difficult for those who lack diligence to understand or know.
Why is this? Those who lack diligence cannot cultivate the equality of all dharmas; if they are not equal, they contend with the Buddha. Pūrṇa!
Who is unable to practice equanimity? Pūrṇa!
All those in the world practice inequality; within the Bodhi of all Buddhas, there is neither equality nor inequality.
Pūrṇa, it is by means of this path that I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, I have stated in my sūtras that all dharmas, within the state of ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), enter into certainty; this is called "entering the gate of bodhi with certainty."
"Therefore, Pūrṇa! All dharmas are bodhi.
At that time, Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare, World-Honored One!

This *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas is both determinate and indeterminate; it both enters into written characters and does not enter into written characters; it both enters into speech and does not enter into speech.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
Having now heard this sutra spoken by the Buddha, I have attained the universal light of certainty regarding all dharmas.
World-Honored One!
I have now thus attained the light of certainty regarding all dharmas; within a single matter I know all matters, and within all matters I know a single matter.
At that time, the Buddha praised Pūrṇa, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Pūrṇa!"

Since you are thus able to swiftly enter into all the benefits of the dharmas of the Buddhas, you should know that in past lives you have already made offerings to the Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and drawn near to them to inquire and seek instruction.
Pūrṇa! I recall that in the past, within this very space of the earth, you have already heard this sutra from sixty-eight thousand buddhas.
"By reason of these roots of goodness and merit, you shall universally attain the light of certainty regarding all dharmas.
"World-Honored One!
If I have already heard this sutra from as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges, why is it that I have not, even for a single thought-moment, resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"I recall that in a past life, during one kalpa, you once gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet, without being mixed with other thoughts, you subsequently fell away from it."
"By virtue of these causes and conditions of merit, I now declare that among all Dharma teachers, you are the foremost.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"What karmic obstacles did I create in my past lives that, having resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* during one eon,
I have now fallen back from it? The Buddha said, "Pūrṇa!"
Because you have followed and relied upon evil associates, and because you were unable to widely disseminate the Dharma, you have regressed and lost your resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Pūrṇa! There are four dharmas that cause one to fall away from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to become a follower of the śrāvaka vehicle.
What are these four?
Because a bodhisattva associates with evil friends, they are able to increase their aversion toward and distance themselves from roots of goodness, saying:
"What is the use of thus generating the mind of enlightenment?"

Birth and death are long and far-reaching, with immeasurable suffering and affliction; as one wanders through the five realms of existence, it is difficult to encounter an age free from calamity, difficult to encounter the Buddhas, and even more difficult to attain pure faith. Although one may encounter a Buddha, it is further difficult to leave the household life.
You have now encountered this time of no calamity; do not lose it again.

Until you have received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddhas, your roots of goodness will not be fixed, you will not attain *nirvāṇa*, and you will continue to transmigrate through the five realms of existence.
When this person hears these words, their mind retreats and sinks; they become indolent and find no joy in the path to bodhi. Pūrṇa!
A bodhisattva who possesses this first quality falls away from bodhi and becomes a follower of the śrāvaka vehicle.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

A bodhisattva does not hear the sūtras appropriate for bodhisattvas—namely, the Sūtras of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, the Sūtras on Generating the Bodhicitta, the Sūtras on Gathering the Bodhisattva Deeds, and the Sūtras corresponding to the Six Pāramitās.

Because they have not heard [the teachings], they do not practice according to what was taught, nor do they train according to what was taught. Such persons do not know which dharmas a bodhisattva should approach and which should be avoided; which dharmas should be accepted and which should not be accepted; or which dharmas constitute the dharma of a bodhisattva and which constitute the dharma of a śrāvaka.

Because they do not know and do not discern in this way, they fail to associate with those dharmas that should be associated with, and instead associate with those dharmas that should not be associated with.

Since these persons fail to associate with the dharmas they should associate with and instead associate with those they should not associate with, they consequently fall away from the Bodhi of all Buddhas; their minds become weak, weary, and disheartened, and they abandon their original vows.
Pūrṇa! If a bodhisattva possesses these two dharmas, they will fall away from bodhi and become followers of the śrāvaka vehicle.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

If a bodhisattva conceives of attaining all dharmas and becomes greedily attached to a self, they will practice false views, fall into extreme views, and sink into evil and deviant states from which they are difficult to extricate.

Upon hearing this profound sutra—which accords with the ultimate truth and is devoid of even the slightest mark—to reject it in disbelief and fail to penetrate its meaning, one incurs the transgression of destroying the Dharma.

By these causes and conditions, they are born in difficult places where they do not encounter a Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, do not meet with the teachings taught by the Buddhas, and do not find virtuous friends.

Because these people do not see the Buddha, they do not hear the Dharma; because they do not hear the Dharma, they do not encounter the teachings instructed by the Buddhas; because they do not encounter the teachings instructed by the Buddhas, they do not find virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); because they do not find virtuous friends, they lose their dwelling in the state of no-affliction and are born in a state of affliction; because they dwell in a state of affliction, they are separated from virtuous friends and encounter evil associates (*pāpamitra*); by associating with evil associates, they forget their original resolve; because these people lose their original resolve, they abandon the Bodhisattva mind, forsake the Bodhisattva vehicle, and consequently regress, forever losing the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). They practice only the dharmas of birth and death and are unable to cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna.
Pūrṇa! If a bodhisattva possesses this third dharma, they will fall away from bodhi and become followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

When a bodhisattva hears such sutras as these, yet is unable to teach and transform others with a profound mind, their spirit becomes discouraged and they take pleasure only in practicing alone; being stingy and withholding the Dharma, they have no desire to preach it, and cannot extensively gather a multitude of people through the Dharma.
Due to these causes and conditions of unwholesome roots, they lose their wisdom and mindfulness.
Having lost their wisdom and mindfulness, they do not recite the sutras and Dharma together with others.
Being unable to share the Dharma with others, such a person, upon changing bodies, loses the bodhicitta and forgets the mindfulness of a bodhisattva.
"Pūrṇa! When a bodhisattva possesses this fourth dharma, they fall away from bodhi and become followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke in verse:
"By associating with evil associates and being indolent regarding bodhi,
through these causes and conditions, they lose the supreme mind of enlightenment.
Giving rise deeply to the false view of self and falling into extreme and heterodox views,"
One incurs the sin of destroying the Dharma and is born in a place of hardship.
Having been born in such a place of hardship, one then severs the bodhicitta and forgets the original mindfulness; for this reason, one loses the bodhi.
Such a person shall not hear the Dharma for generating the bodhicitta;
if this mind were to increase, it could bring about enlightenment.
Having obtained the vast and wondrous Dharma, they are stingy and unwilling to speak of it.
For these reasons, one falls away from bodhi.
A bodhisattva seeking the Mahāyāna should know these four dharmas;
if one knows these four dharmas, bodhi can arise.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from these four evil dharmas;
diligently practice the dharma of emptiness and draw near to virtuous friends.
Having obtained such a sūtra as this, one should not be stingy or parsimonious.
"Explain it for others with a diligent mind; from this, bodhi is born.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will not lose their dedication toward the mind of bodhi, nor will they lose their dedication toward all roots of goodness."
What are the four?

A bodhisattva maintains pure ethical discipline; they achieve mindfulness and possess settled wisdom; they apply themselves with diligent effort without slackening or retreating; and they achieve extensive learning, giving rise to wisdom.
Pūrṇa! When a bodhisattva possesses these four dharmas, they do not lose their dedication toward the mind of enlightenment, nor do they lose their dedication toward all roots of goodness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Bodhisattva fully maintains the precepts; Their mindfulness reaches far back into the past;
With a diligent mind, they should apply themselves with vigor; Abundant learning adorns their wisdom.”
When Bodhisattvas constantly draw near to these four dharmas,
whatever matters arise in their minds will all be successfully accomplished.
Therefore, one should always maintain pure precepts and apply oneself with diligent vigor.
Constantly recollecting the Dharma, one should always diligently seek out much learning.
Pure observance of the precepts purifies one’s place of rebirth; recollecting the teachings purifies wisdom;
diligence purifies the Buddha-dharma, and much learning gives rise to great insight.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should study this supreme Dharma;
having studied this supreme Dharma, they shall turn the unsurpassed wheel. Furthermore, Pūrṇa!
A bodhisattva possesses four dharmas that can benefit awakening:

maintaining the precepts is a dharma that benefits awakening; patience is a dharma that benefits awakening; diligence is a dharma that benefits awakening; and extensive learning is a dharma that benefits awakening.
"Pūrṇa! These are called the four dharmas that benefit bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva’s pure upholding of the precepts benefits awakening;
so too do diligence, patience, and extensive learning.
For one who purely upholds the precepts, all that is wished for shall be accomplished.”
The purity of ethical discipline brings great benefit; awakening is not difficult to attain.
When a bodhisattva practices patience, the marks of the body and wisdom are perfected.
Therefore, one should practice patience, seeking the marks of a Buddha and wisdom.
Vigor likewise can bring great benefit to awakening;
for one who constantly practices vigor, awakening is not difficult to attain.
Hearing much also brings benefit; having heard, one draws near to the Dharma.
Staying far away from what is not the Dharma, enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
These four dharmas are the seeds; from them, enlightenment is born.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should draw near to these beneficial dharmas.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain perfection of physical form, perfection of wealth and possessions, and perfection of retinue; they will never be born in places of evil or hardship, and will always encounter the Buddhas and be praised by those Buddhas."
What are the four?
A bodhisattva practices loving-kindness and does not harbor anger or cause affliction toward any sentient being. Pūrṇa!
What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing loving-kindness so as not to become angry with or to afflict any sentient being?

When a bodhisattva practices loving-kindness, they give rise to a compassion that seeks to save all sentient beings. Seeing that sentient beings experience physical suffering and mental suffering, they should form this thought:
"I shall diligently practice the perfection of vigor to deliver these sentient beings."
"Regarding these sentient beings who suffer within birth and death, I should bestow happiness upon them and I should deliver them, freeing them from the suffering of birth and death.
One should give rise to this mind toward all sentient beings; having given rise to this mind, one should practice with diligent vigor, cultivating the six pāramitās:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Pūrṇa! By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, a bodhisattva attains the fulfillment of the six *pāramitās*.
What is the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva?
"How does a bodhisattva, by means of the perfection of wisdom, diligently exert vigor? "Pūrṇa!
A bodhisattva reflects in this way:"
"What dharma is called 'self,' and what dharma is called 'mine'?
When he reflects in this way, he does not perceive any dharma as self, nor does he perceive any dharma as mine.
He forms this thought:
"Having formed this thought, within these phenomena there is no self-phenomenon and no phenomenon belonging to a self.
Because the Bodhisattva is detached from self and what belongs to a self, he knows the body is empty; because the body is empty, sentient beings are empty.
Why is this? Within all phenomena (*dharma*), even "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*) are empty; how much more so, then, sentient beings?

Because the Bodhisattva thus abandons self and what belongs to self, he knows that sentient beings are empty. Because sentient beings are empty, he knows the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is empty. Because the aggregate of form is empty, the aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-skandha*) are empty.

In this way, because the bodhisattva is detached from "self" and "what belongs to self," he knows that the body is empty; because the body is empty, he knows that sentient beings are empty; and because sentient beings are empty, he knows that the aggregates are empty.

Because the aggregates (*skandha*) are empty, one knows that the elements (*dhātu*) are also empty—namely, the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. The element of earth is empty of the characteristic of the element of earth; the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are each empty of the characteristic of their respective elements.
These seeds have no agent and no instigator; since there is no agent, this dharma is empty. Pūrṇa!

Because the bodhisattva is detached from "self" and "what belongs to self," he knows the body is empty. Because the body is empty, he knows sentient beings are empty. Because sentient beings are empty, he knows the aggregates (*skandha*) are empty. Because the aggregates are empty, he knows the elements (*dhātu*) are empty. Because the elements are empty, he knows the sense bases (*āyatana*) are empty. Because the sense bases are empty, the characteristics of the sense bases are empty.
The various sense bases (āyatana) have no agent and no instigator of action; if a dharma has neither agent nor instigator of action, that dharma is empty.
Pūrṇa! It is by means of this that a bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas as empty.
When contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena, one does not perceive any intrinsic nature of phenomena that could serve as a basis for the arising of anger. Pūrṇa!
This is called the great loving-kindness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Knowing the compassion of the emptiness of the body, the compassion of the emptiness of sentient beings, and the compassion of the emptiness of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements—if a bodhisattva can practice such compassion, it is called practicing the compassion of the emptiness of all phenomena.
Pūrṇa! This is called a bodhisattva practicing great loving-kindness.

In this way, the bodhisattva is detached from "I" and "mine," yet with a mind that deeply gives rise to the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they generate great compassion for all sentient beings.

If there are sentient beings who do not know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all such phenomena, and [the Bodhisattva] dons the great armor in order to cause them to know it, this is called the Bodhisattva practicing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because I rescue them, it is called "loving-kindness" (maitrī); because I act for them, it is called "compassion" (karuṇā).
When a bodhisattva accomplishes such great loving-kindness, they are able to act as a rescuer and a refuge for sentient beings, acting as a shelter, an island, and a final destination.

Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice great loving-kindness in this way: without being greedily attached to sentient beings and without giving rise to anger or resentment. This is called the bodhisattva’s compassion regarding the emptiness of sentient beings, which is free from ill will.

Pūrṇa! If a bodhisattva, by means of compassion, detachment, and emptiness, is able to enter into the non-arising and non-ceasing of all dharmas, this is called a bodhisattva constantly practicing great compassion.
When a bodhisattva thus penetrates all dharmas, neither the māras, nor the māra-folk, nor those sent by the māras can destroy them.
A bodhisattva who accomplishes this first dharma is able to sever the fetters within all merits; because they sever the fetters of merit, they attain the perfection of equanimity (samatā-pāramitā).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva is always thus: Cultivating loving-kindness while contemplating emptiness, Knowing that the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are detached, Within which there is no self."
The two dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self" are definitively unobtainable;
because all dharmas are unobtainable, one practices the mind of loving-kindness.
One does not rely upon any dharmas, nor is it that one does not rely upon them.
This is called the path of all Buddhas, The non-reliance upon any phenomena.
One can attain supreme patience, Patience with the true mark of all phenomena;
That all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, And one is able to skillfully penetrate their principle.
All those who possess great wisdom, by drawing near to this Dharma,
constantly obtain a sublime physical form and also attain the eloquence of joyful speech;
they always encounter the Buddhas and understand the meaning and benefit of all dharmas.
Therefore, this bodhisattva attains the unsurpassed path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, Pūrṇa,

a bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently makes offerings to the stūpas and temples of the Buddhas, with a reverent mind using excellent flowers, incense, garlands, ointments, powdered incense, banners, canopies, music, and various other ritual implements to perform these offerings.
"When a bodhisattva accomplishes this second dharma, they are able to attain the fullness of all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The bodhisattva, with the most excellent and wondrous offerings, Makes worship to the stupas of those of supreme wisdom."
With flowers, incense, banners, and canopies, one seeks supreme wisdom.
By the causal conditions of this merit, one receives a body that is always upright and handsome,
possesses abundant wealth and many rare treasures, and achieves a full assembly of kinsmen.
They will certainly attain enlightenment and always abide securely in the Dharma;
in every place where they are born, their merit will increase ever higher.
They will be revered by all kings and constantly remembered by devas, nāgas, and spirits.
All sentient beings alike shall likewise show them reverence.
Those who make offerings to the Buddha, whether while he is present in the world or after his parinirvāṇa,
will receive offerings wherever they are born and always dwell in places free from calamity.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇa! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should always diligently offer worship to the Dharma.
What is meant by 'Dharma'? "
What is called the "Dharma of offering"?

It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, tranquility and insight, clear knowledge, liberation, the three gates of liberation, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising; these are what is called the Dharma.

What is worship? To act in accordance with what is taught within this Dharma, following it without opposition, and to cultivate it fully through the arousal of desire and diligence—this is called the worship of the Dharma.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

As for making offerings to the Dharma, "Dharma" refers to sūtras such as these; to have faith in, understand, contemplate, discern, and accord with them, while the mind does not oppose them—this is called making offerings to the Dharma.
"When a bodhisattva accomplishes this third dharma, they are able to fully attain all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Constantly and diligently making offerings to the Dharma, Abiding within that which has been taught,"
Hearing the profound and wondrous Dharma of emptiness, their minds do not oppose it;
therefore, their bodies are always upright and handsome, and they also attain the eloquence of joyful speech.
As I have praised this Dharma, by means of it, they grow ever loftier and more exalted.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently makes offerings to the noble assembly of the Tathāgata with flowers or incense, or with necklaces, or with powdered incense, or with ointment, or with banners, canopies, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for life; or by constructing monasteries, or establishing gardens and groves, or by providing places for walking meditation, or with bathing pools, or with wells and springs, or with human attendants—using such various articles of offering as these, they make diverse offerings to this noble assembly."
"When a bodhisattva accomplishes this fourth dharma, they are able to fully attain all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The unsurpassed articles of offering, To offer to the assembly of Tathāgatas,"
By the conditions of these merits, one will possess abundant wealth and treasures in every birth;
one’s physical form will always be upright and handsome, and one will also attain the eloquence of joyful speech.
Endowed with all such virtues, one’s wisdom will grow ever higher and more expansive.
One who makes offerings with an upright mind, free from the notions of "self" and "mine," will,
by virtue of these causes and conditions of wisdom, receive offerings wherever they are born.
Praised by all Buddhas, one should constantly draw near to the four dharmas.
"Those born shall always be noble and honored, and their merit will increase ever higher.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll 77; *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll 78.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Later Qin.
Chapter Four: Endowment with Roots of Goodness. The Seventeenth Assembly: Pūrṇa, Part Two. Chapter Four: Endowment with Roots of Goodness.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇa:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle should always cultivate and draw near to four dharmas; they will then be able to fully encompass all wholesome dharmas and also bring all roots of goodness to fulfillment.”
What are these four dharmas?
Pūrṇa! A son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind cultivates, practices, and draws near to the dharma of patience.

When practicing the dharma of patience in this way, because the mind is impartial, one attains the perfection of equanimity, as well as the perfection of equanimity toward all sentient beings; thus, the bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of mental equanimity and the perfection of wisdom equanimity.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether awake or asleep—should someone come at that time carrying a jar of excrement, a jar of poison, or a jar of boiling water; or carrying various refuse, burning coals, feces and urine, or hot ashes, and strike him upon the head or strike his body—the Bodhisattva should not harbor resentment, allow his mind to become distracted, or give rise to anger. He should not say to himself, "What sin have I committed? nor should he look upon that person with an evil mind. Rather, he should single-mindedly seek the Dharma of self-benefit and remain devoted to his practice without abandoning it.
One should thus subdue the mind, thinking:
"For what reason and by what causal conditions does this person bring this jar of excrement, jar of poison, and embers of fire to afflict my body?"
"My body does not experience pain or affliction because of this object.
At that time, the bodhisattva should contemplate the various causes and conditions in this way: "Who gave this object?"
To whom does this object belong?
By what means is it given?
Thus, when this person reflects according to reality, they do not perceive any phenomenon—neither one who gives, nor one who receives, nor any phenomenon whatsoever.
When one contemplates and reflects with such right mindfulness, because neither this nor that can be apprehended, all phenomena are unapprehendable and invisible.
Because this bodhisattva neither attains nor perceives any phenomena, he does not give rise to anger or resentment. Pūrṇa!
If, despite such reflection, a mind of anger or resentment still arises in the bodhisattva, he should again reflect with correct mindfulness as follows:
"What is the causal condition for contact that causes my body to feel pain?
As for these various contacts, where do they touch?
Do they reside in the body, or do they reside in the mind?"
If it resides in the body, the body is like grass, wood, tiles, or stones—a mere reflection; it is without sensation or cognition, neither "I" nor "another.
If it resides in the mind, the mind has no form or color; it arises and perishes from moment to moment, never abiding for even an instant, neither "I" nor "another."
It is only through false, deluded recollections and conceptual discriminations that one speaks of this as suffering, this as pleasure, and this as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

I should not now give rise to such false, deluded recollections and conceptual discriminations; I should now contemplate the mark of equality and reality; I shall practice what is performed by the noble ones, and should not follow after what is performed by ordinary worldlings.
What is it that is performed by the noble ones?
It is the detachment from and liberation regarding all phenomena.
I train for the sake of detachment, not for the sake of conjunction.
Thus, these false conceptualizations and discriminations are all compounded.
With what are they compounded?
They are compounded with craving.
This is the conjunction of hatred, ignorance, and delusion.
What is meant by the conjunction of greed, hatred, and ignorance?

Because of delusion regarding the body, delusion regarding the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and attachment to the view of a self, when the body undergoes suffering, one feels hatred toward others; this is called the conjunction of hatred.

Because of delusion regarding the view of a self-body and because of craving for the view of a self-body, one gives rise to anger toward others when things do not go as desired; this is called the conjunction with ignorance.
If a person is thus bound by the three poisons and gives rise to such causes and conditions for sinful karma, even the Buddhas cannot save them, let alone other people.
‘I should skillfully contemplate the dharma of all causes and conditions, and contemplate the dharma of emptiness.

Thus, when a bodhisattva correctly contemplates the dharma of all causes and conditions in accordance with reality, they do not perceive any dharma that gives, any recipient who receives, or any object by which one gives.
At that time, the Bodhisattva should form this thought:
"All phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions; their intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty and certainly cannot be apprehended.
How could I, within these unapprehendable and illusory phenomena, give rise to anger or initiate the causes and conditions for conditioned activity by performing actions toward them?"

I should now give rise to a mind free from anger and resentment, practicing the dharma that is unconditioned, unarisen, and unborn; I should contemplate the dharma of emptiness and not follow my own heart's whims.
I should now contemplate the dharma that is unmade, unarisen, and unborn, and should not rely upon dharmas that involve conditioned activity.

I should contemplate all phenomena as they truly are; I should not now forcibly construct phenomena within this which is false and non-existent, for such false and forced construction is called hatred.

Why is this? It is because resentment arises based on the substantial body of phenomena; however, within the ultimate emptiness of the true mark of all phenomena, there is no substantial body of phenomena upon which one can rely.
When the Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena in this way, his mind becomes tranquil and resentment does not arise.

Furthermore, whether this bodhisattva is walking or standing, sitting or reclining, awake or asleep, if someone comes and scatters fine, exquisite powdered incense, incense for burning, and unguents over their body; or if they cover their body with exquisite, fragrant flowers and necklaces—such as *campaka* flowers, *mālatī* flowers, or various flower garlands and necklaces; or if they cover their body with exquisite, soft, and fine garments—namely, *kāśika* cloth, *kauśeya* cloth, *kocamba* cloth, *koseyya* cloth, *kṣauma* cloth, *kārpāsa* cloth, fine *kṣaumapāla* cloth, or fine silk—using such soft and fine garments to cover their body.

If one spreads excellent silken canopies, banners, and streamers over it; if one covers its body with various celestial flowers, incense, exquisite garments, rare jewels, and necklaces; or if one offers up delicious celestial food and drink.

Regarding these various offerings, a bodhisattva should not give rise to craving that causes the mind to become attached, nor should they, on account of these conditions, become intimate with those individuals.
While complying with their wishes by visiting them and exchanging greetings, one should not develop partiality or give rise to attachment.
In this regard, a bodhisattva should employ an impartial mind to penetrate the equality of all phenomena, and should form this thought:
"I should harbor neither hatred nor affection toward sentient beings."
Why is this so? Both hatred and love are afflictions.
I should not now give rise to attachment toward these; rather, I should skillfully and thoroughly understand all phenomena as they truly are.
Why is this so? Among all afflictions, that which is conjoined with the condition of craving is the most heavy.

Such afflictions penetrate deeply to the very marrow of the bones; that is to say, within those phenomena that give rise to fetters and latent tendencies, there is a mind of craving that becomes stained and attached.
Why is this so? If the objects of one's craving and attachment do not accord with one's wishes, then resentment arises.
All people desire to cherish their own bodies; when there is someone who harms or troubles them, resentment arises.
Therefore, you should know that hatred is the retribution for defiled attachment, and craving is the retribution for delusion.
I shall now abandon the evil mind of defiled attachment and remain without any craving or clinging toward any phenomena.

We do not train for the sake of desire, nor do we train for the sake of hatred, nor do we train for the sake of delusion; rather, we shall extensively study the reality of all phenomena, contemplate the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are, and act in accordance with what has been taught.

One should simply rely upon the causes and conditions of karmic retribution; regarding all matters of offerings and afflictions, one should know that these are all the conditions for the practice of past karma. Therefore, one should not give rise to attachment toward favorable phenomena nor hatred toward adverse phenomena. One should only purify the mind so that it is free from resentment, ensuring that evil dharmas following after craving, hatred, or delusion do not arise within the mind.
"Pūrṇa! A bodhisattva who accomplishes this first dharma is able to fully attain all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I have always praised wisdom, and I have also praised those who uphold the precepts;
I have extolled the practice of patience, and I have always praised those of great learning.
I praise those who practice wholesome dharmas, and those whose hearts are compassionate and whose speech is kind."
For the benefit of sentient beings, I praise their various virtues as appropriate to each.
I constantly rebuke those who indulge in the five desires, as well as those who harbor anger and resentment,
and those who are deluded, envious, arrogant, and deceitful— those who defile and disturb sentient beings.
With a mind of indolence and laziness, stubborn and difficult to converse with,
ungrateful and lacking reciprocity, they give rise to great anger over a minor matter.
Greedily seeking gain and offerings, they think, "I shall obtain gain and offerings."
I do not praise those who wish others could not obtain [gain], nor those who,
out of petty wisdom regarding profit and honor, desire to envy what others have;
such people cause suffering for other families, and I do not praise them.
Seeking to obtain gain and offerings, one alters one’s dignified deportment;
such a life is not pure and is far removed from my Dharma.
Those who do not practice the Path incur these various faults.
These conditions for the evil realms are not a single thing worthy of praise.
Without severing the evil view of self, the mind of craving and attachment increases;
because the mind of craving and attachment is great, one diligently seeks profit and offerings.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"By practicing patience, I benefit sentient beings and subdue their stubborn and violent minds, swiftly attaining the path of Buddhahood.
I shall practice a mind of loving-kindness, enduring insults and having compassion for all beings."
Knowing that all phenomena are empty, arising from conditions and belonging to nothing, by what cause do phenomena exist?
These phenomena arise from the mind; through false conceptualization, anger is born; yet when one does not dwell upon them, they are all empty.
Deluded conceptualization gives rise to the three realms, and the continuity of the body is never severed.
If one does not differentiate through conceptualization, then such faults will not exist.
Constantly contemplate all phenomena, knowing that they all arise from conditions.
Constantly contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena, he is able to deliver all beings.
To those who have abandoned the precepts and suffer, and who are harmed by arrogance,
he preaches the Dharma for the cessation of suffering, providing great benefit to many.
If someone comes from the east, or from the south, west, north, or the four intermediate directions,
carrying a jar of excrement and poison and striking me upon my head,
I shall not give rise to a mind of anger; for who is the giver and who is the receiver?
What dharma is called "self"?
Observe it with diligent effort.
Do not look upon others with an evil gaze; for what offense have they committed against you that you should treat them so?
One should simply give rise to firm resolve and cover them with a heart of loving-kindness.
Knowing that this is due to the conditions of past karma and that one now undergoes this retribution,
one should repay it and never do it again, dwelling securely within the path of the Buddha.
Others do not possess this; the matter of being slighted and afflicted must surely be due to karmic conditions, which are not lost even after a long time.
While living beings exist in the world, they constantly give rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma.
I now undergo this suffering; know that it is the result of karmic conditions.
If I were to retaliate with evil, I would again suffer the fruits of misery hereafter.
How could I possibly inflict such evil upon that person?
One should seek the unsurpassed Dharma; having sought it, one should explain it for the sake of others, so as to deliver all classes of sentient beings from every kind of suffering and affliction.
If a person offers me incense, flowers, or jeweled necklaces as an act of worship,
One should not give rise to thoughts of attachment; one should practice the contemplation of equanimity.
Hatred and love are not the Path; one should always cultivate a mind of relinquishment.
One should correctly contemplate all phenomena: who is it that gives, and who is it that receives?
Is emptiness associated with the sensation of emptiness?
Internally empty and externally empty as well—emptiness is without association and without sensation; all things are without self.
Emptiness is free from craving; emptiness is free from afflictions.
There is also no purity; the purity that is free from defilement is emptiness.
Within emptiness there is no discrimination; within emptiness there are no intrinsic natures.
Emptiness is eternally empty and signless—this is the path of purity.
Even if someone were to come and cut my body limb from limb, I would feel no anger within, knowing that it exists through the conditions of karma.
Sentient beings give rise to good and evil; according to their karma, they themselves receive the fruit.
I must have committed evil in previous lives, And now receive this bitter retribution.
Now that I receive this evil retribution, I contemplate the body as being like a reflection, Like foam, a magical illusion, or a mirage; It is not empty, yet ultimately empty.
Even if one's body were to be dismembered, or if someone were to provide for and nurture me,
one who intends to repay such kindness should not regard this as a cause for joy.
One should not take pleasure in gain and offerings, nor harbor anger or resentment toward harsh abuse.
Both of these are obstacles, not the Buddha’s true and correct path.
One should abandon all such things— the mind of craving and the mind of anger—
and constantly cultivate emptiness and stillness, thereby severing all obstacles.
Forbearance is the root of the ten powers, the source of the buddhas' supernormal knowledges,
unimpeded wisdom, and great compassion— all have forbearance as their foundation.
The four truths, mindfulness, right efforts, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment—
All take patience as their foundation; why would one who possesses wisdom not cultivate patience?
At Vārāṇasī, I turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, taking patience as its very basis; all Buddhas always praise patience.
"You all should also cultivate the patience of emptiness and non-arising and non-ceasing;
since the characteristics of all phenomena are eternally thus, you shall attain the merits of a Buddha. Furthermore, Pūrṇa!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to remain detached from the five desires; they always delight in leaving the household life, their minds are inclined toward renunciation, and they advance toward it without craving the five desires.
Having attained the state of a renunciant, they distance themselves from all clamor and bustle, dwelling in remote mountain forests without losing the wholesome Dharma.
"When a bodhisattva accomplishes this second dharma, they will be able to fulfill all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The mind always delights in leaving home, And is thus able to leave home constantly."
Always delighting in mountain forests, the place where merit increases;
staying close to secluded and empty places, one immediately leaves behind attachment to the five desires.
Within these, there is no clamor of the multitude, which causes one to lose the conditions for all wholesome dharmas.
Free from all speech and the affairs of coming and going to inquire after one’s health,
empty, tranquil, and blissful— this is what the Buddhas praise.
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should always draw near to it.
Do not crave the pleasures of the village, nor give rise to a mind seeking gain and offerings.
If one rejoices when gaining offerings and falls into grief and distress when losing them,
such a person may provide for the Buddha, yet it is not called true worship.
"To eliminate such faults, one should abandon all gain and offerings,
dwell in seclusion, and cultivate the dharma of emptiness. Furthermore, Pūrṇa:

A bodhisattva constantly studies and seeks the Dharma; having sought it, they recite it. This means seeking the subtle dharmas of pure precepts and ascetic practices (dhūta), not seeking the dharma of excessive desire and lack of contentment;
