seeking the cessation of greed rather than increasing greed, seeking the destruction of anger rather than augmenting anger, seeking the severance of delusion rather than increasing delusion, and seeking the destruction of arrogance.
One seeks not to give rise to pride, but to destroy the pride of self; one seeks not to increase arrogance, but to sever the dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self.
One seeks the dharma of non-self, not the dharmas of relying upon a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span;
one constantly seeks the dharma that can attain great wisdom, never seeking its loss or decline.
The Dharma of great wisdom constantly seeks to attain the peerless wisdom-dharma; it does not seek to attain the dharma of limited wisdom.
It seeks to attain the fulfillment of all dharmas; it does not seek the non-fulfillment of various meritorious qualities.

Seeking such a Dharma, having sought it, one reads and recites it, contemplates and correctly observes it, practices according to what has been taught, and expounds it for others, without seeking worldly gain or even praise such as "well done," but rather teaching many sentient beings to abide in this Dharma.
"Pūrṇa! When a bodhisattva accomplishes this third dharma, they are able to fully attain all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva delights in leaving the household life, upholding the precepts and practicing the dhūtas;
by these means, wisdom increases, and the rain of wisdom flows forth in endless benefit.
Having attained this profound and pure Dharma, one contemplates its meaning with right mindfulness.”
Regarding that which has been thus taught, one is able to practice exactly as heard.
Always with a pure mind, one extensively explains it for others,
benefiting all sentient beings without harboring any expectation in the heart.
Having attained the flavor of all merits, one abides personally within this Dharma and causes others to abide therein as well; thus, the Buddha-dharma increases.
Whatever merits have been accumulated throughout immeasurable eons—
Causing all [these qualities] to manifest before them, they are gathered into the path of the bodhisattva.
Therefore, one should seek the profound Dharma praised by the Buddha;
constantly expounding it for the sake of sentient beings, merit arises from this.
“Pūrṇa! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide securely in the dhūta practices of upholding the precepts, they are able to fulfill all roots of goodness and merit. Pūrṇa!”

In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Merukūṭa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The Buddha’s lifespan was sixty years.
During a single assembly for preaching the Dharma, eight billion bhikṣus attained the path of arhatship. Pūrṇa!
After the parinirvāṇa of Merukūṭa Buddha, the Dharma remained for five hundred years.
Seven days after his parinirvāṇa, all the great disciples likewise followed the Buddha into nirvāṇa.
Pūrṇa! This Buddha has appeared in a world of the five turbidities, just as I do now.
After the great disciples have entered parinirvāṇa, many sentient beings will all think thus:
"In the Dharma of the śramaṇas there is peace and happiness.
Why do we not all go forth together?
Having thought this, they all shaved their hair and beards and went forth, donning the dharma robes.
After leaving the household life, they practice only three things:

first, they constantly frequent the homes of laypeople; second, they live solely by greedily clinging to gain and offerings; third, they nourish their physical bulk without possessing merit or wisdom.
Practicing these three matters and not cultivating other activities, after a hundred years all the great disciples will have completely passed away.

These bhikṣus will mostly associate with laypeople; they will largely abandon the Buddha’s profound sūtras, the precepts, the dhūta practices, and the subtle dharmas, no longer reciting or studying them.
Pūrṇa! At that time, the community of bhikṣus delighted in practicing the five desires and were greedily attached to food and drink.
At that time, the king had an only son named Dharmasiri, whom the king cherished and held in high esteem. Once, while in a secluded place, he had this thought:
"What dharma has the Buddha Merukūṭa attained?
Now his disciples are all negligent, acting no differently than laypeople.
While he was reflecting with such doubt, a deva came to him, remaining invisible and spoke these words:
"O Prince! The profound Dharma attained by the Buddha Merukūṭa is pure and definitive.
At that time, having heard what the deva said, the prince immediately spoke these words:
"What is the nature of the profound Dharma, pure and definitive, attained by the Buddha Merukūṭa?
He replied, "O Prince!..."

This Dharma is without form, without sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is without aggregates, elements, or sense bases; it is without the five desires, nor is there a mind of desire.
The Buddha Mirokandha attained this profound Dharma of pure certainty and preached it for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, the prince again asked the deva:
"May we be permitted to hear this Dharma?
May we understand it as it is taught and practice accordingly?"
The deity said: "O Prince!
If you can practice with single-minded diligence and vigor, it will not be difficult for you to attain it."
"Pūrṇa! At that time, the prince immediately thought to himself:
'It is now this celestial deity who has awakened my mind; I shall leave the household life to seek this profound Dharma.'"
He immediately went to his parents, prostrated himself with his head at their feet, and said to them:
"I now wish to leave the household life and practice the Way within the Dharma of Maitreya Buddha."
The parents replied,
"Why do you now wish to leave us and go forth into homelessness?
Nowadays, among the followers of the Buddha's Dharma, laypeople are no different from those who have gone forth."
At that time, his parents replied in verse:
"Now these assemblies of bhikṣus, Negligent, indulge in the five desires;
Plowing, sowing, and engaging in trade— They are no different from laypeople."
Those who are impoverished and beset by many afflictions, unable to sustain themselves,
leave the household life for the sake of seeking a livelihood.
You, however, are now born into a royal family, enjoying wealth, pleasure, and the five sensory desires.
"With so many rare treasures and possessions, what is the use of leaving the household life?
Prince Dharmasiri replied to his parents in verse:
"I do not seek honor or rank; even if I were to obtain them, I would renounce them."
Now I seek only this: the profound and pure precepts of the Buddha-dharma.
A deity has awakened me and urged me to go forth;
I hope that I shall come to understand the profound Dharma taught by the Buddha.
"Having heard what the deva has spoken, my heart is filled with great joy;
since the Buddha-dharma is now about to perish, I shall assist in its protection and upholding.
His parents replied to Dharmasiri in verse:
“The profound sūtras have already perished, and there is no one left to recite them;
from whom now shall you hear the Buddha’s profound Dharma?”
"If among the fourfold assembly there be one who recites the profound meaning,
you should first receive it from him, and only then may you go forth into homelessness.
Dharmasiri replied to his parents in verse:
"I now exert myself with diligent vigor, practicing pure precepts and dhūta austerities in remote mountain forests,
seeking the Buddha’s profound and pure Dharma."

"Pūrṇa! After Dharmasiri had spoken this verse, he prostrated himself at their feet, took his leave, and departed to renounce the household life; his parents remained silent and were unable to restrain him."
He immediately went to the bhikṣus, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya robes, and received the precepts. With a heart of reverence, he asked the bhikṣus:
"How does the Buddha Merukūṭa preach the Dharma and instruct his disciples?"
"Having heard this, we shall practice according to what has been taught. Pūrṇa!
Thus did the bhikṣus speak to the bhikṣu Dharmasiri.
"We have not heard the Dharma taught by the Buddha; we merely follow the practices of our preceptors and teachers.
You, too, should now practice such a Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmasiri replied to the bhikṣus, saying:
"You all must have left the household life out of poverty and low status; therefore, you now value only food and clothing, and your conduct is no different from that of laypeople.
You should now seek the profound and pure Dharma of the Buddha together with me."
Then the bhikṣus replied to the bhikṣu Dharmasiri in verse:
"What we have undertaken, all these matters have already been accomplished;
our clothing and food are most abundant, and we are free from the king's corvée labor."
Tranquil and exceedingly joyful, no one dares to treat them with contempt;
the suffering and affliction of their time as laypeople now no longer exist at all.
This is what is called Nirvana, the supreme and most blissful peace.
Beyond these matters, I shall no longer have any use for them.
We possess many robes and alms bowls, and our medicinal decoctions and drugs are very abundant;
laypeople constantly provide us with gifts, and the households of our donors are likewise numerous.
"Pūrṇa! At that time, when the bhikṣu Dharmasiri heard these verses spoken by the bhikṣus, his heart was filled with grief and distress; he shed tears and wept aloud."
He went to another monastery and again asked the bhikṣus about this matter:
"How does the Buddha Merukūṭa preach the Dharma and instruct his disciples?
Having heard it, I shall practice according to what he teaches."
The assembly of bhikṣus answered in the same manner.

Thereupon, the bhikṣu Dharmasiri immediately left those bhikṣus and entered alone into a remote and secluded place within the mountain forests, where he cultivated single-minded sincerity, desiring to seek the profound Dharma.

Formerly, among the disciples of the Buddha Merukūṭa, there was a great disciple named Dṛḍha. He practiced in seclusion, dwelling alone in deep mountains; having few desires and being content, his mind delighted in solitude. Having accomplished what was to be done, he was a Great Arhat endowed with the six supernormal powers and the three types of clear knowledge, just like my Mahākāśyapa here today.
On the wall of a mountain cave where the bhikṣu Sthira resided, he inscribed this verse:
“Because they crave and relish the flavors of desire, The cycle of birth and death is never severed.
Nourishing their enemies, they enter the burial mounds, Vainly enduring all manner of suffering and toil.”
The body stinks like a corpse; from its nine orifices flow impurities.
Just as dung-worms delight in filth, the fool’s craving for the body is no different.
Conceptualization and false discrimination are the very root of the five desires.
The wise do not engage in discrimination, and thus the five desires are severed and extinguished.
From wrong mindfulness arises craving and attachment; from craving and attachment arise afflictions.
Through right mindfulness there is no craving or attachment, and all other afflictions are likewise exhausted.
"Pūrṇa! The bhikṣu Dṛḍha had written these four verses upon the wall of a stone cave.
The bhikṣu Dharmasiri, while traveling through the deep mountains, saw these four verses on the wall of that stone cave."

Having seen it, he recited and contemplated its meaning; before long, he attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and went to the place where the Buddha Merukūṭa had formerly undergone cremation.
Upon arrival, he prostrated, circumambulated the site three times, sat down cross-legged, and made this vow:
"I shall not rise from this spot until I have seen the Buddha and heard the other teachings."
"Pūrṇa! The sūtra spoken by the Buddha Merukūṭa is titled 'The Eight Hundred Thousand Gates,' and Śakra Devānām Indra recited and upheld this sūtra.

Knowing that the bhikṣu Dharmasiri deeply loved the Dharma in his heart, Śakra Devānām Indra descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to where he was and preached for him the sūtra of the Eight Hundred Thousand Gates, as well as the four fundamental phrases of much learning, the seven kinds of repeated phrases, and the fourteen gate-phrases."

Having heard this, the bhikṣu Dharmapriya took it up and recited it; he attained the light of wisdom regarding all dharmas, and the profound and subtle sūtras spoken by the Buddha Merukūṭa—concerning purity, emptiness, and detachment—naturally arose within his mind.

Furthermore, the Buddha Merukūṭa manifested his own body, as well as the assembly of bhikṣus, the monastery where he resided, and the couches and beds; he caused the great assembly of the fourfold congregation—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all others—to behold them all.

The bhikṣu Dharmasiri, having attained the eye of wisdom regarding all phenomena, rose from his seat and traveled by stages until he returned to his native land. Arriving at the place where his parents were, he preached for them profound and wondrous sūtras concerning purity, emptiness, and detachment, extolling and praising the merits of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"Pūrṇa! At that time, the parents, palace attendants, ministers, and officials of the bhikṣu Dharmasiri, having heard this Dharma, developed faith and reverence. They said to the bhikṣu Dharmasiri:
'We pray only that the Venerable One will deliver us, so that we may go forth in the Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha Merukūṭa.'"
"Pūrṇa! At that time, eighty-four thousand people followed the king and the queen and left the household life all at once.
After they had gone forth, they were all known as the community of bhikṣus called Dharmasiri."

Pūrṇa! This bhikṣu Dharmasiri caused the Buddha-dharma of Merukūṭa to continue and blaze forth once more, enabling many sentient beings to dwell within it; this was because in his past lives he possessed a heart of great compassion and made a vow to protect the Dharma.

Thereupon, the bhikṣu Dharmasiri traveled from one village to another, from city to city, and from kingdom to kingdom, wandering about and extolling the merits of the Buddha Merukūṭa and his disciples.
Furthermore, he extensively expounded and explained for the sake of all sentient beings the profound sutras and dharmas that accord with purity, emptiness, and detachment.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmapriya was widely honored, revered, respected, and praised by the multitude, and his fame spread far and wide.
Pūrṇa! After the bhikṣu Dharmapriya had thus extensively benefited all sentient beings, he subsequently passed away.
His disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all gathered together in harmony and prepared a pyre of every kind of fragrant wood to perform the cremation as an offering.

Together they shall erect a stupa ten li in length and breadth, making offerings of various flowers, powdered incense, ointments, necklaces, banners, and canopies, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it.
“Pūrṇa! When the bhikṣu Dharmasiri was approaching the end of his life, he made a vow to be reborn again within this Jambudvīpa.
He immediately fulfilled that vow and was born into a royal family, named Smṛtiprāpta.”

During the Dharma of the three hundredth year after the Buddha Merukūṭa, he left the household life; by virtue of his original vows and his knowledge of past lives, he naturally regained all the gate-words and dhāraṇī-words.

By virtue of having attained the power of dhāraṇī, he is able to expound and explain extensively for sentient beings those sutras he had not previously heard, rather than repeating what he had already spoken in former lives.

Pūrṇa! At that time, among the assembly of Dharmasiri bhikṣus, those who possessed profound wisdom, sharp intelligence, and thick roots of goodness, upon hearing the various sūtras spoken by Smṛti, all rejoiced in their hearts, accepted them with faith, and venerated them; they made offerings to and protected the bhikṣu Smṛti.

Among them were bhikṣus who lacked majestic virtue and possessed dull faculties—those who were stubborn, ignorant, and obstructed, with meager roots of goodness. Upon hearing the new Dharma taught by the bhikṣu Smṛti, they did not believe or accept it, but instead opposed and reviled it, saying:
"We have never heard such sūtras as these from our preceptors or teachers, nor have we ever heard them from the great master Dharmasiri."

"Pūrṇa! Among them, those of profound wisdom who rely upon the meaning do not follow mere words; because they rely on the meaning, their minds do not oppose it, and because they do not oppose it, they protect the Dharma of Mount Meru-Keṭa Buddha and reverently guard the monk Smṛti."
Pūrṇa! At that time, there were eighty nayutas of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who, in accordance with what the bhikṣu Anuprāptasmṛti had preached, attained the Dharma of the sūtras.
Pūrṇa! At that time, the assembly of disciples of Dharmasiri was divided into two groups:
the first was called the community of monks of Dharmasiri, and the second was called the community of monks of Smṛtilabdha.
The bhikṣu Smṛti does not say of himself, "I am Dharmasiri. Why is this?
Because all people consider the bhikṣu Dharmasiri to have attained the path of arhatship rather than being a bodhisattva; if he were to speak of himself [in that way], people would become doubtful.
Everyone knew that the bhikṣu Smṛti was a bodhisattva and not an arhat.
Pūrṇa! After the bhikṣu Smṛti had thus extensively benefited all sentient beings, he later passed away.
The assembly of disciples used all kinds of fragrant wood to build a pyre and performed the offering by cremating his body.

The fourfold assembly gathered from all directions, desiring to make offerings to the Great Teacher, the Bodhisattva; together they erected a stupa five li in length and breadth, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising him with various flowers, powdered incense, unguents, perfumes, necklaces, banners, and canopies.
"Pūrṇa! When the bhikṣu Pratismṛti was approaching the end of his life, he again made a vow to be reborn in this Jambudvīpa.
In accordance with his vow, he was born into the family of a great elder named Yaśas."

By virtue of his original vow, he attained the knowledge of past lives; during the four hundredth year of the Buddha Mervāndana, at the age of seven, he left the household life to pursue the Way and attained all the dhāraṇīs.
By the power of the dhāraṇī, he was able to preach for others sūtras never heard before.

Thereupon, the assembly of bhikṣus known as Smṛti and the assembly of bhikṣus known as Dharmasiri—among whom were those with deep roots of goodness—heard the various teachings spoken by Yaśas; their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all attained the bliss of the Dharma.

Pūrṇa! These bhikṣus rely upon the meaning and do not follow the mere words; therefore, when they hear the Bhikṣu Yaśas recite the profound sūtras on emptiness that they have never heard before—which accord with the primary truth—they accept them with faith and without opposition, and are able to receive, uphold, and recite them, practicing according to what has been taught.

Pūrṇa! Among them, there will be bhikṣus who are dull-witted, obscured by darkness, and possessed of meager roots of goodness. Having heard from the bhikṣu Yaśas discourses never before heard—discourses that accord with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and correspond to the profound emptiness—they will neither believe nor accept them, but instead will oppose, reject, and destroy them, saying:
"We have not heard such teachings from our preceptors or teachers, nor have we heard them from the Great Master Bodhisattva Smṛti."

"Pūrṇa! Those who, having heard the Dharma from the bhikṣu Yaśas, received it with joy and faith, were all [excluded] by the bhikṣus Dharmapriya, Smṛti, and others, who out of malice, envy, and contempt would not allow them to dwell there, nor would they study, recite, or expound the sūtras and Dharma with them. On the contrary, they slandered them, saying:
'This is not the Buddha’s Dharma; this is not the teaching of the Great Master.'"

"Pūrṇa! At that time, the bhikṣu Yaśas widely proclaimed and disseminated the Dharma of Merudhvaja Buddha. Traveling from one village to another, he preached for the sake of sentient beings, bringing great benefit to many, and transformed eighty billion nayutas of people, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Such was the benefit provided by the bhikṣu Yaśas; subsequently, he passed away.

There were seventy thousand people who had followed the bhikṣu Yaśas, and they erected seventy thousand stūpas for him, making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and offering praise with various flowers, incense, perfumes, powdered incense, garlands, banners, and canopies.
"Pūrṇa! When the bhikṣu Yaśas was approaching the end of his life, he again made a vow to be reborn in this Jambudvīpa.
After his death, he attained rebirth in a royal family in accordance with his vow. At the time of his birth, the devas raised a great voice, saying:"
"Since the one now born as a king will bring great benefit to sentient beings," it was said;
thus, following this voice, he took the name *Śāstṛ* (Teacher).
When he reached the age of fourteen, during the fifth century of the Dharma of Maitreyananda Buddha, he left the household life to study the Way.

This guiding bhikṣu extensively recited the sūtras and scriptures; he was deeply learned and possessed profound insight. His phrasing was elegant and eloquent, and he was skillful in preaching the Dharma. Pūrṇa!
This guiding bhikṣu traveled from one village to another, from city to city, and from kingdom to kingdom, spreading the teachings of the Buddha Merukūṭa and bringing great benefit to many.
At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus—Dharmasiri, Smṛti, and Yaśas—all gathered together and approached the Teacher, desiring to refute and destroy [his teachings].
At that time, the guide-monk, knowing that the monks had arrived, spoke these words:
"Monks, what matters do you wish to inquire about?
On account of what matters do you ask?"
"How do you ask such a question?
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they were filled with sorrow and distress; remaining silent and unable to respond, they could not obstruct the Teacher Bhikṣu.
Pūrṇa! As long as this bodhisattva’s lifespan remains in the world, the Buddha-dharma will flourish; following his passing, the Buddha-dharma will then perish.

At the end of time, in the evil age when the Dharma is about to vanish, this guiding bhikṣu will travel from village to village, from city to city, and from kingdom to kingdom, expounding for the sake of many sentient beings the pure and profound sūtras that accord with emptiness. He will transform eight million people, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and at the end of their lives, they will all be reborn in the heavens.
Pūrṇa! Such is the benefit provided by this guide, the bhikṣu.
Tonight his life will end, and tomorrow night the Dharma will perish.
Pūrṇa! Because the Dharma of Merukūṭa Buddha has perished, all those profound, pure, and sūtras corresponding to emptiness have entirely vanished. Pūrṇa!
In this way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of these profound sutras, protects the Buddha-dharma and is able to personally fulfill his own roots of goodness and merit. Pūrṇa!
After the life of this Guide Bodhisattva has ended, he will be reborn in the tenth world upward from that land.
At that time, that Buddha was named Sūryanetra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He immediately renounced the world;

by virtue of the causes and conditions of the roots of goodness and merit from his past lives, he possessed profound wisdom, sharp intelligence, inexhaustible eloquence, and swift, unimpeded discernment.
This guide-monk, within the Dharma of the Buddha Sunetra, practiced all wholesome dharmas for eighty-four thousand years.
At the end of his life, he was reborn and encountered a second Buddha named Vardhamānaskandha.
Thereupon, having left the household life under that Buddha to cultivate and accumulate roots of goodness and seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he was reborn in this land after his death.

He again encountered a subsequent Buddha named Amoghasiddhi Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, under whose Dharma he once more entered the monastic life. For seventy thousand years, he diligently cultivated roots of goodness, seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; at that time, he was known as Śūra-Amoghasiddhi.
The Buddha bestowed upon him this prediction, saying:
"After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu Śūra shall attain Buddhahood; his name shall be Anāvaraṇacakṣus Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Pūrṇa! When a bodhisattva accomplishes this third dharma, they are able to attain the full perfection of all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
When a bodhisattva hears the profound, pure, and definitive Dharma,
they are able to dwell in it themselves and likewise teach others.
Though the world finds no bottom, the bodhisattva does not sink.
Abiding in pure precepts, he extensively benefits all sentient beings.
Through past lives and parables, he reveals the Buddha-way to the multitude.
This is what has been taught by all Buddhas; this is the definitive Dharma.
The Bodhisattva is able to practice what is beneficial and is likewise able to benefit sentient beings;
they protect all Buddha-dharmas and instruct the multitude in bodhi.
Whatever tasks sentient beings perform according to the Dharma, the Bodhisattva performs them all for their sake.
Teaching the multitude the Buddha-way, one draws near to Bodhi.
Protecting and upholding the Way of all Buddhas, one also brings vast benefit to sentient beings;
such a person is revered and sustained by devas, nāgas, spirits, and great men.
Therefore, having heard the pure and profound, wondrous Dharma of all emptiness, one should contemplate and seek it with a single mind;
thus, wisdom will increase. Furthermore, Pūrṇa!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fulfill all practices; because they fulfill all practices, they are able to fulfill roots of goodness and merit.
What are these practices? Pūrṇa!
A bodhisattva draws near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and practices generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means.
What constitutes a bodhisattva’s spiritual friend?

The Buddhas and Arhats from whom a bodhisattva hears such a sutra as this, as well as those bodhisattvas with profound resolve who seek the Buddha-way and provide the skillful means for their transformation—all these are called the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
"When a bodhisattva accomplishes this fourth dharma, they will be able to fulfill all merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The dharmas that bodhisattvas Should practice, I have now explained."
Having given, the mind is joyful, without any regrets.
What is meant by joy? It is a bliss that pervades the entire body; with this ever-joyful mind, one practices the path of the bodhisattva.
Whatever the Bodhisattva gives in charity, he dedicates toward enlightenment to benefit all sentient beings; thus his own benefit is immeasurable.
If he sees a beggar, he conceives of them with the thought of a Buddha.
I reflect that this person has now come to bestow upon me the Buddha-way.
Because of this person, I shall attain a pure buddha-land;
this person shows me the Buddha and instructs me in the Buddha-way.
Now that I have encountered this person, I have swiftly attained great auspiciousness;
joy fills my entire body, and I take no pleasure in anything else.
If anyone comes to visit me, they see me from afar and offer their greetings.
"O Benevolent One, what do you require?
I shall give it all to you.
Even if you say that you have no need for anything, the Bodhisattva will still rejoice."
Desiring to transform and instruct me, he said that he required nothing.
This worthy one, by means of the dharma of few desires and contentment which he delights in,
has now come to awaken me, providing the conditions for me to attain Bodhi.
Because of this person, I have now been able to further teach you the Dharma;
your statement that nothing was required was truly excellent.
Had you said that you needed these things, I would have given them to you.
If a bodhisattva possesses [something], they say with joy, "Take this.
Having practiced giving, they have no regrets thereafter;
because they mindfully recollect the Buddha-way, their minds are always filled with joy.
Having practiced giving, I dedicate the merit so that all sentient beings may have their share,
universally ensuring they lack nothing and causing them all to attain contentment.
If one practices the Bodhisattva path, when sentient beings hear my name,
Naturally knowing contentment, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess or greed.
Now the sentient beings in my land follow the Way and are all satisfied;
having abandoned attachment to the five desires, they all delight in practicing the life of renunciation.
Thus dedicating these immeasurable practices through giving,
may I always practice generosity, and may sentient beings likewise follow my example.
When a Bodhisattva practices giving, they cover all sentient beings with compassion.
In all the worlds, there is no such bliss.
It is like a great wealthy elder who possesses abundant riches and many treasures,
yet has only one son who has been traveling for many long years.
When the elder heard that his son had returned, joy filled his entire body;
having been parted for so long, his return was like being born again.
When the Bodhisattva saw the beggar, his heart was filled with great joy.
The portion of joy belonging to the layperson is not even one-sixteenth of it.
Once one has performed such an act, the mind becomes greatly joyful;
the bliss born of a compassionate heart is beyond compare.
Just as when a king punishes a criminal, commanding his limbs to be severed,
and the executioner leads him to the place of execution with the sword raised, poised to strike—
yet the king pardons him and bestows upon him a position of honor, that person will be filled with great joy.
Still they do not equal the Bodhisattva, who finds joy and happiness in giving to the poor.
When the Bodhisattva practices the Way, he does not seek out fields of merit;
whenever there is one who begs, he gives immediately, and thus attains great joy and happiness.
If a bodhisattva encounters a Buddha, An arhat, or a pratyekabuddha, With a reverent heart, knowing such an encounter is rare, They go to offer worship and gifts.
The bodhisattva possesses majestic virtue; Their mind is sharp, clear, and well-disciplined.
Delighting in meritorious virtues and seeking the Path, they make offerings to the Buddhas and the Sangha;
yet they do not serve the various celestial deities with deep reverence,
except for the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
If there are pratyekabuddhas who have spontaneously attained nirvāṇa, one should likewise practice and make offerings to them; such are these various merits.
The bodhisattva is also able to know whether a field of merit is wholesome or unwholesome.
The wise of the world do not revere evil outsiders;
They abide securely in the category of upholding the precepts, Enveloping all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness,
Possessing peerless diligence, And vast, extensive patience, wisdom, and learning.
Practicing these various merits, one becomes highly honored in the world;
able to realize the Buddha’s bodhi, one turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
When a bodhisattva is able to practice these four supreme dharmas in this way, they attain such excellence.
All roots of goodness, all appear before one.
The various merits cultivated through immeasurable billions of eons—
all are gathered and entered into this path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness;
having left the household life to dwell in mountain forests, they should delight in secluded places.
They should always seek the pure, profound, and definitive Dharma.
"Perfecting the bodhisattva practices, thereby causing them to increase within oneself. Chapter Five:

Supernatural Powers At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernatural powers, emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light from every single pore of his body. Furthermore, from each and every pore, he produced great, fierce flames as large as Mount Sumeru. Moreover, from each and every pore, there issued forth Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the great assembly everywhere beheld such supernatural powers.
Then, having manifested these powers, the World-Honored One returned to his former state and addressed Pūrṇa, saying:
"Did you see the Tathāgata emit these supernatural powers from all his pores?"
“I have seen them, World-Honored One. “Pūrṇa!
The Tathāgata always possesses such supernormal powers without ceasing or interruption.

Now, my disciples merely know that the Tathāgata is here preaching the Dharma; yet in truth, I am constantly performing Buddha-work in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions without rest, and I likewise preach the Dharma in this manner throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Pūrṇa! If one speaks the truth, who is this peerless and incomparable person?

This field of merit among two-legged beings is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; when a practitioner of boundless conduct lifts a single step, all sentient beings are unable to know it and unable to conceive of it.
"With what thought, with what conduct, and with what intention does the Tathāgata lift his foot and set it down?
I shall explain this to you, Pūrṇa!
All sentient beings are unable to fathom the thought, the mind, or the conduct by which the Tathāgata lifts his foot and sets it down."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"With what intention does the World-Honored One act? With what conduct does he lift and set down his feet?"
Whether moving or still, sentient beings never know this matter.
His supernormal powers are immeasurable, and his sphere of activity is likewise immeasurable.
Because his merit is immeasurable, he is the foremost, most exalted, and most venerable.
His great divine wisdom is immeasurable; no one is able to know it exhaustively.
Even if all people possessed wisdom and supernormal powers equal to those of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, [they could not fathom it].
They cannot even know the matter of my lifting and lowering my feet;
even if all people were to become pratyekabuddhas,
they would not know a single step of mine, much less the other profound teachings of the Buddha-dharma.
Even if one were to combine immeasurable suns and moons into a single solar disc,
it could not equal the light from a single pore of the Tathāgata.
Even if there were seventy trillion nayutas of worlds...
The solar disc, equal in length and breadth, shines universally upon immeasurable lands.
Such great suns, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, merge to form a single sun; its single ray of light is like Mount Sumeru.
Thus these great suns constantly illuminate the worlds of the ten directions;
yet compared to the Buddha’s radiance, they do not appear, like trees withered by fire.
These rays of the great suns cannot even penetrate the leaves of a tree.
All mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs are capable of acting as obstructions;
yet where the light of the Tathāgata shines, all Mount Sumerus,
the Iron Ring Mountains, and the Vajra Mountains pass through it without any hindrance.
With the power of his radiant supernormal faculties and immeasurable majesty and virtue,
who would not give rise to the resolve for enlightenment— save for those lacking faith?
When sentient beings see such great divine power of light,
many resolve upon the unsurpassed mind, thinking, "We too shall attain it.
At that time, the Buddha smiled, and Ānanda immediately inquired:
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you smile?
I pray that you, with your unimpeded wisdom, will answer.
Then the Buddha replied to Ānanda:
“Sentient beings who now behold the great supernatural power manifested by me, shall resolve their minds to become Buddhas.
Among the assembly, thirty thousand people vowed to protect and uphold this Dharma, saying:
“After the Buddha’s passing, we shall praise and recite such a sutra as this.”
"After my parinirvāṇa, these people shall hear this Dharma of the sutra;
having heard it during the middle and later periods, they shall practice according to what was taught.
It is difficult to give rise to the mind of enlightenment; it is difficult to take deep delight in the Buddha-dharma."
In future ages, to be able to uphold and recite such sutras as these is even more difficult.
Throughout kalpas numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions, the appearance of Buddhas is extremely rare;
yet in the final dharma-ending age, to preach this sutra is even more difficult.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"I entrust these sūtras such as these to you doubly. Why is this?"
"Within Jambudvīpa, wherever such a Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka exists, there the Buddha-dharma exists.
Ānanda! Because such profound sūtras as these perish, the practice of the Dharma as it has been taught will likewise perish."
As it is said: "Because the practice of the Dharma perishes, the Buddha-Dharma perishes. Ānanda!
You should now honor me with the foremost offering."
What constitutes a disciple’s offering to me with the foremost of all offerings?

You should not think in your heart that excellent flowers, fine incense, powdered incense, ointments, banners, canopies, necklaces, garments, music, or the chanting of praises for the Tathāgata constitute the supreme offering.
Ānanda! This is not called the foremost offering.

If a person hears such profound sūtras as these, receives, upholds, reads, recites, and practices according to what is taught, this is called making offerings, showing respect, honoring, and praising the Buddha with the foremost article of offering.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas together offer worship, reverence, and respect to the Dharma, rather than valuing the various worldly articles of offering.
Therefore, Ānanda!
I now entrust this sutra to you with utmost gravity and earnestness.
Why is this? Ānanda!
I studied such sūtras as these and have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
When the Buddhas of the past were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, they also studied such sūtras as these, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
The Buddhas of the future will also study such sūtras as these, and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

The Buddhas currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions, when they were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, also studied such sūtras as these, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and are now turning the wheel of Dharma.
Therefore, Ānanda! This *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* is called the *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra*; you should uphold it.
It was there, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, that I turned the wheel of Dharma for my śrāvaka disciples.
Ānanda! Here now, within this Bamboo Grove, I turn this non-retrogressive wheel of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra to sever all the doubts of sentient beings. Ānanda!

All the Buddhas of the past have also taught this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra on this very spot of empty ground; all the Buddhas of the future will also teach this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra on this very spot of empty ground; and I, having now attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, likewise teach this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra on this very spot of empty ground.
Therefore, you should know that this place is a great stūpa of the Buddha, a site of veneration for gods, humans, and the entire world.
Ānanda! This place possesses a unique and extraordinary merit: it is here that the Buddhas of the past have preached various profound sūtras.
Ānanda! All sentient beings who possess greed, hatred, and delusion, upon entering this Bamboo Grove, do not give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion. Ānanda!
Although the Tathāgata has resided in various other monasteries, none possess such merit as this.
Why is that? Ānanda!
Now, in this Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, when animals enter, they do not give rise to lustful desires; when flocks of birds enter, they do not cry out out of season.
In the past, when King Bimbisāra of Magadha first ascended the throne, he entered this park with his court ladies to enjoy themselves together.
Upon entering, they attained self-awakening; their minds were free from lustful desires, amusements, and playful diversions.
The assembly of courtesans likewise all attained self-awakening; their minds were free from desire and they took no pleasure in frivolous entertainment.
At that time, the king was filled with joy and constantly thought to himself:
"May a Buddha appear in this world within my kingdom, so that I may behold him;
having beheld him, may my heart find faith."
Having offered it with faith,
you should present this grove to the Buddha,
so that the Buddha may dwell within it.
I shall listen to the Dharma.
Why is this? One worthy of offerings should dwell in this grove; it is not a place where those addicted to the five desires should reside.
"Ānanda! It is because King Bimbisāra entered this Bamboo Grove and gave rise to such a virtuous mind that all past Buddhas dwelt in this grove and preached this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra."
Therefore, all the merits of this garden are not shared with others; all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—should pay them homage and respect. Ānanda!

This grove is free from vipers, snakes, centipedes, mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous stingers; if one dwells within it, the poisonous mind no longer arises—this too is an uncommon merit of the Bamboo Grove.
Even if I were to spend a hundred years proclaiming all the merits of this grove, I could not exhaust them.
Why is this? Ānanda!
"Now this Bamboo Grove Monastery has accomplished immeasurable merit; other places are not so.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "I did not previously know that the Bamboo Grove possessed such merit as this."
"Bhagavān! Originally, I did not wish to be the Buddha’s attendant.
I now repent for and apologize for such transgressions and offenses."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When you first attained the purity of the Dharma-eye regarding the Dharma, at that moment this transgression was already eliminated.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle 78.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Seventy-Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Six: The Chapter on Great Compassion; Part Three of the Seventeenth Assembly, the Assembly of Pūrṇa. The Sixth: The Chapter on Great Compassion.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana had this thought:
"How rare is the World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has perfected such great compassion and is well able to explain the affairs of all bodhisattvas."
"Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva fully cultivates and accumulates the Buddha-dharmas in order to instruct and awaken sentient beings regarding non-arising and non-ceasing.
At that time, the Buddha, knowing what Maudgalyāyana was thinking, addressed him, saying:
"It is so, it is so, Maudgalyāyana!
All Buddhas have accomplished the mind of great compassion."
If my disciples were to hear this teaching on the meaning of being endowed with great compassion, their hearts would become bewildered and distressed, finding no further joy.
Maudgalyāyana!
For now, let us set aside the Tathāgata’s great compassion.
"If I were to describe in full all the great compassion he possessed while he was a bodhisattva, you too would become bewildered and distressed, finding no further joy. At that time,
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha,
saying, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
“I pray that you will explain a small portion of the Great Compassion he manifested while practicing the Bodhisattva path in the past.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“Listen attentively now, and hold this well in mind.”
I shall now describe for you a small portion of the great compassion practiced during my original cultivation of the bodhisattva path; I will explain its meaning through analogies.
The great compassion practiced during the original cultivation of the bodhisattva path is inexhaustible to describe, yet this great compassion relies upon four matters.
What are these four?
This Bodhisattva’s great compassion (mahākaruṇā): wherever the Bodhisattva dwells in compassion, he is able to cultivate the Buddha-dharma; this is called great compassion, Maudgalyāyana!
Originally, I had such great compassion and such a great vow for all sentient beings:

"May I always take upon myself the sufferings within all the great hells on behalf of these sentient beings—whether they are undergoing various afflictions in the Avīci Great Hell, the Kālasūtra Great Hell, the Saṃghāta Hell, the Sañjīva Hell, the Raurava Hell, the Mahāraurava Hell, the Tapana Hell, or the Pratāpana Hell—even until their karma is exhausted—and may my mind remain free from sorrow or regret while enduring those sufferings."
Maudgalyāyana!
If it were possible through such causes and conditions to deliver sentient beings, I could take their place entirely, causing all those beings to emerge from the great hells.
Even if I must enter hell alone to undergo suffering in their stead and exhaust all the karmic offenses committed by those beings, at that time my heart would feel no sorrow or regret.
Maudgalyāyana!
I have made such a great vow, and with diligent effort I have questioned those who possess wisdom—namely, the Buddhas and their disciples:
"Is there such a principle or causal condition by which one might undergo suffering on behalf of others, thereby enabling all sentient beings to escape from hell?"
"Maudgalyāyana!

When the wise have heard this, they will only praise and speak of my extensive learning, the profound arousal of the mind for enlightenment, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence, as well as praising the cultivation of intimacy with spiritual friends."
Maudgalyāyana!

Having heard this, I aroused great diligence; for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I gave rise to a profound desire for it, seeking to attain and accomplish the Great Dharma of all Buddhas, practicing with diligent effort to fulfill the various pāramitās, and deeply cultivating patience.
Maudgalyāyana!
How did I originally practice patience so deeply?
When I was originally a bodhisattva, I gave rise to this thought:

"Suppose all sentient beings throughout the ten directions—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception—were all to obtain human bodies and come to my presence, saying:
'O Benevolent One, you have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; we are greatly lacking in the five objects of desire, pleasures, and the necessities of life.'"
"If you cannot give everything to me, you shall not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, those sentient beings all spoke with harsh words, reviling and abusing me with bitter insults and false accusations of evil deeds; because they were dissatisfied, they harmed my body with swords, staves, tiles, and stones.
At that time, I should not give rise to anger, nor should I feel regret or retreat; rather, I should thus discipline my mind:
"These sentient beings are deluded; they do not know how to initiate actions born of delusion."
If I were to give rise to anger or resentment toward these ignorant sentient beings, how would I differ from them?

They have not entered the Path, whereas I have entered the Good Path. Now, regarding these sentient beings, I shall endure all sufferings and refrain from creating karmic actions of anger; my mind shall be like the earth, receiving both the pleasant and the unpleasant with equanimity.
"Maudgalyāyana!
I originally practiced such patience deeply.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!"
Throughout the long night, I have always regarded all sentient beings as if they were my only child.

Just as a great elder of immense wealth and vast riches, possessing many rare treasures, servants, and laborers, might undergo a hundred kinds of precepts to obtain a single son, cherishing him with a deep heart and never tiring of his affection.
"Maudgalyāyana!
This elder always seeks what is beneficial for his son, always provides what is beneficial, and always bestows profit rather than decline or distress.
It is just so, Maudgalyāyana!"

Throughout the long night, I have always regarded all sentient beings as my only child; throughout the long night, I have always sought all that is good for sentient beings, benefiting them and never causing them decline or distress.
"Maudgalyāyana!
For the sake of sentient beings who have lost the way and those on false paths throughout the long night, I show them the right path and cause them to abide in the right path.
Maudgalyāyana!"
For this reason, you should know that throughout the long night, the Tathāgata has cherished all sentient beings with a profound heart, regarding them as his only son.
Maudgalyāyana!
In a past life, there was a company of merchants who, traveling by night, lost their way and entered upon a wrong path.
Because of the darkness of night, they did not know where they were going, and all spoke these words:
"We have lost our way; we have no rescue, no refuge, and no place of reliance.
Which beings—whether devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or humans or non-humans—will show us the path and lead us to the right way?"
"Who can have compassion for us and benefit us by providing light within this dark, perilous, and narrow path during the night? Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist seer dwelling in a grass hut in a forest glade; hearing the sounds of the merchants' piteous cries in the darkness of the night, he spoke these words:

"Now these merchants have lost their way in this empty forest during the darkness of night; if I do not rescue them, it would be improper. These merchants may be harmed or even deprived of their lives by tigers, wolves, lions, elephants, wild oxen, and other such malevolent beasts."
"Maudgalyāyana!
The seer immediately addressed the merchants with a loud voice:
'Do not be afraid; I shall now rescue you and provide light to show you the right path.'"

At that time, after the rishi had comforted the merchants, he wrapped his two arms in cotton cloth, drenched them thoroughly with oil, and set them ablaze, providing light for the merchants as he showed them the way.
"Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, all the merchants thought to themselves:
'This seer is truly rare; for our sake, he does not spare his own life.'"
"Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, after the seer had illuminated and shown the merchants the way with the light of his arm, his compassion for all sentient beings increased further, and he thought:
'When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall act as a guide for those sentient beings on wrong paths and show them the right path.'"
"Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, although my two arms were gone, my body and mind were no different [from before]. Why was this?"
Maudgalyāyana!

Because this Bodhisattva of profound resolve does not cling to his own body or life in seeking the benefit of others, through the causal conditions of his pure-hearted giving, his arm was restored to its original state without any scar or mark.
The merchants immediately attained the right path. When dawn broke, they saw that the seer’s two arms were free of any scars or sores, and they were struck with wonder, thinking:

"This seer possesses great supernormal power; he was able to burn his two arms all night long to illuminate us so that we might attain the right path, yet his arms were not burned at all. He must surely have achieved a great practice and must surely possess great virtue."
"Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, the merchants said to the rishi:
'Excellent, O Rishi!'"
"You have been able to perform the foremost of difficult practices and austerities;
what is it that you now desire through these deeds? The seer replied:

"O merchants! By virtue of this merit, I vow that once I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall deliver you from the suffering of birth and death, and I shall proclaim the Right Path to those sentient beings who have entered onto false paths."
At that time, the merchants were filled with great joy and all said to one another,
"By what means shall we repay this seer? The seer replied:
"You all should together practice the wholesome Dharma with single-minded devotion; be careful not to be negligent.
The merchants replied, "We respectfully follow your instructions."
The merchants, filled with reverence and joy, then took their leave.
Maudgalyāyana!
Do you think that the non-Buddhist seer who, for the sake of the merchants, set his own arm on fire to illuminate the path at that time was anyone else? It was none other than myself.
Do not think thus; it was I myself who was he.
Those merchants were the present twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, Maudgalyāyana!

Throughout the long night, the Tathāgata bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings who are terrified; he shows the correct path to those on false paths; he enables those without eyes to obtain pure vision; and he is able to treat and heal sentient beings with grievous illnesses.
For these reasons, you should know that throughout the long night, the Tathāgata has harbored profound great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
In the distant past, during this Jambudvīpa, a kalpa of great illness arrived, and all sentient beings were universally afflicted by this great sickness."
At that time, there was a king of Jambudvīpa named Mahesena, who possessed eighty-four thousand great cities and held sovereign power over them.
At that time, the king’s principal queen became pregnant; whenever she touched the bodies or hands of those who were ill, their diseases were all cured.
When the moon was full, he gave birth to a son who, immediately upon being born, spoke, saying:
"I am able to cure all sick people.
Furthermore, at the time of his birth, all the devas and spirits within Jambudvīpa cried out in unison:
"The one now born to the King is indeed a human medicine.
Because this sound spread everywhere, he was named Manuṣyabhaiṣajya (Human Medicine).

At that time, people all brought their sick relatives to show them to this prince; whenever the patients arrived, if the prince touched them with his hand or with his body, they were immediately healed and attained peace and happiness.
In this manner, throughout Jambudvīpa, they all brought sick people to show them to the prince.
Whenever the prince touched them with his hand, their illnesses were entirely cured, and they became peaceful, secure, and happy.
"Maudgalyāyana!
The Prince Rājaputra Manuṣya-bhaiṣajya treated diseases in this manner for a thousand years, after which he passed away.
Following his death, various sick people came; hearing that he had died, they were filled with grief and wept."
"Who will deliver us from this suffering and affliction of illness? The sick people said,
"Where did Prince Renyao burn his body?"

Having been informed of his whereabouts, they went to the place where he was burning himself, retrieved his bones, ground them into powder, and applied it to their bodies; immediately, they were all healed.
They then proclaimed: "Prince Manuṣyabhaiṣajya is still able to cure the sick even now."
"Maudgalyāyana! By treating various patients through such causes and conditions, his bones gradually wasted away until they were entirely consumed.

After his bones were exhausted, he went to the place where his body had been burned, took the ashes and charcoal from the ground, and smeared them upon their bodies; thus, all their illnesses were cured."
Maudgalyāyana!
In this manner, during the kalpa of great illness, Prince Rūpya treated all the sick through these skillful means.
Maudgalyāyana!
Do you think that the Prince Manuṣyarāja at that time was someone else?
Do not conceive such a thought; he was none other than myself.
At a time when sentient beings were beset by many illnesses and afflictions, being without rescue or reliance, I healed their diseases.
"Now that I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I likewise treat all sentient beings with the medicine of great wisdom to bring their suffering to an ultimate end.
Maudgalyāyana!"
I take on a body for the sake of sentient beings, providing benefit whenever it can be beneficial.
Maudgalyāyana!
By this cause and condition, you should know that I intentionally take on a body for the sake of sentient beings to bring them benefit.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
Long ago in the distant past, I was once traveling alone when a fierce beast came and took my life, intending to devour my flesh.
As I approached death, I made this vow in my heart: "
"After my death, I shall be reborn in this empty forest marsh as the body of a great beast; if any wicked beasts should take my life, may they all be fully satisfied and satiated."
"Why is this? These various evil beasts constantly harm small insects to devour their flesh; they commit many acts of killing yet remain unsatisfied.
At that time, I made a vow: "I shall be born here in the form of a great beast, so that all these sentient beings who eat flesh and drink blood may all be fully satisfied."

Immediately upon death, he was reborn by transformation within that place with the body of a great beast, causing all the predatory beasts to drink his blood and eat his flesh until they were fully satisfied.
In this manner, for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of lifetimes, he intentionally took on such a body to benefit sentient beings for as long as one kalpa.
Maudgalyāyana!

If I were to speak of my own past practice of the path—how I gave my own flesh and blood to hungry and thirsty beings to satisfy them—I could not finish describing it even in one kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa.
"Maudgalyāyana!
It was thus that I originally gave rise to a profound heart of compassion for all sentient beings suffering in affliction.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!"
In the distant past, I recalled my former existence and saw sentient beings suffering in various ways; upon seeing them, I immediately thought:
"I must not now abandon them and fail to save them."
He immediately went to where he was and asked him:
"What suffering do you have? What do you desire?"
He replied, "O virtuous one!
We are now extremely hungry and thirsty."
Having heard this, I immediately said to them:
"What kind of food and drink do you require now?
They replied:
"We only wish to drink blood and eat flesh.
If you can provide us with the flesh and blood of your own body, we shall be happy and free from all pain.
I immediately granted their request and cut my own flesh and drew my own blood to give to those sentient beings.
Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, my heart felt no regret or stinginess, nor did I feel sorrow or despondency; I thought only this:
"By cutting this flesh now, I shall also extinguish an equal portion of the suffering of birth and death."
"I have always, throughout the long night, delighted in such giving; having given in this way, I have attained profound joy and happiness.
By this cause and condition, you should know that the Tathāgata possesses great compassion for all sentient beings."
“Maudgalyāyana!
I recall that in a past age there was a king named Mahābala, who possessed great power of virtue and had deeply planted roots of goodness.
At that time, King Mahābala had this thought:”
"What if I were now to establish a great assembly of giving to satisfy all sentient beings?

Having formed this thought, he established a great assembly of giving, allowing them to take as much as they desired: to those who needed food, he gave food; to those who needed drink, he gave drink; to those who needed clothing or bedding, gold, silver, precious objects, vehicles, or wealth, he gave them; and to those who needed treasures such as musāragalva, aśmagarbha, sphaṭika, vaidūrya, coral, or amber, he was able to give them all.

Flower perfumes, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, silken banners and canopies, men and women, young and old, male and female servants and laborers, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, fields, and property—all these he gave away entirely.
Maudgalyāyana!
King Mahābala performed such a great act of giving.
At that time, Śakra made this reflection:
"What if I were now to create obstacles for this king so that his purpose is not fulfilled?
Thinking thus, he immediately transformed himself into a brahmin, went to where the king was, and asked him:
"What is being given as alms in this great assembly?"
He replied: "Brahmin!
All that I possess I have given away in charity; I cherish nothing."
The brahmin said: "Regarding your aspiration, can I now receive what I am begging for?
King Mahābala replied:
"I have already spoken these words; I shall give you everything I possess.
The brāhmaṇa said, "If the king is such as this, I now require a portion of the king's own body."
The king then thought to himself:
"This brahmin does not require wealth; he has come now solely with the intent to disrupt my great act of giving.
If I do not grant him a portion of my own body, I shall be the one who ruins this great assembly of offerings."
Having formed this thought, he said to the brahmin, "I shall give you a portion of my body; cut it off and take it with you. The brahmin said:
"Great King, having now spoken these words, do you perhaps have no regrets?
King Mahābala replied,
"My heart has no regrets."
"However, since many beggars have now gathered from all directions, I ought to ensure that they are all fully satisfied.
The brāhmaṇa said, "I am not even sufficient for myself alone; what need is there to mention others?"
"Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, King Mahābala immediately took a sharp blade and cut off his own arm to give to the brāhmaṇa, saying:
'You may take this one arm.'"
"Maudgalyāyana!
When King Mahābala cut off his own arm, his mind remained unaltered and he felt no regret.
Because he practiced such single-minded generosity and was able to relinquish everything, his arm was restored to its original state."
At that time, King Mahābala used a sword to cut off his own limbs and gave them to the brāhmaṇa; once given, they grew back again.
Maudgalyāyana!

Because of these causes and conditions, Śakra’s heavenly merit was exhausted; his mind became feverish with suffering and distress, and he cried out loudly, his very body immediately falling into the Avīci Great Hell.
Maudgalyāyana, do you think that the King Mahābala, who at that time gave his body as an offering, was anyone else?
Do not entertain such a thought; he was none other than myself.
"At that time, was he who wished to obstruct my great assembly for giving anyone else?
Do not think so; it was Devadatta himself, Maudgalyāyana!"
At that time, the foolish Devadatta gave rise to a mind of jealousy and malice; though he sought to obstruct my giving, he was unable to do so and fell into the great hell.

Now that I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and am establishing this great Dharma-giving, the foolish Devadatta still gives rise to anger and jealousy; for the sake of profit and offerings, he has conspired with a multitude of people, desiring to kill me together.
At that time, while I was walking up and down on the slopes of Vulture Peak, he climbed to the summit of the mountain and released a stone from a mechanical device.
Having destroyed his own roots of goodness and conceived malice toward me, he lost his gains, his noble status, and his power, and his body fell into the Avīci Great Hell.
Maudgalyāyana!

Although that foolish man, Devadatta, harbored no evil in body, speech, or mind toward me, he regarded me as an enemy throughout the long night. In life after life, he obstructed my cultivation and accumulation of wholesome dharmas; yet, he was unable to obstruct my own practice of virtue.
Throughout the long night, I have constantly covered and nourished them with compassion, yet I am unable to cause them to regard me as their kinsman.
Maudgalyāyana!

From lifetime to lifetime, Devadatta has failed to recognize my kindness; even now, when I raise my hand, those such as Devadatta likewise fail to recognize the kindness of devas, humans, and asuras of the world. Such people as these have entered the fixed state of error.
Maudgalyāyana!
When Devadatta was about to enter the Great Avīci Hell in the future, he conceived toward me a deep, sincere, and wholesome heart; this, too, is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Devadatta was foremost among those who do not recognize kindness or righteousness; as he was about to enter the Great Avīci Hell, he heard a great voice say:
"Foolish Devadatta! You harbored hatred toward the Buddha; though one should not kill a person, you recklessly created the causes and conditions for murder."
"Because of these sins, I have now fallen into the Avīci Great Hell.
Upon hearing this, he was struck with great terror and his mind was immediately subdued; he then spoke these words:
"I now offer my life, flesh, and bones with single-minded devotion, taking refuge in the Buddha."
His mind immediately attained joy and conceived faith in the Buddha; he let out a great cry and entered the Avīci Great Hell.
By this cause and condition, he later emerged from hell and was reborn among human beings. He left the household life to study the Way and became a Pratyekabuddha named Asthimajjā (Marrow).
"Maudgalyāyana!
I now bestow upon Devadatta the prediction that he shall become a pratyekabuddha; thus, he has already crossed over the suffering of birth and death.
Maudgalyāyana!"
I have delivered Devadatta in accordance with my original vow. Why is this?
Because in a previous life, I vowed to deliver Devadatta.
"I shall deliver you; there is no one else who can deliver you.
Maudgalyāyana! Devadatta has planted the causes and conditions for nirvāṇa only with me, and not with anyone else.
From that time forward, Devadatta no longer cultivated any other roots of goodness; he merely developed pure faith in me and declared, "I take refuge in the Buddha."
By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, he later attained the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
"Maudgalyāyana!

Throughout the long night, I have always regarded all sentient beings as my own parents. I take pity on their solitude and poverty, their lack of wealth, and their wandering through the perilous and evil paths of birth and death; they are foolish and ignorant, forever blind and sightless—who can show them the way?"
"Who can rescue and protect them?
Only I alone should show them the way and save them,
Maudgalyāyana!"
Having reflected upon this, if there are sentient beings who revile me with harsh speech, I do not retaliate.
If they reproach me with bitter severity, I likewise do not retaliate.
Whether they are angry or strike me, I never retaliate.

Why is this? I ought to constantly bestow definitive peace and happiness upon all sentient beings and eliminate all their suffering, afflictions, and misfortunes; therefore, I must not now inflict these sufferings and afflictions upon them.
"Among all these sentient beings, who is able to endure?
Only I am able to endure.

I shall now train in the dharma of patience of sentient beings, the dharma of sublime tranquility, and the dharma of gentleness and compliance; I shall be like a well-tamed great elephant, and not like an untamed elephant."
Maudgalyāyana!

It is like a well-trained great elephant that, when entering the ranks of battle, does not retreat in heart; it can endure the sounds of drums, conchs, horns, and loud shouts. Hearing such terrifying sounds as these, it is neither startled nor afraid.

They are able to endure cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, venomous insects, wind and rain, hunger and thirst; they can endure being wounded by various sharp swords, bows, crossbows, arrows, spears, blades, halberds, iron wheels, and whips. They are able to bear all these things without alarm or fear, charging directly into the ranks of battle without retreating or shrinking back.
Maudgalyāyana!
A tamed great elephant does not think:
"I am unable to charge into the midst of the enemy ranks."
He merely formed this thought:
"I shall defeat this enemy host. Maudgalyāyana!
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I made a great vow just like this: to tame the minds of all sentient beings.
If any sentient beings revile me with harsh speech, I shall not retaliate.
If others provoke me with disputes, I shall not retaliate.

Even if they strike me with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, or even deprive me of my life, at that time my mind shall not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I shall not discriminate, thinking, "This may be accepted" or "this may not be accepted," or "this should be approached" or "this should not be approached. Regarding these matters, I shall have no sorrow, no regret, and no resentment; my mind shall never grow weary or turn away from the path of a bodhisattva.
He does not think:
"I am now unable to enter the ranks of the great bandits. He thinks only this:
"I am able to shatter this array of great evil thieves; I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and deliver immeasurable sentient beings from the three realms."
"Maudgalyāyana!

The patience I practiced when I was originally cultivating the bodhisattva path, and all the loving-kindness and compassion I had for all sentient beings—these could not be fully exhausted even if one were to speak of them."
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
In the distant past, there was a non-Buddhist seer named Kṣāntibala who received this teaching: 'I shall not give rise to anger or resentment toward sentient beings.'"
At that time, there was a Māra named Evil Intention who thought to himself:
"Why do I not now go to the seer and destroy his dharma of patience, causing him to give rise to anger and resentment so that he abandons his patient mind?"

He immediately dispatched a thousand men skilled in reviling to surround him from front and back, using foul language and insults to falsely recount his faults, employing filthy words and vulgar expressions with the utmost severity.

He reviled him while walking; he reviled him upon arriving at the village; he reviled him as he entered the village; he reviled him while eating; he reviled him after having eaten; he reviled him as he rose from his seat; he reviled him as he departed from the village; he reviled him as he returned to his dwelling in the forest grove; he reviled him while standing; he reviled him while sitting; he reviled him while lying down; he reviled him while walking in meditation; indeed, he reviled him even during his inhalations and exhalations. Thus he followed him constantly, reviling him with all manner of impure, loathsome, and abusive words without ceasing.
Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, a thousand people, driven by Māra, reviled and abused the Rishi Kṣāntivādin with harsh words for eighty-four thousand years.

Then, while the Rishi Kṣāntivādin was entering a village, the evil-minded Māra personally poured excrement over his head, placed it in his bowl, smeared it upon his robes, his bowl, and his body, and sprinkled filth over his head.

At that time, although the Rishi Kṣāntivādin was reviled with harsh words, insulted, and treated with contempt by eight thousand four hundred people who were skilled at abuse for eighty-four thousand years, his mind never gave rise to anger or resentment; he did not even conceive a thought of retreat or despondency, nor did he say to himself, "What sin do I possess? and he never gave rise to malice.
For eighty-four thousand years, they did not look upon the Evil-Minded Māra with malevolent eyes, nor did they say to themselves, "What sin do I have?
Maudgalyāyana!

After these one thousand people who were skilled at reviling had reviled the Seer of Enduring Power for eighty-four thousand years, they realized he was indestructible; they conceived pure faith, repented to remove their sins, and spoke these words:
"What dharma do you seek to attain through this matter?
I, too, wish to attain that same dharma," [said the Buddha]. "Maudgalyāyana!"
These thousand fierce revilers attained a pure mind toward the seer, making offerings to him, honoring, respecting, and praising him.
Although the seer received these offerings, he did not give rise to a heart of craving or attachment.
Maudgalyāyana!
Do you think that the Seer of Endurance at that time was someone else?
Do not harbor such a thought; it was none other than myself.

At that time, as I was practicing this Dharma of patience, a thousand men dispatched by the evil-minded Māra reviled me with foul language without ceasing and constantly treated me with contempt; yet they were unable to cause my mind to waver.
Maudgalyāyana!

After those thousand people who had reviled him gave rise to a pure mind toward the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, they repented for their offense of reviling him, followed his example by practicing patience, and resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, I taught and transformed them, causing them to abide in the Buddha-dharma; these thousand people have fully perfected the six pāramitās and will successively attain Buddhahood, all having already entered into nirvana without remainder.
Maudgalyāyana!
Do not think that the evil-minded Māra at that time, who constantly dispatched a thousand people to revile me, was anyone else;
do not entertain such a thought, for he was none other than Devadatta.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
I recall that in past lives, I gave my own body to sentient beings and served as a slave for the people of the world.

At that time, the multitude of people employed me in various ways: some had me separate excrement and urine; some had me act as a scavenger; some had me remove earth; some had me gather grass; some had me take grain, rice, milk, curd, ghee, oil, and honey; some had me take firewood, charcoal, fire, and water. In such ways, they had me perform all manner of tasks."
Maudgalyāyana!

I do not recall ever having such a thought at that time: "If someone asks me to carry away excrement or urine, I will not follow them; but if someone asks me to take flowers, incense, garlands, unguents, powdered incense, food, drink, fruits, or grain, I shall follow them."
Maudgalyāyana!
I do not recall that at that time I ever followed after those tasks I liked to perform, nor did I fail to follow after those tasks I did not like to perform.
Maudgalyāyana!

I do not recall that at that time I followed the kṣatriyas and did not follow the brāhmaṇas, or followed the brāhmaṇas and did not follow the kṣatriyas; that I followed the vaiśyas and did not follow the śūdras, or followed the śūdras and did not follow the vaiśyas; that I followed the kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas and did not follow the vaiśyas and śūdras, or followed the vaiśyas and śūdras and did not follow the kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas.
Nor did he harbor thoughts of such distinctions as, "This person is great" or "this person is small," or "I shall follow this person" and "I shall not follow that person.
Maudgalyāyana!
He simply followed whoever first called out his name, going along with joy.
Maudgalyāyana!

I recall that when I was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, I did not think of anyone who might have a task for me according to the Dharma that I should perform; there was never a time when I lacked the strength to do what was required.
Maudgalyāyana!

I recall that when I was practicing the path of a bodhisattva in the past, there was no task involving conditioned activity that I did not bring to completion, and no good deed that I did not carry through to its ultimate conclusion.
To state the essentials: I recall that when I was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, I never craved my own body, much less material wealth.
While practicing the bodhisattva path, I did not give rise to the notion of "mine" regarding material things; I simply possessed wealth as the result of the ripening of past karma.
Regarding such wealth, I gave rise to this thought: "This property shall be shared in common with all sentient beings; whatever portion belongs to me within this property also belongs to them."
"Maudgalyāyana!
Following my practice of the bodhisattva path, one draws near to the Buddha-dharma by not forming such thoughts as:
'Among these things belonging to me, I have a share and sentient beings have a share. Rather, one should think only: 'All these things belong to sentient beings; I have no share in them.'"

"Maudgalyāyana! As I draw near to the Buddha-dharma, I find joy therein without craving or attachment, without grasping or seizing. I delight in being detached from all phenomena and do not delight in receiving them; I delight in the emptiness of all phenomena and do not delight in the existence of all phenomena; I delight in the stillness of all phenomena and do not delight in the characteristics of phenomena; I delight in the non-existence of the fundamental nature and do not delight in the existence of the fundamental nature."
Maudgalyāyana!

I recall that when I was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, I spontaneously illuminated my own body in the darkness of night to show the way to sentient beings who had lost their path.

Maudgalyāyana, I recall that when I was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, I cut off my own flesh and gave it as a gift to sentient beings who ate meat.
Maudgalyāyana.
I recall that when I was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past,
for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes,
I would draw my own blood and give it as a gift to sentient beings who subsisted on blood.
He causes them to obtain fullness and happiness.
Maudgalyāyana!

To state the essentials: regarding all material wealth and necessities for life within the world, he never feels greed or stinginess toward sentient beings; rather, it is all for the sake of not afflicting or harming sentient beings, as permitted by the wise and praised by the noble ones.
"I have always, throughout the long night, deeply practiced compassion toward all sentient beings in this way.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, I recall that in the past I was a merchant leader named Kṣemaṅkara; I entered the great ocean to retrieve precious treasures and returned safely to my native land."
