When this person entered the city and arrived before his house gate, there were many beggars in the city who surrounded him and spoke thus:
"Welcome, O peaceful, auspicious, and virtuous great donor!"
"We wish to ask for something.
If you grant us permission, we shall make our request. Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, Kṣema spoke to the beggars, saying:
"You may ask for whatever possessions I have; I shall give them to you without any greed or regret.
Then the beggars said to Kṣema:
"Give all the treasures you have obtained from the great ocean to us; if we do so, we shall all attain prosperity.
Thus, Maudgalyāyana, Kṣemadatta immediately gave all his precious jewels to the beggars—there were eighty billion maṇi pearls in total, each worth ten billion taels of gold.
Maudgalyāyana!
After Kṣema had given away these many things, his mind remained unchanged and he felt no doubt or regret.
At that time, having given the many precious objects to the beggars, Kṣema did not enter his house, but returned once more to the sea to gather treasures.
After entering the sea, he obtained even more treasures and returned to his native country at the age of eighty.

As he was about to enter the city, he saw a criminal who had been executed being bound by the executioners; they beat a drum of ill omen and proclaimed the announcement through the streets and alleys, leading him to the place of execution to be put to death.
At that time, the one who was to die saw Kṣema from afar and spoke these words:
"Master merchant, grant me fearlessness; save me from the death penalty and give me my life."
"You are a great donor, a virtuous and good person.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa said to those who were to be executed: "Ho, men!"
"I now grant you fearlessness and shall save you from the death penalty.
He then went to the executioners and gave each person one maṇi jewel, worth one hundred million taels of gold.
"Wait here for a moment; wait until I have returned from the King's side.
At that time, Kṣema quickly went to the King's presence and said to him:
"Great King, I wish to purchase this man's life with excellent treasures."
The King replied to Kṛtaka:
"This man's crime is unforgivable; he cannot be ransomed.
If you must have him, you shall give me all your possessions and submit yourself to death as well, and only then may he be released."
"O Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, having heard this, Kṣema rejoiced, thinking: 'I have obtained great benefit and fulfilled my wish; I am able to save this person and act in accordance with my own intent.'"

Immediately, Kṣemadatta obtained deliverance for this man, sparing him from the death penalty; he then took all the wealth belonging to his household, as well as the rare treasures obtained from the great ocean—immeasurable thousands of billions of gold, silver, and precious objects—and presented them all to the king.
He said to the Great King,
"You may release this man.
All that I possess is here before you."
Having received the object, the king said to the executioner,
"Take Kṣemaka and kill him. He replied:
"So be it," he replied.

Having received the king's command, he immediately bound Kṛkin and led him to the place of execution. Raising a sword in his right hand, he was about to strike Kṛkin when his arm remained straight and would not descend.
Stricken with wonder and terror, he immediately informed the king of this matter.
Maudgalyāyana!
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately took up a sword, intending to kill Kṣemaṅkara.
As he raised the blade to strike, both of the king's arms fell to the ground; overcome by great distress, he cried out and died.
Maudgalyāyana!
Do you think that the merchant leader Kṣema at that time was someone else?
Do not entertain such a thought; he was none other than myself.
The king at that time was none other than this foolish Devadatta.
Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, Devadatta sought to take my life, but he was unable to do so.
As for the present age, since I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, even those who wish to take my life are unable to do so. Why is this?
Among all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—there is no one who can harm the Tathāgata, let alone the foolish Devadatta.

Although Devadatta has now conspired with wicked men to come and kill me, and has also used his own means to seek my death, he has lost his offerings, reputation, and power, and shall enter the Avīci Hell alive.
Maudgalyāyana!

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I did not see anyone who benefited sentient beings as much as Devadatta; yet Devadatta did not recognize the kindness or the righteousness [of my actions].

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I regarded all sentient beings as my own parents; by this causal condition, you should know that the Tathāgata’s heart of compassion for all sentient beings is profound and deep.
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

Long ago in the distant past, on the slopes of the King of Snow Mountains, there was a herd of five hundred elephants. Among them was a great elephant king who served as their leader; his physical form was lovely, and he possessed great strength and wisdom."
At that time, this elephant herd was staying overnight in a mountain pass that was steep, narrow, and difficult to traverse, where there was only a single path.
When the hunter saw this elephant herd, he immediately dug a large pit in the middle of the narrow path during the night, thinking to himself:
"These elephants will fall into this pit; they shall then belong to me, and I may take them as I please."
Having dug the pits at night, he drove the herd of elephants toward a treacherous path and the pits.
As the herd of elephants attempted to escape, they saw the great pits and were unable to pass over them.
Maudgalyāyana!
At that time, the leader of the elephant herd lay his body across the pit to serve as a bridge, allowing five hundred elephants of the herd to pass over his back.
Once the elephants had passed, he leaped up with great vigor.
At that time, the mountain deity spoke these verses:
“The wicked man has dug a deep pit; within it dwells a wise elephant king.
Having crossed over it himself, he enables others to cross as well—thus his labor in digging the deep pit was in vain.”
“Maudgalyāyana! Do you think that the elephant king of sharp faculties and great strength at that time was someone else?
Do not entertain such a thought; it was none other than myself.”
The five hundred herd of elephants at that time were these very five hundred bhikṣus who were corrupted by Devadatta.
The hunter of that time was Devadatta and his four hundred and ninety-nine followers—namely, Khaṇḍadravya, Kāṅkara, Samudradatta, and Kokālika.

Maudgalyāyana! Throughout the long night, I see those who are terrified and bestow upon them fearlessness; I see those who suffer and grant them peace and happiness; I bestow wealth and goods upon those who are impoverished; I show the right path to those who have fallen into wrong paths; I remove the suffering of illness from those who are sick; I provide food and drink to those who are hungry; and to those who eat flesh and drink blood, I give my own flesh and blood.
"Maudgalyāyana!
Whatever I have vowed, I have made it all come true; I have granted that sentient beings shall not give rise to indolence.
Maudgalyāyana!"

I have set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; throughout this interval, all the truthful words I have spoken shall never be otherwise. If I were to ever grow weary, slacken, or rest in my diligent exertion, may I not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Maudgalyāyana!
I act according to my words, and I speak according to my actions.

Chapter Seven: Responding to Difficulties At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Hastin. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having heard this difficult matter from the Tathāgata, the hairs on my body stand on end and tears flow down.
I now wish to ask about one thing.”
The World-Honored One himself said: "When I was a bodhisattva, I acted according to my words and spoke according to my actions.

Since the World-Honored One has made the vow from the beginning to deliver all sentient beings, if he were to enter nirvana now while the beings he vowed to deliver are not yet exhausted, [that vow would be unfulfilled].
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, there may be someone who comes to challenge the bhikṣus, saying:
"The original vow of your Great Teacher was that he would deliver all sentient beings;
yet before all beings have been delivered, he has himself entered parinirvāṇa."
“If such an objection is raised, how should one respond?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu Hastaka:
“If such an objection is raised, you should ask him in return:”

"By what dharma do you define a sentient being? If that person should say, "The aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) are sentient beings," [the response is: "If the aggregates, bases, and elements were themselves sentient beings, then when they are separated from one another, each would be a sentient being. If he should say, "A collection of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is a collection, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, a collection is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The continuity of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is a continuity, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, continuity is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The self-nature of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is a self-nature, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, self-nature is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The characteristics of the aggregates, bases, and elements are a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is a characteristic, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, characteristics are not a single thing, nor are they many things; they are neither permanent nor impermanent, and they are neither internal nor external. Therefore, they cannot be sentient beings. If he should say, "The arising of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is arising, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, arising is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The cessation of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is cessation, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, cessation is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The combination of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is a combination, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, a combination is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The separation of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is separation, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, separation is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The existence of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is existence, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, existence is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The non-existence of the aggregates, bases, and elements is a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is non-existence, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, non-existence is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The aggregates, bases, and elements as they are in their true nature are a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is the true nature, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, the true nature is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The aggregates, bases, and elements as they are in their suchness are a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is suchness, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, suchness is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The aggregates, bases, and elements as they are in their reality are a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is reality, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, reality is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. Furthermore, ultimate truth is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. Furthermore, wishlessness is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. Furthermore, non-arising is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The aggregates, bases, and elements as they are in their non-cessation are a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is non-cessation, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, non-cessation is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. Furthermore, non-self is not a single thing, nor is it many things; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, and it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it cannot be a sentient being. If he should say, "The aggregates, bases, and elements as they are in their non-dharmas are a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is non-dharmas, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, non-dharmas are not a single thing, nor are they many things; they are neither permanent nor impermanent, and they are neither internal nor external. Therefore, they cannot be sentient beings. If he should say, "The aggregates, bases, and elements as they are in their non-entities are a sentient being," [the response is: "If it is a non-entity, then it is merely a designation; it is not a substantial entity. Furthermore, a non-entity is not a single thing
One should then ask him in return:
"Is this sentient being the combination of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements,
or is it the sentient being apart from them?"
If that person should say,
"The combination of the aggregates, bases, and elements is the sentient being," one should reply to them:
"You have already answered this yourself.
Why is that? Because the combination [of factors] constitutes a sentient being, whereas the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) are not themselves sentient beings."
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is for the sake of separation, not for the sake of conjunction.
The World-Honored One delights in the practice of separation and does not delight in conjunction; within conjunction, there are no sentient beings.
If that person should say,
"Only the aggregates, bases, and elements are sentient beings," one should reply by asking:
"If that were so, then all grasses, trees, tiles, and stones would be sentient beings.

Why is this? You state that the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) constitute sentient beings, and yet these [grasses, trees, tiles, and stones] also possess aggregates, bases, and elements."
That person replies:
"In this there is no mind and no mental factors; therefore, it is not a sentient being.
One should then question him in return:
"If that were so, all sentient beings would be a single sentient being.
Why? Because the Tathāgata does not say that the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) are different."
If that person should say:
"The Tathāgata has stated in the sūtras that there are sentient beings; therefore, sentient beings exist," one should reply to them as follows:
"You have already answered for yourself.
Why is this? For the Tathāgata’s sūtras state that one must transcend both existence and non-existence."
If that person should say,
"If that were so, there would be no fruit of the path," one should ask him in return:

"What do you take to be the fruit? If that person says, "I declare that the definitive ultimate truth (paramārtha) is the fruit," [the Master should respond: "If that were so, then all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) would be the fruit. Why? Because they are all established by means of the ultimate truth. If he says, "The ultimate truth is not a fruit," then he contradicts his own thesis. Furthermore, if one asks, "What is the ultimate truth? and he replies, "It is the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (prapañca)," then this cessation is itself the fruit. Therefore, it is established that the ultimate truth is indeed the fruit. If he says, "The ultimate truth is neither a cause nor a fruit," then he contradicts his own thesis. Moreover, if one asks, "What is the ultimate truth? and he replies, "It is the non-arising of all dharmas," then this non-arising is itself the fruit. Therefore, it is established that the ultimate truth is indeed the fruit. If he says, "The ultimate truth is neither a cause nor a fruit," then he contradicts his own thesis. Furthermore, if one asks, "What is the ultimate truth? and he replies, "It is the absence of both existence and non-existence," then this absence is itself the fruit. "You now describe the characteristics of a Buddha. If that person says:

My original vow was to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and deliver all sentient beings.

When I sat at the site of enlightenment, I realized only the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: because this exists, that exists; because this does not exist, that does not exist.
Because what exists, does what exist?

What phenomenon arises without a cause? There is no such thing. That is to say: with ignorance as a condition, there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as a condition, there is consciousness; with consciousness as a condition, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as a condition, there are the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as a condition, there is contact; with contact as a condition, there is feeling; with feeling as a condition, there is craving; with craving as a condition, there is clinging; with clinging as a condition, there is becoming; with becoming as a condition, there is birth; with birth as a condition, there are old age and death; and with old age and death as a condition, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. Thus, through this succession, there is only this great mass of suffering that accumulates.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease; with the cessation of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Within this, I gave birth to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening; I attained penetration into such liberation that is without middle, without end, and without destruction.
Because the Tathāgata has penetrated this liberation, he does not obtain any other dharma, but obtains only dharmas produced by various causes and conditions.
"Elephant-Hand!
The Tathāgata has thoroughly realized all dharmas and teaches them to sentient beings accordingly.
Elephant-Hand!"

Whether Buddhas arise or Buddhas do not arise, the nature and characteristics of all phenomena remain eternally constant and unchanging; that is to say, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is neither lost nor contradicted, and it is neither produced nor originated.
"Elephant-Hand!
I have always taught the Dharma in this manner; you should also understand it according to my intention.
I have preached such a Dharma for you all; you should simply practice it with diligent effort."
"Hastika! Whatever duties a great teacher ought to perform for his disciples, I have fulfilled them all.
You should practice according to what has been taught, and you shall attain the light of wisdom regarding all phenomena."
At that time, Hastin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there should be someone who says:”
"Because the True Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata has perished, who shall provide guidance?

Because there is no teaching and no guidance, it is called the extinction of the True Dharma; because the True Dharma has perished, it is called the extinction of the Tathāgata; thus, it is also said that all sentient beings are not delivered."
The Buddha told Hastin: "If someone asks such a question, you should answer thus: 'The Buddha is the All-Knowing One;
he knows all and sees all. He always waits for the proper time to deliver sentient beings, and even though he has entered nirvana, he is still able to be of benefit.'"
Furthermore, the Buddha now bestows upon the Buddhas of future ages the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood; thus, the lineage of the Buddhas continues without interruption.
All Buddha-dharmas are the Dharma of a single Buddha; for this reason, they are called the Tathāgata-dharma, and the Tathāgata-dharma is itself the Buddha-dharma.
"Therefore, you should know that when the Tathāgata was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he acted according to his words and spoke according to his actions.
Elephant-Hand addressed the Buddha,
saying, "How rare, World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata is perfectly able to penetrate and investigate all dharmas.
Because he is perfectly able to penetrate all dharmas, his actions of body, speech, and mind have wisdom as their foremost guide and all follow after wisdom.
"When the World-Honored One was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he acted according to his words and spoke according to his actions.
The Buddha told Hastika: "So it is, so it is."
"Elephant-Hand!
It is as you have said.
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I acted according to my words and spoke according to my actions."

"Elephant-Hand! If one were to speak truthfully, who would not be mistaken? He who has appeared in the world for the benefit of sentient beings, bringing peace and happiness to gods and humans; he who is the Great Teacher who proclaims the Right Path; he who possesses right knowledge and liberation, free from conceptual proliferation; he who has reached the further shore and delivers those who have not yet crossed over—the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, should declare of himself: 'I am he. He alone is the speaker of truth."
"Elephant-Hand!
If one speaks the truth, who is it that does not deceive?
One who recognizes kindness and repays kindness—such a person should say, 'I am he'; this is my truthful speech."
"Elephant Hand! If there are sentient beings who have even a small matter of faith in me, that matter shall not be lost.

Since I first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, throughout that interval my mind has never regressed, nor have I ever entertained thoughts of delighting in the vehicles of the *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*, thinking, 'I shall obtain such dharmas.'"
It was merely by generating a single thought, desiring to instruct his disciples to seek the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Elephant-Hand!

In the distant past, I was at that time an external-path seer (tīrthika ṛṣi), possessing brilliant wisdom, great learning, eloquence, and having attained the profound dharma-patience (dharmanidhyānakṣānti).

At that time, there were five hundred young brahmins who, seeing the faults and perils of the five desires within the household life and seeing the benefits of leaving home to study the Path, all came to me.

I immediately preached the Dharma for him; he attained the requisites of a Pratyekabuddha and the six supernormal powers, his mind attained mastery, and he was endowed with the bases of psychic power. Constantly using his supernatural might, he flew into cities and villages to beg for food, making offerings to me.
I had this thought:
"Since these people who have accomplished such great pure wisdom are worthy of receiving my offerings,
yet it is through my own teaching that these sages attained such a Dharma while I did not, I ought not to accept their offerings."
"Because I sought to attain this Dharma and, though not yet realized, intended to realize it, I practiced with diligent vigor.
Elephant-Hand!
While I was practicing with such diligent vigor to realize this Dharma, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven appeared before me and said to me:"
"Do not covet this wisdom.
You should attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and deliver immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
Thus spoke Hastin.

Having heard this at that time, I no longer practiced the path; my mind attained the foremost joy and happiness, and for half a month, as I sat in stillness, that bliss pervaded my entire body, Elephant-Hand!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, the devas awaken them and they attain a heart of joy, knowing for themselves that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are the four?
First, the bodhisattva personally and deeply resolves their mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and also teaches others to cause them to deeply resolve their minds.
Second, upon seeing those who have resolved to attain the Great Vehicle, one does not give rise to envy, nor does one harbor such thoughts as:
"Only I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; others should not attain it."
"Third, one instructs sentient beings according to their conduct, speaking with kind intent to protect and nurture their goodness.
Fourth, one constantly exerts oneself to seek all dharmas extensively, preaching them for others without any stinginess."
"Hastikarṇa!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish these four dharmas, the devas will awaken them, knowing that they shall become Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke in verse:
"With a firm mind, the Bodhisattva abides in the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
he is also able to transform sentient beings, causing them to abide in this vehicle.
When originally practicing as a Bodhisattva, he was always free from envy and anger."
Diligently practicing and exerting vigor, his joyful mind increases further.
Seeing the evils of sentient beings, he knows the proper time to transform and instruct them;
always maintaining a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he is free from anger.
Constantly and diligently seeking the Dharma, To disseminate it among all sentient beings;
Filling all things with the Dharma, Like rain that flows everywhere to moisten the earth.
Those who practice these four dharmas Are enlightened by the various devas.
"You shall surely attain Buddhahood; do not give rise to a doubting mind.
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva roused courageous diligence, thinking:
"This matter must surely be true; I shall certainly become a Buddha."
In this way, these bodhisattvas, through diligence and aspiration,
mindfulness, knowledge, and wisdom, cause themselves to grow ever more sublime.
Whenever there are Tathāgatas who appear in the world, [they encounter them].
This bodhisattva possesses such meritorious virtues; revered by great beings,
all kings, ministers, and subjects give rise to hearts of joy, knowing him to be one who has attained the Way.

Regarding the meanings of the chapters and verses of the sūtras, as well as matters of prose, verse, and calculation, he has thoroughly mastered them all; he is the most supreme among sentient beings.
Being sagacious and possessed of wisdom, he accomplishes his deeds not through physical force.
It is solely through their strategic counsel that they are able to achieve success.
They crush and subdue all battle arrays not by the strength of their bodies or hands,
but by the power of wisdom alone, thereby bringing them down spontaneously.
All the kings, ministers, and subjects marveled at what they had never before experienced, saying:
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, he has been born into this world.
Everyone recognized him and said that he was conversing with the gods.
Why is this known to be so?
Because [the Buddhas] know my mind.
This Bodhisattva constantly succeeds in encountering and meeting all Buddhas.
Going to them to inquire and ask questions, one can greatly benefit sentient beings.
Once the Buddhas have answered these questions, they sever all doubts;
benefiting all sentient beings, they cause them all to attain joy.
The Buddha manifests his supernormal powers and grants the prediction that he shall become a Buddha;
for this reason, the mind of this bodhisattva attains great joy.
Regarding all cherished and precious things, both internal and external, he feels no greed or attachment.
Therefore, with great joy, he knows for himself that he shall become a Buddha.
With universal compassion covering all, always free from anger and resentment,
therefore, with great joy, he knows for himself that he shall become a Buddha.
Praised by all Buddhas, having already attained profound and wondrous patience,
they are thus filled with great joy, knowing for themselves that they shall become Buddhas.
They do not rely on any phenomena, knowing that phenomena cannot be relied upon.
Having attained such wisdom, the body is able to fly through the void.
The mind is neither within nor without;
having transcended all conceptualizations, one thus attains the supreme patience (*anuttara-kṣānti*).
Throughout the long night, with compassion, I have universally kept all sentient beings in mind;
by virtue of this merit, I have been able to see immeasurable Buddhas.
All bodies whatsoever are the Buddha-body, without distinction.
One who can attain such patience increases themselves through the Dharma.
Who would not follow and learn from those who have resolved their minds upon Bodhi?
By abiding firmly in the True Dharma, one attains such merit as this.
Therefore, those who seek the Way should always diligently seek the Dharma;
by seeking self-benefit through the Dharma, they increase their bodhi.
Chapter Eight: Pūrṇa At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
When the World-Honored One practiced the bodhisattva path in past lives, he was well able to firmly abide in various wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Pūrṇa! When I practiced the bodhisattva path for a long night, I remained firmly established in wholesome dharmas."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke in verse:
"Seeking the Dharma and being able to attain the Dharma—this is the root of the Buddha-way."
Constantly and diligently practice the Dharma, And remain far removed from what is not the Dharma;
Always walk upon the True Path, And stay far removed from all deviant paths;
Constantly cultivate the path That all Buddhas have approached and relied upon.
This is how one leaves behind all hardships and attains a state free from difficulty.
Having attained a state free from difficulty, one’s diligence will surely not be in vain;
being most noble among the two, one is supreme among all forms and colors.
Fully accomplished in his retinue, he excels in all things.
With a firm mind, he dwells ever securely in the category of ethical discipline and the category of patience;
he likewise abides in the category of diligence, increasing his meditative concentration and wisdom.
"Among all sentient beings, he is always able to be their leader;
among merits, he is likewise supreme; having realized the definitive meaning, he is fearless.
At that time, Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Who would not study such a sublime Dharma?

It is only that we reflect upon our past indolence; we did not aspire to the Buddha’s wisdom, nor did we have confidence that we could attain such buddha-wisdom ourselves, and so we sought our own deliverance by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle.”
"Bhagavān! From this day forward, I shall instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden the assembly of bodhisattvas, causing them to abide in the Buddha-dharma. Why is this? Because—"
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perform what is difficult to perform.

When the World-Honored One was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, for the sake of sentient beings, he constantly performed such extremely difficult and great deeds; such deeds as these do not even exist among all arhats and pratyekabuddhas, let alone among other sentient beings.
World-Honored One!

Such extremely difficult and great matters are undertaken solely because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, out of compassion and for the benefit of all sentient beings, encounter such immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) extremely difficult and great matters while practicing the bodhisattva path.
World-Honored One!

All bodhisattvas perform such a most difficult great task; having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are able to turn the wheel of Dharma and deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Pūrṇa!”
It is as you have said.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have deeply resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for the sake of seeking benefit, profit, and peace for all sentient beings, they possess great compassion for all sentient beings.
When practicing the bodhisattva path for the sake of all sentient beings, there are such immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, profound, extremely difficult, great vows and great undertakings.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the venerable Pūrṇa, along with the fourfold assembly gathered there—the devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others—were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted the Buddha’s words.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Seventy-nine;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
18. The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, Part One of Eighteen.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
There were five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom had attained unimpeded eloquence, achieved great forbearance, and subdued the hosts of Māra;
they were close to the wisdom of the Buddha, being in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).
They had all attained dhāraṇīs, boundless eloquence, powers, fearlessnesses, and sovereign supernormal powers, even unto...
They were fully endowed with all merits, their names being: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva,
Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantāloka Bodhisattva, Parimaṇḍalābha Bodhisattva, Adhyāśaya Bodhisattva, Anantāśaya Bodhisattva,
Vistīrṇāśaya Bodhisattva, Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, and Dharaṇīdhara Bodhisattva.
There were five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present, including the bodhisattvas Bodhisattva, Lokadhara, Manojña, Manicintin, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjuśrī, and others—
sixty inconceivable bodhisattvas— as well as the sixteen bodhisattvas beginning with Bhadrapāla. Thus,
these and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were assembled together.

Furthermore, there was Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, as well as Śakra Devendra, the Four World-Protecting Kings, the Son of Virtue (*Puṇyadeva*), the Son of Right Mindfulness (*Samyakcitta*), all the heavenly kings, all the nāga kings, all the kinnara kings, all the gandharva kings, all the yakṣa kings, all the asura kings, and all the garuḍa kings; each of these kings came together with their respective retinues of hundreds of thousands to assemble at this gathering.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the precious lion throne of the treasury of merit. Among the great assembly, his physical form appeared like Mount Sumeru; he illuminated the world universally like the Sun Deity, and manifested throughout the worlds like the Moon Deity. His virtue was as serene as that of Brahmā, and his majestic power was difficult to behold, like that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas. He was fully endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment like a wheel-turning monarch, and in proclaiming the dharma of signlessness, emptiness, and wishlessness, his mind was fearless like a lion king. The radiance of his body shone forth like a great mass of fire, and he further emitted light like the most supreme and unsurpassed maṇi jewels of the devas, illuminating the trichiliocosm. With the Great Brahma-voice, he caused all sentient beings to attain complete joy.

He understands the profound meaning of all dharmas and expounds the Dharma within the great assembly; it is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, its meaning is subtle and wondrous, and it is complete, unadulterated, and pure Brahma-conduct.

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Pramuditarāja, who sat within the gathering. He beheld the Tathāgata seated upon the lion throne, emitting a great radiance like that of a hundred thousand suns, which shone universally upon all things, causing the light of the devas and humans to be eclipsed and rendered invisible.

Having seen this, he leaped for joy with such overwhelming delight that it pervaded his entire body and mind; unable to contain himself, he rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
“The World-Honored One eclipses this great assembly— The devas, nāgas, asuras, and gandharvas;
The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas lack his majestic splendor, As he universally illumines all like a mountain of gold.”
Just as the various devas dwell together upon Mount Sumeru, so too does the Buddha abide within the great ocean;
the World-Honored One dwells in the ocean of compassion and emits hundreds of thousands of kinds of great radiance.
Abiding in the holy life like the King of Brahmā, with radiance and majesty surpassing all devas,
dwelling securely in meditative concentration and liberation, he illuminates the world as the most excellent of beings.
Just as Śakra among the celestial hosts is supreme in form, appearance, and radiance,
so too is the Buddha beyond the world, endowed with all the marks of excellence and merit.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King rules over the four realms, when the World-Honored One illuminates the world and preaches the Dharma,
he causes all sentient beings to enter the Noble Path, manifesting his heart of compassion.
The radiance obscures the fire-mani jewel, Like the autumn sun traversing the void;
The Buddha surpasses a thousand suns in excellence, The Buddha-sun shines universally upon the world.
Like the full autumn moon in the darkness of night, the Buddha’s light is likewise pure;
his face is perfectly round like the moon, eclipsing the radiance of all devas and humans.
Like a mass of fire atop a mountain peak at night, Purely manifesting throughout boundless realms,
Able to extinguish all the darkness of ignorance— The light of the World-Honored One’s wisdom shines everywhere.
The Buddha’s voice pervades the mountains and valleys; like a lion, he subdues the non-Buddhists.
Proclaiming selflessness, emptiness, and wishlessness, he causes all the non-Buddhists to tremble with fear.
His majestic radiance is like that of a sovereign maṇi jewel, eclipsing the light of all other maṇis;
the Tathāgata’s body is the color of pure gold, universally illuminating the world and surpassing all lights.
The Tathāgata has no equal in the world, much less anyone superior to the World-Honored One;
in merit, wisdom, diligence, skillful means, and all other virtues, none can surpass him.
Great Being who protects and delivers the world, I now behold the ocean of your virtues;
this fills me with joy and inspires deep reverence, and so I prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One.
I have praised the Supreme Tamer, The World-Lamp of perfected merit;
By all the merit I have now acquired, May all sentient beings realize Bodhi.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Joy had praised the Buddha in verse, he joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation and gazed intently at the Buddha’s body without for a moment averting his eyes. He contemplated the Dharma-realm—profound, difficult to understand, difficult to practice, and difficult to enter—a state of quiescence and subtlety that is inconceivable and hard to know, the realm of all Buddhas beyond the reach of thought or measurement.
Internally observing the entire dharma-realm, one contemplates that the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the World-Honored One, is peerless and beyond compare.

Having performed this contemplation, one enters the skillful practice within the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, share the same single dharma-nature and are without distinction.
One contemplates and observes that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are entirely free from attachment, like empty space.
When performing this contemplation, one enters into the realization of the essential nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*); the nature of all phenomena is exactly thus.

Having given rise to such faith, they take delight in the gateways of the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; they know the eternal, blissful, self, and pure, and they know the body of the Buddha. They reflect thus:
"The body of the Tathāgata pervades all lands and appears before all sentient beings; the merits of the Buddhas cannot be fully described even in immeasurable eons."
After the Bodhisattva King of Joy had formed this thought, he remained silent and dwelt contemplating the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Ratnapāla (Protecting the Nation), a venerable son of noble life (*āyuṣmat*), who, having completed the three-month summer retreat in the city of Śrāvastī, took up his robes and bowl and traveled through various countries with several junior novice bhikṣus until he reached Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the venerable Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he praised him with these verses:
"Homage to the most supreme emitter of light! Homage to the one whose mind is like space!
Homage to the one who can sever the net of others' doubts! Homage to the Honored One who transcends the triple world!"
Throughout the countless lands of the ten directions, Hearing the praises of the Tathāgata’s meritorious deeds,
All the bodhisattvas dwelling in those realms Rejoice and come to make offerings to the Buddha.
Having made offerings according to the Dharma, the Bodhisattvas listen with single-minded devotion to the teachings spoken by the Buddha;
hearing the Dharma, they rejoice and return to their own lands, praising the Tathāgata’s manifold merits.
The Tathāgata accumulated practices for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas;
while seeking bodhi for the benefit of others, his mind never experienced weariness or fatigue.
The World-Honored One practices giving and maintains the precepts with steadfastness; He dwells in patience and diligence, traversing the various dhyānas;
Wisdom and skillful means are both fully perfected; Therefore, I prostrate before the Great Holy Honored One.
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the four bases of power, the faculties, the powers, and the liberations;
furthermore, he knows the minds, consciousnesses, and cognitions of sentient beings. Therefore, I prostrate to the Great Ocean of Wisdom.
Knowing the thoughts in the minds of all sentient beings, And the good and evil deeds performed by body and speech,
As well as the means for liberation and so forth, The World-Honored One, having known these, preaches the Dharma for them.
Greed, hatred, and delusion confuse sentient beings, Causing them to enter the three evil realms;
The Tathāgata, having known this, taught their abandonment, Causing those beings to be born in the happy destinies.
All the World-Honored Ones of the past, revered by devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās,
and those of the future who are fully endowed with merit— the World-Honored One knows them all with complete clarity.
The pure lands where all Buddhas are born, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas,
their celestial and human retinues and lineages, and the length of their lifespans— all these he knows completely.

After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain; those who build temples and stupas to honor his relics, and the various kinds of people who receive the treasury of the Dharma—the Great Sages who discipline men know them all.
With the wisdom of the ten powers free from obstruction, you fully comprehend all matters of the three periods of time;
having entered into the knowledge of all phenomena, I bow my head to you, the great ocean of wisdom.
The Buddha is peerless and beyond compare; his Tathāgata body is adorned with all the marks, like stars set in the void. Therefore, I pay homage to the Supreme Being.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form has no equal; it outshines the radiance of the gods and humans in the great assembly.
In the presence of the Buddha, the majesty and virtue of Śakra and Brahmā are eclipsed, so that all their splendors vanish and do not appear.
The body is like a mountain of gold, free from all defilement; His deep blue hair is soft and curls to the right.
The Buddha’s crown is as prominent as Mount Sumeru, A mass of light from immeasurable merit.
From the tuft of hair between his brows he emits a great light, immeasurable, boundless, and beyond counting;
his Buddha-eyes are long and wide like blue lotuses, gazing upon all sentient beings with great compassion.
Like the full autumn moon traversing the void, so too is the face of the Tathāgata;
sentient beings who gaze upon it can never tire. Therefore, I pay homage to the King of Faces.
Like a lion, a swan, or a peacock, he walks with steady, slow steps like a king of elephants;
as he moves and rests, he causes the great earth to tremble—to him, the One of Ten Powers who performed great ascetic practices, I pay homage.
Fingers slender and tapering, all-lovely; webbed hands with the hue of coral and red copper;
arms long and reaching past the knees—homage to the Tathāgata’s golden body.
Your feet are endowed with the marks of wheels and webbed fingers; when you walk, your footprints appear like painted designs.
If there are those who prostrate before the World-Honored One, the Buddha’s radiance will illuminate them so that they may be reborn in heaven.

The Dharma King is fully endowed with the seven treasures; He constantly tames the mind through the gift of Dharma, And teaches and illuminates sentient beings through Dharma practice; I now prostrate to the Dharma King.
Taking compassion as armor and mindfulness as a sword, with the precepts as a bow and wisdom as arrows,
one can thus destroy the enemy of afflictions and the seeds that increase craving within birth and death.
Having crossed over oneself, one delivers billions of sentient beings;
Liberating them from all fetters and bonds, One can show the path of fearlessness and tranquility, Causing them to reach the way of eternal bliss.
Those who practice this vehicle sever birth and death; they suffer no more the pain of parting from those they love.
Having attained the subtle and wondrous state of the unconditioned, they preach the Dharma with a compassionate heart for the sake of sentient beings.
Having praised the most supreme World-Honored One, the one who possesses mastery over all phenomena,
may all sentient beings realize Bodhi through these roots of goodness born from this praise.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla had praised the Buddha with verses, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have a doubt and wish to question the Tathāgata; I only pray that you will grant me leave to do so."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Rāṣṭrapāla Bodhisattva:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall analyze and explain it for you, severing your doubts and causing you joy."

At that time, having received permission, Rāṣṭrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying: “By practicing what does a bodhisattva mahāsattva increase merit in all dharmas, reach the ultimate state, and attain mastery;

realize swift wisdom and obtain decisive wisdom; clearly understand the Dharma and enter into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); teach and transform sentient beings by being able to resolve their webs of doubt; comprehend omniscience and deliver sentient beings through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); act according to one’s words and always proclaim the truth; attain the buddha-anusmṛti-samādhi; skillfully inquire about all profound meanings and, having heard them, be able to retain them; and swiftly realize all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)?”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The practices of the bodhisattva are always resolute; from what does this true resolve arise?”
O Great Being, may you explain for me the distinctions within the ocean of wisdom.
Your Buddha-body is subtle and exquisite like pure gold; supreme among humans and devas, a great mass of merit, you are our compassionate and great refuge—please explain for us the conduct of purity.
How can one attain inexhaustible benefit, And give rise to the ambrosia of awakening, the path, and dhāraṇī?
How can one become an ocean of pure wisdom, And sever all the doubts of sentient beings?
For immeasurable billions of kalpas remaining in birth and death, they feel no weariness, regret, or distaste;
observing the pressing sufferings of all sentient beings, they constantly act for their benefit.
The pure buddha-fields and the Buddha’s retinue, The most excellent lands and lifespans,
And all matters of the subtle and wondrous realms— I pray that you will explain the pure practices of bodhi.
Subduing all māras and destroying false views, Drying up the ocean of craving to attain liberation,
With the continuity of the Dharma practice never severed— O Unsurpassed and Most Victorious One, speak for my sake!
Possessing physical strength, wealth, treasures, and the four analytical knowledges, With compassionate and gentle words, you bring joy to all beings;
Like clouds of loving-kindness and compassion, you moisten everything— I pray that you will explain for me the realm of the Buddha.
May you utter the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, And with the thunderous sound of Great Brahmā, shatter all false views.
The assembly has come, thirsting for and yearning for the Dharma; We pray that you bestow the nectar-juice of liberation.
I now wish to accomplish the subtle and wondrous Way; if you do not delight in the Dharma, I shall not request it.
Now that the time has come to hear the Dharma, I await with reverence; I only pray that you will preach the great treasure of the Dharma for me.
"Bhagavān, I vow to attain Bodhi; the Tathāgata deeply knows my aspiration and delight.
It is not for the sake of causing disturbance that I question the Buddha; how excellent! I pray that you will explain the most supreme practice."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
“Excellent, Rāṣṭrapāla!

That you are now able to inquire about such a meaning benefits many people and brings peace and happiness to devas and humans; it also greatly benefits future generations and sustains all bodhisattvas.”
"Listen attentively and receive this well;
I shall speak for your sake. Rāṣṭrapāla replied, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I pray that you will explain this to me.
The Buddha said, "Rāṣṭrapāla!"
There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can accomplish the aforementioned pure deeds. What are these four?

First, a sincere mind free from flattery and crookedness; second, practicing equanimity toward all sentient beings; third, contemplating emptiness in one's thoughts and actions; and fourth, acting in accordance with one’s words.
"Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know that these four kinds [of practices] can bring about the pure dharmas of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“If there is a bodhisattva whose mind is free from guile, who never regresses from the path to enlightenment,
and who possesses no stubbornness or arrogance, they are called one of boundless wisdom.”
Seeing all sentient beings without protection, Harassed and oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death,
He resolved to cross the ocean of existence, And became able to act as a Dharma-boat for all.
Taming all beings with equanimity, he regards all sentient beings as his only child;
resolving to deliver them all and bring them to liberation, the Supreme Man gives rise to this mind.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one contemplates the gate of emptiness; the notions of a life-span and a self are entirely absent.
All worlds are like illusions, yet sentient beings are deluded by ignorance.
The words spoken by the Bodhisattvas of great wisdom— Those who practice in accordance with them without error,
Tamed, serene, and free from all faults, And able to seek awakening, are called sons of the Buddha.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he addressed the Bodhisattva Guardian of the Nation, saying: "Good son,
there are furthermore four kinds of fearlessnesses for a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
What are these four?
First, the attainment of dhāraṇī; second, encountering virtuous friends; third, attaining profound dharma-patience; and fourth, the purity of ethical conduct.
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s four dharmas of fearlessness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva of great renown, By virtue of attaining dhāraṇī,"
Those who uphold the most excellent Dharma proclaimed by the Tathāgata,
never forgetting it, increase their wisdom;
their knowledge becomes unimpeded, transcending all phenomena.
May they always encounter spiritual friends, who increase the dharmas that aid the path and constantly preach of bodhi, the sphere traversed by all Buddhas;
may they regard evil associates as fire and, fearing being burned, remain far removed from them.
If one hears the Dharma of the mark of emptiness, one should courageously fortify the mind.
The Bodhisattva, free from the notions of self and person, as well as all views and the like, maintains the precepts without flaw; their mind is disciplined and tranquil.
"Teaching and transforming all sentient beings, They abide securely in the Buddha’s precepts.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he further addressed Rakṣita:
"When the practices of the assembly of bodhisattvas reach their ultimate perfection, there are four merits that cause the mind to rejoice."
What are the four?

First, the bodhisattva gives rise to joy upon seeing the Buddha; second, they give rise to joy upon hearing the true Dharma; third, they give rise to joy upon relinquishing all things; and fourth, they give rise to joy through the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
"These are the four dharmas that give rise to joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"In whatever place a bodhisattva is born, They always see the most supreme person."
His majestic radiance pervades all, illuminating the world.
Having seen him, their hearts are filled with reverence, as if gods were honoring Śakra.
This was when he sought bodhi for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Having heard the True Dharma from the Buddha, one is neither terrified nor does one feel only joy;
having cultivated single-minded faith and reverence, one follows the Buddha’s teaching.
Hearing the Dharma of compliance, one attains the mind of patience and becomes free from doubt.
All phenomena are devoid of a sentient being; the notion of a self is likewise so.
Having constantly contemplated this, one abandons the perception of signs and gives rise to joy.
Since one no longer grasps at the mark of a self, the heart leaps with delight upon seeing a beggar.
"When giving away cities and kingdoms, the great earth, his wife and children,
and even his very life— at all times of such universal giving,
his mind never once felt regret. Having spoken this verse, the Buddha further addressed Rāṣṭrapāla:
“A bodhisattva who speaks thus should abandon four kinds of things. What are these four?

First, the bodhisattva abandons the household life; second, having gone forth, he does not crave gain and offerings; third, he distances himself from all donors; fourth, he does not cherish his own body or life.”
"These are the four dharmas that should be abandoned.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The Bodhisattva, seeing the faults of the household, Abandons it and goes forth into homelessness."
Dwelling and resting in mountain forests, in solitary places where no people dwell;
far removed from men and women, from kin and great crowds;
alone without equal companion, like the single horn of a rhinoceros.
Dedicate your mind solely to seeking the path of purity; remain free from anxiety regarding gain or loss.
Be moderate in desire and content with what you have; abandon flattery and eliminate arrogance.
Strive with diligence for the sake of sentient beings; practice generosity to tame the mind.
Practicing asceticism and meditative concentration, he sought the Buddha’s wisdom with single-minded devotion.
Disregarding both body and life, he distanced himself from his loved ones and kin;
with a steadfast mind seeking bodhi, his resolve was like a diamond.
"If someone comes to cut and maim them, they harbor no thought of resentment;
their courageous mind increases as they seek all-encompassing wisdom.
After the Buddha had spoken this verse, he further addressed Rakṣita:
"Bodhisattvas have four kinds of dharmas that lead to freedom from regret. What are the four?

First, the dharma of freedom from regret through not violating the prohibitive precepts; second, the dharma of freedom from regret through dwelling in an araṇya; third, the dharma of freedom from regret through practicing the four noble lineages; and fourth, the dharma of freedom from regret through extensive learning."
"These are the four dharmas that bring freedom from regret.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Maintaining precepts with purity and stainlessness, Like a mani jewel,"
One should not give rise to a conceited mind, thinking, "I am able to uphold the precepts.
Furthermore, using the goodness of these precepts, one teaches them to many others.
Always harboring such an aspiration, one brings the Buddha’s precepts to fulfillment.
Dwelling in seclusion, in pure forest hermitages,
they do not give rise to the notion of a self, nor the notion of a living being.
Observing the forms of men and women as being like grass and wood, [they remain detached].
Without conceiving thoughts of male or female, nor of a self;
abiding in the four noble lineages, free from indolence and deceit,
practicing with a sincere heart at all times, and remaining far removed from negligence.
Seeking the merit of extensive learning, Diligently and constantly practicing,
May I fulfill the aspiration for all-knowledge, The state of supreme merit.
Sentient beings dwell in a prison, Without any protector or refuge.
Wandering through birth and death, they seek wealth to provide for themselves.
I shall instead seek the ship of the Dharma to ferry across those sentient beings in the ocean of afflictions and birth-and-death, leading them to the further shore.
Sentient beings have no refuge, nor is there anyone to protect them;
while sentient beings remain within the conditioned, none can cause them to emerge.
I shall act as their guide, rescuing them and bringing them to liberation.
"Therefore, I have resolved my mind to seek the path to Bodhi.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he further addressed Rakṣa:
"A bodhisattva has four kinds of practices for self-discipline that should be carried out."
What are these four?

First, to vow to be born in favorable realms and always encounter the Buddhas; second, to make offerings to teachers and elders without seeking recompense; third, to always delight in secluded places and renounce gain and honor; fourth, to attain unimpeded eloquence and the dhūta practices of patience.
"These are the four methods of subduing.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The Bodhisattva is courageous and delights in mountain forests; He never seeks gain or offerings from others."
May they always attain profound wisdom and unimpeded eloquence, And be well able to penetrate the characteristics of all phenomena.
They shall constantly make offerings to their teachers and elders, Following their instructions without ever contravening them.
In whatever place they are born, may they encounter the Buddhas, Making offerings and paying respect as they seek Bodhi.
One will always be born in superior realms with a name renowned and far-reaching;
if born in the heavens, one will be honored among the gods, and furthermore, having accomplished the path to Bodhi, one will teach all sentient beings to practice the ten wholesome deeds.
Rejoicing constantly in the merit of recollecting the Buddha, I too shall before long attain the Way of Buddhahood;
once I have realized perfect enlightenment and my merit is fulfilled, I shall deliver sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he further addressed Rakṣa:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the bodhisattva practice. What are these four?"

First, when practicing for enlightenment, one’s mind is free from anger and resentment; second, having renounced one's kin, palace, wealth, and treasures, one dwells in mountain forests and does not proclaim one's own merits; third, although one practices giving, one does not seek its karmic reward; fourth, one is diligent and delights in the Dharma, never perceiving faults in the teacher.
"These are the four dharmas that purify the practice of bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"His mind is pure and free from resentment, Nor does he seek out the faults or transgressions of others."
Free from flattery and crookedness, untainted by attachment, he practices the Great Path seeking Bodhi.
Deeply observing that dwelling at home is the root of suffering, and that associating with evil friends leads to a lack of right mindfulness,
he therefore abandons it all to go forth as a renunciant, dwelling in mountain forests to seek liberation.
Wandering through empty, secluded, and tranquil places, forever severing thoughts of attachment to kin and loved ones,
he disregards both body and life, walking alone and fearless like a lion.
Begging for food to sustain the body, one is always content;
like a bird that makes no store, one takes no pleasure in birth among gods or humans, seeking only the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
Wandering alone without companion, he is solitary; He is ever without fear like a lion, Yet fears all afflictions as one fears wild beasts; If he gains profit or sustenance, his mind feels no joy.
Observing that all sentient beings are constantly heedless, I vow with compassion to shatter this state;
for the sake of protecting all sentient beings, I shall always exert myself with fervent diligence.
Whatever words you utter, always do so with compassion; toward those you love or hate, always maintain a smile.
Unattached to anything like the wind, you should seek only the conduct of a great man.
Always delighting in practicing emptiness and signlessness, Observing conditioned phenomena as like illusions and transformations,
With faculties subdued and a vast mind, In walking and staying, they always delight in the nectar-like Dharma.
Always relying on the Buddha’s teachings, practice the Great Way;
Constantly purify the inner mind, seeking dhāraṇīs and eloquence; Bear all sufferings upon your shoulders, seeking bodhi.
A bodhisattva constantly contemplates such practices; seeing benefit before them, they give rise to joy.
If one does not love and delight in bodhi, there is no evil that such a person will not commit.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he further addressed Rakṣita:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that lead to the downfall of a bodhisattva. What are these four?"
First, lack of respect for others; second, ingratitude and sycophancy; third, excessive pursuit of gain, offerings, fame, and reputation; fourth, feigning goodness and proclaiming one's own virtues.
"These are the four factors that lead to downfall.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Regarding their parents and teachers, They constantly harbor arrogance and lack respect."
Contrary to the heart of gratitude, their minds are crooked and devious; their faculties are scattered and they are full of ignorance.
Constantly thinking of gain and support without ceasing, they feign the appearance of diligence through deceit.
Claiming for themselves that they uphold the precepts and practice austerities, they say, "There is no one like me in all things."
Using harsh speech and coarse words, delighting in strife and contention, they constantly seek out the faults of others without ceasing.
They perpetually violate the conduct of a śramaṇa, busying themselves with farming and trade.
In future ages, there will be monks who abandon merit and virtuous conduct;
because they harbor jealousy and engage in strife, they shall obscure, destroy, and ruin my True Dharma.
They are exceedingly far removed from Bodhi, And likewise distant from the seven noble riches;
Turning their backs on the Eightfold Path of liberation, They wander through the cycle of birth and death within the five realms.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further addressed Rakṣa:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that obstruct the path for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
"First is indolence, second is lack of faith, third is pride, and fourth is anger.
These are the four dharmas that obstruct the Path.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Lax, lacking faith, and dull-witted in mind, Constantly possessed of pride and anger,
Upon seeing bhikṣus who practice patience, They drive them out and banish them from the stūpas and monasteries.”
If, upon gaining profit and offerings, their hearts are filled with joy, and each says,
"I am one who abides eternally," constantly employing skillful means to seek out the faults of others, thinking, "Whoever has a transgression, I shall punish them."
Such persons as these are far removed from the Dharma; hating and envying merit, they fall into the three miserable realms.
Loathing the subtle and wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas, these people shall enter into fierce flames.
Those who commit evil without ceasing will surely experience every form of suffering within suffering;
therefore, you who seek awakening must not later regret it by falling into the evil realms.
A Buddha appears only once in immeasurable billions of kalpas to bring benefit to all sentient beings;
since you have now obtained bodies in the fortunate realms, you should abandon negligence and seek liberation.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further addressed Rāṣṭrapāla:
"A bodhisattva must abandon four kinds of persons (pudgala) and must not associate with them."

What are the four? First, one must not associate with evil friends; second, one must not associate with those who cling to dogmatic views; third, one must not associate with those who slander the Dharma; fourth, one must not associate with those who crave gain and offerings.
"These are called the four kinds of persons whom one should not associate with.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"One who can abandon evil associates And draw near to virtuous associates..."
The path to enlightenment increases, like the moon gradually reaching its fullness.
Those who distance themselves from clinging views and relinquish their lives and all else—
for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way— cast them away as if they were vessels of poison.
One who slanders the Buddha’s Dharma, the tranquil flavor of the nectar of immortality—
if one seeks awakening, one should avoid such a person as one would avoid excrement.
One should distance oneself from those greedy for gain and offerings, and likewise abandon those who practice evil deeds.
These persons should not be approached, just as one avoids a pit of fire.
If you wish to subdue the hosts of Māra, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma,
and seek the supreme benefit, quickly distance yourself from evil associates.
"Abandoning both love and hatred, as well as profit, fame, and envy—
if you seek the unsurpassed path, always cultivate the wisdom of the Buddha.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further addressed Rakṣita:
“Bodhisattvas have four kinds of dharmas that cause them to undergo suffering in the future. What are these four?

First, they treat those with wisdom with contempt; second, they constantly harbor a mind of envy; third, they lack faith in all dharmas; and fourth, they constantly doubt the dharma of pure wisdom, lacking patience while seeking gain and offerings.”
"These are called the four dharmas that bring about future suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The wise person who serves the Buddha Should be honored by all devas and humans."
Yet they instead harbor arrogance and pride; for this reason, they undergo boundless suffering.
Their minds lack patience toward the pure Dharma, and all the gains and offerings they seek are contrary to the Dharma.
Constantly harboring pride and arrogance, they show no respect when they see those who possess wisdom.

Lacking faith and understanding in the Buddha’s Dharma, and likewise toward the assembly of noble sages, such a person constantly wanders through the three evil realms; even if born among humans, they shall be largely deluded.
Having relinquished his human lifespan, he undergoes intense suffering in the great hells;
when this kalpa ends, he is reborn in other regions, and the same is true for the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
If you wish to become a lamp for the world, A supreme man capable of exhausting all suffering,
You must always remain far removed from the karma of the three evil realms, Cultivating all merits to achieve Bodhi.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One further addressed Rakṣita:
"A bodhisattva has four fetters. What are the four?"
First, to treat others with contempt is a bondage for a bodhisattva.
Second, to have a mind that delights in and clings to worldly meditative concentrations, rather than seeking the ultimate, is a bondage for a bodhisattva.
Third, failing to guard one’s own mind and practicing heedlessness before wisdom has been perfected is a bondage for a bodhisattva.
Fourth, entering the homes of others for the sake of seeking gain and offerings is a bondage for a bodhisattva.
"Rāṣṭrapāla!
You should know that these are called the four kinds of fetters for a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Constantly showing contempt for others, Delighting in dwelling amidst worldly virtues,
And being entangled by attachment to various views— Such a person is like an elephant sunk in deep mud.
Delighting in entering the homes of laypeople, Always harboring negligence,"
Lacking wisdom and being dull-witted— this conduct is called bondage.
To sever the suffering of all existence and remain far removed from old age, sickness,
and death, one should abandon arrogance and constantly practice the Bodhisattva path.
Undergoing boundless suffering, Abandoning all pleasant things,
And remaining free from both hatred and love, One attains Buddhahood, untainted by attachment.
"You all should constantly practice the six perfections, As well as the various stages, knowledges, powers, and so forth."
When all merits are accomplished, one shall forever be liberated from the net of death.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I sought Bodhi for the sake of all sentient beings;
constantly practicing generosity to subdue them, I renounced affection and dwelt in the Right Path.
Never forsaking the forest hermitage, emaciated by ascetic practices as he sought bodhi,
with blazing diligence and without indolence, he sought the wisdom of the Supreme Being.

Seeing all sentient beings within the prison of existence, revolving through birth and death within the five realms, he conceived compassionate thoughts for all and gave rise to great pity; for this reason, he sought the path to Bodhi.
He renounced his beloved son and his wives and concubines, And likewise abandoned his wealth, the seven treasures, and so forth,
As well as his life-span, kingdom, and the great earth, For the sake of seeking bodhi and the Buddha-wisdom.
In the past, when I dwelt in a magnificent mountain forest, I was a rishi named Kṣāntivādin;
when King Kali cut off my nose and ears, my blood turned into milk, free from any resentment.
In the past, he was once the son of Śyāma; out of compassionate filial piety, he made offerings to his two parents.
When he was struck by the arrow of Kāśyapa, even then he harbored no thought of anger.
Not sparing even body or life, they cast themselves from high cliffs;
For the sake of seeking the sublime words of all Buddhas, at that time they have no thought of body or life, In order to accomplish the great matter of Bodhi.
In the past, out of compassion for a starving beast, you filled and sustained eight tigers with the flesh of your own body;
at that time, the hosts of devas in the sky praised you, saying, "Excellent, O Great Being!"

In the past, he delighted in practicing great generosity; He was once a Brahmin of pure conduct who, out of compassion for the poverty and suffering of sentient beings, Entered the ocean to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel.

It was then stolen by a sea deity; at that time, I courageously bailed out the great ocean, and immediately recovered the jewel to return to Jambudvīpa, using it to relieve the poverty and suffering of all sentient beings.
I was also once a king named Soma, who would not speak falsely even at the cost of his life;
because of me, all kings attained liberation, and my fame spread far and wide throughout the ten directions.

In the past, I saw a person who was poor; at that time, as a king, I gave my own body to them, causing them to become immensely wealthy with abundant treasures. For this reason, I am called "The Giver of All."
In the past, I was once King Śibi; when a dove came to me in terror, I gave my own flesh in exchange for its life, enabling it to be freed from fear.

In the past, I was a king named Siṃha; when my body was afflicted by a grave illness and a physician prescribed medicine, there was a sick man who begged for this medicine, and out of love for him, I gave it to him before I cared for my own life.
In the past, when I practiced the path for the sake of sentient beings, I was once Prince Sudāna;
at that time, someone came to beg for my wife and children, and without any attachment, I gave them all away.
Formerly, as a bodhisattva named Ghanavyūha, for the sake of transforming King Viśeṣacintin,
he practiced with diligent perseverance for eighty-four thousand years before finally succeeding in converting him.

He was also a prince named Pure Majesty (*Vimalatejas*); before a Buddha stupa, his body manifested spontaneously as he paid reverent offerings to the Unsurpassed, Most Victorious Honored One among Two-legged Beings throughout the ten directions.
Once I was a king named Candraprabha; at that time there was a brahmin named Bhīṣma who begged me for my head and body.
Without any attachment or regret, I gave him my head as an offering.
Furthermore, he became a king named Puṇya, who filled the villages and streets with medicines and food and drink, intending to bestow them upon all sentient beings.

Once he was a great king named Sūryaviśuddha; he had a thousand beautiful female musicians whose bodies were adorned with necklaces of the seven treasures, yet he gave them away in charity without any sense of attachment or regret.

Furthermore, he was a king named Ratnaśikhin, whose head was adorned with a celestial crown of the seven treasures and embellished with the most exquisite flowers and perfumes; these he also gave as alms to all people.

Furthermore, he became a king named Saṃtuṣṭa; his hands and feet were as soft as tūla-cotton, and his complexion was wondrously pure like a lotus flower; he likewise bestowed gifts upon all sentient beings.
Furthermore, he was a caravan leader named Siṃha; when a rākṣasī sought to harm the people, he was able to drive her away through skillful means and settled the merchants on a small island.
