Furthermore, he acted as a caravan leader named Sunetra, who led five hundred followers to gather the seven treasures;
there were rākṣasīs appearing in the form of beautiful women, whom he likewise enabled the merchants to escape from their peril.
Once he was a prince named Puṇyārcis, with hundreds of millions of wives, concubines, and handmaidens;
though they were as upright and exquisite as celestial maidens, he abandoned them and left the home-life without any lingering attachment.
Again, he was a caravan leader named Kanakavarṇa; at that time there was a Tathāgata named Vimala, before whom he burned his ten fingers as an offering to the most supreme among two-legged beings.
Furthermore, he became a king named Flower-Eye, whom all gazed upon with never-tiring hearts;
thus he gave away his wondrous eyes as alms out of compassion for all sentient beings.

Furthermore, he became a bodhisattva named Bahuruci; seeing a woman who had lost her husband, she could not let go of her thoughts of him day or night, and in her intense longing, she remained naked and her mind went mad.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gave rise to compassion; manifesting as a widower who had lost his wife, he gradually transformed that mad woman until she was restored to her senses and regained her original mind.
Furthermore, when I was a bodhisattva named Samantadarśin, I saw a person who was emaciated and suffering from illness;
at that time, I gave rise to compassion and offered my own flesh and blood as a gift to him.
Furthermore, when I was a king named Kusumita, I saw a man suffering from a grave illness;
out of compassion for that person, I broke my own bones and marrow to cure his disease.

Again, he was a king named Śrīsaṃbhava; seeing a man who was extremely impoverished, he bestowed upon him all manner of wealth and treasures, even relinquishing his cherished life without any lingering attachment.
Furthermore, I was a king named Śraddhādhvaja, my two hands soft and endowed with the mark of the wheel;
at that time, someone came and begged for my hand, and for the sake of seeking awakening, I gave it to him as an offering.

Furthermore, he was a king named Samantadarśin; possessing the four continents with abundant wealth and treasures, prosperous, joyful, peaceful, and teeming with men and women, he practiced giving for the sake of seeking awakening.
Furthermore, she was born as a princess named Jñānāśayā; her body was pure white and exceedingly supple.
Out of compassion, joy, and delight, she cut the flesh from her own thigh and gave it away, along with her blood, without a single thought of regret.

Furthermore, I took birth as a woman named Silver-Colored; in the city of Golden Color, there was a woman who had recently given birth and, being hungry and thirsty, desired to eat her child. I cut off both my breasts and gave them to her as an offering.
Furthermore, he was a king named Śrīkīrti, who possessed an abundance of the most excellent necklaces, gold, silver, the seven treasures, and various vehicles;
he was able to give away all those things that are difficult for the world to relinquish.
Furthermore, I was a prince named Jñātakṛtajña; there was a man named Akṛtajña who fell into the sea.
Because Akṛtajña had destroyed my eyes for the sake of a jewel, at that time my heart felt no resentment.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past, when serving as a soldier in the midst of a great battle, I harbored no intent to kill;
I would rather lose my own life than harm another, never even entertaining the thought of killing so much as an ant.

Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was once a pheasant; with reverence, I made offerings to the Venerable One, providing for my fellow creatures—both old and young—and at that time, too, I harbored no arrogant thoughts.

Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was a monkey; while in the mountains I encountered a hunter, and when the entire troop of monkeys came to me for refuge, I, harboring a heart of compassion, saved their lives.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was a king of elephants; at that time, I was captured and bound by a king.
Remembering my parents who were blind and sightless, I sacrificed my own life, refusing to eat even when famished.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past, when I had received the body of a bear, a man lost his way and I rescued and nourished him;
yet that man, leading hunters, instead harmed me—nevertheless, at that time, I harbored no resentment.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was a king of elephants; at that time, I was struck by the arrow of a hunter.
For the sake of the merit of seeking bodhi, I offered my tusks to that man.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was born as a pheasant, dwelling within a sparse forest in the wilderness.
When that forest was consumed by a blazing fire, I rescued it; at that time, flowers rained down from the heavens.

In the past, I was once a nine-colored deer; Drinking water and grazing on grass by the banks of the Ganges, Its waters were deep and wide with swift currents; When someone fell into the river, I rescued him.
That man, greedy for wealth, accepted the king’s bounty and led a great host of soldiers to harm me;
yet as I seek Bodhi and practice compassion, I harbor no resentment toward him.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was once a tortoise; I rescued merchants and enabled them to cross the sea.
When five hundred merchants ate my flesh, at that time I had no thought of anger or resentment.
I recall practicing for enlightenment in the past, when I once took the body of a fish and dwelt within the waters;
out of compassion for all beings, I sacrificed my own life, and hundreds of thousands of sentient beings came to feed upon me.

I see the diseases of hundreds of thousands of beings; manifesting as medicine like a mountain, I wish to cause all beings to eliminate the suffering of illness, thus transforming myself into the body of an insect named Yue (Moon).
I also recall that once I was a lion king, with a massive body and great strength yet possessed of compassion;
at one time, struck by a poisoned arrow, I gave rise to feelings of pity and kindness toward that person.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was a horse-king, my body pure white like jade or snow;
dwelling constantly upon high mountains by the great ocean, I delivered merchants from the perils of rākṣasīs.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past, seeking awakening, I was once a king named Kṣema;
seeing the many afflictions inherent in the five desires, I did not follow the deceitful words of a courtesan.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was once a rabbit; I constantly transformed other rabbits through virtuous deeds.
At that time, dwelling together with a seer, I sacrificed my own body by leaping into the fire to save the seer from hunger.
Furthermore, I recall that in the past I was a parrot, Always dwelling in a forest abundant with flowers and fruit.
To repay the kindness of a withered tree, I did not abandon it; Śakra transformed the withered tree so that it produced flowers and fruit.
Furthermore, I recall that in a past life I was a monkey king;
seeing the monkeys being harmed by a dragon, I taught them to drink from bamboo tubes, whereby all the monkeys were spared from the dragon's calamity.
Furthermore, I recalled again how, when I was a parrot, I gathered people's rice to support my two parents;
the owner of the rice seized me and gave rise to anger, saying:
"Why have you stolen my ripened crops?"
I immediately replied:
"When you planted it, you said, 'I give this to all sentient beings.
I am now taking it to support my parents; therefore, it is not called theft."
The owner of the rice immediately felt great joy and said:
"I am a beast and you are a human being.
Excellent, parrot, you possess wisdom; you are able to cherish filial piety and provide for your parents."
From this day forth, I shall give you rice; you may use it to provide for your two parents.
Thus, throughout immeasurable past lives, there was no ascetic practice I did not perform, nor did I ever harbor a thought of weariness in my quest for the unsurpassed, pure path.
Whether internal or external, there is not a single thing that does not arise:
the precepts, patience, diligence, and dhyāna, as well as immeasurable skillful means and wisdom.
Skin, flesh, marrow, and blood—these he bestowed upon all sentient beings.
In the past, dwelling within mountain forests, his body was withered through courageous and diligent effort;
seeking the Buddha’s teaching of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, he instructed sentient beings and led them into the Way.
I always took delight in the practice of dhūta, never abandoning any of the disciplines I had cultivated;
all such difficult and arduous ascetic practices, there was none that I did not perform in the past.
I say that future sentient beings, upon hearing these words of mine, will give rise to derision;
they will not believe, accept, or practice even a single verse, but instead will further slander such a Dharma.
This arises from being greedily attached to clothing, food, and the like; their minds are constantly engaged in discursive thought and they sleep much;
they are deceitful, crooked, disparage the Dharma, and lack shame or remorse; they destroy the true teaching and possess no merit;
yet upon hearing this subtle and tranquil Dharma, they all dispute among themselves, claiming it is not the Buddha’s word:
"My teacher is of vast learning like the ocean; he is foremost among those who can expound and preach.
Yet he does not practice such a teaching as this; it is certainly not what was spoken by the Buddha."
Even the elders of the past, those renowned and virtuous ones from time immemorial, have never accepted or practiced such a teaching; do not seek after such empty and false matters.
Within this, there is no self and no life-span, nor is there any mention of a *pudgala*;
one merely exhausts oneself in vain without merit or blessing, practicing in toil such as asceticism and strenuous effort.
Since you have already stated that there is a dharma called the Mahāyāna, why do you further say it is empty and selfless?
Because there is no sentient being and no agent, one need not seek anything therein.
"These phrases were composed through mere fabrication, like the false doctrines taught by the heterodox outsiders;
the Tathāgata does not speak such matters.
Thus he reviled and insulted the bhikṣus.
These unwholesome ones, devoid of shame, will commit every kind of fraud, deceit, and deception;
in a future age within my teaching, they shall become bhikṣus in mere outward form.
Inwardly harboring a mind shrouded by jealousy and pride, their hands and feet are restless and they lose all dignified deportment;
the corners of their *kāṣāya* robes constantly hang down, and though clad in the dharma-robes, they are always in the villages.
Wandering among the laity, they are perpetually intoxicated with wine; wearing the dharma-garments upon their bodies, they remain intimate with worldly people.
Abandoning the assembly of merits of the true teaching, they delight in serving as messengers for worldly people;
they keep oxen, horses, and various livestock, as well as slaves, servants, and impure things;
they constantly disturb their minds by planting gardens and fields; their hearts delight in all manner of evils, and they lack virtuous conduct.
They do not draw near to spiritual friends, and their mouths constantly fail to discern what words should be spoken.
There is no evil deed they will not commit with their bodies; they greedily seize the property of the Buddha’s stūpas and the Sangha, let alone being willing to give away their own belongings.
Seeing other bhikṣus who uphold the precepts, they slander them, saying their practice of the holy life is not genuine;
they themselves do not guard the prohibitive precepts and lack majestic virtue, delighting instead in dwelling in lay households and violating the wives of others.
That evil bhikṣu’s greed becomes even more intense; he maintains a wife and children, seeking more without ever being satisfied, no different from worldly laypeople.
He receives clothing, food, medicine, and the like as offerings of faith from others, yet possesses no virtuous intention.
Only increasing their greed, they violate the wives of others;
their minds are constantly bound to the realm of female beauty. Following along with afflictions and lacking noble conduct, they employ skillful means to seduce and deceive women.
To teach and transform worldly people so that they may sever desire—
pointing out that those possessed by greed fall into evil realms such as the hells and the animal kingdom— if one does not abide by this teaching oneself,
how can one transmit desire to transform others?
All his followers were likewise so; day and night they gathered in conversation without ceasing, discussing only the five desires and worldly affairs.
They never offered instruction on the path of goodness, yet he accepted many disciples who surrounded him.
They manifest their own virtues to attract fame and profit; outwardly they display strange marks and feign compassion to gather followers, yet seek no true benefit.
Those afflicted with parching diseases, leprosy, scabies, sores, and the like—these are merely a class of lowly people of mixed origins.
He never teaches the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) and so forth;
he does not perform the duties of a bhikṣu. Neither a practitioner of the Way nor a layman, he has no name, like a piece of wood that is rotten and decayed.
The same applies to those who neglect the *poṣadha* and the *vinaya*, wandering about at will and disregarding the Teacher’s instructions;
they are as reckless as an elephant intoxicated and without a goad.
Their minds are constantly preoccupied with worldly affairs, and the afflictions of the three poisons burn perpetually within them.
Unable to dwell in temporary tranquility,
and with the merit of dhūta practices and the like, pride and arrogance fill their bodies;
they fall into the terrifying Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, they discuss matters of theft and robbery; with body and mind, they devote themselves exclusively to affairs concerning their kinsmen, abandoning meditative concentration and wisdom.
Because their minds are set on their own comfort, they engage in construction—even if it be for the management of a monastery.
Greedy for dwellings, they constantly kick at the lintels;
the assembly, imitating one another, acts in the same way. Those wicked bhikṣus, even when building monasteries, do so solely for themselves and their own kin.
If there is a bhikṣu who complies with them, they will immediately establish and sustain him;
being skillful in means and able to preach the Dharma for the benefit of others, he is himself tamed and also tames others—
such a bhikṣu will ultimately not be accepted.
The remaining rooms are occupied by my disciples; beyond these, they belong to our fellow students.
You have no place to stay among them.
Since each has been assigned to another with whom they are affiliated, there is no further space left to accommodate you.
"Furthermore, there shall be no food or clothing; you must depart.
Since we do not grant even what is required for a brief moment, how much less shall we lend rooms or other goods?
Thus, failing to follow the monastic order of succession, those evil bhikṣus will be like worldly people, accumulating vast amounts of wealth, kin, and the like."
My disciples who act in accordance with the Dharma are driven away from place to place and forbidden to remain;
at that time, remembering what I have taught, they each harbor grief and enter the mountain forests, crying out:
"Alas! Our Teacher’s subtle and wondrous Dharma will before long be entirely extinguished and no longer appear."
There are currently monks who seek great profit; though their bodies lack the practice of Dharma, they quickly acquire virtue.
Yet those who possess the merit of full precepts are treated with contempt and receive no offerings;
thus, they all lament their own misfortune and depart from the cities and towns to dwell forever in empty, quiet mountains and forests.
Those who act with delusion, pride, and arrogance, constantly engaging in strife and double-tongued speech,
deceiving the world to gain profit and offerings, claim for themselves that they are no different from the noble ones.
This treasury of merit of my Dharma teaching, complete with all sublime virtues,
shall be destroyed and no longer appear in future ages, because of the pride of those who do not uphold the precepts.
Just as a treasury of jewels is plundered by others, just as a pond of flowers withers and dries up,
and just as a precious chariot breaks apart on its own— so too shall it be with my Dharma in the future.
Those evil bhikṣus are difficult to subdue; they shall extinguish my Dharma practice until nothing remains.
In such an evil world of the future, they will destroy my Dharma, which is truly terrifying.
Thus, those who delight in various evils distance themselves from gods, humans, and virtuous conduct;
once they have cast off their lives from this body, they fall into the realms of hell and the animal kingdom.
For immeasurable billions of years, they undergo every kind of suffering and affliction;
even if they later happen to obtain a human body, it will be full of many pains, foul and impure, and perpetually unclean.
Whether blind, deaf, or with sightless eyes, their bodies are perpetually afflicted by disease;
their appearance is so hideous that none behold them with pleasure, and they always live in fear while serving others.
Their intentions are difficult to grasp and they lack affection; the words they speak are not trusted or accepted.
If there are such practitioners of evil deeds, they shall be censured and expelled from the assembly.
Such a person will suffer greatly from many ailments, Constantly beaten with sticks and stones and driven away;
His body will always be tormented by hunger and thirst, And those who see him will always treat him with contempt.
If you hear of such manifold sufferings, you should abandon all evil and subdue your mind;
practice wholesome deeds toward all sentient beings, lest you later give rise to regret.

If you have love and reverence for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and for the Noble Assembly who uphold the precepts and the dhūta practices, you should diligently seek such conduct; you should renounce your kin, as well as fame and profit.
All these are inverted and like magical illusions; one should contemplate conditioned things as being like bubbles or dreams.
The union of loved ones must end in separation; all conditioned things do not endure for long.
Do not abandon right effort and the powers; diligently seek the stages and the perfections.
Until you have awakened to sublime bodhi, you should always cultivate and accumulate all practices.

At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Rakṣa-rāṣṭrapāla, saying: “Good son! In future ages, there will be individuals (pudgala) practicing the Mahāyāna who possess such faults and afflictions as these;

you should distance yourself from them. Without seeking diligent cultivation yourself, you associate with such people, failing to apply yourself to right practice. You yourself act with flattery and crookedness, associating with those who act with flattery and crookedness; you yourself lack wisdom and follow those who lack wisdom. You greedily seek worldly gain, never knowing contentment; you are stingy regarding the households of others and harbor envy toward those superior to yourself. You are sycophantic, deceitful, shameless, and without conscience. You falsely manifest the marks of a sage to exalt and honor yourself, while your followers and retinue praise one another to seek fame and profit. For the sake of seeking offerings and sustenance, you constantly enter villages.”
Neither out of compassion for all sentient beings nor for the sake of teaching and transforming them, they constantly say of themselves, "I possess equanimity.
They always harbor this thought:
"How may others know me to be a true spiritual friend to sentient beings, and know me to be one of great learning?"

"In truth, they lack a heart of reverence for the Buddha-dharma and have no desire to seek the Dharma; they are like broken vessels that can no longer serve any purpose, or like indolent people who achieve nothing."
They seek out each other's faults and practice expedient means; lacking wisdom and being indolent, they engage only in evil discursive thought.
They discourse among themselves on matters such as the subversion of the Dharma, stubbornly clinging to their evil minds until death without repentance.
Having accumulated much stinginess and greed, the retinues they maintain also learn from these teachers and surround them;
such practitioners, in all their activities, neither consult the wise nor seek the Buddha-dharma, and because they lack diligent practice, they are born into impoverished families.
Having gone forth from impoverished families, they receive meager offerings within my teaching and feel joy in their hearts, yet lack a sense of shame and remorse.
Since they do not even possess the mind to repent, how could they ever awaken to superior wisdom?
They abandon the virtues of the Buddhas to pursue present fame and profit; because they have obtained such present gain, they claim for themselves, "I am a śramaṇa."
Rāṣṭrapāla! Regarding such individuals and such persons as these, I do not say that they possess even conventional patience, let alone the great wisdom of the Buddhas.
They are far removed from the paths of humans and devas, let alone attaining the path of Buddhahood.
Guardian of the Nation!
For such people as these, I say there are eight kinds of dharmas that create obstacles to bodhi.

What are these eight? First, one will be born in the three evil realms; second, one will be born in a remote region as a lowly person; third, one will be born into poverty; fourth, one’s complexion will be unsightly; fifth, one will be foolish and lacking in wisdom; sixth, one will constantly associate with evil companions; seventh, one will suffer from many ailments; and eighth, one will meet their end through a great and grievous illness.
Rāṣṭrapāla! These eight dharmas are obstacles to bodhi. Why is this so?
Rāṣṭrapāla! I do not say that one attains bodhi merely through verbal expression; I do not say that there is pure conduct in those who falsely manifest themselves as noble ones;
nor do I say that there is the practice of bodhi in those who are deceitful and crooked.
Furthermore, I do not say that those who are excessively greedy for gain and offerings possess the practice of making offerings to the Buddha;
I do not say that those who harbor pride possess the practice of pure prajñā;
I do not say that those lacking wisdom possess the practice of resolving the doubts of others; and I do not say that those who harbor envy and jealousy possess a pure mind.
Regarding practice, I do not say that one who is not diligent can attain the practice of the various dhāraṇīs;
nor do I say that one who does not delight in merit can attain the practice of the good paths;
nor do I say that one who is stingy regarding other households possesses the practice of purity of body and mind; nor do I say that one who falsely manifests an air of majesty...
"Ritual" refers to being able to encounter the assembly of Buddhas. I do not say that those who delight in dwelling at home possess pure verbal karma;
I do not say that those who lack reverence possess pure mental conduct;
I do not say that those who lack contentment possess the practice of delighting in the Dharma; nor do I say..."
Those who cherish their own lives possess the practice of seeking the Dharma. Guo!

Although I may scold, revile, and disparage the six teachers, those non-Buddhists act outside my Dharma yet enter my Dharma to commit various evil deeds; if I were to insult and humiliate them, the resulting harm would be twice that of the six teachers.
Why is this? Because they merely speak with their own mouths, saying, "I am a bhikṣu," yet they deceive all the world, including gods and humans, by lacking actual practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those whose deportment is turbid and disordered, lacking in reverence, Who only increase their pride and greed for fame and reputation,
Whose minds are obscured by afflictions and intoxicated with delusion— Such as these are far removed from the wondrous Bodhi."
Attachment to fame and profit, as well as indolence—through the increase of indolence, right mindfulness is lost;
if there is no right mindfulness, the precepts are lost; if there are no precepts, the good path is lost.
That person was born into a poor family; having managed to leave the household life, they became attached to gain and honor.
It is like a person who discards genuine gold and carries away grass and filth, regarding them as treasures.
Seeking fame and profit, they dwell in mountain forests; having arrived there, they seek out companions instead.
They abandon their supernormal powers, eloquence, and wisdom, seeking only present fame, profit, and followers.
If, at the end of their lives, they fall into evil realms, Or are born among the poor,
the lowly, and the base, Lacking diligence, with ugly countenances and no majesty— All such states arise from the acceptance of self-conceit.
Having distanced themselves from all virtuous deeds and likewise lost right mindfulness through negligence,
they remain within the vast and long-lasting paths of great evil, unable to escape for billions of kalpas.
If one could attain bodhi by seeking fame and profit, Devadatta should have been a Buddha;
just as the fierce Vairambha wind blows away and destroys things, so too it is with those who are indolent and lack precepts.
Having personally lacked virtuous conduct and being greedy for female beauty, their observance of precepts is impure and they have lost their merit;
they are of no use within my Dharma, being as devoid of wisdom as a rotten, decayed log.
If one seeks the Buddha-dharma for the sake of enlightenment, how could one not rely on the practice of liberation?
Just as a monkey is bound by sticky glue, so too is it with those who seek the Way through pride.
In the past, for the sake of seeking even a single phrase of the Dharma, I cast aside my body and life for the sake of Bodhi;
yet those people are indolent and abandon my teaching—such as these find no benefit in my Dharma.
In the past, for the sake of seeking the sublime teaching, I cast myself from high cliffs and into heaps of fire;
having heard it, I practiced according to the Dharma and abandoned all attachment and aversion.

If that person hears my teachings on merit and Dharma, yet does not find joy in even a single phrase, how can they attain Bodhi through a non-existent Dharma? It would be like describing a road before a blind man.

The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 81.
Translated by the Sui Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
The Eighteenth Assembly on the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, Part Two.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed Rāṣṭrapāla, saying: "Rāṣṭrapāla!"

I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, further beyond *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—beyond what can be measured, beyond what can be conceived, beyond all analogy, beyond calculation, and beyond description.

At that time, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Sārthavāhabuddhi, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
At that time, there was a king named Jvalanāśaya.
O Protector of the Nation!
When that King Jvalanāśaya ruled and transformed the realm, this Jambudvīpa measured sixteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, within this Jambudvīpa, there were twenty thousand cities, and in each of those cities there were one thousand koṭis of households. Rāṣṭrapāla!

At that time, King Jvalanānta resided in his own city named Ratnaprabhāsa, which was twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from south to north, and was composed of the seven precious jewels.
It is surrounded by seven tiers of precious walls, each wall being eight paces apart from the next, firm and indestructible.
O Protector of the Nation!
The lifespan of the sentient beings in that land is ten koṭi-nayuta years.

Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, King Arciṣmān first begot a son named Puṇyārcis, who was exceptionally handsome and endowed with a perfect physical form; he was peerless in the world, and those who beheld him never grew weary of looking.
Rāṣṭrapāla!

On the day that prince was first born, seven treasure-treasuries of the seven precious gems spontaneously appeared at his birthplace, and within the royal palace as well, seven treasure-treasuries of the seven precious gems spontaneously appeared, rising to a height of seven men.

Rāṣṭrapāla! When that prince was born, all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa were filled with immeasurable joy and exultation; those sentient beings who were bound in prisons or had shackles placed upon their bodies were spontaneously liberated.
Rāṣṭrapāla! Within seven days, that Prince Puṇyaprabha mastered all the crafts and arts existing in the world. Rāṣṭrapāla!
During the first part of the day, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens came to the prince Puṇyaraśmi and said to him:
"Young man! Do not be negligent;
you should carefully contemplate impermanence."

"O youth! Life does not endure for long; its passage into future lives is so swift that you must constantly observe this and give rise to great dread. Whatever karma you create will certainly be experienced, following you like a shadow follows a form."
Then the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens further spoke this verse for the youth:
“Youth, be prudent and do not be negligent; Nor follow after those who are negligent.
Abandoning negligence is praised by the Buddhas; If one indulges in negligence, all Buddhas condemn it.”
Always self-disciplined and never heedless, capable of giving all things without envy or jealousy,
and mindful of all sentient beings with compassion— such a person shall before long become a Buddha.
"The immeasurable Buddhas of the past, those of the present, and those of the future—
all arise from goodness and abide in the path of heedfulness."
Food, drink, clothing, and gold, silver, and necklaces—
giving these as alms for millions of kalpas in pursuit of the unsurpassed path;
hands, feet, ears, noses, and more, he gives joyfully to those who ask.
If you seek merit with a sincere heart, you shall attain Buddhahood before long.
Royal rank, majestic power, wife, children, and kinsmen—all conditioned things are like illusions; abandon them quickly and do not cling to them.
Life does not endure for long; it is as fragile as a clay vessel.
This borrowed existence is transient, for there is no fixed permanence in it.
Neither parents nor kinsmen can rescue one from the evil realms.
Sentient beings create good and evil, Like shadows that constantly follow forms.
Seeking much within the ocean of desire, They harm one another without gaining benefit;
Yet there is no one to rescue them, And they undergo the suffering of weariness in vain.
Now, desiring to bring benefit to others and seeking the unsurpassed path, though your skin, flesh, and marrow may wither away, do not consider this to be suffering.
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare; the Dharma of cessation is difficult to hear.
By diligently serving spiritual friends, one can destroy the hosts of Māra.
By abandoning evil associates, one can abide in the True Path;
blocking off the paths of evil and heterodoxy—how excellent is abiding in diligence!
Do not begrudge your body or life; hold your mind as firm as a vajra.
Ask the teachers correctly about the Path, and do not abandon the intention of right faith.
All Buddhas of the past always delighted in the aranya.
You should train yourself in accordance with that; you should delight in dwelling in seclusion.
Abandoning affection for wife, children, and kinsmen, as well as your own body and life, seek after vast wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Guardian of the Nation, saying: "Good son!

After Prince Puṇyaprabha had heard these verses from those devas, for ten years he never slept, never laughed or played, never sang or danced, never took pleasure, never leaped for joy, and never indulged in negligence. He did not enter gardens or groves; he took no delight in his retinue and felt no craving for the royal throne. He conceived no fondness for wealth, cities, or castles, and abandoned all such internal and external things without exception. Entering into meditative concentration, he dwelt in a quiet chamber and reflected within himself:”
"All phenomena are impermanent, lacking strength and power, and devoid of solidity; they appear for a moment and then perish. Sovereignty is flavorless and lacks true autonomy.

There is separation from those one loves and encountering those one hates; there is nothing to which one may cling. To falsely give rise to attachment and pleasure is entirely due to ignorance; these things are empty, false, and deceptive, with not a single atom of reality. Only liberation and nirvana constitute true happiness."
Yet ordinary worldlings, intoxicated by ignorance, constantly delight in dwelling therein and arbitrarily give rise to notions of superiority and inferiority.
Now that I am amidst this assembly of the ignorant and foolish, I should remain silent and contemplate non-negligence.
"Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, King Jvalanānta established another city for this youth, named Vijayānanda, which was surrounded by seven tiers of precious walls."

That city has seven hundred streets and alleys running north to south; the walls of these streets are composed of the seven treasures, covered above by nets of golden bells, which are further overlaid with nets of pearls and various other jewels.

At the head of each street, there were eighty-four thousand jeweled pillars; upon these jeweled pillars were fastened sixty thousand jeweled cords, which were interconnected, and between the jeweled cords hung fourteen koṭis of jeweled tala trees. When stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced exquisite sounds, like hundreds of thousands of musical instruments playing spontaneously without being struck.
At the head of each and every street and lane, five hundred young maidens and robust youths, skilled in song and dance, were stationed for the sake of bringing joy and delight to all sentient beings.

The King Jvalanānta further commanded all of them: "From this day forward, none of you shall engage in any other activity day or night, but shall perform only song, dance, and amusements, causing all sentient beings to rejoice and experience happiness."
He caused all who came from the four directions to be filled with joy, not even permitting a single harsh word to escape their lips, desiring to inspire love and delight in the prince’s heart.

Furthermore, at the head of every street, he established various means for giving, namely: clothing, food and drink, necklaces and ornaments, beds, mats, and rugs; vehicles, carriages, and litters; elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; the implements of the five elements; and precious gems such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and pearls, as well as unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, perfumed incense, and various kinds of flower garlands.

If they require clothing, give them clothing; if they require food, give them food; if they require drink, give them drink; if they require a vehicle, give them a vehicle—bestowing upon them whatever they may need.
Furthermore, he established collections of various precious jewels and other treasures in many locations for the enjoyment of the multitude.
He also constructed palaces within the city to serve as places for the prince’s recreation.
The ground was entirely interspersed with various precious jewels, and atop the city were erected great, lofty towers adorned with many treasures.
In the center of the city, a great palace was constructed, within which were arranged ten million couches and mats.
On all four sides of the palace, various gardens were constructed; within these gardens stood many trees, completely filled with every kind of flower, fruit, and tree that provides delight and joy.
“Rāṣṭrapāla! Within that park, he constructed a pond made of the seven precious substances, and on its four sides were stairways made of four kinds of jewels. What are these four?
That is to say: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On one side are two lions, formed of a hundred jewels.
From each of those two lions, fragrant water is emitted, flowing into that pond.
On each of the four sides of that pond, there were likewise two jeweled lions, each drawing water out from the pond; it was always filled with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
The four banks of that pond were surrounded by jewel trees, and further, various trees with flowers and fruits filled the area on all sides.
There were also eight hundred jewel trees, which were interconnected by various jeweled cords; from each individual jewel tree hung silken banners.

On all four sides of that pond, there were further hundreds of millions of precious *tāla* trees; between these trees, they were bound together with jeweled cords from which hung golden bells. When stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced a subtle and wondrous sound, like a hundred thousand musical instruments playing spontaneously without being struck.
Fearing that dust might settle upon it, he covered the ground with a great net of precious jewels.
Within that palace, he arranged ten million couches made of the seven treasures, and upon each jeweled couch, he spread five hundred kinds of cushions.

In the center of the palace, he arranged a high throne made of the seven precious gems, which was taller than seven men; upon this throne, he further spread eighty thousand koṭis of exquisite garments.
Before the high seat, precious incense burners were placed where aloeswood was burned; three times by night and three times by day, various famous flowers were scattered.

A golden silk net covered the palace hall, and along the edges of this net hung golden lotus flowers. Furthermore, a net of pearls was spread over the golden net, and there were eighty thousand bright, pure jewels that provided illumination.
Within that garden, he further established nine million heaps of jewels; each heap was one yojana in height and emitted a great radiance that illuminated that world.

"Rāṣṭrapāla! Within that garden there were also various birds, namely: parrots, mynas, cranes, swans, *kīra* birds, peacocks, geese, wild ducks, as well as ruddy sheldrakes, *kunāla* birds, *kalaviṅka* birds, and *jīvajīvaka* birds."

Whenever those birds wished to call out, they all produced human voices that were subtle, exquisite, and harmonious, like the songs of the birds within the Joyful Garden (Nandana) of the devas; every sound they uttered was intended solely to inspire joy in the prince.
Furthermore, he established a separate kitchen for the prince, preparing five hundred varieties of delicacies every day to provide for him.
At that time, the Great King also issued a decree to all the cities and towns within his realm, commanding that all youths be gathered; the number of youths totaled eighty *koṭis*.

Those youths, some of whom were twenty years of age and others who were older, were all well-versed in every craft and art; having adorned themselves with bright and pure finery, they were all led into the city of Supreme Joy and Bliss.

Each of those youths had their own parents, who further provided tens of millions of *koṭis* of court ladies to serve as attendants for the youths; the youths' own retinues likewise offered tens of millions of young maidens to be their servants, and even the wealthy householders and common people within the kingdom each sent tens of millions of *koṭis* of court ladies.

These court ladies were sixteen years of age; they were neither tall nor short, neither too fair nor too dark, neither coarse nor delicate. All were upright and beautiful, peerless in the world. They were skilled in music, song, and dance, and adept at playful laughter and conversation. Their speech was gentle and their countenances serene and joyful; whether addressing the old or the young, they could always offer comfort and consolation. They were thoroughly proficient in all arts and possessed perfect physical forms. The fragrance of their mouths was like that of the *utpala* lotus, and from every pore of their bodies issued the scent of *candana* sandalwood. Subtle, pure, and refined, they were like celestial maidens.
While Prince Puṇyaraśmi was within this palace, the assembly of court ladies constantly performed music as various offerings.
At that time, having heard this music, the prince had this thought:
"Now these people have become my great enemies, robbing me of the wholesome Dharma;
I must abandon them.
At that time, the prince saw various objects of pleasure but felt neither joy nor delight, just as a man facing execution feels no happiness even when presented with sights of sensual desire.
In this way, and so it was: while Prince Puṇyaprabha was among that assembly of women, his heart felt no joy; even when he gathered together with his kinsmen within that city, he found no pleasure.
From that time onward, ten years have passed; he has not grasped at the marks of form, nor grasped at the marks of sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth, but has thought only this:
"When shall I now be delivered from these enemies?"
"At what time shall I practice heedfulness so that I may attain liberation?
Then the women said to King Jvalanānta:
"Great King, you should know that this prince, though gathered with us, finds no joy nor does he experience pleasure."
The Buddha said: "Rāṣṭrapāla!
At that time, King Arciṣmant, surrounded by eighty thousand minor kings in front and behind, went to where the prince Puṇyarcis was."
Having arrived, his face and entire body were covered in tears; trembling so violently he could not control himself, he fell to the ground in a swoon of grief and distress.
After a short while, he rose again and, turning toward Prince Puṇyaprabha, spoke these verses:
"You possess the most wondrous and great karmic fruit; who could have done you such harm?"
Yet you do not enjoy the most supreme bliss; while you do not receive joy, I suffer in grief.
May you receive joy and grant me gladness; if anyone should disturb or harass you, tell me, and I shall inflict upon them the most severe punishment.
This is what I have contemplated for your sake; whatever the world lacks, speak it forth quickly, for I can manifest it like Śakra.
Your face now resembles a blue lotus; why do you frown, lacking all composure?
The various devas, such as those of subtle and pure form, each excel in all arts and crafts;
they are fully proficient in song, dance, and music.
You should enjoy yourself with them; why do you grieve as if pierced by a poisoned arrow?
You should now quickly enjoy happiness; this is not a time for sorrow or affliction.
The gardens, groves, and ponds are in full bloom, with flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves growing lush and dense, as vast and magnificent as the celestial groves of wondrous fruit.
Now is precisely the season of late spring; your complexion is withered like a faded flower.
You should simply enjoy pleasures and not grieve in suffering.
Bathe your body in exquisite fragrant waters; various flowers bloom as swarms of bees hover around.
Why do you not now take delight?
The exquisite voices of the jīvajīvaka and kuṇāla birds are no different from those of Mount Gandhamādana or the Snowy Mountains;
who, having seen or heard them, would not find joy?
Adorned with lapis lazuli, it is as pure and serene as a celestial palace;
a majestic throne is graced with exquisite garments, and from a lattice of golden bells emerges a wondrous sound—these various melodies are most extraordinary.
Upon the streets, highways, and at the heads of alleys, thousands of court ladies perform music, like celestial maidens in the Joyful Garden;
why are you so bewildered that you do not enjoy this pleasure?
The youths and maidservants, with bodies like those of devas, have gathered here for your sake to enjoy pleasure;
yet your parents weep and shed tears for you, and I am as if I have lost my beloved son—
how can I remain here in such grief, sorrow, and despondency?
At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha replied to his father, the King, in verse:
“Just as one who is fully endowed with merit Contemplates the suffering of conditioned birth and death,
Becomes weary of and detached from afflictions, seeking liberation, And abandons all worldly desires.”
Seeing all sentient beings submerged in the net of death, Constantly seeking liberation and distancing themselves from sensual pleasures,
Reflecting that Bodhi is the most supreme, I only pray that my father, the King, will listen to what I say.
No one has done me any harm; I myself find no pleasure in the delights of desire.
All objects of affection are like enemies; they increase afflictions and lead toward the evil realms.
These female attendants are the pleasures of fools; they increase the activities of Māra and the bonds of entanglement.
They distance one from merit and increase unwholesome states, and furthermore cause one to fall into evil destinies in the future.
The Noble Ones have condemned these five desires; how could I now take pleasure in the root of suffering?
These women are merely external forms, nothing but leather bags filled with sinews and bones, with flesh, blood, excrement, and urine—impurities within. How can one find joy in such a true corpse?
Singing, dancing, music, and the arts are like illusions and dreams that deceive the foolish;
through the discriminations of the foolish, the right path is lost—how could I ever comply with them and perform acts of craving?
When the flowers and fruits of the groves reach winter, they wither, fade, and all fall away;
impermanence scatters and destroys them so that they do not remain long. Life has no fixed duration, yet people are deluded and heedless.
The mind is like the great ocean, never knowing contentment; it increases its attachments to loved ones, seeking them without satiety.
Constantly harming one another for the sake of various desires, I remain as immovable as Mount Sumeru against the wind.
Parents, brothers, sisters, and the like, wives, friends, and all kinsmen, royal thrones,
officials, and power— none of these can save one from falling into the evil realms.
We are now like dew upon the grass, And like a flash of lightning that does not linger;
Our minds are distracted and have no fixed abode— Reflecting on this, we shall practice non-laxity.
Alas, young man, you will not remain for long! Alas, life is like a rushing torrent!
Alas, conditioned things are like floating clouds! Alas, you seek the throne within the three realms!
The wise come to teach: "Do not be negligent! There is no bodhisattva who craves the world;
if you wish to become a Buddha to rescue others, O Father King, do not be negligent and fail to become a Buddha."
If one follows various desires and becomes a slave to craving, they lose their merit and have no path to goodness;
if in this present life one greedily indulges in killing, it is like a bird caught in a net seeking to survive.
Sense objects are like venomous serpents; the aggregates are like hostile thieves.
The mind clings to existence and non-existence, which are of no benefit, like an empty village devoid of refuge.
The father-king’s gardens are like poisonous trees; The torrential waters of impermanence sweep all away.
How could I find any joy in them now?
They are like the blazing fires at the end of an eon, Where sentient beings undergo great suffering.
For the sake of liberating these beings, I shall swiftly prepare a ship according to the Dharma.
Sentient beings have long slept without awakening; sickness has persisted for a long time, and I wish to treat it.
To extract the poisonous arrow and bring them peace and happiness, I shall remove them from those false paths and establish them on the true path.
Bound within the three realms with no way to escape, I preach the Dharma so they may be liberated;
sentient beings are impoverished, lacking the wealth of the Dharma, so I bestow the excellent teaching to make them wealthy.
For those who are lost and submerged within the paths of the evil realms, I shall provide instruction and lead them with skill;
desiring to uproot the trees of craving, I practice compassion and kindle the lamp of wisdom,
causing them to see the great conflagration of the three realms, and further raising clouds of compassion.
Just as the pāramitās provide universal coverage, benefiting sentient beings like flashes of lightning;
with the dharmas of the path and dhāraṇīs as rain, they bring cooling relief that can extinguish the flames of feverish affliction.
For this reason, I was born into a royal family; though dwelling within the conditioned, I took no delight in desire.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I have taken birth in accordance with the world to seek awakening.
I have never taken pleasure in the joys of existence; O Father King, I am now amidst enemies.
How could a wise person delight in such a path?
One with eyes does not fall over a high precipice.
If one seeks enlightenment, one must abandon heedlessness; while all in the world follow the various realms of existence, I alone desire to go against their ways.
Great King, my words shall never prove false; I only pray that you, my royal father, will return to your palace.
Whatever is required for their enjoyment, if one accepts heedlessness and craves the kingship,
I do not desire even hundreds of millions of such thrones; if one remains within the palace, the Way cannot be attained—
only in a place of tranquility and fearlessness can the five desires be transcended.
I have gone to the mountain forests to dwell in tranquility; having reached that place, I seek awakening.
The Tathāgatas of the three times abide in the araṇya; true awakening is not found in desire.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the Bodhisattva Guardian of the Nation, saying:

"Good son! At that time, after Prince Puṇyaprabha had spoken these verses to his father the king, he remained in the palace accompanied by the court ladies; however, his mind was not at ease, and he maintained himself in only three modes of deportment."
What are these three? They are:
whether walking, standing, or sitting, he does not sleep or lie down.

While staying on the eighth floor of a high tower, at the hour of midnight, he sees the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens moving through the air above, praising the merits of the Buddha, and even the merits of the Dharma and the Saṅgha.

Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, having heard the praise of the Buddhas by those devas, the prince Puṇyaprabha’s body hairs stood on end and his entire frame trembled with awe. Joining his ten fingers in palms-together salutation, he addressed those devas in verse:
“Excellent, O assembly of devas! Out of compassion for our suffering, [you have praised the Buddha].”
Do not give rise to weariness; I wish to ask something.

How does one transform sentient beings?

Pure as lapis lazuli, with a wondrous complexion curling to the right;

For the sake of all sentient beings alike, you emit billions of rays of light that fill the trichiliocosm and dry up all the evil realms.

With hundreds of thousands of kinds of sounds, he expounds the Dharma without false speech;

The kalaviṅka and the cuckoo, the ruddy sheldrake and the swan,

Sublime and pure like lapis lazuli, it brings joy to the wise;

With a pure heart, they experience exultation, following the wisdom of others' minds as they inquire.
That Honored One, the King of Dharma, the Sovereign Great World-Honored One, possesses this sublime sound of the Dharma;
his neck is straight and his shoulders are perfectly rounded.

He turns his head like an elephant king; his gait is like that of a lion. His entire body is perfectly proportioned.

The rare and wondrous deeds of the Dharma King: whether gaining profit or loss, experiencing pleasure or pain, receiving fame or insignificance;

"Just like a flower upon the water, and also like the lion king,

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Rakṣa:

Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha again had this thought:

"Such are these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who possess such a great assembly; they have accomplished such supreme and wondrous dharmas of awakening and realization. Yet, I am unable to see such a noble assembly of disciples."
I have now encountered the various evils, sufferings, and afflictions of birth and death; such birth and death are devoid of any meaningful benefit.

All ordinary worldlings cling to the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*); living at home brings many faults and calamities, and insatiable greed is censured by the wise. One is shrouded by the darkness of heedlessness and ignorance.

Thus, these conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are difficult to penetrate; thus, this consciousness-mind is extremely difficult to subdue; thus, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is profoundly deep and difficult to awaken to; thus, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) lack self-mastery; thus, one undergoes and maintains the retribution of unwholesome contact (*spraṣṭavya*); thus, ignorance (*avidyā*) possesses many faults and afflictions; thus, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is a firm bond that is not relinquished; thus, the various graspings (*upādāna*) are extremely difficult to abandon; thus, within these various states of existence (*bhava*), there is no noble path (*āryamārga*); thus, those who are born are extremely difficult to liberate; thus, the aged can destroy the youth; thus, the sick diminish the vigor of physical form; thus, the dead possess no luster; thus, those who are born experience much decay and distress; thus, coming and going brings no benefit.
Such is the subtle and sublime True Teaching of the Tathāgata, which is most worthy of being cherished and delighted in.
How could one, for the sake of such fondness, allow the mind to be deluded by various afflictions, or become turbid, disordered, and impure through various evil thoughts?
Their minds are constantly dissolute; they always take the company of the foolish as their friends;
they engage in unwholesome reflection; their minds are perpetually defiled by and attached to afflictions and the cycle of birth and death;
they delight in evil associates and always dwell together with such wicked ones.
I am not yet able to accomplish even mundane pure virtues, much less attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for me now, I shall cast myself from this tower toward the east; if I were to go out through the gate, I fear my kinsmen would create obstacles for me.

At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha saw himself situated upon that lotus flower.

"Rāṣṭrapāla!

"Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha addressed the World-Honored One in verse, saying:

In the midst of suffering and peril, the World-Honored One has rescued me.
I pray that the Honored One will explain to me: how may one abide within the Dharma and attain great benefit?
I only pray that the Honored One will explain this clearly.
World-Honored One, previously at midnight, various devas came to me and instructed me not to be negligent.
Terror has come upon this place; now I ask the Great World-Honored One:

I have now lost the right path; I pray that you will act as my caravan leader.
I am now like one born blind; may you act as my eyes.
I am now at the edge of a precipice; may the World-Honored One rescue and deliver me.
Grant that I may give rise to right faith, like a person suffering from a grave and terminal illness.
May the Honored One quickly provide healing.
Like a pauper now, may the Honored One take me under his care;

My mind is filled with great doubt; I pray you, sever my web of delusion.
Show me the place of practice: how may I attain bodhi?
I am now submerged in a great flood; I pray you, show me the way to deliverance.

My body has a great ulcer; may you treat it so that it may quickly heal.
My body is pierced by a poisonous arrow; may the World-Honored One be able to extract it for me.
I have constantly fallen into the various evil realms; I pray that your compassion will rescue and deliver me.
May I turn away from the deviant and abide in the Right Path. I am submerged in the river of sorrow and grief;

My lifespan is short and my pursuit of the good is beset by many obstacles;

Now that my body is at ease and tranquil, I have already escaped all perils.
"One who performs meritorious deeds will surely obtain their reward; I pray that you resolve my doubts for me.

Guardian of the Nation!

"Homage to the Honored One of golden hue, whose face is as pure as the full moon;

The hair is pure, radiant, and lustrous; The crown of the head is as high as Mount Sumeru.
Beholders never tire of gazing upon it, For between the brows is the mark of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*).
Its pure and wondrous radiance shines forth, And the eyes are like blue lotus flowers.
Subtle, exquisite, and most extraordinary, with a compassionate and merciful heart,
he gazes upon and reveals all the worlds.
As supple as red copper, it emerges and can completely cover the face.
To those who preach the Dharma and guide the multitude, I pay homage to the one of subtle and wondrous voice.
His teeth are as white as jade or snow, as firm and solid as diamond,
even and closely set, numbering forty.
He transforms and guides immeasurable multitudes; I pay homage to him whose words are beautiful and true, whose honored form is peerless in the world.
His radiance illuminates all lands, such that even the Brahmā heavens and the world-protectors find their own light completely eclipsed.
The Deer King’s arms are slender and supple;
his gait is like that of an elephant king and likewise like that of a lion.
As he moves with serene majesty, the earth trembles and the mountains shake.
His skin is soft, exquisite, and lustrous; his body is like the color of purple gold.
His majestic radiance has no peer, and those who behold him never tire of gazing.
Having practiced austerities for countless eons, he delights in giving without weariness.
With a heart of loving-kindness toward all beings, I pay homage to the Great Compassionate Father.
The Honored One always delights in giving and precepts, Firmly abiding in patience, diligence, Meditative concentration, and wisdom; His dhāraṇī and knowledge are peerless.
Therefore, I pay homage to him who has subdued all non-Buddhists, who dwells among the multitude like a lion,
who as the King of Physicians removes the three defilements, and whom all who hear rejoice.
Therefore, I now pay homage.
Your body, speech, and mind are pure; you are unstained by the three realms, like a lotus in water.

Having crossed to the further shore of the three realms, I therefore pay homage to you.
You who behold all worlds as being like an illusion, like a dream,

Sentient beings and the life-principle are like the moon reflected in water;

For their sake, I employ skillful means through hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates.
Gathering and instructing the assembly with compassion,
he observes that all poisons are constantly ablaze; having perceived this burning affliction,

He delivers countless beings from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, from separation from the beloved,
from meeting with the hated, and from grief, lamentation, pain, and distress.
Having observed the world’s suffering and affliction, he is able to deliver them through his compassion.
Constantly wandering through the world—
among devas, humans, or animals, within the realms of hell and hungry ghosts—
they are deluded and lack a guide.
For their sake, the World-Honored One manifested the supreme guidance.
The Dharma King, transcending the world, likewise proclaimed this noble path,
just as the World-Honored One has now taught.
Surpassing Mahābrahmā, and also surpassing the gandharvas and the celestial maidens—
the Tathāgata’s voice is most supreme, providing explanation for the world.
With true, beneficial patience,
they are endowed with hundreds of thousands of nayutas of merits;
when all sentient beings have heard this, they realize the tranquility of the three vehicles.
If there are those who make offerings to him, they shall obtain supreme and wondrous bliss;
immeasurable devas and humans alike shall attain the true and correct path.
Or they may become kings of men, great wealthy elders, and the like.
Some rule over one world, or two, three, or four worlds as Cakravartin wheel-turning sage-kings;
they transform sentient beings through the ten wholesome paths and enjoy the perfection of the seven treasures— all this arises from making offerings to the Buddha.
Some become Śakra or Brahmā, or dwell among the Four Great Kings;
in Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, or Suyāma— heaven—
these result from making offerings to the Buddha, leading to the attainment of perfect enlightenment in future lives.
Thus making offerings to the Buddha— whether seeing him or hearing his voice—
none shall pass by in vain. They shall remove the suffering of many sentient beings and attain the state of ambrosia, which is most wondrous and free from old age and illness.
The World-Honored One knows the true path; he skillfully explains the locus of the true path.
He is able to sever all evil paths and cause beings to abide on the path of fearlessness.
The stainless, great, and holy path can serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.
If a person seeks merit, they must plant it at the side of the Buddha.
For this reason, they shall obtain an inexhaustible treasury;
for many hundreds of millions of kalpas, that merit shall never be exhausted.
Until they have attained Buddhahood, they shall obtain a pure land as subtle and exquisite as the Heaven of Paranirmita-vaśavartin; having obtained it, they will experience great joy.
Within that wondrous buddha-field, all the beings therein—
Purity of body, speech, and mind—
such merits as these arise from making offerings to the Buddha.
Whether seeking rebirth in heaven, nirvana, or the joys of the human realm, [these are attained thereby].
The retributions of merit and so forth are immeasurable; none of these can ever be exhausted.
With great fame and supreme offerings, amidst hundreds of lands and countless hundreds of thousands of assemblies, one shall proclaim this great renown.
This arises from praising the Buddha’s virtues: the Tathāgata removes the fever of affliction and enables all beings to attain liberation; through his compassion, he brings joy to all who behold him.
His faculties are tranquil and pure; he is the most supreme king among men.
A mass of immeasurable merit; therefore, I prostrate to you.

may gods, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas likewise rejoice.

"Great King!
The prince is currently at that place, prostrating, serving, and making offerings to that Buddha, the World-Honored One.

When King Jvalanānta heard this proclamation from the deva, he immediately set out toward the east, accompanied by the princes, the palace ladies, and his royal retinue of eighty-four thousand *koṭis*, hundreds of thousands, and *nayutas* of beings, to go before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Siṃhavikrāntagāmin.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and praised the Buddha in verse:
“I pay homage to the ocean of merit and wisdom, The peerless Great Being among men,
Supreme in the three realms with no equal, To whom devas and asuras all offer worship.”
Most distinguished and supremely honored among the multitude, beholding the Buddha’s physical marks one never tires;
his body adorned with the thirty-two marks is as pure as Mount Sumeru, a jewel.
The Buddha’s body is subtle and of purple-gold color; those who behold it never tire of it, and I prostrate before him.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, the Tathāgata practiced austerities without weariness or fatigue.

Having made offerings to Buddhas for immeasurable eons—countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis—in the past, his acts of giving were inconceivable; therefore, the radiance of his body is most majestic and pure.
Through generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, through patience, diligence, and skillful means,
the World-Honored One’s physical form is exceedingly pure, surpassing the light of the sun, the moon, and mani jewels.
The radiance of Śakra and Brahmā is eclipsed and no longer appears; the Buddha manifests wondrous forms for the sake of the world.
Sometimes he dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, and sometimes he manifests his descent to be born.
He manifests the body of a pure white elephant, entering the mother’s womb from her right side within a dream.
The manifestation of the Buddha’s body is like space, Like a shadow, the moon in water, a dream, or a magical creation;
The Buddha’s responsive manifestations are likewise so.
Sometimes he takes seven steps to demonstrate his manhood, Proclaiming: "Among gods and humans, I am supreme."
I am able to rescue and liberate all beings from suffering;
free from doubt regarding all phenomena, I manifest for the sake of the multitude the initial learning of writing, and bring them to accomplishment in the tranquil state of meditative concentration.
Manifesting as dwelling among court ladies, yet abandoning parents, wife,
and children while their kinsmen and relatives weep with longing; leaving home to dwell in the forest and always walking alone,
he is constantly surrounded by tens of millions of devas who never tire of praising him.
Long ago you subdued the four kinds of Māras, yet in this land you manifest their subjugation for the first time;
long ago you turned the wheel that has no beginning, yet now through compassion you manifest its initial turning.
Observing that the world is attached to the notion of permanence, And seeing that the multitudes proclaim,
"I shall enter nirvāṇa," While the world delights in the cycle of birth and death, The World-Honored One preaches for them the state of quiescence;
His merit, wisdom, and skillful means are beyond compare, As his body emits radiance that illuminates many lands.
Bodhisattvas from all directions followed the light and came, To prostrate before the World-Honored One’s inconceivable majesty.
The Dharma King preached for them the subtle and wondrous Dharma; Their hearts gave rise to joy as they realized purity.
He manifests a body for the sake of the multitudes, identical to that of the world; yet the Buddha-body neither comes nor goes.
The Tathāgata abides in the Dharma like an illusion or a transformation; therefore, I prostrate to the Great Being.
Excellent is the World-Honored One’s teaching of the wondrous path; for the sake of the multitude, you have revealed the road to Bodhi.
For my sake, you have displayed this supreme Dharma-gate; therefore, I now realize this Dharma.
That which the Tathāgata has manifested for me, I have realized and shall proclaim for the sake of all sentient beings.
O Buddha, the Knower of Wisdom, free from affliction, Honored One of the Three Realms—I now extol the merit of the Buddha’s realization;
may I, together with all sentient beings in the world, swiftly realize the unsurpassed path of quiescent extinction.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further addressed the Bodhisattva Guardian of the Nation, saying:
"Guardian of the Nation!

At that time, having known the profound faith of King Jvālāmati, the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi preached the Dharma as was appropriate, causing him to abide in the stage of non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Rakṣapāla! At that time, the prince Puṇyolkā addressed the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to invite the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus to enter my city; I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant me permission.

"Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, having received the Buddha’s permission, Prince Puṇyaraśmi addressed his parents, his kinsmen, and his court ladies, saying:
'Venerable ones, you should know that I now offer this city of Jyotirāga, together with all its ornaments, to that Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus; I shall never regret it.'"
"I only pray that my parents and all my kinsmen will give rise to a heart of sympathetic joy.
At that time, his parents and kinsmen all spoke with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"I rejoice in all of this. Kṣemadatta!
At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha immediately further adorned the city of Jayasundarī and offered it as a gift to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the prince prepared five hundred kinds of exquisite foods of the finest flavors every day for the Buddha and the Saṃgha to offer as alms to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, he constructed a saṃghārāma for the bhikṣus, adorning all its cells with the seven treasures; within the chambers, he spread various colored silken rugs in hundreds of thousands of layers.
Furthermore, for the sake of the community of bhikṣus, he daily prepared new, pure robes and offered them to the assembly according to their wishes.

He also constructed a place for walking meditation (caṅkrama), adorning its ground with various jewels. Above it was spread a jeweled net, and on both sides of the walkway, he planted various trees and flowers of all kinds—namely, the utpala, padma, and puṇḍarīka—and every variety of flower was present there in full abundance.

At that time, the prince made such offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks for three hundred billion years; during that interval, he never slept and had no regard for his own body or life, thinking of nothing but making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks.

During that time, he was free from thoughts of greed and free from thoughts of malice; he felt no attachment to the position of kingship, and he would relinquish his body and life in every circumstance, let alone other possessions.
Furthermore, regarding all that the Tathāgata has taught, he received and upheld it all without ever forgetting or losing it; not even a single phrase did he ever ask the Tathāgata to repeat.

During that time, he neither bathed nor anointed his body with ghee or oil; he neither washed his feet nor sat or lay down, except for the times of eating and attending to the necessities of nature, until finally he never experienced a thought of fatigue.
When that Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, he himself takes red sandalwood to form a pyre for the cremation of the Tathāgata’s body.
At the site where the Tathāgata’s body is cremated, he makes offerings to the relics with various sublime and excellent articles of worship.

Furthermore, throughout various places within Jambudvīpa, they made offerings to the śarīra with flower garlands, renowned incenses, diverse kinds of music, and even banners, canopies, and precious victory standards.
Having made such offerings, he further constructed ninety-nine koṭis of separate precious stūpas for those relics.
Those stūpas were composed of the seven treasures and were further covered with nets of various jewels and pearls.

Furthermore, he fashioned canopies of the seven precious gems for the various stūpas; for each individual stūpa, he offered five hundred jeweled canopies, and at the site of each and every stūpa, he presented hundreds of thousands of varieties of musical instruments.

Throughout every part of Jambudvīpa, he caused exquisite flowering trees to be planted everywhere; before each and every stūpa, he lit hundreds of thousands of lamps, with each lamp-vessel holding a thousand *hu* of oil.
Furthermore, he again made offerings to that stūpa with all kinds of perfumes—unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, as well as various flower garlands and the like.
After Prince Puṇyaraśmi had performed such offerings for a koṭi of years, he subsequently went forth into the homeless life.

Having gone forth, he possessed only the three robes and constantly practiced alms-gathering; he delighted in the dhūta practices, remained perpetually seated and never lay down, and during other times he never slept. He did not seek anything from others, and when giving to all, his mind expected no recompense; he constantly expounded the True Dharma for the sake of others.
Thus, for four koṭis of years, he would not even accept a single word of praise from anyone, let alone receive any material offerings or sustenance.
If, when listening to the Dharma, one has no thought of weariness, the devas will constantly attend to and make offerings to them.

At that time, within that land, the king, his ministers, queens, court ladies, all the people, and their respective retinues will all follow and emulate that prince in leaving the household life to practice the Way.
"Rāṣṭrapāla! At that time, when the devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens saw this event, they thought to themselves:

'Now all the people within this kingdom are following the prince to leave the household life; thus, this entire kingdom is now the Three Jewels. We should now act as donors to make offerings to them, which is equivalent to making offerings to the Three Jewels and benefiting the world.'"
After that Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for sixty-four koṭis of years, all of which were sustained by the bhikṣu Puṇyaprabha.

From that time forward, the bhikṣu Puṇyaraśmi constantly made offerings in this manner; in this sequence, he made offerings to ninety-four koṭis of Buddhas, performing for each and every Buddha the same acts of offering as described above.
Rāṣṭrapāla, what do you think?
Is that King Arciṣmān anyone other than this person?
Do not harbor any different views; he is none other than the present Tathāgata Amitāyus.
Guardian of the Nation! What do you think?
Who else could that Prince Puṇyaprabha have been?
Do not harbor any doubt; it was none other than myself.
And who else could that guardian deity of the city have been at that time?
"That is Akṣobhya Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Rakṣa: "Rakṣa!"

Therefore, if any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should study the various practices cultivated by Prince Puṇyaraśmi with profound resolve and utmost sincerity, so as to be able to relinquish all feelings of aversion and attachment.
Therefore, because I have constantly and diligently practiced such asceticism, I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

However, in future ages there will be monks who cherish fame and profit, who are greedily attached to their followers, and whose wholesome qualities naturally diminish; they are constantly harmed by the enemy of self-conceit and are truly to be pitied.
For the sake of greed for profit, they distance themselves from the True Dharma; having left the home life in vain, they defile the conduct of a śramaṇa.

They merely say with their mouths, "I am a bodhisattva," yet in their inner hearts they practice nothing but flattery and crookedness. Their body and mind are clouded and turbid, submerged in the mud of afflictions; they possess only the outward form while contradicting the fundamental Path.

Having abandoned their vows, they become greedily attached to matters such as clothing, food and drink, housing, bedding, and medicinal requisites; their minds lack shame and remorse, they do not avoid disgrace, and they possess no dignified deportment.
They remain far from the Buddha’s realm, their minds constantly clinging to greed.
Guardian of the Nation!
If there are those who hear such a teaching as this, they should recognize those evil associates.
"One who is a bad friend seeks fame and covets profit; one should not associate with such a person.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Those who practice much negligence Are far removed from the state of the Ten Powers."
Their minds are constantly greedy for gain and offerings, as well as for various followers and retinues;
they abandon the Buddha’s bodhi and the thousands of kinds of merit.
Pretending to be sages, they seek fame and profit; they are evil-natured and devoid of shame or remorse.
Deceitful and sycophantic, without shame or remorse,
they enter into the Buddha-dharma and, following along with all afflictions,
swiftly fall into the evil realms.
With their mouths they say, "We are great virtuous ones dwelling in the forest," yet in their hearts they constantly think of the village.
Because of their greed, their minds are full of discursive thoughts;
such people are as far from liberation as heaven is from earth.
The practitioner should keep them at a distance, as one fears a venomous snake.
Such persons take no delight in the Buddha-dharma nor in the Sangha of noble qualities;
they abandon and depart from the path of goodness, constantly treading upon deviant ways.
Having lost immeasurable virtues, they are obscured by the various realms of existence.
Hearing of my past conduct, believe it with a true and sincere heart;
you should learn from my practice throughout many koṭis of eons.
Such a Dharma is difficult to encounter; one should therefore give rise to the mind of great patience.
Wherever I have taught, you should diligently practice and uphold it.
If you wish to attain Buddhahood within the wondrous and supreme Mahāyāna, [you must do so].
One should recollect the conduct of that king, whose various merits are immeasurable.
Having contemplated this reality, one should abide within his teaching;
in this way, the path to enlightenment shall be seen just as the Buddha has taught.
Reflect deeply upon all virtues, the locus of the lineage of the noble ones;
one should act according to the teaching.
Otherwise, one will lose the flavor of virtue and shall be born within the evil realms.
Folly is no different [from such conduct]; having been born there, one will surely regret it.
To those who dwell in mountain forests, I urge you:
be careful not to praise yourselves, nor disparage the conduct of others; rather, always reproach yourself.
In the past, I turned my back on billions of Buddhas because of a mind of self-conceit;
do not begrudge your own body or life, but renounce all places of attachment and affection.
As I have spoken this sutra, give rise to a heart of reverence for the Dharma.
If one can practice according to what has been taught, awakening will not be difficult to attain.
This vehicle was proclaimed by the Great Sage; having heard it, do not give rise to doubt.
Therefore, within the Buddha-dharma, one should abide in accordance with the holy teachings.
"Exert yourself with diligence, even at the cost of body and life; do not violate my teaching.
If you do not believe this teaching, it will be of no benefit in your future regrets.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further addressed the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
