“Rāṣṭrapāla! If there is a bodhisattva who constantly practices the five pāramitās without ceasing, and if there is another bodhisattva who, within this sūtra, is able to practice according to the Dharma and abide according to the teaching, and further declares:
‘I abide according to the teaching; I practice according to the teaching.’”

If one were to compare the merit of practicing the five perfections prior to this with this present merit, it would not equal even a hundredth part; it would not equal even a ten-thousandth part; it would not equal even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-th part; it would not equal even a part calculable by number or beyond calculation; it would not equal even a *kalā* part; it would not equal even a part by way of analogy; it would not equal even an *upaniṣad* part.

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, thirty nayutas of devas, humans, asuras, and others who had not previously resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi all generated that resolve and became non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there were seven thousand bhikṣus who, having exhausted all outflows (āsrava), attained liberation of mind.
At that time, the Elder Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the name of this Dharma-fundamental?
How should we receive and uphold it?
Having made this request, the Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Rakṣa:
“Good son! This dharma-text is named ‘The Pure Practice of Non-Empty Vows’; you should uphold it as such.
It is also named ‘The Vinaya of Certainty in the Bodhisattva Practice of the Play of the Good Man’; you should uphold it as such.”
It is also titled "The Endowment of True Meaning"; thus should it be upheld.
It is also titled "The Former Deeds of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Puṇyaraśmi"; thus should it be upheld.

When the Buddha had finished teaching this Dharma, the Elder Protector-of-the-Nation Bodhisattva, along with the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume Eighty-one and Volume Eighty-two,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Sengkai of the Cao Wei Dynasty.
19. The Chapter on the Householder Ugga, the Nineteenth. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, together with a great community of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and five thousand bodhisattvas. Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantamukha Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, and others such as these were their leaders.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma, surrounded with reverence by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands.
Then, the householder Ugga, accompanied by five hundred followers, departed from the great city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to Jeta’s Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also the elder Dharmadatta (in another text, Priyadarśana), the elder Yaśas, the elder Sudatta, the elder Yaśodatta, the elder Sudhana, the elder Priyavimśa, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, the elder Nāgaśrī, and the elder Satyananda; each of these was accompanied by five hundred elders, and together they departed from the great city of Śrāvastī for the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
All of them, together with their retinues, had planted deep roots of goodness in the Mahāyāna and were destined for the unsurpassed, true path.
At that time, the householder Ugga, knowing that all the householders had assembled, received the Buddha’s spiritual power and, joining his palms toward the Buddha, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask something; I pray that you will deign to grant me your attention.
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One said, "Householder!"
“The Tathāgata always permits you to ask whatever you wish.
According to your doubts, I shall explain in response to your questions so as to bring joy to your heart.
When the householder Ugga heard these words, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son or daughter of good family resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, understands and inclines toward the Mahāyāna, has faith in the Mahāyāna, desires to assemble the Mahāyāna, desires to mount the Mahāyāna, and knows the Mahāyāna; if they protect all sentient beings, console and encourage all sentient beings, and act for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings—firmly adorning themselves with resolve, thinking: ‘I must deliver those not yet delivered, liberate those not yet liberated, comfort those who lack comfort, and lead those who have not attained *nirvāṇa* to *nirvāṇa*; I shall bear the burden of all beings and act as a great bridge and boat.’”

Having heard of the wisdom of immeasurable Buddhas and desiring to cultivate that Buddha-wisdom, they give rise to great adornment; knowing the immeasurable sufferings and afflictions within birth and death, their minds remain free from sorrow and vexation throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and their hearts never grow weary as they transmigrate through birth and death for immeasurable kalpas.
“World-Honored One!
Among these, if there are sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle—
whether they are renunciants practicing and accumulating the Dharma-conduct, or householders practicing and accumulating the Dharma-conduct.”
Excellent, World-Honored One! You have compassion for humans, devas, and asuras.
World-Honored One, you protect the Mahāyāna so that the Three Jewels are not interrupted, and you cause all-knowledge to abide long in the world.
"Bhagavān! We pray that you will expound upon the sphere of ethical conduct for lay bodhisattvas.

How may a lay bodhisattva, dwelling in the state of a householder, practice in accordance with the instructions of the Tathāgata without impairing the factors conducive to enlightenment, and how may they attain superior progress in this present life without being obscured by entangling karma?"
"Bhagavān! How does a renunciant bodhisattva abandon what is cherished and dear to go forth?
They should be instructed as follows:"
What is the practice of the Dharma?
How does one cultivate goodness?
And how should a renunciant bodhisattva abide?
"What does it mean to 'not dwell'?
Having thus requested, the World-Honored One then addressed the householder Ugga:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Householder!
What you have asked is indeed appropriate for you.
Householder, listen attentively and reflect upon it well."
"I shall now explain for you the superior practices attained through the training and dwelling of bodhisattvas,
both householders and those who have gone forth. Ugga replied,
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I shall receive the teaching and listen.
The Buddha said, "Householder!"

A lay bodhisattva should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha, dedicating the merit of these Three Jewels toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
"Householder!
How does a lay bodhisattva take refuge in the Buddha?

I must attain the thirty-two marks of a Buddha’s body to adorn myself; I shall gather these roots of goodness to accumulate the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and for the sake of this accumulation, I shall practice with diligent vigor."
"Householder!
This is called a lay bodhisattva taking refuge in the Buddha.
Householder!"
"How does a lay bodhisattva take refuge in the Dharma? Householder!

Such a bodhisattva reveres the Dharma and those who teach the Dharma; they desire the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, and find supreme joy in the Dharma. They assist the Dharma, abide in the Dharma, uphold the Dharma, and protect the Dharma. They are firmly established in the Dharma, praise the Dharma, dwell in the practice of the Dharma, increase the Dharma, and seek the Dharma. They take the Dharma as their strength, bestow the weapons of the Dharma, and make the Dharma alone their primary task."
"Householder! Once I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall bestow the True Dharma as an equal gift upon all humans, devas, and asuras."
This is called the lay bodhisattva’s taking refuge in the Dharma.
Householder!
How does the lay bodhisattva take refuge in the Saṃgha?
"O Householder!

If a bodhisattva sees a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat, as well as ordinary persons or those of the śrāvaka vehicle, they should in all cases show respect and compliance, quickly rise to welcome them, and circumambulate them to the right with pleasant words and a gentle voice."
One should reflect in this way:
"When we attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, we shall preach the Dharma for the sake of accomplishing the merit and benefits of the śrāvakas."
"Although they give rise to a mind of reverence, they do not abide therein.
Householder!
This is called a lay bodhisattva taking refuge in the Saṃgha."
“Householder! A bodhisattva living at home who accomplishes four dharmas takes refuge in the Buddha.
What are these four?
One does not abandon the bodhicitta, nor does one cease exhorting others to generate the bodhicitta; one does not abandon great compassion, and never gives rise to the thought of other vehicles.
Householder!
This is called the householder bodhisattva accomplishing four dharmas to take refuge in the Buddha.
Householder, when a householder bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he takes refuge in the Dharma.
What are the four? They are:

to associate with and rely upon those who are Dharma-preachers; having heard the Dharma, to contemplate it well; to expound the Dharma as one has heard it for others; and to dedicate the merit of this teaching of the Dharma toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
"Householder!
This is called the fourth dharma by which a lay bodhisattva accomplishes taking refuge in the Dharma.
Householder!"
A lay bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas takes refuge in the Saṃgha:

if there are those who have not yet resolved to enter the Śrāvaka vehicle, they encourage them to generate the mind of omniscience; whether through the gathering of material wealth or the gathering of the Dharma, they rely on the Saṃgha of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas and do not rely on the Śrāvaka Saṃgha, seeking the virtues of the Śrāvakas without dwelling in their minds.
"Householder!
These are called the four dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva accomplishes taking refuge in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, householder!"
When a lay bodhisattva, having seen the Tathāgata, practices mindfulness of the Buddha, this is called taking refuge in the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma, they practice mindfulness of the Dharma; this is called taking refuge in the Dharma.
Having seen the Tathāgata and the community of śrāvakas, not forgetting the bodhicitta— this is called taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, householder,
if a bodhisattva vows to always practice giving together with the Buddha, this is called taking refuge in the Buddha.
To practice giving while guarding the True Dharma is called taking refuge in the Dharma.
To dedicate this giving toward the Unsurpassed Way is called taking refuge in the Sangha.
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home performs the deeds of a virtuous person and does not perform the deeds of an unvirtuous person.
Householder!"
What is meant by the karma of a virtuous person, rather than the karma of an unvirtuous person?
Householder!
It is when a lay bodhisattva accumulates wealth and estates in accordance with the Dharma, and not contrary to the Dharma.
He seeks with equanimity, rectitude, and correctness—not with coarseness or malice—and does not oppress others.
Having obtained his domain in accordance with the Dharma, he gives rise to the perception of impermanence; he does not harbor thoughts of stinginess, but delights in relinquishment without parsimony.

One provides for one's parents, wife, children, slaves, and various laborers with wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma; having first provided for those such as close friends, kinsmen, and spiritual teachers, one then bestows the Dharma.
Furthermore, householder!

A bodhisattva living at home bears a heavy burden and exerts great diligence; that is to say, he bears the burden of the five aggregates of all sentient beings, relinquishes the burden of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and teaches and transforms sentient beings without weariness.

Having renounced his own happiness for the sake of sentient beings, he remains unshaken by gain or loss, praise or blame, renown or insignificance, pleasure or pain, thereby transcending worldly dharmas.

Though his wealth is immeasurable, he is free from arrogance and indolence; though he suffers loss of profit or reputation, he feels no grief or distress. He skillfully observes karmic actions and guards right conduct; seeing those who violate the prohibitions, he does not give rise to anger. In all his movements, he dwells well and remains awakened; he eliminates frivolity and fulfills wisdom. He assists in the affairs of others while relinquishing his own tasks; he acts without expectation and, having performed deeds, does not abandon them midway, but knows and remembers their kindness.
One should skillfully perform acts of giving by bestowing wealth and stipends upon the poor; one who possesses power should subdue great arrogance, while comforting those who lack power.

One should remove the arrows of grief from others and endure those who are inferior; one should abandon arrogance and overweening pride, and with reverence and respect, draw near to those of great learning to inquire of their clear wisdom.
Their vision is upright and their conduct is unconditioned, free from illusion or delusion.
They harbor no attachment toward sentient beings; they cultivate goodness without satiety and seek much learning without weariness. Their actions are steadfast, equaling those of the noble sages.
He gives rise to great compassion toward those who are not noble; he is firm as a friend, treating enemies and kin with equality, and regards all sentient beings with an impartial mind.
He is without stinginess regarding any dharma, and as he hears the teachings, he reveals them and contemplates their meaning.

Regarding all sensual pleasures, he gives rise to the perception of impermanence; he does not crave his own body and contemplates life as being like dew; he contemplates wealth and possessions with the perception of them being like illusory clouds; regarding men and women, he has the perception of them as being like a closed prison; regarding his kinsmen, he gives rise to the perception of suffering; regarding fields and houses, he has the perception of them as corpses in the cycle of birth and death; regarding the wealth he seeks, he has the perception that it destroys roots of goodness; regarding his home, he gives rise to the perception of confinement; regarding his relatives, he gives rise to the perception of them as jailers; he gives rise to the perception of no difference between night and day; regarding this unsubstantial body, he gives rise to the perception of giving it away as a substantial gift; regarding this unsubstantial life, he gives rise to the perception of a substantial life; and regarding unsubstantial wealth, he gives rise to the perception of giving it away as a substantial gift.
What is meant by generating the thought of a firm gift toward this non-firm body?
To perform all tasks and carry out all commissions for others is called generating the thought of a firm gift toward this non-firm body.
Not losing one's original goodness and increasing present roots of goodness is to conceive the thought of firm giving regarding what is not a firm life.
Subduing stinginess and practicing generosity is to conceive the thought of firm giving regarding what is not a firm wealth.
"Householder!

This is called the practice of a lay bodhisattva cultivating the conduct of a virtuous man (satpuruṣa). Toward all Tathāgatas, he is entirely without fault; his speech is called 'conformable' and 'in accordance with the Dharma,' and he is free from divergent thoughts regarding the Unsurpassed Way."
"Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva should receive the excellent precepts, namely the five precepts.
He delights in non-killing, laying aside the sword and staff; with a sense of shame and firm vows, he does not kill any sentient beings whatsoever."
He does not afflict anyone, maintains an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, and constantly practices loving-kindness.

He should refrain from stealing; being content with his own wealth, he harbors no longing for the property of others. Having abandoned greed and giving rise to no delusion, he feels no attachment to the emoluments of others, nor does he take even a blade of grass or a leaf that has not been given.

He abstains from sexual misconduct; content with his own wife, he does not covet the wives of others, nor does he look upon the beauty of other women with a defiled mind. His heart feels weary and averse toward it, perceiving it as nothing but suffering, and his mind is constantly turned away from it in renunciation.

If one gives rise to thoughts of desire toward one's own wife, one should instead give rise to thoughts of impurity and dread; this is the power of the fetters (saṃyojana) that constitutes desire, and it is not something I do.
One should constantly cultivate the perception of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
That person should reflect in this way:
"I shall not even give rise to a thought of desire, much less engage in the physical union and mutual contact of two bodies."
"One should abstain from false speech; one should speak truthfully and speak reality, acting in accordance with what one says and not deceiving others.
Accomplished in a virtuous mind, one acts after prior reflection, speaking exactly as one has seen and heard."
Guarding the Dharma, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever speak falsely.

Such a person should abstain from alcohol, remaining sober and undisturbed; they should not speak falsely, nor act with self-deprecation or frivolity, nor engage in mocking or idle chatter, nor provoke others to dispute. They should abide in right mindfulness and then understand this.
If one’s mind desires to relinquish all wealth and property, one should give food to those who need food and bestow drink upon those who need drink.
When giving to others, one should form this thought:
"When I am mindful of this Dānapāramitā, I shall provide whatever they desire."
Furthermore, I shall cause those who seek [my gifts] to be satisfied.
If I give them wine, I shall instead restrain such persons, enabling them to attain right mindfulness so that they are not driven to madness or delusion. Why is this?
"To fully satisfy the desires of others is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Elder!
Therefore, when a bodhisattva gives wine to others, there is no fault in this before the Buddha."
"Householder!
If a lay bodhisattva takes these merits from upholding the five precepts and dedicates them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they will well protect the five precepts."
Furthermore, one should abstain from divisive speech; if there are disputes, one should bring about reconciliation.
One should avoid harsh words, uttering instead words of love and gentleness, greeting others first with inquiries after their well-being, and never disparaging or insulting them.

They speak words that benefit others, words of the Dharma, timely words, truthful words, words of renunciation, words of subduing, and words free from frivolous laughter; they act according to what they say and do not give rise to greed or delusion. They always bring peace to all minds without causing them harm, and they constantly cultivate the power of patience to adorn themselves.
One should always maintain right view, abandon all false views, and not prostrate to other deities, but instead make offerings now to the Buddha.
"Furthermore, householder!

If a bodhisattva living at home dwells among villages, cities, towns, districts, or crowds of people, he should preach the Dharma for the multitude according to his location. To sentient beings who lack faith, he should exhort them to develop faith; to those who are unfilial, who do not recognize their parents, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, who do not distinguish between elders and juniors, and who are defiant toward instruction and devoid of any sense of awe or avoidance, he should exhort them to practice filial piety and obedience."

If there are those who have heard little, he encourages them to hear much; if they are stingy, he encourages them to give; if they violate the precepts, he encourages them to observe them; if they are prone to anger, he encourages them to practice patience; if they are lazy, he encourages them to exert themselves; if their minds are distracted, he encourages them to cultivate concentration; if they lack wisdom, he encourages them to develop it. To the poor, he provides wealth; to the sick, he gives medicine. He acts as a protector for those without protection, a refuge for those without refuge, and a support for those without support.
That person should practice this Dharma by following mindfulness in all such places, so as not to let a single being fall into the evil realms.
Householder, in this way the bodhisattva exhorts each and every one, up to the seventh time, desiring to establish sentient beings in virtuous conduct.

Since they cannot be made to abide in such a state, this bodhisattva should give rise to great compassion for these sentient beings and firmly resolve upon the adornment of all-encompassing wisdom, saying:
"If I do not tame these wicked sentient beings, I shall never attain supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment."

Why is this? It is for this reason that I have made the vow of great adornment; it is not for the sake of being disciplined, free from flattery, free from deceit, and endowed with precepts and virtuous conduct that I have undertaken this great adornment.
"I shall diligently exert such vigor so that my actions are not in vain, and that sentient beings who see me immediately gain faith and respect. Elder!
If a bodhisattva dwells in such towns or villages and does not instruct sentient beings to avoid falling into the evil realms, that bodhisattva is censured by all Buddhas.

"Elder! Therefore, a bodhisattva should thus adorn themselves with the great adornment, thinking: 'I must now practice this conduct and dwell in cities, towns, villages, and districts so that not a single person falls into the evil realms.'"
"O Householder!
It is just as if there were a skilled and renowned physician in a city who, by causing even a single sentient being to die from a poison-disease, were to be rebuked by the multitude.
Thus it is, O Householder!"
If a bodhisattva, wherever they may dwell, does not teach sentient beings so as to prevent them from falling into the evil realms, that bodhisattva will be rebuked by all the Buddhas.
"Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva skillfully practices and trains in conduct.

That which is called 'home' (kula) is named the slayer of roots of goodness; it is named that which does not abandon faults and harms the assistance of wholesome karma. For this reason, it is called 'home.'
Why is it called "dwelling"?
Because all fetters and latent tendencies dwell therein, it is called "dwelling.

Furthermore, because one dwells in unwholesome thoughts, dwells in lack of self-control, dwells as a shameless, ignorant, and petty ordinary person, and dwells in unwholesome conduct and various evil transgressions, it is therefore called a "home."
Furthermore, as for "living at home" (*gṛhastha*), all forms of suffering and affliction manifest therein, and it destroys one's prior roots of goodness; therefore, it is called "living at home.

Moreover, as for "home," dwelling within it, there is no evil that one does not commit; dwelling within it, one fails to properly revere and obey one's parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—this is what is meant by "home."

Furthermore, as for "household" (*kula*): the branches of long-standing attachment, along with sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, all arise therein; it gathers together killing, binding, scolding, beating, reviling, and the production of harsh speech—therefore, it is called a household.

It causes unproduced roots of goodness to waver and fail to be created, and it causes already produced roots of goodness to be entirely dissipated and extinguished. It is censured by the wise; that is to say, if one dwells within this state, one falls into the evil realms, or if one dwells within this state, one falls into greed, hatred, and delusion. Therefore, it is called the "house."

If one dwells within this, it obstructs and causes the abandonment of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; therefore, it is called a "house."

If one dwells within this state, being gripped by craving for parents, wife and children, sisters, relatives, friends, and associates, one constantly thinks of wealth and sensual desires without ever reaching satisfaction; like the ocean swallowing rivers, it is never filled.
If one dwells in the household life, it is like fire consuming fuel; one's thoughts have no fixed place, like the wind that does not stay.

Living at home consumes the body as if one were ingesting poison, for all manner of sufferings come to dwell there. Therefore, one should renounce the household life as one would distance oneself from an enemy.
If one dwells at home, it creates obstacles to the noble Dharma; it gives rise to many conditions for dispute and is constantly characterized by opposition.
Living in a household, one is entangled in a mixture of good and evil conditions and burdened with many worldly affairs.
Living at home is impermanent and cannot endure for long; it is a phenomenon that does not abide.
Life at home is extremely suffering because one must seek protection, leading to manifold anxieties regarding enemies and kin alike.
Living at home, one lacks self-mastery yet falls into the conceit of "mine-ness.
Living at home is deceptive and delusive; there is no reality, yet things appear as if they were real.
Living at home involves separation, for one must pass through many different places.
Living at home is like an illusion, for it gathers together many unreal sentient beings.
Living at home is like a dream, for rise and fall alternate therein.
Living at home is like dew, for it quickly breaks and falls away.
The household life is like a drop of honey, for its flavor lasts but a moment.
The household life is like a web of thorns, for one is greedily attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
The household life is like a needle-mouthed insect, for it consumes food without discernment.
The household is like a venomous snake, for its members mutually encroach upon one another.
The household abounds in expectations, for the mind is made to stumble and yearn.
Life at home is full of fear, for one is plundered by kings, thieves, water, and fire.
"A household involves much debate and many afflictions.
Thus, householder, a bodhisattva who dwells at home is said to be 'one who well understands the household.'"
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home who practices the gift of well-subdued discipline, with discernment and gentleness, should contemplate thus:
'If I have given to that person, then it is mine; as for what remains in my household, it is not mine.'"
That which has been given is firm, while the rest is not;
that which has been given brings happiness in the future, while the rest brings happiness in the present;
that which has been given requires no guarding, while the rest must be guarded.
If one who has already given is not bound by craving, others increase their craving;
if one who has already given has no sense of "mine," others possess the sense of "mine";
that which has been given is without fear, while the remainder is fearful.
That which has already been given is the foundation pillar of the Path, while the rest are the pillars of Māra;
that which has been given is inexhaustible, while the rest are exhaustible;
that which has been given is joy, while the rest—guarding and protecting—is suffering.
That which has already been given is free from fetters, while the remainder increases them;
that which has already been given is a great domain, while the remainder is not a domain;
if that which has already been given is the deed of a true man, the rest remaining is not the deed of a true man.
That which has already been given is praised by all Buddhas; that which remains is praised by ordinary worldlings.
Thus, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home should remain steadfastly established in giving.
"Furthermore, householder!
When a lay bodhisattva sees a beggar, he should give rise to three perceptions.
What are these three?
The perception of spiritual friends, the perception of wealth in future lives, and the perception of the foundation of bodhi.
Furthermore, there are three perceptions:
the perception of compliance with the Tathāgata’s teachings, the perception of the desire for karmic fruition, and the perception of subduing Māra.
Furthermore, there are three perceptions:

one should conceive the perception of kin and relatives toward those who come seeking; the perception of gathering toward the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); and the perception of renunciation toward infinite births.
One should give rise to these three perceptions in this manner.
Furthermore, there are three perceptions. What are the three?
They are the perception of removing greed, the perception of removing hatred, and the perception of removing delusion.
These three perceptions arise. Why is this?
O Householder!
This person’s greed, anger, and delusion all become slight.
Householder!
How do these three things all become slight?
If, when giving wealth, the mind is free from attachment, this is called the thinning of greed.
If one gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward the beggar, this is called the thinning of hatred.
If, after having given, one dedicates the merit toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path, this is called the thinning of delusion.
"Householder!
This is called a donor whose greed, hatred, and delusion are thin.
Furthermore, householder!"
When a lay bodhisattva sees a beggar, they cultivate the mental orientation toward fulfilling the six pāramitās. What are these six?
If this bodhisattva possesses no object whatsoever that they do not intend to give away, this is called cultivating the fulfillment of the dāna-pāramitā.
Giving based on the bodhicitta is called practicing and fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Not giving rise to anger or reproach toward those who seek [gifts] is called practicing and fulfilling the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).

If, when practicing giving, one does not give rise to the thought of one's own deficiency, this is called cultivating and proceeding toward the fulfillment of the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

If, after having given, the mind feels no regret and instead gives rise to redoubled joy, this is called cultivating and proceeding toward the fulfillment of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

If, after having practiced giving, one does not grasp at any phenomena and does not expect a karmic reward, this person of clear wisdom does not abide in any phenomena; following non-abiding, they head toward the unsurpassed path—this is called cultivating and proceeding toward the fulfillment of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is called a bodhisattva seeing a beggar and practicing to fulfill the six pāramitās.
"Furthermore, householder!

A lay bodhisattva should cultivate equanimity toward the eight worldly dharmas; such a person neither gives rise to sorrow nor joy regarding household wealth, property, wife, or children, and even if they are lost or forgotten, they do not give rise to grief."
One should contemplate in this way:

conditioned phenomena are like illusions and are the marks of false conceptualization. Parents, wives, children, servants, employees, friends, and kinsmen are none of mine; I must not commit unwholesome karma for their sake, as it is not appropriate for me.
These are companions for this present life, not companions for future lives; they are companions for pleasure, not companions for suffering; I am not their protector, nor am I protected by them.
Generosity, self-discipline, wisdom, diligence, and heedfulness—these roots of goodness that assist the factors of enlightenment are mine; wherever I go, they shall follow me.

Why is this? Parents, wives, children, male and female relatives, friends, and servants cannot save me; they are not my refuge, not my dwelling, not my island, not my shelter, and not mine or what belongs to me. These aggregates, elements, and sense bases are neither I nor mine; how much less could parents, wives, and children be mine?

"Parents, wives, and children are the products of karma; I too receive retribution according to my own good and evil karma, and they likewise receive good and evil retribution according to their own karma.
Householder!"

Furthermore, whether walking, coming, sitting, or rising, this bodhisattva constantly contemplates these matters; they do not commit even a hair’s breadth of evil or unwholesome karma of body, speech, or mind for the sake of parents, wife, children, relatives, servants, or laborers.
"Therefore, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home should give rise to three perceptions regarding his own wife.
What are these three?
The perception of impermanence, the perception of change, and the perception of decay.
Householder! These are called the three perceptions that a lay bodhisattva generates toward his own wife.
A lay bodhisattva further gives rise to three perceptions regarding his own wife.
What are these three?

She is a companion for pleasure, not a companion for the next world; she is a companion for food and drink, not a companion for karmic retribution; she is a companion for times of happiness, not a companion for times of suffering.
"Householder!
These are the three perceptions that a lay bodhisattva generates toward his own wife.
Furthermore, he generates another three perceptions."
What are the three?
The perception of the unattractive, the perception of the foul and putrid, and the perception of the loathsome.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are these three?
The perception of an enemy, the perception of an executioner, and the perception of a deceptive friend.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of a rākṣasa, the perception of a piśāca, and the perception of a malevolent spirit—
these are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The notion that [what is received] is not "mine," the notion of non-attachment, and the notion of begging.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of holding to misconduct of body, the perception of holding to misconduct of speech, and the perception of holding to misconduct of mind.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of harmfulness—
these are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of darkness, the perception of defiled precepts, and the perception of bondage.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of obstacles to ethical discipline, the perception of obstacles to meditative concentration, and the perception of obstacles to wisdom.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of flattery and crookedness, the perception of a snare, and the perception of a cat on the watch—
these are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
They are the perception of calamity, the perception of feverish affliction, and the perception of illness and disorder.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of seductive charm, the perception of causing decay, and the perception of frost and hail.
These are called the three.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise.
What are the three?
The perception of sickness, the perception of old age, and the perception of death—
these are called the three.
Furthermore, there arise three perceptions:
The perception of Māra, the perception of a māra-maiden, and the perception of something fearsome—
these are called the three.
Furthermore, one gives rise to another three perceptions:
The perception of anxiety, the perception of weeping, and the perception of suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of a great female wolf, the perception of a makara fish, and the perception of a large female cat.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of a black snake, the perception of a corpse-guarding fish, and the perception of one who robs away vital energy.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
One should have no thought of rescue, no thought of refuge, and no thought of protection.
Furthermore, one should give rise to three thoughts:
the thought of her as a mother, the thought of her as an elder sister, and the thought of her as a younger sister.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of an enemy, the perception of a murderer, and the perception of a jailer.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
The perception of a waterfall, the perception of waves, and the perception of whirlpools.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of mud, the perception of being submerged in mud, and the perception of turbidity.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of being blind, the perception of wearing cangues, and the perception of wearing shackles.
Again, three perceptions arise:
The perception of a pit of fire, the perception of a pit of swords, and the perception of a torch of grass.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of lack of benefit, the perception of thorns, and the perception of poison.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of imprisonment, the perception of punishment, and the perception of swords and blades.
Again, three perceptions arise:
The perception of strife, the perception of litigation, and the perception of imprisonment.
Furthermore, three perceptions arise:
the perception of association with the disliked, the perception of separation from the beloved, and the perception of illness.
To speak briefly, this extends even to all perceptions of strife and contention, all perceptions of dregs and turbidity, and all perceptions of unwholesome roots.
Householder!
A bodhisattva living at home should generate such mental images and reflections regarding his own wife.
"Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva should not harbor excessive attachment toward his own children.
Householder!"
If one conceives such extreme affection for one's child that it does not exist for others, this leads to self-destruction.
One should reproach oneself by means of three dharmas.
What are these three?
The path to enlightenment is attained through an impartial mind, not through a partial mind;
it is attained through right practice, not through wrong practice;
it is attained through undifferentiated practice, not through mixed practice.

Furthermore, one should rebuke one's own mind for conceiving thoughts of enmity, thoughts of an evil friend, and thoughts of one who is not a virtuous friend toward one's own child; such thoughts oppose the Buddha’s wisdom and impartial compassion, and they destroy my roots of goodness.
In every situation, he should discipline his own mind, regarding all beings as he would his own child, and regarding all beings as he would himself.
He should cultivate this reflection:
"I have come from another place; my child has come from another place."
Why is this? All sentient beings have once been my children, and I too have been the child of all those sentient beings.
I never give rise to the thought that "these are my children" and "those are not."
Why is this? Having gone through the six realms of existence, one may again become an enemy or a child; therefore, I should treat all beings equally, whether they are kin or non-kin.
For what reason should I give with redoubled affection to those who are my kin, while giving nothing at all to those who are not my kin?
If I give rise to a mind of attachment or aversion, I will not give anything at all to those who are not my kin.
If I give rise to a mind of attachment or aversion, I will be unable to proceed toward the Dharma.
Why is this? Unequal conduct leads to an unequal destination, while practicing equal conduct leads to an equal destination.
I ought not to practice such unequal conduct; I shall train in an equanimous mind toward all sentient beings so that I may swiftly reach omniscience.

“Householder! A bodhisattva living at home does not give rise to the notion of ‘mine’ or the notion of ‘protecting’ regarding various material goods; he is not bound by them, does not conceive of them with longing or affection, and does not produce fetters or afflictions.
"Furthermore, householder!
If a beggar comes to a householder bodhisattva seeking something, the bodhisattva should, in accordance with the wealth being given, reflect with a sincere mind:
'Whether this wealth is given away or not given away, it shall both perish and vanish; my wishes will not be fulfilled, and I must inevitably face death. "
"I shall not abandon my wealth; rather, let my wealth abandon me.
I must now renounce it so that it becomes a lasting wealth, and only then die.
Having renounced this wealth, at the time of death I shall have no regret, but instead feel joy and be without remorse."
If one is unable to give, one should inform the beggar with these four points:

"At present, my strength is inferior and my roots of goodness are not yet mature; within the Mahāyāna, I am but a beginner, and my mind is not yet capable of practicing giving with complete mastery. I am still attached to signs and abide in the notions of 'self' and 'what belongs to self.'"
"O virtuous Great Being!
I now repent before you; do not harbor resentment. I shall practice with such diligent effort as to fulfill all the aspirations of sentient beings."
"Householder! A householder bodhisattva should speak thus to a beggar.
Furthermore, householder!"

When a lay bodhisattva hears the words of the Buddhas of the past, if they do not encounter a Buddha or the noble Saṅgha, they should pay homage to all the Buddhas of the ten directions and give rise to sympathetic joy for all the Buddhas' original practices leading up to their attainment of Buddhahood.

In this manner, three times each day and night, they purify the actions of body, speech, and mind, and purify their loving-kindness and compassion; being endowed with the pure raiment of shame and remorse, they rejoice in the roots of virtue they have accumulated with the bodhicitta, acting with gentleness and goodness, showing reverence, and severing pride.

One should practice the three divisions and recite the Dharma of the three divisions; with single-minded devotion, repent of all unwholesome karmas and refrain from creating new ones, while rejoicing in all meritorious deeds to fully accumulate the marks and signs of excellence.
I entreat all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma, and I shall fully receive and uphold all the teachings they proclaim.
May the Buddhas live long and increase their roots of goodness, and may my own land likewise become so.
"Furthermore, householder!

A lay bodhisattva who observes the eight precepts and practices the conduct of a śramaṇa should draw near to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of pure precepts and virtuous conduct, relying upon them as attendants and not perceiving their faults;
even if he sees a śramaṇa transgressing the rules of conduct, he should not show disrespect."

Furthermore, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is the Worthy One (Arhat) and the Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha), adorned with the practice of ethical discipline, and adorned with concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The *kāṣāya* is free from defilement; all fetters and attachments have been completely relinquished.
One should redouble one's reverence for the banner of the sages and saints, and give rise to great compassion for that bhikṣu, for he ought not to commit such evil deeds.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are named "Tranquil," "Tamed," and "All-Knowing. Their noble banner and attire signify tranquility, taming, subduing, and omniscience; yet these [others] act contrary to the Dharma, being neither tranquil, nor tamed, nor subdued, nor knowing.

As the World-Honored One has said, one should not despise those who have not yet studied; it is not their fault, but rather the fault of their fetters (*saṃyojana*). It is because of these fetters that they manifest such evil deeds.
Within this Buddha-dharma there is a way of transcendence; if a person is able to transcend them, then such a possibility exists.
If one understands these fetters and practices right contemplation to attain the first fruit, one will certainly proceed toward the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
Why is this? Because wisdom can destroy the fetters.
The World-Honored One has further said: "A person should not recklessly disparage others, for that brings harm upon oneself.
What the Tathāgata knows is not what I know; therefore, one should not harbor anger, resentment, or malice toward them."
"Furthermore, householder!
If a bodhisattva living at home enters a monastery, he should stand at the gate and pay homage with his five limbs prostrate before entering.
He should contemplate in this way:

This place is the sphere of practicing emptiness, the sphere of practicing signlessness, the sphere of practicing wishlessness, and the four sublime abodes of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
It is the place where right practice and right dwelling find their rest; when shall I abandon the defilements of the household life?
"When shall I abide in such practice?
I should give rise to this desire for renunciation.

There is no way to cultivate and accumulate the path to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment while remaining a householder; all must go forth from home and enter the secluded forests to cultivate and thereby achieve the unsurpassed right path."
Living at home is full of dust and defilement; leaving home is sublime and excellent.
Living at home is bound by fetters; leaving home is free from obstruction.
Living at home is full of stains; leaving home is renunciation and detachment.
The householder is encompassed by evil; the renunciant is encompassed by goodness.
The householder sinks into the mire of craving and desire; the renunciant remains far removed from the mire of craving and desire.
The householder is associated with the mundane; the renunciant is associated with wisdom.
The householder lives by wrong livelihood; the renunciant lives by pure livelihood.
The householder is full of defilements; the renunciant is free from defilements.
The householder undergoes decline; the renunciant does not decline.
Living at home is dwelling in sorrow; leaving home is rejoicing.
Living at home is a staircase for all evils; leaving home is ascending beyond that staircase.
Living at home is bondage; leaving home is liberation.
Those who live at home dwell in fear; those who have left the home life dwell without fear.
Those who live at home are subject to punishment; those who have left the home life are without punishment.
Those who live at home have many afflictions; those who have left the home life are without affliction.
Living at home is fraught with feverish distress; leaving home is free from such heat.
Living at home involves much seeking and suffering; leaving home is free from seeking and brings joy.
Living at home is characterized by agitation; leaving home is free from agitation.
Living as a householder brings poverty and suffering; leaving home brings freedom from suffering.
Living as a householder brings timidity and weakness; leaving home brings freedom from timidity.
Living as a householder is lowly and base; leaving home is honorable and noble.
Household life is burning; the life of renunciation is tranquil.
In household life one benefits others; in the life of renunciation one benefits oneself.
Those in the household lack vital moisture; those who have renounced possess great nourishment.
For those living at home, there is the pleasure of bondage; for those who have gone forth, there is the pleasure of cessation.
For those living at home, thorns increase; for those who have gone forth, there are no thorns.
Those living at home accomplish minor dharmas; those who have gone forth accomplish the Great Dharma.
Those who live at home are undisciplined; those who have left the home life are disciplined.
Those who live at home are estranged from the precepts; those who have left the home life protect the precepts.
Those who live at home increase the oceans of tears, milk, and blood; those who have left the home life dry up the oceans of tears, milk, and blood.
Householders are censured by all Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, whereas those who have left the household life are praised by all Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
Householders lack contentment; those who have left the household life possess contentment.
The Māra rejoices in the life of a householder; the Māra grieves for one who has left the home life.
The householder is not subdued, while the renunciant is subdued.
The householder is a servant; the renunciant is the master.
The householder dwells at the boundary of birth and death; the renunciant dwells at the boundary of nirvāṇa.
The householder falls into decline; the renunciant uproots decline.
The householder is in darkness; the renunciant is luminously radiant.
Those who live at home have their faculties under no control; those who have left the home life have their faculties under control. Those who live at home are intoxicated and heedless;
those who have left the home life are not heedless. Those who live at home are inconsistent with the Dharma;
those who have left the home life are consistent with the Dharma.
Those who live at home look downward; those who have left the home life look upward.
Those who live at home have many concerns; those who have left the home life have few concerns.
Those who live at home have little strength; those who have left the home life have great strength.
Those who live at home are crooked and deceitful; those who have left home are upright and honest.
Those who live at home have much anxiety; those who have left home are free from anxiety.
Those who live at home are pierced by arrows; those who have left home have removed the arrows.
Those who live at home suffer from illness; those who have left the home life are free from illness.
For those at home, there is the law of aging; for those who have left the home life, there is the law of vigor.
For those at home, life is one of negligence; for those who have left the home life, they cultivate the life of wisdom.
Those who live at home practice deception; those who have left the home life are free from deception.
Those who live at home engage in much activity; those who have left the home life engage in no such activity.
Those who live at home are vessels of poison; those who have left the home life are vessels of nectar.
Household life is fraught with calamities; the life of renunciation is free from disaster.
Those in the household do not relinquish; those who have renounced let go.
Those in the household take up poisonous fruits; those who have renounced take up non-poisonous fruits.
Those who live at home are associated with what is unloved; those who have left the home life are not associated with what is unloved.
For those at home, delusion is heavy; for those who have left the home life, wisdom is light.
Those at home lose skillful means; those who have left the home life possess pure skillful means.
Those who live at home lose right intention; those who have left home purify right intention.
Those who live at home lose supreme intention; those who have left home purify supreme intention.
One who lives at home cannot act as a savior; one who has left home acts as a savior.
Living at home leads to poverty and inferiority; leaving home does not lead to poverty.
Living at home is no shelter; leaving home is the making of a shelter.
Living at home is no refuge; leaving home is the making of a refuge.
Those who live at home are full of anger; those who have left the home life are full of loving-kindness.
Those who live at home carry burdens; those who have left the home life have laid down their burdens.
Those who live at home do not bring all disputes to an end; those who have left the home life bring disputes to an end.
Householders have faults; those who have left the home life are without fault.
Householders are preoccupied with busy affairs; those who have left the home life are free from such busyness.
Householders suffer from feverish affliction; those who have left the home life are free from such heat.
Those who live at home have many enemies; those who have left home have no enemies.
Those who live at home accumulate possessions; those who have left home have no accumulations.
For those who live at home, wealth is solid; for those who have left home, virtue is solid.
Living at home is accompanied by sorrow; leaving home brings tranquility to sorrow.
Living at home leads to depletion and loss; leaving home leads to increase and gain.
Living at home is easy to obtain, whereas for one who has left home, it is difficult to attain even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Living as a householder is easy to do; leaving the household life is difficult to do.
Living as a householder is to go with the current; leaving the household life is to go against the current.
Living as a householder is to dwell within the current; leaving the household life is to possess a boat or raft.
Household life is a river of fetters; the life of renunciation is its crossing.
Household life is this shore; the life of renunciation is the other shore.
Household life is entanglement; the life of renunciation is freedom from entanglement.
Those who live at home harbor resentment; those who have left the home life are tranquil regarding resentment.
Those who live at home follow the laws of kings; those who have left the home life follow the Buddha-dharma.
Those who live at home are defiled by craving; those who have left the home life are free from defilement.
Living at home gives rise to suffering; leaving home gives rise to happiness.
Living at home is shallow and near; leaving home is deep and far-reaching.
Living at home makes companions easy to find; leaving home makes companions difficult to find.
The householder has a wife as his companion; the renunciant has the mind as his companion.
The householder is preoccupied with busy affairs; the renunciant is free from such affairs.
The householder causes suffering to others; the renunciant brings happiness to others.
The laity practice the gift of material wealth; those who have left the home life practice the gift of the Dharma.
The laity uphold the banner of Māra; those who have left the home life uphold the banner of the Buddha.
The laity dwell in a nest; those who have left the home life are free from the nest.
Living at home is the path of non-dharma; leaving home is departing from the path of non-dharma.
Living at home is a dense forest; leaving home is departing from the forest.
Thus it is, householder!

The lay bodhisattva reflects in gradual stages: "Even if I were to perform great sacrifices as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and bestow them all upon sentient beings for a single day, it is within the well-regulated Dharma that the mind of renunciation arises; this is the fulfillment of firm and complete giving."
"I should now resolutely cultivate the precepts and learning.

Upon entering the monastery and paying homage to the Tathāgata’s stūpa, he gives rise to three thoughts: "I, too, shall obtain such offerings; I, too, shall obtain the relics for the sake of compassionately benefiting all sentient beings."
"By training thus, practicing thus, and exerting myself with such diligence, I shall swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having performed all the deeds of a Buddha, I shall enter parinirvāṇa just as the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas do."
He enters the monastic quarters to observe the virtues of all the bhikṣus: who is learned in the scriptures?
Who is a preacher of the Dharma?
Who is a keeper of the Vinaya?
Who upholds the Āgamas?
Which bhikṣus uphold the Bodhisattva-piṭaka?
Who is the forest-dweller (āraṇyaka)?
What kind of bhikṣu has few desires, begs for alms, wears rag-robes, dwells alone, and is secluded from desire?
Who is one who practices?
Who is one who sits in meditation?
Who is the administrator?
Who is the monastery head?
Observe their conduct thoroughly; according to whichever person’s disposition it may be, do not give rise to criticism or reproach.
Whether staying in a monastery or visiting a village, one should well-guard one's verbal karma in whatever one says.
If there are bhikṣus who lack the requisites of robes, alms-bowls, medicine, or other necessities, one should provide them accordingly so as not to cause them to give rise to anger.
Why is this? Because gods and humans possess the fetter of envy and jealousy, they should be protected all the more.
The minds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are not those of Arhats; ordinary persons give rise to transgressions, whereas Arhats do not.

He associates with those of great learning for the sake of cultivating hearing; he stays close to Dharma-preachers to cultivate certainty; he stays close to those who uphold the Vinaya to subdue the fetters and avoid falling into transgressions; he stays close to those who uphold the Bodhisattva-piṭaka to train in and practice the six pāramitās and the cultivation of skillful means; he stays close to forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka) to train in dwelling in solitude; and he stays close to practitioners to train in the practice of sitting upright.

If there is a bhikṣu who has not yet attained the stage of certainty, one should give robes to him if he needs robes, and a bowl if he needs a bowl, and exhort that bhikṣu to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind. Why is this?
This is not a superior state, for wealth and Dharma are what encompass others.
In this way, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home thus skillfully understands the conduct of a śramaṇa.
If there are śramaṇas who are quarreling, disputing, contending, or competing, he reconciles them, even at the cost of his own life, to protect the True Dharma.
Householder!
When a bodhisattva living at home sees a sick bhikṣu, he gives up his own flesh and blood so that the other may recover from their illness.
"Householder!

A bodhisattva living at home who has not yet opened the mind of giving does not first invite others, and feels regret after having given; for all roots of goodness, the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) serves as the foremost."

Householder, when a bodhisattva dwelling in the household stage practices according to the Buddha’s teachings, neither forgetting nor losing the factors that assist awakening, they remain unstained in the present life and attain further superior qualities.
At that time, the householder Ugga and all the other householders raised their voices in unison, joyfully praising him:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
You have well explained the faults and afflictions of the household life; yet we still do not know the precepts and practices of those who have gone forth, nor the merits of the renunciant life."
World-Honored One!
We too observe that there are many faults in the household life and great virtues in leaving the home life.
We only pray that the World-Honored One [will grant us permission].
"Out of compassion for us, we pray that we may be permitted to go forth.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha told the elder:
"To go forth is extremely difficult; it requires single-minded pure conduct."
Then the elders said to the World-Honored One:
“World-Honored One!
It is truly as the Holy Teaching says.”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to leave the household life; I shall act according to your instructions.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately granted him permission to leave the household life.
He then addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva and Sarvaśuddha Bodhisattva:
“O virtuous man! Cause these people to leave the household life.
Then Maitreya and the others caused all nine thousand elders to leave the household life, and these elders received the precepts of renunciation.
At that time, there were also a thousand householders who resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Then, the householder Ugga addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have already spoken of the faults and the merits of the householder's life."
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the practice of the merit of hearing the precepts for renunciant bodhisattvas.
How does a bodhisattva, having been tamed through the sublime Dharma, engage in renunciation, and how do they perform prostrations, rising, staying, coming, going, advancing, and halting?
The Buddha told the householder:
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for you.
A bodhisattva who has gone forth should train in this way, and should dwell and practice in this way."
“Yes, World-Honored One!
We shall receive your instruction and listen. The Buddha said:
“Householder! A bodhisattva who has gone forth should train in this way:
‘For what reason have I abandoned my work to go forth?’”
For the sake of cultivating wisdom, one should apply oneself with diligence as if one's head were on fire.
One should form this thought:
"I must now abide in the four noble lineages and practice the ascetic dhūtas with joy."
"Householder!
How does an ordained bodhisattva cultivate the four noble lineages?
This ordained bodhisattva should give rise to contentment with whatever robes he possesses; he should praise contentment and must not utter false speech for the sake of clothing."
If he does not obtain robes, he does not harbor thoughts of them, does not dwell upon them, and gives rise to no distress;
even if he should obtain robes, his mind does not give rise to attachment.

Although he wears and puts on robes, he is without fettering attachment, neither coveting nor clinging to them; he knows their faults, knows the way of renunciation, and is content in accordance with this.
One does not praise oneself nor disparage others. Householder!

A person who has gone forth, according to whatever alms-food they receive and whatever bedding and seats they obtain, should likewise practice contentment and give rise to appreciation. They do not utter false speech for the sake of bedding and seats; if they do not obtain them, they do not harbor thoughts of them nor give rise to distress. If they do obtain them, they do not become attached, maintaining them with an unattached mind—without stinginess and without being bound by them. Knowing their faults and knowing the practice of renunciation, they follow this contentment and never praise themselves or disparage others.
Delighting in relinquishment, delighting in renunciation, and delighting in cultivation, yet not praising oneself for this delight in relinquishment, renunciation, and cultivation— Householder!
This is called the dwelling of a renunciant bodhisattva in the four noble lineages.
"Furthermore, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva wears his robes while maintaining ten virtues.
What are these ten?

It is for the sake of modesty, for the sake of covering the body, for the sake of warding off mosquitoes and gadflies, and for the sake of protection against wind and storms; it is not for the sake of softness to the touch nor for the sake of beauty. It is for the purpose of manifesting the outward signs of the precepts of a śramaṇa. This dyed robe causes gods, humans, asuras, and others to regard it as a stūpa, and thus one accepts and maintains it. It is dyed for the sake of liberation, not for the sake of desire; it is appropriate for tranquility, not for the fetters. Wearing this dyed robe, one does not give rise to various evils but cultivates various wholesome deeds. One wears the dyed garment not for the sake of vanity, but having realized the Noble Path, thinks: "I act in this way," and in a single moment of thought, one does not harbor the fetters of dye.
"Householder!
These are called the ten meritorious qualities of a renunciant bodhisattva that are embodied in the robes they wear.
Furthermore, householder!"
A renunciant bodhisattva, seeing ten reasons, does not abandon begging for food for as long as their life lasts.
What are these ten?
"I shall now sustain myself by my own means, and not depend on others for sustenance."
If there are sentient beings who offer me food, I require that they first establish themselves in the three refuges before I accept the food.
If they do not offer food, I give rise to great compassion for those sentient beings.
I practice with diligent vigor for the sake of those sentient beings, so that after their tasks are accomplished, they may partake of this food.

Furthermore, I do not contravene the Buddha’s instructions; rather, in order to plant the fundamental causes for fulfillment, and based on the conditions for vanquishing pride and accumulating the cause of the Unseen Summit (uṣṇīṣa), I beg for alms with equanimity, neither for the sake of union with women nor men, nor for the sake of both men and women together.
They give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, because they gather the ornaments of omniscience.
Householder!
The renunciant bodhisattva perceives these ten benefits!
For as long as life lasts, one does not abandon the practice of begging for food.
If someone comes with a sincere heart of reverence and faith to invite one,
then one should go.
If there are those who invite you, but do not do so with a sincere heart,
observe whether there is benefit for yourself;
if there is a cause and condition for benefiting others, you should then go.
"Furthermore, householder!
Because a renunciant bodhisattva sees ten benefits, he never abandons the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
What are these ten?

Because of their sovereign removal [of defilements], because they lack the grasping of a self, because they have abandoned attachment to bedding and requisites, because they are tranquil and free from craving, because there is no gain to be had in their dwelling, because they sacrifice body and life in forest retreats, because they abandon the clamor of crowds, because they perform what is to be done within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, because they find satisfaction in tranquil concentration, and because their focused mindfulness is free from obstacles.
"Householder!
This is called the bodhisattva who has gone forth seeing ten benefits of virtue, and who does not abandon the forest hermitage for as long as life lasts.
Householder!"

If a forest-dweller (āraṇyaka), for the sake of hearing the Dharma, or due to matters concerning his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), or to inquire after the health of the sick, should enter a village settlement, he should form this thought:
"I shall return tonight."
If one stays in a dwelling for the purpose of reciting and chanting, one should form this thought:

"I am now intentionally staying in an araṇya; by dwelling in an araṇya, I am in accord with the Dharma. I have no notion of contention regarding any things, and no notion of obstruction regarding any dharmas; I gather the Dharma without weariness."
"O Householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya should reflect in this way:
'For what reason do I dwell in an araṇya?'"

It is not only those in secluded places who are called śramaṇas; for among them there are many who are undisciplined and lack tranquility, who are neither steadfast nor consistent, yet also dwell therein—namely, deer, monkeys, birds, beasts, lions, tigers, wolves, thieves, and caṇḍālas—who possess none of the virtues of a śramaṇa.

Therefore, I should fulfill the purpose and benefit of a śramaṇa who practices the conduct of an araṇyaka: namely, maintaining mindfulness without distraction, attaining dhāraṇī, cultivating great loving-kindness and great compassion, mastering the five supernormal powers, fulfilling the six pāramitās, not abandoning the mind of omniscience, practicing skillful means, and constantly gathering and transforming sentient beings through the gift of the Dharma.

Not abandoning the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), practicing the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), diligently applying oneself to hearing the Dharma, binding the mind to cultivate and collect practices that are correctly conformed to, not realizing the wisdom of the fruits [of the path], guarding the true Dharma, and having faith in karmic retribution—this is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
To sever all conceptual constructions and discriminations is right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
To expound the Dharma according to one's understanding is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
To exhaust and bring karma to its end is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
To sever the fetters and habitual tendencies is called right livelihood.
To diligently advance toward meditative concentration is called right effort.
To not forget all phenomena is called right mindfulness.
To attain the knowledge of all-knowledge is called right concentration.

To understand emptiness without alarm, signlessness without fear, and wishlessness without timidity; for the mind not to cling to existence; to rely on the meaning and not on the letter, to rely on wisdom and not on consciousness, to rely on the Dharma and not on the person, and to rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not on sūtras of provisional meaning.
"Householder!
This is called a renunciant bodhisattva abiding in the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, householder!"
A renunciant bodhisattva should not associate with large crowds.
Thinking, "I should abandon my own roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings," one cultivates roots of goodness without ever forsaking them.
"Householder!
There are four types of close association for a bodhisattva who has gone forth, permitted by the Tathāgata. What are these four?"
"Householder!
It is permitted by the Buddha for a renunciant bodhisattva to draw near to and listen to the Dharma.
It is permitted by the Buddha to draw near to and bring all sentient beings to maturity."
To make offerings to the Tathāgata is what the Buddha has permitted.
To draw near to and never abandon the mind of omniscience is what the Buddha has permitted,
O Householder!
These are called the four kinds of intimacy with the Tathāgata permitted for a renunciant bodhisattva.
Householder!
Intimate yourself with these four; do not intimate yourself with others.
"Furthermore, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in a forest hermitage should reflect thus:
'For what reason have I come to this place?'"
For what matter have I come here? Out of fear of what have I come?
Is it out of fear of the clamor of the crowd, fear of intimacy, fear of greed, hatred, and delusion, or fear of madness and arrogance?
...fearing affliction and fever; fearing stinginess and greed; fearing forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
fearing the skandha-māra, the kleśa-māra, the mṛtyu-māra, and the devaputra-māra; fearing impermanence within permanence;
fearing self within non-self; fearing pleasure within suffering; fearing purity within impurity; and fearing the mind, intellect, and consciousness in the present.
Fear of being beaten; fear of the view of self; fear of "I" and "mine"; fear of evil associates;
fear of gain and honor; fear of speaking at improper times; fear of claiming to have seen what was not seen; fear of claiming to have heard what was not heard;
fear of claiming to have thought what was not thought; fear of claiming to have known what was not known; fear of the stains of a śramaṇa; [fear of] the desire realm and the form realm.
The fear of the formless realm, the fear of birth and death in all realms of existence, the fear of hell, the fear of animals,
and the fear of hungry ghosts— I now dread such fears as these, and have therefore come to this forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*);
I do not dwell among the clamor and crowds of householders, for if I do not practice and do not cultivate mindfulness, [I shall fall].
Dwelling [in such places] would not be appropriate; it is because they have escaped these fears that they have come to this place.

In the past, immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all dwelt in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka), liberated from all fears and attained fearlessness, thereby attaining the fearless, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Future bodhisattvas will likewise be thus: dwelling in forest hermitages, they shall be liberated from all fears and attain the fearless, unsurpassed right path.
Present bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus: dwelling in forest hermitages, they practice fearlessness and attain the fearless, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, being liberated from all fears.
"Therefore, I now desire to attain fearlessness and be liberated from all fears by dwelling in an araṇya.
"Furthermore, householder,
a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, being without dread or fear, should train in this way."
If there are those who have fear, it arises entirely from attachment to a self and clinging to a self, with the self as the primary cause.
It all stems from loving the self, giving rise to the notion of "I," seeing the self, conceiving the self, and grasping at the self; one falsely conceptualizes the self and seeks to protect the self.
If one dwells in an araṇya while not relinquishing the grasping at a self, this is a loss of benefit.
Householder!
If one dwells in an araṇya without the notion of a self, that is dwelling in an araṇya.
To be without attachment to views is to dwell in the forest retreat (*āraṇyaka*).
To not dwell in the notions of "self" or "what belongs to self" is to dwell in the forest retreat.
Householder, you should know that to be without the notion of *nirvāṇa* is to dwell in the forest retreat, let alone the notion of afflictions (*kleśa*).

"O Householder! What is called the forest-dweller’s abode? It is to be without attachment to any phenomena (*dharma*), not to dwell in any phenomena, and to be unimpeded regarding all phenomena. It is not to dwell in dependence on forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles; it is to dwell in the equality of all phenomena, which is stainless; to dwell with a well-disciplined mind; to cast aside all fear and dwell in fearlessness; to dwell having crossed over the great river of all fetters and outflows; to dwell in the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*); to dwell in fewness of desires, contentment, ease of being satisfied, and ease of being supported; to dwell in the fulfillment of wisdom; and to dwell in practice according to what has been heard.
It is to dwell in liberation by contemplating the gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
He dwells in the knowledge and vision of liberation because he has severed the fetters;
he dwells at the ultimate limit because he accords with dependent origination;
and he dwells having accomplished what was to be done because he is ultimately pure.
"Householder!
Just as medicinal herbs, trees, and forests in an open space are neither afraid nor terrified,
so it is, householder!"

A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in a forest hermitage should give rise to the thought that [the self] is like grass, wood, walls, or fences, and like a magical illusion; within this, who is there to fear and who is there to be terrified?

Therefore, one should contemplate the body with fearlessness: this body is not the self, nor does it belong to a self; it is devoid of a sentient being, devoid of a life-span, devoid of a person, devoid of a man, and devoid of a youth.

As for what is called "fear," it is an empty name without reality; I should not now give rise to fear regarding that which lacks reality, just as in those empty places where medicinal herbs and forests have no owner and no protector.
Having thus understood all phenomena, one should dwell well in the forest retreat (āraṇyaka). Why is this?
Because they have severed sorrow and contention, they are called "forest-dwellers" (āraṇyaka); because they are without birth and without protection, they are called "forest-dwellers."
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva who has gone forth and dwells in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) should train in this way:

gradually conforming to the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha), next cultivating the aggregate of meditative concentration (samādhiskandha), and dwelling in the forest hermitage to gather the aggregate of wisdom (prajñāskandha)."
Dwelling in the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), one practices the aggregate of liberation; dwelling in the forest hermitage, one gives rise to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
dwelling in the forest hermitage, one spreads the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); dwelling in the forest hermitage, one accumulates the twelve dhūta virtues;
and dwelling in the forest hermitage, it is for the sake of the skillful means of truth. Dwelling in the forest hermitage...
Because the son dwells in a favorable place, knowing the aggregates (*skandha*); because he dwells in the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), abiding in the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
because he dwells in the forest hermitage, eliminating the sense-bases (*āyatana*); because he dwells in the forest hermitage, not forgetting the bodhicitta;
because he dwells in the forest hermitage, contemplating emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without fear; and because he dwells in the forest hermitage, he does not lose anything.
By virtue of all roots of goodness, dwelling in forest hermitages is praised by the Buddhas;
dwelling in forest hermitages is commended by Bodhisattvas; dwelling in forest hermitages is extolled by all the Noble Ones;
dwelling in forest hermitages is the reliance for those who seek liberation; and dwelling in forest hermitages is what those who seek omniscience should practice.
Dwelling in this place.
"Furthermore, householder!
