A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) fulfills the six pāramitās by means of very few things."

Why is this? To dwell in the forest hermitage while not begrudging one’s own body or life is called the practice by which a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in the forest hermitage fulfills the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
"O Householder!

When a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in the dhūta-precepts and the precepts of body, speech, and mind, this is called a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, cultivating and fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
"Householder!
How does a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in the forest cultivate and fulfill the perfection of patience?
By maintaining a mind free from malice toward all sentient beings and enduring for the sake of omniscience."
"Householder!
This is called a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, practicing and perfecting the perfection of patience.
Householder!"
How does an ordained bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya cultivate and fulfill the perfection of diligence?
This bodhisattva should train in this way: "I shall not depart from this place until I have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
"O Householder!
This is called a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, cultivating and fulfilling the perfection of vigor.
O Householder!"
"How does a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya cultivate and fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā?
Householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya sets aside meditative absorption to teach and transform sentient beings, cultivating all roots of goodness."
"Householder!
This is called a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, cultivating and perfecting the dhyānapāramitā.
Householder!"
"How does an ordained bodhisattva dwelling in a forest hermitage cultivate and fulfill the perfection of wisdom?
Householder!

An ordained bodhisattva dwelling in a forest hermitage should train in this way: 'Just as this body of mine is empty, so too is that place; just as this body of mine is awakening, so too is that place; just as suchness is free from conceptual construction, so too is emptiness free from conceptual construction.'"
"Householder!
This is called a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, cultivating and fulfilling the perfection of wisdom.
Householder!"
A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya abode thus fulfills the six pāramitās.
Householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas knows the araṇya abode.
What are the four?

Pure ethical discipline, extensive learning, application to contemplation, and practice in accordance with the Dharma—these are called the ways in which a renunciant bodhisattva knows how to dwell in an araṇya.
Furthermore, householder!
If a renunciant bodhisattva’s fetters increase, he should not associate with them; dwelling in an araṇya, he should subdue those fetters.
Furthermore, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in a forest hermitage should cultivate the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) for the sake of transforming devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas.
Furthermore, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva should dwell in forest hermitages as taught by the Buddha.
Therein, I should fulfill all pure virtues and be perfumed by wholesome dharmas; thereafter, I shall go to cities and villages to preach the Dharma.
"Householder!
These are called the four dharmas by which a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya.
Furthermore, householder!"

A renunciant bodhisattva, having risen from his forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) to receive the Dharma and engage in recitation, approaches his preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya), whether they be of superior, middling, or inferior rank; these are my fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
One should not be indolent, for this is one's own duty;
one should not be envious of them, but should serve as their assistant.
One should contemplate in this way: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the field of merit for offerings by all devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.
The Buddha is the father of all sentient beings; the Buddha does not give rise to the thought of seeking service from others.
I now wish to learn this: I too shall act as a servant for all sentient beings, and I shall not seek for others to serve me.
Why is this? Householder!
If a bhikṣu values being served and attended upon, he loses the merit of the Dharma.
If one were to gather others through material wealth, how would that be?
It would be because they wish to have me perform labor for them that they gather me with wealth; it would not be for the sake of the Dharma, and I would lose my own faith.
If one is gathered as a servant through material wealth, there is no great reward or benefit.

If you approach your preceptor or ācārya, you should understand their intentions and act accordingly, ensuring that your preceptor or ācārya does not lose faith in you or cease to hold you in respect and affection.
He sacrificed his body and life for the sake of chanting and reciting the Dharma; he fulfilled their wishes as a merit and benefit, renouncing gain and honor to praise the Dharma.
Householder!

If a bodhisattva, regarding another who has received, upheld, read, or recited even a single four-line verse associated with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom—the path for accumulating bodhi—shows reverence toward that teacher for the sake of the Dharma.

For as many immeasurable eons as there are syllables, phrases, and verses upheld by these aforementioned masters, one should serve them and offer every form of worship without generating any flattery or hypocrisy.
"Elder, you should know that one cannot repay such an act of kindness, let alone fail to revere the Dharma. Elder!

If, out of faith, one gives rise to wholesome thoughts—recalling the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; recalling that which is untainted (*anāsrava*); and recalling tranquility and self-mastery—and serves the preceptor for immeasurable eons, making offerings to him, even then one has not fully repaid the preceptor’s kindness. Elder, you should understand it thus."
"Elder, you should know that if, having heard the Dharma, one obtains immeasurable retribution and immeasurable wisdom, I ought to provide immeasurable offerings to my preceptor.
Furthermore, Elder!"
Householder, a renunciant bodhisattva dwells according to the dharma of renunciation. Householder,
what is meant by "dwelling according to the dharma of renunciation"?
Having heard of the pure precepts, this renunciant bodhisattva should train in and cultivate the four types of pure precepts in this way.
What are the four? They are:
dwelling in the noble lineages and delighting in the dhūtas; not associating with householders or renunciants; and dwelling in forest hermitages without guile or crookedness.
Furthermore, householder!
Once an ordained bodhisattva has heard of the pure precepts, they should further train in these four types of pure precepts.
What are the four?

This means that while maintaining the purity of bodily precepts, one does not apprehend a body; while maintaining the purity of verbal precepts, one does not apprehend speech. Free from all views, one gives rise to the mind of omniscience.
Householder!
These are called the four pure precepts.
Furthermore, householder,
once an ordained bodhisattva has heard of these pure precepts, they should train in the four pure precepts in this manner.
What are these four? They are:
being free from the notion of "I," relinquishing the notion of "mine," distancing oneself from and severing the views of eternalism and nihilism, and understanding the law of dependent origination.
Householder!
These are called the four pure precepts.
Furthermore, householder!
Once a renunciant bodhisattva has heard of these pure precepts, they should train in the four pure precepts in this manner.
What are these four? They are:

that the aggregates (skandhas) are non-existent; that the elements (dhātus) are like the dharma-realm; that the sense-bases (āyatanas) are like an empty village; and that one does not dwell in conventional designations.
Householder!
These are called the four pure precepts.
Furthermore, householder,
once an ordained bodhisattva has heard of these pure precepts, he should train in the four pure precepts in this manner.
What are the four?
Knowing that "I" cannot be found as a self; hearing and awakening others so as to purify their minds; the mind not delighting in dwelling upon any phenomena; and being without fluctuation.
"Householder!
These are called the four purities of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, householder!"
Having heard of the pure precepts, a renunciant bodhisattva should train in the four types of pure precepts in this way.
What are the four? They are:
understanding emptiness; not fearing the signless; giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings; and entering into non-self.
"Householder!
These are called the four kinds of pure precepts of a renunciant bodhisattva.
Furthermore, householder!"
Once a renunciant bodhisattva has heard of the Samādhi of Purity, they should train in this way: What is the Samādhi of Purity?
It is that all dharmas are non-existent;
it is the mind free from duality, the mind of right action, and the one-pointed mind.
With a mind free from agitation, free from conceptual proliferation, free from distraction and clamor, and free from dependence;
possessing mastery over the mind without its wandering or scattering, not dwelling within the realm of the mind, one perceives the mind as being like an illusion.
To contemplate all phenomena as being equal to the dharma-realm—without activity and without abiding, neither arising nor attainable internally or externally—is the equality of samādhi.
To abide in such a dharma is what is called "samādhi."
"In this way, householder!
This is called the renunciant bodhisattva’s contemplation of the pure accumulation of concentration.
Furthermore, householder!"
When a renunciant bodhisattva hears of the accumulation of pure wisdom, having heard it, they should contemplate: what is called the accumulation of pure wisdom?

That bodhisattva should train themselves in this way, knowing the analytical knowledge of conditioned phenomena, eloquent knowledge, swift knowledge, knowledge of sentient beings, and the knowledge of gathering external sentient beings.
In this way, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva contemplates the accumulation of pure wisdom.
Furthermore, householder!
A renunciant bodhisattva should train in this way: that which is called wisdom is "unfettered" because it is without a body;
it is without grasping, without movement, without abiding, without form, without marks, without birth, and without activity, for it is like space.
“Householder!
If one contemplates in this way, it is called a bodhisattva dwelling in renunciation.
When this Dharma was spoken, eight thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These elders attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thirty-two thousand sentient beings were freed from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the elder Ugga, filled with joy and exultation, offered a robe worth hundreds of thousands to the Buddha as an offering and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By means of these roots of goodness, I universally bestow them upon all sentient beings alike, so that all lay bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may accomplish the precepts and dharmas as taught by the Buddha, and all monastic bodhisattvas may fulfill all dharmas, likewise fulfilling them exactly as taught by the Buddha.”
“World-Honored One!
How does a lay bodhisattva, while dwelling in the state of a householder, train in the precepts of one who has gone forth?
Having asked this, the Buddha addressed the elder:
“Householder bodhisattvas who possess five qualities dwell on the level of a householder while training in the precepts of one who has gone forth. What are these five? O Elder!
When a bodhisattva dwells on the stage of a householder, they do not begrudge any of their possessions; being in accord with the mind of omniscience, they do not look for karmic rewards.
Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home, while abiding in the state of a householder, maintains pure brahmacarya; he does not cultivate thoughts of sensual desire, much less engage in the union of two.
Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva, having gone to a secluded place, cultivates the four dhyānas; yet, through the power of skillful means, he does not enter the fixed position [of the śrāvaka].
Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva dwelling on the ground of householders should study wisdom with extreme diligence and accord with all sentient beings through loving-kindness.
Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home, while dwelling in the household stage, protects the Dharma and also encourages others to do so.
Householder!
"This is called the householder bodhisattva dwelling on the stage of a householder who, being endowed with five dharmas, trains in the precepts of renunciation.
At that time, the householder Ugga addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"While at home, I shall abide as the World-Honored One has taught, so as to increase and broaden the Buddha-way; I shall also train myself in all the precepts for those who have left the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they smile, rays of light of various colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—issue from their mouths, illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds. These rays pass upward beyond the Brahma-world, eclipsing the light of the sun and moon, then return to circle the Buddha’s body three times before entering the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
At that time, Ānanda,
seeing the Buddha smile, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes so as to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One, for what reason do you smile?"
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not smile without cause.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see this householder Ugga making offerings to the Tathāgata?"
"I wish to practice the Dharma and let out the lion's roar.
Ānanda replied, "I have seen it."
“World-Honored One!
We have seen them. Sugata!”

“Ānanda! This householder Ugga, while dwelling on the level of a layperson, will constantly provide offerings and pay respect to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who appear in the world during this Bhadrakalpa; he will protect and uphold the True Dharma, and while remaining at home, he will abide by the precepts of one who has gone forth and extensively hear of the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Tathāgata.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Ugga:
"What benefit or happiness do you see in living at home?
Do you possess noble wisdom?"
He replied: "Venerable sir,
one who has not realized great compassion should not claim for himself, 'I am at peace.'"
"Venerable Ānanda!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva endures all sufferings without abandoning sentient beings.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"This householder, the Elder Ugga, while dwelling on the level of a layperson, has transformed many sentient beings during this Bhadrakalpa; this is more than what an ordained bodhisattva could achieve in a hundred or even a hundred thousand kalpas."
Why is this? Ānanda! The merit possessed by hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas who have left the household life does not equal the merit possessed by this householder Ugga.
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of this sutra?”
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is titled 'The Questions of the Householder Ugga,' and it is also titled 'The Bodhisattva Precepts for Laypeople and Monastics,' and also titled 'The Chapter on Reverently Serving Teachers and Elders.'"

Ānanda! If there are bodhisattvas who hear this sutra, they possess great diligence; their inferior diligence cannot match theirs even by a hundred thousand million times as they abide in the holy life.
Therefore, Ānanda!

Those who wish to abide themselves in diligence and wish to encourage others in diligence; those who wish to abide themselves in all meritorious qualities and wish to encourage others to abide in them—should listen to this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain it extensively for others, and practice according to its teaching.
Ānanda! I entrust this Dharma to you, so that you may receive, uphold, read, and recite it. Why is this?
Ānanda! This Dharma is fully endowed with all merits. Ānanda!
If there is a bodhisattva who accords with this Dharma, then they do not depart from accordance with the Tathāgata.
Ānanda! If there is a bodhisattva who departs from this Dharma, then they depart from the Buddha.
If there is a bodhisattva who departs from this Dharma—departing from its reception, upholding, recitation, and practice as taught—they depart from seeing all Buddhas. Why is this?
Ānanda! All matters concerning the appearance of a Buddha in the world are revealed within this sutra. Ānanda!

Even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with raging fires, one should pass through them for the sake of perfect enlightenment, in order to go and hear this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice according to its teachings.

Ānanda! If one were to fill the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them with reverence, it would be for the sake of hearing this Dharma, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, and practicing according to its teaching.
Ānanda! If one were to erect stūpas made of the seven precious substances for all the Buddhas of the past and honor them with every kind of offering— Ānanda!
If one were to provide all manner of requisites for life to the present Buddhas and their assemblies of śrāvakas;
and, Ānanda,
if one were to serve all future Buddhas and bodhisattvas as their slaves or their disciples while making offerings to them.
If one does not hear this sutra, nor receive, uphold, read, recite, propagate, or abide by it—being separated from such dharmas—one cannot be said to make offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

Ānanda! If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this sutra, receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it to others, and practice according to its teachings, these bodhisattvas have already made offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Why is this? Ānanda! To practice according to the teaching is the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s discipline.

When these words had been spoken, the Venerable Ānanda, the householder Ugga, the gandharvas, the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Two;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
20. The Chapter on the Inexhaustible Treasury, Part One of Twenty.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus, all of whom had accomplished supreme merit and were capable of the lion’s roar.

There were five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom had attained the gates of dhāraṇī and unimpeded eloquence, realized the stage of non-arising, and dwelt in non-retrogression; they were endowed with various samādhis and sported with supernatural powers, and were well-versed in knowing the mental activities and inclinations of sentient beings. Their names were as follows:

Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas such as Sūryadhvaja, Candradhvaja, Samantaprabha, Candrarāja, Uccagiri-prabhāsa, Vairocana, Siṃhamati, Guṇaratnaprabha, Sarvārthasiddha, Paripūrṇapūrvapratyaya, Paripūrṇapraṇidhānacaryā, Śūnyatājñāna, Samacitta, Priyaṃkara, Gaṇarata, Saṃgrāmajit, Jñānacaryā, Vidyunmat, Vijayavādin, Siṃhanāda, Susvaraghoṣa, Prabodhana, Cakravartikauśalya, and Nirvāṇacaryā were the leaders of this assembly.

Furthermore, Śakra-devānām-indra, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Brahmā-devaputra, Lord of the Sahā World, and a vast multitude of others—including gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas of great majesty and virtue—were all present together.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vidyudgati, seeing that the great assembly was tranquil and pure and that all the great nāga-elephants had gathered, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
"I have a slight doubt that I now wish to inquire about; I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to listen and grant me permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Elapatra, saying:
"Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, let it be as you wish to ask; I shall explain it for you."
The Bodhisattva Vidyutprāpta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By accomplishing what dharmas can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva fulfill all the desires of sentient beings, remain unstained by any faults, and skillfully guide them according to their faculties and natures? How can he cause those sentient beings, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, not to fall into the evil realms, but to be certain of attaining realization of equality? How can he dwell in the world without defilement like a lotus flower, move through various buddha-fields without wavering from the dharma-realm, never be separated from the Buddhas yet not perceive a physical body, abide in the three gates of liberation without entering the fixed stage [of the śrāvaka], and according to the wishes of sentient beings, adorn and purify buddha-lands, swiftly achieving anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a single kṣaṇa?”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vidyudgati immediately addressed the Buddha in verse before him:
"O Unsurpassed Honored One among Men, Possessor of boundless knowledge and vision,
Abiding in the common dharmas, You bring benefit to all the worlds."
Beholding all sentient beings with an impartial mind, you are the refuge for the world;
You reveal the paths of both error and correctness, causing them to attain ultimate peace and happiness.
You accumulate supreme merit, like a vast heap of various jewels.
The sun of wisdom for the world, the Honored One worthy of offerings in the three realms,
may you please expound the Supreme Vehicle to accomplish the path of the Bodhisattvas;
your countenance is like the full moon, and you are fully endowed with śamatha.
You have revealed the Dharma of tranquility, which can extinguish all afflictions;
we pray that you will speak of the bodhisattva practices for the benefit of all sentient beings.
[Please tell us] of the buddha-fields and the lifespan, as well as the physical body and the retinue.
The three karmas and all phenomena—may they all be pure.
We pray that the Tathāgata will explain the pure conduct of a bodhisattva:
how does one subdue the māras?
How does one preach the Dharma?
How does one avoid forgetfulness? We pray that you will explain this for us:
how does the courageous one enter everywhere into the cycle of birth and death?
Abiding within the state of a single characteristic, how is it that one is always unmoved regarding all phenomena?
How is it that, in the presence of the Buddhas, one draws near and makes offerings,
yet constantly contemplates the Buddha’s form-body while ultimately remaining free from all characteristics?
Though they have realized the three gates of liberation, like birds flying through the realm of space,
as long as they have not yet perfected all merits, they will ultimately not enter nirvana.
Knowing the dispositions and natures of the faculties of beings, they act in accordance with them without fear.
Nor do they give rise to stained attachment; how do they bring those sentient beings to maturity?
First bestowing worldly happiness, they later cause them to develop a pure mind, become endowed with supreme wisdom, and realize unsurpassed bodhi.
"Such profound and wondrous meaning—may the Tathāgata please expound it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vidyutprāpta, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

"Good son! You are indeed able to ask the Buddha about such a meaning as this, for the benefit, peace, and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings, to sustain the devas and humans of the present world, and for the sake of all bodhisattvas in future ages."
"Therefore, Vidyutprāpta!
You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
The Bodhisattva Vidyutprāpta said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told Vidyutprāpta:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have five kinds of treasuries: the great treasury, the inexhaustible treasury, the universally inexhaustible treasury, and the boundless treasury. When bodhisattvas are fully endowed with such treasuries, they are forever free from poverty; they are able to accomplish the aforementioned sublime merits and shall swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with little effort.”

What are the five? They are the treasure-store of those whose conduct is dominated by greed, the treasure-store of those whose conduct is dominated by hatred, the treasure-store of those whose conduct is dominated by delusion, the treasure-store of those whose conduct is characterized by equal proportions [of the three poisons], and the treasure-store of all dharmas.
Dian-de! What is called the "treasury of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s conduct of craving"?

It refers to sentient beings who, bound by the perversions associated with the conduct of craving, give rise to various conceptual discriminations according to the signs they follow; within the various spheres of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, they cling with firm attachment, becoming intoxicated and deluded by their indulgence in pleasure.
A bodhisattva should know, as they truly are, the various mental activities of those sentient beings: what do those sentient beings desire and seek?
In what objects are their attachments and habitual tendencies intensified?
What kind of faith and understanding do they fully possess?
What roots of goodness did they plant in the past?
And toward which vehicle will they set forth?
How long will all these roots of goodness take to mature?
In order to sever all the desires of sentient beings and to cause their virtuous minds to remain in constant succession, the Bodhisattva carefully observes them and provides healing treatment.

Dian, you should know that the distinctions among the faculties and conducts of sentient beings are difficult to discern; they cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, let alone by ordinary people or non-Buddhist practitioners.
Therefore, Vidyutprāpta!
There are some sentient beings who, though attached to various desires, are nonetheless able to bring to maturity *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

There are other sentient beings who, upon merely encountering the objects of desire, or even by uttering words with a defiled mind, immediately attain the maturation of unsurpassed illumination and liberation.

There may be sentient beings who, upon beholding various exquisite forms, give rise to desire and defilement; yet when those forms change and decay, they immediately become aware of it, and their afflictions of desire cease. Deeply contemplating impermanence, they are then able to mature toward unsurpassed enlightenment and liberation.

There may be sentient beings who, although they do not give rise to lustful attachment upon seeing a woman, later conceive a defiled mind by recollecting her and giving rise to love and longing through the mental image of her appearance.
There may be sentient beings who, within their dreams, see pleasing forms and give rise to greedy attachment, fixating their minds on them and pursuing them.

There may be sentient beings who, upon hearing the voice of a woman, immediately give rise to lustful craving; yet at times, by briefly seeing her and becoming free from the mind of defiled passion, they attain maturity in unsurpassed enlightenment and liberation.
Therefore, Vidyutprāpta!

A bodhisattva skillfully understands these various diseases of greed as well as the medicines for greed; yet, within the dharma-realm, there are no two distinct characteristics. Thus, toward those sentient beings who are deluded regarding this dharma-realm, the bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion.
"O Dharmavatsa!
Whether it be greed, hatred, and delusion, or the wisdom of the dharma-realm, there is not the slightest dharma that can be apprehended.
The bodhisattva forms this thought:"

"As I see it, these sentient beings give rise to desire, hatred, and delusion within this collection of dharmas that are established by conventional designation, which are signless, devoid of intrinsic nature, empty, and quiescent."

I shall observe this as it truly is; for the sake of those deluded beings who are attached to desire, I will abide in great compassion to fulfill my former vows, and through non-conceptual wisdom, I will bring them to maturity without wavering from the dharma-realm.

If there is a man who falsely conceives pure thoughts toward that woman and gives rise to heavy lustful attachment, the Bodhisattva immediately manifests a female body, exquisitely beautiful and endowed with perfect physical marks, adorned with various precious jewels and necklaces, such that she is like a celestial maiden never seen before; thus, according to the needs of that sentient being, he causes him to become enamored and attached.
Having observed their extreme attachment, he assessed their capacity and, through skillful means, extracted the poisonous arrow of their craving.

By his power of mastery, he transformed back into a female body, appeared before those people, and preached the Dharma for them, causing those sentient beings to penetrate the Dharma-realm; he then vanished and was no longer seen.

If there is a woman who conceives a mind of passionate attachment toward a man, the Bodhisattva then manifests in the form of that man; he even extracts the poisonous arrow of her craving and preaches the Dharma for her so that she may enter the Dharma-realm, after which he vanishes and no longer appears.

Dian-de! These twenty-one thousand modes of greedy conduct, along with those eighty-four thousand modes of conduct, are all brought forth by the bodhisattva’s effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) through the production of immeasurable billions of dharma-gates. This serves to enlighten and liberate all sentient beings; yet the bodhisattva does not think, "I am preaching the Dharma for sentient beings in this way," nor is there any sentient being who attains liberation.

Dian-de! It is, for example, like the Dragon King Anavatapta, who by the power of his karma causes four great rivers to flow from within his palace. For the sake of all sentient beings dwelling on land or in water, he provides refreshing coolness during the heat of summer; he moistens flowers and fruits and nourishes the five grains, causing all sentient beings to dwell in peace and happiness.
Yet that dragon king does not form the thought:
"I am now causing these river waters to flow out; they have flowed out, or they shall flow out.
Nevertheless, the four rivers are always naturally overflowing for the use of sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva is likewise so: having fulfilled his former vows, he teaches the Four Noble Truths through effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), extinguishing all the feverish afflictions of birth and death, and universally bestowing upon humans and devas the sublime bliss of liberation.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva does not think:
"I am now teaching the Dharma; I have taught it; I shall teach it.
Rather, dwelling spontaneously in a mind of great compassion, they observe sentient beings and teach the Dharma according to their needs.
"Furthermore, Vidyutprāpta!

It is like Śakra, who has twelve nayutas of celestial maidens; by the sovereign power of that Śakra, he manifests many bodies so that all those celestial maidens may have their desires for pleasure fully satisfied, each thinking to herself:
'I am now alone sporting with Śakra.'"
Yet Śakra is truly without any defilement. It is the same for the bodhisattva:
regarding those sentient beings who are ready to be delivered, he brings them to maturity according to their inclinations, yet this bodhisattva remains entirely free from attachment.
Furthermore, Vidyutprāpta!

It is like when the solar orb rises over the mountain peaks, its radiance universally illuminates Jambudvīpa; in all places it shines upon, various forms and colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—all become manifest. Yet that solar orb possesses no marks of differentiation, being of a single color and a single light.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: the sun-disk of wisdom illuminates the dharma-realm and emerges from the mountain peaks of the attachments of those sentient beings. Although it teaches the Dharma according to their inclinations regarding a single object of focus, there are no two distinct characteristics within the dharma-realm.
“Dian-de! This is called the treasure-trove of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s conduct of desire.

Once a bodhisattva has realized this treasure-trove, for one kalpa or more than one kalpa, they manifest immeasurable bodies according to the various inclinations of sentient beings and preach the Dharma to them using various words and phrases; yet, within the dharma-realm, there is no duality.”
Furthermore, Vidyutprāpta!

It is like genuine gold: through the power of craftsmanship, it is fashioned into various ornaments and decorative items according to one's will; although their appearances differ, the nature of that gold remains without distinction.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: skillfully observing the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he manifests immeasurable bodies according to the various inclinations of sentient beings and preaches the Dharma for them using diverse words and phrases; yet, within the dharma-realm, there is no dualistic appearance—this is what is meant by constantly entering the single characteristic of the dharma-realm.
Having obtained such a hidden treasure, the bodhisattva is able to preach various teachings for the sake of sentient beings.
Having heard these teachings, they become fully endowed with the inexhaustible wealth of the noble ones, and the poverty of birth and death is forever severed.
"Furthermore, Vidyutprāpta! What is called the 'treasury of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of aversion'?

It refers to sentient beings who are associated with arrogance, who conceive of 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' and dwell in the distinctions between self and others; who, from time immemorial, have not cultivated loving-kindness or patience; whose minds are ruined by the burning affliction of hatred; who do not give rise to mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; and who, shrouded by the poison of anger, are deluded regarding the Dharma."
Toward those sentient beings who are prone to much anger, the bodhisattva never gives rise to harm, injury, or affliction, but reflects only thus:

"How strange! Sentient beings are deluded and confused; they give rise to perverse resentment within the nature of all phenomena, which is fundamentally quiescent, stainless, without conjunction, without conflict, and far removed from all dharmas."

Having reflected thus, he dwells in a mind of great compassion, constantly feeling personal remorse; even if someone were to dismember his body limb by limb, he remains steadfast in patience for the sake of taming sentient beings who act with anger.

If those immeasurable sentient beings who habitually act with hatred become mutually estranged and harbor resentment in their hearts, once this karma is completed, they shall fall into the evil destinies of venomous serpents.

Bodhisattvas abiding in patience transform these sentient beings through the power of their compassionate mindfulness, enabling them not to undergo the retribution of the evil realms and ensuring they shall certainly realize equality.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means for eliminating the conduct of anger among sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Electra!
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are angry and afflicted, they form this thought:

"All dharmas are by nature pure; yet these sentient beings, following after signs, give rise to false discrimination, and within this state of equality that is free from violation, they give rise to anger."
Those sentient beings are unable to understand the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

If these beings were to see the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they would never give rise to anger or malice toward others; it is precisely because they do not understand the fundamental nature of the dharma-realm that they produce hatred.

Toward those sentient beings who are full of anger, the Bodhisattva increases his compassion and dwells in great pity (*mahākaruṇā*), fulfilling his former vows. By means of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), he reveals and expounds various Dharma gates in order to destroy the conduct of anger in sentient beings, yet he does not even think, "I am preaching the Dharma for sentient beings to eliminate their anger."
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the characteristics of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of extinguishing afflictions by abiding in the undifferentiated characteristic of the dharma-realm.
Dian-de! For example, it is not that light can manifest without first removing darkness, yet there is no one who can remove darkness.
Thus, the natures of both darkness and light are like space, without any distinction between them.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: relying on this non-discriminative wisdom of the dharma-realm, they skillfully preach the Dharma to destroy the various modes of hatred in sentient beings, yet they do not create distinctions within the dharma-realm.
"Elapatra! Just as all the light emitted by the solar disc is encompassed by the solar disc wherever it shines, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
in order to subdue and eliminate the practice of anger, every word they speak is a wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), making no distinction within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)."

In this way, there are twenty-one thousand types of conduct characterized by hatred, as well as eighty-four thousand other such types of conduct. Having accomplished non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), the bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their various modes of hateful conduct, without forming the thought:
"I am now preaching the Dharma for sentient beings; I have already preached it, or I shall preach it."
This is called the "treasure-store of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of aversion.

Once a bodhisattva has realized this treasure-store, whether for the duration of an eon or more than an eon, they may use various kinds of scripts, languages, and skillful means to expound it according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings; yet they cannot reach the limit of that practice of aversion, and the wisdom and eloquence of this bodhisattva likewise remain inexhaustible.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful exposition of the non-differentiated characteristic of the dharma-realm, whereby one obtains such a treasury for subduing anger.
"Furthermore, Vidyutprabha!
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s treasury for subduing delusion?

O Diandide! It is an exceedingly difficult matter for bodhisattvas to practice such conduct as this: namely, for the sake of those sentient beings who follow the path of afflictions, who harm others, who are enveloped in the shell of ignorance, who bind themselves as silkworms in their cocoons, who lack skillful means within the dharma-realm, who do not skillfully observe what ought to be practiced, who are attached to the view of self, who walk upon false paths, who abide in dull faculties, and who find it difficult to achieve liberation—for the sake of such deluded beings, they initiate great application from the moment of their first resolve, never giving rise to weariness or indolence.
He reflects thus:
"By what conditions, by what kind of resolute conviction, and by teaching the Dharma in what manner can I cause these sentient beings to enter the bodhisattva practice and attain liberation?"

"In the past, the Bodhisattva skillfully contemplated the dharma-realm and, abiding in great compassion through effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), recognized that those sentient beings were deluded regarding the dharma-realm; he then preached the Dharma according to their respective capacities to bring them all to subdual."
Nor does he think:
"I am now preaching the Dharma; I have preached it, or I shall preach it.

By the power of his past vows, he skillfully contemplates dependent origination, and the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates spontaneously emerge, severing the ignorance and karmic actions of sentient beings and causing them to attain liberation.

Dian-de! It is like a skilled physician who excels at treating all manner of illnesses. Having first thoroughly mastered the medical treatises and various theories, he understands every manifestation of a disease as soon as he sees it; through the application of mantras and medicines, there is none that is not cured.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: skillfully observing the dharma-realm with effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), for the sake of those sentient beings who have accumulated deluded conduct, he reveals and expounds hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates according to their faculties and natures, causing them all to attain clear understanding.
"Electric Attainment!
This is called the 'Treasury of Deluded Conduct' of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Once the Bodhisattva has realized this treasury, they skillfully contemplate dependent origination and, for the sake of such beings of deluded conduct, may—for a kalpa or more than a kalpa—skillfully expound through various scripts and languages according to their inclinations and dispositions; yet they cannot reach the limit of those beings' deluded conduct, and the wisdom and eloquence of this Bodhisattva likewise remain inexhaustible."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful exposition of the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena, whereby they attain such a treasury of deluded conduct.

There are twenty-one thousand such modes of deluded conduct, and eighty-four thousand other modes of conduct; in order to sever these modes of conduct, the Bodhisattva reveals and expounds hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates.
This is called the bodhisattva’s treasury of deluded conduct. Furthermore, Elapatra,
what is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s treasury of balanced conduct?

It is like a wheel of mirrors on four sides, transparent, brilliant, pure, and free from all defilements or obscurations, suspended at a crossroads; whatever forms and images face it all appear within it without increase or decrease.
Furthermore, this bright mirror does not think or say:
"I am able to manifest these various forms and images.
Nevertheless, once this mirror-disk has been well polished and refined, all phenomena naturally appear within it.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: having thoroughly polished the mirror-wheel of the dharma-realm and abiding in the samādhi of effortlessness, they reveal and expound hundreds of thousands of dharma-gates according to the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, causing them all to understand and attain liberation, without giving rise to the mark of dharmas or the mark of sentient beings.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the characteristics of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he understands, as they truly are, those sentient beings who correspond to these four practices; he then teaches the Dharma to them according to their faculties and dispositions, while observing that within both the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings, there are no two distinct natures.
Because that realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) are clearly seen to be non-dual and without distinction.
Vidyutprāpta! It is, for example, like space, which possesses no characteristics of various distinctions and has no establishment.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: skillfully observing the dharma-realm, they comprehend all dharmas as entering into a single characteristic.
Furthermore, by the power of their past vows, they preach various teachings according to the conduct of sentient beings, yet within the dharma-realm there is no differentiation.
Dian-de! These twenty-one thousand modes of conduct, as well as those eighty-four thousand modes of conduct, the Bodhisattva observes and understands them all with complete clarity.

Just as a skilled physician prescribes medicine according to the illness, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva teaches the Dharma in various ways through effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*); this is called the "treasury of equalized practice" (*sama-bhāga-vibhūti*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Once a bodhisattva has realized this treasury, even if they were to teach it to sentient beings for an eon or more than an eon, using various skillful expressions according to their inclinations and aspirations, they could never reach the limit of those practices; likewise, the bodhisattva’s wisdom and eloquence would never be exhausted.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful exposition of the non-differentiated characteristic of the dharma-realm, whereby they obtain such a treasury of balanced practice.
*The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra*, Scroll 83;
*The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra*, Scroll 84.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty, Part Two: The Assembly on the Inexhaustible Treasury.
"Furthermore, Vidyutprāpta!
Once the Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom, he skillfully understands the faculties, conduct, and inclinations of all sentient beings.

If he sees sentient beings with excessive greed, in order to subdue them and treat their affliction, he manifests as an ordinary person experiencing various desires, possessing a wife, children, household affairs, and the necessities of life; yet, like a lotus flower, he remains unstained by them.
There are sentient beings who are deluded and lack wisdom; not understanding the skillful means of a bodhisattva, they think:
"How could a wise person greedily indulge in various desires?"
"they are no different from ordinary worldlings," they then claim that the bodhisattva is far removed from awakening.

Because their minds are thus impure, sentient beings give rise to great anger and resentment rather than reverence and faith; due to this karma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the great hells.
Furthermore, once the retribution for offenses has been exhausted through the secret transformative influence of a bodhisattva, one will certainly attain entry into equanimity. Electra!
It is like a fierce fire: wherever grass and wood are cast into it, everything blazes up and becomes fire.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: the fire of wisdom blazes intensely, and whether sentient beings possess greed, hatred, and delusion, or are virtuous or non-virtuous, the Bodhisattva engages in the same conduct as them, so that all these blazing states are transformed into wisdom.
This is called the unique quality of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, it is like the unique characteristic of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, which is composed of four kinds of jewels on its four sides.

According to the various colors and forms of sentient beings—whether blue, yellow, red, or white—if they approach the side of lapis lazuli, they all become one color, identical to that lapis lazuli; if they approach the golden side, they all become golden; and the same applies equally to the silver and crystal sides.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: having attained the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), he accords with sentient beings whether they are characterized by greed, hatred, or delusion, or whether they are wholesome or unwholesome; wherever they go, he accompanies them as their peer and causes them all to enter the wisdom of a Bodhisattva.
Due to the impurity of that mind and their own evil karma, they may fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal realm, or the world of Yama.
Nevertheless, by virtue of this bodhisattva’s unique merit and the power of his vows, once their retribution for these sins is exhausted, they will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Dian-de! In the past, during an immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpa in an age of the five turbidities, a Buddha appeared, named Ratnarāśiguṇasvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, the lifespan of beings will be one hundred and twenty years, just as it is for me today.

Those sentient beings will be utterly shrouded by the afflictions of intense greed, hatred, and delusion; they will oppose their parents, brothers, and friends, and will not obey their preceptors and teachers, remaining ignorant of their kindness and virtue.

Constantly harboring poisonous malice, deceit, and thievish intent, they destroy one another and act unrighteously; they harbor no reverent faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and being stingy, mean-spirited, and base, they practice the ways of hungry ghosts.
In that buddha-field, there are such evil sentient beings who are difficult to subdue.
Yet, by the power of his former vows, that World-Honored One attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this evil world.
That Buddha also had a community of twenty-two thousand great śrāvakas.

At that time, there was a king named Viśvada (Broad Bestowal), a sovereign ruler who governed Jambudvīpa; with pure faith in the Buddha-dharma, he invited that Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus for the summer retreat and provided extensive offerings.

At that time, there was a Dharma-preaching bhikṣu named Vimala, who was endowed with eloquence and skillful in preaching the Dharma such that the assembly delighted in hearing it; he revealed the teachings to sentient beings without ever becoming weary.

In all the teachings they proclaim, there is no seeking of gain; their countenance is serene and joyful, and they are the first to speak words of greeting. Possessing full physical vigor and a dignified appearance, they are a joy for all sentient beings to behold, and are thus honored, revered, respected, and praised.

Furthermore, there were newly ordained young bhikṣus who constantly followed Vimala as he entered and left the royal palace without hindrance, and who provided him with various offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus within that assembly who did not know how to cultivate the discipline of body, mind, and wisdom; they showed no reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha; they held views of eternalism, nihilism, and a self, and they slandered the Buddha's teachings, being fickle and difficult to discipline.

Failing to restrain his sense faculties, he dwelt in what is not the Dharma; lacking the conduct of a śramaṇa, he claimed for himself the title of a śramaṇa, while his actions of body, speech, and mind were entirely deviant and perverse.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had completed the rains retreat, he entered parinirvāṇa.
King Viśāṃpatī performed the cremation offering with red sandalwood and erected eighty koṭis of jewel stūpas, featuring railings made of red sandalwood and golden lotuses on all four sides.
The Vimala Bhikṣu was prophesied by the Buddha as the foremost among those of great learning; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he widely proclaimed the True Dharma.
Wherever he traveled through cities, towns, and villages, he taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them all to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, there were many wicked bhikṣus who did not know how to practice and constantly harbored jealousy; deluded by Māra, they went to the king and spoke these words:
"The Bhikṣu Vimala, whom Your Majesty reveres and honors, enters and leaves the royal palace without any restriction."
Yet that bhikṣu has not yet abandoned sensual desire; he eats at improper times, wears perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, and is truly not one of pure conduct and thus unworthy of offerings.
I have come for this matter to inform the King: do not later develop a lack of faith toward the True Dharma of the Buddha.
At that time, there was a māra named Extremely Evil who immediately transformed his body into the likeness of a bhikṣu and went again to the king’s location to repeat what he had said before.
King Viśāṃtara had heard these words many times; he then thought to himself:
"The stainless bhikṣu is diligent, wise, and one whom I hold in high esteem. If such a thing were to happen, it could never be."
Having formed this thought, at that time the hosts of Māras manifested half their bodies in the sky and, facing the king, spoke these verses:
“The King should train in the arts and be well-versed in timely opportuneness;
one who cannot understand even what has been extensively taught does not possess the marks of a human sovereign.”
The Buddha’s disciples, the Arhats, have already perfected great wisdom;
how could they rely on such words or follow the view of annihilationism?
For your benefit, O Bhikṣu, I tell you these sincere words.
One who holds nihilistic views and belongs to the evil destinies is truly not one who practices the holy life.
That person, within the palace, enjoys himself with the court ladies;
Your Majesty should observe this together with your attendants and put your doubts to rest.
When the king heard these matters, his heart was filled with great alarm and fear;
he immediately took his attendants and hastened to the palace.
At that time, Vimalā was in the palace, expounding the ultimate truth.
All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; they are without self and without a life-principle.
You, O King, along with your host of soldiers, were all deluded by Māra when you saw the palace maidens surrounding the bhikṣu.
His wrath was as fierce as a rutting elephant, and he immediately commanded the *caṇḍāla*:
"A bhikṣu has defiled my palace; you must punish him with harsh measures.
His ministers, aides, and kinsmen were all possessed by Māra.
Toward a faultless bhikṣu, he gave way to malice born of anger.
As the executioner advanced with his sword, Vimala wept;
the King said:
"You act contrary to the Dharma; why do you weep again?
Vimalā said to the king:
"This matter is difficult to explain; wait but a moment, and I shall have clear proof."
When the King heard the bhikṣu’s words, he immediately halted the executioner and said:
"I shall test what you can do; you should quickly declare it.
For one who has accomplished a sublime resolve and practices compassion to benefit the world,"
Joining the ten fingers and palms together, he uttered this vow:
"Great King, you should know: if this is truly not so, may the earth tremble in six ways, and may wondrous flowers rain down from the sky."
When these words were spoken, the great earth shook in six ways, and from the realm of space, celestial flowers rained down; the hosts of Māra were filled with grief and distress.
At that time, the King gave rise to pure faith, prostrated at his feet, and sought his joy:
"I am about to fall into hell; I have no refuge—may you protect me!
Alas, that I have encountered such evil; how could I give rise to such a poisonous mind?
Without protection and with no one to rely upon, I follow only evil companions."
"In the ten directions I have no protector, save for the Great Teacher alone.
I shall renounce my royal throne and remain in refuge for as long as life lasts.
The bhikṣu, knowing the king’s resolve and that of his retinue, [proceeded accordingly].
For his sake, he preached the ultimate truth; hearing it, the king attained right faith.
Together with ten billion followers, he renounced his royal throne and left the household life.
He practiced the dhūta austerities and did not accept invitations from others.
At that time, within the royal harem, eighty thousand court ladies,
having heard the teaching of the ultimate truth, all abided in the stage of non-retrogression.
For twenty-four years, the king relied upon the Buddha’s teachings.
Though they constantly repent day and night, their karmic offenses are still not exhausted.
With a hundred koṭis of followers, they harbor evil intent toward the Dharma Master;
consequently, after their lives end, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Having suffered for many billions of years, he encountered the Tathāgata once his transgressions were exhausted;
yet due to the causes of his former terrors, the residual retribution left him perpetually weak and inferior.
Through gradual cultivation and practice, he made offerings to a thousand billion Buddhas.
In each of the other lands, they all attained perfect enlightenment, sharing one and the same name: Glorious Renown of Merit.
At that time, King Viśāṃpati went to the place of the bhikṣu Maitrīkṣānti.
Due to having conceived a poisonous and harmful intent, for many hundreds of millions of years he underwent the retribution of his past evil karma by falling into the Great Howling Hell.
Once this karmic retribution was exhausted, he again attained a human body.
I encountered the Tathāgata Universal Eye, Whom I approached and constantly made offerings to.
Because of this, I successively served Eighty koṭis of Buddhas;
Thereafter, I attained perfect enlightenment— I am that very person now.
That bhikṣu who sought to harm the Dharma Master free from fault will become a Buddha in the future; he is none other than Maitreya Bodhisattva.
At that time, within the royal palace, there were eighty thousand court ladies.
With pure faith, they have planted manifold virtues and served immeasurable Buddhas;
now, once again, they set forth in practice, making great vows to benefit sentient beings.
They shall serve thousands of billions of Buddhas, each attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
"I now tell you all: do not give rise to harm toward anything.
Cultivate loving-kindness, which is praised by the Buddhas; you shall swiftly attain great Bodhi.
Thus spoke Vidyutprabha!
If one cannot properly know the faculties, natures, and inclinations of sentient beings, one must at all times refrain from giving rise to a harmful mind.
Vidyutprāpta!
For example, among all mountains, Sumeru is the foremost.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise so; it is the most honored and unsurpassed among all forms of wisdom.
It is like the ocean, which is the most excellent among all waters.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise thus; among all forms of wisdom, it is the most profound and vast.
It is also like the universal monarch (cakravartin), who is the most honored and supreme among all kings.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise so; among all forms of wisdom, it is the supreme of the supreme.

Vidyutprāpta, because the Tathāgata has accomplished such wisdom, he fully knows the mental transformations of every sentient being’s thoughts as they engage in greed, hatred, and delusion, and in the mere snap of a finger, he is able to gather them all in.

Dian-de! The Tathāgata has attained all-knowledge; it is as if a person with clear vision were to look at five mango fruits in the palm of his own hand, understanding them clearly and without doubt without the need for effort.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he fully understands the mental activities of all sentient beings and teaches the Dharma in various ways within the great assemblies.

In immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-worlds, I fully know and see those sentient beings whose conduct is associated with greed, who, tormented by the fever of greed, spend their days and nights in vain deliberations as time passes by.
I fully know and see how, driven by the feverish affliction of greed, they give rise to various karmas of body and speech.

I fully know and see how sentient beings who act out of hatred, their minds shrouded by anger and resentment, harbor mutual malice and jealousy; because of this poisonous harm, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
I fully know all those sentient beings who are associated with deluded conduct, who are obscured by the darkness of ignorance, and who, being confused and attached, delight in following false views.

I fully know those who are capable and those who are incapable; those who progress and those who regress; those who plant roots of goodness in the Tathāgata Vehicle, those who plant roots of goodness in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and those who plant roots of goodness in the Śrāvaka Vehicle. I know them all.

The Tathāgata, having accomplished such wisdom, is able within the great assembly to discern the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings; because he knows it is not the proper time, he remains silent and dwells in equanimity, thinking only this:
"These sentient beings are deluded regarding the Dharma and are unable to understand it."

Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of the superior faculties and skillfully knows the proper time, he thoroughly understands those who are capable of being tamed, those whose aspirations are supreme, those who are able to endure, and those who accept wholesome words.
Having understood this, one should gather in and benefit those sentient beings.
Therefore, Vidyutprāpta!

A beginner bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stage of certainty cannot fully understand the superior aspirations and practices of sentient beings, whether they be householders or renunciants; such a person should never give rise to thoughts of aversion or malice, lest they bring about their own decline and affliction for a long night.

Therefore, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, a bodhisattva should regard all those who abide in the Mahāyāna as Buddhas; even if they see other sentient beings committing various evil deeds, they should not give rise to a thought of harm toward them.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has constantly taught that if sentient beings have even the slightest deficiency in pure and wholesome dharmas, they will ultimately be unable to enter nirvāṇa.
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings whose conduct is dominated by greed, they should think:
"That they are scorched by the feverish affliction of desire is my own fault.
Seeing those who are scorched by the feverish afflictions of hatred and delusion, they should likewise think in every case: "This is my transgression."
Why is this? I have witnessed the suffering and illness of all sentient beings and ought to seek medicinal means to treat them.
I previously vowed to eliminate the illnesses of sentient beings; that I now neglect and abandon them is my own fault.
When a bodhisattva has accomplished such an intentionality, they examine their own faults and give rise to a profound mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Even if they encounter someone who kills them or cuts off their limbs, it is impossible for them to harbor a heart of retaliation toward that enemy.
Diande! When a bodhisattva practices correctly in this manner, all unwholesome karma from the past is exhausted without remainder, and unwholesome karma will never arise again in the future.

“Dian-de! In the remote past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Jina-janma Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
The world was named Radiance.
He resided within the groves of the city of King Saṃśaya-vinivartana.

At that time, there was a caṇḍāla named Bhīṣaṇa, who was fierce, cruel, and fond of killing; he was habituated to violence and devoid of compassion, his hands smeared with blood, such that all who saw him were struck with fear.

At that time, a candāla had tied up a cow at his house and was about to enter to slaughter it; seeing this, the cow became terrified, snapped its rope, and fled toward the grove where the Tathāgata Jyotīrasa resided.
At that time, a caṇḍāla followed behind him carrying a sword; the ox, terrified and panicked, fell into a deep pit, its life nearly ending as it bellowed in agony.
Seeing the ox, the caṇḍāla’s anger intensified further, and he entered the pit with his sword, intending to kill it.

Before he had descended, at that time the Tathāgata Jyotiṣprabha was in that grove, surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, extensively analyzing the Dharma-gate of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), namely: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. Thus, through these causes and conditions, all is nothing but a mass of pure suffering.

Dian-de! Within these conditions, ignorance has no volition or cognition regarding formations; formations likewise have no volition or cognition regarding ignorance. This continues until birth has no volition or cognition regarding aging-and-death, and aging-and-death likewise has no volition or cognition regarding birth.

Thus, the nature of all these phenomena is unattainable; they are without activity, without thought, and without self or what belongs to a self. Their fundamental nature is pure, and each is unaware of the others.

Because ordinary beings have not heard of such phenomena, they grasp at form as being the self, or that "I possess forms," or that "forms belong to me"; this applies likewise to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Due to this attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self," one perceives the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the impure as pure, and the non-self as self, thereby giving rise to the four perversions.

Due to inverted views, one is deluded by ignorance and improper reflection; thus, being stained by attachment according to the mind, one cannot break through it, and the bonds of craving keep one bound in the cycle of birth and death, continuing without interruption.

Because the wise skillfully contemplate the characteristics of the dharma-realm, they do not perceive even the slightest existence of a self, a person, a sentient being, or even a life-span, nor can they find birth, old age, sickness, death, bondage, or slaughter.

"Diandei! At that time, the fearsome Caṇḍāla, hearing from afar the sound of the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, immediately awakened and ceased his murderous intent; he cast away the sword he held and emerged from the pit."
He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. He addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now wish to leave the household life to follow the Way within the Buddha-dharma."
The Buddha said, "So be it. Welcome, bhikṣu."
He immediately became a śramaṇa and attained full ordination.
At that time, the Tathāgata Jyotīṣprabha, knowing that his aspirations had gradually matured, extensively expounded upon the various practices of bodhisattvas for him.
Upon hearing this, Bhayaṃkara realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and shall never again regress from the Buddha-dharma.

As for that ox, having heard the verses on dependent origination spoken by the Tathāgata, its mind was filled with joy because of their subtle and wondrous sound; at the end of its life, it was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where it beheld Maitreya and attained right faith.
Thus it is, Vidyutprāpta!
The conduct of sentient beings is profoundly deep, subtle, and secret; it is difficult to discern and difficult to know.
Therefore, Vidyutprāpta!

A bodhisattva who seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should skillfully know the faculties and conduct of sentient beings; dwell with a mind of equanimity and non-obstruction toward all sentient beings; remain forever free from attachment to all phenomena; relinquish all possessions; cultivate and maintain pure precepts; abide securely in patience; exert diligence; enter into various meditative concentrations; and contemplate the nature of all phenomena as they truly are.
Dian-de! When a bodhisattva fulfills these six dharmas, they are able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How does one fulfill them?
This is because they practice by relying upon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Vidyutprāpta! What is the Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas?"
It is said that when a bodhisattva perceives all forms, they understand them as they truly are: fundamentally unarisen and pure by nature.
Because the bodhisattva has attained skillfulness regarding form, they are able to accomplish the four kinds of unhindered eloquence.
What are the four? They are:

non-obstruction regarding meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), non-obstruction regarding phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), non-obstruction regarding expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid), and non-obstruction regarding eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid).
Regarding non-obstruction regarding meaning: it is because one is without hindrance concerning the meanings of all forms.
What is the meaning of "form" (rūpa)?
It refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha). What is the ultimate truth?

This means that because form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, one achieves such knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), which is called unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).

As for unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), it is the thorough investigation and accurate comprehension of all phenomena of form as they truly are; this is called unimpededness regarding phenomena.

Unimpededness in terminology (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) refers to the skillful differentiation of various verbal expressions regarding all forms through unimpeded wisdom; this is called unimpededness in terminology.

Unimpededness in eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) refers to the opening up and exposition of teachings regarding all forms according to the capacities of sentient beings, being untainted and unattached; this is called unimpededness in eloquence.

Once the Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom, they universally teach the Dharma to all sentient beings who are deluded and attached to form-dharmas, according to their dispositions and inclinations, using effortless wisdom as appropriate; yet they do not conceive of duality within the Dharma-realm.
This is extensively explained to apply likewise to odor, taste, touch, and mental objects.
"O Diandei! This is called the Dharma-treasury of all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Once a Bodhisattva has realized this treasury, in order to subdue those sentient beings who are deluded within such realms, they may, according to their inclinations, at each and every location, skillfully proclaim the teaching using various expressions for a single kalpa or even more than a kalpa; yet they cannot reach the limit of those locations, nor does the Bodhisattva’s wisdom diminish. Because they do not depart from the dharmadhātu and accord with its non-duality and non-differentiation, this is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful exposition of the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena."

Having obtained such a treasury of Dharma, one is able to preach the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, enabling them to attain the complete and inexhaustible wealth of the Dharma, and causing the poverty of birth and death to be forever severed.
Dian-de! These are called the five kinds of treasuries of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva: the great treasury, the inexhaustible treasury, the universally inexhaustible treasury, and the boundless treasury.
Because the Bodhisattva has accomplished such a hidden treasury and perfected all supreme merits, he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi swiftly with little exertion of effort.

When this Dharma-gate of the hidden treasury was spoken, the Bodhisattva Vidyutprāpta attained dhāraṇī; five hundred bodhisattvas attained the Vidyutprabhā-samādhi; and thirty-six thousand devaputras resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Candradhvaja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”
"What is the meaning of 'effortless wisdom'?
The Buddha told Candradhvaja:
"If there is a bodhisattva who, within wholesome dharmas, engages in mental and physical application by grasping at objects and performing conditioned acts, this is called 'effortful activity.

If there is a bodhisattva whose body and mind are harmonious and supple, who is without thought, without dependence, and free from the marks of cultivation, then through the fulfillment of their past vows and wisdom, they manifest various displays throughout billions of buddha-fields;
yet they remain unmoved within the dharma-realm, constantly expounding the Dharma without even the slightest mark of a phenomenon."
They bring sentient beings to maturity through the four means of attraction, yet there are no sentient beings to be delivered;
they adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, yet they do not perceive any impure Buddha-fields;
they constantly keep the Buddhas in mind, yet do not contemplate their physical forms.
Wandering through all Buddha-fields without departing from the Dharma-realm—
this is called the bodhisattva’s wisdom of effortlessness (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
Because the bodhisattva accomplishes such wisdom, they fulfill all the hopes of sentient beings, yet remain free from attachment regarding their deeds.

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these words on effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), the trichiliocosm shook in six ways. Śakra Devānām Indra, together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, rained down *māndārava* flowers, *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *padma* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, and powdered sandalwood incense from the sky above, scattering them over the Buddha.
The celestial drums resounded spontaneously and a great light shone everywhere; such had never been seen before, and those sentient beings who encountered it found their bodies cooled.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vidyutprāpta, saying:
"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have, in this very place, revealed and expounded such a Dharma-gate."
In the future, all Buddhas who shall appear in the world will likewise reveal and expound this Dharma-gate at this very place.
Furthermore, the present Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, emit great rays of light so that this Dharma-gate shall not be interrupted.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What should this sutra be named?
How should I receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Inexhaustible Treasury,' and it is also named 'The Exposition of the Non-differentiated Characteristics of All Dharmas. You should uphold it by these names."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva Vidyutprāpta, the Elder Ānanda, and the fourfold assembly—including all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others in the world—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Eighty-Four;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume Eighty-Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
21. The Chapter on Bestowing the Prediction upon the Illusionist Bhadra.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats well-known to the world.

There were fifty bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had attained great supernormal powers and mastery over transformations, who had realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and various *dhāraṇīs*. Their names were:

Bodhisattva Siṃha, Bodhisattva Siṃhamati, Bodhisattva Candra-candana, Bodhisattva Vinayaka, Bodhisattva Mahāvinayaka, Bodhisattva Jyotirjaya, Bodhisattva Jyotirbhāsa, Bodhisattva Jyotirtejas, Bodhisattva Jyotirvyūha, Bodhisattva Vibodhana, Bodhisattva Gaṇottama, and Bodhisattva Sattvavinayaka; as well as all the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, headed by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Maitreya and the Dharma-prince Mañjuśrī.

Furthermore, he was surrounded by the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Mahābrahmā the Lord of the Sahā World, and an immeasurable multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great renown that is heard throughout the world; namely: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He is the knower of all and the seer of all, who has perfected the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharmāḥ*), and great loving-kindness and great compassion. He is fully endowed with the five eyes (*pañcacakṣūṃṣi*) and has completely perfected the miracle of prophecy (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*), and the miracle of supernormal power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).

One is able to place the great earth, cities, towns, grasses, trees, forests, Mount Sumeru, and so forth, along with the great oceans, rivers, and the palaces of the various devas of the trichiliocosm upon the tip of a single hair and cause them to abide in space; whether for the duration of an eon or more than an eon, they remain without tilting or moving according to one's intended wish.
