At that time, the kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and all the people of the city of Rājagṛha conceived deep respect for the Tathāgata, and they reverently made offerings of various superior and exquisite foods, drinks, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
In that city there was an illusionist named Bhadra, who was well-versed in heterodox doctrines and skilled in incantations and arts; he was the foremost among all illusionists.

In the kingdom of Magadha, with the sole exception of those who have realized the Truth and the lay followers—both male and female—who possess right faith, all other ignorant people were deluded by this illusion and there was none who did not return their faith to it.
At that time, the illusionist, having heard of the Tathāgata’s reputation for merit and fame, conceived this thought:
"All the sentient beings in this city now regard me with respect; only the śramaṇa Gautama has yet to believe and submit. I should now go there to test him."
"If he were to return to me, the people of Magadha would surely redouble their respect for me.

At that time, because the karmic conditions for good roots planted by that illusionist in previous lives had reached maturity, and through the power of the World-Honored One’s majestic virtue, he departed from Rājagṛha for Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.

Beholding the Buddha’s radiance, it surpasses that of a hundred thousand suns; his face is as majestic and beautiful as the full moon; his physical form is perfectly complete like a nyagrodha tree; the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa between his brows is pure like the light of a mani-jewel; his eyes are deep blue like the *utpala* lotus; even reaching up to the Brahma-heaven, none can see the crown of his head; and with sixty kinds of pure vocal tones, he preaches the Dharma for the multitude.
Although this illusionist beheld the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue as exceptionally sublime, he still harbored perverse pride and further thought to himself: "I should now test him."
"If you are one who possesses all-knowing vision, you should understand my intention.
Having thought this, he stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and said:
"I pray that you will accept my humble offering tomorrow."

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the faculties of the illusionist and the sentient beings of Rājagṛha had reached maturity, accepted their invitation in silence for the sake of bringing them to spiritual ripening.
At that time, having seen that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation, the illusionist further thought to himself:
"This Gautama does not understand my intention; it is certain that he is not an omniscient one."
Having thus taken his leave and paid his respects, he departed.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was present in the assembly; having witnessed this event, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Bhadrā intends to deceive the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus; I pray only that the World-Honored One does not accept her invitation."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Do not harbor such thoughts.

Indeed, greed, hatred, and delusion are capable of deception and delusion; however, I have long since severed and extinguished these matters, for I have realized that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen."
Having dwelt in right practice for long eons, who could possibly deceive me?
You should now know this: what that person has done is not true illusion; rather, it is the Tathāgata’s doing that is true illusion.
Why is this? Because one has directly realized that all phenomena are like illusions.

Even if all classes of sentient beings were to become masters of illusion like Bhadra, they would not equal the Tathāgata by even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or anything reachable through calculation or analogy.
He further addressed Maudgalyāyana: "What do you think?
Could that illusionist possibly manifest and adorn all the worlds within this trichiliocosm?"
He replied, “No.

“Maudgalyāyana, you should know that although I can now, within a single hair-tip, manifest and adorn worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have still not exhausted the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers.”
Maudgalyāyana, you should know that there is a great wind-circle named *Saṃvartanī*, which is capable of destroying the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named *Vairambha*, which can both destroy the world and establish it once again.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named "Agitation," whose winds are constantly able to rotate the world-system.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named "Abiding," whose winds can travel as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named Disperser, which can disperse Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, as well as the Black Mountains and others.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named Fierce Flame, which, when the fire at the end of the kalpa burns, can waft those fierce flames upward as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Furthermore, there is a wind-wheel named Cessation (*nirodha*), which is able to extinguish the fires of the kalpa when they burn.
Furthermore, there is a wind-wheel named Coolness (*śītalā*), which can cause a single cloud to universally cover the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named Universal Shower, which, when the kalpa-fire burns, pours down great rains everywhere throughout the world.
Furthermore, there is a wind-circle named Drying Up, which, when the kalpa-floods surge, is able to cause all that water to completely evaporate.
Such wind-circles as these, if I were to describe them in detail, would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
Maudgalyāyana, you should know: what do you think?
Could this illusionist remain for even a moment within such wind-circles?
He replied, “No. The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
“The Tathāgata is able to walk, stand, sit, and lie down upon such wind-circles without being shaken.

Furthermore, he can place such wind-circles within a single mustard seed and manifest all the activities performed by those wind-circles; yet, there is neither increase nor decrease in the mustard seed, and the various wind-circles do not obstruct one another.”
“Maudgalyāyana, you should know that the Tathāgata has perfected the dharmas of illusory arts (māyā-vidyā) without limit or end.
When the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the great assembly heard the Tathāgata speak these words, they were struck with wonder; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they cried out with one voice:
“We have now encountered a guide of great majesty and supernormal power, and have obtained great benefit.”

If there are those who, upon hearing of such supernatural powers of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, give rise to profound faith and understanding, these persons will surely obtain great and wholesome benefit, and shall resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the illusionist went to Rājagṛha that very night and, in a most lowly and filthy place, conjured a bodhimaṇḍa that was vast, level, and upright; it was adorned with various silken banners and canopies, strewn with flowers and perfumes, and covered with jeweled curtains.
Furthermore, eight thousand precious jewel-trees appeared; beneath each of these jewel-trees was a lion throne, all exquisitely adorned with immeasurable coverings and furnishings.

Desiring to make offerings to the bhikṣus, he further transformed himself into food and drink of a hundred flavors, and manifested five hundred attendants dressed in white garments and adorned with ornaments.
Having performed this transformation, the Four Heavenly Kings came to the assembly and said to the illusionist:
"Tomorrow, for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgata, you have manifested such immeasurable ornaments; by reason of these causes and conditions, you shall obtain great merit."
"Now, because I wish to assist you, I shall make offerings to the Tathāgata and manifest a second site of enlightenment here.
Will you be able to listen?
When the illusionist heard these words, he was struck with a sense of wonder and immediately gave his consent.
Thereupon, the Four Great Kings immediately manifested immeasurable and exquisite ornaments of adornment, surpassing the magical transformations of the illusionist.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with thirty thousand sons of gods, came to the site of enlightenment and said to the illusionist:
"I too now wish to cause you to adorn the site of enlightenment through your offerings."
The illusionist was struck with awe and granted his permission.
Thereupon, for the sake of the Tathāgata, Śakra, Lord of Devas, manifested a hall that was like the magnificent palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Furthermore, he further manifested the Pārijāta, the Kovidāra, and other celestial wondrous trees, arranged in successive rows.

When the illusionist saw this, he sighed in wonder and regret, wishing to withdraw his manifestations; yet, despite exhausting his incantations and magical arts, the illusory creations remained exactly as they were.
He then thought to himself:
"This is truly marvelous.
From the past until now, the manifestation and concealment of my transformations have always proceeded according to my will."
Yet, at this present time, it cannot be made to vanish; this must surely be because of that Tathāgata.
At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing his thought, said to the illusionist:
“Because you have now adorned the site of enlightenment for the sake of the Tathāgata, it cannot be made to vanish.”

By this you should know that if there is another person who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, gives rise to even a single thought-moment, by virtue of this root of goodness they will ultimately be able to create the cause for parinirvāṇa.
Having heard these words spoken by the Lord of Devas, his heart was filled with great joy.
When the night had passed, he went to the place where the Tathāgata was and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
"I have now completed my preparations; I pray that you will deign to show me compassion.

Then, at the time of dawn, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his bowl, and surrounded with great reverence by the great assembly, entered the city of Rājagṛha to proceed to the site of the illusionist’s performance hall.

The non-Buddhist practitioners, brahmins, and śramaṇas of the kingdom of Magadha all wished that the Tathāgata would be deluded by the illusions of a magician; desiring to witness this, they all gathered together.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, desiring to see and hear the Tathāgata’s supernatural transformations and his lion’s roar, also all assembled there.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the Tathāgata caused that illusionist, Śakra, and the four kings to each see the World-Honored One within the places they themselves had adorned.
At that time, having seen this, the illusionist abandoned his arrogance, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I now repent and confess my transgressions before the Tathāgata.”
"Previously, I falsely deceived the Buddha by conjuring various kinds of magnificent displays through illusion.
Although I have gradually come to repent, I am unable to make them vanish.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the illusionist, saying:
"All sentient beings and all their requisites are illusory transformations, for they are produced by the illusions of karma.
The assembly of bhikṣus is also an illusory transformation, for they are produced by the illusions of the Dharma."
My own body is also an illusion, for it is conjured by wisdom.
All worlds of the trichiliocosm are likewise illusions, for they are collectively conjured by all sentient beings.
All phenomena whatsoever are nothing other than illusions, for they are illusions produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions.
You should now distribute illusory food and drink in due order.

Then that illusionist, together with the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, and their respective retinues, as well as the attendants he had conjured by magic, immediately took food and drink and offered them to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, so that all those gathered there were fully satisfied.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa spoke in verse:
"Knowing that food is an illusory transformation, And that the recipient is likewise so,
When one realizes this state of equality, Only then is it called a pure gift."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "Knowing that the seat is an illusory transformation, and that the one who sits upon it is likewise so—
when this equality is realized, it is then called a pure gift."
Śāriputra said: "Just as with an emanated attendant, so too is the mind of the recipient;
if the giver can be thus, it is called a pure gift."
Subhūti said: "Do not regard the gift as a gift, nor the recipient as a recipient;
when a giver can act in this way, it is called a pure gift."
Ānanda said: "The gift is like space; the recipient cannot be apprehended.
Being far removed from body and mind, that gift is most pure."
The Bodhisattva Prabhāketu said:
“Just as a magician conjures various adorned things through illusion, so too are all phenomena; yet foolish people do not realize this.”
The Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha said:
"Just as this seat and all these trees are produced by the illusory mind,
what slight difference could there be between the illusory mind and empty space?"
The Bodhisattva Siṃha said: "The jackal has never heard the lion’s roar;
its heart feels no fear as it howls amidst the trees of the forest."
Just as upon hearing the roar of a lion, one hides away with nowhere to go,
so it is with this illusionist: unable to stand before the Tathāgata,
he constantly praises himself among the non-Buddhists as surpassing the Buddha.
Although the illusionist creates them, the illusions have their limits;
that which is accomplished by the Tathāgata is an illusion without end.
None of the devas or māras are able to know its boundary.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
"To fully understand that the attendant, the food and drink,
and the eater are all entirely illusory transformations— to practice such sublime giving is unsurpassed."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"Just as fire, when it obtains clarified butter, grows ever more intense,
so too, O World-Honored One, are the magical transformations performed by a magician."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"The virtuous deeds of this assembly are as they have never been before;
all phenomena are likewise always equal to the prior limit."
At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to bring that illusionist to spiritual maturity, manifested a householder who entered the assembly and said to the illusionist:
"What do you intend to do here now?"
The illusionist replied,
"I have prepared various foods and drinks as an offering to the śramaṇa Gautama. The elder said:
"Do not speak thus. The Tathāgata is now with the bhikṣus in King Śreṇika’s palace, accepting offerings and eating.
By the Buddha's supernormal power, he caused that illusionist to see the Tathāgata and the bhikṣus eating there.
Furthermore, he again manifested a second elder and said to the illusionist,
"What are you doing? The illusionist replied:
"I am making this offering to the śramaṇa Gautama.
The elder spoke again: "Do not say such a thing."
"The Tathāgata is now with the bhikṣus, wandering through the streets and alleys of the brahmins to beg for alms.
By the Buddha's supernatural power, the illusionist was made to see again the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones wandering through the streets and alleys to beg for alms.
Furthermore, he again manifested as a third elder and said to the illusionist:
"The Tathāgata is currently in the garden of Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, proclaiming the sublime Dharma for the fourfold assembly."
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the illusionist was made to see all this.
Next, [the Buddha] further manifested as Śakra Devānām Indra, who came to the illusionist and spoke again:
“The Tathāgata is now in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, preaching the Dharma for the assembly.”
At that time, the illusionist again saw the Tathāgata expounding the essentials of all dharmas amidst the assembly of devas.

Then, the illusionist further beheld the Tathāgata, endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence, amidst the flowers and leaves of the forest trees, upon all the lion thrones, and throughout the city of Rājagṛha—in its alleys, streets, walls, houses, halls, palaces, and all other sublime locations.
Furthermore, in the presence of all the Tathāgatas, he saw his own body confessing and revealing his transgressions.

At that time, the illusionist saw only the bodies of the Buddhas and nothing else; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, he immediately attained the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
Rising from samādhi, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"In the past, within Jambudvīpa, my illusory transformations were unsurpassed;
yet compared now to the Buddha’s supernormal powers, they cannot equal even a small fraction."

From this, one finally comes to understand that the inconceivable power of all Buddhas can manifest transformations according to the mind, producing emanation Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All the Tathāgatas who are seen are fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
I pray that the Honored One will reveal: who is the true Buddha?
Among these Tathāgatas, I wish to practice offerings;
I pray that the Honored One will tell me: what constitutes the supreme fruit?
If a person does not give rise to a mind of respect toward the Buddha,
such ordinary worldlings will fall away from peace and happiness.
Now, before the World-Honored One, I confess all transgressions previously committed.
For the sin of rashly testing the Tathāgata, I vow that it shall be extinguished forever without remainder.
May Brahmā, Śakra, and the great assembly all bear witness to me:
for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, I now resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
With the radiance of wisdom, he awakens the world;
Bestowing the nectar of the Dharma, he causes all to be fully satisfied.
If a person, in the presence of the Buddha, Beholds such a miraculous transformation,
Having heard the words of Manojñā, which concern supreme conduct and unimpeded wisdom—
who that possesses clear intelligence would not resolve to attain bodhicitta?
I pray you show me the path to enlightenment and the universally pure practices.
What is the practice that the followers of the two vehicles cannot enter?
What is the sphere of activity that is honored and venerated?
How does one possess dignified deportment and become free from all doubt and regret?
How does one cultivate the firm and substantial through tireless study of the teachings?
How does one speak for others so that they delight in the True Dharma,
being free from the desire for gain and honor, and knowing well how to repay kindness?
How does one always act as an indestructible friend to sentient beings?
How does one draw near to virtuous friends and abandon evil associates?
How does one encounter the Buddhas and offer them worship with a tireless mind?
What are the training rules, and how are they honored and purified?
How does one establish the lineage of meditative concentration and achieve a mind that accords with reality?
And how does one abandon what is contrary to reason and become fully endowed with right reflection?
How is it that one is without cowardice, is not seized by Māra,
contemplates the principles of meaning, and does not abandon sentient beings?
How is it that one should not abandon them, yet takes up what is not taken up?
How does one enter into right practice and become fully endowed with skillful means?
How does one cultivate loving-kindness and compassion, accomplish the various supernormal powers,
realize unimpeded eloquence, and attain the dhāraṇīs?
How does one attain the patient acceptance of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) and pure eloquence (*pratibhāna*),
abandon what should be abandoned, and enter into the profound meaning?
How can all of one's vows be brought to complete fulfillment?
How does one attain non-retrogression regarding the various pāramitās?
Regarding such a Dharma as this, I vow to practice it with diligence;
I pray only that the World-Honored One of Great Compassion will expound it extensively for my sake.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"If one thoroughly understands that all phenomena Are entirely like illusions and transformations,
Such a person can manifest The bodies of ten billion Buddhas."
He travels to millions of lands to deliver all sentient beings.
Like the *bhadra* flower, which manifests various colors while remaining formless,
he neither arises nor ceases, and has no abiding, nor coming or going.
The transformation body of the World-Honored One, along with the assembly of bhikṣus,
is likewise without birth or cessation, even unto nirvāṇa.
All of these are the Tathāgata’s inconceivable supernormal transformations.
It is also like a magical illusion, manifesting as an array of elephant and horse troops.
It deludes all sentient beings, who falsely perceive it as real;
yet these elephant and horse troops have no intrinsic nature and no arising.
The Buddhas have no marks of form; they neither go nor come.
Those who dwell in the view of self and person falsely give rise to the notion of a Buddha.
One should not [recognize them] by means of physical marks, lineage, or place of birth.
Even with a voice like that of Brahmā, one who wishes to perceive the Tathāgata finds it difficult to do so through the consciousness of the mind.
One cannot discern the various Buddhas by means of the Dharma-nature body (dharmatākāya) of the Buddhas, which transcends the three periods of time.
The intrinsic nature is free from all marks and does not fall within the categories of phenomena;
all Tathāgatas who appear have an intrinsic nature that is without arising,
nor do they possess the aggregates, elements, or sense bases, abiding in the state of non-reliance.
Such is the Buddha’s Dharma-body; it cannot be seen by the five eyes.
If one claims, "I see the Buddha," then one does not see him at all.
To take non-seeing as seeing is like the tracks of a bird in the sky.
The Buddhas whom you have seen, as well as those whom others have not yet seen, are equal like space;
they are of one single characteristic, without distinction.
Their morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation— [are likewise equal.]
All Tathāgatas are without distinction in their merit;
they all abide in emptiness and have no attachment to phenomena.
All things are like illusions, lacking intrinsic nature and without arising.
To make offerings to a single Tathāgata is to make offerings to many Buddhas;
for the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is equal and without distinction.
Thus, all these Buddhas are able to produce merit and benefit.
Universally bestowing upon all Tathāgatas, they all attain the great fruit;
together they realize the equality of the pure dharmatā.
Therefore, among all Tathāgatas, there are no various distinctions.
As you previously asked, "Who is the true Buddha?
you should now abandon a distracted mind and listen attentively as I proclaim it.
You should abide in right mindfulness and wisdom, and investigate all phenomena.
All things are without birth; they are falsely perceived as real.
If material forms were subject to birth, they would likewise be subject to cessation;
therefore, all Tathāgatas are ultimately without birth.
He is neither born from himself, nor does he undergo dispersal or extinction.
Thus one contemplates the Tathāgata: to see him through non-seeing is true seeing.
As you have seen the Buddha, he does not depend on any location or direction.
All ordinary beings depend entirely upon the five aggregates;
one should observe those aggregates as one would the Buddha.
This applies to all Buddhas and all dharmas, even down to sentient beings.
Taking the signless as the sign, and having no basis for reliance—if one observes in this way, one will swiftly realize awakening.
All phenomena are non-existent; they arise from false conceptualization.
The nature of causes and conditions is empty, for they are devoid of an agent-nature.
One who can thus thoroughly understand that both causes and conditions and the agent are empty will then be able to realize the dharmas that are free from defilement and are pure.
"By means of the pure Dharma-eye, one shall behold all Tathāgatas.

When the illusionist heard these words, he attained the patient acceptance of the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti); five thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and two hundred bodhisattvas realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished his meal, wishing to fulfill the wish offered by the illusionist, he spoke again in verse:
“If one can regard the object given, the giver, and the recipient with an equal mind free from discrimination, then this constitutes the perfection of giving.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the Tathāgata, through the empowerment of the Buddha’s spiritual power, will cause these arrangements and adornments provided by the illusionist not to vanish for seven days.”

At that time, for the sake of the assembly’s request, the Tathāgata caused the illusionist to manifest a transformed *bodhimaṇḍa*, which remained magnificently adorned as before for a full seven days.

Then, the Tathāgata, surrounded by bhikṣus, great bodhisattvas, and deities such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas who paid him reverent homage, returned to Vulture Peak Mountain to preach the Dharma to the assembly.
At that time, the illusionist again went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
“I pray that you will expound upon the path of the bodhisattvas, so that those who diligently practice may swiftly reach the site of enlightenment.
The Buddha said, “Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for your sake.”
The illusionist replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I am eager and desirous to hear."
The Buddha said:
"Good son! There are four kinds of dharmas that constitute the path of a bodhisattva."
If one is able to practice these, one shall swiftly attain the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). What are the four?

First, never to fall away from the bodhicitta; second, never to abandon any sentient being; third, to seek all roots of goodness without ever becoming weary or satisfied; and fourth, to protect and uphold the true Dharma by exerting great diligence.
"Good son! Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva’s conduct is universally pure. What are these four?

First is purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), second is purity of intention (*āśaya-viśuddhi*), third is purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*), and fourth is purity of rebirth (*upapatti-viśuddhi*).
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that are practiced exclusively by Bodhisattvas and cannot be entered by those of the two vehicles (*yāna*):

What are the four? First, practicing meditative concentration without being reborn [in accordance with its power]; second, the mind being able to discern profound meanings; third, giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings; and fourth, expounding the Dharma with various forms of eloquence without impediment.
Furthermore, there are four practices to be cultivated. What are these four? First, delighting in dwelling in solitude;

second, feeling weary of clamor and bustle; third, giving rise to a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings; and fourth, being able to understand that all conditioned phenomena have no coming or going.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for honoring and making offerings. What are the four?
First, not begrudging one's body or life; second, always maintaining a joyful mind; third, relinquishing arrogance; and fourth, practicing according to the teaching.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for being fully endowed with dignified deportment:
first, knowing the proper time; second, knowing the proper place; third, tranquility; and fourth, truthfulness.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that enable one to be free from doubt and regret.

What are the four? First, one should prevent and guard against unwholesome actions; second, one should joyfully associate with wise persons; third, one should constantly and skillfully contemplate the meaning of what has been heard; fourth, one should not, even out of a spirit of loving-kindness, expose the faults of others.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for which one never tires of hearing much. What are these four?

First, because it increases the right wisdom of both oneself and others; second, because it is able to sever and eliminate the doubts of others; third, because it is able to uphold the Buddha’s true Dharma; and fourth, because it praises all Tathāgatas inexhaustibly.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which extensive learning becomes firm and substantial. What are these four?

First, having heard the true Dharma, one is able to understand it well; second, having heard the true Dharma, one does not commit any evil deeds; third, having heard the true Dharma, one explains and reveals it to others; fourth, having heard the true Dharma, one dedicates the merit toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that bring benefit through the preaching of the Dharma. What are these four?

First, constantly receiving fragrant foods and drinks from others; second, always receiving clothing and various kinds of offerings; third, causing the power and influence of Māra’s retinue to become weak; and fourth, being protected by the devas so that Māra finds no opportunity.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that cause others to have faith and delight in the Dharma one preaches. What are these four?
First, because the mind has few desires; second, because one is always content; third, because one’s speech is gentle; and fourth, because one’s body conforms to the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one can expound the true Dharma without harboring expectations. What are these four?

First, to always maintain a sense of dread toward saṃsāra; second, not to seek worldly gain, offerings, or friends; third, to constantly give rise to a spirit of protection toward all sentient beings; and fourth, to be able to cultivate the noble lineages.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for knowing and repaying kindness. What are the four?

First, exhorting all sentient beings to advance toward Bodhi; second, knowing that the karma one has performed will not be lost or destroyed; third, loving sentient beings with compassion as if they were one’s own body; and fourth, being well able to practice the deeds of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are four qualities by which one becomes an indestructible friend to all sentient beings. What are these four?

First, because one can don the great armor of patience; second, because one benefits and brings welfare to sentient beings without seeking recompense; third, because one never retreats from the mind of great compassion; and fourth, because one does not abandon them even when subjected to much affliction and harm.
Furthermore, there are four qualities by which one should attend upon spiritual friends.

What are these four? First, they have accomplished skillful means; second, they have accomplished a sublime intention; third, they have accomplished the correct conduct of a bodhisattva; and fourth, they have accomplished the exhortation and praise of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are four things that one should abandon regarding evil associates. What are these four?
First, praising and speaking of the two vehicles; second, causing others to regress from bodhicitta; third, increasing unwholesome dharmas; and fourth, destroying all wholesome roots.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one encounters the Buddhas. What are these four?

First, because one constantly and single-mindedly focuses on mindfulness of the Buddha; second, because one praises the various merits of the Tathāgata; third, because the ethical discipline one has received is universally pure; and fourth, because one generates great vows with a superior intention.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one makes offerings to all Buddhas with a mind free from weariness.

What are these four? First, one should rejoice within oneself, thinking: "I am now making offerings to the supreme field of merit. Second, because of my offering, all sentient beings shall also receive offerings. Third, through having made this offering, one shall attain firmness in the bodhicitta. Fourth, upon beholding the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, one's roots of goodness increase.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that give rise to a mind of reverence toward the various precepts. What are these four?
First, transcending the evil realms; second, attaining birth in the happy realms; third, revering the Tathāgata; and fourth, fulfilling all vows.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that should be studied. What are the four?

First, never abandoning the bodhicitta; second, maintaining a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; third, diligently practicing the pāramitās; and fourth, not giving rise to fear upon hearing immeasurable teachings.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for the purification of the precepts. What are these four?
First, not committing any evil; second, deeply understanding the nature of emptiness; third, not slandering the Buddhas; and fourth, destroying all views.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that constitute the lineage of samādhi. What are these four?
First, being free from clamor and bustle; second, delighting in tranquility; third, having a mind free from distraction; and fourth, the increase of roots of goodness.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas of the mind that accord with principle which one should accomplish. What are the four?

First, dedicating the wholesome dharmas one cultivates toward bodhi; second, the mind is constantly tranquil and free from attachment; third, constantly and diligently practicing the gates of liberation; and fourth, never seeking to realize the nirvana of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, there are four things that should be abandoned by one with an irrational mind. What are these four?

First, having fear regarding all of birth and death; second, not giving rise to faith and acceptance toward what is practiced; third, not seeking superior understanding of the secret teachings; and fourth, not cultivating the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that one should properly cultivate and study with right reflection. What are these four?
First, a bodhisattva undergoes the suffering of birth and death for immeasurable eons, even for the sake of a single sentient being.
Second, one should first understand the differences in the faculties and natures of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma so that they may abandon their afflictions;
third, one should sever all evil, cultivate all goodness, subdue the armies of Māra, and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
fourth, for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings in the trichiliocosm, one should expound the essentials of all dharmas with a single Brahma-voice.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one possesses a mind free from timidity that Māra cannot destroy. What are these four?

First, viewing all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations; second, constantly remaining in accord with correct wisdom that accords with reality; third, having no conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena; and fourth, having no attachment to any signs.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for contemplating the meaning. What are the four?

First, knowing that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; second, knowing that there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be called "arising"; third, knowing that phenomena born of conditions are themselves without arising; and fourth, knowing that phenomena are neither born nor do they perish.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one does not abandon sentient beings. What are these four?
First, not abandoning the great vow; second, enduring weariness and suffering; third, not begrudging body or life; and fourth, constantly practicing the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Furthermore, there are four things that should not be abandoned. What are these four?

First, not abandoning all acts of giving; second, not abandoning the maturation of sentient beings; third, never ceasing self-reflection and vigilance; and fourth, not abandoning the cultivation of others' virtues.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that should always be embraced. What are these four?

First, one should cultivate even the most minute roots of goodness; second, one should increase the virtues of others with a mind free from indolence; third, upon hearing the teaching of generosity and morality, one is able to believe and accept them; fourth, one does not seek after any gain, profit, or reputation.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that lead one into correct practice. What are these four?
First, the accomplishment of penetrative wisdom; second, abiding in the great samādhi; third, the cultivation of emptiness; and fourth, the absence of attachment.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas of skillful means. What are the four?

First, regarding all acts of generating the resolve [for enlightenment], the bodhisattva takes the bodhicitta as the foremost; even afflictions are thereby made to incline toward unsurpassed bodhi, let alone the arousal of various wholesome states of mind.
Second, to regard all sentient beings—even those who abide in false views—as vessels for the Dharma;
third, to thoroughly understand that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
and fourth, to cultivate liberation within the gates of samādhi without any notion of attachment.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for cultivating the mind of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). What are the four?

First, cultivating the mind of great loving-kindness to rescue and protect sentient beings; second, cultivating the mind of great loving-kindness to deliver sentient beings; third, cultivating the mind of great loving-kindness to awaken sentient beings; and fourth, cultivating the mind of great loving-kindness in order to cause sentient beings to enter *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for cultivating the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). What are these four?

First, one cultivates the mind of great compassion so that sentient beings may leave all evil realms and dwell in the happy destinies. Second, one cultivates the mind of great compassion so that sentient beings may abandon all evil conduct and practice wholesome dharmas. Third, one cultivates the mind of great compassion so that sentient beings may leave the Lesser Vehicle and enter the Great Vehicle. Fourth, one cultivates the mind of great compassion so that sentient beings may leave birth and death and attain nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for accomplishing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). What are the four?

First, not begrudging one’s body or life because of the absence of attachment; second, understanding that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; third, giving rise to reverence toward all sentient beings; and fourth, cultivating *śamatha* without distraction.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains unimpeded eloquence. What are the four?

First, to accord with the meaning rather than the letter; second, to accord with the Dharma rather than the person; third, to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena as being beyond words and letters; and fourth, to rely on the understanding of words and letters to deliver inexhaustible expositions.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains dhāraṇī. What are these four?

First, never being weary of extensive learning; second, revering and making offerings to those who possess extensive learning; third, explaining the true meaning through various names and expressions; and fourth, being able to correctly enter according to the secret teachings.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one can attain dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*). What are these four?

First, extensively cultivating resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); second, being without regression; third, the perfection of the provisions (*sambhāra*); and fourth, diligent effort without weariness.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains pure eloquence. What are the four?

First, not being in opposition to those who preach the Dharma; second, honoring the Dharma teacher and listening to them with reverence; third, not becoming arrogant because of one's extensive learning; and fourth, not treating those of little learning with contempt.
Furthermore, there are four things that should be abandoned. What are these four?

First, one should abandon greed, hatred, and delusion; second, one should abandon the Śrāvaka vehicle; third, one should abandon the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and fourth, one should abandon the notion of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for entering the profound meaning. What are the four?

First, deeply penetrating dependent origination regarding conditioned phenomena; second, being able to correctly understand the secret meaning; third, deeply generating correct understanding regarding the nature of all phenomena; and fourth, thoroughly comprehending the meaning of emptiness regarding all phenomena.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that cause one's aspirations to be fulfilled. What are these four?

First, purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, the complete purification of evil karma; third, the absence of flattery and deception; and fourth, the increase of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains non-retrogression regarding the pāramitās. What are the four?

First, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one is able to universally penetrate all pāramitās within a single pāramitā; second, through skillful means, one understands one sentient being and thereby universally understands all sentient beings; third, through skillful means, one realizes the purity of a single dharma and thereby universally realizes the purity of all dharmas; fourth, through skillful means, one comprehends a single Buddha and thereby comprehends all Buddhas.
"Why is this? It is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without differentiation.

When the Buddha had spoken these four Dharma-gates for bodhisattvas, the illusionist Bhadra realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). With a heart filled with exultation, he immediately ascended into the air, his body rising seven *tāla* trees above the ground.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance, emitting immeasurable rays of light from his face. These rays illuminated all the Buddha-worlds and returned to vanish into the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not manifest this smile without cause or condition.
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and questioned him in verse:
“O Honored One of Universal Renown and Omniscience, whose majestic virtue and sphere of knowledge are inconceivable,
who have already reached the shore of the merit of Bodhi— what is the cause for Your present smile?”

The sentient beings of the five destinies throughout the ten directions—whether their mental activities and dispositions be superior, middling, or inferior—the Tathāgata understands them all; for what reason do you now manifest a smile?
The various and wondrous sounds produced by the great assemblies of humans, devas, and the eight classes of beings,
when compared to the pure voice of the Tathāgata, do not equal even a *kalā*— a mere infinitesimal fraction— of it.
The World-Honored One’s radiance pervades the ten directions, Universally illuminating immeasurable Buddha-fields;
The light of the sun, moon, mani jewels, and Brahmā heavens— None can compare to that of the Tathāgata.
Having realized the profound Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, There is no self, no person, and no sentient being;
Having abandoned both extremes of existence and non-existence, One skillfully knows the three periods of time to be like the moon in water.
Who now proceeds toward the Supreme Vehicle, continuing the lineage of the Tathāgata’s Dharma and being born within the vast Triple Gem?
We pray that you will proclaim the causes and conditions for your smile.
The light of the smile manifested by the Tathāgata has distinctions for those of the various vehicles;
that which vanishes at the knees or the shoulders is for those of the two vehicles.
The immeasurable light now emitted enters the crown of the Tathāgata’s head;
who is this supreme among gods, who shall receive the prediction of enlightenment in this Buddha-vehicle?
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see this Bhadrā? He replied:
“I have seen it,” [the youth replied]. The Buddha told Ānanda:

“After ninety-two thousand kalpas have passed, this son of good family shall attain buddhahood in the eon of Good Transformation within the world-realm of Great Adornment; he shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śrīvikrīḍitarāja.”

The people of that Buddha-land are numerous, peaceful, secure, and enjoy abundant prosperity. The ground is level, soft, and supple like *tūla* cotton; rows of trees bearing flowers and fruits stand in orderly succession, adorned with banners, pennants, and precious canopies. Various musical instruments resound spontaneously, and exquisite fragrances pervade everywhere. Whatever food and drink is required arrives as soon as it is thought of, and all the various articles for daily use and sustenance are no different from those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
That land is constantly manifested with various kinds of adornments; therefore, it is called the Land of Great Adornments.
All the people within that country abide in the Mahāyāna with deep and firm faith.
The lifespan of that Tathāgata King of Divine Transformations was ten thousand years, and his True Dharma remained in the world for a full hundred billion years.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Renowned Name the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, declaring:
"In a future age, you shall successively become a Buddha, named Sarvāgra-jina Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha."
When Bhadrayā heard this prediction from the Tathāgata, she descended from the air, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these words:
“I now take refuge in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as in the Dharma and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.”
In this manner, he repeated these words with earnest devotion countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of times.
He further spoke thus:

“Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, because there is no difference in *tathatā* (suchness), has taught that all phenomena are not different from *tathatā*, even to the point that they are without distinction, without deficiency, without conceptual differentiation, and without arising or fabrication.”
"My present taking of refuge is also like this.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to Bhadrapāla:
"If you take refuge in accordance with the True Suchness (tathatā) as taught by the Buddha, do you now perceive anything to be attained within the nature of the Buddha-dharma?"
The illusionist replied:
"My own body is the dharmatā of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
I and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction, for all dharmas are true suchness (*tathatā*).
That which is called "true suchness" is the undifferentiated nature of all dharmas; all sentient beings are likewise so.
Venerable sir, you should know that what is called "non-duality" means the absence of conceptual discrimination;
this is non-duality. Why is this?
Because one thoroughly knows that all phenomena exist merely as names, which is the wisdom of a Buddha.
The Venerable Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
This Bhadrā possesses such wisdom and eloquence."
"In the past, you deluded and confused the world through illusory transformations; now, you again delude and confuse it through wisdom.
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
"O son of good family!"
“Is it truly so? Bhadralā replied,
“Just as the Buddha performs acts of delusion and confusion, I likewise delude and confuse the world.”
Why is this? It is because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of "sentient beings" and "lifespan" within the context of non-self; this is a great delusion in the world.
Just as when a Tathāgata has realized awakening, he does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that comes and goes in birth and death, yet he speaks of coming and going in birth and death;
according to my understanding, it is only the Tathāgata who is a great deluder.
The Buddha said:
"Good man, excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said."

The Tathāgatas, among all Buddhas, abide in non-self and even in the absence of coming and going within birth and death, yet they speak of "sentient beings" and so forth in accordance with worldly convention.
Furthermore, there is not the slightest dharma that can be called "nirvāṇa," yet for the sake of realizing the dharma of nirvāṇa, they speak of nirvāṇa.
When Bhadrapāla had heard this teaching, he came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to leave the household life and become a bhikṣu.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"You should shave this son of good family's hair and beard and confer upon him the full precepts.
Maitreya Bodhisattva, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, immediately granted him the going-forth and conferred the full precepts.
Having already gone forth, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This going forth is merely a matter of outward appearance; it is not true going forth."

If bodhisattvas are truly those who have left the home life, it means they dwell apart from all signs within the triple world to bring sentient beings to maturity; only then can they be called truly having left the home life.
When these words were spoken, five thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all attained liberation of the mind from the outflows (*āsrava*).
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?”
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Dharma Gate of Bestowing the Prediction upon the Magician Bhadra,' and it is also named 'The Dharma Gate of Gradually Realizing Bodhi.'"

If there are sentient beings who, in future ages, wish to see the Tathāgata and perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings, they should receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this sutra to others.
Why is this? Such a person has already seen the Tathāgata and has also performed the Buddha-work for others.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and circulate this sutra act out of compassion to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Furthermore, those who wish to set out toward unsurpassed bodhi should also diligently practice and cultivate this sutra.
This sutra can bring forth unsurpassed bodhi; this sutra can give birth to unsurpassed bodhi. For this reason, this sutra is also named "The Birth of Bodhi."
"If there are those who receive and uphold this sutra, one should know that all Buddhas abide within their bodies; how much more so for those who practice accordingly within it.
Then Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This sutra is also titled "Arousing the Roots of Goodness. Why is this?
Because now, having heard this sutra from the Buddha, all roots of goodness manifest before one.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda and Bhadrapāla, along with the great assembly of devas and humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Five;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
22. The Great Display of Supernatural Powers, Part One of Twenty-Two.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Mañjuśrī and the devaputra Śreṣṭhidāraka were also present in the assembly.
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By how many kinds of supernatural transformations does the Tathāgata constantly discipline sentient beings?”
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"I subdue sentient beings through three kinds of miraculous transformations:
first, the transformation of teaching the Dharma; second, the transformation of instruction and admonition; and third, the transformation of supernormal powers."
What is called the miraculous transformation of preaching the Dharma?

It refers to the Tathāgata’s unimpeded great wisdom, which perceives the differences in the mental activities of all sentient beings in future ages, and fully understands their faith or lack of faith in the Three Jewels, as well as their karma and its retributions.

As the Buddha has taught: if one commits evil deeds in the present life, one shall fall into the evil realms, and the retribution for such karma will be received with absolute certainty and without deviation.

Yet, if those sentient beings, by virtue of the causes and conditions of their wholesome karma and the power of their vows, are born from the evil realms into the human or celestial realms, or attain liberation through the vehicles of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or the Mahāyāna; or if they undergo suffering and experience joy throughout such kalpas until they attain nirvāṇa and encounter various Buddhas—such karmic results are likewise determined and without deviation.

If those sentient beings, by virtue of the causes and conditions of their wholesome karma and the power of their vows, are to be born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, they shall attain liberation through such vehicles after the passage of that many eons; through such practices, they shall behold the Buddhas, serve them, and make offerings to them.

In this way, all wholesome and unwholesome karmas—whether superior, middling, or inferior—even those as brief as a single thought-moment—the Tathāgata fully knows and accordingly preaches the Dharma for them; this is called the miraculous transformation of preaching the Dharma.
What is called the miraculous power of instruction? It is when one instructs those who uphold the precepts in this way:

"This should be done; this should not be done. This should be believed; this should not be believed. This should be associated with; this should not be associated with. These dharmas are defiled; these dharmas are pure. This extends even to the gathering of all the provisions for merit and the path of virtue, such that by practicing such a path one attains the vehicle of the śrāvaka or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and by practicing such a path one accomplishes the Mahāyāna. One should abandon what is contrary to the Dharma and abide in accordance with the Dharma, exactly as taught by the Buddha, without any deviation.

"This is karma for the hells; this is karma for animals; this is karma for hungry ghosts; this is karma for humans and devas. One should abandon what is unwholesome and cultivate wholesome dharmas; this is the Noble Path, and one should train accordingly."
These sentient beings, cycling between the human and celestial realms, gradually enter nirvana; thus, his instruction and teaching never go in vain. This is called the miracle of instruction.
What is called the miracle of supernormal power?

If, for the sake of subduing sentient beings who are arrogant, he manifests a single body as many bodies, or manifests many bodies as a single body; passes unimpeded through mountain precipices and walls; emits fire from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part, or emits fire from the lower part of his body and water from the upper part; enters the earth as if it were water and treads upon water as if it were solid ground; touches the sun and moon with his hand despite their majestic power; or manifests a vast body reaching as far as the Brahma-world, even extending so widely as to cover the entire trichiliocosm.
“Manifesting in accordance with what is appropriate to tame sentient beings— this is called the miraculous transformation of supernormal powers.
At that time, the celestial son Śreṣṭhidatta addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!
"Is there any supernatural power that can surpass this?
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"The Tathāgata possesses yet another supreme supernatural power."
He then said to Mañjuśrī:

“You should expound [the Dharma] so that all bodhisattvas may attain profound dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti) and subdue all Māras, and so that the Tathāgata’s bodhi-dharma may long abide in the world.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the Tathāgata were to place the four great oceans of the trichiliocosm within the palm of his hand, and the sentient beings dwelling in the waters were not disturbed or moved, such a supernatural transformation would not yet be considered extraordinary.”

If the Tathāgata, regarding all phenomena—which are inexpressible, nameless, signless, formless, soundless, without activity, without action, without letters, without conceptual proliferation, without representation, beyond mind, intellect, and consciousness, and which are the cessation of all paths of speech, quiescent and illuminating—were nevertheless to distinguish and reveal them through words and language; [this is the inconceivable power of the Buddha].

That which cannot be understood by any in the world, and which causes shock and terror when heard by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—this is called the greatest supernormal transformation (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, if the Tathāgata were to place the trichiliocosm within his mouth, there would be no obstruction to the four continents; the radiance of the sun and moon would not be obscured and would remain as before, and the sentient beings therein would not perceive the direction or location from which he came or where he went.
“World-Honored One!
Such a supernatural transformation is not yet the most excellent.

If the Tathāgata, regarding all dharmas—which are inexpressible, without letters, without names or marks, even transcending mind, thought, and consciousness, where all paths of language are cut off, and which are quiescent and illuminating—were nevertheless to proclaim and reveal them through letters and speech, this is called the greatest supernatural transformation of all Buddhas.”
Furthermore, by virtue of the supernatural power of the Tathāgata’s unique body, he manifests various forms according to the needs of sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
Such miraculous transformations are not yet considered supreme.

What is called the Great Supernatural Transformation of the Tathāgata refers to: where there is no self, he speaks of a self; where there are no sentient beings, he speaks of sentient beings; where there is no person, he speaks of a person; where there is no nourisher, he speaks of a nourisher; where there is no name, he speaks of a name; where there is no form, he speaks of form; where there are no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, he speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; where there are no bases, he speaks of bases; where there are no elements, he speaks of elements. Although he speaks of the emptiness of the eye, the eye does not say it is empty; although he speaks of the emptiness of forms, forms do not say they are empty; although he speaks of the emptiness of eye-consciousness, consciousness does not say it is empty. This extends likewise to the emptiness of the mind and phenomena, and the emptiness of mind-consciousness, and so forth.

To speak of such dharmas as being nameless and signless, unmoving and unknowing, and beyond words—thereby destroying all marks of arising and ceasing—is the Tathāgata’s greatest supernatural transformation.

Such a supernormal transformation is not associated with the eye, nor with forms, nor with visual consciousness; it is not associated with the ear, sounds, or auditory consciousness; nor with the nose, odors, or olfactory consciousness; nor with the tongue, tastes, or gustatory consciousness; nor with the body, tangibles, or tactile consciousness; nor with the mind, mental objects, or mental consciousness.
Such a spiritual transformation is not conjoined with body nor conjoined with mind; it is without activity or volition, transcending all realms, and is something that the entire world cannot believe.
Why is this? That which is called "the world" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Ordinary persons give rise to false attachments toward these, either asserting that the aggregates are permanent or asserting that they are impermanent.
For this reason, all those in the world who falsely perceive the aggregates as permanent cannot produce faith when hearing that they are impermanent;
those who falsely perceive the aggregates as pleasurable cannot produce faith when hearing that the aggregates are suffering;
and those who falsely perceive the aggregates as a self cannot produce faith when hearing that there is no self.
They falsely perceive the aggregates as pure, and thus cannot give rise to faith when hearing them described as impure;
they reckon the aggregates as "mine," and thus cannot give rise to faith when hearing that there is no "mine";
they reckon the five aggregates as real, and thus cannot give rise to faith when hearing them described as unreal.
For this reason, the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations transcend the characteristics of the mind; those who hear of them do not rejoice, and they cannot be believed by anyone in the world.
Furthermore, because they transcend the realm of the eye and are not material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), they are called supernormal transformations.

Because it transcends the sphere of the ear and is not a phenomenon of sound, and so on, up to transcending the sphere of the mind and being not a phenomenon of the mind; because it cannot be displayed and is not known by ordinary cognition—this is called a supernormal transformation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

Furthermore, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are ineffable; yet to speak of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is called a miraculous transformation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

Arisinglessness, non-action, absence of intrinsic nature, absence of characteristics, non-birth, non-extinction, and primordial nirvāṇa are ineffable; yet to speak of nirvāṇa is called a miraculous transformation.
Furthermore, the purity of giving is called a miraculous transformation because it purifies the three spheres.
What are these three? They are:
being free from the mark of self and the mark of sentient beings; not dwelling on bodhi; and maintaining the purity of ethical discipline. This is called a miraculous transformation.
Because the actions of body, speech, and mind are non-active, the purity of patience is called a miraculous transformation (*ṛddhi*).
Because there is no attachment to momentary destruction, the purity of diligence is called a miraculous transformation.
Because there is no going and no coming, and the body and mind are unmoving, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is pure; this is called a spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*).
Because the mind has no basis and is tranquil both internally and externally, wisdom (*prajñā*) is pure; this is called a spiritual transformation.
It illuminates all phenomena because it extinguishes all views.
Furthermore, that the Dharma, which has no characteristic of emergence, is spoken of as the teaching on liberation—this is called a miraculous manifestation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
That the Dharma is without differentiation, yet is analyzed through words and letters—this is called a miraculous manifestation.
To teach that there is cultivation when phenomena have no activity is called a miraculous manifestation.
To teach that there is coming and going when phenomena have no coming or going is called a miraculous manifestation.
To establish various fruits within the realization of the single path is called a miraculous manifestation.
To differentiate the three vehicles within the Dharma of a single flavor is called a miraculous transformation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
That all Buddhas are in fact only one Buddha, yet they speak of immeasurable Buddhas, is called a miraculous transformation.
All buddha-fields are but a single buddha-field; to speak of immeasurable fields is called a miraculous transformation.
Immeasurable sentient beings are but a single sentient being; to speak of immeasurable sentient beings is called a miraculous transformation.
All Buddha-dharmas are the one Buddha-dharma; to preach immeasurable dharmas is called a miraculous manifestation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
The Dharma cannot be shown, yet to reveal all dharmas is called a miraculous manifestation.
"The non-attainment of dharmas, their cultivation, and their realization—this is called a miraculous transformation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"According to my understanding of the meaning of what you have said, all verbal expressions regarding any dharma are entirely termed miraculous transformations."
Mañjuśrī said: “So it is, so it is.
All verbal expressions are in truth nothing that is expressed; this is called a great supernormal transformation.”

When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and five hundred bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra said to the Devaputra Śreṣṭhin:
“Did you not feel fear or terror upon hearing of this miraculous manifestation?
The Devaputra replied:
“I am myself a manifestation of supernatural power;
why should I be terrified? Śāriputra asked, “With what underlying intention does the devaputra say this?”
The deva said:
“All dharmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, move without moving; this is called the great supernormal transformation (mahā-ṛddhi-prātihārya). Therefore, Śāriputra!...”
Those who perform wholesome deeds are born in the heavens with great majesty and power; such wholesome karma is inconceivable.
The coming and going of all sentient beings within birth and death is likewise inconceivable; that which is inconceivable is called a great supernatural transformation (*mahāvikurvita*).
As the Buddha has taught, there are four kinds of realms that are inconceivable:
first, the inconceivable realm of karma; second, the inconceivable realm of nāgas; third, the inconceivable realm of dhyāna; and fourth, the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas.
For this reason, it is said that all dharmas are called a great supernatural manifestation (*mahāvikurvita*),
and one should not be terrified by them. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if the Tathāgata were to manifest this supernatural power, would the realm of empty space ever feel fear?
He replied, “No. The deva said:
"If space is not afraid, why do you ask, 'Are you not terrified? Śāriputra replied,
"Are you perhaps identical to space?"
The deva said:
"According to what the Buddha has taught, if there is internal emptiness and external emptiness, is this space? He replied:
"So it is," the deva said. "For this reason, all sentient beings are of the nature of space."
Śāriputra said: "O Son of Heaven!
Just as you have spoken, before long you too shall manifest this supernatural transformation."
"Why is this? Because transcending all spheres of experience is a great supernormal transformation.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Devaputra Sārthavāha was able to achieve such eloquence because in the past he made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and Mañjuśrī.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is;
it is as you have said. This is the maturation brought about by Mañjuśrī. Śāriputra!”

In the distant past, beyond immeasurable kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Merusammita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The land is named Sukhāvatī, and the eon is named Pramuditā.
Śāriputra, all sentient beings in that Buddha-world are fully endowed with peace and happiness; there is not even the sound of the slightest suffering or affliction.

That Buddha-land is composed of four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; its ground is as level as the palm of a hand, pure and soft like a celestial garment, and free from all places of hardship.
Devas and humans fill the realm, dwelling in peace, prosperity, and immeasurable bliss; therefore, it is named the World of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

Within that Buddha’s Dharma, there are exclusively Bodhisattvas who possess diligent vigor, courageous energy, and the radiance of wisdom. Having attained the *dhāraṇī* of the King of Sūtras, they possess inexhaustible eloquence and skillful means. Through their analytical preaching, supernatural powers, and wisdom, they crush evil Māras and attain unimpeded liberation. Having perfected meditative concentration and patience, they skillfully discern the faculties and natures of beings to prescribe medicine according to the ailment. Endowed with the vast provisions of merit and wisdom, they serve as uninvited friends to all sentient beings.

By means of supernatural powers, they travel throughout all Buddha-fields, enter the ocean of the practice of wisdom, and abide in generosity, ethical discipline, wisdom, and extensive learning. They skillfully dedicate their boundless roots of goodness and dwell in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all Buddha-dharmas, sporting in samādhis, dhyānas, and liberations.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, has such great bodhisattvas as his retinue.
In that world, there was a wheel-turning king named Pure Adornment (*Vimalavyūha*), who ruled the four continents by means of the True Dharma and possessed the seven treasures in their entirety.
The king had a thousand sons, all of whom resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
King Viśuddhālaṃkāra and his harem likewise had all already resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The lifespan of that Tathāgata Sumeru was seventy koṭis of years; at that time, King Viśuddhālaṃkāra served and made offerings to that Buddha-Tathāgata and the assembly of bodhisattvas for a hundred thousand years, providing them with robes, food and drink, and all manner of articles of pleasure.

The king, along with his thousand sons and his harem, attained pure faith; they loved the Dharma with joy and harbored no other thoughts. Constantly making offerings with their own hands before the Buddha and drawing near to listen to the Dharma for over a hundred thousand years, they passed the time.
At that time, the king’s thousand sons and the women of the inner palace attained the four mindfulnesses. What are these four?
First, mindfulness of the Buddha and bodhisattvas; second, mindfulness of giving; third, mindfulness of precepts; and fourth, not forgetting the mind of enlightenment.
Because he had attained this mindfulness, whether by day or by night, he constantly beheld the Buddha and the various bodhisattvas.
Later, on one occasion, King Pure Adornment and his retinue went to the place where the Buddha was in order to hear the Dharma.
At that time, in order to teach and transform the bodhisattvas, that Tathāgata manifested various kinds of supernatural transformations amidst the great assembly.
Then, King Pure Adornment came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is there any supernatural power that can surpass this? The Buddha told the Great King: "The Tathāgata possesses yet another supreme supernatural power:

namely, the thorough knowledge that the past has already ceased, the present does not abide, and the future has not yet arisen; that he speaks of the mental states and mental factors of the three periods of time despite being devoid of such states and factors; that he teaches the three liberations within a single flavor; that he explains the Four Noble Truths within the realization of a single cessation; that he reveals the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of all phenomena; that he brings to maturity sentient beings who are afflicted by delusions and suffering; and that he proclaims the signless and unconditioned to achieve Bodhi."

The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is taught as neither grasping nor rejecting; the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is taught as non-abiding and non-action; the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is taught as the dharma of selflessness; the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) is taught as the tranquility of body and mind; the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is taught as neither distraction nor concentration; the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is taught as being free from this and that shore. One practices skillful means (*upāya*) without stirring a thought; one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) by being free from the mark of dependence; one cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) through the dharma of non-action; one cultivates joy (*muditā*) by being free from elation; and one cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) through the dharma of non-abiding.

By having nothing seen, one gives rise to the divine eye; by having nothing heard, one gives rise to the divine ear; by having no object of attachment, one gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds; by being detached from the prior limit, one gives rise to the knowledge of past lives; and by the immobility of body and mind, one gives rise to the supernormal power of psychic travel.

One cultivates the foundations of mindfulness without dwelling on phenomena; one cultivates the four right efforts through the absence of arising and ceasing; one speaks of faculties where there are no faculties and speaks of powers where there are no powers; one speaks of the factors of enlightenment regarding the quiescence of all phenomena; one cultivates the eightfold noble path without making distinctions; one cultivates śamatha without dwelling in quiescence; one cultivates vipaśyanā while remaining detached from the marks of phenomena; and one speaks of nirvāṇa as being primordially extinguished.

When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached this Dharma of spiritual transformations for the sake of King Viśuddhālaṃkāra and his retinue of a thousand sons, eighty-four thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

King Viśuddhālaṃkāra and his thousand sons realized the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they immediately praised him before the Buddha with these verses:
“Like Mount Sumeru reflecting upon the great ocean, the Tathāgata’s majestic radiance eclipses the entire assembly.”
Like the sun first rising, destroying all darkness, the mark of the World-Honored One’s hair-tuft shines universally throughout the Buddha-fields.
Like the full moon, its radiance blazing intensely, the Buddha’s virtues are perfected, and the light of his wisdom shines everywhere.
Just as a lotus flower is not defiled by water, so the Buddha dwells in the world without any attachment.
Like a lion king who roars in the forest and wilds, the lion among men roars within the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
To teach that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, causing others to leave behind extreme views— this is called the lion’s roar.
Regarding all marks, whether arising or ceasing, to teach that there is no arising or ceasing—
this is called the lion’s roar.
To distinguish this shore, or to point toward the other shore, yet to dwell in no phenomena—this is called the lion’s roar.
To distinguish between the two marks of defilement and purity, while knowing that the nature of all phenomena is pure—this is called the lion’s roar.
The activities of greed, hatred, and delusion arise from conceptual discrimination; not giving rise to such discrimination is called the lion’s roar.
To teach that the phenomena of birth and death are impermanent and without self, arising from inversion, is called the lion’s roar.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are fundamentally quiescent; this is Great Bodhi, which is called the Lion’s Roar.
To reveal the emptiness of intrinsic nature to those bound by various views and wandering through the world is called the Lion’s Roar.
“The Tathāgata, the Guide, is able to fully reveal all the spiritual transformations he manifests; this is called the Lion’s Roar.
‘Regarding all things favorable or unfavorable, his mind does not waver, but remains ever-abiding in equanimity;
this is called the Patience of Accordance with the Dharma.’”
Following the profound and tranquil Dharma as taught by the Buddha,
yet not realizing it therein, is called the "patience that accords with the Dharma.
It is to remain far removed from all faults and evils, while increasing wholesome qualities.
To have no attachment therein is called the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmakṣānti).
To hear the sound of the emptiness of all phenomena and the sound of all [erroneous] views,
yet to have no attachment to either, is called the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma.
The sounds of the boundless Buddha-dharma and the various sounds of afflictions—
when one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding these sounds, it is called the patience that accords with the Dharma (*anulomikī dharmanidhyānaksānti*).
Regarding generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning, as well as diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom...
To practice in accordance with the Dharma is called the patience that accords with the Dharma.
Not abandoning the bodhicitta, viewing all things with equanimity,
