and purifying the path to enlightenment is called the patience that accords with the Dharma.
The Tathāgata speaks according to his own intent, revealing all the Buddha-dharmas;
to have no doubt or hesitation regarding this is called the "patience that accords with the Dharma.
If I realize bodhi, I shall let out the great lion’s roar.
He expounds this miraculous manifestation, just as the Buddha has now spoken.
Within this inconceivable, unsurpassed, and supreme field of merit, I have already planted the seed; I shall never again turn back.
Even if the great earth were to perish and the vast oceans were entirely to dry up,
the roots of goodness I have planted shall never suffer decline or loss.
Fully understanding the minds of sentient beings, I know their nature to be like space.
Deeply planting the seeds of bodhi, one attains boundless merit and virtue.
As my present aspirations and joys are such that only a Buddha can witness and know them,
there is no one among devas, humans, or gandharvas who can understand them.
I now shall never seek the sublime and wondrous rewards of the devas;
I shall attain wisdom such as that of the Buddha, the Honored One among men.
For hundreds of thousands of years, I have drawn near to and made offerings to the Buddhas.
Because I have set out for enlightenment, I cultivate these boundless deeds.
Now, together with my thousand sons and the retinue of the inner palace,
I vow to constantly make offerings to the Buddha, so as to bring enlightenment to maturity.
I have now attained a sublime benefit, having clearly beheld the Buddhas;
I have well heard this Dharma and take delight in Bodhi.
If one takes delight in Bodhi, then one takes delight in the Dharma.
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, he does not abandon the Buddha-vehicle.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Dharmatvarita, who said to King Viśuddhālaṃkāra:
"Great King!..."
"You do not accord with the Tathāgata’s spiritual transformations, nor have you set out toward unsurpassed bodhi.
Why is this? Great King!"

Bodhi abides in the dharma-realm; it neither comes nor goes, is without cognition or activity, is neither form nor characteristic, and is neither grasped nor abandoned. Like painting upon empty space, it is without contact or obstruction, and its intrinsic nature is pure.
"Great King!
Awakening (bodhi) enters all places because all phenomena are equal.
Awakening is without discrimination because it is free from all marks."
Awakening is quiescent, because it is characterized by cessation.
Awakening is pure by nature, because it is free from conceptual attachment.
Awakening is immovable, because it is without confusion.
"Great King!
'Bodhi' is called the equality of the mind, because it does not arise.
'Bodhi' is called the equality of sentient beings, because they are fundamentally unarisen."
"Bodhi" is named "non-arising arising," because causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature.
Bodhi cannot be displayed, because it is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Great King!
Awakening has no sphere of activity, for it transcends all objective realms.
Awakening is free from conceptual proliferation, for it is devoid of the characteristics of discursive thought.
Awakening is emptiness, for its nature and characteristics are empty.
Awakening is signless, because it is free from all signs.
Awakening is wishless, because there is nothing upon which to dwell.
Awakening is unconditioned, because there is no karmic retribution.
Awakening is unconditioned, for it is free from the three marks.
Great King, such is the nature and characteristic of awakening.
If one harbors any aspiration or seeking regarding this Dharma, one will merely exhaust oneself in vain. Why is this?
Because the nature of bodhi is that which a bodhisattva should practice; to be able to practice in such a manner is called "right practice."
At that time, King Viśuddhālaṃkāra said to the Bodhisattva Dharmataraṇa:
"I pray that you will explain to me the correct practice of a bodhisattva. Dharmataraṇa replied:
“Great King! To relinquish all that one possesses is the practice of a bodhisattva, because sentient beings are equal and without discrimination.
To practice the dhūta ascetic virtues and train in the precepts is the practice of a bodhisattva, because the nature of the precepts is equal and there is nothing to be practiced.”
To be free from the feverish affliction of anger is the practice of a bodhisattva, because the nature of patience is equanimity and devoid of mental characteristics.
To be firm and courageous is the practice of a bodhisattva, because diligence is equanimity and free from mental activity.
Samādhi and liberation are the bodhisattva’s practice, because meditative concentration is equal and without any object of focus.
The provisions for the wisdom of hearing are the bodhisattva’s practice, because the nature of wisdom is equal and without any conceptualization.
To be born in the Brahma-abodes is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they are detached from both defilement and purity as being equal.
To give rise to the various supernormal powers is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they do not give rise to conceptual thoughts regarding the equality of these powers.
To possess eloquence is the bodhisattva practice, for it is the equality of the Dharma and its meaning, being free from the characteristics of the mind.
To achieve resolute conviction is the bodhisattva practice, for the dharmadhātu is equal and immovable.
Cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they contemplate equality without indolence.
Arising the four means of integration is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they treat all phenomena as equal and identical.
To maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings is the practice of a bodhisattva, for the nature of the mind is equal and free from discrimination.
To adorn the buddha-fields is the practice of a bodhisattva, for they are pure, equal, and like space.
The thirty-two marks are the practice of a bodhisattva, for they contemplate the signlessness of phenomena and enter into equanimity.
Purifying body, speech, and mind is the practice of a bodhisattva, for they are free from the nature of the three karmas and abide in equality.
Rejoicing in sentient beings is the practice of a bodhisattva, because all sentient beings are equal in their selflessness.
Not wearying of birth and death is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they understand that its nature is equal to a dream.
Constantly cultivating wholesome karma is the practice of a bodhisattva, for they know that karma is equal and devoid of karmic retribution.
Firmly engaging in cultivation is the practice of a bodhisattva, for they contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations.
To endure all sufferings is the practice of a bodhisattva, because by realizing the equality [of all things], suffering does not arise.
To associate with virtuous friends is the practice of a bodhisattva, because the mind maintains equanimity toward both friends and non-friends.
Diligently cultivating the profound mind is the practice of a bodhisattva, for its fruition is equanimity and free from seeking.
Being insatiable in extensive learning is the practice of a bodhisattva, for both preaching the Dharma and listening to it are equal.
The practice of a bodhisattva is the non-attachment to dharmas, because they teach the Dharma with equanimity and without seeking anything for themselves.
The practice of a bodhisattva is the upholding of the true Dharma, because they bring all Buddha-dharmas to maturity with equanimity.
Constantly seeking true wisdom is the practice of a bodhisattva, because the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is equality.
Humbling one’s mind is the practice of a bodhisattva, because of maintaining an equanimous mind that humbles itself toward all sentient beings.
“Universally encompassing all virtuous merits is the practice of a bodhisattva, because such merit is equal and free from conceptualization.

At that time, King Pure Adornment, having heard this exposition of the various practices of bodhisattvas, leaped for joy with rapture and affection; he immediately removed his garments and ornaments and gave them to the Bodhisattva Swift as the Dharma.
At that time, the king’s thousand sons also each removed their own ornaments and offered them to the Bodhisattva, saying these words:
"May all sentient beings accomplish the conduct of a bodhisattva and attain such eloquence."
"We have now gained a great and wholesome benefit, having been able to see such a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and to pay him respectful offerings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Swift-Traveler said to King Pure Adornment:
"The offerings you have made are quite inferior; you should know that there are also superior forms of offering."
Then the Bodhisattva Dharmatara uttered these verses:
“If all sentient beings in the great trichiliocosm were to set out for enlightenment,
and even if one were to offer them as gifts— both men and women— for an entire eon;”
If a person resolves upon the path to enlightenment, leaves the household life out of faith,
and practices in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings, their merit shall surpass that of others.
Throughout the worlds of the past and the future, for all the Tathāgatas—
There is no one who, without abandoning the household life, Can achieve the unsurpassed path.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time Praise the dharma of leaving home.
If you delight in making offerings to the Buddha, You should follow the Buddha and leave the household life.
Even if one were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with precious jewels to offer to the Buddha,
it would not equal a single day of leaving the household life to cultivate tranquility;
such a person draws near to Bodhi and utterly destroys the hosts of Māra’s army.
For one who has gone forth and is heedful, the pure dharmas constantly increase.

Without destroying the various roots of goodness and remaining far removed from all afflictions, they abandon the burdens of domestic life; thus following the Path, they are praised by the Noble Ones.

"Having renounced the home and abandoned the bonds of affliction, having removed affliction and escaped the fetters of Māra, with a liberated mind acting without defilement, one will realize Bodhi before long.
At that time, King Pure Ornament, having heard this verse, completely relinquished his sovereign throne and all desires; he then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to leave the household life and receive the precepts within the Buddha’s excellent Dharma and Vinaya.
At that time, the Tathāgata Equal to Mount Sumeru replied:
"Great King! I have always exhorted and praised the state of homelessness as being free from affliction, whereas attachment to the household life is not what I sanction.
If you still harbor affection for the royal throne, I shall instruct you on how to abide in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, King Viśuddhālaṃkāra addressed his thousand sons, saying:
"Which of you is able to succeed to the royal enterprise?
All the sons replied:
"We also wish to leave the household life; we pray that you will grant us your permission.
The Father King replied, "If all of you were to leave the household life, who would nurture the people of these four continents?"
"If you all possess firm and resolute great compassion, you should become kings and cause all sentient beings everywhere to dwell securely in wholesome dharmas.
At that time, among the thousand sons, there was a prince named Mindful of Great Compassion, who replied to his father the king in verse:
"O Father King, regarding the various merits You have attained within the Buddha-dharma..."
Out of compassion, I have accepted the royal throne; I shall likewise train in this way.
I will constantly practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and observe the eight precepts for as long as I live.
I shall not drink alcohol, nor shall I apply ointments or adorn myself with incense and flowers.
He removed his bodily ornaments, did not lie upon a golden couch,
and did not tread upon golden sandals; he did not adorn his head with a jeweled crown,
nor did he wear celestial, exquisite garments, nor did he gaze upon various performances of music and dance.
He did not dally with strange birds or beasts, nor did he follow after the women of the palace.
He traveled throughout the four continents, proclaiming and practicing the ten paths of wholesome action;
he rebuked the faults and afflictions of the household life and praised the Dharma of renunciation.
Abandoning the pride of self-mastery, drawing near to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
never retreating from the bodhicitta, and always feeling weary of the triple world;
through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and shared purpose, one gathers in sentient beings.
May all beings throughout the Great Vehicle Attain complete maturity.
Six times throughout the day and night, I shall go to the presence of the Buddha To hear the Dharma And make offerings to that Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata Equal to Mount Sumeru praised Prince Mahākaruṇācintin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"

Because you perceive the equality of all phenomena, you abide in great compassion and the right faith of renunciation; as such, you are most excellent among lay bodhisattvas, being equal and no different from those who have gone forth.

At that time, King Pure Adornment immediately established Nian Daibi as his successor to the throne and, together with nine hundred and ninety-nine princes, left the household life to follow the Buddha.

Having gone forth, the Tathāgata Sameru taught him such dharmas of spiritual transformation; before long, he attained the five supernormal powers, as well as mindfulness, dhāraṇī, and the wisdom of great learning.

At that time, mindful of great compassion, he received the position of empowerment on the fifteenth day, and likewise used this Dharma to proclaim and instruct all sentient beings throughout the four continents.

Ninety-two koṭis of sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all of whom went forth from home to practice the Way within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Samasumeru, abiding in the Mahāyāna and attaining non-retrogression.
Śāriputra! Observe these dharmas of immeasurable merit, which bring to maturity all sentient beings who possess roots of goodness. Śāriputra!
Was that King Pure Adornment anyone else?
He is none other than the present-day Son of Heaven, Merchant Leader (Śreṣṭhidāra).
As for the Bodhisattva Dharmavega, he is the present-day Mañjuśrī.
Those thousand sons are the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa.
As for the Prince Mahākaruṇācintin, he was my own self. Śāriputra!
"Because these bodhisattvas practice with a profound mind, correct conduct, and heedfulness, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When he spoke this account of the dharma of past cultivation, thirty-two thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, “Virtuous One,
you and the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta have long cultivated the holy life, made many offerings to the Buddhas, and planted various roots of goodness.”
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable sir!

That which is called 'holy conduct' (brahmacarya) is the Eightfold Noble Path; it is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛtadharma). I, however, am unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); therefore, I do not practice holy conduct for long."
Now, the so-called "practice of the holy life" (brahmacarya) is defined as having something to practice; I have nothing to practice, and for this reason, I have not long practiced the holy life.
Furthermore, the practice of the holy life is characterized by duality; I am without duality, and for this reason, I have not long practiced the holy life.

Furthermore, the "holy life" (brahmacarya) is called the extinction of afflictions; since I have no afflictions, there is nothing to be extinguished, and for this reason I do not practice the holy life for long.
To race after the five desires is what is called the holy life; as for me, I have never engaged in the five desires from the beginning, and for this reason I do not practice the holy life for long.
To transcend the path of Māra is called the Brahma-faring; I constantly abide within all paths of Māra, therefore I have not long practiced the Brahma-faring.
To accomplish wholesome dharmas is called the Brahma-faring; I have attained nothing at all regarding either good or evil, therefore I have not long practiced the Brahma-faring.
The correct station where Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas abide is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*); I have no realization therein, and for this reason I have not long practiced the holy life.
Cultivating the path to Nirvāṇa is called the holy life; I have no aspiration or seeking for Nirvāṇa, and for this reason I have not long practiced the holy life.
Furthermore, Śāriputra! Regarding what you said—
that you have made many offerings to the Buddha—
do you consider that the Tathāgata can be offered to?
Why is this so? The Tathāgata is not form and is invisible; how, then, can one make offerings to the Tathāgata? The Tathāgata is not sensation, having stilled all sensations;

the Tathāgata is not perception, being free from all fetters; the Tathāgata is not mental formations, being ultimately without volitional activity; the Tathāgata is not consciousness, having transcended mind and intellect. How, then, can one make offerings to the Tathāgata?

Furthermore, the Tathāgata walks in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, not within the realm of eye and form; he dwells at the limit of signlessness, not within the realm of ear and sound; he is detached from dualistic characteristics, not within the realm of nose and fragrance; he has no characteristic that can be known, not within the realm of tongue and taste; he has no characteristic of obstruction, not within the realm of body and touch; he enters into equality, not within the realm of mind and phenomena. How, then, can one make offerings to the Tathāgata?

Furthermore, the Tathāgata is called the Dharma-realm; he is named Suchness (Tathatā). He has entered the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), dwells in great emptiness, is immovable in his fundamental nature, has severed all conceptual proliferation (prapañca), and is without any object of attachment. He does not abide in consciousness, nor does he rely on the three realms; he likewise does not dwell in this world or future worlds. He is eternally quiescent and supremely tranquil, detached from body, speech, and mind, formless and signless, beyond praise or blame, without outflows and without loss. Just as space pervades all places, how can one possibly make offerings to the Tathāgata?
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Regarding the planting of various roots of goodness as you have described, these roots of goodness are not the root of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), nor the roots of greed and hatred, nor the roots of inversion, nor the roots of the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the seven stations of consciousness, nor the roots of the eightfold wrong path, the nine afflictions, or the ten unwholesome paths of action.

Those roots of goodness are not the root of training in morality, nor the root of training in concentration, nor the root of training in wisdom; they are not the root of the right path, nor the root of clear knowledge and liberation; they are not the root of the Four Truths and the six supernormal powers, nor the nine successive meditative attainments and the ten roots of one beyond training; they are not the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the root of the Eightfold Noble Path.

Furthermore, these roots of goodness are not the roots of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), nor the roots of hindrances, nor the roots of regret (*kaukṛtya*), nor the roots of views of arising and ceasing, nor the roots of views of annihilationism and eternalism. They are not the roots of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-sustainer. Nor are they the roots of the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*), or the celestial demon (*devaputramāra*).

Those roots of goodness are not the root of false conceptualization, nor the root of ignorance, nor the roots of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, and affliction.

Those roots of goodness are not the roots of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they are not the roots of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom; they are not the roots of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity; nor are they the roots realized by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The roots of merit of a bodhisattva are as follows: the root of omniscience in which the mind dwells nowhere; the root of neither self-agency nor other-agency;
the root of patience and self-mastery; the root that adorns body, speech, and mind; the root of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
the root that brings all sentient beings to maturity; the root that embraces all dharmas; and the root of accomplishment.
The root of all Buddha-dharmas; the root that ensures the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed; the root of relinquishing all possessions without seeking karmic retribution;
the root of accumulating manifold virtues without seeking the status of Śakra or Brahmā; the root of exerting great diligence without delighting in the Lesser Vehicle;
the root of practicing meditative concentration without attachment to its flavor; and the practice of wisdom through non-relinquishment.
The faculty of the roots; the faculty of cultivating skillful means regarding all pervasive conditioned phenomena; the faculty of being endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses;
the faculty of attaining dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence; the faculty of acquiring supernormal powers and purifying buddha-fields;
and the faculty of proceeding to the tree of enlightenment and turning the wheel of Dharma.

When Mañjuśrī had thus spoken these three kinds of definitive meanings, the entire great assembly all exclaimed, “Excellent! They scattered various flowers over the World-Honored One and upon Mañjuśrī, saying:
“If there were no Mañjuśrī within a buddha-field, a Buddha would not appear in the world.”
Were it not for Mañjuśrī, one could not bring to maturity the vast roots of goodness of all sentient beings.

If there are those who hear the Dharma-gate taught by Mañjuśrī and are neither startled nor alarmed, they will remain far removed from all demonic activities and obstacles, attaining pure radiance within this Mahāyāna.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta amidst the great assembly:
"Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said."
“Son of Heaven!
Having heard the miraculous transformations described by Mañjuśrī, you are able to understand other miraculous transformations as well, without further alarm or fear. Why is this? Because—”

That which causes great terror to all the world is as follows: to speak of the perception of impermanence within the perception of permanence; to speak of the perception of suffering within the perception of pleasure; to speak of the perception of non-self within the perception of self; to speak of the perception of impurity within the perception of purity; to speak of the perception of non-existence within the perception of existence; to speak of the perception of emptiness among various views; to speak of the perception of non-conceptualization within the perception of tranquility; to speak of the perception of wishlessness within the triple realm; and to speak of the perception of non-attachment regarding "self" and "what belongs to self."
If one is neither startled nor terrified by this, it is called abiding in right discipline.
Why is this? If one gives rise to alarm or fear, one will be unable to receive and uphold these teachings—namely, because of attachment to a self and what belongs to a self.
If there is no attachment, then there is no dwelling; if there is no dwelling, then there is no movement; if there is no movement, then there is no coming or going;
if there is no coming or going, then there is nothing received; if there is nothing received, then there is nothing grasped;
if there is nothing grasped, then there is no inversion; if there is no inversion, then there is no false view; if there is no false view—
Then there is no right faith; without right faith, there is no right view; without right view, there is no right concentration; without right concentration, there is no distracted mind;
without a distracted mind, there is no place of abiding; without a place of abiding, there is no establishment;
without establishment, there is no characteristic of consciousness; and without the characteristic of consciousness, there is no conceptualization.
Without discursive thought, there is nothing to be attained; without attainment, there is no objective clinging; without objective clinging, there is no discrimination;
without discrimination, one does not perceive self or other; because one does not perceive self or other, there is no continuity;
because there is no continuity, there is no feverish affliction; because there is no feverish affliction, there is no vexation.
Because the cause of affliction—the causes of mental distress—is absent, one attains the vision of light; because one sees the light, one attains wisdom;
because one attains wisdom, one attains a vast mind; because one attains a vast mind, Māra finds no opportunity;
because one subdues Māra, there is no obstruction; and because there is no obstruction, one realizes the first [fruit] before one's eyes.
All Buddha-dharmas.
Thus, O Son of Heaven!
To reveal and expound that all dharmas are without arising and without action—this is what is called the great supernormal transformation.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Regarding what I have asked, do you, O Noble One, speak entirely through secret meaning? Mañjuśrī replied:

“Śāriputra! All dharmas are established as provisional names through the aggregation of syllables; these syllables are inexhaustible and are spoken according to one’s inclination. One should understand that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature, as is appropriate.”
Śāriputra! All dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature; they are without accumulation and without anything perceived. They are merely expounded according to one's inclinations and as is appropriate.
Furthermore, these dharmas come from nowhere and go nowhere; they do not abide in any direction nor are they separate from any direction; they have no gathering and no dispersal.

If one were to explain all Buddha-dharmas and all sentient beings' dharmas by means of words and letters, they do not emerge from the body nor do they emerge from the mind; they arise from causes and conditions.
Just as those syllables have no accumulation, so too the mind and mental factors have no accumulation.
Just as the mind and mental factors have no accumulation, all afflictions and hindrances likewise have no accumulation.
Just as afflictions have no accumulation because they are obstructions, wisdom likewise has nothing to accumulate.
Therefore, both afflictions and wisdom are to be relinquished, for neither afflictions nor wisdom abide anywhere.
"This is what is called 'expounding the great supernormal transformation.
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"What is the wisdom of a bodhisattva?"
Mañjuśrī said: "The knowledge of suffering is so called because it does not weary of the aggregates;
the knowledge of origination is so called because it accumulates roots of goodness."
The knowledge of cessation reveals that there is arising;
the knowledge of the path brings about departure from the evil realms;
the knowledge of causes ensures that what has been accomplished is indestructible.
The wisdom of conditions, because it severs birth and death;
the Buddha-wisdom, because it causes entry into realization;
the wisdom of dependent origination, because it is free from attachment.
Knowledge of the aggregates, because it eliminates the māra of the aggregates;
knowledge of the elements, because the dharma-realm is equal;
knowledge of the sense bases, because one skillfully contemplates them as empty villages.
The wisdom of giving, because there is no such thing as an improper time;
the wisdom of precepts, because it gathers in those who have broken the precepts;
the wisdom of patience, because it protects sentient beings.
The wisdom of diligence, because it performs wholesome karma;
the wisdom of meditative concentration, because it does not depart from a concentrated mind;
the wisdom of wisdom, because it thoroughly understands all phenomena.
The wisdom of skillful means, for the sake of maturing sentient beings;
the wisdom of loving-kindness, for the sake of uprooting all states of existence;
the wisdom of compassion, because it is free from weariness.
The wisdom of joy, because of delighting in the Dharma;
the wisdom of equanimity, because of accomplishing the Buddha-dharmas;
the wisdom of observation, because of abiding in the foundations of mindfulness.
The wisdom of right effort, because it accords with equality;
the wisdom of the bases of spiritual power, because they are devoid of functional activity;
the wisdom of the faculties and powers of faith, because they are free from all attachment.
The wisdom of the faculty and power of diligence is for the sake of crushing and destroying all afflictions.
The wisdom of the faculty and power of mindfulness is for the sake of not losing mindfulness.
The wisdom of the faculty and power of concentration is for the sake of the equality of all phenomena.
The wisdom of the faculty of discernment (*prajñendriya*) is the knowledge of the natures of all faculties.
The wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) is because of spontaneous awakening.
The wisdom of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is because it uproots all evil destinies.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because its roots of goodness are inexhaustible;
the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), because one has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*);
and the knowledge of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛtijñāna*), because one has accomplished the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*).
The wisdom of mindfulness of the Dharma, because it turns the wheel of the Dharma;
the wisdom of mindfulness of the Sangha, because it enters into the assembly of equality;
the wisdom of mindfulness of relinquishment, because it does not abandon any sentient being.
The wisdom of mindfulness of the precepts, because it fulfills all vows;
the wisdom of mindfulness of the heavens, because it is free from all evils;
the wisdom of the faculties of sentient beings, because it thoroughly understands the immeasurable.
The wisdom of fulfillment, because there is no deficiency in ethical discipline;
the wisdom of the medicine for sentient beings, because it accords with reality as it is;
the wisdom of what is possible and what is impossible, because one does not perceive [inherent] possibility.
The wisdom of the ten powers, because it encompasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
the wisdom of fearlessness, because it thoroughly understands what constitutes an obstacle and what does not;
and the unimpeded wisdom regarding the past, because it is free from attachment.
Unimpeded knowledge of the future world, because all phenomena have no destination;
unimpeded knowledge of the present world, because there is no abiding;
and the knowledge of the infinite bodies received by all sentient beings, because they arise from speech.
The wisdom that discerns the differences in the vocal expressions of all sentient beings arises from the mind;
it is the wisdom that can fully comprehend the movements of the minds of all sentient beings;
it is the faultless wisdom that thoroughly understands the faults of all sentient beings.
The wisdom that is free from violence, because it can pacify all forms of strife and contention;
the wisdom that does not lose mindfulness, because it establishes sentient beings with distracted minds in tranquility;
and the wisdom that gathers in sentient beings, because it gathers in those who are indolent.
The Buddha’s unique wisdom knows that which should be transformed;
his great wisdom of skillful means relies upon prajñā.
O Son of Heaven!
"This is called the wisdom of all bodhisattvas.
By means of this wisdom, one shall attain the unimpeded great wisdom of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How rare, how rare!
This wisdom of the bodhisattva is the most preeminent within the three realms; it cannot be accomplished through meager adornments."
If one can give rise to such wisdom, it constitutes a great supernormal transformation. Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva become fully adorned with this Dharma?
Mañjuśrī said: "O Son of Heaven!
If, upon hearing that all sentient beings are primordially quiescent, one does not give rise to alarm or fear, this is called a bodhisattva being fully adorned."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! What is meant by the term ‘bodhisattva’?”
He replied, "If one practices for enlightenment while abiding nowhere, this is called a bodhisattva.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'Mahāsattva'? He replied:
"One who has transcended all conditioned phenomena and perfected great wisdom is a Mahāsattva."
He asked again:
"In what sense are they called 'superior beings'? He replied:
"Because of wisdom, they do not cling to phenomena; because of the power of skillful means, they gather in all beings. For this reason, they are called 'superior beings.
" He asked again:
"What is meant by 'pure beings'?"

He replied: "Because they do not dwell with any afflictions and because they give rise to great diligence in order to eliminate the disease of afflictions in sentient beings, they are called pure sentient beings."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'extremely pure sentient beings'? He replied:
"If one cultivates the factors of the path purely in order to deliver all sentient beings, this is called 'a most pure sentient being.
He asked again:
"How is it that a bodhisattva acts as a guide for the world?"
He replied: "One who is able to abide securely in the path they practice and brings immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to maturity is called a guide.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva abiding in subjugation? He replied:
"If, regarding those sentient beings who ought to be subjugated, one is able to cause them to abide in ultimate subjugation, this is called subjugation."
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain valor? He replied:
"If one can bring all sentient beings to maturity, crushing the enmity of Māra and causing them to emerge from birth and death, this is called 'valiance.
He asked again:
"In what way is a bodhisattva difficult to thwart?"
He replied: "If one can fulfill former vows and does not seek the realization of the paths of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is called a bodhisattva who is difficult to thwart."
He asked again:
"In what way does a bodhisattva excel beyond all? He replied:
“By means of wisdom and skillful means, one protects and upholds the True Dharma and brings sentient beings to maturity; all devas and humans look up to him with reverence—this is called ‘excellence.
He asked again:
“How does one preach the Dharma?”
He replied: "To destroy all various heterodox arguments in accordance with what the Buddha has taught—this is called preaching the Dharma.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'expounding the Vinaya'? He replied:
"To abide oneself in the precepts and to be able to sever the afflictions and evil karma of sentient beings—this is called expounding the Vinaya."
He asked again:
"How does one fully accomplish the benefit of sentient beings? He replied:
"To dedicate all accumulated roots of goodness to all beings is called being fully endowed with the benefit of sentient beings.
He asked again:
"What is the straightforward mind?"
He replied, "I do not give rise to anger or obstruction toward sentient beings who are greedy, hateful, deluded,
or deceitful. He asked again:
"What is meant by 'being without guile'?
He replied: "It is that what one says is truthful."
He asked again:
"How does one become free from deception? He replied:
"Reflect carefully before you speak.
He asked again:
"How does one abandon pride?"
He replied, "It is to not give rise to arrogance toward any sentient being.
He asked again:
"What is the great gift? He replied:
"To give even the unsurpassed enlightenment, which is accumulated with difficulty and is hard to attain, to sentient beings—how much more so all the material things of the world!"
He asked again:
"What is meant by being endowed with ethical discipline? He replied:
"Even at the cost of one's life, one shall never abandon the bodhicitta.
He asked again: "What is patience?"
He replied: "One who can endure oppression and does not oppress or afflict others.
He asked again:
"What is diligence? He replied:
"To discern all phenomena, finding nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended."
He asked again:
"What is meditative concentration? He replied:
“I do not see the realm of desire.
He asked again: “What is wisdom?”
He replied, "There is no discrimination.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'abiding in loving-kindness'? He replied:
"To contemplate that the realm of sentient beings is empty and devoid of anything whatsoever."
“How does one abide in compassion? He replied:
“Knowing that all phenomena are empty, yet not relinquishing diligence.”
“What is dwelling in joy? He replied:
“Dwelling in great tranquil bliss while seeking the Dharma without weariness.”
“What is dwelling in equanimity? He replied:
“Being unstained by worldly dharmas, one is able to rescue the world.”
“What is the purity of the body? He replied:
“It is the body born according to one’s will, manifested equally for all sentient beings.”
“What is purity of speech? He replied:
“Whatever Dharma one preaches never goes to waste; it is able to fully satisfy all sentient beings.”
“What is purity of mind? He replied:
“To be able to fully comprehend all the mental thoughts of all sentient beings within a single moment of mind.”
“What is the divine eye? He replied:
“It is the ability to see all forms, appearances, and radiances without any attachment.”
"What is the divine ear? He replied:
"Hearing all sounds while remaining detached from the characteristics of sound."
“What is the knowledge of others' minds?
He replied: “It is the thorough understanding of the arising, ceasing, and continuous flow of all mental states.”
“What is the knowledge of past lives? He replied:
“It is to know the prior limit without moving from the reality-limit.”
"What are the supernormal powers? He replied:
"They are the unmoving activities that crush and destroy all māras."
“What is meant by ‘subduing’? He replied,
“It is the ability to subdue all that is difficult to subdue.”
“What is meant by ‘protection’? He replied:
“It is not being disturbed or distracted by the sense faculties.”
“What is meant by ‘being well-tamed’? He replied:
“That which cannot be moved by any phenomena.”
“What is tranquility? He replied:
“To dwell amidst the fires of affliction without being burned by them, and to expound the Dharma for those who have crossed over the afflictions.”
“What is pure faith? He replied:
“If it is said that the Buddha’s body is a phenomenon of material form (rūpa-lakṣaṇa), one ultimately does not believe or accept it, and is not corrupted by it.”
“What is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva? He replied:
“If one perceives that the faults of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings are equal to awakening (*bodhi*), this is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva.”

When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
"One who is well able to expound the practices of all bodhisattvas has already encompassed all the immeasurable merits of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta said to Mañjuśrī,
"How many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, did you venerate and make offerings to in the past to obtain such eloquence?"
Mañjuśrī said: "It is, for example, like a person created by illusion whose mental activities have already ceased.
The deva asked:
"If even the mental characteristics of sentient beings cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be the extinction of a mind for an illusory person? He replied:
"The nature and characteristics of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are thus; it is by relying on this Dharma that I make offerings to the Tathāgatas."
The deva asked,
"Virtuous one, how long has it been since you began practicing the dānapāramitā? He replied:
“If a person created by a Buddha were asked, ‘How long or how recently have you practiced the dānapāramitā?
how would you answer? The deva replied, “There is no answer to be given.”
Mañjuśrī said: "I am also like this. Why do you ask about the duration or proximity of my practice?"
The deva asked,
"Do you abide in stinginess? He replied:
"So it is. He asked again, "What do you think?"
He replied, "I do not abandon the Buddha-dharma or all sentient beings; for this reason, I am stingy.
The deva said:
"If the meaning spoken by Mañjuśrī is as you say, does it also constitute breaking the precepts? He replied, "It is so."
The deva asked, "What do you think? He replied:
"One who breaks the precepts falls into the evil realms; because I enter the evil realms for the sake of liberating suffering sentient beings, it is called 'breaking the precepts.
He asked again:
"Did you give rise to a harmful mind?"
He replied, "So it is. The deva said:
"What do you think? He replied:
"One who possesses a harmful mind is called one who lacks loving-kindness."
"I have no affection whatsoever for afflictions or for the two vehicles; therefore, it is called a 'harming mind.
He asked again, "Are you indolent?"
He replied, “It is so. He asked again:
"What do you think? He replied, "I do not initiate actions of body, speech, or mind; I have nothing to pursue, neither grasping nor rejecting. Therefore, it is called indolence."
He asked again, "Are you distracted? He replied:
"So it is," the deva said. "What do you think?"
He replied, "As for what is called 'distraction,' does it not mean that the mind of liberation does not abide?
The deva said:
"So it is," he replied. "Because I do not abide in liberation for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, it is called a 'distracted mind'."
He asked again,
"Are you without wisdom? He replied:
"So it is. He asked again: "What do you think?"
He replied, "Indeed, those who lack wisdom are like the ignorant and deluded; they do not fear birth and death—is this not so?
The deva said:

"So it is," he replied. "I am neither startled nor terrified by birth and death; because I wish to bring deluded sentient beings to maturity, I engage in their same activities, and for this reason I am called 'one without wisdom.'"
The deva asked,
"Are you one who is worthy of offerings by the world? He replied:
"I harbor no thought of killing toward any living being.
He asked again, "What do you think?"
He replied, "Because I have destroyed greed, hatred, and delusion, I am one worthy of offerings by the world.
The deva said:
"What you have said will cause all the world to be utterly terrified.
He replied, "O Devaputra!"
If the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is terrified, then the world is terrified. Why is this?
Because the entire world is itself the reality-limit.
He asked again:
"If there were someone who slanders and disparages this teaching, where would they go? He replied:
"When one attains nirvana.
He asked again, "In what sense?"
He replied: "In the noble liberation there are no words; therefore, by transcending verbal expression, one attains nirvana.
For this reason, all dharmas are primordially liberated and do not need to be liberated again."
He asked again,
"What is the meaning of this? He replied:
"Is one who is already liberated to be liberated yet again?
He asked further:
"Does one who slanders the True Dharma not enter hell?"
He replied, "If one is already liberated, they are free from all defilements; how then could they go to hell?
The deva said:
“Mañjuśrī! As you have said, there is no one who provides praise or assistance. He replied:
"What is praised and supported within emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
He asked again:
"In what should one who practices emptiness abide?"
He replied: "One should abide in loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Why is that? Because..."
“Sentient beings are like illusions, for their intrinsic nature is empty. The deva said, “Mañjuśrī!
"How does one thoroughly understand the realm of all sentient beings? He replied:
"One sees that all sentient beings arise from causes and conditions, being neither annihilated nor eternal; therefore, one universally knows the realm of sentient beings."
He asked again:
"What is the meaning of 'the realm of sentient beings'? He replied:
“The realm of sentient beings is itself the dharma-realm.
He asked again:
“What is the dharma-realm?”
He replied, "The realm of self-nature emptiness is called the dharma-realm.
He asked again:
"What is called the space element? He replied,
"That which transcends all objective spheres is the space element."
He asked again:
"What is that which transcends the realms? He replied:
"This is the realm of the Buddha.
He asked again,
"What is meant by the realm of the Buddha?"
He replied: "The eye-element is the Buddha’s sphere; yet the Buddha’s sphere is not the sphere of the eye, nor of visible forms, nor of eye-consciousness.
The ear-element is the Buddha’s sphere; yet the Buddha’s sphere is not the sphere of the ear, nor of sounds, nor of ear-consciousness."
Even the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is the realm of the Buddha, yet the realm of the Buddha is not the realm of the mind, mental objects, or mental consciousness.
The form-element (*rūpadhātu*) is the realm of the Buddha, yet the realm of the Buddha is not the realm of form.
The realms of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the Buddha’s realm; yet the Buddha’s realm is not the realm of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The realm of ignorance is the Buddha’s realm; yet the Buddha’s realm is not the realm of ignorance.
Even the realm of old age, sickness, and death is the Buddha’s sphere; yet the Buddha’s sphere is not the sphere of old age, sickness, and death.
The desire realm is the Buddha’s sphere, because it is characterized by the absence of greed.
The realm of form is the Buddha’s sphere, because it is not a state of opposition that eliminates greed.
The formless realm is the Buddha’s sphere, because it is not a state of non-seeing due to ignorance.
The unconditioned realm is the Buddha’s sphere, because it is free from dualistic characteristics.
The conditioned realm is the Buddha’s sphere of activity, for it is not characterized by the three marks.
O Son of Heaven!
This is called the Buddha’s sphere of activity.
Such a realm enters all realms, encompassing both the finite and the infinite.
Because the bodhisattva skillfully enters this realm, they constantly traverse all realms within the world while transcending the realm of Māra.
To understand the Buddha-realm and the Mara-realm as they truly are—tranquil and equal—is called the greatest supernatural manifestation (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva does not abide in equality, yet brings sentient beings to maturity through the dharma of equality.
What is meant by equality and non-equality?
All phenomena are empty and quiescent by their very nature; to realize this is called abiding in equality.
To be unable to enter into the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena is called non-equality.
The Bodhisattva brings such sentient beings to maturity, yet does not abide even in the equality of emptiness.

All phenomena are equal in being wishless, equal in being unconditioned, equal in being unborn, equal in being unceasing, equal in being free from defilement, equal in being quiescent, equal in being without intrinsic nature, equal in cessation, and equal in nirvāṇa.
Because they do not fully comprehend this dharma of equality, the bodhisattva brings such sentient beings to maturity, yet does not dwell in equality either.
Therefore, that the bodhisattva neither dwells in equality nor departs from equality is the practice of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Devaputra Sārthavāha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"I pray that you will explain for me the practices of all bodhisattvas. Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
The practice of a bodhisattva is inconceivable.
The Son of Heaven said:
“How does a bodhisattva practice that which is inconceivable? Mañjuśrī replied,
“The practice of desire is the bodhisattva’s practice, because desire is inconceivable.”
The practice of anger is the bodhisattva practice, because anger is inconceivable.
The practice of delusion is the bodhisattva practice, because delusion is inconceivable.
Stinginess is the bodhisattva practice, because there is no notion of giving.
Not violating the precepts is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they do not grasp at the characteristics of the precepts.
Not being resentful or harmful is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they have no notion of patience.
Not being indolent is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they are free from the conceptualization of diligence.
Non-distraction is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they do not abide in meditative concentration.
Freedom from delusion is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they do not form the notion of "wisdom.
Absence of afflictions is the practice of a bodhisattva, because there is nothing to be abandoned.
Freedom from craving is the bodhisattva’s practice, for it is free from the perception of a self-body.
A mind of compassion is the bodhisattva’s practice, for it relinquishes the affection felt toward women.
Freedom from defilement is the bodhisattva’s practice, for it censures the five desires.
To remain free from unrighteousness is the practice of a bodhisattva, because it accumulates roots of goodness.
To be without stinginess is the practice of a bodhisattva, because it involves the relinquishing of body and life.
To extinguish all evils is the practice of a bodhisattva, because it is free from feverish affliction.
To be without attachment is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they are free from the pleasant and the unpleasant.
To be indestructible is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they correctly contemplate afflictions.
To be without fear is the practice of a bodhisattva, because they enter into boundless saṃsāra.
Great diligence is the practice of a bodhisattva, for it bears the burden of all sentient beings.
Non-retrogression is the practice of a bodhisattva, for it brings to fulfillment former vows.
The practice of all jewels is the bodhisattva practice, because it encompasses the Three Jewels.
All practices are the bodhisattva practice, because they diligently cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Non-obstruction is the bodhisattva practice, because it is free from the two extremes.
Being free from fault is the bodhisattva practice, for it is praised by the wise.
Abiding in a settled mind is the bodhisattva practice, for it involves mindfulness of all sentient beings.
Being without discrimination is the bodhisattva practice, for it involves viewing all things with equality.
Being a virtuous man is the bodhisattva practice, because of bearing the burden without weariness.
Being courageous is the bodhisattva practice, because of crushing and destroying all afflictions.
Being firm is the bodhisattva practice, because of not abandoning what has been undertaken midway.
Surpassing is the bodhisattva practice, because of being diligent and non-retrogressive.
Accordance is the bodhisattva practice, because of having no opposition toward one's companions.
Rejoicing is the bodhisattva practice, because of causing those who commit evil to rejoice.
Faithful joy is the bodhisattva practice, because one delights in seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and serving the teacher.
The adamantine armor is the bodhisattva practice, because one does not violate the code of discipline.
Adorning the Buddha-fields is the practice of a bodhisattva, because it purifies the mind.
Transcending all things is the practice of a bodhisattva, because it enters the Supreme Vehicle.
Knowing gratitude and repaying kindness is the practice of a bodhisattva, because it ensures that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
"Wisdom and skillful means are the practice of a bodhisattva, because they gather and sustain [beings] without interruption.
When this bodhisattva practice was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Devaputra Sārthavāha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How wonderful! You have excellently expounded this bodhisattva practice."
"If bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, they have already received the Tathāgata’s prediction of enlightenment.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."
When I formerly attained this practice, the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me a prophecy.
At that time, I attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas; this is called the Tathāgata’s greatest supernatural transformation.
"Only those who have long accomplished pure karma are able to cultivate this bodhisattva practice.
At that time, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by 'non-arising'?
How should one attain this patience regarding non-arising?
The Buddha said:
"Regarding 'non-arising,' it is not that something first arose and was later said to be non-arising; rather, because it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning, it is called non-arising.
It is not that something first originated and was later said to be non-originated; rather, because it is fundamentally unoriginated from the beginning, it is called non-originated."

It is not that there were previously characteristics which were later said to be non-characteristic; rather, because they are fundamentally without characteristics, they are called "non-characteristic.
It is not that there was previously activity which was later said to be non-activity; rather, because they are inherently without activity, they are called "non-activity."
It is not that sentient beings existed first and emptiness was taught afterward; rather, because the nature of sentient beings is empty, they are said to be empty.
To understand in this way that there is neither arising nor ceasing and that there is fundamentally nothing defiled is called "non-arising."
What is patience? To thus accept that all sentient beings and all buddha-lands are fundamentally unarisen—this is called patience.
To thus accept that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are fundamentally unarisen—this is called patience.
To thus accept and affirm that all bodhisattvas and all buddhas are fundamentally unarisen is called "patience.
To thus accept and affirm that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen is called "patience."

"O Son of Heaven! Because all phenomena are unarisen, they are empty moment by moment. Because they are empty moment by moment, they are called signless. Because they are signless moment by moment, form is empty moment by moment. Because form is empty moment by moment, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty moment by moment. Because consciousness is empty moment by moment, the elements are empty moment by moment. Because the elements are empty moment by moment, the sense bases are empty moment by moment."

If a moment is empty, then there is nothing whatsoever; because there is nothing whatsoever, there is no defilement; because there is no defilement, there is detachment from intrinsic nature; and because there is detachment from intrinsic nature, this is called the primordial quiescence of all phenomena.
To be able to endure in this way and enter into equanimity is what is called attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and receiving the prediction of enlightenment.
One who attains this patience has nothing to be attained.
What is meant by "one who has attainment"?
To perceive the two marks of self and what belongs to the self as attainable is called having attainment.
To perceive the two marks of sentient beings and a life-principle—as well as the nourisher, the person, and the individual—as attainable is called having attainment.
What is meant by "non-apprehension"?
To perceive the nature of self and the nature of "mine" as being understood to be non-dual is called non-apprehension; this is what is meant by the accomplishment of patience (*kṣānti*).
"O Son of Heaven!
When a Bodhisattva practices this patience throughout incalculable eons, it is called the Tathāgata’s greatest supernatural manifestation.

As he spoke these words on patience, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great light shone everywhere throughout all worlds; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; and a rain of various exquisite flowers fell from the void.
Forty-two thousand sentient beings all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and ninety thousand bodhisattvas attained the *anulomika-dharma-kṣānti*.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, this Sahā world became exactly like it was when Dīpaṃkara Buddha entered the Lotus City, without any difference whatsoever.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light of various colors issued from his mouth, illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds up to the Brahma realm; the radiance of the sun and moon was no longer visible, and the light circled the Buddha three times before returning and entering the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“I ask the One Adorned with Light, whose radiance is peerless,
Who has shattered the darkness of all afflictions— For what cause and condition do you smile?”
Having crushed the hosts of Māra’s enemies and subdued all the heterodox teachers, I ask the One of Ten Powers: for what reason do you manifest a smile?
The Tathāgata’s exquisite form is endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Venerated by those in the ten directions, for what cause and condition do you smile?
You are an ocean of wisdom and a tree of insight; you guide and lead all living beings.
Your merit is boundless—by what cause do you manifest this smile?
Your fame pervades the three periods of time; free from defilement, you possess the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*).
Having already crossed over to the three liberations (*vimokṣa*), for what reason do you manifest a smile?
O King of Physicians who destroys birth and death, your feet are endowed with the wheels and rims (*cakrāṅka*).
The vajra-body is indestructible; for what cause and condition do you smile?
Who is able to possess such patience?
Who cultivates these pure practices, aspiring to seek the merits of a Buddha?
Because of this, the Honored One has smiled;
what the Teacher has manifested must surely have a cause and condition.
How excellent that you now proclaim with the Brahma-voice, causing all the assembly to rejoice!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“When I taught this Dharma-gate, seventy-two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-kṣānti*).”
"Ānanda! Do you see this Devaputra, the Merchant Leader? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, indeed, I have seen it,” he replied. The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
This Devaputra Sārthavāha has already made offerings to countless Buddhas and has inspired immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Ānanda! After three hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, this Devaputra Śreṣṭhin will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Guṇarājaprabhāsa.
The land is named Pure and the eon is named Stainless.
That realm is composed entirely of the seven treasures; its ground is as level as the palm of a hand, with eight-stepped pathways covered by jeweled nets and adorned in various ways.
In that buddha-field, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor for other outsiders such as the Lekas, Pārilas, or Vyāsas.
There are no demonic activities that destroy the true Dharma, nor is there the sound of the eight difficulties or any voices of unlawful suffering.
Whatever food or drink they think of, it appears spontaneously.
The clothing and precious playthings of the sentient beings in that land are like those of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Their bodies are all golden in color and possess the thirty-two marks; they abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, it is called the Pure World.
The lifespan of that Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabha is forty minor kalpas.
Within his Buddha-dharma, there are sixty-two koṭis of bodhisattvas who, by the power of their vows, enter parinirvāṇa along with the Buddha.

Ānanda! If there are bodhisattvas who resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and attain such forbearance as this, they shall all be born in pure worlds and receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabhāsa.
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Avalokita, who scattered celestial māndārava flowers over the Tathāgata and spoke these words:

“When the Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabhāsa attains the Unsurpassed Way, I shall be born in that pure world as a Cakravartin King. There, I shall serve and make offerings to that Buddha, the World-Honored One, and to the assembly of bodhisattvas; subsequently, I shall succeed him upon the Buddha’s seat and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Prince Vicāra shall become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) within the Dharma of that Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabhāsa, and his name shall be Sudarśana."

Having reverently made offerings to that Buddha-Tathāgata with immeasurable articles of worship, and having fully perfected the factors conducive to enlightenment, you shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in that land, and be known by the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhāsa*).
Ānanda! After King Sudarśana had installed his eldest son to succeed him on the throne, he went forth from home to practice the path under that Buddha.
When that World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bestowed a prophecy upon him:
"This Bodhisattva Sudarśana shall, after my parinirvāṇa, next attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having bestowed this prediction, the Buddha entered nirvana.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta,
"The Tathāgata has already bestowed upon you the prediction of enlightenment.
The devaputra replied:
“Venerable One! Just as a person created by the Buddha is given a prediction [of enlightenment], so too am I.
Just as the nature of suchness neither increases nor decreases, the Tathāgata’s prediction likewise has no increase or decrease.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive, uphold, and widely proclaim this Dharma-gate for the benefit and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings, and for the sake of gathering in all future bodhisattvas."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have received it upon the crown of my head.”
"What should it be named?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is titled 'The Exposition of Great Miraculous Transformations,' and it is also titled 'The Secret Words Spoken by Mañjuśrī,' and it is also titled 'The Questions of the Devaputra Śreṣṭhidatta'; you should uphold it thus."
Ānanda! If a son or daughter of good family can believe in, accept, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra for others, they will have already encompassed all meritorious virtues.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, along with the other bhikṣus, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhin, and immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya nayuta devaputras; Mañjuśrī and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds in the ten directions who had gathered there; and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Translated by Prince Śrutavarman of Ujjayinī during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
23. The Assembly of Mahākāśyapa, Part One of Twenty-Three.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great community of five thousand bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Their names were:

the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Guṇakaraṇḍa, and the Bodhisattva Maitreya; these and other such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas served as the leaders.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly of hundreds of thousands who paid him respectful homage as he preached the Dharma.

Then, Mahākāśyapa, being among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I wish to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha a few questions; if the Buddha grants permission, I shall venture to inquire.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Ask whatever you wish."
“The Tathāgata is fully able to analyze this for you, severing your doubts and causing you to attain joy.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to seek nirvana and go forth into homelessness within the True Dharma, how should they train?
How should they practice?
How should they cultivate contemplation?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!”
You have now skillfully questioned the Tathāgata on such a matter as this.
Your inquiry is for the benefit of all devas and people of the world, so that they may attain peace and happiness.
"Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"So be it. I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“Sons and daughters of good family who seek nirvana and have gone forth in the true Dharma should train in the pure precepts; they should be endowed with the morality of restraint and the teachings of the true Dharma, and they should train thus so as not to transgress even the most subtle points of the pure precepts.”

They accord with the True Dharma and are free from a deceitful mind; they remain far removed from greed and are fully possessed of shame and remorse; they always stand in awe of birth and death, joyfully seeking seclusion, feeling weary of and detached from the cycle of existence, and constantly mindful of Nirvana.

Whether beneath a tree, among mountain crags, in a quiet chamber, or within a cave, when first cultivating right intention, one should bring to mind the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavat—one who is born with a perfected lineage, perfected roots of goodness, and perfected immeasurable pure precepts, immeasurable samādhis, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable liberations, and immeasurable knowledge and vision of liberation; one who is perfected in all the inconceivable, boundless qualities of a Buddha, and perfected in peerless and limitless merit.
He speaks words of truth and speaks words of reality; what he says is non-dual and does not deceive sentient beings.

He is a great king of physicians who can extract the poisoned arrow; he is an uninvited friend endowed with great compassion; he is a great guide who teaches the most profound Dharma to lead others into the profound, and teaches the Dharma of quiescence so that they may attain quiescence.

It is empty and devoid of sentient beings; signless and having severed signs; wishless and detached from wishes; free from conceptual proliferation and having abandoned all conceptual proliferations—profound, difficult to see, and difficult to awaken to.
Its nature is remote and detached, transcending both existence and non-existence; it is without activity and has severed all formations, without speech and is free from discourse.
It is signless and equal, stainless and pure, without grasping or abandoning; it can extinguish all suffering and sever craving, leading one to nirvana.
“Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu such as this, whether for a single day or more than a day, while staying in a quiet chamber, should bring the Tathāgata to mind and reflect thus:
‘I have obtained a human body, I have entered the path of renunciation, and I have received the dharma of a bhikṣu; having drawn near to the Tathāgata, I must not be indolent.’”
Why is this? By practicing the precepts in this way, one shall attain the fruits of the Path.
For this reason, in future ages, if a Buddha appears in the world, one shall behold that Buddha; for a Buddha’s appearance in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower.
“Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu practicing the path should train in the practice of the Venerable Subhūti, whose life is wisdom. Kāśyapa!”
It is rare to behold or hear of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is even more extraordinary to go forth in the True Dharma and be fully endowed with the bhikṣu precepts.
Noble sons and noble daughters who leave the household life within the True Dharma do so for two reasons. What are these two?
First, to attain the fruits of the Path in the present; second, to behold the Buddhas of the future.
Kāśyapa! There are certain deluded people who, while wearing the kāṣāya, oppose the Tathāgata, yet claim of themselves: "I have attained the fruit of the Way and am a noble one (ārya).
Whether in a quiet chamber or within a cave, such a person harbors covetous thoughts, thinking:
Thinking, "All these donors have given me robes and bowls," he reflects:
"The Tathāgata does not know me, does not perceive me, and does not see me."

"Kāśyapa! Whether a bhikṣu is in a quiet room, or within a cave, whether walking, sitting, or lying down, if he gives rise to thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of malice, or various other kinds of evil discursive thoughts."
In whatever place they dwell, the deities therein, knowing those bhikṣus, will feel sorrow and distress in their hearts, thinking:
"These bhikṣus act contrary to the Dharma and what is appropriate."
"Having gone forth within the True Dharma, he contemplates such unwholesome dharmas as these.
Kāśyapa! Those deities, knowing that bhikṣu, each employ expedient means to cause him to be ill at ease.

Kāśyapa! If those celestial deities, by means of meager roots of goodness, attain meager wisdom and yet can still know the minds of others, how much more so the Tathāgata, who has fully practiced wisdom for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas?
Kāśyapa! There is nothing the Tathāgata does not know, nothing he does not see, nothing he does not awaken to, and nothing he does not realize. Kāśyapa!
The Tathāgata is endowed with unimpeded wisdom and fully understands all phenomena of the three periods of time. Therefore, Kāśyapa,
a son or daughter of good family who has gone forth into homelessness within the True Dharma should form this thought:
"All the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, fully know my mind; the present Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions also know my mind. Do not act as a thief among the śramaṇas within the Buddha-dharma."
“Kāśyapa! What is meant by a ‘thief of the śramaṇas’?
There are four kinds of thieves of the śramaṇas.”
What are these four? Kāśyapa!

If there is a bhikṣu who wears the Dharma robes with proper decorum, yet acts like a semblance of a bhikṣu while violating the prohibitions and performing unwholesome deeds, this is called the first thief among śramaṇas.
Second, when after sunset one contemplates unwholesome dharmas with the mind; this is called the second thief among śramaṇas.

Third, having not attained the fruit of sainthood, yet knowing oneself to be an ordinary person, one falsely claims to have attained the fruit of arhatship for the sake of gain and offerings; this is called the third thief among śramaṇas.
Fourth, praising oneself and disparaging others; this is called the fourth thief among śramaṇas.
Kāśyapa! These are the four kinds of thieves among śramaṇas.

Kāśyapa! It is as if there were a person of great power who, regarding all the precious treasures of the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa—such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, coral, and amber—were to inflict harm with swords and staves and seize them all.
Kāśyapa! What do you think? Would this person’s transgression not be considered great?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there is an ordinary person who has not yet attained the fruit of sainthood and knows himself to be an ordinary person, yet for the sake of gain and offerings claims, 'I have attained the fruit of a srotāpanna,' and accepts even a single meal, his transgression is greater than that."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

Regarding this Dharma of discipline taught by the Tathāgata, who, upon hearing this Dharma and not yet having attained the fruit of sainthood, would claim to have realized the Path and accept a single cup of water?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.
Those who wish to transcend birth and death should practice in this way, as if their very heads were on fire."

Kāśyapa! Suppose there is another person who possesses great physical strength and seizes all the necessities for sustaining the bodies of sentient beings throughout the four continents, using blades and clubs to take them away entirely.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
On account of this act of robbery, would that person incur much demerit?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
“Very many,
Sugata! The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

"If an ordinary person who has not yet attained the fruit of a noble one, for the sake of gain and offerings, falsely claims, 'I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin,' and accepts a gift of a single meal, their transgression is greater than that."

Kāśyapa! Suppose there were a person who, within a thousand worlds, were to plunder all the necessities of life for all sentient beings—including gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, conch shells, amber, coral, and various kinds of precious gems; priceless garments, vehicles, palaces, and utensils for food and drink; as well as seizing their swords and staves used for inflicting harm.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Based on the causes and conditions of such karmic injury throughout those kalpas, would that person not incur a great deal of demerit?
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
“Very many,
Sugata! The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there are sentient beings who have not yet attained the fruits of sainthood and know themselves to be ordinary worldlings, yet for the sake of gain and offerings falsely claim, 'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin,' and thereby receive the faithful offerings of others—even as much as a single meal—their transgression is greater than that."

Kāśyapa! Suppose there is another person endowed with great physical strength who, within a medium chiliocosm, seizes and robs all the means of enjoyment belonging to all sentient beings—whether devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans—and inflicts harm upon them with swords and staves.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
By reason of such acts of harm, would that person incur much demerit?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
“Very many,
Sugata! The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there are sentient beings who have not yet attained the fruits of sainthood and, knowing themselves to be ordinary worldlings, falsely claim for the sake of gain and offerings that they have attained the fruit of Arhatship, and thereby receive the faithful offerings of others—even if only a single meal—their transgression is greater than that."

Kāśyapa! It would be better to deprive all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm of every means of enjoyment than to falsely claim for oneself that one has attained the fruits of holiness and accept the faithful offerings of others, even as much as a single meal.
Kāśyapa! In my observation of the dharmas of the śramaṇas, there is no offense more grave than falsely claiming to have attained the fruits of holiness. Kāśyapa!
Śrāvakas have four kinds of evil desires. What are the four?

First, seeking to see the Buddhas of future ages; second, seeking to become a universal monarch (cakravartin); third, wishing to be born into a great kṣatriya clan; and fourth, wishing to be born into a great brāhmaṇa clan.
These are called the four kinds of evil desires.
Even to have a seeking for anything up to and including nirvana is called evil desire; this is what is known as the Tathāgata’s secret teaching.
Kāśyapa! There are four types of dispositions among śrāvakas that must never be engaged in at any time or on any occasion.
What are these four?
First, attachment to a self; second, attachment to a person; third, violating the precepts; and fourth, seeking the Buddha-dharma for the sake of future lives.
These four types of dispositions are things that a śrāvaka should never, at any time or in any circumstance, engage in.
Kāśyapa! If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain pure precepts, I shall preach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to them; I never preach it to those people of evil desires.
For those who uphold the precepts, whose minds are free from flattery and crookedness, and who seek nirvana, I speak this so that they may find peace and security.
