Kāśyapa! I shall now speak further, so that all practitioners, having heard it, may rejoice.

Kāśyapa! Suppose there were another person who, for one kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, were to provide all manner of articles of pleasure as offerings to all sentient beings throughout the four continents.
Kāśyapa! If there should be another person who offers a single vessel of water to one who maintains the precepts and lives by right livelihood,
the merit obtained by that son or daughter of good family will surpass the former gift immeasurably and boundlessly.
Kāśyapa! If such a person of evil desires receives offerings from others, they cause greater harm to people than all other wicked friends or enemies. Kāśyapa!
For those who have left the household life, there are furthermore four kinds of subtle afflictions.
To be possessed of these afflictions is like entering hell while carrying a heavy burden.
What are these four?

First, seeing others obtain benefit, one gives rise to envy in the heart; second, hearing the sūtras and prohibitions, one instead violates them; third, contravening the Buddha’s words, one conceals them and does not repent; fourth, knowing for oneself that one has violated the precepts, yet one accepts the offerings of the faithful.
Kāśyapa! These are called the four kinds of subtle afflictions.
If a person who has left the household life possesses these afflictions, it is as if they were entering hell while carrying a heavy burden.
Kāśyapa! There are four kinds of pseudo-śramaṇas. What are the four?
First, immoral conduct; second, the view of self; third, slandering the true Dharma; and fourth, the view of nihilism.
These are called the four types of pseudo-śramaṇas.
Kāśyapa! There are four forms of negligence for those who have left the household life that lead them into hell. What are these four?
First is negligence due to extensive learning, wherein one becomes negligent by relying on one's own extensive learning.
Second is negligence due to gain and offerings, wherein one becomes negligent because of obtaining gain and offerings.
Third is negligence regarding friends and associates, wherein one becomes negligent by relying upon and depending on friends and associates.
Fourth is negligence regarding ascetic practices (*dhūta*), wherein one exalts oneself and disparages others based on one's own adherence to ascetic practices.
These are called the four kinds of negligence. Kāśyapa!
A renunciant who possesses these four forms of negligence will fall into hell.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, there will be semblance śramaṇas who, though wearing the kāṣāya robe upon their bodies, will destroy the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi cultivated and accumulated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"Do not ask such a question of the Tathāgata. Why is this?"
Kāśyapa! Although those foolish people truly possess faults and evils, the Tathāgata does not speak of them.
Because of their evil desires, their minds falsely cling to perverse conduct and deviousness, and they believe in and accept all demonic activities.
"That foolish person truly has faults and evils, yet the Tathāgata does not speak of them.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will remain long in this world to preach the Dharma for me.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The Tathāgata shall soon enter parinirvāṇa."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the World-Honored One will remain in the world for one kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, to protect and preserve the True Dharma.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:

"As for those foolish people, even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world and teach and transform them through various supernatural powers and discourses on the Dharma, they would still be unable to cause those evil desires to cease."

Kāśyapa! In the future final age, during the last five hundred years, there will be sentient beings who are fully endowed with roots of goodness and whose minds are pure; they will be able to repay the Buddha’s kindness and protect my Dharma.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I would rather carry upon my head all sentient beings, mountains, rivers, stone walls, cities, towns, and villages of the four great continents for an entire kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, than hear the voice of those foolish sentient beings who lack faith.”
"World-Honored One!
I would rather sit upon a single sesame seed for a full kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, than hear the voice of those faithless, deluded people who violate the precepts."
“World-Honored One!

I would rather remain within the great kalpa-fire for hundreds of thousands of billions of years—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—than hear the voice of those faithless, deluded people who violate the precepts.”

"Bhagavān! I would rather endure all manner of anger, abuse, beatings, and injuries inflicted by all sentient beings than hear the voices of those faithless, deluded people—thieves of the Dharma and great violators of the precepts."
"Bhagavān! I have practiced but a little and my wisdom is shallow; I am unable to bear such a heavy burden, Bhagavān!"
Only a bodhisattva is capable of bearing such a heavy burden.
World-Honored One,
I wish to speak a parable regarding this matter.
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person, aged and extremely old, one hundred and twenty years of age, whose body was afflicted by a long-standing disease of goiter, lying upon a bed and unable to rise or move.
At that time, another person who was immensely wealthy and possessed of abundant riches took precious treasures and went to the sick man’s dwelling, saying to him:”
"I have a matter requiring my presence in another land.
I entrust these jewels to you; please guard them for me.
Whether I return in ten years or twenty, wait until my return, and you shall restore them to me."
That old man lay ill upon his bed, having no children and being all alone.

Not long after that person had departed, the sick man’s condition grew critical and he passed away; the wealth he had entrusted was entirely lost and scattered, so that when the traveler returned, he could find nothing of it to claim.
World-Honored One!
It is the same for the śrāvakas: their wisdom is slight and shallow, their practice is minimal, and they lack companions; thus, they cannot remain long in this world.
"If the True Dharma is entrusted [to others], it will not long remain before it disperses and perishes.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Kāśyapa! I have already understood this and have intentionally entrusted it to you, so that when those deluded people hear it, they will give rise to a sense of remorse.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to speak a second parable.
World-Honored One!”

For example, suppose there is a person whose physical strength is robust and flourishing, free from all ailments and suffering, and devoid of every disease; whose lifespan lasts for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years; who is born into a great lineage and possesses abundant wealth and treasures; who well maintains pure precepts, possesses great compassion, harbors joy within, and is able to relinquish the afflictions of all sentient beings.
His mind was courageous, benefiting many people and bringing them peace and happiness, as well as benefiting devas and humans.
At that time, a certain person came to him carrying precious goods and said to him:
"I have some business to attend to and must go to another land."
I entrust these precious seals to you; you must guard them well.
Whether it be ten years or twenty years, wait for my return and then restore the seals to me.
"Suppose that person obtains a treasure trove and guards it; when that person returns from his journey, he immediately restores it [to the owner].
World-Honored One!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: if they entrust the Dharma-treasure to other Bodhisattvas, it will never be lost or destroyed throughout immeasurable thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas. They will benefit immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, the Wheel of Dharma is not interrupted, and the Jewel of the Sangha remains complete."
"World-Honored One!
I am unable to uphold such matters; only a bodhisattva is able to endure and receive them.
World-Honored One!"

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is present here in this assembly; the Tathāgata entrusts him with the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which he has accumulated over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, so that in the future age during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, he may fully protect, propagate, and extensively expound it.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya shall, in a future age, realize the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of a Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!

It is like a king’s eldest crown prince who, having received the consecration and ascended the throne, shall attend to the affairs of state and rule the world according to the Dharma; all the king’s ministers will then come to pay him homage and submit to his authority.
“World-Honored One!
Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva shall likewise do so, governing the throne of the Dharma King and protecting the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mahākāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right hand—which possessed a subtle, golden radiance accumulated through roots of goodness over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and whose fingers and palms were the color of a lotus—and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya.
He spoke these words: "Maitreya! I entrust you with this:

in the future final age, during the last five hundred years when the True Dharma is perishing, you must protect the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and ensure that they are not severed."
At that time, when the Tathāgata extended his golden hand and stroked the crown of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s head, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and its radiance filled the entire trichiliocosm.
At that time, the devas of the earth and the devas of the sky, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, all joined their palms and addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, saying:
"The Tathāgata has entrusted the Dharma to the Noble One; we pray that the Noble One will accept this True Dharma for the benefit of all devas and humans."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For the sake of benefiting even a single sentient being, I would still endure suffering for immeasurable billions of kalpas; how much more so, then, when the Tathāgata has entrusted me with the True Dharma—how could I possibly not accept it?
World-Honored One!
I now receive and uphold [this teaching], and shall expound upon it in future ages the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi accumulated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
When Maitreya Bodhisattva had spoken these words, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
One should not give rise to contentious debate or overweening pride toward other sentient beings. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
One who performs the task correctly means one who protects the true Dharma.
World-Honored One!
If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot bear the heavy burden of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Maitreya!"
Just as you today stand before me and utter the lion’s roar, upholding and protecting the True Dharma of the Tathāgata,
so too did the great bodhisattvas before the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, likewise utter the lion’s roar and protect the True Dharma.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that the World-Honored One will explain how, in future ages, there will be those who are foolish and ignorant, who call themselves bodhisattvas and call themselves śramaṇas, yet for the sake of fame and profit, they harass and disturb donors, spiritual friends, and their own kinsmen.”
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain his faults and evils. Why is this?
If the World-Honored One explains his faults and evils, once I have heard them, I shall restrain my own mind and conduct.
"That foolish person, upon hearing what the Tathāgata has said, may gain faith and understanding, thinking: 'The Tathāgata knows me; the Tathāgata awakens me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya, saying: "Excellent!"
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain for you the faults of those deluded people. Maitreya!
In the future final age, during the last five hundred years, there will be sentient beings who claim for themselves, "I am a bodhisattva."
I shall now declare those various evil desires.
Maitreya, one who possesses four qualities claims for himself to be a bodhisattva.
What are the four? First, seeking gain and offerings; second, seeking fame and reputation; third, flattery and crookedness; and fourth, wrong livelihood. Maitreya!
"By possessing these four dharmas, one calls oneself a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, there will be those who call themselves bodhisattvas while practicing the ways of dogs."

Maitreya! It is like a dog that has first gone to another's house; seeing another dog coming after it, it gives rise to anger and jealousy and barks at it with a snarl, while in its inner mind it conceives the thought, "This is my home."
The Buddha told Maitreya:
“In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, it shall be just the same.

There will be those who call themselves bodhisattvas yet practice the ways of dogs; when they enter the homes of other donors, they conceive the thought that it is their own home, and having given rise to this thought, they immediately develop greedy attachment.”

Having previously gone to another's house and seen a later-arriving bhikṣu, he stared at him with glaring eyes, giving rise to jealousy and anger; he then instigated a quarrel and slandered one another, saying:
"The bhikṣu so-and-so has such-and-such faults."
"Such-and-such a bhikṣu has such-and-such faults.
You must not associate with that bhikṣu.
If you associate with that bhikṣu, you will be despised by all people and will increase the defilement of your transgressions."
Such a person gives rise to envy in their heart; they perform the causes for rebirth as a hungry ghost and the causes for poverty and low status.
For the sake of their own livelihood, they falsely claim themselves to be Bodhisattvas.

For the sake of food and clothing, they praise the wisdom and merit of the Tathāgata to inspire faith in other sentient beings, while internally they themselves violate the precepts and engage in evil desires and misconduct.
The Buddha told Maitreya: "Observe the future world, where there will be such great terrors.

A lion should roar the lion’s roar and perform the lion’s deeds; it should not howl like a jackal and perform the jackal’s deeds. One should praise those who can relinquish all wealth, yet one is stingy oneself and cannot abandon greed; one should praise compassion, yet one practices anger oneself; one should praise patience, yet one practices impatience oneself; one should praise the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), yet one cannot practice giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation oneself. There is only talk, but one cannot learn or delight in the bodhisattva practice of diligence."

“Maitreya! In the past, immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Jñānottara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
“Maitreya! That Buddha appeared in an age of the five turbidities.

At that time, within the Buddha’s Dharma, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Raticandra (Joyful Diligence), who was fully endowed with mindfulness and wisdom. Having few desires and being content, he followed the teachings of the Tathāgata; he traveled through various villages and towns to preach the Dharma for others, and was known to, respected, and venerated by kings, ministers, and all the people.”
At that time, when that bhikṣu wished to enter a city or town, he would first observe for himself; if he expected to receive respect, kind words, and praise, only then would he enter the city.
Furthermore, he might travel to places of wrong views and lack of faith, where he would not receive kind speech or offerings, but would instead encounter only anger, abuse, and physical assault.
And that bhikṣu, donned in the armor of patience, dwells securely in great compassion without abandoning sentient beings; he neither gives way to anger nor gives rise to a mind of regret. Maitreya!
"All the sentient beings transformed by the Bodhisattva Delightful Diligence have become bhikṣus who act as donors, offering robes, food, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"What do you think?"
"At that time, would those bhikṣus not go to other households?
Would there be any jealousy?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Maitreya:

“Observe the Bodhisattva Delight in Diligence’s heart of altruism: with few desires and contentment, he observes with great compassion, refraining from entering cities or villages where he cannot obtain food.”
He converts those with wrong views to become donors (*dānapati*) for other bhikṣus, never again entering [their homes].
He transforms regions of wrong views and lack of faith, causing them to attain right faith; even when met with anger, beating, or abuse, his mind feels no resentment.
Thus it is, Maitreya!
In past ages, the great bodhisattvas entered villages and towns to transform sentient beings, not for their own livelihood. Maitreya!
Do not view this otherwise.
At that time, was the Bodhisattva Delighting in Diligence anyone else? It was I myself.
Maitreya! Therefore, if a bodhisattva enters a village or town wishing to transform sentient beings, they should train in the manner of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Delighting in Diligence.
Furthermore, they should train in the practices of other great bodhisattvas; do not train in the ways of dogs.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, there will be bhikṣus who call themselves bodhisattvas; for the sake of food and clothing they enter villages, not entering villages to transform sentient beings, but only for the sake of wealth and goods, mutually slandering one another."
One rejoices when one gains for oneself, yet feels sorrow, anxiety, and anger when seeing others gain.
One gives rise to sorrow and anxiety when one seeks something but does not obtain it, yet gives rise to joy when seeing others fail to obtain it.
Maitreya! Observe how that person is thus inverted.
For the sake of the bodhisattva dharma, all articles of enjoyment should be completely relinquished to all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because, out of a heart of great compassion, he has made vast vows so that all sentient beings may fully attain happiness. Maitreya!
For example, suppose an elder or householder has an only son who is handsome in appearance, respectful and obedient to his father’s commands, and whom he loves most dearly.
Due to some minor circumstance, the son is imprisoned.
At that time, his father heard of this and personally entered the prison.
Maitreya, what do you think?
"For what purpose has this householder entered the prison?
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"For the sake of seeing his son, he enters the prison to seek release and liberation.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"What is called a 'prison' is none other than birth and death."
The elder householder is a metaphor for all bodhisattvas.
The term "only son" refers to how all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard all sentient beings as they would their own only child.
"Maitreya! Just as that elder or householder enters a prison out of compassion to see his son and rescue him, so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
he enters a village not for the sake of food, drink, clothing, or bedding, but to transform sentient beings and enable them to attain liberation."
The Buddha told Maitreya:

“In the future final age, during the last five hundred years, there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate the mind, do not cultivate ethical discipline, and do not cultivate wisdom.”
"Those bhikṣus enter villages carrying various incenses and flowers as gifts for others in order to seek clothing, bedding, food, and drink.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"It is not the way of a bhikṣu to engage in such lowly occupations and enter villages and towns."

If you enter a village or town, you should do so for the sake of seeking the Dharma and seeking virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra). Do not harbor flattery or crookedness; do not give rise to arrogance. You should speak only of the Dharma; do not speak of worldly affairs, nor of the joys, sorrows, gains, or losses regarding fields and houses; do not speak of matters concerning kings or bandits, nor of cities, towns, villages, or military matters; do not speak of the marriages and social gatherings of men and women. You should speak only of the Dharma—praising the merits of the Buddha, extolling the True Dharma, and praising the Noble Sangha—and discourse upon the dharmas of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"Suppose there were precious jewels and articles of pleasure filling a trichiliocosm, and some sons or daughters of good family were to give these precious jewels and articles of pleasure as gifts to all sentient beings."
If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of others, explain even a single four-line verse so that they may hear it,
the merit obtained by those good sons or good daughters will surpass the former merit by an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"Observe, Maitreya, that this bhikṣu’s entry into the village brings great benefit."
If you enter a city or town, do not distance yourself from praising the Triple Gem or discussing worldly affairs.
Why is this, Maitreya?

If gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, agate, coral, and various other jewels, as well as all manner of musical instruments, cannot cause people to be free from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; [then what need is there to mention other things?]

Maitreya! Only the True Dharma can bring great benefit, liberating one from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; this is called the subtle and esoteric Dharma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If the three thousandfold world system were filled with precious jewels,
and one were to give them all away as alms, the merit obtained would be small;”
If one were to preach even a single verse of the Dharma, its merit would be exceedingly great.

Even if one were to take all the objects of pleasure in the three realms and bestow them entirely upon a single person, it would not equal the merit of giving a single verse; the latter’s merit is supreme.
"This merit surpasses that [previous one], and it can bring about freedom from all suffering and affliction.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"If there were a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, with treasures filling boundless worlds, made offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas."
"If there is a bodhisattva who, with a heart of great compassion, explains even a four-line verse for the sake of a single sentient being, their merit shall surpass that of the former.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with precious jewels,..."
Giving to all the Tathāgatas is not equal to a single gift of the Dharma.
Although the merit of giving jewels is great, it does not equal a single gift of the Dharma;
even the merit of a single verse is superior, how much more so when it is beyond measure?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!
The Tathāgata possesses a light called 'Adorned with All Merits,' which resides within his right palm."

By means of this light, I am able to cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to have every necessary article of enjoyment fully satisfied: to those who need food, I give food; to those who need drink, I give drink; to those who need clothing, I give clothing; to those who need vehicles, I give vehicles; to those who need jewels, I give jewels—I am able to provide all such things as these.
Maitreya! Although all sentient beings may obtain this happiness, they are unable to attain liberation from within birth and death. Maitreya!

Therefore, the Tathāgata does not bestow upon sentient beings the worldly requisites for pleasure, but grants instead the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure that transcends the world; having heard it, sentient beings will ultimately be liberated from suffering.
Therefore, Maitreya!
You all should study the unsurpassed gift of Dharma of the Tathāgata; do not value the worldly gift of material sustenance. Maitreya!

In the future, at the end of the age during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is extinguished, there will be bhikṣus who claim to be bodhisattvas, yet who perform unwholesome deeds with their bodies, unwholesome deeds with their speech, and unwholesome deeds with their minds; they violate the prohibitions with their bodies, violate the prohibitions with their speech, and violate the prohibitions with their minds, creating unwholesome karma and lacking the fruits of the śramaṇa.

Maitreya! For the sake of sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain bodhicitta, I have taught the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva, by which they do not fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or other difficult states.

Good sons and good daughters should apply themselves with diligent vigor and be fully possessed of a sense of shame and remorse. Constantly fearing birth and death, they should always harbor dread toward all places of rebirth, thinking: "How shall I cause the sentient beings of the three realms and six paths to quickly attain liberation?"
Why is this? Maitreya!

The bodhisattva mahāsattva makes a vow to deliver all sentient beings of the three realms and six paths, causing them to attain liberation; those who lack peace, he causes to find peace; and those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa, he causes to attain nirvāṇa.

Maitreya! When I survey all worlds—whether among devas, humans, māras, or brahmās, or among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—I do not see a single person capable of bearing such a heavy burden as this Bodhisattva.
Maitreya! It is as if there were a person who carried upon their head the mountains, rivers, stones, and cliffs of the trichiliocosm.
Someone then said to them:
“Good son! You should now take this trichiliocosm upon your head for one kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, or even for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, carrying it without ceasing.”
“Maitreya! What do you think? Would such a person be considered to possess great power?”
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is most great.”
"World-Honored One!
It is exceedingly great. Sugata!"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"The power of the diligence of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is even more superior than that.
A bodhisattva makes a vow to deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to abide in the bliss of nirvāṇa."
Maitreya! It is as if there were a person who could, all at once, accomplish all the deeds performed by every sentient being throughout the trichiliocosm.
Maitreya! What do you think?
Is the work performed by this person not indeed great?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha:
“It is exceedingly great,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"The deeds performed by a bodhisattva exceed even this.
When a bodhisattva utters a word:"
"Those sentient beings in the three realms who suffer afflictions, I shall cause them to attain liberation.
Maitreya, it is like a householder who has an only son; his appearance is handsome and he is in his youth, and he is filial and obedient toward his parents.
The elder, along with his sons, wives, concubines, retinue, servants, and wealth, were all cast into the king’s prison.
At that time, the great king said to the elder:
"One hundred yojanas from here there is a city named such-and-such; go there in seven days, and after traveling for another seven days, return to my presence."
"If you can do as you have said, we shall restore your wife, children, kinsmen, and wealth to you in their entirety, and grant you official property as well.
However, if you do not arrive here from that city within seven days, we shall execute you and your only son; your relatives and wealth shall all be confiscated by the state."
The Buddha said to Maitreya: "What do you think?

This elder exerted himself with diligent effort because he loved himself, loved his only son, and cherished his wife, concubines, slaves, servants, and wealth, as he traveled from that city with such toil and hardship until he reached here."
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, that person does not think of food, drink, or sleep, but thinks only of traveling swiftly."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Because such a person cherishes their own life, they therefore travel with haste.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"If all sentient beings were to practice with diligence and vigor exactly as that person does,

and if all sentient beings were to exert such diligence, it would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, a ten-millionth part, a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, or a hundred-thousand-ten-million-nayuta part— indeed, not even an incalculable fraction— of the diligence of a bodhisattva."
Why is this? Maitreya!
All sentient beings follow the flow of birth and death, whereas Bodhisattvas go against the flow of birth and death, causing them to abide in unshakable nirvana.

Maitreya! It is like a person of great courage and immense strength, even more powerful than those before, who takes the waters of the four great oceans and all the rivers and returns them all to the Anavatapta Great Lake.
Maitreya! What do you think?
Is the deed performed by this person rare and extraordinary?
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Such a matter is most rare.”
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"The diligence of a bodhisattva that is difficult to perform and rare is even more extraordinary than this.
That a bodhisattva, with a heart of great compassion, transforms all sentient beings and causes them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—this matter is difficult."
If one can have faith in the existence of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, this is difficult.
If there is one who can believe in the karmic fruits of good and evil deeds, this is difficult.
To be able to extinguish the arising of greed, hatred, and delusion—this is difficult.
To be able to renounce one's kinsmen, give rise to a mind of few desires, and set forth to seek renunciation by walking seven steps—this is difficult.
To don the saṃghāṭī robe and, with right faith, renounce the world within the True Dharma, becoming free from the fire of desire—this is difficult.
Not to violate the prohibitive precepts—this is difficult.
To be able to leave behind clamor and bustle to cultivate the practice of seclusion—this is difficult.
To have faith that all phenomena are empty—this is difficult.
To attain the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) regarding the profound Dharma is difficult.
To realize the three gates of liberation is difficult.
To realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship is likewise difficult.
Why is this? Maitreya,
that which is called "difficult" is to leave the home life out of faith within the True Dharma and attain the fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Maitreya! In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, there will be sentient beings who resolve to attain the bodhicitta; yet within the True Dharma, they will leave the household life to study the Path only to find themselves empty-handed with no attainment, abandoning the deeds of a bodhisattva to perform the conduct of ordinary fools.
Maitreya! What are the deeds of a bodhisattva? Maitreya!
There are twenty dharmas pertaining to the practice of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva does not accomplish these twenty dharmas, they will be unable to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
What are the twenty? First, being free from avarice; second, practicing generosity; third, being free from feverish affliction;
fourth, practicing pure ethical discipline; fifth, being free from ill-will; sixth, practicing patience; seventh, being free from laziness...
1. Diligence; 2. Great vigor; 3. Freedom from a distracted mind; 4. Cultivating wisdom through mindfulness while practicing the supportless samādhi;
5. Cultivating profound patience; 6. Being fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā);
7. Practicing the signless practice (animitta-caryā); 8. Practicing the empty practice (śūnyatā-caryā); 9. [And so forth.]
15) practicing the conduct of wishlessness; 16) accomplishing the sphere of wishlessness; 17) not abandoning any sentient beings;
18) cultivating great compassion; 19) not thinking of the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
20) the mind delighting in accomplishing the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
These are called the twenty kinds of karma of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these twenty karmas, they are able to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Maitreya!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four kinds of definitive vows. What are the four?

First, the definitive attainment of Buddhahood and the turning of the wheel of Dharma; second, causing sentient beings in birth and death to attain liberation; third, causing immeasurable sentient beings to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and fourth, relinquishing one’s own bodily pleasure so that all sentient beings may obtain untainted bliss (*anāsrava-sukha*).
"These are called the four kinds of definitive vows.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"Suppose there were two men who were well-versed in medical prescriptions, well-versed in incantations, skilled at distinguishing poisonous drugs, and proficient in identifying ambrosia."

At that time, one person from among the great assembly immediately took poison and consumed it himself, manifesting a rare phenomenon; having eaten it, he suffered pain and his body was not at ease, so he further sought the art of nectar-spells in the hope of eliminating the poisonous vapors.
At that time, that person sought [the remedy] but could not find it; the poisonous vapor intensified, and he subsequently passed away.
Then the second person spoke these words:

"I cannot now consume this poisonous medicine. Since I do not consume the poison, I have no need for the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). I do not wish to dwell among the multitude as an object of wonder, causing my body to suffer and be distressed."
“Maitreya! In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, there will likewise be various lay and ordained bodhisattvas who speak thus:
‘The Dharma that I preach is able to eliminate all sins.’”
Having spoken thus, they further accumulate evil karma and say again: "I repent.
I declare that such a person is called a "dead man" within the True Dharma.
Why is it called death?
It refers to falling away and sinking from the True Dharma; this is what is called death, Maitreya.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva whose mind was pure, who spoke these words:
"I do not commit offenses, so there is no need for repentance.
I shall repent of all offenses of the past and future, but I do not commit them in the present."
"It is just as that person who does not eat poisonous medicine has no need for nectar (amṛta). Maitreya!
That which is called 'poison' refers to violating the precepts within the True Dharma; this is what is meant by poison."
“Maitreya! You all must not become people who consume poison.
Thus the Buddha addressed Maitreya.

“Furthermore, there are four dharmas that cause a bodhisattva to be separated from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and even from the fruit of a śrāvaka, let alone from omniscience itself. What are these four?
First, ingratitude; second, guile and crookedness; third, lying; and fourth, violating the precepts.”
Maitreya! These four kinds of dharmas can cause a bodhisattva to depart from omniscience (sarvajñā) and even from the state of a śrāvaka, let alone from omniscience itself. Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are four things that a bodhisattva should abandon by running swiftly even beyond a hundred yojanas. What are these four?
First, gain and offerings;
Second, evil friends;
third, evil assemblies;
fourth, being together in one place, whether engaging in jesting and laughter, or becoming angry, or quarreling.
One should swiftly abandon [such a person] at a distance of more than a hundred yojanas.
Maitreya, a bodhisattva should not harbor ill will toward other bodhisattvas.
Maitreya, suppose there were a bodhisattva who beat, reviled, and mutilated all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm.
What do you think? Would that person have committed a grave offense?
“Would a bodhisattva incur much demerit by beating, reviling, or cutting all sentient beings in this way?
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If striking a single sentient being incurs so much transgression, how much more so for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm? Why is this,
World-Honored One?
"All Bodhisattvas should not give rise to a mind of anger toward sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya, saying:
"If there were a Bodhisattva who beat, reviled, or mutilated all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, the transgression incurred would still be relatively small."
If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of anger toward another bodhisattva, they shall regress from enlightenment for as many eons as that.
Maitreya, it is like a wooden pillar: if one attempts to cut it with grass or soil, one will not succeed; only with a sharp axe can it be cut.

The roots of goodness of a bodhisattva are likewise thus; they cannot be exhausted by anything else, yet if one gives rise to a mind of anger toward a bodhisattva, it can destroy all those virtues. Maitreya!

"Therefore, a bodhisattva should train in showing reverence toward those bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], giving rise to a mind of respect for them as if they were the World-Honored One.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I shall practice honoring and revering all sentient beings, how much more so bodhisattvas. Why is this?
World-Honored One!

One should abandon ill-will and practice patience; remain free from deceit and crookedness and practice a pure mind; distance oneself from the conditioned and practice the path of non-self and non-grasping; do not prize wealth and treasures but value the practice of the Dharma; and do not seek clothing or food, but seek the wealth of the Dharma.
Abandoning envy, one should feel sympathetic joy upon seeing others in great wealth.
One should not become a śramaṇa merely for the sake of seeking fame; rather, one should train in all the virtues of a śramaṇa.

I shall not merely speak with my mouth, but shall practice true conduct; I shall renounce gain and honor, practice fewness of desires and contentment, and seek the merits of the Buddha. I shall not enter villages for the sake of wealth or profit, but shall enter villages mindful of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
One should not enter villages or towns for the sake of food or clothing to practice deceitful conduct; rather, one should practice right conduct and praise the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
One should not learn the base and inferior mind of ordinary worldlings, but should instead learn the practice of the Buddhas: not observing the faults of others, but only disciplining oneself.
Cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā; abandon the evils of the three karmas and constantly practice the pure conduct of the three karmas.
Free from breaking the precepts, one should study the prātimokṣa.
They do not sustain their lives by relying on the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha, but instead praise the Tathāgata’s true merits for the sake of seeking the Dharma rather than seeking alms.
They constantly praise the True Dharma and practice in accordance with it, and they praise the noble Saṅgha.
They rely on the Sangha of non-retrogression, not on the worldly Sangha of conditioned existence.
They do not seek any worldly requisites for sustaining the body; they seek only the True Dharma and not worldly affairs.
Seeking the supramundane Dharma, one should be free from flattery and crookedness; practicing with sincerity, one should not take pleasure in remaining in a single place.
One should be like a wild deer, having no fixed abode, and leaving behind worldly pleasures to seek the merits of the Buddha.
One should abandon sleep and recite the sūtras during the first and last watches of the night.
One should forsake clamor and dwell in seclusion; one should never conceive a sense of weariness toward meritorious qualities, seeking them with a mind that does not rest for even a moment.
One should abandon the ways of dogs and practice the ways roared by the lion.

One should be a friend for eternity rather than a temporary friend; one should abandon those who are ungrateful and practice gratitude; one should not make friends for the sake of wealth and profit, but should make friends with a pure mind.
Abandoning a deceitful mind, one should practice truthful conduct; relinquishing inferior dharmas, one should seek to achieve the unsurpassed Buddha-body.
One should practice reverence toward the Tathāgata and not give rise to arrogance.

Abandoning double-tongued speech and the discordance between mind and mouth, one should practice truthful and non-dual words; one should not act as a bodhisattva while practicing deceit and crookedness.
One should, with a pure mind, practice śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One should abandon self-conceit and practice reverence;
one should abstain from impure food and maintain the precepts with purity.
Having partaken of the alms of others, one should abandon perverse thoughts and keep the Buddhas' Dharma in mind.
Free from the view of a person, one practices the conduct of emptiness; free from deluded cognition, one practices the conduct of signlessness.
Free from bodily deceit and crookedness, one should practice the conduct of purity in the three karmas.
One expounds the Dharma without seeking wealth or profit, preaching the True Dharma with a heart of great compassion.
One does not make friends through material things, but through the Dharma as one's friend.
Not for one's own benefit, but for the benefit of others so that they may not be harmed;
practicing in an araṇya while remaining free from flattery and crookedness, not practicing flattery when begging for alms, and not practicing flattery when wearing rag-robes.
"Why is this? One who possesses the twelve dhūtas does not seek any worldly gain or honor.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!
You have made this lion’s roar, seeking the qualities of a Buddha with a mind that knows no satiety.”
"Having planted various roots of goodness under past Buddhas, they are able to preach this Dharma and speak of these merits.
At that time, while the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya was preaching this Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa asked the bhikṣus,
"Now that you have heard the Dharma being taught, to what place do you, bhikṣus, wish to go? The bhikṣus replied:
"Venerable Kāśyapa! The Dharma taught by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is profoundly deep and difficult to encounter.
We have formed this thought:"
"We are unable to cultivate and attain this Dharma; we wish to return to lay life. Why is this?
Because it is difficult to digest food given out of faith."
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praised the bhikṣus:
"Excellent, excellent!
O sons of good family!"
This is what you ought to do.
If you cannot digest the food offered out of faith, it would be better to return to lay life a hundred times a day than to break the precepts while accepting the offerings of the faithful.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what kind of person should accept offerings of faith?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"Good son! If there are those who cultivate dhyāna and attain liberation, I permit such persons to accept food offered as an act of faith."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the five hundred bhikṣus:
"You should now quickly engage in practice.
A Buddha-world is difficult to encounter; you must abide in the Buddha-dharma."
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus asked Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī! How should we practice?”
Mañjuśrī addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “You should contemplate in this way:

there is not a single dharma that joins, nor a single dharma that disperses; there is not a single dharma that arises, nor a single dharma that ceases; one neither accepts a single dharma nor rejects a single dharma; one neither increases a single dharma nor decreases a single dharma.”

If one practices in this way, there is no attainment regarding phenomena; where there is no attainment, there is no going; because there is no going, there is no coming; and where there is no coming, there is no going. Bhikṣus!
"This is called neither coming nor going, neither abiding nor not abiding.
When Mañjuśrī had spoken this Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (āsravas).
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Eight;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Eighty-Nine.
Translated by Prince Yueposhouna of Ujjayinī during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Mahākāśyapa-parivarta, Chapter Twenty-three, Part Two.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, what kind of bodhisattvas will practice deceit and crookedness?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!"
"Many people practice deceit and crookedness, associate with evil friends, read and recite the sutras little, and do so only for the sake of seeking food and clothing.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
I only pray that the World-Honored One, for the benefit of many, will explain the faults of those bodhisattvas who are deceitful and lack diligence in practice.
May those bodhisattvas, having heard of these faults, restrain their own thoughts and conduct so that they may attain purity.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying: “Kāśyapa!

In the future, during the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, there will be bodhisattvas who associate with evil friends and read and recite the sutras little; they will perform only the work of making offerings to relics, using incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, canopies, lamps, and lights to make offerings to the stūpas and shrines containing the Tathāgata’s relics.”
Kāśyapa! For the sake of laypeople who lack wisdom, so that they may plant roots of goodness, I have taught the offering of śarīras.
Those foolish people do not understand my intention; they merely perform this ritual act.

Kāśyapa! Among all devas and humans, I have always taught this Dharma: by practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā to bring oneself under discipline, there shall be in the world faithful brahmins and householders who will make offerings to the relics.
Kāśyapa! Those foolish people abandon recitation, meditation, and wisdom, and instead sustain their lives by making offerings to śarīras. Kāśyapa!

If there were a bodhisattva who, with incense, flowers, and lamps filling a trichiliocosm as far up as the Brahma Heaven—each lamp wick being as large as Mount Sumeru—were to offer such things to the Tathāgata.

If there is a bodhisattva who, with a pure mind, upholds the precepts and receives, maintains, reads, and recites even a single four-line verse from a venerable teacher, and practices it with a pure mind for as little as seven steps, their merit will be infinitely and boundlessly superior to that [of the former].

Kāśyapa! Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for a hundred thousand years, during the six periods of day and night, offered flowers, incense, and powdered incense filling the entire trichiliocosm to the Tathāgata.

If there is a bodhisattva who abandons clamor and is deeply fearful of the triple world, and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings resolves to proceed toward an araṇya, even taking seven steps, this merit shall be immeasurable and boundless, surpassing the former.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata make such a statement for the purpose of transforming sentient beings?
Kāśyapa! Do not hold such a view; the Tathāgata speaks the truth. Why is this?
“Because the Tathāgata perceives them directly and knows them with clarity.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mārapuṣpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. That kalpa was also named Mārapuṣpa.”
Kāśyapa! The Tathāgata Supuṣpa had a great assembly of ninety-six billion hundred thousand śrāvakas.
At that time, there was a wheel-turning sage king named Nimi, who ruled the four continents according to the Dharma.
Kāśyapa! At that time, King Nimi possessed a full thousand sons, who were valiant, robust, and majestic. Kāśyapa!
At that time, when the Great King had already possessed his thousand sons, there were further two sons who were born by transformation, sitting cross-legged:
the first was named Dharma, and the second was named Sudharma.

Kāśyapa! At that time, the great king invited the Tathāgata Wonderful Flower and the community of bhikṣus, providing them with robes, bedding, food, and medicine for a full eighty-four thousand years. Setting aside all worldly affairs, he devoted himself solely to making offerings.

After seven days, all the bhikṣus were each provided with new robes and various kinds of food and drink according to their wishes; they extensively constructed vihāras and dwelt therein according to their inclinations.
Each bhikṣu was attended by seven servants, and they were provided with food of a hundred flavors. Kāśyapa!
At that time, the great king constructed a vihāra eighty yojanas in square extent, exquisitely painted and surpassing anything in the world.

While the Tathāgata Wonderful Flower and the community of bhikṣus were seated in that vihāra, various exquisite flowers emerged from beneath the earth, causing the flowers in that vihāra to reach up to their knees.

Kāśyapa! At that time, the great king made offerings to the Tathāgata Supuṣpa in the Inconceivable Merit Vihāra for eighty-four thousand years, reverently making offerings, honoring, and praising him.

Kāśyapa! At that time, after the great king had made offerings to the Tathāgata for a full eighty-four thousand years, on the very last day, following the meal of the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, the two sons Dharmapāla and Sudharmapāla, along with their retinues and the fourfold assembly, went to where the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, was staying. Prostrating themselves with their heads at his feet, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is there perhaps any merit from the roots of goodness of giving that surpasses the merit from the roots of goodness of this Great King Nimi? "Kāśyapa!
At the time when the two princes prostrated before the Tathāgata, the great trichiliocosm shook throughout."
Kāśyapa! At that time, the attendant disciple of the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, named Dharmaprativedha, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition does the great earth tremble?
By what cause and condition do these two princes prostrate before the Buddha and stand there?
At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa addressed Dharmaprativedha:
“Good son! What is the use of this question?

If the Tathāgata were to describe how this prince, with a mind of pure resolve, profound patience, and great compassion, prostrates at the feet of the Tathāgata, all devas and humans would surely fall into confusion and despair.”
"Kāśyapa! At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa addressed a śrāvaka disciple endowed with supernormal powers named Nārāyaṇa, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
“Demonstrate your supernatural power and raise these two boys.

Kāśyapa, at that time the bhikṣu Nārāyaṇa rose from his seat; he took one boy with his right hand and the other boy with his left hand, intending to support them and help them rise, yet he was unable to move them.
At that time, Nārāyaṇa exerted his great supernormal powers, supporting the two youths and wishing to make them rise, yet he could not move them;
it was as if one were to divide a single hair into ten million parts and fail to move even a single part.
Kāśyapa! At that time, the earth of the trichiliocosm shook everywhere, and the mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs all trembled violently, yet they could not move those two youths.

Kāśyapa! At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, Nārāyaṇa caused all the Buddha-worlds in the direction below, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to tremble; yet he did not move even a single hair on the two youths.
"Kāśyapa! At that time, the bhikṣu Nārāyaṇa prostrated before the Buddha Puṣpaśrī and said:
'World-Honored One!'"
"Will I not lose my supernormal powers?
For what reason?
World-Honored One!"

"These two boys have been born for but a short time; though they lie prostrate before the Buddha with their heads touching the ground, I am unable to make them rise, even by exerting my full supernatural power.
At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa addressed the bhikṣu Nārāyaṇa, saying: "Good son!
"You have not lost your supernormal powers. Good son!
The realm of a bodhisattva is inconceivable; it cannot be disturbed nor can it be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

"Good son! If all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm were endowed with great supernormal powers no different from yours, they would be unable to move these two youths from their place even in the course of a hundred million eons."
"Kāśyapa! At that time, when the Tathāgata Subhūṣa spoke these words, four million two hundred thousand sentient beings among the assembly resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Those sentient beings formed this thought:
"The spiritual power of the Bodhisattva is truly rare.
Even though he has not yet attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), his spiritual power is such that it cannot be shaken by the power of the great Śrāvakas, let alone when he attains the Buddha-way."
"Therefore, we should practice the bodhisattva path and vow to realize the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa, at that time,
after these four million two hundred thousand sentient beings had formed this thought, their minds became firmly established in unsurpassed bodhi.

Kāśyapa! At that time, there was a bodhisattva among that assembly named Śubhamati. Rising from his seat in the midst of the great multitude, he bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, and addressed the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will cause these two youths to arise, and that the Buddha will explain as they have asked.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“At that time, the Tathāgata Wonderful Flower produced a great sound from the midst of space, and its resonance pervaded as far as the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
Wherever the sound reached, the worlds and the earth shook in six ways, and a great radiance was emitted, illuminating the ten directions.
Kāśyapa! At that time, having heard this sound, the two youths rose from the ground.

Kāśyapa! When the youth arose, the musical instruments of gods and humans throughout this trichiliocosm resounded spontaneously without being struck, and a rain of various exquisite flowers fell from the void.

Kāśyapa! At that time, the two youths rose from the earth, went to where the Tathāgata was, circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, gazed up at the Tathāgata.
Kāśyapa! At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa addressed the Bodhisattva Sumati, saying:
"O son of good family!"
After these two youths had prostrated at my feet, they asked me this:
"World-Honored One!
Is there any merit from the roots of goodness arising from giving that surpasses the merit and roots of goodness of this Great King Nimi?"
"Having prostrated at my feet, these two youths stood there having asked their questions.
Kāśyapa! At that time, the Bodhisattva Supratisthita addressed the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the Buddha will explain the questions of the two youths, so that all devas and humans may attain peace and happiness.
At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa addressed the Bodhisattva Sumati:
“Good son! Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you. Good son!”

If there were a bodhisattva dwelling in the practice of forest hermitages and the practice of seclusion, who, with slight understanding of all phenomena, attains the patience of non-arising, their merit would be immeasurably and boundlessly superior to that performed by King Nimi.

"Good son! If every single sentient being in the trichiliocosm were to perform meritorious deeds equal to those of King Nimi, the total merit of all such sentient beings in the trichiliocosm would not equal the merit of a bodhisattva who practices seclusion, abides in a pure mind, is endowed with right mindfulness, and understands that all phenomena are empty, neither coming nor going. This merit of even this slight patience surpasses the former merit; the former does not approach one hundredth part, one thousandth part, one hundred-millionth part, one ten-billionth part, one trillionth part, one hundred-thousand-billionth part, or one hundred-thousand-nayuta-billionth part of it—it does not even admit of calculation."
"Good son! Suppose all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were each to perform meritorious deeds equal to those of King Nimi."
Those sentient beings perform meritorious deeds, constantly cultivating merit for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River.
Good son, what do you think?
"Would that son of good family gain much merit?
Kāśyapa! At that time, the Bodhisattva Suprajñā addressed the Tathāgata Puṣpaśrī, saying:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
The parables spoken by the Tathāgata are inconceivable, and these roots of goodness are likewise inconceivable. Kāśyapa!
At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Flower addressed the Bodhisattva Good Wisdom:
"O son of good family!
I now tell you: only those wise people who have accomplished profound patience can believe these words."

The roots of goodness accumulated by all those sentient beings do not equal those of these two youths who, with a pure mind, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata; they surpass the roots of goodness of all those previous sentient beings such that the former do not approach even one hundredth part, one thousandth part, one hundred-thousandth part, one hundred-millionth part, one ten-billionth part, one trillionth part, one hundred-trillionth part, or even one hundred-thousand-ten-billion-nayuta-th part, nor can they be reached even by calculation or analogy.
"Kāśyapa! At that time, within the great assembly of the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, eighty-four thousand bhikṣus spoke with one voice:
'World-Honored One!'"

We rejoice in the merit of that person who has accomplished profound *dharmakṣānti*, who has faith in the emptiness of all phenomena, whose mind delights in seclusion, and who, having set out for an *araṇya*, takes seven steps and resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to accomplish wisdom.
"We rejoice. Kāśyapa! At that time, the Tathāgata Wonderful Flower praised those bhikṣus:
"Excellent, excellent! Sons of good family,

by means of these inconceivable roots of goodness arising from this karma of sympathetic joy, you shall become wheel-turning sage-kings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and thereafter you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and the great assembly all spoke with one voice to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We rejoice in those people who have resolved their minds, who have accomplished profound patience, who believe in the emptiness of all dharmas, and who are far removed from [the notion of] extinction because of the self-nature purity [of all things].”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying: “Kāśyapa!
At that time, the two youths Dharmaka and Sudharmaka said to the Tathāgata Supuṣpa:”
“World-Honored One!

With what dharmas is a bodhisattva endowed so that they give without expecting recompense, do not give rise to jealousy, have no stinginess in mind, and do not produce greedy attachment; such that when seeing others practicing giving, their own minds harbor no expectations; and so as to accomplish the unsurpassed practice of the Tathāgata, attain profound dharma-patience, and achieve unsurpassed wisdom?”
"Kāśyapa! At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa addressed the two youths, the sons of Good Dharma, saying:
'Sons of noble family!'"

When a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas—giving without expecting a reward, being free from envy, being free from stinginess, and not giving rise to greed—and seeing others give, does not harbor expectations, they accomplish the unsurpassed practice of the Tathāgata, attain profound patience, and perceive unsurpassed wisdom.
What are these four?
First, faith in the emptiness of all phenomena; second, detachment; third, profound patience; and fourth, right mindfulness. Good son!

When a bodhisattva is endowed with these four dharmas, they give without expecting recompense; their mind is free from envy and stinginess, and they do not give rise to greed. Seeing others give, they harbor no longing for themselves; they accomplish the unsurpassed practice of the Tathāgata, achieve profound patience, and possess supreme wisdom.

"Good son! Furthermore, there are four dharmas. If a bodhisattva is endowed with these four dharmas, they will give without expecting recompense, their mind will be free from envy, they will not be stingy, and they will not give rise to greed. Seeing others give, they do not harbor expectations; they accomplish the unsurpassed practice of the Tathāgata, and they achieve profound patience and fulfill unsurpassed wisdom."
What are these four?
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva seeks extensive learning; having attained extensive learning, he travels through cities and villages to preach the Dharma without any expectation of gain, nor does he accept even a single word of praise, his mind being free from all craving.

Among all forms of giving taught by the Buddhas, the gift of Dharma is supreme; abiding in this foremost gift, one’s mind is filled with joy, and one does not seek the bestowal of worldly wealth or material goods.
Why is this? Good son! In the countless *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, the Tathāgatas and their assemblies of bhikṣus do not seek the requisites for worldly livelihood.
If there is a bodhisattva who abides in pure precepts, cultivates the true Dharma, possesses great compassion, and does not seek gain or offerings, they will be remembered by all Buddhas.
If there is one who can recite even a single four-line verse, the words and letters of that verse are all empty of intrinsic nature; likewise, all phenomena are also empty of intrinsic nature.

The roots of goodness and merit of this son of good family surpass the previous roots of goodness; the former do not equal even one hundredth part, one thousandth part, one hundred-thousandth part, one hundred-millionth part, one ten-billionth part, one trillionth part, one hundred-thousand-billionth part, one hundred-thousand-nayuta-billionth part, nor even an incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) fraction of it.
"Kāśyapa! At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa addressed the two youths:
'Sons of good family, when a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas, they shall attain the unsurpassed practice of a Tathāgata.'"
What are the four? First, practicing the unsurpassed state; second, preaching the unsurpassed Dharma; third, bestowing the unsurpassed gift; and fourth, believing in the unsurpassed Dharma.
"Good son! These are called the four dharmas.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed practice of a Tathāgata."

“Kāśyapa! When the Tathāgata Supuṣpa was teaching this Dharma to the two youths, having heard this Dharma, the two youths leaped into the air to a height of seven tala trees and praised the Buddha with one voice:
‘The Tathāgata knows all conditioned phenomena, And teaches sentient beings to practice giving.’”
Yet not being attached to giving— this is the unsurpassed gift.
Being able to accomplish unsurpassed patience, wherein there is no self,
no sentient being, no life, and no person— this is rare and great diligence.
By expounding such a Dharma, one accomplishes profound patience and attains the supreme practice; one attains unsurpassed enlightenment,
forever extinguishing all desires and afflictions, with great wisdom purified.
No longer subject to further existence, he speaks of the practice of detachment.
Causing others to dwell in the *āraṇya*, he cultivates the liberation of emptiness;
without generating conceptual discrimination, he constantly and diligently practices giving.
Not giving rise to conceptual discrimination—this is the stainless limit;
far removed from all names and terms, it is called pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Causing one to practice in the state of quiescence—this is the foremost precept.
Awakened to the state of quiescence, one constantly practices patience.
Without discriminating among sentient beings, this is the pure patience;
free from all conceptualization, one cultivates firm diligence.
Detached from all conditioned things—this is what the Buddha calls diligence;
it can accomplish the dharma of seclusion and incinerate all worldly affairs.
Severing existence and non-existence, this is non-conceptual meditation.
Not giving rise to any afflictions, neither this nor that;
not abiding even in the middle—this is the foremost wisdom.
Transcending the three periods of time, one cultivates the perception of quiescence.
Furthermore, one contemplates this perception: from where does this perception arise?
Thus, knowing there is no [inherent] perception, one praises the virtues of the Buddha.
Proclaiming the foremost Dharma, his mind remains free from divergent thoughts.
Listening to and receiving the True Dharma, one explains names and terms inexhaustibly;
since the essence of self-nature is not established and the observation of objects is found to be without reality,
the mind is then liberated.
Those for whom I preach the Dharma will be bound by Māra, for they do not understand the characteristics of phenomena;
this includes those who seek the state of a śrāvaka and those who seek the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
One should train in this Dharma;
with wisdom that is boundless, do not make inferior vows,
but aspire instead to supreme enlightenment.
Adorned with the marks and signs, like the golden body of a Buddha,
one should seek supreme enlightenment;
for no agent can be found, as all phenomena arise from conditions.
"The nature of non-nature is the true nature. "Kāśyapa!
At that time, while the two youths were reciting these verses in mid-air, King Nimi emerged from his city, and all the earth deities and the deities of space gathered together."
At that time, eighty-four thousand beings within the assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) beings planted roots of goodness.
Kāśyapa! At that time, the two youths Dharmasubhūti and Subhadharma descended from the sky and approached the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
We take refuge in the Buddha, we take refuge in the Dharma, and we take refuge in the Saṃgha; we resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practice the bodhisattva path in the form of bhikṣus.
"Bhagavān, one who has truly generated the mind of awakening believes that all phenomena are unarisen. Bhagavān!"
One who has truly resolved their mind does not cling to any phenomena. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
If there is attachment, then dharmas do not arise.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has said that by attaining a mind free from attachment, one realizes that non-arising.
World-Honored One!
This non-arising should also not be said to be "non-arising.
Why? Because where there is verbal expression, there is arising and ceasing.
If one possesses pure wisdom, there is neither arising nor ceasing; that which is free from arising and ceasing is ultimate exhaustion.

Therefore, World-Honored One, one generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the limit of equality (*samatā-koṭi*), without conceptualizing dharmas, and neither attaining any dharma nor failing to attain it. In this way, one attains equality—the equality of non-attainment.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is pure. Kāśyapa!

At that time, while the Tathāgata Supuṣpa was teaching this Dharma to the two youths, ten thousand beings among the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Great King Nimi, along with his thousand sons and five thousand ministers, all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"At that time, after the Tathāgata Supuṣpa had finished his meal and washed his bowl, he addressed the Great King amidst the great assembly, saying: 'Great King Nimi!'"
"I now preach the Dharma.
When the king and the great assembly heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, they leaped for joy and rejoiced greatly. Kāśyapa!

At that time, the two youths Dharmika and Sudharmika, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, were freed from the fire of desire through their pure faith; desiring to seek ordination, they departed from the city and came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he spoke in verse:
"All Tathāgatas praise the dharma of renunciation;
The household life is full of defilements, Which destroy and extinguish the pure and white dharmas."
They increase unwholesome dharmas and destroy wholesome dharmas;
Living at home is full of faults, while leaving home is free from defilement.
Even if one were to experience desires for ten billion eons, One would never reach satiety.
Experiencing sensual desires without satiety, one dies and perishes while remaining at home.
Just as the ocean receives all streams yet never reaches satiety, so too it is with the ordinary person: they experience sensual desires without satiety.
Just as fire consumes dry grass without ever reaching satiety,
so it is with the ordinary person who experiences desire without ever reaching satiety.
Bound by the net of craving, they bring about the destruction of the world.
Therefore, one should abandon bondage for the sake of renouncing the household life.
Remaining at home involves many faults, and the unsurpassed path cannot be attained;
by renouncing the world and practicing seclusion, one then attains bodhi.
The Tathāgatas of the past, Having already entered parinirvāṇa,
Dwelt in the dharma of araṇya And attained great bodhi. Therefore,
following the example of all Buddhas, One should proceed toward the araṇya.
Having renounced craving and left the household life, one thereafter attains peace and security.
Even if the entire trichiliocosm were filled with precious jewels,
and one were to offer this mass of jewels to all the Buddhas while remaining at home—
If, with a mind free from affliction, one recognizes the faults of the household life and follows the example of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas to leave home and seek wisdom;
having already left the household life, one remains far removed from the fires of all desires.
Raising one’s feet and walking seven steps is superior to giving away the three thousandfold world system.
The merit of those three thousand worlds does not equal even this one fraction;
therefore, the Tathāgata praises those who go forth from home.
Having accomplished great wisdom, Far removed from all fetters,
And free from all attachments, One realizes the unsurpassed path.
Quickly dwell in a place of tranquility, And sever all craving for desires.
All the blazing poisons of the mind are entirely extinguished without remainder.
Training in the way of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, knowing all phenomena as they truly are,
one should swiftly leave the household life and dwell in the dharma of the araṇya.
If you wish to seek the Buddha-way, cultivate the practice of seclusion;
you should train as an araṇya-dweller and not delight in the household life.
This is the realm of all Buddhas, the dwelling place of the sages.
One who is able to abide in this path can attain bodhi.
For those who wish to distance themselves from the afflictions that torment sentient beings, such as desire,
they should leave behind the ways of household life and practice in an araṇya.
‘If you wish to realize the Dharma of the Deathless, turn the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma,
and subdue all Māras and enemies, you should practice in an araṇya. “Kāśyapa!
At that time, having spoken these verses, the two youths Dharmika and Sudharmika departed from the city and proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata Supuṣpa resided.
Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and said:
"World-Honored One!
We now wish to seek ordination from the Tathāgata."
"I only pray, World-Honored One!
Out of compassion, please grant me permission to go forth and leave the household life.
"Kāśyapa! [the Buddha replied.]

At that time, the Tathāgata Wonderful Flower, knowing that the two youths possessed pure faith and sought the way of renunciation, immediately granted them permission to leave the household life and dwell according to the dharma of bhikṣus.

Kāśyapa! At that time, having heard that the two youths had attained the going forth, the Great King immediately commanded his crown prince to succeed him to the royal throne. The King, together with nine hundred and ninety-nine sons, eighty-four thousand wives, five thousand ministers, and all the people, with pure faith and free from the fire of desire, abandoned their homes to go forth; they all went together to visit the Buddha Wonderful Flower.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha Supuṣpa, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to seek renunciation; we pray that the Buddha will grant us permission to leave the household life.”

"Kāśyapa! At that time, the Buddha Wonderful Flower, knowing that the faith and minds of the great assembly were pure, permitted them all to leave the household life and dwell according to the Dharma of bhikṣus. Kāśyapa!"
At that time, within seven days of ascending the throne, the eldest son of the great king reflected to himself:
"I shall never abandon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñā-citta*).
Of what use is such a royal position, wealth, and treasures, which bind one to desire?"
"I shall never abandon unsurpassed bodhi.
Having formed this thought, he resolved to leave the household life and travel through the four continents on the fifteenth day, reciting these verses:
"My father and my kinsmen Have all already left the household life."
Countless billions of sentient beings have left the household life for the sake of the Dharma;
I too now delight in leaving the household life and take no pleasure in abiding amidst the five desires.
With a single mind seeking the path to liberation, I wish to go to where the Teacher dwells.
If one resolves to leave the household life and depart from the fires of all desires, they should swiftly follow my Dharma;
for freedom from suffering is extremely difficult to attain.
If one does not resolve to leave the household life and does not distance themselves from the fires of desire, [they shall remain in bondage].
"Find peace while living at home; dwell securely in the true Dharma.

"Kāśyapa! When that youth spoke these verses, not a single sentient being among those in the four continents took pleasure in staying at home; they all resolved their minds and vowed to seek renunciation."

Kāśyapa! At that time, the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, knowing that the minds and faiths of all sentient beings were pure and that they sought to leave the household life, manifested emanated Buddhas and assemblies of bhikṣus in every city, town, and village throughout the four continents.

Kāśyapa! At that time, among all sentient beings in the four continents, there was not a single person who remained a householder; through pure faith, they were freed from the fire of desire and all attained renunciation.

Once those sentient beings have left the household life, they need not plant or cultivate; the earth naturally produces various kinds of non-glutinous rice, the trees naturally produce various garments, and all the devas serve and attend to them.

Kāśyapa!
