At that time, the two bhikṣus Dharmasena and Kalyāṇadharma were courageous and diligent; for sixty-three billion years, they neither sat nor lay down, but instead applied themselves with tireless vigor in their quest for *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and maintained mindfulness of *sarvajñatā*.

After practicing with diligent vigor for sixty-three billion years, he attained the samādhi known as "Pervasive Arrival. The place where he sat was called the "Vajra Site," for that ground was composed entirely of vajra.
They hear and uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions; having heard them, they are further able to explain them for others. Kāśyapa!

At that time, among all sentient beings in the four continents, if there are any who practice and study the Śrāvaka Vehicle, not a single being will die with an ordinary body; even those who are most indolent will attain the stage of Anāgāmin, and upon passing away from this life, be reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.

Those who practiced together with him seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha will, at the end of their lives from this world, be reborn in other regions where no Buddha resides; they will be born into great families with all their faculties complete.

By the power of the roots of goodness from past lives, he departed from the fire of desire and entered the homeless life; seven days later, he attained the path of a pratyekabuddha, benefited immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, and entered parinirvāṇa.
Those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle achieve the five supernormal powers, possess the four immeasurables and unimpeded eloquence, and attain dhāraṇīs.
Kāśyapa, do not harbor other thoughts.
At that time, was the Great King Nimi anyone else?
He was none other than myself.
The crown prince at that time was the present-day Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Kāśyapa! Do not conceive of this as something else. Why is that?
The youth Dharmaka was none other than the present Mañjuśrī;
the youth Kalyāṇadharma was the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja. Kāśyapa!
"Behold, that buddha-field is pure in this way; it is the dwelling place of sentient beings who possess roots of goodness.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"How long was the lifespan of the Tathāgata Supuṣpa?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The lifespan of the Tathāgata Supuṣpa was eight kalpas."
Kāśyapa! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Supuṣpa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for a full kalpa.
All the devas will make offerings to his relics, and there will be no householders.
Kāśyapa! At that time, two bhikṣus were of few desires and content; they did not offer oblations to the śarīras nor pay homage to the Buddha’s stūpas. Kāśyapa!
At that time, the various devas and the great assembly of hundreds of thousands of newly ordained bhikṣus said to one another:
"These two bhikṣus hold wrong views; they do not believe in the Buddha’s relics, they do not offer worship, and they do not pay homage to the Buddha’s stūpas."

"Kāśyapa! At that time, when the various devas and the great assembly of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus spoke these words, the two bhikṣus Dharmma and Saddharma asked the multitude: 'What do you think?'"
"What constitutes an offering that is a true offering to the Tathāgata?
For what reason do the relics of the Tathāgata receive offerings?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Because he cultivated precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, Śāriputra receives offerings.
The two bhikṣus said, "Cultivating precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation is the true offering; [it is not the offering of material things]."
"It is not for the sake of making offerings to the relics.
The bhikṣus said, "So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."
"What are the characteristics of the precepts?
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation?
The two bhikṣus, Dharmadatta and Kalyāṇadharma, replied:
"The mark of non-action is the mark of precepts; even up to the mark of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the mark of non-action is the mark of knowledge and vision. Kāśyapa!
At that time, the two bhikṣus said to the assembly:
"What do you think? Can that which is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) make offerings to that which is unconditioned?
The bhikṣus replied:
"No," replied the two bhikṣus, Dharmā and Sudharmā.
"True worship consists in having no notion of a Buddha and no vision of a Buddha; how much less, then, can there be the act of worship?"
"If one makes offerings to the Buddha, one should make offerings to oneself.
The bhikṣus asked: "How does one make offerings to oneself?"
The two bhikṣus said:
"One should make offerings to oneself as one would to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the object of offerings for all sentient beings."
As the Buddha has trained, so should you train.
Uphold the prohibitive precepts and gather all wholesome dharmas; contemplate all phenomena without grasping at their characteristics.
If one can thus provide for oneself, one shall receive the offerings of gods and humans.
If one wishes to make offerings to the relics of the Buddha, one should offer them oneself.
Just as the Buddha-Tathāgata is endowed with all merits, so too do the relics receive offerings.
If one can accomplish such merits, this is called making offerings to the Buddha.
To give rise to no conceptualizations or signs is called making offerings to the Buddha.
To produce no discrimination regarding whether [the offerings] are many or few is called making offerings to the Buddha.

That which neither departs from a future life nor comes from the present life, which is neither the other shore, nor eternal, nor annihilated, and which is neither grasping nor abandoning—this is what is called making offerings to the Tathāgata.
Neither increasing nor decreasing, neither arising nor ceasing, neither exhausting nor not exhausting—this is called making an offering to the Tathāgata.

Neither mind nor mental factors, neither recollection nor conceptualization, neither self nor grasping nor receiving, neither contention nor non-contention, neither disparagement nor praise, neither duality nor entering—this is called making an offering to the Tathāgata.
It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; this is called making an offering to the Tathāgata.

When there is nothing performed by body, nothing performed by speech, and nothing performed by mind—when these cannot be found within body, speech, and mind—this is called making an offering to the Tathāgata.

To have no perception of the past, and to find no such perception in the future or the present; to be without dependence or attachment, and to have no thought of seeking nor engage in conceptual discrimination—this is what is called making offerings to the Tathāgata.

To have no perception of the Buddha, no perception of the Dharma, and no perception of the Sangha; to have no perception of a person, no perception of self, and no perception of others—this is what is called making offerings to the Tathāgata.
The true body of the Tathāgata is without birth and without marks; one cannot cultivate offerings through the notion of birth.
The true body of the Tathāgata is called the mark of non-action; one does not cultivate offerings by means of the mark of action.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the mark of non-duality; one should not practice offerings based on dualistic marks.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the mark of outflowlessness; one does not practice offerings by means of that which is with outflows.

The body of the True Tathāgata is called the mark of emptiness; one does not make offerings to the Tathāgata through the view of a self, the view of a life-force, the view of annihilationism or eternalism, the view of a self or what belongs to a self, or the view of existence or non-existence.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the markless mark; one cannot cultivate offerings to it by means of marks.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the wishless mark; one cannot cultivate offerings to it by means of wishes.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the signless; one cannot cultivate offerings toward it by means of existence.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the immovable sign; one cannot cultivate offerings toward it by means of movement.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the signless state of non-action; one cannot cultivate offerings through action.
The body of the true Tathāgata is called the state free from greed; one cannot cultivate offerings through greed.
The body of the True Tathāgata is called "free from the mark of hatred"; one cannot cultivate offerings through hatred.
The body of the True Tathāgata is called "free from the mark of delusion"; one cannot cultivate offerings through delusion.

The body of the True Tathāgata is endowed with precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; one cannot cultivate offerings toward it through the violation of precepts, a distracted mind, or ignorance.

The body of the True Tathāgata is characterized by loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; it cannot be honored through offerings made with a mind of anger, affliction, envy, or distraction.

The body of the True Tathāgata is endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; it cannot be honored through offerings made with a mind of stinginess, broken precepts, malice, indolence, agitation, or delusion.

“Kāśyapa! When Dharmasubhūti preached this Dharma in the midst of the great assembly, four million two hundred thousand sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); eighty-four thousand sentient beings attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin through pure wisdom; and two million three hundred thousand sentient beings resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Kāśyapa! Observe the purity of mind of the two bhikṣus, Dharmaka and Sudharmaka. Kāśyapa!”
"You should learn from those noble beings their profound patience and skillful means.
Kāśyapa, when those two bhikṣus were preaching this Dharma in the midst of the great assembly!"
Having heard this Dharma, all the bhikṣus abided in profound patience;
they all practiced the conduct of few desires and contentment,
and did not make offerings to śarīras, Buddha-stūpas, or temples.
Why is this? Because all those bhikṣus delight in the profound Dharma, Kāśyapa!
After seven days, all the Buddha-stūpas will completely disappear, and the reliquaries containing the śarīras will likewise all vanish. Kāśyapa!
“You should train yourself in this way: ‘I shall emulate the profound patience of those true beings. The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“You should know that in the final five hundred years of the末法 (mofa) age, there will be bodhisattvas and bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate the mind, do not cultivate ethical discipline, and do not cultivate wisdom. For the sake of their livelihood, they will make offerings to Buddha-stūpas and the Buddha’s relics; yet they do not practice these offerings for the sake of nirvāṇa or for the sake of detachment from desire. Having themselves violated the prohibitions and being foolish and ignorant, they nevertheless honor and revere the Tathāgata’s relics—which are permeated by the cultivation of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—merely for the sake of their livelihood.”

One who possesses greed, hatred, and delusion might offer worship to the relics of the Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who are themselves free from greed, hatred, and delusion, solely for the sake of maintaining a livelihood; yet that person remains personally possessed of stinginess, greed, envy, malice, indolence, distraction, and folly. Alternatively, a great donor who abides correctly in a single-minded state might, for the sake of maintaining a livelihood, transform others to offer worship to the relics of the Tathāgata.

Kāśyapa! For the sake of teaching and transforming those sons and daughters of good family who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, I have used my supernormal powers to leave behind these relics, so that those who make offerings to them may enjoy the bliss of humans and devas, and establish the causes for future lives until they reach nirvāṇa.

Although those foolish people have gone forth within my Dharma, they do not understand my Dharma; they abandon the practice of renunciation and instead worship stupas, temples, and relics for the sake of their own livelihood, for the sake of obtaining robes and bowls, for the sake of gain and offerings, and for the sake of fame—it is for these purposes that they worship the relics.
What is called the activity of a bhikṣu? Kāśyapa,
the activities of a śramaṇa as described above are of two kinds:
The first is the cultivation of dhyāna; the second is the practice of recitation.
Such an explanation is for the purpose of entering the Path, not the ultimate teaching. Kāśyapa!
If there is a practice that can exhaust all karma, it is called the practice of a śramaṇa.

To be without action and without recitation, without dhyāna; to be without action and without non-action; to be without mindfulness and without non-mindfulness; to be without exhaustion and without arising; to realize the three gates of liberation and not dwell within the triple world; to be without coming and without going—this is the practice of a śramaṇa.
Those sentient beings, having abandoned this right action, practice other actions.
That meritorious action is for the sake of transforming householders; thus, householders who follow the Tathāgata’s teaching shall attain the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
Those foolish people have gone forth into homelessness within my Dharma, yet they do not even practice the teachings that accord with it; how much less could they possibly attain [realization]?
If there were anyone who could attain it, such a thing would be impossible.

“Kāśyapa! In the future age, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who resemble śramaṇas; their robes and physical appearance will be like those of śramaṇas, yet their ethical discipline will not be like it, their meditative concentration will not be like it, and their wisdom will not be like it.”

Kāśyapa! It is like a person who is well-versed in medical formulas and various incantations; he uses an incantation to consecrate a single monastic robe and gives it to someone to wear. Upon seeing it, that person conceives a desire for it and immediately puts it on.
If seven days or eight days have passed, his body becomes as blazing as a mass of fire.
Just as when that incantation has been performed and it is taken and given to someone, and that person, having seen it, immediately conceives a greedy attachment;

so too is it with the bhikṣu: seeing fine robes, he accepts and wears them. Whether after seven days or eight days, whether inside a house, in a lane, or in a forest, the robes he wears blaze like fire and burn away his roots of goodness.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Is there any benefit in that person wearing the kāṣāya?
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One,
it would be of no benefit.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “So it is, so it is.

My *kāṣāya* is the accumulation of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* roots of goodness consisting of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.”
Kāśyapa! In future ages there will be foolish people who, wearing the robes of the noble ones, resemble śramaṇas in appearance and enter among the villages and towns.
When faithful brahmins, elders, and householders see them clad in dharma-robes, they will assume them to be true śramaṇas and will all together respect, support, and praise them.
That foolish person, having received offerings because of his *kāṣāya*, gives rise to joy; when his body perishes and his life ends, he falls into hell.
Having been born in hell, he takes great hot iron plates as clothing, swallows iron balls, drinks molten boiling iron, and sits upon a hot iron bed.
Kāśyapa! Behold, such is the majestic power of the kāṣāya.
Those foolish people who wear the kāṣāya yet indulge in pleasure and negligence, committing evil deeds for themselves, will fall into hell when their bodies perish and their lives end.
Kāśyapa! I have always said: it would be better to wear a garment made of glowing, red-hot iron than to wear the *kāṣāya* with a body that has broken the precepts;
it would be better to swallow hot iron than to consume the offerings of the faithful with a body that has broken the precepts.
Kāśyapa! Observe that those who break the precepts incur such faults by consuming the offerings of the faithful; therefore, you all should cultivate and train in the dharma of pure precepts.
Kāśyapa! What do you think?
Whether it be a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a gandharva, an asura, a garuḍa, a kiṃnara, a mahoraga, a human, or a non-human—could any of them create an image of the Tathāgata’s physical body?
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One.”
"The physical form of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, because he has no physical form.
For this reason, none of these can create it.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“In the future, during the final five hundred years, there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate the mind, do not cultivate ethical discipline, and do not cultivate wisdom. They will create images of the Tathāgata upon cloth or beneath walls and thereby make a living; on account of this karma, they will hold themselves in high esteem and look down upon others.”
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does King Prasenajit gain much merit by creating an image of the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa, the merit obtained is exceedingly great.”
King Prasenajit fashioned an image of the Tathāgata and offered it a priceless robe, yet he did not seek any reward for clothing or food.
Kāśyapa! Those foolish people fashion images for the sake of their livelihood.
Kāśyapa! Even selling livestock is still unwholesome; how much more so for that deluded person who fashions an image of the Tathāgata and peddles it before laypeople to sustain their own livelihood?
Kāśyapa! It is like a person who, being young and ignorant, abandons ambrosia to drink poisonous medicine. Kāśyapa!
That foolish person is just like this: having fashioned an image of the Tathāgata, they sell it for the sake of their livelihood; this is what is called "poison. Kāśyapa!
Regarding what is called "poison," within the True Dharma, craving is its poison. Kāśyapa!

Because of that craving, those foolish people give rise to anger; they contend with one another and mutually slander each other, each claiming, "I am practicing offerings. Due to such disputes, they fall into hell.
Kāśyapa! It is like a person who, lacking skillful means, enters into battle and instead of conquering the enemy, uses the sword he carries to wound himself. Kāśyapa!
Foolish people are likewise; because they lack skillful means, they fall into hell on account of the Dharma. Kāśyapa!

If there were good sons or good daughters who, using the seven treasures, constructed stūpas for the Tathāgata, fully adorned and perfected, each stūpa being as high, vast, and magnificent as Mount Sumeru, filling Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, like a field of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
One who creates an image of the Tathāgata even as small as four finger-breadths will obtain immeasurable merit.”
"How much more so, then, for one who creates an image as large as Mount Sumeru; the merit obtained would be inconceivable.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, through internal contemplation of the Buddha’s body, attains profound dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti), their merit will surpass that [of the former] by immeasurable and boundless degrees."
Kāśyapa! If there is another person who abides in pure precepts and explains a four-line verse to others, elucidating its meaning and intent, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless.
Kāśyapa! How does one contemplate the body of the Tathāgata? Kāśyapa!
If a bodhisattva wishes to contemplate the Tathāgata, they should train like the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya.

Kāśyapa, in the distant past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Prabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Kāśyapa! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Prabhāsa, there was a bodhisattva named Mahāvīrya, born of the Brahmin caste, who was peerlessly handsome.
Kāśyapa! Within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata Prabhāsa, there are bhikṣus who have few desires, are content, and abide in practice according to the Dharma. Kāśyapa!
Those bhikṣus all fashioned and erected images of the Tathāgata.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who painted an image of the Tathāgata upon white cotton cloth, fully adorned with all manner of colors; he then carried it to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya was.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahā-vīrya, seeing this painted image, was filled with great joy and spoke these words:
"The form of the Tathāgata is so exquisitely beautiful; how much more so, then, must be the body of the Tathāgata, the Truly All-Knowing One!"
"May I, in a future life, attain such a body of wondrous form.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahā-vīrya thought to himself:
"I can no longer remain living as a householder."
"One who lives as a householder cannot achieve such a body. Kāśyapa!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya was sixteen years of age, with all his faculties fully developed; he went to his parents, prostrated himself in reverence, and addressed them, saying:
"I now wish to leave the household life and study the Path within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata;
I pray that you will grant me your approval. His parents replied, "Do not speak such words."
"Why is this? I am now old and you are my only son; if you renounce the household life, we shall die. Mahā-vīrya said:
"I shall employ skillful means to ensure my parents survive so that I may go forth into the homeless life. His parents asked,
"What work do you wish to perform?"
The son said to his parents:

"From this day forth, I shall not eat any flavors, I shall not ascend to sit upon a bed, I shall not consume ghee or oil, and I shall not drink gruel or water; whether good or evil, I shall not speak with my mouth, until I have attained the state of going forth."
"Kāśyapa! After the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya had made this vow, he remained silent. Thus he remained silent for one day without eating.
At that time, his parents recited various incantations and offered him food of a hundred flavors, yet he was unwilling to eat and did not speak at all."
Kāśyapa! The Bodhisattva Mahā-vīrya remained thus silent for a second day.
At that time, his parents and five hundred kinswomen brought food of a hundred flavors to his location, reciting various incantations in the hope that he would partake of it.
He did not even look at them, let alone eat them. Kāśyapa!

On the third day, five hundred paternal uncles of Mahā-vīrya brought various kinds of food and urged him to eat, but he likewise remained silent and spoke not; he neither drank nor ate, nor did he even look at them.
On the fourth day, five hundred companions brought food of a hundred flavors and recited various incantations, seeking to bring him under their will.
At that time, Mahā-vīrya remained silent.

On the fifth day, the parents then brought forth their entire treasure storehouse—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and various other precious objects—as well as eighty-four thousand exquisite and magnificently adorned court ladies, and led them to where he was.
His father, mother, and five hundred companions each exhorted Mahā-vīrya, saying: "You should remain at home;
with these treasures, give as much as you wish in alms to create merit, and enjoy yourself together with these court ladies."
At that time, Mahā-vīrya remained silent amidst the great assembly, never casting even a glance about.
On the sixth day, he severed all recollections and thoughts, giving rise to no thought of food, but focused his mind solely on the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyak-saṃbuddha.
Kāśyapa! At that time, his parents, their acquaintances, and eighty-four thousand exquisite court ladies all wept together and paid homage to Mahāvīrya.
At that time, Mahāsthāmaprāpta did not even look back. Kāśyapa!
At that moment, there was a house-deity at the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta was staying; manifesting great supernatural power in the midst of the sky, he spoke these verses:
"With a firm and resolute mind of diligence, as immovable as Mount Sumeru,
he does not abandon the aspiration for renunciation in order to attain bodhi."
The great earth may be shaken, and fire may dwell within the waters;
such things as these may be overturned, but the Bodhisattva cannot be moved.
You all must not undergo such hardship as to commit unwholesome deeds.
Sentient beings lack the eye of wisdom, Abiding for long ages within birth and death.
To benefit all living beings, I therefore seek bodhi;
With a mind that delights in renunciation, I shall surely accomplish the unsurpassed path.
Without seeking worldly rewards, one practices the bodhisattva path,
vowing to achieve the wisdom of great enlightenment to rescue and deliver suffering sentient beings.
Even if the three-thousandfold world system were filled with precious jewels, [it would not equal the merit of this].
And toward all sublime lands, their minds feel no greedy attachment.
You, with your foolish minds, have committed unwholesome deeds;
you should repent of these transgressions yourselves, for Bodhisattvas do not dwell in the mundane world.
“Kāśyapa! At that time, the parents, relatives, friends, and female attendants of the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya, having heard the words of the deva, all repented their faults and said to the Bodhisattva:
‘Leave the household life as you wish.’”
"You should take food and drink; do not let yourself perish.

Kāśyapa! At that time, Mahā-vīrya did not eat for seven days; his radiance was brilliant and joyful, and his complexion remained unchanged. His mind focused solely on recollecting the body of the Samyaksaṃbuddha, while all the devas scattered flowers as an offering.
When the time of Great Diligence had passed seven days, he abandoned all his household affairs as if discarding mucus or spittle.
At that time, his parents, friends, acquaintances, and eighty-four thousand court ladies all wept with grief as they followed him to see him off.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahā-vīrya took the painted cloth image and entered a deep mountain, a secluded place devoid of people and inhabited only by birds and beasts. There he opened and displayed the image, gathered grass to serve as a seat, and sat before the image in the full lotus posture, straightening his body and maintaining right mindfulness as he contemplated the Tathāgata.
Having observed this with discernment, he formed this thought:
"The Tathāgata is thus rare and subtle; if even a painted image is so upright, dignified, and exquisite, how much more so is the body of the Tathāgata, the Truly All-Knowing One!"
Again, he thought to himself:
"How should one contemplate the Buddha?
At that time, the forest deity, knowing what was in the bodhisattva's mind, addressed the bodhisattva, saying:
"Good son! You should reflect in this way: How does one contemplate the Buddha?
If you wish to contemplate the Buddha, you should contemplate a painted image; contemplating this painted image as no different from the Tathāgata is called contemplating the Buddha."
"One who observes in this manner is said to observe correctly.
At that time, Mahā-vīrya thought to himself:
"How should I now observe this painted image so that it is equal to the Tathāgata?"
Again, he had this thought:
"The image of the Tathāgata neither perceives nor knows; all dharmas are likewise neither perceiving nor knowing.
Such an image exists only as a name; all dharmas are likewise only names. These names are by nature empty and quiescent, being nothing at all."
The body of the Tathāgata has such characteristics as these.
This painted image is not realization, not attainment, and not fruition; it is neither one who realizes, nor one who attains, nor one who obtains fruition.

It is neither abiding, nor going, nor coming; neither arising nor ceasing; neither defiled nor pure; neither form nor non-form; neither the exhaustion of greed, nor the exhaustion of hatred, nor the exhaustion of delusion; it is not the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; it is neither beginning, nor middle, nor end.
All dharmas are likewise so, and the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are likewise so.
Just as this painted image is neither conscious nor active, all dharmas are likewise so, and the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are likewise so.
Such a painted image is neither seen, nor heard, nor smelled, nor tasted, nor touched, nor known; it is neither exhalation nor inhalation. All phenomena are likewise thus, having no knower.
This painted image is not comprised within the realm of desire, nor is it comprised within the realms of form or formlessness;

all phenomena are likewise so. This painted image is neither beginning, middle, nor end; neither this nor that; neither conditioned activity nor non-activity; neither grasping nor relinquishing; neither performing nor reciting; neither real nor unreal; neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa—all phenomena are likewise so, and the bodily marks of the Tathāgata are likewise so.

Thus the Bodhisattva contemplates the body of the Tathāgata; sitting cross-legged through day and night, he accomplishes the five supernormal powers, becomes fully endowed with the immeasurable qualities, attains unimpeded eloquence, and achieves the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, possessing great light.
He achieves the divine eye, which surpasses that of ordinary humans; with this divine eye, he sees the Buddhas of the eastern direction, as many as incalculable asaṃkhyeyas.
He attains the pure divine ear, by which he is able to hear and receive all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Because his divine ear was purified, he heard, received, and retained every dharma taught by each of the Buddhas without any obstruction. Kāśyapa!

At that time, Mahā-vīrya practiced diligence for seven full days; taking wisdom as his sustenance, he did not eat the offerings of the world, while all the devas scattered flowers as an offering to him.

Kāśyapa, at that time, Mahā-vīrya did not wear the kāṣāya robe nor did he see the Buddha; he did not receive the prohibitive precepts, but his mind was solely intent on recollecting and training for sarvajñatā.
Kāśyapa! A bodhisattva should contemplate the body of the Tathāgata in this way: neither as an object of contemplation nor as not an object of contemplation. Kāśyapa!

A bodhisattva should contemplate an image of the Tathāgata in this manner, just as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahā-vīrya contemplates an image of the Tathāgata. Having accomplished such contemplation, one attains great wisdom; by means of this wisdom, one perceives all the asaṃkhyeya Buddhas of the ten directions and hears the Buddhas preaching the Dharma.

Kāśyapa! At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya emerged from the mountain and came to a village to preach the Dharma for the people. During one assembly of preaching, twenty thousand sentient beings established themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings established themselves in the merits of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; their parents and kinsmen all established themselves in the non-retrogressive state of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kāśyapa! Do not harbor other thoughts.
As for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāvīrya at that time, could he possibly have been anyone else?
I am that very person. Kāśyapa, for this reason,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the great diligence of the bodhisattva mahāsattva [Vīradatta], and should likewise train in the practices of all other great bodhisattvas.

Kāśyapa, in the future final age, during the last five hundred years, there will be certain sons of good family who seek the bodhisattva path; lacking the mind of skillful means and being full of many attachments, they will paint images of the Tathāgata beneath walls in order to seek gain and offerings.
He speaks thus: "I alone make offerings; no one else makes offerings.
Cultivating only a small amount of merit, he holds himself in high esteem and looks down upon others, sustaining his life by means of such offerings.

"Bhagavān! The Buddha said: “Śāriputra, it is so, it is so; it is just as you have said.”
Śāriputra, this sphere of wisdom, skillful means, and samādhi of these bodhisattvas is that which all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to know.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to manifest the supernatural transformations of all buddhas, fulfilling all the desires and pleasures of sentient beings, while their minds remain unmoved regarding all phenomena.

If there are sentient beings who delight in being householders and are arrogant and heedless, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of bringing them to maturity, manifests the majestic body of a great householder and preaches the Dharma to them.

If there are sentient beings who, relying on their great power and influence, become arrogant, the Bodhisattva, in order to subdue them, manifests the body of Nārāyaṇa with great strength and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are sentient beings who aspire to seek nirvana, the Bodhisattva, at that time, for the sake of delivering them, manifests in the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating dependent origination, the Bodhisattva, at that time, for the sake of delivering them, manifests in the body of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are sentient beings who aspire to seek bodhi, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of delivering them, immediately manifests the body of a Buddha to lead them into the wisdom of a Buddha.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
These bodhisattvas, through various skillful means, bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them all to dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma.

Why is this so? Because there is only the wisdom and liberation of the Tathāgata, the ultimate nirvāṇa; there is no other vehicle by which one may attain deliverance. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because the Tathāgata has awakened to reality as it truly is, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because he knows the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings and is able to manifest them all, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because he has accomplished the root of all wholesome dharmas and severed the root of all unwholesome dharmas, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because he can show sentient beings the path to liberation, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because he can cause sentient beings to leave the false paths and abide in the true path, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because he expounds the true meaning of emptiness regarding all phenomena, he is called the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva thus knows the various inclinations and desires of all sentient beings and teaches the Dharma accordingly so that they may attain liberation.

For the sake of all foolish worldlings, he reveals true wisdom; while remaining unmoved from the dharma-realm, he can manifest various illusory transformations and adornments, causing all sentient beings to gradually reach the shore of nirvana.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a lay bodhisattva who dwells in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, free from malice and harm, should practice two kinds of giving. What are these two?
First is the gift of Dharma, and second is the gift of material wealth.
A renunciant bodhisattva should practice four kinds of giving. What are these four?
First is the gift of brushes, second is the gift of ink, third is the gift of the sūtra texts, and fourth is the gift of the Dharma through preaching.
A Bodhisattva who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) should abide in these three gifts.
What are these three?
They are the giving away of one’s royal throne, the giving away of one’s wife and children, and the giving away of all one’s limbs, including the head and eyes.
Giving in such a manner is called a great gift; it is called a most sublime gift.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

Are these bodhisattvas not afraid of greed, hatred, and delusion?"
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, all bodhisattvas have two kinds of transgressions of the precepts.”
What are these two? First, an offense associated with hatred; second, an offense associated with delusion.
These two types of offenses are called "great violations of the precepts."
Śāriputra! An offense committed due to greed is subtle and difficult to abandon;
an offense committed due to anger is coarse and easy to abandon.
Regarding those who commit offenses due to delusion (*moha*), their transgression is profound and grave, and it is furthermore difficult to abandon. Why is this so?

Because the fetter of greed (*rāga-saṃyojana*) serves as the seed for all states of existence (*bhava*); it causes the creeping vine of birth and death to extend and persist without interruption. For this reason, it is subtle and difficult to sever.
Those who commit offenses out of anger may fall into the evil realms, yet these can be swiftly eliminated.
Those who commit offenses out of delusion shall fall into the eight great hells, from which liberation is difficult to attain.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if there is a bodhisattva who has committed a pārājika offense, they should, before ten pure bhikṣus, repent with a sincere and earnest mind."

If one has been touched by a woman with a defiled mind, or if attachment has arisen due to mutual gazing, one should perform a solemn confession before one or two pure monks.

Śāriputra! if a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of great compassion, they are able to manifest the realms of hell, animals, and the world of Yama in order to bring sentient beings to maturity.

Why is this? Although a bodhisattva manifests in various ways in accordance with sentient beings, they do not perceive the marks of a body or the marks of birth, for these are unobtainable. Śāriputra!

At that time, Upāli arose from meditative concentration, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While sitting alone in a quiet place, I reflected and had this thought:

"Regarding the training in the pure precepts of the Prātimokṣa taught by the World-Honored One, he has declared for those of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva vehicles that they would rather give up their bodies and lives than ever abandon the precepts."
World-Honored One!
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, what is called the prātimokṣa of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
And what is called the prātimokṣa of those who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle?
“The World-Honored One has declared that I am foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya; how then could I possibly master the meaning of skillfulness in the Vinaya?
Only after hearing it directly from the Buddha, receiving and upholding it, and attaining fearlessness shall I be able to explain it extensively for others.”
Now this great assembly of bodhisattvas and the community of bhikṣus have all gathered together. How excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will extensively expound the definitive Vinaya to eliminate doubt and regret.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli:
"You should now know that the minds generated and the practices cultivated by Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas as they train in the pure precepts are different."
Upāli! There are those who uphold the pure precepts of the Śrāvaka vehicle, yet in regard to the Bodhisattva vehicle, this is called a great breach of discipline.
There are those who uphold the pure precepts of the Bodhisattva vehicle, yet in regard to the Śrāvaka vehicle, this is called a great breach of discipline.
What is meant by saying that although a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle maintains pure precepts, they are called one who has greatly violated the precepts in relation to the Bodhisattva vehicle? Upāli!

A person of the Śrāvaka vehicle should not give rise to even a single thought of receiving further future bodies; this is called the pure maintenance of precepts by a Śrāvaka, yet in relation to a Bodhisattva, it is called a great violation of the precepts.
How is it that a bodhisattva who maintains pure precepts is said to be a great violator of precepts according to the Śrāvaka vehicle?

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Mahāyāna, he is able to endure bodily suffering throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas without giving rise to weariness or aversion; this is called a bodhisattva maintaining pure precepts, yet according to the Śrāvaka vehicle, it is called a great violation of precepts.

For this reason, for those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle, it is taught that they do not maintain the precepts exhaustively; for those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, it is taught that they maintain the precepts exhaustively.
For all Bodhisattvas, it is taught the precepts of both permission and prohibition; for all Śrāvakas, it is taught only the precepts of prohibition.
For those of the Bodhisattva vehicle, the precepts of the profound mind are taught; for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the precepts of sequential practice are taught.
Why is it that Bodhisattvas uphold the precepts of inexhaustible protection, while those of the Śrāvaka vehicle uphold the precepts of exhaustive protection?
Although those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle maintain pure precepts, they should accord with all sentient beings, whereas those of the Śrāvaka vehicle should not so accord.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas maintain the precepts of non-exhaustive protection, while those of the Śrāvaka vehicle maintain the precepts of exhaustive protection.
What is meant by a bodhisattva observing the precepts of both permission and prohibition, whereas a follower of the Śrāvaka vehicle observes only the precepts of prohibition?

If a bodhisattva who has set out in the practice of the Mahāyāna commits an offense during the first part of the day, yet does not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) during the middle part of the day, the bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) remains unimpaired.

If one commits a transgression against the precepts during the middle part of the day, yet does not depart from the mind of omniscience during the latter part of the day, the bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline remains unimpaired.

If one commits a transgression against the precepts during the latter part of the day, yet does not depart from the mind of omniscience during the first part of the night, the bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline remains unimpaired.

If one has transgressed the precepts during the first watch of the night, yet does not depart from the mind of omniscience during the middle watch of the night, the bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline remains unimpaired.

If one has transgressed the precepts during the middle watch of the night, yet does not depart from the mind of omniscience during the final watch of the night, the bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline remains unimpaired.

If one has transgressed any precept during the latter part of the night, provided that at the first part of the day one does not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), the bodhisattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) remains unimpaired.

For this reason, those who follow the Bodhisattva Vehicle and uphold the precepts of permission and prohibition should not lose mindfulness even if they have committed a transgression; they must not give rise to groundless anxiety or regret to distress their own minds.
If one commits an offense regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle, one thereby destroys the pure precepts of a Śrāvaka.

Why is this? Because those who uphold the precepts in the Śrāvaka vehicle sever the afflictions as if their heads were on fire; their sole aspiration is to seek nirvāṇa. For this reason, it is said that upholding the prohibitive precepts constitutes the Śrāvaka vehicle.
"Furthermore, Upāli! How is it that a bodhisattva upholds the precepts of profound penetration, whereas a follower of the Śrāvaka vehicle upholds the precepts of sequential progression?

If a person of the Bodhisattva Vehicle enjoys the pleasures of the five desires with sovereign play for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, yet never abandons the mind of enlightenment, such a bodhisattva is not said to have lost the precepts."

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva is well able to guard and abide securely in the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), such that even in dreams all fetters (*saṃyojana*) do not become an affliction for them; rather, all the afflictions of this bodhisattva shall gradually come to an end, yet they should not exhaust all fetters in a single lifetime.
Those of the Śrāvaka vehicle mature their roots of goodness as if their heads were on fire; they do not take pleasure in receiving birth for even a single thought-moment.
For this reason, those of the Mahāyāna maintain the precepts of profound penetration, which include both permissions and prohibitions, and are thus called "incomplete protection."
Those of the Śrāvaka vehicle who maintain the sequential precepts are said to possess "mere prohibition" and are called "those who guard exhaustively.
Why is this so, Upāli?
For those who seek the Mahāyāna, it is extremely difficult to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; only by being fully equipped with great adornments can one achieve it.
Therefore, although Bodhisattvas come and go through birth and death for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they never give rise to a mind of weariness or revulsion.

For this reason, when the Tathāgata observes those of the Mahāyāna, he should not exclusively teach the dharma of wearying detachment, nor should he exclusively teach the dharma for the swift realization of nirvāṇa.

One should preach for them the Dharma associated with loving-kindness and compassion, which is profound, subtle, and untainted; the Dharma that is free from sorrow and regret and devoid of attachment; and the Dharma of non-obstruction and non-hindrance, which is empty by nature.
"Having heard this, the bodhisattva will feel no weariness within saṃsāra and will certainly fulfill unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If there is a bodhisattva who violates the precepts through association with a mind of greed, or a bodhisattva who violates the precepts through association with a mind of hatred, or a bodhisattva who violates the precepts through association with a mind of delusion.
“World-Honored One!
Among these three types of transgressions, which is the most serious?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli, saying:

"If bodhisattvas practicing the Mahāyāna for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges should violate the precepts while their minds are associated with greed, their transgression is still relatively light.
However, if they violate the precepts through a single moment of anger, their transgression is exceedingly grave."
Why is this? Because one violates the precepts out of greed while gathering in sentient beings, and one violates the precepts out of anger while abandoning sentient beings. Upāli!
Regarding all fetters that can bind sentient beings, a bodhisattva should not give rise to fear;
regarding all fetters that can abandon sentient beings, a bodhisattva should give rise to dread.

Upāli! As the Buddha has taught, greed is difficult to abandon, yet its fault is subtle; hatred is easy to abandon, yet its fault is coarse and heavy; delusion is both difficult to abandon and its fault is likewise coarse and heavy.
Upāli! Among afflictions, if it is difficult to abandon a minor offense, a bodhisattva should endure it;
however, if it is easy to abandon a grave offense, such an affliction should not be tolerated even in a dream.
For this reason, when a follower of the Mahāyāna violates the precepts out of desire, I say that such a person is not considered to have committed an offense.
However, violating the precepts out of anger constitutes a grave violation; it is called a great affliction and a great fall, and within the Buddha-dharma, it is a major obstacle.
Upāli! If bodhisattvas lack skillful means regarding the Vinaya, they will feel fear toward offenses associated with greed, yet they will not feel fear toward offenses associated with anger.

If bodhisattvas possess skillful means regarding the Vinaya, they do not give rise to fear toward offenses associated with greed, yet they give rise to great fear toward offenses associated with anger.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, amidst the great assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are ultimately *vinaya*, what is there to be tamed?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If ordinary beings were to fully understand that all phenomena are ultimately *vinaya*, the Tathāgata would never speak of discipline.”
"Because they do not know, the Tathāgata, in order to cause them to awaken to the ultimate vinaya of all dharmas, has gradually taught the various vinaya teachings.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata has preached this definitive discipline (*vinaya*), yet Mañjuśrī has not yet spoken anything within this Dharma.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you would cause Mañjuśrī to provide a brief explanation.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“You should now explain the meaning of skillfulness in the ultimate Vinaya; Upāli wishes to hear it with longing.”
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said to Upāli:
"All dharmas are ultimately quiescent; because the mind is quiescent, it is called ultimate vinaya."
In all phenomena, a self cannot be found; because there is no defilement or attachment, it is called the Vinaya of Non-Regret.
All phenomena are pure by nature; because they are free from inversion, it is called the Supreme Vinaya.
All dharmas are suchness and the limit of reality; because they are free from all views, they are called the pure *vinaya*.
All dharmas neither come nor go; because they are without discrimination, they are called the inconceivable *vinaya*.
All dharmas are without abiding and without attachment; because they perish moment by moment, they are called the Vinaya that purifies all realms of existence (*sarvagati-viśuddhi-vinaya*).
All dharmas abide at the limit of space (*ākāśakoṭi*); because they are free from all marks (*nimitta*), they are called the Vinaya of natural detachment (*svabhāva-vivikta-vinaya*).
All phenomena have no past, future, or present; because they cannot be apprehended, it is called the Vinaya of the Equality of the Three Times.
All phenomena cannot be established, for the mind is equal; thus it is called the Vinaya of the Permanent Severance of Doubt.
Upāli! This is the ultimate *vinaya* of the *dharmadhātu*, upon which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, rely to attain the Way.
If a son of good family does not skillfully examine this Dharma, he will be far removed from the pure precepts of the Tathāgata.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The teachings spoken by Mañjuśrī regarding all dharmas are inconceivable.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli, saying:
“The Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī is based upon inconceivable and unimpeded liberation.”

For this reason, whatever Dharma I teach is free from all mental characteristics and is called the liberation of the mind; it is intended to cause those with overweening pride to become free from that pride.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are those of the śrāvaka and bodhisattva vehicles who possess overweening pride?”
The Buddha told Upāli:
"If there is a bhikṣu who reflects thus:
'I have severed craving.'"
To say, "I have severed anger and delusion," is called overweening pride. To say, "I have severed anger as well as delusion," is called overweening pride.
"To say, 'The phenomena of greed are different, and the phenomena of all Buddhas are different,' is called overweening pride (adhimāna). To say,
'The phenomena of hatred are different, and the phenomena of all Buddhas are different'..."

To say, "The dharmas of the foolish are different, and the dharmas of the Buddhas are different," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*). To say, "The dharmas of the foolish are different, and the dharmas of the Buddhas are different," is called overweening pride.
To claim there is something to be attained is called overweening pride.
To claim there is something to be realized is called overweening pride.
To claim there is liberation is called overweening pride.
To perceive all phenomena as empty is called overweening pride.
To perceive the signless is called overweening pride.
To perceive the wishless is called overweening pride.
To perceive non-arising is called overweening pride.
To perceive that there is nothing to be done is called overweening pride.
To perceive the existence of various dharmas is called overweening pride.
To perceive that phenomena are impermanent is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To say, "Since all phenomena are empty, what is the use of cultivation?
is called overweening pride.
Upāli! These are called those of the Śrāvaka vehicle who possess overweening pride.
What are those of the Bodhisattva vehicle who possess overweening pride?
If bodhisattvas form this thought:
"I shall resolve my mind to seek all-knowledge," it is called overweening pride.
To think, "I shall practice the six pāramitās," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think, "One attains liberation solely by relying on the prajñāpāramitā; there is no other dharma through which one may achieve transcendence," [is likewise overweening pride].
To say, "This is overweening pride.
To say, "This dharma is profound; this is not profound," is called overweening pride.
To say, "This dharma is pure; this dharma is not pure," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*). To say, "These are the dharmas of the Buddhas;
these are the dharmas of the *pratyekabuddhas*; these are the dharmas of the *śrāvakas*," [is likewise overweening pride].
To say, "This is called overweening pride.
To say, "This dharma should be practiced; this should not be practiced," is called overweening pride.
To say, "This is a profound teaching; this is not a profound teaching," is called overweening pride.
To say, "This is an accessible teaching; this is not an accessible teaching," is called overweening pride.
To say, "This is overweening pride," or "This is the right path; this is the wrong path," is called overweening pride.
"To think, 'Will I quickly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment,
or will I not quickly attain it?
is called overweening pride."
To say, "All phenomena are inconceivable and there is no one who can know them,
yet I am able to fully understand them," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Even to the point of giving rise to conceptualization regarding inconceivable *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* constitutes a great attachment; such a person is called a bodhisattva who possesses overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bhikṣu become free from overweening pride?”
The Buddha told Upāli:
"If one has no attachment toward any inconceivable dharmas, this is called ultimate freedom from overweening pride."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All conceptual proliferations arise from the mind; One should not discriminate between what is dharma and what is non-dharma.
Seeing the Dharma in this way as inconceivable, Such a person dwells in the world in constant peace and bliss."
Ordinary beings, deluded, follow the turning of their own minds, Cycling through the various realms of existence for many eons.
If one knows that the nature of phenomena is entirely without self-nature, This is called the truly inconceivable.

If there is a bhikṣu who recollects the Buddhas, yet his reflection is not skillful and his mindfulness is not correct, he gives rise to false conceptualizations regarding the Buddha; these conceptualizations possess no reality.
If there are those who contemplate empty phenomena, such ordinary persons abide in a false path;
they merely speak of emptiness through words, yet how can words and emptiness be found?
If one contemplates the dharma of tranquility, this mind does not exist, for it is fundamentally unarisen;
mental activities of vitarka and vicāra are all mere conceptual proliferation; the absence of such thought is called seeing all dharmas as they truly are.
All phenomena are devoid of thought; where there is mind or recollection, all is empty.
If one delights in observing emptiness, do not give rise to thoughts regarding this non-thought.
Dharmas are like grass and trees, devoid of cognition; If separated from the mind, they cannot be found.
The intrinsic nature of sentient beings does not exist; All dharmas are exactly thus.
Just as the eye can see by means of sunlight, yet at night, due to the absence of conditions, nothing is perceived;
if the eye were inherently able to see forms, why would it require conditions in order to perceive them?
The eye constantly relies on various lights to perceive diverse colors such as blue and yellow;
one should know that the nature of seeing depends on manifold conditions, and therefore the eye itself cannot see.
Should one hear various pleasant sounds, upon hearing them they immediately cease and do not abide;
their place of departure cannot be found, for it is through conceptual discrimination that the perception of sound arises.
All phenomena are merely sounds, with characters provisionally established therein;
these sounds possess neither dharma nor non-dharma, yet the foolish, not knowing this, give rise to false attachments.
I praise the giving of alms for the sake of the world, yet the root of giving cannot be apprehended;
within that which is ineffable, I proclaim it—therefore, the Buddha-dharma is inconceivable.
I constantly praise and speak of upholding the pure precepts, yet there is no sentient being who breaks the precepts;
the nature of breaking the precepts is like empty space, and the pure upholding of the precepts is likewise so.
I declare that patience is supreme; its nature is the vision of non-arising.
Since there is not even the slightest phenomenon toward which one could feel anger, it is for this reason called "supreme patience."
I say that one should always be diligent day and night, maintaining constant awareness whether awake or asleep as the unsurpassed state;
though one may practice with diligence for many kalpas, there is neither increase nor decrease in what has been accomplished.
Dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi—these open the door to the reality of the world as it is;
though the nature of phenomena is fundamentally unmoving, one provisionally speaks of various dhyānas in accordance with conventional usage.
To observe and awaken to this is called wisdom; to thoroughly understand all phenomena is called a person of knowledge.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not exist, nor is there anyone who observes or understands them.
I have always praised the practice of asceticism, Delighting in the dhūta-dharmas and the dharma of tranquility;
One who can know that all phenomena are unattainable— Such a person is called pure and contented.

When I speak of the various sufferings of hell, and how one dies to enter the great terrors of the evil realms, immeasurable sentient beings give rise to a mind of revulsion; yet in reality, there are no evil destinies to come and go between.
Swords, staves, spears, lances, and all manner of instruments of suffering—none of these have any creator;
they appear to exist only through conceptual discrimination, as immeasurable agonies and torments oppress the body.
In the gardens, various wondrous flowers bloom; The palaces, made of many jewels, reflect one another’s brilliance.
Yet there is no person who could have created them; They all arise from the deluded mind of discrimination.
The deceptive dharma deludes the world; ordinary beings, bound by attachment, give rise to perversions.
Just as one discriminates various illusions and mirages, all grasping and rejecting herein are entirely empty.
I say that the arousal of the mind directed toward enlightenment is the most supreme benefit for the world;
yet in reality, enlightenment is unattainable, and there is no one who arouses the mind directed toward enlightenment.
The nature of the mind is pure and ever-luminous; it is true, without falsehood, and free from attachment.
While ordinary beings give rise to craving through their conceptual discriminations, those afflictions are fundamentally empty.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally quiescent; how could there be desire, hatred, or delusion?
Not perceiving the arising of desire nor the state of detachment from it, one is then said to have attained nirvāṇa.
When the mind never gives rise to defiled attachment, by this one accomplishes great bodhi.
Having cultivated myriad practices throughout incalculable eons, you have liberated immeasurable sentient beings;
yet the self-nature of sentient beings cannot be found, for in truth there are no sentient beings to be liberated.
It is like a great illusionist of the world who conjures up boundless billions of multitudes.
Even if one were to harm these manifested beings, there would be no increase or decrease in this illusory transformation.
All sentient beings are like illusions and transformations; their limits cannot be found.
If one knows such boundless nature, that person will dwell in the world without weariness.
Thoroughly knowing the true nature of all phenomena, they constantly dwell within birth and death as nirvāṇa;
though truly untainted amidst all desires, they subdue sentient beings by speaking of the transcendence of desire.
With great compassion, they benefit all sentient beings, yet in reality there is no person and no life-span;
without perceiving a "sentient being," they bring them benefit—know that this matter is exceedingly difficult.
Just as one might entice a small child with an empty fist, Showing it to him and saying there is something inside to make him rejoice;
When the hand is opened and the fist is empty and nothing is seen, The small child cries out in distress once more.
Thus are all Buddhas inconceivable, skillfully taming the various classes of sentient beings;
having realized that the nature of phenomena is non-existent, they provisionally establish names to demonstrate them to the world.
With words of great compassion and exhortation, he said: "Within my Dharma there is supreme peace and happiness;
you should leave the household life and abandon your attachments to kin, for you shall attain the extraordinary fruits of a śramaṇa."
Having gone forth, one diligently practices; through such practice, one attains nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, by contemplating all phenomena as they truly are, one realizes that there is no fruit whatsoever to be attained.
When one realizes that the fruit is non-existent, only then does a sense of wonder arise;
how joyful is the Great Compassionate Lion among Men, who skillfully expounds the Dharma that accords with reality!
All phenomena are like space, yet they establish hundreds of thousands of names, phrases, and meanings;
some are called meditative absorptions and liberations, while others are called faculties, powers, or enlightenment.
Yet these faculties and powers are fundamentally without arising; meditative concentration and bodhi likewise do not exist.
They are formless, shapeless, and ungraspable, yet they are displayed to sentient beings solely through skillful means.
I say that in the practice of cultivation there is realization; one should know that this involves being far removed from all signs.
If one claims that there is something attained therein, then that is not the realization of the fruits of the śramaṇa.
Since all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, where could one say there is realization?
What is called "realization" is in fact non-attainment; to understand this is what is termed "attainment."
Sentient beings who attain the fruit are called "excellent," yet I say that sentient beings are fundamentally unarisen;
since not even a sentient being can be apprehended, how could there be one who attains the fruit?
Just as a fertile field where there is no seed will never produce sprouts,
so too, when sentient beings cannot be found, at what point could one speak of realization?
The nature of all sentient beings is quiescent; there is no one who can grasp its root.
If one can thoroughly understand such a dharma, that person attains parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Throughout the countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas of the past, there has been none capable of delivering sentient beings;
if these sentient beings were truly existent, none would ever be able to attain nirvana.
All phenomena are utterly quiescent; there has never been a phenomenon that can arise.
If one can perceive all phenomena in this way, that person has already emerged from the three realms.
This is the unimpeded Buddha-enlightenment; within it, ultimately nothing exists.
One who can thoroughly understand such a dharma—I call that person a "one who has left desire behind."
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, two hundred bhikṣus who were characterized by overweening pride attained the exhaustion of all outflows, and their minds were liberated.
Sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?"
"How should we receive and uphold it? The Buddha told Upāli:
"This sutra is named 'Definitive Vinaya' and is also named 'Destroying Mind and Consciousness'; you should receive and uphold it."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Upāli, the assembly of bhikṣus, Mañjuśrī together with all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety, and Volume Ninety-One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci by Imperial Decree.
25. The Chapter on Arousing the Supreme Aspiration, Part One of Twenty-Five.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus and an additional five hundred bodhisattvas.

At that time, there were many bodhisattvas within the assembly whose karmic obstructions were deep and heavy, whose faculties were dull and obscured, and whose wholesome dharmas were meager. They delighted in clamor and bustle, discoursed on worldly affairs, and were addicted to sleep. They engaged in much frivolous proliferation and extensively managed various secular tasks. They were attached to all manner of things they ought not to pursue, forgot right mindfulness, cultivated false wisdom, and applied inferior diligence to perform deluded practices.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya was present in the assembly. Seeing that these bodhisattvas were fully engaged in such unwholesome practices, he thought to himself:

"These bodhisattvas have all regressed from the path-factors for the perfection of unsurpassed bodhi; I shall now cause these bodhisattvas to awaken, gain understanding, and give rise to a heart of joy."

Having formed this thought, he rose from meditative concentration in the late afternoon and went to where [the king] was; they exchanged greetings with one another, and he further delighted him by preaching the essentials of the Dharma with various gentle words.
He addressed them, saying: "O virtuous ones!
How is it that you have attained growth and non-retrogression in the factors of the path toward the perfection of unsurpassed bodhi?"
These bodhisattvas spoke with one voice, saying:
"Venerable One!
Regarding the factors of the path for the perfection of unsurpassed enlightenment, we no longer experience growth; there is only regression."
Why is this? Our minds are constantly shrouded by doubt, and thus we cannot comprehend unsurpassed bodhi.
How could we possibly become Buddhas?
"Are we not becoming Buddhas?
We cannot even comprehend the nature of falling away.
How could it be that we would fall away?"
"Will they not fall?
Because of these causes and conditions, wholesome dharmas are about to arise, yet they are constantly entangled and shrouded by doubt.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed him, saying:
"O virtuous ones! Let us go together to the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

That Tathāgata is the all-knowing one, the all-seeing one; he is fully endowed with unobstructed wisdom and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and through his power of skillful means, he thoroughly knows the conduct of all sentient beings."
"I shall preach the Dharma for you all in various ways, according to your respective faculties and natures.

At that time, there were sixty bodhisattvas among the assembly of five hundred who, together with Maitreya Bodhisattva, went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves on the ground, touching their heads to the Buddha’s feet; overcome with grief, they shed tears and could not rise.
Having completed his acts of reverence, Maitreya Bodhisattva withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!
You should all arise; do not continue to wail in grief and give rise to such great torment.

In the past, you committed evil deeds, treating all sentient beings with a heart of malice, reviling, insulting, obstructing, and harming them. Following your own discursive thoughts, you were unable to understand the distinctions of karmic retribution.
"Therefore, you are now entangled and shrouded by karmic obstructions, such that you are unable to practice the various wholesome dharmas.

When the bodhisattvas heard these words, they rose from the ground, bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees upon the earth, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"We pray that you will explain these karmic obstructions for us.
Having recognized our transgressions, we shall discipline ourselves; from this day forward, we dare not commit them again.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:

“Good son! In the past, during the Dharma of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, you left the household life to pursue the Path. Relying on your own extensive learning, you maintained the pure precepts, yet you constantly harbored a mind of arrogance, pride, and self-indulgence.”
Furthermore, while practicing the dhūta austerities with few desires and contentment, one may again give rise to attachment toward these merits.
At that time, there were two monks who preached the Dharma and had many relatives, friends, fame, and gain.
With a mind of stinginess and envy toward this person, you falsely slandered him by claiming he committed acts of sexual misconduct.

At that time, because of your divisive speech regarding his grave transgressions, the Dharma-master’s friends, relatives, and kinsmen were all led to harbor doubts and fail to develop faith or acceptance; those sentient beings consequently lost their inclination toward the Dharma-master and severed all their roots of goodness.
Therefore, by virtue of this evil karma, you have already been born in the Avīci Hell for sixty hundred thousand years.
As the remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, you shall further be born in the Saṃjīva Hell for forty hundred thousand years.
With their remaining karma not yet exhausted, they were reborn for twenty hundred thousand years in the Black Rope Hell.
With their remaining karma still not exhausted, they were reborn for sixty hundred thousand years in the Scorching Heat Hell.
After passing away from that state, he returns to human birth, yet for five hundred lifetimes he is born blind and sightless.

Due to the remnants of his karma, in every place where he is born he is always dull-witted and obtuse; he forgets right mindfulness, his roots of goodness are obscured, his merit is meager, and his physical form is deformed and deficient.
People take no pleasure in seeing them; they slander, despise, mock, and harbor malice toward them.
They are constantly born in remote regions, impoverished and lowly, losing their wealth and treasures while struggling to sustain their lives, and are neither respected nor loved by the multitude.

After passing away from here, during the final five hundred years of the latter age when the Dharma is about to perish, they will again be born into lowly families in remote borderlands; impoverished, starving, and cold, they will be slandered by others, lose their right mindfulness, fail to cultivate wholesome dharmas, and even if they wish to practice, they will encounter many obstacles.
Although you may momentarily give rise to the light of wisdom, because of your karmic obstructions, it will soon subside again.

After those five hundred years have passed, these karmic obstructions will finally be extinguished; thereafter, you shall be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha, at which time that Buddha shall bestow upon you the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, when the bodhisattvas heard what the Buddha had said, the hair on their bodies stood on end and they were deeply moved by remorse. They wiped away their tears and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I now confess and repent for my transgressions.

We have often treated those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle with contempt, jealousy, and anger, as well as other karmic obstructions; we now repent before the Buddha for these sins as they truly are.
"Today, before the World-Honored One, we make this great vow:
'World-Honored One!

From this day forth until the end of the future, if we should see anyone belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle commit a transgression and expose their fault, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.'"
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until the end of the future, if we should mock, deride, intimidate, or treat with contempt those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until the end of the future, if we see lay or ordained persons of the Bodhisattva vehicle sporting and delighting in the pleasures of the five desires, and seeing them enjoying such things, we shall never seek out their faults; we shall always give rise to faith and reverence, regarding them as our teachers.
If we do not act thus, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until the end of the future, if we should be stingy toward those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle regarding their friends’ households or various gains and offerings, thereby distressing their bodies and minds and causing them oppression, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until the end of the future, if we should cause even a single harsh word to displease those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward until the end of the future, if we do not diligently pay homage and serve those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle during the six periods of the day and night, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until the end of the future, we shall not spare our bodies or lives for the sake of upholding this great vow;
if we were otherwise, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until the end of the future, if we should harbor a mind of contempt toward the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, thinking that they are not superior to us, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until the end of the future, if we are not able to thoroughly subdue our bodies and eliminate thoughts of inferiority—such as those of a caṇḍāla or a dog—then we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until the end of the future, if we should praise ourselves or disparage others, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until the end of the future, if we do not flee a hundred yojanas from places of strife and contention as swiftly as a blowing wind, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until the end of the future, if we should personally boast of any merits—whether they be the precepts, extensive learning, the dhūta practices, fewness of desires, contentment, or any other virtues—we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until the end of the future, we shall not boast of the roots of goodness we cultivate, and we shall confess with shame all sinful karma we have committed;
if we do not do so, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the bodhisattvas:
"Excellent, excellent!
O sons of good family!"
You have well expounded such a Dharma of awakening and well brought forth such vast vows.
By being able to abide within them with such a resolute mind, all karmic obstructions will be completely extinguished, and immeasurable roots of goodness shall likewise increase.
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: “Maitreya!
If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to purify all karmic obstructions, they should make such a vast and great vow.”
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Are there any sons or daughters of good family who, by upholding this vow, shall attain its fulfillment and never regress?"
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
