"If there are sons or daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path and uphold this vow, they would rather sacrifice their bodies and lives than ever let it be deficient or diminished, causing them to regress."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva who, during the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age when the Dharma is about to perish, accomplishes how many dharmas so as to attain liberation in peace and security, free from affliction?”
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: “Maitreya!

If there are bodhisattvas who, during the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age when the Dharma is about to perish, shall accomplish four dharmas, they will attain liberation in peace and security, free from affliction.”
What are these four? They are:

not seeking out the faults of sentient beings; never exposing the transgressions of other bodhisattvas that one may have witnessed; not giving rise to attachment toward relatives or the households of donors; and forever severing all coarse and harsh speech.

Maitreya! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva, during the final five-hundred-year period when the Dharma is about to perish in the latter age, achieves security, freedom from affliction, and liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Seeking not the faults of others, Nor exposing the transgressions of men;
Free from harsh speech and stinginess— Such a person shall attain liberation."

“Maitreya! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, during the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age when the Dharma is about to perish, shall accomplish four dharmas, thereby attaining liberation with peace and freedom from affliction.
What are these four? They are:

one should not associate with those who are indolent; one should abandon all crowds and commotion; one should dwell alone in quietude and always apply oneself with diligent vigor; and one should discipline the body through skillful means.

Maitreya! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva, during the final five hundred years of the latter age when the Dharma is about to perish, will achieve peace, freedom from affliction, and liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"One should abandon indolence, Stay far away from all clamor and bustle, Be tranquil and always content; Such a person shall attain liberation."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!

Therefore, in the final five-hundred-year period of the later age, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain liberation without affliction for themselves and to eliminate all karmic obstructions should abandon places of clamor and dwell in the quiet forests of an araṇya."
One should distance oneself from those who practice what should not be practiced, as well as all those who are indolent and lazy.

Rather, one should observe only one's own body and not seek out the faults of others; delighting in tranquility and silence, one should diligently practice conduct corresponding to the Prajñāpāramitā.
"If you wish to give rise to deep compassion for those sentient beings and bring them great benefit, you should preach the Dharma with a pure mind free from expectation.
Furthermore, Maitreya!"

If a bodhisattva practices the gift of Dharma with a mind free from expectation, not clinging to fame, profit, or the fruits of retribution, but taking the benefit of others as the primary motive and constantly proclaiming the True Dharma extensively for the sake of sentient beings, they shall achieve twenty kinds of benefits.

What are the twenty kinds of benefits? They are as follows: accomplishment of right mindfulness; endowment with wisdom; possession of the power of steadfastness; abiding in pure conduct; the arising of the mind of awakening; attainment of supramundane knowledge; not providing an opportunity for any demons to gain the upper hand; having little greed; being free from anger; and likewise being without delusion; being remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; being protected by non-human beings; having immeasurable devas augmenting their majestic virtue; having no one among their retinue or friends able to cause them harm or ruin; whatever they say being surely believed and accepted by others; not being sought out for an opportunity to attack by enemies; attaining fearlessness; possessing much happiness; being praised by all wise people; and being well-able to preach the Dharma such that all people look up to them with reverence.

Maitreya! These are the twenty kinds of benefits that a bodhisattva shall achieve: they do not become attached to fame, profit, or the fruits of retribution; they act as leaders in performing deeds of benefit; and they always preach the Dharma purely to sentient beings with a mind free from expectation.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

When a bodhisattva practices the gift of Dharma with a mind free from expectation, they do not cling to fame, profit, or the fruits of retribution; taking the benefit of others as their primary concern, they constantly proclaim the True Dharma extensively for the sake of sentient beings, and are further able to accomplish twenty kinds of benefits."
What are the twenty kinds of benefits? They are:
eloquence that has not yet arisen is able to arise;
eloquence that has already arisen is never lost;
They constantly and diligently cultivate practice to attain dhāraṇīs;
with little effort, they are well able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings;
and with little effort, they cause all sentient beings to give rise to a superior mind of reverence and respect.
They attain the pure restraint of body, speech, and mind;
they transcend all fears of the evil realms;
and at the time of death, their minds are filled with joy.
He proclaims the True Dharma and subdues heterodox arguments;
even those of all ranks of nobility, majesty, and dignity cannot hope to look upon him with envy, let alone inferior beings of little merit.
His faculties are fully developed and cannot be eclipsed;
he possesses and maintains a sublime intentionality;
and he has attained śamatha and vipaśyanā.
They shall bring all difficult practices to full completion;
they shall arouse diligence to universally protect the True Dharma;
and they shall swiftly transcend the stage of non-retrogression.
Maitreya, dwelling in accordance with all conditioned phenomena, this is how a bodhisattva shall achieve twenty kinds of benefits:

they do not become attached to fame, profit, or the fruits of retribution; they act as leaders in performing deeds that benefit others; and they always preach the Dharma purely to sentient beings with a mind free from expectation.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"Observe that in the future, during the final five hundred years, there will be bodhisattvas who are utterly lacking in wisdom; when practicing the gift of Dharma, they will feel joy if there is gain and sustenance, yet they will not feel joy if there is no gain and sustenance."
When those bodhisattvas preach the Dharma for others, they give rise to such thoughts:
"How might I cause my friends and donors to become dependent upon me?
Furthermore, they think again:
"How may I cause both lay and ordained bodhisattvas to give rise to pure faith in me, and to respectfully provide offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites?"
"In this way, a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to others for the sake of material gain; if they receive no offerings, their mind becomes weary and discouraged. Maitreya!
It is like a person who aspires to purity, yet has a dead snake, a dead dog, or the corpse of a dead human, along with pus and blood and putrefaction, tied around their neck."
This person will experience deep distress and give rise to profound weariness and aversion; because of this opposition, they will become bewildered, despondent, and ill at ease.

Maitreya, you should know that in the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age, those who preach the Dharma will likewise be thus: in all places where there is no gain or support, their minds will find no accord and no flavor, and they will immediately grow weary and abandon them to depart.
Those Dharma masters will think to themselves:
"It is of no benefit for me to preach the Dharma here. Why is that?"
"These people do not give rise to any anxiety regarding the robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines required by me.
For what reason, then, do they merely exhaust themselves in this?"

“Maitreya! These Dharma masters seek for themselves offerings, attendants, respect, and the inclusion of those who dwell with them or near them; they do not include others for the sake of the Dharma or for beneficial purposes.”

These Dharma masters seek for themselves food, drink, clothing, and bedding; they falsely manifest extraordinary signs as they enter royal cities, towns, and villages, yet in reality they do not act for the benefit or the maturation of sentient beings.
Maitreya! I do not say that one who possesses seeking is pure in the giving of the Dharma. Why is this?
If the mind harbors aspiration, then there is no equality in the Dharma.
I do not say that one with a defiled mind can bring sentient beings to maturity. Why is this?
It is impossible that one who has not yet matured themselves can mature others; Maitreya,
I do not say that honoring, making offerings to, and providing physical comfort for those who are greedily attached to and possess impure things constitutes a beneficial act.
Why is this? Because, while seeking their own peace, security, and prosperity, and gathering a multitude of followers, they are unable to cause them to abide in right faith. Maitreya!

I do not say that a person who is hypocritical dwells in an araṇya; nor do I call one of meager merit "one of few desires"; nor do I name one who craves superior flavors "one who is easily satisfied"; nor do I consider one who seeks fine delicacies "one who begs for alms."

Maitreya! I do not say that one should beg for various kinds of exquisite and superior garments; rather, I mean that one should wear such things as robes made from discarded rags (pāṃśukūla). Maitreya!
Maitreya, I do not say that those who lack discernment, whether they be householders or renunciants, are free from worldly clamor.

Maitreya, I do not say that those who are deceitful and crooked, who encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world yet seek out the faults of others, are practicing according to the Dharma. I do not say that those who cause much harm possess the purity of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*). I do not say that those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) are foremost in learning (*bahuśruta*).

Maitreya! I do not say that those who favor their own factions are abiding in the code of discipline; nor do I say that those with arrogant minds are honoring the Dharma masters; nor that those who use frivolous speech and mockery are preaching the Dharma well; nor that those who mingle with the laity can remain free from all faults within the Saṃgha.

Maitreya, I do not say that selecting and excelling in fields of merit constitutes giving without expectation of reward; nor do I say that one who seeks gratitude and recompense is well-restrained in all matters; nor do I say that one who seeks honor and gain is dedicated to pure aspiration; nor do I say that one who engages in much false conceptualization has truly left the household life.

Maitreya! I do not say that discriminating between self and other is called "joyfully upholding the precepts," nor do I say that failing to show respect is called "listening to the Dharma," nor that being attached to worldly classics and incantations is called "receiving the Dharma."

Maitreya! I do not say that those who lack resolute conviction in the various emptinesses can transcend birth and death; rather, it is those with many attachments who, for the sake of abandoning all conditioned formations, [seek liberation].
Maitreya! I do not say that abiding in the factors of enlightenment while perceiving something as existing is called realized wisdom. Maitreya!

I do not say that those who lack power have accomplished patience; nor that those who are free from provocation have donned the armor of patience; nor that those with few afflictions are called pure in their discipline; nor that those with wrong means are practicing according to the teaching.

Maitreya! I do not say that those who delight in verbal discourse abide with a single mind; nor do I say that those who are fond of worldly affairs cause no harm to the Dharma; nor do I say that those whose wills delight in purity fall into the evil destinies; nor do I say that the cultivation of wisdom constitutes a practice of clamor.

Maitreya! I do not say that being endowed with skillful means is called deceitfulness; nor do I say that speaking falsely for the sake of seeking gain and offerings is [deceit]. One who is without attachment slanders the true Dharma; one who protects the true Dharma cherishes their own body and life; and practicing what is inferior is called the pride of thinking oneself superior when one is not.
Thus it is, Maitreya!

In the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age, there will be bodhisattvas of dull faculties and meager wisdom who are sycophantic, deceitful, and fraudulent, dwelling in the conduct of thieves.
"You should protect them.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
In the final five-hundred-year period of the last age, it is only these sixty bodhisattvas who are entangled by karmic obstructions; are there any other bodhisattvas besides them?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!
In the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age, there will be many bodhisattvas who are entangled and shrouded by karmic obstructions."
These karmic obstructions may either be extinguished or further increased. Maitreya!

Among these five hundred bodhisattvas, there are twenty whose karmic obstructions are slight; in the final five hundred years, they will return to be born in cities, towns, villages, marketplaces, mountains, and wilds. They will belong to noble and eminent lineages and possess great majestic virtue. They will be intelligent, wise, and skilled in expedient means; their minds will be harmonious and gentle, and they will always harbor compassion. They will bring benefit to many, with handsome and dignified countenances and pure, wondrous eloquence; they will be proficient in all arts, crafts, and technical skills.
He concealed his own virtues and dwelt securely in the practice of the *dhūta* austerities; in every place where he was born, he left the household life to pursue the Way.

Having accumulated the roots of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-koṭi* kalpas, he protected and upheld the True Dharma without regard for his own body or life. Dwelling in forest hermitages and secluded groves, he was always diligent and energetic, seeking no gain or honor. He skillfully entered into the mental activities of all sentient beings and fully understood incantations and discourses. Regarding all principles and meanings, he attained deep understanding from even a little hearing, and he was fully endowed with eloquence and wisdom.

Those bodhisattvas, through diligent cultivation within this Dharma, attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence; they proclaimed the True Dharma amidst the fourfold assembly. By the power of the Buddha’s majestic virtue and empowerment, they attained unimpeded and sovereign eloquence regarding all that the Buddha has taught: the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas.
Maitreya! Those twenty skillful bodhisattvas, having heard immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sūtras from their preceptors and ācāryas, were able to receive and uphold them all.
When they say these words:
"This Dharma-gate of mine was personally heard and received from such-and-such a preceptor and ācārya; it is free from doubt," Maitreya!

At that time, there will be lay and ordained bodhisattvas who lack wisdom and skillful means; regarding the Dharma spoken by these bodhisattvas who uphold the True Dharma, they will instead give rise to derision, contempt, and slanderous words, saying:
"Such teachings as these are all fabricated at will by you using clever rhetoric; they were certainly not proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
"We are unable to believe or take delight in this, nor can we conceive of it with a sense of wonder. Maitreya!
At that time, immeasurable sentient beings will all give rise to slander toward this Dharma-preacher, abandon him and depart, and say to one another:
"These bhikṣus have no standard of conduct; they propagate many heterodox doctrines and do not rely on the sūtras or the vinaya, being like the deceptive performances of actors."
"You should not give rise to faith or delight therein, nor conceive of it as something marvelous;
it is not the True Dharma. Maitreya! Those foolish people, possessed by Māra, are unable to understand this teaching and claim that it was not spoken by the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, those bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma will give rise to slander and commit the karma of destroying the Dharma.
By reason of these causes and conditions, they shall fall into the evil realms. Therefore, Maitreya!

If bodhisattvas who are skillful in wisdom wish to protect the True Dharma, they should conceal their own virtues; they must maintain mindful concern for those sentient beings who engage in much conceptual proliferation, lest such beings give rise to unwholesome thoughts toward them.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

In the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age, there will be bodhisattvas who are utterly ignorant; amidst the great assembly, they will slander the True Dharma and those who uphold the Dharma, and furthermore, regarding eloquence and dhāraṇīs, they will be unable to believe in or accept these teachings.”
“World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person, parched with thirst and needing water, who went to a spring or pond wishing to drink from it.
Before arriving there, this person had already cast various excrement and filth into that water.”
Later, unaware that he had intended to drink it, he took up the water and smelled it.
Once he perceived its foul odor, he did not drink it.
Having defiled it himself, he further spoke of its faults, even sighing and saying:
"How strange! This water is exceedingly foul and filthy.
Yet this person does not perceive his own fault at all, but instead directs resentment and blame toward the water.
World-Honored One!
You should know that those who are like springs and ponds are precisely the bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma;
through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they are well able to explain this eye of the Dharma.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, it is like that foolish person who, having thrown excrement and filth into a spring or pond, later does not realize it and wishes to drink the water.
World-Honored One!

In the final five hundred years of the last age, there will likewise be certain ignorant bodhisattvas who, having slandered that True Dharma and those who uphold it, will nevertheless listen to and receive the flavor of the Dharma from such persons.

That person, having lost their way, remains entirely unaware of it; because they pollute their faculty of mind with the fault of doubt, that upholder of the Dharma will be mocked or subjected to derision.
He even went so far as to exclaim: "How marvelous!
This Dharma has been defiled by all manner of faults."

Those ignorant persons, being unable to listen to or accept this True Dharma and its teacher, seek out their faults, slander and insult them, and, giving rise to a mind of revulsion and detachment, abandon them and depart.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Maitreya!”
You are well able to expound such parables, and no one can find fault with your exposition. Maitreya!
For this reason, you should know that there are four kinds of eloquence which have been proclaimed by all Buddhas.
There are four forms of eloquence that are all prohibited by the Buddhas.
What are the four forms of eloquence that are proclaimed by all the Buddhas?

That is to say, it is associated with benefit and not dissociated from benefit; associated with the Dharma and not dissociated from the Dharma; associated with the extinction of afflictions and not associated with the increase of afflictions; and associated with the merits of nirvana and not associated with the faults and outflows of saṃsāra.
“Maitreya! These are the four kinds of eloquence proclaimed by all Buddhas. Maitreya!”
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās wish to preach the Dharma, they should abide in such eloquence.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who possess a mind of faith and compliance, they should conceive the thought of a Buddha toward such a person and regard them as a teacher, and from that person they should listen to and receive the Dharma.
Why is this? One should know that all that this person speaks are the truthful words proclaimed by all Tathāgatas and all Buddhas.

Maitreya! If there are those who slander these four forms of eloquence, claiming they were not spoken by the Buddha and failing to give rise to a mind of respect and reverence, such persons, due to their animosity, will slander all the eloquence taught by those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Having slandered the Dharma, they commit the karma of destroying the Dharma; having committed the karma of destroying the Dharma, they shall fall into the evil realms.
Therefore, Maitreya!

If there are sons of good family with pure faith who wish to be liberated from the karmic causes and conditions of slandering the True Dharma, they do not harbor hatred for the Dharma because of their hatred for people; they do not find fault with the Dharma because of the faults of others; and they do not feel enmity toward the Dharma because of their enmity toward people.
“Maitreya! What are the four kinds of eloquence that are all prohibited by the Buddhas? They are:

that which is associated with what is not beneficial and not associated with what is beneficial; that which is associated with what is not the Dharma and not associated with the Dharma; that which is associated with afflictions and not associated with the cessation of afflictions; and that which is associated with birth and death and not associated with the merits of nirvāṇa.”
“Maitreya! These are the four kinds of eloquence that are all prohibited by the Buddhas.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, if eloquence increases birth and death, it is not that which is proclaimed by the Tathāgatas.

Why, then, does the World-Honored One say that the various afflictions can perform the work of benefiting a bodhisattva, and further praise the embracing of birth and death as being able to fulfill the factors of enlightenment?”
"Are such distinctions not indeed what the Tathāgata has taught?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Maitreya!"
I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
If someone were to say that a bodhisattva takes up birth and death for the sake of fulfilling and accomplishing the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), [would that be correct?]
Furthermore, it is said that all afflictions serve as beneficial matters.
Is such a statement consistent with what is beneficial,
or is it inconsistent with what is beneficial?
"Is this in accordance with the Dharma,
or is it not in accordance with the Dharma?
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is explained correctly, it will correspond to benefit and correspond to the Dharma, for it enables the bodhisattva’s factors of enlightenment to reach fulfillment.”
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!

If one says that a bodhisattva takes up birth and death for the sake of fulfilling the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), it is said that the various afflictions (kleśa) can perform beneficial functions for a bodhisattva.”
Such eloquence as this has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Why is that? Maitreya!
These bodhisattvas have attained mastery over all phenomena; thus, the afflictions they give rise to are without fault.
This is the skillful means of a bodhisattva, which is not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Maitreya! If there is affliction that cannot bring benefit to others, nor can it give rise to the fulfillment of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), it is neither consistent with meaningful purpose nor consistent with the Dharma; it serves only as a cause for inferior roots of goodness.
Within this, a bodhisattva would rather sacrifice their own body and life than follow those afflictions.
Why is that? Maitreya!
There are some bodhisattvas who, by virtue of having attained the power of wisdom, manifest objects of perception within their afflictions;
there are other bodhisattvas who, lacking the power of wisdom, harbor intensified attachment toward those afflictions.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if there are bodhisattvas who, during the final five hundred years of the latter age, desire to be free from the entanglements and fetters of karmic obstacles, they will attain liberation without being harmed themselves.”

Such a person shall give rise to deep faith and understanding within the bodhisattva practices; they shall not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the faults of others, but shall instead aspire to seek the true merits of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Maitreya!"
Therefore, one should develop deep faith and understanding toward the skillful means practiced by the bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because the practice of skillful means by bodhisattvas who practice through wisdom is difficult to believe and understand.
Maitreya! It is like a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) who displays the conduct of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
In this way, the ordinary person and the state of a stream-enterer are each distinct from one another.

Ordinary foolish people, being entangled by greed, hatred, and delusion, fall into the various evil realms; however, the Srotāpanna thoroughly understands greed, hatred, and delusion, and thus never falls into the three evil realms.

Maitreya! It is the same for a bodhisattva who practices through wisdom: even though they have not yet severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of greed, hatred, and delusion, they are nonetheless distinct from other bodhisattvas who are beginners.
Why is this? Because their minds are not shrouded by afflictions, unlike those bodhisattvas who are beginners in their practice.
Bodhisattvas of dull faculties lack skillful means; like ordinary worldlings, they are unable to achieve liberation.
Maitreya! A bodhisattva who practices with wisdom can completely destroy all grave offenses through the power of wisdom, and shall not fall into the evil realms because of them.
Maitreya! It is like a person who throws firewood into a great mass of fire and repeatedly adds more.
Having added it in this way, its flames become even more fierce and increasingly bright, without ever being extinguished.
Maitreya! It is the same for a bodhisattva who practices with wisdom: they burn the fuel of afflictions with the fire of wisdom, yet repeatedly add more fuel of afflictions.
Once it has been replenished in this way, the fire of wisdom becomes even more brilliant and remains inexhaustible.
Maitreya, it is just so;
the power of wisdom and the skillful means of a bodhisattva practicing wisdom are difficult to comprehend.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-One;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Twenty-fifth Assembly on the Development of Superior Aspiration, Part Two.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Once a beginner bodhisattva has gone forth and wishes to attain the power of wisdom that they have not yet attained, what dharmas should they abandon and what dharmas should they cultivate so that the power of wisdom not yet arisen may be brought forth, and the power of wisdom already arisen may be made to increase?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!
Once a beginner bodhisattva has gone forth into homelessness, if they wish to cause the power of wisdom to increase, they should recognize the faults of gain and offerings and must relinquish them."
If one delights in the clamor of worldly talk, is addicted to sleep, extensively manages various affairs, or takes pleasure in frivolous disputations—all such faults should be abandoned.
Therefore, one should renounce gain and honor and cultivate few desires; abandon all clamor and delight in tranquility; relinquish worldly affairs and contemplate the ultimate truth.
During the first and last watches of the night, one should distance oneself from sleep, observing, reflecting, practicing, and cultivating accordingly.
Abandoning all worldly affairs and conceptual proliferations, one should cultivate the supramundane path and maintain loving-kindness toward sentient beings. Maitreya!

Once a beginner bodhisattva has gone forth into homelessness, if they have not yet attained the power of wisdom and desire to attain it, these are the dharmas that should be abandoned and these are the dharmas that should be cultivated.
Why is this? Maitreya!

Once those bodhisattvas have gone forth, it is impossible for them to wish to attain the power of wisdom without abandoning gain and honor, or without cultivating few desires; it is impossible for them to cause the power of wisdom that has not yet arisen to arise, or to cause the power of wisdom that has already arisen to increase.

It is impossible that one who does not abandon clamor and does not abide in tranquility could cause the power of wisdom that has not yet arisen to arise, or cause the power of wisdom that has already arisen to increase.

It is impossible that one who does not abandon worldly affairs and does not contemplate the true meaning should give rise to the power of wisdom that has not yet arisen, or cause the power of wisdom that has already arisen to increase.

To be addicted to sleep during the first and last watches of the night without ever awakening; to fix the mind in contemplation while not relinquishing worldly affairs; to delight in frivolous discourse and fail to practice the supramundane path; and to harbor no thoughts of loving-kindness toward sentient beings—such that one who has not yet produced the power of wisdom should produce it, or one who has already produced it should cause it to increase—is impossible.

Maitreya! Therefore, a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the power of wisdom but desires to attain it should abandon those dharmas that ought to be abandoned and cultivate those dharmas that ought to be cultivated.
Why is this? The wisdom of a bodhisattva arises from causes and conditions; if there were no causes and conditions, it could never arise. Only when causes and conditions harmonize can it be produced.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is meant by 'faults within gain and offerings'?"
"When one observes in this way, it enables a bodhisattva to delight in few desires and not give rise to feverish distress.
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
A bodhisattva at the stage of initial practice should contemplate that gain and offerings give rise to sensual desire;

he should contemplate that gain and offerings cause the ruin and loss of right mindfulness and give rise to anger; he should contemplate that gain and offerings lead to thoughts of profit and loss, giving rise to delusion;

he should contemplate that gain and offerings can produce a mind of arrogance, inferiority, jealousy, and envy; and he should contemplate that gain and offerings [arise] within the homes of relatives and friends.

One should contemplate that because stinginess and attachment give rise to deception and delusion; one should contemplate that because gain and profit result in the savoring of craving and the production of flattery and crookedness;
one should contemplate that because gain and profit lead to the abandonment of the four noble lineages and the lack of shame and remorse;

one should contemplate that because gain and profit are not permitted by any of the Buddhas and cause the habitual practice of arrogance and negligence, giving rise to haughtiness; one should contemplate gain and profit...
One should contemplate that receiving offerings from superior fields of merit while giving rise to contempt constitutes siding with Māra;

one should contemplate that offerings are the root of manifold evils and the destroyer of all virtues; one should contemplate that offerings involve much craving and attachment, being like frost and hail;
one should contemplate that regarding the families of friends and relatives, one gives rise to anxiety and distress by watching their facial expressions. One should contemplate the [offerings]...

Because cherishing objects of affection causes the mind to become distracted by the worry of their loss, one should contemplate gain as that which leads to much forgetfulness regarding the four foundations of mindfulness and causes the white dharmas to weaken.
Because it causes much falling away from the four right efforts, one should contemplate gain as that which enables one to defeat all the arguments of others.
Because it leads one to claim for oneself the attainment of supernormal powers and wisdom, one should contemplate gain [in this way].

One should contemplate that gain and honor are contrary to wisdom because they give rise to [defilements]; one should contemplate that gain and honor lead to enmity and aversion because what was first obtained is later lost;
one should contemplate that gain and honor cause mutual resentment and hatred because they involve much discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*);

one should contemplate that gain and honor diminish the peace and happiness resulting from the mental deliberations and calculations involved in engaging in worldly occupations for the sake of livelihood. One should contemplate gain and honor...

One should contemplate that gain—even up to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*)—is like a courtesan, for it can cause one to fall away from the mind;

one should contemplate that gain leads to the abandonment of wisdom and the severance [of roots of goodness], resulting in falling into the evil destinies of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and the realm of Yama; one should contemplate that gain is associated with Devadatta.
Because Udraka likewise abided in [wrong] dharmas and fell into an evil destiny,
Maitreya! A bodhisattva at the stage of initial practice should observe the faults of gain and profit in this way, delighting in few desires and not giving rise to feverish distress.
Why is this? Maitreya!
A bodhisattva with few desires does not give rise to any faults whatsoever and is capable of being a pure vessel for the Buddhas.

Neither bound to the laity nor to those who have gone forth, they abide in the most excellent resolve of reality; they are neither base nor terrified, because they are free from the fear of falling into the evil realms; they cannot be eclipsed, because they have abandoned attachment to flavors; and having attained liberation from the domain of all Māras, they are praised by all Buddhas and cherished and envied by gods and humans alike.
They do not become stained by or attached to any meditative concentrations, because they abide in the ultimate limit.
Their minds are upright and free from guile or crookedness, and they remain heedful even amidst the five desires, because they perceive their faults.
Practicing as taught, one is able to abide in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), and fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārin) shall likewise cherish this. Maitreya!

If there is a bodhisattva who is wise and discerning, and who can understand these merits in this way, they should, with a superior intention (adhyāśaya), renounce gain and honor, and with a superior intention abide in fewness of desires (alpecchatā), so as to give rise to the effort for the sake of severing craving and attachment.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by 'passing through amidst the clamor and bustle'?"
"When he observes in this way, the bodhisattva dwelling alone in seclusion will not give rise to feverish distress.
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
A bodhisattva at the stage of initial practice should observe that there are twenty kinds of faults in bustle and clamor.
When observing them, it enables the bodhisattva to dwell alone in seclusion and stillness, free from the arising of feverish affliction.
Maitreya! What are the twenty kinds of faults associated with delighting in clamor?
First, failure to guard the actions of the body; second, failure to guard the actions of speech; third, failure to guard the actions of the mind.
Fourth, they abound in desire; fifth, they increase ignorance; sixth, they are addicted to worldly affairs;
seventh, they distance themselves from supramundane discourse; eighth, they respect and cultivate what is contrary to the Dharma;
ninth, they abandon the True Dharma; tenth, Māra Pāpīyān gains an opportunity over them; eleventh...
11) those who have never practiced heedfulness; 12) those who always harbor attachment to heedless conduct;
13) those with many discursive thoughts and investigations; 14) those who diminish their learning;
15) those who do not attain meditative concentration; 16) those who lack wisdom; 17) those who are hasty.
It may be that those who practice the holy life do not love the Buddha (18),
do not love the Dharma (19), and do not love the Saṅgha (20).
“Maitreya! These are the twenty kinds of faults that a bodhisattva contemplates regarding the clamor and bustle of society.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Abandon all greed and hatred, and do not dwell amidst the clamor of the crowd;
if one should remain fixedly therein, such faults should not be committed.
Arrogance, as well as discursive thought and investigation, all arise from the clamor of the crowd."
Those who destroy their conduct and lack precepts praise the clamor of the crowd.
Fools delight in worldly discourse and fall away from the ultimate truth.
With negligence and much discursive thought, they commit these faults; such things one should not do.
The bhikṣu who abandons learning, whose discourse is irrational,
who diminishes his meditative concentrations, and constantly contemplates the world—
how can one who is addicted to such contemplation attain tranquility?
Their minds are constantly distracted, forever estranged from right contemplation.
They quickly fall into non-celibate conduct, amidst clamor and a lack of decorum.
Furthermore, they have never loved the Buddha, nor have they loved the Noble Assembly.
I have abandoned and distanced myself from the dharma of desire, yet I remain attached to words of what is not the Dharma.
Throughout my lives, I have constantly sacrificed a thousand bodies, as well as my limbs, head, and eyes;
for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path, I have never grown weary of hearing the Dharma.
These people who do not follow the Dharma, having heard but little, quickly grow weary and abandon it.
In the past, when I was a king, for the sake of seeking even a single four-line verse,
I was able to give away my wife, children, and all my treasures.
What wise person would not diligently listen to the Dharma?
I have renounced all unrighteous frivolous discourse because liberation is difficult to attain even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
You all should rejoice and aspire to seek the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
If you delight in liberation and possess the most supreme merit,
you should not inquire about any worldly affairs whatsoever.
There is no benefit in clothing and food, nor is Nirvāṇa realized thereby;

one should instead praise the Most Victorious One. "Welcome, O Bhikṣus!"—having thus addressed them, one should spread out seats for them to sit upon and together discuss the essential points of the Dharma.
A human body is extremely difficult to obtain; one should practice the white dharmas according to one's capacity through recitation and meditative concentration—this is how you should ask.
When the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, the bequeathed Dharma shall perish and be destroyed.
Many bhikṣus are heedless; they delight in crowds and abandon solitude.
For the sake of food, drink, and gain, they discourse on worldly affairs day and night.
Like fools in their dreams, they are terrified and swept away by the current.
Knowing that one has frequently committed transgressions, One will surely fall into the three evil realms.
Therefore, one should give rise to a heart of joy, Dwelling alone in quiet seclusion;
Whether in an araṇya, One should resolve to seek the unsurpassed path.
One should not look for the faults of others, nor consider oneself most superior;
for pride and self-indulgence are the roots of heedlessness.
Do not despise those who are lowly, for among those who follow the bequeathed Dharma, they may gradually attain liberation.
Even if a bhikṣu has broken the precepts, if he has deep faith in the Triple Gem, this is the cause of liberation; one should not look for his faults.
Having subdued the difficulties of greed and hatred, do not be startled by negligence.
Such is the nature of residual habits; therefore, there is no need to speak of them.
If a pure bhikṣu spies out the faults of others, this is most certainly not true, and he cannot be said to be practicing the True Dharma.
One who practices according to the Dharma should observe themselves:
monks seeking the Path must abandon evil discourse and always dwell alone in quietude with a joyful heart.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!

To be attached to the clamor and bustle of the world is to possess such immeasurable faults and evils; it causes one to lose merit and virtue, rendering it of no benefit, increasing afflictions, leading to rebirth in the evil realms, and distancing one from the pure dharmas."
"How could a bodhisattva who seeks the wholesome Dharma, upon hearing of such faults, not delight in solitary dwelling in a quiet and secluded place?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is called the fault within the worldly?
When examining it, a bodhisattva should abide in the meaning of certainty; by contemplating this meaning, they do not give rise to feverish distress.
The Buddha said,
“Maitreya! A bodhisattva at the stage of initial practice should observe that there are twenty kinds of faults regarding worldly affairs.”
When one observes in this way, it enables the bodhisattva to abide in the definitive meaning; by contemplating this meaning, one does not give rise to feverish distress.
Maitreya! What are the twenty kinds of faults in delighting in worldly affairs?
First, the mind gives rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, failing to respect those of extensive learning; second, one frequently gives rise to attachment regarding various contentious debates;
third, one loses right mindfulness and appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*); fourth, the body engages in excessive agitation through inappropriate actions;
fifth, one quickly fluctuates between pride and deprecation, thereby destroying patience regarding the Dharma; sixth, the mind is constantly rigid.
1. They have never cultivated powerful meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or wisdom (*prajñā*); 2. They are entangled in speech and discourse at inappropriate times;
3. They are unable to firmly realize noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*); 4. They are not revered by devas and nāgas; 5.
Those possessed of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) constantly hold them in contempt; 6. They do not personally realize [the truth] for themselves.
12) being censured by others; 13) not abiding in right faith while constantly harboring regret and resentment;
14) having a mind full of doubt, wavering and unstable; 15) being like a performer who follows after sounds;
16) being stained by and attached to various desires, flowing along with sensory objects; 17) not contemplating the truth.
Seventeenth, they truly slander the True Dharma; eighteenth, whatever they aspire to never succeeds;
nineteenth, their minds are undisciplined and they are abandoned by others; twentieth, they do not know the Dharma-realm and follow evil friends;
twenty-first, they do not understand that the faculties are bound to afflictions.
“Maitreya! These are the twenty kinds of faults for a bodhisattva who delights in worldly affairs.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Proud of one's great learning, clinging to various disputations,
losing mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension— this is called the fault of being difficult to serve.
Far removed from right reflection, body and mind are not at peace."
To fall away from the patient acceptance of the Dharma is called the fault of mental agitation;
for the mind to be untrained and compliant, thereby remaining far removed from *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, is called the fault of mental agitation.
Lacking respect for teachers and elders, delighting in worldly discourses,
and possessing unstable wisdom— this is called the fault of being a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
The devas do not revere such a one, nor do the nāgas and spirits likewise.
One loses eloquence; this is called the fault of worldly attachment.
The Noble Ones always censure such a person who is addicted to it;
their life is spent in vain—this is called the fault of worldly attachment.
All conditioned phenomena are deficient and lack; they distance one from great enlightenment.
At the end of life, one gives rise to sorrow and suffering—this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
A mind of doubt wavers like grass blown by the wind.
When wisdom is not firm, this is called the fault of flattery.
Just as a professional performer praises the prowess of another, so too does such a person; this is called the fault of flattery.
Following after worldly speech, Attached to the objects of desire,
Constantly walking upon the wrong path— This is called the fault of worldly affairs.
When the heart’s aspirations are not fulfilled, One becomes sycophantic, crooked, and full of contention.
To be far removed from noble conduct is called the fault of worldly attachment.
When a fool obtains a small gain, his mind is constantly shaken;
like a restless monkey, he is agitated—this is called the fault of worldly attachment.
Wisdom is frequently lost, and there is no mind of awakening;
held fast by the foolish, this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Confused regarding the eyes and ears, and so it is even for the mind.
Constantly accompanied by afflictions, this is called the fault of worldly entanglement.
The fool delights in worldly entanglement and passes his entire life in constant emptiness;
it would be better to contemplate a single meaningful principle, for the benefit gained would be boundless.
For example, the flavor of sugarcane, though not separate from its skin and joints,
yet is not obtained from the skin and joints;
it is the skin and joints that are like the words, while the underlying meaning is like the superior flavor.
Therefore, abandon empty words and contemplate the true meaning.
Wise Bodhisattvas, who can recognize the faults of worldly affairs,
always delight in contemplating the merit of the ultimate truth.
The flavor of the Dharma and the flavor of its meaning, and liberation as the foremost flavor—
who possessing wisdom would not find joy in their heart?
Therefore, one should abandon all talk that is without benefit.
Always delight in diligent contemplation of the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Such is the foremost Dharma, praised by all Buddhas;
therefore, the wise person should delight in its diligent cultivation.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
You have been able to skillfully explain the faults of worldly affairs and contemplate the benefits and merits of the ultimate truth.”
“World-Honored One!
How could there be a bodhisattva who seeks the Tathāgata’s true wisdom yet still delights in false and deceptive worldly affairs?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘faults while asleep’?
When examining this, a bodhisattva should arouse diligence and not give rise to distress.”
The Buddha said:
"Maitreya! A bodhisattva who is a beginner should observe that there are twenty kinds of faults in sleep."
When observing these, they enable a bodhisattva to arouse a resolute intention for diligence without weariness.
Maitreya, what are the twenty kinds of faults associated with delighting in sleep?

First, indolence and laziness; second, heaviness of body; third, a sallow and haggard complexion; fourth, the increase of various diseases; fifth, weakness of the fire element; sixth, indigestion of food; seventh, the arising of sores and blisters on the body; eighth, a lack of diligent cultivation; ninth, the growth of delusion; tenth, the feebleness of wisdom; eleventh, dark and turbid skin; twelfth, being disrespected by non-human beings; thirteenth, acting with dullness and stupidity; fourteenth, being bound by afflictions (*kleśa*); fifteenth, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) covering the mind; sixteenth, a lack of delight in wholesome dharmas; seventeenth, the diminution of pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*); eighteenth, engaging in inferior conduct; nineteenth, loathing and disparaging diligence; twentieth, being held in contempt by others.
"Maitreya! These are the twenty kinds of faults for a bodhisattva who delights in sleep.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"The body is heavy and lacks decorum, Laziness diminishes one's capability,
And the complexion lacks luster— These are the faults of delighting in sleep.
Such a person is constantly afflicted by illness, With wind and bile accumulating in great measure."
The four great elements become mutually conflicted; this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
Food and drink are not properly digested; the body lacks luster and moisture;
the voice becomes hoarse and unclear; these are the faults of delighting in sleep.
Sores and blisters break out upon his body, and he remains in constant, heavy sleep day and night;
various worms infest his limbs—these are the faults of delighting in sleep.
One loses diligence and becomes destitute of all wealth and treasures.
Dreaming much without awakening—this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
The net of delusion constantly grows, and one takes pleasure in various views;
blazing and difficult to cure—this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
It diminishes all wisdom and increases delusion;
the mind remains perpetually base—such are the faults of delighting in sleep.
Even one who dwells in an araṇya, if they constantly harbor a lazy mind, [is likewise overcome].
Non-humans find their opportunity; this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
One becomes dazed and loses right mindfulness; one’s recitation is not fluent;
one forgets much of what has been taught; these are the faults of delighting in sleep.
Through delusion one gives rise to confusion, dwelling amidst the afflictions;
the mind finds no peace—this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
All virtues diminish, and one constantly gives rise to a mind of sorrow and regret.
The increase of all afflictions is the fault of delighting in sleep;
Being estranged from all virtuous friends and failing to seek the True Dharma,
Constantly practicing within what is contrary to the Dharma— this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
Not seeking the joy of the Dharma, one diminishes all merits and becomes estranged from the pure dharmas; such are the faults of delighting in sleep.
That person’s mind is timid and weak, and they are constantly lacking in joy.
The limbs become excessively emaciated; this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
Knowing one’s own body to be indolent, yet envying those who are diligent and delighting in speaking of their faults and evils—this is the fault of delighting in sleep.
The wise understand these faults and always remain free from sloth;
the foolish increase the net of views, which brings no benefit but harms their merit.
The wise are ever diligent, assiduously cultivating the path of purity.
To leave suffering behind and attain peace and happiness—this is what all Buddhas praise.
All worldly arts and crafts, as well as supramundane skills, arise through the power of diligence; therefore, the wise should cultivate it.
If one aspires to enlightenment, understands the faults of sleep,
abides in the power of diligence, and awakens with a sense of shame and remorse—
for this reason, the wise always give rise to a mind of diligence.
"Abandoning sleep, one guards the seed of enlightenment.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
To be attached to sleep involves such immeasurable faults as these.
If anyone hears this and yet does not give rise to a sense of remorse, weariness, or renunciation, nor exerts diligence, one should know that such a person is profoundly ignorant.

If there should be a bodhisattva who, desiring to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, hears such explanations of the meaning and merit of these true words, it is impossible that they would become indolent regarding all wholesome dharmas, fail to arouse diligence, or remain apart from the factors of enlightenment.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by 'transgressions amidst worldly affairs'?"
"If, when observing, it causes all bodhisattvas to cease their worldly affairs and diligently cultivate the Buddha-way," the Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
A bodhisattva at the stage of initial practice should observe twenty kinds of faults associated with delighting in busy affairs.
When observing them, it will enable the bodhisattva to refrain from busy affairs and diligently cultivate the Buddha-way.
Maitreya! What are called the twenty kinds of faults?
First, being addicted to inferior worldly activities; second, [being preoccupied with] various recitations and practices...
The three things that I, Kāśyapa, hold in contempt are likewise censured by bhikṣus who diligently cultivate meditative concentration:
fourth, constantly giving rise in the mind to karma that perpetuates the beginningless cycle of birth and death;
fifth, consuming in vain the pure offerings of faith provided by householders and brahmins; and sixth, harboring in the heart a desire to seize various material goods.

Thirteenth, one does not give rise to joy when there is no gain or support; fourteenth, one frequently creates karma that brings about affliction, harm, and obstacles;
fifteenth, one constantly delights in associating with male and female lay followers (upāsaka and upāsikā);
sixteenth, one spends day and night merely preoccupied with food and clothing; seventeenth, one frequently inquires about worldly affairs.
Karma: Seventeenth, they constantly delight in initiating unrighteous speech; eighteenth, they rely on managing communal affairs and give rise to arrogance;
nineteenth, they seek only the faults of others without examining themselves;
twentieth, they harbor feelings of contempt toward those who preach the Dharma.
“Maitreya! These are the twenty kinds of faults for a bodhisattva who delights in engaging in worldly affairs.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Abiding in inferior activities, One remains far removed from sublime practice;
Falling away from great benefit— This is called the fault of worldly affairs.
For a bhikṣu who delights in recitation And for one who cultivates meditative concentration,”
All are censured; this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Constantly performing the karma of birth and death, abandoning the causes of liberation, and receiving offerings of faith in vain—this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Delighting in various wealth and treasures, one does not give rise to sorrow or distress;
yet dwelling in inferior conduct, this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Such a person is full of craving and attachment, constantly coming and going to the houses of courtesans.
Like a bird entering a cage, this is called the fault of manifold affairs.
Constantly worrying and sighing over one's household estate, always harboring a heart of burning affliction,
and speaking words that others do not believe— this is called the fault of manifold affairs.
Not accepting the Venerable One’s instruction, one rejects and treats it with contempt;
violating the pure precepts—this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
With a mind full of discursive thoughts, one busies oneself with worldly occupations.
Inability to cultivate wisdom and abandon [defilements] is called the fault of worldly affairs.
A greedy mind that is ever-blazing, delighting in and attached to various flavors,
and lacking any sense of contentment, is called the fault of worldly affairs.
To feel joy upon gaining profit, And to suffer distress when there is no profit;
To be greedy, stingy, and devoid of benevolence— This is called the fault of worldly affairs.
To cause harm without compassion Only increases all manner of evil karma.
Entangled and bound by the creeping vines of craving— this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
To distance oneself from teachers and elders, to associate with evil companions,
and to reject those who uphold the precepts— this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Day and night, without any other thought, one thinks only of seeking food and clothing;
not delighting in various meritorious virtues—this is called the fault of manifold affairs.
Constantly inquiring after worldly wisdom, one does not delight in supramundane discourse.
To be addicted to and cherish false teachings is called the fault of worldly affairs.
To rely on one's own knowledge of worldly affairs and treat the bhikṣus with contempt,
like a person who is crazed or intoxicated, is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Constantly seeking the faults of others while failing to see one's own transgressions,
and disparaging those who possess virtue— this is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Such a foolish person lacks any skillful means.
To treat the teacher of the Dharma with contempt is called the fault of worldly affairs.
Such base activities are replete with all manner of defects;
what person of wisdom would take pleasure in practicing them?
Pure and sublime karma, endowed with all virtues—
therefore the wise person loves and constantly practices it.
If one delights in inferior karma, the wise should censure it.
Just as one might abandon great wealth to greedily seek a mere trifle,
so too should the wise person abandon inferior deeds and instead seek the supreme Dharma, which all Buddhas constantly praise.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

That those bodhisattvas would abandon the practice of supreme diligence and instead initiate inferior matters—let it be known that such persons possess very little wisdom and their insight is shallow.”
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!

I now tell you this in truth: if there is a bodhisattva who does not cultivate various practices, does not sever afflictions, does not practice meditation or recitation, and does not seek extensive learning, I declare that such a person is not one who has left the household life."

Maitreya! If there are those who diligently practice the path of wisdom and abandonment, who give rise to wisdom, who achieve wisdom, and who do not engage in worldly occupations or manage mundane affairs, I say that such persons abide in the teaching of the Tathāgata.

If there are bodhisattvas who delight in performing worldly occupations and managing various affairs—engaging in what is improper—I say that such persons abide in birth and death; therefore, a bodhisattva should not associate with them.
Maitreya! If there is a bodhisattva who busies himself with many worldly affairs and constructs stūpas made of the seven precious gems that fill the trichiliocosm,
such a bodhisattva cannot cause me to feel joy, nor does he offer worship or reverence to me.

Maitreya! If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding the dharmas associated with the pāramitās, even receives and upholds a single four-line verse, reciting and practicing it and expounding it for others, such a person truly makes an offering to me.
Why is this? The bodhi of all Buddhas arises from extensive learning; it does not arise from worldly affairs. Maitreya!

If there is a bodhisattva who busies himself with worldly affairs, causing other bodhisattvas—those who should be engaged in recitation, practice, and exposition—to instead attend to such worldly affairs, you should know that this person increases their karmic obstructions and lacks any spiritual benefit.
Why is this? These three kinds of meritorious action thus described all arise from wisdom.
Therefore, Maitreya!

A bodhisattva engaged in administrative affairs should not obstruct, hinder, or create difficulties for those bodhisattvas who are reading, reciting, practicing, or expounding the teachings; nor should they impede other bodhisattvas from reading, reciting, practicing, or expounding them.
One should not create obstacles or hindrances for those bodhisattvas who are practicing meditative concentration. Maitreya!

If there is a bodhisattva engaged in worldly affairs throughout Jambudvīpa, one should instead approach, make offerings to, and serve a single bodhisattva who is engaged in recitation, practice, and exposition.

If there were as many bodhisattvas in a single Jambudvīpa as there are who recite, practice, and expound the teachings, one should still approach, make offerings to, and serve a single bodhisattva who is diligently practicing meditative concentration.
Such wholesome karma is rejoiced in by the Tathāgata and approved by the Tathāgata.
If one serves and makes offerings to a bodhisattva who is diligently cultivating wisdom, one shall obtain an immeasurable accumulation of merit.
Why is this? Because the activity of wisdom is unsurpassed and most supreme, transcending all that is practiced within the three realms.
Therefore, Maitreya!
"If there are bodhisattvas who initiate diligence, they should diligently practice within wisdom.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata has well explained the faults of initial-stage bodhisattvas who delight in clamor, worldly affairs, sleep, and various activities.
World-Honored One,
what is meant by "faults within conceptual proliferation"?
"If, when observing, a bodhisattva abides in tranquility and is free from all disputes," the Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
The faults of conceptual proliferation for a bodhisattva at the stage of initial practice are immeasurable and boundless; I shall now briefly describe twenty kinds of them.
What are these twenty kinds of faults?
First, one experiences much suffering and affliction in the present life; second, one increases anger and falls away from patience;
third, one is tormented and harmed by adversaries; fourth, Māra and his followers all give rise to joy;
fifth, roots of goodness not yet produced will all fail to arise; sixth, those roots of goodness already produced...
1. The faculties cause one to fall away from what has been attained; 2. they increase all forms of strife, contention, and rivalry;
3. they create karma leading to the hells and evil destinies; 4. they will result in the acquisition of ugly and unwholesome fruits;
5. the tongue is not supple and speech is stammering and halting; 6. one is unable to retain the teachings received.
12. Not understanding what has not yet been heard when hearing the sūtras;
13. Completely abandoning all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); 14. Swiftly encountering all evil associates (pāpamitra); 15.
Practicing the path and finding it difficult to achieve liberation; 16. Constantly and repeatedly hearing unpleasant speech.
Seventeenth, wherever they are born, they will have many doubts and perplexities; eighteenth, they will constantly be born in difficult circumstances where they do not hear the True Dharma;
nineteenth, they will encounter many obstacles in their cultivation of pure dharmas;
twentieth, they will face much resentment and jealousy regarding what they enjoy and use.
“Maitreya! These are the twenty kinds of faults for a bodhisattva who is addicted to conceptual proliferation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

"In this present life one is constantly afflicted by suffering; lacking patience, one is full of anger, and enemies give rise to harmful intent—this is called the fault of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Mara and his retinue all give rise to hearts of joy."
The loss of all wholesome qualities is called the fault of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
That the unarisen wholesome does not arise, that one constantly dwells in strife,
and that one creates karma for the miserable realms— this is called the fault of conceptual proliferation.
The body is often ugly, one is born into an inferior family, and speech is always stammering;
these are called the faults of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
One cannot retain the Dharma when hearing it, or what is heard does not enter the ears.
Constantly being separated from virtuous friends is called the fault of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Encountering evil associates and constantly hearing discordant speech makes it difficult to escape from the path;
this is called the fault of conceptual proliferation.
Wherever they are born, they will always harbor a mind of doubt and be unable to comprehend the Dharma;
this is called the fault of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
They will constantly be born within the eight difficult states (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) and remain far removed from the state of freedom from difficulties.
To be fully possessed of what is unbeneficial is called the fault of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
To encounter many obstacles to the wholesome, to fall away from right reflection,
and to experience much enmity and jealousy— these are called the faults of conceptual proliferation.
All such faults arise from conceptual proliferation;
therefore, the wise should swiftly distance themselves from it.
For those who engage in such proliferation find it difficult to realize great enlightenment.
Therefore, a person of wisdom should likewise not associate with places of frivolous talk and contentious debate, where many afflictions arise;
the wise should distance themselves from such places, even by a hundred yojanas.
Nor do they dwell near them, nor build various houses;
therefore, those who have left the household life should not abide in contentious debate.
You have no fields or houses, nor wives, children, or servants.
Even regarding such things as honor and status, for what reason should one give rise to contentious debate?
Having left the household life to dwell in tranquility and wearing the dharma robes, one is revered by all sages; therefore, one should cultivate a mind of patience.
Those who thus engage in conceptual proliferation increase their poisonous and harmful minds;
they shall fall into the evil destinies. Therefore, one should cultivate patience.
Imprisonment and bondage, execution and flogging—
All such sufferings as these arise from contentious debate.
Those who engage in such frivolous proliferation constantly encounter evil associates;
their reputation does not increase, and they never possess a joyful heart.
If one abandons contentious debate, no one will be able to find an opportunity to exploit them;
their kin and followers will not be estranged, and they shall encounter virtuous friends.
They will attain purity within the vehicle, and their karmic obstructions will be exhausted without remainder.
Having subdued the armies of Māra, one diligently cultivates the practice of patience.
Disputes abound with many faults, whereas non-dispute is endowed with merit;
if there are those who practice, they should abide in patience.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
You are able to skillfully explain such faults, causing all bodhisattvas to give rise to a mind of awakening.”
World-Honored One!

In the final five hundred years of the latter age, will there be any bodhisattvas who, upon hearing such an exposition on the faults of contentious debate, are able to give rise to remorse and abandon their afflictions?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!
In the final five-hundred-year period of the future degenerate age, there will be few bodhisattvas who are able to give rise to remorse and abandon their afflictions."
There will be many bodhisattvas whose minds are stubborn and who do not respect one another; harboring overweening pride, they will engage in mutual criticism.

Although they may hear this teaching of such profound meaning and supreme merit, and even though they uphold, recite, and explain it, because these bodhisattvas have deep and heavy karmic obstructions, they will be unable to give rise to supreme merit. Consequently, they will harbor doubts and lack faith in this sutra, no longer upholding it or explaining it to others.
At that time, when Māra Pāpīyān saw this occurrence, he assumed the form of a bhikṣu for the sake of deception and, coming to where they were, spoke these words:
"All these sūtras were fabricated by those skilled in worldly rhetoric; they were not proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
"Why is this? You shall not obtain any of the merits or benefits described in this sutra.

Because Māra Pāpīyas thus deluded and confused him, he conceived doubts regarding this profound sūtra which accords with the meaning and benefit of emptiness, gave rise to various disputes, and no longer accepted, upheld, recited, or explained it.

Maitreya! Those foolish people do not understand this; because of their own karma, they are unable to protect those sublime merits. Once their own karma has been exhausted, they will certainly attain such merits.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has spoken regarding the merits and benefits of Amitābha Buddha’s world of Ultimate Bliss."

If there are sentient beings who give rise to ten kinds of thoughts, and with each thought focus their mindfulness exclusively upon Amitābha Buddha, such persons shall, at the end of their lives, attain rebirth in that Buddha’s world.
"Bhagavān! What are the ten kinds of minds that are called 'arousing'?
By means of these minds, one shall attain rebirth in that Buddha-world."
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!
These ten kinds of mind cannot be generated by ordinary, foolish, and unvirtuous persons who are possessed of afflictions."
What are the ten?

First, to give rise to great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and a mind free from harm; second, to give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and a mind free from oppression or affliction; third, to cherish the protection of the Buddha’s true Dharma without begrudging body or life; fourth, to generate supreme patience regarding all phenomena and a mind free from attachment; fifth, to have a pure intention that does not crave gain, offerings, honor, or respect; sixth, to seek the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes and never forget it at any time; seventh, to respect and revere all sentient beings without a sense of inferiority; eighth, to remain unattached to worldly discourse and to develop a mind of certainty regarding the factors of enlightenment; ninth, to plant various roots of goodness with a pure mind free from defilement; and tenth, to give rise to a mind of recollection toward all Tathāgatas, having abandoned all signs.
Maitreya! These are called the ten kinds of minds that a bodhisattva generates.
By virtue of these minds, one shall attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Maitreya! If a person, among these ten kinds of minds, achieves even one, and desires to be reborn in that Buddha-world, it is impossible that they would not be reborn there.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
You are able to reveal and expound the true merits of the Tathāgata, thereby inspiring the sublime resolve and aspiration of bodhisattvas.”
"Bhagavān! What should this sutra be named?
How should we receive and uphold it?"
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"This sutra is titled 'Arousing the Exalted Resolve and Joy of Bodhisattvas,' and it is also titled 'The Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva. You should receive and uphold it by these names."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva and all the śrāvakas, along with the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others of the entire world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume Ninety-Two;
The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume Ninety-Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
26. The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Subāhu, Part One of Twenty-Six.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a son of good family named Subāhu, who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and having paid homage, withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Subāhu, saying: "Good son!
These six pāramitās are what a bodhisattva should always fulfill completely."
What are the six?

They are the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
“Good son! These six pāramitās are that which a bodhisattva must always fulfill. Good Arm!”
"How does a bodhisattva fulfill the practice of the perfection of giving? O Subāhu!

A bodhisattva seeks wealth in various villages through right livelihood and not through wrong livelihood; he acts in accordance with others and does not oppose them, nor does he oppress or distress sentient beings."

One practices giving in order to seek wealth and possessions; one does not practice giving for the sake of respect, offerings, or reputation; nor out of shame or fear, nor for the sake of karmic retribution, nor to be reborn in heaven, nor out of flattery.

Regarding those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them, one neither disparages nor praises them; whether they are acquaintances or strangers, one treats them with a mind of equanimity, making offerings, showing respect, honoring, and praising them.

Furthermore, toward those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them, whether they are kin or not kin, acquaintances or strangers, and whether they are enemies or non-enemies, he always maintains profound respect, affection, faith, and joy.

This bodhisattva should always practice giving according to what he possesses: when there is little, he gives little; when there is much, he gives much; when there is coarse, he gives coarse; when there is fine, he gives fine; when there is exquisite, he gives exquisite; and when there is not exquisite, he gives what is not exquisite.

If one were to take exquisite and delicious food and drink worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold and give it as a gift to another, or if one were to divide a single coin into sixteen parts and give away just one part, and yet feel joy in both instances without any difference in their minds; [this is the perfection of giving].
"Good son! This bodhisattva gives food to those who beg for food in order to fulfill the power of the knowledge of all modes;
he gives drink to those who seek drink in order to sever the power of craving in sentient beings."
If one needs clothing, give clothing, for the sake of attaining the supreme garment of shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*).
If one needs a vehicle, give a vehicle, for the sake of attaining the Bodhisattva Vehicle and the Buddha Vehicle.
If one needs incense, give incense, for the sake of attaining the fragrance of the precepts maintained by the Perfectly Awakened One.
To those who require flowers, give flowers, for the sake of attaining the flowers of the Tathāgata’s seven factors of enlightenment.
To those who require powdered incense, give powdered incense, for the sake of eliminating the unwholesome fragrance of all sentient beings.
To those who require ointments, he gives ointments, so that they may attain a body fragrant with the scent of unimpaired precepts.
To those who require canopies, he gives canopies, so as to extinguish the fires of the afflictions of sentient beings.
To those who require leather mats, he provides leather mats, for the sake of enabling them to receive the bliss of immeasurable wisdom.
To those who require couches, he provides couches, for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the power of the bliss of the noble couches of Śakra and Brahmā.
To those who require a place to sit, he gives a place to sit, so that when they sit beneath the Bodhi tree, no demons or fetters (*saṃyojana*) may disturb or disrupt their seat.
To those who require a dwelling, he gives a dwelling, so that sentient beings may obtain a place of shelter and protection, free from fear, and attain the power of non-self (*anātman*).
One offers fine gardens and pavilions to the Buddha and the Sangha for the sake of attaining the power of unsurpassed, tranquil meditative concentration.

One offers various exquisite offerings and manifold adornments to the stupas and temples of the Buddhas for the sake of attaining the power of a Great Man, characterized by the thirty-two marks and eighty minor signs.
If one lights lamps to provide illumination within Buddha-stūpas or in dark passages, it is for the sake of attaining the immeasurable clarity of the Buddha-eye.
