If one makes offerings of various kinds of music to the Triple Gem, it is for the sake of attaining immeasurable divine hearing.
One gives robes and alms bowls for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed majesty of upholding the precepts;
one gives fans, water for washing, and vessels for use to others for the sake of enabling sentient beings to obtain coolness and purity.
One gives paper, pens, ink, and high seats for the sake of attaining unsurpassed great wisdom.
One gives medicine to the sick for the sake of eliminating the diseases of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of sentient beings.
One gives land to others in order to enable sentient beings to attain the nectar-like realm of the three vehicles;
one constructs stupas and images in order to enable sentient beings to hear the True Dharma.
One should swiftly bestow all that one possesses upon others, for the sake of attaining the power of swift supernatural faculties.
One should practice pure giving, so as to encounter no obstacles on the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.
One constantly practices giving without ceasing, in order to attain the power of uninterrupted eloquence (*anācchedya-pratibhāna*).
One gives according to the wishes [of others], in order to cause sentient beings to attain great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

One does not coerce others to seek wealth for the purpose of practicing giving, in order that Māras and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cannot disrupt or disturb one, so that one may spontaneously achieve the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-mārga*).
A bodhisattva practicing generosity should bestow gifts as described above.

If a bodhisattva wishes to perform such giving, even when they themselves possess no wealth, they should resolve to give with the intention of bringing illumination to all immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.

Whether with power or without power, as in the aforementioned acts of giving, [one thinks]: "This is my virtuous deed; I am excellent and supreme; this is my treasure. It is able to cause all the happiness possessed by sentient beings in all worlds to be fully accomplished, namely, the attainment of the joy of harmony.
Being able to relinquish all things without any doubt, may all my vows be fully accomplished and may I attain peaceful conduct.

If there are any sentient beings in the world who desire and seek whatever they require, I shall satisfy them and give it to them; precious jewels, gold, silver, clothing, and wealth shall be like mountains piled high, and provisions of food and drink shall be as vast and boundless as the great ocean.

During each of the three periods of the day and night, this bodhisattva dedicates the karmic fruits obtained from his own practice of material giving and the giving of Dharma to be shared in common with all sentient beings.
They cause all sentient beings with conditioned existence—of the past, future, and present—to be born in sublime realms and attain supramundane bliss.
Although such persons perform this kind of giving, they never harbor expectations or seek its karmic retribution.
He reveals such skillful means in order to transform sentient beings so that they may enter into wholesome dharmas.

"When this bodhisattva practices giving, he makes the vow: 'May all sentient beings attain crossing-over and liberation, for the sake of attaining all-knowledge and becoming fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.'"
If one gives a gift and, having given it, also wishes that all sentient beings may attain crossing-over and liberation, for the sake of attaining all-knowledge and fulfilling all Buddha-dharmas.
Regarding such generosity, if one lacks the strength and is unable to practice it or relinquish wealth,
that bodhisattva should reflect as follows:
"I shall now apply myself with diligent vigor, gradually and at every opportunity, severing the defilements of stinginess, greed, and parsimony."

I shall apply myself with diligent vigor, gradually and from time to time training in the relinquishment of material gifts; may my mind of giving always increase and expand, so that until the end of existence I never grow indolent, but remain ever joyful in heart.

"In this way, when a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, contemplates the mind of enlightenment, cultivates the mind of enlightenment, aspires for enlightenment, and seeks enlightenment with a vow—this is called the bodhisattva’s immeasurable, incalculable great giving, great relinquishment, and great renunciation."
Why is this? Because such giving is the most supreme and foremost among all forms of giving.

It shall cause me, in future ages, amidst all sentient beings in every world, to rain down the rain of Dharma, to rain down the rain of ambrosia; to bestow the rain of Dharma, to bestow the rain of ambrosia; to bring forth the rain of Dharma, and to bring forth the rain of ambrosia.
“Bhadra-bāhu! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving in this manner, they do not regard it as difficult, but rather as joy and delight, thereby swiftly fulfilling the dāna-pāramitā.”
Good son! A bodhisattva cannot give his own body, limbs, or members to a beggar, whether by cutting them himself or instructing another to cut them. Why is this?
If one were to accomplish such karma, it would cause that beggar to undergo immeasurable suffering in the great hells;
therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cherish their own body or limbs.
Why is this? It is because he wishes to cause the beggar to distance himself from vast unwholesome karma.

If a mendicant comes to a bodhisattva seeking what he requires, and at that time the bodhisattva has no wealth of his own, he must not forcibly compel his parents, wife, children, kinsmen, relatives, servants, or slaves to take their property and give it away, thereby leaving them impoverished.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva desires to practice a mind of equanimous compassion toward all sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not compel their parents, wife, children, kinsmen, relatives, servants, or wealth and property to be used for giving as alms, it is at that time that the bodhisattva attains a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward sentient beings.

"Good son! A bodhisattva should not harbor a mind of stinginess toward other sentient beings, nor should they compel others to take their wealth for the sake of giving; this is not praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, let alone cutting off one's own limbs and joints to give them to others."
This is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). "Good Arm!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become fully endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)?"
"Subāhu! This bodhisattva, toward all sentient beings, for as long as life lasts, personally refrains from killing, instructs others not to kill, and vows not to kill."
One does not steal oneself, teaches others not to steal, and vows not to steal.
One does not engage in sexual misconduct oneself, teaches others not to engage in sexual misconduct, and vows not to engage in sexual misconduct.
One refrains from false speech oneself, teaches others not to speak falsely, and vows not to speak falsely.
This continues until the end of one's life: one refrains from drinking alcohol oneself, teaches others not to drink alcohol, and vows not to drink alcohol.
This bodhisattva constantly upholds and focuses his mind upon these five precepts, remaining diligent and energetic without slackening or deficiency.

Likewise, he forever severs and distances himself from acts that terrify others, such as binding, imprisoning, flogging, or executing; the same applies to divisive speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech.
This bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"I should give rise to a heart of affection and care for all sentient beings, just as parents love and care for an only child."
Even if my parents were to inflict various forms of suffering upon me with bows, arrows, swords, or staves, I would never give rise to a thought of retaliation therein.
Toward all sentient beings, I should regard them as a parent cherishes an only child.
"Just as parents, wives, or children who have been separated for a long time experience immeasurable joy and exultation upon seeing one another all at once,
so too does the Bodhisattva feel such joy when beholding all sentient beings."
This bodhisattva upholds the precept against killing because he wishes to cause sentient beings to abide in the precept against killing of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This bodhisattva upholds the precept against stealing because he wishes to cause sentient beings to abide in the precept against stealing of one beyond training.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept against sexual misconduct because he wishes to cause sentient beings to abide in the precept of non-sexual misconduct of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This bodhisattva maintains the precept against false speech because he wishes to cause sentient beings to abide in the precept of truthful speech of those beyond training.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept against drinking alcohol because he wishes to cause sentient beings to abide in the precept against drinking alcohol of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This bodhisattva maintains the precept against causing fear because he seeks to achieve the adamantine concentration (vajrasamādhi).
This bodhisattva maintains the precept of non-binding because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to sever the fetters of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This bodhisattva maintains the precept of non-imprisonment because he wishes to cause sentient beings to escape the five realms of existence (*pañcagati*).

This bodhisattva observes the precept of not using the whip or the staff in order to distance himself from the obstacles of Māra, the fetters, and the afflictions, so as to attain the samādhi of fixed dharma.
This bodhisattva observes the precept of not inflicting execution in order to ensure that his body, speech, and mind do not engage in unprotected karma.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept against divisive speech in order to attain an unbreakable and harmonious assembly.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept against harsh speech in order to attain the five kinds of Brahma-voice.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept against frivolous speech in order to attain unimpeded speech when preaching the Dharma.

This bodhisattva maintains the precept of seeking out those beings who fear death, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, affliction, and terror.
This is the bodhisattva’s precept of cherishing the property of others so that it is not lost or leaked, for the sake of attaining the concentration of the awakening of unsurpassed bodhi.

When other sentient beings have their wives, children, or women detained or imprisoned, the bodhisattva rescues and liberates them therein, for the sake of attaining the dharma of unimpaired concentration.
If this bodhisattva exhorts others to release [the animals], it is for the sake of attaining mastery over the mind.
If this bodhisattva releases them himself or exhorts others to release them, it is for the sake of sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and destroying all the fetters and latent tendencies of Māra.
If this bodhisattva sees sentient beings imprisoned, he either releases them himself or exhorts others to release them, for the sake of attaining mastery over the mind and being free from obstacles.

If this bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are about to be flogged with whips or canes, he either releases them himself or exhorts others to release them, for the sake of attaining the four fearlessnesses.
If this bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are about to be executed, whether he releases them himself or encourages others to do so, it is for the sake of attaining the four kinds of dharma-bodies.

This bodhisattva maintains the precept of non-deception so that, when seated upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, no māras or fetters can obstruct him, because he has attained the certainty of the Dharma.
This bodhisattva skillfully reconciles those in conflict and generates pure joy, for the sake of attaining an indestructible assembly of great sages.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept of kind speech, desiring to cause all sentient beings to hear pleasant words with their ears and attain joy and happiness in their hearts.
This bodhisattva speaks according to pleasant words because he wishes to ensure that his speech is not false.
This bodhisattva upholds and recites the Buddha’s scriptural expressions and precepts in order to attain the majestic power of the sages and bring the great assembly to fulfillment.

This bodhisattva, throughout the three periods of time, receives and upholds the five-limbed prostration to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as the Bodhisattva precepts, in all places throughout the world—past, future, and present—to attain that which is indestructible at the place of the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree; for they dwell single-mindedly in faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, having attained the dharma of fixedness.
This bodhisattva upholds the precept of sweeping and circumambulating stupas during the three periods of the day in order to attain the fullness of all Buddha-dharmas.
This bodhisattva upholds the precept of praising the Dharma in order to turn the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept of praising the Saṅgha for the sake of being surrounded by a great assembly.
This bodhisattva maintains the precept of taking refuge in the Three Jewels at the three times of the day, desiring to cause all sentient beings to attain the supreme refuge.

This bodhisattva, throughout the three periods of time, upholds the precept that desires the Triple Gem, the Bodhisattvas, and the Dharma to always be present in all worlds so as not to be empty, for the sake of attaining the bliss of unsurpassed enlightenment.
This bodhisattva upholds the precept of exhorting all Buddhas to teach the Dharma throughout the three periods of the day, in order to attain the ten stages and cause the rain of the Dharma to fall.

This bodhisattva, throughout the three periods of the day, upholds the practice of repenting for all transgressions and relinquishing all evil, defiled precepts, in order to sever and extinguish all habitual tendencies of craving.
This bodhisattva upholds the precept of harmonizing all roots of goodness throughout the three periods of time, in order to bring all the *pāramitās* to fulfillment.

This bodhisattva upholds the precept of dedicating all roots of goodness—belonging to all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, noble assemblies, and bodhisattvas, down to the sentient beings of the six realms of existence, wherever they may be in the past, future, or present throughout all worlds—throughout the three periods of time, in order to obtain the requisites for unexcelled bodhi.
This bodhisattva upholds the precepts for aspiring to enlightenment throughout the three periods of time, in order to attain the definitive certainty of unsurpassed enlightenment.

This bodhisattva upholds the precepts for the unsurpassed path of all roots of goodness throughout the three periods of time, in order to attain the definitive powers and fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata.
This bodhisattva upholds and provides for their parents and teachers as a precept, in order to attain the dharma of unsurpassed certainty.

If this bodhisattva sees those who are fearful or impoverished, they uphold the precept of providing fearlessness through offerings and gifts, in order to attain the skillful means of indestructible and invincible discourse.
This bodhisattva upholds the precepts for protection against officials, bandits, water, and fire in order to attain the various powers (*bala*) of the *pāramitās*.

If this bodhisattva sees the transformations produced by the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*) of Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, or bodhisattvas, they uphold the precepts accordingly in order to attain the supreme power of supernormal faculties.
This bodhisattva upholds and guards the precepts regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind for the sake of attaining the Tathāgata’s immeasurable power of knowing the minds of others.

If this bodhisattva sees one who is heedless and has lost mindfulness—meaning one who has lost the meaning of the Three Vehicles in the present and the future—they vow to arouse mindfulness and maintain it so that it is not lost.
This bodhisattva maintains the precepts for hearing the Dharma, gathering the Dharma, and expounding the Dharma, in order to attain the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence.

This bodhisattva maintains all roots of goodness from every action of body, speech, and mind, receiving and practicing them, desiring to cause all sentient beings to cross over and attain liberation, and to attain all-knowledge and fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.

May these roots of goodness be undertaken and practiced for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may attain liberation, attain all-knowledge, and become fully endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas.
Thus, one maintains the precepts without deficiency, without breach, and without negligence.
If one lacks the power or capacity to practice and study them, that bodhisattva should reflect as follows:
"Now I shall apply myself with diligent vigor, gradually and at all times distancing myself from killing and all unwholesome dharmas."

I further redoubled my diligence, gradually and at all times skillfully training in and upholding the precepts so that they might increase and reach fulfillment; even unto the end of my existence, I never became indolent nor gave rise to sorrow.

"Subāhu! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus gives rise to the mind of awakening, maintains the mind of awakening, cultivates the path of awakening, aspires for awakening, and seeks awakening with a vow—this is called the immeasurable and boundless root of goodness of upholding the precepts."
Why is this? Such observance of the precepts is the most supreme and foremost among all virtuous precepts.

By receiving and upholding these precepts, one desires to cause all sentient beings throughout the world to initiate untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) and initiate the precepts of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa-śīla*), and to give rise to untainted precepts and the precepts of those beyond training.

"Subāhu! In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes this ethical discipline, they do not regard it as difficult but rather as joy and delight, thereby swiftly fulfilling the perfection of śīla."
“Bhadra-bāhu! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the perfection of patience?
If members of his own retinue or other sentient beings come to take the bodhisattva’s life, at that time, regarding this matter, the bodhisattva never gives rise to a mind of anger or retaliation.”

Or suppose another person comes to seize the Bodhisattva’s wealth, even down to his wife and children; or if they engage in divisive speech, harsh words, lying, and frivolous talk; or if they inflict various sufferings upon the Bodhisattva through intimidation, binding, imprisonment, flogging, or execution.
At that time, the bodhisattva likewise does not give rise to a mind of retaliation.

Whether one’s life-force and all possessions—even including wife and children—are seized; or whether one is subjected to slander, harsh speech, lying, or frivolous talk; or is threatened, bound, imprisoned, flogged, or executed—the bodhisattva reflects upon such matters as follows: "These are the results of my own evil conduct and unwholesome karma, which I myself have created and must myself experience. Whether in a past life or in the present life, having previously committed these acts, I now receive their retribution."
"How can I now feel anger toward another for my own karmic retribution?
Furthermore, O Subāhu,
a bodhisattva reflects in this way:

"If others should deprive me of my life-force and my wealth, even unto my wife and children; or if they should speak words of double-tongued slander, harsh speech, falsehoods, or frivolous chatter; or if they should subject me to terror, binding, imprisonment, flogging, or execution—I should not, in such circumstances, respond with anger or malice toward them by binding or harming my enemies."

Why is this? Even when I experience slight suffering and vexation in this present life, I do not take pleasure in it nor find it agreeable; how much less could I give rise to anger to harm others, thereby incurring various retributions for transgressions in future lives—immeasurable, boundless, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sufferings, which are all unpleasant, undesirable, and disagreeable results?
"Furthermore, Subāhu! A bodhisattva reflects in this way:

'Because there is the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), one cuts off the life-faculty; because there are material possessions, one seizes and robs them; because there is a wife and children, one takes away their wife and children; because there is the ear-faculty (śrotrendriya), one hears double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, and frivolous chatter; and because there is this body, there is fear, bondage, imprisonment, flogging, and execution.'"
"Now that I myself am experiencing the sensation of suffering through the life-faculty, the ear-faculty, and the body, how can I inflict harm upon others out of anger? Furthermore, Subāhu,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:
"The eye-faculty is itself the earth-element, itself its own substance, itself the dharma-realm, and itself its own nature.
Moisture is water, heat is fire, and motion is wind; these are themselves one's own substance, themselves the dharma-realm, and themselves one's own nature."
In this way, all life is of a nature to decay, a nature to perish, and a nature to be exhausted.
Likewise, all the sense-faculties are of the nature of suffering, of the nature of painful contact, and of the nature of experiencing suffering.

The entire body is the nature of suffering, the nature of contact with suffering, and the nature of experiencing suffering; it is one's own property, it is the dharma-realm, and it is one's own nature.

This life of mine is a phenomenon subject to decay, a phenomenon subject to cessation, a phenomenon subject to exhaustion, and a phenomenon of suffering; these six sense faculties are phenomena of painful contact, that is, contacts of evil touch.

How can I, while my own life is subject to destruction, the Dharma is subject to extinction, and all phenomena are subject to exhaustion, give rise to anger and malice toward others, or bind myself to enemies?
For what reason?
"It is one's own property; it is the dharma-realm;
it is one's own nature. Furthermore, O Subāhu!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:
"The internal eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not self, nor do they belong to a self;
the external eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise not self, nor do they belong to a self."
How can a person of wisdom, regarding these six sense faculties—which are neither self nor belonging to a self—adorn them with attachment and give rise to anger and malice toward others?
"Furthermore, Subāhu!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:

'The suffering among humans is slight; the suffering among hungry ghosts is great; the suffering among animals is even greater still; and the suffering and affliction in the hells are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculably many times more.'"
If one does not wish to undergo even a small amount of suffering in the human realm, how much less should one endure the immeasurable afflictions of the three evil paths in future lives?
Therefore, I should not now give rise to anger or inflict harm upon others.
"Furthermore, Bhadrajālin!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:
'If I can now benefit even a single person, I should not become angry, nor should I harm others or bind my enemies.'"

How much more so shall I, for the sake of benefiting all the immeasurable sentient beings of the world through the profound meaning of the Dharma, don the great armor; having donned this great armor, may I receive the prediction of enlightenment, proceed toward the Mahāyāna, and fully attain the unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas.

Within this Buddha-dharma, one should not be intolerant, nor should one harm others, harbor malice or jealousy, or engage in strife and litigation. Herein, one should practice patience for the benefit of others, skillfully reconciling disputes and harboring no envy.

"Subāhu! If a son or daughter of good family were to undergo all manner of agonies even in the Avīci Hell, they should not give rise to anger or inflict harm or injury upon an enemy; how much less, then, should they give rise to anger or malice toward others when experiencing slight suffering and affliction among human beings?"

If these sons or daughters of good family are met with anger by others, or are reviled, scolded, rebuked, slandered, despised, or have their ill repute spread, they should endure all such evils. They should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion that is pure and stainless, desiring to attain the mind of a Tathāgata.

When this bodhisattva undergoes the terrors of being whipped, beaten, bound, or imprisoned, they should endure all such matters and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, for the sake of shattering the shell of all obscurations of ignorance within a single moment of thought.
This bodhisattva practices patience and a mind of compassion in order to cause all sentient beings to sever craving and hatred.
Even when his ears are being cut off, he practices patience and gives rise to a mind of compassion, desiring that all sentient beings hear the Dharma and have faith.

When the nose is being cut off, one should likewise practice patience and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, for the sake of receiving the fragrance of supreme, majestic upholding of the precepts.

When the feet are being severed, one should likewise practice patience and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, for the sake of attaining the Tathāgata’s four bases of spiritual power.

If one's hands are severed, one should likewise practice patience and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, desiring to gather in all sentient beings so that they may attain tranquility.
If one's limbs and joints are dismembered, one should likewise practice patience and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, in order to bring the six *pāramitās* to fulfillment.
If one's eyes are gouged out, one should still practice patience and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, for the sake of attaining the eye of wisdom.
If one's head is severed, one should still practice patience and give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, for the sake of attaining the head of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.

This bodhisattva, through such patient endurance and directed reflection, vows to enable all sentient beings to cross over and attain liberation, so that they may achieve omniscience and be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
Having thus reflected upon this patience,
I now direct my mind toward it, wishing that all sentient beings may attain crossing-over and liberation, so that they may obtain all-knowledge and fulfill the Buddha-dharmas.
Regarding such patience—unbroken, unimpaired, and undegenerated—if one lacks the power or strength to practice it, at that time the bodhisattva should reflect thus:
"I shall now apply myself with diligent vigor, gradually and from time to time, distancing myself from and abandoning the state of impatience."

Now, I shall apply myself with diligent effort, gradually and at all times training in patience; I will cause this patience to increase, expand, and become fully perfected, so that until the end of existence I shall never be indolent nor give rise to sorrow.

"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the mind of awakening, recollects the mind of awakening, and cultivates the mind of awakening; they long for awakening and aspire to seek awakening. This bodhisattva initiates right practice and such immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) virtues and forbearances (*kṣānti*), desiring to cause all sentient beings in the entire world to initiate untainted (*anāsrava*) forbearance and initiate the forbearance of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and to give rise to untainted forbearance and give rise to the forbearance of one beyond training."
"Subāhu! In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, they do not regard it as difficult but instead find joy and delight in it, thereby swiftly fulfilling the pāramitā of kṣānti."
“Bhadra-bāhu! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the vīrya-pāramitā?
Bhadra-bāhu!”
This bodhisattva should reflect in this way:
"In each of the ten directions today, there are immeasurable worlds in every quarter; in each world, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings gathered together, without limit."
I shall now generate an adornment so that these sentient beings may obtain great benefit and also attain happiness.

Furthermore, because I perceive the dharmas that serve as the objects for the benefit and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings, and because I give rise to the dharmas of the roots of goodness, throughout immeasurable days and nights—whether my mind is negligent, or when other thoughts arise, or even during sleep—I constantly increase my merit and virtue in every moment of thought. In each and every thought-moment, I give rise to immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness as provisions for awakening.
I now understand that because I shall, in every single thought-moment, give rise to and increase immeasurable roots of goodness, it will not be difficult for me to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Now, for this reason, I see that it is very easy to encounter a bodhisattva; therefore, those who wish to attain the unsurpassed path should not be indolent for as long as their lives last.
"Furthermore, Subāhu!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'If a bodhisattva could cause even a single world among the sentient beings of immeasurable and boundless worlds to be free from all sufferings, I would still, in every single moment of thought, initiate and increase immeasurable roots of goodness; how much more so if one causes the sentient beings of immeasurable and boundless worlds to distance themselves from and eliminate birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from loved ones, meeting with those one hates, and the sufferings of the three evil realms.'"
"Furthermore, Subāhu!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:

'If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in a single thought-moment, desires to cause all sentient beings in immeasurable and boundless worlds to distance themselves from and eliminate all sufferings, this bodhisattva will likewise, within that single thought-moment, give rise to and increase immeasurable roots of goodness; how much more so when they desire to cause the sentient beings of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons in immeasurable and boundless worlds to distance themselves from and eliminate birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from loved ones, meeting with those one hates, and the sufferings of the three evil realms.'"
"Furthermore, Subāhu!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect in this way:

'If there are those who wish to attain the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they still gain an increase of immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness in every single thought-moment; how much more so for good sons and good daughters who wish to achieve and perfect the immeasurable and boundless majestic power and authority of the Buddha-dharmas.'"

Good sons and good daughters, through four causes, four conditions, and four objects, whether during the day or night, even when their minds are lax, when other thoughts arise, or when they are asleep, they cultivate and accumulate immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness in every single moment of thought, thereby initiating and augmenting the provisions for awakening.
I now understand that if, in every single thought-moment, I give rise to and increase the four immeasurable roots of goodness, then attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi will not be difficult.
For this reason, I see that awakening (bodhi) is very easy to attain.
Therefore, those who wish to attain the path to awakening should not be indolent for as long as their life lasts.

For example, the four great oceans—whether to the south, north, above, or below—may have their limits easily found; yet, the great ocean of the roots of goodness of the four immeasurables, which serves as the provision for awakening, has its limit difficult to find.
"Why do I not now, in every single thought-moment, give rise to the great ocean of the roots of goodness of the four immeasurables as provisions for enlightenment?
Therefore, those who wish to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way should not be indolent until the end of their lives."
"Furthermore, Subāhu!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'If even those such as lions, foxes, wolves, vultures, magpies, crows, birds, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas can attain the unsurpassed path, how much more so should I, who am now born among human beings, not be indolent? "
"Therefore, those who wish to accomplish the unsurpassed path should not be indolent for as long as their life lasts. Furthermore, Subāhu,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in this way:
"Since even those numbering from a hundred to a thousand have already attained the Unsurpassed Way, how could I alone fail to attain it?

Furthermore, there are the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—who have already attained or will attain [enlightenment] in the present and future; therefore, for as long as this life lasts, I must not be indolent."
This bodhisattva should further reflect in this way:

"Whether it be a dharma spoken by the Buddha, spoken by a śrāvaka, spoken by a bodhisattva, or even spoken by a mad person for the sake of the Buddha—namely, the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā."

This bodhisattva, in order to fulfill the Buddha-dharmas, desiring to achieve the unsurpassed path and desiring to attain all-knowledge, applies himself with diligent vigor in these dharmas as if his head were on fire; he studies and maintains them until they are mastered, contemplates and analyzes them to explain them to others, and reflects with a single-minded focus through wisdom and diligence.
If there is any place where sentient beings preach the Dharma—even if it involves hardships such as blades or staves—this bodhisattva will certainly go to that place to listen to what they say.

If there are sentient beings who cultivate karma for pleasant retribution—whether for happiness in the present life or happiness in future lives—the Bodhisattva at that time assists them in accordance with the Dharma through the sublime meaning of wholesome teachings, and likewise applies himself with diligent and vigorous effort toward those wholesome dharmas.
This bodhisattva personally gives his own body to sentient beings, enabling them to attain mastery over it.
It is like the four great elements, within which all sentient beings exercise mastery according to their needs and uses.
It is likewise with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who gives his own body to others, making them master over it.

Through wisdom and diligence—even amidst the perils of swords and staves—he constantly increases his offerings, respect, and veneration toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as toward teachers and elders, those who are weak, aged, afflicted by illness, and the poor and unprotected; he causes them to apply themselves with diligent vigor, as if their very heads were on fire.

In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, he practices giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation; according to those whom he thus gathers, if there are those who wish to attain the Śrāvaka Vehicle, he disciplines and establishes them in the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
if there are those who wish to attain the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, he disciplines and establishes them in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle;
if there are those who wish to attain the Bodhisattva Vehicle, he disciplines and establishes them in the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
Their wisdom and diligence are like those who rush to extinguish a fire on their own heads.

For the sake of wholesome dharmas and for the sake of the causal conditions of the six *pāramitās*, these bodhisattvas disregard cold and heat, hunger and thirst, the stings of mosquitoes and gadflies, wind and sun exposure, harsh contacts, slanders, and insults; nor do they dwell upon various afflictions, exhaustion, or sleep. Throughout this process, until the end of their lives, they never give such things a thought. Their wisdom and diligence are like those who rush to extinguish a fire on their own heads, remaining untiring even amidst the perils of swords and staves.

For the sake of the causal conditions for unsurpassed enlightenment, this bodhisattva is able to undergo various sufferings—namely, the sufferings of asuras, humans, and the three evil realms—without regarding them as difficult, applying wisdom and diligence as if putting out a fire on one's head.
This bodhisattva possesses firm and powerful diligence, a courageous and steadfast mind, and the power of supreme diligence to emerge from the world and attain Buddhahood.

This bodhisattva desires to attain the *vīrya-pāramitā* and to advance toward the *vīrya-pāramitā*, for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to cross over and attain liberation, and to attain all-knowledge and fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.

Now that I have set out toward the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), I vow that all sentient beings may attain crossing-over and liberation; and for the sake of attaining omniscience and being fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, I shall practice such diligence—unbroken, unimpaired, and undegenerated.
If a bodhisattva lacks the strength and power to fully master the training, they should reflect thus:
"I shall now apply myself with diligent vigor, gradually and at all times eliminating indolence and laziness."

Furthermore, one should apply oneself with diligent effort, training gradually and steadily in effort from time to time, so that this effort may increase, expand, and become complete, such that until the end of existence one never becomes indolent nor gives rise to sorrow.

"In this way, when a bodhisattva gives rise to the bodhicitta, maintains the bodhicitta in mind, cultivates the bodhicitta, and aspires toward enlightenment, this is called the immeasurable, boundless, incalculable perfection of wholesome diligence."
Why is this? Such diligence is the most supreme and foremost among all other forms of diligence toward wholesome dharmas.

It is intended to cause all sentient beings, wherever they may be throughout the entire world, to initiate untainted diligence and initiate the diligence of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and to give rise to untainted diligence and give rise to the diligence of one beyond training.
"Subāhu! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence in this way, not regarding it as difficult but regarding it as joy and delight, they will swiftly fulfill the *vīryapāramitā*."
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Three;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
The Twenty-sixth Assembly: The Bodhisattva Subāhu, Part Two. “Subāhu!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the practice of the dhyānapāramitā?”

If a bodhisattva, upon seeing forms with the eye, does not grasp at their signs, yet at times the faculty of the eye is pulled by external conditions, they should correctly practice its protection so as not to follow those conditions; without dwelling the mind on ignorance or craving for the world, they maintain this precept.
At that time, they fully attain the precept of the eye-faculty.
It is the same for hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tangibles with the body, and cognizing phenomena with the mind.

Whether this bodhisattva is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether speaking the Dharma or remaining silent, they never depart from a mind of tranquil concentration (*samādhi*). They skillfully guard their hands and feet so as not to be distracted; they always maintain a sense of shame and remorse to skillfully guard their verbal karma; they look straight ahead with composure, and their mind is ever tranquil, taking no pleasure in frivolous laughter. They skillfully govern the actions of body, speech, and mind, causing them to be peaceful and still.
Whether in private and secluded places or in public and exposed places, he has no divergent thoughts.
Regarding necessary things—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—his mind is always content; he is easy to support, easy to satisfy, and easy to direct.

Practicing wholesome conduct with tranquility and seclusion, he remains free from worldly clamor; his mind is without variation toward gain or loss, defamation or praise, renown or insignificance, suffering or pleasure;
he is neither elated nor dejected. He maintains an impartial mind regarding life and death, feeling neither hatred nor attachment.
One regards enemies as if they were one's own infants, maintaining a mind of constant equanimity toward both patience and impatience.
It is likewise with regard to the voices of the noble and the ordinary, and the sounds of silence and chaos.

In the midst of forms that provoke aversion or affection, his mind neither exalts nor deprecates; being free from passion, hatred, and attachment to the pleasant and unpleasant, it is likewise with sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
This Bodhisattva contemplates desire as a skeleton, [seeing] that such a mind is aroused by false conceptualizations.
One contemplates desire as a lump of meat, because it gives rise to much resentment and hatred.
One contemplates desire as a torch of fire, because it is a dharma of suffering characterized by attachment that distances one from happiness.
One contemplates desire as fruit upon a tree, because many people are fondly attached to it.
One contemplates desire as a loan, because it cannot be possessed with autonomy.
One contemplates desire as a dream, because it perishes moment by moment.
One contemplates desire as an abscess, because one conceives the notion of pleasure within the perversion of suffering.
He contemplates desire as being like a hook, for by practicing various unwholesome dharmas one falls into the evil realms.
He contemplates desire as being like a river of ashes, for it increases the defilement of desire and one never knows satisfaction.

Therefore, having contemplated in this way, the bodhisattva leaves behind desires, unwholesome states, and evil dharmas; with directed thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, joy and happiness, he accomplishes the practice of the first dhyāna.

Free from applied and sustained thought, with internal clarity and confidence, the mind becomes one-pointed; without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, there is joy and bliss, and thus the practice of the second dhyāna is accomplished.

Free from joy, abiding in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, one experiences bliss with the body; this is that noble state which the noble ones describe as "abiding in equanimity, mindful, and dwelling in bliss," and thus the practice of the third dhyāna is accomplished.

Abandoning the intention toward pleasure and pain, and having first extinguished sorrow and joy, one practices equanimity and pure mindfulness, thereby accomplishing the practice of the fourth dhyāna.
One contemplates the perception of happiness toward all sentient beings, thereby accomplishing immeasurable and boundless loving-kindness.
Contemplating the perception of suffering among sentient beings, one accomplishes immeasurable and boundless compassion.
Contemplating the perception of joy among sentient beings, one accomplishes immeasurable and boundless sympathetic joy.
Among sentient beings, he abandons the perceptions of suffering and pleasure, accomplishing an immeasurable and boundless mind of equanimity.
This bodhisattva does not contemplate perceptions of form, accomplishing the tranquil practice of the sphere of infinite space.
Without contemplating the perception of emptiness, one accomplishes the tranquil practice of the sphere of consciousness.
Without contemplating the perception of consciousness, one accomplishes the tranquil practice of the sphere of nothingness.
Without conceptualizing the perception of the sphere of nothingness, he accomplishes the practice of tranquility in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Regarding the inhalation and exhalation, whether following them or abiding with them, he knows them as long when they are long and short when they are short, thereby accomplishing the practice of tranquility in inhalation and exhalation.
This bodhisattva contemplates the perception of the impurity of the body and accomplishes the practice of the tranquility of impurity.
This bodhisattva contemplates the defects of birth, old age, and sickness through the perception of impermanence and accomplishes the practice of the tranquility of the perception of impermanence.
Contemplating the immeasurable faults and afflictions arising within food, one accomplishes the tranquil practice of the perception of the impurity of food.

Contemplating and discerning that amidst the various adornments of worlds, cities, towns, and villages, all must inevitably return to ruin and decay, one accomplishes the tranquil practice of the world's lack of delight.

This bodhisattva, having the perception of internal forms, perceives external forms as limited, whether beautiful or ugly, grasping their characteristics; thus he accomplishes the practice of the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

This bodhisattva, having the perception of internal forms, perceives external forms as manifold, whether beautiful or ugly, grasping their characteristics; thus he accomplishes the practice of the second sphere of mastery.

If this bodhisattva dies or is burned, and is reduced to dust and soil by wind and sun, or is carried away by water, or is broken, destroyed, and worn away, or if the three realms of existence are severed—this is called "having no perception of internal form while observing external forms as limited," whether beautiful or ugly, grasping their characteristics; thus one accomplishes the practice of the third stage of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

This bodhisattva, being internally without the perception of form, externally perceives forms that are manifold—whether beautiful or ugly—and grasps their characteristics; thus they accomplish the practice of the fourth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

This bodhisattva, being internally without the perception of form, externally perceives blue forms that are immeasurable and boundless, delighting in them and grasping their characteristics; thus they accomplish the practice of the fifth sphere of mastery.

This bodhisattva, being internally without the perception of form, externally perceives forms that are red, immeasurable and boundless; delighting in them and grasping their signs, they accomplish the practice of the sixth sphere of mastery.

This bodhisattva, being internally without the perception of form, externally perceives forms that are yellow, immeasurable and boundless; delighting in them and grasping their signs, they accomplish the practice of the seventh sphere of mastery.

This bodhisattva, being internally without the perception of form, externally perceives forms that are white, immeasurable, and boundless; delighting in them and grasping their signs, they accomplish the practice of the eighth sphere of mastery.

This bodhisattva enters into these immeasurable and boundless spheres of all places (*sarvatraga*), not dwelling on their distinct characteristics, thereby accomplishing the first practice of the spheres of all places.

This bodhisattva enters into the immeasurable and boundless spheres of water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, space, and consciousness, not dwelling on their distinct characteristics, thereby accomplishing the ten practices of the spheres of all places (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatanāni*).

When this bodhisattva enters into the dharma of suffering, his mind takes as its object all roots of goodness, namely: great loving-kindness and great compassion; upholding the true Dharma; ensuring the non-interruption of the Three Jewels; adorning the body of a Buddha; purifying the Brahma-voice; fulfilling former vows; teaching and transforming sentient beings; purifying Buddha-fields; sitting beneath the Bodhi tree; turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma; and severing all fetters and afflictions of sentient beings—such are the objects upon which his mind focuses.

When this bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, he is detached from the four stations of consciousness; he does not rely on the great elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness, nor does he rely on this world or future worlds. Entering such concentration, he has no dependence whatsoever.
When this bodhisattva enters dhyāna, his mind is filled with joy because he desires to enter the unsurpassed samādhi of liberation.
This bodhisattva practices dhyāna with the vow that all sentient beings may attain deliverance and liberation, and for the sake of attaining all-knowledge and perfecting all Buddha-dharmas.

Whether contemplating or having already contemplated, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain crossing-over and liberation, and for the sake of attaining all-knowledge and being fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
If one lacks the power to train in this meditative concentration, that bodhisattva should reflect as follows:

"I shall now, from time to time, gradually and diligently apply myself to vigor in order to distance myself from a distracted mind; from time to time, I shall gradually and diligently apply myself to vigor in training in single-mindedness, so that this single-mindedness may expand and become fully perfected, such that until the end of existence I never grow indolent nor give rise to sorrow."

This bodhisattva arouses the mind of enlightenment, contemplates the mind of enlightenment, and cultivates the mind of enlightenment; they long for enlightenment and aspire to seek enlightenment. This is called the immeasurable and boundless meditative concentration of the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, intended to cause all sentient beings, wherever they may be throughout the entire world, to arouse untainted meditative concentration and arouse the meditative concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and to give rise to untainted meditative concentration and give rise to the meditative concentration of one beyond training.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this meditative concentration, they do not regard it as difficult but rather as joy and bliss, swiftly fulfilling the dhyāna-pāramitā. "Saubhūti!
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the perfection of wisdom? O Subāhu!

If there is a person of keen intelligence and wisdom who, having studied, is able to retain [the teachings], and having heard them, practices recitation; who skillfully studies the profound characteristics and meanings of all dharmas and is also able to discern them; and who, regarding the dharmas as they were heard, reflects upon their meaning after hearing them."

When there are such persons as these, the Bodhisattva at that time should draw near to them, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising them; he should not even distance himself from them, even at the risk of swords or staves.

Because this bodhisattva has studied the teachings, understood their definitive meaning, contemplated that meaning, and made offerings to and honored his teachers and preceptors, he will not avoid various difficult and painful matters—even unto death—such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, the stinging of mosquitoes and gadflies, wind, sunburn, harsh physical contact, verbal abuse, and slander.

This bodhisattva conceives the thought of a mass of jewels regarding the True Dharma; the thought of a treasury of jewels regarding the teacher of the Dharma; the thought of one difficult to encounter regarding those who listen to the Dharma; the thought of the life of wisdom regarding those who inquire about its meaning; the thought of wisdom regarding those who, through extensive learning, eliminate ignorance; and the thought of the eye of wisdom arising through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes regarding those who discern all phenomena.

When this bodhisattva hears these various dharmas, having received, upheld, practiced, studied, and extensively analyzed them, he comes to know the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the four noble truths; the twelve links of dependent origination; and the three periods of time and the three vehicles—thus he attains such knowledge.
"How does one know the elements?
One knows two elements:
the conditioned element and the unconditioned element; these are called the two elements."
What is the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*)?
Any phenomena that arise, abide, and cease are called the conditioned realm.
What is the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*)?
If phenomena are without arising, abiding, or ceasing, this is called the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).
This is called knowing the conditioned and unconditioned realms.
Furthermore, one knows the three realms: the wholesome realm, the unwholesome realm, and the indeterminate realm.
What is the wholesome element?
If it is non-greed associated with non-greed, or non-hatred associated with non-hatred, or non-delusion associated with non-delusion, this is called the wholesome element.
What is the unwholesome element (*akuśaladhātu*)?
If greed is accompanied by greed, or hatred is accompanied by hatred, or delusion is accompanied by delusion, this is called the unwholesome element.
What is the indeterminate element (*avyākṛtadhātu*)?
Excluding the wholesome and the unwholesome, if there are any remaining phenomena, these are called the indeterminate realm (*avyākṛta-dhātu*).
Furthermore, one should know the three realms, namely: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What is the desire realm?

It consists of the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

If, within this, there is desire, defilement, attachment, hatred, delusion, longing, and the mental activities arising from the wish to obtain [objects], this is called knowing the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
What is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?

The Brahmā Heaven, the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers, the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue, the Great Brahmā Heaven, the Heaven of Light, the Heaven of Limited Light, the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, the Heaven of Radiant Sound, the Heaven of Purity, the Heaven of Limited Purity, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, the Heaven of Universal Purity, the Heaven of Abundant Fruit, the Heaven of Limited Fruit, the Heaven of Vast Fruit, the Heaven of Immeasurable Fruit, the Heaven of Non-perception, the Heaven Without Heat, the Heaven Without Affliction, the Heaven of Good Vision, the Heaven of Excellent Good Vision, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
If, within this context, there is attachment to form, delusion, and longing, and the activity of the mind that seeks to obtain [form], this is called the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
What is the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
The devas of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If, within these, there is formless defilement, delusion, and longing, and the desire to produce mental karma, this is called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These are called the three realms.
Furthermore, one knows the four realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, the formless realm, and the unconditioned realm; this is called knowing the four realms.

Furthermore, one knows the six elements, namely: the element of desire, the element of ill-will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill-will, and the element of non-cruelty; this is called knowing the six elements.
Furthermore, one knows the six elements, namely: the earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements; these are called the six elements.

One contemplates that the earth element is impermanent and subject to transformation and decay, possessing neither solidity nor stability. If it is impermanent, it is suffering; if it is suffering, it is without self.

The great elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and lack any mark of solidity. That which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self.
This is called knowing the six elements.
“After this bodhisattva has heard such a Dharma, having received, upheld, practiced, and extensively analyzed it, he immediately understands the five aggregates—
namely, the aggregate of form, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
Form is like foam on water; it arises and perishes, unable to endure for long.
Feeling is like a bubble on water; it arises and perishes, unable to endure for long.
Perception is like a mirage; it arises and perishes, unable to endure for long.
Formative activity is like a plantain tree; it is subject to arising and ceasing and cannot endure for long.
Consciousness is like a magical illusion; it is subject to arising and ceasing and cannot endure for long.
This is called knowing the five aggregates.
“After this bodhisattva has heard this Dharma, received and maintained it, practiced and studied it, and extensively analyzed it, he immediately knows the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
These are the eye base, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases; these are called the six internal sense bases.”

The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is itself the nature of suffering, the nature of aging, and the nature of death; it is empty, selfless, and devoid of what belongs to a self; it is ablaze with the three poisons.

Birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress are likewise able to set ablaze all phenomena of suffering. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: they are ablaze with the three poisons, and so on, up to all forms of suffering.
This is called knowing the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*).

Furthermore, knowing the six external sense bases: the forms seen by the eye are called the external sense bases; the sounds heard by the ear, the odors smelled by the nose, the tastes tasted by the tongue, the tangibles felt by the body, and the mental objects known by the mind—these are called the external sense bases.

The forms seen by the eye are external sense bases; they are of an unstable nature, without support, and devoid of power. All are impermanent, as they truly are and not otherwise, like illusions and like magical transformations.

The sounds heard by the ear, the odors smelled by the nose, the flavors tasted by the tongue, the tangibles felt by the body, and the mental objects known by the mind are also like this; this is called knowing the six external sense bases.
“Once this bodhisattva has heard such a Dharma, having received, upheld, practiced, and extensively analyzed it, he immediately knows the Four Noble Truths.
That is to say: the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin, the Noble Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path; these are called the Four Noble Truths.”
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering?
The five aggregates, the six elements, the six internal sense bases, and the six external sense bases—these are called suffering.

This suffering is impermanent; it is like a hostile thief, like an abscess, like an arrow, like imprisonment in a prison, and like the breaking of a vessel. This lack of self-mastery is itself non-self.
Having attained such knowledge, this is called knowing the Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is the Noble Truth of the Origin?
It refers to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and the conceit of "I am," which consist of a persistent grasping at a self and the definitive reckoning that the self is permanent and indestructible.
"The self is form; the self is distinct from form. The self is perception;
the self is distinct from perception. The self is neither perception nor non-perception;
the self is distinct from neither perception nor non-perception."
The self is identical to the aggregates; the self is distinct from the aggregates.
The aggregates are within the self; the self is within the aggregates.
The self is identical to the elements and sense-bases; the self is distinct from the elements and sense-bases.
The self exists within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases exist within the self.
The self is identical to sensation, yet the self is distinct from sensation.
The self is identical to cognition, yet the self is distinct from cognition.
"I am without feeling; I am distinct from feeling.
"I am limited in form; I am distinct from limited form.
"I am infinite in form; I am distinct from infinite form."
"I am permanent; I am impermanent;
I am both permanent and impermanent; I am neither permanent nor impermanent.
I am finite; I am infinite; I am both finite and infinite; I am neither finite nor infinite."
The Tathāgata exists after death; the Tathāgata does not exist after death; the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
Life is identical to the body, and the body is identical to life.
From where do these sentient beings come, and to where do they go?
These sentient beings are subject to annihilation and possess no continuity; what one has done oneself, one receives oneself, and what another has done, another receives.
One who conceives of a self necessarily has what belongs to a self; one who has what belongs to a self necessarily has a self.
In this way, they grasp at the view of a self and the view of a body, whether as fetters or latent tendencies, or as "I" and "mine."

I receive the root of greed, hatred, and delusion; whether it be the aggregate of bodily, verbal, and mental karma, or meritorious karma, or non-meritorious karma, or karma of the desire realm, or karma of the form and formless realms—this is called the Noble Truth of Origination.
What is the noble truth of cessation?
The exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion; the exhaustion of "I" and "mine"; and the exhaustion of grasping, becoming, and existence—this is called the noble truth of cessation.
What is the noble truth of the path?

When one sees the cessation of suffering and its origin, contemplates the faults and perils of all conditioned phenomena, perceives the tranquility of Nirvana, and has accomplished what was to be done—abiding in such a state, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are called the Noble Truth of the Path.
Thus one knows the Four Noble Truths; when this bodhisattva discriminates and contemplates the Four Noble Truths, he sees that conditioned phenomena are suffering, impermanent, empty, and non-self.
One perceives that unconditioned dharmas can provide protection, serving as a shelter and a refuge; yet, although one performs such contemplation, one does not realize nirvana.
In this way, one knows the Four Noble Truths.
“After this bodhisattva has heard such a Dharma, having received, upheld, practiced, and extensively analyzed it, he immediately understands the twelve links of dependent origination.

That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging and death. These are called the twelve links of dependent origination.”
If one does not know and does not see the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

If there are actions of body, speech, and mind—whether meritorious actions, non-meritorious actions, or those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—these are called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
If there is mind, thought, and consciousness, this is called *vijñāna* (consciousness).
If there is feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention, this is called *nāma* (name).

If there are the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—from the *kalala* stage up to birth by transformation, whether produced by action or not produced by action—this is called *rūpa* (form).
The union of name and form is called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
If there are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, these are called the "six sense bases" (ṣaḍāyatana).
When the eye conditions visible forms to produce visual consciousness, the coming together of these three factors produces contact; this is called "contact" (sparśa).
If there is painful feeling, pleasant feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, this is called feeling (*vedanā*).
If there is craving and attachment, this is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
If there is craving, views, or adherence to precepts and rituals, this is called clinging (*upādāna*).
If there is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is called existence (*bhava*).
If this existence arises, this is called birth (*jāti*).
If this existence decays and changes, this is called old age (*jarā*).
If this existence undergoes dissolution and destruction, it is called death.

When a bodhisattva thus discriminates and contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not give rise to attachment toward the earth as being "I" because of what is seen, heard, sensed, or known; nor do they give rise to attachment toward themselves as being "the earth," nor do they harbor any longing for it.
Water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are also like this.

Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that *nirvāṇa* is not the self, one does not give rise to attachment; that the self is not *nirvāṇa*, one does not give rise to attachment, nor does one harbor any longing for it.

This bodhisattva perceives that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; knowing the three gates of liberation, they extensively cultivate and study the vision of all phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless.
When this bodhisattva sees that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, knows the bliss of cessation, and has diligently practiced and extensively analyzed them, then ignorance ceases.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease.
In this way, although the bodhisattva contemplates the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not realize cessation.
The bodhisattva thus understands the twelve links of dependent origination.

Having heard this Dharma, the bodhisattva single-mindedly receives, maintains, practices, and studies it; having extensively analyzed it, they immediately know the three periods of time—namely, the past, the future, and the present.
What is the past? If a phenomenon has arisen and ceased, it is called the past. What is the future?
If a phenomenon has not yet arisen and not yet originated, it is called the future world.
What is the present world?
If a phenomenon has already arisen but has not yet ceased, it is called the present world.
This bodhisattva reflects upon the various unwholesome roots of the past, regarding them with contempt and revulsion, and thus rejects and abandons them.
Regarding unwholesome roots of the future, he recognizes that they will result in unwholesome retributions, which he finds neither pleasing nor desirable and which are not to his liking.
He shall ensure that unwholesome roots do not arise in the present.
This bodhisattva is able to restrain and protect the actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as the six sense faculties, constantly giving rise to wholesome karma without interruption.

Regarding past roots of goodness, this is the bodhisattva’s bodhicitta: being single-mindedly mindful of bodhi, longing for bodhi, and desiring to attain bodhi; out of deep and profound love and joy, vowing that all sentient beings may cross over and attain liberation, for the sake of attaining all-knowledge and fulfilling all Buddha-dharmas.
The same applies to the future and the present; one should never depart from this mind, remaining ultimately free from indolence, loss of mindfulness, and negligence.
As for the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of the past, these are utterly extinguished, unreal, non-existent, without self, and without what belongs to a self.
If the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of future lives have not yet arisen and have not yet emerged, they are without self and without what belongs to a self.
As for the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the present, they do not abide from moment to moment.
Why is this? Among worldly phenomena, there is not a single moment that abides.
If there were such a moment, even within that single moment there would be arising, abiding, and ceasing; and these very processes of arising, abiding, and ceasing likewise do not abide.

Just as within arising, abiding, and ceasing there are the internal and external aggregates, elements, and sense bases, so too these internal and external aggregates, elements, and sense bases possess arising, abiding, and ceasing.
If they do not abide in this manner, then they are neither self nor what belongs to a self.
If the past has ceased and perished, being unreal and non-existent, it is neither self nor what belongs to self.
If the future has not yet arisen or occurred, it is neither self nor what belongs to self.
If the present moment does not abide from instant to instant, it is neither "I" nor "mine.
To see that the three periods of time are neither "I" nor "mine" is what is called true wisdom.

Not perceiving "I" or "mine," nor what belongs to "I" or "mine," one thus practices non-self and non-mine regarding all states of existence (*bhava*). One practices the perception of dispassion, the perception of abandonment, and the perception of cessation; yet, although one performs these practices, one does not realize *nirvāṇa*.
This is called knowing the three periods of time.
Having heard this Dharma, the bodhisattva receives, maintains, practices, and extensively analyzes it, thereby immediately coming to know the three vehicles:
namely, the celestial vehicle, the Brahma vehicle, and the noble vehicle.
What is the celestial vehicle?
The first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna—these are called the celestial vehicle.
What is the Brahma vehicle?
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are called the Brahma-vehicle.
What is the Noble Vehicle?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are called the Noble Vehicle.

When this bodhisattva from time to time cultivates and accumulates the celestial vehicle, the Brahma vehicle, and the noble vehicle, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they abide in the three vehicles, yet at that time does not personally realize liberation for themselves—this is called "knowing the three vehicles."
Furthermore, one knows the three vehicles, namely: the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna.
What is the Śrāvaka vehicle?

Those of dull faculties who seek liberation; in a single thought-moment, they depart from the dwelling-place of the three realms of existence. Desiring to transcend the world and attain nirvāṇa, they perceive the state of quiescent extinction and apply themselves with diligent vigor as if their heads were on fire.

If one has not yet understood the Four Noble Truths, and desires to shoot at the targets of the Four Truths with the arrows of wisdom, seeking realization and understanding through profound aspiration and diligent effort, this is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.
What is the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle?

Those of middling faculties who seek liberation, desiring to attain tranquility by dwelling alone in a solitary place, who benefit themselves by entering into tranquil meditative absorption, and who skillfully analyze the twelve links of dependent origination—desiring to attain the path of the pratyekabuddha and realizing the state of a pratyekabuddha—this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
What is the Mahāyāna?

It is for those of superior faculties who seek liberation and desire to bring all sentient beings across to deliverance and liberation; it is for the attainment of omniscience and the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas through the six pāramitās; it is the desire to benefit all worlds and to sever the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings. Such a person regards even the five sensual pleasures of all worlds as utterly contemptible, let alone the immeasurable sufferings of the world.

I desire to cause sentient beings to uphold the unsurpassed precepts, and to enable them to hear and see the Mahāyāna sūtras, so that they may receive, uphold, practice, study, contemplate, and discern them; and by reciting them, they may become proficient, applying themselves with diligent and vigorous effort.

If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), one should approach and attend upon them, desiring to cause sentient beings to grasp true wisdom and abide in the four methods of attraction.
One should constantly seek to hear the essential points of all profound dharmas, receiving, upholding, and discerning them.

Desiring to lead all beings into meditative concentration, he personally relinquishes his own happiness to benefit sentient beings; wishing to use his own power to accord with the inclinations of others, he causes them to abide in the Three Vehicles.
Although they manifest such transformations, they always abide securely within the unsurpassed path, their minds indestructible and unshakable like a vajra.
Constantly aspiring to attain unsurpassed bodhi and seeking bodhi—this is called the Mahāyāna.
This is called knowing the three vehicles.
Having heard this Dharma, the bodhisattva receives, maintains, practices, and extensively analyzes it, thereby immediately understanding skillful means.
With body and mind prostrate before the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, he makes this his primary practice; regarding all that he does, he vows for the unsurpassed path.

Having thus taken refuge and generated the bodhicitta, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or while eating, drinking, bathing, or washing, one should have no other thought than this: may there be only the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi. One should always practice such extensive and vast cultivation.

Whether this bodhisattva has first entered meditative concentration or has already entered it, they constantly aspire for all sentient beings to attain crossing-over and liberation; for the sake of attaining all-knowledge and fulfilling all Buddha-dharmas; desiring to be honored within the world; desiring to subdue all sentient beings; desiring to be unsurpassed among all sentient beings; desiring to attain the most supreme state; desiring to instruct and admonish all sentient beings; desiring to cause all sentient beings to attain quiescence; and desiring to achieve perfect enlightenment regarding all dharmas.

When this bodhisattva is endowed with training, he makes a vow that all his roots of goodness performed shall cause all sentient beings to be free from fear, to emerge from the three evil realms, to extinguish immeasurable suffering, and to sever all afflictions.
May those who, in the present and the future, desire to attain the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, be granted its full fulfillment.
May those who, in the present and the future, desire to attain the Mahāyāna, be granted its full fulfillment.

I pray that all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the present and future throughout all worlds, may remain in the world for an eon to preach the Dharma, so that the assembly of noble ones may attain harmony while following the Buddhas as they dwell in the world.
This bodhisattva reflects in this way:

"In whatever place there may be, regarding all the roots of goodness cultivated by sentient beings—whether they wish to be born among humans or in the heavens, or whether they abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or abide in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas—I vow that they shall be fully endowed with loving speech, generosity, beneficial conduct, and cooperation."
By means of this Dharma, that bodhisattva, throughout the three periods of the day, recites, masters, and contemplates this teaching. That is to say:
"I now take refuge in all Buddhas, Dharmas, Saṅghas, and Bodhisattvas, wherever they may be throughout all worlds; I prostrate with my head at their feet in reverent salutation."
The majestic power of all Buddhas is unsurpassed, and their marks are most wondrous.

A Bodhisattva should constantly maintain this thought regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha: "May there be no empty space anywhere throughout the world; may there always be Buddhas in every direction, so that I may exhort them to remain for an eon, preaching the subtle and wonderful Dharma and censuring all evils."
