Whether performed in the past or being performed now, I have already attained freedom from all evil; even for the duration of a single thought-moment, I vow that by means of all roots of goodness, may all sentient beings attain immeasurable lifespans and abide within all wholesome dharmas.
Just as all bodhisattvas swiftly turn the wheel of Dharma, causing the noble ones to attain morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
may the Buddha-dharma abide forever in the world to benefit sentient beings.
May all those born in the five realms of existence obtain roots of goodness, even unto prostrating before all Buddhas,
and may they always abide in this vow.
May all the virtuous vows of these bodhisattvas cause other sentient beings as well as their own bodies to attain wondrous majesty and virtue.
May all the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Sangha Treasures of the future and present worlds abide for one kalpa without any obstacles.
Furthermore, may all the Bodhisattva Treasures swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās and quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, likewise without any hindrance.

I desire to cause all sentient beings to sever suffering, affliction, and fear, and to practice joy and bliss; to sever all unwholesome roots and accomplish all wholesome roots; to achieve the three vehicles according to their respective vows; to swiftly perfect the various pāramitās; and to attain liberation through immeasurable life-span, thereby accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way.
Up until prostrating before all Buddhas, they constantly make this vow:

"May I cause all sentient beings to sever all suffering and affliction. Whatever Buddhas exist throughout every place in all worlds, even including those of the Dharma-body, I vow to offer my own body as a gift to those Buddhas. Desiring to enable all sentient beings to attain liberation and achieve the Unsurpassed Way, may they, in whatever place they are born, have faith and reverence for the Triple Gem."

They offer celestial fragrant flowers to serve and sustain Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise make offerings to the Dharma, the Sangha, and all Bodhisattvas, such that the jewels they present are like Mount Sumeru.

Wherever there may be sentient beings throughout all the worlds, whatever they may require—be it dwellings made of the seven treasures, clothing, food and drink, medicine, or bedding—I shall provide them with everything so that none shall lack for anything.

If there are those who delight in patience, diligence, and the observance of precepts, I shall explain the Dharma according to their inclinations so that they may achieve the supreme Dharma, causing them to be fully endowed with the Three Jewels, to cultivate the six pāramitās, and to swiftly attain the Buddha-way.

Free from all unwholesome dharmas, they practice the true meaning of wholesome conduct through the actions of body, speech, and mind; they do not regress from bodhi and delight in bodhi; wherever they may be, they see Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and constantly cultivate roots of goodness, establishing sentient beings securely within wholesome dharmas.

This bodhisattva, knowing for himself and for others all roots of goodness, directs them toward wisdom and the wisdom of reflection; this is because he vows to cause all sentient beings to attain crossing-over and liberation, and to attain all-knowledge and fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.

Having directed his thoughts toward this, the bodhisattva makes a vow so that all sentient beings may attain crossing-over and liberation, and so that he himself may attain all-knowledge and be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
If this bodhisattva lacks the power to study with such wisdom, they should reflect as follows:
"I shall now apply myself with diligent vigor, gradually severing ignorance from time to time."

I shall now further redouble my diligence, training in this wisdom gradually from time to time, so that this wisdom may increase, expand, and become fully perfected; until the end of existence, I shall never be indolent or give rise to sorrow.

"In this way, when a bodhisattva generates the bodhicitta, contemplates the bodhicitta, cultivates the bodhicitta, and aspires for the bodhicitta, this is the immeasurable and boundless wholesome wisdom of that bodhisattva."

Why is this? Because this wisdom is the most supreme and foremost among all other virtuous wisdoms; it causes all sentient beings in the world to give rise to immeasurable wisdom and to give rise to the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna), producing untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) and producing the wisdom of one beyond training.
"Subāhu! When a bodhisattva practices this wisdom in this way, they do not regard it as difficult, but rather find joy and delight in it, thereby swiftly fulfilling the prajñāpāramitā."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Subāhu joyfully praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! He then accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Four;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
27. The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Suśīla. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, surrounded with great reverence by a vast assembly of five hundred śrāvakas and ten thousand bodhisattvas.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the city of Śrāvastī named Śūradatta (Good Compliance). Having planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past and having served and made offerings to them, he had attained non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He dwelt in great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) without anger; he dwelt in great compassion (*karuṇā*) with tireless, vast salvation; he dwelt in great joy (*muditā*) in the peaceful stabilization of the *dharmadhātu*; he dwelt in great equanimity (*upekṣā*) with the equality of suffering and pleasure. Moderating his food intake and eating at the proper times, he had few desires and was content; he was always a joy for sentient beings to behold.

He constantly used the five precepts and the eightfold fast-day observances to compassionately teach and transform people within a certain city; thereafter, he further exhorted them to practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity, and pure brahmacarya.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣemaṃkara, in order to enable sentient beings to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, was surrounded by a multitude of people as he proceeded toward the Buddha’s dwelling.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beheld this bodhisattva with his pure divine eye; seeing that he dwelt in the practice of supreme diligence and the dhūta austerities, possessed pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), and was firm in his great resolve for universal salvation, he thought to himself:
"This Kṣemaṃkara has never been weary or idle in his holy life (*brahmacarya*); could it be that he does not seek the station of Śakra?"
"Or is he coveting the throne of a king and sensual pleasures?

Having had this thought, he immediately manifested himself as four men and approached the Bodhisattva, reviling and abusing him with various foul words, and further assailing and harming him by striking him with swords, staves, tiles, and stones.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, abiding in the power of loving-kindness and patience, endured it all without ever harboring anger or resentment.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again manifested four great men and came to speak to the Bodhisattva:
"O virtuous and compliant one! Alas!"

Those wicked people have reviled you with unwholesome speech and have wantonly struck and harmed you with tiles, stones, swords, staves, and the like; why do you not command me to take revenge for you?
"I shall sever your life-faculty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to those people:
"O sons of good family, do not speak such words."
If one commits killing, they accomplish evil karma.
Even if someone were to dismember this body of mine limb by limb, like slicing dates or leaves, I would never give rise to a thought of killing.

Why is this? Those who commit murder fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; even if they subsequently obtain a human body, their parents will not love or care for them, and they will be constantly loathed by all people.
Good son! All dharmas are of two kinds:
first, wholesome dharmas; second, unwholesome dharmas.
"By unwholesome dharmas one falls into the evil destinies; by relying on wholesome dharmas, one obtains benefit and merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śūnyatānulomika, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as planting seeds, both good and evil, All arise according to karma."
How could there be bitter seeds that produce sweet fruit?
Such is the nature of phenomena as they appear; the wise should reflect upon this:
suffering is the retribution for evil conditions, while doing good brings constant peace and happiness.

At that time, having heard these words, the person manifested by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself, "I am unable to cause that bodhisattva to commit an act of killing," and suddenly vanished.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, again transformed himself into heaps of gold and silver treasures and sent the men to the Bodhisattva’s location, saying to them:
"You may employ skillful means to take these precious treasures and use them as you please."
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to those people:
"Good sons, do not speak thus. Why is this?
Now, the practice of theft can cause sentient beings to become impoverished, lowly, and without refuge or protection.
Even if I were so poor that my life could not be sustained, I would never engage in the act of taking what is not given.
"Friends, you should know that ordinary people are ignorant and deluded, obscured by their greedy cravings; how could a wise person practice taking what is not given?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śūrasena spoke these verses:
"Though one may accumulate wealth amounting to hundreds of billions, If the mind of greedy attachment is not relinquished,"
The wise say that such a person, though living in this world, is always poor and suffering;
yet although they possess not a single thing, they abide in a mind of renunciation.
The wise say that such a person is the most wealthy in the world.
The wise person, free from all evils, is entirely dignified;
the fool, by committing sins, has his entire body made ugly.
The wise person exhorts the cultivation of goodness, while the fool constantly commits evil.
"It is better to endure the insults of the wise than to receive the praise of fools.
Having heard these words, the person conjured by the Lord of Devas departed with a heavy heart.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again personally tested him by bringing ten million pieces of gold to where the Bodhisattva was and speaking these words:
"Previously, in this great city of Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit had a dispute with another man, and he required a person to serve as a witness for me."
"If you are able to act as my witness, I shall offer this gold to you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Śakra:

"Virtuous one, you should know that one who speaks falsely commits an unwholesome karma; having deceived oneself, one also deceives the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas."

Because false speech serves as the root of all evils, it leads one toward unwholesome realms and destroys pure precepts; it can ruin the physical body, cause the breath to be perpetually foul, and result in one's words being despised by others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke again in verse:
"The person who speaks falsehoods has breath that is always foul; Entering the miserable and evil realms, there is no one able to save them."
Now, as for those who speak falsehoods, they deceive themselves and likewise deceive the devas, nāgas, mahoragas, and others.
One should know that false speech is the root of all evils; it destroys the pure precepts, and at death, one enters the three miserable realms.
"Even if you were to give me as much gold as fills Jambudvīpa,
I could never utter a falsehood.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard these words, he suddenly vanished from sight.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, again commanded Queen Śacī, Queen Āditya, and the five-headed queens and others to go to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling to further test and refine him, seeking to cause him to violate his precepts.

Then Śākī and the others took five hundred women in the prime of their youth, anointed their bodies with perfumes, and adorned them with floral ornaments; during the final watch of the night, they approached the Bodhisattva and spoke these words:
"We women are in the full bloom of our youth and beauty; we pray that you will take us as your pillow and mat, and grant us your pleasure."
At that time, the Bodhisattva gazed upon those women with an undefiled eye and addressed them, saying:

"In the realms of hell, animals, and Yama, there are those who are deranged and of unrighteous mind; they are addicted to the foul, stinking, impure pus and blood, and take delight in the evil rākṣasīs as their kin. They do not have the pure retinues of devas and humans as their kin."
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke again in verse:
"Fools, deluded and confused, dwell upon impurity; They are addicted to and defiled by this stinking body of pus and blood.
All desires swiftly perish and return to impermanence, Causing them to sink forever into the realm of Yama and hell."

Even if there were emanations like you, with physical forms so sublime as to fill the world, I would not harbor a single thought of lustful attachment; I would always regard them as being like dreams or enemies.

At that time, although Śacī and the others displayed every kind of seductive transformation, the Bodhisattva remained entirely free from any desire or attachment. Each returned to his celestial palace and said to Śakra:
"I observe that his virtuous resolve is firm and steadfast; he shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment, of this there is no doubt."
"Why is this? He has not the slightest craving or affection for us; he merely feels weary of and detached from us.
At that time, although Śakra heard these words, he still harbored distress as if an arrow had pierced his body, constantly thinking:
"That man will surely seize and plunder me; of this there is no doubt.
I should now go and test him further: among all his vows, which one does he truly desire?"
Having thought thus, he approached the Bodhisattva, cast off his pride, prostrated with his head at the Bodhisattva’s feet, and asked him in verse:
“You now diligently practice the pure brahma-faring; In regard to all desires, what do you seek?”
"Are you seeking the status of the Sun, Moon, Śakra, or Brahmā?
Or are you seeking the royal thrones within the three realms of existence?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Suśīla replied in verse:
"I observe the sun, moon, Śakra, and Brahmā, The royal thrones of the world, and the retributions of the three realms of existence;
All are impermanent and lack solidity— What wise person would make such a vow?"
At that time, having heard these verses, Śakra, Lord of Devas, again addressed the Bodhisattva:
"If it is as you have said, what vow do you seek?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"I originally did not crave worldly pleasures, but sought only the body that is neither born nor extinguished;
diligently practicing skillful means to save all beings, I vow that we may ascend together upon that path to Bodhi."
At that time, having heard these verses, Śakra, Lord of Devas, felt peace and joy in his heart; he knew for certain that the Bodhisattva did not seek the position of Śakra.
Overjoyed and leaping with delight, he praised him in verse:
"You speak of vast salvation for the sake of all living beings; This mind of yours is so expansive, there is none equal to it."
"May you defeat the armies of Māra and realize the nectar of immortality; through this, may you forever turn the supreme Wheel of Dharma.
When the Lord of Devas had spoken these verses, he circumambulated the Bodhisattva with reverence, prostrated at his feet, and suddenly vanished.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śūradatta entered the city of Śrāvastī in the early morning to wander for the sake of teaching and transforming others. There he obtained a bell made of Jambū-river gold from the beginning of the kalpa; the value of that bell exceeded the entire land of Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took this golden bell and, at a crossroads, proclaimed in a loud voice:
"Who in this city of Śrāvastī is the poorest? To them I shall give this bell as a gift."
At that time, there was a most eminent elder who, having heard these words, came running and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"I am the poorest person in this city; you may take this bell and give it to me."
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the elder: "You are not poor. Why is this so?
"In this city, there is a son of good family who is the poorest among the poor;
you should give these bells to him. The elder asked, "Who is this person?"
The Bodhisattva replied,
"King Prasenajit is the poorest person in this city.
Then that elder said to the Bodhisattva:
"Do not speak thus. Why is this?
King Prasenajit is wealthy and noble, his treasuries overflowing with riches, and his rare treasures and goods are inexhaustible."
"Why do you say that he is the poorest among the poor?
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied in verse before the great assembly:
"Even if one possessed billions of hidden treasures, / Because of a greedy and loving heart, there is no satisfaction."
Just as the great ocean swallows all streams, so too is the foolish person most impoverished.
Because of this, craving further increases; spreading and entangling, it arises in continuous succession.
In both the present life and the future, that one lacking wisdom is ever poor and destitute.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Śūradatta had spoken these verses, he and the great assembly immediately went to visit King Prasenajit.
At that moment, the king was together with more than five hundred elders, calculating and accounting for the treasures and wealth in his treasury.
At that time, the Bodhisattva came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"While I was traveling through and teaching in this city, I obtained a Jambūnada-gold bell from the beginning of the kalpa; the value of that bell exceeds the entire land of Jambudvīpa."
At that time, I secretly thought to myself:
"In this city, there is one who is the poorest; I shall take this bell and give it to him.
Then I reflected further:
"Among those in the city, none is poorer than the King.
Now I bring this bell and wish to offer it to you; since the King is impoverished, please accept it for my sake.
Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva further recited a verse:
"If a person is full of greedy seeking, accumulating wealth without ever being satisfied,
such a person in a state of madness is called the most impoverished.
When the king constantly imposes heavy taxes and inflicts unjust punishments upon the innocent,"
Attached to kingdoms and cities, he does not contemplate the karma of future lives;
though he has attained mastery over the world, he cannot provide shelter for the multitude of beings,
and upon seeing those in poverty and suffering, he never feels a thought of compassion.
Addicted to women, they fear not the evil realms;
never awakening to their own depravity and confusion, are they not truly the poor?
If a person possesses pure faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, [they shall not be so].
Regarding the body, life, and wealth, one should constantly reflect that they are not firm.
Having known them to be not firm, one will not be deluded by them;
thus, regarding body, life, and wealth, one can forever attain what is eternally firm.
If one can diligently abide in mindfulness and delight in heedfulness, that person is called wealthy and noble; their virtuous wealth is ever peaceful and happy.
Just as when fire burns, it never tires of the forest trees.
The King is now just like this, his craving never reaching satiety.
As the clouds are never sated with water, nor the ocean ever sated with its waters, so it is with the King now;
when will there ever be a time of satisfaction?
The sun and moon constantly traverse their courses, never wearying of the four quarters;
so too is it with you now, O King, who until the end of your life shall find no rest.
Just as fire, when it burns, never tires of consuming grass and wood.
The wise person is also like this: they never fail to practice goodness.
Just as water never tires of clouds, and just as the ocean never tires of water, so too the wise person never tires of increasing their goodness.
"Though sovereignty over a kingdom may be attained, it ultimately returns to impermanence;
all things are impure—thus the wise should renounce them.
When King Prasenajit heard these words, he felt deep shame within and said to the Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, O virtuous one!
Although you have exhorted me well, I still do not yet believe.
Now, as for these words of yours, did you speak them yourself?”
"Is there any proof of this?
The Bodhisattva replied, "Have you not heard?

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who possesses all-knowledge, is now present together with immeasurable devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, at the great city of Śrāvastī; he shall testify that you, Great King, are indeed a poor man.
The king said: "Virtuous one!
If it be as you say, I wish to go with you to see the Tathāgata, to hear his instructions, and to take refuge in him and make offerings."
The Bodhisattva replied:

"Great King, you should know that the realm of the Tathāgata cannot be fathomed by ordinary fools. Having destroyed afflictions and pride, and out of compassion for sentient beings, he—through his noble wisdom—knows this world and the worlds to come."
If there are those with roots of goodness and superior intention, the Buddha will constantly bestow his protection upon them even from afar.
If he knows my mind and wishes to inspire faith in me within the Great King, he must surely come here to serve as my witness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, before the King, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Tathāgata in verse:
“The Tathāgata possesses true wisdom And compassion for all living beings;
I pray you know my deep intention And grant your grace as witness.”
At that time, after the Bodhisattva had finished requesting with these verses, the great earth suddenly split open.

Five hundred śrāvakas, ten thousand bodhisattvas, the various devas of Brahmā and Śakra, as well as nāgas and spirits—immeasurable sentient beings surrounded by them—all leaped forth from the earth before the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Śūrasena joined his palms in reverence and, approaching the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Previously, while traveling and teaching within this city of Śrāvastī, I obtained a Jambūnada-gold bell from the time of the kalpa’s beginning; the value of that bell exceeds the entire land of Jambudvīpa.”
At that time, I thought to myself:
"If there is a being in Śrāvastī who is the most impoverished, I shall give this bell to them."
He further reflected to himself:
"King Prasenajit is the poorest person in this city. Why is that? Because—"

Relying on his royal throne, he has never shown compassion toward sentient beings; instead, he has plundered, cheated, and seized from them, inflicting violence and injury at will, all while greed and craving shroud his mind so that he knows no satiety.
"I considered this king to be the poorest of all, and wished to bestow upon him the golden bell as a gift.
The king asked me, 'Who can testify that I am poor?'"

I replied again: "The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has abandoned all afflictions and the stains of hatred without remainder; he is entirely impartial toward all sentient beings—he shall bear witness for you."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct, benefit, and gladden me.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to subdue King Prasenajit, addressed him, saying:
“Great King, you should know that regarding certain dharmas, poverty may be wholesome and compliant, while kingship is considered wealth and honor.”
There are some who, regarding the Dharma, become kings through poverty yet attain wealth and honor through virtuous compliance. Why is this so?
Because they ascend to the royal throne and possess mastery over the world, with their treasuries overflowing with gold, silver, mani-jewels, musaragalva, and coral.
At this time, one should properly accord with the state of poverty and the sovereignty of kingship as wealth and honor.

Diligently cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), delight in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), renounce the household for extensive learning, remain free from all negligence, observe the eightfold fast and the five precepts, and provide vast relief without weariness.
In this regard, O King, you are truly poor, whereas Susīma is rich and noble.

Your Majesty should know that all the wealth and treasuries of every living being in the kingdom of Kośala do not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a *koṭi*th part of the firm and pure observance of the five precepts and the eightfold fast by Susīma.

At that time, King Prasenajit, having personally heard the Tathāgata’s true instruction, cast aside his arrogance and, with palms joined in earnest devotion, gazed up at him with respectful compliance and spoke these verses:
“Excellent! You have subdued my pride; I shall attain the most supreme body of a Tathāgata.
I relinquish this royal throne to you; May I always be among your assembly for enlightenment.”
I am truly poor while you are wealthy; now I know this saying is no false word.
Sovereignty is but a cause of manifold sufferings, turning one’s back on the white dharma and leading to rebirth in the evil realms.
At that time, after King Prasenajit had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhi, vowing to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings and to liberate them from the bonds of birth and death.”

I now wish to divide my wealth, treasuries, gold, silver, and other assets into three portions: one portion shall be offered to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, and the community of bhikṣus; one portion shall be given to the poor, the suffering, and the helpless within the city of Śrāvastī; and one portion of the wealth shall be retained to support the needs of the state.
Whatever gardens, ponds, flowers, and fruits I possess, I vow to offer them all to the Most Victorious Tathāgata and his assembly of bhikṣus.
I pray only that the World-Honored One will deign to show compassion and accept them.
At that time, after five hundred elders of the kingdom of Kośala had witnessed this event, they all gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
Then, the Bodhisattva Suśīla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will expound the essential points of the Dharma for the great assembly, so that all sentient beings who encounter the Tathāgata shall not do so in vain.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the multitude, saying:

“Good sons, there are three immeasurable stores of merit regarding the Tathāgatas; even if they were to be described by the Tathāgatas themselves, they could not be exhausted, let alone by the śrāvakas or those of the other three vehicles.”
What are these three?
First, to protect and uphold the True Dharma; second, to give rise to the bodhicitta; and third, to exhort all sentient beings to form the unsurpassed aspiration.
Furthermore, there are thirty-two dharmas; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family can diligently cultivate them, they will have seen the Tathāgata not in vain.
First, to give rise to indestructible faith in all Tathāgatas; second, to protect and uphold the True Dharma so that it may endure for a long time;
third, to respect the Saṃgha and not treat them with contempt; fourth, to reverently approach those worthy of offerings;
fifth, to maintain a mind that is always impartial toward both the beloved and the hateful; sixth, to constantly [abide] in the Right...
1. Delighting in the Dharma and hearing it with reverence; 2. Abiding in tranquility and remaining free from clamor;
3. Expounding the Tathāgata-yāna without weariness; 4. When teaching the Dharma, not doing so for the sake of fame or profit; 5.
Resolutely seeking the truth and diligently practicing in accordance with the principle; 6. Generosity; 7. Observance of the precepts.
13. Forbearance; 14. Diligence; 15. Meditative Concentration; 16. Right Wisdom; 17.
Protecting and mindful of all sentient beings according to their inclinations; 18. Maturing sentient beings without forgetting the Dharma;
19. Constantly and skillfully subduing oneself; 20. Subduing [others] through the essentials of wholesome dharmas.
Twenty-one: subduing others; twenty-two: being untainted by afflictions; twenty-three: constantly delighting in leaving the household life;
twenty-four: dwelling in araṇya; twenty-five: rejoicing in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa); twenty-six:
diligently practicing the dhūta austerities; twenty-seven: relinquishing unwholesome dharmas; twenty-eight: firmness in great vows.
Twenty-eighth, never being indolent in the araṇya; twenty-ninth, planting the roots of all virtues; thirtieth, always remaining free from negligence;
thirty-first, distancing oneself from the views of the two vehicles; and thirty-second, praising the Mahāyāna.
Thereupon, when the five hundred bhikṣus had heard this Dharma, they were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, twelve thousand sentient beings likewise gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had taught the Dharma to edify all sentient beings and enabled them to obtain wholesome benefits, he and the bhikṣus, along with the rest of the assembled multitude, suddenly vanished from sight.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having witnessed this event, leaped for joy and, taking two robes worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, bestowed them upon the Bodhisattva Śūradatta, saying:
"Excellent, O Benevolent One!"
"I pray that you will compassionately accept [my request].
Bodhisattva Śūliṣeṇa addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know that I ought not to accept these robes."

Why is this? Because I myself possess a robe made of a hundred patches, which I constantly hang from a tree branch to serve as a chest; no sentient beings have any thought of deceiving me or seizing it.
"Since I myself am free from the mind of stinginess, I shall also cause others not to give rise to attachment; such a giver is said to perform a pure gift.
At that time, King Prasenajit spoke again, saying:
"If you will not accept it, I pray that you will step upon it with your foot for my sake, so that I may have peace, happiness, and benefit throughout the long night."
At that time, for the sake of the king, the Bodhisattva stepped upon these two garments with both feet.
Then King Prasenajit said to the Bodhisattva:
"These garments shall now serve your body; you have accepted them on my behalf."
"What shall I do with it? The Bodhisattva Śūrasena replied to the king,
"Take this robe and give it to those who are poor, suffering, and without protection within the city."
At that time, King Prasenajit followed the Bodhisattva’s instruction and took these two robes to assemble the poor and bestowed them upon them.

When those poor people touched these robes, the insane regained their sanity, the deaf regained their hearing, the blind regained their sight, and those with impaired faculties all became fully endowed with them, due to the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the multitude raised their voices together and said,
"By what means shall we now repay the Bodhisattva’s kindness?
Then, a voice from the sky proclaimed:

"O people, you should know that the Bodhisattva Śūrasena cannot have his debt of gratitude repaid by means of flowers, incense, food, or drink; rather, you should simply and swiftly resolve to attain bodhicitta."
At that time, when the five hundred poor men heard such a voice in the air, they all spoke in verse:
"We who are now Arousing the bodhicitta, Shall attain perfect enlightenment And preach the supreme Dharma."
"To all sentient beings, I bestow peace and happiness; I delight in Bodhi, for the sake of attaining the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, O Benevolent One!"
"If you go there and behold the Tathāgata, I pray that you inform me at once; I shall follow you.
The Bodhisattva Suśīla replied, "Great King, you should know that Buddhas are difficult to encounter and the True Dharma is difficult to hear. How could it be right for the Great King alone to go?"
"You should act as a virtuous friend to sentient beings.
Your Majesty should issue a decree to all the people within this city of Śrāvastī that they must all follow you; those who disobey your command shall be punished according to the royal law."
"Why is this? For even ordinary bodhisattvas are surrounded by and adorned with retinues, let alone a king.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the bodhisattva, saying:
“Who are the attendants of a bodhisattva?
The bodhisattva replied,
“Exhorting [others] toward the bodhicitta is the attendant of a bodhisattva, for it causes them to awaken.”
Exhorting others to see the Tathāgata is a retinue of bodhisattvas, because it is not false.
Exhorting others to hear the True Dharma is a retinue of bodhisattvas, because it results in great learning.
Exhorting one to see the noble assembly is a retinue of the bodhisattva, because it results in obtaining virtuous friends.
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are a retinue of the bodhisattva, because they gather in sentient beings.
The six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are a retinue of the bodhisattva, because they increase awakening.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the retinue of the bodhisattva, for they lead toward the site of awakening.
When a bodhisattva possesses this retinue as adornment and protection, he is able to crush the armies of Māra, reach the lion’s roar, and ascend to the most supreme place.

At that time, King Prasenajit and the great assembly were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; nine thousand sentient beings were freed from the defilements of affliction and attained the pure eye.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva Suśīla, King Prasenajit, and all the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Five;

28. The Discourse on the Householder Ugga. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, and had attained perfect self-mastery; they were like great dragons, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, achieved their own welfare, and completely severed the fetters of existence.
Possessing right wisdom and liberation, his mind attained mastery; he was the supreme Arhat worthy of offerings, renowned by all.
Only Ānanda remained on the stage of a learner (śaikṣa).
Their names were as follows:
Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Mahā-aśvaji, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākapphiṇa, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahābrahmā, Rāhula, Nanda—these and others were the leaders.
Furthermore, there were five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present, all of whom had attained samādhi and dhāraṇī.

At that time, in the great city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder named Śūradatta, who was wealthy with treasures and whose storehouses were overflowing with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musāragalva, emerald, coral, amber, maṇi-jewels, pearls, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, slaves, servants, and merchants—all in great abundance.
At that time, Vīradatta was enjoying a banquet with five hundred elders when they held this discussion, saying:

"O virtuous ones! Rare is the appearance of a Buddha in the world; rare is the attainment of a human body; rare is the encounter with such a time. To leave the home life out of faith in the Buddha’s Dharma is also difficult; to attain the nature of a bhikṣu is likewise exceedingly difficult; to practice in accordance with the Dharma is also difficult. A person who knows gratitude, repays kindness, and does not forget even small favors is hard to find; a person who can give rise to a heart of faith and delight in the Buddha’s Dharma is hard to find; for one to achieve such faith and delight is again difficult; to adorn the Buddha’s Dharma is difficult; and to be liberated from birth and death is twice as difficult."
"Shall we seek extinction through the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or shall we set out toward the supreme Buddha-vehicle?
They all cried out again:
"We would rather attain nirvāṇa by proceeding toward the unsurpassed path of the Buddha."

Having deliberated thus, they surrounded him from front and back and departed from the city of Śrāvastī toward the Jeta Grove. Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer] yet asking on purpose, addressed the elder, saying:
"For what reason have you all come to my presence now?
Then, the five hundred elders led by Vīradatta rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees upon the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
We, all these people, gathered together at the same time and deliberated thus:
‘A Buddha appearing in the world is difficult to encounter; a human body is difficult to obtain; and even liberation from birth and death is doubly more difficult.’”
"Shall we seek extinction through the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, or shall we set out toward the supreme Buddha-vehicle?
They all spoke these words:
"We would rather attain nirvāṇa by proceeding toward the unsurpassed path of the Buddhas."
"Because of this deliberation, we have now come to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is resolved to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi train?"
"How should one dwell?
How should one practice?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
You who have set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and have come to me—
listen attentively and reflect upon this well.”
"I shall explain to you how all bodhisattvas should train, how they should abide, and what they should practice.
At that time, the elders received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha told the householder:

"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses a superior aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings; they should practice extensively and diligently cultivate themselves."

Therefore, a bodhisattva should be without attachment to their body, life, and wealth; to their wife and children, storehouses and dwellings, food and drink, clothing, vehicles and bedding, flower garlands, ointments and perfumes, and all objects of pleasure.
Why is this? Because sentient beings cling to the body and thereby produce evil karma; due to that evil karma, they fall into the hells.
If one gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings, one will not cling to body, life, or wealth, and will thus be born in the happy realms.

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses a superior aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, having given rise to loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, should cultivate great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*) without seeking recompense. One who does not seek recompense should abide in the precepts; with the threefold purity of the precepts, one should be endowed with patience (*kṣānti*). Being able to endure all evils, one should arouse diligence (*vīrya*) without begrudging body or life. One should cultivate single-mindedness and dwell securely in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), cultivate wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and should completely relinquish [the notions of] self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
For the sake of sentient beings, one should practice giving and maintain pure ethical discipline.
For the sake of sentient beings, one should cultivate patience and arouse diligence.
For the sake of sentient beings, one should enter meditative concentration and cultivate wisdom and skillful means.
Then the elders spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding our own bodies, as well as our wives, children, and all our wealth and means of livelihood, our hearts are constantly attached to them and cherish them.”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva observe so that he can be free from greed and stinginess regarding his body, life, and wealth?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder, saying:
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who aspires to the supreme resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should contemplate this body as having immeasurable faults and afflictions:
it is a collection of atoms that arises, abides, changes, and perishes from moment to moment.”
The nine orifices of the shifting flux are like the dwelling holes of venomous snakes; they are without a master, like an empty village;
they are ultimately fragile, like an unbaked clay jar; they overflow with foul secretions, like a vessel of filth;
they receive all impurities, like a latrine; and they are not to be touched, like a malignant ulcer.
Craving for beauty is a calamity like food mixed with poison; failing to recognize kindness and virtue is like the Prince Ajātaśatru;
deceiving and misleading others is like a wicked friend; the harm of deluded attachment is like a monkey companion;
severing the life-force of wisdom is like a murderer; robbing one of all wholesome dharmas is like a bandit; constantly seeking out another's vulnerabilities is...
Like an enemy, they possess no heart of compassion; like a butcher, they are difficult to serve; like a violent and wicked person, they are hard to attend to;
like an arrow lodged in the body, which causes pain when touched; like a dilapidated house, requiring constant repair;
like an old or weak horse, difficult to urge forward; like a casket of venomous snakes, which must not be approached; like a rebellious...
The lodging is a gathering place for exhaustion and suffering; it is like a shelter for the solitary with no one to rely upon; it is like a jailer watching for the opportunity to harm;
it is like a king worrying over his state; it is like a frontier city in a state of alarm and fear; it is like a wicked country full of calamities; it is like a broken vessel difficult to maintain;
it is like a sacrificial fire that knows no satiety; it is like a mirage, empty and deceptive; it is like a magical illusion.
To transform and delude people: it is like splitting open a plantain tree to find no solid core within; like a mass of foam upon water that cannot be grasped;
like bubbles on the surface of water that arise and vanish in an instant; like a tree on a riverbank, precariously poised and swaying;
and like a swift-flowing river that ultimately flows into the sea of death.
He further addressed the elder:

"Next, observe the causes and conditions preceding and following this body. It was initially produced from the union of desire and craving; for the sake of its growth and nourishment, it consumes solid food, which reaches the stomach and is digested by the element of phlegm."
Next, when it reaches the yellow storehouse (*pīta-kośa*) and is about to mature, it turns into sourness.

Next, it reaches the wind storehouse (*vāyu-kośa*), where the wind separates the liquid from the dregs, causing them to flow separately to form feces and urine; the liquid transforms into blood, blood transforms into flesh, fat arises from the place of flesh, bone is formed from the place of fat, and marrow is produced within the bone. Thus, the body is a succession of impurities from beginning to end.
When Bodhisattvas contemplate in this manner, they should further reflect: "This body is composed of three hundred and sixty clusters of bones, like a dilapidated house."

The various joints are supported by four subtle channels that spread out and encircle them. The five hundred portions of flesh are like a coating of mud; six vessels are interconnected, five hundred sinews are entwined, and seven hundred subtle channels form a network of binding cords. Sixteen coarse channels are linked together like hooks and straps. There are two cords of flesh, three *krośas* and a half in length, which are knotted within. Sixteen intestines and stomachs wind around the receptacles for the raw and the cooked. Twenty-five vital energy channels (*prāṇa-nāḍī*) are like the gaps between window panes. One hundred and seven joints and pores are like broken vessels. Eighty thousand hair-pores are like a covering of tangled grass. The five sense organs and seven apertures are filled with impurities. Enveloped by seven layers of skin and nourished by the six flavors, it is like a sacrificial fire that consumes its offerings without ever being satiated.
Such a body is by its very nature all stench and filth, decaying from within; who would cherish it or harbor pride toward it?
One should view it only as a borrowed vessel, like a cart for transport, existing merely for the sake of nourishment until the attainment of Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“This body is a vessel of manifold impurities, Just like a jar filled with excrement;
Ordinary people, lacking wisdom, Rely on their physical form and give rise to arrogance.”
Mucus flows constantly from the nose, The breath is always foul and stinking;
Eye-secretions and worms cover the entire body— Who could ever conceive a pure notion of it?
It is like a person holding charcoal, Polishing it in hopes of making it white.
Even when one reaches the end of life, the physical form never changes.
Should one wish to purify the body by emptying rivers to wash it, the body cannot be cleansed even when exhausted; the matter is just like this.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further addressed the five hundred elders, saying:
"If there are bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the supreme aspiration and seek to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should contemplate this body in forty-four ways."
What are the forty-four kinds?
First, this body is of a nature to be loathed because it lacks any true integration; second, this body is foul and impure because pus and blood constantly flow from it;
third, this body is not solid because it is ultimately subject to decay; fourth, this body...
1. Because the limbs and joints are held together by weakness; 2. because this body is impure and foul, with filth overflowing from it; 3.
because this body is like an illusion, deceiving the foolish and ignorant; 4. because this body is a wound, with nine orifices constantly discharging fluids;
5. because this body is ablaze, with the fire of desire raging within; 6. because this body is... [text truncated]
10. Because the fire of anger is fierce; 11. because the body is entirely ablaze due to the pervasiveness of the fire of delusion;
12. because the body is blind and darkened by greed, anger, and delusion; 13.
because the body is a mass of sores, being completely filled with sores; 14. because the body is unstable.
15) Because of the four hundred and four diseases; 16) because it is the dwelling place of eighty thousand families of worms;
17) because this body is impermanent and ultimately ends in death; 18) because this body is dull and ignorant, lacking knowledge of the Dharma;
19) because it is like a clay vessel, subject to arising, abiding, and destruction. 20) Because...
Twenty: because this body is oppressed by much sorrow and affliction; twenty-one: because it has no protector and is destined for destruction;
twenty-two: because this body is treacherous, evil, deceitful, and difficult to know;
twenty-three: like a bottomless pit, its various desires are difficult to satisfy; twenty-four: like fire receiving fuel, its craving for forms is insatiable.
Because of weariness: twenty-fourth, the body is never satiated because of greedily receiving the five desires;
twenty-fifth, it follows harm as if being beaten; twenty-sixth, this body is unstable, fluctuating between flourishing and decline, increase and decrease;
twenty-seventh, the body turns according to the mind due to improper reflection; twentieth—
Eighth, because the body is ungrateful and will inevitably be abandoned in the cemetery; twenty-ninth, because the body becomes food for others, being devoured by foxes and wolves;
thirtieth, because the body is like a mechanical device, held together by tendons and bones;
thirty-first, because the body is not to be looked upon, being filled with pus, blood, excrement, and filth; thirty-second, because the body is not self-...
31) Because it arises dependent upon food and drink; 32) because the body is a false entanglement that ultimately perishes;
33) because the body is an evil friend that frequently acts with hostility and harm;
34) because the body is a killer that inflicts injury upon itself; 35) because the body is a vessel of suffering, oppressed by pain.

17. This body is a mass of suffering, because it arises from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). 38. This body is without a master, because it arises from a multitude of conditions (*pratyaya*). 39.
This body is without a life-principle (*jīva*), because it is devoid of the characteristics of male and female.
40. This body is empty; one should contemplate it as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*). 41. This body is void.
Forty-second, because delusion is like a dream; forty-third, because this body is unreal, like a magical illusion;
forty-fourth, because the body is a deceptive delusion, like a mirage; and forty-fifth, because the body is a fraud, like a reflected image.
These constitute the forty-four kinds.

When a bodhisattva performs this contemplation, all attachment to body and life, to desires, to wife and children, to house and home, to food and drink, to clothing, to vehicles, to fragrant garlands, and to all objects of pleasure, are entirely renounced without lingering attachment; they are thus able to swiftly accomplish the six pāramitās and quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Extremely difficult is it to obtain a human body; Do not commit manifold evils for the sake of this body.
In the end, you shall be food for foxes and wolves in the cemetery; Do not give rise to craving through false views."
Because ordinary fools are deluded and insane, they create various karmas out of attachment to this body;
yet this body, in turn, knows no gratitude, increasing only the conditions for manifold suffering day and night.
The machinery of the body is constantly weary and exhausted; mucus, saliva, excrement, and urine are perpetually full within.
Tormented by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—who among the wise would cherish such a body?
This body is insatiable like a great pit; it serves only to nurture all manner of enmity and harm.
Because of this body, one constantly commits evil deeds and undergoes various sufferings for immeasurable eons.
One should mindfully contemplate certain death and cultivate supreme merit; with right faith, one is born into the Buddha-dharma.
Food, drink, clothing, and ointments have long sustained this body.
Who can uphold it so that it does not decay? One should know that what is useless is not worth indulging in;
the Muni, the World-Honored One, is difficult to encounter, appearing only once in the course of immeasurable kalpas.
One should give rise to pure faith in the Buddha-dharma;
even if one’s lifespan were a thousand billion years, one would still fear impermanence and feel weary detachment—
how much more so when life cannot be preserved for even a moment, as one might fall and sink into the evil realms?
Or perhaps an evil friend comes to urge you: "A human body is difficult to obtain, yet now it has been gained;
seek out abundant wealth and treasures to enjoy yourself, and during these prime years of life, indulge in pleasure and play."
How can there be one who seeks wealth and yet finds joy?
Even if it is obtained, guarding it remains a source of toil and suffering.
Such foolish people speak in vain; therefore, the wise should investigate this.
Wealth and possessions are like illusions and like dreams; foolish sentient beings are deceived and deluded by them.
Gained in one moment and lost in the next, what wise person would give rise to a heart of attachment?
Just as the magical illusions of a conjurer, or the various colors of a city of Gandharvas, so too do wealth and treasures deceive the foolish; within such falsehoods, what reality can there be?
Seeking wealth and profit through various forms of suffering, one is constantly plundered by water, fire, kings, and thieves;
since this serves as the cause for manifold miseries, what wise person would give rise to attachment or delight?
There are those who constantly harbor greed and attachment, Chasing after wealth and profit without ever reaching satiety;
They lack compassion for their own parents, And even give rise to enmity and harm toward their kinsmen.
Their speech is smooth and compliant while their minds are contrary; they create all manner of conditions for deception.
Whether studying heterodox treatises or malevolent incantations, they boast of their skills like a courtesan.
Some may display flattery and deceit with a gentle appearance, while others may act with rigidity and manifest fierce power;
such immeasurable evil karmas as these do not all arise from wealth and profit.
Coral, gold, jade, and mani-jewels—these things are by nature like foam and bubbles;
unable to understand that they are like illusions and transformations, beings fall into the three miserable realms because of these false deceptions.
When the World-Honored One Maitreya appears, he shall succeed me in this very life;
his realm shall have the ground spread with gold—from where do these beings come?
When the kalpa ends and the world is utterly consumed by fire, when Mount Sumeru, the rivers, and the oceans are all parched and withered,
and everything is ultimately extinguished and returns to emptiness— from where would these precious objects go?
Through various evil deeds one seeks wealth and property, raising and supporting wife and children, deeming it joy;
yet when the end of life approaches and suffering oppresses the body, neither wife nor children can provide any rescue.
Amidst those terrors of the three miserable realms, one sees neither wife nor kin;
chariots, horses, wealth, and treasures belong to others—whom can one share in their suffering?
Parents, brothers, wives, and children, Friends, servants, and precious wealth— Upon death, none of these will come to accompany one; Only one's dark karma follows constantly.
The wise person never, for the sake of those they love, commits various evil deeds that lead to the Avīci Hell;
only when their karma is exhausted can they emerge, for no relative is able to take their place.
The messengers of Yama examine only one's karma; they do not inquire after relatives or friends.
Having obtained a human body, you did not abandon evil; now you must endure this extreme suffering with patience.
Yama constantly tells those sinners: "There is not even the slightest offense upon which I can inflict punishment;
you have committed these sins yourselves and now come before me yourself. You have invited this karmic retribution; there is no one to take its place."
Neither parents nor wife nor children can provide salvation; one must only diligently cultivate the causes for renunciation.
Therefore, one should abandon the karma of shackles and chains, and with skillful knowledge, distance oneself from worldly pursuits to seek true peace and happiness.
One should feel dread toward the household and its wife and children, and always rely upon the Buddha’s teachings to practice correctly.
Living at home is a blazing fire, the root of suffering; it is like a glowing furnace, most truly fearsome.
Body and mind are parched with heat, perpetually burning; what wise person would give rise to craving and attachment?
Delighting in the practice of all the Buddhas’ teachings, one finds happiness in having nothing to seek or strive for.
Ignorant and deluded ordinary people do not realize this; they recklessly crave the home, which is the root of suffering.
Amidst skin, sinews, bones, and flesh, they are confused and falsely give rise to the notion of husband and wife.
Unable to comprehend that things are like illusions and transformations, ordinary people give rise to craving and attachment toward them.
The wise are able to recognize these faults; they cast aside all worldly desires and pleasures.
One should seek the Dharma as one seeks medicine, and should swiftly abandon the bonds of the household life.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the five hundred elders attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Elated and leaping with joy, they spoke these verses:
"How wonderful! We have obtained great benefit, The most supreme among all benefits.
Regarding the Buddha’s Dharma, We have all given rise to hearts of joy."
Setting out for enlightenment, to bring benefit and happiness to all classes of sentient beings;
sustaining one's life through virtue, with awakened wisdom resting in peace.
Out of compassion for all beings, may I attain the path of Buddhahood.
We have all already resolved to attain Unsurpassed Bodhicitta.
Adorned with the marks of golden hue, Illuminating the world,
those who delight in Bodhicitta Shall obtain the body of a Tathāgata.
The great mind of bodhicitta is supreme among all minds;
it liberates one from all bonds and is fully endowed with every merit.
Sentient beings with meager fortune find no joy in this.
Not observing the faults of birth and death, one does not delight in the mind of awakening.
If the merit of the mind of awakening were to have physical parts,
such that it pervaded the entire realm of space, who would be able to contain it?
Even if one were to spread precious jewels throughout as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges to make offerings to all the Buddhas,
if another were able to join their palms once and dedicate that merit toward the Bodhicitta, [the latter would generate far greater merit].
The merit of that [latter] exceeds the former, its limit cannot be found.
It is not only the merit of making offerings; other merits are likewise so.
Such is the nature of the bodhicitta, as taught by the Supreme Sage.
The bodhicitta is supreme; like the agada medicine, it can eliminate all illnesses and bestow all peace and happiness.
I see all sentient beings tormented by the three fires.
For immeasurable eons, the wise have diligently and constantly practiced;
like a valiant king of physicians, they fulfill the conduct of enlightenment to rescue sentient beings from suffering and forever free them from all grief and affliction.
In all places of birth, we shall never abandon this mind;
diligently cultivating all practices and vows, we courageously seek the Buddha-dharma.
We have attained a sublime benefit; our hearts are filled with joy.
"Now that you have encountered the Lion of the Śākyas, you shall attain the body of a Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his face he emitted various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, and crystal—which illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds. Even the majestic radiance of the sun and moon in the Brahma-world was completely eclipsed; the light then circled back three times and entered the crown of the Buddha’s head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do you manifest this smile?
As manifested by the Buddha, it is not without cause or condition.
He then spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"The Buddhas, the supreme guides, do not manifest a smile without cause.
O benefactors who have compassion for the world, please explain the reason for this."
For sentient beings impoverished of the wealth of Dharma, you should preach the supreme gift of the Mahāyāna;
you can act as eyes for those blinded by the darkness of the world—please explain the cause and condition of your smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Do you see these five hundred elders who have now resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in my presence?"
Ānanda replied, “Indeed, I have seen it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"These five hundred elders have, in the past, served and made offerings to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness; now, having heard this Dharma, they have attained the patience of non-arising."
From this time forward, these elders shall not be reborn in the evil realms, but shall constantly experience happiness among humans and devas.
Furthermore, in a future age, they shall make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise Maitreya Buddha.

Furthermore, they shall serve, revere, and make offerings to all the Buddhas throughout the Bhadrakalpa; in the presence of those Buddhas, they shall hear the True Dharma, receive and uphold it, recite it, and explain it extensively for others.
After twenty-five kalpas have passed, each shall attain unexcelled bodhi within their respective buddha-fields; they shall all bear the same name: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jina-padma-garbha.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare it is, World-Honored One!”
"How rare, O Sugata!
What shall this vast Dharma-gate be named?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Dharma gate is named 'The Yogācārabhūmi of the Bodhisattva,' and it is also named 'The Inquiry of the Householder Vīradatta. You should receive and uphold it by these names."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the bhikṣus, the five hundred elders, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and the devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Six;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
29. The Assembly with King Udayana, Part Two. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī at the Ghosira Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, King Udayana’s first queen, named Śyāmā, constantly maintained deep faith and reverence for the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones, attending upon and making offerings to them, while also constantly praising the virtues of the Tathāgata.

At that time, the king had a second queen named Dinnā, who was constantly harboring flattery and jealousy; she went to the king and falsely claimed that the Tathāgata and his disciples had behaved improperly toward the chief queen.
Upon hearing these words, the king became exceedingly enraged and immediately shot Queen Śyāmā with an arrow.

At that moment, out of compassion for the king, the queen entered the *maitrī-samādhi*. Consequently, the released arrow turned back and came to rest in the air above the king’s head; its flames blazed fiercely like a mass of fire, most terrifying to behold.
This continued until he had discharged three arrows, each of which was met with the same result.
At that moment, King Udayana, seeing this occurrence, his hair stood on end; filled with alarm and regret, he said to the lady:
"Are you a goddess, or are you a daughter of the nāgas?"
"Are you perhaps a yakṣī, a gandharvī, a piśācī, or a rākṣasī? The lady replied,
"I am not a celestial maiden, nor indeed am I the daughter of a rākṣasa."

"Great King, you should know that I have heard the True Dharma from the Buddha, have received and upheld the five precepts as a laywoman (upāsikā), and out of compassion for you, have entered the samādhi of loving-kindness."
"Although the King conceived unwholesome thoughts toward me, by virtue of my compassionate vow, he has remained unhurt.
Thereupon, she praised the King, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
"One should take refuge in and prostrate before the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; one will certainly obtain peace and security.
King Udayana then thought to himself:

"If even she, having heard the True Dharma from the Buddha and become a laywoman (upāsikā), possesses such majestic spiritual power, how much more so must it be for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha!"
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and said:
“World-Honored One!

Due to the causal conditions of lustful defilement, I was deceived and deluded by the false words of that woman, and consequently gave rise to a mind of malice toward the Tathāgata and the various noble ones.”
Having related all this in detail,
he further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones will grant me joy and accept my repentance, so that these transgressions and faults may be swiftly extinguished."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the king, saying:

"As you have said, because you perceive faults and afflictions in the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones as an ordinary, foolish person would, you have falsely given rise to the poison of anger toward this field of merit."

If you can now rely upon the Noble Law and Discipline, repent of your transgression with a heart free from concealment, and refrain from committing it again for all future time, I shall accept you and cause your wholesome qualities to increase in the future.
King Udayana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have been deluded and overturned by a woman; driven to madness and ignorance, I gave rise to coarse and fierce poisonous hatred. Due to this karmic offense, I shall surely fall into hell.”

We only pray that the World-Honored One, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, will out of compassion reveal the faults of women’s flattery, crookedness, and deceit, so that we may not associate with women and may be spared from all suffering throughout the long night.
The Buddha said:
"Set this matter aside for now.
Why do you insist on asking this and not asking anything else?"
The king said:
“World-Honored One!
I have no further questions.”
Women have caused me to create the karma for hell; now, I seek only to understand the faults of women, their flattery, their deceit, their falsehood, and their seductive guile.
"I pray that you will explain this for me.
He made this request three times, speaking in the same manner each time.
The Buddha said:
“Your Majesty should first understand the faults of men, and only then examine the failings of women.
King Udayana replied: “So be it, Blessed One.”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said,
"All men are deluded and distracted by women due to four kinds of unwholesome transgressions."
What are the four?

First, they are insatiably addicted to and attached to various sensual desires; they take pleasure in gazing at women and indulge themselves in self-indulgence, failing to know how to approach śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess pure precepts and cultivate meritorious deeds.
By not associating with such persons, one will completely fall away from pure faith, pure ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom.

Devoid of these qualities—faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom—they are no longer noble beings; they follow the ways of hungry ghosts, lack wisdom, and are addicted to desire and negligence. Governed by desire, bound by desire, and sustained by desire, they associate with fools, distance themselves from the wise, take evil friends as companions, and engage in what is improper. Clinging to the impure realm of women, they are eventually brought under the sway of women.
They are like slaves bound to fallen women;

they lack shame and dread of blame as they frequent and dwell near the gates of their festering wounds, where pus, blood, filth, mucus, and saliva flow constantly, like the impure realms found amidst a cemetery.
As for those who oppose their parents’ benevolent nurturing, abandon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and fail to give rise to earnest respect or to offer them worship;
who practice the ways of beasts and do not produce pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—they shall forever fall away from the realm of nirvāṇa.

Such persons as these shall enter the Saṃghāta and other great hells up to the Avīci hell; they shall likewise fall into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, where there is no protection or refuge.
Although they have heard my teaching, they still repeatedly think of wicked women who sing, dance, and laugh; they do not give rise to revulsion or detachment.
You should know that they practice the ways of fools and take no pleasure in performing the deeds of virtuous men.
"Great King!
You should know that when a man associates with women, he is associating with the ways of the evil realms.
This is the foremost affliction for a man."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All desires are suffering; They are base, vile, and foul, Impure like pus and blood— Truly loathsome and fearsome."
A place where a multitude of faults and calamities converge— what wise person would take delight in this?
It is overflowing with impurity, like a dead dog, or a dead jackal,
or a charnel ground filled everywhere with filth.
The affliction of sensual desire is likewise to be loathed.
Those who are foolishly deluded, harboring attachment to women, are like dogs that never abandon their own offspring;
they are also like flies that settle upon food and drink spat out by others.
Furthermore, just as a herd of swine greedily seeks after filth and impurity,
so too can women destroy pure precepts; they cause one to fall away from merit and renown,
acting as the cause for rebirth in hell and obstructing birth in the heavenly realms.
What wise person would find joy in this?
It is like someone who has ingested a poisonous drug; their body and mind are racked with pain and distress, and they are unable to move.
Because of this cause of desire, it becomes the root of suffering; like poison within the body, the ignorant do not understand it.
Just as they do not understand, they falsely seek after illusory phenomena, only to exhaust themselves in weariness and pain.
Fools are likewise; constantly stained by desire, they exhaust themselves in weary toil and craving, falling into the various hells.

Whether providing food and drink, performing songs, dances, and music, or marrying the daughters of others to take them as their own wives, they accumulate a multitude of harmful and painful things that yield no benefit.
Fools perform these deeds, which bring no benefit; they increase all manner of transgressions and cause them to fall away from their roots of goodness.
Because of this, they plummet into the deep pits of the evil realms and thereby invite rebirth in hell.
Fierce flaming iron balls, Sharp-edged mountains of blades, And the various sufferings of poisoned arrows—
A woman can amass these many painful things, Yet she adorns herself with flowers and perfumes as if they were ornaments.
Associating with and praising inferior dharmas, one loses wisdom and falls into the three miserable realms.
This arises from being deluded by ignorance, like a weary bird at sea that is lost regarding the shore beyond.
Furthermore, it is like a fool who takes up glowing iron and places it around his neck, as if he were an ox yoked to a cart.
Desire is like various intoxicating liquors that drive people to madness; how can a fool not know it to be the root of suffering?
Or toward one's parents, they fail to recognize their kindness and compassion; all this arises from the defilement of desire, giving rise to such calamities.
Constantly praising and practicing such perverted methods of desire, they are devoid of shame and remorse.
Because they are deluded and distracted by ignorance, having committed such sins,
they shall go to the three miserable realms.
Those who are intoxicated with and deeply addicted to desire can even cast aside the kindness of their parents.
If one has defiled craving and associates with sensual desires, one then turns away from the supreme field of merit.
From this, immeasurable koṭis of deluded thoughts and disturbances arise, leading to successive afflictions.
Or again, they may long for worldly wealth and status; by means of such unrighteousness, they exhort one another.
Because of this, they incur in the present the suffering of being beaten and struck, and at death they will surely fall into the Avīci Hell.
Beholding all manner of sufferings now gathered upon this body, separated from virtuous friends and forever losing the celestial palaces—
what wise person would find joy in such a state?
It would be better to cast oneself into an iron prison, rush across a mountain of knives, or lie down within a furnace of flames than to indulge in female beauty.
If one is constantly stained by greed and pursues perverse desires, one will fall away from and lose many things that bring benefit and happiness.
Women can create the causes of manifold sufferings; desire can destroy all peace and happiness.
The accumulation of unwholesome dharmas and the estrangement from virtuous friends—all have their root in the craving for women.
One who can develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward women will thereby adorn the pure heavenly realms and shall also swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
"Furthermore, Great King!

Since parents always desire the benefit, happiness, and well-being of the children they have born, they are able to perform what is difficult to do and endure all that is difficult to endure; they can even endure all manner of impurities and foul odors."

Furthermore, desiring that his son’s physical form and strength may quickly increase, she causes him to see the excellent and wondrous things of Jambudvīpa, nourishing and sustaining him with milk and food without ever feeling weary or satiated.

Or, for the sake of enabling their children to obtain various sublime pleasures, they undergo hardships to seek and acquire wealth and goods, providing and preparing the necessities of life, and even going to other families to arrange marriages.

Once he has married, he becomes enamored of and attached to other women; because of this attachment, his mind is clouded and intoxicated. He may see his parents gradually growing old and yet act in opposition to them or treat them with contempt. He squanders all their wealth without shame, or causes his parents to no longer remain in the home.
Thus, all this arises from being deluded and inverted by desire.
Great King!

You should know that for this reason, one abandons and turns one's back on the kindness and nourishment of one’s own parents, while honoring, serving, and providing for other women with various offerings without weariness; this is precisely the root that brings about rebirth in hell.
"This is the second fault of a man.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"You should know that those who honor and make offerings to their parents..."
Such a person is always supported by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors,
who enable their household life to be peaceful, secure, and joyful.
Or perhaps through trade, traveling safely to and from distant lands across the great ocean, one obtains various forms of wealth and profit.
This is described as a priceless great treasure that can yield fruit in the present;
it is called the supreme field. Thus, in this present life, there is the precious jewel of karmic fruition.
All this is obtained by making offerings to one's parents.
Furthermore, in future lives, one shall be able to remain far removed from such forms as camels and donkeys, which are driven to labor under heavy burdens.
Furthermore, they shall not suffer the torments of corpses, excrement, the river of ashes, the mountain of blades with its sharp edges, molten copper, and the like.
They shall possess abundant wealth and treasures, an ample supply of grain and silk, and be surrounded by wives, children, and kinsmen.
All were harmonious and cordial.
Within the palaces and gardens, music arose spontaneously; they indulged their desires in joy and amusement, experiencing every kind of exquisite pleasure.
"What wise person, having heard this sound of the Dharma, would not diligently make offerings to the field of their parents?
Furthermore, Great King!"
If certain men, due to wrong views, do not realize that their own bodies will soon perish and yet commit various evils, they deceive themselves.
Those deluded people pass their long nights in vain, like figures carved from wood or stone; though their forms resemble humans, they possess no consciousness.
"To indulge in various sensual desires is to accomplish the karma that leads to rebirth in the evil realms;
this is the third fault of a man.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Men, deluded by desire, commit various kinds of sins because of it.
Obscured by the darkness of inverted views, their minds are shrouded; driven by this, they shall be born into the prisons of the evil realms.”
Furthermore, they will distance themselves from all worthy sages and fail to show respect to the various śramaṇas.
Driven by greed, they will even harm or kill the spirits of mountains and rivers.
All birds and beasts sacrifice to the gods and spirits;
with inverted views as their cause, they seek blessings through what is not the Dharma. Because of this, they are forever deprived of all peace and happiness.
