If, within this [teaching], one commits evil, lacking pure faith, cruel and shameless—
such a person is forever separated from the noble ones and shall surely fall into the Raurava Hell.
Or, for the sake of sensual desires, they oppress and afflict others; such persons shall fall into the Scorching Hell and the Hell of Intense Scorching.
Furthermore, due to their inverted views, they are unable to approach, revere, or make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
they do not listen to the true teaching, which is the Jewel of the Dharma.
One who distances oneself from the noble ones falls into the various evil realms.
Therefore, the wise person, having obtained a human body, should no longer harbor such inverted and false views;
by diligently practicing generosity and purifying ethical discipline, one shall be reborn in heaven.
"to realize the path to enlightenment.
Furthermore, Great King, there may be a man who,
for the sake of his own body and life, exerts himself to the utmost to accumulate precious wealth."

Later, because they are entangled and controlled by women, they serve and attend to them like servants; for this reason, they become stingy with their wealth and treasures, failing to give to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and they even endure the punishments of royal law, accepting all insults, slights, and humiliations.
Whether struck or rebuked by women, or even driven to fear and compelled to serve them with submissive intent,
upon seeing their sorrow and distress, he reflects to himself:
"How may I now cause her to be joyful?"
"One should regard such a person as a slave to desire, who conceives pure perceptions toward this impure and inferior object and gives rise to passionate attachment.
When one draws near to such a woman, it is the fulfillment of karma leading to the miserable realms."
"This is the fourth fault of a man.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The person who is intoxicated by indulgence in desire Truly possesses no peace or happiness."
Because they associate with unwholesome dharmas, they are not called virtuous men.
If a person is self-indulgent and lacks restraint,
following whatever the mind desires, they will ruin their own welfare and merit.
Those people lacking wisdom act according to the ways of animals;
they rush toward female forms of beauty, just as a pig delights in filth.
The fool is unable to perceive the faults and perils of being stained by desire.
Giving rise to thoughts of deep reverence is like being a person in blind darkness;
bound by form, one increases craving for desire,
just as a jackal does not leave the vicinity of a cemetery.
Regarding sounds, scents, flavors, and tangibles, they give rise to a mind of attachment;
thus they revolve within birth and death, like a monkey tied to a pillar.
Because they are shrouded by ignorance, they are deluded and distracted by women.
Like those seeking profit in a marketplace who feign intimacy through deceit,
the fool who associates with sensual desire enters the realm of Māra;
he is like a *cātaka* bird that wallows in filth and excrement.
Just as a torrential hailstorm can damage the crops,
and a potter who stays too close to the fire is often consumed by its flames,
so too those who have not yet seen the Truth lose the pure dharmas through their craving.
Just as the wind blows away fine chaff, such is the meaning of this.
Even if a virtuous man were seized by an executioner,
he would rather endure such torment than consort with a woman.
If one views the beauty of women with delight, One's greedy seeking increases all the more.
Ordinary people who grasp at signs Grow ever greater in their sensual craving,
Just like when, in the heat of summer, One wanders through the midst of a vast wilderness.
Driven by thirst, one drinks salt water; having drunk it, the thirst increases all the more.
Those who have not seen reality live in vain through their folly, for they draw near to women, and their craving and attachment become firm.
If a person touches a venomous insect, they will be harmed by its poison;
likewise, when ordinary worldlings violate their desires, it is just the same.
It is like a painted jar filled within with deadly poison.
Within this, there is truly something to be feared, yet outwardly it manifests as dignified and beautiful.
Adorned with ornaments, women are called "exquisite and wonderful," but within them is extreme filth and corruption, like a leather bag filled with gas.
Furthermore, it is like wrapping a sharp blade in fine silk;
the adornment of that woman is of the same meaning.
It is like a deep pit filled with fire, which can burn and cause harm even without smoke.
Women are also like this: violent, cruel, and devoid of compassion.
Like dead dogs or dead snakes, foul-smelling, loathsome, and putrid;
or like burnt excrement, which all people detest.
A dead snake, excrement, or a dog— though these are indeed loathsome—
women are even more loathsome than those. Just as when the kalpa is destroyed,
fire breaks out across the entire great earth, so too are women a source of burning affliction.
The various plants and trees of the forests are all completely scorched;
the abode of those with massive bodies has its seawaters entirely dried up,
and the world, including Mount Sumeru and other jewel mountains, is everywhere consumed by fire and destroyed.
Thus, at the time of the kalpa-fire, when mountains and seas are consumed by flames,
there is no sentient being capable of providing protection.
It is because of this woman’s desire that all foolish men are burned and harmed.
Just as the fire at the end of an eon blazes, burning everything to ashes;
this body is a constant flow of impurities—saliva, mucus, pus, and blood.
How can those foolish people be so attached to it?
The skeletal frame serves as its supporting pillars, covered over by skin and flesh;
it is so foul and loathsome that it is like discarded leftover food,
or like the door of a granary where husks and chaff are constantly strewn about in disarray.
This body is filled with all manner of filth and impurities; likewise, it contains the stomach,
spleen, kidneys, liver, and gallbladder, as well as the intestines, lungs, excrement,
marrow, brain, pus, and blood, along with eighty thousand families of worms.
Constantly devouring within, the blind and ignorant fools are entangled and shrouded by their own nets of delusion; thus they cannot understand.
They consume the impurities of various leftovers, as the nine orifices constantly flow and discharge.
Such is this body of afflictions, resulting from past impure karma.
Fools, regarding women, become bound by attachment to their sounds and forms;
through this they give rise to defiled clinging, never knowing them as they truly are.
Just as a fly sees vomit and conceives a mind of attachment, so too do fools crave women; their sensory realms are likewise.
They fall prostrate before female beauty, constantly defiling their own bodies.
How can those foolish people find pleasure and dwell here?
Like a bird seeking food that does not know how to avoid the net,
they are likewise harmed by their craving for women.
Just as a fish in the water, swimming before a fisherman,
is caught by him— how could this not be self-inflicted harm?
If a woman were like a fisherman, her flattery and deception would be like a net.
A man is like a fish; being caught in a net is likewise.
Though the sharp blade of a killer is indeed most fearsome, the blade of a woman is even more terrifying, for her harm exceeds that of the former.
Like moths casting themselves into a lamp-flame, or when a house is consumed by fire,
insects and other creatures are incinerated, left without refuge or rescue.
Those who are intoxicated by women are likewise harmed and scorched by the fire of greed.
Because of this, they fall into the evil realms, remaining likewise without refuge.
Foolish people of perverse conduct who lust after the wives of others falsely conceive thoughts of delight, like domestic chickens.
Just like a pheasant in the wilderness that wanders recklessly into a place of slaughter,
injury arises from its own actions and there is no one to rescue it; so too,
those who abandon the Buddha’s Dharma and draw near to women [meet with such ruin].
Due to the causal conditions of these karmic actions, one falls into the evil realms.
Furthermore, just as various monkeys leap and bound among crags and trees,
inevitably causing themselves injury— is this not due to ignorance and delusion?
Thus, those who are addicted to desire, being ensnared by the net of delusion regarding those women, repeatedly undergo the suffering of birth and death.
Like worldly criminals placed upon the torture of the sharp stake, they endure their lot.
Those who are intoxicated by lust shall be suspended in the forest of sword-trees.
Just as with a fierce fire, they are scorched in that cauldron of boiling water;
sesame and wheat are cast therein, and they float and sink along with the seething waves.
Thus, those who are addicted to desire do not recognize the path of goodness;
at death they shall fall into the evil realms, being boiled in cauldrons of boiling water.
The number of such cauldrons is sixty-four koṭis.
Those who have committed evil deeds take those [cauldrons] as their dwelling place.
Each of these individual cauldrons measures one yojana in size;
fierce fires burn throughout, reaching both the bottom and the four surrounding edges.
Some remain for a full hundred years, or two, three, or four hundred;
they undergo the suffering of being scorched and boiled, all caused by their own karma.
The hell-wardens, using sharp hooks, periodically lift them up and cast them out.
The skin and flesh are all rotted and fallen away, and their bones are white as jade;
thereupon the various hell-wardens further place them in iron troughs and pound them with pestles,
such that no one can provide rescue or protection.
At that time, all the marrow in their bones was ground to dust;
blown by the winds of karma, though dead, they were restored to life once more.
If there are those who violate others—whether their wives, concubines, or young daughters—
One who has violated another’s wife shall suffer this punishment: being forced to climb a tree of iron thorns,
receiving the calamity of axes and pestles, and being impaled upon a three-pronged iron fork, or one with four or five tines.
Furthermore, there are iron-beaked crows that deeply peck at the marrow and brain;
jackals and various other beasts vie with one another to devour them.
Such people of perverse desire shall fall into the Hell of Corpses and Excrement.
They rush upon blades and likewise ascend mountains of knives;
such people of perverse desire fall headlong into the Hell of Intense Heat,
and once they have been burned and harmed there, they proceed further to the Cold Ice Hell.
Such people of perverse desire shall likewise fall into the Extremely Hot,
the Howling, and the Great Howling hells, as well as into the Black Rope hell.
Such people of perverse desire shall sink into the briny, scalding river.
Furthermore, they pass through the Hell of Hot Ashes, dying before even reaching the bottom.
In that hell there are thorns with five points, exceedingly sharp;
driven by dogs, they run in panic through their midst.
Those who are infatuated with women fall into places of great terror;
they may swallow iron balls or drink molten copper.
There are two mountains of hot iron that come together from opposite sides.
Those who were once addicted to desire suffer the calamities therein.
When they undergo such torment, there is no one at all to provide protection;
that they receive such retribution for their sins is entirely due to the conditions of their own karma.
Those who once shared in joy and love—where are they now?
I alone endure this calamity, yet they do not come to rescue me.
Because in previous lives I myself created such karma, [I must suffer the consequences].
Even if one has parents and the like, there is no one who can provide rescue;
because in previous lives one created such karma for oneself.
Even if one has sons, daughters, and the like, there is no one who can provide rescue.
Because in a previous life, one has performed such karma oneself,
even if there were brothers and the like, none would be able to save one.
Because in a previous life, one has performed such karma oneself...
Even if one has sisters and the like, there is no one who can provide rescue;
because in previous lives one created such karma for oneself.
Even if one has friends and the like, there is no one who can provide rescue.
Fools, driven by perverse desire, greedily pursue women;
thus they undergo such various sufferings within the Avīci Hell.
To speak of these impure and loathsome women—
That which fools frequent, the wise all keep far from;
to associate with such women is most base and inferior—
the worst of evils— so what is there in it to rejoice?
Ordinary people, addicted to sensual pleasures, Constantly carry a sack of filth;
Due to the causes and conditions of these karmic deeds, They shall undergo immeasurable suffering.
Fools, for the sake of women, Undergo all manner of punishments.
Though imprisoned and beaten, they have no heart of weary detachment.
For the sake of women, fools are subjected to all manner of burning harms;
yet they can endure such suffering, remaining without a heart of weary detachment.
Some are placed upon sharp stakes; some are killed or cast into water, or thrown into great pits, undergoing every kind of bitter suffering.
Even while witnessing such agony, they still remain amidst lustful desires.
Praising women, one never gives rise to weary detachment.
There may be those of little wisdom who know her to be the root of manifold suffering,
yet upon seeing her, they draw near again, like lacquer encountering fire.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, though they may give rise to faith and acceptance,
they still keep many women, their assembly like a flock of sheep. Or,
having heard the teachings of the Buddhas, they only just manage to give rise to a mind of weariness and regret.
In an instant, craving arises again, like the resurgence of a virulent poison.
It is like a frightened pig that stops for but a moment;
yet when it sees filth and excrement, its greedy attachment arises once more.
When fools have heard the Dharma, their hearts are momentarily struck with alarm;
yet later, upon seeing various forms of desire, their craving arises once more.
It is like a man who, from his own head, [cuts off his hair...]
Casting aside the garland of golden flowers, they instead wear hot iron;
because these fools are addicted to desire, they abandon all the Buddha’s teachings,
greedily seeking inferior dharmas, and commit all manner of sinful deeds.
Those intoxicated by various desires fall into the realm of Yama;
they constantly swallow glowing iron balls and drink molten copper.
Those intoxicated by desire turn their backs on the good and practice what is wrong.
Abandoning purity, one will forever proceed to the realm of Yama.
If there is a person of wisdom who hears me preach this Dharma,
they should renounce all desires and swiftly seek liberation.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, King Udayana immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What we have just heard is truly rare, truly rare!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has skillfully explained these faults and afflictions of sensual desires.”

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and become a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
May the World-Honored One graciously accept me.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Udayana and the great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others of the world—having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-seven;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
30. The Chapter on the Girl Prajñāvatī, Number Thirty.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was the daughter of an elder named Prajñāvatī. She was eight years of age, with a handsome countenance and a beautiful complexion; she was endowed with all the auspicious marks, bringing joy to all who beheld her. In the past, she had personally attended upon and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness.
Then that woman went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these verses:
“O Unsurpassed, Perfectly Awakened One, You are the great bright lamp for the world;
Regarding the conduct of Bodhisattvas, I pray you will listen to my questions.”
The Buddha told Miaohui:
"I grant you leave to ask whatever you wish.
I shall explain it for you so as to sever the web of doubt."
At that time, Prajñāśrī immediately addressed the Buddha in verse, asking:
"How does one obtain a handsome form, A body of great wealth and noble status?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions Does one’s retinue become difficult to disperse?"
How does one behold one’s own body as being born through transformation upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower, personally attending all the World-Honored Ones?
How can one realize and attain the supreme, sovereign supernormal powers?
How does one travel to immeasurable lands to pay homage to all Buddhas?
How does one become free from enmity, so that what one says is trusted and accepted by others?
How does one purify the obstacles to the Dharma and forever leave behind the works of Māra?
How is it that at the time of death, one may behold the Buddhas,
hear them preach the pure Dharma, and not undergo suffering?
O Great Compassionate, Unsurpassed Honored One, I pray that you will explain this for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the young girl Prajñākūṭī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have skillfully asked about this profound and subtle meaning."
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for your sake. Wondrous Wisdom replied, “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said to Miaohui:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will receive a handsome body."
What are these four?
First, not giving rise to anger toward evil associates; second, abiding in great compassion; third, deeply delighting in the True Dharma; and fourth, fashioning images of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Hatred destroys the roots of goodness; do not let it increase. With a mind of loving-kindness, delight in the Dharma and fashion images of the Buddha.
You shall obtain a body adorned with the marks of excellence, Which all sentient beings will always joyfully behold."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will obtain a body of wealth and nobility. What are these four?
"First, one should practice giving at the proper time; second, without a mind of contempt or arrogance; third, bestowing with joy; fourth, without hoping for a karmic reward.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Giving at the proper time, free from contempt, Bestowing with joy, without seeking reward."
"One who can constantly and diligently cultivate this practice shall obtain great wealth and status in every birth.
Furthermore, O Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will obtain an indestructible retinue."

What are the four? First, being well able to abandon and relinquish divisive speech; second, causing sentient beings with wrong views to abide in right view; third, protecting the true Dharma so that it remains long when its extinction is imminent; and fourth, teaching all sentient beings to aspire toward the Bodhi of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Abandoning divisive speech and wrong views, Able to protect and uphold the True Dharma as it nears extinction,
Establishing sentient beings in Great Bodhi— Such a one shall attain an indestructible retinue.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they shall receive birth by transformation in the presence of the Buddha and dwell upon a lotus seat.
What are these four?

First, to offer various flowers, fruits, and fine powdered incense, scattering them before the Tathāgata and all stūpas and temples; second, never to falsely inflict harm upon others; third, to create images of the Tathāgata and place them upon lotus flowers; fourth, to give rise to profound pure faith in the Bodhi of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Scattering flowers and incense before the Buddha and the caityas, Not harming others and fashioning images,
Having deep faith and understanding in Great Bodhi— One shall attain birth from within a lotus flower in the presence of the Buddha."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas travels from one buddha-field to another.
What are these four?

First, seeing others cultivate goodness, one does not create obstacles or cause them distress; second, when others preach the Dharma, one never hinders or obstructs them; third, one offers lamps as an offering to the stupas of the Tathāgata; fourth, one constantly and diligently practices all meditative concentrations.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When one sees others practicing goodness or preaching the True Dharma, One should not give rise to slander or create obstacles for them;
By offering lamps at the stupas and temples of the Tathāgata, One cultivates various meditations and wanders through Buddha-fields."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will live in the world without enmity. What are these four?

First, to attend upon spiritual friends with a mind free from guile; second, to have no heart of envy toward the superior dharmas of others; third, to always feel joy in one's heart when others attain renown; and fourth, to have no mind of disparagement toward the bodhisattva practices.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One does not cultivate intimacy with friends through flattery; One harbors no envy toward the superior dharmas of others.
One always rejoices when others attain renown; By not slandering Bodhisattvas, one remains free from enmity."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, people believe what they say.
What are these four?

First, one's speech and practice should always be in accord; second, one should not conceal any of one's evils from virtuous friends; third, one should not seek out faults in the Dharma one hears; fourth, one should not give rise to malicious thoughts toward those who preach the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Speech and practice are always in accord; One does not conceal one's own faults from virtuous friends.
Upon hearing the sutras, one seeks not the faults of persons or dharmas; All that is spoken is received with faith."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they can leave behind the obstacles to the Dharma and swiftly attain purification. What are these four?

First, to encompass the three types of restraint through profound intention; second, not to give rise to slander upon hearing profound sutras; third, to give rise to the mind of omniscience upon seeing bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds; and fourth, to maintain great and impartial compassion toward all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"By means of profound aspiration, one upholds the discipline; Hearing the most profound sutras, one is able to believe and understand them.
Revering those who have first resolved their minds as if they were Buddhas, With a heart of universal compassion, all obstacles are eliminated."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they are able to remain free from all māras. What are these four?

First, thoroughly understanding the equality of the nature of phenomena; second, initiating diligence; third, constantly and assiduously recollecting the Buddha; and fourth, dedicating all roots of goodness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Able to know the equality of all phenomena, Constantly arousing diligence and mindfulness of the Tathāgata,
Dedicating all roots of goodness— The various Māras cannot find an opportunity to harm them.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, at the time of death, the Buddhas will appear before them.

What are these four? First, to fulfill the requests of others by giving; second, to develop deep faith and understanding in all wholesome dharmas; third, to bestow ornaments upon other bodhisattvas; and fourth, to diligently cultivate offerings to the Triple Gem."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Fulfilling the needs of others when they seek help, Believing and understanding the profound Dharma while relinquishing ornaments,
Diligently making offerings to the Triple Gem, the field of merit— At the moment of death, the Buddha will appear before them.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the maiden Prajñāśrī addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall practice and uphold all the bodhisattva deeds as taught by the Buddha.”
World-Honored One!
If I were to omit even a single one of these forty practices and fail to cultivate it, I would be contravening the Buddha’s teaching and deceiving the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed Miaohui, saying:
"The conduct of a bodhisattva is extremely difficult to practice.
Now that you have made such an excellent and great vow, do you possess mastery over this vow?"
At that time, Prajñā said: "Venerable One!

If my great vow is true and not false, and if it can cause all practices to reach fulfillment, may this trichiliocosm tremble in six ways, may the heavens rain down exquisite flowers, and may the celestial drums sound of their own accord."
When these words were spoken, flowers rained down from the void like a shower, celestial drums resounded of their own accord, and the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, Prajñāvatī addressed Maudgalyāyana once more:
"By virtue of these words of truth of mine, may I attain Buddhahood in a future age, just as the Tathāgata Śākyamuni has done today."

"In my kingdom, there shall be no occurrence of demonic activities nor even the name of women of the evil destinies; if these words of mine are not false, may the bodies of this great assembly all become golden in color."
When these words had been spoken, the entire assembly became golden in color.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"I now first pay homage to the bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], as well as to the assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, said to Sudhīmatī:
"In what dharma do you abide to make such a sincere vow?"
妙慧 (Pratibhānā) replied:
"Mañjuśrī! This is not what was asked."
Why is this? Because within the dharma-realm there is no place of abiding.
He asked again:
"What is called 'bodhi'? He replied, "The dharma of non-conceptualization is called bodhi."
He asked again:
"What is meant by the term 'bodhisattva'? He replied:
"All dharmas are equal to the characteristic of empty space; this is called a bodhisattva.
He asked again:
"What is called the practice of bodhi?"
He replied, “The practice of the bodhi-path is like the movement of a mirage or an echo.
He asked again:
"With what underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) was this said? He replied:
"In this regard, I do not perceive even the slightest dharma that is either secret or non-secret."
He asked again:
"If this is so, then all ordinary beings should be identical to bodhi. He replied:
"Do you think that awakening is different from that of ordinary persons?
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?"
"All these share the same characteristic of the single Dharma-realm; they are neither grasped nor rejected, for they are without arising or ceasing.
He asked again:
"Among those who can understand this meaning, how many are there?"
He replied: "As many as are the measures of illusory minds and mental factors, so many illusory sentient beings can understand this meaning. Mañjuśrī said:
"Since illusions and transformations are fundamentally non-existent, how could there be such mental states and mental factors? He replied:
"The Dharma-realm is likewise neither existent nor non-existent; even the Tathāgata is thus."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Subhūti is truly most rare, for he is able to accomplish such a dharma-patience.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is; it is truly as you have said.
However, this young girl has already resolved upon bodhicitta for thirty kalpas, whereas I only set out toward unsurpassed bodhi [afterward].”
"She will also cause you to abide in the patience of non-arising.
At that time, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, paid homage to her, and said to Prajñādarśin:
"In the past, incalculable eons ago, I have already made offerings to you; I did not expect that today I would again be able to draw near to you."
The Girl Prajñā said:
"Mañjuśrī! You should not now give rise to such conceptual discrimination."
"Why is this? Because by means of non-discrimination, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
He then asked Subhūti again:
“Have you still not transformed your female body?
Wondrous Wisdom replied, “The characteristics of a woman are utterly unattainable; what, then, is there to transform?”
Mañjuśrī! I shall eliminate your doubts and dispel your perplexity.

By virtue of this truthful speech of mine, when I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age, the bhikṣus within my Dharma who hear the command "Come, well-come! shall go forth from home into the path.

All sentient beings within my land have bodies that are golden in color; their clothing, ornaments, and requisites are like those of the Sixth Heaven, and their food and drink are abundant, arriving according to their thoughts.
There are no demonic activities nor any evil realms, nor even the name of "woman" exists there.
There are groves of the seven treasures draped above with jeweled nets, and lotuses of the seven treasures covered by jeweled canopies.
Just as the pure buddha-field accomplished by Mañjuśrī is adorned and embellished, let it be exactly like that, without any difference.
If these words of mine are not false, may the bodies of this great assembly all become golden in color.
"My female body shall be transformed into that of a man, like a thirty-year-old bhikṣu who knows the Dharma.

When these words were spoken, this entire great assembly all turned golden in color; the Bodhisattva Wondrous Wisdom transformed her womanhood into manhood, becoming like a thirty-year-old bhikṣu who knows the Dharma.
At that time, the hosts of earth-dwelling devas praised one another, saying:
"How great, how great!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Subhūti attains enlightenment in a future age, such shall be the merit by which he purifies and adorns his Buddha-field."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"In a future age, this Bodhisattva Subhūti shall attain equal and perfect enlightenment, appearing in the world under the name Tathāgata Viśiṣṭaguṇaratnagarbha."

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, thirty koṭis of sentient beings became established in non-retrogression regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; eighty koṭis of sentient beings were freed from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and eight thousand sentient beings all attained realization through wisdom.

Five thousand bhikṣus who had set out on the bodhisattva vehicle and whose minds were inclined toward regression, upon seeing the excellence of the Bodhisattva Prajñā’s noble intention, roots of goodness, and majestic power, each removed the upper robe they were wearing and offered it to the Tathāgata.
Having made such offerings, they uttered this great vow:
"By these roots of goodness, we resolutely aspire to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment."

Because those sons of good family dedicated these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi, they transcended the suffering of birth and death for ninety kalpas and became non-retrogressive from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately bestowed this prophecy upon them:

"In a future age, after a thousand kalpas have passed, during the Stainless Radiance Kalpa, in the world-system called Mirage within the Buddha-field of Hard to Endure, you shall all successively attain Buddhahood within a single kalpa. You shall all share the same name, Tathāgata Adorned with Eloquence, appearing in the world."
Mañjuśrī! This Dharma gate possesses great majestic power; it is able to bring great benefit to both Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and those of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Mañjuśrī! Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, seeking bodhi, practice the six pāramitās for a full thousand kalpas without skillful means.

Furthermore, if there should be someone who, for half a month, copies and recites this sutra once every period, the mass of merit they obtain compared to the former merit is such that it exceeds it by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, a koṭi-fold, and even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! This subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate is the very foundation of the sūtras for all bodhisattvas.
I now entrust it to you; in future ages, you should receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others.
For example, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, all seven treasures are present before him; once the king passes away, the treasures likewise vanish.

In the same way, while this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate circulates in the world, the Dharma-eye of the Tathāgatas—the seven factors of enlightenment and so forth—will not perish; however, if the True Dharma does not circulate, it shall perish.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! If good sons and good daughters seek awakening, they should rouse diligence to copy this sūtra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and expound it for others.
"This is my teaching; do not harbor regrets in future lives.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and the great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
31. The Chapter on the Upāsikā Gaṅgottarā. Chapter Thirty-one. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a female lay follower (upāsikā) in Śrāvastī named Gaṅgottarā; she came from her residence to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Gaṅgottarā,
“From where have you come?
That upāsikā then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one were to ask a manifested person, ‘From where have you come?
how should such a questioner be answered?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"One who is a transformed being has no coming or going, nor is there any arising or ceasing; how, then, could it be said that such a being comes from anywhere?
He asked again:
“Are not all phenomena indeed like transformations?
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is; it is as you have said.”
Gaṅgottarā said: "If all phenomena are like magical illusions, why do you ask, 'From where have you come?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This illusory person does not go to the evil realms, is not born in the heavens, and does not realize nirvāṇa.
Gaṅgopari! Are you also like this?"
He replied: "If I were to perceive the body as distinct from an illusion, then I might say that one goes to the realms of good or evil, or realizes nirvana.
Since I do not perceive the body as distinct from an illusion, how can I speak of going to the various evil realms or even attaining nirvana?"
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Just as the nature of nirvāṇa ultimately never again gives rise to rebirth in the good or evil realms nor to parinirvāṇa, I observe my own body to be likewise."
The Buddha said,
"Do you not aspire toward the realm of nirvana? Gaṅgottarā replied:
“If one were to ask this same question of one who has attained non-arising (*anutpāda*), how should they answer?
The Buddha said:
“Non-arising is itself nirvāṇa.”
Gaṅgottarā said, “Are not all phenomena identical to nirvāṇa?
The Buddha said:
“So it is, so it is. “World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are identical to nirvāṇa, why do you ask, ‘Do you not proceed toward the realm of nirvāṇa?’”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
It is as if a conjured person were to say to another conjured person:
'Do you not proceed toward the realm of nirvāṇa?'"
"How should one answer when asked this?
The World-Honored One replied:
"That which is asked here has no object of dependence."
Gaṅgottarā said: "How could the Tathāgata have asked this question while still having some object of attachment?
The World-Honored One replied:
"However, my question likewise has no objective support (*ālambana*).
It is only because there are sons and daughters of good family who ought to be brought to maturity in this assembly that I have posed this question."
Why is this? Since even the names of those dharmas cannot be apprehended by the Tathāgata, how could there be any dharmas, or anyone who can proceed toward parinirvāṇa?
Gaṅgottarā said: "If that is so, how does one accumulate roots of goodness for the sake of awakening? [The Buddha replied:
"If both the bodhisattvas and those roots of goodness are unapprehendable, then at the time of accumulation there is no mind; it is likewise when they are not being accumulated."
Gaṅgottarā said: "Regarding what you have called 'mindlessness,' what meaning do you wish to clarify?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This Dharma cannot be known through thought, nor can it be attained through thought.
Why is this? Because within this [state], even the mind itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the phenomena produced by the mind."
Because the mind cannot be apprehended, it is described as the inconceivable realm.
This inconceivable realm is without attainment or realization; it is neither defiled nor pure.
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has always taught that all dharmas are like empty space, being without obstruction. Gaṅgottarā said:

“If all dharmas are like space, why does the World-Honored One speak of the existence of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; as well as the elements, the sense bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, the outflowing and the non-outflowing, the defiled and the pure, and birth-and-death and nirvana?”
The Buddha told Gaṅgottarā:
"For example, although I speak of a 'self,' in reality no characteristic of a self can be apprehended.
When I speak of various forms (*rūpa*), in reality no characteristic of form can be apprehended; it is even so up to and including *nirvāṇa*."
Furthermore, just as a mirage has no water to be found, I say that all forms, up to and including Nirvana, are likewise so. O Gangottara!
Within my Dharma, one who practices the holy life sees that all phenomena are unobtainable; only such a person can be said to truly practice the holy life.
Those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) claim there is something to be attained; they cannot be said to abide in true holy life (*brahmacarya*).

I say that such persons of overweening pride, upon hearing this profound Dharma, will give rise to great alarm and doubt, and will be unable to liberate themselves from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"O Ganges-Top!

After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be one who can proclaim such a profound Dharma that cuts off the cycle of transmigration, and if there are those who are foolish and, due to wrong views, give rise to thoughts of anger and malice toward this Dharma-preacher, they shall, by reason of these causes and conditions, fall into the various hells."
Gaṅgottarā said: "Regarding the Dharma of severing the cycle of existence as spoken of by the Buddha, for what reason is it called 'severing the cycle of existence'?
The Blessed One replied:

That which severs the cycle of transmigration is called the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the inconceivable realm; this dharma cannot be pierced or destroyed, and for this reason it is called the dharma that severs transmigration.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with serene joy, and from his face he emitted various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and the color of crystal. These lights shone universally throughout immeasurable realms, ascending as far as the Brahma world before returning to enter through the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not manifest a smile without cause or condition."
Having had this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"By what causes and conditions do you manifest this smile?"
The Buddha said, “I recall that in the past, there were a thousand Tathāgatas who also preached this Dharma at this very place.

In each of those assemblies, there was likewise a laywoman named Gaṅgottarā as the leader. After that laywoman and the great assembly heard this Dharma, they all left the household life and attained parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What should this sutra be named?
How should we receive and uphold it?”
The Buddha said, “This sutra is named ‘Stainless Purity’; you should receive and uphold it by this title.
When this sutra was being spoken, seven hundred bhikṣus and four hundred bhikṣuṇīs had all their outflows forever exhausted, and their minds attained liberation.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm manifested various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, saying:
"This upāsikā is truly rare; she is able to engage in dialogue with the Tathāgata and has attained fearlessness."
"This person has already, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, drawn near to them, made offerings, and planted various roots of goodness.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the laywoman Gaṅgottarā, along with the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Scroll Ninety-Eight;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Scroll Ninety-Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
32. The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Abhayaguna. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavat was dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a community of five hundred bhikṣus.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas were immeasurable and boundless; furthermore, there were eight thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who served as their leaders, all of whom had attained samādhi and dhāraṇī, skillfully entered the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and were adept in the various supernormal powers, having attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

They were as follows: the Bodhisattva Meru, the Bodhisattva Mahāmeru, the Bodhisattva Nityasamāhita, the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Nityapramuditendriya, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Rāhu, the Bodhisattva Devendra, the Bodhisattva Varuṇa, the Bodhisattva Adhyāśaya, the Bodhisattva Vijayāśaya, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Uttaryāśaya; these eight thousand individuals and others served as their leaders.
At that time, the Bhagavān was residing in Rājagṛha; kings, princes, brahmins, elders, and householders honored, praised, and made offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a multitude of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings, who respectfully encircled him as he preached the Dharma.

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Upāli, the Venerable Rāhula, the Venerable Ānanda, and other such immeasurable śrāvakas, having dressed themselves in the morning and taken up their alms bowls, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food from house to house according to the Dharma, without any other purpose.
At that time, as the śrāvakas were thus begging for alms, they gradually made their way to the palace where King Ajātaśatru resided.
Having arrived at the king’s location, they stood to one side in silence, neither speaking of begging for alms nor of not begging for alms.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru had a daughter named Abhayamati, who was incomparably beautiful, peerless, matchless, and without equal, having perfected the most excellent and sublime virtues. Being twelve years of age, she sat upon a gabled pavilion of her father the king, wearing golden jeweled sandals.

At that time, Vīryaśrī saw that the śrāvakas did not rise or welcome him; they remained silent, neither engaging him in conversation nor welcoming him, nor prostrating to him, nor yielding their seats.
When King Ajātaśatru saw the virtue of fearlessness, he remained silent for a moment and then addressed him, saying:
"Do you not know that these are all the foremost disciples of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni who have accomplished the Great Dharma?"
"Are you not a field of merit for the world?
You wander for alms out of compassion for all sentient beings.
Having now seen you, why do you neither rise, nor go forward to meet me, nor pay homage; why do you neither exchange greetings nor offer me a seat?"
"For what reason do you not rise to greet me now that you have seen me?
At that time, Abhayaguna addressed his father, the King, saying:
"I do not know, Great King, whether you have ever seen or heard of a Wheel-Turning Sage King rising to greet minor kings when he encounters them?"
The king said, “No. He spoke again:
“Great King! Have you ever seen or heard of the lion, the king of beasts, rising to greet a jackal when he sees it?
The King replied:
"No," he replied. He spoke again: "Great King!"
"Have you ever seen or heard of Śakra, King of the Devas, welcoming other devas?
Or has Mahābrahmā ever paid homage to other assemblies of devas?
The King replied:
"No, indeed. He spoke again: "Great King!
“Have you ever seen or heard of the deity of the great ocean paying homage to the deities of rivers,
streams, and ponds? The King replied, “No.”
He spoke again: "Great King!
Have you ever seen or heard of Sumeru, the king of mountains, paying homage to any other minor mountain kings?"
The king said, "No. He spoke again:
“Great King! Have you ever seen or heard of the deities Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha ever having paid homage to a firefly?
The King replied:
"No," the woman said, "Great King!"

In this way, when a bodhisattva resolves their mind to advance toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, having first generated the mind of great compassion as a universal monarch (cakravartin), how could they pay homage to the śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna who are devoid of great compassion?
"Great King!

Have you ever seen the Lion, the King of Beasts—who has already sought the path of unsurpassed, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment—paying homage to a human jackal of the Lesser Vehicle? Great King!"
"Is it appropriate for one who has already sought the path of the Great Brahmā and set out upon it to associate with a śrāvaka who possesses only meager roots of goodness?
"Great King! [the Buddha replied.]

Is it possible that one who wishes to reach the ocean of great wisdom and seeks to thoroughly understand the collection of the Great Dharma would instead seek after the śrāvaka, who is like a cow’s footprint?
For he has heard the sounds from another.

“Great King! Is there anyone who, desiring to go to the Buddha’s Mount Sumeru to seek the Tathāgata’s boundless form-body, would further seek out śrāvakas to pay them homage, merely for the sake of the power of the ‘hollow mustard seed’ samādhi?”

“Great King! Is it possible that one who has heard of the merit and wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, which is like the light of the sun and moon, would, having heard this, pay homage to śrāvakas who are like fireflies?”
Because the śrāvakas can only moisten themselves and illuminate themselves, having attained liberation by hearing sounds from others. "Great King!
Even when the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa, one would not yet pay homage to the śrāvakas; how much less so now while the World-Honored One is still in the world."
Why is this? Great King!
If there is one who associates with those who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle, that person will immediately give rise to the mind of a Śrāvaka.
If a person associates with those who are pratyekabuddhas, that person will immediately give rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha.
If one associates with the Truly and Fully Awakened One, one will immediately give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
After the maiden Abhayamati had spoken thus, she replied to her father, King Ajātaśatru, in verse:
"Just as a person who has reached the ocean might take up a single coin—
so do I see the conduct of all these śrāvakas."
Having reached the great ocean of the Dharma, they abandon the precious hoard of the Mahāyāna and give rise to narrow and inferior minds, practicing the path of the Hīnayāna.
It is like a person who, having gained the favor of a king, enters and exits without any hindrance; yet, [if he were to act otherwise], he would be cast into a pit of excrement.
One who begs a single coin from a king is merely a relative by proximity;
one who approaches a Wheel-Turning King with a heart of reverence and begs for hundreds of thousands of riches,
thereby moistening the suffering of immeasurable poverty— this is called a true, virtuous relative.
Just as a person seeking a single coin, so too are the śrāvakas:
they do not seek true liberation, but instead take up a minor nirvāṇa.
If they give rise to a narrow and inferior mind, they deliver themselves but do not deliver others.
Just as a minor physician Treats only his own person,
So too is the great King of Physicians, Who heals and cures many people;
Having well aroused a heart of compassion, He attains reverence and a good reputation.
That physician gains worldly profit because he has mastered medical formulas;
yet, having crossed over himself but not others, the wise do not revere him.
But like a skilled king of physicians who has thoroughly mastered all methods,
They rescue immeasurable thousands of billions of sentient beings suffering from illness.
That physician gains the world’s respect and renown;
likewise, those who resolve for Bodhicitta universally cure the disease of the afflictions.
Great King, the castor-oil forest—its flowers, fragrance, and shadows are not sublime;
the śrāvakas are like castor trees, for they have not resolved to save the world.
But if one reaches the king of trees, the great multitude gains benefit.
So too it is with all Bodhisattvas, who are able to benefit all beings.
Just as the autumnal sun’s heat cannot dry up small pools of water,
yet once it reaches the great ocean, it can moisten immeasurable multitudes.
The path of the śrāvakas is narrow and inferior, like the print of an ox’s hoof;
it cannot extinguish all the afflictions of sentient beings.
It is not upon these minor hills that the golden-hued body appears.
Only by ascending Mount Sumeru can one see his entirely golden body.
Great King, the various bodhisattvas are likewise like Mount Sumeru;
because they abide in the world, the world attains liberation.
All possess this single body of form, fully endowed with all-encompassing wisdom;
the wisdom of the śrāvakas is not so, being like the morning dew.
It cannot moisten the world, for they have not realized the Dharma.
Just as the earth increases and nourishes immeasurable multitudes,
the śrāvaka is like dew on a flower, while the bodhisattva is like a great rain.
By drawing near, one attains the Great Dharma, like the moistening power of the ocean.
Just as the *karavīra* flower lacks that subtle fragrance,
which neither men nor women delight in, but only cherish the *campaka*;
so too is it like seeking the blue lotus, whose floral scent is most wondrous.
The *dhatura* flower is like the śrāvaka; its wisdom does not moisten the multitudes.
Just as the *campaka* flower is, so too are the bodhisattvas;
out of compassion for sentient beings, they are able to transform the masses of beings.
Great King, have you ever known what is most extraordinary?
It is when a single person dwells in the wilderness as one who benefits many.
If you wish for true peace and security, and to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, [you must practice thus].
One should resolve to attain bodhicitta, And not take up the path of the two vehicles.
In the vast wilderness of the world, They are able to rescue those who have lost their way;
Just like a skilled guide, So too are all Bodhisattvas.
Great King, have you ever seen a small raft cross the great ocean?
Only by riding upon that great ship can one ferry across immeasurable multitudes.
Great King, the śrāvakas are like rafts; the bodhisattvas are like the great ship.
Once the Dharma of the Path of Cultivation has been perfumed, it enables one to cross the ocean of hunger and thirst.
Great King, have you ever seen one riding a donkey enter the fray?
One sees only those riding elephants or horses who achieve victory in battle.
The śrāvakas are like donkeys on a journey, while the bodhisattvas are like dragon-elephants;
having subdued Māra and sat beneath the tree of enlightenment, they deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
It is just as when the night sky is empty and the various stars do not appear.
Because the full moon appears, it is able to illuminate Jambudvīpa.
The śrāvakas are like the stars, while the bodhisattvas are like the full moon;
out of compassion for sentient beings, they manifest the path to nirvāṇa.
The light of a firefly cannot accomplish much;
the sun’s radiance illuminates Jambudvīpa, enabling all manner of deeds.
Śrāvakas are like fireflies; they cannot bring great benefit.
The Buddha possesses the light of liberation and compassionately regards all beings.
A jackal’s cry cannot frighten the king of beasts;
only the lion king, with a single roar, causes even the flying birds to fall.
O Great King, the various śrāvakas do not resolve upon bodhicitta;
they do not act for the benefit of sentient beings, but merely eliminate all afflictions.
Because the Great King perceives this, he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka.
Having already resolved upon the Great Mind, how could one give rise to a lesser one?
O Great King, you have well obtained this body; being able to resolve upon the Unsurpassed Mind, you shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings and abandon the path of the Lesser Vehicle.
Having well attained a worldly body, you have further gained the benefit of the world;
having come well into this world, you have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind.
Seeking the unsurpassed path, you rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
If one can benefit both oneself and others, that person is truly worthy of praise;
they shall attain worldly renown as well as the ultimate path.
For this reason, I do not now pay homage to the śrāvakas.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to the girl Vīradevī, "You possess great arrogance;
why is it that you see these great śrāvakas and yet do not go out to welcome them?"
The woman said: "Great King!
Do not speak such words."
"The Great King is also arrogant; why does he not welcome the poor within the city of Rājagṛha?
The king said to his daughter, "They are not of my kind; how could I welcome them?"
The woman said: “Great King!
A bodhisattva at the initial stage is likewise; he is not of the same class as any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
The king said to the girl,
"Do you not see that all the bodhisattvas pay homage to all sentient beings?
The girl replied:

“Great King! A Bodhisattva, in order to deliver all sentient beings who are afflicted by pride and anger, causes them to give rise to the mind of dedication; for this reason, he pays homage to all sentient beings.”
In order to foster the various roots of goodness in sentient beings, the bodhisattva pays homage to them.
Yet, although the śrāvakas are free from malice and resentment, they are nonetheless unable to increase their own roots of goodness.
"Great King!
Even if hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were to preach the sublime Dharma for him, there would be no increase in the precepts, meditative concentration, or samādhi he has attained.
Great King!"
The śrāvaka is like lapis lazuli, while the bodhisattva is like a precious vessel.
Great King!
It is like a jar that is full; when the heavens send down rain, it does not receive even a single drop.
Thus it is, Great King!

Even if hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, were to preach the sublime Dharma for the śrāvakas and others, they would receive no nourishment from it; they could not increase their morality, concentration, and wisdom, nor could they cause sentient beings to resolve upon the mind [of awakening] and reach all-knowledge.
Great King!
It is like the great ocean, which can receive all rivers, clouds, rain, and so forth. Why is this?
Because the great ocean is an immeasurable vessel,
O Great King!
When the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas preach the Dharma, those who hear it accordingly obtain great benefit and merit, and all roots of goodness increase.
"Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas are vessels for boundless discourse.
At that time, having heard the girl's words, King Ajātaśatru remained silent.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:
“This girl, Fearless Virtue, has attained great eloquence and is thus able to speak in such an inexhaustible manner.”
"I shall now go before him and question him briefly.
For now, I will ask:
'Have you attained patience?'"
Having formed this thought, he approached and asked the woman,
"Do you now abide in the Śrāvaka-yāna? She replied:
"No. "Do you now abide in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas? He replied:
"No. "Do you now abide in the mind of the Great Vehicle? He replied:
"No," Śāriputra said. "If that is so,
by abiding in which vehicle is one able to let out such a lion's roar?"
The woman replied to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"If I were currently abiding anywhere, I would not be able to roar the lion's roar.
Because I abide nowhere, I am able to roar the lion's roar."
Yet Śāriputra spoke thus: "In which vehicle do you abide?
How could there be any differentiation of vehicles within that Dharma which Śāriputra has realized?
"Is this the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or is it the Mahāyāna?
Śāriputra said: "Listen as I speak."
"The Dharma realized by me has no distinction between vehicles and non-vehicles, because it is of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
The girl Abhayā said: "Venerable Śāriputra!"
"If dharmas are signless, how can they be sought?
Śāriputra said, "O Girl Fearless Virtue!"
"What distinction or difference in superiority or inferiority exists between the Dharma of the Buddhas and the Dharma of ordinary beings?
The woman said to the Venerable Śāriputra,
"What difference is there between emptiness and tranquility?"
Śāriputra said, "There is no distinction. Abhayaguṇa said:

“Śāriputra! Just as space is quiescent and devoid of any signs of distinction, superiority, or inferiority, so too the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of ordinary beings are devoid of any signs of distinction, superiority, or inferiority.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as space can receive all forms without distinction, so too there is no distinction and no difference between the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of ordinary beings.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the girl Abhayamati:

"What difference do you perceive between the Buddha-dharma and the Śrāvaka-dharma, such that you see these great Śrāvakas and neither rise to welcome them, nor respond to them, nor offer them a seat?"
The girl Abhayamati replied to Maudgalyāyana:

"Suppose the stars were to fill the three-thousandfold world system; they would be unable to illuminate it clearly. It is the same with the śrāvakas: they are able to perceive through the wisdom of meditative concentration, but if they do not enter concentration, they do not perceive."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"If one does not enter meditative concentration, one cannot know the minds of sentient beings.
The woman said to Maudgalyāyana:

"The Buddha enters no meditative absorption yet teaches the Dharma as appropriate throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to deliver all sentient beings, for he possesses excellent knowledge of the mind;
how much more so, then, for the śrāvakas who possess but the slight radiance of the stars?"
This is the supreme feat of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
is there any among the śrāvakas who can know how many world-systems are forming and how many world-systems are disintegrating?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said, “I cannot know it.
The woman said to Maudgalyāyana:
“Do the śrāvakas know how many Buddhas have already entered parinirvāṇa, how many Buddhas will enter parinirvāṇa in the future, and how many Buddhas are entering parinirvāṇa at present?”
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I cannot know it. The woman said to Maudgalyāyana:
“Do the śrāvakas know how many sentient beings have much greed,
how many sentient beings have much anger,
and how many sentient beings have much delusion?”
"How many sentient beings are there who possess equal proportions of the [three] defilements?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"I am unable to know."
The woman said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Does a śrāvaka know the number of sentient beings who take up the Śrāvaka Vehicle,
and the number of sentient beings who take up the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle?"
"How many sentient beings have received the Buddha Vehicle?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"I am unable to know."
The woman said to Maudgalyāyana:
“Do the śrāvakas know how many beings are delivered by the śrāvakas?
And how many beings are delivered by the pratyekabuddhas?”
"How many sentient beings can the Buddha deliver?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "I cannot know."
The woman said to Maudgalyāyana,
“Does a śrāvaka know how many beings are in the group of those fixed in rightness who possess right view,
and how many beings dwell in the group of those fixed in error?”
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I cannot know. The woman said to Maudgalyāyana:

"Only the Tathāgata, the Truly and Perfectly Awakened One, knows the realms of all sentient beings as they truly are and teaches the Dharma accordingly; such a matter is not within the sphere of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, much less that of other sentient beings."
Maudgalyāyana!

You should know that this is a preeminent matter of the Tathāgata; because the Tathāgata has fully attained all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), it is something that none of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas possess.
Then the girl Abhayā spoke again to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“The World-Honored One has always declared that among those with supernormal powers, you, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, are the foremost.”

Does Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal power enable him to know of and reach the world of Gandhahastin, and does he know whether all the trees in that world produce the most sublime and wondrous sandalwood fragrance?
Maudgalyāyana replied, “I have only now heard the name of that world; how could I possibly go there?
Maudgalyāyana asked the girl:
"What is the name of that Buddha who is preaching the Dharma in that world?
The girl replied, "That Buddha is named Fragrant Light Emitting Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is preaching the Dharma there."
Maudgalyāyana said to the girl,
"How can you now see that Buddha? At that time,
the fearless girl, without rising from her seat or altering her dignified posture, made this vow:

"If this Bodhisattva, at the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, can surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, by virtue of this vow, may that Tathāgata Emitting Fragrant Light manifest his body here, causing all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to see that World of Fragrant Elephants and to smell the sublime and wondrous sandalwood trees."
When the girl Abhayā had made this vow, the Tathāgata Gandhaprabhāsa emitted light from his body.

Because of that emission of light, all the śrāvakas were able to see that world of Gandhahastin, as well as the Buddha surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas; there, the Buddha, having concealed his form behind a lattice-work canopy, was preaching the Dharma to the assembly, and the Dharma he preached was heard here in its entirety.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, she was further able to smell the exquisite fragrance of *candana* sandalwood from those trees.
The Buddha of that world spoke these words:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as the fearless woman has said."
"When a bodhisattva thus first resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they have already transcended the realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
While this Dharma was being taught, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By what causes and conditions does that fragrance of the wondrous tree come?
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!”

When the fearless woman Abhayā engaged in a discussion according to the Dharma with the śrāvakas and made her vow, that Buddha, having known it, used his supernatural powers to manifest such fragrances and that world.
"And that exquisite, sublime sandalwood fragrance pervades this entire trichiliocosm.
Then the girl Abhayā said to Maudgalyāyana,

"If one beholds such inconceivable and supreme merits as these, yet still gives rise to the narrow and inferior mind of a śrāvaka of the Lesser Vehicle, seeking only one's own liberation, you should know that their roots of goodness are exceedingly meager."
Who, upon seeing the deeds of a Bodhisattva who has accomplished immeasurable merit, would not resolve to attain enlightenment?
Maudgalyāyana!
Do you know how far that Buddha-world is from here?
He replied, "I do not know. The woman said:
“Maudgalyāyana!
Even if one were to employ various supernormal powers for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it would be impossible to know or see that Buddha-world.
It is, for example, like the countless groves of bamboo and reeds.”
"Only after passing through such Buddha-worlds as these will one reach that world of Fragrant Elephants.
At that time, that Buddha withdrew his radiance.
Once the light was withdrawn, the world of Fragrant Elephants and that Tathāgata suddenly vanished from sight.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to Abhaya,
"Have you ever seen that world of Fragrant Elephants, as well as that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
The woman then replied: "Mahākāśyapa!
Can the Tathāgata be seen?"
As the Buddha has taught: "Those who see me by means of form, or seek me by means of sound, all follow a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Since the essence of all Tathāgatas is the Dharma-body, and the Buddha-dharma is neither visible nor audible, how can it be known or seen?
By whatever means sentient beings may find joy, the Buddha manifests an unobstructed body, for he abides in skillful means.
Yet Mahākāśyapa said to me:
"Do you see that world and that Buddha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
I saw that Buddha, not with the physical eye, for he is not a form perceived by the physical eye;
nor did I see him with the divine eye, for he is without sensation.
It is not seen by the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), because it is free from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
It is not seen by the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), because it is free from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
It is not seen by the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), because it is free from the perception of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Mahākāśyapa! My vision of the Tathāgata is just as the Venerable Kāśyapa sees him, because I have extinguished the mind of ignorance, craving, and views. Mahākāśyapa!
"I see that Buddha just as the Venerable Kāśyapa sees him; furthermore, I also see 'I' and 'mine,' and so forth.
Kāśyapa said to the woman:
"If dharmas are eternally non-existent, how can ignorance, craving, and the characteristics of 'I' and 'mine' arise?"
"Because all sentient beings are invisible.
The woman said, "Mahākāśyapa!"
"If all these phenomena are eternally non-existent,
how can they be seen? Mahākāśyapa replied,
"If all Buddha-dharmas are ultimately non-existent, how can they be seen?"
The woman said:
"Mahākāśyapa! Do you see the meaning of the increase of all Buddha-dharmas?"
Mahākāśyapa said, “I do not even know the dharmas of ordinary persons, let alone the Buddha-dharmas.
The fearless maiden said:
"Therefore, Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
Since that dharma is not established, how could there be any interruption or continuity such that one who has not realized it would see it? Mahākāśyapa!"
All phenomena are eternally non-existent and cannot be manifested.
Therefore, Mahākāśyapa, all dharmas are utterly void.
If phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, how can that pure dharma-realm be perceived? Mahākāśyapa!
If one wishes to see the pure Tathāgata, those sons and daughters of good family should purify their own minds.
Then Mahākāśyapa said to Abhayā,
"How does one purify one's own mind well?
The woman replied:

“Mahākāśyapa! Just as with the suchness of one’s own self and the suchness of all phenomena, if one has faith in them, there is neither making nor losing, because one thus perceives the purity of one’s own mind.”
Kāśyapa asked, "What is the essence of one's own mind?
The woman replied:
"Emptiness is its essence.
If one realizes that emptiness and gains confidence in one's own body, one then gains confidence in the emptiness of true suchness (*tathatā*), because the nature of all phenomena is quiescent.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the fearless woman, saying:
“From which Buddha did you hear such a Dharma that you attained right view?
As the Buddha has taught, there are two causes and conditions for the arising of right view:
hearing the Dharma from others and internal reflection.”
The woman said: "Mahākāśyapa!
It is by relying on those external sounds and hearing those external sounds that one subsequently engages in internal reflection."
"Mahākāśyapa! Since a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not rely on the words of others nor on sounds, how can it be said that they 'abide in cessation'?
Kāśyapa addressed the woman, saying:
"Because one observes the Dharma according to what has been heard, it is called 'contemplative practice' (vipaśyanā-caryā).
Then Mahākāśyapa again asked the woman:
"How does a bodhisattva reflect within themselves?"
The woman said: “Mahākāśyapa!

If, while engaging in the same activities as other bodhisattvas in preaching the Dharma, one does not give rise to the notion of sentient beings, a bodhisattva thus practices internal contemplation; for this reason, it is called the accomplishment of internal contemplation.”

Mahākāśyapa! All dharmas are complete with the past limit, the middle limit, and the future limit, because all dharmas have the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*), and all dharmas have the nature of present true suchness.
"If one observes in this way, it should be known that this bodhisattva is called 'one who has accomplished internal contemplation.
Kāśyapa said to the woman,
"How are these dharmas established?"
The woman said: "Mahākāśyapa!
It should be done in this way: just as that suchness is seen to be neither bound nor liberated."
Mahākāśyapa asked, "In what way is seeing called right view?
The woman replied:
“Mahākāśyapa! Because one is free from the views of the two extremes, neither acting nor not acting—seeing in this way yet not seeing—is called right view.”
"Mahākāśyapa! Dharmas possess only names, yet because they are apart from names, they can never be realized.
Then Mahākāśyapa again asked the girl:
“How does one come to see for oneself?
The fearless maiden replied,
“Just as the Venerable Mahākāśyapa sees.”
Mahākāśyapa said: "I do not perceive a self, nor do I perceive what belongs to a self.
The woman spoke to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"One should view all phenomena in this way, because they are devoid of self and what belongs to a self.
When this teaching was spoken, the Venerable Subhūti was filled with great joy and said to the fearless woman,
"You have attained a great benefit, being able to achieve such eloquence."
Then the girl Abhayā addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: “Subhūti,
can phenomena that are obtainable or unobtainable be sought after?”
And he said to me, "You have well attained eloquence.
I possess this eloquence such that, if I were to say there is nothing to be cognized, whether internally or externally, then I would truly possess eloquence."
Then Subhūti spoke to the woman, saying:
"What have you realized?
What dharma have you attained that you possess such swift and wondrous eloquence?"
The woman replied:
"Because I do not know them myself, I do not perceive from others the distinguishing characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

Knowing dharmas in this way, I do not see defilement or purity, the outflowing or the outflow-free, the conditioned or the unconditioned, the mundane or the supramundane, nor the dharmas of ordinary beings; for because I do not see them, [I do not grasp them]."
Because that dharma-body is itself the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma, one attains the Buddha-dharma yet does not perceive a Buddha.
Subhūti, if it is thus, there is nothing to be awakened to or perceived; such is this eloquence.
Subhūti asked, "What is eloquence? The woman replied:
“Subhūti! Just as you have attained it, so should you eliminate [all afflictions].
The woman spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Just as that dharma-body is neither heard nor attained, yet there is something spoken.
The woman said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Can the dharma-body abide?"
"Furthermore, can one increase or decrease it while still possessing such eloquence?
At that time, Subhūti spoke to the woman, saying:
"If one realizes the untainted (anāsrava), there is no distinction in phenomena (dharma), nor is there any eloquent discourse, because the essence of those phenomena is ineffable."
The woman said to the Venerable Subhūti:
“How can such thoughts and words arise regarding all phenomena?
You have skillfully attained their benefit and gained such eloquence.”
Subhūti said to the woman:
"Do you speak because you have attained eloquence,
or do you speak because you have not attained it?"
The woman said to the Venerable Subhūti,
"Is it as the Buddha has taught— that all dharmas are like echoes? Subhūti replied:
"I believe this matter.
The woman asked,
"Are echoes and reflections possessed of eloquence or devoid of eloquence?"
Subhūti said: "Because there is internal sound, there is external resonance.
The woman said to Subhūti:
"Because sound exists as a condition, there is that echo; what nature or characteristic does that echo possess?
Yet, that echoing sound has no nature or characteristic. Why is this?"
"If it arises through conditions, then it has the meaning of being unarisen. Subhūti said:
"All phenomena arise through conditions."
The girl Abhayā said:
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-arising. Subhūti said:

"If the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is thus ultimately non-existent, why does the Tathāgata speak in this way, saying that Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges shall attain perfect enlightenment?"
The woman asked,
"Can the dharma-realm be produced? Subhūti replied:
"It cannot arise. The girl Fearless said:
"All Buddhas and Tathāgatas are entirely of the nature and characteristics of the dharmadhātu."
Subhūti said: "I do not perceive any dharma-realm.
The fearless maiden said:
"All that you have spoken consists of untainted words, yet you say that Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges shall attain perfect enlightenment.
To what does this refer? For what reason?"
Because the dharma-realm is neither born nor extinguished;
because all speech and non-speech are ultimately pure;
because it is not a functional entity, it is inexpressible and transcends the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Subhūti said: "How extraordinary you are!
To be a householder and yet able to skillfully teach the Dharma in such a way, and furthermore to possess such inexhaustible eloquence!"
The girl Abhayā said: “Subhūti,
for a bodhisattva there is no grasping or non-grasping, no hearing or non-hearing, whether they be a householder or one who has gone forth, yet they possess eloquence.”
"Why is this? Because through the purity of the mind, wisdom is made manifest; and because wisdom is made manifest, eloquence is revealed.
The woman spoke thus to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Now you may well explain the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti said, "Speak, and I shall listen. The Fearless Woman replied:
“Subhūti! Because bodhisattvas accomplish eight kinds of dharmic practices, they cannot be said to be either householders or renunciants.
What are these eight dharmas?
Subhūti! First, a bodhisattva attains purity of body and gains settled faith in bodhi;
second, they accomplish great loving-kindness and great compassion while never abandoning sentient beings.
Third, because they have accomplished great compassion, they are skillful in all worldly affairs;
fourth, they are able to relinquish their bodies, lives, and limbs, and they accomplish skillful means;
fifth, they are skillful in making immeasurable vows.
Sixth, they accomplish the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) because they are free from all views;
seventh, they possess great courageous diligence because they never tire of cultivating all wholesome deeds;
eighth, they attain unobstructed knowledge because they have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
