Subhūti! Because a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight dharmas, one cannot say whether they are a householder or one who has gone forth; regardless of which deportment they abide in, they dwell within bodhi without any hindrance.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula said to the fearless maiden:
"These words are indeed impure speech.
Yet you, wearing jeweled sandals and seated upon a high couch, are able to engage in such dialectical discourse with the śrāvakas."
“Have you not heard that one must not preach the Dharma to those who are not ill, nor should one preach the Dharma to those seated on high couches?
Then the girl Vīradattā addressed the Venerable Rāhula, saying:
“Do you truly know what is pure and what is impure?”
"Venerable Rāhula! Is this world pure? Rāhula replied:
“There is neither purity nor impurity.
The girl Abhayā said:
“I shall receive and practice the precepts as established by the Tathāgata.”
"If one violates those precepts, is it pure or impure?
And if another person does not violate those precepts, is it neither pure nor impure?
The girl Abhayā replied:
“Stop, stop; do not speak thus. If one practices according to how the Dharma is taught or according to how the precepts are laid down, that is called impurity.”
Rāhula! Because he has realized the untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma), he does not commit any transgression.
Since he does not commit transgressions, for him there is neither purity nor impurity.

Why is this? Because the various śrāvakas have transcended all formal teachings and transcended all disciplinary precepts; it is for the sake of those śrāvaka learners that the Tathāgata has come into the triple world and preached for them.
Yet those śrāvakas have already transcended the three realms; for this reason, it is said that they have transcended what is not transcended.
Since the realms are thus, because they cannot realize the precepts, it is said that they are pure or impure.
"Furthermore, space consists only of verbal expression and only the vision of the power of wisdom;
therefore, it can be described as pure or impure. Rāhula said, "What is the difference between purity and impurity?"
The girl Abhayā said:
"For example, suppose there is pure gold that has been cleansed of all impurities; whether it is fashioned into an ornament or left unworked, what difference is there in its color?"
Rāhula said, "There is no distinction.
The fearless maiden said:
"Purity and impurity are distinguished only by name; there is no other distinction.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is free from all defilements, being without stain and without attachment."
The woman said to the Venerable Rāhula:
"One should not preach the Dharma while seated upon a high or broad seat.
All Bodhisattvas sit upon a grass mat rather than a high seat; they are superior to Śrāvakas who abide in the Brahma-heaven."
Rāhula asked, "For what reason? The woman replied:
“Rāhula! Have you ever seen upon what seat a bodhisattva sits to attain bodhi? Rāhula replied:
"He shall sit upon a seat of grass. The woman said, "When the Bodhisattva sits upon the seat of grass,

all those in the trichiliocosm— the Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, and the Four Great Kings, as well as other devaputras, up to those in the Akaniṣṭha heaven and beyond— will all come to prostrate with their ten fingers joined like palms, and arrive at the Bodhisattva's location to worship his feet."
Rāhula replied, “So it is, so it is. Then the girl Abhayā asked Rāhula:

"Having accomplished such dharmas as these, the Bodhisattva sits upon a seat of grass; this surpasses sitting upon high, vast, and grand couches, and it surpasses Śrāvakas dwelling in the Brahma Heaven."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to the girl Vīradattā:
"Do you not know that this is the son of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, who is foremost among those training in the precepts?"
Then the girl Abhayā said to her father, the King: "Stop, Great King!
Do not speak thus, saying that Rāhula is the son of the Tathāgata."
"Great King!
Have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?
Has a lion king ever given birth to a jackal?"
The king said, "I do not see her.
The woman said:
"Great King! Have you ever seen or heard of a Wheel-Turning Sage King paying homage to other minor kings? He replied:
"I have not seen it.
The woman said, "Great King!"
In this way, the Tathāgata, the lion-king, turns the great wheel of Dharma, surrounded by śrāvakas. Great King!
If one speaks according to the royal law, who is considered a true son of the Tathāgata?
One should then answer: "It is the bodhisattvas.
Therefore, Great King, one must not say that the Tathāgata has a son, nor that the Tathāgata has no son.
"If one speaks of those who are the true sons of the Tathāgata, one should say that those who give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are the sons of the Tathāgata.
When this Dharma-gate was being taught, twenty thousand women within King Ajātaśatru’s palace gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Twenty thousand devaputras fulfilled that Dharma, and having heard this daughter’s lion’s roar, they resolved upon Bodhicitta.
The King spoke again, saying:
"These are the sons of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; though they have abandoned all afflictions and train in the precepts of the śrāvakas, how can they be true sons?"
At that time, those devaputras scattered flowers over the Buddha throughout the city of Rājagṛha as an offering to the girl Abhayā.

Then, the girl Abhayā descended from her couch and paid homage to the great śrāvakas, providing them with various kinds of exquisite food and drink—whether to be licked, smelled, or sipped—offering them in accordance with the Dharma.
When those śrāvakas had finished making their offerings, they spoke these words:
"We do not know, Venerable Great Śrāvakas, for what reason you have left the presence of the Tathāgata at this early hour and come here?"
"You should listen to the Dharma first, and only then go for alms.
Venerable sir, please depart; I shall arrive there in just a moment.

At dawn, the lady Bhaya-datta, together with King Ajātaśatru, her mother, and an immeasurable multitude of people from Rājagṛha as her retinue, went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Those śrāvakas also went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This daughter of noble family, Abhayā, is truly marvelous; she has attained such great benefit.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Śāriputra:

"This daughter Abhayā has already resolved her mind toward Bodhi under ninety billion Buddhas in the past, planting various roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas for the sake of seeking unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment."
Śāriputra said, “World-Honored One!
Is this girl able to transform her female body?”
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! Do you see that woman? Is she truly a woman?”
You should not now hold such a view. Why is this?
It is because by the power of their vows, these bodhisattvas manifest in female bodies in order to deliver sentient beings.
Thereupon, the girl Abhayamati made this vow:
"If all dharmas are neither male nor female, may I now manifest the body of a man, so that the entire great assembly may behold it."
Having spoken these words, he immediately extinguished his female form and manifested a male body; he ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees and remained there without descending.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra,
do you see that Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue?"
"It remains in the void and does not descend.
Śāriputra said, "I have seen it."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
After this Bodhisattva Abhayaguṇa has passed seven thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall attain perfect enlightenment and be known by the name Vimala Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
That Buddha-world is named Radiance.
The Buddha’s lifespan is one hundred kalpas, and the duration of the True Dharma is ten kalpas.
It consists solely of a community of bodhisattvas, including thirty thousand non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.

The ground of that Buddha-world is of pure lapis lazuli, adorned with the eightfold paths and covered by lotus flowers; there is not even the name of any of the evil realms, and it is filled with devas and humans.
“Śāriputra! Just as the gods of Tuṣita Heaven experience subtle and wondrous bliss and the flavor of the supreme Dharma, so too do those sons of heaven experience such bliss.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue’s mother, named Sūryacandraprabhā, together with King Ajātaśatru, joined their palms with ten fingers extended and went to where the Buddha was, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have obtained great benefit; though I have carried this son in my womb for nine months, this good man now utters such a great lion’s roar.”
I now dedicate these roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; after this, I shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment in that world called Vimalaprabhā.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra,
do you see this now?”
He replied, “I have seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! After this daughter Candraprabhā has cast off this body, she will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as a son of the gods named Ābhāsa-vardhana.
When Maitreya Bodhisattva attains bodhi, she will be the eldest son of King Darśana; having made offerings to that Buddha Maitreya, he will immediately go forth into the homeless life.”
He saw that prince, at the place where Maitreya Buddha preached the Dharma, being able to fully remember and uphold everything taught—the beginning, middle, and end.
He saw him successively encounter all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa and receive offerings from them all.

Having thus gradually made offerings to the Buddhas, he will subsequently become a great king at the time that the Tathāgata Vimala attains bodhi; he will possess the seven treasures and be named Dharanidhara.

Having seen that Prince make offerings to these Tathāgatas, he too shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, receiving the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha Vairocana (Universal Radiance). He will fully accomplish a Buddha-world such as was described above.

At that time, Lady Candraprabhā was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; she immediately removed a wondrous jewel necklace worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold and offered it to the Buddha.
Having spoken thus to the Great King, she received the five pure precepts and fully cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue stood before the Tathāgata and spoke these words:
"By the power of the causal conditions of this vow, may it be so that when I attain bodhi in the future, all bodhisattvas shall likewise be clad in the dharma-robes."
"By the power of these causes and conditions of this vow, may all those born by transformation cause the Tathāgata to appear like a young bhikṣu of eight years' standing.
After the Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue had manifested his body and spoken these words, he donned the robes of the True Dharma and immediately became a bhikṣu, fully endowed with dignified deportment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue addressed his own father, King Ajātaśatru, saying: "Great King!
All dharmas are exactly like this."
"Immediately, she suddenly manifested the appearance of one born by transformation, free from all signs arising from conceptual discrimination and devoid of all delusions. 'Great King!
At that very moment, she again manifested the body of a woman.'"
"Did Your Majesty see it?
The King replied,
"I have seen it."
"I do not perceive me by means of the marks of the physical body.
Having now seen you in the form of a bhikṣu, I further see you in the form of a woman.
The Buddha asked the king:
"What is the truth? Great King!
You should train yourself in this way: abiding within all phenomena, you should perceive all things with right view."

Furthermore, because you have been burned by the afflictions and have failed to comprehend the power of the Dharma, and because of this lack of comprehension, you have given rise to doubt and regret regarding matters that do not warrant suspicion.

You should repeatedly draw near to the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; through the majestic power of those Bodhisattvas, you shall enable the Great King to receive his confession of transgression.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Receive and uphold this Dharma-gate of the prophecy for the Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue; read and recite it without forgetting."
Ānanda! If there were good men or good women who, possessing the seven treasures, made offerings to all the Tathāgatas throughout a trichiliocosm as vast as the three-thousandfold world system;

If there should be another person who is able to receive and uphold this Dharma-gate of the Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Fearless Virtue, receiving and upholding even a single phrase or a single verse upon hearing it, they will obtain merit exceeding that [of the former]; how much more so if they fully master it, whether by reading or reciting, extensively explaining it for others, and practicing it according to the Dharma.

When the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma-gate of the prophecy for the Bodhisattva Abhayaguṇa, Lady Candraprabhā—the mother of Abhayaguṇa—along with the devas, nāgas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume Ninety-nine;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred.
Translated by the Western Jin layman Nie Daozhen.

33. The Chapter on the Exposition by the Bodhisattva Vimaladatta, Part One: The Introductory Chapter, Number Thirty-Three. Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus.

All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions. They had attained mastery over all dharmas; they had accomplished what was to be done and laid down the heavy burden. Having realized their own benefit, they had exhausted the fetters of existence. They had attained liberation through right knowledge; their minds were well-liberated and their wisdom was well-liberated. Their minds were tamed like those of great elephant kings; they had attained mastery of mind and reached the further shore, entering the eight liberations.
With the sole exception of Ānanda,
there were also various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who were all greatly adorned, well-known to all, attained to the stage of non-retrogression, and were all but one birth away from buddhahood.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Guṇakośa, Bodhisattva Prajñālaṃkāra, Bodhisattva Manojña, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Pramuñcaghoṣa Kumārabhūta, Acintyavimokṣacaryā Kumārabhūta, Sarvadharmacintanānāvaraṇa Kumārabhūta, Bodhisattva Maitreya, Bodhisattva Viśoka-dāna, Bodhisattva Amūḍhadarśin, Bodhisattva Apāyavarjita, Bodhisattva Anāvaraṇacaryā, Bodhisattva Tamo’ntakara, Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Bodhisattva Pratibhānalaṃkāra, Bodhisattva Ratnaguṇatejorāja, Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpadharmaprabhāsaśrī, and Bodhisattva Anāvaraṇacintin. Together with these twelve thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, they were all present.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Aniruddha, and the Venerable Ānanda—along with the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Avidyādṛṣṭi, the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Apāyavivarjita, the Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇaviśodhana, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānavyūha, and the Bodhisattva Avidyācaryā—these eight great bodhisattvas and eight great śrāvakas, taking up their robes and bowls at dawn, were about to enter the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Then, while on the road, they each formed this thought and discussed the matter together.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said:
"Having entered such a meditative concentration, I shall go to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms; may all sentient beings within the city hear the Four Noble Truths."
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana said:
"I shall enter such a meditative concentration and go to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms, wishing that all sentient beings within the city may be free from the works of Māra."

Mahākāśyapa said: "I shall enter such a meditative concentration and go to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms, so that all sentient beings within the city who give to me may obtain inexhaustible rewards, even unto Nirvāṇa."
The Venerable Subhūti said:

"I shall enter such a meditative concentration and go to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms; may all sentient beings within the city who see me, by virtue of this cause and condition, experience various joys among gods and humans and reach the end of suffering."
The Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"I shall enter such a meditative concentration and go to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms, wishing that all the non-Buddhist brahmins and nirgranthas within the city may attain right view."
The Venerable Rahula said:
"I shall enter such a meditative concentration that, when I go to Śrāvastī to beg for alms, may all sentient beings within the city attain the bliss of non-contention."
The Venerable Aniruddha said:
"I shall enter such a meditative concentration and go to Śrāvastī to beg for alms, wishing that all sentient beings within the city may recognize the retribution of their past karma."
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"I shall enter such a meditative concentration and go to Śrāvastī to beg for alms, wishing that all sentient beings within the city may have the teachings they previously heard manifest before them."
The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī thought to himself:

"I shall cause all the gates, windows, walls, vessels, trees, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as the garments and necklaces within the city of Śrāvastī, to all emit the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-existence, selflessness, the absence of conceptual proliferation, and the absence of intrinsic nature."
The Bodhisattva Vimaladarśana thought to himself:

"I shall cause all sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī who are destined to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to perceive whatever objects they see as the image of the Tathāgata, and I shall cause them to become definitively resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Bodhisattva Ratnākāra made this reflection:
"I shall cause all the treasuries within the houses and residences of every clan in the city of Śrāvastī to manifest and produce the seven precious jewels."
The Bodhisattva Free from Evil Destinies (Durgatipariśodhana) thought to himself:
"I shall cause all sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī who are destined to fall into evil destinies to undergo their suffering lightly in this present life and be swiftly liberated from it."
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin formed this thought:
"I shall cause all sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī to completely eliminate the five hindrances.
Then the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara formed this thought:

"I shall cause the sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī who are imprisoned and confined to be swiftly liberated; those facing death shall immediately find their lives saved; and those who are terrified shall immediately attain fearlessness."
The Bodhisattva Prajñābhadraka thought to himself:
"I shall cause all sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī who see me to attain eloquence, so that they may engage in mutual dialogue using various sublime verses."
The Bodhisattva Avidyācaryā (Vigilant Conduct) formed this thought:
"I shall cause every sentient being within the city of Śrāvastī who beholds me to attain non-deluded vision and become resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Thus, these eight great bodhisattvas and eight great śrāvakas discussed the aforementioned matters together until they reached the gate of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a daughter of King Prasenajit within the city named Vimaladattā; she was only eight years old, yet her countenance was so upright and majestic that it was rarely seen in the world.

On the eighth day of the second month, on the day when the Puṣya constellation appeared, the daughter, together with five hundred Brahmins, carrying jars filled with water, went outside the city to bathe the image of the deity.
At that time, the five hundred brahmins saw the bhikṣus standing outside the gate; having seen them, they all considered it inauspicious.
Then, the most senior among the assembly of brahmins, who was one hundred and twenty years old and named Brahmā, said to the girl Vimaladattā:
"Now these bhikṣus are standing outside the gate."
"This matter is inauspicious; we should return to the city and need not behold this.
Once this has been seen, all matters such as sacrifices, offerings, prosperity, and auspiciousness will become inauspicious."
At that time, the maiden Vimaladattā replied to the brahmin in verse:
"These are all without grasping, The foremost objects of praise;
They are able, for the sake of many sentient beings, To wash away all evils."
All these are pure, having fully seen the Four Noble Truths;
the non-Buddhists are not pure, being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.
To the Field of Merit, the Most Honored among Two-legged Beings, giving to them brings immeasurable reward.
Those who plant [roots of virtue] within this, shall never exhaust them throughout the three realms of existence.
With pure and complete observance of the precepts, they emerge from the mud unattached;
moving through the world like a skilled physician, they heal and rescue sentient beings from their ailments.
The Buddha is the most excellent in the world, the sovereign of all dharmas;
these are his sons who have accomplished the state of arhatship.
How could a wise person practicing such bodhisattva conduct ever abandon them?
Those who practice this sublime conduct are worthy of praise by the world;
they are the wise ones who have long practiced giving.
For the Brahmin who honors such as these, all matters will be auspicious without doubt.
"Praising this one who possesses these marks, whose mind is pure and who is a fertile field of merit—
if a brahmin has faith, he shall obtain joy and the bliss of freedom from sorrow.
At that time, the brahmin again answered the girl Vimaladattā in verse:
"Do not follow the narrow-minded and foolish; do not visit the shrine where you see śramaṇas with shaven heads wearing saffron robes who seek only their own pleasure.
Your parents will not be pleased, and we shall be filled with shame."
"If you wish to practice giving, that matter will likewise not be auspicious.
It is well that you do not show respect to these various bhikṣus.
Then, the girl Vimaladattā replied to the brahmin in verse:
"If I should fall into an evil realm, neither my parents, nor my kinsmen,
nor my wealth and treasures, nor even my brave and strong men could save me;
except for that assembly of majestic power, who else could rescue me?"
"Out of reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, I would sacrifice my body and my life;
yet apart from the Honored Triple Gem, there is no other path upon which I can rely.
At that time, the brahmin asked the girl Vimaladattā:
“You have never seen the Buddha or the Saṅgha, nor have you ever heard the Dharma; by what means do you possess such faith?
The girl Vimaladattā replied to the brahmin:

“Seven days after my birth, while I was on a high palace atop a golden-legged couch, I saw five hundred devaputras flying through the air, praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha with immeasurable merit. At that time, I heard them.”
Furthermore, there was a certain devaputra who had never seen the Buddha, heard the Dharma, or beheld the Saṃgha;
he asked the other devaputras, "What is the Buddha like?"
Those devaputras, knowing my sincere heart and in order to answer the question posed by one devaputra and to inspire joy in me, spoke these verses:
“His hair is deep blue-black, pure and curling to the right;
The Buddha’s face is like the full moon, with the color of a hundred-petaled lotus.”
The hair-tufts are like white jade or snow, curling to the right for all to behold with joy;
black bees swarm around blue lotuses, and his eyebrows and eyes are likewise.
His jaw is like that of a lion, and the blinking of his eyes is like that of a bull-king.
His lips are like the *bimba* fruit; his teeth are white, dense, and even.
His gait is like that of a swan; his tongue is broad and covers his face.
His voice is exceedingly pure and clear; all who hear it rejoice.
The cries of peacocks, geese, and swans; A sound like a lapis lazuli lute;
The chiming of the *kiṃnara* hosts’ bells; The voice of the *kalaviṅka*, The song of the *kuṇāla* bird, And the calls of the *jīvaṃjīvaka* and *kukila*.
And with various kinds of music, the Buddha’s voice is likewise.
His roar is like that of a lion; it can shatter all rival doctrines, remove all defilements and afflictions, and through truthful speech, sever all views.
Abiding amidst the great assembly, he is able to exhaust all questions and doubts;
being unerring and gentle, he gladdens the hearts of the multitude.
Having departed from the two extremes, he correctly teaches the Middle Way.
He constantly speaks words that are pleasing to the mind; all who hear his voice rejoice.
His speech is free from deceit or crookedness, and each listener gains understanding according to their own capacity.
The Buddha’s words are adorned with wisdom, like a garland of various exquisite flowers.
His neck is rounded and his arms are long and straight; his palms are level with the mark of the wheel clearly pure;
his fingers are slender, long, and exquisite; his nails have the color of red copper.
The Buddha’s body is firm, level, and full; his waist is slender with the physique of a lion.
The private parts are deep-seated, even, and perfectly rounded; his male organ is concealed as that of a horse-king.
His body is like a mountain of gold, with a single hair growing from each pore, curling to the right and pointing upward; he is comparable to a dragon-elephant.
"The thighs are fleshy and the calves are like those of a deer; the ankles are level and the bones are like interlocking hooks;
the soles of the feet are level, displaying the mark of the wheel, complete with its thousand spokes clearly defined.
"O Brahmin! [he said.]
At that time, the sons of the gods in the void praised the Tathāgata for these matters.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, who has delivered all beings from existence to the further shore and attained great compassion, is like a great king of physicians who protects all sentient beings.
Untainted by hatred or love, like a lotus in the water;
I have merely praised a small fraction of the World-Honored One’s merits, O Brahmin!

"Since I was born only seven days ago and heard of such true merits of the World-Honored One, from that time forth I have never known sleep, nor have I ever experienced thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, or thoughts of harm."

From that time forth, I have been entirely devoid of any affection or attachment toward my parents, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen; toward wealth, jewels, necklaces, and clothing; toward cities, gardens, and groves; and even toward my own body and life—except for mindfulness of the Buddha.
"Wherever the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, you shall go with focused mind to listen and receive it all in its entirety; whether in letter or in meaning, you shall not lose a single word, O Brahmin!"
Day and night, I have never failed to see the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
O Brahmin! I gaze upon the Buddhas without weariness, listen to the Dharma without satiety, and serve the assembly without fatigue.
At that time, the daughter Vimaladattā praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha in these various ways.
Then, five hundred people, including the Brahmin Brahmādeva, all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then the girl Vimaladattā descended from her carriage and proceeded on foot toward the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Having arrived, she prostrated herself at their feet with all her head; then, with a mind of reverence and respect, she approached the venerable Śāriputra.
Having arrived, she stood before him and said to Śāriputra:
"I am a woman; my wisdom is slight and shallow, I have many afflictions, and I am often heedless, delighting in base matters and led astray by improper reflection."
Excellent, Venerable Śāriputra!
Out of compassion for me, you have expounded this subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Having heard it, I shall derive long-lasting benefit and increasing peace and happiness throughout the night.
Just as this discussion began, King Prasenajit arrived at that place.
Having heard what was being said, the king addressed the girl Vimaladattā, saying:
"You possess every happiness and lack nothing; why do you have such a sorrowful countenance, neither sleeping nor finding joy in worldly pleasures?"
Then King Prasenajit spoke these verses for his daughter:
“Resplendent as a celestial maiden, Having bathed, anointed with fragrant unguents,
and arrayed in garments and necklaces, Why do you grieve and find no sleep?”
The country is wealthy with abundant treasures, and your parents have attained freedom;
what is there that is not delightful, that you do not sleep?
You gladden the hearts of your many kinsmen, and all people look toward you with respect and hope.
I am adorned in various ways; why do you not find joy?
What have you seen or heard that causes you to harbor such sorrow and grief?
How excellent! What is your wish?
“Tell me of this matter.
Then the girl Vimaladattā replied to her father, the king, in verse:
“The King does not perceive within his own house The frailty of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.”
Dwelling in the world is like a phantom dancer; human life does not pause for a moment.
Who could sleep after drinking poison?
Who could find joy while dwelling in death?
Having fallen from a cliff, what hope is there for life?
Such is the nature of all worldly phenomena. Like a person caught among snakes, how could there be sleep or desire?
The four great elements are like venomous snakes; how can there be a heart of joy?
Surrounded by all manner of enemies, like one who is starving, how can there be pleasure?
Being a captive in the land of enemies, O Father King, how can there be joy?
"Since seeing the World-Honored One, I have resolved to attain Buddhahood.
O King, I have never heard of such a thing: That a Bodhisattva would ever be heedless for even a moment.
Chapter Two: On the Śrāvakas At that time, the girl Vimaladattā said to Śāriputra:
“Venerable Sir!
I wish to ask a few questions; I pray that you will explain them for me out of compassion.
The World-Honored One has declared that you are the foremost among those possessed of wisdom.”
Is this wisdom conditioned or unconditioned?
If it were conditioned,
it would be deceptive and not a real dharma.
If it were unconditioned, then as an unconditioned dharma it would have no arising; and for a dharma that has no arising, there is no origination.
Because there is no origination, Great Virtue’s wisdom would be non-existent.
Śāriputra then remained silent.
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana said to Śāriputra,
"Venerable One!..."
"Why did you not answer the question posed by the girl Vimaladatta?
Śāriputra replied to Maudgalyāyana, "This girl did not ask about conditioned phenomena; she asked about the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)."
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no verbal expression; therefore, it cannot be answered with words.
Then, the girl Vimaladattā said to Maudgalyāyana, "The World-Honored One has prophesied that you, Great Virtue, are the foremost among those possessed of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*)."
When the Venerable One rides upon the divine foot (ṛddhipāda), does he conceive the notion of sentient beings,
or does he conceive the notion of dharmas?
If he dwells in the notion of sentient beings, then since sentient beings have no reality, those divine feet likewise have no reality.

"If one dwells in the perception of dharmas, dharmas are without change; if there is no change, then there is nothing to be attained; if there is nothing to be attained, then there is no discrimination.
Thereupon, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana remained silent.
Mahākāśyapa said to Maudgalyāyana: "Venerable one,
why do you not answer the questions posed by the maiden Vimaladattā?"
Maudgalyāyana said: "This woman did not ask about the analytical supernormal powers (*ṛddhivibhūti*).
The awakening (*bodhi*) of all Tathāgatas is unconditioned and non-conceptual; it is inexpressible."
Then the girl Vimaladattā said to Mahākāśyapa, “The World-Honored One has declared that you, Great Virtue, are the foremost among those who practice *dhūta* austerities.

Furthermore, Great Virtue, out of compassion for sentient beings, you enter the eight liberations before receiving offerings; even when receiving the gift of another for a single thought-moment, do you repay them with your body?”
Is it through the mind that one repays?

If it were through the body, the nature of the body is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), no different from grass, trees, walls, tiles, or rubble; therefore, it cannot necessarily repay the kindness of a benefactor.
If one seeks to repay with the mind, the mind does not remain still for even a single thought-moment, and thus it cannot repay either.
If one sets aside both body and mind, that is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If it is the unconditioned dharma, who is there to repay?
Mahākāśyapa remained silent. The Venerable Subhūti said to Mahākāśyapa:
"Why do you not answer the question posed by the girl Vimaladattā?"
Mahākāśyapa replied to Subhūti: "The question asked by this woman concerns the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of phenomena.
This principle cannot be proclaimed or answered through words."
Then the girl Vimaladattā said to Subhūti:
"The World-Honored One has declared that you, Great Virtue, are the foremost among those who dwell in non-contention (*araṇa*).
Does this practice of non-contention enter into the realm of existence?"
Does one enter into suchness?
If one enters into suchness, suchness is not a characteristic of arising, nor is it a characteristic of cessation.

That which is neither a characteristic of arising nor a characteristic of cessation is equality. That which is equality is suchness. That which is suchness is non-action. That which is non-action is beyond verbal expression. That which is beyond verbal expression is inconceivable. That which is inconceivable cannot be proclaimed.
"If there were such a thing as 'having a nature,' then having a nature would be deceptive.
If it were deceptive, it would not be the sphere of activity of the Noble Ones.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti remained silent.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Subhūti:
"Why do you not answer the questions posed by the woman Vimaladattā? Subhūti replied to Pūrṇa:
"It would be improper for me to provide an answer; silence alone is my preferred state.
The question this woman has asked concerns the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); were there to be any verbal expression, it would give rise to faults."
“The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is beyond verbal expression;
this is the practice free from contention. Then the girl Vimaladattā said to Pūrṇa:
“The World-Honored One has prophesied that the Venerable One is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.”
When teaching the Dharma, do you teach that dharmas have objective referents,
or that dharmas lack objective referents?
If you teach that dharmas have objective referents, then you are the same as ordinary worldlings.
Why is this? Because ordinary people speak of the existence of objective realms; therefore, Venerable Sir, you do not depart from the dharmas of ordinary people.
If there were no objective realms, then nothing would exist at all.
"If there is nothing at all, how can one be called the foremost among those who preach the Dharma?
Pūrṇa then remained silent. The Venerable Revata said to Pūrṇa:
"Venerable sir!
Why do you not answer the question posed by the girl Vimaladattā? Pūrṇa replied to Revata:
"This girl does not ask about the conditioned, but asks about the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Within the ultimate truth, there is no verbal expression; therefore, there is no principle by which an answer can be given.
Then, the girl Vimaladattā said to Revata:
“The Blessed One has declared the Venerable One to be the foremost among those who practice meditation.
When the Venerable One meditates, does he rely on a state of consciousness or a state devoid of consciousness?”
If one enters dhyāna based on the mind, and the mind is like an illusion or a magical transformation—unreal—then this concentration is likewise unreal.
If one were to enter dhyāna without a mind, then all external phenomena, such as grasses, trees, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, should also be able to attain dhyāna.
"Why is this? Because they are equally without mind.
Thereupon, the Venerable Revata remained silent.
The Venerable Aniruddha said to Revata,
"Why did you not answer the questions posed by the maiden Vimaladattā? Revata replied to Aniruddha:
"What this girl has asked regarding the sphere of practice of the Buddhas is not something that can be answered by a śrāvaka.
Then the girl Vimaladattā said,
"Is there a difference between the Dharma of the Buddhas and the Dharma of the śrāvakas?"
If there were difference, would the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) be twofold?

All noble ones (ārya) practice the unconditioned, and the nature of the unconditioned is that there is no arising. If there is no arising, then there is no duality; if there is no duality, then it is suchness (tathatā).
"Since suchness is non-dual, for what reason, Venerable Revata, have you made this statement?
Then the girl Vimaladattā said to Aniruddha:
"The World-Honored One has declared that the Venerable One is the foremost among gods and humans regarding the divine eye."
"Venerable sir, as for that which is seen by the divine eye, does it exist as a thing or not?
If one sees it as existing, that is the view of permanence; if one sees it as non-existent, that is the view of annihilation. To be free from these two extremes is to be without views."
The Venerable Aniruddha remained silent.
The Venerable Ānanda said to Aniruddha,
"Why do you not answer the question asked by the girl Vimaladattā?"
Aniruddha replied to Ānanda:
“The question asked by this girl concerns the destruction of conventional designations; therefore, it cannot be answered by means of conventional designations.
Then the girl Vimaladattā said to Ānanda:
“The World-Honored One has declared that the Venerable One is the foremost among those of great learning.
Is this Dharma of great learning the ultimate reality,
or is it merely words?”
If it were a real meaning, that meaning would be inexpressible.
If a dharma cannot be expressed, then it is not known by the auditory consciousness.
If it is not known by the auditory consciousness, it furthermore cannot be expressed.
If one relies on the literal text, then the World-Honored One has said that one should rely on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on the literal text.
Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda would neither be "one of great learning" (*bahuśruta*) nor one who possesses the definitive meaning.
The Venerable Ānanda remained silent.
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"Why do you not answer the question posed by the girl Vimaladattā?"
Ānanda said: “The questions asked by this woman concern the much-heard [scriptures] that are free from words; these cannot be answered with sounds.
She asks about equanimity; equanimity is not the mind, for it is free from the characteristics of the mind.”
"This is not the dharma of those on the stage of training; how could I possibly answer?
This is the dharma of the Tathāgatas, the Dharma Kings, who have reached the further shore.
Chapter 3: The Bodhisattva Chapter At that time, the girl Vimaladattā addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
“The World-Honored One has declared you to be the foremost among bodhisattvas who possess profound understanding.
Is it because the twelve links of dependent origination are profoundly deep that you are so,
or is it because the ultimate truth is profoundly deep?”
If one considers the twelve links of dependent origination to be profound, there is no sentient being who can bring about the profundity of the twelve links of dependent origination. Why is this?

Because the twelve links of dependent origination neither come nor go; they are not known by visual consciousness, nor are they known by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness. Within this, the twelve links of dependent origination are not conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"If one considers the ultimate depth to be deep, then that ultimate depth is not deep, nor is there anyone who attains ultimate depth.
Mañjuśrī replied to the girl Vimaladattā:
"It is deep because the limit of beginning is deep."
The girl Vimaladattā asked Mañjuśrī,
“Since the beginning limit is not a limit, therefore your knowing is also not knowing.
Mañjuśrī replied to the girl Vimaladattā:
"Because one attains non-attainment through non-knowing, it is called the 'initial limit'.
The girl Vimaladatta asked Mañjuśrī, "Within non-attainment there is no portion of speech; transcending the path of language, there is nothing that can be said."
Mañjuśrī replied to the girl Vimaladattā,
“It is merely spoken by means of conventional words.
The girl Vimaladattā said to Mañjuśrī:
“The awakening of the Buddhas transcends words, phrases, and verbal expression; therefore, awakening is ineffable.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā addressed the bodhisattva Asangadarśana, saying:
“O son of good family, you have said this:”

I thought to myself: "I shall go to the city of Śrāvastī, wishing that all sentient beings within the city who are destined to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* shall see whatever objects they behold as entirely the image of the Tathāgata, and further, that they shall become certain of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"When one sees the Tathāgata, does one contemplate him as the form-body (rūpakāya), or does one contemplate him by means of the dharma-body (dharmakāya)?

If one contemplates him by means of the form-body, then one does not see the Buddha. As the World-Honored One has said: 'If one sees my form-body or hears my voice, that person possesses extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) and does not truly see me.'"
If one speaks in terms of the Dharma-body, the Dharma-body cannot be seen. Why is this?
Because the Dharma-body is free from seeing and hearing and cannot be grasped; therefore, it cannot be seen or heard.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladarśana remained silent.
The Bodhisattva Ratnākāra addressed the Bodhisattva Vimaladarśana, saying:
“O son of good family!
"Why did he not answer the questions posed by the girl Vimaladattā?
The Bodhisattva Amohadarśana replied:
"The girl Vimaladattā asked about the dharma of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This dharma of non-nature is inexpressible; therefore, he did not answer."
The girl Vimaladattā said, “Noble son!
I do not ask about dharmas that lack intrinsic nature, for dharmas that lack intrinsic nature cannot be questioned.”
"Once you have studied this, your answers will be without obstruction.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā said to the bodhisattva Ratnaketu, "Noble son!..."

You said: "I shall form this thought: 'Upon arriving in the city of Śrāvastī, may all the lineages, households, and treasuries within the city produce and bring forth the seven precious jewels in their full abundance.'"
"In your mind as you give these jewels, is there attachment or is there no attachment?
If there is attachment, then you are the same as ordinary, ignorant people."
Why is this? It is because ordinary beings possess attachment.
If there were no attachment, then within the state of non-attachment, there would be no giving of jewels.
Then the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa remained silent.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā said to the Bodhisattva Vigata-durgati: "Noble son!
You said: "I made this thought:

'I shall go to the city of Śrāvastī, and I vow that if there are any sentient beings within the city who are destined to fall into the evil realms, may they all experience their retribution lightly in this present life and be swiftly liberated from suffering.'"
“The Tathāgata has said that karma is inconceivable; can this inconceivable karma be swiftly severed?
If it could be severed, it would contradict what the Tathāgata has taught.”
If you do not know [the nature of things], how can you lightly accept them and swiftly sever [attachment]?
If you are able to sever them, then among these phenomena that have no master, you yourself would be the master.
If you are able to sever them, you should likewise be able to not sever them.
The Bodhisattva Virāgagati replied to the girl Vimaladattā, “By the power of my vows,
I am able to cause [the karma] to be experienced lightly and swiftly severed.
The girl Vimaladattā then asked the Bodhisattva Virāgagati:
“Good son! The suchness-nature of all phenomena cannot be received through the power of aspiration.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Free from Evil Destinies remained silent.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā said to the bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin: "Noble son!
You said:..."
"I should form this thought: 'May all sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī completely eliminate the five hindrances.
You should form this thought:
'Having entered this samādhi, I shall enable sentient beings not to be obscured by the five hindrances.'"
"In this meditative absorption, is one's own self sovereign,
or is another sovereign?
If it is one's own self that is sovereign, there is no means by which it could reach that [other]."
Since all phenomena have no one who reaches them, how can you enter meditative concentration to remove the five hindrances for others?
If another were autonomous, you could not benefit them.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin replied to the girl Vimaladattā:
"This practice has loving-kindness as its foremost principle.
The girl Vimaladattā then asked the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin:
"All Buddhas practice acts of loving-kindness. Good son!
Is there any Buddha who, because of sentient beings, does not take the five hindrances as an affliction?"
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin remained silent.
Then the girl Vimaladattā said to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, “Noble son!

You said: "I shall form this thought: 'May the sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī who are imprisoned and confined quickly obtain liberation; may those facing death immediately find their lives saved; and may those who are terrified immediately attain fearlessness.'"
Now, as for what is called "fear," does it involve grasping or not?
If it involves grasping, then ordinary foolish people also possess grasping; therefore, that cannot be the case.
"If there is no grasping, then there is nothing to bestow; within the dharma of non-bestowal, how could there be any removal?
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva then remained silent.
Prajñābhadraka Bodhisattva said to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
“Good son! Why do you not answer the question posed by the daughter Vimaladattā?
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said:
"This girl does not inquire about the dharma of arising and ceasing; therefore, it is not possible to answer her.
The girl Vimaladattā asked Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
"Is there such a question as one concerning neither arising nor ceasing?"
Avalokiteśvara replied to the girl Vimaladattā:
"Within that which is neither born nor extinguished, there are no letters, words, or speech.
The girl Vimaladattā then asked Avalokiteśvara:
“Those of wisdom provisionally employ words regarding that which is wordless, yet they do not cling to words.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unimpeded; therefore, the wise are not obstructed by words.”
Then the girl Vimaladattā said to the bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin: "Noble son,
you said:..."
"I should form this thought: 'May all sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī who see me attain eloquence, so that they may engage in mutual dialogue with one another using exquisite verses.'"
"Good son! Does this eloquence of yours that you have bestowed arise from *vitarka* (applied thought)?
If it arises from *vitarka*, then since all conditioned phenomena arise from *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought), it is therefore not tranquil."
"If that which arises from craving were to give, then the gift would be empty.
Bodhisattva Prajñābhadrā replied to the girl Vimaladattā:
"This was my first aspiration when I initially resolved upon bodhicitta: 'May all who see me attain eloquence, so that we may question and answer one another with sublime verses.'"
Then the girl Vimaladattā asked the bodhisattva Viśeṣamati:
“Noble son, do you yourself now possess the aspiration that has set forth for awakening?”
"If it already exists, that would be the view of eternalism; if it does not exist now, it cannot be given to others. Therefore, one's vow would be in vain.
At these words, Bianyan became silent.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā said to the bodhisattva Amoghadarśin: "Noble son!
You have said:..."

"I formed this thought: 'I vow that if there are any sentient beings within the city of Śrāvastī who see me, they may attain vision free from delusion and become certain of attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"Is this bodhi existent, or is it non-existent? If it were existent,
it would be a grasping at extremes regarding conditioned bodhi."
"If it were non-existent, it would be false and one would fall into an extreme view.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vimaladarśana replied to the girl Vimaladattā: "This bodhi is called wisdom."
The girl Vimaladattā asked the bodhisattva Amoghadarśin:
"Is this wisdom called 'arising' or is it 'non-arising'?"
If it is called "arising," then it is not that which is produced by wholesome and compliant reflection; it is conditioned knowledge, known only by the foolish and ignorant.
If it is called "non-arising," then within non-arising there is nothing at all.

If there is nothing that exists, then there is no conceptual differentiation; there is no conceptual differentiation among the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the awakening (bodhi) of the Tathāgatas.
Foolish ordinary people differentiate awakening, but those with wisdom do not differentiate it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avidyādṛṣṭi remained silent.
Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the venerable śrāvakas and the great bodhisattvas, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"We should return; there is no need for us to enter the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
Why is this? What the girl Vimaladattā has spoken is itself the Dharma-food of the wise."
"Today we delight in the food of the Dharma; we have no need for morsel-food.
The girl Vimaladattā asked Subhūti, "If it is said that all dharmas are neither superior nor inferior, what is there to be sought within these dharmas for which one would go on alms-round?"
"Venerable sir!
The non-proliferation of conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*) is the practice of a bhikṣu; one should not delight in proliferation.
This is the dharma that is without support (*anāśrita*); it is not the practice of those who rely [on supports]."
“The conduct of the noble ones is without regression.

At that time, the eight great śrāvakas, the eight great bodhisattvas, five hundred brahmins including Brahmā, the girl Vimaladattā, King Prasenajit, and the entire great assembly together went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The maiden Vimaladattā circumambulated him seven times separately, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood with palms joined, questioning the Buddha in verse:
“I ask the Peerless Honored One, The Worthy One of Immeasurable Renown.”
Bestowing the joy of ambrosia upon all beings, how does a Bodhisattva practice?
How does he abide beneath the tree of enlightenment, shattering Māra and subduing his weary enemies?
How does he cause the heavens and earth to tremble, as well as the kings of mountains and the forest thickets?
How does one emit radiant light, And manifest immeasurable renown?
I pray that the World-Honored One of Great Compassion Will explain the conduct corresponding to awakening.
How does one attain dhāraṇī, And the wondrous voice of the Tathāgata?
How can one cultivate and maintain The pure, wondrous, and supreme concentration?
How can practitioners Attain the power of the divine feet?
I now entreat the World-Honored One To explain the true practice of these people.
How does one attain single-minded mindfulness and a firm, resolute heart?
How does one attain responsive eloquence, perfected in its subtle refinement?
How does one attain accordance with principle, encompassing all meanings in their full perfection?
He eloquently expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma; the wise have no obstructions.
How does one delight in giving and wisdom, in pure precepts and patience, in skillful diligence and meditative concentration, and how does wisdom illuminate the world?
How does one recollect past lives? How does one see with the clear and luminous divine eye?
How does one possess the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, and the supernormal power to traverse all buddha-fields?
How is it that one does not dwell in a womb, but is born through transformation within a lotus?
Why do you constantly stand before all Buddhas to preach the Dharma of emptiness and non-self?
How do you treat enemies and kin as equals, severing both craving and defilement,
with a will and conduct free from high or low, just like wind and earth?
Gain and loss, defamation and fame, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure—
how does one relinquish these eight worldly dharmas and move through the world like the sun?
How does one avoid flattery and contention, eliminate the self, and abandon arrogance?
In the state of meditative concentration within a secluded place, why does the wise one delight in the true meaning?
Why is there no fondness for wife, children, and wealth?
Why do those who practice the path take pleasure in quiet and solitary places?
How is it like a bird in flight? And how is it like the single horn of a *kiṃnara*?
How does one delight in the True Dharma, and how does one delight in a joyful mind?
How do those who possess wisdom contemplate earth, water, fire, and wind?
Without wavering or discrimination, dwelling in dhyāna like space,
one does not engage in unrighteous conduct nor take pleasure in observing the conduct of others;
rather than abandoning body or life, one would never forsake the Dharma.
How can one conceive of awakening as being like the World-Honored One?
Having conceived of the World-Honored One, how can one give rise to the vow for awakening?
How can one obtain a pure land and a pure saṃgha?
The wise attain long life; by chanting their names, one gains peace and happiness.
Through skillful means they reach the further shore, yet though they have seen the Truth, they do not realize final extinction.
Able to deliver immeasurable multitudes, how can they encourage others to joyfully practice roots of goodness?
How does one attain a handsome appearance, as well as birth through transformation;
how does one possess great wisdom and abundant wealth, and come to know the minds of sentient beings?
How does one recollect past lives and constantly meet with all the Buddhas?
Throughout thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, how can one never be born in difficult places?
How does one obtain the excellent marks and the thirty-two primary characteristics?
How does one attain skillful eloquence and the analytical eloquence of a Buddha?
How does one cultivate the pure land and bring about a community of bhikṣus,
so that by following wherever one’s wishes and joys lie, one may be born there?
What practices must a leader perform to attain a beautiful form and a renowned name?
Having attained power through diligence and the like, how can one remain unshakable?
How can one be free from hesitation and be able to practice the bodhisattva path,
having abandoned all agitation and regret, and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
Within the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, how may one attain supreme excellence?
One would rather sacrifice their own body and life than ever slander the Dharma.
The World-Honored One knows all—of this world and the future.
"I pray that the World-Honored One of Great Wisdom will next explain the conduct of Bodhisattvas.
Chapter Four: On the Conduct of Bodhisattvas At that time, the World-Honored One praised the girl Vimaladatta, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

For the sake of establishing the great peace, happiness, and benefit of all sentient beings, and out of compassion for the gods and humans of the world, you have questioned the Tathāgata regarding such conduct of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā and the entire great assembly all exclaimed, "Excellent!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke for him:
"A bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas is able to destroy all māras."
What are these four? They are:

not giving rise to resentment or envy toward the gains and offerings of others; refraining from divisive speech; exhorting many sentient beings to plant roots of goodness; and generating a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings.
“Vimaladattā! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the power to destroy all māras.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Without giving rise to thoughts of malice or envy, nor engaging in divisive speech,
one can teach many sentient beings to plant the roots and seeds of wholesome dharmas;
one can cultivate a vast mind of loving-kindness that extends universally throughout the ten directions."
One who practices this conduct well is able to crush all Māras and enemies.
"Stainless Giver, Daughter!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they can emit light that transcends immeasurable buddha-fields."
What are the four? They are:

being able to give the light of lamps; protecting and upholding the True Dharma when the Dharma is about to perish; being able to go to the places where beings are negligent or fallen into difficult circumstances to preach the Dharma for them; and being able to offer precious ornaments and necklaces to the Buddha’s stūpas and temples.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the ability to emit light that transcends the lands of the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one can give lamps, And protect the Dharma during the final age of the Dharma,"
Guiding others and difficult to be negligent, they offer precious ornaments to the Buddha temples;
for this reason, these Bodhisattvas are able to emit pure light that passes through immeasurable Buddha-lands, its illumination reaching to boundless horizons.
"Those who are touched by this light all attain peace and happiness, and immediately give rise to the unsurpassed resolve.
'Stainless Bestower of Alms!
If a bodhisattva can accomplish four dharmas, they will be able to cause immeasurable and boundless buddha-fields to tremble.'"
What are these four? They are:

practicing according to what has been taught; attaining profound dharmakṣānti; firmly upholding wholesome dharmas; and transforming immeasurable sentient beings so that they practice for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the ability to shake immeasurable and boundless buddha-fields.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Practicing according to what has been taught, Skillfully understanding the patience regarding profound dharmas,"
Desiring to attain pure and white dharmas, Firmly maintaining all sublime practices,
Able to teach immeasurable multitudes To give rise to the bodhicitta—
One who practices these four dharmas Can shake immeasurable lands.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain dhāraṇī. What are these four?

They are able to bestow various pure and wonderful necessities; they give whatever is required to adorn the female attendants; they constantly praise all Tathāgatas with various dharmas; and they draw near to and extensively cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā.
"This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of four dharmas by which one attains all dhāraṇīs.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one practices various kinds of giving, One can attain dhāraṇīs."
Adorned with beautiful maidens, they can fully satisfy all their needs at will;
they constantly praise the Tathāgata and cultivate true wisdom, as permitted by the World-Honored One.
By means of these four matters, one immediately attains dhāraṇī;
throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, what has been heard will never be forgotten,
and all that is spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions can be fully received and remembered.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to attain samādhi.
What are these four?
Having great weariness toward birth and death, always delighting in secluded and quiet places, constantly exerting diligent effort, and being well able to accomplish all tasks undertaken—
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can attain samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having abandoned all states of existence, He wanders alone like a *kiṃnara*.
The son of good family practices with diligence, And accomplishes the deeds he has undertaken."
The wise are able to accomplish these four supreme and wondrous dharmas;
they draw near to bodhi and seek all most excellent teachings.
Those who possess a tranquil mind are able to attain all samādhis.
"Awakening to supreme bodhi is the sphere of practice of all Buddhas.
Daughter of Vimaladattā!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to attain the bases of psychic power."
What are the four?
Because the body is light, because the mind is light, because there is no dependence upon any phenomena, and because one experiences the four elements as the element of space.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the power of the divine feet.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The body and mind are likewise light; The wise do not cling to dharmas."
Perceiving these four elements as equal to the realm of space,
one who possesses these four dharmas can attain the power of the divine feet;
in a single thought-moment, they pass through billions of lands and make offerings to that many Buddhas.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain exquisite and upright beauty. What are these four?

They eliminate all filth and refuse to give way to anger; they delight in purifying Buddhist stupas and temples, providing exquisite ornaments as offerings; they abide in dignified deportment and uphold the precepts, always being the first to inquire with kind words; they do not disparage those who preach the Dharma, but always maintain the perception of them as the World-Honored One.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves exquisite and sublime physical beauty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Without angering or vexing others, One departs from and abandons coarse and defiled conduct."
Sweeping and sprinkling the temple of the World-Honored One, reverently offering precious ornaments,
always maintaining pure precepts, and first offering greetings when setting forth the resolve;
being unhindered toward the Dharma Master, one regards him with a mind of reverence as toward the World-Honored One.
"One who practices these four wholesome deeds is called a courageous and steadfast person;
most excellent and supreme, those who see them cannot help but rejoice. Girl Vimaladatta!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to attain birth by transformation. What are these four?

Carving and sculpting lotus flowers and images of seated Buddhas; and with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as well as various other kinds of diverse and exquisite flowers, filling their cupped hands to scatter them over the Tathāgatas and all their stūpas and shrines.
One aspires to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, constantly practicing harmony and respect without disparaging the faults of others;
one plants roots of goodness for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to many sentient beings so that they may be liberated from the suffering and affliction of birth and death;
and one vows to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves birth through transformation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Carving flowers upon a seated image, Making offerings of various kinds of flowers,"
Benefiting others without afflicting the multitude, manifesting birth in the buddha-fields of all Buddhas,
constantly making great vows to deliver sentient beings of the ten directions—
by means of these four sublime practices, one is always born in the buddha-fields of all Buddhas.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain great wealth. What are these four?

He does not reject supplicants; he feels no attachment or stinginess toward the objects he gives away; he constantly wishes that all sentient beings may obtain abundant wealth and treasures; and he abandons all views to accord with right faith.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves great wealth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"With a mind of giving free from obstruction, Without stinginess regarding wealth,"
Having faith and understanding in all Buddha-dharmas, one obtains wealth and riches in every birth;
having faith and understanding free from flattery and envy, one does not litigate over the faults of others;
with a single-minded and exclusive faith, for this reason one acquires treasures and jewels.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain great wisdom. What are these four?

One does not give rise to hatred or envy toward the teachings of others; one explains the methods for removing faults so that there is no doubt or regret; one encourages those who are diligent in their efforts so as not to let them falter; and one personally always delights in frequently cultivating the dharma of emptiness.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves great wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Not being envious of the true Dharma, Teaching others to eliminate doubt and regret..."
Constantly leading sentient beings, they cultivate the various empty practices of the Buddhas.
The wise delight in this Dharma, attaining wisdom and a renowned reputation;
skillfully understanding the words of all Buddhas, they swiftly become Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will remember their past lives. What are these four?
For those who have forgotten or lost what they have studied and recited, he provides them with mindfulness and explains what they have forgotten;
he constantly produces pleasant and agreeable sounds that people delight to hear;
and he always practices the gift of Dharma without fail, for the sake of liberating beings from birth and death and leading them toward Nirvana.
"I vow that I shall enter the skillful means of dhyāna like Sudhana.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva is able to recollect past lives.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Causing those who have forgotten to remember, Constantly producing sounds that please the mind,
Preaching the Dharma without weariness, And constantly cultivating the characteristics of meditative concentration—
By means of these four dharmas, All shall attain the knowledge of past lives."
They can remember immeasurable eons and swiftly awaken to the sphere of the Buddhas' conduct.
"Stainless Bestower of Alms!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will always encounter all Buddhas."
What are these four? They are:

rather than sacrificing one's body and life, not to slander the Dharma; rather than sacrificing one's body and life, not to revile bodhisattvas; rather than sacrificing one's body and life, not to associate with evil friends; and to recollect all Buddhas without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva always encounters all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Not slandering awakening, Nor disparaging bodhisattvas,"
Delighting in leaving behind evil associates, One should mindfully contemplate all Buddhas without weariness.
Practicing this conduct of great virtue, One shall encounter all Buddhas;
Until the moment of attaining perfect enlightenment, One will always be in the company of the Buddhas.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will obtain a body endowed with the thirty-two marks. What are these four?
They gathered various precious jewels and scattered them over the Buddha’s stūpas and temples;
they anointed the bases and pedestals of the stūpas with various kinds of fragrant oils;
they adorned the stūpas and temples with diverse flower garlands and made offerings with all manner of musical performances.
"Always attending upon the worthy and holy ones without ever departing from them—
this is the fourth dharma by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Collecting jewels to scatter over stupas and temples, And further anointing them with fragrant oils;
With various flowers and manifold music, Providing service to suit the Worthy and Holy Ones.
His body is adorned with the complete marks, Elegant, exquisite, and most exceptionally beautiful."
By this, one attains the various marks, thereby adorning the Honored One among Men. "Stainless Giver!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they attain the eighty secondary signs."
What are these four? They are:

stripping off various exquisite garments to spread as a Dharma seat; serving all beings without ever becoming weary; approaching the place where the Dharma is taught without any thought of superior debate, but regarding the assembly with reverence as if they were the World-Honored One; and exhorting many sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the eighty minor marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Spreading seats with various exquisite garments, Making offerings without weariness,"
Do not compete with those who uphold the Dharma, but exhort the multitude to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind.
Those able to practice this Dharma will swiftly attain the various marks of excellence;
by practicing what the Bodhisattvas have personally cultivated, they shall be endowed with the eighty minor characteristics.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain eloquence that is well-suited. What are these four?
They uphold and draw near to the Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas;
they recite the *Tri-skandhaka-sūtra* during the six periods of day and night;
and although the awakening of all buddhas—being neither born nor extinguished—is difficult for the world to believe, they are nonetheless able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it.
He extensively explains them to others so that they may attain joy, being without attachment even to his own body or life.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves skillful and appropriate eloquence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Upholding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, Valiantly reciting the three aggregates,
Pursuing the world’s signs of non-arising, Teaching with skillful means to bring joy,
Having no attachment to body or life, One upholds the True Dharma of the Ten Powers.”
Acting without doubt, one attains the most supreme and excellent enlightenment.
By practicing this profound Dharma, one is able to obtain responsive eloquence;
it is like a garland of various flowers, which gods and humans delight to behold.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain a pure buddha-field. What are these four?
Because they are free from envy, because they possess an impartial mind, because they protect the practice of awakening, and because they do not associate with the fourfold assembly—
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves a pure land.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Do not envy others; Seeing them obtain gain, rejoice.
With an impartial mind, practice great compassion, Transforming the multitudes without attachment."
“Practicing these four immeasurables, the wise one guards them well;
they will attain a pure land without difficulty and swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed path.
Daughter Without Stain!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will obtain a pure assembly. What are these four?

They do not covet the followers of others; they gather those who are discordant and cause them to reconcile; they provide for the needs of those who study and recite; and they abandon divisive speech.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves a pure assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"He never hopes for others' assemblies; He brings together those who have separated."
Providing for the needs of those in training, And not alienating sentient beings—
One who can practice these four things Will obtain a pure assembly.
For the sake of such a pure assembly, One would not abandon them even through extreme suffering.
“Vimaladattā! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be born in whatever buddha-field they have vowed to attain, in accordance with their aspiration.
What are these four?
One does not give rise to resentment or envy regarding the reputation, gain, or offerings of others;
one cultivates the six pāramitās with single-minded devotion;
and one regards all bodhisattvas as the World-Honored One.

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, one constantly maintains equanimous contemplation, never for the sake of gain, reputation, flattery, or false praise.
This is the fourth dharma by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the fulfillment of their vow to be reborn in whichever buddha-field they desire.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Without begrudging the fame and profit of others, seeking the pure six perfections,
regarding Bodhisattvas as equal to the Honored One, one shall never flatterously seek renown.”
“The Bodhisattva who practices this goodness can see the worlds of the ten directions;
according to whatever their heart desires, they shall immediately be born therein.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall practice the bodhisattva conduct as it has been taught.

If, regarding the bodhisattva conduct taught by the World-Honored One, one does not practice even a single dharma within this teaching, then one would be deceiving all the Buddhas currently preaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions.”
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana said to the girl Vimaladattā, “You dare to let out a great lion’s roar before the Buddha; do you not know the difficult practices of a bodhisattva?”
"One shall never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while in a female body.
At that time, the girl Vimaladattā replied to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:

"I now make this vow of truth before the Buddha: if in a future age I shall certainly attain Buddhahood as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to a Buddha, World-Honored One, and Teacher of Gods and Humans, by virtue of this vow of truth, may this trichiliocosm tremble in six ways, without causing any affliction or disturbance to sentient beings."

"As the World-Honored One has taught regarding the practices of all bodhisattvas, may I practice them throughout my entire life. By this true vow, may a rain of various celestial flowers fall from the void, may hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resound without being struck, and may I transform this female body into that of sixteen youths."

After the maiden Vimaladattā had made this sincere vow, the trichiliocosm immediately shook in six ways, a rain of various celestial flowers fell from the sky, and hundreds of thousands of divine musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. Thereupon, the maiden Vimaladattā transformed her female body into that of sixteen boys.
Then the Venerable Maudgalyāyana bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now pay face-to-face homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, from their first aspiration until their arrival at the site of enlightenment."
“World-Honored One!
This woman possesses such great majesty and the power of supernormal faculties that she is able to make great vows, and once these vows have been made, they are all fulfilled according to her wish.”
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“It is so, it is so; it is as you have said.

From the first resolution until the seat of enlightenment, the Bodhisattva is honored by gods and humans like a Buddhist stūpa or temple, serving as the unsurpassed field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene and joyful countenance. According to the constant law of all Buddhas, when they smile, various colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal—issue forth from their mouths, illuminating immeasurable and boundless Buddha-fields.
