The splendor of the suns, moons, and palaces of devas and māras is no longer visible; the light then withdraws and enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, asked in verse:

"With the voice of a deva, a nāga, or Brahmā, and the lion’s roar, With the sound of the kalaviṅka and the thunderclap, You dispel greed, hatred, and delusion, giving rise to joy; I pray, O Ocean of Ten Powers, tell the cause of your smile."
The earth shook in six ways without causing any distress, raining down exquisite celestial flowers that gladdened the hearts of all;
the World-Honored One subdued all the non-Buddhists, just as a lion subdues the jackals.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for me the cause and condition of this smile.

Though the light of ten billion suns, moons, jewels, and lightning, and the radiance of devas, nāgas, and Brahmā kings may exist, the pure light issuing from Śākyamuni’s mouth surpasses all these lights; the Buddha’s light is supreme.
The tuft of hair between the eyebrows is like a white gem or the moon; It is perfectly round and soft, comparable to celestial robes.
The white hair emits light that illuminates the infinite; I pray you tell us, for what reason do you emit this light?
The Blessed One’s teeth are pure, free from defilement; Square, even, closely set, and white as snow.
From the Buddha’s mouth should issue rays of variegated light— Blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal.
Even if the world-system were to perish and the sun and moon should fall, even if the earth were to fill the void leaving no dwelling place,
the nature of water could be made to change into fire, and the nature of fire could likewise be changed into water,
and the great ocean could be entirely made to dry up— yet the Tathāgata’s words of truth are never otherwise.
Suppose all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were simultaneously to become pratyekabuddhas;
and suppose each of those pratyekabuddhas were to gather together millions of questions of hundreds of thousands of kinds over the course of billions of kalpas,
and they all assembled before the Tathāgata at once, each asking their questions simultaneously in different voices.
The Tathāgata immediately replied with a single voice, Able to sever the immeasurable doubts of that assembly.
Having accomplished wisdom and reached the further shore, Adorned by all forms of wisdom,

“Mañjuśrī! Regarding the three vehicles, what kind of equality have you realized?
He replied:
"The Buddha-realm is equal; I have realized it thus.
The Buddha asked, "Have you attained the realm of the Buddha?"
He said, "If the World-Honored One has attained it, I too shall attain it.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti spoke to Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Does the Tathāgata not attain the realm of a Buddha?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Do you, however,
have anything attained within the realm of the śrāvakas?”
Subhūti said: "The liberation of the Noble One is neither attainment nor non-attainment. He asked:
"So it is, so it is. The liberation of the Tathāgata is neither possessed of an objective sphere nor devoid of an objective sphere. Subhūti said:
“Mañjuśrī! You do not protect bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to attain awakening as you preach the Dharma. Mañjuśrī replied:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Suppose there were a physician who,
while attending to a patient, did not administer medicines that are sour, pungent, bitter, or astringent.”
"Would that physician cause the patient to recover,
or would he cause him to die? Subhūti replied:
"This brings about the suffering of death; it does not bestow peace and happiness.
Mañjuśrī replied, "The one who preaches the Dharma is likewise so."

If, out of concern that others might become terrified, one conceals such profound meanings and instead expounds them using only miscellaneous phrases and flowery rhetoric, one bestows upon sentient beings the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, rather than granting them the health, peace, and bliss of Nirvana.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus were liberated through the exhaustion of the outflows (āsrava-kṣaya) by no longer grasping at any phenomena.
Eight thousand devas and humans became free from dust and removed of defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Seven hundred devaputras resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made this vow, saying:
"In a future age, may we obtain such eloquence as Mañjuśrī has attained."
At that time, the Elder Subhūti said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you not teach the Śrāvaka vehicle to the śrāvakas?”
He replied, "The vehicle of all dharmas is the vehicle upon which I ride. Subhūti said:
"Are you a śrāvaka? Are you a pratyekabuddha?
Or are you a samyaksaṃbuddha?"
He replied: "I am a śrāvaka because my understanding does not arise from the voice of another.
I am a pratyekabuddha because I do not abandon great compassion and fearlessness."
"I have become a Samyaksaṃbuddha because I did not abandon my original vow.
Subhūti said, "How then can you be called a śrāvaka?"
He replied,
"Because those sentient beings have never heard the Dharma before and I cause them to hear it,
I am a śrāvaka. He asked again:
"How do you act as a pratyekabuddha?
He replied, "I cause sentient beings to have faith in and awaken to the dharma-realm; for this reason, I am called a pratyekabuddha."
He asked again:
"How do you define one who is a Samyaksaṃbuddha? He replied:
"Because I have thus realized that all phenomena are equal within the dharmadhātu, I am the One Truly and Fully Enlightened. Subhūti said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"In what stage do you definitively abide?
He replied, "I abide in all stages."
Subhūti said: "Do you, too, dwell in the stage of an ordinary person? Mañjuśrī replied:
“I too am definitively established on the stage of an ordinary person.
Subhūti asked: “With what underlying intention do you say this?”
He replied: "Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is equal, it is said thus. Subhūti said:

"If all dharmas are entirely equal, upon what basis should one establish the various dharmas—this stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, or the stage of the Buddha?"

Mañjuśrī said: "For example, within the realm of empty space throughout the ten directions, one may say, 'This is the empty space of the eastern direction,' and the same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir."
Such various distinctions in verbal expression do not introduce any difference into space.
Therefore, O Noble One!
Although one establishes the characteristics of the various stages based on the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena, there is likewise no differentiation within emptiness itself.
Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī! Have you already entered the state of certainty beyond regression?"
He replied: "I have already entered [the state], yet I have also emerged from it. Subhūti said:
"How does one enter and then emerge again?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Virtuous one,
you should know that this is the wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva."
They enter into the correct nature of transcendence (*samyaktva-niyāma*) as it truly is, and emerge through skillful means. Subhūti,
it is like a person skilled in the art of archery, against whom an enemy intends to do harm.
A master archer had a son whom he loved and cherished most deeply.
Once, while his beloved son was in the wilderness, the father mistakenly took him to be an enemy and released an arrow to shoot at him.
The son then cried out loudly, saying, "I am without fault; why are you harming me?
At that time, the master archer possessed great swiftness of action; he hurried to the son's side and pulled the arrow back from him.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: in order to discipline Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he enters the stage of certainty and then emerges from it, yet he does not fall into the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.
"For this reason, it is called the Buddha-ground.
Subhūti asked: "How does a bodhisattva attain this ground?"
Mañjuśrī said: “If bodhisattvas abide in all stages while abiding nowhere, they thereby attain these stages.
If they can expound upon all stages yet do not dwell in inferior stages, they thereby attain these stages.”

If there are those who practice in order to exhaust the afflictions of all sentient beings, yet the dharma-realm is inexhaustible; though they abide in the unconditioned, they act within the conditioned; and while amidst birth and death, they regard it as a pleasure garden rather than seeking nirvana—this is for the sake of attaining this stage.
To fulfill all aspirations, to attain the patience of non-self (*anātma-kṣānti*), and to bring sentient beings to maturity, one seeks this stage.
To attain the wisdom of a Buddha and not give rise to anger or resentment toward those who lack such wisdom, one seeks this stage.
For the sake of those seeking the Dharma, they turn the wheel of Dharma, yet there is no differentiation within the dharma-realm; practicing in this manner, they attain this stage.
Furthermore, if bodhisattvas subdue the Māras and manifest as the four Māras, they attain this stage.
Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī! This bodhisattva practice is extremely difficult for all the world to believe."
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.
These bodhisattvas act within the world while transcending worldly dharmas."
Subhūti said: "Mañjuśrī, you should explain how this transcends the world."
Mañjuśrī said: "The so-called 'world' refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Within these aggregates, form has the nature of a mass of foam, feeling has the nature of a water bubble, perception has the nature of a mirage, mental formations have the nature of a plantain tree, and consciousness has the nature of an illusion. One should know that such is the fundamental nature of the world: it is like a mass of foam, a mirage, a bubble, an illusion, and a plantain tree. Within this, there are no aggregates and no names for aggregates; there are no sentient beings and no names for sentient beings; there is no world and no transcending of the world."

If one correctly knows the five aggregates in this way, it is called resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); if there is correct resolute conviction, then one is liberated from the very beginning; if one is liberated from the very beginning, then one does not cling to worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*); if one does not cling to worldly phenomena, then one transcends the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the five aggregates are empty of intrinsic nature.

If they are empty of intrinsic nature, then there is no self and nothing belonging to a self. If there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, then there is non-duality. If there is fundamentally no duality, then there is neither grasping nor abandoning. Because there is neither grasping nor abandoning, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, one transcends the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, these five aggregates belong to causes and conditions.

That which belongs to causes and conditions does not belong to a self, nor does it belong to sentient beings. That which does not belong to a self and does not belong to sentient beings is without an owner. Being without an owner, there is no grasping; being without grasping, there is no contention. This absence of contention is the Dharma of the śramaṇa, like a hand drawing in space, where there is no contact or obstruction.
Practicing such emptiness and equality transcends the world.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when the five aggregates and the dharma-realm enter equally into the dharma-realm, this is "no realm. If it is no realm, then there is no earth element, water, fire, or wind element; there is no self, no sentient beings, and no life-span; there is no desire realm, nor the form or formless realms; and there is no realm of the conditioned or unconditioned, nor of birth-and-death or nirvāṇa.
"Having entered this realm, one dwells together with the world yet has no abiding place; if there is no abiding place, one transcends the world.

When he spoke these words on the dharma of transcending the world, two hundred bhikṣus, through non-clinging to all dharmas, attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind. Each of them took off his *uttarāsaṅga* robe and covered Mañjuśrī with it, saying:
"If one does not give rise to faith and understanding in this Dharma-gate, they shall have nothing to attain and nothing to realize."
At that time, Subhūti addressed those bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones! Have you attained or realized anything at all?"

The bhikṣus said: "If one possesses overweening pride, it may be said that they have attainment and realization; for a śramaṇa who is free from overweening pride, there is neither attainment nor realization."
In what respect could he give rise to such a movement of thought as to say of himself:
"I have attained this; I have realized this"?
If there were any movement of thought therein, it would be the work of Māra.
Subhūti said: "Venerable sir! According to what you understand, what have you attained and what have you realized that you speak thus?"
The bhikṣus said: “Only the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, and Mañjuśrī know what we have attained and know what we have realized,
O Virtuous One!”
As I understand it, if one does not comprehend the characteristic of suffering, yet says, "Suffering is what I should know," this constitutes overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Likewise, to say that "origination should be abandoned," "cessation should be realized," or "the path should be cultivated" [without such comprehension] constitutes overweening pride.
Because they do not understand the characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path, they make such statements as, "I have cultivated the path," which constitutes overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
What is the characteristic of suffering?
This refers to the characteristic of non-arising.
Thus, if the characteristics of origin, cessation, and the path are characterized by non-arising, they are signless and unapprehendable.
Within them, there is not the slightest suffering to be known, nor origin to be abandoned, nor cessation to be realized, nor a path to be cultivated.
If one is not startled, terrified, or afraid when this meaning of the Noble Truths is explained, one does not possess overweening pride;
if one gives rise to alarm and fear, one possesses overweening pride.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those bhikṣus,
saying, "Excellent, excellent! and addressed Subhūti:
"These bhikṣus previously heard Mañjuśrī expound such profound teachings within the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Because these bhikṣus practiced this profound Dharma in the past, they are now able to understand it quickly upon hearing it in accordance with their former training."
In this sequence, those within my Dharma who hear this profound teaching and give rise to faith and understanding shall all, in the Dharma of Maitreya, attain entry into the ranks of the assembly.
At that time, the Devaputra Śubhavyūha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Virtuous One, you frequently preach the Dharma here in this Jambudvīpa. We pray that you would go to the Tuṣita Heaven."
Those devaputras have also long cultivated vast roots of goodness; had they heard the Dharma, they would have understood it.
Yet, because they were attached to pleasure, they were unable to come to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma, thereby causing themselves harm and decline.

At that time, Mañjuśrī immediately manifested a supernatural transformation, causing the Devaputra Śubhavyūha and the entire assembly to each perceive themselves as having entered the Tuṣita Heaven palace, where they beheld its groves, palaces, towers, railings, and windows, all interspersed with exquisite adornments.

These various jeweled terraces were twenty stories high and wide, draped with nets and canopies of manifold jewels and strewn everywhere with celestial flowers; diverse species of birds gathered there, soaring and perching while singing in harmony.
In the midst of the void, there were celestial maidens scattering mandārava flowers, singing praises, and enjoying themselves in play.
Having witnessed this, the Devaputra Sudhana addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How rare, Mañjuśrī!"
"How is it that we have so swiftly arrived at the Tuṣita Heaven palace and behold this grove and the assembly of devas?
Mañjuśrī, we pray that you will preach the Dharma for us."
At that time, the Elder Subhūti said to Śīlaguṇa:
"O Son of Heaven!
You did not leave this assembly to go elsewhere; it was through the supernatural transformations of Mañjuśrī that you saw yourself enter the Tuṣita heaven palace."
At that time, the Devaputra Śubhavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
The playful mastery of samādhi and the supernatural transformations of Mañjuśrī have manifested this entire assembly within a single kṣaṇa as entering the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.”
The Buddha said,
“Devaputra! Do you truly see the supernatural transformations and miraculous powers of Mañjuśrī?”

As I understand it, Mañjuśrī, if you wish to gather the meritorious adornments of as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges and manifest them all within a single Buddha-land, you are entirely capable of doing so.

Or, with the tip of a finger, they lift as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, carry them beyond as many Buddha-lands in the zenith as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and place them in empty space; furthermore, they cause all the waters of the four great oceans within those Buddha-fields to enter a single pore, yet sentient beings who dwell in water feel no constriction, each perceiving themselves as not having left the sea.

All the Sumeru Kings of the various worlds were entirely placed within a single mustard seed; yet the devaputras who dwell upon those Sumerus all believed they were each in their own original palaces.

Furthermore, all sentient beings of the five destinies within all Buddha-fields were placed entirely within his palm, and he caused them all to behold exquisite provisions and requisites, just like those in the Land of Universal Joyful Adornments.
Furthermore, all the masses of fire existing in all worlds can be entirely placed within a single tuft of tūla-cotton.
Moreover, all the suns and moons existing in all Buddha-worlds can be completely eclipsed within a single pore.
"Whatever is to be done according to the circumstances, all that shall be performed.
At that time, Māra the Evil One transformed himself into a bhikṣu and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We wish to see Mañjuśrī manifest such supernatural transformations before us.
Of what use are these empty and boastful words, which no one in the entire world can believe?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"You should manifest a supernatural transformation within this assembly.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, without rising from his seat, entered the samādhi called "The Adornment of All Dharmas through Sovereignty over the Mind."
At that time, all the supernatural transformations as described by the Buddha were manifested, and Māra, the assembled multitude, and the Devaputra Sudhana all beheld them.
When the great assembly witnessed these miraculous manifestations, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and spoke thus:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Because the Buddha has appeared, this noble being exists, who opens this Dharma-gate and manifests various supernatural transformations within the world.
At that time, the Evil Māra, through the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, spoke these words:
“How rare, World-Honored One!”
Mañjuśrī possesses such supernormal powers, and this assembly is likewise rare, having attained faith and understanding in the supernormal transformations of Mañjuśrī.
World-Honored One!

Even if there were as many Māras as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they would be unable to create obstacles for these sons and daughters of good family who possess such faith and understanding.
I am also the evil Māra Pāpīyān, who constantly seeks an opportunity to afflict and disturb sentient beings.

From this day forward, I make this vow: wherever this Dharma-gate circulates, I shall not pass within a hundred yojanas in the four directions of any place where there are those who give rise to faith and understanding, who love and delight in it, and who uphold, read, recite, and expound it.
“World-Honored One!

However, because there are those among my followers who wish to sever and extinguish the Dharma of the Tathāgata, causing the minds of practitioners to become distracted, I shall now speak this dhāraṇī in order to subdue them.”

If sons or daughters of good family write down, read, recite, and explain this Dharma-gate to others, the hosts of devas and māras shall obtain excellent benefit; they shall cause the speaker of the Dharma to have joy in body and mind and to practice with diligent application, bestowing upon them unimpeded eloquence and dhāraṇīs, and providing service and offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions so that they lack for nothing.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying: "Tadyathā | Amale ||"
Vimala-sati-te ā-kāpe.
Tatoṣṭhuru ṣaṭśaye duryavati bhūtapatigamiḷi.
Hṛdye (9) suphṛdye (10) phuphusi (11)
12. Dhṛisukhi, 13. Vaiti, 14. Kāyi.
15. Mī-si-li 16. Yang-ju-li-ba-li 17. Hu-lu-hu-mo-di.
Sakhe (18) śuṣmiṃ te dīdharat (19) ānava te tittiriścaṇi (20)
Kṛtāri-te (21) kṛti-pate (22) hrū-che-du-pate-maṃtrā-pracīna-taruka (23)
Āvara-mukta-va-sūrya (24). “World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family single-mindedly receives and upholds this dhāraṇī without allowing the mind to become distracted, they will always be protected by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others; no evil spirits will be able to find an opportunity to harm them.”
When Māra Pāpīyān recited this mantra, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Māra Pāpīyān:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You should know that such eloquence as yours is the realm of Mañjuśrī’s supernatural powers.
Thereupon, while Mañjuśrī manifested his supernatural powers and Māra Pāpīyān recited the incantation, thirty-two thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Then Mañjuśrī withdrew his supernatural power, causing this entire assembly to see themselves once again as they were before.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Devaputra Śubhavyūha, saying:
"O son of good family!
"Go to the Tuṣita Heaven and announce to the assembly of devas that I shall come there.

When the Devaputra Śubhavyūha heard these words, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, as well as those of the Bodhisattvas and the venerable Śrāvakas. Surrounded respectfully by his retinue, he suddenly vanished before the assembled multitude and, in an instant, arrived in the Tuṣita Heaven.
At that time, Śubhavyūha addressed all the devaputras, saying:
"You should know that Mañjuśrī, out of compassion for you, wishes to come here."
"You all should renounce all sensual pleasures, distance yourselves from arrogance, and listen to the Dharma with reverence, respect, and compliance.
At that time, the Devaputra Śubhavyūha prepared the site of enlightenment as was appropriate, then joined his palms and spoke these words: "Mañjuśrī!
"Now is precisely the right time.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, surrounded before and behind by ten thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and vanished from the assembly. He appeared in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he sat upon the prepared seats together with the great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas at that place of practice.

At that time, the entire great assembly heard the sons of the gods from the palaces of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin; as well as the hosts of Māras, the hosts of Brahmās, and even those up to the Peak of Existence, all calling out to one another:
"Mañjuśrī is now in the Tuṣita Heaven and is about to preach the Dharma."
Upon hearing this, hundreds of thousands of gods all gathered together; the celestial palaces of this desire realm were no longer able to contain them.
Then Mañjuśrī, by means of his supernatural power, caused those gods to perceive for themselves a vast expanse where they could dwell without obstructing one another.
At that time, the Devaputra Kalyāṇakārin addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"The great assembly has gathered; we pray that you will preach the Dharma for them.
Mañjuśrī replied to the Devaputra Kalyāṇakārin:
“There are four kinds of dharmas which a bodhisattva who abides in heedfulness is able to gather: what are the four?

First, abiding in the precepts while possessing great learning; second, abiding in meditative concentration while practicing wisdom; third, abiding in supernormal powers while giving rise to great knowledge; and fourth, abiding in tranquility while constantly observing.”
"Son of Heaven!
There are eight kinds of dharmas that enter into the Vinaya. What are these eight?"

First, purity of body; second, purity of speech; third, purity of mind; fourth, purity of view; fifth, purity of the dhūta virtues; sixth, purity of livelihood; seventh, purity through abandoning all pretenses of manifesting unusual signs for the sake of seeking profit from profit; eighth, purity of never forsaking the mind of omniscience.
These are called the eight dharmas that enter into the precepts.
O Son of Heaven!
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that enter into extensive learning.

What are the eight? First, respect; second, humbling one's mind; third, initiating diligence; fourth, not losing right mindfulness; fifth, receiving and upholding according to what is heard; sixth, skillfully observing with the mind; seventh, teaching others as one has heard; eighth, neither praising oneself nor disparaging others.
These are called the eight dharmas for entering into extensive learning.
O Devaputra! Furthermore, there are eight dharmas for entering into meditative concentration.

What are the eight? First, dwelling in tranquility within an araṇya; second, abandoning clamor and bustle; third, remaining unstained by sensory objects; fourth, physical and mental pliancy; fifth, the mind taking a meditative object as its focus; sixth, severing all signs of sound; seventh, reducing food to sustain the body; eighth, not grasping at noble bliss.
These are called the eight dharmas for entering meditative concentration.
O Son of Heaven!
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas for entering wisdom.

What are these eight? First, skillfulness regarding the aggregates; second, skillfulness regarding the elements; third, skillfulness regarding the sense bases; fourth, skillfulness regarding dependent origination; fifth, skillfulness regarding the truths; sixth, skillfulness regarding the three periods of time; seventh, skillfulness regarding all vehicles; and eighth, skillfulness regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
These are called the eight dharmas that enter into wisdom.
Celestial Son!
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that enter into the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
What are the eight?
First is the supernormal power of the divine eye, because one sees without obstruction;
second is the supernormal power of the divine ear, because one hears without obstruction.
Third is the supernormal power of reading the minds of others, because one contemplates the minds of all sentient beings;
fourth is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, because one remembers the limits of the past;
fifth is the supernormal power of the spiritual bases, because one manifests all manner of miraculous transformations.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, because of exhausting the outflows of all sentient beings;
seventh is neither abiding in afflictions nor grasping at liberation, due to the power of skillful means;
eighth is entering nirvana without relying on the liberation of the śrāvakas.
These are called the eight dharmas for entering into supernormal powers.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that can lead one into wisdom. What are these eight?

First is the knowledge of suffering; second is the knowledge of its origin; third is the knowledge of its cessation; fourth is the knowledge of the path; fifth is the knowledge of causes; sixth is the knowledge of conditions; seventh is the knowledge of the three periods of time; eighth is all-encompassing knowledge.
These are called the eight kinds.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that enter into tranquility. What are these eight?

First is internal tranquility; second is external tranquility; third is tranquility regarding craving; fourth is tranquility regarding grasping; fifth is tranquility regarding existence; sixth is tranquility regarding birth; seventh is tranquility regarding all afflictions; and eighth is tranquility regarding the three realms.
These are called the eight dharmas.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that enter into contemplation. What are these eight?
First is morality, second is learning, third is meditative concentration, fourth is wisdom, fifth is supernormal powers, sixth is knowledge, seventh is tranquility, and eighth is heedfulness.
"O Son of Heaven!
These are called the eight dharmas. Because a bodhisattva dwells securely in heedfulness, he shall attain all the buddhas' enlightenment and the factors of enlightenment."
Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
You should abide in heedfulness according to this.
"O you Sons of Heaven, by abiding in heedfulness, the three kinds of happiness will never diminish."
What are these three?
First is the bliss of the heavens, second is the bliss of meditative concentration, and third is the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
Those who abide in heedfulness attain liberation from the three types of suffering.
What are these three? They are the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Furthermore, one who is heedful transcends three kinds of fear.
What are these three?
They are the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Furthermore, those who are not negligent attain transcendence of the three realms of existence (*bhava*). What are these three?
They are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!
Those who dwell in heedfulness attain freedom from the three stains.
What are these three?
These are the stain of greed, the stain of hatred, and the stain of delusion.
Furthermore, by being heedful regarding the three trainings, one shall attain fulfillment.
What are these three?
These are known as higher morality (*adhiśīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
One who is heedful constantly draws near to and makes offerings to the Triple Gem.
What are these three?
These are the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Sangha-jewel.
Furthermore, one who abides in heedfulness attains freedom from the three obstacles to the perfections (*pāramitā*).
What are these three?
First, being stingy oneself;
second, giving rise to hatred and envy toward those who practice generosity;
and third, following along with stingy people.
They themselves break the precepts, yet they harbor hatred and envy toward those who uphold them, while following those who break them;
they themselves are prone to anger, yet they harbor hatred and envy toward those who practice patience, while following those who harbor ill will;
they themselves are indolent, yet they harbor hatred and envy toward those who are diligent, while following those who are indolent.
They themselves are distracted, yet they harbor hatred and envy toward those who practice meditative concentration and follow those who are distracted;
they themselves lack wisdom, yet they harbor hatred and envy toward those who possess wisdom and follow those who lack wisdom.
"O you sons of the gods!
This is called 'dwelling in reliance upon heedfulness,' by which one shall attain the distancing of the three obstacles to the pāramitās.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods!"
One who dwells in heedfulness shall obtain the assistance of three kinds of perfections as companions. What are these three?

They are: the increase of giving by dedicating it toward enlightenment without seeking karmic rewards; [the increase of morality by dedicating it toward enlightenment without seeking karmic rewards]; and [the increase of patience by dedicating it toward enlightenment without seeking karmic rewards].
Increasing in ethical discipline, one dedicates it toward awakening without seeking rebirth in the heavens;
increasing in patience, one dedicates it toward awakening without giving rise to thoughts of harm toward any sentient being;
increasing in diligence, one dedicates it toward awakening with no sense of satiety regarding various roots of goodness.
As meditative concentration increases, one dedicates it toward enlightenment with an undistracted mind;
as wisdom increases, one constantly cultivates wholesome deeds and dedicates them toward enlightenment.
This is called relying on heedfulness to abide in and obtain these three auxiliary companions to the pāramitā.
Therefore, O sons of the gods!
Abiding in heedfulness increases all wholesome dharmas; this is what the Buddha has approved.
Furthermore, all dharmas are like space; thus should one contemplate these four right efforts.
What are the four? They are:
the arousal of diligence so that unwholesome states that have not yet arisen do not arise—because all phenomena are without agency;
and the arousal of diligence to eliminate unwholesome states that have already arisen—because the nature of phenomena is pure.
All phenomena are quiescent; one initiates diligence so that wholesome dharmas not yet arisen may arise.
All phenomena have no location and no activity; one initiates diligence so that wholesome dharmas already arisen may remain without being lost.
“O Son of Heaven!
These four right efforts of the bodhisattvas are approved by the Buddha.
Furthermore, O Sons of Heaven!”
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equal, without arising or ceasing.

Relying on this nature of phenomena, because there is nothing to be attained, one does not commit any evil; because one accords with the nature of phenomena, one diligently cultivates all manner of goodness. One who practices in this way is practicing without anything to practice.
Furthermore, not grasping at nor rejecting any phenomena is called right effort.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods,
you should contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness, which are as follows:
There is no dwelling place of the body, no dwelling place of sensation, no dwelling place of the mind, and no dwelling place of phenomena.
Being without a dwelling place and without a basis for establishment—this is called the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Furthermore, one should contemplate the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*):

first, because the body and mind are untiring and delight in cultivating wholesome dharmas; second, because one initiates diligence for the sake of accomplishing all sentient beings and thereby cuts off craving and desire; third, because all dharmas are unattainable yet one realizes all Buddha-dharmas; and fourth, because the mind is like an illusion or a transformation, having no basis and transcending all grasping and attachment.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the five faculties (*pañcendriya*):
first, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), because it takes precedence by being decisively established within all phenomena;
second, the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), because it universally cultivates all practices to accomplish the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*).
Third is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), because it fully possesses all dharmas and the mind is well-tamed and supple, being free from forgetfulness;
fourth is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), because it remains far removed from discursive攀缘 (*ālambana*) and does not follow after drowsiness or sleep;
fifth is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), because it decisively discerns all dharmas, with correct contemplation manifest before one, and does not rely on others.
What are called the powers?
It is said that when one dwells securely within the suchness of the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), no afflictions whatsoever can obstruct or destroy them; this is called power.
By dwelling in this power, one attains the supreme Dharma; knowing things as they truly are—neither different nor identical—it is called a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

If one realizes all phenomena in accordance with awakening and practices progressively by means of this path, penetrating the secret and remaining unshakable regarding the Dharma, it is called the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
Therefore, O sons of the gods!
You should thus cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; transcending all conditioned activities without further obstruction, your wisdom shall blaze forth and reach ultimate tranquility.
What is called ultimate tranquility?

It means that all phenomena neither arise nor cease; because they do not cease, there is nothing to be done; because there is nothing to be done, there is neither non-action nor reception, and there is no recipient and no designation—this is called ultimate tranquility.
When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the devaputra Kalyāṇakirti addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How should a bodhisattva cultivate the Path?"
Mañjuśrī said: “O Devaputra!

If bodhisattvas do not abandon birth and death yet cause sentient beings to enter nirvāṇa; if they do not abandon craving and grasping yet pull sentient beings out [of saṃsāra] and establish them in the Noble Path—this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the path.”
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
One who cultivates the Path skillfully abides in the purity of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Why is this?

With a mind of tranquility, the bodhisattva perceives that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure; for the sake of sentient beings who delight in and cling to various views, who dwell in latent tendencies, and who lack skillful means, they expound the meaning of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Why is this? It is because these sentient beings give rise to views regarding that which is empty of intrinsic nature.

This bodhisattva, through the signless, the wishless, and the unconditioned—the fact that all phenomena are by their very nature non-arising—causes those ordinary people who have long been habituated to the views of arising and ceasing due to afflictions to gain faith and delight in this non-arising, while remaining unmoved even by arising and ceasing.
"O Son of Heaven!
This is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the path.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"
"One should perceive the path by which Bodhisattvas come and go.
The sons of the gods said, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What is the path by which a bodhisattva comes and goes? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!..."
The Bodhisattva departs having realized bodhi, and returns to preach the Dharma as appropriate.
He departs having attained the various dhyānas and liberations, and returns manifesting birth within the desire realm.
They depart because they have entered the Noble Path; they come because they bring sentient beings to maturity through great compassion.
They depart because they have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); they come because they endure and accept sentient beings.
He departs because he has transcended all phenomena; he comes because he uproots sentient beings.
He departs with firm vows; he comes with the realization that vows have no intrinsic nature.
He departs by means of the three gates of liberation, and he comes for the sake of taking birth.
He departs for the sake of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and he comes in order to establish sentient beings in enlightenment.
"O Son of Heaven!
This is called the path by which all bodhisattvas come and go.
When this bodhisattva path was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Devaputra Śubhavyūha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"We have previously heard of a world named Sarvaguṇaprabhāsa; where is it located?"
“What kind of Dharma does the Tathāgata teach therein? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!...”
That world of Universal Radiance of All Merits is located above, beyond twelve Ganges-sands of Buddha-fields; there, the Tathāgata Samantabhadra preaches the Dharma.
The devaputras said, “We wish to see that world and that Tathāgata.

At that time, Mañjuśrī immediately entered the Samādhi of Radiant Adornment; by the power of this samādhi, he emitted a great light that passed through Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges Rivers, illuminating everywhere the World of Universal Radiance of All Merits.
Then that bodhisattva asked:
"From where does this light come? That Buddha replied:

“Good son! Below, past as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā. In that land, there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells in the world preaching the Dharma.”

In that world there is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī who has entered the Samādhi of Radiant Adornment; he emits great rays of light that universally illuminate immeasurable Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, and it is this radiance that comes to illumine this assembly.
Those bodhisattvas then addressed the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, saying:
"We wish to behold the World-Honored One Śākyamuni and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī."

At that time, the Tathāgata Samantabhadra emitted a great radiance that illuminated twelve *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* buddha-fields, reaching as far as the Sahā world, so that those bodhisattvas could clearly see this assembly of bodhisattvas.
Then that Blessed One addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Who among you is able to go to that Sahā world?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmolkādharin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to go to that Sahā world.
The Buddha said:
"Now is precisely the right time.

At that moment, the Bodhisattva Dharmanetrīdhara, together with ten billion bodhisattvas, vanished from that land and appeared in the Tuṣita Heaven, emitting a great radiance that shone throughout the world.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protecting devaputras, and the great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas attained what they had never experienced before, and spoke these words:
"The playful exercise of supernatural powers by these bodhisattvas is truly rare and marvelous."

At that time, by means of this radiance, the assembly beheld the world-system of Universal Radiance of All Merits, as well as the adornments of the realm of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, which could not be fully described even in an eon.
When Mañjuśrī manifested these supernatural transformations, seven nayutas of devaputras and others resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmolkādhara addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
“We should go together to pay homage to and visit the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Then Mañjuśrī,

having brought to liberation all those among the devaputras who were ready to be saved, proceeded with the assembly of Bodhisattvas led by Dharmolkādhara, as well as the great śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, to where the Buddha was staying.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmolkādhara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"Samantabhadra Tathāgata inquires after the World-Honored One’s health, asking whether you have little illness and little affliction, whether your daily life is light and easy, and whether you dwell in peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons!"

As for this Mañjuśrī and the noble being Dharmolkadhara, their supernormal transformations, the radiance of their wisdom, their maturation of sentient beings, and their service to all Buddhas—no bodhisattvas whatsoever can know the limits of the depth of their wisdom and skillful means.
"You, son of good family!

You should train in the supernatural powers, eloquence, and wisdom of this Mañjuśrī, the noble being who holds the torch of the Dharma, as well as those of all the bodhisattvas, in order to serve the Buddhas and bring sentient beings to maturity."
These noble beings, throughout incalculable eons, have traveled from one buddha-field to another constantly performing the work of a Buddha.
If sentient beings enter the sphere of these noble beings, they shall never again fall into the realm of Māra in the future.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Ānanda:
"You should well uphold this Dharma-gate, so as not to sever the lineage of the Three Jewels.
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmolkādhara rose from this assembly and, together with his retinue, returned to his own Buddha-field.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Devaputra Sudhana, the Elder Ānanda, and all the world’s devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred One;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
36. The Thirty-Sixth Assembly: The Assembly of the Devaputra Susthitamati. Chapter One: The Prologue.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were virtuous elders endowed with supernatural powers, with the great śrāvakas as their leaders.
At that time, there were also forty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose names were:
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Siṃhadhvaja Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Mahāpratibhānaskandharāja Bodhisattva, and Dhāraṇī... [Bodhisattva].
Vīśvadeva Bodhisattva, Satpuruṣa Bodhisattva, Meruśikhara Bodhisattva, Merudhvaja Bodhisattva, Acalācala Bodhisattva,
Arthasamvicintin Bodhisattva, Arthasamvicintimati Bodhisattva, Sucintita Bodhisattva, Cintācitta Bodhisattva, Vīramati Bodhisattva, and Kalyāṇa... [Bodhisattva].
The Bodhisattva Citta, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, the Bodhisattva Parvatarāja-saṃghaṭṭita,
the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Ratnamati, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta,
the Bodhisattva Nityanikṣiptahasta, the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, the Bodhisattva Sattvatāraka, and the Bodhisattva Uttamavīrya.
Sāgaramati, Yathā-vādi-tathā-kārin Bodhisattva, Adhyāśaya-praṇidhāna Bodhisattva,
Pradīpa-hasta Bodhisattva, Samacitta Bodhisattva, Apāya-vinodana Bodhisattva, Sarva-śoka-tamo-vinodana Bodhisattva,
Anikṣipta-dhur Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Candragarbha Bodhisattva, and Vajra-pada Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Anantapada, the Bodhisattva Amitapada, the Bodhisattva Acyutagatipada, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva Jayamati, the Bodhisattva Hitamati, the Bodhisattva Adhimatramati,
the Bodhisattva Cāritramati, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, and the Bodhisattva Candradhvaja.
...the Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī, the Bodhisattva Vairocana, the Bodhisattva Śūramgama,
the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍitagarjitaghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Asaṅgapratibhāna, the Bodhisattva Anulomapratibhāna,
the Bodhisattva Tīkṣṇapratibhāna, the Bodhisattva Varasena, the Bodhisattva Sūryacandraprabhāntarita, and the Bodhisattva Anālambana.
...the Bodhisattva Asaṅgamati, the Bodhisattva Nityahāsa, the Bodhisattva Pramuditendriya,
the Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavivaraṇa, the Bodhisattva Strīvivarta, the Bodhisattva Maṇiratna, the Bodhisattva Pradīpa,
the Bodhisattva Vairocana, the Bodhisattva Jvālana, the Bodhisattva Gaṇajyeṣṭharāja, and the Bodhisattva Gambhīra...
The speaker was the Bodhisattva, with such bodhisattvas mahāsattvas as his chief attendants.

At that time, there were also the four great kings of the heavens, Śakra, the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, and Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world; with these as their leaders, they were accompanied by an assembly of sixty thousand devas.

Furthermore, there were the Devaputra Susthitamati, the Devaputra Sudatta, the Devaputra Maheśvara, and others such as these who served as leaders; together with a multitude of thirty thousand devas, they had all long since established themselves in the bodhisattva path.
Furthermore, there were twenty thousand asura kings, with Rāhu Asura King and Sumeru Asura King as their leaders; they, too, had all already established themselves upon the bodhisattva path.

Furthermore, there were sixty thousand great nāga kings, with the nāga king Anavatapta and the nāga king Vijayacandra as their leaders, all of whom had already established themselves upon the bodhisattva path.

Along with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and even all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—an immeasurable great assembly—all came together for this gathering.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was surrounded by such an immeasurable assembly of hundreds of thousands and was preaching the Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī entered into the samādhi of the "Removal of the Mind through Non-contention" within his own chamber, remaining serene and unmoving.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, with a mind of single-minded composure, arose from samādhi; at that moment, the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable and boundless, shook in six ways.
Then Mañjuśrī, having arisen from samādhi, thought to himself:
"In those immeasurable and boundless world-systems, there appears in the world but one Buddha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he manifests as rarely as the udumbara flower."

In this way, these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world most rarely and with great difficulty; the Dharma they teach is the cessation of all existence, which is nirvāṇa—incalculable, non-conceptual, profoundly deep, beyond analogy, and difficult to understand or know.
However, because the Buddhas do not appear in the world, this cannot be heard; and because it is not heard, the sufferings of sentient beings are difficult to bring to an end.

I should now go to the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and inquire about this matter. By asking about this matter, I shall cause all sentient beings to accomplish roots of goodness, and also cause all who practice the bodhisattva path to no longer have doubts regarding those profound and inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, so that they may all fully realize the goal of Buddha-enlightenment.

However, the sentient beings of this Sahā world are for the most part full of desire, possessed of anger, and characterized by ignorance; they have severed the pure dharmas, being stubborn, dull-witted, and deceitful; they lack shame and remorse, and are arrogant and conceited; they distance themselves from the Buddhas and oppose the Dharma and the Sangha. May those beings hear such profound and wondrous Dharma and thereby attain the eye of pure wisdom.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again thought to himself:

"I should now assemble the bodhisattvas from the ten directions in a great gathering, so that they may all hear this wondrous Dharma-gate spoken by the Tathāgata and realize the profound patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti)."
At that time, having formed this thought, Mañjuśrī immediately entered the Samādhi of Universal Radiance and Stainless Adornment.

Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great light that illuminated Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; all were universally softened, moistened, and purified, becoming bright, stainless, subtle, and beyond praise.

This radiance shines universally throughout the worlds of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—the ten directions—so that all places therein, whether dark, obscure, or hidden, including mountain precipices, forests, and mountains large and small; Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, and other Black Mountains; as well as Mount Sumeru and Mount Mahāsumeru—all such places are rendered brilliantly clear by this light, without any obstruction.

At that time, all the Buddhas currently preaching the Dharma in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, had their respective disciples each address their Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
For what cause and condition has such a great auspicious radiance appeared in the world?
World-Honored One!
From the past until now, I have never before heard of or seen such light—so pure and so subtle.
“World-Honored One!
What is this radiance?

It causes us to experience great joy throughout our entire bodies and brings purity to our minds; it also causes sentient beings to no longer harbor greed, anger, or delusion, so that all afflictions and evils are no longer committed.”
World-Honored One!
By whom was this radiance created?
By whose empowerment has it appeared here?
After those attendants had made this request, the World-Honored Ones remained silent and gave no reply.

At that moment, all the various sounds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions—namely, the voices of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as the sounds of elephants, horses, and various beasts—all ceased entirely.

Whether it be the sound of wind, the sound of fire, the sound of water, the sound of the waves of the great ocean, the sound of music, or the sound of songs of praise—at such times, by the power of the Buddha, all these sounds likewise cease and everything becomes utterly tranquil.
Then the attendants of those Buddhas of the ten directions again requested their respective Buddhas, saying:
"World-Honored One!

We pray that out of great compassion, for the sake of pitying all devas and humans, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all devas and humans, and for the sake of benefiting all devas and humans, you will proclaim for us the origin from which this light comes, which is able to universally illumine all Buddha-lands."

At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions, using the voices of all Tathāgatas throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions—voices all identical to the Brahma-sound—spoke with the vocal activity of a single Tathāgata; the matters they spoke of were likewise without any difference. Using these wondrous sounds, they each reported [the matter] to their own attendants.

When those Buddhas uttered their voices, all Buddha-fields trembled; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments sounded all at once, and even all the music of the devas, humans, and asuras resounded spontaneously without being struck.

Furthermore, from within those various musical sounds, the sounds of all dharmas emerged—namely, the sound of impermanence, the sound of suffering, the sound of non-self, the sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of detachment, the sound of liberation, the sound of the dharma-realm, the sound of suchness, the sound of the limit of reality, the sound of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the sound of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the sound of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the sound of the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the sound of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), the sound of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), the sound of great loving-kindness, the sound of great compassion, the sound of great sympathetic joy, the sound of great equanimity, the sound of harmony, the sound of benefit, and the sound of renunciation. Thus, hundreds of thousands of such diverse sounds of the dharmas issued forth.

Furthermore, when those various sounds issued forth, immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings all attained the stage of non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, there are those who achieve the state of a pratyekabuddha, those who become śrāvakas, and even those who attain the status of Mahābrahmā, Śakra Devendra, or a universal monarch (cakravartin).
At that time, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions each addressed their attendant disciples, saying: "Good sons!
You should not now inquire about this matter."
Why is this? Because this causal condition of the light is not within the sphere of experience of any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others.
If I were to explain it, even the world’s devas, humans, and asuras would immediately become bewildered and lost; therefore, you should not inquire about this matter.

When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of the causes and conditions of such radiance, it is that which can produce and bring to fruition inconceivable and supreme roots of goodness; it also arises by depending upon such inconceivable and supreme roots of goodness, namely the practices of the perfections (*pāramitās*) such as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
These conditioned phenomena are born from this light and are also accomplished by this light.
Therefore, even if we Buddhas and Tathāgatas were to spend an entire eon, or slightly less than an eon, praising and expounding upon the merits of such light, we could never reach their end.
Furthermore, through the power of these roots of goodness—compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—cultivated together, this radiance is able to give rise to joy.
At that time, the attendants of the Buddhas of the ten directions each earnestly entreated him, saying three times:
“We pray only that the World-Honored One [will grant this].”

Out of compassion for all devas and humans, for the sake of the peace and happiness of all devas and humans, for the benefit of all devas and humans, and for the maturation of the various roots of goodness of bodhisattvas, please explain to us the causes and conditions of this light.
After those bodhisattvas had made this request, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, each addressed their attendant disciples, saying:
"O sons of good family!
"You should listen attentively; I shall speak for you.
The attendants replied, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
"We wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, each of those Buddhas addressed their respective attendants, saying: "Virtuous sons!"

There is a world named Sahā; in that land there is a Buddha, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who has appeared in an age of the five turbidities.
The sentient beings in that land are largely possessed of greed, anger, and delusion, and are oppressed by manifold afflictions.
Those beings lack reverence; they do not recognize shame or modesty, being entirely devoid of a sense of guilt, and the karmic actions they perform are for the most part unwholesome.
You were able to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within such a defiled and evil world, and now you currently dwell among the assembly preaching the Dharma.
"Good son! In that world,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata has a great disciple, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mañjuśrī,
who possesses great merit, is endowed with wisdom, and is courageous and diligent."
Through majestic spiritual power (*anubhāva*), they are able to cause all bodhisattvas to attain joy;
to cause bodhisattvas to fulfill their practice; to cause the majesty and power of all bodhisattvas to increase;
to cause all bodhisattvas to arouse diligent vigor; to skillfully discern all dharma-terms; and to reach unimpeded wisdom.
Because he has reached the further shore and is able to fully attain unimpeded eloquence; because he has attained mastery over all dhāraṇīs;
and because he has already perfected all the inconceivable merits of a bodhisattva—he caused that bodhisattva to wish to inquire of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
This profound Dharma gate is for the sake of bringing the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas to fulfillment,
and for the sake of enabling those who practice the Bodhisattva Vehicle to attain the perfection of those inconceivable Buddha-dharmas.

"Good son! Furthermore, Mañjuśrī emits this radiance because he wishes to cause the great assembly of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions to gather, and to cause those bodhisattvas to attain the supreme Dharma."
"For this reason, that Mañjuśrī emits a great radiance that illuminates all Buddha-lands.
At that time, the attendants of the Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions again each questioned their respective Buddhas, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In what samādhi does that Mañjuśrī abide to emit this radiance?
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed their attendant disciples, saying:
"O sons of good family!
"Because that Mañjuśrī has entered the Samādhi of Universal Radiance and Stainless Adornment, he emits this light.
The attendant bodhisattva again addressed the Buddhas, saying:
"World-Honored Ones!"
"I have never before seen such radiance, such purity, nor such a power to bring joy to body and mind.
The Buddhas then addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Does he not intend to instruct the bodhisattvas in the arousal of practice?"
"Will he not wish to assemble a great multitude of bodhisattvas?
Will he not wish to gather these bodhisattvas to proclaim such a sublime sūtra as this?

At that time, from immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, there were in each world immeasurable asaṃkhyeya assemblies of bodhisattvas who each went to where those World-Honored Ones were and prostrated themselves at the Buddhas' feet.
Having completed the prostrations, he again addressed those Buddhas, saying:
"World-Honored Ones!
Who possesses this light?"
"Who possesses such merit?
We have never before seen or heard of this; suddenly this light has appeared, illuminating all the worlds.
Then those Buddhas further addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
“Good sons! There is a world named Sahā;
its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.”

In that place there is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, endowed with great majestic virtue; it is he who has emitted this radiance for the purpose of assembling the great multitude of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Then those bodhisattvas again addressed those buddhas, saying:
“World-Honored Ones!

We now wish to go to the Sahā world, desiring to behold Śākyamuni Tathāgata in order to pay him homage and show reverence, to make offerings and serve him, and to inquire about the principles of the Dharma; furthermore, we wish to see Mañjuśrī and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas there.”
Those World-Honored Ones then addressed those bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!
You may go as you please."
"You should know the time.

At that moment, immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, incalculable, inexpressible, unfathomable, and countless billions of nayutas of koṭis of pāramas of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from the ten directions each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, they each vanished from their respective worlds and appeared here in this Sahā world-system.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from the ten directions all approached the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Among them, some were able to rain down various perfumes—namely, scented unguents, powdered incense, and fragrant garlands—and came into the presence of the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Or there were bodhisattvas who rained down various exquisite flowers, namely:

the utpala flower, the padma flower, the kumuda flower, the puṇḍarīka flower, the campaka flower, the pāṭalī flower, the dhanuṣkāra flower, the atimuktaka flower, the sumanā flower, and the bā... [flower].
Liśika flowers, māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, pāruṣaka flowers, mahāpāruṣaka flowers, cāndraka flowers, mahācāndraka flowers,
exquisite cāndraka flowers, cakraka flowers, and mahācakraka flowers.
Raining down such various flower garlands as these most exquisite *cakra* flowers, they approached the place where the World-Honored One,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha was.

There were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, able to produce hundreds of thousands of sublime and wondrous sounds, came to the place where the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, was staying.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, able to fill the trichiliocosm with a single voice, sing praises of the Buddha’s virtues as they approach the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Adorned with such various ornaments, they all proceeded to where the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, was residing.

At that time, the great assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had come from the ten directions gathered here in this Sahā world. All sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—whether in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the world of Yama—became entirely tranquil; their bodies and minds were at peace and free from desire, hatred, and delusion. They were far removed from all poisons, envy, flattery, deception, pride, and the burning afflictions of distress; all sentient beings gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness and were filled with joy.
Why is this? It is because of the majestic spiritual power of those great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; such is the nature of the matter.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from the ten directions all gathered at the place of the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated with his head at the ground in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and remained suspended in mid-air. He then entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Invisibility.

Having entered this samādhi, he manifested according to his will countless hundreds of thousands of various exquisite-colored great lotus thrones upon which he sat cross-legged; then, he entirely concealed his body so that it was no longer visible.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa beheld those extraordinary and rare auspicious signs and the great supernormal feats; he further saw that great rain of flower-fragrance falling upon the assembly, and he also saw them producing immeasurable musical sounds. He likewise saw them emitting great radiance, and he also saw that throughout this trichiliocosm, in all four continents, there fell a rain of exquisite flowers piled as high as the knees. Furthermore, he saw that the entire great assembly—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all had fully attained bodies endowed with the golden-colored mark.

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, maintaining perfect deportment; he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, praised him in verse:
"Ever bringing joy and all happiness, With a face that is full, stainless, and pure— O Great Being, heroic in the Ten Powers, Endowed with the hundredfold marks of adamant virtue."
Wandering through the three realms among humans and devas, there is none who can equal the Buddha;
you are inconceivable and beyond measure—only pray that you sever my doubts.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, you constantly practiced giving to gather in the world;
free from attachment and without dependence, you maintained the precepts with peerless purity.
Fully cultivating patience, you transcend the world; among all powers, the Ten Powers are supreme.
With merit complete and full, there is none who surpasses you; I pray only that you forever sever my doubts.
Having cultivated myriad practices for more than a hundred thousand kalpas, Seeing sentient beings undergo all manner of sufferings,
They remain courageous and diligent without ever wearying, Constantly giving rise to immeasurable joy.
I offer my head, eyes, marrow, and brain; I renounce my sons, daughters, and wives;
I grow weary of and abandon my kingdom, city, and all possessions—only pray, sever and untangle the net of my doubts.
When the World-Honored One practiced giving in the past, The elephants, horses, carriages, and litters were beyond counting;
Passing on garments of the *nayuta* grade and above, He constantly bestowed them upon the world with joy.

The World-Honored One has always practiced giving with a prior intention, such as these various goods and manifold treasures, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, as well as fields and houses; for this reason, today I inquire of you.
In the past, when his body, ears, and nose were severed, his inner mind remained stainless and free from anger;
even when questioned by others, he spoke according to the Dharma, skillfully explaining the power of patience.
Because you have thoroughly realized the dharma of profound emptiness, Your mind is subtle and difficult to measure;
O person of merit who can bestow happiness upon others, Therefore, I now question you, the Stainless One.
All outflows long since exhausted, all afflictions entirely removed, He deeply perceives sentient beings submerged in various sufferings—
Those shrouded by darkness, the ignorant, Who give rise to defilement, as well as the notions of self and person.

Out of compassion for all beings, you give rise to a heart of loving-kindness; having diligently practiced through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have opened up the shore of perfect awakening and bodhi. I pray only that you will sever the doubts I now hold.
Skillfully entering and emerging from the gates of supernormal powers, He dwells with mastery in concealment and manifestation;
Having realized non-self and shattered the mark of selfhood, He destroys all phenomena, yet they are not empty.
The Buddha is unstained by the world; his true practice and right reflection are subtle, tranquil, and free from all defilement. I pray only that you will resolve this doubt for me.
When the World-Honored One practiced in former times, He never for a moment neglected giving, precepts, patience, or diligence;
He also constantly cultivated meditative concentration and wisdom, Benefiting all living beings beyond compare.
The mass of your merits is difficult to fathom; Deep and vast as the ocean, it is inexhaustible.
You are skillful in coming and going, and well-established in your abiding; I pray only that you will act as my refuge.
In the past, the Immaculate One cultivated great compassion; when a terrified dove sought refuge with him, he did not abandon it.
He carved his own body and sliced his thigh until blood flowed profusely, offering his flesh to the hawk to take its place.
Weighing his entire body against that [enemy], the pigeon was still heavier while his own body remained light;
O Greatly Enlightened One, who acts with skillful means and compassion, I pray only that you resolve my doubts for me.
Mount Sumeru trembles and the myriad stars fall; The palaces of all the devas are utterly destroyed;
The waters of the four great oceans dry up in a single day, And the abodes of the asuras on high in the heavens vanish.
Even if the sun were to fall to the earth, And the bright moon in the sky were suddenly to grow dark,
The words of the Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, Are true and sincere, and possess no duality.
At that time, after the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had praised with these verses, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Virtuous World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition does this subtle and wondrous radiance exist in the world?"
“Furthermore, by what causes and conditions have these unprecedented auspicious signs suddenly appeared so clearly?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying: “Kāśyapa!”
You should not inquire about this matter now. Why is that?

Such a realm is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; if I were to explain the meaning of this light, all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—would become startled and doubtful, falling into a state of confusion and ruin. Therefore, you should not ask this now.
Then Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that out of great compassion, for the sake of pitying all devas and humans, for the benefit of all devas and humans, and for the peace and happiness of all devas and humans, you will explain the profound causes and conditions of this radiance so that I may attain understanding.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for you. Mahākāśyapa replied:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it; please deign to expound it.
Then the Buddha again addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:

“Kāśyapa! Now, my Mañjuśrī has entered the Samādhi of Universal Radiance and Stainless Adornment. By the power of this samādhi, he has emitted this light, which shines throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in order to gather those immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and unfathomable asaṃkhyeya great Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and bring them here to this Sahā world.”
They all prostrated at my feet, circumambulated me three times to the right, and remained in the air at a height of one tala tree, each sitting cross-legged upon their respective great lotus seats.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

What bodhisattva-mahāsattvas now possess such majestic spiritual power and virtue that they cause such subtle and wonderful fragrant flowers to rain down, and furthermore produce these hundreds of thousands of musical instruments that sound spontaneously without being struck?"
The Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa!

It is by the majestic spiritual power of the bodhisattvas of the ten directions that such sublime and wonderful flowers and incense rain down, and even within the space above, immeasurable sounds of music resound spontaneously."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Within this assembly, I do not see even a single bodhisattva; why then does the World-Honored One further speak of the bodhisattvas of the ten directions?”
“Kāśyapa! All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like can never see those multitudes of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Why is this?
Kāśyapa! Among these, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others do not abide in great compassion.

If one can abide within this ground of compassion, then one is able to perform deeds for the benefit of others, and is likewise able to practice the various pāramitās, such as giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
"Once they have entered the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they can never again practice these stages traversed by bodhisattvas. Kāśyapa!

All these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have entered the samādhi of invisibility; therefore, no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can see those bodhisattvas, except for the Buddhas and the great bodhisattvas who dwell on this stage."
Kāśyapa! Even bodhisattvas who have newly entered the Great Vehicle cannot see it, let alone all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"If one were to see it, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

“Blessed One, how many dharmas must a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill, what roots of goodness must they cultivate, and what merits must they acquire in order to enter this ‘Concealment of the Body’ samādhi?
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will be able to attain this samādhi of invisibility. What are these ten?
First, their disposition is gentle and flexible, and they dwell deeply in right faith.
Second, never abandoning or forsaking any sentient being;
third, ultimately bringing the mind of great compassion to full completion;
fourth, awakening to the understanding that all things are without attachment to manifold marks.
Fifth, although they seek after all Buddha-dharmas, they never grasp at them falsely;
sixth, they do not even contemplate the wisdom of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
seventh, they are able to relinquish everything in the world, even their own bodies and lives without any stinginess, let alone other things which they would not give away.
Eighth, although they undergo immeasurable births and deaths and afflictions, they remain unstained by and unattached to all conditioned activities;
ninth, they constantly cultivate immeasurable generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, yet do not differentiate between the various *pāramitās*;

tenth, they constantly give rise to this thought: "Only after I have established all sentient beings in Bodhi shall I sit beneath the Bodhi tree," without grasping at the marks of either Bodhi or sentient beings.
“Kāśyapa! These are the ten dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enable them to attain the samādhi of invisibility.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
You have so skillfully expounded this matter.
It is truly fitting that the World-Honored One should speak in such a way."
“World-Honored One!
Even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have never once given rise to such a thought as: ‘I shall establish all sentient beings in the stage of arhatship,’ let alone in the Buddha-dharma.”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa, it is so, it is so.”
