Therefore, none of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are able to enter the bodhisattva’s samādhi of invisibility.
They do not even know the name of this samādhi; how then could they enter it?
"If one were able to enter it, such a thing would be impossible.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
We now deeply wish to behold those great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Why is this? Because such Great Beings are difficult to encounter.
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa, you should stay for a while.”
"If you must wait for Mañjuśrī to arrive, those bodhisattvas shall emerge from their meditative absorption, and only then will you see them.
Nevertheless, Kāśyapa!"
You too have attained these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi; you should now concentrate your mind and seek out those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to see where they are.
"In what posture do they abide?
What activities do they perform?

Then, having received this holy instruction, Mahākāśyapa, relying upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and his own supernormal powers, immediately entered twenty thousand samādhi doors and sought in this manner: "Where are those bodhisattvas now located?"
In what posture does he abide?
Is it while walking?

Yet, in the end, one does not see him standing; nor does one see him reclining or lying down; nor does one see him sitting upright; nor does one see him, nor even know by what speech he speaks or what activity he performs, from where he comes or to where he goes.
Thereupon, he arose from his meditative concentration and approached the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
How extraordinary, World-Honored One!"
"I have already experienced twenty thousand gates of samādhi, yet in my search for these bodhisattvas, I have seen none at all.
World-Honored One!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet realized the state of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and yet they have already attained such subtle and wondrous samādhis; how much more so when they realize unsurpassed bodhi!"
“World-Honored One!
It is impossible that any good man or good woman who sees or hears such a miraculous transformation would not swiftly resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“World-Honored One!

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is able to attain such a samādhi of invisibility dons the armor of diligence with the desire to deliver all those sentient beings, yet they never depart from this wondrous concentration.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.
This is not even within the sphere of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone other sentient beings.”
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has declared me to be the foremost among his śrāvakas in wisdom; I should now seek out where these bodhisattvas currently reside."
In what posture does he abide?
What activities does he perform?
Would it not be well if we were able to behold him?

At that time, having formed this thought, Śāriputra—relying on both the Buddha’s majestic power and his own strength—immediately entered thirty thousand samādhi-doors and circled about, observing where those bodhisattvas were now and what kind of deportment they maintained; yet he did not know even so much as a hair’s breadth of their characteristics.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti had this thought:
"I should now also seek out where these bodhisattvas are and what kind of deportment they maintain."
"What have they done? Would it not be well if we could see them?

At that time, having formed this thought, Subhūti, through the majestic power of the Buddha and by his own strength, entered forty thousand samādhi-doors. He searched everywhere for those bodhisattvas—where they were located and what kind of deportment they maintained—but he did not see even their walking, standing, sitting, or reclining; nor did he perceive from where they came or to where they went.
Thereupon, emerging from meditative absorption, he went before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has declared that among my śrāvakas, I am foremost in the samādhi of non-contention; I have also attained this gateway of samādhi."
"So it is, World-Honored One!

If I have entered meditative concentration, even if someone possessed of great supernormal power were to take ten billion sets of four continents to make a single great drum, and take Mount Sumeru to make a single great mallet, and while I am in concentration, cause a giant man to stand before me holding that great mallet to strike that great drum without ceasing for as long as an eon—even such a sound of the drum would not enter my ears, let alone a distracted mind being able to cause me to emerge."
"If that sound of the drum could ever cause me such affliction as to pull me from my concentration, it would be impossible.
World-Honored One!
The universal and vast nature of the *araṇā-samādhi* attained by me now is just like this."

I have experienced forty thousand samādhis and searched everywhere for those bodhisattvas, yet in the end I could not see them; indeed, I did not perceive even a single person’s sign of coming or going for even a moment.
"So it is, World-Honored One!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, seeking such inconceivable wisdom, would enter into the hells for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges to undergo all manner of sufferings for the sake of each and every sentient being."
"Bhagavān! Because they seek the bodhisattva path, although they undergo manifold sufferings, they do not abandon such profound and inconceivable wisdom.
It is thus, Bhagavān!"

If today my outflows of mind are not yet exhausted, if I have not attained liberation, or if there remains anything among the Buddha-dharmas that I have not yet known, may I remain forever within birth and death in the future, never again abandoning that inconceivable, great, and wondrous vehicle.
Thereupon the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! It is truly as you have said.
You have spoken thus out of faith.”

I cause this body of yours not to enter *nirvāṇa*, so that by means of these roots of goodness, after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in a future world, you shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) who rules the world with the True Dharma, and only thereafter attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
As for the number and types of sentient beings in this present trichiliocosm, would they not be many? Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is.”

Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings in these worlds were endowed with wisdom like Śāriputra, foremost in the understanding of emptiness like Subhūti, and preeminent in ascetic practices like Mahākāśyapa; and suppose such great śrāvakas were to collectively exhaust their knowledge and vision in seeking that bodhisattva for one eon, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons, or even for immeasurable eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—they still would not be able to see him.
If one could see it, such a thing is impossible. Why is this? Subhūti!
Whatever those bodhisattvas do is not within the sphere of activity of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; therefore, those of the two vehicles can never perceive it.
When this Dharma was being taught, eighty-four thousand devas and humans within that assembly all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, while in his own dwelling, reflected thus:
"Now these hundreds of thousands of millions of great bodhisattvas from the ten directions have all assembled here."
"I shall further summon the great assembly of devas to gather like clouds.
Would this be acceptable?

Having thus reflected, Mañjuśrī immediately employed his supernatural powers to miraculously transform eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* of exquisite jewel lotuses, as large as chariot wheels, with stems of pure gold and petals of white silver, adorned with nets of *vaidūrya* and supreme treasures.

Within each of these flowers there were transformed Buddhas and various Bodhisattvas, sitting cross-legged upon lotus pedestals; their bodies were purple-gold in color, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, their majestic virtue towering high as they radiated brilliant light everywhere.

Then that lotus flower ascended to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and all the Brahmā heavens, up to the Peak of Existence.

To speak briefly in this way, throughout this entire trichiliocosm—including ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion sets of four continents, and the celestial palaces of the desire realm and the form realm—there is nowhere that these emanated lotuses do not reach.
From these sites of transformation and the assembly of bodhisattvas, a great sound issued forth, proclaiming throughout the trichiliocosm, and they spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One, sun of clear wisdom, Rarely appears in the world;
Like the udumbara flower, He is even more difficult to encounter.”
The Lion of the Śākyas, the Hero among Men, now appears in this world;
he proclaims the profound and wondrous Dharma to forever uproot the source of all suffering.
Though the heavens possess joy, who can guarantee its permanence?
Driven by karma, one returns to the three miserable realms, once again undergoing manifold sufferings and poisons.
Regarding the various objects of desire one has practiced, craving alone increases;
though there is fundamentally no pleasure in the three realms, the foolish remain steeped in attachment to them.
Having already attained the supreme rarity— namely, the appearance of the Buddhas—
how can those who are foolish and heedless fail to perceive that suffering is not yet severed?
You all should quickly seek to see the Buddha and hear the True Dharma.
If the Sage has already entered nirvana, though one regrets, it is difficult to catch up.
The net of Māra is deeply fearsome; you have been negligent and are now ensnared—when will there ever be a time for liberation?
Only those who seek the Buddha-dharma, you shall be the sustenance for sentient beings;
you all must quickly seek the thirty-two wondrous marks.
The Buddha can save the world; there is nothing else upon which one may rely.
The Hero of the World is most rare; his great compassion is beyond measure.
For immeasurable billions of eons, his conduct has been unfathomable;
having accumulated merit and wisdom, he has perfected himself as the Lion of the Śākyas.
He proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma, Profound and difficult to perceive.
Wherein are there sentient beings, Or self, person, and life-span?
Thus he shatters the view of permanence; Once severed, nothing remains.
Having relinquished all signs, he speaks this for the sake of sentient beings.
He proclaims the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), wherein the mental activities of the world have ceased;
it is solely that which is empty and signless, wishless, and without volitional action.
Space is fundamentally formless; it neither arises nor ceases, neither comes nor goes—this is what the wise have taught.
It is inexhaustible and unproduced, primordially pure and non-existent.
No characteristics can be seen, and no thoughts can express it.
Sentient beings are fundamentally unborn; how then can one speak of death?
In quiescent extinction there are no sentient beings; where, then, do sentient beings abide?
Speech and sound are used to expound the Dharma, yet the Dharma does not abide in speech and sound, nor can it be found in written characters; thus has the World-Honored One taught.
Though one searches everywhere throughout all realms, one does not perceive wind, water, or fire.
The ground is likewise without discrimination; this is what the eye of wisdom proclaims.
Form, sensation, and perception, volition and consciousness are like empty space;
though they are conventionally called the five aggregates, in reality there is no accumulation.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, And the mind— these and all other faculties—
Though said to be empty by nature, Even emptiness cannot be apprehended.
Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, As well as all various phenomena,
These arise from conceptual discrimination, yet the essence of discrimination is empty and quiescent.
The realm of desire, the realm of form, and those heavens of the formless realm—
all are said to be like illusions and transformations, deceptive and not real.
"In this way, all these World-Honored Ones preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
those who wish to escape from all sufferings should quickly take refuge in the Great Teacher.
When those emanated Buddhas spoke this verse, it was heard throughout this entire trichiliocosm.

Ninety-six billion devas of the desire and form realms attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; twenty thousand sons of gods grew weary of and renounced all desires; thirty-two thousand sons of gods all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and ten thousand sons of gods who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the immeasurable, boundless, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of great assemblies of devas, who had been summoned by that manifested Tathāgata, all gathered like clouds in an instant at the place where Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was.
They prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Taking celestial flowers and fragrances—namely, utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, māndārava, and mahāmāndārava flowers—as well as various flower garlands, powdered incense, and unguents, they scattered them over the World-Honored One and performed other offerings.
Furthermore, with various kinds of celestial and exquisite musical sounds, they sang praises that filled the entirety of space.

At that time, the great assembly was so numerous as to be beyond calculation; it completely filled these four continents such that there was not even a space the size of a staff-tip that was not pervaded by them.
These devas and humans, endowed with great majesty and virtue, scattered various flowers that filled the four continents, piling up to the knees.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 102; *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 103.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Two: Revealing the True Meaning; The Thirty-sixth Assembly of the Son of Heaven Sudhīmat, Part Two.

At that time, within the great assembly was a preeminent deva, namely the Son of Heaven Sudhīmat, the Son of Heaven Praśāntamati, and the Son of Heaven Hrīvyavatrāpin, together with ninety-six billion such sons of heaven. All of them were practicing the path of the bodhisattva, and they all went together to the place where Mañjuśrī was, arriving outside his gate and circumambulating him seven times to the right.
Having circumambulated [the Buddha] seven times, he then rained down celestial *mandārava* flowers.
The falling rain of flowers completely covered the void to a height of ten *yojanas*, forming a flower-canopy pavilion shaped like a precious stūpa.
Then Mañjuśrī took this flower platform and made an offering to the World-Honored One.

Having made the offering, he immediately employed his supernormal powers to cause a network of flowers to completely cover the void of all lands within this trichiliocosm. The radiance of these flowers shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm, making it all brilliantly and intensely bright, and furthermore, they rained down celestial māndārava flowers.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, serene, composed, and dignified, emerged from the vihāra; by means of his supernatural power, he caused a magnificent seat made of the seven treasures to appear spontaneously upon the ground where he stood, a seat towering and fully adorned with all splendors.
Mañjuśrī composed his countenance, adjusted his robes, and ascended this precious seat.
When the Devaputra Susthitamati saw Mañjuśrī having ascended the precious seat, he immediately prostrated at Mañjuśrī’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
All the devas also prostrated at the feet of Mañjuśrī.
At that time, Mañjuśrī reflected thus:
"Who today is capable of engaging in a dialogue with me before the World-Honored One regarding the profound Dharma?"

Who is the vessel of the Dharma capable of receiving such inconceivable phrases: the phrase that is extremely difficult to realize, the phrase that has no location, the phrase that is without attachment, the phrase that is free from conceptual proliferation, the phrase that is unattainable, the phrase that is ineffable, the phrase that is profound, the phrase that is true reality, the phrase that is unimpeded, the phrase that is indestructible, the phrase that is emptiness, the phrase that is signlessness, the phrase that is wishlessness, the phrase that is suchness, the phrase that is the limit of reality, the phrase that is the realm of phenomena, the phrase that is formless, the phrase that is non-appropriation, the phrase that is non-rejection, the phrase that is the Buddha, the phrase that is the Dharma, the phrase that is the Saṅgha, the phrase that is the fulfillment of wisdom, the phrase that is the equality of the three realms, the phrase that all phenomena are unattainable, the phrase that all phenomena are unborn, the phrase that is the lion, the phrase that is the courageous, and the phrase that is the absence of phrases?
"Having spoken thus, who is there to listen?
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī reflected further:

"Now, here there is only the Devaputra Susthitamati, who has made offerings to many Buddhas in the past, has entered the profound *dharmakṣānti*, and is fully endowed with eloquence; he shall be able to discourse with me on the true meaning before the World-Honored One."
At that time, having reflected thus, Mañjuśrī addressed the Devaputra Susthitamati, saying: "Devaputra!
You have now attained the profound dharma-patience and are further endowed with unimpeded eloquence."
"Shall we now go together with me to the presence of the World-Honored One to discuss such profound and subtle meanings?
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati replied to Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Great Being!"

I speak thus: if one toward me is without speech, does not provide exposition, does not maintain inquiry nor offer response; if there is no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha; if the three vehicles are severed and extinguished; if there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; if there is no union and no dispersal, no opening and no initiating, and no production of sound, being free from all words and letters—only with one who speaks in such a manner shall I engage in discourse.
Mañjuśrī said to the Devaputra Susthitamati: "Devaputra!

When I speak in this way, one is able toward me neither to hear nor to listen, neither to read nor to recite, neither to receive nor to uphold, neither to contemplate nor to mind, neither to grasp nor to reject, and neither to perceive nor to know; such a one does not hear my words, nor does he speak them for others."

Why is this so? Because the Bodhi of all Buddhas is fundamentally without words or letters, without mind and free from mind, and without any awakening; though it is spoken of by way of provisional names, even those names are empty.
Susthitamati spoke again: "O Great Being!
For now, please speak for the sake of these sons of the gods; these sons of the gods desire to hear what you, Great Being, have to say."
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra! I never speak for those who merely wish to listen, nor do I speak for those who merely hear and receive.”
Why is this? For anyone who hears and receives [the teaching] acts out of grasping and attachment.
What constitutes grasping and attachment?
That is to say: attachment to a self, attachment to a person, attachment to a sentient being, attachment to a life-span, and attachment to a soul.
Because of such grasping and attachment, there is listening and receiving; one should know that through such listening and receiving, they abide within three kinds of bonds.
What are the three fetters?
First, the fetter of viewing a self; second, the fetter of viewing sentient beings; third, the fetter of viewing phenomena.
O Son of Heaven!
If one listens to the Dharma without these three kinds of fetters of views, it should be known that such a person abides in the three kinds of purity.
What are the three purities?

First, not seeing oneself, not conceptualizing, not reflecting upon, and not realizing; second, not seeing the speaker, not conceptualizing, not reflecting upon, and not realizing; third, not seeing what is spoken, not conceptualizing, not reflecting upon, and not realizing.
"O Son of Heaven!
These are what are called the three kinds of purity.
O Son of Heaven!"
"If there are those who can listen in this manner, it is listening with equanimity, not with partiality.
At that time, the Devaputra Suvimalavikrāntagāmin praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You have spoken most skillfully."
"O Mahāsattva!
If there is anyone who can speak in such a manner, you should know that this is the teaching of non-retrogression. Mañjuśrī said:
“Cease, O Son of Heaven!
You should not now engage in false conceptualization or discrimination regarding the regression of bodhisattvas. Why is this?
If a bodhisattva were to undergo regression, they would ultimately never be able to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
Because within this awakening (bodhi), there is no dharma of regression.
Susthitamati spoke again:
"Great Being! If it is so, in what place could there be such a turning back?"
Mañjuśrī said: “O Devaputra!

You should know that there is regression because of desire; there is regression because of hatred; there is regression because of delusion; there is regression because of craving for existence; there is regression because of ignorance; and even so, there is regression because of being born from the twelve links of dependent origination within saṃsāra.”
There is regression from causes; there is regression from views; there is regression from names;
there is regression from forms; there is regression from the desire realm; there is regression from the form realm;
there is regression from the formless realm; and there is regression from the practice of the śrāvakas.
"Reversal" refers to turning back from the practice of the pratyekabuddhas;

it is turning back from conceptual discrimination, turning back from attachment, turning back from signs, turning back from grasping at signs, turning back from the view of annihilationism, and turning back from the view of eternalism. From...
There is regression because of grasping; there is regression because of relinquishing; there is regression because of the notion of a self;
there is regression because of the notion of a sentient being; there is regression because of the notion of a life-span;
there is regression because of the notion of a person; there is regression because of the notion of a *pudgala*; there is regression because of volition...
There is regression because of conceptualization; there is regression because of bondage; there is regression because of inversion.

There is regression because of the view of self; there is regression because of the sixty-two views rooted in the view of self; there is regression because of the hindrances; there is regression because of the aggregates; there is regression because of the sense bases; there is regression because of the elements.
Because of the notion of a Buddha, there is regression; because of the notion of the Dharma, there is regression; because of the notion of the Saṃgha, there is regression.

Likewise, even up to the notions: "I shall become a Buddha," "I shall preach the Dharma," "I shall deliver sentient beings," "I shall destroy Māra," and "I shall attain wisdom"—because of all such notions, there is regression.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

If one can refrain from discriminating the ten powers of the Tathāgata, refrain from discriminating the four fearlessnesses, refrain from discriminating the eighteen unique qualities, refrain from discriminating all faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path; refrain from discriminating the various marks and signs of excellence, refrain from discriminating the adornment of the Buddha-land, refrain from discriminating śrāvakas, refrain from discriminating bodhisattvas, and even refrain from discriminating all that leads to regression—this is called non-regression.
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Great Being! If this is so, in what place shall one attain non-retrogression?"

Mañjuśrī said: "O Son of Heaven, you should know that one attains non-retrogression by virtue of penetrating the Buddha-wisdom; one attains non-retrogression by virtue of emptiness, non-retrogression by virtue of signlessness, non-retrogression by virtue of wishlessness, non-retrogression by virtue of suchness, non-retrogression by virtue of the dharma-nature, non-retrogression by virtue of the limit of reality, and non-retrogression by virtue of equality."
Susthitamati said: "O Mahāsattva! If it is as you say, then all conceptualization and non-conceptualization are both not different."
Why is this so? Because all [phenomena] arise from conceptualization and discrimination, it can therefore be said that they are subject to regression.
He asked again:
"Is such a retrogression a dharma, or is it a non-dharma? Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is neither existent nor non-existent that such a one thus regresses. Sudhīmat said, "O Mahāsattva!"
“If that is so, from what does one regress?

Mañjuśrī replied, “To say ‘it exists’ or ‘it does not exist’ is a false grasping, an inverted grasping, and an improper grasping. Since that is neither grasping nor non-grasping, for this reason it can be said that one regresses.”
Furthermore, that state of being subject to regression (parihāṇadharman) cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist. Why is this?
If there were regression within the realm of existence or non-existence, that would constitute a logical fallacy.

Why is this? If there were a phenomenon that undergoes retrogression, one would fall into the extreme of eternalism; if there were no phenomenon that undergoes retrogression, one would fall into the extreme of nihilism.
Yet the World-Honored One teaches neither abiding in eternalism nor abiding in nihilism; what the World-Honored One has taught is that which is neither annihilated nor eternal.
"O Devaputra!
If one realizes that what was previously perceived as unreal is indeed so, then it is called neither annihilated nor eternal.
O Devaputra!"
"This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s retrogression.
When this teaching was spoken, ten thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
**Chapter Three: Mañjuśrī’s Miraculous Transformations** At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "O Mahāsattva!..."

"Now we may go together to the place where the Tathāgata resides, to pay him homage, seek his instruction on what we have not yet heard, and also take this opportunity to pose questions according to the Dharma. Mañjuśrī said,
"O Son of Heaven!"
"Do not engage in conceptual discrimination or attachment regarding the Tathāgata.
Sudhīmat said, "O Mahāsattva!"
"Where is the Tathāgata, that you say one should not be attached? Mañjuśrī replied,
"He is right here before us."
Susthitamati said, "If it is so, why do I not see it? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! If you can now not see anything at all, this is what is called truly seeing the Tathāgata. Suvimalaprabha said:
"If you are present before me, why do you admonish me not to grasp the Tathāgata?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Devaputra!..."
"What do you say exists presently before us? Sudhīramati replied,
"The realm of empty space exists."
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so, O Devaputra! That which is called 'Tathāgata' is the realm of empty space."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are equal, like empty space.
Therefore, empty space is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is empty space; empty space and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction.
"O Son of Heaven!
For this reason, if anyone wishes to see the Tathāgata, they should form this contemplation:
realize the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) as it truly is; therein, there is not a single thing that can be differentiated."

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī again, by means of his supernatural power, manifested thirty-two multi-storied jeweled halls complete with carriages and litters. They were square on all four sides with pillars at the four corners, surrounded by railings and interlaced with jeweled nets; they were exceptionally wonderful, lofty and majestic, fully adorned, and most delightful.
Within all the halls and pavilions there were excellent couches made of various jewels, covered with celestial garments.
Upon each couch sat a manifested bodhisattva, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

At that time, after Mañjuśrī had thus universally manifested these matters of adornment, he then proceeded together with those transformed lotus-buddhas and transformed bodhisattvas, as well as this precious palanquin, the multi-storied pavilions, the halls, and the assembly of bodhisattvas, toward the place where the Buddha was. They circumambulated the Buddha seven times, and having also encircled the assembly of bhikṣus, they leapt into the air, their radiance illuminating the entire assembly and the site of enlightenment, and remained stationed on all four sides.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, who had set out later, suddenly arrived at the Buddha’s presence before Sudhāparipṛccha.
Sudhāparipṛccha, the Devaputra, arrived even later and said:
“Great Being!...”
"I set out before you, yet I have arrived later.
By what path did you come to this place? Mañjuśrī replied:

“Devaputra! Even if one were to make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, prostrating and paying homage to them all, one would ultimately never perceive my coming, going, or staying.”
At that time, the emanated bodhisattvas upon the flower pedestals and the assembly of bodhisattvas within the jeweled hall spoke these verses in unison to praise the Tathāgata:

"Having already made offerings to inconceivable World-Honored Ones More numerous than the sands of the Ganges, He practiced with fervor to seek awakening; Therefore, he has transcended all gods and humans."
The Muni of wondrous radiance and sublime form, the hero of the three realms, possesses truly extraordinary marks;
for the sake of the multitude he proclaims the most profound Dharma, that there is no life-span, nor self, nor person.
The World-Honored One practices giving and maintains pure precepts; With patience and diligence, he fully cultivates dhyāna;
His wisdom is pure, transcending the three realms; I pay homage to the Most Victorious Honored One who has reached the other shore.
Those who resolve their minds to seek Bodhi shall receive the sublime offerings of devas and humans;
if they harbor no doubt regarding profound emptiness, they shall succeed to the position of the Great Dharma King who transcends the world.
The Buddhas of the past, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, And all the Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings in the present,
Constantly proclaim that all phenomena are empty, Primordially signless and without fabrication.
The essential nature of sentient beings cannot be apprehended; how, then, could there be birth or death?
Since they originally have neither coming nor going, all phenomena are like empty space.
Just as a conjured person observes various phenomena, which, though manifested, lack any reality;
so too is the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One— all these are empty and deceptive, identical to illusions and dreams.
If one were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with jewels and bestow them as alms upon all people,
yet another could practice patience and skillfully explain emptiness— the latter’s practice of giving would surpass that of the former.
Furthermore, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one makes offerings to the Buddhas, the supreme among gods and humans,
presenting incense, flowers, and various requisites, seeking bodhi and departing from the world.

Having heard such a profound Dharma, wherein there is no sentient being, life, or person—one should know that they have attained clear and pure patience; this is the offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Though one practices giving for countless eons— bestowing clothing, food, elephants, horses, and various treasures—
know that these are not the cause of liberation, for they are based on the notions of a self, a person, and sentient beings.
I take refuge in the Honored One among men who has attained parinirvāṇa, Who rescues and delivers immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings;
All phenomena are empty and fundamentally pure, Thus adorned with the wisdom of liberation.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is extremely rare to encounter; it is difficult to hear the True Dharma and give rise to faith.
A human body is difficult to obtain, yet now you have acquired it. How excellent! O son, practice in accordance with the Buddha-Dharma.
Having already attained the removal of these eight difficulties, Forever severed from narrow confines, dwelling in leisure and seclusion,
And having gained faith and practice in all the true dharmas, One should rouse courageous and vigorous diligence.
Having heard the Dharma, you should contemplate it correctly; do not grasp at the sound as soon as you hear it.
You all should constantly practice in the araṇya, and you will surely and swiftly become heroes among men.
Draw near to virtuous friends and Dharma masters, and you should swiftly distance yourself from all evil companions.
Maintain an attitude of equanimity toward all sentient beings, and take great care not to give rise to the mind of self and others.
Always delighting in much learning and upholding the prohibitive precepts, Abandoning home and dwelling among the forest trees;
Using aged medicine to treat illness without feigning virtue, And constantly begging for food while accepting robes made of discarded rags.
All conditioned phenomena are themselves unconditioned; they are equal in their single characteristic, like a mirage.
If one realizes the limit of reality and perceives suchness, one will swiftly accomplish the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
One should contemplate the five aggregates as being like an illusion, And the internal and external sense bases as being like empty huts.
The World-Honored One has always taught such a Dharma; Regarding phenomena as equal to these, do not give rise to attachment.
Greed and hatred are empty by their very nature; ignorance and pride arise from conceptual discrimination.
Those dharmas have already ceased and are now non-existent; one who knows thus shall attain Buddhahood.
When these emanated bodhisattvas had spoken this verse,
twenty-two thousand beings within that assembly all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Five hundred bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and their minds liberated, attained liberation of mind.
Three hundred bhikṣuṇīs, free from dust and defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye.

Seven thousand upāsakas and upāsikās, as well as twenty-five thousand devaputras, were likewise freed from dust and defilement, and their Dharma-eyes became pure. Furthermore, three hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Thereupon, the great earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways: namely, it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; and so it was likewise for roaring, rising, awakening, and the rest.
Chapter Four: Destroying Māra. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By whom has this auspicious sign been manifested?”
They were able to cause the great earth of this trichiliocosm to quake in six ways.

Furthermore, the various bodhisattvas upon the lotus thrones within these precious palanquins and halls emitted great radiance that illuminated this assembly, as they expounded such subtle and profound Dharma.
Furthermore, he caused an immeasurable number of billions of devaputras to assemble, and another billion bodhisattvas and others also gathered there.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This is due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, by which he has manifested such wondrous adornments and caused the bodhisattvas and devas to gather like clouds."
Why is this so? Śāriputra, it is because Mañjuśrī and the Devaputra Susthitamati,

leading a great assembly, wish to come to my presence to inquire about this Dharma-gate of the Samādhi that Shatters and Scatters All Māras, in order to fully accomplish all inconceivable and profound Buddha-dharmas.
Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If this is so, for what cause and condition do I, though observing this assembly, ultimately not see that Mañjuśrī?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You should wait for a moment.

Mañjuśrī has already brought about great ruin and decline for all the Māras, all the hosts of Māras, and all the palaces of Māras. The miraculous transformations he performs are most wondrous and magnificent; he is approaching my dwelling, and you shall see them for yourself."
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī entered the Samādhi of Shattering and Dispelling All Māras.

By the power of this samādhi, at that very moment, the ten billion Māra palaces within the trichiliocosm became dilapidated, dark, and as if on the verge of collapse; their transformations having manifested, they were stripped of all majestic splendor. This caused all the Māras to find no pleasure in their abodes, each seeing himself as decrepit, emaciated, and walking with the aid of a staff, while the celestial maidens were transformed into old women.
When all the Māras saw this event, their hearts were filled with great sorrow and the hair on their bodies stood on end; struck with terror, they thought:

"What strange and miraculous transformation is this that makes both our internal and external conditions so inauspicious? Could it be that the time of our death has arrived, and we shall suffer the retribution of our dispersal?"
"Is this because the world is about to undergo the calamities of a kalpa of destruction?

While those hosts of māras were thinking thus, Mañjuśrī, by means of his supernatural power, immediately manifested ten billion devaputras standing before the māras and addressed the host of māras, saying:
"Do not be anxious or afraid."
"This is neither your misfortune nor the end of the kalpa. Why is this so?

It is because there is currently present here the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, who has entered the samādhi-dharmaparyāya of 'Shattering and Dispelling All Māras. He possesses great majestic power and spiritual virtue that transcend the world."
"Such is the power of that Great Being’s samādhi; there is nothing else behind it.

When these transformed devaputras spoke these words, all the Māra kings and their demonic hosts, hearing the names of the Great Being Mañjuśrī spoken by the transformed devas, became even more terrified, trembling with anxiety and unease, and all the palaces of Māra shook violently.
Then the various Māra kings replied to the emanated devas, saying, "We only pray that you,
in your benevolence and compassion, will rescue us from this perilous distress.
The emanated sons of the gods spoke again to the Māras, saying:
"Do not fear, do not fear!
You should now proceed with all haste to the presence of the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha. Why is this?
That Buddha-Tathāgata possesses great compassion.

If any sentient beings are tormented by anxiety and fear, they need only go to him for refuge; they shall all receive peace and happiness, and their various anxieties and sufferings will be eliminated.
When the emanated devas had spoken thus, they suddenly vanished from that place.

At that time, all the Māra kings and their demonic hosts, hearing the instruction of the emanated devas, were without exception filled with joy. With one mind, in a mere instant, they all arrived before Śākyamuni Buddha—though frail and leaning on staffs—and spoke with one voice, saying:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
"May we be saved! May we be saved! Deliver us from these strange portents, afflictions, and great calamities.
World-Honored One!
We would rather endure the names of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas than wish to hear the name of that single Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī."
"Why is this? As soon as I heard the name of this Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, I was struck with great terror, as if my own life were being lost.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the various Māras, saying:
“Pāpīyān! Why have you suddenly uttered such words?
For what reason?”

Whatever guidance and benefit for sentient beings the Great Being Mañjuśrī provides is something that hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas have not done in the past, do not do now, and will not do in the future.

It is solely this Mañjuśrī who, throughout the past, future, and present, constantly establishes such great deeds for the sake of sentient beings, placing them within liberation once they have reached maturity; therefore, although you have heard the names of those hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, you should not give rise to suffering or distress, nor should you feel any alarm or fear.
"Why do you say that we have all suddenly become greatly terrified upon hearing the name of Mañjuśrī?
Then those hosts of Māras replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is out of sincere shame for this wretched, aged body, and further driven by fear and trepidation, that I have uttered these words.
World-Honored One!”
"From this day forward, we take refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One; we only pray that you will have compassion for us and restore our original forms.
The Buddha told them, "Wait but a moment."
Once Mañjuśrī has arrived, he will personally remove your shame.

Thereupon Mañjuśrī arose from samādhi and was accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others, surrounding him before and behind. They produced immeasurable hundreds of thousands of subtle and wonderful musical sounds and rained down such immeasurable exquisite flowers—namely, utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers. Possessing great adornment, great supernormal powers, and infinite majesty, they all came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
Have you entered this samādhi that shatters and disperses all māras?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “World-Honored One,
indeed, they have already entered.”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! From which Buddha did you hear this samādhi?"
"For how long must one practice until it is fully perfected? Mañjuśrī replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Before I had originally resolved to attain Bodhicitta, I heard of such a samādhi from the Buddha. He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the name of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, who preached this samādhi so that you might hear it? Mañjuśrī replied,
"World-Honored One!"

I recall that in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mandāravagandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. When he appeared in the world, he proclaimed this samādhi for the dispersal and destruction of all Māras.
"At that time, I first heard it.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"How is this samādhi cultivated and attained?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva fully accomplishes twenty kinds of dharmas, he will be able to attain this Samādhi for Shattering Māra.”
What are the twenty? They are:
first, reviling and disparaging desire to destroy the mind of greed; second, reviling and disparaging anger to destroy the mind of hatred;
third, reviling and disparaging delusion to destroy the mind of ignorance; fourth, reviling and disparaging envy...

1. To revile and destroy envy, thereby destroying the mind of envy; 2. To revile and destroy anger, thereby destroying the mind of anger; 3. To revile and destroy malice, thereby destroying the mind of malice; 4.

To revile and destroy the mind of jealousy, thereby destroying the mind of jealousy; 5. To revile and destroy pride, thereby destroying the mind of pride; 6. To revile and destroy the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), thereby destroying the mind of the hindrances;

7. To revile and destroy feverish affliction, thereby destroying the mind of affliction; 8. To revile and destroy conceptualization, thereby destroying the mind of conceptualization; 9. To revile and destroy all views, thereby destroying the mind of views.
Tenth, the censure and destruction of conceptualization to break the mind of conceptualization; eleventh, the censure and destruction of grasping at objects to break the mind of grasping;
twelfth, the censure and destruction of attachment to break the mind of attachment; thirteenth, the censure and destruction of various marks to break the mind of marks;
fourteenth, the censure and destruction of existing phenomena to break the mind of existence; fifteenth, the censure and destruction...

16. Criticizing and disparaging the eternal dharma to destroy the mind that clings to permanence; 17. Criticizing and disparaging the doctrine of annihilation to destroy the mind that clings to annihilation; 18.

Criticizing and disparaging the aggregates (*skandha*) to destroy the mind that clings to the aggregates; 19. Criticizing and disparaging the sense bases (*āyatana*) to destroy the mind that clings to the sense bases;
20. Criticizing and disparaging the elements (*dhātu*) to destroy the mind that clings to the elements; 21. Criticizing and disparaging the three realms to destroy attachment to the three realms.
“O Bhagavan, it is because the mind [is thus].
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, possessing twenty dharmas, ultimately achieves such a samādhi.”
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas which, when fully practiced by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, enable them to attain this samādhi.
What are these four?”

First, establishing mental activity that is pure, disciplined, and supple; second, a mental nature that is sincere and straightforward, free from all guile and crookedness; third, a mind free from攀缘 (pān-luán-yán, clinging/fixation) that enters into profound *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to the Dharma); fourth, the ability to give away everything, both internal and external.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the samādhi.
World-Honored One,
there are further four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can attain samādhi.
What are the four? First, ultimate and profound faith; second, the accomplishment of truthful speech; third, constant delight in secluded places; and fourth, non-apprehension of all signs.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills and accomplishes this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves and attains this samādhi. What are these four?
First, associating with virtuous friends; second, always knowing contentment; third, sitting alone in contemplation; fourth, not delighting in clamor and vulgarity.
These are the four dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva, bring about the accomplishment of samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas which, when accomplished by a bodhisattva, enable the attainment of this samādhi. What are these four?
First, the precept of non-destruction; second, the precept of non-violation; third, the precept of non-reliance; and fourth, the precept of not seeking recompense.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills and achieves samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas that a bodhisattva accomplishes to attain this samādhi. What are these four?
First, abandoning the mind of a śrāvaka; second, distancing oneself from the mind of a pratyekabuddha; third, abiding in the patience of a bodhisattva; fourth, not forsaking sentient beings.
These are the four dharmas that a bodhisattva must fulfill to achieve this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas which, when accomplished by a bodhisattva, enable them to attain this samādhi. What are these four?
First, cultivating emptiness and relinquishing the self; second, being signless and detached from signs; third, being wishless and eliminating wishes; fourth, relinquishing all that is possessed.
"These are the four dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva, enable one to attain samādhi.
'World-Honored One!
At that time, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maṇḍāravagandha spoke this Dharma-gate for Dispelling and Scattering All Māras, I heard it from that Buddha and first began its practice.'"
Next, there was another Buddha named Sarvaratnavidyutādityacandraprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; at that time, I fully accomplished [the path] under him.
"When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught this gate, ten thousand bodhisattvas within that assembly all attained the accomplishment of this samādhi-gate.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!"
Now this Mañjuśrī has been able to accomplish such a Samādhi for subduing Māra over a vast period of time.
By the power of this samādhi, he has brought it to pass that Pāpīyān and his host of māras have become white-haired and aged, their physical forms and wills both decayed, even to this extent.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "What do you think?
Do you now say that this Mañjuśrī alone has transformed all these māras in this trichiliocosm into such decrepit old men?"
Śāriputra! You should not now hold such a view. Why is that?

Śāriputra! All the Māras currently existing in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all been thus transformed and destroyed; this is entirely due to the majestic power of Mañjuśrī.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
You should now temporarily withdraw your supernatural power so that those māras may regain their original forms.”
At that time, Mañjuśrī, having received the Buddha’s instruction, addressed the māras, saying:
“O virtuous ones!
Do you truly feel weary of this bodily form?”
The various Māras replied,
"Indeed it is so,
Great Being!"
Mañjuśrī said: "If it is so, you too should now feel weary of and distressed by desire, and not be attached to the triple world. The Māras replied:
“Excellent, Great Being!
We have respectfully heard your noble instruction; how could we dare to disobey it?
We only pray that you will briefly lend us your majestic power to remove this painful shame.”
Mañjuśrī then withdrew his supernatural power, causing all the Māras to regain their celestial forms and their former adornments.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Māras, saying: "Pāpīyan!
Regarding all that you have called "eye," what is the eye?
What is the conceptualization of an eye?
Likewise, where is this eye-attachment, and what is this characteristic of an eye?

"This eye is an object of clinging; this eye is an obstacle; this eye is volition; this eye is a self; this eye is a basis; this eye is delight; this eye is conceptual proliferation; this eye is 'mine'; this eye is protection; this eye is mindfulness; this eye is grasping; this eye is relinquishing; this eye is discrimination; this eye is deliberation; this eye is accomplishment; this eye is arising; this eye is ceasing; and so on, up to this eye coming and going."
Such dharmas as these constitute the sphere of your activity and the obstacles of Māra.
As it is with the eye, so it is likewise for the body and the mind.
Furthermore, as it is with forms up to tangibles and mental objects (*dharmas*), they constitute the sphere of your activity and the obstacles of Māra; it is also thus.
You all should understand this as it truly is.
Furthermore, Pāpīyan!
That which you call "eye" is in fact not an eye; it is also without an eye.

One should cultivate the perception of no eye, no attachment to the eye, no characteristic of the eye, no objective support for the eye, no obstruction regarding the eye, no thought of the eye, no "I" in the eye, no dependence on the eye, no craving for the eye, no conceptual proliferation regarding the eye, no "mine" in the eye, no protection of the eye, no mindfulness of the eye, no grasping at the eye, no relinquishing of the eye, no discrimination of the eye, no deliberation regarding the eye, no determination of the eye, no arising of the eye, no cessation of the eye, no going away of the eye, and no coming of the eye.
Such dharmas as these are not within your domain; you cannot exercise mastery over them, for they lack any basis or power in you, and you have no autonomy regarding them, nor do you grasp at them.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the body and the mind;
as it is with visible forms, so it is with tangibles and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
You all should understand this according to reality.

When Mañjuśrī had spoken this Dharma, ten thousand Māras, including Pāpīyān, among the assembly all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and eighty-four thousand members of the Māra’s retinue were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Chapter Five: The Bodhisattva’s Physical Conduct. At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We pray that Mañjuśrī may cause us to behold those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Why is this,
World-Honored One?"
“Such great beings are difficult to encounter.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“You should know that this great assembly is all thirsting with longing, desiring to behold the bodies of all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have come from the ten directions.”
"Now is precisely the right time; you should manifest yourself.

Thereupon, having received this holy instruction, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Dharmacakra, Candraprabha, Māramathana, Gadgadasvara, Vimala, Śānti, Vicaya, and Dharmarājasiṃhanāda, as well as these and countless other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, saying: "O Great Beings!"
"You should now each manifest your own bodies within your palaces, clearly displaying the forms of your respective lands.
After Mañjuśrī had spoken these words, the assembly of bodhisattvas arose from samādhi and each manifested their original bodies, so that the entire great assembly could see them all.

There are some bodhisattvas whose bodies are as tall and vast as Sumeru, the king of mountains; some have bodies eighty-four thousand yojanas in height; some have bodies of one hundred thousand yojanas, or ninety thousand, down to fifty, forty, thirty, or twenty thousand yojanas.
Some have bodies ten thousand yojanas in size, and even some that are five thousand, four thousand, three thousand, or two thousand;
some have bodies one thousand yojanas in size, and even some that are five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, or two hundred.
Some have bodies one hundred yojanas in size, and others fifty, forty, thirty, or twenty;
some have bodies ten yojanas in size, and others five, four, three, two, or even one yojana.
In this manner, there were even some bodhisattvas whose physical dimensions—whether large or small, long or short, broad or narrow—were no different from those of the human beings in this Sahā world.
At that time, this trichiliocosm was so densely filled with the great assembly that there was not even a space as small as the tip of a staff left empty.

Among them were all the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the most part possessed of towering merit and profound wisdom, endowed with majestic power and accomplished in supernatural faculties; they emitted great radiance that illuminated throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddha-worlds in the ten directions. Furthermore, the assembly was completely filled with all those of great majesty and virtue—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—as well as kings of both great and small stature.
At that time, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes so as to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now wish to briefly inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding certain doubts in my mind.
I do not know whether the World-Honored One would deign to listen.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you, resolve your doubts, and bring joy to your heart.”
Mañjuśrī said: “So be it, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will proclaim it for me; I shall listen and receive it.”
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
what is meant by the term ‘bodhisattva-mahāsattva’?”
"What is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "You ask, 'What constitutes a bodhisattva?'"
Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of 'Bodhisattva'?"—
it is because they are able to awaken to and understand all phenomena that they are called Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. Mañjuśrī!
All those phenomena that a bodhisattva awakens to are what is called "verbal expression. Mañjuśrī!
How does a bodhisattva awaken to all phenomena?
This refers to the awakening of the eye, the awakening of the ear, the awakening of the nose, the awakening of the tongue, the awakening of the body,
and the awakening of the mind. Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva awaken to the eye, the ear, and so forth, up to the mind?
Mañjuśrī! This is because a bodhisattva awakens to the fact that the intrinsic nature of those eye-phenomena is empty.
Having awakened in this way, they never give rise to the thought, "I am able to awaken to and know this."
In this way, one awakens to the ear and so forth, up to awakening to the mind; all are empty by their very nature.
Having awakened in this manner, one does not give rise to the thought, "I am able to perceive.
When a bodhisattva has thus awakened to the eye and so forth, they further awaken to the fact that those forms are empty by their own nature.
Having awakened in this way, one does not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to perceive.
Thus, from perceiving sounds up to perceiving mental phenomena (*dharma*), all are empty by their very nature; one likewise does not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to perceive."
This is how a bodhisattva awakens to all dharmas.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva awaken to those five aggregates?"
That is to say, when a bodhisattva perceives that the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) is inherently empty, through such awakening he contemplates signlessness (*animitta*);
through such awakening he contemplates wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); through such awakening he contemplates desirelessness (*anabhilāṣa*);

through such awakening he contemplates tranquility (*śānti*); through such awakening he contemplates detachment (*viveka*); and through such awakening he contemplates non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
There is: because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of substantiality; because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of movement;

because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of arising; because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of coming; because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of going;
because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of reality; because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of a master; because of such...
Because of awakening, one contemplates non-attainment; because of such awakening, one contemplates non-knowing; because of such awakening, one contemplates non-seeing;
because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of a person; because of such awakening, one contemplates the absence of conceptualization;
because of such awakening, one contemplates the ineffable.

Because one awakens in this way, one realizes that awakening is merely a name; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates non-self; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates that which arises from discrimination; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates that which is born of conditions; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates it as being like an illusion; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates it as being like a transformation; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates it as being like a dream; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates it as being like a reflection in a mirror; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates it as being like an echo; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates it as being like a plantain tree; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates its lack of long-term endurance; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates its lack of solidity; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates its falsity; because one awakens in this way, one contemplates its insubstantiality.
Because they awaken in this way, this is called the bodhisattva’s awakening to all phenomena. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to greed, hatred, and delusion?

This means that one awakens to the fact that greed arises from conceptual discrimination, awakens to the fact that hatred arises from conceptual discrimination, and awakens to the fact that delusion arises from conceptual discrimination; furthermore, one awakens to the fact that this conceptual discrimination itself is empty and non-existent, being without substance, without discursive proliferation (*prapañca*), ineffable, and unattainable.
This is how a bodhisattva awakens to all phenomena. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to the three realms?

This means awakening to the fact that the desire realm is devoid of self or person; awakening to the fact that the form realm is without activity; awakening to the fact that the formless realm is empty and non-existent; and awakening to the fact that all three realms are utterly remote and detached.
This is the bodhisattva’s awakening to all phenomena. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to the conduct of sentient beings?

That is to say: awakening to the fact that sentient beings act out of greed; awakening to the fact that sentient beings act out of anger; awakening to the fact that sentient beings act out of ignorance; and awakening to the fact that sentient beings act with equal proportions of these three poisons.
Having awakened thus, he realizes it thus, explains it thus, teaches and transforms sentient beings thus, and causes them to attain liberation thus.
This is the bodhisattva’s awakening to all dharmas.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken all sentient beings?
It means awakening to the fact that all sentient beings exist as mere names; apart from those names, there are no distinct sentient beings."
Therefore, all sentient beings are one sentient being, and that one sentient being is all sentient beings; thus, these sentient beings are non-sentient beings.
If one can be thus without conceptual discrimination, this constitutes the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s awakening to all dharmas.
Furthermore, how does one awaken to all dharmas?
Because they are able to awaken to the bodhisattva path in this way, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to awaken to all dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning further, spoke in verse:
“Awakening to the eye and the ear, Their very nature is eternally empty and quiescent.”
Not claiming "I am able to awaken" is what defines a bodhisattva.
Contemplating the nose and the tongue, seeing that their fundamental nature is non-existent,
and not discriminating "I am awakening"— this is what defines a bodhisattva.
Observing the body with wisdom, one also realizes that the mind is naturally so;
having realized this, one explains it to others—such a person is called a bodhisattva.
Regarding forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and all sensory objects that the mind delights in,
One who realizes that the nature of things is empty is called a bodhisattva.
One who realizes that form, sensation, perception, volitional formations,
and consciousness are all like illusions is called a bodhisattva.
The aggregation of the five aggregates is like a dream;
awakening to the fact that they possess not a single characteristic and not discriminating "I know" is what is called a bodhisattva.
Neither arising nor emerging, without action and without speech—this is the state of a bodhisattva.
Thus it is said that there are only names, and those names are not things either.
The awakening of desire and hatred arises from conceptual construction;
yet that construction has no intrinsic substance and is ultimately and forever empty of itself.
Delusion also arises from conceptualization, and conceptualization arises from causes and conditions;
based on these, various views arise, yet no such views can be found.
One awakens to the emptiness of the three realms, realizing that nothing possesses any true reality.
Being unshakable therein, one is thus called a bodhisattva.
The realm of desire is not established; it all arises from conceptual discrimination.
The realms of form and formlessness—none of them are solid or secure.
The conduct of all sentient beings, including greed, hatred, and delusion, the wise fully comprehend.
All sentient beings are, in truth, but a single sentient being.
The wise have no perception; they do not think of those sentient beings.
The arising of all phenomena occurs entirely due to inversion;
one who perceives that inversion knows the true nature of inversion.
Their wisdom is most subtle; they do not grasp at sounds.
Having awakened, they have no attachments; therefore, they are called Bodhisattvas.
They can relinquish their own physical bodies and ultimately have no place of reliance.
One who thus awakens to reality is called a bodhisattva.
Having reached the other shore of ethical discipline, they do not even think of that "other shore.
Awakening to the suchness of the dharmas of ethical conduct, they are neither born nor extinguished.
With a mind of loving-kindness pervading all sentient beings,
yet perceiving no mark of a "sentient being," one awakens to the limit of those beings, declaring it only through provisional words.
With courageous and great diligence, the profound mind grows weary of the conditioned.
Seeing the three realms as empty and void, one realizes unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Constantly entering subtle and wondrous dhyāna, free from attachment and without dependence,
without dwelling and without grasping at objects— such is the concentration of the wise.
With the sword of sharp wisdom, one cuts through the bonds of all views;
observing the nature of the dharma-realm, there is neither cutting nor wounding.
If a person truly awakens to and realizes all phenomena as they truly are, [they will not be harmed].
"Benefiting sentient beings at the appropriate time—this is what is called a bodhisattva.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, fascicle 103; *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, fascicle 104.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Refuting the Characteristics of a Bodhisattva. The Third Part of the Thirty-sixth Assembly: The Discourse of the Devaputra Susīma. Chapter Six:
Refuting the Characteristics of a Bodhisattva. At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, regarding a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved their mind [upon enlightenment], by what meaning is it called ‘the first resolution of the mind’?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the arising of all perceptions within the three realms in this manner, one may say that they have generated the initial resolve for the first time.
Mañjuśrī! This is called the bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind.”
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of desire, this is the first production of the thought of enlightenment; if a mind of hatred arises, this is the first production of the thought of enlightenment; if a mind of delusion arises, this is the first production of the thought of enlightenment.”
"What the World-Honored One has spoken— could it not be that this refers to the initial arousal of the mind?
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī,
"Great Being!..."

If those bodhisattvas who give rise to greed, anger, and delusion are called "those who have first resolved their minds," then all ordinary beings bound by every fetter would likewise be called bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds.
"Why is this? Because those ordinary worldlings have constantly given rise to such minds of the three poisons—greed, anger, and delusion—from the past until now. Mañjuśrī said to Sudhīmat:
“Devaputra! As for your statement that all ordinary beings have constantly been able to give rise to these three poisons since time immemorial, this meaning is not so. Why is this?
The mental power of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is weak and inferior, and thus they cannot give rise to this greed, hatred, and delusion.

Only the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, all Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) are able to give rise to this greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, ordinary beings cannot give rise to them.
Susthitamati said: "O Great Being! Why do you now speak in such a manner?"
"May the assembly in this gathering neither recognize nor understand, thereby falling into the net of doubt, which is truly terrifying.
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Sudharmamati:
"O Son of Heaven!..."
What do you think?
When a bird flies back and forth through the air, does that bird leave footprints in the empty sky?
Is there any movement involved?
"Is there no practice of exertion?
Sudhīramati replied, "It is not that there is no practice of exertion."
Mañjuśrī said: “So it is, so it is, O Devaputra!”
For this reason, I have made this statement:
if there are those capable of giving rise to desire, hatred, and delusion, it is only those Buddhas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas who are able to give rise to them.
"Son of Heaven, you should know!
That which has no basis of reliance is called 'setting forth'; that which has no grasping or attachment is called 'setting forth.
Since there is neither reliance nor grasping, this absence of verbal formulation is what is termed 'setting forth. This is non-existence."
The phrase "discrimination" is called "setting forth"; the phrase "that which is unarisen" is called "setting forth"; the phrase "that which is unreal" is called "setting forth";
the phrase "that which is not a thing" is called "setting forth"; the phrase "that which does not come" is called "setting forth";
the phrase "that which does not go" is called "setting forth"; the phrase "that which is without birth" is called...
To set forth is to be without objects of dependence; this is called setting forth. To set forth is to be without realization;
this is called setting forth. To set forth is to be without contention; this is called setting forth. To set forth is to be without thought;
this is called setting forth. To set forth is to be without disintegration; this is called setting forth. To set forth is to be without words; this is called setting forth. This is not...
To break the verse is called "setting forth"; this is the wordless phrase, which is called "setting forth"; this is the phrase of non-attachment, which is called "setting forth";
this is the phrase of non-abiding, which is called "setting forth"; this is the phrase of non-appropriation, which is called "setting forth";
this is the phrase of non-rejection, which is called "setting forth"; this is the phrase of non-extraction, which is called "setting forth."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know that this is the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind of awakening.
O Son of Heaven!"

If a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind does not feel attachment toward any such dharmas, does not conceptualize them, does not see or know them, does not hear or recognize them, neither grasps nor rejects them, and neither gives rise to nor extinguishes them, this is what is called the true resolution of the mind.
“O Son of Heaven!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can rely upon such a dharma-realm, such equality, such reality-limit, and such skillful means, then those [afflictions] such as greed, hatred, and delusion will arise.”

Furthermore, if one is indeed able to rely [on the path] in this manner, then the eye, ear, mind, and so forth will arise, and the grasping at forms up to the grasping at consciousness and so forth will arise.

In this way, all views arise; ignorance and craving arise; even the factors of the twelve links of dependent origination arise; the various matters of the five desires arise; attachment to the three realms arises; the view of self arises; the view of "mine" arises; the sixty-two views, rooted in the view of self, arise; the notion of a Buddha arises; the notion of Dharma arises; the notion of Saṅgha arises; the notion of self arises; the notion of others arises; the notion of earth arises; the notion of water arises; the notion of fire arises; the notion of wind arises; the notion of space arises; the notion of consciousness arises; the four perversions arise; the four stations of consciousness arise; the five hindrances arise; the eight wrong paths arise; the nine afflictions arise; and the ten unwholesome courses of action arise.

"Son of Heaven, you should know that I shall now speak of the essentials: all conceptualizations, all bases of conceptualization, all verbal expressions, all marks, all modes of engagement, all aspirations, all attachments, all thoughts, all mental intentions, and all obstacles—these are all that a bodhisattva must bring forth."
"You should know this as it truly is, O Son of Heaven!
For this reason, if you can now remain without attachment and without conceptualization toward these dharmas, this is what is called 'truly setting forth.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
That you are now able to fully proclaim for the sake of all bodhisattvas such a meaning of the initial resolve is truly remarkable. Mañjuśrī!
It is because you have already, in the past, made offerings to immeasurable, boundless, and more numerous than the sands of the Ganges Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, that you are able to speak thus.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding these two matters now spoken of by Mañjuśrī—the initial arousal of the bodhicitta by a bodhisattva and the attainment of the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas—are they equal and without distinction?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said, Śāriputra.”
In the past, the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction, saying: "Māṇava!
In the future, after the passing of incalculable kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Śāriputra! At that time, I also did not depart from this mind to attain the patience of non-arising.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!"
“You should know that the meaning of the initial resolve of all those bodhisattvas is no different from what Mañjuśrī has said.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, all these are initial arousals of the mind. Why is this?
As the World-Honored One has said, all initial arousals are non-arousals; that which is a non-arousal is precisely the Bodhisattva’s first arousal of the mind.

When this Dharma was being taught, twenty-three thousand bodhisattvas realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); five thousand bhikṣus attained liberation through the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) regarding all dharmas; and sixty billion devaputras became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Now this Mañjuśrī has once again performed what is difficult to perform, by proclaiming such a profound Dharma-gate and bringing great benefit to all sentient beings."
Mañjuśrī said to Kāśyapa: "Venerable Kāśyapa!
I truly do not perform any difficult task."
Why is this? Because all dharmas are without action; furthermore, there is no that which has been done, is being done, or will be done. O Mahākāśyapa!
Regarding all phenomena, I neither act nor refrain from acting; the meaning is likewise so.
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa, among sentient beings, I have neither those to be liberated nor those who are bound.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are non-existent. Kāśyapa!
"How is it that you speak such words before the World-Honored One as 'I can do what is difficult to do'?
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa!
I have done nothing; be careful not to say that I can do what is difficult to do."
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa!
I truly do not create it.
It is not only I who do not create it; the Tathāgata does not create it, the Pratyekabuddha does not create it, and the Arhat also does not create it.
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa!
What kind of people are able to perform what is difficult to do?
If one wishes to speak correctly of those who can perform what is difficult to do, they are none other than all infants and ordinary worldlings.
To speak in such a manner is called speaking well. Why is this?

Because for all Tathāgatas, there is nothing that has been attained, is being attained, or will be attained; even all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have no attainment whatsoever, whereas all those ordinary worldlings attain everything.
Then Mahākāśyapa again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "O Great Being!
