What is it that all Buddhas do not attain?"

Mañjuśrī said: "All Buddhas do not apprehend a self, do not apprehend a *pudgala*, do not apprehend a sentient being, do not apprehend a life-span, do not apprehend a person (*puruṣa*), do not apprehend annihilation, do not apprehend permanence, do not apprehend the aggregates (*skandha*), do not apprehend the sense-bases (*āyatana*), do not apprehend the elements (*dhātu*), do not apprehend name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), do not apprehend the desire realm, do not apprehend the form realm, do not apprehend the formless realm, do not apprehend discrimination, do not apprehend reflection, do not apprehend the foundations of mindfulness, do not apprehend dependent origination, do not apprehend inversion, do not apprehend greed, hatred, and delusion, do not apprehend this world, do not apprehend that world, do not apprehend a self, do not apprehend 'mine,' and so on, up to not apprehending any phenomena whatsoever."
Venerable Kāśyapa!
In this way, all these dharmas are neither sequentially obtained nor lost; they are neither bound nor liberated, neither grasped nor discarded, neither near nor far.

Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should awaken to and understand this Dharma-gate: if the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not attain anything at all, then those [dharmas] are neither dharmas nor have they been heard.

Ordinary persons attain all of these; therefore, ordinary persons are able to perform what is difficult to do—this is not performed by Buddhas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Arhats; this is precisely what is called "the work of ordinary persons."
Kāśyapa asked again, "What is it that you do? Mañjuśrī replied:

“Constructing [the notions of] annihilation and permanence; constructing [the notion of] defilement as a basis; constructing recollection and grasping or rejecting; and even constructing all such conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), such as the mental discriminations that accord with high and low states.”
Therefore, Venerable Kāśyapa!

Regarding these dharmas, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perform no action; there is nothing they have done, are doing, or will do. It is only those ordinary worldlings who are capable of performing what is difficult to do.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘the patience of non-arising’ (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), why is it named the patience of non-arising?”
World-Honored One!
For what further reason is it called the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas"?
How does a bodhisattva attain this dharma of patience?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "In truth, there is no person who attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) within the phenomena of arising.
What is called 'attaining' is merely a matter of words and names."
Why is this? Because the dharma of non-arising is unattainable and free from objective conditions, one does not "attain" the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).
Since one attains that which is unattainable—neither gaining nor losing—it is therefore said that one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
That which is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is the patience that all phenomena are without arising;
it is the patience that all phenomena are without coming; it is the patience that all phenomena are without going; [it is the patience] with respect to the One...
Because of such patient acceptance that all phenomena are without self; because of such patient acceptance that all phenomena are without a master;
because of such patient acceptance that all phenomena are without grasping; because of such patient acceptance that all phenomena are without relinquishing;
because of such patient acceptance that all phenomena are without anything possessed; because of such patient acceptance that all phenomena are without reality;
Because all phenomena are without equal, one thus accepts them with patience; because all phenomena are unequaled with the unequaled, one thus accepts them with patience;
because all phenomena are without comparison, one thus accepts them with patience; because all phenomena are unstained like space, one thus accepts them with patience;
because all phenomena are indestructible, one thus accepts them with patience; because all phenomena are without interruption...
Because of such patience, all phenomena are without defilement; because of such patience, all phenomena are without purity;
because of such patience, all phenomena are empty; because of such patience, all phenomena are signless;
because of such patience, all phenomena are wishless; because of such patience, all phenomena are free from greed and hatred.
Because one thus endures ignorance; because one thus endures the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; because one thus endures the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
and because one thus endures the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena.

Because all phenomena are thus: without discrimination, without association, without recollection, without conceptual proliferation, without thought, without agency and without power, weak, inferior, and deceptive; like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a reflected image, like a plantain tree, like a mass of foam, and like a water bubble—such is their acceptance.

That which is to be endured is itself nothing that can be endured; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma, but is merely spoken of as such by means of names. Yet even those names cannot be apprehended, for their intrinsic nature is inherently detached.

Thus, regarding this patience of speech, one enters with faith and understanding; being without delusion or doubt, without alarm or fear, and without agitation or sinking, it pervades the entire body. One then dwells in right reception and acts, neither perceiving a self nor abiding anywhere.

Mañjuśrī! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the forbearance of the non-arising of all phenomena, up to and including the point where they do not engage in any conceptualizations whatsoever.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called 'patience' (kṣānti), what constitutes patience?"
"Because one is not destroyed by sense objects even unto the end, it is called 'patience' (kṣānti).
Then, the Devaputra Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī: "O Mahāsattva!"
"What is it that is not destroyed by sense objects? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
Regarding what is called the eye: by what dharma is the eye destroyed?
It is said that pleasant forms (*śubha-rūpa*) and unpleasant forms (*aśubha-rūpa*) are what destroy the eye.
Just as forms destroy the eye, so too do sounds destroy the ear, and so on, up to mental objects (*dharma*) destroying the mind (*manas*).
"Son of Heaven!

If a bodhisattva sees forms with the eye, they do not grasp at their signs nor become attached to their beauty; they do not discriminate or conceptualize them, nor do they feel desire or aversion. Knowing that their fundamental nature is empty and devoid of thought or perception, they are not harmed or defeated by various forms;
this applies even to mental objects and the mind."
"O Son of Heaven!
If one’s six sense-faculties are without attachment, without bondage, without destruction, and without injury, such a bodhisattva dwells in the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).

Because they dwell in the patience of dharmas, they do not engage in any discrimination regarding all phenomena: there is no arising or non-arising, no outflow or non-outflow, no wholesome or unwholesome, and no conditioned or unconditioned. They do not dwell upon worldly or world-transcending phenomena; they neither discriminate nor reflect upon them. This is what is called the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*)."

When this Dharma was being taught, sixty-three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Great Being! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva initiate superior practice, so as to transcend and progressively enter the various stages?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! Who among them is able to initiate superior practice such that one could say there is a 'leaping transition' between the stages?"
Susthitamati said: "O Great Being!
Do you not know that the practices of the Bodhisattvas are supreme and increasingly sublime, even transcending them until they fulfill the ten stages?"
Mañjuśrī said to Sudhīmat: “It is not so, O Devaputra!”
"I have heard the Buddha say that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations.
Do you not believe this? Sudhīmat replied:
"O Mahāsattva! Since these are the sincere words of the World-Honored One, who would dare not believe them? Mañjuśrī said:
“Son of Heaven!
Just as with that illusory person and the illusion itself, could there be any superior practice, transcendence, or progression, even unto the fulfillment of the ten stages?
Suvimalamatir replied:
"No, Great Being! Mañjuśrī said.
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
If a phantom person and the power of illusion were able to transcend and enter [the stages], then we too would likewise transcend and enter."
Why is this? As the World-Honored One has taught, all dharmas are like illusions and transformations; therefore, there is no transition or entry.
O Devaputra!
Therefore, if one says that there is a transition between the stages, that is not a transition.
I also do not say that there is a transition between the stages. Why is this so?
Because all dharmas do not transition into one another, a dharma cannot transition into another dharma.

That is to say, form does not transition into feeling, feeling does not transition into form; perception does not transition into formations, formations do not transition into perception; consciousness does not transition into form, and form does not transition into consciousness.
"O Son of Heaven!
In this manner, even regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), one should formulate fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) in this way:
'Furthermore, the eye does not enter into the ear, nor does the ear enter into the eye.'"
The nose does not enter into the tongue, nor does the tongue enter into the nose.
The body does not enter into the mind, nor does the mind enter into the body.

Why is this so? Because all phenomena have distinct natures that operate within their own respective domains; they are dull, ignorant, and devoid of conscious awareness. They are like grass, trees, walls, tiles, and stones; like reflections in a mirror; like illusions and transformations. They cannot be perceived or touched, being of a single mark which is markless.
For this reason, all phenomena have no transcending or shifting; they neither emerge nor enter, neither go nor come.

O Son of Heaven, you should know that if Bodhisattvas understand and realize in this way that all those phenomena have no transcending or shifting, they will no longer have further conceptual distinctions regarding the stages (*bhūmi*). There is no entering the path, no abandoning of stages, and no regression; within that transcending and shifting of awakening (*bodhi*), there is no loss or extinction.
Why is this? If a person views those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) as being real, they will not transcend or transform them. Why is that?
Because the nature of all dharmas is fundamentally pure,
O Devaputra!
This is called the bodhisattva’s stage of the transcendent path.
"O Son of Heaven!
It is like a master illusionist who conjures ten-tiered palanquins and palace towers, and immediately causes illusory people to dwell within them.
O Son of Heaven!"
"What do you think?
Does that person’s palace have a fixed location? Sudhīmat replied:
"No, Great Being! Mañjuśrī said.
"It is so, it is so, O Son of Heaven! That one perceives the stages of a bodhisattva as being subject to transcendence and transformation is precisely like this."
Chapter Seven: Refuting the Characteristics of the Two Vehicles, Part One. At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati again asked Mañjuśrī: “O Mahāsattva!
Suppose at some time there is a person who comes to the Great Being seeking to leave the household life; how should the Great Being then respond?
How should he explain the Dharma for leaving the household life and attaining deliverance?
"How does one confer the precepts and instruct in their observance? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
If there should be someone who comes to me seeking to leave the household life, I shall instruct them by saying:
"O sons of good family!
You should not now give rise to the mind of leaving the household life."
"If you do not give rise to the mind of renunciation, I shall teach you the true Dharma of renunciation. Why is this so?
O Devaputra!

If one seeks to leave the household life, one seeks the desire realm, as well as the form realm and the formless realm; furthermore, one seeks the pleasures of the five worldly desires and seeks various matters regarding future retributions.
If a son of good family has something to seek, he does not realize the Dharma; because he does not realize the Dharma, he perceives the mind.
Therefore, O Devaputra, if there is nothing to grasp, that constitutes the realization of the Dharma.

Because one realizes the Dharma, one does not perceive the mind; because one does not perceive the mind, one does not go forth; because one does not go forth, there is no intention to go forth; because there is no intention to go forth, that [intention] does not arise; because it does not arise, there is no birth; because there is no birth, one exhausts suffering; because one exhausts suffering, there is ultimate exhaustion; because there is ultimate exhaustion, there is no further exhaustion; because there is no further exhaustion, it cannot be exhausted; that which cannot be exhausted is space.
"O Son of Heaven!
At that time, I gave such instruction to that son of good family.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"
Furthermore, if there should be someone who comes to me seeking to leave the household life, I shall instruct them with these words:
"O sons of good family!
You should not now give rise to the mind of leaving the household life."
Why is this? Because that mind is unborn and cannot be brought forth; do not, out of a sense of difference, cling to this mind.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
If there should be another person who comes to me seeking to go forth, I would further instruct them, saying:
"O sons of good family!
If you do not now cut off your beard and hair, in that way you will truly have gone forth."
At that time, the Devaputra Susīma again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Great Being! For what reason do you speak in this way?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra! The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma involves nothing to be severed or eliminated.”
Susthitamati asked again: "What is it that is neither severed nor eliminated? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
The dharma of form is neither severed nor eliminated; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither severed nor eliminated.
O Son of Heaven!”
If, moreover, there is someone who thinks:
"I have gone forth by shaving off my hair and beard," you should know that such a person dwells in the mark of self (*ātman*). Because they dwell in the mark of self, they do not perceive equality.

Furthermore, because one sees me, one sees sentient beings; because one sees sentient beings, one sees the hair of the head and beard; and because one sees the hair of the head and beard, the thought of shaving them arises.
O Devaputra!

If one does not perceive the mark of a self, then one does not perceive the mark of another; because there is no mark of another, there is no conceit of "I"; because there is no conceit of "I," there is no sense of "mine"; because there is no sense of "mine," there is no discrimination; because there is no discrimination, there is no agitation; because there is no agitation, there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because there is no conceptual proliferation, there is no grasping or rejecting; because there is no grasping or rejecting, there is no doing or not doing, no ceasing or not ceasing, no separation or union, no decrease or increase, no gathering or dispersing, no thinking or recollecting, and no speaking or verbalizing. This is what is called abiding in reality.
Susthitamati said: "Great Being!
What is the true meaning?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!
That which is called 'reality' is itself empty space; it is this very empty space that is designated as reality."

It is without arising and without ceasing, without decrease and without increase; for this reason, it is said that space is real, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is real, suchness is real, the dharma-realm is real, and the limit of reality is real.
That which is thus real is also not real. Why is this?
Because it cannot be apprehended within that reality, it is called "not real."
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Sudhīmati:
"O Son of Heaven!
If there should be someone who comes to me seeking to go forth from the household life, I shall instruct them to speak as follows:"
"O sons of good family!
If you can now refrain from grasping or becoming attached to that monastic robe, I shall consider you as truly having left the household life. Sudhīramati said:
“Great Being! For what reason do you speak thus? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no grasping at phenomena; whatever they proclaim is not for the sake of attachment.
Thus spoke Susthitamati.
"What is it that is not grasped? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
That is to say: not grasping at form as either permanent or impermanent, up to and including not grasping at consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;
not grasping at the eye as either permanent or impermanent, up to and including not grasping at the mind as either permanent or impermanent;
and not grasping at forms, up to and including not grasping at mental phenomena (*dharma*).
One does not grasp at desire, one does not grasp at hatred, one does not grasp at delusion, and one does not grasp at perversions.
O Devaputra!
In this way, one does not grasp at any phenomena whatsoever, nor does one abandon them; they are neither conjoined nor separated.
"O Son of Heaven!
If one grasps at the kāṣāya, you should know that he possesses great signs of views.
O Son of Heaven!"
Therefore, I say that one does not attain purity or liberation by means of attachment to the kāṣāya.
Why is this so? O Devaputra!
"In the great seat of enlightenment of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
there is no saffron robe. Sudhīmat said,
"O Great Being!"
"What dharma is the kāṣāya? Mañjuśrī replied, "Devaputra!"

As for your question regarding what constitutes the *kāṣāya*: greed is the *kāṣāya*, hatred is the *kāṣāya*, delusion is the *kāṣāya*; causes are the *kāṣāya*, all views are the *kāṣāya*, name-and-form is the *kāṣāya*, conceptualization is the *kāṣāya*, attachment is the *kāṣāya*, grasping at signs is the *kāṣāya*, and speech is the *kāṣāya*. In this way, even up to all dharmas of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), these are all the *kāṣāya*.
If one knows that all phenomena are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and are without volition or thought, this is called being "without the saṃghāṭī.

If there is no saṃghāṭī, then there is nothing; if there is nothing, then there is no defilement; if there is no defilement, then there is no obstruction; and because there is no obstruction, there is also no action—this is what is meant by "deliberation."
Susthitamati said: "Great Being! Regarding what you call 'deliberation,' for what reason is it termed 'deliberation'?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! That which is called 'deliberation' is so called because, within the equality of all phenomena, there is neither increase nor decrease, and neither doing nor non-doing."
"O Son of Heaven!

If one can neither increase nor decrease regarding the Dharma, as the World-Honored One has taught that one should no longer give rise to conceptualization or discrimination, it is therefore called 'deliberation'."
Susthitamati said: "What is meant by 'neither adding nor subtracting'? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! It transcends equality.
Having transcended equality, phenomena cannot be apprehended; that is to say, the past cannot be apprehended, the future cannot be apprehended, and the present cannot be apprehended.”

Those dharmas are not such as they appear; there is no action of increase or decrease, no action of a self (*ātman*), no action of a person (*pudgala*), no action of a sentient being (*sattva*), no action of a life-span (*jīva*), no action of annihilation, and no action of permanence. There is no conceptualization regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*); there is no conceptualization regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Furthermore, there is no thought that "this is the action of observing precepts," "this is the action of breaking precepts," "this is the action of afflictions," "this is the action of purity," "this is the action of attaining the fruit," "this is the action of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)," "this is the action of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*)," "this is the action of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*)," "this is the action of an arhat," or "this is the action of a pratyekabuddha," up to and including: "this is the action of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)," "this is the action of signlessness (*animitta*)," "this is the action of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)," "this is the action of clear liberation (*vidyā-vimukti*)," or "this is the action of detachment from desire."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
All these teachings are spoken for the sake of those unlearned ordinary people who engage in conceptualization and discrimination.

You should know that these are the deluded thoughts and attachments of the most inferior and ignorant people who seek to grasp at phenomena through desire; therefore, the Tathāgata has expounded this teaching on the conceptualization and discrimination of what is done and what is not done in order to sever their attachment.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Susthitamati praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, Great Being!
You have most excellently expounded such a profound Dharma-gate."
At that time, the World-Honored One likewise praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Mañjuśrī!"
"It is well that you are now able to speak in this way.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again to Sudharmamati, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!
Furthermore, if anyone comes to me seeking to leave the household life, I shall instruct them to speak as follows:
"O sons of good family!
If you can now refrain from receiving full ordination, this is what is called true renunciation."
The Well-Established-Mind said:
"Great Being! For what reason do you speak these words?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! As the World-Honored One has taught, there are only two ways of receiving full ordination."
What are these two? First, receiving the correct and equal precepts; second, receiving the deviant and unequal precepts.
Among these, what are the deviant and unequal precepts?

That is to say: falling into the view of a self, falling into the view of a person, falling into the view of a sentient being, falling into the view of a life-span, falling into the view of a soul, falling into the view of annihilationism, falling into the view of eternalism, falling into wrong views, falling into pride, falling into desire, falling into hatred, falling into delusion, falling into the desire realm, falling into the form realm, falling into the formless realm, and falling into grasping and conceptual discrimination.
"O Son of Heaven!

This is a brief explanation of falling into all unwholesome dharmas, falling into following evil associates and falsely grasping at all dharmas, and falling into not knowing the essential way out and the place of liberation."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know that this is called receiving the heterodox and unequal precepts.
O Son of Heaven!
In this regard, what is the receiving of the correct and equal precepts?"
That is to say: emptiness is equanimity, signlessness is equanimity, and wishlessness is equanimity.
O Devaputra!
If one can thus enter the three gates of liberation, awakening to them as they truly are, without conceptualization or mental construction, and without regressing from any dharma—O Devaputra!
This is called receiving the precept of correct equanimity. Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

If greed arises, or if anger arises, or if delusion arises; if craving and ignorance arise; if the view of self arises, or the sixty-two views rooted in the view of self arise; if the three types of wrong conduct arise, or the four perversions arise; even down to the eight wrong paths, the nine afflictions, and the ten unwholesome courses of action arising—this is therefore called receiving the correct precepts.
"O Son of Heaven!
It is like all seeds, grasses, trees, and forests, which all grow and flourish depending upon the great earth; yet that earth is impartial and possesses no intentional thought."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
If one correctly receives the precepts within the Buddha-dharma, one will fully accomplish them. Devaputra!
Just as all seeds of grasses and trees depend upon the great earth to abide and grow,
O Devaputra,
you should likewise fully receive and maintain the true precepts.
Why is this? Because by abiding in the precepts, the factors of the Path increase; the precepts are just like that seed.
Furthermore, as a seed grows and is thus called "accomplished," so it is with the precepts.
"Because they abide thus in the precepts, O Devaputra, all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) arise, increase, and attain the name of accomplishment.

This, O Devaputra, is the pure morality received by all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their Śrāvakas of the past, future, and present; that is to say, it is the entry into those three gates of liberation, the place where all conceptual proliferation and verbal expression cease."
"Son of Heaven, you should know that if one can receive the full precepts in this manner, it is called receiving them correctly, not incorrectly.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Son of Heaven, Sthāmitra: "Son of Heaven!
I now further address those who have thus gone forth and thus received full ordination, instructing them as follows:
"Sons of good family!
If you are now able not to uphold the prohibitive precepts, this shall constitute the true upholding of them."
The Bodhisattva Susthitamati said:
"O Great Being! For what reason do you speak in this way?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! Because all dharmas are entirely without anything to be grasped, there is nothing that can be maintained."
"How is it that this precept alone is to be maintained?
O Devaputra!
If a precept can be maintained, then one maintains the three realms."
"Son of Heaven!
In your view, what constitutes precepts? Sudhīramati replied:
“O Mahāsattva! If one can be fully endowed with the *prātimokṣa*, this is called morality. Mañjuśrī said:
“O Son of Heaven!
What is meant by ‘prātimokṣa’? Sudhīmat replied:
“O Mahāsattva! That which is called maintaining the body, as well as speech and mind—when these three karmas are fully perfected, this is what is termed *pratimokṣa*. Mañjuśrī said:
“Devaputra! What do you think?
Where, in this present moment before us, is there any such bodily action to be performed?”
In this way, the past and the future likewise have no agency.
Since they are all without agency and without form or appearance, can one say that they exist as blue, yellow, red, white, or the color of crystal?
Susthitamati said: "No, Great Being!"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! What is that name?"
"How can it be explained?
Sudhīramati replied, "That which is called 'unconditioned' (asaṃskṛta) is truly inexpressible; the same applies even to that which is produced by the mind."
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra, what do you think?"
"Can that which is unconditioned be made conditioned? Sudhīmat replied, "No."
"O Great Being! Mañjuśrī said, "O Son of Heaven!"
For this reason, I speak thus: if one does not grasp at them, that is true upholding of the precepts.
O Devaputra!
If one speaks of the training in higher morality, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom, it is for the sake of training in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

One should understand it thus: because there is nothing to be grasped, it is called the training in higher ethics; because there is nothing to be known, it is called the training in higher mind; because there is nothing to be seen, it is called the training in higher wisdom.
Because the mind does not engage in conceptual discrimination, does not engage in recollection, and does not give rise to distinctions, it is called the supreme training of the mind.
As it is with the training of the mind, so it is with ethical discipline and wisdom.

"O Son of Heaven! If one does not apprehend the mind, then one does not contemplate the precepts; if one does not contemplate the precepts, then one does not reflect upon wisdom; if one does not reflect upon wisdom, then no further doubts or delusions arise; since there are no doubts or delusions, one does not uphold the precepts; and if one does not uphold the precepts, this is what is called truly upholding the precepts."

"Son of Heaven, you should know this: that upholder of the precepts has no desires; because he has no desires, he does not regress; because he does not regress, he is pure; because he is pure, he attains liberation; because he is liberated, he attains diligence; because he is diligent, he is without outflows; because he is without outflows, he abides in right practice; because he abides in right practice, he is without form; and being without form, he is precisely space."
Why is this? Because that space is devoid of form and characteristics.
Therefore, O Devaputra!
If there is anyone who can train in this way, it is non-training; because they have no training, it is true training.
In what place does one train? It is by training in no place.
What is "no location"?
It is the equality of emptiness,
O Devaputra!
"If one can dwell correctly in the equality of emptiness, this is what is called truly dwelling in the training of ethical discipline.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Devaputra Susthitamati, saying: "Devaputra!"
If a person can renounce the world and receive full ordination in this manner, I further instruct them to say these words:
"O sons of good family!

If you can now accept all the offerings and requisites provided by faithful donors throughout the entire trichiliocosm, yet remain free from discrimination regarding them and harbor no thought of seeking recompense, this is what is called the pure upholding of the precepts."
The Bodhisattva Susthitamati said:
"Great Being! For what reason do you speak in this way?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!
If a person grasps at those three things—the giver, the recipient, and the material gift—it is for this reason that it is called 'repaying kindness.'"

Furthermore, O Devaputra, if one perceives that [the Buddha] as being for the sake of repaying kindness, if one contemplates that as being for the sake of repaying kindness, or if one discriminates that as being for the sake of repaying kindness—[this is true gratitude].
O Devaputra!
If one does not see that, does not grasp that, does not contemplate that, and does not conceptualize that, what is there to repay? Why is this?
Because it is ultimately pure from the very beginning; such is the repayment.
"O Son of Heaven!
If one grasps, perceives, contemplates, discriminates, or even recalls the retribution [of actions], such a person is called an ordinary worldling, not an Arhat."

Why is this so? Because these ordinary worldlings always act with grasping and attachment at all times, conceptualizing and discriminating between "this is received" and "that is given," or "this is defiled" and "that is pure. Due to such discrimination, there is the requital of kindness.
What is meant by repaying kindness?
It refers to the fact that ordinary worldlings take up a body for future birth within the cycle of birth and death; therefore, one desires to practice repaying kindness toward them.
O Devaputra!

All Arhats do not undergo further existence; they ultimately do not see, do not conceptualize, and do not discriminate. Being without "this" or "that," they will no longer receive a body—where, then, could one repay their kindness?
"O Son of Heaven!
If you accept that offering, you should practice the three purities before doing so.
What are the three purities?"
First, not perceiving one's own body means there is no giver; second, not perceiving others means there is no recipient; third, not perceiving material wealth means there is no act of giving.
"O Son of Heaven!
Such triple purity is ultimate purity; once purified in this way, what further recompense would there be for it?
O Son of Heaven!"

For this reason, I have spoken thus: if one receives all the requisites from faithful donors throughout the trichiliocosm, yet remains without discrimination and without thoughts of reward, this is called the truly supreme field of merit in the world; this is true renunciation; this is pure observance of the precepts.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Devaputra Susthitamati, saying: "Devaputra!
Having granted such renunciation and such precepts to that person, I shall further instruct him, saying:"

"O sons of good family! If you are now able not to dwell in forest hermitages nor remain in villages; not to stay near nor reside far away; not to sit alone nor dwell in crowds; not to speak much nor remain silent; not to beg for food nor accept invitations; not to attend to rag-robes nor receive other robes or alms-bowls; not to have great greed nor few desires; not to seek much nor be insatiable; not to stay under trees nor in the open air; and not to consume decomposed medicines nor receive meat or ghee—then, O sons of good family!"

"If you can practice in such a way that you do not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding any of the dhūtas, then you are said to be fully endowed with the practice of the dhūtas. Why is this so?
If one practices by means of recollective discrimination, that is the prideful mind perceiving various signs.

O Devaputra! If one practices in this way, one will think thus: "I accept rag-robes; I practice alms-gathering; I dwell at the foot of a tree; I sit in the open air; I practice in an araṇya; I take decomposed medicine; I have few desires; I am content; I practice the dhūta-penance."
"O Son of Heaven!
One who practices correctly does not give rise to such thoughts. Why is this? Because..."
Because they are entirely free from all conceptual discrimination,
even at that time they do not perceive a self, let alone calculate the existence of the merits of dhūta practices;
if they were to perceive such things, it would be impossible.
"O Devaputra!
Therefore, if there is one who practices such dhūta austerities without recollecting or discriminating, I declare that person to be a true dhūta."
Why is this? O Devaputra!

If such a person sweeps away greed, sweeps away hatred, sweeps away delusion, sweeps away the three realms, sweeps away the five aggregates, sweeps away the twelve bases, and sweeps away the eighteen elements—of such a person, I say that he is a true dhūta.

Why is this? Because that dhūta does not grasp nor reject, does not contemplate nor think, does not cultivate nor practice, and is neither dharma nor non-dharma; for this reason, I call him a true dhūta.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Devaputra Susthitamati: "Devaputra!
After I and those people have thus gone forth and thus practiced, I shall further instruct them, saying:..."
"O sons of good family!

If you are now able not to contemplate the Four Noble Truths, not to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, not to cultivate the four right efforts, not to cultivate the four bases of power, not to cultivate the five faculties, not to cultivate the five powers, not to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment, not to cultivate the eightfold noble path, and not to cultivate the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, then do not realize the three gates of liberation."
Why is this? O Devaputra!
Those Noble Truths enter into the mark of non-arising; they cannot be known through recollection, nor can they be cultivated or realized.
Why is this so? Within that which is non-arising, how can one speak of "realization"?
O Devaputra!
Therefore, I say that as for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they are neither mindfulness nor thought regarding all phenomena; thus they are called "foundations of mindfulness.
O Devaputra!

If a bhikṣu does not abide in the desire realm, does not abide in the form realm, and does not abide in the formless realm, it is said that the bhikṣu does not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness while contemplating and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness.
What is the cultivation through reflection?
It is called "cultivation through reflection" precisely because there is no [inherent] reflection or cultivation.
One should understand that this sequence applies up to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
"O Devaputra!

If that bhikṣu practicing dhyāna finds nothing at all to be obtained among all dharmas, then because there is nothing to be obtained, he does not contemplate, does not discriminate, does not cultivate, and does not realize."
Why is this? O Devaputra!
Those dharmas possess nothing but names.
Just as with the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, although they have names, they cannot be apprehended; they arise solely through the conditions of conceptual discrimination.
Being of one mark and yet markless, they are spoken of by means of such names, yet even that speech is non-existent.

Therefore, although these are realized through names and designations, they are ultimately unattainable; this is what is called the realization of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are.
Then the Devaputra Susthitamati again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "Great Being!
Regarding what you call a 'bhikṣu who practices dhyāna,' what is meant by a bhikṣu who practices dhyāna?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra!
If that bhikṣu, regarding all phenomena, grasps only a single practice that is most conformable—namely, non-arising—this constitutes the practice of dhyāna.”
Furthermore, there is not even the slightest dharma to be grasped; this is the practice of dhyāna.
Moreover, what dharma is not grasped?
That is to say, one does not grasp at this world or that world, one does not grasp at the three realms, and so on, up to not grasping at any dharmas whatsoever.
Such equanimity is the practice of dhyāna. O Devaputra!
For one who practices dhyāna, there is not even a single dharma with which they are associated; this absence of conjunction and absence of dispersion is the practice of dhyāna.
At that time, there were many hundreds of thousands of beings in that assembly who all harbored doubts, thinking:
"Now, such as this is what Mañjuśrī has spoken; how can it be in accord with the teachings of the Noble One?"
Why is this? The World-Honored One has constantly taught that if a person can enter the three gates of liberation, it is called nirvana.
Furthermore, as the Buddha has said, if one practices the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, one will realize nirvana.
However, now Mañjuśrī further speaks thus: "One should not cultivate these practices that assist toward enlightenment, nor should one enter those three gates of liberation."
"Could it be that Mañjuśrī is speaking falsely?
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, knowing that the bhikṣus and the entire assembly were all in doubt, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"O Mahāsthavira!..."
"You are now most worthy of being trusted; the World-Honored One has declared you to be foremost in wisdom.
Venerable sir, at what time did you realize the dharma of freedom from desire?"
"Furthermore, when one realizes the Dharma, does one not see the Four Noble Truths? Śāriputra replied, "No."
“Is it not that one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? He replied, “No.”
“Have you not entered the three gates of liberation? He replied, “No.”
"O Mahāsattva!
At that time, there was not even a single dharma to be seen, to be eliminated, to be cultivated, to be realized, or to be selected. Why is this so? "
"All dharmas are unconditioned, unborn, ineffable, and empty.
If they are empty, what is there to be realized?
When this Dharma was spoken, thirty thousand bhikṣus among the assembly attained liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows regarding all phenomena.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 142;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 145.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
The Thirty-sixth Assembly of the *Susthitamati-devaputra-paripṛcchā*, Part Four; Chapter Seven, Part Two:
"Breaking the Characteristics of the Two Vehicles. At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Mahāsattva!
You are truly wise and possessed of sharp, penetrating intelligence to have so eloquently expounded such profound patience regarding emptiness. Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
I am not one of such clever eloquence or sharp intelligence.
Indeed, those who possess such sharp intelligence are merely all the infants and ordinary worldlings."
Why is this? O Devaputra!
All ordinary worldlings are called those who possess the wisdom of names.
What is sharp wisdom?
It refers to the sharp wisdom of hell beings, the sharp wisdom of animals, the sharp wisdom of hungry ghosts, the sharp wisdom of Yama, and even the sharp wisdom of all within the three realms.
One who is thus associated with grasping and attachment may be said to possess sharp intelligence. Why is this?
Because they do not know the prior limit of birth-and-death and afflictions.
"O Devaputra!

Therefore, those ordinary worldlings are attached to the profit of greed, attached to the profit of hatred, and attached to the profit of delusion; they are even associated with the grasping at name-and-form (nāmarūpa) through various views. For this reason, they are said to possess 'sharp wisdom' [in a conventional sense]."

It is not said that the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas who have attained patience possess this wisdom of grasping at signs; rather, this is called the wisdom of grasping at signs possessed by all ordinary worldlings.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Susthitamati again asked Mañjuśrī:
"Great Being! What do you intend to manifest by what you have just said—is it wisdom?"
Mañjuśrī replied, "No. Sudhīmat said, "Do you wish to follow [the path]?"
Mañjuśrī said, "No. Suvicintitārtha said:
"Do you wish to follow the phrases? Mañjuśrī replied, "So it is, so it is."
"O Devaputra!
I do so by means of words and syllables. Sudhīmat replied:
“O Mahāsattva! For what reason do you now speak in such a manner? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!

If Bodhisattvas do not move from even a single word or phrase at the outset, yet they know the gates of meaning, locations, proximities, distances, shallownesses, and depths of those words and phrases exactly as they are—namely, knowing the sphere of emptiness, the sphere of signlessness, the sphere of wishlessness, the sphere of detachment, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of non-arising, and the sphere of suchness—and within these they experience neither reception nor action, and possess neither conceptualization nor cognition, for this reason it can be said that there are only words and phrases.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"Because you have now attained the dhāraṇī, you are able to explain with such discernment.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I truly have not attained that dhāraṇī. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
If there were anyone who could obtain this dhāraṇī, they would be called a foolish ordinary person (pṛthagjana);
it is not the Buddha, the World-Honored One, nor the various bodhisattvas who obtain this dhāraṇī.
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
Those ordinary persons and deluded sentient beings obtain the dhāraṇī because they possess attachment.
What is it that they grasp at?
It is said that they attain dhāraṇī by grasping at a self; they attain dhāraṇī by grasping at a person;
they attain dhāraṇī by grasping at a life-force; they attain dhāraṇī by grasping at a man.
One attains dhāraṇī through the grasping at annihilation; one attains dhāraṇī through the grasping at permanence;
one attains dhāraṇī through the grasping at desire; one attains dhāraṇī through the grasping at hatred;
one attains dhāraṇī through the grasping at delusion; and one attains dhāraṇī through the grasping at ignorance.
One attains dhāraṇī through attachment to craving; one attains dhāraṇī through attachment to the view of a self;
one attains dhāraṇī through attachment to the five aggregates; one attains dhāraṇī through attachment to the twelve bases;
one attains dhāraṇī through attachment to the eighteen elements; one attains dhāraṇī through attachment to recollection.
Noble women, because they grasp at and differentiate, they attain dhāraṇī; because they grasp at the sixty-two views, they attain dhāraṇī;
and so on, up to grasping at all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they attain dhāraṇī.
For this reason, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) attain dhāraṇī.

Why is this so? If a dharma is grasped and clung to by that ignorance, it is something obtained by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); it is not what is obtained by Buddhas, nor by Śrāvakas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Bodhisattvas. For this reason, only those ordinary persons obtain the dhāraṇī.
"Why is this? Because those ordinary worldlings, due to their ignorance, speak of there being 'acquisition' and 'attainment,' whereas the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the bodhisattvas do not.
At that time, the Son of Heaven, Sustained by Good Intent, again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“O Mahāsattva! If you do not attain the dhāraṇī, will you not fall into the state of dullness and insentience? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Thus it is, O Devaputra!
I am indeed dull-witted. Why is this?
Now, those who are dull and obtuse are said to have no knowledge because they cannot know the sphere in which I act.
Therefore, all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, are all dull and obtuse; it is not the case for ordinary worldlings.
Why is this so? Because all ordinary worldlings are included within the reckoning, and all other wise ones are likewise categorized as dull-witted.

Since even the mental conduct of craving belonging to a *srotāpanna*—due to its obstructive nature—is still counted among these, how much more so for ignorant ordinary worldlings who would not be excluded from that reckoning?
"O Son of Heaven!
For this reason, one may say that I am dull-witted.
I truly have not attained that dhāraṇī."
"Why is this? Because I have not attained even a single dharma.

When this teaching was spoken, among that great assembly there were five hundred bhikṣus who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, were unable to believe or accept it. They gave rise to great terror and a mind of slander; having conceived such evil thoughts, they abandoned [the teaching] and departed, immediately seeing themselves fall into the great hells.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Mahāsattva! May you please wait; do not speak such a profound sūtra as this."

Why is this? Because within this assembly, five hundred bhikṣus, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, were unable to believe or accept it; they gave rise to great fear and a mind of slander, and immediately perceived themselves as already dwelling in hell.
Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra: "Śāriputra!
You should not now give rise to false conceptual discrimination."
Why is this? Because there is not even a single dharma that falls into hell. For what reason?
Since all dharmas are unarisen,
why have you now suddenly spoken these words, commanding me to desist and not proclaim this Dharma? Śāriputra!

If a son or daughter of good family, relying on the view of a self, relying on the view of a person, relying on the view of a sentient being, relying on the view of a life-span, and relying on various views, were to make offerings to Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as their communities of bhikṣus, providing all necessary requisites according to their needs, and were to continue such offerings for the remainder of their lives without ceasing; [this would not equal the merit of the former].

Furthermore, if there are those who hear this profound Dharma-gate taught by me—which cannot be believed by anyone in all the worlds—namely, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action; which is vast, tranquil, without arising or ceasing, and devoid of self, person, sentient being, or life-span; and which consists of impermanence, suffering, and non-self—if they slander such teachings after hearing them, they shall fall into hell.
However, Śāriputra!
Once these sons and daughters of good family have heard such a profound Dharma as this, even if they fall into hell, upon emerging from hell they will swiftly attain nirvāṇa.

If a son or daughter of good family, despite making offerings to as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, should still grasp at a self and fail to hear such a profound sūtra-dharma, they will ultimately not be liberated and will not swiftly realize nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
It is so, it is so; it is truly as you have said.
Should anyone hear such a profound and subtle sūtra as this, it is no different from encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Why is this? If one wishes to realize the fruit of srotāpanna, it must be by means of this sutra;
if one wishes to realize the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat, one must hear this sutra.
Why is this? Because it is by not clinging to a self that one is able to realize the Dharma.
When realizing this Dharma, there is nothing seen and nothing attained.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra,
you should know that although these five hundred bhikṣus have fallen into hell, they will emerge from that hell and swiftly realize nirvāṇa."
Śāriputra, it is not those foolish ordinary persons—who are submerged in views, fallen into doubt, and attached to gain—who can attain liberation by making offerings to the Tathāgata. Śāriputra!
These bhikṣus, by returning once more to this [practice], will even attain liberation and quickly achieve nirvāṇa; others are not able to attain quick liberation. Why is this?
Because they have not heard this profound Dharma-gate, Śāriputra!

If there are good sons or good daughters who hear such a profound Dharma-gate even once, though they do not believe or accept it and consequently fall into hell, they will nevertheless be swiftly liberated.
"Those who fall into views and enter hell have not yet attained liberation.
Chapter Eight: Destroying the Marks of the Ordinary Person. At that time, the Crown Prince Sudhīmat addressed Mañjuśrī again, saying:
"O Great Being!"
“O Benevolent One, will you now permit me to practice the holy life? Mañjuśrī replied,
“It is so, O Devaputra!”
"If you can now refrain from thinking of seeking and cease from intending to advance, then I shall grant you the holy life. Sudhīmat said,
"O Great Being!"
"For what reason is it said thus? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
If that which is conditioned can be called the holy life (*brahmacarya*), what could that which is unconditioned be called?
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
If that which is attained through views can be called the holy life, what could that which is attained without views be called?
Susthitamati said: "Great Being!
Do you now perhaps lack the holy life?"
Mañjuśrī said: “So it is, so it is, O Devaputra!”
I have no Brahma-conduct. Why is this?
For that which is Brahma-conduct is not Brahma-conduct; because it is not Brahma-conduct, I call it Brahma-conduct.
Then the Devaputra Susthitamati praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Great Being!”
“Because you, O Benevolent One, are endowed with the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), you are able to deliver such unobstructed discourse. Mañjuśrī said,
“O Son of Heaven!...”
If I were to possess unimpeded eloquence, it would itself become an obstacle. Why is this?
For all grasping at a self and what belongs to a self arises from conceptual discrimination.
"Because all conceptualization is nothing other than an obstruction.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Devaputra Susthitamati, saying: "Devaputra!..."

If you are now able to sever the life-faculty of all sentient beings, yet do so without wielding a sword, without carrying a staff, without grasping a cudgel, and without holding a clod of earth while performing this deed, I shall practice the holy life together with you.
The Bodhisattva Susthitamati said:
"Great Being! For what reason do you speak in this manner?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra! Regarding what is called 'sentient beings,' what do you think?"
Susthitamati said: "O Mahāsattva!
When I speak of 'sentient beings,' these sentient beings—even including all things—exist merely as names, for they are all grasped through conceptualization."
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! Therefore I say to you:

you must now slay the notion of a self, slay the notion of a person, slay the notion of a sentient being, and slay the notion of a life-span; even to the point of eradicating notions such as names—this is what it means to 'slay'."
Susthitamati said: "Great Being!
With what instrument of killing should one carry out the act of killing?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra! I always employ that sword of sharp wisdom to carry out the act of killing."

"Devaputra!

"By what dharma do you define the equality of defilement?

without action, without regression, and without falling— this is called the equality of defilement."
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra! Furthermore, by what dharma is 'pure equality' constituted?"
Susthitamati said: "The suchness, the dharmatā, and the limit of reality—these three gates of liberation are called the equality of purity. Mañjuśrī said:
“Son of Heaven!

"No, Great Being! Mañjuśrī said.

Susthitamati said: "Great Being!

"What is this head?

This is what can be slain,

If a person maintains single-minded concentration and self-restraint, they should immediately recognize the arising of a mind of greed and, through skillful means, dispel it and restore it to tranquility.

Seeking the place where this desirous mind arises and the place where it ceases:
from where does it come? To where does it go?
Within this, who is defiled; who is the one who undergoes defilement; and what is the phenomenon that constitutes defilement?

When observing in this way, one does not see the defiler, does not see the defiled, and does not see the object of defilement. In this way, it should be understood that all feelings and states of mind are also explained in the same manner.

O Son of Heaven, you should know that such a method of killing kills and gives birth simultaneously; therefore, one may say that when one performs the act of killing, first severing the head constitutes true killing. It is for this reason that I speak thus.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Devaputra Susthitamati: "Devaputra!

Susthitamati said: "O Great Being!
For what reason do you now speak thus again?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! According to your own understanding, what do you take to be a Buddha?"
Susthitamati said: "O Great Being!
That which is suchness and the dharma-realm, I call the Buddha."
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra, what do you think?”
"Can suchness, the dharma-realm, be stained or attached to?
Sudhīmat replied, "No."
"O Great Being! Mañjuśrī said, "O Son of Heaven!"
"For this reason, I have spoken thus: if you can now slander all the Buddhas, I shall likewise practice the holy life (brahmacarya) together with you.
Mañjuśrī said, "O Devaputra!"
"What do you consider to be the Dharma? Sudhīramati replied,
"O Great Being!"
"Detachment from desire and tranquility— this, I call the Dharma. Mañjuśrī said, "O Devaputra!"
"What do you think?
Can that dharma of tranquility be stained by attachment? Sudhīmat replied:
"No, Great Being! Mañjuśrī said.
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
For this reason I speak thus: if you are now able to revile the True Dharma, I shall likewise practice such a holy life together with you."
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra! According to your understanding, what do you take to be the Saṃgha?"
Susthitamati said: "Great Being!
Unconditioned dharmas are what is called the Noble Saṃgha."
"As the World-Honored One has said, all noble ones receive their name from the unconditioned; therefore, the unconditioned dharma is called the Sangha of Śrāvakas.
Mañjuśrī said, "O Son of Heaven!..."
"What do you think?
Can these unconditioned dharmas be grasped? Suvimalaprabha replied:
"No, Great Being! Mañjuśrī said.
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
For this reason I have spoken in this way: if you are now able to destroy the noble Saṃgha, I shall practice such a holy life together with you."
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!

If a person perceives the Buddha, they are attached to the Buddha; if a person perceives the Dharma, they are attached to the Dharma; if a person perceives the Saṅgha, they are attached to the Saṅgha."
Why is this? Because the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are not something that can be acquired.
O Son of Heaven!

If a person does not see the Buddha, does not hear the Dharma, and does not recognize the Sangha, they do not turn their back on the Buddha, do not slander the Dharma, and do not disrupt the Sangha. Why is this?
Because they do not perceive the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha.
O Devaputra!
If a person loves the Buddha, loves the Dharma, and loves the Sangha, they are thereby defiled by attachment to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
"Son of Heaven, you should know that if a person does not become attached to the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha, this is what is called 'detachment from desire' and 'nirvāṇa.
Son of Heaven, for this reason I speak thus: if you can now remain unstained by attachment to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, then I shall practice this same holy life together with you."
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Great Being! How rare, how rare!"
"Today you have been able to proclaim such a profound locus of meaning.
How may I repay your kindness, O Great Being? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Son of Heaven!

“O Mahāsattva! How could I now fail to repay you? Mañjuśrī said:

"O Son of Heaven!
If you are able not to requite such a favor, that itself constitutes a requital.
Thus spoke Suvikrāntamati.
"O Mahāsattva! Can you truly not repay his kindness now? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
It is so, it is so; I neither repay my debt of gratitude, nor do I fail to repay it.
Thus spoke Suvimalaprabha.
“O Mahāsattva! For what purpose do you speak these words again? Mañjuśrī replied:

Furthermore, O Devaputra!

As for one who does not repay kindness, it is as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has proclaimed regarding equality: that all dharmas are entirely without action, without a locus of action, and all enter into equality without returning or turning back; they are neither transcendent nor immanent, neither self nor other, and are without doing or non-doing. For this reason, I am one who does not repay kindness.
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:

"Is it by abiding in patience that one speaks, or is it by abiding in the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
That in which I abide is neither patience nor non-Dharma.

The one named Well-Established-Mind said: "Great Being!
Upon what does that emanated person rely for his abiding?"

"Son of Heaven!
If it is so, why do you ask where one dwells, whether it is through patience or through the Dharma?"
To such a question, O Devaputra,
that which I call "patience" exists only as a name; even that name has no place of abiding.
The Dharma is likewise: it has no place of abiding, no movement or shifting, and no conceptual discrimination.

Why is this so? As the Buddha has taught, the Tathāgata dwells within that dharma of suchness (tathatā).
All sentient beings are likewise; they dwell in suchness, remaining as immovable as it is.

"The suchness of sentient beings is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of sentient beings. There is no duality and no distinction between the suchness of sentient beings and the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Mahāsattva!"

If one is neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa, then that person is called a true śramaṇa. Why is this so?
Because such a person is not attached to the realm of desire, not attached to the realm of form, and not attached to the formless realm; for this reason, I call them a true śramaṇa.

If one’s eye does not leak, the ear does not leak, the nose does not leak, the tongue does not leak, the body does not leak, and the mind does not leak, I further declare such a person to be a true śramaṇa."
"O Devaputra!

O Devaputra!"

O Devaputra!

Then the Devaputra Susthitamati again praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

"Because you, O Benevolent One, have long made offerings to various Buddhas in the past and planted many roots of virtue,
you are thus able to proclaim such sublime teachings. Mañjuśrī said, "O Devaputra!"
I have made no offerings to the Buddhas and have not cultivated roots of goodness. Why is this?
I do not see what was done in the past, nor do I know what will be done in the future; though there is that which is done, there is no act of doing.
“Since one has never established oneself within any of the Buddha-dharmas, how can one plant the roots of all virtues?
Chapter Nine: The Exposition Verified by Supernatural Powers At that time, the Crown Prince Sudhīmat addressed Mañjuśrī again, saying:
“O Great Being!
"I have previously heard of the Illusion-like Samādhi; I only pray that you will deign to show us this right concentration out of your compassion.
Mañjuśrī said, "O Son of Heaven!"
“Do you wish to see and hear the profound realm of the Illusion-like Samādhi?
Sudhīramati replied, “O Mahāsattva!”
"I truly wish to see it.
At that moment, Mañjuśrī entered the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) as he had spoken.
Instantly, all realms throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, naturally manifested before him.

Thereupon, the Devaputra Susthitamati beheld all the Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, and all the various phenomena therein. Just as it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—in all ten directions—there are likewise all such activities in Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of which are exactly equal and without difference;
all of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati, having beheld all such realms within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, was so filled with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself.

"I have just seen that in the immeasurable realms of the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, the Buddha-activities are likewise diverse, yet each proclaims such a sutra as this.

"What do you think?

"No, Great Being! Mañjuśrī said.
"Is it likewise with the eastern direction and the other nine directions— that all such realms throughout the ten directions are also real?
Sudhīramati replied, "O Mahāsattva!"
All things are empty and devoid of reality. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are fundamentally without birth; they are like illusions and transformations that deceive the world.

“Excellent, excellent, O Devaputra!”
"It is exactly as you say.
At that time, there were five hundred bodhisattvas in the assembly who had already attained the four dhyānas and accomplished the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Clearly perceiving these other karmic consequences, they give rise to deep remorse that never leaves their minds; thus, they are unable to enter into the profound Dharma.

"I shall certainly be harmed; I am being harmed for the sake of doing good.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!"
From the very beginning, there has been no self, no person, and no individual; it is only that the internal mind perceives a self and a person.
When the internal mind arises, it already harms the self, and this is what is called "harming."
When the bodhisattvas had heard what the Buddha had said, they all thought to themselves:

"All phenomena are entirely like illusions and transformations; herein there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span, no man, no mānuṣya, no mānava, no father, no mother, no arhat, no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Saṅgha. There is no such thing as a heinous crime, nor is there anyone who commits a heinous crime—how could there be one who falls into such a crime?"
Why is this so? This Mañjuśrī is now intelligent, sagely, and profoundly wise, surpassing his peers, and is praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

He has already attained the profound and unimpeded *dharmakṣānti*, and has previously made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. He skillfully discerns and understands the teachings of all Buddhas and is able to expound such a true Dharma. While he maintains equal mindfulness and reverence toward all Tathāgatas, he has suddenly drawn a sword, intending to threaten the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One suddenly said: "Wait, wait! Mañjuśrī!"
"You have not harmed me. If you must harm me, you should harm me well. Why is this so?

In this regard, if there were even a single dharma that could be gathered and assembled to definitively achieve what is called the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the father, the mother, or an Arhat—something that could certainly be grasped—then it would not be subject to extinction.

Within this there is nothing at all; all phenomena are empty.
Through inverted and false conceptualization, the deluded grasp at a self-mind.
Reflecting upon my past transgressions, the karma I have created is most grievous.

Sentient beings trapped in the net of doubt, upon hearing the Dharma, may have their remorse removed.

"As the sword is, so too is the Buddha; they are of one mark and have no duality.

Because that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has employed the sword of wisdom to preach the profound Dharma, he causes immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to purify their Dharma-eye, attain liberation of mind, realize the profound patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and dwell securely in Bodhi.

"When this karma ripens, where will it be experienced?
Then Mañjuśrī addressed Śāriputra, saying,
"O Great Virtuous One, it is like this:"
As you have said, I can now only perform such extremely grave evil karma, yet I truly do not know where I shall undergo its retribution.
However, Śāriputra!
As I see it, when the karmic maturation of a person created by transformation or illusion occurs, I experience it in this very way.
Why is that? Because that illusory person has no mental discrimination and no conceptual thoughts; for all phenomena are like illusions and transformations.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I now ask you; answer according to your own understanding.
What do you think?
"Do you truly see the sword, as you think? Śāriputra replied, "No."

"In this way, Śāriputra!

"And yet you instead ask me about the place where one receives retribution? Śāriputra said,
"O Mahāsattva!..."

"O sons of good family!

At that time, when the assembly of bodhisattvas from the ten directions had heard these words from Mañjuśrī, they each looked toward their own original buddha-worlds and beheld Mañjuśrī standing before their respective buddhas, expounding such a Dharma to the great assemblies. "O sons of good family!

Having become thoroughly proficient in the *prajñāpāramitā*—the illusory nature of phenomena—they are able, within all such illusory phenomena, to manifest their physical form and perform the deeds of a Buddha in any of the buddha-fields of the ten directions, exactly as they wish.
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; for this reason, what is produced follows the mind.

It is, for example, like the palaces and wheels of the sun and moon abiding in the realm of space: they never descend into the various vessels [of the world], yet their light shines everywhere, reaching all places without exception.

The Bodhisattva thus abides immovably, manifesting universally before the Buddhas of the ten directions according to his will; he may manifest the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or the forms of Brahmā kings and Śakras, or the affairs of the Four Heavenly Kings and wheel-turning monarchs, or the governance and civilizing influence of sovereigns and ministers. In this way, he is able to manifest the various forms and species of all sentient beings in the evil realms at will, yet from the very beginning, he harbors no thought of deliberate effort or fabrication.

"I pray that the Buddha will proclaim it for us.

The Great Collection Sutra, Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Assembly on the Skillful Means of the Mahāyāna (Part One). Translated by the Eastern Jin Indian layman Zhu Nanti. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park Monastery, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were śrāvakas, both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

There were twelve thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom had attained supernatural powers and were well known to the multitude; they had attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, had realized the patience regarding all phenomena, and had fully accomplished immeasurable merits.
At that time, the Tathāgata arose from samādhi and, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings who paid him reverent homage, preached the Dharma for them.

At that time, among the assembly there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Jñānavijaya, who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I wish to ask about one matter; I only pray that you will grant me leave.
If the Buddha permits it, I shall venture to consult you.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya:
“Good son! Ask whatever you wish;
I shall explain it for you and sever your doubts.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘skillful means,’ what constitutes the skillful means of a bodhisattva?”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice skillful means?
Having asked this, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

For the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, you have asked about the meaning of skillful means; this brings great benefit and great peace and happiness. Out of compassion for the world, you seek to benefit and bring peace and happiness to gods and humans, and you do so to gather the wisdom of future bodhisattvas as well as the teachings of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.”
"Good son! I shall now speak for you.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
The Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya received the instruction and listened. "Good son!
A bodhisattva who practices skillful means gives a single morsel of food as a gift to all sentient beings."

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva practicing skillful means gives even a single morsel of food as alms, down to the level of animals, while aspiring for all-knowledge; thus, the bodhisattva shares it with all sentient beings and dedicates it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By means of these two causes and conditions, they gather in all sentient beings; that is to say, the mind that seeks omniscience and the skillful means of aspiration.
Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices skillful means, if he sees one who practices giving and gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), he vows that these roots of goodness from sympathetic joy be shared with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This skillful bodhisattva also vows that neither the giver nor the receiver shall be separated from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñā-citta*).
Even if the recipient is a person of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), he vows that they likewise shall not be separated from the mind of omniscience.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
Furthermore, son of good family,

when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices skillful means, if they see flower trees without owners and various kinds of incense within the worlds of the ten directions, they gather them together with the vow to offer them to all Buddhas.

If one sees in the worlds of the ten directions any flowers or leaves with fragrance belonging to a master, which are being blown by the wind, may they all be gathered together and offered as an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of these roots of goodness—whether for oneself or for the sake of all sentient beings—one possesses the mind of omniscience.
Through the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, one attains immeasurable morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
Furthermore, son of good family,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means, if they see sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions receiving various rewards of happiness, having seen this, they form this thought:
"May all sentient beings attain the bliss of omniscience.

If one sees sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions undergoing various retributions of suffering, one should perform repentance for the transgressions of those beings and make this great adornment:
"Whatever sufferings these sentient beings endure, may I receive them all in their stead so that they may attain bliss."
"By these roots of goodness, may I attain all-knowledge and eliminate the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings.
For this reason, one ultimately does not undergo any suffering but experiences only pure happiness.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means, if they pay homage to a single Buddha, reverently making offerings, honoring, and praising him, they form this thought:
"All Tathāgatas share one Dharma-realm, one Dharma-body, one morality, one concentration, one wisdom, one liberation, and one knowledge and vision of liberation."

Having formed this thought, you should know that if one pays homage to a single Buddha, and with reverence, makes offerings, respects, and praises them, this is itself to pay homage, make offerings, respect, and praise all Buddhas.
If one makes offerings to a single Buddha, it is equivalent to making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Having thus made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions,
this is called the practice of skillful means by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means, he should not disparage himself even if he is of dull faculties; rather, if he can master even a single four-line verse, he should form this thought:
'If I understand the meaning of one four-line verse, I thereby know all the Buddha-dharma.'"
"All the Buddha-dharmas are entirely subsumed within the meaning of this single verse.

Having thus attained thorough understanding, one’s mind shall not be indolent. Whether arriving at various kingdoms, cities, towns, or villages, one shall extensively expound it for others with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, seeking no gain, offerings, fame, or praise, and making this vow:
"May these four lines of verse be heard by others."
"By means of these roots of goodness and through skillful means, I vow that all sentient beings shall become as learned as Ānanda and attain the eloquence of the Tathāgata.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
"Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means, even if he is born into a poor family, that bodhisattva may go so far as to beg for food; if he obtains a single morsel, he uses it to give to the Sangha."
If one gives to a single person and feels no shame, one should form this thought:
"As the Buddha has taught, the expansion and excellence of the mind surpasses the giving of material wealth.

Although my gift of material wealth is small, by means of the mind of omniscience, I vow that these roots of goodness shall result in omniscience, and cause all sentient beings to obtain a 'jewel-hand' just like that of the Tathāgata."
For this reason, one fulfills the bases of merit consisting of giving, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration.
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
Furthermore, good son!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means, if he sees śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas receiving abundant offerings, honor, and praise, that bodhisattva consoles his own mind by means of two considerations.
What are these two? They are as follows:
because of the bodhisattvas there are the Tathāgatas, and because of the Tathāgatas there are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One should reflect in this way:
"Although those of the two vehicles obtain offerings and sustenance, I am still superior to them.
What they consume is my father’s property; how could I harbor expectations for such things?"
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
Furthermore, son of good family,
when the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices skillful means, they are endowed with the six pāramitās at the time of practicing giving.
What are the six?
Son of good family!
