When a bodhisattva practices skillful means, if he sees a beggar and eliminates the mind of stinginess and attachment, fully accomplishing great giving, this is called dānapāramitā.

To personally maintain the precepts and give them to those who maintain the precepts; to see those who have broken the precepts and exhort them to uphold them, and only after they have been exhorted to uphold the precepts does one provide them with gifts—this is called śīlapāramitā.

To personally eliminate ill will and practice loving-kindness and compassion, with a mind free from defilement and impurity, bestowing gifts with an impartial mind that seeks to benefit all sentient beings—this is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

If one gives food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, one immediately becomes fully endowed with physical and mental diligence; whether going or coming, advancing or halting, bending or stretching, looking down or looking up—all these are called the *vīryapāramitā*.
If, having practiced giving, one's mind attains concentration, being joyful, delighted, and focused without distraction, this is called the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Having given in such a manner, one discerns all phenomena: "Who is the giver?"
Who is the recipient? Who is the one who experiences the retribution?

Having observed in this way, one finds that there is not a single dharma that can be called a giver, nor a person who receives the gift, nor one who experiences the retribution; this is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means while being endowed with the six pāramitās.
At that time, the bodhisattva Jñānavijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is unprecedented.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices skillful means, at the very moment of giving, by means of this gift, they encompass all Buddha-dharmas as well as all sentient beings.”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya: "Good son,
it is as you have said."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means, by the power of those skillful means, even though they practice only a small amount of giving, the merit they obtain is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya: “Good son!
Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has reached the stage of non-retrogression, they still practice giving through skillful means; this is called a bodhisattva practicing skillful means.”
"Good son! There may be a time when an evil friend instructs a bodhisattva, saying:
'Why do you remain for so long in birth and death?'"
"You may enter nirvana early within this very body.
Having understood this, the Bodhisattva should immediately distance himself from it, thinking:
"I am thus greatly adorned as I teach and transform all sentient beings, yet this person creates various obstacles for me."
"If I were not within the cycle of birth and death, how could I teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings?
The Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there are sentient beings who, due to deluded thoughts, commit the four grave offenses," the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya,
"O son of good family!"
If a renunciant bodhisattva commits the four grave offenses due to deluded conceptualization, a bodhisattva who practices skillful means is able to completely eliminate them.
I now also declare that there is neither one who commits an offense nor one who undergoes retribution.
The Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva commit an offense?”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya:

"Good son! Although a bodhisattva practices the precepts of liberation, even if for hundreds of thousands of kalpas he eats only fruit and grass, he is able to endure the good and evil words of sentient beings."
If one contemplates the Dharma together with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, son of good family!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva committing a grave offense.
Son of good family!
Just as a śrāvaka who violates a grave precept cannot attain nirvāṇa in that very body,
so too, son of good family,
a bodhisattva who does not eliminate the shared contemplations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and who neither abandons nor regrets them, will ultimately never achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"If one were to attain the Buddha-dharma, such a thing would be impossible.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Early this morning, as I entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms in regular succession, I saw the Bodhisattva Saṃpūjya-rāja sitting on the same couch as a woman.
As Ānanda had finished speaking these words, the great earth immediately shook in six ways.
The Bodhisattva Saṃgharāja rose into the air to a height of seven tala trees amidst the great assembly and said to Ānanda:
"Venerable One,
how could one who has committed an offense abide in the sky?"
Ānanda! You may inquire of the World-Honored One regarding this matter: what constitutes an offense, and what does not constitute an offense?
At that time, Ānanda, filled with grief, approached the Buddha; kneeling on his right knee and grasping the Buddha’s feet with his hands, he said:
“World-Honored One!
I now repent my transgression.”
"Such a great dragon, I say, has committed an offense.
Such a bodhisattva, I seek out his faults.
World-Honored One!"
"I now repent my transgression; I only pray that you will grant me forgiveness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should not seek out faults in a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
Ānanda! You, as a śrāvaka, practice the meditative absorption of cessation in a place of obstruction; there shall be no hindrance to severing all fetters. Ānanda!

A Bodhisattva practicing skillful means thus accomplishes the mind of omniscience; even while enjoying himself among the ladies of his inner palace, he gives rise to neither demonic activities nor obstacles, and thereby attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Ānanda!

A bodhisattva who practices skillful means never fails to receive such sentient beings and exhort them toward the Three Jewels, or toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Ānanda! If a son or daughter of good family who trains in the Mahāyāna does not depart from the mind of omniscience, even if they see the five desirable sensual pleasures that appeal to them, they may immediately enjoy themselves together with them.
Ānanda! You should form this thought:
"A bodhisattva such as this is precisely the root capable of accomplishing a Tathāgata."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
For what reason did the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Saṃgharājarāja sit on the same seat as this woman?"
Ānanda! In the past, throughout five hundred lifetimes, that woman was the wife of the Bodhisattva Saṃmārta-rāja.
Due to her former habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), upon seeing the Bodhisattva Saṃmārta-rāja, her heart gave rise to attachment; she was bound by it and could not let go.

Because of the power of the Bodhisattva Saṃgharāja’s majestic virtue, his upright appearance, and his observance of the precepts, [the king], having seen him, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
while dwelling in solitude, he gave rise to this thought: "If the Bodhisattva Saṃgharāja would sit upon the same seat as me, I shall resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Ānanda! At that time, the Bodhisattva King of the Multitude of Honored Ones (Saṃgharāja), knowing the thoughts in the mind of that woman, and having known them thus, put on his robes and took up his bowl in the early morning, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in sequence, and upon reaching her house, he entered it."
At that moment, he contemplated this Dharma-gate:
"Whether it be the internal earth-element or the external earth-element, they are one and the same earth-element.
Because the mind of the earth-element grasps the hand of a woman and sits together upon a single bed, the Bodhisattva Sarvarājasa immediately spoke these verses while seated there:"
“The Tathāgata does not praise the desires practiced by ordinary people;
by abandoning desire and craving, he became the Teacher of Gods and Humans.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“At that time, having heard this verse, the woman was filled with great joy and boundless exultation. She rose from her seat, approached the Bodhisattva Saṃghāṭa-rāja, prostrated at his feet in reverence, and spoke this verse:
‘I do not crave sensual desire; Sensual desire is censured by the Buddha.’”
"Having abandoned desire and craving, one becomes a Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Having spoken this verse, he said:
"I now repent for the evil desires that arose within me previously."
Immediately, she gave rise to a wholesome desire and resolved her mind upon Bodhicitta, vowing to benefit all sentient beings.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, after the Bodhisattva King of the Multitude of Honored Ones had exhorted that woman to resolve her mind upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he rose from his seat and departed."
Ānanda! Behold the karmic reward of this woman’s single-minded devotion.
Now, by means of my perfect and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna*), I prophesy that this woman, at the end of her life here, shall transform her female body and become a man.

In a future age, after ninety-nine kalpas, he shall make offerings to hundreds of thousands of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas, fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, and attain Buddhahood, with the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalakleśa.
After that Buddha attained enlightenment, during that era, not a single person gave rise to unwholesome thoughts.
Ānanda, you should know that the retinue gathered by a Bodhisattva who practices skillful means shall never fall into the three evil realms.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Saṃgharājarāja descended from mid-air and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Having completed his prostration, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva practices skillful means, if for the sake of a single person they give rise to great compassion and gather together wholesome dharmas—whether appearing to have committed an offense or having actually committed one—they may fall into the great hells for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva is capable of enduring all evils and the sufferings of hell; by means of these roots of goodness, he vows not to abandon a single person.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva King Honoring the Multitude, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, noble son!

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such a mind of compassion, although they may experience the five desires, they do not commit grave offenses; they remain free from all transgressions and far removed from all karma that leads to rebirth in the evil realms.”

"Good son! I recall that in the past, beyond incalculable kalpas and even more than that number, there was a brahmin named Jyotiṣka who, for forty-two billion years, constantly practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya) in a forest clearing."
At that time, after the year had passed, the brahmin emerged from the forest and entered the city of Sukhāvatī. Having entered the city, he saw a woman.

When that woman beheld the brahmin’s dignified and majestic appearance, she immediately conceived a desire for him; she approached the brahmin, grasped his feet with her hands, and instantly collapsed to the ground.
"Good son! At that time, the brahmin said to the woman:
'Sister, what do you seek?'"
The woman said,
"I seek a brahmin. The brahmin replied:
"Sister! I do not engage in sexual desire.
The woman said:
"If you do not follow me, I shall die this very day.
Good son! At that time, the brahmin Jyotiṣka thought thus:
"This is neither my dharma nor my time.
Having cultivated the pure brahma-conduct for forty-two billion years, how could I now allow it to be destroyed?"
At that time, the brahmin dragged himself away by force for seven paces; having gone those seven paces, he gave rise to a heart of compassion and thought to himself:
"Though I have violated the precepts and fallen into the evil realms, I am able to endure the sufferings of hell."
"I cannot bear to see this woman suffer such agony; I will not allow this man to cause my death.
Son of good family!
At that time, having thought thus, the brahmin returned to the woman's side, took her by the right hand, and spoke these words:
"Sister, arise; do as you wish. Good son! At that time, the brahmin lived as a householder for twelve years.

When the twelve years had passed, he immediately left the household life once more. He then restored his four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and having completed them, at the end of his life he was reborn among the Brahmā gods.
"Good son! Do not harbor any doubt.
At that time, the brahmin was none other than my own self, and that woman is now Gopī."

"Good son! At that time, because I briefly gave rise to a heart of compassion for that woman, I immediately attained transcendence from the suffering of birth and death for ten hundred thousand kalpas."
"Good son! You should observe in this way: while other sentient beings fall into the hells due to craving and desire, a bodhisattva who practices skillful means is born in the Brahma Heaven."
"This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya: "Good son!"
If Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others had practiced skillful means, they would not have caused Kokālika to fall into hell. Why is this?
O son of good family!
I recall that in a past life, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu named Vimala who dwelt in a cave within a forested wilderness.
Not far from his cave, there were five rishis.

At that time, a great cloud suddenly arose and sent down heavy rain; there was a poor woman who, encountering this torrential rain on the road, became cold, naked, and terrified, and immediately entered the cave where Vimala resided.
When the rain had ceased, the monk Vimala emerged from the cave together with this woman.
Upon witnessing this, the five sages felt a sense of revulsion and said to one another,
"The monk Vimala harbors deceitful intent and has committed an impure act."
At that time, the bhikṣu Vimala, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sages, immediately leaped into the air to a height of seven tala trees.
When the five sages saw the bhikṣu Vimala ascending into the sky, they said to one another:
"According to the scriptures and treatises we have studied, if a person engages in impure conduct, they cannot fly up into the sky like this."
"If one cultivates pure conduct, one can do so.
At that time, the rishi immediately prostrated himself before Vimala with his five limbs touching the ground, joined his palms, and confessed his transgression, not daring to conceal it.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya: "Good son!
At that time, if the bhikṣu Vimala had not employed such skillful means to fly up into the void, these five sages would have entered hell in their very present bodies."
Good son, at that time, was the bhikṣu anyone else?
He was none other than Maitreya Bodhisattva. Good son!
You should know this now: if Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had employed such skillful means to fly up into the air, the bhikṣu Kokālika would not have fallen into hell.
"Good son! You should now know that the skillful means practiced by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are not possessed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

Good son! It is like a courtesan who is well-versed in the sixty-four gestures; for the sake of wealth and treasures, she uses flattering words to entice others, falsely promising to surrender her body, and without any sense of stinginess or regret, she gives away her most prized possessions until she finally obtains those goods.
Having obtained those objects, he drives them away without giving rise to a mind of regret.
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva who practices skillful means knows how to act with appropriate skillful means; he thus teaches and transforms all sentient beings, manifesting his body according to their desires. Regarding necessary objects, his mind is free from stinginess, even to the point of sacrificing his own body for the sake of sentient beings. He delights in roots of goodness and does not seek their karmic rewards.

Having known that sentient beings have cultivated roots of goodness, his mind never regresses; at that very moment, he gives rise to a spirit of renunciation, and regarding the five sensory desires that appear, he is forever free from attachment.

Good son! It is like a black bee among the animals: although it passes through the fragrance and flavor of all flowers, it has no thought of dependence toward them and no attachment; it does not carry away the scent of the petals, leaves, or stalks as it departs.

Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means, it is likewise so: in order to transform sentient beings, he dwells amidst the five desires yet perceives the impermanence of all phenomena; thus, he does not give rise to craving through the notion of permanence, nor does he harm himself or harm others.
"Good son! Just as a small seed, though it produces a sprout, does not lose its original nature nor produce anything different from itself;

so too, good son, the seeds of wisdom—emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-self—though a bodhisattva may have afflictions regarding the pleasures of the five desires, do not produce the sprouts of the three evil realms, nor do they diminish the color of the roots of goodness, nor do they lead to regression."
"Good son! It is like a fisherman who coats his net with bait and casts it into the deep abyss; once he has obtained what he seeks, he immediately pulls it out. Good son!"

The Bodhisattva who practices skillful means is also like this: using the wisdom of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-self, he cultivates his mind and binds it into a net; taking the mind of omniscience as his sustenance, although he may be cast into the mire of the five desires, he draws himself out from the realm of desire according to his vow, and after his life ends, is reborn in the Brahma world.

"Good son! It is like a person who is well-versed in incantations and, having been seized by officials and bound with the fivefold fetters, immediately severs those five bonds by the power of his own incantations and departs according to his wish."

"Good son! Thus, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices skillful means, although he dwells among the five desires and enjoys them together with others, for the sake of transforming sentient beings according to their needs, he uses the mantra of omniscience to sever the bonds of the five desires and is born in the Brahma world."
"Good son! It is like a man well-versed in the arts of war who, concealing a sharp sword, escorts a traveler.

Yet among that crowd, not a single person knows that this man secretly harbors a wondrous stratagem; instead, they treat him with contempt, even feeling pity for him rather than respect, and say to one another:"
"Since that man possesses neither weapons nor allies, he is no valiant hero and lacks any power; unable to save even himself, how could he possibly rescue others?"
"It is impossible that this man could defeat the bandits;
he will surely encounter many hardships.
Then, when that man reached the desolate wilderness, the bandits all rose up together.

At that time, the man, having firmly armed himself, immediately drew the hidden sword; with the first throw of the blade, the bandits were all slain, and once the thieves were destroyed, he returned the sword to its place of concealment.

"Good son! A bodhisattva who practices skillful means well-conceals the sword of wisdom, yet through skillful means dwells among the five desires and enjoys them together with others in order to transform sentient beings."

When śrāvakas see these skillful bodhisattvas dwelling amidst the five desires and enjoying them together, they give rise to turbid thoughts because they do not understand skillful means; or else, out of pity, they consider them to be indolent, thinking:
"If such people cannot even save themselves, how much less can they rescue all sentient beings?"
"It is impossible that one could destroy Māra.

At that time, the Bodhisattva skillfully employs the sword of wisdom and expedient means; according to his aspirations, he severs all afflictions and utterly annihilates them. With the sword of wisdom, he reaches a pure Buddha-field where there are no women, nor even a single thought of desire.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Priyakāra who entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms in due order, eventually arriving at the house of a certain elder.
The elder had a daughter named Guṇavardhanā, who was staying atop a high tower.
At that time, when the woman heard the Bodhisattva’s voice, she immediately took the food and went out toward the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana.

Upon seeing the Bodhisattva, she beheld his physical form, his marks and signs of excellence, and his voice; lustful desire arose instantly, and consumed by passion, her life ended at once and her bones and joints fell apart.
When the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana saw the girl Guṇavardhanā, he too gave rise to unwholesome thoughts of lustful desire.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana reflected to himself: "What is that dharma?"
The Dharma consists of attachment.
What is that eye? What is this eye?
The nature of the eye is not cognition; it is merely a mass of flesh—without affection or knowledge, without thought or awareness, without discrimination, its nature fundamentally empty.
"The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental objects.

Having observed in this way—from the thin skin and thick skin, the blood, flesh, fat, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, marrow, bones, tendons, and veins, from the feet to the crown of the head—whether internally or externally, there is not a single dharma that is to be cherished or clung to, nor any object of anger or delusion.
Observing all phenomena as they truly are, he immediately became free from desire and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

Having attained the patience of non-arising, his mind was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation; he then ascended into the air to the height of a *tāla* tree and circumambulated the city of Śrāvastī seven times.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana soaring through the air like a king of geese, unimpeded by anything.
Having seen this, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!
“Did you see the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana fly through the air, soaring like a king of geese without any obstruction?
Ānanda replied, “Indeed, I saw him.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Because this Bodhisattva Priyadarśana gave rise to a mind of desire and sought after all dharmas, he shall immediately destroy the hosts of Māra and turn the wheel of Dharma.”

After the girl Guṇavardhanā passed away, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; her female body was transformed, and she became a man. He naturally came to dwell in a palace made of the seven precious jewels, twelve yojanas in length and breadth, with fourteen thousand celestial maidens serving as his attendants.
The devaputra Guṇavardhana attained the knowledge of past lives and investigated his prior karmic conduct, reflecting:
"By what karmic conditions have I come to be born here?

Having thus reflected, he saw that he had been the daughter of a householder in the city of Śrāvastī; because he had seen the Bodhisattva Maitreya and conceived a mind of lustful desire, his lustful mind having become intense, his life ended immediately, and he was transformed from a female body into a male.
"By means of this matter, I have attained immeasurable supernormal powers.
At that time, the devaputra Vardhamāna thought to himself:
"It is by giving rise to sexual desire that one obtains such a reward."
"Now, my mind is profoundly pure toward the Bodhisattva Prema; I pay him homage and offer worship to him.
If I were now to remain and first enjoy the five sensual pleasures, this would not be appropriate for me."
Having reflected thus, he intended to go to the Tathāgata to see him, pay homage, and make offerings to the Bodhisattva Priyakāra.

Then, at the beginning of the night, the Devaputra Puṇyavardhana, together with his retinue, took celestial flowers, incense, ointments, and powdered incense, and came to the place where the Buddha was. Using his own radiance, he illuminated the Jetavana Grove in its entirety. He entered to visit the World-Honored One and to see Priyakāra; he then made offerings to the Buddha with celestial flowers, powdered incense, and ointments. He prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Priyakāra, as well as the entire assembly, circumambulated them three times to the right, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“The Honored One of gods and men, Inconceivable, The conduct of a Bodhisattva...”
It is also inconceivable.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; even those of great renown are likewise inconceivable.
In the past, in Śrāvastī, I was once a young girl named Puṇyavardhanā, living in the house of an elder.
I was young in years and possessed of a handsome appearance; my parents loved me dearly and provided me with protection.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is free from frivolity; he possesses a fatherly affection and great majestic power.
Entering the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms, he gradually arrived at the house where my father resided.
At that time, hearing his beautiful and wondrous voice, my heart was filled with great joy,
and I immediately took the food and went out.
I then approached the one who practices the Great Mind, the Son of the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
When I saw the Bodhisattva, he was already within my heart; as I contemplated his pure and wondrous form, a defiled desire arose in my mind.
If I do not obtain him—the object of my inner wish—then at that very moment, my life shall perish.
At that time, my mouth was unable to speak, and the food held in my hand could not be given to him.
My inner heart burned with fever, and lustful desire arose; at that moment, my body grew hot, and I immediately passed away.
At that time, when my life ended, within the span of a single thought-moment, I immediately attained rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having left behind the lowest state of a woman's body, I became a man, praised by all people.
A magnificent and wondrous palace appeared spontaneously, adorned with various exquisite jewels, treasures held dear by men.
It was fully provided with ten thousand [beings] and four thousand court ladies;
such a retinue as this is my possession.
By means of this condition, I immediately examined my past lives and reflected within myself, thereby knowing the causes of the past.
Having obtained such a retribution, I, with a defiled mind, gazed upon Priyakārin;
yet, by seeing the Bodhisattva, I attained the light of joy.
The flames of light emitted from my body are the result of those karmic conditions, for which I have received such retribution.
I never wish to seek the Two Vehicles; that which I aspire to, only the Buddha knows.
If the retribution for a mind of lustful desire is still such as this, how much more so for one who can cultivate a virtuous mind and offer worship?
Just as I now, before the World-Honored One, have made such a vow to seek all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā).
Even if one were to practice for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, never regressing from the wisdom of the Buddha;
having encountered a virtuous friend, such as the Bodhisattva Maitreya, I shall now [act] accordingly.
The true offering is the offering of the Dharma; any other offering is not a true offering. Only the arousal of the bodhicitta is the true offering.
Practicing for enlightenment, most excellent and most venerable, I shall no longer look upon women with desire; such is my vow—to be free from the female body.
I spoke to the Buddhas of the four fearlessnesses; my parents immediately perceived me, their bodies broken and withered, as they wailed and wept in grief.
The parents said to him, "This is what a bhikṣu has done; we cry out in resentment and reproach the bhikṣu.
By the Buddha's divine power, he caused that devaputra to go to his parents' place and rebuke and admonish them with parables:
"Do not give rise to anger toward this bhikṣu; do not suffer various afflictions for a long night.
The woman Guṇavardhanā, having passed away first, has immediately attained rebirth in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
Having left behind this female body, you shall attain the state of a man; with a celestial body, your radiance will shine afar.
Your parents should now go to the presence of the World-Honored One and repent for their former unwholesome thoughts.
"Except for the Tathāgata, there are no other Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, upon whom one can rely.
With a fearless heart, he exhorted his parents, and immediately his parents heard the name of the Buddha.
Seeking harmony and union, they arrived at the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resided.
Having reached the Buddha’s presence, they bowed their heads in reverent salutation to the Honored One among two-legged beings.
"I now repent of my former mind of anger;
I pay respectful homage to the Honored One among men.
I shall now ask what should be asked; the Tathāgata knows it himself."
How does one make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
How does one practice and cultivate virtuous conduct?
Regarding these questions, I pray that you will explain them; having heard this, [I shall practice accordingly].
“Dedicate yourself single-mindedly to practice.
The Buddha, knowing that the hearts of his parents were firm and resolute, the Teacher of Gods and Humans spoke these words:
“If you wish to make offerings to all Buddhas, dedicate your mind with steadfast resolve and give rise to the bodhicitta.”
The parents of Guṇavardhana, together with their entire retinue numbering five hundred,
having heard these words from the Teacher of Gods and Men, gave rise to the bodhicitta and made great vows.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Ānanda:
“Listen now attentively to what I shall say.
The conduct of a bodhisattva is inconceivable; it is unsurpassed wisdom.”
And through skillful means,
when women see me, if they should give rise to a mind of desire, they shall immediately be freed from it;
regarding their female bodies, they shall become men and be honored by others.
Ānanda, observe: such is the power of virtue; had one committed what is contrary to the Dharma, one would have fallen into the evil realms.
A valiant person practices this, whereby they destroy the hosts of Māra, cause others to be born in heaven, and themselves become gods among humans.
Now this son of heaven makes offerings to me; his mind is reverent and he is rightly directed toward Bodhi.
He shall make offerings to immeasurable World-Honored Ones, and in a future age he will attain Buddhahood, named Sudarśana.
These five hundred people, who are directed toward Bodhi, shall also become Buddhas and serve as teachers of gods and humans.
Since the Buddha possesses such virtues, who would not make offerings to him?
In this place, through deep faith, one attains immeasurable bliss.
Not by one woman, nor two, nor three, but by immeasurable hundreds of thousands,
nayutas, and billions, upon seeing Priyakāra, they gave rise to thoughts of lustful desire.
He immediately passed away and was reborn as a man.
A great king of physicians with a vast reputation—whom would not revere such a bodhisattva?
"Even if one gives rise to a desire-filled mind, one still attains further happiness; how much more so for a Bodhisattva who gives rise to a mind of reverence.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle 106.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 107,
translated by the Eastern Jin Indian layman Zhu Nanti,
Part Two of the Thirty-eighth Chapter on Mahāyāna Expedient Means.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is like Mount Sumeru; if various colors reach its slopes, they all become one golden color.”
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who come before a bodhisattva—whether with a mind of anger, a pure mind, or a mind stained by desire—all such states are entirely of one and the same color: the color of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).”
"Bhagavān! From this day forward, I shall give rise to a mind of reverence toward all bodhisattvas as lofty as Mount Sumeru. Bhagavān!"
It is like a king of medicines named Sarvadarśin; whether one takes it with a mind of anger or a pure mind, all shall be healed, for that medicine can eliminate all poisons.
World-Honored One!

It is the same for a bodhisattva: if there are those with minds of anger or minds of purity who come before a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva is able to eliminate for them all the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said.
Then Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is unprecedented.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is most honored and supreme.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the various dhyānas and, having cultivated these dhyānas, returns to the desire realm to teach and transform sentient beings—even while practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness to transform sentient beings and lead them to become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—he never, by virtue of his great compassion, departs from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) until the end.

"Bhagavān! The skillful means practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inconceivable; thus, although they may experience the bonds of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, they have no attachment or craving therein."
“World-Honored One!
I shall now, by means of my eloquence of joyful speech, speak of a small portion of the merits of all bodhisattvas.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Speak as you wish. “World-Honored One!

Suppose there were a vast, desolate wilderness of hunger with a great high wall reaching up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). In that great, desolate wilderness of hunger there was but a single gate, and within this wilderness there were many sentient beings.”

Not far from the marsh, there was a great city—abundant, joyful, and flourishing, magnificent, pure, and exquisite; if any sentient beings entered that city, they would be free from old age, sickness, and death.
The road leading toward the city was only one foot wide, yet it was perfectly straight.

Among the multitude in that marsh, there was a wise man—sharp-witted and sagacious—who suddenly gave rise to a thought, desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings through his great compassion.
This person then cried out in a loud voice from within the empty wilderness:
"All you people, you should know that not far from here there is a great city, prosperous, flourishing, magnificent, pure, and exquisite, where many devas and humans dwell."
"If there are sentient beings who enter that city, they shall be free from old age, sickness, and death, and I can also preach the Dharma for transcending old age, sickness, and death.
You all should come; let us go there together, and I shall serve as the great guide for you all."
In that empty marsh there was a lowly being who conceived a longing to seek understanding and spoke thus:
"If you can cause me to remain in this marsh, I shall accept your instruction;
but if you wish to lead me out of this marsh, I cannot accept it."
A superior being spoke thus: "I shall go with you to the place where you are going.
When the beings of little merit in this empty marshland heard such a proclamation, they did not believe it upon hearing it, nor did they follow the wise person.
“World-Honored One!

At that time, the wise man emerged from the empty wilderness and looked in the four directions; he saw a path only one foot wide, narrow and constricted, with great deep pits on both sides of it, each a hundred thousand cubits deep.”
The wise person braces the path on both sides with wooden planks; crawling forward upon it, he does not look to the left or right.
Although hostile bandits follow behind and terrify him, at that time he does not look back either, for his mind is courageous and sharp, giving rise to no fear.
Having gradually passed through [the obstacles], he finally beheld that city; having seen the city, his mind was free from fear.
After entering the city, there was no old age, sickness, or death, and he brought great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings by preaching the Dharma for transcending old age, sickness, and death.
“World-Honored One!
The great empty wilderness of famine is the famine of birth-and-death.
The great high wall reaching up to the formless realm is ignorance and craving for existence.”
The many sentient beings within this marsh are all ordinary worldlings caught in the cycle of birth and death.
The path toward the city that is only one foot wide is a side track.
Those among the multitude in that marsh who are wise people are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Those inferior beings who hope to understand and remain unmoved within the marsh are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Those superior beings who say, "I shall go with you to the place you are bound for," are other bodhisattvas.
Those beings of meager merit who hear this and do not believe are all those of wrong views, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and their disciples.
Those who emerge from the great empty marsh are those who diligently cultivate the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñā-citta*).
The one-fathom narrow path is the gateway to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-mukha*).
On both sides of that path are great, deep pits a hundred thousand cubits deep; these are the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The propping of the path on both sides with wooden planks represents wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).
Crawling forward represents the Bodhisattva gathering in all sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

"The hostile bandits following behind and pursuing those who are afraid" refers to Māra and his followers, as well as those sentient beings who have deeply given rise to the sixty-two views and those who slight and slander the Bodhisattvas.
Not looking behind signifies the fulfillment of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) with single-minded devotion.
Not glancing to the left or right signifies not praising the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The great city is the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).

Having gradually passed through [the obstacles] and finally beholding that city, the fact that his mind is free from fear once he has seen the city means that this bodhisattva, having seen the Buddha and the Buddha’s conduct, single-mindedly reveres the wisdom, majesty, and virtue of the Buddha; having skillfully studied the *prajñāpāramitā*, he employs expedient means (*upāya*) to gradually and appropriately draw near to all sentient beings without any doubt or difficulty.

That there are none who grow old, fall ill, or die upon entering the city signifies that this bodhisattva benefits immeasurable sentient beings by causing them to transcend old age, illness, and death.
That he preaches the Dharma signifies that he is a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“World-Honored One!
I now pay homage to all bodhisattvas.
Having spoken these words, ten thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mahākāśyapa, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are able to exhort and inspire all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; you are able to accomplish immeasurable merit.”
If an action can harm oneself or harm others, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will never perform it;
if there is speech that can harm oneself or harm others, they likewise will not engage in it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇottara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are actions or words that can harm oneself or harm others—things which no Bodhisattva would ever do—World-Honored One!”

For what reason did he, in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, while practicing the bodhisattva path with only one lifetime remaining, act as a great brahmin named Jyotiṣka and speak these words:
"The path to bodhi is extremely difficult to attain"?
"How could a bald-headed man accomplish such a task?
I have no desire to see him.
What is the meaning of the World-Honored One’s words spoken at that time?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Puṇyavardhana: “Good son!
You must not give rise to doubt regarding the Tathāgata or the Bodhisattvas.”
Why is this? Because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have accomplished inconceivable skillful means; Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell in various skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings.
"Good son! Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well.
There is a sutra titled 'The Perfection of Skillful Means' (Upāya-pāramitā); I shall now expound it for you."
At that time, the Bodhisattva gradually learned skillful means from Dīpaṃkara Buddha; now, I shall also provide you with a brief explanation and analysis. Noble son!

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva saw Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). From that time forth, he has been free from error or delusion, jesting, and loss of mindfulness; he has had no unconcentrated mind, and his wisdom has never diminished.

"Good son! Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) according to his original vow, he is able to achieve unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) after seven days;
if he so desires, he can also achieve it after a hundred eons."

For the sake of sentient beings, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas undergo all forms of existence; wherever they may be, by means of the power of wisdom, they fulfill their aspirations according to their seekers' needs, and only thereafter do they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son! By the power of skillful means, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the world for immeasurable billions of kalpas, yet they feel no sorrow and never grow weary or seek to depart.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
Furthermore, good son,
regarding all the meditative concentrations of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, if a śrāvaka enters them, his body and mind become unmoving, and he thinks to himself that he has already entered nirvāṇa.

If a bodhisattva enters [this state], they apply physical and mental diligence without indolence; they gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and out of great compassion, they teach and transform sentient beings by means of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.

Furthermore, good son, it is according to his original vow that the bodhisattva dwells in the Tuṣita heaven palace; he is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the wheel of Dharma—it is not that he is unable.
While in the Tuṣita Heaven, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:
"The people of Jambudvīpa cannot come to this Tuṣita Heaven to hear and receive the teaching of the Dharma; however, the devas of Tuṣita can descend to Jambudvīpa to hear the Dharma."
For this reason, the Bodhisattva leaves the Tuṣita Heaven and attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in Jambudvīpa.
This is called the practice of skillful means by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva, in accordance with his original vow, may come from the Tuṣita Heaven without entering a mother’s womb, and is likewise able to immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If he were not to enter, sentient beings might give rise to doubt and say:
"From where has this bodhisattva come?
Is he a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a gandharva, or is he a magical transformation?"
Having harbored such doubts, one is unable to listen to the Dharma, nor can one practice to sever all afflictions.
Therefore, it is not that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not enter the mother’s womb; rather, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
Good son, do not think that the bodhisattva truly dwells in the mother’s womb; do not give rise to such a view.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not truly enter the mother’s womb. Why is that?
When the Bodhisattva enters the Immaculate Samādhi and does not arise from this concentration until he descends from Tuṣita and sits beneath the Bodhi tree, the devas of Tuṣita think to themselves:
"The Bodhisattva’s life has come to an end; he will never return here again."

At that time, while the Bodhisattva was actually remaining unmoved in the Tuṣita Heaven, he manifested entering the womb, experiencing the five desires, being born, leaving home, and practicing austerities.
All sentient beings regard these as real, yet for a bodhisattva, they are all transformations.

A bodhisattva’s entering the womb, experiencing desire, manifesting personal enjoyment, leaving home, and practicing austerities—all these are performed through the power of a bodhisattva’s transformations.
Why is this? Because at that time, the conduct of the bodhisattva is so pure that he will never again enter a womb, having long since become weary of and detached from such existence.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
"For what reason does he manifest entry into the mother's womb appearing as a white elephant? Good son!

Because he is the most honored among Bodhisattvas in this trichiliocosm and has perfected pure and white dharmas, he manifests entry into the mother's womb appearing as a white elephant; no other deva, human, ghost, or spirit is able to enter the mother's womb in such a manner."
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason does the bodhisattva remain in the womb for a full ten months before emerging?
"Good son! There may be other sentient beings who give rise to this thought:
'If the ten months are not completed, this boy's body will perhaps not be fully formed.'"
For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests dwelling within the womb for a full ten months.
From the initial entry into the womb until the completion of those ten months, throughout that interval, various devas constantly come to the mother’s side to pay homage and surround her.
At that time, the devas beheld the high tower where the Bodhisattva’s body was situated, adorned entirely with the seven treasures—a sight not possessed by the devas themselves.
Having witnessed this auspicious omen, twenty-four thousand sons of gods resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
For what reason, son of good family, does the bodhisattva enter the womb from the right side?
Son of good family!
There may be sentient beings who harbor such doubts, thinking that the Bodhisattva was born from the union of the parents' vital essences.
To sever those doubts and to manifest birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), he entered through the side.
Once he had entered her side, there was no further place for him to enter; yet Queen Māyā experienced such physical and mental bliss as she had never before attained.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means (*upāya*).
"For what reason does a bodhisattva take birth in a secluded place, rather than in a household or within a city? Good son,

it is because a bodhisattva has from the outset always delighted in secluded places, praised such places, and praised the quietude of mountain forests and hermitages, practicing therein the state of cessation."

If a bodhisattva is born into a household, devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, and others will come to make offerings, bearing flowers, powdered incense, and unguents, as well as hundreds of thousands of immeasurable celestial musical performances.
At that time, all the people of the city of Kapilavastu were mentally distracted, negligent, and arrogant, such that they were unable to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva was born in a secluded place, rather than within the city or inside a house.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason did the mother of the bodhisattva give birth to the bodhisattva while leaning back and grasping a branch of the śāla tree?
"Good son! Sentient beings harbor doubts, thinking that when Queen Māyā gave birth to the Bodhisattva, she experienced various sufferings and afflictions just like other women.
To demonstrate to those beings that she experienced supreme bliss, she reached up and grasped a branch of the tree while giving birth to the Bodhisattva."
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason does the bodhisattva emerge from the right side with right mindfulness, rather than from any other part of the body?

"Good son! The pure conduct of a bodhisattva is the most honored and supreme within the trichiliocosm; it does not abide because of the female organ, nor does it emerge because of the female organ. A bodhisattva in his final birth manifests in this way, and no other practitioner of the holy life does so. For this reason, the bodhisattva emerges from the right side."
Once born, there is likewise no place from which he emerges; as it was before, so it is after.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
For what reason, when the Bodhisattva was first born, did Śakra Devānām Indra receive him with precious robes, and not some other deva?
"Good son, in the past Śakra Devānām-indra made this vow:
'If a Bodhisattva is born, I shall receive him upon a precious robe.'"
Because the bodhisattva’s roots of goodness are sublime, they increase the faith, respect, and offerings of the other devas.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
"For what reason, when the Bodhisattva was born, did he immediately take seven steps, neither six nor eight?

Good son! It is because the Bodhisattva possesses great supernormal power and the marks of a Great Man of diligent vigor, which he desires to manifest to sentient beings; no other person is able to manifest in such a way."
If there are other sentient beings to benefit by seven steps, the Bodhisattva takes six;
if there are other sentient beings to benefit by eight steps, he then takes seven.
Therefore, there was no one to support the Bodhisattva as he took seven steps—not six, nor eight.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means (upāya).
"For what reason did the Bodhisattva, having taken seven steps, proclaim these words:
'I am the most honored and most supreme in the world; I am free from old age, sickness, and death'?"

"Good son! At that time, among the assembly, Śakra, Brahmā, the various devas, and the sons of devas harbored conceit in their hearts, saying to themselves: 'We are the most honored ones in this world.'"
At that time, those devaputras were arrogant and conceited, lacking a mind of reverence; the Bodhisattva then thought:
"These devaputras possess such pride, and because of this pride, they will fall into the three evil realms for a long night."
Therefore, the Bodhisattva spoke these words:
"I am the most honored and supreme in the world; I am free from old age, sickness, and death.
When the Bodhisattva uttered these words at that time, their voice was heard throughout the entire trichiliocosm.
There were also various devas who had not yet gathered when the Bodhisattva was born; upon hearing this sound, they all assembled.
At that time, the devas of the desire realm and the form realm joined their palms in reverence and paid homage to the Bodhisattva, each saying to one another:
"It is unprecedented! It is marvelous!"
Therefore, after the Bodhisattva had taken seven steps, he made this true declaration:
"I am the most honored and supreme in the world; I am free from the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death."
"This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason, after taking seven steps, did he laugh so loudly?
Good son!..."
The Bodhisattva does not smile out of desire, nor does he smile out of pride, nor does he smile out of contempt.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"These sentient beings possess desire, anger, and ignorance, as well as all other afflictions, just as they did originally; now they are likewise so."

I originally exhorted them to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and I have now attained it myself; yet those sentient beings remain indolent and lazy, and thus they still dwell within the ocean of suffering in saṃsāra, having not severed their afflictions.

These sentient beings and I simultaneously gave rise to the bodhicitta; yet while I have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, those sentient beings remain in the ocean of suffering and affliction within saṃsāra due to their indolence and laziness.
These inferior beings, for the sake of gain and offerings, do not diligently apply themselves to seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Although these beings still now pay homage to me and make offerings to me, at that time I gave rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); I have now fulfilled my vow.
For these reasons, the Bodhisattva laughed heartily.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing skillful means (*upāya*).
"By what cause and condition was the Bodhisattva’s body pure at birth, free from any impurity, such that Śakra Devendra and Brahmā Sahāmpati bathed him?"

Good son! Because the Bodhisattva desires to cause Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas to offer worship, and because he also follows worldly custom—just as a newborn infant ought to be bathed—the Bodhisattva, though his body is free from impurity, causes Śakra and Brahmā to bathe him.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason does the bodhisattva, while in a secluded place, not proceed immediately to the site of enlightenment but instead returns to the palace?

"Good son! Because he wishes to demonstrate the fulfillment of the sense faculties, he manifests dwelling in a palace and enjoying himself with the five desires; subsequently, he renounces the four continents and goes forth into homelessness.

Furthermore, desiring to transform others by causing them to abandon the five desires, he shaves his hair and beard, dons the dharma robes, and leaves the household life; for these reasons, he makes such a manifestation."
Therefore, the bodhisattva returns once more to his home rather than proceeding directly to the site of enlightenment from a secluded place;
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
"For what reason did Lady Māyā pass away shortly after the Bodhisattva was born, when he was only seven days old?
Good son! This was because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of Lady Māyā had reached its end; it was not the fault of the Bodhisattva."

When the Bodhisattva was previously in the Tuṣita Heaven, he observed with his divine eye that Queen Māyā’s life-force would remain for seven days after the ten months were complete; at that time, the Bodhisattva descended from the Tuṣita Heaven.
Because the Bodhisattva, through skillful means, knows that Queen Māyā’s life-force was about to end, he descended to be born; this is not the fault of the Bodhisattva.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
"For what reason does a bodhisattva skillfully study writing, treatises, games of chance, archery, charioteering, military strategy, tactical planning, and various arts and crafts? Good son,
it is for the sake of learning worldly dharmas."
Within the trichiliocosm, there is not a single matter that the Bodhisattva does not know.

Whether it be verses, eloquence in speech, responsive eloquence, incantations, jesting, singing, dancing, music, or crafts, the Bodhisattva already fully understands them all from the moment of his birth.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason does the bodhisattva take a consort, female attendants, and a retinue?
O son of good family!
A bodhisattva does not act out of desire.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva is a man who has transcended desire.
At that time, if the Bodhisattva were not to manifest a wife, children, or grandchildren, sentient beings would say that the Bodhisattva is not a man.
If sentient beings harbor such doubts, they will incur immeasurable sin.
To sever that doubt, he took a woman of the Śākya clan and manifested the appearance of having Rāhula.
If anyone should think that Rāhula was born from the union of father and mother, let them not hold such a view.
Furthermore, Rāhula descended from his life in the heavens to enter the womb; he was not born through the union of his parents.
Moreover, because Rāhula had made a fundamental vow, that whenever there is a Bodhisattva in their final birth before Buddhahood, he shall act as that Bodhisattva’s son.
Gopī originally made this vow at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, until I reach the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood, may you always be my husband and I your wife, for the sake of this brahmin."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having accepted the seven stalks of *utpala* flowers, spoke these words:
"Although I do not accept them, I shall now fulfill the aspiration of this virtuous woman."
Having made this vow, he did not depart from the roots of goodness of the seven flowers; for this reason, the Bodhisattva accepted her as his consort.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva in his final birth accomplishes the manifestation of dwelling amidst palace ladies within the inner chambers.

At that time, the Bodhisattva had achieved a wondrous physical form and was honored by the devas; he had accomplished his renunciation. Seeing all these matters thus fulfilled, the Śākya maiden focused her mind single-mindedly and made this vow, generating the bodhicitta:
"May I also be endowed with such accomplishments as these."
For this reason, the Bodhisattva took Gopī as his wife in order to cause her to give rise to this thought.

Furthermore, there are beings of great resolve who dwell in the household life; having experienced the various pleasures of the five desires, wealth, servants, and kin, the Bodhisattva manifests these matters so that he may cause those beings to renounce the household life, its five desires, wealth, servants, and kin, and instead go forth into homelessness.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva manifests living as a householder amidst the five desires, wealth, treasures, servants, and kin, only to renounce them and leave the home life.
When sentient beings see this, they reflect:
"The Bodhisattva possesses the most exquisite and unsurpassed five desires, yet he is still able to renounce them and go forth; how much more so should we not also go forth?"
"Furthermore, all the wives, sons, and daughters that a bodhisattva possesses were those whom he transformed through various wholesome dharmas while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past.
These sentient beings also made this vow:
'If this bodhisattva reaches his final birth, we shall always serve as his wife, children, and kinsmen.'"
Furthermore, because he wishes to increase the pure, white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) of such people, the Bodhisattva dwells among his wife, children, and retinue.

Moreover, as for the Bodhisattva dwelling in the palace, it is because he desires to transform and guide the forty-two thousand ladies-in-waiting so that they may resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and also so that other people shall not fall into the evil realms; therefore, the Bodhisattva remains within the palace with his wife, children, and retinue.
Furthermore, all women are consumed by the fire of desire; yet upon seeing the Bodhisattva, they immediately become free from lustful passion.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva transforms himself into various bodies, such that their facial features, height, and proportions are no different from those of his original form.

Those women enjoyed themselves together with the emanated bodhisattva, each thinking to herself that she was enjoying herself with a real bodhisattva; meanwhile, at that time, the bodhisattva remained constantly in meditative concentration, cultivating the practice of peaceful and blissful conduct.

Just as an emanated bodhisattva experiences the five desires without any thought of desire, so too is the true bodhisattva; from the time of Kāśyapa Buddha until his final birth, he has already been free from sexual desire.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
The original vows of Chandaka and Kanthaka were likewise so.
For what reason did the Bodhisattva contemplate beneath the tree in Jambudvīpa?
"Good son! It is for the sake of teaching and transforming seven hundred million devas.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva wishes to let his parents know that he will certainly shave off his hair and beard, don the Dharma robes, and leave the household life."

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva wished to manifest the increase of wisdom, the Jambu tree followed him with its shade; desiring to cause sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness, the Bodhisattva therefore sat in meditation and contemplation beneath the Jambu tree.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason does the bodhisattva not take pleasure in the five desires for himself, but instead leaves the city to go on an excursion?

"Good son! It is because he wishes to manifest the sight of old age, sickness, and death that he causes his kinsmen to know that the Bodhisattva has left home to study the Way out of fear of old age, sickness, and death; it is not that he has left home out of arrogance or to diminish his kin, but rather that he has left home out of a desire to benefit them."
The Bodhisattva perceives the faults and afflictions of the household life, and for this reason leaves the home.

Yet, in order to demonstrate to all sentient beings the suffering of old age, sickness, and death, the Bodhisattva does not delight in the five desires and departs from the city to go on a tour of observation.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason does the bodhisattva go forth from home at midnight? Good son!
Desiring to manifest the roots of goodness that benefit sentient beings, the Bodhisattva increases the roots of goodness of sentient beings wherever he dwells. Noble son!
Furthermore, for the sake of pure and wholesome dharmas, he abandons the five desires and leaves the household life without informing his retinue.
Having departed from all worldly pleasures, one never departs from the pure and white Dharma; for this reason, the Bodhisattva leaves home at midnight.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
"For what reason did the Bodhisattva cause his palace women and female musicians to fall asleep before he renounced the world?
Good son! It was because he wished to ensure that the blame for the faults of renunciation would fall entirely upon the devas."
If there are kinsmen or relatives who, upon seeing the Bodhisattva renounce the household life, give rise to a mind of anger and resentment, the Bodhisattva should reflect thus:
"This person harbors an evil heart toward me; they shall consequently suffer for a long night and fall into the three evil realms."

His kinsmen and relatives understood it thus: "These were the devas who, because [the Bodhisattva] was shrouded in sleep, opened the gates, led the way, and ascended into the sky; it was not the fault of the Bodhisattva."
At that time, the people’s faith would have increased, while their lack of faith toward the celestial beings would have arisen.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva, seeing such faults, covered the palace ladies and female musicians with sleep before departing the home life.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason did the bodhisattva send Chandaka, the white horse, and the precious robes and necklaces back home?
Good son! He desires to let his retinue know that the Bodhisattva does not crave the fame, fine garments, superior clothing, or various precious necklaces of household life.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects in this way: "I now practice such training so as to cause all people to follow my example in relinquishing all possessions and going forth from home into the Buddha-dharma."
Having trained in this manner, these people distance themselves from all beloved objects and practice the four noble lineages;
they do so except when their parents do not permit them to go forth into the homeless life.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
For what reason, son of good family, does the bodhisattva use a blade to shave off his own hair?
Son of good family!
Within this trichiliocosm, there is no deva, nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, human, or non-human who can approach the majestic power of the Bodhisattva, much less be able to shave his hair.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva manifested this in order to inspire deep faith in sentient beings; wishing to leave the household life, he himself took up a blade and shaved his hair.
Furthermore, it was for the sake of King Śuddhodana.
At that time, King Śuddhodana conceived an evil thought; relying on his own noble lineage, he spoke with arrogance:
"Whoever shaves my son's hair shall be executed."
At that time, when King Śuddhodana heard that the Bodhisattva had personally taken up a blade to shave his hair, his malevolent thoughts were immediately extinguished.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing skillful means (*upāya*).
“Good son! Listen well now.
For what reason did the Bodhisattva practice austerities for six years?”

Good son! It is not that this Bodhisattva undergoes this suffering as a residual retribution for past karma; rather, he does so to cause sentient beings to give rise to a sense of dread regarding all karmic retributions for evil deeds and to turn toward the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, good son!
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Bodhisattva spoke these words:
"I do not wish to see this shaven-headed mendicant."
"How could one who is bald attain bodhi?
The path to bodhi is profoundly deep and difficult to attain.
Such individuals as these are also Bodhisattvas manifesting skillful means.
One should understand the meaning of what has been said here.
For what reason does the bodhisattva utter such harsh and offensive words?
O son of good family!
At that time, when Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world, there was a son of a brahmin named Jyotiṣka.
He had five close friends, all of whom were sons of great brahmins who had previously studied the Mahāyāna.
At that time, because those five men had long associated with evil friends, they lost their bodhicitta. Good son!

At the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, those five men served non-Buddhist practitioners and did not believe in the Buddha-dharma; they understood the language of non-Buddhists but did not understand the language of the Buddha, and they understood the teachings of non-Buddhists but did not understand the teachings of the Buddha.
At that time, five men served a teacher of non-Buddhist paths.
That teacher claimed of himself:
"I am a Buddha, a World-Honored One; I am the All-Knowing One."
"I too possess the path to enlightenment.

At that time, the brahmin Jyotiṣka, employing skillful means, desired to lead the five men back so they might become precious vessels; wishing to turn away the heterodox and erroneous minds of those five men, he went to the potter's workshop by way of skillful means and spoke these words:
"I now wish to see the shaven-headed mendicant."
"How can one who is bald attain bodhi?
The path to bodhi is extremely profound and difficult to attain.
"Good son! [he said].
After these words had been spoken, after a short time had passed, while the brahmin Jotipāla was with those five men in a secluded place, the potter arrived at that spot.
Having arrived at that place, he immediately praised the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa Buddha in the presence of the brahmin Jyotiṣka, and further addressed Jyotiṣka as follows:
"You should go with me to the place where the Buddha is."
"Good son! At that time, the brahmin Jyotiṣka thought to himself:
'These five men's roots of goodness are not yet mature.'"

If I were to praise Kāśyapa Buddha as not being the teacher of non-Buddhists, these five people would surely give rise to doubt; for it would be impossible for them to reach the presence of the Buddha [with such uncertainty].
At that time, because Śuddhodana protected his original vow and practiced the skillful means of the retribution of the *prajñāpāramitā*, he spoke these words:
"I do not wish to see this shaven-headed practitioner."
"How can one who is bald attain bodhi?
The path to bodhi is extremely profound and difficult to attain.
How does the Prajñāpāramitā reward the practice of a bodhisattva?"

In the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no notion of enlightenment (bodhi) and no notion of a Buddha. At that time, one does not perceive a Buddha, nor does one perceive enlightenment; furthermore, one does not perceive enlightenment internally, nor does one perceive enlightenment externally, nor does one perceive enlightenment both internally and externally. Thus, one fully knows that enlightenment is empty and devoid of any dharma.
At that time, knowing that all phenomena are non-existent, Jyotiṣka practiced skillful means and spoke these words:
"I do not wish to see a shaven-headed mendicant."
"How can one who is bald attain bodhi?
The path to bodhi is exceedingly profound and difficult to attain.
"O son of good family!"
Again, at another time, the brahmin Jyotiṣka and those five men went to the bank of a river.
At that moment, the potter, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority and desiring to transform those five men, went to their location once more and spoke thus to the brahmin Jyotiṣka:
"You should come with me to the presence of the Buddha to pay him homage, make offerings, and show him reverence, respect, and praise."
"The appearance of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the world is extremely rare.

Hearing the potter’s praise, the brahmin Jotipāla was unwilling to leave. At that time, the potter immediately stepped forward, seized the brahmin by the hair with his hand, and forcibly led him toward the Buddha's dwelling; at that moment, the five men followed Jotipāla with devoted hearts and likewise arrived at the Buddha's dwelling.
At that time, according to the established law of the kingdom, if one seized another by the hair and reported it to the authorities, the seizer was liable to death.
Then, five men conceived wrong views; seeing the brahmin Jyotiṣka seize [the Buddha’s] hair, their minds were swayed and they followed after him.

"What merit does that Tathāgata’s Dharma possess that it causes this potter to disregard the penalty of death, seize Jyotiṣka by the hair, and bring him before the Buddha to pay homage, make offerings, and show reverence, respect, and praise?"
At that time, the five men directed their minds toward the presence of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Having seen the Buddha, their original vows were reawakened and they gave rise to faith and reverence.
Once faith and reverence had arisen, they immediately rebuked Jyotiṣka before the Buddha:
"Since the World-Honored One possesses such majestic virtue as we have heard described, how could our minds not give rise to faith and reverence? "Good sons!
At that time, the five men, having witnessed the majestic virtue of Kāśyapa Buddha and heard his eloquence, again resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

At that time, Kāśyapa Buddha, seeing that the five men had attained single-minded concentration, preached for them the *Dhāraṇī of the Non-retrogressive Wheel of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka*, the Vajra-words, and the *Anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, teaching them in successive order.
At that time, the five men immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Good son!

I have now fully attained the wisdom of a Buddha; had the brahmin Jyotiṣka praised the Buddha Kāśyapa instead of praising his own non-Buddhist teachers at that time, it would have been impossible for those five men to have gone to the Buddha’s presence, let alone have given rise to a heart of faith and reverence.

"Good son! The brahmin Jyotiṣka, in order to transform five people who were studying the Bodhisattva Vehicle, employed the skillful means of the karmic fruition of the *prajñāpāramitā* and spoke these words:
'I do not wish to see shaven-headed mendicants.'"
"How can one who is bald attain bodhi?
The path to bodhi is extremely profound and difficult to attain. "Good son!..."
The non-retrogressive bodhisattva has no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding awakening, and no doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years due to karmic obstructions, in order to transform five people and to demonstrate the retribution of his own karma; this was not like other sentient beings who neither know nor see [the truth].

Because these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts have uttered such evil words—whether knowingly or unknowingly, whether intentionally or unintentionally—those beings will undergo various sufferings and afflictions for a long night, fail to obtain any benefit, and fall into the three evil realms.
For the sake of those sentient beings, he manifests the performance of karma and the experiencing of its retribution; therefore, the Tathāgata manifests the experiencing of this retribution.

A bodhisattva has no karmic retribution that constitutes any obstacle; yet because there are sentient beings who slander śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts, their minds are shrouded by grief and affliction, preventing them from attaining liberation or the fruits of the Path.
In order to eliminate the sorrow and affliction in the minds of sentient beings, he manifested the experience of such karmic retribution. Those sentient beings then thought:
"If even a Bodhisattva in his final birth was slandered by Kāśyapa Buddha yet still attained liberation, how much more so for one like me who spoke evil words unknowingly?"
"Therefore, I shall now repent of my own transgressions and henceforth never commit any evil deeds again.
Furthermore, good son, it was for the sake of subduing the various non-Buddhists that I practiced austerities for six years; this was not a true obstacle to my karma.
Why is this? There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who claim to attain pure liberation by eating only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day.
In order to subdue them, the Bodhisattva manifests the practice of eating only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day.
If a bodhisattva eats coarse and astringent food, they cannot even attain the Noble Path, let alone pure liberation.
For this reason, the bodhisattva speaks these words:
"I do not wish to see shaven-headed practitioners."
"How could one who is bald attain Bodhi?
The path to Bodhi is extremely profound and difficult to attain.

For this reason, by means of these circumstances, the Bodhisattva manifested six years of ascetic practice in order to subdue fifty-two hundred thousand deities of coarse conduct, as well as non-Buddhist seers and Bodhisattvas of coarse conduct.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 107; *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Volume 108.
Translated by the lay devotee Zhū Nántí of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
*Mahāyāna-sūtra on the Chapter of Expedient Means*, Chapter Thirty-Eight, Part Three.
"For what reason does a bodhisattva, having eaten, obtain sufficient strength to reach the Bodhi tree, rather than reaching the Bodhi tree in a state of emaciation?"
"Good son! A bodhisattva is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi even with a body so emaciated from abstaining from food and drink; how much more so when consuming sesame and rice?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva, out of compassion for sentient beings of the future, partook of this most excellent food. Why was this?

Because the roots of goodness of those beings were not yet matured; they sought the Way without consuming food and drink, and due to the suffering of hunger and thirst, those beings were unable to attain wisdom.
If the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*) can attain wisdom and illuminate all phenomena, it is not an ascetic practice (*duṣkara-caryā*).

Therefore, the Bodhisattva demonstrates to sentient beings that by practicing peaceful conduct one attains wisdom; furthermore, out of compassion for future sentient beings, he desires to cause them to emulate him by consuming this sublime food. Thus, after eating the *śyāmāka* grain, he perfected the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The woman who offered the food likewise accomplished the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of joy while dwelling in the first dhyāna, they are able to remain without food for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing skillful means.
"For what reason did the Bodhisattva seek grass from the Devaputra Śivika to spread as a seat?
Good son, the Buddhas of the past did not use fine silken fabrics to spread their seats of liberation; furthermore, he wished to fulfill for the Devaputra Śivika the dharmas that assist awakening."
At that time, after Kṣemaṅkara had given the grass to the Bodhisattva, he resolved his mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"O son of good family!
Now I shall grant you this prediction:"
"That Devaputra Śāntamati shall, in a future age, attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimala.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing skillful means (upāya).

"For what reason did the Bodhisattva, while sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, cause the evil Māra Pāpīyas to arrive at the foot of the Bodhi tree, not wishing for the Bodhisattva to immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"Good son! Mara was originally unable to reach beneath the Bodhi tree.
It would be impossible for him to come here without my summoning him."
"Good son! At that time, the Bodhisattva sat beneath the Bodhi tree and reflected thus:
'Among the four continents, who is the most honored and supreme?'"
"To whom now do these four continents belong?
