The Bodhisattva then knew that Māra Pāpīyān was the most honored in the realm of desire.
He thought: "Now I shall battle with Māra; if Māra is defeated, then all sentient beings within the entire realm of desire will likewise be defeated."
At that time, a great assembly of devas will gather and arrive at the foot of the Bodhi tree; having arrived, they will surely give rise to faith.
The hosts of Māras, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—all such beings will come and surround the Bodhi tree.

When those multitudes behold the Bodhisattva’s lion-like play, upon seeing him, some may resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, some may resolve their minds on the bodhisattva path, and some may give rise to faith; by virtue of having seen the Bodhisattva, all such persons attain liberation.
"Good son! Having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva emits light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which causes the palaces of Pāpīyān to become dark."

At that time, because the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system was illuminated by this radiance, it became universally and brilliantly bright. From within this radiance, such a voice issued forth:
"That son of the Śākyas has left the home life to study the Way; he shall now attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Having transcended the realm of Māra and surpassed the hosts of Māra, he shall diminish all future hosts of Māra.
Now that Bodhisattva is engaged in battle with Māra.
"O son of good family! [Thus it was said.]
At that time, having heard this sound, Pāpīyān’s heart was filled with great sorrow, as if an arrow had pierced it.
Then the Māra Pāpīyān arrayed his fourfold army to a distance of thirty-six yojanas; they all came to surround the Bodhi tree, wishing to create great obstacles for the Bodhisattva.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, abiding in great compassion and great wisdom, grasped his golden hand with wisdom and struck the earth; having struck it, the entire host of Māras was instantly dispersed and destroyed.

Once the hosts of Māra had been defeated, eighty-four trillion devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, and other such great assemblies, beholding the Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue, his subtle and exquisite body, his dignified and handsome countenance, and his courageous power, gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means.
For what reason did the Tathāgata, for seven days and seven nights, not relinquish his cross-legged posture, gazing up at the Bodhi tree with eyes that did not blink for even a moment?

"Good son! At that time, there were devas of the form realm who practiced the conduct of quiescence. When those devas saw the Tathāgata sitting cross-legged, joy arose in their hearts. Having given rise to joy, they reflected thus:
'Now we should seek to know upon what the mind of the śramaṇa Gautama relies.'"
After those devas and humans had sought in this manner for seven days and seven nights, they could not find even a single moment’s point of reliance of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the devas were redoubled in their joy; thirty-two thousand sons of gods resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made this vow:
"In a future age, may we attain such practice of quiescence as this, and gaze upward at the Bodhi tree."
Therefore, after the Tathāgata had attained the Way, he sat cross-legged for seven days and seven nights, gazing up at the Bodhi tree with his eyes never blinking for a moment.
This is called the skillful means of the Tathāgata.

For what reason? Because when the Tathāgata was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he cultivated immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya vows and practices in order to bestow the bliss of liberation upon all sentient beings.
Why must you wait for the invitation of Brahmā before preaching the Dharma?
Good son, the Tathāgata knows this: there are many devas and humans who take refuge in Brahmā and revere Brahmā.
Those sentient beings will think thus:
"The Brahmā King has manifested us by transformation; he is the most honored in the world, for apart from Brahmā, there is no one else capable of creating the world."
"Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata, having known this, thought: 'Now I shall wait for the Brahmā King’s exhortation.
If that Brahmā King were to merely incline his head, all those beings who take refuge in the Brahmā King would likewise take refuge."
They shall say to one another:
"The Brahma King exhorted the Tathāgata to teach the Dharma; it was not that he did not request it.
O son of good family!
Because the Tathāgata possesses great majesty and virtue, the Brahmā King came to my place and exhorted me to preach the Dharma and turn the wheel of the Dharma.
Son of good family!
If I had not employed my supernatural power to cause the Brahmā King to request it, that Brahmā King would not have had the intention beforehand to come and entreat the Buddha.

Good son! Because sentient beings rely upon the Brahma King, [the Buddha] desires to lead them away from reliance on the Brahma King; thus, he awaits their request, taking the Brahma King as a witness.

"Good son! At that time, when the Brahma King exhorted the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma, sixty-eight hundred thousand Brahmās conceived the aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and spoke these words:
'This one is truly the Buddha, the most honored and most supreme among all sentient beings.'"
Making such a vow, he says:
"In a future life, may I achieve such wisdom and majestic virtue.
This is called the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata.

“Good son! Previously, I explained and demonstrated to sentient beings the causal conditions of the ten karmas; whether it be a bodhisattva or a Tathāgata, they manifest skillful means within these ten. Only those who possess wisdom can understand this meaning.”
"Good son! You should not give rise to the thought that a bodhisattva might possess even subtle transgressions.
If a bodhisattva who has accomplished such subtle unwholesome dharmas were to sit at the site of enlightenment and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, such a thing is impossible."
Why is this? Son of good family!

The Tathāgata has accomplished all wholesome dharmas and severed all unwholesome dharmas; he possesses no habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from the karmic retribution of birth and death. It is impossible that there should remain any residue that is not completely extinguished, let alone any obstructive karmic retribution.

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who claim there is no retribution for karma and do not believe in the retribution of karma, for the sake of these beings, I manifest the causes and conditions of karmic retribution.
In truth, the Tathāgata has no karmic retribution; yet even I, the Dharma King, still undergoes the retribution of karma—how much more so would other sentient beings not undergo it?"
It is for the sake of those sentient beings that he manifests such a display; therefore, the Tathāgata manifests his own karmic conditions.
Son of good family!
The Tathāgata has no karmic obstructions whatsoever.

It is like a master calligrapher who, having skillfully studied the treatises on writing, instructs young children; he praises various calligraphic styles according to the children's needs, yet it is not that the master calligrapher has any obstruction regarding those calligraphic styles.
The writing master thought to himself:
"These young children shall follow me in their studies. Good son!
That scribe did not utter such a proclamation because he lacked understanding.
Son of good family!
The Tathāgata is also like this: having thoroughly studied all dharmas, he speaks and demonstrates in this way for the sake of other sentient beings, so that their karmic actions may become pure.
Good son! It is like a great physician who is well able to cure all manner of illnesses.
Though he has no illness himself, upon seeing those who are ill, he takes bitter medicine before them.
When those who were ill saw that this physician had already taken the bitter medicine, they followed his example and took it, each of them being cured of their illness.

Good son, the Tathāgata is also like this: having himself eliminated all diseases of affliction and being without obstruction regarding all phenomena, he is able to manifest all dharmas, [showing] that such a retribution is obtained because of unwholesome karma.
Manifesting such conditions, he desires to cause sentient beings to eliminate all obstacles of body, speech, and mind, and to practice pure conduct.
Good son! It is like the son of an elder or the son of a householder whom his parents, out of love and affection, provide with a wet nurse.
At that time, this wet nurse was free from illness, yet for the sake of the infant she took bitter medicine herself, wishing to make her milk pure.

Son of good family! The Tathāgata is also like this; he is the father of all worlds. In order to teach and transform sentient beings who do not understand karmic retribution, the Tathāgata, though free from illness, manifests sickness for the sake of sentient beings, saying: "By such karma one receives such retribution; by such karma one receives such retribution."
Upon hearing this, sentient beings will give rise to fear and awe in their hearts, thereby eliminating all evil karma and refraining from creating conditions for further evil.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya: “Good son!
In the distant past, he encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha. At that time, there were five hundred merchants who had entered the great ocean in search of precious treasures.
Son of good family!

Among those merchants was a wicked man—deceitful and full of guile—who constantly committed evil deeds without ever feeling remorse. Well-versed in the arts of war, he perpetually acted as a bandit, seizing the property of others as his livelihood. In appearance, he resembled a merchant and traveled on the same ship with the other merchants.
At that time, that wicked man thought to himself:
"These merchants have obtained a great deal of rare treasure; I shall now kill these merchants, take their treasure, and return to Jambudvīpa."
Having reflected thus, he desired to kill all those people. Good son!
At that time, there was a man named Mahākāruṇika (Great Compassion) who served as the great leader among that multitude.
At that time, in a dream during the night, the leader saw a sea spirit come and speak these words:
"In this assembly of yours, there is one wicked man with such-and-such appearance who constantly acts as a bandit, plundering the wealth of others."
That person has now conceived such an evil thought:
"Once I have killed these five hundred people, I shall take their wealth and return to Jambudvīpa.
If this wicked person succeeds in his original intent and kills the five hundred people, he will commit a great act of parricide and rebellion.
Why is this? These five hundred people are all bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogression toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If these evil persons were to kill such bodhisattvas, due to the obstructive karma and transgressions of that act, each and every bodhisattva—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—the evil person would remain constantly in hell throughout that entire interval.
"You are a guide; you should employ skillful means so that those evil persons do not fall into hell, and so that those five hundred bodhisattvas may likewise preserve their lives."
"Good son! At that time, the Great Compassionate Guide thought to himself:
'By what skillful means can I prevent those evil men from falling into hell, while ensuring that the five hundred bodhisattvas preserve their lives? "
Having reflected thus, he did not speak of this matter to anyone.
At that time, while waiting for the wind, there were seven days remaining before he was to return to Jambudvīpa.
After seven days had passed, he reflected thus:
"There is no other expedient; only by removing this one evil person can these five hundred people be made to preserve their lives."
He further thought: "If I were to speak of this to others, these five hundred people would give rise to malicious thoughts.
Having given rise to malicious thoughts, they might kill this wicked man, and those people would consequently fall into the evil realms."
"Good son! The Great Compassionate Guide thought thus:
'I shall now kill him myself.'"
"Because I have killed this person, even if I must fall into the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of kalpas and undergo the sufferings of hell, I am able to endure it.
I will not allow an evil man to harm five hundred bodhisattvas and, by creating such evil conditions, cause them to suffer in hell."

"Good son! At that time, the Great Compassionate Guide gave rise to a heart of pity and employed this skillful means, thinking: 'For the sake of protecting these five hundred people, I shall harm this evil man.'"
At that time, the guide immediately struck and killed the evil man with his spear, enabling all the merchants to return safely to Jambudvīpa.
"O son of good family!
Do not harbor any doubt.
The guide at that time was none other than myself.
The five hundred merchants were these very five hundred bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, who shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within this kalpa.
"Good son! Because I practiced skillful means and great compassion at that time, I immediately transcended the hardships of birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Then, after that evil man’s life ended, he was reborn in the heavens of the good realms."
"Good son! You should now know this:

do not think that it is because a bodhisattva possesses such obstructive karmic retribution that they are able to transcend the hardships of birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; rather, it is immediately due to the power of that bodhisattva’s skillful means."
“Good son! For the sake of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata employs such skillful means as to manifest the khadira thorn. Good son!”
At that time, the kharjūra thorn pierced the Tathāgata’s foot. O son of good family!
It was by the Buddha’s spiritual power that the thorn was made to enter his foot. Why is this?
The Tathāgata’s adamantine body cannot be destroyed. Good son!
Formerly, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were twenty people, all of whom were in their final existence.
Those twenty people had another twenty enemies, each of whom thought to himself:
"I shall go to their house as a friend, take their lives, and not tell anyone."
"Good son! At that time, those twenty who were in their final births, together with the twenty enemies, arrived at the place where the Buddha was by the power of the Buddha's spiritual authority."
"Good son! At that time, in order to subdue these forty men, the Tathāgata addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana in the midst of the great assembly, saying:
'Now, from within this ground, a khadira thorn has emerged, wishing to pierce my right foot.'"
Before he had even reached the ground, this khadira thorn immediately sprang up from the earth, one cubit in length.
As it emerged, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I shall now take this thorn and cast it into another world-system.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"This is not within your power."
"This khadira thorn is now in this ground; you cannot pull it out.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana used his great supernormal power to go forward and pull at the thorn. Then the trichiliocosm shook violently, and all worlds were lifted up along with the thorn, yet he could not move the thorn even by a single hair's breadth.
"Good son! At that time, by means of his supernatural power, the Tathāgata ascended to the realm of the Four Great Kings, and the khadira thorn also followed the Buddha there.

Then the Tathāgata proceeded further to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the thorn likewise followed him to each of these places."
It was likewise so even up to the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, when the Tathāgata returned from the Brahma Heaven to his original seat within the city of Śrāvastī in Jambudvīpa, the thorn also followed him back and stood upright toward the Tathāgata upon this very spot.

At that time, the Tathāgata took hold of the khadira thorn with his right hand, placed his left hand upon the ground, and stepped upon it with his right foot; thereupon, the trichiliocosm shook violently.
Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated before the Buddha, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
"What kind of karma did he perform in the past to receive such a retribution?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In a past life, I entered the great ocean and, wielding a sharp stake, struck a man and severed his life-root."
"Ānanda! It is by reason of these karmic conditions that such a retribution was obtained.
"Noble son! [the Buddha continued.]
When I had finished explaining these karmic conditions, those twenty hostile bandits who intended to kill twenty people thought to themselves:
"If even the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, receives such retribution for evil karma, how much more so must we receive it?"
These twenty people immediately rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these words:
“We today repent our transgressions before the Buddha; we dare not conceal them.”
“World-Honored One!
Previously, with an evil mind, I desired to harm that person; now, repenting deeply, I dare not conceal my transgression.
At that time, for the sake of that person, the World-Honored One explained the conditions for the production of karma and the conditions for the exhaustion of karma.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the twenty people immediately attained right understanding, and forty thousand others likewise attained right understanding.
For this reason, the Tathāgata showed the kharjūra thorn piercing his foot; this is called the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata.
"For what reason did the Tathāgata, who previously had no ailments, request the *utpala* flower from Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, to smell it so as to induce its descent?
Good son!..."

At that time, not long after the Tathāgata had established the Prātimokṣa precepts, there were five hundred bhikṣus in their final existence who were constantly practicing the path in various other forests.
When those bhikṣus contracted such illnesses, they could not be cured by the medicines prescribed for chronic conditions.
Those bhikṣus, out of reverence and caution for the Buddha’s precepts, did not seek other medicines nor take any other medicines.
"Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata thought to himself:
'By what skillful means can he be made to take and consume other medicines?'"
If I permit it, those bhikṣus will seek other medicines and consume other medicines. Why is this?
If the Tathāgata does not permit it, people in the future will transgress the noble Dharma.
"Therefore, because the Tathāgata employs skillful means, he requested blue lotuses from the physician Jīvaka and smelled them to cause [the discharge] to come down.
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven immediately went into the midst of that assembly of bhikṣus and spoke these words:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"You may seek other medicines; do not remain with this illness and die.

The bhikṣus replied, "We dare not disobey the World-Honored One’s teaching. We have no autonomy; we would rather die than disobey the Buddha's instruction. We do not seek superior or abundant medicines."
When he had spoken thus, the Śuddhāvāsa devaputra addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, seeks other excellent medicines and discards those that are old and worn."
"Venerable sirs, you may seek other medicines.

Having heard these words, the bhikṣus cast aside their doubts and sought other medicines; having taken those other medicines, their illness was cured. Once their illness was cured, within no more than seven days, they realized the fruit of arhatship.
"Good son! If the Tathāgata does not seek other medicines, those bhikṣus likewise shall not seek other medicines.
If they do not seek other medicines, it is impossible that they could eliminate all illnesses, sever all fetters, and realize the fruit of arhatship."
This is called the skillful means of the Tathāgata.
"For what reason, son of good family, does the Tathāgata enter the city for alms and depart with an empty bowl? [The Buddha replied:
"Son of good family!"

The Tathāgata has no karmic obstructions; at that time, the Tathāgata, out of compassion and protective mindfulness for future bhikṣus, considers those bhikṣus who enter cities, towns, or villages to beg for food but, lacking merit themselves, are unable to obtain any.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way:

"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has accomplished all merits; yet when he entered the city to beg for alms, he returned with an empty bowl. How much more so for us, whose roots of goodness are so meager?"
"We should not give rise to distress, vexation, or fever because we fail to obtain alms.
For this reason, the Tathāgata manifested entering the city to beg for food and departing with an empty bowl.
"Good son! If you think that it was because the evil Māra Pāpīyān obscured the minds of the elders and brahmins in the city so that they would not give even a single morsel of food, good son!..."
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?
The evil Māra Pāpīyān cannot cut off the Tathāgata’s food.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the evil Māra Pāpīyas caused the people in that city to be obscured; this was not something that could have been accomplished by the power of Māra alone.
At that time, I was entirely free from karmic obstructions, yet for the sake of transforming those sentient beings, I manifested an empty bowl as I went forth.
At that time, after I and the community of bhikṣus had finished our meal, all the Māras, devas, and other celestial beings thought to themselves:
"Now that the Buddha and the assembly of monks have finished their meal, will they perhaps feel any distress?"

That very night, he beheld the Buddha and the Sangha; not even for a single thought-moment did he experience anxiety or distress, and his mind was neither elated nor depressed, remaining exactly as it had been before.
"Good son! At that time, there were seven thousand devaputras who, inclining toward the Tathāgata, gave rise to a mind of faith and reverence.
I then preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena."

"Good son! Not long thereafter, that brahmin householder again heard that the World-Honored One possessed great majestic virtue; conceiving a heart of yearning and reverence, he immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and repented before him."

At that time, the Tathāgata immediately taught him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; upon the first teaching of the Dharma, twenty thousand people attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata enters the city to beg for alms and leaves with an empty bowl, this is called the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*).
For what reason did the Brahmin woman Ciñcā tie a wooden bowl to her belly and slander the Tathāgata, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has caused me to become pregnant; he ought to provide me with clothing, bedding, food, and drink"?
"Good son! Regarding this matter, the Tathāgata has no karmic obstruction whatsoever.
If there were such a karmic obstruction, I could have cast this Brahmin woman Cañcā beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The Tathāgata manifests this karmic obstacle through skillful means in order to transform sentient beings who lack understanding.

Why is this? In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who have left the household life to study the Path within my Dharma; at that time, some may be slandered by others, and because of these circumstances, they will feel shame and remorse, or they may lose their delight in the Buddha-Dharma, abandon the precepts, and return to secular life.

If those bhikṣus are slandered, they should reflect upon the Tathāgata: "Even the Tathāgata, who has accomplished all wholesome dharmas and possesses great majestic virtue, is still subject to slander; how much more so for us that we should not be slandered? Having reflected thus, they will eliminate shame and remorse; having eliminated shame and remorse, they shall be able to cultivate the pure and sublime brahmacarya.

"Good son! Because the Brahmin woman Ciñcā is constantly shrouded by evil karma, her nature is largely characterized by lack of faith. This woman’s body has not attained taming within the Buddha-dharma; she is perpetually obscured by evil karma, such that she even gives rise to slander within her dreams, feeling joy in her heart upon waking."
"This woman, upon the end of her life, shall fall into hell.
Good son! I am able, through other skillful means, to eliminate this woman's various unwholesome karmas, enabling her to transcend birth and death and providing for her salvation."
Good son! There are times when the Tathāgata does not rescue other beings. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has no partiality toward any sentient being; this is called the skillful means of the Tathāgata.
For what reason did the brahmins kill the brahmin girl Sundarī and bury her in the moat of the Jetavana Garden?
Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that such a matter existed, set it aside and did not speak of it.
The Tathāgata has perfected the mind of omniscience and is without any obstruction; by means of his supernormal powers, he could have caused this sword not to enter the woman’s body.

At that time, I knew that the life-force of the woman Sundarī was about to end and that she would certainly be killed by another; through this expedient means, I caused the unwholesome deeds of the various non-Buddhists to be exposed, leading them to fall into an unfavorable state.
Such matters as these are known only to the Buddha; by abiding in these matters, he causes many sentient beings to give rise to pure faith and increase their roots of goodness.
At that time, the Tathāgata did not enter the great city of Śrāvastī for seven days.
After not entering the city, at that time, sixty billion devas who had been tamed came together with the gods and worldlings to my dwelling after seven days had passed.
At that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly; having heard this teaching, eighty-four thousand people attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
This is called the skillful means of the Tathāgata.
"For what reason, noble son, did the Tathāgata and the Saṃgha eat horse barley for three months while staying in the Brahmin village of Verañjā?"

In the past, I knew that this brahmin would certainly abandon his initial intention to invite the Buddha and the Sangha and fail to provide them with food and drink; nevertheless, I intentionally went to accept his invitation. Why was this?
It was for the sake of those five hundred horses.

In previous lives, these five hundred horses had already trained in the Bodhisattva vehicle and had previously made offerings to the Buddhas of the past; however, due to associating with evil friends, they created the conditions for unwholesome karma, and by reason of that unwholesome karma, they fell among the animals.
Among the five hundred horses was one great horse named Sūryagarbha, who was a mahāsattva.

In past lives, while in the human realm, this Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha had already exhorted these five hundred small horses to resolve upon bodhicitta; desiring to deliver these five hundred horses, he manifested birth among them.
"By virtue of the Great Horse's majestic power, he caused five hundred horses to recognize their own past lives and recover the minds they had previously lost.
Son of good family!
Out of compassion for those five hundred bodhisattvas who had fallen among the horses and wished to enable them to escape this animal state, the Tathāgata knowingly accepted the invitation."
"Good son! At that time, the five hundred horses reduced their consumption of barley by half and offered it as alms to the Saṃgha; the great horse offered his own half-portion to the Tathāgata.
Then, for the sake of the five hundred horses, the great horse preached the Dharma using the voice of a horse and also instructed them in repentance."
"Now we shall pay homage to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
Having said this, he further spoke these words:
"You all should offer half of your food as an alms-offering to the Saṃgha."
At that time, after the five hundred horses had repented their transgressions, they conceived pure faith toward the Buddha and the Sangha.
After three months had passed, not long thereafter, these five hundred horses died and were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

Those five hundred devaputras then came from the heavens to the place where the Buddha was to make offerings to the Tathāgata; at that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for them, and having heard this teaching, they were certain to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, those five hundred horse-boys had well-tamed their minds and would attain the state of a pratyekabuddha in a future age.

That great horse, Sūryagarbha, will in a future age make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, accomplish the factors conducive to enlightenment, and thereafter become a Buddha named Well-Tamed (Suvinita) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Good son! There is no superior, exquisite flavor in the world that the Tathāgata does not obtain. Good son!"

Although the Tathāgata may consume grass, wood, earth, clods of soil, or shards of pottery, within this trichiliocosm there is no flavor like that of the grass, wood, earth, clods, or shards consumed by the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Son of good family!

The Tathāgata, the Great Being, has attained the mark of the supreme taste among all tastes; even when the Tathāgata places the coarsest food in his mouth, the flavor he experiences surpasses that of the exquisite food of the devas.
"Good son! For this reason, you should know that what the Tathāgata eats is the most supreme and wondrous. Good son!"
At that time, Ānanda felt distress in his heart, thinking:
"The offspring of a Universal Monarch has left the household life to study the Way, yet he eats this horse-barley like a person of low station.
At that moment, I perceived Ānanda’s mind.
Having perceived Ānanda’s mind, he immediately gave him a single grain of barley and said to Ānanda:
"Taste this barley; what is its flavor like?
After Ānanda had tasted it, a sense of wonder arose within him, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I was born into a royal family and raised in a great royal household, yet I have never before tasted such a flavor.
After Ānanda had eaten this barley, for seven days and seven nights he neither ate nor drank, yet he felt no hunger or thirst.
"Good son! Therefore, you should know that this is the skillful means of the Tathāgata, and not an obstacle of karma. Good son!"

There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who observe the precepts as I do and, having accepted an invitation from another, know that the host is distracted and unable to provide for them, or they are unwilling to remain.
For this reason, wherever the Tathāgata has already given his consent, he will certainly attend the invitation; furthermore, it is because he wishes to manifest the conditions of karmic retribution.

Son of good family, you should know that it is the constant law of the Tathāgata that even if he accepts an invitation from another and does not receive the provisions, he will not cause the host to fall into the evil realms.

Good son! Among those five hundred bhikṣus who, together with the Tathāgata, spent the summer retreat eating horse barley, four hundred bhikṣus gave rise to thoughts of lust because they perceived impurity as pure.
If those bhikṣus eat refined food, their desire increases; if they eat coarse food, their minds are not overwhelmed by greed.
After three months have passed, those bhikṣus abandon the mind of sensual desire and realize the fruit of arhatship.

"Good son! It was for the sake of subduing five hundred bhikṣus and delivering five hundred bodhisattvas that the Tathāgata, through the power of skillful means, accepted horse-barley for three months; this was not the result of karmic retribution."
This is called the skillful means of the Tathāgata.
For what reason did the Tathāgata, on the fifteenth day when the precepts were being recited, say to the Elder Kāśyapa:
"I now have a backache"?
"You now teach the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment. Good son!
At that time, there were eight thousand devaputras who had disciplined themselves through the Śrāvaka Dharma, sitting together in harmony within that assembly.
"Good son! Those devaputras were those who, in past lives, were taught and transformed by Mahākāśyapa; they are not negligent regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
Those devaputras have repeatedly heard the Kāśyapa bhikṣu expound the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Good son! With the exception of the Kāśyapa bhikṣu, even if hundreds of thousands of buddhas were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not be able to bring about their understanding.

At that time, Kāśyapa extensively expounded the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment to the sons of the gods; having heard the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment from the bhikṣu Kāśyapa, the sons of the gods attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

"Good son! If there are sentient beings whose bodies are entangled by the suffering of illness, such that they are unable to go to the place where the Dharma is being preached to listen to the teaching with reverence,
those people should form this thought:"

"The Buddha is the Dharma King; he still listens to the teachings of the seven factors of enlightenment to eliminate his ailments, so how much more should we not fail to go and listen to the Dharma or fail to revere the Dharma?
O son of good family!
In order to subdue the devas and eliminate the suffering and afflictions of humans, and furthermore to demonstrate reverence for the Dharma, the Tathāgata spoke these words: "Kāśyapa!..."
"I now have a backache;
you should expound the Dharma of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment. Why is this?"
"Because they respect the Dharma.
The Tathāgata possesses no coarse body of the four great elements; how much less could he have illness?
This is called the skillful means of the Tathāgata.
"For what reason did the Tathāgata say, 'I have a headache,' when the Śākya clan was being destroyed?
Good son! There may be sentient beings who speak thus:"

“The World-Honored One cannot benefit his kinsmen; he feels no compassion for them, nor does he wish for their peace and security. Having gone forth, he has severed all ties to his clan and has no desire to rescue or protect them.”
"These sentient beings speak thus because they do not understand. Good son!

The Tathāgata has already reached the very limit of all roots of suffering; yet, because the Tathāgata knows the thoughts in the minds of these sentient beings, he sat beneath the Śāla tree and said of himself that his head ached."
"Good son! At that time, I immediately told Ānanda that I had a headache.
At that moment, three thousand devaputras with nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and immeasurable others who were fond of killing all gathered together."
For the sake of those devas who hold nihilistic views and those who delight in killing, he manifests karmic obstacles and speaks these words:
"Because I saw others killing living beings and rejoiced in their intent with my own eyes, I now suffer from a headache."
When he had spoken this Dharma, seven thousand devas and humans were all tamed.
This is called the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata.
"For what reason did the Tathāgata, having heard it, remain patient when the Brahmin Potalaka reviled him with five hundred kinds of insults?"

"Good son! The Tathāgata can, by means of his supernormal power, cast this brahmin into another world; he can also, by means of his supernormal power, cause the brahmin to be unable to utter even a single word of abusive speech."

"Good son! At that time, many among the assembly of devas and humans saw that the Tathāgata was able to endure abusive speech without speaking or replying; they gave rise to a mind of equanimity, a mind of impartiality, a mind of benefit, and a mind of forbearance, such that the beginning was like the end and the end was like the beginning."
At that time, four thousand people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The Tathāgata, perceiving this significance, and seeing that the Brahmin Phalada had uttered five hundred kinds of evil abuse yet still conceived a mind of equanimity toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [was moved].
"Good son! Having seen this, that brahmin gave rise to a mind of faith and reverence;
he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, planting the roots of liberation."
This is called the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata. "Good son!
Devadatta has lived together with the Bodhisattva in every lifetime; such instances are also the skillful means of the Bodhisattva."
Why is this? It is because of Devadatta that I have fulfilled the six pāramitās and have also greatly benefited immeasurable sentient beings.
How is this known?
"Good son! At that time, sentient beings were so happy that they did not know how to practice giving, nor did they know who was a recipient.

The Bodhisattva then wished to teach them to practice generosity; at that moment, Devadatta, having conceived a heart of jealousy, went to the Bodhisattva’s abode and requested his kingdom, cities, wife, children, head, eyes, hands, and feet."
At that time, the Bodhisattva joyfully gave his gift.
Then, there were immeasurable sentient beings who, seeing the Bodhisattva’s giving, felt joy in their hearts and developed faith and understanding regarding generosity, saying:
"Just as the Bodhisattva gives, I too shall practice such giving; may I become a Bodhisattva."
"Good son! When Devadatta perceives that the Bodhisattva maintains pure precepts and knows this, he desires to break the precepts upheld by the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva does not violate his pure precepts."
At that time, there were immeasurable sentient beings who, seeing the Bodhisattva upholding the precepts, likewise emulated him in upholding the precepts.

When the Bodhisattva upholds the precepts and does not give rise to an evil mind even when treated with contempt, disparagement, or verbal abuse by others, he is then fully endowed with the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Countless sentient beings, seeing the Bodhisattva tame his mind through patience, likewise emulated the Bodhisattva’s practice of forbearance.
Good son! You should know that Devadatta brought great benefit to the Bodhisattva.
Good son! Just as Devadatta has now released a large, intoxicated elephant intending to harm the Tathāgata,
and has also hurled down a great boulder from Vulture Peak Mountain!
These are all manifestations through the skillful means of the Tathāgata and are not offenses resulting from karmic retribution. Why is this?
Because through these skillful means, immeasurable sentient beings are benefited.
“Good son! The Tathāgata has spoken in summary of ten karmic causes and conditions; all of these are the Tathāgata’s skillful manifestations and are not actual karmic retributions. Why is this?
Sentient beings do not know that the fruits of retribution are obtained through the causes of karma.

For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata manifests such karmic retributions, showing: "Having performed this karma, one obtains this retribution; having performed that karma, one obtains that retribution; by performing such karma, one obtains such retribution."
Having heard this, sentient beings perform such actions and abandon such actions; they desist from unwholesome karma and cultivate wholesome karma. Good son!

Now that these skillful means have been explained and these skillful means have been demonstrated, these various skillful means must be firmly maintained as a secret treasury and should not be taught to inferior persons whose roots of goodness are meager.
Why is this? This sutra is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, much less can inferior ordinary persons believe and understand it. Why is this?
This person is unable to learn these various skillful means.

Why is this? Because these sūtras on skillful means are not for their use; they cannot receive or uphold them, as they are like other earthenware vessels. Only a bodhisattva is able to explain and learn these teachings on skillful means.
"Good son! It is like lighting a great bright lamp in the darkness of night; one is then able to see everything that exists within the room. Good son!"

Having heard these various skillful means, the bodhisattva immediately perceives the path practiced by all bodhisattvas; within this Dharma, he knows what he should study, and having reached the further shore of all the practices of the Tathāgatas and the practices of bodhisattvas, one who skillfully practices the bodhisattva path does not consider it difficult.

"Good son, I shall now speak for those who wish to attain the various wholesome dharmas of the path to bodhi. That is to say, good sons and good daughters, upon hearing that there is a place even a hundred thousand yojanas away where this *Upāya-sūtra* is being preached, they should go there to listen."
Why is this? Because if a bodhisattva, having heard this sūtra of skillful means, attains the practice of illumination and eliminates doubt and regret regarding all dharmas,
then at that time the fourfold assembly and all the devas and humans who have become vessels of jewels will hear and fully understand it when this sūtra is preached.

Those who are not vessels for the jewels, though present in this assembly, neither hear nor know; they do not even hear the name of this sutra with their ears, let alone speak it aloud, because they are not vessels for the jewels.
"Therefore, when the Tathāgata preached this Dharma, they did not hear it nor did they know it, because they had not received the Buddha’s spiritual power.
When this sutra was spoken, seventy-two thousand people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?”
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Perfection of Skillful Means,' and it is also named 'The Chapter on Turning Skillful Means,' and it is also named 'Explaining Skillful Means for Taming'; uphold it thus."

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya felt great joy in his heart. Likewise, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who were training, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who were training in the bodhisattva vehicle, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—having heard this teaching, they exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! as the Mahāyāna *Upāya-kauśalya Sūtra* was now concluded.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 108;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 109.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
39. The Assembly of the Elder Bhadrapāla, Part One of Three.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying in the great city of Rājagṛha, at the Bamboo Grove of the elder Kalandaka, together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus who had accomplished what was to be done and were no longer subject to further existence; the elder Śāriputra was the leader of the assembly.
At that time, the bhikṣus surrounded the World-Honored One, desiring to hear and receive the Dharma; their bodies and minds were harmonious and compliant, free from drowsiness.
At that moment, the countenance and complexion of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, were like a lotus flower blooming at sunrise—dignified, radiant, smiling, and serene.
At that time, those bhikṣus had this thought:
"What dharma-gate does the Bhagavān now wish to proclaim, such that his countenance is thus radiant with light?"

At that time, there was a son of a very wealthy merchant leader and elder named Bhadrapāla (translated into Chinese as Xiangu 賢護), who, surrounded by a retinue of one thousand followers and possessing a majestic power that seemed to shake the great earth, approached the World-Honored One with a calm and steady gait.

At that time, the son of the elder Bhadrapāla, having received celestial retribution due to the causal conditions of his past merit, approached the Buddha; his body was as supple as a newly emerged tender flower branch.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he beheld the Tathāgata’s most supreme and wondrous countenance and his body—a treasury of merit, tranquil and serenely concentrated—shining with a brilliance like that of a golden tree, its radiance pervading the entire bamboo grove.
At that time, Bhadrapāla conceived pure faith toward the Buddha and, joining his ten fingers in palms-together gesture, thought thus:
"That one who has attained great renown throughout the world does not speak falsely; it is indeed true that he is called Sarvajña, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

At that time, Bhadrapāla immediately bowed his head and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; with both knees touching the ground, he raised his head with a single-minded focus, gazing intently at the World-Honored One without blinking his eyes.
While gazing upon the Tathāgata in this manner, his body remained solemn, neither leaning nor moving.
At that time, seeing that the elder Bhadrapāla had thus given rise to such longing and veneration within his heart, the Tathāgata immediately emitted a wondrous light from his body once more.

When that radiance shone forth, the elder Bhadrapāla immediately attained fearlessness; he rose from the ground, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and once again prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One.
Having completed his prostrations, he knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity upon me; I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct me.
O Great Sage, World-Honored One!"
My faith in the Buddha has not yet been long-standing; therefore, World-Honored One, you should teach me a single Dharma-gate based solely on immediate, present matters.

Now I am thirsty for and yearn to hear all dharmas, for I am oppressed by afflictions within birth and death, filled with many doubts, and my mind is constantly engaged in discrimination. For this reason, I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, will preach the Dharma for me so as to resolve my doubts.
O Great Sage, World-Honored One!
Because I lack correct knowledge, I am deluded; I do not know the ford for crossing the ocean of afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Only the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, possesses all-knowledge; he is rare in the world, like a wish-fulfilling jewel, for he is able to bestow all happiness upon sentient beings and cause them to achieve it.
"Furthermore, the World-Honored One is like a father and mother; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to obtain wholesome karmic fruits, he is their very root.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"
"If there be any who have doubts, you may now ask as you wish; I shall analyze and explain them for you.

At that time, the elder Bhadrapāla, having received the Buddha’s approval, felt joy within his heart and, wishing to inquire about his mental doubts, immediately rose from his seat and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stood to one side, his body was endowed with a perfect and full majesty of light.
At that time, the elder bhikṣu Ānanda, having seen him, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”

This son of a householder, Bhadrapāli, surpasses the majesty of all kings with the power of his physical radiance and virtue; he is exceptionally sublime and peerless in his beauty, so upright and lovely that he has no equal within this world.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Elder Ānanda!
Do you now wish to hear of all the various joyful matters within the home of this householder Bhadrapāla?"

To speak fully of the fruit of the bliss he experiences, even Śakra, the King of Gods in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, cannot equal it; how much less could anyone in this Jambudvīpa among human beings ever attain such a state—such a thing is impossible.
"Except for one person, the son of a householder named Somabuddhi (translated in the Sui language as 'True Moon' [Zhenyue]).
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"What extraordinary excellence exists within the house of this householder Bhadrapāli that the World-Honored One praises it so highly?
At that time, the Buddha told the Elder Ānanda:
"You should listen attentively and receive this with a sincere mind."
The wealth and roots of goodness possessed by this son of a householder are vast; I shall now explain them to you in sequence. Ānanda!
This son of a householder is constantly followed by sixty thousand preeminent merchant lords, each of whom possesses immeasurable and extraordinary treasures of various kinds in great abundance.

Within the household of Bhadrapāli, sixty thousand exquisite six-panel couches were perpetually laid out; they were covered with multi-colored quilts and bedding, and further adorned with crimson and variegated silks used as backrests. On both sides, fine garments such as *kauśeya* silk and other multicolored fabrics were provided—four sets at each station—as well as fire-resistant cloth (*agnimanthaka*) and coarse hemp.
All kinds of garments and various miscellaneous items produced in the lands of the four directions completely adorned his house.
Those clothes were all soft and supple, as smooth and lustrous as the palm of a hand.
Throughout his residence, everywhere was adorned with hanging strings of true pearls as ornaments.

Furthermore, there were sixty thousand court ladies, exquisite and peerless in beauty, their bodies soft, supple, and smooth. They were skilled in laughter and jesting, adept in speech, and possessed a graceful and radiant charm that captivated the hearts of others. Upon seeing them, those prone to anger naturally became joyful; those who encountered them while grieving felt comfort and solace. Their playful words and tones opened the heart and delighted the eye. All were filial and respectful toward their husband, maintaining perfect wifely decorum, and they remained free from desire for any other man.
At times, they may feel shame and modesty within themselves; with palms joined, brows lowered, and bodies bowed in reverence, they focus exclusively upon their husbands without looking elsewhere.

At other times, because each feels a particular affection for her own husband, jealousy arises and they quarrel and resent one another; with furrowed brows and knitted foreheads like deep hooks, they feign this as sport, though in truth they harbor no jealousy.

Her fingers were long and slender with rounded joints; her ankles and wrists were delicate and well-proportioned, giving her body an intoxicating grace. She cast coquettish glances as she moved with measured steps, her gait flowing and elegant.

Her hair was deep blue-black, fine, smooth, and soft; she was skilled at braiding and styling it in ways that could bewitch people, and she stood among such female attendants, either serving them or leaning upon them.
All those court ladies were devoted solely to their husbands, and their pure reputations spread everywhere.
Moreover, these ladies came from the most eminent lineages; they possessed great renown within their own families and were all worthy of becoming the principal wives of great houses.
With such various adornments as these, the house of the elder Bhadrapāla was immeasurably vast and spacious.

Furthermore, whenever the elder desired to eat, there would appear sixty thousand varieties of soups, stews, rice, and delicacies, exquisitely fragrant and delicious, no different from the cuisine of the celestial kitchens.

The rice was entirely made of husked grain, yet it was replete with color and flavor, possessing the eight meritorious qualities; it could be eaten at will and would dissolve as soon as it entered the mouth. Having eaten, it followed along smoothly without causing any obstruction, and its karmic fruition brought forth results that were naturally and perfectly satisfying to the mind.
Furthermore, after eating, his body became radiant and free from all foul odors.

Moreover, within the house of that elder, there were sixty thousand palanquins, each adorned with various rare and precious things; they were interspersed with pearls and were perfectly uniform in height and width, all covered with exquisite cloths and strewn with fragrant flowers.
Water was sprinkled upon the ground so that there was no dust, and it became pure and moist.

Furthermore, within the house there were various kinds of supreme sounds produced by hand-strikes, finger-plucks, and breath-blown instruments; their resonance was subtle, brilliant, and soul-stirring. The songs were perfectly pitched, like the voice of a white dove—a sound the heart delights to hear—and in this way, the house was exquisitely adorned.
Furthermore, within his household, the trees of the gardens and groves were luxuriant and flourishing, with flowers intermingling in brilliant shades of red and purple.

Amidst these forested groves there were various birds, each uttering beautiful songs; their voices were so harmonious and elegant that they were like those in a celestial palace, or like Mount Sumeru composed of myriad jewels, no different from a dragon’s lair.
Furthermore, various kinds of lamps were lit; their light was undisturbed by the wind, penetrating everywhere and illuminating the night so brilliantly that it was no different from day.
Moreover, within the kingdom where his residence was located, there were sixty thousand cities, each with its streets and lanes aligned, and fully equipped with watchtowers and defensive battlements.

In every part of that city, merchants from various countries gathered and congregated; with their diverse appearances, diverse languages, and a multitude of rare and miscellaneous precious goods, they traded with one another, filling the city to overflowing with hundreds of thousands of millions of people beyond counting.

Furthermore, surrounding those cities on all four sides were hundreds of thousands of species of orchards and various trees; their flowers and fruits were lush and abundant, and their branches and leaves spread out in profusion, while swarms of bees vied with one another to gather their fragrances and essences.
Furthermore, those cities abound with elephants, horses, and various vehicles. "Ānanda!

Within those cities, all the wealthy householders, lay devotees, merchant leaders, and traders constantly and single-mindedly praise all the virtues of Bhadrapāla; with palms joined, they prostrate and extol him. How much more so, then, for those who have heard his fame and whose hearts longingly desire to behold him!"

Furthermore, the king of that country, Prasenajit, seeing that the elder Bhadrapāla possessed abundant wealth, resources, influence, and merit, humbled himself before him like a poor man envying another's treasures.

“Ānanda! Whenever that youth, the householder Candra, partakes of a meal, there are a thousand kinds of exquisite flavors; whatever is required by his side, morning and evening, appears spontaneously.”
Furthermore, five thousand court ladies surrounded and attended him for his amusement. Ānanda!

The joy experienced by the youth of the householder Candra is a thousand times superior even to that of Śakra, Lord of Devas; yet when compared to the physical appearance, complexion, treasuries, wealth, and the karmic fruit of enjoyment of Bhadrapāla, it does not equal even a hundredth part of the latter.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
This householder Bhadrapāla possessed a magnificent carriage named 'Captivating the Mind,' which was so exquisitely crafted and splendid that it was without peer among those of the human world."
Within this chariot was a celestial jewel throne.

The chariot was entirely adorned with an interlacing array of various celestial jewels—lapis lazuli, diamond, pearl, and precious shells—their radiance shining as brightly as the stars in the sky; such was its magnificence.
When that chariot travels, it is as swift as the wind. Ānanda!

When Bhadrapāli intends to go within the ocean to gather precious jewels, he reaches his destination by merely sitting in that chariot according to his wish; and having enjoyed his pleasures, if he wishes to return home, he arrives as soon as he thinks of it.
At that time, Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness did this elder Bhadrapāla cultivate in the past, such that in this present life he receives such a karmic retribution?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Elder Ānanda!
If you wish to know, you should listen attentively."
These causes and conditions all arise from having planted roots of goodness in the presence of various Buddhas in the past, whereby they now obtain such supreme and exalted retribution. Ānanda!
I recall that in the distant past, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Sukhābha (Light of Joy), an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Ānanda! At that time, this householder Bhadrapāli became a śrāvaka monk under that Buddha, named Dharmakoṭi. Although his observance of the precepts was incomplete and he had many lapses and deficiencies, he was skilled at proclaiming the Buddha’s teachings and revealing what had not been heard before.

This great Dharma Master, upon hearing the *dhāraṇī* and the *sūtra-piṭaka*, as well as upholding the *vinaya-piṭaka*, constantly expounds the essentials of the Dharma for all sentient beings. Possessing vast knowledge, eloquence, and keen intelligence, his meaning and flavor are profoundly deep; his voice is clear and penetrating, causing those who hear it to delight in listening. Those who hear the Dharma give rise to joy in their hearts and shall never again fall into the various evil realms.
Ānanda! By virtue of such causes and conditions from giving the Dharma, for ninety-one kalpas he was constantly reborn among gods and humans as one who was handsome, noble, and wealthy. Ānanda!
I shall further explain to you in due order the causes and conditions for the wondrous carriage obtained by this son of a householder.

Ānanda! When the householder Bhadrapāla was a Dharma teacher during the era of that Buddha Prabhāsa, he saw various fellow practitioners of the holy life—monks who maintained the precepts—who were emaciated, exhausted, weak, and incapable of enduring their burdens. Whatever they required, he gave it all as alms; furthermore, he joyfully provided them with shoes, sandals, boots, and other such items.
By virtue of this merit, one now experiences the wondrous fruit of retribution: the wish-fulfilling chariot.
Furthermore, Ānanda, in the past there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, that Buddha addressed the elder, saying:
"In a future age there shall be a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; that Blessed One shall bestow upon you a prophecy."
"Ānanda! This householder Bhadrapāla must be instructed by me so that he may give rise to understanding.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!

This son of a householder is so wealthy and possesses such vast stores of property, yet his nature is gentle and mild; he does not give rise to arrogance, and his mind remains unstained by the five desires."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“You should now know that any wise person does not give rise to arrogance in their mind because of wealth or the five objects of desire.”
"Ānanda! Because this son of a householder has used the Dharma as a cause, he shall receive many kinds of inexhaustible rewards of merit.

At that time, the householder Bhadrapāla, having received the Buddha’s permission, wished to ask about his doubts; he immediately focused his mind before the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, you embrace all sentient beings and have pity for them.
Now, there is a doubt in my mind that I wish to ask; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for me so that my doubts may be severed.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elder’s son Bhadrapāla, saying:
“Bhadrapāla! If you have doubts in your mind that you wish to sever and eliminate, now is precisely the right time.”
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, the elder Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All sentient beings know that there is a conscious spirit, yet this conscious spirit is like a precious casket that has not yet been opened; they do not know what kind of treasure is within it.
World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of this consciousness?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it called "consciousness"?
World-Honored One!

When a person dies and is without hands, feet, or eyes, at the moment of the end of life when the sense faculties are about to cease and the great elements are about to disperse, how does this consciousness depart from this body?
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, what is the color of this consciousness,
and what is its substance?
How is one separated from this body?
How does this consciousness abandon this body and achieve another body?
How does it abandon these elements (*mahābhūta*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) to proceed toward future lives, and how does it achieve each respective individual body?
World-Honored One!
Now that a person has died, how do the future sense bases (āyatana) arise in accordance with it?
How is it that by performing various roots of goodness in this life, one receives their karmic fruit in a future life?

Since one has already cultivated roots of goodness through the various bases and aggregates of this present life, how could that person subsequently receive their karmic retribution within other, distinct aggregates?
"How does this consciousness obtain a body in that place?
How do the bases (āyatana) follow the substance of that place?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the elder, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Bhadrapāla! It is so, it is so, just as you have asked.”
Listen now with a sincere mind and receive this attentively; I shall explain for you the coming, going, shifting, and ceasing of the spirit-consciousness (vijñāna). Bhadrapāli!
It is just as the element of wind, which, though lacking form or color and being invisible, nevertheless manifests form and color through causes and conditions.
What is the meaning of "manifesting form and color"?

It is like the wind blowing and moving various trees, or striking against mountains, walls, water, and cliffs to produce sound; because it is produced by the conditions of cold and heat, it is capable of being perceived, yet the substance of that wind cannot be seen.
The hands, feet, eyes, and so forth are likewise thus unobservable; one superimposes superior qualities upon various forms, such as black or white. Bhadrapāli!

In this way, in this way, this realm of consciousness is likewise: it cannot be seen by means of form, nor does it reach the substance of form; it manifests as form only by taking the activities of its entry as its substance.
This consciousness-element is likewise so.
One must understand how this consciousness-element receives the designation "contact" and "dharma-element" in that state;
furthermore, how does this consciousness-element, after abandoning this body, receive pleasant contact and so forth?
For example, just as the element of wind can carry fragrance, we know that the scent of these flowers comes from being blown by the wind.
Yet, this element of wind does not actually grasp the floral fragrance and bring it here; nor is it the case that the fragrance can come without the wind.
That fragrance is formless, that wind is also formless, and the faculty that perceives the fragrance is likewise formless. Bhadrapāli!

Even so, when the consciousness of a dying person is about to depart, having taken up sensation, contact, and the various elements, it is only through the union of the parents in that world that the existence of consciousness can subsequently be known. Because that consciousness exists, one knows that there is sensation and contact, which combine to form [a new being].
It is just as when a superior person possesses a powerful consciousness, there is a superior root of fragrance; because the root of fragrance is superior, there is a superior fragrance.
Furthermore, because two bodies are superior, two things that are superior can be seen; these two superior things are namely visible form (*rūpa*) and tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*).

Because the wind is abundant, the fragrance is also abundant; in this same way, because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is great, sensation (*vedanā*) is also great; because sensation is great, consciousness is also great; because consciousness is great, the various elements (*dhātu*) are also great, yet one thereby knows what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.

For example, suppose a painter has already skillfully prepared his board; whenever he desires to produce something, he can do so immediately because of his excellent understanding, and he can create whatever colors he wishes.

Yet, if that painter had no colors, he could not manifest any forms. In the same way, this consciousness accomplishes the six types of "form-bodies": namely, the consciousness and cognition that sees forms by means of the eye; yet for one who sees forms by means of the eye, there is actually no form. For one who hears sounds by means of the ear, there is likewise no form. For one who smells odors by means of the nose, there is likewise no form. For one who knows tastes by means of the tongue, there is likewise no form. For one who perceives tangibles by means of the body, those tangibles are also without form. For one who possesses the great elements by means of the mind, those too are without form. All that is known is also without form; one should know that within those objective spheres (*viṣaya*) as well, there is no form whatsoever.
In this sequence, you should know that this consciousness is likewise formless; it should be contemplated in this way.
As for your question, Bhadrapāla, regarding how this consciousness leaves this body and goes to the next world: [it is as follows].

At the time of death, this consciousness is sustained by karma; when this karma and the life-force are exhausted, it is like a person who has entered the samādhi of cessation, whose body still possesses consciousness. Once this conscious body has ceased, one subsequently enters and abides within the internal state of cessation.

In this way, in this manner, this consciousness abandons the body and the primary elements at the side of the deceased; having abandoned them, there remains only the power of mindfulness, whereby it knows: "I am such-and-such a person."
When an ordinary person abandons the body, there are two kinds of contact with right mindfulness. What are these two?
First is right mindfulness; second is contact.
At the time of that person's death, there are two types of tactile sensations within the body:
first, physical sensation; second, mental sensation.
After death, there remains only mental tactile sensation.
"Furthermore, as to your question regarding the meaning of 'consciousness' (vijñāna):

there is a seed that can produce a sprout; from wisdom (jñāna) consciousness arises, which is precisely what is called 'mindfulness' (smṛti). Therefore, because of both wisdom and the seed, it is termed 'consciousness'."
Thereafter, it again experiences contact; because it cognizes suffering and pleasure through knowledge, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Subsequently, it further experiences the wholesome and the unwholesome; because it is also able to cognize wholesome and unwholesome objects, it is called consciousness.
Just as a sprout grows from a seed, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because its body is thereby accomplished.

Furthermore, Bhadrapāli, as to your question regarding how this consciousness abandons the body and migrates toward another: it is like the reflection of a physical form appearing in a mirror; or like a physical form being cast from within a mold using a lump of clay; or again, like the rising of the sun which is able to dispel all darkness.

When that sun has set, darkness arises once more; yet that darkness has no fixed permanence, nor does it abide in a state of impermanence. Furthermore, that darkness is without form, without sensation, and invisible.
Thus, once this consciousness has produced a body, it is like a body being produced when darkness departs from light;
that person does not see this consciousness, yet the consciousness receives this body.

For example, it is like a woman who has conceived, yet she does not know whether the child she carries will be male or female, dark or fair, whether its faculties will be complete or incomplete, or whether its hands and feet will be symmetrical.
It is not so; for one who is in the womb may move immediately upon being touched by hot food.

In this manner and that, this consciousness comes and goes, expands and contracts, and moves together with the opening and closing of the eyes; due to various karmas performed in the past, it experiences all objects such as laughing and speaking.
In all instances where a consciousness arises that dwells within the acquired physical body, sentient beings do not know what the essence of this consciousness dwelling within my body is. Bhadrapāli!
Because this consciousness is perfectly accomplished, it flows through all states of existence (*bhava*), yet it is not defiled by or attached to those states of existence. Bhadrapāli!
These states of existence and the objects of the six sense faculties consist of the six elements (*dhātu*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Bhadrapāli! You should understand the objects of consciousness and so forth in this way, Bhadrapāli!
For example, suppose there were a wooden man who, by means of a single mechanism, performed all manner of tasks, running, leaping,
and displaying various kinds of acrobatic feats.
Bhadrapāli, what do you think?
"What causes and conditions led that wooden man to perform such an act?
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"What the Tathāgata has asked is not within my domain;
I lack the wisdom to answer. The Buddha spoke again: "Bhadrapāli!"
Just as that artisan performs various tasks through the power of skillful wisdom,
yet that skilled work has no physical form because it is produced by intelligence;
even so, this body arises for a person through the skill of consciousness, and these various bodies are produced by consciousness.
This consciousness arises because it constructs the body, yet this consciousness is inexhaustible.
Because of the cultivation and perfuming of the dharma-realm, the mental faculty that recollects all past bodies is accomplished.
Just as the light of the sun, this consciousness must be seen in this way.
For example, just as the sunlight shines upon foul, turbid, and putrid corpses yet is not defiled by them, and yet that stench and filth do not exist apart from the light of the sun produced therein.

In this way and that way, when this consciousness first seeks birth, it enters a womb within the filth of excrement and various impurities, or even within the bellies of pigs, dogs, and the like; yet, that consciousness is not defiled by such stench or impurity.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāli! Once this consciousness has abandoned the body, it follows according to its good or evil conduct.
What is the meaning of this?
When this consciousness abandons this body, it immediately undergoes those karmic results of both merit and demerit.

It is like the element of wind arising from a mountain peak and reaching the Campaka grove; because of contact, it receives a subtle fragrance, yet upon reaching a place of filth or a place where corpses stink, O Bhadrapāli!
That wind reaches many places and takes up much fragrance; as it reaches them, the fragrance becomes abundant.
Just as that wind element carries that fragrance along, yet that wind element has no form, and that fragrance likewise has no form.
It is just so, just so. Once this consciousness has abandoned the body, it departs carrying its good and evil karma, proceeding in this sequential manner.
When that consciousness intends to depart, it is like a person in a dream who perceives all things as existing, yet the body does not move from its original location.
In this way and that way, merit also arises.

When consciousness is about to transfer, it is like seeing various things in a dream; yet this consciousness does not emerge from the throat, nor does it emerge from the various apertures, and as it emerges, it likewise seeks no such apertures.
At that time, Bhadrapāla prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when chicken eggs or goose eggs are within their shells and those shells have no holes, one can distinguish them by consciousness without the shells being broken?”
"How does that consciousness migrate? The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"It is like when one perfumes sesame seeds with various flowers such as the Campaka; once they are well-ripened, one presses them to extract the oil, and then says, 'This is Campaka flower oil.'"

Just as that fragrance does not destroy the sesame seeds while its scent is transferred to them—yet that fragrance does not adhere to the sesame seeds, but rather the scent adheres because of the union of the seeds and the flowers—so too, that fragrance does not enter by seeking a pore from the side of the sesame seed; rather, through those two factors, the fragrance is transferred.
In this way, in this manner, this consciousness does not break the eggshell.
Just as the subtle fragrance is transferred, so too is this consciousness transferred; you should understand it thus.
"Furthermore, this consciousness does not migrate; it should be viewed as being like the radiance of the sun, fire, or a mani-jewel.

Furthermore, this consciousness migrates, just as a seed reaches a particular place where that seed is cast into the ground, and there sprouts, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits arise—whether white, red, or black—each with its own specific taste, potency, and maturation."
Furthermore, just as that earth element is one, so too are the elements of water, fire, and wind.

In this same way, this consciousness possesses a single dharma-element; having achieved a body within any of the various realms of existence, it subsequently arises, appearing in colors such as black, white, or red, and possessing a nature that is either harsh and rigid or gentle and compliant.

"Furthermore, Bhadrapāli! At the time of death, once this consciousness has abandoned the body, it becomes the causal seed for a subsequent body, intending to form the physical structure of hands, feet, and so forth."

At that time, no distinct physical parts yet existed; rather, those elements abandoned their status as earth and took on the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), with all those realms merging in harmony through mindfulness.

Yet, by the power of faith and reverence, that mindfulness merged in harmony with the dharma-realm; it grasped consciousness without departing from consciousness, whereby the dharma-realm became visible, and there was a cause for consciousness that did not depart from the dharma-realm.

"However, with that wind of consciousness acting as an aid, all other realms of phenomena become subtle and wondrous—namely, the realm of mindfulness, the realm of sensation, the realm of phenomena, and the realm of form.
At that time, Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In what way does that consciousness possess form? The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"There are generally two kinds of form:"
The first is internal, and the second is external.
What is meant by "internal form"?
It refers to the eye.
The external refers to form (*rūpa*).
If there is eye-consciousness, that is called internal form;
sound is external to the ear, fragrance is external to the nose, flavor is external to the tongue, tangibles are external to the body, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) are external to the mind.

Bhadrapāli! It is like a person born blind who, while sleeping at night, dreams of various kinds of celestial and wondrous forms, most excellent and supreme; having seen them, that person gives rise to the most excellent joy and bliss.
Having awakened from sleep, he no longer saw it; yet when dawn broke, he spoke to others, saying: "O people!
Listen to my dream from last night while I was sleeping."
I saw the forms of women who were most wonderful, supreme, and beautiful; I also saw hundreds of thousands of men, and I saw groves and gardens.
All these things I saw here and there in my dream.

"Or there may be people whose bodies are soft and supple, whose hands and feet are dignified, whose arms are long and well-proportioned, whose bodies are slender, and whose waists and hips are perfectly symmetrical.
Thus, he described in full detail the physical forms and the ornaments and necklaces of all those people whom the man born blind had seen in his dream.
At that time, the forms described by that person born blind are not seen because consciousness has not yet arisen. What do you think?
How could that person born blind see anything in a dream while asleep?
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain this matter for me: how may it be seen?"
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: "Bhadrapāla!
You should know that it is by means of the power of wisdom derived from the internal eye that those born blind see in their dreams; it is not seeing with the physical eye."
Bhadrapāli! Just as a person in a dream who sees forms for a brief moment correctly recollects their own death, so too is it for a person who sees internal forms. Furthermore, Bhadrapāli!
I shall explain this further for you.
