The consciousness of a dead person is like a seed being transferred.

Just as a seed scattered upon the ground receives the four great elements, so too does this consciousness receive right mindfulness, receive sensation, and receive both the wholesome and the unwholesome; only after it has abandoned the body does it transfer.
Bhadrapāla asked the World-Honored One again:
"How does this consciousness receive wholesome and unwholesome cognitions before it migrates?
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"It is like a lotus-colored maṇi jewel that changes according to the color of its reflection: if it is placed against a black form, it immediately turns black; if placed amidst white, it turns white. Wherever the reflected form may be, that maṇi jewel becomes identical in color to it; wherever it is set, its color changes in accordance with the color of that location."
"In this same way, this consciousness receives both good and evil and then departs; it is just like that.
At that time, Bhadrapāli again asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is the substance of this divine consciousness that manifests?
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: “This divine consciousness is formless;
it has no place of aggregation and no place of accumulation. Ultimately, it cannot be apprehended and cannot even be described as such.”
This consciousness has birth, has cessation, and has affliction; it cannot be described [in simple terms]. Bhadrapāli!

It is like a sprout growing from a seed: one cannot say that a rotten seed produces a sprout, nor that a damaged seed produces a sprout; rather, it is from a sound, intact seed that the sprout is produced and brought to completion.
Bhadrapāli! What do you think? Where does that sprout of the seed abide?
Is it in the stem, or in the leaves, or in the roots? Is it in the branches for the sake of that fruit?
In this same way, this consciousness has no place of dependence within the body; it does not abide in the eye, nor in the ear, nor in the nose, and so on, up to and including the mind.

It is just as a sprout grows from a seed; that sprout which is produced has grasping (*upādāna*) as its root. Because of grasping in that state, one immediately undergoes conception (*garbhāvakrānti*). Once conception has occurred, there is contact (*sparśa*). Just as once a sprout has grown, branches, leaves, and flowers appear in due time, and when branches, leaves, and flowers exist, there is fruit.

In this way and that way, this consciousness first brings about the formation of the body; once the body has been formed, the spiritual consciousness has no place to dwell, yet the body does not exist apart from the spiritual consciousness.

Just as those seeds from a tree appear only after it has matured and then produce fruit—rather than the fruit possessing seeds at the time of its birth—in this very way, when this life ends, this consciousness manifests from within the body to undergo rebirth.

Bound by the marks of craving and grasped by the marks of mindfulness, whether through a wholesome connection or an unwholesome connection, it is sustained by the element of wind; impelled by the perfuming of wisdom and pursued by karmic conditions, it then manifests upon the union of the parents.

Bhadrapāli! It is like a well-polished, excellent mirror that reflects the image of a face; it is not that the face does not exist for there to be a reflection of the face, nor is it that the mirror does not exist for there to be a reflection of the face.

Just as when a bright mirror and a face come together through the conjunction of these two conditions, the form of a face appears; yet that facial form has no color, no sensation, and no consciousness. Nevertheless, as the body moves, the form within the mirror also moves. Just as the body speaks, shifts, moves, extends, contracts, bends, or looks up and down—whatever actions it performs—the form of the face within the mirror likewise manifests those same activities.
Bhadrapāli! What do you think? For what reason does that facial form manifest its image within a mirror?
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Because of the human body, such a form appears within that mirror; according to the color of the body, the face also has such a color, and that form likewise has such a color. Whether the various sense faculties are complete or incomplete, the features of that facial form likewise appear in the clear mirror.”
“Bhadrapāli! Just as a clear mirror achieves the form of a face because there is a body, so that a form appears within that clear mirror;
in this same way, this body is achieved through the body itself, which is brought about by consciousness, sensation, grasping, consciousness, and the various formations of volition.”
As for that "bright mirror," it refers to the conditions of the union of the father and mother.
One should know that just as when the body has perished there is no longer a form of consciousness,
so too, after a facial image has appeared in a bright mirror, one may again see the facial image in clear water.
When this consciousness has abandoned this physical body, it proceeds to another existence and again receives the other aggregates (skandhas).
It is like the seeds of the nyagrodha tree or the udumbara tree and others; though they are extremely small, they are able to produce the branches of a vast tree.
Once the great tree has grown its branches, it abandons that form and is born again in another place.
When those seed-essences have abandoned the form of the tree, they wither and dry up according to the seasons, no longer possessing their original flavor.
Once its fundamental flavor has ceased, that tree immediately withers and decays.
In this same way, this consciousness—subtle, without fixed color or form—having produced various bodies, is again abandoned and further accomplishes a different body before it.
It is just as when seeds such as those of barley, wheat, sesame, small grains, or large grains are scattered in a particular location; they immediately take root in that very place.

In this way, indeed, this consciousness moves from within the bodies of sentient beings to another place; there it abides with grasping and receiving, experiencing either merit or demerit, as it shifts from this world to that world.

It is just as a honeybee, seeing the flavor within a flower, takes its nectar and fragrance and leaves the flower to move to another; or, abandoning an inferior flower, it moves to one that is excellent.
Having sat upon the flower, one becomes attached to that flower and seeks its fragrance and flavor.
In this same way, this consciousness, by means of many roots of goodness, may receive a celestial body.

Having received a celestial body, due to the ripening of evil fruits, one may further receive the bodies of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; having received these, one receives yet other bodies.
How, then, should this divine consciousness be contemplated?

It is like the seed of saffron, or the seed of red madder, or the seed of the white lotus; their substance is originally indeterminate in its various colors, yet within those seeds neither sprout nor fixed color can be seen.
When that seed enters the earth and obtains the moisture of water, it immediately produces a sprout; once there is a sprout, flowers subsequently arise.
Yet that color cannot be seen in the seed, nor does the sprout and its color exist apart from the seed.

In this way, and so it is: when this consciousness has abandoned this body and is about to form that other body, the various sense faculties do not yet exist within that mass of flesh, let alone the various sense bases.
Since there are neither sense faculties (*indriya*) nor sense bases (*āyatana*), how could there be divine sight, divine hearing, or [the objects of] odor, flavor, and touch?
Even if one were to possess the principle of cognition by way of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), how could it be known?
"At that time, I performed such various karmas; my past body was thus"—this is experienced solely through consciousness (*vijñāna*).
For example, just as a silkworm produces silk filaments from its own mouth to form a cocoon, wrapping itself within it and then dies therein;

even so, this consciousness, having produced a body for itself, creates karma for itself just as the silkworm produces silk to wrap itself up, and then, its own body being extinguished, it migrates toward that [new state].
For example, just as a lotus flower arises from within water and possesses exquisite color, fragrance, and flavor, yet the actual substance of the water cannot be seen within that flower;
once the flower has perished, if one places its seeds upon the ground, there will be the presence of color and fragrance therein.
In this way, in this way: wherever this consciousness is transferred, none of the sense faculties or their objects are transferred along with it, nor is sensation transferred;
that which is transferred is solely the dharma-dhātu.
For example, wherever a wish-fulfilling jewel goes, whatever object is required is obtained immediately according to one's thought.
It is like the radiance of the sun; it follows the sun of its own accord, and wherever the sun reaches, the light also reaches there.
In this way, wherever this consciousness is transferred, the perceived objects, the dharma-realm, and their characteristics follow it and do not depart.
Furthermore, once this consciousness has abandoned the body, it takes up all forms of existence.
Having gathered and grasped [the aggregates], being without flesh or bone, they approach their subsequent existence.
They grasp the physical body, existence (*bhava*), and various objects of contact; with the divine eye, they behold the taking up of good and evil.

For example, when the fruits of the jujube, the *sahasrābdika* (thousand-year) jujube, the *āmra*, the *kapittha*, and so forth have reached maturity, each possesses a single taste—whether bitter, sour, sweet, salty, or any of the other six tastes.
When those various fruits have ripened, their flavor resides within them; as the seeds are moved to different locations, each possesses its own flavor.
In this very way, wherever the seed of this consciousness is moved, it naturally possesses contact according to merit or demerit, moving along with its own existence and mindfulness.
"Furthermore, when this consciousness abandons the body, it forms such a thought:
'Just as I now abandon this body, therefore this thought is called "consciousness. "
"To discern and know wholesome and unwholesome karma; to know that this karma follows one's self, and to know that one follows this karma.
Because of such cognitions, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
"Furthermore! This body is called 'consciousness' (vijñāna) because it knows and performs all various karmas.

It is like the element of wind (vāyu-dhātu), which at times is cold and at times is hot; at times it possesses a scent following what is foul, and at times it possesses a scent due to fragrance; therefore, it is known as wind."

Thus, although this consciousness itself has no form, because it takes form as its cause for grasping—whether through the cause of grasping desire, the cause of grasping views, or the cause of grasping at the rewards of observing precepts—and so on up to sensation (*vedanā*), the physical form of the body is accomplished by virtue of sensation being its cause; therefore, it is called "consciousness."

At that time, there was a young householder among the assembly named Somabhadra (in the *Yindu* [Sanskrit] pronunciation; translated in the Sui period as "True Moon"), who rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
How should one contemplate its form?
How should one contemplate grasping?
How should one contemplate the grasping for sensual desire?
"How should the grasping at views be contemplated?
How should the grasping at precepts and observances be contemplated?
The Buddha told Candracchattra:
“O True Moon! Any wise person who wishes to understand what you have asked should understand it in this way:

Whether it be a beautiful form or an unattractive form, from the time it is a mere mass of flesh, one must contemplate its sinews and blood, its veins and channels, the sutures of the skull and the brain, the large and small intestines, the lungs, heart, liver, kidneys, spleen, gallbladder, and all the internal organs, as well as the fat, grease, marrow, and blood, the phlegm, mucus, and saliva—all of which are impure, foul-smelling, transient, and terrifying.”
The hair of the head, the beard, the whiskers, and the skin form a covering and aggregate; once aggregated, all these forms are composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
These four great elements take up form to constitute the body; therefore, they are called "form-appropriating" (*rūpopādāna*).
Sujāta! That part of the body which is formed from the union of the father and mother and is solid and firm is the earth element (pṛthivī-mahābhūta).
All that is moist and soft is called the water element (ab-dhātu).
All that is warm and brings to maturity is called the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*).
All that moves, bends, and extends is called the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
All that is cognized is called the spheres (*dhātu*) of sound, odor, taste, and tangibility.
"That which cognizes what is being thought of is therefore called consciousness.
At that time, Soma-bhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How does one abandon that form realm at the time of death?
How does that consciousness depart from that body?
And how, having abandoned that body, does it perceive: "This is my body"?
The Buddha replied to Candracchattra: “Candracchattra!
When this body is first received and remains present, the karmic activities of the body have already ceased and the primary elements (mahābhūta) have been relinquished.”

For example, when milk is mixed with water and boiled over a fire, through the heat, the milk and the water separate; yet, while the milk possesses the essence of its fat and flavor, that [water] has no such color.
Candraprabha!
It is so, it is so. When a person dies, the body is distinct, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are also distinct, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is likewise distinct.

Nevertheless, once that consciousness has grasped the great elements and taken up the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it perfumes the mind with the dharma-realm; thus, having grasped both good and evil, it proceeds to the next world.

It is like the mahā-kalyāṇaka medicinal ghee—translated in the Sui language as "Great True Medicine Ghee"—which is prepared by boiling various medicinal ingredients for their flavor and potency. Within it there may be pungent, bitter, sour, salty, bland, or sweet tastes; yet once these various flavors have been extracted and assimilated, they ripen within the body.
Just as after the tastes such as color and fragrance have been apprehended, the substance of that ghee is relinquished and transformed into the taste of medicine, so too is this consciousness:
having relinquished the body, it apprehends the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the dharma-realm, and then this consciousness migrates away.
To speak of the essence of that ghee's flavor is to use it as a metaphor for the body.
To speak of those various medicines being blended and gathered together is a metaphor for the various sense faculties (*indriya*).
To speak of the color, fragrance, taste, and texture of those medicines is a metaphor for consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is called "consciousness" because it migrates away.
That all flavors are about to depart is precisely the shifting of consciousness;
one should contemplate it in this way.
As for what is called the differentiation of human forms, these may be either virtuous forms or non-virtuous forms.
Alternatively, when it enters the body and the great true medicinal ghee is digested and assimilated, this is a metaphor for wholesome karma;
one should contemplate it in this way.
If it is said that after consuming that great true medicinal ghee, emaciation and a yellowish complexion emerge, this is a metaphor for unwholesome karma.
One should contemplate it in this way:
just as the great mahā-ghṛta medicinal ghee is like this consciousness, one should contemplate it as follows:

just as that great ghṛta medicinal ghee takes up the colors and flavors of various medicines and, once processed, becomes a great true medicinal ghee, yet that ghee has no hands, feet, or sense faculties, but merely takes up those flavors.
In this way, in this manner, when this consciousness has abandoned the body and abandoned the various elements (*dhātu*), it takes up only the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Having taken up sensation, it departs, taking with it both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Candraprabha!

After that person has relinquished the body, in a future life they will attain right mindfulness and celestial recollection; they may see the various devas of the six desire realms, or see the sixteen great hells, or see their own body with all its faculties complete.
At that time, he knows thus: "This is my body.
When that person’s life comes to an end, they perceive various signs, either seeing a sublime palanquin or seeing a sublime grove.
Within those groves were various kinds of trees, lush and beautiful as they sprouted anew; there were also exquisite ponds, and one could see all manner of things accomplished therein.
Seeing such signs as these, his heart gives rise to joy.
Having given rise to joy, he passes away peacefully and in accordance with the Dharma; that person’s consciousness is like one riding a horse.
One should contemplate in this manner.
Regarding the phrase "riding a horse," it is like a person on a battlefield who is clad in fine, sturdy armor and skillfully holds the reins and bridle while swiftly mounting the steed.

In this way, this consciousness—clad in the armor of attachment to objects of perception and the ripening of wholesome fruits—swiftly mounts the inhalation and exhalation, and abandons the various elements (*dhātu*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).
Having abandoned them, it takes up rebirth in the higher Brahma heavens, even reaching the sublime realms of the Akaniṣṭha and other celestial abodes.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 109;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 110.
Translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
The Thirty-ninth Assembly of the Householder Bhadrapāla, Part Two.
At that time, in the assembly, there was the youth Candraketu-pravararāja, who rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is the cause for seeing forms?
What is the cause for desire? What is the cause for seeing?
"What is the cause for the view of clinging to precepts and observances?
The Buddha told Candraprabha:
"The wise perceive the realm of wisdom; the foolish perceive the realm of folly."

When the wise see various beautiful and lovely forms, they understand them to be foul and loathsome—merely lumps of flesh, sinews, bones, pus, and blood; large and small vessels; large and small intestines; lymph, marrow, and membranes; kidneys, heart, spleen, gallbladder, liver, lungs, stomach, and abdomen; the raw and cooked viscera; yellow phlegm, saliva, tears, and mucus; hair of the head, beard, body hair, and nails; and excrement and urine, all wrapped in a thin skin, exposed as impure filth, terrifying and detestable.
All forms whatsoever are born from the four great elements; these are the causes of form. Candraprabha!

Just as parents give birth to a body, the solidity of the body is the earth element, its moisture is the water element, its warmth is the fire element, and its movement is the wind element; whatever is perceived through cognition, including the spheres of sound, smell, taste, and touch—all these constitute consciousness.
The youth Candravrata again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At the time of death, how does consciousness depart from the body?”
"How does consciousness migrate to the body?
How does consciousness know that it is now abandoning this body?
The Buddha told Candraprabha:
“Sentient beings receive retribution according to their karma; the stream of consciousness flows in succession, sustaining the body without interruption.
When the allotted time ends and the retribution is exhausted, consciousness abandons the body and migrates to receive another existence according to its karma.”
For example, when water and milk are mixed and boiled, by the power of the heat of the fire, the milk, the water, and the cream each separate.
In this same way, Moon-essence!
When the life of sentient beings comes to an end, by the power of karma, the physical body, consciousness, and the various sense bases and elements each separate.

Consciousness serves as the basis; by grasping the dharma-realm and the mindfulness of the dharma-realm, together with wholesome and unwholesome karma, it transmigrates to receive the retribution of others.
Moon-Reality!
It is like the great and auspicious ghee, which is produced through the blending of the powers of various excellent medicinal herbs and the efficacy of the refining process.

The great auspiciousness and goodness of *sūksma-sūkṣma* (subtle-subtle) nature sustain the power of excellent medicines; through the six flavors—pungent, bitter, sour, salty, astringent, and sweet—they nourish the human body, providing it with color, fragrance, and taste.
When consciousness abandons this body, it carries along its wholesome and unwholesome karma as well as the fruits of the Dharma; its transition to and reception of further retribution is likewise so.
Moon-essence!
The *sūci* is like the body, and the various medicines blended together constitute great auspiciousness and goodness.
Just as various factors and sense faculties combine to produce an action, and as the flavors and textures of various medicinal herbs contribute to the formation of ghee;

so too does karma sustain consciousness. Just as one who consumes [ghee] that is greatly auspicious, delightful, nourishing, radiant, beautiful, peaceful, and free from affliction, so too does consciousness, when sustained by wholesome [karma], obtain all manner of pleasant retributions.

Consuming ghee in violation of the Dharma causes one’s countenance to change for the worse, becoming wretched and devoid of the luster of blood and breath; one becomes as white as dead soil, just as an evil consciousness reaps various bitter retributions.
Moon-essence!

Just as the auspicious and virtuous jewel *sū* lacks hands, feet, eyes, or other limbs, yet is able to grasp the color, fragrance, flavor, and potency of excellent medicines, so too is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

It grasps the dharmadhātu, sensations, and various wholesome karmas; it abandons this physical body and its sensations to receive them within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Therein, it attains sublime celestial mindfulness and beholds the six heavens of the desire realm and the sixteen hells. It sees its own body with hands and feet perfectly formed and the sense faculties exquisitely beautiful, and it perceives the discarded corpse, saying: "This was my body in a previous life."

Furthermore, he beheld celestial palaces of lofty and sublime appearance, adorned with various flowers, fruits, shrubs, and trees; covered by climbing vines, they shone with brilliant splendor, like freshly refined gold inlaid with myriad precious gems.
Having seen this, his mind was filled with great joy; because of that great joy and love, consciousness then took rebirth there.
This person of wholesome karma, when casting off one body and receiving another, experiences peace and happiness without suffering, like a horse rider who abandons one mount to mount another.
It is like a mighty warrior fully endowed with martial skill who, seeing the enemy forces approaching, dons sturdy armor and mounts a swift steed; wherever he goes, he is without fear.

In the same way, when consciousness relies upon roots of goodness, abandons inhalation and exhalation, and relinquishes the elements, sense bases, and the body, it migrates to receive superior bliss and is reborn therein, from the Brahmakāyika Heaven up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra).
At that time, the Prince Mahauṣadha rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
when consciousness departs from the body, what color or form does it take?”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent,
Great Medicine!
"What you have now asked concerns the most profound realm of the Buddhas; apart from the Tathāgata, there is no one else capable of understanding it.
Thereupon, the youth Bhadrapāla, the Supreme, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The questions posed by Prince Mahauṣadha are profoundly deep; his wisdom is subtle, keen, sharp, and decisive."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"This Prince Mahauṣadha has already planted roots of goodness under the Buddha Vipaśyin; he was once born into the families of non-Buddhist practitioners for five hundred lifetimes."
When he was a non-Buddhist, he constantly contemplated the meaning of consciousness.
What is consciousness? In what way is it consciousness?
Throughout five hundred lifetimes, you have been unable to resolve the coming and going of consciousness, nor do you know its underlying causes.
Today, I shall shatter your web of doubt and enable you to attain understanding.
Thereupon, the youth Bhadrapāla, Supreme and Excellent, addressed Prince Mahauṣadha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
What you have now asked is subtle and profoundly deep."
Candraprabha’s question was shallow and narrow in meaning, like that of an infant; his mind roamed among external objects while remaining ignorant of the internal.

The True Dharma is rarely heard and the Buddhas are difficult to encounter; the Buddha’s perfect and vast wisdom and unfathomably deep insight—this most sublime principle—should be sought through dedicated inquiry.

At that time, Prince Mahauṣadha, seeing the Buddha’s radiant countenance, his features relaxed and joyful like a blooming autumn lotus, leaped for joy with great delight. With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I cherish the profound Dharma and thirst for the profound Dharma; I constantly fear that the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa before I have heard the True Dharma. Among the sentient beings of this final age of turbidity, they are ignorant and know nothing, failing to distinguish between good and evil. They cannot discern what is wholesome or unwholesome, nor what is matured or immature, and thus they wander in confusion through the painful realms of saṃsāra.
The Buddha told Prince Mahābhaiṣajya:
“The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter and difficult to obtain.

In the past, for the sake of even half a verse, I climbed a mountain and threw myself down, sacrificing my life; thus, in seeking the True Dharma, I have undergone immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various hardships.”
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Whatever you desire to ask, feel free to inquire; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Prince Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, we shall do as you command,
World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of consciousness?”
"I pray that you will grant me an exposition.
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:

"It is like a person's reflection appearing in water; this image cannot be grasped, it cannot be distinguished as either existent or non-existent, and is like the form of a *kuraṅga* deer or the likeness of a mirage."
The Prince Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One, what is craving?”
The Buddha said:
"It is like a person facing a pleasing form; the eye-faculty pursuing it is called craving.
It is just as when one holds a bright mirror to view the reflection of one's own face: if the mirror is removed, the reflection does not appear."
The migration and movement of consciousness is likewise thus: the forms of good and evil karma, as well as the color and image of consciousness, are all invisible.
It is like one born blind who knows nothing of the rising and setting of the sun, nor of day and night, light and darkness.
It is likewise that consciousness cannot be seen; within the body, craving, feeling, perception, and volition are all unseeable.
The great elements, the sense bases, and the aggregates of the body—all these are consciousness.

All those with material bodies—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body, as well as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—and likewise the immaterial bodies that experience pleasure and pain, are all consciousness.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
It is like a person whose tongue receives food and discerns the six tastes—sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and astringent.
While both the tongue and the food possess form and color, taste itself has no form."
Furthermore, one perceives various sensations through the body’s bones, marrow, flesh, and blood; while the bones and so forth possess form, the sensations themselves lack form.
The same applies to the knowledge of the fruits of merit and demerit.
Then the youth Bhadrapāla, supreme among youths, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Can this consciousness discern merit and non-merit?”
The Buddha said: "Listen well.
It is not that one who has not yet seen the Truth can see consciousness."
Consciousness cannot be seen; it is not like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of one's hand, nor does consciousness reside within the eyes and other sense organs.
If consciousness were located within the eyes and so forth, one should be able to see consciousness upon dissecting the eyes and other organs.
"Bhadrapāla! Just as the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, perceive consciousness as formless, I likewise perceive consciousness as formless.
Consciousness cannot be seen by ordinary, ignorant people; it is merely revealed through metaphors."
Bhadrapāla! If you wish to know the merits and demerits of consciousness, you should now listen.
For example, Bhadrapāla, it is as if there were a person possessed by various devas, gandharvas, or spirits such as skandhas. Bhadrapāla!
"What do you think?
If one were possessed by a deity, a ghost, or a spirit, could the essence of that possession be found within the body and perceived?
Bhadrapāla replied to the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One!
When one is possessed by devas or other spirits, the essence of that possession has no color and no form; whether sought within or without the body, it cannot be seen."

“Bhadrapāla! For one who is possessed by a great celestial deity of superior merit, one must prepare excellent incense and flowers, burn various renowned types of incense, and arrange pure, fragrant food and drink. All sacrificial implements and offerings must likewise be fragrant and clean.”

Thus, when this consciousness is supported by merit, one obtains the fruits of nobility and happiness—whether as a king of men, or a high minister, or one of great renown and status, or one with mastery over wealth, or a leader among various groups, or a great merchant chief, or one who attains a celestial body and enjoys the superior fruits of the heavens; for it is because consciousness is supported by merit that the body receives such pleasant retribution.

Just as when one is possessed by a deity of superior merit, one immediately becomes joyful upon obtaining exquisite flowers, fragrances, and delicious food and drink, and the patient finds peace and stability;
so too, one should know that this present attainment of nobility, wealth, and sovereignty is entirely due to the merit that supports the consciousness-body, thereby yielding the fruit of happiness.

Bhadrapāla! Those who are possessed by inferior and evil spirits such as the pūtana and others will come to crave impure things such as excrement, filth, putrefaction, nasal mucus, and saliva; if these are used for their sacrificial offerings, they will be delighted and the illness will be cured.
Just as that person, through the power of ghosts and spirits, follows the desires of ghosts and spirits to delight in impurity, stench, decay, and filth;

so too is consciousness supported by the provisions of sin. It may be born into poverty, or among hungry ghosts and various foul-eating animals within the manifold evil realms; because consciousness is supported by sin, the body obtains the fruit of suffering.
Bhadrapāla! The physical bodies of the victorious celestial deities are without substance and without form, yet they receive various fragrant and pure offerings.
That consciousness is formless, and that it receives the retribution of supreme bliss is likewise so.
When those possessed by inferior and evil spirits such as the Pūtanas and others, they partake of impure, foul, and evil food and drink.
Just so, when consciousness is nourished by sinful karma, it likewise reaps the bitter retribution of consciousness.

Bhadrapāla, you should know that consciousness has no physical form, just as the bodies possessed by devas and other spirits do not; and just as one obtains good or bad results from offerings and food, so too does one receive the retribution of suffering or pleasure based on the accumulation of demerit or merit.
Prince Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does one perceive the causes of desire?”
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!
Desire arises through mutual dependence, just as fire is produced when two pieces of wood used for kindling depend upon each other and human effort is applied."
In this way, desire arises conditioned by consciousness and conditioned by the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles of male and female.
It is like fruit arising from a flower: the fruit was not present within the flower, yet when the fruit arises, the flower perishes.
In this way, consciousness is manifested through the body; yet when one seeks consciousness by following the body, consciousness cannot be seen.
Once the body has arisen as the fruit of the karma of consciousness, it then passes away and perishes; the impure substances such as the bones and marrow all completely dissolve and disperse.
Furthermore, just as a seed carries forward the taste, color, fragrance, and texture of its future fruit, transplanting and giving rise to them;
so too is it with consciousness: when it abandons this body, it carries the karma of good and evil, along with feeling, perception, and mental attention, to receive the retribution of a future birth.
Furthermore, it is like a man and a woman who, having met in the joy of desire, part ways and depart.

The consciousness-body, through its union, becomes bound by attachment, relishing and craving its objects with stinginess; yet when the retribution is exhausted, they separate and undergo their respective karmic fruits. Amidst the conditions of father and mother, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) encounters them, and by the power of karma, consciousness arises to obtain the fruit of a body.
Both passion and karma are devoid of form or substance; when desire and its characteristics act as mutual causes, they give rise to further desire—this is the cause of desire.
"Great Medicine!
What is the view of clinging to precepts and rituals as the cause?"

"Precepts" refers to the precepts established by the Teacher, such as the practices of not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking intoxicants.
"Grasping" refers to the clinging to these precepts, forming such a view as:
"By virtue of maintaining these precepts, I shall attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin)."
For this reason, one attains superior existence, namely, receiving the bodies of humans, devas, and so forth.
These are all tainted virtues (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and not untainted virtues (*anāsrava-kuśala*); for untainted virtue has no ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) consisting of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Now, this attachment to precepts and rituals is a type of outflow (āsrava); when planted within consciousness, it results in the retribution of good and evil karma.
Because consciousness is not pure and serves as a cause for affliction, one undergoes the suffering of feverish distress; this constitutes the cause of the view of attachment to precepts and rituals.
Mahābhaiṣajya said to the Buddha,
“How does consciousness take on the body of a deva, and even the body of a hell-being?
The Buddha said:
“Mahābhaiṣajya! Consciousness and the dharma-realm maintain a subtle vision; it is not that which the physical eye relies upon as the cause for seeing.

When this subtle vision unites with a field of merit, one sees celestial palaces, sensual pleasures, and playful diversions. Having seen them, one rejoices, and consciousness becomes bound by attachment, forming such a thought:”
"I shall go there. This stained attachment and longing serve as the cause for existence.
Having seen his own former body lying discarded in a charnel ground, he reflects thus:
"This corpse is my great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); because he accumulated various virtuous deeds, I have now obtained this celestial retribution.
Mahābhaiṣajya said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
"Since this consciousness already has such affection for and attachment to this corpse, why does it not take up residence there?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!..."
“Suppose, for example, one has cut off and discarded their beard and hair; even if they appear glossy black and fragrant, could they ever be replanted on the body to grow back again?
Great Medicine replied to the Buddha, “No, World-Honored One.”
“World-Honored One!
Once the beard and hair have been cast off, they cannot be replanted upon the body to grow again.
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Great Medicine! Once the corpse has been discarded, consciousness can no longer be entrusted with it to receive retribution."
Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This consciousness is dark, profound, and subtle; it has no substance that can be grasped and no form that can be sought. How is it able to sustain sentient beings of massive bodies, such as elephants?”
"Even though his body is as firm and solid as a diamond, he is able to pierce through the body of a strong man and, possessing strength equal to nine elephants, is able to hold him.
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!"

For example, the element of wind has no substance and no form; it may abide within deep valleys or narrow crevices, yet when it emerges, it can be violent and fierce, even toppling Mount Sumeru and pulverizing it into fine dust.
“Mahauṣadha! What are the color and appearance of the wind-mahābhūta of Mount Sumeru?
Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The wind element is subtle, without substance and without form.
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!..."
The wind element is subtle and wondrous, lacking substance and form.
Consciousness is likewise: wondrous and without substance or form, it is capable of sustaining both large and small bodies, whether receiving the body of a mosquito or the body of an elephant.
For example, it is like a bright lamp whose flame is subtle and refined; when placed within a room, all darkness is dispelled according to the size of that room.
Consciousness is likewise: it sustains itself according to the magnitude of its various karmic causes.
The Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for the characteristics and nature of these various karmas, what are they like?”
"By what causes and conditions does it manifest?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!..."
To be born in the palaces of the various devas, partaking of celestial delicacies and dwelling in peace and happiness—all this is brought about by the results of karma.
It is like a person wandering through a vast wilderness in parching thirst: one who finds cool, sweet water experiences relief, while another who finds nothing endures the suffering of thirst.

Those who obtain cold water receive it as no one brings it to them; those who suffer from thirst likewise encounter no obstruction or refusal when seeking water. Each receives the retribution of pleasure or suffering according to their own karmic causes.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!

You should view wholesome and unwholesome karma in this way: like the two phases of the moon in the sky, white and black; or like a raw fruit that, through the increase of the fire element, ripens and its color changes."

Thus, because of the increase of merit, this body is born into a noble family with abundant assets and overflowing gold and jewels, manifesting excellent and flourishing marks; or it is born in the palaces of the various devas, enjoying happiness and sovereignty—all of these are the manifestations of the auspicious signs of virtuous karma and merit.
It is like planting a seed in the earth, where the fruit appears at the top of the tree.

Yet that seed does not travel from branch to branch to reach the top; even if one were to dissect the trunk of the tree, the seed would not be found. No one carries the seed and places it upon the branches; once the tree has grown and its roots are firm, the seed cannot be seen.
In this way, all wholesome and unwholesome karmas depend upon the body; yet, though one seeks them within the body, the karma is not seen.

It is like flowers existing because of seeds, yet flowers are not found within the seeds; or like fruit existing because of flowers, yet fruit is not found within the flowers. As the flowers and fruit develop, their development is not seen.
Because there is karma due to the body, and because there is a body due to karma, it is likewise that there is no karma within the body and no body within karma.
Just as when a flower ripens and falls, its fruit then appears; so too, when the body ripens and perishes, the karmic fruit then emerges.

Just as a seed possesses the causes for flowers and fruits, so too does this body possess the causes of wholesome and unwholesome karma within those karmas; they are formless and lack any manifest sign of ripening.

Just as a human shadow has no substance and is unimpeded, cannot be grasped, and does not cling to the person; yet it moves forward and backward, coming and going, in accordance with the person's movements, nor is it seen to emerge from the body.

The karmic body is also like this: it possesses the body and possesses karma, yet one does not perceive the karma; though bound to the body and not separate from the body, it is capable of producing karma.
It is like medicinal herbs with bitter, pungent, or astringent flavors that can cleanse the body and eliminate all diseases, causing the body to become full and joyful, with a radiant complexion.

Those who see it know they must take excellent medicine; though the flavor of the medicine can be tasted, its matured efficacy is formless—it cannot be seen by looking, nor can it be grasped by touch, yet it can nourish a person’s complexion and luster.
That karma, though formless, can sustain the body is likewise so. As for that which is sustained by wholesome karma:

food, drink, clothing, and all internal and external requisites are abundant and beautiful; the hands and feet are well-proportioned and the physical appearance is exquisite; dwellings are magnificent and opulent; mani-jewels, gold, silver, and various treasures are accumulated in abundance; one enjoys peace, happiness, and pleasure according to one's heart's desire. One should know that these are the characteristics of wholesome karma.

To be born into a lowly station, a remote borderland, or in poverty; to lack basic necessities and long for the happiness of others; to have coarse and poor food, or to go without food; to have a wretched appearance and dwell in a humble place—one should know that these are the signs of evil karma.
It is just as a bright mirror reflects the beauty or ugliness of a face; yet the reflected image has no substance and cannot be apprehended.
In this same way, consciousness, supported by wholesome or unwholesome karma, gives rise to birth among humans or devas, or among those in the hells, animals, and so forth.
"Mahābhaiṣajya, you should thus perceive the union and transformation of karma and consciousness.
Mahābhaiṣajya said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How can a subtle consciousness sustain the various sense faculties and grasp a vast body?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!
It is like a hunter who enters the mountain forest, taking up a bow and a poisoned arrow to shoot a fragrant elephant.

As the poison from the arrow mingles with the blood and spreads through the elephant’s body, its limbs become paralyzed and its sensory faculties and objects of perception are simultaneously lost; as the venom flows to its vital organs, the color of its body turns bluish-red.
It is like a case where a poisonous clot of blood kills an elephant, and the elephant then passes away.
What do you think?
Can the amount of the poison be compared to the size of the elephant’s body? Can they be measured against one another?
Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The amount of poison compared to the body of an elephant differs so vastly in measure that they cannot be equated, just as Mount Sumeru is compared to a mustard seed.”
"Great Medicine!
In this same way, consciousness abandons this body to take up the various sense faculties; it abandons these various elements and undergoes transformation according to karma, just so."
The Great Medicine further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How is it that the subtle consciousness sustains this vast body without becoming weary?"
The Buddha said, “Great Medicine!

Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas high. The two great nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, each encircle it three times. When these two nāgas breathe heavily, they cause Sumeru to tremble and shake, and the waters within the inner ocean all turn into poison.”
These two nāga kings are long, powerful, and strong; the two great nāga kings, Andhaka and Takṣaka, are also equal to them.
What do you think?
“Would there be any difference between the consciousness of the four dragon kings and the consciousness of a mosquito? Mahauṣadha replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"The four dragons and the mosquito have no difference in their consciousness. "Great Medicine!
Suppose a single small drop of vatsanābha poison enters the mouths of the four dragons; the four dragons would then die."
"What do you think?
Between a small drop of medicinal poison and the poison in a dragon’s mouth, which poison is greater?
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The venom in the dragon’s mouth is great, while the poison of a small drop of medicine is extremely slight. “Great Medicine!

A sentient being with a massive body possesses strength equal to nine elephants; yet the subtle consciousness, being colorless and formless, is beyond the measure of conceptual discrimination, and its maintenance according to karma is likewise so.”
Suppose there were a *nyagrodha* seed, extremely minute; yet when planted, it gives rise to a tree that spreads out vast and wide, with branches and twigs numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
What do you think?
Is the seed and the tree similar in size?
Mahābhaiṣajya said:
“World-Honored One!
The disparity between that seed and the tree is like comparing the hole of a lotus fiber to the realm of space.”
"Thus it is, Great Medicine!
One cannot find the tree within the seed, yet without the seed, the tree would not grow.

A tiny *nyagrodha* seed can produce a great tree; so too, a subtle consciousness can produce a great body. While searching for the body within consciousness, the body cannot be found; yet apart from consciousness, the body does not exist."
Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can consciousness, which is adamantine, firm, and indestructible, abide within this body that is fragile and quickly decays?
The Buddha said:

"Mahābhaiṣajya! It is like a poor man who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel; by the power of that jewel, there spontaneously appear lofty buildings with carved trees and exquisite palaces, lush gardens and groves with flourishing flowers and fruits, and elephants, horses, attendants, and all necessary articles of enjoyment."
Later, that person lost the wish-fulfilling jewel, and all their resources and articles of pleasure were completely extinguished.

The divine wish-fulfilling jewel is firm and enduring; even a thousand vajras could not destroy it, yet the resources and enjoyments it produced were false and impermanent, dispersing and perishing with great speed.
"Consciousness is likewise firm and indestructible, yet the body it produces quickly decays and quickly perishes.
Great Medicine said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How can this supple and subtle consciousness penetrate into coarse and rigid matter?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!
The nature of water is extremely supple, yet its surging currents and cascading springs can pierce mountain rocks.
What do you think?
How do the qualities of hardness and softness compare between water and stone?
Mahābhaiṣajya said:
“World-Honored One!
The substance of stone is hard and rigid like a vajra, while the substance of water is soft and supple, providing a pleasant touch.”
“Great Medicine! Consciousness is likewise most subtle and most supple; it can penetrate the form of the rigid and massive body and migrate into it to receive retribution.
Great Medicine again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When sentient beings cast off their bodies, how are they born among the various devas?
And even how are they born in places such as the hells?”
The Buddha said, “Great Medicine!

When sentient beings approach the end of their lives, those supported by meritorious karma abandon their ordinary vision and attain a divine, wondrous vision. With this divine, wondrous vision, they see the six heavens of the desire realm; furthermore, they see the movements of their bodies within the six destinies, as well as celestial palaces, the Garden of Joy (Nandana), the Variegated Flower Garden, and so forth.”

Furthermore, he saw the various devas dwelling in lotus palaces, surrounded by beautiful maidens who attended them with laughter, jesting, and play. Their ears were adorned with various flowers, and they wore garments of kauseya silk; their arms were decorated with various ornaments such as seals, rings, and bracelets. Flowers were in constant bloom, and all manner of requisites were fully provided.

Upon seeing the goddess, his heart was immediately filled with passion and attachment; he was joyful and content, his countenance relaxed and pleasant. His face was like a lotus flower, his gaze steady and undisturbed, his nose neither crooked nor deficient, and his breath was not foul. The color of his eyes was bright and fresh like the petals of a blue lotus. There was no pain in the joints of his body; blood did not flow from his eyes, ears, nose, or mouth. He did not lose control of his excrement or urine, nor did his body hairs stand on end. The palms of his hands were not deathly yellow, his nails were not bluish-black, and his hands and feet were neither disordered nor curled up; auspicious signs were clearly manifest.

He saw in the midst of space a vast and lofty palace, with hundreds of thousands of variegated pillars arranged in exquisite array and draped with nets of bells; as a gentle breeze blew over them, they produced clear and delightful sounds. Various fragrant flowers adorned the jeweled palace, where many celestial youths, their bodies embellished with various gems, were sporting within the hall.

Having seen this, he was filled with joy; his smile revealed teeth like *kunda* flowers, which were neither too wide open nor too tightly closed. His voice was harmonious and smooth, his body was neither excessively cold nor excessively hot, and though surrounded by his kinsmen, he felt no sorrow or distress.
When the sun first rises, one shall relinquish their life; what they see will be bright and clear, free from all darkness, as exquisite fragrances waft from the four directions.

Beholding the venerable form of the Buddha, they will feel joy and profound reverence. Having seen him, they will part with their loved ones in joy, like one who departs for a brief moment and immediately returns, comforting their kin and acquaintances so that they do not fall into sorrow or distress.
It is the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that those who are born must inevitably die; do not give rise to suffering and affliction through conceptual discrimination.
Great Medicine!

When a person of virtuous karma approaches the end of life, they delight in giving, reciting various *gāthās*, various hymns of praise, various mantras, and repeatedly proclaiming the teachings of the True Dharma; like one who is asleep yet not truly sleeping, they pass away in peace and tranquility.
When he was about to relinquish his life-span, the celestial father and celestial mother were seated together on one seat, and flowers spontaneously emerged from the hand of the celestial mother.
Seeing the flowers, the celestial mother looked at the celestial father and said:
"This is most auspicious, rare, and a supreme fruit."
"O Devī, you should know now that the time for your joy at your son’s celebration will not be long.
As the mother of the deva thus toyed with the flower with both hands, her life came to an end at that very moment.

The formless consciousness abandons the sense faculties; it sustains the activities of the objects while abandoning the elements, and sustaining the affairs of the elements, it migrates to receive diverse retributions. It is like a rider on horseback abandoning one mount to mount another; like the sun’s rays drawing forth light; like fire arising from wood; or like the reflection of the moon appearing in clear, still water. When consciousness is supported by wholesome karma, it migrates to receive celestial retribution, transferring with the speed of a pulse or the wind to take rebirth within a flower.

The Heavenly Father and Mother sat together and gazed upon it; for seven days, the wind of desire for nectar blew over the flower. Adorned with precious earrings that shimmered and dazzled, the radiant and pure celestial youth appeared in the hand of the Heavenly Mother.
Mahābhaiṣajya said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
How can formless consciousness, by relying on the power of causes and conditions, give rise to that which has form?”
"How is it that that which has form abides within causes and conditions?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!"
It is like fire produced when pieces of wood come together and rub against one another.

This fire cannot be found by searching within the wood, yet if the wood is removed, the fire likewise cannot be found. Fire arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions; if the causes and conditions are not complete, the fire does not arise.
Within wood and other such materials, one may search for the characteristics of fire but ultimately cannot see them; yet everyone sees fire emerge from within the wood.
In this same way, Great Medicine!

Consciousness arises through the conjunction of the conditions of parents and gives rise to a physical body. Within the physical body, consciousness cannot be found; apart from the physical body, there is likewise no consciousness.
"O Mahauṣadha!
Just as when fire has not yet emerged, the signs of fire do not appear, and there is neither the sensation of heat nor any other characteristics—
so it is, O Mahauṣadha!"
If the body does not yet exist, consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, and volition do not all manifest.
Great Medicine!

It is like seeing the brilliant radiance of the solar disc, yet ordinary people do not see the substance of the sun; they cannot know whether it is black, white, yellowish-white, or yellowish-red, but they know that the sun exists through its functional activities, such as its shining heat, its light, its rising and setting, and its cyclical movements.
"Consciousness is also like this; it is known to exist through its various functions.
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying, "What are the functions of consciousness?"
The Buddha said:
"Great Medicine!
Feeling, perception, mental formations, volition, sorrow, suffering, and affliction—these are the functions of consciousness."
"Furthermore, there are wholesome and unwholesome karmas that perfume [the mind] to become seeds, which manifest as the functioning consciousness.
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that consciousness, having departed from the body, quickly receives another body?"
"When consciousness has abandoned the old body but has not yet received a new body— at that moment, what is the characteristic of consciousness?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!..."

Suppose there were a man, long-armed, brave, and strong, clad in sturdy armor and riding a horse as swift as the wind into battle; when weapons clashed and his mind grew distracted, he fell from his horse, yet by virtue of his martial skill and agility, he immediately leapt back onto it.
The consciousness abandoning the body and swiftly taking up another body is likewise like this.
Furthermore, it is like a coward who, seeing an enemy and becoming terrified, flees on horseback;
the consciousness, supported by wholesome karma, seeing the celestial parents sitting together upon a seat, swiftly transferring its rebirth there is likewise like this.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Regarding what you have asked: when consciousness has abandoned the old body but has not yet received a new body—at that moment, what is the characteristic of consciousness?
Mahābhaiṣajya!"

For example, when a person’s reflection appears in water, it has no substantiality that can be grasped; yet its hands, feet, face, eyes, and various features are no different from those of the person. Within the reflection, there is no physical substance or activity; it is neither cold nor hot, nor does it possess any tactile sensations. Furthermore, it lacks fatigue, flesh, or the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and it is devoid of the sounds of speech, bodily sounds, or sounds of pleasure and pain.
"Consciousness abandons the old body before the new body has been received; the characteristics are likewise so, O Great Medicine!
This is the support for those who, by means of wholesome karma, are born among the devas.
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does consciousness arise in the hells?
The Buddha said,
“Great Medicine!
Those who perform evil deeds enter hell.
Listen attentively,
Great Medicine!
Among these beings, those who have accumulated roots of unwholesomeness form this thought at the time of death:
"Now that I die in this body, I shall abandon my parents, relatives, and loved ones, which brings me immense grief and suffering."

Seeing the various hells and seeing his own body as one destined to enter them, he saw his feet above and his head inverted and pointing downward; furthermore, he saw a place where the ground was entirely composed of blood.

Having seen this blood, the mind becomes attached to its flavor; conditioned by this attachment, one is born in hell, and by the power of the causes of putrid, foul water and stench, consciousness takes rebirth therein.
For example, just as insects are born within foul-smelling filth, stinking curd, or putrid wine due to the power of various causes of stench,
so too do those entering hell take birth by resorting to foul substances.
The youth Bhadrapāla, the Supreme and Noble, joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the physical appearances of the sentient beings in the hells?
Furthermore, what is their form?”
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine! Those who,
out of craving, are born in the Blood-Earth Hell have blood-light radiating from their entire bodies, and their bodies are the color of blood."
Those born in the Hot Spring Moat have bodies like black clouds.
Those born in the River of Flowing Milk have bodies marked with various mottled colors; their bodies are extremely soft and delicate, just like the body of a noble infant.

His body was so tall that it exceeded eight cubits; his beard, hair, and body hairs were all long enough to trail on the ground, and his hands, feet, face, and eyes were deformed and incomplete. When the people of Jambudvīpa saw him from afar, they would die instantly.
Mahābhaiṣajya said to the Buddha,
“What do the sentient beings in the hells take as food?
The Buddha replied:

“Mahābhaiṣajya! The sentient beings in the hells experience not the slightest pleasure; in their terror they flee in all directions, and seeing from afar molten copper and red liquid, they think it is blood and rush toward it in great numbers.”
Furthermore, a voice cried out:
"All you who are hungry, come quickly to eat!

They then rushed toward that place; having arrived, they stood there and cupped their hands to their mouths, whereupon the hell-wardens poured molten copper into their cupped palms and forced them to drink it.
When molten copper enters their bellies, their bones and joints burst apart and flames erupt from their entire bodies.
Great Medicine!
Whatever food the sentient beings in hell consume only increases their suffering; there is not the slightest bit of peace or happiness.

The suffering of the sentient beings in hell is such that consciousness does not abandon them nor is it destroyed; the body is like a heap of bones upon which consciousness rests and does not depart, for as long as the karmic retribution is not exhausted, the body of suffering is not relinquished.
Oppressed by the suffering of hunger and thirst, they suddenly see a grove where flowers and fruits flourish in profusion and the foliage is vast and lush.
Having seen it, they laugh with joy and say to one another:
"This grove is lush and verdant; its pure breeze is cool and beautiful."

The multitude hurriedly entered the garden for a brief moment of pleasure; however, the leaves, flowers, and fruits all turned into swords and blades that hacked and severed the sinners. Some had their bodies split in two, while others cried out in great terror and fled in all directions.

The hell-wardens rise up in a crowd, grasping vajra-clubs, or iron clubs, iron axes, and iron staves; biting their lips in rage, flames issue from their bodies as they strike and beat the offenders, blocking them and preventing their escape.
All these things are seen as the result of one's own past karma.
The hell-wardens follow behind the offenders and say to them: "Where are you going?"
"You should remain here and not wander east or west again.
Where do you intend to flee?
This garden is adorned by your own karma; can you possibly leave it?"
"Thus it is, Great Medicine!

The sentient beings in the hells undergo various kinds of suffering; after seven days they die and are reborn again in hell. By the power of their karma, they are like wandering bees that, having gathered nectar from flowers, return to their original place."

Sentient beings with sinful karma who are destined for hell, at the moment of their initial death, see the messengers of death arrive to bind their necks and drive them away. Their bodies and minds experience great suffering as they enter a vast darkness, like being seized and led off by bandits, crying out:
"Alas! Alas! What a calamity! How bitter!"
I now abandon all my various beloved relatives and friends of Jambudvīpa to enter hell.
I no longer see the path to heaven, but see only suffering; I am like a silkworm spinning its own thread to entangle itself until death.
"I have committed sins myself and am bound by my karma; like one caught in a snare with a cord tied around the neck, I am dragged and driven away, being led into hell.
O Bhadrapāla! Such is the nature of suffering for beings born in hell due to their sinful karma.
At that time, when Bhadrapāla and Prince Mahauṣadha had heard this teaching, their bodies trembled and their hair stood on end. They both rose, joined their palms, and spoke these words:

"We now take refuge together in the Buddha; we pray that you will grant us protection. By the merit of having heard this Dharma, may we not remain within the flow of existence while wandering in the wheel of birth and death, nor fall into the three miserable realms or enter hell."
Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; I only pray that you will grant me leave.
The Buddha said:
"As you desire, ask whatever you wish.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is an accumulation?
What is a collection? What is an aggregate?
"What is meant by 'the body does not transmigrate'?
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:

"The element of wisdom, the element of vision, the element of mind, and the element of clarity—by the combination of these four elements the body is formed. The consciousness of the objects of these four elements is called 'accumulation.'"
The "aggregate" refers to the six elements, the six sense bases, and the six objective fields; it is the cause of the three elements and two sense bases.

That is to say, the combination and accumulation of hair of the head, beard, body hair, nails, skin, flesh, pus, blood, mucus, saliva, yellow phlegm, fat, grease, marrow, lymph, hands, feet, face, eyes, and the various large and small joints is called an aggregate.
Just as grains, beans, sesame, and wheat, when accumulated and stored together, become high and large and are thus called a "heap" (rāśi),
so too are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness termed the "six elements" (ṣaḍ-dhātu).
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are called the six objective spheres (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Greed, hatred, and delusion are called the causes of the three realms.
Furthermore, wind, bile, and phlegm are also called the three causes.
The two entrances refer to precept and faith.
There are also two causes, namely equanimity and giving.
Furthermore, there are two causes, namely effort (*vīrya*) and concentration (*samādhi*).
Again, there are two causes, namely the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*).
As for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these four are called the formless aggregates (*ārūpyaskandha*).

Feeling (*vedanā*) refers to the experiencing of the characteristics of suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither painful nor pleasant; perception (*saṃjñā*) refers to the cognition of the characteristics of suffering and pleasure; mental formations (*saṃskāra*) refer to present mindfulness, attention, and contact; and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the master of this body that pervades all its constituents—there is nothing the body does that is not due to consciousness.
"Non-transmigration" refers to the purification of body, speech, and mind, whereby one realizes and attains the fruits of the Path.

When such a person dies, consciousness abandons the aggregates of existence (*skandhas*) and does not again undergo existence or flow into the various realms of rebirth. Transmigrating to the Ultimate Bliss, they do not transmigrate again; this is called non-transmigration.
Thereupon, Bhadrapāla and Prince Mahauṣadha prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!
This collection of teachings spoken by the Buddha, the All-Knowing One, shall bring great benefit, welfare, and happiness to sentient beings in the future.”
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma-aggregate of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and not subject to cessation; those who possess all-knowledge know this and do not act [to destroy it].

Having accumulated the light of wisdom through immeasurable toil and suffering over many kalpas, I now proclaim this sūtra, this sun of the True Dharma, to provide great illumination for all sentient beings. Its virtue and renown flow universally throughout the ocean of omniscience; it is taught for those who are able to discipline their minds and direct their mental streams."

Wherever this sutra is recited, read, or explained, it shall be protected by all devas, ghosts and spirits, asuras, and mahoragas, who will all come to pay their respects; and no fears of water, fire, kings, or thieves shall be able to cause harm.

"From this day forward, O bhikṣus, do not preach this sūtra before those who lack faith; be careful never to show it to those who seek out faults; do not preach it among the Nirgranthas, the followers of the Nirgrantha sect, or among other non-Buddhists; nor should you preach it to those who are disrespectful or who do not request it with longing."
If one violates my teachings and causes harm to the Dharma, such a person is thereby harming the Tathāgata.
Bhikṣus, if there are those who pay homage to and make offerings to this sutra, you should honor and support them; such persons are holders of the Tathāgatagarbha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One should courageously transcend the burdens of worldly dust, Diligently cultivate the Buddha’s True Teaching,
And utterly destroy the host of the army of death, Just as an elephant tramples through reeds and rushes."
"Uphold the Dharma and observe the precepts; with single-minded diligence, do not be negligent.
By doing so, you shall cast off the cycle of birth and death, exhausting all suffering and reaching the end of existence.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the youth Bhadrapāla-uttara, the prince Mahauṣadha, along with the bhikṣus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred and Tenth. At that time, there was among the assembly a prince, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Mahauṣadhi. He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"When that consciousness departs from this body, what form will it have?
The Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Mahābhaiṣajya, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Mahābhaiṣajya! It is so, it is so. The meaning of what you have asked is exceedingly profound; only the Tathāgatas are able to know it.
Yet, apart from the Tathāgata, there is no one else who can know this consciousness."
At that time, Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is rare indeed that this Prince Mahauṣadha is able to inquire about such profound matters—so subtle, so minute, so profound, and so secret.”
The Buddha replied to Bhadrapāli: “It is so, Bhadrapāli!
Because this Prince Mahauṣadha had already made offerings to the World-Honored One Vipaśyin in the past and planted roots of goodness.”
Bhadrapāli! In five hundred past lives, this Prince Mahauṣadha was once a non-Buddhist practitioner; at that time, he frequently inquired about the meaning of this consciousness.
However, at that time, this Prince Mahauṣadha will likewise be unable to discern within this consciousness where it comes from or where it goes;
since he does not understand this matter, I shall now resolve this meaning for him.
At that time, the elder’s son Bhadrapāla praised Prince Mahauṣadha, saying: “Mahauṣadha!
Excellent, excellent!”
"O Benevolent One, your wisdom is vast and boundless; thus you are able to inquire about the profound meaning from the World-Honored One.
I now exhort Great Medicine to request this meaning from the World-Honored One."

He who has entered into all difficult-to-know matters skillfully understands their profound meaning; do not let this Somaśubha, with his trivial amusements, be the first to question the Buddha. Why is that?
The reason is that you have repeatedly troubled [the Buddha] by asking improper questions of the World-Honored One.

However, it is extremely rare for a Buddha, the World-Honored One, to appear in the world, and it is likewise difficult for such a Dharma assembly to convene in this world. Therefore, you should now entreat the World-Honored One to explain these points of profound meaning.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prince Mahābhaiṣajya gazed up at the World-Honored One and saw that the World-Honored One was joyfully smiling, as pure and radiant as a fresh autumn lotus flower just beginning to bloom.
Having seen this, he was filled with joy. At that time, the Bodhisattva Prince Mahauṣadhi addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! Because of my thirsting longing, I delight in hearing the True Dharma. Yet I fear that the World-Honored One may not fully reveal the essentials of the Dharma to me nor resolve my doubts; furthermore, I fear that the World-Honored One will soon enter parinirvāṇa; and I fear that sentient beings will be unable to understand the retribution of good and evil karma, and will perpetually undergo birth and death, unable to abandon their afflictions.”
The Buddha said to Mahābhaiṣajya: "Mahābhaiṣajya!

It was for this very reason that in the past I recited these verses, threw myself from the precipice of a great mountain as an act of giving, and further performed hundreds of thousands of billions of various other deeds, including immeasurable and boundless difficult ascetic practices."
“Mahābhaiṣajya!
Whatever doubts you may have, simply ask me; do not consider it difficult. I shall explain them to you in detail according to your wishes.
At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the color of this consciousness?
The Buddha addressed Mahābhaiṣajya, saying:

"Mahauṣadhi! This consciousness is like the fire of a magician, like a person's reflection in water, and like the wind-circle which has no fixed location; it possesses no fixed color, like the way sentient beings perceive empty space, and it is like craving."
Mahābhaiṣajya asked again:
"What is that craving? The Buddha said:
"It is like a person shooting an arrow; because they possess the faculty of sight, they see the arrow as it flies away.
It is also like a person holding a bright, clear mirror and seeing the reflection of their own face within that mirror; once the mirror is removed, the reflection is no longer seen."
This consciousness is likewise; when it transfers from a human body, its cognitive realm perceives only sins and merits.

It is like one born blind, who does not see the sun-god at its rising, at midday, or after midday; nor does he see the moon-god at night, nor does he see it during its rising or its darkening—he sees none of these at all.
This consciousness is likewise: within this body, it cannot be seen. O Mahābhaiṣajya!
Within this body, there is attachment, grasping, and perception; for the wise, there is only consciousness.

All that constitutes this body—the aggregation and collection of the various elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and aggregates (*skandha*), including all forms; as well as the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and the sensations of form and so forth, whether painful or pleasant, along with the mind and all other such forms—this is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
It is as when a person knows a taste with the tongue, whether it be bitter or pungent; while that person's tongue has form, that taste is without form.
All that exists within this body—bones, marrow, flesh, and blood—is with form, whereas that which is experienced is without form."
"This is what is called consciousness that experiences transgression and merit.
At that time, Bhadrapāli prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Who is it that experiences the retribution of sins and merits? The Buddha told Bhadrapāli:
"Listen attentively and receive this well; I shall explain it for you."
Those who perceive reality see this consciousness, yet this consciousness cannot be apprehended.
It is like the fruit of the *āmra* tree, which can be seen in the palm of one's hand; this consciousness does not abide within the path of the eye, nor can it be seen by the eye.
Those Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, perceive this consciousness; I likewise am formless and invisible.
It is only because the ignorant do not know and do not see that I speak of it as being merely "consciousness," which cannot be seen.
Bhadrapāli! This consciousness experiences both merit and demerit; I shall explain this to you, so listen attentively.
It is, for example, as if there were someone possessed by a *yakkha*, or a *rakkhasa*, or a *gandhabba*, or a deity.
Bhadrapāli! What do you think? Can those various ghosts or *yama-preta*s within that person's body be seen?
Bhadrapāla said: “World-Honored One!
That ghost, whether within or without the human body, is truly invisible.”
“However, those ghosts within the human body likewise have no physical form. Bhadrapāli!

Just as when that most excellent deva resides within a human body, it takes the finest fragrant flowers, unguents, powdered incense, as well as various flower garlands and food and drink—all of the highest and most superior quality.”
Thus, when this body takes up the most excellent karma, it experiences it by means of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Whether one takes up the position of a king to rule with sovereign power, or takes up birth in the family of a wealthy and prosperous great householder, or receives the karmic fruit of the heavens—in such ways does this consciousness experience such merit.

The most supreme deity resides within the human body and receives the most excellent offerings; whether receiving royal sovereignty or abundant wealth, it moistens that human body and causes it to rejoice.
In this same way, the consciousness that receives the retribution of merit is also like this, Bhadrapāli!

Just as that impure piśāca ghost dwells within a human body and partakes of impure things and foul odors, or receives various offerings in a latrine or a secluded place, and upon receiving those offerings, immediately gives rise to joy.
Because that person is under the influence of impure spirits and deities, they constantly delight in foul, filthy, and unclean places.
Since their mind finds such things pleasing, they feel joy whenever they obtain foul and filthy objects.

Thus, this consciousness undergoes an evil retribution and gives rise to an impure mind; it may be born into a poor or lowly family, or into the realm of hungry ghosts, where it constantly eats filth and excrement with a heart full of delight.
Nevertheless, this consciousness experiences such evil retribution;
just as that supreme deity, though lacking form or shape, receives the most excellent and highest offerings.
In this way, although this consciousness has no form, it receives the most supreme and wondrous retribution, taking on a body according to its karma.
It is like that formless *pūtana* ghost who clings to a human body and constantly delights in eating various kinds of filth.
In this way, this consciousness dwells within impure karma and constantly delights in lowly and base places. Bhadrapāli!
You should know that this impure consciousness is thus.
