Bhadrapāli! Just as that ghost-form exists within a human body yet has no physical color, so too does this consciousness receive the retributive fruits of good and evil, like that ghost or spirit; you should understand and perceive it in this way.
At that time, Prince Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is it to experience sensual desires?"
The Buddha replied to Mahābhaiṣajya:
"One should observe that desire arises from the mutual conjunction of various factors.
It is like drilling wood to produce fire; it is only through the physical effort of a person that fire is subsequently brought forth."
When one desires to experience sensual pleasure, it arises from a man’s intention and the subsequent contact; thereafter, the matter of desire is produced.
It is like a flower that gives rise to a fruit: although there was originally no fruit within that flower, because the flower exists, the formation of the fruit can subsequently be seen.
Thus, once this body has been born, consciousness can then be perceived; yet within this body, no consciousness is itself visible.

Because of consciousness, there exist within the body impure things such as marrow, bones, flesh, and blood, just as when a seed is sown and produces a flower, one subsequently receives its color, fragrance, and flavor because of that flower.

Just as once a fruit has been produced it returns to extinction, so too this consciousness, having formed the body, likewise returns to extinction; yet, grasping at wholesome and unwholesome sensations, perceptions, intentions, and mental consciousness, it proceeds to that other world. It enters into union with a male and female, giving rise to a heart of joy; through their congress and mutual embrace, impurity is emitted; once the impurity has been emitted, they again separate from one another.

When those two experience sensual pleasure, their minds give rise to joy; yet once they have experienced it, the thought of desire no longer remains, and they either separate from one another or develop a sense of weary detachment.
The perception of desire is like this.

In this way, this consciousness arises in dependence upon the body as its object, giving rise to a joyful mind and increasing sensation and perception. It is just as when a person sees a woman's form and immediately gives rise to the perception of desire, each becoming attached to the body; once the desire has been experienced, they subsequently feel weary and detached and depart.
This consciousness is likewise: having already received a body, it eventually abandons it and gives rise to the thought of weary detachment.

Furthermore, due to the sexual desire of the parents, the intermediate state (antarābhava) receives a body by grasping at karma; this consciousness enters from within, and through the fulfillment of its causes of desire, the body is formed.
That karma is formless, and the cause—the man or woman—is likewise formless; however, because they grasp at sensory objects, thoughts of desire arise, and thus it becomes possessed of form.
Therefore, it is said that one experiences the perception of desire.
Because one experiences the perception of desire within form, it is called "experiencing desire.
Furthermore, Great Medicine!
Because one takes up the precepts as an object of focus, one receives subsequent retribution. How is this so?
I shall explain it for you.

Regarding the observance of precepts: one physically refrains from killing, does not steal the property of others, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not drink alcohol or cause strife; one is thus cautious and free from negligence.

This constitutes clinging; desiring to receive the fruit of a *srotāpanna* or the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin* in a future life, one thereby undergoes further existence, whether as a celestial being or as a human being.

Furthermore, those who possess wholesome karma—whether it be with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—accomplish the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, which moisten the consciousness (*vijñāna*) in that state.

Having performed and maintained various karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, which accomplish consciousness and the rest, and having experienced the objects of desire, they subsequently develop weary detachment toward them.
"For this reason, it is said that because one maintains the precepts, one receives this subsequent retribution.
At that time, Prince Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
"How does this consciousness receive a celestial body?
And how does it receive a body in hell?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Prince Mahauṣadha, saying:
“Mahābhaiṣajya! Listen attentively now; I shall explain this matter for you.
Mahābhaiṣajya!”
This consciousness arises because it is sustained by the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), forming the mental perception of a celestial being.

That celestial perception does not reside in the physical eye; rather, that which is perceived by the essence of that perception is itself the cause of sensation. Therefore, it is called the "perception of the cause of sensation."

As for this person who perceives the heavens, it is through the successful accomplishment of meritorious objects of focus that they perceive the celestial palaces; therein, within the desire realms, they experience various kinds of pleasures of the five senses.
Having seen this, he immediately gives rise to a desire; consequently, he arouses a cognition of thought:
"I must now go to that place.
Once he has given rise to such a desire, he produces an afflicted attachment, and his mind grasps at signs of existence.
Furthermore, he sees his former body abandoned within the Śītavana charnel ground. Having seen this, he then thinks:
"This is my celestial consciousness."
"Having performed these roots of goodness, I shall now desire to go to the heavens.
At that time, Prince Mahauṣadha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Since that consciousness is thus attached to the corpse, why does it not immediately enter the corpse?
The Buddha said to Prince Mahauṣadha: "Mahauṣadha!"
It is, for example, as if a person were to shave off their hair and beard.
Having seen the hair and beard fallen upon the ground, they would think:
"This hair and beard of mine was beautiful, black, fragrant, and clean; I wish that this hair of mine might grow back upon my head just as it was before."
"O Mahauṣadha! What do you think?
Would those hairs be able to grow back onto the head again?"
Mahābhaiṣajya said: “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “Great Medicine! It is so, it is so.”
“Once that person’s consciousness has abandoned the body, it is impossible for it to desire to re-enter and dwell within it again.
At that time, Prince Mahauṣadha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Since this consciousness is subtle, lacking any distinct color and being vast and boundless, how can it come to approach the body of the Great White Elephant,
and furthermore, how can it shatter a vajra body?
“Since he does not possess the strength of a thousand elephants, how can a human being be born with the ability to sustain the strength of a thousand elephants?
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:
“It is like the element of wind, which is formless and invisible, yet dwells within mountain valleys.”
And once that wind has emerged from those mountain valleys, it can crush, topple, and shatter even great mountains as high as Mount Sumeru.
Great Medicine!
What do you think? What color does that wind element have,
and what color does that mountain have?
The Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That wind is subtle and weak, and moreover lacks a physical form; it should be viewed in this manner."
The Buddha again addressed Mahābhaiṣajya, saying:

"Mahābhaiṣajya! Just as that wind element is soft, weak, and formless, so too is that consciousness; it is likewise soft, weak, and without a physical body. Nevertheless, it is not obstructed in its ability to accomplish a great body or to accomplish a subtle and minute body."
Yet that consciousness is of one and the same nature whether in a mosquito or in an elephant.
Great Medicine!
It is like the light of a small lamp or candle, whether on a wall or within a room, which is able to dispel great masses of darkness.
"This consciousness is also like this: although it is minute and subtle, it can produce large and small forms and colors, all because it undergoes [the results of] karma.
At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What color does that karma have?
What is its substance?
How many kinds of causes does it have?
"You should observe this," the Buddha replied to Mahābhaiṣajya.
"The realm of karma consists of experiencing subtle and exquisite pleasures, and receiving celestial food and drink."
It is like two people traveling together who come upon a vast wilderness.
There, one of them suddenly encounters cool, clear water and drinks it, while the other dies of hunger and thirst.
Yet that water cannot enter the mouth of one person by itself, nor is there anyone among them who does not receive a drink.
It is solely due to causes and conditions that one person encounters the cool, refreshing water and drinks it, while another does not encounter it.
In this way, in this manner, these wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are likewise.
Just as with the dark fortnight and the bright fortnight, one must perceive the wholesome and the unwholesome accordingly.
For example, when raw fruit has ripened, it transforms into a different color; yet that color comes about because the power of heat brings it to maturity.
In just this way, through the power of merit, this body is born into the family of a wealthy householder, possessing abundant wealth and treasures and experiencing happiness in the present life.
While dwelling in the celestial palaces, one manifests the experience of divine bliss;
yet subsequently, upon losing that sovereign power of the heavens, one manifests the state of lacking merit.

It is just as when a seed is sown in the earth: after the tree has grown, that seed no longer appears upon the tree; it does not move from branch to branch, nor does it manifest within the trunk, nor is there anyone who takes the seed in hand and places it on the tree, nor does it shift from the root.
Those seeds may become manifest.
In this way and that way, these various karmas— whether wholesome or unwholesome— reside within the body without being apparent,
just as flowers arise from seeds and fruits arise from flowers.
The flower does not exist within the seed, nor does the seed exist within the flower; yet the seed and the flower do not have two separate entities.

In this same way, the various karmic existences within this body arise from karma, and while the body exists because of karma, that body cannot be seen within the karma, nor can the karma be seen within the body.
Just as a flower must reach maturity before it can produce fruit,
so too, once the body has matured, various karmas can manifest.
Just as wherever a seed exists, there a flower will appear, and only after the flower appears does the fruit come into being.
In this way, in whatever place this body is born, whatever good or evil is seen in that place immediately manifests; yet those roots of karma have no form.
It is like a person who has a shadow because of their body; that shadow is neither fixed nor possesses color, yet it follows the person as they move.
That shadow does not rest upon the person, nor can a shadow be manifested apart from the body.
Thus, within this body, the manifestations of good and evil appear together, never separating from one another; wherever the body goes, they follow in its wake.
That karma follows it everywhere; that karma does not exist apart from the body, nor can karma manifest apart from the body.
Just as various medicines—whether pungent, sweet, bitter, or otherwise—can eliminate all diseases once a person has drunk or taken them;
having thus removed the various evils from the body, they bring about suppleness and a radiant complexion.
Those who see him can discern his physical appearance; this person has encountered a potent medicine.

Yet, those various medicines have no color in their taste or potency; their taste, potency, and color cannot be manifested. It is only through the person’s own physical form that they can be made manifest as upright and handsome.

In this way, indeed, this wholesome karma reaches the human state even though it is formless; because of fine food and drink, because of wearing beautiful clothing, and because that person’s faculties are complete, they experience pleasure with their body.
Furthermore, to have this body adorned with gold, silver, and rare treasures, and to possess the status and influence of the wealthy and noble—all these are the realms of wholesome karma.

To lose such status and lack meritorious karma, to be impoverished and distressed, to be far removed from resources and wealth, to constantly lack necessities and seek the property of others, to have coarse and unpalatable food and drink, and for all one’s movements—walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—to be inferior; to lack the fine karmic rewards to nourish the body, and to be born with an ugly appearance—all these are the realms of unwholesome karma.
Just as a bright mirror, by virtue of its clarity, causes the beauty or ugliness of a face to appear distinctly, yet the reflection within that mirror has no color;
even so, by the power of good and evil, this consciousness manifests among humans, or in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"O Mahauṣadha!
These various karmas follow this consciousness.
O Mahauṣadha!"
"One must know and see it in this way.
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How does this consciousness accomplish the various sense faculties and receive a great body?
How does it abandon the various sense faculties?
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:
"It is like a hunter who enters a deep forest, takes up a powerful bow, and coats the tip of an arrow with poison to shoot a great elephant.

Although the drop of poison is small, once it has entered the skin and reached the blood, its toxic vapor spreads throughout the body, reaching the range of all the sense faculties. It causes the faculties to become obstructed and the joints to contract, changes the color of the blood throughout the limbs, and finally results in the abandonment of the body."
The poison returns to its original point of entry and naturally emerges from it.
Great Medicine!
That single drop of poison is extremely minute, yet the body of the elephant is immense.
"What do you think? Mahauṣadha replied to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!
"Although the poisonous medicine is extremely minute, its manifestation is as vast as Mount Sumeru.
The poison migrates throughout, which is why it pervades the entire body.
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:
"In this way, when this consciousness abandons the body, it abandons the sense faculties and abandons the elements; the sequence is likewise such and such.
Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that you can accept such a vast body without fear or difficulty?
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Suppose there were Mount Sumeru, eighty-four thousand yojanas high, and upon that mountain there were two dragon kings:"
One was named Nanda and the other Upānanda; they circled that mountain three times and remained there.
The breath from the sighs of those dragon kings made the seawater undrinkable.
When that nāga king breathes in and out, Mount Sumeru trembles.
Just as that nāga king’s body is vast and possesses great strength, so too it is with the nāga kings Vāsuki and Takṣaka.
"Mahābhaiṣajya! What do you think?
Would the consciousness of those dragon kings be equal to the consciousness of a mosquito?"
"Do not perceive it otherwise.
Prince Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"As it appears to my mind, the consciousness of that dragon king and that of a mosquito are equal and without distinction.
The Buddha further addressed Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Suppose there is a poison named Vatsanābha, and another poisonous drug named Halāhala."
If one were to give such mustard seeds as food to Nanda, Upananda, and their like, they would immediately and swiftly meet their end.
Great Medicine! What do you think?
Between the poison of a dragon and the poison of medicine, which poison has the greater power?
Is the dragon's poison greater,
or is the medicinal poison greater?
Mahābhaiṣajya replied,
“World-Honored One!
According to my view, Nanda and Upananda possess much poison, whereas Vatsanābha possesses little poison.”
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya: "It is so, it is so.

Although there is a great body with the strength of nine thousand elephants, this does not hinder the fact that its consciousness, though minute, lacks a fixed form and is invisible; yet, through the conditions of karma, this consciousness brings about the accomplishment of the great body."
"Mahābhaiṣajya!

It is like the seed of a nyagrodha tree: although its form is small, it is not incapable of producing a great tree whose branches and twigs are so long and wide that they cover hundreds of thousands of lands."
"Mahābhaiṣajya! What do you think?
Between the form of that seed and the trunk of the tree—of these two, which is greater?"
Mahābhaiṣajya replied to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It would be like comparing a small hole to empty space."
The Buddha again addressed Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Furthermore, that tree cannot be seen within the seed, nor does it arise apart from the seed.
Mahābhaiṣajya!"

Just as from that minute seed there arises a vast tree, so it is that the formless consciousness accomplishes a great physical body; because of consciousness, the physical body manifests, and the physical body cannot be seen apart from consciousness.
At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Since this consciousness is as firm and solid as a vajra, how does it come to achieve such a frail body?"
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Suppose there is a person who is so poor that he cannot support himself, yet suddenly encounters a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).

Having obtained the jewel, he takes it and makes his wish; immediately, there appear multi-storied pavilions, ponds, and terraces, city gates, moats, and high gateways surrounding them, as well as gardens where flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves grow luxuriantly, covering everything above. Furthermore, all other necessities and wealth are spontaneously manifested according to his heart's desire."
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
All those things are utterly frail; they are phenomena that quickly perish and disperse.
Then, as soon as that person's hand suddenly loses the wish-fulfilling gem, those pleasant things immediately vanish and no longer appear."
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Just as that wish-fulfilling gem cannot be destroyed even by a thousand vajras, it possesses such power that whatever one contemplates according to one's wishes will all be successfully realized."
"In this way, in this way, this consciousness is as firm as a diamond, whereas that which receives the body is not firm.
At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya again asked the World-Honored One:
"Since that consciousness is so weak, how does it destroy the firm body and migrate to that other world?"
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Suppose, for example, that a stream of water flows downward within a mountain and then pierces through the mountain to emerge on the other side.
Mahābhaiṣajya!"
"What do you think? What solidity does that water possess?
Great Medicine replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
That mountain body is as hard, firm, and solid as a diamond, yet the nature of those water drops is soft and pliant.
“It is like applying medicine to one who has been touched by a dream.”
"In this way, in this way, the essential nature of that consciousness is supple; it can break through the great body and immediately depart.
At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya again asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
Whenever any sentient being, having cast off their body and brought their life to an end within the realm of sentient beings, how do they receive the bodies of various devas?
And how do they further receive the bodies of the various realms of existence?
The Buddha said to Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Mahābhaiṣajya! Listen attentively; I shall explain this matter for you."
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Whenever sentient beings cast off their sentient body after death, they receive a new body by virtue of having performed meritorious deeds.
Having again cast off that body, their consciousness leaves the human body and perceives itself as having attained a celestial body."
Having attained the divine eye, he sees the various devas of the six desire realms and also sees the celestial palaces of those six desire realms.
He sees when that person’s body is destroyed, and he further sees the celestial gardens and groves, such as the Nandana Grove and the Vimāna Grove.
In that place, there are high thrones covered with celestial garments; everywhere there are terraces, palaces, and exquisite groves of trees, and in every spot gather beautiful jade maidens.
That consciousness perceives these things constantly adorned with flowers, which bring joy to the mind as they behold them—various necklaces, earrings, and armlets.
Then he saw a celestial youth upon the seat; both the jade maiden and the deva son looked upon him with joy.
Once that celestial youth had been born, they further beheld the birth of a celestial maiden.

When that celestial youth saw the maiden, he immediately conceived a mind of desire; having conceived a mind of desire, he attained joy; having attained joy, his entire body and mind experienced rapture; and with his mind and body filled with rapture, his physical form then transformed at that moment, becoming like the color of a lotus flower.

At the time of that person's death, they immediately attain non-perverted vision; their nose is not crooked or twisted, and their breath is not foul. That person's eyes and ears resemble the color of the blue lotus, and the limbs and joints of their body do not fall apart.

He did not shed blood, nor did he produce excrement or urine; the pores of his body were not rubbed or torn, and his nails no longer had a bluish tint, nor were his hands yellowed. His hands and feet remained motionless, neither extending nor contracting, as he passed away.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
At the time of that person's death, there are premonitory signs from the heavens; namely, they see a palanquin appearing before them.
That palanquin is adorned with thousands of pillars and hung with networks of bells, which emit a beautiful and subtle sound."
Various kinds of subtle and exquisite fragrant flowers were scattered upon it, and they emitted a wonderful and sublime fragrance.
Furthermore, various kinds of necklaces and ornaments adorned its surface.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable celestial youths who,
upon seeing this, gave rise to a heart of great joy.
Having given rise to a heart of joy, two teeth appeared upon their bodies, white and pure like the kunda flower.
He manifested his two eyes, neither too wide open nor too closed;
his voice was subtle, mournful, and beautiful;
and the soles of his two feet were like the color of a lotus.
After that corpse has passed away, its body and mind are neither cold nor hot.
The deceased person’s kinsmen do not grieve for them excessively.

When that person, according to the Dharma, is about to take up [a new] life at the time of death, at that moment the sun is just rising and there is no darkness in any direction; one clearly perceives all forms and colors.
Furthermore, excellent and wondrous fragrances from all directions will pervade and arrive.
When that person is on the verge of death, their two eyes do not close, and they experience no confusion regarding the various directions they behold.
Upon seeing the image of the Tathāgata, they immediately gain faith and give rise to a pure intention.
They further see their beloved kinsmen and embrace them with a heart of joy, as if a dead person had returned to life, or like a traveler returning from afar who comforts his kin, saying:
"O kinsmen, do not grieve, do not lament; for all who are born possess this law of separation."

"O Mahauṣadha! If those sentient beings possess powerful meritorious karma, or if they have internally generated the intention to give, their eloquence will repeatedly praise and sing of the merit of giving, or of various causes and conditions for merit."
When that person has spoken these words, his intention is to sleep; his body and mind attain peace and happiness that pervade his entire being, and he relinquishes his body and life with tranquility.
At the moment he relinquishes his body and life, he looks upward and sees the various devas sitting together upon the same couch.
Having seen them sitting together, the jade maiden places her hand upon his body.
With both hands cupped full of fragrant flowers, and having thus gathered the flowers, she says to that deva:
"Excellent, most excellent!
May there be auspiciousness; the time has come for you, O youth, who desire rebirth in heaven.
Having spoken these words, that jade maiden immediately reached for a flower with her hand, and having reached for it, she reached for it again.

At the moment of extracting the flower, those sentient beings immediately reach the end of their lives; when they relinquish the sense faculties and their common consciousness, relinquish the objects of the sense faculties, and relinquish the great elements, the four aggregates remain without a fixed substance and are formless.

It is like a person wishing to mount a horse, or like the sun-god, or like a bright jewel, or like a flame, or like the moon reflected in water, or like a magical illusion; with the body taking hold of wholesome karma, it departs as swiftly as air escaping from a tube.
As that consciousness was about to be born in that place, it saw its parents sitting upon a celestial couch because of that flower.
Seeing those two deities in union, the consciousness took form within the flower.
At that time, a subtle wind, blended with the flavor of nectar, blows forth.
Once it has arisen, that consciousness, within seven days, becomes a young deva boy wearing a celestial crown upon his head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since that consciousness has no form, by what causes and conditions is form brought to completion?”
“How is it that they appear through causes and conditions?
The Buddha said,
“Great Medicine!”

For example, when two pieces of wood are joined and rubbed against one another, fire is produced; yet that fire cannot be seen within the wood, nor can the fire be obtained apart from the wood. Furthermore, fire is not produced by a single cause alone, nor is it obtained without a cause, nor is its color visible upon the wood itself.
Because of causes, it emerges; upon emerging, it perceives forms. Yet, apart from the wood, no separate form can be found.
In this same way, Great Medicine!

That consciousness, through the union of father and mother, achieves the acquisition of a body. That consciousness is not to be seen within the body, nor does that consciousness exist apart from the body.
"Mahauṣadhi! It is like this: only after fire has emerged does one see forms; yet it is not because of its heat that forms can be seen, nor can it be said that forms are seen because of its redness."
Thus it is, Great Medicine!

That consciousness exists as "consciousness" because it has accomplished a body; yet it cannot be perceived by means of sensation (*vedanā*), nor can it be perceived by means of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
It is like the sun, whose perfect radiance shines forth with great majesty and brilliance that can be clearly seen.
Yet ordinary people do not perceive its true color; some say it is black, some say it is white, some say it is yellowish-white, and others say it is green."
"Mahābhaiṣajya!

One cannot perceive the consciousness within the body as being either black or white through physical sight; it is like the analogy of the sun, which cannot be seen by its heat or its radiance. That which can be perceived is merely its appearance and disappearance as it moves—thus should it be contemplated."
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Whenever this consciousness wishes to observe, it merely takes up its various natures.
Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the various natures of that consciousness?
The Buddha said to Mahauṣadha:
"Those natures of feeling, grasping, conditioned formations, sorrow, reflection, affliction, joy, and lack of joy."
One should contemplate the various natures of this consciousness in this manner.
Furthermore, the spiritual consciousness possesses an intrinsic nature that can be contemplated.
What is this fundamental nature?
"That which is called 'wholesome mind,' 'unwholesome mind,' and so forth, takes these as its basis.
At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Once that consciousness has departed from this body, how does it so swiftly take up birth in that new place?
Having departed from this body, before it reaches that other body at the time of taking birth, where does it abide?
"How should one contemplate this divine consciousness?
The Buddha answered Mahābhaiṣajya:

"Suppose there is a man whose arms are slender and long, and whose hands and feet, from top to bottom, are all perfectly proportioned; he mounts a subtle, exquisite, and swift steed and gallops into the midst of battle."
Having entered the ranks, he is wounded by swords, spears, bows, and arrows, and his mind becomes distressed and confused.
While within those ranks, his mind grows bewildered and faint, causing him to fall from his horse and collapse upon the ground.
That man was skilled in handling weapons; having fallen to the ground, he rose with great speed, seized his horse with his hand, and immediately mounted it.
Just as that man swiftly regained his horse upon falling, and having regained it, immediately rode it, so too did that horse swiftly attain its swiftness and swiftly carry him.
One should know that the consciousness of that deity is also like this:
just as that person, pursued by bandits and filled with terror, mounts a horse and flees with great speed.
When this consciousness first abandons the body and is about to reach that [new] state, it is likewise so.

If one is to be born in a heavenly realm, one immediately grasps at the thought of heaven; seeing the parents of the gods seated together on a single throne, and having seen them, one grasps at that object with such speed that one immediately attains rebirth.
Furthermore, Great Medicine!

Regarding your question as to where consciousness abides at the moment an ordinary person first transfers it, and what its nature should be observed to be before that consciousness has yet arrived—[I shall explain].
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
It is like a person's reflection appearing in water; although it manifests a form, it is not the actual form of a person. You should view things in this way, Mahābhaiṣajya!"
The person's shadow, with its head, feet, hands, and limbs perfectly proportioned, appears in the water at the same time as the form is produced; yet it does not give rise to such thoughts as:
"I am afflicted by heat," "I am frozen by cold," or "My body is exhausted."
That [reflection] does not have such a thought as to say:
"I am the true body, just as it was previously in the womb as a mass of flesh.
Furthermore, that reflection has no place of disturbance.
When that person’s body and shadow are reflected in the water, no sound issues forth—neither a cry of pain nor a cry of joy.
Great Medicine!
This consciousness, having departed from this body but not yet reached the next body, possesses such a form and such a nature.
"O Mahauṣadha!
Whenever a fortunate consciousness first intends to take on a celestial body, it undergoes such an experience.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahauṣadha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This consciousness desires to take birth in hell; how does it undergo [rebirth]?
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Listen attentively now as I explain for you how beings who lack merit seek rebirth in hell.
Great Medicine!

Whenever a sentient being commits unwholesome karma, they are bound by the conditions of that karma. When such a being wishes to cast off their body in this place, at the moment of casting it off, they form this thought:
"I am that very person; having cast off my body from this hell, these are my parents.
And at the moment that person casts off the body, they achieve a physical form exactly as it naturally exists.
That person’s body is manifested as its original form, and they immediately perceive their own limbs.
Yet, as soon as that person first casts off the body, they are overwhelmed by sorrow and immediately perceive various hells.
Once that consciousness has first abandoned the body and is already in that hell, it immediately accomplishes the karma of existence and immediately perceives that hell.

Or, seeing something like blood being sprinkled from another direction, it immediately gives rise to a perception of attachment; having given rise to this perception of attachment, it immediately takes on a hellish body.

That consciousness is like a body of worms produced because of low-lying, damp, foul, and rotting ground; it is like worms produced from hidden filth and decay, or like various worms produced within spoiled curd.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
It is the same for sentient beings who wish to be born in hell.
At that time, Bhadrapāla joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for those beings who are in the hells, what is the color of their bodies?
How do they receive their physical forms?”
The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who are stained by the place of blood, their bodies will take on a blood-colored hue.
If there are sentient beings who are stained by the river Vīraṇī, their bodies will immediately take on the color of clouds that are neither white nor black."
If there are sentient beings who become stained by and attached to the Ash River, their bodies will develop mottled discolorations.
Yet, the bodies of those sentient beings in that place remain soft and supple, as if they were princes being raised in comfort and ease.

Bhadrapāli! There, the sentient beings take on massive bodies, eight and a half cubits in height; their beards, whiskers, and hair are extremely long, and their feet are terrifying, pointing backward.
If there were a person from Jambudvīpa who wished to go to the hells to observe them, upon seeing those hell-beings, they would immediately die of terror.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāli!
"Although the sentient beings in the hells have food, they possess not even a moment of happiness.
At that time, Mahauṣadha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When those sentient beings eat, what food do they have?
The Buddha replied to the Bodhisattva Mahābhaiṣajya, saying: "Mahābhaiṣajya!"
While those beings are wandering through the hells, they see from afar something red—either molten copper or molten brass—and having seen it, they cry out to one another: "Alas!..."
"O virtuous ones, who desires food?
Come here and eat together.
Having heard these words, they gathered in one place; having approached the hall where molten copper was being prepared, they stood there and, seeking food, opened their mouths to eat.
Furthermore, that molten copper and brass, blazing and emitting light, produce such sounds as "tata-tata" as they enter their mouths and burn their entire bodies.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Those sentient beings undergo such miserable conditions for the sake of food.
Furthermore, Mahābhaiṣajya!"

At that time, the consciousness of those sentient beings within that hell resides solely within their skeletal remains; their consciousness does not depart from the bones, and because their consciousness does not depart from the bones, they do not undergo death.
Nevertheless, those beings remain afflicted by hunger, and there is no food to be found there.

In that place, there are exquisite groves; with their eyes they see various flowers and fruits, and various trees lush and deep green, as well as vast, exquisite regions covered with soft green grass.
Seeing such a garden and place so exquisite, they each rejoiced with smiles; each gave rise to a thought and called out to one another: "O you people!..."
"Such gardens and groves are exquisite and provide sublime pleasure, and there is also a cool, refreshing breeze.
Having heard and seen this, they quickly gathered together and entered those gardens and groves.

Having entered, they experience pleasure for a short time; however, all the flowers, fruits, and leaves upon those trees then turn entirely into iron, and those sentient beings have their bodies split and torn apart by those iron branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
When those sentient beings in that hell have their bodies split open like bamboo roots by the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, they cry out loudly and run about in every direction.

At such a time, there appear behind them various henchmen of King Yama, holding sharp axes or great iron clubs; their eyes are terrifying, their teeth are extremely sharp, and their hair is ablaze with fire. The flames are high and vast, burning their entire bodies as they hold various kinds of weapons and staves in their hands.
The sinners are born according to their karma, and that person pursues them from behind, shouting these words:
"People, stop! Stop! Do not run away.
This grove was created by your own karma; why do you flee in such distress instead of experiencing this retribution here?"
"O Mahauṣadha! You should contemplate those sentient beings in hell as undergoing such suffering and affliction in this way.
Furthermore, O Mahauṣadha!"
After seven days have passed, those in the hells undergo the sufferings of hell in their entirety, just as bees gather nectar from flowers to produce honey. Why is this?
Because it is formed through the various causes of existence (*bhava*); consciousness (*vijñāna*) first begins to receive and take upon itself the various sufferings of hell.
Yet that consciousness, when first leaving the body, lacks autonomy; oppressed by various sufferings, it finds no joy in its heart.
Upon first seeing the great darkness and arriving at that place, it is as if a person were being driven and dragged away by bandits, thinking to itself: "Alas!"
For what reason do I now abandon this exquisite Jambudvīpa and forsake my beloved kin and companions to proceed with such haste toward hell?
I no longer see the path to the heavens.
At that time, like a silkworm entangled in its own silk, it swiftly seeks a place of rebirth.
Lacking autonomy and bound by karma, it is unable to remain still.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Those sentient beings in the hells have such causes and conditions that they undergo such various sufferings and afflictions.
At that time, having heard these words, Prince Mahābhaiṣajya and the merchant’s son Bhadrapāli’s hair stood on end; with palms joined, they took refuge in the Buddha.
The Prince Mahauṣadha and the others made this aspiration upon generating the mind of enlightenment:

"By virtue of these causes and conditions of hearing the Dharma, while within the cycle of birth and death amidst the afflictions, may we never be born in the evil realms, and may we never undergo the sufferings of hell."
At that time, Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I wish to ask the Buddha further about the doubts that have long resided in my mind."
The Buddha said: "Bhadrapāli!
Ask whatever you doubt; let your mind question freely."
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called a ‘collection’ (rāśi), and what is called an ‘accumulation’ (caya)?”
"What is called the aggregates (skandha)?
What is called shifting?
The Buddha said:
"Bhadrapāli! There are four kinds of dharmadhātus that bring this body into existence. What are these four?
The conjunction of the various elements (*dhātu*), the perception by wisdom and the mental faculty, ignorance, and the consciousness of various objects—
this is the general meaning, which I have already explained.
"Aggregation" refers to the six elements and the various spheres of entry.
Within the six elements, three are coarse:
first, the sense bases (*āyatana*), which further comprise two kinds of grasping.

Internally, there are hair of the head, beard, and mustache; various body hairs, skin, flesh, pus, blood, mucus, saliva, and fat; the five viscera; the hands, feet, head, face, and the various limbs and joints. Because these are combined together, they are termed an "aggregate" (*rāśi*).
For example, just as various grains—whether sesame, wheat, barley, beans, or peas—are called a "heap" because they are gathered together;
in the same way, this body is called a "heap" because it is a gathering of bodily parts, limbs, and joints.
Regarding the six elements, what are the six?
First, the earth element; second, the water element; third, the fire element; fourth, the wind element; fifth, the space element; and sixth, the consciousness element.
Regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), what are the six?
First, the eye; second, the ear; third, the nose; fourth, the tongue; fifth, the body; sixth, the mind.
Regarding the objects of the six sense bases, what are the six?
First, form; second, sound; third, fragrance; fourth, flavor; fifth, touch; sixth, mental phenomena (*dharma*).
These are called the objective spheres of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana-viṣaya*).
As for what is said regarding the three fundamental natures of all coarse elements (*sthūla-dhātu*), which three are they?
First is desire, second is hatred, and third is delusion.
Their arousal is threefold; what are these three?
First is wind, second is phlegm (pitta), and third is mucus and saliva.
Regarding what is called "grasping at the sense bases," there are two types. What are these two?
First is the observance of precepts; second is faith.
Furthermore, there are six types. What are these six?
First is giving, second is wealth, third is diligence, fourth is meditative concentration, fifth is the wholesome, and sixth is the unwholesome.
Regarding the term "aggregates" (skandha), why are they called aggregates?
First is feeling (vedanā), second is perception (saṃjñā), third is formations (saṃskāra), and fourth is consciousness (vijñāna);
these four aggregates are formless.
What is called "feeling" is the act of experiencing.
What is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is the cognition that distinguishes between pleasure and pain.
What are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*) are seeing, hearing, touching, and feeling.
This is named "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); it acts as the master of the body, attaining sovereignty because it exercises mastery over all things.
Regarding the term "transference" (*saṃkrānti*): it refers to one who has successfully accomplished the pure precepts of bodily, verbal, and mental action.

At the time of death, when the faculties and life-force are withdrawn, at that moment that consciousness abandons the aggregates and no longer undergoes rebirth; because it does not return and experiences exclusively bliss, it is called "transference."
This is what is called "shifting.
To be free from this is not called "having shifting."
"Such sequential distinctions are not called 'transference.
Having spoken these words, Bhadrapāla and the Bodhisattva Mahābhaiṣajya prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have skillfully expounded such a meaning for my sake—the truth of omniscience.
World-Honored One!”
"In future ages, this Dharma gate shall provide benefit and nourishment for all deluded and ignorant sentient beings.
The Buddha replied to those two persons, saying, "Bhadrapāli!"
These Tathāgatas, who possess wisdom, are free from falsehood; yet those who are not omniscient cannot know this true essence.
In the past, I practiced immeasurable asceticism to cultivate the radiance of this wisdom, and what I have spoken today is no different from that.

This is the Dharma of the Light of Wisdom, which spreads forth from its own place; it is taught by the Ocean-Treasury of All-Knowledge for the sake of transforming and guiding all sentient beings through its merit and renown.

In whatever place it is located and in whatever place it is taught, that place shall be protected by non-humans, as well as by devas, asuras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others who come to protect that location.
"By prostrating there, one shall be free from all terrors; officials shall be unable to do evil, and bandits shall be unable to cause harm.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus! You all..."

If you know that from this time forward, this Dharma-gate must not be spoken to those who lack faith; it must not be spoken to those who seek out faults; it must not be spoken to outsiders such as the Nirgranthas; it must not be spoken to the disciples of the Nirgranthas; it must not be spoken to those dwelling in forest hermitages or empty, secluded places; and it must not be spoken to those who do not request it with a sincere heart.
Why is this? It is because they might seek out faults;
yet the Tathāgata is truly without fault.

If there are ordained bhikṣus or lay householders who believe in, accept, and follow this matter, one should accord with those people and arouse a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward them exactly as one would toward the Tathāgata.
"One should give rise to such a thought: 'This person upholds the treasury of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Because one has resolved to leave the home life, One ought to practice the Buddha-dharma."
Having subdued the hosts of Māra, like an elephant destroying a bamboo hut,
if one can practice this Dharma, being heedful of matters of negligence,
extinguishing the afflictions of birth and death, one shall bring all suffering to an end.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the elder’s son Bhadrapāla, the bodhisattva Prince Mahauṣadha, the great assembly of bhikṣus, and the devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 111, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty. Chapter 40:
The Assembly of the Faithful Maiden Viśuddhaśraddhā. Chapter Forty: The Assembly of the Faithful Maiden Viśuddhaśraddhā.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

All of them were renowned throughout the world, had attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, were fully endowed with the various patiences, had subdued Māra and his enemies, and had realized the dharmas attained by all Tathāgatas.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Sustaining the World, Bodhisattva Sustaining the Path, Bodhisattva Sustaining the Earth, Bodhisattva Sustaining the Great Earth, Bodhisattva Delighting in Wisdom, Bodhisattva Causing Faith and Joy, Bodhisattva Adorned with Sublime Color, Bodhisattva Jewel Flame, Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, Bodhisattva Jewel Thought, Bodhisattva Jewel Abode, Bodhisattva Jewel Wisdom, Bodhisattva Jewel Virtue, and Bodhisattva Jewel Light; there were also the various bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, with Bodhisattva Maitreya as their leader.
Furthermore, there were sixty bodhisattvas with incomparable minds, with Mañjuśrī as their leader.
There were also sixteen great beings, with Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva as their leader.

Furthermore, twenty thousand devaputras from Tuṣita were present in the assembly. At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon a lion throne of great majestic adornment, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands.

His radiance shone brilliantly like the sun and moon; his majesty and virtue were preeminent like those of Śakra and Brahmā; he rose high above the crowd like Mount Sumeru; his blazing splendor was as fierce as a great torch; his gaze was calm and composed like that of a great elephant king; his preaching of the Dharma was fearless like the roar of a lion; and he overshadowed the entire assembly like Rāhula, the lord of stars. Adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, his majestic light blazed intensely. Emitting a Brahma-voice that filled the trichiliocosm, he preached the Dharma within the great assembly, desiring to awaken all sentient beings and cause them to dwell securely in the definitive, supreme meaning.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a beloved daughter named Śraddhā, who was of tender age and possessed a countenance so upright and majestic that she was a joy for all sentient beings to behold.

Having planted roots of goodness in past lives and cultivated the Mahāyāna, she was surrounded by five hundred young maidens, each holding a golden garland; they departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jeta Grove.

Arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side. He then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Having long accumulated pure karma of merit and goodness, Fulfilling an ocean of boundless virtues, Causing all beings to have faith, delight, and joy— Therefore, I prostrate to the Honored Muni.”
Manifesting a majestic radiance of wondrous appearance, Revealing the gateway to the Dharma, the treasury of all jewels;
With a bodily light shining one fathom in every direction, I pay homage to the Great Wisdom, the Cool Lake.
A great tree of merit with inexhaustible blessings, most honored among men and praised by the world;
since your original vows and precepts are already perfected, I prostrate to you, the Honored One worthy of offerings.
Abiding securely in the sublime Dharma, ever serene, With an impartial mind toward the world as toward an only child,
Possessing wisdom and skillful means to understand all conditioned phenomena, He shows the level path like a skilled guide.

If there are those who are firm and courageous, Who bring benefit to all classes of sentient beings through compassion— Such bodhisattvas practice correctly; I pray that the Tathāgata will explain this for them.
How shall one attain firm strength to dwell securely within birth and death and subdue the hosts of Māra?
How shall one attain the Dharma of equality?
And how shall one bring all sentient beings to maturity?
How is it that you are like the earth, like space, And likewise like wind, water, and fire?
How do you attain faith and abide in the Dharma, Like Mount Sumeru or the lion king?
How does one distance oneself from love and hate, With a pure mind, upright and free from flattery?
How does one give rise to generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, Vigor, meditative concentration, and liberation?
How does wisdom shatter the darkness of all afflictions, While always abiding securely in great skillful means?
Samādhi, dhāraṇī, and unimpeded eloquence— Abiding in the four immeasurables and the five supernormal powers?
How can one stand before all Buddhas, Constantly receiving birth by transformation and knowing past lives?
Practicing *dhūta* and dwelling in non-contention within the forest hermitage, you have tamed your mind and extinguished the afflictions;
upholding the precepts and cultivating the path to enlightenment, you have realized the extinction of the nectar-like *nirvāṇa* and subdued the demonic enemies.
Bestowing peace and happiness upon all beings, you turn the wheel of Dharma—such a true path, we pray, you will proclaim.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the young girl Viśuddhaśraddhā, saying:
"If a bodhisattva can accomplish eight powers, they will be firm and courageous amidst birth and death, remaining free from weariness."

What are the eight? First, the power of aspiration, because it is free from flattery and deception; second, the power of resolute conviction, because it is detached from all evils; third, the power of application, because it constantly cultivates the wholesome; fourth, the power of pure faith, because it deeply believes in the retribution of karma; fifth, the power of the bodhicitta, because it does not seek the Lesser Vehicle; sixth, the power of great loving-kindness, because it does not harm sentient beings; seventh, the power of great compassion, because it is able to endure all evils; eighth, the power of virtuous friends, because they provide timely admonitions.
"O maiden! These are called the eight powers.
Because a bodhisattva accomplishes such powers, they are firm and courageous, remaining unstained by anything within the cycle of birth and death."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"With a mind of courageous resolve, free from all flattery and deception, always acting with integrity,
one correctly advances toward Bodhi."
By the power of resolute conviction, one distances oneself from all evils and purely cultivates wholesome conduct, abiding in right effort.
With the full complement of application, constantly observing with skill, one’s diligence is firm and steadfast as one brings peace and happiness to sentient beings.
By the power of pure faith, one thoroughly understands karmic retribution; through faith in the Buddha’s wisdom, one gathers and sustains the world.
By the power of the bodhicitta, one remains far removed from the Lesser Vehicle, never severing the lineage of the Buddhas, and abides securely in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
By the power of great loving-kindness, they regard all sentient beings with equanimity; without love or hatred, they give rise to neither anger nor harm.
By the power of great compassion, they endure all evils; unstained by birth and death, they feel no weariness or exhaustion.
Through the power of virtuous friends, they are constantly alerted and awakened; their minds do not regress or sink, but dwell securely in bodhi.
Those who exert themselves with vigor, having attained these eight powers, shall sit at the site of enlightenment and destroy the hosts of Māra.
"Furthermore, maiden!
By accomplishing eight qualities, a bodhisattva abides in equanimity.
What are these eight?

First, the equality of all sentient beings, because they are fundamentally without self; second, the equality of all phenomena, because all dharmas are quiescent; third, the equality of all lands, because they enter the realm of emptiness; fourth, the equality of all wisdoms, because they preach the Dharma with equanimity; fifth, the equality of all practices, because causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature; sixth, the equality of all vehicles, because they are equally unconditioned; seventh, the equality of the mind, because the mind is like an illusion; eighth, the equality of all Māras, because afflictions, being primary, are ultimately ungraspable.
"These are the eight dharmas that abide in equanimity.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Sentient beings are fundamentally without self; In every thought-moment, nothing can be apprehended."
One who dwells in equanimity should contemplate in this way:
all phenomena are equal, their intrinsic nature eternally empty and still;
though words involve conceptual distinctions, all dharmas are fundamentally without difference.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, No boundaries can be found;
Their nature is like empty space, And the Buddha-lands are eternally equal.
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time Dwell in the equality of the Dharma-realm.
Boundless wisdom and liberation—every Buddha is thus.
Sentient beings are fundamentally dependent origination; all are equal.
Skillfully knowing their conduct, he brings them to awakening as is appropriate.
Sentient beings are of various kinds; One understands them to be like illusions and transformations.
Internally and externally there is nothing to be grasped; Their intrinsic nature is eternally pure.
The various vehicles are taught in diverse ways, Yet the unconditioned nature is equal.
The Teacher, through skillful means, distinguishes and teaches the three vehicles.
Though he appears to dwell amidst the demons of affliction, afflictions are non-existent;
likewise, the celestial demons, the aggregates, and death—all objective realms—are entirely empty.
"Furthermore, maiden!
By accomplishing eight kinds of dharmas, a bodhisattva is free from all hatred and attachment.
What are these eight?

First, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, constantly practicing what is beneficial; fourth, being unstained by worldly dharmas; fifth, not being attached to one's own person; sixth, constantly cultivating a concentrated mind; seventh, relinquishing body and life; eighth, observing the afflictions.
"By practicing these eight dharmas, one can become free from hatred and attachment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Robed firmly in the armor of loving-kindness, Compassionately grieving for all beings,"
Abiding in a mind of equanimity, one gives rise to neither hatred nor attachment.
The wise person acts for the benefit of others, constantly bestowing peace and happiness upon them;
when gaining profit, they do not become arrogant, and when slighted or reviled, they harbor no resentment.
Unmoved by the eight winds, one gives rise to neither hatred nor attachment.
Toward oneself as toward others, one does not conceive thoughts of hatred or attachment;
having relinquished all such perceptions, one remains unattached to any sensory realm.
Constantly observing one's own body, one does not begrudge even life itself;
the wise person remains unmoved by suffering or pleasure, like empty space.
Skillfully examining the afflictions, they are free from both "I" and "mine."
Maintaining conduct ever like the earth, one gives rise to neither hatred nor attachment. Furthermore, maiden,
because a bodhisattva accomplishes eight qualities, they experience no weariness within the cycle of birth and death.

What are the eight? First, because their roots of goodness are vast; second, because they observe sentient beings; third, because they always see the Buddhas and cultivate offerings; fourth, because they perceive immeasurable Buddha-fields; fifth, because they constantly seek the wisdom of the Buddhas; sixth, because they understand that birth and death are like a dream; seventh, because they have no timidity regarding the sublime Dharma; and eighth, because they observe the past and the future as being identical to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If there are those who practice the Way, Cultivating goodness free from blemish or stain,
Pure as the moon in the sky, They deliver suffering sentient beings."
Because they encompass all merits, they never grow weary in the cycle of birth and death.
Observing the nature of sentient beings, they practice diligence with steadfast resolve;
throughout immeasurable Buddha-fields, they reverently make offerings to the Buddhas.
Therefore, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, Is never weary throughout birth and death.
Throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, He proclaims the inconceivable Dharma, Ensuring that the seeds of the Triple Gem are not severed; He shall surely become a King of Dharma.
Those who steadfastly maintain the prohibitive precepts feel no weariness in the cycle of birth and death.
Having realized the nature of birth and death to be like a dream, a cloud, or a flash of lightning,
they attain liberation from all phenomena and feel no weariness in the cycle of birth and death.
Abiding securely in bodhi, with a joyful mind always serene,
they cross to the shore of skillful means without weariness amidst birth and death;
constantly cultivating the sublime Dharma, they wax like the moon in the sky.
Delighting in the Buddha’s virtues, one never tires amidst birth and death.
Though birth and death are boundless, one abides eternally in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
through the union of wisdom in a single thought-moment, one never tires amidst birth and death.
"Furthermore, maiden!
One accomplishes the equality of the mental realm by means of eight dharmas. What are these eight?

First, the mind is like the earth; second, the mind is like water; third, the mind is like fire; fourth, the mind is like wind; fifth, the mind is like space; sixth, the mind is equal to the dharma-realm; seventh, the mind is equal to liberation; eighth, the mind is equal to nirvana.
"This is called the eightfold equality of the mind-realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The equal mind is like the earth, bearing all things; toward both good and evil,"
Without increase or decrease, their equanimity is like water: it washes away all defilements, nurtures the world, and removes the thirst of afflictions.
The equanimous mind is like fire, burning away and extinguishing afflictions; it is a great torch of radiance that leaves nothing unincinerated.
The equanimous mind is like the wind, having no fixed place and no dependence; it wafts the fragrance of precepts and learning, flowing throughout the three periods of time.
With a mind equal like space, free from views and pure, they enter everywhere yet do not follow Māra.
With a mind equal to the Dharma-realm, they dwell securely in well-attained stability; neither increasing nor decreasing, they always enter into equanimity.
The liberation attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas involves neither one who is bound nor one who is liberated.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa have no coming and no going; abiding in tranquility, they roam throughout the three periods of time.
"Furthermore, young woman!
There are eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the birth of bodhi.
What are these eight?

First, giving gives rise to [the state of] relinquishing all modes of existence; second, ethical discipline gives rise to being free from transgressions; third, patience gives rise to being free from malice; fourth, diligence gives rise to being free from indolence and retreat; fifth, meditative concentration gives rise to the practice of skillful means; sixth, wisdom gives rise to upholding the precepts and extensive learning; seventh, the Brahma-abodes give rise to liberation and tranquility; eighth, the supernormal powers give rise to constant abiding in meditative absorption.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Those who constantly practice giving, Free themselves from all greed and the torment of feverish affliction;
Without seeking karmic rewards, They dedicate their merit toward the Bodhi of the Buddha.”
Observing the precepts constitutes the Great Vehicle; though limbs may be severed, one remains free from anger and resentment.
Aiming for the attainment of great peace and bliss, one eliminates habitual tendencies to realize true cessation.
The Bodhisattva practices diligence, acting for the sake of sentient beings throughout many eons.
Enduring suffering while wandering through the world, his power of diligence increases.
The practitioner of meditative concentration remains far removed from all conceptual proliferation;
having reached the further shore of the dhyānas, he is not reborn according to those states of absorption.
Great wisdom is peerless, forever free from all extreme views;
realizing that the world is empty and quiescent, the darkness of delusion is extinguished without remainder.
Cultivating the Brahma-abodes in tranquility, one purifies all evil realms.
Constantly serving as Śakra and Brahmā, he diligently cultivates all that is meaningful and beneficial.
With supernormal powers, he travels through Buddha-fields, attending upon Buddhas to hear the Dharma.
Skillfully knowing the dispositions and desires of all beings, he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
"Furthermore, maiden!
By accomplishing eight kinds of dharmas, a bodhisattva attains dhāraṇī and unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
What are these eight?

First, out of respect for the Dharma; second, out of service to one's preceptors and ācāryas; third, out of seeking the Dharma without weariness; fourth, out of expounding the teachings as they have been heard; fifth, out of not being stingy with the Dharma; sixth, out of not proclaiming the faults of others; seventh, out of loving and revering the Dharma teacher as one does a preceptor; and eighth, out of not seeing the transgressions of others and encouraging them to leave such transgressions behind.
"These are called the eight dharmas; when a bodhisattva accomplishes and fulfills them, they possess total retention (*dhāraṇī*) and unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Always seeking the Dharma with a resolute mind, Serving one's teacher and associating with virtuous friends,"
Staying far away from evil associates, one attains the mastery of the inexhaustible treasury.
Never weary of extensive learning, one courageously and diligently seeks the Dharma;
expounding it just as it was heard, one does not crave gain or offerings.
Attaining pure eloquence,
they joyfully practice the gift of Dharma; Far removed from stinginess and envy,
they practice the Dharma without attachment, And thereby obtain dhāraṇīs.
Guarding the precepts and observing oneself, Not seeking out the faults of others,
Taking compassion as one's reliance, And speaking words that are not untimely—
One shall attain unimpeded eloquence.
"Regarding those who preach the well-spoken Dharma, one should love and respect them as if they were teachers;
by concealing their faults and encouraging them to leave evil behind, one attains the retention of an inexhaustible ocean.
Furthermore, young woman!"
Because Bodhisattvas accomplish eight dharmas, they are born by transformation upon lotus flowers in the presence of all Buddhas.

What are these eight? First, not to speak of the faults of others even at the cost of one's life; second, to exhort and transform sentient beings so that they take refuge in the Triple Gem; third, to establish all beings in the bodhicitta; fourth, to maintain pure conduct free from defilement; fifth, to fashion images of the Buddha and place them upon lotus seats; sixth, to cause sentient beings who are afflicted by sorrow and distress to have their afflictions removed; seventh, to always remain humble before those who are arrogant; and eighth, not to trouble or vex others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Even if suffering should oppress the body, One shall never speak of the faults of others;
Constantly praising the Triple Gem, One will be born by transformation before all Buddhas."
Exhorting others to resolve for Bodhicitta, Causing them to seek all-encompassing wisdom,
Constantly practicing the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), They are born through transformation before all Buddhas.
Adorning Buddha-images with gold, Seated upon precious lotus thrones.
Dispelling the grief and affliction of sentient beings, they are born by transformation before all Buddhas.
Toward those who are arrogant, they remain humble like a disciple;
not causing others to feel distress, they are born by transformation before all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, young woman!
There are eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the merit of *dhūta* practices and constantly delights in dwelling in an *āraṇya*.
What are these eight?

First, having few desires; second, being content; third, fulfilling wholesome dharmas; fourth, nourishing oneself with what is wholesome; fifth, constantly maintaining the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*); sixth, seeing the perils of birth and death and always feeling weary of and detached from them; seventh, constantly contemplating impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; eighth, possessing deep and firm faith that does not follow the teachings of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Having few desires and being content, remaining heedful, Taking joy in the Dharma and various virtues as one's sustenance,
Delighting in constantly practicing the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), And seeing the perils of birth and death, giving rise to a mind of fear."
Therefore, one should always delight in practicing the dhūtas, like the single horn of a rhinoceros, solitary and without companion.
Conditioned phenomena are suffering and without self; with a mind of wisdom and deep faith, one abides in right diligence.
Seeing for oneself the nature of the Dharma, one does not follow others; dwelling constantly in empty seclusion is praised by the Buddha.
The dhūta practitioner dwells in seclusion, free from affliction and distress;
Devoid of all disputes and manifold faults, Having distanced himself from kin and severed praise, He thus delights in dwelling in an araṇya.
"Furthermore, young woman!
By accomplishing eight kinds of dharmas, a bodhisattva subdues the enmity of Māra.
What are these eight?

First, entering into the emptiness of nature; second, having faith in signlessness; third, having faith in wishlessness; fourth, thoroughly understanding non-action; fifth, being free from internal doubt; sixth, exercising patience toward the non-arising of phenomena; seventh, decisively realizing the absence of intrinsic nature; eighth, skillfully observing all dharmas without violating suchness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“In emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, One attains the three liberations and subdues the enemy Māra.
In the conditioned and the unconditioned, there are no dualistic marks; Realizing non-arising, one attains liberation.”
Those who possess such patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena subdue all demonic adversaries.
Within this state of neither arising nor ceasing, the aggregates and elements are selfless, like an illusion;
having definitively realized that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they do not deviate from suchness through skillful means.
To differentiate between phenomena is the work of Māra; by abandoning differentiation, one subdues Māra.
Practicing both wisdom and skillful means, abiding neither in existence nor in emptiness, one cultivates such a sublime Dharma and attains a wondrous form-body through excellent skillful means.
"Furthermore, maiden!
Because a bodhisattva accomplishes eight kinds of dharmas, they do not depart from bodhi.
What are these eight?
First is right view, because it brings to maturity those sentient beings with wrong views;
second is right mindfulness, because it feels compassion for those sentient beings with wrong thoughts;
third is right speech, because it takes pity on all forms of wrong speech.
Fourth is right action, because it subsumes all wrong actions;
fifth is right effort, because it delivers those who exert themselves wrongly;
sixth is right livelihood, because it does not abandon sentient beings who lead wrong livelihoods.
"Seventh is right intention, because it causes one to leave behind wrong intention;
eighth is right concentration, because it gives rise to and advances those who possess wrong concentration.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Those who have accomplished right view transform all those with wrong views;
constantly practicing right mindfulness, they take pity on those with wrong mindfulness;
speaking pure and correct words, they compassionately regard those with wrong speech."
Abiding securely in right action, they gather in those of wrong action;
constantly practicing right effort, they do not abandon those of wrong effort;
corresponding with right livelihood, they gather in those of wrong livelihood.
The wise one rightly reflects and compassionately pities those of wrong reflection;
ever abiding in right concentration, they gather in those of wrong concentration.
By means of the unsurpassed Eightfold Noble Path, they cross the turbulent flood in safety.
Furthermore, crossing over those who drift is the path of Great Bodhi.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cross over themselves alone with grass rafts;
the Bodhisattva carries others across extensively, like a great master mariner.
"Furthermore, maiden!
By accomplishing eight kinds of dharmas, a bodhisattva realizes the path to the deathless (amṛta). What are these eight?

First, dwelling in the dharma of non-contention; second, skillfully guarding the unobstructed mind; third, constantly contemplating the meaning of reality as it is; fourth, dwelling in the bodhicitta and practicing the six recollections; fifth, diligently practicing the various pāramitās; sixth, accumulating roots of goodness and maturing sentient beings; seventh, dwelling in great compassion and embracing the true dharma; eighth, attaining the stage of non-arising and abiding in non-retrogression.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Constantly cultivate the practice of non-contention, Abide in the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa,
Distance yourself from the fault of anger, And accumulate all roots of goodness."
Skillfully contemplating the meaning of reality as it is, One attains all inexhaustible eloquence;
Abiding securely in the bodhicitta, One constantly dwells in non-thought.
In all the pāramitās, One practices with diligence, never regressing.
Having attained the power of various skillful means, one thereby delivers sentient beings.
Able to bestow the wealth of the Dharma King upon all with a compassionate heart,
one swiftly realizes the patience of non-arising and does not regress from bodhi.
"If one can practice in this way, the Buddha-dharma will not be difficult to attain;
before long, one shall subdue the hosts of Māra and realize supreme Bodhi.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the maiden Viśuddhaśraddhā was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By maturing how many dharmas can one transform the female body?
The Buddha told the girl:
"If one accomplishes eight dharmas, one shall transform the female body.
What are these eight? First, freedom from envy;

second, freedom from stinginess; third, freedom from flattery; fourth, freedom from anger; fifth, truthful speech; sixth, freedom from harsh words; seventh, relinquishing greedy desire; eighth, being free from all false views."
"O maiden! By practicing these eight dharmas, you shall swiftly transform your female body.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Do not envy others; being free from stinginess, always delight in the Dharma.
Do not practice flattery or deception, and feel weary of the female body.
With a mind of loving-kindness, abandon anger, and constantly cultivate truthful speech."
Abandoning greed and leaving harsh speech behind, dwell securely within right view.
If you loathe the female body, you should practice this Dharma;
then you shall swiftly undergo transformation and receive the body of a virtuous man.
"Furthermore, maiden!
By accomplishing eight dharmas, one can transform the female body. What are these eight?

First, to revere the Buddha and take profound delight in the Dharma; second, to respect and make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess ethical discipline, patience, and extensive learning; third, to give rise to no attachment toward husbands, sons, daughters, or one’s household; fourth, to uphold the prohibitive precepts without any transgression; fifth, to give rise to no improper thoughts toward any person; sixth, to cultivate a superior resolve that brings weary detachment from the female body; seventh, to abide in the bodhicitta and the qualities of a mahāsattva; and eighth, to contemplate the family business as being like an illusion or a dream.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Revering the Buddha and deeply delighting in the Dharma, Honoring the precepts and extensive learning,
Without giving rise to thoughts of greed or attachment— The female body shall swiftly be transformed."
Maintaining the precepts with a sense of shame and remorse, not harboring improper thoughts of others,
dwelling securely in the bodhicitta, and taking no pleasure in the vehicles of other paths—
by these means, one can swiftly transform this impure female body.
With superior resolve, one attains a mind of disenchantment; all things are like illusions.
All phenomena are fundamentally unmoving, for their nature is empty and quiescent through causes and conditions.
By diligently practicing the Dharma as it truly is, one swiftly attains the body of a Great Man.

At that time, the young girl Viśuddhaśraddhā scattered the golden garland she held over the Buddha; it transformed in mid-air into a palace and pavilion of pure gold, within which a manifested Tathāgata sat upon a golden throne.

At that time, the five hundred young maidens each removed their personal ornaments and scattered them over the Buddha; they also transformed into golden pavilions in mid-air, adorned with various precious canopies and parasols.
At that time, the five hundred young girls, having witnessed this great supernatural manifestation, spoke these verses with one voice:
“The World-Honored One is the most supreme among men; Out of compassion, he benefits all sentient beings.
We have now resolved to attain Bodhicitta; With our aspirations and joys in accord, we abide in self-mastery.”
As the Teacher of the World who bestows peace and bliss, I shall make offerings to the Honored One among Men.
Having heard the Dharma, we are now free from the dust and defilements; we no longer harbor any doubts.
Only by leaving behind this female body and its manifold pollutions shall we forever shatter afflictions and subdue the enemy Mara.
To the immeasurable koṭis of Buddhas throughout the ten directions, I shall always joyfully make offerings;
abiding securely in generosity and precepts, exerting diligent effort, with patience and meditative concentration skillfully taming the mind,
and employing wisdom and skillful means to gather in sentient beings, I shall realize the path of supreme bodhi.
Benefiting immeasurable multitudes of humans and devas, Causing them all to give rise to the Mahāyāna mind, We shall be able to let out the lion’s roar; We shall become teachers of humans and devas.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a smile. According to the constant law of all Buddhas, rays of light of various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, and crystal-like—issued from the Buddha’s mouth, illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds up to the Brahma realm. They circled the Buddha three times and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what cause and by what condition do you manifest this smile?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see the girl Śraddhā? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, I have seen it,” he replied. The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
