When the lifespans of these five hundred maidens, including Śraddhā, come to an end, they shall cast off their female bodies and be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where they will serve and make offerings to Maitreya, the World-Honored One, and to all the Tathāgatas of the Bhadrakalpa.
After eighty-four thousand koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, this girl of pure faith shall become a buddha in the world-system called Lightning Radiance, named King Adorned with Light Tathāgata.
The eon is named Constant Light.

The lifespan of that Buddha is twelve thousand years, as measured by the gods of Tuṣita Heaven. His land consists exclusively of a retinue of immeasurable and boundless great bodhisattvas, among whom these five hundred maidens are the foremost;
they are just as my sixty bodhisattvas are now, with Mañjuśrī as their leader.

Ānanda! If there are women who hear this sutra, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, they shall not undergo another female body after this life ends, and will swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the five hundred maidens, including Pure Faith, as well as all the devas, humans, and asuras in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

41. The Forty-first Assembly on the Eight Dharmas, from the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*: The Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as ten thousand bodhisattvas mahāsattvas and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain matter; I wonder if the World-Honored One would grant me permission to do so?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: "Maitreya!"
"Ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha whatever you desire in your mind; I shall analyze and explain it for you, so as to bring joy to your heart.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Thus it is, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear this.

How many dharmas must bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish so that they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, do not fall back or turn away from the dharma of supreme progress, subdue all demonic adversaries while practicing the bodhisattva conduct, know the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are, and have no weariness of mind toward any world? Because their minds are unwearied, they do not rely on the knowledge of others, but swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!”
"It is well that you are now able to ask the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning.
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
"You should now listen with single-minded attention; I shall analyze and explain this profound meaning for you."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so; I wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: “Maitreya!

If bodhisattva mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish eight dharmas, they shall not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they shall neither regress nor turn back from the dharma of supreme progress; while practicing the bodhisattva conduct, they shall subdue all māras, enemies, and adversaries; they shall know the self-nature and characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are; their minds shall not grow weary regarding the various worlds; and because their minds do not grow weary, they shall not rely on the wisdom of others, but shall swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these eight?
Maitreya! They are:

that which consists in the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ accomplishment of the profound mind, accomplishment of the mind of practice, accomplishment of the mind of relinquishment, accomplishment of the mind that skillfully knows the means of dedication, accomplishment of the mind of great loving-kindness, accomplishment of the mind of great compassion, accomplishment of skillful knowledge of means, and accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Maitreya! How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the profound mind? Maitreya!”
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha, their minds remain ultimately firm and unshakable regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
upon hearing praise or disparagement of the Dharma, their minds remain ultimately firm and unshakable regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and upon hearing praise or disparagement of the Saṅgha, their minds remain ultimately firm and unshakable regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the profound mind. Maitreya!"
"How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind of practice? Maitreya!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas distance themselves from killing, distance themselves from stealing, distance themselves from sexual misconduct, distance themselves from false speech, distance themselves from divisive speech, distance themselves from harsh speech, and distance themselves from frivolous speech, Maitreya!"
In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the mind of practice.
"Maitreya! How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind of relinquishment?"

Maitreya! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are masters of relinquishment and donors who give to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, to the poor, beggars, and those of low station, as well as whatever is required such as clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for the sick—Maitreya!
In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately achieve a mind of equanimity.
"Maitreya! How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve a mind that skillfully understands the method of dedication?"
Maitreya! If all the roots of goodness cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— namely, the actions of body,
speech, and mind— are entirely dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Maitreya!
In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately achieve a mind that thoroughly understands the skillful means of dedication.
"Maitreya! How do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve a mind of great loving-kindness?"

Maitreya! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished the bodily action of great loving-kindness, ultimately accomplished the verbal action of great loving-kindness, and ultimately accomplished the mental action of great loving-kindness, Maitreya!
In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the mind of great loving-kindness.
"Maitreya! How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the mind of great compassion?"

Maitreya! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished irreproachable bodily action, have ultimately accomplished irreproachable verbal action, and have ultimately accomplished irreproachable mental action, Maitreya!
In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the mind of great compassion.
"Maitreya, how do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish skillful knowledge of expedient means?"
Maitreya! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are well-versed in the conventional truth, well-versed in the ultimate truth, and well-versed in both truths, Maitreya!
In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ultimately accomplished the skillful knowledge of means.
"Maitreya! How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of wisdom?"

Maitreya! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive in this way—that depending on this dharma, this dharma exists; depending on this dharma, this dharma arises—namely: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—in this manner, there is only the arising of this great mass of suffering.

Maitreya! This dharma being absent, that dharma is absent; this dharma ceasing, that dharma ceases. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease. In this way, there is only the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
“Maitreya! In this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately accomplish the perfection of wisdom. Maitreya!”

This is called the ultimate accomplishment of the eight dharmas by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whereby they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Within the dharmas of supreme progress, they neither regress nor turn back; while practicing the bodhisattva conduct, they subdue all māras and hostile adversaries. They know, as it truly is, the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all dharmas; their minds do not grow weary toward any world, and because their minds do not grow weary, they do not rely on the wisdom of others, but swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

42. The Chapter on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva from the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, the Forty-second Chapter on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were well-known to the multitude.
Their names were:
Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Ānanda, Rāhula, and others, who served as the leaders.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present together, with the following as their leaders:

Bodhisattva Good Intention, Bodhisattva Superior Intention, Bodhisattva Firm Intention, Bodhisattva Lion Intention, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Accumulated Eloquence, Bodhisattva Beautiful Sound, Bodhisattva Victorious Banner, Bodhisattva Faith-Wisdom, Bodhisattva Varuṇa, Bodhisattva Indrājit, Bodhisattva Indradeva, Bodhisattva Non-Dependent, Bodhisattva Endowed with Eloquence, Bodhisattva Wondrous Flower of Supernatural Powers, Bodhisattva Maitreya, and the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who paid him homage and veneration as he preached the Dharma for them.

Then, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, being present within that assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have a slight doubt that I now wish to inquire about; I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to grant me his hearing.
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"If you have any doubts, ask whatever you wish now; I shall explain it for you so that you may attain joy."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s permission, Maitreya Bodhisattva was filled with joy and leaped for gladness as he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By accomplishing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva leave behind all evil realms and evil associates, and be able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!"
Out of your desire now to have compassion for all beings and to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans, you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning.
You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear [it].”
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes one dharma, they will leave behind all evil realms and evil associates, and will swiftly be able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
What is the one? It is the generation of the bodhicitta of superior intention;
this is called the one.
Maitreya! Furthermore, there are two dharmas by which one may leave behind all evil realms and evil associates, and swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are the two? First, one constantly and diligently cultivates śamatha; second, one attains skillfulness in vipaśyanā.
These are called the two.
Maitreya! Furthermore, there are three dharmas by which one leaves behind all evil realms and evil associates, and is able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these three?
First, the accomplishment of great compassion; second, the cultivation of the dharma of emptiness; and third, the non-arising of discrimination regarding all phenomena.
These are called the three. Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one leaves behind all evil realms and evil associates, and is able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are the four? First, abiding securely in pure precepts; second, being free from the net of all doubts; third, delighting in the araṇya; and fourth, giving rise to a mind of right view.
These are called the four. Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which one leaves behind all evil realms and evil associates, and is able to swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

What are the five? First, dwelling in the dharma of emptiness; second, not seeking the faults of others; third, constantly observing oneself; fourth, loving and delighting in the true dharma; and fifth, gathering in and protecting others.
These are called the five. Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are six dharmas by which one leaves behind all evil realms and evil associates, and is able to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

What are the six? First, being free from desire; second, not giving rise to anger; third, not engendering delusion; fourth, constantly refraining from coarse speech; fifth, abiding in emptiness; and sixth, having a mind like space.
These are called the six. Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas by which one leaves behind all evil realms and evil associates, and is able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

What are the seven? First, abiding in right mindfulness; second, achieving the discernment of phenomena; third, initiating diligence; fourth, constantly giving rise to joy; fifth, attaining physical pliancy; sixth, dwelling in various meditative concentrations; and seventh, being fully endowed with equanimity.
These are called the seven. Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas by which one leaves behind all evil realms and evil associates, and is able to swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are the eight? First, right view;
second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right mindfulness; and eighth, right concentration.
These are called the eight. Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are nine dharmas by which one leaves behind all evil realms and evil associates, and is able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are the nine?
First, quickly departing from all desires and unwholesome, evil states, one dwells in the first dhyāna—characterized by applied and sustained thought, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
Second, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, one dwells in the second dhyāna—characterized by internal serenity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
Third, being detached from joy, one dwells in the third dhyāna with equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind;

fourth, being detached from both sorrow and suffering as well as joy and bliss, one dwells in the fourth dhyāna with pure equanimity and mindfulness, free from suffering and bliss, and one-pointedness of mind;
fifth, transcending perceptions of form and having no further objective referents, one dwells in the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
Sixth, having transcended the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, he is able to abide in the meditative absorption of infinite consciousness;
seventh, having transcended the meditative absorption of infinite consciousness, he is able to abide in the meditative absorption of nothingness;
eighth, having transcended the meditative absorption of nothingness, he abides in the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Ninth, having transcended the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is able to abide securely in the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is called the ninth. Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which one may leave behind all evil realms and evil associates, and swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are these ten?

First, they are well able to accomplish the Vajra Samādhi; second, they accomplish the Samādhi corresponding to the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); third, they accomplish the Samādhi of expedient practice; fourth, they accomplish the Samādhi of universal illumination; fifth, they accomplish the Samādhi of universal radiance; sixth, they accomplish the Samādhi of pervasive illumination; seventh, they accomplish the Jewel Moon Samādhi; eighth, they accomplish the Moon Lamp Samādhi; ninth, they accomplish the Samādhi of renunciation; tenth, they accomplish the Samādhi of the Supreme Banner Arm Seal.
These are called the ten. Maitreya!
When a bodhisattva has accomplished these dharmas, they will leave behind all evil realms and evil associates, and will swiftly be able to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, having heard this Dharma, was filled with great joy. He bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, he immediately praised the Buddha before him with these verses:
"In past kalpas, the Buddha Gave up his beloved wife and children, His head, eyes, marrow, and bones, Until he reached the further shore of giving."
The Buddha constantly guards the prohibitive precepts, Like a yak cherishing its tail;
most supreme and peerless, He has reached the further shore of ethical discipline.
By the power of patience, the Buddha Abandons all conflict and contention.
Seeking not the faults of others, one reaches the further shore of patience.
Through the power of diligence, the Buddha attained supreme tranquility;
having reached the further shore of effort, he abides in ultimate and eternal bliss.
By the power of meditative concentration, the Buddha is able to extinguish all defilements of sin;
as a guide for devas and humans, he has reached the further shore of concentration.
By the power of wisdom, the Buddha thoroughly understands all phenomena.
With no inherent nature whatsoever, he has reached the further shore of wisdom.
At the Bodhi tree, the Buddha subdued the hosts of Māra;
possessing supreme knowledge, he accomplished the unsurpassed path.
The Guide, with the power of fearlessness, turned the pure wheel of Dharma in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, shattering all the heterodox teachers.
His unsurpassed, great wisdom transcends the world.
Able to emit pure radiance, He skillfully expounds the essentials of all dharmas.
The Tathāgata’s pure form, His wisdom and his merit,
Surpass all worlds, And are able to reach the further shore.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Bodhisattva Maitreya is truly rare, for he has been able to accomplish immeasurable eloquence; he preaches the Dharma with equality according to the thoughts of sentient beings, yet remains unattached to words and letters.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said. Ānanda!”
Maitreya Bodhisattva, it is not only today that you have been able to praise the Buddha before me with verses.

In the distant past, ten incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha named Jvalanaprabhāvikrīḍitasvaraviśeṣarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, there was a son of a brahmin named Bhadrayuṣa, who was endowed with all the auspicious marks and brought joy to those who beheld him.

As he emerged from the park, he saw that Tathāgata—exceedingly handsome and sublime, with his sense faculties in perfect tranquility; having attained *śamatha*, he was like a pure pool free from all impurities; adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks, he was like a *sāla* tree in full bloom; surpassing all others like Mount Sumeru; his countenance was serene and joyful like the full moon; his majestic radiance was brilliant like the shining sun; and his physical proportions were perfectly symmetrical like a *nyagrodha* tree.
At that time, Bhadrayuśas beheld the sublime marks of the Buddha Tathāgata, and with a heart of pure faith, he thought:
"How rare it is that the World-Honored One has been able to achieve such adornment of immeasurable merit!"
"I, too, vow that in a future age, I shall achieve such a body endowed with merit.
Having made this vow, he threw himself upon the ground and further thought to himself:
"If in a future age I am to attain the body of a Buddha, I pray only that the Tathāgata will tread upon me with his feet."

At that time, the Buddha, knowing the intention of Bhadrayu, stepped upon Bhadrayu’s body with his foot. As soon as the foot was placed down, Bhadrayu attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The World-Honored One turned back and addressed the bhikṣus:
"None of you shall step upon Bhadrayu with your feet."

Why is this? Because these are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have now already realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and are further able to accomplish the supernormal knowledges of the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the power of miraculous transformations.
At that time, Bhadrayuśas immediately praised the Buddha in his presence with these verses:
"The Buddha, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, Is most honored and unsurpassed;
Transcending all the worlds, I now prostrate in worship."
The Great Radiance of the Tathāgata eclipses the sun and moon;
transcending all worlds, I now prostrate in worship.
Like the roar of a lion, all beasts are struck with fear.
The World-Honored One of great majestic power subdues all non-Buddhists.
The white tuft of hair between his brows is like the radiance of crystal;
it shines universally throughout the world, surpassing all things.
The World-Honored One is without equal; with feet marked by the thousand-spoked wheel, he purifies and transforms the world, able to shake the great earth.
Having accomplished the path of renunciation, he has transcended the ocean of afflictions.
With all treasures of merit, he bestows them as he wishes.
The Tathāgata’s pure precepts are like the great earth;
they give birth to all virtues, free from any thought of love or hatred.
By the power of wisdom, one thoroughly understands that all phenomena are empty;
sentient beings and a life-span cannot be apprehended through conceptual differentiation.
One skillfully understands the nature of sentient beings, their mental activities, and their destinies.
Acting as a bright lamp for the world, you bring benefit to all.
To those oppressed by the sufferings of the world and drifting in the violent torrent,
you constantly exert the power of great diligence for the sake of all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One is free from afflictions, Birth, old age, sickness, and death;
He dwells in the world like empty space, Untainted by anything at all.
With the great majestic light of wisdom, He is able to shatter all darkness.
"Forever free from greed, hatred, and delusion, I now prostrate and pay homage to you.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From that time forward, the supernatural powers attained by the Bodhisattva Bhadrayus have never again declined."
What do you think?
Was that person named Bhadrayu at that time anyone else?
He was none other than this very Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in this assembly today.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Bodhisattva Maitreya has long since realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), for what reason has he not yet attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Bodhisattvas have two kinds of adornments and two kinds of gathering: namely, gathering sentient beings and adorning sentient beings; gathering buddha-fields and adorning buddha-fields.”
In past lives, when Maitreya Bodhisattva cultivated the bodhisattva path, he always delighted in grasping Buddha-lands and adorning Buddha-lands.
In the past, when I cultivated the bodhisattva path, I always delighted in grasping sentient beings and adorning sentient beings.
However, while Maitreya practiced the bodhisattva path for forty kalpas, I then resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By the power of my courageous and diligent exertion, I bypassed nine kalpas and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within this Bhadrakalpa.
Ānanda! I have realized awakening by means of ten dharmas. What are these ten?

First, one is able to give away that which is beloved; second, one is able to give away one’s beloved wife; third, one is able to give away one’s beloved son; fourth, one is able to give away one’s beloved head; fifth, one is able to give away one’s beloved eyes; sixth, one is able to give away one’s beloved royal throne; seventh, one is able to give away one’s beloved precious jewels; eighth, one is able to give away one’s beloved flesh and blood; ninth, one is able to give away one’s beloved marrow and bones; tenth, one is able to give away one’s beloved limbs.
"These are called the ten.
By practicing these dharmas, I was able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Ānanda!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that can realize bodhi. What are these ten? First, attaining the merit of ethical discipline;

second, accomplishing the power of patience; third, initiating diligence; fourth, attaining all meditative concentrations; fifth, possessing great wisdom; sixth, never abandoning any sentient beings; seventh, giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; eighth, constantly practicing the dharma of emptiness; ninth, being skillfully able to accomplish true emptiness; and tenth, being skillfully able to accomplish signlessness and wishlessness.
These are called the ten.
By practicing these dharmas, I am able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Ānanda!

When Maitreya Bodhisattva was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he was unable to relinquish his hands, feet, head, or eyes; rather, he accumulated unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the path of skillful means and peace and happiness.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How was it that when Maitreya practiced the bodhisattva path in the past, he was able to accumulate unsurpassed bodhi solely through the path of skillful means and peace?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, when Maitreya was practicing the bodhisattva path, during the six periods of day and night, he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in prostration, and before all the Buddhas recited these verses:
'I now take refuge and pay homage To all the Buddhas of the ten directions. "
The assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, and the Great Sages with their divine eyes,
likewise pay homage to the bodhicitta; it causes one to leave behind all evil realms,
enables rebirth in the heavens, and leads even to the realization of Nirvāṇa.
If I have committed even a slight transgression, arising from the movements of my mind,
I now, before the presence of all Buddhas, repent so that it may be extinguished.
Whatever merits I have accumulated through my body, speech, and mind, I now [dedicate].
May this become the cause for awakening, so that I may attain the unsurpassed path.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, those who make offerings to the Tathāgata and to the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom— I now rejoice in them all.
I confess all my transgressions; I rejoice in all this merit.
I now pay homage to all Buddhas, wishing to attain supreme wisdom.
To the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who have realized the ten stages—
I now prostrate with my head in homage, Vowing to swiftly realize Bodhi.
Having realized Bodhi, May you subdue the armies of Māra,
Turn the pure Wheel of Dharma, And bring benefit to all classes of sentient beings.
May I always vow to dwell in the world for immeasurable *koṭi* eons,
Beating the great Dharma drum to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
I am submerged in the mire of desire, bound by the cords of greed;
Bound by manifold fetters, I pray that the Buddha will look upon me with compassion.
Though sentient beings are heavily defiled, the Buddhas never weary of them or abandon them;
may you, through great kindness and compassion, deliver us from the ocean of birth and death.
The paths of the Bodhisattvas traversed by all the World-Honored Ones of the present, the Buddhas of the past,
and those of the future— may I now vow to practice and study them.
May I fulfill the *pāramitās* and achieve the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Delivering all sentient beings, they realize the unsurpassed path.
They thoroughly understand that all phenomena are empty, signless, and devoid of intrinsic nature;
they neither abide nor can be designated, being neither born nor extinguished.
Furthermore, like the Great Sage, he thoroughly understands non-self,
the absence of a person (pudgala), and even the absence of a life-principle (jīva).
Regarding all matters of giving, he does not cling to "I" or "mine."
To bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, I give without stinginess or parsimony.
May the objects I bestow arise without effort;
observing and realizing their emptiness, may I fulfill the perfection of giving.
Maintaining the precepts without deficiency, one attains the pure śīla of a Buddha;
because there is no abiding, one fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
Enduring with patience like the four great elements, one does not give rise to a discriminating mind.
Because of being free from ill-will, one fulfills the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
May one, through the power of body and mind, give rise to great diligence (vīrya),
remaining firm and without indolence, thus fulfilling the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
Through the samādhis of being like an illusion, like a magical transformation,
and like a vajra, as well as through courageous diligence, may they be endowed with the perfection of dhyāna.
May they realize the wisdom of the three vidyās and enter the three gates of liberation.
Having realized the equality of the three times, Possessing the perfection of wisdom;
The wondrous form-bodies of all Buddhas, With their radiance and great majestic power— May I,
through the bodhisattva’s practice of diligence, Attain the fulfillment of them all.
"Regarding the one named Maitreya, who diligently cultivates such practices,
is endowed with the six pāramitās, and dwells securely in the ten stages," the Buddha told Ānanda:
“Maitreya Bodhisattva, by abiding in such skillful means, has accumulated the prerequisites for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Ānanda!
In the past, when I sought the Way, I underwent immeasurable suffering before I was able to accumulate the prerequisites for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Why is this? In the distant past, there was a prince named Sarvārthadarśin, who was handsome and exquisite, endowed with all the primary marks, and whom all who saw him rejoiced to behold.
While out strolling in the gardens and groves, he saw a sick person suffering from manifold heavy afflictions; moved by a heart of compassion, he asked him:
"For this illness of yours, is there no medicine that can cure it?"
At that time, the sick man addressed the prince in verse, saying:
"The medicine for my illness is difficult to find; it cannot be obtained in this world, nor does even the king possess it—how much less one afflicted by disease."
"Though one may master all treatises and be skilled in explaining medical prescriptions,
even if they wish to provide treatment, the medicine may be difficult to obtain.
At that time, the Prince again addressed the sick man in verse:
"Gold, silver, and mani-jewels, even up to elephants and horses—
whatever you seek, speak it forth, and I shall remove your sorrow and distress."
At that time, the sick man addressed the prince again in verse, saying:
“If I drink the blood of the prince, I shall surely attain peace and happiness.”
"I pray that you give rise to a heart of joy, And grant me freedom from sorrow and affliction.
At that time, the Prince again addressed the sick man in verse:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, I would fall into the Avīci Hell; I would endure all manner of suffering, Provided it might bring them peace and happiness."
"I could endure even many kalpas [of suffering], let alone this blood from my own body!
At that moment, the Prince took a sharp blade and pierced his body to draw blood, allowing the sick man to use it as he pleased, without giving rise to even a single thought of regret or resentment.
Ānanda, you should know this: was the Prince Sarvārthasiddha at that time anyone other than myself? He was none other than I.
While the waters of the four great oceans may still be measured, the blood I have sacrificed from my own body while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past is beyond calculation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, there was a crown prince named Māndārava, who was handsome and exceptionally sublime, endowed with all the marks of excellence, such that all who saw him were filled with joy."
Emerging from the garden grove, he saw a sick man whose body was emaciated; moved by a heart of compassion, he asked him:
"For this illness of yours, is there no medicine that can provide a cure?"
At that time, the sick man addressed the prince in verse, saying:
"Though there be skilled physicians in the world, there is no medicine to cure my illness.
I only pray that you will give rise to compassion and remove my sorrow and distress for my sake."
At that time, the Prince addressed the sick man with these verses:
“For the benefit of the world, I shall give everything away—my own body parts as well as precious treasures. Whoever has need of anything, let them speak.”
At that time, the sick man addressed the prince again in verse:
"Just like a great king of medicines, He heals all ailments according to one's needs;
And just like the light of the sun and moon, He shines universally upon all worlds."
"If you could give me your own marrow and smear it all over my body,
this illness would be eliminated, and I would find peace and happiness for a long night.
At that time, the Prince again addressed the sick man with these verses:
“If there are sentient beings who crush my body to extract my marrow for the benefit of the world,
my mind shall not give rise to sorrow or affliction.”

At that time, the Prince immediately shattered his own body to take the marrow from within it, giving it to the sick man for him to use as he pleased, without giving rise to even a single thought of regret or resentment.
Ānanda, you should know this: who else could the Crown Prince Supuṣpa have been at that time?
It was none other than my own self.

While the waters of the four great oceans may still be measured, the instances in which I sacrificed my body’s marrow and bones while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past are beyond calculation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, there was a king named Candraprabha (Moonlight), who was handsome and exquisite, endowed with all the marks of perfection, and whom all who saw him rejoiced."
Emerging from the garden grove, he saw a blind man who was poor and begging for alms;
moved by compassion, he asked him, "What do you require? I shall give it to you."
"Whether it be food, drink, clothing, ornaments, or articles of utility, gold, silver, mani-jewels, or various precious gems—whatever you desire, I shall grant it all to you.
At that time, the blind man addressed the king in verse:
"The Great King is like the sun and moon, His radiance illuminating the world."
Endowed with supreme merit, you shall before long be reborn in the heavens.
All pure and wondrous forms, I now see them no more;
I pray that Your Majesty will arise in compassion and grant me my beloved eyes.
At that time, the Great King addressed the blind man with these verses:
"Come quickly to take my eyes, so that you may attain peace and happiness."
May I, in a future age, attain the pure eye of a Buddha.
As I practice the path of a bodhisattva, I shall relinquish everything;
if I do not give this to you, it would violate my original vow.

At that time, King Candraprabha immediately took a sharp blade and gouged out his own eyes, giving them to the blind man to use as he pleased, without giving rise to even a single thought of regret or resentment.
Ānanda, you should know this: who else could that King Candraprabha have been at that time?
It was none other than myself.
Even Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, can be measured; yet the number of times I gave away my beloved eyes while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past is beyond calculation.
Ānanda! When Maitreya Bodhisattva was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this vow, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who diminish lust, anger, and delusion and accomplish the ten wholesome actions, it is only at such a time that I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Ānanda! In a future age, there will be sentient beings who, with diminished lust, anger, and delusion, have accomplished the ten wholesome paths of action; at that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Why is this? It is because of the power of that bodhisattva's original vow.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, while practicing the bodhisattva path, I made this vow:

'May I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi at that time when the five turbidities prevail in this evil world, when the defilements of greed and anger are heavy, and when sentient beings commit all manner of evils—such as being unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, and even lacking harmony among their own kin and dependents.'"

"Ānanda! Because of this vow, whenever I now enter a city or a village, there are many sentient beings who revile me, as I gather assemblies by teaching the Dharma that avoids the extremes of eternalism and nihilism."
"If they smear me with dust and soil while I am begging for alms, or give me food mixed with various poisons to eat, or slander me by means of a woman— Ānanda!"
"Now, by the power of my original vow, I give rise to great compassion for such evil sentient beings as these and preach the Dharma for them.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to perform what is difficult to do and endure what is difficult to endure; he brings to full discipline those who are undisciplined, and he takes upon himself the burden of sentient beings defiled by such faults and evils, preaching the Dharma for them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.
For what reason?"
“Because they are embraced by the great compassion of the Tathāgata.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Hearing of the Tathāgata’s firm and steadfast vows, the hairs on my body stand on end.
World-Honored One,
what shall this sutra be named?
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The name of this sutra is 'The Questions of Maitreya,' and it is also called 'The Causes and Conditions of Past Vows. You should receive and uphold it by these names."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva, the Venerable Ānanda, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 111;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume 112.
Translated by an unknown translator, appended to the Qin Records and included here after collation.
43. The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, the Forty-third.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus.

There were sixteen thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), who had gathered from various buddha-fields; they were all destined to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment after only one more birth.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
“There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva falls away from wisdom. What are these four?
They do not respect the Dharma nor revere the Dharma teachers;
they keep secret the profound teachings they have received instead of explaining them in their entirety;
and when there are those who delight in the Dharma, they create obstacles for them, using various causes and conditions to discourage and break their resolve.
Kāśyapa, being arrogant and self-exalting while disparaging others—
this is the fourth dharma by which a bodhisattva falls away from wisdom.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains great wisdom. What are these four?
They always revere the Dharma and honor the Dharma teachers;
they extensively expound for others the teachings they have heard with a pure mind, seeking no fame, reputation, or material gain whatsoever;
knowing that wisdom arises from extensive learning, they seek it diligently and without slackening, as if their hair or clothing were on fire.
Hearing the sutras, reciting and upholding them, delighting in practicing according to what is taught rather than following mere words— Kāśyapa,
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains great wisdom.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva loses the bodhicitta. What are these four?

Having deceived their teachers and elders, they do not show reverence for the sūtras and the Dharma they have received; where there is no cause for doubt or regret, they cause others to feel doubt and regret; toward those who seek the Mahāyāna, they revile, slander, and spread their ill repute; and with a mind of flattery and crookedness, they associate with others.
Kāśyapa! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva loses the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which they do not lose the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) from lifetime to lifetime, until the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) spontaneously appears before them.
What are these four? When faced with circumstances that would cost them their lives, they do not speak falsely, much less in jest.
He always engages with others with a straightforward mind, free from all flattery and crookedness;
he conceives the thought of World-Honored Ones toward all bodhisattvas and is able to proclaim their names in the four directions;
he does not take pleasure in the various Small Vehicle teachings himself, and causes all sentient beings whom he transforms to abide in unsurpassed bodhi.
Kāśyapa! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not lose the mind of awakening from lifetime to lifetime, until the site of enlightenment naturally appears before them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
There are four dharmas by which the wholesome qualities produced by a bodhisattva perish and do not increase.
What are these four? They are:

reciting, studying, and practicing the Lokāyata scriptures with a mind of arrogance; approaching donors with a mind greedy for gain and offerings; disparaging other bodhisattvas; and rejecting and disbelieving sūtras that one has not previously heard.
Kāśyapa! These are the four dharmas by which the wholesome dharmas that have arisen perish and do not increase.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which the wholesome dharmas they have produced increase and are not lost.
What are these four? They are:
abandoning false teachings and seeking the true scriptures, the six pāramitās, and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
With a mind free from arrogance toward all sentient beings, one remains humble and lowly; receiving offerings in accordance with the Dharma, one knows moderation and contentment;

remaining free from wrong livelihoods, one dwells securely in the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*); one does not proclaim the faults of others, whether real or unreal, nor does one seek out the shortcomings of others;
and if one’s mind does not penetrate the various dharmas, one forms this thought:
"The Buddha-dharma is immeasurable; he expounds it according to the inclinations of sentient beings. This is known only by the Buddha and is not something I can understand.
Thus, taking the Buddha as one's witness, one does not give rise to opposition.
Kāśyapa! These are the four dharmas by which the wholesome qualities born within a bodhisattva increase and are not lost.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four types of crooked minds that they should distance themselves from. What are these four?

To give rise to doubt and regret regarding the Buddha’s Dharma; to harbor arrogance and resentment toward sentient beings; to give rise to a mind of jealousy regarding the gains and offerings of others; and to revile Bodhisattvas and spread their ill repute.
Kāśyapa! These are the four crooked states of mind that a bodhisattva should distance themselves from.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four characteristics of a straightforward mind. What are these four?
Whatever transgressions they have committed, they never conceal them; they confess them openly to others with a mind free from the entanglements of hypocrisy.
Even if one loses one's kingdom, life, or wealth, in such urgent matters one will never speak falsely, nor utter any other evil words;

when subjected to insults, slander, beatings, binding, or various forms of injury, one accepts this suffering by blaming only oneself, relying on the retribution of one's own karma and harboring no resentment toward others;
abiding in the power of faith, if one hears the profound and difficult-to-believe Buddha-dharma, one’s own mind being pure, one is able to receive and uphold it all.
Kāśyapa! These are the four signs of the upright mind of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
Bodhisattvas have four signs of ruin. What are these four?
Reciting and studying the scriptures while giving rise to frivolous conceptualization, rather than practicing in accordance with the Dharma;
They are unable to serve, obey, or show reverence to their teachers and elders so as to bring them joy; they diminish the offerings given by others;
they accept the faithful offerings of the laity while violating their own original vows;
and upon seeing virtuous bodhisattvas, they treat them with contempt and lack respect.
Kāśyapa! These are the four signs of a bodhisattva’s ruin.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four marks of wholesome conformity. What are these four?
Hearing a sutra not previously heard, they immediately believe and accept it, practicing according to what is taught; they rely on the Dharma and do not rely on mere words.
They accord with the teacher’s instructions and can comprehend their intent; they are easy to converse with, and all their actions are virtuous, never failing the teacher’s wishes.
They do not regress from precepts or meditative concentration, receiving offerings with a disciplined and compliant mind.
Upon seeing virtuous bodhisattvas, they show reverence and affection; they follow after virtuous people and receive their noble conduct and virtue.
Kāśyapa! These are the four signs of a bodhisattva’s wholesome compliance.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four errors. What are the four?
To agree with those who are untrustworthy is an error of a bodhisattva;
To preach the profound Dharma to sentient beings who are not vessels for it is an error of a bodhisattva;
to praise the Lesser Vehicle to those who delight in the Great Vehicle is an error of a bodhisattva;
and when practicing generosity, to give only to those who observe the precepts and to honor the virtuous while excluding the wicked is an error of a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa! These are the four errors of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four right paths. What are these four?

They maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; they universally transform all sentient beings equally by means of the Buddha-wisdom; they preach the Dharma with impartiality to all sentient beings; and they cause all sentient beings to dwell equally in right practice.
Kāśyapa! These are the four right paths of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four types of those who are not spiritual friends and not virtuous companions. What are these four?

Those who seek the state of a śrāvaka desire only their own benefit; those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha delight in few activities; those who study non-Buddhist scriptures such as the Lokāyata, which are adorned with ornate rhetoric; and those whom one associates with increase only worldly benefits and do not augment the benefits of the Dharma.
Kāśyapa! These are the four who are not good spiritual friends and not good companions for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four kinds of spiritual friends and four kinds of virtuous companions. What are these four?
Those who come seeking [help] are spiritual friends, because they provide the causal conditions for the Buddha-way.
One who is able to preach the Dharma is a spiritual friend, because they give rise to wisdom;
one who is able to instruct others to leave the household life is a spiritual friend, because they cause wholesome dharmas to increase;
all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are spiritual friends, because they cause all the Buddha-dharmas to increase.
Kāśyapa! These are the four virtuous spiritual friends and the four virtuous companions of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
There are four types of bodhisattvas who are not bodhisattvas but resemble them.
What are these four? They are:

those who crave gain and offerings rather than seeking the Dharma; those who crave reputation rather than seeking merit; those who crave their own pleasure rather than rescuing sentient beings by means of the Dharma that extinguishes suffering; and those who delight in gathering followers rather than delighting in solitude.
Kāśyapa! These are the four who are not bodhisattvas but resemble bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
There are four kinds of true Bodhisattvas. What are the four?
They are those who are able to believe in and understand emptiness, while also believing in the retribution of karma.
Knowing that all phenomena are devoid of a self, yet giving rise to great compassion for sentient beings;
deeply delighting in nirvana while wandering through saṃsāra;
and practicing all acts of giving for the sake of sentient beings without seeking any karmic reward.
Kāśyapa! These are the four kinds of true merit of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four great treasuries. What are these four?

If a bodhisattva encounters the Buddhas and is able to hear the six pāramitās along with their exegesis; if they regard the Dharma-preacher with an unobstructed mind; and if they delight in the practice of seclusion with a mind free from indolence.
Kāśyapa! These are the four great treasuries of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can transcend the works of Māra.
What are these four? They are:
never abandoning the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), and having no malice or obstruction toward any sentient beings.
Awakening all forms of knowledge and vision;
not disparaging any sentient being in one's mind. Kāśyapa!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can transcend the works of Māra.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva gathers all roots of goodness."
What are these four? They are:

dwelling in secluded places while remaining free from a deceitful mind; practicing the four methods of attraction among all sentient beings without seeking recompense; not sparing one's body or life for the sake of seeking the Dharma; and cultivating various roots of goodness with a mind that never tires.
Kāśyapa! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva gathers all roots of goodness.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Bodhisattvas have four immeasurable adornments of merit.
What are these four? They are:

practicing the gift of Dharma with a pure mind; giving rise to great compassion for those who break the precepts; extolling and praising the bodhicitta among all sentient beings; and cultivating patience toward those who are inferior.
Kāśyapa! These are the four immeasurable adornments of merit of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
One who is called a bodhisattva is not so named merely by title; one who can practice wholesome dharmas and maintain a mind of equanimity is called a bodhisattva.
Briefly stated, one who accomplishes thirty-two qualities is called a bodhisattva.
What are the thirty-two dharmas?
Constantly seeking profound peace and happiness for all sentient beings, causing them all to abide within omniscience; not harboring hatred toward the wisdom of others;
destroying arrogance and deeply delighting in the Buddha-way; and loving and respecting [the Dharma] without falsehood.
Cultivating ultimate intimacy, his mind remains impartial toward both enemies and kin until he reaches *nirvāṇa*.
He always maintains a smile and greets others with courtesy; his activities never cease midway.
Universally practicing great compassion for all sentient beings, his mind never tires, and he is insatiable in his learning. He seeks out his own faults rather than speaking of those of others.
He shortens [the duration of] his life by practicing all modes of conduct with the bodhicitta; he practices generosity without seeking its reward;
he observes the precepts not for the sake of rebirth; he practices unimpeded patience toward all sentient beings;
he exerts himself in diligence for the sake of cultivating all roots of goodness; and he gives rise to meditative concentration that is free from birth in the formless realms.

Practicing the wisdom of skillful means, they accord with the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); they regard sentient beings, whether virtuous or evil, with a compassionate mind free from fear;
with a single mind they listen to the Dharma, their minds abiding in seclusion; their hearts take no pleasure in or attachment to the various affairs of the world;

they do not crave the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), but constantly perceive great benefit within the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*); and they distance themselves from evil associates while drawing near to virtuous friends.
He accomplishes the four Brahma-vihāras and sports in the five supernormal powers;

constantly relying on true wisdom, he never abandons sentient beings whether they engage in wrong or right conduct; his speech is always definitive, he prizes the Dharma of reality, and in all that he does, bodhi is his primary concern.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
If a person possesses these thirty-two qualities, they are called a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
The merit of a bodhisattva is immeasurable and boundless; this should be understood through the causes and conditions of analogy.
Kāśyapa, it is like the entire great earth, which serves all sentient beings with no discriminatory mind and without seeking any recompense.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until sitting at the site of awakening, all sentient beings receive benefit, yet the Bodhisattva’s mind remains free of discrimination and seeks no recompense.
Kāśyapa! Just as all varieties of water cause the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and trees to grow, so too is the bodhisattva:
because his own mind is pure, he universally covers all sentient beings with loving-kindness and compassion, causing them all to increase in every wholesome dharma.
Kāśyapa! Just as all kinds of fire can ripen the hundred grains and fruits, so too is the wisdom of a bodhisattva: it can ripen all wholesome dharmas.
Kāśyapa! Just as all varieties of wind are able to establish all worlds, so too is the skillful means (*upāya*) of a bodhisattva; it is likewise able to establish all Buddha-dharmas.
Kāśyapa! Just as when the moon first appears, its radiance and form increase day by day, so too it is with the bodhisattva’s pure mind: all wholesome dharmas increase day by day.
Kāśyapa! Just as when the sun first rises it emits its light at once, universally illuminating all sentient beings,
so too does the bodhisattva emit the light of wisdom, simultaneously and universally illuminating all sentient beings.
Kāśyapa! Just as the lion, the king of beasts, is neither startled nor afraid wherever he goes, so too is the bodhisattva:
through pure observance of the precepts and true wisdom, he is neither startled nor afraid wherever he dwells.
Kāśyapa! Just as a well-trained king of elephants can accomplish great tasks without his body becoming exhausted, so too is the bodhisattva:
because he has well trained his mind, he is able to bring about great benefit for sentient beings without his mind ever growing weary.
Kāśyapa! It is like various lotus flowers that grow in water yet cannot be defiled by it.
So too is the bodhisattva: though born into the world, he cannot be defiled by worldly dharmas.
Kāśyapa! It is like a person who cuts down a tree; if the root remains, it will grow again.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: although they have severed the fetters and proclivities through the power of skillful means, because of their attachment to roots of goodness, they may still be reborn within the three realms.
Kāśyapa! Just as the flowing waters from all directions, once they have entered the great ocean, become of a single taste;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: by gathering all roots of goodness through various gateways and dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all become of a single taste.

Kāśyapa! Just as the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Four Great Kings all rely upon and dwell within Sumeru, the King of Mountains, so too is the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva: it is that upon which sarvajñatā relies and dwells.
Kāśyapa! It is just as a great king, by means of his ministers' power, is able to accomplish the affairs of state.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is likewise; through the power of skillful means, they are able to accomplish all the works of a Buddha.
Kāśyapa! Just as when the sky is clear and bright, free from clouds and obscurations, there will certainly be no sign of rain;
likewise, a bodhisattva of little learning has no sign of the rain of Dharma.
Kāśyapa! Just as when the heavens are overcast with clouds, rain will surely fall to satisfy all sentient beings, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
from the cloud of great compassion, they raise the great rain of Dharma to benefit sentient beings.
Kāśyapa! For example, wherever a wheel-turning monarch appears, there the seven treasures are found.
In the same way, Kāśyapa!
When a Bodhisattva appears in the world, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment manifest in the world.
Kāśyapa, it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (maṇi): wherever it is located, there will be immeasurable gold, silver, and precious treasures.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: wherever he arises, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jewels of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa, it is just as when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven enter the Garden of Equality; all the objects they use are entirely equal.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; because of his truly pure mind, he teaches and transforms sentient beings with impartiality.
Kāśyapa, it is like the power of incantations and medicinal herbs, which prevents poison from harming people.
The poisonous fetters of a bodhisattva are likewise; by the power of wisdom, they do not fall into the evil realms.
Kāśyapa, it is as if the discarded filth in a great city, if placed within a field of sugarcane or grapes, becomes beneficial.
The fetters of a bodhisattva are also like this; whatever remains is entirely for the sake of being a causal condition for *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
"Thus it is, Kāśyapa!"
A bodhisattva who wishes to study this *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* should practice the correct contemplation of all phenomena.
What is meant by "correct contemplation"?
It refers to the genuine reflection upon all phenomena.
One who practices true and correct contemplation does not contemplate a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; this is called the Middle Way of true and correct contemplation.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, one who contemplates truly observes that form is neither permanent nor impermanent; they observe that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent; this is called the Middle Way of true and correct contemplation.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, as for true contemplation:

one contemplates the earth element as neither permanent nor impermanent; one contemplates the water, fire, and wind elements as neither permanent nor impermanent. This is called the Middle Way, the true and correct contemplation.
Why is this so? Permanence is one extreme;

impermanence is another extreme. Between permanence and impermanence, there is neither form nor shape, neither manifestation nor cognition; this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.

"Self" is one extreme; "non-self" is another extreme. Between these two, there is neither form nor shape, neither clarity nor cognition; this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if the mind is real, this is one extreme; if the mind is unreal, this is another extreme. That which is without mind-consciousness and without mental factors is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.

In this same way, whether it be wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas, worldly dharmas and world-transcending dharmas, faulty dharmas and faultless dharmas, outflowing dharmas and non-outflowing dharmas, conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas, and even soiled dharmas and stainless dharmas, they are likewise free from the two extremes; they cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed. This is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all dharmas.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, "existence" is one extreme and "non-existence" is another extreme. That which lies between existence and non-existence—formless, shapeless, without illumination, and without cognition—is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the Dharma I have taught is the twelvefold dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair."
Through such causes and conditions, there is merely the accumulation of this great mass of suffering. If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease;

because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases; because name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; because contact ceases, feeling ceases; because feeling ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, clinging ceases; because clinging ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; and because birth ceases, thus old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and the multitude of afflictions—all this great mass of suffering—cease.
Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual and without distinction; one who knows them thus is said to have the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Likewise, conditioned activity and non-activity, consciousness and the object of consciousness, name-and-form and the visible and invisible, the six sense bases and the six supernormal powers, contact and the object of contact, feeling and the cessation of feeling, craving and the cessation of craving, grasping and the cessation of grasping, existence and the cessation of existence, birth and the cessation of birth, and aging-and-death and the cessation of aging-and-death—all these are non-dual and without distinction. One who knows them thus is said to have the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, as for true contemplation:
it is not by means of emptiness that all phenomena are made empty; rather, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is itself empty.
It is not by means of signlessness that phenomena are made signless; rather, phenomena themselves are signless."
One does not cause phenomena to be wishless by means of wishlessness; rather, phenomena themselves are inherently wishless.

One does not cause phenomena to be without arising, without birth, without self, without grasping, and without intrinsic nature by means of being without arising, without birth, without self, without grasping, and without intrinsic nature; rather, phenomena themselves are inherently without arising, without grasping, and without intrinsic nature.
To contemplate in this manner is called true contemplation.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is not because there are no persons that it is called empty; rather, emptiness is itself empty.
The past limit is empty, the future limit is empty, and the middle limit is also empty; one should rely upon emptiness and not rely upon the person.
If, having attained emptiness, one then relies upon emptiness itself, this constitutes a falling away from the Buddha-dharma.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
It would be better to give rise to a view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to overweening pride through a view of emptiness. Why is this so?
All views are liberated through emptiness; however, if one gives rise to the view of emptiness, it cannot be removed.
Kāśyapa, it is like a physician who administers medicine to cause the illness to stir, yet the medicine remains within and does not come out.
"What do you think? Would such a patient ever recover? "No."
“World-Honored One!
If this medicine does not come forth, the illness will only increase further. “It is so, Kāśyapa!”
All views can only be extinguished by emptiness; however, if one gives rise to the view of emptiness itself, it cannot be removed.
It is like a person who fears empty space, wailing and beating their breast while saying:
"I renounce empty space!"
"What do you think? Can this space be abandoned? "No, it cannot."
“World-Honored One!
‘It is so, Kāśyapa! If one fears the dharma of emptiness, I say that such a person is deranged and has lost their mind.’”
Why is this? Because they constantly practice within emptiness yet fear emptiness.
It is like a painter who, having personally painted an image of a yakṣa demon, becomes terrified upon seeing it, faints, and falls to the ground.

All ordinary beings are likewise; because they themselves create forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, they wander through birth and death, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions without realizing it.
It is like a magician who, having conjured illusory people, returns to devour them himself.
So it is with the bhikṣu who practices the Way: whatever phenomena he contemplates are all empty, all quiescent, and devoid of solidity; even this contemplation itself is empty.
Kāśyapa! It is like two pieces of wood that, when rubbed together, produce fire, which then burns those very pieces of wood.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
Because of the contemplation of reality, noble wisdom is born; once noble wisdom has arisen, it in turn consumes that very contemplation of reality.

It is like lighting a lamp: all darkness naturally vanishes; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere—it does not come from the east, nor upon departing does it go to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below; it does not come from those places, nor upon departing does it go to them.
Yet this lamp-light has no such thought as, "I am able to extinguish darkness.
It is simply that by the nature of the lamp-light, darkness is naturally absent; both light and darkness are empty, without action and without grasping.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
True wisdom arises and ignorance is extinguished; both wisdom and ignorance are empty of dual characteristics, being without action and without grasping. Kāśyapa!
Suppose there has been a dark room for a thousand years that has never seen light.
If a lamp were lit at that time, what do you think?
Would that darkness think: "I am here"?
“Do you mean that I have dwelt here for a long time and do not wish to depart? “No,
World-Honored One.”
"If, when a lamp is lit, darkness is powerless and, though it does not wish to depart,
must inevitably be extinguished; so too, Kāśyapa,
the karmic fetters practiced over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas are all utterly eliminated by a single contemplation of reality."
That which is the lamp-light is holy wisdom;
that which is darkness consists of all fetters and karmic actions. Kāśyapa!
For example, it is as impossible as for a seed planted in the air to grow; from the very beginning, such a thing has never occurred.
It is likewise impossible for a bodhisattva to attain realization and cause the Buddha-dharma to increase in such a manner.
Kāśyapa! Just as seeds sown in fertile soil are able to grow, so it is, Kāśyapa!
The Bodhisattva is also like this: although they possess various fetters and worldly dharmas, these can cause the Buddha-dharma to grow. Kāśyapa!
It is, for example, as lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he does not give rise to the Buddha-dharma. Kāśyapa!
It is, for example, like a lotus flower that grows from within low-lying, damp mud.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: from the mire of birth and death, and from sentient beings fixed in wrong determination, he can give rise to the Buddha-dharma. Kāśyapa!
It is like the four great oceans, which are filled with ghee produced therein.
The conditioned roots of goodness of a bodhisattva are likewise exceedingly many and immeasurable. Kāśyapa!

For example, if one hair were split into a hundred parts, and with one such part one were to take a single drop from the ocean, the conditioned roots of goodness of all śrāvakas would be just like that.
Kāśyapa! For example, just as there is space within the hole of a small mustard seed, so too is the conditioned wisdom of all śrāvakas. Kāśyapa!
Just as the empty space of the ten directions is immeasurable and boundless,
so too is the power of the conditioned wisdom of a bodhisattva, which is exceedingly great and immeasurable. Kāśyapa!
Suppose, for example, there were a great consort of a Kṣatriya king who conceived and gave birth to a son through a man of lowly status.
What do you think? Would he not be a prince?
"No, World-Honored One. "So it is, Kāśyapa!"

My assembly of śrāvakas is also like this; although they have attained realization together and are born from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they are not called the Tathāgata’s true sons. Kāśyapa!
For example, suppose a Kṣatriya great king has a liaison with a messenger and conceives a son; although he is of low birth, he is still called a prince.

A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is likewise: though they have not yet fully perfected merit and wisdom, they come and go within the cycle of birth and death, benefiting sentient beings according to their power and capacity; such a person is called a true son of the Tathāgata.

Kāśyapa! It is, for example, as if a wheel-turning sage-king had a thousand sons, yet not a single one among them possessed the marks of a sage-king; the sage-king, amidst them, did not conceive the notion that they were his sons.

The Tathāgata is likewise: although he may be surrounded by hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of śrāvaka followers and lack any bodhisattvas among them, the Tathāgata does not conceive the notion of "sons" toward those within that assembly.
Kāśyapa! It is like this:

suppose the chief queen of a wheel-turning sage king has been pregnant for seven days, and the child possesses all the marks of a wheel-turning king; the devas would honor him more than any other sons who possess physical strength.
Why is this? This prince in the womb will surely succeed to the sovereign position and continue the lineage of the holy king.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is also like this: although they have not yet perfected the faculties of all bodhisattvas, they are deeply respected by the devas and celestial kings—just as one would respect a prince in the womb—surpassing even the great arhats of the eight liberations.
Why is this? Such a bodhisattva is called one who succeeds to the position of honor and does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, Kāśyapa!
For example, a single lapis lazuli gem surpasses a mountain of crystal as Mount Sumeru does;
so too is the bodhisattva, for from the very first moment of generating the mind of awakening, they surpass the assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa! Just as on the day a great king’s queen gives birth to a son, the subordinate kings and ministers all come to pay their respects;
so it is with a bodhisattva: when they first resolve to attain enlightenment, all devas and people of the world should likewise pay them homage and respect.

Kāśyapa! It is like the various medicinal herbs that grow on the King of Mountains, the Snowy Mountains; they belong to no one and are without discrimination, yet whatever is taken according to the illness, all can provide a cure.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: the medicinal wisdom he has gathered is free from discrimination, universally providing equal protection and salvation for all sentient beings.
Kāśyapa, it is like when the moon first appears; the affection and respect of all people exceed that for the full moon.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
Those who believe my words should love and revere the bodhisattva even more than the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because it is from Bodhisattvas that Tathāgatas arise. Kāśyapa,
it is like a foolish person who abandons the moon to worship the stars.
The wise are not like this; they never abandon the practice of a bodhisattva by paying homage to śrāvakas.
Kāśyapa, it is as if all the gods and humans in the entire world, though they may skillfully polish a counterfeit pearl, cannot cause it to become a precious lapis lazuli gem.

Those who seek the state of a śrāvaka are also like this: even if they maintain all the precepts and achieve meditative concentration, they will ultimately never be able to sit at the site of enlightenment and realize the Unsurpassed Way.
Kāśyapa! Just as a well-polished lapis lazuli gem can produce hundreds of thousands of immeasurable precious treasures,
so too does the teaching and training that brings a bodhisattva to maturity produce hundreds of thousands of immeasurable jewels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Mahākāśyapa:

"A bodhisattva should always seek to benefit sentient beings, and furthermore, correctly cultivate all existing roots of merit and goodness, bestowing them equally upon all sentient beings with an impartial mind."
The medicinal wisdom thus attained reaches throughout the ten directions, treating all sentient beings so that they all attain ultimate liberation.
What is meant by "ultimate medicinal wisdom"?

That is to say: one uses the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to counteract lustful desire; the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) to counteract ill-will; the contemplation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) to counteract ignorance; the contemplation of the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to counteract all false views; the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) to counteract all recollections, conceptualizations, and conditional thoughts; the contemplation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) to counteract all aspirations for existence within the three realms; the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) to counteract all [other] inversions; the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are impermanent to counteract the inversion of perceiving permanence within the impermanent; the fact that conditioned phenomena are suffering (*duḥkha*) to counteract the inversion of perceiving pleasure within suffering; the fact that there is no self (*anātman*) to counteract the inversion of perceiving a self within the non-self; and the tranquility of *nirvāṇa* to counteract the inversion of perceiving purity within the impure.
