“Kāśyapa! What is a *kaṇa-śramaṇa*? Kāśyapa!”
It is like wild barley growing in a field of wheat; its form resembles wheat so closely that it cannot be distinguished.
At that time, the farmer thinks to himself, "All this wild barley is good wheat."
Only later, when the ears of grain appeared, did he realize his error; he could no longer say that everything was barley.

Kāśyapa, in the same way, there are tares among the śramaṇas who appear to be those who maintain the precepts and possess virtuous conduct; when donors see them, they believe them all to be true śramaṇas.

Yet that deluded person is not truly a śramaṇa, though he claims to be one; he is not a practitioner of the holy life, though he declares himself to be so. Having long been ruined and fallen away from the observance of precepts, he does not even count among the assembly. Within the Buddha-dharma, he lacks the life-force of wisdom and shall fall into the evil realms.
It is just like weeds among good grain.
At that time, devas, nāgas, and spirits who possess the divine eye see that foolish person falling into hell; having seen this, they say to one another:

"This is a foolish person who previously appeared to be a śramaṇa while practicing unwholesome dharmas; now he shall fall into the great hells, and from this day forward, he will never again be able to attain the virtues or the fruits of a śramaṇa."
"It is just like weeds among good grain.
Kāśyapa, this is called the 'weed śramaṇa'."
“Kāśyapa, what is a śramaṇa who has abandoned birth? Kāśyapa, [it is as follows:]”
For example, it is like the "pustules" (pūti) of rice seedlings; because they do not ripen, they are called "pustules.
Because they lack substance, they are blown away by the wind; lacking firmness or strength, they resemble rice but are not rice.

Kāśyapa! Such a "pseudo-monk" (pūti-śramaṇa) merely resembles a monk in outward form; he lacks anyone to instruct or rebuke him, possesses no power of virtue, and is blown about by the winds of Māra. Lacking the vital strength of observing the precepts, he is devoid of extensive learning, has lost his power of meditative concentration, and is far removed from wisdom. Unable to destroy the thieves of the various afflictions (kleśas), such a person is called weak, inferior, and powerless; he belongs to Māra and is caught by Māra’s hook, submerged within all manner of afflictions, blown about by the winds of Māra like the *pūti* rice.
Kāśyapa! Rice that has been stored for too long is unfit to be sown, nor will it produce sprouts. Kāśyapa!
In this way, the *pūtiśramaṇa* has no seed of the Path within the Buddha-dharma and does not attain liberation within the Dharma of the noble ones.
Kāśyapa, as for the *pūtiśramaṇa*, it refers to one who breaks the precepts and practices evil; such a person is called a *pūtiśramaṇa*.
“Kāśyapa! What is it to resemble a śramaṇa? Kāśyapa!”

For example, it is like a skilled craftsman who coats copper with gold; its color resembles gold, yet its value is not that of gold, and only when it is rubbed and polished does one know it is not gold. Kāśyapa!

Thus, those who resemble śramaṇas take pleasure in adorning themselves; they constantly bathe their bodies and wear their robes in a neat and orderly fashion. They are fully endowed with all the protocols of a śramaṇa, maintaining correct deportment in every movement—whether going or coming, bending or stretching.

Yet they are constantly harmed by greed, anger, and ignorance; they are also harmed by gain, offerings, respect, and praise; and they are harmed by all afflictions, such as pride and overweening pride.

Though held in high esteem by others, he does not value the Dharma; he constantly exerts himself to adorn his body and craves food and drink, seeking not the noble Dharma and fearing nothing of the future world. He is respected in the present but not in the life to come; he merely increases his flesh and fat, relying on gain and offerings rather than relying on the Dharma.

Bound by various fetters, they diligently engage in domestic labor; following the inclinations of householders, they likewise undergo their experiences, suffering when there is suffering and enjoying pleasure when there is pleasure, being harmed by love and hatred.
Having no intention to practice the dharma of a śramaṇa and having abandoned all formal observances, such a person will inevitably fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
That person possesses neither the reality of a śramaṇa nor the title of a śramaṇa; they are not equal to a śramaṇa.
Kāśyapa! This is called a pseudo-śramaṇa. Kāśyapa!
"What is it that causes one to lose the vital energy of a śramaṇa?

Kāśyapa, it is like a man or a woman, or a boy or a girl, whose blood and vital energy are drunk by a non-human being; that person becomes emaciated and lacks physical vigor because they have lost their blood and vital energy."
Kāśyapa! Because such a person has lost their vital blood and energy, they cannot be cured by any medicines, incantations, or even by weapons; they will inevitably die.

Kāśyapa! Such śramaṇas lack the vital essence of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; they also lack the vital essence of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; furthermore, they lack the vital essence of practicing generosity, self-restraint, and guarding the actions of body, speech, and mind; they lack the vital essence of abiding in the four noble lineages; they lack the vital essence of ritual decorum; and they lack the vital essence of purifying body, speech, and mind.
Kāśyapa! This is called a śramaṇa who has lost his vital energy. Kāśyapa!
It is like a śramaṇa who has lost his blood and vital energy; though he receives the Dharma-medicine of the Tathāgata, he does not achieve liberation for himself.

As for this Dharma-medicine: if lust arises, one should contemplate impurity; if anger arises, one should practice loving-kindness; if delusion arises, one should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination. One should apply correct reflection toward all afflictions, abandon the delight in crowds, and relinquish all that belongs to the self.
The three matters of one who has left the household life should be cherished and protected.
These three matters are: maintaining pure precepts, taming the mind, and entering meditative concentration without distraction.
Kāśyapa! This medicinal Dharma, which I have taught and which I permit you to take, though you receive this medicine, you shall not attain liberation by means of it alone. Kāśyapa!

Furthermore, there are supramundane dharmas, namely: the contemplations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; knowledge of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the four noble truths; and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Kāśyapa! Even with such a medicine of the Dharma, that person likewise does not achieve self-deliverance. Kāśyapa!
Thus, this śramaṇa is foul-smelling, filthy, and impure; because he has violated the precepts and possesses meager merit, he is born in an extremely low place due to his arrogance.
When his life here ends, he will not be reborn elsewhere, but will certainly fall into the great hells.
Just as a person who has lost their vital blood and energy will certainly die, so too a śramaṇa who ends his life in this manner will necessarily fall into hell.
Kāśyapa, this is called the "blood-and-energy-depleted śramaṇa."
When he had spoken thus, five hundred bhikṣus abandoned the precepts and returned to lay life.
At that time, other bhikṣus rebuked those bhikṣus, saying:
"If the Venerable Ones retreat from the Buddha-dharma and return home, such as this is not good; such as this is contrary to the Dharma."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak such words. Why is that?"
If it is thus, it is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu does not wish to accept the faithful offerings of others and returns home, this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
Because those bhikṣus possessed much faith and understanding, they gave rise to a sense of remorse.
When these words were spoken, having heard them, they thought to themselves:
"We may have engaged in impure conduct while receiving the offerings of the faithful; we ought to feel remorse and withdraw to return home."
“Kāśyapa! I now declare that these bhikṣus, having passed away from this life, will be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven in the presence of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
When the Tathāgata Maitreya appears in the world, those bhikṣus shall be among the number of his first assembly.”
Chapter Four: The Chapter on the Bhikṣu Who Manages Affairs. At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how can a bhikṣu be capable of managing the affairs of the Saṃgha?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I permit two kinds of bhikṣus to manage communal affairs. Which two?
First, one is able to purely maintain the precepts; second, one fears the future life as much as one fears a vajra.
Furthermore, there are two other kinds. What are these two?
First, knowing and understanding the retribution of karma; second, possessing a sense of shame, dread of blame, and a mind of remorse.
Furthermore, there are two other kinds. What are these two?
The first is the arhat; the second is one who is able to cultivate the eight liberations.
Kāśyapa, regarding these two kinds of bhikṣus, I permit them to manage affairs without incurring any blemish.
Why is this? Kāśyapa, because it is difficult to guard the minds of others.

Kāśyapa! Within the Buddha-dharma, there are various forms of renunciation, various dispositions, various mentalities, various liberations, and various ways of severing the fetters. Some are forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), some are alms-seekers (piṇḍapātika), some delight in dwelling in mountain forests, and some delight in staying near villages while purely maintaining the precepts.

Some were able to transcend the four yokes; some diligently cultivated extensive learning; some eloquently expounded all dharmas; some were skilled in upholding the Vinaya precepts; some were skilled in maintaining the ritual procedures of the Vinaya; and some traveled through various cities and villages to preach the Dharma for others.
When there are such monks as these in the Saṃgha, the monk who manages affairs should skillfully discern the mental dispositions of these people. Kāśyapa,
if an araṇya-dwelling bhikṣu delights in secluded places, the monk who manages affairs should not command him to perform any labor or service.
Sometimes, when an araṇyaka bhikṣu is assigned labor duties within the order of bhikṣus, the administrative bhikṣu should perform them on his behalf.
If he does not do so himself, he should hire another person to act as his substitute.
One should not employ forest-dwelling bhikṣus in labor; however, if it is not a time for practicing the Way, one may have them perform a small amount of work. Kāśyapa!
If there is a bhikṣu who begs for alms, the bhikṣu who manages affairs should provide him with excellent food.
If there is a bhikṣu who is able to remain free from the four yokes, the bhikṣu who manages affairs should provide him with whatever he requires, namely: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.

In the dwelling place of a monk who has abandoned the yokes, a monk engaged in administrative affairs should not raise his voice or shout loudly, nor should he cause others to do so, for the sake of protecting the monk who has abandoned the yokes.
The *karmadāna* bhikṣu should conceive a sense of reverence toward the bhikṣu Vigatāṅgaṇa as if he were the Blessed One, and should give rise to this thought:
"Such a bhikṣu is able to act as a pillar of the Dharma within the Buddha's teachings; I shall provide him with whatever he requires."
"Kāśyapa! If there is a bhikṣu who diligently cultivates much learning, a bhikṣu who manages affairs should exhort him, saying:
'Venerable one, diligently cultivate much learning and recitation so that they become proficient; I shall provide for all the needs of the Venerable ones.'"

If the venerable ones diligently cultivate extensive learning, this is a fine ornament among the community of bhikṣus; they are able to ascend the high seat and extensively expound the True Dharma, thereby generating wisdom within themselves as well.
The *karmadāna* bhikṣu should not employ them at improper times, but should protect and support them so that they may cultivate extensive learning. Kāśyapa!

If there is a bhikṣu who expounds the Dharma, the *karmadāna* bhikṣu should provide him with all necessary supplies. He should lead the Dharma-expounding bhikṣu to cities, towns, and villages, exhorting the people to come and listen to the Dharma. He should also provide for the place where the Dharma is taught, arranging a fine and elevated seat for the Dharma-preacher.

If there is a bhikṣu who, by force of his own power, seeks to disrupt one who is preaching the Dharma, the bhikṣu in charge of affairs should go to mediate and reconcile them; he should also frequently visit the place of the Dharma-preacher and praise him, saying, "Excellent!"

Kāśyapa! If there is a bhikṣu who well upholds the precepts and well understands the meaning of the Vinaya, a bhikṣu engaged in administrative affairs should go to him frequently and inquire about the meaning:
"How may I manage affairs so that I do not incur offense, neither harming myself nor harming others?"

The bhikṣu who upholds the meaning of the Vinaya should observe the mind of the administrator of affairs and preach the Dharma to him in accordance with those affairs, namely: "This should be done; this should not be done."
A *karmadāna* bhikṣu should, with single-minded faith, pay homage and make offerings to those who uphold the Vinaya.

Regarding whatever property belongs to the Saṃgha, he should provide it to the Saṃgha at the appropriate time and must not hoard or withhold it. He should distribute according to what the Saṃgha requires; he should give when it is the proper time to give. He should give without malice, not give contrary to the Dharma, not give with desire, not give with anger, not give with delusion, and not give out of fear. He should act in accordance with the Saṃgha’s rules and not follow the ways of householders; he should act in accordance with the Saṃgha’s regulations and not act according to his own arbitrary rules.
One should not conceive the thought of ownership over the property of the Saṃgha; even for minor matters, one should decide them in consultation with the Saṃgha and not decide them independently.

Regarding the items used—namely, the permanent property of the Saṃgha, the property of the Buddha, or the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha of the four quarters)—that monk in charge of affairs should distinguish between them: the permanent property of the Saṃgha should not be given to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*, nor should the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* be given to the permanent property of the Saṃgha. The permanent property of the Saṃgha should not be mixed with the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*, nor should the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* be mixed with the permanent property of the Saṃgha.

The property of the permanently resident Sangha and the property of the Sangha of the four quarters must not be mixed with the property of the Buddha; likewise, the property of the Buddha must not be mixed with the property of the permanently resident Sangha or the property of the Sangha of the four quarters.

If the property of the permanent saṃgha is abundant while the saṃgha of the four quarters has a need, the *karmadāna* bhikṣu should convene the saṃgha, distribute voting sticks, and solicit their consent; if the saṃgha is in harmony, he should divide and bestow the property of the permanent saṃgha upon the saṃgha of the four quarters.

Kāśyapa! If there is something required for a Tathāgata’s stūpa, or if it is in a state of decay, and if the property of the permanent resident community (*saṃgha*) or the property of the universal community (*cāturdisa-saṃgha*) is abundant, the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* bhikṣu should assemble the community, distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*), and seek their consent, saying:
"This Buddha-stūpa is decaying; now there is a need for [repairs]."

The property of this permanent monastery and the property of the *caitya* (the Sangha of the four quarters) are abundant. Venerable Sangha, please listen: if it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, and if the Sangha does not begrudge these bestowed items—whether they be the property of the permanent monastery or the property of the *caitya* Sangha—I shall now take them to repair and maintain the Buddha-stūpa.
"If the Saṃgha is in harmony, the *karmadāna* (steward) bhikṣu should repair the Buddha-stūpa using the property of the Saṃgha.
If the Saṃgha is not in harmony, the *karmadāna* bhikṣu should exhort other laypeople to seek out wealth and materials to repair the Buddha-stūpa."

Kāśyapa! If there is a great abundance of the Buddha’s property, an administrative bhikṣu must not divide and distribute that property of the Buddha to the *sthavira-saṃgha* (the permanent community) or the *cāturmahārājika-saṃgha* (the universal community). Why is this?
Regarding these objects, one should conceive of them as belonging to the World-Honored One.

Every possession of the Buddha, even down to a single thread, was bestowed upon the Buddha by donors out of faith; therefore, gods and humans alike regard these items as stupas for the Buddha, let alone precious objects.

If one has previously offered a robe to a stūpa, that robe should rather be allowed to be blown away by the wind or rotted and destroyed by the rain within the stūpa; one must not trade this robe for precious objects.
Why is this? Because no one is able to place a price upon the property of a Tathāgata’s stūpa, and furthermore, because the Buddha has no need for anything. Kāśyapa!
For one who is such a person of pure and skillful administration, the property of the Triple Gem should not be allowed to become intermingled with their own.
Furthermore, they should always be content with their own gains and sustenance, never giving rise to the thought of ownership regarding the property of the Triple Gem.

Kāśyapa! If an administrative bhikṣu gives rise to a mind of anger toward a person of great virtue who maintains the precepts, yet because of his authority, he compels that person—who circumambulates and pays homage to him—to perform menial labor.
Therefore, because of the condition of their angry minds, monks who manage monastic affairs fall into the great hells.
If they should obtain a human birth, they become the slaves of others, constantly driven and coerced by their masters, and subjected to the lashings of those who employ them.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if a *karmadāna* bhikṣu,
acting out of self-will, establishes further heavy regulations that exceed the monastery's usual limits, and punishes bhikṣus by forcing them to work at improper times."
Because of these unwholesome roots, this monk who manages monastic affairs falls into the Small Hell of Many Nails.
Having been born therein, his body is pinned and stretched out with hundreds of thousands of nails; his body blazes intensely, emitting great flames like a massive conflagration.

If one speaks with a mind of anger to those of great virtue who uphold the precepts, using grave matters to intimidate them, that monk who manages affairs will be reborn in hell. There, his tongue shall be five hundred yojanas long, and it shall be pinned with hundreds of thousands of nails, from each of which great flames of fire erupt.

Kāśyapa! If a monk in charge of affairs repeatedly receives property belonging to the Saṃgha and, out of stinginess, hoards it; or if he gives it to the Saṃgha at an improper time, or gives it with difficulty, or gives it with hardship, or gives only a small portion, or does not give it at all; or if there are those to whom he gives and those to whom he does not.
Because of these unwholesome roots, the bhikṣu in charge of monastic affairs will fall among the foul and evil hungry ghosts who constantly eat balls of excrement.
When this person’s life ends, he shall be born therein; at that time, other hungry ghosts will show him food but will not give it to him.

At that time, this ghost, longing and desiring to obtain it, gazes intently at this food without blinking its eyes; yet, for hundreds of thousands of years, suffering the pains of hunger and thirst, he never obtains food. Should he occasionally obtain some, it turns into excrement and urine, or becomes pus and blood.

Why is this? Because there are those who maintain the precepts and are honored and saluted by others; since they have mastery over the property belonging to the Saṃgha, it is difficult for them to give it away. Kāśyapa!

If a bhikṣu in charge of monastic affairs arbitrarily misappropriates and uses the property of the resident saṃgha, the property of the saṃgha from the four quarters, or the property of the Buddha for his own purposes, he will receive a retribution of great suffering for one kalpa or more than one kalpa.
Why is this? Because they have misappropriated the property of the Triple Gem. Kāśyapa!
If a bhikṣu in charge of monastic affairs hears of such an offense or knows of such an offense, yet deliberately gives rise to a mind of anger toward one who upholds the precepts,
I declare now that this is something even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot cure.
Kāśyapa! Therefore, when a bhikṣu who manages affairs has heard of such unrighteous offenses, he should well protect the actions of his body, speech, and mind, protecting both himself and others.
“Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who manages affairs would rather eat his own flesh than ever use the property of the Triple Gem for clothing, bowls, food, or drink.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is truly unprecedented.

The Tathāgata himself, out of a heart of compassion, has preached such a Dharma: for those who lack shame and remorse, he preaches the Dharma of shamelessness and lack of remorse; for those who possess shame and remorse, he preaches the Dharma of shame and remorse.”
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sūtra, Volume 113 and Volume 114.
Translated by the Northern Liang śramaṇa Shi Daogong.
Chapter 44: The Assembly on the Jewel Banner; Chapter 5: On Aranyaka Bhiksus.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [The Blessed One]”
“World-Honored One! If there is a bhikṣu who calls himself an araṇyaka bhikṣu, to what extent is one called an araṇyaka bhikṣu?
To what extent is one called a piṇḍapātika bhikṣu?”
To what extent is one called a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes?
To what extent is one called a bhikṣu who dwells at the foot of a tree?
To what extent is one called a bhikṣu who dwells in a cemetery?
"To what extent, Kāśyapa, is one called a 'monk dwelling in the open air'?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"An araṇya-monk must delight in the araṇya and dwell in the araṇya."

Kāśyapa! If there is a forest hermitage that is free from loud noises and the clamor of crowds; where it is devoid of deer, wild boars, tigers, wolves, and various birds; and which is far removed from thieves, robbers, and those who tend cattle and sheep.
In accordance with the sphere of conduct for śramaṇas, one should practice in such forest hermitages (āraṇya).
If that bhikṣu wishes to go to a forest hermitage, he should contemplate eight dharmas.

What are the eight? First, I shall relinquish my body; second, I should relinquish my life; third, I shall relinquish gain and honor; fourth, I shall depart from all places of attachment and delight; fifth, I shall die among the mountains like a deer; sixth, in an araṇya, I shall practice the conduct of an araṇya-dweller; seventh, I shall sustain myself by means of the Dharma; eighth, I shall not sustain myself by means of afflictions.
Kāśyapa! These are called the eight dharmas that a forest-dwelling bhikṣu should contemplate; having contemplated them, he should go to a forest dwelling. Kāśyapa!

Once the forest-dwelling bhikṣu has reached the forest hermitage, he practices the dharma of the forest-dweller; by means of eight modes of practice, he cultivates loving-kindness and gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.

What are the eight? First, compassion that benefits; second, compassion that brings joy; third, compassion free from malice; fourth, correct compassion; fifth, impartial compassion; sixth, compliant compassion; seventh, compassion that contemplates all phenomena; eighth, compassion pure as space.
Kāśyapa! By means of these eight practices, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings. Kāśyapa!
Once an araṇya bhikṣu has reached an araṇya dwelling, he should reflect in this way:
"Although I have come to a remote place and am alone without a companion, if I practice what is wholesome or what is unwholesome, there is no one to instruct or reprove me."
Again, he thought: "There are the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who know my single-mindedness; they shall serve as my witnesses."
"I am now practicing the dharma of the araṇya here, yet my unwholesome mind does not attain mastery.

If I go to this most remote place—solitary, without companions, without those with whom I am intimate, and possessing nothing—I must now awaken to thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of malice; I must likewise awaken to all other unwholesome dharmas."

I should not now be no different from those who delight in crowds, nor should I be no different from those who dwell near villages; if I am thus no different, I would have deceived the devas, nāgas, and spirits, and even the Buddhas would not be pleased with me upon seeing me.
"If I now abide according to the dharma of an araṇya-dweller, then the devas, nāgas, and spirits will not reproach me, and when the Buddhas see me, they too will be joyful. Kāśyapa!

An araṇya bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya place practices the dharma of the araṇya: with single-minded persistence he upholds the precepts of liberation, skillfully guarding the assembly of precepts; he purifies body, speech, and mind, acting without flattery or deceit; he purifies his right livelihood and directs his mind toward the various meditative concentrations. In accordance with the Dharma as he has heard it, he should maintain mindfulness and diligently engage in right reflection, proceeding toward the renunciation of desire, tranquility, and nirvāṇa.
Fearing birth and death, one contemplates the five aggregates as enemies, the four great elements as venomous snakes, and the six sense bases as an empty village.

Skillfully knowing the means, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination to remain free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism; one contemplates the absence of sentient beings, self, persons, and life-force, understanding the characteristic of the emptiness of phenomena and practicing the signless, gradually diminishing conditioned activity while proceeding toward non-action.

The mind should always be filled with apprehension regarding conduct within the three realms; one should constantly and diligently practice as if one’s head were on fire, practicing with such vigor that one never regresses.

One should contemplate the true nature of the body and give rise to this mind to contemplate these dharmas: one must know the root of suffering, sever all accumulations, realize cessation, and diligently cultivate the path.

Practicing loving-kindness, they dwell securely in the four foundations of mindfulness; leaving unwholesome states, they enter the gateway of wholesome dharmas; dwelling securely in the four right efforts, they enter the four bases of psychic power and guard the five wholesome faculties, attaining mastery within the five powers.

He awakens to the seven factors of enlightenment, diligently practices the eightfold noble path, upholds meditative concentration, and uses wisdom to discern the characteristics of all phenomena. Kāśyapa!
I have taught such a Dharma to adorn the araṇya bhikṣu.

Having thus adorned himself, he dwells in the mountain forests; during the first and last watches of the night, he diligently cultivates all practices and should not sleep, constantly mindful of desiring to attain the supramundane Dharma.

Kāśyapa! Wherever an araṇya bhikṣu dwells, he should constantly practice the Path. He does not adorn his own body or his robes; he gathers dry, withered grass to use as a seat, employing it as his own sitting mat, and he remains detached from the property of the resident monastic community (saṃgha) and the universal monastic community (cāturmahārājika saṃgha).
In the forest hermitage (āraṇya), one should be content with clothing, obtaining only what is sufficient to cover the body for the sake of practicing the Noble Path. "Kāśyapa,
if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu goes to a city or village for alms, he should form this thought:
"I have come from the forest hermitage to this city or village; whether I obtain food or not, my mind shall be free from sorrow or joy.

If he does not obtain food, he should give rise to a joyful mind and reflect upon the retribution of past karma, thinking: "I must now diligently cultivate meritorious deeds," and further reflect that even the Tathāgata obtained no food when he went on his almsround.
When that forest-dwelling bhikṣu enters a city or village to beg for food, he should do so adorned with the Dharma; having been adorned with the Dharma, he may then beg for food.
What is the adornment of the Dharma?
If one sees a pleasing form, one should not become stained by attachment; if one sees an unpleasing form, one should likewise not give rise to anger.

If one hears a pleasing sound or an unpleasing sound, if one smells a pleasing fragrance or an unpleasing fragrance, if one tastes a pleasing flavor or an unpleasing flavor, if one touches a pleasing tactile object or an unpleasing tactile object, or if one encounters a pleasing phenomenon or an unpleasing phenomenon, the mind remains unstained and does not give rise to anger.

Guarding the sense-doors, he gazes only a yoke’s length ahead and subdues his mind; he does not allow the dharmas he has contemplated to depart from his mind, and he does not beg for alms with a defiled mind, but should practice sequential begging.
If one obtains food, one should not give rise to attachment; if one does not obtain food, one should not give rise to anger.
Whether one visits ten houses or more than ten houses and fails to receive food, one should not feel sorrow, but should instead form this thought:
"These householders and brahmins have many affairs and do not give me food."
"Furthermore, this householder and all these brahmins have never even conceived the thought, 'I [should give],' let alone 'give me food. Kāśyapa!
If an araṇya bhikṣu can be thus, he will not give rise to alarm or fear while begging for alms."

Kāśyapa! When an araṇya bhikṣu goes for alms, if he sees sentient beings—whether men, women, boys, girls, or even animals—he should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward them, thinking:
"I practice such diligence and make such vows."
"If sentient beings see me or receive food from me, they shall all be reborn in the heavens. Kāśyapa!

When a forest-dwelling bhikṣu receives coarse food or refined food, having accepted this food, he should look toward the four directions: "Who in this village or town is poor? I should set aside some of this food to give to them."

If one sees a poor person from whom one may beg for alms, one should immediately divide one's portion in half and give it to them. If one does not see such a poor person, one should generate this thought:
"For those sentient beings who are not seen by my eyes, I vow to bestow upon them the finest portions of the food I have obtained."
"I am the donor and he is the recipient. "Kāśyapa!

When an araṇya bhikṣu goes for alms and receives food, he carries it to his araṇya dwelling. Having washed his hands and feet, he maintains the pure conduct of a śramaṇa and fulfills all pure dharmas. Having taken grass according to the Dharma, he sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka). Once seated, he eats with a mind free from attachment and free from arrogance; he has no anger and no turbid or distracted mind."
When about to eat, one should reflect in this way:
"There are now eighty thousand families of worms within this body; these worms will all find peace and happiness by obtaining this food, and I now sustain these various worms with this food."
"When I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall gather [beings] through the Dharma.
Kāśyapa, furthermore, at times an araṇya bhikṣu may find his food insufficient; he should then form this thought:

"Now my body is light and I am able to practice patience; I have severed all evils and have little need for excrement or urine. Having attained lightness of body, I have also attained lightness of mind; furthermore, I sleep little and do not give rise to thoughts of desire."
"One should reflect in this way.
Kāśyapa! If a forest-dwelling bhikṣu receives much almsfood, he should give rise to the thought of contentment."
One should take a single morsel from the food and place it upon a clean stone, reflecting thus:
"There are birds and beasts capable of eating this; I give it to them, and they are the recipients."

"Kāśyapa! After the forest-dwelling bhikṣu has finished eating, he washes his bowl, rinses his mouth, and washes his hands. He thoroughly cleans his alms-bowl, wipes it dry with his hand, and then takes up his saṃghāṭī robe to proceed toward the forest dwelling, never departing from the Dharma-characteristics he had originally contemplated."

Kāśyapa! When a forest-dwelling bhikṣu practices the conduct of a forest dweller, if he is an ordinary person who has not yet attained the fruits of śramaṇaship, and if at times tigers or wolves come to his place, upon seeing them he should not give rise to fear. He should reflect thus:

"When I originally came to this forest dwelling, I already surrendered my body and life. I should not be startled or afraid; I should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, remain free from all evil, and remain free from fear."

If tigers or wolves should sever my life-root and devour the flesh of my body, I should give rise to this thought: "I have attained a great benefit; by means of this non-durable body, I shall obtain a durable body."
"I have not given food to these tigers and wolves; now that they have devoured my flesh, their bodies have attained peace and happiness. Kāśyapa!
An araṇya bhikṣu practicing the dharma of the araṇya should thus relinquish his body and life.

“Kāśyapa! When a forest-dwelling bhikṣu practices the dharma of the forest, if non-human beings—whether appearing in beautiful forms or in hideous forms—should come to his dwelling, he should harbor neither thoughts of attachment nor thoughts of aversion toward those non-humans.”
Kāśyapa! There may be certain devas who have previously seen the Buddha and come to the araṇya to pose various questions and challenges.
Having posed their questions and challenges, the araṇya bhikṣu explains the Dharma to those devas according to his own capacity and the teachings he has studied.
If at times the devas pose profound questions and the araṇya bhikṣu is unable to answer them, he should not give rise to a mind of pride, but should say:
"I am not learned; do not despise me."
"I shall now diligently practice and study the Buddha-dharma; once I have attained mastery of the Buddha-dharma, I will be able to answer all things.
Furthermore, one should exhort the devas:
"May you now preach the Dharma for me, and I shall listen and receive it with devotion."
Furthermore, one should express gratitude by saying:
"I pray that you do not disdain me. Moreover, Kāśyapa!
An araṇya bhikṣu practicing the dharma of the forest dweller should skillfully cultivate the perception of the forest.

Just as grass, wood, tiles, and stones have no owner, no self, and no belonging, so too is this body: it has no self, no life-principle, no person, and no sentient being; it is free from contention, for all such phenomena arise only from the conjunction of conditions.
If one reflects well upon this Dharma, I shall be able to sever all views; one should constantly contemplate the dharmas that are empty, signless, and wishless. Kāśyapa!
When a forest-dwelling bhikṣu practices the dharma of the forest, how do the medicinal herbs, grasses, and various groves come together,
and how do they disperse and perish?

In this way, external things have no owner, no self, and no sense of "mine," nor do they involve dispute; they arise spontaneously and perish spontaneously, yet there is no one who arises or perishes. Kāśyapa!

Just as grass, trees, tiles, and stones have no self, no master, and nothing to which they belong, so too is this body: it has no self, no life-force, no person, and no sentient being; it is free from dispute. It arises from a multitude of conditions and ceases when those conditions disperse. Within this reality as it truly is, there is not a single dharma that either arises or ceases.
Kāśyapa! Regarding such a Dharma as this, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu should practice it upon reaching a forest hermitage. Kāśyapa!

When an araṇyaka bhikṣu practices such a dharma, if he trains in the Śrāvaka-yāna, he will swiftly attain the fruits of śramaṇaship. Even if there are obstructing dharmas such that he does not attain the fruits of śramaṇaship in the present life, he will, after seeing no more than one, two, or three Buddhas, certainly succeed in severing all outflows (āsravas).

If one studies the Bodhisattva vehicle, they will attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the state of being free from obstructions in the present life; they will certainly behold the Buddhas of the future and swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When this "Chapter on the Aranyaka" was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus severed all outflows (*āsrava*) and their minds attained liberation.
**Chapter Six: The Bhikṣu Who Begs for Alms** The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
"How does a bhikṣu beg for alms?"
Kāśyapa! If there is a bhikṣu who has first established this fundamental vow:
"I have gone forth in reliance upon alms-gathering."
"I now abide by my former vow.
That bhikṣu, with single-minded mindfulness free from flattery and deceit, remains detached from all invitations to meals and detached from all offerings within the Saṃgha, firmly adorning himself.

A bhikṣu who begs for alms should not give rise to the perception of "delicious flavors" regarding any tastes. Furthermore, even when presented with exquisite food, he should exhort his own mind to form this thought:
"I am like a caṇḍāla; I should purify my body and mind, but I should not purify my food and drink."
Why is this? Because once fine food has been consumed, it all becomes excrement;
since it is foul, filthy, and impure, I should not seek fine food.
Having thus disciplined the mind, when entering cities, towns, or villages to beg for food in succession, one should not give rise to such thoughts:
"A man gives me food, not a woman; a woman gives me food, not a man; a young boy gives me food, not a young girl; a young girl gives me food, not a young boy."
One should obtain fine food, not coarse food; one should obtain excellent food, not inferior food.
At the proper time, one should be given food intentionally, not unintentionally; one should find food easily, not with difficulty; one should obtain food quickly, not slowly.

"When I enter a village, I should receive honor and not dishonor; I should obtain fresh food and not stale food; I should obtain food from wealthy families and not from poor families; and crowds of men and women should come out to welcome me."
"Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who begs for alms should not contemplate such unwholesome dharmas. Kāśyapa!"
A bhikṣu who begs for alms should thus adorn himself; this is the constant practice of one who begs for alms.
When begging for alms, whether he receives food or not, he should feel neither sorrow nor joy, and he should not give rise to the notion of food being coarse or fine.

Why is this? Because many sentient beings are greedily attached to delicious flavors; due to this attachment to flavor, they commit various evil karmas, and by reason of these evil karmas, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.

One who is content does not crave exquisite flavors; they should abandon fine food and accept coarse food, removing the tongue's attachment to taste so that the mind remains content. Even when obtaining extremely coarse food, one should remain satisfied.
If such a person should pass away, they will be reborn in the heavens or among human beings; having been born in the heavens, they will partake of celestial delicacies.
Kāśyapa, in this way, a bhikṣu who begs for alms is free from craving for flavors and has tamed his mind; even if he eats beans for seven days, he does not give rise to distress.
For what reason?
It is for the sake of sustaining the body; having eaten now, I am sufficient for the practice of the path. It is for this reason that I eat, Kāśyapa.

When a bhikṣu who begs for alms receives this portion of food that falls into his bowl—being obtained in accordance with the Dharma and being a righteous gain—he should eat this food together with fellow bhikṣus who practice the holy life.
Kāśyapa! If a bhikṣu who lives on alms should at times fall ill and have no one to assist him so that he is unable to go begging for food, he should thus discipline his mind:
"I am alone and without a companion; having gone forth as a single individual, the Dharma is my only companion, and I should keep the Dharma in mind."
Now that I am afflicted by the suffering of illness, as the World-Honored One has taught, the bhikṣus should attend to the Dharma.
Regarding the Dharma I have heard, I should reflect upon it well.
How should one reflect well?
"One contemplates the body as it truly is.
Having contemplated the body as it truly is, for one who possesses wisdom, it is possible that, being alone and single-minded, they may attain the first dhyāna.
Having attained the bliss of the first dhyāna, whether for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, they take dhyāna as their sustenance and their mind is filled with joy."
Kāśyapa! If a bhikṣu who begs for alms practices such dharmas and yet does not attain dhyāna, he should diligently practice and abide in wholesome dharmas in this manner.
Many people will know of him, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits will send food to him; this is because he has received the retribution for being free from the yokes.

Kāśyapa! If a bhikṣu who begs for alms encounters heavy rain or a great wind and dust such that he is unable to beg for food, at that time he should adorn himself by taking loving-kindness as his sustenance and dwell in contemplation upon the Dharma he practices.
If one is unable to eat for two or three nights, one should form this thought:

"There are many sentient beings who have fallen among the hungry ghosts; because they have committed evil karma, they are tormented by suffering so severe that they do not obtain even a single drop of saliva for as long as a hundred years."

Now that I abide within these various Dharma-gates, I should give rise to this thought: "Though my body and mind are weak and frail, I shall now endure hunger and thirst; I must diligently cultivate the Noble Path and must not regress."
"Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who begs for alms should not associate with householders—neither men nor women, nor boys nor girls. Kāśyapa!"
If a bhikṣu who goes for alms has a layperson remove all impure items from the food, he should sit at his seat and preach the Dharma to them.
Once the food has been purified and he has received it again, he should rise from his seat and depart.
Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who begs for alms should not manifest flattery.
What is meant by manifesting flattery?
If one speaks these words to others:
"I have now obtained coarse and poor food through begging, and moreover it is insufficient for me to share with many people;
I eat little, and I am now hungry and thirsty, my physical strength being weak and inferior."
"Kāśyapa! This is called self-displaying flattery. Kāśyapa!"
A bhikṣu who begs for alms should avoid such matters as these.
"Kāśyapa, a bhikṣu who begs for alms should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all things."
If food falls into the bowl—whether coarse or fine, whether small or large, whether pure or impure—one should accept it all with a mind free from both sorrow and joy.
One should always purify the mind and contemplate the characteristics of all phenomena; one partakes of food for the sake of sustaining the body in order to practice the Noble Path.

Kāśyapa, when a bhikṣu who begs for alms enters a city or village to beg in succession and departs with an empty bowl because he receives no food, he should reflect that the Tathāgata possesses great majestic virtue: having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch to go forth into homelessness, and having severed all unwholesome dharmas and accomplished all wholesome dharmas, He still entered villages to beg for alms and departed with an empty bowl.
How much less so for me, who am of little merit and have not planted roots of goodness—how could I return with an empty bowl?
Therefore, you should not give rise to sorrow. Why is this?
"It is impossible for one who has not planted roots of goodness to obtain coarse or fine food.
That I have not obtained food must be because either Māra himself, or one sent by Māra, or Māra’s concealment of the brahmins and householders has prevented me from obtaining alms."
I shall diligently cultivate the practice of remaining free from the four māras and severing all afflictions.
Once I have diligently cultivated this path, neither Māra Pāpīyān nor those sent by Māra will be able to create obstacles.
“Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who begs for alms should uphold the noble lineages in this way.
Chapter Seven: The Bhikṣu Who Wears Rags from Dustheaps. The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
“A bhikṣu who wears rag-robes should gather discarded items from refuse heaps with this reflection:

‘It is for the sake of shame and modesty, not for the sake of adorning myself with clothing; it is to ward off the wind, the sun’s heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, and other harmful contacts; it is to abide securely in the Buddha’s teaching, not out of a desire for purity or excellence; thus do I gather discarded things from amidst the refuse.’”
When receiving [alms], one should give rise to two kinds of thoughts.
What are these two?
First, the thought of contentment; second, the thought of being easy to support.
Furthermore, two perceptions arise:
first, the perception of being without pride; second, the perception of maintaining the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
Furthermore, two perceptions arise:
First, it is not for the purpose of adorning the body; second, it is to purify the mind.

Kāśyapa, when a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes picks up discarded items from among the refuse, if he sees his kinsmen or acquaintances at that place, he shall stop immediately and not take them, thinking thus:
"Kāśyapa! These people may rebuke me, saying: 'You are an impure person.'"
I say that this bhikṣu does not attain pure conduct. Why is this?
Because the mind of a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes is as firm as stone; external things cannot enter it, nor can they move it.

Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who wears rag-robes should pick up items from among the refuse, wash them thoroughly to remove all dirt and grease, and after washing, dye them well. Having dyed them, he should fashion them into a saṃghāṭī, joining the pieces skillfully, patching them skillfully, and sewing them skillfully. Once it is accepted, he should wear it so that it does not become torn or ruined.
Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who wears rag-robes and dwells in the contemplation of impurity wears rag-robes for the sake of abandoning desire.
He wears rag-robes with a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of abandoning hatred.
One wears the rag-robe while contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in order to abandon delusion;
one wears the rag-robe while engaging in right reflection in order to sever all afflictions.
One wears the refuse-rag robe to guard the sense faculties; one wears the refuse-rag robe to understand the six sense bases;
and one wears the refuse-rag robe without flattery or deceit, so as to bring joy to the devas, nāgas, and spirits.
Kāśyapa! For what reason is it called "rag-robe" (pāṃśukūla)? Kāśyapa!
It is like dead ashes, which people do not covet and for which they do not give rise to the thought of "mine"; by nature, they should be discarded. Kāśyapa!

Likewise, these rag-robes are neither "I" nor "mine. They are easily obtained, are not acquired through wrong livelihood, are not sought from others, and do not require observing the facial expressions of others.
Things discarded are no different from refuse; they belong to no one, and for this reason they are called "rag robes" (pāṃśukūla).
Kāśyapa! Rag robes are the banner of the Dharma, because they belong to the Great Sages.
This is a lineage, because it belongs to the noble ones.
This is a state of abiding, because it is the noble heritage.
This is focused mindfulness, because it is the ritual practice of wholesome dharmas.
This is well-guarded because of the aggregate of ethical discipline;
this is the gateway because of the aggregate of concentration;
this is the secure abiding because of the aggregate of wisdom.
This body is for the sake of the assembly of liberation;
this is conformity with the Dharma, for the sake of the assembly of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Kāśyapa!
In this way, one who wears rag-robes gains great merit; having nothing to seek and nothing to crave, they are able to abandon arrogance and cast off the heavy burden. Kāśyapa!
If there is a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes out of contentment, the devas, nāgas, and spirits will long to see him with joy.

Kāśyapa! When a bhikṣu wearing rag-robes enters meditative concentration, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings kneel, join their palms, and prostrate themselves before him; how much more so for other minor deities.

Kāśyapa! If there are wicked bhikṣus who diligently seek clothing to adorn their bodies, appearing outwardly to practice pure conduct while inwardly being fully possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Although he thus adorns his body with such fine ornaments, the devas, nāgas, and spirits do not come to him to pay homage or offer worship.
Why is this? Because it is known that this bhikṣu diligently seeks clothing to adorn his body, yet does not remove the defilements of the mind and mental factors.
Because the devas knew [of his intent], they departed from afar. "Kāśyapa!
You saw the śrāmaṇera Cunda picking up impure, foul-smelling, and filthy items from a dust-heap; having finished his alms-round, he went to Lake Anavatapta, wishing to wash them."
At that time, there were resident devas by the side of the pond who all came from afar to welcome him, bowing their heads to the ground in salutation.

Those devas, being fond of cleanliness, took the impure rag-robe held by the śrāmaṇera Cunda and washed it until it was free of filth; they then took the wash-water and used it to bathe their own bodies.

The devas know that Cunda is able to maintain the pure precepts, enters into various meditative absorptions, and possesses great majestic virtue; for this reason, they welcome him, pay homage, and prostrate themselves before him. Kāśyapa!

When you saw the brahmin Subhadra, having dressed in clean garments after begging for alms, intending to go to the Great Anavatapta Lake, the ever-abiding devas stationed themselves on all four sides of the lake at a distance of five li each, far off obstructing the brahmin so that he could not approach the lake, fearing that his impure food or leftover scraps would defile this great lake.
Kāśyapa! You now see this with your own eyes: it is through the power of the noble ones’ correct practice that such a fruit is obtained.
Whatever impure items of refuse-rag cloth the śrāmaṇera Cunda possesses, the devas take them to wash, and they also wash their own bodies with the washing water.
The brahmin Subhadra was kept five li away from the pond and not allowed to approach it.
Kāśyapa! Who, having heard this, would not diligently practice and study within the Noble Dharma?
All those noble ones, devas, and people of the world come to pay homage with their heads at his feet, to revere and make offerings to him.
Kāśyapa! It is because he seeks such noble virtues that he wears robes made of discarded rags.

Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who wears rag-robes and dwells securely in the noble lineages should not give rise to anxiety. Regarding rag-robes, he should conceive of them as a stūpa, as the World-Honored One, as that which transcends the world, and as being without self or what belongs to a self. Having contemplated in this way, he should wear the rag-robes and thus discipline his mind.
Because the mind is pure, the body attains purity; it is not because the body is pure that the mind attains purity.
Kāśyapa! Therefore, you should purify the mind and not adorn the body.
Why is this? Because the mind is pure, one is said to possess the "holy life" (brahmacarya) within the Buddha-dharma. Kāśyapa!
If a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes can train in this way, he trains as I have trained and as you have trained.
Kāśyapa! If you can wear such coarse robes, you will then practice contentment and live according to the noble lineages.

Kāśyapa! Whether your saṃghāṭī is placed upon a bed or at your seat, or while you are walking in meditation wearing your uttarāsaṅga, ten million devas will pay homage to that saṃghāṭī; for this saṃghāṭī is the garment that covers the body, perfumed by morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Kāśyapa! You should know that even your robe deserves such respect and veneration; how much more so, then, your own person? Kāśyapa!

I have renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and study the Way; I have already put on all my former fine, superior, and exquisite silken garments, head-dresses, fine cotton cloths, and various other magnificent robes.
I now practice contentment within the noble lineages; for the sake of others, I have cast aside fine garments and wear robes from cemeteries.
If future bhikṣus hear this teaching of mine, they will immediately be able to follow my example.
Kāśyapa! You originally possessed an upper garment of golden thread; I requested it from you, and you brought it to me. Kāśyapa!
Out of compassion for you, I have accepted it from you; it was not out of greed, nor for the sake of adorning my body. Kāśyapa! There are wicked bhikṣus who neither learn from me nor learn from you;

they are shrouded by greed, accumulating many robes and bowls, hoarding food and drink, and storing them away without relinquishing them. They also keep gold, silver, lapis lazuli, grain, rice, oxen, sheep, chickens, pigs, donkeys, horses, carriages, plows, and all other implements required for a household livelihood, seeking to possess them all.
Kāśyapa! A person of wisdom, though remaining at home, can increase wholesome dharmas; a foolish person who has left the household life cannot attain such a portion of goodness.
How is it that a person of wisdom, while at home, can cause wholesome dharmas to increase?

Kāśyapa! If there are those who have left the household life and wear the saṃghāṭī draped around their necks, yet lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and are preoccupied with many worldly affairs, being bound by various attachments as they seek fine food and clothing.

Once they have donned the kashaya, householders see them and pay homage, provide them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, and come and go to welcome and escort them. Kāśyapa!
Householders may attain such wholesome dharmas,
but those who have gone forth do not possess them. Why is this?
Because those renunciants seek many things for themselves and are unable to give to others.

Kāśyapa, in the future there will be bhikṣus who store up many robes and bowls and possess many goods; at that time, those bhikṣus will be frequently seen by householders receiving their salutations, respect, veneration, and praise.
Why is this? It is because that bhikṣu has received many offerings from others or holds them for me, and whenever I have need, he is able to give them to me at the proper time. Kāśyapa!

There may be a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, perceives the faults and afflictions of the world, and diligently cultivates wholesome dharmas to abandon all outflows as if his head were on fire; his mind is contented, he has few worldly concerns, and he diligently cultivates self-benefit while remaining free from all habitual conditions for evil.
Yet that bhikṣu has no one who goes to his place, no one who approaches him, and no one who pays him homage, respects, honors, or praises him.
Why is this? Because those householders are fickle and shallow; they see the benefits of the present life but do not see the benefits of future lives.
Those householders will give rise to such thoughts:
"No benefit is to be gained from this bhikṣu; what is the use of associating with him?
What is the use of paying homage, honoring, or praising him?"
“Except for those who are impoverished and possess few roots of goodness, or those whose past conditions dictate that they should pay respect; Kāśyapa!
Such people as these will draw near to, prostrate to, honor, and praise the precept-keeping bhikṣus, taking them as their spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).”
Kāśyapa! Having spoken thus, it accords with the minds of two kinds of people. Which two?
First, seeing the Four Noble Truths; second, seeing the faults and perils of birth and death.
Furthermore, there are two more:
first, diligently practicing with the desire to abandon the four yokes; second, desiring to attain the fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, there are two:
first, to focus one's mindfulness on karmic retribution; second, to desire to know the characteristics and meanings of all phenomena. Kāśyapa!

I now shut the gates of all those who are indolent—namely, those who do not understand karma and do not understand the retribution of karma; those who have abandoned virtuous conduct; those for whom the faults of future lives appear as adamantine as they do not see them; those who see the benefits of the present life but do not see the benefits of future lives; and those who do not give rise to even a single thought directed toward the gate of liberation.
Kāśyapa! I now say that such evil bhikṣus should not be expected to encounter such a teaching, nor to hear such a Dharma being expounded.

Having heard this Dharma, they recognize their own conduct; yet, failing to understand the profound Dharma, they slander it, claiming, "This was not spoken by the Buddha; it was composed by a master of treatises," or "It was spoken by Māra," and they use this to instruct others.
That evil bhikṣu thus harms himself and also harms others; he defiles himself with impurities and also defiles others.
Such an evil bhikṣu is unable to benefit himself, nor can he benefit others.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Just as all Buddhas, out of great compassion, have spoken of the bhikṣu who practices with single-minded devotion and attains mastery over all dharmas, the Tathāgata has already explained this at length in this sutra.”

"Bhagavān! If there are sentient beings who, having heard this sutra, believe, understand, read, and recite it while turning toward the Dharma as it truly is, you should know that these sentient beings have already been taken into the care of all the Buddhas."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"If there are those who receive and uphold this sutra, because they have already planted various roots of goodness under previous Buddhas, they now desire to obtain this sutra and master it through reading and recitation, and they desire liberation. These are good men and good women, whether they are practitioners of the homeless life or practitioners living at home; this Dharma-gate can sever all outflows (āsrava) and also lead to nirvāṇa."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to receive and uphold this sutra.”
"What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is titled 'The Selection of All Precious Dharmas,' and it is also titled 'The Ritual for Abiding in the Noble Lineages,' and also titled 'The Gathering of Those Who Uphold the Precepts,' and also titled 'The Severing of Those Who Break the Precepts,' and also titled 'Jewel Peak,' and also titled 'Jewel Gathering,' and also titled 'Jewel Treasury,' and also titled 'The Dharma Gate of All Jewels.'"

When Mahākāśyapa had finished questioning on the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, the Jewel Peak (Ratnaśikhara), the assembly of bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Scroll 114; Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Scroll 115.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Assembly of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, the Forty-fifth.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there were also ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present, namely:
Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner, Dharma Banner, Moon Banner, Sun Banner, and Boundless Banner.
Furthermore, there were sixteen lay bodhisattvas, with Bhadrapāla as their leader.
There were also sixty bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of incomparable mind, with Mañjuśrī as their leader.
Furthermore, there were all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, with Maitreya Bodhisattva as their leader.
There were also sixty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with Akṣayamati Bodhisattva as their leader.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet. He scattered various precious flowers over the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called "bodhicitta," for what reason is it called bodhicitta?
By how many factors does a bodhisattva further accomplish bodhicitta?
And what is this bodhicitta?

The bodhicitta cannot be apprehended within the mind, nor can the mind be apprehended within the bodhicitta; apart from the bodhicitta it cannot be apprehended, and apart from the mind the bodhicitta also cannot be apprehended.
Awakening is without form and without marks, and is ineffable; the mind likewise is without form and without marks, and cannot be demonstrated; sentient beings are also thus, for all are ungraspable.
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are thus, by what principle should one practice?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Listen attentively now.
That which I call ‘bodhi’ is fundamentally without name or verbal expression.”

Why is this? Because within awakening (bodhi), names and verbal expressions cannot be apprehended; the same applies to the mind and sentient beings. To know them in this way is to know the bodhicitta.
Enlightenment is neither past, future, nor present; likewise, the mind and sentient beings are also neither past, future, nor present. One who understands this meaning is called a bodhisattva.
Yet, even therein it cannot be apprehended; since there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended among all phenomena, this is called "attaining the bodhicitta.

It is like an arhat who attains the fruit of arhatship, yet therein there is absolutely nothing to be attained—except for the conventional expression that one has attained the fruit, for regarding all phenomena, there is nothing whatsoever to be attained.

Attaining the bodhicitta is likewise thus: for the sake of attracting and gathering beginner bodhisattvas, the bodhicitta is taught; yet within it, there is no mind and no name of "mind," no enlightenment and no name of "enlightenment," no sentient beings and no name of "sentient beings," no śrāvakas and no name of "śrāvakas," no pratyekabuddhas and no name of "pratyekabuddhas," no bodhisattvas and no name of "bodhisattvas," no Tathāgatas and no name of "Tathāgatas," no conditioned phenomena and no name of "conditioned phenomena," no unconditioned phenomena and no name of "unconditioned phenomena," and neither present attainment nor future attainment.

"Good son! I now expound this according to conventional expression: if there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are vast and surpass all others, like Mount Sumeru rising above everything, the initial arousal of the mind for them is the cause for the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)."
Just as the great earth is well able to sustain all undertakings, this second generation of the bodhicitta serves as the cause for the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

With courageous resolve, one accepts afflictions with composure; like a lion king who subdues all beasts with its majesty and remains free from fear, this third generation of the bodhicitta serves as the cause for the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

Possessing power and swiftness, it is able to subdue the afflictions, just as Nārāyaṇa crushes and subdues opposing hosts; this fourth arousal of the mind is the cause for the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*).

The various roots of merit and goodness unfold like the blossoming flowers of the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees; this fifth arousal of the mind is the cause for the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā).

Dispelling the darkness of ignorance, it is like the solar disc whose radiance is boundless; this sixth production of the thought of enlightenment is the cause for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Its meritorious intentions and all adornments are fully perfected, like a great caravan leader who possesses abundant wealth and is able to extricate beings from perilous difficulties through skillful means; this seventh production of the thought of enlightenment is the cause for the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*).
With hindrances eliminated and the mental disposition fully perfected like the pure full moon, this eighth resolve is the cause for the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).

With all buddha-fields and sentient beings thoroughly purified, and with wholesome qualities complete so that all tasks are accomplished—like a poor person finding an inexhaustible treasury and having their aspirations fulfilled—this ninth resolve is the cause for the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

With merit and wisdom as boundless as space, possessing mastery over all phenomena like a consecrated universal monarch, this tenth arousal of the mind serves as the cause for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

"Good son! If one cultivates and achieves these ten kinds of arousal of the mind, they are called a bodhisattva; they are called a most excellent being, an unobstructed being, and a being who is not inferior."
However, because the ultimate reality cannot be apprehended, within it there are no sentient beings, no mind, and no bodhi.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving, ten factors are primary:

first, the faculty of faith; second, the power of faith; third, the resolute intention (*āśaya*); fourth, the superior resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*); fifth, benefiting sentient beings; sixth, great loving-kindness (*maitrī*); seventh, great compassion (*karuṇā*); eighth, practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); ninth, delighting in the Buddha-dharma; and tenth, seeking omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). These are the ten.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), ten dharmas are foremost:

first, purity of physical action; second, purity of verbal action; third, purity of mental action; fourth, the absence of a mind of enmity or harm; fifth, the purification of the evil destinies; sixth, the distancing from the eight adversities; seventh, transcending the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; eighth, abiding securely in the merits of a Buddha; ninth, fulfilling all aspirations; and tenth, accomplishing the great vows."
These are the ten.
Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience, he takes these ten dharmas as primary:

First, abandoning anger and hatred; second, not being attached to the body; third, not being attached to life; fourth, faith and understanding; fifth, maturing sentient beings; sixth, the power of loving-kindness; seventh, the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma; eighth, the patient acceptance of the profound Dharma; ninth, the vast and supreme patient acceptance; tenth, destroying the darkness of ignorance. These are the ten.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), ten dharmas are foremost: first, acting in accordance with whatever sentient beings do;

second, constantly generating sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind; third, being free from indolence; fourth, striving for progress; fifth, cultivating right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*); sixth, cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*); seventh, destroying the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*); eighth, observing all phenomena (*dharma*); ninth, bringing all sentient beings to maturity; and tenth, seeking omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."
These are the ten.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva practices the dhyāna-pāramitā, they take ten dharmas as primary:

First, abiding securely in wholesome dharmas; second, the mind taking a single object as its focus; third, attaining meditative equipoise through that focal object; fourth, right concentration; fifth, dhyāna and liberation; sixth, the faculty of concentration; seventh, the power of concentration; eighth, destroying the enemies of the afflictions; ninth, the perfection of the accumulation of concentration; tenth, the samādhi of protecting the Dharma. These are the ten.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, ten dharmas are foremost:

first, skillfully observing the aggregates; second, skillfully observing the elements and sense bases; third, right view; fourth, right mindfulness; fifth, thorough knowledge of the noble truths; sixth, relinquishing all views; seventh, the faculty of wisdom; eighth, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena; ninth, the power of wisdom; and tenth, unobstructed gnosis."
These are the ten.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of skillful means, these ten dharmas are foremost:

First, entering into the mental activities and inclinations of all sentient beings; second, exerting power over all sentient beings; third, great loving-kindness and great compassion; fourth, maturing sentient beings without weariness; fifth, relinquishing the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; sixth, superior wisdom and vision; seventh, practicing the various pāramitās; eighth, contemplating all phenomena as they truly are; ninth, encompassing inconceivable powers; tenth, the stage of non-retrogression. These are the ten.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of power, ten dharmas are foremost:

First, knowing the dense forest of the mental activities of all sentient beings; second, knowing the dense forest of the afflictive activities of all sentient beings; third, knowing the dense forest of the activities of the inclinations and resolutions of all sentient beings; fourth, knowing the dense forest of the activities of the faculties of all sentient beings; fifth, knowing the dense forest of the activities of the various elements of all sentient beings; sixth, knowing the dense forest of the activities of the secondary afflictions of all sentient beings; seventh, knowing the dense forest of the activities of birth and death of all sentient beings; eighth, knowing the dense forest of the activities of karmic retribution across the three times of all sentient beings; ninth, knowing the dense forest of the activities of habitual tendencies and afflictions of all sentient beings; tenth, maturing the activities of the faculties of all sentient beings with a mind free from weariness. These are the ten.
"Good son! The bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of vows has ten dharmas as its foremost:

first, knowing that all phenomena are unborn; second, knowing that all phenomena are signless; third, knowing that all phenomena are unceasing; fourth, knowing that all phenomena are non-existent; fifth, having no attachment to any phenomenon; sixth, knowing that all phenomena have no coming; seventh, knowing that all phenomena have no going; eighth, knowing that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; ninth, knowing that all phenomena are equal in having no beginning, middle, or end; and tenth, having no discrimination regarding the beginning, middle, or end of any phenomenon."
These are the ten.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, these ten dharmas are foremost:

First, being well able to thoroughly understand and discern all phenomena; second, being well able to bring the white dharmas (*śukladharma*) to full completion; third, accumulating the immeasurable provisions of a bodhisattva; fourth, accomplishing the vast provisions of merit and wisdom; fifth, the perfection of great compassion; sixth, entering various differentiated worlds; seventh, entering the afflictive conduct of all sentient beings; eighth, applying the mind to enter the realm of the Tathāgata; ninth, entering the supreme realm of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-dharmas; tenth, receiving the position of empowerment and accomplishing the most excellent marks of omniscience. These are the ten.
“Good son! These are the ten dharmas that serve as the foremost for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the ten pāramitās.
Furthermore, good son!”
What is the meaning of *pāramitā*?
It refers to clearly demonstrating the transcendence of all practices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the vast and perfect wisdom of the Tathāgata;
non-attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned; and knowing birth as it truly is.
Because they have transcended death; because they cause all who have not yet awakened to awaken; because they attain the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible treasury of Dharma;
because they attain unimpeded liberation; because they deliver all sentient beings through the perfection of giving;
because they fulfill their original vows through the perfection of ethical discipline; and because they possess the marks of sublime beauty through the perfection of patience.
Because diligence brings all Buddha-dharmas to ultimate fulfillment; because meditative concentration gives rise to the four immeasurables;
because wisdom eradicates all afflictions; because skillful means accumulate all Buddha-dharmas;
because vows can cause the Buddha-dharmas to reach perfection; because powers can cause sentient beings to attain pure faith; and because...
Because they are endowed with the wisdom of a Tathāgata’s omniscience; because they have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
because they have attained the stage of non-retrogression; because they have purified Buddha-fields; because they have brought sentient beings to maturity;

because they have perfected all the wisdom of the Tathāgatas at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); because they have subdued all Māras; and because they traverse by means of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Therefore, because one abides in neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; because one transcends all the merits of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
because one subdues all heterodox disputants; because one accomplishes the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma);
because one realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); and because one turns the [wheel of Dharma]—ten...
Because there are two kinds of wheels of Dharma,
all such things as these constitute the meaning of the *pāramitās*.
"Furthermore, son of good family!..."

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is about to dwell in the first stage, the Stage of Joy, there is first this sign: he sees all the hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of treasures hidden within the trichiliocosm.

When a bodhisattva is about to dwell in the second stage, the Stainless, there is first this sign: they see the ground of the trichiliocosm as level as the palm of a hand, adorned with the pure splendor of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of jewel lotuses.

When a bodhisattva is about to dwell in the third stage, the Luminous (Prabhākārī), there first appears this sign: he sees himself clad in armor, holding a staff, courageous and steadfast, subduing his enemies.

When a Bodhisattva is about to dwell in the fourth stage, the Radiant (*Arciṣmatī*), this premonitory sign first appears: he sees winds blowing from the four directions, scattering various kinds of named flowers upon the ground.

When a Bodhisattva is about to dwell in the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*), this premonitory sign first appears: he sees women with their heads adorned with garlands of *atimuktaka*, *pāriyātrika*, and *campaka* flowers, and wearing various kinds of ornaments upon their bodies.

When a Bodhisattva is about to dwell in the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), there first appear these signs: he sees a lotus pond filled with the water of eight virtues, clear and pure, its bottom strewn with golden sand and adorned with four stairways of jewels. Furthermore, within the pond he sees *utpala*, *padma*, and *kumuda* flowers, as well as *puṇḍarīka* flowers serving as ornaments; he further sees his own body sporting therein.
When a bodhisattva is about to dwell in the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā, there is first this sign: they see hell on both their left and right sides, yet they pass beyond it without being harmed.

When a Bodhisattva is about to dwell in the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), there first appears this sign: he sees his own two shoulders adorned with the marks of the lion king, such that all other beasts are struck with terror.

When a bodhisattva is about to dwell in the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), there first appears this sign: he sees himself as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) teaching and transforming others through the True Dharma, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kings, with various jewel-adorned, pure white parasols held over the bodhisattva’s head.
