When a Bodhisattva is about to dwell in the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), there first appears this sign: he sees his own body as the color of pure gold, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), with a halo extending one fathom, seated upon a high and broad lion throne, surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Brahmās, who pay him respectful homage and offerings while listening to his preaching of the Dharma.
“Good son! By the power of samādhi, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifests such preliminary signs of the ten stages.
Furthermore, good son!”

Bodhisattvas of the first stage fulfill the perfection of giving; Bodhisattvas of the second stage fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; Bodhisattvas of the third stage fulfill the perfection of patience; Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage fulfill the perfection of diligence; Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage fulfill the perfection of wisdom; Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage fulfill the perfection of skillful means; Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage fulfill the perfection of power; Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage fulfill the perfection of aspiration; and Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage fulfill the perfection of knowledge.

"Furthermore, noble son! When a bodhisattva first generates the mind of awakening, they attain the *ratnābhāsa* samādhi; with the second generation of the mind, they attain the *susthitā* samādhi; with the third, the *acala* samādhi; with the fourth, the *avaivartika* samādhi; with the fifth, the *ratnapuṣpa* samādhi; with the sixth, the *sūryamaṇḍalāvabhāsa* samādhi; with the seventh, the *sarvārthasiddha* samādhi; with the eighth, the *jñānolkā* samādhi; with the ninth, the *pratyakṣabuddhadharma* samādhi; and with the tenth generation of the mind, they attain the *śūraṅgama* samādhi."

"Furthermore, noble son! In the first stage (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva attains the *dhāraṇī* of supreme empowerment; in the second stage, the *dhāraṇī* of invincibility; in the third stage, the *dhāraṇī* of excellent abiding; in the fourth stage, the *dhāraṇī* of indestructibility; in the fifth stage, the *dhāraṇī* of stainlessness; in the sixth stage, the *dhāraṇī* of the lamp of the wheel of wisdom; in the seventh stage, the *dhāraṇī* of supreme conduct; in the eighth stage, the *dhāraṇī* of pure discernment; in the ninth stage, the *dhāraṇī* that manifests infinite dharma-gates; and in the tenth stage, the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma."

At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Unobstructed Radiance Lion Banner (*Anāvaraṇaprabha-siṃhadhvaja*). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous, Sugata!
This Dharma-gate is so profound and vast that it is able to encompass all Buddha-dharmas.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Lion Banner of Unobstructed Radiance, saying:
"It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
Son of good family!
If there is a bodhisattva who can even briefly listen to and receive this Dharma-gate, they will certainly not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? Because those sons and daughters of good family have previously planted various roots of goodness and have brought those roots of goodness to maturity; thus they are able to hear such a sutra as this, for they are sealed by this sutra.
"Good son! If there are men or women who hear this sutra, all the roots of goodness they have planted will become completely pure.
They shall attain the non-abandonment of seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings to the Sangha, and they shall bring sentient beings to maturity."
He does not abandon the *sāgaramudrā-dhāraṇī*; he attains the *anantaprabhavā-aparityāga-dhāraṇī*; he attains the *sattvāśayacaritapraveśa-aparityāga-dhāraṇī*;
he attains the *vimalasūryaprabhāketu-dhāraṇī*; and he attains the *vimalacandraprabhāketu-dhāraṇī*.
The bhikṣuṇī attained the dhāraṇī of never abandoning the cessation of all fetters;

she attained the dhāraṇī of never abandoning the destruction of boundless afflictions as firm as a mountain of diamond; she attained the dhāraṇī of never abandoning the discourse that enters the equal nature of phenomena;
she attained the dhāraṇī of never abandoning the entry into the sounds and voices of true speech.
He attained the dhāraṇī of the seal of infinite purity manifesting like space, which is never to be abandoned;
he attained the dhāraṇī of the manifestation of the infinite bodies of Buddhas, which is never to be abandoned.

"Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes such dharanis, he can manifest the body of a Buddha in all lands throughout the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings; yet, within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is neither coming nor going, nor is there any teaching or transforming of sentient beings."

Regarding the Dharma that is taught, they do not cling to words, remaining equanimous and unmoving; although they manifest birth and death within saṃsāra, there is no arising or ceasing, nor is there even the slightest phenomenon that comes or goes. They thoroughly understand that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are originally quiescent and abide in the Buddha-dharma.
"Why is this? Because all those dharmas are without discrimination.

When this Dharma was being taught, thirty thousand bodhisattvas among the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); immeasurable bodhisattvas obtained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); and immeasurable bhikṣus attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, along with the bhikṣus, the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

46. The Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Exposition of Prajñāpāramitā, Part One of the Forty-sixth Chapter of the Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, translated by the Liang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering a full thousand.
There were ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all adorned with the great adornments and each having already established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression.
Their names were:
Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Unobstructed Eloquence Bodhisattva, and Not Abandoning the Burden Bodhisattva; together with such great bodhisattvas as these.
When the first light of dawn appeared, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta came from his dwelling place to where the Buddha was staying and stood outside.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, and other such great śrāvakas, each came from their respective dwellings together to where the Buddha was staying and stood outside.
When the Buddha knew that the assembly had all gathered, the Tathāgata emerged from his dwelling, arranged his seat, and sat down. He addressed Śāriputra:
"For what reason are you standing outside the gate at this early hour?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva arrived here earlier and has been standing outside this gate; it was only later that I arrived in the evening.”
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Mañjuśrī,
“Did you truly arrive at this dwelling place first, wishing to see the Tathāgata?
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
I have indeed come here desiring to see the Tathāgata.
For what reason?
I delight in right contemplation for the benefit of sentient beings.

I contemplate the Tathāgata as having the mark of suchness (tathatā) without marks of difference, the mark of immovability without marks of activity, the mark of non-arising and the mark of non-cessation, the mark of neither existence nor non-existence, the mark of neither abiding in a direction nor departing from a direction, being neither of the three periods of time nor not of the three periods of time, neither dualistic nor non-dualistic, and neither defiled nor pure. By means of such right contemplation of the Tathāgata, I benefit sentient beings.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If one can see the Tathāgata in this way—the mind neither grasping nor not grasping, neither accumulating nor not accumulating."
At that time, Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“If one can see the Tathāgata in the manner you have described, it is truly rare.”
One beholds the Tathāgata for the sake of all sentient beings, yet the mind does not grasp at the mark of sentient beings;
one transforms all sentient beings toward nirvāṇa, yet likewise does not grasp at the mark of tending toward nirvāṇa;
one gives rise to great adornment for the sake of all sentient beings, yet the mind does not perceive the mark of adornment.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra:
“So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.”
Although they don the great armor for the sake of all sentient beings, their minds never perceive the mark of a sentient being;
although they don the great armor for the sake of all sentient beings, the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.

Suppose a single Buddha remains in the world for an eon or more than an eon; and suppose that in this same Buddha-world there are likewise immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each of whom preaches the Dharma day and night without ceasing for even a moment, for an eon or more than an eon, each delivering immeasurable beings—numerous as the sands of the Ganges—into nirvana, yet the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.

Even so it is throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; each and every Buddha preaches the Dharma to teach and transform others, delivering immeasurable beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges into nirvana, yet there is neither increase nor decrease in the realm of sentient beings.
"Why is this? Because a fixed characteristic of sentient beings cannot be apprehended; therefore, the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.
Śāriputra spoke again to Mañjuśrī, saying:

"If the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases, for what reason do bodhisattvas seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings and constantly practice the preaching of the Dharma?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If all sentient beings possess the characteristic of emptiness, then there would be no bodhisattva seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor would there be any sentient beings for whom one might preach the Dharma.”
"Why is this? Because within the Dharma I teach, there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"If there are no sentient beings, how can one speak of the existence of sentient beings and the realm of sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied,
"The characteristic of the realm of sentient beings is like the realm of the Buddhas."
He asked again:
"Is the realm of sentient beings finite? He replied:
"The measure of the realm of sentient beings is equal to the measure of the realm of the Buddhas.
He asked again:
"Does the measure of the realm of sentient beings have a location?"
He replied: "The measure of the realm of sentient beings is inconceivable.
He asked again:
"Does the characteristic of the realm of sentient beings abide? He replied:
"Sentient beings have no abiding; they abide like space."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“When practicing the prajñāpāramitā in this manner, how should one abide in the prajñāpāramitā? Mañjuśrī replied:
"To dwell in the perfection of wisdom by means of non-dwelling dharmas.
The Buddha again asked Mañjuśrī:
"In what way is non-dwelling in dharmas called dwelling in the perfection of wisdom?"
Mañjuśrī said: "By means of the mark of non-abiding, one abides in the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha again addressed Mañjuśrī:
“When one abides in this manner within the *prajñāpāramitā*, how do these roots of goodness increase?
How do they diminish? Mañjuśrī replied:

"If one can abide in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, there is neither increase nor decrease in any roots of goodness, nor is there any increase or decrease in any phenomena; likewise, the nature and characteristics of this *prajñāpāramitā* are also without increase or decrease."
World-Honored One!
Practicing the prajñāpāramitā in this way, one neither abandons the dharmas of ordinary beings nor grasps the dharmas of the noble ones. Why is this?
In the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive any dharma that can be grasped or abandoned.
Practicing the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, one likewise does not perceive nirvāṇa as something to be delighted in, nor saṃsāra as something to be loathed.

Why is this? Because they do not perceive birth and death, how much less could they feel weary of or seek to leave them; because they do not perceive nirvāṇa, how much less could they delight in or become attached to it.

Practicing the prajñāpāramitā in this way, they do not perceive any defilement or affliction to be abandoned, nor do they perceive any merit to be grasped; regarding all phenomena, their mind neither increases nor decreases.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the dharma-realm as having increase or decrease.
World-Honored One!
If one can act in this way, it is called the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
Not perceiving that any phenomena have arising or ceasing—this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Bhagavān! Not seeing any phenomena as having increase or decrease is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā. Bhagavān!"
When the mind has no desire for grasping and does not perceive any characteristic of phenomena as something to be grasped, this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
One does not see beauty or ugliness, does not give rise to notions of high or low, and does not engage in grasping or rejecting.

Why is this? Because phenomena have neither beauty nor ugliness, as they are free from all marks; phenomena have neither high nor low, as they are equal in their dharmatā; phenomena have neither acceptance nor rejection, as they abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
"This is the cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Are these dharmas of the Buddhas not unsurpassed?"
Mañjuśrī said: "I do not perceive any phenomenon as having the characteristic of superiority or inferiority.
That the Tathāgata has personally realized that all phenomena are empty is something that can be verified and known."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "So it is, so it is.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has personally realized the dharma of emptiness."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Within this dharma of emptiness, can any distinction of superiority or inferiority be found?"
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
"Is that which you have spoken the true Dharma?
He then addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Anuttara is the name for the Buddha-Dharma."
Mañjuśrī said: "As the Buddha has taught, 'Anuttara' is the name for the Buddha-dharma. Why is this so?"
"No dharma can be named 'Anuttara'. Mañjuśrī said:

"To practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner is not called being a vessel for the Dharma; it is neither the method for transforming ordinary beings, nor is it the Buddha-dharma, nor is it a method of increase—this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive any dharma that can be conceptually distinguished or contemplated.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you not contemplate the Buddha-dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, "No."
World-Honored One, as I contemplate it, I do not perceive the Buddha-dharma, nor can it be differentiated:
"this is the dharma of ordinary persons," "this is the dharma of śrāvakas," or "this is the dharma of pratyekabuddhas. It is precisely in this way that it is called the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive the characteristics of ordinary beings, does not perceive the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma, and does not perceive any fixed characteristics in all phenomena; this is what constitutes practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive the desire realm, one does not perceive the form realm, one does not perceive the formless realm, and one does not perceive the realm of cessation.
Why is this? Not perceiving any dharma as having the characteristic of exhaustion or cessation is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, when cultivating the *prajñāpāramitā*, not perceiving one who bestows a favor and not perceiving one who repays a favor, contemplating these two aspects with a mind free from discrimination—this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive any Buddha-dharma to be grasped, nor does one perceive any dharma of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to be abandoned; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive any dharmas of ordinary beings that are to be extinguished, nor does one perceive the dharmas of the Buddhas; yet the mind realizes and knows them—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “Excellent, excellent!

You have been able to thus skillfully explain the characteristics of the profound Prajñāpāramitā. This is the Dharma-seal (dharmamudrā) in which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train; even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—whether those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—should likewise not depart from this seal when cultivating the fruits of the path.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If there are those who, upon hearing this Dharma, are neither startled nor terrified, they have not merely planted roots of goodness under a thousand Buddhas; rather, having long cultivated the foundations of virtue under hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, they are then able to remain neither startled nor terrified by this profound Prajñāpāramitā.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall now further explain the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said, “Speak then.
“World-Honored One! [he replied.]

When practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive any dharma as something in which one should abide or from which one should refrain; nor does one perceive any objective sphere characterized by that which is to be grasped or abandoned. Why is this?

Just as all Tathāgatas do not perceive the marks of the objective realm of any phenomena, they do not even perceive the realm of the Buddhas, let alone grasp at the realms of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or ordinary beings.

They do not grasp at the mark of the conceivable, nor do they grasp at the mark of the inconceivable; they do not perceive that dharmas possess various marks. Having personally realized the inconceivable dharma of emptiness, such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have already made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and planted all manner of roots of goodness; thus, they are neither startled nor terrified by this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one perceives neither bondage nor liberation; yet, regarding ordinary beings up to those of the three vehicles, one does not perceive any marks of differentiation—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“How many Buddhas have you already made offerings to? Mañjuśrī replied:
“I and all Buddhas are like illusory transformations; I see neither the offering nor the recipient.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “Do you now not abide in the Buddha-vehicle?”
Mañjuśrī said, “As I contemplate it, I do not perceive even a single dharma; how, then, could I abide in the Buddha-vehicle?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Have you not attained the Buddha-vehicle? Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Buddha-vehicle is merely a name; it cannot be obtained, nor can it be seen.
How then could I obtain it? The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!
"Have you attained unimpeded wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I am myself unimpeded; how could that which is unimpeded attain what is unimpeded?"
The Buddha asked,
"Do you sit at the site of enlightenment? Mañjuśrī replied:
"All Tathāgatas do not sit upon the site of enlightenment; how then could I alone sit upon the site of enlightenment?
Why is this? Because I perceive that all phenomena abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
The Buddha asked,
“What is called the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)? Mañjuśrī replied:
“The view of a self and so forth are the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
The Buddha asked:
“In what way is the view of a self the limit of reality?”
Mañjuśrī said: "The view of a self is like the mark of suchness;
it is neither real nor unreal, neither coming nor going, and neither a body nor not a body—this is called the limit of reality."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one has attained definitive and certain realization regarding this meaning, such a person is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”

"Why is this? Because they are able to hear the characteristics of such profound *prajñāpāramitā* without their minds being startled, terrified, submerged, or regretful. Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
To hear such Prajñāpāramitā and to be fully endowed with its characteristics of the Dharma is to be near the seat of the Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has directly awakened to these characteristics of the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one hears this profound Prajñāpāramitā and is able to be neither startled, nor terrified, nor submerged, nor regretful, you should know that such a person is one who beholds the Buddha.”
At that time, there was also the laywoman Viśākha, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Whether it be the dharmas of ordinary persons, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all these dharmas are without marks (animitta). For this reason, regarding the Prajñāpāramitā from which one hears it, one is in no way startled, terrified, cowed, or regretful.”
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are fundamentally without marks.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing such profound Prajñāpāramitā, attain certainty of mind and are not startled, not terrified, not despondent, and not regretful, you should know that these persons abide in the stage of non-retrogression."

If a person, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is neither startled nor terrified, but listens with faith and joy, receiving it without weariness, they are thereby fully endowed with the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, they are able to reveal and analyze it for others, practicing according to what has been taught.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“By observing what meaning do you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and in what do you abide within *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
Mañjuśrī said: "I have not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Since I do not abide in the Buddha-vehicle, how could I ever attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"What I have spoken is precisely the characteristic of bodhi.
The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You are able to skillfully explain this meaning within this most profound Dharma.
You have long planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas, and you have purely cultivated the Brahma-faring through the dharma of signlessness."

Mañjuśrī said: "If one perceives signs, one speaks of signlessness; yet I now perceive neither signs nor signlessness. How, then, can you say that one purifies the holy life by means of the dharma of signlessness?"
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you perceive the precepts of the śrāvakas? He replied:
“I see it. The Buddha asked, “How do you see it?”

Mañjuśrī said: “I do not form the view of an ordinary person, nor do I form the view of a noble one; I do not form the view of one in training, nor do I form the view of one beyond training; I do not form the view of greatness, nor do I form the view of smallness; I do not form the view of the disciplined, nor do I form the view of the undisciplined; I neither see nor do I not see.”
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, “If you now contemplate the Śrāvaka Vehicle in this manner, how would you contemplate the Buddha Vehicle?”
Mañjuśrī said, “I do not perceive the dharma of a bodhisattva, nor do I perceive one who practices for awakening or realizes awakening. Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī:
“What is meant by ‘Buddha,’ and how does one contemplate the Buddha? Mañjuśrī replied:
"What is meant by 'self'? Śāriputra replied, "The 'self' exists only as a name; the characteristic of a name is empty."
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is. Just as I have only a name, the Buddha also has only a name."
The emptiness of the characteristics of names is itself bodhi; one does not seek bodhi by means of names.
The characteristic of bodhi is beyond words and beyond description. Why is this?
Because both speech and bodhi are empty.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, as to your question regarding what is called a Buddha and how one contemplates a Buddha: that which is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither name nor sign—this is called a Buddha.
"Just as one contemplates the true reality of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha;
only the wise are able to know this, and this is called 'contemplating the Buddha. *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Scroll 115 [and] Scroll 116.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa of the Liang Dynasty.
The Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Exposition of Prajñā, Part Two of Forty-Six.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā as spoken by Mañjuśrī is not something that can be understood by a bodhisattva who is a beginner. Mañjuśrī said:
"Not only is this beyond the comprehension of novice bodhisattvas, but even those of the two vehicles who have completed their tasks are likewise unable to fully understand it.
Thus, there is no one capable of knowing such a teaching of the Dharma."
Why is this? Because regarding the characteristic of bodhi, there is truly no dharma that can be known. It is without seeing and without hearing;

without attainment and without thought; without arising and without ceasing; without speaking and without listening. Thus, the nature and characteristics of bodhi are empty and quiescent; it is without realization and without knowledge, without form and without marks. How, then, could there be one who attains bodhi?
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, “Does the Buddha not realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the dharma-realm? Mañjuśrī replied:
"No, Śāriputra! Why is that?
The World-Honored One is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
If one were to realize the dharma-realm by means of the dharma-realm, that would constitute a contentious dispute. Śāriputra!
The characteristic of the dharma-realm is itself bodhi.
Why is this? Because within this dharma-realm there is no characteristic of a sentient being, and all dharmas are empty.
The emptiness of all phenomena is itself bodhi, because it is non-dual and without discrimination.

Śāriputra, within non-discrimination there is no knower; if there is no knower, there is neither speech nor discourse. The absence of the characteristics of speech and discourse is neither existence nor non-existence, neither knowing nor not knowing.
All phenomena are likewise thus. Why is this?
Because all phenomena have no location, due to their definitive nature.
The characteristics of such an offense as this are inconceivable. Why is this?
Because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena cannot be destroyed.
Likewise, these heinous crimes have no intrinsic nature; they do not arise in the heavens, nor do they fall into hell, nor do they enter nirvana.
Why is this? All karmic conditions abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); they neither come nor go, and they are neither cause and effect nor not cause and effect.
Why is this? Because the dharma-realm is boundless, having neither beginning nor end. Therefore, Śāriputra!
If one sees that a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense does not fall into hell, and a practitioner of pure conduct does not enter nirvāṇa—
such a bhikṣu is neither worthy of offerings nor unworthy of offerings, neither one who has exhausted outflows nor one who has not exhausted outflows.
"Why is this? Because one dwells in equanimity toward all dharmas. Śāriputra said:
“What is called the patience of non-retrogression? Mañjuśrī replied,
“Not perceiving even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of arising or ceasing is called the patience of non-retrogression.”
Śāriputra asked, "What is meant by a 'monk who is not disciplined'? Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Arhat whose outflows are exhausted is called ‘untamed.
Why is this? Because all fetters have been extinguished and there is nothing further to be tamed, he is therefore called ‘untamed.’”
If one's mental activity exceeds [the proper measure], they are called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Why is this?
Because ordinary beings do not accord with the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is called "exceeding."
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent!
You have now skillfully explained for me the meaning of 'Arhat' as one whose outflows are exhausted."
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is.
I am indeed a true Arhat whose outflows are exhausted."

Why is this? Because he has severed the desire for the state of a śrāvaka and the desire for the state of a pratyekabuddha; by these causes and conditions, he is called an Arhat who has attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"When the bodhisattvas sit upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), do they awaken to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Mañjuśrī replied, "When bodhisattvas sit upon the seat of enlightenment, there is no awakening to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? Because, according to the nature of bodhi, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Since bodhi is signless (*animitta*), who could sit upon it, and likewise, who could rise from it?
"For this reason, one does not see a bodhisattva sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), nor does one perceive the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Awakening is the five heinous crimes, and the five heinous crimes are awakening.
Why is this? Because awakening and the five heinous crimes have no dual characteristics.
Without thought and no thinker, without vision and no seer, without cognition and no cognizer, without discrimination and no discriminator—such characteristics are called bodhi.
Seeing the signs of the five heinous crimes is likewise so; if one says they see bodhi and thereby realize it, you should know that such people are those of overweening pride.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"When you say, 'I am the Tathāgata,' do you also consider me to be the Tathāgata? Mañjuśrī replied:
"No, World-Honored One! I do not consider the Tathāgata to be a 'Tathāgata'."
There is no characteristic of suchness that can be named "suchness," nor is there any Tathāgata-knowledge capable of knowing suchness.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata and knowledge are without dual characteristics.
“Emptiness is the Tathāgata; it exists only as a name. How then could I say that this is the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “Do you doubt the Tathāgata?”
Mañjuśrī said: “No, World-Honored One.”
"I observe that the Tathāgata has no determinate nature; being without birth and without cessation, I have no cause for doubt.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, "Do you not now say that the Tathāgata appears in the world?"
Mañjuśrī said, "If a Tathāgata appears in the world, the entire dharma-realm should likewise appear.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you say that the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have entered nirvana? Mañjuśrī replied,
"The single characteristic of all Buddhas is inconceivable."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “So it is, so it is.
The Buddha is of one mark, the inconceivable mark.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does the Buddha now abide in this world?”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, “So it is, so it is. Mañjuśrī said:
"If the Buddha remains in the world, the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges should likewise remain in the world.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas possess the same single characteristic—the inconceivable characteristic—and that which is the inconceivable characteristic is neither born nor extinguished."
If all future Buddhas appear in the world, all Buddhas likewise appear in the world. Why is this?
Within the inconceivable, there are no marks of past, future, or present; it is only because sentient beings grasp at them that they speak of an appearance in the world or of a Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“This is what is understood by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and irreversible Bodhisattvas. Why is that?
"These three kinds of people, upon hearing the profound Dharma, are able neither to slander it nor to praise it.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Since it is thus inconceivable, who would disparage it,
and who would praise it?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The Tathāgata is inconceivable, and ordinary beings are also inconceivable.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Are ordinary beings also inconceivable?
The Buddha said,
"They are also inconceivable."
"Why is this? Because all mental characteristics are inconceivable. Mañjuśrī said:
"If it is said that the Tathāgata is inconceivable, then ordinary beings are also inconceivable.
Now, the countless Buddhas who seek nirvāṇa are merely exhausting themselves in vain."
"Why is this? Because the inconceivable dharma is itself nirvāṇa; they are equal and without distinction. Mañjuśrī said:

"In this way, the inconceivability of ordinary beings and the inconceivability of the Buddhas can only be understood by good sons and good daughters who have long cultivated roots of goodness and drawn near to virtuous friends."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you wish for the Tathāgata to be the most supreme among all sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied:
“I wish to cause the Tathāgata to be the most supreme among all sentient beings, yet even the mark of a sentient being cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said,
“Do you wish to cause the Tathāgata to attain the inconceivable Dharma?”
Mañjuśrī said: “One would wish for the Tathāgata to attain the inconceivable Dharma, yet there is no accomplishment regarding any dharmas.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do you wish for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha, "I do wish for the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings; yet, both this preaching and the listener are ultimately unattainable."
Why is this? Because they abide in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
There is no distinguishing characteristic between the dharma-realm and sentient beings.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Do you wish for the Tathāgata to be the unsurpassed field of merit? Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Tathāgata is an inexhaustible field of merit, an inexhaustible characteristic; this inexhaustible characteristic is the unsurpassed field of merit.
It is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit; it is called a ‘field of merit.’”
Being devoid of such characteristics as light and darkness, arising and ceasing, and so forth, this is called the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
If one can understand the characteristics of the field of merit in this way, then even when planting seeds of goodness deeply within it, there is neither increase nor decrease.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“In what way are the seeds planted neither increasing nor decreasing? Mañjuśrī replied:

“The characteristics of the field of merit are inconceivable; likewise, it is inconceivable when a person cultivates goodness therein according to the Dharma. Planting seeds in such a manner is called ‘neither increasing nor decreasing,’ and it is also the unsurpassed, most supreme field of merit.”
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the great earth shook in six ways, manifesting the signs of impermanence.

Sixteen thousand people all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); seven hundred bhikṣus, three thousand upāsakas, forty trillion upāsikās, and sixty quadrillion nayutas of devas from the six desire realms became free from dust and removed of stains, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions does this great earth tremble in six ways?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I have taught that the characteristics of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) are without distinction; therefore, I manifest this auspicious sign.
In the past, the Buddhas of former ages also spoke thus regarding the characteristics of the field of merit at this very place to benefit sentient beings, and all worlds shook in six ways."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! Mañjuśrī is inconceivable.”
"Why is this? Because the characteristics of the Dharma that have been taught are inconceivable. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Just so, just so. As Śāriputra has said, what you have spoken is truly inconceivable.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The inconceivable is ineffable, and the conceivable is also ineffable; thus, both the nature of the conceivable and the inconceivable are ineffable.”
“The characteristics of all sounds are neither conceivable nor inconceivable.
The Buddha said,
“Have you entered the inconceivable samādhi?”
Mañjuśrī said, “No, World-Honored One.”
I am indeed inconceivable.

Since I do not perceive any mind capable of conceiving or deliberating, how can it be said that I have entered the inconceivable samādhi? When I first resolved to enter this concentration, I now reflect that, in reality, there is no characteristic of mind by which I enter samādhi.
It is like a person learning archery: through long practice they become skilled, such that later, even without conscious intent, their arrows invariably hit the mark because of that long training.

I am also like this: when first learning the inconceivable samādhi, I bind my mind to a single object; once long practice has brought it to fulfillment, there is no further mental activity, and I am constantly in a state of meditative concentration.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, “Is there yet another samādhi of sublime and wondrous quiescence? Mañjuśrī replied:
"If there were such a thing as an inconceivable concentration, you might ask whether there is yet another concentration of cessation.
As I understand it, even an inconceivable concentration cannot be found; how then can one ask if there is a concentration of cessation?"
Śāriputra asked, "Is it that the inconceivable samādhi cannot be apprehended? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Concentrative absorption that is conceivable has the characteristic of being attainable; concentrative absorption that is inconceivable has the characteristic of being unattainable.
All sentient beings truly accomplish inconceivable concentrative absorption."
Why is this? Because all mental characteristics are themselves not mind; therefore, it is called the inconceivable samādhi.
For this reason, the characteristics of all sentient beings and the characteristics of the inconceivable samādhi are equal and without distinction.
The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have long planted roots of goodness under various Buddhas and purified your brahmacarya; thus you are able to expound this profound samādhi.”

"Do you now abide in this prajñāpāramitā? Mañjuśrī replied, "If I were abiding in prajñāpāramitā while being able to speak thus, that would be to have a conceptualization; I would then be abiding in the notion of a self."
If one dwells within the perception of existence or the notion of a self, then the Prajñāpāramitā would have a locus.
If the Prajñāpāramitā dwells in non-existence, that too is the notion of a self and is likewise called a locus.
Free from these two positions, one dwells in non-dwelling, abiding as all Buddhas abide: peacefully established in cessation, a realm beyond conceptual thought.
Such inconceivability is called the dwelling place of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In the sphere of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all phenomena are without marks (*animitta*) and all phenomena are without activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

The *prajñāpāramitā* is itself the inconceivable; the inconceivable is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); the dharma-realm is without marks; that which is without marks is the inconceivable; and the inconceivable is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the dharmadhātu; they are non-dual and without distinction.
That which is non-dual and without distinction is the dharmadhātu; the dharmadhātu is signlessness (animitta); signlessness is the realm of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The realm of prajñāpāramitā is the inconceivable realm; the inconceivable realm is the realm of neither arising nor ceasing; and the realm of neither arising nor ceasing is the inconceivable realm.
Mañjuśrī said: “The realm of the Tathāgata and my own realm are non-dual in nature.
One who cultivates the prajñāpāramitā in this manner does not seek awakening.”
Why is this? Because the characteristic of bodhi is dissociated from it, which is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
World-Honored One.
If one knows the mark of self yet does not cling to it—being without knowledge and without clinging—this is the inconceivable knowledge of the Buddha.
To be without knowledge and without clinging is precisely what the Buddha knows.
Why is this? Because one knows that the essential nature has no marks of existence; how, then, could it transform the dharma-realm?
If one knows that the essential nature is without substance and without attachment, it is termed "non-thing."

If there is no entity, it is without location, without support, and without abiding; being without support and without abiding is precisely the absence of arising and ceasing; and the absence of arising and ceasing is precisely the merit of both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
If one knows in this way, then there is no mental conception.
One who has no mental conception—how could they know of conditioned or unconditioned merits?

This lack of knowing is the inconceivable. That which is inconceivable is what the Buddha knows; it is neither grasping nor non-grasping. One does not perceive the marks of the three periods of time, such as going and coming, nor does one grasp at arising and ceasing or any formative activities. Furthermore, it is neither annihilation nor permanence.

One who knows in this way is said to possess right knowledge and inconceivable knowledge; like space, it is without "this" or "that" and cannot be compared, being without good or evil, without equal or unequal, and without marks or features.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
“If one knows in this way, it is called non-retrogressive wisdom. Mañjuśrī said:
"Non-active wisdom is called non-retrogressive wisdom.
It is like gold ore: only after it has been subjected to hammering does one come to know its quality; if it is not refined through striking, no one can know it."

The characteristics of non-retrogressive wisdom are likewise thus: they manifest only when one acts within the sphere of objects without recollection or attachment, without arising or fabrication, fully possessing immovability, and neither born nor extinguished.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“If the Tathāgatas were to speak of their own wisdom themselves, who would be able to believe it? Mañjuśrī replied:

"In this way, the wise one neither possesses the dharma of nirvana nor the dharma of saṃsāra; this is the practice of quiescence, the practice of immovability, which neither abandons nor does not abandon greed, hatred, and delusion."

Why is this? Because it is neither exhausted nor extinguished; it is not separate from birth and death, yet it is not not separate; one does not cultivate the path, yet it is not that one does not cultivate the path. One who forms such an understanding is said to possess right faith.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: “Excellent, excellent!
It is as you have said; you have deeply understood this meaning.”
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In a future age, if such a profound and true Dharma is preached, who will be able to believe and understand it, and receive and practice it as they have heard?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“Those among the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās in this assembly who have heard this sutra—such persons as these will, in future ages, if they hear this Dharma, certainly be able to believe and understand it; they will be able to read, recite, believe, understand, accept, and uphold the profound Prajñāpāramitā, and will also be able to analyze and expound it for others.”
For example, it is like a householder who, having lost a maṇi jewel, suffers with grief and distress; yet if he later recovers it, his heart is filled with great joy.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, it is for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who possess a mind of faith and delight: if they do not hear the Dharma, they give rise to suffering and distress.
If, upon hearing it, one believes, understands, accepts, and upholds it, constantly delighting in its recitation and study with great joy,
you should know that such a person is seeing the Buddha and is likewise drawing near to and making offerings to all Buddhas.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"It is like when the buds of the pārijātaka tree first appear in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; upon seeing this tree, all the devas therein are filled with great joy, for they know that before long this tree will surely blossom."

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās hear this Prajñāpāramitā and are able to give rise to faith and understanding, it will be just the same for them; before long, these people shall also cause all Buddha-dharmas to bloom and flourish.

In future ages, there will be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, will believe, accept, read, and recite it with minds free from regret or despondency. You should know that such persons have already heard and received this sūtra from this assembly; they are also able to explain and propagate it widely for others in villages and cities. You should know that these persons are protected and remembered by the Buddha.

Within this profound Prajñāpāramitā, those sons and daughters of good family who are able to believe and delight in it with minds free from doubt and uncertainty have long since practiced and studied under past Buddhas and have planted all manner of roots of goodness.
It is like a person who, while stringing beads with their hands, suddenly encounters a supreme, true maṇi jewel and feels great joy in their heart;
one should know that this person must have seen such a jewel before.
In this same way, Kāśyapa,

if a son or daughter of good family who has been practicing other teachings suddenly hears the profound Prajñāpāramitā and is able to give rise to joy, it should be known that this person likewise has heard it in the past.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, are able to believe and accept it with hearts full of great joy, such persons as these have also previously attended upon countless Buddhas and have practiced and studied it after hearing the Prajñāpāramitā.

For example, suppose there is a person who first sees from afar a city or a village; later, they hear others praising that city, saying that its gardens, various ponds and springs, flowers, fruits, groves, and trees, as well as its men and women, are all delightful and worthy of affection.

Upon hearing this, the person was filled with great joy and further urged [the Buddha] to describe the city’s gardens and groves, adorned with every excellence: various flowers, ponds, and springs; many sweet fruits; and all manner of rare, wondrous, and delightful things.
When such people hear this, they are filled with profound joy, for they have all seen [the Buddhas] in the past.

If good sons or good daughters hear the Prajñāpāramitā, receive it with faith, and are able to give rise to joy, delighting in hearing it without weariness and further encouraging others to explain it;
"You should know that these individuals have previously heard such profound *prajñāpāramitā* from Mañjuśrī.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If, in a future age, sons or daughters of good family hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, believe in it, delight in it, and receive it with devotion, one should know by these signs that such persons have also heard, studied, and practiced it in the presence of past Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha has taught that all dharmas are without action, without marks, and supremely quiescent.”

If a son or daughter of good family can thus clearly understand this meaning and speak it as they have heard it, they will be praised by all Tathāgatas; such speech does not contravene the characteristics of dharmas, and is therefore the word of the Buddha and is also "blazing."
"The characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* is also called 'blazing'; it is fully endowed with the Buddha-dharmas, penetrates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and is inconceivable.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I cultivated all roots of goodness; desiring to abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*; desiring to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."

If good sons or good daughters wish to understand the characteristics of all phenomena and wish to know that the mental realms of all sentient beings are entirely equal, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Mañjuśrī! Those who wish to study all Buddha-dharmas so as to fulfill them without obstruction should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who wish to study all the marks and signs, majestic deportment, and immeasurable ritual methods of all Buddhas when they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to know how all Buddhas do not fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and [to understand] all ritual methods and modes of deportment, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because within these dharmas of emptiness, one does not perceive the bodhi of the Buddhas and so forth.
If good sons or good daughters wish to know such characteristics as these without doubt or confusion, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this? Because in the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not perceive any phenomena as arising or ceasing, nor as defiled or pure; therefore, sons and daughters of good family should train in the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner.
If one wishes to know that all phenomena lack the characteristics of past, future, and present, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of the dharma-realm do not exist within the three periods of time.
If one wishes to know that all phenomena enter equally into the dharma-realm with a mind free from obstruction, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to attain the wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects, and likewise to realize it for oneself without grasping or attachment, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to attain a mind of loving-kindness that pervades all sentient beings without limit or partiality, yet does not form the notion of a mark of "sentient being," one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to not give rise to contentious debate regarding any sentient being, nor even to grasp at the mark of "non-contention," one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to know the ten powers and the fearlessnesses concerning what is possible and what is impossible, and to abide in the Buddha’s wisdom to attain unimpeded eloquence, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! I contemplate the True Dharma as unconditioned and signless;

it is without attainment and without benefit, without arising and without ceasing, without coming and without going. There is no knower, no seer, and no doer. I do not perceive the Prajñāpāramitā, nor do I perceive the realm of the Prajñāpāramitā. It is neither realization nor non-realization; it is free from conceptual proliferation and devoid of discrimination. All dharmas are inexhaustible and transcend exhaustion; there is no dharma of ordinary beings, no dharma of śrāvakas, and no dharma of pratyekabuddhas. The Buddha-dharma is neither attained nor unattained; it does not abandon saṃsāra and does not realize nirvāṇa; it is neither conceivable nor inconceivable, neither created nor uncreated.”
“Since the characteristics of dharmas are thus, how should one study the Prajñāpāramitā?
At that time, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If one can understand the characteristics of all dharmas in this way, this is called studying the Prajñāpāramitā.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to study the Samādhi of Sovereignty over Bodhi, and having attained this samādhi, desires to illuminate all profound Buddha-dharmas, know the names of all Buddhas, and fully comprehend all Buddha-worlds without obstruction, they should train in the Prajñāpāramitā as taught by Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, for what reason is it called ‘Prajñāpāramitā’?
The Buddha said:

“The Prajñāpāramitā is boundless and limitless, nameless and signless; it is beyond thought, without refuge, without island or shore, without transgression and without merit, without darkness and without light. Like the dharmadhātu, it has no boundaries and no finite number; this is called the Prajñāpāramitā.”

It is also called the sphere of practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is neither a sphere of practice nor a non-sphere of practice, for all are entered into the One Vehicle and thus termed a "non-sphere of practice. Why is this?
"Because it is without thought and without action.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should one practice to be able to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!..."
By practicing as taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one can swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there is the *Ekavyūha Samādhi*; if a son or daughter of good family cultivates this samādhi, they too will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
what is meant by the ‘samādhi of one practice’?”
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma-realm is of a single characteristic; to bind one's conditions to the Dharma-realm is called the Samādhi of One Practice.

If good men or good women wish to enter the Samādhi of One Practice, they must first hear the Prajñāpāramitā and practice and study according to its teachings; only then can they enter the Samādhi of One Practice."
As with the conditions of the dharma-realm, it is non-retrogressive, indestructible, inconceivable, unimpeded, and signless.

Sons and daughters of good family who wish to enter the Samādhi of One Practice should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and not grasp at appearances. They should bind their minds to one Buddha, single-mindedly reciting that Buddha’s name; following the direction of that Buddha, they should sit upright and face toward him, being able to maintain the mindfulness of that one Buddha continuously from thought to thought.
Within this very mindfulness, one is able to see all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Why is this? Because the merit of mindfulness of a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, and it is no different from the merit of immeasurable Buddhas.

The inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are equal and without discrimination; all ride upon the one suchness to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, fully possessing immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence.
One who enters the Samādhi of One Practice in this manner fully knows that the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is characterized by non-differentiation.

Although what Ānanda has heard of the Buddha’s teachings, his attainment of mindfulness, dhāraṇī, eloquence, and wisdom, is the most preeminent among the śrāvakas, he still dwells within the realm of numerical measurement and thus remains subject to limitation and obstruction.

If one attains the Samādhi of Single Practice, one will distinguish each and every dharma-gate of all the sutras, understanding them all with certainty and without obstruction; day and night, one will constantly expound wisdom and eloquence that never ceases.
Compared to Ānanda’s extensive learning and eloquence, even a hundred thousandth part would not equal one-hundredth of his.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should form this thought:
"How may I attain the inconceivable merit and immeasurable renown of the *ekavyūha-samādhi*?"
The Buddha said, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should mindfully contemplate the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi), constantly exerting themselves with diligence and without indolence.
By practicing and training in this sequence, one will gradually be able to enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi* and realize its inconceivable merit;
however, those who slander the True Dharma or are hindered by the heavy karmic obstacles of disbelief cannot enter it.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! It is like a person who obtains a maṇi jewel and shows it to a jeweler.
The jeweler replies:"
"This is a priceless, genuine mani-jewel," he said,
and then requested of his teacher,
"Please polish it for me so that its luster and color are not lost."
"Once the jeweler has finished polishing it, as he grinds it, the color and radiance of the jewel will shine through from both sides. Mañjuśrī!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who cultivate and study the inconceivable merit and immeasurable renown of the One-Practice Samādhi, then as they cultivate and study it, they will know the characteristics of all dharmas; their clear penetration will be unimpeded and their merit will increase in exactly the same way."
Mañjuśrī! For example, just as the radiance of the solar orb pervades everywhere and possesses no characteristic of extinction, so too is it when one attains the *ekavyūha-samādhi*:
one is able to fully possess all merits without deficiency, and likewise illuminates the Buddha-dharma like the light of the solar orb.
Mañjuśrī! All the teachings I have expounded are of a single flavor, the flavor of detachment, the flavor of liberation, and the flavor of quiescent extinction.

If a son or daughter of good family attains this Samādhi of Single Practice, their own discourse shall likewise be of a single flavor, the flavor of detachment, the flavor of liberation, and the flavor of quiescent extinction, conforming to the True Dharma without any sign of error.
Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this One Practice Samādhi, they will completely fulfill all the dharmas that assist the path and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the dharma-realm as having either differentiated characteristics or a single characteristic, they swiftly attain the inconceivable characteristic of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet within that bodhi, there is also no attaining of Buddhahood."
One who understands in this way will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If one believes that all phenomena are entirely the Buddha-dharma, and neither gives rise to alarm nor harbors doubt, such a person of patient endurance will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does one swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of such causes?”
The Buddha said:
"One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* neither by means of causes nor by means of non-causes. Why is this?"
The inconceivable realm is obtained neither by means of causes nor by means of non-causes.

If a son or daughter of good family, upon hearing such an exposition, does not give rise to indolence, you should know that this person has already planted various roots of goodness under previous Buddhas.
Therefore, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā being taught and do not give rise to fear or alarm have truly gone forth from the Buddha.
If an upāsaka or upāsikā hears such profound prajñāpāramitā and their mind is not startled or terrified, they have thereby accomplished true refuge.
Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family does not practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they are not cultivating the Buddha-vehicle.
It is, for example, like the great earth, upon which all medicinal herbs and trees depend for their growth.
Mañjuśrī! It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva: all roots of goodness increase by depending upon the prajñāpāramitā, and they do not conflict with anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In which cities, towns, or villages of this Jambudvīpa should such a profound Prajñāpāramitā be expounded?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If there are those in this assembly who, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, all make a vow, saying: ‘In future ages, may we always be in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā,’ then through this faith and understanding, they will be able to hear this sūtra in future ages.”
You should know that such a person has not come from any other minor roots of goodness, yet is able to endure and receive this teaching, and having heard it, they rejoice. Mañjuśrī!
If there is another person who hears this Prajñāpāramitā from you, you should say to them:
"In this Prajñāpāramitā, there is no Dharma of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor is there any Dharma of the Buddhas, nor even any dharmas such as the arising and ceasing of ordinary beings.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās should come to question me, saying:
"In what manner does the Tathāgata teach the Prajñāpāramitā?"
I should answer: "All dharmas are characterized by the absence of contention; how then could the Tathāgata speak of the Prajñāpāramitā? Why is this?
I do not perceive any dharma with which one might engage in dispute, nor is there any sentient being’s consciousness capable of knowing it.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, I shall further explain the ultimate reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Why is this? Because all dharmas equally enter into the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and for an arhat there is no distinct, superior dharma. Why is this?
Because the dharmas of an arhat and the dharmas of an ordinary person are neither identical nor different.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
according to this teaching of the Dharma, there are no sentient beings who have already attained nirvāṇa, are now attaining it, or will attain it in the future.
"Why is this? Because there is no determinate characteristic of a sentient being. Mañjuśrī said:

"If anyone wishes to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, I shall speak thus: those who listen should not think or cling, and should be without hearing or attainment; they should be like a phantom person, free from all discrimination. To speak in this manner is to truly teach the Dharma."

Therefore, listeners should not form dualistic conceptions; they should not abandon their various views while practicing the Buddha-dharma, nor should they grasp at the Buddha-dharma or reject the dharmas of ordinary beings. Why is this?
The two dharmas—the Buddha and the ordinary person—are empty of characteristics because there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
If someone asks me about this, I shall speak in this way, thus providing comfort and thus establishing them.

Good sons and good daughters should inquire in this manner and maintain their minds in this way so that they do not regress or sink; you should know that these characteristics of phenomena are taught in accordance with the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said.
If good sons and good daughters wish to see the Buddhas, they should study this Prajñāpāramitā in this manner."
If one wishes to draw near to the Buddhas and make offerings to them in accordance with the Dharma, one should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to say, "The Tathāgata is my World-Honored One," one should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one says that the Tathāgata is not my World-Honored One, one should likewise study this Prajñāpāramitā;
if one desires to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should likewise study this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes not to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should likewise study this *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one wishes to accomplish all *samādhis*, one should study this *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one wishes not to achieve any samādhi, one should likewise study this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the samādhi of non-action has no distinct characteristics, and because all dharmas are without arising and without emergence.
If one wishes to know that all phenomena are merely provisional designations, one should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to know how all sentient beings cultivate the path to awakening, yet do not seek the marks of awakening and their minds do not regress or sink, they should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are the characteristic of bodhi.

If one wishes to know the characteristics of the conduct and non-conduct of all sentient beings, non-conduct is itself bodhi; bodhi is itself the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm is itself the limit of reality. With a mind that does not retreat or sink, one should study such prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to know that the supernormal powers and transformations of all Tathāgatas are signless, unimpeded, and without location, one should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās wish not to fall into the evil destinies, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā; they should receive, uphold, read, and recite even a single four-line verse, and explain it to others in accordance with the true nature of reality.”
In this way, good sons and good daughters should know that they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and shall dwell in the Buddha-land.

If, upon hearing this *prajñāpāramitā*, they are not startled, not terrified, and give rise to faith and understanding, one should know that such persons are approved by the Buddhas; this is the Mahāyāna Dharma-seal practiced by the Buddhas.
If sons or daughters of good family study this Dharma-seal, they will transcend the evil realms and not enter the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Because they have thus transcended, at that time Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven will take celestial, exquisite flowers—Utpala, Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, and divine Māndārava flowers—as well as celestial sandalwood incense, other powdered perfumes, and various kinds of gold and jewels, and perform celestial music to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, all the Tathāgatas, and Mañjuśrī, scattering them upon them.
Having made this offering, he made this vow: "May I always hear the Dharma-seal of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra-devānām-indra further made this vow:

"May the sons and daughters of good family in Jambudvīpa always be able to hear this sutra; may they definitively understand and believe in all Buddha-dharmas, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others, and may all devas provide them with protection."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: “Kauśika! It is so, it is so.”
“Good sons and good daughters shall attain the definitive Bodhi of all Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"In this way, sons and daughters of good family who uphold [this teaching] shall obtain great benefit and immeasurable merit.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the entire earth shook in six ways.
The Buddha then smiled, emitting a great radiance that shone throughout the trichiliocosm.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This is precisely the seal of the Tathāgata upon the mark of the Prajñāpāramitā. The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

It is so, it is so. Once the Prajñāpāramitā has been taught, these omens all appear as a seal upon the Prajñāpāramitā, so that people may receive and uphold it, ensuring it remains free from praise or disparagement.
Why is this? Because the Dharma-seal of signlessness cannot be praised or disparaged.
By means of this Dharma-seal, I now ensure that none of the devas or māras can find an opportunity to cause harm.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly, having heard the exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred Sixteen;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.

Chapter Forty-Seven: The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin (Part One) Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of forty-two thousand bhikṣus and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.

They had all come together from the various buddha-worlds of the ten directions; they were all those who had reached the stage of being "born only once more" before attaining Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), having attained non-attachment and non-obstruction. They had emerged from the Samādhi of Valiant Subjugation and had acquired the Samādhi of the Supreme Lotus, the Samādhi of the Vajra Maṇḍala, the Samādhi of Firm Abiding, the Samādhi of Pure Cultivation, the Samādhi of the King of Banner-Flowers, the Vajra Samādhi, and the Samādhi of Pure Virtuous Deeds. Having distinguished their skillful means and practices, they had all gained intimate access to the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued many and delivered beings from the realms of Māra, thereby establishing the lands of all Buddhas.

He attained the *dhāraṇī* of inexhaustible discourse and came to know the fundamental origins of all sentient beings. With his wondrous eloquence, he could delight all hearts; he strode with the lion’s gait, fierce and fearless.
When entering an assembly, one should proclaim words and phrases appropriate to the occasion to accomplish all practices, thereby adorning oneself with majestic marks.
Having renounced worldly wealth and abandoned all non-Buddhist paths, one’s meritorious achievements are widely manifested and their fame reaches the ten directions.

The virtues praised by all Buddhas are immeasurable; they are all accomplished through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, having been cultivated through the practice of the path for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of incalculable kalpas.
Beholding the ailments of all sentient beings, they dispense medicine according to their illnesses so that all may be healed.
They enter into the profound and subtle principle of dependent origination, thereby relinquishing and severing all notions of annihilationism and eternalism.

Their conduct is pure and their resolve is without blemish; their mental nature is brilliant as they transform and enlighten all living beings, each one gathering and protecting them so that they find their proper place, while clearly understanding instructions and attaining mastery of mind.

Possessing powerful and firm resolve, they do not destroy their compassionate heart; endowed with the seven riches of faith, precepts, learning, generosity, shame, remorse, and wisdom, they desire to transform sentient beings and manifest dwelling in seclusion through skillful means.
The power of their practice, their virtuous vows, and their holy merit are immeasurable, with minds as vast as space.
Their names are:
Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Nityaprabhāsa, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The Bodhisattvas: Siṃhamati, Siṃhagati, Siṃhagarjitasvara, Ugratejas, Vajramati, Vajragati, Vajradhvaja, Vajrāśaya, Akampitagatipadma, and Ekacārin.
The Bodhisattva Lokasundara, the Bodhisattva Suvimalaprabha, the Bodhisattva Padmanetra, the Bodhisattva Padmaviśuddha,
the Bodhisattva Ratnaviśuddha, the Bodhisattva Śṛṅkhalādhara, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, the Bodhisattva Ratnakārya, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta,
the Bodhisattva Guṇaprabharāja, the Bodhisattva Viśuddharāja, and the Bodhisattva Vigataparigraha.
The Bodhisattva King of Mind, the Bodhisattva Adorned with Lightning Light, the Bodhisattva Space Treasury, the Bodhisattva Gentle Sound, the Bodhisattva Rain Sound,
the Bodhisattva Unwavering Sound, the Bodhisattva Pure Mind, the Bodhisattva Lightning Sound,
the Bodhisattva Liberated from Bonds, and so forth— these sixteen noble beings, including Mañjuśrī and others, numbering sixty.
The noble sons such as Gandhahastin and others, and the thirty-two pure practitioners such as Maitreya and others,
were all bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa. There were also twenty thousand celestial sons of similar class,

including the celestial son Mārajit, the celestial son Viśuddha-viśuddha, the celestial son Sumati, the celestial son Bhadrapāla, the celestial son Vijayī, the celestial son Manojavā, the celestial son Śāntikṛtadhvani, and the celestial son Sucintita— all of whom followed the Mahāyāna.

The gods of the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, the Brahmā Sahāmpati, Māraputra Nandika, and the son of the gods Sunirmita, along with other gods, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and humans and non-humans, were beyond calculation.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon a great, pure lion throne, surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands; he preached the sūtra with courage and fearlessness, uttering the lion’s roar like the sun shining everywhere, like the full moon in its brilliance, and like fire dispelling the darkness.
His seat was brilliantly radiant and majestic in its awesome splendor, surpassing that of Śakra and Brahmā.
The Buddha’s body appeared exceptionally prominent, like Mount Sumeru emerging from the great ocean.

The scriptures he preached—whether in their introductory, intermediate, or concluding sections—were all sublime and virtuous; their meanings were beautiful and complete, ultimately pure, as he constantly cultivated the holy life and extensively manifested kindness and compassion.
He proclaims the bodhisattva practices and expounds the bodhisattva dharma; that which one should follow and cultivate is called "Pure Conduct" (śuddhacaryā).

At that time, nine million two hundred thousand buddha-lands away from this buddha-field in the eastern direction, there was a world named Sunirmita. Its Buddha was named Śuddhavāsas Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva to the left and right of the Buddha named Rādhañjuna (translated in Chinese as Bǎojì, "Jewel Topknot"), who, together with eight thousand bodhisattvas, suddenly vanished from his buddha-field and arrived here in this Sahā world, dwelling in the Brahma Heaven.
With a single precious canopy covering this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold great thousand worlds, he rained down celestial flowers of various colors.
Standing in the Brahma-heaven, he spoke these verses:
“May all devas and humans obtain wholesome benefit; Their hearts aspire to behold the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas.”
To eliminate the heat of affliction from worldly affairs, they resolve their hearts with firm intent upon the Buddha-way.
Countless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, through the power of diligent practice, transcend all obstacles;
they subdue hundreds of thousands of millions of māras and attain the Buddha-way, free from defilement and sorrow.
I have come forth from the east; my world is named Suvikrānta, situated beside the Buddha Viśuddhasthita.
I have come desiring to prostrate before the Lion of the Śākyas.
Should anyone wish to hear the Dharma, or behold the bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
or desire to pay homage to those World-Honored Ones, let them come swiftly to Vulture Peak Mountain.
The appearance of the various Guides is difficult to encounter; the essentials of the scriptures are very hard to find.
A human body is difficult to obtain, as is leisure; firm faith in the prohibitions and precepts is likewise truly rare.
If one were to cultivate the roots of virtue at this very moment, and seeing sentient beings dwelling in the darkness of error,
were able to open their minds and lead them to nirvāṇa, they would swiftly proceed together toward the Most Victorious One.
If you wish to abandon the three evil realms, Attain the secure and peaceful abodes of devas and humans,
And reach the unconditioned state that extinguishes birth and death, Then you should go to the Peerless One.
Acting as a king of physicians, he bestows the nectar of immortality; like a guide, the Honored One shows the correct path.
As a King of Dharma, he wields the supreme jewel to subdue all realms of sentient beings.
When Ratnaśikhin had spoken these verses, he made them heard throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system by the sound of his voice.
Upon hearing these verses, the Venerable Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!”
"From where does the meaning of this sublime verse originate?
