The Buddha said, "To the east of here, nine million two hundred thousand Buddha-fields away, is a realm named Good Transformation. There dwells a Buddha named Pure Abode Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently teaches the Dharma."

To the left and right of that Buddha is a bodhisattva named Ratnaśikhin, who, together with eight thousand bodhisattvas, has come to this Sahā world-system desiring to see the Buddha, prostrate, inquire after his well-being, and receive the sūtras; furthermore, wishing to see the bodhisattvas gathered from the assemblies of the ten directions, he dwells in the Brahma-heaven and speaks these verses.
The sound of these verses was heard throughout the trichiliocosm, causing countless classes of sentient beings to plant the roots of various virtues and come together to approach the Buddha.

Thereupon, Ratnaśikhin, surrounded by eight thousand bodhisattvas and an immeasurable multitude of devaputras, played hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, rained down various exquisite flowers, and emitted a great radiance that shook the trichiliocosm. He proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and each circumambulated him seven times before standing upright before the Buddha; the eight thousand bodhisattvas did likewise, with the entire host of devaputras attending as their retinue.
The Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Viśuddhavihāra respectfully inquires after you: Are you free from all ill? Are your aspirations peaceful and secure? Do you dwell in ease and lightness? Is your strength at peace?”

Having been permitted by the God among Gods to come here with this humble body, I pray that you will bestow your compassionate grace and proclaim for the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas the teachings of the Way that ought to be practiced.

When a bodhisattva dwells herein, they attain ultimate fulfillment and complete purity; they universally don the armor of all virtues, accumulate the equal practice of manifold goodness, and purely cultivate their person.

They perceive the thoughts of all living beings and, observing their characteristics and conduct, they transform them accordingly; thus, by means of wisdom, they preach the Dharma for the sake of lust, anger, and ignorance, causing them to attain sublime practice.
If there are multitudes dwelling in false dharmas, he then demonstrates for them the teaching of equality.

Covered by the vision of all Tathāgatas, all classes of sentient beings receive their protection and reliance; no māras can find an opportunity against them, and they attain the unimpeded vision of all Buddhas.
"Whatever one dares to follow and cultivate shall all become the pure conduct of a Tathāgata.
By what cause is such a meaning brought about?
The Buddha told Ratnaśikhin:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
It is well that you ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall explain the pure conduct practiced by all the bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"A bodhisattva has four dharmas by which their conduct is pure. What are these four?

First is the perfection of practice; second is always following and cultivating the various factors of the path of the Buddhas; third is being fully endowed with supernormal powers; and fourth is transforming and enlightening sentient beings.
These are the four.
The practice of the Perfection of Conduct is that which encourages and assists all things without exception, entering universally into the root of all virtues.
As for the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment, one dwells in great compassion and clearly understands the entry of wisdom according to the appropriate time.
Those endowed with supernormal powers discern the mental activities and the karmic deeds—both good and evil—of sentient beings.
Those who transform sentient beings possess firm great compassion and clearly recognize the inclinations and destinies of their natures.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is meant by the purity of practice in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving?
It means that whatever habits of stinginess and greed one may have cultivated, one completely abandons them and cultivates a mind of generosity."
Having already been able to relinquish and abandon base, defiled matters characterized by greed, they encourage the practice of giving, bestowing all that they possess without stinginess.
Having practiced such generosity, they do not create any distinctions regarding the four requisites.

What are the four? First, that the categories of sentient beings have no diversity; second, that all sūtras and dharmas are not distinct from one another; third, that there is no differentiation in what can be encouraged and assisted; and fourth, that the application of one's will and nature is likewise without diversity.
What is meant by having no distinctions among all sentient beings?
It is not to give rise to this thought:
"I shall give to such-and-such a person, but I shall not give to so-and-so."
Giving to B produces much merit; giving to A produces little merit.
One gives generously to B and sparingly to A.
One makes offerings to B with delight, while giving to A merely as a matter of course.
One should always give to A, while giving to B only occasionally.
One personally deliberates and bestows gifts upon A, whereas one does not trouble oneself to bestow them upon B.
One gives everything to A, while giving only coarse things to B.
"This person upholds the precepts; that person violates the prohibitions.
This person has abundant blessings; that person has meager blessings.
This person is able to bring the virtues of abundant blessings to completion; that person cannot."
"This person cultivates the correct path; that person practices the deviant.
This person carries out the karma of equanimity; that person falls into and follows the karma of perversion.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"In this way, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they should discard all such mentalities and cultivate an impartial resolve, harboring no distinctions."

One should always maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and respond accordingly, using this to enlighten and transform them through the precepts of even-mindedness. One should practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and protective equanimity without ever forgetting them.
What is called "equanimity" is like space, entirely devoid of increase or decrease; this is what is meant by saying that sentient beings possess no diversity.
The Buddha told Ratnaśikhin:
"What is meant by 'all phenomena are not distinct from one another'?
It means that even when teaching the Dharma, one proclaims equality and does not harbor thoughts such as:"
"To those who respectfully practice the Dharma, I shall grant this sutra; however, I will not bestow it upon those who cannot accord with the Dharma.
If one is able to fully embody all dharmas, I shall grant it to them; I will not grant it to those who cannot fully embody the Dharma."
"One who wishes to promote the Way and practice the gift of Dharma does not consider it a loss when giving to ordinary beings, nor do they consider it an increase when giving to sages and worthies.
Furthermore, calculating that all dharmas are fundamentally pure, equal, and without distinction—for this reason, what is given should be equal."
In this regard, all phenomena are not distinct from one another;
the requisites offered as gifts and the assistance rendered therein are likewise without differentiation.
When practicing generosity, one does not form such thoughts:
"I shall obtain merit, hoping for the rank of Śakra, Brahmā, or a heavenly being.

He does not wish to be a sovereign, a noble, or a wealthy elder; nor does he long for or seek after the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, or fine touch. He does not set his mind on abundant wealth, rare treasures, precious goods, retinues, or attendants, nor does he covet or envy the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies.
In all places where he wanders, he does not seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Whatever he may bestow, he applies his will to seeking the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
This is called encouraging and assisting without making distinctions.

Regarding all things that may be relinquished, their fundamental nature resides in the Way without any distinction; whether in union or separation, there is from the outset neither increase nor decrease. They do not hope for any recompense, desiring only to deliver those who have not yet reached it and lead them across to the other shore.
His mind was simple and honest, free from flattery; he harbored profound faith and an inherently pure and virtuous nature that never wavered or changed.
He gave away what he cherished with a joyful heart, and whenever anyone came to seek something, he was able to bestow it upon them with a sense of great delight.

"The disposition and nature of this son of good family in his practice of giving are likewise without distinction; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), which is without variety.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, there are eight matters by which one abandons deviant paths and practices the work of giving."
What are these eight? They are:
not perceiving a self, not perceiving a person, not perceiving a life-span, not perceiving annihilation, not perceiving permanence, not dwelling in the three states, and not perceiving non-existence.
If one practices giving, one should purify these eight matters.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they abandon the karma of the four abodes. What are these four?
First, to abandon what is not the Dharma, thereby using the scriptures to transform and enlighten ordinary people;
second, to abandon the mindset of the śrāvakas and set one's will upon the Great Way;
third, to abandon the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas and cultivate equanimity.
The fourth is to distance oneself from all attachments and dependencies regarding one’s dwelling place; these are the four.
One should further abandon four types of mental preoccupation.
What are the four? First is the perception of permanence; second is the perception of bliss; third is the perception of purity; fourth is the perception of self.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters that constitute pure giving. What are these four?
First is purity of body; second is purity of speech; third is purity of mind; and fourth is purity of nature.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of giving that transcend all hindrances.
What are these three?
The first is to abandon longing; the second is to cast off resentment; the third is to distance oneself from the Hīnayāna—these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three things by which one abandons what should be given and leaves behind all fears.
What are these three?
First is arrogance, second is contempt, and third is the work of Māra;
these are the three.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of giving that are sealed by the vision of the Dharma. What are these four?
First is internal emptiness; second is external emptiness; third is the emptiness of persons; and fourth is the emptiness of the Path.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of giving characterized by exclusive dedication to diligence. What are these four?

First is to satisfy all sentient beings; second is to be fully endowed with the teachings of all Buddhas; third is to completely achieve the marks and signs of physical excellence; and fourth is to purify Buddha-fields.
These are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of giving whose intention is never abandoned. What are these four?

First, the mind constantly contemplates the Way; second, the constant desire to see the Buddha; third, the cultivation of great compassion; and fourth, the eradication of the defilements and afflictions of sentient beings.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of giving that adorn and purify the site of enlightenment. What are these three?
The first is purity of self; the second is purity of others; the third is purity upon reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
these are the three.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of giving that result in purity for the recipient.
What are the four? First is giving with wisdom;
second is being able to gladden the hearts of sentient beings; third is understanding how to provide encouragement and assistance; fourth is clearly understanding and observing the scriptures.
These are the four.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"This is the dharma to be practiced by a bodhisattva; it is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) that brings about the practice of ultimate purity.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), there is one thing that leads to purity.

What is this one thing? It is to understand the bodhisattva’s mind as being without equal; its mind transcends all worlds, being most honored and peerless, surpassing the intentions of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This mind can subdue all māras; it enters into the reach of sentient beings, whose renowned virtue is an immeasurable treasure; and while universally protecting those who follow and practice the Dharma, the mind never forgets."
This is the first.
Furthermore, there are two matters: the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) as pure conduct. What are these two?
First, to always harbor compassion and refrain from harming sentient beings; second, to set one's mind upon the Way with a pliant and gentle nature.
These are the two. Furthermore, there are three matters for the purity of the *śīlapāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline).
What are the three?
First is purity of body: the three matters of bodily purity are without deficiency or omission, being perfected and complete.
Second is purity of speech: all that is spoken is free from flattery and deceit.
The third is purity of mind, which eliminates all defilements, covetousness, and harmful intent.
These are the three.
Furthermore, there are four matters of the purity of the perfection of precepts.

What are the four? First, their precepts are pure; second, they uphold the prohibitions without violation; third, they teach and transform sentient beings by means of these precepts; fourth, when they see those who uphold the precepts, they revere them as if they were Buddhas.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are five matters of the purity of the perfection of precepts.

What are these five? First, not praising oneself; second, not disparaging others; third, relinquishing the aspiration for the stage of a śrāvaka; fourth, distancing oneself from the intent of a pratyekabuddha; and fifth, being free from all greedy attachments.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are six matters of the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). What are these six?

First, to constantly mind the Buddha and not violate the prohibitions and precepts; second, to constantly mind the Dharma and practice accordingly; third, to constantly mind the Sangha and not contravene the Buddha's teachings; fourth, to constantly mind giving and universally relinquish worldly desires; fifth, to constantly mind the prohibitions and precepts and no longer covet anything within the five realms of existence; sixth, to constantly mind the various devas and proclaim the roots of all virtues. These are the six.
Furthermore, there are seven matters of the purity of the perfection of precepts (*śīlapāramitā*). What are these seven? First, to have firm faith and delight in all Buddha-dharmas;

second, to constantly maintain self-reflection and a sense of shame, undertaking heavy responsibilities for the sake of the multitude; third, to be mindful of a sense of remorse, contemplate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and not be conceited; fourth, to be benevolent and harmonious, not causing affliction to others or oneself; fifth, to be free from malice and to fear the calamities and sins of future lives; sixth, not to disturb or harass others, but to still the mind and cease grief and sorrow; seventh, upon seeing sentient beings suffering in affliction, to feel compassion and pity for them.
These are the seven.
Furthermore, there are eight matters of the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). What are these eight?

First is to be free from flattery and deceit; second is to be free from a mind of expectation; third is not to crave gain and offerings; fourth is to abandon stinginess and pride, having no place of dependence; fifth is to know contentment with whatever one possesses; sixth is to practice the dhyāna of the noble ones, fully endowed with tranquility and detachment; seventh is to dwell in seclusion, not sparing even body or life; eighth is to delight in solitary dwelling, distancing oneself from crowds, taking pleasure in the Dharma, fearing the three realms while not grasping at the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
These are the eight.
Furthermore, there are nine matters of the purity of the perfection of precepts (*śīla-pāramitā*). What are these nine?

First, the discipline of having no fixed destination, which teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they may attain liberation; second, gradually practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to cultivate and purify its source; third, bringing the mind to ultimate completion so that it harbors no affliction or feverish distress; fourth, seeking profound stillness to bring the thoughts of the mind to rest; fifth, practicing the correct observance of dignified deportment and ritual propriety; sixth, transcending prohibitive precepts so as not to perceive a self; seventh, never deceiving or deluding others, but out of compassion for all living beings, fully embodying the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*); eighth, ultimately accomplishing the karma of the dharma of precepts so that it remains without deficiency or leakage; ninth, constantly maintaining mindfulness of and encouraging the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
These are the nine.
Furthermore, there are ten matters of the purity of the *śīlapāramitā*. What are these ten?
First, the three matters of purifying the body;
second, the four matters of purifying the mouth;
third, the three matters of purifying the mind.
The fourth is to maintain mindfulness of abandoning flattery and deceit;
to be upright in character and disposition rather than narrow-minded or fickle.
The fifth is for the nature of the mind to enter everywhere so that none fail to receive deliverance.
Sixth, to know the limits of all that is perceived while taking compassion as the foundation, thereby fully resolving all fetters;
seventh, for the mind to be free from rigidity, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that their karmic activities are entirely harmonized;
eighth, to constantly cultivate one's own person, and upon seeing fellow beings, to treat them with sincerity and reverence.
Ninth is to exhort and demonstrate the matters of the Dharma to all benefactors;
tenth is to provide them with food and clothing so that they may be free from worldly occupations. These are the ten.
Furthermore, there are two matters by which the perfection of precepts is purified. What are these two?

First, if one encounters those who revile or insult them, they would rather lose their body and life than ever break the precepts; they do not give rise to such thoughts, nor do they covet wealth or worldly affairs.
The second is to neither wander about nor greedily seek after anything, for all dharmas are empty, signless, and without form.
Furthermore, there are two other matters. What are these two?
The first is internal purity, which eliminates the sense bases;
the second is external purity, which relinquishes all objective spheres.
These are the two.
Furthermore, there are two matters:
first, purifying the mind of the Way by understanding the characteristic of spontaneity;
second, maintaining the purity of the precepts by being free from all signs.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"This is the pure practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is meant by the purity of conduct in the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience?
If one is reviled, to remain silent and not retaliate is purity of speech.
If one is struck or beaten, to accept it without resentment is purity of body."
If one encounters those who are angry, yet feels compassion rather than resentment, this is purity of mind.
If one encounters those who revile or insult, yet harbors no hatred, this is purity of nature.
Furthermore, if one hears others utter coarse and violent words, one does not give rise to anger or malice for the sake of protecting sentient beings.
Even if blades and staves were brought against his body, or he were struck and pelted with tiles and stones, he would protect himself for the sake of future lives and harbor no malice.
Even if his body were dismembered limb by limb, he would feel no sorrow or distress, for he follows the Path.
Seeing those who beg for alms, one does not give rise to anger, for the sake of fulfilling the four debts of gratitude.
One gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and does not cause affliction or resentment, for the sake of drawing near to the Buddha-way.
One cultivates a mind of compassion, for the sake of perfecting one's vows.
His meritorious achievements spread abroad such that there are none who do not receive his commands; this is because he has great compassion for many.
The benevolent mind and virtuous reputation through which he practices giving are for the sake of performing the path of the Dharma and casting off the heavens of Māra.
Furthermore, one practices patience while recollecting the Buddha-way, for the sake of attaining the body of a Buddha.
If one practices patience while recollecting the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), it is for the sake of perfecting the ten powers (*daśabala*).
If one practices patience while recollecting wisdom (*prajñā*), it is because one desires to be fully equipped with the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividya*) without obstruction.
One practices patience by contemplating compassion, for the sake of accomplishing great kindness;
one practices patience by contemplating the crossing over of delusions, for the sake of perfecting great pity;
one practices patience by contemplating being like a lion without fear, for the sake of being free from dread.
One practices patience while mindful of the invisible crown of the head, because one does not harbor self-importance toward sentient beings.
One practices patience while mindful of possessing the primary and secondary marks, because one universally desires to rescue and deliver all in the world.
"One practices patience while being endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, for the sake of accomplishing supernormal wisdom.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"There are two dharmas that purify the power of patience: [text missing]"
The first is to cultivate the path of practice with diligence; the second is to gather the power of righteousness (*artha*). As for what can be said therein:
if one is able to practice patience such that body and mind have no dependence, this is the gathering of the power of righteousness.
To practice patience without attachment toward any phenomena is the meaning of cultivating the path.

One who possesses pure patience can endure sentient beings; knowing that there is no person who can master any phenomena, as they are all entirely tranquil and quiescent, this is called pure patience.
Why is this? Because therein there is neither anything to be endured nor anything not to be endured; when one attains nothing at all regarding any phenomena, that is called "patience" (kṣānti).
Even the concept of "patience" (kṣānti) cannot be apprehended; that which is unattached to all phenomena is what is called patience.
This patience that has no dependence and no location, which does not accept any phenomena, is what is termed patience; it is not by means of grasping at anything that one practices patience.
That which does not calculate in terms of self, person, or life-span is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Not being attached to body or life, and observing them as mere things such as walls, tiles, or stones—this is what is meant by patience.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“A bodhisattva has two kinds of patience:

first, the thorough understanding of the disintegration of the constituent parts of the body; second, the clear realization that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, whereby one achieves patience.”
"This is the purity of the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
“What is called the purity of the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā)?”

Not abandoning the mind of the Way, the undertakings they initiate are never timid or weak; they always abide in diligent cultivation without sleep, never departing from the roots of virtue as they accumulate merit, and do not retreat from the *pāramitās*.

If one practices with skillful means to seek the Dharma, is capable of expounding the sutras for others, protects the true Dharma and delivers many beings, does not weary of great wisdom in transforming sentient beings, purifies Buddha-lands and transcends the Lesser Vehicle, and fulfills original vows through ultimate noble wisdom.

Never failing in generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning; having approached skillful means and wisdom and already reached the house of merit—what intention should one maintain to diligently rescue all sentient beings so that they are free from arrogance? This is called diligence.

What is meant by purity? It is when one clearly understands that the body is like a shadow or an echo; when one’s speech is gentle and the consciousness does not grow weary; when one’s wisdom is ultimate and the mind is pure and tranquil; when one is clear regarding conduct such that it is forever inexhaustible; when one discerns all cessations and dissolves them through wisdom, thereby achieving a single-mindedness in which wisdom does not arise.
He abandons diligence through three matters:
first, attachment to causes and conditions; second, performing inverted actions; and third, the cessation of expectations and imaginings.
If one has no dependence or attachment toward the three realms, this is diligence.
Furthermore, there are three matters. What are these three?
The eye has no attachment; it does not rely on forms nor crave consciousness.

It is likewise with the ear and sound-consciousness, the nose and odor-consciousness, the tongue and taste-consciousness, the body and tactile-consciousness, and the mind and mental-object-consciousness—all are entirely without attachment.
He has nothing to receive and nothing to practice; therefore, it is called diligence (*vīrya*).

There is no giving that is not free from stinginess, no precept that is not free from violation, no patience that is not free from contention, no vigor that is not free from indolence, no meditation that is not free from distraction, and no wisdom that is not free from folly. He does not cultivate roots of virtue, nor does he possess unwholesomeness; he seeks neither the Buddha-way nor attains the stages of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*. Since he has nothing to practice and yet nothing that he does not practice, he thereby achieves the purity of the two kinds of diligence.
What are the two?
First, to have no internal dwelling while giving rise to various causes and conditions; second, to relinquish external views, manifold perceptions, and all consciousnesses.
These are the two forms of diligence.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of purity.
What are these two purities?
The first is internal tranquility and concentration; the second is not wandering externally and being free from negligence.
These are the two purities.
When one's faculty of diligence is such that, regarding all activities, there is no activity and no frivolous play, this is the bodhisattva’s practice of the purity of the perfection of vigor.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure perfection of tranquility?
It is to diligently gather the matters of a single mind, observing that which should be examined through right concentration."
If he practices dhyāna with a single mind, he does not cling to form, and he abandons feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If he practices dhyāna, he does not cling to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness.
If one practices dhyāna, they do not crave forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or textures. If one practices dhyāna, they do not cling to earth, water, fire, wind, or space;

they do not cling to the positions of Śakra, the sun, the moon, Brahmā, or the noble and powerful; they do not cling to the realms of desire, form, or formlessness; they do not rely on this world or the world beyond; they do not dwell in the body nor have any fixed location; they do not rely on words and their minds are neither weary nor lax; they abide nowhere, are neither abrupt nor violent, and by not dwelling in extremes, they attain the state of non-conceptualization.

If he is a practitioner of dhyāna, he does not conceive of a self-body, does not give rise to various views, does not crave for a self, a person, or a life-span; he does not perceive subtle matters as acceptable or unacceptable, does not perceive annihilation, does not observe impermanence, and does not perceive arising and ceasing, existence or non-existence, or place and no-place.

If he practices dhyāna, he does not eternally exhaust the source of all outflows (*āsrava*), nor does he cling to the Buddhas, nor enter the traces of the realization of the fruit of nirvāṇa, nor does he dwell perpetually in non-action.

If one practices dhyāna, they single-mindedly understand emptiness but do not take emptiness as a realization; they seek signlessness and wishlessness but do not take signlessness and wishlessness as realizations.
Donning the great armor of virtue, practicing infinite compassion, and abiding in great pity, they fulfill all requirements and carry out the practice of emptiness.
What is meant by fulfilling the practice of emptiness?

It is not to conceive of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom; it is not to conceive of skillful means or any methods of transformation; it is not to conceive of kindness, compassion, joy, or equanimity; nor is it to hope for entry into noble wisdom.

One does not think that the bodhicitta has anything to observe; one does not think that the will, nature, or mind has anything to respond to; one does not think of the four debts of gratitude, wise giving, benevolence, or love, nor of benefiting others, benefiting all equally, or providing universal salvation.

One does not conceive of the mind as being at ease or as having anything stored within it; nor does one conceive of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path.

They do not seek the silence of withdrawal while observing the Dharma; they do not seek the conduct of tranquility, concentration, or gentleness; they do not seek shame or remorse for their faults; yet they dwell perpetually in the Buddha-way, never ceasing.

Following the teachings of the Dharma-eye, they grasp the radiant torch; constantly cultivating purity through the precepts of the noble assembly, they establish themselves in the contemplation of sentient beings to bring about the fulfillment of the Buddha-body. Adorned with virtues, they follow the Hero of the World; hearing the perfect sound, they revere the Buddha-samādhi. Attaining the eloquence of the supernormal powers of right enlightenment, they receive the ten powers and abide in fearlessness. They reach the subtle and wondrous eighteen unique qualities of all Buddhas, which are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Having uprooted all the defilements of desire within their dwelling places, they do not depart from supernatural powers as they guide sentient beings; with the four analytical knowledges and clear diligence, they teach and transform sentient beings through the dharmas that deliver one from this world and the world beyond.

Transcending the common crowd, he left the household life with straightforward integrity; he crossed over the swift waters and passed beyond the surging currents, severing all that exists and all places of dwelling. Naturally tranquil and serene, his Dharma-teaching was profound and still; observing the phenomena of the body, he felt no craving or attachment, and his resolve was fixed upon the Buddha-dharma, fully comprehending the thought of spontaneity.

Transcending all stages of abiding and practice, as well as the silence of speech and words, whatever he speaks is always the proclamation of the Buddha’s word; through this utmost sincerity, he extinguishes the state of constant burning and transforms sentient beings.
"This is called being fully endowed with the practice of emptiness.
The Buddha told the son of good family: "Suppose all the people in the trichiliocosm were painters.

Each would have his own training, their skills differing and their specialties unequal. Some might be skilled at painting houses but unskilled at painting figures; some might be able to copy but unable to paint in colors; some might excel at hands and feet but be clumsy with ears and eyes; some might have ill-proportioned heads but beautiful bodies, while others might be incapable of it at all."
Their training was each different; some were pleasing to people while others were not, their knowledge varied, and their appearances were distinct.
The King summoned all the painters, and they arrived immediately.
The King ordered that the various forms of the three realms be depicted, and he instructed them, saying:
"Each of you must paint an image and bring it to show me.
All the masters gathered in one place and each painted a form.
The one teacher has attained the essence of all that is supreme.
Son of noble family!
What do you recall?
"Are you able to universally prepare for all that can be done? He replied,
"Indeed, I am able."
The Buddha said:
"I shall provide an analogy to explain this meaning.
It is like a painter who depicts all manner of forms, each capturing its true essence without losing the intended character."

The study of this Dharma is likewise so: through diligent and energetic cultivation of the pure conduct (brahmacarya), one attains the Buddha-dharma, wherein all matters are fully accomplished through a single correct practice.

For this reason, being fully endowed with the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-caryā*), there is nowhere it does not reach; one thereby achieves all Buddha-ways, completely eliminating worldly desires, inverted perceptions, and various conceptualizations. One is free from arrogance and conceit, takes no pleasure in negligence, and although dwelling amidst manifold defilements, does not associate with them. This is called the Bodhisattva being fully endowed with the practice of emptiness.
When these words were spoken, eight thousand bodhisattvas became fully endowed with the practice of emptiness and attained the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti).
This is the pure practice of the bodhisattva’s perfection of tranquility (śamathapāramitā).
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is called the pure practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom?
There are twelve matters that constitute this pure practice."

What are the twelve? Wisdom that sees the past without obstruction; wisdom that sees the future without obstruction; wisdom that sees the present without obstruction; being able to clearly comprehend both the conditioned and the unconditioned; possessing clear understanding of all arts and crafts existing in all worlds, as well as the karmic actions that should be performed and the means of transcending the world; and explaining with discernment the meaning of the ultimate truth.

Knowing their habitual tendencies, he proclaims their fundamental and derivative aspects; regarding the inclinations of the faculties of all sentient beings—whether those who are pliant and inferior, those who are clear and penetrating, or those of moderate capacity—he possesses wisdom concerning the past and future that is free from all obstruction, his sagely majesty towering far above worldly knowledge.

They fully perceive the inclinations, natures, and conducts of sentient beings, as well as their physical forms and transformations; they comprehend the profound meanings that are difficult to understand and difficult to attain, thereby dissolving all views.
Free from all heterodoxies, all dwelling places, and all obstructing matters, they enter into noble wisdom that universally encompasses all sentient beings and enter into the wisdom of the Dharma.
He clearly understands the ultimate destination of the meaning of the noble treasury and realizes the true realm of entry.
His illumination is free from confusion and encounters no obstruction; as he observes the immeasurable delights of the seasons, all that he perceives is perfectly clear and without error.
Awakened consciousness is truly and actually neither extinguished nor exhausted; whatever it observes, there is nothing rejected. By means of a single practice, there is no practice.
It perceives all the observances, dignified deportment, and ritual propriety of sentient beings; the inclinations of the minds of the people of the world are all seen by the Bodhisattva.

Without departing from the world, they transcend all worldly realms; yet, before even achieving the Buddha-lands, they have already surpassed all conditioned causes and conditions. They transform and guide sentient beings beyond all conditioned activities, universally perfecting all virtuous practices, and extensively delivering all mental activities associated with causes and conditions.

They perceive all that sentient beings think in their minds; they protect the worldly dharmas without exception; they do not abandon the practices of the mundane world but enter with faith into the thoughts of sentient beings. Their wisdom is calculated to be free from sudden violence; they do not fall into perilous pitfalls, for their faculties are tranquil and settled; they never grow weary or indolent, nor do they allow themselves to become distracted.

Eternally contemplating holy wisdom, he is ever in accord with virtue; he approaches the Bodhi tree and sits at the site of enlightenment, subduing all demons and abandoning external paths. His practice involves that which is received, yet his holy radiance penetrates everywhere without anything being grasped.

The Great Sage has attained the abodes of all Buddhas that bring joy to sentient beings; he perceives all through concentration and wisdom, universally entering into all meanings. All dharmas are of one and the same flavor, as he employs the skillful means of expedient power and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to transcend to the other shore beyond measure.
This is what is called the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).

It is able to fully comprehend all causes and conditions, the various thoughts that arise, auspicious signs, extraordinary transformations, and the mental activities and intentions of beings, thereby enabling them to cross over; this is what is called "crossing to the other shore."
Furthermore, it is reckoned that this wisdom possesses two kinds of purity:
first, the practice of the purity of the perception of unimpeded wisdom; second, the adornment and purification such that no person can equal its marks of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of purity:
first, the purification that eliminates inversions; second, the purification that removes all views.
Moreover, the wisdom practiced by those bodhisattvas enters everywhere; their noble clarity is complete and thorough, as they understand sentient beings and master the knowledge of the scriptures.
These Bodhisattvas, through this wisdom, understand that nothing exists; yet they enter into the dust of worldly toil to personally transform those bound by desire.

Abiding in all places of birth and within all realms, they establish wisdom as they traverse various lands, fully comprehending all spheres of experience. With this authentic and true wisdom, they do not cross over from this shore to that, nor do they dwell in between.
His wisdom enters everywhere; he perceives the ten directions without obstruction, and through the absence of concealment, he reaches the boundless limit.

He perceives the wisdom of ultimate truth (*satya*), clearly understanding the beginning, end, categories, and temporal sequences of all phenomena (*dharma*). Having been able to discern the wisdom of true reality, he knows the destination of its meaning: there is neither correspondence nor non-correspondence, neither conjunction nor distinction, neither laxity nor exertion, neither duality nor singularity; even when reckoning all phenomena, there is no correspondence or conjunction.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If a bodhisattva practices the activities of wisdom, taking wisdom as his dwelling, he establishes a hall of merit; he makes the chamber of the Dharma of renowned virtue and the Path his abode, and abiding in *dhāraṇī* and analytical knowledge and eloquence, he becomes fully endowed with all matters of wisdom."
"O son of good family!
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure conduct of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Having spoken these words, at that time twenty-two thousand people in the assembly all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); five thousand bhikṣus exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind; and ten thousand devaputras were freed from dust and defilement, and their Dharma-eye became pure.
At that time, the sons of the gods raised their voices in praise, saying:

"If there are sentient beings who attain the hearing of this Dharma-gate of the path of the pure practices of the various perfections (pāramitās), they shall be granted a prediction of enlightenment by all the Buddhas."
"How much more so for those who hear it, are able to receive, uphold, recite, and chant it, and practice according to the instructions above!
The Buddha said to Ratnaśikhin:
"What is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of purity regarding the dharmas of the Buddha-way category?"
To observe one's own body and know that it is fundamentally without a self is the application of mindfulness; thus, one establishes one's resolve through two matters.
What are these two? The first is the examination of impurity; the second is the contemplation of pure conduct.
What is meant by "filthiness"?
This body is impermanent and filled with impurities; this body is of meager strength, weak, and powerless; this body is constructed like a house that is leaning and on the verge of collapse.
What is meant by contemplating purity?
I shall, through this impure body, apply diligent effort to realize emptiness and attain the Tathāgata’s body, the Dharma-body.
This Dharma-body is majestic, a body of infinite virtue, manifesting physical forms for the sake of all sentient beings to bring joy to everyone.
O son of good family!
Contemplate two matters regarding the body to establish your resolve.
Furthermore, O son of good family!
When a bodhisattva contemplates the body and realizes it is ultimately without a self, they attain two pure dharmas. What are these two?
First, seeing impermanence; second, observing permanence.
This body is impermanent and cannot endure for long; it is subject to both old age and sickness, and must inevitably return to death.

Having realized this truth, one should not commit unwholesome deeds for the sake of the body. By not identifying with the body, one cultivates what is firm and essential, practicing the three essentials:
first, the essential of the body; second, the essential of life; and third, the essential of wealth.
This body is impermanent, yet all sentient beings hold it as precious; what benefit does it bring?
One should practice compassion.
What is the essential purpose of the body?
One’s body does not commit evil; one is humble, reverent, and obedient, bowing one’s head before those of broad wisdom.
What is the essential precept?
It is to take refuge in the Triple Gem and to practice the ten virtues, the six perfections, and the four immeasurables.
What is meant by the essential wealth?
It is to renounce one's own possessions and practice giving to provide for those who are poor and destitute.
One’s body is not one's own; as for what is spoken from the mouth, there are many errors, leading to flattery, coarse words, and that which is improper.
For this reason, they completely abandon these practices and no longer commit further transgressions.
Having realized that there is no self and that life cannot be preserved, even if they are harmed, they do not commit evil deeds.
He realized that the body is impermanent and subject to separation; he did not transgress what was improper, and gave away all his possessions without any greed.
Having understood that there is no self, the meritorious virtues and glorious achievements he attained were so manifest as to be beyond measure.
What is meant by "permanence"?

If one contemplates the body and realizes it is devoid of a self, then by means of the wisdom realized through the mind at that time, one encourages all-encompassing knowledge, does not contravene the Buddha’s teachings, does not lose the words of the Dharma, and does not harm the Sangha; one exhorts and transforms the multitudes and governs the people—this is called permanence.
It is for this reason that it is called "constant," because it cannot be exhausted.
What is called "inexhaustible" refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Being in accord with the Way, without end and without beginning, it is profound, subtle, and eternally existing; this is what is meant by the unconditioned.
That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is indeed permanent.
When a bodhisattva dwells therein, observing all the roots of virtue and all the supernormal knowledges until reaching the unconditioned, this is called "having permanence."
It is for this reason that it is called "constant": because of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Cultivating the Bodhisattva path, one constantly upholds the practice of emptiness; contemplating signlessness, one does not cling to wishlessness; universally perfecting all practices of diligence—this is what is meant by "having constancy."
That which is called "constant" refers to being like space.

When a bodhisattva’s mind is equal to space—without distinction and free from conceptual thought—one who practices in this manner is a bodhisattva; this is called the constant, unsurpassed, right, and true state.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“When a bodhisattva contemplates the body and realizes that it is fundamentally without a body, this is called the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).

All human bodies are fundamentally empty; by understanding the emptiness of the body, the mind has no attachments. One contemplates the bodies of sentient beings as being established within the Buddha-body.”
One should contemplate in this way: "If the body of the Tathāgata is free from all outflows (āsrava), my own body is likewise so.
Examining all phenomena (dharma), one should practice the path and its meaning without failing the Buddha's teaching.

Having attained the untainted body (*anāsrava-kāya*), one observes sentient beings and discriminates among their various marks; yet because the untainted body is untainted and pure, its fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is likewise pure.

Just as one establishes various practices based on the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), one encourages and assists those roots of virtue so that they too are free from outflows. One who is able to achieve the untainted dharmas is thus able to abide within all outflows.
What are the outflows?
First is the outflow of desire, second is the outflow of existence, and third is the outflow of views.
Having severed the outflow of desire, he is born in the desire realm to transform and guide sentient beings.
If one cuts off the outflows (āsrava), yet wanders through birth and death to instruct all beings in what they receive;
furthermore, that which is seen as an outflow is the outflow of ignorance and the darkness of delusion.
The Bodhisattva applies himself to that diligence without slackening, perfecting his vigor until its very root is uprooted.

If he contemplates the body and practices the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), he transcends all past unwholesome conduct, leaves behind all defilements, and adheres to tranquility. Thus, when contemplating the body, there is nothing to be transcended; there is no arising, and thus no purposeful action—this is what it means to contemplate the body.

If, having observed thus, one does not perceive a body nor anything to be examined, one abandons attachment to the body and no longer conceives of a self. Being without a self, there is nothing to crave; being without craving, there is no contention; being without contention, there is no calamity or fault. Being without calamity or fault, one attains the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). Having attained the patience of the Dharma, there is nowhere to which one returns; being without a place of return, there is no violence. Being without violence and not abiding in self-conceit, one abides in the Dharma; one who abides in the Dharma does not practice what is non-Dharma.

One who practices in accordance with the Dharma is always conjoined with the Dharma; one who cultivates the path of the Dharma attains the compassion of the Dharma. Having received the compassion of the Dharma, one hears the sound of the Dharma; having practiced the sound of the Dharma, one does not hear the sounds of the realms. Having stilled the sounds of the realms, one then attains samādhi; having attained right reception, one observes with profound discernment. Having observed with profound discernment, there is no conceptualization; having no conceptualization, there is no action; having no action, there is no non-action. Having reached the truly authentic Dharma through neither acting nor non-acting toward all actions, one then becomes equal toward all dharmas.
Having realized the equality of all phenomena, one attains the omniscience of universal wisdom.
O son of noble family!
When a bodhisattva contemplates the body, they understand that fundamentally there is no self, and thus their practice of mindfulness is purified.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is called the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to sensation?
It means observing that sensation is fundamentally without sensation; this is the application of mindfulness."
Beholding all forms of suffering and seeing all sentient beings amidst their various calamities and hardships, he sheds tears for them and attains great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
He reflects thus: "Beings are in distress;
if they were to attain peace, they would be free from pain and sensation."
Thus, one eliminates all harm and reaches the point of contemplating pain and knowing that, fundamentally, there is no pain.

When the application of mindfulness has ceased all sensations, one dons the great armor for the sake of all sentient beings; first, one personally eliminates unrighteous conduct within one's own body, and furthermore, one does not even conceive of the cessation of sensations.

If there are those who encounter suffering, he universally exercises great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for all of them, demonstrating eternal peace to cause their manifold afflictions to be forever extinguished.

For those who are greedy and lustful, he gives rise to great compassion; first eliminating his own greed, he is not bound by desire, and even when his own body encounters suffering, he does not regard it as a hardship.
For those who are prone to anger, he arouses great compassion to sever his own fetters of anger; he then perceives sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant.

For those who act in folly, he arouses great compassion to extinguish his own bonds of delusion; he contemplates pain and pleasure without attachment, destroying all fetters to abide in freedom and peace.

If one encounters suffering and pain without becoming distressed, and relinquishes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), then one can practice in accordance with the path so as to be free from both suffering and pleasure, thereby destroying ignorance.

If one encounters pleasant sensations without accumulation, and upon meeting various afflictions realizes the body is impermanent, one contemplates painful and itchy sensations, observing that within pain there is no self.

He contemplates pleasant sensations as being peaceful in their cultivation, yet he views painful sensations as being like sores and diseases; for this reason, it is called "neither pleasant nor painful.
Furthermore, should he observe that all existing states of ease ultimately revert to impermanence.
Regarding those who possess manifold sufferings, if one reckons that which is suffering as being neither painful nor pleasant, then there is likewise no self.
If a bodhisattva perceives various matters of peace and happiness, clearly recognizing that all are fundamentally without peace, this is the contemplation of sensation (vedanā).

One knows that suffering has no root, arising only to vanish immediately; one clearly understands that all phenomena cannot endure for long; one observes that all things arise like flames and suddenly perish; one views the birth of all dharmas as being like shadows—from where do they come, and why do they disperse and cease?
Contemplating the fundamental nature of all phenomena as clearly as one gazes upon the palm of one's hand—whence do they come, and whither do they go?
One immediately realizes that they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
By contemplating all phenomena as not being a source of affliction, and by universally perceiving that all things are brought to rest through profound faith, one thereby attains the Way.
Having attained the Way, there is nothing further to be acquired, and one never again falls back.
Why is this? Because he is able to perceive the root from which all beings arise and seeks its cessation; he does not seek cessation for his own sake alone.
O son of good family!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through skillful means and great compassion, observes sensations and realizes that, from the very beginning, there is no sensation; this is the practice of the stationing of the mind (smṛtyupasthāna).
He eliminates all views and clearly recognizes this: he does not encounter the various sufferings of the triple world, nor does he seek to realize a limit through their cessation.

Regarding these manifold sufferings, he contemplates the Buddha and praises the fundamental nature; he understands that all sufferings are silent and tranquil, fundamentally non-existent, and that there is no encountering of affliction, nor will there ever be an encountering of affliction.

All dharmas are empty and devoid of a self; they are seen merely as aggregations dependent upon causes and conditions. They have no master and no self; having abandoned all that is perceived, there is nothing to be nurtured or increased.
When he contemplates in this way, he attains the vision of ultimate truth.

Since that which is produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions is entirely unapprehendable, and having become unapprehendable, he investigates thus: as the causes and conditions are empty, so too are all phenomena that arise and are established from them empty.
Having already attained the meaning of emptiness, one then contemplates that suffering is fundamentally without sensation; this constitutes the application of mindfulness.
What is called "tranquility" refers to the body being serene and calm; thus, one selects the various meanings through the noble wisdom of the Path. This, O son of good family!

“The Bodhisattva contemplates the body and sensations, realizing fundamentally that there is no sensation; this is the practice of pure conduct through the stationing of mindfulness. The Buddha told the son of good family:

“The Bodhisattva contemplates the mind and realizes fundamentally that there is no mind; this is the practice of the stationing of mindfulness. Establishing oneself in the mind of the Way, one attains the establishment of the mind; by means of one’s own mental wisdom, one seeks the root of the mind, seeing neither the inner mind nor the outer mind, and dwelling in neither the internal nor the external.”
Examining the nature of that mind, one does not perceive the five aggregates; there are no sense-bases and no sense-fields, for that mind is tranquil and settled.
When seeking its point of support, from where does it arise?
He then further contemplated that the mind arises from conditions;
he immediately further contemplated whether the mind was distinct [from its conditions], or whether the causes and conditions were distinct.
Thereupon, he understood it for himself.
If causes and conditions were different from the mind, then there would be two minds;
if causes and conditions were the mind and the mind were causes and conditions, for this reason, the mind does not perceive the mind.
To reckon within the mind is not to fail to see the mind; it is like false and unreal sensory objects abiding in empty space.
Just as a sharp blade may wound a finger, causing a sore at that time, once the sore on the finger has healed, there is no longer any affliction or suffering.
In this way, son of good family! The mind is also like this; for this reason, the mind does not see the mind.

That which is seen by the mind is nothing seen. One should contemplate the dwelling place of such a mind in this manner: it neither gives rise to offenses nor is seen as subject to annihilation; one does not conceive of it as eternally existing, nor does it possess a self-body.
The body is like a wall; its causes and conditions are neither disordered nor separated from compassion. It is neither this nor different—this is what constitutes the mind.
One should maintain the mind in this way.
The movement of the mind constitutes phenomena; the mind has no place of abiding and no place of activity. The mind cannot be seen, for the characteristics of the mind are spontaneous.

To understand this clearly—such that what is perceived is like this, not departing from what is perceived—and for the mind to be tranquil, with clear awareness that it has no fundamental basis: this is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the mind as being without mind, which constitutes the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If the mind does not arise and cannot be seen, then there is no perception, neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate; there is also no arrogance, and thus one is not negligent. This is called observing the mind and knowing that fundamentally there is no mind, which constitutes the application of mindfulness to the mind."
Furthermore, just as the mind is formless, so too are its causes and conditions, as well as its eloquence.
Since the root of virtue is formless, and just as the mind is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and virtue is likewise formless, the bodhicitta that is thus exhorted is also formless.

If the mind of the Way and the assistance rendered therein have no form or color, and the Way itself is likewise entirely non-existent, for this reason it is said: "As is the mind, so is its practice."
If one calculates that encouraging and assisting the mind of the Way is likewise so, then just as the mind of the Way is so, the fundamental purity of the human mind is also thus.
Since the mind of the Way is fundamentally pure, all dharmas are also like this.
This mind is understood as universally penetrating; this is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the mind as being no-mind, which constitutes the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

It is afflicted by manifold sufferings and never remains still, like a monkey or the swift current of a river. It is also like the radiance emitted from an oil lamp that suddenly travels far away; it has no physical form and is subject to constant shifting and turning. Greed and stinginess toward the various realms and the afflictions of the six sense-faculties serve as its dwelling place; in an instant it changes, each according to its respective conditions.

The mind has no fixed location and wanders alone; it possesses neither solidity nor essentiality, yet it is not without them. It observes in profound stillness and solitude—this is called observing the mind as being without mental activity, wherein the cessation of thought is pure.
The mind enters the dharma-realm of wisdom; the wisdom-mind dwells in its fundamental luminosity, which is pure, pristine, and undefiled.

Knowing the true reality of the mind and comprehending the present, that which is seen by the eye is equal to the mental phenomena. Wisdom is likewise like the mind, and the mind is equal across the three periods of time. Having attained this equanimity, one then knows what is truly real. Mind and wisdom are spontaneous, beyond the need for protection or maintenance, and their observation is invisible. This is called the contemplation of the mind as no-mind, which constitutes the foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

When one reckons its fundamental purity, it is spontaneous; the mind is also fundamentally pure and thus understands the minds of sentient beings. Because the mind is pure, one transforms and guides the people by preaching the Dharma for them, so that they may understand and know their own minds are spontaneous, and that all sentient beings are likewise spontaneous.
If one can discern the mind in this way, one perceives its characteristics and preaches the Dharma accordingly.

Just as the characteristics of the mind are naturally so, the characteristics of the minds of sentient beings are naturally so as well. If one can penetrate these characteristics, then for that person the preaching of the Dharma results in the realization that one's own mind is empty, and the minds of sentient beings are likewise empty.
Having understood this emptiness, one preaches the Dharma for them, maintaining equanimity within one's own mind.

If one can maintain such equanimity while preaching the Dharma, one’s own person becomes equal; having equalized one's own mind, one then equals all sentient beings; having equalized all sentient beings, one then equals all phenomena; and having equalized all phenomena, one then equals all Buddhas.
Having realized this true reality, one does not allow the mind to depart from non-attachment nor dwell within desire.
When the mind has attained stillness, one enters the Dharma-realm and proceeds toward spontaneity; the mind abides nowhere, and regarding all phenomena, it remains unmoving.
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the mind as being without mind, which is the purity of the station of mindfulness.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"When a Bodhisattva contemplates phenomena and knows that they are fundamentally non-existent, this constitutes the practice of the station of mindfulness; he then reflects to himself:"

"When dharmas arise, they arise; when dharmas cease, they cease. When one calculates from the beginning to the end, there is no self-body, nor person, life-span, or vital principle, nor the born or the unborn, nor birth, old age, sickness, death, or the destination of passing away. Within these various dharmas, it is merely the conjunction of dharmas."

Because they come together, habits and customs are formed; if there were no convergence of conditions, these would not exist. Following the causes of habitual pleasure, conditions converge to give rise to the roots of both good and evil. Since all things return to impermanence and lack such convergence, no phenomena arise from the absence of habituation.

Thus observing and clearly understanding all phenomena, he sees that even the destination toward which they tend is non-existent; whether it be the meritorious deeds performed through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, or those that are not meritorious, all such practices are like illusions and impermanent. Therefore, one should reverently practice diligence and establish the causal conditions.
There are ten supreme and unsurpassed practices that eliminate causal conditions and resolve one’s will upon the Great Dharma.
What are these ten? The body is pure and free from defilement; its various marks and secondary characteristics are such that no one can see the crown of its head.
They deliver all who have been oppressed or wronged; their nature and disposition are pure and they are endowed with ten matters.
Their minds are pure and they are perfected in right conduct; the sixty billion voices spoken from their mouths bring joy to sentient beings.
Those whose minds are pure always harbor compassion and benevolence, feeling pity for all beings and never inflicting harm upon them.
Their thoughts are constantly settled and never disturbed; their eloquence is pure, and whatever they preach accords with the Dharma and its meaning, their skill in discourse being inexhaustible.
Great compassion is pure, exhorting and transforming all sentient beings so that they may find joy in the realm of Nirvana.
Great pity is pure, never wearying of birth and death throughout incalculable eons.
He purifies the ten powers and clearly understands that the faculties, origins, and thoughts of sentient beings are each different.
With pure fearlessness, he discerns and governs the infinite multitudes of sentient beings, desiring to be endowed with the unique qualities of all Buddhas.
The wisdom of the past, future, and present is unimpeded throughout the three periods of time; the pure application of the Buddhas' Dharma is sovereign because it returns to noble wisdom.
These are the ten.

Having attained these ten practices of the supreme, most excellent, and unsurpassed Great Dharma, he contemplates them with weighing reflection without weariness; he accumulates meritorious deeds without falling into ruin, and his conduct of virtue is characterized by earnest diligence.
What is meant by causing all dharmas to have no place of origin or arrival?
It is to transcend all habitual defilements in which one dwells, and having realized that all things are entirely impermanent, to be able to give rise to and accomplish the samādhi of impermanence.

One who attains this samādhi is free from the perception of solidity and remains undisturbed; according to their original vows, they manifest where they are to be born, entering various realms and then being reborn, thereby proclaiming the practice of merit to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
O son of good family!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), universally expounds the sūtras and contemplates all dharmas; realizing that fundamentally no dharma exists, he establishes the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*).

If there are those who attain the Way and follow the cultivation of the scriptures, and if they can clearly understand the dharmas of the stages of the path (mārgāṅga), they do not perform various good deeds nor perceive anything as permanent; they have no attachments yet do not eliminate unwholesome dharmas. What the mind of the Way perceives is uninterrupted wherever it may be; they neither reckon things as eternal nor fall into the view of annihilationism.
If there is a bodhisattva who abandons views of permanence and annihilation, maintains a mind of equanimity, and dwells nowhere in the middle—
what is meant by "the middle"?
One should not dwell upon mental formations; when the manifold darkness of ignorance is entirely removed, this is called the intermediate state.
Where there is no instruction and nothing to be taught, where there is no speech and no discourse, this is called the intermediate state.

To speak briefly: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and the afflictions of old age, sickness, death, and sorrow—all such distresses that cannot be encountered have been completely eliminated; this is called the "intermediate."
That which is taught has neither wisdom nor location; this is called the intermediate state.
Within that intermediate state, there is neither a messenger nor one who sends.

Thus, regarding that which is reckoned as one's dwelling place and its contents, there is no one who commands or instructs; reckoning this from beginning to end, it cannot be definitively determined. Having no fixed location, it cannot be grasped or held, and thus there is no attachment. It is tranquil, serene, and suddenly extinguished—this is called the "intermediate."
O son of good family!

Just as an echo has no fixed location, yet it arises in response when one approaches its source; so too, for one who perceives the Truth, the distinction between the true and the false falls away—this is what is meant by the "intermediate."
Without speech and without discourse, that is neither seeing nor abiding anywhere. Thus, noble son!

Regarding the matters of consciousness and form that arise and are instigated, and the conditions through which they are synthesized from the encounter of two factors—the interval between them is without instruction and without discourse; this is called the "intermediate."

When causes and conditions combine, they do not rely on conceptual principles; those principles are unattainable. That which is unattainable does not come again, and this non-returning is called the "intermediate."

Furthermore, one who calculates the self realizes that there is no self; here, it is extinguished and stilled. Regarding the self and non-self, they are naturally pure. In this intermediate state, one calculates the person and their lifespan; yet regarding the person and their lifespan, there is nothing to be seen, being naturally pure. This is called the "intermediate."
To have no attachment to the pleasure of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the intermediate state.
That which arises from perversion and yet is found to be nothing at all is the intermediate state.
That which is false, deluded, and ignorant, as well as the teaching of ultimate sincerity—none of these can be apprehended; this is called the middle way.

To dissolve one's own self so that there is no attachment between this shore and the further limit, and to neither engage in conditioned phenomena nor unconditioned phenomena, nor to practice any habitual tendencies—this is called the middle way.
To eliminate birth and death and depart from nirvana entirely without verbal instruction—this is the middle way.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

“One who contemplates the dharmas and realizes that the dharmas are fundamentally unconditioned attains the stationing of the mind; without destroying the dharma-realm, their mind spontaneously attains the stationing of the mind.”

That guide of the dharma-realm thoroughly understands all phenomena; when he considers both the dharma-realm and the realm of persons, he neither destroys nor disintegrates that dharma-realm, nor does he destroy the realm of persons. These two things—the realm of persons and the dharma-realm—are equal to the realm of empty space.
He perceives all phenomena universally through a single realm; seeing with the eye of wisdom, he employs the contemplation of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) to observe the conduct of the Buddha.

Suppose there were a person who did not discern phenomena—they would have no vision. For this reason, although phenomena are manifold, one sees that there is no fundamental substance and does not contemplate their multiplicity.
If one perceives fundamental non-existence through the contemplation of dharmas, it is not seen by the fleshly eye, nor by the divine eye, nor by the wisdom eye. Why is this?
Because that which causes the eye to function does not undergo conceptualization and thus is not seen by the fleshly eye; that eye does not fall into the conduct of birth and death.
If one sees nothing with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one does not employ that eye to practice negligence.

If one sees nothing with the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), one contemplates phenomena (*dharma*) and realizes that phenomena are fundamentally non-existent; one universally perceives that all phenomena have no location and that phenomena have no abiding place. Having seen that all phenomena have no abiding place, one then acts according to the intent of the Dharma, thereby not violating or losing the vows made in the past. This is for a bodhisattva to establish their own resolve in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas, so as to be able to observe the profound and subtle Dharma, never abandoning the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
"This is the noble son’s bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the pure conduct of mindfulness on the fundamental non-existence of phenomena.
The Buddha told the noble son:
"These four foundations of mindfulness practice the four kinds of diligence."
What are the four?
Contemplating the body as being without a self, one abandons the inverted perception that conceives of what is not pure as pure.
Contemplating sensation as being without sensation, one abandons the inverted perception that conceives of suffering as pleasure.
Contemplating the mind as no-mind, one eliminates the perception of permanence within impermanence.
Contemplating phenomena as non-existent, one abandons the notion of self within that which is non-self.
By cultivating equanimity toward the four inversions, one becomes free from all attachment.
If a bodhisattva is able to practice equanimity, they can purify all conditioned activities.

When a bodhisattva upholds this pure and subtle practice of equanimity, they attain the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti); it is called the four right efforts (catvāri samyakprahāṇāni), and through them, one also attains the patience regarding dharmas.
What is meant by the purity of the abandonment of mental states?

When a practitioner expounds the Dharma of the Path, through these causes and conditions they skillfully cultivate the practice of the fundamental [wholesome] roots, naturally conforming to them; they do not follow unwholesome roots nor give rise to defilements. As for the sprouts of various unwholesome roots that have not yet arisen, they do not allow them to emerge, thereby practicing diligence.
Whenever unwholesome and unlawful matters arise, one immediately extinguishes them; this constitutes the cultivation of diligence.
As for wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, one encourages their production.
To further increase one's diligence in giving rise to wholesome dharmas, so that they may be fully perfected and not forgotten, this is the practice of diligence.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva’s fundamental practice of pure karma enables them to exercise self-restraint and protection, so as not to lose wholesome dharmas and to dwell in mastery; gradually cultivating and nurturing them, they manifest and proclaim wholesome dharmas, and once these wholesome dharmas have arisen, they are never again lost.

When that son of good family thus practices these four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) with purity, his bodhisattva practice attains mastery of mind and undistracted diligence. Being pure, he does not associate with defilement; being stainless and pure, he does not contradict the Buddha’s wisdom. Thus, following the Way and teaching, he practices great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); mind and mind meet as they perceive one another’s thoughts. Having not lost his diligence, he practices equanimity; this is called attaining the right efforts.

Why is this? Because one proceeds with equanimity and does not resort to perversity; by relying on equanimity and not following perversity, one attains the samādhi of the equality of mental relinquishment.
"Having attained samādhi, it is called the 'Equanimity of the Four Right Efforts' (catvāri samyakprahāṇāni).
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"If one can practice these four right efforts, then one will be able to uphold and fulfill the four bases of psychic power (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ)."

By severing greed and practicing diligence, one causes the mind of the Way to become tranquil and free from defilement; thoughts become sparse and diminished, and having abandoned what is unrighteous, one attains lightness and ease, thereby achieving great compassion and the buoyancy of diligence.

Having attained skillful means, one is cautioned against rash action; for this reason, one accomplishes the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) and ascends to the hall of the Way to attain the four masteries (*vaśitā*). What are these four?

Regarding mastery over lifespan: having attained long life that is itself limitless, they possess immeasurable longevity even within a short life to transform sentient beings; within a long life, they listen to and contemplate the teaching of the Dharma; or, manifesting a short life when there might be weariness, they cause others to thirst for the Dharma and earnestly seek its meaning; in every place of rebirth, whether in the heavens or among humans, they attain mastery over their own lifespan.
This is the first attainment of mastery.
Furthermore, noble son!

There is mastery over body and speech; such a person’s body and speech are brought about by their own self. The mind does not rely on the body, yet it manifests forms through the faculty of thought. It displays physical appearances according to their features, and based on the deportment, etiquette, physical beauty or ugliness, height or shortness, and virtue or vice of sentient beings, they contemplate right concentration to determine by what discipline they may be transformed.

The Bodhisattva then transforms his physical appearance; in the mere instant of a thought, whether sitting, rising, or moving about, he transforms all people—beings that crawl, breathe, or are otherwise animate—so that their bodies and complexions become uniform as he preaches the Dharma to them.
This is the second attainment of mastery. Furthermore, one attains mastery over the Dharma;

dwelling within the three realms, one upholds and governs the sublime scriptures that transcend the world rather than practicing worldly dharmas.
