Thus, while manifesting transformations everywhere in accordance with worldly customs, one does not abandon or distance oneself from the wisdom that transcends the world. Nor does one lose the profound path of unimpeded wisdom or become deluded regarding the dharma of dependent origination through the twelve links of causality.

Whether born in the heavens or within the human world, he causes countless people to follow his teachings through their respective languages; according to their inclinations, those with superior, middling, or inferior aspirations each obtain what they seek, attaining such majestic and sovereign mastery as this.
This is the third attainment of mastery.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who establish their minds so that they act according to their own will; as for this mastery, they may gather all the great oceans of existence within the trichiliocosm into a single ocean and establish it therein, manifesting transformations without any coming or going.

He consolidated all the Mount Sumerus of the three-thousandfold world system into a single mountain, such that the Four Heavenly Kings and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were unaware of its merging, dispersing, coming, or going.

Thereupon, he manifested transformations throughout the trichiliocosm, establishing all its inhabitants and beings so that they could know the number of every tree, flower, and fruit; he caused water and fire to fill the void of space, or transformed them into various jewels, establishing these according to his manifestations.
Having already established this, at the very moment they resolve their minds, there is none who does not receive deliverance;
yet it is as if nothing has changed. This is the fourth attainment of mastery.
Furthermore, son of good family!

By means of these four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), the bodhisattva practices and establishes himself, conversing with the Buddhas of the ten directions who remain by his side whether sitting, rising, or walking. He accompanies and engages in conversation with all beings—Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Great Kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—as they sit, rise, and walk.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers are subtle, sublime, and preeminent, standing out as distinct.
This has been attained through the practice of the principles of wholesome dharmas in the past, without any deficiency or omission.
What is meant by the meaning of practicing wholesome dharmas in the past as a basis for the supernormal power of psychic travel?

It means making one’s body supple and light, showing reverence to elders, serving the assembly of benefactors, and running errands or attending to their needs without finding it difficult; being humble and lowly in mind, harboring no self-importance; speaking kind words that please and win the respect and affection of all; returning to them with prostrations and performing every ritual courtesy; ensuring that one's speech accords with one's actions; having a mind that is light and agile; harboring no arrogance or indulgence; and maintaining a heart free from malice or harm.

He cultivates humility and subdues his own will; he listens to and receives the words of the Honored One, complying with the teachings by kneeling and prostrating; maintaining a supple mind, he restrains his resolve and practices with diligence, never abandoning it.
That person is fully endowed with the etiquette of the precepts; his physical conduct is extraordinary compared to the masses, and his mind is neither indolent nor negligent.
Having eliminated the defilements of greed, anger, and delusion that arise from desire, he is free from covetousness and envy.
When gluttony is eliminated and the underlying tendencies do not arise, the illness will be cured and one will transcend all worldly affairs.
The heavy burden one carries results from weakness and inferiority, leading to this affliction; by covering over these worldly affairs through the practice of *śamatha*, one removes that burden.

Regarding the five matters of receiving offerings, one bestows grace by means of bridges and pathways; one crosses the four great rivers with a large vessel, ferrying across all classes of sentient beings beyond the surging currents.

His transformative influence was transcendent and extraordinary: he rectified the chaotic, stabilized the wayward, established the biased, and brought laughter to those who disparaged; he did not obstruct the returning waves but resolved all doubts, and through his marvelous teachings, he brought peace to all who were restless.
He brings to mind all realms to awaken those who have not yet awakened; whatever he holds dear, he always gives away as a gift without later regret.
Seeking to rescue sentient beings, he encourages them toward the aspiration for the Way; if he sees others accumulating roots of virtue, he rejoices on their behalf.
He never praises himself for having attained peace for his own person; seeing others at peace, he rejoices in it and commends it.
Easy to support and contented, he does not look for profit from others; delighting in the life of renunciation, he encourages others to leave the household life and study the Way.
Cultivating great and universal compassion, they constantly maintain the aspiration for the Way; regarding enemies and friends with equanimity, their joy is like space.
Seeing those who are exhausted, they provide them with vehicles, thereby bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
Upon seeing those who study and learn, he honors them as if they were Buddhas; toward those who have not yet studied, he does not treat them with contempt.
To those who are impoverished, he gives wealth and means of livelihood; to those who are ill, he provides medical treatment to save their lives.

Seeing those who provide protection and rescue, one should repay their kindness with filial piety; seeing those who observe the prohibitions and precepts, one should be able to cultivate self-restraint.

In making offerings and serving them, one must not fail to accord with their intentions; as for those who lack reverence and diligence, one should encourage and rescue them, leading them through the ways of the world.
Wherever he travels and wanders, he commits no evil; he remains unattached to worldly affairs and practices all virtues.
O son of good family!
He cultivates the subtle and sublime supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), maintaining such conduct so as not to lose these powers, always accompanied by them until he attains the Way of the Buddha.
"This is the pure practice of the bodhisattva’s supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
*The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, fascicle 117 [and] fascicle 118.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Forty-seven, Part Two: The Assembly of the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What are called the five roots of pure practice for a bodhisattva?
To cultivate the meaning of the Path without grasping at any dharmas is the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya).
To vow to cross over to the other shore without requiring a driver is the faculty of diligence (vīryendriya)."
Not abandoning the aspiration for enlightenment for the sake of all beings is the faculty of intention (*chanda-indriya*).
To govern great compassion with the desire to rescue those in peril and distress is the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*).
To be able to receive and uphold all dharmas while cultivating profound stillness is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*).
Furthermore, son of good family!
To have deep faith in all the teachings of the Buddhas and to follow the tracks of the Path is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
To serve the teachings of the Buddhas without ever becoming weary is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
To keep in mind the sacred meanings of all Buddha-dharmas, never forgetting or abandoning them, is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
To practice the meditative concentration of the Buddhas without ever becoming lax or negligent is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
To be able to eliminate the knots of doubt in all sentient beings and to be free from conceptual longing is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, to aspire to the Buddha-way without harboring hesitation is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
That its nature is harmonious and supple, and that it cultivates diligence without ever turning back, is the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*).
That it encourages and assists the roots of virtue so that they grow and are never diminished is the faculty of mind (*manendriya*).
To universally manifest radiance that illuminates sentient beings and rescues them from turmoil is the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*).
To discern the fundamental origins of all persons and preach the Dharma accordingly is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*).
To transcend all hindrances and remain without attachment is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
To understand the fetters of sentient beings so that they are freed from all bonds is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
To practice what one's will upholds without attachment, walking alone through the three realms with a preeminent distinction—this is the faculty of intention (*manas-indriya*).
To know the causes and conditions by which all obstructions arise—this is the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*).
To fully comprehend all attachments and to possess an intelligence that reaches everywhere without obstruction—this is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, to cause that which one follows to be free from delusion—this is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
To transform others so they are not deluded, to abandon what is untimely, and to always maintain joy—this is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).

To always practice with purity according to the teachings one has received, not to be deluded by the defilements of the multitude regarding the subtle and wondrous Dharma, and to never forget the meaning of the Way while increasing one's cultivation day by day—this is the faculty of mind.
When one’s mind is pure and practices impartiality, attaining liberation through the equanimity of right concentration and noble wisdom, this is the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*).

When one realizes that there is nothing obstructive within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), departing from all untimely states and abiding in the clear understanding of the Dharma, this is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*).
To eliminate all roots of non-virtue and cultivate a multitude of virtues is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
To adhere to the roots of virtue and comply with the scriptures is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Accumulating manifold virtues without transgressing or losing the Dharma is the faculty of intention (*manendriya*).
A concentrated mind that is joyful, yet does not crave pleasure or tranquility, and which discerns the roots of all virtues in sentient beings, is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
To practice all manner of wholesome deeds through skillful means and cultivate the dharmas of the path accordingly is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

Furthermore, to believe and diligently cultivate the relinquishing of all laziness and negligence; for the mind to have no seeking and no forgetfulness; to protect and sustain the concentrated mind so that it does not become confused; and to practice wisdom in order to enlighten and transform ignorance—this is the faculty of wisdom.

Furthermore, those who practice faith cast aside false teachings; those who practice diligence relinquish the notion of self; with a mind focused on a single point, they cross beyond attachment to the body.
By being able to practice meditative concentration, they tear asunder the net of all sixty-two views.
As for those of wisdom and insight, they eliminate all attachments and the bonds of affection.
O son of noble family!
This is the pure practice of the five faculties cultivated by a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s purification of the five powers?

It is when one calculates that these can establish the five faculties, practices them without abandoning them, subdues and casts off the four Māras, does not follow the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and never regresses from the Mahāyāna; it is when one eliminates the defilements of various cravings and worldly toil, makes one's vows firm, attains mastery over the mind, and maintains a courageous resolve; it is when one's body is healthy and robust with strength, and one's faculties are tranquil, unimpaired, and rooted in steadfast faith."
"Noble son! This is called the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).
To refrain from doing what ought not to be done, and to control one's nature so that it becomes balanced and harmonious—this is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*)."
To practice all that ought to be cultivated and to possess a powerful mental resolve—this is the power of intention (*cittabala*).
To never forget the path-work one has undertaken and thereby to deliver all beings—this is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).
To be unharmed by the manifold thoughts of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects; to transcend all hesitation, fetters, and the dwelling places of the mind—this is the power of wisdom.
Furthermore, the power of faith is that which does not receive anything from the instruction of others.
The power of diligence is that which one should maintain and never forget or abandon.
The power of intention is that which attains dhāraṇī and the uncommon path of mind.
As for the power of meditative concentration, it is that one preaches the Dharma with impartiality, without following any factionalism.
As for the power of wisdom, it is that one resolves all doubts and unties the bonds of the net of afflictions that shackle sentient beings.
Furthermore, the power of faith is that which can fully possess the momentum of sincere trust.
The power of diligence is that which brings about liberation through firm strength for those who have not yet crossed over.
The power of intention is that which fully possesses the power of liberating wisdom and the knowledge and vision of deliverance.
As for the power of concentration, it is fully endowed with the power of ultimate resolve and nature.
As for the power of wisdom, it is fully endowed with the source of all various practices.
Furthermore, as for the power of faith, it can subdue the afflictions of stinginess, greed, and defilement.
As for the power of diligence, it is the ability to relinquish all that one possesses.
As for the power of intention, it is the manifestation of the roots of virtue that encourages and assists the mind of enlightenment.
As for the power of concentration, it is the practice of equanimity through the renunciation of all seeking.
As for the power of wisdom, it is that one never expects a reward for any practice one may perform.
Furthermore, as for the power of faith, it is that one relinquishes all accumulations of broken precepts.
As for the power of diligence, it is that one assiduously cultivates the prohibitions without ever transgressing them.
As for the power of intention, it fully possesses the mind of enlightenment so that it remains without deficiency or omission.
As for the power of concentration, one immediately attains entry into the ground of benevolence and harmony.
As for the power of wisdom, one severs birth and death in all that is practiced.
Furthermore, the power of faith is to remain free from the roots of contention and anger.
The power of diligence is to practice patience in accordance with right mindfulness.
The power of intention is to be fully endowed with the practices of the Path and not to disparage the Dharma.
As for the power of concentration, one first restrains the mind to ensure non-negligence and protects all classes of sentient beings.
As for the power of wisdom, one does not conceive of a self nor entertain the notion of a person.
Furthermore, the power of faith consists in casting off indolence and all defiling dust and grime.
The power of diligence consists in being able to transcend all causal conditions and not being deluded by evil deeds.
As for the power of intention (*chanda-bala*), it consists in practicing the Path so as to bring it to fulfillment.
As for the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*), it consists in the body attaining rest and being able to subdue the Māras.
As for the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*), it consists in there being nothing among all that is to be done which is not accomplished.
Furthermore, the power of faith is that which digests all defilements and various heterodox practices.
The power of diligence is that which gathers sentient beings together and transforms them.
The power of intention is that which always unifies one's resolve and provides encouragement and assistance.
As for the power of concentration, it constantly practices stillness and tranquility, never becoming turbid or distracted.
As for the power of wisdom, it clearly understands the dharmas practiced by all people.
Furthermore, as for the power of faith, it abandons all views and the various defilements of what is known.
As for the power of diligence, it is to constantly and zealously practice in order to seek extensive learning.
As for the power of intention, it is to purify one's thoughts so that one's actions accord with what is appropriate.
As for the power of concentration, it is to attain that state wherein the mind gives rise to nothing at all.
As for the power of wisdom, it consists of diligent study and capability that leads to accomplishment.
Furthermore, the power of faith is to constantly attain the wealth of the seven riches through sincerity.
The power of diligence is to clearly understand and discern so as to bring about the seven factors of enlightenment.
As for the power of his intention, his mind is always orderly and never confused.
As for the power of his concentration, it brings about transcendence beyond the abidings of the seven consciousnesses.
As for the power of his wisdom, he surpasses the eight heterodoxies and remains unattached.
That which cannot be destroyed and whose mind remains ever pure is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).
To practice purity without retreating, being without distinction between pure and impure, or appropriate and inappropriate, is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).
To purify the mind so that it accords with the dharmas of the path-factors for all classes of beings, being without intention and without thought—this is the power of the mind (*cittabala*).
To apply diligent effort with the mind toward the cultivation of stillness and attain right meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—this is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).
If one can maintain purity and is not deluded by various views, honoring all roots of virtue, this is the power of wisdom.
O son of good family!
This is the purification of the five powers practiced by a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is meant by the purification of the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) of a bodhisattva?
By manifesting the factor of enlightenment of intention (saṃkalpa-bodhyaṅga), he attains mastery in the unique wisdom of the path."
Regarding the factor of awakening of dharma: one observes one's conduct so that it accords with the appropriate time and remains unattached.
Regarding the factor of awakening of vigor: one diligently practices until reaching the state of non-obstruction.
Regarding the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): the mind becomes free from attachment to worldly pleasures.
Regarding the factor of faith (*śraddhā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): body and mind find rest and reach the ultimate goal.
Regarding the factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): one is detached from the savor of mental volition and attains penetration.
The Chapter on the Awakening of Contemplation refers to the complete accomplishment of whatever karma one creates.
Furthermore, the mind that seeks the Way neither gains anything nor loses anything; this is the awakening of intention.
If one’s diligent effort in protecting and upholding the Dharma becomes ever more refined day by day, this is the awakening factor of dharma-discernment (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
To transform and enlighten sentient beings without weariness or fatigue is the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
To establish joy in the Dharma and to contemplate it with earnest application is the awakening factor of rapture (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
If one transforms sentient beings to eliminate their afflictions and establishes them in the Way, this is the factor of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
If one dwells in equanimity with a mind free from distraction, this is the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
If one can examine and practice the wisdom of the sages and worthies to establish all people, this is the category of the awakening of observation (*vipaśyanā*).
To be free from sorrow and without discursive thought, like a lion, surpassing the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, this is the category of the awakening of intention (*manas*).
All phenomena are entirely pure; one who clearly understands this possesses the factor of enlightenment of Dharma.
When one's conduct is pure, guarding body, speech, and mind so as not to commit transgressions, this is the factor of enlightenment of vigor.
Purity, non-attachment, and freedom from harm constitute the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Thoroughly cultivating one's practice and fully accomplishing all that ought to be done constitutes the factor of enlightenment of faith (*śraddhā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Never conforming to the world’s adherence to worldly dust (*rajas*), yet maintaining equanimity toward all forms and appearances—this is the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Never dwelling in the practice of dualistic dharmas, remaining free from drifting in the currents of saṃsāra, and constantly protecting and rescuing sentient beings—this is the factor of awakening of discernment (*dharma-pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The Buddha addressed the son of good family: "Why is it called the 'Factor of Enlightenment' (bodhipakṣa)?

It is because one clearly understands all phenomena without failing to penetrate them; one discerns, weighs, and cognizes their destination; one understands the proper deportment and etiquette and where they lead; and one transforms sentient beings. Dwelling in that state, one personally and diligently cultivates the broad practice of righteous principles, removing the fetters and all points of entanglement—this is the Factor of Enlightenment of the Mind."
This, then, constitutes the practice of the worthy and the sages, not that which is cultivated by foolish men.

To speak of these holy practices, they are not the conduct of Māra, nor are they the conduct of those who are arrogant and conceited; as for the practice of the holy sages, this is not something that can be attained by non-Buddhists or followers of heterodox schools.
The conduct of the noble ones does not involve the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, or tactile sensation.
For those who practice as noble ones, there is no attachment to the causal conditions of manifold conceptualizations.
The practitioner of the noble path has no selective attachment to places or directions, nor does he suffer any loss of mindfulness.
The practitioner of the noble path is devoid of the activities of mind, consciousness, thought, and speech.
The practitioner of the noble path is free from the dharmas of seeing, hearing, recollecting, and cognizing.
The practitioner of the noble path has no conceptualization or mental construction regarding nirvāṇa.
To have no activity toward any dharma whatsoever—this is the practice of the noble ones.
To cultivate the scriptures such that there is nothing—whether appropriate or inappropriate, to be remembered or not remembered—and no other thoughts, is the practice of the noble ones (ārya).
To abide nowhere among all phenomena and not to long for a position of honor is the practice of the wise.
To be undeluded regarding all phenomena, to act in accordance with the right principle so that each thing finds its proper place—this is the practice of the noble ones.
To never engage in dispute regarding any phenomenon, but to dwell in harmony and concord—this is the practice of the noble ones.
To practice all dharmas without the perception of dharmas, and not to lose the resolve for the Way—this is the conduct of the noble ones.
O son of good family!
Cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment, the pure conduct of the noble ones.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure conduct of the eightfold path?
That which is called the eightfold path consists of: first, right view."
What is called right view?
It is when one is able to practice all dharmas, neither abiding in self nor in non-self, and not dwelling in the contemplation of emptiness. Why is this so?

When one examines the body, it is equal to the self (ātman) without distinction; furthermore, one does not abide in the contemplation of the emptiness of the person who contemplates the body. Why is this?
Because the body, the person, and emptiness are likewise equal.
Furthermore, one does not abide in the contemplation that human life and lifespan are distinct from emptiness.
Why is this? Because human life and lifespan are empty.
One contemplates the equality of the mind, and likewise does not contemplate any birth-and-death, being free from the notion of emptiness regarding beginning and end.
Why is this? Because all that exists in birth-and-death and the afflictions of beginning and end, as well as that which is seen as empty, are all equal.
One does not dwell in the contemplation of emptiness by severing the views of annihilationism or eternalism, nor by clinging to a self or what belongs to a self. Why is this?
Because the views of annihilationism and eternalism are, in fact, equal.
Furthermore, one does not calculate the body or the emptiness that is observed, nor does one dwell therein. Why is this?
Because the body, the self, and emptiness are all equally empty.
Furthermore, one does not abide in the view that there is a distinction between the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, nor in the practice of contemplating emptiness. Why is this?
Because the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as the emptiness that is contemplated, are all entirely equal.
O son of good family!

To have views of "this" and "that," and to observe even up to nirvāṇa, is what constitutes right view regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; those with wrong views do not depart from perversion.
If one has no conceptualization regarding superior, middling, or inferior views, this is called right view.
Why is this? Because when one observes in such a manner, there is likewise no perversion.
What constitutes "view"?
One who holds such views should contemplate equality.
To view the dharmas of ordinary beings as base and lowly, while viewing the dharmas one has studied as noble and exalted—to view things in this manner is erroneous contemplation.

To perceive the dharmas of ordinary beings as having impure conduct that has not yet been eliminated, while perceiving the dharmas of bodhisattvas as being free from defilement—to view things in this way constitutes a false view.

To perceive the dharmas of ordinary beings as being with outflows (*sāsrava*), while perceiving the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as being without outflows (*anāsrava*)—to view things in this way constitutes a false view.
To perceive that the dharmas of ordinary beings involve seeking food and clothing, while the dharma of pratyekabuddhas does not expect offerings—to view things in this way is a false view.
To perceive that there is a limited mind characterized by expectation, while the mind of a bodhisattva is free from all expectation—to view things in this way is a false view.
To view the dharmas of ordinary beings as being characterized by negligence, and the dharmas of Bodhisattvas as being characterized by desirelessness—such a view constitutes a false view.
To view the dharmas of ordinary beings as entirely conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and the Buddha’s True Dharma as the unconditioned path (*asaṃskṛta-mārga*)—such a view constitutes a false view.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"To be able to examine that the dharmas of ordinary persons and all dharmas are fundamentally pure, and that the dharmas studied by them are also fundamentally pure; to contemplate that all dharmas are entirely spontaneous—this constitutes right view."
The dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of training are also empty; to realize that the dharmas of training are empty is right view.
The dharmas of ordinary beings are equal to causes and conditions; to clearly understand that the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha are likewise equal to causes and conditions is right view.
The dharma of ordinary beings is quiescent silence; the dharma of bodhisattvas is likewise profound stillness—this is right view.
The dharma of ordinary beings has no attainment, and the dharma of the Buddhas has no ultimate end—this is right view.
As for right view: when the mind does not enter into duality and does not perceive duality; when one is without a person and does not perceive a self, that is right view.

To be without manifold views and not to regard manifold things as distinct views constitutes the contemplation of equality. Thus, one does not conceive of all phenomena as having superior, middling, or inferior qualities. To have no conceptualized perceptions regarding any phenomenon is right view.
As for right view, it is the absence of manifold views and the absence of anything seen; that which is without anything seen is indeed right view.
That which is to be examined has no form or color; seeing all phenomena as being without form or color is indeed right view.
"Noble son! One who contemplates all dharmas and understands them in this way is said to be one who proclaims the Dharma and Vinaya.
When these words were spoken, five hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and their minds were liberated.
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa:

"What is called right mindfulness is the elimination of all thoughts, wherein both thought and non-thought are gathered together in stillness; it is the observation of the wisdom-virtue that reaches the dharma of profound serenity, clearly understanding what is observed as it pertains to all phenomena."
Regarding those who possess faith and contemplation: what is called "Dharma" and what is called "non-Dharma"?

To understand that all phenomena are each distinct and do not associate with one another, and to clearly realize this non-contemplation as equality—how much less could there be any such thing as faith in what is false?

"In all thoughts, there is neither thought nor non-thought; there is nothing further to be contemplated, and no distinction between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate—this is right mindfulness.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"What is called right speech is that which, when spoken, does not perceive one's own body, does not perceive others, and is not attached to self or other; it does not harm oneself nor does it harm others—this is called right speech."

Furthermore, right speech means to understand all phenomena equally, knowing that all phenomena reach the state of cessation, and knowing that all phenomena return to the Dharma of the noble ones and to liberation; this is called right speech.

Practicing a mind of loving-kindness and further increasing compassion, making no distinction between kin and enemy; teaching that even correct speech is empty, expounding all dharmas as signless, wishless, entirely without action, neither arising nor originating; that the words for all dharmas are equal, and that the teaching on all dharmas is impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

As for their correct speech: they declare that all dharmas are devoid of a person or a life-span; they teach equally that all dharmas arise from the conditions of the mind, such that according to what one sows, one reaps its fruit; and the Bodhisattvas manifest themselves before sentient beings to proclaim the sutras and teachings so that they may practice the Buddha-way.
When one’s right speech is pure, one is protected by all the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called right speech.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

“What is called right action is that which dissolves all karmic deeds created, never again establishing the foundations for such deeds; it is the practice of karma that extinguishes all suffering and affliction, causing all habitual actions to become empty and non-substantial. It does not give rise to wrong action, remains free from worldly toil and defilement, and is without turbidity—this is called right action.”

If there is a bodhisattva who thoroughly understands these karmas as well as all phenomena, and who cultivates virtuous conduct without performing any [deliberate] acts toward the roots of goodness, this is called "non-action" which constitutes the performance of practice; it is the abode of emptiness, voidness, and non-substantiality. This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the supreme, honored path, which is right action.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is called right livelihood (samyag-ājīva) is not reckoning there to be a self, nor reckoning there to be a person; this is called right livelihood.
One who possesses right livelihood does not accumulate any of the afflictions (kleśa)."

The right livelihood of a bodhisattva enables the pure cultivation of the mental dispositions of sentient beings; having purified those dispositions, they do not conceive of a self, nor do they conceive of a life-span and so forth. For the sake of others, themselves, and all phenomena, they practice the meaning of purity—this is called right livelihood.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"What is called 'right effort' (samyak-pradhāna) means that herein one does not perform unrighteous deeds; the mind does not abandon the skillful means of virtue; it is peaceful and free from cowardice; and one cultivates right conduct with purity and approaches it closely—this is called right effort."

That which is right expedient means does not constitute a false expedient; the skillful means employed accord with what is spoken. One does not calculate whether dharmas are equal or unequal; being neither active nor inactive, one abides as all dharmas abide, establishing skillful means in accordance with their course of action.

According to this principle, the Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise so: taking such quiescence as the means (*upāya*), all dharmas are equal and without distinction, and their practice is also equal. To eliminate the deviant means for all sentient beings, one thereby encourages and assists them toward universal wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*); this is the correct means practiced by Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"What is called right intention refers to recollecting the Buddha-way and being mindful of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, wisdom, and loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; this is called right intention."
Maintaining diligent mindfulness, he does not listen to any defilements of worldly toil nor yield to the influence of Māra.

As for that which he contemplates, wherever he is reborn, he does not fall into wrong views; he skillfully governs his mind and restrains his thoughts, like a gatekeeper who knows the proper time for closing and opening.
To eliminate all unwholesome thoughts and reflections, and not to entertain erroneous thoughts—this is called right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
When a bodhisattva abides in this right intention, they do not seek to realize the fruit within the nature of the path of cessation; this is the pure practice of a bodhisattva’s right intention.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"What is called the right concentration of a bodhisattva is to follow the practice of the noble ones, knowing the truth of suffering, severing the seeds of the truth of origination, realizing the seeds of the truth of cessation, and cultivating the seeds of the truth of the path; this is right concentration."
If he enters right concentration, his own body is equal [to others] and all phenomena are also equal.
His own body is pure and all phenomena are also pure; his own body is empty and all phenomena are also empty.
One who is able to thus maintain meditative concentration and right attainment enters into equanimity without falling into cessation; this is the pure practice of a bodhisattva’s right concentration.

At the very moment the mind is aroused, one acts with equanimity, fulfills wisdom and all noble merits, and awakens to the realization of all phenomena; this is the pure practice of a bodhisattva’s right concentration.

When the Buddha had spoken this discourse on Right Concentration and Awakening, one thousand six hundred disciples—both gods and humans—who had previously delighted in the Lesser Vehicle and entered its teachings, now changed their resolve and gave rise to the aspiration for Unsurpassed, Right, and True Enlightenment.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s awakening of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga)?

It is to nourish the mind so that it does not give rise to [defilements], to eliminate lust, anger, and ignorance, and to depart from attachment to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Abiding in the three bases without attachment, one walks alone through the triple world, transcends the three gates of liberation, and attains the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā). Beholding the past, future, and present without obstruction, one delivers sentient beings and removes all impurities, just as the brilliance of the sun shines upon everything."

Through skillful means and wisdom, they manifest themselves according to the occasion, moving through the three periods of time like a lotus in water; they transform and enlighten all beings, causing them to resolve upon the path. This is the pure practice of a bodhisattva who guards the intention for awakening.
The Buddha told Ratnaśikhin:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva accomplishing supernormal powers as a pure practice?
Furthermore, one possesses five things that enable thorough vision."

What are these five? Attaining radiance is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*); it universally illuminates the ten directions, exhausting all darkness so that nothing remains unseen or unilluminated. It perceives all Buddhas and those whom they transform and deliver; therefore, it is called the divine eye.
Beholding from afar the destinations of sentient beings throughout their beginnings and ends, and adorning their resolve, is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).

It perceives all forms, colors, appearances, and species throughout the ten directions—whether beautiful or ugly, long or short. This divine eye is without obstruction; its mental activity is quiescent and its characteristic is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It surpasses that of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, seeing both the origins and the ends of things without anything being beyond its reach.
"Noble son! By means of such analogies, one attains the five supernormal powers; reaching this divine eye constitutes the eye of a bodhisattva.
This is the purity of the bodhisattva’s divine eye."
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"Furthermore, by means of five things, one achieves such penetrating hearing that there is nothing one does not hear. What are these five?

They hear human voices, and they also clearly hear the voices of non-humans; they hear the sounds of suffering from those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, and they hear all the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma. They are able to hear and comprehend all the various languages and expressions throughout the ten directions, each distinct and different, numbering in the hundreds of millions of kinds.
"These are the five matters by which a bodhisattva’s supernormal power of clairaudience is purified.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"Furthermore, there are five matters by which one knows the thoughts and intentions of others' minds."
What are these five?

They are the ability to fully comprehend the origins and causes of all beings—whether gods, humans, hell-dwellers, hungry ghosts, or animals—as well as their mental inclinations toward good or evil, and how they shall receive further bodies in future lives.

He knows the direction in which the mental intentions of the past, future, and present incline; he determines their origins and sees that they return to unwholesome karma. He fully understands the good and evil deeds performed by the mental intentions of sentient beings.
Observing their mental states, if they harbor greed, lust, anger, or delusion, the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma according to their fundamental conduct as is appropriate.
This is the pure practice of a Bodhisattva who knows the thoughts and intentions of others.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s pure supernormal knowledge of the past?
It means knowing the ancient worlds through five matters."
Those who experience lust, anger, and delusion do so entirely as a natural consequence of failing to engage in mature reflection;

they simply fail to understand that their own bodies have undergone countless transmigrations. Instead, they should focus exclusively on practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, wisdom, and the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
By relying on that concentrated mind, one attains this; furthermore, from having already brought about its reception, one contemplates the various marks through the causal conditions of mindfulness.
Those causal conditions of the marks are also spontaneously received by oneself through action, as one reflects upon the mind and observes its own resolve.

Their entry into the gate of delusion is likewise spontaneous; having become mindful of this consciousness, they experience all things—be they physical forms, retinues, power, reputation, nobility, poverty, lowliness, suffering, or pleasure—as natural occurrences of their own being, thereby undergoing these afflictions.
"This is called the bodhisattva’s pure supernormal power of knowing the thoughts of past minds.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with the bases of psychic power?"
Thus, one attains the spiritual powers (ṛddhipāda) by means of five matters. What are these five? They are:

the sovereign mastery of manifesting physical forms; the attainment of spiritual power through consciousness and vocal resonance; and the universal pervasion of the spiritual power exercised by the mind.
The spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) by which all sentient beings find delight are each distinct; through the spiritual power of approaching what is seen, they reach everywhere.

Seated, they behold the countless lands of the ten directions, pervading the realms of all Buddhas. According to local customs, they manifest their physical forms; their bodies pervade all sentient beings of the ten directions as they preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain understanding and resolve to awaken to the Great Way.
"O son of good family!
This is the purity of the psychic powers practiced by a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“The Bodhisattva’s eye of wisdom is endowed with the purity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
As for that divine eye, it abides in the consciousness of the spirit without any attachment, thereby attaining the fundamental and ultimate purity of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*)."
Abiding in non-obstruction, they immediately know the mental inclinations of sentient beings without fail; they fully know the locations of the past and the future, and are able to verify them all.
Abiding in non-action, one exhausts all outflows and the activities of birth and death, thereby purifying the bases of psychic power and attaining the clarity of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
What are called these superknowledges are the gateway to the noble wisdom that brings an end to all outflows.
The Bodhisattva takes delight therein through these five supernormal powers, yet his mind does not dwell upon the wisdom that exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*).
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:

"Suppose there were a great capital city located a hundred thousand *yojana* away from a populated district along a winding road; the path is perilous and fraught with countless hardships, obstructed by deep ravines and narrow defiles where bandits lie in ambush to plunder, and where lions, tigers, and wolves prey upon one another."
If one emerges from this path and can reach that country, entering its great city, one will be completely liberated from all afflictions and attain immeasurable peace and security.

At that time, there was a man who heard of the fame, virtue, merit, and happiness of that kingdom and city, which were renowned far and wide. This man had an only son born to him, whom he loved and cherished deeply, never tiring of gazing upon him; yet, hearing the name of that kingdom, he abandoned his son and departed. Exerting himself with all his might, he endured various hardships and the sufferings of many difficulties, never flagging day or night, until he encountered a cool shade. Mastering the six arts and wielding the five weapons, he was then able to cross over.
He arrived at the city gate and stood upon its lintel; proceeding slightly further to the second gate, he opened that city gate and stood there alone, then immediately reflected:
"The one son born to me has not yet come."
"Because of his affection for his son, he does not enter the great city; instead, he immediately returns and brings his son back with him to the Land of Bliss. The Buddha told the clansman:

"The Bodhisattva thus dons the armor of the infinite, and through great diligence and a firm nature, by means of sincere devotion, manifests the Great Way. He purifies the karma of the mind and practices pure and virtuous conduct. Having exhausted all outflows (āsrava), he gives rise to a heart of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), transforming and enlightening sentient beings by preaching the Dharma for them. Through wisdom, he cuts off birth and death, attaining the ultimate accomplishment of the state beyond outflows (anāsrava)."
Out of compassion for sentient beings and the desire to rescue and protect them, he returns once more to manifest in the stage of an ordinary person.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"That city is a metaphor for the towering noble wisdom in which all outflows have been exhausted."

"To travel through difficult terrain for hundreds of thousands of *yojana*s on a dark and remote path" refers to wandering through the immeasurable hardships of birth and death, rescuing and liberating sentient beings without being constrained by them.
"Robbers, thieves, tigers, and wolves" refers to the afflictions of the various Māras, false views, and unrighteousness.
"Devouring one another" refers to the calamities of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the three realms.
"Encountering cool shade" refers to the practice of equanimity (*samatā*).
"The six arts and five weapons" refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
"That person" is the Bodhisattva.

Arriving at that city, he stood upon the threshold of the gate; then, proceeding gradually from the outer gate to the middle gate, he stood there and did not advance further. This signifies that the Bodhisattva proceeds from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); with all outflows (*āsrava*) exhausted and his mind luminously penetrating, he does not abandon his original vow to deliver the beings of the ten directions as if they were his only child.

Regarding those who do not enter the city but return: the Bodhisattva takes pity on all sentient beings, regarding them in his heart as a father regards an only son. He eliminates the hardships of the outflows (*āsrava*) of birth and death and dwells transcendentally at the summit of the Dharma (*dharmakūṭa*). Although he has emerged from birth and death, he does not exhaust the outflows; instead, he returns immediately to dwell within the five destinies (*pañcagati*) to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
"This is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s skillful means and great compassion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"It is unprecedented, O God among Gods!"

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, harboring great compassion in his resolve, does not delight in [personal] liberation; desiring to deliver sentient beings as if gazing upon the palm of his own hand, he returns to the cycle of birth and death without feeling aversion or weariness.
He again asked the Buddha,
"What dharmas does a bodhisattva practice so as not to grow weary of birth and death?
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“Bodhisattvas have twenty matters for which they do not weary of birth and death.
What are these twenty matters? They are:
practicing the roots of virtue up to the ultimate of great compassion; maintaining great loving-kindness to gather in those in great peril; cherishing [all beings]...”
With great compassion, they embrace those who do not practice broad pity; they transform sentient beings and deliver all. They constantly use diligence to embrace the timid and weak;
with a nature of harmony and regulation, they embrace those harboring fetters; with skillful means, they embrace those who do not know moderation;
with wisdom, they embrace the ignorant and deluded; and with a single mind, they embrace those who are heedless.
He is able to gather in those who are obstructed by means of supernormal powers; he is able to gather in those who are mired in darkness by means of holy wisdom;
he is able to gather in those who are purposeless by means of acting according to the occasion; his mind is single-mindedly intent on gathering in those who are agitated and confused;

he honors the aspiration for the Way to gather in those who have not studied; he practices the four debts of gratitude to gather in those who have no protector; and he gathers in the poor by means of giving.
Through poverty, one gathers those who lack propriety by means of reverence and precepts; through extensive learning, one gathers those of little wisdom;

through dhāraṇī-retention, one gathers those prone to forgetfulness; through eloquence, one gathers those who are stubborn and stammering; and through superior virtue, one gathers those with little merit.
It is for this reason that one achieves great wisdom.
"O son of good family!
These are the twenty practices by which a bodhisattva does not grow weary of birth and death.
Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin again asked the Buddha:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being appropriately situated within birth and death to bring benefit to countless beings?
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"If a bodhisattva adorns themselves with virtue while being appropriately situated within birth and death, they moisten those who are impoverished and in peril with the moisture of merit."
Adorned with extensive learning, one is well-suited for the cycle of birth and death; through eloquence, one brings great benefit to many.

Being able to maintain one’s resolve without negligence or forgetfulness, one attains *dhāraṇī* and is well-suited for the cycle of birth and death, causing all people to each attain the wisdom of hearing.
Having attained the Treasure Hand, he adorns himself with excellent giving; his wealth is never depleted, and he uses these treasures to bring great benefit to many.
Furthermore, remaining heedful within the cycle of birth and death, he tirelessly expounds the Dharma, bringing vast benefit to all people.
Furthermore, one should appropriately gather all marks within the cycle of birth and death, adorning all sentient beings with the cultivation of wisdom.

One’s words and deeds should correspond, acting appropriately within the cycle of birth and death; whatever one does should be timely and maintain its proper measure, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.
One should practice giving all things without stinginess, appropriately transforming beings within birth and death so that each attains their proper place.

Through the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), one brings great benefit to all sentient beings; one should observe pure precepts appropriately within birth and death, adorning oneself with the holding of precepts to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
"Patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are appropriate for the cycle of birth and death; through these six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), one brings great benefit to all sentient beings.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"In the distant past, incalculable and immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Puhuai Shi (Universal Destroyer of the World) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
The world was named Celestial Contemplation (*Devadarśana*), and the eon was named Joyful Delight (*Prītivardhana*). Why was that eon called Joyful Delight?
Because during that eon sixty thousand Buddhas appeared, and at that time the Śuddhāvāsa devas heard countless voices proclaiming the virtues of those Buddhas.

In this kalpa, there were sixty thousand Buddhas; at that time, both devas and humans together sang praises of them, and all who heard these sounds of admiration felt joy and gave rise to wholesome minds. For this reason, the kalpa was named "Joyful."
The Buddha told the son of noble family:

"That buddha-world is peaceful, secure, and blissful; its virtues are so magnificent that the devas and humans never tire of beholding it. For this reason, the world is named 'Heavenly Contemplation' (Devadarśana)."
That land is subtle, supremely sincere, and magnificently adorned; its ground is composed of various kinds of incense and is capable of sustaining the foundation of a thousand worlds.
Furthermore, the fragrance emitted by that buddha-field pervades immeasurable and innumerable lands throughout the ten directions.
In that land, within the shade of sandalwood smoke, there naturally arise infinite lotus flowers named "Radiant Brilliance.
The light of these lotuses constantly illuminates that world with great splendor.

The people, both great and small, possess the power of spiritual travel (ṛddhi). The dwellings of those of long-standing virtue consist of fragrant towers, lecture halls, and monasteries, with eaves, doors, windows, and lattices, as well as couches, beds, rugs, and mats of exquisite fineness and elegance.

That Buddha’s land likewise has no states, cities, districts, counties, villages, or hamlets; furthermore, all its people have attained supernatural powers and walk upon the void, while its towers, pavilions, and lecture halls are also situated in space. Seated within these towers and halls, they single-mindedly contemplate the Way, reciting, chanting, and discussing it.

There are no women there, nor is there the womb; all beings are born by transformation and the very name of "woman" is unheard of. Furthermore, there is not even the mention of the three miserable realms or evil destinies, nor are there the afflictions or sufferings of toil and hardship.

All the people take meditative concentration and joy as their food and drink; they have profound faith in the subtle and wondrous, aspiring toward the Mahāyāna, and among them there is no other vehicle, nor even the names of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The people of that land all wear crowns and caps; their clothing and complexions are like those of celestial beings.
Even when they go out to study, they immediately abandon worldly toil and sensual desire, remaining free from the burdens of sorrow.
Furthermore, that Tathāgata does not command the bodhisattvas to don the dharma-robes.
Why is this? It is because those individuals do not give rise to defiled or turbid minds.

The physical form and majestic countenance of that Tathāgata appeared like those of Brahmā; the assembly of bodhisattvas was fully endowed with every dignified deportment and ritual propriety, remaining composed and serene as they sat, rose, and expounded the Way of the Sūtras.

Suppose that bodhisattvas possessing infinite transformations and supernatural powers from the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions were to travel to the world of Devadṛśa; passing through various kingdoms to come and visit the Tathāgata, they would bow their heads in prostration and take refuge in him to hear the sūtras. Upon seeing that the Buddha-land was peerless, its virtues transcendent and sublime, vast and immeasurable, and marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, they would raise their voices in praise and then depart.
The Buddha addressed the son of noble family:

"If that Tathāgata were to proclaim the transformative teachings of the Way for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he would ascend into the void to a height of sixty-six *zhang* above the ground and sit upon a subtle, pure, and magnificently adorned lion throne. For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he would discourse on the supreme Dharma-teachings by briefly outlining their essentials, rather than extensively analyzing them or repeatedly refining their intermediate meanings, as I have done here with much elaboration and earnestness."

Why is this? Because all these noble beings have entered into holy wisdom; with a single phrase or verse, they are able to understand and penetrate hundreds of thousands of meanings. Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims the teachings of the sūtras by means of concise statements rather than through many words.
That Buddha expounded for him the four practices of purity:

the purity of the perfections (pāramitās), the purity of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas), the purity of supernormal powers (abhijñā), and the purity of transforming sentient beings; these are the four.
The Buddha told Ratnaśikhin:
"At that time, there was a bodhisattva in that buddha-field named Ratna who addressed the Tathāgata Lokavināśana, asking:
'What is meant by a bodhisattva who should remain within saṃsāra for the sake of bringing great benefit to all sentient beings?'"

At that time, the Tathāgata extensively analyzed and explained the meaning of these two phrases for the Bodhisattva: "In this Great Wisdom, no one can prevail; the conduct of a Bodhisattva constantly dwells within birth and death, yet they attain the radiance of wisdom which brings great benefit and nourishment."
As soon as the Buddha had spoken these words, sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
The Buddha said to Ratnaśikhin:
"The Bodhisattva Ratnaka further asked:"
"What is meant by a bodhisattva adorning and purifying the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and sitting beneath the tree of awakening?
The Tathāgata Huaishe replied to Zhenbao:
"One adorns and purifies the site of enlightenment and sits beneath the tree of awakening by means of non-negligence."
"What is meant by 'one who is heedful'? The Buddha replied, "One who practices the sūtras.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'practicing the sūtras'? He replied:

"It is the correspondence between speech and action, which is non-negligence; furthermore, being non-negligent, one does not run wild, but cultivates the armor of immeasurable great virtue, remaining ununited with the aggregates and transcending the five aggregates."
Generosity is immeasurable because it is inexhaustible;
ethical discipline is immeasurable because it is for the sake of those who have not yet trained;
patience is immeasurable because it endures all sufferings.
Diligence is immeasurable because it is the activity of true beings;
meditative concentration is immeasurable because there is no falling back;
wisdom is immeasurable because there is no obstruction.
Immeasurable loving-kindness, because it transforms and guides sentient beings without limit;
immeasurable compassion, because it pities sentient beings and relieves their destitution;
immeasurable sympathetic joy, because it gladdens sentient beings with the Dharma.
One practices immeasurable protection for the sake of rescuing, aiding, and nourishing all sentient beings;
one undergoes immeasurable births and deaths for the sake of long-term cultivation of all the dharmas of the Buddha-way;
and one transforms immeasurable people for the sake of bringing peace to both self and others.
The True Dharma is immeasurable, for one follows it according to the times through steadfast diligence;
virtuous wisdom is immeasurable, for one wields skillful means equally in accordance with the times;
one serves immeasurable Buddhas, for one is fully endowed with wisdom.
He seeks immeasurable learning because his wisdom is preeminent;
his mind enters the immeasurable because he perceives the aspirations, natures, and conducts of sentient beings;
his virtuous conduct is immeasurable because his will dwells in the tranquility that transcends all limits.
"His dwelling in seclusion is immeasurable, because he accords with his mind;
his silent stillness is immeasurable, because his investigation is vast and universal, swiftly and completely perfecting all supernormal powers and wisdom.
The Buddha told Precious Jewel:

"This is the dharma that should be followed through heedfulness; for a bodhisattva who practices this heedfulness, it means to adorn and purify the site of enlightenment and sit beneath the Bodhi tree."
Furthermore, son of good family!
Non-laxity is the foundation upon which all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are established, and it is the source that leads to the noble wisdom of non-laxity.
One attains the essential and steadfast Dharma by accumulating the roots of virtue through non-laxity.

Being able to practice without negligence, they never forget the teachings heard in the distant past; they are universally able to uphold all sūtras and digest all afflictions and immeasurable hindrances.
Regarding the meanings of all paths, they are free from obstruction.

Those who are without negligence are able to incinerate the vast wilderness of accumulated darkness of ignorance; they are fully capable of protecting all the teachings of the sutras, eliminating all manifold signs, and subduing the sense faculties.

Those who are heedful abandon the deviant paths and practice all manner of goodness; their power and majesty are preeminent, fully endowed with the ten powers, and like space, their strength is without equal.
Those who are heedful attain fearlessness, fully accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, and reach the ultimate summit.
Those who are heedful are able to obtain the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms of the Buddhas.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“When that Buddha preached this discourse on heedfulness, twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.”
What do you think, noble son?
Was the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha at that time anyone else?
Do not view it in such a way.
Why is this? It is because your very body is it.

For this reason, you should form this contemplation: if a bodhisattva is free from negligence, they shall appropriately adorn and purify the site of enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter the immeasurable path of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin:

"Regarding what is called a bodhisattva’s transformation of sentient beings: if a bodhisattva practices purity, and perceives that the conduct and minds of sentient beings harbor both good and evil, they are then able to transform immeasurable, limitless, and inconceivable classes of beings, causing each to practice the Dharma of the Infinite."
Those bodhisattvas, whose natures are disciplined and gentle, enter into profound discernment and freely transform and guide countless people.
O son of noble family!
Because the faculties of people differ and their perspectives vary, the bodhisattvas manifest accordingly to lead them forward.

There may be those who achieve transformation through firm and upright precepts; or those who receive instruction because of their violation of precepts; or those who receive the transformative influence of the Way through the exchange of clothing and goods; or through gentleness, or through harshness; or while harboring a poisonous mind, or through fear, or through suffering and affliction, or through peace and security, they receive transformation.

Sometimes through speech; sometimes from attaining victory; sometimes from arising due to causes; sometimes from disposition; sometimes from affliction; sometimes from what is agreeable to the mind; sometimes from existence; sometimes from non-existence; sometimes from prosperity; sometimes from that which is received; sometimes from that which is not received; sometimes from livelihood through wealth and occupations; sometimes from tranquility and the absence of anything to be grasped; sometimes from longing for and seeking exquisite countenances; sometimes from ugly forms; or sometimes they are brought to transformation through the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and subtle touch.
Some attain awakening through anger, verbal abuse, foul odors, unpleasant tastes, coarse or hard textures, or impure phenomena;

some are transformed through living together or staying overnight with others; some through coming and going or frequent mutual encounters; some through hearing the Buddha’s Dharma and the noble Saṃgha; some through joy, some through sorrow, some through the realization of non-self, or through silent stillness; and some receive transformation through the sounds of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom.
Some are transformed through the afflictions of sentient beings and conditioned existence; some are transformed by hearing of the peace and security encountered in the heavens and the world;
some hear the teachings of the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and some hear of the Mahāyāna and are thereby transformed.

Some follow from constant joy rather than sorrow; some follow from grief rather than gladness; some follow from wealth and profit; some follow from exultation yet do not perceive love or respect; some follow from gaining profit, or from suffering decline; and there are also those who are transformed through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Some are transformed through internal karma, some through external karma, and some receive instruction and transformation through the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, hands, and feet.
Some are transformed by means of entertainment, song, and play, while others are transformed by means of flowers and incense.
Some encounter suffering and affliction through his body; some receive transformation and enlightenment through his constant bliss.

Some attain the skillful means of tranquility through his mind; some receive transformation and enlightenment through his manifestation in the form of a bhikṣu, or again, through his transformation into the forms of a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā.
"Or again, he may manifest in the form of a Buddha’s countenance to transform and guide them;
or he may manifest in the form of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Wheel-Turning Sage King to transform and guide them.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"If one were not to manifest various kinds of transformations, but instead sought to convert others by observing their dispositions and following their mental inclinations, one would be unable to deliver them.

One must clearly understand the dispositions and behaviors of sentient beings and provide medicine according to their ailments; only then will those delivered be vast in number. If a bodhisattva practices the *pāramitā* of deliverance, they can then receive and uphold the dharmas of the Buddha-way and clearly comprehend the wisdom of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); only thereafter do they peacefully convert sentient beings."
“Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they transform and enlighten sentient beings. What are these four?

First, never wearying of the afflictions of beginning and end, they guide those who have not yet reached understanding. Second, not being greedy for their own peace, they vow to bring peace to all. Third, they always proclaim the teachings of the Way according to the appropriate time and circumstances. Fourth, they discern the various types of sentient beings and the conduct of their respective mental natures.”
These are the four. Furthermore, there are another four:

first, the speech one utters is gentle and its words are worthy of respect; second, the observance of the precepts is pure like the radiance of the sun; third, one's countenance is always joyful and one never harbors resentment; fourth, one constantly maintains a heart of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there are four:
first, the mind harbors no malice; second, the will is set upon great compassion; third, the intention abounds in pity and sorrow for others; fourth, one constantly harmonizes the mind.
Furthermore, there are four:
first, purity of character and conduct; second, freedom from flattery and deceit; third, firmness and vigor in diligence; and fourth, endurance of suffering and joy, as well as good and evil.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva transforms and guides sentient beings; one should cultivate this contemplation, for only then can one be capable of rescuing and delivering all.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:

"In the distant past, incalculable, immeasurable, and inconceivable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vimalaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The world was called *Jiran* (Tranquil), and the eon was named *Aijing* (Affectionate Respect).
The world of *Jiran* was abundant, joyful, and peaceful; the five grains were plentiful and inexpensive, happiness was immeasurable, and the populations of devas and humans flourished.
The Buddha Vimalaprabha had a community of ninety-six billion śrāvakas and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.
The lifespan of that Buddha was three hundred and thirty-six thousand years.
At that time, there was a brahmin who was a great king. The king had a crown prince named Karmamukha, who was handsome and beautiful, such that those who saw him could never tire of the sight.

At the age of sixteen, infatuated with his own appearance and deluded by his noble status and wealth, he became dissolute and arrogant; he refused to go to visit the Buddha Vimalaprabha and would not practice reverence or prostrate himself in salutation.
The Buddha thought to himself:

"Why has Prince Karmaprabhāsa suddenly lost his aspiration for the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and his roots of merit? Unaware of his former lives, he calculates in terms of 'self' and 'mine,' becoming infatuated with physical appearance, wealth, and noble status, and harboring such arrogance that he no longer visits the Buddha."
Having come here, they are unwilling to take refuge, thereby violating the rules of propriety.
If one were to earnestly proclaim their past conduct to them, they would surely recognize their former lives and frequently visit the Tathāgata to prostrate and receive his teachings.

At that time, the Tathāgata Vimalaprabha invited all eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly and had them cast the dharma-votes, asking: "Who among you is able to go to the place of Prince Karmamukhya for eighty-four thousand years to teach and preach the Dharma, without becoming weary or distressed by any suffering or oppression encountered?"
"Even though you went there to teach him, he did not receive you; you obtained nothing but abuse, insults, humiliation, and slander regarding your seating, conversation, and discourse.
The Buddha told the son of noble family:
"At that time, although this tally was employed, among the eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, not a single bodhisattva was willing to accept the Dharma-tally."

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Supreme Exquisite Diligence (Paramavīrya). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I am capable of enduring eighty-four thousand years of coming and going with Prince Karmasena, meeting him repeatedly; I shall renounce all peace and endure every suffering, and though I encounter various calamities, I shall not regard them as a hardship."

As soon as the most wondrous and sublime diligence uttered these words, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways at that very moment; hundreds of thousands of devas and humans dwelling in the void raised their voices in praise, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Clad in the armor of great vows with boundless diligence," the Bodhisattva Supreme Wondrous Diligence then went to the gate of Prince Karmendra and stood there.

When the prince saw him, he reviled, insulted, and abused him with anger and slander; his words poured forth without restraint, as he threw handfuls of dust upon him, struck him with tiles and stones, and assailed him with swords and staves.

At that time, although the Bodhisattva was thus humiliated, he harbored no anger, felt no resentment, and had no regrets; instead, he further strengthened his resolve, donned the armor of diligence, increased his power of wisdom, and gave rise to great compassion, feeling pity for them.
In this manner, after a thousand years, he was finally able to advance and enter the first gate.
Having endured the hardships of suffering, oppression, and contempt for ten thousand years without weariness or fatigue, he proceeded further until he reached the first courtyard of the royal palace.
Furthermore, after twenty thousand years, he reached the second courtyard.
Following this pattern, it took eighty-four thousand years to reach the seventh courtyard.
After seven days and seven nights, Prince Karmamukha saw him once again and immediately questioned him:
"Monk, from where have you come, and what do you seek by coming here?
The Bodhisattva replied,
"I have come specifically to visit you and to inquire about your reputation and merit."
At that time, the Prince thought to himself:
"How extraordinary and unprecedented!
This bhikṣu’s virtue of precepts is immeasurable, such that none can equal him; yet he has never felt weary or ashamed despite being subjected to all manner of insults and humiliations."
The one of supreme and wondrous diligence, Joyful Leader of Deeds, immediately spoke in verse:
“O Prince, I now seek nothing; I desire neither food nor drink nor clothing.
You should manifest a heart free from fear, For I have come here for the sake of the Dharma.”
The Honored One among Men is named Vimalaprabha; the Great Sage appears in this world to bring great benefit.
By preaching the Dharma, he eliminates suffering and affliction; should anyone hear it, they shall attain the Ambrosia.
The appearance of the Buddhas is extremely difficult to encounter; they are hard to meet even in countless thousands of kalpas.
They guide all people so that they may receive the Dharma, acting as the torches of illumination for the world.
On the contrary, they pursue their desires with heedlessness, indulging themselves in wealth and beauty;
deluded by the arrogance of nobility and the pursuit of royal rank, they refuse to go and see the Dharma King.
Wealth and possessions are impermanent, and life is difficult to preserve; the Buddha has said that human life is like the morning dew.
Prince, observe for yourself that it is likewise ever thus; why, having heard the Buddha, do you still indulge in negligence?

O Benevolent One, since you have long set your will upon the Buddha-way and summoned all sentient beings with the desire to deliver them, for what reason now do you allow yourself to be led astray? How can you remain in negligence while seeking to deliver sentient beings?
I now wish to return to the Most Victorious One, To subdue my mind and extinguish worldly desires;
May you, O Benevolent One, exert diligence out of compassion for all, So that I may not later harbor regrets or feel distress.
At that time, the prince of the land, having heard this verse, immediately humbled his mind and gave rise to reverence;
with utmost diligence, he prostrated at [the Buddha’s] feet and said:
"I shall renounce all worldly pursuits; I will no longer long for nobility or crave the kingdom."
"I shall go to the place of peace and security, casting off all flaws and impurities to seek further benefit.
Together with one hundred and eighty million people, each holding various flowers and bearing incense,
they went as one to the presence of the Most Victorious One, to behold the Stainless Light, the Supreme among Men.
Having all arrived at the place of peaceful dwelling, they prostrated at his feet in worship and withdrew to stand to one side beside the Buddha.
At that time, the Prince spoke these words:
"Exquisite and supreme diligence is my teacher; with a heart free from weariness, he encourages me with a gentle countenance.
This debt of gratitude cannot be surpassed; even such offerings as these are insufficient to repay it."
I return and repent, confessing my transgressions to protect the world;
having violated the commands and teachings of the Dharma King, I now take refuge in you with total sincerity. May the Buddha graciously accept this confession of my heart.
Thereupon, they resolved their minds to seek Buddhahood for the sake of all beings, giving rise to compassion;
no longer committing evil or indulging in negligence, they now establish merit to attain the Way of the Buddha.
At that time, the Prince renounced his glorious rank and, together with one hundred and eighty-four million people,
became śramaṇas under the Most Victorious One, vowing in his mind to seek the Buddha-way.
At that time, the Buddha, knowing their aspirations, expounded for them the supreme practice of the Buddha-way;
those who heard the pure Dharma attained compliance, and all the noble beings dwelt in the dharma of non-self.
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa:
"If you wish to know who that Suvarṇavīrya was at that time, it was my own self.
The prince Karmamukha was Maitreya."
O son of noble family!
