In the past, the Bodhisattvas transformed and enlightened sentient beings without weariness; their majestic virtue was as lofty and immeasurable as this, and their learning deepened daily with a diligence that had no peer.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to deliver sentient beings should mindfully practice and study the virtues of that Bodhisattva of Utmost Sublime Diligence from the past.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“A bodhisattva possesses four activities through which they attain mastery; by means of these four activities, they gather in the path and dharmas of all Buddhas.”
What are these four?

First, to transcend all māras so that none do not submit; second, to contemplate the purification of Buddha-fields so as to cultivate pure teachings; third, to adorn body, speech, and mind in accordance with the fundamental nature of a bodhisattva; and fourth, to gather together all the factors of the path of the Buddhas.
These are the four dharmas of the karma of mastery.
Furthermore, there are four matters that constitute the work of a bodhisattva. What are these four?

First, their wisdom clearly understands the inclinations and dispositions of those they enter; second, they universally perceive the roots and origins of sentient beings and where they ultimately return; third, they distinguish all realms of existence according to their causes and conditions, administering medicine according to the illness; and fourth, they clearly recognize all paths and practices so as to attain tranquility and harbor no anger.
"These are the four matters that constitute the bodhisattva’s practice of the sovereign path of karma.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin took from his hair-tuft a bright moon pearl—planted over countless kalpas as the root of merit for hundreds of thousands of boundless virtues, its value equaling this entire trichiliocosm—and offered it to the Tathāgata, speaking these words:

"I offer this jewel from my crown to the Tathāgata. By virtue of this root of merit, may no one be able to behold the mark of my crown, and may I attain the crown of the inconceivable, holy wisdom of all Buddhas."

The Buddha immediately smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating countless buddha-lands. It then returned at once, circled the Buddha three times, and suddenly vanished into the crown of his head.
Thereupon, a bodhisattva named Kṣiprapratibhāna rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and praised the World-Honored One,
inquiring with a verse: "Most honored and without peer, Transcending all that is mundane, Stainless and free from defilement— The Three Realms extol your virtue."
Your compassion is peerless, surpassing even Mount Sumeru;
for what reason do you now smile with joy?
I pray that your wisdom will explain this to me.
With true Dharma, precepts, and disciplined concentration, you who possess a steadfast nature speak with reverence;
may my aspirations find peace, for through skillful cultivation, I shall attain sublime tranquility.
Here resides the Honored One of Gods and Humans, whose resolve is most firm and wondrous.
By what cause and condition do you manifest this response, showing compassion by smiling now?
Your universal power is supreme throughout the ten directions;
with the majesty of radiant merit and light, you are a valiant lion who destroys the darkness, wandering among the multitudes without fear.
In the three realms there is no peer; how could there be anyone superior?
You have expounded the Dharma-abode for us—why do you smile with such joy?
Having departed from defilement, your nature dwells in peace; your countenance is ever serene and pleasant.
Your fame and virtue pervade the void; your swift course is beyond limit.
You dispel all darkness, and there is nowhere your radiance does not shine.
Abiding solely for the sake of liberation, for what reason do you smile with joy?
Cultivating virtue with a pure mind, his vows are like a mountain of gold and jewels;
he constantly instructs those who have not yet reached him, and all people of the world universally make offerings to him.
He is thus the most excellent field of merit, a refuge for the multitude, a sage who transcends the world.
The Lion of the Śākyas manifests the essential; that which he expounds is like space.
Among all devas and human beings, none can equal his excellence.
His equanimity is exceedingly firm, and his sense of shame and dread of blame are most abundant and auspicious.
Sublime are your virtues, numbering in the hundreds of thousands; Your marks are as flourishing as flowers.
O Most Victorious and Benevolent One, you smile— I pray that you grant us an explanation.
Your wisdom is unimpeded, Pervading throughout the three periods of time.
Abiding amidst various bodies and minds, his heart is free from attachment.
He understands all things simultaneously and acts in accordance with what is appropriate.
O Lion of Benevolence, why do you smile? What is the meaning of this?
The devas dwelling in the air harbor joy within their hearts;
the people upon the earth join their palms in self-surrender.
The Victorious One, the Capable Sage, speaks alone of this extraordinary flavor of the nectar of immortality.
When the various devas and humans heard this, their afflictions and darkness were extinguished.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Swift Eloquence: "Did you not see Ratnaśikhin?"

"By offering this Jewel-Crested Pearl to the Tathāgata and aspiring for the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, one thereby makes an offering to the primordial wisdom of the Buddha.
He replied, "Indeed, I have seen it."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“This is the noble son, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin!”

For as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, one makes offerings to as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; constantly practices the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and transforms and enlightens countless classes of sentient beings, establishing them in the Three Vehicles.

After ten *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, receiving the names Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat, known as Ratnasaṃbhava.
The world was named Vimalaprabhā, and the eon was called Vimala.
That world Vimalaprabhā was composed of the seven treasures, all of which emitted light that illuminated immeasurable Buddha-lands in the ten directions.
Its radiance is purple-gold; if sentient beings encounter this light, all their afflictions (*kleśa*) will be entirely extinguished.

That land is abundant and joyful, and all its bodhisattvas are entirely free from attachment. There are no followers of heterodox paths to provoke conflict, as they universally cultivate the treasure of the Path. For this reason, the Tathāgata is named Ratnasaṃbhava (Treasure-Accomplished).

All these bodhisattvas have attained supernatural powers and possess eloquence; the devas and people of that land shall all be pure and virtuous, following the awakening of equality, such that there will be no one lacking in attainment or bearing the name of ignorance.
That land has no sovereign; the World-Honored One alone is the unsurpassed Dharma King.
All devas and humans are born through spontaneous transformation; there are no women, nor even the name of "desire."

The people of that land all cultivate the roots of virtue; there is no one without merit. Their faculties are all complete, and they all adorn their bodies with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
At that time, the Tathāgata and his assembly of bodhisattvas are beyond calculation.
The Buddha’s lifespan was fourteen kalpas.

From the beginning, he spoke nothing else; what he taught consisted solely of proclaiming the wisdom of bodhisattvas and the various *pāramitās*, with eloquence and great compassion, as a single, pure teaching.
All these bodhisattvas have previously received instruction; their faculties are clear and penetrating, enabling them to universally enter the path of all Buddhas through a single phrase.
The Tathāgata has expounded for them the teachings of dhāraṇī, his compassionate mind being like the earth.
What is meant by the "dhāraṇī of the verbal teaching"?
It is to universally enter all chapters through a single verse-line.
What is meant by "one sentence"?
This refers to the sublime and sacred phrases of the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment, which cannot be exhausted.
What is meant by "inexhaustible phrases"?
It means that within the Buddha-way, there is nothing that can be fully fathomed.
What is meant by "inexhaustible"?
To discourse on "non-existence" is called the phrase of inexhaustibility.
Having been able to enter non-existence and universally enter into all syllables—this constitutes a single phrase.
All written characters are inexhaustible; yet there are two characters that have never before been heard of nor practiced, which are proclaimed as issuing from a single character.
That which is a single character does not share its momentum with two characters; therefore, through a single character, instruction is proclaimed.
Were one to proclaim this instruction, there would be no thought and no non-thought, no response and no non-response; in this phrase, there is neither thought nor non-thought.
To accomplish enlightenment through the phrase of non-thought is for a son of noble family to enter the teaching of the *dhāraṇī*.
The Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava taught these *dhāraṇī* phrases for the sake of all bodhisattvas; those who train in and enter this single phrase shall thereby universally enter the intent of all Buddhas.
Were I to spend an eon, or even more than an eon, distinguishing and extolling the praises of the merits of the world Stainless Light, I could not exhaustively reach its limits.
The Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava preached a sūtra called "The Wisdom of Renowned Virtue," which is inconceivable and cannot be bestowed.
That Buddha’s great and noble land is pure, majestic, transcendent, and unsurpassed.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s bestowal of the prediction of his future enlightenment, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin leaped for joy and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“O All-Knowing One, you who see all, You have crossed over the infinite dharmas;
The Tathāgata has transcended All defilements and impurities.”
It is a great marvel, O Mahāmati, that all know my past lives and the number of Buddhas I have made offerings to; the Buddha has explained them all in detail.
Regarding the past, future, and present, their origins and endings are just like this.
Furthermore, knowing that this degenerate age and all its people have been granted the prediction of Buddhahood by the Buddha, they no longer harbor any doubt;
they transform and deliver the world, [discerning] the fundamental and derivative aspects of the various faculties.
Throughout all these lands, even the sun and moon might fall;
yet that which is proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth shall never be altered.
The words spoken by the Buddha are utter sincerity; what he expounds is never false.
He bestowed upon me the path to supreme enlightenment, so that I might become a Buddha, the highest among men.
Just as I had vowed in my aspiration to adorn and purify a buddha-field,
he knew all the thoughts within my mind and spoke accordingly.
Having heard this teaching, his face was joyful and free from hesitation;
the practice he cultivated was supreme, for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
"Just as I have practiced, I shall further increase it immeasurably."
Thoroughly cultivating its fundamental limit, I personally uphold pure conduct.
Arising and practicing to attain Buddhahood, I cross over all dharmas to the infinite;
through diligent effort without cowardice, one arrives there by means of vigor.
Worthy of receiving offerings, they all know that in my past lives I never abandoned diligence until I reached the Tathāgata of Great Compassion.
For the sake of all sentient beings, the beginning and end [of their practice] are thus.
"I shall fully transform and guide them all, so that they may attain Buddhahood and deliver those of other schools.

When the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin spoke this verse, seventy-two thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and they all vowed to be born in that world of Stainless Light. Simultaneously, they raised their voices together and said:
"When the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava attains the Way of the Buddha, may he cause us all to be born in that buddha-field."
The Buddha prophesied for each of them that they would be born in that land.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"Receive this sūtra, uphold it, recite it, and explain its meaning to the multitude. Diligently encourage and assist this essential sūtra, which is that to which all in heaven and earth turn in submission and together offer worship."
Why is this? Those who hear this sutra shall all receive my prediction of enlightenment.
Those who do not believe have meager roots of virtue from their past lives; those who accept this sutra possess roots of virtue that are no ordinary ones.

It is already a great fortune to encounter a Buddha in every lifetime merely by hearing of this sutra; how much more so for those who hear it, uphold it, practice it, and explain it—their merit shall be limitless.
If sons or daughters of noble family were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them as alms at all times, continuing in this manner for hundreds of thousands of years;
"Whoever hears this sutra and joyfully believes and upholds it, their merit shall surpass that [of the former].
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"What is the name of this sutra?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said: "Its name is 'The Inquiry of Ratnaśikhin on the Pure Conduct of Bodhisattvas'; you should uphold it as such."
Thus spoke the Buddha.

The Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin and the assembly of bodhisattvas from the ten directions, the Venerable Ānanda, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and humans, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with joy.
The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume 118; The Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra, Volume 119.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
48. The Assembly of Queen Śrīmālā, the Forty-eighth.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala and Queen Mallikā, having newly realized the Dharma, said to one another:
"Our daughter, Viśākhā!
She is compassionate, wise, learned, and endowed with insight; if she were to see the Tathāgata, she would quickly comprehend the profound Dharma and be free from all doubt."
"I must now cause the eloquent one to give rise to sincerity and faith.
Having deliberated thus, the King and his consort immediately composed a letter extolling the true merits of the Tathāgata.
At that time, he dispatched an envoy named Candrāvatī, who carried the king’s letter to the city of Ayodhyā to present it to Queen Śrīmālā.
When Queen Śrīmālā opened and read the letter, she received it upon her head with joy and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder; she then addressed the envoy Candrāvatī with these verses:
"I have heard the voice of the Tathāgata, Which is indeed difficult to encounter in this world."
If these words are true, you shall be granted robes.
If that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared for the benefit of the world,
he must surely show compassion and allow me to behold his true form.
In the brief span of a moment’s thought, the Buddha manifested an inconceivable body in the midst of space and radiated great light everywhere.
Queen Śrīmālā and her retinue all gathered together at that assembly.
With palms joined, gazing up in reverence, they praised the Great Teacher:
“The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is peerless in the world;
It is incomparable and inconceivable; Therefore, we now pay homage.”
The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so;
all phenomena are eternally abiding—therefore, I take refuge.
He has well subdued the faults of the mind and the four kinds of bodily [faults].
Having reached the inconceivable stage, I now pay homage to you.
Knowing all phenomena as they truly are (*tathatā*), your wisdom-body is unimpeded;
With no loss or forgetfulness regarding the Dharma, I now pay homage to you.
I prostrate to you who transcend all measure; I prostrate to you who are without peer;
I prostrate to you, sovereign of the Dharma; I prostrate to you who have transcended thought.
Out of compassion, protect and shelter me, and cause the seeds of the Dharma to flourish.
Reaching my final body, may I always remain before the Tathāgata.
Through the merit I have cultivated in this life and in other births,
by the power of these roots of goodness, may the Buddha ever accept and sustain me.
When Queen Śrīmālā had spoken these verses, she and her entire retinue of the great assembly prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Śrīmālā:
"In the past, for the sake of Bodhi, I have already revealed this to you."
"Now you have encountered me once more, and it shall be so in future lives as well.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately bestowed upon Lady Śrīmālā the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within that assembly:

"Because you have now praised the Tathāgata’s supreme merits, by these roots of goodness you shall become a sovereign king among devas and humans for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, with all necessities and enjoyments fully provided. In every place where you are born, you shall always encounter me and praise me in my presence, no different from what you have done just now."

Furthermore, you shall make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; after twenty thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood, named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Universal Radiance (Puguang).
In that Buddha-land, there are no evil realms, nor the sufferings of old age, decay, or illness; furthermore, even the names of unwholesome or evil paths of action do not exist.

The sentient beings therein possess dignified and majestic physical forms, are endowed with the five sublime sensory objects, and experience pure happiness that surpasses even that of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
"All those sentient beings therein are oriented toward the Mahāyāna; all who thus study the Mahāyāna shall come to be born in that world.
When Lady Śrīmālā had received this prediction, immeasurable devas and humans were filled with exultation, and they all vowed to be reborn in that Buddha-world.
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed predictions upon them all that they would be born in that land.
Having heard the Buddha’s prediction, Lady Śrīmālā stood before the Tathāgata with palms joined and made ten great vows, speaking thus:
“World-Honored One!
"From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of transgression regarding any precepts I have received.
World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of pride toward any teachers or elders."
"Bhagavān! From this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall not give rise to a mind of anger toward any sentient being. Bhagavān!"
"From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to envy toward those who are superior or toward their superior accomplishments.
World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, although I may have but little food, I shall not give rise to a mind of stinginess."

"Bhagavān! From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not accept or possess wealth and goods for my own sake; whatever I may receive, I shall do so solely to relieve the poverty and suffering of sentient beings."

"Bhagavān! From this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) without seeking gratitude or recompense; with no mind of greedy profit, no mind of insatiability, and no mind of obstruction, I shall gather in and sustain sentient beings."

"Bhagavān! From this day forth until I attain bodhi, whenever I see sentient beings who are without refuge, imprisoned, afflicted by illness, or beset by various perils and calamities, I shall never abandon them; I vow to ensure their peace and security, benefiting them with goodness so that they may be freed from all suffering."

"Bhagavān! From this day forth until I attain bodhi, if I should see any who follow evil disciplines or violate the pure prohibitions of the Tathāgata, within all the cities and villages under my jurisdiction, I shall subdue those who need subduing and gather in those who should be gathered."

Why is this? Because through taming and gathering [disciples], the True Dharma abides for a long time; because the True Dharma abides for a long time, gods and humans flourish while those in the evil realms diminish, enabling the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma to turn perpetually.
"Bhagavān! From this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall uphold the true Dharma and never forget it. Why is this?"
If one forgets the True Dharma, one forgets the Mahāyāna; if one forgets the Mahāyāna, one forgets the pāramitās; and if one forgets the pāramitās, one abandons the Mahāyāna.

If bodhisattvas lack certainty regarding the Mahāyāna, their embrace of the True Dharma will not be firm, and they will be unable to transcend the realm of ordinary beings; this would be a great loss.
“World-Honored One!
All bodhisattvas who uphold the True Dharma in the present and the future will possess boundless and vast benefit.

Although the Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, personally witnesses and knows this as they make such great vows, sentient beings with meager roots of goodness may give rise to a web of doubt, for these ten great vows are difficult to accomplish.”

Having practiced unwholesome dharmas for a long night and thus experienced various sufferings and afflictions, he now makes a sincere vow before the Buddha out of a desire to benefit such sentient beings.
"Bhagavān! I now utter these ten great vows; if they are true and not false, may heavenly flowers rain down upon this great assembly and may the sublime sounds of the heavens resound."
After Queen Śrīmālā had spoken these words before the Tathāgata, celestial flowers immediately rained down from the sky and divine, wondrous sounds issued forth, praising her:
"Excellent, Queen Śrīmālā!"
"What you have said is true and without error.
At that time, the assembly, having witnessed this auspicious omen, was free from all doubt and gave rise to great joy. With one voice they proclaimed:
"May we share the same vows and practices as Queen Śrīmālā in all our future births."
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestowed upon the entire assembly prophecies according to their respective aspirations.
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā again made three great vows before the Buddha:
"By the power of these vows, may I benefit all sentient beings without limit."
The first vow is: by means of my roots of goodness, may I attain the wisdom of the true Dharma in all my births.
The second vow is: once I have attained this true wisdom in whatever birth I take, may I expound it for the sake of all sentient beings without weariness.
"The third vow is that, for the sake of gathering in and protecting the True Dharma, I shall not begrudge my body or life in whatever form I am born.
At that time, having heard this vow, the World-Honored One addressed Śrīmālā, saying:
"Just as all forms enter the realm of space, so too do the vows of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all enter into this vow; these three vows are truly vast and great."
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Now, relying upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the strength of eloquence, I wish to speak of my great vows; I pray that you will graciously grant me your hearing and permission."
The Buddha said, “Śrīmālā, speak as you wish.”
Queen Śrīmālā said: "All the vows of a bodhisattva, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are entirely contained within one great vow.
This one great vow is what is called 'upholding the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.'"
"Thus is the upholding of the True Dharma; it is truly vast.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Śrīmālā!"
You have practiced for a long time; your wisdom and skillful means are profoundly deep and subtle.
Those who are able to understand the meaning of what you have spoken have planted the roots of all that is wholesome throughout the long night.
What you have said regarding the upholding of the True Dharma has all been taught by the Buddhas of the past, is being taught by those of the present, and will be taught by those of the future.

When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, I too shall constantly teach the upholding of the True Dharma through various aspects. Thus, the merit of praising the upholding of the True Dharma is boundless, and the wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise boundless.
"Why is this? Because upholding the True Dharma possesses great merit and great benefit.
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, I shall further expound the vast meaning of upholding the True Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"Listen to what you have to say," [the Buddha said]. Queen Śrīmālā replied:
"The vast meaning of upholding the True Dharma consists in attaining all the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, even to the point of being able to encompass the eighty thousand aggregates of practice."

Just as at the beginning of a kalpa, clouds of various forms arise and rain down a multitude of precious jewels, so too do the clouds of roots of goodness from embracing the True Dharma rain down an immeasurable rain of meritorious rewards.
World-Honored One! Furthermore, just as within the great waters at the beginning of a kalpa, the storehouse of the trichiliocosm and four hundred billion varieties of continents can arise,

so too does the upholding of the True Dharma give birth to the immeasurable storehouse of the Mahāyāna realm, along with the supernormal powers of all bodhisattvas and various dharma-gates, which fully provide all mundane and supramundane requisites for peace and happiness— things never before experienced by any devas or humans.
Furthermore, it is like the great earth bearing four heavy burdens. What are these four?
First, the great oceans; second, the various mountains; third, the grasses and trees; and fourth, sentient beings.

In this way, those sons and daughters of good family who embrace the True Dharma are capable of bearing four kinds of heavy responsibilities that exceed even that of the great earth. What are these four?

That is to say, apart from [those who have] abandoned virtuous friends, lack learning, and follow what is not the Dharma, he brings all classes of sentient beings to maturity through the roots of virtue of humans and devas; to those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he grants the śrāvaka-yāna; to those seeking the pratyekabuddha, he grants the pratyekabuddha-yāna; and to those seeking the Mahāyāna, he grants the Mahāyāna.

These are called the sons and daughters of good family who embrace the true Dharma; they are capable of bearing the four kinds of heavy responsibilities, surpassing even the great earth, O World-Honored One!

In this way, sons and daughters of good family who embrace the true Dharma establish the great earth; they are capable of bearing the four kinds of heavy responsibilities, acting as uninvited friends to all sentient beings, and serving as mothers of the world’s Dharma through their great compassion, benefit, and pity for sentient beings.
Furthermore, the great earth is the source from which four kinds of jewels arise. What are these four?
First, those of priceless value; second, those of superior value; third, those of middling value; and fourth, those of inferior value.

In this way, when sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma establish the great earth, sentient beings who encounter them obtain four great treasures, which are the most preeminent among all treasures.
What are these four?

They are that when sentient beings encounter such a virtuous friend, some may acquire the roots of goodness of humans and devas; some may realize the roots of goodness and merit of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; or [some may realize those] of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

This is called the establishment of the great earth by sons and daughters of good family who embrace the true Dharma; when sentient beings encounter it, they are able to obtain four kinds of great treasures.
World-Honored One!
To bring forth the great jewel is called the true upholding of the True Dharma.
World-Honored One!

Regarding what is called "upholding the true Dharma," it means that there is no difference between the true Dharma and upholding the true Dharma; the true Dharma itself is the upholding of the true Dharma.
World-Honored One!
There is no difference between the pāramitās and the embracing of the true Dharma; the embracing of the true Dharma is itself the pāramitās. Why is this?

When sons and daughters of good family embrace the true Dharma, they bring to maturity through generosity those who should be matured by generosity, even to the point of sacrificing their own bodies to conform to the inclinations of others and thereby bringing them to maturity, causing those sentient beings to abide in the true Dharma. This is called the dāna-pāramitā.

Those who are to be matured through ethical discipline should be matured by guarding the six sense faculties, purifying body, speech, and mind, and even one’s deportment, acting in accordance with their inclinations to establish those sentient beings in the True Dharma; this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

Those who are to be matured through patience: if those sentient beings should revile, insult, slander, or disturb one, one should—through a mind free from anger and with a mind intent on their benefit—employ the power of supreme patience such that even one’s facial expression does not change; by complying with their inclinations, one matures them and causes those sentient beings to abide in the True Dharma. This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Regarding those sentient beings who are to be matured through diligence, one should not give rise to a mind of indolence or inferiority toward them; rather, one should generate a great aspiration and supreme diligence, maturing them in accordance with their inclinations throughout the four modes of deportment, and causing those sentient beings to abide in the True Dharma. This is called the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

Those who are to be matured through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are brought to maturity by means of non-distraction and the accomplishment of right mindfulness toward those sentient beings; never forgetting what has been done, one acts in accordance with their inclinations to mature them, causing those sentient beings to abide in the True Dharma. This is called the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Those sentient beings who are to be matured through wisdom ask about the meaning of various dharmas for their own benefit; for their sake, one expounds all treatises, all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and even various arts and crafts with an untiring mind. One brings them to ultimate maturity by acting in accordance with their inclinations, causing those sentient beings to abide securely in the True Dharma; this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Therefore, World-Honored One!
There is no difference between the pāramitās and the upholding of the true Dharma; the upholding of the true Dharma is itself the pāramitās.
At that time, Lady Śrīmālā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now, relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the strength of my eloquence, I shall further expound upon the great meaning.
The Buddha said:
"What is the great purpose?
"World-Honored One,
there is no difference between upholding the True Dharma and that which is upheld as the True Dharma."
There is no one else who upholds the True Dharma; rather, when sons and daughters of good family uphold the True Dharma, they are themselves the upholding of the True Dharma. Why is this?

If sons or daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma sacrifice their bodies, lives, and wealth for the sake of that Dharma, such persons—by virtue of having sacrificed their bodies—realize the ultimate limit of birth and death, become free from old age and illness, and attain the indestructible, eternal, unchanging, and ultimately quiescent, inconceivable Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.

By virtue of relinquishing life, they realize the ultimate limit of birth and death as being forever free from death, thereby attaining the infinite and eternal; they accomplish inconceivable meritorious virtues and dwell securely in the miraculous transformations of all Buddha-dharmas.

By means of relinquishing material wealth, one realizes the perfection of the fruit of retribution that transcends the future limit of birth and death, surpassing sentient beings and being inexhaustible and undiminished; endowed with the adornment of inconceivable merit, one becomes an object of honor and veneration for all sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!
Those sons and daughters of good family who sacrifice their bodies, lives, and wealth to uphold the True Dharma shall receive the prediction of enlightenment from all Tathāgatas,
World-Honored One!”

If, when the True Dharma is about to perish, there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who form factions and engage in disputes, should any son or daughter of good family—with a mind free from flattery and deceit, loving and cherishing the True Dharma, and upholding the True Dharma—enter among those virtuous friends.
"One who enters into the company of virtuous friends will certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas.
World-Honored One!

I see that the upholding of the True Dharma possesses such great power; the Tathāgata takes this as his eye, as the root of the Dharma, as the guide to the Dharma, and as the means for penetrating the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing what Lady Śrīmālā had said regarding the great power of embracing the True Dharma, exclaimed: "So it is, so it is."
Excellent, Śrīmālā!

It is as you have said: the power of the great majesty of upholding the True Dharma is such that it is like a strong man who, by the slightest touch upon one's *marmans*, produces great agony and further aggravates a grave illness.
In this way, Śrīmālā!
Even if one were to uphold the True Dharma for but a small portion, causing Māra Pāpīyān to suffer intense anguish, grief, lamentation, and sighing, it would be just like this.
"Śrīmālā! I have never seen any other single wholesome dharma that causes Māra such grief and distress as the partial upholding of the True Dharma. Śrīmālā!"
For example, just as a bull king is handsome in form and color, with a stature so extraordinary that it overshadows all other oxen;
even so, Śrīmālā, one who practices the Mahāyāna, even if they only slightly embrace the true Dharma, is able to overshadow all the wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Śrīmālā! Furthermore, just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, is high, vast, majestic, and beautiful, overshadowing all other mountains;
so it is, Śrīmālā!"

From the very beginning of entering the Mahāyāna, by means of a mind intent on benefiting others that disregards one’s own body and life to embrace the True Dharma, one is then able to surpass all roots of goodness within the Mahāyāna that, while regarding their own body and life, seek long-term endurance.
Therefore, Śrīmālā!
You should, by means of embracing the True Dharma, reveal and instruct all sentient beings.
Thus it is, Śrīmālā!
One who upholds the true Dharma attains great benefit and great fruit. Śrīmālā!

Even if I were to praise all the merits of upholding the true Dharma for countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I could not reach their limit; therefore, upholding the true Dharma accomplishes such immeasurable merit.
The Buddha told Śrīmālā:
"You should now further expound what I have taught regarding the embracing of the True Dharma, which is beloved and cherished by all Buddhas. Śrīmālā replied:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
One who upholds the True Dharma is called a follower of the Mahāyāna. Why is this?
The Mahāyāna gives birth to all the wholesome dharmas of both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those of the mundane and supramundane realms.

Just as the Lake Anavatapta gives rise to the eight great rivers, so too does the Mahāyāna give birth to all the wholesome dharmas of both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those of the mundane and supramundane realms.
"Bhagavān! Furthermore, just as all seeds, grasses, trees, and forests grow depending upon the great earth,
so too do all the wholesome dharmas— whether mundane or supramundane— of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas grow depending upon the Mahāyāna."
Therefore, World-Honored One!

To abide in the Great Vehicle and embrace the Great Vehicle is itself to abide in and embrace all the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as all mundane and supramundane phenomena.

As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught regarding the six bases—namely, the abiding of the True Dharma, the extinction of the True Dharma, the Prātimokṣa, the Vinaya, right renunciation, and the reception of full ordination—it is for the sake of the Mahāyāna that he spoke of these six bases.
Why is this so? The abiding of the True Dharma is for the sake of explaining the Mahāyāna; the abiding of the Mahāyāna is precisely the abiding of the True Dharma.
The extinction of the True Dharma is for the sake of explaining the Mahāyāna; the extinction of the Mahāyāna is precisely the extinction of the True Dharma.
Prātimokṣa and Vinaya—these two dharmas have the same meaning but different names.
Vinaya is precisely the training of the Mahāyāna. Why is this so?

Having gone forth for the sake of the Buddha and received full ordination, therefore, the aggregate of precepts of the Mahāyāna is the Vinaya; this is true going forth and this is receiving full ordination, World-Honored One!
An Arhat does not go forth or receive full ordination.
Why is this? Because an Arhat does not go forth or receive full ordination for the sake of the Tathāgata.
Arhats possess the perception of fear and take refuge in the Tathāgata. Why is this?

Because arhats perceive all conditioned activities and dwellings as fearful, like a person holding a sword who intends to come and harm them; therefore, arhats do not realize the ultimate peace and happiness of liberation.
World-Honored One!
Relying on that which does not seek reliance—just as all sentient beings, having no refuge, seek a refuge for the sake of peace and security when they are terrified by this or that [fear].
“World-Honored One!
Because such Arhats still possess fear, they take refuge in the Tathāgata.

Therefore, because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have a remainder of birth-dharmas, their holy life is not yet established, what was to be done is not yet accomplished, and that which was to be abandoned is not yet finalized, they remain far from Nirvāṇa.”

Why is this? Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized nirvāṇa and accomplished immeasurable, inconceivable, and all-encompassing merits; that which was to be abandoned has been entirely severed, reaching ultimate purity; he is an object of veneration for all sentient beings, transcending the realms of both the two vehicles and bodhisattvas.
The Arhats and others are not like this; it is said that their attainment of nirvāṇa is a skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddha, and for this reason, the Arhats and others remain far from nirvāṇa.

When the World-Honored One speaks of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas who, having contemplated liberation, have reached the ultimate through the four knowledges and attained rest, these are all the Tathāgata’s intentional speech (*saṃvṛti-vāk*) spoken according to the inclinations of others, which is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Why is this? There are two kinds of death. What are these two?
The first is the death of segmented existence (*paricchinna*), and the second is the death of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
The death of segmented existence refers to sentient beings in continuous succession.
The death of transformation refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and sovereign Bodhisattvas, from the time they assume bodies born at will until their attainment of enlightenment.
Among the two kinds of death, by means of *pariccheda-maraṇa* (death in segments), one gives rise to the knowledge that "my births have been exhausted" regarding Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.

Because they are able to realize the fruit with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-phala*), they give rise to the knowledge that "the holy life has been established. This is something no ordinary fool can do, nor have the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*) yet accomplished; because the afflictions of the continuum have been utterly severed, they give rise to the knowledge that "what was to be done has been done."

When the World-Honored One speaks of the wise one who is born without receiving further existence, he means that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to sever all afflictions and have not fully realized the wisdom regarding the taking of birth.
Why is this? Because these Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet completely severed or exhausted their remaining afflictions, they are unable to fully comprehend all forms of rebirth.
There are two kinds of afflictions: namely, the afflictions of the underlying ground (*āśraya-bhūmi*) and the active afflictions (*samudācāra*).
There are four underlying grounds. What are these four?
That is to say, the Dwelling Place of Seeing One Realm, the Dwelling Place of Attachment to Desire, the Dwelling Place of Attachment to Form, and the Dwelling Place of Attachment to Existence.
World-Honored One,
these four dwelling places can give rise to all pervasive afflictions.
World-Honored One, the afflictions that arise are associated with the mind moment by moment; however,
the ground of the abiding of ignorance has been dissociated from the mind since beginningless time.
World-Honored One!
The power of the four stages of abiding can serve as the basis for the universal arising of afflictions; compared to the stage of ignorance, it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
World-Honored One!
Thus, this ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) possesses the greatest power over the ground of the abiding of craving for existence (*bhavarāga-vāsabhūmi*).

It is, for example, like the King Māra, with his physical strength, majestic virtue, and retinue, who eclipses the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

In this way, the ground of the abiding of ignorance (avidyā-vāsabhūmi) obscures the four grounds of abiding and serves as the basis for afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges; it also causes the four types of afflictions to endure for a long time.
The wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot sever it; only the wisdom of the Tathāgata can sever it.
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; the power of the ground of abiding ignorance is the greatest.
World-Honored One!”
Just as the three realms of existence arise from the cause of out-flowing karma conditioned by grasping,
so too do the bodies born at will of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and powerful Bodhisattvas arise from the cause of non-out-flowing karma conditioned by the ground of ignorance.
The bodies produced at will and the untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) of these three stages both take the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) as their basis.
Although that [ground] possesses conditions, it is also able to act as a condition for them.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, the three kinds of bodies born of mental autonomy and untainted karma all take the ground of ignorance as their condition, being identical in nature to craving for existence.
“World-Honored One!
The ground of abiding in craving does not share the same karma as the ground of abiding in ignorance; the ground of abiding in ignorance is distinct from the four grounds of abiding.
Only a Buddha is able to sever that which is distinct from the four grounds of abiding.”

Why is this? Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have severed the four stages of abiding, yet they do not attain mastery over the power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-bala), nor can they realize it through direct manifestation. Why is this?

The Blessed One spoke of "the designation for the exhaustion of outflows" (āsravakṣaya-paryāya). Therefore, because Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas in their final existence are shrouded by the ground of ignorance, they do not know and do not see those various phenomena.
Because one does not know and does not see those various phenomena as they truly are—one does not abandon what should be abandoned and does not exhaust what should be exhausted.
Since one does not abandon and exhaust those various phenomena, there is only partial liberation rather than universal liberation;
there is only partial purification rather than universal purification.
“World-Honored One, because one possesses only partial merit rather than all merit;

because one possesses only partial liberation rather than all liberation— and so on, up to possessing only partial merit rather than all merit— one knows there is remaining suffering, abandons the remaining origin, realizes the remaining cessation, and cultivates the remaining path.”
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If one further knows the remaining suffering, abandons the remaining accumulation, realizes the remaining cessation, and cultivates the remaining path, this is called partial parinirvāṇa; it is the realization of partial nirvāṇa and the orientation toward the realm of nirvāṇa.”

If one knows all suffering, abandons all its origination, realizes all its cessation, and cultivates the entire path, one will realize the eternal, quiescent, and cool nirvana within this impermanent and decaying world.
World-Honored One!
In this world that is without protection and without refuge, they act as protection and as refuge. Why is this?
Those who perceive high and low among all phenomena do not realize nirvana; only those whose wisdom is equal, whose liberation is equal, and whose purity is equal realize nirvana.
Therefore, nirvāṇa is called "equal and of one taste.
What is this single taste?
It is the taste of liberation.
World-Honored One!
If the stage of ignorance is neither severed nor exhausted, one cannot attain the single flavor or equal flavor of nirvana. Why is this?

Because the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is neither severed nor exhausted, all transcendent dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges—which ought to be severed—are not severed, and those which ought to be exhausted are not exhausted.

Because these transcendent dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges are neither severed nor exhausted, the various meritorious dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges are neither realized nor attained.

Therefore, because the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) serves as the source for the arising of all defilements (*upakleśa*) that are to be abandoned, [the afflictions] arise from it; they are the afflictions that obstruct the mind, the afflictions that obstruct calm abiding (*śamatha*), the afflictions that obstruct insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the afflictions that obstruct meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). In this way, they even obstruct the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the realization of the fruit of the preparatory knowledge of the attainments (*samāpatti*).
All afflictions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, can be severed by the Bodhi of the Tathāgata and the Buddha’s adamantine wisdom (*vajrajñāna*).
All arising afflictions depend entirely upon the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), because the ground of ignorance serves as their causal condition.
"Bhagavān! These arising afflictions are associated with the mind moment by moment. Bhagavān!"
"Bhagavān, the ground of the abiding of ignorance has been dissociated from the mind since beginningless time.
Furthermore, Bhagavān,

all those dharmas that are to be abandoned by the bodhi of the Tathāgatas and the vajra-wisdom of the Buddhas— more numerous than the sands of the Ganges— are all supported and established upon the ground of the abiding of ignorance."
For example, just as all forests of seeds grow depending upon the great earth, and if the earth is destroyed, they too are destroyed along with it;

so too, the dharmas to be severed by the Tathāgatas’ bodhi and the Buddha’s vajra-wisdom—which exceed the sands of the Ganges—all grow depending upon the ground of the dwelling-place of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).

If that ground of abiding ignorance is severed, then all those dharmas that are to be severed by the Tathāgatas’ bodhi and the Buddha’s adamantine wisdom—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—are likewise severed accordingly.

Because all dharmas that should be abandoned—equal in number to those exceeding the sands of the Ganges—as well as all afflictions and the arising of afflictions, have already been severed, one is then able to realize the inconceivable dharmas of all Buddhas, equal in number to those exceeding the sands of the Ganges.

He is able to realize unimpeded supernormal powers regarding all phenomena; he attains all wisdom and vision, free from every fault; he acquires all meritorious qualities and becomes a Great Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma; he realizes the stage of mastery over all phenomena and gives the true lion’s roar: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
Therefore, the World-Honored One, with the lion’s roar, gives a definitive declaration based on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
World-Honored One!
There are two kinds of knowledge regarding the non-existence of further existence (*anupapatti-jñāna*).
What are these two? First, all Tathāgatas, by the power of their mastery, subdue the four māras and transcend all worlds, becoming objects of veneration for all sentient beings;

they realize the inconceivable and pure *dharmakāya*, attain mastery over the phenomena of the ground of the knowable, and being most supreme and unsurpassed, have nothing further to do and perceive no further ground to be realized.

Endowed with the ten powers, he has ascended to the most supreme ground of fearlessness; he observes all phenomena without obstruction, roars the true lion’s roar, and will not undergo further existence.
The second refers to arhats and pratyekabuddhas, who have attained deliverance from the fear of immeasurable birth and death and experience the bliss of liberation; they form this thought:
"I have now departed from the fear of birth and death and shall no longer undergo various sufferings."
"World-Honored One!
Arhats and pratyekabuddhas observe in this way, thinking that they will not undergo further existence, yet they do not realize the supreme nirvāṇa of rest.

Because they have not encountered the Dharma regarding the stage of non-realization, they are able to understand for themselves: 'I have now realized the stage with remainder; I shall certainly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

Why is this? Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas all enter the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is itself the Buddha-vehicle; therefore, the three vehicles are identical to the One Vehicle. Those who realize the One Vehicle attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself Nirvāṇa. What is called Nirvāṇa is the Tathāgata’s pure Dharmakāya, and those who realize the Dharmakāya are the One Vehicle. There is no difference between the Tathāgata and the Dharmakāya.
That which is called the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; he who realizes the ultimate Dharma-body is the ultimate One Vehicle; and the ultimate One Vehicle is that which is free from continuity.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

The duration of the Tathāgata’s abiding is immeasurable, equal to the limit of the future; the Tathāgata is able to benefit the world through infinite great compassion and infinite vows. To speak thus is called speaking well.
Furthermore, if it is said that the Tathāgata is permanent, is an inexhaustible dharma, and the ultimate refuge for all the world, this too is well-spoken.

Therefore, one who is able to serve as an inexhaustible refuge, a permanently abiding refuge, and an ultimate refuge throughout the future limit within this unprotected and supportless world is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Dharma is the path of the One Vehicle, and the Saṃgha is the assembly of the Three Vehicles; these two refuges are not ultimate refuges and are termed "partial refuges. Why is this so?
It is taught that the One Vehicle path realizes the ultimate Dharma-body; thereafter, there is no further teaching of the One Vehicle path because those of the Three Vehicles would experience fear.
They take refuge in the Tathāgata to seek liberation through practice and cultivation, for they have tasks to perform and are directed toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The second is the reliance on that which is not ultimate; it is a limited reliance.

When sentient beings are disciplined by the Tathāgata, they take refuge in the Tathāgata and receive the nourishment of the Dharma; through a mind of faith and joy, they take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
These two refuges are entered through the moistening of the Dharma;
the Tathāgata is not entered as a refuge through the moistening of the Dharma. To speak of the Tathāgata is to speak of the true refuge.
These two refuges, in their ultimate sense, are called the ultimate refuge in the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is not different from these two refuges; therefore, the Tathāgata is himself the three refuges.
Why is this? Because they proclaim the Single Vehicle path, the Tathāgata’s supreme state, endowed with the four fearlessnesses, and roar the true lion’s roar.
If the Tathāgatas, according to the inclinations of beings, employ skillful means to speak of the two vehicles, these are themselves the Great Vehicle.
In the ultimate sense, there are no two vehicles; those of the two vehicles enter together into the One Vehicle, and the One Vehicle is the vehicle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-yāna*).
World-Honored One!

When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas first realize the Noble Truths, it is not by means of a single wisdom that they sever all the stages of abiding (*bhūmi*), nor is it by means of a single wisdom that they realize the four types of perfect knowledge (*parijñā*) and their various merits. Furthermore, it is not by means of [ordinary] dharmas that they can thoroughly understand the meaning of these four dharmas.
World-Honored One!
Regarding supramundane wisdom, there are no four kinds of wisdom that approach gradually or take objects gradually.
World-Honored One!
World-Honored One, supramundane wisdom has no gradual progression, being like the diamond simile.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas eliminate the various stages of dwelling through their knowledge of the various noble truths, yet they do not possess the supramundane wisdom of the ultimate truth.
Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—not the domain of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—can, through the wisdom of inconceivable emptiness, shatter the shell of all afflictions.
"World-Honored One!
The ultimate wisdom that shatters the shell of afflictions is called the supramundane wisdom of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
The wisdom of the first Noble Truth is not ultimate wisdom; it is the wisdom directed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
World-Honored One!
That which is the true meaning of "noble" is not the Two Vehicles. Why is this so?
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are called "noble ones" (ārya) only because they have accomplished a limited portion of merit.
World-Honored One!
That which is called the "Noble Truths" (āryasatya) is not the truth or the merit of those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, regarding these truths, only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha first fully realizes them; he subsequently reveals and expounds them for the sake of the world-dwellers who are enclosed within the shell of ignorance. Therefore, they are called the Noble Truths.
World-Honored One!

These noble truths are profound and subtle, difficult to see and difficult to understand, beyond conceptual differentiation, and not an object of discursive thought; they cannot be believed by anyone in the entire world.
It can be known only by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this?
Because this teaching is the profound Tathāgatagarbha.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the domain of the Buddhas; it is not within the sphere of activity of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, the meaning of the Noble Truths is taught; this Tathāgatagarbha is profoundly subtle, and the Noble Truths thus taught are likewise profound and wondrous. They are difficult to see and difficult to comprehend, beyond conceptual differentiation, and not an object of discursive thought. They cannot be believed by any in the world, but can be known only by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

If one has no doubt regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, which is enveloped by immeasurable afflictions, then one will likewise have no doubt regarding the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, which is the emergence from the storehouse of all afflictions.

"Bhagavān! If there are those who attain ultimate realization of the mind regarding this Tathāgatagarbha and the inconceivable, secret realm of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, they will be able to believe in, comprehend, and give rise to resolute conviction in the meaning of the two noble truths as they have been taught."
What are the meanings of the two noble truths?
They are the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The conditioned noble truth refers to the meaning of the four noble truths that is incomplete.

Why is this? Because they are protected by others, they are unable to know all suffering, abandon all its origins, realize all its cessations, and cultivate all paths; therefore, they do not know the conditioned and the unconditioned, nor do they know nirvana.
World-Honored One!
The truth of non-action explains the meaning of the four noble truths in their perfection. Why is this so?
Because they are able to protect themselves, they know all suffering, abandon all its origin, realize all its cessation, and cultivate all its path.
These meanings of the Eight Noble Truths thus explained, the Tathāgata has taught by means of the Four Noble Truths alone.

Regarding this meaning of the four noble truths of non-action, only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has brought his task to completion; it is not within the capacity of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? It is not by means of dharmas that are superior, inferior, middling, or sublime that one can realize nirvāṇa.
How then does the Tathāgata attain the ultimate realization of the truth of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra-satya)?

It means that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have fully known all suffering, abandoned all afflictions, and transcended the accumulation of suffering comprised by those afflictions; they are able to realize the cessation of all suffering within the aggregates of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), and they cultivate the path to the cessation of all suffering.
World-Honored One!
It is not because of the destruction of phenomena that it is called the cessation of suffering. Why is this?

What is called the cessation of suffering is without beginning and without action, without arising and without exhaustion, eternally abiding and immovable, pure by nature, and emerged from the shell of afflictions.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has accomplished that which exceeds the sands of the Ganges, possessing the inconceivable dharmas of the wisdom of liberation; this is designated as the Dharma-body.
World-Honored One!
This Dharma-body, when not separated from afflictions, is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
World-Honored One,
the Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the wisdom of the emptiness of the Tathāgata.
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgatagarbha has never been seen nor attained by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is known and realized only by the Buddha."
Furthermore, this wisdom of the emptiness of the tathāgatagarbha is of two kinds. What are these two?
They are the empty tathāgatagarbha, which is that which is free from all afflictions that consist of non-liberated wisdom.
World-Honored One!
The non-empty tathāgatagarbha possesses inconceivable dharmas of the liberative wisdom of Buddhas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges.
World-Honored One!
Regarding these two types of wisdom of emptiness, all the great śrāvakas are able to enter them through faith.
World-Honored One!

All such wisdom regarding the emptiness of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas operates by taking the objects of the four inversions as its focal point; therefore, it has never been seen nor realized by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
The cessation of all suffering is personally realized only by the Buddha, who destroys all afflictions by cultivating the path to the cessation of suffering.
World-Honored One!
Among these Four Noble Truths, three truths are impermanent, while one truth is permanent.
Why is this? These three truths enter into the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), and that which has the characteristics of the conditioned is impermanent (*anitya*).
That which is called impermanent is a phenomenon subject to destruction; that which is subject to destruction is not a truth, is not permanent, and is not a place of refuge.
Therefore, O World-Honored One, the first three truths, from the perspective of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), are not truths, are not permanent, and are not objects of refuge.

The truth of the cessation of suffering alone is free from conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). Being free from conditioned characteristics, its nature is eternally abiding; that which is eternally abiding in nature is not a phenomenon subject to destruction. That which is indestructible is the truth, is permanent, and is the object of refuge.
"Bhagavān! For this reason, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is, by way of ultimate meaning, a truth, it is permanent, and it is a place of refuge. Bhagavān!"

This Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is inconceivable; it transcends the cognitive domain of the minds and consciousnesses of all sentient beings, and it is also beyond the reach of the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
For example, one born blind does not see various forms, and a seven-day-old infant does not see the solar disk.

The Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is likewise: it is not an object of perception for the mental consciousnesses of ordinary beings, nor is it the domain of the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The consciousness of ordinary beings refers to the views of the two extremes; the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is termed "pure wisdom.
As for the view of extremes, it consists of grasping at the five aggregates of clinging as a self and giving rise to divergent conceptualizations.
There are two types of extreme views. What are these two?
They are the view of eternalism and the view of nihilism.
World-Honored One!
If there is another who views saṃsāra as impermanent and nirvāṇa as permanent, and does not hold the views of annihilationism or eternalism, this is called right view. Why is this?

Those who engage in speculative theorizing perceive that the body, the sense faculties, the experiencer, and the thinker perish in this very life; failing to understand the continuity of existence, they are blind and lack the eye of wisdom, giving rise to the view of annihilationism.

Regarding the momentary destruction of the continuity of the mind, the ignorant and deluded do not understand the objective sphere of mental consciousness and thus give rise to the view of eternalism.
World-Honored One!

Yet those various meanings transcend all conceptualization and inferior views; it is due to the false imaginings and inverted attachments of foolish people that they speak of annihilation or eternity.
“World-Honored One!

Sentient beings who are subject to inversion perceive the five aggregates of clinging as permanent when they are impermanent, as pleasant when they are suffering, as self when they are non-self, and as pure when they are impure.”
The pure wisdom possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas has never before seen the realm of the Tathāgata or the Buddha’s dharmakāya.

There may be sentient beings who, out of faith in the Tathāgata, conceive notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity regarding the Tathāgata; such views are not inverted, but are indeed right view.
Why is this? Because the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is the perfection of permanence, the perfection of bliss, the perfection of self, and the perfection of purity.

If sentient beings form such a view, it is called right view; those with right view are called true sons of the Buddha—they are born from the mouth of the Buddha, born from the True Dharma, transformed by the Dharma, and have obtained a share of the Buddha’s Dharma.
World-Honored One!
That which is called "pure wisdom" refers to the perfection of wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This pure wisdom does not even have the truth of the cessation of suffering as its objective domain, let alone the truth of the cessation of suffering itself.
This is the sphere of activity for the wisdom of those who have entered the stream. Why is this?
Those of the three vehicles who are beginners and not deluded regarding the Dharma will be able to realize and fully comprehend that meaning.
World-Honored One!
For what purpose do you speak of the four types of stream-enterers?
World-Honored One!
"These four ways of entry are worldly dharmas, World-Honored One!

There is only one way of entry that is supreme and foremost among all ways of entry; by the ultimate truth, this is the way of entry, this is the refuge, and this is the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering."
“World-Honored One!
Birth and death depend upon the Tathāgatagarbha; it is because of the Tathāgatagarbha that one says the prior limit (pūrvakoṭi) cannot be known.
World-Honored One!”
“Because the Tathāgatagarbha exists, there is birth and death; this is called a well-spoken teaching.
World-Honored One!
As for birth and death: the cessation of the various faculties of sensation followed immediately by the arising of other faculties of sensation—this is what is called birth and death.”
World-Honored One!
The two dharmas of birth-and-death are the Tathāgatagarbha; in conventional terminology, they are called "birth-and-death.
World-Honored One!

In those who die, the various faculties of sensation cease; in those who are born, the various faculties of sensation arise. The Tathāgatagarbha, however, is neither born nor dies, neither ascends nor falls, and is free from the characteristics of the conditioned.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha is eternal and indestructible;
therefore, World-Honored One, the Tathāgatagarbha is the refuge and support for the treasury of non-separable liberating wisdom, and it serves as its foundation.
Furthermore, it serves as the support and foundation for all conditioned phenomena that are external, detached, and characterized by the lack of liberating wisdom.
World-Honored One, if there were no *tathāgatagarbha*, there would be no weariness with suffering nor any aspiration to seek nirvāṇa.

Why is this? Because these seven phenomena—the six consciousnesses and that which is known—do not abide for even a moment, do not undergo manifold sufferings, and are incapable of generating weariness with cyclic existence or aspiring for nirvana.
The Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit; it is unborn and unceasing, yet it experiences various sufferings.
Out of weariness with suffering, it aspires for and seeks nirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha is not a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.

The Tathāgatagarbha is not within the sphere of experience for those sentient beings who hold the view of a body, those sentient beings who are subject to inversions, or those sentient beings who hold the view of emptiness.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha is the Dharma-realm treasury, the Dharma-body treasury, the supramundane treasury, and the naturally pure treasury; this intrinsic nature is pure.
Regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, as I understand it, even when it is defiled by adventitious afflictions, it remains the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
World-Honored One!
From moment to moment, the wholesome and unwholesome mind cannot be defiled by adventitious afflictions. Why is this?
“Afflictions do not touch the mind, and the mind does not touch afflictions.
How, World-Honored One, can a defiled mind arise without there being any mutual contact between phenomena?”
Because there are afflictions, there is a mind that follows along with defilement;

this defilement of secondary afflictions is difficult to understand and difficult to comprehend. Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One—who is the eye, the wisdom, the root of the Dharma, the venerable one, the guide, and the refuge of the True Dharma—knows and sees it as it truly is.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Lady Śrīmālā, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said.
The intrinsically pure mind being defiled by secondary afflictions is difficult to comprehend.”
Furthermore, Śrīmālā,
there are two kinds of dharmas that are difficult to comprehend. What are these two?
That is to say, the intrinsically pure mind is difficult to comprehend, and that the same mind is defiled by afflictions is likewise difficult to comprehend.
Regarding these two dharmas, you and the bodhisattvas who have accomplished the Great Dharma are able to hear and receive them; other śrāvakas can understand them only through faith.
“Śrīmālā! If my disciples possess superior faith and accord with the wisdom of the Dharma, they shall attain the ultimate within this Dharma.

Those who accord with the wisdom of the Dharma observe the faculties, consciousnesses, and objects; they examine karmic retribution; they observe the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of arhats, the mastery over the mind, and the delight in the bliss of dhyāna; and they observe the noble supernormal powers and transformations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

By accomplishing these five skillful contemplations, the present and future śrāvaka disciples, through superior faith and in accordance with the knowledge of the Dharma, will be well able to understand that the inherently pure mind is defiled by afflictions, thereby attaining the ultimate state.
"Śrīmālā! This ultimate state is the cause of the Mahāyāna.
You should now know that those who have faith in the Tathāgata do not give rise to slander regarding the profound Dharma."
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
there is yet another matter that can bring great benefit.”
"I shall, by receiving the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, expound upon this matter.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"Now, speak as you please. Queen Śrīmālā said:
"There are three kinds of sons and daughters of good family who, regarding this profound Dharma, avoid self-injury and generate abundant merit, thereby entering the path of the Mahāyāna."
What are these three?

If good sons or good daughters are able to personally achieve profound knowledge of the Dharma, or achieve knowledge that accords with the Dharma, or if they are unable to comprehend this profound Dharma and defer to the Tathāgata, saying, "This is known only by the Buddha; it is not within my sphere."

Aside from these three types of sons and daughters of good family, all other sentient beings, regarding this profound Dharma, grasp at it according to their own preconceptions, adhering to false explanations, contravening the True Dharma, and practicing the ways of non-Buddhists.
"Any rotten seeds, wherever they may be located, should be removed and destroyed.
Such corrupt things should be suppressed by all devas and humans together.
Having spoken these words, Queen Śrīmālā and her retinue prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, praised her, saying:
“Excellent, Śrīmālā!
You skillfully protect the profound Dharma through expedient means and are well-versed in subduing adversaries.
Having personally attended hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Tathāgatas, you are able to expound this meaning.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a supreme radiance that illuminated the entire assembly; his body ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees, and by means of his supernormal powers, he walked through the air back toward Śrāvastī.

At that time, Queen Śrīmālā and her retinue gazed upon the World-Honored One without averting their eyes for even a moment. Once he had passed beyond the range of their vision, they were filled with joy and exultation; they praised the Tathāgata’s merits to one another and, with single-minded devotion, called the Buddha to mind as they returned to the city of Ayodhyā, where they exhorted King Amitra to establish the Mahāyāna.

Among the women in the city, those aged seven and above were converted to the Mahāyāna; likewise, the king’s friend converted all men aged seven and above to the Mahāyāna. Consequently, there was no one among the people of the entire kingdom who did not study it.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Jeta Grove and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, mindful of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his retinue, arrived as soon as he was thought of and stood before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, saying:
“Kauśika! You should receive, uphold, expound, and reveal this sutra for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens.”
He further addressed Ānanda:
"You too should receive and uphold this, and explain it in detail for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?”
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"This sūtra accomplishes boundless merit; it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone other sentient beings."
Kauśika, you should know that this sutra is a profound, subtle, and magnificent mass of great merit; I shall now briefly state its name for you.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Venerable Ānanda addressed him, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall surely receive your instruction.”
The Buddha said:
"This sutra praises the true merits of the Tathāgata; it should be upheld in this way.
It sets forth ten kinds of inconceivable great vows; it should be upheld in this way."
One should uphold it thus: that one great vow encompasses all vows;
one should uphold it thus: that the inconceivable reception of the true Dharma is taught;
one should uphold it thus: that entry into the One Vehicle is taught.
When the infinite truths are taught, they should be upheld in this way;
when the Tathāgatagarbha is taught, it should be upheld in this way;
when the Buddha’s Dharmakāya is taught, it should be upheld in this way.
The teaching on the meaning of emptiness conceals the ultimate reality; it should be upheld in this way.
The teaching on the meaning of the single truth should be upheld in this way.
The teaching on the eternally abiding, immovable, quiescent, and sole reliance should be upheld in this way.
When it is said that the truth is inverted, it should be held in this way;
when it is said that the intrinsically pure mind is obscured by afflictions, it should be held in this way;
when it is said that one is a true son of the Tathāgata, it should be held in this way.
One should uphold this teaching that Lady Śrīmālā uttered as the true lion’s roar.
Furthermore, Kauśika,
what is taught in this sutra cuts through all doubts, is of definitive meaning, and leads one into the path of the Single Vehicle.
Kauśika! I now entrust to you this *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* which has been preached; until the Dharma remains, you shall reveal and expound it throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the Venerable Ānanda, and the great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred Nineteen;
The Great Treasure Accumulation Sutra, Volume One Hundred Twenty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
49. The Assembly of the Sage Viśāla. Chapter Forty-Nine. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on the bank of the Gaṅgā River in the city of Ayodhyā.

At that time, there was an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus, including the Venerable Ānanda, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Bakula, Revata, Ajñātakauṇḍinya, and others. Having accomplished what was to be done and being free from all defilements, their outflows were exhausted and they were no longer subject to regression. They never ceased for a moment from meditation, recitation, or walking practice; some moved about as silently as a flock of geese, while others dwelt constantly in meditative concentration within the forests. Abiding securely in the gateways of the Tathāgata’s luminous teaching, they had subdued their faculties and attained fearlessness.

At that time, the branches and leaves of the sāla trees in Kalinga were lush and flourishing, with fragrant flowers carpeting the ground; kokila birds, kalaviṅka birds, royal geese, and swarms of bees gathered there, warbling in harmony, able to cause sentient beings to leave behind all states of delusion and decline.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should diligently perform what is to be done, so as to shield yourselves with the precepts and decorum.
