At that moment, a brilliant radiance suddenly appeared from the west, like the light of the sun’s orb. Because the Venerable Ānanda had not yet abandoned desire, he spoke, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of sign is this radiance now appearing?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! This most excellent and supreme among the five-attainment seers, the son of Kṛṣṇagandha, is named Vipula.

Restrained in diet and emaciated, his body lacks luster; accompanied by five hundred of his followers—namely the seer Avaśyapa, the seer Devamānuṣa, the seer Śambhavya, the seer Tāṇḍya, the seer Kāmavya, the seer Mekhalāsvin, the seer Vicikitsāsava, and the seer Dūraga—and surrounded by them from before and behind, he shall come to me.”
At that time, the seer Vipula beheld from afar the World-Honored One, his body and mind serene, dwelling amidst the forest thickets and attended by the bhikṣus.
He then reflected to himself:
"How marvelous and noble! "

Endowed with the physical marks of one destined for omniscience, he renounced his ministers, the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, and sixty thousand court ladies as if discarding poisoned food; he practiced austerities in the mountain forests, leaving behind all sensual pleasures, and his fame has spread everywhere—truly, it is not in vain.
At that time, there was a seer among the assembly named Nārada. Gazing from afar at the Tathāgata, his heart was filled with joy, and he spoke in verse:
“Beneath that grove of blue-flowering trees, who is this person who resembles a mass of purple gold?”
"The Meru mountain of wondrous jewels flows with blazing light, / Just like the autumn moon, free from all mist and clouds.
At that time, all the sages were filled with joy; with palms joined in reverence, they gradually approached the Buddha’s dwelling.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Observe those sages in Jambudvīpa who have disheveled hair hanging down, dwell among the thickets of the forest, smear themselves with ash, and abstain from grains; some eat only at the end of a month or a fortnight until they become emaciated, using deer skins or tree bark as clothing, leaving their hair and nails uncut, and squatting in the open air."
Some have complexions like smoke, charcoal, or black bees; they perform incantations and fire sacrifices as auspicious rites and dwell anywhere—on empty ground or beneath trees.

Some throw themselves from high cliffs or cast themselves into deep waters; they torment their bodies with blazing fires and the scorching heat of the sun, yet rely on their caste rather than seeking unsurpassed wisdom.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that these sages possess impure vision; being attached to the various realms of existence, they wander through birth and death and are unable to achieve liberation.
When the bhikṣus had heard the World-Honored Buddha speak these words, they spoke with one voice, saying:
“We, by relying upon the Tathāgata, shall now diligently cultivate the holy life and forever achieve liberation from all realms of existence.”

At that time, the rishi Vipula and his companions gradually approached the Buddha’s dwelling; beholding the majestic and solemn majesty of the arhats, they were inwardly filled with awe and trepidation, bowing their bodies and casting down their gazes.

Each has their hair tied up in disarray and wears white cords upon their bodies; their countenances are dark and sallow, their two eyes are yellowish-green, and their hair is parched and withered. They carry the three-pronged trident, their forms are lowly and ugly, and some travel through the void.
Or, while discussing secular scriptures, they came before the Tathāgata and said:
"World-Honored One!
In this present assembly, we pray that the Buddha will know the proper time."
The Buddha said,
“Vipula! I have already fully understood all forms of rebirth as well as their intrinsic nature.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Who is this being surrounded by a multitude of sages, whose eloquence and wisdom are penetrating and敏捷 (agile), and whose hair on the crown of his head flows upward?"
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! This is extensive;
it constitutes the Vedas, upholds and practices the Śākalā teachings, and creates various kinds of worldly scripts.”
At that time, the various arhats said to one another:
"What has this seer attained that he practices such asceticism yet remains unliberated from birth and death?"
He further reflected to himself:
"This assembly of sages has now come to the Buddha's presence; what will they ask?
Will it concern causes and conditions?"
"Is it because there is no self?
At that time, the Rishi Vipula joined his palms toward the Buddha and said to him,
"World-Honored One!"
"The appearance of a Buddha is rare, and the gathering of this assembly is likewise rare.
I now have a few questions; I pray that you will deign to show me compassion.
The Buddha said:
“Great Seer! Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you.
The Seer Vipula said:
"What is giving? What is the meaning of giving?
And what is a donor?"
What is the meaning of "donor" (dānapati)? Why is it that a giver is not called a donor?
And why is it that a donor is not called a giver?
How does one obtain a meritorious reward from a recipient when practicing generosity?
How is it that once given, whether in the present life or after the end of life, the merit of the gift follows the practitioner and accumulates into a mass?
“World-Honored One!
After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, who will receive the offerings made to the stupas and shrines and thereby obtain the karmic reward of merit?
The Buddha said:
“Great Seer! The question you have now asked is most rare; it is intended to awaken those who have newly resolved their minds.
At that time, Śāriputra was among the assembly, his hair white and his face wrinkled; he raised his eyebrows with his right hand, looked around, and after a long pause, spoke:
"I have heard in the past that the sage Viśvāmitra was praised by the world; why is it that today you do not speak or inquire like one who knows, but instead act like a small child?
Why do you not ask about the profound and subtle meaning of non-self and its causal conditions, but instead ask about the karmic retribution of giving?"
The Venerable Ānanda went forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
That seer is attached to giving; I wish to explain the meaning of giving for his sake.”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! If the Tathāgata is questioned and a śrāvaka answers, it is not the teaching of the Tathāgata.”
Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This seer now has various doubts; I wish to explain them for him.
The Buddha said:

"Not so. You are the foremost among the śrāvakas; if you were to offer an explanation before me that causes sentient beings to fall into evil destinies, it would be slanderous to say that the Tathāgata does not possess definitive wisdom, or that the Tathāgata still harbors pride despite having fully realized the nature of awakening."
At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the bhikṣus gave rise to pure faith and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Ṛṣi Vipaśyin has certain doubts; we pray that you will resolve them for us.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the seer Vaipulya, saying:
“Listen attentively now to the karmic distinctions regarding the fruits of giving.
If those who receive [the gift] can cause the donor to produce a fruit of retribution, this constitutes the true meaning of giving.”

If there are sentient beings who give rise to a pure mind and, using their own wealth and treasures, have an attendant distribute them according to the needs of recipients, the owner of that wealth and treasure is called the donor (*dānapati*), while the attendant is called the giver (*dātṛ*).
Furthermore, if there is a person who, with a pure mind, gives their own belongings as an offering, they become a donor and are also called a giver.
Moreover, O Great Sage!
Listen now attentively to the thirty-two kinds of impure giving.
Furthermore, if there is a person who gives with inverted views, it is not called pure giving.
If it is done for the sake of repaying a debt of gratitude, it is not called pure giving.
If it is done without compassion, it is not called pure giving.
That which is done for the sake of sensual desire is not called a pure gift.
If one gives into fire, it is not called a pure gift.
If one throws it into water, it is not called a pure gift.
A gift given out of fear is not called a pure gift.
A gift given to the five types of households is not called a pure gift.
A gift given with poison is not called a pure gift.
Giving weapons and staves is not called pure giving.
Giving for the purpose of killing and harming is not called pure giving.
Giving for the sake of exercising control over others is not called pure giving.
That which is given for the sake of praise is not called a pure gift.
That which is given for the sake of singers and performers is not called a pure gift.
That which is given because of divination or physiognomy is not called a pure gift.
That which is sought for the sake of ornamentation is not called a pure gift.
That which is intended to bind one in friendship is not called a pure gift.
That which, when birds or beasts come to eat from one's gardens or dwellings, does not bring joy, is not called a pure gift.
One who studies the arts and crafts does not practice pure giving.
Giving medicine because of illness does not constitute pure giving.
Giving wealth after having previously struck or reviled someone does not constitute pure giving.
If one harbors doubt, thinking, "Will this gift of mine now have a reward, or will it have no reward?
such giving is not called pure giving.
If, after having relinquished the gift, one harbors within a burning affliction of stinginess, attachment, regret, or resentment, it is not called pure giving.
If one says that the recipient shall later become a cow or an animal for one's sake, it is not called a pure gift.
If one says that one will personally receive the karmic reward of the merit, it is not called a pure gift.

If a person lacks pure faith while in their youth and vigor, yet later encounters the suffering of illness or stands at the threshold of death—with agonizing pain in their body and their limbs falling apart, with the messengers of Yama taunting them before them, and their relatives weeping piteously as they gaze upon one another—it is only at such a time that they begin to practice giving; this is not called "pure giving."
Some may think that if one intends for other cities and towns to know of one's giving, it is not called pure giving;
likewise, if one gives with an increase in envy and jealousy, it is not called pure giving.
To give gifts of gold, silver, silk, cloth, and garments out of a desire to form a marriage alliance with another noble family is not called a pure gift.
To give gifts for the sake of seeking sons, daughters, or other miscellaneous worldly conditions is not called a pure gift.
If one has the thought, "I give now so as to receive retribution in a future life," it is not called a pure gift.
If, upon seeing the poor and destitute, one fails to give rise to compassion and instead takes wealth to give to those who are wealthy and noble, it is not called a pure gift.
If one gives out of greed for flowers or fruits, it is not called a pure gift. Good son!
These thirty-two kinds of tainted giving are like a person carrying seeds and sowing them wherever they please in a field of weeds and filth.

"However, when those seeds rely upon the great earth element and encounter the moisture of rain from the heavens, they will certainly sprout; yet as for the flowers and fruits, one may harvest only a small amount.
At that time, the Rishi Vipula again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can one give such that it neither destroys nor corrupts those who observe the precepts or those who violate them?"
The Buddha said: "Great Seer!

If there is another person who, with pure faith in cause and effect, gives rise to a heart of joy, acts for the sake of all sentient beings without regret or stinginess, and does not discriminate between those who uphold the precepts and those who break them."
Furthermore, good son,
there are five kinds of giving that are called "great giving. What are these five?

First is giving at the proper time; second is to those traveling on a journey; third is to the sick and those who tend to them; fourth is to those who preach the Dharma of the Right; and fifth is to those traveling to other lands.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of food; third, the gift of shelter; fourth, the gift of lamps; and fifth, the gift of incense and flowers.
Purṇa spoke again: "What is purity? The Buddha said:
"If one gives rise to faith, harbors compassion within for all sentient beings, and dedicates [the merit] toward Bodhi for the sake of universal purity and liberation, one attains purification.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of unsurpassed giving."
What are these five?
First, giving to the Tathāgata—this gift is unsurpassed;
second, giving to the Saṃgha—this gift is unsurpassed.
Third, giving to those who preach the Dharma is a supreme gift;
fourth, giving to one's father is a supreme gift;
fifth, giving to one's mother is a supreme gift.
Furthermore, there is a giver whose gift is called a "great gift," namely: giving to a king who has lost his throne is called a great gift;
giving to one who is oppressed by government officials and has no one to rely upon, or to one who is tormented by the pains of illness—to give to such persons is called a great gift.
If one is abandoned by a king, or at the time of execution, or when facing other life-threatening dangers, to sacrifice one's own life to save another’s life is called the "Great Gift."
To bestow medicine upon those who are ill is also called a great gift;
to bestow offerings at the proper time upon the assembly of monks who possess the precepts is also called a great gift.
Furthermore, giving to those who seek wisdom is also called a "great gift.
Moreover, giving to those among the animal realm—such as frogs, leeches, crows, and other birds and beasts—is also called a "great gift."
To give to those who are destitute or deficient so as to bring them full satisfaction is also called a great gift.
Furthermore, if someone encourages others to practice pure giving and rejoices in their merit, this too is called a great gift.
Furthermore, O Great Sage!
Regarding what you previously asked— how one may plant roots of merit to obtain a reward of blessings after my parinirvāṇa—
listen, son of good family!
All Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body and not the form-body; whether they remain in the world or have passed into extinction, there is no difference in the merit of all offerings made to them.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch proclaims these words throughout the great earth:
"Within my realm, no one shall kill living beings nor speak falsehoods."

"The people of that kingdom, although they have not yet seen the king nor personally served him as attendants, will immediately comply with his instructions upon merely hearing them; the king will consequently feel great joy toward these people."
Because this man was not executed by the king, he obtained the retribution of rebirth in heaven; those who oppose him fall into the evil realms.
Thus it is, O Great Seer!
Although there may be sentient beings who behold my physical body, what can they attain if they do not protect their precepts?
Just as Devadatta, despite having encountered me, fell into hell;
if there should be anyone in a future age who diligently practices my teaching, that would be truly rare, no different from seeing my own body.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
Regarding your question as to whether the causes and conditions of merit constitute an accumulation:
it is like the flames produced by burning reeds and rushes; these flames cannot be said to be an accumulation or a heap."
In this way, the donor accumulates the provisions like a shadow following a form, yet it is not seen.

It is also like grapes or sugarcane: before they are pressed, the juice cannot be seen; even if one searches for the accumulation of juice within each joint or every second joint, nothing at all is seen. Nevertheless, that juice is not obtained from the outside.
The karmic fruit of merit is likewise: it does not reside in the hands, the mind, or the body of the donor, yet it is never separate from them.
It is also like the seed of a nyagrodha tree before it has matured; at that time, its sprout cannot be seen.
It is like a merchant who, carrying a small amount of goods, travels to a great city and, through trade, acquires vast wealth and profit.
The retribution of merit is likewise: it is like a bee gathering from flowers without damaging their color.
"Who can perceive the accumulation of clouds that contain rain and moisture?
Yet, when they arise, their purpose is necessarily accomplished.
At that time, the Rishi Vastu addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have already understood the distinctions among forms of giving.
How is it that this consciousness dwells within the body with attachment?”
The Buddha said: "Great Seer!

It is just as when a king resides within his city, fearing the arrival of an enemy army, he first constructs moats and trenches, amasses provisions, and trains his warriors. He raises various banners and flags, disciplines his intoxicated elephants, and strictly exhorts his troops to maintain vigilance. Clad in armor and focused on combat, they stand with sharp weapons drawn, their blades bared."
Because the king’s merit is exhausted, his army, though once powerful, is utterly destroyed.

In this same way, the King Consciousness dwells within the city of the body; seeing the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) being assailed by impermanence, he breaches the moat of faith, dons the armor of right mindfulness, controls the elephant of intoxication, and trains the horse of the mind. He then addresses the six sense bases, saying:

"Now the powerful army of impermanence is approaching; you must quickly don the armor of generosity, take up the sword of wisdom, prepare the bow of shame and remorse, and establish the embankment of ethical discipline."

At that time, those six sense bases are gradually oppressed by the army of impermanence; then, like a king whose merit is exhausted, that consciousness abandons the city and flees to dwell in another realm.
The Rishi Vaipulya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should one thoroughly understand which is a city of merit and which is not a city of merit, so that I may abandon the latter?
The Buddha said:

“Great Sage! It is like a person who, having boarded a great ship intending to cross the vast ocean, encounters wind and waves surging and tossing him about, while soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, whales, and monsters vie with one another to cause peril and harm.”
By means of this boat, the person eventually reached the other shore; having attained fearlessness, he circumambulated the boat three times, made offerings with reverence, and proclaimed:
"Excellent! It is by means of this boat that I have crossed the great ocean."
"Thus it is, O Great Seer!
Beings possessing merit, after the end of their lives, reflect in this way:
'This body of mine has now been reborn in the higher realms of the heavens; the human life I have obtained has not been spent in vain.'"
"By means of this body-boat, one crosses the ocean of evil destinies; how excellent was that previous life, truly worthy of the highest reverence!
If there are those who fall into the evil destinies, it is like crossing the sea in a rotten, decayed boat, which sinks or floats within the great ocean, tossing about and overturning.
Although this person’s remaining life has brought them to the shore, they again encounter lions, tigers, and wolves filling the area, who scold them, saying: "Alas!
This rotten, old ship was driven backward into the great ocean, causing me such terror and making me witness such suffering."
The consciousness that falls into the evil realms is likewise; it reviles its own body, saying:
"I have reared myself in vain and now encounter this evil retribution.
For a long time in this world, I have carried filthy grass upon my back, binding myself in vain like a silkworm making a cocoon."
"Why have I become so deeply immersed in this?
At that time, when that consciousness has just entered the mother's womb for its second existence, within seven days it can form this thought:
"I have passed away from that place and have come to be born here."
"Because of his wholesome karma, his mind is filled with joy, which causes his mother to possess three signs.

Namely: her face is radiant and her countenance is exquisite; she is free from all blemishes or dark spots; her right foot feels twice as heavy when it presses upon the ground, and she repeatedly strokes her right flank with her hand; furthermore, though she wears white garments, they appear even more beautiful."
The consciousness that has created evil karma also reflects for seven days, thinking:
"In such-and-such a city, I once committed such-and-such a sin.

Having formed this thought, it gives rise to grief and distress, causing its mother to manifest various evil signs: namely, her body becomes foul-smelling, emaciated, and jaundiced; she is constantly filled with sorrow and lamentation, frequently vomiting; calamities fill her door, misfortunes press upon her, and she is beset by many illnesses.
"At the time of delivery, she may either lose her life or die herself.
Then the Seer Vipula addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"When that consciousness first enters the womb, what kind of mindfulness and wisdom does it possess?

The Buddha said, "Once this consciousness has entered the womb, it perceives the gardens, groves, palaces, and ponds of Jambudvīpa as being everywhere filled with adornments; seeing its kinsmen gathered together, it feels an extreme longing and joy."

Furthermore, by means of the light of celestial wisdom, he recollected through mindfulness his various births throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, knowing: "That one was my mother; she gave birth to me for five hundred lifetimes."
Having formed this thought, he gave rise to a mind of weary detachment and cried out: "Alas!
Enough of birth and death in this world; I vow that my toil within the various realms of existence shall forever come to rest."
At that time, the seer Vaiśravaṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since that consciousness is already able to feel such weary detachment, will it not surely transcend birth and death?”
The Buddha said: "No, Great Seer!"
That consciousness lacks the characteristic of renunciation; it is impossible for it to attain liberation.
Although that element of consciousness may thus feel weary of and detached from birth-and-death within the cycle of existence, one who is truly able to renounce should not undergo rebirth.
If it were not so, then those who cultivate merit as well as those who commit transgressions would all necessarily proceed toward nirvāṇa.
As you have stated, that which is called "consciousness-thought" (vijñāna-cetanā) is the predominance of consciousness, not the predominance of wisdom.

"Why is this so? Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to differentiate, while wisdom (*jñāna*) is able to comprehend; it is through the union of consciousness and wisdom that things are as you have described.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"It can ward off all enemies and robbers— those who accumulate afflictions;
it brings to an end both knowledge and ignorance, as well as wisdom alongside folly,
views, pride, and nescience— all such things as these."
There is no wisdom that exists apart from consciousness; it is by means of consciousness that one can understand.
Wisdom and consciousness are never separate; I have always taught that they are conjoined.
A single wheel does not constitute a chariot, nor do two wheels alone suffice.
Nor does it arise from anything else; it requires a person and an ox,
together with spokes and linchpins, two rims joined in mutual support,
and both shafts, yokes, and thongs— only then can it be called a chariot.
The body-cart is likewise thus: born from the conjunction of the various elements, with all the sense faculties fully complete, it is by consciousness that it is drawn along.
Its limbs and joints are interconnected, and its sinews and veins are constantly pervading it.
Covered by skull, skin, and hair, with intestines, lungs, heart, and spleen, and the liver and stomach all joined together, a provisional body is established.
The King of Consciousness dwells within it; it is not the body that acts as the charioteer.
To thoroughly understand the nature of all entities is called the union of wisdom and consciousness.
Furthermore, Great Seer, this consciousness is subtle and cannot be seen as a form; it possesses no sense faculties, yet it is not separate from them.
"If any person feels timid, or gives rise to fear, or engages in discursive thought, all of these are functions of consciousness and not the operation of wisdom.
At that time, the seer Vaipulya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How does one observe those among all sentient beings who come to be born from the hell realm, up to those who come to be born from the human realm?
By what distinctions of karma are they born as devas, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, or in the hells?
The Buddha said: "Great Seer!

That the fundamental nature of sentient beings sinks here and arises there is the realm of the Buddhas; it is not something that can be known by seers possessing the five supernatural powers, nor is it something that can be realized by devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, those in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, or any other Śrāvakas."
"O Great Sage!
Even the realm experienced when one attains the first fruit within my Dharma—having become free from the three impurities—is beyond the comprehension of Śakra, Nārāyaṇa, or you great sages."
When the Tathāgata had spoken thus, the Rishi Vipaśyin reflected to himself:
"Within this cycle of saṃsāra, such a realm of noble wisdom has never before been encountered."
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said, “World-Honored One!
I am now decayed and have lost my mindfulness; I cannot attain the fruit, nor am I capable of bearing the burden of upholding bodhi.”

I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the stainless Saṅgha. From this day forth, together with my disciples and retinue, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. May the World-Honored One please instruct, benefit, and gladden us; may you remain forever in this world with the sun of noble wisdom to dispel the cataracts of affliction.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound for us on all sentient beings who fall from the heavens.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively.
Now is the very time.
If there are sentient beings who firmly accomplish the offering of incense and flower garlands, such persons shall certainly be reborn among the Mālādhāra devas."

At the time of death, their bodies emit a wondrous fragrance and they perceive fresh flowers; furthermore, they see various colored blossoms coming to scatter upon them. Some may see multi-storied pavilions and palaces adorned with hanging bells, tassels, and diverse flowers, wherein hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens reside.
After his life ended, he saw the parents of the Mālādharas deities united like those of Jambudvīpa; then, driven by the wind of craving, he entered the womb.
Seven days after the mother of that deity had become pregnant, she gave birth to her son from beneath her right side.

As soon as he is born, a celestial *manojñā* flower spontaneously forms a garland upon his chest, possessing seven colors—namely white, black, yellow, red, celestial azure, crimson lotus, and like fire-copper—which are brilliantly radiant; its fragrance, carried by the wind, pervades one *yojana*. Therefore, that deity is called Mālādhara (The Garland-Bearer).
In the palace there is a tree whose sap is fragrant and delicious like nectar (*amṛta*).
The fruits in the gardens possess eight superior flavors and are as large as *bīnaḷu* beans.
Whatever those devas eat consists entirely of sweet fruits and no other solid food; whenever they feel hunger, fruit spontaneously appears upon the trees.
The ground they tread upon is free of thorns; fresh flowers and tender grasses are spread everywhere in purity.
There may be palaces resembling clusters of white flowers, or houses made of gold with gilded eaves.
Those celestial maidens, adorned with radiant beauty, gaze out from the balconies and railings as they enjoy one another’s company.
Their lifespan lasts for two hundred celestial years; when their time is near its end, two signs appear:
the leaves of the tree upon which they dwell wither and droop, and the fragrance of its flowers naturally vanishes.
The flower garlands he wore suddenly withered and turned yellow; the cool breeze changed into a poisonous heat;
and he abandoned the most excellent city of the gods and departed.
At that time, the celestial maidens, seeing these signs of decay, surrounded him and wailed in grief, exclaiming:
"Alas! How can that impermanent one lack even a trace of compassion? Now, regarding us whom he holds so dear, he has brought himself under constraint and will abandon us in an instant."

At that time, the deva-son was gradually oppressed by a feverish illness, and fire manifested throughout his entire body; yet, despite the addition of these blazing flames, he felt no heat or distress, and with a mind still full of joy, he passed away from that realm and took birth in the human world within a womb, causing his mother to crave fragrant flowers, garlands, and various fruits.
Furthermore, in dreams he constantly sees cities, marketplaces, and shops adorned and draped everywhere with flower garlands.

Once born, his physical form is radiant and smooth; he is always fond of white garments and flower wreaths. He delights in visiting relatives and is addicted to sensual pleasures; he is infatuated with women and his movements are light and fickle. There is no fine clothing, exquisite garments, or gardens that he does not crave and enjoy; seeing those who are wealthy and noble, he feels redoubled joy.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

Regarding those who proceed toward the realm of the Four Great Kings: if there are sentient beings who, with a heart of compassion, give food and clothing to the poor, provide medicine according to their needs to the sick, or construct wells and springs, or bestow ponds and pools."

When that person is about to die, their body does not wither or emaciate, their complexion remains unchanged, and there is no filth or sweat upon them. Their voice does not crack or break, nor do they suffer from the discharge of urine or feces. The six sense objects remain sufficient and the faculties are unimpaired; they are able to see themselves amidst the assembly of devas.

When his life has ended, his complexion is like that of a red lotus and a wondrous fragrance issues from his mouth; furthermore, a pure breeze blows, wafting the fragrance of exquisite flowers over his corpse.
Thereupon, his consciousness perceives the Four Heavenly Kings and their parents sporting joyfully, intoxicated by and immersed in sensual desire.
Then the father of that deity stroked the back of the mother with his right hand, and she immediately conceived in her thigh.
After seven days had passed, he was born, fully adorned with celestial ornaments.

Great Seer, you should know that the land where the gods of the Four Great Kings dwell is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is adorned with an intermingling of gold, silver, orpiment, and realgar, filled with hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, and possesses hundreds of thousands of flowers and fruits shaped like human forms.

In those gardens, the light of celestial mani-jewels constantly shines; the branches and trunks of the trees hang with *kalpa*-garments and exquisite silks, and the trees are so smooth and lustrous that all who see them are filled with joy.
In their grotto-dwellings, musical instruments are constantly suspended, and flutes and pipes of various kinds spontaneously produce sounds.
Those celestial youths take solid food for sustenance; the fragrant and delicious *śāli* rice is the color of a red lotus and its flavor exceeds that of nectar.
The utensils for their food are of two kinds:
first, golden vessels; second, silver vessels.
Whatever colors, fragrances, and delicious flavors they desire all appear within them.
Furthermore, there is a celestial beverage called Flower-Wine, whose fragrance and coolness are extraordinary; even those who merely smell it naturally become intoxicated.

Each of those devas has a sleeping palace named Early Autumn, draped everywhere with flowering branches and *sāla* and *kīcaka* trees made of gold, silver, and various jewels, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and covering the space above; there are also various kinds of seats and bedding for reclining.

Sixty thousand celestial maidens possessed exceptionally beautiful countenances and wore garments of radiant brilliance; their voices were clear and resonant, harmonizing with celestial music. Created by the various desire-deities, they engaged in singing, dancing, and performance, conversing and interacting with laughter, such that all who beheld them would find their passions and attachments increased.
Before his palace, a *stūpa*-pillar was erected, adorned with alternating gold and silver and embellished with silken banners; various precious streamers hung from it, fluttering in the wind.
There were four Heavenly Kings:
the first is called Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Nation), the second Virūḍhaka (Increasing Growth), the third Virūpākṣa (Terrifying Eye), and the fourth Vaiśravaṇa (Great Hearing).
These Four Heavenly Kings, within that celestial realm, were fully endowed with the pleasures of chanting, whistling, singing, dancing, banqueting, and sporting.

At that time, among the assembly were many divine youths of exceptional strength and skill, possessing exquisite celestial bodies; they walked back and forth with arms dangling like intoxicated elephants, their body fragrances so intense as to pervade an entire yojana.
Their lifespan is five hundred celestial years, and none suffer premature death.

The gardens, groves, and trees are lush, radiant, and pure, adorned with *kādamba* flowers that are all fragrant and free from any foul odor. The stairways and paths on all four sides are composed of various jewels, and hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens constantly perform as singers and musicians; from their precious instruments, wondrous sounds emerge.
"Good son! When the lifespan of those devas is about to end, there are three signs:
first, the radiance of their bodies fades away; second, their flowers lose their fragrance; and third, they no longer hear the celestial maidens playing various musical instruments."

The gardens and palaces where they once constantly delighted in roaming now have only the harmonious and elegant songs of birds; these pleasant places they once loved are no longer dear to them. Their flower garlands wither, the celestial maidens wail in grief, and their garments become soiled. As they gaze upon the objects of former joy and play, their distress intensifies until they faint. Sweat flows from their bodies and their eyes become parched and withered; like fish taken from water and placed in the midday sun, they are oppressed by burning anguish as they writhe upon the ground.
At that time, seeing the celestial youth suffering in such distress, all the women came to surround him and wailed with one voice, crying out: "Alas! Alas!"
"How can it be that those we love are thus? How has that which we cherished and delighted in turned instead into sorrow and suffering?
Why now do you abandon us and our places of recreation?"
Then the goddesses praised him in verse:
“With various exquisite adornments, this place where the Benevolent One enjoys his pastimes is a city of supreme merit, with multi-storied pavilions on all four sides.”
Celestial maidens are ever-present, and the gardens remain perpetually lush;
why then abandon joy and love?
Alas! Such is this impermanence.

At that time, after the goddesses had spoken these verses, they looked at one another and choked with emotion; each took various flowers with her right hand and scattered them from afar upon him, further saying:
"O Benevolent One!
"Because you possess merit, you shall be reborn among humans; that is a land of merit where you should plant the seeds of all virtues with a mind of faith.

At that time, seeing that the women had all turned their backs and departed, the deva’s feverish affliction increased even further, his body and mind burning intensely. Like a drop of clarified butter placed upon glowing iron, he was suddenly extinguished, leaving behind only a trace of fine ash. This was then scattered by the winds of karma, becoming as invisible as a minute particle divided into a thousand billion parts.
Thereupon, that consciousness descends from the heavens; seeing the union of its parents at the place of rebirth, it conceives joy and enters the womb.

As soon as it is situated within the womb, signs appear in the mother: her appetite for food increases, she abstains from eating flesh and blood, she takes pleasure in wearing crimson garments, she loves places of assembly, and she feels a redoubled affection for her kinsmen.
Although she carried the child, she never experienced pain or distress; her mouth did not flow with saliva, nor did her body feel heavy.
Once the child was born, his human features were dignified and handsome; his eyes were a deep azure, like a celestial blue gem, a sight that all delighted to behold.

Having heard of the affairs of the Four Heavenly Kings in the higher realms, they naturally feel joy and always delight in giving; they love exquisite fragrant garments and are by nature fond of frequent eating; they constantly take pleasure in song, dance, gardens, and groves, and there is nothing—be it women or sensual beauty—they do not cherish with lingering attachment.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

If there are sentient beings who, with pure faith, distance themselves from killing and stealing, and practice giving by offering food, drink, exquisite requisites, clothing, and treasures, and who diligently and sincerely scatter flowers and prostrate before the Buddha-stūpas."

When their lifespan comes to an end, their bodies are free from the pain of illness, filth, or foul odors; they do not forget the karmic deeds they have practiced; their faces are like the color of gold, their noses are not sunken or crooked, their minds are not agitated or distressed, and their throats are neither constricted nor gasping for breath; they are not cut asunder by the "wind-blades" of death, their voices do not crack, and their sleep and meals remain peaceful and tranquil.
Great Seer, you should know that for such a person, poison cannot cause harm; their food and drink are digested, and they are entirely free from injury, calamity, or untimely death.

When that person’s life comes to an end, because of their celestial consciousness, they behold the hundreds of thousands of multi-storied pavilions of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The gates and pillars are adorned with golden makaras, and the ground is sprinkled with snake-victorious sandalwood perfumed water. The earth is soft, pure, and whiter than frost or snow, as clean as a pearl necklace. Rows of yellow sandalwood trees and celestial jewel lamps are interspersed in orderly lines, while celestial men and women frolic in the gardens, intoxicated by their sensual delights.
Having seen this, she felt great joy; it was as if a string of pearls had been taken by someone and placed into the hand of the Mother of Heaven to serve as a fetal treasury.

At that moment, flowers immediately blossomed upon the Mother’s palm. She held them up to show the Father of Heaven, and they rejoiced together. Then, as she rubbed and massaged those flowers with both hands, the child was conceived.
Then the mother of that deity said to the father of the deity:
"Today I have given birth to a boy who shall increase our noble lineage.
Thereupon, she assembled her kinsmen to celebrate with joy.

Upon being born, after seven days have passed, his celestial marks are fully perfected; he recollects his previous life, knowing from such-and-such a place he passed away and has now been reborn here, identifying "such-and-such is my father," "such-and-such is my mother," and "I previously cultivated such-and-such merit."

When they had this thought, they were filled with a towering joy; they then gave rise to deluded craving toward the various sensual desires, and within the celestial realms, they naturally perceived the palaces, gardens, and groves with greed, delight, and attachment.

At that time, the youth’s arms hung down long and curved like the trunks of elephants; his chest was firm and full like the breast of a lion; his waist and abdomen were rounded and slender, without any sagging or folds; his spine was straight and level, with no bones protruding higher or lower; his two thighs were round in form like the stalks of a plantain tree; his flesh was radiant and pure, free from any dark spots or blemishes; he had no body hair, nor any foul odors, for a sublime fragrance flowed forth from his body.
Flower garlands, necklaces, and celestial robes were light and fine, naturally covering his body without the need for external seeking.
At that time, all the celestial maidens within the palace who had no celestial males saw this youth approach and surround them together, and they all spoke these words:
"Welcome, O Benevolent One!"
"This palace is entirely yours.
We daughters have previously had no one to rely upon; we wish to serve and follow you.
Among them, some said:
"These women are in the prime of their youth; their breasts are like golden jars and their faces are like red lotuses.
Within this garden, such celestial trees as the *kovidāra* forest hang down in lush splendor, surrounded on all sides by sixty thousand celestial maidens."
"Excellent, O virtuous one!
You may enjoy yourself with us forever, though like lightning in the clouds, you do not remain constant.

In some palaces, various celestial instruments such as flutes, drums, and lutes spontaneously produce sound; there are exquisite rugs and lion thrones, adorned with pearl necklaces and draped with silken streamers, yet these silken fabrics were not produced by silkworm cocoons.
At that time, when the young boy beheld those precious ornaments, he sat upon the throne like a consecrated king.
Once he had ascended the throne, all the precious playthings uttered voices, saying:
"This person of virtuous karma has come to be born here because he cultivated celestial merit while in Jambudvīpa."
"You all should come here to serve him with song, dance, and entertainment, so that this person of merit may rejoice without weariness.

Once these words were spoken, sixty thousand celestial maidens from the gardens and palaces appeared, holding celestial flowers and garments of radiant splendor. The fragrance emanating from their bodies was like grape wine, honey wine, and flower wine; those who smelled it became intoxicated.
Singing in unison, they cried out: "You have accumulated heavenly merit; we pray you, accept our service at this time!"

Thereupon, the youth, together with the host of celestial maidens, wandered through the Forest of Joy, the Forest of Variegated Flowers, the Forest of Yellow Carpets and Stone Crags, the Forest of Utmost Radiant Adornments, the Garden of the Solar Palace, the Garden of the Sound of Springs, the Garden of Music, and the Garden of Clusters of Flowers.
They roam through such sublime and wondrous groves and gardens, which are delightful and cool, free from all harsh winds, and fragrant with the scent of flowers.

Blue *maṇi* jewels serve as lamps, while various bees and bird-kings produce exquisite sounds; the plumage of these birds resembles a variety of precious gems, and their beaks are made of celestial lapis lazuli. As they fly and frolic in groups, they fill the trees throughout the groves.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

In that realm there is a pond that waxes and wanes with the moon, endowed with the eight meritorious qualities; it is pleasing to the mind, stainless, cool, and crystal clear. Within it, fragrant flowers with a hundred petals bloom, and rows of trees line its banks, filled everywhere with various blossoms."

In that pond, numerous celestial maidens sport and enjoy themselves; various precious vessels and other items appear according to their wishes. There is exquisite food of color and fragrance known as the "celestial nectar" (*amṛta*), which is whiter than the *kumuda* flower or snow, endowed with sweet aroma and easy to digest, free from any bitter, astringent, or unwholesome flavors.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

Among the devas and humans, there are those whose karmic retributions are not uniform; though they eat from the same vessel, some may experience red, some azure, and even yellow or black, and various other mixed colors. While their celestial appearances remain indistinguishable, it is only their food that differs."
Great Seer, you should know that those sentient beings, although they had previously practiced giving, later felt regret; it is due to this retribution that they obtain such a fruit.

Furthermore, there is a garden named Saṃkusumita, adorned with a mixture of branches, flowers, and leaves; its hundreds of thousands of groves are pure and soft, like crystal, and its flowers and fruits are ever-luxuriant.
Within the groves of that forest dwell the Munis who possess bodies of profound tranquility and have transcended desire;
the gods and goddesses who constantly enter there do so without being driven by the pleasures of craving or sensual passion.
"Great Seer, you should know that my disciple, the foremost śrāvaka Kātyāyanīputra, is a pure-born son of a brāhmaṇa family who dwells in a mind of meditative concentration and loving-kindness."
Through that meditative concentration, he opened his compassionate eyes and entered *samādhi*, manifesting inhalation and exhalation only once every seven days.

When he entered this state of absorption, a wind that accords with his intention would arrive at will; even if the fire at the end of an eon were to burn the great earth into a single conflagration, it could not harm even a mustard-seed’s portion of his dhyāna-body, while his limbs remained as immovable as Mount Meru.

The Nanda Dragon King and Upananda possess great power and fierce vigor; by their exhalation and inhalation, Mount Meru, the king of mountains, is shaken, and they cause the waters of the four great oceans to turn salty.
When the arrogant Vaṃpati entered meditative absorption, those two dragon kings exerted all their power but were unable to disturb him.

My disciple here, while in the Śāla grove, was beheld by the celestial maidens; though they were immersed in sensual desire, upon seeing this Venerable One, they gave rise to pure hearts and scattered *mandārava* flowers and various lotuses over him, joining their palms in reverent homage.
The youths of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven also came to surround him, providing and offering celestial ambrosia as sustenance.

This Venerable One constantly expounded for the devas in the Saṃkīrṇa Grove various sūtras, including those of the *Adbhutadharma*, *Itivṛttaka*, *Udāna*, *Veyyakaraṇa*, *Jātaka*, *Nidāna*, *Vaipulya*, *Geya*, *Vyākaraṇa*, *Avadāna*, and *Upadeśa*.
At that time, when the devas and humans heard this essential teaching, there were none who did not respond with earnest reverence, respect, and honor.
"Furthermore, O Great Sage!

In the Heaven of the Thirty-three there is an assembly hall; that hall has eighty-four thousand pillars, all constructed from gold, silver, vaiḍūrya, agate, fine jade, and the heartwood of sandalwood."

Hanging bells and suspended chimes emitted subtle and wondrous sounds; various celestial garments were arrayed, and banners and streamers were erected; the exquisite sounds of flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, zithers, cymbals, gongs, conchs, and drums resounded forth.
The men and women of that heaven love and respect one another; with harmonious countenances and compassionate joy, they constantly gather together.

Within those halls, they are adorned with *maṇi* jewels; the emerald-green lapis lazuli is pure, smooth, and like a mirror. It is everywhere covered with fragrant ointments, powdered incense, and various flowers. Furthermore, there is neither blowing wind nor any scorching heat, and venomous snakes, mosquitoes, and gadflies are all far removed.
Those who dwell there harbor no thoughts of drowsiness or indolence.
A subtle, pure, and harmonious breeze permeates the groves and pavilions.
The various multi-storied towers are draped with canopies and nets, while exquisite jewel necklaces hang down and various fragrant flowers are scattered about.

Although the hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens were full of passion, they were free from jealousy and strife; their countenances were as upright and beautiful as the full moon, their bodies and heads adorned with flower garlands and precious jewels, and they sang exquisite, pure songs without ceasing as they moved to and fro.
"Furthermore, O Great Seer!
That celestial assembly hall is square and regular on all sides; its long corridors are wide and spacious, and tall trees stand densely packed like overhanging clouds.

On the four sides of that hall there are gardens, each measuring one hundred yojanas, interspersed with various golden lotuses and miscellaneous flowers that emit wondrous songs, bringing joy to those who hear them."
It is surrounded by groves of *kukānada* trees, *pāriyātra* trees, and *kovidāra* trees. Great Seer!

The furnishings and ornaments of the Sudharmā assembly hall are all made of gold, silver, and various precious gems; its terraces and pavilions are constructed of piled lapis lazuli. Its treasuries are filled with rare and wondrous treasures, and its hundreds of thousands of palaces adorn the gardens. From near and far, one constantly hears of peace and happiness, free from all illness, suffering, and other calamities.
After those devas have finished sporting in the various gardens and groves, they return to this hall to enjoy their pleasures.

Furthermore, O Great Seer, among the Trāyastriṃśa devas there is another palace named Sudarśana (Good View). It is as bright as the midday sun and as pure as a clear mirror; its four sides are completely adorned with flower garlands suspended all around.
There were a thousand celestial maidens adorned with various flowers and shimmering pearl bells; they wore crowns decorated with nets and tassels of gold and emerald.
Elephants, horses, and chariots trampled back and forth, scattering golden dust that turned every place yellow.

In that hall there were sixty thousand pillars, with capitals and bracket-sets layered and interlaced, reflecting one another’s brilliance; interspersed with rare treasures and painted in vermilion hues, the ground was anointed with the richly fragrant and intense scents of sandalwood, aloeswood, and storax.
Śakra Devānām Indra, holding his vajra and surrounded before and behind by hundreds of thousands of women, ascends the jeweled palace to enjoy himself in pleasure and merriment.

Great Seer, you should know that among the Trāyastriṃśa devas there is a celestial king named Indra. His strength is valiant and robust, equal to nine thousand elephants; his hanging arms are slender and beautiful like the trunks of celestial elephants. His body is like pure gold, with firm and dense muscles and sinews that do not protrude. His chest is like that of a lion, his belly is neither bulging nor sagging, and his waist is slender and tapered.
He wears a head ornament fashioned from necklaces strung with golden threads; his celestial garments are radiant with pearl pendants and flow down in elegant folds.
His divine renown has long been universally established; he composes treatises and scriptures, partakes of ambrosia, and constantly travels mounted upon the elephant Airāvaṇa.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

That Śakra’s physical body is not composed of flesh and bone, but is formed entirely of flowers; his voice is clear and beautiful, and the fragrance of his body is extraordinary, such that even if a mad elephant were to smell its scent, it would become naturally tamed and well-behaved. His appearance is upright and majestic, just like the body of a Buddha."
Its brilliant radiance outshines all collections of gold, stripping them of their luster and rendering them dark.
The Seer Vaiśravaṇa said,
“It is truly rare that the Tathāgata now praises the Lord of Devas in such a manner.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Pṛthu:
"That Devendra possesses an impermanent body, an inferior body.

It is like a vessel made of fragile grass, or like a paper-cut flower; it is like a painting artist's decorative murals, or like a craftsman's carved wooden image; it is also like a woven flower that soon withers and perishes—how could it be worthy of praise?"
Furthermore, Great Seer!

Among my disciples, there is one named Aniruddha who possesses supernormal powers; by means of his very body born of father and mother, even the strength of a single limb and joint exceeds that of Śakra.
At that time, Aniruddha was among those seated in the assembly; hearing the Tathāgata speak these words, he thought to himself:
"Now the World-Honored One has awakened me."

He immediately entered samādhi; his bodily radiance was brilliant like freshly refined celestial gold. He wore a most excellent crown whose pearl light shone with resplendent reflection; his face was more lustrous than clarified butter (sarpis); his eyes were deep blue like vaidūrya; he wore armlets made of maṇi, agate, and sūryakānta gems; and the fragrance of his bodily light perfumed everywhere as it shone forth in universal brilliance.

At that time, when the seer Vipula beheld this phenomenon, his heart was greatly struck with amazement. He immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, gazed upward with a sense of rare wonder, and cried out in a loud voice:
"How marvelous! How excellent!"
"I have not lived my human life in vain;
now that I have encountered the World-Honored One’s gathering and exposition, I behold today what I have never seen before.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pṛthu:
“Between the body of that Śakra and that of Aniruddha, which is superior and which inferior?
The Seer Vaiśravaṇa replied:
“If one were to compare the body of that Śakra with that of Aniruddha, even a hundredth part of the latter would not equal the former, nor indeed would even a thousandth part.”
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer! It is not at all extraordinary for such a body to be attained; those who have acquired merit achieve the marks of their physical form in accordance with their aspirations."
At that time, the assembly gave rise to a heart of joy and all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will further explain for us the realm of the devas.
The Buddha said:
"In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, its Lord, the Great King, has a chief queen named Śacī who dwells in the Nandana Grove.

Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial nymphs, her beauty is exquisite like a flower in full bloom; her cheeks are like red lotuses and her face is like gold as she sports in the gardens, wearing garments of brilliant colors and fine, soft textures."

He wears celestial, exquisite jewel flowers as head ornaments; his pearl necklaces, bracelets, and pendants emit wondrous sounds. His forehead is broad and level, from which hang golden tassels and chains; his eyes are slender and long, like flowers about to bloom.

Her sincere devotion was focused entirely upon the Lord of Devas; she was never subject to anger, strife, frowning resentment, or jealousy, nor did she suffer from the afflictions associated with pregnancy.

Great Seer, you should know that this lady’s defilement of attachment was twice as heavy as that of other celestial maidens, and her mind was so haughty and arrogant that it remained as inaccessible and difficult to behold as Mount Meru and Mount Mandara.
Neither fat nor thin, neither tall nor short, her physical constitution was fragrant and pure, free from all impurities; the wind carried exquisite flowers that formed a canopy above her.
This lady was always able to manifest the lineage of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are free from all afflictions and burdens, and they constantly sport within their towers, pavilions, and palaces.
Their lifespan there is one thousand celestial years."
When his life was about to end, five ominous signs appeared:
first, the clear and cool ponds were as pure as crystal; those who touched them felt a sense of joy, and gentle breezes lightly swayed the various flowers, which shimmered with radiant light.
As he was about to bathe in this pond, his body turned into fat and grease; seeing this omen, the deva was struck with fear, leaped out of the water, and fled into the forest.

At that time, seeing his agitation, the celestial maidens also hurriedly followed him and stopped beneath a tree; with hearts filled with distress and voices choked with sobs, they spoke to him in unison:
"O Benevolent One!..."
"How can you so quickly abandon us and dwell here in such solitude?
Then that celestial youth, his voice gradually becoming piteous, spoke these words:
"Since time immemorial, I have never before manifested a body with such impurities."
Having spoken these words, sweat suddenly welled up from beneath both his armpits. Seeing these signs of decay, those celestial maidens immediately departed.

Thereupon, the deva, seeing the maidens leave, was filled with distress and gasped for breath; the inner heat of his affliction increased, the flower garland upon his head withered away, the celestial robes he wore suddenly became soiled and greasy, and he found no pleasure in his celestial bed, furnishings, or various playthings.

When those celestial maidens beheld such signs, they knew for certain that he was about to die; smelling the foul odor from afar, they merely gazed at one another, wailing with choked sobs and bitter grief, crying out:
"Alas, what suffering!"

This delicate and supple body formerly roamed and enjoyed itself with us; in the celestial ponds it was like a ruddy sheldrake, in the Sudharmā Hall like a king of geese, in the Nandana Grove like a kalaviṅka bird, and as it wandered by the Mandākinī River it was like a fragrant elephant. In the Pāruṣyaka and Cūḍāmaṇi groves it was like a king of bees, and amidst the various trees it was like a celestial flower crown.
"Now why are you being afflicted by the five signs of decline? Having abandoned us, where will you go?

When that celestial being heard this lamentation, his anger and distress increased further, and he was seized by a fever of great terror; his entire body withered away, and his eyes became distraught with fear.

It is like a merchant who has lost his caravan; like one crossing the ocean whose ship has been wrecked; like a person who has lost a wish-fulfilling jewel; or like a tree on a perilous peak that is rotten and decayed, being shaken and battered by fierce winds.
Furthermore, like a young nāga being pecked and seized by a garuḍa, he was filled with agitation, trembling, and fear.
Joining his palms, he addressed those celestial maidens, saying:
"Come forward! I pray that you may touch me with your hands so that I might find some slight relief."
Although he spoke these words, the women merely wept piteously from afar and none came forward; each grasped a branch of a tree and threw it toward his heart, saying:
"Your heavenly merit is exhausted; you shall soon be reborn in that Jambudvīpa."
Then, having heard these words and realizing he had been cast aside, that deva cried out in resentment:
"Alas! What a tragedy! Within this place, I was bound by various provisions, gardens, palaces, and my retinue of women."
"Now that my life has ended and I am about to travel the path of death, why do you stand so far off and merely say to me, 'You shall be reborn in Jambudvīpa'?
When that deva had spoken these words, he again beheld the places where he used to roam; moment by moment he reflected upon them, trembling with grief and lamentation, and cried out in a loud voice:
"Alas, Sudharmā Hall!"
Alas, the Nandana Grove! Alas, the Miśrakāvana Grove!
Alas, the Kūṭāgāraśālā Grove!
Alas, Pāruṣyaka Grove! Alas, Pāriyātra Grove! Alas, Vaijayanta Grove and the others!
Alas, Mandākinī River, palaces, halls, chambers, and towers!
At this moment, I am no longer master of myself; I am suddenly forsaking you all and falling away from here.

Before his lamentation had ended, he again saw the women coming and going in a state of alarm, wiping away their tears with their hands; they were sobbing and sighing, their countenances filled with terror.
He further uttered words of sorrowful complaint: "Alas, my beloved!"
Alas, my kinsmen!
Why do you see me about to tread the path of death and yet fail to speak with me?
As I now stand at this long road of birth and death, you do not deign to come and bid me farewell; I and you shall never see one another again.
Alas! Because my merit and karma are now exhausted, I see this dwelling as if it were pitch-black and desolate emptiness.
Alas, why do the celestial music and songs no longer play?
"Why is it that I now hear nothing at all in this silence?

Alas! This is the place of supreme delight among the heavens, where all the devas and gandharvas attend upon me. O Vajradhara of firm and wondrous form, alas, shall I ever again behold the Thousand-Eyed One amidst the assembly?"
"Alas! Why have the pāriyātra flowers and kovidāra flowers upon my head withered away?
At that time, seeing this deva so distressed and sorrowful, the entire assembly of devas all sighed in grief.

"At that time, as for the one named Wondrous-Ear Earring (Sudarśana-karṇa-kuṇḍala), Śakra Devānām Indra was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts; together with Queen Śacī, her various court ladies, and the gandharvas, they followed him on his journey, performing beautiful music."
Seeing them in that heaven, oppressed by the five signs of decline and approaching the path of death, all felt deep compassion and sighed in unison, saying:
"Alas, how strange!"
"That impermanent one lacks even the slightest compassion; he is violent, evil, and harmful.
Śakra Devānām-Indra addressed those devas with a Brahma-like voice, saying:
"Stop, stop!"
"O Son of Heaven!
We shall all likewise follow this path; do not give rise to attachment, lest you fall into the evil realms.
At that time, the assembly of devas also spoke in unison:
“O Benevolent One!
You should fully perform all manner of wholesome deeds so as to be reborn among humans, the ground where all sentient beings cultivate meritorious karma.
Thereupon, having heard these words, that deity reflected to himself:
"I am now certain to fall. Joining his palms, he addressed the various devas who had gathered there, saying:
"May you who dwell among the heavens rejoice with me; for the time of my fall has now arrived."
Having spoken these words, he sighed deeply and gazed about; then two signs appeared:
first, his eyes became like red lotuses; second, the ornaments adorning his body suddenly vanished.
When the other devas perceived these signs, each took celestial flowers and scattered them upon him while playing celestial music.

At that time, the one facing death saw the hosts of other devas providing a send-off with drums, music, banners, and flowers, and encouraging him to go; he immediately felt joy at being born in Jambudvīpa, and his weeping and sorrow ceased from that point on. From this point forward is the latter part of the *Viyāsaparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
When his life has ended and he has died, the Gāthana wind blows upon that deceased deva; that wind of exquisite fragrance blows him away until he is dispersed.
Once thus dispersed, he immediately departs from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, unknown in location and without a fixed abode, such that others can neither perceive him nor know of him.

Once they have fallen from that state, they are born among humans within a womb; their mother then manifests signs such as smiling, laughing, singing, and dancing. Her mind is stained with desire and she is constantly joyful; she delights in places of flowers, fruits, and groves, takes pleasure in various multicolored garments, and always enjoys food and drink.

Although dwelling within the womb, she experiences no pain; she takes no pleasure in improper desires, her mind delights in fine fragrances and flower garlands as adornments, and when she lies down, she has auspicious dreams free from distorted visions.
Great Seer, you should know that at the time when those from the Heaven of the Thirty-three devas pass away and are reborn, such signs appear while they dwell within their mother’s womb.
Great Seer, you should know that at that time, the mother is entirely free from all the defects of pregnancy, and subsequently, the child is born.

Great Seer, you should know that when the boy was born, his limbs were well-proportioned, his palms were marked with auspicious lines, and he was lovely, supple, and delicate. His waist was slender, his teeth were closely set, and his body was soft. His mind delighted in superior virtues and aspirations; by nature he loved the affairs of desire and cherished fine garments. He took pleasure in forest groves and possessed a sublime fragrance upon his body. He was of great wealth and abundant riches, fully endowed with gold and jewels, and belonged to a noble lineage—yet those who habitually practice giving and precepts while possessing much desire are born into poor families. His heart rejoiced in generosity; he was neither dark nor pale, and his hands and feet were even and level. All who saw him felt love and respect for him, and by nature he delighted in philosophical discourse.

His mind is supple and possesses little anger; he delights in consorting with the wives of others and feels no affection for his own wife or concubines; nor does his heart harbor attachment toward his kinsmen, brothers, or retinue.
"Great Seer, you should know that it is the inherent nature of those who fall from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and are reborn among humans to be thus.

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking, the seer Vyāsa—also known as the seer Vighuṣṭa in the new scriptures, the difference being merely a matter of dialect between the Tang and Sanskrit pronunciations—together with the entire assembly of seers, felt joy in their hearts and exclaimed, "Excellent!"

Recently, while perusing the texts, I observed that this portion was missing; though I consulted the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* of the Tripiṭaka, my doubts remained unresolved. I subsequently examined the old scriptural collections and recovered the *Vaiśya Sūtra*, which is identical to this Sanskrit manuscript. Although the translations differ in their sequence, a comparison of the two versions reveals no difference in their underlying principles. Therefore, I have used the old text to supplement this new lacuna.
Those who examine this later will, I hope, not be led astray.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the Western Capital during the Wuchen year of the Kaiyuan era.
